EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers)
Event.summary: From roughly the mid-2000s through the early 2010s, Indian poultry farms reported significant infectious bursal disease outbreaks linked to genetically drifting vvIBDV strains and reassortant viruses, despite widespread use of vaccination. These outbreaks were characterized by high morbidity, variable mortality, and severe bursal lesions in young chickens, leading to immunosuppression and production losses in both broiler and layer sectors across several Indian states. As monitoring improved, molecular characterization guided updates in vaccine strain selection and control strategies, which helped reduce disease severity in many large operations, although novel variants continued to arise and cause re-emergent disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expanding commercial poultry production with high bird densities, complex live-bird marketing chains, and variable vaccine handling and coverage allowed ongoing circulation and selection of IBDV variants; economic pressures sometimes limited optimal vaccination schedules. Internal mechanisms: Accumulation of genetic drift and reassortment events in Indian IBDV populations, including unique VP1 and VP2 constellations that likely evolved from combinations of classical and vvIBDV segments (novel strain/genotype emergence, reassortment), altered antigenicity compared with vaccine strains, and maintained high immunosuppressive capacity (increased virulence/pathogenicity), driving re-emergence in vaccinated flocks.
Review: retain: The Indian re-emergence event (mid‑2000s to early 2010s) is well supported by molecular work documenting genetic drift and reassortment in vvIBDV strains, and the coding as re-emergence without geographic novelty is consistent with the project definitions. No corrections to geography, timing, or classification were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hydatidosis, Hydatid disease
Countries: China – high‑altitude western and north‑western provinces/autonomous regions including Sichuan (Ganzi, Shiqu), Qinghai, Tibet (Xizang), Xinjiang, Gansu, Ningxia, Inner Mongolia, Yunnan, Shaanxi [2000s]
Host: Dogs (owned and semi‑feral, definitive host); foxes and other wild canids (definitive hosts, especially in pastoral areas); sheep, yaks, goats and other livestock (intermediate hosts for CE); small mammals (intermediate hosts for AE); humans (accidental intermediate host; high village‑level prevalence)
Event.summary: From roughly 2000 to the mid‑2010s, large‑scale ultrasound and serological surveys in western China documented extremely high co‑endemicity of cystic and alveolar echinococcosis, especially among Tibetan pastoral communities on the eastern Tibetan Plateau (western Sichuan and adjoining Qinghai) and in other western and north‑western provinces. In Shiqu County, Sichuan, village‑based surveys between 2000–2002 found overall human echinococcosis prevalences exceeding 10% with both CE and AE present, and subsequent national surveys during 2012–2016 estimated around 170,000 human cases and tens of millions at risk, with particularly high prevalence in Tibet and Qinghai. By 2016, China accounted for the majority of global AE cases and a major share of CE burden, with sustained high transmission in dogs, foxes, livestock and small mammals despite intensified control in some areas.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847145/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional transhumant and sedentary pastoralism with large dog populations, home slaughter of yaks and sheep, feeding of uncooked viscera to dogs, limited dog deworming and slaughterhouse controls, poverty, and ecological conditions favouring high densities of small mammal intermediate hosts all promoted intense transmission; remoteness limited access to diagnosis and care.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847145/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Long‑standing E. granulosus s.l. and E. multilocularis lineages maintained in high‑altitude ecosystems, with geographic expansion into additional counties documented; the very high force of infection reflects ecological suitability and dense host networks more than emergence of novel genotypes, so the episode is best characterised as re‑occurrence in a pre‑existing endemic zone.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This episode captures the exceptional CE/AE burden in Tibetan and other western Chinese pastoral areas and is clearly among the most impactful global events. However, I reclassified it as pure re‑occurrence: western China was well known to be endemic for CE and AE before 1990, and the high prevalences observed from 2000 onward represent amplification and better documentation of long‑standing transmission, not first detection or spread to a new continent/sub‑region, nor emergence of a new strain. Thus intra‑continental and inter‑continental emergence and re_emergence were set to “No.” Geographic scope (western and north‑western Chinese provinces within Eastern Asia) and years remain appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Multiple pathogens
EPP.common.name: Varroosis, Tropilaelaps infestation, Foulbrood (Diseases of bees)
Host: Managed western honey bee (Apis mellifera) colonies (brood)
Event.summary: From about 2000 onward, Switzerland experienced a prolonged epidemic of European foulbrood caused by Melissococcus plutonius, with annual numbers of infected apiaries rising sharply compared with earlier decades and reaching several hundred newly infected apiaries per year by the mid‑2000s. This epidemic persisted through much of the 2000s, leading to frequent destruction of symptomatic colonies and extensive sanitation measures in affected cantons. Following intensified control efforts and stricter biosecurity measures, reported case numbers declined in the early 2010s, marking the end of this peak epidemic phase.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high local apiary densities, frequent movement of colonies and equipment among beekeepers, and management practices that delayed early detection in subclinically infected colonies likely facilitated horizontal spread of M. plutonius. Internal mechanisms: molecular studies indicate the presence and expansion of more virulent M. plutonius strains and shifts in strain distribution, which are considered to have contributed to the unusually high clinical expression and spread of European foulbrood during this period.
Review: retain – Swiss federal and peer‑reviewed sources confirm that European foulbrood reached epidemic proportions in Switzerland between roughly 2000 and 2010, with case numbers far exceeding historic baselines and then declining after strengthened control measures. The episode is appropriately coded as a re‑emergence driven by changes in pathogen strain composition and virulence, rather than as inter‑ or intra‑continental spread. Event remains one of the clearest, highly documented re‑emergence episodes for European foulbrood and should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis spiraecola
EPP.common.name: black bean aphid
Host: Citrus spp. (particularly clementine and grapefruit) in northwestern and northeastern Algerian orchards
Event.summary: By the 2010s, field studies in northwestern and later northeastern Algeria showed that Aphis spiraecola had become the predominant aphid on citrus, whereas earlier surveys had recorded more balanced communities with Aphis gossypii and other species. Monitoring in 2012–2017 documented high densities of A. spiraecola on young grapefruit and clementine flushes, with multiple peaks each year and relatively low parasitism rates compared with other aphids. The species now dominates aphid assemblages in many Algerian citrus orchards, causing foliage distortion, honeydew and sooty mould problems and contributing to the local risk of Citrus tristeza virus spread, prompting increased attention to biological control options and selective insecticides.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Changes in citrus management in Algeria (including shifts in insecticide use and variety composition), together with favourable temperatures and flush patterns, likely promoted A. spiraecola relative to other aphids in citrus orchards. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive potential on citrus under local climatic conditions and relatively weak regulation by parasitoids and predators compared with some competing species underpin its current predominance; no specific resistance alleles or new strains have yet been implicated.
Review: review – Retain as a North African resurgence event, but reclassify it from re-emergence to re-occurrence. A. spiraecola was already present on citrus in Algeria and neighbouring North African countries by the 1980s, so the 2010s episode reflects a marked increase in abundance and dominance, apparently driven by management and ecological changes rather than documented genetic shifts. The approximate start period (early 2010s) and host emphasis are consistent with Algerian aphid fauna studies, but the precise onset year and the extent of spread beyond surveyed regions should be validated.

EPP.scientific.name: Bemisia tabaci
EPP.common.name: sweetpotato whitefly
Host: greenhouse vegetables and ornamentals, some field vegetables
Event.summary: During the 2010s, MED lineages of Bemisia tabaci, initially dominated by Q1, became widespread in Korean greenhouse crops, and more recently a MED Q2 subgroup of eastern Mediterranean origin was detected invading and spreading within the country. Over roughly 2010–2020 these MED populations caused increasing problems in protected vegetable and ornamental production, with rising insecticide resistance and concerns about displacement of existing biotypes. By the end of this period, Q2 had established in multiple regions, prompting renewed focus on resistance management and biological control in Korean IPM programs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of greenhouse vegetable and ornamental production with frequent import of plant material and limited crop rotation, plus intensive insecticide use creating strong selection pressure. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of new MED haplotypes, particularly Q2, with higher insecticide resistance and competitive ability, representing novel strain/genotype emergence and enhanced transmission capacity in local conditions.

EPP.scientific.name: Bradybaena similaris
EPP.common.name: Asian trampsnail
Countries: Brazil (southern states – including Rio Grande do Sul, Paraná, Santa Catarina) [2010s]
Host: Strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) and other fruit and vegetable crops, including vines, citrus, banana, coffee, and leafy vegetables
Event.summary: During the 2010s, Bradybaena similaris was increasingly reported as a damaging pest in commercial strawberry fields and other horticultural crops in southern Brazil, culminating in studies published around 2019 that identified it among the principal terrestrial gastropods attacking strawberries and a wide range of other crops. Field surveys in Rio Grande do Sul and neighboring states documented heavy nocturnal feeding on strawberry fruits and foliage, as well as on vines, citrus, banana, coffee, and leafy vegetables, with growers reporting economic losses and contamination of harvested produce. Subsequent adoption of targeted molluscicide use, improved field sanitation, and modifications to irrigation and mulch practices helped moderate the most severe outbreaks, although the snail remains entrenched as a key gastropod pest in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of fruit and vegetable production with drip irrigation, plastic mulches, and abundant ground cover created moist refuges ideal for snail survival; regional transport of planting material and produce likely redistributed B. similaris among farms. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive capacity and broad host range increased its ability to exploit diverse crops, contributing to pronounced resurgence as an economically important pest in southern Brazilian horticulture.
Review: Review – retain with reclassification and minor wording clarification. Confirmed from the Ciência Rural paper and regional pest information that B. similaris has long been present in Brazil but emerged during the 2010s as a prominent pest of strawberries and other horticultural crops in southern states, with clear evidence of crop damage and grower concern. Updated event-type coding to re_occurrence = true and re_emergence = false, because the outbreak reflects resurgence and spread within an already infested country/subregion driven by production intensification and favorable microhabitats, not a new host jump (strawberry was already known as a host) or documented evolutionary change. Adjusted the countries string slightly to make clear that multiple southern Brazilian states are involved while still treating Brazil as the country unit. Recommended action: keep as one of the main South American agricultural impact events, but human reviewer should confirm that it is not better merged with the citrus-nursery episode into a single, broader southern-Brazil horticultural outbreak period.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia spp.
EPP.common.name: Lyme borreliosis
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Primarily humans and wildlife (rodents, birds, cervids) with domestic dogs and, in some areas, horses serving as exposed hosts/sentinels; transmission maintained by Ixodes ricinus and related ticks feeding on wild vertebrates and domestic animals.
Event.summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, Europe experienced a substantial increase and northward/altitudinal expansion of Ixodes ricinus populations and associated Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato transmission, leading to higher Lyme borreliosis incidence and emergence of new risk areas in northern and central Europe, including parts of Scandinavia and high-altitude sites. Field studies in Sweden in the early 1990s documented efficient transmission of Borrelia burgdorferi s.l. from reservoir mammals to I. ricinus, while multi-country analyses later in the 2000s showed rising Lyme incidence in at least nine European countries, coinciding with tick range expansion and increased reports of disease in humans and animals in newly suitable habitats. By around 2010, these processes had produced a continent-wide pattern of geographic expansion, with Lyme borreliosis now established further north and at higher elevations than previously recorded, and endemic transmission persisting in expanded foci rather than ending as a simple outbreak.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climate warming (milder winters and longer vegetation seasons) allowed I. ricinus survival and activity at higher altitudes in central Europe and higher latitudes in Scandinavia; changes in land use and habitat connectivity (reforestation, fragmentation creating ecotones) favored ticks and hosts; increases and redistribution of deer and other cervids provided abundant tick reproductive hosts; and human behavior (recreation in forested landscapes, outdoor work, pet ownership) increased exposure of people and domestic animals. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent adaptation of ticks and Borrelia to new climatic envelopes) and enhanced transmission efficiency in local enzootic cycles; no single novel Borrelia strain has been definitively linked to the overall expansion, though local differences in Borrelia genospecies composition influence host range and pathogenicity.
Review: review – This event appropriately summarizes a large, multi-country expansion of Ixodes ricinus and Lyme borreliosis risk across northern, central and parts of southern Europe, which is among the most impactful global emergence episodes for this pathogen complex in both humans and domestic animals. To comply with the event-type definitions (which treat re_occurrence as mutually exclusive with intra- and inter-continental emergence), I changed the classification by setting re_occurrence from true to false so that the event is coded purely as intra_continental_emergence, reflecting that the defining feature is spread into previously unaffected northern and high-altitude sub-regions rather than resurgence in historically endemic areas. I also replaced the non-specific tick-borne encephalitis Wikipedia link with a review focused on zoonotic tick-borne pathogens in domestic animals in temperate and cold regions of Europe, while retaining the key Ixodes ricinus range-change and Swedish Borrelia transmission studies and a modeling paper on Borrelia dynamics; countries, sub-regions, dates and narrative remain consistent with the literature. Because of these classification and source adjustments, this row is flagged for review but should be retained in the final top-10 list.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus
EPP.common.name: FP-associated herpesvirus, CFPHV
Countries: Mexico (Laguna San Ignacio, Baja California Sur – eastern Pacific [2000s]
Host: Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas)
Event.summary: During the 2000s, FP was first reported in green turtles along the Baja California Peninsula at Laguna San Ignacio, representing an important early record for the eastern Pacific foraging grounds of Mexican green turtles. Over the following decade, additional reports from the region and from the southwestern Gulf of Mexico documented histologically and virologically confirmed ChHV5‑associated FP in green turtles near Veracruz, indicating that clinically apparent FP had become established in both Pacific and Gulf foraging aggregations. By around 2016, FP was recognized as an emerging but still patchily distributed disease in Mexico, extending the known range of FP in both the eastern Pacific and Gulf of Mexico portions of the Central America sub‑region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Mexican FP cases have been reported from nearshore foraging areas influenced by fisheries, coastal development and localized pollution or eutrophication, but detailed multi‑site driver analyses remain sparse. Internal mechanisms: Histopathology and PCR confirmed classical FP lesions and ChHV5 infection in Mexican green turtles, and viral typing studies from northern Sinaloa and other sites show ChHV5 haplotypes closely related to Atlantic and Pacific lineages rather than a novel Mexican strain. This episode is therefore best viewed as an intra‑continental emergence of clinically expressed FP into the Central America sub‑region rather than a new viral lineage.
Review: retain – Mexico’s combined eastern Pacific and Gulf of Mexico FP emergence is important for documenting expansion of clinically expressed FP into the Central America sub‑region and eastern Pacific basin. Event type has been adjusted to intra‑continental emergence only, with re‑emergence removed because this represents first well‑documented establishment in that UNSD sub‑region rather than a reappearance. One Africa‑focused article that was previously listed in the event’s sources has been removed as irrelevant; remaining sources directly describe Baja California and Gulf of Mexico cases. Flagged for review mainly to refine local timing as more Mexican datasets become available.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonellosis
Continent: Europe; North America; South America; Asia; Africa
Sub.regions: Europe: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; North America: Northern America; South America: South America; Asia: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Western Asia; Africa: Northern Africa; Eastern Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa
Host: Commercial layer hens and broilers (poultry); indirectly eggs as product
Event.summary: During the 1980s and 1990s, Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis emerged and then dominated as the leading Salmonella serovar in commercial poultry flocks, with major egg‑associated epidemics in North America and Europe by 1990 and rapid expansion into poultry production in South America, Asia and Africa during the 1990s. The epidemic was driven by infection of layer hen reproductive tissues, allowing transovarian contamination of intact shell eggs and widespread human disease linked to eggs and poultry meat. By the late 1990s, coordinated control programs, including surveillance in poultry breeding and layer flocks, culling of infected flocks and stringent egg refrigeration, reduced prevalence in some high‑income countries, although S. Enteritidis remained established in poultry industries worldwide.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Industrialization and global consolidation of poultry breeding, centralized sourcing of breeding stocks, poor on‑farm biosecurity in some regions, and large‑scale international trade in live poultry enabled inter‑continental dissemination of an epidemic S. Enteritidis lineage. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced ability of certain phage types/lineages to colonize ovaries and oviducts of laying hens and survive in egg contents facilitated vertical and food‑borne transmission; no single resistance determinant dominated this event, but adaptation to intensive poultry environments and high egg contamination potential underpinned re‑emergence.
Review: Review – Event correctly captures the late‑20th‑century global Salmonella Enteritidis epidemic in commercial poultry and eggs. The 1990–2000 window is acceptable as the main phase within the post‑1990 scope, but the event‑type classification has been clarified: the epidemic lineage is treated as a re‑emergent, egg‑adapted clone with major inter‑continental spread (inter_continental_emergence = Yes; re_emergence = Yes), while intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence are set to No to respect the classification scheme.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonellosis
Continent: Europe; North America; South America; Asia; Africa; Oceania
Sub.regions: Europe: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; North America: Northern America; South America: South America; Asia: Western Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Africa: Southern Africa and other affected subregions; Oceania: Australia and New Zealand
Host: Broiler chickens and turkeys (commercial flocks and slaughterhouses); poultry meat and offal; occasionally other livestock and environmental reservoirs
Event.summary: From the early 2000s onward, a clonal lineage of Salmonella enterica serovar Infantis carrying a large pESI or pESI‑like megaplasmid encoding multidrug resistance, heavy‑metal resistance and additional virulence and fitness factors emerged in broiler production systems. First characterized in broiler‑associated isolates from Israel in the mid‑2000s, this lineage subsequently established itself in broiler flocks and broiler meat in multiple European countries, North America and South America, with pESI‑positive Infantis becoming a predominant serovar in broiler meat in the European Union and increasing sharply in raw chicken and turkey products in the United States during the 2010s. By the 2010s, pESI‑carrying S. Infantis had been detected in poultry, meat and human infections across parts of Asia, Africa and Oceania as well, indicating global dissemination of this adapted, multidrug‑resistant broiler‑associated lineage.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and vertical integration of global broiler production, international trade in breeding stocks, and widespread antimicrobial use in poultry created strong selection and dissemination pathways for a successful S. Infantis lineage. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of the pESI megaplasmid (and related pESI‑like plasmids) carrying extended‑spectrum beta‑lactamase genes such as blaCTX-M-65, other antimicrobial‑resistance determinants, metal‑resistance genes, siderophore systems and additional fitness/virulence genes increased persistence in broiler farms and carcasses and facilitated adaptation to intensive poultry environments, constituting a major re‑emergent and inter‑continental clone.
Review: Review – New event added to capture the global emergence of pESI‑positive multidrug‑resistant Salmonella Infantis in broiler production from the early 2000s through the 2010s and into the 2020s. This lineage is now a dominant Salmonella serovar in broiler flocks and broiler meat in the EU and a major contributor to poultry‑associated salmonellosis in the United States and other regions, and it fits the definition of an inter‑continental re‑emergence driven by acquisition of a megaplasmid conferring extensive resistance and enhanced fitness. Country lists and dates are simplified and should be checked by subject‑matter experts, but omission of this event would likely leave out one of the most impactful modern Salmonella emergence episodes in food animals.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
EPP.common.name: gonoccocus
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Australia and New Zealand; Northern America; Western Europe
Host: Humans (sexually transmitted infection in heterosexual and MSM populations)
Event.summary: From the early 1990s, fluoroquinolone-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae emerged in East and South‑East Asia and the Western Pacific and was soon detected in Hawaii and other parts of the United States, largely among infections linked to travel in Asia. Over the mid‑ to late‑1990s and early 2000s these resistant lineages became established across Asia and Oceania and then in Northern America and Western Europe, with rapidly rising resistance proportions in sites such as Honolulu, California and the United Kingdom. By about 2007, fluoroquinolone resistance exceeded stewardship thresholds in many settings, leading countries (including a 2007 national change in US CDC guidelines) to stop recommending fluoroquinolones for gonorrhoea and leaving extended‑spectrum cephalosporins as the only routinely recommended class.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy and often indiscriminate use of fluoroquinolones to treat gonorrhoea and many other community infections in East/South‑East Asia and later globally; high partner change rates and dense sexual networks facilitating rapid dissemination; international travel and sex tourism linking Asian epicentres with Hawaii, North America and Europe. Internal mechanisms: Stepwise accumulation of mutations in gyrA and parC conferring high‑level fluoroquinolone resistance; selection and clonal expansion of successful resistant lineages with adequate fitness that could compete with susceptible strains.
Review: Review – Major global emergence of fluoroquinolone-resistant N. gonorrhoeae correctly identified and supported by primary sources. Corrected the continent label to use 'Northern America', extended the end year to 2007 to reflect the US CDC decision to stop recommending fluoroquinolones, and reclassified the episode purely as re-emergence (removed intra- and inter-continental emergence) because resistance arose within an already global pathogen.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
EPP.common.name: gonoccocus
Host: Humans (primarily men who have sex with men in urban centres)
Event.summary: Across the 1990s, several Western and Northern European countries reported declining gonorrhoea incidence in the general population but a simultaneous rise in cases among men who have sex with men, particularly in major cities. Sentinel surveillance from nine Western European countries documented increasing gonorrhoea diagnoses among MSM in the mid‑1990s even as heterosexual rates continued to fall, and these MSM‑focused resurgences persisted into the 2000s. Targeted prevention campaigns and integration of STI services into HIV care and community settings partially stabilised incidence but did not fully reverse the upward trend.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Behaviour change among MSM following the introduction of effective HIV therapy, including reduced condom use and more frequent partner change; concentration of sexual networks in urban gay venues and, later, online platforms; improved testing in MSM communities that increased case detection; stigma and access barriers that delayed care for some groups. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel resistance mechanism defined this resurgence, but many circulating strains carried accumulated resistance to penicillin, tetracycline and later fluoroquinolones, allowing persistent transmission where outdated regimens were still used.
Review: Retain – Appropriately captures the MSM-focused gonorrhoea resurgence in Western and Northern Europe during the 1990s–2000s; timing, geography and classification as re-occurrence (behaviourally driven resurgence without a single defining new strain) are consistent with surveillance reports, and no structural corrections were required.

Event.summary: Between 2020 and 2024, WHO’s global GASP/EGASP and related systems documented sharp increases in resistance or decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone, cefixime and azithromycin in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, with resistant isolates reported from a growing number of countries on all inhabited continents. From 2022 onward, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported an upsurge of ceftriaxone‑resistant, multidrug‑resistant and extensively drug‑resistant gonorrhoea in the EU/EEA and United Kingdom, including clusters with clear evidence of domestic transmission rather than purely imported cases. By 2025 these patterns prompted strong international warnings that continued spread of such strains could severely compromise standard gonorrhoea treatment, leading to updated guidelines, intensified surveillance and renewed calls for vaccine and drug development.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Ongoing heavy use of ceftriaxone and, in many countries, azithromycin, sometimes at suboptimal doses; disrupted STI services and treatment interruptions during the COVID‑19 pandemic leading to delayed care and possible inappropriate antibiotic use; global travel and interconnected sexual networks enabling rapid international dissemination of resistant clones such as FC428‑like strains; limited culture‑based testing capacity in many low- and middle‑income countries, which allowed resistance to spread before detection. Internal mechanisms: Further expansion of mosaic penA alleles conferring ceftriaxone and cefixime resistance, often combined with macrolide resistance mutations and other determinants to produce MDR and XDR phenotypes; selection of clones with high biological fitness that can transmit efficiently despite carrying multiple resistance mutations; incremental elevation of MIC distributions, so that a rising fraction of isolates approach or exceed clinical breakpoints for last‑line drugs.
Review: Review – Appropriately summarises the recent global escalation of ceftriaxone-, cefixime- and azithromycin-resistant gonorrhoea documented by WHO GASP/EGASP and ECDC, and correctly treats this as a re-emergence episode driven by increasingly fit resistant clones rather than as new continental emergence. The continent field was standardised to list all inhabited continents explicitly, and intra-/inter-continental emergence flags were removed to align with the event-type definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: Haemophilus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Haemophilus influenzae infection
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Northern America
Host: Humans (patients with invasive disease and community‑acquired respiratory infections; adults and children)
Event.summary: Over roughly the last decade, surveillance and genomic studies from East Asia, Europe and North America have documented the emergence and spread of multidrug‑resistant (MDR) nontypeable H. influenzae (NTHi) responsible for invasive disease and difficult‑to‑treat respiratory infections. A detailed study from northern Taiwan of invasive NTHi collected between 2011 and 2020 showed that most isolates were ampicillin resistant and over half were MDR, with novel resistance transposons carrying up to seven antibiotic-resistance genes, while European and North American series reported increasing proportions of BLNAR, BLPACR and fluoroquinolone- or macrolide-resistant NTHi among invasive and otitis media isolates. EPP.common.name: Enterococcus faecium infection

Review: retain – Event appropriately summarizes the spread and establishment of hospital‑adapted VREfm (CC17/A1) across multiple European sub‑regions in the 1990s–early 2000s. Geography matches UN sub‑regions, and classification as intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence is consistent with the definitions. Sources are relevant and event impact is clearly among the largest for this EPP.

Event.summary: From the early 1990s through about 2015, the high‑risk Pseudomonas aeruginosa clone ST235, together with related epidemic lineages such as ST111, ST175 and ST244, expanded from initial foci in Europe and Asia into hospitals worldwide. Over this period, these clones became leading causes of multidrug‑resistant and extensively drug‑resistant P. aeruginosa infections in ICUs and other high‑risk wards across Europe, Asia, the Americas, Africa and Oceania, driving rising carbapenem resistance and worse clinical outcomes. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence in the form of high‑risk sequence types, especially ST235 (often ExoU‑positive) and ST111/ST175, which combine multiple acquired β‑lactamases (ESBLs and carbapenemases such as VIM and IMP) with intrinsic resistance mechanisms and virulence factors, enhancing both resistance and pathogenicity; enhanced transmission and environmental persistence due to biofilm formation and fitness traits; geographic range expansion enabled by this combination of resistance and virulence.

I have therefore set intra_continental_emergence and inter_continental_emergence to false and retained re_emergence = true to reflect emergence of new resistant/virulent lineages. The continent field has been simplified to “Multiple continents (global)” to acknowledge worldwide distribution while keeping sub‑continent detail in the sub_regions field. This event should be retained as one of the major AMR-driven P. aeruginosa emergence events but merits expert review of clone lists and country coverage if more detailed comparative burden data become available.

Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Western Asia; Northern America; South America; Northern Africa; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults and children, especially ICU, burns, and immunocompromised patients)
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through about 2015, the high‑risk Pseudomonas aeruginosa clone ST235, together with related epidemic lineages such as ST111, ST175 and ST244, expanded from initial foci in Europe and Asia into hospitals worldwide. Over this period, these clones became leading causes of multidrug‑resistant and extensively drug‑resistant P. aeruginosa infections in ICUs and other high‑risk wards across Europe, Asia, the Americas, Africa and Oceania, driving rising carbapenem resistance and worse clinical outcomes. By the mid‑2010s, genomic and surveillance studies demonstrated that ST235 and other high‑risk clones had established endemic transmission on all inhabited continents, after which local infection‑control programs and antibiotic‑stewardship efforts began to limit spread in some centers but did not eliminate these clones globally.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive and often inappropriate use of broad‑spectrum β‑lactams and fluoroquinolones in hospital settings selected for multidrug‑resistant clones; high connectivity of healthcare networks, international travel and patient transfer allowed inter‑regional spread; inadequate infection‑prevention infrastructure and overcrowding in some hospitals facilitated endemic transmission. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence in the form of high‑risk sequence types, especially ST235 (often ExoU‑positive) and ST111/ST175, which combine multiple acquired β‑lactamases (ESBLs and carbapenemases such as VIM and IMP) with intrinsic resistance mechanisms and virulence factors, enhancing both resistance and pathogenicity; enhanced transmission and environmental persistence due to biofilm formation and fitness traits; geographic range expansion enabled by this combination of resistance and virulence.
Review: review – Event correctly captures the global emergence and spread of high‑risk P. aeruginosa clones (notably ST235, ST111, ST175) across multiple continents and is well supported by clone-focused reviews and genomic studies.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1368764615000369?utm_source=openai)) However, the original classification as both intra‑continental and inter‑continental emergence conflicts with the project definition, which specifies that these categories should only be used when the EPP organism itself is new to a subregion/continent; ST235 and related clones are novel genotypes of an already endemic species. I have therefore set intra_continental_emergence and inter_continental_emergence to false and retained re_emergence = true to reflect emergence of new resistant/virulent lineages. The continent field has been simplified to “Multiple continents (global)” to acknowledge worldwide distribution while keeping sub‑continent detail in the sub_regions field. This event should be retained as one of the major AMR-driven P. aeruginosa emergence events but merits expert review of clone lists and country coverage if more detailed comparative burden data become available.

Internal mechanisms: introduction and clonal expansion of CA‑MRSA lineages (ST30 and USA300‑Latin American variant) carrying PVL and other virulence factors, representing novel strain/genotype emergence, increased virulence/pathogenicity, and enhanced community transmission; diversification and adaptation of these clones within the region over time.

EPP.scientific.name: Staphylococcus aureus
EPP.common.name: Staphylococcus aureus infection
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Humans (community-associated skin and soft tissue infections; some invasive infections; plus healthcare-associated infections caused by CA-MRSA strains)
Event.summary: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, Europe, which already faced entrenched hospital MRSA epidemics, began to detect increasing numbers of CA‑MRSA infections, often associated with PVL‑positive clones imported or related to lineages circulating in other continents. Through the 2000s, CA‑MRSA outbreaks and sporadic cases were reported in multiple European countries—including the UK, France, Spain, Italy, Germany and the Netherlands—with some spread of USA300 and other virulent CA lineages into both the community and healthcare facilities. By the mid‑2010s, CA‑MRSA remained less dominant in Europe than in North America or parts of Oceania, but had become a recognized and sometimes severe cause of skin, soft tissue, and invasive infections across several European subregions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: international travel and migration introducing epidemic CA‑MRSA clones, antibiotic selection pressure in both community and hospital settings, and opportunities for transmission in households, sports teams, military settings, and hospitals. Internal mechanisms: introduction and secondary spread of PVL‑positive CA‑MRSA lineages (including USA300 and related strains) into a region already dominated by hospital MRSA clones, representing novel strain/genotype emergence and increased virulence/pathogenicity relative to traditional hospital lineages.
Review: retain – Appropriately summarizes the emergence of PVL-positive CA-MRSA lineages (e.g., ST80, ST30, USA300 introductions) in Europe during the 2000s with moderate but geographically broad impact, and correctly classifies this as re_emergence in a continent where MRSA was already endemic in hospitals. EPP.scientific.name: Treponema pallidum
EPP.common.name: Syphilis
Sub.regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Eastern Asia
Host: Humans with syphilis receiving macrolide therapy (primarily MSM and other sexually active adults)
Event.summary: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, clinically significant macrolide-resistant Treponema pallidum was identified, with azithromycin treatment failures linked to A2058G mutations in the 23S rRNA gene first reported in patients in San Francisco and then elsewhere in North America and Europe. During the 2000s, surveillance documented rapidly increasing proportions of macrolide-resistant strains in U.S. and Canadian cities and in several European and Chinese settings, making macrolide monotherapy unreliable for syphilis treatment. By around 2010, macrolide-resistant T. pallidum had become prevalent on multiple continents, and international guidelines moved away from macrolides toward penicillin-based regimens except in narrowly defined circumstances.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread, often empiric use of azithromycin and other macrolides for STI and respiratory infections, including off-guideline use of single‑dose azithromycin as a convenient alternative to injectable benzathine penicillin for syphilis in some settings; overlapping high‑transmission sexual networks in MSM facilitated dissemination of resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and clonal spread of point mutations (A2058G and later A2059G) in the 23S rRNA gene of T. pallidum conferred high-level macrolide resistance, a clear example of antimicrobial resistance–driven re-emergence.
Review: review – Retain as a key global re-emergence event driven by antimicrobial resistance, but the type-of-emergence coding has been aligned with the project rules: intra_continental_emergence and inter_continental_emergence have been set to false, because the species was long present on all affected continents and this episode reflects the emergence and spread of resistant lineages (re-emergence) rather than first occurrence in new regions. Country list has been slightly expanded to name major documented sites (e.g. Seattle, Baltimore) while still summarising other affected European locations in aggregate.

EPP.scientific.name: Histoplasma spp.
EPP.common.name: histoplasmosis
Host: Humans living with HIV, especially with advanced HIV disease (AIDS)
Event.summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, disseminated histoplasmosis emerged as a leading AIDS-defining opportunistic infection and cause of death among people with advanced HIV in several Latin American settings, notably French Guiana and likely other South and Central American countries. Longitudinal cohorts from French Guiana documented hundreds of microbiologically proven disseminated cases from the early 1990s through the 2010s, with incidence rates up to 15 cases per 1,000 person‑years in HIV cohorts and case‑fatality comparable to or exceeding tuberculosis when diagnosis was delayed. Modelling and multicountry data later showed that, by around 2012, HIV-associated histoplasmosis incidence and deaths in Latin America rivalled or exceeded those due to tuberculosis in people living with HIV, cementing its role as a major, previously neglected killer in this region.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6958354/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The HIV epidemic created large populations of profoundly immunosuppressed individuals in endemic Histoplasma regions of Latin America, dramatically increasing the probability of progression from latent or subclinical infection to disseminated disease. Health-system factors—limited awareness, misdiagnosis as tuberculosis, and poor access to rapid antigen testing and effective antifungals—contributed heavily to high mortality, making histoplasmosis a neglected opportunistic infection. External social drivers included poverty, delayed HIV testing, and late presentation to care. Internal mechanisms: No single new fungal genotype is implicated; rather, established Histoplasma lineages caused severe disease in immunocompromised hosts, demonstrating host-population expansion (high-risk HIV group) and clinical re-expression of an old pathogen under new immunologic conditions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10687118/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This event summarizes the very large burden of HIV-associated disseminated histoplasmosis in Latin America and the Caribbean, which modelling shows to cause incidence and mortality comparable to or greater than tuberculosis among people with HIV in the region. The classification as re-occurrence (resurgence in already endemic subregions driven mainly by external factors: HIV epidemic, weak diagnostics, late ART) is appropriate; intra-/inter‑continental emergence are rightly not used. Countries and subregions match the UNSD structure for Latin America, though the country list is necessarily selective rather than exhaustive; this could be further detailed in future iterations but does not warrant exclusion.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptococcus neoformans
EPP.common.name: cryptococcosis
Host: Humans (primarily HIV-infected adults with suspected meningitis)
Event.summary: Between roughly 2004 and 2014, studies from Botswana, South Africa, Zambia, and Uganda demonstrated that cryptococcal meningitis had become the leading identified cause of adult meningitis in much of southern and eastern Africa. National and referral-hospital data from Botswana indicated that cryptococcal meningitis accounted for about 90% of microbiologically confirmed adult meningitis cases, mirroring earlier and contemporaneous data from high-HIV-prevalence provinces in South Africa and from Zambia. In a Ugandan cohort of HIV-infected adults with suspected meningitis (2010–2012), cryptococcal meningitis accounted for about 60% of all meningitis diagnoses, with bacterial and tuberculous meningitis much less common. Over this period, bacterial meningitis incidence declined with introduction of conjugate vaccines, but cryptococcal meningitis persisted as the dominant cause of adult meningitis in these settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high prevalence of advanced HIV disease, incomplete ART coverage and adherence, late care-seeking, and limited diagnostic capacity for alternative meningitis etiologies concentrated adult meningitis burden in cryptococcal disease. Introduction of bacterial conjugate vaccines reduced bacterial meningitis, increasing the relative share of cryptococcal meningitis among adult meningitis cases. Internal mechanisms: No strong evidence for major pathogen evolution; the patterns reflect changing host susceptibility and competing etiologies rather than new cryptococcal strains.
Review: review: The overall event concept (cryptococcal meningitis becoming the leading cause of adult meningitis in parts of southern and eastern Africa) is well supported by Botswana national data and adult meningitis cohort studies from South Africa and Uganda.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6679721/?utm_source=openai)) Corrections made: (i) the Ugandan country period was changed from “Uganda [2004–2012]” to “Uganda [2010–2012]” to match the prospective cohort that found 60% of meningitis cases due to cryptococcal meningitis,([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4347329/?utm_source=openai)) and (ii) the Countries field was clarified to give explicit date ranges for South Africa and Uganda rather than vague descriptors such as “pre-ART era comparator.” Source URLs were updated to replace the Uganda 2015–2017 paper with the more relevant 2010–2012 cohort description (PMC4347329). The episode remains classified as re-occurrence; flagged for review to confirm the exact date ranges for Zambia and for consistency with any additional national datasets.

EPP.scientific.name: Talaromyces marneffei
EPP.common.name: talaromycosis
Host: Humans – primarily adults with advanced HIV/AIDS
Event.summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, talaromycosis expanded from northern Thailand into a belt of neighboring Southeast Asian countries, with autochthonous AIDS-associated cases documented in Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, Vietnam and later the Philippines. In Vietnam, the first AIDS-related talaromycosis cases were reported in 1996–1997, followed by a large cohort of patients managed at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases in Ho Chi Minh City between 1996 and 2009, where talaromycosis became a common AIDS-defining illness. By the late 2000s, talaromycosis was recognized as an established endemic opportunistic mycosis across much of mainland South-eastern Asia, with incidence gradually modified by improving HIV testing and antiretroviral therapy programs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional spread and maturation of the HIV epidemic throughout mainland South-eastern Asia, combined with ecological suitability (presence of bamboo rat reservoirs and favorable climate) and improvements in mycology diagnostic capacity in referral centers. Internal mechanisms: No specific new fungal genotype identified; the emergence is best explained by geographic expansion of recognized human infection due to increased exposure and susceptible hosts and by improved recognition rather than biological change of the pathogen.
Review: review – Event appropriately captures the multi-country spread of HIV-associated talaromycosis within South-eastern Asia and should be retained as one of the largest regional episodes; however, the emergence type has been corrected from re_emergence to re_occurrence because expansion into additional countries within the same UNSD sub-region is driven by HIV epidemiology and improved detection rather than documented pathogen change, and it does not qualify as intra-continental emergence under the given rules.

EPP.scientific.name: Talaromyces marneffei
EPP.common.name: talaromycosis
Host: Humans – primarily HIV-negative adults with adult-onset immunodeficiency due to anti–interferon-γ autoantibodies; other inborn errors of immunity and iatrogenic immunosuppression
Event.summary: From around 2004 onwards, clinicians in Thailand, Taiwan, Hong Kong and southern China began reporting clusters of disseminated talaromycosis in HIV-negative adults with unexplained susceptibility to intracellular pathogens, which were later linked to high-titer neutralizing anti–interferon-γ autoantibodies and related adult-onset immunodeficiency syndromes. Over the 2000s and 2010s, multiple case series confirmed T. marneffei as a leading fungal pathogen in this new host group, often presenting with recurrent or relapsing talaromycosis and co-infections such as nontuberculous mycobacteria and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. By around 2020, talaromycosis associated with anti–IFN-γ autoantibody–mediated adult-onset immunodeficiency and other inborn errors of immunity was widely recognized across endemic regions in East and Southeast Asia, representing a major re-occurrence of the pathogen in a non-HIV immunodeficient population and contributing to substantial morbidity and mortality despite antifungal therapy.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Emergence and recognition of adult-onset immunodeficiency syndromes due to anti–IFN-γ autoantibodies and increased use of advanced immunosuppressive therapies for cancer and autoimmune diseases; improved immunologic and genetic diagnostics revealed underlying immune defects in previously unexplained non-HIV talaromycosis cases. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of recognized disease into new immunologic niches within the human host population (adult-onset neutralizing anti–IFN-γ autoantibody–mediated immunodeficiency and other inborn errors of immunity); no specific fungal genetic change has been definitively linked, so the episode is treated as re-occurrence driven by changes in host immunity and medical practice.
Review: review – This event is retained as it captures a major shift of talaromycosis into HIV-negative adults with anti–IFN-γ autoantibody–mediated and other immunodeficiencies across East and South-eastern Asia; the emergence type is standardized to re_occurrence (first_detection and re_emergence set to false), reflecting that the fungus exploits newly recognized human immune defects within already endemic subregions rather than representing a new global detection or documented pathogen-level re-emergence.

EPP.common.name: Morganella infection
Continent: Asia; Europe; Africa; North America; Oceania
Sub.regions: Southern Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Eastern Africa; Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Hospitalized human patients (mixed adult populations, mainly with prior healthcare exposure or recent medical care in the Indian subcontinent) infected or colonized with NDM‑producing Enterobacteriaceae, including occasional Morganella morganii isolates

EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Chickens (broilers and pullets; commercial layer and broiler operations)
Event.summary: During the 1990s, very virulent infectious bursal disease virus (vvIBDV), first recognized in Europe in the late 1980s, caused a continent-wide wave of severe Gumboro disease outbreaks, beginning in Benelux countries and rapidly involving major poultry producers across Western and Northern Europe. The epizootic led to high flock mortality and heavy production losses, exemplified by a 1998 Danish episode affecting 36 broiler farms and causing the loss of over 200,000 broilers, while similar patterns of mortality and immunosuppression were reported in multiple European states. Improved vaccination strategies, biosecurity, and adaptation of control programs to vvIBDV pathotypes gradually reduced overt mortality by the late 1990s, though vvIBDV became enzootic in many European poultry sectors.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and geographic concentration of broiler and layer production, dense poultry populations with high farm connectivity, and movement of live birds and hatching eggs facilitated rapid dissemination of vvIBDV between European countries; gaps in existing vaccination programs, designed for classical strains, left flocks vulnerable. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of very virulent serotype 1 strains with increased virulence (increased virulence/pathogenicity) and enhanced capacity to cause high mortality and severe bursal damage; antigenic differences from classical and U.S. variant strains reduced protection from existing vaccines and favored geographic range expansion within Europe (geographic range expansion, inherent).
Review: review: Retain this event as the major vvIBDV epizootic in Europe, but change 'intra_continental_emergence' from Yes to No because vvIBDV arose within an already endemic IBDV population and, per the project rules, new pathotypes should be treated as re-emergence rather than intra-continental emergence. Geography, timing and impact are well supported by European reviews and outbreak reports, but the revised classification should be quality-checked.

EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Host: Chickens (backyard and commercial flocks)
Event.summary: The first recognized infectious bursal disease outbreaks in Bangladesh were reported at the end of 1992, coinciding with reports of severe Gumboro disease in neighboring South Asian countries and marking the southward spread of vvIBDV within Asia into high-density poultry systems of the subcontinent. Through the 1990s, repeated, large-scale outbreaks with high mortality and marked bursal pathology occurred in broiler and layer flocks across Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, causing heavy production losses and predisposing birds to secondary infections. By around 2000, IBDV—often in very virulent form—was firmly established in South Asian poultry; improved vaccines and control programs subsequently mitigated but did not eliminate recurrent disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of commercial poultry production in South Asia, movement of day-old chicks and hatching eggs, and limited early diagnostic and surveillance capacity supported the introduction and spread of vvIBDV into Bangladesh and neighboring countries; concurrent endemic diseases amplified the impact of IBDV-induced immunosuppression. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and regional expansion of vvIBDV strains closely related to European/Asian very virulent lineages (novel strain/genotype emergence relative to previously circulating or undetected IBDV) with high virulence and strong B-cell tropism (increased virulence/pathogenicity), combined with selection for variants able to escape partial vaccine immunity (antigenic diversification facilitating re-emergence).
Review: review: This South Asian wave of severe IBD (vvIBDV) should be kept as one of the major emergence events, but 'intra_continental_emergence' was set to No because the virus species was already endemic in the region and the new pathotype represents re-emergence rather than spread of a previously absent EPP. Otherwise, the timing (Bangladesh first recognized in 1992 with spread across India and Pakistan in the 1990s) and the listed countries align with primary reports and reviews.

EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Host: Chickens (commercial broilers, layers, and smallholder flocks)
Event.summary: From the mid-2000s through the early 2010s, West African countries such as Nigeria and Ghana reported recurrent, severe outbreaks of infectious bursal disease attributed to very virulent IBDV strains in both commercial and smallholder poultry, often in flocks that had been vaccinated. These outbreaks were characterized by high mortality, marked bursal lesions, and strong immunosuppression that exacerbated other endemic diseases, causing substantial economic losses and undermining farmer confidence in vaccines. Although updated vaccination regimes and improved husbandry gradually reduced disease severity in some large operations, vvIBDV remained enzootic in West Africa, and outbreaks continued to reappear in new locations and production systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of commercial poultry production in West Africa, frequent movement of chicks and live birds with limited biosecurity, and incomplete vaccine coverage or mismatches between field and vaccine strains facilitated resurgence; socioeconomic constraints limited consistent implementation of control measures. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of vvIBDV lineages confirmed by molecular characterization in Nigerian and Ghanaian flocks, including in vaccinated birds (novel strain/genotype emergence relative to earlier classical strains and evidence of vaccine escape); high virulence and immunosuppressive capacity (increased virulence/pathogenicity) supported repeated re-emergence and persistence despite control efforts.
Review: retain: This West African event is well supported by molecular studies and outbreak descriptions documenting vvIBDV in vaccinated flocks in Nigeria and Ghana; coding as both re-occurrence and re-emergence is appropriate because failures of control measures and virulent genotypes both contributed. Geography (Western Africa) and timing (mid‑2000s to early 2010s) are consistent with the literature, so no substantive corrections are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers)
Event.summary: Between the early 2000s and early 2010s, China and other East Asian countries experienced repeated infectious bursal disease outbreaks associated with evolving vvIBDV lineages, including strains with distinctive VP2 and VP1 genomic features and reassortant genomes, in intensively reared chickens. These outbreaks caused significant mortality and bursal destruction in young birds and led to chronic immunosuppression problems in broiler and layer operations, despite extensive vaccination efforts. Over time, adaptation of vaccine strains and schedules to circulating vvIBDV and increased biosecurity helped reduce overt mortality, but genetically diverse vvIBDV strains persisted and continued to cause episodic disease and economic losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extremely dense and rapidly expanding poultry industries in China and neighboring countries, high farm connectivity, and intense vaccine usage created selective pressure and opportunities for viral evolution and spread; large integrated systems facilitated the rapid dissemination of successful viral variants. Internal mechanisms: Continued evolution and diversification of vvIBDV strains, including novel VP2 hypervariable-region mutations and evidence of reassortment between classical and very virulent segment lineages (novel strain/genotype emergence and reassortment), sometimes associated with altered antigenicity and pathogenicity (increased virulence/pathogenicity and partial vaccine escape), underpinning repeated re-emergence events.
Review: retain: This event accurately captures the continued evolution and episodic impact of vvIBDV in East Asia during the 2000s, with appropriate classification as re-emergence and no intra- or inter-continental spread. The cited Chinese sequence and pathogenicity studies support both the timing and the description of reassortant vvIBDV lineages, so no major changes were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Babesia spp.
EPP.common.name: Babesiosis
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe
Host: Dogs
Event.summary: From the early 1990s onwards, canine babesiosis caused mainly by Babesia canis expanded from long-standing endemic foci in southern Europe into central, western and northern European countries where cases had previously been rare and largely associated with travelled dogs. Over subsequent decades, autochthonous infections and new endemic foci were documented in Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, the Netherlands, Belgium, Poland and later Baltic countries such as Lithuania and Latvia, in parallel with marked north- and westward expansion of the ornate dog tick Dermacentor reticulatus. By the 2010s, canine babesiosis was recognized as an emerging and in some regions rapidly spreading tick-borne disease across much of central and northeastern Europe, prompting increased surveillance and tick-control recommendations but no prospect of continent-wide elimination.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climate warming with milder winters and longer vegetation seasons, land-use changes that created suitable meadow and riparian habitats, and changing wildlife host densities all favoured expansion of Dermacentor reticulatus into central and northern Europe; increased movement of pet dogs and greater veterinary awareness also contributed to detection. Internal mechanisms: Efficient transovarial and transstadial transmission of B. canis in D. reticulatus and inherent geographic range expansion capacity of this tick species underpinned establishment of new endemic foci, with emerging reports of imidocarb treatment failures in some areas suggesting that drug resistance may be developing locally.
Review: retain – Large, multi-decade expansion of canine babesiosis due to Babesia canis and Dermacentor reticulatus into central, western and northern Europe is well supported by surveys and tick-distribution studies; the listed countries, broad time ranges and event types (intra-continental emergence plus re-emergence) are consistent with UNSD sub-regions and project rules, so no structural changes were made.

EPP.common.name: Babesiosis
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Host: Dogs (including fighting breeds and imported dogs)
Event.summary: In 2003, a dog in Spain with clinical babesiosis was confirmed by molecular testing to be infected with Babesia gibsoni, providing the first PCR-verified record of this predominantly Asian small Babesia species in a European dog. Over the 2000s and early 2010s, additional B. gibsoni infections were identified in dogs in Germany, the United Kingdom and other European countries, often in American Pit Bull Terriers, American Staffordshire Terriers or other fighting breeds, some of which had links to imported dogs or organized dog fighting. Most cases were sporadic and concentrated in specific high-risk populations, but their recognition demonstrated that B. gibsoni had been introduced to Europe and could persist through dog-to-dog transmission, prompting broader diagnostic screening and guidance on preventing spread via bites and contaminated blood.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International movement and trade of dogs, particularly importation of fighting breeds from B. gibsoni-endemic regions in Asia and North America, and contact during dog fighting or other close-contact activities facilitated introduction and localized spread; increasing use of molecular diagnostics allowed differentiation of B. gibsoni from other small piroplasms. Internal mechanisms: Persistence of B. gibsoni in chronically infected carrier dogs and efficient non-tick transmission via blood exposure (bites, transfusions) enabled establishment in new canine populations despite the apparent absence of its primary tick vector in much of Europe; no clearly novel parasite lineage was implicated, so the event is best interpreted as inter-continental geographic spread of an existing lineage rather than true re-emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia spp.
EPP.common.name: Lyme borreliosis
Countries: Morocco [1990s] (sporadic human Lyme borreliosis cases and B. lusitaniae-infected ticks)
Host: Humans (small case series with erythema migrans, neurologic and articular manifestations), domestic dogs and horses as potential exposed hosts, and wildlife including small mammals and lizards (e.g. Psammodromus algirus) serving as reservoirs; infection maintained mainly in Ixodes ricinus and Ixodes inopinatus in North Africa and, in some eastern African sites, in Hyalomma rufipes associated with migratory birds and livestock.
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, clinical and serological studies in Tunisia identified patients with erythema migrans and compatible neurological and articular symptoms, together with high seroprevalence for Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato, providing the first recognized Lyme borreliosis cases in North Africa and coinciding with detection of Borrelia lusitaniae and related genospecies in Ixodes ticks. Subsequent work in the 1990s and 2000s documented very high prevalence of B. lusitaniae in I. ricinus and I. inopinatus ticks in Tunisia and Morocco and additional detections of Lyme-group Borrelia in ticks from Algeria and Egypt, while small human case series and serosurveys confirmed that Lyme borreliosis was present but non-endemic and likely underdiagnosed. During the 2000s, Lyme-group Borrelia, including B. garinii, were also reported from ticks along the Indian Ocean coasts of Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique, associated with migratory birds and Hyalomma rufipes, indicating limited but genuine autochthonous establishment of Lyme-group Borrelia cycles in selected North and East African coastal ecosystems rather than mere importation of cases from Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Suitable Mediterranean and coastal climates in North African Maghreb countries and along parts of the western Indian Ocean coast provide humidity and vegetation structure favorable to Ixodes spp. and other ticks, while migratory birds moving between Europe and Africa likely introduced and help maintain Lyme-group Borrelia across the Mediterranean and into East Africa; local land use and presence of lizards, small mammals and livestock create additional reservoir and vector habitats. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of Lyme-group Borrelia and their tick vectors into African coastal environments, including adaptation of Borrelia lusitaniae to reptile reservoirs and Ixodes species prevalent in Mediterranean habitats, and possible spillover via Hyalomma ticks that feed on migratory birds and savanna animals. Overall incidence remains low and focal, but this represents the first documented establishment of Lyme-group Borrelia transmission cycles in African wildlife and domestic-animal systems.
Review: review – This is a new row added during peer review to capture first detections and limited emergence of Lyme-group Borrelia and Lyme borreliosis in Africa, based on clinical series from Tunisia in the 1990s and high Borrelia lusitaniae infection rates in Ixodes ticks in Tunisia and Morocco, together with later reports of Lyme-group Borrelia along the Indian Ocean coasts of Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique. Dates and country list are approximate and derived from regional reviews rather than harmonized surveillance data, so confidence is set lower (0.7) and this row is flagged for review in future iterations, but including it aligns the dataset with the rule that first continent-level detection events may be retained even when case numbers are modest.

Host: Ornamental koi carp; farmed and wild or stocked common carp
Event.summary: In autumn 2013, the first Dutch cases of koi sleepy disease due to CEV were confirmed in koi, signalling spread of the virus into Western Europe beyond the UK. Over the early to mid‑2010s, France experienced increasing reports of winter and early-spring mortality events in adult carp in ponds and lakes linked to CEV, and in 2014 Germany documented its first clinical outbreak in koi showing classic lethargy, gill necrosis and high mortality. These outbreaks demonstrated that CEV had become widely established in Western European koi and carp populations, contributing to substantial losses in recreational and production fisheries.([library.wur.nl](https://library.wur.nl/WebQuery/groenekennis/2048251?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intense trade in ornamental koi and movements of stocking carp among Western European countries facilitated repeated introductions and secondary spread; overwintering or early-spring holding of carp at low yet permissive temperatures favored disease expression; carp angling and restocking practices moved infected fish between waters with limited health screening. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of CEV genogroup I viruses adapted to common carp and genogroup II viruses carried in koi provided a viral background able to exploit these trade and management pathways; no clearly novel Western European lineage is required to explain the emergence, so this event is treated as intra‑continental spread rather than re‑emergence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4431602/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review. The Netherlands start date has been corrected to 2013, when first KSD/CEV cases were reported there; France and Germany timing remain approximate but consistent with early Western European detections. This episode clearly reflects spread into a new European subregion following UK introduction, so intra_continental_emergence has been set to true and re_emergence reset to false.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus
EPP.common.name: FP-associated herpesvirus, CFPHV
Host: Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas); additional ChHV5 infections documented in hawksbill (Eretmochelys imbricata) and olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea) turtles at Mabul Island
Event.summary: In the 1990s, a large abattoir‑based survey of 4,407 green turtles landed in Indonesia documented FP in 21.5% of individuals, with affected turtles bearing multiple tumors but generally remaining in fair to good body condition, revealing a substantial, previously under‑recognized disease burden in Southeast Asian foraging stocks. Subsequent work in Asia confirmed clinically apparent FP and active ChHV5 infection in endangered green turtles from Taiwan and, by 2015–2019, in green, hawksbill and olive ridley turtles foraging around Mabul Island, Sabah, where FP tumors were present but relatively rare while ChHV5 DNA prevalence in clinically healthy turtles rose from ~8% to over 40%. Collectively, these findings show that FP and ChHV5 have become established across multiple Asian foraging areas, with moderate but regionally important tumor prevalence and evidence of multi‑species infection.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Indonesian and Malaysian study areas include heavily fished, nearshore foraging grounds subject to varying degrees of coastal development and pollution, yet FP has also been reported in relatively clear waters, suggesting that eutrophication and water quality may modulate, but do not solely determine, disease expression. Internal mechanisms: The Indonesian abattoir survey and later Asian virological work demonstrate that CFPHV/ChHV5 is endemic in regional green turtle populations and capable of infecting multiple turtle species; phylogenetic analyses show Asian ChHV5 sequences clustering with strains from Hawaii, Brazil and the Atlantic, consistent with long‑distance dispersal via turtle migrations rather than a unique Asian lineage. The 1997–2019 Asia event is therefore interpreted as a re‑occurrence and broad recognition of an existing global virus in Asian foraging grounds rather than a true first emergence.
Review: retain – A substantial 1990s Indonesian survey (21.5% FP prevalence in 4,407 green turtles) together with more recent ChHV5‑FP reports from Taiwan and Mabul Island demonstrates a major, long‑lasting Asian FP presence that is missing from the original dataset and should be among the top 10 events by impact. This new event row has been added, coded as a re‑occurrence in Asia (true first Asian FP observations date back to the 1950s in Malaysia) rather than as inter‑continental emergence. Years span 1997–2019 to capture both the Indonesian survey and later Taiwan/Mabul work; country list and sub‑regions follow UNSD conventions. Flagged for review to refine exact start/end years if more detailed temporal data are compiled.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus
EPP.common.name: FP-associated herpesvirus, CFPHV
Host: Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas)
Event.summary: Historically, FP was rare or absent along the northwestern Gulf of Mexico, but by about 2010 the first FP‑affected green turtle was reported on the Texas coast, followed by increasing numbers of affected juveniles in in‑water capture and rehabilitation datasets, indicating in situ disease occurrence rather than isolated imports. Concurrently, histological and molecular confirmation of ChHV5‑associated FP in green turtles from Veracruz in the southwestern Gulf of Mexico showed that FP and ChHV5 had become established along both the U.S. and Mexican coasts of the western Gulf. By the late 2010s, FP was recognized as an emerging health concern for green turtles in the northwestern Gulf, with prevalence still lower than in Florida or Brazil but clearly rising in some Texas embayments and Mexican foraging grounds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: As elsewhere, western Gulf FP cases are concentrated in shallow bays and estuaries near industrialized and urbanized coastlines affected by oil and gas activities, agricultural runoff and sewage inputs, suggesting that water‑quality degradation and eutrophication may promote tumor development in infected turtles. Internal mechanisms: Viral sequence data indicate that Gulf of Mexico cases share ChHV5 variants with other western Atlantic and Caribbean populations, supporting the view that this episode represents geographic and demographic expansion of an existing virus and re‑occurrence of disease within the broader Northern America and Central America sub‑regions, not a distinct inter‑continental or intra‑continental emergence event.
Review: retain – The western Gulf of Mexico (Texas plus Veracruz) episode captures an important, more recent range expansion and increasing FP prevalence in a previously low‑incidence part of the species’ range, with substantial sample sizes in Texas studies. Event types have been corrected: it is now coded as re‑occurrence only (expansion within already affected continental regions), removing the previous intra‑continental emergence flag, which is reserved for first detections in new UNSD sub‑regions. The continent and sub‑region fields have been updated to reflect that the event spans both Northern America (USA) and Central America (Mexico). An unrelated West Africa paper was dropped from the event‑level source list. Flagged for review primarily to confirm whether future data suggest splitting U.S. and Mexican Gulf events.
