EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus
EPP.common.name: FP-associated herpesvirus, CFPHV
Host: Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas)
Event.summary: In the 2010s, FP was increasingly reported from green turtle foraging aggregations in the western Indian Ocean, including the Diani–Chale National Marine Reserve in Kenya, where long‑term photo‑ID monitoring documented multiple individuals with tumors and allowed tracking of progression and regression of lesions. Expert surveys and regional reports highlighted additional FP observations from Seychelles, Madagascar’s Barren Islands (where high FP incidence was noted around Maroantaly Island), and other western Indian Ocean sites, indicating that clinically apparent FP and ChHV5 infection had become widespread across key eastern African and island feeding grounds. By the early 2020s, FP was recognized as an established but spatially heterogeneous disease in these regions, with ongoing work to quantify prevalence and population‑level impacts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Popular reef‑associated tourism destinations and coastal developments, such as Kenyan marine reserves and Seychelles beaches, bring increased sewage, runoff and boat traffic to nearshore turtle foraging areas, potentially degrading water quality and promoting eutrophication, similar to other FP hotspots globally. In Madagascar’s Barren Islands, FP has been reported in association with important foraging and developmental habitats whose environmental status is poorly characterized but may be affected by local fisheries and land‑use changes. Internal mechanisms: Photo‑ID and case‑tracking studies show both progression and spontaneous regression of tumors in individual turtles, highlighting dynamic host–virus interactions and the importance of immune responses. Limited molecular data suggest that eastern African ChHV5 variants are closely related to other Atlantic and Indo‑Pacific lineages, consistent with spread via turtle movements rather than a distinct new strain.
Review: retain – This event captures the first substantial, multi‑site establishment of FP in eastern Africa and the western Indian Ocean, which is a major range expansion into the Eastern Africa sub‑region following earlier Atlantic African records. Event type has been restricted to intra‑continental emergence (new UNSD sub‑region for Africa) without re‑emergence, and the countries list expanded to include Madagascar’s Barren Islands and other regional sites mentioned in expert surveys. Sources now include a recent Kenya photo‑ID study, the global expert overview, and documentation of high FP incidence in the Barren Islands. Flagged for review to refine participating countries and dates as more regional data become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus multilocularis
EPP.common.name: Alveolar echinococcosis
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Red foxes (Vulpes vulpes); voles and other small rodents; humans (sporadic and emerging cases in newly affected countries)
Event.summary: During the 1990s and early 2000s, Echinococcus multilocularis expanded its known range in European fox populations from four core endemic countries (Austria, France, Germany, Switzerland) to at least eight additional central, western, northern and southern European countries, with first records in foxes in Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, Italy and several central‑eastern states. As surveillance of red foxes and small mammals intensified, more newly infected areas were documented and occasional human cases began to be recognized in some of these countries. By the early 2000s, ecological and surveillance data confirmed that the parasite’s geographic range in Europe was far wider than previously thought, establishing new endemic foci across western and central Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large increases in red fox populations across Europe driven by oral rabies vaccination, hunting changes and urbanization, combined with high rodent densities in agricultural and peri‑urban landscapes, allowed the parasite to spread along expanding fox ranges and colonize new territories. Intensified wildlife surveillance and improved diagnostic tools (necropsy, copro‑PCR) increased detection probability and helped map the expanding range. Internal mechanisms: This episode reflects geographic range expansion of existing sylvatic cycles rather than a clearly distinct strain, although local adaptation of the parasite to new ecological settings likely supported establishment.
Review: Decision: review – Event is real and high‑impact, but several geographic details needed correction. (1) Sub‑regions expanded to include Northern and Southern Europe because Denmark and Italy are affected as documented in Oksanen et al. 2016 and subsequent Italian fox studies.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Event window extended to 1990–2002 so that Italy’s first fox detections in the early 2000s fall within the episode, consistent with Manfredi et al. and later confirmations from Alto Adige.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7789758/?utm_source=openai)) (3) Country list edited to remove non‑standard tags like “[historic]” and to reduce spurious precision (e.g. “Belgium [1991]”→“Belgium [1990s]”; “Netherlands [1996]”→“Netherlands [1998]” to match first published Dutch fox detections).([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304401798002635?utm_source=openai)) Event type kept as intra‑continental emergence only, which matches spread to multiple new European sub‑regions; no re‑occurrence flag is used because these are genuinely new endemic areas rather than resurgence in previously endemic ones. Because of these adjustments and remaining approximate dating for some central‑eastern countries, this row should be checked against national fox surveillance summaries before final use.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus multilocularis
EPP.common.name: Alveolar echinococcosis
Sub.regions: Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Humans (in most listed countries); red foxes; domestic dogs; small rodents
Event.summary: From the 1990s through the 2000s, human alveolar echinococcosis emerged in central‑eastern and Baltic Europe and in several western and southern European countries that had previously reported no or very few locally acquired cases, including Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, Lithuania, Latvia, Slovenia, Romania, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and parts of northern Italy. These new human reports coincided with confirmation of Echinococcus multilocularis in foxes and small mammals in many of the same countries, often first detected in the mid‑1990s or early 2000s, while in Denmark and Sweden the parasite was found only in wildlife with no confirmed autochthonous human cases during this period. By around 2015, several hundred human AE cases had been collated from these newer endemic areas, indicating that the parasite’s public health impact had expanded well beyond the historic Alpine foci into much of central, northern and eastern Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued spread and densification of infected fox populations across Europe, facilitated by rabies vaccination, landscape change, agricultural intensification and high rodent prey densities, enabled colonization of new subregions and countries. Greater diagnostic awareness, improved imaging and serology, and the creation of national and multinational registries led to better identification and reporting of AE cases in countries where the disease had previously gone unrecognized or had been misdiagnosed. EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hydatidosis, Hydatid disease
Host: Dogs and other canids (definitive hosts); sheep, goats, cattle, camels and other livestock (intermediate hosts); humans (accidental intermediate host, indicator of intense dog–livestock transmission)
Event.summary: After the dissolution of the Soviet Union around 1991, cystic echinococcosis (CE) due to Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato re‑emerged across the newly independent Central Asian republics, with sharp rises in human surgical cases and high infection prevalences in dogs and livestock documented during the 1990s and 2000s. In Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, official data showed rapid post‑1991 increases followed by sustained high incidence of human CE (often 5–25+ cases/100,000/year) and high infection levels in rural dogs by the 2000s, while similar resurgences were reported in neighbouring post‑socialist Mongolia. By the mid‑2010s, CE remained highly endemic across Central Asia and Mongolia despite some control efforts, indicating long‑term re‑establishment of dog–livestock transmission cycles driven by socio‑economic transition rather than parasite change.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Profound socio‑economic transition after the Soviet collapse led to fragmentation/privatization of collective farms, growth of smallholder flocks, uncontrolled home slaughter, unsafe offal disposal, reduced dog management, and collapse of state veterinary and public‑health services, greatly increasing dog exposure to infected livestock viscera and human contact with infected dogs.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3713972/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Amplification of pre‑existing E. granulosus s.l. lineages under altered transmission conditions, with increased force of infection driven by growth and changed management of dog and livestock populations rather than emergence of novel genotypes.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This event clearly represents one of the largest post‑1990 CE resurgences worldwide and should be retained as a major emergence episode. I removed western China from the country list and narrative to avoid double‑counting with dedicated China events, restricting this episode to the post‑Soviet Central Asian republics plus Mongolia, which share the same socio‑economic transition driver. Based on the definitions, I reclassified the event as re‑occurrence only (no re‑emergence), because the literature documents resurgence due to external socio‑economic and veterinary‑service collapse, with no evidence of novel parasite strains or resistance; intra‑ and inter‑continental emergence appropriately remain “No.” Sub‑regions (Central Asia; Eastern Asia) are still appropriate because Mongolia is assigned to Eastern Asia in the UNSD scheme. Source set is generally appropriate; the scispace link duplicates peer‑reviewed material and could be dropped in later curation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Event.summary: From the late 1990s onward, Baltic and eastern‑central European countries recorded large new foci of Echinococcus multilocularis infection in foxes and raccoon dogs, accompanied by rising numbers of human AE cases, representing a major northward and eastward expansion from the classic endemic core in France, Germany, Switzerland and Austria. Lithuania diagnosed 96 human AE cases between 1997 and 2008 alongside very high fox infection intensities, while Poland documented over 120 human AE cases from 1990–2011 with a marked rise during 2000–2009 and clustering in the north‑east bordering Lithuania; similar first or early autochthonous human AE cases were reported in Latvia, Estonia, Belarus, Hungary and Romania during the 2000s. By around 2010, AE was recognized as emerging across large parts of the Baltic and eastern‑central Europe, with sustained fox infection and continuing human case detection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and urbanization of red fox populations following rabies vaccination campaigns, landscape changes increasing rodent intermediate hosts, expanding raccoon dog populations, and improved imaging/serology together created new and denser E. multilocularis transmission cycles and increased detection of human AE.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of E. multilocularis within Europe, with high worm burdens in foxes indicating enhanced transmission; at continental scale, spread is best explained by wildlife ecology and control of rabies rather than emergence of a single novel strain.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This episode represents a major intra‑European expansion of AE into the Baltic and eastern‑central European countries and is clearly among the largest post‑1990 emergence events. I corrected the emergence‑type classification: first_detection was set to “Yes” in the draft but should be “No” at the global host‑system scale, and there is no strong evidence that parasite evolution (as opposed to wildlife ecology and rabies control) is the primary driver, so re_emergence was changed to “No.” Intra‑continental emergence remains “Yes” because transmission was newly documented in UNSD subregions (Northern Europe – Baltics; Eastern Europe) beyond the pre‑1990 Alpine core. I also recommend removing the general Echinococcosis Wikipedia link in favour of more specific peer‑reviewed sources and have added a key EU‑wide systematic review of E. multilocularis distribution in wildlife as a more relevant source.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hydatidosis, Hydatid disease
Countries: United States of America – north‑central and midwestern states within the historic endemic zone (e.g. Minnesota and neighbouring states) and isolated new foci (e.g. Missouri) with locally acquired canine and occasional human AE cases [2010s]
Host: Wild canids (coyotes, foxes) as definitive hosts; domestic dogs (definitive host with severe clinical AE); small mammals (intermediate hosts); zoo primates and other captive mammals (aberrant intermediate hosts); humans (locally acquired AE cases)
Event.summary: From 2009 onward, Echinococcus multilocularis exhibiting European‑type genotypes was detected in dogs and wild canids in western and central Canada, including British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and later Ontario, extending well beyond the historically recognized Arctic and north‑central endemic zones. Molecular studies of a 2009 dog case in British Columbia showed the parasite to be closely related to European strains rather than traditional North American lineages, and subsequent surveys found increasing E. multilocularis prevalence in urban coyotes around Calgary and other cities, along with a growing number of severe canine AE cases and at least several locally acquired human AE cases in Alberta and sporadic locally acquired infections in the United States.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3358155/?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2010s, Canadian experts characterized E. multilocularis, particularly introduced European‑type strains, as an emerging and costly zoonotic problem in North America with expanding geographic range and host spectrum.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International and interprovincial dog movements (including imported dogs from Europe and endemic regions without mandatory Echinococcus testing or treatment), urban expansion into wildlife habitats, increasing and urbanizing coyote and fox populations, and low awareness and deworming coverage in dogs facilitated introduction and establishment of European‑type E. multilocularis in new regions.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1471492212000517?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of more pathogenic or highly zoonotic European‑type haplotypes into North America, followed by geographic range expansion and enhanced transmission in urban and peri‑urban canid–rodent cycles; this represents strain‑level re‑emergence of AE risk in regions where the species was previously absent or rare, rather than first continental introduction of E. multilocularis itself.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (borderline for inclusion). This event describes the strain‑level invasion of European‑type E. multilocularis into western and central Canada (and, to a lesser extent so far, parts of the USA). I corrected the emergence‑type classification: North America has long been endemic for E. multilocularis, so this is not an inter‑continental or intra‑continental emergence at the species level, nor a first_detection event globally. Instead, it is best treated as re‑emergence driven by introduction of more zoonotic European haplotypes and their establishment in new urban and peri‑urban canid–rodent cycles; accordingly, only re_emergence is set to “Yes.” I also refined the country list to focus on provinces and states where European‑type strains and locally acquired AE have been documented. Although the absolute number of human cases remains small compared with China, Central Asia or South America, the combination of novel genotype introduction, wide geographic spread in wildlife and dogs, and high per‑case costs gives this event strategic importance; whether it should remain among the top 10 highest‑impact events depends on how strictly impact is defined (current DALYs vs future risk), so it is flagged for further expert review rather than automatic exclusion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Foot-and-mouth disease virus
EPP.common.name: FMDV, Aphthovirus
Sub.regions: Southern Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, and other cloven‑hoofed livestock
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through 2001, a single genetic lineage of FMDV serotype O (topotype ME‑SA, PanAsia strain) that emerged in northern India expanded its range, first spreading across South Asia and the Middle East and then into East Asia, the Russian Federation, and parts of Africa. Between 1998 and 2001 this PanAsia strain caused widespread outbreaks across multiple Asian subregions, reached South Africa, and culminated in major incursions into previously FMD‑free or long‑free areas of Europe in 2001, including the large United Kingdom epidemic and additional outbreaks in Ireland, France, and the Netherlands, with millions of animals ultimately culled and severe trade disruption. Control relied on rapid slaughter policies, emergency vaccination in some settings, strict movement controls, and coordinated international surveillance, after which the pandemic wave subsided although related ME‑SA lineages remain endemic in parts of Asia and the Middle East.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and globalization of livestock production and trade; long‑distance movement of live animals and animal products across Asia, the Middle East, and into Europe; porous borders and informal trade networks; limitations in regional vaccination coverage and strain matching at the time of spread. Internal mechanisms: emergence of the highly successful O/ME‑SA PanAsia lineage with genetic changes in VP1 and related regions conferring enhanced fitness, broad host range, and strong transmissibility, enabling rapid geographic range expansion and repeated re‑emergence in regions that were previously disease‑free or had long intervals since the last FMD outbreaks.
Review: review – retained as a single linked episode describing the global spread of the O/ME-SA PanAsia lineage from India across South and West Asia into East Asia, parts of Africa and Europe, consistent with molecular and historical reconstructions([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC387408/?utm_source=openai)). Event_year was broadened from 1998–2001 to 1990–2001 to align with first detection of PanAsia in India. Subregions were expanded (adding South-eastern Asia and Southern Europe) to match the listed countries. Event-type flags were simplified to re_emergence only (intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence set to false) because FMDV itself was already established on all affected continents and subregions; the key feature is emergence and global dissemination of a highly fit new lineage rather than first presence of the virus in those areas.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Gammacoronavirus gallus
EPP.common.name: IBV, Infectious bronchitis virus
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Commercial broiler, breeder and layer chickens
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, a new infectious bronchitis virus variant designated 4/91 (also known as 793B or CR88) was identified in commercial chicken flocks in the United Kingdom and neighbouring Western European countries, where it caused severe respiratory disease, kidney lesions and production losses in flocks routinely vaccinated with Mass‑type strains. Through the mid‑1990s this 4/91 (GI‑13) lineage spread rapidly across much of Western, Northern and Southern Europe, becoming one of the dominant field genotypes and prompting the development and licensing of specific live‑attenuated 4/91 vaccines to restore protection. By about 2000, 4/91‑like viruses—both field strains and vaccine‑derived variants—were entrenched in European poultry populations and continued to contribute to IB outbreaks and to recombination with other IBV lineages.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑density industrial broiler, breeder and layer production in Western and Southern Europe, together with extensive movement of hatching eggs and pullets and initially exclusive use of Mass‑type vaccines, facilitated rapid dissemination of the 4/91 variant once it emerged and created strong selection pressure for vaccine‑escape variants. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – appearance of the GI‑13 (793B/4‑91) lineage with distinct S1 sequences and partial antigenic mismatch to Mass serotypes; Enhanced Transmission and broad tissue tropism allowing efficient spread and respiratory/renal disease; Recombination between 4/91‑like and other IBV genomes and widespread use of live 4/91 vaccines sustained a diverse pool of 4/91‑related viruses in the field.
Review: Added event. The original dataset omitted the major 4/91 (GI‑13, 793B) variant wave in Europe, which is well documented as causing substantial welfare and economic problems in vaccinated flocks and rapidly spreading across many European countries in the 1990s. IBV was already endemic in Europe long before 1990, so this lineage is correctly coded purely as re‑emergence rather than first detection or inter‑continental emergence. Country start years are kept approximate ("1990s" or "mid‑1990s") because precise first‑isolation dates by country are not consistently reported; a specialist could refine these if needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Gammacoronavirus gallus
EPP.common.name: IBV, Infectious bronchitis virus
Host: Commercial broiler and layer chickens
Event.summary: In 1998, a Middle Eastern IBV variant later assigned to the GI‑23 lineage (Var2‑like) was first identified in Israel, following earlier Var1‑type IBV outbreaks in that country and signalling the emergence of a distinct regional genotype. Over the 2000s and early to mid‑2010s, GI‑23 variants spread widely through Middle Eastern poultry industries, becoming a major cause of infectious bronchitis in Israel, Iran, Jordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and neighbouring Western Asian countries and accounting for a substantial fraction of clinical IB cases in regional surveillance. By around 2016, GI‑23 was firmly entrenched across much of the Middle East, co‑circulating with Mass‑like, 4/91‑like and other genotypes and continuing to cause recurrent outbreaks and vaccine failures.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional trade in hatching eggs and live birds, dense broiler and layer production, and partial vaccine coverage allowed repeated introduction and amplification of GI‑23 variants across Middle Eastern countries; limited early genomic surveillance delayed recognition of the widespread lineage. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – evolution of GI‑23 as an indigenous Middle Eastern genotype; Genetic drift and recombination produced Var2‑like strains with enhanced fitness and immune escape; Re‑emergence was driven by antigenic mismatch with vaccines based on Mass and 4/91 strains, leading to onward spread across multiple Western Asian countries.
Review: Flagged for review. The previous version misclassified this lineage as a first detection and intra‑continental emergence, but IBV had been reported in several Middle Eastern countries decades earlier; for the species‑level EPP this wave is best treated as a re‑emergence driven by the rise and spread of the GI‑23 lineage. The country list and time span have been expanded to include additional Western Asian countries (Jordan, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Lebanon, Afghanistan, Syria) where GI‑23/Variant‑2 was documented during the 2000s–2010s, based on phylodynamic and regional genotyping studies; specific start years for some countries remain approximate and could be refined with more detailed national data.
Review.Comment: too long period

EPP.common.name: Bovine tuberculosis, bTB
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990s]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus); European badger (Meles meles); other wildlife (e.g., deer)
Event.summary: From the early 1990s onward, Great Britain and Ireland experienced a marked resurgence of bovine tuberculosis in cattle herds after earlier control successes, with rising herd incidence particularly in southwest England, Wales, and parts of Ireland.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6312888/?utm_source=openai)) During 2003–2015, analyses documented substantial and sustained increases in breakdown rates in high‑risk and edge areas of England and localized hotspots in Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, while Scotland remained largely free.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6312888/?utm_source=openai)) By the mid‑2010s, enhanced testing, badger culling/trial interventions, and tightened cattle movement controls had slowed but not eradicated the epidemic, leaving bovine TB as a major economic and policy challenge.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6312888/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Changing cattle demographics (larger herds, increased movements), historical gaps in testing during the 2001 foot‑and‑mouth disease outbreak, and the presence of a dense badger wildlife reservoir in many high‑incidence areas all contributed to re‑occurrence; social and political constraints on wildlife control also limited rapid intervention.([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2018.00109/full?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No clear novel strain appears to have driven this resurgence; instead, the key internal factor is Enhanced Transmission via long‑standing badger reservoirs and complex cattle–badger–cattle transmission cycles, allowing sustained high incidence despite control measures.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3377356/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Major long‑running re-occurrence episode with large economic impact: marked post‑1990 resurgence of bTB in cattle associated with badger reservoirs in Great Britain and Ireland is thoroughly documented and clearly among the highest‑impact events for M. bovis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6312888/?utm_source=openai)) Event type as re-occurrence (external drivers dominating, no clear novel strain) and the Europe/Northern Europe/UK and Ireland geographic assignment are appropriate; no changes made.

Host: Cattle (Bos taurus); wild boar (Sus scrofa); red deer (Cervus elaphus); other wild ungulates
Event.summary: From the 1990s onward, Spain reported increasing Mycobacterium bovis infection in wild boar and red deer, with some hunting estates reaching extremely high prevalences and frequent spillover to cattle, marking a shift to a multi‑host wildlife–livestock maintenance system in parts of the Iberian Peninsula.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3377356/?utm_source=openai)) In the 2000s, similar patterns were documented in Portugal, where wild boar and red deer became recognized maintenance hosts and new M. bovis clonal complexes (e.g., Eu2, Eu3) emerged and spread among wildlife and cattle across ecological corridors.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10484045/?utm_source=openai)) By the mid‑2010s, high animal TB prevalence in these multi‑host communities persisted despite cattle control programs, forcing adoption of integrated wildlife and livestock surveillance and management strategies.([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-77713-8?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma mycoides subsp. mycoides
EPP.common.name: MmmSC
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo – Ituri region [1990s]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus, Bos indicus and crossbred beef and dairy cattle in pastoral and agropastoral systems)
Event.summary: From about 1990, CBPP re‑emerged explosively in East and parts of Southern Africa, with infection moving from long‑standing foci in Angola, Sudan and the Horn via Uganda and Kenya into northern Tanzania (Ngorongoro, Arusha Region) and then into Kagera on the Uganda border. Over roughly 1990–2003, linked epidemics spread through much of Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda, Burundi, the Ituri region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Namibia, Zambia and Botswana, reinvading countries that had been free for decades and greatly expanding the geographic range of a largely homogeneous African epidemic lineage. By the early 2000s, coordinated regional vaccination, movement control and stamping‑out campaigns had reduced outbreak numbers, but CBPP remained entrenched and endemic in many of these subregions and continued to threaten neighboring free areas.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonellosis
Sub.regions: Europe: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; North America: Northern America; Asia: Western Asia; Oceania: Australia and New Zealand
Host: Primarily cattle; also pigs, poultry (especially turkeys), and sheep
Event.summary: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, a multidrug‑resistant clone of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium definitive phage type 104 (DT104), resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, streptomycin, sulfonamides and tetracycline (ACSSuT), expanded rapidly in cattle and other livestock in the United Kingdom and neighboring European countries. Through trade in animals and animal products and other routes, this DT104 clone spread across Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe and was recognized in multiple livestock species by the mid‑1990s. By 1996, the same multidrug‑resistant DT104 strain had emerged in cattle and humans in Canada, the United States, Israel and, shortly afterward, Australia and New Zealand, becoming a major cause of disease and prompting international control efforts in the late 1990s and early 2000s before incidence declined following interventions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of cattle, pig and poultry production, high use of therapeutic and growth‑promoter antimicrobials in food animals, and extensive trade in live animals and animal products facilitated selection and rapid international dissemination of the DT104 clone. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and stabilization of a multidrug‑resistance cassette (R‑type ACSSuT) associated with class‑1 integrons and the Salmonella genomic island SGI1 increased fitness under antimicrobial pressure and contributed to re‑emergence, and some sublineages developed additional quinolone resistance during the late 1990s.
Review: Review – Event is real and appropriately framed as the global emergence of multidrug‑resistant Salmonella Typhimurium DT104 in livestock. Geography has been corrected by adding Asia/Western Asia because Israel is listed among affected countries, and the event‑type flags were adjusted to reflect an inter‑continental re‑emergence of a multidrug‑resistant clone (inter_continental_emergence = Yes; intra_continental_emergence = No; re_emergence = Yes) in line with the mostly mutually exclusive classification rules.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonid alphavirus
EPP.common.name: SAV
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe
Host: Primarily farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in freshwater (sleeping disease, SD); with later sporadic SAV2 infections in Atlantic salmon in freshwater or seawater
Event.summary: Beginning in the mid‑1990s, a distinct genotype of Salmonid alphavirus (SAV2) associated with sleeping disease was first recognised in freshwater‑reared rainbow trout in France, where outbreaks affected a substantial proportion of farms. Over the late 1990s and 2000s, the same virus was detected in additional Western and Southern European trout‑farming countries including the United Kingdom, Ireland, Spain, Italy and Germany, and first laboratory‑confirmed outbreaks or detections were reported in Poland, Switzerland and Croatia during the early 2010s. Across this linked period, SAV2‑associated sleeping disease caused recurrent farm‑level episodes characterised by lethargy, fish lying on their sides at the tank bottom, variable mortality and pronounced growth retardation, making SAV2 one of the principal infectious constraints on freshwater rainbow trout aquaculture across much of Western, Southern and parts of Eastern Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensification and geographic expansion of rainbow trout aquaculture in Europe, frequent trade and movement of eggs, fry and juveniles between hatcheries and grow‑out sites in different countries, and limited early diagnostic capacity facilitated cross‑border spread and establishment of SAV2. Internal mechanisms: emergence and dissemination of the SAV2 genotype, genetically distinct from SAV1 viruses that cause classic pancreas disease in salmon, represent novel strain/genotype emergence together with host and environmental expansion, as SAV2 shows marked adaptation to rainbow trout in freshwater and can also infect salmon in some production systems. These features justify classification both as intra‑continental emergence (spread into new European sub‑regions) and as re‑emergence (a new subtype and host niche within an already affected continent).
Review: retain – the original event correctly captured the emergence and spread of SAV2/sleeping disease across European trout farming but truncated the period at 2010 and omitted several countries where first outbreaks or laboratory confirmations were documented later (for example, Poland, Switzerland, Croatia). I have extended the event window to 1995–2014, expanded the country list (and added Ireland), and made clear that the country‑specific years are approximate where only decade‑level information is available. Classification as intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence (novel genotype and host niche) is appropriate. Further refinement of first‑detection years by country would improve the entry but is not essential for recognising this as one of the major SAV emergence episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: TBEV
Host: Humans (food-borne and tick-bite associated TBE); small ruminants (goats, sheep, cows as virus source in milk); Ixodes ricinus ticks
Event.summary: Between 2007 and 2016, Slovakia reported the highest documented occurrence of alimentary (food-borne) tick-borne encephalitis in Europe, with multiple outbreaks linked to consumption of unpasteurised goat, sheep or cow milk and cheese, including a large outbreak in eastern Slovakia in 2013 that affected dozens of people. Similar but generally smaller food-borne TBE outbreaks occurred in the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and other countries during this period, highlighting alimentary transmission as a clinically important complement to tick-bite exposure in endemic areas. Most outbreaks subsided rapidly once contaminated dairy products were withdrawn from sale and pasteurisation or boiling of milk was reinforced, although sporadic alimentary events have continued to be reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cultural practices involving consumption of raw milk and artisanal cheeses from small ruminants grazing in endemic forest-edge pastures created opportunities for alimentary TBEV transmission; limited awareness of this route and lack of systematic pasteurisation in some rural settings allowed multi-person outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: The events involved European-subtype TBEV strains capable of surviving and remaining infectious in milk and dairy products; the prominence of alimentary outbreaks represents functional re-emergence via a different transmission route (enhanced transmission through food) rather than a novel genotype, and in some foci may reflect high viral loads in livestock following intense tick exposure.
Review: review - Retained as a distinct re-emergence episode characterised by large alimentary outbreaks, with Slovakia as the main hotspot. Sub_regions was restricted to Eastern Europe because all listed countries fall in this UNSD subregion. The emergence classification was adjusted to re_emergence only (re_occurrence set to false) to reflect the prominence of a re-emerging transmission route (food-borne infection) involving established European TBEV strains, rather than a generic resurgence driven mainly by external factors.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: TBEV
Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus ticks; wildlife reservoirs (rodents, deer)
Event.summary: In the mid‑2010s, Nordic countries documented expansion of human TBE cases into new coastal and higher-latitude foci, including increasing incidence along the Norwegian and Swedish coasts and newly recognised foci in Denmark beyond the long-known endemic island of Bornholm, where autochthonous cases in 2018–2019 highlighted spread to mainland Zealand and Jutland. Case counts in Norway, Sweden and Finland rose over 2015–2019 compared with earlier years, although absolute numbers remained lower than in Baltic or Central European hotspots. These northern foci have persisted, with interannual variability linked to climate and small-mammal population cycles and ongoing gradual spread northwards along the Scandinavian coastline.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Warmer temperatures, longer vegetation seasons and milder winters at higher latitudes have improved overwinter survival and seasonal activity of Ixodes ticks; changes in deer and rodent populations and human outdoor behaviour (recreation, second homes, forestry work) have increased human–tick contact. Internal mechanisms: Expansion represents geographic range expansion of existing European TBEV lineages into newly suitable northern habitats (geographic range expansion – inherent) rather than emergence of novel variants.
Review: review - Retained as a major intra-continental range expansion episode into new foci in the Nordic countries. Kept the focus on spread into new geographic areas (intra_continental_emergence = true) and set re_occurrence to false to comply with the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra-/inter-continental emergence; the main signal is establishment of new northern and western foci rather than mere resurgence in long-recognised localities.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia trifida
EPP.common.name: great ragweed, Texan great ragweed, giant ragweed, tall ragweed, blood ragweed, perennial ragweed, horseweed
Sub.regions: Eastern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Primarily riverbanks and floodplains, roadsides and disturbed land, with localized invasion of maize and sunflower fields; major producer of allergenic pollen affecting nearby human populations
Event.summary: After scattered earlier records in the 19th and 20th centuries, giant ragweed expanded conspicuously in Central and Eastern Europe from about 2000 onward, with particularly rapid spread documented in parts of European Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Hungary and the western Balkans along major river systems and transport corridors. During the 2000s and 2010s, populations increased in agricultural landscapes of Italy and France as well, where dense stands formed in some sunflower and maize fields and produced heavy pollen loads contributing to allergic disease. By the 2010s and early 2020s, Ambrosia trifida was recognized as an emerging invasive ragweed in Europe, added to the EPPO Alert list in 2014 and to the EPPO A2 List in 2019, and first detected as a naturalised invasive population in additional countries such as Montenegro in 2024, prompting regional risk assessments and coordinated early‑warning and control programs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Repeated introduction as a contaminant in grain and seed, increased river traffic and road transport, and regional climate warming favoring warm‑summer annuals all promoted establishment and spread; disturbance of riparian zones, road verges and abandoned fields provided ideal habitats, while limited early awareness of this species (compared to common ragweed) delayed targeted control. Internal mechanisms: strong competitive ability in fertile, disturbed soils, prolific seed production, and potential for long‑distance dispersal along rivers and human transport routes supported range expansion; European field studies suggest shifts in morpho‑functional traits that may enhance invasiveness in some invaded sites, supporting classification as re‑emergence in addition to intra‑continental spread.
Review: review – Retain: this row appropriately aggregates the main European invasion episode since ca. 2000, which, although still locally distributed, spans multiple sub‑regions and has significant agronomic and allergenic impacts where dense populations occur. The event has been re‑typed to intra‑continental emergence + re‑emergence (with re‑occurrence set to No) to reflect spread into new European sub‑regions (Southern and Western Europe) alongside evidence of trait shifts in invaded populations, while respecting the rule that re‑occurrence should not co‑occur with intra‑continental emergence. Countries and timing were checked against EPPO and the 2021 European monograph, including confirmation of the first record for Montenegro in 2024.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/epp.12661?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis spiraecola
EPP.common.name: black bean aphid
Host: Citrus spp. (sweet orange, clementine, satsuma, lemon and other citrus); occasionally other fruit trees and ornamentals in the same orchards
Event.summary: From the 1980s into the 1990s, Aphis spiraecola rapidly built up in Mediterranean citrus orchards in Spain, Italy, Greece and southern France, where it had previously been absent from citrus or regarded as a minor species compared with Aphis gossypii. Through the 1990s–2000s it displaced A. gossypii as the dominant citrus aphid across much of the western Mediterranean, including the Algarve region of Portugal, causing chronic infestations of spring flushes, leaf curling and increased concern about Citrus tristeza virus spread. By the 2010s A. spiraecola was entrenched as the key citrus aphid in most Mediterranean coastal citrus zones and is now managed primarily through conservation biological control, monitoring and selective insecticides rather than broad‑spectrum sprays.

Internal mechanisms: High performance of A. spiraecola on clementine and sweet orange, together with differences in parasitoid and predator complexes compared with A. gossypii, allowed it to attain much larger populations and become an important Citrus tristeza virus vector in Mediterranean citrus.

EPP.scientific.name: Bemisia tabaci
EPP.common.name: sweetpotato whitefly
Host: cotton, vegetables, cassava and other smallholder crops
Event.summary: From about 2000 onward, MED (Q) and invasive MEAM1 lineages of Bemisia tabaci were increasingly detected across sub-Saharan Africa, including West African countries such as Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal and Togo, as well as parts of Eastern and Southern Africa. Through the 2000s and early 2010s these invasive populations became important pests of cotton and vegetables and contributed to renewed problems with virus diseases in cassava and other crops. By the mid‑2010s MED and MEAM1 were widely established in many African cropping systems alongside indigenous cryptic species, making Bemisia control a chronic issue.

EPP.common.name: Asian trampsnail
Host: Peridomestic vegetation, gardens, and agricultural plantations (including various crops in northeastern and east-central Argentina)
Event.summary: Although Bradybaena similaris had a historical record from Misiones Province in the mid-20th century, a 2019 BioInvasions Records study documented nine new localities in Misiones and the first confirmed record in Entre Ríos Province, representing the southernmost occurrence of the species in South America. EPP.scientific.name: Digitaria setigera
EPP.common.name: East Indian crabgrass
Host: Direct-seeded upland and rainfed rice (Oryza sativa) and rainfed maize (Zea mays) in smallholder fields
Event.summary: From the 1990s onward, the expansion of direct-seeded upland rice and intensified rainfed maize production in parts of north-east and eastern India and neighbouring Nepal was accompanied by shifts in weed communities, with Digitaria setigera reported among the dominant grassy weeds in rainfed maize in Odisha and in upland direct-seeded rice in Nagaland during 2009–2010. Weed surveys and management trials in dry/direct-seeded rice in South Asia through the 2000s and 2010s repeatedly listed D. setigera as a frequent late-emerging grass weed that contributed to yield losses where weed control was inadequate. By the late 2010s, integrated weed-management recommendations for these systems (sowing method, stale seedbeds and selective herbicides) explicitly targeted D. setigera together with other competitive grasses, but the species remained a recurrent component of cereal weed floras in parts of Southern Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread adoption of dry/direct seeding in rice and expansion of rainfed maize, driven by labour shortages, water constraints and mechanisation, created aerobic, highly disturbed seedbeds that favour colonising grass weeds; limited or poorly timed weed control further allowed Digitaria setigera to increase in abundance. Internal mechanisms: No specific new biotypes or resistance traits have been reported for D. setigera in these systems; its emergence reflects inherent colonising traits of a native annual grass—high seed production, tolerance of intermittent drought and repeated disturbance, and persistence in the soil seed bank—leading to re-occurrence and increased weed importance in long-cultivated cereal landscapes rather than true geographic or host-range expansion.
Review: Added new high-impact event. Multiple weed-survey and management studies from the 1990s–2010s (e.g. Rout & Satapathy 1996 for maize in Odisha; Kikon & Gohain 2017 for upland direct-seeded rice in Nagaland; Agronomy Journal of Nepal 2021; Paiman et al. 2020) consistently identify D. setigera as one of the dominant grassy weeds in direct-seeded rice and rainfed maize in parts of Southern Asia, affecting staple crops over large areas. Because the species is native/long established in this region and no novel genotypes or resistance have been documented, the event is correctly coded as re-occurrence only (no intra- or inter-continental emergence, no first detection). This pan-regional cereal-weed resurgence was missing from the original file but is likely among the most impactful post-1990 emergence episodes for D. setigera and should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Liriomyza huidobrensis
EPP.common.name: pea leafminer
Host: Potato, peas, beans, lettuce, celery, tomato, alfalfa and numerous other vegetables and ornamentals in Andean and adjacent cropping systems
Event.summary: In its native Andean range, Liriomyza huidobrensis shifted from a background pest to a major outbreak species around 1990, particularly in coastal and highland Peru where insecticide-resistant populations exploded on potatoes and vegetables, and similar problems soon appeared in Ecuador, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil and parts of Chile. Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, these resistant populations caused chronic, severe damage and high yield losses, and simultaneously served as the primary global source for invasive lineages exported with ornamental and vegetable trade. Although some Andean regions adopted improved IPM and biological control, the pest remains highly damaging and continues to exert strong selection on local management practices.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of vegetable and potato cultivation, coupled with heavy and often indiscriminate insecticide use, killed natural enemies and favored L. huidobrensis outbreaks; increased export of vegetables and ornamentals from Peru and neighboring countries disseminated outbreak populations abroad. Internal mechanisms: Evolution of strong insecticide resistance and possibly increased fitness in cool environments turned a native leafminer into a dominant pest, and these resistant genotypes underlie most invasive populations worldwide.
Review: review: Keep this as one of the key global events (native-range pest escalation and source of invasive genotypes), but the emergence type should be coded as re-emergence only (not also re-occurrence) because the change is primarily driven by evolved insecticide resistance and associated strain shifts; Chile was added to the country list to better match regional distribution, and a human reviewer should confirm that the chosen 1990 start year and set of South American countries capture the main high-impact outbreak period.

EPP.scientific.name: Paracoccidioides spp.
EPP.common.name: paracoccidioidomycosis
Host: Humans (primarily adult male rural workers engaged in agriculture, cattle ranching, and deforestation‑related activities)
Event.summary: From the 1990s into the early 2000s, paracoccidioidomycosis was increasingly reported along the eastern border of the Brazilian Amazon, especially in the states of Maranhão, Pará, and Tocantins, where disease had previously been rare. As federal colonization programs, road construction, and expansion of agriculture and cattle ranching drove migration into newly deforested frontier zones, clinical series and sero‑epidemiologic data documented the establishment of new endemic and hyperendemic foci of paracoccidioidomycosis. By the early 2000s this eastern Amazon belt was recognized as part of an expanded endemic area, with sustained transmission among rural populations exposed to disturbed soils.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Government‑promoted colonization of frontier lands, highway building, deforestation, and rapid expansion of coffee, crops, and cattle ranching along the eastern Amazon border increased human encroachment into forest soils harboring Paracoccidioides and generated intense soil disturbance. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of established Paracoccidioides brasiliensis complex lineages into newly deforested and cultivated zones; there is no evidence that a single novel genotype alone drove this spread, but pre‑existing strains colonized new ecological niches created by land‑use change.
Review: retain – Event corresponds to the well‑described expansion of paracoccidioidomycosis into the eastern Amazon border (Maranhão, Pará, Tocantins) linked to agricultural frontiers and migration. Geography (Brazil, South America | South America), time window (1990s–early 2000s), and classification as intra‑continental emergence into new Brazilian sub‑regions are consistent with major reviews. No changes made beyond minor wording; sources are appropriate and high‑quality.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryphonectria parasitica
EPP.common.name: chestnut blight fungus
Host: Castanea spp. (commercial sweet chestnut orchards, primarily Castanea sativa and hybrids; occasional reports on Quercus spp. in the affected region)
Event.summary: In September 2010, chestnut blight was detected for the first time in commercial chestnut orchards in the Ovens Valley of north‑east Victoria, Australia, where laboratory tests confirmed Cryphonectria parasitica on trees across at least six properties, marking the first established field outbreak of the disease in Australia and on the Oceania continent. An intensive eradication programme followed between 2010 and the late 2010s, during which more than 740,000 trees were inspected and over 5,000 diseased or at‑risk chestnut trees were removed under quarantine to protect an industry of roughly 350 growers concentrated in this region. Despite the initial campaign, low‑level infections persisted and additional foci were found in 2017–2019, and in 2019 the National Management Group concluded that eradication was no longer feasible, triggering a Transition to Management phase (2019–2020) and the current status of chestnut blight as an established but locally confined pathogen in Victoria.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected chestnut planting material or scion wood from overseas (likely Europe or Asia) into Australian nurseries in the early 2000s, including an earlier interception in post‑entry quarantine in Victoria in 2001, followed by escape into commercial orchards in the Ovens Valley; dense plantings of susceptible cultivars in a cool, humid montane climate facilitated establishment and spread. Internal mechanisms: high aggressiveness of introduced C. parasitica lineages on Castanea spp., the ability of the fungus to remain latent in bark tissues for prolonged periods and sporulate profusely on cankers, and an apparent absence of established hypovirulent CHV1 strains in Australia, all of which undermined eradication despite rigorous sanitation and tree removal.
Review: review – Newly added event capturing the first established field outbreak of chestnut blight in Oceania and its decade‑long management; classified as an inter‑continental emergence into Australia based on official Agriculture Victoria and IPPC reports, and recommended for expert review of quantitative impact metrics (e.g. industry losses) as more data become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Multiple pathogens
EPP.common.name: Varroosis, Tropilaelaps infestation, Foulbrood (Diseases of bees)
Host: Managed western honey bee (Apis mellifera) colonies (brood)
Event.summary: Throughout the 1990s, American foulbrood (AFB) caused by Paenibacillus larvae was recognised as the most serious honey bee disease in New Zealand, with concern that incidence was increasing as government funding for control programmes was reduced. In response to rising case numbers and industry pressure, the Biosecurity (National American Foulbrood Pest Management Strategy) Order 1998 came into force in 1999, creating a national elimination strategy that mandated systematic inspection and destruction of infected colonies and contaminated equipment. Over the subsequent decade to around 2008, national surveillance and coordinated beekeeper action progressively reduced AFB prevalence, transforming a major resurgence threat into a managed elimination programme, although sporadic cases persisted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: earlier relaxation of government‑funded control efforts and variable beekeeper compliance had allowed AFB prevalence and spore reservoirs in equipment and honey to build up by the early 1990s, increasing disease pressure and threatening export markets for honey and live bees. Internal mechanisms: the extreme environmental persistence of P. larvae spores in hive materials, honey and the environment, coupled with management practices such as exchange of contaminated equipment and robbing behaviour, underpinned the disease’s resilience and necessitated strict destruction‑based control rather than reliance on antibiotics.
Review: retain – Event captures a nationally important resurgence and subsequent large‑scale management response to American foulbrood in New Zealand, supported by government and industry documents. Coding as a re‑occurrence (resurgence driven primarily by external management and compliance factors, not major pathogen change) is appropriate. Time span 1990–2008 reflects both the build‑up phase and the first decade of the national Pest Management Strategy; the event is retained as one of the most impactful AFB episodes in the period.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia psilostachya
EPP.common.name: Cuman ragweed, western ragweed, perennial ragweed
Countries: India [1990s–2010s, first recognised in Tumkur District, Karnataka; subsequent delimiting survey across ≈10 villages in Turuvekere taluk]
Host: Highly invasive alien weed of croplands, pastures, plantation crops and common land in semi‑arid Karnataka, India
Event.summary: During the 1990s–2000s an unfamiliar ragweed was observed invading fields and common lands in Turuvekere taluk of Tumkur District, Karnataka, and was subsequently identified as Ambrosia psilostachya, representing its first confirmed occurrence in India. By the early 2010s surveys showed that western ragweed had colonized around 10 villages and invaded roughly 400 acres of cropland, horticultural and plantation fields and social forestry areas, forming dense stands that displaced grasses and increased management costs. Recognized as a quarantine weed under India’s Plant Quarantine Order (2003), A. psilostachya became the target of a specific delimiting survey and local eradication programme, with herbicide treatments and awareness campaigns reducing some satellite patches but the main infestation remaining a serious emerging threat.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduced with contaminated imported seed, planting material or fodder, then spread within Tumkur District via local movement of soil, machinery, fodder and along road verges under semi‑arid conditions and grazing pressure. External drivers include agricultural intensification, land‑use change and insufficient early detection capacity. Internal mechanisms: The species’ perennial rootstock and extensive rhizomatous system, combined with tolerance of semi‑arid, sandy soils and the ability to regenerate after cutting or grazing, underpin rapid build‑up of dense stands and make control difficult, leading to regional range expansion within Southern Asia once established.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event). Indian sources describe A. psilostachya as a new record for the country, restricted mainly to Tumkur District, but already invading about 400 acres of cropland, pastures and plantations and designated a quarantine weed, with dedicated delimiting surveys and eradication efforts undertaken.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122535/records/65de98846eef00c2cea09c3f)) This outbreak is clearly among the most impactful recent emergence events for the species in Asia and globally. Since Southern Asia already contained A. psilostachya in Iran by the early 1990s, the Indian outbreak is best coded as re_occurrence (a major increase in incidence within a previously affected subregion) rather than as intra‑continental or inter‑continental emergence or global first detection.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia serpens
EPP.common.name: serpent spurge, matted sandmat
Countries: Pakistan – Sindh Province, Khairpur District (cotton‑growing talukas including Kingri, Gambat, Khairpur, Sobhodero, Kotdiji, Thari Mirwah, Faiz Ganj, Nara) [1990s–2007]
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) fields and irrigation margins in semi‑arid irrigated agriculture
Event.summary: Weed surveys in cotton fields of Khairpur District, Sindh, carried out in the 1990s and early 2000s, revealed Euphorbia serpens as one of the six most frequent and dense weeds, with an average frequency of about 67% and high plant densities across multiple talukas.([pakbs.org](https://www.pakbs.org/pjbot/PDFs/39%287%29/PJB39%287%292265.pdf)) The species, together with Trianthema portulacastrum, Dactyloctenium aegyptium and Brachiaria eruciformis, was identified as a dominant and "devastating" weed complex in cotton, indicating a substantial increase in abundance and competitive importance in this irrigated cropping system relative to earlier floristic accounts.([pakbs.org](https://www.pakbs.org/pjbot/PDFs/39%287%29/PJB39%287%292265.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of irrigated cotton in Sindh, combined with inadequate or ineffective weed‑management practices and repeated tillage, created open, nutrient‑rich microsites that favored fast‑growing annual broadleaf weeds such as E. serpens; irrigated, hot conditions allowed multiple weed flushes within a season.([pakbs.org](https://www.pakbs.org/pjbot/PDFs/39%287%29/PJB39%287%292265.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: small, numerous seeds, rapid germination, prostrate growth and the ability to root at nodes enable E. serpens to form dense mats between crop rows, intercepting resources and hindering mechanical weeding, thereby promoting re‑occurrence and increased dominance in cotton fields without documented evolution of herbicide resistance.
Review: review – New event added to represent the emergence of E. serpens as a high‑frequency, high‑density weed in cotton in Khairpur District, Sindh. The Pakistan Journal of Botany survey shows that by the mid‑2000s it ranked among the most assertive weeds across eight talukas, implying substantial agronomic impact. Because the species was already present in Southern Asia, I coded this as 're_occurrence = true' (resurgence of a previously known weed under changing agronomic conditions) rather than intra‑continental emergence. Earlier Pakistani records likely pre‑date the survey, so the 1990–2007 window should be interpreted as the period of documented dominance rather than first arrival.

EPP.scientific.name: Cuscuta campestris
EPP.common.name: field dodder
Countries: India [1990s; severe, widespread infestations documented in 2000s–2020s]
Host: Rainfed and irrigated pulses (lentil, chickpea, greengram, blackgram), oilseeds (niger/Guizotia abyssinica, linseed), chillies and other vegetables, and forage legumes (lucerne, Egyptian clover)
Event.summary: From at least the 1990s, field dodder became one of the most serious parasitic weeds in pulses, oilseeds and fodder crops in parts of India, with weed‑science reports noting its spread across several central and eastern states. By the 2000s, experiments and reviews documented widespread infestations in crops such as lentil, chickpea, niger and linseed, with yield losses in heavily infested fields frequently estimated in the tens of percent and, for some hosts, up to around 80% in research trials. Through the 2010s–2020s, C. campestris has remained a chronic constraint on production in affected regions, with management relying on clean seed, crop rotation, tolerant varieties and pre‑emergence herbicides rather than any prospect of eradication.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of pulse and oilseed cultivation under rainfed and irrigated systems, widespread use of farm‑saved and locally traded seed contaminated with dodder seed, and movement of infested hay and machinery facilitated the build‑up and regional spread of C. campestris. Internal mechanisms: Very small, hard seeds that survive for years in soil, plus an exceptionally broad host range on annual crops and weeds, underpin persistent re‑occurrence without clear evidence of novel biotypes or resistance evolution in this period.
Review: review – Newly added high‑impact event. Indian weed‑science reviews and field experiments document C. campestris as a major parasitic weed of pulses, oilseeds (especially niger and linseed), chillies and forage legumes across multiple states, with very large yield losses in susceptible crops after 1990; event years and subnational spread are approximated and should be refined against national floras and survey data.

EPP.scientific.name: Elsinoë fawcettii
EPP.common.name: citrus scab fungus
Countries: China [2010s, major citrus-growing provinces including Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Sichuan, Yunnan, Zhejiang]
Host: Multiple Citrus spp. (including satsuma mandarin, pomelo, lemons, tangelos and other commercial citrus cultivars)
Event.summary: In the early 2010s, Chinese researchers collected Elsinoë fawcettii isolates from major citrus‑growing regions across China to investigate serious scab problems on a range of citrus cultivars. By 2014, pathogenicity and molecular analyses revealed at least 11 distinct pathotypes in China, including a newly described SM pathotype and additional host‑specialised variants affecting key commercial citrus types. Recognition of these diverse and sometimes newly defined pathotypes highlighted that citrus scab had diversified and adapted to different citrus hosts in China, prompting renewed efforts to tailor cultivar choice and fungicide programmes to local pathotype structure and helping stabilise disease impacts where those measures were adopted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large-scale, diverse citrus production across humid regions of China provided multiple host niches and continuous inoculum; climate conditions (warm, wet) favoured repeated infection cycles and selection for locally adapted strains. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (identification of at least one new pathotype – SM – and additional host-specialised pathotypes of E. fawcettii); host expansion and increased host specificity across different citrus cultivars; underlying genetic diversification documented by ITS and ISSR markers.
Review: Decision: Retain. Hou et al. (2014) and Hyun et al. (2009) document substantial pathotype and genetic diversity of E. fawcettii in China and worldwide, including the description of new pathotypes (such as SM) and evidence of host-specialised variants, which fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by internal evolutionary change rather than simple geographic spread. The geographic assignment (Asia, Eastern Asia, China) accords with UNSD classifications, and the sources used (primary Chinese pathotype study, global pathotype study, and supporting molecular/physiological work) are appropriate for this event. No corrections to event type or geography are required, but specific years of isolate collection (early 2010s) are inferred from the paper and thus the 2014 end date should be treated as approximate.

EPP.scientific.name: Parvovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: CPV, FPV
Sub.regions: North America: Northern America. Europe: Southern Europe; Western Europe.
Countries: Netherlands [2010s, recurrent feline panleukopenia outbreaks in Dutch animal shelters highlighted in a 2018 outbreak-management article].
Host: Domestic cats in animal shelters and rescue facilities (mainly kittens and juveniles).
Event.summary: Around 2010–2013, multiple large feline panleukopenia (FPV) outbreaks were documented in shelter populations in North America and Europe. In the USA, an adoption-guarantee shelter experienced a 10-month series of confirmed and suspected FPV cases with high morbidity and mortality in kittens, while in north-western Italy a multi-year outbreak originating in a single large shelter generated 177 hospitalised FPV cases over three years and became effectively endemic. Similar recurrent outbreaks and associated guidance on outbreak management were published for Dutch animal shelters, together indicating that FPV remained a leading cause of severe disease and death in shelter kittens despite long-standing availability of effective vaccines.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High turnover and crowding of cats in open-admission and large municipal or charity shelters; intake of many unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated kittens; delays in vaccination at intake; incomplete adherence to isolation, cohorting and sanitation protocols; high environmental stability of FPV with inadequate disinfection of rooms, cages and fomites. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel FPV genotype has been consistently implicated in these outbreaks; FPV and occasionally CPV-like strains were already endemic, so these episodes are best interpreted as re-occurrence events driven largely by management and population-risk factors rather than by major viral change.
Review: Decision: review (retain event). I refined the continent and subregion coding to “North America; Europe” with explicit reference to Northern America, Southern Europe (Italy) and Western Europe (Netherlands), and updated the country list to name the specific shelters and regions described in the main case-series and guideline papers. The event type has been changed from a generic multi-type coding to “re-occurrence only”, because FPV was long endemic in all these subregions and the outbreaks are best explained by shelter-level drivers (crowding, intake of unvaccinated kittens, breakdowns in vaccination and biosecurity) rather than by the emergence of a distinct new viral strain. The cited sources are appropriate for a composite shelter-outbreak episode, but human review is advised to confirm that aggregating multiple shelters and countries into a single 2010–2013 re-occurrence event meets the project’s expectations for event granularity.

EPP.scientific.name: Parvovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: CPV, FPV
Sub.regions: Asia: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia. Africa: Western Africa; Northern Africa. Europe: Southern Europe; Eastern Europe. North America: Northern America.
Countries: Thailand [2010s, CPV-2c of Asian lineage reported in dogs and cats]
Host: Primarily domestic dogs (puppies and juveniles with hemorrhagic gastroenteritis); occasional infections documented in wild canids and non-carnivoran wildlife such as pangolins, but these are not the main drivers of the event.
Event.summary: Phylogeographic analyses indicate that an “Asian” CPV-2c lineage originated in Asia around 2008 and remained largely confined there until roughly 2012, when it underwent a marked expansion in population size and geographic range. Over the following decade, viruses from this lineage became widespread and often predominant in many parts of Asia (including China, Viet Nam, Thailand, Myanmar and India), and were introduced repeatedly into Africa, Europe and North America, with documented establishment in countries such as Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Egypt, Italy, Romania and Canada. This lineage displaced earlier CPV-2 variants in many settings, contributed to numerous outbreaks and endemic cases of severe canine parvoviral enteritis and further diversified into regional sublineages, representing a second major CPV-2c-driven re-emergence wave superimposed on existing CPV endemicity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increasing international and regional trade and movement of pet dogs (including import of dogs from Asian countries to Europe and Africa), rescue and rehoming chains, and informal dog movements; sustained pools of unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated dogs in many low- and middle-income regions; urbanisation and dense free-roaming dog populations; limited molecular surveillance delaying recognition of the lineage’s spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – the “Asian” CPV-2c lineage harbours a characteristic constellation of VP2 and non-structural gene mutations (e.g. at residues 5, 267, 324 and 370) associated with enhanced receptor binding and possibly increased fitness, enabling it to outcompete earlier CPV-2a/2b and prototype CPV-2c strains in multiple regions. EPP.scientific.name: Plasmodium spp.
EPP.common.name: malaria parasites
Countries: United Republic of Tanzania [1990s highland epidemics]

Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climate variability (including El Niño and Indian Ocean Dipole–related warm, wet anomalies), land‑use change (deforestation, swamp cultivation and agricultural expansion), rapid population growth and migration between lowland endemic zones and highland settlements, antimalarial drug resistance (notably to chloroquine and later sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine), and weakening of vector‑control and health‑care systems all increased epidemic risk. EPP.scientific.name: Eriosoma lanigerum

EPP.scientific.name: Cyperus esculentus
EPP.common.name: chufa flatsedge, chufa, yellow nutgrass, yellow nutsedge

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus toscanaense

EPP.scientific.name: Iltovirus gallid2

Event.summary: From late 2007 onward, eastern Australia experienced an unprecedented series of ILT outbreaks in commercial poultry in Victoria and New South Wales, with many flocks showing severe respiratory disease and high mortality.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1567134816301952?utm_source=openai)) Molecular epidemiology demonstrated that most outbreaks between 2007 and 2009 were caused by two novel, highly virulent recombinant ILTV genotypes (classes 8 and 9) that arose through recombination between pre‑existing Australian live vaccine strains (SA2, A20) and the newly introduced European Serva vaccine strain; by 2009–2015, an additional recombinant (class 10) emerged and became predominant in parts of New South Wales.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1567134816301952?utm_source=openai)) Despite intensive control measures and changes in vaccine policy, these vaccine‑derived recombinants displaced previously circulating class 2 field strains and continued to cause economically important outbreaks over several years before improved vaccination strategies and regulatory changes reduced their impact.

Review: Decision: retain. Reason: The Australian recombinant‑vaccine epizootic is one of the most impactful and scientifically important ILT events worldwide, illustrating vaccine‑driven re‑emergence of more virulent genotypes; geography, timing and classification as re‑emergence are consistent with primary molecular epidemiology studies.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1567134816301952?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida

Event.summary: Between 2007 and 2015, retrospective surveillance in Ethiopia’s Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples’ Regional State documented 1,496 reportable cattle disease outbreaks, with haemorrhagic septicaemia accounting for 393 outbreaks (26.3%) and thousands of bovine cases and deaths across multiple zones. HS outbreaks occurred in diverse agro-ecological zones and were concentrated after the long rainy season, indicating persistent endemic circulation with periodic large flare-ups that together caused substantial productivity losses. Geography (Africa/Eastern Africa, Ethiopia; SNNPRS) and timeframe are consistent with the retrospective study; classification as re-occurrence is appropriate since environmental seasonality and incomplete vaccination, not pathogen change, explain the pattern. Removed a redundant Mendeley catalog URL in favor of the primary journal PDF and WOAH manual.

EPP.scientific.name: Proboscivirus elephantid1

Review:
RETAIN – This multi-year episode appropriately summarizes India’s emergence and subsequent high burden of EEHV-HD, including early recognition in 1997, extensive molecular documentation of lethal and subclinical cases, and major clusters such as the 2019 Nandankanan/Odisha events. Coding as intra_continental_emergence (new Asian sub-region: Southern Asia) and re_emergence (diverse local genotypes, broader host range including wild calves) is justified and consistent with the definitions.
No corrections to country, sub-region, or event-type coding were necessary. Additional primary Indian references (e.g., extended genotypic evaluation and Assam case series) could be cited for even greater detail but are not essential for this high-level event row.

EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus

EPP.scientific.name: Covert mortality nodavirus
EPP.common.name: CMNV
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (L. vannamei, F. chinensis, M. japonicus) and multiple wild and farm-associated crustaceans including ridgetail white prawn (Exopalaemon carinicauda), red swamp crayfish (Procambarus clarkii), swimming crabs and intertidal crabs.

EPP.scientific.name: Abutilon theophrasti
EPP.common.name: velvetleaf, butterprint, buttonweed, Indian mallow, velvetleaf Indian mallow, China jute, Indian hemp, pie-marker
Countries: New Zealand (national outbreak linked to contaminated fodder beet seed; properties affected across at least 11 regions, with more than 1,200 South Island properties traced to contaminated seed lines)

Event.summary: In the 2015/16 season, a major biosecurity incursion of velvetleaf was detected in fodder beet crops in the South Island of New Zealand, when plants were found in numerous paddocks sown with pelleted fodder beet seed imported from Europe that was later confirmed to be contaminated with velvetleaf seed. Countries and sub‚Äëregion coding (New Zealand within Australia and New Zealand, Oceania) are correct, and classification as re‚Äëoccurrence is appropriate given earlier New Zealand presence. EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus sindbis

Host: Wild birds (e.g. hooded crow and other passerines); ornithophilic mosquitoes; incidental equids and other mammals; potential but as yet rarely documented human exposure
Event.summary: From 2009 onward, Sindbis virus was repeatedly detected in Germany, beginning with isolation of SINV from Culex and Anopheles mosquitoes in the Upper Rhine valley in 2009 and, in 2010, from a hooded crow in Berlin, followed by multiple detections in mosquitoes and resident birds through at least 2016 during nationwide arbovirus monitoring.
