Despite serological evidence of past infection in blood donors and widespread enzootic circulation along river floodplains and wetlands, only isolated or no confirmed autochthonous human Sindbis fever cases were recognised, and the episode transitioned into low‑level endemicity while public and veterinary health attention increasingly focused on emerging flaviviruses such as West Nile and Usutu viruses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: westward expansion of SINV‑infected migratory birds from long‑established foci in Fennoscandia and eastern Europe; suitable wetland and floodplain habitats along German river systems supporting high densities of ornithophilic mosquitoes; enhanced entomological and wildlife surveillance from 2011 onward as part of broader mosquito‑borne virus monitoring. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses show German SINV strains to be closely related to other European genotype I viruses, indicating geographic range expansion and local establishment of existing lineages rather than emergence of a distinct, more virulent variant.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Germany represents the first well-documented establishment of enzootic SINV circulation in Western Europe; the original time span (2011–2014) has been corrected to 2009–2016 to reflect initial mosquito detections in 2009 and subsequent findings in wild birds and mosquitoes. Classification as intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD subregion is appropriate, but the near-absence of recognised human disease and the exact end year of the linked episode should be checked against national surveillance before final use.

EPP.scientific.name: Caprine arthritis encephalitis virus

Host: Domestic goats in commercial and breeding herds

EPP.scientific.name: White spot syndrome virus

Gaps in vaccination left cohorts of young cattle and wildlife susceptible while older animals remained partially immune, favouring maintenance of low‑level transmission. Internal mechanisms: The virus in this focus belonged to African lineage 2 and showed an unusually mild clinical phenotype in cattle yet retained the capacity to cause severe disease in certain wild artiodactyls. In response, provincial authorities and growers implemented stricter movement controls, promoted aggressive removal of infected trees, and began an extensive replanting program with resistant cultivars and improved management practices, allowing slow recovery of production while the pathogen remains endemic in the region. ([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CRSPAN/distribution/CA_bc?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The primary driver of this event was long‑distance movement of infected Corylus planting stock or propagative material across the U.S.–Canada border from infested Pacific Northwest orchards into British Columbia, despite domestic and import phytosanitary regulations aimed at protecting the province. I have reclassified the event type from re_emergence=Yes to re_occurrence=Yes (re_emergence=No), because the outbreak is best explained by cross‑border movement of an existing Pacific Northwest pathogen population and conducive climate and production systems in the lower Fraser Valley, with no evidence of a newly evolved strain; this fits the project definition of re‑occurrence. Review: retain (newly added): This high‑impact, multi‑island invasion (Nauru, Palau, French Polynesia) was previously omitted despite clear evidence of severe fruit damage, major management interventions and classical biological control programmes. It constitutes the first confirmed establishment of B. dorsalis in Oceania (UNSD Micronesia and Polynesia) after 1990 and clearly belongs among the top global emergence events; dedicated row added with continent/sub‑region coding aligned to UNSD and supported by primary Pacific fruit fly literature.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis

Countries: Italy [2018-2024 – Campania (Salerno and Napoli provinces), with later detections in other municipalities and regions under official eradication and surveillance]
Host: Citrus, persimmon and other fruit trees in mixed orchards and gardens where traps were deployed; larvae and emerging adults have been recovered from infested citrus and other fruits in some monitored orchards.
Event.summary: In 2018, official surveys in the Campania region of southern Italy trapped multiple male Bactrocera dorsalis complex flies in mixed fruit orchards, with morphological and molecular analyses confirming the first record of oriental fruit fly in Europe. Follow‑up monitoring in Italy captured additional adults in Campania and other regions, and in 2022 adults emerged in the laboratory from fruit collected in citrus and pear orchards, indicating at least transient local reproduction, although populations have remained localised and are subject to official eradication and containment measures. Internal mechanisms: typical B. dorsalis traits of high fecundity, wide host range and strong dispersal underpin its incursion potential; available genetic data indicate that Italian populations are closely related to Asian source populations, consistent with recent introductions rather than long-term cryptic establishment or major evolutionary change. EPP.common.name: Candida glabrata

Event.summary: From the early to late 2010s, Chinese tertiary hospitals reported the first documented invasive infections caused by pan‚Äëechinocandin-resistant Candida glabrata and later conducted a multicentre genomic analysis of echinocandin non-susceptible C. glabrata clinical isolates collected between 2014 and 2019. Although echinocandin resistance remained uncommon overall, these studies showed that pan‚Äëechinocandin-resistant and multidrug‚Äëresistant C. glabrata had emerged in China and were associated with invasive candidiasis in high‚Äërisk patients.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased use of echinocandins for invasive candidiasis in Chinese hospitals, particularly in patients with prior azole exposure and complex comorbidities; expansion of intensive care and oncology services; and limited therapeutic alternatives for resistant Candida infections. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of FKS hot‚Äëspot mutations during or after echinocandin therapy and, in some cases, concurrent azole resistance produced pan‚Äëechinocandin-resistant or multidrug‚Äëresistant C. glabrata, constituting re‚Äëemergence driven by antifungal resistance and enhanced tolerance to echinocandin pressure.
Review: retain ‚Äì Event captures the first reported pan-echinocandin-resistant C. glabrata invasive infection in China and subsequent multicentre genomic work on echinocandin non-susceptible isolates; the timing, geography and re-emergence classification are supported by the cited Chinese case series, CHIF-NET surveillance and genomic study.

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter jejuni
EPP.common.name: campylobacteriosis
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Between 1992 and 1998 in Minnesota, USA, surveillance detected the first locally acquired quinolone‚Äëresistant Campylobacter jejuni infections among patients who had not received quinolone therapy, after years in which no such resistance had been observed. Over this period, the proportion of human C. jejuni isolates resistant to fluoroquinolones rose markedly, in parallel with increasing detection of resistant strains in retail poultry products. Resistance levels remained elevated thereafter, indicating establishment of a resistant zoonotic reservoir and a sustained shift in the epidemiology of human campylobacteriosis in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Licensing and widespread use of fluoroquinolones in poultry production in the United States created strong selection pressure; contaminated poultry meat became a major vehicle for resistant C. jejuni into humans. Internal mechanisms: Stepwise accumulation of mutations mediating fluoroquinolone resistance in C. jejuni, with resistant strains increasingly recovered from both human stool samples and chicken meat.
Review: Review ‚Äì Event accurately reflects the early emergence of fluoroquinolone‚Äëresistant C. jejuni in the U.S., including its link to poultry. Classification as re‚Äëemergence (AMR‚Äëdriven) is appropriate, and geography is correct. Impact is substantial for antimicrobial resistance but modest in terms of documented outbreak case counts. Consider consolidating this with the Finland traveler‚Äëassociated resistance event as a single global fluoroquinolone‚Äëresistance emergence episode in the final top‚Äë10 list.

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter jejuni
EPP.common.name: campylobacteriosis
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From the early 2000s, New Zealand experienced a prolonged national epidemic of campylobacteriosis, with notification rates peaking around 2003‚Äì2006 at roughly 380‚Äì400 cases per 100,000 population, the highest national incidence reported in the literature. Most cases were attributable to poultry, and the epidemic caused tens of thousands of illnesses annually, hundreds of hospitalizations, and measurable mortality and economic costs. In 2006‚Äì2007, a national Campylobacter risk‚Äëmanagement strategy targeting poultry production and processing was implemented, and by 2007‚Äì2008 notifications and hospitalizations declined by more than 50% compared with 2002‚Äì2006, ending the epidemic phase although campylobacteriosis remained the country‚Äôs most common foodborne illness.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High per‚Äëcapita poultry consumption, high contamination levels of fresh chicken meat, industrial consolidation of poultry processing, and initially limited regulatory controls sustained a prolonged high‚Äëincidence epidemic; coordinated regulatory and industry interventions (process‚Äëhygiene criteria, carcass‚Äëcontamination monitoring, and risk‚Äëmanagement targets) subsequently reduced human exposure. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic was driven mainly by established poultry‚Äëassociated C. jejuni genotypes; molecular epidemiology showed that reductions in poultry contamination translated into reductions in poultry‚Äëattributed human infections rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: Retain ‚Äì National epidemic and subsequent sharp decline following poultry‚Äëfocused interventions are very well documented and represent a major high‚Äëburden re‚Äëoccurrence event with clear control impact. Temporal span and classification as re‚Äëoccurrence (driven by food‚Äësystem changes, not pathogen evolution) are appropriate; minor wording in the summary was aligned more closely with reported incidence figures, but no structural changes were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis
EPP.common.name: Bd
Host: Wild native frogs, especially stream-breeding species (e.g., Taudactylus spp., Litoria spp.)
Event.summary: Around 1993, mass mortality of rainforest frogs was first observed in upland eastern Australia, and histology later revealed chytridiomycosis as the cause, with Bd subsequently being formally described in 1998‚Äì1999 from material associated with these die-offs. Over the mid‚Äë1990s the fungus spread along the Great Dividing Range in Queensland and New South Wales, causing rapid, wave-like population crashes and extinctions or near-extinctions in multiple high-elevation frog species. By the late 1990s the initial epidemic wave had passed through many sites, leaving relict or extirpated populations and prompting national recognition of chytridiomycosis as a key threatening process for Australian amphibians.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely human-mediated translocation of infected amphibians (including via the pet and research trades) and contaminated equipment, combined with favorable cool, moist montane climates and high host density along stream networks, facilitated rapid establishment and spread once Bd arrived in eastern Australia. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of the highly virulent Global Panzootic Lineage (BdGPL), with enhanced transmission and pathogenicity in na√Øve Australian frog communities, underpinned the severity of this first widely recognized chytridiomycosis epizootic and led directly to the initial description of Bd as a new species.
Review: retain ‚Äì Event appropriately captures the first recognized chytridiomycosis epizootic in eastern Australia and the period during which Bd was first formally described (1998‚Äì1999), with correct continent/sub-region/country coding and a plausible 1993‚Äì1999 window. Treating this as the global 'first_detection' episode is consistent with the literature on Bd discovery; no changes were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus
EPP.common.name: FP-associated herpesvirus, CFPHV
Countries: United States of America (Hawaiian Islands, especially KƒÅne ªohe Bay on O ªahu and coastal pastures at Palaau, Moloka ªi)
Host: Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas)
Event.summary: Fibropapillomatosis had been recognized at low prevalence in Hawaiian green turtles since at least the 1950s, but around 1989 the disease erupted in juvenile foraging aggregations, most notably in KƒÅne ªohe Bay on O ªahu and at Palaau on Moloka ªi. Capture‚Äìmark‚Äìrecapture and transect studies in 1989‚Äì1995 documented some of the highest FP prevalences recorded globally, with local values ranging from near 0% to nearly 100% at specific sites, and high burdens of external and internal tumors linked to mortality and strandings. Prevalence peaked around the mid‚Äë1990s and has since declined but remained a major chronic conservation concern, with FP identified as a leading cause of green turtle strandings in the Hawaiian archipelago over multi‚Äëdecadal monitoring.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Hawaiian FP hotspots are strongly associated with semi‚Äëenclosed, nutrient‚Äëenriched bays and lagoons influenced by urban runoff, wastewater and altered macroalgal communities; work linking FP risk to eutrophication indices, nitrogen footprints and proliferation of certain macroalgae and biotoxin‚Äëproducing dinoflagellates supports a role for anthropogenic nutrient loading and natural tumor promoters. Internal mechanisms: Molecular and phylogenetic studies show distinct yet long‚Äëestablished CFPHV/ChHV5 lineages in Hawaii compared with Florida, with no evidence that recent viral mutation alone triggered the epizootic; instead, chronic environmental stress and perhaps host immune responses are considered key determinants of disease expression in latently infected turtles.
Review: retain ‚Äì The Hawaiian FP epizootic is clearly one of the most impactful global events, with extreme local prevalences and strong conservation concern. Event type has been corrected to re‚Äëoccurrence only (environmentally driven resurgence in a region with prior FP) rather than also re‚Äëemergence, as current evidence does not support a newly evolved, more virulent virus as the primary driver. Countries and sub‚Äëregion coding are consistent with the UNSD scheme. Event summary and sources are appropriate and focused on the main 1989‚Äì1995 outbreak.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic haematopoietic necrosis virus
EPP.common.name: EHNV
Countries: Australia (multiple commercial rainbow trout farms in the Murrumbidgee River catchment, New South Wales, and at least one farm in the Shoalhaven River catchment, plus affected farms in Victoria)
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), mainly 0+ post‚Äëhatchery fingerlings and small growers, with infection pressure maintained by co‚Äëendemic EHNV reservoirs in nearby wild redfin perch populations.
Event.summary: Between 1986 and 1992, EHNV was repeatedly detected on commercial rainbow trout farms in south‚Äëeastern Australia, particularly in the Murrumbidgee and Shoalhaven River catchments of New South Wales, following establishment of the virus in redfin perch within the same drainage systems.([research.ed.ac.uk](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/epidemiology-of-epizootic-haematopoietic-necrosis-virus-ehnv-infe?utm_source=openai)) Outbreaks typically involved low‚Äëto‚Äëmoderate increases in mortality among 0+ fingerlings less than 125 mm long, with laboratory testing showing high proportions of clinically affected and dead fish positive for EHNV but very low prevalence in in‚Äëcontact survivors. As awareness and surveillance improved, farms adopted stricter biosecurity and stocking practices, and subsequent cohorts often cleared the virus, limiting long‚Äëterm persistence on farms but demonstrating that EHNV had expanded its effective host range from wild redfin to intensively reared salmonids in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of live trout fingerlings between hatcheries and grow‚Äëout farms, use of potentially contaminated transport water, and proximity to EHNV‚Äëinfected wild redfin perch populations in shared catchments created repeated opportunities for spillover into aquaculture facilities. Poor water quality, high stocking density and low water‚Äëexchange rates on some farms were correlated with clinical disease expression.([research.ed.ac.uk](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/epidemiology-of-epizootic-haematopoietic-necrosis-virus-ehnv-infe?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: EHNV is highly virulent but relatively poorly transmissible in rainbow trout, leading to outbreaks characterized by low infection prevalence but high case‚Äëfatality among infected fingerlings; the virus‚Äôs ability to infect both redfin and trout represents a host‚Äëexpansion dynamic and justifies classification of this multi‚Äëyear farmed‚Äëfish episode as re‚Äëemergence rather than simple re‚Äëoccurrence.
Review: REVIEW ‚Äì correct and retain, but adjust timing and classification. The main epidemiological work on EHNV in farmed rainbow trout documents five outbreaks on a New South Wales farm from 1986‚Äì1992 and similar episodes on other farms, with no strong evidence that outbreaks continued through the late 1990s; the event period has therefore been corrected from 1990‚Äì1999 to 1986‚Äì1992 to match the published data.([research.ed.ac.uk](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/epidemiology-of-epizootic-haematopoietic-necrosis-virus-ehnv-infe?utm_source=openai)) To reflect that this event primarily represents host expansion from wild redfin to farmed trout rather than a simple resurgence in an already affected host, re_emergence is set to true and re_occurrence to false. Users who wish to strictly enforce the 1990‚Äëonward time window could, if necessary, treat this as a 1990‚Äì1992 subset of the same multi‚Äëyear episode, but epidemiologically the 1986‚Äì1992 interval is more coherent.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Feline leukemia virus
EPP.common.name: FeLV
Host: Florida panther (Puma concolor coryi) in south Florida
Event.summary: After an apparent absence of FeLV cases in Florida panthers between 2004 and late 2010, FeLV infections reappeared in the population from 2010 to 2016, with six of 214 necropsied panthers testing FeLV‚Äëantigen positive and at least one death attributed primarily to FeLV‚Äëassociated disease. These contemporary cases occurred west of the historic outbreak zone and mostly involved animals killed by vehicle collisions in more human‚Äëpopulated areas, indicating renewed spillover rather than simple persistence of the earlier virus. Continued vaccination of panthers and local domestic cats, combined with surveillance and case management, limited the scale of this re‚Äëemergence and FeLV remained at low prevalence, although repeated introductions from domestic cats remain a recognised threat.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The re‚Äëemergent FeLV infections arose in south and southwest Florida where panthers increasingly overlap with free‚Äëranging domestic cats around ranches, rural residences, and roads, consistent with repeated cross‚Äëspecies transmission driven by human land‚Äëuse change, expanding residential development, and incomplete vaccination and management of local domestic cat populations. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses of FeLV from contemporary (2010‚Äì2016) panthers showed viruses clustering with domestic cat FeLV‚ÄëA strains and provided evidence of FeLV‚ÄëB recombinant virus, indicating multiple introductions from domestic cats and ongoing viral evolution. This episode is therefore classified as re‚Äëemergence involving repeated host expansion (domestic‚Äëcat‚Äìto‚Äëpanther spillover) and novel strain/genotype dynamics in a population that had already experienced a prior FeLV outbreak.
Review: Review ‚Äì Retain this as the second, lower‚Äëintensity FeLV episode in Florida panthers, characterised by six antigen‚Äëpositive necropsied animals during 2010‚Äì2016 after a six‚Äëyear period with no detected cases. Classification as re_emergence is consistent with the event‚Äëtype definitions and molecular evidence for repeated domestic‚Äëcat spillover and the presence of FeLV‚ÄëB; no intra‚Äë or inter‚Äëcontinental emergence is involved because FeLV was already present in North America and in Florida. Geography and timing (North America / Northern America, United States; 2010‚Äì2016) match the primary sources, but a human reviewer should confirm whether any post‚Äë2016 FeLV‚Äëpositive panthers represent additional linked episodes or isolated cases that would warrant updating the end year or adding a new event row.

EPP.scientific.name: Cacopsylla pruni
EPP.common.name: plum psyllid
Host: Apricot (Prunus armeniaca) in experimental and commercial orchards in Languedoc‚ÄëRoussillon, with nearby wild Prunus domestica, P. cerasifera and P. spinosa acting as reservoirs.
Event.summary: From 1994 to 2000, a major ESFY epidemic in apricot orchards in Languedoc‚ÄëRoussillon (southern France) prompted detailed epidemiological studies combining large‚Äëscale insect trapping and molecular diagnostics. These studies identified Cacopsylla pruni as the main vector of ESFY in the region and linked its early‚Äëspring flights from infected wild Prunus stands into orchards with primary infections in apricot seedling blocks. Although annual spread in monitored experimental orchards was modest, cumulative infection over several years led to significant tree loss and demonstrated that without early removal of infected trees and better management of nearby wild Prunus and psyllid populations, ESFY could progressively compromise regional apricot production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High density of susceptible apricot plantings, close juxtaposition of orchards and wild Prunus stands harbouring both C. pruni and ESFY phytoplasma, and initial lack of awareness of the vector‚Äôs overwintering and spring migration behaviour allowed sustained transmission. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation ‚Äì overwintered C. pruni adults moving from conifers back onto Prunus in early spring were shown to be important carriers of ESFY, with their migration phenology closely matching the window of host susceptibility and making them particularly effective vectors under southern French conditions.
Review: review ‚Äì Event accurately reflects the Languedoc‚ÄëRoussillon epidemic and the French work that first quantified C. pruni‚Äôs role as ESFY vector. Adjusted the event classification from re_emergence to re_occurrence to match the definitions (vector and pathogen were already established in Southern Europe; the outbreak was driven by high local infection pressure rather than a new strain or host shift). Retained the Plant Pathology 2001 article as the main source and kept the period, geography and host description unchanged.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cochliomyia hominivorax
EPP.common.name: New world screwworm myiasis
Host: Primarily cattle, but also small ruminants, horses and dogs
Event.summary: In July 1998, following decades of endemic New World screwworm myiasis and mounting economic losses, Jamaica launched a national eradication programme with FAO/IAEA and USDA support, targeting an island-wide population that caused year‚Äëround infestations in cattle, goats, pigs, horses and dogs. From November 1998 to October 2004, surveillance recorded on the order of hundreds of animal screwworm cases per month, prompting progressive intensification of control, including weekly releases of about 16 million sterile flies from August 1999, farmer outreach and improved wound management. Despite logistical challenges and slower-than-expected progress, these area‚Äëwide measures substantially reduced infestation pressure and transformed the problem from an acute burden into a managed endemic threat, laying the groundwork for longer‚Äëterm suppression and protection of screwworm‚Äëfree areas in the wider Caribbean.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: long‚Äëstanding endemicity of C. hominivorax in Jamaica, high densities of susceptible livestock, inadequate wound management and limited early access to SIT created persistently high screwworm burdens and significant economic losses, motivating an intensive eradication campaign. Internal mechanisms: no evidence indicates a novel strain, resistance or increased virulence; this episode reflects severe re‚Äëoccurrence of typical screwworm populations until area‚Äëwide integrated pest management and sterile‚Äëfly releases began to reverse the trend.
Review: Review ‚Äì This event represents a major, well‚Äëdocumented re‚Äëoccurrence in an already endemic Caribbean territory and merits inclusion among the top episodes. However, the original row mis‚Äëstated timing and case numbers. The event year has been corrected to 1998‚Äì2004 to match the national eradication programme (start of government programme in July 1998, sterile fly releases from 1999, and surveillance data reported through October 2004), and the summary has been revised to rely on Jamaica‚Äëspecific surveillance and economic impact rather than misattributing regional case totals from other countries. Classification as re‚Äëoccurrence (without intra/inter‚Äëcontinental emergence) remains appropriate because the parasite was long established in Jamaica and no novel strain was involved. Sources (FAO/IAEA monograph, IAEA/Jamaica documents and subsequent analyses) remain suitable, but this corrected row should be checked by a human reviewer before finalization.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus kyasanurense
EPP.common.name: Alkhurma virus
Countries: Saudi Arabia – Mecca and Jeddah regions (including Alkhumra district) [1994-1999]
Host: Humans (butchers, abattoir workers and other residents exposed to sheep, goats and camels, ticks, and raw animal products); livestock (sheep and camels) implicated as sources of infected blood or milk; ticks suspected as vectors.
Event.summary: From 1994 through 1999, a series of patients from Mecca and Jeddah, notably clusters of male butchers working in the Alkhumra district who had recently slaughtered imported sheep or handled camel products, were hospitalized with acute severe hemorrhagic febrile illness, prompting investigation for known viral hemorrhagic fevers. Virologic testing in Saudi Arabia and at international reference laboratories led to isolation and sequencing of 11 closely related strains of a previously unrecognized tick‑borne flavivirus distinct from but related to Kyasanur Forest disease virus, establishing Alkhumra hemorrhagic fever virus as a novel human pathogen and defining an initial endemic focus in western Saudi Arabia. The recognized cases resolved with supportive care or resulted in death, and no sustained human‑to‑human chains were identified, but the discovery triggered formal recognition of Alkhurma hemorrhagic fever and the development of national surveillance and research programs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑risk occupational exposure of butchers and slaughterhouse workers handling viremic sheep and camels, including frequent contact with fresh blood and raw meat, as well as consumption of unpasteurized camel milk, created opportunities for zoonotic spillover; importation and movement of livestock into Mecca and Jeddah abattoirs likely introduced or amplified virus circulation; presence of Ornithodoros and Hyalomma ticks in animal resting places provided an efficient bridge for virus maintenance. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) from an enzootic tick‑livestock cycle to humans; molecular analyses across 1994–1999 isolates showed low diversity and supported a recent divergence from Kyasanur Forest disease virus, consistent with a relatively new tick‑borne flavivirus lineage rather than a long‑circulating but previously unrecognized human pathogen.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Adjusted event year from a single year (1995) to 1994–1999 and expanded the geographic description to include both Mecca and Jeddah, based on detailed epidemiologic data showing 11 virologically confirmed cases beginning in May 1994; removed the first_detection flag so that this episode is coded solely as first global emergence in humans, which better matches the definitions and available historical evidence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus kyasanurense
EPP.common.name: Alkhurma virus
Countries: Saudi Arabia – predominantly Najran, with additional cases from Jeddah, Makkah, Taif and other western/southwestern provinces [2011-2016]
Host: Humans (men and women, including housewives, housemaids, students and workers with and without direct animal-contact occupations) exposed to livestock, ticks and possibly other vectors; livestock (sheep, goats, camels) and ticks (Ornithodoros savignyi, Hyalomma spp.) as key components of the enzootic cycle.
Event.summary: From 2011 onward, implementation of a dedicated national Alkhurma hemorrhagic fever surveillance system in Saudi Arabia revealed a marked resurgence of reported AHFV infections, with 93 laboratory‑confirmed cases in 2011 and continued transmission concentrated in Najran but also involving Jeddah, Makkah, Taif and other western/southwestern regions. During 2011–2014, surveillance data documented 281 laboratory‑confirmed human cases, followed by a further 169 confirmed cases between 2014 and 2016, with Najran accounting for roughly three‑quarters of cases overall and an increasing proportion of patients being women, housewives/housemaids and persons without formal animal‑handling occupations, indicating broader community exposure and greatly improved case ascertainment. By 2015–2016 annual case counts had fallen to several dozen per year and case‑fatality rates had dropped below 1%, but persistent endemic transmission in Najran and periodic detections elsewhere led Saudi health authorities and researchers to characterize AHFV as a re‑emerging tick‑borne zoonosis requiring sustained, integrated surveillance and control rather than episodic outbreak response.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and geographic expansion of small‑ruminant and camel husbandry in Najran and other western/southwestern provinces, continued household animal keeping and informal slaughtering, urbanization at the livestock–human interface, and cross‑border livestock movements with neighboring Yemen maintained frequent human exposure to infected animals and ticks; introduction and scale‑up of national AHFV surveillance and laboratory capacity from 2011 onwards substantially increased detection, especially of milder cases and cases in women and children. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies across Saudi isolates up to the mid‑2010s demonstrate low genetic diversity and no clear evidence of a novel, more virulent genotype, so this multi‑year wave is best interpreted as re‑occurrence driven by ecological factors and enhanced surveillance rather than true viral re‑emergence; efficient maintenance of AHFV in local tick and livestock populations reflects inherent ecological suitability rather than recent viral adaptation.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: New event added to capture a major multi‑year resurgence documented by Saudi national surveillance, comprising approximately 281 confirmed cases in 2011–2014 and 169 confirmed cases in 2014–2016 (roughly 450 cases total), with transmission centered in Najran but extending to other western/southwestern provinces; classified as re‑occurrence within the same continent and sub‑region because case increases are explained by ecological drivers and enhanced surveillance rather than emergence of a distinct viral lineage.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Carp edema virus
EPP.common.name: CEV
Host: Ornamental koi carp in tanks and ponds co-cultured with goldfish and Indian major carps
Event.summary: In June 2015, a severe disease outbreak with lethargy, gill necrosis and high mortality was reported in adult koi on a farm in Kerala, and nested PCR plus sequencing confirmed CEV, constituting the first report of koi sleepy disease in India. Over subsequent years, additional large-scale mortalities of koi were documented in ornamental fish farms in eastern India, including a major event in Odisha described in 2020, revealing that CEV infection had become widespread in the Indian ornamental carp sector. These outbreaks prompted increased diagnostic efforts and biosecurity guidance to limit further spread into India’s extensive carp-farming regions.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27902384/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of India’s ornamental fish industry, with substantial importation of koi from East Asia under limited health screening, likely introduced CEV; high stocking densities, transport and handling stress, and variable water quality in small-scale ornamental facilities promoted disease expression; internal distribution of ornamental koi disseminated infection across Southern India and into the eastern region. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies to date show close similarity between Indian CEV isolates and established international genogroups, suggesting that emergence in India reflects long-distance movement of existing high-virulence lineages rather than evolution of a distinct Indian variant.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27902384/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review. The original event incorrectly suggested outbreaks from around 2013; this has been corrected to 2015–2020 based on the first confirmed case in Kerala and later documented farm outbreaks in eastern India. Classification as intra‑continental emergence is appropriate because India represents first spread of CEV into the Southern Asia subregion; sources now align closely with the updated timeframe.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Cattle and domestic buffalo in southern Indian states (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala)
Event.summary: During the early 1990s, rinderpest persisted mainly in the southern Indian states despite decades of vaccination, with recognized infection from at least 1990 and the last bovine outbreak reported in Karnataka in January 1995. Transmission occurred as sporadic outbreaks in pockets with low vaccination coverage, but overall incidence fell sharply after India launched the National Project on Rinderpest Eradication and Operation Rinderpest Zero. No clinical cases were detected after late 1995, allowing India to document freedom from clinical rinderpest and ultimately achieve official recognition as free from infection by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH/OIE) in 2006.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Incomplete and uneven vaccine coverage, very large cattle and buffalo populations, and logistical constraints in reaching smallholders and remote areas allowed continued low-level circulation into the early 1990s. Progressive improvements in funding, organization and coverage under national eradication programmes closed immunity gaps and strengthened surveillance, accelerating fade-out of infection. Internal mechanisms: Available virological evidence does not indicate emergence of a new strain or altered virulence; the pattern is best interpreted as declining re-occurrence of long-established endemic lineages under gradually intensifying control rather than re-emergence driven by viral change.
Review: retain – This is a major endemic focus and “endgame” episode for South Asia, with timing and geography well supported by FAO and Government of India sources (last outbreaks in southern states with disappearance by late 1995). Classification as re-occurrence (control-system driven fade-out of existing lineages) rather than re‑emergence is appropriate. No structural corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus/indicus), water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis)
Event.summary: From 2000 to 2005, participatory disease surveillance across Pakistan documented haemorrhagic septicaemia as one of the most prevalent and economically important livestock diseases, with high reported prevalence and perceived importance in many districts of Punjab, Sindh, North-West Frontier Province/Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Azad Jammu and Kashmir and the Northern Areas, and annual economic losses in Punjab alone estimated at more than 2.17 billion Pakistani rupees. HS was identified as a leading cause of cattle and buffalo mortality in susceptible stock, with farmers consistently ranking it above or alongside other major transboundary diseases in terms of economic impact. The episode represents a period of intense endemic circulation and repeated local outbreaks, which spurred calls for improved vaccination coverage, surveillance and coordinated national control strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of cattle and buffalo in smallholder systems, seasonal monsoon-associated humidity, fodder scarcity, heavy work stress in draught animals, and gaps in vaccination coverage and surveillance enabled widespread HS transmission and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: Outbreaks were attributed to endemic Pasteurella multocida serotypes B:2/E:2; there is no evidence that novel genotypes or resistance profiles were central to this period, so the episode is best characterized as large-scale re-occurrence driven by environmental and management factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Added as a new multi-year national episode because participatory disease surveillance (2000–2005) shows HS as one of Pakistan’s most prevalent and economically important bovine diseases, with very large estimated annual losses. Classified as re-occurrence (endemic disease with external drivers; no evidence that novel strains drove this period). Geography (Asia/Southern Asia, Pakistan) and timeframe follow the surveillance and economic-loss data; sources focus specifically on HS epidemiology and impact in Pakistan.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonellosis
Host: Sheep (ewes and lambs) in ovine flocks
Event.summary: Between 1996 and 2001, Salmonella enterica serovar Abortusovis, an ovine host‑adapted serovar already known in parts of Europe and western Asia, caused multiple epidemic abortion episodes in ovine flocks in Spain, with isolates recovered from numerous geographically distinct herds during this period. The infection was introduced and maintained in flocks primarily by movement of carrier sheep and contact with infected animals during seasonal migration, leading to repeated clusters of late‑term abortions, stillbirths and weak lambs. Control actions involving flock management, removal of infected animals and improved biosecurity eventually reduced the number of reported epidemic outbreaks after 2001, although the pathogen remained endemic in some areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movements of replacement ewes and rams, transhumance/seasonal grazing that mixed flocks from different regions, and inadequate control of aborting animals contributed to spread of Salmonella Abortusovis within and between Spanish ovine flocks. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects amplification of existing host‑adapted clones rather than clearly documented novel genotypes; plasmid‑encoded virulence factors that promote systemic infection and abortion in ewes underlie the severity of disease.
Review: Review – Epidemic Salmonella Abortusovis‑associated ovine abortion episodes in Spain (1996–2001) are real and well documented, but the main drivers are animal movements and flock management (external drivers) rather than documented pathogen change. Accordingly, the event has been reclassified as re_occurrence = Yes and re_emergence = No, and the sub‑region label has been standardized to 'Europe: Southern Europe'. The overall global impact of this ovine‑specific event, relative to large poultry‑ and cattle‑associated Salmonella clones, should be reviewed when prioritizing the final top‑10 list.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Host: Saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica), with related bovine HS strains in cattle
Event.summary: From 2010 to 2015, several mass mortality events affected saiga antelope populations in Kazakhstan, culminating in an unprecedented die‑off in May 2015 in the Betpak‑Dala population in which around 200,000 animals died within weeks, wiping out entire calving aggregations and reducing the global population by more than two-thirds. Necropsy, bacteriology and molecular work confirmed haemorrhagic septicaemia caused by Pasteurella multocida serogroup B as the proximate cause of death, with earlier, smaller die‑offs in 2010–2012 also linked to P. multocida. Following the 2015 catastrophe, surviving saiga populations began to recover under intensive conservation measures, but the events highlighted the potential for an opportunistic bovine pathogen to cause explosive, climate‑triggered mortality in a wild antelope host already under demographic pressure.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unusually warm and humid conditions during calving in 2015 (and likely in earlier events), high animal density at calving sites, and limited dispersal are inferred to have triggered systemic activation of normally commensal P. multocida in saiga tonsils, leading to synchronized septicemia and mass mortality; historical over‑exploitation and habitat pressures left populations especially vulnerable. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed that saiga isolates were P. multocida serogroup B closely related to bovine HS strains (e.g. ST64) with multiple virulence genes; this represents host expansion and re-emergence of haemorrhagic septicaemia in a wild ungulate, where bacterial traits and host physiology under climatic stress enabled rapid progression from commensal carriage to fatal septicaemia across entire calving aggregations.
Review: Retain – This is an exceptionally high-impact event, with ≈200,000 saiga deaths in 2015 plus earlier die-offs, and clear attribution to P. multocida-associated haemorrhagic septicaemia under extreme climatic conditions; it also represents a major host expansion for a classical bovine pathogen. Corrected the emergence classification so that only re-emergence is marked "true" (reflecting host expansion and altered disease expression), removing the simultaneous re-occurrence flag to comply with the project rule that re-emergence should not co-occur with re-occurrence. Geography (Asia/Central Asia, Kazakhstan; Betpak-Dala and Ural saiga populations) and timeframe are consistent with the EID, Science Advances and BMC Microbiology analyses.

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia mallei
EPP.common.name: Malleus (glanders)
Host: Equids (horses, mules, donkeys)
Event.summary: After India had remained free of reported glanders for about eight years, the disease reappeared in 2006 with outbreaks among equids in northern states such as Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Punjab, followed by spread to additional states over the next several years. Between 2006 and 2010–2011, surveillance and outbreak investigations confirmed 164 infected equids in at least eight states, with major foci including a large outbreak in Maharashtra and repeated episodes in Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand, leading to extensive euthanasia of working and cart horses. Under strengthened national legislation, infected animals were culled and biosecurity and movement controls were tightened, reducing incidence but not preventing subsequent sporadic cases and later resurgence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Relaxation or uneven enforcement of historical glanders control laws, uncontrolled movement of working and pack equids between endemic and previously free districts, and increased movements for brick-kiln work and religious pilgrimages facilitated re-introduction and spread. Economic disincentives to report disease and cull infected animals, together with limited early diagnostic capacity, delayed containment in some states. Internal mechanisms: Available studies emphasize circulation of existing B. mallei strains without evidence of a novel genotype or marked change in virulence; the episode is therefore best viewed as a major re-occurrence driven by management and movement factors rather than re-emergence due to pathogen change.
Review: review – Retained as one of the largest modern glanders episodes, but emergence types adjusted. Intra_continental_emergence was set to No because India lies within the already affected Southern Asia sub-region; the outbreak represents resurgence within that sub-region, not first occurrence in a new one. Re_occurrence remains Yes and re_emergence is set to No, because the literature attributes the 2006–2011 resurgence to horse movements and control gaps, with no clear evidence for new strains or host shifts.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Seeded by viruses from the 2004–2006 Indian Ocean outbreaks, chikungunya re‑appeared in India in 2005–2006 after roughly three decades of apparent absence, spreading to at least 16 states and causing about 1.3–1.4 million suspected cases in 2006 alone. From 2006 onward, related East/Central/South African lineage viruses caused major epidemics in Sri Lanka and the Maldives and then moved through parts of Indonesia, Malaysia and southern Thailand, where large outbreaks occurred in 2008–2009 after more than a decade without transmission. By around 2010, incidence had declined or become sporadic in many of these areas, but the virus established new endemic foci and left large cohorts with post‑epidemic rheumatologic sequelae.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2006_10_17-en?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of Aedes aegypti in tropical urban and peri‑urban environments, inadequate vector control infrastructure, and intense human travel within South and South‑East Asia facilitated rapid dissemination once reintroduced. Large, immunologically naive populations supported explosive transmission, especially in densely populated Indian states and major cities in Indonesia and Thailand. Internal mechanisms: Continued spread of the ECSA/Indian Ocean lineage, including viruses bearing E1‑A226V and related mutations, increased fitness in Aedes albopictus and may have enhanced transmissibility, supporting re‑emergence across a wide climatic range in Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4754000/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event narrowed to Asia only and extended through 2010 to capture the full South and South‑East Asian re‑emergence wave. Pacific island introductions (New Caledonia, Papua New Guinea, Yap) were removed from the country list and are treated separately in Oceania‑focused events. Emergence‑type flags were simplified to re‑emergence only: chikungunya was already known in Southern and South‑eastern Asia, and spread to new countries within the same subregions does not qualify as intra‑continental emergence under the project rules. Wikipedia and a Western Hemisphere EID paper were replaced with region‑specific WHO and peer‑reviewed sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Pastoral cattle herds and wild bovids (notably African buffalo and antelopes) in the southern Sudan ecosystem and contiguous areas of Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia
Event.summary: From 1993 to the late 1990s, classic rinderpest persisted in the southern Sudan ecosystem and neighbouring pastoral areas of Uganda, Kenya and western Ethiopia, forming one of the last major African reservoirs of virulent lineage‑1 virus. Widespread outbreaks in cattle and associated wildlife occurred in southern Sudan and Karamoja (Uganda) in 1993–1995, with further activity in border districts of Kenya and Ethiopia, before intensive control efforts reduced incidence. The final laboratory‑confirmed outbreak in this ecosystem was recorded near Torit in what is now South Sudan in 1998, after which no further confirmed rinderpest occurred, paving the way for verification of eradication in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Protracted civil conflict in southern Sudan, insecurity in parts of Uganda and Kenya, and very limited state presence severely constrained veterinary services, vaccination coverage and disease reporting. Large, mobile pastoral herds moved across porous borders with little control, sustaining transmission in an ecological “southern Sudan axis” even as other African regions became free. Only with the introduction of community‑based animal health workers, targeted vaccination in high‑risk corridors and improved surveillance under PARC/PACE and GREP was this reservoir finally extinguished. Internal mechanisms: Virological data indicate circulation of established lineage‑1 rinderpest viruses rather than a novel strain; the episode is thus characterized as re-occurrence of classic rinderpest maintained by conflict and pastoral ecology rather than re-emergence driven by virus evolution.
Review: review – This major East African focus, often described as the “southern Sudan axis,” was missing from the original output despite being identified in GREP analyses as one of the last two African reservoirs of classic virulent rinderpest. A new row has been added summarizing widespread outbreaks in southern Sudan and contiguous parts of Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia during 1993–1998, culminating in the final confirmed outbreak near Torit. Country list and time ranges are approximate and should be cross‑checked against national datasets; emergence-type classification as re-occurrence is supported by lineage‑1 virology and the strong influence of conflict and service breakdown.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Poxvirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Pox viruses infection
Sub.regions: Eastern Europe; Central Asia; Western Asia
Host: Cattle; domestic water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis, limited)
Event.summary: From 2015 lumpy skin disease virus spread north and east from the Middle East and Türkiye into the Caucasus and the Russian Federation, with the first Russian outbreaks reported in 2015 and a major epidemic in 2016 that caused nearly two thousand recorded outbreaks and substantial cattle losses in southern regions. In 2016 LSDV was also confirmed in western Kazakhstan, marking the first occurrence of the disease in Central Asia, and in subsequent years the Russian epidemic front advanced along the border with Kazakhstan, with recurrent seasonal clusters through about 2020. Intensive vaccination campaigns using homologous and later recombinant vaccines, combined with movement controls and surveillance, progressively reduced outbreak numbers, though LSDV and recombinant vaccine-like strains have persisted locally in parts of Russia and neighbouring countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of cattle and vectors between endemic areas of Türkiye, the Caucasus and southern Russia; summer conditions favourable to blood-feeding insects; limited prior immunity in Russian and Kazakh cattle; delayed deployment and suboptimal coverage of homologous vaccines during early years; possible contribution of illegal or heterologous vaccines. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of LSDV into new subregions (Eastern Europe and Central Asia) accompanied by the emergence and maintenance of recombinant vaccine-like strains detected in Russia and Kazakhstan, consistent with re-emergence driven partly by viral genetic change.
Review: Review – New event added to capture the large and well-documented LSD epizootic in the Russian Federation and Kazakhstan (plus neighbouring Caucasus states), which is comparable in scale and impact to the Balkan and Asian LSD waves and should be among the top events for this EPP. Classified as intra-continental emergence (new subregions in Europe and Asia) and re-emergence (appearance and spread of recombinant vaccine-like strains); recommended for expert review of country list and exact end year.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Ipomoea imperati
EPP.common.name: beach morningglory, beach morning-glory
Countries: Italy – south‑western Sicily (Gorgo Cottone, Modione River mouth, Triscina) [2015-2020]
Host: Coastal sandy-beach and dune plant communities (embryonic and shifting dunes with Ammophiletea vegetation in Spain, Italy, Balearic Islands and Madeira)
Event.summary: From the early 2000s, Ipomoea imperati re-appeared and expanded within Southern Europe, first through rediscovery of a small but persistent Sicilian population at the mouth of the San Leonardo River and subsequent records along the Calabrian Tyrrhenian coast, following earlier extinction of mainland Italian populations.([biodiversityjournal.com](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2021/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04_899-903.pdf)) In parallel, Spanish botanists documented the species as an alien strandline plant along Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, with a 2005 note reporting it as a new adventive in Doñana National Park and a 2015 study describing incipient naturalized stands of 300–750 m² on Cádiz dunes at Barbate and Algeciras, already rated as high-risk invaders of Natura 2000 dune habitats.([biolveg.uma.es](https://www.biolveg.uma.es/abm/Volumenes/vol40/40_Garcia_de_Lomas_Ipomoea.pdf)) Over the 2010s–early 2020s, additional dense mats of 1,500–3,000 m² were recorded at Castilnovo and Los Lances (Tarifa) and the species was newly reported as part of the alien flora of the Balearic Islands, while three small but nearly monospecific dune populations were found along the south‑western Sicilian coast; by 2025, I. imperati remained localized but clearly expanding within selected Spanish and Italian dune systems and subject to active monitoring and control in some protected areas, with no indication that the invasion episode has yet ended.([biodiversityjournal.com](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2021/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04_899-903.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Repeated introductions and secondary spread along heavily used Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts via ornamental or landscaping plantings, beach restoration works, shipping and tourism-related activities have increased propagule pressure of Ipomoea imperati in Spain, Italy, Balearic Islands and Madeira, while intense disturbance and fragmentation of dune systems (walkways, parking areas, beach bars, residential development) create open sandy microsites that favor establishment and clonal expansion.([biolveg.uma.es](https://www.biolveg.uma.es/abm/Volumenes/vol40/40_Garcia_de_Lomas_Ipomoea.pdf)) External management responses (inclusion in national invasive-plant atlases, targeted removal in Doñana and other Andalusian sites) both reflect and influence the trajectory of this episode.([juntadeandalucia.es](https://www.juntadeandalucia.es/medioambiente/contenidoExterno/Pub_renpa/boletin69/parques/parques7.html?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – buoyant seeds, vegetative stolons and a deep, robust rhizome system enable long-distance hydrochorous dispersal along coasts and rapid local mat formation on embryonic and shifting dunes; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – tolerance of salt spray, burial and sand movement makes the species particularly well adapted to colonize disturbed dune fronts; Competitive exclusion of some native strandline and foredune species arises from its dense, nearly monospecific mats, which can smother other vegetation and stabilize sand in ways that alter natural dune dynamics.([biodiversityjournal.com](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2021/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04_899-903.pdf))
Review: REVIEW – Retain this event but with substantial corrections. (1) Changed the event type from intra-continental emergence + re-emergence to re-occurrence only, because Ipomoea imperati has long been present in the Southern Europe subregion (e.g. historical Italian and eastern Mediterranean records) and there is no evidence of a novel strain or host shift; the post‑2000 spread in Spain and reappearance in Italy represent renewed incidence within an already affected UNSD subregion, not movement into a new subregion or biological re-emergence.([biodiversityjournal.com](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2021/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04_899-903.pdf)) (2) Adjusted the time span from 2005–2021 to 2001–2025 to reflect the first modern Sicilian record (Turrisi 2001), earlier Spanish coastal records synthesized by Sanz Elorza et al. (2001, 2004), the 2005 Doñana adventive report, subsequent Cádiz xenophyte populations (2011–2015) and new Andalusian and Balearic localities documented up to 2023–2025.([biolveg.uma.es](https://www.biolveg.uma.es/abm/Volumenes/vol40/40_Garcia_de_Lomas_Ipomoea.pdf)) (3) Simplified and standardized the countries field, removing nested subnational descriptions that belong in the event summary and aligning country assignments with the UNSD Southern Europe list while still indicating key coastal areas and first-record years. (4) Pruned and updated event-level source URLs to prioritize primary floristic and invasion-ecology papers (Garcia-de-Lomas et al. 2015; Garcia-de-Lomas et al. 2024; Caldarella et al. 2021; Cennamo et al. 2013), Macaronesian and Balearic alien-flora notes, the Andalusian invasive-plant control portal, and POWO for range context, while de-emphasizing duplicate ResearchGate copies and general Wikipedia summaries.([biolveg.uma.es](https://www.biolveg.uma.es/abm/Volumenes/vol40/40_Garcia_de_Lomas_Ipomoea.pdf)) (5) Overall, this episode clearly qualifies as one of the main modern emergence events for this species but should be re-checked by a coastal weed specialist for completeness of country list and precise dating of earliest Spanish records.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Rodents and possibly lagomorphs contaminating surface water, domestic animals exposed to contaminated water, humans (primarily rural villagers)
Event.summary: Beginning in 2005, Türkiye experienced a marked resurgence of tularemia, with 431 human cases reported that year and multiple waterborne outbreaks in rural villages, after decades of sporadic or unreported disease activity. Epidemiologic investigations linked clusters of oropharyngeal tularemia to ingestion of untreated spring or creek water contaminated by rodents and other wildlife infected with Francisella tularensis, indicating active epizootic cycles in local small-mammal populations. Over subsequent years, improvements in surveillance, chlorination of village water supplies, and public education on water safety and rodent control led to a substantial decline in reported cases by 2008, though localized outbreaks and sporadic cases have continued, reflecting persistent wildlife reservoirs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Inadequate treatment of village water systems, use of unchlorinated springs and streams, and increased exposure of rural populations to contaminated surface water facilitated large waterborne outbreaks; land-use and climatic changes likely favoured rodent reservoirs. Internal mechanisms: The pattern is consistent with renewed amplification of existing F. tularensis subsp. holarctica lineages in Western Asia rather than documented emergence of a novel strain or host jump, so it primarily reflects re-occurrence driven by infrastructure and ecological conditions.
Review: review – event retained as a major re-emergence of tularemia in Türkiye, involving thousands of cases over several years, but emergence-type coding was adjusted. Because tularemia has been recognised in Turkey and the wider Western Asia region since the mid-20th century, the 2005–2010 wave does not qualify as intra-continental emergence; it is best treated as re-occurrence driven by water infrastructure and ecological factors. Sources already appropriately emphasise the epidemiology and scale of the resurgence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonellosis
Continent: Europe; North America; South America; Asia; Africa
Sub.regions: Europe: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; North America: Northern America; South America: South America; Asia: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Western Asia; Africa: Northern Africa; Eastern Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa
Host: Commercial layer hens and broilers (poultry); indirectly eggs as product
Event.summary: During the 1980s and 1990s, Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis emerged and then dominated as the leading Salmonella serovar in commercial poultry flocks, with major egg‑associated epidemics in North America and Europe by 1990 and rapid expansion into poultry production in South America, Asia and Africa during the 1990s. The epidemic was driven by infection of layer hen reproductive tissues, allowing transovarian contamination of intact shell eggs and widespread human disease linked to eggs and poultry meat. By the late 1990s, coordinated control programs, including surveillance in poultry breeding and layer flocks, culling of infected flocks and stringent egg refrigeration, reduced prevalence in some high‑income countries, although S. Enteritidis remained established in poultry industries worldwide.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Industrialization and global consolidation of poultry breeding, centralized sourcing of breeding stocks, poor on‑farm biosecurity in some regions, and large‑scale international trade in live poultry enabled inter‑continental dissemination of an epidemic S. Enteritidis lineage. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced ability of certain phage types/lineages to colonize ovaries and oviducts of laying hens and survive in egg contents facilitated vertical and food‑borne transmission; no single resistance determinant dominated this event, but adaptation to intensive poultry environments and high egg contamination potential underpinned re‑emergence.
Review: Review – Event correctly captures the late‑20th‑century global Salmonella Enteritidis epidemic in commercial poultry and eggs. The 1990–2000 window is acceptable as the main phase within the post‑1990 scope, but the event‑type classification has been clarified: the epidemic lineage is treated as a re‑emergent, egg‑adapted clone with major inter‑continental spread (inter_continental_emergence = Yes; re_emergence = Yes), while intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence are set to No to respect the classification scheme.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Coccidioides spp.
EPP.common.name: Coccidioides fungi
Countries: United States of America (Washington State ‚Äì Benton, Franklin, Yakima, and Spokane counties)
Host: Humans (local residents and outdoor workers)
Event.summary: Around 2010, Washington State identified its first suspected locally acquired human cases of coccidioidomycosis in residents with no travel to known endemic areas. Subsequent investigations between 2010 and 2015 detected multiple autochthonous cases in eastern Washington and confirmed Coccidioides immitis in soil samples at exposure sites, with whole‚Äëgenome sequencing linking environmental and clinical isolates. After these detections, Washington instituted enhanced surveillance, and reported case counts slowly increased, indicating persistent but relatively low‚Äëlevel endemic transmission in this newly recognized northern focus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Possible climate warming and altered precipitation patterns enabling survival of Coccidioides further north; land disturbance from construction, agriculture, and recreational vehicle use in arid canyons; and increased clinical awareness once initial cases were recognized. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of Coccidioides immitis beyond its historic range in the southwestern United States; genomic analyses show Washington isolates nested within Californian lineages, consistent with relatively recent colonization rather than a long‚Äëstanding cryptic focus, but without evidence of a distinctive, more virulent clone.
Review: review ‚Äì This row appropriately captures the first recognized autochthonous human infections and environmental isolations of Coccidioides in Washington State, a key northward range expansion, and justifies classification as intra-continental emergence. Re_emergence has been set to false, since this represents colonization of a new area within Northern America rather than reappearance in a previously affected subregion due to pathogen change; a Washington State Department of Health guideline has also been added as a primary source for timing and case counts.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida albicans
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Humans (primarily people with advanced HIV infection receiving chronic fluconazole for recurrent oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis)
Event.summary: In the early 1990s in the United States, clinicians began to report failure of fluconazole therapy for recurrent oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis in people with advanced HIV infection, linked to fluconazole‚Äëresistant Candida albicans isolates with markedly elevated MICs.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7814530/?utm_source=openai)) Prolonged, repeated azole use in large HIV‚Äëpositive cohorts selected for resistant C. albicans strains, which then became an important cause of refractory mucosal and occasionally invasive disease in major urban HIV treatment centers. As combination antiretroviral therapy and more judicious azole use were adopted in the mid‚Äëto‚Äëlate 1990s, the incidence of highly resistant C. albicans in HIV clinics stabilized or declined but remained a clinically significant problem in heavily pre‚Äëtreated patients.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread, long‚Äëterm fluconazole use for therapy and prophylaxis of recurrent mucosal candidiasis in people with AIDS; very high burden of immunosuppression and frequent healthcare exposure before effective ART. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance via stepwise azole resistance mechanisms (ERG11 target‚Äësite mutations, efflux pump overexpression, loss of heterozygosity at ERG11), with clonal expansion of resistant lineages in some patients or centers; possible selection for strains with enhanced persistence at mucosal surfaces under drug pressure.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7814530/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain ‚Äì Appropriately captures an early 1990s emergence of fluconazole‚Äëresistant C. albicans in U.S. HIV populations, a major drug‚Äëresistance milestone with substantial clinical impact. Classification as re‚Äëemergence (pathogen change via azole resistance) and geography (United States, Northern America) are consistent with source literature; no structural changes beyond added citations are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida albicans
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients with invasive candidiasis treated with the echinocandin caspofungin)
Event.summary: After caspofungin was approved in 2001, echinocandins were rapidly adopted in the United States as first‚Äëline or salvage therapy for invasive candidiasis, including infections due to C. albicans.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.01653-05?utm_source=openai)) Between roughly 2001 and 2006, scattered clinical and laboratory reports documented the first C. albicans isolates with markedly reduced susceptibility to caspofungin, carrying FKS1 hot‚Äëspot mutations and sometimes associated with treatment failure in animal models or patients. Following these early cases, echinocandin‚Äëresistant C. albicans remained rare but became an established resistance phenotype, prompting routine susceptibility testing and development of molecular assays targeting FKS hot‚Äëspot mutations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and increasing use of echinocandins (particularly caspofungin) for empiric and targeted therapy of invasive candidiasis in high‚Äërisk inpatients. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance through novel FKS1 hot‚Äëspot mutations in the 1,3‚ÄëŒ≤‚ÄëD‚Äëglucan synthase complex, leading to elevated echinocandin MICs and reduced drug activity; early clonal expansion of mutant lineages within some hospital environments.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.01653-05?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain ‚Äì Represents the initial emergence of FKS1‚Äëmediated echinocandin resistance in C. albicans following caspofungin introduction in the U.S., a key mechanistic and clinical turning point. Classification as re‚Äëemergence (new resistance phenotype in an existing pathogen) with no intra‚Äë or inter‚Äëcontinental component is appropriate; existing sources are relevant and sufficient.

EPP.scientific.name: Nakaseomyces glabratus
EPP.common.name: Candida glabrata
Host: Humans (adults with candidemia identified through population-based surveillance in metropolitan Atlanta, Georgia, and Baltimore, Maryland, and in other North American hospital registries)
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through the early 2000s, U.S. population-based surveillance in metropolitan areas such as Atlanta and Baltimore showed a 10‚Äì40% increase in candidemia incidence together with a species shift toward non‚Äëalbicans Candida, particularly Candida glabrata. Around 2000‚Äì2005, C. glabrata accounted for roughly one quarter to one third of adult candidemia cases in many North American centers, and azole-resistant isolates became more common, establishing a high baseline burden of C. glabrata disease before echinocandins came into widespread first-line use.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased survival of patients with cancer, transplants, complex abdominal surgery, and other immunosuppressive conditions; extensive use of broad-spectrum antibacterials; central venous catheterization; and prolonged fluconazole prophylaxis all favoured non‚Äëalbicans species over C. albicans. Internal mechanisms: C. glabrata‚Äôs intrinsically reduced fluconazole susceptibility, together with the capacity to acquire azole-resistance mechanisms (e.g. PDR1 gain-of-function and efflux pump upregulation), enabled the species to expand under azole pressure; this episode is classified as re‚Äëemergence because it reflects both external drivers and the increasing contribution of azole‚Äëresistant C. glabrata to the candidemia burden.
Review: review ‚Äì Retain this episode as an early‚Äë2000s North American emergence of C. glabrata as a leading cause of candidemia and rising azole resistance; keep the re-emergence classification but clarify in the text that it reflects both external drivers and increasing azole resistance. Updated the Source URLs to emphasize the 1998‚Äì2000 U.S. population-based candidemia study, the MD Anderson hematogenous candidiasis paper, the MMWR surveillance summary, and a focused C. glabrata resistance review, and removed a generic Wikipedia link.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Nakaseomyces glabratus
EPP.common.name: Candida glabrata
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with invasive candidiasis in Madrid hospitals from which sequential Candida glabrata isolates were analyzed)
Event.summary: In the early to mid‚Äë2010s, Spanish tertiary hospitals in Madrid reported sequential Candida glabrata isolates from individual patients that evolved from echinocandin-susceptible to echinocandin-resistant during therapy, with detailed molecular characterization of FKS2 mutations and resistance phenotypes. These clinical series documented in-host development of echinocandin resistance associated with clinical and microbiological failure in invasive candidiasis due to C. glabrata and highlighted the emergence of echinocandin-resistant C. glabrata in Spain.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy use of echinocandins as first-line therapy for invasive candidiasis in haematology/oncology and intensive care patients who often had prior azole exposure, limited alternative antifungal options, and frequent need for prolonged treatment of complex intra‚Äëabdominal and bloodstream infections. Internal mechanisms: In-host selection of C. glabrata clones carrying FKS2 hot‚Äëspot mutations (such as D666H and related substitutions) that raised minimum inhibitory concentrations to anidulafungin and micafungin, sometimes combined with azole resistance, exemplifying re‚Äëemergence driven by treatment-associated antifungal resistance.
Review: review ‚Äì Retain this as a representative Southern European example of in-host echinocandin resistance emergence in Spain, but correct the event years from 2010‚Äì2017 to 2012‚Äì2017 to reflect the reported collection period for sequential and susceptible isolates. The geography and re-emergence classification remain appropriate, and the Source URLs are focused on the Spanish molecular characterization study and complementary echinocandin-resistance case reports and reviews.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Brucella spp.
EPP.common.name: brucellosis
