Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of the Chinese poultry industry, high flock densities, and frequent co‑infections with other respiratory pathogens (e.g. avian influenza, Newcastle disease virus, infectious bronchitis virus) created favourable conditions for repeated ILT outbreaks and wide geographic spread of existing viruses.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7241549/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Most outbreak isolates were low‑virulence or vaccine‑related ILTV strains with limited genetic divergence; there is no indication of a single novel recombinant dominating nationwide, so this period is best interpreted as multi‑province re‑occurrence of previously established lineages rather than intra‑continental emergence into a new subregion.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: Event is retained as a representative multi‑province ILT episode in China, but the original classification as intra‑continental emergence has been corrected to re-occurrence, because ILT has been present in China and Eastern Asia for decades and the 2010–2014 isolates mainly reflect endemic circulation of field and vaccine‑related strains.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1040638715618230?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Iltovirus gallid2
EPP.common.name: Gallid alphaherpesvirus 1, ILT virus
Countries: Türkiye [2014-2018] (Konya and other commercial poultry regions; commercial layers, broilers and some backyard flocks)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial layers and broilers; backyard flocks in some studies)
Event.summary: In the mid‑ to late 2010s, Türkiye documented multiple ILT outbreaks and high seroprevalence in commercial layer flocks, particularly in the Konya region where ELISA surveys found ILTV antibodies in over 40% of sampled birds and 64% of sampled farms.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29424631/?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent investigations detected ILTV DNA in broiler and layer flocks with respiratory disease in several Turkish provinces, and nationwide surveys reported PCR‑positive ILTV in about 14% of 119 flocks examined, indicating widespread endemic infection in the country’s commercial poultry.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40101513/?utm_source=openai)) Control responses have focused on improved surveillance, strain characterization and targeted vaccination, with ILT now recognised as an economically significant contributor to respiratory disease in Turkish poultry.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of the Turkish poultry industry, high stocking densities, incomplete biosecurity, and possible spillover between commercial and backyard flocks facilitated the spread and entrenchment of ILTV in previously under‑recognised areas.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11960647/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Sequencing of Turkish ILTVs has revealed genetic diversity in gB, gG and ICP4 genes but does not yet point to a single dominant vaccine‑derived recombinant; available data are most consistent with geographic expansion and increased detection of existing and imported genotypes rather than major novel‑strain emergence.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: Türkiye has reported ILT since at least 2003, and 2014–2018 episodes represent expansion and intensification within an already affected Western Asian country rather than first introduction to a new subregion.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17449712/?utm_source=openai)) The intra‑continental emergence flag has therefore been set to "No" and the event reclassified as re-occurrence, while retaining it as one of the larger recent ILT episodes in Western Asia.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Poxvirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Pox viruses infection
Countries: Greece [1994-1998] (Evros prefecture near the border with Türkiye)
Host: Sheep (Ovis aries)
Event.summary: Between 1994 and 1998 a protracted epidemic of sheep pox caused by capripoxvirus affected the Evros prefecture in northern Greece, with repeated seasonal waves in local sheep flocks near the Turkish border. The epidemic caused major economic losses from mortality, culling, movement bans and trade restrictions on small ruminants and their products. Intensive stamping-out, movement control, and biosecurity improvements gradually interrupted local transmission by the late 1990s, although sheep pox remained a regional threat in neighbouring countries and sporadically reappeared in Greece in later years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of susceptible sheep flocks with limited prior immunity; cross-border movements of animals and products from endemic areas in neighbouring countries; environmental conditions favouring mechanical vector transmission and farm-to-farm spread; limited early vaccination coverage. Internal mechanisms: This episode is best characterised as a re-occurrence of an established capripoxvirus in a known region, driven by external factors rather than clear viral change; no specific novel strain has been consistently implicated.
Review: Retain – Well-documented multi-year sheep pox epidemic in Evros, Greece with large numbers of affected flocks and substantial economic impact; timing, geography and classification as re-occurrence within Southern Europe are consistent with primary sources. No structural changes made.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonellosis
Continent: Europe; North America; South America; Asia; Africa
Sub.regions: Europe: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; North America: Northern America; South America: South America; Asia: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Western Asia; Africa: Northern Africa; Eastern Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa
Host: Commercial layer hens and broilers (poultry); indirectly eggs as product
Event.summary: During the 1980s and 1990s, Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis emerged and then dominated as the leading Salmonella serovar in commercial poultry flocks, with major egg‑associated epidemics in North America and Europe by 1990 and rapid expansion into poultry production in South America, Asia and Africa during the 1990s. The epidemic was driven by infection of layer hen reproductive tissues, allowing transovarian contamination of intact shell eggs and widespread human disease linked to eggs and poultry meat. By the late 1990s, coordinated control programs, including surveillance in poultry breeding and layer flocks, culling of infected flocks and stringent egg refrigeration, reduced prevalence in some high‑income countries, although S. Enteritidis remained established in poultry industries worldwide.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Industrialization and global consolidation of poultry breeding, centralized sourcing of breeding stocks, poor on‑farm biosecurity in some regions, and large‑scale international trade in live poultry enabled inter‑continental dissemination of an epidemic S. Enteritidis lineage. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced ability of certain phage types/lineages to colonize ovaries and oviducts of laying hens and survive in egg contents facilitated vertical and food‑borne transmission; no single resistance determinant dominated this event, but adaptation to intensive poultry environments and high egg contamination potential underpinned re‑emergence.
Review: Review – Event correctly captures the late‑20th‑century global Salmonella Enteritidis epidemic in commercial poultry and eggs. The 1990–2000 window is acceptable as the main phase within the post‑1990 scope, but the event‑type classification has been clarified: the epidemic lineage is treated as a re‑emergent, egg‑adapted clone with major inter‑continental spread (inter_continental_emergence = Yes; re_emergence = Yes), while intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence are set to No to respect the classification scheme.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia trachomatis
EPP.common.name: Chlamydia
Sub.regions: Europe | Northern Europe; Europe | Western Europe
Host: Humans – sexually active adolescents and adults with genital chlamydia infections detected in routine screening and diagnostic programmes.
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, Sweden observed unexpected declines in reported Chlamydia trachomatis cases in some counties despite stable or rising test volumes, prompting investigation into potential diagnostic problems. In 2006, investigators discovered a new C. trachomatis variant (nvCT) with a 377‑bp deletion in the cryptic plasmid that removed the single NAAT target sequence used by Abbott m2000 and Roche Amplicor/TaqMan assays, allowing the strain to spread largely undetected for several years and to reach high prevalence in counties using these tests, while remaining detectable in counties and countries using alternative assays. After recognition of nvCT, Sweden and a few other European countries where sporadic nvCT cases were identified rapidly updated NAATs to include additional targets, undertook recall testing and partner notification, and by the late 2000s the proportion of nvCT among all chlamydia diagnoses in Sweden declined substantially as the diagnostic escape advantage was removed, with only limited transmission documented in Norway, Denmark, Ireland and France.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The emergence was facilitated by widespread use of single‑target nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) in routine chlamydia screening, creating strong diagnostic selection pressure in regions relying on Abbott and Roche assays that failed to detect the new variant; high screening coverage and sexual network connectivity in Sweden further supported rapid dissemination. Internal mechanisms: The nvCT strain carried a 377‑bp deletion in the plasmid region targeted by these NAATs, representing Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence with Diagnostic Escape, leading to apparent drops in case notifications and substantial under‑diagnosis until multi‑target assays and specific nvCT tests were introduced, after which its fitness advantage waned and its prevalence began to fall.
Review: Decision: review. The Swedish nvCT diagnostic‑escape episode is correctly included as a major re‑emergence event driven by a novel plasmid deletion variant and by NAAT testing practices, and classification as re_emergence (with all other emergence‑type flags set to false) is appropriate. However, the original row overstated the geographic extent and timing of nvCT spread outside Sweden by listing the United Kingdom and unspecified “other European countries” and by implying broader circulation. Based on national investigations and a Europe‑wide survey, there is strong evidence that nvCT transmission remained largely confined to Sweden, with only small numbers of confirmed cases in Norway, Denmark, Ireland and France, and no confirmed circulation in the UK. I therefore (i) removed the United Kingdom and the vague “other European countries with sporadic detections” from the country list; (ii) restricted countries to Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Ireland and France with starting years aligned to documented detections (Sweden 2002–2006 period of undetected spread; other countries 2007); and (iii) removed “Europe | Southern Europe” from sub_regions, as no Southern European country with nvCT circulation is well‑documented. Event years (2002–2009), host description and mechanism/driver text remain valid. Given these corrections, the event should be retained but flagged for expert review of the exact end year and any very small additional national clusters that do not substantially change its impact ranking.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyclospora cayetanensis
EPP.common.name: cyclosporiasis
Host: Humans (adults and children consuming fresh imported berries at social events, restaurants and via retail)
Event.summary: From spring through summer 1996, a very large multinational outbreak of cyclosporiasis occurred in North America, with approximately 1,465 outbreak-associated cases reported from 20 U.S. states, the District of Columbia, and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Québec; epidemiologic investigations in both countries consistently implicated fresh raspberries imported from Guatemala as the vehicle of infection. Similar but somewhat smaller raspberry‑linked outbreaks recurred in 1997 and again in 1998, including a 192‑case, 13‑cluster event in Ontario, Canada, and further clusters in the United States, and in 2000 a 54‑case outbreak in Philadelphia and other clusters were again traced to Guatemalan raspberries or blackberries. This multi‑year episode ended only after Guatemalan growers, the Guatemalan Berry Commission, and U.S. and Canadian regulators suspended spring raspberry exports, implemented a stringent Model Plan of Excellence with improved water quality, hygiene and field sanitation, and restricted exports to vetted farms, after which raspberry‑associated Cyclospora outbreaks in North America ceased.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of international trade in high‑value fresh berries from Cyclospora‑endemic Guatemala to North American markets; use of inadequately treated irrigation and wash water and poor sanitary infrastructure on some exporting farms; fragile raspberries with complex surface morphology that are difficult to wash effectively; and initially low awareness of Cyclospora among clinicians and laboratories in the United States and Canada, which delayed case recognition. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel strains or increased virulence during this episode; emergence was driven by repeated contamination of produce in endemic areas and its distribution into a naïve, high‑consumption market. Mechanism categories: Enhanced transmission via contaminated fresh berries entering new consumer markets and geographic range expansion of exposure (but not necessarily of long‑term parasite establishment) into Northern America.
Review: retain: This row correctly captures the large 1996–2000 North American epidemic linked mainly to Guatemalan raspberries, but the emergence type was misclassified. North American outbreaks were already recognized in 1990 and 1995, so this episode is not the first inter-continental occurrence on the continent. I reclassified it as re_occurrence, removed Peru from the country list (no strong evidence it was a major produce source in this specific episode), narrowed sub_regions to Northern America and Central America, and clarified that multiple years and clusters are grouped because they share a common Guatemala–North America raspberry supply chain. Event should be retained as one of the highest-impact global episodes for this parasite.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterococcus faecium
EPP.common.name: Enterococcus faecium infection
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia
Host: Humans (hospital inpatients; ICU, hematology/oncology, and surgical wards)
Event.summary: Between the late 1990s and mid‑2000s, Asia saw its first documented cases and outbreaks of vancomycin‑resistant E. faecium, beginning with high‑level vancomycin‑resistant strains in Japan and then spreading to Korea, Taiwan and mainland China. By 1998–2004, tertiary hospitals in Korea reported nearly 100 VREfm isolates, mostly belonging to epidemic clonal groups, and from 2001 to 2005 hospitals in several Chinese cities isolated VanA‑type VREfm, indicating wider establishment. During this period, localized ICU and ward outbreaks were increasingly recognized, including major events in Singapore, prompting hospitals to introduce targeted screening and infection‑control interventions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: growth of large tertiary hospitals, intensive antibiotic use (including glycopeptides) in ICUs and oncology units, and regional patient referral networks facilitated establishment and spread of VREfm in previously largely VRE‑free health systems. Internal mechanisms: importation and expansion of hospital‑adapted VREfm clonal complexes (e.g. CC17/related groups) carrying vanA/vanB genes, with further diversification in Asian hospitals, reflecting both clonal spread and within‑hospital evolution under antibiotic selection (Inter‑continental emergence; Re‑emergence; Antimicrobial Resistance; Enhanced Transmission; Geographic Range Expansion – inherent).
Review: review – Retain as a key event capturing the first documented VREfm cases and subsequent spread across Asian sub‑regions (Japan, Republic of Korea, mainland China, Taiwan, Singapore). To respect the mostly mutually exclusive event‑type scheme, intra‑continental emergence was set to No and inter‑continental emergence kept as Yes, reflecting the first sustained establishment of VREfm in Asia; re‑emergence remains Yes. Country list and timing are broadly correct, though the exact naming for Taiwan may need alignment with the Country sheet.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Treponema pallidum
EPP.common.name: Syphilis
Sub.regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Eastern Asia
Countries: United States of America (San Francisco, Los Angeles, Seattle, Baltimore) [1998–2002]
Host: Humans with syphilis receiving macrolide therapy (primarily MSM and other sexually active adults)
Event.summary: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, clinically significant macrolide-resistant Treponema pallidum was identified, with azithromycin treatment failures linked to A2058G mutations in the 23S rRNA gene first reported in patients in San Francisco and then elsewhere in North America and Europe. During the 2000s, surveillance documented rapidly increasing proportions of macrolide-resistant strains in U.S. and Canadian cities and in several European and Chinese settings, making macrolide monotherapy unreliable for syphilis treatment. By around 2010, macrolide-resistant T. pallidum had become prevalent on multiple continents, and international guidelines moved away from macrolides toward penicillin-based regimens except in narrowly defined circumstances.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread, often empiric use of azithromycin and other macrolides for STI and respiratory infections, including off-guideline use of single‑dose azithromycin as a convenient alternative to injectable benzathine penicillin for syphilis in some settings; overlapping high‑transmission sexual networks in MSM facilitated dissemination of resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and clonal spread of point mutations (A2058G and later A2059G) in the 23S rRNA gene of T. pallidum conferred high-level macrolide resistance, a clear example of antimicrobial resistance–driven re-emergence.
Review: review – Retain as a key global re-emergence event driven by antimicrobial resistance, but the type-of-emergence coding has been aligned with the project rules: intra_continental_emergence and inter_continental_emergence have been set to false, because the species was long present on all affected continents and this episode reflects the emergence and spread of resistant lineages (re-emergence) rather than first occurrence in new regions. Country list has been slightly expanded to name major documented sites (e.g. Seattle, Baltimore) while still summarising other affected European locations in aggregate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ehrlichia sp.
EPP.common.name: ehrlichiosis
Host: Humans (patients with undifferentiated febrile illness, some HIV-infected), domestic dogs and ticks as implicated reservoirs/vectors
Event.summary: In the 1990s and early 2000s, isolated case reports from Mali and serologic surveys from several African countries suggested that human ehrlichial infections might be occurring but lacked definitive molecular confirmation. Between approximately 2004 and 2008, investigators in Cameroon conducted a systematic study of patients with undifferentiated febrile illness and detected Ehrlichia chaffeensis–specific DNA in a subset of blood samples, providing the first clear molecular and clinical evidence of human monocytic ehrlichiosis in sub‑Saharan Africa. These findings, together with prior serologic evidence and detection of E. chaffeensis and E. canis in local dogs and Rhipicephalus sanguineus ticks, showed that human‑pathogenic Ehrlichia spp. are present and occasionally cause disease in African settings with high tick and HIV burdens, although diagnosed case numbers remain low and likely under-represent the true burden.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close human contact with dogs and livestock, abundant tick vectors (including Rhipicephalus sanguineus), and high prevalence of HIV infection in some sub‑Saharan settings increase both exposure to Ehrlichia spp. and susceptibility to severe disease; historically limited diagnostic capacity meant that ehrlichial infections were often misclassified among undifferentiated fevers. Internal mechanisms: The E. chaffeensis/E. canis lineages detected in African patients, dogs and ticks appear similar to those found elsewhere, suggesting long‑standing but previously unrecognized endemicity or historical inter‑continental spread rather than recent de novo evolution; this event is best interpreted as inter‑continental emergence in terms of human recognition and first confirmed autochthonous cases.
Review: Decision: review. This event appropriately represents the first molecularly confirmed human E. chaffeensis infections in Africa (Cameroon) against a background of earlier serologic hints from Mali and other countries, and qualifies as the inter-continental emergence of clinically recognized HME in Africa. I turned off the first_detection flag so that the row now cleanly encodes inter_continental_emergence, and I removed a duplicate PDF URL for the Frontiers review while retaining the main HTML article plus the earlier serosurveys as supporting context. The balance between treating the imported Mali case and the Cameroonian series as part of the same emergence episode versus separate events could be reconsidered, but the current aggregation is defensible.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Caprine arthritis encephalitis virus
EPP.common.name: CAEV, Small ruminant lentivirus
Host: Domestic goats (dairy and meat) in semi-arid smallholder and breeder herds
Event.summary: Between the mid‑2000s and around 2010, several epidemiological and serological studies in Northeast Brazil documented CAEV as an important emerging infection in goat herds, starting with surveys in the Cariri region of Paraíba state that found notable seroprevalence across 60 herds, followed by broader studies of breeder goats in seven Northeastern states. These investigations showed that CAEV was present in multiple states with herd-level seroprevalence associated with more technified/intensive production, buck use, and inter‑herd animal movement, implying that the virus had spread widely through regional trade and breeding networks. Recognition of CAEV as endemic in major goat‑producing areas of Northeast Brazil led to calls for control programmes focused on testing, culling or segregating positives, and adjusting breeding practices, but full eradication has not been implemented and subsequent work continues to find CAEV in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of goat production in the semi‑arid Northeast, movement of breeding animals among states, shared use of bucks, and limited historical testing all facilitated regional dissemination; semi‑intensive and intensive management systems were associated with higher seroprevalence. Internal mechanisms: Circulating SRLV strains in Northeastern Brazil were phylogenetically related to CAEV‑type lentiviruses; no uniquely more virulent variant was reported, and the main internal factor was the virus’ capacity for persistent infection and efficient transmission in dense herds.
Review: retain – this episode aggregates the earliest large-scale serosurveys in the Cariri region of Paraíba and subsequent multi‑state breeder surveys in Northeast Brazil, which together represent one of the most substantial documented CAEV emergence/re-occurrence events in South America in terms of herd numbers and regional spread. Geographic scope, timing and host description are consistent with the cited Brazilian studies; no major corrections to dates, regions or emergence-type classification (re_occurrence in an already affected continent) are needed. Event is appropriately counted among the top global CAEV emergence episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus
EPP.common.name: FP-associated herpesvirus, CFPHV
Host: Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas); additional ChHV5 infections documented in hawksbill (Eretmochelys imbricata) and olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea) turtles at Mabul Island
Event.summary: In the 1990s, a large abattoir‑based survey of 4,407 green turtles landed in Indonesia documented FP in 21.5% of individuals, with affected turtles bearing multiple tumors but generally remaining in fair to good body condition, revealing a substantial, previously under‑recognized disease burden in Southeast Asian foraging stocks. Subsequent work in Asia confirmed clinically apparent FP and active ChHV5 infection in endangered green turtles from Taiwan and, by 2015–2019, in green, hawksbill and olive ridley turtles foraging around Mabul Island, Sabah, where FP tumors were present but relatively rare while ChHV5 DNA prevalence in clinically healthy turtles rose from ~8% to over 40%. Collectively, these findings show that FP and ChHV5 have become established across multiple Asian foraging areas, with moderate but regionally important tumor prevalence and evidence of multi‑species infection.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Indonesian and Malaysian study areas include heavily fished, nearshore foraging grounds subject to varying degrees of coastal development and pollution, yet FP has also been reported in relatively clear waters, suggesting that eutrophication and water quality may modulate, but do not solely determine, disease expression. Internal mechanisms: The Indonesian abattoir survey and later Asian virological work demonstrate that CFPHV/ChHV5 is endemic in regional green turtle populations and capable of infecting multiple turtle species; phylogenetic analyses show Asian ChHV5 sequences clustering with strains from Hawaii, Brazil and the Atlantic, consistent with long‑distance dispersal via turtle migrations rather than a unique Asian lineage. The 1997–2019 Asia event is therefore interpreted as a re‑occurrence and broad recognition of an existing global virus in Asian foraging grounds rather than a true first emergence.
Review: retain – A substantial 1990s Indonesian survey (21.5% FP prevalence in 4,407 green turtles) together with more recent ChHV5‑FP reports from Taiwan and Mabul Island demonstrates a major, long‑lasting Asian FP presence that is missing from the original dataset and should be among the top 10 events by impact. This new event row has been added, coded as a re‑occurrence in Asia (true first Asian FP observations date back to the 1950s in Malaysia) rather than as inter‑continental emergence. Years span 1997–2019 to capture both the Indonesian survey and later Taiwan/Mabul work; country list and sub‑regions follow UNSD conventions. Flagged for review to refine exact start/end years if more detailed temporal data are compiled.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Classical swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: Hog cholera virus, CSFV
Host: Domestic pigs (backyard and commercial herds)
Event.summary: After roughly two decades without recognised cases, Cuba reported re‑emergence of classical swine fever in 1993, with virus introduction into commercial and backyard pigs leading to an epizootic that became endemic and generated several hundred recorded outbreaks nationwide between 1993 and 1997. From this focus, CSF spread to neighboring Haiti in 1996 and to the Dominican Republic in 1997, where more than two hundred outbreaks were reported in 1998, causing high mortality in smallholder herds and prompting regional trade restrictions and concern about spread toward the mainland Americas. Control relied on intensive vaccination, stamping‑out in affected foci, and movement controls, which progressively reduced outbreak numbers but did not fully eliminate CSF, leaving the virus endemic in parts of the Caribbean.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Regional trade in live pigs and pork between Cuba and Hispaniola; insufficient and inconsistently applied vaccination and biosecurity in backyard and smallholder systems; informal movement of animals and pork and feeding of uncooked swill; limited veterinary infrastructure in some affected areas. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of CSFV genotypes within Caribbean pig populations, followed by local diversification and adaptation to backyard production and marketing networks, facilitating long-term persistence and repeated seeding of new foci.
Internal mechanisms coded: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (regional establishment and diversification of new genotypes); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through adaptation to dense informal trade and backyard systems.
Review: retain – new event added to capture the 1993–1998 Caribbean epizootic centred on Cuba with subsequent spread to Haiti and the Dominican Republic, which together generated hundreds of outbreaks and substantial pig losses and clearly rank among the most impactful post‑1990 CSF episodes. Countries, timing and epidemiological linkage are based on OIE/USDA documentation and Cuban molecular‑epidemiology studies; classified as re-emergence in an already affected subregion rather than as intra-continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Sub.regions: Northern Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) in commercial and backyard systems; occasional wild/feral rabbits
Event.summary: In February 2015, RHDV2 was first reported in Africa during severe outbreaks in commercial rabbit farms in Kairouan, Tunisia, where it caused high mortality and major economic losses, and molecular data showed multiple introductions of GI.2-like strains from Europe. Over the next several years genetically related viruses were detected in North African countries including Morocco, Algeria and Egypt, and by 2015–2020 RHDV2 had appeared in multiple West African nations such as Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria and Senegal, where large outbreaks—most notably the 2019 epidemic in Ghana and the 2020 wave in Nigeria—devastated rapidly growing rabbit industries. By 2022, RHDV2 had also been confirmed in South Africa, with outbreaks in wild and domestic lagomorphs, indicating that the new genotype had become established across several African subregions with recurrent, often high-mortality production losses rather than remaining a series of isolated incursions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: importation of live rabbits and rabbit genetic stock from Europe and Asia, movement of rabbit meat and byproducts into coastal West African port cities, rapid expansion of semi-intensive rabbit production as a protein source, and limited biosecurity in smallholder and peri-urban farms facilitated introduction and onward spread. Internal mechanisms: introduction and onward dissemination of the globally successful GI.2 genotype with high transmissibility, broader age susceptibility, and partial vaccine escape relative to earlier GI.1-based vaccines, together with largely naïve African rabbit populations, underpinned severe production losses. Mechanisms include novel genotype-driven geographic range expansion, enhanced transmission, and, in some countries, further diversification via recombination documented in African RHDV2 genomes.
Review: review – Updated the time span from 2015–2019 to 2015–2022 and corrected several country-specific first-detection windows (e.g. Nigeria from 2017–2019 to 2020–2021, Senegal to 2020, South Africa to 2022, Algeria to 2018–2021, Tunisia to 2015–2018) in line with WOAH and recent outbreak reports. Re-coded the episode as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by the GI.2 genotype in an already RHD-affected continent, removing previous inter- and intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence flags to comply with the event-type definitions; the event should be retained but remains flagged for expert review of exact country-year ranges.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Continent: North America; South America (Central America and Caribbean)
Host: Domestic European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) in pet, backyard and commercial settings; multiple native North American lagomorphs including black-tailed jackrabbit (Lepus californicus), cottontail rabbits (Sylvilagus spp.), and endangered riparian brush rabbit (Sylvilagus bachmani riparius)
Event.summary: RHDV2 was first detected in the Americas in 2016 during an outbreak among feral rabbits in Mont-Joli, Québec, Canada, which was rapidly contained, followed by a genetically distinct 2018 outbreak centred on feral and domestic rabbits in British Columbia. In March 2020, after earlier detections in Cuba (2019) and isolated U.S. pet rabbit cases in 2018–2019, a large, sustained epizootic began in New Mexico and spread across domestic and wild rabbits and hares in the southwestern United States, northern Mexico and later additional U.S. states, causing hundreds of reported outbreaks and substantial mortality in jackrabbits, cottontails and endangered riparian brush rabbits. By 2022, RHDV2 was established across a broad swath of western North America and parts of the Americas, triggering emergency vaccination campaigns, movement restrictions and long-term surveillance before incidence began to decline somewhat with increased awareness and vaccine uptake.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement of infected domestic rabbits and possibly contaminated fomites between Canada, the United States, Mexico and the Caribbean; limited early access to RHDV2 vaccines in North America; and dense populations of susceptible wild lagomorphs in arid southwestern landscapes all facilitated widespread transmission once the virus arrived. Internal mechanisms: the broad host range of RHDV2 across lagomorph species, high environmental stability and contagiousness, and partial immune escape from prior GI.1-based immunity enabled rapid multi-species spillover and establishment in novel native hosts, leading to severe mortality in jackrabbits, cottontails and endangered brush rabbits. Mechanisms include host expansion (spillover), enhanced transmission, and geographic range expansion, with re-emergence in continents that had previously experienced only sporadic or eradicated RHD incursions.
Review: review – Harmonised event-type coding so this North America–Central America–Caribbean episode is treated solely as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by the GI.2 genotype and host expansion, removing previous inter- and intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence flags. Adjusted country-year annotations to distinguish early, self-limited Canadian incursions (Québec 2016, British Columbia 2018–2019) from the large 2019–2022 epizootic affecting the southwestern United States, Mexico (from 2020) and Cuba (2019). This row intentionally aggregates several genetically and spatially linked outbreaks for parsimony; a human reviewer may consider splitting early Canadian incursions into a separate, lower-impact event if finer temporal resolution is required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Cattle and other domestic bovines (with some involvement of small ruminants and camels in parts of the Arabian Peninsula)
Event.summary: In the early to mid‑1990s, rinderpest caused a series of outbreaks on the Arabian Peninsula following introduction from endemic foci to the north. Oman reported a large epidemic in 1992 with well over 100 outbreaks, and rinderpest continued to be detected there until the mid‑1990s. Related incursions affected cattle in Saudi Arabia, and rinderpest remained present in hill cattle in Yemen until at least 1995 despite annual vaccination campaigns, with additional outbreaks reported in the United Arab Emirates in the mid‑1990s. Coordinated regional efforts under the West Asian Rinderpest Eradication Campaign (WAREC) and GREP, including intensified vaccination, movement control and improved surveillance, progressively eliminated these foci, so that by the late 1990s rinderpest was believed to persist only in Yemen.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing trade and movement of live cattle and other livestock from endemic areas in South and West Asia into Gulf states, combined with incomplete routine vaccination and weaknesses in border control, allowed repeated re-introduction of rinderpest. The early 1990s regional instability following the Gulf War likely exacerbated gaps in veterinary services. In Yemen, difficult terrain and dispersed hill cattle systems impeded high vaccine coverage, favouring endemic persistence until targeted campaigns closed remaining immunity gaps. Internal mechanisms: There is no indication that these outbreaks were driven by a novel strain or altered virulence; they are best interpreted as re-occurrence of known Asiatic lineages in a high‑risk trade hub.
Review: review – This multi‑country Arabian Peninsula focus, including a large epidemic in Oman and persistent endemic infection in Yemen with additional outbreaks in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, was absent from the original dataset but is clearly highlighted in FAO/OIE sources as one of the remaining rinderpest reservoirs in the mid‑1990s. A new row has been added with approximate year ranges and country‑specific last-report dates based primarily on regional summaries and OIE workshop data. Because detailed national outbreak timelines are heterogeneous and not always fully accessible, this event is flagged for human review to confirm the per‑country start years and relative weighting of Oman versus Yemen.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Pastoral cattle herds and wild bovids (notably African buffalo and antelopes) in the southern Sudan ecosystem and contiguous areas of Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia
Event.summary: From 1993 to the late 1990s, classic rinderpest persisted in the southern Sudan ecosystem and neighbouring pastoral areas of Uganda, Kenya and western Ethiopia, forming one of the last major African reservoirs of virulent lineage‑1 virus. Widespread outbreaks in cattle and associated wildlife occurred in southern Sudan and Karamoja (Uganda) in 1993–1995, with further activity in border districts of Kenya and Ethiopia, before intensive control efforts reduced incidence. The final laboratory‑confirmed outbreak in this ecosystem was recorded near Torit in what is now South Sudan in 1998, after which no further confirmed rinderpest occurred, paving the way for verification of eradication in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Protracted civil conflict in southern Sudan, insecurity in parts of Uganda and Kenya, and very limited state presence severely constrained veterinary services, vaccination coverage and disease reporting. Large, mobile pastoral herds moved across porous borders with little control, sustaining transmission in an ecological “southern Sudan axis” even as other African regions became free. Only with the introduction of community‑based animal health workers, targeted vaccination in high‑risk corridors and improved surveillance under PARC/PACE and GREP was this reservoir finally extinguished. Internal mechanisms: Virological data indicate circulation of established lineage‑1 rinderpest viruses rather than a novel strain; the episode is thus characterized as re-occurrence of classic rinderpest maintained by conflict and pastoral ecology rather than re-emergence driven by virus evolution.
Review: review – This major East African focus, often described as the “southern Sudan axis,” was missing from the original output despite being identified in GREP analyses as one of the last two African reservoirs of classic virulent rinderpest. A new row has been added summarizing widespread outbreaks in southern Sudan and contiguous parts of Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia during 1993–1998, culminating in the final confirmed outbreak near Torit. Country list and time ranges are approximate and should be cross‑checked against national datasets; emergence-type classification as re-occurrence is supported by lineage‑1 virology and the strong influence of conflict and service breakdown.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma agalactiae
EPP.common.name: Contagious agalactia
Host: Domestic dairy sheep and goats (small ruminants)
Event.summary: Over the four-year period ending in 2018, Iran reported a cumulative 968 outbreaks of contagious agalactia to the OIE, the highest officially notified CA burden worldwide in that interval. These outbreaks, affecting dairy sheep and goat flocks across multiple provinces, reflected intense circulation of Mycoplasma agalactiae and related mycoplasmas in a major small‑ruminant‑producing country, with substantial but incompletely quantified losses from milk reduction, animal deaths and disease control expenditures. Despite ongoing vaccination and treatment, CA remained entrenched in Iranian small‑ruminant systems during this period, highlighting gaps in surveillance, vaccine performance and farm‑level biosecurity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: very large national populations of sheep and goats managed in extensive and semi‑intensive systems, seasonal movements of flocks, frequent trading of animals, and variable access to high‑quality vaccines and diagnostics favoured persistent transmission and repeated outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: the epidemic wave is best interpreted as a high‑intensity re‑occurrence of established CA in Iran; there is no indication from available summaries that a single new strain with markedly altered virulence or host range dominated the 2014–2018 outbreaks.
Review: review – new aggregated national event added to represent the exceptionally high burden of CA in Iran (968 outbreaks reported over 2014–2018), which is clearly among the most impactful recent emergence waves; classified as a large-scale re‑occurrence in an already affected Southern Asia country rather than as first detection or inter‑continental emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma agalactiae
EPP.common.name: Contagious agalactia
Host: Domestic sheep and goats (pastoral small ruminants)
Event.summary: During the same four-year period to 2018, Mongolia officially reported 380 outbreaks of contagious agalactia in small ruminants, indicating substantial Mycoplasma agalactiae activity in pastoral sheep and goat systems of Eastern Asia. These outbreaks occurred in predominantly nomadic or transhumant livestock systems and added to the burden of other endemic diseases, contributing to milk losses, morbidity and the need for culling in affected flocks. Control remained challenging because of the vast grazing areas, flock mobility, limited laboratory infrastructure and economic constraints on sustained vaccination, allowing CA to persist as a recurrent problem.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive nomadic and semi‑nomadic management of sheep and goats, large flock movements over long distances, harsh climatic conditions and constrained veterinary resources impeded early detection and systematic control of CA outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: as in Iran, the wave is best viewed as a re‑occurrence of known M. agalactiae infection; existing evidence does not single out a novel genotype as the main driver, but aggregated OIE data indicate that CA reached a nationally significant level of impact during 2014–2018.
Review: review – new national-level event added for Mongolia, which reported 380 CA outbreaks over 2014–2018; this represents one of the largest recent epidemic waves outside the Mediterranean basin and merits inclusion as a major re‑occurrence episode in an Eastern Asian pastoral system.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus sindbis
EPP.common.name: Sindbis virus
Host: Humans; mosquitoes (e.g. Culex univittatus); wild and domestic animals in shared ecologies
Event.summary: Between 2006 and 2010, South Africa recorded continuous laboratory‑confirmed Sindbis fever cases in humans, with a marked increase in 2010 when 208 of 2,025 suspected arboviral cases tested IgM‑positive for SINV, representing a sharp rise compared with 2006–2009 and indicating a substantial though under‑recognised outbreak mainly on the central plateau. The episode unfolded largely in late summer and early autumn in provinces such as Free State and Northern Cape, where SINV is endemic and where above‑average rainfall simultaneously fuelled a large Rift Valley fever epidemic in livestock and humans, suggesting shared climatic drivers for both arboviruses. As vector populations declined and drier conditions returned, Sindbis case detections fell back to background sporadic levels, with no severe or fatal human cases reported in this series but highlighting ongoing endemic transmission and the potential for larger future outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: unusually high rainfall and flooding in 2009–2010 that increased breeding sites for Culex mosquitoes, coinciding with an extensive Rift Valley fever epizootic; agricultural and outdoor occupational exposure of farmers and farm workers in the central plateau; limited awareness and routine diagnostic testing for Sindbis fever leading to substantial under‑ascertainment except during intensified arbovirus investigations. Internal mechanisms: established South African SINV lineages maintained in bird–mosquito cycles with no evidence for new, more virulent genotypes; the 2010 spike is best interpreted as a climate‑driven re-occurrence of endemic SINV activity rather than true re-emergence due to viral change.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2010 peak in Sindbis fever detections in South Africa (208 IgM-positive cases) is the largest well-characterised post-1990 outbreak there and clearly linked to climatic conditions that also drove widespread Rift Valley fever; geography, timing and classification as climate-driven re-occurrence are appropriate and supported by national surveillance data.

EPP.scientific.name: Parvovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: CPV, FPV
Sub.regions: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand. Asia: Western Asia.
Countries: Australia [2014-2018, multiple large FPV outbreaks in eastern states including Victoria and New South Wales after decades without major epizootics]
Host: Domestic cats (mostly unvaccinated kittens and young cats, many in shelters, rescue facilities and urban stray colonies).
Event.summary: Clinical feline panleukopenia (FPV infection) had become rare in Australia by the early 2010s, with no large reported outbreaks for roughly four decades, largely due to widespread vaccination. In 2014, severe FPV outbreaks re-emerged in eastern Australia and continued through 2015–2018 in multiple regions, causing hundreds of cases and high mortality, while contemporaneous outbreaks were reported in New Zealand (2016–2018) and the United Arab Emirates (2017). Sequence analysis showed that the Australian and New Zealand outbreaks were caused by closely related FPV lineages distinct from those in the UAE, and that intensified vaccination and outbreak control subsequently reduced reported case numbers, although FPV remains a recurrent threat in under-vaccinated cat populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Declining or inconsistent FPV vaccination coverage in pet, shelter and stray cats; accumulation of large populations of unvaccinated urban strays and feral colonies; high-density housing and population turnover in shelters and rescue facilities; movement of cats between shelters, rescue groups and regions; probable introduction of FPV into naïve subpopulations via inter-regional movement of cats (particularly relevant for the UAE outbreak). Internal mechanisms: While phylogenetic studies identified distinct FPV lineages associated with the Australian/New Zealand and UAE outbreaks, the major drivers appear to have been immunity gaps and management factors rather than a clearly more virulent virus, so this is best considered a re-occurrence event; nonetheless, ongoing evolution of FPV with regional clustering underscores the potential for future strain-related changes in epidemiology. Enhanced Transmission – high environmental stability and heavy faecal shedding of FPV facilitated rapid spread once vaccination gaps existed.
Review: Decision: review (retain event). The timing and geography (eastern Australia 2014–2018, New Zealand 2016–2018, United Arab Emirates 2017) match well-documented large FPV epizootics after decades of low clinical incidence in these regions, clearly qualifying this as a major re-emergent episode. I changed the event-type coding from a combination of intra-continental emergence, re-occurrence and re-emergence to “re-occurrence only”, because FPV was historically present in both Oceania and Western Asia and the literature identifies waning population immunity and vaccination lapses, rather than a fundamentally new viral phenotype, as the primary drivers of these outbreaks. The source list was also refocused on the key outbreak and seroprevalence papers and a general shelter-medicine FPV guidance resource. A human reviewer should confirm that the balance between external drivers and any putative strain effects is appropriately reflected in the re-occurrence classification.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyclospora cayetanensis
EPP.common.name: cyclosporiasis
Countries: Guatemala [1996–2000, as source of imported raspberries and other berries]
Host: Humans (adults and children consuming fresh imported berries at social events, restaurants and via retail)
Event.summary: From spring through summer 1996, a very large multinational outbreak of cyclosporiasis occurred in North America, with approximately 1,465 outbreak-associated cases reported from 20 U.S. states, the District of Columbia, and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Québec; epidemiologic investigations in both countries consistently implicated fresh raspberries imported from Guatemala as the vehicle of infection. Similar but somewhat smaller raspberry‑linked outbreaks recurred in 1997 and again in 1998, including a 192‑case, 13‑cluster event in Ontario, Canada, and further clusters in the United States, and in 2000 a 54‑case outbreak in Philadelphia and other clusters were again traced to Guatemalan raspberries or blackberries. This multi‑year episode ended only after Guatemalan growers, the Guatemalan Berry Commission, and U.S. and Canadian regulators suspended spring raspberry exports, implemented a stringent Model Plan of Excellence with improved water quality, hygiene and field sanitation, and restricted exports to vetted farms, after which raspberry‑associated Cyclospora outbreaks in North America ceased.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of international trade in high‑value fresh berries from Cyclospora‑endemic Guatemala to North American markets; use of inadequately treated irrigation and wash water and poor sanitary infrastructure on some exporting farms; fragile raspberries with complex surface morphology that are difficult to wash effectively; and initially low awareness of Cyclospora among clinicians and laboratories in the United States and Canada, which delayed case recognition. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel strains or increased virulence during this episode; emergence was driven by repeated contamination of produce in endemic areas and its distribution into a naïve, high‑consumption market. Mechanism categories: Enhanced transmission via contaminated fresh berries entering new consumer markets and geographic range expansion of exposure (but not necessarily of long‑term parasite establishment) into Northern America.
Review: retain: This row correctly captures the large 1996–2000 North American epidemic linked mainly to Guatemalan raspberries, but the emergence type was misclassified. North American outbreaks were already recognized in 1990 and 1995, so this episode is not the first inter-continental occurrence on the continent. I reclassified it as re_occurrence, removed Peru from the country list (no strong evidence it was a major produce source in this specific episode), narrowed sub_regions to Northern America and Central America, and clarified that multiple years and clusters are grouped because they share a common Guatemala–North America raspberry supply chain. Event should be retained as one of the highest-impact global episodes for this parasite.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia spp.
EPP.common.name: Lyme borreliosis
Host: Humans (small case series with erythema migrans, neurologic and articular manifestations), domestic dogs and horses as potential exposed hosts, and wildlife including small mammals and lizards (e.g. Psammodromus algirus) serving as reservoirs; infection maintained mainly in Ixodes ricinus and Ixodes inopinatus in North Africa and, in some eastern African sites, in Hyalomma rufipes associated with migratory birds and livestock.
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, clinical and serological studies in Tunisia identified patients with erythema migrans and compatible neurological and articular symptoms, together with high seroprevalence for Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato, providing the first recognized Lyme borreliosis cases in North Africa and coinciding with detection of Borrelia lusitaniae and related genospecies in Ixodes ticks. Subsequent work in the 1990s and 2000s documented very high prevalence of B. lusitaniae in I. ricinus and I. inopinatus ticks in Tunisia and Morocco and additional detections of Lyme-group Borrelia in ticks from Algeria and Egypt, while small human case series and serosurveys confirmed that Lyme borreliosis was present but non-endemic and likely underdiagnosed. During the 2000s, Lyme-group Borrelia, including B. garinii, were also reported from ticks along the Indian Ocean coasts of Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique, associated with migratory birds and Hyalomma rufipes, indicating limited but genuine autochthonous establishment of Lyme-group Borrelia cycles in selected North and East African coastal ecosystems rather than mere importation of cases from Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Suitable Mediterranean and coastal climates in North African Maghreb countries and along parts of the western Indian Ocean coast provide humidity and vegetation structure favorable to Ixodes spp. and other ticks, while migratory birds moving between Europe and Africa likely introduced and help maintain Lyme-group Borrelia across the Mediterranean and into East Africa; local land use and presence of lizards, small mammals and livestock create additional reservoir and vector habitats. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of Lyme-group Borrelia and their tick vectors into African coastal environments, including adaptation of Borrelia lusitaniae to reptile reservoirs and Ixodes species prevalent in Mediterranean habitats, and possible spillover via Hyalomma ticks that feed on migratory birds and savanna animals. Overall incidence remains low and focal, but this represents the first documented establishment of Lyme-group Borrelia transmission cycles in African wildlife and domestic-animal systems.
Review: review – This is a new row added during peer review to capture first detections and limited emergence of Lyme-group Borrelia and Lyme borreliosis in Africa, based on clinical series from Tunisia in the 1990s and high Borrelia lusitaniae infection rates in Ixodes ticks in Tunisia and Morocco, together with later reports of Lyme-group Borrelia along the Indian Ocean coasts of Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique. It is coded as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence because it represents the first autochthonous establishment of Lyme-group Borrelia cycles on the African continent in humans, wildlife and domestic animals, while remaining low-incidence and geographically restricted. Dates and country list are approximate and derived from regional reviews rather than harmonized surveillance data, so confidence is set lower (0.7) and this row is flagged for review in future iterations, but including it aligns the dataset with the rule that first continent-level detection events may be retained even when case numbers are modest.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Hepatovirus A
EPP.common.name: Hepatitis A virus
Countries: United States of America (multiple states including California, Kentucky, Michigan, Utah, West Virginia and many others)
Host: Humans, predominantly people who use drugs (injection and non-injection) and people experiencing homelessness or unstable housing, with spillover to the general adult population
Event.summary: Starting in 2016, the United States experienced widespread, protracted hepatitis A outbreaks across dozens of states, primarily affecting people who use drugs and people experiencing homelessness, with about 37,500 outbreak-associated cases during August 2016‚ÄìDecember 2020 and over 380 reported deaths, and approximately 44,900 cases and 424 deaths when extended through 2022. The outbreaks began as localized clusters (e.g. in California, Kentucky, Michigan, Utah, West Virginia) and expanded geographically as HAV spread via person-to-person contact in encampments, shelters, jails, and drug-using networks, marking a shift from foodborne to large community transmission among marginalized populations in the vaccine era. Intensive public health responses‚Äîincluding large-scale vaccination campaigns targeting at-risk groups, improved sanitation and handwashing facilities, vaccination programs in emergency departments, correctional facilities and shelters, and public awareness‚Äîeventually reduced incidence in many affected areas, and by 2020‚Äì2022 many states were able to declare their outbreaks over.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growing populations of people who use drugs and people experiencing homelessness with poor access to sanitation, hygiene facilities, and healthcare; low baseline HAV immunity and vaccination uptake among adults at risk; crowded living conditions in shelters, encampments, and correctional settings; mobility of at-risk populations spreading infection across jurisdictions. Internal mechanisms: Circulation mainly of HAV genotype IB strains without clear evidence of increased intrinsic virulence; the main mechanisms were social determinants (homelessness, drug use, incarceration) and gaps in adult vaccination coverage, combined with historically low immunity in middle-aged adults.
Review: retain ‚Äì This prolonged series of person-to-person outbreaks (‚âà37,553 cases and 380 deaths through 2020; ‚âà44,937 cases and 424 deaths by 2022) is one of the largest HAV emergence events globally in the vaccine era, driven by homelessness and drug-use syndemics. Time span, geography, host groups, and classification as re-occurrence are consistent with CDC analyses; no structural corrections required, though the summary could note the higher final case count through 2022. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/wr/mm7139a1.htm))

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter jejuni
EPP.common.name: campylobacteriosis
Countries: United States of America (multistate: at least 18 states)
Host: Humans; companion dogs (puppies)
Event.summary: From 2016 to 2018, and again in 2019‚Äì2020, the United States experienced multistate outbreaks of extensively drug‚Äëresistant Campylobacter jejuni infections linked to contact with puppies sold through commercial pet stores, with at least about 113‚Äì120 confirmed human illnesses, around 17‚Äì24 hospitalizations, and no deaths documented during investigated periods. Whole‚Äëgenome sequencing identified a persistent clone (REPDBR01) circulating in puppies within the commercial breeding and pet‚Äëstore distribution chain, with isolates resistant to multiple first‚Äëline antibiotic classes including macrolides and fluoroquinolones. The outbreaks subsided after enhanced infection‚Äëcontrol and antimicrobial‚Äëstewardship measures in the pet industry and public‚Äëhealth advisories, but the resistant clone has continued to cause sporadic illnesses, indicating ongoing zoonotic risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‚Äëdensity commercial dog‚Äëbreeding and distribution networks, frequent movement of puppies between breeders, distributors, and pet stores, and widespread prophylactic and therapeutic antibiotic use in puppies created conditions for amplification and dissemination of resistant C. jejuni. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance and enhanced transmission‚Äîwhole‚Äëgenome sequencing identified a persistent, extensively drug‚Äëresistant C. jejuni clone (REPDBR01) with resistance to multiple antibiotic classes that caused repeated multistate outbreaks; efficient colonization of puppies facilitated zoonotic spillover to humans.
Review: Retain ‚Äì Event is well documented by CDC and peer‚Äëreviewed studies as an ongoing multistate outbreak series caused by an extensively drug‚Äëresistant C. jejuni clone associated with puppies. Classification as re‚Äëemergence (AMR and host‚Äëassociated clone) is appropriate; inclusion adds an important AMR‚Äëand‚Äëzoonosis dimension beyond large waterborne outbreaks.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira spp.
EPP.common.name: Leptospira bacteria
Countries: Thailand (nationwide, with focus on northeastern provinces)
Host: Humans (mainly male agricultural workers, especially rice farmers)
Event.summary: From the late 1990s through the early 2000s, Thailand experienced a nationwide leptospirosis epidemic. Reported human cases rose from roughly 2,230 in 1998 to 6,080 in 1999 and about 14,286 in 2000, with most cases in northeastern rice‚Äëgrowing regions, before gradually declining after 2003 as control efforts took effect. The epidemic was linked to intense monsoon seasons, increased exposure of farmers to flooded rice fields, and improved recognition and reporting of leptospirosis through national surveillance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: heavy monsoon rains and flooding, high rodent reservoir density in rice ecosystems, barefoot and unprotected work in paddy fields, and heightened clinician awareness plus strengthened surveillance which increased detection. Internal mechanisms: molecular typing during the epidemic identified a widely distributed clone of L. interrogans associated with many cases, but available evidence still points primarily to environmental and occupational drivers in a country where leptospirosis was already endemic; classification as large-scale re‚Äëoccurrence is therefore reasonable.
Review: retain ‚Äì National surveillance data confirm this multi‚Äëyear epidemic with peaks of >14,000 cases as one of the largest leptospirosis outbreaks ever recorded. Geography and classification as re‚Äëoccurrence are consistent with definitions; although a dominant clone was reported, evidence for a clearly novel strain is limited. Recommended to retain as a core high‚Äëimpact event.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira spp.
EPP.common.name: Leptospira bacteria
Countries: Sri Lanka (nationwide, with spread from historically high‚Äëincidence southern districts into northern and central districts)
Host: Humans (agricultural workers and rural residents, as well as peri‚Äëurban populations exposed to contaminated water)
Event.summary: After a decade of elevated but relatively stable leptospirosis incidence, Sri Lanka entered a new phase of intensified transmission beginning in 2020, when 8,323 cases were reported nationally. Case counts remained high in 2021‚Äì2022 and then surged to 9,630 cases in 2023 and a record 13,328 cases in 2024, with high‚Äëincidence clusters spreading from traditional rice‚Äëgrowing southern districts into previously low‚Äëincidence northern and central areas. Although stronger surveillance contributed to higher detection, spatiotemporal analyses suggest that increased rainfall and evolving agricultural and land‚Äëuse patterns helped drive this multi‚Äëyear resurgence, which was ongoing as of 2024.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: long‚Äëterm climatic trends with heavier seasonal rainfall, expansion and intensification of paddy cultivation, changes in rodent and livestock ecology, and improved surveillance and diagnostic capacity that enhanced case ascertainment and revealed spread into new districts. Internal mechanisms: rodent reservoir studies document circulation of pathogenic L. interrogans and L. borgpetersenii in multiple small-mammal hosts, but available evidence points mainly to geographic expansion and environmental drivers rather than emergence of a distinctly new strain; the episode is therefore best classified as large‚Äëscale re‚Äëoccurrence in a hyperendemic country.
Review: review ‚Äì Added to represent Sri Lanka‚Äôs recent multi‚Äëyear resurgence, with national surveillance documenting 8,323 cases in 2020 and peaks of 9,630 cases in 2023 and 13,328 cases in 2024, the highest annual totals yet reported. Classified as re‚Äëoccurrence driven by climatic and agricultural factors in an already hyperendemic setting. This episode clearly ranks among the most impactful global leptospirosis events since 1990 and should be considered for inclusion in any top‚Äë10 list, but the new data and interpretation should be reviewed in context with earlier Sri Lankan outbreaks.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
EPP.common.name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
Host: Adult kidney transplant recipients
Event.summary: In the mid‚Äë2000s, an Australian renal transplant service documented a cluster of 14 Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia cases among kidney transplant recipients, far exceeding the centre‚Äôs prior experience and occurring predominantly late after transplantation. Many affected patients required intensive care, two died and several lost their grafts, and contact mapping showed that cases were temporally and spatially linked through a busy outpatient transplant clinic and shared ward areas. Once the cluster was recognised, the service instituted blanket trimethoprim‚Äìsulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for all potentially exposed kidney transplant recipients and extended routine prophylaxis duration, together with strengthened infection-control measures, which was followed by rapid cessation of new outbreak-associated PCP cases. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22129760/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growing cohort of chronically immunosuppressed kidney transplant recipients, many years out from transplantation; limited baseline use or early discontinuation of PCP prophylaxis owing to toxicity concerns; dense patient contact networks in outpatient clinics and inpatient wards. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (epidemiologic clustering and multilocus sequence data consistent with person-to-person spread of closely related strains); no evidence of a unique, more virulent genotype driving the outbreak. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22129760/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: The Australian kidney-transplant cluster, involving 14 cases with high morbidity and strong epidemiologic evidence for clinic-based nosocomial transmission, is real and among the larger transplant-unit outbreaks; the event is retained but its type has been changed from re-emergence to re-occurrence, since no novel strain or resistance mechanism was shown, and the summary has been aligned more closely with the details reported by Phipps et al. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22129760/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
EPP.common.name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
Host: Adults with and without HIV infection, including patients with hematologic malignancies, solid-organ transplants, autoimmune diseases, chronic lung disease and other immunosuppressive conditions
Event.summary: From 2008 to 2012, national hospital discharge data from Spain identified 4,554 admissions with Pneumocystis pneumonia, and a nationwide analysis showed that while overall incidence remained relatively stable, the proportion and incidence of PCP among HIV-negative patients increased, whereas incidence among persons with HIV infection declined. Among HIV-negative cases, most had identifiable risk factors such as haematologic malignancies, chronic lung diseases and non-haematologic cancers, and mean in-hospital mortality and costs were high, highlighting PCP as an emerging public health problem in non-HIV immunocompromised Spaniards. This multi-year pattern represents a substantial re-occurrence of PCP in new patient groups at the national level, analogous to trends documented in the United Kingdom and France during overlapping periods. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31637227/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Changing epidemiology of immunosuppression in Spain, with more patients receiving chemotherapy, steroids and other immunosuppressants for cancers, autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, and chronic lung conditions; declining HIV-related PCP due to effective antiretroviral therapy and prophylaxis; underuse or late initiation of prophylaxis in non-HIV risk groups. Internal mechanisms: No specific new P. jirovecii strain was implicated; the emergence is best explained by host- and health-system-level changes. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31637227/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: This newly added event summarises the first nationwide Spanish analysis of 4,554 PCP admissions during 2008‚Äì2012, which demonstrated rising incidence and high mortality among HIV-negative immunocompromised patients despite stable overall rates; it is classified as re-occurrence, driven by expanding and changing non-HIV risk groups, and merits inclusion among the major post‚Äë1990 emergence events for P. jirovecii because of its national scale and clinical burden. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31637227/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Rubivirus rubellae
EPP.common.name: Rubella virus
Host: Humans (primarily adolescents and young adults, including pregnant women; infants with CRS)
Event.summary: Beginning in 1997, Brazil experienced a large rubella epidemic with about 30,000 reported cases nationally as rubella became notifiable and immunity gaps among adolescents and young adults were revealed. Between 1999 and 2001, multiple states reported outbreaks, and suspected congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) cases rose from roughly 200 to 600 as virus circulation intensified among women of reproductive age. The epidemic subsided after intensified surveillance, postpartum vaccination, and catch‚Äëup campaigns, but left a documented cohort of CRS‚Äëaffected infants and highlighted major immunity gaps in young adults.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Incomplete and heterogeneous rubella vaccine introduction focused on children, leaving large cohorts of susceptible adolescents and young adults, especially women of childbearing age; strengthening of case and CRS surveillance increased detection; high population mixing in urban centers facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype was identified as driving this wave; the event is best characterized as resurgence due to an expanding pool of susceptible young adults rather than viral change.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Well-supported by Brazilian Ministry of Health data and peer-reviewed analyses describing ~30,000 rubella cases in 1997 and rising suspected CRS between 1999 and 2001; geography (Brazil, South America) and timing are correct, and classification as a re-occurrence (no documented novel strain driving the epidemic) matches the definitions. Note that the later Rio Branco/Para√≠ba 2000‚Äì2001 subnational episode is nested within this national epidemic and is flagged separately for possible exclusion or merging.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis
EPP.common.name: Bd
Host: Wild Malagasy frogs (multiple endemic species sampled across lowland and montane sites)
Event.summary: Between 2005 and 2010, intensive surveys across Madagascar failed to detect Bd despite global concern about its potential arrival on the island. In 2010, Bd was first detected at low prevalence in wild amphibians from the Makay region and subsequent surveys up to 2014 documented patchy but increasing presence at additional sites, indicating recent introduction and early spread without clear, documented mass die-offs. By the mid‚Äë2010s, Bd was considered present but not yet widely established or clearly epizootic in Madagascar, prompting ongoing surveillance and contingency planning to prevent or respond to large-scale chytridiomycosis outbreaks in the island‚Äôs highly endemic amphibian fauna.

Internal mechanisms: Introduction of Bd (likely BdGPL or a related lineage) into a na√Øve, highly endemic amphibian fauna represents geographic range expansion of the pathogen, but to date there is limited evidence for strong virulence expression or epidemic dynamics at the island scale, suggesting either an early invasion stage, lineage-specific differences, or host and environmental factors moderating disease expression.
Review: review ‚Äì Retain this as the first confirmed detection and early spread of Bd in Madagascar, with Africa/Eastern Africa coding, a 2010‚Äì2014 window, and narrative all consistent with Bletz et al. (2015) and Kolby et al. (2015). 'First_detection' has been set to false because global first detection of Bd occurred in the late 1990s; classification as an intra-continental emergence within Africa (from other African or external sources into Madagascar) more accurately reflects its status and limited documented impact to date.

EPP.scientific.name: Covert mortality nodavirus

Host: Wild and farm-associated fish and invertebrates including the goby Mugilogobius abei, Japanese flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), cyprinid fish such as goldfish/carp (Carassius auratus), sea cucumber (Apostichopus japonicus), large yellow croaker (Larimichthys crocea), crabs and other non-penaeid hosts, with later reports of infection in additional invertebrates such as bivalves.
Event.summary: From 2018 onward, CMNV was detected for the first time in a widening range of non-penaeid hosts in and around shrimp-farming areas in China, beginning with natural infection of the intertidal goby Mugilogobius abei collected near affected ponds and soon followed by reports of CMNV infection in farmed Japanese flounder, cyprinid fishes, and coastal crabs. By around 2022, experimental and field data showed that these new hosts could harbor CMNV with associated histopathological changes, implying that CMNV had undergone substantial host expansion and established additional reservoirs in coastal ecosystems adjacent to shrimp farms.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continuous discharge of CMNV-contaminated effluents and sediment from shrimp ponds into surrounding coastal and estuarine waters, plus physical connectivity between ponds, drainage canals and nearshore habitats, repeatedly exposed wild fish and invertebrates to high viral loads; mixed and proximate aquaculture of shrimp with fish, sea cucumbers and other species increased inter-species contact, while growing demand for polyculture systems intensified these interfaces. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) ‚Äì CMNV successfully infected and replicated in new vertebrate and invertebrate hosts (e.g. gobies, Japanese flounder, cyprinids, sea cucumbers, bivalves), indicating a marked broadening of its host range beyond penaeid shrimp and pond crustaceans; enhanced transmission/vector adaptation ‚Äì infection of wild fishes, echinoderms and other invertebrates created additional reservoirs and potential biological or mechanical vectors capable of reintroducing virus into shrimp ponds; increased virulence/pathogenicity in some new hosts is suggested by observed lesions in nervous, muscular and other tissues, though the full production impact in these species is still being elucidated.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Changes made: (1) Adjusted Year from 2015‚Äì2020 to 2018‚Äì2022 to align more closely with the timing of published host-jump reports: natural infection of the goby Mugilogobius abei (2018), farmed Japanese flounder (2019), sea cucumber (2021), and large yellow croaker (2022), as well as more recent evidence of CMNV in bivalves. (2) Expanded the Host description and event summary to explicitly mention key new vertebrate and invertebrate hosts documented in the literature, framing this as a major multi-phyla host expansion within Eastern Asia. (3) Updated sources to prioritize primary research articles on cross-species transmission and new host detections, while retaining one recent Aquaculture article on CMNV in bivalves as support for later host range broadening. Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Changes made: (1) Reclassified this episode from first_global_emergence = Yes and first_detection = Yes to first_global_emergence = No, first_detection = No, re_emergence = Yes, to reflect that CMNV was first detected and globally emerged in farmed shrimp in China in 2014; the human POH‚ÄëVAU association represents a later host expansion and re‚Äëemergence in a new host species within an already affected subregion, consistent with the definition of re-emergence (changes in the EPP such as host expansion). EPP.scientific.name: Marteilia refringens
