Host: Ostrea edulis (European flat oyster) in natural beds and coastal fishing grounds of the Gulf of Thessaloniki / Thermaikos Gulf (northern Aegean Sea)
Event.summary: Between about 1994 and 1998, native flat‚Äëoyster beds in the Gulf of Thessaloniki (Thermaikos Gulf) in northern Greece suffered progressive, multi‚Äëyear mass mortalities and a dramatic decline in landings, leading to closure of the local O. edulis fishery and functional extinction of natural beds. Review: review: Added this event as a major, previously omitted emergence episode: the marteiliosis‚Äëassociated collapse of Greek flat‚Äëoyster beds in the Gulf of Thessaloniki / Thermaikos Gulf during 1994‚Äì1998, explicitly cited in the DFO synopsis as a dramatic decrease in O. edulis production linked to M. refringens.([dfo-mpo.gc.ca](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/aah-saa/diseases-maladies/madoy-eng.html))  Classified it as re‚Äëoccurrence (not intra‚Äëcontinental emergence) because the parasite was already endemic in the Southern Europe sub‚Äëregion (France, Spain, Italy) and there is no evidence of a distinct strain or host jump in this case, even though it was the first detection in Greece.([dfo-mpo.gc.ca](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/aah-saa/diseases-maladies/madoy-eng.html))  A national expert review is recommended to refine the exact starting year (the production decline begins in the mid‚Äë1990s and some Greek sources frame the extinction of oyster beds as occurring over the preceding decade) and to ensure that the role of co‚Äëoccurring stressors (other diseases, pollution) is properly weighted relative to marteiliosis in the event summary.

EPP.scientific.name: Abutilon theophrasti
EPP.common.name: velvetleaf, butterprint, buttonweed, Indian mallow, velvetleaf Indian mallow, China jute, Indian hemp, pie-marker
Countries: New Zealand (Auckland and Waikato regions; >60 infested properties traced by 2014)
Host: Maize and maize silage on dairy and arable farms in Auckland and Waikato, with secondary spread into pastures where contaminated maize silage was fed out.
Event.summary: Around 2011, a serious velvetleaf infestation was recognised on a Waikato farm where the weed was severely depressing maize yields, and subsequent tracing revealed that it had been present in the region for some time but misidentified or overlooked. Over the following years, investigations by the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), Waikato Regional Council and the Foundation for Arable Research (FAR) linked the incursion to movements of contaminated maize or maize silage and identified more than 60 infested properties across North and South Auckland and Waikato, leading to its declaration as an Unwanted Organism in 2012 and inclusion in regional pest management plans by 2014. Internal mechanisms: No evidence suggests a novel genotype or herbicide‚Äëresistant strain; instead, the same traits that make velvetleaf a major weed elsewhere‚Äîvigorous seedling growth, rapid height gain, strong competitive ability in tall summer crops and long‚Äëlived seed banks‚Äîenabled establishment once it was accidentally introduced into Waikato maize systems. EPP.scientific.name: Cacopsylla pruni

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis
Host: Humans (three adults with comorbidities)
Event.summary: From July 2020 through 2023, three adults living near the Mississippi Gulf Coast developed severe melioidosis without travel to endemic countries, and B. pseudomallei with near‑identical genomes was isolated from both patients and nearby household soil and water, confirming local environmental establishment. EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus mayaro
EPP.common.name: Mayaro virus
Host: Humans (residents of multiple communes in French Guiana, including peri-urban and forest-fringe areas)

EPP.scientific.name: BSE prion

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans; sylvatic and peri-urban cycles with Aedes spp. mosquitoes and non-human primates
Event.summary: Beginning in September 2017, Nigeria detected confirmed yellow fever cases in Kwara State after many years without large reported outbreaks, signalling a resurgence that over 2017–2019 expanded to dozens of states with thousands of suspected cases and multiple confirmed clusters. Despite phased preventive and reactive vaccination campaigns under the EYE strategy, new foci continued to appear in 2019–2020, including high-fatality clusters in Delta and Enugu states and additional confirmed cases across several other states. EPP.scientific.name: Cyperus esculentus

Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) and other irrigated summer crops at risk in the Italian rice-growing region
Event.summary: In the mid‑2010s, rice farmers in north-western Italy began reporting control failures of yellow nutsedge despite repeated applications of ALS-inhibiting herbicides (halosulfuron and azimsulfuron), which previously had provided effective control in Italian rice. Review: Decision: review. Event is retained as the first confirmed ALS-inhibitor-resistant Cyperus esculentus population in Europe but its timing and source set have been aligned more closely with primary data. The year range is adjusted to 2017–2020 and the country label to "Italy [2017–2020]" to match the herbicide-resistance database, which lists 2017 as the first year of confirmed resistance in rice in the Piedmont region, and the period over which failures and characterisation studies were reported. The event remains classified as re_emergence because it involves a documented ALS target-site mutation and altered herbicide response within an already widespread weed. Source URLs now explicitly include the open-access Agronomy article and the international resistance-database case entry, alongside the original CNR abstract, to strengthen documentation of both mechanism and timing. EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Countries: Bangladesh [2009-2012] (primarily districts Pabna, Sirajganj, Tangail, Rajshahi, Bogra, Rajbari and neighbouring north‑western districts)
Host: Humans exposed via slaughtering, butchering, processing or consuming infected cattle and other livestock
Event.summary: After relatively low reported activity since the 1980s, anthrax re‑emerged in Bangladesh in August 2009 with linked livestock and human cutaneous outbreaks in Pabna District, followed by at least 14 animal–human outbreaks across multiple north‑western districts by October 2010. National surveillance then documented 607 human cutaneous anthrax cases in 2010, 278 in 2011 and 176 in 2012, often associated with slaughtering or handling sick cattle, informal meat marketing, and limited carcass disposal control. Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Endemic environmental contamination with B. anthracis spores in grazing lands; economic pressure and cultural practices of slaughtering and consuming moribund or suddenly dead livestock; inadequate carcass disposal and limited routine vaccination coverage; gaps in veterinary and public‑health coordination prior to 2009.
Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing showed closely related strains in animals and humans between 2009 and 2010, consistent with local transmission from endemic foci rather than introduction of a novel genotype; the event mainly reflects increased exposure and improved detection rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – Multi‑year anthrax re‑emergence in Bangladesh from 2009–2012 (including the 2010 wave with 607 human cutaneous cases and linked livestock outbreaks across ≥12 districts) is one of the largest documented post‑1990 human anthrax episodes; coding as re‑occurrence in Southern Asia with no intra‑/inter‑continental emergence is appropriate, and country/sub‑region information and time span match national and FAO/WHO summaries.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9151811/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Iltovirus gallid2
EPP.common.name: Gallid alphaherpesvirus 1, ILT virus
Countries: United States of America [2005-2008] (Central Valley, California – 57 broiler ranches from two integrators)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial broilers on large integrator ranches)
Event.summary: Beginning in 2005, a large vaccinal ILT outbreak in California’s Central Valley affected 57 broiler ranches belonging to two integrators, with birds showing respiratory disease, increased mortality and condemnation losses, and viruses indistinguishable from chicken‑embryo‑origin (CEO) vaccine strains.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/41120550_Intervention_Strategies_for_Laryngotracheitis_Impact_of_Extended_Downtime_and_Enhanced_Biosecurity_Auditing?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak persisted through multiple production cycles despite standard cleaning, disinfection, and vaccination, leading companies and state authorities to implement a coordinated regional depopulation, extended down‑time, and intensive biosecurity audit programme across affected ranches.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/41120550_Intervention_Strategies_for_Laryngotracheitis_Impact_of_Extended_Downtime_and_Enhanced_Biosecurity_Auditing?utm_source=openai)) After completion of extended down‑time and strengthened sanitation in early 2008, ILT diagnoses fell sharply; only two of the previously affected ranches recorded further cases, and both integrators subsequently regained LT‑free status.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high broiler densities in multi‑house ranches, reuse and movement of contaminated litter, incomplete down‑time between flocks, and frequent movements of personnel and equipment facilitated sustained circulation of vaccinal ILTV over a wide area.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/41120550_Intervention_Strategies_for_Laryngotracheitis_Impact_of_Extended_Downtime_and_Enhanced_Biosecurity_Auditing?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was driven by CEO‑vaccine–like viruses that had spread and persisted in the field; there is no evidence for a novel recombinant genotype, so this episode is best classified as re‑occurrence of vaccine‑origin ILTV maintained under intense production pressure.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: Event is correctly identified as a major vaccinal ILT epizootic in California, but the event period has been adjusted from 2005–2007 to 2005–2008 to reflect the documented duration of coordinated control efforts in Chin et al. 2009.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/41120550_Intervention_Strategies_for_Laryngotracheitis_Impact_of_Extended_Downtime_and_Enhanced_Biosecurity_Auditing?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (rather than re-emergence) is retained because the causative viruses were CEO‑like and not novel recombinants.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus/indicus), water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis)
Event.summary: During the early 2000s, India experienced intense HS activity in bovines, with particularly high incidence in Karnataka state, where retrospective analysis of outbreak and farm-level data showed HS outbreaks increasing from 2002 and peaking in 2005. Numerous farm outbreaks caused high morbidity and mortality and substantial economic losses via reduced milk production, loss of draught power and replacement costs, with state-level projected economic losses from HS running into tens of millions of US dollars under high-incidence scenarios. Following this peak, targeted mass vaccination campaigns and improved management and awareness led to a marked decline in reported HS outbreaks and associated financial losses in Karnataka.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense bovine populations in small and medium farms, suboptimal housing and nutrition, and monsoon-associated humidity and temperature were linked to repeated HS outbreaks; limited vaccine coverage at the start of the period contributed to high susceptibility, while expanding vaccination programs later reduced incidence. Internal mechanisms: Outbreaks were caused by endemic Pasteurella multocida serotype B:2; there is no evidence of a novel genotype or resistance trait driving emergence, so the episode reflects re-occurrence driven by environmental stress and inadequate herd immunity rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Large, well-documented regional episode with quantified outbreak trends and substantial projected economic losses for Karnataka, making it one of the most impactful HS episodes in India during 1990–2010. Updated the 'countries' field to explicitly indicate India [2002–2005] and Karnataka state as the focal area; classification as re-occurrence (environmental and vaccination-coverage driven) is consistent with the epidemiological analysis and no evidence for novel strains.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia miyamotoi
EPP.common.name: Borrelia miyamotoi disease
Host: Humans (immunocompromised and immunocompetent patients with tick exposure in Western and Northern Europe)
Event.summary: Following the Dutch index case, multiple countries in Western and Northern Europe reported autochthonous Borrelia miyamotoi disease between about 2015 and 2018, including neuroborreliosis-like CNS infections in Germany and Sweden and increasing numbers of systemic cases in France. A large French study of 824 patients with persistent polymorphic symptoms after tick bites identified 43 with B. miyamotoi DNA in blood, while additional single cases were documented in countries such as Norway and Poland and in Austria (where a European-type strain was detected in a patient reporting a tick bite in the United States). Together, these reports demonstrated that B. miyamotoi was widely established in Ixodes ricinus across Europe and capable of causing both acute febrile illness and meningoencephalitis in immunocompromised and immunocompetent persons, leading several centers to add B. miyamotoi testing to diagnostic algorithms for tick-associated fever and neuroborreliosis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7059645/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Broad distribution and increasing densities of I. ricinus in Western and Northern Europe; high recreational and occupational exposure to ticks; and rising interest in non-Lyme tick-borne infections that prompted targeted PCR and GlpQ-based serology in patients with compatible syndromes. Internal mechanisms: Stable transovarial maintenance of B. miyamotoi in Ixodes populations and its ability to cause invasive CNS disease as well as persistent polymorphic symptom complexes; the emergence pattern here reflects geographic and diagnostic expansion of existing genotypes rather than appearance of a clearly novel strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7827671/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Review. Clarified that this multi-country episode represents extension of B. miyamotoi disease from the earlier Eastern and Western European foci into additional Western and Northern European settings, which supports 'intra_continental_emergence = true' at the UNSD subregional level. Expanded the country field to indicate that the Austrian case was probably imported after a tick bite in the United States (despite a European genotype) and to acknowledge other Western/Northern European countries with sporadic cases (e.g., Norway, Poland) that are not assigned separate rows. No further type flags were added. Because the included French cohort focuses on patients with chronic polymorphic symptoms and the clinical significance of B. miyamotoi DNA in that context is debated, this grouping and its interpretation as a major emergence event should be reviewed by a subject-matter expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia mallei
EPP.common.name: Malleus (glanders)
Host: Equids (horses, donkeys, mules)
Event.summary: Between 2015 and 2018, India conducted extensive risk-based serological surveillance for glanders and clinical investigations in working and indigenous equids, testing more than 7,700 animals across multiple states and detecting an overall seroprevalence of about 1%. Surveillance revealed ongoing transmission in previously affected states such as Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab and Maharashtra, as well as new foci in additional districts, with seasonal peaks in cases from March to June. Progressive culling of seropositive equids, movement restrictions and awareness campaigns were implemented, reducing apparent prevalence in some areas but not achieving national elimination, and underscoring the chronic endemic status of glanders in parts of India.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued movement of low-value working equids between endemic foci and new districts, reluctance of owners to present animals for testing or accept euthanasia due to economic constraints, and incomplete enforcement of the Prevention and Control of Infectious and Contagious Diseases in Animals Act contributed to persistent low-level transmission and repeated re-introduction into nominally cleared areas. Climatic seasonality and peaks in work demand may also have influenced temporal clustering of cases. Internal mechanisms: Studies did not identify clearly novel B. mallei lineages or increased virulence during this period; the pattern reflects recurrent flare-ups of existing strains under imperfect control and surveillance, fitting the definition of re-occurrence.
Review: review – Retained as a distinct later episode of national-scale surveillance and resurgence in India, but intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because the disease was already established in Southern Asia; this is not first occurrence in a new sub-region. Re_occurrence remains Yes, with re_emergence No, reflecting recurrent outbreaks driven by equid movements and incomplete control rather than documented pathogen change.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus
EPP.common.name: FP-associated herpesvirus, CFPHV
Countries: Brazil (northeastern coast – Potiguar Basin, Rio Grande do Norte and Ceará [2012–2015]
Host: Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas); occasional other sea turtle species
Event.summary: From the early 2000s onward, FP emerged as a major health issue for juvenile green turtles along the Brazilian coast. Systematic monitoring by Projeto TAMAR and associated programs documented rising numbers and proportions of FP‑affected strandings in northeastern Brazil; for example, in the Potiguar Basin, FP was recorded in 610 of 2,688 stranded turtles between 2012 and 2015, with relative frequency increasing from roughly 13% to 35%. Underwater and capture surveys near industrial thermal effluent discharges in southeastern Brazil reported local FP prevalences of 34–76%, while Babitonga Bay in southern Brazil experienced prevalences often exceeding 50% and became one of the most highly affected sites globally outside Hawaii and Florida. Previously FP‑free oceanic sites such as Fernando de Noronha recorded their first FP/ChHV5‑positive turtles in the 2010s. By around 2020, clinically apparent FP was established along large stretches of the Brazilian coast.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Brazilian FP hotspots are consistently associated with anthropogenically altered nearshore environments, including areas influenced by industrial thermal and chemical effluents, heavy urban runoff, and eutrophication. Analyses linking FP prevalence to indices of environmental quality and to distances from pollution sources support a central role for degraded water quality and possibly harmful algal blooms in promoting tumor development. Internal mechanisms: Extensive molecular surveillance confirms widespread ChHV5 infection among Brazilian green turtles, with regionally structured viral variants; however, current evidence supports long‑standing viral circulation rather than a newly emergent, more virulent strain. The large Brazilian episode is thus best regarded as an intra‑continental emergence into the South America sub‑region followed by sustained establishment and high local prevalence driven by environmental cofactors.
Review: retain – Brazil hosts some of the highest FP prevalences documented worldwide outside Hawaii and Florida, with large numbers of affected turtles and clear conservation significance, so this is rightly one of the top 10 events. Event type has been simplified to intra‑continental emergence (into the South America sub‑region) without additional re‑occurrence/re‑emergence flags, because this episode primarily reflects first large‑scale establishment and subsequent intensification rather than pathogen change or reappearance in a previously known South American sub‑region. Wording of the summary was slightly tightened, and the countries field standardized to emphasize Brazil as the sole country with key states listed. Sources are appropriate and focused on Brazilian datasets and environmental analyses.

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis
Host: Humans (three adults with risk factors) and livestock (two animal cases)
Event.summary: Between 2018 and 2021, Southern Africa documented an emergence cluster of three human and two animal melioidosis cases in South Africa and Namibia, with whole‑genome sequencing showing substantial diversity among B. pseudomallei isolates and supporting long‑term regional persistence. The episode unfolded as sporadic but clinically severe infections in persons with diabetes and other risk factors and in livestock, all initially unexpected because melioidosis had not previously been recognized in Southern Africa. Following these detections, the event stabilized into sporadic recognized cases with calls for enhanced environmental sampling and improved diagnostic capacity rather than a continuous high‑incidence outbreak.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: improved clinical awareness and reference laboratory support leading to identification of a pathogen that likely had been underdiagnosed; regional climatic and land‑use conditions conducive to B. pseudomallei survival; and common risk factors such as diabetes and hazardous alcohol use. Internal mechanisms: phylogenomic analyses indicate diverse B. pseudomallei lineages of Asian origin have become established in Southern Africa, reflecting geographic range expansion and long‑term environmental adaptation rather than a single recently introduced epidemic clone.
Review: Review – Retain and keep coded as intra-continental emergence. Prior African human cases and environmental detections were in other sub-regions (principally Eastern and Western Africa), whereas these are the first confirmed human and ovine cases from Southern Africa (South Africa and Namibia), representing spread into a new UN African sub-region. Countries were slightly standardized to “South Africa [2018-2021]; Namibia [2019]”; sources are appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Aparavirus tauraense
EPP.common.name: Taura syndrome virus, TSV
Host: Farmed giant tiger prawn (Penaeus monodon), Pacific white shrimp (L. vannamei) and other penaeids in mixed or sequential culture (e.g. Metapenaeus ensis in Taiwan)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, molecular surveys in Taiwan identified distinct TSV isolates in P. monodon and Metapenaeus ensis as well as in L. vannamei, showing that the virus had expanded beyond its original principal host into additional penaeid species with different susceptibility profiles. In Thailand, the first confirmed TSV outbreak in farmed L. vannamei was detected by RT‑PCR in early 2003, and subsequent work documented TSV infections in both L. vannamei and P. monodon, often as co‑infections with WSSV in mixed or sequential culture systems. Between about 2000 and 2006, increasing reports of TSV in P. monodon and other regional species contributed to complex disease presentations and additional losses in farms that had previously considered TSV primarily a risk for L. vannamei.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: diversification of shrimp farming in East and South‑East Asia, with overlapping culture of P. monodon, L. vannamei and other penaeids in shared water bodies and farm systems, created ecological opportunities for cross‑species transmission; limited species‑specific biosecurity measures meant viruses introduced with L. vannamei could spill over to resident species. Internal mechanisms: host expansion (spillover) of TSV from its principal host L. vannamei into P. monodon and other penaeids, accompanied by genetic variation in capsid genes that affected host range and replication efficiency, represents a re‑emergence mediated by viral adaptation to new hosts rather than a purely geographic spread event.
Review: Review (host-range expansion; impact somewhat uncertain). Evidence from Taiwan (field and experimental infections in P. monodon and Metapenaeus ensis) and Thailand (molecular detection of TSV in P. monodon and L. vannamei, often with WSSV co‑infection) supports genuine host expansion and additional disease burden, justifying classification as re_emergence driven by host expansion and viral genetic variation. However, quantitative estimates of incremental production loss attributable specifically to TSV in non‑vannamei hosts are limited, and geographic coverage beyond Taiwan and Thailand is less clear. The event is retained as one of the main re‑emergence episodes but flagged for expert review of its relative ranking among the top 10 TSV events and for potential refinement of the country list if stronger data on impacts in other South‑East Asian countries become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus
EPP.common.name: FP-associated herpesvirus, CFPHV
Host: Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas)
Event.summary: Between 1998 and 2006, monitoring of foraging green turtles in Corisco Bay on the border of Equatorial Guinea and Gabon documented FP prevalences averaging around 17%, providing the first histopathologically confirmed FP hotspot in Central/West Africa and overturning the previous assumption that the region was FP‑free. By 2005, FP‑like tumors were observed on green turtles off the Republic of the Congo, and by the early 2010s, histological and virological work from Príncipe Island in Sao Tome and Principe confirmed ChHV5‑associated fibropapillomas there. Further surveys and case reports across the 2010s documented FP and/or ChHV5‑positive turtles in Ghana, Guinea‑Bissau, and Mauritania, indicating that clinically apparent FP had spread along much of the Gulf of Guinea coastline. Although reported prevalences generally remained lower than in Hawaii or Florida, this series of detections marks the establishment of FP across multiple Atlantic African foraging grounds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The Gulf of Guinea is undergoing rapid coastal development associated with oil and gas extraction, port expansion, urbanization and artisanal fisheries, all of which can alter water quality and increase turtle exposure to pollutants and eutrophication—conditions similar to FP hotspots elsewhere. Internal mechanisms: Histopathology and PCR from Príncipe Island and other sites confirmed classic FP lesions and ChHV5 infection, and global phylogeographic analyses of CFPHV show African haplotypes clustering with those from other Atlantic basins, suggesting that FP in Atlantic Africa reflects geographic expansion and local expression of an existing herpesvirus lineage rather than the emergence of a novel strain.
Review: retain – This event correctly identifies the first confirmed establishment and subsequent spread of FP in Atlantic Africa, which represents the first inter‑continental emergence of FP into the African continent. Event type has been reclassified from intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence to inter‑continental emergence only, aligning with the definition of a first occurrence in a new continent. Countries were expanded to include Guinea‑Bissau and Mauritania based on later surveys documenting FP and/or ChHV5 there. Flagged for review to refine timing for West African sites as more precise dates become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Sub.regions: Northern Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) in commercial and backyard systems; occasional wild/feral rabbits
Event.summary: In February 2015, RHDV2 was first reported in Africa during severe outbreaks in commercial rabbit farms in Kairouan, Tunisia, where it caused high mortality and major economic losses, and molecular data showed multiple introductions of GI.2-like strains from Europe. Over the next several years genetically related viruses were detected in North African countries including Morocco, Algeria and Egypt, and by 2015–2020 RHDV2 had appeared in multiple West African nations such as Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria and Senegal, where large outbreaks—most notably the 2019 epidemic in Ghana and the 2020 wave in Nigeria—devastated rapidly growing rabbit industries. By 2022, RHDV2 had also been confirmed in South Africa, with outbreaks in wild and domestic lagomorphs, indicating that the new genotype had become established across several African subregions with recurrent, often high-mortality production losses rather than remaining a series of isolated incursions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: importation of live rabbits and rabbit genetic stock from Europe and Asia, movement of rabbit meat and byproducts into coastal West African port cities, rapid expansion of semi-intensive rabbit production as a protein source, and limited biosecurity in smallholder and peri-urban farms facilitated introduction and onward spread. Internal mechanisms: introduction and onward dissemination of the globally successful GI.2 genotype with high transmissibility, broader age susceptibility, and partial vaccine escape relative to earlier GI.1-based vaccines, together with largely naïve African rabbit populations, underpinned severe production losses. Mechanisms include novel genotype-driven geographic range expansion, enhanced transmission, and, in some countries, further diversification via recombination documented in African RHDV2 genomes.
Review: review – Updated the time span from 2015–2019 to 2015–2022 and corrected several country-specific first-detection windows (e.g. Nigeria from 2017–2019 to 2020–2021, Senegal to 2020, South Africa to 2022, Algeria to 2018–2021, Tunisia to 2015–2018) in line with WOAH and recent outbreak reports. Re-coded the episode as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by the GI.2 genotype in an already RHD-affected continent, removing previous inter- and intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence flags to comply with the event-type definitions; the event should be retained but remains flagged for expert review of exact country-year ranges.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Cattle and other domestic bovines (with some involvement of small ruminants and camels in parts of the Arabian Peninsula)
Event.summary: In the early to mid‑1990s, rinderpest caused a series of outbreaks on the Arabian Peninsula following introduction from endemic foci to the north. Oman reported a large epidemic in 1992 with well over 100 outbreaks, and rinderpest continued to be detected there until the mid‑1990s. Related incursions affected cattle in Saudi Arabia, and rinderpest remained present in hill cattle in Yemen until at least 1995 despite annual vaccination campaigns, with additional outbreaks reported in the United Arab Emirates in the mid‑1990s. Coordinated regional efforts under the West Asian Rinderpest Eradication Campaign (WAREC) and GREP, including intensified vaccination, movement control and improved surveillance, progressively eliminated these foci, so that by the late 1990s rinderpest was believed to persist only in Yemen.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing trade and movement of live cattle and other livestock from endemic areas in South and West Asia into Gulf states, combined with incomplete routine vaccination and weaknesses in border control, allowed repeated re-introduction of rinderpest. The early 1990s regional instability following the Gulf War likely exacerbated gaps in veterinary services. In Yemen, difficult terrain and dispersed hill cattle systems impeded high vaccine coverage, favouring endemic persistence until targeted campaigns closed remaining immunity gaps. Internal mechanisms: There is no indication that these outbreaks were driven by a novel strain or altered virulence; they are best interpreted as re-occurrence of known Asiatic lineages in a high‑risk trade hub.
Review: review – This multi‑country Arabian Peninsula focus, including a large epidemic in Oman and persistent endemic infection in Yemen with additional outbreaks in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, was absent from the original dataset but is clearly highlighted in FAO/OIE sources as one of the remaining rinderpest reservoirs in the mid‑1990s. A new row has been added with approximate year ranges and country‑specific last-report dates based primarily on regional summaries and OIE workshop data. Because detailed national outbreak timelines are heterogeneous and not always fully accessible, this event is flagged for human review to confirm the per‑country start years and relative weighting of Oman versus Yemen.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis
Host: Wild boar (Sus scrofa); occasionally free-range pigs
Event.summary: From roughly 2013 to 2016, Italy recorded several trichinellosis outbreaks linked to wild boar hunted in regions previously classified as negligible risk for Trichinella, including a well-described outbreak in southern Italy in which consumption of undercooked wild boar sausages led to dozens of human cases caused by T. britovi. Retrospective analysis of Italian data from 1985–2016 indicates that most animal Trichinella detections (n≈354) involved wild boar, with occasional domestic pigs and other species, but these 2013–2016 outbreaks signalled a southward shift of enzootic foci into new hunting areas. Italian and EU reference laboratories subsequently emphasized systematic testing of wild boar carcasses from all regions and reinforced public advisories on thoroughly cooking game meat.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and increased density of wild boar populations, spread of boar into new habitats, growth of recreational hunting, and inconsistent application of Trichinella testing to animals from putatively low-risk regions facilitated renewed human exposure. Internal mechanisms: No novel species or genotypes were identified; the outbreaks represent re-occurrence of T. britovi in wild boar at the periphery of its known range rather than parasite evolution, although the geographic shift broadened the realized endemic area within Italy.
Review: Decision: review. The original event has been reclassified as re-occurrence only (re_emergence set to No) because the evidence points to geographic spread and increased detection of existing T. britovi foci in wild boar, without clear parasite change. These Italian wild-boar outbreaks are epidemiologically important for Europe but involve tens rather than hundreds of human cases and modest numbers of infected animals compared with the very large episodes in Romania, Argentina, China and Türkiye; they may or may not fit within a strict global top ten and are therefore flagged for expert review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia prostrata
EPP.common.name: prostrate spurge, prostrate sandmat, blue weed, ground spurge
Countries: Russian Federation – Tomsk Region and other localities [2018–2021]
Host: Weed of anthropogenic habitats: wastelands, lawns, parks, gardens, fields, fallow lands, sidewalks, roadsides, railway embankments and river banks
Event.summary: Around 2012 Euphorbia prostrata was first recorded from the Almaty Region of Kazakhstan, marking its documented arrival in Central Asia and showing that this American species had reached a previously uncolonised Asian sub-region. By 2018–2019 it was found as a weed in anthropogenic habitats in Uzbekistan and by 2018–2021 it was newly recorded in several localities in the Russian Federation, mostly along railway rights-of-way and urban disturbed sites. These findings together document a coordinated eastward and northward expansion across Central Asia and into continental parts of Russia, where the species is currently assessed as an alien of minor impact but clearly increasing its range.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of transport infrastructure, urbanization and trade across Central Asia and the Russian Federation has increased movement of contaminated soil, road materials and plant propagules, facilitating long-distance dispersal of ruderal aliens. Irrigation schemes, parks and gardens provide persistently disturbed, watered microsites in otherwise harsh continental climates. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion through pre-adaptation to hot, dry, nutrient-poor and compacted substrates typical of anthropogenic sites, with enhanced transmission via persistent seed banks and accidental transport with gravel and railway ballast enabling stepwise spread along transport corridors.
Review: Review – Retain this episode as an intra-continental emergence, because it documents the first confirmed records in the Central Asia sub-region (Kazakhstan and later Uzbekistan) and new records in Russia, within continents where the species was already established elsewhere. EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma agalactiae

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus toscanaense
EPP.common.name: Toscana virus

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Countries: Mauritius [1996–1999: first African record of B. dorsalis near Camp Carol close to the international airport, followed by rapid spread within the island and successful eradication after a nationwide control campaign]
Host: Mango, lychee, guava and other cultivated and wild fruits in Mauritius’ humid lowland and mid‑altitude production zones
Event.summary: In June 1996 Bactrocera dorsalis was detected for the first time in Mauritius near Camp Carol, close to the main international airport, representing the earliest confirmed occurrence of this species in Africa. Within a short period the fly was found infesting mango, lychee and other fruits in several parts of the island, raising the risk of severe yield losses and export restrictions and prompting the launch of a nationwide male‑annihilation and bait‑spray programme. By 1999 B. dorsalis was no longer detected and the pest was officially declared eradicated, but this incursion highlighted the high vulnerability of African horticulture to oriental fruit fly invasions and foreshadowed later, more extensive colonization of mainland Africa and neighbouring islands.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The initial introduction likely occurred via imported infested fruit or luggage arriving by air, as suggested by first detection near the airport, with abundant hosts and suitable tropical climate on Mauritius enabling rapid establishment. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, broad host range and strong dispersal ability typical of B. dorsalis facilitated quick spread within the island; however, intensive, well‑resourced area‑wide control (male‑annihilation, bait sprays, sanitation) was sufficient to overcome these biological advantages and achieve eradication.
Review: retain (newly added): The 1996–1999 Mauritius outbreak was the first confirmed African occurrence of B. dorsalis and required a nationwide eradication programme; it is explicitly highlighted in the invasion‑history literature for the Indian Ocean and Africa and should be treated as the inter‑continental emergence event for the African continent. This critical event was missing from the original dataset and has now been added with UNSD‑consistent coding and primary sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Parvovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: CPV, FPV

Countries: Italy [2010-2013, multi-year FPV outbreak in a large feline shelter in north-western Italy with 177 hospitalised cats and high mortality]
Host: Domestic cats in animal shelters and rescue facilities (mainly kittens and juveniles).
Event.summary: Around 2010–2013, multiple large feline panleukopenia (FPV) outbreaks were documented in shelter populations in North America and Europe. In the USA, an adoption-guarantee shelter experienced a 10-month series of confirmed and suspected FPV cases with high morbidity and mortality in kittens, while in north-western Italy a multi-year outbreak originating in a single large shelter generated 177 hospitalised FPV cases over three years and became effectively endemic. Similar recurrent outbreaks and associated guidance on outbreak management were published for Dutch animal shelters, together indicating that FPV remained a leading cause of severe disease and death in shelter kittens despite long-standing availability of effective vaccines.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High turnover and crowding of cats in open-admission and large municipal or charity shelters; intake of many unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated kittens; delays in vaccination at intake; incomplete adherence to isolation, cohorting and sanitation protocols; high environmental stability of FPV with inadequate disinfection of rooms, cages and fomites. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel FPV genotype has been consistently implicated in these outbreaks; FPV and occasionally CPV-like strains were already endemic, so these episodes are best interpreted as re-occurrence events driven largely by management and population-risk factors rather than by major viral change.
Review: Decision: review (retain event). I refined the continent and subregion coding to “North America; Europe” with explicit reference to Northern America, Southern Europe (Italy) and Western Europe (Netherlands), and updated the country list to name the specific shelters and regions described in the main case-series and guideline papers. The event type has been changed from a generic multi-type coding to “re-occurrence only”, because FPV was long endemic in all these subregions and the outbreaks are best explained by shelter-level drivers (crowding, intake of unvaccinated kittens, breakdowns in vaccination and biosecurity) rather than by the emergence of a distinct new viral strain. The cited sources are appropriate for a composite shelter-outbreak episode, but human review is advised to confirm that aggregating multiple shelters and countries into a single 2010–2013 re-occurrence event meets the project’s expectations for event granularity.

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine indica
EPP.common.name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass

Host: Oil palm plantations and nurseries; maize (corn) fields
Event.summary: By the early 2010s, Indonesian oil palm nurseries and plantations were reporting Eleusine indica becoming dominant after repeated herbicide use, with early work noting poor control by glyphosate and the need for alternative graminicides. In 2012–2019, glyphosate‑ and paraquat‑resistant goosegrass was confirmed in North Sumatra oil palm, and subsequent studies showed additional resistance to ammonium glufosinate and widespread multiple‑resistant populations in Riau and West Kalimantan. By 2023–2025, greenhouse screening of maize‑field populations across six major maize‑producing provinces found widespread atrazine resistance and emerging mesotrione resistance in goosegrass, indicating multiple resistance across PS II and HPPD inhibitors on top of previously documented glyphosate and paraquat resistance and raising concerns for both oil palm and maize productivity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Monoculture oil palm with frequent non‑rotated use of glyphosate, paraquat and glufosinate in plantation inter‑rows; intensification of maize production with heavy reliance on atrazine–mesotrione mixtures; lack of crop and herbicide rotation; limited awareness of resistance principles among smallholders. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence with documented glyphosate and paraquat resistance indices up to ~4–6, confirmed glufosinate resistance in some biotypes, and greenhouse evidence of PS II (atrazine) and HPPD (mesotrione) resistance; involvement of both target‑site and metabolic (non‑target‑site) mechanisms; Enhanced Transmission through extensive seed production and local movement on contaminated machinery within plantation and maize landscapes.
Review: Decision: retain – Indonesian oil palm and maize studies consistently report glyphosate-, paraquat- and glufosinate-resistant goosegrass in North Sumatra, Riau and West Kalimantan and more recent atrazine/mesotrione resistance in maize across multiple provinces, justifying a single linked national event. The timing, geography and classification as re-emergence due to multiple herbicide resistance are appropriate; minor clarifications were added to the country field to make the provincial spread explicit but no re-typing was needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Coccidioides spp.
EPP.common.name: Coccidioides fungi
Countries: United States of America (California ‚Äì southern San Joaquin Valley counties, especially Kern and Tulare)
Host: Humans (residents of southern San Joaquin Valley counties, particularly Kern and Tulare)
Event.summary: After several years of relatively low reported incidence, central California experienced a marked coccidioidomycosis upsurge beginning in 1991 following a prolonged drought and unusually wet winters in the southern San Joaquin Valley. During 1991‚Äì1994, annual reported coccidioidomycosis cases in California rose roughly tenfold above the historical baseline to more than 4,500 cases per year, with the great majority occurring around Bakersfield and neighboring Kern and Tulare counties, leading to thousands of illnesses and substantial healthcare costs. By 1995, case numbers declined toward pre‚Äëepidemic levels, although they remained higher than in the 1980s, and subsequent analyses concluded that the epidemic reflected environmentally driven amplification of endemic strains rather than emergence of a single new clone.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Interaction of a multi‚Äëyear drought in the late 1980s followed by periods of heavy rainfall in 1991‚Äì1992, which favored fungal growth and later dust generation, combined with population growth and housing expansion in high‚Äërisk valley locations, increased occupational and outdoor recreational soil exposure, and many residents lacking prior immunity. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing of clinical isolates during the epidemic showed high genetic diversity and little linkage disequilibrium, indicating that no novel hypervirulent clone was responsible and supporting an interpretation of environmentally driven population increase of existing Coccidioides immitis lineages rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain ‚Äì New row added to capture the large 1991‚Äì1994 coccidioidomycosis epidemic in central California, during which annual reported cases rose from a long-term baseline of a few hundred to >4,500 per year, mainly in Kern/Tulare counties; this episode is clearly among the most impactful modern events and is well documented in CDC and J Clin Microbiol analyses. Classified as re-occurrence driven by climatic and demographic factors with no evidence for a novel epidemic clone.

EPP.scientific.name: Brucella spp.
EPP.common.name: brucellosis
Host: Humans (slaughterhouse workers and other exposed individuals in Paran√° State)
Event.summary: In 2014, a large outbreak of human brucellosis occurred among workers at a slaughterhouse in Pai√ßandu, Paran√° State, southern Brazil, where exposure to infected cattle carcasses and aerosols led to dozens of symptomatic infections. Over the ensuing three years, more than 3,500 potentially exposed workers and contacts across the state were evaluated, and 754 individuals were found seropositive for Brucella, making this the largest recorded human brucellosis outbreak in Brazil and revealing a substantial previously unrecognized burden. Review: review ‚Äì New event added for the 2014‚Äì2017 Pai√ßandu slaughterhouse outbreak in Paran√°, Brazil, described as the largest human brucellosis outbreak in the country, with 51 clinically defined outbreak cases and 754 seropositive individuals among more than 3,500 at‚Äërisk workers and contacts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6161910/?utm_source=openai)) Treated as a multi‚Äëyear occupational re‚Äëoccurrence in an endemic setting; there is no evidence of novel strains or spread to new continents. EPP.scientific.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
EPP.common.name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
Host: Adult renal and liver transplant recipients
Event.summary: Between 2007 and 2010, Denmark‚Äôs largest transplantation centre (Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen) experienced a major outbreak of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, with 29 cases among renal and liver transplant recipients in a setting where routine PCP prophylaxis was not used. Multilocus genotyping of respiratory specimens from cases and controls showed several distinct P. jirovecii genotypes circulating, with three predominant genotypes shared across clusters of renal and liver recipients, consistent with repeated nosocomial transmission along shared inpatient and outpatient pathways. After the outbreak investigation, the centre introduced systematic cotrimoxazole prophylaxis and enhanced infection-control measures for solid-organ transplant recipients, resulting in a marked decline in new PCP cases in this population. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23903011/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High volume of solid-organ transplantation and follow-up without standard long-term PCP prophylaxis; shared outpatient facilities and inpatient wards linking renal and liver recipients; intensive immunosuppressive regimens including treatment for rejection and cytomegalovirus infection. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (molecular evidence for clustering of specific P. jirovecii genotypes within and between organ groups); multiple pre-existing strains were involved rather than a single novel outbreak lineage. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23903011/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain: The 29-case Rigshospitalet outbreak in renal and liver transplant recipients (2007‚Äì2010) is accurately timed and located, and is clearly one of the largest documented nosocomial PCP outbreaks in solid-organ transplantation; it is retained as a key high-impact event, with classification adjusted from re-emergence to re-occurrence because several existing genotypes circulated under conditions of absent prophylaxis and intense patient contact. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23903011/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
EPP.common.name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
Host: Adult renal transplant recipients
Event.summary: In the early 2010s, a tertiary-care renal transplant centre in South India reported what was described as the first recognised outbreak of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia among its kidney transplant recipients, with a cluster of hospitalised patients developing PCP over a relatively short period after years in which the infection had been rare. Many affected patients were admitted for reasons other than suspected respiratory infection and only later developed respiratory failure with radiologic changes, underscoring low baseline awareness of PCP risk in this setting. After the cluster was recognised, the centre implemented more systematic cotrimoxazole prophylaxis and strengthened infection-control procedures, which were followed by a marked reduction in new PCP cases among their transplant recipients. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4165050/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of renal transplantation activity in India with limited routine use of prolonged PCP prophylaxis; high patient density and shared inpatient facilities in a large multispecialty hospital; delayed recognition of PCP as an important opportunistic infection in non-HIV immunocompromised patients in the region. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission is suspected based on temporal and spatial clustering in the transplant ward, but no detailed genotyping was reported; thus the episode is better framed as re-occurrence in a previously low-recognition setting. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4165050/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: The South Indian renal-transplant outbreak is genuine and important as the first reported cluster in this population, but the exact outbreak window is not clearly stated in the abstract and may be shorter (around 2012‚Äì2013) than the 2010‚Äì2013 span used here; the event is therefore retained but coded as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence, and its start and end years should be verified against the full text if precise dating is required. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4165050/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Varicellovirus humanalpha3
EPP.common.name: Varicella-zoster virus, Human alphaherpesvirus 3
Countries: United States of America (multiple Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centers, including South Texas Family Residential Center and Port Isabel Service Processing Center)
Host: Detained migrants (children and adults) in U.S. ICE facilities
Event.summary: Between January 1, 2017 and March 22, 2020, varicella circulated persistently across U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention centers, with 1,052 chickenpox cases identified among detained migrants and 26 distinct outbreaks documented in nine facilities. One family detention center in South Texas experienced a chickenpox outbreak that lasted 33 months, and nearly half of all varicella cases occurred in just two Texas centers. Transmission declined only after heightened awareness, limited vaccination efforts, and population turnover reduced the susceptible pool within affected facilities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extreme crowding, high population turnover, and frequent transfer of detainees between facilities; poor access to routine immunizations; many migrants originating from countries without universal varicella vaccination or with disrupted health services. Internal mechanisms: no novel VZV variants identified; outbreaks are driven by setting-related transmission dynamics and baseline susceptibility.
Review: Decision: retain, but note aggregation. Reason: this event aggregates 1,052 varicella cases and 26 outbreaks across interconnected ICE facilities over a 3-year period and is one of the largest documented VZV burdens in a detention system. Although individual outbreaks are spatially distinct, the prolonged, transfer-fueled transmission within the ICE network reasonably fits the "linked, recurrent episode in the same outbreak system" concept. Emergence type as re-occurrence is appropriate; no inter-continental or intra-continental emergence is involved because VZV was already endemic in North America.

EPP.scientific.name: Feline leukemia virus
EPP.common.name: FeLV
Host: Florida panther (Puma concolor coryi) in south Florida
Event.summary: Between 2001 and 2004, FeLV was detected for the first time in free‚Äëranging Florida panthers in south Florida after almost two decades of negative surveillance, with infections clustered in and around Okaloacoochee Slough, the Florida Panther National Wildlife Refuge, and parts of Big Cypress. Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The epizootic was most likely initiated by cross‚Äëspecies transmission from an FeLV‚Äëinfected domestic cat at the wildland‚Äìurban interface, facilitated by landscape fragmentation, increasing overlap between free‚Äëranging domestic cats and panther habitat, and the very small, genetically depauperate Florida panther population that heightened vulnerability to infectious disease. This episode represents host expansion (spillover) from domestic cats into Florida panthers coupled with novel strain/genotype emergence in this host, resulting in severe disease and high case fatality.

Geography (North America / Northern America, United States) and host specification (Florida panther) are appropriate. The J Wildl Dis epizootiology paper has been added as a key source alongside the EID articles and FWC summary. A human reviewer should verify the preferred start/end years and reconcile minor discrepancies among sources in the exact number of FeLV‚Äëattributed deaths.

EPP.scientific.name: Coccus pseudomagnoliarum
EPP.common.name: citricola scale
Countries: United States of America (California: Davis and surrounding areas in the northern Central Valley)
Host: Chinese hackberry (Celtis sinensis) and other ornamental/amenity trees; citrus present in the broader region but this study focused on hackberry infestations.
Event.summary: Following a severe population decline of citricola scale in northern California attributed to very cold winter conditions in 1990‚Äì1991, populations on Chinese hackberry trees in Davis, California began to recover starting in 1991. Between 1991 and 1994, a field study documented steadily increasing densities of female scales and crawlers on untreated hackberry trees each year, indicating a strong resurgence of this introduced subtropical species in urban landscapes. By 1994, high densities were again causing heavy honeydew and sooty mold accumulation, prompting evaluation of control options such as horticultural oil sprays and systemic insecticide trunk implants.

EPP.scientific.name: Helicoverpa armigera
EPP.common.name: cotton bollworm
Host: Cotton, maize, soybean, peanut and other smallholder field crops
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, northern China experienced exceptional Helicoverpa armigera population explosions, with particularly severe first and second generation outbreaks in Hebei Province in 1992 that infested nearly 800,000 ha of cotton and about 600,000 ha of wheat, with larval densities locally reaching nearly 200 larvae/m¬≤.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-4546?utm_source=openai)) These outbreaks, linked to favorable weather, abundant host crops and escalating insecticide resistance, persisted through the mid‚Äë1990s and caused major yield losses, making cotton bollworm the principal constraint on cotton production. In response, the Chinese government launched a major Bt‚Äëcotton development program in 1992 and commercial Bt cotton planting began in 1997, after which H. armigera pressure and related yield losses in cotton and associated crops declined sharply.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive monoculture of cotton, wheat and other hosts in northern China, with heavy reliance on chemical insecticides and favorable climatic conditions in 1991‚Äì1992 that enhanced overwinter survival and early season population build‚Äëup. Internal mechanisms: significant pre‚Äëexisting and further evolving resistance in H. armigera populations to widely used insecticides, combined with high dispersal capacity and fecundity, which produced a dramatic re‚Äëemergence of bollworm outbreaks in a long‚Äëinfested subregion and set the stage for Bt‚Äëcotton adoption.

EPP.scientific.name: Helicoverpa armigera

Event.summary: In 1994, cotton‚Äëgrowing areas of Pakistan experienced a major Helicoverpa armigera outbreak, during which growers responded with very frequent applications of pyrethroids and other insecticides; resistance monitoring showed that moderate resistance levels present in 1991‚Äì1993 escalated to very high levels from 1994 onwards.([cotton.org](https://www.cotton.org/beltwide/proceedings/1998/abstracts/483.cfm?utm_source=openai)) Over the 1994‚Äì1997 seasons, H. armigera remained one of the most destructive pests of Pakistani cotton, with widespread control failures and substantial yield losses reported across several cotton‚Äëproducing regions. EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio cholerae
EPP.common.name: Cholera bacterium
Host: Humans (internally displaced persons, drought‑affected rural and peri‑urban populations in Somalia)
Event.summary: After years of fragile health services and chronic WASH deficits, Somalia experienced a very large cholera outbreak in 2017, with over 78,000 suspected cases and about 1,150 deaths reported across 16 regions during a severe drought and food‑insecurity crisis. EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
EPP.common.name: gonoccocus
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2016-2018]
Host: Humans (pharyngeal and urogenital gonorrhoea, mainly in heterosexual men and women)
Event.summary: In 2016, the United Kingdom documented the first confirmed global failure to cure pharyngeal gonorrhoea using WHO‑recommended dual therapy with ceftriaxone (500 mg intramuscularly) plus azithromycin (1 g orally), in a patient infected with a highly resistant strain. In 2018, England reported an additional "super gonorrhoea" case with high‑level azithromycin resistance and ceftriaxone resistance that failed standard treatment and required alternative regimens, attracting wide public and professional attention. After intensive partner tracing, targeted testing and tailored high‑dose or alternative antibiotic regimens, onward transmission of these specific dual‑therapy‑resistant strains appeared limited, but the events underscored the fragility of last‑line treatment options.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reliance on dual therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin in response to rising cephalosporin MICs; frequent pharyngeal gonorrhoea in sexual networks where orogenital contact and limited condom use are common; subtherapeutic antibiotic exposure in the pharynx due to lower tissue drug levels and patient adherence issues; international travel importing highly resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Concurrent resistance to ceftriaxone (via mosaic penA and accessory mutations) and high‑level azithromycin resistance (23S rRNA mutations and efflux), resulting in extensively drug‑resistant N. gonorrhoeae; enhanced survival in the pharyngeal niche where reduced drug penetration and asymptomatic infections facilitate persistence and onward spread.
Review: Retain – This event highlights globally important dual-therapy treatment failures and extensively drug-resistant cases first documented in the UK (and contemporaneously in Australia) and is well supported by WHO, ECDC and NEJM reports. Classification as a re-emergence event linked to dual ceftriaxone and azithromycin resistance is appropriate, and no structural corrections were necessary.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans in multiple rural districts; Pteropus fruit bats (reservoir)
Event.summary: From 2003 through 2005, Bangladesh experienced recurrent winter–spring Nipah seasons in western and central districts including Naogaon, Manikganj, Rajbari, Faridpur and Tangail, together accounting for on the order of 90 human cases with very high case‑fatality ratios; the largest cluster occurred in Faridpur in 2004, with around 36 cases and 27 deaths, alongside smaller outbreaks in 2003 and 2005. Investigations showed that many primary cases had consumed fresh date palm sap shortly before illness, and several outbreaks featured clear family and neighbourhood transmission chains, consolidating recognition of the western "Nipah belt". Each seasonal episode waned as date‑palm sap harvesting ended and ad‑hoc risk‑communication campaigns were implemented, but these years established an almost annual pattern of Nipah emergence in Bangladesh.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: seasonal harvesting and consumption of raw date palm sap contaminated by bat urine or saliva, bat roosts located in and around affected villages, and intensive caregiving and funeral practices with little infection‑control infrastructure enabled repeated spillover and localized transmission. Internal mechanisms: stable circulation of Bangladesh‑lineage Nipah virus capable of direct bat‑to‑human foodborne transmission and limited person‑to‑person spread; no clear evidence of a distinct new genotype driving these particular seasons.
Review: retain – appropriately aggregates closely spaced 2003–2005 outbreaks in the same Bangladesh "Nipah belt" into a linked recurrent episode and classifies it as re‑occurrence within Southern Asia; geography, timeframe and qualitative magnitude match WHO and national summaries.

EPP.scientific.name: Scedosporium spp.
EPP.common.name: scedosporiosis
Host: Humans (previously healthy adults who nearly drowned in the March 11, 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami and developed delayed invasive scedosporiosis)
Event.summary: After the Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami of March 11, 2011, several near-drowning survivors developed severe Scedosporium infections, including a 59‑year‑old woman with lung and multiple brain abscesses due to S. apiospermum and later patients with tsunami-associated S. aurantiacum brain abscess and S. apiospermum vertebral osteomyelitis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223506/?utm_source=openai)) These cases occurred weeks to months after aspiration of heavily contaminated seawater mixed with soil and oil, and they were initially misdiagnosed as bacterial or Aspergillus infections before culture and molecular testing revealed Scedosporium spp.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223506/?utm_source=openai)) Following heightened awareness and targeted antifungal therapy (often voriconazole-based combinations), additional tsunami-related Scedosporium cases were not reported from the same coastal communities once acute disaster conditions and environmental contamination subsided.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223506/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large-scale coastal flooding and infrastructure destruction from the 2011 tsunami, which created stagnant, oil- and sewage-contaminated seawater and debris fields where Scedosporium spp. thrive; near-drowning with aspiration of this water; prolonged intensive care and broad-spectrum antibiotics; and delays in recognising mold infection because of its subacute course and initial similarity to bacterial pneumonia or common molds.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223506/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Enhanced adaptation of S. apiospermum and S. aurantiacum to polluted aquatic environments and damaged lung tissue; intrinsic resistance to amphotericin B with variable susceptibility to triazoles; and strong neurotropism and osteotropism leading to CNS abscesses and vertebral osteomyelitis after hematogenous spread.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24238227/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event). This row isolates the Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami–associated near-drowning scedosporiosis cases as a discrete emergence event in Eastern Asia, rather than aggregating them with the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, which occurred in a different subregion and time period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223506/?utm_source=openai)) The coding as re-occurrence is appropriate because Scedosporium was already established in Japan, and the event reflects disaster-driven resurgence rather than new geographic or host-system introduction. Event years (2011–2013) are inferred from case-report timelines and the disaster date and should be double-checked against the full texts during final curation.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria meningitidis
EPP.common.name: meningococcus
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From 2013 to 2015, the Australian state of Victoria and later other jurisdictions noted a sharp rise in invasive meningococcal disease caused by serogroup W Neisseria meningitidis, after many years in which this serogroup was rare. Molecular analysis showed that most MenW isolates belonged to the ST‑11 clonal complex and were closely related to the South American/UK lineage, indicating international spread of a hypervirulent clone into Australia. In response to increasing case numbers and severity, Victoria and then other Australian states implemented MenACWY conjugate vaccination programmes in adolescents and selected high‑risk groups, after which MenW incidence in vaccinated populations fell, though ST‑11 MenW persisted at lower levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of the MenW ST‑11 lineage through international travel into a population without routine MenW vaccination, combined with typical adolescent and young adult social mixing and high mobility within Australia, facilitated rapid establishment and spread. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of the globally circulating hypervirulent MenW ST‑11 ‘South American/UK’ strain into Oceania, with inherently high virulence and transmissibility, represents clonal re-emergence rather than true inter‑continental emergence of the species in a country with long‑standing meningococcal disease.
Review: review – Retain as an important extension of the MenW ST‑11 wave into Oceania but correct emergence typing. Australia has had endemic meningococcal disease for decades; this event concerns the introduction and expansion of a particular MenW ST‑11 lineage, not first continental occurrence of the species. I therefore set both inter_continental_emergence and intra_continental_emergence to false and kept re_emergence as true. The countries, time span and sources remain appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis

Over 2010–2012, case investigations, serosurveys and environmental sampling identified multiple autochthonous human infections and isolated B. pseudomallei from soil, confirming that melioidosis is regionally endemic in parts of Puerto Rico rather than limited to imported infections. After these studies, sporadic locally acquired cases continued to occur, but heightened clinician awareness and environmental data allowed more rapid diagnosis and management instead of large undiscovered outbreaks.

Internal mechanisms: recognition of established environmental foci of B. pseudomallei in Puerto Rico and probable long‑standing low‑diversity local strain circulation, rather than emergence of a novel genotype.

Earlier sporadic human cases and environmental detections in the wider Caribbean meant the sub-region was not new; this 2010–2012 cluster, investigations, and soil isolation fit the definition of re-occurrence driven by external factors (rainfall and improved surveillance). Event.summary: Beginning in 2001, enhanced surveillance for viral hemorrhagic fevers around Makkah and the nearby Alkhumra district identified a cluster of suspected Alkhurma hemorrhagic fever cases among residents and visitors with occupational or household exposure to livestock and ticks. The episode subsided after 2003 with no evidence of sustained human‑to‑human transmission, but AHFV was recognized as an endemic zoonotic threat in the western region and incorporated into national hemorrhagic fever surveillance and control guidelines.

Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel viral genotype or major change in virulence was reported during this period; the pattern is best explained by re‑occurrence driven by environmental and behavioral factors plus improved surveillance rather than intrinsic viral change, so it is classified as re‑occurrence and not re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event appropriately summarizes the 2001–2003 Alkhumra/Makkah cluster (37 suspected, 20 confirmed cases), with correct continent/sub‑region (Asia | Western Asia), country assignment (Saudi Arabia) and classification as re‑occurrence in a previously affected western Saudi focus; no changes required.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus B

Event.summary: Around 2008, Japan reported a large echovirus 30–associated aseptic meningitis outbreak in the Tokyo metropolitan area, contributing a substantial proportion of meningitis cases that year. EPP.scientific.name: Alcelaphine gammaherpesvirus 1

Event.summary: From 2014 to 2016, Kapiti Plains Ranch in south‑eastern Kenya recorded recurrent seasonal peaks of wildebeest‑associated malignant catarrhal fever in ranch cattle, with 325 animals showing clinical signs over three years and a substantial proportion confirmed as AlHV‑1 infections by PCR and ELISA. Disease incidence rose each year following the wildebeest calving season as cattle grazed within mixed wildlife–livestock landscapes, generating annual herd‑level losses that in some years approached 10% in parts of the ranch. Incidence declined after implementation of wildebeest‑avoidance measures and participation in experimental vaccination trials, but WA‑MCF remained an important seasonal constraint on cattle production in this ecosystem.

The cited BMC Veterinary Research paper documents recurrent outbreaks in Kapiti Plains Ranch (Kenya) from 2014–2016 with 325 clinically affected cattle; it does not provide evidence for a single epidemiologically linked 2014–2016 outbreak in Tanzania. EPP.scientific.name: Aphanomyces invadans

Host: Farmed snakeheads (Channa punctata and other Channa spp.), Indian major carps (Labeo rohita, Cirrhinus mrigala, Cirrhinus reba) and small cyprinids (Puntius spp.) in earthen ponds and connected Indus River floodplain systems in Punjab and Sindh provinces.
Event.summary: In April 1996, Pakistan reported severe ulcerative disease outbreaks in farmed snakeheads in Punjab that were confirmed histologically as epizootic ulcerative syndrome caused by Aphanomyces invadans, representing the first recognised occurrence of EUS in the country but within an already affected South Asian region.([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jsfp1966/33/4/33_4_321/_article?utm_source=openai)) During 1996–1998, EUS spread rapidly through pond systems and into the Indus River floodplain, with subsequent confirmation in Indian major carps and other cyprinids in Sindh and estimates that around 20% of farms were affected in some divisions following major floods.([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jsfp1966/33/4/33_4_321/_article?utm_source=openai)) By the late 1990s, the disease was considered endemic in parts of the Indus basin, with ongoing but more localised outbreaks and continuing concerns about long‑term impacts on inland fisheries and rural livelihoods.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy monsoon flooding in 1996 facilitated movement of infected fish and water between ponds and river channels; extensive use of surface water, poor pond biosecurity and expanding semi‑intensive carp and snakehead aquaculture increased host density and connectivity, enabling rapid spread.([oie.int](https://www.oie.int/fileadmin/Home/eng/Health_standards/aahm/current/chapitre_aphanomyces_invadans.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Available evidence indicates Pakistan’s outbreaks were caused by the same Asian clonal genotype of A. invadans described elsewhere, without evidence of a novel strain; disease emergence here chiefly reflects geographic and host‑population expansion within Southern Asia, mediated by environmental and management factors, rather than evolutionary change in the pathogen.

Because EUS was already established in Southern Asia (Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka) before 1990, Pakistan’s 1996 outbreak is not an intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD sub-region and should not be tagged as first_detection; it is best classified as a regional re-occurrence driven by flooding and aquaculture expansion.([oie.int](https://www.oie.int/fileadmin/Home/eng/Health_standards/aahm/current/chapitre_aphanomyces_invadans.pdf))
