EPP.scientific.name: BSE prion
EPP.common.name: Mad cow disease, BSE
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event.summary: In May 2003, Canada confirmed BSE in a native-born beef cow in Alberta, the first recognised indigenous North American case and evidence of domestic feed-borne transmission. Intensive tracing, culling of cohorts, and expanded surveillance over 2003–2005 uncovered additional infected cattle from the same high-risk birth cohorts, while more than 30 countries imposed partial or total bans on Canadian beef and live cattle exports, causing severe economic disruption. Canada responded with stricter feed controls, specified-risk-material removal, and a large national surveillance programme, after which BSE incidence declined to very low levels and the country progressed toward, and ultimately achieved, negligible BSE risk status.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Historical use of ruminant MBM in Canadian cattle feed prior to the 1997 ruminant-to-ruminant feed ban; possible importation of contaminated MBM from Europe; high-intensity commercial beef and dairy production; strong trade incentives that encouraged rapid surveillance and policy tightening once indigenous BSE was detected. Internal mechanisms: Inter-continental emergence of classical BSE in North American cattle herds with sustained amplification via contaminated feed; long incubation periods allowing infected birth cohorts to persist after initial control measures, until enhanced bans and removal of specified risk materials broke the cycle.
Review: retain – This is a major global BSE emergence episode: the first recognised indigenous classical BSE outbreak in North America, with substantial trade and production impacts. The inter_continental_emergence flag is appropriate because this is the first evidence of sustained feed-borne BSE transmission in a new continent (earlier Canadian and Omani cases were imported-only). The original re_emergence = Yes has been corrected to re_emergence = No, as there is no evidence of a new strain or prior elimination and reappearance in the same subregion; this is the initial establishment of classical BSE in North America.

EPP.scientific.name: Canine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Canine distemper virus, CDV
Host: Santa Catalina Island fox (Urocyon littoralis catalinae); domestic dogs and/or raccoons as likely introduction vectors
Event.summary: In the late 1990s, a virulent CDV epidemic swept through the endemic island fox population on Santa Catalina Island, California. Fox numbers on the island crashed from an estimated ~1,300 adults in 1990 to roughly 100 animals by 1999–2000, with foxes east of the Two Harbors isthmus suffering an ~85–90% decline following detection of CDV in carcasses. The epidemic burned through the immunologically naïve population until emergency measures—including captive breeding, translocation of foxes from the unaffected western subpopulation, and widespread CDV vaccination—stabilized numbers and initiated a slow recovery, though CDV remains a central long‑term threat.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of CDV to an isolated, previously unexposed island fox population via an infected domestic dog or raccoon arriving by boat from mainland California; high local fox densities and close proximity to human settlements facilitated rapid fox‑to‑fox transmission once CDV was introduced; small population size and restricted range greatly increased extirpation risk. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a dog-lineage CDV strain into an insular canid with no prior immunity, producing very high case fatality and a population crash; subsequent models and monitoring show that even infrequent CDV incursions can drive quasi‑extinction without continued vaccination and biosecurity.
Review: review - Newly added event. A CDV epidemic on Santa Catalina Island (USA) in 1998–2000 reduced the endemic island fox population by ~85–90% (from ~1,300 to ~100 animals) and is widely regarded as a near-extinction event that triggered ESA listing and intensive management, so it clearly qualifies among the top global CDV emergence events post-1990. Classified as 're_emergence' (host expansion and severe impact in a new wildlife host within the animal system) rather than first_detection or inter-continental emergence. Years, geography (North America | Northern America; United States) and host assignment follow King et al. 2014, Kohlmann et al. 2005 and related sources and should be retained but could be fine-tuned further if more precise onset dates are desired.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyvirus cyprinidallo3

Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of CyHV‑3 into African freshwater systems through infected hosts, facilitated by the virus’s environmental stability in water and its capacity for subclinical infection and latency that allow long‑distance movement and later recrudescence.
Review: retain – Event appropriately captures the first documented emergence of CyHV‑3 in Africa (South Africa 2001–2003), with correct continent/subregion coding and classification as an inter‑continental emergence episode. Updated the country-year annotation to New Zealand [2017–2019] in line with retrospective detection and circulation studies. The event clearly remains one of the major emergence episodes for this EPP in Oceania and merits retention, but is flagged for expert confirmation of the end date as RHDV2 continues to circulate at lower levels.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica

Host: Sheep (ewes and lambs) in ovine flocks
Event.summary: From the 2003/2004 to 2004/2005 lambing seasons, several sheep flocks in western Switzerland experienced large abortion storms, with up to 70% fetal losses in some flocks, and Salmonella enterica serovar Abortusovis was identified as the causative agent after decades during which this serovar had not been officially reported in the country. Internal mechanisms: Available data point to re‑introduction and expansion of existing ovine‑adapted lineages rather than emergence of a novel, genetically distinct strain.

Based on detailed Swiss outbreak and seroprevalence studies, the event window has been broadened to 2003–2005 rather than a single year, the sub‑region label standardized to 'Europe: Western Europe', and the event type set to re_occurrence only (re_occurrence = Yes; re_emergence = No). EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans and non-human primates; sylvatic cycle with Haemagogus/Sabethes mosquitoes, with substantial spillover risk to urban Aedes aegypti
Event.summary: From late 2016, Brazil experienced a massive sylvatic yellow fever epidemic starting in Minas Gerais and spreading through São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo, Bahia and other states, causing 778 confirmed human cases and 262 deaths in 2016–2017 and 1,376 confirmed cases and 483 deaths in 2017–2018, along with extensive die‑offs of non-human primates. The virus advanced southward and eastward into the Atlantic Forest and coastal belt, reaching areas close to major urban centres that had been considered risk‑free for decades, and numerous unvaccinated international and regional travellers (including from Argentina, Chile and Europe) acquired infection while visiting affected Brazilian states. Large‑scale emergency and preventive vaccination campaigns, adoption of a single‑dose policy and, in some areas, use of fractional doses, together with strengthened epizootic surveillance and vector control, eventually reduced transmission, and seasonal case numbers declined after 2018, though low‑level activity has recurred.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Encroachment into forested areas, ecological conditions favouring sylvatic vectors, low or uneven vaccination coverage in newly affected coastal and southeastern regions, and national and international travel of unvaccinated people into forested recreational and occupational settings all contributed to the magnitude and geographic expansion of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic work indicates that a yellow fever virus lineage from the Amazon region was introduced into southeastern Brazil and spread efficiently through multiple neotropical monkey species but does not demonstrate novel virulence or vaccine escape, so the event is best characterised as a large re-occurrence with major geographic range expansion rather than re-emergence driven by intrinsic viral change.
Review: retain – Confirmed by WHO, PAHO, ECDC and CDC as the largest yellow fever epidemic in Brazil for many decades (over 2,100 confirmed human cases and hundreds of deaths) with major geographic expansion toward the Atlantic coast; this clearly fits among the top 10 global events. Event types have been adjusted so that only re-occurrence is marked (no strong evidence for intrinsic viral re-emergence), and the country list has been restricted to Brazil, with infections in travellers from Argentina, Chile and elsewhere treated as travel-related exposures rather than separate transmission foci.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans; non-human primates and mosquitoes in sylvatic and peri-sylvatic cycles
Event.summary: Following the 2013 episode, Ethiopia experienced renewed yellow fever activity with an outbreak in August 2018 in Wolayita Zone (SNNPR) that caused 35 reported cases, and a larger outbreak in 2020 in Enor-Ener Woreda, Gurage Zone, with around 85 suspected cases and four deaths. These events occurred in districts identified as high‑risk in sub‑national risk assessments, reflecting expanding zones of sylvatic transmission and very low population immunity in parts of SNNPR and adjacent Oromia. Reactive vaccination campaigns in 2018 and 2020, embedded within Ethiopia’s engagement in the EYE strategy and combined with strengthened surveillance and risk mapping, halted active transmission in the newly affected areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of human settlement and agriculture into ecologically suitable zones for yellow fever transmission, very low routine vaccination coverage before EYE implementation, and incomplete preventive mass vaccination in high‑risk districts facilitated spread into previously unaffected woredas. Internal mechanisms: Available data point to geographic range expansion and spatial clustering of existing viral lineages within an endemic country, without evidence of a distinct new genotype or resistance phenotype; therefore this is best described as re-occurrence rather than pathogen-level re-emergence.
Review: review – Retained as a combined 2018 and 2020 Ethiopia episode because together they represent a notable expansion of yellow fever risk zones within an endemic country and prompted substantial vaccination activities, but total case numbers remain modest relative to Sudan 2005/2012, Angola 2015–2016, Brazil 2016–2018 and Nigeria 2017–2020. Event-type has been corrected from re-emergence to re-occurrence, since available evidence points to spatial spread of existing lineages rather than intrinsic viral change.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia graminea
EPP.common.name: grassleaf spurge
Host: Weed in disturbed and urban habitats (Eleuthera and New Providence Islands), likely associated with horticultural sites.([phytoneuron.net](https://www.phytoneuron.net/2013Phytoneuron/20PhytoN-BahamaEuphorb.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Event.summary: Between about 2011 and 2013 botanists discovered grassleaf spurge on Eleuthera and New Providence in the Bahamas, where it was growing as a weedy species in disturbed habitats, and in 2013 it was formally reported as new to the Bahamian flora. The species appears to have been introduced through the horticultural trade, consistent with its ornamental use elsewhere, and was observed in multiple localities on the two islands by the time of publication. The report highlighted it as an invasive alien requiring attention, but long‑term spread or control outcomes in the archipelago have not yet been fully described.([phytoneuron.net](https://www.phytoneuron.net/2013Phytoneuron/20PhytoN-BahamaEuphorb.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction and repeated dispersal via horticultural imports and nursery trade within the Bahamas; secondary spread facilitated by disturbance around resorts, residential areas and roads. Internal mechanisms: generalist weed traits, including tolerance of dry, sandy soils and strong seed production, allow successful establishment in coastal and urban environments; this event represents geographic range expansion within the Caribbean where the species is already native in other islands (e.g., Cuba, Dominican Republic).([phytoneuron.net](https://www.phytoneuron.net/2013Phytoneuron/20PhytoN-BahamaEuphorb.pdf?utm_source=openai))

EPP.common.name: grassleaf spurge
Host: Weed in disturbed habitats on a research farm and other disturbed sites near Tripoli (Faculty of Agriculture research farm, University of Tripoli).([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/401132662_Euphorbia_graminea_Jacq_Euphorbiaceae_-A_new_distributional_record_for_the_flora_of_Libya))
Event.summary: Between about 2023 and 2025 botanists in Tripoli observed an unusual Euphorbia in disturbed habitats on the University of Tripoli’s agricultural research farm, later confirmed as grassleaf spurge and described in 2026 as a new distributional record for Libya. Internal mechanisms: characteristic invasive‑weed traits such as prolific seed production, explosive dehiscence and tolerance of disturbed, semi‑arid Mediterranean conditions enable naturalization in Northern Africa without evidence of new genetic change.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/401132662_Euphorbia_graminea_Jacq_Euphorbiaceae_-A_new_distributional_record_for_the_flora_of_Libya))

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopneumovirus hominis
EPP.common.name: Human Respiratory syncytial virus, RSV
Countries: France [2023-2025] (nationwide infant nirsevimab programme with reduced RSV bronchiolitis hospitalizations and surveillance-detected RSV-B variants carrying nirsevimab resistance-associated substitutions)
Host: Humans (infants in their first RSV season; focus on medically vulnerable and general infant population)
Event.summary: Beginning in mid‑September 2023, France implemented one of the first nationwide programmes offering the long‑acting monoclonal antibody nirsevimab (Beyfortus) to almost all infants entering their first RSV season, which led to a substantial reduction in RSV bronchiolitis hospitalizations during the 2023–2024 season compared with pre‑programme years. Intensive virologic surveillance of infants with breakthrough RSV infections during 2023–2024 identified rare RSV‑B viruses carrying substitutions at the nirsevimab binding site (notably F:N208D and an I64M+K65R combination) that conferred marked reductions in in‑vitro susceptibility to nirsevimab. Subsequent national multicentre analyses across the first two programme seasons (2023–2025) documented additional resistant RSV‑B variants but still found resistance‑associated substitutions in only a small minority of sequenced breakthrough cases, highlighting the early emergence—but as yet limited spread—of monoclonal antibody–resistant RSV under large‑scale prophylactic pressure. ([santepubliquefrance.fr](https://www.santepubliquefrance.fr/en/node/35309?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Policy decisions to introduce universal or near‑universal nirsevimab prophylaxis for infants in France from 2023–2024 onwards, together with intense RSV circulation in the early post‑COVID period and strong laboratory surveillance networks, created both strong selective pressure at the F‑protein antigenic site Ø and the capacity to detect emerging escape variants. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial / monoclonal antibody resistance, via RSV‑B variants with amino‑acid substitutions in the nirsevimab binding site (e.g. N208D and related patterns) that substantially reduce neutralization in vitro; emergence and onward transmission of these escape variants represents a form of re‑emergence, although current data suggest that fitness costs are sufficient to keep their prevalence low so far. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39419046/?dopt=Abstract&utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. I recommend retaining this event as an important early example of monoclonal‑antibody resistance emerging in RSV under national‑scale prophylaxis, but with caveats: resistant RSV‑B variants remain rare (a small fraction of sequenced breakthrough infections) and the clinical impact on overall RSV burden is limited so far. I kept the timeframe as 2023–2025 to capture the first two programme seasons and the 2026 multicentre resistance analysis, standardised country/region naming, and refocused the event summary on documented resistance frequencies rather than suggesting that resistant viruses account for a “meaningful minority” of all breakthrough cases. Classification as ‘re-emergence’ driven by antimicrobial resistance is appropriate, but continued surveillance will be needed to determine whether this ultimately qualifies among the ten highest‑impact emergence events for RSV.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: EEEV, EEE virus
Countries: Canada [2008-2010] (primarily Quebec, Nova Scotia and parts of Ontario)
Host: Horses; emus and other ratites on affected farms
Event.summary: Between 2008 and 2010, Eastern equine encephalitis emerged as an important epizootic disease in eastern Canada, beginning with an outbreak in southern Quebec in fall 2008 that killed multiple horses and emus after decades in which EEE had been only sporadically recognized in the country. Follow‑up surveillance and case reports documented additional clusters of equine disease in Quebec, localized outbreaks in Nova Scotia and further confirmed cases in Ontario, with Canadian reviews estimating on the order of several dozen equine cases in Quebec and more than ten in Nova Scotia over this three‑year period. These episodes led provincial and federal authorities to expand mosquito and equine surveillance, alert veterinarians and horse owners, and promote vaccination programs in newly affected areas; equine case numbers declined after 2010, but serological and pathology data indicated that EEEV had become established in local bird–mosquito cycles.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Northward dispersal of infected birds and mosquitoes from long‑standing U.S. foci, together with suitable wetland habitats in southern Quebec and the Maritimes and low baseline equine vaccination coverage, likely facilitated establishment of EEEV transmission in eastern Canada; warm, wet summers during 2008–2010 probably increased vector abundance and contact between vectors and horses. Internal mechanisms: Available Canadian and U.S. sequence data are consistent with circulation of typical North American EEEV strains introduced from U.S. source populations rather than the emergence of a novel genotype, so these outbreaks are best classified as geographic and incidence re‑occurrence within the Northern America subregion rather than as genetic re‑emergence or intra‑continental emergence.
Review: review – New event added because multiple Canadian sources describe unprecedented clusters of EEE in Quebec and Nova Scotia from 2008–2010 (roughly 40–50 horses plus emus affected), characterizing this period as emergence of EEE as an epizootic disease in eastern Canada; coded as re‑occurrence in the Northern America subregion (the project’s rules specify that spread to new countries within a subregion is not scored as intra‑continental emergence). Approximate provincial counts and the choice of 2008–2010 as a linked episode window should be verified by a domain expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: EEEV, EEE virus
Countries: United States of America [2011-2013] (Vermont – primarily Rutland and Addison counties)
Host: Emus (ratites on a commercial farm); horses; humans (linked but dead-end hosts)
Event.summary: In 2011, Vermont documented its first recognized outbreak of Eastern equine encephalitis when an emu farm in Rutland County experienced high mortality among birds that tested positive for EEEV, and virus was isolated from emu brain tissue. The following year, Vermont reported its first two human EEE cases, both in residents of the Rutland–Addison area who developed severe neuroinvasive disease and died, and additional equine cases in 2012–2013 confirmed that EEEV had become established in local mosquito–bird cycles in parts of western Vermont. After 2013, no further human or equine cases were detected for nearly a decade, but the 2011–2013 episode led to implementation of statewide mosquito surveillance, sustained public‑health messaging and incorporation of equine and ratite vaccination and mosquito control into Vermont’s arbovirus response planning.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Spread of infected birds and mosquitoes from established EEEV foci in neighboring New York and New Hampshire, combined with suitable wetland habitats and seasonal mosquito abundance in the Otter Creek and Lemon Fair watersheds, likely permitted establishment of local transmission; outdoor ratite flocks and unvaccinated horses in these areas were highly exposed to biting mosquitoes. Internal mechanisms: Available sequence data indicate that the Vermont viruses belong to typical North American EEEV lineage I without evidence of a novel genotype, so this linked 2011–2013 episode is best viewed as geographic and incidence re‑occurrence in a newly affected state within an existing Northern America focus rather than genetic re‑emergence.
Review: review – Original event year and summary incorrectly implied that two fatal human cases occurred in 2011; these have been corrected by expanding the event window to 2011–2013 and explicitly describing the 2011 emu‑farm outbreak followed by two fatal human cases and several equine cases in 2012–2013. Type coding as a re‑occurrence (not first detection or intra‑continental emergence) is preserved, in line with the project rule that spread to a new U.S. state within Northern America is not coded as intra‑continental emergence. A subject‑matter expert should confirm the chosen 2011–2013 episode boundaries.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Maconellicoccus hirsutus
EPP.common.name: hibiscus mealybug
Host: Cacao (Theobroma cacao) as a newly emphasized, economically important host, alongside other perennial crops and associated shade or border plants
Event.summary: After hibiscus mealybug had been present in Mexico on ornamentals and other hosts since the late 1990s, severe infestations were reported in cacao plantations in Tabasco in the mid‑2010s, where the pest damaged shoots, leaves and pods and caused noticeable yield loss and dieback. The mealybug exploited both cacao and associated shade or border plants, and its emergence as a key pest in cacao systems prompted detailed studies of damage symptoms, host associations and local natural enemies. By the late 2010s, management recommendations specific to cacao (monitoring, cultural measures and compatible biological and chemical controls) were being developed, illustrating the pest’s capacity to re‑emerge as a serious problem on new, high‑value perennial crop hosts within an already infested region.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281034453_Biological_Control_of_Pink_Hibiscus_Mealybug_Project_Manual?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of cacao cultivation in warm, humid lowland regions with diverse shade trees and border vegetation that serve as alternative hosts; movement of infested planting material and pruned branches between farms; limited initial monitoring of mealybugs in cacao systems, allowing populations to build before being recognized as a major problem. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and re‑emergence on a major new economic host (cacao) within an already infested landscape; high adaptability and polyphagy of M. hirsutus, enabling successful exploitation of cacao tissues and associated shade plants; potential development of locally adapted populations or shifts in natural enemy complexes that increased its prominence in cacao relative to earlier ornamental‑focused infestations.
Review: review – This cacao‑focused episode is real and well documented for Tabasco, Mexico, and illustrates a clear host‑range driven re‑emergence of M. hirsutus within an already infested country, so it is appropriate to keep it as one of the major events. The main correction needed was geographic: Mexico belongs to the Central America sub‑region within the South America continent group in the project’s country list, so the sub‑regions field has been restricted to Central America rather than “Central America; South America.”([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/media/data/reporting/rs-2011-04-en.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re‑emergence (rather than a new inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence) is consistent with the fact that the pest had been present in Mexico on other hosts since 1999 and that the novelty here lies in its rise to prominence on cacao. Recommended action: retain but keep flagged for review to confirm the relative importance of this host‑shift episode compared with other possible crop‑specific re‑emergence events (e.g. on grapes or mulberry in Asia).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Duck herpesvirus 1, Duck plague virus
Host: Commercial and backyard ducks (especially Muscovy and local breeds) of various ages in multiple provinces
Event.summary: From 2016 to 2018, Egypt experienced widespread duck viral enteritis outbreaks across several provinces, with examined flocks showing approximately 75% mortality and a 40% drop in egg production; diagnosis was confirmed through characteristic lesions, virus isolation in embryonated duck eggs, and PCR targeting the DEV DNA polymerase gene.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense duck production in the Nile Delta, inadequate or improperly implemented vaccination programs, poor biosecurity in both commercial and backyard systems, and potential involvement of migratory waterfowl contributed to high DVE incidence and severe flock-level impacts. Internal mechanisms: Sequenced isolates showed typical virulent DEV genomic features without strong evidence of a radically novel genotype, indicating re-occurrence of pathogenic field strains in a vulnerable production system rather than emergence of a taxonomically new variant.
Review: retain – Added as a major recent African epizootic: multi-province outbreaks with ~75% mortality and substantial production losses make this one of the largest documented DVE events in Egypt. Correctly coded as re-occurrence in Africa/Northern Africa, Egypt; provinces are listed explicitly from the primary study. Exact flock counts per outbreak are not given in the abstract and should be consulted in the full paper for precise quantitative ranking.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Seeded by viruses from the 2004–2006 Indian Ocean outbreaks, chikungunya re‑appeared in India in 2005–2006 after roughly three decades of apparent absence, spreading to at least 16 states and causing about 1.3–1.4 million suspected cases in 2006 alone. From 2006 onward, related East/Central/South African lineage viruses caused major epidemics in Sri Lanka and the Maldives and then moved through parts of Indonesia, Malaysia and southern Thailand, where large outbreaks occurred in 2008–2009 after more than a decade without transmission. By around 2010, incidence had declined or become sporadic in many of these areas, but the virus established new endemic foci and left large cohorts with post‑epidemic rheumatologic sequelae.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2006_10_17-en?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of Aedes aegypti in tropical urban and peri‑urban environments, inadequate vector control infrastructure, and intense human travel within South and South‑East Asia facilitated rapid dissemination once reintroduced. Large, immunologically naive populations supported explosive transmission, especially in densely populated Indian states and major cities in Indonesia and Thailand. Internal mechanisms: Continued spread of the ECSA/Indian Ocean lineage, including viruses bearing E1‑A226V and related mutations, increased fitness in Aedes albopictus and may have enhanced transmissibility, supporting re‑emergence across a wide climatic range in Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4754000/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event narrowed to Asia only and extended through 2010 to capture the full South and South‑East Asian re‑emergence wave. Pacific island introductions (New Caledonia, Papua New Guinea, Yap) were removed from the country list and are treated separately in Oceania‑focused events. Emergence‑type flags were simplified to re‑emergence only: chikungunya was already known in Southern and South‑eastern Asia, and spread to new countries within the same subregions does not qualify as intra‑continental emergence under the project rules. Wikipedia and a Western Hemisphere EID paper were replaced with region‑specific WHO and peer‑reviewed sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Sub.regions: Caribbean; Central America; South America; Northern America
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Following the 2013–2014 Caribbean introduction, chikungunya reached mainland South America in early 2014, with French Guiana reporting imported and then locally acquired cases and an estimated >16,000 clinical cases in Cayenne and surroundings. Over 2014–2016, autochthonous transmission was documented across most Central and South American countries and parts of Mexico, as well as small clusters of local transmission in Florida, USA; by late July 2016, the Region of the Americas had recorded roughly 2.9 million suspected and confirmed cases and nearly 300 deaths since the virus’s arrival. Co‑circulation with dengue and later Zika complicated diagnosis and strained health systems but also prompted major investments in Aedes control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5137246/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high Aedes aegypti densities in urban centers across Latin America, coupled with water storage practices, inadequate housing and vector control gaps, allowed chikungunya to follow pathways previously established by dengue. Rapid regional air and land travel facilitated dissemination from Caribbean foci into mainland countries, where climatic conditions and existing vector populations supported sustained transmission. Internal mechanisms: The same Asian lineage that seeded the Caribbean was the main driver of epidemics across mainland Americas; its traits supported efficient replication in Aedes aegypti but no single novel mutation was uniquely implicated. This event is best classified as intra‑continental emergence within the Americas following the initial inter‑continental introduction.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5137246/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retained as one of the highest‑impact events globally (>2.9 million reported cases across the Americas by mid‑2016). The continent field was cleaned (removal of duplicate “South America (including Central America and the Caribbean)” label), and the emergence type was recoded as intra‑continental emergence only, because the inter‑continental jump into the Americas is already captured in the 2013–2014 Caribbean event. Country list focuses on heavily affected mainland countries and the small but epidemiologically important Florida clusters.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Betainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza B virus
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans, with continued susceptibility in children but markedly reduced overall influenza activity in 2020–2021
Event.summary: Following the onset of the COVID‑19 pandemic in early 2020, global influenza activity collapsed, but among the few influenza B detections almost all were B/Victoria-lineage and virological surveillance recorded no confirmed naturally occurring B/Yamagata-lineage viruses after March 2020.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7976381/?utm_source=openai)) During the 2020–2021 and 2021–2022 seasons, countries in East Asia, Europe, North America and Oceania that did observe influenza circulation reported overwhelming dominance of B/Victoria, while B/Yamagata remained undetected despite continued typing and sequencing.([who.int](https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/influenza-update-n-381?utm_source=openai)) By 2023–2024, WHO and national advisory bodies concluded that inclusion of a B/Yamagata antigen in seasonal vaccines was no longer warranted and recommended a transition back to trivalent vaccines containing only a B/Victoria component, marking a major reconfiguration of global influenza B ecology.([cdn.who.int](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/influenza/who-influenza-recommendations/vcm-southern-hemisphere-recommendation-2024/202309_recommendation.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=2c2cbebd_7&utm_source=openai))

Review: Decision: review – updated sub-regions to remove unsupported 'South-eastern Asia' (no specific countries listed) and reclassified the episode as re-emergence, reflecting the lineage-level restructuring of influenza B (apparent disappearance of B/Yamagata and dominance of B/Victoria) rather than a simple re-occurrence of typical seasonal activity; descriptions now align more closely with WHO and national vaccine‑composition recommendations.

EPP.scientific.name: Hepatovirus A
EPP.common.name: Hepatitis A virus
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; South America; Northern America
Countries: United States of America (selected MSM clusters) [2016-2018]
Host: Humans, predominantly men who have sex with men (MSM), with some spread to other adults
Event.summary: Between mid-2016 and 2018, an unusual wave of hepatitis A outbreaks occurred across at least 22 EU/EEA countries and extended into the Americas, disproportionately affecting men who have sex with men (MSM), with over 4,400 outbreak-confirmed cases reported in Europe alone and hundreds of related cases in Chile, Argentina, Brazil, the United States and Canada. The outbreaks began with clusters at MSM social venues and events in Western Europe and spread through sexual networks and international travel, with molecular typing showing three closely related HAV genotype IA strains (VRD_521_2016, RIVM-HAV16-090 and V16_25801) shared between European and American MSM outbreaks. Intensified vaccination campaigns targeting MSM, sexual health messaging, and depletion of susceptibles gradually reduced transmission by 2018, though some countries in Latin America continued to report MSM-associated clusters into 2019.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High susceptibility among adult MSM in low- or medium-endemicity countries due to limited prior natural infection and incomplete vaccination coverage; dense sexual networks and large MSM gatherings (e.g. Pride events); international travel connecting European and American MSM communities; global HAV vaccine shortages that hampered rapid scale-up of targeted immunisation. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of specific HAV genotype IA strains capable of efficient person-to-person transmission via sexual and close contact routes, but without clear evidence of fundamentally increased virulence; overall pattern is best characterized as behavioral and immunity-pattern-driven re-occurrence rather than emergence of a new viral lineage.
Review: review – This represents a major, well-documented global outbreak wave among MSM (≈4,475 outbreak-confirmed cases in 22 EU/EEA countries plus large MSM-associated epidemics in Chile and other American countries) and clearly belongs among the highest-impact events. Classification as re-occurrence (rather than inter-continental emergence or re-emergence) is appropriate, since HAV was long established in all affected regions and no fundamentally new genotype emerged. However, the countries column uses a placeholder (“other EU/EEA countries”) and mixes European and American MSM clusters that are epidemiologically linked but sometimes treated as separate sub-episodes; there is also potential overlap with the Latin America MSM 2017–2019 event row. Recommend: (i) replacing the placeholder with the explicit 22 EU/EEA country list from ECDC; and (ii) agreeing at dataset level whether all MSM outbreaks linked to the three IA strains (Europe + Americas) should be merged into one global MSM episode (2016–2019) or kept as regional sub-events to avoid double counting. ([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/news-events/epidemiological-update-hepatitis-outbreak-eueea-mostly-affecting-men-who-have-sex-men-0?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Hepatovirus A
EPP.common.name: Hepatitis A virus
Host: Humans, predominantly men who have sex with men (MSM), with some cases in other adults
Event.summary: Between roughly 2017 and 2019, several Latin American countries, notably Argentina, Brazil and Chile, experienced hepatitis A outbreaks predominantly affecting men who have sex with men, temporally related to and in many cases genomically linked with the contemporaneous European MSM outbreaks. In Chile, an MSM-focused outbreak starting in late 2016 produced more than 700 reported cases by mid-2017 and was shown by molecular analysis to be caused by genotype IA strains closely related to the European MSM strains, while Argentina and Brazil reported clusters of adult cases in MSM during 2017–2019 amidst reduced childhood endemicity and incomplete adult vaccination. Targeted vaccination of MSM, enhanced surveillance, and public health messaging in sexual health services gradually curtailed transmission, and incidence among MSM declined by 2019 even though isolated clusters continued in some cities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Epidemiologic transition with decreased childhood HAV exposure and incomplete adult vaccination in middle-income Latin American countries, leading to susceptible young adult cohorts; concentration of transmission within MSM sexual networks; travel links to Europe and other regions; limited initial awareness and uptake of MSM-specific HAV vaccination recommendations. EPP.scientific.name: Clostridioides difficile
EPP.common.name: Clostridioides difficile infection
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with healthcare‑associated CDI, including dialysis patients; multiple hospital outbreaks)
Event.summary: From 2008 onward, Polish hospitals recorded a rapid rise in CDI driven by hypervirulent PCR ribotype 027 and its closely related ribotype 176, with some centers reporting 027 accounting for 48–65% of toxigenic isolates and numerous hospital outbreaks, including a documented 2012 nephrology‑ward outbreak among dialysis patients. National surveillance between 2011 and 2013 showed very high CDI incidence rates and a predominance of 027/176 across multiple regions, while broader nosocomial‑infection reports for 2011–2015 identified C. difficile as the leading cause of reported hospital outbreaks. Implementation of targeted infection‑control bundles and antibiotic stewardship is ongoing to curb 027/176 transmission and reduce the heavy CDI burden in Polish healthcare facilities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High hospital antibiotic use with frequent fluoroquinolone and cephalosporin exposure, aging inpatient populations, and limited early CDI diagnostics contributed to the rapid establishment of 027/176 and under‑recognition of cases. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – expansion of 027 and related 176 lineages; Antimicrobial Resistance – high rates of resistance in 027/176 compared with other ribotypes; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – association with severe disease and outbreaks; Enhanced Transmission – efficient hospital spread, as indicated by numerous nosocomial outbreaks and high ward‑level prevalence.
Review: retain – Correctly summarises the expansion of ribotypes 027 and 176 and the high CDI burden in Polish hospitals from 2008 onwards, including dialysis‑ward outbreaks and national data showing C. difficile as the most common cause of reported nosocomial outbreaks in 2011–2015. Coding as re‑emergence in Poland (Eastern Europe) is appropriate given the emergence of new epidemic genotypes in a country with pre‑existing CDI.

Host: Humans (adults and children consuming fresh imported berries at social events, restaurants and via retail)
Event.summary: From spring through summer 1996, a very large multinational outbreak of cyclosporiasis occurred in North America, with approximately 1,465 outbreak-associated cases reported from 20 U.S. states, the District of Columbia, and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Québec; epidemiologic investigations in both countries consistently implicated fresh raspberries imported from Guatemala as the vehicle of infection. Similar but somewhat smaller raspberry‑linked outbreaks recurred in 1997 and again in 1998, including a 192‑case, 13‑cluster event in Ontario, Canada, and further clusters in the United States, and in 2000 a 54‑case outbreak in Philadelphia and other clusters were again traced to Guatemalan raspberries or blackberries. This multi‑year episode ended only after Guatemalan growers, the Guatemalan Berry Commission, and U.S. and Canadian regulators suspended spring raspberry exports, implemented a stringent Model Plan of Excellence with improved water quality, hygiene and field sanitation, and restricted exports to vetted farms, after which raspberry‑associated Cyclospora outbreaks in North America ceased.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of international trade in high‑value fresh berries from Cyclospora‑endemic Guatemala to North American markets; use of inadequately treated irrigation and wash water and poor sanitary infrastructure on some exporting farms; fragile raspberries with complex surface morphology that are difficult to wash effectively; and initially low awareness of Cyclospora among clinicians and laboratories in the United States and Canada, which delayed case recognition. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel strains or increased virulence during this episode; emergence was driven by repeated contamination of produce in endemic areas and its distribution into a naïve, high‑consumption market. Review: retain: This row correctly captures the large 1996–2000 North American epidemic linked mainly to Guatemalan raspberries, but the emergence type was misclassified. North American outbreaks were already recognized in 1990 and 1995, so this episode is not the first inter-continental occurrence on the continent. I reclassified it as re_occurrence, removed Peru from the country list (no strong evidence it was a major produce source in this specific episode), narrowed sub_regions to Northern America and Central America, and clarified that multiple years and clusters are grouped because they share a common Guatemala–North America raspberry supply chain. EPP.scientific.name: Treponema pallidum
EPP.common.name: Syphilis
Sub.regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Eastern Asia
Host: Humans with syphilis receiving macrolide therapy (primarily MSM and other sexually active adults)
Event.summary: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, clinically significant macrolide-resistant Treponema pallidum was identified, with azithromycin treatment failures linked to A2058G mutations in the 23S rRNA gene first reported in patients in San Francisco and then elsewhere in North America and Europe. During the 2000s, surveillance documented rapidly increasing proportions of macrolide-resistant strains in U.S. and Canadian cities and in several European and Chinese settings, making macrolide monotherapy unreliable for syphilis treatment. By around 2010, macrolide-resistant T. pallidum had become prevalent on multiple continents, and international guidelines moved away from macrolides toward penicillin-based regimens except in narrowly defined circumstances.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread, often empiric use of azithromycin and other macrolides for STI and respiratory infections, including off-guideline use of single‑dose azithromycin as a convenient alternative to injectable benzathine penicillin for syphilis in some settings; overlapping high‑transmission sexual networks in MSM facilitated dissemination of resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and clonal spread of point mutations (A2058G and later A2059G) in the 23S rRNA gene of T. pallidum conferred high-level macrolide resistance, a clear example of antimicrobial resistance–driven re-emergence.
Review: review – Retain as a key global re-emergence event driven by antimicrobial resistance, but the type-of-emergence coding has been aligned with the project rules: intra_continental_emergence and inter_continental_emergence have been set to false, because the species was long present on all affected continents and this episode reflects the emergence and spread of resistant lineages (re-emergence) rather than first occurrence in new regions. EPP.scientific.name: Cryptococcus neoformans
EPP.common.name: cryptococcosis
Host: Humans (primarily HIV-infected adults with suspected meningitis)
Event.summary: Between roughly 2004 and 2014, studies from Botswana, South Africa, Zambia, and Uganda demonstrated that cryptococcal meningitis had become the leading identified cause of adult meningitis in much of southern and eastern Africa. National and referral-hospital data from Botswana indicated that cryptococcal meningitis accounted for about 90% of microbiologically confirmed adult meningitis cases, mirroring earlier and contemporaneous data from high-HIV-prevalence provinces in South Africa and from Zambia. In a Ugandan cohort of HIV-infected adults with suspected meningitis (2010–2012), cryptococcal meningitis accounted for about 60% of all meningitis diagnoses, with bacterial and tuberculous meningitis much less common. Over this period, bacterial meningitis incidence declined with introduction of conjugate vaccines, but cryptococcal meningitis persisted as the dominant cause of adult meningitis in these settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high prevalence of advanced HIV disease, incomplete ART coverage and adherence, late care-seeking, and limited diagnostic capacity for alternative meningitis etiologies concentrated adult meningitis burden in cryptococcal disease. Introduction of bacterial conjugate vaccines reduced bacterial meningitis, increasing the relative share of cryptococcal meningitis among adult meningitis cases. Internal mechanisms: No strong evidence for major pathogen evolution; the patterns reflect changing host susceptibility and competing etiologies rather than new cryptococcal strains.
Review: review: The overall event concept (cryptococcal meningitis becoming the leading cause of adult meningitis in parts of southern and eastern Africa) is well supported by Botswana national data and adult meningitis cohort studies from South Africa and Uganda.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6679721/?utm_source=openai)) Corrections made: (i) the Ugandan country period was changed from “Uganda [2004–2012]” to “Uganda [2010–2012]” to match the prospective cohort that found 60% of meningitis cases due to cryptococcal meningitis,([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4347329/?utm_source=openai)) and (ii) the Countries field was clarified to give explicit date ranges for South Africa and Uganda rather than vague descriptors such as “pre-ART era comparator.” Source URLs were updated to replace the Uganda 2015–2017 paper with the more relevant 2010–2012 cohort description (PMC4347329). The episode remains classified as re-occurrence; flagged for review to confirm the exact date ranges for Zambia and for consistency with any additional national datasets.

EPP.scientific.name: Rubivirus rubellae
EPP.common.name: Rubella virus
Host: Humans (primarily young adult men; pregnant women; infants with CRS)
Event.summary: Beginning in 2007, several South American countries that had recently implemented rubella vaccination strategies focused largely on women experienced linked rubella outbreaks among under‑vaccinated young adult men. Brazil reported 8,739 confirmed rubella cases in 2007 alone, with marked outbreaks in São Paulo and other states and documented CRS cases, while Chile experienced nationwide spread with more than 4,000 confirmed cases between 2007 and 2009, and Argentina reported around 90 cases, for a regional total of roughly 13,000 confirmed infections. The outbreaks, driven by long‑standing cohort gaps among adult men and amplified by urban social mixing, subsided by 2009 following intensified surveillance and large‑scale measles–rubella or MMR catch‑up campaigns targeting adult men and women, coinciding with interruption of endemic rubella transmission in the Americas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Historical vaccination strategies in Argentina, Brazil, and Chile that initially prioritized women of childbearing age and young children left large cohorts of adult men unvaccinated; urban crowding and mobility promoted adult‑to‑adult spread; regional elimination targets prompted enhanced surveillance, revealing the full extent of the epidemics. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and regional predominance of genotype 2B rubella virus in South America during this period, representing a novel lineage in this regional context and facilitating tracking of virus spread between countries; although no clear change in virulence was documented, the genotype replacement in combination with large adult-male epidemics supports classification as a re‑emergence episode.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Updated to treat the 2007–2009 adult-male epidemics in Brazil, Chile, and Argentina as a single linked South American event, with countries and years now specified in the Countries field and summary. This tri-country resurgence produced ~13,000 confirmed cases and multiple CRS cases and is clearly among the most consequential post-1990 rubella events. To comply with the typology, only re_emergence is marked yes, reflecting documented regional predominance of genotype 2B together with large-scale resurgence in previously vaccinated populations; intra-/inter-continental categories remain no because rubella was long established in this continent.

EPP.scientific.name: Morganella spp.
EPP.common.name: Morganella infection
Continent: Asia; Europe; Africa; North America; Oceania
Sub.regions: Southern Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Eastern Africa; Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2008-2010]
Host: Hospitalized human patients (mixed adult populations, mainly with prior healthcare exposure or recent medical care in the Indian subcontinent) infected or colonized with NDM‑producing Enterobacteriaceae, including occasional Morganella morganii isolates
Event.summary: From 2008 onward, New Delhi metallo‑β‑lactamase‑1 (NDM‑1) was first recognized in carbapenem‑resistant Enterobacteriaceae in patients linked to healthcare in the Indian subcontinent, and early collections of NDM‑1 producers already included a Morganella morganii isolate among predominantly Klebsiella and Escherichia coli strains. Over 2008–2010, NDM‑1‑producing Enterobacteriaceae spread rapidly from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh to hospitals in the United Kingdom and other European centers via travelers and medical tourists, with Morganella occasionally identified among colonizing or infecting species. By roughly 2010–2012, NDM‑positive Enterobacteriaceae carrying blaNDM‑1 (and related NDM variants) had been reported from health‑care settings across multiple continents—including Western Asia, East and South‑East Asia, Northern Europe, Northern America, Eastern Africa and Oceania—establishing the potential for Morganella to participate in globally disseminated, carbapenem‑resistant Enterobacterales lineages.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: growth of high‑intensity tertiary care and medical tourism in the Indian subcontinent; extensive broad‑spectrum antibiotic use in hospitals; widespread carriage of blaNDM‑bearing plasmids in Enterobacteriaceae; international travel and cross‑border patient transfers facilitating export of NDM‑producing strains to Europe, North America, Africa and Oceania. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – acquisition of blaNDM genes on promiscuous plasmids by Morganella morganii; Antimicrobial Resistance – emergence of high‑level carbapenem resistance mediated by NDM; Enhanced Transmission – efficient horizontal transfer of NDM plasmids across diverse Enterobacterales in healthcare environments, allowing Morganella to join multispecies AMR clones; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – no change in the organism’s ecological niche is proven, but plasmid‑mediated carbapenem resistance allowed survival under intense carbapenem selection pressures worldwide.
Review: review: Event retained but reinterpreted as a re-emergence episode driven by acquisition of NDM-type carbapenemases in Morganella rather than as first detection or true inter-continental emergence of the organism itself. Corrected type-of-emergence coding by setting first_detection and inter_continental_emergence to No and re_emergence to Yes, consistent with the project’s guidance that new resistance determinants should not be classified as inter-/intra-continental emergence of the EPP. Sub-region list was cleaned to remove the non-standard entry “Northern Europe (Nordic countries)”; the countries list was pruned to drop “Nordic countries (unspecified)” and “Taiwan, Province of China”, which lacked specific Morganella data in the cited sources. Country-specific years remain approximate for some sites (e.g. “2010s”) and should be refined if more detailed Morganella-focused NDM surveillance data become available.

EPP.scientific.name: Aparavirus tauraense
EPP.common.name: Taura syndrome virus, TSV
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp, especially L. vannamei (with involvement of other cultured species where co‑cultured)
Event.summary: Following its establishment in Taiwan and coastal China, TSV was detected in Indonesia in 2002 soon after the official introduction and rapid expansion of L. vannamei culture, and in Thailand around 2003 as farmers shifted from P. monodon to L. vannamei. By about 2004, TSV had been reported from additional coastal provinces in China and from farms in the Republic of Korea, Myanmar and Viet Nam, where it contributed to high disease losses as the virus entered naïve shrimp‑farming areas. Over subsequent years, TSV became endemic in many East and South‑East Asian shrimp‑farming zones, co‑circulating with other major viral pathogens such as white spot syndrome virus (WSSV).
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intra‑Asian movement and trade of live L. vannamei postlarvae and broodstock, often sourced from previously infected regions within Asia, combined with rapid regional expansion and intensification of shrimp farming, drove TSV spread to new Asian subregions; limited biosecurity, water exchange among farms, and co‑culture or sequential culture of different penaeid species facilitated virus maintenance and spread. Internal mechanisms: TSV’s ability to infect multiple penaeid hosts and its efficient horizontal transmission allowed rapid establishment and persistence in new Asian production systems once introduced.
Review: Review (approximate timing). This event appropriately captures intra‑continental expansion of TSV within Asia from its initial foci in Taiwan/China to Indonesia, Thailand, Korea, Myanmar and Viet Nam and is clearly among the major impact events. Countries and sub‑regions have been standardised to the UNSD list. However, the specific year assignments for Myanmar and Viet Nam are approximate (sources document that TSV was endemic in these countries by 2004 rather than giving exact first‑detection years), so the event is flagged for expert review of country‑specific start years while being retained as a major Asian spread episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Aparavirus tauraense
EPP.common.name: Taura syndrome virus, TSV
Host: Farmed giant tiger prawn (Penaeus monodon), Pacific white shrimp (L. vannamei) and other penaeids in mixed or sequential culture (e.g. Metapenaeus ensis in Taiwan)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, molecular surveys in Taiwan identified distinct TSV isolates in P. monodon and Metapenaeus ensis as well as in L. vannamei, showing that the virus had expanded beyond its original principal host into additional penaeid species with different susceptibility profiles. In Thailand, the first confirmed TSV outbreak in farmed L. vannamei was detected by RT‑PCR in early 2003, and subsequent work documented TSV infections in both L. vannamei and P. monodon, often as co‑infections with WSSV in mixed or sequential culture systems. Between about 2000 and 2006, increasing reports of TSV in P. monodon and other regional species contributed to complex disease presentations and additional losses in farms that had previously considered TSV primarily a risk for L. vannamei.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: diversification of shrimp farming in East and South‑East Asia, with overlapping culture of P. monodon, L. vannamei and other penaeids in shared water bodies and farm systems, created ecological opportunities for cross‑species transmission; limited species‑specific biosecurity measures meant viruses introduced with L. vannamei could spill over to resident species. Internal mechanisms: host expansion (spillover) of TSV from its principal host L. vannamei into P. monodon and other penaeids, accompanied by genetic variation in capsid genes that affected host range and replication efficiency, represents a re‑emergence mediated by viral adaptation to new hosts rather than a purely geographic spread event.
Review: Review (host-range expansion; impact somewhat uncertain). Evidence from Taiwan (field and experimental infections in P. monodon and Metapenaeus ensis) and Thailand (molecular detection of TSV in P. monodon and L. vannamei, often with WSSV co‑infection) supports genuine host expansion and additional disease burden, justifying classification as re_emergence driven by host expansion and viral genetic variation. However, quantitative estimates of incremental production loss attributable specifically to TSV in non‑vannamei hosts are limited, and geographic coverage beyond Taiwan and Thailand is less clear. The event is retained as one of the main re‑emergence episodes but flagged for expert review of its relative ranking among the top 10 TSV events and for potential refinement of the country list if stronger data on impacts in other South‑East Asian countries become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Host: Chickens (broilers and layers, often subclinically affected)
Event.summary: From the mid‑2010s, a novel variant IBDV genotype (nvIBDV, classified as A2dB1b) emerged in China and subsequently spread through East and parts of Southeast Asia, generating a large-scale epidemic characterized largely by subclinical infections with severe bursal atrophy and immunosuppression rather than classic high-mortality Gumboro disease. Over this period, nvIBDV became widespread in Chinese broiler and layer flocks and was detected in other countries such as Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Malaysia, undermining vaccine programs targeting classical and vvIBDV strains and contributing to increased susceptibility to other poultry pathogens. Adjustments to vaccination strategies, including development and deployment of variant-adapted vaccines and improved monitoring, have begun to address this challenge, but nvIBDV remains an important, immunosuppressive re-emergent form of the virus in Asian poultry systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High vaccine pressure against classical and vvIBDV phenotypes, dense poultry production, and extensive movement of birds and products across East and Southeast Asia promoted emergence and spread of variants better adapted to partially immune flocks; intensive production favored viruses that cause subclinical yet immunosuppressive infection. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of the novel variant genotype A2dB1b with distinct VP2 antigenic properties and altered pathogenic profile (novel strain/genotype emergence), associated with strong bursal atrophy but often reduced overt mortality; partial escape from existing vaccine-induced immunity (antigenic variation/functional vaccine escape) allowed successful regional expansion (enhanced transmission/geographic range expansion).
Review: review: Retain this event as the major emergence of the Chinese novel variant nvIBDV (A2dB1b) and its subsequent spread in East and South‑eastern Asia, but update the period to 2015–2022 to match analyses showing reappearance of variants as novel strains in the mid‑2010s and their rapid expansion thereafter. The country list was refined to include only locations with documented nvIBDV (China, Japan, Republic of Korea, Malaysia), and 'intra_continental_emergence' was switched to No so the episode is coded purely as re-emergence of a new genotype within an already endemic virus species; Source URLs now point to primary Chinese and global analyses of A2dB1b rather than Middle East–focused papers.

EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers)
Event.summary: From the early 2020s, molecular surveillance revealed rapid spread of the novel variant IBDV genotype A2dB1b from its origin in East Asia into the Near East and North Africa, with first detections in Jordan and Lebanon in late 2023, followed by rapid establishment in the United Arab Emirates and evidence of related nvIBDV strains in Iraq. In parallel, Egypt reported nvIBDV A2dB1b in poultry flocks alongside existing vvIBDV strains, indicating further geographic expansion and leading to outbreaks characterized mainly by subclinical infection, bursal atrophy, and immunosuppression rather than high mortality. Ongoing circulation of these variants in the Middle East and North Africa has complicated control strategies based on classical and vvIBDV vaccines and raised concern about their long-term impact on vaccine performance and poultry health.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Trade in live birds and hatching eggs and regional integration of poultry supply chains between Asia, the Near East, and North Africa facilitated long-distance movement of nvIBDV; limited early awareness and diagnostic targeting of this genotype allowed silent spread before it was molecularly characterized. Internal mechanisms: The A2dB1b genotype possesses distinct VP2 antigenic signatures and is adapted to infect partially immune flocks previously vaccinated against classical and vvIBDV (novel strain/genotype emergence and vaccine escape), with a tendency toward subclinical yet strongly immunosuppressive disease (increased pathogenicity in terms of immune dysfunction rather than overt mortality), enabling re-emergence in regions where IBDV was already endemic and geographic expansion across Western Asia and into North Africa.
Review: review: This event is retained as the spread of nvIBDV A2dB1b into the Near East and North Africa, but the dates and geography were corrected using recent molecular surveillance: the wave now spans roughly 2021–2025, with nvIBDV first detected in Egypt around 2021–2023 and then in Jordan, Lebanon and the UAE from late 2023 onward, and Iraq added based on A2dB1b-classified sequences; Oman and Qatar were removed because current data primarily show other genotypes there. 'First_detection', 'intra_continental_emergence' and 'inter_continental_emergence' were all set to No so the episode is treated strictly as re-emergence of a new genotype in continents where IBDV was long established; the sources now cleanly support these corrections and should be reviewed by a domain expert for final confirmation.

EPP.scientific.name: Canine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Canine distemper virus, CDV
Host: Rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta) in breeding farms and research facilities; cynomolgus monkey (Macaca fascicularis) in a Japanese facility
Event.summary: In 2006, a measles‑like respiratory disease emerged among rhesus macaques at a breeding farm in Guangxi, southern China, where subsequent investigations identified CDV as the etiologic agent, marking one of the first confirmed natural CDV outbreaks in nonhuman primates at scale. Related CDV outbreaks then occurred in rhesus monkeys at a Beijing animal center and in 2008 in cynomolgus monkeys at a facility in Japan, with genetic analyses showing closely related strains circulating across facilities. Control was achieved through culling, quarantine and enhanced biosecurity, but these events established CDV as an emerging pathogen of captive Old World monkeys in East Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density housing of macaques in breeding and research facilities, with frequent animal movements between farms and centers, created ideal conditions for CDV amplification; likely contact with infected dogs or contaminated materials introduced canine lineages of CDV into naïve primate colonies; limited prior recognition of CDV risk in primates delayed diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover and subsequent adaptation) of CDV into nonhuman primates; molecular analyses showed that monkey strains clustered with contemporary dog CDV lineages (Asia‑1), with specific mutations in the H gene associated with altered receptor usage that may facilitate infection of primate SLAM receptors; ongoing chains of CDV transmission within primate colonies highlight efficient transmission in the new host once established.
Review: review - Retain as a top-impact event because outbreaks in Chinese breeding farms and a Japanese primate facility involved ~10,000 infected monkeys with substantial mortality, and represent a clear, well-characterized host expansion of CDV into nonhuman primates. Corrected event-type coding by setting 'first_detection' to false (CDV was long known in the animal host system); the event is best classified as 're_emergence' driven by host expansion and viral adaptation in primates. Geographical coding (Asia | Eastern Asia; China and Japan) is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Caprine arthritis encephalitis virus
EPP.common.name: CAEV, Small ruminant lentivirus
Countries: Brazil – multiple Northeastern states (Piauí, Maranhão, Sergipe, Alagoas, Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba, Ceará) [2008-2010]
Host: Domestic goats (dairy and meat) in semi-arid smallholder and breeder herds
Event.summary: Between the mid‑2000s and around 2010, several epidemiological and serological studies in Northeast Brazil documented CAEV as an important emerging infection in goat herds, starting with surveys in the Cariri region of Paraíba state that found notable seroprevalence across 60 herds, followed by broader studies of breeder goats in seven Northeastern states. These investigations showed that CAEV was present in multiple states with herd-level seroprevalence associated with more technified/intensive production, buck use, and inter‑herd animal movement, implying that the virus had spread widely through regional trade and breeding networks. Recognition of CAEV as endemic in major goat‑producing areas of Northeast Brazil led to calls for control programmes focused on testing, culling or segregating positives, and adjusting breeding practices, but full eradication has not been implemented and subsequent work continues to find CAEV in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of goat production in the semi‑arid Northeast, movement of breeding animals among states, shared use of bucks, and limited historical testing all facilitated regional dissemination; semi‑intensive and intensive management systems were associated with higher seroprevalence. Internal mechanisms: Circulating SRLV strains in Northeastern Brazil were phylogenetically related to CAEV‑type lentiviruses; no uniquely more virulent variant was reported, and the main internal factor was the virus’ capacity for persistent infection and efficient transmission in dense herds.
Review: retain – this episode aggregates the earliest large-scale serosurveys in the Cariri region of Paraíba and subsequent multi‑state breeder surveys in Northeast Brazil, which together represent one of the most substantial documented CAEV emergence/re-occurrence events in South America in terms of herd numbers and regional spread. Geographic scope, timing and host description are consistent with the cited Brazilian studies; no major corrections to dates, regions or emergence-type classification (re_occurrence in an already affected continent) are needed. Event is appropriately counted among the top global CAEV emergence episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Carp edema virus
EPP.common.name: CEV
Host: Farmed common carp; ornamental koi carp in pond and garden systems
Event.summary: From 2013 onward, CEV-associated disease outbreaks were recognised in common carp and koi on Czech farms, with retrospective and prospective testing confirming virus circulation in Central European carp culture. In 2013–2014, Austria reported koi sleepy disease in koi and common carp from pond systems, while 2013–2015 surveillance in Poland documented multiple CEV-positive outbreaks and revealed substantial viral diversity; Slovakia then confirmed its first CEVD case in 2019. Together, these linked epizootics caused significant mortalities in pond-reared carp across Central and Eastern Europe and established CEV as an important transboundary disease in major regional carp-producing countries.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/tbed.12293?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of pond-based carp aquaculture in Central and Eastern Europe increased host density and stress; regional trade in stocking material and broodstock, often via Czech and Polish hatcheries, dispersed CEV among farms and across borders; seasonal temperature patterns in spring and autumn favored outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Genetic studies identified multiple CEV genogroups in Poland and neighbouring countries, including a divergent lineage (genogroup III) found only in common carp, indicating viral diversification within Europe; nonetheless, because these are first detections in the Eastern Europe subregion, they are classified as intra‑continental emergence rather than re‑emergence.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27453481/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review. Country timings for Czechia and Slovakia were incorrect in the original row; these have been aligned with first-confirmed CEVD cases (Czechia from 2013, Slovakia 2019) and the event period adjusted to 2013–2019. The episode is best described as intra‑continental emergence into the previously unaffected Eastern Europe subregion; re_emergence was therefore set to false, with viral diversification retained as part of the mechanism rather than as a separate emergence type.
