EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Host: Cattle; domestic small ruminants to a lesser extent; wild red deer (Cervus elaphus), fallow deer (Dama dama) and mouflon (Ovis orientalis musimon)
Event.summary: In autumn 2022, epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 8 closely related to the Tunisian 2021 EHDV‑8 TUN 2021 strain was detected for the first time in Europe in cattle in Sardinia and Sicily (Italy) and in southern Spain, marking the first incursion of EHD into European livestock and wildlife. During 2022–2023 the same EHDV‑8 lineage spread widely across mainland Spain, into neighboring regions of Portugal and southern France and into mainland Italy, causing numerous outbreaks in cattle herds with fever, oral lesions, edema, milk drop and occasional deaths, as well as significant mortality and clinical disease in European red deer, fallow deer and mouflon. By late 2023 the disease had affected all regions of mainland Spain and multiple regions in Portugal, France and Italy, with control responses including movement restrictions and accelerated development and deployment of inactivated EHDV‑8 vaccines; activity continued into 2024 and beyond, raising concern that EHD may become endemic in parts of southern and western Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely wind‑borne dispersal of infected Culicoides midges across the Mediterranean from North Africa into southern Europe, in the context of a warming climate and shifting vector distributions, followed by dense livestock networks and game‑estate management practices that facilitated virus amplification and within‑continent spread between Italy, Spain, Portugal and France. Internal mechanisms: Inter‑continental emergence and rapid geographic range expansion of the EHDV‑8 TUN 2021 lineage into naïve European cattle and cervid populations, with marked pathogenicity in both domestic and wild hosts, alongside rapid development and deployment of new inactivated EHDV‑8 vaccines that may influence future viral evolution and disease dynamics.
Review: Review – classification was adjusted by setting first_detection to No (global first detection predates this event) while retaining inter_continental_emergence as Yes to reflect the first occurrence of EHDV in Europe and intra_continental_emergence as Yes to capture subsequent spread from initial foci in Southern Europe (Sardinia, Sicily, Andalusia) into Western Europe (France). The event is clearly one of the most impactful in the history of EHD, with multi‑country spread, severe cattle and wildlife disease, and major regulatory and vaccination responses, and should be retained as a cornerstone emergence episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Sub.regions: Northern Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) in commercial and backyard systems; occasional wild/feral rabbits
Event.summary: In February 2015, RHDV2 was first reported in Africa during severe outbreaks in commercial rabbit farms in Kairouan, Tunisia, where it caused high mortality and major economic losses, and molecular data showed multiple introductions of GI.2-like strains from Europe. Over the next several years genetically related viruses were detected in North African countries including Morocco, Algeria and Egypt, and by 2015–2020 RHDV2 had appeared in multiple West African nations such as Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria and Senegal, where large outbreaks—most notably the 2019 epidemic in Ghana and the 2020 wave in Nigeria—devastated rapidly growing rabbit industries. By 2022, RHDV2 had also been confirmed in South Africa, with outbreaks in wild and domestic lagomorphs, indicating that the new genotype had become established across several African subregions with recurrent, often high-mortality production losses rather than remaining a series of isolated incursions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: importation of live rabbits and rabbit genetic stock from Europe and Asia, movement of rabbit meat and byproducts into coastal West African port cities, rapid expansion of semi-intensive rabbit production as a protein source, and limited biosecurity in smallholder and peri-urban farms facilitated introduction and onward spread. Internal mechanisms: introduction and onward dissemination of the globally successful GI.2 genotype with high transmissibility, broader age susceptibility, and partial vaccine escape relative to earlier GI.1-based vaccines, together with largely naïve African rabbit populations, underpinned severe production losses. Mechanisms include novel genotype-driven geographic range expansion, enhanced transmission, and, in some countries, further diversification via recombination documented in African RHDV2 genomes.
Review: review – Updated the time span from 2015–2019 to 2015–2022 and corrected several country-specific first-detection windows (e.g. Nigeria from 2017–2019 to 2020–2021, Senegal to 2020, South Africa to 2022, Algeria to 2018–2021, Tunisia to 2015–2018) in line with WOAH and recent outbreak reports. Re-coded the episode as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by the GI.2 genotype in an already RHD-affected continent, removing previous inter- and intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence flags to comply with the event-type definitions; the event should be retained but remains flagged for expert review of exact country-year ranges.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Continent: North America; South America (Central America and Caribbean)
Host: Domestic European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) in pet, backyard and commercial settings; multiple native North American lagomorphs including black-tailed jackrabbit (Lepus californicus), cottontail rabbits (Sylvilagus spp.), and endangered riparian brush rabbit (Sylvilagus bachmani riparius)
Event.summary: RHDV2 was first detected in the Americas in 2016 during an outbreak among feral rabbits in Mont-Joli, Québec, Canada, which was rapidly contained, followed by a genetically distinct 2018 outbreak centred on feral and domestic rabbits in British Columbia. In March 2020, after earlier detections in Cuba (2019) and isolated U.S. pet rabbit cases in 2018–2019, a large, sustained epizootic began in New Mexico and spread across domestic and wild rabbits and hares in the southwestern United States, northern Mexico and later additional U.S. states, causing hundreds of reported outbreaks and substantial mortality in jackrabbits, cottontails and endangered riparian brush rabbits. By 2022, RHDV2 was established across a broad swath of western North America and parts of the Americas, triggering emergency vaccination campaigns, movement restrictions and long-term surveillance before incidence began to decline somewhat with increased awareness and vaccine uptake.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement of infected domestic rabbits and possibly contaminated fomites between Canada, the United States, Mexico and the Caribbean; limited early access to RHDV2 vaccines in North America; and dense populations of susceptible wild lagomorphs in arid southwestern landscapes all facilitated widespread transmission once the virus arrived. Internal mechanisms: the broad host range of RHDV2 across lagomorph species, high environmental stability and contagiousness, and partial immune escape from prior GI.1-based immunity enabled rapid multi-species spillover and establishment in novel native hosts, leading to severe mortality in jackrabbits, cottontails and endangered brush rabbits. Mechanisms include host expansion (spillover), enhanced transmission, and geographic range expansion, with re-emergence in continents that had previously experienced only sporadic or eradicated RHD incursions.
Review: review – Harmonised event-type coding so this North America–Central America–Caribbean episode is treated solely as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by the GI.2 genotype and host expansion, removing previous inter- and intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence flags. Adjusted country-year annotations to distinguish early, self-limited Canadian incursions (Québec 2016, British Columbia 2018–2019) from the large 2019–2022 epizootic affecting the southwestern United States, Mexico (from 2020) and Cuba (2019). This row intentionally aggregates several genetically and spatially linked outbreaks for parsimony; a human reviewer may consider splitting early Canadian incursions into a separate, lower-impact event if finer temporal resolution is required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Pastoral cattle herds and wild bovids (notably African buffalo and antelopes) in the southern Sudan ecosystem and contiguous areas of Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia
Event.summary: From 1993 to the late 1990s, classic rinderpest persisted in the southern Sudan ecosystem and neighbouring pastoral areas of Uganda, Kenya and western Ethiopia, forming one of the last major African reservoirs of virulent lineage‑1 virus. Widespread outbreaks in cattle and associated wildlife occurred in southern Sudan and Karamoja (Uganda) in 1993–1995, with further activity in border districts of Kenya and Ethiopia, before intensive control efforts reduced incidence. The final laboratory‑confirmed outbreak in this ecosystem was recorded near Torit in what is now South Sudan in 1998, after which no further confirmed rinderpest occurred, paving the way for verification of eradication in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Protracted civil conflict in southern Sudan, insecurity in parts of Uganda and Kenya, and very limited state presence severely constrained veterinary services, vaccination coverage and disease reporting. Large, mobile pastoral herds moved across porous borders with little control, sustaining transmission in an ecological “southern Sudan axis” even as other African regions became free. Only with the introduction of community‑based animal health workers, targeted vaccination in high‑risk corridors and improved surveillance under PARC/PACE and GREP was this reservoir finally extinguished. Internal mechanisms: Virological data indicate circulation of established lineage‑1 rinderpest viruses rather than a novel strain; the episode is thus characterized as re-occurrence of classic rinderpest maintained by conflict and pastoral ecology rather than re-emergence driven by virus evolution.
Review: review – This major East African focus, often described as the “southern Sudan axis,” was missing from the original output despite being identified in GREP analyses as one of the last two African reservoirs of classic virulent rinderpest. A new row has been added summarizing widespread outbreaks in southern Sudan and contiguous parts of Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia during 1993–1998, culminating in the final confirmed outbreak near Torit. Country list and time ranges are approximate and should be cross‑checked against national datasets; emergence-type classification as re-occurrence is supported by lineage‑1 virology and the strong influence of conflict and service breakdown.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma mycoides subsp. mycoides
EPP.common.name: MmmSC
Countries: Ethiopia – western highlands (Boji district, West Wellega Zone) [2000-2002]
Host: Cattle in mixed crop–livestock systems in the Ethiopian highlands and north‑western export‑oriented zones
Event.summary: Around 2000, Ethiopian veterinary services reported a resurgence of CBPP in the western highlands (Boji district, West Wellega), where a 16‑month longitudinal study from June 2000 to January 2002 documented that about one‑third of cattle in monitored herds seroconverted and that clinical cases and mortality were substantial. In the early to mid‑2000s, additional outbreaks were documented on the southern edge of a planned north‑western disease‑free export zone, with official records noting one outbreak in 2003 and at least two more in 2004–2005 that threatened Ethiopia’s ambitions to establish a CBPP‑free export region. Strengthened surveillance, targeted vaccination along trekking routes from endemic pastoral areas, and movement management into the proposed free zone subsequently reduced reported outbreak numbers, although CBPP remained an important constraint on Ethiopia’s cattle sector.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of trekking routes and cattle trade from more heavily infected southern and western lowland areas into highland districts such as Boji and into the periphery of the north‑western export zone underpinned these resurgence events, with mixed crop–livestock systems and communal grazing favoring local spread. Farmer responses centered on informal antibiotic treatment and ad hoc isolation, which, combined with gaps in formal vaccination coverage and diagnostic capacity, were insufficient to interrupt transmission. Internal mechanisms: Epidemiological and modeling work from Boji shows typical CBPP dynamics dominated by chronic carriers and slow within‑herd spread, without evidence of a novel strain; the key internal factor is the ability of MmmSC to persist in chronically infected animals and to spread insidiously in smallholder herds, allowing geographic range expansion of existing African lineages within Ethiopia.
Review: REVIEW – Retain this as an important Ethiopian resurgence episode, but correct the timing and structure: (i) adjusted the start year to 2000 to match the Boji district longitudinal study (June 2000–January 2002) rather than 2003–2004; (ii) treated the Boji highlands (2000–2002) and the 2003–2005 outbreaks at the southern edge of the proposed north‑western disease‑free zone as a single linked national episode of re‑occurrence; and (iii) kept the classification as re‑occurrence, since the evidence indicates resurgence of existing African CBPP lineages driven by cattle movements and control gaps, not emergence of a new strain.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus marinus
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis (Dermo disease of oysters)
Countries: Brazil [2015-2017] (continued detections in native Crassostrea sp. and farmed Crassostrea gigas in Santa Catarina aquaculture areas)
Host: Introduced Crassostrea gigas (Pacific oyster in aquaculture) and native Crassostrea spp. along the Santa Catarina coast, southern Brazil
Event.summary: From about 2013 onward, histological and molecular surveys in Santa Catarina, Brazil’s principal bivalve aquaculture state, revealed Perkinsus marinus infections at high prevalence in native Crassostrea sp. and, at lower prevalence, in farmed Crassostrea gigas at sites such as São Francisco do Sul and Balneário Barra do Sul. These findings constituted the first confirmed reports of P. marinus infecting C. gigas in South America and documented southward spread of the parasite into a temperate farming region where C. gigas dominates production. Although recorded C. gigas mortalities were relatively limited and infections often light to moderate, the establishment of P. marinus in both native and introduced oysters raised serious concerns about chronic production losses and trade restrictions in Brazil’s main oyster-farming hub.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance movements of live oysters and seed for aquaculture, together with shared coastal water bodies and infrastructure, likely facilitated introduction and subsequent dissemination of P. marinus from northeastern Brazil or Mexican sources to Santa Catarina. Local temperature and salinity regimes in southern Brazil proved permissive for parasite establishment in both native Crassostrea sp. and introduced C. gigas. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence via host expansion and geographic range expansion within the South America subregion, as P. marinus successfully infected the non-native C. gigas and persisted in multiple oyster species, indicating robust adaptability and potential for chronic, production-limiting disease rather than acute die‑offs alone.
Review: review - The original row mixed northeastern Brazilian spread with later detections in Santa Catarina and gave a 2013–2019 time span. Here the event has been restricted to Santa Catarina, with timing (2013–2017) and locations aligned to Cunha (2016) and Leibowitz et al. (2019), which document high P. marinus prevalence in native Crassostrea sp. and lower prevalence in farmed C. gigas. 'Intra_continental_emergence' has been set to 'No' because these detections occur within an already affected UNSD subregion; the event is retained as a re-emergence episode marked by host expansion and southward spread and should be reviewed by a domain expert for final phrasing.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Poxvirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Pox viruses infection
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus, Bos indicus and crossbreds); water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis, limited)
Event.summary: In August 2015 lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) was confirmed for the first time in the European Union in cattle herds in Evros, northern Greece, following progressive northward spread from endemic foci in Africa and the Middle East. During 2016 the disease spread rapidly across the Balkans, affecting Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Serbia, Albania and Montenegro and causing thousands of outbreaks, production losses and extensive trade restrictions. Mass vaccination campaigns using live homologous capripox vaccines and movement controls from 2015–2017 progressively contained the disease, and by 2018 the Balkans were considered free of active LSDV transmission although the virus remained endemic in parts of Africa and Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of live cattle trade and informal animal movements between Türkiye and neighbouring Balkan countries; abundant blood-feeding arthropod vectors (biting flies, mosquitoes) favoured by warm, wet summers; limited prior immunity in Balkan cattle populations; initial gaps in vaccine supply and rollout; high-density dairy and beef systems facilitating spread. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of LSDV from Africa–Middle East into the European continent; available genomic data indicate that the viruses in south‑eastern Europe were closely related to Middle Eastern field strains without major adaptive change.
Review: Review – This event has been refocused to the 2015–2017 Balkan and EU epidemic only (first occurrence of LSD in Europe), with Israel and Türkiye now covered under the Western Asia event. The year span was corrected from “2012–2016” to “2015–2017”, continent simplified to “Europe”, and inter-continental emergence is retained as “Yes” because this represents the first establishment of LSDV on the European continent. Kosovo*, while epidemiologically affected, is not listed as a separate country because it is absent from the provided Country sheet.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonellosis
Sub.regions: Europe: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; North America: Northern America; Asia: Western Asia; Oceania: Australia and New Zealand
Host: Primarily cattle; also pigs, poultry (especially turkeys), and sheep
Event.summary: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, a multidrug‑resistant clone of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium definitive phage type 104 (DT104), resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, streptomycin, sulfonamides and tetracycline (ACSSuT), expanded rapidly in cattle and other livestock in the United Kingdom and neighboring European countries. Through trade in animals and animal products and other routes, this DT104 clone spread across Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe and was recognized in multiple livestock species by the mid‑1990s. By 1996, the same multidrug‑resistant DT104 strain had emerged in cattle and humans in Canada, the United States, Israel and, shortly afterward, Australia and New Zealand, becoming a major cause of disease and prompting international control efforts in the late 1990s and early 2000s before incidence declined following interventions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of cattle, pig and poultry production, high use of therapeutic and growth‑promoter antimicrobials in food animals, and extensive trade in live animals and animal products facilitated selection and rapid international dissemination of the DT104 clone. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and stabilization of a multidrug‑resistance cassette (R‑type ACSSuT) associated with class‑1 integrons and the Salmonella genomic island SGI1 increased fitness under antimicrobial pressure and contributed to re‑emergence, and some sublineages developed additional quinolone resistance during the late 1990s.
Review: Review – Event is real and appropriately framed as the global emergence of multidrug‑resistant Salmonella Typhimurium DT104 in livestock. Geography has been corrected by adding Asia/Western Asia because Israel is listed among affected countries, and the event‑type flags were adjusted to reflect an inter‑continental re‑emergence of a multidrug‑resistant clone (inter_continental_emergence = Yes; intra_continental_emergence = No; re_emergence = Yes) in line with the mostly mutually exclusive classification rules.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Obolodiplosis robiniae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia in urban plantings and street trees in southwestern France and Belgium
Event.summary: After initial detection in Belgium and then France in the mid‑2000s, Obolodiplosis robiniae populations built up dramatically in 2007 in parts of southwestern France, especially Dordogne and Gironde, where black locust trees experienced heavy galling and premature leaf drop. During the 2007 growing season, high densities of galls were reported in streetside and ornamental plantings, drawing attention from plant protection services and leading to targeted monitoring. By 2008, however, field surveys recorded a sharp decline in visible damage in the same areas due to high parasitism by the introduced parasitoid Platygaster robiniae, and the outbreak subsided to lower, more stable levels of infestation.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense planting of susceptible black locust in urban and peri‑urban landscapes, combined with the recent arrival of the gall midge and initially low levels of natural enemies, allowed rapid population growth in southwestern France; mild climatic conditions further supported multiple generations per season. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was reported, but enemy release followed by subsequent build-up of the specialist parasitoid Platygaster robiniae created a boom‑and‑bust dynamic, with the initial outbreak representing a re‑occurrence driven largely by ecological imbalance (low parasitism) rather than genetic change in the pest.
Review: Decision: review. The 2007–2008 outbreak and subsequent collapse of O. robiniae populations in southwestern France (Dordogne, Gironde) and previously infested Belgium is well documented by EPPO RS 2008/202 and associated national reports, and its classification as a re-occurrence (not a new inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because populations were already established in Europe. Country timing has been corrected so France is now listed as [2007–2008] instead of [2005–2007], aligning with EPPO’s account of first French records in 2007 and high damage followed by parasitoid-driven decline in 2008, while Belgium remains [2005–2007] to reflect earlier detection with confirmation and peak damage by 2007.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Spodoptera frugiperda
EPP.common.name: fall armyworm, "légionnaire d’automne"
Host: Maize (Bt and non-Bt), primarily Zea mays
Event.summary: Around 2006, unexpectedly severe damage by fall armyworm was observed in Cry1F Bt maize in Puerto Rico, marking the first documented case of field-evolved resistance of S. frugiperda to a Bt maize event and leading to withdrawal of TC1507 maize there. During the early 2010s, subsequent monitoring and bioassays documented high levels of Cry1F resistance in fall armyworm populations in mainland USA (Florida, North Carolina) and in Brazil, with larvae surviving on Bt maize plants in the field. This resistance has persisted in Puerto Rico despite removal of Cry1F maize and contributed to reduced efficacy of single-toxin Bt hybrids across parts of the Americas, driving shifts to pyramided Bt traits and integrated resistance-management strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive and continuous planting of single-toxin Cry1F Bt maize hybrids (TC1507 and related events) in warm tropical and subtropical production systems with high fall armyworm pressure; inadequate refuge compliance in some areas; year-round cultivation enabling multiple pest generations. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – field-evolved resistance to the Cry1F Bt toxin (and cross-resistance to some other Cry1 toxins) mainly via changes in midgut receptors such as ABCC2 and reduced Cry1F binding, increasing larval survival and damage on Bt maize.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (retain, with modifications). Changes made: (1) Updated Event Year from "2006" to "2006-2013" so the row clearly covers the linked Cry1F resistance episode in Puerto Rico, southeastern USA and Brazil, consistent with reports of initial field-evolved resistance in Puerto Rico from 2006 onward and subsequent confirmations in Florida/North Carolina and Brazil around 2012–2013.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22537834/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Corrected continent and sub-region fields to follow the UNSD scheme: Puerto Rico is placed under South America | Caribbean, the United States under Northern America | Northern America, and Brazil under South America | South America. (3) Refined country-year annotations to Puerto Rico [2006–2008], USA [2012–2013], and Brazil [2013], which better matches the timing of documented resistance detections. Event-type classification as re-emergence (due to evolution of Bt resistance in an already established pest within its native continental range) and not as intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate and has been retained. Rationale: This is clearly one of the most impactful post-1990 events for FAW because it marks the first field-evolved resistance to a Bt maize event globally and triggered major changes in resistance management; it should be kept as a major re-emergence episode but flagged for the minor structural corrections above.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Duck herpesvirus 1, Duck plague virus
Host: Commercial Muscovy and local balady ducks on multiple farms in Gharbia Governorate
Event.summary: Between 2002 and 2004, six outbreaks of duck viral enteritis with high mortality were diagnosed in commercial Muscovy and balady duck flocks in Gharbia Governorate, Egypt, with affected birds showing classic gross and histologic lesions of duck plague and confirmation by virus isolation and histopathology.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density commercial duck production in the Nile Delta with limited biosecurity, probable contact with infected wild or backyard waterfowl, and suboptimal vaccination facilitated repeated re-occurrence of DVE on multiple farms. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was reported; lesions and virologic findings were consistent with established virulent Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1 strains circulating in Egypt since the first national report in the 1980s.
Review: retain – Added as a major African epizootic: six high-mortality outbreaks in commercial Muscovy and balady ducks in Gharbia (2002–2004) represent one of the best-documented, larger-scale DVE episodes in Egypt post‑1990. Classified as re-occurrence in Northern Africa/Egypt, where DVE has been present since 1986; event magnitude (multiple farms with high mortality) justifies inclusion, but exact flock sizes should be extracted from the full Benha Vet. Med. J. article for precise impact ranking.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic haematopoietic necrosis virus
EPP.common.name: EHNV
Host: Wild juvenile European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis); endangered Macquarie perch and other native species in nearby catchments were considered at high risk but no confirmed EHN cases in natives were reported from this lake.
Event.summary: In December 2008, EHNV was confirmed as the cause of a large mortality event in juvenile redfin perch in Lake Ginninderra in the Australian Capital Territory, marking a clear resurgence of EHN at a site with severe epizootics documented in the early 1990s.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) A further outbreak in December 2010 again produced conspicuous die‑offs of juvenile redfin, demonstrating that EHNV persisted within the upper Murrumbidgee endemic focus and could periodically re‑emerge when susceptible cohorts accumulated. Intensive surveillance conducted between 2007 and 2011 found EHNV to be absent from redfin outside the upper Murrumbidgee endemic area, underscoring the localised but persistent nature of this focus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued dominance of invasive redfin perch in Canberra‑region lakes, frequent movement of anglers and recreational craft between impoundments, and stable cool‑water conditions that favour EHNV replication and transmission all contributed to periodic re‑appearance of disease at Lake Ginninderra.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Long‑term environmental persistence of EHNV in endemic catchments and its high virulence for juvenile redfin underpin episodic mass‑mortality events when large naive cohorts are present, even if overall prevalence in the redfin population remains low between outbreaks.
Review: REVIEW – retain event but adjust classification. Evidence from Becker et al. (2019) and associated surveillance shows that these 2008 and 2010 Lake Ginninderra outbreaks are classic re‑occurrence in an established endemic focus, with no indication of a novel strain, new host, or inter‑/intra‑continental spread; accordingly, re_emergence has been set to false while re_occurrence remains true.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) All other fields, including timing, location and host, align well with published data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Sprivivirus cyprinus
EPP.common.name: Spring viraemia of carp virus
Host: Percocypris pingi (an endangered cyprinid fish endemic to the upper Yangtze River) reared in culture; SVCV is also known to infect multiple other cyprinids in China.
Event.summary: In April 2016, a severe haemorrhagic disease with more than 35% mortality was observed in cultured Percocypris pingi in Leshan County, Sichuan Province, prompting investigation of a suspected emerging pathogen in this conservation‑relevant species. Histopathology, virus isolation, RT‑PCR and sequencing identified SVCV genogroup Ia as the aetiological agent, representing the first documented SVCV infection and mass mortality in P. pingi and confirming that SVCV circulating in Chinese carp could spill over into this native cyprinid. Control efforts centred on culling affected stocks, improving hygiene and husbandry in P. pingi farms, and raising awareness of the risks that SVCV poses to endemic cyprinids as carp aquaculture continues to expand in the upper Yangtze basin.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensification and geographic expansion of aquaculture for the high‑value but conservation‑sensitive Percocypris pingi increased exposure to SVCV‑contaminated water, co‑reared carp, or shared equipment, while habitat degradation in the wild has shifted more of the species’ biomass into farms where transmission is facilitated. Internal mechanisms: this outbreak reflects host expansion (spillover) of an established SVCV Ia lineage from carp into P. pingi without major detectable genomic divergence, consistent with re_emergence driven by extension of host range rather than evolution of a new genotype.
Review: retain – This row accurately captures the 2016 SVCV‑associated mass mortality event in cultured Percocypris pingi in Sichuan, China, as described by Xiao et al.
