Event.summary: Between January 2003 and December 2005, the Australian Scedosporium (AUSCEDO) Study conducted a nationwide, laboratory-based surveillance across 49 laboratories and documented 180 episodes of scedosporiosis, including 62 episodes meeting criteria for invasive disease, establishing Scedosporium spp. as a leading non-Aspergillus mold pathogen in Australian high‚Äërisk patients.([researchers.westernsydney.edu.au](https://researchers.westernsydney.edu.au/en/publications/population-based-surveillance-for-scedosporiosis-in-australia-epi?utm_source=openai)) Molecular typing of 146 clinical isolates from this period and earlier case collections showed that most infections were due to S. prolificans or S. apiospermum, but also revealed a third cluster corresponding to the newly described species Scedosporium aurantiacum, which accounted for about one‚Äëthird of clinical isolates in some centres and was prominent among cystic fibrosis lung isolates.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2600218/?utm_source=openai)) After 2005, awareness of scedosporiosis, improved culture conditions and new PCR assays led to better recognition and targeted management, but Scedosporium remained associated with substantial morbidity and mortality among Australian transplant, hematology and chronic lung disease populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3122855/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increasing numbers of adults with advanced chronic lung disease and cystic fibrosis, expanding solid-organ and lung-transplant programs, and widespread use of amphotericin B and triazoles active against Aspergillus but less effective against Scedosporium spp., creating ecological niches for these intrinsically less susceptible molds.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3122855/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (formal description and clinical recognition of S. aurantiacum as a distinct species within the P. boydii/S. apiospermum complex in 2005, with high environmental abundance in Australia and frequent recovery from CF lungs); antimicrobial resistance (reduced susceptibility of S. prolificans and S. aurantiacum to most systemic antifungals); enhanced colonisation of structurally damaged airways and transplanted lungs facilitating persistent infection and occasional dissemination.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jcm.43.10.4930-4942.2005?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. This row accurately summarises the large AUSCEDO population-based surveillance study (2003‚Äì2005) and the contemporaneous recognition of S. aurantiacum as a distinct, clinically important species in Australia, which together constitute one of the most substantial scedosporiosis emergence events worldwide.([researchers.westernsydney.edu.au](https://researchers.westernsydney.edu.au/en/publications/population-based-surveillance-for-scedosporiosis-in-australia-epi?utm_source=openai)) The continent, subregion and country coding are correct, and classifying the event as re-emergence is appropriate because it captures both the rise of a new species (S. aurantiacum) and the marked increase in burden and clinical recognition, rather than first detection in humans. To keep the event sheet focused on the single, country‚Äëscale surveillance episode, I did not create separate rows for earlier non-clonal case clusters at Alfred and Westmead hospitals, but note them in the underlying literature; this choice is consistent with the definition of linked, country‚Äëlevel episodes and should be reviewed if finer within-country resolution is later required.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/14/2/pdfs/07-0920.pdf))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
EPP.common.name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
Host: Adult renal transplant recipients and HIV-infected adults sharing a renal/immunology/HIV building
Event.summary: Between 1994 and 1996, a Lyon hospital building that housed both renal transplant services and HIV care units experienced a cluster of ten PCP episodes in renal transplant recipients alongside 36 cases in HIV-infected patients, after only one transplant PCP case in the preceding seven years. Molecular typing of Pneumocystis isolates showed that a single genotype (type 1) was disproportionately common among transplant recipients and was shared between several transplant and HIV-infected patients who had overlapping hospital stays, pointing to nosocomial person-to-person transmission within the building. After the outbreak was recognized, the centre implemented systematic trimethoprim‚Äìsulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for susceptible patients and HAART for HIV-infected individuals, and no further PCP cases occurred in renal transplant recipients through at least 2003. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/10/04-0453_article))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High density of HIV-infected patients with PCP and renal transplant recipients in the same building; lack of, or suboptimal, anti-PCP prophylaxis in both groups during much of the period; intense immunosuppression in transplant recipients because of rejection episodes. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (molecular evidence that a predominant P. jirovecii type circulated between HIV and transplant patients); possible selection of type 1 in this local setting, but without clear evidence of novel virulence traits. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/10/04-0453_article))
Review: review: This event has been corrected to reflect the Lyon Edouard-Herriot Hospital outbreak in 1994‚Äì1996 rather than 1998‚Äì2001, matching the period when ten renal transplant and numerous HIV-infected patients developed PCP in a shared building; it is reclassified as re-occurrence since it reflects nosocomial spread of an existing genotype (type 1) under inadequate prophylaxis rather than emergence of a new strain, and remains highly informative for transmission dynamics despite modest absolute size. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/10/04-0453_article))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Rubivirus rubellae
EPP.common.name: Rubella virus
Host: Humans (children and adolescents, young adults, pregnant women; infants with CRS)
Event.summary: In 2010‚Äì2011, Viet Nam experienced a large nationwide rubella epidemic, with thousands of reported cases and an estimated 7,000 or more infections in 2011, concentrated in older children and young adults who had not been reached by earlier measles-focused immunization efforts. Many pregnant women were infected during this wave, leading in 2011‚Äì2012 to a major congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) epidemic: surveillance in tertiary hospitals identified over 400 suspected CRS infants, of whom 279 were laboratory-confirmed and 5 had congenital rubella infection, with high frequencies of low birthweight, congenital heart disease, cataracts and hearing impairment. The rubella and CRS epidemics waned after 2012, and in 2014 Viet Nam introduced a nationwide measles‚Äìrubella vaccination campaign for children 1‚Äì14 years of age followed by routine MR immunization, leading to sharp declines in rubella and CRS incidence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Absence of rubella-containing vaccine in the national immunization programme before 2014 left large susceptible cohorts of adolescents and young adults, including many women of childbearing age; high birth rates and concentration of cases in urban and industrial areas increased the number of pregnant women exposed; improvement of CRS and case-based surveillance during and after the epidemic enhanced detection and reporting of outcomes. Internal mechanisms: Available studies describe circulation of rubella virus genotypes consistent with strains circulating elsewhere in the region, without evidence that a novel, more virulent strain drove the event; thus the epidemic is best characterized as a re-occurrence of endemic rubella manifesting as a large nationwide wave once sufficient susceptibles accumulated.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This large nationwide rubella wave and subsequent CRS epidemic in Viet Nam, with 7,000+ reported rubella cases in 2011 and nearly 300 laboratory-confirmed CRS infants in 2011‚Äì2012, was previously missing and clearly qualifies as one of the most impactful rubella events globally in the vaccine era. Geography (South‚Äëeastern Asia; Viet Nam), timing (2010‚Äì2012) and classification as a re-occurrence driven by the absence of RCV and large susceptible cohorts are consistent with the definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: Varicellovirus humanalpha3
EPP.common.name: Varicella-zoster virus, Human alphaherpesvirus 3
Countries: United States of America (New York City; multiple migrant shelters and residential facilities)
Host: Recently arrived migrants (children, adolescents, and adults) living in New York City shelters and residential facilities
Event.summary: After three linked varicella cases were identified in October 2022 among recent migrants in a New York City residential facility, health authorities detected an expanding multi-facility outbreak involving asylum-seekers arriving largely from Central and South America and other regions without routine varicella vaccination. Between September 12, 2022 and March 6, 2024, surveillance documented 873 outbreak-associated chickenpox cases, predominantly in children and adolescents, with 28 hospitalizations for complications such as encephalitis, pneumonia, bacteremia, and severe skin infection; one large family shelter alone reported nearly 200 cases. Transmission within major shelters subsided following intensive on-site varicella vaccination campaigns, which raised documented immunity among resident children from roughly one-quarter to over four-fifths, alongside improved isolation and linkage to primary care, although sporadic imported cases continued with new migrant arrivals.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: sustained migration from countries where varicella vaccine is not routinely provided or where immunization programs have been disrupted; extreme crowding and mixing in NYC shelters and other temporary accommodations; initially limited systematic screening and vaccination of new arrivals. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of novel VZV strains; the outbreak reflects rapid spread of endemic VZV in a highly susceptible migrant population and demonstrates the effectiveness of large-scale catch-up vaccination in curtailing transmission.
Review: Decision: retain. Reason: with 873 reported cases and substantial morbidity in a large, multi-facility shelter system, this NYC migrant outbreak is among the largest documented varicella episodes in a high-income urban setting in the varicella vaccine era. Timeline, case counts, and hospitalization figures align with CDC MMWR reports. Emergence type as re-occurrence (re-surgence in a previously endemic subregion driven by under-immunized migrants and overcrowding) is appropriate; imported cases without onward spread outside shelters are correctly not coded as inter-continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus cacheense
EPP.common.name: Cache Valley virus
Countries: United States of America (Alabama ‚Äì urban Alabama)
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) ‚Äì 16-year-old male with IKZF1-related combined immunodeficiency (adolescent with prior immune thrombocytopenic purpura)
Event.summary: In early 2023, a 16‚Äëyear‚Äëold boy with cerebral palsy and a history of immune thrombocytopenic purpura, later found to have IKZF1‚Äëassociated combined immunodeficiency, was hospitalized in urban Alabama with dysarthria, aphasia and dysphagia after several weeks of respiratory symptoms and progressive neurologic decline. Brain MRI showed diffuse atrophy and subsequent metagenomic sequencing of cerebrospinal fluid identified CVV; despite monthly intravenous immunoglobulin and a prolonged course of the antiviral molnupiravir, he experienced fluctuating neurologic improvement and deterioration over 2023‚Äì2025, with eventual recurrence of CVV in CSF and death under hospice care. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/ofid/article/13/5/ofag217/8658568)) This case represents the first reported pediatric CVV encephalitis with longitudinal molecular monitoring and experimental antiviral therapy, further expanding the spectrum of CVV disease manifestations and vulnerable host groups.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Residence in Alabama with presumed local mosquito exposure, combined with unrecognized underlying combined immunodeficiency (IKZF1 variants) and prior B‚Äëcell‚Äìmodifying therapy for immune thrombocytopenic purpura, created marked susceptibility to chronic CVV CNS infection; diagnostic delay also reflected the rarity of the disease and limited routine testing for CVV. Internal mechanisms: The case demonstrates that CVV can cause prolonged, relapsing neuroinvasive disease in a severely immunocompromised adolescent and that viral RNA may clear from CSF during molnupiravir treatment but recur after cessation, supporting classification as re_emergence driven by altered host‚Äìvirus dynamics and novel therapeutic responses within the established North American range.
Review: Decision: review (newly added event). This row has been added to capture the recently reported pediatric CVV encephalitis case from Alabama with IKZF1-related immunodeficiency and molnupiravir treatment, which materially expands the known clinical and host spectrum of CVV disease and should be included among the major post-1990 human emergence events for this virus.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Duck herpesvirus 1, Duck plague virus
Countries: Bangladesh (Haor/wetland districts in the north-eastern region)
Host: Semi-scavenging and free-ranging domestic ducks (mixed local and commercial breeds) in village and small commercial flocks
Event.summary: Between December 2012 and November 2014, recurrent duck plague outbreaks were documented on 50 farms among 450 investigated in five Haor (wetland) districts of north-eastern Bangladesh, affecting an estimated 175,467 ducks; PCR confirmed duck plague virus in 36 outbreaks, with farm-level morbidity of about 52%, mortality near 30%, and case fatality around 57%, indicating very large aggregate losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of ducks in Haor wetlands, extensive mixing of village and nomadic flocks on communal water bodies, low and irregular vaccination coverage, and weak biosecurity favored sustained transmission and repeated large-scale outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization showed Bangladeshi field isolates clustering with virulent strains from Vietnam and China without clear evidence of a distinct new genotype, supporting classification as re-occurrence driven mainly by environmental and management factors.
Review: retain ‚Äì One of the best-quantified, highest-impact modern DVE episodes, with >170,000 ducks at risk and tens of thousands estimated dead; geography, host system, and classification as re-occurrence in Southern Asia/Bangladesh are correct and clearly supported by epidemiologic and molecular studies.

EPP.scientific.name: Baylisascaris procyonis
EPP.common.name: Baylisascariasis
Host: Captive raccoon (Procyon lotor)
Event.summary: Between 2011 and 2013, surveys of captive raccoons at multiple zoological and breeding facilities in China identified Baylisascaris procyonis eggs and adult worms, confirmed morphologically and by molecular sequencing, representing the first confirmed detection of this zoonotic parasite in the country. Infections were detected in several facilities, indicating that imported raccoons had introduced and maintained the parasite in captivity. No human cases were recognized during this period, but the study highlighted substantial environmental contamination potential and the risk of future spillover to humans and wildlife as raccoons spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: importation and breeding of raccoons for zoo display and the pet trade in China without systematic parasite screening or quarantine, and growing numbers of captive raccoons increasing environmental contamination. Internal mechanisms: efficient fecal‚Äìoral transmission and high egg production enabling establishment in captive populations; genetic analyses showed close relatedness to North American and European B. procyonis, consistent with recent introductions rather than long‚Äëstanding endemic strains.
Review: Review ‚Äì Retained as the first confirmed detection of B. procyonis in China, but removed the intra_continental_emergence flag. Japan and China are both classified in the same UN Eastern Asia subregion, and by definition intra‚Äëcontinental emergence in this project refers to spread into a new subregion, not merely into an additional country within the same subregion. First_detection is kept to indicate first documented occurrence in China.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Baylisascaris procyonis
EPP.common.name: Baylisascariasis
Host: Humans (children and adults) with neural and ocular larva migrans; raccoon (Procyon lotor) as definitive host
Event.summary: From May 2013 through December 2015, CDC identified seven confirmed or probable human Baylisascaris procyonis infections with central nervous system or ocular disease in patients from six U.S. states, compared with 22 cases reported in the preceding four decades. Cases occurred in young children and adults living in raccoon‚Äëprevalent areas of Oklahoma/Arkansas, Ohio, Massachusetts, California, Virginia and Minnesota, most with documented or likely exposure to raccoon latrines or contaminated soil. The cluster of severe, highly publicized cases prompted new clinical alerts and public‚Äëhealth messaging but did not signal control of the parasite in raccoons, which remains widespread across North America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increasing raccoon densities and human‚Äìraccoon contact in suburban and peri‚Äëurban settings, limited public awareness of latrine‚Äëassociated risks, and improved diagnostic tools and surveillance (including use of a recombinant antigen immunoblot at CDC) that enhanced recognition of human cases. Internal mechanisms: pronounced neurotropism of B. procyonis larvae in paratenic hosts leading to severe neural larva migrans even with low‚Äëlevel exposure; no novel strain was reported, but existing virulence combined with changing exposure patterns produced a perceptible re‚Äëoccurrence of severe disease.
Review: Review ‚Äì Retained as a major human baylisascariasis episode but corrected geography and type. The original row listed several U.S. states that did not appear in the 2013‚Äì2015 case series; the countries field is now limited to ‚ÄúUnited States of America,‚Äù with specific states described in the narrative, consistent with MMWR 2016. Because the cluster occurred in an already endemic North American subregion and there is no evidence for a novel strain, intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence were set to No and the event is coded purely as a re_occurrence driven by exposure and surveillance changes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Border disease virus
EPP.common.name: BDV, Pestivirus D
Host: Pyrenean chamois (Rupicapra pyrenaica pyrenaica)
Event.summary: Beginning in mid‚Äë2005, a second major wave of BDV‚Äëassociated disease in Pyrenean chamois was detected in the Cad√≠ and Cerdanya‚ÄìAlt Urgell hunting reserves and neighboring areas of northeastern Spain, spreading over more than 120,000‚Äì130,000 hectares of alpine habitat. Over roughly 31 months, an estimated 3,000 chamois died and in the worst‚Äëaffected reserve numbers fell from about 3,458 animals in 2004 to 1,281 by mid‚Äë2006 (‚âà63% decline), after which the outbreak gradually subsided as surviving chamois developed immunity and BDV‚Äë4 transitioned to endemic circulation at lower prevalence. This multi‚Äëyear epizootic confirmed BDV‚Äë4 as a key population driver for Pyrenean chamois and demonstrated the capacity for repeated, spatially expanding die‚Äëoffs in connected subpopulations.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/17726/cdc_17726_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement and spatial connectivity of chamois subpopulations across contiguous mountain reserves, high densities in preferred ranges, and limited feasibility of controlling infection in free‚Äëranging wildlife facilitated re‚Äëintroduction and spread of BDV‚Äë4 beyond the initial outbreak area. Internal mechanisms: continued circulation of the previously emerged BDV‚Äë4 genotype in a largely immunologically na√Øve metapopulation, with no evidence for a fundamentally new strain but with demographic feedbacks (recruitment of susceptible juveniles) enabling a large re‚Äëoccurring epizootic. This fits the project definition of re‚Äëoccurrence in the same subregion driven primarily by ecological and management factors rather than additional viral change.
Review: Retain: Major follow‚Äëon epizootic with very large wildlife mortality and range expansion within the Pyrenees. Re‚Äëclassified as re_occurrence (Yes) and re_emergence (No) because it reflects re‚Äëappearance and geographic spread of the same BDV‚Äë4 lineage rather than emergence of a new genotype.

EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus
EPP.common.name: FP-associated herpesvirus, CFPHV
Countries: Australia (Moreton Bay, Queensland and nearby inshore foraging grounds)
Host: Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas); loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta)
Event.summary: Health surveys of marine turtles in Moreton Bay, Queensland, in 1998‚Äì2000 revealed FP tumors in around 17% of examined green turtles and 8% of loggerheads, demonstrating a pronounced local epizootic in an area where FP had previously been rarely reported although present elsewhere along the Queensland coast since the 1970s. Subsequent monitoring showed that FP remained established but with variable prevalence among inshore foraging sites, prompting concern that the disease could become a significant contributor to morbidity in eastern Australian turtle populations and spurring broader Great Barrier Reef health investigations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Moreton Bay is a highly modified estuarine‚Äìcoastal system influenced by urban development, port and industrial activities, and riverine runoff, all of which can degrade water quality and favor eutrophication and macroalgal blooms; these factors mirror environmental correlates of FP hotspots in other regions and are suspected to promote tumor expression in CFPHV‚Äëinfected turtles. Internal mechanisms: Histopathology and PCR confirmed typical FP lesions and ChHV5 infection in Australian turtles, and subsequent genetic work across Queensland foraging grounds has shown that viral variants are structured by foraging area rather than reflecting a novel, more virulent strain. The Moreton Bay episode is therefore best characterized as a regional re‚Äëoccurrence of FP within an already affected sub‚Äëregion, linked to environmental cofactors and high turtle density.
Review: retain ‚Äì Moreton Bay represents the clearest, well‚Äëdocumented FP epizootic in eastern Australia and is widely cited as a key Great Barrier Reef‚Äìadjacent hotspot. Event type has been changed from intra‚Äëcontinental emergence plus re‚Äëemergence to re‚Äëoccurrence only, reflecting that FP was already known from Queensland in earlier decades and that current evidence points to environmental, not viral, change as the dominant driver. Sources remain appropriate, anchored on the original survey and subsequent Queensland‚Äëfocused work.

EPP.scientific.name: Encephalomyocarditis virus
EPP.common.name: EMCV, Cardiovirus A
Host: Multiple captive zoo mammals in the southeastern United States, including an African elephant, an East African hippopotamus, and a common brown lemur (Eulemur fulvus), plus associated rodents on zoo grounds
Event.summary: Between approximately 2018 and 2020, a series of fatal EMCV infections occurred in US zoological collections in the southeastern states, including an East African hippopotamus at a Texas zoo in 2018 (isolate N‚Äë19‚Äë013), a common brown lemur at a south Florida facility in 2020 (N‚Äë20‚Äë413), and an index African elephant case (N‚Äë037‚Äë19) that prompted detailed investigation and vaccine development. Within at least one affected institution, multiple susceptible species died over a period of only a few weeks, with necropsies showing severe necrotizing myocarditis and pulmonary edema consistent with EMCV. Following diagnosis, zoos implemented intensive rodent control, improved enclosure and feed‚Äëstorage hygiene, and, in at least one case, an autogenous inactivated EMCV vaccine program for elephants and other high‚Äëvalue species; after these measures, EMCV‚Äëassociated deaths in the involved collections declined sharply, though EMCV remains a recognized recurrent threat in North American zoos.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Co‚Äëhousing of diverse, often immunologically naive zoo mammals in outdoor or semi‚Äëoutdoor enclosures where synanthropic rodents can access feed and bedding created repeated opportunities for spillover; shared feed sources and occasional animal transfers may have contributed to within‚Äë and between‚Äëfacility spread. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses of N‚Äë037‚Äë19, N‚Äë19‚Äë013, and N‚Äë20‚Äë413 showed that these viruses belong to EMCV serotype 1 and share close capsid antigenic profiles with other recent EMCV‚Äë1 strains rather than representing a novel species or serotype; the episode is therefore best viewed as a re‚Äëoccurrence of endemic EMCV in high‚Äëvalue zoo hosts with enhanced transmission at the wildlife‚Äìrodent interface, rather than emergence of a fundamentally new lineage.
Review: Decision: retain. The timeframe (2018‚Äì2020), host range (elephant, hippopotamus, lemur), and characterization of this as a multi‚Äëfacility zoo outbreak cluster are consistent with the recent "zoological transmission" study; no substantive corrections were needed beyond phrasing. Classification as re‚Äëoccurrence is appropriate, given long‚Äëstanding EMCV presence in North American pigs and zoo mammals and the lack of evidence that these isolates constitute a new serotype; intra‚Äë or inter‚Äëcontinental emergence is not supported. Because the event description aggregates several closely linked fatal cases across facilities but the exact start and end dates are approximate, a human reviewer may wish to refine the date range if more detailed facility‚Äëlevel timelines are needed, but the event clearly qualifies as a major modern zoo emergence episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma agalactiae
EPP.common.name: Contagious agalactia
Countries: North Macedonia ‚Äì Debar and Gostivar regions
Host: Domestic sheep and goats (small ruminants)
Event.summary: From 1997 to 1999, severe outbreaks of contagious agalactia occurred first in the Debar region and later in the adjoining Gostivar prefecture of what is now North Macedonia, affecting almost 80% of local small‚Äëruminant flocks. Laboratory investigation of the 1999 incidents, including bacterial isolation and serology, confirmed Mycoplasma agalactiae as the causative agent, documenting the pathogen‚Äôs presence in this Balkan country within a broader Southern European endemic zone. The episode prompted proposals for serological surveillance and control measures, and CA has since been recognised as present but not among the most commonly reported small‚Äëruminant diseases nationally.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: cross‚Äëborder animal movements and trade within the western Balkans, traditional transhumant grazing systems and limited prior diagnostic capacity likely allowed unnoticed introduction and amplification of CA in local flocks before confirmation. Internal mechanisms: the available data do not indicate novel strain characteristics; this episode is best interpreted as a marked regional re‚Äëoccurrence of classical M. agalactiae‚Äëassociated CA within an already affected Southern European subregion rather than a first detection or intra‚Äëcontinental emergence under the UN sub‚Äëregion definitions.
Review: review ‚Äì corrected the event years to 1997‚Äì1999 (matching the reported Debar and Gostivar outbreaks) instead of 2001, clarified that the affected areas were Debar and Gostivar within North Macedonia, and reclassified the episode as a re‚Äëoccurrence in the Southern Europe sub‚Äëregion rather than as a 'first detection' or 'intra‚Äëcontinental emergence', which would conflict with the instruction not to treat spread to a new country within the same sub‚Äëregion as intra‚Äëcontinental emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cacopsylla pruni
EPP.common.name: plum psyllid
Host: Mother‚Äëplant orchard of apricot (Prunus armeniaca), Japanese plum (P. salicina), European plum (P. domestica), peach and nectarine (P. persica) in the Primorska region, plus surrounding wild Prunus spp.
Event.summary: Between 2004 and 2006, a mother‚Äëplant orchard established in 2001 with virus‚Äëfree material in the Primorska region of Slovenia experienced a severe ESFY outbreak. Molecular surveys showed that 70% of sampled apricot trees and all sampled Japanese plum trees were infected with ‚ÄòCa. Phytoplasma prunorum‚Äô, while about half of sampled European plums and a smaller proportion of peaches and nectarines were also infected, often without clear symptoms; sudden wilting and dieback affected more than half of the apricot trees, which were subsequently removed. Cacopsylla pruni adults trapped near the orchard all tested positive for ESFY phytoplasma, indicating very high local infection pressure and revealing that the surrounding wild Prunus and vector populations posed a serious threat to the production of healthy planting material.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Establishment of a multi‚Äëspecies mother‚Äëplant orchard in a landscape with abundant wild Prunus and established ESFY, combined with use of material tested for viruses but not necessarily for phytoplasmas, allowed rapid build‚Äëup of infection once the pathogen and vector were present. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/Vector adaptation ‚Äì local C. pruni populations reached high densities on wild and cultivated Prunus and showed 100% infection in tested samples, so their seasonal movement between wild reservoirs and mother plants created an intense and self‚Äësustaining ESFY focus that was difficult to control by tree removal alone.
Review: review ‚Äì Added this Slovenian mother‚Äëplant‚Äëorchard outbreak because the extremely high ESFY incidence in apricot and Japanese plum, the documented infection of C. pruni and the need to remove large parts of the orchard make it one of the most consequential ESFY/C. pruni events in Central‚ÄìSouthern Europe. Classified it as a re_occurrence in a region where both vector and pathogen were already present, driven by high infection pressure in a critical planting‚Äëmaterial source rather than by a new introduction or vector lineage. Sources were chosen to reflect the primary case study and broader distribution context, and this new row should be reviewed to confirm that the timing and host details match national surveillance data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Helicoverpa armigera
EPP.common.name: cotton bollworm
Host: Bt cotton (Cry1Ac‚Äëexpressing cultivars)
Event.summary: By about 2010, after more than a decade of widespread Bt cotton cultivation in northern China, resistance monitoring detected reduced susceptibility of Helicoverpa armigera populations to Cry1Ac and provided evidence of field‚Äëevolved resistance in at least one area (Qiuxian, Hebei).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19764057/?utm_source=openai)) Over the next few seasons, these resistant populations contributed to localized increases in boll damage and higher larval survival on Bt cotton in some counties, though large‚Äëscale crop failure was avoided through continued refuge cropping and integrated pest management. Continued resistance monitoring, adjustments to refuge strategies and diversification of control tactics have since limited the spread and impact of high‚Äëlevel Cry1Ac resistance, but this episode marked a clear evolutionary shift and ongoing re‚Äëemergence risk in Bt‚Äëbased cotton systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extremely high adoption rates of single‚Äëtoxin Cry1Ac Bt cotton across northern China with relatively limited and spatially patchy structured refuges, imposing strong and prolonged selection pressure on H. armigera. Internal mechanisms: genetic changes conferring resistance to Cry1Ac (including increased frequency of resistance alleles and altered midgut receptor interactions), documented as field‚Äëevolved resistance in at least one region, representing a re‚Äëemergence of the pest in Bt‚Äëcotton systems despite previous successful suppression.
Review: retain ‚Äì Keep as a major event. Evidence from resistance‚Äëmonitoring and early‚Äëwarning studies in northern China clearly documents field‚Äëevolved Cry1Ac resistance in H. armigera by around 2010, with localized agronomic impacts and substantial implications for long‚Äëterm Bt‚Äëcotton sustainability.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19764057/?utm_source=openai)) The existing classification as re‚Äëemergence (without intra‚Äë or inter‚Äëcontinental components) is appropriate, and the geographic and temporal framing is consistent with the underlying literature. No structural corrections were needed; only flagged for continued monitoring as resistance frequencies evolve.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoebolavirus zairense
EPP.common.name: Ebola virus
Host: Humans in conflict-affected communities in North Kivu, Ituri and South Kivu Provinces, including health-care workers
Event.summary: In August 2018, Ebola virus disease due to Zaire ebolavirus was detected in North Kivu Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, only days after a smaller Equateur outbreak elsewhere in the country ended, marking DRC‚Äôs tenth recorded Ebola outbreak and its first large epidemic in the densely populated, conflict-affected eastern provinces of North Kivu and Ituri (later also South Kivu). The epidemic spread across health zones in these provinces and ultimately caused around 3,470 cases and 2,280 deaths, with persistent transmission fueled by insecurity, attacks on health facilities, community mistrust, and frequent population movement; a small number of cases were detected in neighboring Uganda as cross-border importations without sustained local transmission. Deployment of a ring-vaccination strategy with rVSV-ZEBOV-GP, novel therapeutics in Ebola treatment units, and gradual improvements in community engagement and security eventually reduced case incidence, and WHO declared the outbreak over on 25 June 2020.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: complex humanitarian emergency in eastern DRC with ongoing armed conflict, population displacement, and attacks on health workers and treatment centers; weak and fragmented health infrastructure; high mobility across porous borders; burial and caregiving practices involving close contact; initial mistrust of response teams. Internal mechanisms: outbreak caused by Zaire ebolavirus, with genomic data consistent with a single spillover event followed by human-to-human transmission and ongoing within-epidemic evolution; despite viral diversification, social and security conditions, rather than a qualitatively more transmissible strain, explain the scale of the epidemic. Because cases detected in Uganda were importations with no sustained chains of transmission, the episode is classified as a large re-occurrence in Middle Africa rather than as intra-continental emergence into Eastern Africa.
Review: Status: retained with modification. Uganda has been removed from the country and sub-region fields and the intra-continental emergence flag is set to false because the few cases detected in Uganda during this period were cross-border importations without sustained in situ transmission; the episode is best characterized as a very large re-occurrence in a previously affected country and sub-region driven by conflict and health-system weaknesses.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio cholerae
EPP.common.name: Cholera bacterium
Host: Humans (rural and peri‑urban populations, especially in northern and north‑eastern states, including conflict‑affected areas)
Event.summary: After years of intermittent outbreaks, Nigeria experienced exceptionally large cholera waves during October 2020–October 2021, with about 93,600 suspected cases and roughly 3,300 deaths reported nationwide across 33 of 37 states, making it the largest documented cholera epidemic in the country’s history. The outbreaks disproportionately affected northern states with poor WASH infrastructure, insecurity and population displacement, and were further complicated by the concurrent COVID‑19 pandemic, which strained surveillance and response capacity. Intensified case management, risk communication, and WASH interventions, together with seasonal declines in transmission, brought case numbers down after late 2021, although Nigeria continues to report recurrent cholera activity and remains one of the countries with the highest estimated cholera burden.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Inadequate access to safe water and sanitation, particularly in rural northern states; conflict and displacement in the north‑east; heavy rainfall and flooding in some regions; overlapping health emergencies (COVID‑19 and others) diverting resources from cholera control. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of endemic seventh‑pandemic strains; possible contribution of antimicrobial resistance in some isolates, but epidemiologic patterns are primarily explained by environmental and systemic drivers.
Review: retain – Nigeria’s 2020–2021 epidemic (~93,600 cases and ~3,300 deaths) is the country’s largest documented cholera outbreak and one of the largest recent national epidemics globally, particularly notable for its interaction with the COVID‑19 response and for the breadth of states affected.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11770646/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re‑occurrence in a long‑affected sub‑region is appropriate. No geographical corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: After several decades of mainly sporadic activity, chikungunya virus caused two large urban outbreaks in 1999–2000 in the Matete and Kingabwa townships of Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo, following periods of heavy rain. Contemporary investigations estimated around 50,000 human cases of febrile arthralgia, and virologic work confirmed chikungunya virus of a Central African lineage as the etiologic agent. Transmission declined after 2000 as vector densities fell and population immunity increased, but the episode signaled renewed epidemic potential in Central African cities and preceded later large outbreaks around the Indian Ocean and in Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5384432/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid urban growth in Kinshasa, poor drainage, and heavy rainfall created extensive Aedes breeding sites in densely populated neighborhoods, facilitating intense human–mosquito–human transmission. Limited arboviral surveillance and diagnostic capacity meant the chikungunya etiology was only recognized after substantial spread. Internal mechanisms: Virus isolates from this outbreak formed a distinct Central African chikungunya lineage, indicating evolutionary divergence from earlier East African strains and supporting classification as re‑emergence rather than simple recurrence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5384432/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added because the 1999–2000 Kinshasa outbreaks (≈50,000 cases) are widely cited as a major modern re‑emergence in Africa and are among the most impactful post‑1990 chikungunya events. Classified as re‑emergence in Middle Africa with no inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence flags, since chikungunya was already established on the continent. Recommend retaining this event after manual verification of case estimates and locality.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In May 2014, the first chikungunya infection in French Polynesia was detected in a traveler returning from Guadeloupe, and local transmission was documented from October 2014 onward. The virus then spread rapidly across Tahiti and most archipelagos, ultimately infecting an estimated 60,000–70,000 people (about one quarter of the population) and causing notable numbers of severe and atypical cases, including ICU admissions and deaths, as well as an increase in Guillain–Barré syndrome. Transmission declined by early 2015 as vector control was reinforced and a high proportion of residents became immune, but chronic rheumatologic sequelae persisted in many patients.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1341321X16301428?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of an Asian‑lineage virus from the Caribbean via air travel, together with high densities of Aedes aegypti and climatic conditions favoring year‑round vector abundance, enabled rapid amplification in densely populated island communities. Concurrent dengue and later Zika circulation complicated clinical recognition and further strained health services. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed an Asian genotype closely related to Caribbean strains, indicating long‑distance human‑mediated movement of an existing lineage rather than the emergence of a novel mutant; this outbreak is best characterized as intra‑continental emergence into the Polynesian subregion of Oceania.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6407142/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retained as the major high‑impact Pacific outbreak, with case numbers and severity (including ICU admissions and neurological complications) well documented. Emergence type recoded as intra‑continental emergence (Polynesia within Oceania) rather than first detection or inter‑continental emergence, because chikungunya had already established local transmission in Melanesia and Micronesia by 2011–2013. No changes to geography or timing; sources remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Pakistan reported its first recognized chikungunya outbreak in December 2016 in Karachi, Sindh Province, after weeks of unexplained febrile illness with severe arthralgia in densely populated neighborhoods. Over subsequent months, thousands of suspected cases were reported in Karachi and additional foci in Balochistan and other provinces, with WHO documenting roughly 1,000 suspected cases by March 2017 while local health authorities and clinical studies estimated more than 30,000 people affected. Transmission decreased later in 2017 as surveillance improved, vector control measures were intensified and seasonal declines in Aedes populations occurred, but chikungunya became established as a recurrent arboviral threat in major Pakistani cities.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6986857/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid, often unplanned urbanization in Karachi and other cities, poor solid‑waste management and abundant water‑holding containers favored proliferation of Aedes aegypti; weak baseline arboviral surveillance delayed recognition and response. High human mobility within and between provinces facilitated spread from initial foci. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses linked Pakistani strains to ECSA/Indian Ocean lineage viruses carrying additional mutations (including E1:K211E and E2:V264A) associated with enhanced transmission efficiency in urban Aedes populations, consistent with re‑emergence of an adapted lineage in a previously unaffected national setting.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8638460/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retained as a major first national outbreak in a large, densely populated South Asian country, but “first_detection” and “intra‑continental emergence” flags were removed because chikungunya had long been recognized in humans and in the Southern Asia subregion (India, Sri Lanka, etc.). The episode is more accurately classified as re‑emergence of an adapted ECSA lineage into a new national setting within an already affected subregion. Case‑number statements were harmonized with WHO EMRO and peer‑reviewed estimates.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: After its first documented autochthonous chikungunya outbreak in 2015–2016, Paraguay experienced a much larger resurgence beginning in October 2022, with national surveillance recording roughly 71,000–80,000 suspected, probable or confirmed cases by March 2023 and about 118,000 suspected and confirmed infections by early April. The epidemic, concentrated initially in Asunción and the surrounding Central Department, caused high hospitalization rates and at least 46 deaths, with severe disease observed particularly in infants and older adults, and coincided with co‑circulating dengue. Transmission declined later in 2023 as vector control was intensified and seasonal conditions became less favorable, but the wave highlighted the potential for high‑impact resurgence of chikungunya in subtropical South America.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7223a5.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High Aedes aegypti densities in urban Paraguay, warm and wet seasonal conditions and gaps in sustained vector control campaigns favored rapid amplification, while socioeconomic factors such as limited access to secure water and air‑conditioning increased human–mosquito contact. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses showed that the 2022–2023 wave was driven by an ECSA lineage that had circulated in Paraguay since mid‑2010s; the surge appears to reflect climatic and demographic drivers acting on a persisting lineage rather than a markedly altered viral phenotype, and is therefore classified as re‑occurrence rather than a distinct re‑emergence event.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8084490/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retained as a major recent resurgence with very high incidence and notable severity in Paraguay. Emergence type recoded as re‑occurrence only: available genomic data indicate epidemic expansion of an established ECSA lineage rather than emergence of a substantially new variant. Event summary updated to reflect more precise case and death counts from CDC MMWR and EID reports.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida parapsilosis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Very low birthweight and preterm neonates in a tertiary hospital neonatal intensive care unit
Event.summary:
From 1987 to 1991, a prolonged outbreak of Candida parapsilosis colonization and infection affected the neonatal intensive care unit at the Children’s Hospital, University of Helsinki, with a total of 58 colonized or infected infants; the 1990–1991 period falls within the tail of this episode, during which very low birthweight infants frequently developed C. parapsilosis sepsis and had markedly increased mortality compared with uninfected controls.
([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8559627/?utm_source=openai)) Epidemiologic investigation found C. parapsilosis on the hands of several nurses but not in environmental reservoirs, supporting sustained patient-to-patient transmission in the unit.
([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8559627/?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak subsided after reinforcement of infection-control measures and the introduction of prolonged parenteral fluconazole prophylaxis for extremely preterm infants, which coincided with cessation of new cases.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Expansion of intensive care for extremely preterm, very low birthweight infants, extensive use of central venous catheters and parenteral nutrition, and high exposure to broad-spectrum antibiotics created a setting highly permissive for exogenous C. parapsilosis transmission in the Helsinki NICU; hand contamination of nurses provided a key transmission route.
([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8559627/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No specific antifungal resistance mechanism was documented during this episode; instead, the outbreak reflected the intrinsic ability of C. parapsilosis to colonize skin and catheter surfaces, form biofilms, and persist as one or a few successful clones in the unit.
Review: review – Added as a new high‑impact event capturing the 1990–1991 portion of a 55‑month NICU outbreak in Helsinki with 58 colonized/infected neonates and high mortality, which is repeatedly cited as a landmark C. parapsilosis outbreak. Classified as re-occurrence (no documented antifungal resistance), with continent/subregion/country fields aligned to the UN scheme. Although the outbreak began in 1987, only the 1990–1991 period is represented here to respect the ≥1990 time window; recommend curator confirmation that including this truncated yet epidemiologically coherent episode is acceptable.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland – Northern Ireland [2000-2001]
Host: Humans (residents served by three separate public drinking‑water systems in the greater Belfast area)
Event.summary: From April 2000 to April 2001, three epidemiologically unrelated drinking‑water‑associated cryptosporidiosis outbreaks occurred in different supply zones in the greater Belfast area of Northern Ireland. Outbreak A in spring 2000 produced at least 129 laboratory‑confirmed cases, outbreak B later that year produced 117 cases, and outbreak C in early 2001 produced 275 cases, together resulting in several hundred confirmed infections in communities served by distinct water treatment works with varying vulnerabilities. Once investigations linked these clusters to specific supplies and genotyping showed involvement of both bovine and human C. parvum genotypes, targeted boil‑water advice, remedial treatment and distribution‑system improvements were implemented at the affected works, after which outbreak incidence declined and routine cryptosporidiosis surveillance returned toward baseline.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: multiple deficiencies in drinking‑water systems in a region with endemic Cryptosporidium in both humans and livestock, including contamination of surface‑water sources by agricultural runoff or sewage and weaknesses in filtration or distribution‑system integrity, rather than a single shared source. Internal mechanisms: circulation of established bovine and human C. parvum genotypes capable of waterborne spread; although different genotypes and subgenotypes were involved in the three outbreaks, they were already present in the region and there is no clear evidence of a novel, more virulent strain emerging during 2000–2001.
Review: review – Existing row substantially revised. Original text understated the total number of cases across the three Northern Ireland outbreaks and did not clearly convey that they were epidemiologically unrelated events in separate supply zones. Case counts and linkage to specific waterworks have been aligned with the EID article; classification as a re‑occurrence in an already endemic region remains appropriate. Consider whether to keep these three linked but moderate‑size outbreaks as a single aggregated event if a strict top‑10 global list is enforced.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Countries: Sweden – Östersund and neighboring municipalities on the same supply [2010-2011]
Host: Humans (municipal drinking‑water consumers in Östersund and adjacent communities)
Event.summary: Beginning in November 2010, residents of Östersund in northern Sweden developed widespread acute diarrheal illness that investigation quickly traced to the public drinking‑water supply, with C. hominis subtype IbA10G2 detected in patient stool and environmental samples. Over late 2010 and early 2011, approximately 27,000 people in the municipality and neighboring communities served by the same supply were estimated to have been infected, in what became the largest documented waterborne cryptosporidiosis outbreak in Europe, prompting a long‑lasting boil‑water advisory, school and workplace disruptions, and sustained health‑care demand. The outbreak ended after enhanced treatment barriers, including UV disinfection, were installed, contaminated water was flushed from the distribution system, and the contamination source was controlled; follow‑up studies documented persistent gastrointestinal symptoms in a subset of affected individuals months to years later.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: contamination of a surface‑water source and/or distribution system with human sewage in a system that lacked adequate barriers to protozoa, limited routine testing for Cryptosporidium, and climatic conditions that may have contributed to contamination pulses. Internal mechanisms: a highly transmissible C. hominis subtype, low infectious dose, and the resilience of oocysts in cold surface waters allowed widespread distribution of infection via municipal tap water; however, the subtype IbA10G2 was already globally distributed and does not represent a novel lineage in Sweden, so the episode is classified as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: retain – This is the largest documented waterborne Cryptosporidium outbreak in Europe and one of the top global events by case count. Geography, timing, and classification as a re‑occurrence driven by water-treatment and sewage issues are consistent with Swedish and CDC reports; case-count estimates (~27,000 infections) are in line with primary sources. No structural corrections were needed, so the row can be retained as a key reference event.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans in northern and central districts; Pteropus bats (reservoir)
Event.summary: During the 2010–11 and 2011–12 Nipah seasons, Bangladesh experienced some of its largest and deadliest recurrent outbreaks, notably in northern districts including Lalmonirhat, Rangpur and Dinajpur and later Joypurhat and neighbouring areas, with about 44 cases and 40 deaths in 2011 and a further 12 cases and 10 deaths in 2012. Many index cases reported drinking fresh or fermented date palm sap, and extended household and neighbourhood transmission chains were documented, including clusters involving school‑aged children. These seasonal outbreaks subsided each year after targeted risk‑communication campaigns, changes in sap‑drinking behaviour and the end of the sap‑harvesting period, but they confirmed the entrenched winter seasonality and high lethality of Nipah in Bangladesh.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: entrenched cultural practices of consuming raw and fermented date palm sap contaminated by bat excreta, limited adoption of sap‑protection measures, and delayed recognition and isolation of Nipah cases in remote districts led to large multi‑district clusters. Internal mechanisms: continuing circulation of Bangladesh‑lineage Nipah virus with efficient person‑to‑person transmission in close‑contact settings; increased incidence is best explained by ecological and behavioural factors rather than documented viral evolution.
Review: retain – appropriately treats the 2011 and 2012 northern Bangladesh outbreaks as a linked recurrent episode confined to Southern Asia, with correct order‑of‑magnitude case counts and emphasis on raw/fermented date palm sap and person‑to‑person spread; classification as re‑occurrence is consistent with definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: Scedosporium spp.
EPP.common.name: scedosporiosis
Host: Humans (previously healthy or mildly comorbid adults and children who survived near-drowning during the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and aspirated heavily contaminated seawater and sludge)
Event.summary: Following the December 26, 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, several near-drowning survivors in southern Thailand developed severe Scedosporium apiospermum/Pseudallescheria boydii complex infections weeks after aspirating polluted tsunami waters, including cases of vertebral osteomyelitis and brain abscess with antecedent pneumonia (“tsunami lung”).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3366756/?utm_source=openai)) A review of near-drowning-associated scedosporiosis identified at least two such tsunami survivors among 20+ global cases, highlighting extremely high mortality (≈70%) and a strong tendency for CNS dissemination, even in immunocompetent hosts.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17714363/?utm_source=openai)) As environmental contamination receded and acute disaster conditions resolved, no ongoing local transmission chains were documented, but these sentinel cases established Scedosporium spp. as key causes of invasive fungal disease in tsunami and near-drowning victims in tropical coastal settings.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3366756/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extreme environmental disturbance from the Indian Ocean tsunami, which mixed soil, sewage, hydrocarbons and marine waters into stagnant pools and debris fields, producing high inocula of Scedosporium conidia in water aspirated by victims; prolonged entrapment in contaminated water, traumatic injuries and delays in definitive care that favoured tissue necrosis and secondary infection; and intensive antibacterial therapy that may suppress bacterial competitors while sparing Scedosporium.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3366756/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission/host adaptation (ecological adaptation of S. apiospermum/P. boydii to sewage and polluted brackish water, enabling massive exposure during near-drowning); increased virulence/pathogenicity (marked angioinvasiveness with a strong propensity for hematogenous CNS and bone dissemination and delayed, insidious clinical presentation).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17714363/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event). This row extracts the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami–related scedosporiosis cases in Thailand as a distinct, temporally and geographically bounded emergence episode, in line with the guideline that events should only be merged when epidemiologically linked or continuous within the same outbreak area.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3366756/?utm_source=openai)) It is correctly coded as re-occurrence rather than inter-continental or first-emergence, because Scedosporium was already present in South-eastern Asia and the spike in cases is driven by an external environmental catastrophe rather than novel pathogen traits. Countries and subregion follow the UNSD scheme, and the main sources now focus tightly on tsunami/near-drowning–associated disease rather than general Scedosporium epidemiology.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria meningitidis
EPP.common.name: meningococcus
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From December 2016 to June 2017, Nigeria experienced the largest documented epidemic of serogroup C meningococcal meningitis globally, centred in several northern states of the meningitis belt. Over this period, approximately 14,518 suspected cases and 1,166 deaths were reported, with laboratory-confirmed cases overwhelmingly due to the same ST‑10217 serogroup C lineage that had caused earlier, more localised outbreaks in 2013–2015 in north‑west Nigeria and in Niger in 2015. Intensive case management, reactive vaccination campaigns with C‑containing polysaccharide and conjugate vaccines, and the eventual onset of the rains brought the epidemic under control by mid‑2017, although further localised NmC outbreaks continued to occur.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climatic conditions of the meningitis belt, persistent household crowding, limited early access to care, and delays in obtaining sufficient serogroup C vaccine doses contributed to rapid spread once ST‑10217 became established in multiple northern Nigerian states. Internal mechanisms: This epidemic represents further geographic and demographic expansion of the hyperinvasive ST‑10217 serogroup C lineage that had emerged earlier in north‑west Nigeria and Niger, clearly fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by a novel strain with high epidemic potential in previously affected subregions.
Review: review – New major event added. The 2016–2017 Nigeria NmC epidemic, with >14,000 suspected cases and >1,000 deaths, is widely cited as the largest MenC outbreak ever recorded and is epidemiologically linked to the earlier ST‑10217 emergence in north‑west Nigeria and Niger. It was missing from the original dataset. I classified it as re‑emergence (expansion of a novel clone in previously affected subregions), without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence flags, and limited the country field to Nigeria, where this particular wave was concentrated.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus machupoense
EPP.common.name: Machupo virus
Host: Humans in Beni Department (Magdalena, Huacaraje, San Ramón and nearby rural communities), including residents and health‑care workers
Event.summary: From early 2007 into 2008, Beni Department experienced the largest recognized resurgence of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever since the 1960s. Surveillance first detected around 20 suspected BHF cases with three deaths near Magdalena and neighboring areas of Iténez Province, followed in February 2008 by reports of roughly 200 additional suspected cases and 12 deaths from municipalities including Huacaraje and San Ramón; a joint investigation by Bolivian authorities and CDC ultimately confirmed Machupo virus infection in five patients (three fatal), demonstrating active viral circulation across multiple rural communities. Intensive rodent‑control campaigns, reinforcement of infection‑prevention measures in local health facilities, and community education were deployed, and by late 2008 reported incidence had fallen back to low endemic levels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2819859/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion and improved road connectivity of rural communities in Beni, climatic variability and land‑use changes that likely boosted C. callosus populations, and persistent gaps in rodent‑proofing of homes and food‑storage structures created conditions for widespread human–rodent contact; limited infection‑prevention capacity in small health centers contributed to local amplification and infection of health‑care workers. Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses of 2007–2008 Machupo isolates show close continuity with earlier strains rather than a distinct new genotype, and no evidence of altered virulence or host range, so this multi‑year episode is best understood as a pronounced re‑occurrence driven by ecological and social factors rather than intrinsic viral evolution. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2819859/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain / Review: This row correctly captures the key 2007–2008 resurgence and classifies it as a major re‑occurrence in the endemic Beni focus rather than inter‑continental spread. I have revised the narrative to distinguish suspected from laboratory‑confirmed cases and to align more closely with the CDC Emerging Infectious Diseases investigation and Bolivian surveillance reports, and I have pruned less authoritative sources (e.g., language‑specific Wikipedia and tertiary summaries) in favor of primary CDC and Ministry of Health documents. Because of discrepancies between suspected and confirmed counts, the event should remain flagged for expert review but clearly belongs among the top post‑1990 Machupo events. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2819859/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus machupoense
EPP.common.name: Machupo virus
Host: Humans in endemic communities of Iténez Province, Beni Department (notably Magdalena and San Ramón)
Event.summary: From 2012 through 2013, Beni Department experienced another notable re‑occurrence of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever concentrated in the endemic municipalities of Iténez Province, especially Magdalena and San Ramón. Bolivia’s Programa Nacional de Enfermedades Transmitidas por Roedores reports that 2012 had the highest recent burden, with 17 laboratory‑confirmed BHF cases and a case‑fatality of about 40%, followed in 2013 by four confirmed cases, all fatal, on a background of dozens of suspected infections each year; departmental summaries similarly describe seasonal outbreaks with many suspected and a handful of confirmed cases in these municipalities. Targeted rodent‑control operations, health‑education campaigns, and improved case management were implemented, and by 2014–2016 no further confirmed human Machupo cases were reported in Beni, indicating that this multi‑year resurgence was brought back under control. ([minsalud.gob.bo](https://www.minsalud.gob.bo/component/jdownloads/?Itemid=465&catid=9&id=99%3Aanuario-epidemiologia-2016&task=download.send))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: persistent ecological suitability for the C. callosus reservoir in Beni’s savanna and forest‑edge agricultural landscapes, high levels of rodent infestation in homes and food‑storage areas, and socioeconomic constraints limiting structural improvements contributed to recurrent seasonal outbreaks in 2012–2013; limited access to advanced diagnostics in remote municipalities may have delayed confirmation of some cases. Internal mechanisms: Ministry of Health analyses and virologic data emphasize continuity with the long‑established Machupo lineage, without evidence of new genotypes, altered virulence, or host expansion, so this episode is interpreted as a pronounced but mechanistically typical re‑occurrence driven by environmental and behavioral factors. ([minsalud.gob.bo](https://www.minsalud.gob.bo/component/jdownloads/?Itemid=465&catid=9&id=99%3Aanuario-epidemiologia-2016&task=download.send))
Review: Review (retain but substantially corrected): The original row characterized 2012–2013 as involving only sporadic cases based largely on narrative reviews and generic ProMED references, underestimating the magnitude documented in official Bolivian surveillance. Ministry of Health and SEDES Beni reports show that 2012 had 17 confirmed cases and 2013 four confirmed cases (all in Iténez Province), with high case‑fatality. I have rewritten the event summary to reflect these data, replaced vague ProMED references with Ministry of Health documents, and retained the classification as a re‑occurrence in the existing endemic area; the episode clearly belongs among the major post‑1990 emergence events but should remain flagged for expert checking of exact counts and municipal attributions. ([minsalud.gob.bo](https://www.minsalud.gob.bo/component/jdownloads/?Itemid=465&catid=9&id=99%3Aanuario-epidemiologia-2016&task=download.send))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis
Host: Humans (adults and children, many with diabetes, alcohol use, chronic lung and renal disease)
Event.summary: During the 2009–2010 monsoonal wet season, the Top End region of the Northern Territory, Australia, experienced record rainfall and simultaneously recorded its highest annual incidence of human melioidosis since prospective surveillance began in 1989. Case counts and severity rose sharply, with Royal Darwin Hospital reporting markedly increased admissions for pneumonic and septicemic melioidosis compared with the preceding 20 years, but intensive care and optimized therapy limited mortality to under 10%. As rainfall returned closer to normal in subsequent seasons, the incidence of melioidosis declined toward its long‑term endemic baseline, though strong rainfall‑incidence associations persisted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: record or near‑record wet season rainfall and associated flooding, which strongly increased environmental exposure to B. pseudomallei in soil and surface water, especially among people with diabetes, hazardous alcohol consumption, chronic lung disease or renal disease. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of a new genotype driving this surge; instead, enhanced transmission due to climatic anomalies in a highly endemic setting explains the re‑occurrence peak.
Review: Review – Retain this as one of the most impactful melioidosis seasons globally; coding as a re-occurrence in an already endemic sub-region is appropriate. Only a minor formatting change was made to the countries field (country plus years, without subnational detail) to align with the Excel specification; sources remain appropriate and event-level data are consistent with the primary MJA report.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis
Host: Humans (adults in Madagascar; contextual links to other western Indian Ocean island cases)
Event.summary: In 2012 and 2013, two adult patients from the coastal city of Mahajanga, Madagascar, were diagnosed with fatal autochthonous melioidosis, with B. pseudomallei of novel sequence types confirming local environmental circulation on the island. These cases, together with earlier recognition of a first autochthonous human case in nearby Mauritius in 2004 and several imported cases to Réunion Island epidemiologically linked back to Madagascar, collectively indicated previously unrecognized endemicity of melioidosis in the western Indian Ocean islands of Eastern Africa. After these sentinel events, awareness campaigns and limited environmental studies suggested ongoing but sporadic transmission rather than large, sustained outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: tropical climate with heavy rains, intensive exposure to wet soil and surface water in peri‑urban and rural settings, and high prevalence of diabetes and other comorbidities, combined with historically weak diagnostic capacity for melioidosis in African laboratories. Internal mechanisms: emergence and recognition of diverse, previously undescribed African B. pseudomallei sequence types with phylogenomic evidence of an Asian origin, consistent with re-emergence driven in part by pathogen diversity in a previously known African sub-region.
Review: Review – Retain this as a key western Indian Ocean emergence episode but adjust its scope and type. The original row inappropriately bundled the separate 2004 Mauritius case (already captured in its own event) and coded the episode as intra-continental emergence. Restricted the countries field to Madagascar [2012-2013] and reclassified the event as re-emergence (novel sequence types in an African sub-region where melioidosis had already been recognized historically), with intra_continental_emergence set to false.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridium botulinum
EPP.common.name: Botulism
Countries: United States of America (San Diego County, California) [2017-2018]
Host: Humans (people who inject drugs, primarily black‑tar heroin users via subcutaneous or intramuscular injection)
Event.summary: Between September 2017 and May 2018, San Diego County, California, experienced a prolonged outbreak of wound botulism among people who injected black‑tar heroin, many via ‘skin‑popping’ or intramuscular injection. Public‑health surveillance identified at least 13 confirmed wound botulism cases with typical neurologic signs and laboratory evidence of botulinum neurotoxin, all reporting recent black‑tar heroin injection and no shared food exposures. Intensive clinical alerts, harm‑reduction outreach, and education for people who use drugs and clinicians, along with prompt access to antitoxin, facilitated early recognition and treatment of additional cases and contributed to a decline in incidence after mid‑2018, although sporadic wound botulism continues to occur in association with black‑tar heroin in western North America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: widespread use of black‑tar heroin and injection practices (particularly skin‑popping and intramuscular injection) that introduce spores from the environment or contaminated drug supply into devitalized tissue under anaerobic conditions; limited access to sterile injection equipment and wound care; and ongoing circulation of contaminated heroin lots. Internal mechanisms: colonization of wounds by C. botulinum with in situ production of neurotoxin; no evidence of new toxin types or increased intrinsic virulence, so the outbreak reflects behavioral and drug‑market changes rather than microbial evolution.
Review: Decision: review. This San Diego black‑tar heroin–associated wound botulism cluster (≥13 cases) is one of the larger wound botulism outbreaks reported and is epidemiologically important for the growing injection‑drug–linked botulism burden. However, in terms of total case numbers it is still smaller than several massive foodborne outbreaks now included. It should be retained if the dataset aims to represent all major transmission routes (foodborne and wound); otherwise it could be deprioritized in a strictly size‑focused top‑10.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Legionella pneumophila
EPP.common.name: Legionnaires’ disease
Host: Humans (community residents in the Lens/Harnes industrial area, many with chronic lung disease)
Event.summary: From November 2003 to February 2004, a major community outbreak of Legionnaires’ disease occurred in and around Harnes and the Lens region of Pas‑de‑Calais in northern France, after local authorities detected an unusual cluster of severe pneumonias. Detailed epidemiologic and microbiologic investigations ultimately identified 86 confirmed cases of Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 infection within a radius of about 10–12 km of the Noroxo petrochemical plant, and 17–18 patients died, giving a case‑fatality rate of roughly 20% and making this the worst legionellosis outbreak recorded in French history. Aerosol sampling and environmental testing implicated the plant’s large industrial cooling towers as the principal source; following plant shutdowns, tower disinfection and broader preventive measures at nearby installations, new cases declined and the outbreak was declared over in early 2004, triggering stricter French regulations for industrial cooling systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large petrochemical cooling towers emitting high volumes of aerosols over a densely populated urban–industrial area, use of inadequately treated industrial water and insufficient monitoring and biocide control, meteorologic conditions favouring long‑distance plume dispersal, and a local population with substantial underlying respiratory and occupational exposures. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic strain was L. pneumophila serogroup 1; genotyping showed a predominant clone but no evidence of radically increased virulence, host range, or antimicrobial resistance, so the event is best characterised as environmental amplification and aerosol spread of an existing lineage rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – The Pas‑de‑Calais/Harnes 2003–2004 petrochemical‑plant outbreak (86 confirmed cases, 17–18 deaths and ≈20% case‑fatality) is described in French public‑health reports and international reviews as the largest and deadliest Legionnaires’ disease epidemic in France and one of the most severe globally, yet it was missing from the original dataset. Adding this event corrects that omission. It is correctly located in Europe/Western Europe and France and classified as re‑occurrence; the multi‑month, two‑wave pattern is reflected in the year field “2003‑2004”.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Legionella pneumophila
EPP.common.name: Legionnaires’ disease
Host: Humans (community residents of Manzanares, predominantly older adults and people with chronic disease)
Event.summary: In December 2015, public health authorities in Castilla‑La Mancha, Spain, detected an explosive community outbreak of Legionnaires’ disease in the town of Manzanares (Ciudad Real province) after several residents presented with severe pneumonia. Over subsequent weeks, regional reports recorded 593 notified cases and roughly 237–277 laboratory‑confirmed legionellosis cases, with four deaths, making this one of the largest Legionnaires’ disease outbreaks worldwide and notable for an exceptionally high attack rate of about 14–15 cases per 1,000 inhabitants. Rapid epidemiologic and environmental investigations focused on multiple aerosol‑generating installations, and a contaminated cooling tower together with an ornamental fountain were identified as the most likely sources; after their shutdown, cleaning and disinfection, along with intensified surveillance and public communication, incident cases declined and the outbreak was considered over by early February 2016, prompting further tightening of Legionella control regulations in Castilla‑La Mancha.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High density of potential aerosol‑generating installations (cooling towers, decorative fountains) within a small urban area, ageing and susceptible population structure, favourable winter meteorological conditions (including thermal inversion and high humidity) that trapped aerosols near ground level, and incomplete prior risk assessment and maintenance of risk installations.
