Internal mechanisms: Environmental and technical investigations identified L. pneumophila serogroups 2–14 (including serogroups 8–10) in some samples, but available data do not show a uniquely virulent or drug‑resistant lineage; the event appears driven primarily by environmental amplification, meteorological factors and host susceptibility rather than clear evolutionary change in the pathogen.
Review: Retain – Spanish public‑health reports and a detailed scientific investigation describe the Manzanares 2015–2016 outbreak (≈237–277 confirmed cases, 4 deaths, very high attack rate) as one of the largest Legionnaires’ disease clusters worldwide and the community outbreak with the highest attack rate reported in the literature, yet it was missing from the original dataset. Adding this event corrects that omission. It is properly located in Europe/Southern Europe and Spain, and coded as a re‑occurrence; the year field “2015‑2016” reflects the documented December 2015 to February 2016 duration. Differences between contemporaneous press releases and later technical reports on the exact number of confirmed cases are acknowledged in the summary but do not affect emergence‑type classification.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus B
EPP.common.name: enterovirus infection
Countries: Italy (multiple regions; outbreak linked to nursery school cluster) [2012–2013]
Host: Humans (children and family members with aseptic meningitis or febrile illness)
Event.summary: Around 2012–2013, Italy experienced a documented outbreak of echovirus 30–associated aseptic meningitis, including clusters linked to a nursery school where parents and close relatives of preschool children developed febrile upper respiratory illness and meningitis. Molecular analysis showed that the Italian outbreak strains were closely related to echovirus 30 viruses circulating elsewhere in Europe, consistent with participation in a broader European E30 wave. The outbreak resolved over the course of the year with standard supportive management and no indication of sustained high‑level transmission beyond the epidemic period.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24051044/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: child‑care and household transmission in nursery school–associated clusters, with onward community spread; seasonal patterns of Enterovirus circulation in Southern Europe. Internal mechanisms: participation of Italian strains in the European E30 lineage that has repeatedly generated new variants, suggesting re‑emergence driven by lineage turnover and genetic drift/shift, rather than introduction of a completely novel serotype.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24051044/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus sindbis
EPP.common.name: Sindbis virus
Host: Wild birds (African thrush, Turdus pelios, in wetland and savanna-edge habitats); ornithophilic mosquitoes (implied); potential incidental human exposure (not yet documented in this focus)
Event.summary: During field sampling campaigns in 2022–2023 in and around the Amurum Forest Reserve in central Nigeria, Sindbis virus RNA was detected for the first time in West Africa in wild birds, with three of 504 sampled African thrushes testing positive and one yielding a complete SINV genome. These findings documented an enzootic transmission focus in Nigeria that had not previously been recognised, despite earlier serological evidence of human exposure from the 1970s, and indicated active local virus circulation rather than isolated introductions. No associated human Sindbis fever cases were reported during the study period, and after the surveillance campaign ended the extent and persistence of SINV transmission in Nigeria remained uncertain, but the detection nevertheless marked a clear intra‑continental range expansion of SINV into the Western Africa subregion with ecologies suitable for future spillover to humans.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely long‑distance introduction via migratory birds connecting eastern and southern African SINV foci with West African wetlands; suitable wetland and forest‑edge habitats and mosquito fauna in central Nigeria enabling local SINV maintenance; expanded ornithological surveillance and molecular diagnostics that increased the probability of detecting low‑prevalence infections in wild birds. Internal mechanisms: the detected Nigerian SINV strain clustered phylogenetically with known SINV genotype I lineages from Algeria, Spain and Kenya, suggesting geographic range expansion of existing genotypes rather than emergence of a novel lineage; any future human disease risk will depend on local vector competence, bird reservoir dynamics and human–mosquito contact patterns.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This event represents the first confirmed detection of Sindbis virus in wild birds in Nigeria and, more broadly, in West Africa, marking a major expansion of the known enzootic range with clear relevance for future human risk. The original dataset mis-dated the event to 2024; the event year has been corrected to 2022–2023 to reflect the documented sampling period, and the classification as intra-continental emergence (new African subregion) is appropriate, though continued surveillance will be needed to quantify its long-term importance.

EPP.scientific.name: African swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: ASFV
Host: Domestic pigs (village and smallholder); feral/free‑ranging pigs
Event.summary: In March 2020, Papua New Guinea officially confirmed its first African swine fever outbreaks in free‑ranging village pigs in the Southern Highlands province, marking the arrival of ASF in Melanesia and the Oceania region and raising major concerns for Pacific biosecurity. The disease caused high mortality among village pigs in affected provinces, with reports of hundreds to around a thousand deaths in some areas and significant livelihood impacts for subsistence farmers. Intensive awareness campaigns, movement controls and targeted response efforts helped to limit the geographic extent of the outbreak, and authorities later reported that ASF was under control, though ongoing vigilance remained necessary.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely introduction via infected pigs or pork products from ASF‑affected parts of Asia, combined with free‑ranging pig husbandry, communal scavenging, low biosecurity and limited veterinary infrastructure in rural Highlands communities. Internal mechanisms: high virulence and environmental stability of genotype II ASFV enabled rapid local spread once introduced into naive pig populations, but no evidence suggests novel viral traits beyond those circulating in Asia and Europe; the main significance of this event lies in its role as the first occurrence of ASF in the Oceania continent.
Review: retain – Verified as the first confirmed occurrence of ASF in Oceania (Papua New Guinea) and therefore an inter‑continental emergence event despite the relatively modest absolute number of pigs affected. Corrected the start year from 2019 to 2020 and aligned the country‑specific dates accordingly using WOAH/FAO reports, and changed the emergence‑type coding to 'inter_continental_emergence' = Yes and 'intra_continental_emergence' = No, since there was no prior ASF in Oceania. Replaced a Reddit link with an official and trade‑press confirmation (The Pig Site) for stronger sourcing.

EPP.scientific.name: Alcelaphine gammaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Commercial American bison (Bison bison) finished in a large Midwestern feedlot
Event.summary: From early 1998 through late 1999, a large feedlot in the American Midwest experienced a devastating enteric disease syndrome in American bison, ultimately attributed to sheep‑associated malignant catarrhal fever caused by OvHV‑2. Retrospective and prospective necropsy and PCR investigations showed that malignant catarrhal fever had been present in the yard since at least 1993, but an intense epizootic began in January 1998, with an estimated 150 bison dying of the syndrome over two years and MCF becoming the leading cause of death in the 1,101‑animal consignment under study. A concurrent cohort study found that, among 300 monitored bison, 7.3% died and 15 of 22 necropsied animals had classic MCF lesions, and across the full consignment 75 of 98 deaths (75.5%) were attributable to MCF, underscoring its major impact on the commercial bison industry.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high animal density and prolonged confinement in a commercial feedlot, shipment and handling stress, and prior exposure of some bison to OvHV‑2‑infected sheep at source ranches likely increased susceptibility and triggered clinical disease; once infected animals arrived at the yard, repeated handling and other stressors were temporally associated with peaks in mortality. Internal mechanisms: Extreme species susceptibility of American bison to OvHV‑2, with a high proportion of infected animals developing fulminant alimentary‑form MCF and near‑100% case fatality; there was no evidence that a novel viral genotype caused the outbreak, so this represents a severe re‑occurrence of established SA‑MCF rather than a true viral re‑emergence.
Review: Retain: Added as a new event because the 1998–1999 sheep‑associated MCF epizootic in a US bison feedlot killed an estimated ~150 animals and accounted for >75% of deaths in a monitored 1,101‑head consignment, making it one of the most impactful malignant catarrhal fever outbreaks worldwide in terms of mortality and economic loss. Classified as a re‑occurrence in Northern America because OvHV‑2 and MCF were already established in North American bison prior to this outbreak and there is no evidence of first emergence or inter‑/intra‑continental spread.

EPP.scientific.name: Alcelaphine gammaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: American bison (Bison bison) from eight Saskatchewan farms sold through a public auction market and mixed with resident bison on destination farms
Event.summary: Following a November 2000 public auction of 163 bison from eight Saskatchewan farms at a market where 211 lambs were briefly present, an outbreak of sheep‑associated malignant catarrhal fever occurred on seven destination farms over the subsequent 7–8 months. Forty‑five of 163 sale bison (27.6%) became acutely ill and died between 50 and 220 days after the sale, with 21 animals confirmed as MCF cases by pathology and OvHV‑2 PCR and the remaining 24 classified as suspect cases based on clinical history; no cases occurred in unsold bison on the farms of origin or in resident bison mixed with the sale animals. The episode illustrated that a single short aerosol exposure to carrier lambs in an enclosed auction facility can cause high‑mortality SA‑MCF outbreaks in highly susceptible bison with no onward transmission between bison.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Brief but intense airborne exposure of naïve or subclinically infected bison to a large group of lambs shedding OvHV‑2 at a public auction market, followed by transport stress, regrouping and mixing on multiple destination farms, created conditions for widespread clinical disease after a common exposure event. Internal mechanisms: As in other SA‑MCF outbreaks, OvHV‑2 replicated in highly susceptible bison, producing a high case fatality rate with peracute to acute clinical courses; there was no evidence of virus adaptation or sustained transmission among bison, consistent with bison remaining dead‑end hosts.
Review: Retain: Added as a new event because detailed investigation showed that 45 of 163 bison (27.6%) exposed to sheep for less than a day at a Saskatchewan auction died of SA‑MCF, making this one of the best‑documented and most severe OvHV‑2 outbreaks in North American bison. Classified as a re‑occurrence within Northern America, since OvHV‑2 was already endemic in regional sheep and MCF had been reported previously in Canadian and US bison; there is no evidence of novelty in geographic range or viral genotype.

EPP.scientific.name: Alcelaphine gammaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Dairy cows, pregnant dairy youngstock and calves in two intensive dairy herds co‑housed with lambing sheep (OvHV‑2 reservoir)
Event.summary: Beginning in May 2012 and extending into early 2013, two large Dutch dairy herds that co‑housed cattle with lambing sheep experienced severe outbreaks of sheep‑associated malignant catarrhal fever. In the first herd, 10 dairy cows, 10 of 21 pregnant youngstock, one non‑pregnant heifer and one calf died or were euthanized over approximately three months; in the second herd, 5 cows, 20 pregnant youngstock and 10 calves died or were euthanized between September 2012 and January 2013. Clinical signs, pathology and OvHV‑2 PCR confirmed SA‑MCF, and mortality declined only after sick cattle were removed and strict separation from sheep was implemented, demonstrating the capacity of SA‑MCF to cause large multi‑animal losses in Western European dairy systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close indoor co‑housing of susceptible dairy cattle and calves with high densities of lambing sheep, especially during and after lambing when OvHV‑2 shedding peaks, combined with limited ventilation and lack of management awareness of MCF risk in mixed sheep–cattle enterprises. Internal mechanisms: High OvHV‑2 burden and intense virus shedding from lambs in enclosed barns, leading to efficient aerosol transmission to cattle; histopathology and virology indicated typical SA‑MCF without evidence of a novel viral strain, so the scale of losses reflects management‑driven exposure in herds located in a region where the virus was already endemic in sheep.
Review: Review: Retain as a major SA‑MCF outbreak but with corrected geography and sources. The Juniper paper documents two large outbreaks in Dutch dairy herds only; it does not describe a linked Belgian event, so Belgium has been removed from the countries field and the row is now restricted to the Netherlands. The Juniper URL has been corrected from an incorrect manuscript ID to JDVS.MS.ID.555672, and a Reddit mirror of the article has been treated as non‑primary and omitted from the source list. Event year (2012–2013), Western Europe subregion and classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate. A separate row would be needed if the large peracute MCF outbreak in Belgian Blue cattle were to be included explicitly.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Aparavirus tauraense
EPP.common.name: Taura syndrome virus, TSV
Host: Farmed L. vannamei and L. stylirostris (including TSV- and IHHNV-selected resistant lines)
Event.summary: In western Mexico, where TSV had already become endemic, a new strain of TSV emerged around 1998–1999 and caused massive epizootics in Penaeus stylirostris that had been selectively bred for resistance to earlier TSV variants. These outbreaks led to severe crop failures and effectively ended commercial interest in farming P. stylirostris in much of western Mexico, while also increasing disease pressure on co‑cultured L. vannamei. Through the early 2000s this more virulent strain contributed to renewed high mortalities and economic losses until producers shifted species and management strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high‑density shrimp culture in western Mexico with heavy reliance on a limited number of selectively bred TSV‑resistant P. stylirostris lines, combined with persistent endemic TSV circulation and concurrent introduction of WSSV in 1999, created strong selection pressures favouring TSV variants capable of overcoming host resistance. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel TSV strain/genotype (Type B) with altered antigenicity and increased virulence/pathogenicity in P. stylirostris is well documented, representing viral adaptation that negated prior genetic resistance and constitutes a clear re‑emergence driven by evolutionary change in the pathogen.
Review: Review (geographic scope narrowed). This event is strongly supported as a major re‑emergence driven by a new, more virulent TSV strain in western Mexico that overcame resistance in P. stylirostris, but the original JSON over‑generalised its spread to unspecified “multiple Latin American countries” and “USA–Mexico border regions” without clear primary evidence. The Countries field has been restricted to Mexico [1998–1999], and the timeframe adjusted to match WOAH and review‑article descriptions (1998–1999 with impacts continuing into the early 2000s). Classification as re_emergence = Yes remains appropriate. Further regional genetic/epidemiologic data could refine whether this strain caused major, distinct emergence episodes outside Mexico.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: BSE prion
EPP.common.name: Mad cow disease, BSE
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event.summary: In December 2003, the United States confirmed its first BSE case in a Holstein cow slaughtered in Washington State, which tracing showed had been imported from Canada and exposed there before the 1997 North American feed ban. The announcement triggered immediate domestic and international concern, leading many trading partners, including Japan and South Korea, to suspend imports of U.S. beef and provoking intensive media coverage and consumer anxiety. Through 2004, U.S. authorities implemented an expanded BSE surveillance programme, stricter feed and specified-risk-material rules, and trace-back investigations that found no additional classical BSE cases linked to the imported cow, helping to stabilise markets and lay the groundwork for gradual reopening of key export markets.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Pre-ban trade in live cattle between Canada and the United States; historical use of ruminant MBM in feed prior to the 1997 feed ban; limited pre-2003 active BSE surveillance in the U.S.; strong trade dependence on foreign beef markets that magnified the economic impact of a single confirmed case. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of classical BSE into the U.S. via an already-infected imported cow, with no evidence of sustained domestic amplification through U.S. feed chains during this episode; subsequent U.S.-born BSE cases were atypical and are treated as a separate, low-prevalence emergence pattern.
Review: retain – This row has been narrowed to focus on the 2003–2004 U.S. experience with its first detected BSE case (a Canadian-born classical BSE cow in Washington State) and the associated trade and policy response. The original version mixed this episode with later U.S.-born atypical cases (Texas 2005, Alabama 2006), which are now handled in a separate atypical-BSE event to avoid duplication. Event types have been simplified: first_detection = Yes (first BSE detected in the U.S.), with inter_continental_emergence = No (because continental emergence is attributed to Canada’s indigenous 2003 outbreak) and re_emergence = No (no prior U.S. BSE episode in this subregion).

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Host: Cattle, goats, sheep, and humans exposed through handling and consuming meat from sick or dead livestock
Event.summary: From August 2009, multiple anthrax outbreaks began in cattle and small ruminants in northwestern Bangladesh (especially Pabna, Sirajganj and Tangail districts), leading to numerous animal deaths and slaughter of sick animals. Through 2009–2010, at least 14 linked village-level outbreaks were documented in these districts with 39 confirmed and 234 probable human cutaneous anthrax cases, and nationally about 607 suspected human cases were reported during August–October 2010 across 12 districts, all strongly associated with butchering and eating meat from diseased livestock. Emergency public health messaging, guidance on carcass disposal, and expansion of livestock vaccination gradually reduced human and animal case numbers after late 2010, although anthrax remains endemic in Bangladeshi livestock with recurrent smaller outbreaks in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-standing endemic spore foci in floodplain and riverine soils; high densities of cattle and small ruminants linked to intensive dairy and draft use; historically low routine livestock vaccination coverage; economic pressure on poor households leading to slaughter and consumption of moribund animals; informal meat markets and unsafe carcass disposal. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing indicates circulation of several closely related B. anthracis genotypes but no evidence of a novel, more virulent lineage; the 2009–2010 spike reflects environmental and social drivers and heightened recognition rather than genetic re-emergence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row correctly captures the nationally important 2009–2010 wave of zoonotic anthrax outbreaks in Bangladesh, with timing, geography, host range and event-type (re-occurrence driven by endemic spores, low vaccination and risky slaughter/consumption practices) consistent with primary epidemiologic reports. I simplified the countries field to “Bangladesh [2009-2010]” to match the guidance for linked single-country episodes; no other structural changes were needed and the cited sources remain appropriate primary descriptions of the event.

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Countries: United Republic of Tanzania (Songwe Region, Momba District) [2018-2019]
Host: Cattle in affected villages; humans infected after consuming or handling meat from cattle carcasses
Event.summary: Between early December 2018 and 7 January 2019, anthrax was confirmed in a cluster of human and livestock cases centered on Nzoka ward in Momba District, Songwe Region in Tanzania’s southern highlands, following slaughter and consumption of sick cattle. Epidemiologic investigation documented 81 suspected human cutaneous anthrax cases, four fatalities and 16 cattle deaths linked to two uninspected carcasses that had been shared within the community, prompting a multisectoral outbreak response and an economic impact assessment. Health education campaigns, safe carcass disposal, extensive livestock vaccination (over 60,000 animals in and around the district) and strengthened surveillance in both human and animal sectors were implemented, after which no further human or livestock cases were reported and the outbreak was declared over.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Endemic soil contamination with anthrax spores in agropastoral landscapes; slaughter and consumption of cattle that died suddenly or were visibly ill, driven by poverty, lack of awareness of anthrax risks and limited veterinary inspection; gaps in routine vaccination coverage prior to the outbreak and inadequate carcass disposal practices. Internal mechanisms: The episode involved typical zoonotic transmission of endemic B. anthracis from cattle to humans via handling and consumption of contaminated meat; there is no evidence of a novel genotype or altered virulence, so the event reflects social and health-system drivers of re-occurrence rather than pathogen re-emergence.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This event is notable for its substantial human case load (81 suspected cases, four deaths) and inclusion in detailed multisectoral cost analyses, but the original row under-specified the scale and livestock involvement. I have updated the summary and mechanism to incorporate WHO-AFRO and national figures (81 human cases, 4 deaths, 16 cattle deaths) and to clarify the link to two infected cattle carcasses and subsequent large-scale vaccination. Geography (Eastern Africa / United Republic of Tanzania), host description and event-type as re-occurrence remain appropriate; the source list now gives greater weight to the One Health cost-analysis paper and WHO outbreak bulletin.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Host: Hippopotamuses in Queen Elizabeth National Park and Lake Mburo area; additional wildlife species (buffalo, zebra, kob, waterbuck, warthog, elephant) affected; nearby human communities at risk from carcass meat consumption
Event.summary: Beginning in August 2004, an unusual wave of hippopotamus mortality was observed in the Kazinga Channel and adjacent Lakes George and Edward within Queen Elizabeth National Park in western Uganda, and veterinary investigations confirmed anthrax as the cause. Over the course of 2004–2005, approximately 306 hippos (about 11–12% of the local population) and substantial numbers of other wild herbivores—around 63 zebras, 60 African buffalo, 13 warthogs, 12 Uganda kob, three waterbuck and five elephants—died in Queen Elizabeth and nearby Lake Mburo National Park, representing one of the largest recorded wildlife anthrax outbreaks in East Africa. A national multisectoral task force coordinated carcass burning and burial, decontamination of sites, ring vaccination of surrounding cattle and sheep and intensive community sensitization on avoiding consumption of carcass meat; with the onset of rains and exhaustion of highly susceptible hosts, the outbreak was brought under control, although a further, smaller hippo anthrax epizootic re-occurred in 2010.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very dry conditions and low water levels in the Kazinga Channel and adjacent lakes that forced dense aggregations of hippos and other large herbivores onto receding shorelines and grazing lawns where soils were heavily contaminated by spores; long-term environmental anthrax foci in the Queen Elizabeth Protected Area (with documented smaller hippo outbreaks in 1959, 1962 and 1991); opportunistic use of carcass meat by local communities raising concern for human exposure. Internal mechanisms: The event is consistent with repeated environmental re-activation of persistent spores in a known wildlife focus; there is no indication of a novel genetic variant or host jump, so it represents large-scale ecological re-occurrence rather than genetic re-emergence.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The original row treated this as an approximate “around 2004” hippo die-off with limited detail and cited sources that actually referred to other countries’ outbreaks. I have (a) updated the year field to 2004–2005, (b) specified Uganda [2004-2005] in the countries field, (c) revised the event summary to reflect published estimates of 306 hippos and ~150 other large herbivores killed in Queen Elizabeth and Lake Mburo National Parks, and (d) replaced generic media links with primary ecological/epizootiologic sources (Wafula et al. 2008; Driciru et al. 2018; contemporaneous news and park management reports). Classification as re-occurrence in a long-established East African wildlife anthrax focus remains appropriate, but the corrected figures and sources should be reviewed by a subject-matter expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bovine leukemia virus
EPP.common.name: BLV, Bovine leukaemia virus
Host: Dairy cattle (Holstein Friesian)
Event.summary: In 1988–1989, a closed Holstein Friesian dairy herd of 220 pregnant heifers and bulls was imported from Minnesota, USA, to a governmental farm at Arab El‑Aoumar near Assiut in Upper Egypt, at a time when Egypt was considered free of enzootic bovine leukosis.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1046/j.1439-0450.2002.00517.x)) In November 1996, cows in this herd developed weight loss, reduced milk yield, lymphadenopathy and other signs, and subsequent serological screening and PCR testing demonstrated high within‑herd BLV seroprevalence (≈38% in cattle <2 years and ≈73% in older animals) and confirmed BLV proviral DNA, establishing the first recorded outbreak of enzootic bovine leukosis in Egypt.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1046/j.1439-0450.2002.00517.x)) Following diagnosis, strict quarantine and test‑and‑cull measures were implemented; OIE reported 46 clinical cases among 418 susceptible imported dairy cows in Assiut with 45 animals destroyed, and Egypt was later able to re‑establish official BLV‑free status by 1997 after stamping‑out.([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/downld/infos_san_archives/eng/1997/en_970613v10n24.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of BLV‑infected pregnant dairy cattle from the USA into a previously BLV‑free national herd, limited pre‑import and post‑arrival testing in the late 1980s, and close contact, shared needles and equipment within an intensively managed dairy herd facilitated rapid within‑herd transmission.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1046/j.1439-0450.2002.00517.x)) Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was implicated; the outbreak reflects geographic range expansion of an existing BLV lineage into a new country, aided by the virus’s inherent ability to establish lifelong infection and efficient blood‑mediated transmission in high‑density dairy systems rather than documented genetic change.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13151565/))
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The event correctly describes the first recorded BLV/enzootic bovine leukosis outbreak in Egypt and is likely among the most important post‑1990 country‑level emergence events, but the original classification of this row as a 'first detection' event has been changed to 'No' because BLV was identified as the cause of enzootic bovine leukosis globally in the late 1960s, long before this episode. The outbreak represents introduction into a new country within a continent and sub‑region where BLV was already established, which does not fit the definitions of first/global, intra‑continental or inter‑continental emergence; all type‑of‑emergence flags are therefore left as 'No' and the event is retained but flagged for expert review of this categorisation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bovine leukemia virus
EPP.common.name: BLV, Bovine leukaemia virus
Host: Yaks (Bos mutus/Bos grunniens)
Event.summary: Until the 2010s, enzootic bovine leukosis was considered primarily a disease of cattle, and little was known about BLV status in domestic yaks grazing the high‑altitude rangelands of north‑western China. Between April 2013 and March 2014, a large serological survey of 1,584 black and white yaks from Gansu province found BLV antibody prevalence of about 21%, with similar infection levels in both colour types and no strong associations with age, sex or management factors, representing the first report of BLV infection in yaks in China. Subsequent molecular studies on nearly 800 yaks from Gansu, Qinghai and Sichuan confirmed BLV proviral DNA and identified multiple env genotypes (notably genotypes 6 and 10), indicating established, genetically diverse BLV circulation within yak populations on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau rather than sporadic spillover alone.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional yak husbandry in Gansu, Qinghai and Sichuan involves communal grazing, shared watering points and frequent contact with BLV‑infected cattle and other ruminants, while routine BLV testing is rare in yak herds; these practices facilitate cross‑species transmission and silent establishment of infection. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects host expansion and maintenance of existing BLV genotypes in yak rather than emergence of a novel viral lineage, although env‑gene diversity suggests repeated introductions from cattle and subsequent adaptation to high‑altitude yak populations; this justifies classification as re‑emergence driven by host expansion rather than as a first‑detection or geographic emergence event.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This new row captures a major host‑range emergence event—documented BLV infection with moderate prevalence and multiple genotypes in large yak populations on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau—based on robust serologic and molecular surveys. The timing, geography and host classification are consistent with the primary studies, and labelling the episode as re‑emergence (via host expansion into yak) without intra‑/inter‑continental or first‑detection tags is aligned with the provided definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: Bovine leukemia virus
EPP.common.name: BLV, Bovine leukaemia virus
Host: Dairy cattle in intensive production systems
Event.summary: In China, enzootic bovine leukosis had been a major cause of neoplastic disease in cattle before 1985, but national control measures introduced in the late 1980s substantially reduced BLV prevalence through the 1990s. From around 2000 onward, however, surveys began to show renewed spread of BLV in rapidly expanding intensive dairy herds, culminating in large cross‑sectional studies in 2013–2014 that reported high infection levels in Chinese dairy cattle and widespread herd‑level positivity across multiple provinces. Subsequent molecular work on BLV env genes from dairy cattle in Henan and Ningxia provinces identified several genotypes (including genotype 4 newly recognised in China) and substantial sequence diversity, confirming that BLV had re‑established itself as an important endemic pathogen in China’s modern dairy sector after a period of relative decline.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of China’s dairy industry since the 1990s, increased long‑distance movement and importation of breeding stock, high animal densities, reuse of needles and obstetric equipment, and limited BLV‑specific control policies created conditions that favoured resurgence of BLV transmission after earlier reductions. Internal mechanisms: Multiple BLV genotypes (at least 1, 4, 6, 7 and 10) have been detected in Chinese dairy cattle, indicating repeated introductions and genetic diversification, but there is no clear evidence that a single novel, more virulent strain triggered the re‑emergence; the episode is therefore best classified as re‑occurrence driven primarily by management and trade factors, with novel genotype detection noted as an internal mechanism but not treated as a separate emergence type.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This added row summarises the large‑scale post‑2000 re‑emergence of BLV in China’s dairy herds, documented by national and regional prevalence surveys and molecular data, which likely represents one of the highest‑impact BLV events in terms of numbers of infected cattle and economic consequences. It is appropriately classified as a re‑occurrence event (resurgence in a previously affected sub‑region driven by management and industry changes) without intra‑/inter‑continental or first‑detection labels; nonetheless, the exact start year of the resurgence is approximate and could be further refined by future country‑specific historical work.

EPP.scientific.name: Bovine leukemia virus
EPP.common.name: BLV, Bovine leukaemia virus
Host: Water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) and co‑managed cattle
Event.summary: By the mid‑2010s, bovine leukemia virus was already endemic in Colombian cattle herds, but its status in the rapidly expanding water‑buffalo industry of the central‑western coffee‑growing region remained unclear.([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2020.00608/full)) During 2016–2017, a field study sampled 140 buffaloes from eight herds plus nearby cattle, sheep and humans, and nested PCR targeting the BLV env gene detected proviral DNA in 33.6% of buffalo blood samples and 3.4% of cattle, representing the first molecular confirmation of natural BLV infection in water buffaloes in Colombia and, according to the authors, the first PCR‑based report of BLV in buffaloes in the Americas.([scielo.org.mx](https://www.scielo.org.mx/scielo.php?pid=S2007-11242021000200419&script=sci_arttext&tlng=en)) The outbreak did not manifest as a recognized clinical leukosis epidemic in buffaloes, and no immediate large‑scale control program was implemented, but the finding highlighted silent BLV circulation in mixed buffalo–cattle systems and prompted recommendations for enhanced surveillance and management changes to limit further cross‑species spread.([scielo.org.mx](https://www.scielo.org.mx/scielo.php?pid=S2007-11242021000200419&script=sci_arttext&tlng=en))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of water‑buffalo production in Colombia’s coffee‑growing region, frequent co‑grazing and co‑housing of buffaloes with infected cattle, shared handling equipment, and limited BLV testing in buffalo herds created ecological and management conditions favoring cross‑species transmission and establishment of infection in buffalo populations.([scielo.org.mx](https://www.scielo.org.mx/scielo.php?pid=S2007-11242021000200419&script=sci_arttext&tlng=en)) Internal mechanisms: This event reflects host expansion and geographic range consolidation of existing BLV lineages into water buffalo within South America rather than emergence of a clearly novel genotype; BLV’s inherent capacity for lifelong infection and efficient blood‑borne spread underlies its successful spillover and maintenance in this new livestock host.([woah.org](https://www.woah.org/en/disease/enzootic-bovine-leukosis/))
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The Colombian buffalo event represents an important regional host‑expansion episode with substantial within‑herd infection documented by PCR, and it is reasonable to include it among major post‑1990 BLV events. However, the narrative should be interpreted carefully: earlier reports provide serologic and virologic evidence of natural BLV infection in water buffaloes in Brazil and elsewhere, so phrases implying a global 'first' in buffalo should be read as referring specifically to PCR confirmation in Colombia or the Americas rather than worldwide novelty. The event type (re‑emergence via host expansion) remains appropriate, but the row is flagged for human review to ensure wording is adjusted if the dataset text is edited.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia mallei
EPP.common.name: Malleus (glanders)
Host: Horses
Event.summary: In 2018–2019, serological surveys of horses in central and eastern Mongolia found glanders seroprevalence of about 7–8% using rose Bengal test and complement fixation, indicating substantial ongoing transmission in a country that had historically reported eradication of the disease. Positive animals were detected across multiple districts, demonstrating that B. mallei infection was more widespread than previously recognized. Following identification of seropositive horses, Mongolian authorities introduced targeted restrictions on horse movements from affected areas and considered renewed eradication campaigns, although full national elimination has not yet been documented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased regional horse trade and movement for tourism, racing and traditional events, along with free-ranging husbandry practices and limited routine surveillance after earlier eradication campaigns, likely facilitated re-introduction or unnoticed persistence of B. mallei in Mongolian equids. The logistical difficulty of testing and culling free-ranging horses over vast areas hampers rapid control. Internal mechanisms: Available reports have not yet provided detailed genotyping of Mongolian isolates, and there is no evidence of novel virulence or host shifts; the episode is therefore best interpreted as re-occurrence in Eastern Asia, with renewed recognition of infection in a country previously considered free rather than emergence of a fundamentally new strain.
Review: review – Retained as a major modern event documenting relatively high seroprevalence in Mongolian horses, but classification adjusted: intra_continental_emergence set to No because B. mallei was already present in Eastern Asia (e.g. China) and this represents renewed detection in a previously free country, not first entry into a new sub-region. Re_emergence was changed to No and re_occurrence to Yes, as no internal pathogen changes have yet been demonstrated; the emphasis in the literature is on re-introduction or persistence under limited surveillance.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Canine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Canine distemper virus, CDV
Host: African wild dog (Lycaon pictus) in a captive breeding program
Event.summary: In December 2000, an acute infectious disease compatible with CDV swept through a captive breeding group of African wild dogs in Tanzania, beginning shortly after routine handling and vaccination procedures. Within two months, 49 of 52 animals died, and serology and virology confirmed CDV infection as the primary cause of the epizootic. The outbreak burnt out as almost the entire captive pack succumbed, resulting in a severe setback for African wild dog conservation efforts in the region and prompting changes in vaccination and management strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High animal density and close confinement in the captive facility allowed rapid CDV spread once introduced; intensive handling and recent vaccination may have caused stress and transient immune suppression; circulation of CDV in surrounding domestic dogs and wild carnivores provided a likely reservoir. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence of CDV in an extremely susceptible, immunologically naïve endangered host; potential vaccine–wild-type interactions were investigated but evidence supported infection by a field virus closely related to regional dog and wildlife strains; high virulence in African wild dogs magnified conservation impact even though absolute case numbers were modest.
Review: retain - This outbreak (49 of 52 captive African wild dogs dying in Mkomazi Game Reserve, Tanzania) is well documented and remains one of the most consequential CDV events for this endangered species. Event-year range, geography (Africa | Eastern Africa; United Republic of Tanzania) and re_emergence classification are consistent with primary sources; no field corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Canine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Canine distemper virus, CDV
Host: Ethiopian wolf (Canis simensis); domestic dogs as source reservoir
Event.summary: In late 2005, CDV spilled over from local domestic dogs into Ethiopian wolves in Bale Mountains National Park, initiating an outbreak that spread rapidly through multiple contiguous packs. During 2005–2006, mortality reached catastrophic levels in affected subpopulations, with some wolf packs losing most or all members and the event described as the most severe single disease episode recorded for the species. The epizootic declined as infected packs collapsed and limited reactive vaccination and dog control were implemented, but it left Bale’s wolf population greatly reduced and more vulnerable to subsequent disease waves.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High contact rates within tightly social wolf packs promoted very efficient within-pack CDV transmission after spillover from unvaccinated village dogs; continued encroachment of people and dogs into Afroalpine habitat increased cross‑species contact; recent severe rabies outbreaks had already reduced wolf numbers, limiting demographic resilience. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence of CDV in an endangered canid with no prior widespread immunity; high virulence and possible interaction with prior rabies‑driven demographic thinning intensified population impact; CDV’s broad carnivore host range enabled establishment in sympatric dogs and carnivores, sustaining the threat.
Review: retain - This 2005–2006 epizootic in Ethiopian wolves caused 43–68% mortality in affected subpopulations of one of the world’s rarest canids and is clearly among the highest-impact CDV events in wildlife post-1990. Its coding as re_emergence (host expansion into an endangered canid within the animal system) and geographic placement (Africa | Eastern Africa; Ethiopia) are aligned with primary sources; no field-level corrections were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Canine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Canine distemper virus, CDV
Host: Farmed American mink (Neovison vison); red fox (Vulpes vulpes), raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides) and wild ferret (Mustela putorius furo) as key wildlife reservoirs
Event.summary: Following several years with little or no detected disease, a major CDV outbreak began in Danish farmed mink in late summer 2012 and continued into early 2013, ultimately affecting 64 mink farms on the Jutland peninsula. The same CDV strain was also detected in local wildlife—especially red foxes, raccoon dogs and a wild ferret—indicating that a wildlife reservoir seeded infections on multiple farms. Although precise mink mortality numbers were not reported, high morbidity and mortality on large commercial farms resulted in substantial production losses before the outbreak waned under improved vaccination and tightened biosecurity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense housing of thousands of mink per farm, coupled with incomplete vaccination and lapses in farm biosecurity (e.g. wildlife access across fences), allowed rapid farm‑level amplification once CDV was introduced; a widespread, endemic reservoir of infected red foxes and other wild carnivores provided repeated opportunities for farm introduction; management practices that did not fully exclude wildlife or their feces facilitated between‑farm spread. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of a European‑lineage CDV strain that had likely persisted in regional fox populations since at least 2008, with high genetic identity across mink and wildlife isolates; although some mink viruses carried an Y549H substitution in the H gene, the outbreak is best viewed as a re-occurrence of CDV in a previously affected subregion and host group, rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: review - Newly added event. The 2012–2013 Danish outbreak, which involved 64 commercial mink farms and parallel infection in local foxes, raccoon dogs and ferrets, is one of the most significant CDV epizootics in production animals in the post-1990 period and thus warrants inclusion among the top-10 events. Classified as 're_occurrence' because Denmark had prior mink outbreaks and the 2012–2013 wave reflects resurgence of a European-lineage virus from wildlife reservoirs under suboptimal biosecurity, rather than a first or inter-continental emergence. Years, geography (Europe | Northern Europe; Denmark) and host description are based on Trebbien et al. 2014 and Gregers-Jensen et al. 2015.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Canine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Canine distemper virus, CDV
Host: Giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca) in captivity; domestic dogs and other carnivores as potential reservoirs
Event.summary: Between December 2014 and March 2015, an outbreak of CDV occurred at the Shaanxi Rare Wildlife Rescue and Breeding Research Center in China, initially affecting one giant panda and then spreading to other pandas in the facility. Five infected giant pandas that developed clinical signs—characterized by respiratory, gastrointestinal and neurological disease—died within 7–34 days of onset, and genomic sequencing of virus from one panda (giant panda/SX/2014) showed it belonged to the Asia‑1 CDV cluster with mutations associated with cross‑species infection. After aggressive quarantine, relocation of uninfected pandas, and strict biosecurity, the outbreak was contained, but it highlighted that any future CDV incursion in panda range could endanger both captive and wild populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Housing of pandas in a rescue/breeding facility near human settlements and domestic dogs likely facilitated introduction of CDV; limited use of CDV vaccination in pandas before the outbreak meant high susceptibility; fragmented wild panda habitats and increasing numbers of captive animals magnify the consequences of disease introduction. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of an Asia‑1 canine CDV lineage into giant pandas, with H‑gene mutations such as Y549H implicated in overcoming host barriers; the strain showed high virulence in pandas, causing rapid progression and death despite intensive care; genomic work demonstrated that the panda virus was closely related to dog‑origin CDV, underlining the role of ongoing viral evolution and adaptation in enabling new host jumps.
Review: review - Retain as a key emergence event because the 2014–2015 Shaanxi outbreak is the best-documented example of CDV causing fatal disease in giant pandas and has significant conservation implications. Corrected event-type coding by setting 'first_detection' to false (CDV was long recognized in animals); categorized as 're_emergence' via host expansion into pandas (Asia-1 lineage with Y549H in the H gene). Years, geography and host description remain appropriate and should be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Caprine arthritis encephalitis virus
EPP.common.name: CAEV, Small ruminant lentivirus
Host: Domestic goats in commercial and smallholder farms
Event.summary: From January 2021 to December 2022, a nested PCR survey of 1,334 goats from 24 farms across Luzon, Philippines, detected CAEV proviral DNA in 31.4% of animals and 91.7% of farms, revealing a high positivity rate and suggesting that CAEV is widespread in the main goat‑producing island. Farm-level infection ranged from about 1.5% to over 90% of sampled animals, and many farms reported histories of arthritis, pneumonia, mastitis and emaciation in goats, consistent with chronic CAE. These findings led Philippine authorities and researchers to classify CAE as an emerging/re‑emerging notifiable disease in the country and underscored the need for surveillance, movement control and improved kid‑rearing and biosecurity practices to limit further spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growth of goat production in Luzon, inter-farm trade in breeding animals, and a lack of prior systematic testing allowed CAEV to become established and disseminate widely before this molecular survey. Internal mechanisms: The very high within-farm positivity detected by nested PCR reflects the sensitivity of proviral detection in chronic lentiviral infections and long-standing circulation of CAEV in intensive and semi‑intensive herds rather than emergence of a novel strain; standard SRLV features (lifelong infection, efficient milk‑borne and horizontal transmission) underpin the observed high prevalence.
Review: retain – added this event because the Luzon nested-PCR study is one of the most striking recent CAEV re-occurrence episodes globally, with 31.4% of 1,334 goats and 22 of 24 farms testing positive, and CAE recognised as a notifiable emerging/re-emerging disease in the Philippines. Classified correctly as a regional re_occurrence in South‑eastern Asia, since CAEV had already been detected in the subregion (Malaysia and Thailand). Years, geography and host system are consistent with the VirusDisease 2024 report; event is clearly within the top ten CAEV emergence events by impact.

EPP.scientific.name: Capripoxvirus ovis
EPP.common.name: Sheep pox virus, Goat pox virus
Host: Sheep (predominantly) and goats
Event.summary: In September 2022, Spain reported its first sheep and goat pox outbreak in more than 50 years in a sheep farm in Andalusia, followed by a series of outbreaks through May 2023 in Andalusia and Castilla–La Mancha. In total, 30 outbreaks were confirmed, leading to the slaughter of approximately 51,800 sheep and 770 goats under EU stamping‑out rules, with extensive protection and surveillance zones established. Intensive clinical surveillance, movement restrictions and culling successfully eradicated the virus from Spain by mid‑2023, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability of high‑density Iberian sheep systems to incursions from neighbouring endemic regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely introduction from nearby endemic areas in North Africa or the eastern Mediterranean via movements of animals, vehicles or contaminated fomites, combined with high connectivity between holdings through lamb collection and transport networks, delays in reporting mild clinical signs and variable farm‑level biosecurity. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses showed the Spanish virus clustering with other recent European SPPV strains but did not identify major novelty; the event is best classified as first_detection in Spain and a significant new incursion into Southern Europe rather than a distinct re‑emergent strain.
Review: review – New event added for the 2022–2023 Spain outbreak (30 outbreaks; ~52,500 animals culled), which represents first_detection of SGP in Spain after decades of freedom and is clearly among the most impactful recent incursions. Classified only as first_detection (no new continent or sub‑region under UNSD definitions). Outbreak counts and culling numbers should be kept aligned with the final Viruses and EU Implementing Decision summaries.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Carp edema virus
EPP.common.name: CEV
Host: Farmed common carp in earthen ponds
Event.summary: In 2020–2021, mortality events in pond-reared common carp in Iran were investigated and CEV DNA was detected and sequenced, representing the first report of carp edema virus in the country and extending the known range of koi sleepy disease into the Middle East region of Southern Asia. Affected carp showed typical gill lesions and lethargy, and phylogenetic analysis placed Iranian isolates within CEV genogroup I alongside strains from several European countries and the USA. Following these findings, Iranian researchers highlighted CEV as an emerging threat requiring inclusion in national fish health surveillance and improved management to limit future economic losses.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0044848622004975?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional movements of carp seed and broodstock, and possible importation of koi or common carp from Europe or neighbouring countries where CEV is established, likely introduced the virus; pond environments with temperature regimes favorable for CEV replication and other stressors facilitated disease expression. Internal mechanisms: The Iranian viruses’ close similarity to established genogroup I strains indicates geographic range expansion and reintroduction of existing lineages into a new country within an already-affected Southern Asia subregion, consistent with classification as re_occurrence rather than emergence of a distinct variant.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0044848622004975?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review. The original row incorrectly extended the event back to 2018; this has been corrected to 2020–2021 in line with the outbreak years in the Iranian Aquaculture paper. Coding as re_occurrence within Southern Asia is appropriate because CEV was already present in the subregion (India) and there is no evidence for a novel Iranian lineage.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Classical swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: Hog cholera virus, CSFV
Host: Domestic pigs
Event.summary: Belgium, which had previously reduced CSF to low levels, experienced a substantial resurgence in 1993–1994 when virus introduced via regional pig movements spread in high-density pig areas, particularly in northern Belgium. Over roughly four months, around two dozen herds became infected and several hundred thousand pigs were slaughtered or destroyed under EU stamping-out policies, resulting in multi-million-euro losses and trade disruption. Following strict movement controls, tracing of animal movements and intensified surveillance, the outbreaks were eliminated and Belgium later regained CSF‑free status in domestic pigs, although it was affected again on a much smaller scale during the wider 1997–1998 Western European epizootic.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: High pig density and strong trade and animal‑movement links with neighboring countries, particularly Germany and the Netherlands; rapid spread once the virus entered integrated production systems; delays in early detection on some farms. Internal mechanisms: Infection involved genotype 2 CSFV similar to strains circulating elsewhere in Western Europe; there is no evidence that unusually high virulence, rather than trade and husbandry factors, drove the epidemic.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via interconnected production and trade networks.
Review: retain (after correction) – original row mis-dated the main Belgian epidemic as 1995–1998 and over-emphasised the 1997–1998 wave. Timing has been corrected to 1993–1994, when ≈23 outbreaks and large-scale culling occurred, and the summary/mechanism text updated accordingly. Geography and classification as re-occurrence in Western Europe remain appropriate; recommend expert review of final outbreak and loss estimates.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyvirus cyprinidallo3
EPP.common.name: Koi herpesvirus (KHV)
Host: Farmed common carp in net pens and ponds (e.g. Lake Kasumigaura and other culture sites) and wild/feral common carp in Lake Biwa and connected water bodies
Event.summary: Beginning in October 2003, large market‑size common carp reared in net pens in Lake Kasumigaura, Japan, experienced mass mortalities with koi herpesvirus disease confirmed by PCR and experimental infections, prompting major depopulation and disinfection campaigns. In spring 2004, CyHV‑3 spread into wild and feral common carp in Lake Biwa, Japan’s largest lake, where approximately 70–80% of the wild carp population (on the order of 100,000 fish) died, and viral DNA and histopathologic lesions consistent with CyHV‑3 infection were documented. Intensive control measures, including removal of dead fish, culling of farm stocks and movement restrictions, reduced acute mortality by mid‑2004, but CyHV‑3 became established in both cultured and wild carp populations in Japan, with continued low‑level outbreaks and evidence of latent infection in survivors.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high‑density carp culture in lakes and connected waterways, movement of infected carp between farms and regions within Japan, and seasonal water temperatures in spring and early summer that favor CyHV‑3 replication. Internal mechanisms: pronounced host and ecological expansion of CyHV‑3 from cultured koi and carp into large wild and feral carp populations (spillover), together with inherent geographic range expansion within Japan; genetic and ecological differences between domesticated and indigenous carp lineages may have contributed to particularly severe impacts in wild stocks.
Review: review – Retain this event as a distinct major episode in Japan characterized by very high mortality in lake‑pen culture and unprecedented die‑off of wild carp in Lake Biwa, but classify it purely as re‑emergence (due to host/ecosystem expansion within an already affected Eastern Asia subregion) rather than as both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence. Timing, magnitude and ecological context were cross‑checked against Japanese fish pathology reports and CDC/EID analyses of the Lake Biwa mortality.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Host: White‑tailed deer, other wild cervids, and domestic ruminants (especially cattle, but also bison, yak, elk and sheep)
Event.summary: In the summer and autumn of 2012, the United States experienced an unusually large EHD outbreak that affected both domestic ruminants and wild white‑tailed deer across much of the country, with 129 cattle herds, 65 captive deer herds, and additional bison, yak, elk and sheep flocks confirmed PCR‑positive. Clinical disease in cattle and bison was concentrated in the central Great Plains and Midwest, while captive and free‑ranging deer were heavily affected in several Midwestern and eastern states. Virological testing showed that EHDV‑6 accounted for the majority of isolates from diseased deer, displacing historically dominant serotypes. Transmission decreased over the winter of 2012–2013, and while localized activity and residual population impacts persisted into early 2013, cases returned to baseline as Culicoides activity fell.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Severe drought and record high temperatures in 2012 across large parts of the central United States, which shortened the extrinsic incubation period of EHDV in Culicoides and concentrated deer and cattle at limited water sources, amplifying transmission. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence characterized by dominance of the relatively recently introduced EHDV‑6 serotype in both wildlife and domestic ruminants, reflecting a shift in the serotype landscape and possible fitness advantages of EHDV‑6 in North American hosts and vectors.
Review: Review – country list was corrected to remove Canada, as the 2012 domestic ruminant epizootic is documented from the United States, whereas Canadian detections in 2013 represent separate, small‑scale events. Classification was updated to remove intra_continental_emergence (this is not a spread into a new UNSD sub‑region) and emphasize re_occurrence plus re_emergence driven by the rise of EHDV‑6. Event is clearly among the highest‑impact global episodes and should be retained after checking that the revised description and coding match project conventions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds); Barbary red deer (Cervus elaphus barbarus); Culicoides vectors
Event.summary: In late September 2021, Tunisian authorities detected outbreaks of bluetongue‑like disease in dairy and beef cattle herds in central‑western Tunisia, and laboratory investigations identified a novel epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 8 strain (EHDV‑8 TUN 2021) not previously detected in the field since the prototype strain was isolated in Australia in 1982. During 2021–2022, this EHDV‑8 lineage spread among Tunisian cattle, causing fever, facial edema, oral ulcers, respiratory distress, reduced milk production, reproductive problems and occasional deaths, and was also confirmed in Barbary deer and in Culicoides midges along the Tunisian–Algerian border. As vector activity decreased and targeted control and surveillance measures were implemented, clinical cases declined, but virological and serological evidence showed that the new EHDV‑8 lineage had become established in North Africa and posed a risk of onward spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climatic and ecological conditions in central‑western Tunisia favorable for Culicoides vectors, including irrigated agriculture and high cattle densities, together with limited pre‑existing immunity to EHDV‑8 in local ruminant populations and animal movements within border regions. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence of EHD via the first field detection in decades of a genetically distinct EHDV‑8 lineage (EHDV‑8 TUN 2021) capable of infecting cattle, wild Barbary deer and Culicoides vectors, representing novel strain/genotype emergence within a region already known for EHDV‑6 activity.
Review: Review – corrected first_global_emergence and first_detection to No, because EHDV was recognized decades earlier and EHDV‑8 had been described as a prototype strain in Australia; this event instead represents the first documented field circulation of a new EHDV‑8 lineage since 1982 and a major re‑emergence in a region already affected by EHDV‑6. Classification as re_emergence only (without intra/inter‑continental emergence) now aligns with project rules; event remains one of the most consequential recent EHD episodes and should be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: RHD virus, RHDV (RHDV1/GI.1 and RHDV2/GI.2)
Sub.regions: Australia and New Zealand (New Zealand focus for this event)
Host: Wild and domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event.summary: New Zealand, which had experienced illegal introduction of RHDV1 in 1997, remained free of RHDV2 until its first confirmed detection in 2018 during surveillance following the legal release of RHDV1‑K5, with retrospective evidence of circulation in wild rabbits since at least late 2017. From 2018 to 2021, RHDV2 spread widely through feral rabbit populations and occasionally affected domestic rabbits across multiple regions, co‑circulating with several RHDV1 variants. By the early 2020s, RHDV2 was considered established across much of New Zealand, prompting updated vaccination strategies for pet and farmed rabbits.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: probable unauthorized or inadvertent introduction of an exotic RHDV2 strain, movement of infected carcasses and rabbits within New Zealand, and extensive feral rabbit populations already under selection pressure from RHDV1 biocontrol. Internal mechanisms: introduction and onward spread of a distinct New Zealand RHDV2 recombinant lineage (GI.3P‑GI.2) capable of efficiently infecting wild rabbits and co‑circulating with RHDV1, representing a clear re‑emergence driven by novel strain emergence and competitive replacement dynamics within an already infected sub‑region.
Review: review – Retain as a major RHDV2 event in Oceania but adjust event‑type classification. Because the UN sub‑region "Australia and New Zealand" already contained RHDV2 from 2014 via Australia, spread to New Zealand represents expansion to a new country within the same sub‑region rather than to a new sub‑region. Under the project rules, such spread should not be labeled intra‑continental emergence. Accordingly, intra_continental_emergence has been set to "false" and the episode is treated purely as re‑emergence driven by introduction and establishment of a new GI.3P‑GI.2 lineage in a country where RHDV (the EPP) was already present (via RHDV1).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Cattle and domestic buffalo in the Northern Areas (now Gilgit‑Baltistan) and adjoining regions
Event.summary: Between April 1994 and November 1995, northern Pakistan experienced the most severe rinderpest epidemic reported globally for more than a decade, affecting cattle and buffalo in remote highland districts and killing an estimated tens of thousands of animals. Infection spread along roads and trade routes as livestock were moved for markets and social obligations, overwhelming local veterinary capacity and threatening spread into neighbouring countries. Emergency vaccination campaigns, movement controls and intensified surveillance under the GREP framework eventually curtailed transmission, and Pakistan later documented absence of circulation leading up to official recognition as free from rinderpest.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Major gaps in prior vaccination coverage, challenging mountainous terrain and remote communities, and extensive cattle and buffalo movements along trade and social networks allowed rapid spread once the virus was introduced. Delays in detection and laboratory confirmation, combined with limited resources for mass vaccination, greatly amplified the epidemic’s scale. Internal mechanisms: Virological evidence indicates circulation of a known Asian lineage of rinderpest without clear signs of increased virulence or a novel genotype; the epidemic is therefore categorized as dramatic re-occurrence driven by failures in vaccination coverage and surveillance rather than re-emergence arising from viral evolution.
Review: retain – This is clearly one of the largest and best-documented rinderpest outbreaks of the 1990s, with magnitude and chronology supported by detailed clinical and modelling studies. Geography, host range and emergence-type (re-occurrence) are appropriate. No structural corrections were needed; sources are highly relevant and event-specific.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus schmallenbergense
EPP.common.name: Schmallenberg virus, SBV
Host: Domestic ruminants (cattle and sheep) on dairy and mixed farms, and Culicoides biting midges, in multiple regions of Israel
Event.summary: Origin: As part of national arbovirus surveillance, monthly sampling of Culicoides biting midges and diagnostic testing of malformed newborn ruminants between June 2018 and December 2019 in Israel revealed SBV RNA in multiple pools of C. imicola, C. oxystoma and other Culicoides species and in the brains of three malformed lambs and one malformed calf, demonstrating local viral circulation and congenital disease in Israeli ruminants. Development: Positive midge pools and affected farms were distributed across several climatic regions, and phylogenetic analysis showed the Israeli SBV sequences to be closely related to European strains, suggesting recent introduction followed by in situ transmission rather than long‑standing endemicity; although the total number of confirmed congenital cases was limited, the combined entomological and clinical findings indicated that SBV had become established in parts of Israel’s ruminant and vector populations. Ending: After 2019, published reports suggest continuing but low‑level SBV activity rather than large‑scale outbreaks, and Israel is now considered part of the broader Western Asian region in which SBV or closely related Simbu viruses episodically circulate, warranting ongoing surveillance in both vectors and livestock.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely external drivers for this episode include windborne spread of infected Culicoides from neighbouring endemic regions (e.g. Türkiye or Mediterranean Europe), cross‑border movement of infected ruminants or semen, and favourable ecological conditions for C. imicola and allied species in Israel’s coastal and Jordan Valley regions. Internal mechanisms: Genomic data indicate that the viruses detected in Israeli midges and ruminants belong to known SBV lineages rather than a novel variant, so this event primarily represents re‑occurrence of SBV within the already affected Western Asia sub‑region, driven by repeated introductions and vector‑borne circulation in largely naïve local herds.
Review: Review – New event added to recognize the well‑documented 2018–2019 SBV circulation in Israel confirmed by genomic detection in both Culicoides vectors and malformed ruminant neonates. Classified as a re‑occurrence within Western Asia (the sub‑region was already affected via Türkiye), not as a new inter‑continental or intra‑continental emergence. Evidence is strong, but the scale of clinical impact appears moderate; experts may wish to confirm that its inclusion among the top SBV events is appropriate based on impact criteria.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: White spot syndrome virus
EPP.common.name: WSSV
Host: Farmed Indian white shrimp (Fenneropenaeus indicus) and other penaeids in semi‑intensive coastal ponds
Event.summary: Origin: Around 2001–2002, white spot disease was first confirmed in shrimp farms in Khuzestan Province (Abadan area) in southwestern Iran, representing the first documented WSSV outbreaks in the Middle East region. Development: The 2002 epidemic caused near‑total crop losses (approaching 100% mortality) in affected farms and led to a drastic reduction—by roughly two‑thirds—in Iranian shrimp production and exports, with PCR and histopathology confirming WSSV as the etiologic agent. End: Iranian authorities responded with emergency measures including harvest bans, movement controls, and later adoption of improved biosecurity and seed screening, which reduced but did not eliminate WSSV risk; white spot disease has since remained an ongoing constraint on shrimp farming in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation or regional transfer of infected broodstock or post-larvae from WSSV-endemic Asian sources; rapid expansion of semi‑intensive shrimp farming in coastal lagoons without robust health surveillance or quarantine; environmental stressors such as fluctuating salinity and temperature that increased disease expression. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a virulent WSSV genotype into a naïve shrimp population; high within-farm transmission via water and handling, facilitating near-total pond losses once infection was established.
Review: Decision: Review. The event description and impact are well supported, but the subregion has been corrected from 'Western Asia' to 'Southern Asia' to match the UNSD classification that places Iran in Southern Asia. The episode remains coded as an intra‑continental emergence within Asia (first documented WSSV outbreaks in the Middle East region), with other fields unchanged.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: White spot syndrome virus
EPP.common.name: WSSV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) in coastal pond farms in southern (Santa Catarina/Laguna region) and later other Brazilian states
Event.summary: Origin: After remaining free of WSSV during the 1999–2001 Latin American pandemic, Brazil experienced its first confirmed outbreaks in 2005, when farms in Santa Catarina (Laguna region) and subsequently other areas reported acute mortalities of L. vannamei and official notifications to the OIE confirmed WSSV. Development: The incursion led to the near collapse of the shrimp industry in southern Brazil, with production in the affected region reportedly falling from more than 4,000 tonnes in 2004 to well under 500 tonnes by 2006, and follow‑up studies detected WSSV in wild penaeid shrimp and other decapods in nearby estuaries, indicating establishment in local ecosystems. End: Brazil gradually rebuilt shrimp production by emphasizing health-screened or resistant stocks, strict biosecurity and surveillance, but WSSV remained enzootic in some areas and a continuing threat in combination with other viral pathogens such as infectious myonecrosis virus (IMNV).
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of WSSV into a previously WSSV‑free national industry, most likely via infected live shrimp or broodstock and/or contaminated products from other Latin American or Asian sources; high stocking densities and limited initial pathogen screening; co-circulation of IMNV that further stressed stocks and may have exacerbated losses. Internal mechanisms: High virulence and environmental stability of WSSV allowed rapid pond‑to‑pond spread through effluents and carcasses, while establishment in local wild shrimp populations created a persistent reservoir for reinfection of farms.
Review: Decision: Retain (newly added event). Multiple Brazilian case studies and global reviews highlight the 2005 WSSV incursion as causing the collapse of the shrimp farming industry in southern Brazil and as the first confirmed WSSV outbreaks in the country after earlier success in keeping WSSV out. This episode involves very large regional production losses and represents a key step in the spread and establishment of WSSV in the Americas, so it merits inclusion among the top ten global events. It is correctly coded as a re‑occurrence within an already affected South American subregion rather than as a separate inter‑continental or intra‑continental emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans; intermediate and sylvatic cycles with Aedes spp. mosquitoes and non-human primates
Event.summary: From September 2012 to early 2013, a major yellow fever outbreak unfolded across all five Darfur states in western Sudan, initially detected as clusters of haemorrhagic fever with high mortality. By January 2013, health authorities and WHO reported around 847 suspected cases and 171 deaths, making it the largest documented yellow fever outbreak in Africa in more than 20 years at that time and leading to spillover cases into neighbouring Chad. A large-scale emergency vaccination campaign covering millions of people, combined with intensified surveillance and vector control, progressively reduced transmission and the outbreak was eventually declared over.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-standing conflict and population displacement in Darfur, very low yellow fever vaccination coverage, limited health infrastructure, and delayed recognition of the outbreak allowed extensive spread before control measures were initiated; cross-border movement heightened the risk of international spread. Internal mechanisms: Epidemiologic and laboratory investigations indicate circulation of endemic African yellow fever virus lineages; the scale of the epidemic is attributed to social and environmental factors rather than emergence of a novel, more virulent or transmissible strain.
Review: retain – Added because the 2012–2013 Darfur epidemic (≈849 suspected cases and 171 deaths) is explicitly described in peer‑reviewed and WHO reports as the largest African yellow fever outbreak in decades and is therefore unquestionably one of the ten most impactful post‑1990 events. Classified as re-occurrence in Northern Africa (Sudan), with no evidence for pathogen-level re-emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia serpens
EPP.common.name: serpent spurge, matted sandmat
Host: Weed of gardens and cultivated ground in urban environments (Baghdad city, including university gardens and adjacent fields)
Event.summary: During field surveys in 2021–2022, Euphorbia serpens was observed for the first time in Iraq at multiple garden and field sites around the University of Baghdad (Al‑Jadriyah campus), where it formed local population patches; the species had not previously been mentioned in Iraqi floras.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/366067711_New_record_for_Iraqi_Flora_from_the_Family_Euphorbiaceae_the_species_Euphorbia_serpens_Kunth_in_Iraq)) Herbarium specimens were deposited in the University of Baghdad herbarium (BUH 50470–50471), and the species was formally reported as a new record for the Iraqi flora in 2022, by which time it already occurred in several urban sites in Baghdad.
