Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely accidental introduction through contaminated horticultural material (ornamental plants, potting soil or seed) into urban gardens and institutional plantings, combined with irrigation and soil disturbance that favor warm‑season ruderal weeds.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/366067711_New_record_for_Iraqi_Flora_from_the_Family_Euphorbiaceae_the_species_Euphorbia_serpens_Kunth_in_Iraq)) Internal mechanisms: the plant’s ability to root at stem nodes, produce numerous seeds over a long flowering period (late April to early September) and tolerate trampling and heat supports rapid establishment and local spread once introduced, representing geographic range infill within Western Asia rather than expansion into a new continent or subregion.
Review: review – Evidence clearly supports this as the first national record for Iraq, but according to the project definitions 'first_detection' and 'intra_continental_emergence' should not be used for each new country when the species is already established elsewhere in the same subregion (here, Western Asia: e.g. Iran, Gulf States, Palestine). I therefore set 'first_detection' and 'intra_continental_emergence' to false and left all emergence‑type flags off; the event is best treated as a nationally important range infill rather than a continental‑scale emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia glyptosperma
EPP.common.name: ridgeseed spurge, ribseed sandmat
Host: Ruderal weed in disturbed sites, roadsides and agricultural surroundings on sandy soils in the Sabha and Ariggiba regions of south-western Libya.
Event.summary: Between 2023 and 2024, Euphorbia glyptosperma was collected from multiple localities in the Sabha and Ariggiba regions of south-western Libya, where it formed naturalized populations in disturbed sandy habitats, roadsides and fields. These finds represent the first confirmed records of the species for Libya but follow earlier reports that it had already become a naturalized weed in neighbouring Tunisia since the 1990s, indicating expansion within the Northern Africa subregion rather than a continent-wide first arrival. By the time of publication, Libyan populations were mapped and discussed as a potentially expanding alien weed, though their distribution was still limited to a cluster of sites in the south-west and no large-scale agricultural impacts had yet been documented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Probable accidental introduction into Libya via contaminated seed or grain shipments, or other traded plant materials moving within the Mediterranean basin and between North African countries, assisted by road transport networks radiating from Sabha and Ariggiba and by local agricultural disturbance creating bare, sandy ground. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the species’ prostrate, seed-prolific growth form and tolerance of hot, arid, sandy soils allow it to establish in semi-arid Libyan environments once introduced; there is currently no evidence for novel genotypes, herbicide resistance or host-range shifts relative to other extra-limital populations.
Review: review – Original event retained but reinterpreted: evidence from the Libyan paper indicates that E. glyptosperma had already been naturalized in Tunisia since the 1990s, so the Libyan records represent re-occurrence within the Northern Africa subregion rather than an inter-continental emergence for Africa. Accordingly, the emergence-type flags were changed from inter-continental emergence to re-occurrence, and the summary now frames Libya as the first national record within a region where the species was already established. A regional expert should confirm the Tunisian status, check for any other earlier African records, and validate whether this Libyan expansion should be kept as one of the major emergence events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia graminea
EPP.common.name: grassleaf spurge
Host: Roadsides and disturbed sites in lowland agricultural landscapes in southern Taiwan (Pingtung County).([taiwania.ntu.edu.tw](https://taiwania.ntu.edu.tw/abstract/456?utm_source=openai))
Event.summary: Field surveys in 2004 discovered two populations of grassleaf spurge in Pingtung County, southern Taiwan, leading to its formal publication in 2005 as a newly naturalized species and the first confirmed establishment in Asia. The species was found naturalized along roadsides and disturbed sites, indicating successful reproduction and spread beyond cultivation. By the late 2000s it was incorporated into Taiwanese catalogues of naturalized flora, with concern about further expansion though detailed eradication outcomes were not yet reported.([taiwania.ntu.edu.tw](https://taiwania.ntu.edu.tw/abstract/456?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction via international horticultural trade or contaminated planting material, consistent with many other American Euphorbia species naturalized in Taiwan; expansion facilitated by high levels of disturbance in agricultural and roadside habitats. Internal mechanisms: generalist ecology and high reproductive output, plus effective seed dispersal by explosive capsules, allow rapid colonization of disturbed ground; no specific novel genotype was identified.([taiwania.ntu.edu.tw](https://taiwania.ntu.edu.tw/pdf/tai.2005.50.131.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia graminea
EPP.common.name: grassleaf spurge
Host: Roadsides and disturbed sites in subtropical urban landscapes of Guangdong Province, China mainland.([yrdzwkx.com](https://www.yrdzwkx.com/EN/10.3969/j.issn.1009-7791.2018.04.013))
Event.summary: Around 2017–2018 botanists documented naturalized populations of grassleaf spurge in Guangdong Province, representing the first confirmed record for mainland China and an extension of its previously known Asian range beyond Taiwan. A 2018 paper described the species as newly naturalized in Guangdong and summarized its prior status as a weed naturalized in Pacific Islands, Nigeria, Italy and Taiwan, highlighting its invasive potential. By publication, the species was already established along roadsides and disturbed urban sites, with concerns about further spread but no comprehensive management yet in place.([yrdzwkx.com](https://www.yrdzwkx.com/EN/10.3969/j.issn.1009-7791.2018.04.013))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely introduction via horticultural trade or contaminated planting material into the Pearl River Delta’s highly connected urban landscape; extensive disturbed land and subtropical climate in Guangdong provide suitable conditions for establishment. Internal mechanisms: preadaptation to warm, humid climates and disturbed soils and efficient reproductive biology (ballistic seed dispersal, rapid growth) support secondary spread from initial foci.([yrdzwkx.com](https://www.yrdzwkx.com/EN/10.3969/j.issn.1009-7791.2018.04.013))

EPP.scientific.name: Ipomoea imperati
EPP.common.name: beach morningglory, beach morning-glory
Countries: Tunisia – coastal dunes near Mahdia (central-eastern coast) and Tabarka (north-western coast) [2023-2024]
Host: Coastal sandy-beach and dune plant communities on Mediterranean littoral dunes (embryonic to primary dunes with Ammophiletea vegetation in north-western and central-eastern Tunisia)
Event.summary: Between 2023 and 2024, extensive surveys of Tunisian coastal dunes documented Ipomoea imperati for the first time in the country, with two sizeable populations (each exceeding 500 individuals and together occupying more than two hectares) on the dunes of Mahdia and Tabarka.([revistas.uma.es](https://revistas.uma.es/index.php/abm/article/download/22192/22470/126608)) These findings filled the last geographic gap along the southern Mediterranean shore, as the species was already known from other North African coasts (Egypt, Libya, Algeria, Morocco), indicating an increase in known incidence within the Northern Africa subregion rather than a new continental introduction.([revistas.uma.es](https://revistas.uma.es/index.php/abm/article/download/22192/22470/126608)) During the period 2023–2025 the Tunisian populations formed dense mats within typical Ammophiletea dune communities but remained confined to a limited stretch of coast, with no eradication reported and the longer-term invasion trajectory still uncertain.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The appearance of extensive Tunisian dune populations likely reflects a combination of long-distance sea-drift dispersal from existing Mediterranean or Atlantic source populations and chronic anthropogenic disturbance of coastal dunes (tourism infrastructure, trampling, dune restructuring) that opens habitat niches for rhizomatous strandline species; the new records also highlight previous under-sampling of Tunisian dunes compared with other North African coasts.([revistas.uma.es](https://revistas.uma.es/index.php/abm/article/download/22192/22470/126608)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – buoyant seeds, salt tolerance and creeping, rooting stems allow I. imperati to establish and form large mats on newly available dune habitat; clonal growth and high cover (70–80% in comparable Sicilian stands) facilitate local dominance once established, although seed set and spread may be limited and populations may depend heavily on vegetative persistence.([revistas.uma.es](https://revistas.uma.es/index.php/abm/article/download/22192/22470/126608))
Review: REVIEW – New event added. This row was not present in the original dataset but has been included because (1) Acta Botanica Malacitana 50 (2025) documents the first clearly illustrated and confirmed records of Ipomoea imperati in Tunisia, with two large dune populations (>500 individuals over >2 ha), making this one of the most substantial post‑1990 expansions known for the species in North Africa, and (2) the authors explicitly note that the species was already reported from all other North African coastal countries and that this Tunisian record completes its continuous occurrence along the southern Mediterranean shore.([revistas.uma.es](https://revistas.uma.es/index.php/abm/article/download/22192/22470/126608)) The event is therefore classified as a re-occurrence (increase in incidence within the Northern Africa subregion) rather than intra- or inter-continental emergence, which would require colonization of a previously uninvaded continent or UNSD subregion. No evidence was found for a novel strain, host shift, or resistance trait, so re-emergence is set to false. The time span 2023–2025 reflects collection dates in 2023–2024 and publication in 2025; the episode is likely ongoing but currently documented over this interval. This event should be reviewed by regional botanists to confirm whether any older, overlooked Tunisian herbarium material exists and to verify the magnitude of the invaded area relative to other North African sites.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Giardia intestinalis
EPP.common.name: Giardia lamblia, Lamblia intestinalis
Countries: United States of America [1995-1996] (community in Montgomery County, New York State)
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Between December 1995 and February 1996, a community of roughly 20,000 residents in Montgomery County, New York State, USA, experienced a large drinking-water–associated outbreak of giardiasis. Epidemiological investigation attributed an estimated 1,449 illnesses to inadequate filtration of a surface-water source supplying a community water system, with heavy rainfall and elevated post-filtration turbidity preceding and during the outbreak; chlorination alone was insufficient to control Giardia despite the system operating within its usual parameters. After the contamination was recognized, remedial actions including correction of filtration deficiencies and strengthened regulatory oversight were implemented, and outbreak-related cases subsided.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy rains and runoff, combined with suboptimal filtration performance in a community surface-water system, led to breakthrough of Giardia cysts into treated drinking water; turbidity limits were exceeded, but no interruption of chlorination occurred and the system initially remained in operation.([nepis.epa.gov](https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPURL.cgi?Dockey=P1003QZP.TXT)) External drivers included aging treatment infrastructure and insufficient operational control under then-current regulations. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or increased virulence was reported; this was a large-scale re-occurrence of established Giardia transmission facilitated by treatment and source-water vulnerabilities, not a phenotypic re-emergence event.
Review: Review – Added new event. This Montgomery County, New York, outbreak is one of the best documented and largest post‑1990 giardiasis outbreaks globally, with ~1,449 cases linked to a community drinking-water supply; it clearly meets the criteria for inclusion among the most impactful events.([nepis.epa.gov](https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPURL.cgi?Dockey=P1003QZP.TXT)) Classified as re-occurrence only, since Giardia was long established in humans in North America and no new genotype or host system is implicated. Geographic attribution (Northern America, USA) and the 1995–1996 date range follow EPA summaries and outbreak reviews. Event characterization and impact are well supported, but final confirmation of its rank within a global top‑10 list and any additional local morbidity data should be done during expert curation. Retain as a flagship North American waterborne outbreak.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Giardia intestinalis
EPP.common.name: Giardia lamblia, Lamblia intestinalis
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Between November 2018 and April–May 2019, a municipality of about 7,400 inhabitants (Sant’Agata Bolognese, Municipality A) in the metropolitan city of Bologna, Italy, experienced a large community outbreak of giardiasis. Enhanced surveillance and case-finding ultimately identified around 200–228 laboratory-confirmed cases, making it Italy’s first documented large giardiasis outbreak, with illness strongly associated with drinking municipal tap water.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8414958/?utm_source=openai)) Following public health investigation and environmental assessment, suspected deficiencies in the local water distribution system were addressed, residents were advised on safe water use and hygiene, and the outbreak subsided after several months.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Contamination of the municipal drinking-water distribution network in a small town, likely facilitated by infrastructure defects or backflow events, enabled Giardia cysts to reach a substantial fraction of the population; delayed recognition of giardiasis as the etiologic agent contributed to the scale of the outbreak.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8414958/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel assemblage or increased virulence was presented; the event is best viewed as a major re-occurrence of endemic Giardia in Italy, amplified by water-distribution vulnerabilities and diagnostic delay rather than evolutionary change in the parasite.
Review: Review – Added new event. The Sant’Agata Bolognese (Municipality A) outbreak is a well-documented, recent large community giardiasis outbreak in Southern Europe, with roughly 200–228 laboratory-confirmed cases and clear association with municipal tap water.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8414958/?utm_source=openai)) It is explicitly highlighted by ECDC as Italy’s first large giardiasis outbreak and thus meets the criteria for inclusion among high-impact post‑2005 events. Classified as re-occurrence, since Giardia was long present in humans in Italy and there is no evidence of genotype-driven re-emergence or spread into a new host system. Geographic coding (Europe, Southern Europe, Italy) follows the UNSD and provided country list. Strongly recommended to retain as a major European emergence episode; final quantitative ranking within a global top‑10 should be revisited once a complete global list is assembled.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women and infants of particular concern)
Event.summary: From late 1994 through mid‑1995, health authorities in Greater Victoria, British Columbia detected an unusual cluster of acute toxoplasmosis and ultimately identified 110 laboratory-confirmed recent infections among residents, with serologic and epidemiologic evidence that several thousand persons were infected overall. Investigation linked illness to a large unfiltered surface reservoir supplying municipal drinking water, probably contaminated with oocysts shed by cougars and domestic cats, making this the first documented and, at the time, largest toxoplasmosis outbreak associated with a city water system. Following closure and structural remediation of the implicated reservoir, improvements in water treatment, and public advisories, incident cases declined, though some affected individuals— including congenitally infected infants—experienced long-term ocular complications.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of unfiltered surface water in a vulnerable reservoir, high local densities of felids shedding oocysts, heavy rainfall and turbidity events that facilitated contamination, and absence of treatment barriers specific for protozoan oocysts. Internal mechanisms: High-dose environmental oocyst exposure via drinking water; no evidence for a novel parasite genotype or intrinsic change in virulence beyond typical oocyst-borne disease severity.
Review: Retain. Verified as a major global waterborne toxoplasmosis outbreak with ≈110 confirmed recent infections and an estimated 2,900–7,700 total infections, clearly among the most impactful post‑1990 events in terms of persons affected. Geographic coding (North America | Northern America | Canada) is correct, and classification as re-occurrence (waterborne oocyst exposure in a region where T. gondii was long established) is appropriate. Source set centered on the Lancet report and Canadian/BC public health documents is suitable; no changes required beyond clarifying case numbers in the summary.

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Countries: Brazil [2001-2002] (Paraná State; Santa Isabel do Ivaí)
Host: Humans (municipality residents, including pregnant women and children)
Event.summary: Beginning in November 2001, a physician in Santa Isabel do Ivaí, Paraná, reported clusters of patients with fever, myalgia, lymphadenopathy, and positive Toxoplasma serology, triggering an outbreak investigation. Among 2,884 urban residents who volunteered for testing, 426 (11.5%) had IgM and IgG antibodies indicating recent infection, 176 of whom met a clinical case definition, and mapping showed strong spatial clustering in areas supplied by one municipal reservoir. T. gondii was isolated and genotyped from water samples as a highly virulent type I strain, confirming the outbreak as a large waterborne event; closure and replacement of the defective reservoir, coupled with public guidance on drinking water and ice-cream prepared with it, were followed by cessation of new cases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Structural deterioration of an aging concrete reservoir, removal of roofing tiles, and heavy seasonal rains allowed rainwater contaminated with cat feces to infiltrate the tank, in the absence of effective filtration and with chlorination insufficient to inactivate oocysts. Internal mechanisms: High-dose exposure to a type I T. gondii genotype associated with high virulence in animal models and substantial rates of ocular involvement, representing re-emergence through circulation of a particularly virulent strain in a community-scale water system.
Review: Retain. This is one of the largest documented outbreaks worldwide, with 176 symptomatic cases and 426 serologically defined recent infections, and the only event in which T. gondii was definitively isolated and genotyped from the human drinking-water source. Classification as re-emergence is appropriate because a highly virulent type I lineage was demonstrated in the water, indicating parasite genotype as a key driver, while intra-/inter-continental emergence categories remain ‘No’ given long-standing regional endemicity. Event year range, geography (South America | South America | Brazil), and sources (EID dispatch and subsequent reviews) are correct; no structural corrections needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Countries: Suriname [2003-2004] (Patam village near French Guiana border)
Host: Humans (small forest village population including pregnant women)
Event.summary: From late December 2003 through mid‑January 2004, the remote village of Patam on the Surinamese bank of the Maroni River experienced a cluster of severe multivisceral illnesses among previously healthy adults and pregnant women. Investigation documented 11 acute toxoplasmosis cases among 38 inhabitants: eight immunocompetent adults with disseminated disease (one fatal), two lethal congenital infections (a fetus and a neonate), and one symptomatic child; only three villagers had evidence of prior T. gondii exposure. Molecular and mouse-inoculation studies showed that at least five cases were caused by the same highly atypical Amazonian strain, and although no single vehicle could be confirmed, environmental or foodborne oocyst exposure linked to forest felids and hunted game was considered most likely. The event subsided as exposures changed and affected individuals were treated, but it highlighted the capacity of rainforest strains to cause life-threatening disease in small, immunocompetent communities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Subsistence hunting of wild game, close proximity to rainforest felids, lack of treated water and sanitation, and limited access to healthcare permitted intense exposure to oocysts in a remote Amazonian setting. Internal mechanisms: Infection with a highly virulent, atypical T. gondii genotype maintained in a sylvatic cycle, causing unusually severe disease and death even in immunocompetent adults and fetuses—an archetypal re-emergence event driven by parasite genetic diversity and high virulence.
Review: Retain. Although the absolute case count (11) is modest, this Patam/Maroni River outbreak is heavily cited because of its extreme severity, high attack rate in a tiny community, multiple deaths (including two congenital), and clear linkage to an atypical Amazonian genotype. Geography (Suriname; South America/South America) and classification as re-emergence are correct. Source selection (original Clin Infect Dis report plus outbreak reviews) is appropriate; no structural corrections needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Host: Humans (immunocompetent patients with acquired ocular toxoplasmosis)
Event.summary: Beginning in late 2004, clinicians at Aravind Eye Hospital in Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, noted a dramatic rise in patients presenting with primary toxoplasmic retinitis, many with a history of preceding flu-like illness suggestive of recent systemic infection. Over a 12‑month period spanning 2004–2005, between roughly 180 and 250 patients were diagnosed with acquired ocular toxoplasmosis in association with recent serologic conversion, far exceeding baseline numbers for the region. Epidemiologic investigation and temporal association with intense rainfall pointed toward contamination of municipal drinking water (from the Siruvani reservoir) with oocysts as the most plausible common source, although T. gondii was not directly detected in the water. The outbreak tapered as water treatment and source management improved and as the transient cohort of exposed individuals either recovered or developed sequelae.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy rainfall events, vulnerability of a surface-water supply and distribution system, and inadequate barriers against protozoan oocysts likely allowed contamination of municipal drinking water with cat-derived oocysts, exposing a large urban population. Internal mechanisms: High-dose oocyst exposure leading to systemic infection and unusually frequent ocular involvement; although a parasite genotype predisposing to eye disease is suspected, genotyping data are limited, so this event is conservatively treated as re-occurrence rather than confirmed re-emergence.
Review: Retain (added). A large ocular toxoplasmosis epidemic in Coimbatore, with >200 patients over about a year and strong circumstantial evidence implicating municipal water, is widely cited as one of the most consequential outbreaks globally in terms of clinical burden. It was missing from the original dataset and is now added with Asia/Southern Asia/India coding and classification as re-occurrence (no definitive strain data). Sources include the primary Arch Ophthalmol case series, the earlier Indian J Ophthalmol report, and expert reviews. Flagged for review only to refine case counts if the user wishes to choose a single canonical number (e.g., 248) for the Excel sheet.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Escherichia coli
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1996-1997] (central Scotland, including Wishaw and surrounding areas)
Host: Humans (primarily older adults and nursing-home residents consuming cooked meats and other foods from a contaminated butcher’s shop)
Event.summary: In late November 1996, public health authorities in Lanarkshire, central Scotland, detected a cluster of bloody diarrhoea cases and confirmed Escherichia coli O157:H7 infections among residents of Wishaw, with epidemiologic investigation rapidly implicating cooked meats and pies supplied by a local butcher, John Barr & Son, as the common source. The outbreak expanded through retail sales and catered events such as a church lunch and nursing-home meals, ultimately affecting roughly 500 people across central Scotland and causing 21 deaths, mostly among elderly patients, making it at the time the world’s deadliest recorded E. coli O157 outbreak. The epidemic waned after the implicated butcher’s premises were closed, contaminated products withdrawn, and a national inquiry led to new UK hygiene regulations and licensing for butchers and meat retailers, substantially strengthening food-safety controls.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross-contamination of ready-to-eat cooked meats with raw beef at a small butcher’s shop; inadequate separation of raw and cooked areas and shared slicing equipment; failures in local food-safety inspection; high exposure of vulnerable elderly populations through institutional catering. Internal mechanisms: infection with a highly virulent E. coli O157:H7 phage type 2 clone already present in regional cattle; no evidence that a fundamentally novel genotype emerged, so the extreme impact reflected dose, distribution, and host vulnerability rather than new bacterial traits.
Review: retain – Newly added high-impact event: the 1996–1997 central Scotland/Wishaw E. coli O157:H7 outbreak (~500 cases and 21 deaths) linked to a single butcher’s shop. This outbreak is widely recognized as one of the deadliest STEC events globally and clearly belongs in a top‑10 list. Geography (UK/Scotland, Northern Europe), timing and classification as a large re‑occurrence (no novel strain or new region) are supported by FAO/WHO case reports, the Pennington inquiry and peer‑reviewed summaries.

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Host: Humans exposed via slaughtering, butchering and consuming infected cattle and handling contaminated animal products
Event.summary: In 2018–2019, two anthrax outbreaks were investigated in Ethiopia’s Amhara Region, where livestock deaths were followed by 22 and 18 human illnesses respectively, including several suspected deaths in people who had butchered or eaten the carcasses. These events were not the first anthrax outbreaks in Ethiopia but were the first to be laboratory‑confirmed by PCR in both humans and animals, allowing detailed characterization of transmission pathways. After public‑health teams identified exposure routes and implemented community education, carcass‑handling restrictions, and antibiotic treatment for human cases, the outbreaks were brought under control, informing new national approaches to anthrax surveillance and confirmation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8865639/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Continued endemic presence of anthrax in cattle; slaughter and consumption of animals that died suddenly or showed signs of illness; limited prior laboratory capacity for anthrax, resulting in under‑recognition before 2018.
Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of a new strain; the main change is improved diagnostic capacity (PCR confirmation) and outbreak investigation, which re‑revealed established zoonotic transmission patterns (re‑occurrence with first laboratory confirmation in this subregion).
Review: review – Amhara 2018–2019 outbreaks (22 and 18 human cases, with several suspected deaths) are correctly located in Eastern Africa (Ethiopia) and important as the first PCR‑confirmed anthrax outbreaks documented in this region, but they are modest in size compared with other known post‑1990 events. First_detection has been set to No because human anthrax was recognized in Ethiopia long before 2018; the event is best characterized as re‑occurrence with improved diagnostic capacity. Retain for now, but consider downgrading if the event list must be restricted strictly to the highest‑impact outbreaks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8865639/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus toscanaense
EPP.common.name: Toscana virus
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with severe encephalitis and meningoencephalitis)
Event.summary: During the summers of 2017 and 2018, clinicians in Bucharest, Romania identified eight hospitalized patients with severe neuroinvasive Toscana virus infection confirmed by real-time RT-PCR, representing the first documented human cases of TOSV in the country and in Eastern Europe. Most patients were elderly with comorbidities, and five of the eight cases were fatal, highlighting an unexpectedly high case-fatality rate and severe clinical course. After targeted investigation and reporting, Romania recognized TOSV as an emerging neurotropic arbovirus, and while sporadic circulation likely continues, the acute two-year cluster marked a clear emergence event in a new European subregion.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Presence of competent sand fly vectors in southeastern Europe, urban heat-island effects and warm summers enhancing vector activity in and around Bucharest, and expansion of molecular diagnostics for unexplained encephalitis that enabled TOSV detection. Internal mechanisms: Sequence data placed Romanian viruses within known Mediterranean lineages rather than indicating a unique highly virulent strain; the high mortality appears linked largely to host age and comorbidities rather than confirmed increases in intrinsic virulence.

EPP.scientific.name: Caprine arthritis encephalitis virus
EPP.common.name: CAEV, Small ruminant lentivirus
Countries: Oman [2007-2008] (Batinah, Dakhiliya, Sharqiya, Dhahra, Wusta regions)
Host: Domestic non-dairy indigenous goats (slaughtered and field herds)
Event.summary: Between 2007 and 2008, a large serological survey of 1,638 indigenous goats from five regions of the Sultanate of Oman found that 5.1% of samples were positive for antibodies against CAEV, providing the first serological evidence that CAEV was circulating in Omani goat populations. Seropositive animals were detected in several regions, with older age classes more frequently positive, indicating that infection had been present for some time and was not confined to a single imported herd. The findings confirmed that CAEV had become established in the Gulf region and prompted recommendations for improved biosecurity, control of animal movements from endemic source countries and better management of colostrum and kid rearing, although no formal national eradication programme has yet been implemented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing importation of live goats from countries such as Somalia and other CAEV‑affected areas into Oman, combined with traditional extensive or pastoral management that allows mixing between indigenous and imported animals, likely introduced and disseminated the virus. Internal mechanisms: Standard SRLV biology (lifelong infection, delayed seroconversion and persistent shedding) facilitated silent establishment of CAEV in indigenous goats without overt clinical indicators, rather than emergence of a new strain or host jump.
Review: retain – added this event as a major regional re_occurrence in Western Asia, representing the first documented CAEV serological evidence in Oman based on a large, multi‑region survey with >1,600 goats and clear management-related risk factors. Classified as re_occurrence (not intra_continental_emergence) because CAEV had already been reported in the same UN subregion (Western Asia) in Jordan and Saudi Arabia before 2007. Countries, years and host system align with Tageldin et al. 2012; event should be considered among the globally important post‑1990 CAEV emergence episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Caprine arthritis encephalitis virus
EPP.common.name: CAEV, Small ruminant lentivirus
Host: Domestic goats (dairy, meat and breeding herds)
Event.summary: Between March 2011 and October 2012, a large-scale serological survey of 3,437 goats from 65 goat farms across Taiwan found an overall CAEV seropositive rate of 61.7% and herd-level infection in 98.5% of farms, demonstrating that CAEV infection was widespread in both dairy and meat goat operations. Prevalence was highest in dairy herds (over 80% of animals positive in some regions), and positive farms were detected in northern, central, southern and eastern parts of Taiwan, with only one surveyed farm remaining negative. These results provided the first national-level picture of CAEV infection in Taiwan and led to recognition that the virus was endemic and a major constraint on goat productivity, highlighting the need for ongoing surveillance and targeted control measures, particularly in intensive dairy systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of dairy goat farming in Taiwan, including importation of high-yield breeds from CAEV-endemic countries and frequent animal movements between regions, likely underpinned the high prevalence detected in the survey. Internal mechanisms: The study did not identify a novel genotype driving spread; rather, the very high within-herd and herd-level prevalence is consistent with long-standing circulation of typical CAEV strains in dense dairy herds, aided by efficient transmission via colostrum/milk and close contact.
Review: retain – added this event because the 2011–2012 nationwide survey in Taiwan is one of the largest and highest-prevalence CAEV datasets worldwide (3,437 goats, 65 farms, 61.7% individual and 98.5% herd seropositivity), making it clearly among the top ten post‑1990 CAEV emergence/re-occurrence events by impact. Classified as a regional re_occurrence in Eastern Asia, since CAEV had already been present in China and Japan; not marked as intra_continental_emergence. Noted Taiwan as “China (Taiwan)” to align with UN-style nomenclature, but this may need harmonization with the project’s country list.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: EEEV, EEE virus
Countries: United States of America [2023-2024] (Vermont – Franklin, Addison, Orleans and a neighboring northwestern county for human cases; New York – one horse infected while residing in Vermont)
Host: Horses; humans (linked but dead-end hosts)
Event.summary: After several years without detected equine or human disease following the 2011–2013 Vermont episode, EEEV activity resurged in 2023–2024 in northern Vermont, where an unvaccinated horse in Franklin County died of infection and a New York horse that had recently resided in Vermont was confirmed infected, alongside renewed detections of EEEV‑positive mosquito pools. In 2024, two additional unvaccinated horses from Addison and Orleans counties died from EEE and two men from a northwestern county developed neuroinvasive EEE (one fatal), representing the first human cases in Vermont since 2012 and coinciding with a sharp increase in positive mosquito pools across multiple northern and western towns. With the close of the 2024 mosquito season, reported equine cases subsided, but authorities elevated EEE risk classifications for affected counties, strengthened recommendations for annual equine vaccination and personal mosquito‑bite prevention and prepared contingency plans for aerial adulticiding should future seasons show similarly intense activity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Favorable climatic conditions for vector mosquitoes and the presence of extensive wetland habitats in northern Vermont, coupled with low or inconsistent equine vaccination coverage and human residence or recreation near swampy areas, likely allowed re‑amplification of EEEV in local bird–mosquito cycles and spillover into horses and humans; interstate movement of horses between Vermont and neighboring New York helped reveal the geographic extent of local transmission. Internal mechanisms: Surveillance and phylogenetic information to date are consistent with continued circulation of endemic North American EEEV lineages rather than emergence of a novel strain, so the event is classified as a re‑occurrence in an already affected state with an expanded geographic footprint and increased incidence rather than as genetic re‑emergence.
Review: review – Event retained but wording adjusted to align with CDC’s 2026 MMWR description, which reports three equine cases and two human neuroinvasive cases in Vermont during 2023–2024 and documents substantial increases in EEEV‑positive mosquito pools. Classification as a re‑occurrence in a previously affected state remains appropriate, and the countries/subnational areas field has been clarified to distinguish Vermont horses and human cases from the New York horse that acquired infection while in Vermont.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Iltovirus gallid2
EPP.common.name: Gallid alphaherpesvirus 1, ILT virus
Countries: United States of America [2002-2003] (Mississippi broiler belt – 5 broiler-breeder and 29 broiler flocks)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial broilers in an immunologically naïve broiler industry; breeder flocks also affected)
Event.summary: From December 2002 to March 2003, a localized infectious laryngotracheitis outbreak occurred in Mississippi, United States, affecting five broiler‑breeder and 29 broiler flocks in a state that had been free of ILT for the preceding 15 years.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232227630_Factors_Associated_with_Introduction_of_Infectious_Laryngotracheitis_Virus_on_Broiler_Farms_During_a_Localized_Outbreak?utm_source=openai)) The virus spread among closely spaced farms in an otherwise immunologically naïve commercial broiler population, leading to marked respiratory disease, mortality, and production losses.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232227630_Factors_Associated_with_Introduction_of_Infectious_Laryngotracheitis_Virus_on_Broiler_Farms_During_a_Localized_Outbreak?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak was controlled by depopulating infected flocks, implementing ring vaccination with live CEO vaccines around affected sites, tightening movement controls on litter and personnel, and improving house cleaning and down‑time, after which no further ILT‑positive flocks were detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of ILTV into a naïve broiler region, high farm density, movement of company service crews and suppliers between farms, and shared litter‑removal equipment were all statistically associated with ILT introduction on case farms.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232227630_Factors_Associated_with_Introduction_of_Infectious_Laryngotracheitis_Virus_on_Broiler_Farms_During_a_Localized_Outbreak?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The viruses were typical CEO‑like field/vaccine strains; there is no evidence of a novel genotype, and the episode is best interpreted as amplification of existing ILTV lineages under intensive production and suboptimal biosecurity.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: Event clearly represents one of the larger post‑1990 US ILT epizootics (34 commercial flocks) and should be retained, but event description was updated to include the documented number and types of flocks and to rely primarily on the Mississippi risk‑factor study.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232227630_Factors_Associated_with_Introduction_of_Infectious_Laryngotracheitis_Virus_on_Broiler_Farms_During_a_Localized_Outbreak?utm_source=openai)) Non‑specific or tangential sources were removed from this row.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Iltovirus gallid2
EPP.common.name: Gallid alphaherpesvirus 1, ILT virus
Countries: Brazil [2002-2003] (Bastos region, São Paulo State – intensive commercial layer area of ~14 million hens)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial laying hens in large multi-age layer farms)
Event.summary: At the end of 2002 and throughout 2003, a severe ILT epidemic struck the Bastos region of São Paulo State, Brazil, the country’s largest egg‑production hub with around 14 million commercial layers, causing typical respiratory disease, high flock morbidity and mortality reported up to 20%, and major egg‑production losses.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) Molecular characterization showed that most outbreak isolates grouped into distinct field virus clusters, clearly differentiated from some vaccine strains used in Brazil at that time.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21154050/?utm_source=openai)) Following extensive vaccination with live attenuated vaccines, strengthened biosecurity, and regulatory control on bird and litter movements, clinical disease declined, although ILTV has remained endemic in Brazilian commercial poultry.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very dense layer populations in multi‑age complexes, frequent movement of personnel, equipment and litter between barns and farms, and pre‑existing respiratory co‑infections created ideal conditions for rapid farm‑to‑farm spread and large cumulative losses.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Outbreak viruses belonged mainly to established field lineages rather than novel recombinants; subsequent Brazilian work documents long‑term persistence of both field and vaccine‑origin ILTV, with latency and vaccine virus maintenance contributing to continued re‑occurrence in the same production region.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9679056/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Reason: This São Paulo (Bastos) epidemic is widely cited as one of the largest modern ILT outbreaks, affecting an exceptionally dense layer region and causing substantial mortality and production loss; geography and emergence type (re-occurrence within an already affected country/continent) are correct. Minor wording changes were made to emphasise scale and to align with Brazilian primary sources.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Iltovirus gallid2
EPP.common.name: Gallid alphaherpesvirus 1, ILT virus
Countries: Brazil [2010-2011] (Mantiqueira Highlands egg-production region, Minas Gerais State – multi-age layer complexes)
Host: Domestic chickens (large multi-age commercial laying-hen flocks)
Event.summary: In November 2010, an extensive ILT outbreak was reported in a high-density egg‑production area in the Mantiqueira Highlands of Minas Gerais, Brazil, where approximately eight million layers were housed in multi‑age complexes with individual farm sizes up to 2.9 million birds.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) Over subsequent months, multiple farms experienced increased mortality (roughly 1–9% per month) and sudden drops in egg output, with necropsy revealing characteristic necrotic and fibrinous laryngotracheitis and molecular tests confirming ILTV infection.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) As movement restrictions, improved biosecurity, and (later) vectored‑vaccine programmes were implemented by producers and the official veterinary service, mortality gradually returned toward baseline, although ILTV persisted in the region and prompted long‑term surveillance and control efforts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12172900/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extremely dense layer populations in multi‑age systems, restrictions on removal of birds and litter once the disease was recognized, and co‑circulation of other respiratory pathogens created a setting in which ILTV could spread rapidly and cause large cumulative losses.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicate involvement of virulent field strains related to earlier Brazilian ILTV genotypes rather than a fundamentally new recombinant; this episode therefore represents major re‑occurrence of established lineages in a new high‑density production pocket within the same country and subregion.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: This large Minas Gerais outbreak, affecting an egg‑production region with ~8 million hens, was missing from the original list despite being highlighted in Brazilian surveillance papers as a major ILT episode distinct from the Bastos epidemic.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/pvb/a/NtkCwHwQLMvQ9XWGfKsD47t/?utm_source=openai)) A new row has been added and classified as re-occurrence in South America; geography and timing follow Brazilian primary reports.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus schmallenbergense
EPP.common.name: Schmallenberg virus, SBV
Host: Wild ruminants (red deer, roe deer, mouflon) in western Germany, with presumed concurrent infection in domestic ruminants given the enzootic status of SBV
Event.summary: Origin: After earlier post‑epidemic re‑circulation events in 2014 and 2019, serologic surveillance of wild red deer, roe deer and mouflon in western Germany during the 2022–2023 and 2023–2024 hunting seasons found a low SBV antibody seroprevalence of about 4.9% in 2022 but a dramatic increase to roughly 40% overall in 2023, with around 32% of juveniles seropositive, indicating intense SBV transmission in summer–autumn 2023. Development: Parallel monitoring of Culicoides biting midges from 2019–2023 showed continuous low‑level detection of SBV RNA with a marked rise in minimum infection rates in 2023, supporting a substantial re‑circulation wave in vector populations; given Germany’s dense domestic ruminant herds and enzootic SBV status, these wildlife and vector data strongly imply widespread re‑infection of naïve cattle and small ruminants in affected regions, even though only a fraction of clinical cases would be detected. Ending: As in previous cycles, this 2022–2023 wave is expected to subside as younger cohorts acquire immunity, reinforcing the pattern of SBV as an enzootic virus in central Europe with cyclic re‑occurrence every 2–3 years and highlighting the need for continued surveillance and targeted vaccination of susceptible breeding animals to mitigate fetal losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The primary external driver is the progressive decline in herd‑level immunity in both domestic and wild ruminants as immune animals from earlier waves are replaced by naïve youngstock; favourable weather patterns for Culicoides activity and high densities of susceptible hosts in western Germany further facilitate explosive local transmission when virus is re‑introduced or persists at low levels. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses from earlier re‑circulation episodes (e.g. 2019) show that circulating SBV strains remain highly similar (≈99–100% nucleotide identity) to earlier European lineages, suggesting that cyclic re‑occurrence is driven more by immunity dynamics and vector ecology than by major viral change; accordingly, this event is classified as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: Review – New event added because the 2022–2023 increase in SBV seroprevalence in German wild ruminants (from ~5% to ~40%) and associated high infection rates in Culicoides vectors indicate a large, recent re‑occurrence wave with substantial though incompletely quantified impact on ruminant populations. Classified as re‑occurrence (driven mainly by waning immunity and vector dynamics) rather than re‑emergence, since available data show little genomic change. Domestic livestock impacts are inferred rather than explicitly quantified, so experts should confirm whether this episode ranks among the top SBV emergence events by the chosen impact metrics.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
EPP.common.name: gonoccocus
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Humans (sexually active population in EU/EEA, including both MSM and heterosexual men and women)
Event.summary: From around 2008, EU/EEA surveillance began to record renewed increases in gonorrhoea notifications in many Western and Northern European countries after previous declines, with France and Portugal experiencing roughly six‑fold rises and Denmark and Ireland more than tripling reported cases by 2017. Through the 2010s, diagnoses rose across most EU/EEA states, driven by high rates among MSM but also marked increases among young heterosexual men and women, leading to more than 89 000 confirmed cases in 2017 and around 118 000 cases in 2019, the highest annual total recorded since EU‑level STI surveillance began. This multi‑country resurgence prompted intensified testing, partner notification and prevention campaigns as well as ongoing updates to European and national STI strategies, but incidence remained high until temporarily disrupted by COVID‑19–related changes in sexual behaviour and service access in 2020.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Behavioural changes including increases in partner numbers, condomless sex and use of geospatial networking apps; reduced fear of HIV due to effective antiretroviral therapy and wider availability of PrEP; high background prevalence of bacterial STIs in core networks; expanded use of highly sensitive nucleic acid amplification tests and dual chlamydia/gonorrhoea testing, which increased case detection; strengthened EU/EEA surveillance improving ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of multiple N. gonorrhoeae lineages, many with resistance to older antibiotics; however, no single novel strain or resistance mechanism uniquely defines this resurgence, so it is best characterised as a behaviour- and system-driven re-occurrence.
Review: Review – Added as a new high-impact event to capture the large, multi-country resurgence of gonorrhoea incidence across the EU/EEA culminating in record notifications in 2017–2019. Classified as re-occurrence (behavioural and system drivers, without a single defining novel strain) and linked to specific EU/EEA reports; should be retained among the top events, but details (country list and exact start year) may warrant further refinement with full access to surveillance datasets.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3314658/?utm_source=openai))

Internal mechanisms: Novel strain / genotype emergence (ON1 with a 72‑nt G‑gene duplication introducing additional O‑glycosylation sites and altered antigenic structure), followed by rapid lineage diversification and apparent fitness and/or immune‑escape advantages that allowed ON1 to out‑compete predecessor RSV‑A genotypes in most regions. Event.summary: With the introduction of stringent COVID‑19 non‑pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) in early 2020, RSV circulation collapsed in many countries: the usual 2020–2021 winter RSV season was largely absent in Northern America, Europe, parts of South America and Asia, and several African and Oceanian settings. As NPIs were eased and schools and childcare reopened, a delayed and often off‑season reappearance of RSV activity was observed from late 2020 into 2021, typically at lower or moderate intensity compared with pre‑pandemic winters. This globally linked episode of suppression followed by atypical, shifted‑timing epidemics set up unusually large susceptible cohorts of infants and toddlers for subsequent RSV seasons. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/pdfs/mm7029a1-H.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Broad implementation of COVID‑19 NPIs (lockdowns, stay‑at‑home orders, school and daycare closures, mask use, reduced travel and gatherings) sharply reduced contact rates and RSV transmission, while later relaxation of these measures and reopening of schools altered the timing and strength of resurgent epidemics. Internal mechanisms: No major new RSV genotype has been implicated; changes are best explained by altered human behaviour and contact patterns, together with accumulation of RSV‑naïve children who missed exposure during 2020, rather than by viral evolution. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/pdfs/mm7029-H.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. This event captures a clearly bounded, globally important re‑occurrence episode in which RSV activity was almost absent during the 2020–2021 winter and then reappeared in delayed, off‑season epidemics as COVID‑19 NPIs were relaxed. I standardised the continent label to “Northern America” to match the Country sheet and updated the source list to include key multi‑country and US surveillance analyses. Classification as ‘re-occurrence’ driven by external factors (NPIs and changed contact patterns) without evidence of a new genotype is appropriate; it should not be labelled inter‑continental emergence, because RSV was long endemic on all involved continents and imported cases were part of a single, globally disrupted episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Western Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Primarily mango and other tropical fruits (mango, citrus, guava, papaya) in smallholder and commercial orchards, but also a wide range of cultivated and wild fruit hosts across African agroecosystems
Event.summary: In 2003 routine field surveys on the Kenyan coast detected an unknown Bactrocera of Asian origin that was later described as Bactrocera invadens and is now synonymized with B. dorsalis, marking the first major establishment of this species complex on the African mainland following the earlier but eradicated Mauritius incursion. Within just a few years the fly spread rapidly through East Africa and into West, Central and eventually Southern Africa as well as archipelagos such as the Comoros, Mayotte, Madagascar and, after earlier eradication, back into Mauritius, being recorded from more than 30–40 African countries by the early 2010s. Across much of sub‑Saharan Africa B. dorsalis quickly became the dominant fruit fly of mango and many other hosts, causing substantial yield and quality losses, market rejections and new phytosanitary barriers, so that by around 2015 it was widely regarded as a permanent, high‑impact pest and management focus shifted from eradication to long‑term integrated control and quarantine.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Transcontinental introduction from Asia, likely via infested fruit from the Indian subcontinent, initiated the Kenyan coastal outbreak, and subsequent rapid spread across Africa was facilitated by extensive regional trade in fresh fruit, weak internal quarantine, year‑round availability of highly suitable hosts (mango, guava, citrus, papaya) and broadly suitable tropical to subtropical climates. Internal mechanisms: The invading populations shared typical B. dorsalis traits of very high fecundity, strong flight and polyphagy; genetic studies show limited differentiation and signatures of recent demographic expansion, indicating one or few founding events followed by rapid range expansion and high gene flow across Africa. Compared with pre‑invasion fruit fly complexes dominated by Ceratitis spp., the arrival of this invasive B. dorsalis lineage represented a major re‑emergence of fruit fly damage driven by biological invasion and, after the earlier Mauritius episode, constitutes a continent‑wide intra‑continental emergence into new African subregions.
Review: retain (modified): This event is correctly among the largest global emergence events for B. dorsalis, but the original entry mis‑classified it as the inter‑continental emergence and understated the prior African incursion in Mauritius. The event has been reclassified as a major intra‑continental emergence and re‑emergence within Africa following the earlier 1996–1999 Mauritius episode, sub_regions have been simplified to the four relevant UNSD African subregions, and countries have been expanded and annotated with example first‑record years using EPPO and regional syntheses. The narrative has been updated to acknowledge the Mauritius precedent and the role of both mainland and island invasions; sources remain appropriate and highly relevant. Flag for review to confirm the chosen 2003–2015 temporal window and country list capture the most impactful phase.

EPP.scientific.name: Maconellicoccus hirsutus
EPP.common.name: hibiscus mealybug
Host: Wide range of ornamentals and crops (especially Hibiscus spp. and other Malvaceae, plus major crops including citrus, cocoa, cotton and soursop)
Event.summary: Starting with its detection in Grenada in 1994, hibiscus mealybug caused severe damage to ornamentals, fruit trees and field crops and then spread rapidly north and south through the Lesser Antilles, reaching many eastern Caribbean islands, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, and jumping to Belize, Mexico and northern South America (Guyana, French Guiana, Venezuela) by the late 1990s. Internal mechanisms: Extreme polyphagy and high reproductive potential; inherent capacity for geographic range expansion in tropical climates; efficient local dispersal of crawlers by wind, animals and on contaminated plant material, allowing rapid build‑up and spread in newly invaded territories.

Event.summary: Cholera re‑emerged in August 2008 in Chitungwiza and high‑density suburbs of Harare, Zimbabwe, against a backdrop of economic collapse, water system failure, and health‑system breakdown. The epidemic rapidly expanded nationwide, affecting all 10 provinces and leading to approximately 98,600 reported cases and over 4,300 deaths in Zimbabwe, while cross‑border spread caused additional cases in neighbouring South Africa, Mozambique, Botswana and Zambia, making it one of Africa’s largest cholera epidemics in recent decades. Intensified international response, repair of key water and sewage infrastructure, cholera treatment centres, and seasonal decline in transmission led to control of the epidemic by mid‑2009, although Zimbabwe and neighbouring countries have since experienced recurrent smaller outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Severe deterioration of municipal water treatment and sewage systems; collapse of solid‑waste management; health‑worker shortages and lack of basic medicines; high HIV prevalence and malnutrition; extensive cross‑border population movements and trade. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of circulating seventh‑pandemic El Tor lineages in a region with past cholera outbreaks; while some antimicrobial resistance was documented, the magnitude of the epidemic is best explained by infrastructural and socio‑economic collapse rather than major genetic changes.
Review: retain – Robustly documented as one of the largest modern African cholera epidemics with nearly 100,000 cases and >4,000 deaths.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Zimbabwean_cholera_outbreak?utm_source=openai)) The original classification as an intra‑continental emergence was incorrect because Zimbabwe, South Africa, Mozambique, Botswana and Zambia had all reported cholera in previous decades; this has been corrected to re‑occurrence only.([wrc.org.za](https://www.wrc.org.za/wp-content/uploads/mdocs/1398-1-051.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Countries and sub‑regions remain appropriate and are retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio cholerae
EPP.common.name: Cholera bacterium
Host: Humans (communities across all 29 districts of Malawi, with high impact in peri‑urban slums and flood‑affected rural areas, and affected border regions in Mozambique and Zambia)
Event.summary: In March 2022, Malawi declared a cholera outbreak that initially affected a limited number of southern districts but rapidly expanded following tropical storms and cyclones that damaged water and sanitation infrastructure and displaced communities. By mid‑2023 the country had reported roughly 59,000 cases and around 1,770 deaths, making this the largest and deadliest cholera outbreak in Malawi’s recorded history, with transmission documented in all 29 districts and linked spread to neighbouring Mozambique and Zambia as part of a wider southern Africa wave. Intensified national and international response—including large oral cholera vaccination campaigns, expanded treatment capacity, and WASH interventions—eventually brought cases down, and by mid‑2024 Malawi declared the outbreak contained, though the broader regional upsurge and underlying vulnerabilities persist.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Severe tropical cyclones and flooding damaging water systems and contaminating wells; chronic underinvestment in WASH; population displacement and crowding in temporary shelters; overstretched health services due to concurrent emergencies (including COVID‑19 and polio responses). Internal mechanisms: Genomic studies indicate introduction of a newly imported late‑wave seventh‑pandemic O1 Ogawa 7PET lineage distinct from historical local strains (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence) combined with Geographic Range Expansion and Enhanced Transmission via widespread environmental contamination, enabling unusually sustained nationwide and regional spread.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-50484-w?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Malawi’s 2022–2023 outbreak (~59,000 cases, ~1,770 deaths) is the largest and deadliest in the country’s history and forms a key component of the 2021‑present multi‑country cholera upsurge in southern Africa, with documented genomic evidence of a newly imported 7PET lineage.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-50484-w?utm_source=openai)) Event type has been simplified to re‑emergence (driven by introduction of a new lineage and exceptional expansion) rather than re‑occurrence + re‑emergence, to keep types mutually exclusive in line with the general guidance. EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In 2004, chikungunya virus re‑emerged on the Kenyan coast (Lamu Island and Mombasa) after years of limited activity, then spread across the Comoros and other southwest Indian Ocean islands during 2004–2005. In 2005–2006 the same East/Central/South African lineage drove massive epidemics on Réunion (infecting roughly one third of the population, ≈200,000–260,000 persons) and large outbreaks in Mayotte, Mauritius, Seychelles, Madagascar and, slightly later, the Maldives, together totaling on the order of half a million cases. Transmission subsided by mid‑2006 as vector control intensified and susceptible populations were depleted, although low‑level circulation and sporadic cases persisted.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2006_03_17-en?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Drought conditions, water storage practices and rapid urbanization in coastal East Africa and the Indian Ocean islands increased household Aedes breeding sites, while intense human movement between Kenya and the islands enabled rapid seeding of new foci. Internal mechanisms: The East/Central/South African genotype acquired key envelope mutations (notably E1‑A226V) that enhanced replication in and transmission by Aedes albopictus, increasing epidemic potential in settings where this vector predominated and helping to explain the unprecedented scale of the Indian Ocean epidemics.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/214/suppl_5/S436/2632642?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Geographic scope and timing retained, but subregions corrected (removed incorrect “Western Africa” and nonstandard “Eastern Africa (island territories)” and restricted to Eastern Africa and Southern Asia). Emergence type recoded as re‑emergence only (no intra‑continental emergence) because affected territories all lie within already known African and Asian subregions. Source list pruned to keep Indian Ocean–focused WHO and JID articles; a Western Hemisphere–focused EID paper was dropped as less directly relevant.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Seeded by viruses from the 2004–2006 Indian Ocean outbreaks, chikungunya re‑appeared in India in 2005–2006 after roughly three decades of apparent absence, spreading to at least 16 states and causing about 1.3–1.4 million suspected cases in 2006 alone. From 2006 onward, related East/Central/South African lineage viruses caused major epidemics in Sri Lanka and the Maldives and then moved through parts of Indonesia, Malaysia and southern Thailand, where large outbreaks occurred in 2008–2009 after more than a decade without transmission. By around 2010, incidence had declined or become sporadic in many of these areas, but the virus established new endemic foci and left large cohorts with post‑epidemic rheumatologic sequelae.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2006_10_17-en?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of Aedes aegypti in tropical urban and peri‑urban environments, inadequate vector control infrastructure, and intense human travel within South and South‑East Asia facilitated rapid dissemination once reintroduced. Large, immunologically naive populations supported explosive transmission, especially in densely populated Indian states and major cities in Indonesia and Thailand. Internal mechanisms: Continued spread of the ECSA/Indian Ocean lineage, including viruses bearing E1‑A226V and related mutations, increased fitness in Aedes albopictus and may have enhanced transmissibility, supporting re‑emergence across a wide climatic range in Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4754000/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event narrowed to Asia only and extended through 2010 to capture the full South and South‑East Asian re‑emergence wave. Pacific island introductions (New Caledonia, Papua New Guinea, Yap) were removed from the country list and are treated separately in Oceania‑focused events. Emergence‑type flags were simplified to re‑emergence only: chikungunya was already known in Southern and South‑eastern Asia, and spread to new countries within the same subregions does not qualify as intra‑continental emergence under the project rules. Wikipedia and a Western Hemisphere EID paper were replaced with region‑specific WHO and peer‑reviewed sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In December 2013, autochthonous chikungunya transmission was first reported in the Western Hemisphere on the island of Saint Martin/Sint Maarten, where an Asian‑lineage virus caused locally acquired cases in residents without travel history. Over 2013–2014 the virus spread explosively throughout the Caribbean, with PAHO and CARPHA reporting several hundred thousand suspected and confirmed cases and some territories (e.g. Dominican Republic) recording hundreds of thousands of infections. By late 2014 transmission had declined in many islands, but the epidemic established chikungunya as an endemic arbovirus in the Caribbean basin and marked the first inter‑continental emergence of the virus into the Americas.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5137246/?utm_source=openai))

Seasonal conditions favorable for dengue transmission similarly promoted Aedes proliferation and chikungunya spread. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic was driven by an Asian‑lineage virus already well adapted to transmission by Aedes aegypti, without evidence of a major new mutation; the key mechanism was geographic range expansion with efficient transmission in permissive vector and host populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4624217/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Confirmed as the first autochthonous chikungunya outbreak in the Americas and therefore appropriately classified as inter‑continental emergence. The previous use of “first_detection” for this regional introduction was removed to avoid confusion with global first detection in humans (1950s East Africa). Geography (Caribbean subregion under the South America continent code) and timing are consistent with PAHO/ECDC documentation.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Sub.regions: Caribbean; Central America; South America; Northern America
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Following the 2013–2014 Caribbean introduction, chikungunya reached mainland South America in early 2014, with French Guiana reporting imported and then locally acquired cases and an estimated >16,000 clinical cases in Cayenne and surroundings. Over 2014–2016, autochthonous transmission was documented across most Central and South American countries and parts of Mexico, as well as small clusters of local transmission in Florida, USA; by late July 2016, the Region of the Americas had recorded roughly 2.9 million suspected and confirmed cases and nearly 300 deaths since the virus’s arrival. Co‑circulation with dengue and later Zika complicated diagnosis and strained health systems but also prompted major investments in Aedes control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5137246/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high Aedes aegypti densities in urban centers across Latin America, coupled with water storage practices, inadequate housing and vector control gaps, allowed chikungunya to follow pathways previously established by dengue. Rapid regional air and land travel facilitated dissemination from Caribbean foci into mainland countries, where climatic conditions and existing vector populations supported sustained transmission. Internal mechanisms: The same Asian lineage that seeded the Caribbean was the main driver of epidemics across mainland Americas; its traits supported efficient replication in Aedes aegypti but no single novel mutation was uniquely implicated. This event is best classified as intra‑continental emergence within the Americas following the initial inter‑continental introduction.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5137246/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retained as one of the highest‑impact events globally (>2.9 million reported cases across the Americas by mid‑2016). The continent field was cleaned (removal of duplicate “South America (including Central America and the Caribbean)” label), and the emergence type was recoded as intra‑continental emergence only, because the inter‑continental jump into the Americas is already captured in the 2013–2014 Caribbean event. Country list focuses on heavily affected mainland countries and the small but epidemiologically important Florida clusters.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans (pig farmers, abattoir workers), pigs (amplifying host); Pteropus fruit bats (reservoir, implicated epidemiologically)
Event.summary: From September 1998, a new syndrome of encephalitis and respiratory disease emerged among pig farmers in Perak and later in major pig‑farming districts of Negeri Sembilan and Selangor, Malaysia, and was traced to a novel bat‑borne paramyxovirus that had spilled over into intensively raised pigs. Movement of infected pigs disseminated infection between farms and across the border to abattoir workers in Singapore, ultimately causing roughly 265–276 human cases and more than 100 deaths. The outbreak was halted by mass culling of pigs, closure of affected farms, and strict movement restrictions, after which no further large pig‑associated human Nipah outbreaks occurred in Malaysia or Singapore.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid intensification and high density of commercial pig production, planting of fruit trees near pig sheds, and frequent movement of live pigs between farms and to Singapore abattoirs allowed repeated contact between Pteropus fruit bats, pigs, and humans. Internal mechanisms: host expansion from bats to pigs and humans, high viral shedding in pig respiratory secretions, and Nipah virus’s strong neurotropic and pneumotropic properties enabled efficient pig‑to‑human transmission and severe disease in humans.
Review: retain – correctly describes the first recognized human Nipah virus outbreak in Malaysia and linked cases in Singapore, with appropriate geography, timing, event typing (first/global emergence and first detection), and high‑quality primary sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Escherichia coli
Countries: Canada [2017-2018] (Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador)
Host: Humans (consumers of romaine lettuce and leafy greens, mainly in North America)
Event.summary: Between November 2017 and January 2018, Canada reported an outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 infections linked to romaine lettuce, with 42 confirmed cases in five eastern provinces, while the United States detected a genetically related multistate outbreak of STEC O157:H7 infections linked to leafy greens, with 25 cases in 15 states. Molecular subtyping showed that Canadian and U.S. isolates were closely related, suggesting a shared contamination source in romaine or mixed leafy greens distributed on both sides of the border. The episode ended after public health agencies issued advisories, product was withdrawn, and seasonal changes in supply reduced exposure, but it foreshadowed later, larger romaine-associated outbreaks caused by closely related O157:H7 lineages.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Concentrated production of romaine lettuce and other leafy greens in a few U.S. growing regions; likely contamination of fields or wash water with bovine fecal material; centralized processing and broad distribution of bagged salads; high consumption of raw romaine. Internal mechanisms: involvement of a strongly adapted STEC O157:H7 lineage closely related to strains that reappeared in subsequent romaine outbreaks, consistent with a re‑emergence pattern driven by a persistent environmental strain with good survival on plants and in water.
Review: review – Retain as a major leafy-green–associated O157 episode but corrected several issues. Restricted geography to North America/Northern America and removed speculative references to Caribbean/South America, since reported cases were confined to Canada and the United States. Simplified countries and timing to Canada and USA [2017–2018]. Also revised the event_summary to focus on the late‑2017 to early‑2018 cross‑border outbreak only (omitting narrative about the separate fall‑2018 romaine outbreak, which is represented elsewhere) and re-coded the event solely as re‑emergence (re_emergence = true, re_occurrence = false) to keep emergence categories mutually exclusive and emphasize the role of a persistent adapted strain.
