Event.summary: Following the onset of the COVID‑19 pandemic in early 2020, global influenza activity collapsed, but among the few influenza B detections almost all were B/Victoria-lineage and virological surveillance recorded no confirmed naturally occurring B/Yamagata-lineage viruses after March 2020.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7976381/?utm_source=openai)) During the 2020–2021 and 2021–2022 seasons, countries in East Asia, Europe, North America and Oceania that did observe influenza circulation reported overwhelming dominance of B/Victoria, while B/Yamagata remained undetected despite continued typing and sequencing.([who.int](https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/influenza-update-n-381?utm_source=openai)) By 2023–2024, WHO and national advisory bodies concluded that inclusion of a B/Yamagata antigen in seasonal vaccines was no longer warranted and recommended a transition back to trivalent vaccines containing only a B/Victoria component, marking a major reconfiguration of global influenza B ecology.([cdn.who.int](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/influenza/who-influenza-recommendations/vcm-southern-hemisphere-recommendation-2024/202309_recommendation.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=2c2cbebd_7&utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Non-pharmaceutical interventions against COVID‑19 (travel restrictions, masking, school closures and distancing) dramatically reduced influenza transmission worldwide and disrupted the usual reseeding of influenza lineages between hemispheres; differences in local timing and stringency of these measures, along with prior immunity and vaccine use, appear to have favored persistence and reintroduction of B/Victoria viruses while pushing B/Yamagata to extremely low, and possibly zero, effective circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7976381/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Pre‑existing antigenic properties and fitness of contemporary B/Victoria clades, together with B/Yamagata’s tendency to infect older age groups and its relatively antigenically stable vaccine strain, may have interacted with pandemic-era behavior changes to produce the first documented disappearance of an influenza B lineage in the genomic surveillance era, effectively re‑establishing a single-lineage influenza B population dominated by B/Victoria.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12325168/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review – updated sub-regions to remove unsupported 'South-eastern Asia' (no specific countries listed) and reclassified the episode as re-emergence, reflecting the lineage-level restructuring of influenza B (apparent disappearance of B/Yamagata and dominance of B/Victoria) rather than a simple re-occurrence of typical seasonal activity; descriptions now align more closely with WHO and national vaccine‑composition recommendations.

EPP.scientific.name: Hepatovirus A
EPP.common.name: Hepatitis A virus
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; South America; Northern America
Host: Humans, predominantly men who have sex with men (MSM), with some spread to other adults
Event.summary: Between mid-2016 and 2018, an unusual wave of hepatitis A outbreaks occurred across at least 22 EU/EEA countries and extended into the Americas, disproportionately affecting men who have sex with men (MSM), with over 4,400 outbreak-confirmed cases reported in Europe alone and hundreds of related cases in Chile, Argentina, Brazil, the United States and Canada. The outbreaks began with clusters at MSM social venues and events in Western Europe and spread through sexual networks and international travel, with molecular typing showing three closely related HAV genotype IA strains (VRD_521_2016, RIVM-HAV16-090 and V16_25801) shared between European and American MSM outbreaks. Intensified vaccination campaigns targeting MSM, sexual health messaging, and depletion of susceptibles gradually reduced transmission by 2018, though some countries in Latin America continued to report MSM-associated clusters into 2019.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High susceptibility among adult MSM in low- or medium-endemicity countries due to limited prior natural infection and incomplete vaccination coverage; dense sexual networks and large MSM gatherings (e.g. Pride events); international travel connecting European and American MSM communities; global HAV vaccine shortages that hampered rapid scale-up of targeted immunisation. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of specific HAV genotype IA strains capable of efficient person-to-person transmission via sexual and close contact routes, but without clear evidence of fundamentally increased virulence; overall pattern is best characterized as behavioral and immunity-pattern-driven re-occurrence rather than emergence of a new viral lineage.
Review: review – This represents a major, well-documented global outbreak wave among MSM (≈4,475 outbreak-confirmed cases in 22 EU/EEA countries plus large MSM-associated epidemics in Chile and other American countries) and clearly belongs among the highest-impact events. Classification as re-occurrence (rather than inter-continental emergence or re-emergence) is appropriate, since HAV was long established in all affected regions and no fundamentally new genotype emerged. However, the countries column uses a placeholder (“other EU/EEA countries”) and mixes European and American MSM clusters that are epidemiologically linked but sometimes treated as separate sub-episodes; there is also potential overlap with the Latin America MSM 2017–2019 event row. Recommend: (i) replacing the placeholder with the explicit 22 EU/EEA country list from ECDC; and (ii) agreeing at dataset level whether all MSM outbreaks linked to the three IA strains (Europe + Americas) should be merged into one global MSM episode (2016–2019) or kept as regional sub-events to avoid double counting. ([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/news-events/epidemiological-update-hepatitis-outbreak-eueea-mostly-affecting-men-who-have-sex-men-0?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012-2013]
Host: People who inject heroin (humans)
Event.summary: In 2012–2013, new clusters of injectional anthrax were detected among heroin‑injecting drug users in northern Europe, including the United Kingdom, Germany, Denmark and France, several years after the large 2009–2010 outbreak had subsided. These cases again presented with severe injection‑site soft‑tissue disease and systemic involvement, and genomic analyses showed close relatedness to the earlier Ba4599 lineage, indicating re‑introduction of similarly contaminated heroin into European markets. Targeted clinical alerts, intensified surveillance of severe soft‑tissue infections in PWID, and temporary disruption of implicated heroin batches were followed by a decline in new cases by 2013, though sporadic cases continued to appear subsequently.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3901468/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Renewed distribution of B. anthracis–contaminated heroin along the same or similar trans‑Eurasian trafficking routes; ongoing vulnerability of PWID populations and limited routine screening for rare injection‑related pathogens.
Internal mechanisms: Recurrence of the same or closely related B. anthracis genotype as in 2009–2010 suggests persistence or reintroduction from a contaminated production or transit node rather than de novo evolution, consistent with renewed exploitation of the heroin‑injection exposure route rather than appearance of a new strain.
Review: review – 2012–2013 cluster of heroin‑associated injectional anthrax in the UK, Germany, Denmark and France represents a smaller second wave related to the 2009–2010 outbreak. Event is retained but re‑typed as re‑occurrence only (same genotype and exposure route re‑introduced to previously affected subregions) with intra‑continental emergence set to No; wording in the mechanism/driver field was adjusted accordingly. Because this wave is closely linked to the 2009–2010 episode, consider merging into a single 2009–2013 European injectional anthrax episode if a coarser event aggregation is preferred.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3901468/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.common.name: Acinetobacter baumannii infection
Countries: Italy [2020-2021] (Rome Umberto I teaching hospital ICUs with MDR A. baumannii superinfections)
Host: Humans (mechanically ventilated COVID-19 patients and other ICU patients with CRAB or MDR A. baumannii infections and colonization)
Event.summary: During the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic (approximately late 2020 to 2021), a large COVID-19 hub ICU in the Milan area experienced a clonal outbreak of carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii among mechanically ventilated patients, with whole‑genome sequencing confirming closely related CRAB strains and prompting a tailored infection-control strategy that successfully reduced transmission. Concurrently, Italian ICUs including the Umberto I teaching hospital in Rome reported high rates of MDR A. baumannii colonization and infection among COVID-19 patients, with molecular studies documenting sustained clonal transmission across multiple ICUs from 2020 into at least 2022. These COVID-associated episodes represented a significant resurgence of CRAB and MDR A. baumannii in Italian critical care units superimposed on an already hyperendemic national background.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Overwhelmed ICUs due to COVID-19, prolonged mechanical ventilation, heavy empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic and corticosteroid use, staffing shortages, and disruptions to pre-existing infection-prevention programs all favored expansion of CRAB and MDR A. baumannii in Italian ICUs. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance (endemic CRAB and MDR A. baumannii clones carrying carbapenemase genes and multidrug resistance profiles), Enhanced Transmission (efficient clonal spread within and between ICUs, with environmental persistence and cross-contamination in high-acuity COVID-19 units), Re-occurrence (marked increases in incidence of established resistant lineages driven mainly by external pressures of the pandemic).
Review: review – Italian COVID-19 ICU CRAB/MDR A. baumannii episodes in Milan and Rome are substantiated by genomic and epidemiologic studies and are correctly coded to Italy (Southern Europe/Europe). Because these outbreaks involve surges of already-established resistant clones in the context of pandemic-related ICU overload and care disruptions, they are more consistent with re-occurrence rather than re-emergence; re_occurrence is therefore set to true and re_emergence to false, with other descriptors unchanged. The event is flagged for review to confirm treatment of these linked COVID-era outbreaks as re-occurrence within an existing hyperendemic context.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia trachomatis
EPP.common.name: Chlamydia
Sub.regions: Europe | Western Europe; Europe | Northern Europe; Europe | Southern Europe; Europe | Eastern Europe; Northern America | Northern America; Oceania | Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans – primarily men who have sex with men (MSM), with occasional bisexual men; infection type mainly anorectal and inguinal lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) due to C. trachomatis serovar L2b.
Event.summary: Around 2003, public health authorities in the Netherlands detected an unusual cluster of severe proctitis among men who have sex with men, which was confirmed as lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by a C. trachomatis serovar L2b strain that previously had been rarely recognized in industrialized countries. Subsequent enhanced surveillance and molecular typing showed rapid expansion of this L2b epidemic among MSM across multiple Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern European countries and then to North America and Australia over the mid‑2000s, with hundreds to thousands of anorectal LGV cases reported in large urban sexual health clinics. The outbreak was gradually brought under better control after targeted awareness campaigns, improved diagnostic testing for rectal chlamydia in MSM, and guideline‑based doxycycline treatment of LGV cases and contacts, though L2b‑LGV remains an established STI among MSM in many affected countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The resurgence was linked to dense international sexual networks among MSM, high‑risk sexual practices (e.g. unprotected receptive anal intercourse, group sex, use of sex venues), overlapping HIV and STI epidemics, and increased travel between major cities in Europe, North America, and Australia, which facilitated long‑distance spread of an LGV strain that had previously been rare in these populations. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses identified a distinct L2b variant of C. trachomatis responsible for nearly all investigated LGV cases in MSM during this epidemic, indicating Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence combined with Enhanced Transmission within specific sexual networks rather than introduction of an entirely new species to these regions.
Review: Decision: review. The LGV L2b epidemic among MSM in Europe, North America and Australia is correctly identified as a major, epidemiologically linked re‑emergence episode of C. trachomatis. However, the event was misclassified as an inter‑continental emergence, which conflicts with the instructions that new serotypes/manifestations of an already‑endemic EPP in a continent should be treated as re‑emergence rather than inter‑continental emergence. I changed inter_continental_emergence from true to false and retained re_emergence = true to reflect a novel epidemic strain expanding within existing C. trachomatis–endemic regions. I also corrected the country name to “Netherlands (Kingdom of the)” to match the Country sheet. The listed countries and sub‑regions (including Poland as Eastern Europe) and approximate timing are supported by multi‑country LGV reviews and outbreak summaries and are appropriate to retain; no additional LGV‑related emergence events of greater impact were identified that would displace this episode from a top‑10 list for this EPP.

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridioides difficile

Event.summary: In 2009, Australia confirmed its first isolation of epidemic C. difficile PCR ribotype 027 in a patient in Western Australia who had apparently acquired the infection overseas, followed by the first locally acquired 027 infection in a Melbourne hospital in 2010, signalling the local establishment of the hypervirulent lineage. Event.summary: Between the late 1990s and mid‑2000s, Asia saw its first documented cases and outbreaks of vancomycin‑resistant E. faecium, beginning with high‑level vancomycin‑resistant strains in Japan and then spreading to Korea, Taiwan and mainland China. By 1998–2004, tertiary hospitals in Korea reported nearly 100 VREfm isolates, mostly belonging to epidemic clonal groups, and from 2001 to 2005 hospitals in several Chinese cities isolated VanA‑type VREfm, indicating wider establishment. EPP.scientific.name: Staphylococcus aureus

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria meningitidis
EPP.common.name: meningococcus
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From late 1995, a pandemic wave of serogroup A Neisseria meningitidis subgroup III strains reappeared in Niger and neighboring Sahelian countries and, during the 1996 dry season, exploded into the largest recorded meningitis epidemic in the African meningitis belt. Across heavily affected countries including Burkina Faso, Niger, Nigeria and Chad, an estimated quarter‑million suspected cases and roughly 25,000 deaths were reported during 1995–1997, with some districts experiencing attack rates approaching 1% of the population and health systems rapidly overwhelmed. Widespread reactive A/C vaccination campaigns and the onset of the rainy season eventually curtailed transmission, but serogroup A remained endemic in the belt, leading to further cyclical epidemics until MenAfriVac and other control measures were introduced in the 2000s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Classic meningitis‑belt risk factors—hyper‑arid, dusty dry seasons, cool nights, household crowding, and poverty—combined with very low baseline immunity to serogroup A in large cohorts allowed explosive spread once the epidemic clone was established. Internal mechanisms: Regional re-expansion of a highly epidemic-prone serogroup A subgroup III/ST‑5 lineage, which had already been responsible for earlier 20th‑century pandemics, drove the exceptional scale of this re-occurrence without representing a new serogroup or host jump.
Review: review – Event correctly captures the enormous mid‑1990s serogroup A epidemic but needed geographic and temporal corrections. I (i) expanded the event years to 1995–1997 to reflect the documented start of subgroup III activity in 1995 and continued epidemic activity into 1997; (ii) added Nigeria, which contributed tens of thousands of cases and is consistently cited among the worst‑affected countries; and (iii) removed ‘Eastern Africa’ from the sub‑regions, as the listed countries lie in Western and Middle Africa. Classification as a re‑occurrence (rather than re‑emergence or inter-/intra‑continental emergence) is appropriate because both the species and serogroup A were long‑established in these subregions and the surge is mainly attributed to ecological and demographic drivers.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria meningitidis
EPP.common.name: meningococcus
Sub.regions: Western Asia; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Northern America
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2000-2001]
Host: Humans
Event.summary: During the 2000 Hajj pilgrimage in Saudi Arabia, an outbreak of invasive meningococcal disease due to an unusual serogroup W135 ST‑11 clone emerged among pilgrims and local residents despite A/C vaccination, with cases rapidly detected in Mecca and Medina and neighboring Oman. Over 2000–2001, this ‘Hajj clone’ was exported by returning pilgrims, their household contacts and, later, persons with no direct pilgrim link, causing around 300 cases spread across multiple European countries, North America and parts of the Middle East and prompting extensive chemoprophylaxis campaigns. The outbreak subsided after intensified rifampicin prophylaxis, revised vaccine recommendations requiring quadrivalent ACWY vaccine for pilgrims and close contacts, and the end of the Hajj season, but the clone went on to seed longer-term circulation of serogroup W ST‑11 lineages in Africa, South America, Europe and Oceania.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Mass gathering of over a million Hajj pilgrims from many countries, intense crowding in accommodation and transport, and close contact during rituals created ideal conditions for high‑density carriage and rapid dissemination, amplified by global air travel to home countries. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of a hypervirulent serogroup W ST‑11 clone—previously rare and considered a minor serogroup—featuring high invasiveness and transmission potential represents a clear clonal re-emergence of meningococcal disease, rather than first introduction of the species into new continents.
Review: review – Retain as a major event (first large global emergence of serogroup W ST‑11), but correct classification and geography. I removed the inter‑continental emergence flag because N. meningitidis (and even serogroup W) were already present in Europe and North America; the Hajj‑related cases abroad are best viewed as part of a single linked outbreak and a clonal re‑emergence, not first continental introductions. I also removed Africa from the continent list and ‘Northern Africa’ from sub‑regions, where no specific African countries were listed, and expanded the country list to include the nine affected European countries and Oman that are clearly documented in outbreak reports. Sources now focus on the primary Hajj W135 outbreak descriptions and WHO guidance.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria meningitidis
EPP.common.name: meningococcus
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From early 2009, a large serogroup A meningococcal epidemic swept across parts of Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and especially northern Nigeria, triggering what is often described as the worst meningitis outbreak in the region since 1996. Over the 2009–2010 season these four core countries together reported more than 13,000–80,000 suspected cases (depending on surveillance source) and around 900–1,300 deaths, with Nigeria alone recording over 9,000 cases and hundreds of deaths, and emergency vaccine stockpiles were rapidly depleted. Massive reactive vaccination campaigns and the arrival of the rainy season helped end the outbreak, which is widely regarded as the last major serogroup A wave in the belt before MenAfriVac mass campaigns were rolled out from 2010 onward.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The usual meningitis‑belt climatic pattern (very dry, dusty conditions), structural factors such as household crowding and poor access to early treatment, and gaps in pre‑epidemic polysaccharide A/C vaccination coverage allowed rapid build‑up and spread of susceptible populations, so that once the epidemic started it exceeded local vaccine and care capacity. Internal mechanisms: This episode represents another large cyclical resurgence of established serogroup A ST‑5/7 lineages rather than a novel strain, so the main drivers are ecological and demographic rather than new pathogen traits, fitting the definition of re‑occurrence.
Review: review – New major event added. A large serogroup A epidemic in 2009–2010, primarily affecting Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Nigeria, is consistently described as the worst outbreak since 1996 and is therefore clearly among the most impactful post‑1990 meningococcal events. It was missing from the original dataset. I classified it as a re‑occurrence (same serogroup A epidemic lineage in long‑affected belt countries) with no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence flags, and limited the country list to the four states universally recognised as the core of this outbreak.

Event.summary: Beginning in mid‑2022, France detected an unusual rise in severe neonatal infections due to a new echovirus 11 variant, with at least nine neonates hospitalized for sepsis‑like illness and hepatitis between July 2022 and April 2023, seven of whom died. By mid‑2023, additional severe neonatal E11 cases were reported from several EU/EEA countries including France, Croatia, Sweden, Spain, Italy, and the United Kingdom, prompting European and WHO alerts about a multi‑country event. The outbreak has persisted with fluctuating intensity, though increased clinical awareness, perinatal testing, and infection‑prevention measures in maternity and neonatal units aim to limit further severe neonatal cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10236930/?utm_source=openai))

Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of a new echovirus 11 variant associated with severe hepatitis and high case‑fatality in neonates; genomic studies indicate a distinct recombinant variant with apparent increased virulence/pathogenicity and possibly enhanced transmission in the perinatal setting. The multi‑country spread within Europe reflects both intra‑continental emergence of this variant and re‑emergence in subregions with prior E11 circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10236930/?utm_source=openai))

Event.summary:
Following the 2014 North American epidemic, several European countries documented increased EV-D68 detections in children hospitalized with severe respiratory disease, including Norway where about 11% of pediatric respiratory samples in one hospital were EV-D68-positive and two children developed severe AFM.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/rapid-risk-assessment-enterovirus-68-detected-usa-canada-and-europe-second-update?utm_source=openai))

During late 2014 and through 2015, France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden and Italy (along with Denmark and Germany reporting clusters of respiratory illness) all recorded EV-D68 circulation with smaller respiratory outbreaks and sporadic but severe neurologic cases, including the first recognized EV-D68–associated AFM clusters in Europe.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/microbiolspec.ei10-0018-2016?utm_source=openai))
By late 2015, European EV-D68 activity declined seasonally, but the region had transitioned from sporadic detections to a recognized pattern of EV-D68 outbreaks with associated AFM, preparing the ground for the larger pan-European AFM wave documented in 2016.

Drivers: increased clinician and laboratory awareness after the U.S. 2014 epidemic led to targeted EV-D68 PCR and sequencing in respiratory and AFM cases; school-term mixing and autumn seasonality favored transmission; and travel links with North America likely seeded introductions of the same or closely related clades.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/rapid-risk-assessment-enterovirus-68-detected-usa-canada-and-europe-second-update?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses showed European strains in 2014–2015 clustering with North American clade B1/B2 viruses and, in some locations, emerging B3-like lineages, consistent with rapid global dissemination of fitter variants that possessed enhanced respiratory tropism and, in a small subset of infections, neuroinvasive potential—supporting classification as re-emergence driven by novel strains with increased virulence/pathogenicity and enhanced transmission.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5792700/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Retain as the description of the initial European EV‑D68/AFM activity following the 2014 North American epidemic. The countries list has been expanded to include Denmark [2014] and Germany [2014], which reported EV‑D68 respiratory clusters during the same wave, while keeping Norway, the Netherlands, France, the United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden and Italy; sub‑regions and classification as re‑emergence remain appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers)
Event.summary: From the early 2020s, molecular surveillance revealed rapid spread of the novel variant IBDV genotype A2dB1b from its origin in East Asia into the Near East and North Africa, with first detections in Jordan and Lebanon in late 2023, followed by rapid establishment in the United Arab Emirates and evidence of related nvIBDV strains in Iraq. In parallel, Egypt reported nvIBDV A2dB1b in poultry flocks alongside existing vvIBDV strains, indicating further geographic expansion and leading to outbreaks characterized mainly by subclinical infection, bursal atrophy, and immunosuppression rather than high mortality. Ongoing circulation of these variants in the Middle East and North Africa has complicated control strategies based on classical and vvIBDV vaccines and raised concern about their long-term impact on vaccine performance and poultry health.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Trade in live birds and hatching eggs and regional integration of poultry supply chains between Asia, the Near East, and North Africa facilitated long-distance movement of nvIBDV; limited early awareness and diagnostic targeting of this genotype allowed silent spread before it was molecularly characterized. Internal mechanisms: The A2dB1b genotype possesses distinct VP2 antigenic signatures and is adapted to infect partially immune flocks previously vaccinated against classical and vvIBDV (novel strain/genotype emergence and vaccine escape), with a tendency toward subclinical yet strongly immunosuppressive disease (increased pathogenicity in terms of immune dysfunction rather than overt mortality), enabling re-emergence in regions where IBDV was already endemic and geographic expansion across Western Asia and into North Africa.
Review: review: This event is retained as the spread of nvIBDV A2dB1b into the Near East and North Africa, but the dates and geography were corrected using recent molecular surveillance: the wave now spans roughly 2021–2025, with nvIBDV first detected in Egypt around 2021–2023 and then in Jordan, Lebanon and the UAE from late 2023 onward, and Iraq added based on A2dB1b-classified sequences; Oman and Qatar were removed because current data primarily show other genotypes there. 'First_detection', 'intra_continental_emergence' and 'inter_continental_emergence' were all set to No so the episode is treated strictly as re-emergence of a new genotype in continents where IBDV was long established; the sources now cleanly support these corrections and should be reviewed by a domain expert for final confirmation.

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2009-2010]
Host: Humans who inject heroin (persons who inject drugs), exposed via contaminated heroin; the source animal reservoir is presumed to be livestock in heroin-producing regions outside Europe
Event.summary: In late 2009, clinicians in Scotland detected severe soft-tissue infections and sepsis among people who inject heroin, which were confirmed as anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis associated with contaminated heroin batches, marking the first recognized large cluster of injectional anthrax. Over 2009–2010, 119 affected heroin users were identified across Scotland, England and Germany (about half laboratory-confirmed), with a high case-fatality ratio, and molecular typing showed all isolates belonged to a single clonal strain contaminating the heroin supply. The outbreak waned by late 2010 after public health alerts, harm reduction messaging and depletion or removal of contaminated heroin batches, although sporadic cases and a later smaller multi-country wave in 2012–2013 demonstrated that this novel transmission route into a high-risk human subpopulation had not been completely eliminated.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Contamination of heroin during production or transit in regions where anthrax is endemic in livestock; globalized illicit drug trafficking that distributed contaminated product to multiple European countries; high-risk injection practices (“skin popping,” intramuscular injection into deep soft tissues) that create anaerobic conditions favorable for toxin production. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by a single clonal strain (e.g., Ba4599, Trans-Eurasian clade) without clear evidence of enhanced virulence compared with classical zoonotic strains; the public health importance lies in host expansion into people who inject drugs and the emergence of a new clinical presentation, not in a new genotype or geographic range.
Review: Decision: retain (but mark for thematic review). Rationale: This entry represents the defining, largest-ever outbreak of injectional anthrax globally (≈120 affected heroin users in Scotland, England and Germany) and is widely cited as a novel anthropogenic manifestation of B. anthracis infection in a new human risk group. I corrected the countries field to list “United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2009-2010]; Germany [2009-2010]” and removed the subnational “England” label, while keeping the sub-region coding (Northern Europe; Western Europe) consistent with the UNSD country list. Event-type as re-emergence (host expansion/new clinical form) without intra- or inter-continental emergence remains appropriate. Because this episode is dominated by human cases but ultimately originates in animal-derived contamination, it should be cross-checked against the separate human-host anthrax sheet for consistency.

EPP.scientific.name: Betaarterivirus suid 1
EPP.common.name: PRRSV, Blue-ear pig disease
Sub.regions: Asia | Eastern Asia; Asia | South-eastern Asia
Host: Domestic pigs (breeding and grower-finisher herds) in commercial and smallholder systems
Event.summary: Following its emergence in China in 2006, highly pathogenic PRRSV-2 spread into neighbouring East and South‑East Asian countries beginning around 2007, with early severe outbreaks reported in Viet Nam and subsequently in other Indochina countries. Between 2007 and 2011 multiple countries in the Greater Mekong and broader South‑East Asian region—including Viet Nam, Lao PDR, Cambodia and Thailand—experienced large HP‑PRRSV epidemics with high pig mortality, substantial numbers of outbreaks (e.g. over 500 outbreaks in Viet Nam in 2010) and major economic losses. After these epidemic waves, HP‑PRRSV became entrenched in regional pig populations, with continued circulation and localized outbreaks reported in several South‑East Asian countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intense regional trade and movement of pigs and pig products among China and South‑East Asian countries, informal cross‑border movements, rapid growth of pig production in the Mekong region, and gaps in veterinary services and biosecurity facilitated geographic spread. Internal mechanisms: dissemination of the Chinese HP‑PRRSV-2 lineage into new sub‑regions represented geographic range expansion of this highly virulent variant, with phylogenetic studies indicating multiple introductions and subsequent diversification into distinct HP‑PRRSV clades in Thailand, Lao PDR, Cambodia and Viet Nam; these changes reflect both enhanced transmission and ongoing viral evolution within an already highly pathogenic background. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0021997515003370?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia mallei
EPP.common.name: Malleus (glanders)
Host: Equids (horses); dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius) in Bahrain
Event.summary: Around 2010–2011, glanders was detected in equids in Kuwait and Bahrain, countries that had been regarded as free of the disease for decades despite its presence elsewhere in the Middle East. In Kuwait, surveillance initiated in 2010 identified infected horses and led to culling of positives, with the last confirmed case reported in December 2010. In Bahrain, an outbreak that began in April 2010 in horses imported via Kuwait resulted in multiple equine cases and, during a 2011 recrudescence in the same region, a total of about 50 horses and at least one dromedary camel testing positive for B. mallei. Intensive test-and-slaughter programmes, quarantine of affected premises and strict restrictions on equine imports were implemented, enabling both countries later to regain official freedom from glanders.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of horses from endemic areas (notably Syria and Pakistan) through regional trade and movement for racing and leisure, coupled with inadequate pre-import testing and quarantine prior to 2010, appears to have seeded the Kuwait and Bahrain outbreaks; high-value horses kept in dense stable environments amplified transmission once infection was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses showed that strains from Bahrain’s horses and the infected camel were closely related to the UAE 2004 Dubai 7 strain but clustered into at least two distinct lineages, suggesting multiple introductions. The documented natural infection of a dromedary camel, with lesions indistinguishable from those in horses, highlights host expansion/spillover during this outbreak and justifies classification as re-emergence involving host-range expression of an established equine lineage.
Review: review – Event retained but re-dated and merged. Year span changed from 2008–2010 to 2010–2011 to match WOAH and regional reports indicating that Kuwait’s investigation programme and positive cases occurred in 2010 and Bahrain’s large outbreaks with camel involvement occurred in 2010–2011. Countries are now listed as Kuwait [2010] and Bahrain [2010–2011], and the camel spillover is included in this single multi-host, multi-country episode as per the project’s guidance on linked events. Intra_continental_emergence is set to No (glanders was already present in Western Asia), while re_emergence is kept Yes to reflect the host expansion to camels and the presence of at least two distinct B. mallei strain clusters in Bahrain.

EPP.scientific.name: Canine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Canine distemper virus, CDV
Sub.regions: Central Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Europe
Host: Caspian seal (Pusa caspica)
Event.summary: Beginning with a mass mortality in 1997 and followed by larger epizootics in 2000 and 2001, CDV emerged as a major cause of death in Caspian seals, with thousands of animals found dead along the coasts of Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, Iran and the Russian Federation. The 2000 event was characterized by acute respiratory and neurological disease, widespread CDV infection confirmed by serology and RT‑PCR, and mortality affecting a large proportion of hauled‑out seals across the basin. Outbreaks subsided after 2001 as immediate susceptible cohorts were removed, but CDV has since been recognized as an ongoing conservation threat to this endemic marine mammal, with sporadic deaths and concern about future die‑offs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High seal aggregation at breeding and molting haul‑outs promoted intense transmission once CDV was introduced; possible nutritional stress and contaminant burdens (e.g. organochlorines such as PCBs and DDTs) may have compromised immunity and increased mortality; proximity to coastal dog and carnivore populations likely provided the initial spillover route. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a terrestrial CDV lineage into a naïve marine mammal population, with a distinct Caspian strain detected from 1997 onward; high viral transmissibility in dense moulting aggregations and age structure effects led to repeated mass mortality events, consistent with re‑emergence in a new host rather than first emergence at the animal‑system level.
Review: review - Retain and correct. This multi-year, multi-country series of epizootics caused CDV-attributed mortality in the thousands (>10,000 seals estimated dead in 2000) and is clearly among the most impactful CDV emergence events since 1990. Updated 'continent' from 'Asia' to 'Asia; Europe' because the affected coasts span Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan (Central Asia), Azerbaijan and Iran (Western Asia), and the Russian Federation (Eastern Europe) under the UNSD scheme. To respect the event-type rule that only inter-/intra-continental emergence can co-occur with re_emergence, set 're_occurrence' to false and retained 're_emergence = true', reflecting sustained host expansion of CDV into Caspian seals across recurrent die-offs.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Carp edema virus
EPP.common.name: CEV
Host: Farmed common carp; ornamental koi carp in pond and garden systems
Event.summary: From 2013 onward, CEV-associated disease outbreaks were recognised in common carp and koi on Czech farms, with retrospective and prospective testing confirming virus circulation in Central European carp culture. In 2013–2014, Austria reported koi sleepy disease in koi and common carp from pond systems, while 2013–2015 surveillance in Poland documented multiple CEV-positive outbreaks and revealed substantial viral diversity; Slovakia then confirmed its first CEVD case in 2019. Together, these linked epizootics caused significant mortalities in pond-reared carp across Central and Eastern Europe and established CEV as an important transboundary disease in major regional carp-producing countries.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/tbed.12293?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of pond-based carp aquaculture in Central and Eastern Europe increased host density and stress; regional trade in stocking material and broodstock, often via Czech and Polish hatcheries, dispersed CEV among farms and across borders; seasonal temperature patterns in spring and autumn favored outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Genetic studies identified multiple CEV genogroups in Poland and neighbouring countries, including a divergent lineage (genogroup III) found only in common carp, indicating viral diversification within Europe; nonetheless, because these are first detections in the Eastern Europe subregion, they are classified as intra‑continental emergence rather than re‑emergence.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27453481/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review. Country timings for Czechia and Slovakia were incorrect in the original row; these have been aligned with first-confirmed CEVD cases (Czechia from 2013, Slovakia 2019) and the event period adjusted to 2013–2019. The episode is best described as intra‑continental emergence into the previously unaffected Eastern Europe subregion; re_emergence was therefore set to false, with viral diversification retained as part of the mechanism rather than as a separate emergence type.

EPP.scientific.name: Classical swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: Hog cholera virus, CSFV
Host: Domestic pigs (backyard and commercial herds)
Event.summary: After roughly two decades without recognised cases, Cuba reported re‑emergence of classical swine fever in 1993, with virus introduction into commercial and backyard pigs leading to an epizootic that became endemic and generated several hundred recorded outbreaks nationwide between 1993 and 1997. From this focus, CSF spread to neighboring Haiti in 1996 and to the Dominican Republic in 1997, where more than two hundred outbreaks were reported in 1998, causing high mortality in smallholder herds and prompting regional trade restrictions and concern about spread toward the mainland Americas. Control relied on intensive vaccination, stamping‑out in affected foci, and movement controls, which progressively reduced outbreak numbers but did not fully eliminate CSF, leaving the virus endemic in parts of the Caribbean.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Host: Cattle; domestic small ruminants to a lesser extent; wild red deer (Cervus elaphus), fallow deer (Dama dama) and mouflon (Ovis orientalis musimon)
Event.summary: In autumn 2022, epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 8 closely related to the Tunisian 2021 EHDV‑8 TUN 2021 strain was detected for the first time in Europe in cattle in Sardinia and Sicily (Italy) and in southern Spain, marking the first incursion of EHD into European livestock and wildlife. During 2022–2023 the same EHDV‑8 lineage spread widely across mainland Spain, into neighboring regions of Portugal and southern France and into mainland Italy, causing numerous outbreaks in cattle herds with fever, oral lesions, edema, milk drop and occasional deaths, as well as significant mortality and clinical disease in European red deer, fallow deer and mouflon. By late 2023 the disease had affected all regions of mainland Spain and multiple regions in Portugal, France and Italy, with control responses including movement restrictions and accelerated development and deployment of inactivated EHDV‑8 vaccines; activity continued into 2024 and beyond, raising concern that EHD may become endemic in parts of southern and western Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely wind‑borne dispersal of infected Culicoides midges across the Mediterranean from North Africa into southern Europe, in the context of a warming climate and shifting vector distributions, followed by dense livestock networks and game‑estate management practices that facilitated virus amplification and within‑continent spread between Italy, Spain, Portugal and France. Internal mechanisms: Inter‑continental emergence and rapid geographic range expansion of the EHDV‑8 TUN 2021 lineage into naïve European cattle and cervid populations, with marked pathogenicity in both domestic and wild hosts, alongside rapid development and deployment of new inactivated EHDV‑8 vaccines that may influence future viral evolution and disease dynamics.
Review: Review – classification was adjusted by setting first_detection to No (global first detection predates this event) while retaining inter_continental_emergence as Yes to reflect the first occurrence of EHDV in Europe and intra_continental_emergence as Yes to capture subsequent spread from initial foci in Southern Europe (Sardinia, Sicily, Andalusia) into Western Europe (France). The event is clearly one of the most impactful in the history of EHD, with multi‑country spread, severe cattle and wildlife disease, and major regulatory and vaccination responses, and should be retained as a cornerstone emergence episode.

EPP.common.name: FMDV, Aphthovirus
Countries: Brazil (notably Rio Grande do Sul State) [2000-2001]
Host: Cattle, pigs, sheep, and other domestic ruminants and swine

Through coordinated regional control—mass vaccination, movement controls, and surveillance—countries progressively contained the outbreaks, regained FMD‑free status over subsequent years, and incorporated lessons learned into updated regional eradication strategies.

Internal mechanisms: introduction of at least two distinct FMDV type O viruses into the Southern Cone, with efficient transmission in naïve or partially vaccinated cattle populations; these introductions represented re‑emergence of epidemic strains in previously controlled zones rather than new serotypes, but their high transmissibility in large, concentrated cattle systems amplified impact.

Event.summary: Beginning in 2013, FMDV serotype O, topotype ME-SA, lineage Ind‑2001d was detected in Libya after emerging from the Indian subcontinent and Middle East; over the following two years closely related viruses spread westward across the Maghreb. Event.summary: In 1994, a novel H1N2 swine influenza A virus emerged in pigs in the United Kingdom, generated by reassortment between human seasonal H1N1 and existing European swine H3N2 and avian-like H1N1 lineages and causing outbreaks of respiratory disease in pig herds. Over the late 1990s and early 2000s, this reassortant H1N2 lineage spread widely across western, northern and parts of southern and eastern Europe, becoming detectable in pigs in countries including France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Italy, Spain, Denmark, Sweden, Czechia and Poland and co-circulating with avian-like H1N1 and human-like H3N2. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence via reassortment between human seasonal H1N1 and existing European swine H3N2 and avian-like H1N1 lineages produced a new H1N2 virus with human-origin HA and NA and internal genes from established swine lineages, representing a clear re-emergence event driven by genetic innovation rather than introduction of influenza A into a naïve host system.

This event correctly captures the emergence of European H1N2 SIV in UK pigs in 1994 and its spread across much of western and northern Europe, supported by ECDC and EID data on the UK origin and subsequent endemic establishment in continental Europe and by seroprevalence data from multi-country surveys in 2002–2003.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/swine-influenza/factsheet?utm_source=openai)) The classification as re-emergence (a novel reassortant genotype within an already SIV-endemic continent) and the decision not to label this as intra- or inter-continental emergence are consistent with the project rule that new serotypes or manifestations in regions where the organism is already present should be treated as re-emergence. EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Host: Domestic and wild European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event.summary: In 2010, a new pathogenic lagovirus variant, later designated Lagovirus europaeus GI.2 (RHDV2), was first identified during rabbit haemorrhagic disease outbreaks in domestic rabbits in France, where it caused high mortality despite vaccination against classical RHDV. Over 2011–2013 the virus spread explosively through Iberia (Spain, Portugal), Italy, the Netherlands, the UK, and other European countries, and by 2013–2014 it had reached several Atlantic islands including the Azores and Canary Islands, causing large die-offs in both farmed and wild rabbits. By about 2014–2015, RHDV2 had become widely established across Europe and many island systems, partially or fully replacing classical RHDV (GI.1) as the dominant cause of rabbit haemorrhagic disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive rabbit production and trade, movement of live rabbits and rabbit products, high hunting and translocation pressure in wild rabbit populations, and dense, interconnected European rabbit metapopulations facilitated rapid geographic spread on the continent and to offshore islands. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel genotype (GI.2/RHDV2) with distinct antigenic properties and partial vaccine escape relative to GI.1, increased ability to infect younger rabbits, and evidence of recombination with non-pathogenic lagoviruses likely enhanced its fitness and allowed it to outcompete endemic GI.1 strains. Mechanisms include novel strain/genotype emergence, enhanced transmission, and geographic range expansion inherent to the lineage.
Review: review – Corrected event-type coding so this early multi-country European wave of GI.2/RHDV2 is treated solely as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by a new genotype, rather than as first/global emergence, first detection and intra-continental emergence. EPP.common.name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)

Host: Domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) in commercial and backyard systems; occasional wild/feral rabbits
Event.summary: In February 2015, RHDV2 was first reported in Africa during severe outbreaks in commercial rabbit farms in Kairouan, Tunisia, where it caused high mortality and major economic losses, and molecular data showed multiple introductions of GI.2-like strains from Europe. Over the next several years genetically related viruses were detected in North African countries including Morocco, Algeria and Egypt, and by 2015–2020 RHDV2 had appeared in multiple West African nations such as Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria and Senegal, where large outbreaks—most notably the 2019 epidemic in Ghana and the 2020 wave in Nigeria—devastated rapidly growing rabbit industries. By 2022, RHDV2 had also been confirmed in South Africa, with outbreaks in wild and domestic lagomorphs, indicating that the new genotype had become established across several African subregions with recurrent, often high-mortality production losses rather than remaining a series of isolated incursions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: importation of live rabbits and rabbit genetic stock from Europe and Asia, movement of rabbit meat and byproducts into coastal West African port cities, rapid expansion of semi-intensive rabbit production as a protein source, and limited biosecurity in smallholder and peri-urban farms facilitated introduction and onward spread. Internal mechanisms: introduction and onward dissemination of the globally successful GI.2 genotype with high transmissibility, broader age susceptibility, and partial vaccine escape relative to earlier GI.1-based vaccines, together with largely naïve African rabbit populations, underpinned severe production losses. Mechanisms include novel genotype-driven geographic range expansion, enhanced transmission, and, in some countries, further diversification via recombination documented in African RHDV2 genomes.
Review: review – Updated the time span from 2015–2019 to 2015–2022 and corrected several country-specific first-detection windows (e.g. Nigeria from 2017–2019 to 2020–2021, Senegal to 2020, South Africa to 2022, Algeria to 2018–2021, Tunisia to 2015–2018) in line with WOAH and recent outbreak reports. Re-coded the episode as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by the GI.2 genotype in an already RHD-affected continent, removing previous inter- and intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence flags to comply with the event-type definitions; the event should be retained but remains flagged for expert review of exact country-year ranges.

EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Sub.regions: Eastern Europe; Central Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Asia
Host: Domestic cattle
Event.summary: From 2017 onwards, molecular surveillance in Russia and Kazakhstan identified multiple vaccine‑like recombinant LSDV strains emerging in cattle populations that had been vaccinated with live‑attenuated capripox vaccines. These recombinant viruses caused field outbreaks and then spread eastward, with related genotypes later detected in parts of Asia including western China and Mongolia during the first local LSD incursions. Control measures in affected countries were progressively adjusted, including review of vaccine strains and strategies, as outbreaks linked to these recombinants were brought under better control by around 2020.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive use of live‑attenuated capripox vaccines in settings with concurrent circulation of field strains created ecological conditions favorable for recombination, while large cattle populations and imperfect vaccination coverage allowed onward spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via recombination between vaccine and field LSDV strains led to multiple distinct vaccine‑like recombinant lineages with field‑virus behavior; these represented genuine viral re‑emergence with altered genomes and in some cases possibly modified virulence or transmission potential.
Review: review – Event retained as a distinct re-emergence episode driven by vaccine–field strain recombinants, but the sub-region list was expanded to include Eastern Asia because recombinant-derived strains seeded initial outbreaks in western China and Mongolia. Emergence type remains correctly set to re-emergence (novel genotypes) without marking additional intra-/inter-continental spread, which is handled in separate geographic events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Host: Domestic cattle
Event.summary: After several years without EU cases following successful control of the Balkan outbreaks, LSDV reappeared in 2025 with a first case reported in Sardinia (Italy), followed shortly by outbreaks on mainland Italy, a major epizootic in France beginning in summer 2025, and detections in Spain later that year. The French outbreak caused significant trade disruptions and required large‑scale vaccination, movement restrictions and emergency response measures over roughly eight months. By early 2026, French authorities reported that the national crisis was largely under control and remaining regulated zones were being lifted, although surveillance and vaccination remained in place to prevent renewed spread in Western Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reintroduction of LSDV into previously free parts of Western and Southern Europe likely occurred via importation of infected animals or vectors, possibly linked to trade or movement of cattle or vector‑carrying goods under climatic conditions that allowed vector activity well into autumn. High cattle densities, intense trade within the EU and initial gaps in immunity in Western European herds facilitated rapid spread before emergency vaccination scaled up. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence suggests involvement of strains related to recombinant and field lineages circulating in Asia and eastern Europe; the event is best characterized as re‑emergence in a previously cleared region and intra‑continental emergence into new European subregions, with viral traits sufficient for efficient transmission via European vector species but without clear proof of substantially increased virulence.
Review: review – Retained as a major re-emergence and intra-continental emergence event in Western and Southern Europe (Italy, France, Spain) starting in mid‑2025, consistent with WOAH and EU/Swiss summaries. The source list was revised to prioritise WOAH, EFSA, EU and UK official outbreak assessments plus detailed French press reports, and to remove reliance on Wikipedia for this recent episode. Emergence typing as both intra-continental emergence (new European subregions) and re-emergence (return to a previously cleared continent) is justified.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Pastoral cattle herds and wild bovids (notably African buffalo and antelopes) in the southern Sudan ecosystem and contiguous areas of Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia
Event.summary: From 1993 to the late 1990s, classic rinderpest persisted in the southern Sudan ecosystem and neighbouring pastoral areas of Uganda, Kenya and western Ethiopia, forming one of the last major African reservoirs of virulent lineage‑1 virus. Widespread outbreaks in cattle and associated wildlife occurred in southern Sudan and Karamoja (Uganda) in 1993–1995, with further activity in border districts of Kenya and Ethiopia, before intensive control efforts reduced incidence. The final laboratory‑confirmed outbreak in this ecosystem was recorded near Torit in what is now South Sudan in 1998, after which no further confirmed rinderpest occurred, paving the way for verification of eradication in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Protracted civil conflict in southern Sudan, insecurity in parts of Uganda and Kenya, and very limited state presence severely constrained veterinary services, vaccination coverage and disease reporting. Large, mobile pastoral herds moved across porous borders with little control, sustaining transmission in an ecological “southern Sudan axis” even as other African regions became free. Only with the introduction of community‑based animal health workers, targeted vaccination in high‑risk corridors and improved surveillance under PARC/PACE and GREP was this reservoir finally extinguished. Internal mechanisms: Virological data indicate circulation of established lineage‑1 rinderpest viruses rather than a novel strain; the episode is thus characterized as re-occurrence of classic rinderpest maintained by conflict and pastoral ecology rather than re-emergence driven by virus evolution.
Review: review – This major East African focus, often described as the “southern Sudan axis,” was missing from the original output despite being identified in GREP analyses as one of the last two African reservoirs of classic virulent rinderpest. A new row has been added summarizing widespread outbreaks in southern Sudan and contiguous parts of Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia during 1993–1998, culminating in the final confirmed outbreak near Torit. Country list and time ranges are approximate and should be cross‑checked against national datasets; emergence-type classification as re-occurrence is supported by lineage‑1 virology and the strong influence of conflict and service breakdown.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus schmallenbergense
EPP.common.name: Schmallenberg virus, SBV
Host: Domestic ruminants, especially dairy and beef cattle and sheep, in previously exposed regions of western and northern Europe
Event.summary: Origin: After several years of very low clinical incidence following the initial 2011–2013 epidemic, Schmallenberg virus activity reappeared around 2016 in western and northern Europe, with renewed detection of SBV RNA and congenital malformations in calves and lambs in Ireland, Great Britain, France, Germany, the Netherlands and neighbouring countries. Development: Molecular sequencing of SBV from malformed lambs and calves in Great Britain in 2016–2017 revealed a second distinct genetic clade circulating alongside viruses closely related to the original epidemic strain, while bulk‑milk and serologic surveillance in Ireland and France documented substantial re‑circulation in cattle herds and the birth of congenitally affected offspring, indicating that waning population immunity and the accumulation of naïve youngstock had created conditions for a new wave of infection. Ending: By late 2017, reported clinical cases again declined and serologic data suggested increasing immunity in affected regions, with SBV returning to a pattern of low‑level endemic circulation and reinforcing the need for ongoing vector and serologic surveillance to detect future re‑emergence episodes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Key external drivers included the gradual replacement of highly immune adult animals from the 2011–2013 epidemic by susceptible youngstock, waning herd immunity over time, favourable climatic conditions for Culicoides midges in 2015–2016, and continued high densities of susceptible ruminants in intensive production systems. Internal mechanisms: Whole‑genome analyses comparing SBV sequences from the 2011–2013 outbreak with those from 2016–2017 in Great Britain and elsewhere identified a second distinct genetic clade, indicating viral diversification during the inter‑epidemic period; this genetic divergence, together with altered population immunity, supports classification of this episode as a re‑emergence driven partly by novel or diverged genotypes, even though clinical severity and manifestations remained broadly similar to the original epidemic.
Review: Retain – The 2016–2017 western/northern European wave is correctly captured as a major re‑emergence event with good support from genomic and surveillance data, and classification as “re‑emergence” (without co‑flagging re‑occurrence or inter/intra‑continental emergence) is appropriate given the identification of a distinct SBV clade during this period. No substantial corrections were needed beyond clarifying that affected countries are those with documented renewed circulation and congenital cases.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hantavirus, HCPS, HFRS
Host: Rattus norvegicus (pet and breeder rats); humans
Event.summary: Beginning in late 2016 and recognized in early 2017, health authorities in the United States detected Seoul virus infections among workers at home‑based rat‑breeding facilities in Wisconsin and Illinois, with subsequent tracing revealing additional human cases and many infected pet rats across multiple U.S. states. The investigation ultimately identified dozens of facilities in at least 15 U.S. states and Canada linked by rat movements, and multiple confirmed human HFRS cases, representing the first documented outbreak of Seoul virus associated with pet rats in North America. Quarantine, culling of infected rat colonies, trade restrictions and public guidance for rat owners were implemented and gradually stopped further human cases linked to the affected ratteries, though low‑level Seoul virus circulation in wild rats persists.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of the “fancy rat” hobby, interstate and cross‑border trade of live rats, limited biosecurity in small‑scale ratteries, and lack of prior awareness of Seoul virus risk in pet rats allowed widespread dissemination before detection. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and efficient transmission of Seoul orthohantavirus within dense pet‑rat breeding networks (host‑system expansion) constituted a significant re‑emergence in North America, with phylogenetic analyses linking U.S. pet‑rat strains to European Seoul virus lineages introduced via international trade.
Review: retain – The 2016–2017 Seoul virus outbreak in pet rats across the United States and Canada, with 17 confirmed human infections and 31 facilities identified as infected, is the first recognized large pet-rat-associated Seoul virus outbreak in North America and illustrates international host-system expansion. Intra_continental_emergence has been changed from 'true' to 'false' because Orthohantavirus (including Seoul virus in wild rats) was already present in Northern America; the event is best coded as re_emergence due to spread in a new managed host network. Despite modest case numbers, its cross-border scope and novelty justify retaining it.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hantavirus, HCPS, HFRS
Host: Oligoryzomys longicaudatus and related sigmodontine rodents; humans
Event.summary: From late October 2018 through early 2019, a large outbreak of Andes virus HPS centered in Epuyén, Chubut Province, Argentina, produced around 30–34 confirmed cases and 11 deaths, with one linked case detected in Chile. Detailed epidemiologic reconstruction and genomic sequencing showed multiple generations of person‑to‑person transmission within households and social gatherings, making it the largest documented human‑to‑human Andes virus outbreak to date. Aggressive contact tracing, prolonged isolation and quarantine of contacts, and community‑level control measures eventually halted transmission and ended the outbreak, after which HPS incidence in Patagonia returned toward its usual sporadic levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close‑contact social events in small communities, delayed recognition of the outbreak, and limited early infection‑control measures allowed transmission chains to establish; rural housing conditions and rodent exposure likely seeded initial human cases. Internal mechanisms: A particular Andes virus South lineage strain (Epuyén/18–19) with high viral loads in some patients was associated with efficient person‑to‑person spread (enhanced transmission/host adaptation), representing a clear re‑emergence of Andes virus with expanded human transmission potential, although sustained community transmission remained self‑limiting.
Review: retain – The 2018–2019 Epuyén Andes virus outbreak (≈30–34 cases, 11 deaths, clear multi-generation person-to-person transmission) is accurately summarized and widely regarded as the largest documented human-to-human Andes virus event. Geography (Argentina with one linked case in Chile), classification as re_emergence (enhanced transmission) without new continental spread, and sources (WHO DON, NEJM, CDC) are appropriate. This clearly belongs among the highest-impact Orthohantavirus emergence events.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus marinus
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis (Dermo disease of oysters)
Countries: Brazil [2013-2014] (Santa Catarina State, coastal farms around Balneário Barra do Sul and São Francisco do Sul)
Host: Introduced Crassostrea gigas (Pacific oyster in aquaculture) and native Crassostrea spp. along the Santa Catarina coast, southern Brazil
Event.summary: From about 2013 onward, histological and molecular surveys in Santa Catarina, Brazil’s principal bivalve aquaculture state, revealed Perkinsus marinus infections at high prevalence in native Crassostrea sp. and, at lower prevalence, in farmed Crassostrea gigas at sites such as São Francisco do Sul and Balneário Barra do Sul. These findings constituted the first confirmed reports of P. marinus infecting C. gigas in South America and documented southward spread of the parasite into a temperate farming region where C. gigas dominates production. Although recorded C. gigas mortalities were relatively limited and infections often light to moderate, the establishment of P. marinus in both native and introduced oysters raised serious concerns about chronic production losses and trade restrictions in Brazil’s main oyster-farming hub.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance movements of live oysters and seed for aquaculture, together with shared coastal water bodies and infrastructure, likely facilitated introduction and subsequent dissemination of P. marinus from northeastern Brazil or Mexican sources to Santa Catarina. Local temperature and salinity regimes in southern Brazil proved permissive for parasite establishment in both native Crassostrea sp. and introduced C. gigas. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence via host expansion and geographic range expansion within the South America subregion, as P. marinus successfully infected the non-native C. gigas and persisted in multiple oyster species, indicating robust adaptability and potential for chronic, production-limiting disease rather than acute die‑offs alone.
Review: review - The original row mixed northeastern Brazilian spread with later detections in Santa Catarina and gave a 2013–2019 time span. Here the event has been restricted to Santa Catarina, with timing (2013–2017) and locations aligned to Cunha (2016) and Leibowitz et al. (2019), which document high P. marinus prevalence in native Crassostrea sp. and lower prevalence in farmed C. gigas. 'Intra_continental_emergence' has been set to 'No' because these detections occur within an already affected UNSD subregion; the event is retained as a re-emergence episode marked by host expansion and southward spread and should be reviewed by a domain expert for final phrasing.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Poxvirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Pox viruses infection
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus, Bos indicus and crossbreds); water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis, limited)
Event.summary: In August 2015 lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) was confirmed for the first time in the European Union in cattle herds in Evros, northern Greece, following progressive northward spread from endemic foci in Africa and the Middle East. During 2016 the disease spread rapidly across the Balkans, affecting Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Serbia, Albania and Montenegro and causing thousands of outbreaks, production losses and extensive trade restrictions. Mass vaccination campaigns using live homologous capripox vaccines and movement controls from 2015–2017 progressively contained the disease, and by 2018 the Balkans were considered free of active LSDV transmission although the virus remained endemic in parts of Africa and Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of live cattle trade and informal animal movements between Türkiye and neighbouring Balkan countries; abundant blood-feeding arthropod vectors (biting flies, mosquitoes) favoured by warm, wet summers; limited prior immunity in Balkan cattle populations; initial gaps in vaccine supply and rollout; high-density dairy and beef systems facilitating spread. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of LSDV from Africa–Middle East into the European continent; available genomic data indicate that the viruses in south‑eastern Europe were closely related to Middle Eastern field strains without major adaptive change.
Review: Review – This event has been refocused to the 2015–2017 Balkan and EU epidemic only (first occurrence of LSD in Europe), with Israel and Türkiye now covered under the Western Asia event. The year span was corrected from “2012–2016” to “2015–2017”, continent simplified to “Europe”, and inter-continental emergence is retained as “Yes” because this represents the first establishment of LSDV on the European continent. Kosovo*, while epidemiologically affected, is not listed as a separate country because it is absent from the provided Country sheet.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: White spot syndrome virus

Event.summary: Origin: Around 1991–1992, intensive marine shrimp farms in coastal Fujian Province (China) and in Taiwan experienced sudden, pond-wide mortalities in penaeid shrimp, with histopathology and electron microscopy revealing a previously unrecognized large bacilliform DNA virus later named white spot syndrome virus (WSSV). Development: The outbreaks rapidly caused catastrophic losses in Chinese white shrimp and other cultured penaeids, with many ponds suffering 80–100% mortality within days, leading to collapse of major segments of the Chinese shrimp industry and the first detailed descriptions of white spot disease. End: By the mid‑1990s, WSSV was widely recognized as endemic in Chinese and Taiwanese shrimp aquaculture, and production partially recovered only after shifts in species, stocking practices and the adoption of improved biosecurity and diagnostics rather than true elimination of the virus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very intensive pond culture with high stocking densities, deteriorating water quality, and rapid expansion of shrimp farming created ideal conditions for amplification of a newly introduced virus; extensive movement and trading of live post-larvae and broodstock between hatcheries and farms facilitated farm-to-farm spread. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a highly virulent nimavirus capable of infecting multiple penaeid species; enhanced transmission via high viral shedding in water and cannibalism among shrimp; inherent capacity of the virus to persist in multiple crustacean hosts enabling establishment once introduced.
Review: Decision: Retain. This row correctly captures the earliest well-documented WSD outbreaks in Fujian (China) and Taiwan in 1992, with some reviews describing the onset as between 1991–1992. Country and subregion coding are consistent with the UNSD list, and classification as first global emergence (without a separate 'first detection' flag) matches the fact that WSSV appears to be a genuinely new pathogen in shrimp rather than a long-undetected agent.

EPP.scientific.name: White spot syndrome virus
EPP.common.name: WSSV
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (mainly Penaeus monodon, P. japonicus, Fenneropenaeus indicus and related species)
Event.summary: Origin: Following the initial emergence in China and Taiwan, WSSV spread in 1993 into shrimp farms in Japan and the Republic of Korea and, over the next few years, into Thailand, India, Malaysia, Indonesia, Viet Nam and the Philippines, primarily via movement of infected broodstock and post-larvae across East and South-East Asian shrimp-producing regions. Development: Between about 1993 and 1997, these countries experienced repeated, often nationwide waves of white spot disease with acute pond mortalities of 80–100%, causing collapse or severe contraction of intensive shrimp industries in several nations and reshaping regional aquaculture practices. End: By the late 1990s, WSSV was entrenched across most Asian shrimp-farming zones, and although large epidemics continued, producers adapted through changes in stocking density, species choice (e.g. increasing use of Litopenaeus vannamei), and implementation of basic biosecurity and diagnostic screening, converting WSSV from an epizootic to an endemic constraint.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid regional expansion and intensification of shrimp aquaculture; extensive transboundary movement of live shrimp broodstock and post-larvae with limited or no pathogen screening; poor farm-level biosecurity and water exchange practices that allowed virus to spread via canal and coastal waters. Internal mechanisms: High virulence and broad host range of WSSV enabling infection of multiple penaeid species and other crustaceans; efficient waterborne and oral transmission (via cannibalism of moribund shrimp) leading to explosive within-pond epidemics; likely selection of genotypes well adapted to intensive Asian pond conditions.
Review: Decision: Retain. The timing, geography and qualitative impact of the 1993–1997 Asian pandemic are consistent with major reviews: WSSV moved rapidly from China/Taiwan into Japan, Korea, Thailand, India, Malaysia, Indonesia, Viet Nam and the Philippines and caused industry-crashing losses. Continent and subregion labels are correct, and classification as intra‑continental emergence (spread to new Asian subregions) is appropriate. Note that other affected countries (e.g. Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Cambodia) are not listed but this does not change the ranking of this episode among the largest global events.

EPP.scientific.name: White spot syndrome virus
EPP.common.name: WSSV
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (mainly Litopenaeus vannamei and P. stylirostris)
Event.summary: Origin: In January 1999, WSSV was first detected causing white spot disease in farmed shrimp in Nicaragua, Honduras and Guatemala; within months it was found in farms in Panama and spread into major shrimp-farming areas of Ecuador, where by April 1999 it triggered an explosive epidemic. Development: Between 1999 and 2001 the virus disseminated rapidly throughout Central and South American shrimp industries (including the other listed countries), causing acute pond die-offs and, for example, an estimated 42% loss of production capacity in Ecuador alone (about 63,000 tonnes and US$280 million in the first year) and massive job losses regionally. End: By the early 2000s, WSSV had become endemic in much of Latin American shrimp aquaculture; Brazil and Venezuela initially remained exceptional by imposing strict bans on live crustacean imports, while affected countries rebuilt production via improved management, domesticated SPF stocks, and selective breeding for disease tolerance rather than eradication of the virus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-volume transboundary movement of live broodstock and post-larvae of L. vannamei and P. stylirostris from multiple Latin American sources with limited health certification; rapid expansion and intensification of shrimp farms in estuarine systems; weak early-warning and contingency planning for exotic viral diseases. Internal mechanisms: Highly virulent WSSV genotypes capable of causing nearly 100% mortality within 3–10 days post-onset; efficient transmission via water and carcasses that allowed entire farm clusters and coastal embayments to be infected during a single production cycle.
Review: Decision: Retain. This episode is widely recognized as one of the largest and most economically devastating WSSV pandemics, affecting most shrimp-farming countries in Central and South America from 1999 onward. The list of countries and timing (1999–2001) matches FAO and review sources; coding as an inter‑continental emergence into the South America continent (as defined in the project’s country list, including Central America) is appropriate. No changes to geography or classification were needed.
