Event.summary: Around 2007–2009, yellow fever virus activity surged in several South American countries, with intense sylvatic transmission in parts of Brazil and Bolivia and smaller human outbreaks in Paraguay and northeastern Argentina, accompanied by widespread non-human primate die‑offs. Human cases occurred both in rural forested zones and, in Paraguay, in and around the metropolitan area of Asunción, raising concerns about urban yellow fever re‑establishment for the first time in decades. Coordinated emergency vaccination campaigns, enhanced surveillance of human and primate cases and focused vector control in high‑risk municipalities curtailed transmission and prevented sustained urban cycles.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Deforestation, agricultural expansion and human encroachment into forest habitats increased contact with infected sylvatic mosquitoes and primates; movement of unvaccinated people between forested areas and towns infested with Aedes aegypti created opportunities for peri‑urban and limited urban transmission, particularly in Paraguay. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses indicate circulation of established South American genotypes; the episode is best characterised as re-occurrence with geographic range fluctuations of existing lineages rather than emergence of a distinct new strain.
Review: review – Kept as a multi-country South American episode because Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina experienced increased human cases and extensive epizootics; however, case numbers (on the order of hundreds regionally) are smaller than in the 1995 Peru epidemic, Brazil 2016–2018, Angola/DRC 2015–2016 or Sudan 2012. Event type has been corrected from re-emergence to re-occurrence (no evidence for intrinsic viral change), and the country name has been standardised to “Bolivia (Plurinational State of)” to match the provided list.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans; predominantly urban Aedes aegypti cycle with contribution from sylvatic reservoirs
Event.summary: In December 2015, yellow fever cases were detected in Luanda, Angola, heralding the country’s largest outbreak in 30 years and the biggest African epidemic since at least the early 1990s, which spread to many Angolan provinces and into urban areas of neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo. By late 2016, more than 7,000 suspected cases, 962 confirmed cases and almost 400 deaths had been reported across Angola and DRC, and viraemic travellers exported cases to Kenya, China, Morocco and other countries without seeding sustained local transmission. Massive emergency vaccination campaigns using standard and fractional dosing, combined with intensified vector control and global coordination under the newly launched Eliminate Yellow Fever Epidemics (EYE) strategy, eventually interrupted transmission and ended the epidemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid unplanned urbanization in Luanda and Kinshasa with high densities of Aedes aegypti, low vaccination coverage in many districts, intense intra‑African and international travel of unvaccinated workers, and limited global vaccine stockpiles all contributed to explosive spread and exportation. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses linked outbreak viruses to lineages previously circulating in Angola, indicating resurgence of existing strains; enhanced transmission resulted from dense human–vector contact and human mobility rather than documented increases in virulence or vaccine escape.
Review: retain – Confirmed as one of the largest and most disruptive modern yellow fever epidemics (≈7,334 suspected cases, 962 confirmed, ~393 deaths), depleting the global vaccine stockpile and directly triggering the EYE strategy; it clearly belongs in the top 10. Sub-regions have been narrowed to Middle Africa, reflecting that sustained transmission occurred in Angola and DRC, while Kenya, China and Morocco are correctly kept in the country list as imported cases without reclassifying the event as inter-continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: Plague bacillus
Host: Humans; peridomestic and wild rodents; fleas.
Event.summary: During the 1996–1997 transmission season, the southern African plague belt experienced a pronounced regional upsurge, including a large bubonic outbreak in Namwala District, Southern Province, Zambia, where roughly 267 human cases and 26 deaths occurred between December 1996 and February 1997, and major epidemics in neighbouring Malawi and Mozambique. Malawi reported an outbreak totalling about 582 cases and 11 deaths in 1997 across Nsanje, Chikwawa and Ntchisi districts, while Mozambique notified approximately 825 cases and 18 deaths the same year, with most cases clustered in Mutarara and other districts after years of lower activity. These concurrent epidemics in adjacent countries prompted WHO‑supported responses with intensified case‑finding, antibiotic treatment, rodent and flea control, and community risk communication, after which reported case numbers declined markedly in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High rodent densities associated with seasonal agricultural production, poor rodent‑proofing of grain stores and dwellings, and favourable climate for flea survival drove epizootics in the border regions of Zambia, Malawi and Mozambique, while limited access to health care and weak early surveillance allowed human outbreaks to grow large before recognition. Internal mechanisms: Investigations in Namwala and affected districts documented infection in multiple rodent and flea species but did not identify major new genotypes; the events are best interpreted as amplification and geographic spread of long‑standing plague foci under conducive environmental and socio‑economic conditions rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review: This row has been revised to (i) restrict the sub‑region to Eastern Africa, consistent with the UNSD classification of Mozambique, Malawi and Zambia; (ii) extend the event year to 1996–1997 to cover the Zambian Namwala outbreak that began in December 1996; and (iii) add Malawi, which experienced 582 cases and 11 deaths in 1997 and forms part of the same regional upsurge in the southern African plague belt. The event is still coded as re‑occurrence rather than intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or re‑emergence because all three countries had prior plague foci and there is no evidence of a novel lineage; however, grouping three national epidemics into a single regional episode is an analytical choice based on temporal and geographic contiguity rather than documented cross‑border transmission chains, and should be reviewed by a regional specialist.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Primarily mango, but also citrus, guava, papaya and many other cultivated and wild fruit crops (over 250 host plants documented in Africa).
Event.summary: In 2003, an unknown Bactrocera species later synonymised with B. dorsalis (B. invadens) was first detected on the coast of Kenya, signalling the start of a major invasion from Asia into the African mainland and rapidly damaging mango and other fruit crops. Over the following decade, the species spread quickly from East Africa across much of Central, West and parts of Southern Africa, becoming the dominant fruit fly in many mango-producing regions and displacing native Ceratitis species, with severe yield losses, increased insecticide use and trade disruptions. By the mid‑2010s, B. dorsalis was established across most of tropical sub‑Saharan Africa, with only some southern fringe areas remaining free or under transient incursion status, and it continues to cause chronic high infestation levels and high management costs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: repeated introductions from Asia (probably from the Indian subcontinent) followed by intense intra‑African trade in fresh fruit, weak phytosanitary controls, extensive plantings of highly suitable hosts (especially mango) and favourable tropical climates across large areas of sub‑Saharan Africa. Internal mechanisms: introduction of an invasive genotype within the B. dorsalis complex (historically described as B. invadens) with very broad host range and high reproductive capacity, leading to competitive displacement of native fruit flies and very rapid geographic range expansion into a previously unoccupied continent. (Summarised from Lux et al. 2003, Drew et al. 2005, African invasion syntheses and EPPO distribution data.)
Review: review – Event retained as the main Africa-wide mainland invasion episode but reclassified as intra-continental emergence only: it captures spread from initial African foci (post‑Mauritius) into additional African UN sub-regions (Middle, Western and Southern Africa). Inter_continental_emergence and re_emergence flags were removed because first continental occurrence is already represented by the 1996 Mauritius event, and this wave reflects subsequent within-continent expansion rather than reappearance in a previously known sub-region. The country list and approximate dates are broadly consistent with EPPO and regional reviews, but some southern fringe countries (e.g. Botswana, Eswatini) with more recent detections are not listed and could be added in a future refinement if judged among the top-impact events.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia prostrata
EPP.common.name: prostrate spurge, prostrate sandmat, blue weed, ground spurge
Host: Weed of anthropogenic habitats: wastelands, lawns, parks, gardens, fields, fallow lands, sidewalks, roadsides, railway embankments and river banks
Event.summary: Around 2012 Euphorbia prostrata was first recorded from the Almaty Region of Kazakhstan, marking its documented arrival in Central Asia and showing that this American species had reached a previously uncolonised Asian sub-region. By 2018–2019 it was found as a weed in anthropogenic habitats in Uzbekistan and by 2018–2021 it was newly recorded in several localities in the Russian Federation, mostly along railway rights-of-way and urban disturbed sites. These findings together document a coordinated eastward and northward expansion across Central Asia and into continental parts of Russia, where the species is currently assessed as an alien of minor impact but clearly increasing its range.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of transport infrastructure, urbanization and trade across Central Asia and the Russian Federation has increased movement of contaminated soil, road materials and plant propagules, facilitating long-distance dispersal of ruderal aliens. Irrigation schemes, parks and gardens provide persistently disturbed, watered microsites in otherwise harsh continental climates. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion through pre-adaptation to hot, dry, nutrient-poor and compacted substrates typical of anthropogenic sites, with enhanced transmission via persistent seed banks and accidental transport with gravel and railway ballast enabling stepwise spread along transport corridors.
Review: Review – Retain this episode as an intra-continental emergence, because it documents the first confirmed records in the Central Asia sub-region (Kazakhstan and later Uzbekistan) and new records in Russia, within continents where the species was already established elsewhere. I simplified sub_regions to 'Central Asia; Eastern Europe' (dropping the non-standard 'Eastern Europe – Russia') and removed re_emergence, which is not supported by evidence of strain change. The Botanica Pacifica paper plus POWO provide adequate support for timing and geography.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Cydia pomonella
EPP.common.name: codling moth
Host: Organic and integrated apple orchards (and other pome fruits) heavily reliant on CpGV-based biopesticides in southwest Germany and southeast France.
Event.summary: Around 2003, an organic apple orchard in southwest Germany reported serious codling moth damage despite repeated applications of commercial Cydia pomonella granulovirus (CpGV) formulations based on the Mexican isolate CpGV‑M, and similar failures were soon observed in France. Laboratory bioassays on larvae collected in 2003–2005 confirmed an at least 1000‑ to >60,000‑fold reduction in susceptibility to CpGV‑M compared with susceptible strains, marking the first documented field resistance of any insect to a commercial baculovirus product. Over 2003–2006, resistant field populations were reared and characterized (e.g. CpR/CpRR1 in Germany and RGV in France), and genetic studies showed that this "type I" resistance was dominant and largely linked to the Z sex chromosome, explaining its rapid rise and severe control failures in affected organic orchards.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Nearly two decades of intensive CpGV‑M use in European organic and low‑input orchards, often as the cornerstone control tactic, created strong selection pressure; high codling moth pressure in some orchards and limited rotation with alternative effective modes of action compounded this pressure. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of high-level resistance to CpGV‑M, with 1,000–100,000‑fold resistance factors; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – not applicable to the pest, though resistance forced selection and deployment of more virulent CpGV genotypes; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – emergence of resistant codling moth genotypes carrying a Z‑linked, dominantly inherited resistance trait (type I CpGV resistance) that sharply reduced mortality from CpGV‑M.
Review: retain – This event accurately captures the first documented field resistance of any insect to a commercial baculovirus (CpGV-M), originating in an organic apple orchard in southwest Germany around 2003 and shortly thereafter in France, with extremely high resistance ratios and clear evidence of dominant, Z-linked inheritance. The geographic scope, timing and classification as re-emergence (resistance-driven resurgence in previously well-controlled orchards) are well supported by primary literature and need no correction.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630735/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Obolodiplosis robiniae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia in urban plantings and street trees in southwestern France and Belgium
Event.summary: After initial detection in Belgium and then France in the mid‑2000s, Obolodiplosis robiniae populations built up dramatically in 2007 in parts of southwestern France, especially Dordogne and Gironde, where black locust trees experienced heavy galling and premature leaf drop. During the 2007 growing season, high densities of galls were reported in streetside and ornamental plantings, drawing attention from plant protection services and leading to targeted monitoring. By 2008, however, field surveys recorded a sharp decline in visible damage in the same areas due to high parasitism by the introduced parasitoid Platygaster robiniae, and the outbreak subsided to lower, more stable levels of infestation.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense planting of susceptible black locust in urban and peri‑urban landscapes, combined with the recent arrival of the gall midge and initially low levels of natural enemies, allowed rapid population growth in southwestern France; mild climatic conditions further supported multiple generations per season. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was reported, but enemy release followed by subsequent build-up of the specialist parasitoid Platygaster robiniae created a boom‑and‑bust dynamic, with the initial outbreak representing a re‑occurrence driven largely by ecological imbalance (low parasitism) rather than genetic change in the pest.
Review: Decision: review. The 2007–2008 outbreak and subsequent collapse of O. robiniae populations in southwestern France (Dordogne, Gironde) and previously infested Belgium is well documented by EPPO RS 2008/202 and associated national reports, and its classification as a re-occurrence (not a new inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because populations were already established in Europe. Country timing has been corrected so France is now listed as [2007–2008] instead of [2005–2007], aligning with EPPO’s account of first French records in 2007 and high damage followed by parasitoid-driven decline in 2008, while Belgium remains [2005–2007] to reflect earlier detection with confirmation and peak damage by 2007.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Spodoptera frugiperda
EPP.common.name: fall armyworm, "légionnaire d’automne"
Countries: United States of America (Florida, North Carolina) [2012–2013]
Host: Maize (Bt and non-Bt), primarily Zea mays
Event.summary: Around 2006, unexpectedly severe damage by fall armyworm was observed in Cry1F Bt maize in Puerto Rico, marking the first documented case of field-evolved resistance of S. frugiperda to a Bt maize event and leading to withdrawal of TC1507 maize there. During the early 2010s, subsequent monitoring and bioassays documented high levels of Cry1F resistance in fall armyworm populations in mainland USA (Florida, North Carolina) and in Brazil, with larvae surviving on Bt maize plants in the field. This resistance has persisted in Puerto Rico despite removal of Cry1F maize and contributed to reduced efficacy of single-toxin Bt hybrids across parts of the Americas, driving shifts to pyramided Bt traits and integrated resistance-management strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive and continuous planting of single-toxin Cry1F Bt maize hybrids (TC1507 and related events) in warm tropical and subtropical production systems with high fall armyworm pressure; inadequate refuge compliance in some areas; year-round cultivation enabling multiple pest generations. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – field-evolved resistance to the Cry1F Bt toxin (and cross-resistance to some other Cry1 toxins) mainly via changes in midgut receptors such as ABCC2 and reduced Cry1F binding, increasing larval survival and damage on Bt maize.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (retain, with modifications). Changes made: (1) Updated Event Year from "2006" to "2006-2013" so the row clearly covers the linked Cry1F resistance episode in Puerto Rico, southeastern USA and Brazil, consistent with reports of initial field-evolved resistance in Puerto Rico from 2006 onward and subsequent confirmations in Florida/North Carolina and Brazil around 2012–2013.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22537834/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Corrected continent and sub-region fields to follow the UNSD scheme: Puerto Rico is placed under South America | Caribbean, the United States under Northern America | Northern America, and Brazil under South America | South America. (3) Refined country-year annotations to Puerto Rico [2006–2008], USA [2012–2013], and Brazil [2013], which better matches the timing of documented resistance detections. Event-type classification as re-emergence (due to evolution of Bt resistance in an already established pest within its native continental range) and not as intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate and has been retained. Rationale: This is clearly one of the most impactful post-1990 events for FAW because it marks the first field-evolved resistance to a Bt maize event globally and triggered major changes in resistance management; it should be kept as a major re-emergence episode but flagged for the minor structural corrections above.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Spodoptera frugiperda
EPP.common.name: fall armyworm, "légionnaire d’automne"
Sub.regions: Western Africa; Middle Africa; Eastern Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Primarily maize (Zea mays), but also sorghum, millet and other cereals and some vegetable crops
Event.summary: In early 2016, fall armyworm was detected for the first time outside its native Americas on São Tomé and Príncipe and nearly simultaneously in maize fields in southwestern Nigeria, Benin and Togo, where severe outbreaks on maize were initially misattributed to indigenous Spodoptera species and then confirmed as S. frugiperda by morphological and molecular diagnosis. Over 2016–2018 the pest spread rapidly across Western and Middle Africa into Eastern and Southern Africa, becoming established in most sub-Saharan countries and causing extensive damage to smallholder maize and other staple crops. By 2018, fall armyworm infestations and associated yield losses had stabilized at high levels across much of the region, prompting FAO and partners to launch the Global Action for Fall Armyworm Control and national IPM programs to reduce its impact.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Accidental introduction of S. frugiperda from the Americas to West Africa, likely via trade or transport of infested plant material or contaminated cargo; favorable tropical and subtropical climates with year-round host availability (maize and other cereals); widespread monoculture maize, limited early detection capacity, and constrained access to effective, safe control tools in many smallholder systems. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – strong flight capacity (on the order of tens of kilometres per night) and broad host range facilitated rapid colonization across diverse African agro-ecological zones; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – adaptation of invasive populations to local climatic regimes and cropping calendars, enabling continuous breeding and spread across Western, Middle, Eastern and Southern Africa.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (retain, with corrected event-type classification). Changes made: (1) Adjusted emergence-type flags so that this episode is coded solely as an inter-continental emergence (first establishment in Africa outside the native Americas), with first_detection and intra_continental_emergence set to "false". This follows the rule that event types should generally be mutually exclusive, and that spread within Africa to additional sub-regions (Western, Middle, Eastern, Southern Africa) is considered part of the same inter-continental invasion episode rather than separate intra-continental events.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5082806/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Confirmed that the listed countries and years (Nigeria, Benin, Togo, Sao Tome and Principe in 2016; Zambia, DRC and others in 2016–2017; East and Southern African countries mainly in 2017–2018) are consistent with EPPO, IPPC and FAO reporting, though additional African countries experienced outbreaks in the same period. (3) Continent and sub-region fields already matched the UNSD classification and were left unchanged. Rationale: This is unequivocally one of the largest FAW emergence events globally in terms of area affected, yield loss and number of countries, and should definitely be retained; the corrections concern only the technical coding of the emergence type.

EPP.scientific.name: Spodoptera frugiperda
EPP.common.name: fall armyworm, "légionnaire d’automne"
Sub.regions: Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Eastern Asia; Western Asia
Host: Primarily maize; also sorghum, rice, sugarcane and some vegetable and forage crops
Event.summary: In mid-2018, fall armyworm was first reported from Yemen and soon after from maize fields in southern India (Karnataka), marking the pest’s arrival in Asia following its invasion of Africa and the Near East. Over late 2018 and 2019, it spread rapidly across Southern Asia and South-eastern Asia, with confirmed detections and damaging outbreaks in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand and neighboring countries, and by early 2019 it was detected in China’s Yunnan Province before spreading into many maize-producing provinces and other East Asian territories. By 2020–2021, fall armyworm had become established throughout much of Asia, including countries such as Viet Nam, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Japan and the Republic of Korea, causing significant damage to maize, sorghum and other crops and triggering regional action plans, national emergency responses and FAO-coordinated training and monitoring under the Global Action for Fall Armyworm Control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance migration of moths from already infested regions (likely via the Arabian Peninsula and/or eastern Africa into the Indian subcontinent), aided by monsoon wind systems; intense regional and cross-border trade in plant products; continuous availability of host crops in tropical and subtropical agro-ecosystems; limited initial awareness and preparedness among farmers and extension systems. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – high dispersal ability, broad thermal tolerance and polyphagy allowed colonization across diverse Asian climates and cropping systems; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – rapid build-up of populations in multi-cropping systems, with some evidence of adaptation to local cropping calendars and possibly differing host-use patterns between the so-called ‘rice’ and ‘corn’ strains.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (retain, with geography and type corrections). Changes made: (1) Corrected the continent field to "Asia" only and removed the reference to "Africa (Near East/North-east Africa)"; under the UNSD scheme, Yemen is classified in Asia | Western Asia, so this episode is purely Asian in the continent column, even though it is epidemiologically linked to the African invasion.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-6437?utm_source=openai)) (2) Replaced the informal "Asia (Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Eastern Asia; Western Asia); Africa (Eastern Africa – Yemen often grouped with Western Asia/Near East in FAO reporting)" wording with a standardized sub-region list: "Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Eastern Asia; Western Asia". (3) Updated the country list to explicitly include Malaysia [2019] and the Republic of Korea [2019], which are highlighted by FAO’s FAW map and EPPO/Scientific Reports as part of the early invasion front in East and South-east Asia, and removed any implication that Yemen belongs to Africa.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/fall-armyworm/monitoring-tools/faw-map/en/?utm_source=openai)) (4) Adjusted emergence-type flags so this event is classified solely as an inter-continental emergence (first establishment in Asia), with first_detection and intra_continental_emergence set to "false" to respect the rule that event types are generally mutually exclusive. Rationale: This Asia-wide invasion, which rapidly involved more than a dozen countries and large maize areas, clearly ranks among the most impactful FAW emergence events and should be retained. EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
EPP.common.name: Zika virus
Sub.regions: South America; Central America; Caribbean; Northern America
Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women; fetuses/newborns with congenital Zika syndrome; Guillain–Barré syndrome patients)
Event.summary: In early 2015, Brazil confirmed autochthonous Zika virus transmission, likely introduced from the Pacific by travellers, and over the following months the virus spread explosively through Brazil with an estimated 1.5 million infections and an unprecedented surge in microcephaly and other congenital central nervous system malformations in infants. Between mid‑2015 and late 2016, Zika spread throughout South and Central America, the Caribbean and parts of Northern America, with PAHO/WHO documenting hundreds of thousands of reported autochthonous cases and 40+ countries and territories in the Region of the Americas affected, while locally acquired cases also occurred in Florida and Texas in the continental United States. By 2017, incidence declined sharply across the region as a result of accumulated population immunity, aggressive mosquito-control campaigns and public health warnings, and WHO declared the Public Health Emergency of International Concern over in late 2016, although sporadic transmission and congenital Zika syndrome cases continued to be reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of the Asian lineage of Zika virus into a highly urbanized region with widespread Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes; large-scale international travel and mass events that facilitated viral movement; dense urban populations with inadequate water, sanitation and housing that favoured vector breeding; limited prior Zika immunity in the Americas; and health-system constraints in vector control and prenatal screening. Internal mechanisms: Strong neurotropism and teratogenicity of the circulating Asian/American lineage leading to congenital Zika syndrome and microcephaly; possible increased transmissibility in urban Aedes populations; geographic range expansion across an entire new continent, including first documented autochthonous transmission in Northern America; enhanced recognition of sexual transmission as an additional, though minor, route of spread compared with vector-borne transmission.
Review: review – This event appropriately aggregates the large 2015–2017 epidemic across South America, Central America, the Caribbean and Northern America and correctly marks it as an inter-continental emergence because it includes the first autochthonous transmission in Northern America (continental United States). The continent label has been corrected from “South America; North America” to the defined “South America; Northern America”, and some country labels were standardized (e.g. Puerto Rico, United States of America), but the overall structure and impact description are sound and should be retained.

EPP.common.name: Duck herpesvirus 1, Duck plague virus
Host: Domestic ducks (primarily local meat and egg-type breeds reared in paddy-field-based systems) on commercial and smallholder farms
Event.summary: During 2015–2016, a natural duck plague outbreak occurred in the high-density duck-farming Kuttanad region of Kerala, India, leading to significant mortality in domestic duck flocks and prompting isolation of a virulent strain designated DEV/India/IVRI-2016 from liver tissues of affected birds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional free-grazing of large duck flocks on flooded paddy fields, frequent flock movements, and close contact with wild waterfowl in a region already stressed by repeated avian influenza outbreaks created conditions for DVE re-occurrence and spread among commercial and backyard holdings. Internal mechanisms: Genomic sequencing of DEV/India/IVRI-2016 showed a virulent field strain closely related to Chinese and other Asian lineages rather than a vaccine-derived or novel species, fitting re-occurrence of a highly pathogenic lineage in an intensively farmed area.
Review: retain – Added because the Kuttanad outbreak from which DEV/India/IVRI‑2016 was recovered represents an important epizootic in one of India’s densest duck-farming regions; classification as re-occurrence in Southern Asia/India is appropriate. The year range and scale are inferred mainly from virological reports rather than a dedicated outbreak description, so flock numbers and losses should be refined if more detailed epidemiological data become available.

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Wild rodents and hares (European brown hare, mountain hare), mosquitoes and other biting insects, humans (rural residents and outdoor workers)
Event.summary: In the summer of 1995, Finland experienced a major tularemia epidemic with 467 laboratory-reported human cases in central and southern regions, followed by another high-incidence season in 1996, signalling intense amplification of Francisella tularensis subsp. holarctica in local wildlife and vector populations. Transmission was predominantly mosquito-borne, although exposure to contaminated hay dust and aerosols during farming activities also contributed, reflecting widespread circulation of the bacterium in small mammals and their aquatic or terrestrial habitats. As vector activity waned with the onset of colder weather and awareness and personal protective measures improved, human case numbers declined, but subsequent surveillance confirmed that enzootic foci persisted and that Finland remained at high risk for recurrent large mosquito-borne tularemia outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unusually favourable summer weather and hydrological conditions for mosquito breeding, high densities of susceptible small mammals and hares in rural landscapes, and intensive outdoor and farming activities increased human exposure to infected vectors and aerosolised contaminated material. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence for a novel bacterial lineage; the epidemics appear to reflect ecological amplification and geographic range expansion of existing F. tularensis subsp. holarctica foci within Finland, representing re-occurrence in a historically endemic Northern European sub-region.
Review: review – new high-impact event added. Combined the 1995 (467 cases) and 1996 (397 cases) Finnish epidemics into a single linked episode in central and southern Finland, which clearly ranks among the largest modern tularemia outbreaks. Classified as re-occurrence (not first detection or intra-continental emergence) because tularemia was long established in Northern Europe and no novel strain or host jump was demonstrated. Recommended for inclusion among the top-impact events for F. tularensis.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Wild lagomorphs (Iberian hares, wild rabbits), humans (hunters and handlers), small mammals (voles and other rodents implicated environmentally)
Event.summary: In late 1997, tularemia was identified for the first time in Spain during a large outbreak in Castile and León, where hunters and game handlers were exposed to infected Iberian hares and wild rabbits, revealing previously unrecognized circulation of Francisella tularensis subsp. holarctica in northwestern Spain. Through early 1998, several hundred human cases were recorded and infection was also confirmed in multiple animal hosts, establishing a new endemic focus in Castile and León within the broader Southern European tularemia region. Control actions, including restrictions on hare hunting and intensified wildlife surveillance, gradually reduced case numbers and the outbreak subsided, but F. tularensis became established in local wildlife reservoirs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of recreational hunting, high densities of hares and rabbits, and game management practices that increased close contact with infected carcasses and aerosols during skinning promoted spillover to humans. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of F. tularensis subsp. holarctica within Southern Europe into a previously unaffected agro-ecosystem in northwestern Spain and establishment of a new wildlife reservoir system in local lagomorph and small-mammal populations, representing re-occurrence in a known continental sub-region rather than a new intra-continental emergence.
Review: review – event retained as a major outbreak (>500 human cases) and first documented tularemia epidemic in Spain, but emergence-type classification was corrected. Tularemia was already known from other Southern European countries, so the event does not qualify as first detection globally or as intra-continental emergence into a new UN sub-region. Re-coded as re-occurrence within Southern Europe, and the mechanism text was updated accordingly. Countries field was expanded to reflect the full 1997–1998 span and the small associated Cuenca cluster.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Commensal and field rodents (e.g., mice, rats), possibly lagomorphs; humans exposed through contaminated food and water
Event.summary: In the immediate post‑war period of October 1999 to May 2000, the Kosovo region experienced a large water- and food-borne tularemia outbreak that had not been previously recorded there, with hundreds of serologically confirmed human cases. Investigations linked human disease to heavy contamination of household food stores and water supplies by rodents shedding Francisella tularensis, indicating widespread epizootic transmission in local rodent populations. As rodent numbers and food contamination were reduced and public health measures (rodent control, food protection, and water safety) were implemented, human incidence gradually declined, although low-level transmission persisted in some rural areas in the following decade.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: War-related disruption of housing, food storage, and sanitation, combined with population displacement and poor rodent control, allowed rodent populations to proliferate and contaminate grain and water in rural households. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence for a novel strain; the event is best explained by ecological amplification of endemic F. tularensis in rodent hosts and intense environmental contamination, representing re-occurrence of tularemia within the Southern Europe sub-region rather than first detection or intra-continental emergence.
Review: review – outbreak is real and clearly among the most impactful recent tularemia events in Europe (~327 human cases), so it should be retained. However, the country label was changed from “Kosovo” (not listed in the Country sheet) to “Serbia – Kosovo region” for consistency with the UN-based country list. Emergence type was re-coded from first_detection and intra-continental_emergence to re_occurrence, because tularemia was long known in Europe and Southern Europe, and this event reflects war-driven resurgence rather than first global or sub-regional emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Rodents and other small mammals contaminating village water sources; humans in affected villages
Event.summary: In 2006–2007, a tularemia outbreak with approximately three dozen human cases occurred in the Gori region of Georgia, particularly affecting the village of Zemo Rene, within an area where Francisella tularensis is considered endemic in small-mammal reservoirs. Localised clusters of human disease were linked epidemiologically to consumption of untreated water from an unprotected village reservoir that was contaminated by rodents, superimposed on a background of low-level enzootic transmission. As control measures such as chlorination of the water supply, rodent control, improved food and water hygiene, and community education were implemented, reported case numbers declined and the outbreak was considered over, though tularemia remains enzootic in wildlife in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Poorly protected communal water sources easily contaminated by rodents, limited water treatment, poor housing and food-storage conditions, and close contact between people and commensal rodents allowed amplification of an endemic zoonotic cycle into a recognisable human outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Available reports indicate the outbreak was due to re-activation of pre-existing F. tularensis foci rather than introduction of a new strain or host jump, fitting re-occurrence in an endemic Western Asian focus.
Review: review – event verified and its timing corrected from 2005–2006 to 2006–2007 based on detailed Georgian surveillance studies. Classification as re-occurrence in a long-endemic Western Asian focus remains appropriate. However, with only ~35 human cases, this outbreak is small compared with large Finnish, Swedish, Spanish, and Turkish epidemics; it may fall below a strict top-10-by-impact threshold and should be reconsidered for inclusion if a tight cap on event numbers is enforced.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Common voles (Microtus arvalis) and other small rodents, lagomorphs, domestic animals (sheep, dogs) and humans
Event.summary: Ten years after the initial 1997 hare-associated tularemia outbreak, Castile and León in Spain experienced a second major tularemia episode during 2007–2008, coinciding with a massive irruption of common voles in agricultural landscapes. The epizootic involved widespread infection in voles, other small mammals, and domestic animals, with over 1,000 associated human cases showing predominantly typhoidal and pneumonic forms of tularemia, indicating intense environmental exposure to Francisella tularensis. Once vole populations crashed and targeted rodent management, agricultural hygiene measures, and public health interventions were implemented, both animal infection and human case numbers decreased, although F. tularensis has persisted in the regional wildlife community with further, smaller outbreaks reported up to 2020.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Irruptive population dynamics of common voles linked to agricultural intensification and favourable climatic conditions created extremely high rodent densities and contamination of crops, soil, and water, leading to extensive human and animal exposure; mechanised harvesting likely aerosolised contaminated dust. Internal mechanisms: Clear ecological host shift and amplification, with vole populations becoming dominant reservoirs and vehicles for transmission, representing re-emergence driven by host expansion and enhanced transmission within an already endemic Spanish focus.
Review: retain – event description, geography, and classification as re-emergence (through host expansion from hares to common voles and altered transmission routes) are consistent with the primary literature and with the project’s definitions. Case numbers and timing match published accounts of the 2007–2008 Castile and León epidemics. Recommended to retain as one of the most impactful recent tularemia events.

EPP.scientific.name: Sprivivirus cyprinus
EPP.common.name: Spring viraemia of carp virus
Host: Indian carp species farmed in Iran – rohu (Labeo rohita), mrigal (Cirrhinus mrigala) and catla (Catla catla) in pond aquaculture.
Event.summary: Between May 2006 and September 2007, mortality events in Indian carp (rohu, mrigal and catla) on farms in Khuzestan and Gilan provinces in Iran were investigated and confirmed as spring viraemia of carp by nested PCR targeting the SVCV glycoprotein gene and supporting histopathology. All sampled Indian carp from affected farms were PCR‑positive, indicating active SVCV infection in multiple carp species within these freshwater systems and representing the first documented SVCV presence in these hosts and in Iranian carp aquaculture. Control focused on improved diagnostics, on‑farm hygiene, and quarantine/isolation of infected stocks, and the findings prompted concern about further spread of SVCV within the Middle East and highlighted the need for regional surveillance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of warm‑water carp aquaculture in Iran using dense pond systems and movements of seed and broodstock, likely including fish or eggs sourced from regions where SVCV was already present, created pathways for virus introduction into Indian carp farms. Internal mechanisms: this episode reflects both geographic range expansion within Asia from earlier foci in Eastern Europe/China into Southern Asia and host expansion of SVCV into Indian major carps, qualifying as re_emergence driven by host range extension; available data do not indicate a distinct novel genotype, but the virus showed typical SVCV genetic features.
Review: review – New row added to represent 2006–2007 SVCV outbreaks in Indian carp species in Iran, documented by Haghighi‑Khiabanian Asl et al. (2008), which provide the first confirmed SVCV detections in Iranian carp aquaculture. Classified as intra_continental_emergence (new UNSD subregion within Asia) and re_emergence (host expansion into Indian carps); provincial timing and any subsequent control outcomes should be double‑checked against the original article and national reports.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma agalactiae
EPP.common.name: Contagious agalactia
Host: Domestic goats (predominantly) and sheep (does, bucks, kids and lambs)
Event.summary: Between August 2001 and January 2002, two major outbreaks of contagious agalactia occurred in dairy goat and mixed goat–sheep herds in Paraíba state, north‑eastern Brazil, with mastitis, agalactia, polyarthritis, keratoconjunctivitis, fever and high morbidity affecting adults, kids and lambs and causing notable mortality and culling. Mycoplasma agalactiae was isolated from milk, joint fluid, nasal swabs and external ear‑canal washings, and its identity confirmed by immunoperoxidase and PCR, establishing it as the causative agent in both outbreaks. This study documented the first confirmed occurrence of M. agalactiae‑associated contagious agalactia in Brazil, signalling inter‑continental spread of the pathogen into South America’s small‑ruminant dairy sector and raising concern about its potential endemic establishment there.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction of infected animals from commercial dairy goat herds in other Brazilian states into previously unaffected flocks in Paraíba, together with intensive dairy management, close confinement and shared milking equipment, favoured within‑herd transmission once the agent was introduced. Internal mechanisms: the outbreaks were caused by classical M. agalactiae strains without evidence of novel virulence factors; their significance lies in geographic range expansion and inter‑continental emergence into South America (first detection in this continental small‑ruminant host system) rather than in documented strain evolution.
Review: review – added as a missing high-impact event: the first confirmed M. agalactiae‑associated contagious agalactia outbreaks in Brazil (2001–2002), which also represent inter‑continental emergence into South America; classified as 'first detection' and 'inter‑continental emergence' rather than as a generic re‑occurrence, based on explicit wording in the Brazilian report that these were the first such cases detected in the country.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.
