EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus mayaro
EPP.common.name: Mayaro virus
Host: Humans (school children and community members in rural/semirural areas of southern Haiti)
Event.summary: From 2014 to 2015, during cohort surveillance for acute febrile illness among school children in the Gressier–Léogâne area of southern Haiti, investigators identified the first autochthonous human Mayaro virus infections documented in Haiti and the Caribbean. These infections occurred alongside major chikungunya and dengue outbreaks, with at least one child co-infected with dengue and Mayaro virus and epidemiologic features suggesting local transmission possibly involving Aedes aegypti in rural or periurban settings. After this period, only sporadic additional Mayaro detections were reported in Haiti, and there was no documented progression to a large, sustained epidemic across the island.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The introduction of Mayaro virus into Haiti likely occurred via movement of infected travellers or vectors from endemic continental South America, with local amplification favored by high densities of Aedes mosquitoes, widespread circulation of other arboviruses, and limited diagnostic capacity that masked Mayaro within a broader febrile-illness burden. Internal mechanisms: Experimental and field data suggest that Aedes aegypti and potentially other urban/periurban vectors can transmit Mayaro virus, representing enhanced transmission potential via adaptation to anthropophilic mosquitoes; however, there is no clear evidence of a distinct genotype with substantially increased virulence, so the key internal mechanism is vector adaptation and possible expansion from a strictly sylvatic to a more periurban cycle.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Brucella ovis
EPP.common.name: Ovine epididymitis
Countries: Croatia [2002–2003, large‑scale survey documenting first confirmed presence]
Host: Domestic sheep (rams and ewes in multiple counties)
Event.summary: During 2002–2003, a national survey in Croatia tested 14,404 sheep from six counties and identified 1,014 seropositive and 2,060 suspect animals for Brucella ovis by serology, providing the first rigorous proof that B. ovis infection was widespread in Croatian sheep flocks. Clinical and pathological examinations of seropositive rams and some ewes found typical epididymal lesions, confirming ovine brucellosis due to B. ovis as an important reproductive disease. Control measures focused on flock‑level management, castration or culling of positive rams, and ongoing surveillance rather than rapid eradication, and B. ovis has persisted as an endemic infection requiring continued monitoring in Croatia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Implementation of organized serosurveys and improved diagnostics revealed substantial infection that had likely circulated undetected, while animal movements and transboundary trade within the Balkans probably facilitated spread before formal recognition. Internal mechanisms: Reports do not indicate emergence of a novel genotype, increased virulence, or host shift; the episode is best interpreted as a major re‑occurrence and recognition of B. ovis within an already affected European subregion.
Review: Decision: review. Updated the year field from 2002 to 2002–2003 to match the survey period and changed the emergence‑type classification from first_detection to re_occurrence, because B. ovis was already globally and regionally established and FAO/OIE yearbooks list B. ovis in Croatia before this detailed survey. The event remains appropriate to retain as a large‑impact episode, given the very large sample size, high numbers of seropositive animals, and national implications for control programmes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Brucella ovis
EPP.common.name: Ovine epididymitis
Countries: Serbia [2008–2009, first identification in northern districts; 2014, confirmed outbreak in Pirot municipality]
Host: Domestic sheep (rams and ewes in traditional flocks)
Event.summary: Brucella ovis infection was first identified in Serbia in 2008–2009 during serological investigations in the northern region (South Bačka and Srem districts), where ELISA surveys detected substantial seroprevalence in rams and sheep, revealing B. ovis as an under‑recognized cause of reproductive disease in the country. Subsequent work characterized the epizootiological, clinical and pathological features of infected Serbian flocks, and in 2014 a detailed investigation in Pirot municipality in southern Serbia confirmed additional infected rams and flocks, indicating wider geographic spread at the national level. Control strategies have focused on improved diagnosis, culling of seropositive rams, and surveillance, but no national eradication has been achieved and B. ovis is now regarded as an endemic reproductive pathogen of Serbian sheep.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased awareness and availability of serological tests, together with targeted surveys, enabled detection of previously unrecognized infection, while movements of breeding stock between regions (north–south) likely contributed to dissemination. Internal mechanisms: The reports describe typical B. ovis strains without evidence of new genotypes, resistance, or altered virulence; the episode is best interpreted as re‑occurrence and geographic spread within an already affected Southern European subregion.
Review: Decision: review. Changed emergence‑type classification from first_detection to re_occurrence, since B. ovis had long been present in Europe and the event reflects country‑level detection and spread within an already affected subregion, not global first detection in the host system. The timing (2008–2014) and geography are supported by Serbian surveillance and case‑report papers; the event remains appropriate to retain given the relatively high reported seroprevalence and national implications.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Query fever
Host: Domestic goats (primary animal source), sheep (present but less implicated), humans (spillover cases)
Event.summary: In late 1992 and early 1993, after an influenza epidemic, a very large community outbreak of Q fever occurred around the town of Panagyurishte in southern Bulgaria, with goats in their periparturient period identified as the main animal reservoir and period of intense environmental contamination. During spring 1993, human cases of atypical pneumonia and febrile respiratory illness peaked from April to June, coinciding with goat kidding and sporadic abortions, while sheep grazing further from town were considered less likely sources. The outbreak subsided after the kidding season and with implementation of control measures and changing exposure patterns, but subsequent waves in the mid‑1990s showed that Q fever remained endemic in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Post‑communist economic and social changes in Bulgaria led to a tripling in goat numbers, closer contact between goat owners and animals, and increased consumption of raw goat milk and products, which shifted the main source of human C. burnetii infection from cattle and sheep to goats; seasonal concentration of kidding and abortions near populated areas amplified airborne exposure. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel strain was highlighted; the event is best characterized as re-occurrence driven by intensified goat husbandry and environmental aerosolization rather than a new genotype.
Review: retain – This row correctly captures the major Panagyurishte outbreak described as the largest Bulgarian/European Q fever outbreak of the early 1990s, with goats as the main source and >2,000 acute respiratory cases where Q fever contributed substantially.([cureus.com](https://www.cureus.com/articles/150529-a-narrative-review-of-q-fever-in-europe?utm_source=openai))  Country (Bulgaria), subregion (Eastern Europe) and years (1992–1993) are consistent with published accounts, and classification as re-occurrence (rather than first detection or inter-/intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because Q fever had been recognized in Bulgaria for decades.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2640784/?utm_source=openai)) No structural changes made; retained as one of the top global events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyvirus cyprinidallo3
EPP.common.name: Koi herpesvirus (KHV)
Countries: Canada [2007-2008 – extensive mass mortalities of wild common carp in the Kawartha Lakes region of Ontario (Lakes Scugog, Pigeon, Katchewanooka) and in Lake Manitoba, Manitoba]
Host: Wild common carp (Cyprinus carpio) in large lake systems and connected waterways in Ontario and Manitoba
Event.summary: In 2007, an extensive mortality of wild common carp occurred in the Kawartha Lakes region of Ontario, Canada, particularly in Lakes Scugog and Pigeon, followed by additional mortality events in 2008 in nearby Lake Katchewanooka and in Lake Manitoba. Affected carp showed severe gill lesions and systemic pathology, and PCR with sequencing confirmed infection with CyHV‑3 strains identical to known European/U.S. KHV‑U and KHV‑I genotypes. These die‑offs removed large proportions of local carp populations and highlighted the ability of CyHV‑3 to drive major wild‑fish mortality events in temperate North American lakes. After the acute outbreaks, the virus was considered established in Canadian wild carp populations, posing ongoing risks of further re‑occurrence and ecological impacts in connected watersheds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: probable introduction of CyHV‑3 into Canadian waters via movement of infected koi or common carp across borders or through trade, high densities of carp in shallow, eutrophic lakes, and summer water temperatures favorable for viral replication and transmission. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of CyHV‑3 within the Northern American subregion through establishment in wild carp populations, with efficient carp‑to‑carp transmission and persistence that allows periodic large die‑offs without the need for new external introductions.
Review: review – New event added to capture the first confirmed CyHV‑3 outbreaks in Canada, which caused large‑scale mortalities of wild carp in multiple Ontario and Manitoba lakes in 2007–2008 and are widely cited as major KHV events in North America. Classified as re‑occurrence within Northern America (the virus was already established in the USA), with timing and geographic scope based on Garver et al. 2010 and subsequent OIE summaries; recommended for inclusion among the globally most impactful emergence episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Poxvirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Pox viruses infection
Countries: India [2008–2009, especially Rajasthan (Barmer, Bikaner, Jaisalmer) and Delhi]
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius); humans (camel attendants and handlers)
Event.summary: In 2008–2009 a major outbreak of camelpox occurred among dromedary camels in north‑western India (Rajasthan and Delhi), with widespread skin lesions and production losses in affected herds. During this episode, several camel attendants developed pox‑like lesions on their hands and fingers, and laboratory investigations confirmed camelpox virus infection, providing the first conclusive evidence of zoonotic transmission of camelpox to humans. Veterinary control measures, including isolation of sick camels, improved hygiene and, in some areas, vaccination, helped bring the outbreak under control, but camelpox remains endemic in camel-rearing regions of South Asia and the Middle East.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of camels in arid pastoral systems with close daily contact between animals and handlers; seasonal stress and climatic fluctuations after the monsoon; limited prior vaccination and veterinary access in remote camel-rearing areas; animal movements for trade and cultural uses. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak reflects re-emergence of endemic camelpox virus with documented Host Expansion (Spillover) to humans under close-contact conditions, rather than emergence of a clearly distinct viral strain; available molecular analyses show Indian isolates clustering with known CMLV lineages.
Review: Review – Retained as an important regional event and as the first confirmed zoonotic transmission of camelpox to humans, but event-type flags were modified: intra-continental emergence was set to “No” (the disease was already endemic in Southern/Western Asia), and re-emergence was set to “Yes” to reflect reappearance with new host range (humans).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Poxvirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Pox viruses infection
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius); humans (camel attendants and handlers)
Event.summary: In 2008–2009 a major outbreak of camelpox occurred among dromedary camels in north‑western India and in Delhi, with widespread skin lesions and production losses in affected camel herds. During this episode, several camel attendants developed pox‑like lesions on their hands and fingers, and laboratory investigations confirmed camelpox virus infection in humans as well as camels, providing the first conclusive evidence of zoonotic camelpox. Veterinary measures such as isolation of sick camels, improved hygiene and vaccination in selected herds helped bring the outbreak under control, but camelpox remains endemic in camel-rearing regions of South Asia and the wider Middle East.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High camel densities in pastoral and paramilitary herds with close human–animal contact; seasonal stress after the monsoon; historically low vaccine coverage and limited veterinary services in remote camel-rearing areas; transhumant and trade-related animal movements. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence of endemic camelpox virus with demonstrated Host Expansion to humans, rather than emergence of a genetically novel virus; molecular analyses show Indian human and camel isolates clustering with existing CMLV strains.
Review: Review – This camelpox event is regionally important and documents first confirmed zoonotic transmission, but the original classification (intra-continental emergence plus re-occurrence) conflicted with the scheme. It has been reclassified as re-emergence only (no intra-continental emergence or re-occurrence) because the disease was already endemic in Southern/Western Asia and the key novelty was expanded host range.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia psilostachya
EPP.common.name: Cuman ragweed, western ragweed, perennial ragweed
Countries: Taiwan, Province of China [2000–2001, Panpingshan, Zuoying District, Kaohsiung]
Host: Small naturalized population in open coastal grassland and disturbed ruderal habitats in southern Taiwan
Event.summary: In 2000 botanists collected Ambrosia psilostachya from a feral population on Panpingshan in Zuoying District, Kaohsiung, and additional specimens in 2000–2001 confirmed that the species was naturalized at this site. The records documented a small but established alien population in coastal grassland and ruderal habitats in southern Taiwan, adding a new country to the East Asian distribution of A. psilostachya, which had already been introduced elsewhere in the region (e.g. Japan). Since then the species has persisted locally on Taiwan but there are no published reports of extensive spread, major agricultural damage or large‑scale eradication campaigns.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction most likely via contaminated seed, ornamental or horticultural material, or other traded goods through southern Taiwan’s ports, with establishment favoured by open, disturbed coastal grassland. Internal mechanisms: Perennial life history with rhizomatous spread and wind‑dispersed pollen and seeds supports persistence of local foci once introduced, but available evidence points to a geographically limited naturalization rather than broad regional invasion.
Review: Decision: review (likely exclude). Tseng & Peng (2004) and subsequent Taiwanese databases clearly document a newly naturalized A. psilostachya population in Kaohsiung in 2000–2001, but show only a single small focus with no evidence of large‑scale spread or major impacts.([for.nchu.edu.tw](https://for.nchu.edu.tw/en/uploads/file/thesis/3eea2741-5e0b-44e3-bebb-f48042f27f4e.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Asia already harboured A. psilostachya (e.g. Japan, and later Iran) before 2000, so this Taiwanese record is not a global first detection and does not qualify as intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence. The earlier coding of first_detection=Yes and re_occurrence=Yes was inconsistent with project definitions and has been corrected to first_detection=No and re_occurrence=No. Because the event appears minor compared with the major invasions in Italy, France, Iran and India, it is flagged for review as a candidate for exclusion if the dataset is restricted strictly to the ten most impactful emergence events.
Review.Comment: single small focus with no evidence of large‑scale spread or major impacts.

EPP.scientific.name: Frankliniella occidentalis
EPP.common.name: western flower thrips
Countries: India [2014–2015 (first confirmed records), later detections in the Nilgiris and other localities]
Host: Tomato (initial detection near Bengaluru, Karnataka) and occasional records on other crops and ornamental hosts, with potential to utilise a wide range of vegetables, field crops and ornamentals
Event.summary: In 2014–2015, western flower thrips was formally reported for the first time from India on tomato near Bengaluru, Karnataka, based on morphologically and molecularly confirmed specimens, although earlier reports are considered doubtful. Subsequent surveys initially struggled to relocate the species around Bengaluru, suggesting a transient or localised population, but by 2016 a breeding population including males was confirmed on Erythrina in the Nilgiris, indicating establishment at least in parts of southern India. By around 2020, F. occidentalis was recognised by Indian researchers and NPPOs as a high‑risk invasive thrips with the potential to spread widely across India’s large horticultural and field‑crop systems and to vector multiple tospoviruses, prompting development of surveillance and management recommendations even though documented large‑scale outbreaks remain limited so far.([databases.nbair.res.in](https://databases.nbair.res.in/insectpests/Frankliniella-occidentalis.php))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increasing imports and domestic movement of ornamental and vegetable planting material, including cut flowers and nursery stock; rapid expansion of polyhouse and net‑house cultivation that favours invasive thrips; and limited initial diagnostic capacity to distinguish F. occidentalis from morphologically similar native thrips. Internal mechanisms: invasion by genetically distinct F. occidentalis lineages documented by barcoding; strong polyphagy enabling use of many Indian crop and non‑crop hosts; and a high potential to vector TSWV and other tospoviruses, raising concern that small current foci could seed much larger future epidemics.([databases.nbair.res.in](https://databases.nbair.res.in/insectpests/Frankliniella-occidentalis.php))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Event retained as a country‑level first‑detection episode of high strategic importance, but the strength of evidence for widespread establishment and major economic impact by 2020 is weaker than for other events. Corrections: intra‑continental emergence set to “No” because F. occidentalis was already present in the Southern Asia subregion (Sri Lanka from 1996 and Iran from 2004). The summary now more explicitly reflects the current uncertainty around distribution and impact, so this row should be re‑evaluated as more post‑2020 data on establishment and damage in India become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera zeae
EPP.common.name: corn cyst nematode
Countries: Pakistan [2004–2005 nationwide cyst-nematode surveys; high prevalence confirmed again in later studies in Punjab and other provinces up to at least 2019]
Host: Zea mays (maize); Triticum aestivum (wheat); Saccharum officinarum (sugarcane) and other rotational cereals in surveyed fields
Event.summary: In the mid‑2000s, national surveys of cyst nematodes in Pakistan documented Heterodera zeae as widespread on maize, wheat and sugarcane, with the species detected in roughly three quarters of sampled localities across major cereal-growing regions, confirming it as a key constraint on maize production. Subsequent community-analysis work in Punjab and other provinces through the 2010s showed H. zeae to be the most frequently encountered plant-parasitic nematode in maize fields and rotational crops, with occurrence exceeding 50% of sampled sites and strong associations with stunting and poor plant growth. Over this period, H. zeae became firmly recognized as a major maize cyst nematode in Pakistan, prompting recommendations for improved rotations, tolerant cultivars and nematode-aware management to limit chronic yield losses rather than any realistic attempt at eradication.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive maize and wheat cultivation in warm irrigated systems, cereal-based rotations with limited non-host breaks, and low adoption of nematode-targeted management have favoured sustained high densities and broad dissemination of H. zeae in Pakistan. Movement of infested soil and planting material between farms, as well as irrigation-water spread in canal systems, likely contributed to its detection in many localities during 2004–2005 surveys and beyond. Internal mechanisms: Evidence from host-range and population studies suggests the presence of physiological races and some capacity to reproduce on non-cereal hosts (e.g. vetiver, tomato, almond), but no distinct new strain is clearly tied to this period. The episode is best treated as a large-scale re-occurrence and consolidation of an already established pest within Southern Asia.
Review: review – New event added to represent Pakistan, where H. zeae is documented as widespread and a major maize nematode based on 2004–2005 national surveys and later community analyses. Classified as re-occurrence within an already affected subregion (Southern Asia). Start and end years (2004–2019) approximate the main survey and analytical period; given limited quantitative yield-loss data, this row is flagged for expert review of impact ranking and temporal bounds.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera zeae
EPP.common.name: corn cyst nematode
Host: Zea mays (maize)
Event.summary: Around 2015–2016, Heterodera zeae was found for the first time in China in a maize field near Laibin in Guangxi Province, marking its emergence in the Eastern Asia subregion of its native continent. Follow‑up surveys and diagnostic work subsequently documented the nematode in additional maize fields in Henan Province (reported in 2020) and most recently in Sichuan Province (reported in 2024), demonstrating establishment and gradual spread within China’s warm maize-producing zones. By 2024, H. zeae was officially considered present with a restricted distribution in China, and extension recommendations emphasize surveillance, crop rotation, and quarantine measures to slow further expansion rather than complete eradication.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via infested soil or planting material from already infested countries in Southern or South‑eastern Asia, combined with rapid expansion and intensification of maize production in warm regions of southern and central China. Movement of farm machinery and soil between fields, and limited prior awareness of the pest, facilitated local spread once introduced. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype has been highlighted; instead, the event reflects geographic range expansion of H. zeae into previously uninfested warm-temperate and subtropical maize zones of Eastern Asia enabled by its inherent adaptation to high soil temperatures and maize roots.
Review: retain – Event correctly summarizes first detection and subsequent spread of H. zeae in China (Guangxi 2015/2016, Henan, Sichuan) as an intra-continental emergence into the new Eastern Asia subregion. Country, sub-region and timing align with EPPO and Plant Disease notes; classification and sources are appropriate, so no structural changes were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Parvovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: CPV, FPV
Sub.regions: Europe: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Eastern Europe. Asia: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia. North America: Northern America.
Countries: United States of America [2006-2007, CPV-2c detected in multiple states alongside CPV-2b].
Host: Domestic dogs (primarily puppies and young dogs with hemorrhagic gastroenteritis); occasional domestic cats infected by CPV-2c in parts of Europe.
Event.summary: Around 2000, a new antigenic variant of canine parvovirus type 2 carrying a Glu-426 substitution in VP2 (later designated CPV-2c) was first recognised in dogs in Italy, with retrospective data showing closely related 426E strains already circulating in Germany in the mid-1990s. Over the following decade CPV-2c spread across much of Europe—being documented in Spain, Switzerland, the Czech Republic and later Sweden—and progressively replaced earlier CPV-2a/2b variants in many dog populations. By the mid-2000s to early 2010s, CPV-2c had also been reported from Asian countries such as Viet Nam and China and from North America, where it co-circulated with CPV-2a/2b, contributing to large numbers of severe enteritis cases in puppies despite vaccination and establishing multiple regional CPV-2c lineages.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of companion-dog populations; intensive breeding and shelter environments with high densities of susceptible puppies; global movement and trade of dogs; incomplete or improperly timed vaccination leading to windows of susceptibility; environmental persistence of parvoviruses in kennels and public spaces. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – CPV-2c (Glu-426 VP2 mutant) exhibits distinct antigenic properties relative to CPV-2a/2b and shows evidence of strong fitness, enabling replacement of earlier variants in many regions. Enhanced Transmission/Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – very high environmental stability, intense faecal shedding and efficient dog-to-dog transmission allowed CPV-2c lineages to disseminate and become endemic across diverse climates and husbandry systems.
Review: Decision: review (retain event). Corrections made: (i) restricted this event to Europe, Asia and North America and moved South American details to the dedicated South American CPV-2c event to avoid double counting; (ii) updated country timelines (CPV-2c first recognised in Italy in 2000 with retrospective detection in Germany in 1996; first report in Spain in 2006; first CPV-2c detections in China around 2009–2010; CPV-2c predominance in Viet Nam documented for 2016–2018 rather than the mid-2000s); (iii) reclassified the event from “inter-continental emergence + re-emergence” to “re-emergence only”, in line with the project rule that new antigenic variants of an already established EPP should not be coded as inter-continental emergence; and (iv) pruned and refocused the source list on primary molecular-epidemiology studies rather than Wikipedia or duplicate PDF links. The episode clearly represents a major CPV-2c-driven wave of disease and should remain among the key post-1990 emergence events for this EPP, but final coding should be checked by a human reviewer.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Plasmodium spp.
EPP.common.name: malaria parasites
Countries: Rwanda [2018–2019, therapeutic efficacy studies and in vitro confirmation of artemisinin partial resistance]
Host: Humans (Plasmodium falciparum)
Event.summary: From 2012 to 2015, molecular surveillance in Rwanda detected Pfkelch13 R561H and P574L mutations in Plasmodium falciparum, suggesting local emergence of genotypes analogous to Southeast Asian artemisinin-resistance markers; by 2018–2019, therapeutic efficacy studies linked R561H to delayed parasite clearance and ring-stage survival assays confirmed reduced susceptibility to dihydroartemisinin in isolates from southern Rwanda. The prevalence and geographic distribution of R561H increased over time, indicating clonal expansion and establishment of partial artemisinin resistance within Rwanda’s parasite population, although artemether-lumefantrine remained clinically efficacious in most sites. National control programs responded by intensifying therapeutic-efficacy monitoring, updating treatment guidelines as needed, and strengthening vector control and surveillance to track further spread of resistance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High ACT drug pressure in a setting of intense transmission, possible reductions in population immunity following earlier control successes, and limited capacity to rapidly change first-line regimens or fully enforce rational drug use created conditions favouring selection of resistant parasites. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of Pfkelch13 R561H and related alleles in African parasite populations, conferring partial artemisinin resistance as shown by delayed clearance and in vitro survival assays; genetic analyses support independent evolution in Rwanda rather than simple importation from Southeast Asia.
Review: retain – event accurately summarizes the independent emergence and spread of Pfkelch13 R561H (and related mutations) in Rwanda and is a key African evolutionary milestone. Dates (first detection in 2012–2015, clinical association and in vitro confirmation by 2018–2019), geography (Eastern Africa; Rwanda), and classification as re-emergence only (new genotype in an endemic pathogen) match the cited clinical, genetic, and in vitro evidence. No structural corrections were necessary, though precise end year (2020) is somewhat arbitrary and reflects the period over which data are available.

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia mallei
EPP.common.name: Malleus (glanders)
Host: Working equids (horses, donkeys, mules)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, a cross-sectional serosurvey of nearly 1,000 working equids in central Ethiopia found approximately 3–4% seropositive for glanders using complement fixation and Western blot, demonstrating previously unrecognized but widespread infection in an area thought to be largely free of the disease. Subsequent WOAH reports from Eastern Africa recorded official presence of glanders in Eritrea in 2010 and suspected infection in Ethiopia in 2011, confirming that Burkholderia mallei was established in local horse and donkey populations. These findings revealed endemic foci of glanders in Eastern Africa and prompted increased attention to equine health surveillance, although resource constraints have limited comprehensive eradication efforts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High reliance on working equids for transport and draught power, congregation of animals at markets and watering points, low biosecurity, and limited access to veterinary services favoured silent persistence of B. mallei infection in Eastern Africa. Cross-border movements of animals and trade in equids from endemic parts of Asia or the Middle East may have contributed to historical introduction, but the modern event largely reflects recognition of long-standing infection rather than a discrete introduction. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of new strains, resistance, or altered virulence was reported; hence the event is best interpreted as re-occurrence of a long-established pathogen in a previously affected continent, newly documented through improved serological surveys.
Review: review – Added new event to capture a major, previously omitted modern focus of glanders. This row summarises serological evidence for endemic infection in working equids in central Ethiopia (≈3–4% seropositive) and official WOAH notifications from Eritrea and Ethiopia around 2010–2011, which collectively represent the main documented re-occurrence of B. mallei in Eastern Africa. Classified as re-occurrence (no internal pathogen changes demonstrated) and intra/inter-continental emergence set to No because Africa had historical glanders foci. Sources emphasise the original Ethiopian serosurvey, WOAH regional reports, and authoritative disease overviews.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Host: Domestic pigs; humans (pig farmers, abattoir workers); fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir); companion animals (dogs, cats)
Event.summary: From late 1998, intensive pig farms in peninsular Malaysia experienced a new respiratory–neurological disease in pigs accompanied by highly fatal encephalitis among pig handlers, initially misdiagnosed as Japanese encephalitis. Movement of infected pigs spread infection between major pig-producing states and into abattoirs in Singapore, leading to roughly 265 human encephalitis cases with over 100 deaths and the culling of more than a million pigs. The epidemic ended after aggressive pig depopulation, movement bans, farm closures and slaughterhouse controls removed the amplifying host populations and stopped human exposure.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification and high density of pig production, frequent live-pig movements between Malaysian states and to Singapore, and siting of pig farms under fruit trees created close interfaces between Pteropus fruit bats and pigs; early misattribution to Japanese encephalitis delayed targeted control. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of a bat-borne henipavirus into pigs and then humans; enhanced transmission through high-titer virus shedding in pigs acting as amplifying hosts; inherent ability of the Malaysia genotype to spread efficiently within pig herds and from pigs to humans through close contact.
Review: retain – Correctly represents the first recognized NiV emergence in pigs and humans in peninsular Malaysia with linked cases in Singapore; continent, sub-region and countries match UNSD classifications; event-type coding as first global emergence/first detection (without intra- or inter-continental flags) is appropriate and the outbreak is clearly one of the two largest Nipah events globally.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus monkeypox
EPP.common.name: MPXV, Mpox virus, Monkeypox virus
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From February 1996, a large outbreak of human mpox occurred in villages of the Katako-Kombe and Lodja health zones in Kasai-Oriental, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with hundreds of suspected cases and several deaths in a region where the virus was already known to be endemic. The outbreak developed with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission across multiple villages over 1996‚Äì1997, alongside sporadic zoonotic spillover, ultimately becoming the largest documented mpox outbreak to that time. Transmission declined after intensified surveillance and control measures, and case numbers fell by late 1997‚Äì1998, though mpox continued to be reported sporadically in the DRC thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: cessation of smallpox vaccination leading to a growing cohort with no cross‚Äëprotective orthopoxvirus immunity, fragile health systems, and high dependence on bushmeat and wildlife contact in forest villages. Internal mechanisms: no clear evidence of a novel strain; the event is best explained by increased susceptibility and opportunities for transmission (extended human-to-human spread) rather than major viral change.
Review: retain ‚Äì Event correctly captures the large 1996‚Äì1997 Kasai-Oriental outbreak in DRC, with appropriate geography (Middle Africa, Democratic Republic of the Congo) and classification as re-occurrence in an already endemic subregion; no substantive changes were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus monkeypox
EPP.common.name: MPXV, Mpox virus, Monkeypox virus
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Beginning in September 2017, Nigeria detected its first confirmed human mpox cases since the 1970s in Bayelsa State, with rapid recognition of a large, multi-state outbreak after decades of epidemiologic silence. The outbreak expanded during 2017‚Äì2018 to involve at least 118 confirmed cases (and many more suspected) across numerous states and the Federal Capital Territory, with several deaths and clear evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission, including in healthcare settings. By late 2018 incidence declined but mpox became newly established in Nigeria, with ongoing sporadic cases in subsequent years and this lineage later linked to exported cases and the 2022 global clade IIb outbreak.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: urbanization and changing land use in southern Nigeria, increased human‚Äìwildlife contact, weak routine surveillance, and waning population immunity after cessation of smallpox vaccination contributed to unnoticed re‚Äëemergence and spread before detection. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses indicate that the clade II (West African) viruses circulating in Nigeria from around 2014 evolved into the lineage (clade IIb) that later drove the 2022 global outbreak, implying adaptive changes associated with enhanced human‚Äëto‚Äëhuman transmissibility and geographic spread.
Review: review ‚Äì Changed re_occurrence from true to false so that this event is classified primarily as re-emergence (involving an evolved clade II lineage with altered epidemiology) in a subregion where human mpox was known historically but absent for decades; years, geography, and sources remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus monkeypox
EPP.common.name: MPXV, Mpox virus, Monkeypox virus
Host: Humans (including many children and women; evidence of sexual and close household transmission)
Event.summary: From early 2023, the Democratic Republic of the Congo experienced a marked surge of clade I mpox, with suspected cases reported in the majority of provinces and a rapid rise in incidence compared with previous endemic levels. Over 2023‚ÄìApril 2024, DRC reported on the order of 15,000‚Äì20,000 suspected cases and hundreds of deaths, with increasing reports of sexual transmission, spread into large urban centers including Kinshasa, and cases among children and women, indicating changing epidemiology and transmission contexts. The outbreak continued into 2024 but with intensified national and international response planning, including enhanced surveillance, risk communication, and preparations for vaccination and clinical management to reduce incidence and mortality.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: persistent zoonotic reservoir in forested regions, high poverty and mobility, weak health systems, and limited access to vaccines and antivirals, combined with under-detection during the COVID-19 era, facilitated widespread re‚Äëemergence and geographic expansion within DRC. Internal mechanisms: clade I viruses associated with higher case-fatality rates; recent analyses describe distinct clade I sublineages (e.g. Ia and Ib) and document sustained human-to-human transmission including sexual transmission in mining areas and urban centers, supporting classification as re‚Äëemergence with altered transmission dynamics rather than simple re‚Äëoccurrence.
Review: review ‚Äì Simplified the countries field to 'Democratic Republic of the Congo' (province-level spread, including Kinshasa, is now described only in the summary) and changed re_occurrence from true to false so that this large nationwide surge associated with new clade I lineages and sexual transmission is classified as re-emergence rather than both re-occurrence and re-emergence; magnitude, timing and mechanisms align with WHO and CDC sources, but ongoing evolution of the outbreak warrants continued monitoring.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Coccidioides spp.
EPP.common.name: Coccidioides fungi
Countries: United States of America (California ‚Äì especially southern and Central Valley counties)
Host: Humans (California residents, with high incidence in southern Central Valley and southern coastal counties)
Event.summary: In 2016 and 2017, California experienced a pronounced resurgence of reported coccidioidomycosis, with statewide case counts more than doubling compared with 2014‚Äì2015 and reaching historically high levels in several counties of the southern Central Valley and central coast. The increase manifested as a sharp rise in community‚Äëacquired pneumonia due to Coccidioides, overwhelming some local public health resources and prompting statewide alerts to clinicians. After 2017, annual incidence in California declined somewhat but remained elevated compared with the early 2000s, indicating a re‚Äëoccurring pattern tied to environmental and demographic conditions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unusual weather patterns in preceding years (severe drought followed by wet winters that may have promoted fungal growth and subsequent dusty seasons); expansion of residential and occupational activities in highly endemic areas; and improved laboratory reporting and clinician awareness. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of a new, more virulent or resistant strain; the surge appears driven largely by environmental and surveillance factors superimposed on established endemicity.
Review: retain ‚Äì This row accurately summarizes the documented resurgence of coccidioidomycosis in California in 2016‚Äì2017, including record or near-record incidence in southern Central Valley and coastal counties, and it is well aligned with CDC and CDPH analyses; treating it as a major re-occurrence driven by drought‚Äìrain cycles, exposure, and reporting changes is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Coccidioides spp.
EPP.common.name: Coccidioides fungi
Countries: United States of America (Arizona ‚Äì particularly Maricopa, Pima, and Pinal counties)
Host: Humans (Arizona residents, especially in major metropolitan and surrounding desert counties)
Event.summary: Following several years of fluctuating incidence, Arizona experienced a substantial increase in reported coccidioidomycosis during 2017‚Äì2018, with case counts climbing notably above prior years in key counties such as Maricopa and Pima. The surge coincided with heightened clinician testing for Valley fever among patients with community‚Äëacquired pneumonia and with meteorologic conditions favorable for dust generation. Subsequent years showed variable but generally high levels of disease, suggesting that the 2017‚Äì2018 period marked a significant re‚Äëoccurrence of coccidioidomycosis in Arizona‚Äôs already hyperendemic environment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climatic conditions influencing soil moisture and dust storms in central and southern Arizona; urban sprawl and construction in desert fringes; and increased provider awareness and testing. Internal mechanisms: No definitive evidence of new virulence or resistance traits; the pattern is most consistent with environmentally driven re‚Äëoccurrence superimposed on a long‚Äëstanding endemic focus.
Review: retain ‚Äì This event reflects the well-described 2017‚Äì2018 increase in Arizona coccidioidomycosis cases, including a >50% rise in reported cases during October 2017‚ÄìMarch 2018 in Maricopa, Pima, and Pinal counties, and justifiably classifies it as a major re-occurrence driven by climate, land use, and testing practices rather than pathogen evolution.

EPP.scientific.name: Hepatovirus A
EPP.common.name: Hepatitis A virus
Host: Humans (general population, especially children and young adults)
Event.summary: In 2003‚Äì2004, Argentina experienced a nationwide hepatitis A outbreak with a very high incidence (over 60,000 reported cases in 2004 alone) and a heavy burden of fulminant hepatitis requiring pediatric liver transplantation. Incidence rose sharply across the country, particularly among young children, as a large susceptible cohort accumulated in the context of improving sanitation but no routine childhood vaccination. Following introduction of a single-dose universal childhood hepatitis A vaccination program in 2005, incidence and pediatric liver transplants due to hepatitis A dropped dramatically and the outbreak subsided over the subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Transition from high to intermediate endemicity with improved sanitation reduced early-life exposure, leaving many older children and young adults susceptible; high household and community contact rates and suboptimal water and sanitation facilitated fecal‚Äìoral transmission; lack of routine childhood vaccination before 2005 allowed a large susceptible cohort to form. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel HAV strain; the outbreak reflected demographic and epidemiologic shifts and accumulation of susceptibles rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain ‚Äì This is a well-documented, very large nationwide outbreak (incidence 139 and 172.7/100,000 in 2003‚Äì2004; >60,000 reported cases in 2004) with major clinical impact and clear policy consequences (introduction of single-dose universal childhood vaccination). Geography, time span, host, and classification as re-occurrence for a long-endemic virus are appropriate; no column-level corrections needed, though the narrative could note that total cases over 2003‚Äì2004 likely exceeded the 43,000‚Äì60,000 range cited. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3846416/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter jejuni
EPP.common.name: campylobacteriosis
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Between August 2016 and mid‚Äë2017, Sweden reported a large nationwide increase in domestic Campylobacter jejuni infections, with surveillance estimating approximately 5,000 excess notified cases above expected baseline levels. The surge was temporally associated with changes in poultry production and processing that allowed higher Campylobacter contamination levels on broiler carcasses, and whole‚Äëgenome sequencing showed that many human and poultry isolates belonged to closely related lineages from a major producer. Case numbers gradually declined after enhanced control measures and stricter process‚Äëhygiene criteria were introduced in the poultry sector, although incidence remained elevated compared with pre‚Äëoutbreak levels for some time.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Changes in poultry production and slaughter practices, including problems with cleaning and disinfection of transport crates and processing equipment at a major producer, and high national poultry consumption, contributed to increased contamination of retail poultry meat and widespread foodborne transmission. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak largely involved existing poultry‚Äëassociated C. jejuni lineages; no single fundamentally novel strain was identified, so the event is best characterized as a large re‚Äëoccurrence driven by food‚Äëchain and industry changes rather than new pathogen traits.
Review: Retain ‚Äì Event is real, clearly described by the Swedish Public Health Agency, and represents a large, nationally important re‚Äëoccurrence driven by poultry‚Äësector changes, with thousands of excess human cases. Classification as re‚Äëoccurrence and assignment to Sweden, Northern Europe are correct; Wikipedia has been supplemented with the primary national outbreak report to strengthen sourcing.

EPP.scientific.name: Brucella spp.
EPP.common.name: brucellosis
Host: Humans (residents and workers near an animal vaccine manufacturing plant; students and staff at a nearby veterinary research institute); livestock not directly involved in primary transmission
Event.summary: In mid‚Äë2019, residents and workers near the Zhongmu Lanzhou biopharmaceutical plant in Lanzhou, Gansu Province began to test seropositive for Brucella after a failure in disinfecting exhaust gases during production of live animal brucellosis vaccines (Brucella suis strain 2, S2) led to aerosol release of Brucella into surrounding neighbourhoods. Between late 2019 and November 30, 2020, more than 10,000 people in the vicinity‚Äîincluding students and staff of the nearby Lanzhou Veterinary Research Institute and local residents‚Äîwere found seropositive, making this one of the largest recorded brucellosis laboratory‚Äërelated outbreaks, though most cases were asymptomatic or had mild disease. Authorities halted vaccine production and revoked the plant‚Äôs licences, provided long‚Äëterm clinical follow‚Äëup and compensation to affected residents, and implemented stricter biosafety and waste‚Äëgas treatment standards to prevent recurrence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Industrial and biosafety failures at an animal vaccine factory, specifically the use of expired or ineffective disinfectant in 2019 that allowed viable Brucella suis S2 vaccine organisms to persist in waste gas and be carried by prevailing winds, combined with dense surrounding residential and institutional populations, created large‚Äëscale airborne exposure.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/75/10/1845/6604450)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved a live attenuated B. suis S2 vaccine strain whose biological traits permit environmental survival in aerosols; while not a novel species, this vaccine lineage illustrates how established Brucella genotypes can cause extensive subclinical infection when released at scale from manufacturing failures rather than through natural transmission cycles.
Review: review ‚Äì Retain as a major laboratory‚Äërelated outbreak but adjust classification and the country field: re_occurrence is set to ‚ÄòYes‚Äô and re_emergence to ‚ÄòNo‚Äô, because the event reflects accidental aerosol release of an established live vaccine strain (Brucella suis S2) rather than emergence of a novel lineage, and ‚Äòcountries‚Äô is normalised to ‚ÄòChina‚Äô with plant location kept in the summary to match the Country sheet.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/75/10/1845/6604450))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
EPP.common.name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
Host: Renal transplant recipients (HIV-negative adults)
Event.summary: Around 1990‚Äì1991, a Swiss renal transplantation programme reported five cases of Pneumocystis pneumonia among HIV-negative kidney transplant recipients over a 22‚Äëmonth period, after years with no PCP in this cohort, while AIDS patients with active PCP were being seen in the same outpatient facility. A case‚Äìcontrol analysis showed that affected transplant recipients had more encounters in shared waiting and treatment rooms with AIDS patients who had, or later developed, PCP, suggesting transmission from HIV-infected patients to other immunosuppressed hosts. Following recognition of this unusual cluster, greater emphasis was placed on chemoprophylaxis and separation of high-risk transplant patients from AIDS wards, and no similar cluster was reported from this centre in subsequent years. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1777173/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Co-location of renal transplant recipients and AIDS patients with PCP in the same outpatient clinic areas; lack of routine PCP prophylaxis for kidney transplant recipients beyond the early post-transplant period; episodes of acute graft rejection requiring intensified immunosuppression. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (epidemiologic evidence suggesting patient-to-patient spread from AIDS patients with PCP to renal transplant recipients); no specific novel genotype documented at that time. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1777173/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: The Lausanne cluster of five renal transplant recipients with PCP temporally associated with outpatient contact with AIDS patients is real and historically important for suggesting cross-group transmission, but small in absolute size; the year has been approximated to 1990‚Äì1991 to better align with the 22‚Äëmonth period described in the 1991 AIDS report, the host field has been restricted to HIV-negative renal transplant recipients, the event type has been changed from re-emergence to re-occurrence (no evidence of a novel strain), and the PubMed URL has been corrected. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1777173/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
EPP.common.name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
Host: Pediatric renal transplant recipients and an infant with severe underlying disease
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, a pediatric renal transplant unit in Heidelberg, Germany, which had reported virtually no PCP for two decades, experienced three consecutive cases of PCP among kidney transplant recipients over about five months, along with an infant on the same ward who developed PCP in the context of a mitochondriopathy. Single-strand conformation polymorphism typing showed that the three transplant recipients shared two identical P. jirovecii strains, and that the infant harboured multiple strains including these, strongly supporting nosocomial transmission from the infant index case or between the transplant patients themselves. Following recognition of the cluster, the unit introduced routine trimethoprim‚Äìsulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for pediatric renal transplant recipients and reinforced infection-control measures, after which no further linked PCP cases were reported in this population. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/11/2/04-0820_article))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Absence of routine PCP prophylaxis in pediatric kidney transplant protocols owing to concerns about drug toxicity; close spatial clustering of highly immunosuppressed children and an index PCP case on the same ward; prolonged hospitalisations enabling repeated exposures. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (molecular evidence of interhuman spread of specific P. jirovecii strains among paediatric patients); no novel resistance or genotype with clearly altered virulence was identified. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/11/2/04-0820_article))
Review: review: The Heidelberg pediatric renal transplant outbreak, with three paediatric graft recipients and one infant index case, is correctly described and supported by detailed molecular work; it is retained because it provides pivotal evidence for nosocomial transmission in a pediatric setting, but is reclassified as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence and flagged as a relatively small event compared with later national-level incidence shifts, so could be deprioritized if a strict top‚Äë10-by-case-count rule is enforced. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/11/2/04-0820_article))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
EPP.common.name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
Host: Adult kidney transplant recipients
Event.summary: Over an 11‚Äëmonth period from July 2019 to May 2020, a US kidney-transplant centre (Yale) identified an outbreak of 19 Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia cases among kidney transplant recipients, many years after transplantation, in a setting where baseline PCP incidence had been low. Deep multilocus sequence typing with next-generation sequencing of respiratory samples from nine patients revealed coinfection with up to seven distinct P. jirovecii strains per patient and overlapping strain sets across cases, indicating multiple overlapping nosocomial transmission clusters rather than a single clone. A case‚Äìcontrol analysis highlighted frequent transplant-clinic visits, belatacept-based immunosuppression, lower lymphocyte counts and non-White race as important risk factors, and implementation of extended trimethoprim‚Äìsulfamethoxazole prophylaxis and enhanced infection-control measures was followed by interruption of further outbreak-associated PCP cases. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012955/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-volume kidney transplant clinic with chronically immunosuppressed patients, including many receiving monthly belatacept infusions requiring frequent in-person visits; incomplete or time-limited PCP prophylaxis; dense patient‚Äìpatient and patient‚Äìstaff contact networks in outpatient and inpatient settings. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (NGS-based molecular epidemiology demonstrated repeated interhuman spread and complex coinfections with multiple genotypically related strains); no evidence that a single novel, more virulent strain was responsible. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012955/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review: This US kidney-transplant outbreak has been substantially corrected: the event is now dated 2019‚Äì2020 rather than 2010‚Äì2015, the summary emphasises the 19 cases occurring over an 11‚Äëmonth period with next-generation sequencing evidence for multiple overlapping transmission clusters, and the event type has been changed to re-occurrence since the outbreak was driven by clinic exposure and immunosuppression patterns rather than emergence of a single new strain; it should be retained as a major recent example of nosocomial PCP in North America. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012955/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus choriomeningitidis
EPP.common.name: Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus
Host: Human solid-organ transplant recipients; reservoir rodents (likely house mice) not directly identified
Event.summary: In December 2003, four solid-organ transplant recipients in the United States who shared a common donor developed severe febrile illness with meningoencephalitis, hepatitis, and multiorgan failure within weeks of surgery. Laboratory workup identified infection with an identical strain of LCMV in all recipients and in archived donor material, confirming donor-derived transmission in this cluster with high case fatality. The episode concluded without onward community spread but led to heightened awareness of LCMV as a cause of unexplained post‚Äëtransplant encephalitis and multisystem disease and informed subsequent donor‚Äëevaluation guidance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: modern solid-organ transplantation providing an efficient iatrogenic route for LCMV transmission from a single infected donor to multiple highly immunosuppressed recipients; absence of routine LCMV screening in organ donors and unrecognized rodent exposure in the donor‚Äôs environment.
