EPP.scientific.name: Orthomarburgvirus marburgense
EPP.common.name: Marburg virus
Host: Humans (single adult male farmer in Guéckédou Prefecture; extensive traced contacts)
Event.summary: In late July 2021, a 46‑year‑old farmer from Temessadou M’Boké village in Guéckédou Prefecture, southern Guinea, developed acute febrile illness with haemorrhagic signs and died in the community in early August; post‑mortem testing confirmed Marburg virus disease. Intensive investigation and contact tracing identified no additional cases, and the outbreak was declared over after one incubation period plus 21 days had elapsed without new infections. The case represented the first recorded Marburg virus disease in Guinea and in West Africa.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: close human interaction with forest ecosystems in Nzérékoré Region where fruit bats, including Egyptian rousettes, are present; rural health services initially focused on other endemic conditions; but strengthened VHF surveillance after recent Ebola outbreaks enabled rapid laboratory confirmation and targeted response. Internal mechanisms: first documented human spillover of MARV in West Africa, with viral genomes related to Angola‑like bat lineages from Sierra Leone, representing geographic range expansion of existing African lineages rather than emergence of a new species or dramatic shift in virulence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Correctly identified as the first documented Marburg virus disease event in West Africa (Guinea, Western Africa subregion), justifying inclusion despite only a single human case; classified appropriately as intra_continental_emergence for a new subregion, with no intra‑ or inter‑continental spread beyond West Africa.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2021-DON331?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Orthomarburgvirus marburgense
EPP.common.name: Marburg virus
Host: Humans (adult men and a 1‑year‑old child in Ashanti, Savannah and Western regions; healthcare and community contacts)
Event.summary: In June–July 2022, Ghana’s health authorities reported two fatal cases of haemorrhagic fever in Ashanti Region that tested positive for Marburg virus, leading to declaration of the country’s first Marburg virus disease outbreak on 7 July 2022. Further investigation identified a third confirmed case linked to the initial cluster, with infections spanning Ashanti, Savannah and Western regions. Robust surveillance, contact tracing and isolation of suspected cases limited the outbreak to three confirmed infections and two deaths, and Ghana declared the event over in September 2022.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: livelihoods and travel in forest and savannah landscapes where fruit bats occur; population movement between affected regions; concurrent public‑health pressures (COVID‑19, yellow fever, mpox) that complicated response but also left strengthened surveillance infrastructure in place. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of MARV in the Western Africa subregion following the 2021 Guinea case, with genomic analyses showing Ghanaian sequences clustering with the Guinea 2021 virus and other Angola‑like MARV lineages, consistent with repeated spillover from a regional bat reservoir and limited human‑to‑human spread, without clear evidence of major changes in virulence or host range.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event is accurately described (three confirmed cases, two deaths across Ashanti, Savannah and Western regions) and correctly classified as re_occurrence within the Western Africa subregion following Guinea 2021. The previously cited 2021 ECDC CDTR PDF was not Ghana‑specific and has been replaced by WHO and national sources that more directly describe this outbreak.([afro.who.int](https://www.afro.who.int/countries/ghana/news/ghana-declares-end-marburg-virus-disease-outbreak?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Orthomarburgvirus marburgense
EPP.common.name: Marburg virus
Host: Humans (community members in Kie‑Ntem, Litoral, Centro Sur and Wele‑Nzas provinces; healthcare workers and family caregivers)
Event.summary: From late 2022 into early 2023, Equatorial Guinea experienced clusters of unexplained deaths from a haemorrhagic illness in villages of Nsok Nsomo and Ebibeyín Districts, Kié‑Ntem Province, and later in Bata and other districts. On 13 February 2023 the Ministry of Health declared a Marburg virus disease outbreak after a laboratory‑confirmed case, and subsequent investigations documented 16 laboratory‑confirmed and 23 probable cases across multiple mainland provinces with a very high case fatality. After several months of intensive response, including establishment of treatment centres, improved laboratory capacity and extensive contact tracing, the outbreak was declared over in June 2023.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely zoonotic spillover in forested areas of Kié‑Ntem followed by delayed detection in a health system with limited prior filovirus experience; expansion to several widely separated districts, including Bata—an economic hub with major transport links—under conditions of constrained surveillance, incomplete IPC, and funeral‑related exposures. Internal mechanisms: a single MARV lineage causing multiple, partly unlinked chains of transmission with CFR around 90%, representing re‑occurrence of MARV in Middle Africa; despite severity, genomic data support a virus related to known Angola‑like lineages rather than a fundamentally novel variant.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Event exists and is correctly located in Middle Africa/Equatorial Guinea with multiple affected provinces; however, the start year has been updated from 2023 to 2022–2023 and the country start year to [2022] to reflect evidence of a probable index case with symptom onset in late December 2022. Classification as re_occurrence within Middle Africa remains appropriate, as the subregion was already affected (DRC, Angola). Wikipedia links have been replaced by WHO and peer‑reviewed sources.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/31/5/24-1749_article))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthomarburgvirus marburgense
EPP.common.name: Marburg virus
Host: Humans (community members and healthcare workers in Bukoba Rural District, Kagera Region)
Event.summary: In March 2023, the United Republic of Tanzania reported a cluster of severe febrile illness and deaths in villages of Bukoba Rural District, Kagera Region; laboratory testing confirmed Marburg virus disease. The outbreak involved nine cases (eight confirmed, one probable) and six deaths, including infections among healthcare workers, all confined to Bukoba District. Rapid deployment of national and international teams, establishment of a Marburg treatment unit, and strengthened surveillance and border screening enabled containment within weeks, and the outbreak was declared over in June 2023.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: probable exposure to bat reservoirs or contaminated environments in rural Kagera, a region with caves and mining sites; close caregiving and health‑facility contact before MVD was suspected; limited prior national experience managing Marburg outbreaks despite experience with other VHFs. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of MARV in Eastern Africa, with genomes clustering with Ugandan bat and human strains and later with Rwanda 2024 and Tanzania 2025 viruses, indicating repeated localized spillover followed by short human‑to‑human chains rather than a qualitatively new viral phenotype.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event description (nine cases, six deaths, all in Bukoba district) and Eastern Africa/Tanzania coding align with WHO and CDC data, and classification as re_occurrence in an already affected subregion (Kenya, Uganda) with no inter‑continental spread is appropriate. This outbreak remains one of the more substantial post‑2000 events by case numbers and geographic significance.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2023-DON467))

EPP.scientific.name: Orthomarburgvirus marburgense
EPP.common.name: Marburg virus
Host: Humans (predominantly healthcare workers and hospitalized patients in Kigali, plus community contacts in affected districts)
Event.summary: In September 2024, Rwanda declared its first-ever Marburg virus disease outbreak after a cluster of severe viral haemorrhagic fever cases was detected among intensive-care patients and staff in Kigali. Investigation traced the index case to a young adult man with bat‑cave exposure, followed by extensive nosocomial transmission across two major hospitals and limited community spread. By December 2024 the outbreak had caused 66 confirmed cases and 15 deaths, with an unusually high proportion of infections among healthcare workers, and was declared over after 42 days without new cases following the last patient’s recovery.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: zoonotic spillover linked to exposure in a cave inhabited by Egyptian rousette bats, followed by substantial nosocomial amplification in urban ICU settings where VHF-specific triage and full barrier precautions were initially absent; high patient turnover and close staff–patient contact in Kigali hospitals; heavy reliance on invasive procedures; and intense population movement in and out of the capital. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of a MARV lineage in Eastern Africa that was phylogenetically close to viruses from the 2014 Kampala case and later Tanzanian outbreaks, with limited genetic diversity within the outbreak; the scale of transmission was driven primarily by healthcare-associated exposure rather than demonstrably increased viral transmissibility.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Newly added event capturing Rwanda’s first and globally the third‑largest documented MVD outbreak (66 cases, 15 deaths), correctly coded to Eastern Africa/Rwanda with 2024 start and end. Classified as re_occurrence because Eastern Africa was already affected (Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania), and available genomic analyses show close relatedness to earlier regional strains rather than a novel species; clearly among the top‑impact events and should be included.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2024-DON541))

EPP.scientific.name: Orthomarburgvirus marburgense
EPP.common.name: Marburg virus
Host: Humans (rural residents in Katerela and Ruziba villages, Biharamulo District, including women and children; healthcare contacts)
Event.summary: Between December 2024 and January 2025, a cluster of severe haemorrhagic illness and deaths occurred in villages of Biharamulo District, Kagera Region, northwestern Tanzania. On 20 January 2025 the government declared a Marburg virus disease outbreak after laboratory confirmation of a case, and retrospective investigation linked eight additional probable deaths to the same event. In total, ten cases (two confirmed and eight probable), all fatal, were identified, confined to Biharamulo District, and the outbreak was declared over on 13 March 2025 after 42 days without new cases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: limited early recognition of Marburg virus disease in a rural district with recent experience of other VHFs, late health‑seeking behavior with many deaths occurring before diagnostic sampling, and close household caregiving and funeral contact; proximity to wildlife reserves and bat habitats within the Kagera River basin ecosystem; but relatively rapid mobilization of national and international support once the outbreak was declared. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of MARV in Eastern Africa and in Tanzania specifically, with genomic data showing the 2025 viruses to be highly similar to those from the 2023 Tanzanian and 2024 Rwandan outbreaks, indicating repeated localized spillover and limited human‑to‑human transmission; the 100% observed CFR likely reflects under‑ascertainment of milder infections rather than a step‑change in virulence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Newly added event; timing (symptom onset from December 2024 with outbreak declared January 2025), location (Biharamulo District, Kagera Region) and final size (10 cases, all fatal) match WHO and peer‑reviewed genomic analyses. Correctly classified as re_occurrence in Eastern Africa and in a country that already experienced MVD in 2023; not an intra‑continental emergence. Impact (10 cases, 100% CFR) places it clearly among the major post‑1990 events.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2025-DON559))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthomarburgvirus marburgense
EPP.common.name: Marburg virus
Host: Humans (community members and healthcare workers in Jinka, Malle and Dasench woredas, South Ethiopia Region, and Hawassa in Sidama Region)
Event.summary: In November 2025, Ethiopia declared its first-ever Marburg virus disease outbreak after laboratory confirmation of suspected viral haemorrhagic fever cases in Jinka town, South Ethiopia Region. The outbreak, which began with symptom onset in late October 2025 in an adult patient, eventually involved 19 cases (14 confirmed and five probable) and 14 deaths across South Ethiopia Region and Hawassa in Sidama Region. Following intensive response efforts – including activation of national and regional emergency operations, deployment of a mobile laboratory, contact tracing of hundreds of exposed individuals, and establishment of treatment centres – the outbreak was declared over on 26 January 2026 after 42 days without new cases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: emergence in a remote area with limited prior VHF experience, likely linked to bat reservoirs in caves or other roost sites; delayed early recognition and health‑seeking, with several deaths before laboratory confirmation; movement of patients between woredas and to Hawassa; and constrained IPC capacity in some facilities prior to surge support. Internal mechanisms: first documented human MVD outbreak in Ethiopia but occurring in an already affected Eastern Africa subregion; MARV sequences cluster within known African lineages, and transmission patterns indicate one or a few zoonotic introductions followed by human‑to‑human spread in households and health facilities, without evidence of a qualitatively new viral phenotype.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Newly added high‑impact event accurately summarized as Ethiopia’s first MVD outbreak (19 cases, 14 deaths) starting in late 2025, correctly coded to Eastern Africa/Ethiopia and classified as re_occurrence within an already affected subregion. Given its size, geographic novelty and documented multi‑district spread, it clearly belongs among the major emergence events and should be retained, while not being misclassified as intra‑continental or inter‑continental emergence.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON592))

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus C
EPP.common.name: Poliovirus (poliovirus 1; poliovirus 2; poliovirus 3)
Host: Humans, predominantly children in conflict-affected and hard‑to‑reach areas of Borno State
Event.summary: In 2016, after more than two years without detected wild poliovirus, Nigeria’s Borno State reported four WPV1 cases in children from areas long inaccessible due to Boko Haram–related insecurity, revealing that low-level transmission had persisted undetected since at least 2011 and that circulating type 2 vaccine‑derived poliovirus (cVDPV2) was also present in the same region.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/06-october-2016-polio-nigeria-en?utm_source=openai)) These detections prompted declaration of a national and Lake Chad subregional public health emergency and triggered large-scale synchronized outbreak responses using bOPV and mOPV2, with intense efforts to reach children in partially liberated settlements and among displaced populations.([afro.who.int](https://www.afro.who.int/news/polio-outbreak-response-assessment-and-lake-chad-coordination-review-meeting-underway-abuja?utm_source=openai)) Through innovative surveillance (including environmental sampling and mobile-phone–supported AFP reporting) and multiple SIAs, WPV1 transmission in Borno was again interrupted after 2016 and cVDPV2 incidence fell markedly, allowing Nigeria to be certified free of wild poliovirus in 2020, although other cVDPV2 lineages later emerged elsewhere in the region.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/66/wr/mm6607a2.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Armed insurgency, population displacement around Lake Chad, and areas inaccessible to health workers left large pockets of children unreached by both routine immunization and SIAs, permitting long-term undetected circulation of WPV1 and OPV2‑derived lineages.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/66/wr/mm6607a2.htm?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of residual WPV1 and genetically divergent cVDPV2 strains (with multiple nucleotide changes from Sabin 2 and restored neurovirulence) represents viral evolution under selection in severely under‑immunized populations, fitting the re-emergence category through novel strain/genotype emergence coupled with geographic persistence in a security‑compromised reservoir.
Review: review – Event correctly highlights the discovery of hidden WPV1 transmission and cVDPV2 in Borno in 2016 and the intensive Lake Chad response, but the original version incorrectly implied confirmed cases in Niger, Chad, Cameroon and the Central African Republic starting in 2016; those countries mainly participated in synchronized response activities, and their later cVDPV2 outbreaks are better captured under the broader 2017–2023 African cVDPV2 event.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/66/wr/mm6607a2.htm?utm_source=openai)) Countries and subregion have therefore been restricted to Nigeria / Western Africa, and the row is flagged for review because, while epidemiologically important, its small paralytic case count (four WPV1 cases plus limited cVDPV2) means it may fall below the top ten post‑1990 polio emergence events when ranked purely by impact.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus C
EPP.common.name: Poliovirus (poliovirus 1; poliovirus 2; poliovirus 3)
Host: Humans, mainly children in conflict-affected governorates with very low type‑2 immunity
Event.summary: In June 2017, Syria detected an outbreak of circulating vaccine‑derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) causing paralytic disease in Deir ez‑Zor governorate, years after the country had eliminated wild polio and following the global withdrawal of type‑2–containing OPV in 2016.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927908/?utm_source=openai)) Genomic analysis showed the outbreak strain differed by about 22 VP1 nucleotides from Sabin 2, indicating roughly a year of undetected circulation in an extremely under‑immunized population before the first recognized case, ultimately paralyzing 74 children in Deir ez‑Zor, Raqqa and Homs.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927908/?utm_source=openai)) A focused emergency response—with multiple rounds of mOPV2 in affected and neighboring areas and IPV campaigns among young children—interrupted transmission by late 2017, with no new cases in 2018 and the outbreak declared stopped after extensive follow‑up and external review.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927908/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Prolonged civil conflict, mass displacement, difficult access for vaccinators, and pre‑existing gaps in routine immunization led to very low type‑2 immunity, especially after the global tOPV–bOPV switch removed OPV2 from routine use; these conditions allowed a vaccine‑derived lineage to circulate unchecked.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927908/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreak virus was a cVDPV2 lineage with substantial genetic divergence and restored neurovirulence relative to Sabin 2, representing classic novel strain/genotype emergence from vaccine virus and therefore qualifying as re-emergence driven by internal viral evolution.
Review: retain – Large cVDPV2 outbreak (74 paralytic cases) in a conflict setting that directly illustrates the risks created by the tOPV-to-bOPV switch and severe immunity gaps; appropriately classified as re-emergence with high-quality WHO and CDC documentation.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927908/?utm_source=openai)) Minor source refinement has been made by replacing general background articles with EMRO outbreak situation reports; no further structural changes needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (ostrich farm and abattoir workers in Oudtshoorn, Western Cape Province)
Event.summary: In October–November 1996, South Africa reported a large occupational CCHF outbreak among workers at an ostrich farm and slaughterhouse in the Oudtshoorn area of Western Cape, with around 17 laboratory‑confirmed human cases, more than 30 hospitalizations and at least one death. Infection was linked to handling of viremic ostriches and crushing of Hyalomma ticks during slaughter, and secondary transmission in healthcare settings was limited by the rapid institution of barrier nursing once the etiology was recognized. The outbreak led to temporary restrictions on South African ostrich meat exports and prompted extensive changes to tick‑control and biosafety practices in the ostrich industry, preventing further abattoir‑based clusters of similar magnitude.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high densities of Hyalomma ticks on ostriches, intensive handling of tick‑infested birds and their blood in an abattoir with initially limited awareness of CCHF risk, and strong market demand for ostrich products combined to amplify occupational exposure. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak was caused by long‑established Africa‑2 lineage CCHFV circulating in South African livestock and wildlife; there is no evidence for a novel strain or marked change in viral virulence, so this is best interpreted as a major re‑occurrence driven by work practices and trade patterns rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain: Newly added event capturing the largest documented human CCHF outbreak in South Africa and its associated trade impact on the ostrich industry. Classified as re‑occurrence in a long‑endemic country, consistent with historical data showing human CCHF in South Africa since the early 1980s and absence of evidence for a novel viral variant.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (rural residents, agricultural workers and healthcare staff in southern Russia, especially Stavropol and Rostov regions)
Event.summary: After a period of relatively low reported incidence, CCHF re‑emerged in southern Russia in 1999 with a localized outbreak in Rostov Province and additional cases in Stavropol, marking renewed activity in long‑known foci. Through the early 2000s, sustained transmission in the Southern and North Caucasus federal districts produced hundreds of cases and dozens of deaths; for example, in 2006 the Southern Federal District alone reported about 190–200 human cases, and cumulative 1999–2006 counts in Stavropol and Rostov each reached several hundred cases. Increased awareness, improved laboratory diagnosis and targeted vector control later reduced reported incidence somewhat, but sporadic cases and smaller clusters continued beyond 2006 and up to at least 2020.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion and increased activity of Hyalomma tick populations in southern steppe zones, climatic warming, changes in land use and livestock management, and greater human presence in tick habitats drove higher exposure, while socioeconomic changes after the Soviet period weakened some public‑health and veterinary controls. Internal mechanisms: sequencing shows circulation of Europe‑1 CCHFV lineages that have been present in the region for decades; the surge in human disease reflects re‑occurrence and geographic spread of existing genotypes rather than emergence of a novel viral strain.
Review: retain: Newly added high‑impact event summarizing re‑occurrence and geographic expansion of CCHF in southern Russia, with large cumulative case numbers and substantial mortality. Classified as re‑occurrence in a historically endemic subregion (Eastern Europe), consistent with molecular data showing long‑standing Europe‑1 lineages and with WHO/EID descriptions of increasing incidence rather than a new introduction.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (livestock workers, butchers, household contacts and healthcare workers)
Event.summary: Although CCHFV infection in livestock and ticks had been recognized in Iran since the 1970s, the first diagnosed human CCHF case was reported in 1999, quickly followed by additional cases and recognition of endemic transmission in several provinces. Between 1999 and 2011, around 870 human cases were reported nationally, with intense activity in Sistan‑va‑Baluchestan and notable nosocomial clusters in Fars, Isfahan, Mashhad and Birjand during the 2000s. Strengthened national surveillance, laboratory capacity and infection‑prevention measures in referral hospitals reduced the size of hospital outbreaks over time, but Iran continues to report sporadic and cluster‑based human CCHF cases annually.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of livestock trade and slaughter (often without adequate tick control), traditional animal‑handling practices, and initial gaps in barrier precautions in hospitals facilitated both zoonotic spillover and nosocomial transmission once human cases began to be recognized. Internal mechanisms: Asia‑1 lineage CCHFV strains had been enzootic in Iranian livestock and ticks for decades, and there is no clear evidence for a new viral genotype underlying the 1999 re‑appearance; the pattern is best explained as re‑occurrence in a previously known subregion driven by external and healthcare‑system factors.
Review: retain: Event accurately describes the major re‑occurrence of CCHF in Iran in 1999 and subsequent endemic transmission, which accounts for hundreds of cases and frequent nosocomial clusters. Emergence type has been corrected from first_detection/re_emergence to re_occurrence to align with project definitions and the documented long‑standing presence of CCHFV in Iranian livestock and ticks; geographic coding (Southern Asia, Iran) and sources are appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (abattoir workers, butchers, livestock handlers, rural residents and healthcare workers)
Event.summary: Following the first recognized human CCHF cases in 1976, Pakistan saw a marked rise in reported cases and outbreaks from around 2000 onwards, including notable nosocomial clusters such as a 2002 Rawalpindi outbreak linked to a surgical patient. Throughout the 2000s and early 2010s, dozens of cases were reported most years, with heightened activity around Eid‑ul‑Azha when large numbers of animals are slaughtered and moved through informal channels. By 2013, Pakistan was considered one of the highest‑burden CCHF countries globally, with persistent seasonal outbreaks and frequent infections among healthcare workers despite progressive improvements in surveillance and infection‑prevention practices.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high volumes of animal movement and slaughter during religious festivals, weak tick control in smallholder and cross‑border livestock trade, and gaps in hospital infection‑control programs facilitated repeated zoonotic and nosocomial transmission. Internal mechanisms: Pakistan’s CCHFV strains belong mainly to the Asia‑1 lineage and appear long‑established; resurgence after 2000 reflects re‑occurrence and geographic spread of existing genotypes, not emergence of a novel viral variant.
Review: retain: This row captures Pakistan’s substantial CCHF burden since 2000, which ranks among the highest globally by case counts. The previous dual coding as both re_occurrence and re_emergence has been simplified to re_occurrence only, consistent with evidence that endemic Asia‑1 lineages, not new genotypes, underlie these outbreaks; all geographic fields and the main WHO/EMRO and EID sources remain appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (mainly rural residents and agricultural workers in the Kelkit Valley and surrounding north‑central provinces)
Event.summary: CCHF was first recognized clinically in Türkiye in 2002, when an outbreak of severe febrile illness in the Kelkit Valley was confirmed virologically, and thereafter the country experienced the largest recorded national CCHF epidemic worldwide. Between 2002 and late 2015, nearly 9,800 human cases with around a 5% case‑fatality ratio were reported, peaking in the mid‑2000s and concentrated in north‑central Anatolia where Hyalomma ticks and livestock exposures are common. Intensive public‑health response including tick‑bite prevention campaigns, clinician training, strengthened laboratory diagnosis and better supportive care gradually reduced annual incidence and mortality, although seasonal cases have continued.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: agro‑ecological conditions in the Kelkit Valley favorable to Hyalomma ticks, extensive smallholder livestock farming, and increased human–tick contact in rural areas allowed rapid amplification once CCHF was recognized, while heightened surveillance initially inflated reported incidence. Internal mechanisms: Europe‑1 lineage CCHFV strains circulating in Turkish ticks and livestock appear closely related to those in neighboring Balkan countries; current evidence indicates re‑occurrence and geographic expansion of existing genotypes rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: retain: Türkiye’s prolonged epidemic is the single largest CCHF event globally by number of reported cases and is essential for a top‑10 list. Event type has been reclassified from first_detection/re_emergence to re_occurrence to reflect that CCHFV was already established in the wider Western Asia–Balkans region and that available data do not support a distinct new viral lineage in Türkiye. A generic German‑language Wikipedia URL was removed from the source list, leaving primary outbreak and review articles as the main references.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (butchers, livestock handlers, family caregivers and urban residents in Nouakchott and nearby areas)
Event.summary: Between February and August 2003, Mauritania experienced a major CCHF outbreak with 38 human cases (confirmed and probable) and an overall case‑fatality ratio near 30%, the majority of cases residing in the capital, Nouakchott. The epidemic began with a hospital‑based cluster linked to a butcher, followed by further nosocomial and community cases among butchers, livestock workers and family members, revealing previously unrecognized urban transmission. Rapid implementation of barrier nursing, case isolation, slaughterhouse hygiene measures and public risk communication helped to halt the outbreak, and only sporadic CCHF cases have since been reported from the country.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high‑risk slaughtering practices and direct exposure to blood and tissues of infected small ruminants in and around Nouakchott’s abattoirs, combined with limited early recognition of CCHF and inadequate infection‑control measures in hospitals, facilitated both animal‑to‑human and nosocomial transmission. Internal mechanisms: sequence data place Mauritanian viruses within Africa‑3 lineages that also circulate in other West and southern African countries; the 2003 epidemic is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence and amplification of established regional genotypes rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: retain: Newly added event representing the first large, predominantly urban CCHF outbreak recognized in West Africa, with substantial mortality and clear public‑health impact. Classified as re_occurrence within Western Africa, consistent with earlier evidence of CCHFV in the region; geographic fields align with the UNSD Western Africa subregion and sources are high‑quality outbreak descriptions.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (rural resident in northeastern Greece exposed to ticks and possibly livestock)
Event.summary: In June 2008, Greece reported its first recognized fatal CCHF case in a woman from the Rhodopi area of northeastern Greece, despite previous isolation of a seemingly low‑pathogenic CCHFV strain (AP92) from ticks and high human seroprevalence in parts of the country. The patient likely acquired infection from a tick bite or contact with infected animal tissues in a rural setting, and virologic analysis showed that the responsible strain (Rhodopi‑2008) clustered with pathogenic Balkan CCHFV lineages and differed substantially from AP92. After this event, enhanced surveillance documented continued virus circulation in ticks and livestock but no further severe confirmed human cases for many years, suggesting persistent but low clinical incidence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movements of infected livestock and ticks across Balkan borders and expansion of Hyalomma‑infested habitats created opportunities for introduction of pathogenic CCHFV lineages into northeastern Greece, where people engage in outdoor agricultural activities. Internal mechanisms: the emergence of a pathogenic CCHFV strain distinct from the historically detected AP92 genotype in Greece is consistent with re‑emergence driven by strain differences within the Europe‑lineage viruses rather than de novo evolution after arrival in Greece.
Review: review: This single‑case but virologically important event marks the first severe, laboratory‑confirmed CCHF in Greece and the appearance of a pathogenic strain distinct from the earlier AP92 genotype. It has been re‑classified as re_emergence (reflecting strain change in a previously known Southern Europe subregion) and intra_continental_emergence has been set to No to comply with the rule that spread to a new country within an already affected subregion should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence. Given its small case count compared with Turkey, Iran, Russia, Afghanistan and Iraq, it is flagged for review if a strict top‑10 cut is enforced, but is epidemiologically informative for Europe.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (rural residents, relatives caring for patients, and healthcare workers in Kordofan region)
Event.summary: In late 2008, a nosocomial outbreak of hemorrhagic fever in a rural hospital in Al‑Fulah, West Kordofan, was confirmed as CCHF, with multiple healthcare workers and family caregivers infected while caring for a butcher who likely acquired infection from slaughtering infected livestock; additional sporadic cases and small clusters were recognized in nearby areas through 2009. Molecular characterization revealed CCHFV strains belonging to Africa‑3 lineages related to viruses from other parts of Africa, indicating previously unrecognized enzootic circulation in Sudan. Subsequent Sudanese epidemics in 2010–2011 involved larger numbers of cases in Kordofan, but the 2008–2009 events represent the first documented human CCHF emergence in Northern Africa and led to heightened clinical awareness and infection‑control measures in affected hospitals.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intense contact between pastoralist communities and viremic livestock, traditional bedside caregiving practices in rural hospitals, and severe limitations in infection‑prevention infrastructure allowed efficient nosocomial and household transmission once CCHF reached healthcare settings. Internal mechanisms: multiple Africa‑3 lineage variants were detected, suggesting long‑standing enzootic maintenance and movement of viruses with livestock rather than recent evolution of a novel strain; emergence in humans in Sudan is therefore best interpreted as intra‑continental emergence into a previously unaffected African subregion.
Review: review: Event correctly captures the first recognized human CCHF outbreaks in Sudan and, by UNSD definition, the first emergence of CCHF in the Northern Africa subregion; thus intra_continental_emergence has been set to Yes and re_emergence to No (earlier coding as re_emergence was inconsistent with lineage data showing established Africa‑3 viruses). However, case numbers (tens rather than hundreds) are modest compared with the largest national epidemics, so this row is flagged for review if the dataset must be pruned to 10 globally most impactful events; users may alternatively wish to expand the time span to 2008–2011 to encompass the larger 2010–2011 Sudan epidemics.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (index livestock handler, family members and hospital staff in and around Ahmedabad, Gujarat)
Event.summary: In December 2010–January 2011, India detected its first confirmed human CCHF outbreak near Ahmedabad in Gujarat, beginning with a probable livestock‑exposed index patient and followed by secondary nosocomial infections in a nurse, a physician and other hospital contacts; about five confirmed and several additional suspected cases were reported, with high case‑fatality. Molecular investigations identified CCHFV of the Asia‑1 lineage closely related to strains from Pakistan and Afghanistan in patient samples, local ticks and domestic animals, demonstrating establishment of a new endemic focus in western India. Aggressive infection‑control measures, contact tracing and tick‑control interventions limited onward transmission, although sporadic cases and small rural outbreaks have since been reported from Gujarat and neighboring states.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction or amplification of CCHFV‑infected livestock and ticks around Ahmedabad, close human contact with animals, and initial lack of CCHF‑specific infection‑control protocols in hospitals enabled both zoonotic spillover and nosocomial spread. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses show that Indian viruses fall within the Asia‑1 lineage without clear evidence of novel genetic traits; the episode is best viewed as re‑occurrence and geographic range expansion of existing regional genotypes into India, with healthcare‑associated transmission acting as an amplifying context.
Review: review: This event is epidemiologically important as the first confirmed human CCHF outbreak in India and demonstrates spread of Asia‑1 viruses from neighboring countries into Gujarat, but involves relatively few cases compared with major national epidemics. Event type has been adjusted from first_detection/re_emergence to re_occurrence within Southern Asia to align with project rules (no intra‑continental emergence for spread to a new country inside an already affected subregion). Retain if geographic expansion into India is a priority; otherwise, it is a candidate for exclusion under a strict top‑10 impact cut.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (livestock owners, butchers, household contacts and healthcare workers, mainly in Herat, Kabul and other high‑risk provinces)
Event.summary: Although Afghanistan reported sporadic CCHF cases from the late 1990s onward, national surveillance documented a marked surge between 2016 and 2018, with 163 reported cases in 2016, 245 in 2017 and 483 in 2018, many of them severe and with high case‑fatality. Cases clustered in provinces such as Herat and Kabul and were strongly associated with animal slaughter, particularly around Eid‑ul‑Adha, as well as with contact with infected livestock, ticks and blood products; healthcare workers were also affected. Reactive control efforts—including public risk communication, improved infection‑prevention practices and limited tick‑control campaigns—helped reduce incidence somewhat after 2018, but recurrent seasonal spikes continue, and Afghanistan remains one of the highest‑burden CCHF countries globally.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of small‑scale livestock keeping in peri‑urban areas, unregulated slaughter during religious festivals, conflict‑related disruption of veterinary and public‑health services, and limited laboratory capacity for early diagnosis contributed to large seasonal outbreaks once surveillance intensified. Internal mechanisms: Afghan viruses belong mainly to Asia‑1 lineages closely related to strains circulating in Iran and Pakistan; the 2016–2018 surge is best characterized as re‑occurrence and amplification of endemic lineages under changing social and ecological conditions, not emergence of a novel strain.
Review: retain: Newly added event capturing one of the largest recent national CCHF burdens, with nearly 900 reported cases over three years and very high mortality. Classified as re_occurrence in a long‑endemic Southern Asia country and strongly recommended for inclusion among the global top 10 in terms of impact; dates, subregion coding and sources were checked against Afghanistan’s National Disease Surveillance and Response data and recent analytical studies.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (rural residents and health‑facility patients in Mopti Region)
Event.summary: In January–February 2020, Mali notified WHO of an outbreak of suspected CCHF in Mopti Region, with 14 suspected cases and seven deaths, three of which were laboratory‑confirmed as CCHFV infection, yielding an apparent case‑fatality of about 50%. The index cases were linked to rural villages with livestock exposure, and investigation suggested both tick‑borne infection and person‑to‑person transmission through blood contact, raising concern about previously undocumented CCHFV circulation in central Mali. Rapid implementation of case isolation, contact tracing, community risk communication and reinforcement of infection‑prevention practices in local healthcare facilities appears to have prevented a larger secondary wave, although the true extent of enzootic virus circulation remains uncertain.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: unregulated livestock movements, minimal tick‑control practices and weak diagnostic capacity likely allowed silent circulation of CCHFV in animals prior to the recognition of severe human disease; concurrent attention to the emerging COVID‑19 pandemic may also have delayed thorough investigation. Internal mechanisms: available sequence data link Malian viruses to Africa‑3 lineages already found in West Africa, suggesting re‑occurrence and geographic spread of existing regional genotypes into a new national focus rather than emergence of a novel variant.
Review: review: This small but high‑fatality outbreak documents the first confirmed human CCHF cases in Mali and extension of Africa‑3 lineage viruses into a new West African country, but involves few confirmed cases relative to larger regional epidemics (e.g. Mauritania 2003, Afghanistan 2016–2018, Iraq 2022–2023). Emergence type has been re‑coded from intra_continental_emergence/re_emergence to re_occurrence in Western Africa, reflecting previous CCHFV activity in neighboring countries. The row is flagged for review if only the very largest global events are to be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: Crimean Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Host: Humans (butchers, livestock handlers, rural residents and healthcare workers across multiple governorates)
Event.summary: CCHF has been recognized in Iraq since at least 1979, but in 2022–2023 the country experienced its largest recorded outbreak, with WHO reporting over 200 cases and around 27 deaths by May 2022 and later national and regional summaries indicating roughly 1,300–1,400 suspected cases and more than 100 deaths for 2022 alone. Cases occurred across many governorates, especially in the south, and were strongly associated with slaughtering and handling of cattle, sheep and goats, with multiple nosocomial infections among healthcare workers during the peak. A multi‑sectoral One Health response involving intensified tick‑control on animals, safer slaughterhouse practices, improved laboratory capacity and broad public risk communication reduced incidence somewhat in 2023, but Iraq remains a major CCHF focus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: suspension or reduction of routine veterinary tick‑control and livestock spraying during the COVID‑19 pandemic, high demand for animal slaughter around religious festivals, and weak occupational protections for butchers and farmers markedly increased human exposure to infected ticks and animal blood. Internal mechanisms: Iraq’s CCHFV strains fall within Asia‑1 lineages already known from the region; the 2022–2023 surge is interpreted as a re‑occurrence and geographic/intensity expansion of endemic viruses rather than emergence of a new genotype, although higher exposure intensity likely contributed to severe disease and high case‑fatality.
Review: retain: This is Iraq’s largest documented CCHF epidemic and one of the highest recent global case burdens, with over a thousand suspected cases and more than 100 deaths, making it clearly among the top 10 events by impact. Event type has been simplified to re_occurrence only (earlier co‑coding as re_emergence lacked evidence for major viral change), and geographic fields and WHO/EMRO sources remain appropriate and specific to this episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In summer 2007, a traveler returning from India introduced chikungunya virus into the Emilia‑Romagna region of northeastern Italy, where Aedes albopictus was already established. Local transmission in the villages of Castiglione di Cervia and Castiglione di Ravenna produced about 200 symptomatic confirmed or probable cases, representing the first documented autochthonous chikungunya outbreak in Europe. Intensive vector control, blood safety measures and the onset of cooler weather helped interrupt transmission by late September 2007.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/82980/cdc_82980_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑established Aedes albopictus populations in temperate Italy, combined with importation of a viremic traveler from an epidemic area in India, created conditions for local transmission. Warm summer temperatures, suburban housing with gardens and water containers, and high human mobility within Emilia‑Romagna facilitated mosquito–human contact. Internal mechanisms: The imported virus belonged to the ECSA/Indian Ocean lineage, adapted for efficient transmission by Aedes albopictus, demonstrating that this lineage could sustain transmission in a temperate European setting and highlighting the role of vector adaptation in enabling inter‑continental emergence.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/82980/cdc_82980_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Confirmed as the first documented autochthonous chikungunya outbreak in Europe and therefore classified as an inter‑continental emergence event for this continent. The previous “re‑emergence” flag was removed because Europe was not a previously affected subregion. A nonessential Italian‑language Wikipedia link was dropped in favor of peer‑reviewed and official national/European sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: plague bacillus
Host: Humans (bubonic plague in rural Maharashtra and primarily pneumonic plague in the city of Surat and clusters in other states and Delhi).
Event.summary: In late August 1994, after decades without recognised human plague in India, bubonic cases appeared in Mamla village, Beed District (Maharashtra), followed by a large urban pneumonic outbreak in Surat (Gujarat) and smaller clusters in several other states and the National Capital Territory of Delhi. Over the following two months, India reported thousands of suspected cases nationally; WHO and CDC analyses estimate 693 laboratory‑supported cases and 56 deaths from Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Delhi, although the epidemic’s social impact was magnified by mass migration and international alarm. By late October 1994, intensified antibiotic treatment, vector control, disinfection, and environmental sanitation campaigns halted transmission and WHO declared the outbreak over.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: urban flooding, refuse accumulation and poor drainage in Surat and other towns, which caused rodent die‑offs and flea dispersal; very high population density and overcrowded housing; inadequate early surveillance, clinical suspicion and laboratory capacity for plague; rapid mass internal migration that spread fear and may have disseminated infection; and intense media coverage that amplified socio‑economic disruption. Internal mechanisms: epidemiologic patterns are compatible with reactivation or importation of existing Y. pestis lineages into ecologically favourable urban environments, with flea‑borne transmission and person‑to‑person spread in pneumonic foci, but there is no strong evidence of a new genotype, increased intrinsic virulence or drug resistance.
Review: retain – This is correctly identified as one of the most impactful modern human plague outbreaks by case numbers and global socio‑economic disruption, with ≈693 lab‑supported cases and 56 deaths and substantial internal migration.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5585619/?utm_source=openai)) I recommend removing the non‑authoritative aggregator site (everything.explained.today) from the source list and relying on WHO and CDC primary reports and peer‑reviewed analyses instead.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: plague bacillus
Host: Humans (predominantly pneumonic plague with substantial numbers of bubonic and septicemic cases) in urban and peri‑urban settings across multiple districts, including Antananarivo and Toamasina, as well as traditional highland foci.
Event.summary: In August 2017, an index patient with plague illness travelled by public transport from the endemic highlands to the coastal city of Toamasina via the capital Antananarivo, seeding pneumonic cases along the route and triggering an unprecedented urban epidemic. Between August and November 2017, Madagascar reported roughly 2,400–2,700 suspected, probable and confirmed plague cases and about 200 deaths nationwide, with around three‑quarters classified as pneumonic and many occurring in densely populated urban districts that had little prior experience with plague. Massive multi‑sectoral control measures—including rapid case detection and free antibiotic treatment, chemoprophylaxis of tens of thousands of contacts, cancellation of mass gatherings, large‑scale vector and rodent control, and international logistical support—brought the urban pneumonic wave under control by late 2017, although seasonal bubonic cases continue to recur annually in highland foci.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intense human mobility between endemic rural highlands and major cities in overcrowded public transport; high population density and poor sanitation in urban neighbourhoods of Antananarivo and Toamasina; delayed recognition and laboratory confirmation of early pneumonic cases, allowing substantial exposure before control measures were activated; limited baseline preparedness for plague in large cities that had previously seen mainly sporadic imported cases. Internal mechanisms: repeated introductions of Y. pestis from highland foci into urban centres, with a clinical distribution skewed strongly toward highly transmissible pneumonic disease, but genetic investigations indicate multiple existing genotypes rather than a single novel strain, and susceptibility to frontline antibiotics remained generally preserved.
Review: review – This event is unquestionably one of the largest and most consequential modern plague outbreaks, with ≈2,400–2,700 reported cases and ≈200 deaths and a unique pattern of widespread urban pneumonic transmission.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/02-october-2017-plague-madagascar-en)) I have reclassified it from re_emergence to re_occurrence because available genomic and epidemiologic analyses indicate expansion of existing highland lineages into new urban settings under favourable social and environmental conditions, without clear evidence of a novel strain, resistance phenotype, or new host system. Duplicate WHO URLs were removed from the event’s source list, and reliance is placed on WHO DONs and peer‑reviewed outbreak reports; the Wikipedia entry is acceptable as a secondary source but not essential for core epidemiologic data.

EPP.scientific.name: Plasmodium spp.
EPP.common.name: malaria parasites
Host: Humans (mainly Plasmodium vivax)
Event.summary: After Greece was certified malaria-free in the mid-20th century, clusters of locally acquired Plasmodium vivax cases reappeared beginning in 2009 in agricultural and wetland areas such as Evrotas (Laconia, Peloponnese), followed by further foci and sporadic autochthonous infections through 2013. Transmission persisted over multiple seasons with more than 60 locally acquired cases documented and additional introduced cases among migrant workers, indicating re-establishment of limited P. vivax transmission in receptive areas. Intensified vector control, active case detection, and targeted chemoprophylaxis campaigns eventually interrupted these local chains of transmission, and no large sustained foci have been reported afterwards, although occasional introduced or sporadic local cases continue to be detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of P. vivax by migrant agricultural workers from endemic countries, combined with receptive ecological conditions (wetlands, irrigated agriculture, presence of competent Anopheles vectors) and reduced vigilance in a country considered malaria-free; economic austerity may have further constrained public-health capacity. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for markedly novel parasite genotypes or drug resistance driving this event; it is best characterized as geographic range re-occupation driven by human movement and ecology rather than parasite evolutionary change.
Review: retain – event appropriately describes the re-occurrence of locally acquired P. vivax malaria in Greece after mid-20th-century elimination and is among the most salient post-1990 European malaria events. Geography (Southern Europe; Greece), timing (2009–2013), and classification as re-occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence or re-emergence) are consistent with WHO/ECDC reports. No data corrections required; minor case-count uncertainties (exact total of locally acquired vs introduced cases) are within the acceptable range for this level of aggregation.

EPP.scientific.name: Plasmodium spp.
EPP.common.name: malaria parasites
Host: Humans (Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum)
Event.summary: Following unprecedented monsoon rains and flooding starting in June 2022, Pakistan experienced a dramatic surge in malaria, with WHO reporting more than 3.4 million suspected cases by August and subsequent estimates indicating roughly a five-fold increase in incidence and about 2–2.6 million additional malaria cases in 2022 compared with 2021. The outbreak was concentrated in heavily flooded provinces such as Sindh and Balochistan, where large displaced populations were exposed to extensive mosquito breeding sites in stagnant water and had limited access to health services. Emergency responses included mass distribution of rapid diagnostic tests and antimalarials, deployment of mobile clinics, and intensified vector control in camps and flood-affected communities, which gradually reduced, but did not fully eliminate, the elevated transmission risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extreme rainfall and large-scale flooding linked to climate variability and climate change, destruction of housing and health infrastructure, population displacement into temporary shelters with poor vector protection, and expansion of Anopheles breeding habitats in flooded areas all contributed to the surge. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel parasite genotype or drug-resistance trait has been identified as driving this increase; it represents a classic environmentally and socially driven re-occurrence of malaria in endemic areas.
Review: retain – event correctly highlights one of the largest recent environmentally driven malaria surges worldwide and a clear example of climate- and disaster-driven re-occurrence. WHO and World Malaria Report data confirm an approximately four- to five-fold increase in malaria incidence and roughly 2–2.6 million additional cases in 2022 compared with 2021 in Pakistan following catastrophic monsoon flooding. Classification as re-occurrence (with no intra-/inter-continental emergence or re-emergence) is appropriate; no corrections to timing, geography, or drivers were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Mucorales
EPP.common.name: mucoralean fungi
Host: Humans, predominantly adults with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus and hematologic malignancies, including transplant and cancer patients in tertiary centers
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through around 2010, India experienced a steady and marked rise in reported invasive mucormycosis cases, particularly among patients with poorly controlled diabetes and immunocompromising conditions. Multi-center case series and autopsy studies documented increasing incidence in tertiary care hospitals over this period, with mucormycosis transitioning from a rare curiosity to one of the most frequent invasive mold infections in some Indian centers. By the late 2000s and early 2010s, India’s estimated mucormycosis incidence had risen to many times higher than that of most developed countries, setting the stage for later explosive outbreaks during the COVID-19 era.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid urbanization, high and growing prevalence of poorly controlled diabetes, expanded use of corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapies, and improved mycological diagnostic capacity contributed both to true increases in incidence and to better recognition; environmental exposure to thermotolerant Mucorales in tropical/subtropical climates may further elevate baseline risk. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain was identified as the primary cause of this long-term increase; rather, existing Mucorales species (notably Rhizopus arrhizus and Apophysomyces spp.) expanded their clinical impact in susceptible human hosts as underlying risk factors became more common.
Review: Retain – This row appropriately summarizes the well-documented long-term increase in mucormycosis incidence in India from the 1990s through about 2010 using large tertiary-centre series and burden estimates; geography and timeframe are reasonable, classification as re-occurrence (driven by rising diabetes, steroid and immunosuppressive use, and improved diagnostics) is consistent with definitions, and the sources are suitable. No substantive corrections are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Mucorales
EPP.common.name: mucoralean fungi
Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2004]
Host: Adults and pediatric patients with hematological malignancies and bone marrow transplantation in a hematology–oncology unit
Event.summary: In the mid-2000s, a hematology–oncology and bone marrow transplant unit at Queen Mary Hospital in Hong Kong identified a 6‑month outbreak of intestinal infection and colonization by Rhizopus microsporus in 12 patients receiving chemotherapy or transplant care. Intensified surveillance and a case–control study linked disease to ingestion of heavily contaminated oral allopurinol tablets and, to a lesser extent, certain prepackaged ready-to-eat foods, with isolates from patients, tablets, food and cornstarch excipient sharing closely related ITS genotypes. After switching to an alternative allopurinol manufacturer, enforcing boiled-food diets for high-risk patients, and confirming clearance of contamination, no further R. microsporus intestinal cases were detected during several months of follow-up.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Contamination of an oral allopurinol formulation and some ready-to-eat foods with high burdens of thermotolerant R. microsporus spores, combined with intense mucosal damage, neutropenia and immunosuppression in hematologic malignancy and transplant patients, enabled intestinal colonization and invasion. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain biology beyond the thermotolerance and digestive-tract survival typical of R. microsporus was identified; this episode represents point-source amplification and exposure rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Added because this 12‑patient intestinal Rhizopus microsporus outbreak in a Hong Kong hematology/BMT unit is one of the largest single-hospital mucormycosis clusters described and illustrates high-impact, medication/food-borne transmission in immunocompromised hosts. Event is correctly classified as a healthcare-associated re-occurrence; the calendar years are approximated as 2004–2005 based on surveillance periods in the original report and should be checked against primary data in any downstream curation.

EPP.scientific.name: Mucorales
EPP.common.name: mucoralean fungi
Host: Immunocompromised pediatric inpatients, mainly oncology and transplant patients, in a tertiary children’s hospital
Event.summary: Between August 2008 and July 2009, a U.S. tertiary pediatric hospital observed five cases of fatal cutaneous or wound mucormycosis in oncology and other immunocompromised children, far exceeding background incidence. A CDC-led investigation showed that all five infections were hospital-associated and epidemiologically linked to exposure to ostensibly clean linens contaminated with Rhizopus species, with roughly 40% of environmental samples from freshly laundered linens, delivery carts and storage areas yielding Mucorales. After changing the external laundry vendor, modifying linen handling and storage practices, and implementing targeted use of sterile linens for highest-risk patients, no further outbreak-related mucormycosis cases were identified.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavily contaminated reusable linens from an off-site laundry, inadequate protection of clean linen during transport and storage, and a high-risk pediatric oncology and transplant population created repeated high-dose environmental exposure. Internal mechanisms: Infections were due to typical Rhizopus species without evidence of novel virulence traits or host expansion; the outbreak reflects high inoculum and host susceptibility rather than evolutionary change in the fungus.
Review: Retain – New row capturing the 2008–2009 U.S. pediatric hospital linen-associated outbreak (five hospital-associated cases, all fatal), which is among the most consequential healthcare-associated mucormycosis clusters documented before the Arkansas event. Geography, timeframe, case numbers and linen-related mechanisms are well supported by the primary Clin Infect Dis report and follow-on remediation study; classification as re-occurrence is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Mucorales
EPP.common.name: mucoralean fungi
Host: Severely injured U.S. and coalition military personnel with blast-related traumatic wounds, often with lower-extremity amputations and extensive soft-tissue damage
Event.summary: From June 2009 through August 2011, during combat operations in southern Afghanistan, 77 U.S. military casualties met a case definition for invasive fungal wound infection, with fungi from the order Mucorales isolated from roughly 40% of culture-positive wounds. Cases clustered among soldiers with dismounted blast injuries, large contaminated wounds and delayed wound closure, and were associated with higher amputation revision rates, longer times to wound closure and substantial mortality compared with similar trauma patients without mold infection. Development of a trauma-specific invasive fungal infection classification scheme, aggressive serial debridement protocols and early dual antifungal therapy, together with changes in battlefield evacuation and resuscitation practices, were followed by a decline in new IFI cases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-energy improvised explosive device blasts causing massive soft-tissue injury, soil and organic debris heavily contaminating wounds, large transfusion requirements, and delayed definitive wound closure created ideal conditions for invasive mold infection; intensive care settings and prolonged broad-spectrum antibacterial exposure further increased risk. Internal mechanisms: Diverse Mucorales (notably Saksenaea spp. and other genera) were recovered without a single dominant outbreak clone; the event represents amplification of environmental molds in a unique trauma setting rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: Retain – Added to represent the large series of combat-related invasive fungal wound infections in Afghanistan (77 IFI patients between 2009 and 2011, with Mucorales recovered from about 40% of culture-positive wounds), which is a major modern trauma-associated mucormycosis episode. The event is correctly treated as a trauma-driven re-occurrence in Southern Asia rather than first emergence or inter-continental spread; users should note that reported case counts refer to all IFIs, with only a subset proven to be due to Mucorales.

EPP.scientific.name: Mucorales
EPP.common.name: mucoralean fungi
Host: Civilians with severe traumatic injuries sustained during the 22 May 2011 EF5 tornado in Joplin, Missouri
Event.summary: Following the 22 May 2011 EF5 tornado in Joplin, Missouri, clinicians identified a cluster of necrotizing soft-tissue infections among severely injured survivors, and 13 patients ultimately met a definition for tornado-associated cutaneous mucormycosis. Most patients had multiple deep lacerations and penetrating injuries contaminated with soil and debris; ten required intensive-care admission, and five died despite aggressive surgical debridement and amphotericin B–based therapy. After heightened clinical awareness, prompt debridement of contaminated wounds and targeted antifungal treatment were implemented, no further tornado-associated mucormycosis cases were detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: An extremely violent tornado that lofted and injected soil and vegetative debris into traumatic wounds, creating massive, highly contaminated soft-tissue injuries, prolonged field exposure and delayed definitive surgical care, together with broad-spectrum antibiotic use, enabled mucormycete establishment. Internal mechanisms: Cases were caused predominantly by Apophysomyces trapeziformis, an environmental Mucorales fungus; no new genotype was implicated, and disease severity was driven by inoculum and host/wound factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – This 13‑case, 5‑death cluster of tornado-associated cutaneous mucormycosis in Joplin, Missouri, is a landmark natural-disaster–related mucormycosis event with strong primary documentation and clearly defined environmental drivers. It is appropriately represented as a major re-occurrence in Northern America rather than an inter-continental emergence episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Mucorales
EPP.common.name: mucoralean fungi
Host: Adults with major burns in the University Hospital of Lille burn center
Event.summary: Between approximately 2013 and 2016, the burn unit at the University Hospital of Lille, France, documented multiple cases of cutaneous mucormycosis, mainly due to Lichtheimia species, in severely burned patients. Two temporally distinct mini-outbreaks and individual cases prompted an investigation, which identified frequent contamination of unused, non-sterile crepe and elasticized bandages with Lichtheimia DNA and viable spores. After changes in bandage procurement, stricter wound-dressing protocols, and enhanced environmental monitoring, these clusters of burn-associated mucormycosis decreased and no further temporally linked outbreaks were reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Repeated use of non-sterile, fungi-contaminated bandages on large burn wounds and underlying severe tissue damage, often with concurrent broad-spectrum antibiotics and intensive care, provided favorable conditions for mucormycosis outbreaks; hospital supply-chain and sterilization gaps were central external drivers. Internal mechanisms: The isolates were typical Lichtheimia spp. adapted to high temperatures and necrotic tissue; no specific new genotype was required to explain the outbreak, which stemmed from point-source contamination and extreme host susceptibility.
Review: Retain – The seven-case Lichtheimia mucormycosis outbreak in the Lille burn unit (2013–2016) is clearly documented, correctly geolocated in France (Western Europe), and appropriately attributed to contaminated non-sterile bandages; classification as re-occurrence without inter-/intra-continental spread fits the definitions. It represents one of the major burn-unit mucormycosis episodes and should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Mucorales
EPP.common.name: mucoralean fungi
Host: Severely burned adults cared for in the burn intensive care unit at Hôpital Saint-Louis in Paris and a related military burn unit in Clamart
Event.summary: From late 2013 through early 2016, the burn intensive care unit at Hôpital Saint-Louis in Paris, with related cases in the nearby military burn unit at Hôpital d’Instruction des Armées Percy (Clamart), experienced an invasive wound mucormycosis outbreak due mainly to Mucor circinelloides f. circinelloides. Multiple patients developed deep wound infections within weeks of admission, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates showed numerous, largely patient-specific strains, consistent with repeated acquisition from a local environmental reservoir rather than single-strain transmission. After intensified infection-prevention measures, repeated environmental investigations, improved early molecular diagnosis, and changes in dressings and equipment handling, no additional linked cases were reported and incidence returned to baseline.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive burn injuries requiring repeated debridement, high fungal exposure in the burn-unit environment, and likely contamination of dressings or equipment created conditions for repeated Mucorales inoculation; hospital infrastructure and infection-control gaps were central external drivers. Internal mechanisms: Isolates represented diverse environmental M. circinelloides strains with no clearly hypervirulent clone; the outbreak reflected environmental amplification and heavy exposure of highly susceptible burn patients rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Review – The original row mis-timed this outbreak (early 2010s) and vaguely described a single “military-affiliated” burn unit; the corrected version now reflects data from genomic and clinical studies showing an invasive wound mucormycosis outbreak spanning roughly 2013–2016 in the Saint-Louis Hospital burn ICU in Paris with related cases at the Percy military burn unit in Clamart. Classification as re-occurrence remains valid, but the updated dates and multi-centre nature of the event should be verified against national surveillance and burn-registry data; the row is recommended for retention with this clarification.

EPP.scientific.name: Mucorales
EPP.common.name: mucoralean fungi
Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2015]
Host: Immunosuppressed adult inpatients (including oncology and transplant patients) at a tertiary hospital
Event.summary: From 2 June to 18 July 2015, a tertiary hospital in Hong Kong SAR reported six immunosuppressed patients with pulmonary and/or cutaneous zygomycosis caused by Rhizopus microsporus, an unusually high number for such a short period. Epidemiologic investigation linked all cases to exposure to hospital linens supplied by a single substandard external laundry; cultures showed that roughly 28% of freshly laundered clothing and a smaller proportion of laundered linens were contaminated with R. microsporus. After the hospital suspended use of the implicated laundry, replaced linens, and tightened linen-processing and infection-control standards, no additional Rhizopus-related mucormycosis cases associated with that laundry source occurred and the outbreak ended.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of heavily contaminated hospital clothing and linen from a substandard commercial laundry, coupled with intensive care and immunosuppression, served as the main driver; excessive microbial loads on laundered fabrics far exceeded hygienic standards and enabled both inhalational and cutaneous exposure.
