From 2016 through 2021, clinical and screening cases rose sharply—CDC data show clinical cases increasing from 53 in 2016 to 330 in 2018 and then to more than 1,400 by 2021—as the pathogen spread from initial foci in New York and Illinois to more than half of U.S. states, particularly in long-term acute-care and ventilator-capable skilled-nursing facilities. Enhanced surveillance, contact precautions, cohorting, and environmental disinfection slowed transmission in some jurisdictions, but by 2021 C. auris had become widely established as a major multidrug-resistant healthcare-associated pathogen in the country.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Global patient movement and medical care abroad leading to introduction of multiple C. auris clades; high device use and antibiotic exposure in ICUs and long-term care; lapses or variability in infection control and environmental cleaning; COVID-19–related ICU strain amplifying spread in 2020–2021. Internal mechanisms: Multidrug resistance (especially azoles; some amphotericin and echinocandin resistance), environmental survival and skin colonization enabling health-facility endemicity, and geographic range expansion of South Asian and South American clades into North America.
Review: Review: Simplified the country field to a single 'United States of America [2013]' entry (the initial U.S. case year) and removed the duplicate 'multi-state spread' country token, which is better described in the event summary. Corrected emergence typing by dropping the global 'first_detection' and 're_emergence' flags while retaining 'inter_continental_emergence' to reflect the first sustained in situ transmission in North America and subsequent nationwide spread.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/65/wr/mm6544e1.htm?utm_source=openai)) Event clearly represents one of the largest global episodes and should be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candidozyma auris
EPP.common.name: Candida auris
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with candidemia, especially in ICUs during the COVID-19 pandemic)
Event.summary: During 2019–2021, South Africa experienced an accelerated increase in C. auris bloodstream infections, with the proportion of C. auris among all candidemia cases rising markedly, particularly in ICUs managing large numbers of COVID-19 patients. National surveillance showed that C. auris shifted from causing localized outbreaks to accounting for a substantial share of candidemia nationwide, with high azole resistance and substantial mortality. As awareness grew, national surveillance, updated treatment guidelines, and strengthened infection-prevention practices were implemented, which began to slow growth in some hospitals but left C. auris firmly entrenched as a major cause of invasive candidiasis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: COVID-19–related ICU pressures, prolonged mechanical ventilation, corticosteroid and broad-spectrum antibiotic use, and strained infection-prevention capacity against a backdrop of existing C. auris endemicity. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of the established African clade with multidrug resistance and strong environmental persistence, leading to a marked shift in the candidemia ecology toward C. auris dominance in an already affected subregion.
Review: Review: Retained the 2019–2021 focus but linked it explicitly to national analyses showing a sharp COVID‑19–associated acceleration in C. auris bloodstream infections in South Africa.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/32/4/pdfs/25-1407.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Reclassified the event as 're_occurrence' only, reflecting a resurgence in an already affected subregion driven mainly by external healthcare-system stressors rather than new pathogen genotypes, and replaced a Reddit link with the primary Emerging Infectious Diseases article on the accelerated increase. Event remains a major re‑occurrence episode and should be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candidozyma auris
EPP.common.name: Candida auris
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults and children with candidemia and ICU patients with colonization and invasive infection)
Event.summary: From around 2011 onward, a tertiary hospital in Nairobi, Kenya, began to see C. auris emerge as a leading cause of candidemia, with a single-center analysis reporting that C. auris accounted for roughly one third of bloodstream Candida isolates over several years. By 2017–2019, enhanced surveillance and outbreak investigations documented dozens of additional C. auris cases, including at least 57 microbiologically confirmed isolates from an ICU-associated outbreak, with both bloodstream infections and widespread skin colonization. Implementation of targeted infection prevention measures, environmental decontamination, and intensified screening ultimately controlled the recognized outbreak, but C. auris remained a prominent cause of invasive candidiasis in this Eastern African setting and highlighted regional spread beyond South Africa.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-risk ICU care with frequent central venous catheters, broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, and prolonged hospital stays; limited early access to species-level identification resulting in misclassification of C. auris and delayed response; referral patterns drawing complex patients from across East Africa. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and geographic expansion of an African clade of C. auris with multidrug resistance and environmental persistence into Eastern Africa, enabling establishment as a major cause of candidemia in at least one large referral hospital.
Review: Review (added event): Added a new Eastern Africa event to capture the substantial Kenyan emergence, which was missing despite evidence that C. auris caused 70+ fungemia cases at a Nairobi facility between 2011 and 2016 and that a 2017–2019 ICU outbreak yielded at least 57 confirmed isolates.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/femspd/article/80/1/ftac012/6572357?utm_source=openai)) Classified this as an intra‑continental emergence (spread into a new African subregion) rather than re‑occurrence, because it represents the first establishment of sustained transmission in Eastern Africa following earlier emergence in Southern Africa. Given the case burden and role in demonstrating wider African dissemination, this should be included among the top global emergence events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Aspergillus fumigatus
EPP.common.name: aspergillosis
Host: Humans with chronic respiratory disease and invasive aspergillosis; environmental A. fumigatus in agricultural and peri-hospital soils and air
Event.summary: In a referral chest hospital in Delhi, India, clinical isolates collected between 2005 and 2010 from patients with chronic respiratory disease yielded the country’s first documented multi-triazole–resistant A. fumigatus strains harboring TR34/L98H cyp51A mutations in azole-naïve patients, implying environmental acquisition. By 2012, a wider environmental survey across northern, southern, and eastern India found around 7% of environmental A. fumigatus isolates carried TR34/L98H and were cross-resistant to multiple medical triazoles and several agricultural DMIs, indicating a substantial environmental reservoir. Subsequent genetic studies showed clonal expansion of TR34/L98H lineages in Indian environments and patients, highlighting re-emergence of aspergillosis as a more difficult-to-treat disease in a country with a very large underlying burden of post-TB and other chronic lung disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive and often poorly regulated use of triazole fungicides in Indian agriculture and horticulture (e.g., tea gardens, rice paddies, fruit orchards, nursery and hospital grounds) selected for multi‑azole‑resistant A. fumigatus in soil and plant waste; very high prevalence of cavitary or structurally damaged lungs after tuberculosis and other infections created a large pool of susceptible hosts; limited access to fungal diagnostics and susceptibility testing delayed recognition and facilitated undetected spread. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via the TR34/L98H cyp51A promoter-repeat and coding mutation conferring high-level cross-resistance to itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and several agricultural azoles; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and clonal expansion of resistant environmental lineages distinct from local wild-type backgrounds; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as these resistant clones became established across multiple agro-ecological zones in India.
Review: review – Retain this event as a major description of the emergence of environmentally selected azole-resistant A. fumigatus in India. Corrected the event-type classification by setting inter-continental emergence to “false”, because the EPP (A. fumigatus) was long present in Asia and this episode represents emergence of a resistant genotype, which should be classified as re-emergence according to the protocol. Kept the 2005–2012 window and the India [2005] tag as an approximation to the period from which isolates were collected and the timing of early TR34/L98H detections, but note that the earliest resistant isolates in the key JAC study date from the latter part of this interval (e.g. VPCI 1042/09), so precise first-detection years could be refined in future curation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida parapsilosis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Hospitalized adult patients, predominantly intensive care unit patients receiving central venous catheters and total parenteral nutrition
Event.summary:
In 2001, a large outbreak of Candida parapsilosis bloodstream infections occurred in a community hospital in Mississippi, with 22 adult patients (15 confirmed, 7 possible cases) developing candidemia between April and October 2001, mostly among intensive care unit patients receiving total parenteral nutrition and central venous catheters.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC522355/?utm_source=openai)) Molecular typing showed that nearly all case isolates belonged to a single clonal strain that also colonized the hands of a health-care worker and exhibited reduced (though not high-level) susceptibility to fluconazole and voriconazole, confirming sustained nosocomial transmission.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC522355/?utm_source=openai)) Following intensified infection-control measures and reinforcement of hand hygiene, incident cases declined and the outbreak resolved, although related strains continued to be sporadically recovered from blood and catheter tips.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: High use of central venous catheters and parenteral nutrition in ICU patients, suboptimal hand hygiene, and possible contamination of devices created conditions that favored nosocomial transmission of C. parapsilosis in the Mississippi community hospital.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC522355/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: A single hospital-adapted clone with modestly decreased azole susceptibility and strong adhesion/biofilm capacity on catheters and skin dominated the outbreak, but high-level resistance was not the primary driver; hence the event is interpreted mainly as a control failure (re-occurrence) rather than resistance-driven re-emergence.
Review: retain – Event accurately represents the well-documented 2001 adult community-hospital outbreak in Mississippi (22 bloodstream infections linked to a single clone with moderately elevated fluconazole MICs); geocoding, host description and classification as a re-occurrence driven by ICU care, TPN, and hand transmission are consistent with primary sources, so only a narrative cross-check was needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida parapsilosis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Neonates in a tertiary hospital neonatal intensive care unit
Event.summary:
From 2002 through 2008, a tertiary-care university hospital NICU in São Paulo, Brazil, recorded 36 cases of Candida parapsilosis fungemia in neonates, with a marked outbreak peak between 2002 and 2004 when incidence rose to nearly 20 episodes per 1,000 admissions in some years.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3425904/?utm_source=openai)) Almost all affected infants were premature, had central venous catheters, and received total parenteral nutrition, and 30-day mortality reached 45%.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3425904/?utm_source=openai)) An infection-control program was implemented during the outbreak, including reinforcement of catheter care and hand hygiene, after which incidence fell but C. parapsilosis remained an important neonatal pathogen in the unit.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Increased survival of very low birthweight neonates, extensive use of central venous catheters and parenteral nutrition, prolonged antibiotic exposure, and crowding in the NICU created a highly favorable environment for C. parapsilosis transmission and infection.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3425904/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No specific resistance mutation was highlighted; the episode is best interpreted as amplification and persistence of one or more hospital-adapted clones with strong skin and device colonization and biofilm-forming capacity, consistent with a re-occurrence rather than resistance-driven re-emergence.
Review: review – Corrected the event window from “2003–2005” to “2002–2008” to match the full 7‑year NICU case series, in which the statistically significant outbreak peak occurred between 2002 and 2004, and simplified the 'countries' field to 'Brazil [2002]'. Classification as re-occurrence (no documented antifungal resistance) remains appropriate; event size and mortality justify retaining this outbreak among the largest C. parapsilosis emergence episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida parapsilosis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Neonates and other hospitalized patients with candidemia, particularly in intensive care and neonatal units
Event.summary: From around 2009 onward, South African sentinel surveillance and outbreak investigations documented a striking emergence of fluconazole-resistant Candida parapsilosis causing bloodstream infections, especially in public-sector neonatal units, with fluconazole resistance rates in some centers exceeding 50–60%.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11973574/?utm_source=openai)) Many resistant isolates carried the ERG11 Y132F substitution and belonged to clonal lineages that persisted and spread within and between hospitals, making C. parapsilosis the leading cause of neonatal candidemia in some settings.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11973574/?utm_source=openai)) Despite targeted infection-control and antifungal-stewardship efforts, Y132F-bearing clones remained entrenched into the late 2010s, indicating durable re-emergence of resistant lineages rather than transient outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Heavy reliance on fluconazole for treatment and prophylaxis, combined with high burdens of ICU and neonatal patients with central lines, prolonged hospital stays, and challenges in infection prevention and control, created strong selective pressure and ample opportunity for clonal spread of resistant strains.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11911919/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and clonal expansion of ERG11 Y132F substitutions, often together with additional resistance determinants, conferred high-level fluconazole resistance and sometimes cross-resistance to other azoles, allowing resistant clones to outcompete susceptible strains and persist in hospital environments and on patient skin; this pattern fits a re-emergence driven by novel resistant genotypes.
Review: review – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'South Africa [2009]' while keeping 2009–2020 as the event window for the multi-hospital wave of fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis, which surveillance data show to be among the highest-prevalence FRCP settings worldwide. Classification as re-emergence only (rather than intra-/inter-continental emergence) is consistent with definitions, because the species was long established in Southern Africa and the key novelties are resistant clones and their clonal spread.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Candida parapsilosis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Hospitalized adults with candidemia and other invasive Candida parapsilosis infections, including hematopoietic cell transplant recipients and ICU patients
Event.summary:
Analysis of 2,318 Candida parapsilosis isolates collected between roughly 2010 and 2019 from 83 hospitals across China showed that, although overall fluconazole resistance remained low (~2–5%), resistant isolates were clustered in multiple hospitals and belonged to at least 10 clonal genotypes that persisted and transmitted for up to 29 months, many carrying ERG11 Y132F and additional resistance-associated mutations.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10761258/?utm_source=openai)) In parallel, echinocandin susceptibility testing of more than 2,500 C. parapsilosis isolates (2014–2019) identified decreased echinocandin susceptibility in a subset and documented the first pan-echinocandin- and multi-azole-resistant C. parapsilosis bloodstream isolate in China, carrying an FKS1 S656P mutation that conferred high-level echinocandin resistance in functional assays.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9793909/?utm_source=openai)) Together, these findings indicate a re-emergence of C. parapsilosis in Chinese hospitals in a more drug-resistant, clonally expanding form over the 2010s and into the early 2020s.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Increasing use of fluconazole and echinocandins for empiric and prophylactic treatment of invasive candidiasis, rapid growth in the number of high-risk ICU and hematology/oncology patients, and the ability of C. parapsilosis to persist on skin and hospital surfaces favored selection and spread of resistant lineages in Chinese hospitals.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10761258/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Emergence of multiple fluconazole-resistant clones harbouring ERG11 Y132F and other azole-resistance mutations with clear evidence of clonal transmission, along with FKS1 hotspot mutations (e.g., S656P) mediating pan-echinocandin resistance in at least one invasive case, exemplify re-emergence driven by new multidrug-resistance mechanisms and enhanced tolerance rather than simple recurrence of susceptible strains.
Review: retain – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'China [2010]' but otherwise retained this event, which accurately reflects multi-hospital surveillance demonstrating emergence and clonal transmission of ERG11 Y132F–bearing fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis clones and a rare pan-echinocandin-resistant FKS1 S656P isolate. Classification as re-emergence driven by new resistance mechanisms is consistent with the underlying studies and with the event-definition framework.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida parapsilosis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Adult intensive care unit patients with candidemia
Event.summary:
Between July 2011 and February 2012, a tertiary hospital intensive care unit in Brasília, Brazil, experienced a dramatic increase in candidemia, with 40 cases identified, 28 (70%) caused by fluconazole-resistant Candida parapsilosis that represented a sharp shift from the preceding five-year period.
([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/fungal-biology/articles/10.3389/ffunb.2022.1010782/pdf)) Molecular analysis showed that most resistant isolates were closely related, consistent with dissemination of a single or few clonal FRCP strains among ICU patients who commonly had diabetes, central lines and prior antifungal exposure. After the outbreak was recognized, reinforcement of infection-control practices, catheter management and antifungal policies led to control of the cluster and a reduction in new fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis candidemia episodes.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: High empiric and prophylactic fluconazole use, extensive central venous catheter utilization, and intense patient–health care worker contact in the ICU, particularly among patients with multiple comorbidities, provided strong selective and transmission pressures for a resistant clone.
([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/fungal-biology/articles/10.3389/ffunb.2022.1010782/pdf)) Internal mechanisms: A hospital-adapted clone of C. parapsilosis with elevated fluconazole MICs, mediated by ERG11 target alterations and/or efflux-related changes, spread within the ICU and re-established the species as a difficult-to-treat pathogen in this setting, fitting the definition of re-emergence via a more drug-resistant lineage.
Review: review – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'Brazil [2011]' and left the 2011–2012 window unchanged; the description matches the published ICU outbreak in Brasília with 28 fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis candidemia cases. Classification as re-emergence (resistant clone) remains appropriate, and the event is of sufficient scale and impact to retain among the top episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida parapsilosis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Hospitalized adults, especially intensive care unit and surgical patients with invasive candidiasis
Event.summary:
From 2012 to 2016, a Brazilian public university hospital medical center documented a prolonged outbreak and clonal persistence of azole-resistant Candida parapsilosis sensu stricto causing invasive candidiasis, particularly in ICU patients, with retrospective analysis revealing that a single dominant resistant clone had silently circulated for several years.
([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/fungal-biology/articles/10.3389/ffunb.2022.1010782/pdf)) During this period, C. parapsilosis complex became a leading cause of candidemia in the institution, and a substantial subset of isolates exhibited high MICs to fluconazole and other azoles; genotyping confirmed long-term clonal persistence across ICU and other wards. After recognition of the outbreak and characterization of resistance mechanisms, intensified infection-prevention measures and antifungal stewardship were implemented, which reduced but did not completely eliminate the resistant lineage.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Prolonged hospitalization, widespread use of intravascular catheters, high fluconazole exposure in a resource-limited setting, and unrecognized environmental reservoirs in high-dependency units allowed a resistant clone to persist and spread.
([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/fungal-biology/articles/10.3389/ffunb.2022.1010782/pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Emergence and long-term maintenance of azole-resistant C. parapsilosis sensu stricto clones with ERG11 mutations and likely efflux pump upregulation produced high azole MICs and enabled these clones to outcompete susceptible strains under local drug pressure, representing a clear re-emergence of the species in a more drug-resistant form.
Review: review – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'Brazil [2012]' and retained the 2012–2016 time span, which matches the clonal ICU outbreak and long-term persistence of azole-resistant C. parapsilosis at a Brazilian teaching hospital. Classification as re-emergence, driven by resistant clones documented with ERG11 mutations, is consistent with the primary study; the event remains one of the larger and better-characterized FRCP outbreaks and should be kept.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Candida parapsilosis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Hospitalized adults and some pediatric patients with invasive candidiasis, many in ICU and emergency services
Event.summary:
Between 2014 and 2016, a general hospital in Mexico City (Hospital General Dr. Manuel Gea González) experienced a major increase in invasive candidiasis, with at least 74 cases identified; 38% were due to Candida parapsilosis and more than half of these C. parapsilosis infections were caused by fluconazole-resistant isolates.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8257413/?utm_source=openai)) Molecular analysis showed that many resistant isolates carried the ERG11 Y132F substitution and that microsatellite typing revealed a clonal cluster consistent with a hospital outbreak of azole-resistant C. parapsilosis. Following recognition of the outbreak, strengthened surveillance, infection-control measures and antifungal-stewardship interventions were implemented, which contributed to containment of the resistant cluster and a reduction in new fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis cases.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: High case loads in ICU and emergency departments, substantial empirical use of fluconazole, widespread central venous catheter use, complex surgeries and delayed recognition of the outbreak all promoted selection and dissemination of resistant strains within the hospital.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8257413/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and expansion of ERG11 Y132F-mutant C. parapsilosis conferred fluconazole resistance, and some isolates also showed reduced susceptibility to other azoles, consistent with additional ERG11 overexpression or efflux-pump upregulation; these features support classifying the event as re-emergence via a resistant clone rather than simple recurrence.
Review: retain – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'Mexico [2014]' but otherwise kept this well-supported event, which mirrors the published Mexico City general-hospital outbreak with dozens of invasive candidiasis cases and a dominant ERG11 Y132F fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis clone. Classification as re-emergence is appropriate, and the event clearly ranks among the major FRCP episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida parapsilosis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Hospitalized patients with candidemia and other invasive or mucosal Candida parapsilosis infections
Event.summary:
During a three-year multicentre laboratory-based surveillance study (2015–2017) in nine Indian tertiary hospitals, Candida parapsilosis emerged as a prominent cause of candidemia and other infections, with 32% of 199 isolates found to be non-susceptible to fluconazole and concentrated in clonal clusters in seven hospitals.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10512360/?utm_source=openai)) Many fluconazole-non-susceptible isolates carried a novel ERG11 K143R substitution or the previously known Y132F mutation, and genotyping showed two major resistant clusters circulating across multiple centres, indicating ongoing clonal transmission of resistant strains. Publication of these findings led to calls to enhance routine susceptibility testing, infection control, and antifungal stewardship across Indian hospitals.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Extensive use of fluconazole for empiric and prophylactic therapy, high burdens of ICU and post-operative patients with central lines, and limited routine antifungal susceptibility testing and molecular surveillance allowed resistant clones to spread between wards and hospitals.
([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10512360/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of ERG11 K143R in 92% of fluconazole-non-susceptible isolates and of ERG11 Y132F in others directly conferred high azole MICs; genotyping showing multi-hospital clusters is consistent with re-emergence via clonally expanding resistant genotypes.
Review: retain – Simplified the 'countries' field to 'India [2015]' and kept the 2015–2017 window, which exactly matches the multicentre surveillance describing high (≈32%) fluconazole non-susceptibility and clonal spread of ERG11 K143R and Y132F mutants. The event is clearly a major resistance-driven re-emergence episode and merits inclusion among the top global events.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida tropicalis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Hospitalized adults and children with bloodstream infection in a tertiary‑care center (New Delhi)
Event.summary: Between roughly 2004 and 2008, a large tertiary‑care hospital in New Delhi, India, observed a marked rise in candidaemia due to non‑albicans Candida, with C. tropicalis becoming the single most common species in later years and accounting for around 29% of bloodstream isolates, overtaking C. albicans.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3612330/?utm_source=openai)) This shift occurred alongside increasing ICU admissions, widespread use of central venous catheters and total parenteral nutrition, and heavy empirical fluconazole and broad‑spectrum antibacterial use, and was accompanied by notable fluconazole non‑susceptibility across Candida isolates. Even after the pattern was recognized and antifungal stewardship and catheter care were emphasized, C. tropicalis remained a dominant bloodstream pathogen in this center, signaling a broader regional shift toward non‑albicans Candida candidemia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of intensive care capacity, frequent central venous catheterization, parenteral nutrition, prolonged hospitalization, and broad‑spectrum antibacterial use created ecological niches favoring non‑albicans Candida, particularly C. tropicalis, over C. albicans. Internal mechanisms: sustained exposure to fluconazole and other triazoles selected for more tolerant or less susceptible non‑albicans species, including C. tropicalis, although well‑defined azole‑resistant genotypes had not yet been systematically characterized in this period and resistance appeared polyclonal.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3612330/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain – This single‑center New Delhi episode captures an early, well‑documented shift from C. albicans to non‑albicans candidemia with C. tropicalis emerging as the leading species and substantial case numbers, appropriately classified as a regional re‑occurrence driven by intensive care expansion and antifungal/antibacterial selective pressure; geography (Southern Asia, India) and timeframe are consistent with the cited surveillance study.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida tropicalis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Adult hospitalized patients with C. tropicalis bloodstream infection (National Taiwan University Hospital and other Taiwanese centers)
Event.summary: Between 2011 and 2017, National Taiwan University Hospital and collaborating centers documented a rising proportion of fluconazole‑nonsusceptible C. tropicalis bloodstream isolates, with many azole‑resistant isolates belonging to a limited set of multilocus sequence types (e.g. DST225, DST506) within a clonal lineage (clade 4).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6711239/?utm_source=openai)) Molecular typing showed that these fluconazole‑nonsusceptible strains were highly related to each other and to resistant isolates previously reported from mainland China, suggesting regional dissemination of a drug‑resistant clonal population in Eastern Asia. Despite targeted antifungal therapy and infection‑control interventions, resistant C. tropicalis candidemia remained entrenched, highlighting a shift from sporadic resistance to clonal expansion of a high‑risk lineage.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intense clinical use of triazoles over preceding decades, high burdens of hematologic malignancy and ICU care, and frequent central‑line‑associated bloodstream infections fostered selection and nosocomial spread of azole‑resistant C. tropicalis in Taiwanese hospitals. Internal mechanisms: ERG11 mutations (including Y132F) and overexpression, together with upregulation of efflux pumps, conferred fluconazole and broad azole resistance; multilocus sequence typing and whole‑genome data demonstrated a clonal clade 4 lineage with reduced susceptibility and possible enhanced virulence, representing a clear novel strain/genotype emergence and re‑emergence in a previously affected subregion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6711239/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain as a major event but correct geography and event type: the underlying EID study is restricted to Taiwan, so the country list has been narrowed from “China, Taiwan Province of China” to “Taiwan Province of China” only, and the event is now classified solely as re‑emergence driven by a novel azole‑resistant clonal lineage in an already affected Eastern Asia subregion, not as intra‑continental emergence of the species.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida tropicalis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Humans with candidemia and colonization linked to environmental reservoirs in fruit orchards and hospital environments in Taiwan
Event.summary: From 2012 to 2018, surveys of mango and other fruit orchards in Taiwan identified widespread contamination by a predominant fluconazole‑resistant C. tropicalis clade 4 genotype that matched the main azole‑resistant lineage causing human candidemia, with detection frequencies increasing over time.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11521182/?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent hospital environmental surveillance around 2020 found the same genotype persisting in ICU environments, indicating that orchard and healthcare settings formed a linked reservoir for human infection. This multi‑year episode thus represents the establishment of a stable, environmentally and nosocomially maintained azole‑resistant C. tropicalis population that continues to seed invasive human disease despite enhanced surveillance and more cautious azole use.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: long‑term agricultural use of triazole fungicides in Taiwanese orchards, environmental contamination of fruits and soils, and sustained clinical azole prescribing created a One‑Health selection gradient favoring the clade 4 genotype; persistence on hospital surfaces and in ICUs further promoted human exposure and transmission. Internal mechanisms: tandem duplications of ERG11 carrying the Y132F mutation and other ergosterol pathway alterations underlie high‑level azole resistance in clade 4 isolates, and genomic analyses demonstrate that these mutations are stably inherited within an expanding lineage that circulates between environmental niches and human hosts, illustrating novel genotype emergence, enhanced survival, and ecological range expansion within Eastern Asia.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43380-2?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain as a key One‑Health re‑emergence episode showing environmental and hospital reservoirs of a resistant clade 4 genotype, but intra‑continental emergence has been set to ‘No’ because C. tropicalis was already long established in Eastern Asia; this event reflects expansion and ecological diversification of a resistant lineage, not first occurrence of the species in a new Asian subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida tropicalis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Hospitalized patients (ICU and non‑ICU) with invasive C. tropicalis infection across 27 hospitals in Delhi National Capital Region and neighboring states
Event.summary: Between 2014 and 2022, a multicenter Indian surveillance program across 27 hospitals in Delhi and the surrounding National Capital Region collected 1,016 clinical C. tropicalis isolates and showed that C. tropicalis remained a leading cause of invasive yeast infection, with a substantial fraction demonstrating azole resistance. Whole‑genome sequencing and MLST revealed that a single azole‑resistant clade 4 lineage predominated among resistant isolates and was closely related across hospitals, indicating a smoldering regional outbreak with clonal spread facilitated by patient movement and suboptimal infection‑control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13059750/?utm_source=openai)) The episode underscored high morbidity and mortality, treatment challenges and the need for routine species‑level identification and susceptibility testing, leading to recommendations for more restrictive azole use and enhanced fungal stewardship in Indian hospitals.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high candidemia incidence in Indian ICUs and wards, widespread empiric fluconazole use, delays in accurate species identification, frequent patient transfers among Delhi‑NCR hospitals and limited early fungal stewardship promoted the rise and persistence of the clade 4 lineage.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13059750/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: clade 4 isolates harbored ERG11 mutations, copy‑number variation and transcriptional changes that increased azole resistance and upregulated virulence‑associated genes (e.g. adhesins, secreted proteases), consistent with emergence and regional dissemination of a specific high‑risk genotype with enhanced pathogenicity and transmission fitness.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13059750/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain as a key Indian re‑emergence event dominated by clade 4, but re‑occurrence has been set to ‘No’ so that this episode is classified purely as re‑emergence driven by a novel resistant and virulent lineage; this aligns with project rules that re‑emergence (pathogen change) should not be conflated with re‑occurrence (purely external drivers) and reflects the genomic focus of the underlying mBio study.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Candida tropicalis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Critically ill adult and pediatric ICU patients with ICU‑acquired candidemia across a multicenter Indian ICU network
Event.summary: From approximately 2018 through the early 2020s, multicenter ICU surveillance in India, including a large network of ICUs monitored before and during the COVID‑19 pandemic, reported that C. tropicalis accounted for roughly 25–45% of ICU‑acquired candidemia episodes and was often the single most common Candida species, with 30–60% mortality in high‑risk groups.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39278818/?utm_source=openai)) These studies documented increasing proportions of non‑albicans Candida, high azole resistance and frequent need for echinocandin therapy; many C. tropicalis infections developed within 1–2 weeks of ICU admission and were linked to invasive procedures, broad‑spectrum antibiotic and corticosteroid use, and strained infection‑prevention resources during COVID‑19 surges. The episode represents a sustained, high‑burden re‑occurrence of C. tropicalis candidemia in Indian ICUs within an already clade‑4‑dominated resistance landscape.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensification and expansion of ICU care (including for COVID‑19), very high use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics and systemic corticosteroids, heavy reliance on central venous catheters and mechanical ventilation, and pandemic‑related pressures on staffing and infection‑prevention programs all promoted Candida colonization, transmission and progression to candidemia, with national surveillance indicating cross‑facility dissemination of high‑risk clones.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39278818/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: continued selection and spread of azole‑resistant clade 4 and other resistant lineages underlie rising non‑susceptibility, but by this period those genotypes were already established; this ICU‑focused event is therefore classified as re‑occurrence, driven largely by external clinical and health‑system stressors rather than by the first appearance of a new C. tropicalis genotype.
Review: Review – Retain as a distinct ICU‑focused high‑burden episode but reclassify it as re‑occurrence only: the excess burden of C. tropicalis candidemia during 2018–2023, especially around the COVID‑19 period, is best explained by external factors (ICU expansion, broad antibiotic and steroid use, infection‑control strain) acting on an already established resistant clonal background, rather than by emergence of a new genotype. This avoids double‑counting clade 4 emergence, which is captured in the 2014–2022 Delhi‑NCR and Asia‑Pacific events.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Host: Humans (general population of metropolitan Milwaukee; severe outcomes concentrated among immunocompromised persons, especially people with AIDS)
Event.summary: In late March–early April 1993, the municipal drinking‑water supply serving Milwaukee, Wisconsin became heavily contaminated with Cryptosporidium oocysts, probably via sewage overflow into Lake Michigan combined with inadequate filtration at the Howard Avenue Water Purification Plant, producing the largest documented waterborne disease outbreak in U.S. history. Over roughly two weeks an estimated 403,000 of 1.61 million area residents developed acute gastrointestinal illness, thousands were hospitalized and excess deaths occurred among immunocompromised persons, before a boil‑water advisory and plant shutdown halted further exposure. The outbreak waned after the contaminated plant was taken offline and a package of treatment upgrades and regulatory changes for surface‑water supplies was implemented, substantially reducing the risk of similar large‑scale Crypto contamination.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: combined sewer overflow and runoff carrying human sewage into Lake Michigan near the drinking‑water intake, along with suboptimal turbidity control and filtration performance at a large surface‑water treatment plant and delayed recognition of a waterborne outbreak. Internal mechanisms: the low infectious dose, environmental robustness, and chlorine resistance of Cryptosporidium (likely C. hominis) allowed high-intensity transmission via a single municipal water supply once oocysts entered the system; no novel strain is implicated, and impact was driven primarily by exposure scale and host vulnerability.
Review: retain – This is the largest documented cryptosporidiosis outbreak globally in the period considered and clearly belongs among the top 10 events by impact. Geography, timing, and classification as a re‑occurrence (infrastructure‑driven resurgence of an established pathogen) are appropriate; no corrections were required beyond minor wording, and core sources (NEJM, CDC) are highly relevant.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Host: Humans (visitors to a chlorinated water park in Georgia, many of them young children and their families)
Event.summary: In summer 1995, a cryptosporidiosis outbreak associated with a water park in Georgia followed a probable fecal accident in a shallow children’s pool, seeding Cryptosporidium into recirculated, chlorinated water used by thousands of visitors. Epidemiologic investigations linked illness to park attendance, with national surveillance summaries estimating roughly 2,500–5,000 outbreak-related cases and several dozen laboratory-confirmed infections, making it one of the largest recreational-water cryptosporidiosis outbreaks documented in the United States. After the park was closed, hyperchlorination and other remedial measures were undertaken and the outbreak subsided, and the episode helped catalyze strengthened guidance on management of fecal accidents and supplemental disinfection in pools and water parks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extremely high bather loads in a shallow children’s pool, at least one fecal accident by an infected child, and reliance on standard chlorination without supplemental disinfection or rapid fecal-incident response, allowing contamination of the shared recirculation system. Internal mechanisms: the very low infectious dose and chlorine resistance of Cryptosporidium oocysts enabled extensive transmission from a single contamination event; no novel strain or host jump is implicated, so this is best interpreted as re‑occurrence driven by facility design and management rather than evolutionary change in the parasite.
Review: review – Newly added event. Multiple CDC and EID sources agree that a very large recreational-water-associated outbreak occurred at a Georgia water park in 1995, with thousands of illnesses, so it likely ranks among the top global outbreaks by case count. However, published estimates differ (≈2,500 vs. ≈5,400 cases), and the park location is summarized generically; a human reviewer should verify preferred case-count figures and wording before finalizing.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Countries: United States of America – Utah, Idaho, Colorado and other western states [2007]
Host: Humans (swimmers using chlorinated pools and other treated recreational water venues in Utah and neighboring western states; secondary cases in households and childcare settings)
Event.summary: In summer 2007, Utah experienced a very large statewide cryptosporidiosis outbreak primarily linked to treated recreational water venues such as public swimming pools and water parks, with over 1,300 laboratory‑reported cases (far above the typical annual baseline of ≈30) and additional increases documented in adjacent Rocky Mountain states including Idaho and Colorado. Transmission spread over several months via fecal contamination of pools by symptomatic swimmers, especially young children, and subsequent person‑to‑person spread in households and childcare facilities, with reported cases peaking in August before comprehensive control measures took effect. Widespread pool closures and hyperchlorination, restrictions on diaper‑aged children’s pool access, and intensive public campaigns on "healthy swimming" practices were implemented across affected states, after which reported cryptosporidiosis incidence declined toward baseline in the 2008 season.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intense summertime use of chlorinated recreational water, inadequate exclusion of ill swimmers, high levels of community mixing in pools and spray features, and initial under‑recognition of a multi‑county outbreak, all of which favored sustained transmission. Internal mechanisms: prolonged shedding of large numbers of oocysts, chlorine resistance, and low infectious dose allowed efficient spread via pools even when conventional disinfection targets were met; there is no indication that a novel strain or host jump occurred, so this event is best classified as re‑occurrence in an established pathogen facilitated by behavioral and infrastructure factors.
Review: review – Existing row adjusted. The original version cited an estimated 5,700 outbreak-related cases in Utah but did not distinguish clearly between reported and modelled counts, and listed U.S. states as if they were separate countries. The revised row treats this as a single U.S. event, notes >1,300 reported Utah cases and qualitatively acknowledges that true illnesses were likely higher, and keeps classification as a large recreational‑water re‑occurrence episode. A reviewer should confirm the preferred numeric description for Utah and whether to treat linked increases in Idaho/Colorado as part of the same episode or as parallel outbreaks.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Host: Humans (residents supplied by the Abborrverket municipal water treatment plant in Skellefteå)
Event.summary: In early 2011, Skellefteå municipality in northern Sweden experienced a large waterborne outbreak of gastroenteritis subsequently attributed to Cryptosporidium hominis IbA10G2 in the public drinking‑water supply fed by the Skellefteå River. Retrospective analyses and telephone advice-line data suggest that roughly 18,500–20,000 residents were infected, many in a specific water‑distribution zone, and cases persisted for several months before Cryptosporidium was formally recognized as the cause. A prolonged boil‑water advisory, provision of alternative water, and installation of UV disinfection and other treatment improvements were implemented; the outbreak subsided as contaminated water was flushed from the system, and epidemiologic and genotyping work suggested possible links through human travel and wastewater between Skellefteå and the earlier Östersund outbreak.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: sewage overflow and poorly separated drainage during periods of heavy rain, allowing human-source oocysts to contaminate a river‑fed waterworks; insufficient treatment barriers to protozoa at the Abborrverket plant; and delayed outbreak recognition in the absence of routine Crypto testing. Internal mechanisms: the same highly infectious C. hominis IbA10G2 subtype seen in Östersund, with robust environmental survival and low infectious dose, facilitated extensive waterborne spread; no evidence indicates that a new strain emerged specifically in Skellefteå, so this is treated as a re‑occurrence.
Review: retain – Together with Östersund, the Skellefteå 2011 outbreak is one of the largest waterborne cryptosporidiosis events ever recorded (≈18,500–20,000 infections) and clearly belongs among the top global episodes. The existing description and classification as a re‑occurrence are consistent with Swedish public health and BMC Public Health analyses; no substantive corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland – England (Lancashire) [2015]
Host: Humans (about 300,000 customers on the affected United Utilities public water supply in Lancashire)
Event.summary: In August 2015, routine monitoring detected Cryptosporidium oocysts in treated water from the Franklaw treatment works operated by United Utilities in Lancashire, England, prompting a large precautionary boil‑water notice affecting more than 300,000 customers in areas including Blackpool, Chorley, Fylde, Preston, South Ribble and Wyre. Although only a relatively small number of laboratory‑confirmed cryptosporidiosis cases were identified compared with classic outbreaks, the incident caused major disruption, extensive bottled‑water distribution, and substantial economic costs as the advisory remained in place for several weeks while investigations were conducted and treatment barriers were strengthened. The episode concluded after enhanced treatment, flushing, and operational changes reduced the risk of oocyst contamination below regulatory concern, and UK regulators later imposed fines and compensation requirements on the water company for the failures that led to the incident.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: contamination of a large surface‑water‑supplied treatment works with Cryptosporidium (likely from agricultural or environmental sources), combined with inadequate protozoa removal or barrier performance and a reliance on downstream monitoring rather than robust upstream control and validated UV/filtration barriers. Internal mechanisms: the resilience of oocysts to standard chlorination meant that even low-level contamination triggered a large-scale public‑health response; no novel parasite genotype was described, and the public-health impact was driven more by infrastructure and regulatory failures than by biological change.
Review: review – Existing row retained but flagged. The Lancashire 2015 incident involved very large numbers of people under a boil‑water notice and major economic impact, but relatively few confirmed cases, so in terms of illnesses it is smaller than several other events now included. Sources used are appropriate (regulator reports and reputable news coverage), but if the dataset must be trimmed to ten highest‑impact events primarily by case numbers, this row is a candidate for exclusion despite its policy significance.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus hantanense
EPP.common.name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans (rural residents and farmers in multiple Chinese provinces; principal reservoir Apodemus agrarius)
Event.summary: From 1994 to 1998, China experienced a large national cluster of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), with statistically significant high-incidence spatial clusters in many rural counties across northeastern, central and eastern provinces where Hantaan virus is enzootic in Apodemus agrarius. The epidemic period was characterized by thousands of reported human cases annually and clear geographic clustering of high-risk counties, reflecting intense human–rodent contact in agricultural landscapes. Incidence declined somewhat after the late 1990s as vaccination, improved housing, and rodent control programs were expanded, although HFRS remained endemic in many of the same foci.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: agricultural expansion and intensification, high rodent (Apodemus agrarius) densities in rural fields and peri-domestic settings, and climatic variability influencing rodent population dynamics and human exposure patterns; improvements in surveillance also increased case ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: no clear evidence for a novel HTNV genotype dominating this period—disease resurgence is best explained by ecological and socio-environmental factors rather than a major viral shift, so this is classified as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: retain: Correctly represents the mid‑1990s national HFRS cluster in mainland China based on spatial analysis of 1994–1998 surveillance data, with China as the only affected country in the event and HTNV long-established there; classification as a large re-occurrence (rather than intra-continental emergence) is appropriate and sources are well chosen.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus hantanense
EPP.common.name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans in multiple Chinese provinces (notably Shaanxi, Heilongjiang, Inner Mongolia and other northeastern and central provinces)
Event.summary: Between 2004 and 2019, China reported 199,799 HFRS cases nationwide, with the burden concentrated in traditional HTNV-endemic areas of northeastern and north-central China and in emerging high-incidence clusters such as Shaanxi and parts of Inner Mongolia. The epidemic exhibited pronounced spatial–temporal clustering, with recurrent seasonal peaks and intensification of disease in several high-risk regions despite long-standing endemicity and vaccination programs. Toward the end of this period, some regions showed declining incidence attributed to expanded vaccination and rodent control, but others continued to experience substantial case numbers, maintaining HTNV-associated HFRS as a major public health problem.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: changing agricultural practices, rapid urbanization at rural fringes, climatic fluctuations that favored rodent population booms, and demographic shifts (e.g., migrant workers) increasing exposure in high-risk landscapes, along with incomplete vaccine coverage and variable implementation of environmental management. Internal mechanisms: HFRS in China during this period was caused mainly by Hantaan and Seoul viruses; while phylogenetic analyses show regional HTNV lineages, there is no strong evidence that a single novel high-virulence genotype drove the nationwide burden, so this period is best characterized as a large-scale re-occurrence linked to ecological and socio-economic drivers.
Review: retain: Correctly summarizes the 2004–2019 national HFRS burden in China (≈200,000 cases) and identifies high-incidence HTNV-dominated provinces; treating this long, spatially structured epidemic as a single major re-occurrence episode is consistent with the project rules for linked multi-year episodes, though users could further subdivide it if more granular ranking of peaks is needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus hantanense
EPP.common.name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans (college students and surrounding community in Xi’an, Shaanxi Province)
Event.summary: From 2005 onwards, Xi’an City in Shaanxi Province experienced an increasing risk of HFRS associated with Hantaan virus, culminating in a documented outbreak among college students in 2012 in the northern urban area of the city. The outbreak involved multiple confirmed HFRS cases in students and residents; molecular typing of viruses from patients and local rodents showed they were all Hantaan virus closely related to strains circulating in the region since at least the 1980s. Following the outbreak, targeted HFRS vaccination of incoming freshmen and enhanced rodent control and education campaigns were implemented, which contributed to a reduction in cases in subsequent years in that campus population, although the wider region remained endemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high densities of rodent reservoirs (Apodemus agrarius and commensal rodents) in and around student dormitories and campus green areas, suboptimal rodent-proofing and hygiene, and low initial vaccine coverage among students (0.29% in one college versus 72% in another). Internal mechanisms: sequence analysis showed the HTNV strains were closely related to earlier regional strains rather than representing a novel genotype with markedly increased virulence, so the event reflects re-occurrence driven by ecological conditions and gaps in vaccination rather than viral re-emergence.
Review: retain: Accurately reflects the 2012 Xi’an college outbreak (6 student cases, 2 deaths) and the broader 2005–2012 increase in HFRS risk around Xi’an, with virologic confirmation of HTNV and clear ecological and vaccination drivers; scale is modest but justified as a well-characterized urban re-occurrence hotspot rather than a new emergence, so the classification is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus hantanense
EPP.common.name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans (civilians and military personnel in multiple regions of the Republic of Korea, including newly affected southwestern areas)
Event.summary: Between 1999 and 2003, reported HFRS cases in the Republic of Korea increased compared with the early 1990s, with 392 cases reported in 2003 and a notable shift in the geographic pattern of disease to include a substantial number of cases in the southwestern part of the country, in addition to traditional endemic areas near the Demilitarized Zone. The rise affected both civilians and military personnel and reflected wider spatial distribution of HTNV-infected rodents and human exposure. Ongoing use of inactivated Hantaan/Seoul vaccines, improved clinical management and public health education helped to stabilize incidence after the early 2000s, although year‑to‑year fluctuations persisted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: changes in land use and agricultural practices, urban expansion into rural rodent habitats, and favorable climate and food availability for Apodemus agrarius may have allowed HTNV-infected rodent populations to expand into new parts of South Korea, while broader recognition and surveillance also increased reported case numbers. Internal mechanisms: available data implicate endemic HTNV and Seoul virus without clear evidence of a novel genotype, so the event is considered a re-occurrence and geographic range expansion within the same UNSD subregion (Eastern Asia), rather than a distinct intra-continental emergence to a new subregion.
Review: retain: Supported by Korean surveillance data showing an increase to 392 reported HFRS cases in 2003 with a shift toward southwestern regions, and consistent with HTNV/SEOV co-circulation; treating this as a re-occurrence with intra-national range expansion (but not intra-continental emergence, since all locations remain in the same UNSD subregion of Eastern Asia) is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus hantanense
EPP.common.name: Korean hemorrhagic fever virus, Hantaan virus
Host: Humans (rural residents in Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, especially northeastern districts)
Event.summary: From 2000 to 2006, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region in northern China was part of a second major regional HFRS epidemic: reported cases in the region peaked at 661 in 2000, the highest annual total on record there, and substantial numbers of cases continued in the early 2000s with marked spatial clustering. Phylogenetic analyses indicated that Hantaan virus was the principal cause of HFRS in northeastern Inner Mongolia, while Seoul virus predominated in central and western districts that first reported HFRS in the mid-1990s. During 2003–2006, targeted rodent and virologic surveys confirmed widespread circulation of HTNV in Apodemus agrarius in the northeast and SEOV in Norway rats elsewhere. Subsequently, rodent surveillance and public health interventions were strengthened, helping to delineate endemic foci and inform control efforts, although HFRS remained an important zoonosis in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: agricultural expansion and human settlement in grassland and forest–steppe habitats harboring Apodemus agrarius, along with climate-driven rodent population fluctuations, created favorable conditions for HTNV transmission to humans; enhanced surveillance in 2003–2006 also increased detection of cases and virus diversity, especially in newly affected central and western districts. Internal mechanisms: multiple hantaviruses were found co-circulating in rodents, including distinct HTNV lineages, but available data point to ongoing circulation and spread of existing HTNV variants rather than emergence of a radically novel strain, so the event is categorized as a large regional re-occurrence with geographic intensification in established and newly recognized HTNV-endemic zones.
Review: review: Original row dated the event as 2001–2006, but the Inner Mongolia analysis shows that the second major regional HFRS epidemic peaked at 661 cases in 2000 and that 2003–2006 rodent surveys documented HTNV and SEOV circulation; the time window has been adjusted to 2000–2006 and the summary updated to emphasize the 2000 peak and subsequent outbreaks, while retaining the classification as re-occurrence within an already endemic Chinese subregion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
EPP.common.name: gonoccocus
Host: Humans (general sexually active population, with disproportionate impact on MSM and some racial/ethnic minority groups)
Event.summary: After a decline in the early 2000s, estimated gonorrhoea incidence in the United States plateaued around 2006–2009 and then increased sharply, with a roughly two‑thirds rise in per‑capita incidence between 2013 and 2019 and record‑high case counts reported by CDC. The resurgence particularly affected men, including men who have sex with men, but concurrent increases among women indicated growing heterosexual transmission. By 2019 the United States was experiencing its highest gonorrhoea burden in decades, prompting renewed national prevention initiatives and revised treatment guidelines focusing on higher‑dose ceftriaxone monotherapy and intensified partner services.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Changes in sexual behaviour including decreased condom use, growth of online dating and hookup apps, and network effects among MSM; structural factors such as reduced public health STI clinic capacity, health‑care access barriers, and socioeconomic inequities; possible risk compensation associated with HIV pre‑exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) use; high prevalence of asymptomatic infections and limited screening, especially in men. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain dominated nationally, but widespread circulation of diverse lineages, many with resistance to older antibiotics and some with reduced susceptibility to cephalosporins and azithromycin, made treatment more complex and may have modestly increased transmission duration when suboptimal regimens were used.
Review: Review – This is an appropriately major re-occurrence event (large national resurgence in incidence without a single defining new strain). The only substantive correction was to align the continent label with the Country sheet ('Northern America'). Content, timeframe and classification as re-occurrence (not re-emergence) otherwise look sound.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
EPP.common.name: gonoccocus
Host: Humans (heterosexual men and women)
Event.summary: Between April and May 2016, Hawaii detected a cluster of Neisseria gonorrhoeae isolates with both high‑level azithromycin resistance and decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone in seven patients on Oahu. The cluster appeared to arise from local transmission within a small heterosexual network, with all eight isolates sharing a highly resistant phenotype and β‑lactamase production. Prompt public health investigation, partner tracing and use of higher‑dose ceftriaxone with test‑of‑cure helped contain the cluster, and no sustained broader spread of this specific strain was documented in Hawaii thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of dual therapy with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin in a setting with ongoing importation of resistant strains via travel to Asia and substantial local STI burden; limited routine culture‑based surveillance meant the cluster was initially detected through targeted resistance testing. Internal mechanisms: Combination of 23S rRNA mutations and efflux changes conferring high‑level azithromycin resistance (MIC >256 µg/mL) together with alterations in penA and other loci producing elevated ceftriaxone MICs; multidrug‑resistant plasmid‑mediated β‑lactamase production; clonal expansion within a small sexual network demonstrating that strains with dual resistance determinants can remain transmissible.
Review: Review – Sentinel dual-resistant cluster (high-level azithromycin resistance plus decreased ceftriaxone susceptibility) in Hawaii is accurately described and appropriately classified as a re-emergence event. Updated the continent label to 'Northern America'; otherwise no structural concerns, though its relative rank among the ten most impactful events is somewhat judgment-based and could be revisited if further prioritisation is needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans (village residents); Pteropus fruit bats (reservoir, implicated); possible livestock exposure (notably a sick cow) investigated
Event.summary: In April–May 2001, a cluster of severe febrile encephalitis with a high case‑fatality ratio occurred in Chandpur village, Meherpur District, western Bangladesh; retrospective testing confirmed Nipah virus infection in 13 patients, nine of whom died, representing the first recognized Nipah outbreak in the country. Cases were concentrated in a few households and close neighbours in a rural farming community, with epidemiologic investigations pointing to proximity to bat roosts, possible contact with a sick cow, and close caregiving of ill family members as risk factors. Transmission chains burned out within about a month without wider spread, but this event triggered establishment of dedicated Nipah surveillance and outbreak‑response capacity in Bangladesh.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: smallholder farming close to Pteropus bat roosts, intimate contact with sick livestock and family members, and absence of structured infection‑prevention measures in homes facilitated bat‑to‑human spillover and limited human‑to‑human spread. Internal mechanisms: circulation of Nipah virus closely related to the Malaysian strain with inherent potential for severe encephalitis; available data do not show major viral change, so recurrence is best explained by ecological and behavioral factors.
Review: review – event is correctly placed as the first recognized Nipah outbreak in Bangladesh, but the type of emergence has been reclassified from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence at the Southern Asia sub‑regional scale because the earlier 2001 Siliguri, India outbreak in the same UN sub‑region is treated as the initial intra‑continental emergence; still retained because it is the country’s first detection and a major event.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans (hospital patients, visitors, health‑care workers)
Event.summary: Between late January and late February 2001, Siliguri in West Bengal, India, experienced a large outbreak of febrile encephalitis centered around a referral hospital; subsequent serologic and RT‑PCR testing confirmed Nipah virus infection. About 66 probable and confirmed cases with a high case‑fatality ratio were identified, and most patients were hospital staff, inpatients or visitors, indicating extensive nosocomial transmission and some spread into the surrounding community. The outbreak subsided after barrier‑nursing practices and other infection‑control measures were introduced, and no further cases were detected locally that year, establishing Nipah as an emerging threat in India and Southern Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: severe crowding in wards, lack of patient isolation, limited use of personal protective equipment, and delayed recognition of Nipah virus allowed repeated high‑risk exposures among health‑care workers, patients and visitors. Internal mechanisms: efficient person‑to‑person transmission of Nipah virus via respiratory droplets and contact with body fluids in close‑contact healthcare environments, with viruses genetically closer to Bangladesh than Malaysian strains but not representing a distinct lineage at that time.
Review: retain – correctly represents the first recognized Nipah outbreak in India and the earliest outbreak documented in the Southern Asia sub‑region, with appropriate classification as intra‑continental emergence and accurate timing, geography and transmission description.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans (village residents, caregivers, health‑care workers); Pteropus bats (reservoir)
Event.summary: In early 2010, a notable Nipah virus outbreak arose in Faridpur and Gopalganj districts, Bangladesh, beginning with sap‑exposed village residents and expanding into clusters among family caregivers and health‑care workers, for a total of 17 cases and 15 deaths. Field and hospital investigations documented multiple routes of transmission including household caregiving, nosocomial spread within district hospitals, and corpse‑to‑human infection during funeral rituals. Following rapid case isolation, contact tracing, community education to avoid raw date palm sap and high‑risk funerals, and reinforcement of infection‑control practices in health facilities, transmission was interrupted within several weeks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: wintertime consumption of raw date palm sap, frequent close caregiving of severely ill patients without protective equipment, overcrowded hospital wards with weak infection‑control programmes, and traditional washing and embracing of bodies during funerals supported household, nosocomial and corpse‑to‑human transmission. Internal mechanisms: high viral loads in respiratory and oropharyngeal secretions enabled efficient person‑to‑person and corpse‑to‑human transmission, but viral sequences remained within the known Bangladesh lineage rather than representing a novel variant.
Review: retain – accurately captures the Faridpur/Gopalganj 2010 outbreak, including case numbers, transmission routes (household, nosocomial, corpse‑to‑human) and classification as re‑occurrence within an already endemic sub‑region; sources are well chosen (EID articles and WHO/ICDDR,B‑based summaries).

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans across multiple districts (Gaibandha, Natore, Rajshahi, Naogaon, Rajbari, Pabna, Jhenaidah, Mymensingh and others); Pteropus bats (reservoir)
Event.summary: From January to early April 2013, Bangladesh reported its largest Nipah season since 2011, with 24 cases and 21 deaths across roughly a dozen districts including Gaibandha, Natore, Rajshahi, Naogaon, Rajbari, Pabna, Jhenaidah and Mymensingh, indicating widening geographic involvement within the country’s "Nipah belt". Most primary case‑patients had a documented history of drinking raw date palm sap before illness onset, and several small family and community clusters with limited person‑to‑person transmission were identified. As in previous years, cases declined sharply after the sap‑harvesting season ended and risk‑communication campaigns were intensified, but the 2013 season reinforced Nipah’s status as an endemic, highly lethal zoonosis in Bangladesh.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: continued wintertime collection and communal consumption of unprotected raw date palm sap across a growing set of districts, together with dense household living and traditional caregiving practices, supported multiple primary spillover events and short human‑to‑human chains. Internal mechanisms: persistent circulation of the established Bangladesh‑lineage Nipah virus with very high case‑fatality ratio; no specific novel genotype has been uniquely linked to the 2013 outbreaks, so re‑occurrence is attributed primarily to ecological and behavioural drivers.
Review: review – new event added because the 2013 Bangladesh season (24 cases, 21 deaths across many districts) is one of the largest documented Nipah outbreaks and was missing from the original dataset; geography, timeframe, and classification as re‑occurrence are supported by WHO baseline data and contemporaneous national reports.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans (horse owners, slaughterers, caregivers); horses; Pteropus bats (reservoir)
Event.summary: In March–April 2014, an outbreak of henipavirus infection occurred in two villages of Sultan Kudarat Province, Mindanao, Philippines, where at least 10 horses died of acute neurologic disease followed by 17 human cases, mainly among people who slaughtered sick horses, handled carcasses or consumed horse meat. Serologic testing demonstrated Nipah‑neutralizing antibodies and IgM in several patients and domestic animals, and a short sequence of the Nipah P‑gene was detected, indicating infection with Nipah virus or a very closely related henipavirus, although full genome characterization was not achieved. After cessation of horse slaughter and consumption, restrictions on animal movement, and intensified public‑health messaging, no further human or equine cases were detected and the episode was declared over.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: pasturing horses in areas used by fruit bats, lack of awareness of henipavirus risks in equids, slaughter and butchering of acutely ill horses, consumption of undercooked horse meat, and minimal infection‑prevention measures in rural health‑care facilities fostered bat‑to‑horse and horse‑to‑human transmission, with some human‑to‑human spread among caregivers and health‑care workers. Internal mechanisms: infection by a henipavirus antigenically and genetically closest to Nipah virus that was able to infect horses and humans, illustrating a bat–horse–human transmission pathway similar to Hendra virus, although the precise taxonomic status of the virus (NiV versus NiV‑like) remains unresolved.
Review: review – event is retained as a major probable Nipah (or Nipah‑like) henipavirus outbreak introducing the virus into the Philippines with a new equine amplifying host, but the type of emergence has been corrected from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence within South‑eastern Asia because Nipah was already established there (Malaysia/Singapore); virus identity and host expansion justify flagging the row for expert review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans (index family, health‑care workers, close contacts); Pteropus medius bats (reservoir, evidenced by serology)
Event.summary: In May–June 2018, an outbreak of Nipah virus disease occurred in Kozhikode and neighbouring Malappuram districts of Kerala, India, beginning with a family cluster and extending to health‑care workers and other close contacts; around 18–23 cases and 17–21 deaths were reported. Genomic analysis showed that the virus belonged to the Bangladesh lineage, and field investigations detected Nipah‑reactive antibodies in local Pteropus medius bats, indicating local bat reservoirs rather than importation of infected pigs. Intensive case isolation, ring surveillance, quarantine of contacts and reinforcement of hospital infection‑control rapidly curtailed transmission, and no further cases were detected after June 2018, though Kerala remained on high alert for future spillover.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: overlap of Pteropus medius colonies with peri‑urban human settlements, close family caregiving in small homes, and early unprotected contact of health‑care workers with severely ill encephalitis patients allowed both initial spillover and nosocomial spread. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of Bangladesh‑lineage Nipah virus into southern India and efficient human‑to‑human transmission in high‑exposure clinical and household settings, although sequencing did not reveal a Kerala‑specific divergent strain.
Review: retain – correctly describes the first Nipah outbreak in Kerala and a major re‑occurrence in India, with appropriate classification as re‑occurrence in Southern Asia and well‑supported epidemiologic and virologic details from national and WHO sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans in multiple districts; Pteropus bats (reservoir)
Event.summary: From early January to mid‑February 2023, Bangladesh experienced its largest documented Nipah outbreak since 2015, with 11 cases (10 confirmed and 1 probable) and 8 deaths reported from seven districts across two divisions. Most primary case‑patients had a clear history of consuming fresh date palm sap or related products, and some limited person‑to‑person transmission occurred among close contacts, reflecting established Bangladeshi Nipah patterns.
