Intensive public‑health messaging on avoiding raw sap, rapid outbreak investigation, and seasonal decline in sap harvesting contributed to termination of the outbreak by mid‑February 2023.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: continued wintertime consumption of raw date palm sap contaminated by bat saliva or urine, incomplete adoption of sap‑protection measures (such as bamboo skirts over collection pots), and high‑risk caregiving behaviours in rural households permitted recurrent spillover and small clusters. Internal mechanisms: stable circulation of Bangladesh‑lineage Nipah virus with inherently high case‑fatality rate and capacity for person‑to‑person transmission in close‑contact settings; no published evidence suggests a novel variant emerging specifically in 2023, so this event is classified as re‑occurrence driven largely by ecological and behavioural factors.
Review: review – event is correctly characterized as Bangladesh’s largest Nipah outbreak since 2015 and a re‑occurrence in an endemic sub‑region, but the primary WHO source has been updated from a 2025 general situation report to the 2023 Disease Outbreak News (DON442) that specifically details the 11 cases and 8 deaths; otherwise the row is appropriate to retain.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella enterica
Host: Humans (consumers of contaminated frozen dairy products)
Event.summary: In September–October 1994, health authorities in Minnesota detected a sharp increase in Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis infections that was traced to nationally distributed ice cream produced by Schwan’s Sales Enterprises, leading to identification of cases in multiple US states. Epidemiologic and microbiologic investigations showed that contamination occurred when pasteurized ice‑cream premix was transported in tanker trailers that had previously carried raw, unpasteurized liquid eggs, and national surveillance data were used to estimate that approximately 224,000 people across the United States developed gastroenteritis after eating the contaminated products. A nationwide recall of all implicated ice‑cream products, temporary closure of the Marshall, Minnesota plant, and changes to tanker‑cleaning and transport practices terminated the outbreak, and no further cases linked to this production practice were reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A change in bulk transport logistics that allowed tanker trailers to alternate between hauling raw eggs and pasteurized ice‑cream premix, coupled with inadequate cleaning, sanitation and inspection of tankers, enabled cross‑contamination of a pasteurized product that was then distributed widely across the United States. Internal mechanisms: No novel serovar or genotype was implicated; instead, the event illustrates the ability of S. Enteritidis to survive in high‑fat frozen dairy matrices and remain infectious throughout cold storage and long‑distance distribution, i.e. enhanced transmission via persistence in processed foods rather than changes in host range or virulence.
Review: Review: ADD & RETAIN. This event was missing and has been added because the 1994 Schwan’s ice‑cream outbreak is the largest common‑source salmonellosis outbreak ever recognized in the United States, with an estimated 224,000 symptomatic infections nationwide, and is clearly among the top ten human Salmonella emergence events globally since 1990 in terms of case numbers.([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM199605163342001?utm_source=openai)) Classified as 're_occurrence' (large foodborne outbreak driven by external factors in a region where S. Enteritidis was already endemic) with no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence component. Countries and sub‑region fields have been restricted to the United States, consistent with where human cases occurred, while the event summary and sources capture the national scale and production‑chain drivers.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella enterica
Host: Humans (general population; egg consumers)
Event.summary: In 2010, a major US outbreak of Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis infections associated with shell eggs began, with illness clusters detected in multiple states. Epidemiologic and traceback investigations linked many restaurant and event‑related clusters to eggs from large Iowa producers (Wright County Egg and an affiliated company), prompting nationwide recalls of about 550 million eggs and identification of roughly 1,900 culture‑confirmed illnesses across dozens of states, with CDC estimating the true number of outbreak‑related cases to be substantially higher. After contaminated egg lots were withdrawn from the market and on‑farm control measures strengthened, including depopulation of flocks and improved biosecurity and environmental testing, the number of new cases declined and the outbreak was declared over later in 2010.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑density layer‑hen production with inadequate biosecurity and sanitation, internal contamination of eggs from infected hen ovaries, and nationwide distribution of shell eggs without sufficiently robust on‑farm vaccination or testing programs enabled wide spread of a single contamination source. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was singled out; instead, this event illustrates the established capacity of S. Enteritidis to colonize poultry reproductive tracts and contaminate intact eggs, combined with environmental persistence along egg packing and distribution chains (Enhanced Transmission through food‑chain adaptation).
Review: Review: RETAIN. No structural changes were needed other than clarifying that the approximate illness range cited in the summary aligns with CDC’s description of about 1,900 outbreak illnesses linked to shell eggs, with likely higher true case numbers.([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/08/01/cyclospora-lettuce-outbreak-foodborne-illness-record)) Emergence type as 're_occurrence' (large egg‑associated outbreak in an endemic setting) is appropriate, and egg‑production drivers and control measures are well described. Added an explicit reference to the MMWR Vital Signs analysis to support statements about the relative size of this outbreak among US multistate foodborne events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
EPP.common.name: pneumococcal disease
Host: Humans (adults and children, including high-prevalence HIV-infected populations)
Event.summary: From 1993 onward, surveillance at Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital and later nationally in South Africa documented large increases in invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) and high proportions of penicillin-nonsusceptible and multidrug‑resistant S. pneumoniae, particularly among adults and children living with HIV infection. As the HIV epidemic expanded during the 1990s and early 2000s, HIV‑associated IPD incidence and resistant childhood serotypes (e.g., 6A/B, 9V, 14, 19A/F, 23F) rose sharply, with additional emergence of ceftriaxone‑nonsusceptible meningitis isolates by the mid‑2000s. After scale‑up of antiretroviral therapy and introduction of PCV7 in 2009 followed by PCV13 in 2011, national data to about 2012 show major declines in vaccine‑type and drug‑resistant IPD, although resistant strains and excess risk among people with HIV persisted. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9402377/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of the HIV epidemic generated a large immunocompromised population highly susceptible to pneumococcal disease, while heavy use of beta‑lactams, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis, and other antibiotics in both community and hospital settings created intense selection pressure for resistant lineages and facilitated spread in overcrowded facilities. Internal mechanisms: Progressive accumulation and clonal expansion of antimicrobial resistance (penicillin, cotrimoxazole, and, for a subset, third‑generation cephalosporins) within established serotypes and lineages increased fitness under treatment pressure, resulting in re‑emergent, difficult‑to‑treat IPD until countered by ART scale‑up and PCV introduction.
Review: review – updated event years from 1993–2008 to 1993–2012 so that the episode now spans the period of rising multidrug-resistant IPD in South Africa, its amplification by the HIV epidemic, and the early post‑PCV7/PCV13 decline documented up to 2012; geography (Southern Africa/South Africa), focus on HIV‑associated disease, and classification as re-emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
EPP.common.name: pneumococcal disease
Host: Humans (primarily children <5 years, but also adults via herd effects)
Event.summary: After the introduction of the 7‑valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV7) in the United States in 2000, rates of IPD from vaccine serotypes fell sharply by the early 2000s. Between about 2001 and 2008, however, IPD caused by non‑PCV7 serotypes—especially multidrug‑resistant serotype 19A, including ST320/CC320 and related clones—rose substantially in children and adults, partially offsetting vaccine gains. This replacement disease later declined after introduction of PCV13 in 2010, which directly targeted 19A and additional serotypes, leading to major reductions in 19A IPD and associated resistance. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5641a2.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread PCV7 use removed common, often resistant vaccine serotypes from carriage and disease, opening ecological space for non‑vaccine serotypes, while continued antibiotic pressure (e.g., macrolides, beta‑lactams) favored resistant lineages. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and expansion of multidrug‑resistant serotype 19A clones (e.g., ST320/CC320) with enhanced fitness under vaccine and antibiotic selection, along with beta‑lactam and macrolide resistance, drove increased incidence and severity of 19A IPD.
Review: retain – the post‑PCV7 emergence of multidrug‑resistant serotype 19A IPD in the United States is very well documented and clearly among the most impactful modern pneumococcal emergence events; years, geography, and classification as re-emergence via vaccine-driven serotype and genotype shifts are appropriate, and sources are highly relevant.

EPP.scientific.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
EPP.common.name: pneumococcal disease
Host: Humans (primarily pediatric and adult respiratory and invasive infections)
Event.summary: Between 2011 and 2016, multicenter surveillance from 17 Chinese cities showed very high rates of macrolide and multidrug resistance among S. pneumoniae isolates from children and adults, with many strains also non‑susceptible to other commonly used agents. During this period, macrolides were widely employed as first‑line empiric therapy for community‑acquired pneumonia, and conjugate pneumococcal vaccines were not yet broadly incorporated into the national infant program, allowing circulation and expansion of resistant lineages. By the mid‑2010s, Chinese expert guidance increasingly recommended against macrolides as first‑line monotherapy for pneumococcal infection, and growing attention was given to PCV13 introduction and broader stewardship as complementary control strategies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5747162/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive and often inappropriate outpatient macrolide use, incomplete pneumococcal vaccination coverage, and dense urban healthcare utilization created strong selection pressure and opportunities for clonal spread of resistant pneumococci. Internal mechanisms: Very high macrolide resistance mediated largely by erm(B) and mef genes, together with multidrug resistance across several antibiotic classes and expansion of successful resistant serotypes and sequence types, resulted in re‑emergent, difficult‑to‑treat pneumococcal disease across China.
Review: retain – China’s nationwide multicenter data clearly demonstrate extremely high macrolide and multidrug resistance rates in pneumococci and major implications for empiric therapy; years, geography, and classification as re-emergence via antimicrobial resistance are appropriate, and the selected sources are specific and relevant.

EPP.scientific.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
EPP.common.name: pneumococcal disease
Host: Humans (mainly older children and adults with pneumococcal meningitis)
Event.summary: During the 2015–2016 meningitis season, Ghana experienced a large outbreak of pneumococcal meningitis in the Brong‑Ahafo region—outside the traditional meningitis belt—followed by increased pneumococcal meningitis incidence in the Northern and Upper West regions during 2015–2017, five years after infant PCV13 introduction. Across two seasons, most confirmed pneumococcal meningitis cases occurred in persons ≥5 years of age, and approximately 60%–70% of serotyped isolates were serotype 1, despite high infant PCV13 coverage using a 3+0 schedule without booster or catch‑up. These outbreaks and elevated incidence demonstrated that, in this high‑transmission setting, infant PCV13 had not yet generated sufficient herd protection against serotype 1 in older children and adults, raising concerns about schedule design and the need for complementary strategies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6128537/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent meningitis‑belt climatic conditions (dry season, dust, crowding), high baseline carriage and transmission, and use of a 3+0 infant PCV13 schedule without booster or catch‑up limited indirect protection for older age groups; health‑system constraints delayed detection and response. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of highly invasive serotype 1 lineages (including ST217‑related clones) rather than a clearly novel variant suggests that external and programmatic factors predominated, so the episode is best characterized as re‑occurrence of epidemic serotype 1 disease in a known high‑risk subregion.
Review: review – new event added to represent the high-incidence serotype 1 pneumococcal meningitis outbreaks in Ghana (Brong-Ahafo and meningitis-belt regions) during 2015–2017 in the PCV13 era; classified as re-occurrence because the main drivers are climatic and programmatic (schedule and age targeting) rather than emergence of a completely new serotype 1 lineage, and its inclusion ensures that major African epidemic episodes are represented among the top events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
EPP.common.name: pneumococcal disease
Host: Humans (children and older adults with invasive pneumococcal disease and carriage)
Event.summary: After Belgium switched its pediatric program from PCV13 to PCV10 in 2015–2016, surveillance recorded a rapid re‑emergence of serotype 19A invasive pneumococcal disease and carriage by 2017–2018. Whole‑genome sequencing of 19A isolates from children and adults showed diverse sequence types distinct from the earlier 19A clones that had expanded after PCV7 introduction, indicating a new wave of 19A lineages. As evidence accumulated of increased 19A disease following PCV10 use, Belgium and other countries reassessed vaccine policy, and some reverted to or favored higher‑valent formulations including 19A. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7014673/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The national policy change from PCV13 to PCV10 removed direct vaccine pressure on serotype 19A, allowing 19A lineages to expand again in a population where other vaccine serotypes remained suppressed; ongoing antibiotic use further supported selection of fit clones. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and diversification within 19A, including multiple new sequence types and frequent antimicrobial resistance, underpinned re‑emergence of 19A IPD and carriage despite prior control in the PCV13 era.
Review: retain – this Belgium-specific episode is clearly documented as a policy-driven re-emergence of serotype 19A after a switch from PCV13 to PCV10, with measurable increases in IPD and carriage and distinct new 19A clones; although more localized than some other events, it is informative for vaccine policy and currently fits within the top‑10 limit, but curators may reconsider its inclusion if future global ranking across many pathogens demands stricter impact thresholds.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: Rift Valley fever virus
Host: Humans (rural residents and pastoralists) and livestock (sheep, goats, cattle, camels, donkeys) in and around Aioun El Atrouss, Hodh El Gharbi Region.
Event.summary: In September 1998, Mauritanian health authorities detected clusters of febrile illness with hemorrhagic and icteric signs in the Aioun area of Hodh El Gharbi, and laboratory testing confirmed RVFV infection, following an earlier 1987 national epidemic. Between mid‑ and late September, approximately 300–400 human cases and six deaths were reported, concurrent with very high rates of abortion and mortality in sheep, goats and other livestock, with virologic investigations isolating multiple RVFV strains from humans, animals and vectors. Human and animal case numbers declined by late October as the unusually heavy rains that had triggered extensive flooding abated, mosquito populations decreased, and control measures such as animal movement restrictions, vector control and risk communication were implemented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Exceptionally heavy rainfall in September 1998—roughly three times the 10‑year average—created extensive temporary ponds in the arid Hodh El Gharbi region, supporting large populations of RVFV‑competent mosquitoes; dense pastoral livestock populations and close human–animal contact facilitated amplification and spillover. Internal mechanisms: Virologic work documented active circulation of RVFV with multiple virus isolates from humans, livestock and vectors, but these belonged to known West African lineages, indicating re‑occurrence of endemic virus strongly amplified by environmental conditions rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: Review – Added major 1998 Mauritania outbreak (≈300–400 human cases, six deaths), which is explicitly listed among the nine largest RVF outbreaks 1997–2010; classified as re-occurrence in Western Africa. Should be retained when constructing a top-10 global events set.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: Rift Valley fever virus
Host: Humans (rural residents, farmers, herders) and livestock; large numbers of small ruminants and cattle were affected.
Event.summary: In October 2007, Sudan’s Federal Ministry of Health requested international assistance to investigate a suspected hemorrhagic fever outbreak in several states, and RVFV was identified as the causative agent. The outbreak expanded across at least three states along the Nile and its tributaries, with official hospital records capturing hundreds of cases and over 200 deaths, while subsequent analyses estimated up to 75,000 human infections during this epidemic, concurrent with substantial livestock disease and abortions. Human and animal cases diminished by early 2008 as floodwaters receded and emergency control measures—including vector control, bans on animal movement from affected areas, and public education—were implemented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy rainfall and flooding along river systems, including areas influenced by irrigation and dam infrastructure, generated extensive mosquito breeding sites and sustained transmission among livestock, with socio‑economic dependence on livestock, close animal handling, and limited health infrastructure contributing to high human exposure and mortality. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate a distinct new RVFV genotype in Sudan; instead, the large epidemic appears to reflect re‑introduction or persistence of endemic virus amplified under favorable environmental and ecological conditions.
Review: Retain – Large, well-documented outbreak in Sudan within the already affected Northern Africa subregion (following Egypt 1977–78 and later recurrences); classification as re-occurrence is appropriate and no geographic or timing corrections are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: Rift Valley fever virus
Host: Humans (rural residents and people with contact to livestock) and livestock (mainly ruminants) with evidence of infection in animals and humans.
Event.summary: During the rainy seasons of January–May 2008 and November 2008–March 2009, Madagascar experienced successive RVF outbreaks with laboratory‑confirmed human cases and concurrent livestock infections following unusually heavy rains. The outbreaks developed across several districts, including Fianarantsoa and areas near Lake Alaotra, with hundreds of laboratory‑confirmed and probable human infections reported across the two seasons, alongside serologic evidence of widespread animal infection. Transmission subsided after the rainy seasons ended and entomologic conditions became less favorable, though gaps in surveillance and reporting limited precise estimation of total human disease burden.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Above‑normal rainfall and flooding during consecutive rainy seasons in Madagascar’s highland and lowland areas expanded mosquito breeding habitats, facilitating RVFV amplification in local livestock and spillover to humans; limited veterinary and public health surveillance reduced early detection and control. Internal mechanisms: Genetic characterization indicated that viruses from the 2008–2009 outbreaks clustered with Kenya‑1/1a East African lineages rather than earlier Madagascar strains, consistent with renewed introduction and replacement of prior lineages, so this episode is best viewed as re‑emergence driven by importation of distinct viral genotypes plus favorable climatic conditions.
Review: Review – Reclassified from re-occurrence to re-emergence because sequence data show that 2008–2009 strains in Madagascar belong to Kenya-1/1a East African lineages distinct from earlier Madagascar viruses, indicating genotype replacement rather than simple climate-driven resurgence; geography and years are correct and sources remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: Rift Valley fever virus
Host: Humans (farmers, veterinarians, abattoir workers and rural residents) and livestock (especially sheep, goats, and cattle) across multiple South African provinces.
Event.summary: Beginning in 2008, South Africa reported renewed RVF activity with a cluster of human cases linked to a dairy farm outbreak, foreshadowing larger epidemics in subsequent years. The situation escalated into widespread epizootics and epidemics during 2010–2011, when more than 14,000 animal cases were recorded across 8 of 9 provinces and at least 302 laboratory‑confirmed human infections, including around 25 deaths, were documented among people with close contact to infected livestock. Outbreak activity decreased after 2011 as rainfall normalized, vector populations declined, and control measures—such as targeted livestock vaccination, movement controls, and occupational protections—were strengthened, though sporadic smaller outbreaks (e.g., on a farm in 2018 with several human cases) have continued to occur.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Periods of above‑average rainfall and localized flooding in traditionally endemic regions triggered epizootics among sheep and other ruminants; high densities of susceptible livestock due to lapses in vaccination, animal movement between farms, and occupational exposure among farmers, veterinarians, and abattoir workers facilitated widespread zoonotic transmission. Internal mechanisms: Available molecular data suggest circulation of endemic RVFV lineages without clear emergence of a novel variant; the scale and geographic spread reflect environmental suitability and gaps in animal immunity rather than major viral change, with possible minor adaptations in local vector–virus–host interactions enhancing transmission efficiency.
Review: Retain – Multi-year South African cycle correctly summarized around the large 2010–2011 human epidemic; Southern Africa classification and re-occurrence status are consistent with a long history of RVF in the region and supported by national and CDC investigations.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: Rift Valley fever virus
Host: Humans (rural residents, livestock handlers) and livestock (small ruminants, cattle, camels) across southern Mauritania.
Event.summary: In 2010, Mauritania experienced a major RVF outbreak affecting both animals and humans following heavy rainfall in southern regions, with cases reported from multiple wilayas. Epidemiologic investigations identified dozens of confirmed and probable human cases, including 13 deaths, along with widespread livestock abortions and deaths, representing one of several large RVF episodes the country has faced since the late 1980s. Human case reports declined towards the end of the year as rains diminished, vector densities decreased, and joint animal–human health responses were implemented, though RVFV has since continued to re‑emerge periodically in the country.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Exceptional rainfall events in the Sahelian and Saharan fringe zones of southern Mauritania created temporary ponds and flooded depressions that favored amplification of RVFV in domestic ruminants, with pastoral livelihoods and close animal contact exposing humans to infected blood and tissues; limited routine vaccination and vector control contributed to recurrent large‑scale outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Virus isolates from Mauritania during different outbreaks cluster with other West African RVFV lineages, consistent with persistence and local evolution of endemic strains rather than emergence of a radically new variant; the primary driver is climate‑mediated amplification and spread in livestock populations with accumulating susceptible animals.
Review: Retain – 2010 Mauritania outbreak is explicitly listed among major RVF epidemics (≈63 reported human cases, 13 deaths) and remains a relevant Western Africa re-occurrence; geography, timing and classification are correct.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: Rift Valley fever virus
Host: Humans (rural residents, herders, people with animal contact) and livestock in multiple southern regions of Mauritania.
Event.summary: Following heavy rains and flooding in southern Mauritania in 2012, human cases of febrile and hemorrhagic illness were detected in several regions and laboratory testing confirmed RVFV infection. The outbreak unfolded between September and November 2012, with at least 34–41 confirmed human cases and 13–17 deaths reported across regions such as Tagant, Brakna, Trarza, Assaba, and Hodh El Gharbi, alongside evidence of livestock infection and ongoing animal abortions. Transmission diminished by late November as environmental conditions changed and a multisectoral response—strengthening surveillance, improving case management, and implementing measures in slaughterhouses and among farmers—was put in place.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Above‑average rainfall and flooding created extensive breeding sites for RVFV mosquito vectors in southern Mauritania, leading to rapid amplification in local livestock; socio‑economic reliance on pastoralism and informal slaughter practices increased human contact with infected animals, and limited preventive vaccination enabled recurrent outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses indicated that the 2012 outbreak viruses were related to previous Mauritanian RVFV strains, suggesting re‑emergence of locally circulating lineages rather than a novel genotype, with geographic range expansion driven primarily by environmental and husbandry factors.
Review: Review – Moderate-scale Western Africa outbreak (≈34–41 cases, 13–17 deaths) with correct geography and classification as re-occurrence; however, once larger events such as Mauritania 1998, Mayotte 2018–2019 and the 2025 Mauritania/Senegal epidemic are included, this episode is unlikely to rank among the global top-10 by impact and could be excluded if strict prioritization is required.
Review.Comment: Not top 10

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: Rift Valley fever virus
Host: Humans (rural residents, pastoralists) with concurrent livestock infections (small ruminants and camels) in Tahoua Region, Niger.
Event.summary: In August–September 2016, health authorities in Niger’s Tahoua Region detected clusters of severe febrile illness with hemorrhagic signs in pastoral communities, and laboratory testing confirmed RVFV infection, marking the country’s first documented RVF outbreak. The outbreak centered on Tchintabaraden and neighboring departments, with reports of approximately 78 human cases and 26 deaths during August–September and additional suspected cases identified through expanded surveillance, alongside evidence of widespread livestock disease. Case numbers declined after September 2016 as vector control, movement restrictions, and public health messaging were implemented and as seasonal ecological conditions became less favorable, but the event demonstrated RVFV’s expansion eastward within Western Africa into previously unaffected areas of the Sahel.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy seasonal rains in the Sahel produced temporary ponds and flooded grazing areas in Tahoua Region, promoting mosquito proliferation among transhumant herds; extensive livestock movements and trade from neighboring endemic areas likely facilitated virus introduction, followed by local transmission to humans through handling of sick animals and exposure to vectors. Internal mechanisms: Genetic sequencing of outbreak viruses showed close relatedness to known West African RVFV lineages from earlier Mauritanian outbreaks, suggesting geographic range expansion of existing strains rather than major evolutionary change, with successful establishment in a largely naïve human and livestock population.
Review: Review – Corrected emergence-type classification: removed previous ‘first_detection’ and ‘intra_continental_emergence’ flags (RVFV was already established in the Western Africa subregion via Mauritania and Senegal) and set ‘re_occurrence’ to true to reflect range expansion within an existing subregion into a new country (Niger). Event remains epidemiologically important but is smaller than several other global outbreaks; may be de-prioritized if only the very largest events are retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: Rift Valley fever virus
Host: Humans (residents of pastoral and agro‑pastoral communities in Wajir, Marsabit, and Siaya counties) and livestock (goats, sheep, cattle, camels).
Event.summary: In May–June 2018, after reports of livestock abortions and deaths in northern Kenya, an RVF outbreak was confirmed in Wajir and Marsabit counties and later in Siaya, with human cases presenting with acute febrile and sometimes hemorrhagic illness. Over the course of the outbreak, investigations identified around 106 human RVF cases (probable and confirmed) across the three counties, with several fatalities, while thousands of small stock were reportedly lost and serologic studies revealed substantial infection in goats and other livestock. Human case numbers declined by late June as joint animal–human health teams implemented vector control, livestock movement restrictions, and risk communication, and as rains decreased and temporary breeding sites for mosquitoes dried up.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy rainfall and localized flooding in arid and semi‑arid counties of northern Kenya increased mosquito breeding, while high densities of susceptible small ruminants and camels enabled rapid amplification of RVFV; pastoral practices involving slaughtering, butchering, and consumption of sick animals, combined with limited vaccination, facilitated spillover to humans. Internal mechanisms: Epidemiologic and serologic investigations indicate involvement of RVFV strains consistent with earlier Kenyan lineages rather than a novel variant, with environmental suitability and livestock management practices—rather than new viral traits—driving the observed resurgence and spread into multiple counties.
Review: Review – Outbreak is well described and classification as re-occurrence within an already endemic Eastern Africa subregion is appropriate. With 106 human cases and single-country spread, its impact is intermediate compared with the largest global RVF epidemics; depending on how strictly a top-10 threshold is applied, this event is a reasonable candidate for retention or exclusion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: Rift Valley fever virus
Host: Humans (residents of Mayotte with frequent livestock contact or exposure to animal fluids) and livestock (cattle and small ruminants) on the island.
Event.summary: From November 2018 through July 2019, Mayotte, a French overseas department in the Comoros archipelago, experienced a prolonged RVF outbreak with autochthonous human transmission following increased virus circulation in local cattle. A total of about 142–145 laboratory‑confirmed human cases were reported, most in central and north‑western communes, with the majority of patients reporting direct or indirect contact with livestock, consumption of raw milk or involvement in slaughtering; more than 120 animal infection foci were also detected. Human case numbers and new animal outbreaks declined after mid‑2019 as vector control, animal health measures and risk communication were strengthened and the rainy season ended.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A tropical climate with abundant competent vectors, close proximity to RVF‑endemic areas in East Africa and the Comoros, importation and local movement of cattle and small ruminants, and intense human–animal contact around small backyard herds created favorable conditions for virus amplification and spillover; preceding increases in bovine seroprevalence signaled rising transmission. Internal mechanisms: Virologic and modeling studies indicate that the outbreak was driven by circulation of RVFV strains typical of Eastern Africa, with no evidence of a radically novel lineage, so the event represents a substantial re-occurrence in an area with prior evidence of endemic virus rather than a first detection in the human host system.
Review: Review – Newly added major island outbreak with ≈142–145 confirmed human cases and extensive animal involvement in Mayotte, classified as re-occurrence within Eastern Africa (Mayotte is listed under Eastern Africa in the provided country table). This episode is one of the larger RVF outbreaks since 2010 and should be considered among the top-10 global events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus hominis
EPP.common.name: Measles morbillivirus
Host: Humans (primarily unvaccinated and undervaccinated children)
Event.summary: Beginning in early 2018, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) experienced a protracted nationwide measles epidemic driven by low routine immunization coverage and gaps after supplementary campaigns. The outbreak intensified through 2019, ultimately affecting all 26 provinces and causing more than 450,000 suspected cases and over 8,000 reported deaths before large-scale vaccination and response activities gradually brought transmission under control by late 2020, when incidence declined and the epidemic was declared over.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: chronically low measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) coverage (around or below 60% in recent years), gaps in supplemental immunization activities, weak health systems, poverty, and concurrent crises that diverted resources, allowing accumulation of large susceptible cohorts. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of a fundamentally novel genotype driving this outbreak; the main mechanism is re-occurrence due to immunity gaps, with the inherently high transmissibility of circulating B3/H1-lineage strains facilitating rapid geographic expansion.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Large DRC epidemic (≈460,000 suspected cases and >8,000 deaths) is clearly among the most impactful modern measles events and is well documented by UNICEF and WHO/CDC sources. ([unicef.org](https://www.unicef.org/drcongo/en/press-releases/measles-deaths-democratic-republic-congo-top-4000)) Geographic, temporal and host information are correct; classification as re-occurrence (no first/inter-continental or intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because measles has long been endemic in Middle Africa. No structural changes made beyond confirming that emergence-type flags remain all "No" except re_occurrence=Yes.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus hominis
EPP.common.name: Measles morbillivirus
Host: Humans (mainly children, many unvaccinated)
Event.summary: In September 2018, Madagascar detected an unusually large measles outbreak starting in Antananarivo that rapidly spread nationwide due to very low vaccination coverage. By late 2019, estimates suggested roughly 220,000–250,000 cases and over 1,000 deaths, making it the largest measles outbreak in the country’s history. The epidemic waned after multiple mass vaccination campaigns and strengthened surveillance, and incidence gradually returned toward pre‑outbreak levels once large susceptible cohorts had been partially depleted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: long‑standing low MCV1 coverage (around 58% in 2017), high prevalence of childhood malnutrition, urban crowding, poverty, and overlapping health emergencies that strained the health system, allowing accumulation of susceptible children. Internal mechanisms: B3 genotype viruses already circulating in Africa were responsible; there is no evidence of a substantially novel measles strain, so the event is appropriately characterized as re-occurrence driven by immunity gaps and adverse socio-environmental conditions.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Madagascar’s 2018–2019 epidemic (≈225,000+ cases, >1,000 deaths) is one of the largest national measles outbreaks this century and fits the selection criterion based on burden. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/17-january-2019-measles-madagascar-en)) Country, sub-region (Eastern Africa), timing and drivers are consistent with WHO/UNICEF reporting. Classification as re-occurrence only is correct; measles has long circulated in Madagascar and no novel strain was implicated. No field changes required.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus hominis
EPP.common.name: Measles morbillivirus
Host: Humans (primarily children, both unvaccinated and undervaccinated)
Event.summary: From around 2013, the Philippines entered a large measles epidemic cycle as immunity gaps from declining vaccination coverage accumulated in successive birth cohorts. In 2014, WHO recorded more than 57,000 suspected cases and over 21,000 confirmed measles infections with about 110 deaths nationwide, with major outbreaks centered in Metro Manila and other urban areas. Intensified vaccination efforts and outbreak response activities in 2014–2015 reduced incidence, but persistent immunity gaps contributed to renewed resurgence in 2018–2019.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: declining routine measles vaccination coverage, high population density in urban centers, and health‑system constraints that hindered follow‑up campaigns and outbreak response. Internal mechanisms: circulating measles genotypes (notably D8) were not fundamentally new for the region; the outbreak reflects re-occurrence due to large susceptible cohorts rather than viral evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2013–2014 Philippines epidemic (tens of thousands of cases and >100 deaths) is a major Western Pacific/SE Asia event and seeded numerous international outbreaks, including in the U.S. and other high‑income countries. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/news/item/15-05-2019-new-measles-surveillance-data-for-2019?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate; measles was long-established nationally. No corrections to geography, timing or emergence-type flags were required, but users should note that case/death figures vary slightly by source and are approximate.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus hominis
EPP.common.name: Measles morbillivirus
Host: Humans (mainly infants and young children)
Event.summary: In early 2019, the Philippines experienced another major measles epidemic, with outbreaks declared in multiple regions including Metro Manila, Central Luzon, CALABARZON, Western Visayas and Central Visayas. By late February 2019, more than 12,000 suspected cases and over 200 deaths had already been reported, and national totals by year’s end reached many tens of thousands of mainly young, unvaccinated children. Aggressive emergency vaccination campaigns and risk‑communication efforts gradually curtailed transmission over 2019, but the episode underscored severe immunity gaps and eroded public trust in immunization following recent vaccine controversies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: substantial drops in measles vaccination coverage due to long‑term program weaknesses and, more recently, loss of public trust in vaccines, high birth rates, and intense urban crowding. Internal mechanisms: no fundamentally new measles variant was implicated; the epidemic reflects re-occurrence driven by large susceptible cohorts and frequent seeding between regions, with highly transmissible D8 genotypes already circulating in the Western Pacific Region.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2019 Philippines resurgence again produced very large national case and death burdens and contributed materially to global measles resurgence, so it is reasonable to include as a separate high-impact event following the 2013–2014 epidemic. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/news/item/15-05-2019-new-measles-surveillance-data-for-2019?utm_source=openai)) Emergence-type flags (re_occurrence only) and geographic classification are consistent with definitions and WHO reporting; no structural field changes made.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia burgdorferi
EPP.common.name: Lyme disease
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From the early 1990s onward, Lyme disease in the United States intensified in the Northeast, Mid‑Atlantic, and Upper Midwest, building on foci first recognized in the 1970s and 1980s. Over roughly 1990–2010, incidence rose steadily and geographic foci expanded into suburban and peri‑urban areas as infected Ixodes scapularis ticks spread, leading to several hundred thousand treated human infections per year by the 2010s. The event has persisted through at least the mid‑2020s with high and fluctuating annual case numbers and no clear return to pre‑epidemic baselines.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: suburbanization and forest fragmentation that increased edge habitat and human exposure to ticks; recovery and high densities of white‑tailed deer and competent rodent reservoirs; increased outdoor recreation; and regional climate warming that lengthened tick activity seasons and favored Ixodes scapularis survival. Internal mechanisms: highly efficient enzootic transmission cycles of B. burgdorferi sensu stricto in Peromyscus and other small mammals and continued geographic range expansion of competent tick vectors (enhanced transmission/vector adaptation and inherent geographic range expansion), without strong evidence for a single novel hypervirulent strain dominating this period.
Review: retain – This row appropriately captures the long‑running increase and spread of Lyme disease incidence in the northeastern, mid‑Atlantic and upper midwestern United States from the early 1990s through at least the mid‑2020s, with correct continent/subregion/country coding and classification as a re‑occurrence event driven primarily by ecological and behavioral factors rather than pathogen change.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia burgdorferi
EPP.common.name: Lyme disease
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Beginning around 2009, Canada experienced a marked emergence of Lyme disease as locally established Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes pacificus populations expanded northward from the United States and from coastal refugia. Reported human cases increased from 144 in 2009 to over 2,000 by 2017, with national incidence reaching roughly 5–6 per 100,000 and cumulative reports exceeding tens of thousands of cases by the early 2020s as risk spread across multiple provinces. Enhanced surveillance, public health responses, and some regional climatic plateauing have moderated but not reversed this upward trend by the mid‑2020s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: climate warming enabling northward range expansion and overwintering of Ixodes scapularis; changes in land use, forest cover, and deer/rodent host distributions; and increased awareness and surveillance that improved detection and reporting. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of established B. burgdorferi sensu stricto–Ixodes transmission cycles (inherent geographic range expansion and vector adaptation), but no single novel strain has been implicated; the event is best characterized as ecological expansion and re‑occurrence of an existing pathogen into new areas within the same UNSD subregion.
Review: review – Re‑emergence has been set to "No" because the substantial increase in Canadian Lyme disease incidence since about 2009 is well explained by climatic and ecological drivers and northward spread of existing Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto–tick cycles, with no clear evidence of major pathogen change; the row should be retained as a major re‑occurrence event with appropriate geography and approximate timing but flagged for expert confirmation of the start year and burden estimates.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia burgdorferi
EPP.common.name: Lyme disease
Host: Humans
Event.summary: Following the first documented human Lyme disease cases in Heilongjiang Province in the mid‑1980s, northeastern China (e.g., Heilongjiang, Jilin, Inner Mongolia) experienced growing numbers of Lyme borreliosis cases through the 1990s and 2000s. Over roughly 2005–2020, systematic reviews and mapping studies documented wide distribution of Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato exposure and clinically compatible Lyme cases across at least 29 provinces, with particularly high seroprevalence and reported incidence in forested northeastern and some central regions. By around 2020, Lyme borreliosis had become a recognized endemic tick‑borne disease across large parts of mainland China, although underdiagnosis and variable reporting remained substantial challenges.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive forest and grassland landscapes supporting Ixodes persulcatus and Ixodes ricinus ticks; expanding human activity in tick‑infested habitats; increasing clinical awareness and surveillance that raised detection rates; and socio‑economic shifts that increased both occupational and recreational exposure to ticks. Internal mechanisms: circulation of multiple B. burgdorferi sensu lato genospecies, including B. garinii, B. afzelii and others, in Ixodes ticks and vertebrate reservoirs; the apparent geographic broadening is largely due to improved mapping and ecological spread rather than emergence of a single new genotype, so this period is treated as re‑occurrence and range expansion within Asia.
Review: review – The country field has been simplified to mainland China only; evidence for locally acquired human Lyme borreliosis in Hong Kong and Macao remains limited and many reported cases likely reflect imported infections, so those territories were removed from this event. Otherwise, the row gives a reasonable approximation of the post‑1980s recognition and expansion of Lyme borreliosis across China and is retained as a major re‑occurrence event, with timing and burden estimates to be checked against Chinese surveillance sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia burgdorferi
EPP.common.name: Lyme disease
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In the 2000s, sporadic serologic and clinical reports began to indicate the presence of human Lyme disease in southern Chinese provinces previously considered non‑endemic. Around 2010 and into the late 2010s, targeted studies in Hainan and other southern provinces documented Lyme disease antibodies and locally acquired cases among patients with arthritis or neurological symptoms, confirming autochthonous transmission in these subtropical and tropical settings. Although case numbers remained low compared with northeastern China, these findings through roughly 2020 marked a southward ecological expansion of the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato–Ixodes system within the country.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement of infected hosts and ticks via livestock, wildlife and human travel; land‑use changes and development of forested, agricultural and plantation habitats capable of supporting Ixodes and other potential vectors in subtropical/tropical zones; and increasing use of serologic testing for Lyme disease in southern clinics. Internal mechanisms: geographic and ecological range expansion of B. burgdorferi sensu lato and its tick vectors into lower‑latitude habitats (inherent geographic range expansion), possibly facilitated by local adaptation of vectors and strains (enhanced transmission/vector adaptation), consistent with a re‑emergence pattern in new ecological niches within the same national and UNSD subregion context.
Review: review – The event years were extended to 2005–2020 (from 2005–2015) to capture ongoing serologic and clinical evidence of Lyme disease in Hainan and other southern provinces into the late 2010s; the country field was simplified to China because the spread described is within‑country rather than to new UNSD subregions, and 'first_detection' was set to 'No' since Lyme borreliosis was already recognized in China by the mid‑1980s. The event is retained and flagged as a re‑emergence episode representing southward ecological expansion, but it should be reviewed because case counts are relatively low and some reports rely heavily on serology.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: West Nile virus
Host: Humans (adult and elderly urban residents, mainly in Bucharest and southeastern Romania)
Event.summary: In summer–autumn 1996, Romania experienced a large outbreak of West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease centered on Bucharest and southeastern districts, marking a dramatic return of WNV encephalitis to Europe after decades of mainly silent circulation. The epidemic developed rapidly between July 15 and October 12, with 393 serologically confirmed or probable human cases, 352 presenting with central nervous system infection and 17 deaths predominantly among persons over 50 years of age. Transmission subsided with the end of the mosquito season and intensified vector control, after which only sporadic cases were reported until later European re-emergence episodes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: hot summer conditions, high densities of Culex mosquitoes in urban settings, and peri‑domestic bird populations facilitated intense local amplification; limited prior population immunity after a long inter-epidemic period likely increased the pool of susceptible adults. Internal mechanisms: no clearly novel lineage was identified compared with earlier European/Mediterranean WNV lineage 1 strains, so the event is best characterized as a geographic and intensity resurgence without major documented viral genetic change (re-occurrence rather than re-emergence).
Review: retain: Major early European West Nile neuroinvasive outbreak (~393 confirmed cases, 17 deaths) in Eastern Europe; geography and classification as re-occurrence (no new continent or clearly novel strain) are consistent with published accounts, so no structural changes were made.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: West Nile virus
Host: Humans (primarily older adults in New York City and surrounding counties)
Event.summary: In late August 1999, unexplained clusters of encephalitis with muscle weakness were detected in Queens, New York City, and investigation identified the first domestic human cases of West Nile virus in the United States and the Americas. The outbreak evolved over August–September with around 60 hospitalized human cases and 7 deaths, accompanied by extensive bird mortality and WNV‑positive mosquito pools across New York City and neighboring counties, demonstrating rapid local establishment of a new zoonotic arbovirus. Human transmission waned with cooler weather and mosquito control measures, but the virus overwintered and seeded its subsequent continent‑wide spread across North America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely introduction of an infected human, bird or mosquito via international air travel or trade into New York, followed by amplification in abundant urban Culex pipiens mosquitoes and local bird populations; warm late‑summer conditions and dense human populations enhanced exposure. Internal mechanisms: the introduced lineage 1 strain was highly neuroinvasive in humans and birds, but genetic analyses suggest it belonged to the existing lineage 1 clade circulating in the Mediterranean rather than representing a fundamentally new genotype; the key mechanism was geographic range expansion and establishment in a naïve ecological and human context.
Review: review: Corrected event typing so that first_detection is set to "false" (the first detection of WNV in humans was Uganda 1937); retained inter_continental_emergence = "true" to represent the first establishment of WNV in North America. Event is appropriately kept despite modest case numbers because of its pivotal role in inter-continental spread.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: West Nile virus
Host: Humans (country‑wide, mainly older adults)
Event.summary: Between August 1 and October 31, 2000, Israel experienced a nationwide epidemic of West Nile fever, following earlier animal outbreaks and detection of WNV activity in birds in 1998–1999. The epidemic involved 417 laboratory‑confirmed human cases, 326 hospitalizations and about 33 deaths, representing one of the largest and most severe WNV outbreaks recorded globally at that time. Human transmission declined with the end of the mosquito season and intensified vector control, but the event signaled renewed high‑impact WNV activity in an area with documented historical circulation.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high late‑summer temperatures, irrigated agriculture and peri‑urban wetlands supported large Culex mosquito populations feeding on birds and humans; demographic aging and urbanization increased the proportion of susceptible older adults; prior detection of WNV in geese and migratory birds points to avian migration and local ecological change as key drivers. Internal mechanisms: sequence data indicate co-circulation of closely related lineage 1 clusters, including variants similar to those detected in Israel in 1998 and in New York and Russia in 1999, but without definitive evidence that a single new genotype alone explains the outbreak’s severity; the event is therefore treated here as a major re-occurrence in a region with prior human WNV activity.
Review: retain: Large 2000 nationwide outbreak in Israel (~417 confirmed cases, ~33 deaths) is well documented and clearly among the historically largest WNV outbreaks; geography and classification as re-occurrence (no new continent or sub-region, and only modest genotype differences within lineage 1) are acceptable for this dataset, so no structural changes were made.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: West Nile virus
Host: Humans (widely across the United States, especially Midwest and South)
Event.summary: By 2002, three years after its 1999 New York introduction, West Nile virus had spread westward across much of the continental United States, culminating in a massive epidemic and epizootic that summer and autumn. National surveillance documented 4,156 laboratory‑confirmed human cases (including about 2,942 meningoencephalitis cases) and 284 deaths, with virus activity detected in 44 states, tens of thousands of dead birds, thousands of infected mosquito pools and over 14,000 equine cases, reflecting rapid intra‑continental expansion from the Atlantic seaboard into the Midwest and Great Plains. Transmission declined with the onset of colder weather and large‑scale mosquito control, but the virus had become firmly endemic across most of the contiguous United States by the end of the season.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: dispersal via migratory birds, increasing competence and abundance of Culex species in varied habitats, and widespread urban and agricultural irrigation enabled the virus to colonize new ecological zones; lack of herd immunity in both birds and humans and limited early mosquito control in newly affected regions amplified impact. Internal mechanisms: the epidemic was driven largely by the same lineage 1 strain introduced in 1999, with evidence of local adaptation of virus–vector–host systems but no single defining novel genotype; the key mechanisms were geographic range expansion and a high force of infection in a largely naïve continent, consistent with intra-continental emergence into new subregions.
Review: review: Removed re_occurrence = "true" so this epidemic is coded solely as intra_continental_emergence into new North American subregions, in accordance with the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra-/inter-continental emergence. Mechanism text was adjusted to match this interpretation; event is retained as the major 2002 transcontinental expansion of WNV in the United States.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: West Nile virus
Host: Humans (northern Greece, especially Central Macedonia; mainly older adults)
Event.summary: In summer 2010, Greece reported its first recognized outbreak of West Nile virus disease, with autochthonous human cases detected in Central Macedonia after decades of largely silent circulation in parts of Europe. Over the season, 262 probable and confirmed human infections were notified, including 197 neuroinvasive cases and 35 deaths, making it the largest documented European WNV outbreak since Romania 1996 and signalling establishment of an endemo‑epidemic focus in northern Greece. Transmission subsided by October with colder weather and intensified vector control, yet seasonal outbreaks recurred in subsequent years, demonstrating ongoing re‑emergence of lineage 2 WNV in southeastern Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive irrigated agriculture, rice fields and wetlands in Central Macedonia provided ideal habitats for Culex mosquitoes, while high summer temperatures and socio‑economic factors (aging population, outdoor evening activities, and limited early awareness) increased human exposure; migratory birds likely introduced or amplified the virus. Internal mechanisms: molecular analyses showed that the outbreak was caused by a WNV lineage 2 strain closely related to viruses previously detected in wild birds in Hungary and Austria, representing a relatively recent introduction of lineage 2 into humans in this region; higher neuroinvasive potential and adaptation of lineage 2 to European birds and mosquitoes underlie its designation as a re-emergence driven by novel strain/genotype spread and enhanced transmission capacity.
Review: retain: Greece 2010 (262 cases, 35 deaths) is widely recognized as a hallmark lineage 2-driven re-emergence event in Southern Europe; geography and coding as re-emergence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence) match published descriptions, so no structural changes were made.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: West Nile virus
Host: Humans (widely across the U.S., with a major hotspot in Texas, especially Dallas–Fort Worth)
Event.summary: In 2012, more than a decade after West Nile virus first appeared in New York, the United States experienced its largest WNV epidemic since 2003, with concentrated transmission in Texas and other central states. National surveillance recorded 5,674 human cases (2,873 neuroinvasive) and 286 deaths, with Texas alone reporting 1,868 cases and 89 deaths, particularly around the Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex, where intense urban mosquito activity drove sustained community transmission. The outbreak tapered off in late autumn as mosquito populations declined and emergency vector-control measures were expanded, but it underscored that substantial WNV epidemics remain possible in an endemic context.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: exceptional heat and drought during the 2012 summer in Texas and surrounding states were associated with high Culex mosquito infection rates, altered bird–mosquito–human contact patterns, and increased outdoor evening exposure; urban infrastructure (storm drains, standing water) and delayed detection in some jurisdictions exacerbated spread. Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses suggested continued circulation of North American lineage 1 WNV with local evolution but no single new strain explaining the outbreak; heightened transmission appears to reflect climatic and ecological amplification and focal population susceptibility, in line with re-occurrence due primarily to external drivers rather than clear viral innovation.
Review: retain: The 2012 U.S. season (5,674 cases, 286 deaths) is one of the largest WNV epidemics recorded and is appropriately coded as re-occurrence in an already endemic continent driven largely by climatic and ecological factors; no structural changes were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Gammainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza C virus
Host: Humans (primarily children with acute respiratory illness)
Event.summary: In early 1996, surveillance of children with acute respiratory illness in Yamagata City, Japan, identified a cluster of laboratory-confirmed influenza C infections marking a localized community outbreak after years of sporadic detections. The outbreak spread among children over the winter season, with multiple isolates belonging to a single antigenic group (C/Yamagata/26/81-like) recovered from pediatric outpatients and inpatients. Transmission declined by late spring 1996 as susceptible hosts were depleted and respiratory virus circulation shifted to other agents, and routine surveillance detected few or no influenza C cases in subsequent immediate seasons.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Periodic accumulation of susceptible children in the community and winter respiratory seasonality favored localized transmission once influenza C was introduced or reintroduced into Yamagata; limited routine testing in prior years likely allowed low-level circulation to go unrecognized. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak viruses were antigenically and genetically similar to previously circulating C/Yamagata/26/81-like strains, suggesting no major novel genotype, and periodic epidemic peaks are thought to reflect population immunity dynamics rather than marked changes in virulence or transmissibility.
Review: Decision: retain. This Yamagata City outbreak is a well-documented pediatric community epidemic with multiple C/Yamagata-lineage isolates and clear winter seasonality; timing, location, host, and classification as re-occurrence (not first or inter-/intra-continental emergence) are consistent with primary sources, so no corrections are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Gammainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza C virus
Host: Humans (primarily children with acute respiratory illness)
Event.summary: In 1998, Yamagata City, Japan, experienced a second documented outbreak of influenza C virus among children, following a relatively quiescent period after the 1996 epidemic. The 1998 outbreak again involved clusters of pediatric respiratory illness, with virologic surveillance detecting multiple closely related influenza C isolates in the same community setting. As with the earlier episode, circulation waned after the winter–spring peak, and the outbreak resolved without evidence of sustained high-level transmission into the following seasons.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Similar to 1996, a build‑up of susceptible young children and seasonal winter conditions favored renewed community transmission once influenza C re-circulated. Internal mechanisms: Antigenic and genetic analyses showed 1998 strains highly homologous to the 1996 Yamagata outbreak viruses, indicating persistence of the same lineage rather than emergence of a distinct novel variant; the pattern is consistent with recurrent epidemic waves driven largely by host immunity cycles.
Review: Decision: retain. Represents the second Yamagata pediatric outbreak in the same community and lineage, with good virologic characterization; event timing, geography, and classification as a re-occurring wave of an established lineage are appropriate and require no changes.

EPP.scientific.name: Gammainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza C virus
Host: Humans (children and adults with acute respiratory illness)
Event.summary: During the 1999/2000 winter season in Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan, clinicians and public health laboratories documented an increased number of influenza C virus isolations from patients with respiratory illness, indicating a regional epidemic wave. Cases were identified across age groups, with most infections detected in the winter months through targeted virologic surveillance. As winter ended and overall influenza activity declined, influenza C detections fell, and the epidemic wave subsided without documented major spread beyond the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Routine winter respiratory virus seasonality, indoor crowding, and the presence of a susceptible pediatric population likely contributed to the regional 1999/2000 wave once influenza C began circulating. Internal mechanisms: Genetic characterization showed these Hiroshima strains were antigenically related to C/Yamagata-lineage viruses circulating in Japan through the 1990s, supporting a pattern of periodic re-occurrence of existing lineages rather than emergence of a new genotype with distinct virulence properties.
Review: Decision: retain. The Hiroshima 1999/2000 winter cluster is a clearly described regional epidemic with multiple confirmations; start year, location, and interpretation as a re-occurring wave of established Japanese lineages are appropriate, with no apparent misclassification or geographic errors.

EPP.scientific.name: Gammainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza C virus
Host: Humans (infants <24 months hospitalized with respiratory infections)
Event.summary: From September 1999 through July 2003, a prospective study at Severo Ochoa Hospital in Madrid, Spain, followed infants under 24 months admitted with respiratory tract infections and identified influenza C virus as a non‑negligible cause of serious disease, including bronchiolitis and pneumonia. Among 706 hospitalized infants, 30 had influenza virus infections, of whom six were confirmed with influenza C, sometimes as co-infections with RSV or adenovirus. Seasonal circulation and hospital-based respiratory diagnostics showed that influenza C activity fluctuated over the four-year period, with occasional detections requiring hospitalization but no evidence of a large community-wide epidemic driven uniquely by influenza C.

([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/reports-publications/canada-communicable-disease-report-ccdr/monthly-issue/2022-48/issue-9-september-2022/invasive-group-a-streptococcal-disease-surveillance-canada-2020.html?utm_source=openai))

Event.summary: During the 2022–2023 respiratory virus season in the United States, CDC’s Active Bacterial Core surveillance and other systems detected an early and pronounced resurgence of invasive group A streptococcal (iGAS) infections, with particularly notable increases among children and adolescents beginning in autumn 2022 in states such as Colorado and Minnesota. A December 2022 CDC Health Alert Network advisory highlighted pediatric iGAS increases above recent years, often occurring alongside high levels of respiratory syncytial virus and influenza activity, and by 2023 CDC estimated that the national number of serious group A strep infections had reached a roughly 20‑year high compared with pre‑pandemic seasons. Although incidence rose in all age groups, the surge in children was of special concern and prompted intensified surveillance, clinical alerts and public communications, after which activity gradually returned toward typical seasonal levels as the 2023–2024 winter progressed. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/han/2022/han00484.html?utm_source=openai))

([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/groupastrep/igas-infections-investigation.html?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New row added to capture the large 2022–2023 U.S. iGAS surge, which CDC reports as reaching approximately 20‑year highs in serious infections and which parallels the European post‑pandemic wave. Classified as re-occurrence (not re-emergence) because available CDC reports and MMWR analyses describe increases in common emm types without a new genotype or resistance pattern; continent, sub‑region and country fields follow the provided UN/CDC geography.

Event.summary: In 2023, Japan recorded a record number of reported streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (STSS) cases—around 941 in total—substantially exceeding the previous national high from 2019, with a large proportion attributable to group A streptococci and a high case‑fatality risk. Hospital‑based and regional studies from multiple Japanese centres documented parallel post‑pandemic increases in invasive GAS and severe paediatric GAS infections, again in the context of heavy circulation of respiratory viruses and relaxation of COVID‑19 control measures, leading domestic authorities and international commentators to characterise the situation as an unprecedented national surge in severe GAS disease. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11261432/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Ageing demographics, high prevalence of comorbidities, and post‑COVID changes in social mixing and respiratory virus circulation likely contributed to the large pool of susceptible adults and older adults at risk for STSS and other iGAS manifestations; reductions in GAS transmission during 2020–2021 may have created immunity gaps that became evident when non‑pharmaceutical interventions were lifted. Internal mechanisms: Surveillance and early genomic investigations highlight increased contributions of emm1 and other established emm types, and Japanese risk assessments have raised the possibility that M1UK‑like sublineages may be present, but no single nationwide clone has yet been conclusively identified as the primary driver of the surge; at present the event is best interpreted as a pronounced re‑occurrence of severe disease caused by circulating GAS lineages under altered host‑population and ecological conditions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11261432/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New row added because Japan’s 2023–2024 STSS/iGAS surge, with record national case counts and high mortality, represents one of the largest recent country‑level increases in severe GAS disease. Classified as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence since current NIID and hospital‑based reports emphasise post‑pandemic epidemiologic drivers and increased incidence of known emm types; genomic work to clarify the role of M1UK‑like lineages is ongoing, so this classification should be revisited as more data emerge.

Early case reports in the early 1990s established B. mandrillaris as a cause of opportunistic meningoencephalitis in humans and other mammals, largely diagnosed at autopsy. By the mid‑1990s, Balamuthia was accepted as a distinct human pathogen with a very high case‑fatality rate, setting the stage for subsequent recognition of cases worldwide.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Improvements in neuropathology, immunohistochemistry, and reference‑laboratory support (e.g. at CDC) made it possible to distinguish Balamuthia from other free‑living amoebae in brain tissue, and publication of index cases raised global awareness. Internal mechanisms: Available data suggest this event primarily reflects recognition and characterization of a pre‑existing environmental amoeba rather than emergence of a new, more virulent strain; no specific genetic or phenotypic changes were linked to the initial human cases.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures first recognized human Balamuthia infections in the United States around 1990, consistent with J Clin Microbiol/J Eukaryot Microbiol descriptions and CDC summaries; geography, timing, and event‑type classification (first global emergence and first detection) are appropriate and no substantive corrections were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Balamuthia mandrillaris

Internal mechanisms: Serologic studies suggest prior Balamuthia exposure in parts of Africa, but this child’s infection appears to represent the first molecularly proven autochthonous human case on the continent rather than emergence of a novel African lineage; the principal mechanism is thus documentation of continental range expansion and spillover from an environmental reservoir into a human host.

Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of fresh salad vegetables into European food service from Cyclospora-endemic regions, combined with growing year-round consumer demand for raw mixed salads; limited familiarity with Cyclospora among European clinicians and diagnostic laboratories, which delayed recognition of locally acquired disease; and the intrinsic difficulty of detecting low-level contamination on mixed salad ingredients. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel parasite genotypes or increased virulence; the outbreak is best explained by contamination of one or more salad ingredients during production or packing outside Germany. Mechanism categories: Inter-continental emergence of foodborne cyclosporiasis into Europe via globalized fresh-produce trade, with in situ transmission to consumers in a previously unaffected continent.
Review: retain: Corrected the year to 2000 (the German outbreak was confined to that year), restricted geography to Western Europe (Germany only), and removed an unsupported attribution of salad ingredients to Peru. Retained classification as inter_continental_emergence because this represents the first documented locally acquired foodborne outbreak in Europe. Given some remaining uncertainty about the exact produce origin and total case count, this row should be kept but could be revisited against the full EID article if further precision is needed.

Event.summary: During May–August 2018, U.S. public health authorities recorded 2,299 laboratory-confirmed cyclosporiasis cases without recent international travel, the largest annual number since cyclosporiasis became nationally notifiable. Given the small case count (8), a reviewer should confirm that including this as one of the top events is justified on the basis of being Europe’s first clearly described MSM outbreak.
