EPP.scientific.name: Entamoeba histolytica
EPP.common.name: amebiasis
Host: Humans, predominantly HIV-1–infected men who have sex with men (MSM), but also other adults living with HIV or with high‑risk sexual behavior
Event.summary: In Taiwan, invasive amebiasis emerged as a significant opportunistic infection in people living with HIV from the mid‑1990s onward. A 9‑year retrospective review at a major referral hospital (1994–2003) identified 51 episodes of invasive amebiasis among 49 HIV‑infected patients, with markedly higher seroprevalence and intestinal colonization by E. histolytica among HIV‑positive MSM compared with HIV‑negative controls. Subsequent national analyses for 2006–2013 showed that a growing proportion of male amebiasis cases were diagnosed around the time of HIV infection and that sexual transmission (particularly male–male sex with oral–anal contact) had become a dominant route of acquisition. This multi‑year trend represents a re‑occurring, sexually transmitted niche for E. histolytica in a relatively low‑endemic, high‑income setting, with continued incident cases reported into the 2010s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of HIV epidemics in MSM, high‑risk sexual behaviors including oral–anal sex, dense urban sexual networks, and improved access to HIV care and diagnostics together facilitated recognition and onward sexual transmission of E. histolytica. Increased use of serology and antigen/PCR tests in HIV clinics raised detection of both invasive disease and asymptomatic carriage. Internal mechanisms: No consistent evidence for a novel strain or drug resistance; risk appeared driven by host factors (HIV‑related immunity, sexual network structure) and exposure rather than intrinsic parasite evolution, supporting classification as re-occurrence.
Review: review – New event added to capture the well‑documented emergence of invasive and sexually transmitted amebiasis among HIV-infected MSM in Taiwan, which is consistently highlighted in the literature as a major focus of post‑1990 E. histolytica re-occurrence. Classified as re-occurrence (not re-emergence) because drivers are behavioral and host‑related, with no clear parasite genotype shift. A reviewer should confirm time bounds (1994–2013) are appropriate for representing this multi‑year episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Entamoeba histolytica
EPP.common.name: amebiasis
Host: Humans, exclusively men who have sex with men (MSM), most living with HIV, with invasive colitis and liver abscess
Event.summary: Between December 2006 and October 2007, clinicians at a tertiary hospital in Sydney, Australia, reported five cases of invasive amebiasis (three amebic colitis, two liver abscesses) in MSM, four of whom were HIV‑infected, with minimal or no recent travel to highly endemic regions. These cases, together with earlier locally acquired infections and high background carriage of Entamoeba spp. in MSM, provided evidence that E. histolytica had established sexual transmission networks in Australian MSM, representing a shift from imported to autochthonous invasive disease in an otherwise low‑endemic country. All patients recovered with metronidazole followed by a luminal agent, but delays in diagnosis and severe complications in some cases highlighted limited awareness among clinicians.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑risk sexual behaviors in MSM (including oral–anal sex and sex‑on‑premises venues), intersecting HIV and STI epidemics, and under‑recognition of amebiasis as a sexually transmissible infection created conditions for local establishment and spread of E. histolytica in Sydney MSM. Internal mechanisms: No unique genotype or resistance pattern was identified; infections corresponded to typical invasive E. histolytica, again supporting classification as re-occurrence due to social/behavioral drivers.
Review: review – New event added to reflect the first clearly documented locally acquired invasive amebiasis in MSM in Australia (Sydney, 2006–2007), which is repeatedly cited as evidence that sexually transmitted E. histolytica has become established in MSM networks in several Asia–Pacific countries. Classified as re-occurrence; magnitude (small case series) is modest but important in the context of limited post‑1990 discrete outbreaks for this pathogen. A reviewer should confirm its inclusion among the top events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Entamoeba histolytica
EPP.common.name: amebiasis
Host: Humans (secondary school students at Upper Hill School, Nairobi)
Event.summary: In early March 2023, a large cluster of acute gastrointestinal illness occurred among students at Upper Hill School, a boys’ secondary school in Nairobi, Kenya, with around 90–100 students developing stomach pain, diarrhea and vomiting after eating rice, beans and beef in the school. Initial concern focused on cholera, but county health officials reported that rapid cholera tests were negative and that affected students instead tested positive for amoebiasis, with about 16–20 hospitalised at several facilities and the remainder treated and discharged. Public health teams collected water and food samples to investigate contamination of the school’s water supply or kitchen, and the outbreak subsided after supportive treatment and control measures; the episode occurred against a backdrop of water scarcity and broader cholera activity in Nairobi.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Acute water shortage and reliance on potentially unsafe sources, combined with inadequate food and water hygiene in a crowded boarding‑school environment, likely enabled fecal contamination of drinking water or food with E. histolytica cysts. Broader infrastructure challenges in Nairobi (drying boreholes, intermittent municipal supply) and concurrent enteric disease activity increased vulnerability to such outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: No data indicate a new strain or resistance; this is a typical water/food‑borne re-occurrence of invasive amebiasis in a high‑burden region.
Review: review – New event added to capture the 2023 amoebiasis outbreak at Upper Hill School in Nairobi, where close to 100 students were reportedly affected and cholera was ruled out in favour of amoebiasis. While laboratory methods and species‑level confirmation are not fully detailed in media reports, the scale and clear attribution justify inclusion as a major recent re-occurrence event in Eastern Africa; a reviewer should confirm species assignment and any subsequent official investigation reports.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas vaginalis
EPP.common.name: Trichomoniasis
Host: Humans (women attending STD clinics in multiple U.S. cities)
Event.summary: In 2009–2010, the U.S. CDC Sexually Transmitted Disease Surveillance Network conducted the first multisite evaluation of nitroimidazole susceptibility in T. vaginalis isolates from women in six U.S. cities, documenting clinically relevant metronidazole resistance and low-level tinidazole resistance across geographically diverse locations.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/22726?utm_source=openai)) Thousands of women with trichomoniasis were enrolled and a subset of isolates were tested, revealing metronidazole resistance in a measurable minority of samples and confirming that resistant parasites were no longer just sporadic case reports but a distributed problem in the national STD clinic population. In the years that followed, CDC developed reference susceptibility testing services and incorporated guidance on managing nitroimidazole-resistant T. vaginalis into national STI treatment guidelines,([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/parasites/hcp/laboratories/trichomonas-vaginalis-susceptibility-testing.html?utm_source=openai)) marking a shift from isolated case management to systematic recognition of resistance as a re‑emerging therapeutic threat.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive, long-term use of a single class of nitroimidazole therapy (metronidazole and tinidazole) for trichomoniasis and related infections; suboptimal partner treatment and reinfection, leading to repeated exposure of the same parasite populations to drug pressure; and limited routine resistance surveillance prior to 2009 that allowed resistant strains to circulate largely undetected. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance – stable low- and high-level resistance to metronidazole, and rarer resistance to tinidazole, linked to alterations in hydrogenosomal and redox pathways that reduce activation of 5‑nitroimidazoles; these mechanisms represent biological re‑emergence through treatment failure and geographic dissemination of resistant genotypes.
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects the first systematic U.S. multisite surveillance of nitroimidazole resistance in T. vaginalis, with correct timing (2009–2010), geography (STD clinics in multiple U.S. cities), emergence-type classification (re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance), and highly relevant CDC/EID and guideline sources. No changes were made to the original event fields; it is appropriate to keep this as a major resistance-related emergence episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma spp.
EPP.common.name: Trypanosomiasis
Host: Humans (acute T. brucei rhodesiense sleeping sickness in rural communities); cattle (major reservoir influencing human risk)
Event.summary: In late 1998, a new focus of acute human African trypanosomiasis due to Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense was detected in Soroti District in eastern/central Uganda, north of the traditional Busoga focus, in an area previously considered essentially free of this form of sleeping sickness.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673601057786?utm_source=openai))  Over the following years, cases spread into neighbouring Kaberamaido and the southern edge of Lira District, with more than 400–428 human cases reported between 1998 and 2004 and additional unreported cases inferred, making this one of the largest recent rHAT outbreaks in East Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3828156/?utm_source=openai))  Intensive interventions in the early–mid 2000s, including mass treatment of cattle reservoirs and localized tsetse control under the Stamp Out Sleeping Sickness (SOS) campaign, substantially reduced rHAT incidence in these newly affected districts by around 2005, although low‑level risk persisted and surveillance remains necessary.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Post‑conflict restocking schemes and unregulated cattle trade moved T. b. rhodesiense–infected cattle from endemic southeastern Uganda into Soroti, Kaberamaido and Lira, all lying within the tsetse belt but previously free of human rHAT; high infection prevalence in market cattle seeded the new focus and drove its northward expansion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3851531/?utm_source=openai))  Weak veterinary services and limited clinical awareness in the newly affected districts led to delayed recognition of cases, with most patients presenting in late stage, and initial vector‑control measures were insufficient to prevent spread beyond Soroti.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1289320/?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence indicates a novel parasite strain; molecular analyses suggest a genetically homogeneous population consistent with a founder effect from the existing Tororo/Busoga focus, so this episode reflects geographic range expansion within Eastern Africa driven by livestock movements rather than evolutionary change in the parasite.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3828156/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – The Soroti–Kaberamaido–Lira rHAT focus is a well‑documented, high‑impact emergence within Uganda, and the time span (1998–2005) and country assignment are appropriate. However, under the project definitions, this should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence because it occurs within an already endemic UNSD sub‑region (Eastern Africa); instead it represents a major resurgence and geographic spread inside that sub‑region. The emergence type has therefore been corrected from intra‑continental emergence + re‑emergence to re‑occurrence only, reflecting strong external drivers (post‑conflict cattle restocking and weak surveillance) and lack of evidence for parasite change. Users should review and confirm this reclassification.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma spp.
EPP.common.name: Trypanosomiasis
Host: Humans (locally infected individuals via vectors, congenital transmission or transfusion); triatomine bugs; wildlife and domestic animal reservoirs (e.g. woodrats, raccoons, armadillos, dogs)
Event.summary: Although Trypanosoma cruzi has circulated in wildlife and vectors in the southern United States for centuries, the early 2000s marked a period of heightened recognition of locally acquired human Chagas disease, with clusters of autochthonous acute and chronic infections documented in states such as Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee, California, Arizona and Missouri.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6614205/?utm_source=openai))  Systematic reviews and public‑health reports identified roughly 29–31 confirmed and 47–47+ suspected locally acquired human cases during 2000–2018 (i.e. ≈76–78 persons), alongside high infection prevalence in triatomine bugs and peridomestic animal reservoirs, suggesting ongoing but hypoendemic vector‑borne transmission.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001706X19313166?utm_source=openai))  Introduction of routine blood‑donor screening for T. cruzi antibodies in 2007 (with nationwide coverage by 2012), together with state‑level notifiable‑disease systems and targeted investigations of suspected autochthonous cases, reduced transfusion‑related risk and improved detection, but many infections in exposed US residents—both imported and locally acquired—likely remain undiagnosed.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Ecological interfaces where humans live, work or recreate in close proximity to infected wildlife and triatomine habitats—such as substandard rural housing, peridomestic dog kennels, outdoor sleeping, hunting and military training—create opportunities for sylvatic cycles of T. cruzi to spill over into humans in the southern USA.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7470559/?utm_source=openai))  Urban and peri‑urban expansion into wildlife habitat, along with climate and land‑use changes that may alter vector distributions and seasonal activity, further modulate risk, while greater clinical and public‑health awareness and the advent of blood‑donor screening have increased case ascertainment relative to the past.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6614205/?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: Long‑standing enzootic transmission in wildlife and domestic animals provides a reservoir for host expansion to humans, and some triatomine species (e.g. Triatoma sanguisuga, T. gerstaeckeri) show adaptation to peridomestic environments; however, no specific novel parasite lineage or clear shift in virulence has been linked to these human cases, so the pattern is best interpreted as re‑occurrence driven by ecological and surveillance changes rather than parasite evolution.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7470559/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – The pattern of increased recognition of autochthonous Chagas disease in the southern United States from 2000–2018 is well supported by multiple systematic reviews and CDC reports, and the event appropriately highlights a new appreciation of endemic (though low‑level) T. cruzi transmission in North America. However, the original row set both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence to “Yes”. Given longstanding evidence of enzootic T. cruzi circulation in US wildlife and vectors and the absence of clear parasite change, this episode fits the definition of re‑occurrence driven by ecological and surveillance factors rather than re‑emergence due to genetic or phenotypic shifts in the parasite. The classification has therefore been corrected to re‑occurrence=Yes and re‑emergence=No; inter‑ and intra‑continental emergence remain “No” because neither a new continent nor a new UNSD sub‑region is involved.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterococcus faecium
EPP.common.name: Enterococcus faecium infection
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults and children; mainly intensive‑care and high‑antibiotic‑exposure wards)
Event.summary: From 1989 to 1993, vancomycin‑resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) rapidly emerged in U.S. hospitals, with the proportion of enterococcal isolates resistant to vancomycin in the National Nosocomial Infections Surveillance System increasing roughly 20‑fold over this period. Hospitals across multiple states reported rising numbers of nosocomial bloodstream and other invasive infections due to VREfm, particularly among patients with heavy prior antibiotic exposure. By the early 1990s, VREfm had become established as an endemic multidrug‑resistant hospital pathogen in many U.S. centers, with sustained transmission controlled only partially by enhanced infection‑control and stewardship measures.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive in‑hospital use of vancomycin (both intravenous and oral) and cephalosporins, high antibiotic selection pressure in ICUs and oncology/transplant units, and increased use of invasive devices facilitated selection and spread of VREfm in hospitals. Internal mechanisms: acquisition of plasmid‑encoded vanA/vanB glycopeptide resistance determinants and earlier acquisition of ampicillin resistance enabled emergence of multidrug‑resistant, hospital‑adapted E. faecium lineages with enhanced survival and persistence in the hospital environment (Re‑emergence; Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion – inherent).
Review: review – Retain as a major event capturing the rapid rise of VREfm in U.S. hospitals from 1989–1993, supported by NNIS/MMWR and review data. Updated event type to mark this as an inter‑continental emergence (first sustained VREfm transmission in North America) co‑occurring with re‑emergence, while keeping other fields unchanged. Note that the start year 1989 slightly predates the 1990 cut‑off but is appropriate here because the 1989–1993 NNIS surveillance period represents a single linked emergence episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterococcus faecium
EPP.common.name: Enterococcus faecium infection
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults in a large German university hospital; multiple wards)
Event.summary: In 2004, a large outbreak of vancomycin‑resistant E. faecium occurred in a German university hospital, with hundreds of colonized and infected patients identified over the year. The outbreak began with sporadic VREfm detections that were not initially recognized as the start of a major event, then expanded across wards with substantial nosocomial transmission and multiple bloodstream infections. After extensive screening, isolation precautions, environmental decontamination and antibiotic‑stewardship adjustments, transmission was brought under control, but the episode generated an estimated avoidable cost of about 1 million Euros and highlighted the high impact of uncontrolled VREfm spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: delayed recognition of early VREfm cases, high use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics, patient transfers between wards, and crowded tertiary‑care settings increased colonization pressure and facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: expansion of a multidrug‑resistant VREfm clone carrying vanA and esp and adapted to the hospital environment, with enhanced persistence and transmissibility compared with background strains (Re‑emergence; Antimicrobial Resistance; Enhanced Transmission; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: retain – Large single‑hospital outbreak in Germany with hundreds of affected patients and high economic cost is well documented and among the more impactful hospital‑level VREfm events. Classification as re‑emergence (in a previously affected European sub‑region) is appropriate, geography is correct, and the sources used directly describe the event.

EPP.scientific.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
EPP.common.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection
Host: Humans (critically ill intensive-care and other hospitalized patients)
Event.summary: From February 1997 to February 1998, the University Hospital of Verona in northern Italy experienced a small but pivotal outbreak of carbapenem‑resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa producing VIM‑1, a novel transferable metallo‑β‑lactamase. Eight isolates from seven patients in different wards showed very high-level resistance to imipenem and other broad‑spectrum β‑lactams, and molecular work confirmed carriage of the newly described blaVIM‑1 gene on mobile elements. After targeted infection‑control measures, the immediate outbreak was controlled, but subsequent work from the same center and elsewhere showed that VIM‑type carbapenemases had seeded a broader endemic pool of metallo‑β‑lactamase‑producing P. aeruginosa in Italian and other European hospitals.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy carbapenem use in a tertiary‑care setting with a high baseline burden of P. aeruginosa infections, combined with standard ICU risk factors (invasive devices, prolonged stays), favored selection and spread of carbapenem‑resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of the blaVIM‑1 metallo‑β‑lactamase gene on integron-associated mobile genetic elements in a hospital P. aeruginosa lineage, creating one of the earliest documented metallo‑β‑lactamase‑mediated carbapenem‑resistant P. aeruginosa outbreaks outside Japan and marking a key step in the global evolution of carbapenem-resistant strains.
Review: review – The Verona VIM‑1 outbreak is real and well documented as one of the first hospital outbreaks of carbapenem‑resistant P. aeruginosa due to a metallo‑β‑lactamase, with eight isolates from seven patients between February 1997 and February 1998.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11073738/?utm_source=openai)) The original event year range (1997–2000) has been tightened to 1997–1998 to match the primary report, and the event summary has been aligned with the Clin Infect Dis description. The source list has been updated to include the specific Verona outbreak article and to rely on metallo‑β‑lactamase reviews for broader context. Classification as re_emergence (new resistance mechanism in an established pathogen) remains appropriate, with no intra/inter‑continental emergence flags. This event should be retained as a key early AMR emergence, but the revised dates and sources should be checked at curation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
EPP.common.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients, particularly in vascular surgery, hematology and intensive-care wards)
Event.summary: Between 2004 and 2010, large Spanish tertiary hospitals documented successive waves of multidrug‑resistant and extensively drug‑resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa outbreaks dominated by high‑risk clones. An initial VIM‑2‑producing outbreak strain spread on vascular surgery and other wards, followed by a colistin‑only‑susceptible ST235 clone producing GES‑1 and GES‑5 extended‑spectrum β‑lactamases and, later, a VIM‑2‑producing ST175 clone that became the predominant carbapenem‑resistant lineage across multiple units. These clones caused numerous healthcare‑associated infections with limited therapeutic options. After enhanced screening, cohorting, environmental decontamination and antimicrobial‑stewardship interventions were implemented, the contribution of the dominant outbreak clones declined, although carbapenem‑resistant P. aeruginosa remained endemic in many centers.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High use of carbapenems and broad‑spectrum cephalosporins in tertiary‑care hospitals, frequent device‑associated care, and crowding in high‑dependency units created strong selection pressure and opportunities for nosocomial spread; delayed recognition of clonal outbreaks and limited initial infection‑control measures allowed extensive dissemination. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and clonal replacement of high‑risk sequence types ST235 and ST175, each carrying potent β‑lactamases (GES‑type ESBLs or VIM‑2 metallo‑β‑lactamase) and additional resistance determinants, leading to colistin‑only susceptibility or extensive drug resistance; fitness traits and environmental persistence facilitated long‑lasting transmission within and between hospitals.
Review: retain – Multiple primary studies document large hospital outbreaks and subsequent inter‑hospital dissemination of VIM‑2‑ and GES‑producing high‑risk clones (ST235, ST175) in Spain during 2004–2010, with substantial local burdens of MDR/XDR infections.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1368764615000369?utm_source=openai)) The geographic assignment (Southern Europe, Spain) and classification as re_emergence (new resistant clones of a known pathogen) are consistent with project definitions, and no intra/inter‑continental emergence flags are warranted. The event clearly ranks among the major P. aeruginosa AMR emergence episodes in Europe. No structural corrections are required, though exact case counts are not available and could be added if found in national surveillance data.

EPP.scientific.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
EPP.common.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients, various wards including ICUs)
Event.summary: In 2006, a multicenter survey across India found high rates of carbapenem‑resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa carrying diverse VIM‑type metallo‑β‑lactamases (VIM‑2, VIM‑5, VIM‑6, VIM‑11 and the newly described VIM‑18), indicating that multiple carbapenem‑resistant clones had become widely endemic in tertiary‑care hospitals. Through the late 2000s, these carbapenem‑resistant and often multidrug‑resistant strains caused serious hospital‑acquired infections in ICUs and other high‑risk wards nationwide, with limited treatment options and increased morbidity and mortality. By around 2010, national and international reports characterized India as a hotspot for metallo‑β‑lactamase–mediated carbapenem resistance in P. aeruginosa, and surveillance plus stewardship efforts were scaled up, although resistance remained entrenched.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread and often unregulated use of carbapenems and other broad‑spectrum antibiotics, a high burden of severe infections requiring hospitalization, and variability in infection‑control capacity in tertiary‑care hospitals promoted selection and spread of carbapenem‑resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and diversification of VIM metallo‑β‑lactamase genes (including the novel VIM‑18) on mobile genetic elements across multiple P. aeruginosa lineages, creating a broad endemic pool of carbapenem‑resistant strains; clonal expansion and co‑selection with other resistance determinants (e.g. aminoglycoside and fluoroquinolone resistance) enhanced persistence and spread.
Review: retain – The nationwide emergence of multiple VIM‑producing P. aeruginosa clones in India is well supported by the 2006 multicenter survey and subsequent regional resistance analyses, which show high carbapenem‑resistance rates and diverse VIM alleles.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/8/2/pdfs/01-0163.pdf?utm_source=openai)) The event is appropriately classified as re_emergence driven by novel and diversified resistance mechanisms, without intra/inter‑continental emergence flags (the species was already long established in India). The country and sub‑region coding (India, Southern Asia) are correct. No structural corrections are required, although more granular temporal trends (post‑2010) could be added in future updates.

EPP.scientific.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
EPP.common.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients, especially in tertiary-care hospitals and ICUs)
Event.summary: Between 2008 and 2010, Colombia’s national bacterial resistance surveillance network identified widespread dissemination of extensively drug‑resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa high‑risk clones, particularly ST111 and ST235, across multiple tertiary hospitals. These clones, carrying metallo‑β‑lactamase VIM‑2 or carbapenemase KPC‑2 on mobile elements, caused healthcare‑associated infections with resistance to nearly all standard anti‑pseudomonal agents, leaving colistin and a few other drugs as last‑line options. The study documented clonal spread across several Colombian cities, and subsequent clinical reports indicated that these XDR clones remained important causes of severe infections in the early 2010s despite infection‑control and stewardship interventions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased use of carbapenems and other broad‑spectrum antibiotics in Colombian tertiary‑care centers, coupled with constrained infection‑prevention resources and inter‑hospital patient transfers, favored establishment and spread of XDR P. aeruginosa. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and clonal expansion of high‑risk lineages ST111 and ST235 carrying blaVIM‑2 and blaKPC‑2 on integrons and transposons, creating highly resistant strains with strong hospital fitness; mobile genetic elements facilitated rapid dissemination of these resistance determinants among P. aeruginosa populations.
Review: review – The Colombian XDR high‑risk clone emergence is robustly supported by surveillance data from 2008 and 2010 showing multi‑hospital dissemination of ST111 and ST235 carrying VIM‑2 and KPC‑2.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4356786/?utm_source=openai)) However, the original event years (2010–2014) and country timing (“Colombia [2010]”) overstated the documented start date and implied a longer, precisely dated episode than the primary study supports. I have therefore adjusted the event span to 2008–2010 and set the country timing to Colombia [2008], matching the surveillance collection years while still noting persistence into the early 2010s in the narrative. In line with project rules that treat new strains and resistance mechanisms as re‑emergence rather than inter‑continental emergence, I have changed inter_continental_emergence from true to false. The event remains a major regional emergence of XDR P. aeruginosa and should be retained, but final dates and continued post‑2010 impact should be reviewed against any additional Colombian data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
EPP.common.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2011]
Host: Humans (neonates in neonatal intensive-care units)
Event.summary: In December 2011 and early 2012, several neonatal units in Northern Ireland reported clusters of Pseudomonas aeruginosa bloodstream infections, with four neonatal deaths attributed to P. aeruginosa bacteraemia. Environmental investigations demonstrated heavy colonization of tap outlets and flow straighteners in affected units, and variable number tandem repeat (VNTR) typing showed that many tap and patient isolates were closely related, implicating water outlets as an important source. In response, contaminated taps and components were replaced, water systems were remediated, and enhanced infection‑control measures were introduced across neonatal units. These incidents prompted UK‑wide development of a Water Action Plan, technical guidance on P. aeruginosa risks in augmented care units, and specific national recommendations for managing Gram‑negative outbreaks in neonatal units, after which outbreak‑related cases declined.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Complex tap and mixer designs, inadequate monitoring of water quality, and use of hand‑wash outlets in close proximity to highly vulnerable preterm infants allowed biofilm‑associated P. aeruginosa to contaminate clinical environments and equipment; high device use and invasive procedures in NICU patients amplified the consequences of contamination. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain features were uniquely implicated; rather, the event illustrates P. aeruginosa’s inherent ability to form dense biofilms and persist in tap and mixer components, acting as a reservoir for recurrent introduction into susceptible hosts. The episode is therefore best characterized as a re‑occurrence driven by environmental and infection‑control factors rather than by emergence of new genotypes.
Review: review – The original event described a very broad 2005–2015 episode of sink‑associated P. aeruginosa outbreaks across “Western Europe,” with vague country attribution and sources drawn from several unrelated ICU outbreaks. This conflicted with the project rule that multi‑site events should be merged only when epidemiologically linked or representing continuous occurrence in the same area.([researchportal.ukhsa.gov.uk](https://researchportal.ukhsa.gov.uk/en/publications/investigation-of-healthcare-acquired-infections-associated-with-p/?utm_source=openai)) I have re‑scoped the event to focus on the well‑documented 2011–2012 neonatal outbreaks in Northern Ireland, where four neonates died and tap biofilms were clearly implicated, and to highlight the subsequent UK‑wide technical guidance and Gram‑negative outbreak management recommendations. Continent, sub‑region and country fields have been corrected to Europe / Northern Europe / United Kingdom, and the host description, time span, event summary, mechanism and source URLs have been updated accordingly. The event is now coded purely as re_occurrence, reflecting environmental contamination and infection‑control failures without evidence of novel genotypes. This episode remains an important high‑impact event for P. aeruginosa, but the narrowed geographic scope and dates should be reviewed against any additional UK neonatal outbreak documentation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
EPP.common.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with serious infections in tertiary-care hospitals)
Event.summary: From 2020 to 2022, hospitals in eastern China reported clonal spread of a high‑risk Pseudomonas aeruginosa sequence type 463 (ST463) co‑producing KPC‑2 and AFM‑1 carbapenemases, causing difficult‑to‑treat healthcare‑associated infections. During this period, ST463 became predominant among carbapenemase‑producing P. aeruginosa in the affected institutions, with isolates resistant to nearly all standard anti‑pseudomonal agents and only limited remaining therapeutic options. After recognition of the outbreak and its molecular characteristics, infection‑control measures and antimicrobial‑stewardship programs were reinforced, but ST463 persisted as an important driver of carbapenem‑resistant P. aeruginosa in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High use of carbapenems and other broad‑spectrum antibiotics in Chinese tertiary‑care hospitals, frequent device‑associated care, and crowded wards favored selection and spread of carbapenemase‑producing strains; regional patient movement and referrals facilitated inter‑facility dissemination. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and clonal expansion of ST463 co‑producing two potent carbapenemases, KPC‑2 and AFM‑1, representing convergence of class A and metallo‑β‑lactamase mechanisms in a single lineage and leading to extensively drug‑resistant phenotypes; associated mobile genetic elements and fitness traits enhanced survival and transmission in hospital environments.
Review: retain – The emergence of ST463 co‑producing KPC‑2 and AFM‑1 in eastern China during 2020–2022 is described in detail in an Emerging Infectious Diseases report and supported by broader reviews of carbapenemase genes and high‑risk clones in Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10068724/?utm_source=openai)) The geographic and temporal fields match the primary report, and classification as re_emergence (new highly resistant clone of an established pathogen) is consistent with project rules, with no intra/inter‑continental emergence flags. This event clearly represents a major recent AMR emergence episode for P. aeruginosa and should be retained as is.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
EPP.common.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection
Host: Humans (users of over-the-counter artificial tears; hospitalized patients with ocular and systemic infections)
Event.summary: Between January 2022 and mid‑May 2023, U.S. public‑health authorities investigated a multistate outbreak of extensively drug‑resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections caused by a Verona integron‑mediated metallo‑β‑lactamase and GES β‑lactamase–producing strain (VIM‑GES‑CRPA) linked to contaminated over‑the‑counter artificial tears. A total of 81 case‑patients from 18 states were identified, many with severe keratitis or systemic infections; four patients died within 30 days of culture, and several others experienced vision loss or required enucleation. Whole‑genome sequencing showed that isolates belonged to sequence type 1203 carrying novel resistance genes blaVIM‑80 and blaGES‑9, and that outbreak strains were present in multiple unopened and opened bottles of the implicated eye‑drop product manufactured overseas. Following recalls, public advisories and strengthened infection‑control guidance, no further outbreak‑associated cases were detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Contamination of a widely distributed preservative‑free artificial‑tears product during manufacturing or packaging, combined with global distribution and over‑the‑counter access, created an efficient vehicle for community and healthcare‑associated exposure to an extensively drug‑resistant P. aeruginosa strain; lapses in quality assurance and sterility control at the manufacturing facility were central non‑biological drivers. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of VIM‑80 and GES‑9 β‑lactamase genes in a high‑risk ST1203 background, yielding extensively drug‑resistant phenotypes nonsusceptible to nearly all standard anti‑pseudomonal agents; ability of the clone to survive in ophthalmic solution and cause severe ocular and systemic disease after topical use enhanced its transmission and clinical impact.
Review: review – This event clearly represents one of the most impactful recent P. aeruginosa outbreaks, involving 81 case‑patients across 18 U.S. states, four deaths, and multiple cases of vision loss and enucleation, all linked to a contaminated artificial‑tears product.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/79/1/6/7601234)) The original description underestimated case numbers and deaths based on early CDC HAN data; I have updated the event summary to reflect final counts and the formal case definition period (1 January 2022–15 May 2023) reported in the subsequent Clinical Infectious Diseases analysis. An additional source (Grossman et al. 2024, CID) has been added, while maintaining CDC HAN and supplementary materials for epidemiologic and genomic details. Classification as re_emergence (novel XDR clone and new product‑associated transmission route) without intra/inter‑continental emergence flags is consistent with project rules. The event should be retained, but future updates may refine counts if later public‑health reports revise estimates.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Caliciviridae
EPP.common.name: norovirus
Host: humans (predominantly school‑age children and adolescents consuming catered meals, but also staff and some household contacts)
Event.summary: In September–October 2012, eastern Germany experienced an exceptionally large foodborne norovirus outbreak linked to school and kindergarten catering, with nearly 11,000 cases of vomiting and diarrhoea among children and adolescents reported to health authorities, constituting the largest recorded foodborne outbreak in the country. Epidemiologic and virologic investigations traced the outbreak to imported frozen strawberries from China supplied in a specific batch to multiple large‑scale kitchens serving educational institutions, and identical or closely related GII norovirus sequences were recovered from both clinical samples and berries. After the contaminated batch was identified and withdrawn, affected facilities implemented control measures including exclusion of ill food handlers and intensified hygiene and the outbreak subsided over subsequent weeks, although the event spurred European audits and strengthened controls on frozen soft‑fruit imports.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Globalized food supply chains and import of frozen soft fruit from China, combined with centralized catering for many schools and kindergartens, enabled a single contaminated strawberry batch to seed thousands of cases across multiple federal states; the high environmental stability of norovirus and inadequate heat treatment of frozen berries contributed to persistence and transmission. Internal mechanisms: No major novel variant was implicated; instead, this was a classic re-occurrence event driven by foodborne exposure to an existing GII norovirus genotype without evidence of substantially altered virulence or transmissibility compared with contemporaneous strains.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This was Germany’s largest recorded foodborne outbreak with nearly 11,000 cases linked to a single contaminated frozen strawberry batch, making it a justifiable inclusion among the highest-impact norovirus emergence events despite its confinement to one country. Classification as re-occurrence (no evidence of a novel strain, with external drivers—globalized food trade and centralized catering—underpinning the event) is appropriate, and geographic labeling (Europe, Western Europe, Germany) is correct. Source set is focused and highly relevant (BfR and RKI primary reports); no field changes were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Q fever
Host: Humans (residents of Panagyurishte and surrounding communities; exposure linked to infected goats and sheep)
Event.summary: Beginning after a regional influenza wave in late 1992 and peaking in spring 1993, the town of Panagyurishte in central Bulgaria experienced a large epidemic of febrile respiratory illness. More than 2,000 residents were affected, hundreds had radiologically confirmed atypical pneumonia, and serologic testing of a convalescent cohort showed Coxiella burnetii antibodies in about 60% of patients, indicating that Q fever accounted for a major share of the epidemic. Control measures focused on investigating and managing heavily infected goat and sheep flocks around the town and improving public‑health awareness; after the spring peak, case numbers declined, although Panagyurishte has remained an endemic focus of Q fever.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: dense populations of goats and sheep around Panagyurishte, spring kidding and abortion coinciding with dry, windy conditions, and heavy contamination of pastures and village margins with birth products and manure that facilitated long‑range aerosol spread into town. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through the high environmental persistence and aerosolization potential of C. burnetii in contaminated dust, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) within Bulgaria as infection amplified from rural herds into predominantly non‑occupational urban and peri‑urban residents.
Review: Retain – major 1992–1993 Panagyurishte epidemic with >2,000 acute respiratory cases and a high proportion attributable to Q fever, clearly among the largest human Q fever outbreaks; newly added because it was missing from the original file. Classified as re-occurrence (not first detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence) since Q fever was already established in Bulgaria; countries/region and timing were aligned with UNSD geography and published outbreak descriptions.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Q fever
Host: Humans (general population and patients with community‑acquired pneumonia in Cayenne and nearby municipalities)
Event.summary: In the mid‑1990s clinicians in French Guiana noted an unexpected rise in acute febrile respiratory illness and community‑acquired pneumonia around Cayenne, prompting systematic testing for atypical pathogens including Coxiella burnetii. Surveillance between 1996 and 2000 documented a very high annual Q fever incidence (around 37 cases per 100,000 inhabitants) and showed that C. burnetii accounted for roughly a quarter of community‑acquired pneumonias, revealing French Guiana as a hyperendemic hotspot with the highest reported Q fever incidence worldwide and a locally unique C. burnetii genotype. Although incidence has remained elevated, empiric doxycycline treatment for pneumonia, continued clinical awareness and ongoing ecological investigations into the wild reservoir have helped stabilise severe disease burden even as the exact environmental source continues to be defined.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of suburban settlements into rainforest fringes around Cayenne, creating interfaces between humans and a still‑uncertain wild reservoir (likely involving forest mammals), environmental conditions favouring survival and aerosolisation of C. burnetii, and historical under‑recognition of Q fever before targeted testing began. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (identification of a distinctive local genotype linked to unusually severe pneumonia), Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) in the sense of a newly recognised large, sustained human transmission focus in the Guiana Shield, and Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through efficient airborne spread from environmental reservoirs rather than classical domestic ruminant sources.
Review: Retain (with corrections) – strong evidence from surveillance and clinical studies that French Guiana became a hyperendemic Q fever focus with very high incidence and a distinct local genotype in the late 1990s, so this episode belongs among the major events. However, Q fever had been reported in humans and livestock in French Guiana and other South American countries since the 1950s, so the original first_detection and inter_continental_emergence flags have been set to No and the event reclassified as re-emergence in a previously affected subregion; summary wording was adjusted accordingly.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Q fever
Host: Humans (visitors and vendors at a farmers’ market; exposure linked to a single heavily infected ewe)
Event.summary: In May 2003 a large outbreak of atypical pneumonia was reported among persons who had visited an outdoor farmers’ market near Soest, Germany, leading to a focused epidemiologic investigation. A total of 299 notified Q fever cases were linked to the market, and analytic studies estimated roughly 500 symptomatic infections overall, with dramatically higher attack rates among vendors and visitors within a few metres of a small petting area containing a pregnant ewe that lambed during the event. After removal of the animals, cessation of similar displays, clinical follow‑up of affected persons and targeted public‑health messaging, no further cases associated with the market were detected and the episode was recognised as a classic, extremely large point‑source superspreading event.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: temporary co‑location of a heavily infected pregnant ewe with dense crowds in a confined market area, lack of physical barriers or respiratory protection for vendors and visitors, and unrecognised Q fever risk in an agritourism‑like setting. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via intense aerosolisation of C. burnetii during lambing and handling of contaminated bedding, producing highly efficient short‑range exposure, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) from typical farm environments into a mass‑gathering setting; no novel strain has been demonstrated.
Review: Retain (with reclassification) – the Soest farmers’ market outbreak produced 299 notified and an estimated ≈500 clinically ill Q fever cases, making it one of the largest point‑source Q fever events worldwide and clearly within the global top‑10 by case burden. The emergence type is adjusted from re-emergence to re-occurrence because investigations implicate a single infected ewe and environmental/behavioural conditions, with no evidence for a novel strain or host shift.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Q fever
Host: Humans (prison inmates, prison staff, nearby residents and veterinary personnel in the Como urban area)
Event.summary: From January to February 2003, clinicians in Como, northern Italy, observed a cluster of severe pneumonia cases among inmates at the local prison and some neighbouring residents, triggering investigation for atypical pathogens. Serologic testing subsequently identified 133 cases of acute Q fever linked to this outbreak, involving prisoners, guards, local residents and veterinary staff, with epidemiologic tracing implicating a flock of infected sheep and goats that had grazed in meadows adjacent to the prison in the weeks before the epidemic as the most likely airborne source. After management and treatment of the infected flock, environmental measures and heightened clinical awareness, no new outbreak‑related cases were reported, and the event was recognised as a large urban Q fever outbreak in a population with little direct animal contact.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: seasonal pasturing of a large small‑ruminant flock on fields bordering an urban prison and residential area, lambing and abortions near the town, dry conditions that favoured aerosolisation of contaminated dust, and lack of prior awareness of Q fever risk in this urban setting. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via massive shedding of C. burnetii in birth products and manure with windborne spread, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) of infection from traditional rural reservoirs into an urban, largely non‑occupational human population; no change in strain or host range has been reported.
Review: Retain – the 2003 Como prison/urban outbreak with 133 serologically confirmed human Q fever cases is one of the larger post‑1990 epidemics and merits inclusion among the major events. Classified as re-occurrence because Q fever was already endemic in Italy; the outbreak reflects amplification from infected sheep and goats grazing adjacent to the city rather than spread into a new continent or UNSD subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Q fever
Host: Humans (U.S. military personnel and other deployed forces; exposure to local livestock and dust in endemic rural environments)
Event.summary: During the early phase of Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2003, investigation of severe pneumonia among deployed U.S. soldiers first highlighted Coxiella burnetii infection as an under‑recognised cause of febrile respiratory illness in coalition forces, in a region where Q fever was already endemic in livestock and local populations. Subsequent surveillance and case‑finding documented more than 200 acute Q fever cases among U.S. military personnel over the 2003–2004 period and beyond, associated with exposures to sheep, goats and cattle, animal birthing sites, and dust‑laden environments during field operations, convoy movements and base construction. Increased awareness, preventive guidance for deployed personnel and improved clinical recognition and treatment of compatible febrile illnesses led to better case management and likely reduced incidence over time, although sporadic infections continued to occur in deployed forces.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive military activity in rural and peri‑urban Iraqi environments where C. burnetii is endemic in livestock, frequent close contact with sheep, goats and cattle or their contaminated environments, high dust and aerosol exposure during patrols and base work in arid conditions, and limited initial awareness of Q fever as a threat among deployed medical staff. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) in the sense of high‑intensity zoonotic spillover from endemic animal reservoirs to large numbers of immunologically naïve foreign military personnel, and Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via persistence of C. burnetii in dust and aerosols that facilitated long‑range exposure in windy, semi‑desert environments.
Review: Retain – >200 acute Q fever cases reported in U.S. military personnel deployed to Iraq since 2003 constitute a substantial, well‑documented outbreak in a highly exposed, previously unexposed risk group and plausibly belong in the ten most impactful recent events when considering impact on a single host population. Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate because Q fever was already endemic in Iraq and there is no evidence that this episode represented first detection or spread into a new continent or subregion; geographic and temporal details were cross‑checked against CDC advisories and military surveillance reports.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Q fever
Host: Humans (residents of Botevgrad and neighbouring towns; exposure linked to sheep and goat flocks grazing in or moving through urban areas)
Event.summary: Between May and early June 2004, public health authorities in western Bulgaria investigated an outbreak of acute febrile illness and pneumonia in the town of Botevgrad. Case finding and serologic testing identified 220 human Q fever cases (168 from Botevgrad and the remainder from nearby villages), and epidemiologic investigation implicated flocks of sheep and goats that grazed in, or were herded along, town streets and gardens as the most likely source of airborne exposure. Control efforts, including restricting animal movements through residential areas, improving management and monitoring of small‑ruminant herds and increasing clinician and community awareness, were followed by a decline in incident cases and eventual cessation of the urban outbreak.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: unusually close intermixing of small‑ruminant flocks with an urban population (sheep and goats grazing in streets and gardens), inadequate separation of livestock areas from residential zones, and slow initial recognition of Q fever leading to delayed implementation of control measures. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via heavy environmental contamination and aerosolisation of C. burnetii from infected flocks, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) from rural enzootic foci into a densely populated town; no evidence supports a novel strain or change in host range.
Review: Retain – the May–June 2004 Botevgrad outbreak with 220 human cases is one of the largest documented Q fever epidemics in Europe after Panagyurishte and the Dutch epidemic and was missing from the original dataset. It is correctly classified here as re-occurrence in an already endemic country and not as a first or inter‑continental emergence event.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Q fever
Host: Humans (residents of Jena‑Winzerla suburb; exposure linked to nearby grazing sheep flock)
Event.summary: In June 2005, general practitioners in Winzerla, a suburb of Jena in Thuringia, Germany, reported clusters of adults with acute febrile respiratory illness who lived near a hillside where a flock of sheep grazed and lambed, prompting an outbreak investigation. Investigators identified a large community outbreak with 331 reported Q fever cases, high attack rates among residents closest to the sheep pastures and strong epidemiologic evidence that lambing on pastures bordering housing had generated contaminated aerosols drifting over the residential area. Control measures included moving the flock away from homes, restricting access to contaminated pastures and providing clinical management and education for affected residents; after these interventions, incident cases declined, although follow‑up studies documented chronic Q fever and chronic fatigue syndrome in a subset of patients.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: close proximity of a sizeable sheep flock to a densely populated residential area, lambing on open pastures immediately adjacent to housing, and favourable topography and wind conditions promoting down‑slope transport of contaminated aerosols; initial lack of awareness of Q fever risk in this suburban context delayed specific interventions. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through intense shedding of C. burnetii in birth products and environmental contamination from lambing sheep, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) into a suburban community in which large Q fever outbreaks had not previously been recognised; no novel genotype has been shown to drive this event.
Review: Retain (with reclassification) – the 2005 Jena‑Winzerla community outbreak with 331 reported Q fever cases is one of the largest European events and should remain in the major‑event set. The emergence type has been changed from re-emergence to re-occurrence because available analyses attribute the epidemic to high local sheep density, lambing beside residential areas and meteorologic factors rather than to documented changes in the bacterium.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Q fever
Host: Humans (students and staff at a religious boarding high school in an urban area of central Israel)
Event.summary: In June 2005 health authorities in central Israel were notified of numerous febrile illnesses among students and staff at a religious boarding high school located in a densely populated urban area. A case–control investigation and serologic testing showed that 187 of 303 individuals reported compatible recent illness and 144 of 164 tested had evidence of acute C. burnetii infection, confirming a large Q fever outbreak likely linked to contamination of the school’s air‑conditioning system by infected stray cats or other animal reservoirs. After cleaning and modification of the ventilation system, restricting animal access to the premises and providing targeted clinical management and advice, no further school‑associated cases were detected, and the outbreak highlighted that Q fever can cause sizeable urban epidemics with little or no direct livestock contact.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high‑density boarding‑school environment with shared dining and residential facilities, proximity of stray cats and other potential animal reservoirs in an urban setting, and contamination of a central air‑conditioning system that efficiently disseminated infectious aerosols throughout the school. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via the ability of C. burnetii to persist in dust and be aerosolised within ventilation systems, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) of infection into an institutional urban population with limited traditional livestock exposure; there is no evidence of a novel strain.
Review: Retain – the 2005 Q fever outbreak in an urban boarding school in central Israel, with 187 ill individuals and 144 serologically confirmed infections, is one of the larger post‑1990 Q fever epidemics and was absent from the original file. It is correctly classified as re-occurrence in an endemic country, representing amplification in a specific institutional setting rather than spread to a new continent or UNSD subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Q fever
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2006]
Host: Humans (workers at a meat processing plant in Scotland; exposure linked to a sheep lairage)
Event.summary: In July 2006 a large outbreak of Q fever was detected among workers at a co‑located slaughterhouse and meat‑cutting plant near Stirling in Scotland, after a high proportion of staff developed febrile respiratory illness. National surveillance and outbreak reports identified approximately 138–142 human cases, making this the largest recorded UK Q fever outbreak since 2000, and epidemiologic investigation pointed to airborne transmission from a sheep lairage area processing post‑parturient ewes as the most likely source. Following modification of lairage and plant operations, enhanced environmental and engineering controls, and appropriate medical management of affected and at‑risk staff, no further plant‑associated Q fever cases were detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: heavy throughput of small ruminants, including recently lambed ewes, in a large industrial slaughter facility, inadequate containment of aerosols generated in the sheep lairage and cutting areas, and limited prior recognition of Q fever risk in this workforce. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via massive aerosolisation of C. burnetii from heavily contaminated lairage environments and carcass handling, and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) into a concentrated meat‑processing workforce; no evidence indicates a novel strain or altered host range.
Review: Retain (with reclassification) – the 2006 Scottish meat‑processing plant outbreak, involving roughly 140 cases, is the largest documented UK Q fever incident in the 2000s and belongs among the major post‑1990 events. The emergence type has been corrected from re-emergence to re-occurrence because the outbreak is explained by heavy occupational exposure to infected sheep in an endemic country, without evidence of pathogen change or expansion into a new continent/subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Q fever
Host: Humans (community residents and risk‑occupations; infection source linked to dairy goats and dairy sheep)
Event.summary: The epidemic began in spring 2007 when clinicians in the southern Netherlands (notably Noord‑Brabant) reported clusters of atypical pneumonia among adults living near areas of intensive dairy‑goat farming, marking the onset of an unprecedented community Q fever epidemic. Over the following years, notified acute Q fever cases rose sharply to 168 in 2007, 1,000 in 2008 and 2,354 in 2009 (with >4,000 reported cases cumulatively and an estimated tens of thousands of infections), with strong spatial association to infected dairy‑goat and dairy‑sheep farms and environmental spread via aerosols from birthing products and manure; major veterinary measures, including mandatory vaccination of small ruminants and culling of more than 50,000 goats, were implemented. After large‑scale animal vaccination, movement controls, targeted culling and a suite of public‑health interventions, human case numbers declined steeply by 2010 and the epidemic was considered controlled, although chronic Q fever cases and associated mortality continued to be detected in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid intensification and expansion of dairy‑goat farming in the southern Netherlands, very high goat herd densities close to residential areas, delayed recognition of Q fever as a major zoonotic risk, and environmental dissemination of C. burnetii through contaminated aerosols and possibly manure management and particulate matter. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (dominance of a hyperabortigenic C. burnetii genotype in dairy goats and sheep), Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (very high bacterial loads in birth products and manure facilitating efficient aerosol transmission to humans), and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) within the Netherlands as the intensive goat sector expanded into new localities.
Review: Retain – the 2007–2010 Netherlands epidemic (>4,000 notified acute Q fever cases and at least dozens of acute and chronic Q fever–related deaths) is unequivocally the largest human Q fever outbreak ever reported and is correctly classified as re-emergence associated with a hyperabortigenic goat‑associated genotype and rapid intensification of dairy‑goat farming. Geographic scope, time span, case counts and control measures were cross‑checked against national (RIVM) and peer‑reviewed sources and are consistent.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans living, working or recreating in forested regions of the Russian Federation, especially in Siberian and Ural natural-foci areas where Ixodes persulcatus is abundant
Event.summary: From 1990 through the late 1990s, Russia experienced persistently high national tick-borne encephalitis incidence, representing the culmination of a roughly sevenfold increase in notified cases since the mid-1970s. Annual TBE case counts during this decade ranged from about 5,600 to over 10,000, with 89–166 deaths per year, and the burden was heaviest in Siberian and Ural regions where incidence far exceeded national averages.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article)) Although incidence fluctuated seasonally and geographically, by the end of the 1990s TBE was recognized as one of Russia’s most important natural-focal infections before beginning to decline somewhat in the early 2000s in response to vaccination and other control efforts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A combination of ecological and societal factors, including extensive forested landscapes supporting dense Ixodes persulcatus populations, expansion of human activity into tick-infested habitats, changing forestry and agricultural practices, and incomplete vaccination coverage, contributed to high transmission intensity in Siberia and the Urals.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article)) Internal mechanisms: Available genetic data suggest co-circulation of established Siberian and Far Eastern TBEV subtypes rather than the emergence of a single novel lineage; the national-scale increase is best interpreted as a re-occurrence driven predominantly by external ecological and socio-economic drivers acting on long-established foci.
Review: retain – Added because Russia’s 1990s TBE experience (5,593–10,298 cases and 89–166 deaths annually, with a sevenfold increase since the 1970s) clearly ranks among the most impactful global TBE emergence episodes in terms of absolute burden.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article)) Classified as re-occurrence within an already endemic Eastern Europe subregion, driven by ecological and socio-economic factors; no evidence that this decade represented first/global emergence or intra-/inter-continental spread.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans living in or visiting coastal, archipelago and woodland areas of Sweden, especially Stockholm County and eastern coastal regions
Event.summary: From the mid‑1980s into the 1990s and early 2000s, Sweden saw a substantial rise in TBE incidence, particularly in Stockholm County, with a tripling of human cases compared to earlier decades and record high years in the early–mid 1990s. The epidemic developed as milder springs and longer warm seasons favored higher densities and wider distribution of Ixodes ricinus ticks, while growing outdoor recreation in archipelago and forest areas increased human exposure. Expansion of risk areas and improved vaccination efforts in some high‑incidence regions, combined with public health messaging, helped stabilize or reduce incidence after peaks in the 1990s, though TBE remained an important endemic disease and has continued to increase again in the 21st century.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673600052508?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Documented regional warming with earlier springs and longer periods of tick activity, changes in wildlife host populations, and increased outdoor leisure and residence in peri‑urban forested areas all contributed to increased human–tick contact. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of established TBEV foci toward higher latitudes and altitudes, facilitated by climate suitability for Ixodes ricinus; no specific new viral genotype is implicated, so this represents climate‑ and behavior‑driven re-occurrence rather than a strain-driven re-emergence.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673600052508?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Sweden’s marked increase in TBE incidence from the mid‑1980s through the 1990s, especially around Stockholm, is well documented and commonly cited as a key climate‑associated resurgence in Northern Europe.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673600052508?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (no evidence for a novel strain) and focus on Northern Europe/Sweden are appropriate; no corrections to geography or timing are required. Sources from The Lancet and JAMA are suitable primary references; the French Wikipedia link is background only but not essential.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans (primarily coastal residents and visitors in southern Norway exposed to Ixodes ricinus ticks)
Event.summary: In 1997, Norway reported its first recognized human case of tick‑borne encephalitis, marking the appearance of clinically apparent TBE in a country previously considered non‑endemic despite proximity to Swedish foci. Over the following years, additional autochthonous cases were documented along the southern coastal areas, indicating establishment of local transmission in new natural foci at the north‑western fringe of the known TBEV range. The number of cases remained relatively low (0–2 per year through 2003) but persistent, and surveillance and vaccination recommendations were gradually adapted as TBE became an acknowledged emerging tick‑borne infection in parts of Norway.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/12/04-0598_article))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely interplay of milder coastal climate, changing tick and wildlife host distributions, and increased human use of coastal recreational areas, enabling exposure where infected ticks were newly established. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of TBEV into coastal habitats in southern Norway that were previously unsuitable or unrecognized; available data do not demonstrate a distinct new viral genotype, so this is best considered re-occurrence of a known pathogen in a newly affected country within an already endemic Northern European subregion.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/12/04-0598_article))
Review: retain – Norway’s first documented autochthonous human TBE cases from 1997 onwards are important for tracking northwestward spread of the disease, but incidence remained low.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/12/04-0598_article)) Reclassified this episode from re-emergence to re-occurrence because published reports attribute it mainly to climate- and ecology-driven range expansion and improved testing, without evidence of a novel, more virulent TBEV strain. No changes to continent/subregion or timing are needed; sources (especially the CDC EID paper) are appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans in Novosibirsk Region, western Siberia, developing severe encephalitis with prominent hemorrhagic manifestations after tick bites
Event.summary: During the summer of 1999, an unusual cluster of eight fatal tick-borne encephalitis cases with marked hemorrhagic syndrome was identified in Novosibirsk Region, Russia, among 447 serologically confirmed TBE patients. Affected individuals developed typical TBE symptoms followed by massive gastrointestinal and mucosal bleeding and multi-organ hemorrhages, and sequencing of viral E-gene fragments from archived brain samples showed that the responsible variants were closely related to the Far Eastern subtype but carried unique mutations.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article)) In the following two years, hundreds of TBE cases continued to occur in the region but no further hemorrhagic forms were documented, indicating that this severe phenotype represented a short-lived re-emergence of a more virulent TBEV variant within an already highly endemic area.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The 1999 cluster occurred against a background of intense TBEV transmission in western Siberia, where forest ecosystems, abundant ticks and rodent hosts, and frequent human exposure already sustained high incidence. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analysis of E-gene sequences demonstrated that the hemorrhagic cases were caused by TBEV strains within the Far Eastern subtype that possessed distinct mutations compared with typical regional strains, and the abrupt appearance and disappearance of hemorrhagic TBE strongly suggest re-emergence linked to increased viral virulence or altered pathogenicity rather than to changes in surveillance alone.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article))
Review: retain – Added as a separate high-impact event because it represents the first well-documented cluster of hemorrhagic TBE, with eight fatal cases and molecular evidence of a distinct Far Eastern TBEV variant, thus fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by a change in pathogen virulence.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/9/6/03-0007_article)) Geography and timing are clear; no intra-/inter-continental spread is involved.

Review: retain – Added to capture a major Asian TBE episode: more than 2,000 reported cases and 19 deaths across 189 counties in 17 Chinese provinces (2006–2013), with a pronounced 2009–2011 peak and clear southwestward spatial expansion in the northeastern endemic focus.([eprints.soton.ac.uk](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/408106/1/1_s2.0_S1877959X1730167X_main.pdf)) This ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 TBE events outside Europe and Russia. Classified as re-occurrence within Eastern Asia (no evidence for a fundamentally new TBEV subtype), with environmental and occupational drivers.

Review: retain – The Dutch emergence, with first TBEV-positive ticks and first confirmed autochthonous human cases in 2016 followed by continued local transmission, marks a genuine addition of a new endemic country in Western Europe.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5356422/?utm_source=openai)) Reclassified the event from re-emergence to re-occurrence, because published analyses attribute it mainly to westward spread of existing European subtype strains and ecological suitability, without evidence of major viral change. Geography, timing and sources are appropriate.

Review: retain – Belgium’s emergence, starting with two possible/probable autochthonous infections in 2018, three confirmed autochthonous cases in 2020, accumulating additional local cases by 2024, and a household cluster in 2025, represents the establishment and early growth of TBEV transmission in a previously unaffected Western European country.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8314842/?utm_source=openai)) Updated the event period to 2018–2025 and slightly revised the summary to reflect newer data.
