EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus sinnombreense
EPP.common.name: Sin Nombre virus
Host: Humans (primarily young adults; reservoir: deer mouse Peromyscus maniculatus / P. sonoriensis)
Event.summary: In early 1993, clinicians in the Four Corners region of the southwestern United States (New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Utah) noted a cluster of previously healthy young adults presenting with rapidly progressive respiratory failure and high mortality, prompting an intensive epidemiologic investigation. The outbreak led to identification of a novel hantavirus, later named Sin Nombre virus, in association with deer mice and recognition of a new disease entity, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, with at least two dozen laboratory-confirmed cases and roughly half resulting in death in that initial episode. Intensive rodent control and public health education, along with the natural waning of the epizootic in deer mice after an El Niño–driven population boom, were followed by a marked decline in new human cases in the region, although sporadic cases have continued to occur in subsequent years across western North America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unusually high precipitation and subsequent increases in vegetation and rodent (deer mouse) populations in the early 1990s in the Four Corners region increased human–rodent contact opportunities; many affected persons had substantial peridomestic or occupational exposures to rodent-infested dwellings or outbuildings, and limited prior awareness of hantavirus risk likely contributed to intense exposures. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate that a newly evolved, more virulent Sin Nombre strain triggered the event; instead, the outbreak represents first clinical recognition and laboratory detection of a long-circulating zoonotic virus with inherent capacity for severe pulmonary disease when aerosolized rodent excreta are inhaled by humans, i.e., geographic range and host association were pre-existing but previously undetected rather than newly evolved.
Review: retain – This row correctly represents the 1993 Four Corners outbreak of severe respiratory illness in the southwestern United States that led to the discovery of Sin Nombre virus and the definition of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, with appropriate geography and case-fatality characterization. Treating it as a first_detection (rather than first/global emergence) is justified because retrospective investigations have identified earlier HPS cases attributable to New World hantaviruses in the United States dating back to at least 1978 and even 1959, indicating that the virus was present in humans before 1993 but unrecognized. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/11/pdfs/18-0381.pdf))

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus sinnombreense
EPP.common.name: Sin Nombre virus
Host: Humans (HPS/HCPS cases in western Canada; reservoir: deer mouse Peromyscus maniculatus / P. sonoriensis)
Event.summary: Following media coverage of the 1993 Four Corners outbreak, clinicians in Canada retrospectively reviewed unexplained acute respiratory failure cases and prospectively investigated new severe respiratory illnesses, leading to laboratory confirmation of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in Canadian patients in 1994, including cases in British Columbia and Alberta. These early Canadian cases were linked ecologically and virologically to Sin Nombre virus maintained in local deer mouse populations, establishing SNV-associated HPS as a cause of severe disease across western Canada rather than being confined to the southwestern United States. After this first recognized Canadian emergence, active surveillance for HPS began in 1994 and the disease became nationally notifiable in 2000, with a low but persistent annual incidence of mostly sporadic Sin Nombre virus infections reported in western provinces.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Shared ecological conditions across western North America—semi-arid to montane environments favoring deer mouse populations and human activities that disturb rodent-infested structures—enabled detection of Sin Nombre spillover into humans in Canada once awareness increased after the U.S. outbreak; enhanced clinical suspicion and laboratory capacity after 1993 were key drivers of detection. Internal mechanisms: Evidence supports that the Canadian HPS cases were caused by Sin Nombre virus strains closely related to those in the U.S. Four Corners area, implying geographic recognition and improved detection of an existing virus–host system rather than emergence of a novel variant; no clear changes in virulence, transmissibility, or host range were identified for this event.
Review: retain – This row accurately summarizes the first recognized Sin Nombre virus–associated hantavirus pulmonary syndrome cases in Canada in 1994 (initially in British Columbia and Alberta) and correctly places the event in Northern America with Canada as the affected country. The note that active surveillance began in 1994 and that HPS became nationally notifiable in Canada in 2000 is supported by national surveillance documents. Because this episode represents spread to a new country within the same UNSD subregion (Northern America) rather than to a new subregion or continent, and it is not a resurgence within a previously affected subregion, it does not map cleanly onto any of the six emergence-type categories; leaving all type flags as “no” is therefore acceptable, and no changes to the coded event types, geography, or sources are recommended. ([bccdc.ca](https://www.bccdc.ca/health-info/diseases-conditions/hantavirus-pulmonary-syndrome-hps))

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus sinnombreense
EPP.common.name: Sin Nombre virus
Host: Humans (visitors to Yosemite National Park; reservoir: deer mouse Peromyscus maniculatus / P. sonoriensis)
Event.summary: In summer 2012, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome occurred among overnight visitors to Yosemite National Park in California, United States, with confirmed Sin Nombre virus infection in at least ten persons who had stayed in certain tent cabins in Curry Village during June–August. Epidemiologic and environmental investigations linked the cases to heavy deer mouse infestation and structural design features of the insulated tent cabins that facilitated rodent nesting and human exposure to contaminated excreta; the outbreak was notable as the largest recognized Sin Nombre virus cluster in the United States since the 1993 Four Corners emergence. The affected tent cabins were permanently closed and removed, enhanced rodent control and public communication measures were implemented in the park, and no further large clusters associated with Yosemite lodging were reported in subsequent years, although sporadic Sin Nombre virus cases continue to occur in the western United States.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Structural features of the Yosemite Curry Village signature tent cabins, including double walls and insulation that permitted extensive deer mouse nesting, combined with high visitor density during peak tourist season, created an environment with intense human exposure to aerosolized rodent excreta; limited awareness of hantavirus risk among visitors and the park lodging sector likely contributed to inadequate rodent exclusion and control before the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by established Sin Nombre virus strains carried by deer mice rather than a new variant; the key mechanism was enhanced transmission opportunity through environmental and infrastructural factors (rodent infestation in human sleeping quarters) rather than evolutionary change in the virus, so it is best classified as a re-occurrence driven by ecological and structural conditions rather than re-emergence via viral change.
Review: retain – This row correctly describes the 2012 Yosemite National Park outbreak among overnight visitors staying in Curry Village tent cabins, including the approximate number of confirmed Sin Nombre virus infections (10, with eight HPS cases and three deaths), the structural cabin design and rodent infestation as key drivers, and the implementation of cabin closure and enhanced rodent control as control measures. Classifying this as a re-occurrence (resurgence of disease within an already affected subregion of Northern America driven by ecological and infrastructural factors, without evidence of viral change or spread to a new continent) is appropriate, and primary sources from CDC MMWR, CDC Emerging Infectious Diseases, and Public Health Agency of Canada documents consistently identify this episode as the second major Sin Nombre virus outbreak after 1993. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6146a5.htm))

Internal mechanisms: multiple outbreak PFGE/WGS subtypes but no evidence of a novel hypervirulent lineage; risk was primarily related to pathogen survival and multiplication on moist melon surfaces during storage and distribution (re‑occurrence via new food vehicle and handling practices).
Review: retain – Event accurately summarizes the 2011 Jensen Farms cantaloupe outbreak (147 cases, 33 deaths, 1 fetal loss across 28 US states) and its control measures, in agreement with CDC and NEJM reports. Geography and classification as a severe re‑occurrence in an already affected region, involving a new produce vehicle but no clearly novel strain, are appropriate; clearly one of the top global listeriosis outbreaks.

After removal of implicated products, deep sanitation at the facility and strengthened routine WGS‑based surveillance for human and food isolates, the outbreak subsided and incidence returned to background levels.

Internal mechanisms: outbreak caused by a single L. monocytogenes clone without reported novel resistance traits; impact arose from persistence and high exposure in vulnerable populations (re‑occurrence). The event illustrates the value of whole‑genome sequencing for outbreak detection and source attribution.

Geography (Northern Europe/Denmark) and classification as a severe re‑occurrence are appropriate. Given its high case‑fatality ratio and influence on adoption of routine WGS, this outbreak is a strong candidate for inclusion among the top global events and should be considered alongside other large outbreaks when finalizing the list.

Geography (Oceania/Australia) and classification as a severe re‑occurrence via a produce vehicle are appropriate, with WHO, CSIRO and national reports as sources. EPP.scientific.name: Streptococcus agalactiae

By the late 2000s, invasive GBS in nonpregnant adults had become a major and growing component of the overall GBS disease burden in North America, prompting concern about adult-targeted vaccination and prevention strategies.

Internal mechanisms: no single new lineage identified as causal; rather, expansion of multiple existing invasive lineages under changing host and healthcare conditions (enhanced opportunities for invasive infection).
Review: retain – Event captures a major, well-documented rise in invasive GBS disease in nonpregnant adults in the United States, with incidence doubling between 1990 and 2007 and high case counts and mortality. Geography (Northern America), years, and classification as re-occurrence (driven by demographic and comorbidity changes without a clearly novel clone) are consistent with surveillance data and reviews; no corrections to countries, event type, or timing are required, and sources are appropriate for this large-scale trend.

EPP.scientific.name: Streptococcus agalactiae
EPP.common.name: Group B Streptococci
Host: Humans – primarily pregnant women and neonates with invasive and colonizing GBS
Event.summary: In Beijing and other parts of mainland China, susceptibility testing of clinical Streptococcus agalactiae isolates in the late 1990s documented substantial and increasing resistance to erythromycin and lincomycin, with erythromycin resistance rising from roughly 8% to 16% between 1998 and 1999 and notable proportions of isolates carrying ermB and mefA resistance genes. Over the early 2000s, additional studies across China showed persistently high macrolide resistance rates in GBS, mirroring trends in other streptococci in the country. By the mid‑2000s, macrolide- and lincosamide-resistant GBS had become entrenched in Chinese obstetric and pediatric populations, constraining alternative prophylaxis options for penicillin-allergic patients.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive macrolide use in China for respiratory and other community infections created strong selection pressure for resistance among streptococci, including GBS. Internal mechanisms: acquisition and spread of ermB and mefA genes mediating ribosomal modification and active efflux, often on mobile elements, leading to high-level macrolide resistance and reduced susceptibility to related agents (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission via selection of resistant clones).
Review: retain – The event describes the emergence and consolidation of macrolide/lincosamide-resistant GBS in mainland China in the late 1990s–early 2000s, supported by susceptibility and genotypic data and representing a large population with substantial implications for prophylaxis. Geography (Eastern Asia, China), timing (1998–2005), and classification as re-emergence driven by acquired resistance (not spread to a previously naïve region) are appropriate; no corrections to countries, subregions or event type are required, and sources are suitable.

EPP.scientific.name: Streptococcus agalactiae
EPP.common.name: Group B Streptococci
Host: Humans – predominantly previously healthy adults; freshwater fish used in ready-to-eat raw dishes (e.g. Asian bighead carp, snakehead) as the vehicle and reservoir
Event.summary: In mid‑2015, hospitals in Singapore detected an abrupt epidemic of invasive group B streptococcal infections in adults, many presenting with sepsis, meningitis, and septic arthritis, which was rapidly linked epidemiologically and microbiologically to a serotype III ST283 clone and recent consumption of raw freshwater fish dishes. The outbreak peaked at around 26 reported invasive GBS cases per week and affected at least 140–150 persons, before public health authorities issued advisories in July 2015 and implemented bans on the sale of raw freshwater fish in ready‑to‑eat dishes in December 2015. Following removal of raw freshwater fish from the retail food chain, the incidence of invasive ST283 infections in Singapore fell sharply back toward baseline, although sporadic cases and low-level circulation of the clone in humans and fish have persisted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: widespread consumption of ready-to-eat raw freshwater fish dishes, inadequate sourcing and hygienic handling of freshwater fish, and co-mingling of contaminated fish in markets created an efficient foodborne transmission route; delayed recognition of GBS as a foodborne pathogen allowed amplification before control. Internal mechanisms: the hypervirulent ST283 clone is capable of causing invasive disease in immunocompetent adults after gastrointestinal exposure; genomic analyses show close relatedness between human and fish ST283 isolates, supporting efficient cross-species transmission and adaptation to survival in aquatic hosts and human gastrointestinal tracts (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion/Spillover; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via carried determinants).
Review: retain – The 2015 Singapore ST283 outbreak is a clearly defined, high-impact foodborne epidemic (≈140–150 invasive cases, sharp temporal spike, and major policy response) and must be retained as a distinct re-emergence event of a hypervirulent clone with foodborne transmission. Countries, timing, and host description are accurate, classification as re-emergence (novel clone/route in a region where GBS was already present) without intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate, and the cited outbreak investigations and genomic analyses are the most relevant sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Streptococcus agalactiae

Event.summary: Between September and November 2021, public hospitals in Hong Kong detected an unusual cluster of invasive group B streptococcal infections in adults, more than half of which were caused by the hypervirulent sequence type 283 lineage previously associated mainly with Southeast Asia. During this period, ST283 was also isolated from freshwater fish and environmental samples from wet markets, indicating a shared or linked source similar to that seen in Singapore. After public health investigations, heightened food safety messaging and control of contaminated fish sources, the short‑term spike in invasive ST283 cases subsided, though Hong Kong authorities continue to monitor this lineage as an emerging foodborne and invasive pathogen.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: importation and sale of freshwater fish from regions where ST283 is established, combined with traditional culinary practices and handling of raw or undercooked fish in wet markets, facilitated local introduction and amplification; high ambient temperatures during late summer and early autumn may have favored bacterial growth in fish and market environments. Internal mechanisms: dissemination of the same hypervirulent ST283 clone with demonstrated capacity for efficient foodborne transmission and invasive disease in adults, with genomic evidence of close relatedness between human and fish isolates, suggesting ongoing host switching and adaptation (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion/Spillover; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion within Asia).
Review: review – Event appropriately describes the 2021 Hong Kong surge of invasive ST283 infections (95 iGBS cases, 57 due to ST283) with linked detection of the same clone in freshwater fish and wet market environments, and it is clearly a major regional episode. However, the event type required correction: intra_continental_emergence has been set from Yes to No because ST283 had already been present in Hong Kong since the 1990s and this cluster represents a re-emergence/large flare-up of an existing hypervirulent lineage in a previously affected subregion, not first establishment of the species or lineage in a new Asian subregion. Classification as re_emergence (driven by a known hypervirulent clone and foodborne/handling exposures) and the geographic coding (Eastern Asia, Hong Kong SAR) and year (2021) are otherwise consistent with the outbreak description and added genomic/epidemiologic sources, including the detailed EID 2025 cluster report.

EPP.scientific.name: Treponema pallidum
EPP.common.name: Syphilis
Host: Humans (general sexually active population, including sex workers, clients, MSM, and pregnant women)
Event.summary: Following near-elimination of syphilis in China by the 1960s through mass screening and treatment, reported cases began to rise again in the 1980s and accelerated in the 1990s, reaching a national incidence of around 5 per 100,000 by the early 2000s. The epidemic expanded through coastal urban centers and along migration corridors, with high prevalence documented in sex workers, MSM and other key populations during the 1990s and 2000s. By the late 2000s and around 2010, syphilis had re-established as a major nationwide STI with sustained high incidence, prompting renewed government attention and control programs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid economic liberalization, large-scale internal migration, growth of the sex industry, rising disposable income and new sexual networks, and initially weak STI surveillance and control systems all contributed to syphilis resurgence; concurrent HIV expansion, particularly among MSM, increased co-infection burdens. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain was identified as initiating the epidemic; the event reflects geographic and behavioral spread of existing T. pallidum lineages. Later in the period, increasing macrolide resistance was documented but played a secondary role in driving incidence.
Review: retain – Well-documented large-scale resurgence after near-elimination in China, with correct continent/sub-region, country, timing and classification as re-occurrence. No corrections needed; sources (national surveillance analyses and narrative reviews) are appropriate for one of the major global syphilis events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Treponema pallidum
EPP.common.name: Syphilis
Host: Humans – pregnant women and newborns (congenital syphilis)
Event.summary: After very low congenital syphilis incidence in the late 1990s and early 2000s, reported U.S. congenital syphilis cases began to rise sharply from around 335 cases in 2012 to 3,761 in 2022, representing more than a tenfold increase. The epidemic expanded across many states, with disproportionate impacts in the U.S. South and West and among marginalized populations including people with substance use disorders and those with limited prenatal care access. By 2023 the United States recorded its highest number of congenital syphilis cases since the early 1990s, prompting urgent federal and state responses focused on prenatal screening and treatment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large increases in maternal syphilis linked to the broader adult epidemic, gaps in prenatal care coverage and quality (late or no prenatal care, missed or delayed testing, inadequate treatment), social determinants such as poverty, unstable housing, and methamphetamine or opioid use, and constraints in public health infrastructure and penicillin supply in some areas. Internal mechanisms: No specific new T. pallidum variant has been implicated; this is a classic re-occurrence driven by failures in prevention and care delivery rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – This is a major, well-documented emergence event in terms of impact (tenfold increase and hundreds of preventable fetal and neonatal deaths). Geography, time window (2012–2023), and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate and supported by CDC data; no structural corrections required.

EPP.scientific.name: Treponema pallidum
EPP.common.name: Syphilis
Host: Humans – general sexually active population, pregnant women, and newborns (congenital syphilis)
Event.summary: From the early 2000s, Brazil documented rising rates of acquired syphilis, syphilis in pregnancy, and congenital syphilis, with over 300,000 congenital syphilis cases reported nationally between 2001 and 2022 and more than half occurring from 2017–2022. Throughout the 2010s, incidence of congenital syphilis increased in all macro-regions, particularly in the Northeast, and was associated with substantial fetal and infant mortality and adverse pregnancy outcomes. National action plans launched around 2010 and 2016 slowed growth in some regions but did not fully reverse trends, and high burdens persisted into the early 2020s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent social and regional inequalities, challenges in access to and quality of prenatal care, gaps in timely maternal testing and treatment, and delayed implementation of robust syphilis surveillance (acquired syphilis became notifiable nationwide only after 2010); contributing factors include urbanization, internal migration, and coexisting HIV and other STIs. Internal mechanisms: No specific resistant or more virulent T. pallidum lineage has been demonstrated as the main driver; the epidemic is mainly a re-occurrence fueled by health-system and social determinants.
Review: retain – Brazil’s large and sustained increase in acquired, gestational, and congenital syphilis is one of the most impactful national-level events, with very high case numbers and mortality. Geography, time span and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate; event is strongly supported by multiple national and regional analyses.

EPP.scientific.name: Treponema pallidum
EPP.common.name: Syphilis
Host: Humans – heterosexual men and women and MSM; small numbers of congenital cases
Event.summary: After a long decline with only a few hundred annual cases by the early 2000s, Japan experienced a rapid increase in reported syphilis beginning around 2013, with annual cases rising from about 1,200 in 2013 to over 5,000 by 2017 and surpassing 10,000 by 2022. The surge was initially concentrated in major urban centers such as Tokyo and Osaka and, unusually compared with Western countries, involved large numbers of heterosexual men and women as well as MSM. By the early 2020s, syphilis had re-established as a major STI in Japan with sustained high incidence despite intensified public health messaging and surveillance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Changes in sexual behavior including increased casual and commercial sex, widespread use of smartphone dating apps, reduced condom use, and underestimation of syphilis risk due to historically low incidence; limitations in targeted prevention and early diagnosis for high‑risk groups also contributed. Internal mechanisms: High prevalence of macrolide-resistant T. pallidum (A2058G mutation in 23S rRNA) was documented in Japanese strains by the late 2010s, but penicillin remained effective; resistance may have complicated use of macrolides but is not thought to be the primary driver of incidence.
Review: retain – A well-supported major resurgence in Japan, with very large relative and absolute increases in national case counts and distinctive heterosexual involvement. Geography, years and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate; sources include national surveillance summaries and peer-reviewed analyses.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Treponema pallidum
EPP.common.name: Syphilis
Host: Humans – initially Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in remote northern and central Australia, later also urban MSM and heterosexual populations including pregnant women and newborns
Event.summary: After years of relatively low incidence, an outbreak of infectious syphilis was declared in 2011 among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities in north‑west Queensland, followed by outbreak declarations in the Northern Territory (2013), northern Western Australia (2014) and parts of South Australia (2016), with spread across much of northern and central Australia over the following decade. National notification rates rose roughly fourfold from about 6 per 100,000 population in 2011 to around 24 per 100,000 by 2019, and congenital syphilis, previously rare, re-emerged with at least dozens of affected infants and multiple deaths reported since the mid‑2010s. By 2025 syphilis was affecting every state and territory, with particularly high rates among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and rising incidence in women of reproductive age, leading Australia’s Chief Medical Officer to declare syphilis a Communicable Disease Incident of National Significance and prompting a coordinated national response for 2023–2030.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-standing social and structural inequities affecting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities (including overcrowded housing, limited access to culturally safe sexual health services, and poverty), under-resourced regional public health systems, increased mobility between remote communities and towns, and later, broader behavioral and network changes in urban MSM and heterosexual populations contributed to the resurgence. Gaps in antenatal screening and timely treatment in affected regions facilitated a parallel rise in congenital syphilis. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence that a novel, more virulent T. pallidum strain caused the Australian outbreaks; they are best understood as re-occurrence driven by social and health-system factors, with macrolide resistance present but not the primary driver of incidence.
Review: review – New event added. The multi-jurisdictional infectious syphilis outbreak beginning in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities in 2011, and evolving into a nationwide resurgence with re-emergent congenital syphilis and a formal declaration as a Communicable Disease Incident of National Significance in 2025, represents a major Oceania-region event in terms of public health impact. Classified as re-occurrence (no new strain, but marked failures of prevention and care) with correct continent/sub-region and country coding. A human reviewer should confirm the chosen 2011–2025 window and whether any additional Pacific countries should be included or whether this row should remain Australia-specific.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Histoplasma spp.
EPP.common.name: histoplasmosis
Host: Humans (including many with and some without HIV or other immunosuppression)
Event.summary: From 1990 onward, clinicians in mainland China increasingly reported cases of histoplasmosis in patients who had never left the country, revealing that the fungus was locally acquired rather than only imported from the classic endemic Americas. Through case series and national reviews, more than 300 human cases were collated by 2011, with around three‑quarters from provinces along the Yangtze River basin and most considered autochthonous based on lack of travel to known endemic regions. By the end of this period, China was being described as a new or newly recognized endemic area for histoplasmosis, with accumulating evidence of widespread exposure and ongoing sporadic disease in Eastern Asia.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23216676/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased HIV prevalence and other causes of immunosuppression in China, combined with greater clinical awareness and wider use of culture, histopathology and antigen testing, led to better detection of a previously under-recognized endemic mycosis. Environmental drivers include suitable ecological niches for Histoplasma along the Yangtze River basin, such as bat- or bird-guano enriched soils that favor fungal growth. Internal mechanisms: This event mainly reflects geographic range recognition rather than clear evidence of novel genotypes; phylogenetic work suggests multiple lineages in East Asia, likely introduced or dispersed over time by human activity or animal migration rather than a single new strain.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23216676/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the post‑1990 recognition of autochthonous histoplasmosis in China as a newly appreciated endemic focus in Eastern Asia. Classification as intra‑continental emergence (new UNSD subregion within Asia) is appropriate because histoplasmosis was already known elsewhere in Asia (e.g. India, Southeast Asia) but not previously documented as locally acquired in China. Timeframe (1990–2011), geography (China, Eastern Asia) and sources are consistent with major reviews and mapping papers; no higher‑impact Asian emergence event was identified that would displace this one.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Histoplasma spp.
EPP.common.name: histoplasmosis
Host: Humans (single documented autochthonous case: immunocompetent adult with laryngeal and probable disseminated histoplasmosis)
Event.summary: Although Histoplasma had been isolated decades earlier from bat guano in a cave in northern Israel, no human infections were believed to be locally acquired in the Middle East. In 2018, clinicians reported an adult man from northern Israel with chronic hoarseness, weight loss and laryngeal lesions, with no travel history outside the country, whose biopsy, culture and molecular testing confirmed Histoplasma capsulatum infection, representing the first documented autochthonous histoplasmosis case from Israel and the wider Middle East. This report, together with older environmental isolates, triggered re‑evaluation of regional endemicity and raised the likelihood that additional pulmonary or disseminated cases in Western Asia had previously gone unrecognized or been misdiagnosed.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: This emergence signal is driven mainly by improved clinical suspicion and access to histopathology and molecular mycology in Israeli tertiary hospitals, which allowed recognition of a case that might previously have been mistaken for malignancy or tuberculosis. Environmental drivers include bat‑inhabited caves and guano‑contaminated soils in northern Israel that can support Histoplasma growth, indicating that the fungus has likely been present locally for decades. Internal mechanisms: No novel lineage has been implicated; genetic data are limited, and the case is best interpreted as geographic range recognition and intra‑continental emergence into a new Asian subregion (Western Asia), rather than evolution of a new, more virulent strain.
Review: review – This is a newly added row to capture the first documented autochthonous human histoplasmosis case in Israel and the broader Middle East, which was previously folded into a combined Europe–Israel event. Classification as intra‑continental emergence (new UNSD subregion within Asia) is appropriate: histoplasmosis was already known from other Asian subregions (Indian subcontinent, Southeast and East Asia), and the case demonstrates in situ infection in Western Asia rather than an imported episode. Because only a single autochthonous case is documented so far, this event is small in case count but justified as a key geographic range extension; it should be retained but flagged for expert review of the time window and whether additional Middle Eastern cases merit inclusion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Histoplasma spp.
EPP.common.name: histoplasmosis
Host: Humans receiving tumor necrosis factor‑α (TNF‑α) blockers or other biologic immunosuppressive therapies; also people with HIV and other immunosuppression
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, the widespread introduction of TNF‑α blockers and other biologic agents for autoimmune diseases in the United States led to recognition of a new high‑risk group for severe histoplasmosis within endemic areas. Analyses of U.S. hospitalizations for histoplasmosis from 2001–2012 showed substantial morbidity and mortality, while a multicenter review of nearly 100 patients on TNF‑α blockers who developed histoplasmosis between 2000 and 2011 found that over three‑quarters had disseminated disease, prompting the U.S. FDA in 2008 to issue a boxed warning about endemic mycoses with TNF‑α inhibitors. By the end of this period, histoplasmosis had re‑emerged as a significant iatrogenic opportunistic infection in biologic‑treated patients, altering risk profiles in endemic parts of Northern America.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/38201/cdc_38201_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid uptake of TNF‑α inhibitors and related biologic therapies for rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and other conditions created a growing population with impaired cell‑mediated immunity living in long‑established Histoplasma‑endemic zones. Clinical practice patterns (e.g. intensified immunosuppression prior to adequate screening or counseling about fungal risks) and limited early awareness of this association contributed to severe disease. Internal mechanisms: Histoplasma did not acquire known resistance or virulence changes in this setting; rather, host-population expansion to a new iatrogenically immunosuppressed group led to increased incidence and severity, fitting the definition of re‑emergence driven by host expansion and enhanced opportunity for dissemination.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/38201/cdc_38201_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This event appropriately highlights emergence of a large, clearly defined new risk group (patients receiving TNF‑α blockers and related biologic therapies) in a long‑endemic region. The classification as re-emergence (driven by host expansion rather than geographic spread or pathogen change) matches the definitions; intra-/inter‑continental emergence are correctly left as false because the fungus and disease were long established in North America. Timeframe (2001–2012) and sources align with hospitalization data and the TNF‑blocker case series and FDA warnings; no higher‑impact North American event of similar type was identified that would supersede this one.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptococcus gattii
EPP.common.name: cryptococcosis
Host: Humans (both immunocompetent and immunocompromised adults), with linked infections in domestic animals and wildlife in the same region
Event.summary: Beginning in 2004, clusters of autochthonous human C. gattii infections were recognized in Oregon and Washington, USA, in patients without travel to Vancouver Island, indicating that the pathogen had established environmental reservoirs in the U.S. Pacific Northwest in addition to those in British Columbia. Over 2004–2010, public health investigations documented dozens of locally acquired human cases, including infections caused by a novel VGIIc subtype apparently confined to Oregon alongside VGIIa and VGIIb strains closely related to the Vancouver Island outbreak lineage, and showed that clinical disease ranged from severe pneumonia to central nervous system cryptococcomas with substantial mortality.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) By around 2010, C. gattii was recognized as an endemic pathogen in parts of the U.S. Pacific Northwest, with ongoing sporadic cases and heightened clinical and laboratory awareness rather than unchecked epidemic growth.

Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence, notably the VGIIc subtype in Oregon, representing a genetically distinct lineage associated with severe pulmonary and CNS disease; geographic range expansion within the Northern America subregion; and possible increased virulence/pathogenicity and environmental fitness of specific VGII lineages that enabled successful colonization of new microclimates and hosts.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13))
Review: retain – This row appropriately highlights the substantial number of autochthonous C. gattii cases and the emergence of the distinct VGIIc subtype in the U.S. Pacific Northwest, which together constitute a major re‑emergence episode within the broader Vancouver Island–Pacific Northwest outbreak.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) To better align with the event definition and country‑format rules, the countries field has been restricted to “United States of America [2004]” (removing Canada, which is already covered in the 1999–2013 event), and the summary has been lightly edited to emphasize that this episode reflects establishment and diversification of C. gattii in the U.S. rather than a separate inter‑continental emergence. The classification as re_emergence = Yes and intra_/inter‑continental emergence = No is appropriate, so the event is retained but flagged for review due to its partial overlap with the Vancouver Island episode; depending on how much granularity is desired, the two North American rows could alternatively be merged into a single linked episode in a later harmonization step.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptococcus gattii
EPP.common.name: cryptococcosis
Host: Humans (predominantly adults with advanced HIV infection, but including some HIV‑negative patients) in a high‑HIV‑prevalence province; no specific livestock production impacts documented in this series.
Event.summary: Between March 2002 and February 2004, population‑based laboratory surveillance for cryptococcosis in Gauteng Province, South Africa, identified 46 patients infected with C. gattii, representing one of the largest documented series of C. gattii disease globally and occurring in the context of a generalized HIV epidemic.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) Most patients presented with subacute meningitis or meningoencephalitis, often with severe immunosuppression due to AIDS, and cases were identified across multiple hospitals, indicating province‑wide risk rather than a single point‑source outbreak. After 2004, C. gattii has continued to account for a small but important fraction of cryptococcal disease in South Africa, but the 2002–2004 enhanced surveillance period remains the key episode defining the burden and clinical profile of C. gattii infection in this high‑HIV, Southern African setting.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high prevalence of advanced, untreated HIV infection in Gauteng during the early 2000s greatly increased the susceptible human population for cryptococcal disease, while the implementation of active, laboratory‑based surveillance and species‑level identification exposed the contribution of C. gattii within the broader cryptococcosis burden; environmental reservoirs of serotype C (VGIV) C. gattii in southern Africa, documented in earlier mycologic and environmental studies, likely provided longstanding exposure that became clinically manifest as HIV prevalence rose.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) Internal mechanisms: There is no clear evidence that a novel genotype or major change in virulence drove this episode; instead, infections predominantly involved existing serotype C lineages, so the episode is best characterized as a re‑occurrence driven by external host and surveillance factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – This newly added event captures a major, temporally bounded episode in Gauteng Province, South Africa, where population‑based surveillance during 2002–2004 identified 46 C. gattii infections, making it one of the largest documented series outside Australia and the Pacific Northwest and clearly within the top tier of global emergence episodes by case count.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) Classification as re_occurrence = Yes (driven largely by the HIV epidemic and enhanced surveillance) with intra_/inter‑continental emergence = No and re_emergence = No appropriately reflects current evidence that C. gattii (especially serotype C/VGIV) was already present in southern Africa before 2002 and that no single new genotype has been implicated in this increase. Country, subregion and timeframe follow the original surveillance definitions; additional local series from Botswana and other provinces exist but have much smaller case numbers, so they are not added as separate top‑10 events.

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Host: Humans—mainly adults with hematologic malignancies (acute leukemias and other hematologic cancers) and one patient with prosthetic valve endocarditis
Event.summary: Between 1989 and 1994, six Spanish tertiary centers documented 16 deep infections due to Scedosporium prolificans (now Lomentospora prolificans), largely in neutropenic patients with hematologic malignancies and including one prosthetic valve endocarditis case, providing the first substantial European case series and making this mold visible as a serious pathogen in oncology and hematology services. Most patients progressed quickly from localized infection or transient colonization to disseminated disease involving blood, lungs, central nervous system and skin, with all tested isolates showing high MICs to all available antifungals and an 87.5% mortality, which highlighted L. prolificans as an intrinsically multiresistant, highly lethal invader. After this multicenter experience, awareness, diagnostics and reporting improved, and while the initial surge abated, Spain and other European countries continued to report sporadic severe and disseminated lomentosporiosis in similar high‑risk populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of intensive chemotherapy and complex hematologic care in Spain, creating large numbers of profoundly neutropenic patients; use of invasive devices and prolonged hospitalization in environments where the fungus was already present in soil and dust. Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic resistance to amphotericin B, azoles and flucytosine left clinicians with almost no effective fungicidal options; strong angioinvasiveness and ability to disseminate hematogenously favored multiorgan involvement and very high mortality.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Adjusted event_year from “1990–1994” to “1989–1994” to match the primary case-series, which reports 16 deep infections between 1989 and 1994 in six Spanish centers; this slightly predates the nominal 1990 cut-off but the majority of cases fall within the target window and the episode is the key early European emergence signal.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9279332/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Removed the previous ‘re_emergence = true’ flag, as this episode represents the first substantial recognized emergence in Europe and is best classified as inter-continental emergence into a new continent rather than re‑emergence driven by documented pathogen change. (iii) Left geography (Europe, Southern Europe, Spain) and host description unchanged, as they are consistent with the source article. Flagged for manual review specifically regarding acceptance of the 1989 start year under the “1990 onwards” rule, but the event itself is valid and should be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Fusarium spp.
EPP.common.name: fusariosis
Host: Humans (hematology/oncology and transplant patients in a tertiary‑care hospital)
Event.summary: During the 1990s, a US university hospital caring for patients with hematologic malignancies, severe neutropenia and stem‑cell or solid‑organ transplants experienced recurrent invasive fusariosis cases without an obvious source. A detailed environmental investigation cultured the hospital water distribution system, documenting extensive Fusarium solani and Fusarium oxysporum colonization of storage tanks, plumbing, sink drains, faucets and showers, and molecular typing showed that multiple patient isolates were closely related to waterborne strains, establishing a prolonged, water‑associated cluster of fusariosis. After recognition of the potable water system as a reservoir and implementation of water‑management measures (including restrictions on tap‑water exposure for high‑risk patients and engineering controls), the facility reduced fusariosis risk and this work helped prompt broader guidance on waterborne mold prevention in high‑risk hospital units.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Complex hospital plumbing and storage systems permitted persistent Fusarium biofilm formation and inadequate disinfection for filamentous molds, while frequent exposure of profoundly neutropenic or transplant patients to unfiltered tap water via showers, sink use and other contacts created an unrecognized transmission pathway; intensification of chemotherapy and transplantation programmes expanded the susceptible host population. Internal mechanisms: A diversity of Fusarium solani complex and related genotypes was found in both water samples and clinical isolates, indicating environmental opportunism rather than a single emergent strain, but the ability of these molds to adapt to and persist in biofilms within chlorinated hospital water networks, with aerosolization from showers and faucets, supported efficient environmental persistence and exposure in this niche.
Review: review – Retain this event as a major hospital‑associated fusariosis cluster in a US tertiary‑care center where colonization of the potable water system was linked to invasive infections in highly immunocompromised patients. Event year 2001 reflects the principal Clinical Infectious Diseases investigation and publication rather than the full 1990s exposure window described in the paper; the precise start and end years of the cluster should be checked against the original article if finer temporal resolution is required. Geographic coding (North America, Northern America; United States of America) and host description are appropriate, and classification as re‑occurrence is justified because Fusarium infections in US hematology patients were already known and the increase was driven by environmental reservoir recognition and expanding high‑risk populations, not spread to a new region or a demonstrably novel genotype. Source URLs have been streamlined to focus on the original CID outbreak report and a major human fusariosis review, dropping a redundant ResearchGate link and a broad mycology review that added little event‑specific detail; flagged for review mainly to refine the exact temporal bounds if needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Fusarium spp.
EPP.common.name: fusariosis
Host: Humans (patients undergoing cataract surgery with ophthalmic viscoelastic devices)
Event.summary: In late 2020, ophthalmologists and public health authorities in the Republic of Korea detected an unusually large number of fungal endophthalmitis cases following cataract surgery across multiple hospitals nationwide. A national investigation identified around 150–160 affected eyes, most with Fusarium oxysporum isolated from intraocular specimens, and epidemiologic and microbiologic evidence linked cases to specific lots of a sodium hyaluronate ophthalmic viscoelastic device produced by a single manufacturer and distributed widely for cataract operations. Once the implicated viscoelastic batches were recalled and use was halted, along with intensified surveillance and treatment, the incidence of new Fusarium endophthalmitis cases associated with those products declined sharply and the outbreak gradually resolved, although many patients suffered substantial visual morbidity despite aggressive therapy.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Contamination of widely distributed ophthalmic viscoelastic device lots used routinely in cataract surgery provided a direct route for intraocular inoculation of Fusarium spp., converting a rare opportunistic pathogen into the cause of a nationwide, iatrogenic outbreak; centralised procurement and rapid diffusion of the contaminated product across many facilities amplified the number of exposed patients. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was identified as Fusarium oxysporum, with genotypic identity between isolates from patients and from contaminated product, but the available data support clonal contamination and direct inoculation rather than the emergence of a distinctly more virulent or transmissible Fusarium lineage; disease severity mainly reflected the highly vulnerable intraocular site and delayed recognition rather than fundamental changes in pathogen biology.
Review: retain – This event accurately captures the nationwide 2020 fungal endophthalmitis outbreak in the Republic of Korea linked to contaminated ophthalmic viscoelastic devices. Event years (2020–2021), geographic coding (Asia, Eastern Asia; Republic of Korea) and the host description align with national investigations and case series, and the approximate case numbers and linkage to specific viscoelastic lots are consistent with published data. Classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate, because Fusarium ocular infections pre‑dated this episode in East Asia and the outbreak reflects contamination of a medical product rather than spread to a new region or a novel Fusarium lineage. Source URLs already point to the primary EID outbreak investigation and a large JAMA Ophthalmology clinical series and are suitable for documenting this event; no additional higher‑impact outbreaks of Fusarium endophthalmitis were identified that would supersede this episode in scale.

EPP.scientific.name: Fusarium spp.
EPP.common.name: fusariosis
Host: Humans (predominantly obstetric and surgical patients receiving epidural or spinal anesthesia in Durango)
Event.summary: From mid‑2022 into early 2023, clinicians in the state of Durango, Mexico, recognized an unusual cluster of subacute meningitis and meningoencephalitis, largely among women who had undergone cesarean sections or other procedures under neuraxial (epidural or spinal) anesthesia in several private hospitals. A retrospective cohort investigation identified roughly 1,800 patients exposed to neuraxial blockade between May 2022 and February 2023, of whom 80 developed Fusarium solani complex meningitis and 41 died, representing a case‑fatality rate of just over 50 percent; molecular testing of cerebrospinal fluid and anesthetic materials implicated contamination of specific bupivacaine batches used by one anesthesiologist as the source. After the contaminated anesthetic lots were withdrawn, exposed patients were traced and evaluated, and prolonged combination antifungal therapy was instituted for confirmed and probable cases, the incidence of new Fusarium meningitis cases declined and the outbreak was gradually controlled, although many survivors had severe neurologic sequelae.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Manufacturing or handling failures that led to contamination of bupivacaine batches used for neuraxial anesthesia, combined with high volumes of obstetric and surgical procedures and delayed recognition of a fungal etiology, created an efficient, high‑dose route of direct central nervous system inoculation; gaps in regulation and quality control for local anesthetic supplies and infection‑prevention practices in private clinics contributed to the scale and severity of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: The Fusarium solani species complex strains involved showed the expected high minimum inhibitory concentrations to many systemic antifungals and marked neurotropism once introduced into the subarachnoid space, but available data suggest intrinsic resistance characteristics and route of exposure, rather than emergence of a demonstrably novel genotype, were the dominant drivers; the event is therefore best classified as a severe healthcare‑associated re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence of a new strain.
Review: review – Retain this event as it represents the largest documented outbreak of Fusarium solani meningitis, associated with neuraxial anesthesia in Durango, Mexico. The description has been updated to reflect more recent data from the Clinical Infectious Diseases cohort (approximately 1,801 exposed patients, 80 meningitis cases, 41 deaths), which supersede earlier provisional counts of 79 cases and around 35 deaths; the time window (mid‑2022 to early 2023), location (Mexico, Central America sub‑region under the South America continent grouping) and host profile are consistent with primary reports. Classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate: Fusarium was already known as a human pathogen in Mexico, and this event reflects contaminated anesthetic and procedural practices rather than first detection in a new region or emergence of a new strain. Source URLs have been refined to centre on the open‑access CID outbreak report, and less authoritative secondary summaries (for example general Wikipedia pages) have been removed; flagged for review mainly so that any future updates to case counts or follow‑up outcomes can be incorporated if the primary cohort is re‑analysed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pichia kudriavzeveii
EPP.common.name: Candida krusei
Host: Humans – predominantly adults with hematologic malignancies and other cancers receiving intensive chemotherapy and fluconazole prophylaxis
Event.summary: At the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, USA, clinicians noted that Candida krusei, previously an uncommon cause of fungemia, began to account for an increasing proportion of bloodstream infections in cancer patients between 1989 and 1996. Over this 7‑year period, 60 cases of C. krusei fungemia were identified, with the proportion of fungemias due to C. krusei rising from about 5% in 1989–1992 to 10% in 1993–1996, and infections were strongly associated with leukemia, bone‑marrow transplantation, profound neutropenia, central venous catheters and widespread prophylactic use of fluconazole. The escalation was recognized as a serious therapeutic problem because of high mortality (~49% infection‑related) and intrinsic fluconazole resistance, leading to greater use of amphotericin B–based regimens and heightened awareness of drug‑resistant candidemia in high‑risk oncology settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of intensive chemotherapy and hematopoietic stem‑cell transplantation programs created a large population of profoundly immunocompromised patients with central venous catheters and prolonged hospitalizations; widespread use of fluconazole prophylaxis and therapy exerted strong selective pressure favoring intrinsically fluconazole‑resistant Candida species; intensive antibiotic exposure and invasive procedures further disrupted host microbiota and barriers, increasing susceptibility to fungemia. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance/selection – intrinsic fluconazole resistance of C. krusei and selection of this species under azole prophylaxis and therapy; enhanced transmission – likely healthcare‑associated spread within a high‑risk oncology population (temporal clustering and shared risk factors), although clonality was not formally assessed in this series.
Review: review – retain this event but correct the emergence‑type classification. This episode represents a marked re‑occurrence of C. krusei fungemia within an already affected subregion, driven mainly by external factors (introduction of fluconazole prophylaxis, expansion of intensive chemotherapy and transplant programs) rather than by a new strain or resistance mechanism. Accordingly, re_occurrence has been set to true and re_emergence to false; year range, geography, host description and case numbers match the MD Anderson series, and the cited sources remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pichia kudriavzeveii
EPP.common.name: Candida krusei
Host: Humans – adults with hematologic malignancies and profound neutropenia in a hematology service receiving intensive chemotherapy and fluconazole‑containing antifungal prophylaxis
Event.summary: At Erasmus MC University Medical Center in Rotterdam, Netherlands, a sudden rise in Candida krusei colonization and infection was observed among neutropenic hematology patients in the early 2000s, triggering a longitudinal outbreak investigation. During the study period, 39 patients were diagnosed with C. krusei carriage and/or candidemia, 13 developed bloodstream infection and three died, and genotyping showed that 25 patients shared a predominant outbreak genotype, indicating substantial nosocomial transmission under conditions of intensive fluconazole use. After antifungal prophylaxis was modified and stricter infection‑prevention measures were introduced, the incidence of new C. krusei colonization and candidemia dropped rapidly and the outbreak was brought under control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Concentration of highly immunocompromised hematology patients with central venous catheters, mucosal damage from intensive chemotherapy and prolonged hospitalization; routine fluconazole‑based prophylaxis that suppressed susceptible yeasts and permitted intrinsically fluconazole‑resistant C. krusei to thrive; opportunities for cross‑transmission within shared inpatient wards. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance/selection – intrinsic fluconazole resistance of C. krusei enabled it to escape azole prophylaxis and predominate once selected; enhanced transmission – clonal spread of a dominant genotype (genotype 1) among 25 of 39 patients demonstrated efficient healthcare‑associated transmission, although no novel resistance mechanism beyond baseline azole nonsusceptibility was identified.
Review: review – added as a new row to capture one of the largest documented C. krusei hospital outbreaks in Europe (39 colonized or infected hematology patients, 13 candidemias, three deaths). The time window is represented here as 2002–2003 to reflect the early‑2000s outbreak described by Vos et al. 2006, but exact start and end dates should be verified from the full text; therefore this row is flagged for review. Classified as re‑occurrence (a sharp increase within a previously affected Western European subregion driven by fluconazole prophylaxis and nosocomial spread) rather than re‑emergence, because no clearly novel strain or resistance mechanism is shown to underlie the outbreak.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pichia kudriavzeveii
EPP.common.name: Candida krusei
Host: Humans – adults with acute leukemia, other hematologic malignancies and selected solid tumors admitted to a hematology unit, many with severe mucosal injury, neutropenia and intensive cytotoxic therapy
Event.summary: In February 2005, clinicians at the hematology unit of Oulu University Hospital in Finland recognized an unusual cluster of Candida krusei infections, with six patients developing bloodstream infection and a further six showing significant C. krusei growth from deep sites, in addition to several more patients with heavy mucosal colonization. Weekly surveillance cultures of all hematology patients between April and November 2005 identified widespread gastrointestinal colonization by C. krusei (up to 25% of patients in some months), but molecular typing showed mostly patient‑specific genotypes rather than a single dominant clone, suggesting repeated endogenous infections rather than a point‑source outbreak. After intensified hand hygiene, patient cohorting and discontinuation of routine fluconazole prophylaxis, invasive C. krusei infections ceased and no new colonization clusters were detected in subsequent surveillance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑intensity chemotherapy and resulting mucosal injury in acute leukemia and other hematologic patients created portals of entry for gut colonizers; substantial prior antibacterial and some fluconazole exposure altered the mycobiota and likely favored intrinsically azole‑nonsusceptible C. krusei; close contact within a busy hematology ward provided opportunities for intermittent cross‑transmission. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance/selection – intrinsic resistance of C. krusei to fluconazole enabled it to persist under azole use, although this study did not demonstrate a new resistance mechanism; enhanced colonization of damaged gut mucosa and a tendency for endogenous invasion from the gastrointestinal tract rather than a single highly transmissible clone were emphasized.
Review: review – newly added event representing a well‑described 2005 cluster in a Finnish hematology unit (22 patients with C. krusei colonization or invasive infection, including 6 bloodstream infections), which is among the larger published C. krusei clusters in Northern Europe. Year and geographic classification follow Hautala et al. 2007; the event is classified as re‑occurrence because it reflects a surge within an already affected subregion driven mainly by host factors, chemotherapy‑associated mucosal damage and care practices, with no evidence for a fundamentally new strain or resistance phenotype. Sources focus on the original outbreak description; detailed case counts and relative contribution of colonization versus invasive disease should be checked in any downstream quantitative use, hence flagged for review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pichia kudriavzeveii
EPP.common.name: Candida krusei
Host: Humans – predominantly neonates and children (paediatric emergency and paediatric wards) with serious underlying illnesses
Event.summary: At the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER) in Chandigarh, North India, clinicians detected a sudden and sustained surge of Candida krusei candidemia beginning in early 2014, during which 316 candidemia cases were recorded over one year and C. krusei emerged as the single most common species (96 of 316 cases, 30%), especially among paediatric patients. Within this one‑year period, 82 paediatric C. krusei bloodstream infections occurred, with most isolations from the neonatal unit of the paediatric emergency department, and environmental and hand‑wash cultures identified C. krusei on a healthcare worker’s hands and in a washbasin; molecular typing (FAFLP) demonstrated clonality between blood and environmental isolates, confirming extensive cross‑transmission. After recognition of the outbreak, infection‑control measures (enhanced hand hygiene, environmental decontamination, and process changes for device care and antibiotic use) were intensified, which reduced C. krusei candidemia in subsequent years, although sporadic new strains continued to appear, indicating ongoing risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Marked overcrowding in the paediatric facility with high admissions and baby‑to‑bed ratios, frequent use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics – particularly carbapenems – and invasive devices created strong selection pressure and opportunities for bloodstream infection; lapses in hand hygiene and environmental cleaning allowed contamination of sinks and healthcare‑workers’ hands, enabling sustained nosocomial spread; heavy reliance on intensive care for critically ill neonates and children further increased exposure to central lines and parenteral nutrition. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance/selection – intrinsic fluconazole resistance of C. krusei, combined with extensive antecedent antibiotic use, favored this species over more susceptible Candida spp.; enhanced transmission – clonal expansion of a single strain across patients and environmental reservoirs, demonstrated by FAFLP, reflects adaptation to the hospital environment and efficient healthcare‑associated transmission rather than a fundamentally new genotype with altered virulence.
Review: retain – this row accurately captures the very large 2014 paediatric C. krusei candidemia outbreak at PGIMER Chandigarh (96 C. krusei episodes, 82 in children) and is clearly among the highest‑impact events for this species worldwide. Geographic assignment (Asia/Southern Asia, India) and the 2014 time frame match the primary report; classifying the episode as re‑occurrence (a dramatic increase in incidence in a known subregion driven by overcrowding, antibiotic exposure and infection‑control failures) is consistent with the definitions, since no novel strain or resistance mechanism beyond intrinsic fluconazole resistance is implicated. No structural changes were needed; the event is recommended for retention as is.

EPP.scientific.name: Pichia kudriavzeveii
EPP.common.name: Candida krusei
Host: Humans – neonates and young infants in a tertiary‑care neonatal unit (Gauteng Province) with very low birthweight, prematurity, necrotizing enterocolitis and other serious comorbidities
Event.summary: In 2014, a large tertiary neonatal unit in Gauteng Province, South Africa, experienced an explosive outbreak of Candida krusei candidemia, with 48 bloodstream infections occurring over just 4 months among highly vulnerable neonates, representing complete replacement of other Candida species during the peak months. Despite outbreak recognition and infection‑prevention interventions, the unit then experienced a second large C. krusei candidemia outbreak during April–July 2015 with 41 additional cases, in the context of recurrent fungal and bacterial bloodstream‑infection outbreaks linked to overcrowding and infrastructural constraints. The C. krusei outbreaks were eventually curtailed only after strengthened infection‑prevention and control, environmental remediation, and system‑level changes were implemented, although subsequent smaller fungal and bacterial clusters continued to occur through 2016.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Severe overcrowding (patient census above unit capacity), intermittent water supply, and structural limitations that prevented proper isolation of infected infants created conditions for sustained transmission; high baby‑to‑staff ratios and lapses in infection‑prevention and control practices (hand hygiene, handling of central lines, blood transfusions and total parenteral nutrition) promoted spread; the unit cared for extremely preterm and very low‑birthweight infants with fragile skin and mucosal barriers and frequent need for TPN and invasive devices, all recognized risk factors for candidemia. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission – epidemiologic patterns and repeated isolation of C. krusei from multiple infants over short intervals are consistent with nosocomial spread via healthcare workers’ hands and contaminated fomites, even though a specific environmental source was not identified; antimicrobial resistance/selection – intrinsic fluconazole resistance of C. krusei likely conferred a survival advantage in a setting where fluconazole had been commonly used for empiric or prophylactic therapy, favoring persistence once the species was established.
Review: retain – the description, geography and timing of this event match the Emerging Infectious Diseases report of two linked C. krusei candidemia outbreaks in a Gauteng neonatal unit (48 cases in July–October 2014 and 41 cases in April–July 2015). Aggregating these closely spaced waves into a single 2014–2015 linked episode is consistent with the project’s definition of temporally and epidemiologically connected events, and classifying it as re‑occurrence within Southern Africa (rather than inter‑continental emergence) aligns with the fact that C. krusei was already known from the region. No corrections were required beyond adding this review note; the event should be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pichia kudriavzeveii
EPP.common.name: Candida krusei
Host: Humans – preterm and low‑birthweight neonates in a 24‑bed neonatal intensive care unit requiring intensive care, central venous access and broad‑spectrum antibiotics
Event.summary: In a neonatal intensive care unit in Delhi, India, investigators using whole‑genome sequencing documented a protracted series of Pichia kudriavzevii (Candida krusei) bloodstream infections in hospital‑born neonates between 2015 and 2020, comprising at least two outbreak clusters separated in time. Across this five‑year period, 24 neonates were affected in two main clusters (one in 2015–2016 and another in 2020), and genomic analyses showed that infections were caused by multiple but closely related strain clusters that persisted and reappeared within the unit, with some isolates exhibiting higher fluconazole and itraconazole MICs and characteristic loss‑of‑heterozygosity events. Following recognition of these outbreaks and the implementation of strengthened infection‑prevention practices and antifungal stewardship in the NICU, transmission was reduced, though the study highlighted the potential for continued adaptation and persistence of P. kudriavzevii in this high‑risk setting.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High occupancy and prolonged hospitalization of critically ill neonates in a resource‑constrained NICU, extensive use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics and central venous catheters, and intermittent use of azole antifungals created strong ecological niches for intrinsically azole‑nonsusceptible P. kudriavzevii; repeated admissions and overlapping stays facilitated within‑unit transmission. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance/selection and genomic adaptation – whole‑genome and transcriptomic analyses identified distinct strain clusters with differing fluconazole and itraconazole MICs and frequent loss‑of‑heterozygosity events, indicating rapid evolution and selection of better‑adapted hospital lineages; enhanced transmission – recurrence of closely related genotypes across separate outbreak years suggests persistent colonization of the unit and repeated healthcare‑associated spread rather than de novo introduction each time.
Review: review – added as a new row to represent genomically documented P. kudriavzevii outbreaks in a Delhi NICU, involving roughly 24 neonates across two main clusters during 2015–2020, which places this episode among the more impactful neonatal C. krusei events worldwide. The time span and approximate case burden are drawn from Jain et al. 2025 and a recent neonatal invasive candidiasis review; finer subdivision into separate 2015–2016 and 2020 rows could be considered in future iterations. Classified as re‑occurrence within Southern Asia because the species was already established in India and the surge is driven by NICU ecology and adaptation of existing strains rather than first introduction to the region; users should verify exact case counts and any local mortality data before quantitative use, so this row is flagged for review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Talaromyces marneffei
EPP.common.name: talaromycosis
Host: Humans – mainly adults with advanced HIV/AIDS; later smaller numbers of non-HIV immunocompromised patients
Event.summary: From 1990 onwards, northern Thailand (especially Chiang Mai) experienced a sharp rise in disseminated Talaromyces marneffei infections as the HIV epidemic expanded, with talaromycosis becoming one of the leading AIDS-defining opportunistic infections in the country. Over 6,700 cases were diagnosed nationally between 1984 and 2004, with at least 1,843 cases seen at Chiang Mai University Hospital alone, and incidence peaked before widespread access to antiretroviral therapy. As antiretroviral therapy coverage improved in the early 2000s, incidence and mortality from talaromycosis began to decline, although the infection remained a major cause of morbidity and death among people with late-presenting HIV.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Thailand created a large population of severely immunosuppressed adults, particularly in northern provinces, with high exposure to environmental niches harboring T. marneffei; limited early access to antiretroviral therapy and delayed HIV diagnosis amplified risk. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of a novel fungal strain; emergence reflects opportunistic infection in an existing human host species (people with advanced HIV) rather than genetic change of the fungus itself.
Review: review – Retain this as a major high-impact event (nationally >6,000 Thai cases 1984–2004) but reclassify it from re_emergence to re_occurrence, because the post-1990 surge is best explained by external drivers (the HIV epidemic and delayed ART access) without evidence for fungal genetic change; continent, sub-region, country, years, host, and sources are consistent with major epidemiologic reviews and national surveillance.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Talaromyces marneffei
EPP.common.name: talaromycosis
Countries: Viet Nam (Ho Chi Minh City and southern provinces) [1996]
Host: Humans – adults with advanced HIV/AIDS
Event.summary: Between 1996 and 1997, the first four AIDS patients with disseminated talaromycosis were reported from Ho Chi Minh City, marking the first recognition of the disease in Vietnam. In the following years, as HIV incidence rose and diagnostic capacity improved, hundreds of additional talaromycosis cases were managed at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases in Ho Chi Minh City between 1996 and 2009, and the infection became a common cause of hospitalization and death among people with advanced HIV. With the rollout of Vietnam’s National Strategy on HIV/AIDS prevention and expanded antiretroviral therapy from the mid-2000s, talaromycosis incidence began to stabilize but remained a major opportunistic mycosis in southern Vietnam.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growing HIV epidemic in southern Vietnam, delayed HIV diagnosis, and limited early access to antiretroviral therapy, combined with ecological suitability similar to neighboring endemic countries; strengthening of referral hospital laboratories enabled recognition and reporting. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of major genetic change in the fungus; emergence is due to opportunistic infection in a susceptible host population within an already endemic subregion and improved detection.
Review: review – Retain this as a separate high-impact event because large cohorts from Ho Chi Minh City document hundreds of AIDS-associated talaromycosis admissions and high mortality, but correct the emergence typing: this is a re-occurrence within the already endemic South-eastern Asia sub-region, not a first_detection or intra-continental emergence, and there is no evidence for pathogen-level re-emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Talaromyces marneffei
EPP.common.name: talaromycosis
Host: Humans – predominantly HIV-negative adults with hematologic malignancies, autoimmune disease, or other immunosuppressive conditions; some HIV-positive patients
Event.summary: From 2003 to 2014, hospitals in Guangxi, a highly endemic southern Chinese province, documented a growing number of disseminated T. marneffei infections in HIV-negative patients with underlying hematologic malignancies, autoimmune diseases, organ transplantation or other immunosuppressive states, alongside the ongoing burden in people with HIV. Retrospective analyses from the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University showed that these HIV-negative infections could be severe and frequently fatal, challenging the previous view of talaromycosis as almost exclusively HIV-associated. By the mid-2010s, talaromycosis in HIV-negative immunocompromised hosts was recognized as a distinct and expanding clinical problem in southern China, prompting calls for broader diagnostic vigilance and prophylactic strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased use of immunosuppressive therapies for cancer, autoimmune disease and transplantation in Guangxi, coupled with better mycological diagnostics and awareness among clinicians. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of recognized disease into HIV-negative but immunocompromised human hosts; available data do not demonstrate a new fungal genotype or resistance phenotype, so this is treated as re-occurrence driven by changes in host populations and medical practices rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – This event usefully highlights the emergence of severe talaromycosis in HIV-negative but immunocompromised adults in Guangxi; classification has been adjusted from re_emergence to re_occurrence because the shift is best attributed to increased iatrogenic immunosuppression and improved diagnostics rather than documented fungal adaptation, while geographic fields and timing remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Microsporidia
EPP.common.name: microsporidiosis
Host: Primarily HIV-seronegative infants and young children (≈3–26 months old) with and without diarrhea attending primary care clinics in Niamey; surveys also included a small series of immunocompromised adults with chronic diarrhea.
