Event.summary: From 1992 to 1993, investigators in Niamey, Niger conducted stool surveys for microsporidia among nearly 1,000 young, HIV-seronegative children at two primary care centers and in a smaller series of hospital patients. Using chromotrope-based staining and electron microscopy they detected Enterocytozoon bieneusi spores in about 0.8% of children and in roughly 7% of 60 mainly diarrheic, immunocompromised adults, showing that intestinal microsporidiosis was already established in both pediatric and adult populations in West Africa. The work ended as cross-sectional investigations rather than a defined outbreak, but provided some of the first well-documented evidence of endemic human microsporidiosis in West Africa and stimulated further surveys in African HIV and pediatric cohorts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Poor sanitation, limited access to safe drinking water, and high fecal–oral exposure in peri‑urban Niamey likely facilitated transmission of environmentally resistant microsporidian spores; limited diagnostic capacity meant infections in children and adults had previously gone unrecognized. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was identified; the episode mainly reflects improved detection of existing Enterocytozoon bieneusi infections in a new African subregion and in largely immunocompetent young children, rather than documented pathogen evolution.
Review: review – Original row mis-characterized this event as involving HIV-positive adults only, mis-located it as an inter-continental emergence, and labeled it as a global “first detection.” Updated the timing to 1992–1993 with country tag Niger [1992], corrected the host to primarily HIV-seronegative young children (with a smaller adult series), rewrote the event summary and drivers to match the published Niamey surveys, changed the emergence classification to intra-continental emergence within Africa (first well-documented detection in West Africa) with first_detection and inter_continental_emergence set to false, and replaced hard-to-access or generic sources with focused reviews that explicitly summarize the Niamey data. Because these reconstructions rely on secondary summaries of the original AIDS 1993 abstract and related work, they should be cross-checked against the primary articles by Bretagne et al. and colleagues.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Microsporidia
EPP.common.name: microsporidiosis
Host: Adults with HIV infection and chronic unexplained diarrhea attending HIV clinics in Rio de Janeiro.
Event.summary: Beginning in 1992, clinicians in Rio de Janeiro identified intestinal microsporidiosis in HIV-positive adults with chronic unexplained diarrhea and then undertook cohort and cross-sectional studies through the mid‑1990s. These investigations showed that microsporidia, predominantly Enterocytozoon bieneusi, were present in a substantial fraction of Brazilian AIDS patients with diarrhea and helped establish microsporidiosis as an endemic opportunistic infection in South American HIV care settings. The episode reflects a shift from isolated case reports to routine recognition of microsporidia as a significant cause of morbidity in Brazilian AIDS clinics rather than a contained outbreak with a clear end point.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of the HIV epidemic in Brazil increased the population of severely immunosuppressed persons, while urban crowding and deficiencies in water and sanitation likely supported fecal–oral transmission of microsporidian spores. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype or virulence change was implicated; the emergence reflects geographic range expansion and clinical recognition of existing microsporidia in a new continent and high‑risk host population.
Review: review – Event is well-supported by Brazilian cohort and prevalence studies and appropriately captures the first well-documented human microsporidiosis series from South America. However, the original row incorrectly flagged this as “first_detection” in humans; global first detection occurred decades earlier in Japan and Europe/North America. Kept the classification as inter-continental emergence for South America but set first_detection to false and removed inline citation markup from the summary; geography (continent, subregion, country) remains correct.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Microsporidia
EPP.common.name: microsporidiosis
Host: Humans with advanced HIV infection and chronic diarrheal disease (outpatients and inpatients at major US HIV centers).
Event.summary: Between 1993 and 1997, multiple US HIV treatment centers reported increasing numbers of patients with enteric microsporidiosis, including a multicenter chart review that identified 73 HIV-infected patients with gastrointestinal disease and confirmed intestinal microsporidia. During this period, intestinal microsporidiosis became established as a relatively common AIDS-associated opportunistic infection in North America, typically causing severe chronic diarrhea and wasting in patients with very low CD4 cell counts. Incidence declined sharply in the late 1990s and early 2000s as combination antiretroviral therapy became widely available, restoring immune function and reducing susceptibility to chronic microsporidial infection.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The HIV/AIDS epidemic created a large immunocompromised population highly susceptible to opportunistic infections, and improved diagnostic tools (light microscopy, special stains, small-bowel biopsies) in the early 1990s increased detection of microsporidia that previously went unnoticed. Internal mechanisms: No specific new strain was implicated; the episode primarily reflects host population-level immunosuppression and better recognition of an existing pathogen rather than documented microbial evolution.
Review: retain – This row accurately summarizes the large pre-HAART burden of intestinal microsporidiosis among US HIV patients, uses appropriate US-focused clinical sources, and correctly classifies the event as a re-occurrence (marked increase in incidence in a previously affected subregion driven by the HIV epidemic and improved diagnostics) without mislabeling it as first detection or inter-/intra-continental spread. No geographic or major classification corrections required.

EPP.scientific.name: Microsporidia
EPP.common.name: microsporidiosis
Host: Humans with and without HIV infection, including pregnant women, exposed to contaminated segments of the municipal drinking-water distribution system in Lyon.
Event.summary: In the summer of 1995, a large outbreak of intestinal microsporidiosis occurred in Lyon, France, with roughly 200 symptomatic cases among residents served by specific branches of the municipal water distribution network, including both HIV-infected and immunocompetent individuals such as pregnant women. Epidemiologic investigation linked illness to consumption of tap water from one of three water distribution subsystems, and Enterocytozoon bieneusi was identified as the etiologic agent in affected patients, making this the largest documented water-associated human microsporidiosis outbreak. The outbreak subsided after changes to water treatment and distribution and after the implicated water source was bypassed, and no sustained transmission outside the affected distribution area was documented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Contamination of a municipal drinking-water distribution system, likely from human or animal fecal sources, combined with the environmental resistance of microsporidian spores and limitations in standard water treatment and disinfection, permitted widespread exposure; use of inadequately treated surface or groundwater was implicated. Internal mechanisms: Efficient fecal–oral transmission of E. bieneusi via environmentally resilient spores facilitated waterborne spread, but no specific novel genotype or change in intrinsic virulence was demonstrated in association with this outbreak.
Review: review – The Lyon outbreak is correctly identified as the largest documented human microsporidiosis outbreak and the geographic information is accurate, but the original row misclassified it as “re-emergence.” Given that no new strain, host jump, or clear pathogen-level change was implicated, the episode fits the definition of re-occurrence (major increase in incidence in a previously affected subregion driven by environmental and infrastructure factors) rather than re-emergence. Updated the emergence-type flags accordingly and removed inline citation markup from the summary; underlying sources remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Microsporidia
EPP.common.name: microsporidiosis
Host: Renal (kidney) transplant recipients, with additional cases among other solid organ transplant recipients, predominantly infected with Enterocytozoon bieneusi.
Event.summary: From 2005 to 2019, the French TRANS-SPORE registry and associated surveillance networks documented a growing number of microsporidiosis cases among kidney transplant recipients, ultimately reporting 68 renal transplant patients with intestinal E. bieneusi infection across multiple centers. Over this 15‑year period, microsporidiosis emerged as an important cause of chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and acute kidney injury in this population, prompting routine inclusion of microsporidia in the differential diagnosis of post-transplant diarrhea. As awareness, diagnostic capacity, and treatment with fumagillin plus adjustment of immunosuppression improved, clinicians were better able to recognize and manage infections, and incidence appeared to stabilize despite the expanding transplant population.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of solid organ transplantation and chronic immunosuppressive therapy created a growing population at risk for opportunistic intestinal infections; increased clinical awareness and access to molecular diagnostics improved case detection; ongoing exposure to contaminated water, food, or animal reservoirs likely provided sources of infection. Internal mechanisms: No clearly novel strain was linked specifically to transplant recipients; the episode primarily reflects recognition of an existing human-adapted E. bieneusi pool in a new high-risk host group rather than a demonstrated pathogen-level change, although certain genotypes (e.g., genotype C and related group 1 genotypes) are particularly successful in immunosuppressed hosts.
Review: review – The French transplant episode is a major emergence event in a new high-risk human group and is well supported by the TRANS-SPORE registry paper and related reviews. However, the original row labeled it as re-emergence, even though available data point to expansion of a pre-existing human pathogen into a medically created at-risk group without clear evidence of new strain properties. Reclassified it as re-occurrence in a previously affected European subregion driven by changes in host population and clinical practice (transplantation and immunosuppression) and cleaned up the summary text; geography and sources are otherwise appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Microsporidia
EPP.common.name: microsporidiosis
Host: Primarily immunocompetent adults who ate at a hotel restaurant; some individuals had underlying conditions; infections were due to Enterocytozoon bieneusi genotype C.
Event.summary: In October 2009, Swedish authorities investigated an outbreak of gastroenteritis among guests who had eaten at a hotel restaurant, with over 100 persons meeting the clinical case definition and at least 7 of 11 laboratory-investigated patients testing positive for Enterocytozoon bieneusi genotype C. Epidemiologic analysis linked illness to consumption of food served at the hotel, and the cluster was reported as the first documented foodborne outbreak associated with microsporidia in humans. Illness was generally self-limited over days to weeks, and once the implicated meal service ceased and hygiene measures were reinforced, no further transmission was detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A point-source contamination event, most likely involving fresh, ready-to-eat food items or ingredients handled or irrigated with contaminated water, combined with buffet‑style service that exposed many diners at once; the absence of specific food safety standards or monitoring for microsporidia in food allowed the contamination to go undetected. Internal mechanisms: Efficient fecal–oral transmission of E. bieneusi genotype C and its ability to infect immunocompetent hosts under conditions of high-dose exposure contributed to the outbreak, but there was no clear evidence that this genotype had acquired new virulence traits relative to other human-adapted strains.
Review: review – The Swedish hotel outbreak is a well-documented and widely cited first recognized foodborne microsporidiosis outbreak; continent, subregion, and country are correctly coded, and the host description is appropriate. The original row, however, marked this as re-emergence without evidence of pathogen change; given that the event reflects a foodborne point-source outbreak of an already circulating genotype in a previously affected region, it fits the definition of re-occurrence. Updated the emergence-type flags accordingly and removed an apparently invalid PMCID URL from the source list while retaining core outbreak references.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Microsporidia
EPP.common.name: microsporidiosis
Host: Solid organ transplant recipients (kidney and lung transplant recipients) who acquired disseminated Encephalitozoon cuniculi infection from infected donors; several developed severe neurologic disease and at least one death occurred.
Event.summary: In 2012, US public health authorities investigated a cluster of three solid organ transplant recipients who developed febrile illness and organ dysfunction several weeks after receiving organs from a common donor and were eventually found to have disseminated Encephalitozoon cuniculi infection, confirming donor-derived microsporidiosis. A subsequent investigation in 2014 described another cluster of three transplant recipients from a single donor who developed a severe neurologic syndrome due to donor-derived microsporidiosis, with one recipient dying despite intensive care. These linked clusters highlighted transplantation as a previously under-recognized transmission route for microsporidia, led to updated guidance to consider microsporidiosis in unexplained post‑transplant febrile or neurologic syndromes, and spurred increased awareness among transplant programs, effectively limiting further spread through enhanced vigilance and targeted treatment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growth in solid organ transplantation and the use of potent immunosuppressive regimens created highly susceptible hosts, while the absence of routine donor screening for microsporidia and initially low clinical suspicion allowed donor-derived infections to occur and be misattributed to other pathogens. Internal mechanisms: The events demonstrate how existing microsporidia can exploit new iatrogenic transmission pathways (via viable spores in donor organs) rather than documenting emergence of a novel strain; host susceptibility and medical practices, rather than clear pathogen evolution, are the primary drivers.
Review: review – Donor-derived microsporidiosis clusters in US transplant recipients are real, well-documented events and qualify as major emergence episodes because they revealed a new iatrogenic transmission route with severe outcomes. The original row’s geography and narrative are sound, but classifying the episode as re-emergence overstates pathogen-level change; available evidence points instead to re-occurrence in a previously affected region mediated by changes in medical practice and host susceptibility. Adjusted the emergence-type flags accordingly and retained focused transplant and outbreak-investigation sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Microsporidia
EPP.common.name: microsporidiosis
Host: Predominantly immunocompetent adult employees at a single company who consumed catered food; infections were due to Enterocytozoon bieneusi genotype C.
Event.summary: In November 2020, Danish public health authorities investigated a gastrointestinal illness outbreak among employees of a company and ultimately attributed the event to foodborne infection with Enterocytozoon bieneusi after at least 11 individuals tested PCR‑positive. Epidemiologic investigation linked cases to consumption of shared company meals, and detailed follow‑up characterized a median incubation period of around 9 days, prolonged fecal spore shedding in some individuals, and predominantly self‑limited diarrhea and abdominal discomfort in otherwise healthy adults. Once the contaminated food source was removed and workplace hygiene measures were strengthened, no additional transmission was detected, and the outbreak was reported as Denmark’s first recognized foodborne outbreak due to microsporidia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A point-source contamination of catered food, likely through ingredients or food handlers exposed to contaminated water or environments, combined with indoor shared meal settings, enabled clustered exposure among employees; the absence of regulatory controls or routine testing for microsporidia in food meant the contamination was not detected until illness occurred. Internal mechanisms: The human‑adapted E. bieneusi genotype C showed efficient fecal–oral transmission and prolonged shedding in immunocompetent adults, reflecting robust environmental survival and transmission potential rather than clearly novel virulence traits; together with the earlier Swedish outbreak, this event underscored the foodborne potential of existing genotypes.
Review: review – The Danish company outbreak is accurately described, with correct geographic coding and host characterization, and represents an important confirmation of foodborne microsporidiosis in Northern Europe. As with the Swedish outbreak, however, the original row incorrectly treated it as re-emergence; available data indicate a foodborne point-source outbreak of an already common human genotype rather than emergence of a new strain. Reclassified it as re-occurrence in a previously affected region, retained relevant national and peer‑reviewed sources, and removed inline citation markup from the summary.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Scedosporium apiospermum
EPP.common.name: Eumycetoma
Host: Humans, mainly immunocompetent rural adults with Madura foot–type lesions referred to a tertiary center in Rio de Janeiro; a minority had comorbidities or advanced bone involvement
Event.summary: From 1991 to 2014, the Evandro Chagas National Institute of Infectious Diseases (FIOCRUZ) in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, recorded 21 mycetoma patients, including 13 eumycetoma; Scedosporium apiospermum species complex was isolated in three of these, making it the most common identified fungal agent in the series. Cases originated mainly from semi‑arid rural areas of the Southeast and Northeast regions, presenting after years of evolution with tumefaction, draining sinuses and frequent bone involvement, and often requiring prolonged azole therapy plus surgery or even amputation. By the end of the period, increased clinical awareness and access to itraconazole and terbinafine allowed more limb‑sparing management, but morbidity, long treatment duration, and occasional treatment failure remained substantial.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Occupational exposure of agricultural workers walking barefoot in thorny, semi‑arid environments, low awareness of mycetoma among front‑line providers, and long travel distances to referral centers led to late presentations with extensive disease. Poverty and limited access to imaging and microbiology delayed diagnosis and contributed to chronicity. Internal mechanisms: The event does not reflect a new S. apiospermum strain; rather, it highlights the species’ longstanding ability to establish chronic, deep tissue infection with white grains and its intrinsic reduced susceptibility to many antifungals, which together make eumycetoma difficult to cure once established.
Review: Review – retain event, but updated source URLs to use the primary Rio de Janeiro mycetoma series on PMC and clarified that the UN sub-region is simply South America (cases largely originating from Brazil’s Southeast and Northeast macroregions). Classification as re-occurrence (and not first detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because S. apiospermum mycetoma had been documented in Brazil before 1990 and these 1991–2014 cases represent ongoing low-incidence disease in an already affected country. No larger Brazilian S. apiospermum eumycetoma cluster was identified that would displace this event among the top-impact episodes post‑1990.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Scedosporium apiospermum
EPP.common.name: Eumycetoma
Host: Humans, including immunocompetent patients with white‑grain eumycetoma and immunocompromised or chronically ill patients with lung fungus balls, sinusitis, peritonitis, brain abscess and other forms of scedosporiosis
Event.summary: Between approximately 1990 and 2012, Brazilian clinicians reported an accumulated national experience of scedosporiosis due to Scedosporium apiospermum / Pseudallescheria boydii complex, synthesised in a 2013 case report and literature review that identified 24 Brazilian patients overall. Earlier reports had almost exclusively described subcutaneous eumycetoma in immunocompetent hosts, whereas post‑1982 and especially after 1990, additional cases appeared as pulmonary fungus balls in healed tuberculosis cavities, localized invasive infections in cancer and transplant patients, and a fatal central nervous system infection after near-drowning, alongside a new eumycetoma case successfully treated with oral voriconazole. By the end of this period, Brazilian authors recognized scedosporiosis as a diverse clinical entity with high morbidity and mortality in severely immunocompromised patients but potentially curable localized disease when diagnosed promptly and managed with surgery plus modern triazoles.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of transplant programs, chemotherapy, and intensive care in Brazil increased the pool of profoundly immunosuppressed patients at risk for invasive mould infections; chronic lung disease, especially post‑tuberculosis cavities, created niches for intracavitary colonization (fungus balls). Strengthening of mycology laboratories and case-reporting improved recognition of S. apiospermum in specimens previously labeled generically as hyalohyphomycosis or Aspergillus. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects the broad tissue tropism and intrinsic antifungal tolerance of S. apiospermum rather than a new genotype; its long-recognized capacity to cause both eumycetoma in immunocompetent hosts and invasive disease in compromised hosts underpins this re-occurring spectrum of disease. Voriconazole’s superior activity over older agents improved outcomes but does not represent a pathogen-level change.
Review: Review – retain event but corrected the event_year field to "1990-2012" (the original mixed the 1982–2012 literature window with a note about restricting to ≥1990) and set only re_occurrence = true, re_emergence = false, because the Brazilian series documents recurrent and increasingly recognized scedosporiosis by a historically known pathogen in an already affected country, without clear evidence for a novel strain or host jump. Event-level sources were updated to the primary Brazilian scedosporiosis review on SciELO plus the global Clinical Microbiology Reviews article on Scedosporium infections; the earlier semanticscholar PDF links are no longer needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Scedosporium apiospermum
EPP.common.name: Eumycetoma
Host: Humans, mainly adults with chronic lung disease (including cystic fibrosis and post-tuberculosis cavities), hematologic malignancies, solid-organ transplants and other forms of severe immunosuppression; a minority were immunocompetent with localized cutaneous or subcutaneous infection
Event.summary: During 2003–2005, a nationwide, prospective, population-based surveillance study across 49 laboratories in Australia identified 180 episodes of scedosporiosis, of which 108 phenotypically and molecularly corresponded to the Scedosporium apiospermum / Pseudallescheria boydii complex and 72 to Lomentospora (Scedosporium) prolificans. About one-third (62 episodes) met criteria for invasive disease, including lung, disseminated, bone and joint, and CNS infections, with substantial mortality especially among patients with hematologic malignancy and profound neutropenia. This surveillance quantified an overall incidence of scedosporiosis of roughly one case per million population and highlighted S. apiospermum/P. boydii as an important opportunistic mould in Australian patients with chronic lung disease and post-transplant immunosuppression. By the study’s end, Australia was recognized as one of the countries with the highest documented burden of scedosporiosis worldwide.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of organ and stem‑cell transplantation, intensive chemotherapy, and survival of patients with cystic fibrosis and advanced chronic lung disease in Australia markedly increased the number of susceptible hosts, while national mycological surveillance and reference-laboratory support improved detection and species-level identification of Scedosporium isolates. Environmental exposure to nutrient‑rich, polluted soils and waters in urban and peri‑urban settings provided reservoirs for colonization and infection. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects the known propensity of S. apiospermum/P. boydii to colonize abnormal airways and cause invasive disease in immunocompromised hosts, together with intrinsic reduced susceptibility to many antifungals; no specific new genotype or resistance pattern was identified that would justify classifying this as re-emergence driven by pathogen evolution.
Review: Review – added this new event to correct an omission: the 2003–2005 Australian nationwide population-based surveillance for scedosporiosis, which documented 180 episodes (with the majority of isolates belonging to the S. apiospermum/Pseudallescheria boydii complex) and an incidence of about one case per million population. This clearly represents one of the most impactful post‑1990 emergence episodes for this pathogen in terms of case numbers and quantified burden. It is coded as re_occurrence (and not first detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence) because S. apiospermum infections had already been recognized in Australia before 2003 and the increased burden is largely attributable to growth of immunocompromised populations and enhanced surveillance rather than a new strain; detailed parameterization (e.g. exact S. apiospermum-only case counts) should be double-checked against the full article.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Curvularia spp.
EPP.common.name: Eumycetoma
Host: Humans (adult rural farmer with foot eumycetoma)
Event.summary: In 1999, Indian clinicians reported a 27‑year‑old male farmer from Tamil Nadu with a chronic black‑grain eumycetoma of the right foot, in which fungal culture and histopathology identified Curvularia lunata as the etiologic agent—regarded as the first well‑documented Curvularia eumycetoma in Asia. The lesion had evolved slowly over several years with tumefaction and draining sinuses before Curvularia was recognized and oral ketoconazole instituted, with clinical follow‑up described. This publication marked the first confirmed inter‑continental spread in the literature of Curvularia‑associated eumycetoma outside Africa, although it remained a single sporadic case without evidence of further local transmission or clustering.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term barefoot agricultural work in a warm, semi‑arid mycetoma belt region of South India, with repeated minor penetrating trauma by thorns or plant material contaminated with soil fungi, likely allowed inoculation of environmental Curvularia into subcutaneous tissue; limited early access to mycological diagnostics contributed to delayed species‑level identification. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or resistance phenotype was reported; C. lunata was already known as a saprobic dematiaceous fungus capable of forming black grains in mammals, so this event is best interpreted as geographical range recognition (first Asian human case documented) rather than evolution of a new genotype.
Review: Retain – Well‑documented 1999 Indian eumycetoma due to Curvularia lunata (Mycoses case report) representing the first clearly confirmed Asian case; continent, sub‑region, country and year are correct, and classification as inter‑continental emergence (Africa to Asia) is appropriate. No changes made beyond adding this Review note.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Curvularia spp.
EPP.common.name: Eumycetoma
Host: Humans (older male farmer with foot eumycetoma)
Event.summary: In 2007, a 65‑year‑old Indian male farmer presented to a North Indian tertiary center with long‑standing swelling of the right foot, multiple nodules, and draining sinuses exuding black granules; culture of grains yielded Curvularia lunata, confirming black‑grain eumycetoma due to this dematiaceous fungus. The disease had progressed insidiously for six years prior to diagnosis; after Curvularia was identified, oral itraconazole therapy led to gradual improvement. This case represented a re‑occurrence of Curvularia eumycetoma within India following the 1999 Tamil Nadu report, without evidence of local clustering but reinforcing Curvularia’s role as a rare eumycetoma agent in Indian agricultural workers.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Occupational exposure in agriculture with chronic barefoot or minimally shod contact with thorny, fungus‑contaminated soil in a mycetoma‑endemic climate, combined with delayed specialist referral and limited fungal diagnostics, were key external drivers. Internal mechanisms: The isolate behaved like previously described C. lunata eumycetoma strains (black grains, typical conidial morphology, azole‑responsive), with no evidence of new virulence or antifungal resistance; this fits a pattern of sporadic re‑occurrence rather than evolutionary re‑emergence.
Review: Retain – Accurately captures the 2007 Indian C. lunata foot eumycetoma case (IJDVL 2008) as a sporadic re‑occurrence in Southern Asia; geography, timing, and emergence‑type classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Curvularia spp.
EPP.common.name: Eumycetoma
Host: Humans (middle‑aged woman with ankle/foot eumycetoma)
Event.summary: In 2005, Sri Lankan dermatologists reported a 49‑year‑old woman from a farming community in the North Central Province with a 25‑year history of progressive swelling of the left foot, ankle, and lower leg, multiple nodules, and sinuses discharging black grains. Histopathology showed pigmented fungal grains and culture from tissue biopsy yielded Curvularia lunata, and prolonged itraconazole therapy resulted in substantial clinical improvement. The authors noted that C. lunata mycetoma had previously been reported only from Sudan and Senegal and emphasized that this was the first published C. lunata mycetoma from Sri Lanka. This case thus constitutes a country‑level first detection and regional re‑occurrence of Curvularia eumycetoma within Southern Asia, but as a single, longstanding chronic case rather than a new outbreak.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Residence in a rural agricultural setting with long‑term barefoot exposure to contaminated soil and thorny vegetation in Sri Lanka’s dry zone likely facilitated traumatic inoculation of Curvularia; decades of under‑recognition of mycetoma and limited mycology capacity delayed specific etiologic diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: The strain displayed classical C. lunata grain morphology and itraconazole responsiveness, with no evidence of distinctive virulence or resistance traits; the episode is best interpreted as ecological opportunity plus improved diagnostics revealing a rare agent already present in the mycetoma belt.
Review: Review – Year corrected from 2013 to 2005 to reflect the original Sri Lanka Journal of Dermatology case report date; the patient’s lesion long pre‑dated publication, but 2005 is the first documented country‑level detection. Country and sub‑region remain Sri Lanka / Southern Asia, and classification as re‑occurrence (not intra‑continental emergence) is consistent with definitions, since spread is to a new country within the same sub‑region. Flagged for review to confirm the preferred event year convention (year of diagnosis vs. year of later international re‑publication).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria meningitidis
EPP.common.name: meningococcus
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In early 2002, Burkina Faso experienced the first very large meningitis epidemic dominated by serogroup W135 Neisseria meningitidis, after decades in which serogroup A had caused most major epidemics. During that season the country reported nearly 13,000 suspected meningitis cases and about 1,400 deaths, with laboratory confirmation showing that roughly 80% of meningococcal isolates were W135 ST‑11 related to the Hajj‑associated lineage, marking a major shift in serogroup distribution. The epidemic waned with the end of the dry season and the implementation of mass emergency vaccination with trivalent A/C/W135 polysaccharide vaccine in 2002–2003, after which W135 incidence declined substantially, though the lineage continued to circulate at lower levels in the belt.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Usual meningitis‑belt environmental conditions (hot, dry, dusty season, crowded living conditions) and limited prior population immunity to serogroup W, as control strategies and vaccine stockpiles had focused on serogroup A, favored rapid spread once W135 was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Clonal expansion of a hypervirulent W135 ST‑11 lineage, linked to Hajj‑related strains, produced a novel serogroup pattern of large‑scale disease in the region, representing a strain‑specific re-emergence within an already endemic species.
Review: review – Retain as a key high‑impact event (first large W135 epidemic in Africa) but correct the emergence type. Because N. meningitidis was long established throughout West Africa and W135 had been detected previously at low levels, the 2002 Burkina Faso epidemic should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence; it better fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by clonal expansion of a hypervirulent W135 ST‑11 lineage. I therefore set intra_continental_emergence to false and kept re_emergence as true; geography, timing and burden estimates are consistent with the cited literature.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria meningitidis
EPP.common.name: meningococcus
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In 2012, Chile experienced a marked increase in invasive meningococcal disease in which serogroup W Neisseria meningitidis of the ST‑11 clonal complex became the predominant cause for the first time, replacing serogroup B. That year, 133 IMD cases were reported nationally, and among culture‑confirmed cases about 58% were due to serogroup W ST‑11, which was associated with a case‑fatality rate of roughly 30% and severe meningococcaemia presentations. A national vaccination campaign using a quadrivalent MenACWY conjugate vaccine targeting young children and selected high‑risk groups was launched, after which MenW incidence in vaccinated cohorts declined, although W ST‑11 persisted as an important serogroup in Chile and the wider Southern Cone.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Limited pre‑existing population immunity to MenW, absence of routine conjugate vaccination against serogroup W, and urban crowding in Santiago and other cities facilitated rapid spread once the ST‑11 lineage was introduced, likely via regional travel within South America. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and amplification of a hypervirulent MenW ST‑11 ‘South American’ sublineage characterised by high invasiveness and mortality represents a regional clonal re-emergence and serogroup shift within an endemic meningococcal population.
Review: retain – This event accurately summarises the 2012 Chile MenW ST‑11 epidemic, which had a substantial national impact (high incidence relative to baseline, high case‑fatality, and a major vaccine response) and is part of the globally important South American/UK MenW clonal wave. Countries, timing, serogroup and emergence type (re‑emergence of a new clonal lineage in a country with longstanding meningococcal disease) are appropriate, and the sources are specific and relevant. No structural corrections are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Ehrlichia sp.
EPP.common.name: ehrlichiosis
Host: Humans (general population; disproportionately adults with outdoor tick exposure, including some immunocompromised patients)
Event.summary: Beginning with the first recognized human case at Fort Chaffee, Arkansas, in 1986, and accelerating through the 1990s, human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis (HME) caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis emerged as a major cause of acute febrile illness across the south-central, southeastern, and mid-Atlantic United States, with more than 400 cases documented by the mid‑1990s and over 1,200 cases reported by 1997. Surveillance showed geographic expansion from the initial Arkansas focus to at least 30 states as clinician awareness and availability of serologic testing improved, revealing both sporadic cases and small clusters. By the end of the 1990s, E. chaffeensis infection was firmly established as an endemic tick‑borne zoonosis maintained by enzootic cycles in white‑tailed deer and lone star ticks, with ongoing year‑to‑year transmission rather than disappearance from affected foci.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large 20th‑century increases in white‑tailed deer populations and the geographic expansion and rising abundance of the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum) in the eastern and south‑central United States increased human–vector contact; suburbanization and outdoor recreation in tick‑infested habitats further raised exposure, while improved clinician recognition and use of serologic testing contributed to apparent case increases. Internal mechanisms: No single clearly novel strain was implicated; instead, existing E. chaffeensis lineages circulating in wildlife expanded their geographic range and human contact frequency, representing ecologically driven geographic range expansion and enhanced transmission rather than major microbial change.
Review: Decision: review. This episode correctly captures the emergence of human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis in the United States and is clearly one of the globally most impactful events for this EPP. I reclassified it as the single global first-emergence event for Ehrlichia spp. in humans (first_global_emergence = yes) and turned off the re_emergence flag, which is reserved for later genotype/host shifts. The country-specific start year was updated from 1990 to 1986 to reflect the index Arkansas case, while the overall event window remains 1990–1999 to respect the post‑1990 focus of the dataset; these classification choices should be confirmed by the project team.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus chapareense
EPP.common.name: Chapare virus
Host: Humans (rural residents near Chapare River, Cochabamba Department)
Event.summary: In December 2003, a small cluster of acute hemorrhagic fever cases occurred in rural areas near the Chapare River in Chapare Province, Cochabamba Department, Bolivia, including a fatal index case from whom a previously undescribed arenavirus—Chapare virus—was isolated and identified as the cause of Chapare hemorrhagic fever. Investigations documented limited local transmission among residents during late 2003–early 2004 but no wider spread beyond the immediate outbreak area. The episode ended after supportive care and local control measures, with no further confirmed human cases reported in Cochabamba in the subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Zoonotic exposure to infected wild rodents in rural agricultural settings, including poor-quality housing with rodent intrusion and close contact with rodent-infested crop storage, likely facilitated the initial spillover. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) of a previously unrecognized mammarenavirus from its rodent reservoir into humans; possible inherent capacity for severe hemorrhagic disease but no evidence yet of enhanced transmissibility or distinct genotypic variants at this initial emergence stage.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2003–2004 Cochabamba/Chapare cluster with a single fatal, laboratory-confirmed case is well documented as the first identification and detection of Chapare virus in humans, and the location, timing, and case description match PLOS Pathogens, MedGen, CDC and WHO DON 2025 summaries.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2277458/?utm_source=openai)) Continent, sub‑region, country coding and event-type flags (first_global_emergence and first_detection only) are consistent with definitions, and there is no evidence of any larger Chapare events in this period that should displace this row.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus guanaritoense
EPP.common.name: Guanarito virus
Host: Humans (rural agricultural workers and residents in Guanarito municipality and adjacent areas of Portuguesa State); wild rodent reservoirs including the short‑tailed cane mouse Zygodontomys brevicauda and Alston’s cotton rat Sigmodon alstoni in surrounding agricultural fields and peridomestic habitats
Event.summary: The event began when an epidemic of severe hemorrhagic fever was recognized in September 1989 among farmers near Guanarito, Portuguesa State, Venezuela; between May 1990 and March 1991, about 104 suspected cases with 26 deaths were recorded, almost all in small agricultural communities of the west‑central llanos.([wwwn.cdc.gov](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Arbocat/InformationExchange/54%20-%201991%20December%20searchable.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Virologic work in Venezuelan and international reference laboratories identified a novel arenavirus, later named Guanarito virus (Mammarenavirus guanaritoense), as the etiologic agent and linked infections to local rodent reservoirs, establishing Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever as a new zoonotic disease entity restricted to this rural focus.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/12/11-0393_article?utm_source=openai)) After this initial high‑incidence wave subsided in the early 1990s, transmission declined to a lower but persistent endemic level within the same geographic area.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Agricultural expansion and intensification in the llanos of Portuguesa (grain, bean and cane cultivation) increased populations of the rodent reservoir Zygodontomys brevicauda and facilitated their incursion into fields and dwellings, elevating human exposure to infectious excreta; limited rural housing quality and poor rodent control further amplified risk.([researchexperts.utmb.edu](https://researchexperts.utmb.edu/en/publications/venezuelan-hemorrhagic-fever-eight-years-of-observation/)) Internal mechanisms: The emergence reflects zoonotic spillover from chronically infected wild rodents into humans in an area where Guanarito‑like mammarenaviruses appear to have been enzootic; there is no evidence that a dramatically more virulent or transmissible viral genotype appeared at this time, so environmental and social drivers, rather than viral evolution, are considered primary.
Review: review – Retain this event as the first and largest initial outbreak, but correct several details. Time span adjusted from 1990–1992 to 1990–1991 to match the best‑documented high‑incidence period (104 reported cases between May 1990 and March 1991).([wwwn.cdc.gov](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Arbocat/InformationExchange/54%20-%201991%20December%20searchable.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Country start year in brackets changed from [1989] to [1990] to align with the dataset’s 1990 start rule while still describing the 1989 onset in the text. The cotton rat reservoir species was corrected from Sigmodon hispidus (a North American species) to Alston’s cotton rat Sigmodon alstoni, which is the species documented in Venezuela.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/12/11-0393_article)) The emergence‑type coding was revised to mark this episode as first/global emergence only (first_global_emergence = true, first_detection = false) because there is no long prior history of recognized human disease that would justify classifying it primarily as “first detection” of an ancient pathogen. Overall interpretation and geography (rural Portuguesa State, no spread beyond Venezuela) are well supported, but the event is flagged for expert review of exact year bounds and case counts.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus guanaritoense
EPP.common.name: Guanarito virus
Host: Humans in rural farming communities of Portuguesa State and nearby areas of Barinas State; wild rodent reservoirs (primarily Zygodontomys brevicauda, with co‑circulating arenaviruses in Alston’s cotton rat Sigmodon alstoni) in cultivated fields and peridomestic habitats
Event.summary: After the initial 1989–1991 epidemic, incident Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever cases decreased but did not disappear, and surveillance in the mid‑1990s documented a renewed period of higher transmission within the established focus of the west‑central Venezuelan llanos. Clinical and epidemiologic series covering 1989–1997 report a cumulative total of about 220 cases with a cyclic pattern of epidemic peaks every 4–5 years, indicating that a second wave of increased incidence occurred in the mid‑1990s among agricultural workers in Guanarito municipality and adjacent areas of Barinas State, but still without spread outside this rural region.([researchexperts.utmb.edu](https://researchexperts.utmb.edu/en/publications/venezuelan-hemorrhagic-fever-eight-years-of-observation/)) Toward the late 1990s, case numbers again fell back to the low‑level endemic background typical of inter‑epidemic periods in this area.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The resurgence appears consistent with the cyclical ecology of rodent hosts and agricultural practices in the llanos—periods of favorable climate and cropping patterns lead to increased densities of Z. brevicauda and S. alstoni near human settlements, raising the frequency of exposure during planting and harvest seasons; chronic gaps in rodent control and rural health infrastructure likely allow such cycles to translate into episodic human outbreaks.([researchexperts.utmb.edu](https://researchexperts.utmb.edu/en/publications/venezuelan-hemorrhagic-fever-eight-years-of-observation/)) Internal mechanisms: Genetic studies of Guanarito virus isolates from the mid‑1990s show multiple co‑circulating lineages within western Venezuela but do not identify a clearly distinct, more virulent strain emerging during this period, so the episode is best treated as a re‑occurrence driven predominantly by external ecological and social‑economic factors rather than by major viral change.
Review: review – Retain this event as a mid‑1990s re‑occurrence within the same endemic focus, but flag for review because the exact start/end years and relative size of the mid‑1990s epidemic peak are only indirectly inferred from cumulative series (1989–1997) rather than from a clearly demarcated single‑outbreak report.([researchexperts.utmb.edu](https://researchexperts.utmb.edu/en/publications/venezuelan-hemorrhagic-fever-eight-years-of-observation/)) The narrative, geography (Portuguesa/Barinas), and classification as re‑occurrence (no new sub‑region or continent affected, no strong evidence of a novel strain) are consistent with available data. The host description has been slightly adjusted to remove any implication that Sigmodon hispidus is a local reservoir and to emphasize Z. brevicauda and S. alstoni, which are the documented rodents in western Venezuela.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/12/11-0393_article))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus guanaritoense
EPP.common.name: Guanarito virus
Host: Humans (predominantly male agricultural workers) in endemic rural areas of Portuguesa State; local wild rodent reservoirs including Zygodontomys brevicauda and Alston’s cotton rat Sigmodon alstoni in surrounding fields and peridomestic environments
Event.summary: Following several years of relatively low but persistent background transmission in the established endemic focus, a further upturn in Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever activity was reported around 2001–2002 within Portuguesa State, again affecting mainly young male farmers and rural residents. Spanish‑language epidemiologic summaries citing Ministry of Health data indicate roughly 30 clinically recognized cases during 2001–2002, representing a modest but notable increase over baseline, with cases remaining confined to the known endemic municipalities of Portuguesa (and sporadically Barinas) rather than appearing in new regions or countries.([es.wikipedia.org](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiebre_hemorr%C3%A1gica_venezolana?utm_source=openai)) After this episode, incidence again declined and, although sporadic infections continued to occur, no major geographic expansion was described in the published literature up to the mid‑2000s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: As with earlier waves, this re‑occurrence is plausibly linked to fluctuations in rodent reservoir abundance driven by agricultural cycles, climate variability in the llanos, and deteriorating rural socioeconomic conditions that increased exposure to rodents (e.g. food storage, housing quality), compounded by limited access to diagnostics that delayed recognition until clusters became apparent.([botica.xyz](https://www.botica.xyz/102/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: There is no published evidence of a distinct Guanarito virus lineage with altered virulence or transmissibility emerging in this period, so the episode is classified as a re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence; viral genetic diversity in western Venezuela appears longstanding and not clearly tied to specific human outbreak peaks.
Review: review – Retain this event as a smaller early‑2000s re‑occurrence, but keep it flagged for review. The existence of an early‑2000s uptick with approximately 30 cases is supported by Venezuelan sources cited in the Spanish‑language literature,([es.wikipedia.org](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiebre_hemorr%C3%A1gica_venezolana?utm_source=openai)) but Canada’s biosafety sheet summarizes a Guanarito virus outbreak in 2002–2003 without detailing whether it overlaps entirely with or extends beyond the 2001–2002 episode summarized here.([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/laboratory-biosafety-biosecurity/pathogen-safety-data-sheets-risk-assessment/guanarito-mammarenavirus.html)) The temporal bounds (2001–2002) should therefore be regarded as approximate. Host information has been corrected to refer to Sigmodon alstoni (Alston’s cotton rat) rather than S. hispidus, and the classification as a re‑occurrence (no new country or sub‑region affected, no clear viral change) is consistent with available data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus guanaritoense
EPP.common.name: Guanarito virus
Host: Humans in rural communities of Portuguesa and Barinas States (principally agricultural workers and their household contacts); local rodent reservoirs (Zygodontomys brevicauda and Sigmodon alstoni) in fields and peridomestic settings
Event.summary: Around the third quarter of 2011 and extending into early 2012, Venezuelan health and academic authorities reported a renewed epidemic of Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever in the west‑central llanos, described in university council minutes as a “brote” with 86 cases occurring in the endemic zone of Portuguesa and Barinas.([medicinaucv.com](https://medicinaucv.com/documentos/ACTAS/2012/CF07-12.pdf?utm_source=openai)) This outbreak, occurring more than two decades after the initial emergence, followed the previously described pattern of affecting predominantly agricultural populations in the same municipalities, without spread beyond western Venezuela. After 2012, reported incidence again declined, although routine surveillance for febrile ictero‑hemorrhagic syndromes continued to include Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever as a target condition.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The 2011–2012 outbreak fits the cyclic pattern of increased incidence every 4–5 years described for Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever and likely reflects favorable ecological conditions for rodent population growth (rainfall and agricultural cycles), ongoing poverty in rural communities, and limited rodent‑control and housing infrastructure that increase contact with infected excreta; incomplete public health surveillance and reporting may also have allowed local transmission to continue before the outbreak was widely recognized.([researchexperts.utmb.edu](https://researchexperts.utmb.edu/en/publications/venezuelan-hemorrhagic-fever-eight-years-of-observation/)) Internal mechanisms: Available summaries do not indicate emergence of a novel Guanarito virus strain or major changes in host range, so this episode is most consistent with re‑occurrence due to external ecological and social drivers rather than re‑emergence from viral evolution.
Review: review – New event added. Canada’s biosafety data sheet explicitly lists an outbreak of Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever in 2011–2012 with 86 cases,([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/laboratory-biosafety-biosecurity/pathogen-safety-data-sheets-risk-assessment/guanarito-mammarenavirus.html)) and minutes from the Faculty of Medicine at Universidad Central de Venezuela describe a recent FHV outbreak with 86 cases in the llanos of Portuguesa and Barinas, confirming this as a major epidemic wave within the endemic region.([medicinaucv.com](https://medicinaucv.com/documentos/ACTAS/2012/CF07-12.pdf?utm_source=openai)) This episode clearly meets the criterion of being among the largest post‑1990 events by case count and should be included. It is classified as re‑occurrence (no new sub‑region or continent, no evidence of viral change), with countries restricted to Venezuela; imported or potential cases elsewhere are not documented. Exact monthly start and end dates remain uncertain, so the 2011–2012 interval is approximate and merits expert review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus machupoense
EPP.common.name: Machupo virus
Host: Humans in and around the town of Magdalena, Iténez Province, Beni Department (rural agricultural families and contacts)
Event.summary: In July 1994, after almost two decades without confirmed cases, a Bolivian hemorrhagic fever outbreak began in an extended family in the town of Magdalena in Iténez Province, Beni Department, with seven relatives developing severe febrile hemorrhagic illness and six deaths; additional sporadic cases were identified in other residents of the endemic area, bringing the total to roughly one to two dozen probable infections. Bolivian authorities, assisted by international partners, carried out active case finding, rodent trapping, and environmental sanitation campaigns, and no further confirmed human cases were reported after late 1994, although the Machupo virus reservoir persisted in surrounding rural habitats. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00035133.htm))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: agricultural settlement and expansion around Magdalena into savanna and forest‑edge habitats, substandard housing, and grain‑storage practices that encouraged Calomys callosus infestation of dwellings facilitated intense human–rodent contact; gaps in local health infrastructure delayed recognition of the initial family cluster. Internal mechanisms: available virologic investigations show Machupo virus consistent with earlier strains, with no clear evidence of a novel genotype or change in virulence; the episode is best interpreted as a major re‑occurrence in a long‑endemic focus driven by ecological and social factors rather than intrinsic viral evolution. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00035133.htm))
Review: Retain: This is a well‑documented major re‑occurrence in the historic endemic zone of Beni; timing, geography, case severity, and control measures match the CDC MMWR investigation and later reviews. No changes to event classification or geography are needed, and the source set appropriately prioritizes primary outbreak reports. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00035133.htm))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus machupoense
EPP.common.name: Machupo virus
Host: Humans in endemic rural communities of Beni Department
Event.summary: In 1999, surveillance data summarized in clinical overviews indicate a small resurgence of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever in the traditional Machupo‑endemic zone of Beni Department, with approximately eight human cases reported over the year. Cases occurred in rural agricultural communities already known to harbor the Calomys callosus reservoir, without clear evidence of spread into new municipalities, and incidence declined again after targeted rodent‑control and health‑education activities. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/bolivian-hemorrhagic-fever?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: persistent ecological suitability for C. callosus in smallholder farming settlements, seasonal and interannual fluctuations in rodent densities, and limited rodent‑proofing of homes and grain stores likely enabled renewed spillover in a few foci; local socioeconomic conditions kept residents working and storing food in rodent‑infested environments. Internal mechanisms: no published data indicate emergence of a distinct Machupo lineage, increased virulence, or drug resistance, so this episode is best interpreted as endemic re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence driven by viral change. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/bolivian-hemorrhagic-fever?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain: Multiple standard references mention a cluster of ≈8 BHF cases in 1999 in Beni, with no indication of spread beyond the known endemic area; classification as a small re‑occurrence and the geographic coding are appropriate. Because information comes from secondary summaries rather than a formal outbreak report, case counts should be treated as approximate, but the event remains among the more substantial post‑1990 resurgences. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/bolivian-hemorrhagic-fever?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus machupoense
EPP.common.name: Machupo virus
Host: Humans in endemic rural zones of Beni Department
Event.summary: Around the year 2000, national and regional summaries reported approximately 18 additional cases of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever in Beni Department, again confined to long‑affected rural communities where human–rodent contact is intense. These infections appear to have been scattered cases and small clusters rather than one large focal outbreak, but collectively they represented a noticeable uptick in Machupo virus activity compared with the late 1990s; after strengthened surveillance and continued rodent‑control efforts, reported incidence decreased again until the larger 2007–2008 episode. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/bolivian-hemorrhagic-fever?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: continued agricultural encroachment into suitable rodent habitat, fluctuating C. callosus populations, and variable implementation of rodent‑control and housing improvements in remote communities created recurrent opportunities for spillover. Internal mechanisms: available summaries do not report novel Machupo genotypes or altered virulence, so this year’s activity is interpreted as endemic re‑occurrence driven by environmental and behavioral factors. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/bolivian-hemorrhagic-fever?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain: The ≈18 reported cases in 2000 are consistently cited in clinical overviews and represent one of the larger documented post‑1990 resurgences in the endemic Beni focus. Event type (re‑occurrence), continent/sub‑region, and host coding are appropriate; like 1999, magnitude is approximate because it relies on secondary syntheses rather than a dedicated outbreak report. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/bolivian-hemorrhagic-fever?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus machupoense
EPP.common.name: Machupo virus
Host: Humans in rural localities of Huacaraje and Magdalena, Iténez Province, Beni Department
Event.summary: In mid‑2004, Bolivia’s National Health Information System notified two confirmed cases of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever in the endemic Iténez Province of Beni Department, from the localities of Huacaraje and Magdalena, prompting an epidemiologic alert from PAHO. The patients presented with severe febrile hemorrhagic illness compatible with Machupo virus infection in an area long recognized as endemo‑enzootic for the disease; intensified local surveillance, rodent‑control measures, and community education were implemented, and no additional cases were reported in the immediate aftermath, so the episode remained a small but well‑documented focal re‑occurrence. ([paho.org](https://www.paho.org/es/documentos/1-julio-2004-brote-fiebre-hemorragica-boliviana-bolivia))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: ongoing subsistence agriculture and grain storage practices in Iténez, coupled with dense populations of C. callosus around homes and fields, facilitated sporadic spillover to humans; limited early clinical suspicion contributed to delayed recognition but the small number of cases suggests relatively prompt control. Internal mechanisms: no evidence has been presented for emergence of a new Machupo variant or changes in virulence, so this is interpreted as a localized re‑occurrence in the established endemic area. ([paho.org](https://www.paho.org/es/documentos/1-julio-2004-brote-fiebre-hemorragica-boliviana-bolivia))
Review: Review / Add: This 2004 two‑case outbreak in Huacaraje and Magdalena (Iténez, Beni) is clearly documented in a PAHO epidemiologic alert but was missing from the original dataset; it is among the better‑described post‑1990 recurrences and merits inclusion as a re‑occurrence confined to the known endemic zone. Event coding for geography and type is straightforward, but the small size and limited clinical detail justify flagging the row for expert review of its relative importance among the top events. ([paho.org](https://www.paho.org/es/documentos/1-julio-2004-brote-fiebre-hemorragica-boliviana-bolivia))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus machupoense
EPP.common.name: Machupo virus
Host: Humans in endemic municipalities of Iténez Province, Beni Department (e.g., Magdalena and San Ramón)
Event.summary: In 2010, SEDES Beni surveillance tables compiled for the departmental development plan recorded 52 suspected cases of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever in Iténez Province, of which six were laboratory‑confirmed and two were fatal, with most confirmed cases reported from the municipalities of Magdalena and San Ramón in the long‑endemic Machupo focus. The cases clustered within the usual seasonal window for rodent‑borne transmission; local health authorities strengthened rodent‑control, household sanitation, and community‑education activities, and case numbers fell the following year, although transmission did not cease completely. ([es.scribd.com](https://es.scribd.com/document/849614747/Tomo-i-Diagnostico))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: continued presence of dense C. callosus populations around poorly rodent‑proofed dwellings and grain stores in Iténez, together with land‑use practices that bring farmers into rodent‑infested fields and forest edges, underpinned this multi‑case season; limited access to early laboratory confirmation in remote communities may have delayed some diagnoses. Internal mechanisms: there is no indication of a novel Machupo variant or major shift in virulence or host range; the pattern is consistent with ongoing endemic circulation and environmental drivers of re‑occurrence. ([es.scribd.com](https://es.scribd.com/document/849614747/Tomo-i-Diagnostico))
Review: Review / Add: A 2010 cluster with six laboratory‑confirmed cases and two deaths in Iténez Province is documented in SEDES Beni tables reproduced in the departmental development plan and is referenced in national rodent‑borne disease surveillance summaries, yet it was omitted from the original dataset. I have added it as a re‑occurrence confined to the known endemic area; case counts are moderately well supported but still based on programmatic reports, so the row is flagged for expert review of its relative priority among the top events. ([es.scribd.com](https://es.scribd.com/document/849614747/Tomo-i-Diagnostico))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus machupoense
EPP.common.name: Machupo virus
Host: Humans in Beni Department, primarily Iténez Province with at least one confirmed case reported near Trinidad
Event.summary: In 2011, Bolivia’s national rodent‑borne disease program and SEDES Beni reported seven suspected cases of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, three of which were laboratory‑confirmed and one fatal, all occurring in the historic Machupo‑endemic area of Iténez Province, with at least one confirmed case detected near the departmental capital Trinidad. These small clusters indicated persistent low‑level Machupo virus circulation following the 2007–2008 and 2010 outbreaks; enhanced local surveillance and community outreach were implemented, and no evidence of a large outbreak was recorded that year. ([es.scribd.com](https://es.scribd.com/document/849614747/Tomo-i-Diagnostico))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: ongoing coexistence of humans and reservoir rodents in peri‑urban and rural settings around Trinidad and within Iténez, combined with variable rodent‑proofing of dwellings and food‑storage structures, allowed occasional spillover to humans; under‑recognition of mild cases likely contributed to the small but nonzero burden detected. Internal mechanisms: reports emphasize that these cases fit the pattern of established Machupo virus endemicity, without evidence for a new genotype or increased virulence, so the event is best viewed as a modest re‑occurrence rather than a mechanistically distinct re‑emergence. ([es.scribd.com](https://es.scribd.com/document/849614747/Tomo-i-Diagnostico))
Review: Review (retain but corrected): The original row inaccurately described 2011 as a single isolated case near Trinidad based on secondary web sources, whereas SEDES Beni and the national Anuario Epidemiológico document three confirmed BHF cases (one fatal) in the endemic Iténez area. I have updated the event summary and references to reflect these official data, kept the classification as a small re‑occurrence, and recommend expert review of the precise geographic wording and whether this year should be combined analytically with adjacent years (2010–2013) as one multi‑year episode. ([es.scribd.com](https://es.scribd.com/document/849614747/Tomo-i-Diagnostico))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia miyamotoi
EPP.common.name: Borrelia miyamotoi disease
Host: Humans (hospitalized adults with history of Ixodes persulcatus/Ixodes ricinus tick bites in the Yekaterinburg region)
Event.summary: During the 2009 tick season, clinicians at Municipal Clinical Hospital No. 33 in Yekaterinburg, Russia, evaluated 302 patients admitted with suspected Ixodes-borne infections and identified 46 with PCR-confirmed Borrelia miyamotoi disease, representing the first recognized human cases worldwide. Patients had influenza-like illness with high fever, headache, myalgia and, in some, relapsing fever episodes or erythema migrans, in a region already endemic for Lyme borreliosis and tick-borne encephalitis. After patients received antimicrobial therapy and the tick season ended, case numbers declined, and publication of the findings in 2011 established B. miyamotoi as a human tick-borne relapsing-fever pathogen and spurred similar investigations elsewhere in the Northern Hemisphere.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/10/10-1474_article?source=govdelivery&utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intense human exposure to Ixodes persulcatus (and locally I. ricinus) in mixed forest landscapes of the Ural region where multiple tick-borne agents co-circulate, together with deployment of specific PCR and improved serologic assays that allowed clinicians to distinguish B. miyamotoi from Lyme borreliosis and other febrile illnesses. Internal mechanisms: Spillover from rodent and bird reservoirs to humans via ixodid ticks and the relapsing-fever biology of B. miyamotoi, which supports persistent spirochetemia and recurrent fever episodes in the absence of treatment.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/10/10-1474_article?source=govdelivery&utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Review. Adjusted the event to use 2009 as the year and Russian Federation [2009] as the country-specific start year, reflecting that all 46 patients in Platonov et al. were enrolled during the 2009 tick season even though the paper appeared in 2011. The summary was rewritten to clarify timing and avoid implying that illnesses occurred in 2011, while retaining classification as both first_global_emergence and first_detection in humans. Sources now emphasize the original case series and follow-up Russian work; a domain expert should confirm that using the case year (2009) rather than publication year (2011) is appropriate for this dataset.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia miyamotoi
EPP.common.name: Borrelia miyamotoi disease
Host: Humans (patients with history of Ixodes scapularis tick exposure in the northeastern United States, including an immunocompromised index patient with meningoencephalitis)
Event.summary: In 2013, US clinicians reported Borrelia miyamotoi meningoencephalitis in an elderly immunocompromised man from New Jersey with presumed local Ixodes scapularis exposure and described additional febrile patients with serologic or PCR evidence of infection, providing the first recognized human cases in North America. These reports showed that B. miyamotoi had been silently circulating in blacklegged tick populations in the Northeast and Midwest and that a subset of patients with viral-like summer fevers after deer tick bites actually had hard-tick relapsing fever. Recognition of these cases prompted heightened clinical awareness and targeted testing, although early human infections remained sporadic and geographically focal.([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/abs/10.1056/NEJMoa1209039?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Established and expanding populations of Ixodes scapularis associated with high white-tailed deer and rodent densities, reforestation and suburbanization that increase human–tick contact, and more intensive diagnostic work-ups of unexplained summer fevers in Lyme-endemic regions. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of B. miyamotoi within Ixodes complexes in North America and efficient transovarial transmission in ticks that maintain the spirochete in vector populations; in severely immunosuppressed hosts the organism can invade the central nervous system and cause meningoencephalitis.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/20/7/pdfs/v20-n7.pdf))
Review: Decision: Review. Left 2013 as the event year to align with the timing of the first published US case reports but changed 'first_detection' from true to false so that global first detection is reserved for the earlier Russian event. Retained 'inter_continental_emergence = true' because these were the first recognized human infections in North America with in situ transmission by I. scapularis. The summary was streamlined to focus on documented case series rather than speculative burden. A domain expert may wish to confirm whether illness-onset year (around 2011) should be used instead of publication year for this index US event.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia miyamotoi
EPP.common.name: Borrelia miyamotoi disease
Host: Humans (severely immunocompromised patient with probable local Ixodes ricinus exposure in the Netherlands)
Event.summary: In 2013, clinicians in Amsterdam reported a rituximab-treated patient with severe meningoencephalitis in whom Borrelia miyamotoi DNA was detected in cerebrospinal fluid and blood, constituting the first recognized symptomatic human case in the European Union after the Russian series. The illness was linked to presumed local Ixodes ricinus exposure rather than travel to Russia or Asia and was characterized by persistent fever, neurologic deficits, and inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid findings. The patient gradually improved with intravenous antibiotics, and this case prompted wider investigation of B. miyamotoi in ticks and humans throughout Western Europe.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3987849/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Presence of B. miyamotoi in I. ricinus ticks in the Netherlands, as demonstrated by tick-testing studies, and growing use of molecular diagnostics in immunocompromised patients with unexplained central nervous system infections. Internal mechanisms: Neurotropism and persistence of B. miyamotoi in B-cell–depleted hosts, illustrating its capacity to cause severe CNS disease and highlighting the need to consider BMD in the differential diagnosis of meningoencephalitis in endemic Ixodes regions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3987849/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Retain. Classification as an intra-continental emergence event is appropriate because this was the first recognized human BMD case in Western Europe following the earlier Eastern European (Russian) series under the UNSD regional scheme. No changes were made to timing or type flags; the summary was modestly edited to emphasize local acquisition and its catalytic role for European surveillance. The selected sources continue to center on the original Lancet case report and related Dutch work that quantifies exposure in human-biting ticks.

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis
Host: Humans (four adolescent sisters and additional sporadic adult cases)
Event.summary: In February 2003, a rural family in Tejuçuoca, Ceará State, northeastern Brazil, experienced a cluster of severe pneumonic sepsis in four adolescent sisters, from whom Burkholderia pseudomallei was first cultured, marking the first confirmed human melioidosis outbreak in Brazil. The event developed into a small but high‑mortality cluster and prompted investigation of additional sporadic human cases and environmental sources in Ceará over 2003–2004. Subsequent environmental sampling recovered B. pseudomallei from local soil and water, confirming previously unrecognized endemicity in this South American focus rather than continued large‑scale outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: agricultural and rural exposures to contaminated soil and surface water in a semiarid region with seasonal rains, combined with delayed clinical recognition and limited laboratory capacity in a non‑traditional melioidosis setting. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion and long‑standing cryptic environmental establishment of B. pseudomallei in northeastern Brazil revealed by improved surveillance and environmental sampling, rather than a demonstrably novel strain or major virulence shift.
Review: Review – Retain event but correct emergence type and sources. Autochthonous melioidosis had been reported elsewhere in South America (e.g. Ecuador 1962 and other countries) before 2003, so this Ceará cluster represents a major re-occurrence within an already affected sub-region rather than intra-continental emergence. Updated intra_continental_emergence to false and re_occurrence to true, and removed a non‑event‑specific Australian reference from source_urls.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis
Host: Humans (immunosuppressed adult woman)
Event.summary: In January 2004, Mauritius reported its first autochthonous human melioidosis case when a 40‑year‑old woman on immunosuppressive therapy developed septic illness and B. pseudomallei was isolated, in a country where the organism had never previously been identified. The case evolved with severe systemic disease requiring prolonged hospitalization, and retrospective investigation linked her infection to chronic exposure to wet mud during a period of higher‑than‑average rainfall. After targeted public health and clinical awareness efforts, no large outbreak followed, but the case marked recognition of melioidosis as present in the western Indian Ocean region rather than remaining confined to classical Asian and Australian foci.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: higher‑than‑average seasonal rainfall increasing exposure to contaminated mud and surface water, and widespread diabetes and immunosuppressive conditions in the local population.
