Internal mechanisms: likely long‑standing low‑level environmental presence of B. pseudomallei in the western Indian Ocean islands uncovered through improved diagnostic awareness, without evidence for a distinct hypervirulent genotype.
Review: Review – Retain as a key sentinel case in the western Indian Ocean but adjust emergence classification and clean sources. Earlier human melioidosis exposures and cases linked to East Africa existed before 2004, so Eastern Africa was not a new sub-region for human infection; this event is better coded as a re-occurrence in a previously known African sub-region. Set intra_continental_emergence to false and re_occurrence to true, and removed a duplicate PMCID URL, keeping the primary EID case report and the regional review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis
Host: Humans (adult and elderly patients, many with comorbidities)
Event.summary: From July through September 2005, shortly after a major typhoon brought flooding to southern Taiwan, clinicians identified an outbreak of 40 culture‑confirmed human melioidosis cases, far exceeding baseline incidence. The outbreak progressed with many patients presenting with severe pneumonia, sepsis and high rates of bacteremia and septic shock, and molecular typing showed multiple B. pseudomallei genotypes consistent with intense environmental exposure rather than a single clonal source. As floodwaters receded and targeted public health messaging and clinical management improved, case numbers declined back toward endemic levels in subsequent seasons.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extreme rainfall and flooding associated with a typhoon, which likely mobilized B. pseudomallei from soil into surface waters and aerosols, increasing percutaneous and inhalational exposure; high prevalence of diabetes and chronic diseases in the affected population; and increased environmental disturbance in urban and peri‑urban areas. Internal mechanisms: no single novel strain was implicated; instead, enhanced transmission from multiple environmental sources during an extreme‑weather period explains the outbreak.
Review: Review – Event description and classification as a major re-occurrence in an already endemic area are appropriate, but the country field was standardized to the UN-style name used in the country list. Updated countries to “China, Taiwan Province of China [2005]”; otherwise retain the event and source set, which correctly emphasize the typhoon-associated cluster.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis
Host: Humans (mainly Indigenous Aboriginal adults with comorbidities)
Event.summary: In early 2011, after atypically intense rainfall and flooding in normally arid Central Australia linked to a strong La Niña event, six locally acquired human melioidosis cases were identified over four months in residents of the Alice Springs and Tennant Creek region, an area previously considered only marginally affected. The episode unfolded with severe sepsis and pneumonia in several patients, drawing attention because Central Australia had recorded only a handful of cases in the preceding two decades despite long‑running surveillance. As flood conditions resolved and public health alerts were issued, no sustained cluster persisted, but these cases demonstrated that B. pseudomallei is established in interior desert environments of Australia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: La Niña–associated record wet season in 2010–2011 causing unusual flooding in desert landscapes, increasing exposure to contaminated soil and water for local communities, particularly Indigenous populations with high burdens of diabetes and chronic disease. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion or previously under‑recognized endemicity of B. pseudomallei in arid central Australian soils revealed by extreme rainfall events; no clear evidence of a distinct, more virulent strain in this cluster.
Review: Review – Retain but correct event type and standardize the country field. Because melioidosis had long been endemic in the same UN sub-region (Australia and New Zealand) through Top End transmission, this central Australian desert cluster is best treated as a notable re-occurrence driven by extreme rainfall rather than intra-continental emergence. Updated intra_continental_emergence to false, re_occurrence to true, and simplified countries to “Australia [2011]”.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis
Host: Humans (four adults/children, at least two deaths)
Event.summary: Between March and July 2021, four U.S. residents in Kansas, Texas, Minnesota and Georgia developed severe melioidosis with no travel to endemic regions, and genomic analyses showed their B. pseudomallei isolates were nearly identical, indicating a common source. The investigation progressed over several months until CDC detected the outbreak strain in a bottle of Better Homes & Gardens aromatherapy room spray imported from India found in the Georgia patient’s home, leading to a nationwide product recall and recognition of a novel consumer‑product exposure route. Once the contaminated aromatherapy line was withdrawn and households were advised on safe disposal and decontamination, no further linked cases were identified.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: globalization of consumer products, with contamination of an imported aromatherapy spray manufactured in a melioidosis‑endemic country; use of the product in homes leading to inhalational or contact exposure in persons without travel history; and limited initial clinical suspicion in non‑endemic U.S. states. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak was caused by a single B. pseudomallei strain introduced via a manufactured product (novel exposure pathway), but there is no evidence of enhanced virulence or sustained environmental establishment from this source in the affected U.S. states.
Review: Review – Retain this as a major, widely documented outbreak illustrating a novel exposure route. Because transmission resulted from a contaminated imported consumer product with no evidence of onward environmental establishment in the United States, classification as a re-occurrence in a previously affected sub-region (rather than inter- or intra-continental emergence) is appropriate. The countries field was simplified to “United States of America [2021]” to match the country list; otherwise the event description and sources are suitable.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia psittaci
EPP.common.name: psittacosis
Host: Poultry slaughterhouse workers (abattoir employees, truck driver and maintenance mechanic) exposed to infected chickens or turkeys
Event.summary: In 1990, occupational health authorities in western France investigated clusters of influenza‑like illness and atypical pneumonia among employees of a poultry abattoir and identified slaughterhouse exposure to aerosols from chlamydia‑infected chickens and turkeys as the likely source. Serologic testing of the workforce found 18 of 56 employees with evidence of recent Chlamydia psittaci infection, including six workers with pneumonia and four who required hospitalisation, prompting targeted antibiotic treatment and control measures in the plant. The outbreak subsided after medical management, improvements in hygiene and ventilation, and modifications to evisceration practices, with no evidence that sustained transmission occurred beyond the abattoir.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high‑throughput indoor poultry slaughter and evisceration with inadequate engineering controls, aerosol generation during gutting and defeathering, and limited early recognition of psittacosis risk in abattoir workers, resulting in prolonged unprotected exposure. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype or altered virulence was reported; available data are consistent with exposure‑driven re‑occurrence of endemic C. psittaci in a high‑risk occupational setting rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – New high‑impact occupational outbreak added. In 1990 a poultry abattoir in western France experienced psittacosis among 18 of 56 tested workers (six pneumonias, four hospitalisations) based on summaries in a systematic review of human psittacosis outbreaks; this size places it among the more substantial post‑1990 events. Classified as re‑occurrence in an already affected Western European subregion, with France correctly mapped to Western Europe. Because most numerical details are derived from secondary summaries rather than the original Goupil et al. report, a subject‑matter expert should verify final case counts and plant location against the primary paper before finalising the Excel sheet.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia psittaci
EPP.common.name: psittacosis
Host: Humans (visitors, staff and student interns) exposed to psittacine and other birds in an indoor commercial bird park
Event.summary: In late 2001, public health authorities in Matsue City, Shimane Prefecture, Japan, detected several cases of severe atypical pneumonia among staff, student interns and visitors associated with an indoor bird park, and epidemiologic investigation implicated exposure to ill birds housed under closed‑air‑circulation conditions. Seventeen human psittacosis cases (12 visitors, three staff, two students) were confirmed serologically, most with radiographic pneumonia and many requiring hospitalisation, and environmental testing demonstrated C. psittaci DNA in fecal samples from multiple aviary cages. The bird park was temporarily closed, ill birds were isolated or culled and housing conditions were modified, after which no further human cases linked to the park were detected and operations later resumed under strengthened biosecurity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: very high densities of exotic birds kept in enclosed hothouses with recirculating air, use of dehumidifiers and high‑pressure water sprays that aerosolised contaminated fecal material, absence of quarantine or veterinary oversight for imported birds, and lack of respiratory protection for staff and visitors. Internal mechanisms: no novel strain was described; outbreak behaviour was compatible with re‑occurrence of endemic C. psittaci genotypes under unusually conducive environmental and husbandry conditions.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the largest documented psittacosis outbreak in Japan, with 17 confirmed human cases linked to an indoor bird park in Matsue in winter 2001–2002. Country (Japan), continent (Asia), subregion (Eastern Asia), timing and exposure setting all match the primary outbreak report, and classification as a re‑occurrence (not first detection or inter‑continental spread) is appropriate given the long‑standing recognition of psittacosis in Japan. No corrections beyond verification of details were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia psittaci
EPP.common.name: psittacosis
Host: Humans exposed to free‑ranging wild parrots and other birds in peri‑urban residential settings
Event.summary: From March to June 2002, clinicians in the Blue Mountains district of New South Wales, Australia, noted an unusual surge of community‑acquired pneumonia among residents that was eventually linked to exposure to dead and free‑ranging wild birds, particularly parrots, around homes. Among 95 suspected cases, 59 patients had serologic evidence of acute C. psittaci infection and many required hospitalisation, with residence in the upper Blue Mountains, direct contact with wild birds, and lawn mowing without a grass catcher identified as strong risk factors in a case‑control study. The outbreak waned with the onset of colder winter weather, community advisories about avoiding contact with dead birds and using respiratory protection during high‑exposure outdoor activities, and no further large clusters were detected in the area once the event resolved.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high local abundance and mortality of free‑ranging parrots and other wild birds in a forested peri‑urban area, frequent human contact with bird carcasses and droppings, and aerosolisation of contaminated material during lawn mowing and other yard work; limited baseline awareness of psittacosis risk in an endemic region also delayed recognition. Internal mechanisms: there was no evidence of a novel genotype; epidemiologic patterns are consistent with geographic and intensity‑based range expansion of an endemic strain rather than genetic change, supporting classification as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: retain – This row accurately describes the large 2002 Blue Mountains outbreak (59 serologically supported cases) documented in Emerging Infectious Diseases and subsequent Australian work on endemic psittacosis. Continent, subregion and country coding are correct, and classification as re‑occurrence in an area with known psittacosis fits the definitions. No substantive corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia psittaci
EPP.common.name: psittacosis
Host: Humans exposed to wild and domestic birds (particularly at garden bird feeders) in community settings, with some evidence of secondary transmission
Event.summary: From 12 January to 9 April 2013, southern Sweden experienced an unusual increase in psittacosis notifications, with 25 cases detected—about three times the mean winter incidence in the previous decade—drawing renewed attention to psittacosis as a cause of atypical pneumonia. A matched case–control study found that cases were much more likely than controls to have cleaned wild‑bird feeders or otherwise been heavily exposed to wild‑bird droppings, and a separate investigation described a severe index case who appears to have transmitted infection to multiple close contacts, including family members and healthcare workers, indicating both strong environmental and limited human‑to‑human components. The spike in cases declined as the winter–spring season ended and targeted public‑health messaging on safe bird feeding and clinical awareness was implemented, with national incidence returning toward lower endemic levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: seasonal congregation of wild birds at garden feeders, frequent cleaning of heavily contaminated feeders by householders, and close contact with domestic birds in a temperate Northern European setting; increased clinician awareness and diagnostic testing during and after the outbreak likely amplified case detection. Internal mechanisms: while person‑to‑person transmission was documented from at least one severe index case, molecular data did not clearly implicate a novel, more transmissible strain; the event is best interpreted as an exposure‑driven re‑occurrence with rare secondary spread, rather than a re‑emergence of a new lineage.
Review: review – Retained as one of the larger modern psittacosis outbreaks (25 cases in southern Sweden with strong links to wild‑bird feeders and evidence of limited human‑to‑human spread). The original LLM row correctly captured size, timing, exposures, and classification as re‑occurrence, but relied mainly on a later case‑control paper; a dedicated 2013 Eurosurveillance outbreak report has now been added to the event‑level sources to better document case counts and risk factors. No changes to geography or emergence type were needed, yet the row is flagged for review so that final case numbers and the balance between environmental and secondary transmission can be cross‑checked directly against the Swedish outbreak reports when populating the Excel sheet.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia psittaci
EPP.common.name: psittacosis
Host: Humans with psittacosis (many with pneumonia) exposed mainly to wild birds and their droppings around garden bird feeders, with some cases linked to domestic psittacine birds
Event.summary: Between November 2018 and March 2019, Sweden recorded an unusually high number of psittacosis cases, with around 60 notifications—several times higher than typical winter seasons over the preceding 20 years—predominantly from the southern and western regions of the country. Most affected patients reported direct or indirect exposure to droppings of small wild birds, especially through cleaning or handling garden bird tables and feeders, while a minority of cases were linked to domestic parrots and other captive birds, and many required hospital care for atypical pneumonia. Following public‑health communications advising the public to avoid contact with bird faeces and to take precautions when cleaning feeders, combined with the natural end of the winter wild‑bird feeding season, case numbers declined and the outbreak was declared over by the Public Health Agency of Sweden on 13 March 2019.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: widespread winter feeding of small wild birds in gardens, frequent cleaning and handling of heavily contaminated bird tables and feeders, and heightened diagnostic attention once the signal was recognised, all occurring in a setting where C. psittaci circulates in wild birds; subtle ecological changes in wild‑bird populations may also have increased background infection pressure. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel C. psittaci genotype was reported; the pattern is consistent with an exposure‑ and surveillance‑driven re‑occurrence rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: review – New Swedish national winter 2018–2019 outbreak (approximately 60 reported cases, largely linked to wild‑bird feeders) added because it clearly exceeds normal seasonal incidence and is documented by both Folkhälsomyndigheten and ECDC. The country and subregion coding (Sweden, Northern Europe) and classification as a re‑occurrence in a country with longstanding psittacosis activity are appropriate. Exact numbers of laboratory‑confirmed versus suspected cases and the regional breakdown should be verified against Swedish surveillance tables before final Excel entry.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridium botulinum
EPP.common.name: Botulism
Host: Humans (urban residents consuming traditional uneviscerated salted, fermented mullet fish “feseekh/faseikh” purchased in Cairo)
Event.summary: In April 1991, Cairo hospitals reported 91 patients with severe paralytic illness and high mortality after eating traditional salted, uneviscerated mullet fish (feseekh), and investigation identified type E botulism with at least 18 deaths, making this the largest recorded type E outbreak and the first documented botulism outbreak in Egypt. The outbreak was traced to commercially prepared feseekh from a single shop, and national authorities rapidly banned sales from the implicated producer, inspected similar establishments, and warned the public against consuming uneviscerated salted fish around the Sham El‑Nessim holiday. Withdrawals of implicated product, strengthened regulation of salted‑fish production, and recurring seasonal risk‑communication campaigns ended the episode but did not fully eliminate recurrent, smaller fesikh‑associated outbreaks in later years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: mass seasonal consumption of feseekh during a spring holiday; use of uneviscerated fish stored for prolonged periods under warm, anaerobic, and often putrefactive conditions before salting; inadequate process control and oversight of small commercial producers; and limited public awareness of botulism risk. Internal mechanisms: high‑level production of botulinum neurotoxin type E by nonproteolytic C. botulinum in anaerobic, salted fish tissue; no evidence of a novel strain or host jump, so the event represents an extreme contamination and processing failure of an established pathogen.
Review: Decision: retain. This is a well‑documented, massive type E foodborne botulism outbreak in Cairo with 91 hospitalized patients and 18 deaths, described in a J Infect Dis investigation as the first documented outbreak in Egypt and the largest type E outbreak reported globally; it clearly belongs among the top‑impact human botulism events since 1990. Geography (Africa → Northern Africa → Egypt) and classification as re‑occurrence (long‑established pathogen; failures in traditional fish processing) are appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridium botulinum
EPP.common.name: Botulism
Host: Humans (restaurant patrons consuming potato‑ and eggplant‑based dips at a Greek restaurant in El Paso, Texas)
Event.summary: In April 1994, a large restaurant‑associated outbreak of foodborne botulism in El Paso, Texas, affected 30 people after they ate potato‑ and eggplant‑based dips prepared from foil‑wrapped baked potatoes that had been held at room temperature for many hours to days. Epidemiologic investigation and laboratory testing identified botulinum neurotoxin type A in both dips and linked illness strongly to consumption of the potato dip, with four patients requiring mechanical ventilation, making this the largest U.S. botulism outbreak since 1978. Removal of the implicated foods, clinical deployment of antitoxin, and strengthened food‑safety guidance on time–temperature control of foil‑wrapped baked potatoes in commercial kitchens ended the outbreak and informed later U.S. and international prevention messaging.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: improper restaurant food‑handling, specifically leaving foil‑wrapped baked potatoes at ambient temperature for extended periods before incorporating them into cold dips, creating a warm, anaerobic, low‑acid environment ideal for C. botulinum growth and toxin production; gaps in staff training and regulatory enforcement regarding this specific risk. Internal mechanisms: classic proteolytic C. botulinum type A toxin production in a high‑risk food matrix without evidence of new strain characteristics or increased intrinsic virulence.
Review: Decision: retain. The El Paso ‘hazardous baked potato’ outbreak is a well‑characterized event with 30 cases and four ventilated patients, described as the largest U.S. botulism outbreak since 1978; it reasonably qualifies as one of the highest‑impact human botulism episodes globally in the 1990–present period. Geography and classification as re‑occurrence are correct; only minor textual refinements (explicit case count and state) were added.

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridium botulinum
EPP.common.name: Botulism
Host: Humans (schoolchildren in a rural residential school in Gujarat consuming a gram‑flour snack, sevu, stored at ambient temperature)
Event.summary: In September 1996, 34 of roughly 310 pupils in a residential school in rural Gujarat, India, developed acute neuroparalytic symptoms compatible with botulism after eating several common foods, with epidemiologic and microbiological investigation implicating an improperly stored fried gram‑flour snack, sevu, as the likely vehicle. Toxigenic Clostridium butyricum capable of producing type E botulinum neurotoxin was isolated from leftover sevu and patient specimens, making this the first recognized large outbreak of type E botulism in India and a rare example of human foodborne botulism caused by a species other than C. botulinum. Intensified clinical care, withdrawal of suspect snack batches, and national alerts on safe storage of fried snacks brought the episode under control, and the event spurred debate and further research on neurotoxigenic C. butyricum as an emerging cause of botulism.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: mass catering of sevu in a boarding school, with bulk preparation and prolonged storage of a moist, fried gram‑flour product in inadequately ventilated containers at ambient temperatures; limited awareness among school staff of botulism risks from non‑canned foods. Internal mechanisms: emergence of neurotoxigenic C. butyricum producing type E toxin in human foodborne disease in India, representing a strain‑level change within the broader botulism complex rather than altered host or geography for C. botulinum sensu stricto.
Review: Decision: review. This is a large and influential outbreak (34 affected students, several deaths reported in some sources) linked to sevu contaminated with neurotoxigenic Clostridium butyricum type E and is widely cited as the first recognized foodborne botulism outbreak in India. However, the causative organism is C. butyricum rather than C. botulinum sensu stricto, and some official reviews note incomplete clinical confirmation; therefore inclusion under the species‑specific EPP “Clostridium botulinum” should be decided by project leads. Classification has been set to re‑emergence (novel toxigenic species/strain causing human botulism in this region) rather than simple re‑occurrence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridium botulinum
EPP.common.name: Botulism
Host: Humans (villagers in northern Thailand consuming home‑canned bamboo shoots from a 20‑L can)
Event.summary: In April 1998, 13 adults from two neighboring villages in northern Thailand developed severe neurologic illness consistent with botulism, including two deaths, after eating home‑canned bamboo shoots from a single 20‑liter galvanized container sold locally. Epidemiologic investigation and toxin testing of food confirmed foodborne type A botulism from inadequately processed low‑acid bamboo shoots, representing the first laboratory‑confirmed botulism outbreak reported in Thailand and prompting a provincial ban on remaining cans and public education about safe canning and reheating. Although modest in size compared with later Thai events, the outbreak served as an early warning about the risks of home‑canned bamboo shoots and led to strengthened control of home canning before a much larger 2006 outbreak in the same province.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: informal commercial production of low‑acid bamboo shoots in large, home‑made containers, with only boiling at atmospheric pressure before sealing and long‑term storage at ambient temperature; lack of acidification and pressure canning, limited producer awareness of botulism risks, and minimal regulatory oversight of small‑scale canning. Internal mechanisms: typical proteolytic C. botulinum type A spores surviving inadequate heat treatment, then germinating and producing toxin in an anaerobic, low‑acid environment.
Review: Decision: review. The 1998 Nan Province bamboo‑shoot outbreak (13 cases, 2 deaths) is accurately described here and was historically important as Thailand’s first lab‑confirmed botulism outbreak, but it is much smaller than the massive 2006 Nan outbreak (209 cases) and multiple other global events. With the addition of the 2006 Thai event, this 1998 episode is unlikely to remain among the ten most impactful post‑1990 outbreaks and could be excluded if a strict top‑10 size criterion is enforced; it may be retained if the project values country‑level firsts.
Review.Comment: Not top 10

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridium botulinum
EPP.common.name: Botulism
Host: Humans (residents of Casablanca and other areas consuming commercially produced mortadella sausage)
Event.summary: In August 1999, Morocco experienced a major epidemic of foodborne botulism centred in Casablanca, where consumption of a contaminated commercial mortadella‑type sausage led to dozens of cases of flaccid paralysis and multiple deaths. Clinical series describe around 15 confirmed cases among 45 highly suspect patients with toxin type B detected, while food‑safety compilations cite up to 78 cases and approximately 20 deaths linked to mortadella from a single factory, making this one of the most lethal post‑1990 botulism outbreaks. National authorities seized large quantities of suspect sausage, closed the implicated facility, and intensified meat‑processing inspection and consumer warnings, which gradually ended the outbreak and reshaped botulism risk management for cured meat products in Morocco.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: industrial production of low‑acid cured sausage with inadequate heat treatment, salt/nitrite control, or hygiene, allowing survival and outgrowth of C. botulinum spores; wide distribution of a single contaminated product lot; limited early clinical recognition in a setting with little prior botulism experience. Internal mechanisms: classic proteolytic C. botulinum type B toxin production in a moist meat matrix, without evidence of a novel strain, so the event reflects a severe but conventional processing failure.
Review: Decision: retain. The 1999 Moroccan mortadella‑associated outbreak is a large, high‑fatality episode (on the order of several dozen cases and around 20 deaths) documented in clinical series and international food‑safety reviews, and ranks among the most severe modern botulism outbreaks linked to a commercial meat product. Geography and classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate; case numbers in the literature vary, so they are described qualitatively and should be revisited if national surveillance data become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridium botulinum
EPP.common.name: Botulism
Host: Humans (rural villagers attending a religious event and eating home‑canned bamboo shoots in Nan Province)
Event.summary: From 15–26 March 2006, a massive outbreak of foodborne botulism struck Nan Province in northern Thailand, when home‑canned bamboo shoots served at a religious ceremony caused illness in 209 villagers, 134 of whom were hospitalized and 42 required mechanical ventilation. Investigations confirmed botulinum neurotoxin type A from contaminated bamboo shoots produced in unregulated home canneries, and shortages of antitoxin required urgent international mobilization of heptavalent antitoxin stocks. Emergency prohibition of the implicated bamboo‑shoot product, intensified regulation of home‑canned foods, and nationwide education on boiling and safely sourcing bamboo shoots ended the outbreak and led to creation of regional mechanisms for antitoxin sharing and botulism surveillance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: large‑scale informal production and sale of low‑acid bamboo shoots canned without pressure‑cooker sterilization, stored for long periods at ambient temperatures, and served in bulk at community gatherings; lack of enforcement of canning standards and limited awareness of botulism risks in rural areas. Internal mechanisms: high‑level proliferation of proteolytic C. botulinum type A in inadequately processed bamboo shoots; no new strain properties were reported, so the event reflects extreme exposure to a known hazard in a vulnerable food system.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2006 Nan Province bamboo‑shoot outbreak (209 cases, 42 ventilated) is one of the largest laboratory‑confirmed foodborne botulism outbreaks ever documented and had major implications for international antitoxin logistics and food‑safety policy in Thailand; it clearly belongs in any top‑10 list of impactful human botulism events after 1990. Geography and classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate.
