Event.summary: Between 2013 and 2015, the Spanish National Reference Centre for Microbiology received 119 Citrobacter spp. isolates suspected of carbapenemase production; 63 (52.9%) were confirmed carbapenemase producers, mainly Citrobacter freundii, originating from 27 hospitals in 14 provinces. These isolates carried a wide array of carbapenemases (VIM‑1, OXA‑48, KPC‑2, NDM‑1 and VIM‑2), often in combination with ESBLs, and about half caused clinical infections (mainly urinary and wound infections) while the rest were rectal carriage, documenting a nationwide emergence of CP-Citrobacter as part of Spain’s carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales problem.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jac/article/72/12/3283/4259205))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High carbapenem and broad-spectrum cephalosporin use in Spanish tertiary hospitals, extensive inter-hospital referrals, and the existing dissemination of carbapenemase plasmids (notably VIM‑1 and OXA‑48) in Klebsiella pneumoniae and other Enterobacterales, which facilitated spillover into Citrobacter spp. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence through acquisition of diverse carbapenemase genes on mobile genetic elements by multiple Citrobacter species; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of these resistant clones and plasmids across Southern Europe as reflected by their presence in numerous Spanish provinces.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jac/article/72/12/3283/4259205))
Review: retain – This national multi-hospital emergence of carbapenemase-producing Citrobacter spp. in Spain (63 CP-Citrobacter from 27 hospitals in 14 provinces) is clearly one of the largest and most geographically widespread Citrobacter AMR events, and appropriately classified as re‑emergence driven by diverse carbapenemase plasmids. Event period, geography and mechanisms are consistent with the primary JAC paper; sources are appropriate and focused.

EPP.scientific.name: Citrobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Citrobacter infection
Host: Humans (adult inpatients in a tertiary acute-care facility in Miami, Florida)
Event.summary: In 2014, a tertiary acute-care hospital in southern Florida identified an outbreak of Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase‑3 (KPC‑3)–producing Citrobacter freundii with six affected patients, three of whom were infected with a single clone in the same intensive care unit. The cluster was detected through an existing KPC surveillance program when C. freundii isolates with carbapenem resistance and blaKPC‑3 were recovered from clinical specimens, revealing Citrobacter’s previously under-recognized role in a regional CRE problem dominated by KPC‑producing K. pneumoniae. Enhanced environmental cleaning, temporary unit closure and terminal disinfection, and reinforcement of contact precautions successfully halted further spread.([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/infection-control-and-hospital-epidemiology/article/abs/outbreak-of-klebsiella-pneumoniae-carbapenemaseproducing-citrobacter-freundii-at-a-tertiary-acute-care-facility-in-miami-florida/33FB0CF9AA2B4186DB6DBB04E5B34EFE?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Endemic circulation of KPC-producing Enterobacterales in south Florida, inter-facility transfer of high-risk patients, and substantial carbapenem use in the ICU provided ecological conditions for plasmid-mediated spread of blaKPC‑3 into Citrobacter freundii. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via acquisition of a blaKPC‑3–carrying plasmid by a C. freundii clone, enabling carbapenem resistance and participation in a multi-species KPC plasmid network; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via clonal spread within a single ICU before outbreak recognition and containment.([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/infection-control-and-hospital-epidemiology/article/abs/outbreak-of-klebsiella-pneumoniae-carbapenemaseproducing-citrobacter-freundii-at-a-tertiary-acute-care-facility-in-miami-florida/33FB0CF9AA2B4186DB6DBB04E5B34EFE?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – The Miami KPC‑3–producing C. freundii outbreak (six cases, with a clonal ICU cluster) is well-supported by the Infection Control & Hospital Epidemiology paper and illustrates early KPC plasmid expansion into Citrobacter in North America. Event details and emergence type (re‑emergence via novel resistance plasmid) are appropriate. The event-specific source list has been pruned to include only the primary outbreak report and its institutional repository entry; a Finland CP‑Citrobacter paper and a general Citrobacter AMR review that were previously listed for this row have been removed as they describe different settings.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Citrobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Citrobacter infection
Host: Humans (adult inpatients in a major German university hospital; multiple medical and surgical wards)
Event.summary: From February to June 2016, Jena University Hospital in Germany experienced a large nosocomial foodborne outbreak of Citrobacter freundii expressing a VIM metallo‑β‑lactamase, with 76 colonized patients identified across 14 departments following a sudden rise in carbapenemase-expressing C. freundii detected in rectal swabs. Outbreak investigation traced the source to hospital-prepared cold foods (vegetable salads and puddings) contaminated during processing in a central kitchen mixing machine, and withdrawal of implicated dishes plus strengthened infection control and food hygiene practices led to a rapid decline and eventual disappearance of new cases.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/67/1/58/4809943))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Centralized preparation and distribution of cold hospital meals, inadequate control of contamination in a mixing machine, and widespread distribution of contaminated salads and puddings to multiple wards created a common-source foodborne exposure for inpatients already under antibiotic pressure. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via acquisition of a VIM carbapenemase by an otherwise fluoroquinolone-susceptible C. freundii clone; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through efficient dissemination via the hospital food chain, followed by colonization of the gut and environmental contamination of toilets and patient rooms.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/67/1/58/4809943))
Review: retain – This Jena foodborne outbreak is one of the largest known carbapenemase-expressing Citrobacter freundii events (76 colonized patients across many wards) and fits squarely within the project’s definition of a high-impact, epidemiologically linked episode. Geography, timeframe, and mechanisms are accurately captured from the Clinical Infectious Diseases report; event-type classification as re‑emergence is appropriate given the novel carbapenemase-producing clone and foodborne dissemination route.

EPP.scientific.name: Citrobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Citrobacter infection
Host: Humans (adult haematology patients, many with haematologic malignancies, in a Paris teaching hospital haematology ward)
Event.summary: Between January 2016 and June 2019, the haematology ward of a Paris teaching hospital experienced a large, protracted outbreak of OXA‑48–producing Enterobacterales, primarily Citrobacter freundii sequence type 22, with 37 new carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) cases detected, of which 31 were considered acquired on the ward. Among these, 22 isolates were C. freundii and 21 patients developed infections (mainly urinary tract and bloodstream infections). Environmental investigations in 2018 identified OXA‑48 CPE in seven of 74 toilets and one of 39 drains, and whole-genome sequencing confirmed clonal dissemination of OXA‑48–producing C. freundii from contaminated ward toilets to patients; replacement of toilet bowls and tanks plus intensified cleaning and existing contact precautions were required to finally control the outbreak.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8161731/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A highly immunocompromised haematology population with frequent antibiotic exposure, combined with contamination of ward toilets and drains that acted as persistent environmental reservoirs of OXA‑48 CPE, facilitated repeated acquisition events even after a dedicated CPE unit was created. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via plasmid-mediated acquisition of blaOXA‑48 (and occasionally additional carbapenemase genes) by C. freundii ST22; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through environmental persistence in sanitary installations and repeated seeding of susceptible patients via toilet use and splashes.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8161731/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added to capture the large OXA‑48 C. freundii ST22 outbreak in a Paris haematology ward (37 CPE cases, 22 Citrobacter, 21 infections) and its linkage to contaminated toilets. This is one of the most impactful Citrobacter carbapenemase outbreaks reported, with substantial morbidity in a high-risk population and a clear environmental mechanism. Classified as re‑emergence driven by a novel OXA‑48–producing clone expanding within a previously affected subregion. Internal reviewers should confirm that including this event (and the closely related ST‑22 persistence to 2022) is prioritized over smaller CP‑Citrobacter clusters elsewhere.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Citrobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Citrobacter infection
Host: Humans (inpatients in multiple Finnish healthcare facilities, including acute-care hospitals and long-term care settings)
Event.summary: Between 2016 and 2020, Finland’s national carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales surveillance detected three distinct clusters of carbapenemase-producing Citrobacter freundii: a main cluster of 16 KPC‑2–producing ST18 isolates across five healthcare facilities, and two smaller clusters with two cases each in separate facilities in 2018–2019 and 2020. These clusters showed that CP‑C. freundii, previously considered to have limited outbreak potential, could cause multi-year, multi-facility transmission events in Northern Europe, prompting strengthened screening and infection-control measures for Citrobacter as part of the Finnish CPE program.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34164687/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rising prevalence of CPE in Finland, cross-facility transfer of colonized patients, and selective pressure from carbapenem and broad-spectrum cephalosporin use facilitated the emergence and spread of KPC‑2–producing C. freundii ST18 and other CP‑Citrobacter lineages. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance through acquisition of plasmid-borne carbapenemase genes (predominantly blaKPC‑2) in C. freundii; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of CP‑C. freundii lineages across several hospitals and long-term care facilities within the Northern Europe subregion.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34164687/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – The three Finnish CP‑C. freundii clusters (20 cases across multiple healthcare facilities) are clearly documented and illustrate spread of KPC‑2–producing Citrobacter in a low‑prevalence Northern European country. Timeframe, geography and classification as re‑emergence via new carbapenemase-producing lineages are appropriate; sources are specific to the clusters and well chosen.

EPP.scientific.name: Citrobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Citrobacter infection
Host: Humans (hospital inpatients in multiple Chinese provinces) with linked isolates also detected in animals and water environments in a One Health survey
Event.summary: Between June 2016 and March 2023, a large One Health study in China collected 9,701 samples from humans, animals and water environments across 27 provinces and identified 171 carbapenem-resistant Citrobacter (CRC) isolates, including 50 human-derived strains and 117 from water. Citrobacter freundii was the most prevalent species (≈76%), with sequence types ST116 and ST22 predominating, and carbapenem resistance was mainly driven by blaNDM‑1 and blaKPC‑2 carried on mobile plasmids. The findings revealed widespread dissemination of carbapenem-resistant Citrobacter across hospital ICUs, healthy human carriers, livestock and contaminated wastewater, highlighting China as a major focus of CRC emergence.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924857925000214?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive use of carbapenems and other broad-spectrum antibiotics in Chinese hospitals, antibiotic use in agriculture, and inadequate wastewater treatment created strong selection for CRC strains and allowed persistence in hospital effluents and surface waters, with bidirectional transmission between clinical, animal and environmental reservoirs. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via acquisition of blaNDM‑1, blaKPC‑2 and other carbapenemase genes on diverse plasmids in dominant C. freundii sequence types (e.g., ST116, ST22); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through plasmid-mediated spread across Citrobacter and other Enterobacterales species and niches; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as CRC Citrobacter became established across many provinces and sectors in China.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924857925000214?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – The original row mis-specified the timeframe as 2015–2017; this has been corrected to 2016–2023 based on the International Journal of Antimicrobial Agents study, and the country tag updated to China [2016]. The event summarises a large multi-year, multi-province One Health dataset that convincingly demonstrates emergence and broad establishment of carbapenem-resistant Citrobacter across human, animal and water compartments in China, and likely ranks among the most impactful Citrobacter AMR events. Classification as re‑emergence (novel carbapenem-resistant lineages expanding in a country where Citrobacter was already endemic) is appropriate. Internal reviewers should confirm whether they want to treat this multi-sectoral trend as a single linked episode or subdivide by sector.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Citrobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Citrobacter infection
Host: Humans (preterm and critically ill neonates in a neonatal intensive care unit at a university hospital in Seoul)
Event.summary: On 16 December 2017, four preterm infants in the neonatal intensive care unit of Ewha Womans University Mokdong Hospital in Seoul died within about 80 minutes after receiving an intravenous lipid emulsion (SMOFlipid) that was later shown to be contaminated with Citrobacter freundii; the same strain was isolated from blood (4/4 infants), cerebrospinal fluid (3/4) and the leftover lipid emulsion. Epidemiologic investigation by Korean authorities concluded the infants died of sepsis caused by multidrug-resistant C. freundii transmitted via contaminated lipid infusions, leading to national scrutiny of NICU parenteral nutrition practices and strengthened aseptic preparation requirements.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5832946/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Repeated entry into multi-dose lipid emulsion stock bottles for multiple neonatal infusions outside of a controlled pharmacy environment, inadequate aseptic technique, and extreme vulnerability of very preterm infants created conditions for massive extrinsic contamination and rapid, fatal fulminant sepsis; systemic lapses in NICU infection prevention and pharmaceutical compounding were highlighted in the national investigation. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial Resistance (the outbreak strain was multidrug resistant by Korean CDC investigation) enabling limited treatment options; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation in the sense that C. freundii grew to very high concentrations in nutrient-rich lipid emulsion and was directly infused into the bloodstream of several neonates, delivering a high inoculum; the event does not appear to be driven by a uniquely novel Citrobacter genotype so is better classified as re‑occurrence due to external contamination rather than re‑emergence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5832946/))
Review: review – This catastrophic NICU event (four neonatal deaths from contaminated lipid infusion) is clearly documented and is one of the most severe Citrobacter outbreaks in terms of mortality, but is mechanistically an extrinsic contamination failure rather than driven by a novel Citrobacter strain. The emergence-type classification has been adjusted from both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence to re‑occurrence only, aligning with project definitions (external drivers such as unsafe infusion practices without clear evidence of a new Citrobacter genotype). Sources have been streamlined to include the detailed JKMS case report and a companion national commentary describing the multidrug-resistant C. freundii and investigation findings.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (hospitalized neonates in a neonatal intensive care unit)
Event.summary: From December 1992 through March 1993, a neonatal intensive care unit in a Dutch university hospital experienced an outbreak of Enterobacter cloacae colonization and infection, with six ventilated neonates affected and 21 identical isolates recovered from five of them, all resistant to third-generation cephalosporins. Molecular typing by interrepeat PCR showed a single epidemic clone in the NICU and one additional ICU patient, while pediatric ward isolates were genetically distinct, indicating clonal spread within the intensive care setting. The outbreak was controlled after reinforcing infection-prevention measures and surveillance cultures, and no further cases due to the epidemic clone were detected after 1993.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-risk NICU environment with mechanically ventilated, very preterm infants, invasive devices and frequent broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure; likely lapses in infection-prevention and cross-transmission via healthcare workers and shared equipment. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and clonal expansion of a third-generation cephalosporin-resistant E. cloacae strain (via chromosomal AmpC overexpression and/or ESBLs), representing a resistance-driven re-emergence of Enterobacter as a NICU pathogen rather than first occurrence in the region.
Review: review – Well-described Dutch NICU outbreak of third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacter cloacae; geography, dates and resistance classification match primary sources, but only six neonates were colonized/infected, so this episode is smaller than several later outbreaks (e.g. 23-case NICU bacteremia in Taiwan, 9-fatality outbreak in South Africa) and may not belong among the ten highest-impact global events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (premature infants in an intensive care nursery)
Event.summary: Between 29 November 1992 and 17 March 1993, an intensive care nursery at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania experienced an outbreak of Enterobacter hormaechei infections and colonizations among premature infants, with 10 infants affected (six infected, four colonized). Epidemiologic study and typing supported a clonal nursery outbreak originating within the unit, with environmental contamination and cross-transmission among infants. Following strict infection-control measures, cohorting and environmental decontamination, further transmission was halted and the outbreak ended.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-risk intensive care nursery setting with very premature infants, invasive devices, crowding and intensive nursing care; inadequate early recognition and lapses in hand hygiene and equipment decontamination that facilitated cross-transmission. Internal mechanisms: No unique novel resistance trait was highlighted; the event reflects amplification and spread of an opportunistic Enterobacter spp. in a vulnerable neonatal population driven by infection-control failures rather than by emergence of a distinct new genotype.
Review: review – NICU outbreak with ten affected premature infants and no clearly novel resistance mechanism; classification as control-failure-driven re-occurrence is appropriate, but given modest scale it may fall below the top ten global Enterobacter spp. emergence events and should be weighed against larger NICU and carbapenem-resistant outbreaks.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (high-risk neonates receiving total parenteral nutrition in a newborn intensive care unit)
Event.summary: On June 12, 1995, during a 16-hour period in the high-risk section of the neonatal intensive care unit at the Women’s Hospital of the State University of Campinas in Brazil, 11 hospitalized newborns developed signs and symptoms of septic shock 12–24 hours after receiving total parenteral nutrition. Enterobacter cloacae with identical antibiotic-susceptibility patterns and pulsed-field gel electrophoresis profiles was isolated from blood cultures of 10 affected infants as well as from refrigerated aliquots and in-use bags of the parenteral nutrition solution, confirming intrinsic contamination during preparation as the common source. Immediate discontinuation of the contaminated solution, microbiologic investigation of the compounding process, and tightening of aseptic technique and handling of parenteral nutrition ended the outbreak, with no further E. cloacae sepsis cases linked to this source.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intrinsic contamination of compounded total parenteral nutrition solution in the hospital pharmacy, coupled with widespread use of central venous lines and parenteral nutrition among high-risk neonates, created an efficient point source for rapid sepsis onset; limited early detection and the clustering of all high-risk infants in one room amplified impact. Internal mechanisms: A single E. cloacae clone with the capacity to grow and persist in nutrient-rich parenteral nutrition, but without a uniquely described novel resistance determinant; the event is best characterized as a severe, product-contamination-driven re-occurrence in a previously affected host system.
Review: retain – Newly added major NICU outbreak in Brazil in which 11 high-risk newborns developed Enterobacter cloacae sepsis within 16 hours due to intrinsically contaminated total parenteral nutrition; represents one of the most dramatic single-source Enterobacter outbreaks in South America; classification as re-occurrence (product contamination without a clearly novel genotype) is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (neonates with necrotizing enterocolitis and sepsis in a neonatal intensive care unit)
Event.summary: During September and October 1996, a neonatal intensive care unit in a provincial hospital in Gauteng, South Africa, experienced an outbreak of necrotizing enterocolitis and sepsis in premature infants that resulted in nine deaths. Molecular typing by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis showed that E. cloacae isolates from patient blood cultures, multiple environmental sources and a staff member’s hand belonged to the same genotypic cluster, implicating a single epidemic strain widely disseminated in the unit; the Vamin amino acid parenteral nutrition solution was suspected to have contributed to disease severity. After breaches in basic infection control and shortages of staff, equipment and isolation facilities were identified, infection-prevention practices were strengthened and contaminated or potentially contaminated materials were withdrawn, leading to control of the outbreak and prevention of further deaths.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Resource constraints, overcrowding and inadequate staffing in the NICU, together with poor adherence to fundamental infection-prevention measures (e.g. hand hygiene, alcohol rubs, equipment disinfection) and use of contaminated or high-risk parenteral nutrition solutions, enabled extensive environmental contamination and transmission of a single E. cloacae strain. Internal mechanisms: A clonal E. cloacae population associated with severe necrotizing enterocolitis, but without a specific novel resistance gene described; the event reflects major infection-control failure and high host vulnerability rather than genetic innovation, and is therefore coded as re-occurrence.
Review: retain – Newly added 1996 Gauteng NICU necrotizing enterocolitis outbreak with nine neonatal deaths linked to a clonal Enterobacter cloacae strain and contaminated amino acid solution; high mortality and clear documentation justify inclusion as a top-impact event; classified as re-occurrence driven by severe infection-control failures and contaminated parenteral nutrition, not by a novel resistance mechanism.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (hospitalized adult patients in a university hospital)
Event.summary: Beginning with the first qnrA1-positive Enterobacter cloacae isolate detected in 1999, a large nosocomial outbreak emerged at the University Medical Center Utrecht, peaking from 2001 onward and ultimately involving 83 E. cloacae isolates in a single PFGE cluster and at least 53 affected patients. The epidemic strain carried a 180-kb plasmid (pQC) encoding the plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance gene qnrA1, the ESBL gene blaCTX-M-9, and an aminoglycoside-resistance integron, and this plasmid spread in vivo to multiple Enterobacteriaceae species in colonized patients. The outbreak waned only after active screening, strengthened infection-control interventions and antibiotic-stewardship changes, and it provided early documentation of hospital-wide dissemination of plasmid-borne fluoroquinolone resistance in Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High antibiotic selection pressure in a large tertiary-care hospital, including use of cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides; prolonged hospital stays, invasive devices and close contact among patients on affected wards facilitated colonization and spread. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and expansion of a complex multidrug-resistance plasmid (pQC) carrying qnrA1, blaCTX-M-9 and aadB-containing integrons in E. cloacae and other Enterobacteriaceae, representing plasmid-mediated novel genotype emergence, enhanced resistance to fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins and aminoglycosides, and efficient horizontal gene transfer in the gut.
Review: retain – Large, well-characterized Dutch hospital outbreak (83 isolates, ≥53 patients) caused by an Enterobacter cloacae clone carrying plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance gene qnrA1 alongside ESBL and aminoglycoside-resistance determinants; appropriately coded as resistance-driven re-emergence with correct geography and dates.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (adult surgical intensive care unit patients)
Event.summary: From 1 February to 30 May 2005, a surgical intensive care unit in Tours, France, experienced a cluster of 15 patients infected or colonized with third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacter cloacae, including 12 with clinical infections. Epidemiologic investigation linked the outbreak to contamination of air-fluidized therapy beds and mattresses, which acted as reservoirs for the multiresistant clone. Removal and decontamination of the implicated beds, reinforcement of environmental cleaning and infection-control protocols, and antibiotic-use review led to disappearance of the epidemic strain and resolution of the outbreak.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of complex air-fluidized therapy beds whose internal components were difficult to disinfect, creating a persistent environmental reservoir, together with a population of critically ill surgical ICU patients exposed to broad-spectrum antibiotics and prolonged hospitalization. Internal mechanisms: A multiresistant E. cloacae clone with third-generation cephalosporin resistance, likely mediated by AmpC overproduction and/or ESBLs, enabling survival under cephalosporin therapy and clonal expansion within the ICU; this represents resistance-driven re-emergence and enhanced environmental persistence within the hospital.
Review: retain – ICU outbreak in Tours, France (15 affected patients) associated with multiresistant Enterobacter cloacae residing in therapeutic beds; reasonably among more impactful single-ward Enterobacter outbreaks and correctly coded as resistance-driven re-emergence; no structural changes needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (neonates with bloodstream infection in a neonatal unit)
Event.summary: Between 18 November 2012 and 9 February 2013, a five-bed neonatal unit at Patan Hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal, experienced a cluster of 16 neonates with Enterobacter cloacae bloodstream infections over three months, many of whom were severely ill and six of whom died. Whole-genome sequencing of E. cloacae and Citrobacter isolates revealed two distinct multidrug-resistant outbreaks, including one linked to an NDM-1 carbapenemase plasmid previously identified in a community E. cloacae isolate from 2009, with evidence of in vivo plasmid transfer and clonal spread. After environmental investigations, fumigation of multiple pediatric units, and reinforcement of infection-control practices, the incidence of new E. cloacae bacteremias fell sharply and the outbreak period ended.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Overcrowded, resource-limited neonatal unit with high antibiotic usage, limited infection-control infrastructure and shared equipment, combined with introduction of community-associated drug-resistant strains and contaminated environmental sources (including a soap dispenser). Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of carbapenem-resistant, multidrug-resistant E. cloacae clones carrying NDM-1 and other β-lactamase and resistance determinants, representing novel genotype emergence, greatly enhanced resistance to last-line agents and clonal expansion in a highly vulnerable neonatal population.
Review: retain – Neonatal unit outbreak at Patan Hospital, Kathmandu, with 16 neonates and six deaths due to multidrug-resistant and NDM-1-producing Enterobacter cloacae; one of the most consequential documented Enterobacter carbapenemase outbreaks in low-resource settings and correctly coded as re-emergence through acquisition of an NDM-1 plasmid.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (adult inpatients in an internal medicine unit; gut colonization and infections with Enterobacter cloacae and other Enterobacteriaceae)
Event.summary: In April 2011, an elderly patient transferred from Agadir, Morocco, to the internal medicine unit of Nantes University Hospital in France was found to carry gastrointestinal colonization with ertapenem-resistant Enterobacter cloacae and Escherichia coli producing the carbapenemase OXA-48. Subsequent weekly surveillance identified OXA-48-producing E. cloacae in three additional patients without travel history and OXA-48-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae in two patients, with molecular analysis showing that all OXA-48-producing E. cloacae isolates shared blaOXA-48 and blaCTX-M-15 on the same plasmid and that in vivo horizontal transfer of the OXA-48 plasmid from the index strain to other Enterobacteriaceae occurred in the gut. The cluster was controlled through contact precautions, active rectal-swab surveillance, and continued isolation of colonized patients until discharge, preventing further hospital-wide spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intercontinental transfer of a patient from a region where OXA-48-producing Enterobacteriaceae are endemic (North Africa) into a French hospital ward, combined with antibiotic selection pressure and close contact among inpatients, facilitated introduction and onward transmission of carbapenemase-producing strains. Internal mechanisms: Plasmid-mediated carbapenem resistance via blaOXA-48 combined with ESBL gene blaCTX-M-15 on the same transferable plasmid enabled survival under carbapenem and cephalosporin pressure; this outbreak illustrates horizontal plasmid transfer between Enterobacter cloacae, E. coli and K. pneumoniae in the human gut and represents resistance-driven re-emergence rather than first continental emergence of Enterobacter infections.
Review: review – Nantes internal-medicine-unit cluster is mechanistically important for demonstrating in vivo transfer of an OXA-48 plasmid between Enterobacteriaceae, but modest in patient numbers; inter_continental_emergence has been corrected from true to false because Enterobacter spp. and OXA-48-producing Enterobacteriaceae were already present in Europe, so this cluster is best classified solely as resistance-driven re-emergence linked to cross-border patient transfer.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (adult and one neonatal inpatient across an acute-care hospital and long-term acute-care facility)
Event.summary: Beginning in 2010 and intensifying between December 2011 and December 2012, a health-care system in Fargo, North Dakota, identified 20 patients with infections or colonization by carbapenem-resistant Enterobacter cloacae, all carrying the KPC-3 carbapenemase within the same Tn4401 transposon and belonging to a single clonal outbreak strain. Most patients had recent exposure to the system’s long-term acute-care facility and 13 required intensive care; seven patients died, three deaths being directly attributed to carbapenem-resistant E. cloacae infection. Implementation of enhanced infection-control measures and attention to inter-facility transfer and surveillance practices were used to curb further spread, highlighting long-term care facilities as important reservoirs and amplifiers of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High antibiotic exposure and complex comorbidities in patients moving between an acute-care hospital and an associated long-term acute-care facility, the absence of active CRE surveillance, frequent ICU admissions and device use created conditions for clonal dissemination of carbapenem-resistant E. cloacae. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and clonal spread of a plasmid-borne blaKPC-3 gene embedded in Tn4401d in Enterobacter cloacae, conferring high-level carbapenem resistance and representing resistance-driven re-emergence in a healthcare system where Enterobacter had long been endemic.
Review: retain – Newly added regional outbreak of clonal KPC-3-producing Enterobacter cloacae in a North Dakota health-care system (20 patients, three deaths attributable to infection), representing a major North American carbapenem-resistant Enterobacter event; classification as re-emergence due to acquisition of KPC-3 is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (newborns in a neonatal intensive care unit; colonization and invasive infections due to OXA-48-producing Enterobacteriaceae)
Event.summary: An outbreak of OXA-48-producing Enterobacteriaceae began in March 2012 in a neonatal intensive care unit in Jerusalem, Israel; during the peak period from January to August 2012, 49 infants acquired OXA-48-producing Enterobacteriaceae, including 16 with invasive infections, out of 156 NICU patients. Among 31 patient-unique isolates analyzed, two were Enterobacter cloacae and 29 were Klebsiella pneumoniae ST39, all carrying an IncL/M plasmid co-harboring blaOXA-48 and blaCTX-M-14, which conferred resistance to nearly all β-lactams. Following notification of the Ministry of Health, intensive control measures including cohorting colonized infants, frequent rectal surveillance cultures, and strengthened infection-prevention practices reduced new acquisitions to five additional cases over four months, after which no further cases occurred.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Crowded NICU conditions, high antibiotic use, and regional circulation of OXA-48-producing strains that were introduced into the unit, along with initially limited recognition of silent carriage, allowed rapid spread; national-level intervention and strict cohorting were required to halt transmission. Internal mechanisms: Dissemination of a successful plasmid carrying both blaOXA-48 and blaCTX-M-14 across Klebsiella pneumoniae and Enterobacter cloacae, resulting in near-pan-β-lactam resistance and representing an important resistance-driven re-emergence of Enterobacter infections in Western Asia.
Review: retain – Large NICU outbreak in Jerusalem with 57 affected infants (49 during the main period), 16 invasive infections and documented OXA-48 plasmid spread to Enterobacter cloacae; clearly high-impact and correctly coded as re-emergence driven by acquisition of a blaOXA-48/blaCTX-M-14 plasmid.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (newborns in a neonatal intensive care unit; colonization and systemic infection)
Event.summary: In 2012, a neonatal intensive care unit at Hospital General Universitario Gregorio Marañón in Madrid, Spain, detected a cluster of 14 newborns colonized or infected with multidrug-resistant CTX-M-15-producing Enterobacter cloacae over a defined outbreak period; seven infants developed clinical infection and one untreated infant died. Molecular typing showed that all outbreak isolates were closely related and carried CTX-M-15 extended-spectrum β-lactamases along with additional resistance determinants, and cases clustered in time and space within the NICU. After identification of the ESBL-producing clone, reinforcement of infection-control measures and modification of empirical therapy—including greater use of carbapenems—contained the outbreak and prevented further spread of the epidemic strain.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-risk NICU population with frequent invasive procedures and extensive third-generation cephalosporin exposure selected for CTX-M-15 ESBL-producing strains; close proximity of infants and staff-mediated cross-transmission enabled rapid clonal spread. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and expansion of an E. cloacae strain carrying CTX-M-15 ESBLs on mobile genetic elements, conferring resistance to third-generation cephalosporins and many other drugs; a clear example of ESBL-driven re-emergence of Enterobacter infections in neonates in Southern Europe.
Review: retain – Madrid NICU outbreak involving 14 colonized/infected newborns (seven infections, one death) due to CTX-M-15-producing Enterobacter cloacae; a substantial ESBL-associated neonatal event in Southern Europe and properly classified as resistance-driven re-emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterobacter spp.
EPP.common.name: Enterobacter infection
Host: Humans (adult hematology inpatients in a tertiary-care hospital)
Event.summary: Between 2015 and 2021, a hematology unit in a French university hospital experienced a prolonged intermittent outbreak in which 41 patients became colonized or infected with OXA-48-producing Enterobacter cloacae, and a total of 133 clinical and environmental isolates were collected. Whole-genome sequencing revealed that most isolates belonged to a single ST66 E. cloacae clone harboring a blaOXA-48-like-containing resistance plasmid, and epidemiologic investigation implicated persistently contaminated hospital shower drains and wastewater plumbing as key environmental reservoirs seeding new cases. After extensive environmental sampling, installation of removable and autoclavable shower inserts to avoid contact with contaminated drains, and reinforcement of infection-control measures, new acquisitions declined and the outbreak was successfully contained.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent contamination of hospital shower drains and wastewater infrastructure in a hematology unit caring for severely immunocompromised patients, combined with heavy carbapenem and broad-spectrum antibiotic use, facilitated repeated acquisition of carbapenem-resistant E. cloacae despite routine infection control. Internal mechanisms: A dominant ST66 E. cloacae clone carrying a blaOXA-48-like plasmid conferring carbapenem resistance and broad β-lactam resistance, adapted to persist in wet environmental niches and cause intermittent common-source transmission; a major resistance-driven re-emergence event in Western Europe.
Review: retain – Newly added prolonged common-source outbreak in a hematology unit with 41 patients and 133 clinical/environmental OXA-48-producing Enterobacter cloacae isolates linked to shower drains; one of the largest E. cloacae carbapenemase outbreaks described and appropriately classified as resistance-driven re-emergence via a blaOXA-48-like plasmid and environmental adaptation.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus omskense
EPP.common.name: Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus
Host: Humans (rural residents, muskrat trappers and other residents of lake/steppe districts in Novosibirsk Oblast); wild small mammals (especially muskrats and voles) and ixodid ticks as reservoir/amplifying hosts and vectors within the natural focus
Event.summary: After a prolonged inter‑epidemic period with very low or no recorded Omsk hemorrhagic fever (OHF) incidence following the 1945–1958 epidemic wave, surveillance in western Siberia detected renewed human OHF activity beginning in 1989, with sustained low‑to‑moderate incidence from 1990 through 1998 mainly in Novosibirsk Oblast of the Russian Federation. During this period, national data indicate 2–41 reported OHF cases per year in Novosibirsk, with the highest annual counts in 1990 and 1991, representing a clear resurgence compared with the preceding quiescent decades; most patients were muskrat trappers or rural residents exposed to tick‑infested wetlands and infected muskrats in long‑standing natural foci, while epizootic activity in muskrats and ticks was also documented in neighboring Tyumen, Omsk and Kurgan regions.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262182773_Omsk_Hemorrhagic_Fever_Virus)) By the late 1990s, public‑health messaging, changes in muskrat exploitation and ecological fluctuations appear to have reduced human exposure, and reported incidence declined again even though enzootic circulation of OHFV in wildlife persisted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reactivation of OHF natural foci in western Siberia driven by favorable ecological conditions for muskrats and voles around lakes and marshes, intensive muskrat trapping and skinning, and occupational/recreational exposure to tick‑infested habitats, combined with socio‑economic changes in the late Soviet and early post‑Soviet periods that likely reduced resources for systematic vector and wildlife management.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262182773_Omsk_Hemorrhagic_Fever_Virus)) Internal mechanisms: Genetic and antigenic studies indicate that OHFV strains circulating in the 1990s belong to previously recognized western Siberian genotypes, with no clear evidence of major viral evolution or increased intrinsic virulence relative to earlier strains; the episode is therefore best characterized as a re‑occurrence driven primarily by ecological and behavioral factors rather than a genetic re‑emergence (no strong support for Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence or markedly Enhanced Transmission beyond the long‑established ecology).([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262182773_Omsk_Hemorrhagic_Fever_Virus))
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row appropriately captures the documented resurgence of OHF in the 1990s, with cases concentrated in Novosibirsk Oblast after a long quiescent period, and correctly classifies the episode as re‑occurrence in a long‑known natural focus rather than first emergence or inter‑/intra‑continental spread. I have revised the event summary to rely on primary reviews (Růžek et al. 2013; Control of Communicable Diseases Manual) rather than Wikipedia, removed a poorly sourced numeric estimate of "~240" cases in favor of qualitative wording linked to reported annual ranges, and clarified that most human cases were in Novosibirsk while neighboring oblasts mainly showed epizootic activity. These changes strengthen sourcing and reduce over‑precision but do not alter the basic structure of the event; further refinement of exact case counts would require access to detailed Russian surveillance tables.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus omskense
EPP.common.name: Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus
Host: Humans (patients with meningitis or meningoencephalitis in Almaty city); wild rodents (multiple small‑mammal species) and ixodid ticks (Dermacentor marginatus, Dermacentor reticulatus, Ixodes persulcatus) in Akmola, West Kazakhstan, Almaty region and Almaty city as reservoir hosts and vectors within newly recognized natural foci
Event.summary: Between 2016 and 2019, a cross‑sectional investigation in Kazakhstan provided the first direct evidence that Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus had spread beyond the historically recognized western Siberian focus in the Russian Federation: OHFV RNA was detected in Dermacentor marginatus ticks collected in 2016 from the Sandyktau area of Akmola Region, in additional tick pools from Akmola in 2018, in lung tissue of several rodent species trapped in West Kazakhstan Region in 2018–2019, and in cerebrospinal fluid from two patients with meningitis/meningoencephalitis treated in Almaty city hospitals in 2018–2019.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/3aeb/b4a67588f1da5ba4ab630818570485207679.pdf)) These data demonstrated natural foci of OHFV in multiple regions of Kazakhstan and confirmed human infection up to ~1,600 km from the classic western Siberian endemic area, yet no large recognized outbreak of clinically classical Omsk hemorrhagic fever was described; instead, the virus appears to cause sporadic, previously unrecognized neurologic disease in Central Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The Kazakhstan findings likely reflect a combination of long‑standing ecological continuity across the Russia–Kazakhstan border (shared steppe and forest‑steppe habitats, widespread muskrats and small rodents, and Dermacentor/Ixodes tick populations) and improved molecular surveillance for viral causes of undiagnosed febrile and neurologic illness, as suggested by the authors, with climate‑ and land‑use‑driven shifts in host and vector distributions potentially facilitating south‑ and west‑ward spread or detection of OHFV.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/3aeb/b4a67588f1da5ba4ab630818570485207679.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Sequence analyses to date place Kazakh OHFV sequences within the known diversity of the virus rather than identifying a clearly distinct high‑virulence genotype, so the episode is best interpreted as an inter‑continental emergence (new continent and country for the human host system under the UNSD classification: Europe–Russian Federation to Asia–Kazakhstan) driven by geographic range expansion and improved detection, rather than as genetic re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This new row has been added to capture an important emergence event omitted from the original dataset: the first confirmed detection of OHFV in humans, ticks and rodents in Kazakhstan between 2016 and 2019, which represents inter‑continental emergence from Europe (Russian Federation, per the UNSD classification used in the Country sheet) into Asia (Central Asia, Kazakhstan). The episode is supported by a detailed peer‑reviewed study (Wagner et al. 2022, Viruses) and clearly meets the criteria for an emergence event despite involving only a small number of recognized human cases, because it documents establishment of natural foci and autochthonous human infection in a new country and continent. Classification as inter‑continental emergence (with no first‑global‑emergence or re‑occurrence/re‑emergence labels) and the 2016–2019 time window are based on the sampling years reported in that study.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus usutuense
EPP.common.name: Usutu virus
Host: Humans (mostly asymptomatic or mild infections detected in blood donors; occasional rash or nonspecific symptoms)
Event.summary: From 2016 to 2017, Austria detected multiple Usutu virus infections in blood donors through nucleic acid amplification testing aimed at West Nile virus, revealing widespread but largely silent human exposure in central Europe. In 2016, one of four flavivirus NAT‑reactive blood donations and in 2017 six of seven such donations from eastern Austria were confirmed as Usutu virus infections, all from donors residing in areas with intense enzootic circulation in birds and mosquitoes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5710119/?utm_source=openai)) These findings prompted Austrian blood services to integrate Usutu virus into their risk assessments within West Nile virus screening algorithms, and subsequent seasons showed variable but generally low frequencies of Usutu‑positive donations, largely tracking variations in mosquito abundance and avian epizootics rather than indicating a sustained increase in clinically apparent human disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑intensity enzootic Usutu virus transmission in eastern Austria during warm summers, combined with extensive blood‑donor NAT screening for West Nile virus that cross‑detected or specifically tested for Usutu virus, thereby uncovering asymptomatic human infections; land‑use patterns (wetlands and river plains) and climate variability likely amplified Culex mosquito populations. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of several European Usutu virus lineages (notably Europe 2 and Africa 3) capable of efficient replication in birds and mosquitoes, leading to frequent low‑level human spillover; most infected donors remained asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic, suggesting that genetic changes were associated more with transmission efficiency and overwintering than with a marked increase in virulence in humans.
Review: review – event retained to represent the substantial cluster of asymptomatic Usutu‑positive blood donations in Austria, but its scope and classification were corrected. The episode is now restricted to Austria, with Hungary moved to the 2018 multi‑country event, and the sub‑region set to Western Europe only. Year annotations for the country have been kept as Austria [2016] to reflect the start of donor infections, but the emphasis in the summary is on 2016–2017 when most cases were detected. Because Western Europe already had a documented human infection in Germany in 2012, this Austrian episode has been reclassified from intra‑continental emergence to re‑emergence linked to intensifying enzootic circulation and systematic donor screening. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233929728_Detection_of_Usutu_virus_infection_in_a_healthy_blood_donor_from_south-west_Germany_2012?utm_source=openai)) Source URLs were replaced with primary reports on Austrian donor screening and ECDC synthesis documents.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus andesense
EPP.common.name: Andes virus
Host: Humans (hantavirus pulmonary syndrome / hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome)
Event.summary: In early 1995, physicians in El Bolsón, Río Negro Province, southern Argentina, recognized a cluster of severe respiratory illness consistent with hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, and laboratory testing of autopsy tissue from one patient identified a novel hantavirus—later named Andes virus—as the etiologic agent. The event consisted of a small but severe outbreak centered in rural Andean Patagonia, prompting heightened surveillance, rodent investigations, and genetic characterization of the virus in humans and long‑tailed pygmy rice rats (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus). After this initial cluster subsided, Andes virus remained established in local rodent reservoirs and continued to cause sporadic and clustered human infections in Patagonia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased clinical awareness and expanded laboratory capacity for hantavirus pulmonary syndrome after the 1993 Four Corners outbreak in the United States facilitated recognition of similar severe disease in Patagonia; human encroachment into rodent habitats and agricultural/rural activities in the Andean forest ecotone increased opportunities for zoonotic exposure. Internal mechanisms: This event represents the first recognized spillover of an already circulating Andes virus lineage into humans rather than the emergence of a new genotype; no specific genetic changes were uniquely associated with the initial 1995 cluster.
Review: retain – Event correctly represents the first recognized Andes virus–associated HPS cases in El Bolsón in 1995, with appropriate designation as both first_global_emergence and first_detection and accurate placement in South America/South America; sources confirm timing, location, and etiologic characterization, and no earlier confirmed Andes virus event in humans with greater impact was identified.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus andesense
EPP.common.name: Andes virus
Host: Humans (HPS)
Event.summary: From September 22 to December 5, 1996, a large outbreak of Andes virus–associated HPS occurred among residents and visitors in El Bolsón, San Carlos de Bariloche, Esquel, and, via patient transfer, Buenos Aires, Argentina, following the 1995 recognition of the virus in the region. At least 18–20 epidemiologically linked cases were identified, including household contacts and health‑care workers, and molecular and epidemiologic evidence showed that many cases were connected by chains of person‑to‑person transmission rather than independent rodent exposures. The outbreak ended after isolation of cases, reinforcement of infection‑control practices, and public health interventions, after which only sporadic and smaller clusters continued to occur in southern Argentina.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close household contact, provision of care without adequate respiratory protection, and movement of infectious patients between towns and to Buenos Aires enabled human‑to‑human spread; ongoing rural exposures to infected Oligoryzomys longicaudatus rodents maintained background risk. Internal mechanisms: Sequence analysis identified a specific Epilink/96 strain of Andes virus associated with efficient person‑to‑person transmission during the prodromal phase, consistent with enhanced transmission capability (and possibly increased virulence) relative to more typical purely zoonotic hantavirus infections, and justifying classification as re‑emergence driven by viral lineage characteristics.
Review: retain – This is a well‑documented, high‑impact outbreak (≈18–20 cases) with the first confirmed person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus in Argentina; timing, geography and case numbers match primary reports, and classifying it as re_emergence (linked to the Epilink/96 strain with enhanced human‑to‑human transmission) is consistent with the project’s definition of re‑emergence driven by internal viral changes.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus andesense
EPP.common.name: Andes virus
Host: Humans (HPS)
Event.summary: In October 1995, Chile detected its first confirmed case of Andes virus infection in a patient from southern Chile (Cochamó, Los Lagos Region), shortly after virus identification in neighboring Argentina, marking the recognition of HPS in the country. Between July 1997 and January 1998, a substantial outbreak of 25 Andes virus–associated HPS cases, plus several mild and asymptomatic infections, occurred mainly in Regions X (Llanquihue) and XI (Aysén), including three family clusters with suspected limited person‑to‑person spread. The outbreak declined by early 1998 as rodent populations decreased and public health measures were implemented, establishing Andes virus as the principal cause of HPS in Chile with continuing sporadic and seasonal cases thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rural and peridomestic exposures in Nothofagus forest and agricultural landscapes with high densities of Oligoryzomys longicaudatus and other sigmodontine rodents, combined with improved case recognition and enhanced national surveillance, led to detection of both the first Chilean case and the 1997–1998 outbreak; regional rodent "irruptions" related to bamboo flowering and favorable climatic conditions likely amplified human contact rates. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate that Chilean cases were caused by Andes virus lineages already circulating across southern Argentina and Chile rather than a distinct new genotype, so this episode is best interpreted as geographic recognition and amplification of an existing virus rather than emergence of a fundamentally altered strain.
Review: review – Corrected this row to (i) change the event year from 1997–1998 to 1995–1998 to cover both the first recognized Chilean HPS case in 1995 and the subsequent 1997–1998 southern Chile outbreak, and (ii) simplify the countries field from "Chile [1995], Argentina [1995]" to "Chile [1995]" because the linked Argentine cases are already captured in separate Argentina‑focused events; also set first_detection from true to false so that first_detection is reserved for the 1995 global emergence in Argentina, and left all emergence‑type flags as false since spread from Argentina to Chile occurs within the same South America–South America subregion and does not meet the project criteria for intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence. These corrections align the row with UN subregion rules and outbreak descriptions from Chilean and CDC sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus andesense
EPP.common.name: Andes virus
Host: Humans (HPS)
Event.summary: By the summer of 2000–2001, following earlier outbreaks in southern Chile, Andes virus–associated HPS cases began to appear in and around the more densely populated metropolitan region near Santiago, representing a notable northward expansion in recognized human disease within Chile. The event consisted of sporadic but epidemiologically concerning cases in peri‑urban and rural settings of central Chile, triggering expanded ecological and epidemiologic studies of Andes virus and its rodent hosts across a broader latitudinal range. After this period, reported cases in central Chile remained intermittent, but the virus was recognized as entrenched throughout a wider swath of Chile from Patagonia northwards.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of agriculture, forestry plantations, and human settlement into habitats used by Oligoryzomys longicaudatus and other sigmodontine rodents in central Chile increased human–rodent contact, while strengthened laboratory capacity and heightened clinical suspicion of HPS facilitated detection of cases near Santiago. Internal mechanisms: This episode primarily reflects geographic range expansion and improved detection of existing Andes virus lineages, without clear evidence of a new genotype or major change in virulence, and is therefore classified as re‑occurrence driven by external ecological and human‑behavioral factors.
Review: retain – Event appropriately captures the first recognized appearance of Andes virus HPS in central Chile near Santiago around 2000–2001, which is prominent in Chilean phylogeographic and ecological analyses, and its classification as re_occurrence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) is consistent with the rule that spread within the single South America–South America subregion should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus andesense
EPP.common.name: Andes virus
Host: Humans (HPS)
Event.summary: From July to December 2002, Argentina reported multiple clusters of Andes virus–associated HPS involving 13 cases grouped into four epidemiologically linked family and friend clusters in Buenos Aires and Neuquén Provinces, on top of a broader seasonal increase of 31 HPS cases nationally. Detailed investigation showed clear person‑to‑person transmission in several chains—including a father‑to‑son pair in Buenos Aires and a travel‑associated chain in which infection spread from an index case exposed in Villa La Angostura to seat‑mates and close contacts hundreds of kilometers away—demonstrating that not only the southern (Sout) lineage but also the central Buenos Aires (Cent BsAs) lineage can transmit human‑to‑human. After public health response, including contact tracing and reinforcement of infection‑control measures, no further extended transmission chains were documented, and subsequent Argentine HPS incidence returned to the usual endemic pattern.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rural household crowding, rodent infestation around farms and cabins, and long‑distance travel in enclosed settings (notably a 14‑hour bus journey) created opportunities for both zoonotic spillover and prolonged close contact between infectious cases and susceptible contacts; growing national surveillance meant that spatially separated but temporally related clusters were recognized. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analysis identified both Andes virus Sout and Cent BsAs lineages in these clusters, with 100% sequence identity among cases within each cluster, and provided strong evidence of person‑to‑person transmission for Cent BsAs for the first time, indicating re‑emergence driven by viral lineage properties (enhanced capacity for human‑to‑human spread) rather than purely by external ecological drivers.
Review: review – Added this previously missing 2002 Argentina multi‑cluster event because the combined 13 cases with genetically confirmed person‑to‑person transmission (including the first documentation of such transmission for the Andes Cent BsAs lineage) make it one of the most epidemiologically significant Andes virus episodes after 1996, 1997–1998 and 2018–2019. Classified as re_emergence due to the demonstrated transmission capability of a new lineage, and not as intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence since all transmission occurred within Argentina in the existing South America–South America subregion; field values should be retained but the event merits expert review to confirm treating the four clusters as a single aggregated episode is acceptable within the project rules.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus andesense
EPP.common.name: Andes virus
Host: Humans (HPS)
Event.summary: In 2011, a small but important cluster of five Andes virus infections occurred in southern Chile, beginning with an index HPS case and followed by illness in two household contacts and two health‑care workers after close exposure during the index patient’s prodromal phase. Epidemiologic reconstruction and molecular analysis showed a single viral strain with strong temporal and contact links among cases, providing clear evidence of person‑to‑person transmission in both household and nosocomial settings. After recognition of the cluster and implementation of strict infection‑control measures, including respiratory precautions and active monitoring of contacts, no further secondary cases were detected and the outbreak ended.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close household caregiving, aerosol‑generating procedures, and lack of early recognition of hantavirus infection during the non‑specific febrile prodrome facilitated transmission to family members and health‑care workers; respiratory protection and isolation were not consistently in place until after secondary cases were recognized. Internal mechanisms: The cluster illustrates the inherent human‑to‑human transmission potential of circulating Chilean Andes virus lineages but does not show evidence of a novel genotype or substantial change in virulence compared with earlier strains, so it is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence event driven by circumstances of exposure rather than viral evolution.
Review: review – Updated the emergence‑type coding from re_emergence=true, re_occurrence=false to re_occurrence=true, re_emergence=false because the 2011 southern Chile cluster involved person‑to‑person transmission of an already circulating Andes virus lineage without evidence of a new genotype or altered virulence; under the project’s definitions, this fits a resurgence driven by exposure setting and infection‑control gaps rather than by intrinsic viral change. All other fields (year, location, host, and summary) match the primary outbreak report and can be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Legionella pneumophila
EPP.common.name: Legionnaires’ disease
Host: Humans (community residents of Alcalá de Henares, mainly middle‑aged and older adults)
Event.summary: In September–October 1996, a large community outbreak of severe pneumonia occurred in Alcalá de Henares, in the Madrid region of Spain, and was ultimately attributed to Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 when the bacterium was identified in respiratory and lung tissue samples from affected patients. Over the course of several weeks, more than 220 residents (and up to about 250 in some reports) developed pneumonia compatible with Legionnaires’ disease and around a dozen to 16 people died, making it the largest legionellosis outbreak reported in Spain up to that time. Epidemiologic and environmental investigations traced the main source to two contaminated evaporative cooling towers; after their shutdown and disinfection, hyperchlorination of parts of the municipal water system and remedial work on other risk installations, case numbers declined and the outbreak was declared over later in October, prompting tighter regulation of cooling‑tower maintenance in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Aging municipal water and cooling‑tower infrastructure that allowed colonisation by Legionella, inadequate biocide dosing and maintenance of multiple evaporative cooling towers in a densely populated urban area, warm late‑summer weather favourable for bacterial growth, and initial diagnostic uncertainty that delayed recognition of legionellosis. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was L. pneumophila serogroup 1 (Pontiac subtype) without evidence of a fundamentally novel genotype, resistance profile or new host range; the event is best explained by environmental amplification and aerosol dispersal of an established strain rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – The 1996 Alcalá de Henares community outbreak (≈220–250 cases and roughly 10–16 deaths, traced to contaminated cooling towers) is widely documented as Spain’s largest legionellosis outbreak before Murcia 2001 and is consistently highlighted in national reviews of Legionella epidemiology, so it clearly qualifies among the most impactful post‑1990 L. pneumophila events. Legionella pneumophila was already established in Europe, so classification as re‑occurrence (with no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence flags) is appropriate. Case and death counts differ modestly among Spanish governmental and media sources; the summary uses conservative ranges but does not change any emergence‑type coding.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Legionella pneumophila
EPP.common.name: Legionnaires’ disease
Host: Humans (mainly middle‑aged and older adults visiting a flower show)
Event.summary: In February–March 1999, a very large outbreak of Legionnaires’ disease occurred among visitors and staff at the Westfriese Flora flower exhibition in Bovenkarspel, North Holland, Netherlands, when attendees were exposed to aerosolized water from a contaminated whirlpool spa on display. The outbreak rapidly grew into one of the largest legionellosis outbreaks ever recorded, with hundreds of people becoming ill (about 188 cases meeting the outbreak’s strict case definition and over 30 deaths, with some sources reporting up to 318 ill persons) and at least 32 deaths, prompting extensive epidemiologic, environmental, and serologic investigations to identify the common source. Control was achieved after closure of the exhibition, decontamination of implicated equipment, and implementation of strengthened national surveillance and legionella control regulations for public water systems and spa devices.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Indoor public exhibition with a whirlpool spa producing aerosols in a crowded hall, inadequate disinfection and monitoring of spa water, and environmental conditions favorable for Legionella growth and dispersal. Internal mechanisms: No clearly documented novel strain or resistance; outbreak due mainly to amplification of an existing environmental strain of Legionella pneumophila in the spa system (no specific internal evolutionary change demonstrated).
Review: Retain – This flower‑show outbreak is consistently cited (alongside the 1976 Philadelphia event and the 2001 Murcia outbreak) as one of the largest Legionnaires’ disease clusters ever recorded, with roughly 188 outbreak‑defined cases and >30 deaths, so it clearly belongs among the top global post‑1990 events. Geographic assignment to Europe/Western Europe and the Netherlands is correct, and classification as re‑occurrence (with no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence component) is appropriate given the long‑standing presence of L. pneumophila in Europe. Reported case counts vary because different authors use broader or stricter case definitions; the event summary now notes this but no change to emergence‑type coding is required.

EPP.scientific.name: Legionella pneumophila
EPP.common.name: Legionnaires’ disease
Host: Humans (visitors and passers‑by near a public aquarium)
Event.summary: Between 11 and 27 April 2000, a large outbreak of Legionnaires’ disease occurred in Melbourne, Australia, centered on visitors and people passing near the newly opened Melbourne Aquarium, after aerosols from contaminated cooling towers disseminated Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1. Epidemiologic investigations and case–control studies identified 125 confirmed cases (and more than 140 affected individuals in some reports) and at least 4 deaths, making it the largest legionellosis outbreak recorded in Australia. The outbreak ended after the aquarium was closed, its cooling towers were disinfected, and Victoria introduced stricter regulations and mandatory reporting for legionellosis and cooling‑tower maintenance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Newly commissioned building with poorly controlled cooling‑tower water, high visitor traffic in a confined urban area, favorable warm temperatures, and gaps in regulation/maintenance of cooling water systems prior to the event. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of novel genotype or resistance; the outbreak was driven by environmental amplification and aerosolization of an established L. pneumophila serogroup 1 strain (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) at local scale but primarily environmental/system failure rather than pathogen evolution).
Review: Review – The Melbourne Aquarium outbreak (125 confirmed cases, 4 deaths) is Australia’s largest Legionnaires’ disease event and is frequently highlighted in international reviews, but when global outbreaks since 1990 are ranked by a simple composite of cases plus deaths it falls just below several even higher‑impact events (e.g. Alcalá 1996, Pas‑de‑Calais 2003–2004, Seven Oaks 2005, Quebec City 2012, South Bronx 2015, Manzanares 2015–2016). The event itself is well‑documented, correctly located in Oceania/Australia and appropriately coded as re‑occurrence, so the row should be retained for now but is flagged as a borderline candidate for exclusion if the dataset must be restricted to the absolute top ten global outbreaks.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Legionella pneumophila
EPP.common.name: Legionnaires’ disease
Host: Humans (community outbreak affecting city residents, many elderly or with comorbidities)
Event.summary: In July 2001, an explosive community outbreak of Legionnaires’ disease occurred in the city of Murcia in southeastern Spain, with patients beginning to present on 7 July after exposure to contaminated aerosols in the urban environment. Over 800 suspected cases were reported, of which 449 were laboratory‑confirmed and 6 patients died, making this the largest recorded Legionnaires’ disease outbreak worldwide by number of cases; investigation traced the source to hospital cooling towers located in the northeastern part of the city. After identification and disinfection of the implicated cooling towers and implementation of public‑health control measures, the outbreak subsided within weeks, and Spain strengthened monitoring and regulations for cooling‑tower systems.

The patient experienced persistent bloodstream infection caused by a blaVIM‑1‑positive P. mirabilis strain that was highly resistant to carbapenems and multiple other agents. This case showed that VIM‑1‑producing P. mirabilis had reached Italian hospitals and reinforced concerns about limited therapeutic options for severe Proteus infections in southern Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional dissemination of carbapenemase‑producing Enterobacterales within southern Europe, together with ongoing carbapenem use in Italian hospitals, created opportunities for acquisition of blaVIM‑1 by local P. mirabilis strains; delays in detecting MBL producers and implementing control measures may have allowed silent spread. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence via Novel Genotype – introduction of the blaVIM‑1 metallo‑β‑lactamase into Italian P. mirabilis; Antimicrobial Resistance – broad resistance severely restricted treatment options; Enhanced Transmission – clonal spread and/or plasmid transfer from existing VIM‑1 reservoirs in other species facilitated appearance of resistant P. mirabilis in a new national setting.
Review: Review – Event corresponds to Italy’s first VIM‑1‑producing Proteus mirabilis and documents geographic extension of MBL-mediated carbapenem resistance within southern Europe, but it is based on a single patient and is therefore of limited size. It is nevertheless potentially among the top ten events for this EPP because VIM‑1 carbapenemase in P. mirabilis remains rare. Classification has been corrected by setting Intra‑continental emergence=No (the species was long present in Europe; this is a new resistant genotype) and ensuring the event is treated purely as Re‑emergence=Yes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Proteus spp.
EPP.common.name: Proteus infection
Host: Humans (clinical Proteus mirabilis isolates from two geographically distinct US locations)
Event.summary: Between 2009 and 2015, a novel metallo‑β‑lactamase gene, blaIMP‑27, was identified in unrelated Proteus mirabilis isolates from two geographically distinct sites in the United States, with one isolate recovered in 2009 and another in 2015. Both isolates carried blaIMP‑27 within a class 2 integron, and the later isolate harbored the gene on both chromosome and plasmids, indicating successful integration and potential for horizontal transfer. This marked the emergence of a new carbapenemase lineage in P. mirabilis within North America and expanded the diversity of carbapenem resistance mechanisms documented in this species, even though IMP‑27‑producing isolates remained rare.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued reliance on carbapenems and broad‑spectrum β‑lactams for severe infections in US hospitals created selection pressure for novel carbapenemase producers; integron‑ and plasmid‑mediated gene flow among Enterobacterales facilitated independent emergence of IMP‑27‑positive P. mirabilis in distinct regions. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – first identification of the IMP‑27 metallo‑β‑lactamase in Proteus mirabilis; Antimicrobial Resistance – IMP‑27 conferred resistance to carbapenems and other β‑lactams; Enhanced Transmission – localization of blaIMP‑27 in a class 2 integron and on plasmids increased mobility and the potential for broader dissemination across strains and institutions.
Review: Review – Event accurately summarizes the first reports of IMP‑27, the first IMP‑type metallo‑β‑lactamase identified in Proteus mirabilis, in two US locations over a six‑year span. It is mechanistically important but based on only two known isolates, so its ranking among the ten most impactful events is borderline and should be revisited as more epidemiological data accumulate. Classification has been corrected by changing First detection=No (reflecting that Proteus infections were long recognized) and Intra‑continental emergence=No, with the episode treated as Re‑emergence=Yes (novel carbapenemase genotype) rather than geographic emergence of the species.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Proteus spp.
EPP.common.name: Proteus infection
Host: Humans (community and non‑tertiary‑care urinary tract infections due to Proteus mirabilis)
Event.summary: In the early 2010s, a study of uropathogens causing urinary tract infections in the Andaman Islands, India, reported the first detection of New Delhi metallo‑β‑lactamase‑1 (NDM‑1) in Proteus mirabilis, with two clinical isolates carrying the blaNDM‑1 gene among multidrug‑resistant uropathogens. These infections occurred largely in community or non‑tertiary‑care settings, indicating spread of NDM‑1 into P. mirabilis outside major referral hospitals. The episode signaled that NDM‑1, initially described in other Enterobacterales, had expanded its host range to Proteus spp., adding another highly problematic carbapenemase to the Proteus resistance repertoire in South Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Broad community and hospital use of carbapenems and other antibiotics in India, combined with high regional prevalence of blaNDM‑1 in Enterobacterales and environmental dissemination of NDM‑1 via sewage and water, created conditions for spillover of NDM‑1 into Proteus mirabilis; travel and referral networks likely facilitated wider regional spread of NDM‑positive strains.
