Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – transfer of blaNDM‑1 from other Enterobacterales into Proteus mirabilis; Antimicrobial Resistance – NDM‑1 confers resistance to nearly all β‑lactams (except aztreonam) and is often linked to additional resistance determinants, greatly limiting therapeutic options; Re‑emergence – introduction of a new carbapenemase genotype into an already resistant Proteus population, further increasing the risk of treatment failure and severe outcomes.
Review: Review – Event is supported by a peer‑reviewed study documenting the first NDM‑1‑producing Proteus mirabilis in the Andaman Islands and is highly significant because NDM‑1 is a globally important carbapenemase. Original sources pointing to secondary or less authoritative reports have been replaced with the primary article and major reviews. Classification has been corrected from First detection=Yes to First detection=No and interpreted as Re‑emergence=Yes, consistent with the definition that new resistance mechanisms in an existing pathogen constitute re‑emergence rather than first detection of the EPP in the human host system.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus langyaense
EPP.common.name: Langya virus
Host: Humans (febrile rural patients, mainly farmers; zoonotic spillover from shrews suspected)
Event.summary: Origin: During sentinel surveillance of febrile patients with recent animal exposure at hospitals in Qingdao (Shandong) and Xinyang (Henan), China, in April 2018, metagenomic sequencing of a throat swab from one patient revealed a phylogenetically distinct henipavirus, later named Langya henipavirus (LayV), representing the first recognized human infections with this virus. Development: Expanded testing of similar febrile patients over 2018–2021 identified 35 sporadic human cases in rural parts of Shandong and Henan Provinces, most in farmers with animal contact, presenting with fever and sometimes pneumonia, with LayV as the only detectable pathogen in most acute cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission. Ending/status: By August 2021, the surveillance period underlying the initial report concluded with no deaths and no large clusters, and subsequent monitoring and risk assessments up to at least 2024 describe LayV as an ongoing but rare zoonotic spillover threat confined to eastern China without documented spread to other countries or continents.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Zoonotic exposure of rural farmers to infected small mammals, particularly shrews, likely through occupational or environmental contact in agricultural and peri‑forested settings; increased use of metagenomic next‑generation sequencing and targeted surveillance for febrile patients with animal exposure enabled detection of a pathogen that likely circulated previously at low levels. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – a shrew‑borne henipavirus (with high RNA prevalence in Ussuri white‑toothed shrews, Crocidura lasiura) spilled over into humans, causing sporadic febrile illness; no evidence has yet been found for substantial viral adaptations leading to efficient human‑to‑human transmission, increased virulence, or major antigenic change during this emergence episode.
Review: Decision: Review. Rationale: Retain this event as the single major human emergence episode for Langya virus: 35 sporadic febrile cases detected through sentinel surveillance in Shandong and Henan, China, between April 2018 and August 2021, with no deaths and no sustained human-to-human transmission, consistent with NEJM, ECDC and subsequent reviews. The time window (2018–2021), geography (Asia – Eastern Asia; China [2018]) and host description are correct, and no additional large or distinct human emergence events were identified up to at least 2025. The only substantive correction is to the type-of-emergence coding: to respect the guideline that event-type categories are generally mutually exclusive, this episode is best treated as a first/global emergence in humans (first_global_emergence = true) rather than being simultaneously coded as both first_global_emergence and first_detection, so first_detection has been set to false. Detections of Langya virus RNA in shrews in the Republic of Korea (Gyeonggi and Gangwon provinces) expand knowledge of the wildlife reservoir and geographic range but do not constitute a separate human emergence event and are therefore not encoded as an additional row for the human host system. No other columns or source URLs were changed, but this row is flagged for expert review to confirm the event-type coding choice.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: California encephalitis virus
Host: Human (adult man, 65 years old)
Event.summary: In June 1996, a 65-year-old man residing near brackish marshes in Marin County, California, developed neurologic symptoms including blurred vision and dizziness, and was hospitalized with encephalitis of initially unknown etiology. Over subsequent weeks he recovered clinically, and paired acute and convalescent sera were stored; two years later, retrospective plaque‑reduction neutralization testing demonstrated a fourfold rise in antibody titers specific for California encephalitis virus, confirming the infection and representing the first reported human case due to this prototype virus since three cases in 1945. No additional linked human cases were detected in Marin County or elsewhere, and the episode ended as an isolated, fully resolved case that nonetheless highlighted silent enzootic circulation of California encephalitis virus in coastal California and the potential for rare human disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The case likely resulted from mosquito exposure in coastal salt‑marsh habitats near the patient’s home in Marin County, where several Aedes species are abundant; long‑standing enzootic circulation of California serogroup viruses in California wildlife and horses had been documented, suggesting ongoing environmental suitability for transmission. Increased diagnostic attention and retrospective serologic testing as part of arbovirus research were crucial external factors, enabling recognition of this infection more than two years after illness onset. Internal mechanisms: No evidence was presented for novel strain emergence, increased virulence, host expansion, or enhanced transmission; the case is interpreted as a sporadic human spillover from an existing enzootic cycle of the established California encephalitis virus rather than a biologically driven re‑emergence.
Review: retain – This row correctly captures the only confirmed post-1990 human case attributable specifically to California encephalitis virus (Marin County, California, 1996), with accurate year, continent, subregion, and country coding, and an appropriate host description. Classification as a re-occurrence (and not first emergence, intra-/inter-continental emergence, or re-emergence) is consistent with the historical record, in which the virus and human disease were already documented in California in the 1940s and no viral or epidemiologic shift was reported. No additional major emergence events (outbreaks, geographic spread, or multiple human cases) attributable to this virus were identified for 1990–2025, and the primary source (CDC EID case report) plus supporting background references are appropriate for the event.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus lacrosseense
EPP.common.name: La Crosse virus; California encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (primarily children; pediatric neuroinvasive disease)
Event.summary: From 1997 to 1999, La Crosse virus disease was newly recognized as an emerging cause of pediatric encephalitis in eastern Tennessee and adjacent parts of the central Appalachian region, extending the long‑standing focus centered in West Virginia into new counties in Tennessee and southeastern Kentucky and reinforcing risk in western North Carolina. Case reports in Tennessee increased sharply compared with the preceding three decades, and the affected counties in the Ridge‑and‑Valley and Cumberland Plateau physiographic provinces became recognized as a new southeastern endemic focus. After this period, La Crosse virus remained a recurrent cause of seasonal pediatric neuroinvasive disease in the central Appalachians, with eastern Tennessee and western North Carolina joining West Virginia and Ohio as key endemic areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid suburban and exurban development in mixed hardwood forest created abundant natural and artificial container habitats (tree holes, discarded tires, buckets) close to homes, while relatively low use of air‑conditioning and window screens in rural housing increased mosquito–child contact. Internal mechanisms: Host/vector expansion and enhanced transmission associated with invasive container‑breeding mosquitoes—especially Aedes albopictus, from which La Crosse virus was first isolated in the field in eastern Tennessee during this period, and, as later documented, Aedes japonicus in the broader Appalachian region—likely amplified virus circulation and helped spread human disease into new foci.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This event appropriately represents the late‑1990s emergence of La Crosse virus disease in eastern Tennessee and neighboring Appalachian areas and is among the most consequential recent episodes for this pathogen. I revised the narrative to clarify that West Virginia already had recognized endemic transmission before 1997, to emphasize Aedes albopictus as the invasive vector documented during the 1997–1999 cluster, and to note that Aedes japonicus involvement was demonstrated later rather than coinciding exactly with this outbreak. Classification as re‑emergence driven by vector expansion and ecological change, without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, is retained but should be checked by a subject‑matter expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus lacrosseense
EPP.common.name: La Crosse virus; California encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (children and adolescents; neuroinvasive and non‑neuroinvasive disease)
Event.summary: Between 1999 and 2008, central and southern West Virginia experienced a prolonged period of unusually high La Crosse encephalitis incidence, with 251 reported human cases concentrated in a small number of rural, heavily forested counties. Repeated summer peaks of pediatric disease made La Crosse virus the predominant mosquito‑borne infection in the state and an important cause of childhood central nervous system infection in affected communities. After 2008, annual case counts declined somewhat but the same cluster of counties continued to report recurrent cases, indicating entrenched local transmission rather than a single short‑lived outbreak.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rural housing embedded within mixed hardwood forest, with many natural and artificial container habitats and limited use of window screens or air‑conditioning, created intense exposure of children to tree‑hole and container‑breeding mosquitoes; land‑use change and forest fragmentation around homes further increased mosquito–human contact, while local vector‑control capacity remained limited. Internal mechanisms: High local densities of the primary vector Aedes triseriatus, and possibly additional container‑breeding Aedes species, supported efficient enzootic transmission and spillover to humans, sustaining elevated incidence without evidence of a distinct new viral lineage.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The 1999–2008 West Virginia episode, including the total of 251 reported cases and the restriction of most illness to a small set of rural counties, is well supported by state surveillance data and clearly qualifies as one of the largest La Crosse virus disease clusters since 1990. I changed the emergence‑type coding from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence, because the high incidence appears to be driven mainly by environmental, housing, and socio‑economic conditions in long‑affected areas rather than by documented changes in the virus or a new host jump. Geographic fields (continent, sub‑region, country) are correct and did not require modification.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus lacrosseense
EPP.common.name: La Crosse virus; California encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (predominantly children; nationally reported neuroinvasive cases)
Event.summary: From 2003 through 2012, national surveillance recorded 754 cases of La Crosse virus neuroinvasive disease, representing a peak decade of reporting since the infection became nationally notifiable. Most cases occurred in children, and the burden of severe disease shifted from the historic upper‑Midwestern focus toward the Appalachian region: West Virginia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Ohio together accounted for the great majority of pediatric cases, with more than half of the national burden concentrated in roughly 30 high‑incidence counties within these four states. After 2012, reported case numbers decreased somewhat, but La Crosse virus remained the leading cause of pediatric arboviral encephalitis in the United States, with disease still clustering in the same Appalachian and selected Midwestern communities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased human residence and recreation in newly urbanizing and suburbanizing forest edges across the Appalachian region, together with improved clinical recognition and reporting of arboviral encephalitis, amplified detection of severe pediatric disease due to La Crosse virus; in some years, warmer conditions may also have prolonged mosquito seasons. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion within the eastern United States and altered transmission ecology involving both the native vector Aedes triseriatus and invasive container‑breeding mosquitoes increased overall vectorial capacity in affected communities, sustaining high transmission to children without clear evidence for a novel viral genotype.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This row accurately summarizes the 2003–2012 decade of nationally reported La Crosse virus neuroinvasive disease, including the overall case count, predominance of pediatric illness, and concentration of cases in high‑incidence Appalachian counties. I reclassified the emergence type from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence, because the evidence points to intensified transmission and improved surveillance in regions where the virus was already established rather than to the appearance of a distinct new viral strain or a shift into a new continent or UN sub‑region. The time span and geography overlap with the 2003–2021 persistent‑cluster event, so users who prefer strictly non‑overlapping episodes may wish to merge or restructure these two rows, but both are among the highest‑impact episodes and are retained here for now.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus lacrosseense
EPP.common.name: La Crosse virus; California encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (neuroinvasive and non‑neuroinvasive La Crosse virus disease)
Event.summary: Between 2003 and 2021, county‑level analyses of La Crosse virus neuroinvasive disease showed that most US cases arose from a limited set of persistent hotspots in Appalachia and the upper Midwest. Five states—Ohio, North Carolina, West Virginia, Tennessee, and Wisconsin—accounted for about 87% of reported neuroinvasive cases, and repeated spatial‑cluster analyses identified stable high‑risk groupings of counties in southern Ohio, central and southern West Virginia, eastern Tennessee, and western North Carolina. Many other states with competent vectors reported few or no human cases, indicating that La Crosse virus transmission has become highly focal and entrenched in specific ecological and socio‑demographic settings rather than broadly distributed across all areas where the virus and its vectors could potentially occur.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term persistence of ecologically favorable habitats—wooded residential areas with abundant natural and artificial container breeding sites—combined with socio‑economic and behavioral patterns such as outdoor play by children and limited use of personal protective measures, has maintained high child–mosquito contact in a small number of counties; limited, broadly targeted vector control has allowed transmission to continue for decades. Internal mechanisms: Stable maintenance of La Crosse virus in enzootic cycles involving small mammals and Aedes triseriatus, with additional involvement of invasive container‑breeding Aedes species, supports a durable geographic range and entrenched local transmission, producing persistent high‑risk foci rather than short‑lived outbreaks.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This event correctly captures the long‑term pattern of geographically persistent La Crosse virus hotspots in Appalachia and the upper Midwest from 2003–2021, including the concentration of cases in Ohio, North Carolina, West Virginia, Tennessee, and Wisconsin and the stability of county‑level clusters. I changed the emergence‑type coding from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because the episode describes sustained endemic transmission in previously affected areas, not spread into new continents or UN sub‑regions or the unequivocal emergence of a new viral strain. The period and geography overlap substantially with the 2003–2012 high‑incidence event; together, the two rows describe different facets (peak incidence versus long‑term clustering) of a single broad emergence epoch and may be merged at a later curation stage if desired.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
EPP.common.name: Oropouche virus
Host: Humans (urban and peri‑urban populations in Ariquemes and Ouro Preto do Oeste, Rondônia State, western Brazilian Amazon)
Event.summary: In early 1991, a very large outbreak of Oropouche fever occurred in the municipalities of Ariquemes and Ouro Preto do Oeste in Rondônia State, western Brazilian Amazon, after decades of earlier activity in other parts of northern Brazil, with a randomized household survey in Ariquemes alone estimating around 58,574 infections and later reviews suggesting roughly 94,000 infections across both towns. Transmission spread rapidly through recently urbanized settlements at the forest fringe and then declined over the course of 1991 as vector densities fell and control measures were introduced, with no evidence of comparably large recurrences in the same localities in subsequent years.([wwwn.cdc.gov](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Arbocat/InformationExchange/54%20-%201991%20December%20searchable.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid frontier settlement, deforestation and agricultural expansion in Rondônia created dense human populations living near forest edges with abundant breeding sites for Culicoides paraensis biting midges, enabling explosive urban and peri‑urban transmission once the virus was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Available virological data do not indicate a novel lineage emerging uniquely in this outbreak; the event is best interpreted as a large re‑occurrence in a previously affected Amazonian sub‑region driven mainly by ecological and social factors rather than documented viral evolution.
Review: Retain – This is a well‑documented, extremely large 1991 epidemic in Ariquemes and Ouro Preto do Oeste, estimated at tens of thousands to ~94,000 infections, clearly among the highest‑impact Oropouche events since 1990; location and timing match primary reports, and classification as re‑occurrence (rather than emergence) within an already endemic Amazonian sub‑region is consistent with the project definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
EPP.common.name: Oropouche virus
Host: Humans (residents of Iquitos and surrounding communities in Loreto Department, Peruvian Amazon)
Event.summary: In 1992, Oropouche virus was identified for the first time in Peru during a small outbreak of acute febrile illness in Iquitos, Loreto, with five laboratory‑confirmed human cases and serologic evidence of wider exposure, representing westward spread across the Amazon basin from foci in Brazil and Panama. Subsequent investigations and long‑term serosurveys showed that Oropouche virus became established as an endemic and epidemic pathogen in and around Iquitos, with recurrent local outbreaks in the 1990s and 2000s, although the initial 1992 episode itself involved relatively few confirmed cases.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jme/article/42/4/554/911154?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Population movement and trade along Amazonian river networks and ongoing deforestation and urban expansion near Iquitos likely facilitated introduction from Brazil and favored sustained midges–human transmission once the virus arrived. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicate that early Peruvian strains were closely related to Brazilian genotype II viruses, without clear evidence of a novel reassortant at that time, so this event is interpreted as a re‑occurrence and geographic spread within an already affected South America sub‑region rather than intra‑continental emergence into a new UN sub‑region.
Review: Review – Event is correctly identified as the first recognized Peruvian epidemic in Iquitos and is important for establishing endemicity, but the emergence type has been corrected: because Peru lies in the same UN sub‑region (“South America”) where Oropouche virus was already established, this episode is better classified as re‑occurrence (continued spread within an endemic sub‑region) rather than intra‑continental emergence into a new sub‑region.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
EPP.common.name: Oropouche virus
Host: Humans (residents of rural riverine communities in Parauapebas and Porto de Moz, Pará State, northern Brazil)
Event.summary: From 2003 to 2004, Oropouche fever re‑emerged in Pará State, northern Brazil, with outbreaks detected in rural communities near Parauapebas and Porto de Moz after more than a decade without recognized epidemics in this part of the Amazon; targeted house‑to‑house surveys found dozens of recent febrile illnesses with Oropouche IgM and multiple virus isolates. Phylogenetic analysis showed that outbreak strains belonged mainly to genotype II and suggested either introduction of this lineage from western Amazonia or its expansion after a period of cryptic circulation, after which reported transmission in these localities declined again.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2792853/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased human occupation of forested riverine areas, road building and extraction activities in eastern Pará likely increased human exposure to biting midges and facilitated virus amplification in small, closely connected communities. Internal mechanisms: Molecular data demonstrate the presence and expansion of genotype II Oropouche virus in this region, representing a shift in circulating lineages and justifying classification as re‑emergence driven by viral genotype dynamics rather than simple recurrence of a previously dominant lineage.
Review: Review – New row added to capture the 2003–2004 Parauapebas and Porto de Moz outbreaks, which marked documented re‑emergence of Oropouche fever and genotype II circulation in Pará after a long hiatus and are consistently highlighted in reviews as important post‑1990 events; classified as re‑emergence (genotype shift) within the existing South America sub‑region.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
EPP.common.name: Oropouche virus
Host: Humans (urban and rural residents of Magalhães Barata, Maracanã and nearby municipalities in the Bragantina region, eastern Pará, Brazil)
Event.summary: In 2006, a major Oropouche fever epidemic occurred in the Magalhães Barata–Maracanã area of the Bragantina region in eastern Pará State, Brazil, an area that had not reported such an epidemic since the early 1980s, with estimates of roughly 17,000–18,000 suspected cases based on community surveys and clinical surveillance. Intensive serologic testing and virus isolation confirmed widespread recent infection, and molecular characterization showed co‑circulation of genotypes I and II, indicating the return and amplification of Oropouche virus on a large scale in a previously quiet region of northern Brazil.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1386653208003995?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rural land‑use change, small‑scale agriculture and livestock production, and dense human settlement in the Bragantina region likely increased contact between humans, reservoir hosts and Culicoides vectors, enabling sustained transmission once the virus was reintroduced. Internal mechanisms: Genetic studies documented co‑circulation of distinct Oropouche genotypes and the presence of genotype II in eastern Pará, supporting interpretation of this epidemic as viral re‑emergence involving lineage expansion and dispersal into areas without recognized activity for more than two decades.
Review: Review – New row added for the 2006 Magalhães Barata & Maracanã epidemic, which multiple reviews and outbreak reconstructions identify as a major post‑1990 event (~17,000–18,000 cases) and a key example of Oropouche re‑emergence with documented genotype co‑circulation; previously omitted despite clearly being among the highest‑impact outbreaks in the target period.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
EPP.common.name: Oropouche virus
Host: Humans (primarily urban residents of Manaus, Amazonas State, Brazil)
Event.summary: Between 2007 and 2008, Oropouche fever was recognized as a cause of acute febrile illness in Manaus, the capital of Amazonas State, when testing of 631 dengue‑ and malaria‑negative patients identified Oropouche virus infection in a notable fraction of cases, revealing an under‑recognized outbreak affecting multiple urban neighborhoods. Although the number of confirmed infections was modest compared with historic Amazonian epidemics, the event highlighted Oropouche virus as a significant contributor to non‑specific febrile illness in a large metropolis and prompted strengthened surveillance; reported transmission declined after 2008 as seasonal conditions changed and control measures were implemented.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3044544/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid, often unplanned expansion of Manaus into surrounding forest, high human population density, inadequate vector control and diagnostic focus on dengue and malaria delayed recognition of Oropouche virus circulation and facilitated urban amplification. Internal mechanisms: Available sequence data indicate circulation of previously known genotypes without firm evidence for a distinct new lineage associated uniquely with this outbreak, so it is treated as a large urban re‑occurrence rather than a clear-cut re‑emergence event.
Review: Retain – The Manaus 2007–2008 outbreak is well supported by primary sources, illustrates important urban transmission in a major Amazonian city, and fits the definition of a high‑impact re‑occurrence within an endemic sub‑region; geographic fields and emergence‑type coding (re‑occurrence only) remain appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
EPP.common.name: Oropouche virus
Host: Humans (residents of Bagazán village, San Martín Department, northern Peruvian Amazon)
Event.summary: In May 2010, the remote village of Bagazán (≈1,000 inhabitants) in San Martín Department, Peru, experienced an explosive outbreak of acute febrile illness, where serologic testing during the investigation found Oropouche IgM in 108 of 171 sampled residents, indicating a high attack rate and confirming the third documented Peruvian Oropouche outbreak. The episode, which featured gastrointestinal and hemorrhagic manifestations in some patients, subsided over several weeks as vector control was intensified and seasonal conditions changed, though Oropouche virus has since continued to circulate more broadly in Peru.([revistagastroperu.com](https://revistagastroperu.com/index.php/rgp/article/view/421?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Construction of regional roads and associated deforestation and land‑use change around Bagazán are thought to have altered local ecosystems and favored the spread of vectors and reservoir hosts into human settlements, echoing patterns seen in earlier Oropouche outbreaks linked to environmental disturbance. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genetic variant was reported from this outbreak; available evidence suggests expansion of existing Amazonian lineages into a new focus within the same South America sub‑region, so it is classified as a re‑occurrence driven mainly by ecological and socio‑environmental factors.
Review: Review – New row added for the 2010 Bagazán outbreak, which produced >100 serologically confirmed cases in a small community and is consistently cited as a major modern Peruvian Oropouche epidemic linked to environmental change; classified as re‑occurrence within the endemic South America sub‑region.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
EPP.common.name: Oropouche virus
Host: Humans (residents of multiple districts in northern Cusco Region and parts of Madre de Dios, southeastern Peruvian Amazon)
Event.summary: In early 2016, Peru reported a substantial Oropouche fever epidemic in the Amazonian districts of northern Cusco Region, with 57 confirmed cases, alongside a contemporaneous mixed dengue–Oropouche outbreak in neighboring Madre de Dios that reached around 120 confirmed cases, marking the first time Cusco had recorded Oropouche fever and a larger‑than‑previously documented resurgence in Madre de Dios. Epidemiologic and remote‑sensing analyses linked human case clusters to areas with recent vegetation loss and land‑cover change, and reported transmission declined later in 2016 as control measures were implemented and vector‑favorable conditions waned.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/03-june-2016-oropouche-peru-en?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Road building, agricultural frontier expansion and associated deforestation in the valleys of the Apurímac, Ene and Mantaro rivers and surrounding Amazonian foothills likely increased human exposure to vectors and facilitated movement of infected humans or vectors into new communities. Internal mechanisms: Although Peruvian work has identified reassortant viruses related to Oropouche (e.g., Iquitos and Madre de Dios viruses), the 2016 Cusco/Madre de Dios epidemic is primarily attributed to spread of known Oropouche‑complex viruses into new localities rather than the emergence of a clearly distinct genotype, so it is treated as a re‑occurrence driven mainly by environmental perturbation and ongoing lineage circulation.
Review: Review – New row added to represent the 2016 epidemic affecting Cusco and Madre de Dios, which WHO and subsequent eco‑epidemiological analyses describe as the most recent sizable Peruvian Oropouche outbreak before 2023 and the first recorded in Cusco; coded as re‑occurrence within South America because it reflects resurgence and geographic spread in an already endemic country and sub‑region.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
EPP.common.name: Oropouche virus
Host: Humans (patients in Esmeraldas city and surrounding communities on the Pacific coast of northwestern Ecuador)
Event.summary: In 2016, metagenomic sequencing followed by targeted qRT‑PCR in patients with acute febrile illness in Esmeraldas, on Ecuador’s Pacific coast, identified Oropouche virus RNA and led to isolation of the virus from at least one patient and detection of a cluster of six autochthonous cases, representing the first confirmed human Oropouche virus infections in Ecuador and the first recognized focus on the Pacific coast of South America. Phylogenetic analysis showed that the Ecuadorian strain clustered closely with Oropouche viruses from Peru (2008), indicating spread of an existing Amazonian lineage into a new coastal setting rather than a novel reassortant; no large follow‑on outbreaks were reported immediately thereafter, although later regional data suggest continued low‑level circulation prior to the 2023–2025 expansion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5938787/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of infected humans or vectors along trade and transport routes between Amazonian Peru and Ecuador, combined with suitable humid coastal climate and limited routine arboviral testing, likely enabled silent establishment of Oropouche virus in Esmeraldas before detection. Internal mechanisms: Genomic studies indicate that the 2016 Ecuadorian virus belongs to a lineage already circulating in Peru and is not a novel reassortant, so this event is interpreted as a geographically important re‑occurrence within the existing South America sub‑region rather than intra‑continental emergence into a new UN sub‑region or re‑emergence driven by viral change.
Review: Review – The event (first confirmed human infections in Ecuador and first recognized Pacific‑coast focus) is correctly identified as epidemiologically important, but emergence‑type coding has been revised from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence because Ecuador lies in the same UN South America sub‑region where Oropouche virus had long been established; molecular data support spread of an existing lineage, not a novel reassortant.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
EPP.common.name: Oropouche virus
Host: Humans (adult woman with acute febrile illness in northern Colombia; autochthonous infection)
Event.summary: In 2017, an autochthonous human Oropouche virus infection was retrospectively identified in a 28‑year‑old woman in Colombia who presented with acute febrile illness, providing the first confirmed human Oropouche virus case in the country and evidence that the virus had expanded into northern South America beyond previously recognized foci. Sequencing showed that the Colombian virus was closely related to the 2016 Esmeraldas strain from Ecuador, implying recent cross‑border spread of an Amazonian lineage; no large outbreaks were documented immediately afterward, but later studies have detected additional Oropouche infections in Colombia, indicating ongoing, though under‑recognized, circulation.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/27/6/20-4405_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intense human movement and trade along the upper Amazon and Andean foothills, and limited routine inclusion of Oropouche virus in Colombia’s febrile‑illness diagnostics, likely allowed low‑level transmission to go undetected until this case was sequenced. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic relatedness of the Colombian strain to the Ecuadorian 2016 virus supports stepwise geographic spread of an established lineage rather than emergence of a new genotype, so the episode is classified as a re‑occurrence within the endemic South America sub‑region.
Review: Review – The first confirmed human Oropouche virus infection in Colombia is correctly captured as an important geographic expansion signal, but emergence type has been changed from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence because the virus was already established in the South America UN sub‑region and genetic data show close continuity with earlier Ecuadorian–Peruvian lineages rather than a distinct new genotype.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus toroense
EPP.common.name: Punta Toro virus
Host: Humans (febrile patients; mainly urban and peri-urban residents in Panamá, Panamá Oeste, Veraguas, and Los Santos provinces)([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/5/16-1925_article?utm_source=openai))
Event.summary: In 2009, during a large dengue and influenza outbreak in Panama, the Gorgas Memorial Institute re‑tested 4,852 suspected dengue cases and found 27 laboratory-confirmed human infections with Punta Toro virus species complex, marking a notable reappearance of the virus roughly 40 years after its first human detection in the country.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/5/16-1925_article?utm_source=openai)) These cases were concentrated in the Panama City metropolitan area but also occurred in Veraguas, Los Santos and Panamá Oeste, demonstrating both urban and rural transmission across several provinces.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/5/16-1925_article?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak subsided as the dengue/influenza season waned, with all identified Punta Toro virus infections described as self‑limited febrile illnesses without severe outcomes in this series.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/5/16-1925_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: (1) Co‑circulation with dengue and influenza during a national febrile-illness surge led to extensive sample collection and the subsequent re‑testing of dengue‑negative sera, which enabled recognition of Punta Toro virus as a contributor to the outbreak.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/5/16-1925_article?utm_source=openai)) (2) Urbanization and human encroachment into forested or peri‑urban habitats where sandfly vectors are present likely increased human–vector contact, as most confirmed cases came from urban and peri‑urban zones despite the presumed rural ecology of sandflies.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/5/16-1925_article?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain, virulence shift, or resistance phenotype was reported; infections were attributed to members of the existing Punta Toro virus species complex, so the event is best interpreted as re‑occurrence revealed by improved diagnostics rather than virus evolution.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/5/16-1925_article?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Literature review confirms that during Panama’s 2009 dengue/influenza outbreak, re‑testing of 4,852 suspected dengue cases identified 27 Punta Toro virus species complex infections concentrated in the Panama City metropolitan area and nearby provinces; the geographic coding (South America/Central America, Panama [2009]) and classification as a re‑occurrence in a previously known area after first isolation in the 1960s are consistent with primary sources, so no changes were made.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus toroense
EPP.common.name: Punta Toro virus
Host: Humans (febrile patients with dengue‑negative samples identified through passive arboviral surveillance)([prensa.com](https://www.prensa.com/impresa/panorama/virus-punta-mirada-cientifica-Gorgas_0_5258474189.html))
Event.summary: Following retrospective characterization of the 2009 outbreak, Gorgas Institute and Panama’s Ministry of Health introduced passive laboratory surveillance for Punta Toro virus in dengue‑negative febrile cases, and in 2014 this system detected two additional human infections, confirming continued low‑level circulation after the 2009 rebrote.([prensa.com](https://www.prensa.com/impresa/panorama/virus-punta-mirada-cientifica-Gorgas_0_5258474189.html)) These cases occurred within the same general provinces previously affected (Panamá, Panamá Oeste, Veraguas and Los Santos), but were individual detections rather than part of a large, recognized outbreak.([prensa.com](https://www.prensa.com/impresa/panorama/virus-punta-mirada-cientifica-Gorgas_0_5258474189.html)) The illnesses were self‑limited, and no wider transmission clusters or severe disease were reported, so the episode ended as routine surveillance returned to baseline without specific Punta Toro–targeted interventions.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/5/16-1925_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: (1) Implementation of ongoing passive surveillance that tested dengue‑negative samples for Punta Toro virus directly enabled recognition of sporadic human infections that would otherwise have been misclassified as undifferentiated febrile illness.([prensa.com](https://www.prensa.com/impresa/panorama/virus-punta-mirada-cientifica-Gorgas_0_5258474189.html)) (2) Persistent ecological suitability for sandfly vectors and vertebrate reservoirs in both rural and expanding peri‑urban areas of Panama likely maintained a stable but low‑level zoonotic transmission cycle.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4681062/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No evidence was presented for emergence of a new viral lineage, host jump, or resistance trait; thus this represents re‑occurrence due largely to improved surveillance rather than intrinsic viral change.
Review: retain – The La Prensa interview with Gorgas investigators documents two Punta Toro virus cases detected in 2014 through passive testing of dengue‑negative samples in the same Panamanian provinces that experienced the 2009 outbreak; treating this as a small re‑occurrence within Panama with continent/sub‑region coded as South America/Central America is consistent with the source data, so the row is kept unchanged.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus toroense
EPP.common.name: Punta Toro virus
Host: Humans (one laboratory-confirmed Punta Toro virus infection in a symptomatic contact of an Oropouche virus case, detected through enhanced arboviral surveillance of dengue‑negative samples)([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/32/1/25-1224_article?utm_source=openai))
Event.summary: In 2023–2024, an enhanced surveillance project in Panama re‑analyzed 3,589 dengue‑negative arboviral samples using broad PCR panels, and in August 2024 it detected an Oropouche virus infection in a 31‑year‑old environmental officer working in Soberanía National Park; contact tracing around this index case identified one additional symptomatic contact whose sample was positive for the Phlebovirus genus and subsequently confirmed as Punta Toro virus by sequencing.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/32/1/25-1224_article?utm_source=openai)) The Punta Toro virus case presented with nonspecific febrile illness (fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, retro‑orbital pain and conjunctivitis) and was detected as part of a broader investigation into overlooked arboviruses, rather than a discrete Punta Toro outbreak.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/32/1/25-1224_article?utm_source=openai)) No additional Punta Toro virus cluster or severe disease was reported, but the finding reinforced that the virus continues to circulate cryptically in Panama and is usually missed by routine dengue‑focused diagnostics.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/32/1/25-1224_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: (1) Targeted enhanced arboviral surveillance that systematically re‑tested dengue‑negative samples across 2023–2024 was the principal driver of this event’s recognition, enabling detection of both an early Oropouche virus case and a single Punta Toro virus infection and highlighting under‑diagnosed arboviruses in Panama.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/32/1/25-1224_article?utm_source=openai)) (2) Both case-patients worked in or near mature broadleaf forest adjacent to the Soberanía National Park, underscoring the role of sylvatic or peri‑sylvatic environments and outdoor occupations in bringing humans into contact with sandfly and other arbovirus vectors.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/32/1/25-1224_article?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Sequence comparison showed the 2024 Punta Toro virus strain to be genetically divergent from older reference strains but very similar to a 2004 Panamanian sequence, suggesting gradual evolution rather than emergence of a novel genotype; thus this episode is best interpreted as a small re‑occurrence revealed by more sensitive molecular diagnostics, not evolutionary re‑emergence.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/32/1/25-1224_article?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – This row has been corrected to match the 2026 Emerging Infectious Diseases report: enhanced surveillance over 2023–2024 analyzed dengue‑negative samples but identified a single Punta Toro virus infection in 2024 in a symptomatic contact of an Oropouche virus case, not two PTV infections in an index patient plus contact. The event year has been set to 2024, the countries field updated to 'Panama [2024]', and the host, event_summary and mechanism_or_driver text revised accordingly; classification as a small re‑occurrence within Panama still appears appropriate but should be confirmed by a human reviewer.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bandavirus dabieense
EPP.common.name: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus; SFTSV
Host: Humans (largely older adults with outdoor exposure; infections linked to tick bites and occasionally animal contact)
Event.summary: In 2012, South Korea documented its first fatal human SFTS case, retrospectively linked to SFTSV and reported in 2013, after which national surveillance was established. Over the subsequent years, hundreds of autochthonous cases were detected annually, with notable peaks such as 223 confirmed cases and 41 deaths in 2019, concentrated in rural and peri‑urban areas of Gangwon and Gyeonggi Provinces. By the late 2010s SFTS had become a recognized endemic tick‑borne disease in South Korea with seasonal surges, though public health messaging and clinical management gradually reduced case‑fatality in some cohorts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high densities of Haemaphysalis longicornis and other ticks in forested and agricultural landscapes, an aging rural population engaged in outdoor work, and enhanced diagnostic testing after the index case; recreational and occupational exposures in wooded hills contributed to risk. Internal mechanisms: regional establishment and geographic spread of existing SFTSV lineages from neighboring endemic areas in China; no unique Korean genotype clearly linked to the emergence, but local viral diversity now reflects multiple introductions and in situ evolution.
Review: retain – accurately summarizes emergence and subsequent endemic transmission of SFTS in the Republic of Korea from 2012 onward; coding as re-occurrence within the already affected Eastern Asia subregion rather than intra-continental emergence is appropriate, and no geographic or temporal corrections are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Bandavirus dabieense
EPP.common.name: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus; SFTSV
Host: Humans (primarily elderly residents of rural western Japan; vector Haemaphysalis longicornis and related ticks)
Event.summary: In early 2013, Japan confirmed its first human SFTS case—a fatal illness in a woman from western Japan—followed by retrospective identification of earlier cases and rapid implementation of national surveillance. Between 2013 and 2019, several hundred confirmed SFTS cases were reported, largely from western prefectures such as Yamaguchi, Ehime and Miyazaki, with an overall case‑fatality proportion around 17–20% and strong age skew toward older adults. By the end of the decade, SFTS was recognized as an endemic tick‑borne hemorrhagic fever in western Japan, with annual but geographically focal summer outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: long‑established populations of competent tick vectors (Haemaphysalis longicornis, Rhipicephalus microplus) in western Japan, extensive forest‑agriculture ecotones and outdoor activities of elderly residents, and enhanced laboratory testing after the first recognized death. Internal mechanisms: geographic expansion and establishment of SFTSV lineages closely related to Chinese strains; sequence analyses indicate multiple introductions and local adaptation but no single hyper‑virulent genotype driving the Japanese emergence.
Review: retain – appropriately captures Japan’s recognition of SFTS from 2013 and subsequent high-fatality endemic foci in western prefectures; re-occurrence coding within Eastern Asia is justified and no corrections to time span, geography or sources are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Bandavirus dabieense
EPP.common.name: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus; SFTSV
Host: Humans (elderly man with mountain exposure; additional sporadic cases thereafter)
Event.summary: In October–November 2019, Taiwan confirmed its first indigenous SFTS case in a man in his seventies with frequent mountain activities and no travel abroad, after he presented with fever, vomiting, rash and altered consciousness and was initially investigated for dengue; molecular testing at the Taiwan CDC subsequently identified SFTSV, with viral sequences closely related to Japanese and Korean strains. In the following years, Taiwan implemented targeted human and animal surveillance, and a second autochthonous human infection was reported in 2022, again in a resident without recent overseas travel, confirming limited local transmission. By the end of 2025, Taiwan had detected only a very small number of sporadic indigenous SFTS cases and no large-scale outbreaks, although environmental and animal data indicated that competent tick vectors and infected vertebrate hosts were present.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: presence of competent tick vectors in mountainous and forested areas across northern Taiwan, outdoor recreational exposure of older adults, and heightened clinical suspicion following extensive arboviral surveillance (e.g., for dengue). Internal mechanisms: introduction of SFTSV into Taiwan, likely via infected ticks on migratory birds or animal movements, followed by limited local transmission; phylogenetic similarity to Japanese/Korean strains suggests recent regional seeding events rather than long‑standing cryptic circulation.
Review: review – corrected the event period from 2017–2020 to 2019–2022 to match the first indigenous human case in 2019 and a second domestic case reported in 2022, and clarified that only a few sporadic cases occurred through 2025; added Taiwan’s notifiable disease statistics system as a supporting source. Coding as re-occurrence within Eastern Asia remains consistent with the subregion-based scheme.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (primarily infants and young children with hand, foot and mouth disease and severe neurologic complications)
Event.summary: In 1997, Sarawak State in Malaysia experienced a large outbreak of hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) in children, with about 600 hospitalised cases and multiple pediatric deaths linked to EV-A71 infection and brainstem encephalitis. The outbreak evolved over several months with increasing recognition of severe cardiopulmonary and neurologic complications, leading to regional alarm and detailed clinico-pathologic investigations that confirmed EV-A71 as the principal etiologic agent. The episode ended after targeted public health measures and the natural waning of transmission, but it marked the first major EV-A71-driven HFMD epidemic recognized in South-eastern Asia and presaged further large regional epidemics.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high density of susceptible young children, childcare and household crowding, and regional travel within Borneo and between Sarawak and peninsular Malaysia likely facilitated rapid local and inter-state spread; limited prior population immunity to the circulating lineages increased impact. Internal mechanisms: emergence and regional establishment of neurotropic EV-A71 B genogroup lineages (including B3) with strong CNS tropism and capacity to cause cardiopulmonary collapse represents novel strain/genotype emergence with increased virulence/pathogenicity relative to earlier, largely mild EV-A71 circulation in the region.
Review: Decision: retain. Corrected intra_continental_emergence from true to false because EV-A71 had already been detected in the same Asian sub-region (South-eastern Asia) before 1997, including isolation in Singapore in 1984 and an EV-A71-associated HFMD/aseptic meningitis outbreak there in 1987. The 1997 Sarawak epidemic is therefore a high-impact regional re-emergence driven by new B genogroup viruses rather than first spread to a new sub-region. Year, geography, host description, impact and mechanisms are consistent with outbreak investigations, and the event clearly belongs among the major global EV-A71 emergence episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (children with HFMD, herpangina, and severe neurologic disease including encephalitis and pulmonary edema)
Event.summary: In 1998, Taiwan experienced a nationwide EV-A71 epidemic that caused thousands of HFMD and herpangina cases and at least 405 severe cases with 78 deaths in children, overwhelming pediatric intensive care capacity. The epidemic spread across all regions of the island over the summer, with EV-A71 identified in the majority of severe neurologic and cardiopulmonary cases, while other enteroviruses caused milder disease. Transmission declined with seasonal changes and intensified control measures, but recurrent EV-A71 waves occurred in subsequent years, making this 1998 event a defining severe re-emergence of EV-A71 in East Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: dense urban populations, extensive daycare and preschool attendance, and high contact rates among young children promoted explosive transmission; lack of pre-existing immunity in recent birth cohorts and delayed recognition of severe disease contributed to high mortality. Internal mechanisms: circulation of virulent EV-A71 genogroup C2 and related B lineages with demonstrated neurotropism and cardiopulmonary complications represents novel strain/genotype emergence and increased virulence/pathogenicity compared with background EV-A71 activity in the region.
Review: Decision: retain. Classification as re-emergence (and re-occurrence) without intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate because EV-A71 was already circulating in Asia, including Taiwan, before 1998, and the 1998 epidemic is widely recognized as a large, severe national outbreak caused mainly by genogroup C2/B viruses rather than first detection of the pathogen. Country, sub-region, time frame, and impact description (thousands of HFMD cases, hundreds of severe CNS cases, 78 deaths) match NEJM and CDC/EID reports, and the event is unquestionably among the most impactful globally.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (children with HFMD and neurologic manifestations such as aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and acute flaccid paralysis)
Event.summary: From February to September 1999, Perth in Western Australia recorded an outbreak of HFMD and associated neurologic disease in children, with EV-A71 isolated from many patients with meningitis, encephalitis and poliomyelitis-like paralysis. The outbreak unfolded over several winter months with a noticeable increase in severe CNS disease compared with prior years, prompting detailed virologic and clinical investigations. Transmission subsided later in the year with the end of the enterovirus season, but the episode demonstrated that highly neurovirulent EV-A71 lineages had expanded into Oceania and could cause polio-like outbreaks outside Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: seasonal climatic conditions favorable for enterovirus transmission, high contact rates in schools and childcare, and travel links with the Asia-Pacific region likely facilitated introduction and local spread of the epidemic strain. Internal mechanisms: the responsible EV-A71 strain showed pronounced neurotropism and was part of rapidly diversifying B and C genogroups circulating in the Asia-Pacific region, representing novel strain/genotype emergence with increased virulence/pathogenicity and geographic range expansion (inherent) into temperate southern latitudes.
Review: Decision: retain but mark for review of relative priority. Corrected intra_continental_emergence from true to false, because EV-A71 had already caused outbreaks in south-eastern Australia in the 1980s, so the 1999 Perth episode represents re-emergence within the same 'Australia and New Zealand' sub-region rather than first introduction to Oceania. The outbreak, although modest in absolute size (dozens of EV-A71 cases with 14 documented neurological infections and no deaths), is consistently cited as the first clearly recognized EV-A71 neuroinvasive outbreak in Western Australia and an important signal of spread beyond Asia; it can reasonably be kept among major events, but its impact is smaller than that of the largest Asian epidemics.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (infants and young children with HFMD and herpangina, including fatal neurologic cases)
Event.summary: In 2000, Singapore experienced its largest recorded HFMD epidemic, with many thousands of pediatric cases and several fatal infections, during which EV-A71 was identified as a major causative agent alongside other enteroviruses. The epidemic developed rapidly over that year, with widespread community transmission and clusters in childcare centers, and EV-A71 detected especially in severe or fatal pediatric cases. The outbreak declined after implementation of extensive control measures including temporary childcare closures, public education and hygiene campaigns, but EV-A71 continued to reappear in later HFMD seasons at lower levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high childcare attendance, dense urban living conditions, and intense social mixing of preschool-aged children amplified EV-A71 transmission; strong travel connectivity within South-eastern Asia likely imported epidemic lineages related to the 1997 Malaysian outbreak. Internal mechanisms: introduction and expansion of an EV-A71 genogroup B4 lineage closely related to the Sarawak 1997 strain, associated with severe neurologic disease, exemplifies novel strain/genotype emergence and increased virulence/pathogenicity in a population with limited prior immunity.
Review: Decision: retain. The event represents Singapore’s largest EV-A71-associated HFMD epidemic to date, with nationwide preschool closures and multiple EV-A71-confirmed pediatric deaths, and is consistently highlighted in regional outbreak reviews and seroepidemiologic analyses. Geographic coding and timing are correct. Classification as re-emergence (and re-occurrence) is appropriate because EV-A71 had been isolated in Singapore since 1984 and had caused outbreaks in the late 1980s, but the 2000 epidemic reflected both viral evolution (B4 genogroup) and accumulation of susceptible young children. The cited EID article and Ministry of Health communications are specific and suitable sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (children with HFMD or herpangina, including cases with severe neurologic complications and fatalities)
Event.summary: From February to August 2006, Brunei Darussalam experienced its first reported major outbreak of EV-A71 infection, with numerous pediatric HFMD and herpangina cases and a subset developing severe neurologic disease, including brainstem encephalitis and neurogenic pulmonary edema, leading to at least two deaths. The outbreak unfolded over several months in parallel with EV-A71 activity in neighboring Sarawak and peninsular Malaysia, and virus isolates from Bruneian patients were typed as subgenogroup B5, forming a distinct but related lineage within the regional B5 cluster. Transmission waned with seasonal decline and intensified control measures, but the episode highlighted Brunei’s vulnerability to imported EV-A71 lineages and its role in the wider Asia-Pacific emergence pattern.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: close travel and trade links with neighboring Malaysian states, crowded childcare and household environments, and a largely EV-A71-naive young population facilitated rapid spread once B5 viruses were introduced. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak was driven by subgenogroup B5 viruses that had recently emerged in the region, representing novel strain/genotype emergence and enhanced transmissibility and neurovirulence compared with earlier EV-A71 lineages circulating in South-eastern Asia.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added event). Added a dedicated row for Brunei Darussalam’s 2006 EV-A71 outbreak because primary reports and regional reviews consistently identify it as the country’s first major EV-A71 epidemic with neurologic complications and fatalities, and as part of the broader Asia-Pacific wave of severe disease in the mid‑2000s. The event is coded as a South-eastern Asia re-emergence (no first_detection or intra-/inter-continental flags) because EV-A71 had already been circulating and causing major outbreaks in neighboring Malaysia and Singapore; the key features—year, country, clinical severity and B5 genotype—are drawn directly from the Brunei outbreak investigations.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (children with HFMD, severe neurologic disease, and cardiopulmonary failure; EV-A71 predominant in severe and fatal cases in Viet Nam)
Event.summary: From 2010 to mid‑2012, Viet Nam experienced very large HFMD epidemics dominated by EV-A71, with 174,677 reported cases and about 200 deaths between February 2011 and July 2012 alone, most in southern provinces. The outbreak intensified through 2011 with over 110,000 cases and 170 deaths, many due to brainstem encephalitis and neurogenic pulmonary edema, and continued at high incidence into early 2012 before declining; virologic typing demonstrated widespread circulation of EV-A71 genogroup C4 in hospitalized and fatal pediatric cases. After enhanced clinical management, public awareness, and seasonal decline, HFMD incidence decreased, but EV-A71 remained endemic with later resurgence waves in the mid‑2010s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high birth rate and large cohorts of susceptible young children, rapid urbanization and crowding in southern Vietnamese cities, and intense regional travel and trade with neighboring Asian countries facilitated repeated introductions and sustained transmission; limited ICU capacity and delayed referral increased fatality in early waves. Internal mechanisms: establishment of EV-A71 subgenogroup C4 (and related C4a) as the dominant severe HFMD pathogen represents novel strain/genotype emergence, and its strong association with brainstem encephalitis and cardiopulmonary failure indicates increased virulence/pathogenicity relative to co-circulating coxsackieviruses; evolutionary adaptation may also have enhanced transmissibility in tropical climates (enhanced transmission).
Review: Decision: retain with correction to the country list. Removed Cambodia from the countries field so that this row now cleanly represents the very large national HFMD/EV-A71 epidemics in Viet Nam (2010–2012); the 2012 Cambodian cluster is handled separately in its own row and should not be treated as a satellite country within the same event. The time window 2010–2012 is consistent with Vietnamese surveillance and outbreak analyses that describe intense activity from 2010 with a peak in 2011–2012, and the magnitude (hundreds of thousands of cases and ~200 deaths) clearly places this episode among the most impactful EV-A71 events. Classification as re-emergence (and re-occurrence) in South-eastern Asia is appropriate because EV-A71 had caused earlier outbreaks in Viet Nam (e.g. 2005) but the 2011–2012 wave had much greater national impact.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (primarily children under 7 years with severe encephalitis, cardiovascular collapse, and pulmonary edema, often without classic HFMD rash)
Event.summary: Between April and July 2012, Cambodia reported a cluster of unexplained severe pediatric illnesses with rapid neurologic deterioration, cardiovascular collapse and pulmonary edema, in which at least 54–64 children died before the etiology was clarified. As the investigation progressed, laboratory testing showed that most sampled cases were infected with EV-A71 subgenogroup C4, often alongside other pathogens, leading WHO and national authorities to conclude that a severe form of EV-A71-associated HFMD, frequently lacking full mucocutaneous signs, was the primary cause. Following public health alerts, improved case recognition, and seasonal decline in enterovirus circulation, no further similar clusters were reported after mid‑July 2012, marking this outbreak as the first documented major EV-A71 emergence in Cambodia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: limited early surveillance capacity and diagnostic infrastructure delayed identification of EV-A71, while healthcare access constraints meant many children presented late with advanced disease; high background circulation of enteroviruses and co-infections (including dengue and bacterial sepsis) may have exacerbated severity; regional spread of epidemic C4 lineages from neighboring countries likely introduced the strain. Internal mechanisms: EV-A71 C4 viruses involved showed strong neurotropism and cardiopulmonary toxicity consistent with increased virulence/pathogenicity, and their emergence in a largely naive pediatric population exemplifies novel strain/genotype emergence and severe re-emergence in this national setting.
Review: Decision: retain with revised emergence typing. Cleared first_detection (set to false) and intra_continental_emergence (set to false), leaving re_emergence as true. Although 2012 was the first reported major EV-A71 outbreak in Cambodia and first virologically confirmed EV-A71-associated HFMD cluster by national authorities, serologic work suggests earlier low-level circulation, and EV-A71 was already well established in the South-eastern Asia sub-region. The event is thus best viewed as a severe national re-emergence driven by introduction and amplification of C4 lineage viruses in a largely susceptible pediatric population. Year, country and the description of dozens of EV-A71-associated encephalitis/pulmonary edema deaths are well supported by WHO, ECDC and EID sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (children with HFMD and herpangina; mixed enterovirus etiology including EV-A71 with a minority of severe/fatal neurologic cases)
Event.summary: In 2012, Thailand experienced an extensive HFMD outbreak, with more than 36,000 reported cases and an incidence about three times higher than average, during which EV-A71 was one of several co-circulating enteroviruses. The outbreak progressed nationwide from early in the year, with laboratory-based surveillance showing that coxsackievirus A6 became the predominant agent, but EV-A71 still accounted for around 9% of typed HFMD cases and was linked to at least two fatal encephalitis cases, while overall severe complications remained relatively uncommon compared with neighboring countries. Case numbers fell after intensified surveillance, school-based hygiene measures, and the end of the enterovirus transmission season, though EV-A71 lineages, particularly subgenogroup B5, continued to circulate and contributed to later HFMD peaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: widespread childcare and school-based transmission, seasonal climatic conditions, and regional movement of people and viruses from other Asia-Pacific hotspots facilitated broad HFMD spread; partial pre-existing population immunity to EV-A71 may have limited the proportion of EV-A71 among total HFMD cases but did not prevent localized severe disease. Internal mechanisms: circulation and gradual predominance of EV-A71 subgenogroup B5 and other evolving lineages indicate ongoing novel strain/genotype emergence and enhanced transmission, but with relatively lower intrinsic neurovirulence in this setting compared with the highly lethal C4a epidemics in China and Viet Nam.
Review: Decision: review. The 2012 HFMD outbreak in Thailand was large in terms of total notified cases, but EV-A71 accounted for only a minority of typed infections, with coxsackievirus A6 predominating and relatively few EV-A71-associated severe or fatal outcomes. For a dataset intended to capture the ten most impactful EV-A71-specific emergence events globally, this episode is likely of lower priority than more EV-A71-dominated outbreaks (e.g. Viet Nam 2005 or Brunei 2006) and could be considered for exclusion if a strict top‑10 filter is applied. Nonetheless, the event is real, well documented and informative about ongoing EV-A71 circulation and B5 genotype evolution in Thailand, so it is retained but explicitly flagged for review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (mainly young children with severe neurologic disease including rhombencephalitis, encephalomyelitis, acute flaccid paralysis, and some HFMD/herpangina)
Event.summary: Between April and July 2016, Catalonia and later other regions of Spain experienced a large outbreak of severe pediatric neurologic disease linked to EV-A71 subgenogroup C1-variant, with over 200 laboratory-confirmed EV-A71 cases and the majority presenting with brainstem encephalitis, myelitis or other CNS syndromes rather than classic HFMD. The outbreak began in Catalonia with a sharp increase in rhombencephalitis and acute flaccid paralysis in young children, then cases were detected across Spain as national surveillance intensified, and molecular typing showed a recombinant C1 lineage not previously associated with large neurologic outbreaks in Europe. Transmission declined after the summer enterovirus season, but the episode signaled a marked re-emergence of EV-A71 as a major neuroinvasive pathogen in Europe, driven by introduction of an Asia-linked recombinant strain.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increased international travel and connectivity with Asia likely facilitated importation of the C1-variant lineage; low background EV-A71 seroprevalence in many European pediatric populations and limited prior exposure to this specific lineage may have allowed rapid spread and high clinical severity; heightened clinical awareness and MRI use improved detection of EV-A71-associated rhombencephalitis. Internal mechanisms: the C1-variant (C1v2015) recombinant strain combined structural genes of EV-A71 with non-structural regions from other enteroviruses, representing clear novel strain/genotype emergence with enhanced neurotropism and increased virulence/pathogenicity, and its spread into Spain reflects geographic range expansion within Europe.
Review: Decision: retain with corrected emergence typing. Removed inter_continental_emergence and intra_continental_emergence flags because EV-A71 had been present in Europe for decades (notably the large Bulgaria 1975 and Hungary 1978 outbreaks and subsequent circulation and sporadic cases in the Netherlands, UK, Germany and Spain itself), so the 2016 Spanish outbreak is not the first occurrence on the continent or in Southern Europe. Instead, it represents a severe regional re-emergence associated with introduction and amplification of the recombinant C1v2015 lineage. Year, geography, host description and the emphasis on >200 EV-A71 cases with prominent neurologic disease align well with Eurosurveillance and ECDC reports, justifying retention as a major emergence episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus B
EPP.common.name: enterovirus infection
Host: Humans (primarily children with aseptic meningitis)
Event.summary: In early 2003, a large outbreak of aseptic meningitis caused by echovirus 30 (Enterovirus B) began in northern Jiangsu Province, China, in a population with no prior known E30 endemicity. The epidemic expanded to involve 1,681 clinically diagnosed aseptic meningitis patients over several months, with viral isolates all typed as echovirus 30 belonging to a distinct lineage. The outbreak subsided after mid‑2003 following public health response and natural epidemic burnout, but E30 continued to circulate in China in later years in different provinces.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/pdfs/vol11no4_pdf-version.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction and amplification of echovirus 30 in a previously non-endemic area, likely facilitated by high population density and close contact among school-age children, with limited prior immunity in Jiangsu. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (a distinct E30 lineage with genetic divergence from prototype Bastianni and earlier strains, associated with enhanced virulence and efficient transmission), enhanced transmission in school and community settings, and geographic range expansion within China of this lineage.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/pdfs/vol11no4_pdf-version.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Event.summary: In 2003, multiple U.S. states reported concurrent outbreaks of aseptic meningitis linked to non-polio enteroviruses, notably echovirus 9 and echovirus 30. In New York, hundreds of cases were detected and echovirus 9 was predominant, while echovirus 30 also contributed; similar outbreaks occurred in South Carolina and adjacent Georgia counties. The outbreaks waned later in 2003 as enterovirus circulation declined seasonally and public health messaging on hygiene and supportive management was implemented.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5232a1.htm?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus B
EPP.common.name: enterovirus infection
Host: Humans (children with aseptic meningitis; some AFP and HFMD cases in surveillance)
Event.summary: In 2008, Shandong Province, China, experienced a sizable outbreak of aseptic meningitis in which coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3), an Enterovirus B serotype, was identified as the primary etiologic agent. Molecular epidemiology of 72 CVB3 isolates from 1990–2010, including those from the 2008 outbreak, showed that the epidemic was caused by a genogroup D lineage that had emerged and spread in Shandong. The outbreak was controlled as the seasonal peak passed and public health measures reduced transmission, but CVB3 genogroup D continued to circulate sporadically in subsequent years.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/18733/cdc_18733_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high susceptibility among children, close contact in schools and households, and typical summer seasonality of enteroviruses. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (genogroup D CVB3 with distinct VP1 phylogeny), which appears to have higher fitness in local transmission; possible enhanced transmission efficiency compared with earlier CVB3 lineages, contributing to a large localized outbreak.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/18733/cdc_18733_DS1.pdf?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus B
EPP.common.name: enterovirus infection
Host: Humans (children with aseptic meningitis and febrile illness)
Event.summary: In May–June 2012, Luoding city in Guangdong Province, China, experienced a large echovirus 30–associated aseptic meningitis outbreak involving at least 183 children. Clinical and environmental surveillance linked the epidemic to an E30 lineage (lineage A or h) that had previously caused meningitis outbreaks in Jiangsu, Shandong, and Fujian provinces, demonstrating continued spread and evolution within China. The outbreak ended after several weeks as control measures, school holidays, and growing population immunity reduced transmission, but environmental surveillance showed persistence of closely related E30 strains in local wastewater.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3906529/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction of an epidemic E30 lineage into a medium‑sized city with many susceptible children, facilitated by school and household contact networks; limited pre-existing immunity in Guangdong to this lineage; seasonal climatic conditions favorable to Enterovirus transmission. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and geographic range expansion (lineage A/h E30 spreading across multiple Chinese provinces), with high genetic similarity between clinical and wastewater strains, indicating robust transmission fitness and environmental persistence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3906529/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus B
EPP.common.name: enterovirus infection
Host: Humans (children and adults with aseptic meningitis and non‑specific viral illness)
Event.summary: In 2013, South‑East France reported widespread circulation of a new echovirus 30 variant that caused a marked increase in aseptic meningitis cases and non‑specific viral illness. Molecular epidemiology showed that the outbreak strain belonged to a lineage that had been circulating across Europe since around 2000, but with distinct temporal clustering indicating recent emergence of a successful variant. The upsurge declined later in 2013 as immunity increased and routine infection‑control and supportive care limited further spread, though E30 continued to cause sporadic meningitis in the region.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24973284/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: typical enterovirus seasonality in temperate Europe, school and community contact networks, and possibly under‑immunity to the new E30 variant among younger age groups. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence within the European E30 lineage (phylogenetically distinct variant associated with the outbreak), contributing to re‑emergence with higher incidence; this reflects evolutionary replacement rather than introduction into a new continent or subregion.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24973284/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus D
EPP.common.name: enterovirus D68
Host: Humans (children with acute flaccid myelitis following respiratory illness)
Event.summary:
