As temperatures dropped and mosquitoes disappeared in autumn, human transmission ceased, but the wide spatial footprint of the 2021 epidemic and concomitant serological evidence in birds indicated that SINV had established a wider endemic range within Finland than previously recognised, setting the stage for future cycles of re-occurrence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: a combination of climatic conditions (warm summer temperatures and precipitation patterns) favouring large mosquito populations, high densities of susceptible forest grouse and other birds, and a growing human population engaging in outdoor activities in newly affected areas; increased clinical awareness and laboratory testing likely enhanced case ascertainment compared with earlier years. Internal mechanisms: sequence analysis of 2021 Finnish SINV isolates showed them to belong to the established European genotype I lineage and to be closely related to prior Finnish, Swedish and German strains, implying that the main internal mechanism was geographic range expansion and amplification of existing genotypes rather than emergence of a new, more virulent strain.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2021 Finnish outbreak, with 566 confirmed cases and documented geographic expansion within Finland, is clearly one of the most impactful SINV events globally in the study period; the description, geography and classification as a large re-occurrence in an endemic region are well supported by surveillance and genomic data.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus sindbis
EPP.common.name: Sindbis virus
Host: Humans; likely local wild birds and Culex mosquitoes maintaining the enzootic cycle (not directly sampled in this report)
Event.summary: In July–August 2025, four autochthonous patients living in south‑eastern Tuscany, Italy, were hospitalised with acute neurological symptoms, and next‑generation sequencing of cerebrospinal fluid samples detected Sindbis virus RNA, providing the first unequivocal evidence of human neuroinvasive SINV infection and the first recognised cluster of locally acquired SINV disease in Italy. The cases occurred against a background of established but largely subclinical SINV circulation in southern Europe, where antibodies and viral RNA had previously been detected in birds and mosquitoes but no confirmed human outbreaks had been described. Following hospital management and supportive care, no wider community outbreak was identified, and transmission appeared to be limited to a small focus during the summer mosquito season, but the event highlighted the potential for SINV to cause severe central nervous system disease outside its traditional Northern European and South African strongholds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: seasonal abundance of competent Culex mosquitoes in lowland Tuscany during the warm summer of 2025; local enzootic circulation of SINV in birds that had gone largely undetected in routine surveillance; improved use of unbiased next‑generation sequencing in encephalitis diagnostics that enabled identification of SINV RNA where routine testing for other neurotropic viruses was negative. Internal mechanisms: available data indicate that the Italian viruses belong to the established SINV genotype I lineage known from Europe and Africa, and there is currently no clear evidence of major genetic change specifically associated with neuroinvasiveness; the event is therefore interpreted as a clinically important but probably surveillance‑driven re-occurrence of SINV infection in a region where the virus was already present, rather than emergence of a novel, more virulent strain.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The Tuscany 2025 cluster is small in case numbers but highly significant as the first confirmed neuroinvasive Sindbis virus infections and the first recognised autochthonous human cases in Italy; it therefore merits inclusion among major events. Because detailed clinical and genomic data are still emerging, the classification as re-occurrence (rather than re-emergence) and the absence of an intra-continental emergence label should be revisited once more evidence is available on whether these viruses differ biologically from previously circulating European strains.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus western
EPP.common.name: western equine encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (single severe encephalitis case in Argentina) with evidence of low-level post-epizootic WEEV circulation in local equine and vector populations
Event.summary: In 1996, Argentina detected an isolated but severe human case of western equine encephalitis in a rural resident, occurring more than a decade after the major equine–human epizootics of 1972–1973 and 1982–1983 but within a region where WEEV had been historically established. The case likely arose from sporadic spillover out of residual avian–mosquito–equine transmission foci that persisted after the earlier epizootics, without evidence of a wider human outbreak or substantial onward transmission during that season. Following clinical management of the case and reinforcement of equine vaccination and vector surveillance, no further confirmed human WEE cases were reported in Argentina until the large 2023–2024 re-emergence, and human disease again fell into apparent silence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Post-epizootic persistence of WEEV in avian–mosquito–equine cycles in central Argentina, together with climatic and ecological conditions that intermittently favored local Culex and Aedes vector proliferation, probably enabled sporadic spillover to humans despite the absence of a recognized equine epizootic. Internal mechanisms: Available data link the 1996 infection to the long-established South American WEEV lineage, without evidence for a novel genotype or increased intrinsic virulence, so this episode is best interpreted as a low-intensity re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion driven by environmental and surveillance factors rather than viral genetic change.
Review: retain – Verified that a single clinically and serologically confirmed human WEEV case occurred in Argentina in 1996 after the 1970s–1980s epizootics and that no additional human cases were recorded nationally until 2023. Continent, UNSD subregion (South America), country coding (Argentina [1996]), and classification as a re-occurrence (with no intra-/inter-continental emergence) are consistent with the protocol definitions and with WHO/PAHO and Argentine sources. No larger post‑1990 human WEEV emergence events were identified that would displace this event from the top‑10 list for this EPP.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus western
EPP.common.name: western equine encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (fatal encephalitis in a 14-year-old boy) with evidence of enzootic WEEV circulation in equine and mosquito populations in the broader Southern Cone region
Event.summary: In April 2009, Uruguay recorded a fatal case of viral encephalitis in a previously healthy 14-year-old boy in Montevideo, with molecular testing identifying western equine encephalitis virus as the likely cause and representing the first documented human WEE case in the country. The illness progressed rapidly from febrile symptoms to severe encephalomyelitis and death, and intensive investigation did not identify additional temporally or spatially linked human cases, although serologic and entomologic surveys confirmed WEEV circulation in equine and mosquito populations in Uruguay and the wider Southern Cone. After this episode, Uruguay strengthened arboviral surveillance and vector control, and no further confirmed human WEE cases were reported until the multi-country 2023–2024 regional re-emergence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The 2009 case most likely resulted from spillover from an established enzootic equine–mosquito–avian transmission cycle in the Southern Cone, with local climatic and ecological conditions favoring vector abundance in peri-urban environments around Montevideo and increasing human exposure. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analysis showed that the virus from the 2009 patient clustered within known South American WEEV lineages without marked divergence or evidence of enhanced virulence, indicating that this episode reflects re-occurrence of an existing lineage in a previously affected South American subregion and the first recognized human infection in Uruguay, rather than intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD subregion or a genetically driven re-emergence.
Review: review – Corrected the emergence-type coding. Under the protocol, intra-continental emergence requires spread to a new UNSD subregion within a continent; Uruguay and Argentina both lie in the South America subregion, which was already known to harbor WEEV in humans. I therefore set intra_continental_emergence from “true” to “false” and re_occurrence from “false” to “true,” and rewrote the mechanism/driver text to describe this episode as a re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion and the first documented human case in Uruguay. Geography (South America/South America; Uruguay [2009]) and timing remain appropriate, and the event is retained as one of the small number of well-documented human WEEV emergence episodes after 1990.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Serratia spp.
EPP.common.name: Serratia infection
Host: Humans (recipients of blood and blood components, mainly platelet concentrates and red cell units)
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through the mid‑1990s, multiple U.S. centers reported clusters of severe septic transfusion reactions that were ultimately linked to Serratia liquefaciens contamination of platelet concentrates and other blood components. These episodes, collated in national analyses, showed that S. liquefaciens could proliferate to high titres during room‑temperature storage of platelets, causing fulminant sepsis and death in some recipients and revealing a previously under‑recognized transfusion hazard. In response, blood services introduced stricter donor arm disinfection, diversion pouches and, later, routine bacterial screening of platelet units, which markedly reduced the incidence of Serratia‑associated transfusion sepsis in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Standard transfusion practices at the time—particularly storage of platelet concentrates at room temperature, incomplete donor skin disinfection, and absence of routine bacterial screening—created conditions in which environmental Gram‑negative bacteria introduced at donation could survive and multiply to dangerous levels. Internal mechanisms: S. liquefaciens, an environmental Serratia species not normally part of human flora, proved able to persist and proliferate in platelet bags and other blood components, effectively exploiting this artificial niche; this represents a host/exposure expansion and enhanced transmission in the context of blood products rather than a new geographic range.
Review: Review: Event is real and important as a national recognition of Serratia liquefaciens as a transfusion‑transmitted pathogen and catalyst for major blood safety changes. To comply with the event‑type rules, the classification has been corrected to re_emergence = true and re_occurrence = false (the episode reflects host/exposure expansion and regulatory failure rather than a simple incidence resurgence). Geographic fields and sources are appropriate; recommended to retain as one of the top 10 most impactful emergence events for Serratia spp.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Serratia spp.
EPP.common.name: Serratia infection
Host: Humans (neonates in a governmental hospital NICU, Gaza City)
Event.summary: Between January and December 2005, the NICU of a governmental hospital in Gaza City experienced a massive outbreak of Serratia marcescens septicaemia, with 159 culture‑confirmed nosocomial bloodstream infections in neonates. The outbreak was associated with high mortality—70 deaths (44% of cases)—and strongly linked to very low birthweight, prematurity and mechanical ventilation, indicating widespread transmission in a highly vulnerable population. Following recognition of the epidemic and identification of key risk factors, strengthened infection‑control measures and antimicrobial stewardship were implemented, ultimately reducing S. marcescens incidence, although the report emphasized the ongoing need for prevention in resource‑constrained settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Overcrowded NICU with limited staffing and infection‑control resources, high use of invasive procedures and mechanical ventilation, and broad‑spectrum empirical antibiotic use favored rapid dissemination of S. marcescens. Internal mechanisms: Isolates remained susceptible to imipenem and some fluoroquinolones, and no specific novel resistance determinant was highlighted; this event is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence driven primarily by environmental and health‑system factors rather than by major pathogen genetic change.
Review: Retain: This is one of the largest and deadliest documented Serratia marcescens NICU outbreaks worldwide (159 neonates infected, 70 deaths), clearly among the top 10 by impact. Geographic and temporal fields are correct (Gaza City, State of Palestine, 2005) and event type as re_occurrence (without strong evidence for novel strain properties) is appropriate. Minor clean‑up of secondary URLs was made (nonessential table‑of‑contents and Japanese summary links removed) but no substantive data corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Serratia spp.
EPP.common.name: Serratia infection
Host: Humans (primarily adult oncology and infusion‑center patients with central venous catheters, as well as home‑care patients, exposed to contaminated prefilled heparin or saline syringes)
Event.summary: From October 7, 2007 through February 17, 2008, a multistate outbreak of Serratia marcescens bloodstream infections occurred in the United States, initially detected as clusters at an outpatient chemotherapy infusion center in Texas and in Chicago and subsequently recognized in nine states. Investigation linked 162 probable or definite S. marcescens BSIs to exposure to intrinsically contaminated prefilled heparin and isotonic sodium chloride flush syringes manufactured by a single company, with 4 deaths in which infection may have contributed. After epidemiologic and laboratory evidence implicated the syringes, a national recall of all prefilled heparin and saline syringes from the manufacturer was issued in December 2007–January 2008, and reports of new S. marcescens BSIs declined sharply thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Lapses in sterile manufacturing and quality‑control processes at a compounding/medical‑product company led to intrinsic contamination of nationally distributed prefilled heparin and saline syringes, seeding bloodstream infections across multiple states; extensive outpatient and home‑care use of these products amplified the scale of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was a typical nosocomial S. marcescens capable of surviving and proliferating in aqueous syringe contents; no unusual resistance profile was highlighted, and impact was driven by contaminated product distribution rather than novel pathogen traits.
Review: Review: Major multistate product‑associated outbreak (162 BSIs across 9 US states with 4 associated deaths) that was missing from the original dataset and clearly qualifies as one of the most impactful Serratia events post‑1990. Added as a new event with continent/subregion/country fields and event type (re_occurrence) set according to published descriptions. Recommended to retain in the final top‑10 list; details could be further checked against the companion investigation of the Texas subset (Su et al., Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol 2009) if finer granularity is needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Serratia spp.
EPP.common.name: Serratia infection
Host: Humans (neonates in the NICU of Alexandra General Hospital, Athens)
Event.summary: Between December 2007 and September 2010, the NICU of Alexandra General Hospital in Athens, Greece, experienced three consecutive outbreaks of Serratia marcescens caused by genetically distinct clones. Over the 35‑month period, 57 neonates had S. marcescens isolated (37 colonized and 20 infected), and 9 of the 20 infected infants (45%) died, reflecting severe late‑onset sepsis and other invasive infections. Investigation linked the outbreaks to repeated introductions of new S. marcescens clones, with contaminated sinks and total parenteral nutrition implicated as possible reservoirs during specific waves, and intensified screening, cohorting and environmental control eventually halted the recurrent outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑risk NICU setting with extensive use of central lines and total parenteral nutrition, combined with intermittent environmental contamination (e.g., milk kitchen sink drain) and gaps in infection prevention, facilitated repeated introduction and spread of new S. marcescens clones. Internal mechanisms: Although multiple genetically distinct clones were identified, the report did not emphasize novel resistance determinants or unusual virulence; the event is best interpreted as a series of severe re‑occurrence episodes driven by infection‑control and environmental factors rather than by a single emergent high‑resistance lineage.
Review: Review: Large, prolonged NICU episode (57 colonized/infected neonates, 20 invasive infections, 9 deaths over 3 linked outbreaks) that was not captured previously and clearly ranks among the most clinically impactful Serratia NICU outbreaks post‑1990. Added as a new event, classified as re_occurrence (repeated introduction and spread of different clones without clear evidence of novel resistance). Recommended for inclusion in the top‑10 list, with details drawn from Maltezou et al. 2012 (American Journal of Infection Control).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Serratia spp.
EPP.common.name: Serratia infection
Host: Humans (adult inpatients, predominantly medical and surgical ward and ICU patients in a tertiary hospital, "hospital H1")
Event.summary: Following the introduction of colistin as salvage therapy in several wards of an Argentine tertiary hospital (H1) in 2005, the frequency of Serratia marcescens and Proteus mirabilis—both intrinsically colistin‑resistant species—increased markedly from 2006 onward. Between November 2007 and April 2008, H1 experienced an outbreak of multidrug‑resistant S. marcescens infections caused by a single epidemic cluster (cluster I), involving 32 patients with serious infections such as bloodstream infection and pneumonia and an attributable mortality of approximately 40% among infected patients. Molecular analysis showed that the outbreak clone carried complex class 1 integrons (In132::ISCR1::blaCTX‑M‑2) and additional resistance determinants (e.g., blaPER‑2, qnrB10), and implementation of strict infection‑control measures along with optimization of colistin use terminated transmission.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy colistin use in response to other multidrug‑resistant Gram‑negative pathogens created strong ecological selection favoring intrinsically colistin‑resistant species like S. marcescens, and routine infection‑control measures were initially insufficient to prevent spread of the emerging MDR clone across multiple wards. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic S. marcescens cluster acquired complex class 1 integrons and extended‑spectrum β‑lactamase and plasmid‑mediated quinolone resistance genes, conferring multidrug and likely near pan‑drug resistance; this represents clear novel genotype emergence and re‑emergence of S. marcescens under polymyxin pressure.
Review: Review: Original row mis‑assigned this colistin‑associated outbreak to Italy in 2011 and treated the event dates imprecisely; primary sources show it occurred in an Argentine hospital (H1) with an epidemic period from November 2007 to April 2008 and ~40% mortality among infected patients. Continent, subregion, country and year fields have been corrected, and the event reclassified as re_emergence only (due to acquisition of complex resistance integrons and severe MDR phenotype). This outbreak is a key example of polymyxin‑driven selection of an epidemic S. marcescens clone and should be retained among the top 10 events, but details should be double‑checked against Merkier et al. 2013 (Journal of Clinical Microbiology) by a human reviewer.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Serratia spp.
EPP.common.name: Serratia infection
Host: Humans (children, mostly outpatients and some inpatients, attending a rural health center)
Event.summary: At Basse Health Centre in eastern Gambia, a healthcare‑associated outbreak of Serratia liquefaciens infections was detected in mid‑2010, when laboratory staff noticed a sudden rise in S. liquefaciens isolation from clinical specimens. Between 30 June and 16 September 2010, 44 children had clinical samples (including blood and respiratory specimens) positive for S. liquefaciens, and three infected children died with no other identified cause. Investigation traced the outbreak to contamination of multiple hospital consumables and solutions used for nebulization and intravenous infusion, and after removal and sterilization of the implicated fluids and equipment, the outbreak was brought under control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Poor aseptic technique in preparation and handling of medications for nebulization and intravenous infusion, reuse of multi‑dose vials for multiple patients, and limited infection‑control awareness in a low‑resource rural health center allowed S. liquefaciens to contaminate fluids and spread to many children. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was environmentally adapted and able to persist in moist medical products, but no unusual resistance profile was emphasized; this represents a severe re‑occurrence of an environmental Serratia species in human patients driven by procedural and hygiene failures rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Review: Original event correctly identified this as a major outbreak of S. liquefaciens in The Gambia but mis‑stated the timing (it occurred over 10 weeks in 2010, not 2013–2014) and gave an imprecise country/year notation. Event year has been corrected to 2010 (June–September) with countries updated to "Gambia [2010]" and the summary aligned to the primary report (Ikumapayi et al. 2016). Given 44 infected children, three deaths, and a clear demonstration of product contamination in a low‑resource setting, this event merits inclusion among high‑impact Serratia episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Serratia spp.
EPP.common.name: Serratia infection
Host: Humans (primarily adult cardiac‑surgery and ICU patients in a 600‑bed acute‑care hospital)
Event.summary: Over a roughly 12‑month period beginning in mid‑2012, the 600‑bed Lucerne Cantonal Hospital in Switzerland experienced a hospital‑wide outbreak of Serratia marcescens, with most cases identified from respiratory samples among cardiac surgical intensive‑care patients but additional cases across wards. Standard CDC outbreak investigation, supplemented by Ishikawa "fishbone" root‑cause analysis, identified plausible sources including contamination of a transesophageal echocardiography probe used during cardiac surgery and deficiencies in surface disinfection logistics and products. After comprehensive re‑engineering of disinfection processes, targeted replacement or decontamination of implicated devices and reinforcement of infection‑control practices, the outbreak ended and hospital S. marcescens incidence returned to baseline; Swiss national data indicate approximately 91 cases over the 12‑month period.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Complex cardiac surgical care with repeated use of a shared TEE probe and suboptimal disinfection processes created a persistent environmental reservoir and transmission route for S. marcescens, while broader weaknesses in surface disinfection logistics allowed contamination to spread hospital‑wide. Internal mechanisms: Isolates behaved as typical nosocomial S. marcescens without unique resistance features highlighted; re‑occurrence was driven chiefly by environmental persistence, biofilm formation on inadequately disinfected equipment and workflow problems rather than novel pathogen traits.
Review: Review: Event is real and high‑impact, with about 91 cases over 12 months in a Swiss teaching hospital, but the original row inaccurately dated the outbreak to an approximate 2014–2015 period. Based on the primary article and Swissnoso outbreak summary, the event year has been corrected to 2012–2013, and the country/subregion fields (Switzerland, Western Europe) are retained. Classification as re_occurrence (environmental/device‑associated outbreak without novel resistance) is appropriate. Recommended to keep as one of the top 10 events, with chronology verified by a human reviewer if greater precision is required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Serratia spp.
EPP.common.name: Serratia infection
Host: Humans (neonates and infants in the Targu Mures neonatal/paediatric units, with additional related adult cases in another hospital)
Event.summary: From late 2014 through 2015, a neonatology unit in Targu Mures, Romania, experienced an outbreak of carbapenem‑nonsusceptible Serratia marcescens, characterized by colonization and invasive infections in neonates and infants, with related NDM‑1‑producing Enterobacterales also detected in the hospital and in a second hospital in Cluj‑Napoca. Whole‑genome sequencing of 33 S. marcescens isolates (27 NDM‑1 positive) and other Enterobacterales showed that a pKOX_NDM1‑like IncFIIY plasmid had been imported into Romania and disseminated between K. pneumoniae, E. cloacae and S. marcescens, with a clonal NDM‑1 S. marcescens strain causing a defined outbreak in the Targu Mures neonatal unit. Intensified infection‑control and active screening were used to monitor and contain the outbreak and associated plasmid spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive use of broad‑spectrum β‑lactams and carbapenems in Romanian hospitals, coupled with gaps in infection‑control infrastructure, facilitated introduction and spread of NDM‑1‑producing Enterobacterales, including S. marcescens, in neonatal and adult units. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and subsequent clonal expansion of S. marcescens strains carrying a pKOX_NDM1‑like plasmid conferred high‑level carbapenem resistance and multi‑drug resistance, representing clear novel genotype emergence and a re‑emergence of a more drug‑resistant Serratia lineage in this setting.
Review: Review: Event is real and important as one of the first detailed descriptions of an NDM‑1 S. marcescens neonatal outbreak in Europe and part of a broader multi‑species plasmid transmission network in Romania. The original row slightly simplified the broader context (multi‑hospital, multi‑species) but correctly located the main outbreak in the Targu Mures neonatal unit and classified it as re_emergence. An invalid placeholder PMC URL has been removed, and the summary clarified to match the WGS study. Recommended to retain as a top‑10 event, with any remaining numeric details (exact numbers of infected vs colonized neonates) cross‑checked by a human reviewer from the full article and supplementary tables.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Serratia spp.
EPP.common.name: Serratia infection
Host: Humans (neonates and infants in multiple NICUs, neonatal units and a pediatric ICU at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital, Taoyuan)
Event.summary: Beginning on 14 February 2021, a network of three NICUs and two neonatal units at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital in Taoyuan, Taiwan, experienced an outbreak of carbapenem‑resistant Serratia marcescens in neonates and young infants. Fourteen infants developed serious infections during the acute phase, including sepsis, meningitis and pneumonia, and whole‑genome sequencing as part of longitudinal surveillance (through June 2023) showed that the main outbreak clone carried multiple resistance determinants associated with carbapenem resistance. After a comprehensive infection‑control package—enhanced hand hygiene, cohorting, dedicated staff, active screening and environmental and genomic surveillance—was implemented, the acute outbreak was contained within about 2.5 months, and over two years of follow‑up only one subsequent infection was genetically linked to the original epidemic clone, although unrelated S. marcescens infections continued to occur.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Complex care across co‑located NICUs and neonatal units with high antibiotic exposure provided fertile conditions for the emergence and spread of carbapenem‑resistant clones, and pre‑intervention infection‑control practices were insufficient to prevent rapid dissemination. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain possessed multiple resistance genes, including determinants associated with carbapenem resistance, exemplifying novel strain/genotype emergence and enhanced antimicrobial tolerance that enabled persistence under broad‑spectrum antibiotic pressure, making this a clear re‑emergence of a more drug‑resistant S. marcescens lineage in the NICU ecosystem.
Review: Review: Event is real and recent, documenting a carbapenem‑resistant S. marcescens outbreak in Taiwanese NICUs followed by two years of genomic surveillance. The original row’s basic description (14 infected infants, 2021 outbreak with follow‑up to 2023, multiple resistance determinants including an efflux pump associated with carbapenem resistance) matches the primary report, but one invalid placeholder PMC URL has been removed and the summary updated to align more closely with the Biomedical Journal article. Recommended to retain as a key AMR‑driven re‑emergence event; exact gene lists and case counts across the full 2021–2023 period should be checked by a human reviewer if further granularity is needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Serratia spp.
EPP.common.name: Serratia infection
Host: Humans (primarily older adults with serious underlying conditions cared for in hospitals across Norway; opportunistic infections with S. marcescens complex ct755)
Event.summary: Between June 2021 and February 2023, Norway experienced a national outbreak of Serratia marcescens complex clone type 755 (ct755), first detected as a cluster of bloodstream infections in several hospitals and later recognized through whole‑genome sequencing as a widespread clonal outbreak. A total of 74 ct755 cases were identified across 33 hospitals, mostly in patients aged 60 years and older with substantial comorbidities, presenting with opportunistic infections typical of S. marcescens. Extensive case‑record review and interviews failed to identify common in‑hospital exposures, and the geographic spread and lack of clear nosocomial links suggested a community source, possibly a widely distributed product such as food. Despite the absence of a definitive source, the outbreak was eventually controlled through heightened surveillance and infection‑control vigilance, and S. marcescens complex ct755 highlighted challenges posed by opportunistic pathogens detected via high‑resolution WGS.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased use of clinical whole‑genome sequencing enabled recognition of a widely distributed S. marcescens complex clone that otherwise might have been dismissed as unrelated sporadic cases; the underlying driver appears to be a community‑distributed source (suspected nationally distributed product) rather than classic nosocomial reservoirs, with hospital‑based infection‑control measures playing a supporting role in limiting secondary spread. Internal mechanisms: The ct755 clone was non‑pigmented and largely antibiotic‑susceptible, with no major novel resistance mechanisms highlighted; its impact stems from clonal dissemination in the community and healthcare system rather than pathogen evolution, so this event is best categorized as a large re‑occurrence outbreak of an opportunistic Serratia lineage uncovered by WGS.
Review: Review: Newly added event capturing the recent Norway 2021–2023 national Serratia marcescens complex ct755 outbreak (74 cases across 33 hospitals) that was absent from the original dataset but clearly among the most impactful modern episodes. Classified as re_occurrence (large‑scale clonal spread without notable novel resistance) and located in Northern Europe / Norway based on the Eurosurveillance report. Strongly recommended for inclusion in the top‑10 list, with final details (e.g., exact case counts and ward‑level distribution) to be confirmed from the full article.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (primarily anthroponotic cutaneous leishmaniasis due to Leishmania tropica in Kabul and other cities; zoonotic L. major in some northern foci)
Event.summary: From around 1990 onward, Kabul and several other Afghan cities experienced a prolonged epidemic of anthroponotic cutaneous leishmaniasis, against a backdrop of war-damaged infrastructure, mass displacement and collapsing health services. Cross-sectional surveys and WHO assessments in the early 2000s estimated that roughly 2%–3% of Kabul’s 2.5 million residents had active lesions and 15%–20% had scars at any time, implying tens of thousands of new cases annually and making Kabul the world’s largest single focus of cutaneous leishmaniasis. Through the 2000s, expansion of leishmaniasis clinics, provision of antimonial drugs and insecticide-treated nets and targeted health education gradually improved access to care and began to curb incidence and severity, but large numbers of new infections continued to occur each year, particularly in crowded, impoverished neighborhoods and informal settlements.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Decades of armed conflict, rapid unplanned urbanization, destruction of housing and sanitation, and massive internal displacement produced dense peri-urban settlements with abundant sandfly breeding sites and little vector control; shortages of diagnostic capacity and drugs limited early treatment and prolonged infectiousness. Internal mechanisms: Amplification of long-established L. tropica anthroponotic transmission cycles with humans as the main reservoir, without clear evidence of novel parasite genotypes, so this episode is best viewed as a large-scale re-occurrence driven primarily by socio-political and environmental change rather than intrinsic parasite evolution.
Review: Review – Added as a new event because the prolonged anthroponotic cutaneous leishmaniasis epidemic in Kabul (≈200,000 prevalent infections and ≈67,500 incident cases annually in early 2000s) clearly ranks among the most impactful Leishmania emergence episodes since 1990. Classified as re-occurrence (not first detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence) because leishmaniasis was already endemic in Afghanistan and the surge reflects conflict, urban crowding and collapse of control programmes rather than spread to a new continent/sub-region or parasite change. Time window 1990–2010 is approximate, chosen to encompass the documented multi-decade epidemic described in WHO and EID sources; details should be checked against any country program data before finalization.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (visceral leishmaniasis, mainly L. infantum; zoonotic cycle involving domestic dogs)
Event.summary: From the 1980s into the 1990s and 2000s, Brazil saw a major shift of visceral leishmaniasis from rural endemic foci in the Northeast into urban and peri-urban environments, with large outbreaks in cities such as Teresina, São Luís, Natal, Belo Horizonte, Campo Grande, Araçatuba and Bauru. Between 1980 and 2005, Brazil reported nearly 60,000 VL cases, with an increasing proportion occurring outside the traditional Northeast region as the disease spread along migration and transport corridors and became established in medium and large cities; by 2001–2012, ten major urban centers accounted for about 15% of all Brazilian VL cases. Through intensified surveillance, canine reservoir control and vector-control measures in many municipalities after the mid‑2000s, some urban foci stabilized or declined, but VL remained endemic and highly spatially heterogeneous, with periodic urban outbreaks continuing beyond 2012.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid and often unplanned urbanization, rural–urban migration, peri-urban poverty, accumulation of infected domestic dogs as reservoir hosts, and favorable peri-domestic environments for sandfly vectors fostered the establishment of VL in cities; shortcomings in solid waste management and housing also increased vector density. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and ecological adaptation of phlebotomine vectors (e.g. Lutzomyia longipalpis) and domestic dog reservoirs to urban/peri-urban habitats, representing enhanced transmission and ecological niche expansion of existing L. infantum strains rather than a wholly novel species, justifying classification as re-emergence.
Review: Retain – Appropriately describes the major urbanization and geographic spread of visceral leishmaniasis in Brazil, a key global emergence pattern with tens of thousands of cases and establishment of multiple large urban foci. Classifying this as re-emergence (driven by ecological adaptation and geographic expansion of an existing zoonotic cycle) rather than intra-continental emergence is consistent with the UNSD sub-region scheme (all areas involved lie within the South America sub-region) and with the event definition. No changes to core fields were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (primarily cutaneous leishmaniasis due to an atypical Leishmania donovani variant; occasional visceralized cases)
Event.summary: Around 2001, clinicians in Sri Lanka began to identify increasing numbers of autochthonous cutaneous leishmaniasis cases, which were confirmed between 2001 and 2005 as being caused by L. donovani MON‑37, a parasite classically associated with visceral disease in neighboring India and East Africa. Over the next decade, surveillance documented thousands of CL cases with gradually widening spatial distribution across the island, seasonal transmission peaks, and rare visceralized or atypical presentations, indicating that this atypical L. donovani lineage had successfully established stable human transmission foci in multiple districts. After leishmaniasis was made a notifiable disease in 2008, reporting and control activities intensified, and although incidence remained substantial through at least 2013, enhanced diagnosis, awareness and control efforts helped limit the expansion and provided a clearer picture of the new endemic pattern.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely a combination of environmental changes, land-use and human mobility facilitating introduction or expansion of L. donovani into new ecologic niches on the island; limited early surveillance allowed the focus to grow before full recognition. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of an atypical L. donovani variant that predominantly causes cutaneous rather than visceral disease represents a novel strain/genotype emergence and a shift in clinical tropism; ongoing evidence suggests some capacity for visceralization, indicating altered host–parasite interactions and possibly enhanced transmission in skin tissues.
Review: Review – The original row misclassified this episode as “first detection” for Sri Lanka, but historical work documents leishmaniasis in the country since at least 1904 and modern locally acquired CL cases from 1992 onwards. The event has been reinterpreted as a re-emergence driven by an atypical, dermotropic L. donovani MON‑37 lineage, so the first_detection flag has been set to false while keeping re_emergence as true. Years, geography (Sri Lanka, Southern Asia) and the epidemiologic description are consistent with multiple peer-reviewed sources, but the revised classification should be checked and accepted by domain experts.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (visceral leishmaniasis with rising HIV co-infection; mainly L. donovani)
Event.summary: During the early 2000s, Ethiopia’s long-standing visceral leishmaniasis endemicity evolved into a more complex public health problem as case numbers remained high (estimated 2,500–4,000 new VL cases annually) and VL–HIV co-infection emerged as a major challenge, particularly in northwest foci such as Humera, Metema and surrounding areas. Between roughly 2004 and 2014, national data showed sustained VL transmission across multiple regions (Tigray, Amhara, Oromia, Afar, Somali and SNNPR) and an increasing proportion of VL cases co-infected with HIV, complicating treatment and fueling relapses. In response, Ethiopia established a national leishmaniasis task force and expanded VL and CL treatment sites in the late 2000s and early 2010s, which, together with improved HIV care, began to moderate the impact of co-infection, though both diseases remained entrenched in vulnerable, mobile populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of commercial agriculture and labor migration into endemic lowlands, chronic poverty, malnutrition, and the growing HIV epidemic created large populations at risk of VL and of severe disease; limited access to early diagnosis and effective treatment further increased transmission and mortality. Internal mechanisms: The main mechanism is increased expression of severe VL in immunocompromised hosts rather than a novel parasite genotype; HIV co-infection amplifies parasite burden and transmission potential but does not imply a fundamentally new Leishmania lineage, so this is categorized as re-occurrence driven by host and health-system changes rather than intrinsic parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – Accurately summarizes the evolving national VL situation in Ethiopia, including sustained high incidence, emergence of high VL–HIV co-infection burdens and the public-health response. Classification as re-occurrence (rather than re-emergence) is appropriate because there is no strong evidence of parasite-level change; the surge reflects external drivers (HIV epidemic, labor migration, agriculture projects). No corrections beyond verification were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (primarily cutaneous leishmaniasis among military personnel, mainly L. (Viannia) braziliensis; broader civilian CL and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis transmission)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, Colombia experienced a marked intensification of cutaneous leishmaniasis transmission, particularly affecting army personnel deployed in jungle and forested conflict zones in Meta, Guaviare and surrounding departments, with about 3,400 soldiers incapacitated by leishmaniasis in 2004 alone and roughly 13,000 cases reported nationally that year. Between 2005 and 2009, approximately 45,000 leishmaniasis cases (mostly CL) were reported nationwide, with high incidence in conflict-affected departments, reflecting both civilian and military exposure. After the mid‑2000s peak, case numbers gradually declined in the 2010s, influenced by changes in conflict dynamics and military operations (including the peace process with FARC), as well as improved prevention and treatment within the armed forces, though CL remained an important occupational disease for military and other populations entering enzootic forest areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Prolonged internal armed conflict and intensified military operations in Amazonian and Andean foothill jungles drove large numbers of susceptible soldiers into highly endemic forest habitats, while poverty, deforestation and settlement expansion also altered vector–host contact patterns; healthcare access for front-line troops and rural civilians was limited, increasing the clinical and operational impact of infections. Internal mechanisms: The surge reflects increased human exposure to existing zoonotic Leishmania transmission cycles rather than a clearly documented novel strain; multiple Leishmania (Viannia) species circulate in these areas, but the dominant driver of this emergence episode is socio-political (armed conflict) rather than intrinsic parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – This episode is well supported by military and national surveillance data and describes a clearly defined period of very high CL incidence (including ≈3,400 Colombian soldiers affected in 2004 and ≈45,000 national cases 2005–2009). Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate because transmission intensified in long-endemic forest foci due to conflict-related exposure and limited control, without evidence of a new parasite or expansion into a new WHO/UNSD sub-region. No structural corrections were needed, though reliance on a general Wikipedia article for some figures should ideally be secondary to primary epidemiologic sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (visceral leishmaniasis, primarily L. donovani)
Event.summary: In 2003–2004, visceral leishmaniasis was recognized for the first time in the highland districts of Libo Kemkem and Fogera in South Gondar Zone, Amhara Region, Ethiopia, where VL had not previously been reported, marking the emergence of a new highland focus. The outbreak expanded rapidly through 2004–2005, ultimately affecting thousands of people (over 2,500 treated cases) with high case fatality, before control efforts and natural epidemic dynamics led to a sharp decline in new cases by 2006–2007. Following this peak, surveillance and treatment capacity were strengthened in the region, and subsequent surveys found low prevalence, suggesting that intensive control and partial herd immunity limited continued explosive transmission, though low-level endemicity likely persisted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Population movements from known VL-endemic lowland areas, changes in housing and agricultural practices, and possible climatic shifts enabling sandfly vectors to survive at higher altitudes contributed to the establishment of transmission in previously non-endemic highlands; poverty and limited health infrastructure facilitated rapid spread and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of L. donovani transmission into higher-elevation ecological zones represents geographic range expansion of existing parasite–vector systems, potentially aided by vector adaptation to new climatic conditions; there is no strong evidence of a distinct novel parasite strain, so this event is best interpreted as ecological expansion of an existing lineage rather than a new genotype.
Review: Retain – Correctly characterizes the Libo Kemkem/Fogera highland VL outbreak as a major new ecological focus of L. donovani in Ethiopia, with ≈2,400–2,500 treated primary VL cases between 2005 and 2007. The 2004–2007 time window and classification as re-emergence (geographic range expansion of an existing parasite–vector system within Eastern Africa, rather than first detection in humans) are supported by detailed outbreak investigations; no corrections were necessary.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (autochthonous cutaneous leishmaniasis, mainly L. mexicana and related species; also associated canine leishmaniasis due to L. infantum)
Event.summary: Although sporadic autochthonous cutaneous leishmaniasis had been recognized in southern Texas since the early 20th century, from about 2001–2007 onward new clusters of locally acquired CL were detected farther north in Texas and into southeastern Oklahoma, with multiple confirmed cases prompting health alerts and field studies documenting local enzootic cycles. Between 2007 and the early 2020s, state and literature data indicate a steady trickle of autochthonous CL cases each year in Texas (often 6–15 cases annually) and rare cases in Oklahoma, Arizona and even North Dakota, suggesting gradual northward and westward expansion of Leishmania transmission and its rodent or canine reservoirs within the United States. By the early 2020s, reviews of U.S.-autochthonous leishmaniasis documented on the order of 80–90 confirmed locally acquired human cases (mostly CL) and highlighted concerns that climate change and land-use shifts could further expand suitable habitat for sandfly vectors and reservoir hosts, potentially increasing the frequency and geographic extent of human disease if surveillance and awareness do not keep pace.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Changing climate (warmer temperatures and altered precipitation), land-use changes, expansion of peri-urban habitats, and human encroachment into areas with reservoir rodents and dogs have likely allowed both sandfly vectors and Leishmania reservoirs to expand northward; increased clinical awareness and diagnostics have also contributed to recognizing cases. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of existing Leishmania species (e.g. L. mexicana, L. infantum in dogs) and their vectors into previously unsuitable or marginal zones, potentially reflecting ecological and genetic adaptation to new climates and hosts; this constitutes re-emergence with inherent geographic expansion and enhanced transmission in new foci, superimposed on a background of long-standing but previously under-recognized endemicity in southern Texas.
Review: Review – The event accurately describes the gradual northward and westward expansion of autochthonous cutaneous leishmaniasis within the USA and is correctly reclassified here as re-emergence only (re_occurrence set to false) because it represents geographic and ecological expansion of existing enzootic cycles rather than a simple resurgence in a known focus. However, the absolute number of human cases (<100 confirmed autochthonous cases over several decades) is small compared with major epidemics in Afghanistan, South Asia, Brazil and East Africa. Recommended as a candidate for exclusion if a strict “top 10 by impact” filter is later applied, while still being epidemiologically noteworthy for range-expansion and preparedness in temperate regions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (visceral leishmaniasis, L. donovani)
Event.summary: Starting in late 2009, South Sudan—already known for cyclical VL epidemics—experienced a major new outbreak of visceral leishmaniasis in Upper Nile, Jonglei and other northern states, with more than 6,000 cases and over 300 deaths reported by late 2010 and ultimately over 28,000–30,000 cases reported by 2012. The epidemic expanded rapidly in remote, conflict-affected areas marked by population displacement, severe food insecurity and collapsing health services, overwhelming limited treatment centers until a multisectoral response scaled up diagnosis, case management and vector control. With intensified responses from national authorities, WHO and NGOs, case numbers gradually declined after the 2011 peak, although VL remained endemic with continued smaller outbreaks and substantial under-reporting in subsequent years.

Case–control investigations showed a strong dose‑response relationship between the quantity of horse meat consumed and disease, and parasitologic and typing studies identified Trichinella spiralis. The outbreak ended after the implicated batch of horse meat was withdrawn, and the episode triggered tighter European regulations and more sensitive digestion‑based protocols for systematic Trichinella screening of horse carcasses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: international trade in horse meat, limited sensitivity of then‑standard trichinoscopy and pooled digestion screening of horse carcasses, and strong culinary preferences in parts of France for raw or lightly cooked horse meat, which allowed a heavily infected carcass to seed hundreds of infections across multiple districts. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak strain was identified as T. spiralis, with no evidence of novel genotypes or increased virulence; the episode therefore represents a high‑impact re‑occurrence mediated by food‑safety system failure and consumer behaviour rather than biological change in the parasite.
Review: retain – Restricted this event to the well‑documented 1993 horse‑meat–associated outbreak with 538 cases, rather than combining it with the much smaller 1991 Auvergne outbreak (23 cases), and updated the year to 1993 and the country field to ‘France [1993]’ only.([courses.washington.edu](https://courses.washington.edu/zepi526/Papers09/ancelle_trichinellosis.pdf)) Classification as re‑occurrence in Western Europe is appropriate; this was not a first detection or inter‑continental emergence event because Trichinella was already endemic in European humans well before 1990.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis (human infection with Trichinella spp.)
Host: Humans; wild boar (Sus scrofa) and possibly other game or backyard pigs as source meats, with infection by Trichinella britovi
Event.summary: In 2020, EU/EEA surveillance recorded 117 confirmed trichinellosis cases, with 79 cases notified by Italy and a marked January peak that ECDC attributed largely to a food‑borne outbreak in Italy caused by Trichinella britovi, most likely linked to inadequately cooked meat from wild boar or pigs raised under non‑controlled housing. The outbreak was detected through national notification systems when clusters of patients with febrile myalgia and eosinophilia were found to share consumption of game or pork products, and subsequent trace‑back investigations focused on infected wild boar and backyard pigs. Control actions included tracing and removal of contaminated meat lots, clinical management of cases, expanded testing of wild boar and pigs, and renewed public‑health messaging about the risks of eating raw or undercooked game, which curbed further spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increased recreational hunting and consumption of wild boar and other game meats, incomplete application of Trichinella testing to hunted animals and pigs kept outside controlled housing, and culinary preferences in parts of Italy for undercooked or cured meat products, all of which periodically allow infected carcasses to enter the human food chain despite otherwise low national incidence. Internal mechanisms: the causative agent T. britovi has long circulated in European wildlife; no evidence has been reported of new variants or resistance, so this episode is coded as a re‑occurrence driven by human behaviour and game‑meat handling rather than genetic change in the parasite.
Review: retain – The 2020 Italian outbreak is corroborated by ECDC’s 2020 Annual Epidemiological Report, which notes 79 confirmed cases notified by Italy and a January peak in EU cases linked to a T. britovi food‑borne outbreak there;([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/Trichinellosis-AER_2020_Final.pdf)) while smaller than the large 1990s Eastern European and Argentine waves, it is one of the more substantial recent EU outbreaks and illustrates ongoing re‑occurrence linked to wild‑boar meat in Southern Europe.

EPP.scientific.name: Varicellovirus suidalpha1
EPP.common.name: Aujeszky’s disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1 (pseudorabies virus, PRV)
Host: Human (46-year-old female swineherd with ocular exposure to PRV-contaminated hoggery sewage)
Event.summary: In June 2017, a 46-year-old swineherd from Jiangxi Province, China, developed high fever, headache and rapidly progressive visual loss after her eyes were splashed with sewage from a pig farm experiencing pseudorabies outbreaks. Vitreous humor obtained during vitrectomy yielded thousands of PRV sequence reads by metagenomic next-generation sequencing with over 80 percent genome coverage, findings that were confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing, and subsequent testing showed PRV-specific antibodies in serum and cerebrospinal fluid. The patient’s systemic symptoms resolved but she was left with severe, permanent visual impairment. This case provided the first prospectively investigated, unequivocally molecularly confirmed human PRV infection in China and highlighted direct eye exposure to heavily contaminated farm effluent as a high-risk route, while still showing no evidence of central nervous system involvement or human-to-human spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Direct occupational exposure of the patient’s unprotected eyes to high-titer PRV-contaminated hoggery sewage on a farm with poorly controlled pseudorabies; high PRV prevalence in regional pig herds; limited mandatory vaccination and lack of routine eye and face protection for workers cleaning pig sties; and the growing use of unbiased metagenomic sequencing for atypical ocular infections, which enabled recognition of PRV in this case. Internal mechanisms: Novel genotype II variant PRV strains circulating in Chinese pigs with genetic differences from classical vaccine strains; probable enhanced neuro- and oculotropism of these variants that allows invasion of ocular tissues after mucosal exposure; and host expansion as these pig-adapted variants occasionally cross into humans with intense exposure, yet still without any documented capacity for human-to-human transmission.
Review: Decision: Review. Rationale: Event retained as a discrete, well-documented single-patient emergence episode representing the first widely recognised, molecularly confirmed human PRV infection in China, but first_detection has been changed from true to false because earlier suspected human infections (1914 onward) and at least one retrospectively analysed 2011 encephalitis case predate this event. Host description has been aligned with the case report (adult female swineherd in Jiangxi Province). Event-type coding otherwise remains focused on re-emergence driven by variant strains, with no intra- or inter-continental spread flags. Source list was streamlined to emphasise the primary case report and key contextual reviews.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Varicellovirus suidalpha1
EPP.common.name: Aujeszky’s disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1 (pseudorabies virus, PRV)
Host: Humans (adult farmers, butchers, veterinarians and other workers with recent exposure to PRV-infected pigs or raw pork)
Event.summary: From mid-2016 onward, multicentre Chinese programmes that used metagenomic sequencing to investigate encephalitis of unknown cause began to identify clusters of adults with rapidly progressive panencephalitis, often accompanied by acute retinal necrosis, after close occupational contact with sick pigs or freshly butchered pork. Between 2016 and roughly 2019, at least a dozen such patients from provinces including Henan, Hubei, Shandong and others had PRV sequences detected in cerebrospinal fluid or ocular fluid, with characteristic MRI findings, high mortality and frequent severe neurological or visual sequelae; in 2019, a human PRV strain (hSD-1/2019) was isolated from CSF, showing close phylogenetic affinity to contemporary genotype II variant swine strains and high experimental virulence in pigs. Additional sporadic encephalitis and endophthalmitis cases have continued to be reported through at least 2022–2024, so that on the order of 30–35 molecularly supported human cases are now recognised, consolidating PRV as a rare but severe occupational encephalitic and ocular pathogen in Eastern China.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High prevalence of genotype II variant PRV infection in intensively reared pigs across many Chinese provinces; dense swine production and marketing networks that sustain widespread viral circulation; common occupational practices that expose farmers, butchers and veterinarians with skin breaks or mucosal contact to raw pig tissues, blood and secretions; and the routine introduction of unbiased next-generation sequencing into diagnostic work-ups for encephalitis and severe ocular infections, which markedly increased detection of PRV in human clinical samples. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and subsequent dominance of genotype II variant PRV (clade 2.2) with mutations in key glycoproteins that confer partial immune escape from Bartha-K61-derived vaccines and may enhance neuroinvasiveness; increased virulence and neurotropism in animal models and in affected humans, evidenced by fulminant panencephalitis, respiratory failure and retinal necrosis; and host expansion in the form of rare but severe spillover into heavily exposed adult humans, while remaining incapable of sustained human-to-human transmission.
Review: Decision: Review. Rationale: Event retained as the principal multi-year cluster of severe human PRV encephalitis and ocular disease in China, but the Event Year has been broadened from 2018–2019 to 2016–2024 to reflect published multicentre cohorts, virus-isolation work and systematic reviews showing confirmed cases beginning in mid-2016 and continuing sporadically through at least 2022–2024. Geographic scope remains restricted to China (Eastern Asia), and the event is still coded as re-emergence driven by genotype II variant strains rather than as intra- or inter-continental spread. Source URLs were updated to emphasise the key J Neurovirology cohort study, the Clinical Infectious Diseases report that first isolated a human PRV strain, several detailed case reports and the 2022 systematic review aggregating approximately a dozen encephalitis patients.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: African horse sickness virus
EPP.common.name: AHSV
Host: Horses (working and transport horses in rural Eastern Cape)
Event.summary: From November 2000 through May 2001, a major outbreak of African horse sickness caused by virus serotype 2 struck the Transkei region of South Africa’s Eastern Cape Province, where large numbers of working horses are used for transport and draught. Veterinary reviews estimate that more than 1,000 horses died during this epizootic, making it one of the most severe AHS events in South Africa in recent decades and severely disrupting local rural livelihoods. Emergency vaccination campaigns, restrictions on horse movements and vector control were implemented, and reported cases declined after the 2000–2001 summer–autumn transmission season.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of unvaccinated or poorly vaccinated working horses, together with warm, wet seasonal conditions that favoured Culicoides vector abundance, allowed AHSV-2 to spread rapidly through villages in the coastal Transkei. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was associated with AHSV serotype 2 known from other African regions, with no clear evidence of a novel or unusually virulent lineage; the event is therefore interpreted as a climate- and management-driven re-occurrence of AHS in an endemic country rather than emergence of a new viral variant.
Review: retain – New row added because the 2000–2001 Transkei (Eastern Cape, South Africa) serotype 2 outbreak, with more than 1,000 horse deaths reported in veterinary reviews, is clearly among the largest recent AHS epizootics in South Africa; classified as re-occurrence in an endemic area driven mainly by climatic and management factors, with no strong evidence for novel viral evolution.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: African horse sickness virus
EPP.common.name: AHSV
Host: Horses; donkeys; mules (equids)
Event.summary: Between 2007 and 2010, Ethiopia experienced extensive African horse sickness activity, with retrospective analyses documenting 737 outbreaks across multiple administrative regions and frequent severe disease in horses. Molecular typing showed co-circulation of AHSV serotypes 2, 4, 6, 8 and 9, with serotypes 4, 6 and 8 confirmed in Ethiopia for the first time, indicating substantial diversification of circulating virus populations. Control relied mainly on vaccination of horses and supportive care, and while AHS remained endemic, the intense multi-serotype outbreak activity subsided after 2010 as vaccine coverage and naturally acquired immunity increased.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of susceptible horses and donkeys, environmental conditions highly favourable for Culicoides vectors, and incomplete vaccination coverage—particularly in donkeys, which can sustain subclinical infections—facilitated widespread transmission. Internal mechanisms: The appearance and co-circulation of several additional AHSV serotypes (2, 4, 6, 8 alongside endemic 9) represent re-emergence driven by expanded serotype diversity and genome reassortment, rather than simple resurgence of a single long-established lineage.
Review: review – Event retained but the countries field was standardised to show only the country-specific start year (Ethiopia [2007]) and the source list was streamlined to prioritise primary peer-reviewed articles documenting 737 outbreaks and the first detections of serotypes 4, 6 and 8; classification as re-emergence is appropriate because expansion of serotype diversity clearly contributed to this multi-year epizootic.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: African horse sickness virus
EPP.common.name: AHSV
Host: Horses
Event.summary: Starting in March 2007, African horse sickness virus serotype 2, and to a lesser extent serotype 7, caused a nationwide epizootic in Senegal, beginning around Dakar and then spreading across multiple departments over roughly four months. Retrospective analyses documented 232 outbreaks and about 1,100–1,200 horse deaths, with the overall economic impact of mortality, lost traction power and control measures estimated at around €1.4 million. A large-scale emergency vaccination campaign with polyvalent live-attenuated vaccine, combined with movement restrictions and vector control, brought the epidemic under control by late 2007, after which reported incidence returned to a lower endemic level.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of AHSV-2 (and 7) into a horse population in which previous circulation had been dominated by serotype 9, likely via movements of infected equids from neighbouring West African countries, together with high horse densities in the Niayes and Senegal River valley, abundant Culicoides vectors in the rainy season, and lack of pre-existing immunity to these serotypes, drove rapid spread. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic is best characterised as re-emergence due to the incursion and amplification of new serotypes (2 and 7) in an already AHS-endemic system rather than simple climatic resurgence of serotype 9.
Review: retain – New high-impact event added because the 2007 Senegal epizootic (232 outbreaks, ≈1,100 horse deaths and ~€1.4 million in losses) is one of the largest modern AHS epidemics in West Africa and is explicitly linked to introduction of AHSV-2 (and 7) into a population previously dominated by serotype 9; classified as re-emergence within an endemic region rather than intra-continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: African horse sickness virus
EPP.common.name: AHSV
Host: Horses; donkeys; mules
Event.summary: In 2011, Ethiopia experienced one of its largest recorded African horse sickness seasons, with retrospective veterinary reports indicating 208 outbreaks, 3,036 cases and 1,167 equid deaths across central, northern and western regions. Clinical cases were dominated by the cardiac and horse-sickness fever forms, and virological investigations identified only serotype 9 circulating in the affected areas, differing from the multi-serotype situation documented in 2010. Control consisted of vaccination, movement restrictions and supportive care; incidence decreased after 2011, although AHS remains endemic in Ethiopian equids.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High rainfall and suitable temperatures for Culicoides vectors, large populations of susceptible horses and donkeys, and uneven vaccination coverage created favourable conditions for intense transmission of endemic AHSV-9. Internal mechanisms: No evidence was reported for the emergence of new serotypes or major genomic variants during 2011; the episode is therefore classified as a re-occurrence of endemic serotype 9 driven mainly by climatic and management factors rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain – New row added because the 2011 Ethiopian season, with 208 outbreaks, 3,036 cases and 1,167 deaths, is comparable in scale to the 2007–2010 multi-serotype period and clearly among the country’s largest modern AHS events; classified as re-occurrence of endemic serotype 9, since only AHSV-9 was detected and no substantial genetic novelty was reported.

EPP.scientific.name: African horse sickness virus
EPP.common.name: AHSV
Host: Horses
Event.summary: In 2014, another outbreak of African horse sickness occurred within the African horse sickness controlled area of Western Cape Province, South Africa, with clinical cases confirmed in the Porterville and Robertson areas among horses that should have been protected by strict vaccination and movement controls. Genetic sequencing of AHSV-1 isolates from this outbreak demonstrated close relatedness to components of the polyvalent live-attenuated vaccine, indicating reassortment and reversion to virulence rather than introduction of a wild-type field strain from elsewhere. Rapid implementation of quarantine, expanded movement bans, intensified surveillance and ring vaccination within and around the affected zones led to containment of the outbreak, and horse exports resumed after the required waiting period once no further cases were detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of live-attenuated multivalent AHS vaccines in an endemic country, combined with dense equine populations and suitable Culicoides vectors in the Western Cape controlled area, created conditions in which vaccine-derived viruses could circulate and occasionally escape detection; movements of vaccinated but viraemic horses likely contributed to dispersal before the outbreak was recognised. Internal mechanisms: Whole-genome sequencing confirmed that the 2014 outbreak viruses were reassortants between live-attenuated vaccine strains that had acquired combinations of genome segments associated with increased virulence, representing clear re-emergence through vaccine-derived genome reassortment and reversion to higher pathogenicity.
Review: retain – No major issues identified; the 2014 Western Cape outbreak in the AHS controlled area is well documented as a vaccine-derived AHSV-1 re-emergence episode with relatively limited case numbers but substantial trade and regulatory impact, and its classification as both re-occurrence (within a known AHS risk region) and re-emergence (vaccine-derived strain) without intra- or inter-continental spread is consistent with project definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: African horse sickness virus
EPP.common.name: AHSV
Host: Horses (including racehorses and pleasure horses); zebras in captivity (probable source)
Event.summary: In early 2020, horses in Pak Chong district of Nakhon Ratchasima Province, northeastern Thailand, developed peracute respiratory signs, oedema and rapid death, and laboratory testing in March–April 2020 confirmed African horse sickness virus serotype 1, marking the first confirmed AHS outbreak in Thailand and in South-eastern Asia. WOAH reports and subsequent studies documented 607 cases with an estimated case-fatality rate of about 93% in naïve horses, and spread to multiple provinces before emergency measures took full effect. Large-scale ring vaccination with live-attenuated AHS vaccine, strict movement bans, zoning and vector control were implemented, which eventually curbed further spread within Thailand, although intensive surveillance and vaccination continued over subsequent seasons as authorities sought to re-establish AHS-free status.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely illegal or poorly regulated importation of infected equids—particularly zebras—from Africa into Thailand shortly before the first detected cases, combined with abundant Culicoides vectors, a fully susceptible horse population and extensive local equine movements, facilitated rapid establishment and explosive spread; delays in recognising AHS as the cause further increased impact. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses showed that the outbreak strain was AHSV-1 closely related to southern African lineages rather than a novel serotype, with its impact driven primarily by highly efficient vector-borne transmission into an immunologically naïve horse population, representing intra-continental geographic range expansion within Asia rather than antigenic innovation.
Review: review – Event retained and remains one of the most consequential recent AHS outbreaks (607 cases with ~93% case-fatality in a naïve horse population), but the “first_detection” flag has been set to false because AHS was described and detected in equids long before 2020; the event is more accurately classified as an intra-continental emergence within Asia, representing spread of an established African serotype to a previously unaffected subregion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: African horse sickness virus
EPP.common.name: AHSV
Host: Horses (backyard and sport horses)
Event.summary: In August 2020, horses on a property in Manir, Terengganu State on the Malay Peninsula developed fever and respiratory signs, and by early September the Malaysian veterinary authorities notified WOAH that five backyard horses had tested positive for African horse sickness virus, representing the first confirmed occurrence of AHS in Malaysia. Epidemiologic investigations and sequence data indicated that the Malaysian outbreak was caused by AHSV-1 closely related to the 2020 Thai outbreak strain, suggesting spread from Thailand into Malaysia with a limited number of clinically affected horses. Rapid implementation of quarantine, movement controls, targeted vaccination around affected holdings and heightened surveillance led to containment of the outbreak, with no evidence of wider establishment in Malaysia and subsequent suspension and later restoration of the country’s officially recognised AHS-free status.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional spread of AHSV-1 from Thailand—via either cross-border movement of infected equids or wind-borne dispersal of infected Culicoides midges—into an AHS-free Malaysia, coupled with suitable tropical conditions for vectors and local horse movements, enabled in situ transmission in Terengganu; concurrent COVID-19-related disruptions may have complicated surveillance and logistics. Internal mechanisms: The virus was not a novel serotype but represented geographic range expansion of AHSV-1 within Asia, with high virulence in naïve horses; this event is best viewed as a small, epidemiologically linked extension of the Thai outbreak rather than a separate evolutionary shift.
Review: review – Event retained as part of the 2020 South-eastern Asian emergence episode and the first confirmed occurrence of AHS in Malaysia, but the “first_detection” flag has been set to false because AHS was detected and described in horses long before 2020; the event is best classified as an intra-continental emergence tightly linked to the Thai outbreak, with only limited local transmission in Terengganu.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: African swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: ASFV
Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar (limited detection compared to pigs)
Event.summary: On 3 August 2018, China reported its first African swine fever outbreak in Liaoning Province in northeastern China, with confirmation of genotype II ASFV from affected pigs and rapid identification of further outbreaks along major transport corridors. Over late 2018 and 2019, the virus spread to all provinces, leading to massive culling and mortality that reduced China’s pig herd by an estimated 40–50%, disrupted domestic pork supply and reshaped global pork markets. ASF persisted with recurrent outbreaks through at least 2022, despite large‑scale depopulation, movement controls and biosecurity campaigns, with emergence of additional viral variants and concerns about substandard vaccines contributing to continued virus circulation.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: large, highly integrated but unevenly biosecure pig production sector; long‑distance trucking of pigs and pork; widespread swill feeding and informal slaughter; complex supply chains; and delayed or incomplete reporting in some areas. Internal mechanisms: introduction of highly virulent genotype II ASFV into the previously ASF‑free Eastern Asia subregion, followed by emergence of additional variants/strains within China, potential selection pressure from experimental or illicit vaccines, and inherent viral stability that enabled sustained endemicity and widespread geographic range expansion across all Chinese regions.
Review: retain – This is by far the single most impactful ASF event globally in terms of pigs lost and market disruption. Under the UNSD classification, ASF had already reached Western Asia in 2007, so the appropriate type is intra‑continental emergence into a new Asian subregion (Eastern Asia), not inter‑continental emergence. 'First_detection' was set to No, as global first detection predates 1990. Countries, timing and impact are well supported by WOAH, FAO, USDA and peer‑reviewed sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alcelaphine gammaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Indigenous Tanzanian shorthorn zebu cattle grazing near wildebeest calving grounds
Event.summary: In April–June 2004, pastoral Maasai herds in Enguserosambu village, Ngorongoro District, northern Tanzania, experienced an outbreak of acute malignant catarrhal fever in zebu cattle following the wildebeest calving season. Cattle grazing at the wildlife–livestock interface developed high fever, corneal opacity, mucopurulent nasal discharge and high case fatality, and Alcelaphine herpesvirus 1 was confirmed by molecular characterization from affected animals. Losses subsided after cattle were moved away from wildebeest areas and surviving animals either died or recovered, but the episode highlighted the recurrent seasonal risk of wildebeest‑associated MCF in this pastoral ecosystem.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Seasonal overlap of Maasai cattle with dense migratory wildebeest populations at shared grazing and water sources in Ngorongoro, together with semi‑nomadic management that brings susceptible cattle into close contact with wildebeest calves during peak viral shedding.
