Internal mechanisms: Long‑established circulation of AlHV‑1 in blue wildebeest, with very high viral shedding from calves around calving driving aerosol transmission to cattle; there is no evidence that a novel strain or host shift was involved, so this episode represents a severe re‑occurrence in an endemic risk system.
Review: Retain: Well‑documented wildebeest‑associated MCF outbreak in Maasai cattle in Enguserosambu (Ngorongoro District) with clear epidemiological linkage to wildebeest calving and substantial local livestock losses; continent/subregion/country coding and event‑type classification as re‑occurrence in Eastern Africa are appropriate, and the sources used are directly relevant to the event.

EPP.scientific.name: Anaplasma marginale
EPP.common.name: Bovine anaplasmosis
Host: Dairy cattle (Bos taurus)
Event.summary: In August 2002, a large dairy herd of 286 cows in the canton of Grisons, alpine Switzerland, experienced an outbreak of severe hemolytic disease marked by fever, anorexia, agalactia, anemia and high culling, in a region where bovine anaplasmosis had previously been reported only sporadically and without major economic impact. Microscopy, serology and PCR confirmed Anaplasma marginale infection in nearly half the cows, alongside frequent co-infections with Babesia/Theileria spp. and Mycoplasma wenyonii, making this the first severe bovine anaplasmosis outbreak linked to multiple vector-borne pathogens in alpine Switzerland. After diagnosis, the entire herd was culled and regional surveillance showed very low but non-zero seroprevalence, indicating a dramatic re-occurrence of disease rather than first introduction of the pathogen.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of A. marginale into a largely immunologically naïve high-yield dairy herd north of the Alps, with abundant tick and biting-fly exposure, created conditions for high within-herd transmission and severe clinical disease; regional cattle trade likely contributed to pathogen introduction. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel A. marginale genotype was reported; disease severity appears to have been amplified by polymicrobial co-infections (Babesia, Theileria, haemotropic mycoplasmas) and age-dependent susceptibility in adult cows.
Review: Retain: Well-documented 2002 alpine Switzerland outbreak with substantial morbidity and culling, confirmed by OIE notification and detailed clinical/molecular description, and representing a dramatic resurgence of bovine anaplasmosis in a previously low-impact area of Western Europe. Classification as re-occurrence (not first detection or intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because earlier sporadic Swiss cases and established infection in other Western European countries pre‑date this event. No corrections needed beyond trimming sources to those directly describing the Swiss outbreak.

EPP.scientific.name: Anaplasma marginale
EPP.common.name: Bovine anaplasmosis
Host: Cattle (Leiqiong and Wagyu breeds), water buffalo, and Rhipicephalus microplus ticks
Event.summary: From May to September 2020, researchers in northern Hainan, China collected 151 bovine blood samples (Leiqiong cattle, Wagyu cattle and buffalo) and 63 Rhipicephalus microplus ticks and, using PCR, detected Anaplasma marginale in 10.75% of all samples together with Babesia bovis and B. bigemina, with high mixed-infection rates in Leiqiong cattle. The work was presented as the first molecular detection of A. marginale, B. bovis and B. bigemina in cattle and R. microplus from the sampled northern coastal area of Hainan, complementing earlier province-level evidence of A. marginale circulation. Although not a point-source outbreak, the findings documented a substantial endemic focus of bovine anaplasmosis and piroplasmosis in an important subtropical island cattle area and prompted calls for improved tick control and surveillance to avert clinical losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Warm, humid coastal climate in Hainan favors proliferation of R. microplus, and local husbandry practices with high tick exposure in Leiqiong cattle and buffalo enable persistent circulation of A. marginale and Babesia spp.; increasing animal movement and under-appreciation of tick-borne disease risk likely contributed to under-detection before this survey. Internal mechanisms: No novel A. marginale genotypes were highlighted; the event mainly reflects improved detection and recognition of endemic transmission in a specific region of Hainan rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Review: The study robustly demonstrates A. marginale and Babesia spp. circulation in cattle and R. microplus in northern Hainan and can reasonably be treated as a regional emergence/re-recognition event, but it is a cross-sectional molecular survey rather than a clearly bounded clinical outbreak with quantified production losses. The event is classified as re-occurrence within Eastern Asia, consistent with prior evidence of A. marginale in Hainan and other Chinese provinces; it does not qualify as first detection for China or for the island as a whole. A non-specific Babesia review article previously listed as a source has been removed in favor of the primary preprint and ResearchGate versions of the Hainan study. Consider retaining this event only if the dataset aims to include important detection-based emergence signals alongside major clinical outbreaks.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Anaplasma marginale
EPP.common.name: Bovine anaplasmosis
Host: Dairy cattle (smallholder farms)
Event.summary: In a study published in 2024, investigators conducted the first molecular survey of Anaplasma marginale in healthy dairy cattle from 40 smallholder farms in Khon Kaen Province, north-eastern Thailand, and detected infection in 49 of 385 animals (overall prevalence ≈12.7%), with positives spread across multiple districts. Phylogenetic analysis of msp4 sequences showed Thai isolates clustering with A. marginale strains from Australia, China, Spain and the USA, indicating widespread international strain sharing. The findings demonstrated that bovine anaplasmosis is already endemic in the emerging dairy sector of north-eastern Thailand, where clinical disease may previously have been under-recognized, and led to recommendations for enhanced tick control, farmer awareness and diagnostic capacity to reduce future clinical outbreaks and productivity losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Smallholder dairy systems in north-eastern Thailand with frequent tick exposure, limited acaricide use and increasing cattle movement across the Mekong subregion create favorable conditions for establishment and spread of A. marginale. Internal mechanisms: No distinct Thai-specific lineage was identified beyond global msp4 similarity; the emergence pattern is driven mainly by geographic range expansion and recognition of under-detected endemic transmission rather than documented genetic change, making this a re-occurrence/intensification event rather than re-emergence.
Review: Review: The Khon Kaen study provides solid molecular evidence of established endemic A. marginale infection in dairy cattle in a previously under-studied area of South-eastern Asia, but it describes a prevalence survey rather than a discrete clinical outbreak with quantified production losses. It is therefore a borderline inclusion if the event list is restricted strictly to the most impactful outbreak episodes by cases or economic loss. Classification as re-occurrence within an already affected continent and sub-region is appropriate, and the country, sub-region and year are consistent with the primary article. Recommend retaining if the project values key detection-based emergence signals; otherwise consider deprioritising this event relative to large clinical outbreaks.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Aparavirus tauraense
EPP.common.name: Taura syndrome virus, TSV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei)
Event.summary: In 1992 shrimp farmers in Guayas Province, Ecuador, near the Taura River, observed a new, acute disease in L. vannamei characterised by red tails, soft shells and high mortality, soon termed Taura syndrome. During 1992–1993 the syndrome spread rapidly among coastal farms, becoming the most important disease of farmed L. vannamei in the Western Hemisphere and causing major production losses. Subsequent investigations demonstrated a viral aetiology, and the causative agent was characterised and named Taura syndrome virus (now Aparavirus tauraense), marking its first known emergence in the shrimp host system.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid intensification and expansion of L. vannamei aquaculture in coastal Ecuador, high farm and pond connectivity, and frequent movement of postlarvae and juveniles among farms facilitated the amplification and farm‑to‑farm spread of the newly emerged pathogen. Internal mechanisms: TSV, a positive‑sense RNA virus, likely arose as a novel agent in intensive shrimp culture with high mutation rates and efficient horizontal transmission, enabling rapid establishment in naïve farmed shrimp populations.
Review: Retain (minor corrections). Adjusted Event Year from 1991–1993 to 1992–1993 and standardised the country entry to Ecuador [1992], because multiple authoritative reviews place the first recognised Taura syndrome outbreaks in June 1992 near the Taura River even though phylogenetic work suggests a most‑recent common ancestor around 1991. Sources were focused on primary reviews and the WOAH manual rather than Wikipedia. No change in event type: this remains the first/global emergence in the shrimp host system.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Aparavirus tauraense
EPP.common.name: Taura syndrome virus, TSV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) in grow-out ponds in the Lake Maracaibo and Paraguaná regions
Event.summary: Until the early 2000s, Venezuela remained free of documented TSV despite extensive spread elsewhere in the Americas. In late 2004, farms in western Venezuela (notably in Lake Maracaibo and the Paraguaná Peninsula) experienced a severe epizootic in L. vannamei with classic Taura syndrome signs, high mortalities and pond survivals in some areas reportedly as low as 5–30%. Histopathology and RT‑PCR confirmed TSV infection, and the epizootic spread rapidly across the western shrimp‑farming region through 2004–2005, prompting OIE notifications and calls for urgent biosecurity and stock‑replacement measures. Subsequent genetic work on a Venezuelan isolate (TSV‑VE05) from this outbreak showed it to be a distinct variant within the global TSV phylogeny.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement of infected postlarvae and broodstock from neighbouring TSV‑endemic countries, inadequate on‑farm biosecurity, reuse of pond water, and mechanical transmission by birds and aquatic insects were all implicated in the rapid spread of TSV across western Venezuelan farms. Environmental stressors, particularly episodes of heavy rainfall and associated salinity drops in Lake Maracaibo, were associated with peaks in mortality. Internal mechanisms: the Venezuelan outbreak isolate TSV‑VE05 differed genetically from earlier American isolates (about 7% divergence from the HI94 reference strain in the genome sequence) and has been recognised as a new TSV variant; its virulence in experimental infections was comparable to highly pathogenic reference strains, supporting classification of this episode as a strain‑driven re‑emergence within the South American subregion.
Review: Retain (newly added major event). This large 2004–2005 epizootic in western Venezuela was missing from the original JSON despite clear evidence of severe regional impact (very low pond survivals and rapid spread) and its association with a genetically distinct Venezuelan TSV variant. It has been added as a re_emergence event (not intra‑ or inter‑continental, because TSV was already established elsewhere in South America) driven by novel strain emergence and poor biosecurity. Dates and impact are based on detailed clinical, histopathological and RT‑PCR descriptions from Venezuelan field studies plus genetic characterisation of TSV‑VE05. Further expert review could refine the exact start–end years, but the event clearly belongs among the top TSV emergence episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Aparavirus tauraense
EPP.common.name: Taura syndrome virus, TSV
Host: Cultured Indian white shrimp (Penaeus indicus) in intensive farms on the Red Sea coast
Event.summary: During 2010–2011, intensive P. indicus farms on the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia experienced severe disease outbreaks in which both WSSV and TSV were detected, with TSV first confirmed by RT‑PCR in mid‑2010. At affected farms, shrimp began dying about 30 days after stocking and survivals at harvest dropped to roughly 30–50%, with Taura syndrome disease persisting through 2010 and into 2011 and losses increasing further when WSSV appeared. Molecular analyses showed that Saudi TSV isolates formed a distinct lineage separate from previously described Americas, Belize, South‑East Asia and Venezuelan groups.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of intensive P. indicus culture in Saudi Arabia, coupled with importation of P. vannamei and other shrimp stocks from TSV‑endemic regions, and limited initial biosecurity measures, created conditions for introduction and establishment of TSV in a previously unaffected Western Asian shrimp‑farming zone. High farm density and water exchange among ponds facilitated on‑farm and farm‑to‑farm spread, while co‑infection with WSSV exacerbated mortality and economic losses. Internal mechanisms: Saudi TSV isolates represent a distinct genotype within the global TSV phylogeny, suggesting evolutionary diversification as TSV spread into new environments and host species; this, together with confirmed disease in P. indicus, indicates re‑emergence with host expansion and genotype divergence within a new Asian subregion.
Review: Retain (new intra-continental re-emergence event). This 2010–2011 episode represents the first well‑documented establishment of TSV in Western Asia and in intensive P. indicus culture, with clearly described high mortalities and production losses, and a distinct Saudi TSV genotype. It has therefore been added as an intra_continental_emergence (new UNSD sub‑region within Asia) and re_emergence (new genotype and host expansion). This corrects the original assertion that there were no major 2005–2025 emergence events. The event should be retained as a key later‑phase emergence episode; additional regional surveillance data could clarify whether TSV has since spread widely in the Middle East or remained largely confined to Saudi farms.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphanomyces astaci
EPP.common.name: Crayfish plague
Host: Wild and commercially harvested narrow‑clawed crayfish Pontastacus (Astacus) leptodactylus in major Turkish lakes and reservoirs
Event.summary: In the mid‑1980s, intensive crayfish fisheries in western Anatolia began experiencing unexplained mass mortalities, first reported from Lake Çivril and other western Turkish lakes around 1985. Subsequent diagnostic work and field studies confirmed Aphanomyces astaci as the etiological agent of the disease, and the pathogen spread rapidly through the main lake and reservoir fisheries, driving national landings of Pontastacus leptodactylus down from roughly 5,000–7,000 tonnes in 1984 to a few hundred tonnes by 1991.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0044848603004290?utm_source=openai)) By the early 1990s most commercial crayfish stocks in Türkiye had collapsed, and the acute nationwide epizootic transitioned into a state of chronically depleted, fragmented populations with only localized harvesting.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: strong export demand from European markets led to heavy exploitation and large‑scale live crayfish trade, while translocations of crayfish among Turkish lakes and minimal biosecurity facilitated both the initial introduction of A. astaci from Europe and its rapid spread through inland waters.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0044848603004290?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: the high susceptibility of P. leptodactylus to A. astaci, combined with efficient waterborne zoospore transmission in dense lake fisheries, produced explosive epidemics and near‑total mortality, representing a major geographic range expansion of the pathogen from Europe into Western Asia.
Review: Review – Retain this event as one of the most impactful emergence episodes (collapse of a major crayfish fishery and first well‑documented inter‑continental spread of A. astaci into Asia), but the original row mis‑used the 'first_detection' flag (now set to No, because global first detection occurred in 19th‑century Europe) and lacked clarity on the start year. The event period has been adjusted from 1984–1991 to 1985–1991 based on Turkish harvest and outbreak data, while acknowledging that some sources reference 1984 as the last pre‑plague baseline year; a human reviewer should confirm whether including this pre‑1990‑onset episode is acceptable under the "post‑1990" rule.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Aphanomyces astaci
EPP.common.name: Crayfish plague
Host: Native white‑clawed crayfish Austropotamobius pallipes in three central Italian river systems
Event.summary: In the summer of 2009, dense populations of the native white‑clawed crayfish Austropotamobius pallipes in three watercourses of central Italy suffered sudden mass mortalities over a few weeks. Laboratory examination of moribund and dead crayfish, including culture and PCR, identified Aphanomyces astaci as the cause of disease, representing the first crayfish plague outbreak in Italian A. pallipes populations to be confirmed by isolation of the pathogen in culture.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20481093/?utm_source=openai)) Following the die‑offs, affected reaches were left virtually devoid of native crayfish, and post‑outbreak management focused on local movement restrictions, surveillance and habitat protection rather than attempted eradication of the pathogen.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: long‑term spread of invasive North American crayfish (especially Procambarus clarkii and Pacifastacus leniusculus) in Italian waters and human‑mediated transfers of live crayfish or contaminated fishing gear between catchments likely introduced A. astaci into these central Italian streams.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233799926_Crayfish_in_Italy_Distribution_threats_and_management?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: the extreme susceptibility of A. pallipes to A. astaci and the rapid zoospore‑mediated transmission of the pathogen in small headwater streams led to near‑complete local extirpation once the fungus became established, exemplifying classic crayfish plague re‑occurrence in an already endemic European region.
Review: Review – Added as a new event because a large 2009 outbreak in wild Austropotamobius pallipes is widely documented and represents one of the most important post‑1990 European re‑occurrence episodes. Classified as re‑occurrence (not intra‑/inter‑continental emergence) because A. astaci has been established in Italy since the 19th century and no clear evidence of a distinct new genotype or host shift was identified in this outbreak; a human reviewer may wish to confirm whether concurrent 2009 epizootics in farmed Cherax destructor should be represented in a separate row or referenced only in the narrative.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphanomyces astaci
EPP.common.name: Crayfish plague
Host: Invasive red swamp crayfish Procambarus clarkii (feral pond and reservoir populations) and native burrowing crayfish Parastacus defossus and Parastacus pilimanus (low‑level infections)
Event.summary: Around 2012–2013, molecular surveys of feral Procambarus clarkii populations in reservoirs and irrigation ponds in south‑eastern and southern Brazil provided the first confirmed record of Aphanomyces astaci in South America. Quantitative and conventional PCR assays detected the pathogen in multiple invasive P. clarkii populations and revealed low‑level ('agent level A2') infections in two native burrowing crayfish species, Parastacus defossus and P. pilimanus, occurring in sympatry.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/306248212_First_detection_of_the_crayfish_plague_pathogen_Aphanomyces_astaci_in_South_America_a_high_potential_risk_to_native_crayfish?utm_source=openai)) Although large‑scale crayfish die‑offs had not yet been documented at the study sites, the findings showed that crayfish plague had been introduced to a continent with high endemic crayfish diversity, raising alarm about potential future epizootics and losses of native Parastacus species.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: decades of introductions and spread of P. clarkii for aquaculture, live food and the aquarium trade in Brazil created self‑sustaining invasive populations, and unregulated movements of live crayfish between waterbodies facilitated the silent spread of A. astaci.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/306248212_First_detection_of_the_crayfish_plague_pathogen_Aphanomyces_astaci_in_South_America_a_high_potential_risk_to_native_crayfish?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: chronic, often subclinical carriage of A. astaci by P. clarkii and environmental overlap with susceptible native Parastacus species enabled pathogen spillover and establishment in a new continent (inter‑continental emergence), despite the absence of immediately obvious mass mortality events at the time of detection.
Review: Review – New row added because the Brazilian detection of A. astaci in feral Procambarus clarkii and sympatric native Parastacus species is the first confirmed record of crayfish plague in South America and therefore a key inter‑continental emergence event, even though documented mortality was limited at the time of study. Classified as inter‑continental emergence (South America) with 'first_detection' kept as No because this is not the first global description of the pathogen; a human reviewer should confirm the chosen event window (2012–2013), which follows the timing reported in global syntheses but is approximate in the primary Hydrobiologia paper.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphanomyces astaci
EPP.common.name: Crayfish plague
Host: Farmed redclaw crayfish Cherax quadricarinatus (Australian species introduced into freshwater aquaculture)
Event.summary: Between November/December 2013 and January 2014, five freshwater crayfish farms in northern and southern Taiwan experienced outbreaks of an initially unknown disease in redclaw crayfish (Cherax quadricarinatus), with moderate to very high cumulative mortality and up to 100% losses at most affected farms. Histopathology and PCR with species‑specific ITS primers identified Aphanomyces astaci as the causative agent, confirming the first crayfish plague outbreaks in Asia involving an Australian Cherax species and the first report of C. quadricarinatus naturally infected by A. astaci.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201116300313?utm_source=openai)) Control measures, including fallowing and disinfection of ponds and adjustment of stocking practices, ended the acute mortality episodes, but the outbreaks raised serious concern about further spread of the pathogen in Asian aquaculture.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: international trade in live redclaw crayfish and/or co‑stocked North American crayfish, together with movements of contaminated water and equipment among farms, likely introduced A. astaci into Taiwanese aquaculture, where high stocking density and water reuse favoured rapid farm‑level spread.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201116300313?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: host expansion into a highly susceptible non‑native Cherax species in a warm‑water Asian setting, combined with efficient zoospore production and transmission within dense pond populations, produced fulminant disease with very high mortality, marking the first documented intra‑continental emergence of crayfish plague from Western Asia into Eastern Asia.
Review: Review – Original event correctly highlighted this as a major outbreak but mis‑classified it as both intra‑continental emergence and re‑emergence. Under the provided definitions, the Taiwan episode is best treated purely as intra‑continental emergence (first confirmed crayfish plague outbreaks in Eastern Asia), with 're_emergence' set to No because the sub‑region had not previously been known to harbour the pathogen. Event dates, host description and sources remain appropriate, but a human reviewer should confirm that the country label ('Taiwan (Province of China)') aligns with the project’s Country sheet conventions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphanomyces astaci
EPP.common.name: Crayfish plague
Host: Endemic Japanese crayfish Cambaroides japonicus in streams near Sapporo (Hokkaido), with invasive Procambarus clarkii and Pacifastacus leniusculus acting as reservoir hosts
Event.summary: In October 2014, mass mortality of the endemic Japanese crayfish Cambaroides japonicus was first reported from a stream in Sapporo, Hokkaido, prompting concern about a novel disease threatening this already declining species. Molecular analyses (ITS and mitochondrial rnnS/rnnL regions) and histology confirmed Aphanomyces astaci infection in C. japonicus and in sympatric invasive Procambarus clarkii and Pacifastacus leniusculus, with evidence for both a known d1 haplotype and a novel d3 haplotype associated with P. clarkii.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5884544/?utm_source=openai)) During 2014–2015 multiple C. japonicus populations around Sapporo suffered severe die‑offs, dramatically reducing local abundance and leading Japanese authorities and researchers to warn that crayfish plague now posed a serious extinction risk to Japan’s only native crayfish species.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: long‑standing introductions of North American crayfish (P. clarkii, P. leniusculus) in Japan created persistent reservoirs of A. astaci, and human‑mediated translocations of invasive crayfish, combined with habitat overlap with remnant C. japonicus populations, facilitated cross‑species transmission.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5884544/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel mitochondrial haplotype (d3) in P. clarkii and spillover of A. astaci into highly susceptible native C. japonicus represent pathogen genetic diversification and host expansion within an already infected sub‑region, justifying classification as re‑emergence rather than first introduction to Eastern Asia; the outbreaks caused the first confirmed crayfish plague epizootics in a non‑European native crayfish.
Review: Review – Event retained as a major episode but re‑classified: because A. astaci was already present in East Asia (in invasive crayfish) before the 2014–2015 die‑offs, this outbreak in Cambaroides japonicus is best coded as re‑emergence only, not as a new intra‑continental emergence. The narrative correctly emphasises the appearance of a novel haplotype and host shift, which fit the definition of re‑emergence; a human reviewer may wish to confirm whether earlier (2012–2013) Japanese detections in invasive crayfish should be represented as a separate, smaller emergence event or left as background to this high‑impact native‑host outbreak.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphanomyces astaci
EPP.common.name: Crayfish plague
Host: Native white‑clawed crayfish Austropotamobius pallipes in multiple Irish river catchments (Erne and subsequent rivers)
Event.summary: In August 2015, more than 600 dead white‑clawed crayfish Austropotamobius pallipes were reported from the Bruskey River in the Erne catchment in County Cavan, Republic of Ireland; laboratory testing confirmed Aphanomyces astaci as the cause, marking the first confirmed crayfish plague outbreak in Ireland since an unconfirmed event in 1987.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/303035030_Outbreak_of_crayfish_plague_in_Ireland?utm_source=openai)) Over the following years, additional outbreaks and environmental‑DNA detections of A. astaci occurred in multiple river systems (including the Suir, Deel, Barrow, Nore, Shannon, Moy, Sligo and others), leading to severe declines or local extirpations of A. pallipes populations in affected catchments.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10819094/?utm_source=openai)) By about 2019, Ireland had established a National Crayfish Plague Surveillance Programme and strengthened biosecurity messaging, but once A. astaci became established it remained entrenched, threatening Ireland’s status as a stronghold for the species.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: accidental introduction of non‑native crayfish carrying A. astaci (likely through illegal stocking or releases) and the spread of spores on contaminated angling, boating and other water‑contact equipment between catchments are considered the most plausible drivers of these outbreaks.([fisheriesireland.ie](https://www.fisheriesireland.ie/news/media-releases/investigation-underway-into-cause-of-crayfish-plague-on-river-bruskey-near?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: the extreme susceptibility of A. pallipes to A. astaci and rapid dispersal of zoospores in connected river networks produced rapid, near‑complete mortality once outbreaks began, characteristic of classic crayfish plague re‑occurrence in a region where the pathogen had probably been absent for decades.
Review: Review – New row added because the 2015–2019 Irish outbreaks eliminated or severely reduced many of the last large, relatively intact white‑clawed crayfish populations in Europe, clearly qualifying as one of the most impactful post‑1990 crayfish plague events. Classified as re‑occurrence (not intra‑/inter‑continental) because Ireland experienced at least one earlier outbreak in 1987 and there is no strong evidence that a fundamentally new strain or host shift drove the 2015+ epizootics; a human reviewer may refine the end year or split later outbreaks into a separate episode if more detailed genotyping data suggest multiple independent introductions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphanomyces astaci
EPP.common.name: Crayfish plague
Host: Invasive red swamp crayfish Procambarus clarkii (feral pond population) and coexisting freshwater crabs and shrimps in West Java
Event.summary: Around 2018, field surveys in West Java documented an established outdoor population of the invasive red swamp crayfish Procambarus clarkii and its widespread availability in Indonesian ornamental pet shops. Molecular diagnostics using species‑specific mitochondrial markers confirmed Aphanomyces astaci infection in the feral P. clarkii population and in P. clarkii held in at least one pet shop, and also detected A. astaci DNA in coexisting freshwater crab and shrimp species from the same locality, demonstrating that crayfish plague had entered Indonesian inland waters.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/aqc.2970?utm_source=openai)) No major mass mortality events were reported at the study sites during the survey period, but the combination of invasive host establishment and pathogen detection indicated successful introduction and early establishment of A. astaci in maritime South‑east Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: importation and domestic trade of live P. clarkii for food and as ornamental animals, together with releases into ponds and natural water bodies, facilitated both host and pathogen introduction in Indonesia, where regulations prohibited import of hazardous fish species but allowed aquaculture and internal transport of P. clarkii.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/aqc.2970?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: chronic carrier status of P. clarkii and the ability of A. astaci to infect non‑crayfish decapods allowed the pathogen to persist and circulate in local decapod communities, representing an intra‑continental range expansion within Asia into a previously uninfected sub‑region with high endemic crustacean diversity and substantial aquaculture.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/aqc.2970?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – New row added because the Indonesian detections represent the first confirmed establishment of A. astaci in South‑eastern Asia and thus a key intra‑continental emergence event, even though large die‑offs have not yet been documented. The event is coded as intra‑continental emergence (Asia) with no re‑occurrence/re‑emergence flags, reflecting that this is the first known presence in this sub‑region; a human reviewer should verify the precise onset year based on sampling dates in Putra et al. (2018) and any subsequent OIE reports.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Avian metapneumovirus
EPP.common.name: Avian pneumovirus, TRT virus
Host: Commercial chickens (broilers and layers), later turkeys on Brazilian farms
Event.summary: In the mid‑1990s, avian metapneumovirus (primarily subtype A) was first detected in Latin America, with the earliest confirmed reports from Brazilian poultry flocks in 1995 based on field samples from chickens showing respiratory disease and swollen head syndrome. Over the following few years, serologic and virologic surveys showed the virus becoming established in Brazilian chicken and turkey operations across multiple regions, associated with respiratory signs and egg‑production losses. By the late 1990s the virus was considered endemic in much of the Brazilian poultry sector, prompting the development and introduction of vaccination and improved biosecurity measures to control recurring outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of Brazilian poultry production, high densities of broiler and layer farms, and limited prior immunity or vaccination against aMPV in Latin America facilitated initial establishment and spread; regional poultry movements likely dispersed infection between states. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of aMPV subtype A into a previously naïve continental poultry population (novel strain for the region) with efficient respiratory transmission in chickens and turkeys allowed rapid geographic range expansion and high within‑flock attack rates.
Review: Decision: retain. Evidence from Brazilian virological and serological studies confirms first isolation of aMPV from broiler‑breeder flocks in Brazil in 1995, with rapid spread and establishment in broilers and turkeys over subsequent years; Chilean detections in 1997 appear secondary and smaller in scale. Classification as first detection plus inter‑continental emergence for South America is appropriate, and no larger Latin American aMPV event in 1990–2025 was identified. No structural changes made.

EPP.scientific.name: Avian metapneumovirus
EPP.common.name: Avian pneumovirus, TRT virus
Host: Commercial meat turkeys (Colorado, then Minnesota and other upper‑Midwest states); later other turkey flocks in the region
Event.summary: In May 1996, a severe upper respiratory disease outbreak with sinusitis and conjunctivitis affected commercial meat turkeys in Colorado, and laboratory investigation at the US National Veterinary Services Laboratories identified avian metapneumovirus, later classified as the novel subgroup C, marking the first detection of aMPV in North American poultry. Over the late 1990s the virus spread from Colorado to major turkey‑producing states in the upper Midwest, including Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, Iowa and Wisconsin, with a large proportion of turkey premises testing seropositive and industry losses estimated at roughly US$15 million per year from 1997–2000. As live‑attenuated vaccines and strengthened biosecurity and surveillance were implemented, incidence in US commercial turkeys declined, and by the early 2000s the multi‑state subtype C epizootic had largely subsided, leaving the virus under much better control in US flocks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of commercial turkey production in Colorado and the upper Midwest, movement of birds, equipment and personnel between farms, and concurrent circulation of other respiratory pathogens (e.g., avian influenza, mycoplasmas) promoted rapid farm‑to‑farm spread and exacerbated disease severity. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a genetically and antigenically distinct subgroup C lineage compared with European A/B strains reduced detection by existing serologic assays and suggested prior evolution in wild birds, representing both a novel genotype and an inter‑continental range expansion into a naïve turkey population.
Review: Decision: review. The event window was expanded from 1996–1998 to 1996–2000 to reflect evidence that subtype C aMPV spread from Colorado to Minnesota and neighboring upper‑Midwest states and caused substantial economic losses through about 2000, rather than being confined to Colorado and Minnesota in the first two years. The previous flagging of this episode as 're_emergence' was removed, because the outbreak represents first continental introduction of aMPV into North American poultry rather than reappearance in a previously infected North American subregion. Additional US‑focused overview papers were added to better document the multi‑state extent and economic impact of the epizootic.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Avian metapneumovirus
EPP.common.name: Avian pneumovirus, TRT virus
Host: Muscovy ducks and other farmed ducks in France; subsequent detections in wild ducks and other wild birds in Europe
Event.summary: Around 1999, subtype C avian metapneumovirus was first isolated in farmed Muscovy ducks in France, representing the first detection of this subgroup outside North America and the emergence of a distinct Eurasian aMPV‑C lineage in waterfowl. Over the ensuing several years, aMPV‑C infections were documented in domestic ducks and in multiple wild bird species in Europe, indicating establishment of a duck‑ and wild‑bird–associated lineage that was genetically distinct from US turkey aMPV‑C strains and from European A/B viruses. As knowledge of this lineage grew, management responses focused on enhanced surveillance of ducks and wild birds and on considering duck and wild‑bird reservoirs in control strategies for poultry aMPV in Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close contact between domestic ducks and wild waterfowl, outdoor and free‑range duck production, and shared wetlands facilitated spillover and maintenance of the virus in duck populations and wild‑bird reservoirs. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a distinct Eurasian aMPV‑C lineage with adaptation to ducks and wild waterfowl represents host expansion and genomic diversification within aMPV‑C, enabling efficient transmission and persistence in new host species while remaining antigenically distinct from A/B strains and from North American turkey aMPV‑C.
Review: Decision: review. Timing (starting in 1999) and classification as re‑emergence in a region where aMPV A/B were already endemic remain appropriate, but the event’s source list was revised to prioritize papers that directly describe the French Muscovy duck aMPV‑C isolates and their phylogenetic placement, rather than relying mainly on Chinese or generic systematic‑review articles. No evidence was found for a larger or earlier European duck aMPV‑C episode that would displace this event among the top‑impact post‑1990 episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Avian metapneumovirus
EPP.common.name: Avian pneumovirus, TRT virus
Host: Commercial chickens (broilers, layers, breeders) and turkeys on multiple Brazilian farms
Event.summary: Beginning in the early 2000s, Brazil experienced increasingly frequent outbreaks of respiratory disease and production drops in chickens and turkeys, with aMPV detected by RT‑PCR and virus isolation in multiple geographic regions and production types, including the first confirmed isolation from turkeys. By 2003–2008, surveillance showed circulation of aMPV subtypes A and B in vaccinated and non‑vaccinated chicken and turkey farms across six Brazilian regions, associated with swollen head syndrome, reduced egg production, carcass condemnation from aerosacculitis, and notable economic losses. Subsequent years saw the incorporation of aMPV vaccination into broader respiratory disease control programs and ongoing molecular surveillance to track subtypes and vaccine performance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and geographic expansion of Brazil’s poultry sector, high farm densities, complex vertical integration networks, and incomplete or uneven vaccination coverage allowed aMPV to spread widely and persist; coinfections with Escherichia coli and other respiratory pathogens worsened clinical outcomes and carcass condemnation rates. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation and evolution of subtypes A and B in Brazilian flocks, with adaptation to local production systems, likely increased transmissibility and disease expression in intensively reared broilers and turkeys, representing geographic range expansion within Brazil and re‑emergence driven by subtype diversity and partial vaccine escape.
Review: Decision: review. This episode reflects amplification and geographic spread of aMPV A and B within Brazil, not first occurrence of the virus in a new South American subregion; therefore, 'intra_continental_emergence' has been changed from Yes to No. Retaining 're_emergence' as Yes captures the substantial resurgence and subtype diversification in an already affected subregion with clear production impacts. No other fields were altered, and the event still qualifies as a major post‑1990 aMPV episode in South America.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Avian metapneumovirus
EPP.common.name: Avian pneumovirus, TRT virus
Host: Meat‑type commercial chickens (yellow‑feathered broilers) in southeastern China
Event.summary: During February–April 2012, severe respiratory disease with conjunctivitis, sinus swelling, and up to 80% morbidity was observed in meat‑type commercial chickens on farms in southeastern China, and laboratory investigation identified aMPV subgroup C as the major pathogen. Molecular characterization of the JC strain showed it belonged to the aMPV‑C cluster but formed a distinct subcluster more similar to some wild‑bird and human metapneumovirus strains than to other aMPV‑C isolates, and experimental infection of specific‑pathogen‑free chickens produced marked respiratory lesions, demonstrating higher pathogenicity than previously recognized in chickens. Control of the affected flocks relied on culling and local biosecurity measures, and the episode spurred wider epidemiological studies documenting that aMPV‑C infection was likely widespread in Chinese chicken flocks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of broiler production, limited prior detection of aMPV in Chinese chickens, and possible introduction from wild birds or live‑bird markets facilitated rapid spread once the virus entered commercial flocks; lack of subtype C‑targeted vaccination in chickens likely contributed to high morbidity. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a distinct, highly pathogenic aMPV‑C variant (JC strain) in chickens, with closer genetic relatedness to some wild‑bird and human metapneumoviruses, represents novel genotype emergence, enhanced virulence in chickens, and re‑emergence of aMPV‑C within an already affected Eastern Asian subregion.
Review: Decision: review. The event window was narrowed to 2012 to match the documented period of the JC‑strain outbreaks in southeastern Chinese chickens, rather than the broader 2010–2013 range originally used. 'Intra_continental_emergence' was changed from Yes to No because aMPV (including subtype C) was already present in Eastern Asia (e.g. in Japan and South Korea); this episode reflects spread to a new country within the same subregion plus the emergence of a more pathogenic aMPV‑C variant, which is better captured as re‑emergence with novel strain characteristics. 'First_detection' is retained here to indicate first confirmed isolation of aMPV‑C from chickens in China.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Avian metapneumovirus
EPP.common.name: Avian pneumovirus, TRT virus
Host: Muscovy ducks and other domestic ducks in China
Event.summary: From around mid‑2010, outbreaks characterized by respiratory disease and egg‑production problems were reported in Muscovy ducks on farms in southern China, and virological investigation led to the isolation and characterization of subtype C aMPV strain S‑01 from affected ducks. The isolated virus caused respiratory and reproductive disease in experimental infections and showed close genetic relationships to North American aMPV‑C but clear distinction from subtypes A and B, indicating introduction and adaptation of aMPV‑C in Chinese duck populations. Over the subsequent years of this episode, serologic and molecular surveys suggested that aMPV‑C infection in domestic ducks and possibly wild ducks had become more widespread, raising concern about ducks as a reservoir for continued circulation and spillover to other poultry.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Mixed‑species duck farming, contact between domestic ducks and wild waterfowl in rice‑paddy and wetland systems, and limited prior surveillance of aMPV in ducks enabled undetected introduction and amplification of aMPV‑C. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of the aMPV‑C lineage from turkeys and chickens into domestic ducks, with evidence of efficient replication and disease expression in Muscovy ducks, represents re‑emergence driven by host adaptation and geographic spread of the Eurasian aMPV‑C lineage within Eastern Asia.
Review: Decision: review. The time span was adjusted from 2010–2014 to 2010–2012 to better reflect the period emphasized in the primary S‑01 Muscovy‑duck paper, which describes severe disease beginning in 2010 without clearly documenting continuation of the same outbreak through 2014. 'Intra_continental_emergence' was changed from Yes to No because aMPV was already present in Eastern Asia; the key feature of this episode is emergence of a duck‑adapted aMPV‑C lineage and its spread among domestic ducks, which fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by host expansion and viral adaptation within an already affected subregion. 'First_detection' is retained to denote first documented aMPV‑C isolation from Muscovy ducks in China.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Avian metapneumovirus
EPP.common.name: Avian pneumovirus, TRT virus
Host: Sheldrake ducks (Fujian Province), other domestic ducks in affected area
Event.summary: From about 2021, a novel aMPV subtype C variant, designated aMPV‑FJ21, was isolated from Sheldrake ducks in Fujian Province, China, during outbreaks of a severe hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome with reproductive tract lesions and reduced egg production. Phylogenetic analyses showed that FJ21 formed a distinct lineage within the aMPV‑C group, genetically distant from previously described North American and Eurasian aMPV‑C lineages, suggesting emergence of a new genetic lineage in Chinese ducks. Following characterization, affected flocks were managed through culling or enhanced flock‑level biosecurity, and the discovery prompted recommendations for increased surveillance and reconsideration of vaccine strategies in duck production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive duck production in southeastern China, regional movement of live ducks, and ongoing exposure to wild waterfowl likely created conditions for continued aMPV‑C evolution and the emergence of more pathogenic variants; limited or absent vaccination in ducks left populations immunologically susceptible. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence within subtype C (FJ21 lineage) with distinct genomic features and association with hydrosalpinx and severe reproductive pathology indicates increased pathogenicity and possible altered tissue tropism, fitting the definition of re‑emergence driven by viral evolution in ducks.
Review: Decision: retain. The FJ21 outbreaks in Sheldrake ducks are clearly documented as a newly emerged, genetically distinct aMPV‑C lineage causing significant reproductive disease and egg‑production losses in Chinese duck flocks from 2021 onward. This event is appropriately classified as re‑emergence (new variant in an already affected subregion) and appears to be one of the more impactful aMPV episodes in ducks during 2005–2025. No structural changes were made; sources already include the primary Virulence article and a recent systematic review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Avian metapneumovirus
EPP.common.name: Avian pneumovirus, TRT virus
Host: Broiler breeder chickens in Jiangsu Province, China
Event.summary: In 2022, severe respiratory disease outbreaks occurred in broiler breeder chickens in Jiangsu Province, China, and investigation led to the isolation of an aMPV subgroup C strain designated GX22‑01 from affected flocks. The virus was confirmed by immunofluorescence, Western blotting, and sequencing of the nucleoprotein gene, and was associated with significant respiratory signs and production impacts in breeder flocks. After confirmation, affected farms implemented flock‑level management responses including targeted culling and heightened biosecurity, and the event added to evidence that aMPV‑C has become an important and evolving pathogen in Chinese chicken production systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑density breeder operations, regional poultry movement networks, and ongoing circulation of aMPV‑C in Eastern China facilitated the appearance of outbreaks in previously unaffected breeder farms. Internal mechanisms: Continued evolution of aMPV‑C in Chinese poultry populations and adaptation to broiler breeder chickens, represented by the GX22‑01 strain, underlie this re‑emergence, likely involving genotype diversification and potentially enhanced transmissibility or fitness in breeder flocks.
Review: Decision: review. The event year was narrowed from 2022–2023 to 2022 to match the period explicitly documented in the Jiangsu broiler‑breeder outbreaks from which GX22‑01 was isolated; current evidence does not yet support treating 2023 as part of the same epidemiologically linked episode. Classification as re‑emergence is retained because GX22‑01 represents another distinct aMPV‑C strain emerging in Chinese chickens in a region with prior aMPV circulation. The source list already includes the primary Jiangsu paper plus contextual Chinese aMPV‑C literature, so only the time span was corrected.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Avian metapneumovirus
EPP.common.name: Avian pneumovirus, TRT virus
Host: Commercial turkeys and chickens in the United States (laboratory‑confirmed affected flocks)
Event.summary: In January 2024, the US National Veterinary Services Laboratories confirmed avian metapneumovirus subtype B in poultry samples submitted through the National Animal Health Laboratory Network, marking the first confirmed detection of subtype B aMPV in US commercial poultry, where previous circulation had been dominated by subtype C and had been largely controlled by the late 2000s. Subsequent molecular and field investigations documented that both subtypes A and B had entered US poultry, with subtype B driving major outbreaks of respiratory and reproductive disease in turkeys and chickens in eastern states (including the Delmarva region) and subtype A detected more frequently in some western production areas. Throughout 2024 and into 2025, control efforts focused on intensive surveillance, flock‑level management and depopulation of affected premises, and rapid deployment of inactivated subtype B vaccines under special approvals, while national trade was maintained through targeted rather than nationwide movement restrictions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large‑scale integrated turkey and chicken production, dense networks for interstate movement of poults, hatching eggs, and live birds, and movement of equipment and personnel between complexes created conditions for rapid dissemination once aMPV‑A and aMPV‑B entered US systems; introduction pathways likely involved a combination of imported breeding stock, biologics, and/or wild‑bird reservoirs interacting with biosecurity gaps. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and early spread of genetically distinct aMPV‑A and aMPV‑B lineages into a poultry population where subtype C had been absent for more than a decade created a largely immunologically naive host population; sequence data indicate these lineages differ antigenically from historic US subtype C strains, implying genotype diversification with important consequences for diagnostic test performance and vaccine matching, and justifying classification as re‑emergence in a previously affected subregion.
Review: Decision: review. The event is retained but its description was broadened from 'first detection of subtype B' to cover the concurrent introduction and spread of both subtypes A and B in US poultry, consistent with USDA and recent peer‑reviewed reports. Classification as 'first_detection' (for these subtypes in US poultry) plus 're_emergence' (reappearance of aMPV in a previously affected North American subregion with novel lineages) is appropriate, while 'inter_continental_emergence' remains No because aMPV as a species had already been present on this continent. The source list was updated to include the APHIS program update, detailed molecular epidemiology papers on subtype A and B introductions, and an extension fact sheet summarizing 2024 US subtype distribution and vaccine options.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: BSE prion
EPP.common.name: Mad cow disease, BSE
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event.summary: In 2002, Israel reported its first and so far only BSE case, a 10‑year‑old dairy cow born and raised on a kibbutz farm in the Golan Heights, representing spread of BSE into Western Asia. Epidemiologic investigation suggested infection had probably occurred years earlier via imported feed ingredients that may have been contaminated with European MBM, but no further cases were identified despite extensive testing of slaughtered cattle and fallen stock. Israel quickly implemented precautionary measures including age-based slaughter policies, specified-risk-material controls, and long-term targeted surveillance, and no recurrence of BSE has been detected in its national herd.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dependence on imported protein meals (e.g., poultry or fish meals potentially contaminated with ruminant MBM); limited early awareness of BSE risk in the region; trade patterns linking Israel to European feed suppliers. Internal mechanisms: Intra-continental emergence of classical BSE within Asia, with a single recognised indigenous case and no evidence of sustained in-country amplification, implying a low-level point introduction rather than an established epidemic.
Review: review – The event is real (a single indigenous BSE case in Israel) and correctly described and classified as intra_continental_emergence within Asia. However, its impact in terms of case numbers and trade effects was modest compared with other BSE episodes (e.g., UK, EU 2000–2001, Japan, Canada, U.S., Brazil). It is therefore flagged for expert review as to whether a one‑case, non-epidemic event should remain among the top ten impact-focused emergence events for this EPP, or be deprioritised in favour of higher-burden episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: BSE prion
EPP.common.name: Mad cow disease, BSE
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event.summary: In 2012, Brazil reported its first BSE case, an aged beef cow that had died in the state of Paraná in 2010 and was later confirmed to have atypical BSE after retrospective testing of archived brain tissue by national and international reference laboratories, constituting the first recognised BSE infection in South American cattle. The delayed disclosure led several importing countries to briefly suspend some Brazilian beef imports, despite risk assessments concluding that the case was a spontaneous atypical form with no evidence of feed-borne spread and that the carcass had not entered the food chain. Brazil retained its official negligible classical BSE risk status, but responded by reinforcing surveillance, validation of diagnostic procedures, and international communication to reassure trading partners.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very large, export-oriented beef sector under intense international scrutiny; retrospective review of neurological cases and improved laboratory capacity that enabled detection of a single atypical case after the animal’s death; precautionary trade responses by importing countries sensitive to any BSE report. Internal mechanisms: Inter-continental emergence of atypical BSE in South America, most likely representing a sporadic prion strain arising in an older cow rather than feed-amplified classical BSE; no evidence for onward transmission, but confirmation that atypical BSE can occur at very low background levels in South American herds.
Review: retain – Brazil’s 2012 atypical BSE case is correctly identified as the first reported BSE infection in South American cattle and produced notable, if short-lived, trade impacts given Brazil’s role as a major beef exporter. Inter_continental_emergence = Yes is appropriate for the South American continent. The original re_emergence flag (used to denote a novel strain) has been set to No to avoid conflating first detection on a new continent with global re-emergence; atypicality is captured instead in the mechanism_or_driver narrative.

EPP.scientific.name: Babesia bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine babesiosis
Host: Commercial dairy and beef cattle plus a large feral cattle herd; Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks as vector
Event.summary: In December 2007, Babesia bovis was accidentally introduced into previously babesiosis‑free New Caledonia when cattle vaccinated with a live tick‑fever (babesiosis/anaplasmosis) vaccine from Australia were imported into a territory already infested with the cattle tick Rhipicephalus microplus.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai)) During early 2008, clinical bovine babesiosis was confirmed on 22 commercial farms involving roughly 2300 high‑risk and 1600 suspect cattle, and infection also spread into a large feral cattle herd that served as a persistent reservoir.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai)) An intensive eradication campaign based on quarantine, repeated imidocarb treatment and aggressive tick control eliminated infection from commercial herds within about a year, followed by several years of targeted surveillance and feral‑cattle destocking to contain the last nidus of infection, after which New Caledonia again reported absence of bovine babesiosis.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of live vaccinated cattle into a naïve island territory, gaps in vaccine quality assurance allowing a B. bovis‑containing live vaccine to be used where the parasite was absent, and the presence of abundant competent R. microplus ticks and unmanaged feral cattle created ideal conditions for establishment and local spread of the vaccine strain.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No evidence suggests the involvement of a novel B. bovis genotype or resistance trait; instead, the emergence reflects human‑mediated geographic range expansion of an existing live vaccine strain into a previously unexposed island population with pre‑existing tick vectors (geographic range expansion via host and vector movement).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain as one of the major post‑1990 emergence events. Corrected classification from inter‑continental to intra‑continental emergence because Babesia bovis has long been endemic in northern Australia and other parts of Oceania, so New Caledonia represents spread to a new sub‑region, not a new continent.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babesiosis?utm_source=openai)) Set the 'first_detection' field to No, as global detection in cattle dates back to 1888 in Romania and B. bovis had been recognised in multiple continents well before 1990; this episode is the first detection in New Caledonia only.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4557164/?utm_source=openai)) Event‑level sources were pruned to focus on primary reports of the New Caledonia outbreak and eradication campaign (Barré et al., Hüe et al., WOAH/WOAH‑NC documents), removing generic references such as Wikipedia and broad factsheets that did not add event‑specific detail.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21771538/?utm_source=openai)) Flagged for review only to confirm the chosen end year (2011) against the final eradication status of the feral herd in the most recent local reports.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Babesia bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine babesiosis
Host: Cattle on smallholder and commercial farms on Santa Cruz Island; likely local tick vectors (exact species composition under investigation)
Event.summary: In 2024, a molecular survey of 170 cattle from 19 farms on Santa Cruz Island in the Galápagos detected Babesia bovis DNA in 11.2% of animals, alongside Babesia bigemina (14.7%), Trypanosoma vivax (14.7%) and a high prevalence of Anaplasma marginale (67.1%), documenting B. bovis on the islands for the first time.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11510725/?utm_source=openai)) Earlier work had reported only B. bigemina from pooled tick samples on Santa Cruz, so the new findings indicate that B. bovis has recently been introduced and is now circulating within local cattle populations on at least a quarter of surveyed farms.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0817/13/10/910?utm_source=openai)) The authors highlighted that multiple haemoparasites and frequent co‑infections could impair productivity and potentially threaten endemic fauna if parasite–vector cycles expand further, and recommended Galápagos‑specific surveillance and integrated control strategies.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11510725/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of infected cattle or ticks from mainland Ecuador or other endemic areas, limited biosecurity for introduction of livestock to the islands, and environmental conditions suitable for tick vectors likely facilitated the introduction and establishment of B. bovis and other haemoparasites on Santa Cruz Island.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11510725/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate a novel B. bovis genotype; this event is best interpreted as geographic range expansion and re‑occurrence of a mainland parasite in a previously babesiosis‑free island ecosystem, with enhanced transmission risk due to multiple co‑circulating haemoparasites and naïve cattle hosts rather than documented genetic change in the parasite.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11510725/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Added as a new emergence/re‑occurrence event because molecular surveys on Santa Cruz Island in the Galápagos detected Babesia bovis DNA in 11.2% of sampled cattle and documented this parasite there for the first time, in a setting where only B. bigemina had previously been reported.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11510725/?utm_source=openai)) Although the absolute number of cattle is modest, the introduction affects a previously babesiosis‑free archipelago with conservation value and demonstrates establishment of B. bovis in about a quarter of sampled farms, justifying inclusion among major recent emergence episodes. Classified as re‑occurrence within South America (long‑endemic on the mainland) with no evidence yet of novel strain evolution. Flagged for review to confirm the sampling year underlying the 2024 publication and to monitor whether subsequent clinical outbreaks or spread to additional islands occur.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Babesia spp.
EPP.common.name: Babesiosis
Host: Equids (horses)
Event.summary: In August 2008, equine piroplasmosis caused by Theileria equi (formerly Babesia equi) was detected in a Quarter Horse in Manatee County, Florida, in a country that had been considered free of the disease since 1988. Epidemiological investigation and extensive testing subsequently identified about 20 T. equi-infected horses on several linked premises, all associated with unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing, and tick surveillance did not find competent tick vectors infected with the parasite, pointing instead to iatrogenic transmission. Through 2008 and into 2009, aggressive quarantine, testing, euthanasia or removal of infected horses, and tightened biosecurity allowed authorities to contain and ultimately eradicate this focus, but the outbreak underscored vulnerabilities around blood-borne practices and illegal horse movements in maintaining EP-free status.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected horses, probably from Mexico, into an EP-free state; high-risk management practices in non-sanctioned racing (reuse of needles and syringes, possible blood transfusions, and multi-dose vials contaminated with blood) that amplified blood-borne spread; and initial lack of awareness of EP risk among participants. Internal mechanisms: No novel parasite genotype or change in vector competence was reported; the episode mainly reflects re-introduction and amplification of an established T. equi lineage in a previously cleared system, so it is best categorized as re-occurrence driven by failures in biosecurity and movement control rather than intrinsic parasite change.
Review: review – Event correctly describes the 2008 Florida equine piroplasmosis outbreak in Manatee County and is clearly among the largest recent equine Babesia episodes; I replaced less relevant or unstable URLs with peer-reviewed and official sources (JAVMA outbreak report, APHIS, an Australian EAD bulletin and a veterinary news article) but made no changes to the core timing, geography, host or event-type coding (re-occurrence).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Babesia spp.
EPP.common.name: Babesiosis
Host: Equids (horses)
Event.summary: In 2009, a large Quarter Horse ranch in southern Texas that had not imported horses recently nor reported international travel detected equine piroplasmosis due to Theileria equi in multiple animals. Serologic screening showed that the majority of horses on the index ranch were infected, and field investigations documented heavy infestations with Amblyomma cajennense (now A. cajennense sensu lato/A. mixtum) and other ticks, with experimental work confirming A. cajennense as a competent vector under local conditions. The outbreak demonstrated sustained autochthonous tick-borne transmission of T. equi in a country long regarded as free of endemic EP, and eradication required years of quarantine, intensive tick control and either culling or prolonged imidocarb treatment of infected horses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density management and frequent movement of horses within and from the ranch, combined with abundant populations of Amblyomma cajennense and other ticks in south Texas, allowed efficient spread once T. equi was introduced; historical reliance on serologic surveillance alone may have missed chronically infected carriers. Internal mechanisms: Demonstration that A. cajennense could maintain and transmit T. equi in this ecosystem represents an important vector–parasite adaptation facilitating transmission in a setting where previous control programs had targeted other tick species; the event is therefore best treated as re-emergence in a previously affected subregion driven in part by changes in the effective vector assemblage.
Review: review – Retain this as a major equine piroplasmosis outbreak with well-documented local tick-borne transmission in south Texas; I set re_occurrence to "false" and re_emergence to "true" so that the event type matches the definition (reappearance in a previously affected subregion with clear new vector involvement) and respects the rule that re-occurrence and re-emergence are generally treated as mutually exclusive.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Babesia spp.
EPP.common.name: Babesiosis
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2015]
Host: Dogs
Event.summary: In the winter of 2015–2016, several severe cases of canine babesiosis due to Babesia canis were diagnosed in dogs with no travel history in Harlow, Essex, in the United Kingdom, which had previously been regarded as free from endemic canine babesiosis. Follow-up investigations through 2016–2017 identified additional locally acquired cases in Essex and Romford, and infected Dermacentor reticulatus ticks were found on affected dogs and in popular dog-walking fields, confirming an autochthonous transmission focus. Although local tick control, heightened veterinary awareness and owner education appeared to limit spread from the initial hotspot, the episode demonstrated that B. canis could establish enzootic transmission in parts of the UK given expanding D. reticulatus populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected dogs or ticks from continental Europe into areas of the UK where D. reticulatus populations were already present but under-recognized, combined with high dog traffic at affected recreational sites, created conditions for local transmission; warmer winters may have improved tick survival and activity. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and local establishment of D. reticulatus within the UK provided a competent vector able to sustain B. canis transmission in a country that had previously seen only imported cases, making this a re-emergent focus within a Northern Europe subregion already affected by B. canis in the Baltic states.
Review: review – The Essex/Romford outbreak represents the first clearly documented autochthonous focus of Babesia canis in the UK and should be retained as a distinct high-impact event; however, I changed intra_continental_emergence from "true" to "false" and left only re_emergence="true" because B. canis was already established elsewhere in the Northern Europe sub-region (e.g. Baltic countries), and spread to a new country within the same sub-region should not be classified as intra-continental emergence under the project rules.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.
