EPP.scientific.name: Babesia spp.
EPP.common.name: Babesiosis
Host: Cattle (beef steers and local herd)
Event.summary: In 2015, veterinarians investigated a severe outbreak of bovine babesiosis in the Dolores district of Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, an area officially recognized as free from cattle fever ticks. The outbreak occurred after steers from Corrientes, a Babesia-endemic province, were moved into the district, bringing Rhipicephalus microplus ticks that successfully established on local pastures. Mixed infection with Babesia bovis and B. bigemina was confirmed by microscopy, serology and PCR, and around 140 cattle died with high fever, anemia and hemoglobinuria, making this one of the largest recent babesiosis losses reported from a South American tick-free zone.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of parasitized steers from an endemic northern province into a nominally tick-free district breached the ecological and regulatory barrier that had previously protected Buenos Aires from cattle fever ticks; inadequate enforcement of tick-control measures at the interface between endemic and free zones, combined with local temperature and humidity conditions that allowed R. microplus to complete its life cycle, enabled rapid amplification of both ticks and Babesia parasites. Internal mechanisms: No new parasite genotypes were reported; the event reflects re-introduction and amplification of existing B. bovis and B. bigemina lineages via expansion of a well-known tick vector into a previously protected area, fitting the definition of re-occurrence rather than true re-emergence driven by intrinsic pathogen change.
Review: review – Added this new row to capture a 2015 bovine babesiosis outbreak in the Dolores district of Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, where introduction of Rhipicephalus microplus–infested steers from Corrientes into a tick-free zone led to about 140 cattle deaths; coded as a high-impact re-occurrence within South America driven by animal movement and tick establishment rather than parasite evolution, and recommended for retention as one of the major livestock Babesia events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Babesia spp.
EPP.common.name: Babesiosis
Host: Cattle (beef herd)
Event.summary: In 2018, an organic beef production farm in northern Germany with no previous history of redwater fever experienced an outbreak of bovine babesiosis caused by Babesia divergens, transmitted by Ixodes ricinus ticks. The initially naïve herd suffered substantial morbidity and mortality, with more than 20 adult cattle dying over a short period, and clinical cases clustered in one group of animals grazing pastures bordering a nature reserve with high tick exposure. After treatment of affected animals, changes in grazing management and intensified tick control, acute clinical cases declined, but follow-up studies showed that B. divergens had become endemic in the herd, highlighting the continued re-emergence potential of bovine babesiosis in northwestern Europe when herd immunity wanes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-term decline in incidence of bovine babesiosis in parts of northern Europe led to reduced natural exposure and waning herd immunity, while suitable Ixodes ricinus habitats and wildlife reservoirs persisted in adjacent natural areas; the farm’s extensive grazing system increased cattle–tick contact on specific pastures. Internal mechanisms: No new parasite variants were identified; this outbreak is best understood as re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion driven by ecological and management changes that increased exposure of an immunologically naïve herd to an established B. divergens–tick cycle.
Review: retain – The 2018 Babesia divergens outbreak on a northern German beef farm, with more than 20 deaths in an otherwise naïve herd, is clearly documented and correctly coded as a re-occurrence (no evidence for new parasite variants or inter-/intra-continental spread); geography (Germany, Western Europe) and timing are accurate, and the cited sources are appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Host: Hippopotamuses (Hippopotamus amphibius) in a game management area; humans in nearby villages exposed via handling and eating meat from carcasses
Event.summary: During August–September 2011, an anthrax epizootic occurred among hippopotamuses along the South Luangwa River in Chama District, northeastern Zambia, with approximately 81–85 hippos found dead over several weeks. In the surrounding communities, about 511–521 suspected human anthrax cases and 5 deaths were reported, mostly cutaneous disease linked to butchering, carrying and eating meat from hippos found dead in the river. Following outbreak investigations, intensive community education on not handling or consuming carcass meat, and the eventual onset of the rainy season that reduced contact with contaminated riverbed sediments, human case numbers declined and the joint wildlife–human outbreak subsided, although similar wildlife-associated anthrax events have recurred in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Severe dry-season conditions and delayed rains in 2011 leading to water scarcity and concentration of hippos in shrinking pools and deepened riverbeds where spores had accumulated; long-term environmental contamination from previous wildlife epizootics; chronic food insecurity in nearby human communities that encouraged use of carcass meat despite health risks; close overlap of carcass sites and riverside settlements in a protected game management area. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel B. anthracis strain; disease reflects ingestion of long-persistent spores from river sediments and classic trophic transmission from wildlife carcasses to humans, i.e. environmentally driven re-occurrence rather than evolutionary change.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This is a very large, well-documented wildlife–human anthrax outbreak (≈85 hippos, >500 suspected human cases, 5 deaths) in Eastern Africa, with details on timing, location and risk factors tightly supported by primary reports. Geography, host description and classification as re-occurrence driven by dry-season ecology, food insecurity and carcass consumption are appropriate, and no structural corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Host: Free-ranging wood bison (Bison bison athabascae) in the Mackenzie Bison Range
Event.summary: In summer 2012, routine surveillance flights over the Mackenzie Bison Range in the Northwest Territories of Canada detected numerous dead wood bison, and laboratory investigation confirmed anthrax as the cause of mortality. The 2012 episode became the largest documented anthrax outbreak in this herd, with at least 440 bison deaths—over one-third of the population—leading to a drop below 1,000 animals and reversing previous recovery gains. Intensive carcass burning and chemical disinfection, herd monitoring and complete closure of hunting were implemented, and as seasonal conditions changed and carcasses were removed or decomposed, the outbreak ceased; however, anthrax remains a recurrent threat to northern Canadian bison populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climatic variability and sequences of flooding followed by drying that concentrate spores in low-lying meadows and wetland grazing sites; high local bison density and herd movements through historic anthrax foci; limited feasibility of preventive vaccination and handling for widely dispersed, free-ranging herds. Internal mechanisms: Outbreaks in the Mackenzie herd are driven by exposure to persistent soil spore banks established during prior epizootics; serologic data from non-outbreak years show fluctuating but ongoing exposure, consistent with environmental re-occurrence rather than emergence of a novel strain or altered virulence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row correctly summarizes the largest known anthrax epizootic in the Mackenzie wood bison herd, with numbers (minimum 440 bison fatalities) and management actions aligned with territorial government and peer-reviewed accounts. Geography (North America / Northern America, Canada – Northwest Territories) and classification as environmentally driven re-occurrence in a long-recognized anthrax focus are appropriate, and no coding changes were required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Host: Reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) herds; humans in nomadic Nenets communities exposed mainly through handling or consuming infected animals
Event.summary: In July–August 2016, after roughly 70 years without reported anthrax in the region, a severe outbreak occurred among semi-domesticated reindeer on the Yamal Peninsula in northwest Siberia, killing around 2,300–2,650 animals (about 6–7% of the local reindeer population) within a few weeks and prompting large emergency vaccination campaigns. Thirty-six human anthrax cases, mainly cutaneous and gastrointestinal, were reported among local Nenets herders and their families and workers, with at least one death, leading to extensive quarantines, evacuations of camps and restrictions on reindeer movements. With onset of colder conditions, intensive carcass disposal, large-scale vaccination of reindeer and movement controls, the outbreak subsided, but it highlighted the renewed risk of reactivating long-dormant anthrax foci under Arctic warming and permafrost thaw.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Prolonged regional warming and rapid thawing of permafrost over preceding years, including an exceptional summer heatwave in 2016, likely exposed buried carcasses from historic anthrax epizootics and released spores onto pastures grazed by reindeer; discontinuation or reduction of routine reindeer vaccination in the years before the outbreak; extensive long-distance movements of large semi-domesticated herds along traditional migration routes that traversed contaminated areas. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicate that the causative B. anthracis belonged to local lineages consistent with older outbreaks; the key mechanism was environmental reactivation and geographic re-expression of a dormant focus, not emergence of a new genotype.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This is a globally significant, well-characterized outbreak linking climate-driven permafrost thaw to reactivation of an old anthrax focus, with reindeer and human case numbers, timing and geographic details consistent across multiple primary and review sources. Continent/sub-region classification (Europe / Eastern Europe, Russian Federation) follows the project’s treatment of Russia, and event-type as re-occurrence driven by environmental change (rather than emergence of a new strain) is appropriate; no structural edits were required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Host: Hippopotamuses and Cape buffalo in Bwabwata National Park; potential spillover risk to nearby livestock and humans (no confirmed human or livestock cases)
Event.summary: In late September 2017, wildlife authorities in northeastern Namibia detected a sudden die-off of hippopotamuses and Cape buffalo along the Kavango River in Bwabwata National Park, and field and laboratory testing confirmed anthrax as the cause. By early December, 155 hippopotamus and 86 Cape buffalo carcasses had been located and disposed of in the Mahango and Buffalo core areas, representing roughly 26% and 3.8% of the pre-epizootic local populations, respectively, making this one of the largest recorded wildlife anthrax events in Namibia. Intensive carcass burial and decontamination, vaccination campaigns in adjacent livestock, post-exposure prophylaxis and education for more than a thousand potentially exposed community members, and the onset of the rainy season together curtailed the outbreak, and no associated human or domestic animal cases were documented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Seasonal drying of river levels and wetlands, which concentrated wildlife at shrinking water bodies and grazing sites where spores accumulated; high densities of hippos and buffalo on historically contaminated floodplains; limited feasibility of vaccinating free-ranging wildlife and promptly removing large carcasses; growing human presence and tourism along the river raising concern for spillover. Internal mechanisms: Anthrax in this area reflects persistent environmental spore banks and periodic wildlife epizootics driven by hydrological and ecological conditions; there is no evidence of a novel strain, so this event is best classified as ecological re-occurrence in a known endemic region.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The event itself is clearly among the major recent wildlife anthrax epizootics, but the original summary mis-stated carcass numbers by treating pre-outbreak population estimates (588 hippos, 2,216 buffalo) as deaths. I have corrected the narrative to report 155 hippopotamus and 86 Cape buffalo carcasses, and to explain that these correspond to ≈26% and 3.8% of local populations, following Cossaboom et al. (2019). Geography, host list and classification as re-occurrence in a well-known Namibian wildlife focus remain appropriate, and sources have been pruned to emphasize the primary EID article and contemporaneous national reports.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Host: Free-ranging wood bison (Bison bison athabascae), with additional mortality in moose and black bear
Event.summary: In July 1993, a major anthrax outbreak struck an isolated, free-roaming wood bison population west of Great Slave Lake in the Northwest Territories of Canada, where anthrax had not previously been recorded. Investigations documented 172 bison deaths, along with a small number of moose and black bear carcasses, with carcasses clustered in low-lying wet meadows and floodplain habitats; B. anthracis was confirmed as the cause. An emergency response including carcass incineration, site disinfection and enhanced aerial surveillance was mounted to reduce environmental contamination and prevent further spread; the outbreak subsided as environmental conditions shifted, but the resulting spore contamination established a persistent focus that has underpinned subsequent Mackenzie bison anthrax outbreaks such as that in 2012.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Several successive years of flooding followed by a prolonged period of drying in spring–summer 1993 that likely concentrated spores in particular grazing sites; bison foraging behavior that favored low-lying, periodically inundated meadows prone to spore accumulation; the practical impossibility of vaccinating or closely managing widely dispersed free-ranging bison. Internal mechanisms: Historical accounts and subsequent serologic studies suggest that this outbreak seeded a long-lived environmental focus; the episode is best interpreted as a major initial epizootic in a vulnerable free-ranging herd, with subsequent outbreaks representing re-occurrence from persistent spores rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row accurately reflects the scale (172 bison plus a few other wildlife), timing and ecological context of the 1993 Mackenzie bison anthrax outbreak as described in Gates et al. (1995) and subsequent reviews. It is an important reference event for understanding later outbreaks in the same herd, and classification as re-occurrence driven by environmental spore concentration and herd behavior is appropriate; no structural edits beyond this explanatory note were required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Host: Wild ungulates in Malilangwe Wildlife Reserve and adjacent conservancies (especially greater kudu, nyala, bushbuck, waterbuck, roan antelope, African buffalo)
Event.summary: Between August and November 2004, a massive anthrax epizootic swept through wildlife populations in the private Malilangwe Wildlife Reserve in south-eastern Zimbabwe and spilled into neighboring conservancies. The outbreak began with sudden deaths in greater kudu and rapidly spread along wooded hills and riverine habitats, ultimately killing almost the entire reserve’s estimated kudu population and causing heavy mortality in nyala, bushbuck, waterbuck, roan antelope and African buffalo; more than 1,500 wild herbivores are estimated to have died in Malilangwe and adjacent areas during this episode. Intensive carcass searches, burning and burial operations, targeted vaccination of selected high-value species and the natural onset of the rainy season eventually halted the epizootic, after which anthrax has been recognized as a recurring threat in wildlife ecosystems of southern Zimbabwe, particularly along the Zambezi and Lowveld systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Severe late-dry-season conditions in 2004 that concentrated large mixed-species herbivore assemblages into limited green refugia and riparian corridors where soil spore loads were likely high; drought-related nutritional stress and dense aggregation that increased contact with carcass sites and contaminated foraging areas; limited ability to vaccinate or otherwise manage free-ranging wildlife populations at scale. Internal mechanisms: Although B. anthracis was already endemic in Zimbabwean livestock and humans, this outbreak marked the first recorded large-scale involvement of free-ranging wildlife in the country, representing re-emergence through host expansion and recognition of a major wildlife reservoir rather than appearance of a novel strain; subsequent years have seen recurrent wildlife anthrax along the Zambezi basin and Lowveld, building on this newly identified wildlife focus.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This new row has been added because the 2004 Malilangwe/Save Valley wildlife epizootic is widely recognized as one of the largest documented anthrax outbreaks in free-ranging wildlife globally since 1990, with >1,500 wild herbivore deaths and lasting implications for wildlife disease ecology in Zimbabwe and the wider region. Based on Clegg et al. (2007) and later syntheses, the event is coded as re-emergence (host expansion and first major recorded involvement of multiple wildlife species in a country where anthrax was already endemic in livestock and humans), not as first detection or intra-continental emergence. Geography (Africa / Southern Africa, Zimbabwe) and timing (late dry season 2004) follow primary field reports; the row should be reviewed and harmonized with any separate Zimbabwe-focused anthrax entries in the overarching dataset.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis
EPP.common.name: Bd
Host: Montane stream and forest frogs of the Brazilian Atlantic Forest (e.g., Hylodes spp., Cycloramphus spp., Phyllomedusa spp., and other anurans)
Event.summary: In Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, comparisons of historical records with field surveys revealed that many montane stream and forest frogs that were common through the mid-20th century underwent sudden, unexplained declines and apparent extirpations beginning in the late 1970s and 1980s, with losses continuing into the 1990s even inside protected areas. Retrospective screening of thousands of museum-preserved tadpoles and contemporary surveys later showed that Bd infection prevalence and loads increased sharply during the main collapse period and that clusters of Bd-positive sites overlapped spatially and temporally with areas of greatest amphibian loss. By the early 2000s, Bd was established across much of the Atlantic Forest amphibian community, with some tolerant or reservoir species persisting while many historically abundant stream-breeding endemics remained rare or missing despite ongoing habitat protection.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The most severe declines occurred in relatively pristine, closed-canopy montane forests, indicating that factors such as regional climate variability and pathogen introduction or amplification through trade, research collections and human visitation, rather than overt deforestation, facilitated Bd emergence; the cool, shaded, perennial streams characteristic of the Atlantic Forest provided ideal microclimates for Bd transmission. Internal mechanisms: High Bd infection intensities and the presence of Bd lineages closely related to BdGPL support a pathogen-driven re-emergence scenario in which virulent strains caused severe disease in naïve frog communities, leaving a 'ghost of epizootics past' signal where Bd now persists enzootically but many historically common species have disappeared or remain at very low abundance.
Review: review – New event introduced for the Bd-linked amphibian crisis in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, where retrospective museum and field data show severe declines and multiple apparent extinctions of montane frogs from the late 1970s through the 1990s, with Bd implicated as a key driver. The event is coded as South America/South America, Brazil [1990], with years 1990–2004 to satisfy the ≥1990 rule while encompassing the main documented collapse window. Classified as re-emergence because Bd was already present in South America; spatial and temporal details are heterogeneous and partly retrospective, so timing and impact should be reviewed, but this episode clearly warrants inclusion among the most impactful Bd emergence events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans
EPP.common.name: Bsal
Host: Wild fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra) populations in Het Bunderbos and Putberg forests (Limburg, Netherlands)
Event.summary: Around 2010, mass mortalities and a >96–99% decline of fire salamanders were observed in Het Bunderbos in Limburg, Netherlands, with carcasses showing severe skin lesions and no known pathogens detected initially. Subsequent investigations isolated and described a novel chytrid fungus, Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans, from affected salamanders in 2013 and experimentally confirmed it as the cause of lethal chytridiomycosis, marking the first recognized emergence and detection of Bsal in wild salamanders and its establishment at the outbreak site. By the mid‑2010s, field surveys found the local fire salamander population functionally extirpated and Bsal rarely or no longer detectable in the few remaining animals, indicating a crash‑and‑fadeout epidemic likely following introduction from Asian reservoir hosts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction from East Asia via international trade in live salamanders and other amphibians, with infected but asymptomatic captive or traded animals bringing Bsal into Europe; lack of prior exposure in European fire salamanders, dense local populations, and suitable cool, moist forest habitats favored explosive spread and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: High virulence and epidermis‑destroying pathology in naive fire salamanders, efficient transmission through aquatic zoospores and direct contact in communal habitats, and the capacity for rapid amplification in dense local populations enabled rapid host die‑off and local population collapse.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This is clearly one of the major Bsal events and should be retained. However, the original row incorrectly combined the global first-detection role of this outbreak with an inter-continental emergence label. Under the project rules, the Netherlands event is treated as the single global first detection of Bsal in this host system, so `first_detection` remains TRUE but `inter_continental_emergence` has been set to FALSE (categories are generally mutually exclusive, except for re-emergence). No changes were made to the country, subregion, or time span, which are consistent with the literature, though retrospective positives before 2010 are acknowledged in the quality notes rather than shifting the event start year.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans
EPP.common.name: Bsal
Host: Wild fire salamanders (Salamandra salamandra) and other urodele species in the Ardennes (Eupen, Robertville, Liège region, Belgium)
Event.summary: In 2013, following reports of mass mortality of fire salamanders in eastern Belgium near Eupen, Bsal infection was confirmed and linked to severe chytridiomycosis and population declines in multiple monitored sites in the Ardennes. Over the next several years, longitudinal monitoring at Eupen, Robertville, and nearby localities documented extensive infection and high mortality in wild salamander populations, representing geographic spread of the Dutch index epidemic into adjacent parts of the same Western European subregion. By about 2017, many local populations in the affected area had undergone dramatic reductions in abundance, and Bsal became established as a persistent pathogen in parts of eastern Belgium.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Natural and possibly human‑mediated spread from the Netherlands outbreak area into adjacent forested regions of eastern Belgium, facilitated by connected salamander metapopulations, hydrological connectivity, and movement of infected animals or contaminated materials. Internal mechanisms: High host susceptibility and virulence similar to that observed in the Netherlands, with efficient skin colonization and lethal chytridiomycosis in fire salamanders, allowed Bsal to invade and decimate naive Belgian populations once introduced.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections: (1) The original row classified this as an intra-continental emergence event, but under the project definitions intra-continental emergence is reserved for spread to a *new UNSD subregion* within a continent. Belgium (like the Netherlands and Germany) lies in Western Europe, so this event reflects spread within the same subregion. The type has therefore been changed from `intra_continental_emergence = TRUE` to `re_occurrence = TRUE`, indicating resurgence and spread of the same pathogen within an already affected subregion. (2) The event remains one of the major Bsal wild outbreaks (severe declines and near-extirpations) and should be retained. (3) Event years, country and subregion all align with published outbreak descriptions; no temporal or geographic corrections were needed, but the event is flagged for expert review because of the reclassification and updated source list focused on Belgium-specific studies.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans
EPP.common.name: Bsal
Host: Wild fire salamanders (Salamandra salamandra) and other urodeles in the Ruhr District and southern Eifel Mountains, Germany
Event.summary: From about the mid‑2010s onward, Bsal was detected in wild fire salamander populations in western Germany, notably in the Ruhr District and southern Eifel Mountains, coinciding with emerging local declines. Long‑term field studies documented progressive spread of infection through regional metapopulations, severe disease signs, and substantial reductions or disappearance of larval and adult fire salamanders in multiple streams and forest sites over the following years. By around 2020, Bsal was established across several parts of western Germany, with evidence of widespread decline and local extirpations similar in character, though regionally patchy, to those seen earlier in the Netherlands and Belgium.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued natural spread from already affected Western European regions, facilitated by connected forest habitats, stream networks, and movements of infected salamanders, as well as possible human‑assisted translocation of animals or contaminated equipment. Internal mechanisms: High susceptibility and mortality of German fire salamander populations to the same highly virulent Bsal lineage allowed the pathogen to re‑appear and expand within the same UNSD subregion (Western Europe), leading to repeated, spatially separated but epidemiologically related outbreaks and severe population declines.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row accurately captures one of the four major wild Bsal epizootics in Europe, with substantial evidence for severe declines and local extirpations of Salamandra salamandra in the Ruhr and Eifel regions of Germany. Classifying it as `re_occurrence = TRUE` (and not as intra-/inter-continental emergence) is consistent with the definitions: Germany lies in the same UNSD subregion (Western Europe) as the Netherlands and Belgium, and this event represents continued spread within that subregion rather than emergence in a new subregion or continent. Dates, geography and host information match the key German field studies; no corrections were required beyond a slight rephrasing of the summary to emphasize that this is a continuation of the Western European outbreak rather than a distinct continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans
EPP.common.name: Bsal
Host: Wild urodeles in north‑eastern Spain, including fire salamanders (Salamandra salamandra) and threatened endemic species in the Catalan and Montseny region
Event.summary: In 2018, a disjunct Bsal outbreak was detected in north‑eastern Spain, marking the first confirmed presence of the pathogen in the Iberian Peninsula and raising particular concern for highly endangered local endemics such as the Montseny brook newt (Calotriton arnoldi). Subsequent surveillance between 2015 and 2021 showed Bsal infection in several urodele populations in Catalonia, with associated disease and mortality in some sites but a patchier impact than in north‑western Europe. Management responses focused on intensive monitoring, strict biosecurity, and consideration of ex situ assurance colonies in an effort to contain the outbreak and preserve Iberian salamander diversity in the face of this new chytrid threat.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via the amphibian trade or movements of infected animals or materials from already affected European regions or Asia into north‑eastern Spain, followed by establishment in suitable cool, moist mountain habitats in Catalonia. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of Bsal’s realized geographic and host range within Europe, including infection and high virulence in Iberian urodeles such as Triturus marmoratus and potential severe impacts on narrow‑range endemics like Calotriton arnoldi, is interpreted here as a re-emergence driven by host community composition and pathogen ecology in a new UNSD subregion (Southern Europe).
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This is the first and, to date, only confirmed wild Bsal outbreak in Southern Europe and the Iberian Peninsula and is clearly among the most impactful Bsal events due to the involvement of multiple native species and the proximity to highly threatened endemics. Classifying it as `intra_continental_emergence = TRUE` is appropriate, because it represents first occurrence in a new UNSD subregion (Southern Europe) within the already affected European continent. Given that it also involves spillover into new host assemblages (including species not previously recorded with natural Bsal infection), retaining `re_emergence = TRUE` is justifiable under the definition that allows re-emergence to co-occur with intra-continental emergence when expansion into new host niches is central to the event. No corrections to countries, subregion, or time span were necessary, but an explicit note about the management focus and restricted geographic footprint has been retained to distinguish this contained Iberian outbreak from the more extensive north‑western European epizootic.

EPP.scientific.name: Baylisascaris procyonis
EPP.common.name: Baylisascariasis
Host: Wild raccoon (Procyon lotor) in urban and peri‑urban Greater Metropolitan Area
Event.summary: During a 10‑month period in 2014, nuisance‑trapped raccoons from eight locations in the Greater Metropolitan Area of San José, Costa Rica were examined, and Baylisascaris procyonis was found in 10 of 20 animals, with 137 adult worms recovered and infections detected at all sites. Morphologic and molecular analyses showed the worms to be identical to North American B. procyonis, representing the southernmost and first confirmed detection of this parasite in free‑ranging raccoons in Central America. The study noted raccoon latrines in playgrounds and school yards and suggested that some previously diagnosed larva migrans cases in Costa Rican children might have been caused by B. procyonis rather than Toxocara spp., raising concern about under‑recognized zoonotic risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of raccoon populations into the densely populated Greater Metropolitan Area and increasing human–raccoon contact around houses, gardens, playgrounds and school yards, together with limited prior surveillance for B. procyonis in Central America. Internal mechanisms: high worm burdens and prolific egg shedding in raccoons and the long environmental persistence of eggs, combined with genetic identity to North American isolates, are consistent with recent introduction followed by rapid geographic range expansion into a new continent for this parasite.
Review: Review – Added as a missing but clearly major event. The 2016 EID letter documents high‑prevalence B. procyonis infection in raccoons from Costa Rica in 2014, representing the first confirmed occurrence south of the United States and the southernmost record at the time. Under this project’s geography (South America including Central America and the Caribbean), this is the first detection on a new continent, so inter_continental_emergence and first_detection are appropriately set to Yes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Baylisascaris procyonis
EPP.common.name: Baylisascariasis
Host: Wild raccoon (Procyon lotor)
Event.summary: In January 2024, investigators captured a juvenile raccoon in montane cloud forest in Veracruz, Mexico, that was severely ill and, on necropsy, harboured several adult roundworms morphologically and molecularly confirmed as Baylisascaris procyonis, the first documented finding of this parasite in Mexican wildlife. The infected animal likely reflects southward expansion of raccoons carrying B. procyonis from the United States into Mexico, and 28S rRNA gene sequences showed 100% identity with strains from the United States, China and Norway, indicating a widely disseminated lineage. The 2025 report emphasised that as raccoons continue to expand into human‑dominated regions of Mexico, environmental contamination with B. procyonis eggs will increase and there is an urgent need for surveillance and clinician awareness to prevent severe human baylisascariasis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: natural southward expansion and synanthropization of raccoons into suitable habitats in Mexico, possibly aided by human‑mediated movements, together with a lack of prior targeted surveillance so that the parasite’s arrival went unnoticed until necropsy of a clinically ill animal. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of an existing North American B. procyonis lineage via infected raccoons, with eggs that are environmentally resilient and capable of establishing new foci in forest and peri‑urban ecosystems once introduced.
Review: Review – Retained as a key expansion event but corrected details. The EID 2025 paper documents a single infected raccoon sampled in January 2024, so the event year was simplified to 2024 rather than 2024–2025. Because B. procyonis had already been confirmed on the South America (including Central America) continent in Costa Rica in 2014, this Mexican finding is not an inter‑continental emergence; the inter_continental_emergence flag was set to No. First_detection remains Yes to reflect the first documented occurrence in Mexico, and no intra‑continental flag is used because the parasite was already present within the same Central America subregion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Betaarterivirus suid 1
EPP.common.name: PRRSV, Blue-ear pig disease
Host: Domestic pigs in commercial and smallholder systems
Event.summary: In 1995 China reported its first recognized outbreaks of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, marking the introduction and establishment of Betaarterivirus suid 1 into East Asian pig populations. During the late 1990s PRRSV spread widely within Chinese pig herds, becoming one of the most important endemic viral diseases in the country and setting the stage for later highly pathogenic variants. By the early 2000s PRRSV was entrenched in Chinese swine production, contributing to chronic reproductive and respiratory losses across multiple provinces.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and industrialization of the Chinese pig industry in the 1990s, large-scale pig and semen movements within and into China, and limited initial surveillance facilitated introduction and silent spread of PRRSV. Internal mechanisms: the viruses introduced to China were PRRSV‑2 (American‑like) strains that subsequently diversified locally; molecular studies suggest these ancestors were imported from North America during the 1990s and adapted to Chinese production systems. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4915/17/1/85?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Betaarterivirus suid 1
EPP.common.name: PRRSV, Blue-ear pig disease
Host: Domestic pigs of all ages in intensive and backyard herds
Event.summary: In early 2006 a new, highly pathogenic variant of PRRSV-2 emerged in southern China, causing an epidemic characterized by high fever, severe respiratory disease and unusually high mortality in pigs of all ages, including vaccinated animals. The virus, later termed highly pathogenic PRRSV (HP‑PRRSV) and associated with characteristic deletions in the Nsp2 region, rapidly spread across many Chinese provinces in 2006–2007 and was estimated to have affected more than 2 million pigs with very high morbidity and mortality. By 2007 the initial epidemic wave had peaked, but HP‑PRRSV became endemic in China and continued to cause recurrent outbreaks in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high pig population density, large commercial operations with frequent live‑pig movements between farms and provinces, and widespread but imperfect vaccination created conditions for rapid spread and potential selection of escape variants; limited early recognition and control facilitated broad dissemination. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel highly pathogenic PRRSV‑2 variant (HP‑PRRSV) characterized by ‘1 + 29’ amino acid deletions in Nsp2 and additional genomic changes associated with increased virulence, enhanced systemic replication and high mortality, representing a clear example of increased virulence/pathogenicity and possibly enhanced transmission within the existing PRRSV‑2 lineage. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3165578/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus pandemicum
EPP.common.name: SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19 virus
Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2021]
Host: Pet hamsters (Syrian and dwarf hamsters) in the commercial pet trade and households
Event.summary: In December 2021–January 2022, Hong Kong authorities investigated a COVID-19 cluster linked to a pet shop, where multiple imported hamsters and environmental samples tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant AY.127 and genomic analysis suggested that infected hamsters were the source of infection for several human cases. Subsequent investigations identified co-circulation of Delta AY.127 and a B.1.258-like lineage in hamsters at a wholesale warehouse and pet shops, indicating infection before or during international transport, and further human cases were epidemiologically linked to exposure to hamsters or contaminated environments. To terminate the outbreak and prevent wider spread, authorities ordered the culling of more than 2,000 hamsters and other small mammals in pet shops and warehouses, suspended imports of small mammals, and advised owners to surrender recently purchased hamsters for euthanasia, after which the hamster-associated outbreak was brought under control with no evidence of sustained hamster-to-human transmission beyond the initial cluster.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: international pet trade with hamsters likely infected in Europe or along transport routes before arrival in Hong Kong; dense housing, mixing of batches and high animal turnover in wholesale facilities and pet shops; and close contact between hamsters, shop workers, and customers in a city with otherwise strict COVID-19 controls. Internal mechanisms: host expansion into hamsters, a species experimentally known to support efficient SARS-CoV-2 replication and transmission; co-circulation of two distinct variant lineages within the hamster trade that evolved abroad; and enhanced transmission within hamster populations with at least one documented hamster-to-human spillback event, illustrating the potential of small-mammal trade networks to generate novel transmission chains.
Review: review – retain as a high-impact, well-documented outbreak linked to the international hamster trade in Hong Kong with clear public-health and animal-welfare consequences. Emergence coding has been adjusted by setting re_occurrence to 'No' and keeping re_emergence='Yes', because this episode represents re-emergence in a new, highly susceptible pet-trade host with distinct variant lineages in a subregion where SARS-CoV-2 infections in animals were already known, rather than a simple resurgence of prior animal infections driven solely by external factors.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bluetongue virus
EPP.common.name: BTV
Host: Cattle, sheep and goats on mixed and specialised ruminant farms across multiple Tunisian governorates
Event.summary: In the summer of 2020, after years of enzootic bluetongue with intermittent use of live‑attenuated vaccines, bluetongue virus serotype 4 re‑emerged explosively in Tunisia, with climatic conditions and waning immunity allowing widespread infection of cattle, sheep and goats in numerous governorates. Between August and November 2020 the outbreak produced high morbidity and notable mortality in affected herds and flocks, with farmers reporting substantial losses in milk yield, growth and reproduction as well as treatment and replacement costs, and a detailed survey estimated heavy direct economic losses at the farm level. As vector activity declined with the end of the transmission season and emergency control measures, including vector control and improved clinical management, were implemented, clinical incidence dropped, but bluetongue remained a major ongoing threat in Tunisia within a broader pattern of multi‑serotype BTV circulation in North Africa.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Favourable weather patterns in 2020 in Tunisia, including increased rainfall and temperatures that supported expansion of Culicoides vector populations; cessation of mass vaccination against BTV serotypes 1, 2 and 4 from 2017 onwards, which left large cohorts of susceptible small ruminants and cattle; and widespread smallholder and mixed farming systems with limited biosecurity that facilitated local spread. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence of BTV‑4 in a region with a long history of BTV‑2 and BTV‑4 circulation, with no clear evidence so far that a fundamentally new genotype or host shift was involved; the heavy impact of this event appears to be driven primarily by external drivers and gaps in immunity rather than intrinsic viral change.
Review: Decision: retain. Reasoning: Added as a new event because the 2020 BTV‑4 outbreak in Tunisia generated very substantial direct losses (estimated in the hundreds of millions of euros equivalent) and therefore ranks among the most economically impactful bluetongue episodes in the 2005–2025 period, yet was absent from the original profile. It is coded as re‑occurrence (not intra‑continental emergence or re‑emergence) because BTV‑4 and other serotypes have circulated in Tunisia since at least 1999; the 2020 episode reflects resurgence under favourable climatic and immunological conditions rather than appearance of a new strain in a previously unaffected UNSD sub‑region. This row relies heavily on one detailed economic‑epidemiological study, so it should be reviewed to confirm that no contemporaneous, even larger multi‑country North African BTV‑4 event warrants separate representation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bonamia exitiosa
EPP.common.name: Bonamiosis
Host: Argentinean flat oyster Ostrea puelchana (cultured and wild beds)
Event.summary: Between 1995 and 1996, Bonamia exitiosa caused a severe epizootic starting in a commercial culture of the native flat oyster Ostrea puelchana in San Antonio Bay (San Matías Gulf) and spreading into nearby natural beds along the northeastern coast of the gulf, producing about 95% mortality in cultured stock and high prevalence in wild beds; subsequent surveys showed marked and long‑lasting reductions in oyster density and mean size, with fisheries activity greatly curtailed as beds remained chronically depleted. EPP.scientific.name: Bonamia exitiosa
EPP.common.name: Bonamiosis
Host: Chilean (dredge/Bluff) oyster Ostrea chilensis in the Foveaux Strait wild fishery

EPP.scientific.name: Bonamia exitiosa
EPP.common.name: Bonamiosis
Host: Australian flat (native) oyster Ostrea angasi in farmed and adjacent wild populations in southern Australia (Victoria, New South Wales, South Australia)
Event.summary: After Bonamia‑like disease had devastated experimental native oyster culture and nearby wild Ostrea angasi beds in parts of Australia in the early 1990s, renewed outbreaks occurred between about 2013 and 2017 on intertidal O. angasi farms in southern Australia, where molecular work confirmed the causative agent as Bonamia exitiosa. These more recent epizootics caused substantial mortality on farms and prompted detailed studies of infection dynamics, revealing seasonal patterns and high infection intensities in some cohorts, with concerns that disease in culture could spill over to remnant wild O. angasi populations. Management responses included enhanced biosecurity, movement restrictions, and research into farm design and husbandry practices to limit disease spread, and bonamiosis continues to constrain expansion of native‑oyster aquaculture.

Event.summary: Around 2005, Bonamia ostreae was confirmed for the first time in Morocco, representing the first documented occurrence of the parasite in North Africa and extending its known range from Europe and North America into a new continent. EPP.scientific.name: Bovine leukemia virus
EPP.common.name: BLV, Bovine leukaemia virus
Host: Water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) in mixed buffalo–cattle systems
Event.summary: Around 2000, investigators in northern Brazil sampled water buffaloes and co‑managed cattle from herds in Pará state to clarify whether bovine leukemia virus, long recognised in cattle, also circulated naturally in buffalo populations. Although no discrete clinical leukosis outbreak or national control response was reported, this finding established buffalo as a natural BLV host in South America and highlighted mixed buffalo–cattle systems as a previously unrecognised reservoir for virus maintenance and spread.

Internal mechanisms: The event reflects host expansion and geographic range consolidation of existing BLV lineages into water buffalo rather than emergence of a demonstrably novel or more virulent genotype; buffalo infections appear to involve the same viral types circulating in sympatric cattle, with BLV’s inherent capacity for life‑long, cell‑associated infection enabling persistence in this additional domestic ruminant host.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row has been added because the 2000 Vet Record report of naturally occurring BLV infection in Brazilian water buffalo is widely regarded as the first clear demonstration of natural BLV infection in this major livestock species, with important implications for host range and epidemiology. The country, sub‑region, timing and host are consistent with the primary source, and classifying the episode as re‑emergence (via host expansion) without intra‑/inter‑continental or first‑detection labels aligns with the event‑type definitions.

By the late 2010s, enhanced surveillance and vaccination, along with changes in livestock management, began to slow or partially reverse the expansion, though brucellosis remained a prominent zoonosis in northern China.

EPP.scientific.name: Brucella spp.

Event.summary: In Saudi Arabia, human brucellosis incidence rose through the 1980s to a documented peak of about 72 cases per 100,000 population in 1990, with very high regional rates exceeding 100 per 100,000 in some governorates, reflecting intense transmission from infected sheep, goats, camels, and cattle. EPP.scientific.name: Brucella spp.

Event.summary: Between 2005 and 2007, Bulgaria detected new foci of Brucella melitensis and B. abortus infection in livestock and humans after having been considered free of these forms of brucellosis since 1958, marking a notable resurgence in Eastern Europe. Following this detection, Bulgaria implemented risk‑based surveillance and large‑scale testing of small ruminants and cattle, intensifying controls in border municipalities to contain and eventually eliminate the reintroduced infection.

EPP.scientific.name: Brucella spp.

Event.summary: In 2008, an outbreak of human brucellosis occurred on the island of Thassos in northern Greece, linked to locally produced raw goat cheese contaminated with Brucella melitensis biovar 3 from an infected donor flock. The outbreak involved at least 55 confirmed human cases by mid-June 2008, against a background of endemic brucellosis in rural Greece, highlighting how unsafe artisanal cheese production can trigger concentrated epidemics even in areas considered livestock-brucellosis-free. Following investigation, authorities intensified surveillance of goat herds and enforced stricter controls on milk‑donor flocks and cheese‑processing practices on the island, which helped bring the localized outbreak under control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Consumption of fresh, unpasteurized goat cheese; inadequate veterinary control of donor goat flocks and cheese hygiene; persistence of brucellosis in small ruminants in rural Greece despite formal eradication programs in many areas. Internal mechanisms: Local amplification of an endemic Brucella melitensis biovar 3 strain in a poorly controlled goat flock and contamination of cheese, leading to a point‑source foodborne outbreak in humans; no clear evidence of pathogen evolution, so this is coded as re-occurrence.

Event.summary: From about 2006 onward, Israel documented spillover of Brucella melitensis—traditionally endemic in sheep and goats—into previously brucellosis‑free dairy cattle herds, leading to several farm‑level outbreaks and secondary human infections through milk and direct contact. Israeli veterinary and public‑health authorities responded by intensifying vaccination of small ruminants, culling infected cattle herds, and enhancing cross‑sectoral surveillance to limit further spillover and protect the status of commercial dairy farms.

Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and enhanced transmission of Brucella melitensis from sheep/goats into dairy cattle, with genomic analyses indicating clustering of bovine and human isolates within small‑ruminant‑associated lineages rather than a distinct bovine lineage; this justifies coding the episode as re-emergence (pathogen host expansion) rather than simple re-occurrence.

Event.summary: In 2004, glanders was detected for the first time in the United Arab Emirates in an official equine quarantine facility in Dubai, when imported horses from Syria tested positive and an outbreak spread among quarantined and high-value performance horses. Event.summary: In 2011, Lebanon reported its first occurrence of glanders when horses at the Beirut Hippodrome racetrack and associated premises tested positive for B. mallei, after two recently imported horses from Syria developed clinical signs. Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected horses from endemic Syria, where glanders was still present, into a previously free national herd with limited prior experience of the disease, coupled with racetrack housing that favoured close-contact transmission, seeded the outbreak. Rapid recognition and large-scale testing of almost the entire Lebanese horse population were required to delimit infection and restore export confidence. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel B. mallei lineage or host shift was presented; the event is a re-occurrence in the already affected Western Asia sub-region, driven by equine trade rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – New event added to capture a major, previously omitted outbreak. The 2011 Lebanon episode involved euthanasia of more than 20 horses at the Beirut Hippodrome and testing of almost the entire national horse population, with substantial trade and surveillance impacts, making it one of the largest modern glanders events by scale relative to national herd size. Classified as re-occurrence (re-introduction into Western Asia via horses imported from Syria) with no intra- or inter-continental emergence and no evidence of internal pathogen change. Sources prioritise WOAH bulletins and detailed racetrack outbreak descriptions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus camelpox
EPP.common.name: CMLV
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: Between 1992 and 1994, Eastern Sudan experienced 35 reported outbreaks of camelpox in dromedary herds, with epizootics lasting 2–5 months and showing about 9% morbidity and 1.2% mortality overall, with deaths concentrated in young camels under three years of age. The disease spread mainly by direct contact at communal watering points, producing fever, facial and limb oedema, lymph node enlargement and generalized or localized pox lesions on the head, neck, legs and abdomen. Outbreaks were most frequent in the cooler winter months and eventually subsided as susceptible cohorts recovered and seasonal conditions changed, without evidence of a novel strain or spread to new sub‑regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Endemic circulation of camelpox in camel‑rearing areas of Sudan, seasonal congregation of camels at shared watering points, and higher susceptibility of young stock supported efficient transmission and recurrent epizootics. Internal mechanisms: Clinical and epidemiological patterns were consistent with known CMLV strains, with no evidence for a distinct new genotype; this episode is best interpreted as re‑occurrence of endemic virus in a previously affected sub‑region.
Review: Decision: retain. Added as a new event to capture the large 1992–1994 epizootic in Eastern Sudan (35 outbreaks with 9% morbidity and 1.2% mortality), which is one of the better‑documented, higher‑impact African camelpox episodes within the 1990+ period and was missing from the original dataset; classified as re‑occurrence in Northern Africa with no evidence of a novel strain or new sub‑region, consistent with Khalafalla & Mohamed 1996 and WOAH/WOAH regional distribution data.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus camelpox
EPP.common.name: CMLV
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: In 1999 an eruptive moderate form of camelpox was reported in a dromedary herd in the Al‑Ahsa region of Saudi Arabia, with 100% morbidity but no recorded deaths and extensive skin lesions on the head, neck and limbs. The outbreak developed rapidly within the affected three‑ to four‑year‑old camels following an initial febrile phase and typical pox lesions, but remained confined to the herd without evidence of spread to new areas. Control relied mainly on isolation of sick animals and supportive care, complementing existing broader regional vaccination and surveillance activities, and the episode resolved without wider propagation.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High stocking density and close contact among animals in the affected herd promoted efficient camel‑to‑camel transmission; regional endemicity and partial immunity in surrounding herds likely limited wider spread. Internal mechanisms: Virus isolation and characterization did not indicate a novel strain, and the clinical picture matched typical camelpox, so this event is best interpreted as re‑occurrence of endemic CMLV within a previously affected country.
Review: Decision: review. The 1999 Al‑Ahsa herd outbreak is real and correctly located (Asia/Western Asia) and classified as a re‑occurrence, but it involves a single herd with moderate severity and no deaths, so its overall impact is smaller than multi‑herd epizootics in Sudan, the UAE and Kazakhstan; if a strict ‘top ten’ impact filter is applied, this event is a candidate for downgrading or exclusion in favor of larger or zoonotically significant episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus camelpox
EPP.common.name: CMLV
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: In spring and summer 2005 the first documented outbreak of camelpox in Syria occurred in the provinces of Duma (near Damascus) and Hama, with estimated 30–90% morbidity, 1–15% mortality and very high abortion rates in affected herds. The outbreak began after introduction of infected camels that had been grazing east of Damascus, then spread between herds via communal grazing and contacts, producing generalized skin and mucosal lesions, respiratory signs and deaths mainly in young and pregnant animals. Movement restrictions, improved biosecurity and supportive treatment, together with confirmation of the etiological agent as camelpox virus by electron microscopy, virus isolation and PCR sequencing of the hemagglutinin gene, helped bring the episode under control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of infected camels from desert grazing areas into naive herds, use of shared pastures and watering points, and limited prior immunity in Syrian camel populations enabled rapid spread and high abortion rates; potential involvement of ticks and other arthropods may have amplified transmission. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analysis showed the Syrian CMLV to be closely related to strains from Somalia and Saudi Arabia, indicating geographic range expansion of existing lineages within Western Asia rather than emergence of a novel variant.
Review: Decision: retain. The first documented Syrian outbreak is well supported by primary data (morbidity, mortality, abortions and laboratory confirmation), and mapping to Asia/Western Asia with classification as re‑occurrence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) correctly follows the project rule that spread to a new country within an already affected sub‑region is not coded as intra‑continental emergence; the source set is adequate, though the generic ScienceDirect ‘topics’ page is non‑essential.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus camelpox
EPP.common.name: CMLV
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius) and camel herders (Homo sapiens)
Event.summary: In 2014, typical camelpox outbreaks were observed in two migratory dromedary herds near Showak in Gedarif State, Eastern Sudan, followed between September and December by pox‑like skin disease in three camel herders who worked closely with the affected animals. The human cases presented with erythematous, vesicular and pustular lesions on the hands, arms, legs, back and abdomen that resolved within about two months and showed no evidence of human‑to‑human transmission. Molecular testing, virus isolation and partial genome sequencing confirmed camelpox virus in samples from both camels and herders, demonstrating zoonotic transmission of CMLV in Eastern Sudan against a background of endemic camel infection.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Migratory camel husbandry with close daily contact between herders and sick animals, handling of camels with active skin lesions, and lack of personal protective equipment facilitated camel‑to‑human exposure; endemic camelpox in Eastern Sudan provided a persistent animal reservoir. Internal mechanisms: Comparative sequencing showed high similarity between camel and human CMLV isolates, supporting direct spillover; the event represents re‑occurrence of camelpox in a known sub‑region combined with re‑emergence via host expansion to humans, rather than emergence of a distinct novel lineage.
Review: Decision: retain. Added as a new event to represent the 2014 Showak (Gedarif State) outbreak involving dromedary herds and three camel herders, which provides key evidence for zoonotic CMLV transmission and was missing from the original list; coded as re‑occurrence in Northern Africa and re‑emergence due to host expansion to humans, in line with the primary case‑report and camel zoonosis reviews.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus camelpox
EPP.common.name: CMLV
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: In 2016 an outbreak of pox‑like skin disease occurred in camel herds in the Negev and southeastern Israel, where camelpox had not previously been diagnosed, leading to identification of CMLV as the causative agent. Affected camels showed fever, weakness, abortions and multifocal skin lesions, mainly in females, and infection was confirmed by electron microscopy, cell culture, immunological assays and sequencing of the full viral genome. Following diagnosis, on‑farm control measures including isolation of sick animals, improved hygiene and close monitoring were implemented, and the outbreak remained localized without documented wider spread across Western Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Probable introduction of infected animals or contaminated fomites from neighboring endemic countries, together with naive camel populations and lack of prior vaccination in Israel, allowed localized transmission in affected herds. Internal mechanisms: Genetic characterization showed the Israeli strain to be closely related to other known CMLV genomes within established diversity; this event represents geographic spread of existing lineages within Western Asia rather than emergence of a significantly different genotype.
Review: Decision: retain. The first diagnosed camelpox outbreak in Israel is well documented and appropriately mapped to Asia/Western Asia and classified as re‑occurrence within an already affected sub‑region; genomic data confirm that the virus clusters within known CMLV diversity, with no evidence of a novel lineage or inter‑continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus camelpox
EPP.common.name: CMLV
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: In summer 2020 a severe systemic camelpox outbreak was reported in a large dromedary dairy herd in the United Arab Emirates, where camelpox had previously appeared only sporadically, causing generalized external and internal lesions, respiratory disease and measurable mortality, with about 56 clinically affected camels among 5,085 animals and five deaths (overall mortality 0.1%, case fatality rate ~8.9% among diseased animals). The outbreak developed rapidly after introduction of susceptible animals and coincided with reduced ectoparasite control at the start of the COVID‑19 pandemic and high burdens of Hyalomma dromedarii ticks. Following laboratory confirmation of CMLV, aggressive treatment of secondary infections, restoration of tick control and improved biosecurity measures, the outbreak was brought under control and used as a case study on virulence and pathogenesis of systemic camelpox.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High animal density and constant close contact in a commercial dairy herd, temporary lapses in tick and ectoparasite control associated with COVID‑19‑related disruptions, introduction of likely naive animals and abundant Hyalomma ticks and other vectors enhanced transmission and disease severity; management factors such as animal movement between units further facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: Pathological and genomic analyses suggested particularly virulent circulating strains capable of causing generalized systemic disease, but still within known CMLV diversity; the event is therefore coded as re‑occurrence in an endemic country and re‑emergence with increased virulence/pathogenicity in an intensively managed herd.
Review: Decision: retain. This well‑documented 2020 UAE outbreak in a large commercial herd had modest herd‑level mortality but unusually high case fatality among clinically affected animals and extensive systemic lesions; classification as re‑occurrence plus re‑emergence (increased virulence and severity in an endemic country) is consistent with the primary report and with project definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus camelpox
EPP.common.name: CMLV
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius) – presumed source, and one human case (Homo sapiens)
Event.summary: Around 2023, a 30‑year‑old male migrant worker in Qatar presented with painful pustular lesions on his arms and was diagnosed with camelpox, constituting the first documented human camelpox case in the country and likely linked to occupational exposure to infected or subclinically infected camels. The case occurred against a background of endemic camelpox in regional camel herds but without a reported large concurrent camel outbreak in Qatar, and there was no evidence of onward human‑to‑human transmission. The patient recovered with supportive management and infection‑control measures, and the episode prompted calls for stronger One Health surveillance integrating veterinary and human sectors for early detection of similar zoonotic spillover events.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close occupational contact between camel workers and infected or subclinically infected camels, together with limited use of personal protective measures, enabled zoonotic exposure in an endemic region; regional camel trade and husbandry maintain a persistent animal reservoir. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and clinical data indicate spillover of existing CMLV strains into a human host without evidence of sustained human‑to‑human spread or a novel viral lineage; this event is therefore coded as re‑emergence involving host expansion to humans in Qatar rather than a new continental or sub‑regional presence in camels.
Review: Decision: retain. The first confirmed human camelpox case in Qatar is well documented and epidemiologically linked to camel exposure in a region with established camelpox in camels; mapping to Asia/Western Asia is correct and classification as re‑emergence (host expansion to humans) without re‑occurrence reflects the absence of a major concurrent camel epizootic; the DeepDyve URL from the original draft is redundant given the open‑access PMC article and has not been retained here.

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter fetus
EPP.common.name: Bovine genital campylobacteriosis
Host: Breeding bulls and beef cows in Spanish beef herds managed under dehesa and mountain grazing systems
Event.summary: Between 2011 and 2019, analysis of 5,182 breeding bulls from 1,950 Spanish beef herds submitted to the SALUVET veterinary diagnostic laboratory demonstrated sustained endemic infection with Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis, with about 7.7% of bulls and 12.2% of herds PCR‑positive and infection widely distributed across dehesa and mountain systems. Over this nine‑year period, bovine genital campylobacteriosis was repeatedly confirmed as a major contributor to early reproductive failure in natural‑service beef herds and was frequently detected together with bovine trichomoniasis, reinforcing its economic significance. Control recommendations focused on improved bull testing, biosecurity, strategic culling and increased reliance on artificial insemination, but the persistent detection of positive bulls throughout the study period illustrated the difficulty of eradicating the pathogen in extensive grazing systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive beef production with natural mating, especially under dehesa and communal mountain pastures, older breeding bulls, and co‑infection with bovine trichomoniasis were major risk factors for Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis infection; limited mandatory surveillance and the movement of breeding bulls between herds facilitated ongoing transmission. Internal mechanisms: long‑term, asymptomatic colonization of the bull prepuce and efficient venereal transmission allowed the pathogen to persist endemically without requiring major genetic change, so this episode reflects resurgence and continued detection of an established infection rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: Decision: Retain. This event closely reflects the national‑scale diagnostic‑laboratory dataset reported for Spain from 2011 to 2019, including the numbers of bulls and herds tested and the estimated prevalences (≈7.7% of bulls and 12.2% of herds PCR‑positive for C. fetus subsp. venerealis), and correctly emphasizes dehesa and mountain grazing systems as high‑risk settings. Spain is correctly placed in Europe | Southern Europe and the event is appropriately coded as re‑occurrence, as BGC has been endemic in Spain and other European countries for decades. The cited sources include the primary Spanish study, an official national factsheet and a recent global review, which are suitable references. No larger or more impactful post‑1990 BGC event in Europe was identified that would clearly supersede this episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter fetus
EPP.common.name: Bovine genital campylobacteriosis
Host: Beef cows and breeding bulls in a commercial cow‑calf herd in Saskatchewan, Canada
Event.summary: In 2011, a large commercial beef herd in Saskatchewan, Canada, experienced marked reproductive failure with reduced pregnancy rates and prolonged calving intervals, prompting a detailed outbreak investigation. A new real‑time quantitative PCR assay applied to preputial and reproductive samples identified Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis as the primary cause of bovine genital campylobacteriosis in the herd, confirming venereal transmission from infected breeding bulls to cows. Control measures including segregation and culling of infected groups, changes in bull management and enhanced record‑keeping led to improved reproductive performance in subsequent breeding seasons, illustrating both the substantial potential impact of BGC in North American beef systems and the value of molecular diagnostics in outbreak settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: reliance on natural service with limited pre‑breeding surveillance for venereal pathogens, introduction or persistence of carrier bulls, and large extensively managed breeding groups facilitated unnoticed spread of Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis before diagnosis; the absence of routine vaccination or testing for BGC meant that infertility was initially attributed to other causes. Internal mechanisms: chronic, often asymptomatic colonization of the bull prepuce and efficient venereal transmission underpinned rapid within‑herd dissemination, but there was no evidence of a novel strain, antimicrobial resistance or host shift, so the outbreak represents re‑occurrence of a known pathogen rather than re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: Retain. The description matches the documented Saskatchewan cow‑calf herd outbreak investigated with a novel real‑time PCR test, including the timing, clinical picture (marked reproductive losses) and subsequent improvement following targeted control. Canada is correctly assigned to Northern America | Northern America, and the event is suitably coded as re‑occurrence because BGC had long been present in North America and there is no evidence of first introduction, inter‑continental spread or a novel strain. Although the event involves a single herd, it is one of the better‑characterised high‑impact BGC outbreaks in a region where the disease is relatively uncommon due to widespread artificial insemination, and is reasonable to retain among the limited number of major post‑1990 episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter fetus
EPP.common.name: Bovine genital campylobacteriosis
Host: Bulls in mixed pastoral and other management systems in northern Nigeria (with implications for cows in the same herds)
Event.summary: In 2013, a large cross‑sectional survey in three northern Nigerian states collected preputial samples from 602 bulls in 250 herds and used culture and identification methods to estimate a true animal‑level Campylobacter fetus prevalence of about 16%, with roughly 81% of isolates identified as C. fetus subsp. venerealis and most of these as biovar intermedius, and a herd‑level prevalence of around 25%. Infection was particularly common in older bulls and in herds managed under pastoral systems, and there was a strong positive association with brucellosis, helping explain substantial, previously unquantified infertility and abortion losses. Subsequent work highlighted bovine genital campylobacteriosis as a key differential in reproductive failure investigations in the region and called for improved control programmes, although structural constraints in extensive systems have limited rapid reduction of disease burden.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: dominance of extensive pastoral and agro‑pastoral cattle systems with natural mating, frequent communal grazing and bull sharing, limited access to veterinary infrastructure and diagnostics, and high mobility of herds across porous borders provided ideal conditions for the maintenance and spread of Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis; concurrent brucellosis further exacerbated reproductive losses. Internal mechanisms: predominance of C. fetus subsp. venerealis biovar intermedius strains adapted to the bovine genital tract enabled efficient venereal transmission and chronic carriage in bulls, but surveys did not implicate recent genetic changes as drivers of increased incidence, so the episode is best interpreted as documentation of endemic re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: Retain. This event accurately summarises the 2013 Acta Veterinaria Scandinavica survey in northern Nigeria, which sampled 602 bulls in 250 herds and reported a true animal‑level Campylobacter fetus prevalence of 16.4% and herd‑level prevalence of 25.5%, with most isolates classified as C. fetus subsp. venerealis biovar intermedius and a strong association with brucellosis. Nigeria is correctly assigned to Africa | Western Africa, and categorisation as re‑occurrence (long‑standing endemic infection documented with modern epidemiological methods) is appropriate. The cited sources include the primary paper plus a companion risk‑factor analysis, providing good coverage of both prevalence and drivers. No larger, clearly more impactful BGC event from sub‑Saharan Africa post‑1990 was identified that would unambiguously displace this episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter jejuni
EPP.common.name: Campylobacteriosis
Host: Broiler chickens; turkeys; cattle (secondary)
Event.summary: After fluoroquinolones were approved for use in U.S. poultry in 1995, previously rare ciprofloxacin‑resistant C. jejuni began appearing in human and animal isolates, with state and national surveillance from 1992–2001 documenting a clear upward trend in quinolone resistance linked partly to domestic poultry exposure. Retail chicken surveys in the late 1990s and early 2000s found Campylobacter contamination with notable levels of fluoroquinolone resistance in chicken and turkey products, indicating establishment of resistant strains in poultry production. In response to accumulating evidence that poultry use was driving resistant infections, the U.S. FDA withdrew fluoroquinolone approvals for poultry by 2005, after which monitoring focused on resistance trends in poultry‑associated C. jejuni.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Therapeutic and metaphylactic fluoroquinolone use in broiler and turkey production, high‑throughput poultry processing, and large‑scale distribution of contaminated meat. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via gyrA mutations and related mechanisms; Enhanced Transmission along the poultry production chain sustaining high colonization and contamination rates.
Review: retain – Strongly corroborated by U.S. surveillance data showing no fluoroquinolone‑resistant C. jejuni in 1990, rapid emergence after poultry approvals in 1995, rising resistance in human and poultry isolates in 1997–2001, and withdrawal of enrofloxacin for poultry in 2005.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3367372/?utm_source=openai)) Event framing as a resistance‑driven re‑emergence in U.S. food animals is appropriate and among the globally most consequential episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter jejuni
EPP.common.name: Campylobacteriosis
Host: Broiler chickens; turkeys; beef cattle (retail beef); pigs (retail pork)
Event.summary: Beginning in 2002, the U.S. National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System retail meat program systematically sampled chicken, turkey, beef and pork, finding Campylobacter contamination particularly common in poultry and documenting substantial resistance to fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and other drugs. Over 2002–2007, a large fraction of C. jejuni and C. coli isolates from chicken breast and other meats were resistant to multiple antimicrobial classes, with many widely dispersed clones, defining a major emergence of MDR Campylobacter in U.S. animal‑source foods. This surveillance demonstrated that MDR Campylobacter had become entrenched in retail meat supply chains, informing subsequent control efforts in livestock production and processing.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Previous widespread antimicrobial use in poultry and other livestock, large industrial slaughter and distribution systems that amplify and disseminate colonized flocks and herds, and limited early‑2000s regulatory constraints on non‑therapeutic antimicrobial use. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance with combined resistance to macrolides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and other drug classes; Enhanced Transmission in slaughter and carcass processing environments and along retail distribution networks.
