Review: retain – Supported by NARMS retail‑meat data showing high Campylobacter contamination of poultry and frequent multi‑class resistance in >2,000 isolates collected 2002–2007 across the United States.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3008252/?utm_source=openai)) This represents a distinct, highly impactful phase in which MDR Campylobacter became firmly established in the U.S. meat supply beyond the initial fluoroquinolone‑only emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter jejuni
EPP.common.name: Campylobacteriosis
Host: Sheep (pregnant ewes and fetuses); cattle (reservoir)
Event.summary: From about 2003 onward, investigators in the United States identified a highly virulent, tetracycline‑resistant Campylobacter jejuni clone (clone SA, for sheep abortion) that rapidly became the predominant cause of Campylobacter‑associated ovine abortions, responsible for the vast majority (>90% in some series) of diagnosed cases. Molecular epidemiology showed that clone SA was widely distributed in sheep flocks and also present in beef and dairy cattle and retail meats, indicating broad ruminant reservoirs and potential food‑borne transmission to humans. Through the 2000s and early 2010s, recurrent abortion storms associated with clone SA caused substantial reproductive losses in sheep operations and prompted development of targeted pathogenesis studies and vaccine candidates, marking a major re‑emergence event in ruminant health.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive use of tetracyclines as the main class of antibiotics approved for prevention and treatment of Campylobacter abortion in U.S. sheep, flock management practices that facilitate within‑flock spread, and intensive ruminant production systems. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (uniform tetracycline resistance in clone SA); Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity associated with a distinct capsular polysaccharide and other virulence determinants enabling systemic infection and placental invasion; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of clone SA within U.S. ruminant populations.
Review: review – New high‑impact event added. Multiple studies document that a single hypervirulent, tetracycline‑resistant C. jejuni clone (clone SA) emerged around 2003 as the predominant cause of ovine abortion in the United States, accounting for >90% of cases and being widely distributed in sheep and cattle.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3295108/?utm_source=openai)) This constitutes a major re‑emergence in the animal host system that was missing from the original list and clearly merits inclusion among the top 10 events; timeframe and geography are well constrained but should be checked against any national production‑loss data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter jejuni
EPP.common.name: Campylobacteriosis
Host: Broiler chickens; chicken meat at slaughter
Event.summary: In 2016, a structured national survey of Campylobacter from chicken flocks and carcasses at slaughter across all major Australian meat‑chicken producers unexpectedly identified fluoroquinolone‑resistant C. jejuni and C. coli despite the absence of licensed fluoroquinolone use in Australian poultry. Genomic analyses showed that these resistant isolates carried the canonical gyrA Thr86→Ile mutation and were interspersed among international lineages, suggesting introduction from outside Australia rather than local selection by on‑farm fluoroquinolone use. The survey indicated that these resistant strains had achieved widespread colonization of commercial flocks across companies, marking a notable emergence of fluoroquinolone resistance in a previously largely susceptible national poultry reservoir.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of resistant strains via imported breeding stock, hatching eggs, or other indirect trade/traffic, combined with intensive vertically integrated poultry systems that can disseminate introduced clones widely even without local fluoroquinolone use. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via gyrA mutations; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of resistant international lineages into Australian broiler populations; Enhanced Transmission in large integrated production chains.
Review: review – Event year has been narrowed to 2016, aligning with the national slaughter‑survey that first detected fluoroquinolone‑resistant Campylobacter in Australian chickens, in a setting where such resistance had previously been absent due to lack of licensed fluoroquinolone use.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/AEM.02765-19?utm_source=openai)) The summary has been adjusted to remove implications of multi‑year monitoring before follow‑up studies and to emphasize the survey‑documented widespread colonisation; classification as a resistance‑driven re‑emergence remains appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter jejuni
EPP.common.name: Campylobacteriosis
Host: Dogs (pet store puppies); humans (secondary, zoonotic spillover)
Event.summary: Between 2016 and 2020, U.S. public health investigations identified a multistate outbreak of multidrug‑ and extensively drug‑resistant C. jejuni infections linked to pet store puppies, with 168 epidemiologically or molecularly associated human cases across at least 30 states and strong evidence implicating dogs sourced through commercial breeding and retail chains. The outbreak strains were resistant to all recommended first‑line treatments and many other antibiotic classes and were traced back through puppy supply chains involving multiple breeders, transporters and pet store chains, indicating that high‑level resistant Campylobacter had become established in this companion‑animal network. Control efforts including revised antibiotic use practices, infection‑prevention guidance for pet stores and veterinarians, and public awareness campaigns helped reduce new outbreak‑associated cases after 2018, but XDR outbreak‑related strains continued to be detected through 2020, showing persistence of this new host‑system reservoir.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive commercial breeding and retail distribution of puppies, frequent prophylactic and empirical antibiotic use in puppies before and after sale, high‑density housing and transport stress, and close human–dog contact facilitating zoonotic transmission. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance with extensive MDR and XDR profiles across multiple antibiotic classes; Host Expansion (Spillover) and establishment of highly resistant C. jejuni lineages in companion dogs as a distinct reservoir; Enhanced Transmission through shared kenneling, transport, and retail environments and across the pet trade network.
Review: retain – CDC outbreak reports and subsequent analyses confirm a large, multistate outbreak of MDR/XDR C. jejuni linked to pet store puppies from 2016–2020, with 100+ confirmed human cases and strains resistant to all recommended first‑line therapies.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/67/wr/mm6737a3.htm?utm_source=openai)) This is a clearly defined, high‑impact re‑emergence involving a new companion‑animal reservoir and justifies inclusion as one of the top events.

EPP.scientific.name: Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei
EPP.common.name: NHP bacterium
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp, mainly Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei), with cases also in western blue shrimp (P. stylirostris) and other local penaeids.
Event.summary: After its initial recognition in 1985, necrotising hepatopancreatitis continued to cause recurrent seasonal epizootics in shrimp farms along the Texas coast during the early 1990s, with microscopic and ultrastructural studies on samples collected in 1986–1991 confirming heavy infections of hepatopancreatic epithelial cells by a pleomorphic intracellular Gram‑negative bacterium.([int-res.com](https://www.int-res.com/articles/dao/13/d013p235.pdf)) These outbreaks developed during warm seasons with high salinity and were associated with 20–95% mortality and serious production losses in Pacific white shrimp grow‑out ponds.([units.fisheries.org](https://units.fisheries.org/fhs/wp-content/uploads/sites/30/2017/08/6.2.1-Hepatopancreatitis-2014.pdf)) As better diagnostic tools and management practices were introduced in the mid‑1990s, farms reduced but did not eliminate NHP‑associated losses, and the disease became an endemic constraint in the region rather than an acute epizootic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive pond-based mariculture in Texas with high pond organic loads, elevated summer temperatures and high salinity (20–40 ppt) created favourable conditions for proliferation and transmission of the NHP bacterium; poor biosecurity and reuse of pond water facilitated within‑farm persistence.([units.fisheries.org](https://units.fisheries.org/fhs/wp-content/uploads/sites/30/2017/08/6.2.1-Hepatopancreatitis-2014.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of novel strain emergence; the main factor was high baseline pathogenicity of Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei combined with host stress, leading to severe granulomatous hepatopancreatitis and high mortality in L. vannamei.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC168141/?utm_source=openai))
Review: RETAIN. Evidence from Lightner et al. 1992 and subsequent reviews shows that NHP was first recognised in Texas shrimp farms in 1985 and caused severe seasonal losses (20–90% crop mortality) through the early 1990s, with multiple farms affected nearly every year.([int-res.com](https://www.int-res.com/articles/dao/13/d013p235.pdf)) Treating the 1990–1994 cluster as a linked re‑occurrence episode in an already affected subregion (Northern America) is consistent with the event definitions, and no larger unrecorded NHP events are evident for this period; geography, host list and sources are appropriate and need no correction.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei
EPP.common.name: NHP bacterium
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) and western blue shrimp (P. stylirostris) in coastal ponds in Sonora and Sinaloa, Mexico.
Event.summary: Necrotising hepatopancreatitis was first reported in Mexican shrimp aquaculture in 1999, when farms in Sonora and Sinaloa on the Pacific coast recorded outbreaks of hepatopancreatic disease and confirmed NHP infections in L. vannamei and P. stylirostris.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2607/13/11/2631?utm_source=openai)) During the subsequent 2–3 years, affected ponds experienced summer mortalities ranging from about 20% to 80%, particularly when water temperatures reached or exceeded 34 °C and salinity rose to around 45 g/kg, leading to notable production losses and increased diagnostic and control efforts.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2607/13/11/2631?utm_source=openai)) As farmers improved biosecurity, adjusted stocking densities and modified water management, the intensity of NHP outbreaks declined, and the disease transitioned toward an endemic but better‑managed problem in the main shrimp‑farming regions of north‑western Mexico.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional expansion of intensive shrimp farming in north‑western Mexico, coupled with movements of post‑larvae and possible use of infected broodstock from regions already affected by NHP, likely introduced the pathogen; extreme summer water temperatures and high salinity strongly predisposed ponds to outbreaks and high mortalities.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2607/13/11/2631?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreaks were attributed to the same NHP bacterium later named Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei, with no strong evidence for a distinct Mexican strain; pathogenicity expressed as severe hepatopancreatic necrosis in stressed shrimp populations rather than through documented novel genotypes.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568585/?utm_source=openai))
Review: RETAIN. A recent peer‑reviewed history of shrimp diseases in Mexico clearly states that NHP was first reported there in 1999 in farmed P. vannamei and P. stylirostris in Sonora and Sinaloa, with 20–80% summer mortalities under very warm, hypersaline conditions.([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2607/13/11/2631?utm_source=openai)) This supports the 1999 onset year and the description of impact. Because Peru/Ecuador (South America subregion) were already affected in 1993, the first detection in Mexico (Central America subregion) is correctly classified as intra‑continental emergence within the broader South America continent defined in the Country sheet, rather than as a new inter‑continental event. WOAH and national sources corroborate Mexico as part of the endemic Western Hemisphere range, so no geography or type changes are needed.([woah.org](https://www.woah.org/app/uploads/2021/03/microsoft-20word-20--20nhp-20disease-20card-20-draft-.pdf))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei
EPP.common.name: NHP bacterium
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp including Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) and black tiger shrimp (Penaeus monodon) in coastal ponds in northern Viet Nam (Quảng Ninh) and later other farming areas.
Event.summary: Around 2002, Vietnamese authorities first detected necrotising hepatopancreatitis, caused by a Rickettsia‑like Gram‑negative bacterium referred to locally as NHPB, in farmed penaeid shrimp in Quảng Ninh province, representing the first confirmed occurrence of the disease in Asia.([vbpl.vn](https://vbpl.vn/quangtri/Pages/vbpq-toanvan.aspx?ItemID=26839&Keyword=&utm_source=openai)) In the following years, NHP was recognised as present in parts of the Asia–Pacific region and officially reported from Viet Nam, where affected ponds showed slow growth, lethargy, soft shells and hepatopancreatic degeneration with reported mortalities up to 50–100% over several weeks.([library.enaca.org](https://library.enaca.org/Health/FieldGuide/pdf/Necrotising%20hepatopancreatitis.pdf)) As diagnostic standards and shrimp health management improved and attention shifted to other emerging hepatopancreatic diseases such as AHPND, NHP remained a recognised but comparatively less prominent bacterial threat, managed through biosecurity, pond hygiene and avoidance of extreme temperature–salinity combinations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of penaeid shrimp aquaculture in Viet Nam, combined with imports or movements of seed from regions where NHP was endemic, likely introduced Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei into Asian farms; local pond conditions with high temperature and salinity episodes facilitated disease expression.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7172736/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The agent was described as a Gram‑negative, Rickettsia‑like bacterium consistent with NHPB, implying geographic range expansion of an already virulent lineage into a new continent and additional host species (including P. monodon) rather than evolution of a new strain; host expansion within penaeids is recognised but not clearly linked to novel genotypes.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568585/?utm_source=openai))
Review: REVIEW. NACA’s regional field guide and multiple reviews affirm that NHP has been officially reported from Viet Nam and is the only confirmed focus in the Asia–Pacific region, with Vietnamese regulations indicating first detection on farmed shrimp in Quảng Ninh around 2002.([library.enaca.org](https://library.enaca.org/Health/FieldGuide/pdf/Necrotising%20hepatopancreatitis.pdf)) This justifies classifying the 2002–2005 Viet Nam episode as an inter‑continental emergence event (first establishment in Asia). However, the original OIE disease‑card URL used in this row is now obsolete; I have replaced it with the current WOAH disease page, which links to the Aquatic Code and Manual chapters on infection with Hepatobacter penaei.([woah.org](https://www.woah.org/en/disease/necrotising-hepatopancreatitis-hepatobacter-penaeiv/)) Event timing, geography, and host range look consistent with available sources, but given limited quantitative impact data, human review of the exact year range and severity is recommended.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei
EPP.common.name: NHP bacterium
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) in commercial ponds in Brazil experiencing high mortality attributed to NHP bacterium.
Event.summary: Around 2010, Brazilian shrimp farms reported significant mortalities in L. vannamei stocks, and diagnostic investigations on shrimp from a commercial farm with high losses confirmed necrotising hepatopancreatitis bacterium infection through wet mounts, histopathology and PCR.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1749-7345.2010.00424.x?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak developed as a severe on‑farm epizootic, with high prevalence of advanced NHP lesions in broodstock and grow‑out shrimp that contributed to production declines in parts of the national industry already challenged by other diseases.([globalseafood.org](https://www.globalseafood.org/advocate/disease-risk-factors-shrimp-production-brazil/?utm_source=openai)) Following implementation of improved broodstock screening, pond management and biosecurity, Brazilian producers reduced the impact of NHP, although the pathogen remains present in the region as part of a complex of shrimp bacterial diseases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of infected broodstock and post‑larvae, high stocking densities, and suboptimal pond management likely allowed re‑establishment and amplification of NHP bacterium in Brazilian ponds that had previously reported the disease; environmental stressors and co‑infections may have exacerbated clinical expression.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1749-7345.2010.00424.x?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of a novel Brazilian strain; rather, the episode reflects re‑occurrence of Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei in an already affected subregion, with disease severity associated with high infection loads and host stress rather than documented genetic change in the bacterium.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568585/?utm_source=openai))
Review: RETAIN. The 2010 Brazilian episode is supported by a peer‑reviewed diagnostic study documenting high NHP‑attributed mortalities on a commercial farm, and by broader regional analyses that list Brazil among the Latin American countries where NHP is established.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1749-7345.2010.00424.x?utm_source=openai)) Because South America (Peru/Ecuador) was already affected in 1993, this event fits best as a major re‑occurrence within the same subregion rather than as a new intra‑continental emergence; the current classification reflects that and no geography or host corrections are needed, though the exact national-scale production impact remains less quantified than for the Peru/Ecuador epizootic.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei
EPP.common.name: NHP bacterium
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) in ponds in the Golfo de Nicoya, Costa Rica.
Event.summary: During 2014, an outbreak (brote) of necrotising hepatopancreatitis occurred in L. vannamei cultured in the Golfo de Nicoya, Costa Rica, exacerbated by El Niño–related conditions of unusually high water temperatures and salinities; histopathology confirmed characteristic NHP lesions in affected shrimp.([revistas.uned.ac.cr](https://revistas.uned.ac.cr/index.php/repertorio/user/setLocale/en_US?source=%2Findex.php%2Frepertorio%2Farticle%2Fview%2F2553)) The episode caused significant on‑farm morbidity and mortality and was recognised nationally as an important climatic‑driven disease event in Costa Rican shrimp aquaculture. As environmental conditions normalised and management measures were implemented, mortalities decreased, and NHP remained one of several bacterial diseases monitored in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The 2014 El Niño event produced elevated sea surface temperatures and salinity in the Golfo de Nicoya, stressing shrimp and creating favourable conditions for expression and transmission of NHP in existing farm systems; management practices and stocking densities likely modulated outbreak severity.([revistas.uned.ac.cr](https://revistas.uned.ac.cr/index.php/repertorio/user/setLocale/en_US?source=%2Findex.php%2Frepertorio%2Farticle%2Fview%2F2553)) Internal mechanisms: Available evidence indicates involvement of the typical NHP bacterium (Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei) with no demonstration of novel strains or resistance traits, so this episode reflects environmentally driven re‑occurrence rather than pathogen evolution or host‑range shift.
Review: REVIEW. This new row has been added to capture the well‑documented 2014 outbreak of NHP in farmed L. vannamei in the Golfo de Nicoya, Costa Rica, which the primary case report explicitly describes as a brote associated with El Niño–type high temperature and salinity conditions.([revistas.uned.ac.cr](https://revistas.uned.ac.cr/index.php/repertorio/user/setLocale/en_US?source=%2Findex.php%2Frepertorio%2Farticle%2Fview%2F2553)) Because Central America was already affected via earlier spread to Mexico and other countries, this is best classified as a re‑occurrence event within an endemic subregion driven by climatic factors, not as intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence. Quantitative national production‑loss data are limited, so a human reviewer should confirm that this episode merits inclusion among the top‑impact events for this pathogen, but current evidence suggests it is one of the more significant recent NHP outbreaks in Central America.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Canine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Canine distemper virus, CDV
Host: Ethiopian wolf (Canis simensis); domestic dogs as source reservoir
Event.summary: Around 2010, only about four years after the 2005–2006 CDV epizootic and a major rabies outbreak, CDV re‑emerged in Ethiopian wolves across Bale Mountains National Park. The virus again spread rapidly among closely knit packs, causing high mortality and the eradication of several packs before waning as susceptible animals were exhausted and emergency vaccination and dog control were intensified. This second CDV wave further fragmented and depressed the already weakened wolf population, demonstrating the short inter‑epizootic interval and the chronic threat posed by CDV in this system.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent CDV circulation or repeated reintroduction from surrounding domestic dogs where vaccination coverage was low; rapid demographic turnover and incomplete vaccination of wolves limited the build‑up of long‑term herd immunity; continued land use change and high dog density kept wolves in close proximity to reservoir populations. Internal mechanisms: Reappearance of the same or closely related CDV lineage in a partially recovered but still vulnerable host population, with virus life‑history traits (short infectious period, high transmissibility in social canids) favoring frequent epizootic waves rather than a distinct new genotype.
Review: review - Retain as a major follow-on event in Ethiopian wolves but adjust classification. This 2010 outbreak is a resurgence of CDV in the same Bale Mountains subregion shortly after the 2005–2006 outbreak, driven primarily by external factors (ongoing dog reservoir, incomplete vaccination, demographic recovery after rabies), with no evidence that a novel viral strain or host expansion occurred. Accordingly, recoded as 're_occurrence = true' and 're_emergence = false'; years, geography and host details were left unchanged.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Caprine arthritis encephalitis virus
EPP.common.name: CAEV, Small ruminant lentivirus
Countries: Somalia (Somaliland – Togdheer and Waqoyi Galbed districts) [2008]
Host: Domestic goats in pastoral and agropastoral herds
Event.summary: In 2008, a cross-sectional survey of 1,198 goats from 34 randomly selected herds in northern Somalia (Somaliland) found an overall CAEV seroprevalence of 6.0% and herd-level infection in 24 of 34 herds, providing the first solid evidence that CAEV was circulating in a country with one of Africa’s largest goat populations. Multivariable analysis showed that older age, larger herd size and rearing goats together with sheep were significant risk factors for seropositivity, indicating ongoing within- and between-herd transmission in the main goat-producing districts. The study, set against the backdrop of an earlier global survey in the 1980s that had found no reactors in Somali goats, signalled a substantial regional emergence of CAEV in Eastern Africa and highlighted the need for surveillance and movement control in a livestock-dependent economy.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and commercialization of goat production in Somaliland, close contact between goats and sheep, and regional trade and movements of animals (including imports for slaughter and breeding) likely introduced CAEV into previously negative populations and supported its spread. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was reported; the emergence pattern is consistent with introduction of typical CAEV/SRLV genotypes into high-density pastoral systems, with persistent infection and slow seroconversion leading to under-recognition until systematic serological surveys were undertaken.
Review: retain – added this as a key African re_occurrence event: it documents CAEV establishment in northern Somalia using a large sample (1,198 goats) and herd-level analysis in a country with ~12 million goats, and explicitly contrasts the new positives with earlier global data showing no reactors from Somalia. Classified as re_occurrence (not first_detection or intra_continental) because CAEV had already been reported in Eastern Africa (e.g. Kenya) by the mid‑1980s; the main novelty is the virus’ emergence in Somalia’s large pastoral goat sector. Event clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 CAEV emergence episodes and should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Caprine arthritis encephalitis virus
EPP.common.name: CAEV, Small ruminant lentivirus
Host: Domestic goats (dairy Saanen and other breeds)
Event.summary: Around 2010, a dairy goat farm in South Korea that had been considered free of CAEV began to experience lameness, carpal joint swelling and neurologic signs in goats; nested PCR and sequencing of the gag gene confirmed CAEV infection and the episode was reported as the first recognized outbreak of CAE on a Korean farm. Subsequent testing on the index farm found more than half of the adult Saanen goats and a substantial fraction of kids PCR-positive, while nearby farms keeping only native Korean black goats remained negative, indicating localized establishment of infection in imported dairy breeds. Follow-up serological and molecular work showed that Korean isolates clustered with known CAEV strains, and control on the affected farm focused on testing, culling of positives and improved kid-rearing practices rather than a national eradication programme.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of infected Saanen or other dairy breeding stock into a previously CAEV‑naïve commercial farm, limited historical testing, and increasing interest in intensive dairy goat production created conditions for silent spread before overt clinical disease emerged. Internal mechanisms: The Korean isolates showed close sequence homology to known CAEV strains, suggesting that endemic establishment was driven by efficient lactogenic and horizontal transmission in intensive herds rather than by a novel genotype or increased virulence.
Review: retain – adjusted the event year from an imprecise 2005–2010 range to 2010, corresponding to the first confirmed outbreak and molecular characterization reported by Park et al. (2010) and later detailed clinically in a 2021 case report, and clarified the country/time annotation accordingly. Kept emergence-type coding as a regional re_occurrence (CAEV was already present in Eastern Asia in China and Japan) and not as intra_continental_emergence, which is reserved for first appearance in a new UN subregion. Event remains one of the key post‑1990 CAEV emergence reports in Eastern Asia.

EPP.scientific.name: Capripoxvirus ovis
EPP.common.name: Sheep pox virus, Goat pox virus
Host: Sheep (primarily), goats (exposed and culled in mixed flocks)
Event.summary: In November 1994, sheep pox re‑appeared in Evros Prefecture in north‑eastern Greece, near the land border with Türkiye, after the country had been free of clinical disease for several years. The outbreak evolved into a prolonged regional epidemic lasting until December 1998, involving 249 infected premises in Evros and neighbouring areas, with extensive culling, movement restrictions and other control measures implemented. By late 1998 the epidemic was stamped out through depopulation of affected and at‑risk flocks and strict biosecurity, although a single reappearance in 2000 triggered renewed control before the disease was again eliminated.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: repeated introduction of virus across the Evros land border from endemic areas in Türkiye, high densities of small‑ruminant farms, and practical challenges in enforcing movement controls in a transboundary grazing zone. Internal mechanisms: no novel strain or host shift was described; dynamics reflected high susceptibility of naïve or under‑vaccinated flocks and efficient direct and aerosol transmission within and between holdings.
Review: retain – Well-supported major epidemic in Evros, Greece, 1994–1998 with correct continent/sub‑region assignment and appropriate classification as re‑occurrence in a historically affected area; no structural changes made.

EPP.scientific.name: Capripoxvirus ovis
EPP.common.name: Sheep pox virus, Goat pox virus
Host: Goats (small ruminants, primarily local breeds)
Event.summary: In early 2005, Viet Nam reported its first recognised goatpox outbreaks affecting several northern provinces, marking the first documented presence of capripoxvirus disease in Vietnamese goat populations and in mainland South‑East Asia. The outbreaks caused high morbidity and notable mortality in naïve herds, prompting emergency control measures including movement restrictions, quarantine and culling in affected flocks. After implementation of these measures and targeted vaccination with imported capripox vaccines, the 2005 episode was brought under control, although the virus later re‑appeared in the country.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction of virus via informal or formal trade in small ruminants from endemic neighbouring areas (especially southern China), rapid expansion of goat production in northern Viet Nam, and low baseline immunity due to absence of previous exposure or vaccination. Internal mechanisms: molecular work later linked Vietnamese strains to Chinese goatpox viruses, suggesting regional spread of established lineages rather than de novo evolution.
Review: retain – OIE immediate notification confirms 2005 as the first reported goatpox occurrence in Viet Nam and in South‑East Asia; classification as first_detection and intra‑continental emergence (new UNSD sub‑region within Asia) is appropriate; no corrections required.

EPP.scientific.name: Capripoxvirus ovis
EPP.common.name: Sheep pox virus, Goat pox virus
Host: Goats
Event.summary: In March 2014, after almost a decade without reported disease, a large goatpox outbreak re‑appeared in North Viet Nam’s Ninh Binh Province, eventually affecting more than 1,800 goats across multiple communes with an estimated case fatality of around 6–7%. The outbreak spread rapidly among intensively raised and backyard goats, prompting emergency vaccination, movement restrictions and culling of severely affected animals. Following these measures and heightened awareness, the epidemic was brought under control, but it underscored the vulnerability of Viet Nam’s expanding goat sector to renewed capripox incursions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of goat production in northern Viet Nam, increased animal movements within and between provinces, low baseline immunity due to limited routine vaccination and long absence of disease, and delayed recognition of early clinical cases. Internal mechanisms: molecular characterization showed the 2014 strain was closely related to Chinese and earlier Vietnamese goatpox viruses, indicating re‑introduction of a regional lineage into a largely naïve population (re‑occurrence) rather than a novel genotype.
Review: review – Corrected emergence-type coding: this episode follows the 2005 first detection in Viet Nam and represents re‑occurrence of a regional lineage in the same UNSD sub‑region, so intra_continental_emergence has been set to false and re_occurrence to true; no evidence supports classification as re_emergence (no new host or clearly novel genotype). Retain as a major national outbreak but confirm exact case and mortality figures from the primary papers.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Carp edema virus
EPP.common.name: CEV
Host: Ornamental koi carp on commercial farms supplying the regional market
Event.summary: Around 2015, Brazilian koi farms reported outbreaks of lethargy, gill disease and mortality in ornamental carp, and laboratory testing confirmed CEV infection, constituting the first detection of koi sleepy disease in South America. Affected farms supplying the national and regional ornamental fish trade experienced substantial losses, and detection of CEV in Brazilian koi signalled that the virus had crossed into a new continent. Following confirmation, researchers and authorities highlighted the need for improved diagnostics, quarantine of imported carp and risk assessments to prevent introduction into common carp aquaculture and wild carp populations.([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13567-025-01700-y?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of koi (and possibly goldfish) from CEV-endemic regions in Asia and Europe without targeted CEV screening introduced the virus into Brazilian ornamental aquaculture; climatic conditions with suitable water temperatures, combined with intensive indoor and pond culture, favored clinical disease expression. Internal mechanisms: Available genetic data indicate that Brazilian isolates belong to known international CEV lineages, suggesting successful inter‑continental transfer of established strains rather than emergence of a novel South American variant; this justifies classification as inter‑continental emergence.([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13567-025-01700-y?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain. Brazil’s first CEV detections represent the initial incursion of the virus into South America and had meaningful economic implications for the ornamental sector, justifying inter_continental_emergence classification. Sources (UF/IFAS fact sheet and EAFP abstracts) are appropriate for this broad, continent-level event.

EPP.scientific.name: Carp edema virus
EPP.common.name: CEV
Host: Wild adult common carp in an inland artificial lake
Event.summary: In mid-June 2020, a severe mortality event involving more than 300 adult common carp occurred in a recreational lake in north-eastern Italy, where affected fish showed sleepy behaviour, gill lesions and died over several days at water temperatures around 15 °C; virological testing identified CEV as the likely primary cause. This was one of the first clear demonstrations that CEV can drive significant mortality in free-living wild carp populations in Southern Europe, complementing earlier detections in Italian farmed carp and koi. The findings raised concern that CEV might threaten wild carp stocks as well as aquaculture and informed European risk assessments and surveillance priorities.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33591616/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Prior establishment of CEV in Italian carp aquaculture and ornamental sectors likely led to spillover into wild carp via stocked or escaped fish; environmental conditions in the artificial lake, including temperature near the lower limit of the permissive range and possible eutrophication, may have stressed fish and favored disease expression. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrated ability of CEV to cause high mortality in older, wild carp in open waters suggests either broad baseline virulence or adaptation of existing European genogroup I strains to new ecological contexts; because Southern Europe (Italy) was already affected in culture settings, this wild-fish episode is treated as re_emergence rather than a new intra‑continental emergence.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33591616/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review. The original dataset implied Italian wild carp mortality from about 2017 onward and cited a North American wild-carp paper as a source; this has been corrected to a 2020 event based on the J Fish Dis case report, and the US-focused DAO article has been removed from this row. Classification as re_emergence is appropriate because CEVD had already been present in Italian aquaculture, and this episode reflects a major ecological expansion into wild adult carp.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia abortus
EPP.common.name: Enzootic abortion, EAE, Ovine enzootic abortion
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius) in a large semi‑intensive dairy camel operation
Event.summary: In the 2018–2019 calving seasons a large, semi‑intensive dairy camel farm in northern Saudi Arabia, which had previously recorded ≤2–3% annual abortions, experienced a sudden abortion storm in the last trimester of pregnancy, with 71 of 210 pregnant she‑camels (33.8%) aborting without prominent systemic illness. Field veterinarians implemented enhanced surveillance and submitted sera, placental tissue, amniotic fluid and a preputial wash from a breeding male for laboratory testing; ELISA indicated prior exposure to several abortifacient pathogens, while real‑time PCR performed at a regional reference laboratory detected C. abortus DNA in 6 of 8 sampled aborted females and in one breeding male, and ruled out Toxoplasma gondii, Coxiella burnetii, Brucella spp. and Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis as primary causes, thereby implicating C. abortus as a major contributor to the abortion storm. Following implementation of strict segregation of calving areas, repeated mass doxycycline treatments, removal of the infected male and improved hygiene and disinfection protocols, abortion rates fell back to around 4% in the 2019–2020 season and the episode was considered controlled, although subsequent serologic surveys in the region have confirmed that C. abortus remains an important abortifacient in camels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid growth and intensification of dairy camel production in Saudi Arabia, high stocking densities, shared calving and milking infrastructure, and seasonal movement between grazing and calving units created favourable conditions for efficient transmission, while limited prior abortion investigation meant chlamydial infections in camels were under‑recognised despite earlier serologic evidence in Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries.([researchopenworld.com](https://researchopenworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/IJVB-5-531.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: there is no evidence in this outbreak of a novel genotype, new host jump or antimicrobial resistance; rather, existing C. abortus lineages exploited intensive management conditions to cause high‑level infection and shedding in dromedary camels, leading to a marked but reversible increase in abortion incidence. On this basis the episode is best characterised as a severe re‑occurrence of C. abortus‑associated abortion in an already exposed camel population in Western Asia, not as first detection or host‑expansion re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: review (retain with reclassified emergence type). Changes made: (1) Re‑evaluated the event in light of serologic and uterine‑infection studies demonstrating C. abortus infection in camels in Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries before 2018, which shows that camels were already a recognised host in this region.([researchopenworld.com](https://researchopenworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/IJVB-5-531.pdf)) (2) Set re_occurrence to "Yes" and re_emergence to "No", and left inter_continental_emergence and intra_continental_emergence as "No", because the episode represents an unusually large outbreak in an already infected host population in Western Asia rather than a new host expansion or geographical first. (3) Adjusted the mechanism/driver description to focus on intensive management, high stocking density and gaps in surveillance as key external drivers, and removed the stronger claim of host expansion as an internal mechanism; no novel strain or adaptation specific to camels was documented. The event remains a high‑impact abortion storm (33.8% abortions) and is appropriate to retain among major emergence episodes, but its type has been corrected to align with the project’s definitions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia abortus
EPP.common.name: Enzootic abortion, EAE, Ovine enzootic abortion
Host: Sheep (multiple flocks in Sulaimani province – Kalar, Said Sadiq, Chamchamal)
Event.summary: During the 2017 lambing season, veterinarians in Sulaimani province, northern Iraq, reported widespread abortions in several sheep flocks in districts including Kalar, Said Sadiq and Chamchamal. Thirty aborted fetuses from five affected herds were examined; conventional PCR and embryonated‑egg culture identified C. abortus DNA in one fetus from Kalar, while the remaining 29 fetuses were positive for Brucella abortus, indicating a mixed‑etiology abortion problem dominated by brucellosis but with documented C. abortus involvement in at least one herd. Control recommendations focused on strengthening diagnosis and control of both brucellosis and chlamydial abortion (improved lambing hygiene, biosecurity and strategic antibiotic use), and the acute abortion episode subsided, although subsequent surveys have shown that enzootic abortion and other infectious causes remain important contributors to reproductive loss in Iraqi flocks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high small‑ruminant density with limited biosecurity and vaccination coverage, co‑circulation of multiple abortifacient agents (notably Brucella abortus) in the same flocks, and generally weak surveillance and diagnostic capacity at the flock level in northern Iraq, all of which predisposed to recurrent abortion episodes. Internal mechanisms: no novel C. abortus genotype or clear change in pathogen biology was reported; the single C. abortus‑positive fetus isolated in this study clustered phylogenetically with other regional isolates, and the event is best viewed as a re‑occurrence of C. abortus within an endemic Western Asian sub‑region where the pathogen has long been present alongside other abortifacients.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7256821/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review (candidate for exclusion on impact grounds). Rationale: The Sulaimani study clearly documents C. abortus isolation and molecular characterisation from one aborted fetus and provides useful evidence of the pathogen’s presence in Iraqi sheep.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7256821/?utm_source=openai)) However, only 1 of 30 fetuses (3.3%) was C. abortus positive, whereas 29 (96.7%) were positive for Brucella abortus, indicating that the abortion storm in these flocks was overwhelmingly driven by brucellosis rather than by C. abortus. In comparison with numerous large C. abortus‑dominated abortion outbreaks documented in Europe and Asia (e.g. the many flocks in Iran in which C. abortus was the leading diagnosed cause of abortion),([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9684225/?utm_source=openai)) this episode is unlikely to rank among the top ten most impactful C. abortus emergence events globally. The event type (re_occurrence in a long‑endemic Western Asian sub‑region) and geography are appropriate, but given its relatively small direct C. abortus contribution it is recommended that this row be considered for exclusion if the dataset needs to be restricted strictly to the highest‑impact events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia abortus
EPP.common.name: Enzootic abortion of ewes
Host: Yaks (Bos grunniens)
Event.summary: In 2012, a cross‑sectional study of 674 yak sera from six counties in Qinghai Province found a C. abortus seroprevalence of about 17.7%, indicating widespread infection in yak herds on the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau; subsequent work isolated and genetically characterized C. abortus from aborted yak fetuses and tissues in the same region. Together, these studies showed that C. abortus infection was common in yaks and associated with abortion and reproductive losses, establishing yak as a significant livestock host for this pathogen in Eastern Asia. By the mid‑2010s, enzootic abortion due to C. abortus had been recognized as an important constraint on yak productivity in the high‑altitude pastoral systems of Qinghai and neighboring provinces.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and commercialization of yak husbandry on the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau, co‑grazing of yaks with sheep and goats, and limited biosecurity and veterinary infrastructure likely facilitated spillover and maintenance of C. abortus in yak herds, with environmental and nutritional stressors at high altitude exacerbating abortion impacts. Internal mechanisms: The episode reflects host expansion of existing C. abortus lineages into yaks (Host Expansion (Spillover)) and geographic range expansion within Eastern Asia (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)); available genomic work suggests relatively conserved lineages adapted to local ruminant populations rather than a radically novel genotype.
Review: ORIGINAL EVENT, RETAINED WITH TYPE CORRECTION. (1) Classification: first_detection and intra_continental_emergence have been set to false because C. abortus was long established in Chinese and wider Asian sheep and goats before 2012; this episode documents its characterization in a new livestock host rather than first presence in Eastern Asia. Re_emergence remains true to reflect a host‑expansion event within a previously affected sub‑region, consistent with the definition that links re‑emergence to changes in the pathogen such as expanding to a new host. (2) Content: The summary is slightly reframed to emphasize host expansion and systematic investigation in yaks, noting prior evidence of chlamydial abortion in yak herds but limited characterization before these studies. (3) Impact: Because yaks represent millions of animals in the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau and reproductive rates are intrinsically low, this host‑expansion event is considered one of the most consequential emergence episodes for C. abortus. Flag: RETAIN as a major emergence event.
Review.Comment: Accept after correction

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia abortus
EPP.common.name: Enzootic abortion of ewes
Host: Yaks (Bos grunniens)
Event.summary: Between roughly 2018 and 2020, a survey of 938 yak sera from six areas of the Tibet Autonomous Region reported an overall C. abortus seroprevalence of about 11.1%, with infection detected across age groups and locations, providing the first systematic data on C. abortus in Tibetan yak populations. These findings extended earlier Qinghai and Gansu reports to show that C. abortus infection in yaks is widespread across the broader Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau, with endemic transmission rather than isolated spillover. By the time of publication in 2021, C. abortus was recognized as an established reproductive pathogen of yaks in Tibet, reinforcing its importance in high‑altitude pastoral systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional free‑ranging yak production, communal alpine grazing, seasonal transhumance, and limited segregation of pregnant animals likely facilitated regional spread and maintenance of C. abortus following earlier introduction into yak populations, while sparse veterinary infrastructure and lack of routine abortion diagnostics delayed recognition in Tibet. Internal mechanisms: Available data suggest dissemination of previously established yak‑adapted C. abortus strains from neighboring provinces rather than a new genotype; the episode therefore represents regional geographic range expansion and re‑occurrence of C. abortus‑associated abortion within the same Eastern Asia sub‑region (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: ORIGINAL EVENT, RETAINED WITH TYPE CORRECTION. (1) Classification: first_detection and intra_continental_emergence are set to false because C. abortus infection in yaks had already been documented in other Chinese provinces (Qinghai, Gansu) before this survey. The event is now coded as re_occurrence (ongoing endemic transmission and spread within the same Eastern Asia sub‑region) without re_emergence, as no clear host switch or novel genotype was reported. (2) Event year and countries: Years left as 2018–2020, matching the approximate sampling period underlying the 2021 publication; countries field simplified to Tibet Autonomous Region with bracketed year. (3) Impact: This event is important mainly as consolidation and geographic extension of the earlier yak emergence on the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau, rather than a distinct, higher‑impact wave. Flag: RETAIN but marked for REVIEW when prioritizing a strict top‑10 list, as it could be merged with the Qinghai yak event into a single plateau‑wide emergence episode depending on desired granularity.
Review.Comment: Accept after correction

EPP.scientific.name: Chrysomya bezziana
EPP.common.name: Old world screwworm myiasis
Host: Sheep; goats; cattle; camels; dogs; donkeys; humans (sporadic)
Event.summary: The event originated when Old World screwworm was first officially reported from Yemen in late 2007, after sudden incursions into Sa’dah Governorate near the Saudi border, most likely introduced via movement of infested livestock from neighboring endemic areas into susceptible small‑ruminant and camel herds in Yemen’s north‑western lowlands. During 2008, a severe outbreak of traumatic myiasis developed in sheep, goats, cattle, camels, dogs and other animals across several coastal and adjacent inland governorates, with thousands of cases reported and major concern about southward and highland spread and potential spillover into wildlife and humans; by 2009, further outbreaks were reported from central governorates such as Taiz, Ibb and Dhamar. Coordinated surveillance and control activities under regional AOAD/FAO/IAEA programs, including wound treatment campaigns, larvicide supply, awareness efforts and movement management, reduced reported case numbers after 2008–2009, although C. bezziana likely remained established and Yemen has since been considered at continued risk of screwworm re‑incursion and renewed outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movements of small ruminants and camels from endemic neighboring countries, limited veterinary and surveillance infrastructure, and high livestock densities in climatically suitable coastal and lowland areas fostered establishment once the fly arrived; extensive pastoral systems, frequent untreated wounds (including around docking, branding and other procedures), and delayed treatment amplified local transmission. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak represents geographic range expansion and resurgence of existing Middle Eastern C. bezziana lineages into a previously less‑affected country within the same Western Asia subregion, exploiting the species’ inherent capacity for dispersal and high reproductive output, rather than emerging from a newly evolved strain or a shift in host range; enhanced transmission in dense small‑ruminant populations and along trade pathways was the key biological driver.
Review: retain – Yemen’s 2007–2009 wave is one of the best‑documented large OWSW emergence episodes after 2000, with thousands of animal cases and strong regional concern. Consistent with project rules, it is not coded as intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence because Western Asia already harboured C. bezziana in other Gulf countries; instead, the emergence type has been changed from re_emergence to re_occurrence, reflecting reappearance and dramatic increase within an already affected subregion driven largely by external factors (animal movements, service disruption, climate). Event years and host range are well supported by FAO/IAEA reports and later reviews, but detailed governorate‑level burden estimates remain uncertain and could be refined from national Yemeni data if available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chrysomya bezziana
EPP.common.name: Old world screwworm myiasis
Host: Cattle; sheep; goats; donkeys; dogs; cats; other domestic livestock; wild mammals (various wildlife species reported locally)
Event.summary: The event began during the 2023 rainy season when veterinarians and livestock keepers in several regions of Senegal started reporting unusually aggressive traumatic myiasis in small ruminants, cattle, equids and companion animals, with larvae later confirmed by the national veterinary laboratory and an FAO/IAEA mission as Old World screwworm (Chrysomya bezziana). Between July 2023 and January 2024, the infestation spread across at least five departments, including coastal and inland areas such as Dakar–Thiès–Fatick and parts of Tambacounda and Ziguinchor regions, where field investigations documented about 1,900 confirmed screwworm myiasis cases and many additional farmer‑reported cases, leading to deaths, culling and marked loss of productivity in affected herds. Following emergency support from FAO, WOAH and national services—focused on larvicide treatment of wounds, farmer and veterinarian awareness campaigns, and enhanced surveillance—the wave of cases subsided with the end of the rainy season in early 2024, but authorities highlighted that pupae surviving in the soil, continued animal movements and climatic suitability mean that further outbreaks during future rainy seasons in Senegal and neighboring West African countries remain a significant risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A wet 2023 rainy season, high densities of small ruminants and other livestock, frequent untreated or poorly treated wounds (including around tail docking, castration and traditional husbandry practices), and limited prior awareness of screwworm facilitated rapid amplification once C. bezziana was introduced or re‑introduced into Senegal; animal movements within West Africa and across ecological zones likely aided spread among departments. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak reflects the establishment and resurgence of an already widely distributed African C. bezziana lineage in a country that had not reported the parasite for decades, exploiting its inherent high fecundity, broad host range and capacity to complete multiple generations over a rainy season; there is currently no evidence of a novel strain, resistance, or major shift in host range, so the episode is interpreted as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: review – New event added because FAO and WOAH report that Senegal experienced its first confirmed large outbreak of Old World screwworm between July 2023 and January 2024, with roughly 1,900 recorded cases in five departments and thousands of animals affected during the 2023 rainy season, making this one of the most significant recent emergence events in Africa. Consistent with the project definitions and historical records of C. bezziana in other West African countries, this episode is classified as re_occurrence within the Western Africa subregion rather than intra‑continental emergence or first detection, and there is currently no evidence of a distinct strain or host‑range shift that would justify re_emergence coding. As the situation is relatively recent and surveillance is still being strengthened, case numbers, host range and any subsequent spread to neighboring countries should be revisited when more detailed WAHIS and national data become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Classical swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: Hog cholera virus, CSFV
Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar (Sus scrofa)
Event.summary: After CSF had been close to eradication in much of the EU, Germany experienced a prolonged resurgence beginning in the early 1990s, with 424 outbreaks in domestic pigs and widespread infection in wild boar recorded between 1990 and 1998. Intensive control measures, including culling and movement restrictions, were implemented as CSF became endemic in wild boar in several regions, repeatedly seeding infections into pig farms. By 1998, the last outbreak in domestic pigs was eliminated and Germany regained CSF‑free status for domestic herds, although infected wild boar remained a concern for some time.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: High pig density and extensive trade/movements of pigs and pig products within Germany and neighboring EU states; hunting and feeding practices that facilitated contact between wild boar and domestic pigs; difficulties in biosecurity implementation at small farms. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission via establishment and maintenance of CSFV in wild boar populations, which acted as a wildlife reservoir repeatedly infecting domestic herds rather than a clearly novel viral genotype.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within wildlife reservoirs.
Review: retain – major 1990s German CSF epizootic with >400 domestic-pig outbreaks and a large wild boar reservoir; geography, timing and impact are consistent with primary sources. Event correctly coded as a re-occurrence in Western Europe without intra- or inter-continental spread; no structural changes made.

EPP.scientific.name: Classical swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: Hog cholera virus, CSFV
Host: Domestic pigs; free‑ranging pigs; wild boar
Event.summary: After earlier control successes, Italy continued to report CSF outbreaks in domestic pigs and wild boar through the mid‑ to late‑1990s, with notable activity from about 1995 in mainland regions and in Sardinia. Molecular typing of isolates from outbreaks between 1985 and 2000 showed at least two separate introductions affecting both domestic pigs and wild boar, indicating sustained circulation and repeated spillover. By late 1999, Italy declared itself free from CSF in domestic pigs except on Sardinia, where endemic infection persisted in free‑ranging pigs and wild boar, necessitating ongoing control programs into the 2000s.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Extensive smallholder and free‑ranging pig husbandry in mountainous and forested areas; close contact between domestic pigs and wild boar; challenges enforcing biosecurity and movement controls; mixed infections with other pig diseases complicating surveillance. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicated multiple CSFV lineages but not a single novel hypervirulent genotype; persistence was instead linked to maintenance in wildlife and traditional production systems.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (maintenance in wild boar and free‑ranging pigs); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within island and mountainous habitats.
Review: retain – Italy (including Sardinia) experienced recurrent CSF with substantial involvement of wild boar and free-ranging pigs in the 1990s, forming part of the core Western European problem recognised by WOAH. Countries field has been simplified to 'Italy [1995]' (Sardinia now specified in the narrative), but geography, timing and classification as re-occurrence in Southern Europe remain appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Classical swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: Hog cholera virus, CSFV
Host: Domestic pigs
Event.summary: In February 1997, classical swine fever was detected in a mixed sow and finishing herd in the pig‑dense regions of the Netherlands, triggering one of the largest modern CSF epizootics. The virus spread through intensive pig production areas, ultimately infecting 429 herds and leading to culling of several million pigs, including more than 1.1 million pre‑emptively slaughtered in 1,286 herds at risk. By 1998, strict stamping‑out, movement controls, and pre‑emptive slaughter brought the epidemic to an end and the country regained CSF‑free status, though at enormous economic and social cost to the pig industry.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Very high pig and herd density, frequent animal movements, and complex trade networks within and beyond the Netherlands; late detection in a densely connected production system; policy of non‑vaccination which required extensive culling once virus was established. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by CSFV subgenotype 2.1a, but there is no strong evidence that intrinsic increases in virulence drove spread; rather, management and network factors dominated.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (via dense production and movement networks).
Review: retain – Netherlands 1997–1998 epidemic is correctly characterised as one of the largest CSF outbreaks ever recorded, with ≈429 infected herds and millions of pigs culled; geography and timing match EU and WOAH reports. Coding as a major re-occurrence in Western Europe without inter-continental spread is appropriate and sources are highly relevant.

EPP.scientific.name: Classical swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: Hog cholera virus, CSFV
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2000]
Host: Domestic pigs
Event.summary: In August 2000, the United Kingdom detected classical swine fever in a pig farm in Suffolk, East Anglia, the first confirmed outbreak since national eradication in 1966. The disease spread to a total of 16 farms in the high‑density pig region of East Anglia, leading to the culling of about 75,000 pigs and substantial trade disruption. Through rapid stamping‑out, movement controls, and zoning, the outbreak was contained and officially ended by early 2001, allowing the UK to maintain its overall CSF‑free status.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Reintroduction most likely via movement of infected pigs or contaminated pork products into a previously CSF‑free, high‑density pig production area; high farm connectivity and animal movements facilitated early spread; absence of vaccination meant all control relied on culling and movement bans. Internal mechanisms: No major new genotype or virulence change was identified; the event is best explained by reintroduction and production‑network drivers.
Internal mechanisms coded: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (through dense farm network, not virological change).
Review: retain – UK 2000 East Anglia outbreak is correctly described as a nationally important re-occurrence with 16 infected farms and ~75,000 pigs culled, causing major trade impacts. Geography (Northern Europe/UK) and event-type coding as re-occurrence only are appropriate; no structural corrections were needed.
Country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

EPP.scientific.name: Classical swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: Hog cholera virus, CSFV
Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar (Sus scrofa)
Event.summary: Japan, which had reported no CSF outbreaks since 1992, confirmed re‑emergence of the disease in September 2018 at a pig farm in Gifu Prefecture, central Honshu, after pigs began dying in August. Genetic analysis showed the virus belonged to subgenotype 2.1 and differed from strains causing earlier Japanese outbreaks, and the infection rapidly spread to numerous pig farms and wild boar populations in Gifu and neighboring prefectures, with nearly 900 notifications in domestic pigs and wild boar by August 2019. Through extensive culling, movement controls, vaccination of wild boar, and eventually vaccination of domestic pigs in affected prefectures, Japan progressively brought the epidemic under control, though control and eradication efforts continued beyond 2021.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Dense pig production in central Japan, frequent movements of pigs and vehicles among farms, and contact between farm environments and abundant wild boar populations; probable introduction of CSFV via contaminated live pigs or pig products from endemic regions; delay in recognition due to long absence of CSF. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of a novel CSFV subgenotype 2.1 lineage distinct from historic Japanese strains, with efficient transmission in both domestic pigs and wild boar and genetic evidence of ongoing evolution; maintenance in wild boar created a persistent wildlife reservoir.
Internal mechanisms coded: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion (Spillover and maintenance in wild boar reservoir); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of 2.1 lineage into previously free Japan.
Review: retain – the 2018–2021 Japanese CSF epidemic, with re-introduction of genotype 2.1 after 26 years of freedom and hundreds of notifications in pigs and wild boar, is clearly one of the major modern CSF emergence events. Geography, timing, host range and classification as re-emergence are appropriate, and the source set is strong and outbreak-specific.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: CCHFV
Host: Humans (slaughterhouse and animal-market workers, animal skin processors), dromedary camels, imported cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event.summary: In 1994, a cluster of severe hemorrhagic fever cases occurred among abattoir workers and livestock traders in the United Arab Emirates, leading to investigation of a suspected viral hemorrhagic fever outbreak. Over 1994–1995, more than a dozen human cases with high case-fatality were confirmed as Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever and linked epidemiologically to slaughtering or handling imported livestock infected with CCHFV. Intensified infection-prevention measures in slaughterhouses and better control of animal imports and ticks curtailed the outbreak, after which only sporadic cases were reported in the country.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large-scale importation of cattle, sheep and goats from CCHF-endemic countries in Asia and Africa for slaughter, combined with inadequate tick control and poor abattoir biosafety, created intense exposure of workers to infected animal blood and Hyalomma ticks; earlier nosocomial transmission in Dubai in 1979 shows the virus was already present but under-recognized in the country. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate circulation of existing CCHFV lineages rather than a novel strain, and the event is best explained by amplification of endemic virus in livestock under high-intensity trade and slaughter conditions, increasing spillover risk to humans.
Review: Decision: retain (with reclassification). CCHF was first reported in the UAE in a nosocomial outbreak in Dubai in 1979, so the 1994–1995 abattoir-associated episode cannot be coded as first_detection; first_detection has been set to false and re_occurrence to true while keeping other emergence-type flags as no. The year range, country (United Arab Emirates), subregion (Western Asia) and occupational focus are well supported by outbreak investigations, and the sources are appropriate, but this event should be flagged as borderline if a very strict top‑10-by-impact filter is later enforced because of its moderate case numbers.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: CCHFV
Host: Humans (ostrich abattoir workers), ostriches, cattle, Hyalomma ticks
Event.summary: In October 1996, an outbreak of acute hemorrhagic fever occurred among workers at an ostrich abattoir in Oudtshoorn, Western Cape Province, South Africa, where CCHFV was already known to circulate in livestock and ticks. Seventeen abattoir workers developed compatible illness, with at least one death, and investigations linked infection to handling viremic ostriches and possibly crushing infected Hyalomma ticks during slaughter and processing. Control measures including temporary closure of slaughter operations, improved personal protective equipment, and stricter tick control on ostriches and other livestock ended the outbreak, and subsequent years saw only sporadic occupational cases in South Africa.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of commercial ostrich farming and export in the Klein Karoo increased human contact with ticks and blood from CCHFV-infected birds and other livestock; limited awareness and insufficient protective measures in abattoirs heightened risk. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak reflects amplification of an established South African CCHFV lineage in ostriches and ticks rather than a novel strain, with occupational exposure and high tick burdens driving re-occurrence in a known endemic focus.
Review: Decision: review (borderline for top‑10). This row accurately represents the 1996 ostrich-abattoir outbreak in Oudtshoorn, including timing, location (South Africa, Southern Africa subregion), host range and classification as re_occurrence in an already endemic country, and the cited WHO and South African sources are appropriate. However, with 17 human cases it is smaller than several later multi‑province outbreaks (e.g. Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, Iraq, Mauritania), so it may fall below the ten most impactful global events, although it remains epidemiologically important for the animal host system and ostrich industry.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: CCHFV
Host: Humans (rural residents, healthcare workers, slaughterhouse workers), cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event.summary: In June 1999, clusters of severe hemorrhagic fever were recognized in Sistan and Baluchestan Province in southeastern Iran, triggering investigations that confirmed Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in an area where sporadic human and animal infections had been reported since the 1970s but no large outbreak had been documented. Between 1999 and the early 2000s, hundreds of suspected and confirmed cases, including nosocomial clusters and infections among butchers and animal handlers across several provinces, were reported, making this the first major nationally recognized CCHF epidemic in Iran. Expanded surveillance, public health education, hospital infection-control measures and veterinary tick control gradually reduced incidence after the early 2000s, though the virus remained endemic with recurring human and animal infections in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-standing but under-recognized circulation of CCHFV in livestock and ticks, increased animal movement across the Iran–Pakistan–Afghanistan borders, and poor infection control in rural hospitals led to spillover and nosocomial amplification; enhanced laboratory capacity and surveillance converted previously cryptic transmission into a documented epidemic. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies place Iranian strains mainly within the Asia-1 lineage and do not indicate a major novel variant driving the surge; the episode is best interpreted as a large re-occurrence in an endemic system fueled primarily by external drivers rather than substantial viral change.
Review: Decision: retain (with corrections). National and provincial data show sporadic CCHF infections in humans and livestock in Iran from the 1970s onward, with 1999 marking the first large, multi-province outbreak rather than the first detection; accordingly, first_detection has been set to false and re_occurrence to true, and the narrative has been revised to remove the claim that only ticks and livestock were previously infected. The country, subregion (Southern Asia), time window (1999–2004), scale (hundreds of cases) and external drivers are consistent with primary Iranian and regional sources, justifying inclusion as one of the most impactful CCHF episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: CCHFV
Host: Humans (rural residents, agricultural workers), cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event.summary: In 1999, an outbreak of severe febrile illness with hemorrhagic manifestations occurred in Stavropol Territory in southern European Russia, resulting in about 65 CCHF cases and 6 deaths and representing the first large, laboratory-confirmed CCHF outbreak reported from this region after several decades without recognized disease. During 1999–2000 and subsequent years, additional cases were reported from adjacent regions including Rostov, Astrakhan, Volgograd and Kalmykia, indicating establishment of new endemic foci in southern Russia. Intensified tick-control campaigns in livestock, public education and better surveillance mitigated case numbers over time, though hundreds of cases continued to occur sporadically in 1999–2020.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Agricultural development, increased livestock grazing and human encroachment into steppe and semi-desert habitats favored Hyalomma tick expansion and human exposure; cross-border livestock movements from neighboring endemic areas likely introduced CCHFV into new Russian territories. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses show Russian strains grouped within the Europe 1 lineage, indicating geographic range expansion of known genotypes into new ecological zones rather than the emergence of a novel lineage.
Review: Decision: retain (with corrections). Because CCHF was recognized in Crimea and other parts of the former Soviet Union long before 1999, the Stavropol outbreak cannot be considered first_detection; I set first_detection to false and re_occurrence to true, and removed re_emergence, while keeping the emphasis on renewed activity after a prolonged lull in this territory. The year span (1999–2000), location in southern European Russia (Eastern Europe subregion), and approximate magnitude are in line with WHO outbreak reports and Russian surveillance data, supporting its inclusion as a major re-activation and geographic expansion event.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: CCHFV
Host: Humans (rural residents, family contacts, healthcare workers), cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event.summary: In spring and summer 2001, Kosovo (then part of Yugoslavia/Serbia) experienced a notable outbreak of CCHF, with 69 suspected cases, 18 confirmed or clinically compatible infections, and 6 deaths concentrated in rural areas. The outbreak originated in villages where residents had close contact with livestock and ticks, and spread included nosocomial and household transmission among caregivers and health staff. Enhanced surveillance, barrier nursing and public education on tick avoidance and safe handling of livestock and patients ended the outbreak by late summer, although sporadic cases and smaller clusters continued to occur in later years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High Hyalomma tick densities in pastoral areas, close contact with cattle and small ruminants, and limited infection-control practices in local hospitals allowed virus maintained in livestock and ticks to spill over repeatedly and spread within households and healthcare facilities. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analysis of Kosovo strains indicated continuity with long-established Balkan CCHFV lineages, and the event is best interpreted as a large resurgence in a known endemic focus rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: Decision: retain (with minor source cleanup). This row correctly captures the size, timing and setting of the 2001 Kosovo outbreak and appropriately classifies it as re_occurrence without intra- or inter-continental emergence in a long-recognized Balkan focus. I recommend replacing the earlier Italian-language Wikipedia citation with primary descriptions from Emerging Infectious Diseases and related reviews, as done here, but otherwise the event is well supported and merits inclusion as one of the more substantial European CCHF episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
EPP.common.name: CCHFV
Host: Humans (farmers, animal handlers, healthcare workers), cattle, sheep, goats, Hyalomma ticks
Event.summary: Beginning in 2002, Türkiye detected its first recognized CCHF cases in the Kelkit Valley region of north-central Anatolia, initially as sporadic severe febrile illnesses among rural residents and animal handlers, with virologic confirmation in 2003. Over 2002–2008, a rapidly expanding epidemic produced more than 1,800 confirmed cases by 2007 and over 3,000 by 2008, with a case-fatality rate around 5%, and the virus became endemic across multiple provinces, with most cases occurring in spring and summer among persons exposed to ticks or livestock. Following the establishment of a national surveillance system, clinical guidelines and public health campaigns emphasizing tick avoidance and safe animal handling, incidence stabilized at lower but persistent levels, making Türkiye one of the world’s major CCHF foci.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of livestock grazing in tick-infested hilly regions, increased human interaction with Hyalomma-infested cattle and small ruminants, and limited early awareness of CCHF in the medical community facilitated rapid amplification of infection; occupational exposures among farmers and healthcare workers further propagated the epidemic. Internal mechanisms: Turkish CCHFV strains belong to the Europe-1 lineage, closely related to Balkan viruses, consistent with geographic range expansion and establishment of a large endemic focus; seroprevalence and molecular data suggest long-standing but previously under-recognized circulation that intensified under changing land-use and climate conditions, so this episode is best viewed as the first detected national epidemic driven mainly by eco-epidemiologic change rather than a novel viral genotype.
Review: Decision: retain (with corrections).
