EPP.common.name: EHP
Host: Penaeus (Litopenaeus) vannamei (Pacific whiteleg shrimp) and, later, giant freshwater prawn cultured in Korea
Event.summary: In April 2020, indoor shrimp farms in the Republic of Korea culturing Pacific whiteleg shrimp with growth disorders were confirmed to harbor EHP, representing the first detection of the parasite in Korean aquaculture and extending its known range within the Eastern Asia subregion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8614486/?utm_source=openai)) Follow‑up investigations detected EHP in additional P. vannamei farms and, by 2022, in farmed giant freshwater prawn (Macrobrachium rosenbergii), indicating host expansion beyond marine penaeids.([kci.go.kr](https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/landing/article.kci?arti_id=ART003091386&utm_source=openai)) Phylogenetic analyses showed that Korean EHP isolates formed a distinct clade relative to previously reported strains from Thailand, Viet Nam, China and India, and although overall prevalence remained lower than in heavily affected South‑eastern Asian countries, Korean authorities classified EHP as an emerging disease requiring routine monitoring, biosecurity and quarantine measures to prevent wider establishment.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8614486/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increasing diversification and intensification of shrimp and prawn aquaculture in Korea, together with trade in live shrimp and possibly broodstock or postlarvae from EHP‑endemic regions, likely facilitated introduction of the parasite into indoor and recirculating systems; once present, closed‑system conditions allowed persistent infection but limited wider environmental spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8614486/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: emergence of phylogenetically distinct Korean EHP lineages and confirmed host expansion to giant freshwater prawn are consistent with re‑emergence driven by parasite adaptation, while efficient horizontal transmission within culture systems sustains localized outbreaks and chronic growth disorders.
Review: review – Corrected the event‑type coding: this Korean episode is not a global 'first detection' of EHP, so 'first_detection' was set to 'No'; 're_occurrence' was also set to 'No' because the salient feature is emergence of distinct local lineages and host expansion rather than simple resurgence driven by external factors. 'Re_emergence' is retained as 'Yes' to reflect host expansion to Macrobrachium rosenbergii and the distinct Korean clade reported by phylogenetic analyses. Country, year of first detection (2020), and Eastern Asia sub‑region coding remain consistent with the primary reports but should be double‑checked by an expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus suid 1
EPP.common.name: Swine vesicular disease virus, SVDV
Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event.summary: After the 1992–1995 European resurgence, SVDV remained endemic mainly in central and southern Italy, with sporadic but persistent outbreaks in commercial and backyard pig farms. During 1996–2005, repeated re‑introductions via pig movements and environmental persistence on farms produced a background of low‑level cases that triggered EU safeguard measures and led to the implementation and later strengthening of the Italian national surveillance and eradication programme. These outbreaks gradually declined in number toward the mid‑2000s but the virus was not eliminated, setting the stage for a large epidemic in northern Italy in 2006–2007.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: dense pig production in parts of Italy, frequent movement of pigs and pig transport vehicles, and inadequate cleansing/disinfection of vehicles and premises allowed virus persistence and re‑seeding between herds; non‑compliance in some smallholder and informal production systems hindered eradication. Internal mechanisms: persistence of established Italian lineages with strong environmental stability and long survival in pork products supported ongoing low‑level transmission, but there is no strong evidence that novel, more virulent genotypes drove this phase (primary mechanism: external drivers and environmental persistence rather than major viral change).
Review: retain – Evidence from WOAH/OIE documentation, Italian surveillance data and genomic studies shows that after the early‑1990s European wave, SVDV persisted endemically in central and southern Italy with recurrent low‑level outbreaks through the late 1990s and early 2000s. The chosen time window, country coverage (Italy only) and classification as re-occurrence driven mainly by movement, biosecurity and environmental persistence are consistent with published information, so no structural changes were made.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus suid 1
EPP.common.name: Swine vesicular disease virus, SVDV
Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, SVDV reappeared in the Iberian Peninsula via Portugal, which reported outbreaks in 2003 and 2004 and a further incident in 2007 in pig‑dense regions with active trade links to Italy. Genetic analyses showed that the Portuguese viruses were closely related to contemporary Italian strains, indicating re‑introduction from the long‑standing Italian reservoir rather than the emergence of an independent endemic focus. Through intensified stamping‑out, movement restrictions and targeted serological surveillance, Portugal eliminated SVDV again by the late 2000s, and no further outbreaks have since been reported there.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: cross‑border trade and movement of live pigs and possibly contaminated pork products from infected Italian regions into Portugal, combined with gaps in farm and transport biosecurity and delays in detecting mild vesicular signs, facilitated re‑introduction into Portuguese pig herds and created risks for neighboring Iberian production. Internal mechanisms: the Portuguese viruses belonged to the same European lineage circulating in Italy and do not represent a fundamentally new genotype; the episode is therefore best explained by animal movements and environmental stability of the virus rather than major viral innovation (Re-occurrence driven by trade and environmental persistence).
Review: review – Restricted this episode to Portugal only and removed Spain from the country list and narrative, because WOAH/OIE summaries and later reviews indicate that Spain’s last SVD outbreaks occurred in 1993 and that only Portugal (2003–2004 and 2007) and Italy reported SVD in the 2000s. Updated the event summary and drivers accordingly while retaining the classification as re-occurrence driven by re-introduction from the Italian reservoir via trade.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus suid 1
EPP.common.name: Swine vesicular disease virus, SVDV
Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event.summary: In mid‑2006, a new recombinant SVDV lineage within the long‑circulating European fourth antigenic variant was introduced into northern Italy, probably entering high‑density pig‑producing areas in Lombardy (e.g. Brescia) and remaining undetected for some weeks before the first case was recognized at slaughter in Bergamo. Between 2006 and 2007 this epidemic led to roughly 140 notified outbreaks and the slaughter of more than 150,000 pigs, with spread largely driven by movements of infected animals and contaminated transport vehicles between commercial farms, dealers’ premises and slaughterhouses. Intensive epidemiological tracing, strengthened farm and transport biosecurity, regionalization and stamping‑out measures ultimately contained the epidemic by the end of 2007, although related viruses continued to circulate at lower levels in parts of southern Italy.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction of infected pigs or contaminated transport into intensive pig systems in northern Italy, combined with very high herd density, extensive within‑country pig movements and incomplete cleansing and disinfection of vehicles and premises, allowed rapid farm‑to‑farm spread before controls were tightened; traders’ premises and long‑distance movements played a key role. Internal mechanisms: whole‑genome sequencing shows that the 2006–2007 epidemic was driven by a distinct recombinant lineage within the established European variant, closely related to viruses detected earlier in Portugal and southern Italy, with evidence of recombination and adaptive evolution that may have facilitated its successful spread (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Geographic range expansion within Italy; Enhanced transmission in intensive pig production systems).
Review: review – Restricted the country list for this event to Italy, because WOAH/OIE and genomic analyses treat the 2006–2007 epidemic as an Italian outbreak genetically related to but not epidemiologically continuous with earlier Portuguese cases; Portugal is instead covered in a separate 2003–2007 re-occurrence event. Updated outbreak numbers to align with OIE reports (approximately 140 outbreaks and >150,000 pigs culled) and clarified that this wave represents re-emergence driven by a recombinant lineage within the European variant.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: EHDV
Host: Beef and dairy cattle (Bos taurus)
Event.summary: In late summer 1997, a large epidemic of Ibaraki disease occurred in western Japan when cattle developed fever, salivation, dysphagia and bluetongue‑like oral lesions, and EHDV belonging to a strain later reclassified as serotype 7 was isolated from sick animals and aborted fetuses.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC85817/?utm_source=openai)) Over the 1997–1998 season the virus spread across southern and western Japan, causing widespread clinical disease and more than 1,000 reported abortions and stillbirths in infected pregnant cows, making it one of the most severe EHD‑associated cattle outbreaks recorded.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/epizootic_hemorrhagic_disease.pdf)) The epidemic waned with the end of the vector season and implementation of vaccination against Ibaraki disease, but established EHDV‑associated Ibaraki‑like disease as a major recurring arboviral threat to Japanese cattle.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: warm, humid late‑summer conditions in western and southern Japan favoring Culicoides midges; dense dairy and beef cattle populations with limited prior immunity; movement of animals between affected prefectures. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence—an EHDV lineage now attributed to serotype 7 caused classical Ibaraki disease signs and extensive reproductive losses; host adaptation and increased virulence for cattle compared with earlier Ibaraki virus outbreaks; potential reassortment within the EHDV serogroup.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/epizootic_hemorrhagic_disease.pdf))
Review: Decision: retain (added). Rationale: Major 1997–1998 Ibaraki disease epidemic in Japanese cattle is well documented, caused by an EHDV strain now attributed to serotype 7, and resulted in widespread clinical disease and >1,000 abortions/stillbirths, clearly placing it among the 10 most impactful EHDV emergence events since 1990.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/epizootic_hemorrhagic_disease.pdf)) Classification set to re-emergence (new pathogenic EHDV lineage in a previously affected subregion) with other emergence-type flags left false to align with provided definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: EHDV
Host: Wild white‑tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) and other wild ruminants
Event.summary: In mid‑August to late September 1999, a large epizootic of hemorrhagic disease due to EHDV‑1 occurred along the eastern United States from Georgia to New Jersey, affecting white‑tailed deer across over 100 counties in at least 10 states and causing thousands of deer deaths.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17092892/?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak developed rapidly over late summer with widespread deer mortality and characteristic hemorrhagic lesions, making it the largest documented EHD outbreak in U.S. deer since the 1970s.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17092892/?utm_source=openai)) The epizootic waned as vector activity declined in autumn, but highlighted the potential for large‑scale, climate‑linked recurrence of EHD in North American cervids.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: warm late‑summer conditions and abundant Culicoides vectors in the eastern U.S.; high densities of susceptible white‑tailed deer across multiple states; landscape changes and agricultural water sources favoring midge breeding. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel genotype implicated; this represents a major cyclical re‑occurrence of endemic EHDV‑1 with high transmission intensity rather than a new strain.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17092892/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: 1999 eastern U.S. HD epizootic is well documented as one of the largest modern EHD outbreaks in wild deer, with broad geographic extent and high mortality. Geography (United States, Northern America) and classification as re-occurrence without intra/inter-continental or first-detection flags are consistent with definitions and literature.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17092892/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: EHDV
Host: Dairy cattle (Holstein and other breeds)
Event.summary: In late September 2006, Israel recorded a severe orbiviral outbreak in dairy cattle characterized by fever, oral ulcers, lameness, reduced milk yield and high morbidity; virological investigation identified EHDV‑7 as the causative agent, representing the first confirmed EHD outbreak in Israeli cattle.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article)) Over the summer and autumn, the outbreak spread through multiple dairy farms with substantial production losses, making it one of the first and most severe cattle‑dominated EHD events globally.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article)) The epidemic declined with the onset of cooler weather and reduced vector activity, but EHDV‑7 became established in the region and contributed to subsequent EHDV diversity in Israel.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10885110/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction of EHDV‑7 into densely managed Israeli dairy cattle populations, probably via movement of infected animals or wind‑borne midges from neighboring endemic areas; climatic suitability for Culicoides vectors in summer–autumn; high herd densities favoring local spread. Internal mechanisms: novel strain/host adaptation—EHDV‑7 closely related to Australian strains but showing reassortment with African/Middle Eastern segments and associated with unusually severe clinical disease and milk loss in cattle; enhanced transmission via competent local Culicoides spp.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Set first_detection from true to false, because EHDV had been described in the livestock/wildlife host system long before 2006; this event is the first detection in Israel but not in the host system globally.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false, as EHDV was already present in other Western Asia countries (e.g. Oman) before 2006, and spread to a new country within the same subregion does not meet the definition of intra‑continental emergence.([fr.wikipedia.org](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maladie_h%C3%A9morragique_%C3%A9pizootique?utm_source=openai)) (iii) Kept re_emergence=true to reflect emergence of a new, clinically important EHDV‑7 lineage in a subregion where EHDV was already known.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: EHDV
Host: Cattle
Event.summary: In July 2007, a 7‑week outbreak of bluetongue‑like disease began in cattle in Muğla Province in western Türkiye, with affected animals showing fever, stomatitis, facial edema, lameness, udder erythema and reduced milk yield; laboratory testing confirmed infection with EHDV‑6 closely related to North African strain 318.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article)) Similar clinical cases were soon reported from neighboring provinces including İzmir, Çanakkale and İstanbul, confirming that the North African EHDV‑6 lineage had spread into Western Asia and could cause clinically apparent disease in Turkish cattle.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article)) The outbreak subsided toward the end of August 2007 as temperatures cooled and Culicoides activity decreased, but established EHDV‑6 as part of the regional orbivirus fauna.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: spread of EHDV‑6 strain 318 from North Africa across the eastern Mediterranean, likely via wind‑borne Culicoides and/or movement of infected ruminants; suitable summer climate and vector habitat in western Türkiye; limited pre‑existing immunity in local cattle. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of a fit EHDV‑6 epidemic lineage with demonstrated pathogenicity in cattle; potential enhanced fitness in local Culicoides populations enabling establishment in Western Asia.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Restricted this row to the 2007 cattle outbreak in Türkiye only and removed Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia from the countries field to avoid double‑counting the 2006 Maghreb epizootic already captured in the 2004–2006 event. (ii) Updated continent and subregion to Asia/Western Asia only, which matches the territorial classification for Türkiye. (iii) Set first_detection=false because EHDV was long known in the host system, and inter- and intra‑continental emergence are not appropriate (EHDV was already present in Asia); retained re_emergence=true to reflect expansion of the EHDV‑6 Maghreb lineage into an already affected subregion with a changed strain profile.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/2/08-0572_article))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: EHDV
Host: Wild white‑tailed deer; captive cervids; cattle and other domestic ruminants (limited clinical disease)
Event.summary: In 2007, the United States experienced one of its most extensive orbivirus years, with widespread hemorrhagic disease in white‑tailed deer across eastern and midwestern states and concurrent bluetongue activity, involving EHDV‑2 and detecting EHDV‑6 for the first time in U.S. deer.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai)) Deer mortality was reported from many counties in at least 11 states, with both wild and captive cervid herds affected and sporadic disease in domestic ruminants.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai)) The epizootic declined in late autumn as midge activity fell, but contributed to recognition of a trend toward more frequent and severe EHDV years in North America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: favorable warm, dry late‑summer conditions promoting Culicoides abundance; high deer densities and anthropogenic water sources creating vector habitat; cyclical build‑up of susceptible deer cohorts following lower‑impact years. Internal mechanisms: detection of exotic‑derived EHDV‑6 in North American deer alongside endemic serotypes, but 2007 is best characterized as a major re‑occurrence of multi‑serotype EHDV activity rather than a single novel genotype event.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: 2007 is recognized in surveillance summaries and USAHA reports as a major HD year with extensive deer mortality and the first detection of EHDV‑6 in North American cervids, justifying inclusion among high‑impact events.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai)) Event geography and classification as re-occurrence (without intra/inter-continental or re-emergence flags) are consistent with definitions and current knowledge.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: EHDV
Host: Wild white‑tailed deer; captive cervids; cattle and bison
Event.summary: During the summer and fall of 2012, an unusually large EHD outbreak occurred across the United States, affecting domestic cattle and bison herds as well as wild and captive white‑tailed deer, and involving multiple serotypes including EHDV‑2 and the emerging EHDV‑6.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526531/?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak produced notable cattle morbidity and death in some herds, with average within‑herd morbidity of about 7% in cattle/bison and 46% in captive deer, and viral detections across roughly 15 states in the Midwest and Southeast.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526531/?utm_source=openai)) Transmission declined with the onset of cooler weather, but molecular epidemiology later showed reassortant viruses containing segments from exotic EHDV‑6 and endemic EHDV‑2, raising concerns about future emergence potential.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526531/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: widespread drought and high late‑summer temperatures in 2012 that favored midge breeding and increased wildlife–livestock congregation at remaining water sources; expansion of captive deer farming and dense cattle herds in affected regions. Internal mechanisms: novel strain/genotype emergence—evidence of reassortant EHDV combining exotic (EHDV‑6) and endemic (EHDV‑2) genome segments in U.S. herds; increased virulence/pathogenicity in cattle compared with earlier North American experience; enhanced transmission efficiency of these reassortants through abundant Culicoides vectors.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526531/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Change made: re_occurrence was set from true to false and re_emergence left true, because the 2012 outbreak is distinguished by emergence of reassortant EHDV-6/EHDV-2 strains with altered host impact rather than solely by external drivers; under the provided definitions, this better fits re-emergence (EPP change in a previously affected subregion) rather than simple re-occurrence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4526531/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: EHDV
Host: Cattle (primary); wild cervids likely exposed
Event.summary: Between September and November 2021, Tunisia experienced a severe outbreak of EHD in cattle caused by EHDV serotype 8, representing the first major circulation of this serotype in North Africa and globally.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9866946/?utm_source=openai)) Affected herds showed fever, anorexia, lameness, oral lesions and production losses, with molecular and phylogenetic analyses confirming a distinct EHDV‑8 lineage circulating in Tunisian cattle and Barbary deer.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10383031/?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak waned with the end of the 2021 vector season, but EHDV‑8 remained established and later served as the source for spread into Algeria, Morocco and ultimately southern Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction and local amplification of a previously undetected EHDV‑8 lineage under favorable climatic conditions and abundant vector populations in coastal and inland Tunisian cattle areas. Internal mechanisms: novel strain/genotype emergence (regional emergence of EHDV‑8 with distinct VP2/VP5 signatures); increased virulence/pathogenicity in cattle relative to earlier regional EHDV‑6 events; geographic range expansion of EHDV‑8 within North Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9866946/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Set first_detection from true to false because EHDV was already long known in ruminants; this episode is the first detection of serotype 8 in North Africa but not the first detection of the EPP in the host system.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/epizootic-hemorrhagic-disease-virus?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false in line with the rule that new serotypes in a region where the organism is already present should be treated as re-emergence rather than intra-continental emergence. (iii) Retained re_emergence=true to capture the appearance of a new, epidemiologically important EHDV‑8 lineage in a previously affected subregion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9866946/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Host: Cattle (beef and dairy herds)
Event.summary: Between January and April 2003, a bluetongue‑like disease outbreak occurred in cattle across much of Réunion Island, with 3,607 animals in affected herds and 235 showing clinical signs including fever, lameness and torpor, and occasional death after a protracted course. Virological investigations identified epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus, primarily serotypes 2 and 6, as the causal agent, representing the first recognized EHD epizootic in cattle on Réunion and the wider south‑west Indian Ocean region. As Culicoides activity declined later in 2003 the outbreak subsided, but subsequent surveys documented continued circulation of EHDV alongside bluetongue virus in the island’s cattle population.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and establishment of EHDV‑2 and EHDV‑6 on Réunion via infected Culicoides midges, probably linked to animal and wind‑borne vector movements from nearby African mainlands, combined with climatic conditions favorable to high midge abundance and widespread exposure of largely naïve cattle. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of EHDV into the south‑west Indian Ocean and emergence of clinically apparent disease in cattle, with serotypes and strains showing sufficient virulence to cause overt illness and mortality in a previously unexposed cattle population.
Review: Retain – newly added major cattle epizootic on Réunion (2003) involving >3,600 cattle and confirmed EHDV infection; classified as intra‑continental emergence into Eastern Africa plus re‑emergence due to expansion of pathogenic serotypes into a new island ecosystem. Sources updated to include the original outbreak description and quantitative data on herd involvement.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds); likely subclinical infection in local wild ruminants
Event.summary: In late summer and autumn 2006, a large‑scale outbreak of bluetongue‑like illness occurred in Israeli dairy and beef cattle herds that had not previously experienced confirmed EHDV disease, with reports from dozens of localities along the Jordan Valley and adjacent regions. Laboratory investigations isolated epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 7 (EHDV‑7) from affected cattle, and epidemiologic analyses documented involvement of more than 80–100 herds with fever, oral lesions, lameness, milk drop and occasional deaths, causing major economic losses. Clinical cases declined after the end of the Culicoides transmission season, but EHDV became established in Israel and was followed in later years by additional outbreaks caused by other serotypes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of EHDV‑7 into Israel, probably via wind‑borne dispersal of infected Culicoides midges or regional animal movements from North Africa or the Arabian Peninsula, in a setting of dense dairy cattle populations and favorable summer climate for vector activity. Internal mechanisms: Geographic expansion of an exotic EHDV‑7 lineage from the Asia–Pacific/African–Middle Eastern region into Western Asia, with high pathogenicity in cattle compared to historically mostly subclinical EHDV infections, representing both intra‑continental emergence into a new UNSD sub‑region and re‑emergence through a novel serotype causing severe disease in cattle.
Review: Review – corrected classification: set inter_continental_emergence to No because EHDV was already present in Asia (e.g. Japan) before 2006, and set intra_continental_emergence to Yes to reflect first incursion into the Western Asia sub‑region. First_detection was changed to No because global first detection of EHDV predates this event. Event remains a major outbreak and should be retained after expert review of the revised coding.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Host: White‑tailed deer and other wild cervids; some farmed/captive deer; sporadic cattle
Event.summary: In 2007, an exceptionally widespread hemorrhagic disease epizootic affected wild white‑tailed deer across large areas of the eastern and Midwestern United States, with wildlife surveillance reporting thousands of cases across many counties and multiple states. Virological investigations documented co‑circulation of multiple EHDV serotypes, including endemic EHDV‑1 and EHDV‑2 and the recently introduced EHDV‑6, making this one of the most extensive orbivirus outbreaks in U.S. deer on record. Case reports declined rapidly after the first hard frosts reduced Culicoides vector populations, but local deer populations in some regions suffered substantial short‑term declines and heightened management concern.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Hot, dry summer conditions in 2007 that concentrated deer around shrinking water sources heavily infested with Culicoides midges, along with high deer densities in agricultural and suburban landscapes and limited prior immunity to EHDV‑6. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven by the simultaneous circulation of multiple EHDV serotypes, including the newly established EHDV‑6, with possible serotype‑specific differences in virulence and transmission contributing to unusually broad geographic spread and high deer mortality.
Review: Retain – this event is well supported as one of the largest documented hemorrhagic disease outbreaks in U.S. deer, with multi‑state spread and high mortality. Geographic coding and classification as re‑occurrence plus re‑emergence (due to the recent introduction of EHDV‑6) are consistent with the project definitions and supporting reports.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Countries: United States of America – especially Illinois and neighboring Midwestern states [2013]
Host: Wild white‑tailed deer; some cattle
Event.summary: Following the large 2012 event, another major hemorrhagic disease year occurred in 2013, particularly in the Midwestern United States. In Illinois, wildlife surveillance recorded over 1,200 reported cases of hemorrhagic disease in wild white‑tailed deer across more than 60 counties, with substantial local mortality and hunter‑observed declines in some herds. Similar but patchier activity was reported in neighboring states. As in other temperate outbreaks, reported cases declined sharply after the first hard frosts reduced Culicoides midge populations and terminated transmission for the season.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued high deer densities, favorable summer conditions for Culicoides vectors in the Midwest, and residual susceptibility in cohorts not heavily exposed in 2012, leading to another year of intense localized transmission. Internal mechanisms: This episode is best characterized as a re‑occurrence of cyclical hemorrhagic disease activity in previously affected sub‑regions, with serotypes similar to earlier years; there is no strong evidence that a novel serotype or significantly altered viral phenotype dominated in 2013.
Review: Retain – this event represents one of the largest documented state‑level hemorrhagic disease epizootics in wild deer (e.g. >1,200 reported cases in Illinois alone) and captures the continued high impact of EHD in Midwestern cervid populations after 2012. Classification as re‑occurrence only (without intra/inter‑continental emergence or first detection) aligns with the project definitions; sources were refined to include quantitative Illinois data.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Host: Beef and dairy cattle
Event.summary: From October 2015 over a three‑month period, a febrile illness affecting cattle was reported in Hyogo Prefecture in western Japan, with 46 animals (40 Japanese Black beef cattle and 6 Holstein dairy heifers) on 38 farms showing fever, anorexia, cessation of rumination, swollen eyelids, oral lesions, difficulty swallowing and, in some cases, abortions. Seven cattle died and two were euthanized because of poor prognosis, making this the most substantial EHD‑like disease event in Japanese cattle since classical Ibaraki disease episodes. Laboratory investigations confirmed infection with epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 6 (EHDV‑6), and phylogenetic analyses indicated that the strain belonged to an Asia‑Pacific lineage distinct from the North African/Mediterranean EHDV‑6 cluster.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climatic and ecological conditions in western Japan favorable to Culicoides vectors, with likely introduction or amplification of EHDV‑6 in local ruminant populations that had little recent exposure to this serotype. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence of clinically significant EHD in Japanese cattle driven by an EHDV‑6 lineage with pathogenic features reminiscent of, but genetically distinct from, historic Ibaraki virus (EHDV‑2), representing intra‑continental emergence into parts of Eastern Asia where EHDV‑6 had not previously caused recognized cattle outbreaks.
Review: Review – newly added event to represent a major Eastern Asia emergence of EHDV‑6 in cattle (46 affected animals on 38 farms with multiple deaths), which is highlighted in the primary literature as a notable outbreak. Classified as intra‑continental emergence (first substantial EHDV‑6 cattle outbreak in this part of Eastern Asia) plus re‑emergence due to a new pathogenic lineage; this should be checked by domain experts but appears consistent with regional EHDV history.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Host: Dairy and beef cattle (including pregnant cows); aborted fetuses
Event.summary: In September 2015, a country‑wide epizootic of febrile illness and production loss was recognized in Israeli dairy and beef cattle herds, with clinical signs including reduced milk yield, weakness, drooling, lameness, recumbency, fever, mild oral and nasal mucosal erythema, weight loss and abortions; deaths and cachexia occurred in a minority of animals. Virological testing (ELISA, real‑time RT‑PCR and VP2 sequencing) confirmed epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 6 (EHDV‑6) infection, and the outbreak involved multiple geographic foci including northern Israel and the Dead Sea region. After the Culicoides season ended, the epizootic declined, but serologic data and subsequent detections indicated continued EHDV circulation in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Favorable conditions for Culicoides vectors in Israeli dairy and beef production areas, combined with movement of infected animals or midges from neighboring EHDV‑6‑endemic countries, facilitated spread into densely stocked herds. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence of EHD in Israel associated with a different serotype from the 2006 EHDV‑7 outbreak, with EHDV‑6 causing widespread clinical disease and abortions, reflecting both viral genetic diversification and changing host–virus dynamics in a region where multiple EHDV serotypes now co‑circulate.
Review: Review – newly added event to capture the large 2015 EHDV‑6 epizootic in Israeli cattle, which caused substantial production losses and abortions and is cited as a major cattle outbreak in recent global reviews. Classified as re‑occurrence and re‑emergence within Western Asia rather than new continental emergence; inclusion brings the dataset closer to representing the ten most impactful post‑1990 EHD episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Equid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: EHV-1, Equine herpesvirus 1
Host: Horses (pregnant mares in a riding-school herd)
Event.summary: In early 1991, a riding school in the Netherlands experienced an EHV-1 abortion storm: seven of twelve pregnant mares aborted late-term and one live-born foal died at eight days of age, with virus isolation from aborted foals confirming EHV-1. Most abortions occurred within about two weeks after an initial February abortion, and clinical illness remained largely confined to the affected mares, with no clear evidence of spread beyond the facility. Isolation of aborting mares, strengthened hygiene, and the natural decline in virus shedding led to cessation of new abortions and the outbreak ended later that spring.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High stocking density and close contact in a riding-school setting, including recent transport of at least one pregnant mare, created conditions for rapid respiratory spread and heavy exposure of mares late in gestation. Internal mechanisms: Serologic data and timing support reactivation of latent EHV-1 in an index mare triggered by transport or management stress, followed by typical abortion-storm pathogenesis; there is no evidence for a novel genotype or geographic range expansion, so this is best interpreted as a local re-occurrence of endemic virus.
Review: Review – Event is real, well documented, and correctly coded as a re-occurrence of endemic EHV-1 rather than any form of first emergence. I corrected the country name to the standardized "Netherlands (Kingdom of the)" and updated the summary to reflect the published case numbers (7 of 12 mares aborting plus one foal death). However, this is a single-farm abortion storm with fewer than 10 foal losses and is likely not among the ten highest-impact global EHV-1 events since 1990; retain if a representative abortion-storm example is desired, otherwise consider exclusion under a strict top‑10 criterion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine arteritis virus
EPP.common.name: EAV, Equine arterivirus
Host: Horses at a riding establishment near Barcelona (mixed riding horses, various breeds)
Event.summary: In 1992, an outbreak of equine viral arteritis occurred at a riding establishment near Barcelona, Spain, affecting 31 of 186 horses with fever, depression, edema of the limbs and ventrum, and vesicular–erosive stomatitis but no recorded mortality. Serologic testing confirmed recent infection with equine arteritis virus, representing the first confirmed clinical EVA outbreak reported from Spain, although the virus was already recognized elsewhere in Southern and Western Europe. The outbreak remained confined to the riding establishment and resolved with management measures, after which Spain reported no further major clinical EVA outbreaks for many years despite later serologic evidence of low‑level EAV circulation in horse populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Probable introduction of an infected horse or semen from other European regions into a largely naïve Spanish riding population, together with close housing and intensive use of horses at a single establishment, facilitated efficient respiratory spread. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – efficient horse‑to‑horse respiratory transmission of an established EAV lineage into an immunologically naïve group; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – establishment of clinical EVA in a new national population within Southern Europe without evidence of a novel genotype.
Review: retain – Event is well documented as the first recognized clinical EVA outbreak in Spain and of moderate regional impact. Corrected emergence classification: set intra_continental_emergence to false because EAV was already established in Southern Europe (e.g. Italy) before 1992; treated instead as a re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion with first national recognition.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine arteritis virus
EPP.common.name: EAV, Equine arterivirus
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1993]
Host: Non‑Thoroughbred breeding horses (stallions and mares) on a stud in south Nottinghamshire and horses on five linked premises
Event.summary: In 1993, equine viral arteritis was diagnosed for the first time in the United Kingdom when an outbreak began on a non‑Thoroughbred stud in south Nottinghamshire after use of a recently imported Anglo‑Arab stallion. Infection spread to five additional premises via chilled semen used for artificial insemination and via movement of acutely or subclinically infected mares, resulting in typical EVA signs including pyrexia, depression, conjunctivitis, and limb and genital edema in about 100 horses. Voluntary movement restrictions, tracing of exposed mares, and control measures on the six affected premises contained the outbreak, after which EVA was made notifiable in the UK and long‑term serologic surveillance programmes for stallions and mares were implemented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International trade in breeding stallions and chilled semen from continental Europe into a naïve UK horse population, combined with widespread artificial insemination and return movement of bred mares, enabled rapid dissemination; absence of prior EVA vaccination and limited awareness further amplified spread. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – efficient venereal and respiratory transmission from a persistently infected carrier stallion and acutely infected mares; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – first confirmed establishment of clinical EVA in the Northern Europe subregion with onward spread between multiple premises.
Review: retain – Widely recognised as the first recorded EVA outbreak in the UK, involving six premises and around 100 horses and prompting major regulatory changes. Corrected type classification by setting first_detection to false (global first detection was in 1953 in Ohio); retained intra_continental_emergence as true because this represents spread of clinical EVA into the Northern Europe subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine infectious anemia virus
EPP.common.name: EIAV, Swamp fever virus
Host: Horses (sport and breeding horses treated with or epidemiologically linked to contaminated hyperimmune plasma)
Event.summary: In 2006, equine infectious anaemia was unexpectedly detected in Ireland in a cluster of sport and breeding horses, after several animals on premises in County Meath that had received imported equine hyperimmune plasma developed acute EIA, revealing the country’s first recorded outbreak in many decades. Subsequent investigations showed that the index infections were linked to a contaminated plasma batch, with additional clinically apparent and subclinical cases identified on multiple farms and in referral facilities in Ireland and one linked premises in Northern Ireland through iatrogenic transmission and horse movements. The episode was contained over the following months through extensive tracing, testing and culling of infected horses, strict movement controls, and enhanced surveillance, after which Ireland regained its EIA-free trade status with no evidence of endemic circulation.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International trade in inadequately screened equine hyperimmune plasma and its therapeutic use in multiple horses seeded infection, while subsequent spread was driven by iatrogenic transmission (shared veterinary equipment, surgical procedures) and movement of treated horses between farms and clinics. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses showed that Irish viruses were closely related to those involved in a contemporaneous Italian plasma-associated outbreak, with no evidence of a new, more virulent EIAV strain; the episode reflects re-introduction and amplification of established EIAV lineages rather than evolutionary change.
Review: retain – Real 2006 Irish outbreak seeded by contaminated hyperimmune plasma, with multiple linked premises and cross-border spread to Northern Ireland. Classification as re-occurrence in Northern Europe is consistent with prior EIAV presence in the subregion, and host, geography and timing are correct; sources include national reports and detailed outbreak investigations. Minor nuance: the outbreak ultimately involved more than two premises, but the summary captures the main drivers and control measures, so no structural changes are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine infectious anemia virus
EPP.common.name: EIAV, Swamp fever virus
Host: Horses (mainly sport and working horses in central and other Italian regions)
Event.summary: In 2006, Italy experienced a notable outbreak of equine infectious anaemia when horses that had received contaminated hyperimmune plasma developed EIA in central regions, leading to recognition that EIAV infection was more widespread in the national horse population than previously appreciated. As investigations and follow-up testing proceeded, additional infections were detected on neighbouring and more distant farms, including animals with no direct plasma exposure, implicating mechanical transmission by blood-feeding flies and possible iatrogenic spread, and prompting Italy to launch a comprehensive National Surveillance Plan that actively screened the entire equid population between 2007 and 2012. Over this 2006–2012 episode, testing of over a million equids identified EIAV-seropositive animals on more than a thousand holdings, but systematic serological screening, notification, culling or permanent isolation of positive equids and movement controls progressively reduced infection prevalence, after which surveillance shifted to a risk-based approach and reported occurrence declined to low levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of untested or inadequately screened equine plasma products, combined with horse movements between farms and extensive use of shared equipment, seeded the initial outbreak, while favourable vector conditions and dense equid populations in some rural areas facilitated ongoing mechanical transmission by horseflies and stable flies; the absence of prior nationwide testing meant many inapparent carriers had accumulated undetected. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses of Italian field isolates revealed typical EIAV gag sequences, including close relatedness between the Irish and Italian 2006 plasma-associated strains and other historical North American and Asian isolates, without evidence of a novel hypervirulent genotype; re-occurrence is best explained by persistence and amplification of existing EIAV lineages in high-risk ecologic niches rather than viral innovation.
Review: review – Year span adjusted from 2006–2007 to 2006–2012 to reflect that the initial 2006 plasma-associated outbreak directly triggered Italy’s National Surveillance Plan, during which over 1 million equids were tested and EIAV-positive animals were found on >1,000 holdings through 2012, making this a multi-year national re-occurrence episode rather than a short, two‑year event. Geography, host, and classification as re-occurrence remain appropriate; sources now clearly support the extended surveillance period and magnitude.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Equine infectious anemia virus
EPP.common.name: EIAV, Swamp fever virus
Host: Horses (primarily saddle and sport horses, with some cases on rescue or mixed-use premises)
Event.summary: From 2009 to 2012, France experienced a multi-year episode of sporadic but impactful equine infectious anaemia re-occurrence after a long period of very low prevalence, with around 15 cases in several outbreaks in 2009 (notably in the Var department and one case in Dordogne), 10 infected horses across seven foci in 2010 in multiple regions, and eight cases in two foci in 2012 in the Gard and Vaucluse departments. The episode consisted of geographically scattered clusters affecting mainly saddle and sport horses, including foci epidemiologically linked to imports of Romanian-origin horses via Belgium as well as apparently autochthonous infections, leading to intensive national surveillance and detailed outbreak investigations. Each focus was controlled through euthanasia of positive horses, movement restrictions, tracing and testing of in-contact and neighbouring equids, and expanded testing within affected departments, and by 2014 only two isolated cases were detected in the Gard department, indicating that this re-occurrence phase had been largely contained.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected horses from endemic areas (especially Romania) through intra-EU trade, together with frequent movements of sport and leisure horses for competition and sale, initiated several French outbreaks, while local transmission was favoured by vector exposure and, in some instances, potentially by management practices that allowed blood contamination between animals; heightened surveillance also increased detection of latent carriers. Internal mechanisms: No French-specific EIAV genotype with clearly increased virulence or altered host range has been reported; phylogenetic and serological data suggest that re-occurrence reflects repeated introductions and local persistence of existing EIAV strains rather than emergence of a distinct, more pathogenic lineage.
Review: review – Evidence from French surveillance reports and the RESPE network confirms the cluster sizes and distribution summarised here (≈15 cases in 2009, 10 in 2010, 8 in 2012) and supports classification as a national re-occurrence episode confined to Western Europe. To strengthen sourcing, official French outbreak and surveillance reports (RESPE alert on the 2012 Gard focus; Gaudaire et al. 2012 surveillance overview) have been added alongside the OIE regional report and the French Wikipedia synthesis; the NDCC equine disease alert is no longer relied upon as a primary source. Geography, timing and event type remain appropriate, but the row is flagged for review to allow a future curator to decide whether pre‑2009 French foci (2001, 2005, 2007) should be merged into a longer linked episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Equine infectious anemia virus
EPP.common.name: EIAV, Swamp fever virus
Host: Equids (horses, mules and donkeys, primarily in extensively managed western herds)
Event.summary: Between 2009 and 2012, Canada’s national equine infectious anaemia control program documented a substantial burden of endemic EIAV in western and northern regions when federal disease investigations identified 409 EIA-positive equids on 288 holdings, with 397 of these cases in the western provinces and territories (Yukon, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan) and only 12 in eastern Canada (Québec). The episode unfolded not as a single point-source outbreak but as a concentration of infections detected through case-triggered testing in remote, extensively managed equid populations where owner-requested surveillance coverage was low, prompting concern that EIAV remained entrenched in parts of western Canada despite very low national prevalence. Control measures during this period involved investigation of each positive case, tracing and testing of in-contact equids, mandatory movement restrictions and, where required, destruction or permanent quarantine of infected animals, and the findings contributed to federal discussions and consultations on revising Canada’s national EIA disease control program.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive outdoor management of equids in remote western regions, low levels of voluntary owner-requested testing, and abundant tabanid and stable fly populations facilitated ongoing mechanical transmission of EIAV and allowed infection to persist in sparsely monitored herds; movements of untested or infrequently tested equids between ranches further propagated infection. Internal mechanisms: Available Canadian studies emphasize long-term circulation and genetic heterogeneity of EIAV gag sequences in naturally infected horses rather than the emergence of a new high-virulence strain, so this multi-year pattern represents re-occurrence and persistent endemicity in specific ecological niches rather than viral re-emergence driven by genetic change.
Review: review – New event added to capture a clearly major post‑1990 EIAV episode: 409 positives detected during federal disease investigations from 2009–2012, overwhelmingly in western Canada, which is of greater numerical impact than several small European clusters. Classified as re-occurrence because EIAV has been present in Canada since the 19th century, with no evidence of a novel strain; continent, subregion and host assignments follow the project’s geography schema. Summary and drivers are based on peer‑reviewed analyses of Canada’s EIA control program and CFIA guidance, but the row is flagged for expert review to refine the narrative once full-text Canadian reports are consulted without access limitations.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine infectious anemia virus
EPP.common.name: EIAV, Swamp fever virus
Host: Equids (horses, working equids and other equines)
Event.summary: In 2010, Romania—where EIAV had been endemic for decades—reported a dramatic surge in detected equine infectious anaemia when intensified testing under an eradication program revealed 1,331 outbreaks involving 1,389 seropositive equids during the first half of the year, mainly in rural areas with high densities of working horses. As the episode unfolded, Romanian authorities implemented extensive control measures and the European Commission adopted protective legislation that required pre-movement testing, restricted exports of Romanian equidae and imposed additional safeguards in EU Member States receiving Romanian horses, during a period when infected Romanian-origin horses were linked to outbreaks in Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and the United Kingdom. Through 2011–2012, continued surveillance, culling of positives and strengthened movement controls reduced the number of newly reported outbreaks, but low-level endemicity persisted in some regions, and Romania remained a primary European source of EIAV infection in traded equids.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-standing endemic EIAV in Romania combined with large populations of susceptible working equids, informal horse movements without systematic pre-movement serological testing, and abundant blood-feeding flies created conditions for high local transmission, while Romania’s integration into the EU internal market made it economically important to document infection status, leading to intensified testing that revealed the full extent of infection. Internal mechanisms: Molecular data do not indicate emergence of a novel, hypervirulent EIAV strain in Romania during this period; the apparent ‘explosion’ in case numbers is better explained by improved surveillance superimposed on existing endemicity, combined with continued mechanical transmission and movement of asymptomatically infected equids.
Review: retain – The row accurately reflects the scale of Romania’s 2010 EIAV epizootic (1,331 outbreaks; 1,389 positive equids in the first half of 2010), its role as the main endemic source for subsequent Western European incursions, and the EU protective measures enacted via Decision 2010/346/EU. Classification as a re-occurrence in Eastern Europe is appropriate because EIAV was long-established in the region, and there is no evidence of strain-driven re-emergence; no corrections to geography, timing or event type are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine infectious anemia virus
EPP.common.name: EIAV, Swamp fever virus
Host: Horses (imported Romanian horses and resident horses on affected premises)
Event.summary: In early 2010, Belgium detected equine infectious anaemia in a horse in West Flanders that had been imported from Romania, representing the country’s first recorded occurrence of EIA and triggering concern because many Romanian-origin horses had entered Belgium in preceding years. Epidemiological investigations and targeted serological surveys of horses imported from Romania between 2007 and 2009 revealed additional EIAV-positive animals on several premises, confirming that asymptomatically infected horses had been moved through Belgian dealer networks and sold on to other EU countries. Belgian authorities imposed emergency measures including on-farm quarantine, tracing and testing of contact and similarly imported horses, culling of infected equids and strict movement controls, and were able to demonstrate freedom from infection on affected premises three months after removal of the last positive animals, although re-occurrence with new foci was documented again in 2012.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of live horses from endemic Romania without sufficiently stringent or effectively enforced pre-export testing, coupled with commercial dealer movements of poorly documented animals, was the primary driver of EIAV introduction into Belgium; once in-country, infected but clinically normal horses posed a risk of further spread. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization of Belgian EIAV isolates showed close relatedness to Romanian field strains, consistent with direct introduction rather than in situ viral evolution, and no new genotype with increased virulence or altered tropism was identified; the event thus reflects re-occurrence mediated by trade rather than viral change.
Review: review – The Belgian 2010 episode is real, well documented and of regulatory importance, but the row has been updated to add the national AFSCA epidemiological summary as a primary source describing that seven outbreaks were detected, all involving Romanian-origin horses, and that Belgium considered this its first recorded EIA occurrence. Event classification remains re-occurrence at the Western Europe subregional scale, which already had EIAV via earlier French outbreaks; timing and geography are correct. Flagged for review mainly to ensure future harmonisation of how first-ever detections at country level are handled within the global classification scheme.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine infectious anemia virus
EPP.common.name: EIAV, Swamp fever virus
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2010]
Host: Horses (imported and resident horses, mainly in dealer and livery premises)
Event.summary: In 2010, the United Kingdom confirmed equine infectious anaemia in an imported horse in Northumberland that had been part of a consignment of Romanian-origin horses routed via Belgium and the Netherlands, during a wider period of EIAV incursions into Western Europe linked to trade from Romania. Over 2010–2012, Great Britain detected a small number of additional cases and very small clusters on dealer and livery premises receiving horses from continental Europe, including two linked cases in Devon and Cornwall in 2012, each of which prompted extensive tracing and testing of in-contact horses and horses from the same import consignments. All incursions were managed by immediate euthanasia of infected horses, imposition of movement restrictions and intensive surveillance of associated premises, and by the end of this period Great Britain remained officially free of endemic EIAV, with national guidance documents describing EIA as a rare, sporadic, mostly import-related infection and indicating that the last outbreaks occurred in 2012.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International trade and movement of horses from endemic Eastern European areas, often via intermediary countries such as Belgium and the Netherlands, without fully effective pre-export or pre-movement screening, was the primary driver of EIAV incursions into the UK; concentration of imported horses in dealer premises increased the risk of onward spread to local horses. Internal mechanisms: Sequence data for UK isolates show close relatedness to Romanian and other European strains and do not indicate the emergence of a novel, more virulent lineage; re-occurrence is therefore best attributed to repeated introduction of existing EIAV genotypes combined with opportunities for mechanical and iatrogenic transmission.
Review: review – The UK 2010–2012 incursions are genuine and policy‑relevant, and the event is correctly framed as a series of small, import-related outbreaks rather than a new endemic focus. To better ground the narrative, official Defra guidance (confirming outbreaks in 2010 and 2012 and the UK’s otherwise EIA‑free status) and the detailed epidemiological report on the 2012 Devon/Cornwall cases have been added as sources. Classification as re-occurrence in Northern Europe remains appropriate; the row is flagged chiefly so future curators can consider whether all Romania-linked 2010 incursions in Western/Northern Europe should be consolidated into a single, multi-country episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine infectious anemia virus
EPP.common.name: EIAV, Swamp fever virus
Host: Equids (horses and mules, mainly working animals in Pantanal wetlands and northeastern states)
Event.summary: From 2010 to 2014, multiple large-scale serological surveys in Brazil highlighted an exceptionally heavy endemic burden of equine infectious anaemia, particularly in the Pantanal wetland region and in northeastern states, revealing that EIAV remained widely disseminated despite existing control regulations. In 2010, testing of 5,615 equids from 209 municipalities in the northeastern states of Paraíba, Rio Grande do Norte and Ceará found 151 seropositive animals (2.7%), with infection present year-round and in all three states, while a survey in the Poconé municipality of the northern Pantanal found EIAV antibodies in approximately one-third of sampled equids and on more than half of surveyed farms, with prevalence exceeding 40% among animals kept on regularly flooded pastures. A 2014 statewide study in Mato Grosso, encompassing the Amazon, Cerrado and Pantanal biomes, subsequently reported 6.6% animal-level and 17.2% herd-level seroprevalence among 3,858 equids in 1,067 herds, with the highest infection levels in the Pantanal zone, underscoring that EIAV is entrenched across multiple biomes and prompting calls to re-evaluate Brazil’s EIA control programme and strengthen prophylactic measures.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive, low-biosecurity management of working equids in flooded wetlands and cattle-ranching systems, sharing of saddles, tack and veterinary equipment, incomplete segregation or culling of seropositive animals, and abundant populations of blood-feeding flies in the Pantanal and other humid regions all favoured efficient EIAV transmission and persistence. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies of Brazilian EIAV from Pantanal horses show high genomic variability within endemic strains but do not implicate a single emergent hypervirulent variant; the high prevalence and farm-level clustering reflect long-term adaptation of EIAV to local equid populations and ecologic conditions rather than a recent evolutionary shift, making this a major endemic re-occurrence episode rather than a distinct re-emergence driven by viral change.
Review: review – New event added to represent the very high-burden, post‑1990 endemic situation in Brazil, particularly in the Pantanal/Mato Grosso and northeastern states, where herd- and animal-level seroprevalence (up to ≈52% of farms and ≈30% of animals in parts of Pantanal; ≈6–7% of animals at state level in Mato Grosso) clearly make this one of the most impactful EIAV episodes by numbers infected. Classified as re-occurrence because EIAV has been recognized as endemic in Brazil for decades and the studies describe entrenched infection rather than first introduction or novel-strain emergence. Geography and timing align with survey periods, but the row is flagged for review so that a future curator can refine spatial granularity (e.g. separate Pantanal vs. northeast) if desired.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Verotoxigenic E. coli, STEC
Host: Cattle (feedlot and dairy; healthy carriers)
Event.summary: In 1990, a U.S. study systematically detected and characterized verotoxin-producing E. coli in feces of healthy cattle, showing that roughly 10% of animals carried VTEC/STEC strains and confirming that feedlot and dairy cattle could serve as major asymptomatic reservoirs for human-pathogenic serotypes. Follow‑up work through the early 1990s established similar carriage patterns in other North American herds and helped embed cattle reservoirs into quantitative risk assessments for beef and dairy products. This research phase concluded with STEC being recognized in North American policy and industry guidance as a critical pre‑harvest hazard in cattle production systems rather than a purely human clinical problem.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification of feedlot beef and large dairy operations in North America, high stocking densities, and fecal–oral transmission within herds favoured amplification and maintenance of STEC, while improved laboratory methods (Shiga/verotoxin assays, DNA probes) enabled detection in asymptomatic cattle. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects recognition, rather than de novo evolution, of STEC lineages in cattle; no specific novel strain or host expansion is implicated relative to earlier VTEC reports in calves and other domestic species.
Review: review – Study accurately documents early large-scale detection of VTEC/STEC in healthy U.S. cattle and the role of cattle as reservoirs, but it is primarily a surveillance milestone rather than a discrete, high-impact emergence episode (no single major outbreak, policy shift, or geographic jump is tied to 1990 alone). I removed the previous re_emergence flag so that all emergence-type indicators are now No, because there is no clear evidence of a qualitative pathogen change or new host adaptation compared with earlier 1980s VTEC detections in calves and other animals. Consider excluding this row if a strict “top 10” list of highest-impact events is enforced.
Review.Comment: it is primarily a surveillance milestone rather than a discrete, high-impact emergence episode

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Verotoxigenic E. coli, STEC
Host: Humans (primarily children) infected via undercooked beef patties; beef cattle as upstream reservoir
Event.summary: From late 1992 through early 1993, undercooked beef patties contaminated with E. coli O157:H7 served at a fast‑food chain caused a multistate outbreak in the United States, with more than 700 laboratory‑confirmed cases and at least four child deaths. Investigation traced the outbreak to ground beef produced from cattle carrying O157:H7, revealing widespread contamination risks in centralized grinding and distribution systems. In 1994, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) responded by declaring E. coli O157:H7 an adulterant in raw ground beef and implementing routine regulatory testing, marking a step‑change in how STEC hazards in cattle and beef were managed.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Centralized, high‑volume grinding of beef from multiple feedlot sources, inadequate cooking procedures at retail outlets, and limited pre‑existing regulatory control of STEC in beef dramatically increased human exposure to O157:H7. Public alarm and intense media coverage prompted a strong regulatory response, including FSIS’s 1994 zero‑tolerance policy for O157:H7 in ground beef, which in turn drove major investment in pre‑ and post‑harvest control measures in cattle and the beef supply chain. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was a typical O157:H7 with stx2 and eae; there is no evidence of unusual virulence evolution beyond known EHEC traits, so the episode is best viewed as a large re‑occurrence driven by exposure and processing failures rather than by qualitatively new pathogen biology.
Review: retain – Added as a major re_occurrence episode because the 1992–1993 Jack-in-the-Box O157:H7 outbreak (≈732 cases, 4 deaths) and the subsequent 1994 FSIS decision to classify O157:H7 as an adulterant in ground beef together had enormous impact on cattle/beef STEC control. Classified solely as re_occurrence (no intra- or inter-continental emergence) since O157:H7 was already established in North America; the event’s importance stems from the scale of human disease and the regulatory shift, not from first detection. Sources include the outbreak summary and Microbiology Spectrum review detailing the 1994 adulterant policy.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Verotoxigenic E. coli, STEC
Host: Cattle (beef and dairy; healthy carriers)
Event.summary: Between 1992 and 1994, a large survey of 387 cattle in Japan tested more than 2,000 E. coli isolates and found that roughly one quarter of animals shed verotoxin‑producing E. coli, identifying both O157:H7 and numerous non‑O157 VTEC/STEC serotypes. These data provided the first comprehensive evidence that Japanese cattle were a major reservoir of STEC strains, including those implicated in human disease. Subsequent to these findings, STEC was incorporated into national zoonotic surveillance and food safety programs, laying groundwork for understanding and responding to large school‑based O157 outbreaks later in the decade.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of Japanese cattle production and the introduction of sensitive diagnostic methods (PCR and verotoxin assays) permitted detection of previously under‑recognized STEC carriage. Internal mechanisms: Maintenance of STEC lineages with stx1, stx2 and other virulence genes in the bovine gastrointestinal tract, with efficient fecal shedding but little or no clinical disease in cattle, confirming their role as asymptomatic reservoirs of human‑pathogenic strains.
Review: retain – This event appropriately captures the first large-scale demonstration that Japanese cattle were important reservoirs of STEC, and its timing (1992–1994) precedes and informs Japan’s subsequent large O157 outbreaks. Coding as first_detection (for Japan) and intra_continental_emergence (expansion of known Asian STEC from South Asia to East Asia) is reasonable. No geography corrections were needed; the sources (Itoh et al. Vet Microbiol 1998 plus a later characterization paper) are suitable primary references.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Verotoxigenic E. coli, STEC
Host: Humans (primarily children with HUS and hemorrhagic colitis); cattle as emerging reservoir of sorbitol-fermenting O157:H−
Event.summary: In the mid–late 1990s, sorbitol-fermenting Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H− emerged in Germany as a distinct lineage causing severe hemolytic uremic syndrome in children, with a notable outbreak in Bavaria in 1995–1996. Follow‑up investigations identified cattle as a reservoir for these strains, and by 2000 sorbitol-fermenting O157:H− STEC had been isolated from bovine feces, supporting a zoonotic link. By the end of this episode, this unusual O157 lineage was recognized as an important, highly pathogenic variant established in regional cattle herds and repeatedly causing pediatric HUS.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density cattle production, slaughtering of regionally sourced animals, and close integration of cattle, the food chain and human populations in central Europe facilitated maintenance and transmission of the new lineage. Enhanced clinical and veterinary surveillance following severe pediatric HUS clusters prompted targeted studies that eventually detected the sorbitol-fermenting O157:H− strains in cattle. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of a sorbitol‑fermenting, usually nonmotile O157:H− STEC lineage with distinct phenotypic traits and virulence gene combinations, representing re-emergence of STEC in the same subregion through evolution of a highly pathogenic clade rather than simple spread of pre‑existing O157:H7.
Review: review – This episode correctly describes the emergence of sorbitol-fermenting O157:H− as a distinct, highly pathogenic lineage in Germany and its subsequent detection in cattle. To align with the rules that new strains in already affected regions should be coded as re-emergence rather than intra-continental spread, I set intra_continental_emergence to No and retained only re_emergence as Yes. First_detection is interpreted here as first recognition of this specific SF O157:H− lineage in cattle, not first STEC in Western Europe more generally.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Verotoxigenic E. coli, STEC
Host: Dairy cattle (three pasture-based herds in southeast Queensland; healthy carriers) and farm environments
Event.summary: Over a 12‑month period in the late 1990s, a longitudinal study of three Australian dairy herds in southeast Queensland collected nearly 600 cattle fecal samples and over 140 environmental samples, documenting Shiga toxin–producing E. coli in about 17% of cattle feces and 4% of environmental samples. The work identified serotypes including O26:H11 and O157:H7 and showed persistent contamination of water and pasture on these pasture-based farms. Publication of these findings around 2000 provided the first detailed, large-scale evidence that Australian dairy cattle and their farm environments were an established reservoir of multiple STEC serotypes of human health concern.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and modernization of the Australian dairy sector and increasing concern over export-market requirements for pathogen control motivated systematic surveillance for STEC on dairy farms. Internal mechanisms: Stable colonization of dairy cattle and environmental persistence of STEC serotypes, including O157:H7, in a new continental setting, indicating that globally distributed STEC lineages had become entrenched in Oceania’s ruminant reservoirs even though O157-associated human disease remained relatively rare in Australia.
Review: review – Adjusted the timing to reflect the actual sampling period (a 12‑month longitudinal study in the late 1990s) rather than the 2000 publication year and interpreted this as the first large-scale documentation of STEC (including O157:H7) in Australian dairy cattle. Given the lack of earlier published evidence of STEC reservoirs in Oceania’s cattle and the paper’s prominence in later reviews, I set first_detection and inter_continental_emergence to Yes for the animal host system, while leaving intra_continental_emergence at No. This event is retained as the main representation of STEC establishment in cattle in Oceania.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Verotoxigenic E. coli, STEC
Host: Cattle (dairy and beef; healthy carriers)
Event.summary: In 1999, a survey of 197 fecal samples from healthy dairy and beef cattle and slaughter cattle in Rio de Janeiro State, Brazil, used PCR screening for stx genes and culture on CT‑SMAC to detect STEC. Approximately 71% of samples were positive for stx, with higher prevalence in dairy cattle, and 15 STEC strains representing 11 serotypes were isolated; notably, three O157:H7 strains were recovered. The authors reported this as the first isolation of O157:H7 from cattle in Brazil and highlighted the high background prevalence of STEC in cattle as a potential source of contamination for beef and dairy products.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of dairy and beef production in southeastern Brazil, combined with improved laboratory methods (PCR for stx genes and selective media for O157), allowed detection of widespread STEC carriage that had previously gone undocumented. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects geographic documentation of STEC, including O157:H7, in Brazilian cattle rather than clear evidence of a novel strain; it establishes Brazil as part of the global network of STEC‑infected cattle reservoirs with multiple human‑pathogenic serotypes.
Review: retain – Added to cover South America, using Cerqueira et al. (Vet Microbiol 1999) which showed very high stx gene prevalence in cattle and reported the first isolation of O157:H7 from Brazilian cattle. Classified as first_detection for Brazil without intra- or inter-continental flags, because STEC was already established in South America (notably in Argentina) before 1999. No evidence of a specific new strain or resistance profile was highlighted, so re_emergence was left No.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Verotoxigenic E. coli, STEC
Host: Cattle (feedlot and range; asymptomatic reservoirs of multiple non-O157 and O157 serogroups)
Event.summary: From the mid‑2000s through 2011, large surveys in U.S. feedlot and range cattle documented widespread shedding of multiple non‑O157 STEC serogroups—especially O26, O45, O103, O111, O121, and O145—alongside O157:H7, with these "top-7" serogroups increasingly implicated in severe human illness and outbreaks. Molecular work showed that many cattle isolates carried stx2 and other virulence factors associated with human disease, and by 2011 the U.S. FSIS responded by declaring six non‑O157 STEC serogroups adulterants in non-intact beef. This sequence of surveillance, attribution and regulatory action marked a qualitative shift in how diverse STEC lineages in cattle were viewed and controlled in North America.
