Review: review – This outbreak is appropriately included as one of the most consequential Hendra events because it involved the largest documented horse‑to‑horse transmission cluster after 1994 and caused two human infections with one death. The main correction is to the host field, which now explicitly lists humans as well as horses; classification as re_occurrence remains appropriate, as genomic analyses show no major viral divergence and the severity is attributable to high‑risk clinical settings. The narrative of case numbers, human outcomes and control measures is consistent across Queensland Health, Business Queensland and CDC EID reports.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus hendraense
EPP.common.name: HeV
Host: Horses
Event.summary: In July 2008, shortly after the Redlands clinic outbreak, multiple horses on a property near Proserpine in north Queensland died or became severely ill, and three horses were confirmed infected with Hendra virus, with at least one additional death considered a probable but untested case. This Proserpine outbreak occurred more than 900 km from Redlands yet within the same winter season, and together the two independent multi‑horse incidents signalled unusually broad HeV activity in bat reservoirs and spillover into horses across eastern Queensland. Quarantine of the affected property, destruction of infected and high‑risk horses and movement controls contained the Proserpine outbreak, and no human infections were documented despite substantial equine case numbers.([business.qld.gov.au](https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/service-industries-professionals/service-industries/veterinary-surgeons/guidelines-hendra/incident-summary))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Similar environmental conditions to Redlands—winter season with increased shedding of virus by flying foxes and close proximity of horses to bat foraging areas—likely favoured bat‑to‑horse spillover at Proserpine, while on‑property husbandry practices and delay before recognition of Hendra virus contributed to multiple equine infections. Internal mechanisms: Sequence comparisons indicate that the Proserpine and Redlands viruses represent closely related variants within the known HeV diversity, so this episode is best understood as geographic re‑occurrence and local amplification of an established lineage rather than emergence of a new strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3182206/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added: the Proserpine 2008 outbreak involved three confirmed and at least one probable equine case and is highlighted in ecological and genomic analyses as one of two large, geographically separated outbreaks in winter 2008, placing it clearly among the top HeV emergence events. It is classified as re_occurrence within the same subregion because it represents another multi‑horse spillover without evidence of a distinct strain or new host. Horse numbers, timing and the concurrent nature of this outbreak with Redlands were cross‑checked against Queensland Health, Business Queensland and the Queensland Ombudsman review.([business.qld.gov.au](https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/service-industries-professionals/service-industries/veterinary-surgeons/guidelines-hendra/incident-summary))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus hendraense
EPP.common.name: HeV
Host: Horses; humans
Event.summary: In August 2009, an equine nursery near Cawarral, close to Rockhampton in central Queensland, experienced a Hendra virus outbreak in which four horses were confirmed or strongly suspected to be infected, all of which died or were euthanised. A 55‑year‑old veterinarian who had performed a nasal endoscopy and other procedures on an infected horse without full respiratory protection developed encephalitis and died, becoming the fourth recorded human fatality from Hendra virus. The outbreak was controlled through destruction of affected horses, long‑term quarantine of the property, widespread tracing and risk assessment of human contacts, and a major review of infection‑control practices in equine veterinary medicine.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close confinement of horses in a multi‑paddock nursery, coupled with high‑risk veterinary procedures conducted before Hendra virus was suspected, increased within‑property transmission and intense human exposure to respiratory secretions and blood; the event occurred against a background of increasing horse movements within Queensland. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicate that the Cawarral virus was highly similar to other HeV isolates, so the severity of this outbreak is attributable to exposure conditions rather than novel viral traits; bat‑to‑horse spillover followed by limited horse‑to‑horse transmission in a confined setting best explains the pattern of cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3294518/))
Review: review – This Cawarral outbreak remains one of the highest‑impact events because it involved multiple equine cases and a fatal human infection in a veterinarian. The main correction is to the host field, which now includes humans; the event is still best classified as re_occurrence since viral genome comparisons show high conservation with earlier strains and there is no evidence of a novel genotype. Timing, horse and human case counts and control measures are consistent across Queensland Health, Business Queensland, parliamentary and media reports.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus hendraense
EPP.common.name: HeV
Host: Horses; dog (domestic)
Event.summary: Between June and October 2011, eastern Australia experienced an unprecedented spike in Hendra virus activity, with 17 documented property‑level spillover events in Queensland and New South Wales and 21 horse deaths across multiple locations. Within this cluster, a property near Mount Alford/Boonah in south‑east Queensland with three infected horses also yielded the first naturally infected domestic dog, which was seropositive for Hendra virus antibodies, indicating that the virus’s recognised domestic host range extended beyond horses. Intensive surveillance, property quarantines, destruction of infected horses and enhanced risk communication eventually saw the number of new incidents decline after winter, and no sustained transmission beyond affected properties or any human infections were documented during this surge.([business.qld.gov.au](https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/service-industries-professionals/service-industries/veterinary-surgeons/guidelines-hendra/incident-summary))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Severe weather events in late 2010 and early 2011, including major flooding in south‑east Queensland and northern New South Wales and Cyclone Yasi, likely disrupted flying fox food resources and roosts, increasing nutritional stress and driving bats into closer contact with horses, while heightened awareness and testing probably improved detection of spillovers. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion from horses into a companion dog on the Mount Alford property demonstrated that HeV can infect domestic canids under field conditions, and the marked, climate‑associated increase in spillover incidence within an already affected subregion is treated here as re_emergence even though no specific new genotype was identified.([health.qld.gov.au](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/cdcg/index/hendra))
Review: review – This row is retained as a synthetic description of the June–October 2011 spike, which comprised 17 separate property‑level spillovers causing 21 horse deaths and the first recorded natural HeV infection in a dog. It explicitly aggregates multiple independent bat‑to‑horse spillover events into a single episode because they were temporally clustered, geographically proximate and plausibly driven by shared climatic and ecological conditions; users should note that most incidents are not linked by horse‑to‑horse transmission. The event is kept as re_emergence due to the combination of a marked incidence increase and documented host expansion to a dog, and the overall magnitude and chronology match Queensland Health, Business Queensland and secondary syntheses.([business.qld.gov.au](https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/service-industries-professionals/service-industries/veterinary-surgeons/guidelines-hendra/incident-summary))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus hendraense
EPP.common.name: HeV
Host: Horses; dog (domestic)
Event.summary: In June–July 2013, Hendra virus infection was confirmed in an unvaccinated horse on a property near Macksville on the mid‑north coast of New South Wales, and the farm was quarantined while remaining horses, cats and dogs were monitored. Subsequent testing detected Hendra virus RNA and neutralising antibodies in a quarantined dog that had close contact with the sick horse, confirming the second naturally infected dog recorded and extending recognition of canine involvement to NSW. No human infections occurred, and the outbreak was declared over after follow‑up testing of in‑contact animals remained negative and movement restrictions were lifted.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendra_virus))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued bat–horse interface in coastal NSW, together with low vaccine uptake in the region, created susceptible horse populations in close proximity to flying fox contamination; farm dogs had unrestricted access to paddocks and sick horses, facilitating cross‑species exposure. Internal mechanisms: This event represents geographic re‑occurrence of the previously documented ability of Hendra virus to infect dogs, now in a different state, rather than emergence of a new host species or genotype; available virologic data show no novel variant, and there was no evidence of dog‑to‑human or dog‑to‑horse onward transmission.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/21/12/15-1324_article?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added: the 2013 Macksville outbreak is included because it documents the second naturally infected dog and demonstrates that canine Hendra virus infection can occur outside Queensland, an important host‑range and geographic consideration. It is classified as re_occurrence within the same subregion since dog infection had already been documented in 2011 and no new genotype was identified. Horse and dog involvement, timing and the scope of the public‑health and veterinary response are drawn from CDC EID’s detailed case report, ABC coverage and the Business Queensland incident table.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/21/12/15-1324_article?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus hendraense
EPP.common.name: HeV
Host: Horses
Event.summary: In June 2019, Hendra virus infection was confirmed in an unvaccinated older mare on a small non‑Thoroughbred property near Scone in the Upper Hunter Valley, New South Wales, marking the first equine case in the Hunter region and, at that time, the furthest south that infection in a non‑bat host had been documented. An urgent One Health response involving NSW Health, the Department of Primary Industries and local veterinarians quarantined the property, traced and risk‑assessed ten human contacts and monitored in‑contact horses, with no additional equine or human infections detected. Extensive media and industry communication followed, and vaccination uptake in the Hunter Valley increased, while quarantine was lifted once follow‑up testing of animals remained negative.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7582210/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of flying fox foraging and roosting into the horse‑dense Upper Hunter region, combined with variable adoption of the Equivac HeV vaccine, created conditions for spillover into an area previously believed to be low risk; climate variability and broader environmental changes affecting bat ecology may also have contributed. Internal mechanisms: Viral characterisation did not show a novel genotype, so this event is interpreted as geographic range expansion of spillover within the same subregion rather than emergence of a distinct strain, prompting revised risk mapping and biosecurity guidance for the thoroughbred and broader equine industries.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7582210/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added: the 2019 Scone case is widely recognised as the first equine Hendra virus infection in the Hunter Valley and, at the time, the southernmost non‑bat case, with substantial implications for risk mapping and vaccination behaviour. It is therefore justifiably among the top ten emergence events even though it involved only a single horse, and is classified as re_occurrence within the Australia and New Zealand subregion because no new genotype was identified. The description of the case, One Health response and impact on vaccine uptake is based on NSW Health surveillance reports, veterinary case descriptions, Business Queensland data and ABC news coverage.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7582210/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus hendraense
EPP.common.name: HeV
Host: Horses; flying foxes (fruit bats)
Event.summary: In October 2021, a horse near West Wallsend in the greater Newcastle region of New South Wales died with acute neurological signs and was confirmed infected with Hendra virus genotype 2 (HeV‑g2), the first equine case in which this divergent lineage was prospectively diagnosed and, at that time, one of the southernmost confirmed HeV infections in a horse. Genomic surveillance over the preceding decade had identified HeV‑g2 RNA in grey‑headed and other flying foxes across eastern, southern and western Australia, and application of the new PCR assay also led to retrospective recognition that at least one 2015 horse case in Gympie, Queensland, had been caused by HeV‑g2. The West Wallsend outbreak was confined to the index horse thanks to rapid diagnostic confirmation, property quarantine and risk communication, and surveillance and messaging were expanded southwards to reflect the broader distribution of the variant in bat reservoirs and horses.([business.qld.gov.au](https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/service-industries-professionals/service-industries/veterinary-surgeons/guidelines-hendra/incident-summary))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensified genomic surveillance of flying foxes and horses and the development of an HeV‑g2‑specific molecular assay enabled detection of this genotype in bats across a wide geographic range and its identification in horses, including the Newcastle case; ongoing habitat change and urban encroachment continue to bring flying foxes and horses into contact over a broader latitudinal band. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence—HeV‑g2 is substantially divergent from the prototype Hendra virus yet retains the capacity to infect horses—and inherent geographic range expansion of this lineage in bat reservoirs underpin its classification as re_emergence, with spillover now documented in horses further south and, retrospectively, as early as 2015 in Gympie.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11905374/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – This row is retained as the key description of Hendra virus genotype 2 emergence in horses but updated to reflect subsequent evidence that at least one 2015 Gympie horse case was retrospectively reclassified as HeV‑g2 and that the lineage has a broad distribution in flying foxes. The event remains appropriately classified as re_emergence because it documents recognition of a divergent viral genotype and southward expansion of confirmed spillover into horses, rather than a simple recurrence of the prototype strain. Hosts, geography and timing are consistent with the primary veterinary case report, CSIRO communications and Australian government sources, while the text now clarifies the relationship between the 2021 diagnostic breakthrough and earlier, retrospectively reinterpreted cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11905374/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Infectious salmon anemia virus
EPP.common.name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event.summary: In March 2000, ISA was first suspected and then confirmed in a salmon sea farm in the Faroe Islands, initiating an epidemic that raged from 2000 to 2005 and affected most of the archipelago’s salmon farms. The disease spread widely among marine sites, causing very high cumulative mortalities and leading to near collapse of the Faroese salmon aquaculture industry, with extensive depopulation and trade restrictions imposed by the EU and OIE. A complete restructuring of production with large fallowing zones and strict biosecurity, combined with eradication of infected stocks, eventually ended the epidemic by 2005; no further clinical ISA was seen until a re‑emergent outbreak in 2014.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High concentration of farms in fjords with limited water exchange, lack of pre‑existing ISA‑specific management plans, and extensive movements of fish, equipment and personnel promoted rapid island‑wide dissemination; limited early fallowing and zoning delayed control. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of virulent HPR‑deleted ISAV variants from a background of non‑virulent HPR0 viruses circulating in Faroese broodstock, smolt farms and marine sites, representing a transition from endemic low‑pathogenic infection to highly virulent epidemic strains.
Review: review – The Faroese 2000–2005 epidemic is correctly captured as one of the most severe ISA events globally, with near collapse of the local industry. It is not a global first_detection (Norway 1984) and occurs in a subregion where ISA was already known, so first_detection has been set to false. Given strong evidence that virulent HPR‑deleted variants emerged from endemic HPR0 in Faroese production, coding as re_emergence is appropriate. Country name has been aligned with the Country sheet (“Faroe Islands”) while retaining the first detection year.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Infectious salmon anemia virus
EPP.common.name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event.summary: From 2003 to 2005, Norway experienced a renewed cluster of 32 ISA outbreaks distributed along much of its coast, despite earlier success in reducing cases after the 1990 peak. The disease reappeared at multiple marine sites, with variable clinical severity and substantial local mortalities, prompting renewed concern about farm‑to‑farm spread. Genotyping and epidemiological investigation showed that many outbreaks were linked by shared viral genogroups and risk factors such as proximity and operational contact, and strengthened biosecurity plus rapid depopulation again reduced annual outbreak numbers after 2005.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Horizontal transmission associated with geographic proximity of farms, shared workboats and service infrastructure, and movements of fish contributed to spread; increasing farm biomass and complex contact networks created recurrent opportunities for re‑introduction. Internal mechanisms: Multiple ISAV genogroups circulated, with evidence that virulent HPR‑deleted variants arose repeatedly from non‑virulent HPR0 backgrounds and then spread locally, representing recurrent re‑emergence driven by mutation and selection for virulence under farming conditions.
Review: review – Retained as a major post‑control resurgence in Norway, but recoded from a combined re_occurrence + re_emergence to re_emergence only. The 2003–2005 cluster occurred in a long‑affected subregion, and molecular work shows repeated emergence of pathogenic HPR‑deleted variants from HPR0; this fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by viral change. Using only re_emergence avoids overlapping event‑type labels, which are intended to be mutually exclusive except for co‑occurrence with intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Infectious salmon anemia virus

Review: review – New event row added: the 2007–2008 nationwide Mongolian epizootic, with ≈459,000 equine cases and ≈24,600 deaths, is explicitly described in CDC and Mongolian studies as one of the world’s largest EI outbreaks and was missing from the original list. It is best classified as re-emergence of EI in an already affected Eastern Asia subregion driven by introduction and expansion of Florida clade 2 viruses; the summary and drivers synthesize data from Mongolian field investigations and subsequent phylogenetic analyses.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Equine influenza virus, EIV
Host: Horses (racehorses, breeding stock, pleasure and working horses; some spillover to dogs in close contact)
Event.summary: In August 2007, Australia detected its first-ever outbreak of equine influenza H3N8 when imported horses in a quarantine station near Sydney tested positive and the virus escaped into local horse populations, rapidly causing large-scale outbreaks in New South Wales and Queensland. Within weeks, tens of thousands of horses across eastern Australia developed respiratory disease, prompting nationwide movement bans and the cancellation of major racing events, with the outbreak lasting into early 2008 before intensive surveillance, ring vaccination and strict movement controls succeeded in eradicating the virus. Australia regained equine influenza–free status in 2008 after no further transmission was detected and emergency vaccination programs were halted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: international movement of horses with inadequate or breached quarantine procedures introduced Florida clade 1 H3N8 into a fully naïve national herd; dense horse populations around racing and breeding hubs and frequent long-distance horse transport allowed rapid dissemination. Internal mechanisms: the introduced Florida clade 1 virus was highly transmissible in naïve horses, leading to explosive spread; although not unusually virulent per se, its transmission efficiency and the immunological naivety of Australian horses resulted in an exceptional epidemic, with documented spillover into dogs in close contact with infected horses.
Review: retain – Australia’s 2007–2008 epidemic was the first EI incursion into Oceania and involved roughly 70,000 infected horses on thousands of premises with major economic losses; classification as first detection in the region and inter-continental emergence is well supported by OIE and national reports, and the geographic fields are correct.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Equine influenza virus, EIV
Host: Horses and other equids (including racehorses, police and military horses, and working equids)
Event.summary: Starting in June 2008, India reported widespread outbreaks of equine influenza H3N8, first recognized in Katra (Jammu and Kashmir) and then spreading over the following year to at least ten other states, affecting diverse equine populations. The epizootic caused extensive respiratory disease, disrupting racing, police and military horse operations and equestrian events, and prompted a national response including restrictions on equine movement and emergency vaccination campaigns. By mid‑2009 the outbreak had subsided as vaccination coverage improved and herd immunity increased, but Florida clade 2 viruses became established in Indian equine populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: large-scale movement of horses for religious pilgrimages, military duties, racing and shows, combined with low baseline vaccination coverage and limited early surveillance, facilitated rapid geographic spread across Indian states. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analysis showed the outbreak virus belonged to Florida clade 2 within the American lineage, closely related to viruses in Mongolia and China, reflecting regional circulation and antigenic drift that allowed efficient transmission in India’s equine populations and necessitated vaccine updates.
Review: review – Adjusted emergence-type classification: EI had already caused a major epidemic in India (and Southern Asia) in 1987, so the 2008–2009 multi-state epidemic is best treated as re-emergence driven by introduction of Florida clade 2 viruses rather than intra-continental emergence into a previously unaffected subregion. Country, timing, host description and primary sources appear accurate, but precise national burden estimates should be revisited if finer quantification is required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Equine influenza virus, EIV
Host: Horses (nomadic and semi‑nomadic herds central to pastoral livelihoods)
Event.summary: In mid‑2011, Mongolia experienced another nationwide epizootic of equine influenza H3N8, with outbreaks first detected near Ulaanbaatar and then spreading across multiple aimags following national horse racing events, affecting tens of thousands of horses. The outbreak caused high morbidity, significantly impacting transportation, herding and rural economies, and molecular analyses linked the causative Florida clade 2 virus closely to strains from the 2007–2008 Mongolian and Central Asian outbreaks. As movement restrictions, natural immunity and targeted vaccination took effect, reported cases decreased, and international assessments considered this a recurrence of previously circulating Florida clade 2 lineage rather than a wholly new introduction.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: traditional nomadic management with extensive mingling of herds, mass gatherings at national horse racing festivals (Naadam), and long-distance seasonal movements provided strong opportunities for virus dissemination; limited systematic vaccination programs in rural areas left many horses susceptible. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak virus represented continued evolution within Florida clade 2 but remained closely related to earlier Mongolian strains, suggesting lineage persistence and re-amplification rather than emergence of a novel genetic variant.
Review: review – Re-classified this episode as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence: genetic analyses show 2011 viruses to be very closely related to those from the massive 2007–2008 Mongolian outbreak, with external drivers (mass horse movements and limited vaccination) playing the dominant role. A separate row has been added for the 2007–2008 nationwide epizootic to capture that earlier, even larger event.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: HPAI in wild birds
Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2002]
Host: Wild and park waterfowl (geese, ducks, swans), other free‑living wild birds (egrets, herons, gulls, pigeons, sparrows), plus captive flamingos in urban parks
Event.summary: In December 2002, outbreaks of highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza occurred in waterfowl and other wild birds in two public parks in Hong Kong SAR, China, with deaths in wild migratory and resident birds as well as captive collections. The event expanded through December 2002–January 2003 with continued deaths in ducks, geese, swans, herons, gulls, pigeons and passerines, prompting intensive surveillance and culling of poultry to remove sources of infection. The outbreaks were brought under control by depopulation of poultry in live‑bird markets and enhanced biosecurity, and no sustained transmission in wild birds in Hong Kong was reported thereafter, though the episode highlighted wild birds as a susceptible host system for HPAI H5N1.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close contact between infected poultry and park waterfowl, high bird density in urban parks and live‑bird markets, and mixing of domestic ducks and wild birds facilitated spillover. Internal mechanisms: The re‑emergent 2002 H5N1 lineage showed increased virulence in ducks and the ability to cause systemic infection and high mortality in multiple wild bird species, reflecting novel genotype combinations and increased pathogenicity in waterfowl.
Review: review – Event correctly represents the first well‑documented lethal HPAI H5N1 outbreak in wild birds (Hong Kong parks, 2002–2003). To align with the near‑mutually‑exclusive event‑type rules, 'first_detection' has been set to false, leaving 'first_global_emergence' as the sole primary classification for this host system. Geography, years, host description, and sources remain appropriate; the non‑primary Wikipedia source has been dropped in favor of peer‑reviewed articles.
