EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Swine influenza virus (Influenza A virus of swine; main subtypes H1N1, H1N2, H3N2)
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus)
Event.summary: In 1998, severe respiratory disease outbreaks occurred in multiple US swine herds, and virological investigation identified novel H3N2 triple‑reassortant swine influenza A viruses containing gene segments from human, avian and classical swine lineages. Over 1998–2000 these triple‑reassortant H3N2 viruses rapidly spread across major US pig‑producing regions, displacing classical H1N1 as the dominant cause of swine influenza and generating associated H1N2 and reassortant H1N1 variants. By 2000, the novel H3N2 reassortants were widely established in US swine, fundamentally changing the genetic landscape of swine influenza there.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high‑density, year‑round intensive pig production in the US Midwest, frequent animal movements, and close contact with humans and birds in production systems facilitated co‑infection and reassortment. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (triple‑reassortant H3N2 with human, avian and swine genes), Enhanced Transmission/Adaptation in swine (efficient pig‑to‑pig spread), and rapid Geographic Range Expansion within US herds once established.
Review: retain – Correctly captures the well-documented 1998 emergence and rapid spread of triple‑reassortant H3N2 swine influenza in US pigs; geography, timing and classification as a re‑emergence event in a previously affected subregion are appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Host: Primarily intensively reared turkeys and chickens in high-density poultry areas of northern Italy (Veneto, Lombardia); LPAI H7N1 also detected in other domestic birds (guinea fowl, quail, pheasants, ducks, ostriches).
Event.summary: In late March 1999, low pathogenic H7N1 avian influenza virus was detected in turkeys and chickens in the densely populated poultry regions of northern Italy, marking the start of a large LPAI epidemic that spread through commercial flocks. Over 1999–2000 the virus caused hundreds of outbreaks and, after several months of circulation, mutated to a highly pathogenic H7N1 variant that led to mass mortality in turkeys and chickens and the culling or death of over 13–16 million birds. Intensive stamping‑out, movement controls and depopulation in affected areas progressively eliminated the epidemic lineage, and by 2001 surveillance showed only sporadic detections and eventual disappearance after major changes in industry biosecurity and vaccination policies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high poultry density and intensive turkey and chicken production in the Po Valley, together with extensive movements of live birds and shared equipment between farms and slaughterhouses and limited early surveillance, facilitated rapid spread of LPAI H7N1 before strict control measures were implemented. Internal mechanisms: emergence and evolution of a novel H7N1 lineage within Italian poultry, including stepwise genetic changes in the HA cleavage site that increased virulence and converted an initially low-pathogenic virus into a highly pathogenic form, making this a classic example of re-emergence driven by viral evolution in a densely populated poultry system.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12062787/))
Review: Retain. The Italian 1999–2001 H7N1 epidemic is correctly captured as a major LPAI episode that evolved into HPAI, with appropriate geography (Italy/Southern Europe) and host description. Classification as re-emergence (due to mutation of an LPAI virus to HPAI in a region where avian influenza was already known) is consistent with project definitions and supported by detailed outbreak analyses.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12062787/))

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Host: Commercial broiler, layer and breeder chickens and backyard poultry throughout Pakistan; G1-lineage H9N2 LPAI viruses (particularly genotype A5) becoming the dominant avian influenza subtype.
Event.summary: In 1998, low pathogenic H9N2 avian influenza was first reported in commercial chickens in Pakistan, introducing a new LPAI subtype into a rapidly expanding poultry industry already affected by other avian influenza subtypes. Through the early 2000s, H9N2 spread widely in broiler and layer flocks, causing recurrent respiratory disease outbreaks and substantial mortality and egg-production losses, with major epidemics reported in densely populated poultry areas such as Karachi and Punjab. By the mid-2000s and into the 2010s, H9N2 had become hyper-endemic in Pakistani poultry, prompting widespread vaccination and control efforts, yet the virus continued to circulate and occasionally infected humans, illustrating a long-running re-emergence driven by an established poultry-adapted lineage.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Densely concentrated commercial poultry production near major urban centres, frequent movements of birds and eggs between farms and live bird markets, inadequate farm-level biosecurity, and co-infections with other respiratory pathogens fostered rapid establishment and persistence of H9N2 across Pakistan. Internal mechanisms: introduction and subsequent evolution of G1-lineage H9N2 viruses, with genotype A5 and related variants becoming dominant, acquiring gene segments through reassortment and mutations associated with mammalian receptor binding and efficient replication in chickens, fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by pathogen change in a region where LPAI was already present.([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/world-s-poultry-science-journal/article/abs/emerging-threat-of-h9n2-viruses-in-poultry-of-pakistan-and-vaccination-strategy/FC522C91F1147508165198500E4E2D6C))
Review: Retain (added new event). Pakistan’s long-running H9N2 LPAI epizootic, beginning in 1998 and now endemic with large documented economic losses and occasional human infections, is widely recognised as one of the most important H9N2 foci globally and was missing from the original dataset.([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/world-s-poultry-science-journal/article/abs/emerging-threat-of-h9n2-viruses-in-poultry-of-pakistan-and-vaccination-strategy/FC522C91F1147508165198500E4E2D6C)) It is therefore added as a major re-emergence event in Southern Asia.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Host: Commercial and backyard chickens, turkeys and quail in Egypt; LPAI H9N2 co-circulating with endemic HPAI H5N1 in poultry.
Event.summary: In early 2010, active surveillance in Egyptian poultry first identified H9N2 low pathogenic avian influenza in broiler chickens in northern Egypt, and soon afterwards in turkeys and quail, indicating introduction of this subtype into North African poultry. During 2011–2013 the virus spread widely and became enzootic in commercial and backyard flocks, often detected alongside endemic H5N1, and was associated with respiratory disease, reduced egg production and substantial economic losses. Following this initial explosive spread, H9N2 became entrenched and diversified into several closely related clusters in Egypt, with routine detection in surveillance and concern about reassortment with H5 and other avian influenza viruses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely importation of infected birds or hatching eggs from neighbouring Middle Eastern countries where H9N2 is endemic, dense mixed-species poultry production with limited biosecurity, and co-circulation of multiple respiratory pathogens facilitated establishment and spread; live bird markets and backyard flocks provided additional maintenance reservoirs. Internal mechanisms: introduction of G1-like H9N2 viruses that subsequently diversified within Egypt, with genetic markers for mammalian adaptation and reassortment with wild-bird-origin gene segments, representing a clear re-emergence of LPAI driven by viral adaptation in a new ecological and geographic setting.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6383604/))
Review: Retain with corrections. Multiple sources agree that G1-lineage H9N2 was first detected in Egyptian poultry in 2010, with rapid diversification and endemic establishment thereafter.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6383604/)) In the original row this episode was incorrectly coded as both "first_detection" and "inter-continental emergence"; LPAI (and H9N2) were already well documented globally and in other African countries (e.g. Libya 2006, Tunisia 2010–2012), so under the project rules it should be treated as a re-emergence event within Africa rather than a first or inter-continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Swine influenza virus, SIV
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), with zoonotic spillover to humans at agricultural fairs
Event.summary: Around 2010–2011, U.S. surveillance detected variant H3N2 swine influenza viruses (trH3N2) in pigs that carried the internal TRIG cassette and acquired the matrix (M) gene from the 2009 H1N1pdm09 virus, with infections documented in exhibition and commercial herds and occasional human infections linked to agricultural fairs. Over the next several years, these reassortant H3N2 viruses spread within U.S. swine populations and were repeatedly associated with human variant H3N2 (H3N2v) cases, including a multi-state outbreak in 2012 with hundreds of fair-associated infections, highlighting intense bidirectional transmission at the human–swine interface without causing catastrophic pig mortality but contributing to widespread respiratory disease and production impacts in affected herds. By the mid‑2010s, H3N2 viruses carrying the pH1N1 M gene had become part of the diverse North American SIV landscape, continuing to reassort with H1 lineages in pigs and persisting as an important zoonotic risk during swine exhibitions while being managed in herds through vaccination, improved fair biosecurity, and enhanced surveillance rather than being eliminated.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense mixing of pigs from multiple sources at agricultural fairs and exhibitions, along with close human–pig contact, facilitated amplification and cross‑species transmission of the novel H3N2 variants; movement of pigs between production sites and variable vaccine match further supported their spread and persistence in commercial and exhibition herds. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence via reassortment between endemic triple‑reassortant H3N2 SIVs and the H1N1pdm09 virus resulted in H3N2 viruses carrying the pH1N1 M gene, which may enhance transmissibility and adaptation; this constitutes a re-emergence driven by genetic change and recurrent host expansion (frequent spillover to humans) within an already SIV-endemic subregion.
Review: Review. The event correctly describes the emergence in U.S. pigs of H3N2 variant viruses that carry the H1N1pdm09 M gene and their strong epidemiologic link to H3N2v human infections associated with agricultural fairs from 2011 onward, as documented in CDC MMWR and EID reports.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6051a4.htm?utm_source=openai)) Classifying this as re-emergence only is appropriate, because these viruses represent a new reassortant genotype within an already SIV-endemic subregion and do not meet the criteria for first/global, intra- or inter-continental emergence of the EPP. To improve the relevance of sources, I replaced a tangential Nigerian H5N1/H1N1pdm09 serology paper with targeted CDC MMWR and EID articles on H3N2v transmission at fairs and on subclinical infection in exhibition swine, while retaining the broader CDC swine/variant flu background page. The geography (United States only), time frame (2011–2014) and emphasis on fairs are reasonable simplifications of a complex situation, but this row should be reviewed to confirm that no larger SIV events are being crowded out by this choice.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Swine influenza virus, SIV
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus)
Event.summary: From approximately 2016 onward, surveillance in Chinese pig farms identified a dominant genotype of Eurasian avian-like H1N1 swine influenza, termed G4 EA H1N1, which had arisen through reassortment and began to replace earlier EA H1N1 lineages in pigs, causing endemic respiratory disease across major swine-producing regions of China. Over 2016–2020, G4 EA H1N1 viruses became the predominant H1N1 genotype detected in Chinese pigs and serologic studies found substantial exposure in swine workers, indicating widespread circulation in pigs and frequent human–pig contact with the lineage, though without recognised large human outbreaks to date. By 2020, G4 EA H1N1 was firmly entrenched in Chinese swine populations, continuing to evolve and co-circulate with other SIV lineages and prompting international concern and preparedness activities because of its genetic makeup and demonstrated ability to infect humans, even though pig herds were managed through routine influenza control measures rather than emergency depopulation.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and consolidation of China’s intensive pig industry, high pig densities, and complex live-pig marketing chains favoured replacement of older EA H1N1 lineages by fitter reassortant G4 viruses; relatively sparse systematic swine influenza surveillance before 2016 allowed the lineage to spread widely before its predominance was fully recognised. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence through reassortment between Eurasian avian-like H1N1 swine viruses and internal genes from H1N1pdm09 and triple-reassortant swine influenza lineages created the G4 genotype, characterised by a specific constellation of polymerase, nucleoprotein, matrix and non-structural genes that support efficient replication in pigs and infection of humans; this is a clear re-emergence event involving genetic innovation and geographic range expansion within Chinese pig populations.
Review: Review. This event accurately summarises the emergence and rapid predominance of the G4 genotype of Eurasian avian-like H1N1 swine influenza viruses in Chinese pigs since about 2016, as described in the original PNAS report and subsequent risk assessments and EID analyses that show G4 viruses becoming the main EA H1N1 genotype and infecting a notable fraction of swine workers.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/swine-flu/comm-resources/cdc-prepare-swine-flu.html?utm_source=openai)) Coding it as re-emergence (a novel reassortant genotype within a long‑infected host population) and not as a first or inter-continental emergence event is consistent with the project definitions. To strengthen the evidence base, I replaced the general Swine influenza Wikipedia link with the primary PNAS article on G4 and an EID paper on its zoonotic threat, while retaining the CDC preparedness page that contextualises public-health concern. The year range (2016–2020) captures the documented rise to predominance but may need updating as more recent surveillance shows whether G4 remains dominant; therefore this row is flagged for expert review rather than unconditional retention.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Jaagsiekte sheep retrovirus
EPP.common.name: JSRV, Sheep pulmonary adenocarcinoma virus
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event.summary: Origin: In the mid‑2010s, ovine pulmonary adenocarcinoma was identified histologically and by PCR as an incidental finding in sheep from two flocks in Southern Jutland, Denmark, representing the first documented, laboratory‑confirmed OPA cases in the country. Development: A subsequent national abattoir-based survey of 1,480 sheep and lamb lungs in 2016 found no confirmed OPA cases, suggesting that OPA prevalence remained very low or highly focal despite earlier detections. End: The incidental detections and the negative 2016 survey indicated that JSRV was present but probably at low prevalence in Denmark, prompting recommendations for continued surveillance using histology and immunohistochemistry rather than gross inspection alone.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via live animal trade or shared breeding stock from neighboring European countries where OPA is endemic; diagnostic intensification (histology, IHC, PCR) enabled detection of otherwise overlooked cases. Internal mechanisms: No specific evidence of a novel JSRV strain or altered pathogenicity was presented; the event mainly reflects detection of low‑level endemic infection rather than biological change.
Review: retain – The Danish article explicitly notes that OPA had previously been detected only as incidental PCR‑confirmed cases in two Southern Jutland flocks, and that its national prevalence was unknown before this work, supporting use of first_detection for Denmark. Time and place (Europe, Northern Europe, Denmark) are correct. The 2014 date is inferred rather than directly stated in the source and may need refinement from the original Maedi–Visna prevalence study cited as reference 18, so this event should be kept but the exact year could be checked in a future pass.([dvt.ddd.dk](https://dvt.ddd.dk/bladarkiv/2018/nr-10/proportion-of-ovine-pulmonary-adenocarcinoma-in-danish-sheep-at-slaughter/))

EPP.scientific.name: Jaagsiekte sheep retrovirus
EPP.common.name: JSRV, Sheep pulmonary adenocarcinoma virus
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event.summary: Origin: Increasing numbers of sheep in some Mongolian regions were observed with chronic respiratory signs and lung tumors consistent with pulmonary adenomatosis, prompting efforts to confirm the etiologic agent. Development: A 2021 study performed histopathology and nested PCR on lung tissues from clinically affected slaughtered sheep, demonstrating typical OPA lesions and amplifying JSRV proviral 5′‑LTR sequences, which clustered phylogenetically with Chinese, American, Indian, and Scottish strains, suggesting introduction from abroad rather than a distinct local lineage. End: The work established the presence of exogenous JSRV causing OPA in Mongolian sheep and concluded that rapid molecular diagnostic capacity was needed to manage a disease whose incidence appeared to be rising in some areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via international or regional trade in breeding stock from countries where JSRV is endemic; extensive grazing and limited routine post‑mortem diagnostics may have allowed silent spread before recognition. Internal mechanisms: Sequenced proviral fragments did not form a distinct Mongolian clade but grouped with existing global strains, indicating geographic range expansion via animal movement rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: retain – The Mongolian Journal of Agricultural Sciences paper describes the first molecular confirmation of OPA/JSRV in Mongolia and explicitly interprets the infection as likely imported from abroad, matching the intended use of first_detection at the country level. Eastern Asia/Mongolia coding is correct and the event is a reasonable inclusion among major modern emergence events given the size of the national sheep population and evidence for increasing case recognition.([mongoliajol.info](https://mongoliajol.info/index.php/MJAS/article/view/1910))

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus japonicum
EPP.common.name: JEV
Host: Domestic pigs; Culex mosquitoes; (humans as spillover hosts)
Event.summary: Until the late 2000s, Tibet on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau was considered non‑endemic for Japanese encephalitis because its high altitude was thought to preclude sustained mosquito–vertebrate transmission cycles. In 2009, however, investigations following human JE cases identified JEV‑specific IgM antibodies in one‑third of sampled piglets in Mainling and Medog counties and viral RNA in local Culex mosquitoes, demonstrating that pigs were newly participating in local transmission cycles in this previously unsuitable high‑altitude environment. Subsequent surveillance confirmed ongoing, though still relatively limited, JEV circulation in plateau areas, marking a durable range expansion of the virus in Chinese domestic pig populations rather than a one‑off incursion that disappeared.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Warming temperatures, changes in land use and agriculture, and development of pig production and irrigation in parts of Tibet likely improved habitat suitability for Culex vectors and facilitated introduction and maintenance of JEV. Internal mechanisms: The event represents geographic range expansion into high‑altitude ecological zones where JEV transmission had not previously been sustained, consistent with re‑emergence driven by climatic and ecological shifts combined with the virus’s inherent capacity to exploit new environmental niches, rather than by a specifically identified new genotype unique to Tibet.
Review: retain – This event is well supported by primary data showing IgM‑positive piglets and infected Culex mosquitoes in high‑altitude counties of Tibet previously regarded as JE‑free. Coding as re‑emergence (range expansion into new ecological zones within an already affected country and subregion) without intra‑/inter‑continental tags is appropriate, and Eastern Asia/China placement matches the UNSD regional scheme.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus japonicum
EPP.common.name: JEV
Host: Humans; potential reservoir hosts such as domestic pigs and aquatic birds and local Culex mosquitoes are inferred but were not directly investigated in this event.
Event.summary: In March 2016, during a large yellow fever outbreak in Angola, genomic analysis of blood from a 19‑year‑old man in Cunene Province who had not travelled outside Angola revealed co‑infection with yellow fever virus and Japanese encephalitis virus, with phylogenetic analysis showing the JEV genome to be genotype III closely related to Asian strains; this provided the first documented evidence of locally acquired JEV infection on the African continent. Only this single human case with detectable JEV RNA was identified, but the finding in a rural Angolan resident, in a setting where competent Culex vectors and potential amplifying hosts such as pigs and aquatic birds are present, indicated that JEV had been introduced into, or was newly recognized within, African transmission cycles. After the yellow fever epidemic waned, no further confirmed JEV cases were reported from Angola, but the event prompted international calls for targeted serologic and entomologic surveillance in humans and animals in Angola and neighboring countries to determine whether the virus had become established.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased human movement and trade between Asia and Africa during the 2010s likely provided opportunities for introduction of JEV into Angola, and extensive clinical sampling during the yellow fever outbreak enabled its unexpected detection; the presence of irrigated agriculture, domestic pigs and waterbirds, and competent Culex vectors in southern Angola provides ecological conditions in which JEV could circulate once introduced. Internal mechanisms: The Angolan virus belonged to known genotype III rather than a novel lineage, so this episode is best interpreted as an inter‑continental geographic range expansion of existing Asian JEV lineages into Africa, facilitated by human and possibly bird or mosquito movement, rather than by documented viral genetic innovation.
Review: review – New event added to capture the first documented autochthonous JEV infection in Africa (Angola, 2016), which is widely cited as the continent’s initial evidence of local transmission and is clearly among the most important post‑1990 emergence events despite direct data only from a human case. Classified as inter‑continental emergence into Middle Africa because the infection was locally acquired and not imported. Animal hosts (pigs/birds) are inferred but not directly documented, so this row should be retained but flagged for expert review of host listing and to confirm that including a primarily human case in the animal‑host sheet is acceptable for the project’s cross‑host framing.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus japonicum
EPP.common.name: JEV
Host: Commercially reared domestic pigs
Event.summary: Between about 2017 and 2021, serological surveys of commercially reared pigs in four states of southwestern Nigeria found JEV‑specific IgG antibodies in roughly one‑third of sampled animals, providing the first evidence that pigs in Africa had been naturally exposed to Japanese encephalitis virus. These findings, in unvaccinated pigs across multiple farms and age groups, indicate that local transmission cycles involving pigs and competent Culex vectors had become established or had been introduced into West Africa, even though no large, clinically recognized animal or human outbreaks were reported at the time. Following publication of these data, JEV exposure in Nigerian pigs has been recognized as a potential emerging zoonotic risk, prompting calls for integrated surveillance in pigs, vectors and humans to clarify the extent and dynamics of this new African focus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Presence of JEV mosquito vectors such as Culex tritaeniorhynchus in southwestern Nigeria, growth and intensification of pig farming with limited biosecurity, and suitable climatic conditions likely enabled introduction and silent circulation of JEV in pig herds following its initial appearance in Africa. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not yet identify a distinct novel genotype or phenotype; this event is interpreted as intra‑continental emergence of JEV from its first recognized African focus into a new UNSD subregion (Western Africa) and establishment of transmission in domestic pigs, rather than as a separate inter‑continental emergence or genotype‑driven re‑emergence.
Review: review – The underlying pig serosurvey is robust and documents substantial JEV antibody prevalence in unvaccinated pigs in southwestern Nigeria, supporting inclusion of this event as a major development for animal hosts in Africa. However, the event type has been corrected from inter‑continental emergence to intra‑continental emergence, because the first documented African JEV infection occurred in Angola (Middle Africa) in 2016; the Nigerian findings therefore represent spread into a new UNSD subregion (Western Africa) and first confirmation in domestic pigs, not the initial continental incursion. Given remaining uncertainty about possible cross‑reactivity in serologic assays and limited virologic confirmation, this row should be retained but kept flagged for expert review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus japonicum
EPP.common.name: JEV
Host: Domestic pigs; feral pigs; Culex mosquitoes; sentinel chickens; an alpaca; (humans as spillover hosts)
Event.summary: In late 2021 and early 2022, Japanese encephalitis virus was detected in piggeries across south‑eastern mainland Australia (Victoria, New South Wales, southern Queensland and South Australia), far south of its previous known range in northern Australia and the Torres Strait, signalling a major epizootic in domestic and feral pigs. By late 2022, JEV had been reported from more than 80 commercial piggeries and feral pig populations across multiple states, with concurrent detections in mosquitoes, sentinel chickens, an alpaca and humans; molecular analysis showed involvement of genotype IV, a lineage not previously reported in Australia. With the onset of cooler, drier conditions and implementation of vector‑control, animal movement controls and targeted vaccination of at‑risk humans, reported transmission declined, though JEV is now considered an emerging endemic risk in southern Australia’s pig‑farming and wetland regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Prolonged La Niña conditions and widespread flooding created extensive mosquito breeding habitats along river systems such as the Murray, while high densities of domestic and feral pigs and waterbirds in irrigated agricultural landscapes provided abundant amplifying hosts; movement of infected birds and mosquitoes likely facilitated rapid spread among piggeries. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of JEV genotype IV in Australia, coupled with southward geographic range expansion into temperate regions with largely naïve pig and human populations, constitutes a clear re‑emergence based on viral genetic change and range expansion within an already affected country, with potential implications for transmission efficiency and overwintering in local vectors and hosts.
Review: retain – The large 2021–2022 genotype IV–associated outbreak in eastern and southern Australian piggeries is a clearly major epizootic, with strong documentation of >80 affected piggeries, feral pig involvement and multiple human cases. Treating this as a re‑emergence event (new genotype and major southward range expansion within Oceania, rather than a new continent) is consistent with the definitions and with prior JEV presence in northern Australia; geography and sources are appropriate, so the row should be kept as is.

EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: RHD virus, RHDV (RHDV1/GI.1 and RHDV2/GI.2)
Host: Domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event.summary: In late 1988, rabbit haemorrhagic disease was introduced into Mexico, likely via imported frozen rabbit meat from China, leading to a major epidemic of RHDV1 in domestic rabbitries from 1989 to 1991. Mexican authorities implemented extensive stamping‑out, movement controls, disinfection and serologic surveillance, ultimately destroying more than 120,000 rabbits as part of eradication efforts. The last outbreak was reported in 1992, and Mexico was declared free of RHD thereafter, with subsequent detections linked to later RHDV2 introductions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction through contaminated rabbit meat or live rabbits from endemic regions, rapid spread via movement of animals and contaminated equipment between farms, and lack of prior awareness or immunity. Internal mechanisms: establishment of virulent RHDV1 (RHDVa) in a naïve domestic rabbit population in the Americas; no new genotype is implicated, and disease control relied on depopulation and movement restrictions rather than evolutionary changes in the virus.
Review: review – Retain as the key event representing the first introduction and subsequent eradication of RHDV1 in the Americas. Corrected: (i) event years adjusted from 1990–1992 to 1988–1992 to reflect the documented start of the epidemic in late 1988 with control and eradication completed by 1992; (ii) this remains classified as an inter‑continental emergence because it is the first recognized occurrence of RHDV in the Western Hemisphere. Country and sub‑region coding (Mexico in South America | Central America) are consistent with the project’s country sheet.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: RHD virus, RHDV (RHDV1/GI.1 and RHDV2/GI.2)
Sub.regions: Australia and New Zealand (Australia focus for this event)
Host: Wild and domestic European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event.summary: Serologic data indicate that RHDV2 was circulating in Australian wild rabbits by spring 2014 and was first confirmed virologically in May 2015 in a wild rabbit in New South Wales. Within roughly 18 months, RHDV2 had spread across all Australian states and territories, rapidly displacing existing RHDV1 field strains and causing average declines of around 60% in monitored wild rabbit populations. By 2016–2017, RHDV2 had become the predominant lagovirus biocontrol agent in Australia, complicating planned releases of additional RHDV1 strains but significantly suppressing rabbit numbers in many regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive connectivity of wild rabbit populations across open landscapes, mechanical spread by insect vectors and fomites, and strong selection pressure from existing RHDV1 biocontrol leading to partial host immunity. Internal mechanisms: introduction and rapid geographic expansion of RHDV2/GI.2 with apparent fitness advantages over RHDV1, including infection of younger age classes, broader host range and partial vaccine/immunity escape, resulting in both inter‑continental emergence of GI.2 into Oceania and re‑emergence of RHD as a more effective biocontrol agent.
Review: retain – Keep as a major event, representing the rapid establishment and dominance of RHDV2 as a biocontrol agent in Australia. Classification as both inter‑continental emergence (for GI.2 into Oceania) and re‑emergence (novel genotype supplanting existing RHDV1 in an already affected sub‑region) is consistent with the project rules. Country, timing and impact are well supported by primary sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Humans; reservoir hosts including dogs, rats and other peridomestic mammals; cattle and pigs suspected as additional sources
Event.summary: In October–November 1995, rural communities in western Nicaragua experienced an epidemic of acute febrile illness with severe pulmonary hemorrhage after periods of intense rainfall and flooding, and investigations identified leptospirosis caused mainly by L. interrogans serovars in the Canicola and Pyrogenes groups as the principal etiology, with more than 2,000 febrile illnesses evaluated and dozens of deaths. The outbreak developed rapidly among residents heavily exposed to creeks, irrigation channels and flooded fields contaminated with urine from infected dogs, rodents and livestock, and Leptospira were isolated from both human patients and local animals. Transmission declined after floodwaters receded, risk factors such as walking in creeks and dog ownership were publicized, and targeted environmental and rodent-control measures were implemented, but the episode signalled that severe pulmonary hemorrhagic leptospirosis could emerge in Central America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Exceptional rainfall and flooding inundated rural settlements and farmlands, increasing human contact with water and soil contaminated by urine from infected dogs, rodents, pigs and cattle, while limited sanitation and protective equipment amplified exposure. Internal mechanisms: The event involved highly pathogenic L. interrogans serovars already circulating in local animal reservoirs rather than a demonstrably new genotype, so it represents environmentally driven re-occurrence of virulent lineages rather than de novo microbial evolution.
Review: Retain – Event corresponds to the well-documented 1995 western Nicaragua epidemic with pulmonary hemorrhage; geography and timing match, and classification as re-occurrence (environmentally driven resurgence in an already endemic Central American setting) is appropriate. Minor textual clean-up applied by removing inline citation tags from the host field; case and death magnitudes are within the documented range from CDC/MMWR and subsequent analyses.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Humans; urban rats as primary reservoir; dogs and livestock present in affected communities
Event.summary: In 1996, the city of Salvador in northeast Brazil and the state of Rio de Janeiro experienced major urban leptospirosis outbreaks after heavy seasonal rains and flooding, with Rio de Janeiro alone reporting about 1,425 cases and 22 deaths and other coastal cities also affected. The epidemics were concentrated in densely populated low-income neighborhoods with poor drainage, accumulated refuse and heavy rat infestation, where residents were extensively exposed to contaminated floodwater. As rainfall decreased and municipal authorities implemented emergency rodent control, drainage works and public health messaging, case numbers fell, although flood-associated urban leptospirosis has remained a recurring problem in Brazilian coastal cities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intense rainfall and flooding in rapidly urbanizing, informal settlements with inadequate storm-water and solid-waste management led to explosive growth of rat populations and widespread contamination of floodwaters with Leptospira, while poverty, crowding and limited access to protective gear heightened human exposure. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate efficient transmission of endemic L. interrogans serovar Copenhageni and related serovars maintained in rodents rather than emergence of a novel genotype, so the episode is best interpreted as a severe, environmentally driven re-occurrence.
Review: Retain – Large, well-characterized urban outbreaks in Rio de Janeiro and Salvador with >1,000 cases and documented deaths; regional coding (South America/South America, Brazil) and re-occurrence classification are consistent with PAHO and Lancet descriptions. Only cosmetic change was removal of inline citation markers from the host field.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Humans; cattle and water buffalo as major livestock reservoirs; pigs and dogs; commensal rodents
Event.summary: During the late 1990s, Thailand saw a steep rise in leptospirosis incidence, culminating in a nationwide peak in 2000 with around 14,285 reported human cases, particularly in the northeastern rice-growing provinces. The outbreak was concentrated among agricultural workers exposed to flooded paddy fields and irrigation water contaminated by urine from infected cattle, buffalo, pigs, dogs and rodents, with serosurveys in livestock showing very high infection prevalence in the same regions. After leptospirosis was recognized nationally as a major flood-associated zoonosis and targeted surveillance, health education and some animal-health interventions were implemented, reported incidence declined and stabilized at lower but still substantial levels in subsequent years.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/13/1/06-0718_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of rice agriculture, high-density cattle and buffalo grazing in paddy landscapes, and widespread seasonal flooding greatly increased human–animal–water contact, while earlier under-recognition of the disease meant many cases were previously missed but now captured through improved surveillance. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic primarily reflected intense transmission of existing pathogenic L. interrogans serovars maintained in livestock and rodents, rather than a demonstrably new genotype, fitting re-occurrence driven by environmental and agricultural change.
Review: Retain – Thailand’s 2000 peak (≈14,285 cases) is one of the largest modern leptospirosis outbreaks; geographic coding (Asia/South-eastern Asia, Thailand) and classification as re-occurrence (environmental and occupational drivers without clear evidence of novel strains) are appropriate. Host list and narrative correctly emphasize cattle/buffalo and rodents as key reservoirs; only inline citation text in the host field was removed.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Humans; cattle and buffalo; pigs; rodents; dogs
Event.summary: In 2003, Sri Lanka recorded a marked increase in leptospirosis, with about 2,235 notified cases nationwide, representing the country’s first large modern outbreak since systematic surveillance began in the early 1990s. Cases clustered in wet agricultural districts where rice farmers and other rural workers were exposed to waterlogged fields and irrigation channels contaminated with urine from infected cattle, buffalo, pigs, rodents and dogs. Notifications fell after the main rainy season and acute control and awareness efforts, but the event marked the start of a period of recurrent large seasonal epidemics in the country.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High rainfall, paddy agriculture, close contact with infected cattle and buffalo, and rodent infestation in rural areas created ideal conditions for environmental contamination and human exposure, while improved case recognition and reporting increased apparent incidence. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not implicate a particular novel strain or host jump; the outbreak is best interpreted as re-occurrence of endemic L. interrogans lineages under favorable climatic and occupational conditions.
Review: Retain – Surveillance data confirm a substantial national increase (~2,235 cases) in 2003, making this a reasonable choice as the first large modern Sri Lankan epidemic. Subregion and country coding (Asia/Southern Asia, Sri Lanka) and re-occurrence classification (environmental and occupational drivers, no clear new strain) are appropriate; host list and sources are adequate, though the primary paper "Leptospirosis in Sri Lanka 2003–2012" should be used rather than generic Wikipedia pages.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Humans; cattle and buffalo; pigs; rodents; dogs
Event.summary: In 2008, Sri Lanka experienced its largest recorded leptospirosis outbreak, with about 7,400–7,500 suspected cases and roughly 200 deaths reported nationally, particularly in districts such as Matale, Kegalle, Kandy and Kurunegala. The epidemic followed periods of heavy rainfall and widespread flooding coinciding with intensive paddy cultivation and close contact with cattle, buffalo, pigs and rodents, and many patients presented with severe pulmonary and multi-organ involvement. After the peak, notifications declined but remained much higher than in the pre-2003 era, indicating that leptospirosis had become a high-incidence, frequently epidemic zoonosis in Sri Lanka.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3163869/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extreme rainfall and flooding, extensive rice agriculture, lack of personal protective equipment for farmers, and gaps in livestock vaccination and rodent control were central in amplifying transmission, while heightened awareness improved reporting. Internal mechanisms: Multiple pathogenic L. interrogans serovars were circulating, but no single novel genotype was clearly linked to the epidemic; re-occurrence driven by climatic and agricultural factors remains the most appropriate classification.
Review: Retain – 2008 is clearly documented as Sri Lanka’s largest leptospirosis outbreak (~7,400 cases, ~200 deaths), and thus belongs among the top global events. Regional coding and classification as re-occurrence (strong climatic and occupational drivers, without clear evidence of a new strain) are correct; event summary has been slightly tightened and cross-checked against national surveillance and detailed outbreak analyses.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Humans; primary reservoirs rats (Rattus spp.) in dense urban settlements; dogs and livestock (notably pigs and cattle) as additional sources contaminating floodwaters
Event.summary: After Typhoon Ondoy (Ketsana) caused catastrophic flooding across Metro Manila in late September 2009, a large leptospirosis outbreak occurred, with Philippine Department of Health reports indicating about 2,299 suspected cases and 178 deaths across 15 hospitals, and detailed investigation at San Lazaro Hospital documenting 471 hospitalized patients and 51 deaths. The epidemic developed rapidly among mostly young male residents of low-lying urban districts who had waded through deep floodwaters contaminated by urine from infected rats, dogs and livestock, and many fatal cases showed pulmonary hemorrhage, acute renal failure and multi-organ dysfunction. Case numbers fell to baseline by early November as floodwaters receded, emergency response and clinical management improved, and public warnings were issued, but the event has since been regarded as a benchmark example of flood-associated urban leptospirosis risk in South-east Asia.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/18/1/10-1892_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: An intense tropical cyclone produced extreme rainfall and prolonged flooding that submerged densely populated, poorly drained urban areas with inadequate drainage, sanitation and solid-waste management, greatly increasing contact with Leptospira-contaminated water; delayed access to care and dialysis further increased mortality. Internal mechanisms: Available data implicate pathogenic L. interrogans serogroups already endemic in local rat populations rather than a new genotype, so this episode is best classified as re-occurrence driven by climatic extremes and urban vulnerability.
Review: Review – New event added because the 2009 Metro Manila outbreak (≈2,300 suspected cases, 178 deaths) is one of the most severe modern leptospirosis epidemics globally and clearly meets the “top-10 impact” criterion. Geography and timing (Asia/South-eastern Asia, Philippines [2009]) and classification as re-occurrence (large flood-associated surge in an already endemic country) are appropriate. Recommend retaining as a major event and, if a strict limit of 10 events is enforced later, considering replacement of smaller-scale episodes such as the Italy Hardjo herd outbreaks or the Puerto Rico 2017 cluster.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Humans; cattle and buffalo; pigs; rodents; dogs
Event.summary: In early 2011, Sri Lanka experienced another major leptospirosis epidemic, with surveillance data indicating about 6,700 suspected cases and 100 deaths nationally, and a particularly intense flood-associated outbreak in the dry-zone district of Anuradhapura. The epidemic was driven by extensive flooding of agricultural land and irrigation schemes, exposing farmers to contaminated water, but molecular analyses showed that many cases in Anuradhapura were caused by Leptospira kirschneri, a species not previously recognized as a common cause of human leptospirosis in the country, and associated with severe cardiac and renal complications. Case numbers declined after the rainy season ended and control measures were strengthened, yet the shift in infecting species and severe clinical pattern highlighted a genuine re-emergence phenomenon within Sri Lanka’s long-standing leptospirosis problem.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3894175/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy rainfall and flooding of irrigation schemes and paddy fields, intense human contact with contaminated surface water, high rodent and livestock infection prevalence, and limited personal protective equipment sustained high transmission risk. Internal mechanisms: Unlike earlier outbreaks dominated by classical L. interrogans serovars, the 2011 Anuradhapura cluster was largely due to L. kirschneri, indicating a shift in the infecting Leptospira species and supporting classification as re-emergence driven in part by changes in pathogen populations rather than purely by environmental factors.
Review: Review – Reclassified from re-occurrence to re-emergence because PLOS NTD analyses show that the 2011 Anuradhapura outbreak was predominantly caused by Leptospira kirschneri, previously not a common human pathogen in Sri Lanka, representing a shift in infecting species. Regional coding and overall description remain valid, but the mechanism section was updated to emphasize this internal pathogen change; human expert review is recommended to confirm the balance between environmental drivers and pathogen evolution.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Dairy cattle; humans occupationally exposed to infected herds
Event.summary: Between 2007 and 2011, two documented abortion outbreaks caused by Leptospira serovar Hardjo (Hardjo-bovis/Hardjo-prajitno complex) were detected in dairy cattle herds in northeastern Italy, a region where bovine leptospirosis was already known to occur. Affected herds experienced increased abortions, stillbirths, infertility and milk drop, and investigations confirmed herd-level leptospiral infection with evidence of chronic carrier cows shedding organisms. Implementation of an integrated outbreak management plan including enhanced biosecurity, whole-herd antibiotic treatment and vaccination against Hardjo controlled clinical disease and reduced shedding, but Hardjo-associated leptospirosis remains an endemic production and zoonotic risk in Italian dairy systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density dairy farming with frequent animal movements between farms, incomplete vaccination against Hardjo in some herds, and environmental exposure to contaminated water and possible wildlife reservoirs allowed within-herd transmission and re-introduction. Internal mechanisms: The outbreaks involved a cattle-adapted Hardjo maintenance serovar already established in Italy rather than a novel genotype, so they are better viewed as re-occurrence of endemic infection facilitated by gaps in herd immunity and management rather than true re-emergence.
Review: Review – Reclassified from re-emergence to re-occurrence because the Italian dairy outbreaks involved Hardjo, a long-established cattle maintenance serovar, with no clear evidence of a new strain or host jump; the main drivers were management practices and incomplete vaccination. The event is genuine but relatively localized (a few herds) compared with very large human outbreaks and continent-wide canine re-emergence; it should therefore be considered a candidate for exclusion if the dataset must be trimmed to the 10 highest-impact global events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Humans; livestock (cattle, pigs); dogs; rodents as major maintenance hosts contaminating surface water
Event.summary: In early 2012, two successive tropical depressions caused severe flooding in western Fiji, leading to the largest recorded leptospirosis outbreak in the Pacific region, with approximately 576 reported cases and around 40–44 deaths and a case fatality near 7%. The epidemic was concentrated in flood-affected rural and peri-urban communities where people were exposed to turbid floodwaters and muddy soils contaminated by urine from infected cattle, pigs, dogs and abundant rodents, and many severe cases presented with pulmonary hemorrhage and acute renal failure. Following intensified clinical awareness, public messaging, and environmental and veterinary interventions, case numbers fell, but recurrent flood-associated leptospirosis outbreaks have continued to pose a major One Health challenge in Fiji.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4731082/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Successive extreme rainfall and flooding events in a tropical island setting with limited sanitation, dense livestock and dog populations, and high rodent abundance dramatically increased human contact with contaminated water and soil, while constraints in diagnostic capacity delayed recognition and treatment. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak appears to have been driven by intense transmission of existing pathogenic L. interrogans serovars endemic in local animal reservoirs rather than emergence of a new genotype, so it is best classified as a severe flood-driven re-occurrence.
Review: Review – New event added because the 2012 Western Fiji outbreak (≈576 cases, ~40–44 deaths) is documented as the largest leptospirosis epidemic in the Pacific and represents a major flood-associated zoonotic event. Coding as Oceania/Melanesia (Fiji [2012]) and as re-occurrence is appropriate given pre-existing endemicity; however, inclusion as a top-10 event should be confirmed by subject-matter experts when balancing global human and animal impact.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Humans; reservoir hosts including rats, dogs and livestock (cattle, pigs) contaminating floodwaters
Event.summary: After Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017, causing widespread flooding and severe damage to water and sanitation infrastructure, surveillance data and retrospective reviews documented several dozen to roughly one hundred suspected and confirmed human leptospirosis cases and at least four confirmed deaths, with some analyses suggesting additional undetected fatalities. The outbreak developed as displaced residents, emergency workers and others were forced to rely on unsafe surface and groundwater sources and were heavily exposed to debris and standing water contaminated by urine from infected rats, dogs and livestock. Reported cases gradually decreased as floodwaters drained, emergency response operations restored safer water supplies, and risk communication and clinical awareness improved, although endemic leptospirosis transmission linked to animal reservoirs has continued on the island.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A major hurricane caused prolonged flooding, disruption of piped water supplies, population displacement, and strain on clinical and laboratory systems, substantially increasing opportunities for exposure to Leptospira-contaminated water and delaying diagnosis and treatment. Internal mechanisms: No evidence indicates the emergence of a new Leptospira strain; the event reflects environmentally and infrastructurally driven re-occurrence of pathogenic L. interrogans maintained in rat and domestic animal populations.
Review: Review – Outbreak is real and clearly hurricane-associated, but reported case numbers (tens to low hundreds of suspected and confirmed cases and a handful of confirmed deaths) are modest compared with very large outbreaks in Thailand, Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Fiji. Classification as re-occurrence and Caribbean/South America coding are appropriate; however, given the aim to capture roughly the 10 most impactful events globally, this Puerto Rico episode should be considered for exclusion or down-weighting in favor of larger outbreaks, while still being noted in narrative reviews because of its political and surveillance implications.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira spp.
EPP.common.name: Leptospira bacteria
Host: Pigs (2600-sow commercial breeding herd)
Event.summary: Around 2000, a large outbreak of leptospirosis occurred in a 2600-sow breeding herd in Thailand, where approximately 5% of sows aborted over a short period, causing a marked spike in reproductive losses. Subsequent investigation using expanded serological testing (including additional serovars sejroe, hardjo, and bratislava) identified Leptospira interrogans serovars Bratislava and Sejroe as the cause of the abortion storm. After herd-wide antimicrobial treatment and implementation of rodent control and feed-box protection to reduce contamination, clinical signs and abortions ceased and the outbreak was brought under control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density intensive swine production with inadequate biosecurity and rodent access to feed likely allowed heavy environmental contamination with leptospires, while absence of targeted vaccination against the causative serovars facilitated rapid spread. Internal mechanisms: Infection of a largely naive breeding herd by already circulating Leptospira interrogans serovars Bratislava and Sejroe, which were only identified after an expanded serologic panel was applied, led to a severe abortion storm; this represents re-occurrence of endemic serovars in a susceptible herd rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: review: Event corresponds closely to a documented abortion storm in a 2600-sow herd in Thailand, but it represents re-occurrence of endemic serovars rather than emergence of a novel strain. Reclassified the event from 're_emergence' to 're_occurrence' and rewrote the mechanism/driver text accordingly; timing (publication year 2000 used as an approximation of outbreak year) and geography (Thailand, South‑eastern Asia) are correct.([digital.car.chula.ac.th](https://digital.car.chula.ac.th/tjvm/vol30/iss3/2/)) Impact is substantial at herd level but smaller than continent‑wide canine and pinniped epizootics, so this row should be kept provisionally and revisited when ranking the global top 10 events for this EPP.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira spp.
EPP.common.name: Leptospira bacteria
Host: Dairy cattle (mixed-age cows in a commercial dairy herd)
Event.summary: In 2015, a dairy herd in northeastern Brazil experienced a major leptospirosis-associated reproductive outbreak in which, between January and July, 17% of 106 cows aborted, 5.7% delivered stillborn calves, and 11.3% showed repeated estrus, indicating substantial herd-level reproductive failure. Serological and epidemiological investigation implicated leptospirosis as the likely primary cause of the abortion and stillbirth cluster. Following implementation of control measures including vaccination, antibiotic treatment, and management interventions, the incidence of new reproductive problems declined and the outbreak was contained.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Tropical environmental conditions with high rainfall, pasture flooding, and contact with contaminated surface water, combined with possible wildlife and rodent reservoirs and incomplete prior vaccination, facilitated intense exposure and transmission in the dairy herd. Internal mechanisms: This event represented re-occurrence of endemic bovine leptospirosis leading to a pronounced abortion cluster, driven mainly by high within-herd transmission and persistent renal shedding rather than the documented emergence of a new serovar or genotype; the primary internal mechanism was efficient reproductive-tract and transplacental infection leading to abortion and stillbirths.
Review: retain: The 2015 abortion‑associated outbreak in a Brazilian dairy herd (Maranhão State, Northeastern Brazil), with approximately 17% abortions and additional stillbirths and repeat estrus, is accurately summarized and is well supported by the primary case report and recent reviews of bovine genital leptospirosis.([repositorio.unesp.br](https://repositorio.unesp.br/server/api/core/bitstreams/fce4777b-5e58-4a63-86d8-0248cf91021f/content)) Event type 're_occurrence' is appropriate because bovine leptospirosis is long‑endemic in Brazil and no novel serovar or host jump was documented; geography and timing are correct; no corrections made.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: Tick-borne encephalitis virus (LI subtype)
Host: Sheep (coastal flocks in Sunnhordland and Sørlandet); ticks (Ixodes ricinus); likely involvement of local cervids and willow ptarmigan as reservoir hosts
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, louping ill—previously regarded as a disease of the British Isles—was recognised causing encephalomyelitis in sheep flocks in coastal areas of Sunnhordland and Sørlandet in southern Norway, and virus isolates from affected sheep were shown by antigenic and sequencing studies to be classical louping ill virus closely related to British strains. These outbreaks produced neurological disease and deaths in local sheep and demonstrated that LIV had established at least transient natural foci on the Norwegian coast, with serologic evidence of exposure also detected in game birds and deer. Following these limited epizootics and increased awareness, no further clinical outbreaks in Norwegian livestock have been reported since 1991, although later wildlife and livestock serosurveys show that closely related tick‑borne flaviviruses may continue to circulate at low levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected Ixodes ricinus ticks into coastal pastures in southern Norway—most plausibly via movement of sheep or game animals from infected areas or by migratory birds—combined with humid, tick‑suitable hill grazing and local deer populations, enabled establishment of a new LIV focus outside the British Isles. Internal mechanisms: Molecular comparison of the Norwegian virus with British LIV strains showed >95% nucleotide and >98% amino‑acid identity in the envelope gene, indicating geographic range expansion of an existing lineage rather than emergence of a genetically distinct, more virulent strain.
Review: retain: Added this event to capture the early‑1990s Norwegian outbreaks that confirmed classical louping ill virus outside Great Britain and Ireland. Timing (1991), geography (Norway in Northern Europe) and the description of sheep as the main clinical host with I. ricinus as vector are consistent with Norwegian public‑health and veterinary sources and with Gao et al. (1993). Classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate under the project rules (spread within an already affected UN subregion, no novel genotype), and despite relatively few reported flocks this episode is highly important for geographic range and should be retained as one of the core post‑1990 events.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: Tick-borne encephalitis virus (LI subtype)
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1994]
Host: Sheep (upland hill flocks); ticks (Ixodes ricinus); red grouse as an important wildlife host in the same upland system
Event.summary: In the mid‑1990s, intensive serologic and ecological studies in hill sheep flocks in the Forest of Bowland, Lancashire, England, revealed very high prevalence of louping ill virus exposure and ongoing production losses in an upland grazing system where sheep and red grouse served as key hosts for both ticks and virus. From 1994 onwards a coordinated control programme combining vaccination of lambs and yearlings, acaricide use and grazing management was implemented across multiple farms, and follow‑up surveys through 1999–2000 and into the early 2000s showed marked reductions in LIV force of infection in flocks that sustained these measures, although spatial heterogeneity in risk persisted. As management practices were adjusted based on these findings, disease incidence and tick burdens declined, and this Bowland focus transitioned from a major emergence concern to a better‑controlled endemic system.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of Ixodes ricinus ticks on rough upland pasture, abundant competent hosts (unvaccinated sheep and red grouse) and management geared toward both sheep production and grouse shooting created conditions for intense local LIV circulation, with significant economic impact. Implementation of systematic vaccination, acaricide treatment and tick‑aware grazing regimes then altered host–vector contact rates and reduced virus transmission, illustrating how land use and husbandry practices drive re‑occurrence and control of this endemic flavivirus. Internal mechanisms: Available data show no evidence of a novel LIV strain in this focus; the event reflects amplification and subsequent suppression of an established lineage through ecological and management change rather than genetic evolution of the virus.
Review: retain: This event correctly summarises the Forest of Bowland (Lancashire) focus studied during 1994–2001, where high LIV seroprevalence in hill sheep and associated grouse led to implementation and evaluation of a structured vaccination and tick‑control programme. The year range, location (UK within Northern Europe), hosts and classification as re‑occurrence (intensification and subsequent control of endemic infection) are all consistent with the epidemiologic literature. No corrections to timing, geography, event type or sources are required; the event should be retained as one of the main high‑impact post‑1990 episodes for this EPP.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: Tick-borne encephalitis virus (LI subtype)
Host: Ticks (Ixodes ricinus) collected from goats and sheep in northern Greece; goats and sheep as presumed vertebrate hosts in this natural focus
Event.summary: Greek goat encephalitis virus (GGEV), a louping ill–like member of the LI/TBE complex first isolated from a newborn goat with encephalitis in northern Greece in 1969, was revisited in the early 2000s when large‑scale tick surveys were undertaken in rural northern Greece. Between 2003 and 2006, over 3,000 ixodid ticks collected from goats and sheep were screened by RT‑PCR, and two pools of Ixodes ricinus were positive for GGEV, confirming continued, low‑level circulation of this LIV‑related subtype in livestock‑associated tick populations decades after the original goat case. Because no sizeable contemporary livestock outbreaks were reported during this period, the episode is best regarded as renewed detection of a persistent natural focus rather than a major new epizootic, and its prominence waned once surveillance data had documented the virus’s limited prevalence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional small‑ruminant grazing in wooded, tick‑infested mountainous pastures and limited vaccination or acaricide use maintain ecological conditions under which GGEV can persist at low prevalence in local Ixodes ricinus populations. The main proximate driver of this event was expanded molecular surveillance of ticks in 2003–2006, which revealed viral persistence that had gone undocumented rather than a true surge in incidence. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed that contemporary GGEV sequences clustered closely with the historical Vergina strain and related southern European LIV‑like viruses, indicating evolutionary continuity rather than emergence of a distinct, more virulent genotype.
Review: review: The row accurately reflects the 2003–2006 tick‑survey work in northern Greece, where only two of 3,144 Ixodes ricinus tick pools tested positive for Greek goat encephalitis virus, confirming long‑term persistence of this LIV‑like subtype at very low prevalence but without documented large livestock outbreaks. I corrected the host field to remove explicit mention of the original 1969 goat case (pre‑1990) and instead describe goats and sheep as presumed vertebrate hosts in the surveyed flocks, in line with project rules against mixing hosts from other episodes. Because the impact in terms of clinical cases and production loss appears minimal, this episode is borderline for inclusion among the “top 10” emergence events and should be reconsidered for possible exclusion or down‑weighting in the final dataset.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: Tick-borne encephalitis virus (LI subtype)
Host: Goats (Bermeya breed); ticks (Ixodes ricinus and related species)
Event.summary: In autumn 2011, a severe neurologic disease outbreak occurred in a herd of Bermeya goats in Asturias, north‑western Spain, with 17 goats dying over four months and clinical and pathologic signs closely resembling classic louping ill. Virologic investigation showed that the causative agent was a louping ill–like flavivirus genetically distinct from both British/Irish LIV and the previously recognised Spanish sheep encephalitis virus that had affected Basque sheep in the 1980s, and the new subtype was designated Spanish goat encephalitis virus (SGEV), representing an expansion of recognised LI‑lineage activity into goats in this region. After the affected herd was investigated and management adjustments were made, the outbreak subsided, but the event firmly placed SGEV and north‑western Spain within the wider LI/TBE complex distribution and stimulated targeted surveillance of ticks, wildlife and livestock on the northern Iberian Peninsula.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional grazing of goats on tick‑infested mountainous pastures, animal movements between farms within Asturias and the absence of specific vaccination or awareness of LI‑like flaviviruses in Spain created favourable conditions for intensive local exposure to infected Ixodes ticks. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses showed that the outbreak virus formed a distinct phylogenetic lineage, Spanish goat encephalitis virus, separate from classical British/Irish LIV and from Spanish sheep encephalitis virus, indicating novel strain/genotype emergence within the LI/TBE complex together with clear host expansion to goats as a prominent clinical host in this focus.
Review: retain: This event is well documented by the 2011 Bermeya‑goat outbreak in Asturias caused by Spanish goat encephalitis virus, a novel LIV‑lineage subtype that produced high mortality and expanded both the known host range and geographic range of LI‑like viruses in Iberia. I corrected the host field to restrict it to goats and tick vectors involved in the 2011 episode, removing sheep that relate only to the earlier 1987 Spanish sheep encephalitis virus epizootic (which lies outside the 1990–cut‑off period) in order to avoid mixing hosts from separate events. Classification as re‑emergence (new genotype and host expansion within a subregion where related LI‑like viruses already circulated) is appropriate, and the event clearly belongs among the major post‑1990 emergence episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: Tick-borne encephalitis virus (LI subtype)
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2019]
Host: Sheep (yearling ewes moved to hill grazing); ticks (Ixodes ricinus)
Event.summary: In April 2019, a group of about 200 yearling ewes was moved onto tick‑infested hill grazing on a farm near Oswestry on the English/Welsh border, and within 2–3 weeks 10 animals developed neurological signs including torticollis, fitting, head shaking and recumbency, with several later found dead. Post‑mortem examination of an affected ewe showed non‑suppurative encephalitis, and serology plus RT‑PCR on hindbrain tissue confirmed infection with louping‑ill virus, with sequencing demonstrating >99% identity to existing LIV sequences from Aberystwyth in west Wales and clear distinction from northern‑England isolates. After diagnosis, management changes and heightened awareness limited further losses, but the incident was reported as a North‑East Wales outbreak and underscored the ongoing risk that naïve sheep moved into upland tick habitats can experience significant losses from LIV.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The key external drivers were movement of immunologically naïve, unvaccinated yearling ewes into an upland pasture with high densities of Ixodes ricinus ticks, lack of prior exposure in the flock and environmental conditions favouring tick survival and activity, which together enabled rapid infection and focal outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Genetic characterisation showed the virus to be closely related to previously circulating Welsh LIV strains rather than a novel variant, so this event is best interpreted as ecological re‑occurrence of endemic LIV in a high‑risk grazing system rather than strain‑driven re‑emergence.
Review: retain: This added event reflects the 2019 North‑East Wales outbreak documented in Access Microbiology, where ~10 of 200 yearling ewes developed neurologic disease and some died after being moved onto hill grazing, with LIV confirmed by serology, PCR and sequencing. Geography (United Kingdom within Northern Europe), timing (2019) and classification as re‑occurrence in an already endemic region without evidence of a novel viral lineage are consistent with the primary report. Given its clear clinical impact and formal documentation as an outbreak, it should be retained as one of the principal post‑1990 emergence episodes for this EPP.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: Tick-borne encephalitis virus (LI subtype)
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2025]
Host: Sheep (Cheviot hoggs and lambs); ticks (Ixodes ricinus); possible co‑infection with Anaplasma phagocytophilum causing tick‑borne fever
Event.summary: In spring 2025, SRUC Veterinary Services reported two clusters of louping ill in sheep on neighbouring farms near St Boswells in the Scottish Borders, an area where the disease had not been diagnosed since 2003, marking a notable return after more than two decades. The first cluster involved homebred Cheviot hoggs grazing rough tick‑infested hill ground that developed classic neurological signs and were confirmed as LIV‑positive by serology, PCR and histopathology; the second involved multiple deaths among 4‑week‑old lambs in a bought‑in ewe flock, where non‑suppurative encephalomyelitis and LIV infection were similarly confirmed. Following diagnosis, advice on tick control, flock management and awareness of concurrent tick‑borne fever was implemented, and the outbreaks subsided, but they highlighted renewed LIV activity in the Scottish Borders and prompted calls for greater veterinary vigilance and development of replacement vaccines.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Local land‑use changes that increased suitable tick habitat, rising deer populations, climate warming that may allow Ixodes ticks to complete more life‑cycle stages per year and movement of naïve, unvaccinated ewes into a high‑risk area all likely contributed to renewed LIV transmission in these flocks. Co‑infection with tick‑borne fever (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) in the hoggs probably exacerbated immunosuppression and clinical severity, while the absence of a currently available commercial LIV vaccine in the UK left farmers reliant on acaricides and grazing management. Internal mechanisms: No evidence has been presented for a genetically novel LIV strain in these cases; the pattern is best interpreted as ecological and management‑driven re‑occurrence of endemic LIV at the southern edge of its Scottish range.
Review: retain: This event is well supported by the SRUC Veterinary Services report describing two distinct but nearby farm outbreaks near St Boswells in 2025, after more than 20 years without diagnosed cases in the Scottish Borders. The year, location (Scottish Borders within the UK and Northern Europe), host description and classification as re‑occurrence (reappearance of endemic LIV driven by ecological and management factors, with no evidence of a new strain) are all consistent with that source and broader UK surveillance summaries. No corrections to the row were needed; it should be retained as a recent, clearly defined re‑occurrence episode.
