EPP.scientific.name: Maedi-visna virus
EPP.common.name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Host: Sheep (imported Merino and Awassi; indigenous Menz and other central highland sheep)
Event.summary: From the mid‑1980s, serology at Debre Berhan breeding centres detected Maedi–Visna virus infection for the first time in Ethiopia, initially in imported Merino sheep and then in local Menz and crossbred flocks in the central highlands.([repository.au-ibar.org](https://repository.au-ibar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/efd11302-ba60-4ad1-a656-985d54b21213/content)) During the 1990s and early 2000s, surveys of government ranches and nearby smallholder flocks found very high MVV seroprevalence (often >70%) and increasing chronic respiratory disease, leading to recognition of ovine progressive pneumonia as a major emerging cause of pneumonia in central Ethiopian sheep.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12494555/)) By about 2003, microscopic examination of pneumonic lungs from highland sheep confirmed typical maedi‑visna lesions alongside pulmonary adenomatosis, indicating that MVV had become endemic in improved and crossbred highland flocks while remaining rare in lowland small ruminants.([ilri.org](https://www.ilri.org/knowledge/publications/pulmonary-adenomatosis-and-maedi-visna-ethiopian-central-highland-sheep))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large‑scale importation of exotic wool and dairy breeds (Merino, Awassi, Romney, Dorper) into Ethiopian government ranches from the 1960s onwards, and subsequent dissemination of crossbred rams to farmers around Debre Berhan and other highland areas, introduced MVV and facilitated its spread into previously naïve central Ethiopian sheep populations.([repository.au-ibar.org](https://repository.au-ibar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/efd11302-ba60-4ad1-a656-985d54b21213/content)) Intensive management and housing at breeding centres, with high stocking densities and close confinement at lambing, further amplified transmission before the disease was widely recognised.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12494555/)) Internal mechanisms: No unique Ethiopian MVV lineage has yet been defined; the event reflects typical SRLV biology—lifelong infection, delayed seroconversion, and efficient dam–lamb and close‑contact transmission—which allowed extensive silent spread prior to formal detection.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12494555/))
Review: Decision: review. Corrections made: (i) changed first_detection from Yes to No and flagged re_occurrence as Yes, because MVV was first serologically detected in imported Merino sheep in Ethiopia in 1986 (with subsequent infection in local sheep) and thus global first detection lies decades earlier; (ii) adjusted the time span to 1986–2003 to cover the documented introduction and early establishment phase, while keeping the focus on post‑1990 emergence; (iii) rewrote the event summary to rely on primary Ethiopian studies (Ayelet/Woldemeskel and later surveys) rather than implying that recognition only began “around 1990”; and (iv) updated sources to include the AU‑IBAR review and ILRI microscopic study instead of generic MVV reviews alone. This event remains one of the largest and most consequential modern emergence episodes for MVV and should be retained, but a subject‑matter expert should verify exact start/end years and whether to split additional sub‑events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Maedi-visna virus
EPP.common.name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Host: Sheep (south‑western Finnish flocks)
Event.summary: Finland, previously regarded as free of Maedi–Visna, detected MVV infection in eight sheep flocks in the south‑west during a 1994 serological survey; epidemiological investigation indicated that the virus had been introduced by imported sheep around 1981.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167587700001628)) Over the mid‑to‑late 1990s, infection remained geographically limited while a government‑approved voluntary control programme using repeated ELISA testing, culling of reactors and movement restrictions was implemented in affected and at‑risk flocks.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167587700001628)) By about 2000, Finland reported successful eradication of MVV from programme flocks and regained national MV‑free status, making this a well‑documented incursion and elimination episode.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167587700001628))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected breeding sheep from other European countries into southwestern Finland, followed by local trade of live animals between a small number of flocks, seeded MVV into a country that had been free of the infection.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167587700001628)) The subsequent voluntary control programme—with systematic serological surveillance, removal of positive animals and tight movement controls—minimised further spread and allowed eradication. Internal mechanisms: No novel MVV strain or host shift was reported; the event reflects re‑occurrence of established SRLV genotypes in a previously free national population via trade.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7222820/))
Review: Decision: review. Changes: (i) set first_detection from Yes to No to align with the definition that first detection refers to the host system globally (MVV was already widespread in Europe long before 1994); (ii) set re_occurrence to Yes, as this episode represents a re‑occurrence/incursion into a previously free country within a sub‑region (Northern Europe) where MVV was already endemic; and (iii) clarified in the summary that the event is a national incursion and eradication episode, not a global or continental first. The event is well supported by the Finnish voluntary control programme paper and remains a useful example of successful eradication, so it should be retained among the major events, but the re‑classification should be checked against how other country‑level first‑detections are coded in the broader dataset.

EPP.scientific.name: Maedi-visna virus
EPP.common.name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Host: Sheep (Menz, Awassi and crossbred flocks at Debre Berhan and Amed Guya sheep multiplication centres)
Event.summary: Between 2004 and 2007, a severe Maedi–Visna outbreak forced closure of the Debre Berhan and Amed Guya sheep breed multiplication centres in Ethiopia’s Amhara Region, which had been central to national crossbreeding programmes. MVV serosurveys at Amed Guya during this period found very high flock‑level seroprevalence (around 87%) across Menz, Awassi and crossbred sheep, and concurrent respiratory disease caused major production losses.([globalscientificjournal.com](https://www.globalscientificjournal.com/researchpaper/SEROPREVALANCE_AND_ASSOCIATED_RISK_FACTORS_OF_MAEDI_VISNA_IN_AMEDGUYA_SHEEP_BREED_MULTIPLICATION_CENTER_AMHARA_REGION_NORTHERN_ETHIOPIA.pdf)) The crisis led to suspension of ram distribution, mass culling of seropositive animals—reports indicate that at Amed Guya roughly 2,300 of 3,000 sheep were slaughtered—and temporary closure of both ranches.([globalscientificjournal.com](https://www.globalscientificjournal.com/researchpaper/SEROPREVALANCE_AND_ASSOCIATED_RISK_FACTORS_OF_MAEDI_VISNA_IN_AMEDGUYA_SHEEP_BREED_MULTIPLICATION_CENTER_AMHARA_REGION_NORTHERN_ETHIOPIA.pdf)) By 2007, the centres had been partially restocked with MVV‑negative flocks, but later studies still documented high seroprevalence, underscoring how deeply MVV had become entrenched in these improvement herds.([globalscientificjournal.com](https://www.globalscientificjournal.com/researchpaper/SEROPREVALANCE_AND_ASSOCIATED_RISK_FACTORS_OF_MAEDI_VISNA_IN_AMEDGUYA_SHEEP_BREED_MULTIPLICATION_CENTER_AMHARA_REGION_NORTHERN_ETHIOPIA.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Crossbreeding projects that imported Awassi and other exotic breeds into Debre Berhan and Amed Guya from the 1960s onwards, combined with their mandate to supply thousands of improved rams to surrounding smallholders, created large, densely stocked ranches that acted as both amplifiers and dispersal hubs once MVV was introduced.([globalscientificjournal.com](https://www.globalscientificjournal.com/researchpaper/SEROPREVALANCE_AND_ASSOCIATED_RISK_FACTORS_OF_MAEDI_VISNA_IN_AMEDGUYA_SHEEP_BREED_MULTIPLICATION_CENTER_AMHARA_REGION_NORTHERN_ETHIOPIA.pdf)) Limited early MVV surveillance and biosecurity at these centres allowed infection to reach very high within‑flock prevalence before it was detected and control measures—closure, testing and mass culling—were imposed. Internal mechanisms: There is no clear evidence for emergence of a novel Ethiopian strain; the episode is best explained by typical SRLV dynamics in crowded breeding flocks with high dam–lamb contact and close housing during the cold season, leading to sustained high infection pressure.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12494555/))
Review: Decision: review. New event added. Rationale: multiple Ethiopian sources report that the Debre Berhan and Amed Guya multiplication ranches were closed between 2004 and 2007 because of a major MVV outbreak, with very high seroprevalence and large‑scale culling (about 2,300 of 3,000 sheep at Amed Guya). This represents a discrete, high‑impact episode distinct from the earlier introduction/establishment phase and clearly qualifies as one of the most consequential MVV emergence events globally in the post‑1990 period. I created a dedicated row to capture this outbreak, coded as re_occurrence (no evidence for a new strain), and sourced it directly from detailed seroprevalence and programme reports. A domain expert should verify the approximate numbers culled and ensure there is no double‑counting with the broader 1986–2003 Ethiopia event.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus hominis
EPP.common.name: Measles virus, MeV
Host: Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata) in a closed colony of 53 animals at Everland Zoological Gardens, Yongin, Republic of Korea
Event.summary: Between December 1992 and March 1993, an outbreak of natural measles virus infection occurred in a colony of 53 Japanese macaques at Everland Zoological Gardens in Yongin, Republic of Korea, probably originating from exposure to infected human visitors while the monkeys were on outdoor public exhibit. Over roughly four months, 12 macaques aged 7 months to 22 years developed dermatitis, diarrhea, neurologic signs and systemic disease and died, and necropsy with histopathology, immunohistochemistry, in situ hybridization and electron microscopy confirmed widespread measles virus antigen and characteristic paramyxovirus nucleocapsids in multiple tissues together with frequent opportunistic co-infections. Clinical cases ceased after the most severely affected animals died and the colony was managed in new outdoor enclosures, and no further measles cases were reported from this group, highlighting the high susceptibility of unvaccinated macaques and the risk posed by human visitors. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1354/vp.36-6-594))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of human measles virus into a closed, unvaccinated Japanese macaque colony at a public zoo, most likely via aerosol exposure to infected human visitors, with recent transfers between enclosures and associated handling stress likely contributing to immunosuppression. Internal mechanisms: A standard wild-type human measles virus caused profound immunosuppression in affected macaques, predisposing them to high rates of secondary infections (including disseminated cytomegalovirus infection, bacterial pneumonia and Candida-associated lesions) and contributing to about 21% colony mortality, but there is no evidence of a novel NHP-adapted strain; pathogenesis closely mirrored severe human measles with opportunistic infections. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1354/vp.36-6-594))
Review: review – Newly added high-impact event based on a detailed veterinary pathology case report describing a 1992–1993 measles epizootic in 53 Japanese macaques at Everland Zoological Gardens, Yongin, Republic of Korea (12 deaths; approximately 21% colony mortality). This outbreak clearly meets criteria for inclusion among the largest MeV emergence events in non-human primates since 1990 and fills an omission in the original dataset. Classified here as a re-occurrence in Asia rather than first detection or intra-continental emergence, because measles epizootics in captive NHPs were already well documented in Asia and elsewhere before 1990, but this choice should be confirmed by a human reviewer given incomplete historical reporting for Eastern Asia. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1354/vp.36-6-594))

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus hominis
EPP.common.name: Measles virus, MeV
Host: Old World non-human primates (Cercopithecidae), including cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis), rhesus macaques (M. mulatta), and pig-tailed macaques (M. nemestrina) housed in two primate research facilities
Event.summary: In 1996, a large measles outbreak occurred in two U.S. facilities housing Old World non-human primates, following introduction of wild-type human measles virus during a period of ongoing community measles transmission. Over approximately two months, 94 monkeys developed evidence of acute measles infection, with clinical illness and serologic confirmation indicating rapid within-facility spread. The outbreak was brought under control through quarantine measures, restriction of human–primate contact, and emergency vaccination of both non-human primates and at-risk human staff, after which no further MeV transmission was detected in the colonies. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10090093/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reverse zoonotic transmission from humans to NHPs during a concurrent human measles outbreak in the United States, facilitated by close contact between animal-care staff and primates and incomplete measles immunity among staff; high-density housing of susceptible macaques in indoor research facilities enabled rapid aerosol spread once the virus was introduced. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain specific to NHPs was identified; the outbreak virus was a circulating wild-type human measles virus, so the principal mechanisms were the inherent high transmissibility of MeV and the high susceptibility of Old World primates rather than viral adaptation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10090093/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event is real and extensively documented (94 Old World non-human primates with acute measles infection over about two months in two U.S. research facilities) and is clearly among the most impactful MeV epizootics in NHPs since 1990. Geographical assignment (North America | Northern America; United States of America) and timing (1996) are correct, and classification as a re-occurrence driven by reverse zoonosis and gaps in vaccination or staff immunity is consistent with the literature; no corrections beyond minor wording and citation additions were needed. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10090093/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus hominis
EPP.common.name: Measles virus, MeV
Host: Cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) in a non-human primate quarantine facility south of Manila, with concurrent Reston ebolavirus infection in some animals
Event.summary: In August 2015, a non-human primate quarantine facility south of Manila, Philippines, detected unusual rash illness and sudden deaths in six cynomolgus macaques during routine monitoring, in the context of a large human measles outbreak nationally. Investigation and testing of 174 sera from the colony identified Reston ebolavirus infection in the dead animals and eight macaques with serologic evidence of recent measles virus infection, including two coinfected with RESTV, and the MeV strains corresponded to genotype B3 viruses circulating in humans in the Philippines at that time. The measles component of the outbreak was contained through quarantine, enhanced biosecurity, and close monitoring of the colony, and no onward spread of MeV from this facility to other NHP colonies was reported. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6038738/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reverse zoonotic spillover of measles virus from humans to captive macaques during a large national measles outbreak in the Philippines in 2015, facilitated by close human–NHP contact in a quarantine facility and concurrent biosecurity lapses that also permitted Reston ebolavirus transmission; high animal density and internal movements within the facility likely aided within-group spread. Internal mechanisms: The measles virus detected in macaques was a human genotype B3 strain rather than an NHP-adapted lineage, so cross-species transmission and limited onward spread reflected the inherently high transmissibility of MeV and host susceptibility rather than emergence of a novel variant specific to NHPs; there is no evidence in the report for increased virulence or other viral changes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6038738/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event is real and supported by a detailed Emerging Infectious Diseases case report on the 2015 Reston ebolavirus outbreak in cynomolgus macaques in the Philippines, which documents concurrent measles virus infection in eight animals; this outbreak is one of the few well-characterized post‑2005 MeV events in NHPs and should be retained as a major emergence episode. The original row misclassified this as first detection in the host system; measles infection in non-human primates was documented globally, including in Asia, many decades earlier, so the First_detection flag has been set to false and the event classified as a re-occurrence in an already affected sub-region of Asia driven by a large human measles epidemic and facility-level biosecurity gaps. The source list has been updated to prioritize the peer‑reviewed Emerging Infectious Diseases article (and its CDC stacks/PMC copies) as primary references, with the earlier conference abstract retained only as a supplementary citation; a human curator should verify that the balance between Reston ebolavirus and MeV content in the summary is appropriate for this EPP profile. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6038738/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.common.name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Net‑cage–cultured marine red sea bream (Pagrus major) around the Penghu (Pescadores) Islands off the southwestern Taiwan area
Event.summary: From 1993 onward, outbreaks of a severe viral disease with abnormal swimming, lethargy and cumulative mortalities of 50–90% over roughly two months were reported in net‑cage–cultured red sea bream around the Penghu Islands off southwestern Taiwan. Virological and molecular analyses showed the causative agent to be closely related to Japanese RSIV, indicating introduction of red sea bream iridoviral disease into the Taiwan region. Farm‑level losses declined after affected cohorts were removed and stocking practices were modified, but RSIV/ISKNV‑like megalocytiviruses subsequently became established in Taiwanese marine aquaculture and were detected in additional host species.

Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of an existing RSIV genotype within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 into a new country inside the Eastern Asia sub‑region, with high virulence in red sea bream but no clear evidence for major genomic change relative to Japanese isolates.

EPP.scientific.name: Megalocytivirus pagrus1
EPP.common.name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Freshwater pond‑cultured mandarin fish (Siniperca chuatsi) in southern China
Event.summary: From about 1994, large‑scale outbreaks of a systemic disease with splenic and renal necrosis caused catastrophic mortalities, often 90–100% in affected ponds, in pond‑reared mandarin fish in southern China. The causative agent, later named infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus (ISKNV), was identified as a megalocytivirus and linked to severe economic losses across multiple provinces during the late 1990s. As diagnostic tools and vaccines were developed and disseminated, farmers adopted control measures that reduced the frequency of explosive outbreaks, although ISKNV remained an important constraint on mandarin fish culture.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of high‑value mandarin fish aquaculture with very high stocking densities, warm summer temperatures and frequent live‑fish movements between farms created conditions for efficient introduction and amplification of ISKNV. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a distinct ISKNV genotype within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 able to cause peracute systemic disease in mandarin fish and later infect additional freshwater and marine species, representing a major genotype and host expansion of the species within Eastern Asia.
Review: review – New event added to capture the mid‑1990s emergence of infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus (ISKNV) in pond‑reared mandarin fish in China, which was omitted from the original file despite being one of the most impactful Megalocytivirus pagrus1 epizootics worldwide; classified as re_emergence (new genotype and host within the previously affected Eastern Asia sub‑region).

EPP.scientific.name: Megalocytivirus pagrus1
EPP.common.name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Cultured rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus) and other marine finfish (e.g. red sea bream, sea perch, black porgy, rockfish) in coastal marine farms
Event.summary: By the mid‑1990s, RSIV‑like systemic disease causing mass summer mortalities was recognized in cultured marine fish in the Republic of Korea, with rock bream particularly affected. Through the late 1990s and early 2000s, recurrent epizootics produced annual die‑offs and major economic losses in rock bream and co‑reared species, and experimental infections demonstrated near‑100% mortality at typical rearing temperatures. Expanded surveillance, vaccination and changes in stocking and temperature‑management reduced, but did not eliminate, RSIVD as a major pathogen of Korean marine finfish aquaculture.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of rock bream and other marine finfish farming, frequent movement of juveniles among farms, and seasonal seawater temperatures of roughly 25–30 °C that trigger disease expression in subclinically infected stocks all favoured repeated outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Adaptation and host expansion of RSIV genotype I within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 to rock bream, which shows very high susceptibility and can act as an efficient amplifying host, underpinning re‑emergence of the virus within the Eastern Asia sub‑region.
Review: review – Event retained but emergence‑type flags were corrected: first_detection was set to false (global first detection in Japan), and re_emergence is now used (with re_occurrence = false) to emphasize the marked host expansion and repeated severe outbreaks of RSIVD in rock bream within the same Eastern Asia sub‑region.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Megalocytivirus pagrus1
EPP.common.name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Farmed turbot (Scophthalmus maximus) in intensive cold‑water marine culture in northern China (e.g. Shandong Peninsula)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, turbot farms in northern China began reporting a 'viral reddish body syndrome' in juveniles and adults, characterized by skin reddening, lethargy and high mortality. A new megalocytivirus, turbot reddish body iridovirus (TRBIV), was isolated from affected fish and linked to repeated outbreaks between about 2001 and 2006 that caused substantial production and economic losses in the rapidly expanding turbot industry. Subsequent development of diagnostics, vaccines and improved husbandry reduced the frequency of severe TRBIV epizootics, although the virus remains present in cultured flatfish populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of intensive turbot aquaculture in northern China, high stocking densities in recirculating or flow‑through systems and sub‑optimal husbandry facilitated spread once TRBIV was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a distinct TRBIV lineage within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 adapted to cold‑water flatfish hosts, with high virulence and efficient transmission in turbot, representing a major genotype and host shift within the species.
Review: review – New event added for turbot reddish body iridovirus (TRBIV) outbreaks in farmed turbot in northern China in the early 2000s, which represent a major genotype‑specific emergence of Megalocytivirus pagrus1 with high mortality and economic losses; classified as re_emergence in Eastern Asia.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Megalocytivirus pagrus1
EPP.common.name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Farmed giant sea perch / Asian seabass (Lates calcarifer) fingerlings in coastal cage farms in southern Taiwan area (Kaohsiung and Pingtung)
Event.summary: From April to October 2017, multiple coastal cage farms rearing giant sea perch (Asian seabass, Lates calcarifer) in southern Taiwan experienced epizootics of systemic disease with up to 90% mortality in fingerlings. Molecular characterization showed that the causative agents were megalocytiviruses within the RSIV/ISKNV complex, and one isolate clustered closely with viruses from fingerlings recently imported from Thailand, indicating transboundary introduction through regional seabass seed trade. Mortalities declined after affected cohorts were culled or harvested early and stricter health management and sourcing controls were implemented, although megalocytivirus infection remains an ongoing risk for L. calcarifer culture in the area.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional trade in Asian seabass seed from Southeast Asian hatcheries, high stocking densities of fingerlings in coastal cages and warm seasonal temperatures facilitated introduction and rapid spread of megalocytiviruses into seabass farms in southern Taiwan. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrated host expansion of Megalocytivirus pagrus1 (RSIV/ISKNV genotypes) to Asian seabass, a euryhaline marine–brackish species, with high virulence in fingerlings, representing re‑emergence of the species complex in a new cultured host within Eastern Asia.
Review: review – Event retained but (i) the Country field was adjusted to 'China [2017]' to comply with the project Country list while the narrative retains the southern Taiwan location, and (ii) emergence‑type flags were simplified to re_emergence = true (host expansion within Eastern Asia) with re_occurrence = false.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Megalocytivirus pagrus1
EPP.common.name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Cage‑cultured Asian seabass (Lates calcarifer) in estuarine and coastal farms along the west coast of India
Event.summary: In 2018, severe mortality events (approximately 50–90% losses) were reported in cage‑cultured Asian seabass along the west coast of India, and diagnostic investigations identified red sea bream iridovirus (RSIV) genotype II as the causative agent, representing the first confirmed Megalocytivirus pagrus1 outbreak in Indian marine finfish aquaculture. A second major outbreak in 2020 affected additional seabass farms in the same region, confirming local establishment and spatial spread of RSIVD in Southern Asia. Following these episodes, Indian research institutes and authorities initiated targeted surveillance, diagnostic test development and vaccination trials, which have helped reduce but not eliminate the risk of further high‑mortality outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of RSIV genotype II via importation of infected Asian seabass seed or broodstock from endemic countries, rapid expansion of open estuarine and coastal cage culture with high stocking densities and limited biosecurity, and warm tropical waters promoted efficient transmission and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of RSIV genotype II within Megalocytivirus pagrus1 into a new sub‑region (Southern Asia) and continued adaptation to Asian seabass as a major cultured host, leading to re‑emergence in a new ecological and production context.
Review: review – Event retained but emergence‑type flags were corrected so that the episode is classified as intra_continental_emergence (first major establishment in Southern Asia) with re_emergence (new sub‑region and genotype/host context), while first_detection and re_occurrence were set to false to avoid multiple overlapping categories.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Megalocytivirus pagrus1
EPP.common.name: RSIV (Red seabream iridovirus complex, including ISKNV/TRBIV)
Host: Cage‑cultured Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) and hybrids in intensive floating cages on Lake Volta
Event.summary: From late 2018, intensive tilapia cage farms on Lake Volta in Ghana experienced unprecedented mortalities, with some operations reporting 60–90% losses and daily deaths exceeding 10 tonnes of fish during the peak of the outbreak. Histopathology, virus isolation and PCR confirmed infectious spleen and kidney necrosis virus (ISKNV) as the causative agent, and follow‑up surveys in 2019–2020 showed the virus had become endemic across multiple production zones on the lake. Although mortality rates declined after emergency culling, stocking reductions and adoption of management measures such as heat‑shock treatment and vaccination on some farms, ISKNV continues to cause recurrent losses, particularly in juvenile tilapia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of cage‑based tilapia aquaculture on Lake Volta, very high stocking densities, frequent live‑fish movements among hatcheries and grow‑out sites, and limited initial biosecurity enabled rapid spread once ISKNV was introduced, likely via movement of infected seed or broodstock. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of Megalocytivirus pagrus1 to tilapia in Africa and efficient transmission in high‑density cage systems allowed the virus to establish and re‑emerge in successive cohorts, representing inter‑continental emergence with major production impacts.
Review: review – New event added to represent the large‑scale ISKNV epidemic in cage‑cultured tilapia on Lake Volta, Ghana, from 2018 onward, which accounts for some of the highest reported mortality and production losses for Megalocytivirus pagrus1 worldwide; classified as inter_continental_emergence with re_emergence (host expansion and establishment in Africa).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: MERS-CoV, Betacoronavirus 1
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: Retrospective testing of archived sera from Saudi Arabian dromedary camels collected from 1992 through 2010 showed very high MERS-CoV antibody seroprevalence, revealing that the virus had been endemic in Arabian Peninsula camel populations long before the first recognized human cases in 2012.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4891877/)) Subsequent analyses linked these long-standing camel infections to the clade B MERS-CoV strains associated with human outbreaks in Saudi Arabia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4891877/)) The event is considered ongoing, with continued widespread circulation in Saudi camels and periodic zoonotic spillover into humans.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-established intensive camel husbandry and dense dromedary populations in the Arabian Peninsula, with frequent animal movements for trade and cultural practices (racing, dairy, meat), maintained high transmission.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4891877/)) Internal mechanisms: Long-term adaptation of MERS-CoV to dromedaries with efficient upper-respiratory replication and shedding, but relatively mild disease, favored silent maintenance and geographic expansion (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/21/7/pdfs/15-0070.pdf))
Review: review – Event is valid and should be retained as a major emergence episode, documenting long-term MERS-CoV circulation in Saudi dromedaries and first documented introduction of camel infection into Asia (inter-continental emergence from Africa). However, it was misclassified as a re-emergence; re_emergence has been set to No because there is no earlier recognized camel event in Western Asia and no clear evidence of a novel strain causing a resurgence in this subregion. A more specific primary source (the mBio Saudi camel infection paper) has been added and the generic Wikipedia link removed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: MERS-CoV, Betacoronavirus 1
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: A serologic study of 651 dromedary camel sera from the United Arab Emirates found that 151 samples collected in 2003 and 500 collected in 2013 had high titers of antibodies neutralizing MERS-CoV or a conspecific virus, demonstrating that camels in the UAE had been heavily infected at least a decade before human MERS was recognized.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24655412/)) The 2013 samples confirmed that high camel seroprevalence persisted during the early human epidemic period.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24655412/)) The event illustrates long-standing endemic infection in Gulf-region camel populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive camel farming and trading systems in the UAE, including movements to and from neighboring Gulf countries, likely facilitated stable viral maintenance, while serologic studies initiated after the human epidemic revealed pre-existing infections.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24655412/)) Internal mechanisms: No specific novel viral properties were identified; rather, this event highlights the silent, well-adapted host reservoir state of MERS-CoV in dromedaries (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: review – The UAE serologic evidence for widespread camel infection in 2003 and 2013 is robust and the event should be kept. However, intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because the virus was already established in Western Asia (Saudi Arabia) and the UAE lies within the same subregion; spread to a new country within a subregion does not meet the intra-continental emergence definition. No other changes to timing, geography or sources are needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: MERS-CoV, Betacoronavirus 1
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: In 2013, investigations of two human MERS cases on a farm in Qatar identified MERS-CoV RNA and later virus isolates in nasal swabs from several dromedary camels in the same herd, with near-identical genome sequences between one camel and the human patient, providing direct evidence of active infection and zoonotic transmission on farm premises.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2013_11_29-en)) The farm study showed transient shedding and seroconversion in the camels, confirming ongoing in situ camel-to-camel and camel-to-human transmission.([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/abs/10.1056/NEJMoa1401505)) Subsequent control measures focused on farm biosecurity and reducing close contact with sick camels, but camel infections and intermittent human cases have continued in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close occupational contact between farmers and camels, including handling of camels with respiratory symptoms and use of raw camel products, enabled zoonotic spillover.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2013_11_29-en)) Internal mechanisms: Efficient replication and shedding of MERS-CoV in the upper respiratory tract of camels facilitated high-titer exposure to humans in farm settings (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation), though no distinct new viral genotype was implicated.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/21/7/pdfs/15-0070.pdf))
Review: review – The Qatar farm outbreak is a key event demonstrating direct camel-to-human transmission and should be retained, but it was previously misclassified as re_occurrence. Because Western Asia was already known to host endemic camel infection and there is no documented prior control followed by resurgence in Qatar, re_occurrence has been set to No, leaving this as an important but untyped emergence event in the classification scheme. In addition, the Lancet Infectious Diseases outbreak investigation has been added as a primary source and the generic Wikipedia link removed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: MERS-CoV, Betacoronavirus 1
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: In 2013–2014, studies in Egypt detected very high seroprevalence of MERS-CoV antibodies in domestic and imported dromedary camels and identified near–full-genome MERS-CoV sequences from camel nasal swabs, confirming active infection and viral shedding in North African herds.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24079378/)) Phylogenetic analysis grouped Egyptian camel viruses with other African clade C MERS-CoV strains distinct from Arabian Peninsula clade B.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/)) The event firmly established that African camel viruses formed a separate lineage, with ongoing circulation but no large recognized human outbreaks in Egypt.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large national camel population in Egypt and substantial imports of camels from Sudan, Somalia and other African exporters created mixing of herds and opportunities for viral introduction and persistence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/)) Internal mechanisms: Evolution and maintenance of clade C viruses with distinct phylogenetic signatures compared with Middle Eastern clade B strains (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence), but without evident increase in pathogenicity in camels.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/))
Review: retain – This event correctly describes high seroprevalence and active infection with genetically distinct clade C viruses in Egyptian camels and is appropriately coded as a re_emergence episode (novel strain/genotype emergence within a previously infected Northern Africa subregion). Years, geography, and sources are consistent with the literature, and no corrections are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: MERS-CoV, Betacoronavirus 1
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius; some Bactrian camels also sampled)
Event.summary: Serologic surveys of camels in Punjab, Pakistan, using samples collected from 2012 to 2015, found high prevalence of MERS-CoV–specific antibodies, with evidence of infection in camels born in Pakistan, indicating established local transmission.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28221127/)) A subsequent countrywide survey reported about 76% seropositivity among Pakistani dromedaries, while no neutralizing antibodies were detected in sampled humans, suggesting silent but widespread animal infection without recognized human disease.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6235758/)) This event marks the first documented establishment of MERS-CoV in camels in Southern Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of camels from the Arabian Peninsula and Africa, combined with growth of domestic camel populations and trade within Pakistan, likely introduced and then maintained MERS-CoV in South Asian herds.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382745/)) Internal mechanisms: No distinct South Asian lineage was defined; viruses were similar to known camel strains, suggesting geographic expansion of established genotypes rather than novel evolution (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: review – Pakistan represents the first documented establishment of camel MERS-CoV in Southern Asia and is correctly classified as intra_continental_emergence (spread from Western Asia to a new Asian subregion). The event should be retained, but the “countries” field has been simplified to a single entry, “Pakistan [2012]”, as required by the specification of one country with its starting year per linked episode. Details of the 2014 national survey remain in the event summary. No other changes to timing, geography or sources are needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: MERS-CoV, Betacoronavirus 1
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: In 2015, serologic testing of dromedary camels at livestock markets and quarantine sites in Bangladesh found MERS-CoV antibodies in about 31% of animals, with higher seroprevalence in adults than juveniles, indicating exposure and likely circulation of the virus in Bangladeshi camel populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5938793/)) Many seropositive camels had been imported, but detection in younger animals suggested local transmission as well.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5938793/)) The event represents extension of documented camel MERS-CoV infection into another country of Southern Asia, though no human MERS cases have been confirmed in Bangladesh.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of camels from the Middle East and Africa into Bangladesh for slaughter and religious festivals, together with market crowding and limited biosecurity, provided opportunities for introduction and local spread of MERS-CoV.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5938793/)) Internal mechanisms: The viruses are presumed similar to previously characterized camel strains, with no specific new genotype reported; the event mainly reflects geographic expansion following trade (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: review – The Bangladesh survey documenting MERS-CoV antibodies in market and quarantine camels is well supported and should be kept, as it shows further geographic expansion of camel infection within Southern Asia. However, intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because the subregion “Southern Asia” was already established as infected by 2012–2015 data from Pakistan; spread to an additional country in the same subregion does not satisfy the intra-continental emergence definition. No adjustments to timing, geography or sources are otherwise required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus caprinae
EPP.common.name: PPR virus, PPRV
Host: Domestic sheep and goats
Event.summary: In mid‑2008 Morocco detected its first PPR outbreaks, with more than one hundred foci reported across many provinces and particularly heavy losses in sheep flocks, marking the first recognised incursion of Asian lineage IV PPRV into the Maghreb and a major re‑emergence of the disease in Northern Africa, where PPR had previously been reported in Egypt in the late 1980s. During 2008 the epidemic spread widely within Morocco, threatening millions of small ruminants and posing a risk of further spread across the Maghreb and to southern Europe. A national emergency programme combining mass vaccination campaigns from 2008 to 2010 with strict movement controls and outbreak containment dramatically reduced transmission; subsequent serological surveys indicated high vaccine‑derived immunity and an absence of active virus circulation in previously affected regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction is thought to have occurred via movement of infected small ruminants from endemic regions in sub‑Saharan Africa or the Middle East into Moroccan markets or grazing systems; internal livestock trade and congregation at markets and religious‑festival gatherings amplified spread. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by PPRV lineage IV, a genetic lineage that had recently spread into Africa and represented a shift from the previously circulating African lineages, consistent with re‑emergence driven by introduction of a new genotype into a largely naïve small‑ruminant population.
Review: Retain – this is a key high‑impact event, signalling the jump of lineage IV PPRV into the Maghreb and creating substantial risk for the western Mediterranean.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/Outbreak-of-%27peste-des-petits-ruminants%27-in-Morocco/en)) However, the original record incorrectly treated it as both first detection and intra‑continental emergence for Northern Africa; PPR had already been documented in Egypt in 1987–1989, so Northern Africa was not a new sub‑region by 2008.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10093352/)) The intra_continental_emergence and first_detection flags have therefore been set to false and re_emergence to true, reflecting the introduction and amplification of a new genetic lineage in a previously affected sub‑region. The event summary has been updated to acknowledge prior Egyptian outbreaks while still emphasising the significance of the Moroccan incursion. Recommended decision: retain (with corrected classification and narrative).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Cattle and other domestic bovines
Event.summary: In 1990, rinderpest was diagnosed in cattle in Georgia, representing the first incursion of the disease into this Transcaucasian republic for many decades and the first penetration into the wider European region since 1949. The outbreak occurred amid severe political instability and weakening of veterinary services, raising concern about wider regional spread, but was rapidly identified and stamped out through emergency control and vaccination. Although small in absolute numbers, the episode was epidemiologically important as a warning of renewed transboundary risk in the post-Soviet space and was later linked by molecular studies to Asiatic lineage viruses also detected on the Mongolia–Tuva–Chita border.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Civil unrest and fragmentation of state institutions in the late Soviet period weakened surveillance, animal-movement control and border veterinary services, facilitating re-introduction of rinderpest into Georgian cattle. Informal cross-border livestock trade and transhumance from endemic areas likely provided the source of infection. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization showed the virus belonged to an existing Asiatic lineage rather than a novel strain, and there was no evidence of altered virulence; the event therefore reflects re-occurrence of a known lineage under conditions of reduced control, not viral evolution.
Review: retain – Structured fields (year, geography, emergence-type classification) closely match FAO descriptions of the 1990 Georgian incursion, which was small but epidemiologically significant as the first penetration into the European region since 1949. Georgia is correctly coded to Asia | Western Asia per the project’s UNSD-based country sheet, despite some sources describing this as an outbreak “into Europe.” No structural corrections were needed; wording of the summary was slightly tightened and supplemented with explicit reference to its linkage to Asiatic lineage viruses.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Cattle and domestic buffalo (with prior involvement of small ruminants in earlier outbreaks)
Event.summary: Sri Lanka experienced its last recognized rinderpest outbreak in 1994, following a notable reintroduction in 1987 that had prompted detailed virological studies. The 1994 episode, which occurred against a backdrop of civil conflict and incomplete vaccine coverage, affected cattle and buffalo herds in areas where rinderpest had previously been endemic but was rapidly contained through intensified vaccination and control measures. No further clinical cases were reported after 1994, and Sri Lanka subsequently documented freedom from rinderpest as part of regional eradication efforts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: War-related disruption of veterinary services, difficulties in sustaining high vaccination coverage in conflict-affected and remote areas, and ongoing livestock movements contributed to the re-occurrence of rinderpest up to 1994. Targeted national and international support strengthened surveillance and immunization, enabling elimination. Internal mechanisms: The virus responsible for Sri Lanka’s outbreaks belonged to established Asian lineages; experimental work on the 1987 strain focused on host range and pathogenicity but did not demonstrate a novel genotype capable of explaining the 1994 recurrence. The 1994 event is therefore best interpreted as re-occurrence due to gaps in control rather than re-emergence driven by viral change.
Review: retain – This row accurately captures Sri Lanka’s last rinderpest activity in 1994 as a re-occurrence following the 1987 reintroduction, in line with FAO and national epidemiology bulletins. The emergence-type classification and geographic coding are appropriate, and the sources are specific to the event. No structural corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Cattle and domestic buffalo
Event.summary: In 1995, Afghanistan reported a rinderpest outbreak that was epidemiologically linked to movement of infected cattle from Pakistan, extending the South Asian epidemic zone. The disease spread among local cattle and buffalo herds in areas already stressed by prolonged conflict and population displacement but was limited in overall size compared with the Pakistani epidemic. Emergency vaccination and ad‑hoc control measures, supported by regional GREP activities, eventually interrupted transmission, and Afghanistan subsequently reported no further rinderpest cases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unregulated cross-border livestock movements from Pakistan into Afghanistan, combined with conflict-related displacement, poor veterinary infrastructure and limited vaccination, facilitated re-introduction and local spread of rinderpest. The broader context of civil unrest impeded systematic surveillance and coherent response. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved the same Asian lineage implicated in Pakistan’s epidemic; there is no evidence of a novel genotype or altered virulence, so the event is classified as re-occurrence driven by animal movement and governance factors rather than by viral change.
Review: retain – The Afghan outbreak is correctly portrayed as a spillover from the major Pakistani epidemic, with year, geography and emergence-type (re-occurrence) matching FAO descriptions. While detailed case counts are sparse, its inclusion is justified by its role in extending the South Asian epidemic zone. No structural corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Morbillivirosis
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries) and goats (Capra hircus)
Event.summary: In 2007, China officially reported peste des petits ruminants (PPR) for the first time in small ruminants, with outbreaks in western regions such as Tibet, indicating that small ruminant morbillivirus had spread eastward from endemic areas in South and West Asia. The disease developed with clinical cases and serologic evidence showing that PPR had been circulating for some years before detection and then caused significant local losses in sheep and goats. Subsequent control measures and surveillance reduced reported outbreaks in initially affected provinces, although PPR has since become established in parts of China and required ongoing management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of small‑ruminant trade and transboundary animal movements from endemic South and West Asian areas into western China, combined with low awareness and limited diagnostic capacity that delayed recognition. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of lineage IV PPR virus into a new Asian subregion (Eastern Asia) rather than a clearly novel genotype; high transmissibility and naivety of host populations drove large outbreaks once introduced.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4655833/))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Morbillivirosis
Host: Domestic sheep and goats
Event.summary: In mid‑2008, peste des petits ruminants was reported for the first time in Morocco in central provinces, marking spread of small ruminant morbillivirus across the Sahara into North Africa beyond long‑infected Egypt. The outbreak developed rapidly, with numerous foci across the country and high mortality risks for millions of sheep and goats, prompting concern about further spread across the Maghreb and into Europe. From 2008–2011, Morocco implemented nationwide vaccination campaigns and strict movement controls, after which reported PPR outbreaks ceased and the country effectively eliminated the virus from its small‑ruminant population.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of lineage IV PPRV from East Africa via trade or informal animal movements, aided by porous borders and high densities of small ruminants; limited prior immunity in Moroccan flocks allowed rapid spread before vaccination. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of the Asian/lineage IV virus into a previously unaffected African subregion (Northern Africa), with high inherent transmissibility and virulence typical of PPRV but no evidence for a dramatically altered strain in this event.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/Outbreak-of-%27peste-des-petits-ruminants%27-in-Morocco/en))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Morbillivirosis
Host: Fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus) in the Mediterranean Sea
Event.summary: In 2011 a morbillivirus infection was identified in an emaciated fin whale stranded on the Tyrrhenian coast of Italy, and during 2011–2013 dolphin morbillivirus was molecularly confirmed in multiple stranded Mediterranean fin whales, indicating a significant spillover from infected dolphins. The episode developed in the context of ongoing cetacean morbillivirus circulation in Mediterranean striped dolphins and other odontocetes, but with new involvement of large baleen whales showing systemic infection and lesions. After 2013, reported morbillivirus‑positive fin whale strandings declined, suggesting that this host‑expansion episode was temporally limited, although the virus continues to circulate in odontocetes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High overlap between feeding and migration areas of fin whales and infected odontocete hosts, combined with environmental stressors such as high contaminant loads that may predispose to disease. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) and re-emergence of dolphin morbillivirus into a new large‑whale host species, with enhanced transmission potential across cetacean guilds but without evidence of a separate, fin‑whale‑adapted virus.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/22/2/15-0882_article))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Morbillivirosis
Host: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops aduncus) and other coastal cetaceans in South Australia
Event.summary: Between 2011 and 2013, an unusual mortality event occurred among Indo‑Pacific bottlenose dolphins in South Australia, with morbillivirus infection confirmed in the majority of tested carcasses and described as the largest morbillivirus‑associated cetacean die‑off reported in the Southern Hemisphere. Event.summary: Bovine paratuberculosis was first detected in Japan in an imported dairy cow that died in 1959, and the disease was made notifiable in 1971; case numbers increased gradually through the 1980s, reaching more than 200 diagnosed cases per year in the mid‑1990s. In 1998, Japan strengthened its national control programme by introducing compulsory active surveillance using a Mycobacterium phlei‑absorbed ELISA on all adult cattle at 5‑year intervals, with animals that were repeatedly ELISA‑positive or culture‑positive subjected to compensated slaughter. During 1998–2000 alone, 2,469 ELISA‑ or culture‑positive cattle (about 1,500 dairy and 969 beef) were culled under the programme, and a further 3,181 high‑risk animals (mainly progeny and cohorts of infected cattle) were slaughtered with subsidies, representing a major national test‑and‑cull effort. Through the 2000s and 2010s, this compulsory surveillance and eradication framework continued, with regular testing of infected herds every 3–6 months until all animals tested negative, maintaining pressure on MAP infection and supporting Japan’s broader goals for control of high‑impact bovine diseases and protection of trade.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rising numbers of diagnosed paratuberculosis cases in the 1980s and 1990s, combined with Japan’s emphasis on controlling serious bovine diseases and safeguarding export markets and public confidence in dairy products, led to adoption of an intensive national surveillance and culling programme. Government funding for testing and compensation facilitated producer participation and allowed repeated whole‑herd testing at defined intervals. Internal mechanisms: The programme targeted existing bovine MAP infections; there is no clear evidence that a novel strain or resistance trait emerged in this period—the impact derives from policy‑driven removal of infected and high‑risk animals on a national scale rather than a change in pathogen biology.
Review: Decision: added event, flag for review. Rationale: A major national bovine paratuberculosis control programme in Japan, initiated before 1998 and substantially intensified that year with compulsory ELISA screening of all adult cattle and test‑and‑cull with compensation, resulted in the slaughter of at least 2,469 confirmed infected cattle and 3,181 high‑risk animals during 1998–2000 alone, and continued as an active control framework into the 2010s. Given the scale of culling, compulsory surveillance, and Japan’s sizeable dairy and beef sectors, this episode is among the most impactful MAP control/emergence events globally post‑1990 and was missing from the original dataset. Geographic fields (Asia, Eastern Asia, Japan) and classification as re‑occurrence (intensified control and reduction of an established pathogen driven by external regulatory decisions) are appropriate; no evidence supports first detection or intra/inter‑continental emergence during this period. The chosen year range (1998–2018) is meant to capture both the initial surge of test‑and‑cull and the continuation of the compulsory national programme, but exact end‑year should be confirmed from Japanese regulatory sources. Human expert review is recommended to refine the upper time bound and to check whether this event should be split into separate phases (initial eradication campaign vs. long‑term maintenance).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis
EPP.common.name: MAP, Johne's disease
Host: Mixed pastoral livestock (deer, cattle, sheep)
Event.summary: By the mid‑2000s, Johne’s disease caused by MAP had become a recognised multi‑species problem in New Zealand’s pastoral systems, particularly affecting farmed deer and dairy cattle, leading industry and government stakeholders to seek coordinated solutions. In 2007, the deer industry established Johne’s Management Limited (JML) to support practical control in farmed deer, and from 2008–2016 the Johne’s Disease Research Consortium (JDRC) operated as an industry–science partnership to generate epidemiological, genetic and management tools for Johne’s control across cattle, sheep and deer. Over its lifespan this coordinated programme developed risk‑based management recommendations, improved diagnostic approaches and provided resources to farmers, helping to reduce clinical disease incidence and embed Johne’s control in New Zealand’s broader herd and flock health strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Accumulated economic losses and animal‑welfare concerns from Johne’s disease in high‑value deer and dairy sectors, together with evidence of widespread infection from abattoir and on‑farm data, drove creation of industry‑funded and government‑supported research and management programmes; the collaborative structure allowed coordinated interventions across multiple livestock species. Internal mechanisms: Research under JDRC explored host genetics and MAP–host interactions, but the episode is primarily characterised by improved understanding and control of existing MAP infections rather than clear emergence of novel strains or resistance traits.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Although this event is framed around control initiatives rather than a discrete outbreak, it reflects a major coordinated multi‑species response to a burdensome endemic disease across New Zealand’s pastoral industries, including a national abattoir‑based surveillance system for deer and cross‑sectoral research investment. The 2007–2016 window corresponds to the establishment of JML (2007) and the life of the JDRC (2008–2016). Geographic and host fields are appropriate, and classification as re‑occurrence (ongoing management of a recognised endemic problem) is consistent with definitions. Sources (JDRC website, DRL/JML resources, Gautam et al. 2018) provide good coverage. Because this row sits at the boundary between “emergence event” and “control era,” human reviewers may wish to confirm its inclusion relative to other possible control‑focused events, but its impact on national MAP management justifies retention.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine tuberculosis, bTB
Host: African buffalo (Syncerus caffer); cattle (Bos taurus); other wildlife (e.g., lions, kudu) in and around Kruger National Park
Event.summary: In 1990, bovine tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium bovis was first detected in a free-ranging African buffalo in Kruger National Park, South Africa, indicating recent cattle-to-buffalo spillover into this major wildlife population.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12023572_Prevalence_of_bovine_tuberculosis_in_African_Buffalo_at_Kruger_National_Park?utm_source=openai)) Through the 1990s and early 2000s, infection prevalence increased and spread northwards through the park’s buffalo metapopulation, with subsequent spillover to other wildlife species and concern for transmission to adjacent communal cattle.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12023572_Prevalence_of_bovine_tuberculosis_in_African_Buffalo_at_Kruger_National_Park?utm_source=openai)) By about 2006, the infection front had reached the northern boundary of Kruger, establishing a large, persistent sylvatic reservoir that complicated prospects for regional bovine TB control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7059242/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction from infected cattle at the wildlife–livestock interface, high buffalo density, drought stress in the early 1990s, and park management practices that facilitated within-park animal movements and contacts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2870607/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) from cattle into African buffalo followed by establishment of a new wildlife maintenance host population; Enhanced Transmission via dense, socially structured buffalo herds; and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within the park as infected subpopulations seeded new areas over time.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2870607/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Well-supported major wildlife re-emergence event: M. bovis spilled over from cattle into Kruger African buffalo in 1990 and spread northwards to infect most herds by the mid‑2000s, creating a persistent multi-species wildlife reservoir.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12023572_Prevalence_of_bovine_tuberculosis_in_African_Buffalo_at_Kruger_National_Park?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-emergence (new wildlife maintenance host within a long-endemic region) and the Africa/Southern Africa/South Africa geographic coding are appropriate; no changes made.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine tuberculosis, bTB
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus); farmed deer (Cervus spp.); brushtail possum (Trichosurus vulpecula); other wildlife (e.g., ferrets, feral pigs, wild deer)
Event.summary: During the 1980s and early 1990s, bovine tuberculosis control in New Zealand stalled as widespread infection became established in brushtail possum populations, leading to a rapid rise in infected cattle and farmed deer herds and expansion of wildlife vector risk areas.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4566898/?utm_source=openai)) Herd infection prevalence peaked in 1994–1995 with around 1,700 infected herds (≈3.8–3.9% of all cattle and deer herds) and TB‑infected wildlife occupying roughly a third of the country, threatening export markets and prompting creation of a national pest management strategy focused on wildlife vectors.([ospri.co.nz](https://www.ospri.co.nz/our-programmes/the-tbfree-programme/history?utm_source=openai)) From the late 1990s through about 2011, large‑scale possum control, intensified livestock testing, and movement controls progressively reduced infected herds to under 100 nationwide and shifted programme goals from control to staged eradication of M. bovis from both livestock and wildlife reservoirs.([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00480169.2015.1013581?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reduced funding for possum control in the late 1970s and early 1980s, high possum densities in forest–pasture mosaics, and close spatial overlap between possums, cattle and farmed deer allowed wildlife infection to become widespread and to drive recurrent breakdowns in domestic herds across an expanding vector risk area.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4566898/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) with establishment and consolidation of brushtail possums—and locally ferrets, feral pigs and wild deer—as maintenance hosts of M. bovis; Enhanced Transmission via dense possum populations and shared feeding sites; and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of M. bovis lineages across large areas of New Zealand’s pastoral landscape, although no single novel genotype has been implicated.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4566898/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Added because the 1990s wildlife‑driven bovine TB epidemic in New Zealand (peaking at ~1,700 infected cattle and deer herds and TB wildlife over ~39–40% of the country) is clearly among the most impactful global M. bovis emergence episodes in the post‑1990 period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4566898/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (resurgence driven mainly by external control and policy factors rather than a new strain) and the Oceania/Australia and New Zealand/New Zealand geographic coding are appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine tuberculosis, bTB
Host: Free-ranging sika deer (Cervus nippon); cattle (Bos taurus); European badger (Meles meles)
Event.summary: From the mid‑2000s onward, surveillance in Ireland increasingly detected Mycobacterium bovis infection in free‑ranging sika deer populations co‑occurring with cattle and badgers in endemic bovine TB areas, particularly in County Wicklow.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai)) Through the 2010s, detailed epidemiologic and genetic studies showed that in some foci sika deer had infection prevalences and transmission patterns consistent with an independent maintenance host, rather than acting solely as spillover from cattle or badgers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai)) By around 2020, evidence had accumulated to classify sika deer as a new wildlife maintenance host of bovine TB in Ireland, adding complexity to eradication efforts that had previously focused mainly on cattle and badgers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expanding and increasingly dense free‑ranging sika deer populations in parts of Ireland, habitat overlap with cattle and badgers, and shared pasture and feeding areas created conditions for sustained deer–deer and cross‑species transmission.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) transitioning to a true wildlife maintenance reservoir role for sika deer; Enhanced Transmission via multi‑host networks; and possible Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of local M. bovis strains into new deer habitats, though without clear evidence of a fundamentally novel genotype.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This free‑ranging sika deer event documents the emergence of a new wildlife maintenance host within a high‑incidence area (County Wicklow) and has clear implications for Ireland’s eradication strategy, making it a plausible member of the top‑10 set despite its geographically localized nature.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8027074/?utm_source=openai)) Event type as re-emergence (new maintenance host in a long‑infected region) and Europe/Northern Europe/Ireland geographic coding are appropriate; no field-level corrections needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae
EPP.common.name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Countries: Türkiye (Thrace region – European part of the country) [2002]
Host: Domestic goats (Capra hircus)
Event.summary: From 2002, unusually severe respiratory disease with high morbidity and mortality was observed in goat herds in the Thrace region of Turkey, and laboratory investigations confirmed contagious caprine pleuropneumonia caused by Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae, representing the first recognized CCPP outbreak in Turkish Thrace and the first confirmed occurrence on the European landmass since outbreaks reported in Greece in the 1920s–1930s. Over the following decade the disease spread within Thrace and became established, with serological surveys in 2014 showing an overall CCPP seroprevalence of just over 8% in goats and repeated PCR or culture detections from lung samples up to 2015. After intensified surveillance and control, Mccp was no longer detected from clinical lung samples after about 2015, suggesting local extinction or a marked reduction of clinical circulation in the region. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30964465/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of infected carrier goats through regional trade or informal transboundary movements from endemic areas in Anatolia or the broader Middle East into the relatively naïve goat population of Thrace, followed by local spread facilitated by flock mixing, animal markets and delayed recognition of CCPP. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing indicates close relatedness of Thrace strains to those circulating elsewhere in Turkey and the Middle East, with no evidence of a novel highly divergent lineage, supporting interpretation of this event as geographic re‑occurrence and establishment in a previously free area within an already affected sub‑region rather than de novo evolution of a new strain. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8787594/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event is genuine and important: it captures the first documented CCPP outbreak in Turkish Thrace with subsequent endemic circulation until 2015, consistent with Özdemir et al. 2018 and EFSA assessments. The emergence-type coding has been corrected from inter-continental emergence to re-occurrence, because CCPP was already known from Europe (Greece in the 1920s–1930s) and, under the UNSD scheme used in this project, Türkiye is classified in Asia–Western Asia rather than in the Europe continent. Geography (Asia; Western Asia; Türkiye) and the temporal span 2002–2015 are retained but should be checked against the primary papers for exact start/stop years and prevalence figures.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae
EPP.common.name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Domestic goats (Capra hircus)
Event.summary: Between 2006 and 2007, Iran officially reported to the OIE a large epizootic of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, with about 478 outbreaks and approximately 16,000 goats affected nationwide, indicating that Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae had become widely established in domestic goat populations of the country. These outbreaks occurred across multiple provinces and reflected rapid spread in naïve or insufficiently immunized herds within a region where CCPP has historically been present in neighbouring Southern Asian countries such as India, leading to substantial production losses before systematic diagnosis and reporting were in place. After this two‑year wave, CCPP has continued to be recognised in Iran, with sporadic or localized outbreaks reported and later laboratory confirmation in several provinces, while national control policies and vaccination strategies have gradually been developed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10003596/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of goats within and into Iran from enzootic neighbouring regions of Western and Southern Asia, combined with extensive pastoral and transhumant systems, limited early diagnostic capacity, and gaps in targeted vaccination against CCPP, favoured rapid establishment and spread. Internal mechanisms: Available accounts emphasise typical virulent Mccp strains without evidence for a distinct new lineage; this episode is best interpreted as a major re-occurrence and geographic expansion of existing strain complexes into Iran within an already affected Southern Asia sub-region, rather than as emergence into a previously naïve sub-region or as re-emergence driven by marked genetic change. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10003596/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – This row correctly captures a nationally important CCPP wave in Iran in 2006–2007 (≈478 outbreaks, ≈16,000 goats), as summarised in Abdollahi et al. 2023 and in recent reviews. However, the original classification as intra-continental emergence was inappropriate because CCPP has been reported in the Southern Asia sub-region (e.g. India) since at least the early 20th century; the event reflects a large re-occurrence and spread within an already affected sub-region. Emergence-type coding has therefore been changed to re-occurrence (yes) with intra-/inter-continental emergence set to no; geography (Asia – Southern Asia – Iran) is consistent with the UNSD country list.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae
EPP.common.name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Captive wild ungulates (Nubian ibex Capra ibex nubiana; wild goat Capra aegagrus; Laristan mouflon Ovis orientalis laristanica; gerenuk Litocranius walleri) and domestic goats in a mixed collection
Event.summary: In 2007, an outbreak of severe respiratory disease compatible with CCPP occurred in a large mixed collection of captive wild ungulates and goats at Al Wabra Wildlife Preservation in Qatar, with high morbidity and mortality among wild goats, Nubian ibex, Laristan mouflon and gerenuk as well as domestic goats; Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae was isolated and confirmed as the causative agent. The disease spread rapidly through enclosures housing these conservation‑relevant species, demonstrating that multiple wild Caprinae and related antelopes are highly susceptible once exposed to infected goats and that wildlife collections can act as intense transmission foci. Intensive veterinary intervention, strict biosecurity measures, and separation of species, alongside treatment and culling of affected animals, eventually contained the outbreak, but only after substantial losses in the captive wild populations. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17469281/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑density mixed‑species housing in a wildlife collection, close contact between domestic goats and exotic ungulates, and likely introduction of infected goats or subclinically infected wildlife facilitated cross‑species aerosol transmission of Mccp. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrated ability of circulating Mccp strains to infect multiple wild Caprinae and antelope species indicates host expansion and enhanced transmission across species barriers; this episode fits a re-emergence pattern driven by host expansion into new wild hosts rather than by a clearly novel genotype. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17469281/?utm_source=openai))
