Review: review – Event accurately summarises the well-documented 2007 outbreak in captive wild ungulates and goats at Al Wabra Wildlife Preservation (Qatar), including affected species and confirmation of Mccp as the agent. I updated the source list to prioritise the primary case report (J Zoo Wildl Med 2007, cited via PubMed) plus a recent arid-lands mycoplasma review and the comprehensive CCPP review, and removed reliance on ResearchGate as the main primary-source link. Classification as re-emergence (host expansion into multiple wild species in a region where CCPP is already enzootic) with no intra-/inter-continental emergence is appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae
EPP.common.name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Domestic goats (Capra hircus)
Event.summary: Between 2008 and 2009, Oman experienced a major national epizootic of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, with nearly 600 reported outbreaks affecting about 30,000 goats, making it one of the largest documented CCPP waves in recent decades. Outbreaks were recorded across multiple governorates, with morbidity in affected herds often very high and mortality reported at roughly 10% of clinically affected animals, leading to severe production and livelihood losses in a goat-dense livestock sector. Following recognition of the scale of the problem, Omani authorities strengthened surveillance, introduced or expanded vaccination and treatment campaigns, and began more systematic epidemiological and serological studies, but CCPP has remained an important threat to the country’s goat industry. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6830973/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High national goat densities, frequent internal animal movements, and climatic stressors (high temperatures and seasonal rainfall peaks) likely contributed to increased transmission and the synchronised appearance of many outbreaks, while limited prior vaccination coverage and incomplete diagnostic capacity delayed effective control. Internal mechanisms: Available reports do not indicate emergence of a new lineage; instead, the episode reflects large-scale re-occurrence and amplification of endemic Mccp strains in a previously affected Western Asia country, underscoring how environmental stress and management factors can precipitate very large epizootics without major genetic change. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/374586864_Contagious_caprine_pleuropneumonia_A_review_of_the_global_situation_with_a_special_reference_to_Oman))
Review: review – New event added because multiple authoritative sources (Yatoo et al. 2019; EFSA 2017; Ali et al. 2023) report nearly 600 CCPP outbreaks in Oman during 2008–2009, affecting about 30,000 goats, which clearly qualifies this as one of the largest CCPP epizootics since 1990. It is coded as a re-occurrence in Western Asia rather than as intra-continental emergence, because CCPP and Mccp had been present in Oman and the wider region for decades. Quantitative figures are taken from secondary syntheses of OIE data and should be verified against original national/OIE reports, but the overall scale and timing are well supported.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae
EPP.common.name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Arabian oryx (Oryx leucoryx) and Arabian sand gazelle (Gazella marica) in captivity; proximal domestic goats likely source at regional scale
Event.summary: In 2014, a severely emaciated captive Arabian oryx in the United Arab Emirates died with respiratory signs and pleuropneumonia, and pleural fluid culture followed by genotyping identified Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae, with the sequence type matching that of Mccp strains from an ongoing CCPP outbreak in adjacent sand gazelles housed in a neighbouring enclosure. This episode provided the first documented evidence that members of the Hippotraginae subfamily, specifically Arabian oryx, are susceptible to CCPP, expanding the known wild host range beyond Caprinae and gazelles. After recognition of the link, management measures including separation of susceptible species, improved biosecurity, and control of CCPP in nearby goats and gazelles were implemented to prevent further cross‑species transmission. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378113514003265?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Mixed‑species captive management with close proximity between Arabian oryx, sand gazelles and potentially goats, combined with movement of infected animals into the collection, created conditions for aerosol or close‑contact transmission of Mccp across species barriers. Internal mechanisms: Molecular genotyping confirmed that the oryx infection was caused by the same Mccp strain as in nearby sand gazelles, indicating host expansion of an existing lineage to a new wild host (Arabian oryx) without major genetic divergence; this represents re-emergence driven by host expansion and high virulence in a naïve Hippotraginae species. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378113514003265?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event correctly reflects the first reported fatal CCPP case in an Arabian oryx in the UAE with concurrent infection in sand gazelles, as described by Chaber et al. 2014 and cited in EFSA and WOAH documents. Geography (Asia; Western Asia; United Arab Emirates), host description and classification as re-emergence via host expansion are appropriate, and no structural corrections are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma gallisepticum
EPP.common.name: MG
Host: Commercial broiler breeder chickens, turkey breeders, broiler chickens, growing turkeys and a large commercial egg-layer complex (Gallus gallus domesticus, Meleagris gallopavo)
Event.summary: After Mycoplasma gallisepticum had been largely eradicated from U.S. commercial broiler chicken and turkey breeder flocks, extensive MG outbreaks were detected in the fall of 1999 in North Carolina, involving numerous broiler and turkey breeder flocks as well as associated broiler chicken and growing turkey operations. Over the following 1–2 years, MG infection affected at least 54 breeder and grow‑out flocks in North Carolina and contributed to the first MG outbreaks in over two decades in the Delmarva broiler production region, including infection of a one‑million‑bird commercial egg‑layer complex, prompting large‑scale depopulation, movement controls and intensive regional surveillance. Through aggressive biosecurity measures, culling of infected breeder and layer flocks, and tighter controls on movement and sourcing of MG‑free breeder stock and hatching eggs, these outbreaks were gradually contained by the early 2000s, although MG has continued to cause occasional outbreaks in U.S. commercial poultry thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Re‑introduction of MG into commercial systems via movement of infected broiler breeder stock and hatching eggs, breakdowns in biosecurity and multi‑age production systems allowed rapid farm‑to‑farm spread in a region that had been largely MG‑free for years; dense poultry production in North Carolina and the Delmarva region amplified transmission and economic impact. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak appears to have involved re‑introduction and dissemination of virulent field strains rather than a fundamentally new genotype; MG’s inherent ability for vertical (transovarian) and horizontal transmission in poultry flocks, combined with stressors and co‑infections, contributed to severe respiratory disease and production losses but there is no clear evidence that this episode was driven primarily by novel strain evolution rather than external drivers.
Review: review — The initial LLM output omitted a major late‑1990s re‑occurrence of MG in U.S. commercial poultry, despite its clear impact on flock numbers and industry concern. A new event row has been added to capture the 1999–2001 North Carolina and Delmarva outbreaks, during which MG reappeared in at least 54 broiler and turkey breeder, broiler chicken and growing turkey flocks in North Carolina and caused the first MG outbreak in over 22 years in the Delmarva broiler region, including a one‑million‑bird egg‑layer complex.([nimss.org](https://nimss.org/projects/view/mrp/outline/3840)) This episode fits the definition of re_occurrence (re‑appearance and expansion in a previously controlled subregion driven mainly by external factors such as movement of infected stock and lapses in biosecurity) rather than re_emergence driven by new strain properties; it is therefore coded as re_occurrence=true, re_emergence=false. Because this event is geographically limited to the United States but involves very large numbers of commercial birds and substantial economic impact, it likely ranks among the top MG emergence events since 1990 and should be retained after expert review of flock counts and precise temporal bounds.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma mycoides subsp. mycoides
EPP.common.name: MmmSC
Host: Beef cattle in communal and commercial systems in Ngamiland and adjacent districts, Botswana
Event.summary: In February 1995, after about 50–56 years of national freedom from CBPP, Botswana detected an outbreak in Ngamiland District, with infection traced to transboundary spread from long‑endemic foci in Angola and northern Namibia. The disease spread within northern Botswana during 1995, prompting declaration of an infected zone and the subsequent slaughter, under a stamping‑out campaign in 1996, of roughly 320,000 cattle in Ngamiland to regain international disease‑free status. By the end of 1997, after restocking and continued surveillance, Botswana again reported freedom from CBPP, with trade access progressively restored.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The key external driver was uncontrolled or poorly regulated movement of infected and carrier cattle across the borders from endemic areas in Angola and northern Namibia into Ngamiland, facilitated by porous borders, traditional transhumance routes and the high value of cross‑border livestock trade. Delays in recognizing CBPP, logistical challenges in enforcing movement controls and the need to protect export markets led policy‑makers to adopt an aggressive stamping‑out policy that magnified the economic impact through mass culling. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization of MmmSC isolates from the Botswana outbreak revealed that most strains were closely related to other African epidemic isolates, but at least one isolate showed phenotypic and genotypic properties consistent with a novel biotype distinct from classical strains, supporting classification of this event as re‑emergence driven in part by emergence of a new biotype within the existing species, in addition to re‑introduction from endemic reservoirs.
Review: REVIEW – Retain this event as one of the most impactful CBPP episodes globally because of the slaughter of ~320,000 cattle and severe trade disruption, but simplify the “countries” field to Botswana [1995] only; Angola and Namibia are better treated as endemic source areas described in the narrative rather than as participating outbreak countries in this row. Kept the emergence type as re‑emergence, as molecular work demonstrates a distinct Botswana biotype within MmmSC, consistent with pathogen change contributing to the episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma mycoides subsp. mycoides
EPP.common.name: MmmSC
Host: Cattle in smallholder, pastoral and agropastoral systems in western and north‑western Zambia
Event.summary: Zambia, which had previously controlled CBPP and reported freedom by the mid‑1990s, experienced re‑occurrence of the disease with new outbreaks detected from 1997 onwards in Sinjembela and other areas of Western Province bordering Angola and Namibia. During the late 1990s and early 2000s, serological surveillance and field investigations revealed that CBPP was more widespread than initially thought, with infection extending into North‑Western Province and prompting concern about onward spread into Namibia, Zimbabwe and Botswana. Control campaigns combining vaccination, quarantine, movement restrictions and targeted culling continued into the early 2000s, gradually reducing reported outbreak numbers but failing to completely eliminate CBPP foci within Zambia during this period.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movements of cattle from endemic areas of Angola and, to a lesser extent, from neighboring infected zones in Namibia and Tanzania were the most likely sources of re‑introduction into Zambia’s Western Province, while internal cattle trade and seasonal movements along the Zambezi floodplain facilitated wider dissemination. Limited resources for sustained vaccination and surveillance, logistical difficulties in remote border areas, and broader regional relaxation of structured eradication campaigns in the 1990s contributed to delayed detection and incomplete containment. Internal mechanisms: Available reports do not indicate emergence of a new MmmSC strain in Zambia; instead, the episode is best interpreted as re‑occurrence of CBPP due to re‑seeding by existing African lineages and subsequent local spread, with chronic carrier animals and subclinical infections complicating eradication.
Review: REVIEW – Retain this national‑level event but extend the end year from 2000 to 2003 to align with FAO/OIE reports that CBPP spread beyond Western Province into North‑Western Province and was still being detected in 2002–2003. Kept the classification as re‑occurrence (rather than re‑emergence or intra‑continental emergence) because Zambia had a prior history of CBPP and the resurgence is attributed to re‑introduction from neighboring endemic areas and incomplete control, with no clear evidence of a novel strain.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma mycoides subsp. mycoides
EPP.common.name: MmmSC
Countries: Ethiopia – Western Oromia (Bako Agricultural Research Center and surrounding districts) [2011]
Host: Research and nearby smallholder cattle herds in Western Oromia, Ethiopia
Event.summary: In May 2011 a severe outbreak of respiratory disease consistent with CBPP occurred in the cattle herd of the Bako Agricultural Research Center in Western Oromia, Ethiopia, with many animals becoming sick and some dying before infection with MmmSC was confirmed. Subsequent serological surveys in surrounding districts showed appreciable CBPP seroprevalence, indicating that the research herd outbreak formed part of a wider local focus rather than an isolated incursion. Following this episode, control measures including vaccination, improved biosecurity and movement management were implemented at the research farm and in nearby communities, and later surveys reported lower but still notable CBPP seroprevalence, suggesting partial control but continued endemicity in the broader region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected or carrier cattle from surrounding endemic areas into the Bako research herd, likely through routine purchases or exchanges, combined with close confinement and high contact rates in the research setting, amplified transmission and triggered the severe farm‑level outbreak. Regional cattle movement patterns and trade from higher‑prevalence western zones into Western Oromia created ongoing risk, while delays in etiologic diagnosis slowed implementation of specific CBPP measures. Internal mechanisms: Serological and epidemiological data suggest involvement of endemic Ethiopian MmmSC lineages rather than a novel variant; the key internal feature was the capacity of chronic carrier animals to introduce infection silently into a largely naïve, high‑value herd and to sustain efficient within‑herd transmission under intensive management, making this a clear re‑occurrence rather than a novel emergence.
Review: RETAIN – This event is accurately described and supported by detailed local epidemiological studies documenting the 2011 Bako outbreak and surrounding seroprevalence. Although smaller in geographic scope than the major 1990s and early‑2000s epizootics, it represents one of the best‑characterized post‑2005 CBPP resurgence episodes and reasonably belongs among the top documented emergence/re‑occurrence events for this pathogen.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma mycoides subsp. mycoides
EPP.common.name: MmmSC
Host: Dairy and beef cattle herds in northern Italy (particularly Lombardy and neighboring regions)
Event.summary: In October 1990, after roughly a century of national freedom from CBPP, Italy detected a new outbreak in cattle in northern regions, marking re‑introduction of the disease into Europe’s commercial cattle sector. Between 1990 and 1993 a total of 94 outbreaks were notified, mainly in northern Italy, leading to the slaughter of more than 17,000 cattle under a government‑funded stamping‑out program and strict movement controls. By late 1993 the last Italian outbreak had been eliminated, and following continued surveillance Italy regained official CBPP‑free status in the mid‑1990s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The Italian epidemic is believed to have originated from importation of infected cattle from CBPP‑affected regions, followed by local spread facilitated by intensive cattle movements and farm‑to‑farm contacts in high‑density dairy and beef systems in northern Italy. Rapid implementation of active surveillance, movement restrictions and large‑scale culling was essential to eradicate the disease but also imposed substantial economic costs, including loss of animals and trade disruptions. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses have shown that European MmmSC strains isolated since 1990 form a distinct lineage characterized by an ~8.8‑kb chromosomal deletion affecting the glycerol transporter operon and a surface lipoprotein gene, representing a specific “European” biotype with somewhat different pathogenicity profiles compared with many African strains; thus this episode is best classified as re‑emergence involving a distinct biotype in a region with prior historical CBPP rather than simple re‑occurrence of unchanged strains.
Review: REVIEW – Added this new row because the 1990–1993 Italian CBPP epidemic, with 94 outbreaks and over 17,000 cattle slaughtered, is clearly one of the most impactful modern CBPP events outside Africa and had been omitted. Classified as re‑emergence (not intra‑/inter‑continental emergence), since CBPP had long been known in Europe and molecular data show a distinct European MmmSC biotype rather than a first detection on a new continent.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma mycoides subsp. mycoides
EPP.common.name: MmmSC
Host: Beef and mixed cattle herds in northern Portugal (Iberian Peninsula)
Event.summary: In 1999, Portugal reported new CBPP outbreaks in northern regions, representing a resurgence of the disease in the Iberian Peninsula after earlier control efforts and constituting the last recorded CBPP cases in Europe and the European Union. The outbreaks were controlled through stamping‑out, strict movement restrictions and intensified surveillance, with all affected herds depopulated and trade safeguards imposed until freedom could be demonstrated. Following these measures, CBPP was eliminated in Portugal and the country, along with the rest of the EU, has since been officially recognized as free of CBPP.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The Portuguese outbreak is generally attributed to re‑introduction of infection into Iberia via movements of infected cattle, either from residual foci in southern Europe or from imports originating in endemic regions, with local spread facilitated by animal movements within affected northern zones. High‑value export markets and EU regulations mandated rapid containment and eradication through depopulation, surveillance and movement controls, which, while effective, caused significant though localized economic losses. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence does not indicate emergence of a novel MmmSC strain specific to Portugal; the episode is best categorized as re‑occurrence of CBPP in a previously affected region of Southern Europe driven by re‑introduction of existing European lineages and subsequent limited local transmission.
Review: REVIEW – Added this row because the 1999 Portuguese outbreak is widely documented as the last occurrence of CBPP in Europe and the EU and, although smaller than the Italian epidemic or the major African wave, is highly significant in terms of geographic range and trade impact. Classified as re‑occurrence in Southern Europe (CBPP had been present in Portugal and Spain previously) without strong evidence for a novel strain, and not as inter‑continental emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma synoviae
EPP.common.name: MS
Host: Native Chinese chicken breeds and commercial chickens (layers and broilers)
Event.summary: Beginning in 2010, large numbers of flocks of native‑type and commercial chickens in multiple Chinese provinces developed infectious synovitis with lameness and joint swelling, and epidemiological investigations identified Mycoplasma synoviae as the primary causative agent. Between 2010 and 2015, surveillance and serological surveys showed that MS infection became widespread across at least 16–21 provinces, affecting thousands of broiler and breeder flocks and causing substantial morbidity and production losses, representing a marked increase in incidence and geographic spread compared with earlier sporadic reports. Control efforts based mainly on mass antibiotic medication, improved hygiene and disinfection reduced clinical impact on some farms, but MS remained highly prevalent and continues to be an important production‑limiting disease in Chinese poultry.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of the poultry industry in China with large populations of native and commercial breeds; multi‑age production systems and high flock densities facilitating horizontal MS transmission; extensive movement of birds between farms and regions; limited use of specific MS vaccines during the study period, leading to dependence on antimicrobials and hygiene alone. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission – high within‑flock prevalence and efficient respiratory and contact spread documented during the 2010–2015 outbreaks; possible, though not fully characterized, strain diversity (including a distinct K‑group genotype) contributing to variable clinical severity between flocks rather than a single novel genotype.
Review: review – This event represents a very large, well‑documented wave of MS‑associated infectious synovitis in China between 2010 and 2015 and should be retained as one of the major emergence episodes. I have not altered the geographic scope or event classification (re‑occurrence driven mainly by industry expansion), but I replaced one source that was focused on 2016–2019 antimicrobial resistance with more relevant serological and meta‑analytic studies documenting the scale and distribution of the 2010–2015 epidemic. Recommended for retention with these updated references.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma synoviae
EPP.common.name: MS
Host: Commercial chickens (broilers and layers) in China
Event.summary: From 2016 to 2019, systematic minimum‑inhibitory‑concentration testing of Mycoplasma synoviae isolates from Chinese chicken farms showed that all field strains had very high MIC values to enrofloxacin and variable but sometimes elevated MICs to macrolides and other commonly used drugs, indicating widespread fluoroquinolone resistance and emerging multidrug resistance in circulating MS populations. During the same period, MS infection was recognized as one of the most prevalent and economically important bacterial diseases of chickens in China, and treatment failures with standard antibiotic regimens were increasingly reported in flocks with synovitis and respiratory disease. These findings raised serious concerns about the sustainability of antibiotic‑based MS control and prompted calls for more judicious antimicrobial use, better susceptibility testing, and greater reliance on vaccination and biosecurity to reduce circulation of resistant MS strains.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy and often prophylactic use of enrofloxacin, macrolides, tetracyclines and other antibiotics in Chinese poultry production, frequently without susceptibility testing; large flock sizes and continuous production cycles providing strong selection pressure and transmission opportunities for resistant clones; limited regulatory oversight of on‑farm antimicrobial use. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance – field isolates showed uniformly high MICs to enrofloxacin and variably elevated MICs to macrolides and other classes, with point mutations identified in the quinolone‑resistance–determining regions of parC, gyrA and parE and in 23S rRNA; selection and persistence of multidrug‑resistant MS strains in commercial systems under continued antibiotic exposure.
Review: retain – The time window, geographic focus (China), and classification of this episode as an antimicrobial‑resistance–driven re‑emergence are well supported by MIC data from Chinese isolates collected between 2016 and 2019 and by global reviews of resistance in veterinary mycoplasmas. I have only refined the wording of the summary and mechanism to emphasize the predominance of enrofloxacin resistance and the specific mutations described; no structural changes to the event are needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Nairovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Nairobi sheep disease virus, NSDV
Host: Sheep; goats
Event.summary: In 1993, Nairobi sheep disease virus (NSDV) was officially reported in Côte d’Ivoire, marking the first confirmed epizootic of Nairobi sheep disease in West Africa and indicating spread beyond the long‑recognized East African focus. Based on OIE/WOAH reporting summarized by USDA APHIS, affected flocks of sheep and goats experienced acute hemorrhagic gastroenteritis compatible with classical Nairobi sheep disease. No subsequent large NSDV epizootics have been documented from Côte d’Ivoire, and the event is generally cited as an isolated westward incursion rather than the establishment of a persistent West African focus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely long‑distance movement of infected small ruminants and/or infested Rhipicephalus ticks from endemic East or Central African areas into West African production systems, facilitated by regional trade and transhumance, provided the opportunity for NSDV to reach susceptible flocks in Côte d’Ivoire, though direct movement chains were not documented.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/media/document/2308/file)) Environmental suitability of savanna and mixed crop–livestock systems in West Africa probably allowed short‑term maintenance of the tick–ruminant cycle during the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: The event is best interpreted as geographic range expansion of existing African NSDV lineages into a new African sub‑region; available sequence data do not indicate a distinct Côte d’Ivoire specific genotype or altered virulence compared with East African strains.
Review: retain – The 1993 Côte d’Ivoire outbreak is explicitly listed in the USDA APHIS Nairobi sheep disease technical fact sheet as an officially reported NSD epizootic (“Cote d’Ivoire (1993)”), based on WOAH/OIE data.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/media/document/2308/file)) Coding of continent (Africa), sub‑region (Western Africa), and country is accurate given the UNSD classification, and classification as intra‑continental emergence into a previously unaffected African sub‑region is consistent with available historical distribution data, which place earlier foci in East and Central Africa.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/nairobi_sheep_disease.pdf)) The narrative about introduction via movements of infected animals or ticks is plausible but inferential; no concrete trade tracebacks are reported in the primary sources. No structural changes to this event row are recommended.

EPP.scientific.name: Nairovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Nairobi sheep disease virus, NSDV
Host: Sheep; goats
Event.summary: In 2007, Somalia notified WOAH of an outbreak of Nairobi sheep disease affecting small ruminants in pastoral systems in the Horn of Africa, summarized in USDA APHIS documentation as the most recent officially reported NSD outbreak worldwide. Sheep and goats in affected Somali flocks developed acute febrile illness and hemorrhagic diarrhea typical of NSD, with high mortality in naïve animals. The event occurred in an area already known to be at ecological risk for NSDV, and disease activity subsided after the episode without evidence of wider regional spread or subsequent large-scale epizootics, although enzootic circulation in ticks and livestock is thought to persist.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Pastoral transhumance and cross‑border livestock movement across the Horn of Africa, coupled with heavy rains associated with regional climate anomalies that favor proliferation of Rhipicephalus appendiculatus and other tick vectors, likely underpinned the 2007 Somali re‑occurrence of NSD.([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/downld/infos_san_archives/eng/1998/en_980306v11n10.pdf)) Weak veterinary infrastructure and insecurity in Somalia may have delayed detection and response, allowing considerable flock‑level impact before recognition. Internal mechanisms: No specific genetic or phenotypic viral changes were reported for this episode; it is best viewed as a re‑occurrence of endemic NSDV disease driven by ecological and management factors rather than by major viral evolution.
Review: retain – The 2007 Somalia outbreak is directly cited in the USDA APHIS technical fact sheet as the “most recent outbreak” of Nairobi sheep disease reported to WOAH, with earlier outbreaks in Kenya and Tanzania in 2003.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/media/document/2308/file)) Multiple reviews describe NSDV as historically endemic in the Horn of Africa, including Somalia,([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00330-26)) so coding this event as a re‑occurrence (and not as intra‑/inter‑continental emergence) in Eastern Africa is appropriate. The lack of detailed quantitative outbreak data limits precise impact ranking but does not challenge the event’s inclusion; no field corrections are required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Nairovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Nairobi sheep disease virus, NSDV
Host: Ticks (predominantly Haemaphysalis longicornis and other ixodid ticks collected from sheep and goats); vertebrate maintenance hosts presumed to include sheep and goats, although clinical disease had not yet been reported
Event.summary: In 2013, Nairobi sheep disease virus RNA was first detected in ixodid ticks collected from small ruminants in northeastern China (Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang provinces), revealing previously unrecognized circulation of NSDV in East Asia beyond its known African and South Asian range. Viral metagenomic analysis and segment sequencing showed that the Chinese NSDV ("NSDV China") formed a distinct phylogenetic clade separate from Kenyan and Indian/Sri Lankan strains, indicating a geographically structured lineage established in local tick populations. Although no concurrent clinical outbreaks in sheep or goats were recognized at the time, repeated detection of NSDV RNA in Haemaphysalis longicornis and other ticks in subsequent surveys suggested ongoing, cryptic maintenance cycles in the region, raising concern that ecological change or introduction of highly susceptible flocks could precipitate overt disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and high abundance of Haemaphysalis longicornis and other ixodid ticks in northeastern China, influenced by land‑use change and climate warming, together with growing small‑ruminant production, created suitable conditions for establishment of a NSDV transmission cycle in East Asia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9836300/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses of S, M and L segments showed that Chinese NSDV sequences clustered together yet were distinct from African and South Asian lineages, consistent with geographic range expansion accompanied by local genetic diversification into a Chinese clade; however, this diversification occurred in a new Asian sub‑region rather than representing reappearance in a previously affected area.
Review: review – The 2013 detection of NSDV RNA in ticks from sheep and goats in Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang, China is securely documented by Gong et al. (2015, Emerging Infectious Diseases) and multiple subsequent tick‑virome studies, which together demonstrate a distinct Chinese NSDV lineage in Haemaphysalis longicornis and other ixodid ticks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4378503/?utm_source=openai)) Treating this as an intra‑continental emergence into a new Asian sub‑region (Eastern Asia) is appropriate, because NSDV/Ganjam virus was already recognized in India and Sri Lanka (Southern Asia) by the mid‑20th century.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S004268220291514X?utm_source=openai)) However, the original row incorrectly also marked this event as “re‑emergence”, which by the project definition requires reappearance in a previously affected sub‑region with viral change; China represents a novel sub‑region rather than reappearance, so `re_emergence` has been set to `false`. No other structural fields were altered, but this change in event‑type coding should be reviewed by a domain expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Nairovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Nairobi sheep disease virus, NSDV
Host: Sheep; goats
Event.summary: In the early 2020s, definitively reported in a 2025 Journal of Virology article, Nairobi sheep disease virus was for the first time identified causing infection and clinical disease in sheep and goats in China, converting prior tick‑only detections into recognized livestock disease foci in East Asia. Meta‑transcriptomic sequencing of diseased small ruminants revealed high NSDV abundance in spleen tissue, and follow‑up field investigations documented approximately 4.1% NSDV RNA positivity and around 30% seroprevalence in sampled herds, with some animals experiencing severe hemorrhagic gastroenteritis and mortality.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/abs/10.1128/jvi.00006-25?af=R)) Subsequent control and heightened awareness helped limit the recognized outbreaks to a small number of farms, but the discovery highlighted that NSDV has become established in Chinese small‑ruminant production systems with the potential for broader epizootics.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growth and spatial expansion of small‑scale and medium‑scale sheep and goat farming in China, combined with the established presence of NSDV‑infected Haemaphysalis longicornis ticks since at least 2013 and evidence of wider tick‑borne NSDV circulation in multiple Chinese provinces, created conditions for spillover from ticks into naïve or partially naïve flocks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9836300/?utm_source=openai)) Limited prior awareness of NSDV in China and lack of specific preventive measures likely allowed the virus to circulate undetected until severe cases were investigated with high‑throughput sequencing. Internal mechanisms: Chinese NSDV isolates from ticks and sheep/goats form several distinct but related sub‑clades that are clearly separated from Kenyan and Indian strains, implying local genetic diversification and adaptation to Chinese tick and vertebrate hosts.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00330-26)) This combination of established vector‑borne circulation followed by emergence of clinically apparent disease in livestock driven by locally evolved NSDV lineages supports classification of this episode as re‑emergence within an already infected sub‑region, rather than as a new intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence.
Review: review – First confirmed NSDV infections and clinical Nairobi sheep disease in Chinese sheep and goats are clearly documented by Yao et al. (2025, Journal of Virology), which reports high viral loads in diseased animals, approximately 4.1% RNA prevalence and 29.9% seroprevalence in sampled herds, and experimental confirmation that the isolated Chinese strain is highly pathogenic for sheep.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/abs/10.1128/jvi.00006-25?af=R)) Coding this as a re‑emergence event (appearance of livestock disease in an area where NSDV was already established in ticks and has diversified into a distinct Chinese clade) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is consistent with the project’s definitions and with recent reviews emphasizing eastward expansion and Chinese clade diversification.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00330-26)) The main residual uncertainty is the exact calendar window of field cases and sampling; the article is published in mid‑2025 and does not, in the limited accessible text, clearly delimit outbreak onset and end dates, so the “2023–2024” range in this row should be treated as an informed estimate and validated against the full primary data. No other fields have been altered, but because of this timing uncertainty the event is flagged for expert review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus piscine
EPP.common.name: Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus, VHSV
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in marine sea‑cage aquaculture on the British Columbia coast; associated wild marine fish reservoirs (especially Pacific herring and other pelagic species) in the Northeast Pacific Ocean.
Event.summary: In the mid‑1990s, genotype IVa VHSV, already endemic in wild marine fishes of the northeastern Pacific, was repeatedly isolated from Atlantic salmon held in marine net‑pen farms in British Columbia, marking the first confirmed infections of farmed Atlantic salmon by this virus in the region. Most detections were associated with low to moderate mortality or subclinical infections rather than explosive die‑offs, but they demonstrated that farmed Atlantic salmon could become infected following spillover from wild herring and other marine fishes and prompted enhanced surveillance and risk assessments for the sector. Since about 2000, VHSV IVa has remained an enzootic marine pathogen in Pacific Northwest fish communities, with intermittent detections in farmed Atlantic salmon but few documented large‑scale mortality events.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and high stocking densities of Atlantic salmon sea‑cage aquaculture in coastal British Columbia placed large, naïve farmed salmon populations in close contact with an enzootic marine VHSV IVa reservoir in Pacific herring and other wild fishes; schooling behavior of herring and their tendency to enter net pens likely facilitated viral transfer into cages. Regulatory attention and surveillance increased because of concerns over pathogen exchange between wild and farmed fish and potential impacts on wild salmon. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of genotype IVa VHSV from wild marine fishes to Atlantic salmon; viral persistence in infected Atlantic salmon tissues even when overt disease was limited; and continued low‑level circulation of genetically similar IVa strains in wild and farmed populations, maintaining an ongoing risk of viral adaptation toward greater virulence in this host.
Review: review: Event retained but re‑dated and reframed. Evidence from Canadian and U.S. risk assessments and surveillance documents indicates that genotype IVa VHSV has been periodically detected in farmed Atlantic salmon in British Columbia since the mid‑1990s, with infections acquired from wild marine reservoirs and usually causing low‑level or subclinical disease rather than catastrophic farm losses. The original 1992–1995 timing appears to have conflated the well‑known 1992–1996 IHNV epizootics in Atlantic salmon with VHSV; the year range is adjusted here to 1995–2000 as an approximate window for the first confirmed VHSV detections and early investigations. Because outbreaks have generally been modest in scale compared with other VHSV events, a human reviewer should decide whether this host‑expansion episode merits inclusion among the top 10 emergence events or should instead be treated as contextual background for Pacific Northwest VHSV ecology.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus piscine
EPP.common.name: Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus, VHSV
Host: Farmed Japanese flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus) in marine net‑pen aquaculture in the Seto Inland Sea; wild Japanese flounder and other marine fish in surrounding Japanese coastal waters.
Event.summary: In 1996 a severe rhabdoviral disease outbreak occurred in market‑sized farmed Japanese flounder in the Seto Inland Sea, and the causative agent was identified as viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus, representing the first confirmed VHSV outbreak in cultured fish in Japan and the first recognized VHS disease event in Asia. Over subsequent years, additional VHSV isolates were recovered from both farmed flounder and apparently healthy wild Japanese flounder in the Inland Sea and Sea of Japan, demonstrating establishment of a broader marine reservoir and continued local circulation. Control of the disease in Japanese flounder farms relied on improved biosecurity, husbandry changes and stock management, and VHSV has persisted as an endemic marine pathogen in Japanese coastal waters with ongoing but more localized outbreaks in farmed flounder.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of Japanese flounder mariculture in coastal Japan during the 1990s, combined with high stocking densities and use of local seawater, increased opportunities for contact between farmed flounder and VHSV‑infected wild marine fishes; movements of fish or eggs for aquaculture may also have contributed to viral introduction and spread. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of genotype IVa‑like VHSV from wild marine fishes into intensively cultured Japanese flounder; probable emergence of local strain clusters adapted to this flatfish host as indicated by genetic analyses of Japanese isolates; and enhanced transmission under net‑pen conditions, where crowding and handling stress can amplify clinical disease expression.
Review: review: Event retained and re‑classified as an inter‑continental emergence because the 1996 Seto Inland Sea outbreak in farmed Japanese flounder is widely recognized as the first confirmed VHS disease outbreak in Asia, expanding the virus from its historical European and North American range into a new continent. Re‑emergence is kept as ‘yes’ to reflect the appearance of a new genotype/host combination and marked host‑range expansion within the global fish host system. Dates, geography and main impacts align with primary Japanese fish pathology reports; no corrections to timing or country are needed, but a regional expert could refine the end year of the linked episode if more detailed outbreak chronologies are desired.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus piscine
EPP.common.name: Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus, VHSV
Host: Sea‑reared rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in marine net‑pen farms on the west coast of Sweden; wild Baltic/North Sea herring (Clupea harengus) in adjacent coastal waters acting as a reservoir and putative source of infection.
Event.summary: In 1998, VHSV genotype Ib was detected in diseased sea‑reared rainbow trout on the west coast of Sweden, marking the start of a marine net‑pen epizootic in an area previously considered free of VHS. Despite stamping‑out measures, infection re‑occurred in 2000, and identical or near‑identical VHSV Ib strains were isolated from herring caught close to affected trout farms, implicating spawning herring as a repeated source of virus introduction. Recurrent outbreaks, coupled with the difficulty of excluding infected herring from open cages, ultimately made rainbow‑trout farming in this coastal area untenable, and the affected region transitioned away from this form of aquaculture.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of open marine net‑pen systems for rainbow trout in coastal areas frequented by large schools of spawning herring created sustained opportunities for virus transfer from wild to farmed fish, while repeated restocking of cages and movements of equipment and service vessels facilitated farm‑to‑farm dissemination once VHSV was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of genotype Ib from wild herring into rainbow trout; apparent local adaptation of marine Ib strains to cause clinical disease in trout; and efficient waterborne transmission and amplification within densely stocked sea‑cage populations in relatively confined coastal embayments.
Review: review: New event added to capture the repeated VHSV genotype Ib outbreaks in sea‑reared rainbow trout on Sweden’s west coast around 1998–2000, where infected herring were strongly implicated as a reservoir and where trout farming was ultimately abandoned in the affected area. Classified as re‑emergence in Northern Europe, not intra‑continental emergence, because VHSV was already established in the same UNSD subregion through Danish and other Nordic aquaculture and marine reservoirs. Dates and impact (initial detection in 1998, recurrence in 2000, and eventual cessation of rainbow trout farming) are drawn from later Finnish and Norwegian syntheses citing Nordblom & Norell (2000); a regional expert should confirm the exact number of farms, total production losses and whether any post‑2000 residual cases should be folded into this episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus piscine
EPP.common.name: Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus, VHSV
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in brackish‑water net‑pen farms in the Baltic Sea and Gulf of Finland, primarily in the Åland Islands and selected mainland coastal sites.
Event.summary: In spring 2000, VHSV was diagnosed for the first time in Finland from four rainbow trout farms in brackish water along the Baltic coast, signalling introduction of the virus into Finnish marine‑influenced aquaculture. Between 2000 and 2004 the infection spread despite control efforts, and by the end of 2004 VHSV had been isolated from 24 farms in three separate coastal areas, causing notable production losses and triggering extensive stamping‑out, movement restrictions and the designation of a large restriction zone in the Åland Islands. Following aggressive eradication and progressive strengthening of on‑farm biosecurity, the Finnish brackish‑water VHS epizootic was brought under control, although a nearby marine reservoir in wild fish continues to pose a risk of re‑introduction.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of rainbow trout farming in brackish Baltic coastal waters increased contact between farmed fish and marine VHSV reservoirs, while frequent movements of live fish, shared service vessels and waterborne pathways enabled farm‑to‑farm spread once the virus was introduced; cross‑border trade and regional movements of fish or eggs may also have played a role. Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence of VHSV in a new production niche via spillover from marine lineages closely related to historical Danish freshwater isolates; partial adaptation of genotype Id to rainbow trout under brackish conditions; and enhanced transmission associated with semi‑open net‑pen systems and high stocking densities.
Review: retain: The 2000–2004 Finnish brackish‑water rainbow trout epizootic is well documented (24 farms in three Baltic coastal areas) and clearly ranks among the largest VHSV emergence events in European aquaculture after 1990. Country, subregion, timing and description of control measures match primary Finnish and international sources, and coding as re‑emergence (genotype Id spreading into a new production setting within an already affected Northern European region) is appropriate. No structural corrections are required, though the continuation of low‑level detections in Åland after 2004 is acknowledged in the cited thesis and could be treated as an extended tail of this episode in future, more granular datasets.

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus piscine
EPP.common.name: Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus, VHSV
Host: Sea‑farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in marine net‑pen farms in Storfjorden, western Norway; associated wild marine fish in surrounding fjord and coastal waters.
Event.summary: In autumn 2007, an outbreak of VHS occurred in sea‑farmed rainbow trout in Storfjorden on Norway’s west coast, and the causative virus was identified as a genotype III strain previously known only from wild marine fish in the North Sea and Skagerrak, representing the first confirmed VHS outbreak caused by this genotype in farmed salmonids. The episode involved several farms within one fjord system, with elevated but moderate mortality and clinical signs of both neurological disease and septicemia, and genomic analyses showed that the outbreak strain differed from low‑virulence marine genotype III isolates. The affected farms were depopulated and strict control measures implemented, and while genotype III VHSV remains present in Norwegian marine fish, major outbreaks in rainbow trout farms have been rare or absent since this event.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of rainbow trout mariculture along the Norwegian coast increased contact between farmed salmonids and wild marine fish harboring genotype III VHSV, while waterborne spread within the fjord and routine animal and equipment movements likely connected farms during the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of genotype III from non‑salmonid marine hosts to rainbow trout, with molecular studies identifying specific amino acid substitutions in the nucleoprotein and other genes associated with increased virulence in trout; enhanced transmission in dense sea‑cage populations within a semi‑closed fjord system; and demonstration that even genotypes previously considered low‑pathogenic for salmonids can, after limited genetic change, cause clinical VHS in rainbow trout.
Review: retain: The 2007 Storfjorden outbreak in sea‑farmed rainbow trout is accurately described and supported by detailed virological and epidemiological investigations, with correct timing, geography and identification of genotype III as the causative strain. Classification as re‑emergence (host expansion and increased virulence of a previously low‑pathogenic marine genotype in a subregion where VHSV was already present) is consistent with the event definition, and no changes to the coded emergence types or main narrative are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus piscine
EPP.common.name: Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus, VHSV
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in freshwater raceways and flow‑through farms across multiple major trout‑producing provinces in Iran.
Event.summary: From 2015 onward, Iran—then one of the world’s largest producers of freshwater rainbow trout—began reporting severe viral disease outbreaks in trout farms, and molecular investigations identified VHSV alongside IHNV as causes of multiple clinical epizootics in several provinces. Between 2015 and 2019 at least a dozen VHSV‑positive outbreaks were documented, with farm‑level cumulative mortalities often in the 20–70% range and substantial economic losses in heavily affected regions of this nationally important food‑fish sector. Phylogenetic analyses showed that Iranian VHSV isolates clustered within European genotype I lineages, suggesting introduction via infected eggs or fry, and authorities and industry responded by strengthening surveillance programs, biosecurity measures and controls on imported trout eggs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very rapid expansion and high stocking densities in Iran’s rainbow trout industry, combined with heavy reliance on imported eggs and frequent movements of fry and market fish among provinces, created strong opportunities for introduction and dissemination of novirhabdoviruses; limited early on‑farm biosecurity and warm‑season water temperatures further exacerbated outbreak severity. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of genotype I VHSV lineages in a previously naïve, highly intensive freshwater trout system; co‑circulation and possible interactions with IHNV; and ongoing viral evolution within farms under strong transmission and selection pressures, as suggested by molecular‑epidemiology data.
Review: review: New event added because 2015–2019 VHSV outbreaks in Iran occur in one of the world’s largest rainbow trout industries and involve repeated high‑mortality episodes and multi‑province spread, making them among the most consequential recent VHSV emergence events globally. Classified as intra‑continental emergence (first confirmed establishment of VHS disease in Southern Asia as an UNSD subregion) and re‑emergence (introduction of genotype I lineages into a previously naïve but intensively farmed host population). The number of VHSV‑positive outbreaks, mortality ranges and relative contribution of VHSV versus IHNV are taken from molecular‑epidemiology studies rather than complete national surveillance summaries; a regional expert should cross‑check these figures against official veterinary statistics and consider whether post‑2019 events should be treated as a continuation of the same emergence episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus salmonid
EPP.common.name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in marine net-pen aquaculture; nearby wild Pacific salmonids as reservoir hosts (e.g. sockeye salmon, Oncorhynchus nerka)
Event.summary: In July 1992, IHNV was detected for the first time causing disease in sea-cage–reared Atlantic salmon in British Columbia, Canada, triggering an epidemic that affected multiple marine farms between 1992 and 1996 and caused substantial cumulative mortalities and stock culls. The virus, originating from endemic wild Pacific salmon, spread between net-pen sites via waterborne transmission and farm-to-farm movements of infected fish, prompting area-wide surveillance and control programs. By the mid‑1990s, improved biosecurity, coordinated area management, and fallowing allowed the initial epidemic wave in Atlantic salmon to subside, although IHNV remained endemic in wild salmon and a risk for farms.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of a naïve, highly susceptible host (Atlantic salmon) into IHNV-endemic coastal waters; rapid expansion and high stocking densities of marine net-pen aquaculture; limited early biosecurity, including movement of subclinically infected fish between farms; hydrodynamic connectivity facilitating waterborne spread among sites. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) from native Pacific salmonids into farmed Atlantic salmon; possible selection for variants with enhanced fitness in Atlantic salmon within high-density net-pen conditions, although the epidemic is largely attributed to ecological and management drivers rather than a single clearly defined novel genotype.
Review: retain – Major 1992–1996 epizootic of IHNV in farmed Atlantic salmon in British Columbia; timing, hosts, and drivers match primary outbreak descriptions. Only change was to standardize the sub-region field to 'North America | Northern America'; event-type classification as re-emergence (host expansion into Atlantic salmon within an already endemic sub-region) is consistent with the scheme.

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus salmonid
EPP.common.name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in marine net-pens
Event.summary: In August 2001, a new epidemic of IHNV began in farmed Atlantic salmon in British Columbia, Canada, with the first reported case that year and successive outbreaks through June 2003 across multiple marine farms. The epidemic developed through farm-to-farm spread within coastal production areas, again linked to contacts among net-pen sites and exposure to endemic virus in wild salmon. The wave of outbreaks was eventually controlled by strengthened movement restrictions, culling of affected cages, area-based fallowing, and enhanced surveillance, after which large-scale IHNV epidemics in BC Atlantic salmon subsided.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued intensive Atlantic salmon farming in IHNV-endemic waters; high connectivity among farms through live-fish transfers and shared water masses; initial gaps in coordinated area management; environmental mixing with wild salmon migration corridors. Internal mechanisms: Persistence of IHNV in wild salmonid reservoirs and in farmed stocks; available genetic data indicate continuity with earlier BC strains, so the epidemic is primarily associated with management and ecological risk factors rather than the emergence of a clearly distinct new genogroup.
Review: review – Retain as a major emergence episode, but the event type has been corrected. The 2001–2003 wave represents a large re-occurrence of IHNV in the same sub-region and host species as the 1990s BC epidemic, driven mainly by farm management and connectivity; evidence for a distinct new viral lineage is limited, so 're_occurrence = true' and 're_emergence = false' better match definitions. Sub-region string was also standardized.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus salmonid
EPP.common.name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and grayling (Thymallus thymallus) in freshwater farms
Event.summary: In August 1999, Austria reported an IHNV outbreak in a trout farm with high acute mortality, and over the following decade multiple farms across the country tested positive for IHNV infections. The initial outbreak was linked to recent introduction of infected fish, and subsequent surveillance revealed additional farms infected with European M‑genogroup viruses of two distinct lineages. Through progressive implementation of testing, culling, and movement controls, IHNV-positive farms were reduced and later surveillance of import consignments after 2004 found no further IHNV-positive lots destined for Austria, indicating containment of the earlier wave of introductions and spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Purchase and introduction of infected rainbow trout from other European sources; waterborne spread along connected streams; limited historical health screening prior to stock movements. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of European M-genogroup lineages (including M‑Eur1 and M‑Eur2) in Austrian farms, but available data suggest these lineages reflect diversification of the original European introduction rather than a wholly new strain arising in Austria; the outbreak is therefore best interpreted as re-occurrence due to trade and farm connectivity in a previously affected sub-region.
Review: review – Retain as a significant European episode, but adjust interpretation: IHNV was already present in Western Europe, and Austrian outbreaks are best classified as re-occurrence within that sub-region driven by movements of infected trout rather than as re-emergence due to a newly evolved strain. The re_emergence flag was therefore set to false, while re_occurrence remains true.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus salmonid
EPP.common.name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in freshwater hatcheries and grow-out farms
Event.summary: In 1991, the Republic of Korea recorded its first outbreak of IHNV in a rainbow trout hatchery in Gangwon‑do Province, following earlier establishment of the virus in Japan and China. The outbreak caused mass mortalities in hatchery fry and led to subsequent detection of IHNV in additional Korean trout farms, confirming local establishment of the pathogen. Control efforts comprised culling of affected lots, disinfection, and revised sourcing of eggs and fry, but IHNV has since persisted as a recurrent problem in Korean rainbow trout aquaculture.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected rainbow trout eggs or fry from other IHNV‑endemic regions of East Asia (particularly Japan); intensification of coldwater aquaculture in Korea with high-density hatcheries and farms using shared water sources. Internal mechanisms: Establishment of Asian J‑genogroup IHNV variants in Korean farms with evidence for multiple introductions from Japan and subsequent local diversification, but no clear indication that a novel genotype (as opposed to imported Japanese lineages) drove the 1991 emergence.
Review: review – This event reflects the first detection of IHNV in Korea but not in the animal host system globally. The previous 'first_detection' flag has therefore been removed to keep that category reserved for global first description. Given IHNV was already established in the Eastern Asia sub-region (Japan and China), the Korean outbreaks are better classified as a re-occurrence in a previously affected sub-region associated with egg trade and aquaculture expansion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus salmonid
EPP.common.name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in freshwater hatcheries and grow-out farms
Event.summary: IHNV was first detected in Iranian rainbow trout farms in the early 2000s (around 2003–2004), marking the arrival of the virus in Southern Asia and initiating a period of recurrent outbreaks in trout hatcheries and broodfish facilities. Over the mid‑2000s, IHNV became widespread in Iranian trout-producing regions, with surveillance studies documenting infection in multiple reproduction and grow-out centers. By the late 2000s, the disease had contributed, together with other viral diseases, to a reduction in national rainbow trout production and forced the eradication or restructuring of some farms, after which improved health management, diagnostics, and biosecurity began to stabilize production despite ongoing endemic circulation.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of infected rainbow trout eggs and broodstock from Europe or other IHNV‑endemic regions; rapid expansion and intensification of Iran’s rainbow trout industry with dense stocking and limited early biosecurity; shared water supplies among farms in mountainous regions facilitating downstream spread. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of IHNV of the European E genogroup into naïve trout populations in a new Asian sub-region, with subsequent local diversification documented in Iranian isolates; this fits both intra‑continental emergence (into Southern Asia) and re-emergence driven by spread of a distinct genogroup into new production systems.
Review: review – Retain as a major emergence episode representing the introduction of E-genogroup IHNV into Southern Asia. The earlier 'first_detection' flag has been removed because first detection in the animal host system occurred decades earlier in North America; however, classification as both intra-continental emergence (new Asian sub-region) and re-emergence (spread of a distinct genogroup into new host populations) is appropriate and allowed by the scheme.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus salmonid
EPP.common.name: Salmonid novirhabdovirus, IHNV, Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus
Host: Farmed rainbow trout fry and fingerlings (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in freshwater hatcheries
Event.summary: In 2016, Iran experienced several severe IHNV outbreaks in rainbow trout hatcheries in provinces including Tehran, East Azerbaijan and Kermanshah, with reported cumulative mortalities of up to 90% in fry at some sites and 50–60% at others. These mass-mortality events occurred against a backdrop of broader IHN/VHS-like disease problems that over the preceding decade had reduced national trout production from roughly 140,000 tonnes to about 100,000 tonnes as many farms were depopulated or closed. Enhanced diagnostics, genetic analysis confirming E‑genogroup viruses closely related to Italian isolates, and strengthened control measures were rolled out after this crisis period, helping to reduce catastrophic fry mortalities in subsequent production cycles.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density fry production and continuous throughput in hatcheries; ongoing introduction of infected or subclinically infected broodfish or eggs; limited early vaccination or specific antiviral tools; economic pressures favouring rapid restocking that may have reintroduced virus into recovering farms. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of highly virulent E‑genogroup IHNV strains in Iranian farms, with molecular analyses indicating close relationships to European isolates; the severity of these outbreaks reflects amplification of virulent lineages under favourable environmental and management conditions rather than emergence of a wholly new genotype.
Review: review – The event is retained as a distinct, high-impact wave of IHNV outbreaks in Iran, but the timing has been corrected: the key detailed description of ~90% fry mortality and associated national production impacts refers to outbreaks investigated in 2016, not 2014–2015. Event year and country bracket have been updated accordingly, and the re_emergence flag has been cleared so the episode is treated as a severe re-occurrence within an already affected sub-region driven mainly by management, trade and high infection pressure.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Okavirus flavicapitis
EPP.common.name: Gill-associated virus genotype 1, YHV, Yellow head virus
Host: Penaeus monodon (black tiger shrimp) in intensive coastal pond culture
Event.summary: The event began in 1990 when farmers in central/eastern Thailand observed sudden mass mortalities of grow-out Penaeus monodon with yellowing of the cephalothorax and gills, later termed yellow head disease and associated with a previously unrecognized virus that was formally described in 1991–1993. The disease spread rapidly along the eastern and western coasts of the Gulf of Thailand to southern farming regions, causing near-total crop losses within days of onset and becoming the first major viral disease problem in Asian shrimp farms. By 1993 the epidemic intensity in Thailand declined as management practices changed and white spot syndrome virus emerged as a dominant cause of mortality, and yellow head disease shifted from catastrophic, widespread outbreaks to more sporadic events.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid intensification of P. monodon aquaculture in Thailand during the late 1980s with very high stocking densities, poor biosecurity, and extensive water and stock movements between farms facilitated explosive within-country spread; limited diagnostic capacity initially allowed cryptic circulation before recognition. Internal mechanisms: the virus (later classified as Okavirus flavicapitis genotype 1) is intrinsically highly virulent in P. monodon, with efficient waterborne and cannibalism-mediated transmission, enabling acute epizootics; available evidence suggests the event reflects geographic range expansion and exploitation of a highly susceptible intensively farmed host rather than a newly evolved genotype at that time.
Review: Retain – This row accurately represents the globally first recognized emergence and description of yellow head disease / YHV1 in Thailand around 1990, with timing, geography (central and coastal Thailand), host (P. monodon), and impact (near-total crop losses, first major viral disease of Asian shrimp aquaculture) all well supported by FAO guidance and multiple virology reviews. The classification as both first/global emergence and first detection in the host system is appropriate for this relatively recently evolved pathogen, and no corrections to countries, regions or emergence-type coding were needed. This event clearly belongs among the top-impact emergence episodes for this EPP.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Okavirus flavicapitis
EPP.common.name: Gill-associated virus genotype 1, YHV, Yellow head virus
Host: Litopenaeus vannamei (whiteleg shrimp) farmed in intensive inland freshwater ponds (Ratchaburi Province, central Thailand)
Event.summary: In 2009, high mortalities with classical yellow head disease–like signs were observed in intensive freshwater inland ponds culturing Litopenaeus vannamei in Ratchaburi Province, central Thailand, with affected shrimp testing positive for yellow head virus by RT‑PCR. From June 2009 to January 2010, multiple farms in this inland production zone experienced acute YHV outbreaks, leading to large crop losses and demonstrating that YHV1 could cause severe disease in P. vannamei under Thai farming conditions after earlier decades in which dramatic outbreaks were mainly associated with P. monodon. The outbreaks subsided after emergency control measures, including fallowing, improved biosecurity, and stocking from YHV‑screened hatcheries, although YHV continues to be regarded as an important transboundary risk for inland and coastal P. vannamei culture in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid conversion of inland freshwater ponds in central Thailand to intensive L. vannamei culture, sometimes with suboptimal biosecurity and use of untested post‑larvae, created new ecological niches for YHV; movement of infected seed or exposure to contaminated water or equipment linking inland and coastal areas likely introduced the virus to these inland systems. Internal mechanisms: molecular characterization of outbreak samples showed they were caused predominantly by a distinct subtype, YHV type 1b, with a characteristic deletion in the ORF3 region encoding gp116, indicating a novel genotype within YHV1 that was associated with severe disease in L. vannamei at a range of salinities; this represents viral genetic diversification, host expansion from P. monodon to P. vannamei, and geographic range expansion into freshwater/inland production environments, collectively constituting a re‑emergence driven by novel strain dynamics and host/environmental shift.
Review: Retain – This row accurately describes the well-documented 2009–2010 outbreaks of yellow head disease due to YHV1b in inland freshwater L. vannamei farms in central Thailand, which are widely regarded as a major re‑emergent episode because they involve a new YHV1 subtype, a host shift from P. monodon to intensively farmed P. vannamei, and expansion into atypical low‑salinity inland systems. The timing, location (Ratchaburi Province), host species, and association with the YHV1b genotype are well supported by Thai field studies and subsequent impact assessments. The classification as re‑emergence (rather than inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence) is appropriate because YHV1 was already endemic in Thai shrimp populations, and this event reflects a genotype/host/environment shift rather than initial introduction into a new region. No corrections to geography, host or emergence-type coding were required; the row is retained as one of the major emergence events for this EPP.

EPP.scientific.name: Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola
EPP.common.name: Snake fungal disease
Host: Captive black rat snake (Pantherophis obsoletus, formerly Elaphe obsoleta obsoleta) with severe facial mycotic granuloma
Event.summary: In 2009, veterinarians in the United States investigated a captive black rat snake with chronic facial masses and granulomatous dermatitis, from which a previously undescribed Chrysosporium-like fungus was isolated and characterized. The fungus was formally described as Chrysosporium ophiodiicola (later reclassified into the new genus Ophidiomyces), establishing the first definitive species-level description of O. ophiodiicola as a pathogen of snakes. This index description ended without documented onward transmission in the collection but provided the taxonomic and diagnostic framework that enabled subsequent recognition of snake fungal disease in wild populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased diagnostic capacity and mycological investigation in captive reptile medicine enabled recognition and description of a previously overlooked keratinophilic fungus. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype characterization (formal delineation of O. ophiodiicola from the Chrysosporium anamorph Nannizziopsis vriesii complex) rather than a newly evolved pathogen per se; no specific adaptation event is implicated in this captive case.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola
EPP.common.name: Snake fungal disease
Host: Multiple free-ranging snake species including timber rattlesnake (Crotalus horridus), eastern massasauga rattlesnake (Sistrurus catenatus), mud snake (Farancia abacura), various Nerodia, Pantherophis, Thamnophis and other colubrids and viperids
Event.summary: From 2006 onwards, wildlife biologists in the eastern United States began observing severe facial and body skin lesions and high mortality in timber rattlesnakes in New Hampshire and other pitviper populations, with similar disease later confirmed in eastern massasauga rattlesnakes in Illinois in 2008 and other species across the eastern and Midwestern states. Over the subsequent decade, targeted field studies and diagnostic testing linked these outbreaks to Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola and documented its presence in dozens of wild snake species, with USGS reporting the pathogen in at least 20 eastern states and widespread clinical snake fungal disease by the mid‑2010s. By the end of this episode, some localized populations such as Illinois eastern massasaugas and New England timber rattlesnakes showed marked declines and high disease-associated mortality, while surveillance and management responses (e.g., monitoring and treatment trials) were ramped up but the disease had become entrenched regionally.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Habitat loss and fragmentation, small and isolated snake populations, environmental stressors, and possibly changing climate conditions are thought to have increased host susceptibility and facilitated emergence and recognition of disease; expanding wildlife health surveillance and molecular diagnostics also contributed to detection. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain has been conclusively proven to underlie this emergence, but O. ophiodiicola shows traits consistent with environmental persistence and effective transmission in cool, humid microhabitats, supporting geographic range expansion (inherent) and enhanced transmission in stressed pitviper populations; the event is therefore categorized primarily as re-occurrence driven by external ecological change rather than clear pathogen innovation.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola
EPP.common.name: Snake fungal disease
Host: Free-ranging eastern foxsnake (Pantherophis gloydi/vulpinus) and additional wild snakes in southern and central Ontario
Event.summary: In March 2015, wildlife health authorities in Ontario, Canada, diagnosed an adult female eastern foxsnake near Lake Erie with severe dermatitis caused by Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola, representing the first confirmed case of snake fungal disease in Canada and the first documented wild snake infection outside the United States. Subsequent targeted testing in 2015–2017 detected the pathogen at several other sites in southern and central Ontario, sometimes without overt disease, indicating wider environmental presence and exposure in Canadian snake communities. The episode led to the inclusion of snake fungal disease considerations in provincial survey protocols for species-at-risk snakes and stimulated ongoing monitoring, but no broad-scale Canadian population collapses attributable solely to SFD have yet been documented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely natural or human-assisted movement of infected snakes or contaminated substrates across the U.S.–Canada border within connected Great Lakes and agricultural landscapes; increased awareness and targeted diagnostics following U.S. reports facilitated recognition. Internal mechanisms: No distinct Canadian lineage has been implicated; the event likely reflects geographic range expansion of existing North American clades into adjacent habitats rather than novel strain evolution.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola
EPP.common.name: Snake fungal disease
Host: Captive snakes in Japan (including imported rat snakes and other colubrids held in private collections)
Event.summary: Around 2019–2021, veterinarians in Japan investigated dermatitis outbreaks in multiple captive snakes, some originating from overseas trade, and histopathology and culture identified Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola as the etiologic agent, marking the first confirmed report of ophidiomycosis in Asia. The disease manifested as severe crusting and necrotic skin lesions in several snakes housed in the same facility, suggesting in situ transmission within captivity. Affected animals were treated and biosecurity measures recommended, but the event raised concern that infected captive snakes could act as reservoirs for spillover into native wild snake populations if escapes or releases occurred.
