Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International wildlife trade in live snakes introduced O. ophiodiicola into Japanese collections, with captive-husbandry conditions (high stocking density, shared enclosures, and environmental stress) favoring pathogen transmission and disease expression. Internal mechanisms: This episode illustrates host expansion and geographic range expansion mediated by human movement of hosts rather than documented new strain evolution; available genotyping suggests these Asian cases are closely related to previously characterized lineages.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola
EPP.common.name: Snake fungal disease
Host: Free-ranging coastal carpet pythons (Morelia spilota mcdowelli), eastern bandy-bandy (Vermicella annulata), white-crowned snake (Cacophis harriettae) and other squamates in South East Queensland
Event.summary: Between April 2023 and September 2024, clinicians at the Australia Zoo Wildlife Hospital in South East Queensland received multiple free-ranging snakes with severe, disfiguring dermatomycosis, including a coastal carpet python admitted in August 2024 with extensive crusted lesions and dysecdysis; skin testing identified Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola and confirmed snake fungal disease as the cause, representing the first documented cases of this pathogen in free-ranging Australian snakes. Additional cases in coastal carpet pythons, an eastern bandy-bandy, and a white-crowned snake were subsequently confirmed, indicating that the fungus was already established in local wild reptile communities. By early 2026, these findings had been synthesized in an Australian Veterinary Journal paper and widely publicized, prompting concern over potential long-term impacts on Australia’s exceptionally diverse reptile fauna and calls for rapid surveillance and management responses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The introduction pathway is not definitively proven but is strongly suspected to involve international movement of captive reptiles or contaminated materials, combined with climatic changes in eastern Australia that favor survival of Onygenaceae fungi and high local densities of susceptible hosts; increasing clinical awareness and diagnostic capacity also contributed to detection. Internal mechanisms: The cases demonstrate geographic range expansion of O. ophiodiicola into a new continent and host expansion within Australian squamates, but current data do not yet implicate a uniquely virulent Australian strain; impacts appear linked to the pathogen’s general ability to cause severe, chronic skin disease in ectothermic hosts under suitable environmental conditions.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoavulavirus javaense
EPP.common.name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Domestic poultry (primarily commercial and backyard chickens), with some involvement of other domestic birds
Event.summary: In 1993–1994, South Africa experienced one of its most severe Newcastle disease epizootics when a newly introduced genotype VIIb virus, probably originating from Europe and ultimately the Far East, spread rapidly through commercial and backyard chicken flocks across multiple provinces.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14991446/)) Within months the virus had spread throughout Southern Africa, causing devastating losses in all classes of poultry, with contemporary reports estimating up to roughly one million poultry deaths per week at the epidemic peak.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6238702/?utm_source=openai)) Intensive vaccination campaigns, movement controls and biosecurity improvements eventually brought the 1993/1994 epidemic under control, although genotype VIIb viruses continued to be detected sporadically until the late 1990s.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6238702/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and geographic expansion of intensive poultry production, movement of live birds and hatching eggs between regions, and gaps in vaccination coverage and farm-level biosecurity favored rapid spread once genotype VIIb NDV was introduced.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6238702/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven by the incursion of a novel, highly virulent genotype VIIb lineage that displaced earlier endemic genotype VIII viruses and formed part of the wider fourth ND panzootic caused by genotype VII.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC88381/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Reinterpreted this row to represent the major 1993–1994 genotype VIIb epizootic in South Africa, rather than a generalized 1990–1994 genotype VIII resurgence. Adjusted the event years, emphasized the scale of mortality, and clarified that this is a re-emergence episode driven by introduction of an exotic genotype VIIb virus, not an intra- or inter-continental emergence. Existing South Africa–specific molecular epidemiology sources remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoavulavirus javaense
EPP.common.name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Commercial and backyard chickens (broilers, layers), with occasional infection of other domestic and wild birds
Event.summary: From the mid-1990s, China began to detect class II genotype VII Newcastle disease viruses (notably subgenotypes VIIc and VIId) during severe outbreaks in chickens, and over the late 1990s and early 2000s these viruses spread from eastern into southern and southwestern regions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC88381/?utm_source=openai)) By the early 2000s, genotype VII NDVs had become the predominant field genotype across most of China, associated with frequent vaccine‑break outbreaks and substantial economic losses despite intensive use of traditional LaSota‑like vaccines.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7602024/?utm_source=openai)) After around 2005, genotype VII remained endemic but incidence fluctuated as vaccination strategies were updated and other genotypes co‑circulated, with ND persisting as a major endemic disease rather than a single explosive epidemic.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7602024/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification and geographic expansion of China’s poultry industry, high densities of commercial flocks, and imperfect matching between commonly used genotype II vaccine strains and emerging genotype VII field viruses favored recurrent large outbreaks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7602024/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence and selection—genotype VII viruses with enhanced fitness and partial antigenic divergence under widespread vaccination became dominant and seeded the fourth ND panzootic.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC88381/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Corrected the start year from 1995 to 1996 to align with reports that genotype VII outbreaks in mainland China were first documented in the mid- to late 1990s, while retaining 2005 as an approximate end to the main emergence phase. Classification as re-emergence (novel predominant genotype in a region with longstanding NDV circulation) is appropriate; no intra-continental emergence flag was added because NDV as a species was already established in Eastern Asia.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoavulavirus javaense
EPP.common.name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Domestic poultry (commercial chickens), with possible involvement of backyard flocks
Event.summary: From 1998 to 2000, Australia experienced its first recorded outbreaks of virulent Newcastle disease when previously endemic low‑virulence NDV strains circulating in chickens in New South Wales evolved into highly virulent forms, causing outbreaks on multiple farms in the Mangrove Mountain and western Sydney regions.([www1.health.gov.au](https://www1.health.gov.au/internet/main/publishing.nsf/Content/cda-pubs-cdi-1998-cdi2210-cdi2210i.htm?utm_source=openai)) The initial 1998 outbreaks and subsequent flare‑ups in 1999 and 2000 led to the destruction of around two million chickens and major disruption of regional egg and meat production.([abc.net.au](https://www.abc.net.au/science/news/stories/1999/42994.htm?utm_source=openai)) Through depopulation of affected flocks, strict movement controls, surveillance and enhanced biosecurity, authorities eradicated the virulent viruses and Australia regained ND‑free status, with only low‑virulence NDV remaining in poultry.([outbreak.gov.au](https://www.outbreak.gov.au/prepare-respond/identify-pests-diseases/emergency-animal-diseases-field-guide?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density commercial poultry production, movements of birds and equipment among farms, and prior circulation of lentogenic NDV strains created conditions in which virulent variants could arise and spread rapidly once they emerged.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19184867/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Clear re‑emergence driven by increased virulence/pathogenicity, as molecular analyses showed stepwise acquisition of multiple basic amino acids at the fusion protein cleavage site in a previously low‑virulence genotype I lineage, converting it into a velogenic virus capable of causing severe disease and high mortality in chickens.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19184867/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Retain this event as a key example of in situ evolution of virulent NDV in a previously NDV-free country for velogenic strains, but improve documentation. Replaced generic North American references with Australian outbreak reports and molecular epidemiology papers, and confirmed classification as re-emergence driven by virulence increase in endemic lentogenic viruses rather than by new continental introduction.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoavulavirus javaense

Host: Village chickens and other rural poultry, plus small-scale and commercial chicken flocks across all agro-ecological zones
Event.summary: In 2008, endemic Newcastle disease in Nigeria culminated in a nationwide epizootic in which an estimated 78,526 outbreaks were reported across the country, mostly in village chickens and smallholder or semi‑intensive commercial flocks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5142595/?utm_source=openai)) The epidemic imposed an estimated financial burden of 8.9 billion Nigerian naira on the rural chicken sector alone, underscoring the heavy, often under‑reported toll of ND on poultry‑dependent livelihoods.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5142595/?utm_source=openai)) Despite these losses, ND remained endemic after 2008, with recurrent outbreaks in backyard and commercial systems and growing recognition of the diverse virulent genotypes circulating in West Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5142595/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive movement of live birds through live‑bird markets, weak biosecurity in village and peri‑urban flocks, limited access to quality vaccines, and incomplete cold‑chain and dosing practices created conditions for explosive spread and persistence of NDV nationwide.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5142595/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The event reflects amplification of multiple virulent NDV lineages (including genotype V sublineages and genotype XVII) already present in Nigeria rather than emergence of a single new genotype, so it is best categorized as a large‑scale re‑occurrence driven mainly by management and marketing factors.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19052688/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – Added this row to capture the 2008 nationwide Newcastle disease epizootic in Nigeria, documented to involve more than 78,000 reported outbreaks and very large economic losses, which clearly qualifies as one of the most impactful recent ND events. Classified as re-occurrence driven primarily by systemic control and biosecurity gaps rather than by the appearance of a single novel genotype.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoavulavirus javaense
EPP.common.name: Newcastle disease virus, NDV, Avian paramyxovirus 1
Host: Backyard gamefowl and exhibition chickens, smallholder flocks, and commercial layer operations in California
Event.summary: In May 2018, virulent Newcastle disease was detected in a backyard exhibition flock in Los Angeles County, California, and over the next two years the outbreak spread widely through backyard gamefowl in southern California, with occasional transmission to commercial layer farms.([outbreak.gov.au](https://www.outbreak.gov.au/prepare-respond/identify-pests-diseases/emergency-animal-diseases-field-guide?utm_source=openai)) By the time California and federal authorities declared the state free of virulent ND in 2020, more than 1.2 million birds had been euthanized and hundreds of premises in Los Angeles, Riverside and San Bernardino counties had been affected.([cdfa.ca.gov](https://www.cdfa.ca.gov/ahfss/Animal_Health/newcastle_disease_info.html?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak was eventually contained through extensive depopulation, quarantine zones, movement restrictions and intensive outreach to gamefowl communities, echoing earlier major California outbreaks in 1971–1974 and 2002–2003.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5659000/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense networks of backyard and gamefowl flocks in urban and peri‑urban southern California, frequent informal movement and trade of birds (including illegal imports), and limited biosecurity in small flocks created ideal conditions for sustained transmission and spillover into commercial operations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5659000/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Virus characterisation showed close similarity to virulent NDV lineages circulating in Mexico and to previous California outbreaks, with no evidence of a substantially novel genotype; the event is best viewed as a re‑occurrence driven by anthropogenic movement and management factors rather than by a fundamentally new viral variant.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3993629/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain – This row accurately describes the scale, timing and drivers of the 2018–2020 virulent Newcastle disease outbreak in southern California, including the approximate number of birds culled, affected counties and the predominance of backyard gamefowl, and correctly classifies it as a major re-occurrence rather than emergence of a new genotype.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus schmallenbergense
EPP.common.name: Schmallenberg virus, SBV
Host: Domestic ruminants (primarily beef and dairy cattle, with evidence of exposure in small ruminants) in central Anatolia and later other western and southern Turkish regions
Event.summary: Origin: Following the large 2011–2013 SBV epidemic in Europe, serologic and molecular surveys of cattle herds in central Anatolia in 2013 detected SBV RNA in approximately 3% of blood samples and neutralizing antibodies in about 24% of sera, with S‑segment sequences showing 98–99% nucleotide identity to European SBV strains, indicating introduction of the virus into Turkish ruminant populations. Development: Additional surveys and case reports over the following years found further seropositivity and evidence of exposure in several Turkish regions, and later work in the Eastern Mediterranean region documented around 29% ELISA seropositivity and low‑level PCR positivity in ruminants between 2015 and 2017, but no explosive epidemic with congenital malformations on the scale seen in north‑western Europe was recorded. Ending: After 2017, SBV appears to have circulated at low to moderate levels in Türkiye, with sporadic detections rather than sustained large outbreaks, suggesting that local herd immunity and climatic/vector conditions may have limited clinical impact despite established circulation within the Western Asia sub‑region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely external drivers include windborne dispersal of infected Culicoides midges from affected parts of south‑eastern Europe across the Bosporus and Aegean, cross‑border movement of ruminants and possibly trade in infected semen, combined with limited initial awareness of SBV in Türkiye, which may have delayed its recognition. Internal mechanisms: Sequenced Turkish SBV strains were highly similar to European isolates, indicating introduction of the existing epidemic lineage rather than the emergence of a novel variant; this episode therefore mainly reflects geographic range expansion within Asia and establishment in Western Asia, supported by competent local Culicoides vectors and largely naïve ruminant hosts, rather than viral innovation.
Review: Review – Existing event retained but reclassified from inter‑continental to intra‑continental emergence because earlier serologic data from China indicate that Asia was already affected by SBV (or an SBV‑like virus) by 2012; this Turkish episode is therefore best interpreted as the first confirmed spread into the Western Asia sub‑region rather than the first appearance on the Asian continent. The narrative was updated to reference both early RT‑PCR and later serologic work in Türkiye, and the evidence base (Tonbak 2016 and subsequent regional studies) is appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

The epidemic spread across several central districts and ultimately resulted in 164 cases (142 confirmed and 22 probable), 55 confirmed deaths, and 87 survivors before being controlled. Aggressive public health measures—including isolation of cases, contact tracing, movement restrictions, and enhanced community engagement in the absence of a licensed Sudan virus vaccine—brought transmission to an end and the outbreak was declared over in early 2023.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Zoonotic spillover in a rural area with close interaction with wildlife, delayed detection of the index cluster, suboptimal infection prevention in some facilities, and population movement along trade routes facilitated early spread. Internal mechanisms: This was a re-occurrence of Sudan ebolavirus in Uganda rather than a new virus species; available evidence suggests a typical Sudan virus lineage without major novel genetic traits, but the event underscores gaps in cross-protective vaccination (no licensed Sudan-specific vaccine at the time) and the importance of strain-specific countermeasures.
Review: retain – The 2022 Sudan virus disease outbreak in Uganda (164 cases) is appropriately included as one of the larger recent filovirus outbreaks and as a re-occurrence of Sudan ebolavirus in an already affected Eastern Africa subregion. Event-type coding (re_occurrence only) accords with the definitions, and the WHO and peer‑reviewed sources provide robust epidemiological and molecular detail.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hantavirus, HCPS, HFRS
Host: Peromyscus maniculatus (deer mouse reservoir); humans
Event.summary: In spring 1993, a cluster of acute respiratory failure and high‑fatality illness was detected among residents of the Four Corners region in the southwestern United States. Epidemiologic and laboratory investigations identified a previously unrecognized New World hantavirus, later named Sin Nombre virus, carried by deer mice and causing a new clinical entity termed hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS). Intensive rodent control, public health messaging on rodent exposure, and improved clinical recognition led to a decline from the initial explosive cluster into sporadic, seasonally linked HPS cases in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unusually wet El Niño conditions in the early 1990s increased primary productivity, boosting deer mouse populations and human–rodent contact in rural housing and peridomestic settings. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and first recognition of a previously undescribed Sin Nombre orthohantavirus lineage capable of causing severe pulmonary disease in humans (novel strain/genotype emergence), with efficient aerosol transmission from infected rodent excreta to people.
Review: retain – Major global event: first recognition of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and Sin Nombre virus in humans in North America. Coding as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence is appropriate, geography (United States; Northern America) is correct, and sources are primary (CDC/EID plus supporting reviews), so no structural changes were needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hantavirus, HCPS, HFRS
Host: Oligoryzomys longicaudatus (long‑tailed pygmy rice rat); humans
Event.summary: In September–December 1996, an outbreak of HPS occurred around El Bolsón, Bariloche and Esquel in southern Argentina, involving at least 18 confirmed cases linked by close social and family contact rather than shared rodent exposure. Molecular and epidemiologic investigations demonstrated person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus, providing the first conclusive evidence that a hantavirus could spread directly between humans. Intensive contact tracing, isolation of symptomatic contacts and strengthened infection‑control measures eventually interrupted transmission and terminated the outbreak after several generations of human‑to‑human spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rural housing with high rodent infestation, close‑knit family and social networks, and delayed recognition of secondary cases facilitated chains of transmission. Internal mechanisms: Andes virus lineage with traits permitting limited human‑to‑human transmission via respiratory secretions (enhanced transmission/host adaptation) and higher viral loads in some patients, representing a clear re‑emergence driven by viral properties rather than simple ecological resurgence.
Review: retain – The 1996 El Bolsón/Esquel Andes virus cluster is the first well-documented person-to-person transmission of a hantavirus and is rightly classified as re_emergence driven by enhanced human-to-human spread. Countries have been restricted to Argentina [1996] to avoid implying contemporaneous Chilean involvement in this specific outbreak. Event remains high-impact despite moderate case numbers and should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hantavirus, HCPS, HFRS
Host: Myodes glareolus (bank vole) and other small rodents; humans
Event.summary: From April 1997 through March 1998, the Republic of Bashkortostan in the European part of the Russian Federation experienced an unprecedented epidemic of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, with 10,057 registered cases and extremely high regional incidence peaking in autumn and early winter 1997. The outbreak occurred in an area where hantaviruses had been endemic but typically at much lower incidence; serologic investigations implicated Puumala orthohantavirus and related rodent-borne lineages maintained in bank voles and other small mammals. Emergency rodent-control campaigns, intensified public guidance on avoiding rodent exposure, and subsequent declines in vole populations were followed by a sharp reduction in HFRS incidence, although Russia has continued to experience recurrent multi‑year epidemic peaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Favorable climatic conditions and mast years leading to explosive bank vole population growth, expansion of human housing and agricultural activity into forest-edge habitats, and limited pre-existing immunity in the local population created conditions for intense spillover. Internal mechanisms: Established Puumala and related orthohantaviruses in local rodents caused disease; available data do not support emergence of a fundamentally novel strain, so the event represents very large-scale re_occurrence driven primarily by host and environmental dynamics rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain – Newly added event to represent the extremely large 1997–1998 HFRS epidemic in Bashkortostan (~10,000+ cases), which was missing despite being one of the highest-burden Orthohantavirus outbreaks worldwide since 1990. Coded as re_occurrence in an already endemic Eastern European subregion with no clear evidence for a novel strain; geography (Russian Federation; Eastern Europe) and hosts follow Russian and international epidemiologic reports. This event clearly belongs among the top-impact episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hantavirus, HCPS, HFRS
Host: Peromyscus maniculatus (deer mouse); humans
Event.summary: In summer 2012, a cluster of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome cases was identified among visitors who had overnighted in tent cabins at Yosemite National Park in California. Investigations linked infection to intense deer‑mouse infestation and rodent access into insulated “Signature” tent cabins, ultimately identifying around ten hantavirus infections and three deaths among visitors from multiple U.S. states and abroad. Closure and remediation of the affected cabins, large‑scale notification of past visitors and strengthened rodent‑exclusion measures ended the outbreak and returned case numbers to baseline sporadic levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Park lodging design that allowed nesting of infected deer mice within wall insulation, high visitor turnover, and limited early recognition of the hazard raised exposure risk; ecologic factors supporting high local rodent densities also contributed. Internal mechanisms: Established Sin Nombre orthohantavirus in deer mice caused infection; the event represents re‑occurrence of HPS in a known endemic region without major viral change, though improved environmental investigation clarified the transmission setting.
Review: retain – The Yosemite 2012 HPS cluster (≈10 cases, 3 deaths, thousands of exposed visitors) is well documented and epidemiologically important, illustrating high-risk built environments and multi-state exposures despite modest case numbers. Geography and coding as a re_occurrence in an already endemic area without intra- or inter-continental emergence are appropriate, and sources (NPS, CDC MMWR, EID) are strong. Recommended to retain as one of the key high-impact, well-characterized outbreaks.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hantavirus, HCPS, HFRS
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012]
Host: Rattus norvegicus (pet and breeder rats); humans
Event.summary: In 2012, UK investigators identified human Seoul virus infections linked to a breeding colony of pet rats (the “Cherwell” facility) and associated fancy‑rat networks, alongside earlier detection of Seoul virus in rats from the Humber region. Testing of animals from these and related colonies found a very high prevalence of Seoul hantavirus RNA in rat tissues, confirming widespread infection in the pet‑rat population and implicating these colonies as the source of human disease. Culling of infected colonies, advice to rat owners and enhanced surveillance curtailed further spread from the implicated facilities, although Seoul virus persistence in European pet and wild rats remains a concern.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growth of the pet‑rat hobby and trade, dense rat breeding facilities, and movement of animals between breeders across Europe enabled amplification and dissemination of infected rats. Internal mechanisms: Seoul orthohantavirus, historically associated with commensal wild brown rats and HFRS in Asia, expanded into intensively traded pet‑rat populations (host expansion and enhanced transmission within a new managed host system), with phylogenetic evidence linking UK pet‑rat strains to international trade‑related introductions.
Review: review – The emergence of Seoul virus in UK pet-rat networks is real and important for documenting host-system expansion into companion animals, but human case numbers are small compared with major HFRS epidemics. Sub_region has been corrected from Western Europe to Northern Europe to match UNSD classification for the UK, and intra_continental_emergence has been set from 'true' to 'false' because Orthohantavirus infections were already established within the Northern Europe subregion; the event is best interpreted as re_emergence via host expansion. Retain for now, but it is a borderline choice if only the very largest events are ultimately kept.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus monkeypox
EPP.common.name: Monkeypox virus, MPXV
Host: Humans; likely small mammals (squirrels and other rodents) as reservoirs/spillover sources
Event.summary: In early 1996, human mpox cases began to increase sharply in the Katako‑Kombe and Lodja health zones of Kasai‑Oriental, Democratic Republic of the Congo, in a forested, highly remote area with ongoing zoonotic spillover. Investigations by WHO and CDC through 1997 documented approximately 511 suspected human cases, mainly linked by household contact and exposure to forest animals, making it the largest documented mpox outbreak to that time. Transmission gradually declined by late 1997 as susceptible contacts were exhausted and intensified surveillance and public‑health measures (isolation, reduced bushmeat hunting) were implemented.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/1997_11_14b-en?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Waning population immunity following cessation of smallpox vaccination, civil instability and displacement in rural DRC, and increased hunting and handling of forest wildlife increased human exposure and person‑to‑person spread. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of a novel strain; the outbreak was caused by the existing Congo Basin (clade I) lineage with high transmissibility but primarily reflected a growing pool of immunologically naïve humans and dense household contacts rather than major viral change.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/7/3/01-7311_article?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus monkeypox
EPP.common.name: Monkeypox virus, MPXV
Host: Humans; reservoir small mammals (forest rodents and other wildlife)
Event.summary: Beginning in late 2005, the Democratic Republic of the Congo experienced another extended resurgence of human mpox, with surveillance between November 2005 and November 2007 detecting around 760 laboratory‑confirmed cases concentrated in forested central and eastern provinces. Transmission occurred predominantly through close household contact and ongoing exposure to infected wildlife, superimposed on a young population with little or no smallpox‑derived immunity. Reported incidence decreased after 2007 as surveillance and community awareness improved and the immediate wave of susceptible contacts declined, though endemic transmission in DRC persisted.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpox_in_the_Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High birth rates producing large cohorts unvaccinated against smallpox, poverty and hunting of bushmeat, and limited access to healthcare and surveillance systems contributed to sustained human‑to‑human transmission and repeated zoonotic introductions. Internal mechanisms: The outbreaks were caused by Congo Basin clade I viruses with known high transmissibility and virulence; no single novel genotype was identified as the driver, so the event is best interpreted as re‑occurrence linked mainly to demographic and ecological changes.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpox_in_the_Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Papillomavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Papillomatosis
Host: Dairy cattle (teats of Polish dairy cows)
Event.summary: In the early 2020s (with findings published in 2023), teat papillomatosis in Polish dairy herds was investigated to genetically characterize the bovine papillomavirus types present. Analysis of teat lesions from affected cows demonstrated infection with multiple BPV genotypes and led to the detection of a new putative BPV type in teat papillomas, confirming that teat papillomatosis in Europe is also driven by diverse and partly novel BPV strains. These cases underscored teat papillomatosis as a contributor to mastitis risk and milk production losses in intensive Polish dairy systems, although outbreaks remained manageable with hygiene, supportive care and culling of heavily affected cows.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive milking routines and imperfect sanitation of teat cups and equipment in Polish dairies likely facilitated herd‑level spread of BPVs, in line with patterns described in other countries. Internal mechanisms: Co‑infection with several BPV genotypes and identification of a putative new BPV type in teat papillomas indicate ongoing viral evolution and diversification within European cattle; existing type‑specific immunity may favor the emergence of new genotypes and recurrent disease, justifying classification as re‑emergence rather than simple re‑occurrence.
Review: Review – The original row dated this event to 2013, but the cited Pathogens paper reporting genetic evaluation of BPV types in Polish teat papillomas was published in 2023 and does not support a specific 2013 outbreak. The year has been updated to 2023–2023, using the publication year as a proxy for the investigation period, and the summary wording was adjusted accordingly. Event type remains re‑emergence (new genotype plus co‑infection) and re‑occurrence (increased recognition of disease in an already endemic subregion); there is no basis for first‑detection or intra‑/inter‑continental emergence flags, as bovine papillomatosis has long been present in Europe. Recommend expert review of the exact sampling years once the full article is accessed, but overall this represents a valid, medium‑impact re‑emergent event in Eastern Europe.

EPP.scientific.name: Paramyxovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Paramyxovirosis
Host: Horses (clinical spillover host); flying-fox bats (Pteropus spp., reservoir identified later)
Event.summary: In September 1994, a previously unknown paramyxovirus (later named Hendra virus) emerged in a Thoroughbred training complex in Hendra, a suburb of Brisbane, Queensland, killing 13 horses and a horse trainer with severe respiratory disease. Subsequent investigation linked the outbreak to spillover from flying-fox bats into horses, and extensive testing of nearly 2,000 horses showed no prior circulation, confirming it as a new henipavirus infection of horses and humans. Quarantine, movement controls and culling of affected horses ended the cluster, and no wider spread in Australian livestock occurred at that time.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density racehorse stabling with intense close contact, horse paddocks located under or near trees used by flying-foxes, and encroachment of horse facilities into bat foraging ranges in peri-urban Brisbane. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a novel henipavirus from bats to horses, followed by efficient horse-to-horse transmission via respiratory secretions once spillover occurred; ecological adaptation of the virus to local bat populations allowed long-term maintenance in the wildlife reservoir.
Review: retain – Event correctly describes the first recognized emergence of Hendra virus with accurate location, hosts, and approximate horse and human fatalities. Classification as first_global_emergence and first_detection is appropriate at the virus-species level (Hendra virus), even though paramyxoviruses in general were long endemic in animals. Geographic coding (Oceania; Australia and New Zealand; Australia) and timing (1994) are correct; sources are authoritative (state health departments, WOAH, peer-reviewed reviews).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Paramyxovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Paramyxovirosis
Host: Sheep; goats; wild bharal (Pseudois nayaur) in affected highland areas
Event.summary: In July 2007, peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV), a morbillivirus of sheep and goats, was confirmed for the first time in China during multiple outbreaks in four counties of the remote Ngari region of southwestern Tibet, causing high morbidity and mortality in small-ruminant flocks and infections in free-ranging bharal. Over 2007–2008, diagnostic surveys and molecular testing documented several distinct outbreak foci in Tibetan villages, indicating sustained in situ transmission rather than isolated introductions, and showed the virus belonged to lineage IV circulating in neighboring South Asian countries. Emergency control measures, including movement restrictions and ring vaccination, were implemented and successfully halted reported outbreaks in Tibet by 2008, after which no further Chinese PPR outbreaks were reported until the large epidemic beginning in 2013.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of small ruminants along traditional transhumance and trade routes linking Tibet with infected regions of South Asia; limited veterinary infrastructure, challenging terrain and low prior awareness of PPR in Tibetan pastoral systems impeded early recognition and control. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of endemic lineage IV PPRV into a new Asian subregion (Eastern Asia) and a previously unaffected country (China), with highly efficient transmission and severe disease in naïve sheep and goat populations and demonstrated ability to infect wild caprines.
Review: review – Epidemiologic details (first confirmation of PPR in China in Ngari, Tibet in 2007; lineage IV; involvement of bharal) and spatial coding (Asia; Eastern Asia; China) are correct. Classification as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence is appropriate for PPRV at the country/subregional level. However, in a strict top‑10 ranking for all animal paramyxoviruses, this episode is of moderate scale compared with later China-wide and African PPR epidemics and the large PDV/CDV events; consider retaining for its importance as the first incursion into Eastern Asia, but it could be deprioritized if the list must be reduced to exactly ten events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Paramyxovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Paramyxovirosis
Host: Sheep; goats
Event.summary: In mid-2008, PPR was confirmed for the first time in Morocco, where outbreaks in sheep and goats were reported in numerous provinces and posed a major threat to approximately 22 million small ruminants. FAO and national assessments indicated that this was the first incursion of PPR into North Africa, implying spread across the Sahara from endemic zones further south. Morocco rapidly launched nationwide vaccination campaigns from 2008 to 2010, combined with movement controls and outbreak containment measures, successfully controlling the epidemic, with the last reported case in November 2008.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of infected small ruminants along trans-Saharan pastoral and trade routes from endemic Sahelian countries; difficulty controlling animal movements in nomadic and transhumant systems in southern Morocco and neighboring regions. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of lineage IV PPRV from sub-Saharan Africa into a new subregion (Northern Africa), with high morbidity and mortality in immunologically naïve sheep and goat populations amplifying the impact of the initial incursion.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the first documented occurrence of PPR in Morocco and the broader North African subregion, with accurate timing (summer–autumn 2008), host species, and approximate population at risk. Classification as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence is appropriate for PPRV. Source set has been strengthened by ensuring inclusion of FAO, ONSSA (Moroccan veterinary authority) and a global PPR review, with Wikipedia kept only as supporting historical context.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Paramyxovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Paramyxovirosis
Host: Goats; sheep
Event.summary: From 2008 onward, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), previously considered PPR-free, began experiencing outbreaks of severe disease in goats and sheep across several provinces, culminating in a large epidemic recognized by 2012 that killed more than 75,000 goats and affected tens of thousands more small ruminants. Retrospective molecular studies of tissues from dead goats collected in Tshela in 2012 showed circulation of lineage IV PPRV closely related to viruses from neighboring Gabon and Nigeria, and revealed that at least four of eleven provinces had been affected between 2008 and 2012. FAO and national authorities mounted emergency vaccination campaigns (e.g. in Bandundu Province) and strengthened surveillance and border controls, which reduced but did not immediately eliminate PPR, and subsequent outbreaks in 2016 and 2018 involved additional viral lineages, indicating complex re-emergence dynamics.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Porous borders and largely uncontrolled movements of small ruminants between DRC and infected neighboring countries; limited veterinary services and public awareness; political instability and population displacement facilitating long-distance livestock movements; lack of systematic vaccination and quarantine infrastructure. Internal mechanisms: Intra-continental emergence of lineage IV PPRV into a new central African country followed by re-emergence and diversification of viral lineages (II, III and IV) over time, aided by viral genetic diversity and the ability of PPRV to persist and spread in mixed production systems and at the wildlife–livestock interface.
Review: retain – Well-supported as one of the largest PPR epidemics in central Africa, with >75,000 goat deaths and multi-province spread in a previously PPR-free country. Classification as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence (first incursion into Middle Africa) combined with re_emergence (multiple lineages detected over 2008–2012 and again later) is consistent with the project rules, which allow re-emergence to co-occur with intra-continental emergence. Country, subregion and timing match FAO and peer‑reviewed molecular epidemiology sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Paramyxovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Paramyxovirosis
Host: Sheep; goats
Event.summary: Peste des petits ruminants was first confirmed in northern Tanzania in 2008, and by early 2010 a major wave of outbreaks was recognized in northern and central regions, with FAO warning that the epidemic could spread southward into countries of the Southern African Development Community. The 2010 outbreaks threatened more than 13 million Tanzanian small ruminants and an estimated 50 million sheep and goats in up to 15 southern African countries if not contained, prompting an emergency regional response. Emergency vaccination in northern Tanzania, restrictions on animal movements, and strengthened surveillance in neighboring states helped to limit further southward spread, but PPR has since become endemic in much of Tanzania and remains a source of risk for southern Africa.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities and frequent movement of small ruminants for trade and pastoralism across East Africa; long, porous borders with Kenya and other endemic neighbors; limited prior PPR vaccination and delayed recognition of the disease after its initial introduction to Tanzania in 2008. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence and southward geographic spread of PPRV within the Eastern Africa subregion into new areas of Tanzania that were previously unaffected, driven by high transmissibility of lineage III PPRV in largely unvaccinated flocks rather than by clear viral genetic change.
Review: retain – Revised the event summary to clarify that PPR was first confirmed in Tanzania in 2008, while the 2010 wave represented a large re-occurrence and southward extension with major regional risk (threat to ~50 million small ruminants across up to 15 SADC countries). Classification as re_occurrence (not intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because PPRV was already established in Eastern Africa and in Tanzania by 2008. Event is borderline in a strict global top‑10 ranking but is retained here given its scale, policy importance for the SADC region, and strong FAO documentation; flagged for possible down‑selection if further prioritization is needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Paramyxovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Paramyxovirosis
Host: Sheep; goats; Mongolian saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica mongolica); goitered gazelles and other wild ungulates
Event.summary: In September 2016, Mongolia reported its first-ever PPR outbreaks in domestic sheep and goats in western provinces bordering China, representing a new country incursion of lineage IV PPRV into a naïve small-ruminant population. In early 2017, the virus spilled over into the critically endangered Mongolian saiga antelope and other wild ungulates in the Great Lakes Depression, causing mass mortality that reduced the saiga population from roughly 25,000 animals to fewer than 9,000 within a few months. Intensive vaccination of livestock, targeted carcass disposal and wildlife surveillance eventually interrupted active transmission by mid-2017, but the event left the saiga population severely depleted and highlighted PPR as a major biodiversity as well as livestock threat.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross-border livestock movements from infected areas of China into western Mongolia; close spatio-temporal overlap of domestic sheep and goats with saiga and other wild ungulates on shared rangelands; limited prior PPR vaccination and wildlife health surveillance in Mongolia. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of lineage IV PPRV into a previously unaffected country; highly lethal host expansion into multiple wild ungulate species (especially Mongolian saiga), with intense transmission at the livestock–wildlife interface enabling rapid spread and catastrophic wildlife mortality.
Review: retain – Adjusted event-type flags by setting intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence to false and treating this as first_detection of PPRV in Mongolia. Under the project’s definitions, intra-continental emergence is reserved for first appearance in a new UNSD subregion (Eastern Asia was already affected via China), and re-emergence requires prior presence in the same subregion, which did not apply at the country level. The event’s very high impact on both livestock and critically endangered Mongolian saiga and its status as Mongolia’s first PPR incursion justify retaining it among the major emergence events.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Pasteurellosis
Host: Cattle, pigs, sheep, rabbits, poultry and companion animals with respiratory or systemic pasteurellosis
Event.summary: Between 2012 and 2017, data from the French national veterinary antimicrobial resistance network (RESAPATH) showed that P. multocida isolated from respiratory infections in food-producing animals and pets was widespread, and that in cattle isolates in particular, resistance to several veterinary antimicrobials (notably tetracyclines and some older agents) was present at non-trivial levels. Although overall resistance to critically important antimicrobials such as third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones remained low, the surveillance highlighted distinct resistance profiles in cattle compared with other host species and provided evidence that selection for resistance was occurring despite national efforts to reduce antimicrobial use. These findings informed national guidelines and stewardship initiatives aimed at preserving the efficacy of key BRD treatments in French livestock.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-standing, widespread use of oral and injectable antimicrobials for respiratory disease in cattle and other species in France, including metaphylactic regimens, provided selection pressure for resistance. The structure of French livestock production, with integrated systems and animal movements between farms and regions, facilitated dissemination of successful resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Progressive accumulation and dissemination of resistance determinants in P. multocida, particularly in cattle isolates (e.g., genes mediating resistance to tetracyclines and older antimicrobials), represent antimicrobial resistance–mediated re-emergence of the pathogen as a more difficult-to-treat cause of respiratory disease. Most isolates remained susceptible to high-priority critically important drugs, but the documented resistance patterns signal evolutionary responses to past drug exposure.
Review: Review – This event reflects a large national surveillance dataset (thousands of isolates) and is important for understanding AMR-driven re-emergence. However, the original draft slightly overstated uniformly increasing resistance trends and underplayed that overall resistance to several key classes remained low. The summary has been rephrased for closer alignment with published RESAPATH and EFSA descriptions. Classification as re_emergence via AMR is appropriate. Geographic coding (Western Europe, France) and years (2012–2017) match the main study period, but a human expert should confirm quantitative thresholds and whether France should indeed be prioritized over other European countries with similar surveillance data in a strict top‑10 ranking.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Pasteurellosis
Host: Free-range and intensive pigs and cattle (acute septicemia and respiratory disease due to P. multocida type B)
Event.summary: From 2009 onward, Spain documented the emergence of P. multocida capsular type B, classically associated with hemorrhagic septicemia, as a cause of acute septicemic pasteurellosis in free-range pigs, wild boar and later cattle. An initial outbreak of acute septicemia in free-range pigs in 2009 was followed by additional type B outbreaks in swine and wild boar, and in February 2015 the first documented outbreak of bovine hemorrhagic septicemia caused by P. multocida type B occurred on a free-range beef farm in southern Spain, affecting calves and one cow with characteristic HS lesions. Over the period 2010–2018, at least 70–80 type B isolates from pigs and cattle with acute septicemia were characterized, revealing shared capsular type B biovar 3 profiles and, in many isolates, reduced susceptibility to commonly used antimicrobials. Autogenous vaccination and targeted antimicrobial therapy were implemented to control farm-level outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of free-range and mixed-species livestock systems in parts of Spain, with close contact between pigs, cattle and wildlife (e.g., wild boar, deer), likely facilitated the introduction and circulation of type B P. multocida lineages historically associated with HS in Asia and Africa. Animal movements and environmental conditions in extensive systems also favored persistence and spillover between host species. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization shows Spanish type B isolates clustering with global HS-associated lineages and sharing virulence-associated genes typical of hemorrhagic septicemia, while antimicrobial susceptibility testing of pig and cattle isolates revealed resistance to several commonly used drug classes (e.g., tetracyclines, some older agents). Together, these findings support classification as re-emergence via geographic expansion of HS-associated type B lineages into Iberian livestock and partial evolution of antimicrobial resistance, rather than a first detection of P. multocida in the region.
Review: Review – Spain’s type B episode is epidemiologically important because it marks the appearance and spread of HS-associated P. multocida lineages in Iberian pigs, wild boar and, for the first time, cattle, with documented acute septicemia and economic impact. The event year range has been updated to 2009–2018 to encompass the first reported pig outbreak and the 2015 bovine HS outbreak. Hosts and event summary have been broadened accordingly, and key primary sources (Acta Veterinaria Hungarica short communication on the 2015 bovine HS outbreak and the Vet Microbiol AMR paper on type B isolates) have been added. Classification as re_emergence (host expansion/geographic expansion plus AMR) remains appropriate. A human reviewer should confirm whether to treat pig and cattle outbreaks as a single linked episode (as done here) or as separate events in a more granular dataset.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Pasteurellosis
Host: Pigs with respiratory disease/pasteurellosis
Event.summary: From approximately 2013 to 2018, veterinary laboratories in Viet Nam collected and characterized 83 P. multocida isolates from pigs showing clinical signs of pasteurellosis and respiratory disease, reflecting recurrent outbreaks in commercial herds in central Vietnam. Molecular analysis revealed high prevalence of multiple virulence factors and capsular serotypes among these isolates, together with several antimicrobial resistance genes. The findings suggest that virulent and partially multidrug-resistant P. multocida lineages had become entrenched in Vietnamese pig production, complicating control of respiratory disease complexes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification of Vietnam’s swine industry, high animal densities, and the use of antimicrobials for growth promotion and disease prevention created favorable conditions for emergence and spread of virulent, resistant P. multocida strains. Internal mechanisms: Many isolates carried clustered virulence genes and antibiotic resistance determinants (including genes conferring resistance to tetracyclines and sulfonamides), consistent with re-emergence driven by acquisition of resistance and maintenance of a robust virulence arsenal in pig-adapted lineages.
Review: Retain – This episode documents the establishment of virulent, AMR-associated P. multocida lineages in a rapidly intensifying swine sector, with repeated clinical disease and clear molecular evidence of resistance and virulence factors. Geographic coding (South-eastern Asia, Viet Nam) and years are in line with the study. Event-type assignment as re_emergence (rather than mere re-occurrence) is appropriate given the focus on virulence and resistance genes. No major inconsistencies were identified; human review could strengthen the link to specific production-loss estimates if available from national sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Penaeid shrimp infectious myonecrosis virus
EPP.common.name: IMNV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei (Penaeus vannamei)
Event.summary: From 2002, intensive L. vannamei farms in Piauí State, northeastern Brazil began reporting episodes of idiopathic myonecrosis with whitening of abdominal muscles and slow but high cumulative mortalities that in some ponds approached 70%. Over 2003–2005 the condition spread along Brazil’s northeast coast into additional states, causing repeated crop failures and national losses estimated in the hundreds of millions of US dollars as productivity in affected areas dropped sharply. Investigations during this period purified a 40 nm dsRNA virus from diseased shrimp, which was designated infectious myonecrosis virus (IMNV), and adoption of improved biosecurity, specific-pathogen-free (SPF) stocks and movement controls subsequently reduced the frequency of catastrophic IMN outbreaks, although the virus remained endemic in parts of Brazil.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of L. vannamei aquaculture in northeastern Brazil, with high stocking densities, long grow-out periods, and frequent environmental stressors (temperature and water-quality fluctuations), together with extensive movement of postlarvae and juveniles among farms, created ideal conditions for emergence and farm-to-farm spread of a previously unrecognised virus. Internal mechanisms: IMNV is a novel dsRNA virus tentatively assigned to the Totiviridae, with a chronic infection profile, high viral loads in skeletal muscle and ability to persist in surviving shrimp; these traits support efficient horizontal transmission within ponds (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation) and facilitated geographic range expansion and establishment in Brazilian farmed L. vannamei populations (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Geographic Range Expansion, inherent).
Review: Review – Retain this event as the first global emergence and detection of IMNV in farmed Litopenaeus vannamei in Brazil, but expand the event period from "2002-2004" to "2002-2005" to reflect that IMN-related epizootics and large productivity losses in northeastern Brazil clearly continued through 2004–2005; geography and emergence-type coding remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Penaeid shrimp infectious myonecrosis virus
EPP.common.name: IMNV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event.summary: In 2006, farms in the Situbondo District of East Java, Indonesia, experienced outbreaks of a myonecrosis disease in L. vannamei characterised by whitening of abdominal musculature and chronic mortalities reminiscent of Brazilian infectious myonecrosis. RT-PCR and sequencing of the viral capsid gene from affected shrimp showed IMNV highly similar to the Brazilian reference strain, confirming introduction of the virus into Indonesia and its spread during 2006–2007 to additional shrimp-growing areas with substantial economic losses in intensive farms. Control measures including stricter screening and control of broodstock and postlarvae movements, farm biosecurity upgrades and adjusted stocking practices gradually reduced catastrophic mortality, although IMNV became endemic and later genotypes have continued to be detected in Indonesian production systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: transboundary movement of live L. vannamei broodstock and postlarvae from IMNV-endemic Brazil, often without adequate health certification or screening, combined with rapid intensification of L. vannamei farming in Indonesia, enabled introduction and establishment of IMNV in Southeast Asia. Internal mechanisms: Indonesian isolates from the initial outbreaks were nearly identical to Brazilian strains, indicating direct geographic spread of an existing lineage; chronic infection dynamics and efficient horizontal transmission in high-density ponds (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion, inherent) underpinned rapid farm-to-farm dissemination once the virus entered the country.
Review: Review – Event appropriately represents the first confirmed IMNV outbreaks in Indonesia and the first inter-continental emergence of IMNV into Asia; I set re_emergence to false (previously true) because early Indonesian isolates were essentially identical to Brazilian strains and there is no evidence that a novel variant drove this initial incursion, so this episode is best classified purely as inter-continental geographic spread.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Penaeid shrimp infectious myonecrosis virus
EPP.common.name: IMNV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event.summary: In May 2015, a grow-out facility for juvenile L. vannamei on the Korean coast experienced sudden mortalities in two tanks, with about 40% of 500,000 stocked shrimp dying over three days; histology revealed typical IMN lesions (coagulative skeletal muscle necrosis and lymphoid organ spheroids), and nested RT-PCR followed by sequencing confirmed IMNV infection. A subsequent epidemiological investigation in 2015 tested broodstock, imported polychaete lugworms used as maturation feed, rearing water and surrounding organisms from five hatcheries, detecting IMNV in one of six broodstock and in 25–40% of the imported lugworms but not in culture water or local wild invertebrates, indicating introduction via infected biological inputs. Following diagnosis, Korean authorities implemented quarantine and movement restrictions on affected facilities, strengthened import controls and diagnostics for broodstock and feeds, and later national surveillance has not reported additional large-scale IMNV epizootics in Korean farms.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Korea’s emerging whiteleg shrimp sector relied on imported SPF broodstock and frozen or chilled polychaete lugworms for broodstock maturation; the discovery of IMNV in both broodstock and lugworms from one hatchery indicates that infected live or fresh inputs, rather than the environment, were the most plausible introduction pathway. High-density juvenile culture and limited prior experience with IMNV in Korea facilitated rapid amplification once it entered the facility. Internal mechanisms: IMNV’s capacity to establish persistent infections in broodstock and survive in fresh or frozen biological materials (feeds) allows long-distance movement without obvious clinical signs, and its chronic but often substantial mortality profile in L. vannamei supports its establishment in intensive hatchery and nursery systems when biosecurity is breached (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion, inherent).
Review: Review – Added this event to capture the first confirmed IMNV outbreak in farmed Litopenaeus vannamei in the Republic of Korea in 2015, which is largely omitted from global timelines; classified it as intra-continental emergence into the Eastern Asia subregion with country-level first detection, and based the description on the national epidemiological investigation that links introduction to infected broodstock and imported lugworm feed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Penaeid shrimp infectious myonecrosis virus
EPP.common.name: IMNV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event.summary: In 2016, shrimp farms in Purba Medinipur District, West Bengal, India reported disease outbreaks in L. vannamei characterised by muscle opaqueness, reddish discolouration of distal abdominal segments and gradually increasing mortalities of roughly 20–50%, with routine PCR tests negative for common DNA shrimp viruses. RT-PCR with IMNV-specific primers, histopathology and experimental infection of naïve shrimp identified IMNV as the causative agent, representing the first confirmed report of IMNV in Indian aquaculture and demonstrating local farm-to-farm spread in affected coastal areas. Subsequent surveillance showed that IMNV infections remained sporadic but persistent in Indian L. vannamei culture, prompting inclusion of IMNV in national health management plans and SPF breeding and screening programmes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of L. vannamei farming in India, heavy reliance on imported and domestically multiplied broodstock, and imperfect screening and biosecurity created pathways for IMNV introduction, while high stocking densities, environmental stress and co-infections likely amplified disease impact once the virus was present. Internal mechanisms: available sequence and epidemiological data suggest that Indian IMNV represents geographic range expansion of existing Asian/Brazilian lineages rather than a uniquely Indian variant; the chronic infection dynamics and high susceptibility of L. vannamei favour establishment in new farming regions once introduced (Geographic Range Expansion, inherent; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: Review – Event correctly describes the first confirmed IMNV outbreaks in India in 2016 and treats them as intra-continental emergence into the Southern Asia subregion with country-level first detection; I removed a later generic surveillance paper that did not specifically document these West Bengal outbreaks and retained the primary 2017 J Fish Diseases article and key reviews as sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Penaeid shrimp infectious myonecrosis virus
EPP.common.name: IMNV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event.summary: In 2018, Malaysian authorities reported an outbreak of disease consistent with infectious myonecrosis in cultured L. vannamei in Melaka, Peninsular Malaysia, with affected shrimp showing muscle atrophy and reddish discolouration of the tail region; national reporting to the NACA/WOAH Quarterly Aquatic Animal Disease system listed infection with IMNV as the causative agent. During 2018–2019, IMNV was recognised as a new viral threat for Malaysian shrimp farming, with positive PCR findings in affected farms raising concern over possible introduction from IMNV-endemic neighbours and prompting review of broodstock and postlarvae import controls. In response, Malaysia implemented enhanced biosecurity, tighter regulation of live shrimp imports and inclusion of IMNV among screened and notifiable pathogens, which appears to have limited more widespread epizootics while leaving IMNV as an ongoing regional risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely introduction of IMNV via regional trade in live L. vannamei broodstock or postlarvae from endemic parts of Asia, combined with high-intensity culture and previously limited routine screening for IMNV, facilitated this re-occurrence within the South-eastern Asia subregion. Internal mechanisms: available sequence information and the regional context suggest the Malaysian outbreaks were caused by IMNV lineages closely related to Indonesian/Indian strains rather than a novel variant; the event is therefore best interpreted as geographic range expansion within Southeast Asia, with impact driven by the inherent high susceptibility of L. vannamei and the chronic, production-sapping nature of IMNV infection (Geographic Range Expansion, inherent).
Review: Retain – QAAD 2018/2 and associated Malaysian reports support a genuine IMNV outbreak in farmed Litopenaeus vannamei in Melaka in 2018 with measurable mortality; classification as first_detection for Malaysia and re-occurrence within an already affected South‑eastern Asia subregion (without new subregion or continent) is consistent with the event definitions, and no corrections to timing, geography or emergence type were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Penaeid shrimp infectious myonecrosis virus
EPP.common.name: IMNV
Host: Cultured penaeid shrimp, primarily Penaeus semisulcatus (also posing risk to L. vannamei)
Event.summary: From around 2018, disease outbreaks with muscle necrosis, reduced growth and abnormal appearance were reported in cultured penaeid shrimp (notably P. semisulcatus) on private farms in Damietta and North Sinai provinces along Egypt’s Mediterranean coast. Clinical examination, histopathology and PCR testing of affected shrimp confirmed IMNV infection with typical myonecrosis lesions, representing the first documented presence of IMNV in African aquaculture and indicating local establishment on the north coast. Repeated detections over subsequent production cycles raised concern about the virus’s impact on Egypt’s expanding shrimp industry and its potential spread to other Mediterranean and Red Sea aquaculture areas, prompting recommendations for stricter import controls, targeted surveillance and improved farm biosecurity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely introduction of IMNV into Egypt via importation of infected broodstock or postlarvae from endemic Asian sources, combined with rapid local development of penaeid shrimp aquaculture and limited prior familiarity with this virus, facilitated the first inter-continental jump of IMNV to Africa. Internal mechanisms: IMNV’s ability to infect multiple penaeid species, including P. semisulcatus, and to persist in apparently healthy or mildly affected shrimp promotes establishment in new host populations and environments (Host Expansion/Spillover; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation), even though distinct Egyptian genotypes have not yet been clearly defined.
Review: Retain – Evidence from Aly et al. (2020) and subsequent diagnostic reviews supports genuine IMNV outbreaks with characteristic myonecrosis lesions in cultured penaeid shrimp on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast beginning around 2018; classification as first_detection for Egypt and inter-continental emergence of IMNV into Africa is appropriate, and no corrections to timing, geography or emergence type were needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Penaeid shrimp infectious myonecrosis virus
EPP.common.name: IMNV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event.summary: In July 2020, the first confirmed case of IMNV infection in cultured L. vannamei in China was detected in Liaoning Province, after years in which official surveillance had reported other shrimp pathogens but no IMNV-positive cases. Subsequent targeted and routine surveillance through 2023 identified additional IMNV-positive farms in coastal China, and molecular analysis showed the Chinese CN-20-1 IMNV isolate to be closely related to Indonesian strains, suggesting relatively recent introduction associated with regional trade in broodstock or postlarvae. In response, Chinese authorities incorporated IMNV into national diagnostic proficiency testing and surveillance programmes, and farms increased screening and biosecurity measures to prevent wider dissemination into the country’s large shrimp farming sector.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high-volume importation and domestic movement of L. vannamei broodstock and postlarvae across East and Southeast Asia, combined with the scale and intensity of shrimp aquaculture in China and prior focus on other pathogens, created conditions for delayed but eventual introduction of IMNV into Chinese farms; expanding molecular diagnostic capacity in the early 2020s then facilitated detection. Internal mechanisms: close phylogenetic affinity of Chinese isolates to Indonesian IMNV lineages indicates continued geographic range expansion of established Asian strains rather than emergence of a novel lineage, with IMNV’s chronic infection dynamics and host susceptibility favouring establishment in new intensive farming regions (Geographic Range Expansion, inherent; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: Review – Event accurately represents the first confirmed IMNV case in China in 2020 and subsequent detections in 2020–2023, and its coding as intra-continental emergence into the Eastern Asia subregion with country-level first detection is appropriate; I removed the re_occurrence flag so that it no longer co-occurs with intra_continental_emergence, in line with the event-type definitions that restrict re_occurrence to events confined within an already known subregion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Penstylhamaparvovirus decapod1
EPP.common.name: PstDV1, IHHNV
Host: Wild and farmed Penaeus monodon; other penaeid prawns and hybrids
Event.summary: Archived samples and subsequent surveillance revealed that IHHNV or closely related viruses had been present in Australian penaeid prawns since at least 1993, when an infectious IHHNV strain was retrospectively identified in cultured P. monodon from northern Australia using IHHNV‑specific PCR and sequencing, while later work also demonstrated the presence of integrated, non‑infectious IHHNV‑related sequences in Australian P. monodon. In 2008, an infectious form of IHHNV closely related to South‑east Asian isolates was reported from farmed P. monodon in northern Queensland, prompting official notification to the World Organisation for Animal Health and incorporation of IHHNV into national surveillance and risk assessments. Although no major farm‑level mortality events attributable solely to IHHNV were documented, endemic infection and/or EVE carriage in wild and farmed P. monodon raised concerns about potential growth impacts and about maintaining the health status of Australian shrimp for domestic production and international trade.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expanding prawn aquaculture in northern Australia and associated health surveillance; international concern about shrimp viral diseases stimulating retrospective testing of archived material and targeted screening of wild broodstock. Internal mechanisms: inter‑continental emergence and establishment of infectious IHHNV in Oceania, likely via historical movements of infected stock; coexistence of infectious IHHNV with integrated genotype 3 IHHNV-related sequences in Australian P. monodon, which complicates PCR diagnosis and necessitated development of assays that can distinguish EVEs from active infection.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15584422/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Substantially revised this row to align with the published timeline: (i) earliest infectious IHHNV in Australia is now dated to archived P. monodon from 1993, with official reporting of an infectious strain from farmed P. monodon in 2008, rather than a vaguely defined 2002–2006 window; (ii) the emergence type is set to inter_continental_emergence=Yes to reflect the first confirmed occurrence of infectious IHHNV in the Oceania continent, while first_detection, intra_continental_emergence, re_occurrence and re_emergence are set to No.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15584422/?utm_source=openai)) Because documented production losses in Australia attributable solely to IHHNV appear modest relative to other viruses, but endemic infection and EVEs are epidemiologically important, this event should be retained but flagged for expert review of its relative ranking among the top emergence events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus olseni
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis
Host: Blacklip abalone Haliotis rubra; greenlip abalone Haliotis laevigata; Roe’s abalone Haliotis roei and other abalone spp.
Event.summary: After its original description in South Australian abalone in 1981, Perkinsus olseni was associated with increasing abalone morbidity and localized depletions in South Australia and New South Wales by the late 1990s, prompting dedicated investigations into Perkinsus‑related mortality from about 1997 onward. Through the 2000s, surveys and FRDC projects documented chronic infections and recurring mortality in blacklip and greenlip abalone along much of southern Australia, with substantial impacts on wild fisheries and concern for farmed stocks. By around 2010, P. olseni was recognized as an endemic, economically important pathogen of multiple abalone species in Australia, with management focusing on surveillance, movement controls and improved diagnostics rather than eradication.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High fishing pressure, warming coastal waters and other environmental stressors on nearshore reef habitats likely reduced abalone condition and resilience, while movement of infected abalone and other molluscs facilitated spread among reefs and jurisdictions. Internal mechanisms: P. olseni exhibits efficient transmission among abalone and other molluscs and can reach high tissue burdens; repeated temperature‑associated mortality episodes in the 1980s and 1990s show that environmental forcing of an established parasite, rather than a demonstrably new strain, underlies this long‑running re‑occurrence of disease.
Review: review – This is a key long‑term Australian abalone episode; the timing and impacts are broadly supported by national reports and FRDC studies. I simplified the emergence coding to re‑occurrence only, because recurrent mortality in long‑infected abalone populations is best explained by environmental drivers and host stress, whereas evidence for novel parasite variants in this period is limited; host range within abalone was already established before 1990.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus olseni
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis
Host: New Zealand cockle / little neck clam Austrovenus stutchburyi and other native bivalves
Event.summary: Around 2000, Perkinsus olseni was first confirmed in New Zealand cockles Austrovenus stutchburyi and other native bivalves from estuaries near Auckland, representing the first recognized occurrence of this parasite in New Zealand molluscs. Over the subsequent decade, surveys showed that P. olseni was present in multiple harbours and estuaries and established in several bivalve species, although large‑scale mortality directly attributed to the parasite in New Zealand remained uncommon. Its presence raised concern for potential sublethal effects on growth and reproduction and for possible spillover into commercially important shellfish sectors.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance movement of molluscs and planktonic stages within the southwest Pacific, including historical trade in shellfish seed and ballast water, likely introduced or redistributed P. olseni within the Australia–New Zealand subregion. Internal mechanisms: Broad host range and capacity for chronic, often subclinical infections in several native bivalve hosts facilitated silent establishment and geographic range expansion; this represents re‑emergence of a known parasite species in a new national fauna and host assemblage rather than a novel pathogen.
Review: review – Retain this as an important Oceania range‑expansion/host‑expansion event, but I (i) adjusted the event start to 2000 and the country tag to New Zealand [2000], based on national surveillance reporting P. olseni in clams from Mangamangaroa Stream in May 2000, and (ii) recoded emergence types: first_detection and intra‑continental emergence were set to "No" because the species was already known from the animal host system (abalone in Australia) and Australia and New Zealand fall within the same UNSD subregion, so spread between them does not meet the project definition of intra‑continental emergence; the event is best coded as re‑emergence via host and geographic expansion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.
