EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus olseni
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis
Host: Black-footed abalone Haliotis iris
Event.summary: In July 2013, Perkinsus olseni was first reported from New Zealand’s black-footed abalone (pāua) Haliotis iris in farmed stocks, marking a new host record and raising concerns for the high‑value pāua fishery. Initial detections occurred during targeted health surveillance of cultured abalone, with infected individuals showing histological evidence of systemic infection but no associated large‑scale mortality. Subsequent work confirmed that P. olseni was also present at low prevalence in wild pāua populations, prompting proactive management and ongoing monitoring despite the absence of major die‑offs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Natural or anthropogenic movement of infected molluscs and their larvae within the southwest Pacific, potentially from Australian waters where abalone perkinsosis is endemic, likely introduced or facilitated contact between P. olseni and New Zealand abalone. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of P. olseni to Haliotis iris, facilitated by its demonstrated ability to infect multiple abalone species elsewhere, constitutes a re‑emergence of the parasite in a new high‑value gastropod host within Oceania.
Review: review – Keep this event as it documents a clear host expansion into New Zealand pāua and triggered WOAH immediate notification, but I recoded it: first_detection and intra‑continental emergence are now "No" because those categories apply at host‑system/continent level, not for individual new host species within the same subregion; the event is best classified as re‑emergence through host expansion in an already infected country.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus olseni
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis
Host: Manila clam Ruditapes philippinarum (wild beds, west coast tidal flats)
Event.summary: In the summer of 2015, intertidal Manila clam beds on the west coast of Korea experienced marked surfacing behavior and mortality during a period of unusually high air and sediment temperatures. Field investigations showed that clams with high P. olseni burdens were more likely to surface and die, and infection prevalences in major beds often approached 100% with very high infection intensities. As temperatures declined after the heatwave, mortality subsided, leaving depressed clam densities and reinforcing the role of P. olseni as a key contributor to episodic summer die‑offs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A short but intense summer heatwave raised air and sediment temperatures above about 33–34 °C for roughly ten days, exacerbating physiological stress in dense intertidal clam populations and creating conditions favorable for parasite proliferation and sediment hypoxia. Internal mechanisms: High chronic P. olseni infection loads compromised host immune function and condition; under extreme thermal stress these chronic infections translated into acute mortality, illustrating a re‑occurrence of outbreaks in an already heavily infected region without any demonstrated change in parasite strain or host range.
Review: retain – This is a well‑documented, high‑impact Korean heat‑wave–associated mortality episode in a region with long‑established perkinsosis. The geographic scope, host, timing and classification as a re‑occurrence (environmentally triggered mortality in an endemic area) are appropriate and consistent with the Parasites & Vectors study and related Korean literature.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus olseni
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis
Host: Venerid clam Pitar rostrata (natural beds)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, a health survey of natural populations of the venerid clam Pitar rostrata from the Uruguayan coast revealed infections with a Perkinsus sp. in about 22% of animals, with severe hemocytic infiltration and tissue damage in affected clams. Sequencing of the ITS‑5.8S rDNA region confirmed that the parasite was Perkinsus olseni, providing the first confirmed record of this species in South America and, at the time, the western hemisphere. Although mass mortality of P. rostrata was not explicitly documented, the finding marked a major geographic range expansion of P. olseni into a new continent and host species.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance transfers of molluscs and planktonic stages within global shellfish trade and shipping, as well as regional oceanographic connectivity in the southwestern Atlantic, likely introduced P. olseni into Uruguayan clam populations from previously infected regions. Internal mechanisms: Successful establishment of P. olseni in Pitar rostrata reflects both host expansion (a new venerid clam host for this parasite in South America) and inter‑continental geographic range expansion, making this a key inter‑continental emergence and re‑emergence event despite limited documented production losses at the time of first detection.
Review: review – Added as a missing major event: Cremonte et al. 2005 document the first confirmed occurrence of P. olseni in South America (Uruguayan Pitar rostrata) and this is widely cited as the species’ first record in the western hemisphere. I classified it as an inter‑continental emergence (new continent with in situ infection) and as re‑emergence because it also represents host expansion to P. rostrata. No evidence suggests this event should be excluded, but a human reviewer may wish to confirm its ranking among the ten highest‑impact events relative to less well‑documented Asian and Indian records.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pestivirus bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine viral diarrhea virus, BVDV
Host: Dairy cattle (Holstein heifers)
Event.summary: In May 2004, a large Holstein dairy in California experienced an outbreak among first-calf heifers in late gestation in which 19 of 37 animals aborted or delivered premature calves with striking skeletal and neurologic deformities, and bovine viral diarrhea virus-1 subtype b (Pestivirus bovis) was isolated from affected fetuses and calves. Over a four-week period, multiple stillborn and live premature calves showed brachygnathism, hydranencephaly, hydrocephalus and other malformations, and experimental inoculation of calves with the outbreak strain demonstrated that it induced marked thrombocytopenia, lymphopenia and leukopenia, an unusual phenotype for BVDV-1. Following recognition of the outbreak, management changes and vaccination were implemented and the episode subsided, but the highly pathogenic BVDV-1b strain has since been used as a challenge virus in experimental work and is considered a notable example of increased virulence within BVDV-1.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction of a virulent BVDV-1b strain into a large California Holstein herd, likely via movements of replacement heifers or contact with infected animals, combined with incomplete protection from existing vaccination protocols that did not fully match the infecting strain, resulted in widespread fetal infection in susceptible late-gestation heifers. Internal mechanisms: increased virulence/pathogenicity of a specific BVDV-1b field strain, which, unlike most BVDV-1 isolates, produced severe congenital malformations and experimentally induced thrombocytopenia, expanding the recognized pathogenic spectrum of Pestivirus bovis and fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by viral change rather than by geography alone.
Review: review – Added as a new major re-emergence event capturing a well-documented 2004 California outbreak in which a BVDV-1b strain caused numerous late-term abortions, premature births and congenital defects, and experimentally demonstrated thrombocytopenia. Classified as re_emergence (increased virulence and atypical pathology of BVDV-1b within an already endemic US region), with no intra- or inter-continental spread. Geography (Northern America, United States) and year are taken directly from the case report; a human expert should confirm that this episode is indeed among the top BVDV-1 events by impact compared with other severe but more localized outbreaks.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pestivirus bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine viral diarrhea virus, BVDV
Host: Beef cattle (feedlot and pasture)
Event.summary: In 2008, a severe outbreak of acute bovine viral diarrhea due to a BVDV-1b (Pestivirus bovis) strain was reported in Brazilian beef cattle, with high morbidity characterized by fever, diarrhea, erosive and hemorrhagic lesions of the gastrointestinal tract, and respiratory signs in affected herds. The outbreak spread within and between herds in the affected region of Brazil over a short period, causing substantial clinical and production losses in growing beef cattle in an area where BVDV was already endemic. Clinical disease waned following removal of severely affected animals, enhanced biosecurity, and, in some operations, implementation of vaccination and testing strategies, but BVDV-1b remained part of the bovine pestivirus pool in southern Brazil.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high-density beef production systems with movement of young cattle between farms and feedlots, limited prior vaccination against BVDV, and mixing of animals from multiple sources facilitated rapid within- and between-herd transmission in an endemic setting. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak strain belonged to subtype BVDV-1b and appeared particularly pathogenic in this context, but available data do not indicate a clearly novel genotype or altered host range, so this episode is best interpreted as a severe re-occurrence driven primarily by management, animal movements and contact patterns rather than fundamental viral change.
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects a well-documented severe BVDV-1b outbreak in Brazilian beef cattle and is appropriately classified as re_occurrence in an endemic region, without intra- or inter-continental emergence. Country and subregion match the UN list, and the primary outbreak description plus a general review on persistent infection are suitable sources. No structural corrections were required, but a human reviewer may still wish to compare its impact against other severe but localized BVDV-1 outbreaks in South America.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pestivirus bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine viral diarrhea virus, BVDV
Host: Dairy cattle, beef cattle, yaks (Bos grunniens), and water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis)
Event.summary: Between 2010 and 2013, a large cross-sectional investigation in China documented very high seroprevalence and widespread active infection with BVDV-1 (Pestivirus bovis) across four bovine species—dairy cattle, beef cattle, yaks, and water buffalo—across eight provinces, revealing extensive and often under-recognized circulation of the virus. Molecular typing showed that all characterized field viruses were BVDV-1 but belonged to multiple subtypes, including 1b and 1m and, importantly, a distinct new cluster designated subtype 1u, alongside other work in China around this time describing the first isolation and pathogenic characterization of a BVDV-1a strain in dairy cattle. Although BVDV-1 had been present in China for decades, the discovery of high infection pressure and newly recognized subtypes prompted calls for nationwide control and reconsideration of vaccine strain composition.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of dairy and beef production in multiple Chinese provinces, frequent long-distance movement of calves and replacement stock, and variable or absent vaccination programs allowed sustained transmission and intermixing of BVDV-1 lineages across species and regions. Internal mechanisms: novel strain/genotype emergence and increasing genetic diversity of Pestivirus bovis, with phylogenetic analyses identifying a new subtype (BVDV-1u) and documenting first isolation of subgenotype 1a from Chinese dairy cattle; this constellation of changes supports classification as re-emergence driven by viral diversification rather than simple persistence.
Review: review – Event correctly treats the nationwide 2010–2013 Chinese surveys as a re-emergence episode characterized by high prevalence and the recognition of new BVDV-1 subtypes rather than as first detection. The continent, subregion and country fields have been cleaned so that only China (with its start year) is listed, and the provinces are instead described in the summary. Primary sources documenting prevalence, subtype 1u, and first isolation of BVDV-1a in China are appropriate; a human reviewer should verify that this episode is among the most impactful BVDV-1 events when considering its broad geographic scope and implications for vaccination.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pestivirus bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine viral diarrhea virus, BVDV
Host: Farmed white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) in proximity to cattle operations
Event.summary: On 5 June 2022, a farmed white-tailed deer in central Florida experienced a stillbirth involving two mummified fetuses that were submitted for diagnostic investigation and found to be infected with BVDV-1 (Pestivirus bovis), representing the first confirmed natural case of BVDV-1–associated fetal mummification in farmed white-tailed deer. Subsequent virological and molecular testing of maternal and fetal tissues confirmed vertical transmission of BVDV-1 in this deer herd, in a region with nearby cattle operations in which bovine BVDV is endemic, highlighting ongoing cross‑species circulation at the wildlife–livestock interface. The herd implemented enhanced biosecurity, diagnostic screening, and management changes to reduce contact with cattle and prevent further spillover, and the case has been used to recommend inclusion of BVDV in the differential diagnosis of abortions on deer farms, although broader surveillance data on follow-on cases remain limited.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: close geographic proximity and potential fence-line contact between farmed white-tailed deer and BVDV-infected cattle or contaminated environments, combined with limited routine pestivirus surveillance in deer farms, facilitated spillover of an endemic cattle virus into a managed wildlife population. Internal mechanisms: host expansion (spillover) of Pestivirus bovis from cattle into white-tailed deer with successful vertical transmission and fetal infection; although BVDV infection in wild deer had been recognized experimentally and serologically before, this case documents a natural, clinically significant reproductive outcome in farmed deer and is therefore treated as a re-emergence event at the wildlife–livestock interface rather than a first detection in the species.
Review: review – Event accurately reflects the first reported natural BVDV-1–associated fetal mummification in farmed white-tailed deer in Florida and appropriately classifies it as re_emergence via host expansion in a region where BVDV-1 is already endemic in cattle, not as first detection or inter-continental spread. The country field has been corrected to use only the UN-standard country name with the start year (state-level detail moved to the summary), and primary case and extension reports plus a general host-range consensus paper are retained as sources. Because this is a single-herd event focused on a novel host rather than large case numbers, a human reviewer should assess whether it merits inclusion among the top-impact BVDV-1 emergence events or should instead be reserved for a more host-centric dataset.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: RVF virus, RVFV
Host: Cattle, water buffalo, sheep, goats, camels
Event.summary: In mid‑1993, after a 12‑year lull following Egypt’s massive 1977–1978 Rift Valley fever epizootic, clusters of acute visual loss after febrile illness were recognized in rural Aswan Governorate, and serologic surveys showed recent RVFV infection in roughly 8–12% of villagers together with concurrent abortions in cattle and buffalo. Surveillance subsequently detected additional human and animal infections in multiple Nile Valley and Delta governorates, indicating renewed widespread RVFV circulation in Egyptian ruminant populations along the irrigated Nile corridor. Intensified livestock vaccination, vector control and enhanced animal and human surveillance were implemented from late 1993 onward, and reported human and animal cases gradually declined, although serologic data suggest low‑level enzootic transmission persisted in livestock.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely re‑introduction of RVFV into southern Egypt via movement of infected ruminants from endemic areas in Sudan, combined with dense populations of cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats and camels along irrigated farms and abundant Culex mosquito breeding sites in Nile irrigation canals, facilitated amplification and spread. Limited immunity in younger livestock cohorts and incomplete vaccination coverage contributed to abortion storms and widespread seropositivity. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate recurrence of previously circulating Egyptian/Nile RVFV lineages rather than emergence of a markedly divergent strain, so this episode is best characterized as a trade‑ and irrigation‑driven re‑occurrence rather than viral evolutionary change.
Review: Retain – New row added for the 1993 Egypt recurrence, which is widely documented as a major RVF outbreak with substantial livestock abortions and widespread human and animal serologic evidence along the Nile Valley. Geography (Northern Africa, Egypt), timing (1993) and classification as re‑occurrence (virus already established since the 1977–1978 epizootic, with no strong evidence for a novel strain) are supported by CDC and Egyptian reviews; this episode merits inclusion among the most impactful post‑1990 animal outbreaks.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: RVF virus, RVFV
Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, camels
Event.summary: In October 2007, Sudanese authorities requested international assistance after suspected viral hemorrhagic fever cases were detected in White Nile and Sinnar States, coinciding with reports of abortions and deaths among sheep, goats, cattle and camels. Subsequent investigations confirmed a large Rift Valley fever outbreak centered in irrigated and flood‑prone areas of White Nile, Gezira and Blue Nile States, with extensive livestock disease, trade disruption and a high number of associated human cases and deaths. As surveillance, mosquito control, animal movement restrictions and public health measures were implemented and seasonal flooding receded toward the end of 2007, animal and human case numbers gradually declined and the outbreak was brought under control, though RVFV remained a threat in Sudan’s irrigation schemes and pastoral zones.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy seasonal rains and expanding irrigation projects along the Nile created ideal breeding habitat for RVFV mosquito vectors, while dense mixed herds of sheep, goats, cattle and camels kept close to human dwellings increased human–animal contact; limited vaccination coverage, weak veterinary services and disruption of livestock markets amplified economic and health impacts. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate that the outbreak was driven primarily by ecological and management factors and by amplification of existing East African lineages rather than by emergence of a substantially different viral strain, so it is best categorized as re‑occurrence in an endemic country.
Review: Retain – The 2007 Sudan event is well documented as a large RVF outbreak affecting White Nile, Gezira, Blue Nile and nearby states, with significant livestock and human impact. Assigning Sudan to the Northern Africa sub‑region (per the project’s UN‑based country list) and classifying the event as re‑occurrence (rather than intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) are correct, as RVFV was already known from Sudan. No substantial corrections are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: RVF virus, RVFV
Host: Cattle (zebu), goats, sheep
Event.summary: During the 2008 and 2008–2009 rainy seasons, Madagascar experienced a major Rift Valley fever epizootic after abnormal mortality and abortions were reported in cattle in coastal and central highland districts, with RVFV infection confirmed in ruminants and humans across at least 19 districts. Nationwide serosurveys among high‑risk slaughterhouse workers and livestock demonstrated recent RVFV circulation in all regions and evidence of virus activity in 70–92 of Madagascar’s 111 districts, indicating widespread infection of zebu cattle and small ruminants. As rainfall decreased and targeted animal and human surveillance and movement controls were strengthened, reported animal cases declined by mid‑2009, although subsequent studies show that RVFV has persisted enzootically in Malagasy ruminant populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unusually wet rainy seasons created extensive mosquito breeding sites in coastal and highland rice‑growing areas, while large‑scale trade and movement of zebu cattle between southern, highland and northern regions disseminated infection; limited vaccination and veterinary capacity favored explosive amplification once RVFV was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses indicate that the 2008–2009 Malagasy outbreak viruses clustered with Kenya‑1 lineages from the 2006–2007 East African epizootic, supporting classification as re‑emergence via introduction of established East African strains into Madagascar rather than long‑term local maintenance or a novel genotype.
Review: Retain – New row added for the 2008–2009 Madagascar epizootic. Multiple outbreak and phylogenetic studies identify this as a major RVF event with widespread livestock infection and national‑scale spread, and locate Madagascar within the Eastern Africa sub‑region in the project’s scheme. Classification as re‑emergence (introduction of Kenya‑related lineages into largely susceptible Malagasy herds) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is appropriate. This event should be counted among the most significant post‑1990 livestock outbreaks.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: RVF virus, RVFV
Host: Camels, sheep, goats, cattle
Event.summary: In late 2010, after unusually heavy rains in northern Mauritania, suspected Rift Valley fever was reported in camels and small ruminants in Adrar and Inchiri Provinces along with human hemorrhagic fever cases, marking a notable re‑emergence of RVF in this largely arid region. Further south, a subsequent outbreak in 2012 followed markedly above‑average rainfall in southern Mauritania, with widespread abortions among cattle, sheep and goats and confirmed human infections in several regions, forming a linked multi‑year episode of virus activity in Mauritanian livestock. Vector control, animal movement restrictions, heightened surveillance and the end of the unusually wet conditions helped curtail active transmission after late 2012, although serologic evidence indicates continued low‑level circulation in local ruminant populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Exceptional rainfall events in both northern oasis and southern agro‑pastoral zones created temporary wetlands favoring vector breeding in otherwise dry landscapes, while high densities of camels and small ruminants around oases and in transhumant systems, together with limited vaccination and veterinary oversight, allowed rapid amplification; movement of camels and small ruminants for trade and grazing likely linked northern and southern foci. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses of the 2010 and 2012 viruses show close relationships to earlier West African lineages and to each other, highlighting re‑activation of RVFV with detectable genetic variation and particularly prominent involvement of camels in severe disease, consistent with re‑emergence featuring lineage diversification and host‑impact shifts rather than a purely climatic recurrence.
Review: Retain – The 2010 northern and 2012 southern Mauritania outbreaks are correctly treated as a linked episode in a single country, with Western Africa sub‑region and 2010–2012 time span supported by WHO and EID reports. Genetic work shows that 2012 viruses cluster with 2010 strains, supporting re‑emergence from an enzootic focus rather than independent introductions. Classification as re‑emergence (with camel‑dominated disease and lineage diversification) is appropriate; no changes to core fields are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: RVF virus, RVFV
Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, camels
Event.summary: In May–June 2018, Kenyan authorities confirmed a new Rift Valley fever outbreak after reports of numerous abortions and deaths in small ruminants and camels and suspected human cases in several pastoral counties. The epizootic was concentrated in eastern and northeastern counties such as Wajir and Marsabit, where high livestock mortality and abortions in sheep, goats and camels were documented and human cases were epidemiologically linked to handling or consuming products from sick animals. Implementation of livestock movement restrictions, targeted vaccination in affected herds, and health messaging to reduce high‑risk animal contact during slaughter and milking, together with the end of the rainy season and associated decline in mosquito vectors, helped to bring the outbreak under control later in 2018.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Seasonal heavy rains and flooding in arid and semi‑arid counties created ideal vector‑breeding habitats, and nomadic pastoral systems with dense mixed herds and extensive trade in live animals and animal products facilitated rapid spread and human exposure; prior vaccination coverage was incomplete, leaving many herds susceptible. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence suggests circulation of known East African RVFV lineages rather than a novel genotype, so this event is best characterized as re‑occurrence driven by climatic conditions, livestock movement and immunity gaps (enhanced transmission via favorable ecology and management rather than intrinsic viral evolution).
Review: Review – The 2018 Kenya outbreak caused substantial abortion storms and notable livestock losses (e.g. government estimates of roughly 3,700 small stock lost across several counties) and is one of the larger recent RVF episodes, though still smaller than the 1997–1998, 2006–2007 or 2010 Southern Africa events. Countries, Eastern Africa sub‑region, timing and classification as re‑occurrence are consistent with WHO and national reports, and sources are appropriate. Because its scale is intermediate relative to other candidates (e.g. Egypt 1993, Madagascar 2008–2009, Sudan 2019–2020), its inclusion among the final top ten should be revisited by subject‑matter experts rather than assumed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus riftense
EPP.common.name: RVF virus, RVFV
Host: Sheep, goats, cattle, camels (primarily small ruminants)
Event.summary: In 2019, after unusually heavy rains and flash flooding across much of Sudan, Rift Valley fever re‑emerged with human and animal cases first detected in River Nile State and then in Red Sea and several other northern and eastern states, accompanied by abortions and deaths in goats and sheep. Between late September 2019 and early 2020, national and WHO reports documented around 500–600 confirmed human cases with multiple deaths and laboratory confirmation of RVFV infection in small ruminants in River Nile and Red Sea states, prompting bans and controls on livestock movements from affected areas. Implementation of One Health response teams, enforcement of animal‑movement restrictions, and the end of peak vector season led to a gradual decline in new human and animal cases by early 2020, although Sudan remains at high risk for further RVF activity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive flooding created abundant breeding sites for mosquito vectors in wadis and irrigated zones, and intense movement of sheep, goats and other livestock through major markets such as Eldamar and Port Sudan facilitated dissemination of RVFV between herding areas and export points; limited veterinary surveillance and vaccination exacerbated spread. Internal mechanisms: Available genetic analyses indicate that 2019 Sudan viruses fall within known East African/Nile RVFV lineages, with no compelling evidence of a substantially novel strain, so this outbreak is best described as a large re‑occurrence in an endemic country driven by climatic conditions and livestock‑movement patterns rather than evolutionary change.
Review: Review – New row added for the 2019–2020 Sudan outbreak, which produced approximately 576 confirmed human cases across several northern and eastern states and documented animal infection in goats and sheep, along with major disruption of livestock movements and exports. Assignment to Northern Africa (Sudan) and classification as re‑occurrence (in a country with prior large outbreaks) are supported by WHO and EID reports. Because animal surveillance data are sparse and the precise livestock burden is uncertain, this episode appears to be a substantial recent RVF event but its exact ranking among the top ten should be cross‑checked against other candidates during expert review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Host: Cattle (newborn calves from pregnant cows infected during gestation; similar risk in sheep and goats in affected regions)
Event.summary: In July 1998, Japan experienced a severe epizootic of congenital abnormalities in calves, with numerous herds across southern and other regions reporting newborn calves with arthrogryposis, ataxia and hydranencephaly, leading to widespread reproductive and welfare losses. Pathology and serology from more than a hundred affected calves examined at Miyazaki University showed lesions typical of Akabane disease and high neutralizing antibody titres against Akabane virus, implicating heavy virus circulation in pregnant cows during mid‑gestation. As the 1998–1999 calving season ended, the wave of malformed calves subsided with the decline in Culicoides vector activity and accumulation of immunity in breeding stock, although Akabane virus remained endemic in southern Japan, setting the stage for later episodic outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: After a period of low Akabane activity, several years of births from naïve heifers and cows created a susceptible breeding cohort, and favourable warm, humid conditions in 1997–1998 supported high densities of Culicoides vectors in key cattle‑rearing areas, allowing extensive infection of pregnant cows within a narrow gestational window. Internal mechanisms: Available reports do not point to a single novel Akabane strain; the outbreak is best interpreted as a large re‑occurrence of endemic virus with geographic spread across much of Japan, following the classic teratogenic pattern in which transplacental fetal infection during specific gestational stages leads to arthrogryposis–hydranencephaly rather than a fundamentally altered pathotype.
Review: Decision: review. New event added to capture the severe 1998 Akabane congenital outbreak described as occurring in "most areas of Japan" with numerous malformed calves examined at Miyazaki University, supported by Uchida et al. 2000 and Akabane reviews.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/104063870001200605)) Classified as re‑occurrence (large epidemic of an endemic virus) rather than first/global emergence or intra‑/inter‑continental spread. National scale and quantitative impact (numbers of affected herds/calves) should be cross‑checked against Japanese surveillance data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Host: Cattle (dairy herds; evidence of related infections in other domestic ruminants)
Event.summary: Between 2001 and 2003, Israel experienced a major resurgence of Akabane virus infection in cattle, with outbreaks initially centered in northern regions and subsequently extending to the Arava Rift Valley and other areas, causing waves of abortions, stillbirths and calves with arthrogryposis–hydranencephaly and other congenital malformations. Serologic surveys and virus characterization demonstrated widespread AKAV circulation in affected herds and showed that the 2002–2003 epizootic involved a distinct viral lineage compared with the earlier 1969–1970 outbreak. After this epidemic phase, clinical incidence declined as herd immunity increased, although Simbu‑group viruses, including Akabane and Shuni viruses, continued to circulate in Israel and periodically cause reproductive losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climatic conditions favoring Culicoides and mosquito vectors, including warm, humid seasons and windborne movement of infected midges, facilitated southward and longitudinal spread of Akabane virus within Israel; intensively managed dairy herds with many susceptible pregnant cows amplified the epizootic. Internal mechanisms: Molecular data indicated that a new Akabane virus lineage was responsible for the 2001–2003 outbreak, consistent with re‑emergence driven by viral genetic change and possibly altered antigenicity or tropism, rather than simple cyclical recurrence of the earlier lineage.
Review: Decision: retain (no structural corrections). The 2001–2003 Israel Akabane outbreak is well documented as a major epizootic involving a new virus lineage and large numbers of malformed calves, and classification as re‑emergence is consistent with Stram et al. 2004 and subsequent Israeli reviews.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419647/?utm_source=openai)) The exact start year (2001 vs. 2002) and geographic extent are reasonable but should be re‑checked against full national surveillance data; no changes were made to timing, geography, or emergence‑type flags.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Host: Cattle (adult beef and dairy cattle with encephalomyelitis; background infections in cattle, sheep and goats)
Event.summary: In summer and autumn 2006, southern Japan experienced the first large‑scale epidemic of Akabane virus–associated encephalomyelitis in adult cattle, distinct from the classical congenital malformation syndrome previously linked to the virus, with hundreds of cattle developing acute neurologic signs such as ataxia, recumbency and hypersensitivity. Virologic investigations identified Akabane virus genogroup I a strains in the central nervous system of affected cattle and showed that virus had recently invaded the region after an apparent year without detectable circulation. The epidemic waned as the vector season ended and herd immunity rose, and subsequent control efforts focused on vaccination of heifers and improved vector monitoring in high‑risk areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High seasonal abundance of competent Culicoides vectors in warm, humid regions of southern Japan, coupled with movement of infected animals or vectors from endemic areas, introduced and amplified the encephalitogenic Akabane strain in largely naïve adult cattle populations. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of a genogroup I a strain with increased neurotropism and virulence for postnatal cattle, representing re‑emergence driven by viral genetic evolution that expanded the clinical spectrum beyond in utero teratogenesis to include severe encephalomyelitis in adult animals.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2006 southern Japan outbreak of Akabane encephalomyelitis in adult cattle is a clearly documented, high‑impact event with hundreds of clinical cases and strong evidence for invasion by a genogroup I a strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2443122/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re‑emergence (novel strain with changed clinical expression) and restriction to Eastern Asia/Japan are appropriate, and no corrections to geography, timing or emergence‑type flags were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Host: Sheep (pregnant ewes; malformed lambs), with potential risk to goats and other small ruminants
Event.summary: During the 2011–2012 and 2012–2013 lambing seasons, several sheep flocks in Ontario and Québec, Canada, reported unusually high rates of late‑term abortions, stillbirths and lambs born with severe skeletal and central nervous system malformations, including arthrogryposis, scoliosis and hydranencephaly. Diagnostic investigations by the Animal Health Laboratory and federal laboratories identified Cache Valley virus in fetal tissues by RT‑PCR and virus isolation, and serology of ewes confirmed recent infection, representing the first laboratory‑confirmed outbreaks of CVV‑associated congenital disease in Canadian livestock and implicating a genetic variant distinct from previously described North American strains. Following these seasons, the acute wave of malformed lambs subsided, but serosurveys and later case reports indicated that CVV had become an established, intermittently manifest cause of reproductive loss in small‑ruminant flocks in eastern Canada.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Warm, wet late summers and autumns in 2011 and 2012 favored mosquito proliferation in eastern Canada, overlapping with breeding schedules that placed many ewes in early gestation during peak vector activity, while most flocks had no prior immunity to CVV, resulting in high attack rates among pregnant ewes. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analysis of Ontario isolates demonstrated a CVV genetic variant distinct from existing reference sequences, suggesting re‑emergence via introduction or evolution of a new lineage with efficient vertical transmission in sheep; nevertheless, the teratogenic pattern closely matched previously described CVV‑induced arthrogryposis‑hydranencephaly syndromes in North American flocks.
Review: Decision: review. New event added to represent the first confirmed CVV congenital malformation outbreaks in Canadian sheep flocks (Ontario and Québec, 2011–2013), supported by AHL newsletters and Canadian arbovirus reviews.([uoguelph.ca](https://www.uoguelph.ca/ahl/sites/uoguelph.ca.ahl/files/June%202012.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re‑emergence of an endemic North American virus via a distinct genetic variant in a new national setting; impact is regional but substantial for affected flocks. Quantitative data on numbers of flocks and lamb losses, and the exact temporal linkage between Ontario and Québec cases, should be verified in future curation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Host: Sheep (pregnant ewes; malformed and stillborn lambs)
Event.summary: In late 2015 and the first weeks of 2016, diagnostic laboratories in Ontario again received multiple submissions of stillborn and aborted lambs from flocks across eastern, central and southwestern parts of the province, many showing marked vertebral deformities, arthrogryposis, cerebellar hypoplasia and hydranencephaly. Histopathology of these fetuses closely resembled lesions seen in earlier Cache Valley virus outbreaks, and serologic testing of ewes and fetuses supported renewed circulation of CVV in the region, consistent with a second wave of virus‑induced congenital disease occurring approximately 3–5 years after the first Canadian episode. Clinical cases declined following the lambing period and the end of the autumn vector season, but the event reinforced the need for mosquito‑exposure management and awareness of CVV as a recurrent cause of lamb losses in Ontario.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: An unusually warm and prolonged autumn in 2015 likely extended mosquito activity into the early breeding season, exposing early‑gestation ewes to infected vectors, while replacement of immune ewes with naïve yearlings since the 2011–2013 outbreak created new susceptible cohorts across many flocks. Internal mechanisms: Available reports from Ontario do not clearly demonstrate major viral genetic change relative to earlier Canadian isolates, so this episode is interpreted primarily as re‑occurrence of endemic CVV driven by climatic variability and herd immunity cycles, rather than emergence of a fundamentally altered strain.
Review: Decision: review. New event added to describe the 2015–2016 Ontario outbreak of malformed lambs attributed to Cache Valley virus, documented mainly through AHL diagnostic reports and summarized in later reviews.([uoguelph.ca](https://www.uoguelph.ca/ahl/sites/uoguelph.ca.ahl/files/ANwsl20-1-Mar2016-pub2010.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re‑occurrence in an already affected subregion (Northern America), driven by climatic conditions and immunity gaps rather than proven viral evolution. The exact number of affected flocks and lambs, and any molecular data from this period, should be checked before final ranking of its impact.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Host: Cattle (large Holstein dairy herd; likely spillover risk to nearby sheep and goats)
Event.summary: In November 2021, a very large Holstein dairy farm (about 23,000 cows) on the Mughan plain in Ardabil Province, north‑western Iran, experienced an outbreak characterized by abortions, stillbirths, mummified fetuses and calves born with severe congenital malformations such as hydranencephaly, arthrogryposis and exophthalmia. Laboratory testing of affected calves and herd mates identified Akabane virus infection, confirming a major Akabane disease outbreak in this previously unaffected border region, while concurrent serologic data and prior case reports indicated that the virus had already circulated and caused disease in other parts of Iran, including areas near Tehran. The Mughan outbreak abated as pregnancies turned over, herd immunity increased and vector activity declined, but it highlighted the ongoing risk of Simbu‑group viruses expanding within Iran and across adjacent parts of Southern and Western Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The Mughan plain’s ecology—low‑lying, irrigated pastures near international borders—provides favorable habitat for Culicoides and mosquito vectors, and cross‑border movement of animals or windborne dispersal of infected midges from neighboring endemic countries (e.g. Azerbaijan, Turkey) likely introduced or amplified Akabane virus in this large, previously naïve dairy herd. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence points to geographic range expansion and local amplification of established Akabane virus lineages in the Middle East, rather than emergence of a markedly new genotype; thus the event is best viewed as a major re‑occurrence within an already affected continental and subregional context driven mainly by environmental and management factors.
Review: Decision: review. This event accurately reflects a large Akabane outbreak in a massive dairy herd on Iran’s Mughan plain, but earlier serologic surveys and case reports show that Akabane virus had circulated and caused disease in other parts of Iran before 2021; therefore, the previous classification as first_detection and intra‑continental emergence was inappropriate.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11260222/)) The event has been reclassified as a major re‑occurrence/range expansion within Southern Asia. The magnitude of losses within the herd is well documented, but data on wider national spread remain limited and warrant further review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Porcine circovirus 2
EPP.common.name: Porcine circovirus-associated disease, PCVAD
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) in high-health commercial herds
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, a novel wasting disease later termed postweaning multisystemic wasting syndrome (PMWS) was first recognized in high‑health pig herds in western Canada, characterized by progressive wasting, respiratory signs, and enlarged lymph nodes in nursery and grow–finish pigs. Investigations during 1991–1996 linked the syndrome to a previously unrecognized porcine circovirus now designated PCV2, with acute outbreaks causing marked increases in post‑weaning mortality compared to historical baselines. The event subsided as affected herds implemented improved biosecurity and management, but PCV2 infection became recognized as endemic in Canadian swine populations and a potential driver of future disease outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of pig production in high‑health herds, high stocking density, and extensive movement of pigs likely facilitated efficient transmission; co‑infection with other respiratory and enteric pathogens and immunostimulation were later shown to be key external co‑factors for full expression of PCVAD. Internal mechanisms: Recognition of a distinct pathogenic circovirus lineage (PCV2) separate from the non‑pathogenic PCV1, with PCV2 causing lymphoid depletion and multisystemic lesions that define PMWS; however, this event represents first clinical detection rather than de novo viral emergence, as retrospective serology suggests prior silent circulation of PCV2 in pigs.
Review: Decision: retain. The event appropriately represents the first recognized PMWS/PCVAD outbreaks in western Canada in the early 1990s and their linkage to PCV2, with correct continent/sub‑region assignment, host specification, and classification as the first detection of this disease entity in domestic pigs. No clearly larger or earlier PCVAD emergence event in swine was identified that would displace this episode, and the listed sources are relevant to its documentation.

EPP.scientific.name: Porcine circovirus 2
EPP.common.name: Porcine circovirus-associated disease, PCVAD
Host: Domestic pigs in commercial and breeding herds in New Zealand
Event.summary: In 2003, New Zealand, previously considered free of many major pig diseases, confirmed its first PMWS/PCVAD outbreak in a farrow‑to‑finish herd in the Waikato region, with epidemic non‑responsive wasting and elevated post‑weaning mortality. Over the next several years, further cases were detected and investigations concluded that the outbreak represented a new disease incursion, as PCV2 infection was ubiquitous serologically but clinical PMWS had not previously been seen. Following intensive industry and governmental response, including tightened biosecurity and control measures, PMWS spread remained limited relative to Europe and North America, and New Zealand maintained a reputation for relatively favorable pig health status despite the presence of PCV2.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of pathogenic PCV2‑infected pigs or genetic material into a pig population with high health status and little prior exposure to virulent PCV2 lineages, combined with intensification and relatively naïve herd immunity, enabled clinical PMWS to emerge; concerns about trade and biosecurity prompted rapid governmental response. Internal mechanisms: PCV2 was already widespread serologically in New Zealand herds, but emergence of clinical PMWS likely reflected either introduction of a more virulent strain or changes in co‑infection patterns and management stress, allowing PCV2 to cause the full PCVAD syndrome rather than subclinical infection.
Review: Decision: retain. This event correctly represents the first recognized PMWS/PCVAD incursion into Oceania via New Zealand in 2003 and its limited spread through 2006. The continent/sub‑region assignment ('Oceania' / 'Australia and New Zealand'), the focus on New Zealand, and the classification as an inter‑continental emergence episode are appropriate, and the cited thesis and outbreak reports substantiate the storyline. No structural changes were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Poxvirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Pox viruses infection
Host: Sheep; goats (Capra hircus, to a lesser extent)
Event.summary: In 2010 Morocco experienced a notable epidemic of sheep pox (and associated sheep and goat pox) that represented a major resurgence of capripoxvirus disease in North Africa. The outbreak began in Moroccan sheep flocks with rapid spread in affected regions, causing high morbidity, notable mortality in lambs, and serious trade disruptions for small ruminants and their products. Aggressive control measures including movement bans, culling and vaccination gradually controlled the epidemic over the following years, although sheep and goat pox remained endemic or recurrent in many African and Asian countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large populations of susceptible sheep with limited recent exposure; increased movements related to trade and religious festivals; possible underinvestment in routine vaccination and veterinary services; environmental conditions favouring animal congregation and mechanical transmission. Internal mechanisms: This epidemic is primarily a re-occurrence of endemic sheep/goat pox viruses rather than emergence of a clearly novel genotype; molecular studies show close relatedness between field and vaccine strains despite the unusual nodular clinical form.
Review: Review – Event is real and regionally important, but intra-continental emergence was incorrectly flagged in the original version. Because sheep and goat pox were already long endemic in Northern Africa, the event is best classified as a re-occurrence; intra-continental emergence has been set to “No”.

EPP.scientific.name: Primate lentivirus
EPP.common.name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) – wild communities in Gombe National Park, Tanzania([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.79.7.3891-3902.2005))
Event.summary: Around 2000, non-invasive sampling and virological testing identified the first SIVcpz-infected wild chimpanzees in Gombe National Park, Tanzania, demonstrating that eastern chimpanzees naturally harbored SIV and that prevalence in some communities approached about 20%.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.79.7.3891-3902.2005); [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1061584/)) Over the following years, expanded longitudinal sampling of multiple Gombe communities mapped infection dynamics, showing persistent SIVcpz circulation, sexual transmission, and variable prevalence between neighboring groups.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.79.7.3891-3902.2005)) By the mid-2000s, Gombe had become a key natural field site for SIVcpz research, anchoring our understanding of SIV epidemiology and evolution in wild eastern chimpanzees.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3822437/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Natural social and mating behavior of chimpanzees, including mating networks and aggression, enabled efficient sexual and blood-borne SIVcpz transmission; long-term research presence in Gombe provided the logistical platform and motivation for extensive sampling and detection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1061584/)) Internal mechanisms: SIVcpz is a recombinant lentivirus derived from multiple monkey SIV lineages and adapted to chimpanzees, with sufficient replication competence and transmissibility to persist in small wild communities; viral diversity observed in Gombe reflects ongoing within-host evolution and between-host spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3822437/))
Review: Decision: retain with corrections. Earlier SIVcpz isolates came from captive or sanctuary chimpanzees in West-Central Africa, so the first wild SIVcpz-positive chimpanzee in Gombe was identified only in 2000, not the mid-1990s.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11799233/?utm_source=openai)) I therefore changed the event year to 2000–2005 and updated the country start year to Tanzania [2000]. Because SIVcpz was already known from other African regions, this event is best classified as an intra-continental emergence into a new sub-region (Eastern Africa), not a global first detection, so first_detection=No and intra_continental_emergence=Yes. Text has been lightly adjusted to avoid implying mid-1990s detection.

EPP.scientific.name: Primate lentivirus
EPP.common.name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) – Gombe National Park populations
Event.summary: From the early 2000s through the late 2000s, long-term follow-up of individually known, SIVcpz-infected chimpanzees in Gombe revealed that infection was associated with markedly increased mortality, reduced fertility, and progressive CD4+ T‑cell depletion, overturning the prior assumption that SIVcpz was non-pathogenic in its natural ape host.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08200)) Over roughly nine years of observation of 94 chimpanzees, researchers documented a more than tenfold increase in death risk in infected animals and linked SIVcpz infection to community-level population decline in the most heavily affected subgroup.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08200); [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2944804/)) By 2009, these findings had reframed SIVcpz as a virulent infection in wild chimpanzees, with major implications for ape conservation and for understanding factors controlling virulence in primate lentiviruses.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08200))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: No strong anthropogenic driver is clearly implicated; instead, long-term demographic monitoring allowed detection of the pathogen’s impact, while ongoing habitat pressures and small community sizes may exacerbate vulnerability of chimpanzee populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2944804/)) Internal mechanisms: High virulence of SIVcpz relative to many monkey SIV infections, with AIDS-like immunopathology and shortened lifespan in chimpanzees; viral and host factors underlying this virulence, including recombination origin and immune activation patterns, are central to comparative studies of SIV/HIV pathogenesis.([www.nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08200))
Review: Decision: retain but clarify type. This row captures the recognition of SIVcpz as a pathogenic, AIDS-like infection causing increased mortality and population decline in Gombe chimpanzees over a ~9-year period beginning around 2000.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08200?utm_source=openai)) It does not represent a new introduction, resurgence in incidence, or clear viral change during the study, so I set re_emergence=No and re_occurrence=No, leaving all emergence-type flags as No. Conceptually, this is the continuation and impact assessment of the same Gombe SIVcpz episode described in the previous detection event; the two rows could be merged into a single linked episode in a future refinement.

EPP.scientific.name: Primate lentivirus
EPP.common.name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Black-and-white colobus monkeys (Colobus guereza) in Kibale National Park, Uganda([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/))
Event.summary: Around 2010, intensive virological surveys in Kibale National Park, Uganda, led to the discovery and full genome characterization of two highly divergent SIV lineages infecting black‑and‑white colobus monkeys, designated SIVkcol‑1 and SIVkcol‑2, expanding the known diversity of SIV in natural hosts.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/)) Over the early 2010s, sequencing and phylogenetic analyses confirmed that these viruses formed distinct lineages within the broader SIV radiation, underscoring that East African colobines had been under-sampled and harbored unique SIV variants.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/)) This discovery episode significantly broadened the recognized geographic and host range of SIV in Eastern Africa and provided new comparative models for studying non-pathogenic natural SIV infections.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expanded, targeted wildlife virological surveillance in Kibale National Park, using fecal sampling and high‑throughput sequencing, enabled detection of previously unknown lentiviruses in cryptic primate hosts.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/)) Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence reflected in two highly divergent SIVkcol genomes; long-term coevolution of SIV with colobus hosts likely resulted in largely non-pathogenic, high-prevalence infections, similar to other natural SIV hosts.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23101/))
Review: Decision: flag for possible exclusion. This event describes the discovery of two highly divergent SIVkcol lineages in black‑and‑white colobus monkeys, which is important for understanding SIV diversity but currently involves a limited host range and no demonstrated large-scale morbidity or mortality.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2821968/?utm_source=openai)) To better match the definitions, I reclassified it as re_emergence=Yes (novel strain/genotype emergence in an already SIV-endemic region) and set first_detection and intra_continental_emergence to No. Compared with continental-scale FIV spread and SIVcpz/SIVgor events, this discovery may not rank among the top 10 most impactful emergence events for this EPP; consider excluding if a strict top‑10 list is enforced, while retaining for diversity-of-hosts analyses.

EPP.scientific.name: Proboscivirus elephantid1
EPP.common.name: Elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus
Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – young captive circus elephant
Event.summary: Around 1990, veterinarians in Switzerland reported an acute, rapidly fatal hemorrhagic disease in a young Asian circus elephant with extensive vascular lesions and herpesvirus-like intranuclear inclusions in endothelial cells, which was later recognized as EEHV1-associated hemorrhagic disease based on retrospective molecular work. The case did not spark an immediate outbreak but, in hindsight, represented the first documented occurrence of lethal EEHV-HD in an Asian elephant and provided archival material that would later be re-analysed once EEHV1 had been characterized. This early European case laid the groundwork for linking similar juvenile hemorrhagic deaths in zoo elephants in Europe and North America to a single group of probosciviruses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive veterinary care and necropsy examination in European circuses and zoos enabled detailed histopathology and electron microscopy, allowing recognition of an unusual hemorrhagic syndrome in juvenile elephants. Internal mechanisms: inherent virulence of EEHV1 in immunologically naïve juvenile Asian elephants, with marked endothelial tropism and widespread vascular damage; later genomic work showed EEHV1 to be a deeply divergent proboscivirus, but current evidence suggests this event reflected first recognition of a long-circulating virus rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review:
RETAIN – Event corresponds to the well-documented first recognized EEHV-associated hemorrhagic death in an Asian elephant in a Swiss circus; classification as the global first_detection in the host system is consistent with the definitions and primary reviews.
Minor nuance: the death occurred in 1988 but was published in 1990; using 1990 as the event year is acceptable under the post‑1990 time-window rule but should be interpreted as approximate. No changes to type coding or geography required; URLs are appropriate primary review sources plus a general summary article.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Proboscivirus elephantid1
EPP.common.name: Elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus
Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – zoo calves and young adults
Event.summary: In 1995, the first Asian elephant calf born at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in Washington, D.C. (Kumari) died suddenly of acute hemorrhagic disease; subsequent PCR and sequencing showed a novel herpesvirus, later named EEHV1, in this and a series of similar lethal and nonlethal cases in U.S. zoos, some retrospectively traced to the 1980s. Between 1995 and 1999, multiple young Asian elephants in North American zoos died with comparable clinical and pathological signs, establishing EEHV-HD as a leading cause of juvenile mortality in the region. Publication of the 1999 Science paper describing EEHV1 from these U.S. and European cases marked the first molecular characterization of the virus and the initial well-defined inter-continental emergence of EEHV-HD outside Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion and improved reproductive management of captive Asian elephant populations in North American zoos increased the number of susceptible juveniles reaching the high‑risk age window; access to diagnostic pathology, archival tissues, and molecular virology expertise facilitated identification of the novel virus. Internal mechanisms: EEHV1A and EEHV1B were characterized as highly virulent genotypes with strong endothelial tropism, causing fulminant primary infections in seronegative calves; their characterization led to formal establishment of the Proboscivirus genus and clarified that EEHV1 infections were endemic rather than an acute epidemic introduction.
Review:
REVIEW – Event is clearly real and among the most impactful EEHV episodes (multiple fatal and nonfatal juvenile cases, first molecular description of EEHV1). However, the original coding incorrectly set both first_detection and inter_continental_emergence to “Yes,” contrary to the guidance that categories are generally mutually exclusive.
Change made: first_detection reset to false so that global first_detection is reserved for the earlier Swiss case; inter_continental_emergence remains true to reflect first confirmed occurrence in a new continent (North America) after Europe. Geography and dates are otherwise sound; sources appropriately emphasize Richman et al. and subsequent North American case series.

EPP.scientific.name: Proboscivirus elephantid1
EPP.common.name: Elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus
Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – wild-born juvenile in sanctuary
Event.summary: In May 2004, a wild-born three-year-old Asian elephant at a sanctuary in Cambodia was found dead with acute hemorrhagic lesions consistent with EEHV-HD, prompting detailed necropsy and subsequent molecular testing reported in 2006. PCR and sequencing of liver and other tissues confirmed EEHV1 DNA with very high similarity to European and U.S. strains, constituting the first PCR-confirmed fatal EEHV case on the Asian continent after several earlier but unconfirmed suspect cases in Asia since the late 1990s. This confirmation resolved debate about whether the same pathogenic EEHV1 variants circulated in range-country elephants and demonstrated that lethal EEHV-HD was not confined to zoo populations in Europe and North America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: development of molecular diagnostic collaborations between range-country veterinarians and overseas laboratories allowed archived tissues from suspicious sudden deaths to be tested for EEHV; increased attention to disease in sanctuary elephants ensured that atypical juvenile mortalities were investigated. Internal mechanisms: the Cambodian isolate clustered within the EEHV1A group while showing typical genetic divergence from Western zoo strains, consistent with long‑standing endemic circulation in Asian elephants rather than recent importation; disease in this calf most likely reflected primary infection of an immunologically naïve juvenile rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review:
REVIEW – Event correctly captures the first PCR-confirmed fatal EEHV-HD case in Asia and its importance for demonstrating endemic EEHV1 in range-country elephants. Two issues required correction: (1) the event year should be 2004 (date of death), not 2006 (publication year), and (2) first_detection should not be set to true because global first detection is assigned to the earlier Swiss case.
Changes made: year updated from 2006 to 2004; country tag updated to Cambodia [2004]; first_detection reset to false while keeping inter_continental_emergence = true to mark Asia as a newly confirmed continent following European and North American detections. Sources remain appropriate and include the original Reid et al. case report.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Event.summary: In 2013, the first fatality attributed to EEHV5 in an Asian elephant was reported from Twycross Zoo in the United Kingdom, involving a juvenile male born in 2009 that died of acute hemorrhagic disease after developing progressive oral and perianal lesions. Whole‑genome sequencing of virus from this case revealed a novel EEHV genotype, EEHV5, phylogenetically distinct from EEHV1 and EEHV4 yet associated with similar vascular pathology and rapid clinical decline. This event demonstrated that multiple EEHV genotypes beyond EEHV1 can cause lethal disease in Asian elephants and stimulated broader genotyping of EEHV cases in European and North American collections.

EPP.scientific.name: Proboscivirus elephantid1
EPP.common.name: Elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus
Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – semi-captive juvenile male used in festival
Event.summary: On 23 February 2011, a 2.5‑year‑old domesticated male Asian elephant from Ban Naxeng in Sayabouri Province, Laos, died suddenly after several days of weakness and facial swelling following participation in the country’s largest elephant festival, where about 50 elephants were gathered. Necropsy revealed extensive petechial and ecchymotic hemorrhages in the heart, spleen, liver and submandibular muscles, and subsequent PCR and sequencing of pooled organ samples confirmed EEHV1A DNA that was closely related to strains previously described from Thailand, India and Western zoos. This case was reported as the first PCR-confirmed fatal EEHV infection in Laos and added another South-eastern Asian range country to the list of locations where EEHV-HD kills young semi-captive elephants.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: participation in a multi-day elephant festival exposed the young calf to transport stress, crowding, novel environments and close contact with elephants from other locations, conditions hypothesized by the authors to elevate glucocorticoid levels and facilitate both reactivation and transmission of EEHV strains. Internal mechanisms: the Laos isolate was a typical EEHV1A strain, genetically very similar to pathogenic strains from other Asian countries and Western zoos, indicating that this event reflects re-occurrence of endemic virus under stress conditions rather than emergence of a novel genotype; the severe disease likely resulted from primary infection of an immunologically naïve juvenile.
Review:
REVIEW – This event was missing from the original dataset despite being a well-documented, PCR-confirmed fatal EEHV1A case and the first reported EEHV-HD death in Laos, adding geographic range expansion within an already-affected South-eastern Asian sub-region.
Change made: New row added with year 2011, correct UNSD sub-region (South-eastern Asia), and country name aligned to the Country sheet (Lao People’s Democratic Republic). Event is classified as re_occurrence because it represents EEHV1A causing disease in another country within a previously affected sub-region, with stress and large elephant gatherings suggested as key external drivers rather than a new genotype. This addition should be reviewed by subject-matter experts but clearly belongs among the top 10 episodes by combined impact (mortality and geographic spread).

EPP.scientific.name: Proboscivirus elephantid1
EPP.common.name: Elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus
Host: Borneo elephant (Elephas maximus borneensis) – rescued calves in an elephant orphanage
Event.summary: In May 2016, three two‑year‑old rescued Bornean elephant calves housed at an elephant orphanage in Sabah, Malaysian Borneo, died within a short period from acute hemorrhagic disease with gross and histologic lesions typical of EEHV-HD, while a fourth herdmate survived after apparent infection. PCR and sequencing of multiple conserved and variable loci from necropsy tissues revealed high viral loads of a single, novel EEHV1A-like strain shared by all affected calves. Comparative phylogenetic analysis showed that this Bornean strain diverged by about 2–5% across key genes from previously characterized EEHV1A genomes and possessed features intermediate between EEHV1A and EEHV1B in highly conserved regions, yet retained a highly pathogenic phenotype. Subsequent case reports confirmed these were the first recorded EEHV-HD cases in Malaysia and in the endangered Bornean elephant subspecies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive rescue and hand-rearing operations for orphaned Bornean elephants concentrated susceptible juveniles in close contact, likely enhancing transmission of endemic probosciviruses, while expanding EEHV awareness in Malaysia prompted detailed necropsies and molecular investigation of sudden calf deaths. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses demonstrated that the Sabah cases were caused by a novel, highly diverged EEHV1A variant that appears to have co‑evolved with Bornean elephants over hundreds of thousands of years, yet still causes fulminant hemorrhagic disease during primary infection in naïve calves; this represents a clear example of re-emergence driven by internal viral diversification within an already endemic EEHV1A lineage.
Review:
REVIEW – This national-level emergence in Malaysia, involving three lethal cases in endangered Bornean elephants and a genomically distinctive EEHV1A variant, was omitted from the original dataset but is substantial in both conservation impact and virological novelty.
Change made: New row added with year 2016 (timing of the three Sabah calf deaths reported in workshop proceedings), country coded as Malaysia with sub-region South-eastern Asia, and event type classified as re_emergence to reflect the discovery of a highly diverged EEHV1A strain rather than a new continent or sub-region. Primary sources include the Malaysian case report and workshop abstract describing the Bornean variant. This event should be retained and reviewed, as it likely belongs within the top ten episodes for this EPP when considering deaths and host subspecies significance.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Pseudogymnoascus destructans
EPP.common.name: White-nose syndrome fungus, Pd
Host: Palearctic Asian hibernating bats in northeastern China, including multiple Myotis spp., Murina ussuriensis and other cave-hibernating insectivorous bats
Event.summary: Following recognition of Pd in Europe and the devastating emergence of white-nose syndrome in North America, targeted surveys were initiated in East Asia. During summer 2014 and winter 2015, intensive sampling of bats and cave surfaces across northeastern China revealed widespread environmental contamination with Pd and infections in at least six bat species, some with histopathologic lesions compatible with white-nose syndrome but without mass die-offs. These detections provided the first contemporaneous confirmation of Pd in Asia and, together with genetic work showing shared and distinct haplotypes across Europe, Asia and North America, demonstrated that Pd is broadly enzootic across the Palearctic rather than confined to Europe. After about 2015, research emphasis in Asia shifted from first detection to understanding host–pathogen coexistence, environmental reservoirs and the risk that Asian lineages could seed introductions into naïve bat faunas elsewhere (e.g. Australasia and temperate South America).
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Targeted surveillance of Asian bat hibernacula and cave environments, motivated by concern over the North American WNS crisis and evidence of enzootic Pd in Europe, led to the first systematic sampling in northeastern China and other Palearctic Asian localities. International research collaborations and molecular diagnostics (qPCR, sequencing) were critical external enablers of detection. Internal mechanisms: Similar to Europe, Palearctic Asian bats appear to tolerate Pd infection, with infection commonly documented (including lesions diagnostic for WNS in some individuals) but with limited evidence of large-scale demographic collapse. The fungus’s psychrophilic biology and ability to persist on cave substrates under cold, humid conditions underpin its broad geographic range in Asia, while long-term host adaptation likely prevents the explosive, high-mortality emergence seen in North America.
Review: review: This event previously mis-stated the timing and geography of Asian detections (it cited Russian Federation [Asian part] and China as positive by 2010, plus Georgia and Turkey, with a 2010–2015 window). Available primary sources indicate that the first confirmed contemporaneous detections of Pd in Asia came from intensive surveys in northeastern China in 2014–2015, with widespread environmental and bat infections documented there, and that Asian Pd (including West Siberian sites in Russia) was recognised as part of a broader Palearctic enzootic through combined European–Asian analyses published mid-2010s.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4698868/?utm_source=openai)) Accordingly, the event year has been narrowed to 2014–2015 and the countries field restricted to China [2014], which is the best-documented Asian range state in this period, while Russian Federation sites in the West Siberian Plain are treated under the Eurasian context but, per the UNSD classification used in the project, fall in Eastern Europe rather than Asia. The emergence-type flags are all set to No because Pd is considered long-enzootic in Asia and this episode reflects first systematic detection rather than new occurrence, spread to a previously uninfected continent, or a strain/host shift. Additional Asian range states (e.g. other parts of Russia, and possibly neighbouring East Asian countries) are likely infected but are not added here due to limited, country-specific confirmation within 2005–2015 in the cited literature; these could be incorporated in future updates if stronger evidence becomes available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Psoroptes ovis
EPP.common.name: Sheep scab
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1973]
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event.summary: After approximately two decades during which sheep scab had been eradicated from Great Britain, Psoroptes ovis was reintroduced in the early 1970s (first detected on a farm in Lancashire, England) and spread widely under a regime of compulsory dipping and statutory control.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/psoroptes_ovis.pdf)) Between 1973 and 1992 around 1,480 flock outbreaks were officially recorded, with pronounced winter seasonality and cases distributed across most sheep‑keeping regions of Great Britain.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10423002/)) In this dataset the linked episode is truncated to its 1990–1992 phase to respect the post‑1990 time window, ending when national sheep scab control was deregulated in 1992 and responsibility for management shifted to flock owners, setting the stage for subsequent endemic re‑establishment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reintroduction of infested sheep into a country that had previously eradicated sheep scab; large national sheep numbers with frequent movements between markets and grazing areas; winter environmental conditions favouring off‑host mite survival; and a statutory control system (compulsory dipping and movement restrictions) that reduced but did not eliminate infection due to incomplete compliance.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/psoroptes_ovis.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel strains, host shifts or drug resistance was reported for this period; the episode is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence of a long‑established parasite in the same sub‑region, driven mainly by animal movements and imperfect implementation of control measures rather than evolutionary change.([cfsph.iastate.edu](https://www.cfsph.iastate.edu/Factsheets/pdfs/psoroptes_ovis.pdf))
Review: Decision: review – Event correctly represents the post‑eradication reintroduction and national epizootic of sheep scab in Great Britain, but the event years have been truncated from 1973–1992 to 1990–1992 to comply with the “from 1990 onwards” rule while still summarising outbreak data from the full 1973–1992 period; outbreak counts and reintroduction dates should be cross‑checked against O’Brien (1999) and UK historical control summaries. Re‑occurrence classification (same sub‑region, no clear parasite change) and geographic coding (Europe, Northern Europe, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland) are appropriate and should be retained.([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/271901/2/271901.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Event.summary: From the early 1990s, garden ponds across southern and eastern England began to experience sudden summer die‑offs of adult and metamorphic common frogs with ulcerative skin lesions and internal hemorrhages; virological work identified FV3‑like ranaviruses as the cause, and public reporting through the Frog Mortality Project documented hundreds of affected sites by the late 1990s. EPP.scientific.name: Ranavirus spp.
