Host: Cultured pig frog (Rana grylio) in intensive frog farms in Hubei, Hunan and other southern/central Chinese provinces
Event.summary: From about 1995, Chinese frog farms culturing the pig frog Rana grylio reported "lethal syndrome" with lethargy, skin hemorrhages and mortality often exceeding 90% in grow‑out animals; a novel iridovirus, later named Rana grylio virus (RGV), was isolated from diseased frogs and shown experimentally to reproduce the disease. Subsequent work demonstrated that genetically similar RGV isolates were present on multiple farms and were closely related to FV3, confirming that FV3‑like ranaviruses had become established in Asian amphibian aquaculture. These outbreaks represent the first well‑documented amphibian ranavirus epizootics in Asia and marked inter‑continental spread of ranavirosis into a new region.

Internal mechanisms: emergence of RGV, an FV3‑like ranavirus adapted to pig frogs that caused systemic infection and severe mortality, demonstrating both host expansion of FV3‑like lineages and inter‑continental range expansion of ranaviruses into Asian amphibian production systems.

Rationale: This new row has been added because the mid‑1990s Rana grylio virus epizootics in Chinese pig frog farms were the first reported amphibian ranavirus outbreaks in Asia and caused very high mortality, so they clearly belong among the top 10 global emergence events. EPP.common.name: Ranavirosis
Host: Cultured tiger frog Hoplobatrachus (Rana) tigrina rugulosa tadpoles; other farmed edible frogs in southern China
Event.summary: In May–June 2000, a frog‑culture facility in Guangdong, southern China, experienced a severe outbreak of abdominal distension disease in cultured tiger frog tadpoles, with clinical signs including distended abdomens, reduced feeding and very high mortality; virological investigations led to the isolation of tiger frog virus (TFV), a ranavirus whose complete genome was later sequenced as the first full ranavirus genome from Asian amphibians. Subsequent work showed that TFV and closely related FV3‑like ranaviruses caused repeated high‑mortality events in cultured tiger frogs and other edible frog species in southern China over the early 2000s. These outbreaks marked ranavirus as a major constraint on frog aquaculture in East Asia and a potential source for cross‑species and geographic spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of frog aquaculture in southern China with high stocking densities; shipment of live frogs and tadpoles among farms and regions; limited biosecurity and water treatment. Internal mechanisms: emergence of tiger frog virus and related FV3‑like lineages with high virulence in tadpoles; possible host adaptation to Hoplobatrachus spp. and efficient replication at aquaculture temperatures, representing a clear re‑emergence of ranaviruses in a new managed host system rather than simple recurrence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The TFV outbreak in southern China is a well‑documented, high‑mortality event in frog aquaculture and a key example of re‑emergence via a novel genotype and host system in a region where ranaviruses were already present (RGV). The timing, geography, hosts and mechanisms are consistent with primary sources, and no structural corrections were needed beyond the contextual addition of the earlier RGV event elsewhere in the table.

EPP.scientific.name: Ranavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Ranavirosis
Host: Wild multi‑species amphibian assemblages including common midwife toad (Alytes obstetricans), alpine newt (Ichthyosaura alpestris cyreni), palmate newt (Lissotriton helveticus), sharp‑ribbed salamander (Pleurodeles waltl), Pyrenees frog (Rana pyrenaica) and others
Event.summary: Beginning in 2005, mass mortality events were recorded in Picos de Europa National Park and other Iberian mountain sites, where a common midwife toad virus (CMTV)‑like ranavirus caused recurrent die‑offs of tadpoles, metamorphs and adults in multiple amphibian species, with some populations collapsing to near extinction within a few years. Long‑term monitoring showed repeated, severe outbreaks through at least 2012, with community‑level impacts including the loss or drastic decline of several species at affected ponds. These Iberian epizootics demonstrated that a novel, generalist CMTV‑like ranavirus lineage could drive large‑scale amphibian community collapse and highlighted Iberia as a major European hotspot for ranavirosis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑elevation breeding sites with dense, multi‑species larval assemblages; climatic warming and extreme weather potentially stressing hosts and extending permissive temperature windows for viral replication; possible human‑mediated movement of infected animals among mountain valleys. Internal mechanisms: emergence and spread of CMTV‑like strains with broad host range and high virulence; enhanced transmission in multi‑host communities; probable viral adaptation and/or recombination events distinguishing CMTV from older European FV3‑like strains.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The Iberian CMTV outbreaks are among the most severe ranavirus events known and clearly should be retained. To align with definitions, this episode is best coded as intra‑continental emergence (first major amphibian ranavirosis documented in Southern Europe/mainland Europe) without re‑emergence, because there was no prior ranavirus presence recorded in that UN sub‑region; re_emergence has therefore been set from 'Yes' to 'No'. The event years, hosts and sources are appropriate but should be confirmed during expert review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ranavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Ranavirosis
Host: Wild water frogs (Pelophylax spp., including P. lessonae and P. esculentus) and smooth newt (Lissotriton vulgaris); other amphibian species affected in subsequent years
Event.summary: In September 2010, a pond in Dwingelderveld National Park in the north of the Netherlands suffered a mass die‑off of over 1,000 water frogs and at least 10 smooth newts; necropsy and PCR identified a CMTV‑like ranavirus identical in major capsid sequence to Iberian common midwife toad virus. Follow‑up surveillance in subsequent years documented additional mortality events and widespread ranavirus infection in multiple amphibian species at numerous Dutch sites, indicating an ongoing regional epidemic. The 2010 Dwingelderveld outbreak is therefore regarded as the first major documented emergence of CMTV‑like ranavirus in Western Europe outside Iberia, with substantial mortality in common frog, newt and water frog populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of CMTV‑like virus via movement of infected amphibians (wildlife trade, pet trade or translocation of animals) between European regions; high density of amphibians in eutrophic waterbodies of protected areas; limited initial awareness and control measures. Internal mechanisms: a CMTV‑like ranavirus lineage with high virulence and broad host range, able to cause rapid, multi‑species mortality; evolutionary relationships between Dutch isolates, Iberian CMTV and Asian ranaviruses suggest historical virus movements and recombination that underpin this emergence and intra‑European spread.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: The Dutch CMTV‑like outbreak and ensuing epidemic are rightly treated as one of the major European ranavirus events and fit the intra‑continental emergence category (first significant ranavirosis recorded in Western Europe). To conform to the definitions, re_emergence has been set to 'No' because this was the first known amphibian ranavirus incursion into that UN sub‑region. The single‑year '2010' start is acceptable but the project may optionally choose to extend the year range to cover 2010–2014 surveillance when reconciling with Dutch data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ranavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Ranavirosis
Host: Farmed Chinese giant salamander (Andrias davidianus), both juveniles and adults
Event.summary: From February to May 2010, high‑mortality outbreaks occurred in intensive farms raising the critically endangered Chinese giant salamander in Shaanxi and other provinces, with affected animals showing severe hemorrhagic lesions and almost complete crop loss in some facilities; virological work identified a novel ranavirus, variably termed Chinese giant salamander iridovirus or Andrias davidianus ranavirus (ADRV). Similar ranavirus‑associated disease with summer mortality reportedly exceeding 90% recurred annually from 2010 to at least 2013 in farms across several Chinese provinces. These outbreaks caused dramatic declines in farmed salamander stocks and raised concern about spillover into remaining wild populations via releases of infected captive‑bred animals.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and high stocking densities in salamander farming; poor biosecurity and water reuse; government‑supported release of captive‑bred salamanders into the wild without systematic disease screening, creating risk for pathogen spillover. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel ADRV/CGSIV ranavirus lineage closely related to CMTV and other frog ranaviruses, with high virulence in salamanders; possible adaptation to a new caudate host and to intensive aquaculture conditions, exemplifying re‑emergence via host expansion and increased pathogenicity rather than simple recurrence.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The Chinese giant salamander outbreaks caused very high mortality in a critically endangered species and are well supported by virological and genomic studies. The classification as re‑emergence (novel, highly pathogenic lineage and host expansion within Eastern Asia, where amphibian ranaviruses were already established) is consistent with the project definitions, and no geographic or temporal corrections were identified.

EPP.scientific.name: Ranavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Ranavirosis
Host: Wild native anuran tadpoles plus invasive American bullfrog (Lithobates catesbeianus); co‑occurring fish also affected during the die‑off
Event.summary: Field investigations in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest in the 2010s documented ranavirus infection in wild tadpoles of both native frogs and invasive American bullfrogs, and described a localized mass mortality of amphibians and fish in a natural waterbody where ranavirus was detected. This episode marked the first confirmed detection of ranavirus infection in wild Brazilian amphibians, extending concern from farms to adjacent natural communities. Subsequent surveys have found persistent ranavirus presence in wild and invasive bullfrog populations in southern Brazil, suggesting environmental establishment and ongoing risk to native amphibians.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Escape and release of infected bullfrogs from farms into natural waterbodies; lack of containment around frog‑farming operations; overlap of farm effluents with habitats of native amphibians and fish. Internal mechanisms: environmental persistence of FV3‑like ranavirus introduced through aquaculture; spillover from invasive bullfrogs acting as reservoirs to native amphibians and fish; potential adaptation to local host assemblages, representing re‑emergence and geographic spread beyond initial farm foci within the same continental sub‑region.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This event appropriately captures the first confirmed infections and an associated mass die‑off in wild Brazilian amphibians and fish, an important ecological extension beyond aquaculture. To fit the formal definitions, intra_continental_emergence has been set to 'No' because both farm and wild outbreaks occur within the same UN sub‑region ('South America'); the episode is better characterised as re‑emergence (novel host community and environmental establishment). The exact onset year (here kept as 2013) should be checked against Ruggeri et al. (2019) by the project team.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ranavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Ranavirosis
Host: Cultured black‑spotted pond frog (Rana nigromaculata) tadpoles in frog farms in Sichuan and other provinces; other edible frog species affected in similar FV3‑like outbreaks
Event.summary: Around 2017, frog farms in Sichuan Province reported substantial mortality (up to about 90%) among cultured black‑spotted pond frog tadpoles; virological investigation isolated a new FV3‑like ranavirus, provisionally termed Rana nigromaculata ranavirus (RNRV), closely related to other Chinese FV3‑like ranaviruses. This outbreak followed earlier high‑mortality ranavirus events in cultured bullfrogs and edible frogs in several Chinese provinces, indicating a pattern of recurring, severe ranavirus disease in Asian frog aquaculture. The 2017 RNRV episode was notable for its high mortality in a new cultured host species and for adding to the diversity of documented FV3‑like lineages impacting aquaculture.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued intensification and geographic expansion of frog farming in China; movement of live frogs and tadpoles between farms; shared water sources and limited quarantine facilitating cross‑farm transmission. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a distinct FV3‑like genotype (RNRV) adapted to black‑spotted pond frogs, with high virulence under farm conditions; broader pattern of frequent novel ranavirus genotypes arising and spreading among cultured amphibians in East Asia, representing repeated re‑emergence events in aquaculture settings.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The RNRV outbreaks caused very high mortality in a widely farmed frog species and exemplify ongoing diversification and re‑emergence of ranaviruses in Asian aquaculture, complementing the earlier TFV and RGV episodes. The timing, geography and classification as re‑emergence are in line with the primary description in Archives of Virology, and no inconsistencies with the project definitions were identified.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella gallinarum (fowl typhoid)
Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers)
Event.summary: Between 2000 and 2008, fowl typhoid became one of the major bacterial diseases of commercial chickens in the Republic of Korea, with S. Gallinarum repeatedly isolated from field cases of septicemia and high flock mortality.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20075274/?utm_source=openai)) The disease affected both broilers and layers, with pronounced outbreaks in young birds and recurring farm‑level losses despite vaccination efforts.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20075274/?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2000s intensified vaccination, stricter biosecurity and culling of infected flocks helped reduce the frequency of clinical outbreaks, although S. Gallinarum remained endemic and required ongoing control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of the Korean poultry industry, high bird densities and incomplete biosecurity likely facilitated repeated farm‑to‑farm spread, while vertical transmission from infected breeder flocks sustained infection pressure.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20075274/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype was highlighted, but reliance on the SG‑9R live vaccine raised concerns about vaccine‑derived variants regaining virulence, and the persistence of systemic disease indicates maintenance of highly virulent S. Gallinarum lineages with efficient transovarian transmission.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella gallinarum (fowl typhoid)
Countries: Bangladesh – Rajshahi City Corporation and other commercial poultry areas [2018]
Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers in urban/peri‑urban farms)
Event.summary: In 2018 a detailed survey of commercial poultry farms in the Rajshahi City Corporation area of Bangladesh documented substantial prevalence of fowl typhoid in both sick and apparently healthy birds, with typical lesions and S. Gallinarum isolation confirming ongoing endemic infection.([banglajol.info](https://www.banglajol.info/index.php/RALF/article/view/55490?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent Bangladeshi studies across the late 2010s and early 2020s reported high seroprevalence of Salmonella infection in broilers and layers and emphasised fowl typhoid as one of the major bacterial constraints on poultry productivity, triggering expanded vaccination efforts with live SG‑9R and locally produced vaccines.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/356423577_Sero_Survey_of_Salmonellosis_in_Broiler_at_Sylhet_City_of_Bangladesh?utm_source=openai)) While these interventions reduced mortality in some operations, the disease has remained a recurrent cause of production loss, particularly in small and medium‑scale farms.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very dense poultry populations in peri‑urban Bangladesh, inadequate farm and hatchery biosecurity, and widespread but often unsupervised antimicrobial use have promoted persistent circulation of S. Gallinarum; incomplete vaccination coverage and suboptimal vaccine handling further limited control.([banglajol.info](https://www.banglajol.info/index.php/RALF/article/view/55490?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Heavy reliance on SG‑9R and related live vaccines raises concern about vaccine‑derived variants and selection for antimicrobial resistance; studies emphasise the risk of AMR in Salmonella from Bangladeshi poultry (antimicrobial resistance and possible novel genotype emergence).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9415136/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella gallinarum (fowl typhoid)
Host: Chickens (integrated crop–livestock farms, small commercial and backyard flocks; contamination detected in poultry meat)
Event.summary: Although fowl typhoid was considered eradicated from commercial poultry in the United States by the early 1980s, recent investigations have documented renewed detection of S. Gallinarum and S. Pullorum in US poultry environments and products.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9415136/?utm_source=openai)) A 2020s study of integrated crop–livestock farms and poultry meat found S. Gallinarum/Pullorum isolates with notable prevalence in farm environments and on carcasses, signalling a quiet re‑emergence of host‑specific Salmonella in sectors outside the tightly monitored industrial broiler industry.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11652723/?utm_source=openai)) These findings, along with industry observations of increased bacterial disease in antibiotic‑free or organic production, have prompted renewed discussion of surveillance and control strategies to prevent re‑establishment of clinical fowl typhoid.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Shift toward antibiotic‑free and organic poultry production, with reduced routine antimicrobial use and, in some systems, less stringent biosecurity than integrated industrial complexes; integrated crop–livestock farming may facilitate environmental persistence and cross‑contamination between flocks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11652723/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Studies underline emerging antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella from retail chicken meat and note the presence of S. Gallinarum/Pullorum among resistant isolates, indicating selection for AMR under past antimicrobial pressure (antimicrobial resistance).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11652723/?utm_source=openai)) The re‑appearance of these historically eradicated biovars in US farms also constitutes a clear re‑emergence linked to changes in production systems and drug use.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella pullorum, Bacillary white diarrhoea
Host: Non-commercial (hobby/backyard) chicken flocks
Event.summary: In 2001, Sweden, which had eradicated S. Pullorum from commercial poultry in the early 1960s and considered both pullorum disease and fowl typhoid eliminated, detected pullorum disease in two epidemiologically linked backyard chicken flocks. The event was recognized after increased mortality and clinical signs in the hobby flocks triggered investigation and bacteriological confirmation of S. Pullorum; no infection was found in commercial breeder or layer flocks. The affected backyard flocks were depopulated, movement restrictions and tracing were applied, and enhanced surveillance of non-commercial poultry was introduced, with no further spread detected and Sweden maintaining PD‑free status in its commercial sector.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: growth of backyard and hobby poultry keeping with variable biosecurity in a country whose long-standing eradication programme focused on commercial breeders and layers; informal movement of live birds or eggs between non‑commercial holdings. Internal mechanisms: the ability of S. Pullorum to persist in carrier hens and transmit vertically via eggs and horizontally via faecal contamination (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation) allowed undetected maintenance in a small non‑commercial reservoir until clinical disease drew attention; there is no evidence of novel strain emergence or antimicrobial resistance specific to this episode.
Review: retain – Event is well supported by Swedish surveillance information and the 2018 Vet Microbiology paper: Sweden had eradicated S. Pullorum from commercial poultry, and two linked backyard flocks were found infected in 2001. Geography (Europe – Northern Europe – Sweden) and classification as a re‑occurrence, with no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, are appropriate. Source coverage is adequate (scientific paper and EU reference-laboratory newsletter), and adding the SVA web page mainly strengthens national historical context rather than changing interpretation.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonid alphavirus
EPP.common.name: SAV
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in seawater cages
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, pancreas disease caused by Salmonid alphavirus subtype 1 (SAV1) produced a prolonged epizootic in marine Atlantic salmon farms in Ireland, with well over half of marine sites affected each year and PD‑attributed mortalities frequently in the low‑to‑mid double‑digit percentage range. The episode developed as SAV spread between bays and cohorts, and PD became one of the leading infectious causes of mortality and poor growth in Irish salmon farming, prompting coordinated research and the establishment of detailed farm‑level monitoring. By the mid‑1990s, improved single‑generation stocking and fallowing practices reduced average mortality even though PD remained widely endemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of marine Atlantic salmon aquaculture in Ireland in the late 1980s and early 1990s, high stocking densities, year‑round use of sites without fallowing, and movements of smolts between bays facilitated farm‑to‑farm spread and persistence of SAV1. Internal mechanisms: there is no evidence of a novel SAV subtype emerging during this period; increased impact appears to reflect amplification of an existing SAV1 lineage in an intensifying production system, consistent with a re‑occurrence driven mainly by external management and environmental factors rather than viral change.
Review: retain – the original row described a 1994–2004 re‑emergence in Ireland and Scotland, but surveillance data show that the major early epidemic in Ireland occurred from about 1989–1994 with very high site prevalence and mortality, followed by reduced severity in the later 1990s. I have therefore re‑dated this event to 1990–1994, limited it to Ireland (where quantitative data are available), rewrote the summary and drivers to match published epizootiology, and kept it classified as a re‑occurrence driven mainly by production intensity and management factors. Boundaries remain approximate and should be reviewed, but the event clearly belongs among the most impactful SAV episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonid alphavirus
EPP.common.name: SAV
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in seawater cages
Event.summary: After several years in the late 1990s and early 2000s when pancreas‑disease‑associated mortality on Irish salmon farms had fallen to relatively low levels, pancreas disease re‑emerged strongly from 2002 onwards. In 2002–2004 a majority of marine farms experienced PD each year, and detailed national surveys in 2003–2004 found average PD‑attributed mortalities around the mid‑teens with some pens losing more than a quarter of their fish, alongside significant growth losses. Through 2005–2007 PD remained widespread, with a high proportion of Irish sites affected annually, and the disease again became a major constraint on industry viability until vaccination, fallowing and improved biosecurity began to reduce case severity in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high biomass of salmon on a reduced number of marine sites, frequent movements of fish between sea cages, incomplete fallowing and high sea‑lice burdens increased opportunities for SAV transmission, while economic pressures encouraged continued production in historically affected bays. Internal mechanisms: viruses responsible for this wave belonged to existing SAV1 lineages rather than a new subtype; the resurgence is best explained as a re‑occurrence linked to production practices and environmental drivers rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain – the original dataset did not include the well‑documented re‑emergence of pancreas disease in Irish marine salmon farms from 2002, despite this wave causing large mortality and production losses and clearly ranking among the most impactful SAV episodes. I have added this new event, set its period to 2002–2007 based on national surveillance and epidemiological studies, and classified it as a re‑occurrence driven by external management and environmental factors without evidence for a new viral subtype. Event boundaries could be refined in future, but inclusion of this episode is strongly recommended.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonid alphavirus
EPP.common.name: SAV
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) and rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) in seawater along the Norwegian coast
Event.summary: From about 2003, Norway experienced a marked escalation in pancreas disease outbreaks caused mainly by Salmonid alphavirus subtype 3 (SAV3) in marine salmon and rainbow trout farms, after more localised disease that had previously been confined largely to western counties in the 1990s. Through 2003–2007 the annual number of PD‑diagnosed farms rose several‑fold and the infection front spread northwards from Hordaland and Sogn og Fjordane into counties such as Nordland, Troms and Finnmark, with repeated epizootics in affected fjords and substantial economic losses from mortality, reduced growth and carcass downgrading. Around 2008–2010, Norway introduced PD zoning, including a production‑free corridor, and PD vaccination became widely implemented; these measures helped slow further geographic expansion and reduce new farm infections, although SAV3‑associated PD has remained an important endemic problem for Norwegian salmonid aquaculture.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid growth and northward expansion of salmonid aquaculture along the Norwegian coast, high farm densities with frequent movements of smolts and harvested fish, and seawater conditions favourable for virus survival promoted both local and long‑distance dissemination of SAV3; before zoning and vaccination were introduced, incomplete biosecurity and limited fallowing further facilitated persistence. Internal mechanisms: SAV3 had been present in Norway since at least the late 1980s and genetic studies indicate relatively stable viral lineages, so the mid‑2000s upsurge is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence driven by production intensity and farm connectivity rather than emergence of a markedly more virulent strain.
Review: retain – this row appropriately captures the major SAV3‑associated pancreas disease epidemic in Norway beginning in 2003, which is one of the largest SAV emergence episodes by number of affected farms and production loss. I have made only minor wording adjustments to emphasise the geographic spread from western to northern coastal counties and to align drivers with Norwegian surveillance and risk‑factor studies; the time window 2003–2010 and classification as a re‑occurrence driven by production and connectivity, rather than by a new SAV3 variant, remain justified. Wikipedia has been removed from the event‑level sources in favour of primary and official references.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonid alphavirus
EPP.common.name: SAV
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (Scotland) [2018]
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in freshwater hatchery / pre‑smolt culture (SAV1‑associated pancreas disease)
Event.summary: In May 2018, a freshwater hatchery on the west coast of Scotland reported increased mortality and reduced performance in Atlantic salmon parr and pre‑smolts, initially suspected to be infectious pancreatic necrosis. Diagnostic testing instead detected Salmonid alphavirus subtype 1 (SAV1), and histopathology showed pancreas, heart and skeletal muscle lesions consistent with pancreas disease, representing the first published description of a clinical SAV outbreak causing PD in freshwater‑reared Atlantic salmon. The episode led to removal of affected cohorts and implementation of enhanced hygiene and stocking measures, and although the outbreak was confined to this facility it raised concern that freshwater systems could act as additional reservoirs feeding infection into the marine production phase.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: concentration of large numbers of salmon in intensive freshwater hatchery units, reuse of water and equipment, and movements of fish between tanks likely favoured persistence and spread of SAV1 within the site; seeding from infected marine stocks or other facilities via water or fish movements is a plausible source. Internal mechanisms: expression of overt pancreas disease at the freshwater life stage indicates host/life‑stage expansion and altered epidemiology of an existing SAV1 lineage, fitting the definition of re‑emergence rather than first detection in the host system as a whole.
Review: review – the original row described extensive SAV1‑associated freshwater pancreas disease outbreaks in Ireland during 2011–2017, for which I could not find supporting evidence in the primary or official literature. I have replaced it with the first well‑documented clinical field outbreak of SAV1‑associated pancreas disease in freshwater Atlantic salmon, which occurred in a Scottish hatchery in 2018 and clearly fits the definition of re‑emergence in a new production niche (freshwater life stage). However, this episode involved only a single facility and its overall contribution to system‑wide losses is modest compared with the large marine PD and SD epidemics; I therefore recommend that this corrected event be kept for now but flagged for further review regarding whether it should remain among the top‑impact events for this EPP.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Scrapie prion
EPP.common.name: PrPsc, Scrapie agent
Host: Sheep (with later recognition in goats, but index description is ovine)
Event.summary: In 1998, Norwegian veterinarians identified several scrapie cases in sheep with highly unusual neuropathology and prion protein profiles, later termed Nor98 or atypical scrapie. Detailed characterization showed distinctive cerebellar and cerebral cortical vacuolation and a unique low–molecular weight PrPSc band pattern, clearly separating these cases from classical scrapie. The finding led to recognition of atypical/Nor98 scrapie as a distinct prion strain and motivated adjustments to Norway’s TSE surveillance to ensure such cases would be detected going forward.
Mechanism.or.driver: Internal mechanism – Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (first description of the atypical/Nor98 scrapie strain with distinctive PrPSc phenotype, lesion distribution and biochemical signature). Drivers – Availability and application of improved neuropathological and biochemical diagnostic methods within Norway’s scrapie surveillance allowed recognition of this divergent strain, which likely had been overlooked previously.
Review: retain – Event accurately captures the first recognition of atypical/Nor98 scrapie in Norwegian sheep in 1998, with correct geography (Northern Europe, Norway), host, timing and classification as re_emergence due to a novel strain; no corrections required.

EPP.scientific.name: Scrapie prion
EPP.common.name: PrPsc, Scrapie agent
Host: Sheep (classical scrapie)
Event.summary: After a long period with very few confirmed events, Norway’s national scrapie surveillance programme detected several small classical scrapie outbreaks in sheep flocks beginning in 2001. Through 2009, classical cases recurred intermittently in a limited number of flocks, while atypical Nor98 scrapie was detected more regularly in other holdings, prompting targeted tracing, culling and movement controls around affected premises. By 2009, classical scrapie remained rare and geographically limited, and Norway continued to document its low‑incidence status while maintaining intensive surveillance and control, after which only atypical cases have been reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers – Livestock management and animal movement patterns, as well as environmental persistence of prions, likely facilitated sporadic re‑introduction and within‑flock transmission of classical scrapie into a small number of Norwegian flocks; enhanced surveillance increased the probability of detection and thus the apparent incidence. Internal mechanisms – No strong evidence of a novel strain in these classical outbreaks; these episodes are best interpreted as re‑occurrence of classical scrapie in a country with long‑standing but low‑level presence under stringent control.
Review: retain – Event appropriately characterizes Norway’s small number of classical scrapie outbreaks detected between 2001–2009, uses correct geography and time span, and classifies them as re_occurrence (resurgence of a known disease without evidence of a new strain); despite relatively modest global impact, it is reasonable to retain as one of the main post‑1990 emergence episodes for this EPP.

EPP.scientific.name: Scrapie prion
EPP.common.name: PrPsc, Scrapie agent
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2002]
Host: Sheep (classical and atypical scrapie)
Event.summary: From 2002 onward, Great Britain conducted large‑scale abattoir and fallen‑stock surveys for scrapie alongside the National Scrapie Plan, leading to greatly increased detection of both classical and newly recognised atypical scrapie compared with prior passive reporting. Over the following decade, hundreds of flocks were identified with classical scrapie and more than a hundred holdings with atypical scrapie, revealing substantial underlying infection that had previously gone largely unrecognised. Genotype‑based breeding for resistance, compulsory culling in infected flocks and continued testing progressively reduced classical scrapie incidence even as atypical cases continued to appear sporadically, illustrating shifting strain dynamics under genetic selection and control pressure.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers – Strong policy and surveillance drivers (EU TSE regulations, the UK National Scrapie Plan, and public concern in the wake of BSE) produced intensive testing and PRNP‑genotype‑based breeding for resistance, as well as culling of infected flocks. Internal mechanisms – Re‑emergence dynamics shaped by host genetic selection (favouring ARR and other resistant genotypes) altered the balance between classical and atypical scrapie, and the broader recognition of atypical scrapie highlighted the diversity of circulating prion strains.
Review: review – Reclassified this episode as re_emergence only (removed re_occurrence) because scrapie was already endemic in Great Britain and the apparent rise in case numbers after 2002 was largely due to intensified active surveillance and recognition of atypical scrapie, rather than a true resurgence driven by external failures of control. Geography, time span and overall description remain appropriate, but coding now aligns more closely with the event‑type definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: Scrapie prion
EPP.common.name: PrPsc, Scrapie agent
Host: Sheep (atypical scrapie); historical background of classical scrapie in sheep
Event.summary: Japan, which had recorded classical ovine scrapie outbreaks beginning in the early 1980s, identified its first case of atypical scrapie in a sheep in 2016 during active TSE surveillance using modern immunohistochemical and biochemical assays. The atypical case occurred in a flock in which overall scrapie incidence was very low but surveillance intensity was high due to national concern over prion diseases such as BSE. Following confirmation, authorities refined elements of their prion surveillance strategy, and no large‑scale epidemic of atypical scrapie has been reported, with scrapie remaining a rare diagnosis in Japanese flocks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Internal mechanisms – Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (first detection of atypical/Nor98‑like scrapie in Asia) and re_emergence in a country with prior classical scrapie but a long interval without major outbreaks. Drivers – Enhanced prion surveillance capacity and diagnostic technology in Japan following BSE‑related investments, and sustained testing of fallen stock and risk animals, enabled recognition of a single atypical scrapie case decades after the country’s initial classical scrapie outbreaks.
Review: review – Removed coding as first_detection, intra_continental_emergence, inter_continental_emergence and re_occurrence, because scrapie (classical form) had been present in Japan and Asia since the early 1980s and the 2016 case represents the emergence of the atypical/Nor98 strain in an already affected continent. Event is now coded solely as re_emergence in line with the definitions, while geography, host and timing remain supported by the primary Japanese reports.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Scrapie prion
EPP.common.name: PrPsc, Scrapie agent
Host: Sheep and goats (classical scrapie; large mixed‑flock epidemic)
Event.summary: From the mid‑1980s and throughout the 1990s and 2000s, Cyprus experienced a major epidemic of classical scrapie in sheep and, increasingly, in goats, with disease spreading widely through mixed small‑ruminant flocks across much of the island. By the 2000s, annual case numbers in goats and sheep numbered in the hundreds to thousands, and scrapie was reported from more than 1,000 holdings, meaning roughly one fifth of all Cypriot small‑ruminant farms were affected and around 90% of EU goat scrapie cases in 2007 came from Cyprus. Intensive surveillance, large‑scale culling, movement controls, and the introduction of breeding programmes for PRNP genotypes associated with resistance gradually reduced incidence toward 2010, although many infected flocks still required long‑term management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers – High densities of mixed sheep–goat flocks, extensive within‑island animal movements, and initial lack of effective control measures allowed classical scrapie to amplify and persist at high prevalence. Internal mechanisms – Host genetic susceptibility, particularly PRNP codon 146 polymorphisms in goats that strongly influenced risk, created highly vulnerable goat populations; later, genotype‑based breeding programmes exploited protective alleles as a control tool but only after the epidemic was well established.
Review: retain – New event added to capture the long‑running, high‑prevalence classical scrapie epidemic in Cyprus, which affected >1,000 small‑ruminant holdings and accounted for around 90% of reported EU goat scrapie cases in 2007; this clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 emergence events for the scrapie prion. Coded as re_occurrence in Western Asia (Cyprus) because it represents a large resurgence of an already present disease driven mainly by host genetics and management, without strong evidence for a novel scrapie strain.

EPP.scientific.name: Scrapie prion
EPP.common.name: PrPsc, Scrapie agent
Host: Sheep (single detected case of atypical/Nor98 scrapie)
Event.summary: In 2005, TSE surveillance on sheep in the Falkland Islands identified an animal whose brain tissue showed atypical, Nor98‑like scrapie on histopathology and western blot, despite the absence of any prior reports of classical scrapie in the territory. The case was confirmed based on a distinctive low–molecular weight PrPSc band and cerebellar‑predominant lesions, and was reported as the first atypical scrapie case in the Southern Hemisphere. No additional cases or evidence of flock‑level spread were documented in subsequent years, and the event is interpreted as a rare, sporadic occurrence that nevertheless expanded the recognised geographic distribution of atypical scrapie.
Mechanism.or.driver: Internal mechanisms – Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence expressed as atypical/Nor98 scrapie in an otherwise classical‑scrapie‑free sheep population, with epidemiology consistent with a sporadic, poorly transmissible prion disease. Drivers – Deployment of rapid TSE tests and confirmatory methods as part of international surveillance programmes allowed detection and characterization of this single atypical case in a remote sheep‑farming territory.
Review: retain – New event introduced to represent the first reported atypical/Nor98 scrapie case in the Falkland Islands (2005), which was also the earliest Southern Hemisphere report of this strain. Classified as re_emergence (novel strain in a continent where classical scrapie had already been present for decades, e.g. Brazil) rather than inter‑continental emergence, in accordance with the rule that new strains of an existing EPP in a continent should not be coded as inter‑continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia saginata
EPP.common.name: Cysticercus bovis (bovine cysticercosis)
Host: Cattle (Bos indicus and cross-bred beef and dairy cattle)
Event.summary: From 2005 to about 2016, abattoir-based surveys collated by Hiko & Seifu and later meta-analyses showed bovine cysticercosis to be widely endemic across Ethiopia, with meat-inspection prevalences ranging from roughly 1.9% in Addis Ababa to around 26% in Hawassa and consistent detection in many other slaughterhouses. Published economic assessments from five local studies together reported direct losses of about 4.05 million Ethiopian Birr (≈US$0.21 million) from carcass downgrading, condemnation and human taeniasis treatment, while the authors stressed that these figures substantially underestimate the true national burden. No clear decline was evident by the mid‑2010s, and repeated identification of spatial ‘hotspots’ around urban centres and irrigated areas led to calls for improved sanitation, strengthened meat inspection and integrated human–animal control to curb ongoing losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid urbanisation around abattoirs, widespread open defecation and poor sanitation in rural and peri‑urban communities, free‑grazing systems where cattle access surface water and fields contaminated with human faeces, and limited sensitivity of routine meat inspection all contributed to persistent environmental contamination with T. saginata eggs and infection of grazing cattle. Internal mechanisms: there is no evidence for novel parasite strains or drug resistance; persistence is best explained by entrenched human–cattle transmission cycles and geographic clustering of high‑risk production and sanitation settings (endemic re-occurrence rather than biological re-emergence).
Review: review – Event is clearly real and high impact: Hiko & Seifu (2019) and the Ethiopian meta-analyses document nationwide prevalences from ~1.9% in Addis Ababa up to ~26% in Hawassa and substantial but under-recorded economic losses. I revised the event summary to match the published cumulative loss estimate of ≈4.05 million ETB (~US$0.21M) from five reports instead of the original claim of “several million US dollars nationally”, and aligned the prevalence range to 1.9–26.3%. Time window (2005–2016), country (Ethiopia) and classification as re-occurrence remain appropriate but should be checked against any newer national syntheses.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia saginata
EPP.common.name: Cysticercus bovis (bovine cysticercosis)
Host: Cattle in Belgium (national beef and dairy herds)
Event.summary: Across roughly 1990–2015, bovine cysticercosis remained endemic in Belgian cattle, with abattoir data feeding into national economic modelling that estimated average annual costs of T. saginata bovine cysticercosis and associated taeniosis at around €4.25 million. During these years, the largest share of total economic loss fell on cattle owners, who faced about €3.4 million per year in value losses and insurance costs linked to carcass freezing, downgrading and occasional destruction, while slaughterhouses and the public health sector bore additional inspection and treatment expenses. This sustained financial burden demonstrates chronic re-occurrence rather than a discrete outbreak, but represents one of the best-quantified high‑impact episodes of T. saginata in European livestock.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Longstanding but low‑level human taeniasis, historical patterns of wastewater and manure use near cattle farms, dense cattle populations and continuous trade within Belgium and neighbouring countries maintained T. saginata transmission despite modern meat inspection; economic incentives and the availability of insurance often favoured post‑slaughter management (freezing, deboning) over costly upstream investments in sanitation or behavioural change. Internal mechanisms: no evidence exists for new parasite variants; the burden stems from detecting an old parasite under stringent food-safety and trade regulations, making this a classic re-occurrence driven by regulatory context and residual environmental contamination.
Review: retain – Jansen et al. (2018) provide robust national estimates of annual costs (≈€4.25M total, ≈€3.41M borne by animal owners) and show that bovine cysticercosis remained endemic over many years; the broader European review supports the interpretation as a long-term economic hotspot rather than new emergence. Country, subregion and time span (~1990–2015) are consistent with the underlying datasets and the classification as re-occurrence only is appropriate. No changes made.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia saginata
EPP.common.name: Cysticercus bovis (bovine cysticercosis)
Host: Feedlot and slaughter cattle in commercial South African beef feedlot systems
Event.summary: In the early to mid‑1990s, bovine cysticercosis was reported as the leading health problem in South African feedlot cattle, with meat-inspection data indicating prevalences high enough to make cysticercosis the dominant cause of carcass downgrading and freezing in some intensive systems. Based on these data, Giesecke (1997, cited in later work) estimated that annual losses to the South African feedlot industry alone were on the order of US$3.3 million due to condemnation, refrigeration and reduced carcass value. Although the infection had been present for decades, recognition of its major economic impact in this period prompted investigations into feedlot-specific risk factors and contributed to subsequent risk‑based control efforts, even though endemic transmission persisted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Highly concentrated commercial feedlot operations drawing cattle from diverse sources, combined with contamination of feed and water by human faeces (including sewage overflows and informal settlements near grazing areas), created conditions for ‘cysticercosis storms’ when batches of animals were exposed to heavy T. saginata egg contamination. Inadequate wastewater treatment and occasional use of sewage-irrigated pastures were highlighted as important risk factors. Internal mechanisms: there is no indication of parasite genetic change; the outbreaks and sustained losses reflect intense, human‑driven exposure in feedlots within an already endemic national setting, making this a re-occurrence driven by management and sanitation rather than re-emergence.
Review: review – New event added. The estimate that cysticercosis was the “top health problem” in South African feedlots with annual losses of about US$3.3M for the feedlot industry comes from Giesecke (1997), as cited in Phiri et al. (2002) and later South African feedlot risk-factor work. The temporal window (1990–1997) is approximate and intended to capture the mid‑1990s situation leading up to that estimate; it should be refined if more detailed national time-series become available. Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate, as T. saginata was long-established and the high losses clearly reflect external drivers (sewage-contaminated feed/water, intensive feedlot management), not parasite change.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia saginata
EPP.common.name: Cysticercus bovis (bovine cysticercosis)
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1999]
Host: Cattle in the United Kingdom (primarily beef and cull dairy cattle in England and Wales)
Event.summary: Around 1999, a European review drawing on UK industry data estimated that bovine cysticercosis in the United Kingdom caused losses of roughly £100 per infected carcass and about £4.0 million per year in total when condemnation, downgrading, refrigeration, handling and transport were taken into account. Although meat-inspection prevalences were low, the size and value of the national cattle herd meant that even sporadic infections translated into substantial economic costs. Subsequent UK work focused on farm-level risk factors and cattle movement networks, and while prevalence has since remained low, bovine cysticercosis continues to recur sporadically, prompting interest in risk-based meat inspection rather than reflecting any true emergence into new regions or hosts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Identified UK risk factors include cattle grazing or accessing surface water contaminated with human effluent, use of sewage sludge on farmland, proximity to camping sites and other areas with uncontrolled defecation, and complex movement of cattle through markets and finishing units, which can spread infection from a small number of heavily contaminated source farms. Internal mechanisms: studies have not demonstrated new T. saginata variants; the 1999 cost estimate reflects long‑standing endemic infection recognised under stringent meat-inspection and food-safety requirements, so this episode is best classified as re-occurrence driven by environmental contamination and animal movements.
Review: review – New event added. Laranjo‑González et al. (2016) report that costs due to bovine cysticercosis in England were estimated at about £100 per carcass and £4.0M annually in 1999, which is comparable in magnitude to the Belgian national burden and clearly among the largest quantified economic impacts globally. I set the event year to 1999 to match that estimate and used later UK case–control work only to characterise risk factors. The country/subregion coding is correct and the event is appropriately treated as a re-occurrence episode in an already endemic system, but UK specialists should confirm whether additional years or regional breakdowns warrant separate entries.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia spp.
EPP.common.name: Cysticercosis
Host: Pigs (porcine cysticercosis – Taenia solium)
Event.summary: In 1997, a large abattoir and field survey in the Eastern and Southern provinces of Zambia examined over a thousand pigs and found very high prevalences of porcine cysticercosis, with around a fifth of slaughtered pigs infected by routine meat inspection and substantial proportions positive on tongue examination. The study showed that T. solium transmission in village pig systems was far more intense than previously documented and ranked among the highest prevalences reported globally at the time. These findings drew attention to porcine cysticercosis as a serious constraint on smallholder pig production and a driver of human neurocysticercosis in the region, stimulating subsequent work on risk factors and control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of smallholder pig production with free-ranging husbandry, minimal use of latrines and frequent open defecation allowing pigs access to human feces, informal slaughter without meat inspection, and low awareness of Taenia solium among farmers and traders. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel parasite genotypes or increased virulence; the very high prevalences reflect amplification of long-standing T. solium transmission under changing husbandry and sanitation conditions, consistent with re-occurrence of an under-recognized endemic infection rather than first emergence.
Review: Review – added as a new event. The 1997 survey in Eastern and Southern provinces of Zambia documented some of the highest reported prevalences of porcine cysticercosis worldwide and large absolute numbers of infected pigs, clearly qualifying it as a major post‑1990 animal Taenia solium event. It is correctly coded as re-occurrence in Eastern Africa: T. solium was already endemic, and the study primarily revealed the scale of an existing problem rather than a new introduction or first/global detection. Geography (Africa/Eastern Africa, Zambia) follows the UNSD-based Country sheet.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia spp.
EPP.common.name: Cysticercosis
Host: Cattle (bovine cysticercosis – Taenia saginata, Cysticercus bovis)
Event.summary: In the late 1990s, a sero-epidemiological study was conducted in adult cattle in Zambia to clarify the status of Taenia saginata cysticercosis, using an antigen-detection ELISA to overcome the low sensitivity of routine meat inspection. The survey revealed a seroprevalence of several percent, with higher infection rates in feedlots and traditional management systems than in dairy farms, indicating that bovine cysticercosis was more widespread than suggested by abattoir records alone. These findings increased awareness among veterinary authorities, highlighted the role of close human–cattle contact and casual labour on farms in sustaining transmission, and informed recommendations on improving meat inspection and sanitation, although endemic transmission in rural areas has likely persisted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional and feedlot cattle husbandry overlapping with areas of poor human sanitation, the presence of untreated human T. saginata carriers, and limited diagnostic capacity, which had led to under-recognition of infections by meat inspection alone. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was identified; the key change was the application of more sensitive serological surveillance to quantify an existing endemic infection, so the event is interpreted as re-occurrence and improved detection rather than first detection in cattle.
Review: Review – keep but corrected the event-type classification. The referenced study is a cross-sectional sero-survey that quantified endemic Taenia saginata cysticercosis in Zambian cattle; it does not represent the global first detection of bovine cysticercosis in animals, which predates 1990 by many decades. 'first_detection' has therefore been set to 'No' and 're_occurrence' to 'Yes' to reflect renewed recognition of a long‑established infection driven by husbandry and sanitation factors. The event remains useful as an example of substantial endemic burden revealed by improved diagnostics, but the absolute number of infected animals is modest; if the dataset is later pruned to only the ~10 most impactful events, this one is a candidate for exclusion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia spp.
EPP.common.name: Cysticercosis
Host: Cattle (bovine cysticercosis – Taenia saginata, Cysticercus bovis)
Event.summary: In 2000, a detailed abattoir-based survey in Paraná State, southern Brazil, evaluated 26,000+ cattle from 137 municipalities slaughtered in a federally inspected plant (SIF 1710) and documented measurable prevalence of Cysticercus bovis. The survey showed that bovine cysticercosis was widely distributed across the state and remained one of the most frequently detected lesions at post‑mortem inspection, resulting in carcass trimming and condemnations that caused non-trivial financial losses. Follow-up work and control measures focused on improving sanitation, strengthening meat inspection and raising awareness among producers and abattoir workers, reducing apparent prevalence in some municipalities but not eliminating the parasite.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive cattle production in areas with suboptimal human sanitation and occasional free defecation leading to pasture contamination with T. saginata eggs; movement of cattle from high-risk areas to slaughter without pre-slaughter control; and limited sensitivity of routine meat inspection, which underestimates light infections and allowed sustained transmission. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a new strain or altered pathogenicity; the event reflects persistence and geographic expansion of cattle production into areas with poor sanitation and thus re-occurrence of a long-established parasite.
Review: Review – retain. The 2000 SIF 1710 survey in Paraná is correctly geo-referenced (South America/South America, Brazil) and appropriately coded as re-occurrence of endemic bovine cysticercosis, not first detection. It documents widespread infection and associated condemnations in a major beef-producing state and serves as an early abattoir-based benchmark. Later statewide studies (e.g. 2004–2008 in Paraná, 2009–2012 in Espírito Santo) show even greater aggregate losses; one of these (Espírito Santo 2009–2012) has been added as a new event. Depending on how strictly the final dataset is limited to the single largest episodes, this 2000 episode can be kept as important context or deprioritized.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia spp.
EPP.common.name: Cysticercosis
Host: Pigs (porcine cysticercosis – mainly Taenia solium, with possible contribution from other Taenia spp.)
Event.summary: By the early 2000s, fragmented data suggested that porcine cysticercosis persisted in parts of Eastern Europe despite prior control efforts. In 2003, official veterinary reports from Poland recorded 4,487 porcine cysticercosis cases detected at slaughter, representing an unusually high burden for the region. Subsequent years showed a decline in reported numbers, interpreted as the combined result of improved meat inspection and control measures, changes in pig production systems and possibly underreporting, while low-level transmission likely continued in backyard and smallholder herds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistence of backyard and smallholder pig production with poor sanitation and lack of controlled housing, allowing pigs access to human feces; incomplete surveillance and inconsistencies in meat inspection and reporting in earlier years that had masked the scale of endemic infection. Internal mechanisms: No specific evidence of a novel T. solium genotype or altered virulence; the event is best interpreted as re-occurrence or renewed recognition of a large endemic focus rather than evolutionary change in the parasite.
Review: Review – retain. The 2003 Polish episode is supported by official veterinary notification data collated in a systematic review and represents an exceptionally large number of porcine cysticercosis cases for Europe. It is correctly coded as re-occurrence in an already endemic country (Europe/Eastern Europe, Poland), without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, and the chosen source (systematic review of taeniosis/cysticercosis in Eastern Europe) is appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia spp.
EPP.common.name: Cysticercosis
Host: Cattle (bovine cysticercosis – Taenia saginata, Cysticercus bovis)
Event.summary: Between 2009 and 2012, analysis of records from federal and state‑inspected slaughterhouses in Espírito Santo State, Brazil, showed that bovine cysticercosis remained a significant sanitary and economic problem. Out of roughly 1.34 million cattle slaughtered in the period, just under 1% were condemned or partially condemned for Cysticercus bovis, resulting in more than 1.5 million kilograms of beef being rejected and direct financial losses on the order of 9 million Brazilian reais. The burden was greater during the rainy season and concentrated in particular municipalities, prompting subsequent spatial risk-mapping work and reinforcing the need for improved sanitation and control of human taeniasis to safeguard the beef industry.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High cattle densities in municipalities with inadequate household sewage coverage, reliance on surface water and flood‑prone pastures contaminated by human feces from untreated T. saginata carriers, and incomplete control of human tapeworm infection and rural sanitation. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel T. saginata lineages or altered pathogenicity; the event reflects re-occurrence and spatial clustering of a long‑established parasite under favourable environmental and sanitation conditions, rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Review – added as a new event. The 2009–2012 slaughterhouse analysis from Espírito Santo documented very large absolute economic losses from bovine cysticercosis (over 1.5 million kg of beef condemned and about 9 million BRL in direct losses) and directly informed spatial risk-mapping and control planning for the state. It is correctly geo-coded (South America/South America, Brazil) and classified as re-occurrence in a country where bovine cysticercosis has long been endemic, with no evidence of new strains or inter‑continental spread.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia spp.
EPP.common.name: Cysticercosis
Host: Pigs (porcine cysticercosis – Taenia solium)
Event.summary: Using epidemiological and economic data from across the United Republic of Tanzania, a national burden-of-disease assessment estimated the societal cost of Taenia solium taeniasis/cysticercosis for the year 2012. Modelling suggested that roughly 12% of the national pig population—on the order of 180,000 animals—were infected with porcine cysticercosis, leading to potential production losses of around US$2.8 million in that year, alongside a much larger human health burden from neurocysticercosis-associated epilepsy. The study’s findings highlighted T. solium as a major public health and agricultural problem and spurred calls for a national One Health control strategy integrating human, pig and environmental interventions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of smallholder pig production with predominantly free-ranging husbandry, low latrine coverage and open defecation allowing pigs access to human feces, backyard slaughter and informal pork markets with little veterinary inspection, and limited access to anthelmintic treatment for both humans and pigs. Internal mechanisms: No specific new parasite genotypes or heightened virulence were identified; the high burden is attributed to social, economic and husbandry factors, so the event is best interpreted as re-occurrence of a long‑established infection rather than true re‑emergence.
Review: Review – added as a new event. The 2012 national assessment for Tanzania estimated that porcine cysticercosis affected on the order of 180,000 pigs (about 11–12% of the herd) and caused pig production losses of approximately US$2.8 million in a single year, making it one of the largest well-quantified animal-sector Taenia solium events globally in the post‑1990 period. It is correctly coded as re-occurrence in an already endemic country (Africa/Eastern Africa, United Republic of Tanzania) with no evidence for new parasite strains or new continental spread.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taenia spp.
EPP.common.name: Cysticercosis
Host: Pigs (porcine cysticercosis – Taenia solium)
Event.summary: A national economic evaluation for Mexico using 2015 data estimated the monetary burden of Taenia solium cysticercosis by combining epidemiologic information with cost data for both human disease and animal production. The study concluded that cysticercosis imposed overall societal costs exceeding US$200 million annually, of which roughly US$19.5 million were attributable to porcine cysticercosis through carcass condemnation and price reductions for infected pigs. These findings underscored that, despite long-standing awareness and partial control, porcine cysticercosis continues to generate major economic losses for the Mexican pig industry and provided quantitative justification for renewed investment in integrated control strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistence of traditional pig-rearing systems in many rural regions with free-ranging or backyard pigs, inadequate sanitation and sewage infrastructure, incomplete coverage and enforcement of meat inspection (particularly in informal slaughter), and ongoing human taeniasis maintaining environmental contamination with T. solium eggs. Internal mechanisms: The study did not implicate any novel parasite variants; the large losses reflect the scale of endemic transmission and its economic impact rather than evolutionary change, so the event is classified as re-occurrence in a long‑affected country.
Review: Review – added as a new event because the 2015 national cost-of-illness study for Mexico quantified very large annual losses due to porcine cysticercosis (around US$19.5 million), in addition to substantial human health costs, making it one of the highest documented animal-sector burdens for Taenia solium worldwide. Coded as re-occurrence in an already highly endemic country (South America/Central America, Mexico) with no evidence of new parasite strains or spread to a new continent. Geography follows the UNSD-based Country sheet, where Mexico is grouped under the South America continent and Central America sub-region.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taylorella equigenitalis
EPP.common.name: CEM organism
Host: Horses (mares on affected studs)
Event.summary: In 2001, Türkiye reported its first confirmed occurrence of contagious equine metritis when Taylorella equigenitalis was isolated from infertile or endometritic mares during routine screening and outbreak investigation, representing the first recognised presence of CEM in the country within the Asian continent. The outbreak appeared to be confined to one or a few studs, with infection detected by culture from genital swabs and managed through treatment of positive mares and movement controls on breeding animals. Follow‑up testing did not reveal widespread dissemination, and available reports suggest the episode was limited in scale compared with large outbreaks elsewhere.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of a carrier breeding animal through international horse trade from CEM‑affected European countries into Turkish studs, combined with limited pre‑import or pre‑breeding screening at the time, facilitated the first recognised establishment of Taylorella equigenitalis in Türkiye. Internal mechanisms: Venereal transmission during natural service and the ability of T. equigenitalis to persist in the genital tract of infected mares and stallions without obvious clinical signs underpinned local spread, but no novel strain, host shift or resistance pattern was reported for this event.
Review: review – Event is real and should be retained as one of the major post‑1990 occurrences because it documents the first confirmed detection of CEM in Türkiye and Western Asia. However, according to the event‑type definitions, 'first_detection' refers to the first detection in the host system globally (which occurred in the UK in 1977), not the first detection in an individual country. I therefore changed first_detection from true to false and left intra_continental_emergence as true to reflect spread of an already known pathogen into a new Asian sub‑region. I also replaced generic review‑style URLs with the specific Vet Record case report (Ozgur et al. 2001) and a molecular epidemiology review that explicitly cites this first Turkish isolation as the main sources for this event.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taylorella equigenitalis
EPP.common.name: CEM organism
Host: Horses (Lipizzaner stallions; limited exposed mares)
Event.summary: In 2006, contagious equine metritis was re‑introduced into the United States when several imported Lipizzaner stallions housed at a breeding and research facility in Wisconsin were found culture‑positive for Taylorella equigenitalis during breeding soundness examinations and follow‑up testing. Trace‑back investigations showed that infection was confined to a small number of imported stallions and a limited group of mares, with no evidence of wider spread into the domestic Thoroughbred or Quarter Horse sectors. Federal and state authorities implemented quarantine, testing and treatment of all infected and exposed horses, and the outbreak was declared eradicated, allowing the United States to regain CEM‑free status prior to the larger 2008–2010 incident.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International movement of high‑value breeding horses from endemic European regions, combined with imperfect pre‑export and post‑import testing protocols, allowed carrier Lipizzaner stallions to enter the United States and introduce T. equigenitalis into a previously CEM‑free population. Internal mechanisms: Chronic, asymptomatic colonisation of stallions and efficient venereal transmission to mares enabled silent carriage and limited spread before detection, but there is no evidence that this event involved a novel, more virulent or resistant strain compared with other European isolates.
Review: retain – The 2006 Lipizzaner‑associated incident in Wisconsin is well documented in U.S. reviews and technical factsheets and represents an important re‑introduction of CEM prior to the major 2008–2010 outbreak. Event year, country (United States), and classification as a re‑occurrence following earlier eradication are consistent with WOAH notifications and U.S. summaries. No corrections were needed beyond tightening sources to focus on the JAS review, CFSPH disease card and a 2006 foreign‑animal‑disease bulletin that describe this specific episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Taylorella equigenitalis
EPP.common.name: CEM organism
Host: Horses (stallions and mares in Lipizzaner and sport‑horse populations)
Event.summary: In May 2011, South Africa, previously considered free of contagious equine metritis, reported its first confirmed cases of Taylorella equigenitalis infection to the World Organisation for Animal Health after detection of CEM in stallions at an artificial breeding centre in Gauteng, with epidemiological evidence pointing to introduction via Lipizzaner or Warmblood stallions imported from Europe in the late 1990s. National stallion‑screening and extensive tracing during 2011–2012 identified at least 43 PCR‑ or culture‑positive horses on the index premises and 12 additional properties across three provinces, revealing that T. equigenitalis had silently persisted for years within a closed Lipizzaner population before being disseminated more widely through assisted reproduction and fomites. All infected and exposed horses were quarantined, treated according to WOAH‑aligned protocols and repeatedly re‑tested, and, with industry cooperation, the outbreak was brought under control, although South Africa continues to treat CEM as a controlled disease with ongoing surveillance and import screening.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing importation of Lipizzaner and Warmblood stallions from endemic European regions, combined with limited early surveillance and later adoption of artificial insemination and other assisted reproductive techniques, allowed Taylorella equigenitalis to establish a hidden reservoir in a closed Lipizzaner population and then spread horizontally via contaminated breeding equipment and management practices. Internal mechanisms: Persistent, asymptomatic carriage in stallions and some mares, efficient venereal and fomite transmission, and the ability of particular clonal lineages to circulate for many years without obvious clinical signs underpinned the scale of the South African outbreak, but available molecular typing suggests introduction of existing European genotypes rather than in situ evolution of a novel, more virulent strain.
Review: review – This multi‑premises South African outbreak was missing from the original dataset but clearly qualifies as one of the most impactful post‑1990 CEM events: it represents the first confirmed occurrence of Taylorella equigenitalis in Africa, involved dozens of infected horses across multiple provinces and is repeatedly highlighted in major reviews as a paradigm‑changing episode linked to artificial reproduction. ([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2b4d/7af2faff9c4f908cb8ecc65766072cabd87e.pdf)) At the peak of the epidemic, at least 15 outbreaks in Havana Province alone involved about 23,201 sick pigs, 10,547 deaths and 5,256 culls, after which herd immunity and control measures allowed mortality to subside and TGEV to transition toward lower‑level endemic circulation with sporadic cases reported up to at least 2008. ([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2b4d/7af2faff9c4f908cb8ecc65766072cabd87e.pdf))

Strong evidence from Cuban case reports and molecular analyses shows a large virgin‑soil TGE epidemic beginning in 2003 with >23,000 cases and >10,000 deaths in Havana Province alone; this clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 TGEV events and represents an intra‑continental emergence into the previously TGE‑free Caribbean sub‑region of the South America continent grouping. ([repozytorium.piwet.pulawy.pl](https://repozytorium.piwet.pulawy.pl/bitstream/handle/123456789/724/s12917-024-04364-6.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=2))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers (external): The Argentine episode appears to reflect introduction of TGEV into previously naïve or minimally exposed commercial herds, probably via movement of infected pigs, semen or contaminated transport and equipment from TGEV‑endemic regions, coupled with intensive, high‑density farrow‑to‑finish production and limited awareness and diagnostic capacity for swine coronaviruses in Argentina, which allowed several years of unrecognized circulation before formal notification. ([sedici.unlp.edu.ar](https://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/handle/10915/123763)) Internal mechanisms: Histopathology and limited molecular data indicate a disease pattern consistent with classical enteric TGEV rather than a distinct new genotype, suggesting that the high impact arose from geographic range expansion of a typical, highly virulent TGEV strain into an immunologically naïve pig population, with severe disease concentrated in very young piglets lacking maternal antibodies. ([sedici.unlp.edu.ar](https://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/handle/10915/123763))
Review: review – Event retained but corrected. (1) Adjusted the event time span from 2011–2015 to 2010–2015 and the country tag from “Argentina [2011]” to “Argentina [2010]” to match the Argentine case‑series, which identified three TGEV‑confirmed outbreaks between 2010 and 2015. ([sedici.unlp.edu.ar](https://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/handle/10915/123763)) (2) Set the ‘first_detection’ flag to false because this category refers to the first detection of the pathogen in the host system globally; TGEV was first detected in pigs in the USA in 1946, so Argentine outbreaks represent national‑level and intra‑continental emergence within South America, not global first detection. ([anipedia.up.ac.za](https://anipedia.up.ac.za/publications/transmissible-gastroenteritis/1017.html?utm_source=openai)) (3) Slightly revised the event summary and mechanism to avoid over‑specific, weakly supported details (for example, specific mention of replacement gilt movements) while keeping the core interpretation that this was a major intra‑continental emergence into the South America sub‑region.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Transmissible gastroenteritis virus
EPP.common.name: TGEV, Porcine transmissible gastroenteritis coronavirus
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), including sows and suckling and recently weaned piglets on small farrow‑to‑finish farms on Tahiti Island
Event.summary: In August 2011, two commercial pig farms in Teva I Uta commune on Tahiti Island, French Polynesia, experienced explosive outbreaks of diarrhea and vomiting in sows and piglets, with reported mortality of 100% in non‑weaned piglets and about 50–76% in weaned piglets, resulting in 738 cases and 547 deaths among roughly 2,975 susceptible pigs across the two herds. ([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/wahis/reports/en_imm_0000011107_20111004_104118.pdf)) Differential diagnosis and serology performed in France confirmed infection with transmissible gastroenteritis virus (TGEV) using a differential TGEV/PRCV ELISA, and the territory submitted an immediate WOAH notification classifying the event as the first occurrence of TGE, indicating introduction into a previously TGE‑free island population in Oceania. ([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/wahis/reports/en_imm_0000011107_20111004_104118.pdf)) The outbreaks burned out over time without vaccination, with mortality spontaneously ceasing after affected piglets died and biosecurity measures were reinforced, and no subsequent large‑scale TGE epidemics in French Polynesia have been widely reported.
