([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/wahis/reports/en_imm_0000011107_20111004_104118.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers (external): WOAH’s epidemiologic investigation noted no live‑pig imports in 2011 and identified swill feeding of untreated restaurant waste by an itinerant butcher as the most plausible source of TGEV introduction, implying long‑distance movement of virus in contaminated pork products to a naïve pig population; high pig density within affected farms and absence of prior immunity in French Polynesia then permitted rapid within‑herd transmission and extreme piglet mortality. ([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/wahis/reports/en_imm_0000011107_20111004_104118.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Available information does not indicate unusual genetic changes in the virus; clinical pattern and severity are consistent with classical enteric TGEV infection in immunologically naïve herds, so this event is best interpreted as inter‑continental geographic range expansion of a typical TGEV strain into Oceania rather than emergence of a novel variant. ([web.oie.int](https://web.oie.int/wahis/reports/en_imm_0000011107_20111004_104118.pdf))
Review: review – New event added. WOAH’s immediate notification for French Polynesia in 2011 documents two severe on‑farm TGE outbreaks and explicitly labels them as the first occurrence of this listed disease in the territory; given the absence of prior records of TGE in Oceania, this episode is appropriately classified here as an inter‑continental emergence of TGEV into Polynesia rather than as a re‑occurrence linked to earlier continental epidemics.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis
Host: Horses (Equus caballus); domestic pigs (background endemicity)
Event.summary: In 1993, Trichinella infection was documented for the first time in horses slaughtered in Romania, against a backdrop of well-established Trichinella circulation in domestic pigs and humans. Although no linked human cases were identified from these specific horses, the finding showed that horses in Romania could enter the domestic cycle and potentially act as sources of large epidemics, as had occurred in Italy and France. The detection led Romanian and EU authorities to include horses in Trichinella surveillance and meat inspection schemes, alongside pigs and game.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The post-communist expansion of informal meat production and trade, including horse slaughter, in a context of high Trichinella prevalence in pigs and wildlife increased opportunities for spillover into horses. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of existing Trichinella lineages (mainly T. spiralis) into horses in the domestic cycle; no novel species were implicated, but the event underscored the capacity of horses to serve as food-borne sources of infection.
Review: Decision: review. The event description and classification as re-emergence (host expansion to horses) are broadly accurate and supported by Romanian reviews, but only a small number of horses were infected and no human cases were linked, so the direct impact is modest. Given numerous much larger outbreaks (Romania-wide pig epidemics, Chinese and Argentine pork outbreaks, major horse-meat epidemics, the 2003–2004 Izmir outbreak), this 1993 detection is unlikely to rank among the ten most impactful global emergence events; retain for now as a species–host milestone but consider excluding if the dataset is trimmed strictly to the top ten.
Review.Comment: unlikely to rank among the ten most impactful global emergence events;

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas foetus
EPP.common.name: Bovine trichomoniasis, Tritrichomonas foetus
Host: Beef and mixed‑purpose cattle herds, breeding bulls and cows under natural service
Event.summary: In 1992, pilot and cross‑sectional studies in the two main livestock‑rearing areas of northeastern Costa Rica used the InPouch TF system to detect Tritrichomonas foetus infection in bulls, finding farm‑level prevalences up to around 15–18% and bull‑level prevalences of about 4–7%, and demonstrating that bovine trichomoniasis was common in local cattle herds. The work identified risk factors such as Bos taurus breed and bull age over 4 years and linked infection to management practices based on untested natural‑service bulls, indicating potential for significant reproductive and economic losses in the national herd. Although no discrete epidemic wave was reported, these studies represented the first detailed, country‑level quantification of bovine trichomoniasis in Costa Rica and catalysed recognition of the disease as an important endemic reproductive problem in Central American beef systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: reliance on natural mating in many herds, limited veterinary reproductive monitoring, and movement or sharing of untested bulls between farms facilitated endemic circulation; low prior awareness and lack of systematic bull testing allowed infection to accumulate before detection. Internal mechanisms: no evidence for genotype change; disease patterns were consistent with canonical bovine T. foetus biology, with chronic asymptomatic carriage in bulls and transient but fertility‑reducing infection in cows leading to early embryonic loss and extended calving intervals.
Review: Review – The 1992 Costa Rica work clearly documents significant endemic infection and economic impact but global first emergence of T. foetus in cattle occurred decades earlier in Europe and other regions; the original classification as “first_detection = Yes” has therefore been changed to No, and no intra‑/inter‑continental emergence flag is applied because earlier circulation in the Americas is well documented though not previously quantified in Costa Rica, so this event is best treated as the first detailed national prevalence study rather than discovery of the parasite in the host system.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0167587792900136?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas gallinae
EPP.common.name: Trichomonosis
Host: Pink pigeon (Nesoenas/Columba mayeri) – an endangered endemic columbid on Mauritius; other sympatric columbids (e.g. spotted dove, Madagascar turtle-dove) as reservoirs.
Event.summary: By the early 1990s, trichomonosis caused by Trichomonas gallinae had become established in captive and wild pink pigeons on Mauritius, likely introduced earlier with non-native pigeons and doves, and was increasingly recognised as a major conservation threat to this critically endangered species. Between about 2002 and 2006, necropsy and epidemiological studies showed that trichomonad infections were a leading cause of post‑fledging mortality, with very high prevalence and frequent fatal ingluvitis in chicks, constraining population recovery despite intensive management interventions. Following these findings, conservation programs implemented improved surveillance, targeted treatment, and management of reservoir columbids, which reduced but did not eliminate trichomonosis as an ongoing constraint on pink pigeon recovery.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Historic introduction and persistence of non-native pigeons/doves on Mauritius provided a chronic reservoir for T. gallinae; small, inbred pink pigeon populations with limited genetic diversity were highly susceptible; supplemental feeding, captive-breeding and release practices brought birds into close contact, enhancing transmission. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – parasite spilled over from introduced columbids into a naive endemic columbid; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – infection caused high nestling and juvenile mortality, with trichomonosis the dominant cause of death in some cohorts; Novel Strain/Genotype Presence – molecular work identified multiple lineages in Mauritian columbids, with some associated with severe disease, indicating circulation of particularly pathogenic variants.
Review: Decision: Retain. This is a well-documented, high‑impact conservation event for an endangered endemic columbid on Mauritius, supported by primary studies showing very high T. gallinae prevalence and substantial chick mortality in 2002–2006.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17699078/?utm_source=openai)) The 1992 start year reflects early recognition of trichomonosis in the population and is somewhat approximate but still within the correct decade of establishment; main impact years (2002–2006) are captured in the summary. Emergence type as re-emergence (long‑present parasite spilling over into a new, highly vulnerable host within the same subregion) is appropriate, with no evidence to justify first/global or intra-/inter‑continental emergence labels.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas gallinae
EPP.common.name: Trichomonosis
Host: Purple finch (Haemorhous purpureus), American goldfinch (Spinus tristis), and occasionally other finches (e.g. pine siskin), with T. gallinae also present in sympatric rock pigeons (Columba livia).
Event.summary: Beginning in 2007, widespread mortalities of purple finches and American goldfinches were reported at garden feeders in the Canadian Maritime provinces, and necropsies identified trichomonosis due to Trichomonas gallinae as the primary cause of death. Over the period 2007–2011, at least 18 sites across the region experienced trichomonosis-related mortality events in passerines, and molecular work showed that many isolates belonged to the same finch epidemic strain (subtype A1) responsible for the British greenfinch declines, alongside additional local strains. After initial emergence, trichomonosis became an established, recurrent cause of mortality in Maritime finch populations, raising concerns about long-term welfare and potential population impacts despite more limited documented declines than in Britain.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density congregation of finches at backyard feeders and birdbaths facilitated oral transmission via contaminated seed and water; cool, moist late-summer and autumn conditions favoured parasite survival; proximity to urban pigeons provided a reservoir. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – T. gallinae, historically associated with columbids, caused severe disease and death in wild finches; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – molecular characterisation revealed presence of the European finch epidemic strain A1 in Maritime finches and rock pigeons, along with additional genotypes, indicating introduction and local diversification; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – a high proportion of dead finches at feeders showed severe upper alimentary tract lesions consistent with rapidly fatal trichomonosis.
Review: Decision: Retain (newly added event). The original LLM output merged Canadian Maritime finch emergence with the western U.S. passerine episode, but available data show that Maritime outbreaks from 2007 onward constitute a distinct, well-documented emergence with repeated multi-site mortality events and clear molecular evidence of the European finch epidemic strain A1.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2839828/?utm_source=openai)) Separating this into its own row avoids over-aggregation of epidemiologically unlinked episodes and aligns better with the project rule that linked episodes should be merged only when occurring in the same outbreak area or clearly connected neighbouring countries.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas gallinae
EPP.common.name: Trichomonosis
Host: Pacific Coast band-tailed pigeon (Patagioenas fasciata monilis); with secondary spillover documented in predators such as spotted owls during mortality events.
Event.summary: In winter 2014–2015, Pacific Coast band-tailed pigeons in California experienced the most widespread and longest-duration avian trichomonosis epidemic ever recorded for this species, with mortality events (≥5 birds) reported from 25 counties and total deaths estimated to exceed 18,000 birds. The outbreak began in November 2014, coinciding with severe multi-year drought and unusually warm conditions that concentrated pigeons at a limited number of water sources, and continued through June 2015, with heavy adult mortality documented in both wintering and breeding areas. This epidemic followed earlier but smaller trichomonosis outbreaks in band-tailed pigeons and, together with hunting mortality, has been implicated as a major factor constraining recovery of an already declining upland game bird population.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Exceptional drought and elevated winter and spring temperatures in California reduced surface water availability and concentrated band-tailed pigeons at remaining water sources, greatly increasing contact rates and environmental contamination; high acorn production in preceding years influenced winter aggregation patterns; continued legal harvest added to disease-related mortality in a declining population. Internal mechanisms: Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – T. gallinae subtype A2 was the predominant parasite and, together with the newly described species Trichomonas stableri, produced severe necrotic upper digestive tract lesions and high case fatality; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – trichomonosis epidemics occurred across much of the Pacific Coast band-tailed pigeon range in California; Dual-pathogen Dynamics – co-circulation of T. gallinae and T. stableri complicated the aetiology but both are highly pathogenic trichomonads contributing to the same disease syndrome.
Review: Decision: Retain (newly added event). Large-scale, drought-associated trichomonosis epidemics in Pacific Coast band-tailed pigeons are among the highest-mortality T. gallinae events documented since 1990, with the 2014–2015 epidemic alone estimated to have killed over 18,000 birds across 25 counties and clearly linked to population-level impacts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6068076/?utm_source=openai)) This event was missing from the original LLM output and is added here as a major re-occurrence (not first emergence) in a region where T. gallinae epizootics have recurred for decades; classification as re_occurrence rather than re_emergence is appropriate because the primary drivers are environmental aggregation and drought rather than documented appearance of a new T. gallinae genotype within this host system.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas gallinae
EPP.common.name: Trichomonosis
Host: European greenfinch (Chloris chloris) and European goldfinch (Carduelis carduelis) in wintering flocks; likely spillover from or co-circulation with infected columbids.
Event.summary: In winter 2016–2017, a major outbreak of finch trichomonosis was documented in European greenfinches and goldfinches wintering in the Boulonnais region of northern France, with large numbers of sick and dead birds observed at feeding sites and in nearby habitats. Necropsy and molecular analyses confirmed T. gallinae infection consistent with the finch epidemic lineage, and concurrent mortality in Brittany and other areas indicated that the epidemic extended across a broad area of western France. The outbreak subsided after winter, but highlighted that the finch epidemic strain had spread from earlier foci in the British Isles and Fennoscandia into western continental Europe, potentially contributing to local declines of affected finch populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Winter feeding stations in northern France concentrated mixed-species finch flocks, enabling efficient oral transmission; climatic conditions and high winter bird densities favoured sustained local circulation; long-distance migrants likely introduced the strain from previously affected regions. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – the same highly transmissible finch epidemic lineage appears to have driven mortality in continental finches; Host Expansion (Spillover) – notable involvement of European goldfinch, broadening the susceptible passerine host range; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the epidemic lineage continued its spread into new western European wintering areas.
Review: Decision: Review. The French 2016–2017 outbreak is a genuine high-impact episode with substantial winter mortality in greenfinches and goldfinches and clear molecular confirmation of the finch epidemic lineage.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6452646/?utm_source=openai)) The original classification as both intra‑continental emergence and re-emergence is inconsistent with project rules, because T. gallinae was long established in western European columbids and this episode reflects spread of a known lineage and host expansion within an already affected continent; intra_continental_emergence has therefore been set to false, with re-emergence retained as the primary event type.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma equiperdum
EPP.common.name: Dourine
Host: Horses (primary clinical cases), with donkeys and mules considered resistant carriers in rural equid populations
Event.summary: From around 2000, routine dourine surveillance and clinical reporting in South Africa began documenting renewed widespread infection in equids, reversing earlier expectations that the disease was disappearing from the country. Between 2000 and 2010, national records compiled for the OIE NTTAT network indicate roughly 900 confirmed dourine cases—over 700 in the Eastern Cape alone—with further confirmed complement‑fixation–positive cases recorded in multiple provinces. Over the subsequent years to about 2015, at least 100 additional seropositive horses were detected country‑wide, after which annual case numbers declined but sporadic positives continued to occur under ongoing targeted surveillance, so dourine remains an endemic controlled disease rather than eradicated.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive use of natural breeding in rural and communal horse populations, movement of breeding stallions between provinces, and limited resources for systematic pre‑breeding testing and culling allowed long‑established dourine foci to persist; socio‑economic constraints and the value of horses for transport and livelihood made aggressive stamping‑out difficult outside high‑value studs; surveillance intensity varied over time, contributing to apparent temporal fluctuations in case counts. Internal mechanisms: Available data and the long‑standing presence of the Onderstepoort (OVI) T. equiperdum strain suggest no clearly documented emergence of a novel, more virulent or drug‑resistant lineage during this period; the episode is best interpreted as large‑scale re‑occurrence of endemic dourine driven by management and control factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – New event added to capture a major, well‑documented re‑occurrence of dourine in South Africa, where national reports and NTTAT/WOAH summaries describe approximately 900 confirmed cases from 2000–2010 and about 100 additional cases to 2015, with cases in most provinces. Classified as re‑occurrence in Southern Africa because dourine has been present in this subregion for more than a century and no clear evidence of a novel strain or resistance pattern was found. Time bounds and national case totals should be re‑checked against full WOAH WAHIS series if finer temporal resolution is needed, but the event clearly belongs among the most impactful modern dourine emergence episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma equiperdum
EPP.common.name: Dourine
Host: Horses (primary clinical cases), with donkeys and mules examined for carrier and clinical states
Event.summary: From August 2005 to January 2007, a cross‑sectional field study in the Arsi‑Bale highlands of Ethiopia systematically documented dourine as a major, ongoing health problem of local horses, with disease widely recognized by owners and seasonal peaks during the breeding season. Serological screening of 646 horses showed high seroprevalence (about 19–28% depending on the test used), and characteristic genital and neurologic signs were commonly observed, while donkeys and mules were also examined to identify clinical and carrier infections. The episode reflects intense endemic transmission and substantial productivity and welfare losses in a long‑affected area, with dourine persisting beyond the study period under similar management and limited control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional breeding systems relying on uncontrolled natural mating, communal use of stallions, and absence of systematic pre‑breeding dourine testing maintained a high force of venereal infection; inadequate access to veterinary services and lack of an eradication or movement‑control programme allowed infection to persist at high prevalence; seasonal breeding (June–September) concentrated transmission and clinical case recognition in specific months. Internal mechanisms: No new strain, host expansion or drug resistance was demonstrated; the event is best interpreted as a high‑burden re‑occurrence of long‑established dourine in Ethiopian highland horses rather than an evolutionary shift in T. equiperdum.
Review: retain – Event accurately summarizes the 2005–2007 Arsi‑Bale highlands survey by Hagos et al. and is appropriately classified as re‑occurrence within Eastern Africa, since dourine has been endemic in Ethiopian equids for decades. Country, sub‑region and time span (August 2005–January 2007) are correctly represented, and the selected article is an appropriate primary source; no corrections recommended.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma equiperdum
EPP.common.name: Dourine
Host: Horses (breeding stallions and mares on affected studs)
Event.summary: In May 2011 dourine reappeared in Italy when a Friesian stallion in Sicily tested complement‑fixation–positive during routine stud examinations, leading to the investigation of a clinically affected mare and confirmation of dourine by serology, clinical signs and histopathology. Subsequent tracing and nationwide surveillance from June to December 2011 uncovered several outbreaks in southern Italy and other regions, ultimately identifying around 20 positive horses and demonstrating re‑establishment of infection in a country that had been officially free since the late 1990s. Through 2012, Italian authorities implemented strict movement controls, targeted surveillance and stamping‑out of infected animals; by around 2012 the outbreak was considered resolved and Italy worked toward re‑establishing recognised dourine‑free status.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reintroduction of infection via an imported or previously infected breeding horse, combined with gaps in pre‑import or pre‑breeding dourine testing, allowed the parasite to enter an officially free equine population; intensive natural mating networks among breeding horses facilitated onward sexual transmission before detection, while initial diagnostic limitations delayed confirmation. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterisation of the Italian outbreak strain indicates a T. equiperdum lineage closely related to other Trypanozoon parasites but does not clearly support increased virulence or drug resistance; the episode is best explained by reintroduction of an established parasite into a susceptible horse population rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – Event retained but the time span has been corrected from 2011–2013 to 2011–2012 to better match OIE immediate notifications and EU reference‑laboratory presentations describing a 2011/2012 dourine outbreak in Italy. Classification as re‑occurrence in Southern Europe (infection reappearing in a country previously officially free of dourine) remains appropriate, and no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence flags are warranted because dourine has long been present in Europe. Source list was slightly strengthened by adding the clinical re‑emergence paper while retaining the original outbreak‑diagnosis and case‑report articles.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma equiperdum
EPP.common.name: Dourine
Host: Horses (nationwide horse populations, with first confirmed dourine case in a stallion)
Event.summary: Within a SATREPS‑supported programme running in the mid‑2010s, Mongolia intensified investigation of non‑tsetse‑transmitted horse trypanosomoses, and in 2014 a stallion with genital swelling and neurologic signs was definitively diagnosed with dourine, yielding the first directly confirmed Trypanosoma equiperdum isolate in the country (strain IVM‑t1). Building on this, a nationwide serological survey collected more than 3,600 horse sera across all provinces and found an overall 4–5% seroprevalence for non‑tsetse‑transmitted trypanosomes (surra and dourine combined), with higher prevalence in several central provinces, showing that these infections constitute a widespread endemic problem. By about 2018, Mongolia had mapped the broad distribution of non‑tsetse equine trypanosomosis and confirmed local dourine transmission, but ongoing surveillance was recommended as the disease could not be eliminated and clinical cases continued to appear sporadically.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large free‑ranging horse populations managed under extensive pastoral systems, combined with near‑universal use of natural mating, create favourable conditions for venereal transmission of dourine; historically limited access to specific diagnostics meant dourine likely circulated undetected until targeted projects introduced molecular and serological testing; the strong cultural and economic importance of horses complicates culling‑based eradication. Internal mechanisms: The IVM‑t1 strain shows typical T. equiperdum features, including defective maxicircle kinetoplast DNA, but no clear evidence has been published of novel virulence, expanded host range or drug resistance; the emergence signal largely reflects first confirmed detection and mapping of an existing infection rather than recent evolutionary change.
Review: review – Event retained but the emergence‑type classification has been corrected by setting intra_continental_emergence from true to false, because dourine had already been officially reported in China and other parts of Asia within the same UNSD sub‑region (Eastern Asia), so the first confirmed Mongolian case does not represent spread to a new sub‑region. The first_detection flag is kept to indicate the first confirmed T. equiperdum infection in Mongolian horses, and the summary has been aligned more explicitly with 2014 as the year of the IVM‑t1 case. Countries, continent and sub‑region are correct, and the cited articles and WOAH/NTTAT abstracts are appropriate primary sources for this episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Vairimorpha apis
EPP.common.name: Nosema apis, Nosema ceranae
Host: Apis cerana; Apis mellifera
Event.summary: During the 1990s, a second Nosema species parasitizing the Eastern honey bee Apis cerana was morphologically and molecularly characterized in China and named Nosema ceranae, confirming a long‑overlooked microsporidian distinct from Nosema apis.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0932473996800599?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent work showed that by the late 1990s to early 2000s N. ceranae was already infecting Apis mellifera in Eastern Asia, with PCR and sequencing from Taiwan and mainland China demonstrating that many nosemosis cases previously attributed to N. apis were in fact due to N. ceranae.([apidologie.org](https://www.apidologie.org/articles/apido/pdf/2007/01/m6062.pdf?utm_source=openai)) By around 2004, the parasite had been clearly recognized as a distinct pathogen of A. mellifera in the region, marking a confirmed host expansion from A. cerana to A. mellifera and setting the stage for its subsequent global spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and regional movement of managed honey bee colonies in Eastern Asia; close proximity of Apis cerana and Apis mellifera in shared landscapes and mixed‑species apiaries; limited biosecurity around bee movements and queen trade. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) from Apis cerana to Apis mellifera; enhanced transmission traits facilitating efficient infection and persistence in the new host; inherent capacity for geographic range expansion once established in globally traded A. mellifera stocks.
Review: review – Event correctly describes the description of Nosema (Vairimorpha) ceranae from Apis cerana and its early host expansion into Apis mellifera in Eastern Asia; geography and timing are broadly consistent with Fries et al. 1996 and Huang et al. 2007. I added primary taxonomic and host‑switch references (Fries 1996; Huang et al. 2007) to replace some generic web summaries, but did not alter the core classification (treated here as first detection of the N. ceranae subtype plus re‑emergence of nosemosis in a new host).([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0932473996800599?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Vairimorpha apis
EPP.common.name: Nosema apis, Nosema ceranae
Host: Apis mellifera
Event.summary: After Nosema ceranae had already been reported from African honey bee subspecies in North and West Africa, a focused molecular survey of 69 colonies on two of the Comoros Islands in the South‑West Indian Ocean confirmed that N. ceranae was also established in Eastern Africa.([thehive.icipe.org](https://thehive.icipe.org/all-prp/1478/?utm_source=openai)) The 2023 study found high infection prevalence and spore loads in Apis mellifera colonies on Grande Comore and lower but still substantial prevalence on Mohéli, demonstrating successful colonization of these oceanic islands despite their relative isolation. Over subsequent monitoring, N. ceranae came to be regarded as an important component of the pathogen complex on the Comoros, and together with data from neighboring islands it suggested that N. ceranae‑associated nosemosis is now widespread in the South‑West Indian Ocean region, even though clear links to large‑scale colony losses remain limited.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movements of honey bee colonies, queens and equipment among South‑West Indian Ocean islands and between these islands and continental Africa; traditional, low‑biosecurity beekeeping and honey hunting in Comoros; environmental stressors such as drought and fluctuating forage availability that may influence disease expression. Internal mechanisms: Intra‑continental geographic range expansion of N. ceranae within Africa from earlier foci (e.g. North/West Africa and other SWIO islands) into the Comoros Archipelago; successful establishment in locally adapted A. mellifera lineages; re‑emergence of nosemosis in a region where Nosema infections were poorly characterized previously, now involving a parasite that tends to cause chronic rather than highly seasonal disease.
Review: review – The original Africa event treated the Comoros Islands as the first inter‑continental emergence of N. ceranae into Africa, but more recent syntheses and primary studies show that the parasite was reported earlier in Algeria and Benin. I reinterpreted the Comoros record as an intra‑continental emergence within Eastern Africa/SW Indian Ocean, set the event year and country‑specific year to 2023 to match the published molecular survey, and re‑coded the type fields accordingly (first_detection and inter_continental_emergence set to false; intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence set to true). I also added the recent population‑genetic study of V. ceranae in the SW Indian Ocean as a supporting source.([thehive.icipe.org](https://thehive.icipe.org/all-prp/1478/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Varicellovirus suidalpha1
EPP.common.name: Aujeszky's disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1, Aujeszky's disease virus, Pseudorabies virus, PRV
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus)
Event.summary: From late 2011, large commercial pig farms in northern China that had long used Bartha‑K61 gE‑deleted vaccines began reporting severe pseudorabies outbreaks with high piglet mortality, abortions and respiratory disease despite high vaccination coverage, indicating the emergence of more virulent PRV variants. During 2012 these outbreaks spread rapidly across major swine‑producing provinces in northern and eastern China, and by 2013–2014 highly pathogenic variant strains such as HeN1, TJ and ZJ01 were causing substantial losses in southern China as well, with illness in large numbers of pigs and frequent vaccine failures documented in outbreak investigations. Between roughly 2014 and 2017, molecular surveillance showed these variant genotype II strains becoming dominant across much of the country, prompting development and rollout of updated gE‑deleted vaccines based on variant strains and intensified control programs, which reduced but did not eliminate circulation of variant PRV in Chinese herds. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/20/1/13-0531_article))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of high‑density, industrial pig production in China, frequent live‑pig movements among provinces, and long‑term, near‑universal use of Bartha‑K61‑based vaccines created strong selection pressure and many opportunities for evolution and spread of fitter field strains. Biosecurity gaps, especially in breeding and nursery units, facilitated farm‑to‑farm transmission once variants appeared. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – molecular analyses showed that post‑2011 isolates formed a distinct "variant" clade within genotype II, with characteristic insertions and amino‑acid substitutions in several glycoproteins (notably gC, gD and gE) compared with earlier Chinese and Western strains; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – experimental infections demonstrated higher mortality and more severe respiratory and neurologic disease, including in older pigs, than classic strains; Enhanced Transmission/Immune Escape – variant strains infected pigs previously vaccinated with Bartha‑K61 and induced strong gE antibody responses, indicating partial vaccine escape; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – within China, variants spread from initial foci in northern and eastern provinces to most major swine regions, but remained within an already endemic continental range. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30386699/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review: review. This is clearly one of the largest post‑1990 emergence events for PRV and should be retained, with classification as re‑emergence in an already endemic Asian sub‑region rather than as inter‑continental spread. PRV was long established in Chinese pigs, and outbreak investigations from 2011–2013 demonstrate that a more virulent, partially vaccine‑escape genotype II variant clade drove unprecedented epidemic activity across many provinces. The 2011–2017 time span reasonably captures the emergence, explosive spread and early control period, even though lower‑level variant circulation persists beyond 2017. The geography (Asia – Eastern Asia; China) and host (domestic pigs) are correct. Mechanism/driver text has been edited to remove an incorrect reference to African swine fever–related restocking, which occurred after 2018 and did not drive the initial variant epizootic, and to emphasize molecular evidence for gC/gD/gE changes and vaccine escape documented in primary outbreak reports. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/20/1/13-0531_article))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Varicellovirus suidalpha1
EPP.common.name: Aujeszky's disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1, Aujeszky's disease virus, Pseudorabies virus, PRV
Host: Farmed mink (Neovison vison)
Event.summary: In 2014, a large commercial mink farm in Shandong Province, eastern China, experienced a sudden outbreak of acute respiratory and neurologic disease in which roughly 3,500 of about 4,000 mink (≈87%) died within one week; PRV was isolated from affected animals, and follow‑up PCR testing showed additional PRV‑positive mink on other farms in the province. Around the same time, a separate severe outbreak occurred in farmed mink in Liaoning Province in northeastern China, where animals fed raw pig offal developed diarrhea, neurologic signs and 80–90% mortality, causing major economic losses in the local fur industry. Genetic and phylogenetic analyses indicated that mink isolates clustered closely with contemporary Chinese "variant" PRV strains circulating in pigs and associated with vaccine failure, consistent with spillover from infected swine herds into mink populations via contaminated pig by‑products. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5775606/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high densities of farmed mink in Shandong and Liaoning, routine use of uncooked pig offal and other abattoir by‑products in mink feed, and concurrent circulation of highly pathogenic PRV variants in regional pig herds created repeated opportunities for transmission of virus‑contaminated tissues to a highly susceptible carnivore host. Weak separation between pig abattoirs and fur‑animal operations and lack of heat‑treatment of feed were key proximal risk factors. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – mink isolates belonged to the same variant genotype II lineage that had recently emerged in Chinese pigs and that showed reduced neutralization by antibodies elicited by Bartha‑K61‑based vaccines; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – outbreaks in mink were characterized by per‑acute clinical signs and very high case fatality in clinically affected animals; Host Expansion (Spillover) – these events represent efficient spillover and adaptation of swine‑origin PRV variants to farmed mink, with PCR surveys indicating that infection was widely distributed in regional mink populations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5775606/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review: review. A 2014 outbreak on a Shandong mink farm killed roughly 3,500 of 4,028 animals (≈87% mortality) in a single week, and a contemporaneous Liaoning outbreak in pig‑offal‑fed mink had 80–90% mortality, both caused by genotype II "variant" PRV closely related to vaccine‑resistant swine strains. These episodes produced major, well‑documented losses in China’s fur industry and clearly rank among the most impactful post‑1990 emergence events for this virus, yet they were missing from the original dataset. They have therefore been added as a single linked episode in Eastern Asia, classified as re‑emergence with host expansion (spillover from pigs to mink) in an already endemic country, not as inter‑continental emergence. Geography (Asia – Eastern Asia; China) and year (2014) follow the primary outbreak descriptions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5775606/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Varicellovirus suidalpha1
EPP.common.name: Aujeszky's disease (AD) virus, Suid alphaherpesvirus 1, Aujeszky's disease virus, Pseudorabies virus, PRV
Host: Humans (occupationally exposed farm workers, veterinarians, slaughterhouse workers)
Event.summary: In 2017, clinicians in China reported a first molecularly confirmed human ocular infection with pseudorabies virus in a swine‑exposed worker who developed febrile illness followed by severe bilateral endophthalmitis; sequencing showed the viral strain to be closely related to emergent highly pathogenic PRV variants circulating in pigs. Over the following years, additional patients with acute encephalitis and/or retinal necrosis were identified in several Chinese hospitals, and a multicenter cohort study of 472 encephalitis patients from 2016–2018 detected PRV DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid of six individuals with rapidly progressive panencephalitis, most of whom had occupational contact with pigs or pork. By around 2022, case reports and systematic reviews had compiled more than a dozen well‑documented, often severe or fatal human neuro‑ophthalmic infections linked to PRV exposure in China, coinciding temporally and geographically with the spread of variant genotype II strains in the country’s pig population and raising concern about an expanded zoonotic host range. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/6/pdfs/17-1612.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑intensity swine production in China with persistent circulation of variant PRV strains, close and sometimes unprotected contact between pigs and farm workers, veterinarians, butchers, and slaughterhouse staff, and limited initial awareness of PRV as a potential human pathogen created repeated opportunities for zoonotic exposure. Wider use of metagenomic next‑generation sequencing for unexplained encephalitis increased the likelihood that PRV infections would be detected rather than remaining idiopathic. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – accumulating human case reports, almost all with direct or indirect exposure to pigs or raw pork products in China and with viral sequences clustering within the post‑2011 variant genotype II lineage, suggest that these strains have a greater capacity to infect humans than earlier PRV variants; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – human infections typically manifested as rapidly progressive encephalitis and/or bilateral retinal necrosis with high morbidity and frequent long‑term neurologic or visual sequelae; Novel Strain/Genotype – at least one human PRV isolate (hSD‑1/2019) has been recovered and shown experimentally to be closely related to contemporary Chinese variant strains and highly pathogenic in pigs; Enhanced Transmission – no sustained human‑to‑human transmission has been documented, with infections still appearing to be limited to direct zoonotic exposure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7897889/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review: review. Severe PRV encephalitis and neuro‑ophthalmic disease in humans have been increasingly reported in China since around 2017, with case series and systematic reviews documenting more than a dozen well‑characterized patients and a recent Journal of Virology review summarizing 34 suspected human infections since 2011, all linked to swine exposure and variant genotype II strains. These events are important for this EPP and should be retained, but the original coding of both "first detection" and "re‑emergence" was inconsistent with the project rules. Because this row belongs to an animal‑host entry (pigs as the primary host system) and human infections represent host expansion of a long‑established pathogen rather than first appearance of the virus in the livestock host system, first_detection has been set to "No" and the event is treated purely as re‑emergence with host expansion in an already endemic Eastern Asia sub‑region. Geography, time span (2017–2022 as the initial period of recognized cases), and host description remain appropriate and are supported by the cited medical literature. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/6/pdfs/17-1612.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus venezuelanense
EPP.common.name: VEEV
Host: Equines (horses, donkeys, mules); humans
Event.summary: In late 1992, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) of epidemic subtype IC re‑emerged in western Venezuela, with initial equine and human cases reported in Trujillo State and neighboring Andean valleys, followed by a larger wave of disease in 1993 that also affected Zulia State. Equids developed severe neurologic signs and high mortality, and human cases of febrile and encephalitic illness were reported, but transmission remained geographically confined to western Venezuela rather than spreading continent‑wide. Emergency equine vaccination campaigns and vector‑control activities, together with the end of the rainy season, reduced mosquito densities and susceptible horse numbers, and epizootic activity waned by early 1994.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Nearly two decades without major epizootics allowed substantial cohorts of unvaccinated horses to accumulate in areas where enzootic subtype ID VEEV circulated in rodent–mosquito cycles; favorable rainfall and humidity in 1992–1993 increased vector abundance in lowland forests and agricultural valleys, promoting amplification and spillover into equines and humans. Internal mechanisms: Comparative genetic studies show that the 1992–1993 subtype IC epidemic strains arose from closely related enzootic subtype ID viruses in western Venezuela, acquiring mutations associated with increased equine virulence and viremia, which enabled horses to serve as efficient amplification hosts and drove this episode of viral re‑emergence.
Review: retain – 1992–1993 western Venezuela subtype IC epizootic is well documented as a re‑emergence of equine‑virulent virus derived from enzootic subtype ID, confined to Venezuelan states such as Trujillo and Zulia; geography, timing and classification as re‑emergence rather than intra-/inter‑continental emergence are appropriate and supported by molecular and epidemiologic studies.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus venezuelanense
EPP.common.name: VEEV
Host: Equines (horses, donkeys, mules); humans (sporadic)
Event.summary: In 1993, an outbreak of Venezuelan equine encephalitis in coastal areas of Chiapas State, southern Mexico, produced neurologic disease and high mortality in horses and some human febrile illnesses, representing the first confirmed equine epizootic caused by subtype IE viruses in the region. Virus isolates from sick equines and mosquitoes showed that previously enzootic IE lineages had acquired equine virulence, permitting efficient amplification in horse–mosquito transmission cycles and spread among multiple lowland foci. Targeted equine vaccination and vector‑control measures, combined with depletion of susceptible horses and seasonal declines in mosquito abundance, brought the epizootic under control within that summer.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense mosquito populations in lowland tropical habitats, growth of equine populations with minimal prior exposure or vaccination, and close contact between horses and long‑standing enzootic VEEV foci on the Pacific coastal plain allowed spillover and amplification. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic and experimental infection studies demonstrate that the 1993 outbreak strains belonged to a subtype IE lineage closely related to enzootic progenitors but bearing mutations that conferred equine virulence and higher viremia, enabling horses to serve as effective amplification hosts; this represents re‑emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence rather than simple recurrence of earlier IAB/IC epidemic viruses.
Review: retain – 1993 Chiapas epizootic is correctly placed in South America | Central America (Mexico), accurately described as the first confirmed equine epizootic due to subtype IE with documented genetic adaptation for equine virulence, and appropriately classified as re‑emergence rather than intra‑continental emergence, because VEEV was already established in the Central American sub‑region.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus venezuelanense
EPP.common.name: VEEV
Host: Equines (horses, donkeys, mules); humans (sporadic, mild febrile illness)
Event.summary: In June–July 1996, Venezuelan equine encephalitis recurred in southern Mexico when an outbreak due to subtype IE virus affected horses in several localities in Oaxaca State, with 32 equine cases and 12 deaths among roughly 2,500 animals under observation and virus isolated from clinically affected horses. This epizootic represented geographic spread and renewed activity of the equine‑virulent subtype IE lineage that had caused the 1993 Chiapas outbreak, raising concern that equine disease could become established more widely along the Pacific coast. Rapid implementation of equine vaccination, movement controls and vector control in affected communities contained the outbreak within weeks and prevented extensive human encephalitis or further spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistence of the equine‑virulent subtype IE lineage in southern Mexico following the 1993 Chiapas epizootic, incomplete vaccination coverage among horses, favorable ecological conditions with abundant mosquitoes in lowland tropical and subtropical habitats, and local movement of equids allowed introduction and amplification in Oaxacan foci. Internal mechanisms: Genetic comparisons show that 1996 outbreak strains fall within the same equine‑virulent IE lineage identified in 1993, with no clear evidence of a distinct new genotype; the 1996 event is therefore best interpreted as re‑occurrence of a previously emergent equine‑adapted lineage driven primarily by ecological and husbandry factors rather than a fresh episode of viral re‑emergence.
Review: review – Event (1996 Oaxaca outbreak) is correctly located and quantified, but the emergence type has been adjusted from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because genetic and epidemiologic data indicate continued circulation of the same equine‑virulent subtype IE lineage responsible for the 1993 epizootic, with no new distinct strain arising in 1996; classification change and revised mechanism text should be checked and accepted or reverted by a domain expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus venezuelanense
EPP.common.name: VEEV
Host: Equines; humans (sero‑evidence and sporadic febrile illness); rodents and mosquitoes in enzootic cycles
Event.summary: From 2003 to about 2010, surveillance in the Gulf Coast region of Mexico documented ongoing Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus activity in coastal lowland states such as Veracruz, Tabasco and Tamaulipas, with sporadic equine infections, human seroconversions and frequent virus isolations from mosquitoes, sentinel hamsters and other vertebrates indicating endemic‑enzootic circulation of subtype IE VEEV. Transmission fluctuated seasonally and geographically but repeatedly recurred in similar wetland and floodplain habitats, occasionally infecting horses and people but without the large equine epizootics seen on the Pacific coast in the 1990s. Continued vaccination of horses in high‑risk areas, vector surveillance and targeted public‑health monitoring limited the scale of outbreaks, and by about 2010 documented VEEV activity in these Gulf‑Coast sites had declined to low or serologically inferred levels, although enzootic circulation almost certainly persists.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent enzootic VEEV cycles in rodent–mosquito systems in tropical wetlands and coastal plains of the Gulf Coast region, expansion of equine and bovine populations into floodplain pastures, incomplete routine vaccination, and environmental conditions such as heavy rains and river flooding that boosted mosquito densities all sustained recurrent low‑level transmission. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses of isolates collected during 2003–2010 show continued circulation of subtype IE lineages closely related to earlier Mexican strains, with no evidence that a new more virulent epizootic subtype had emerged; equids generally developed low or undetectable viremias, suggesting they were not the primary amplification hosts in this region. Consequently, the 2003–2010 Gulf‑Coast Mexico activity is best classified as re‑occurrence of established enzootic lineages with intermittent spillover to equines and humans, rather than a distinct episode of viral re‑emergence or inter‑continental spread.
Review: review – Event correctly summarizes long‑term subtype IE activity along Mexico’s Gulf Coast, but continent and sub‑region have been restricted to South America | Central America (Mexico) and the country list simplified to a single Mexico [2003] entry, because documented transmission during 2003–2010 occurred only in Mexican states and northward spread into the United States remained hypothetical; these geographic corrections should be confirmed and accepted.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus venezuelanense
EPP.common.name: VEEV
Host: Humans; rodents (sylvatic reservoirs); mosquitoes (Culex (Melanoconion) spp.)
Event.summary: In the first half of 2006, clinic‑based febrile surveillance in Iquitos, an Amazonian city in northeastern Peru, detected a marked increase in Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus infections, with 63 laboratory‑confirmed human cases representing approximately a five‑fold rise over baseline incidence from 2000–2004. Cases occurred across multiple urban and peri‑urban neighborhoods, many distant from forested areas, indicating that sylvatic subtype ID VEEV was being transmitted in or very near the city rather than only in rural forest habitats as previously recognized. After intensified vector surveillance and public‑health messaging and as mosquito densities and transmission declined later in the year, case numbers returned toward endemic levels, although enzootic VEEV circulation in the surrounding Amazon Basin persisted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of human settlement and housing into forest margins around Iquitos, high rainfall and flooding that increased breeding sites for Culex (Melanoconion) mosquitoes, and increased human use of peri‑urban forested areas created more frequent contact between people and enzootic VEEV transmission sites, leading to an urban‑proximal outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses showed that viruses from the 2006 outbreak belonged to the Panama/Peru subtype ID genotype already circulating in the region, with no clear evidence of a newly evolved epidemic subtype; the episode therefore represents re‑occurrence of an enzootic lineage in a new ecological context (urban and peri‑urban exposure) rather than emergence of a novel equine‑virulent strain.
Review: retain – 2006 Iquitos outbreak, with 63 laboratory‑confirmed human VEEV infections and evidence of urban/peri‑urban transmission of subtype ID, was previously omitted yet clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 VEEV episodes in terms of human case numbers; it is correctly coded as a South America | South America (Peru) re‑occurrence of an enzootic lineage rather than a first detection or epizootic equine event.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus venezuelanense
EPP.common.name: VEEV
Host: Equines (horses, donkeys, mules); humans (suspected sporadic cases)
Event.summary: Between 2009 and 2013, Colombian veterinary surveillance recorded renewed Venezuelan equine encephalitis activity in multiple lowland departments, with 49 laboratory‑confirmed equine cases reported from 13 departments and additional serologically exposed animals, most frequently in Córdoba, Magdalena and Valle del Cauca. These cases occurred against a background of endemic arboviral transmission and extensive equine movements, but represented a clear resurgence of clinically apparent VEE in equids after several years without major reported animal disease or human outbreaks. Outbreak foci were managed through local quarantine, intensified vaccination campaigns in risk areas and vector‑control measures, and although sporadic cases continued, no large human VEE epidemic comparable to 1995 was reported during this period.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased movement and trade of horses, including informal or poorly controlled transport between departments and across borders, created opportunities for spread of VEEV into new herds; suboptimal vaccination coverage, large susceptible equine populations in tropical lowland areas below ~1,200 m elevation, and climatic conditions favorable for mosquito vectors (rainy seasons and flooding) promoted amplification and spillover. Internal mechanisms: Available information from Colombian reports and regional phylogenetic work suggests involvement of established epizootic/enzootic subtype I lineages rather than a novel variant, with no evidence that a new equine‑virulent strain emerged during 2009–2013; this multi‑year episode is therefore best categorized as re‑occurrence of VEEV in previously affected Colombian sub‑regions.
Review: retain – 2009–2013 Colombian equine VEEV activity, with 49 laboratory‑confirmed equine cases across 13 departments and clear evidence of renewed clinical disease in horses, was missing from the original dataset yet is a substantial multi‑year re‑occurrence within South America | South America; coding as a Colombian re‑occurrence rather than intra‑continental emergence is appropriate and brings the event list closer to capturing the ten most impactful post‑1990 episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Vesicular stomatitis virus
EPP.common.name: VSV
Host: Horses, cattle, one llama (epizootic in mixed livestock herds, primarily equids, with cattle affected on many premises)
Event.summary: Beginning in April 1995, vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus (VSNJV) spilled over from endemic foci in northern Mexico into horses and cattle in the southwestern United States, initiating an epizootic that spread along river valleys in New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, Arizona and adjacent areas over the 1995 season. Subsequent years saw additional activity, including Indiana serotype outbreaks in 1997–1998, with repeated introductions and overwintering leading to recurrent disease in western US states and substantial numbers of quarantined operations. The multi‑year cycle waned as cooler weather reduced vector activity and movement controls, surveillance and biosecurity measures were implemented, ending this epizootic lineage in the late 1990s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: seasonal abundance of hematophagous insect vectors (black flies, sand flies, biting midges) along riparian corridors; livestock movements and grazing patterns that brought horses and cattle into high‑vector river valleys; warm climatic conditions favoring vector survival; and management practices concentrating susceptible animals at shared water sources. Internal mechanisms: introduction of a distinct VSNJV lineage from endemic Mexico, followed by emergence of an Indiana serotype lineage later in the cycle, representing viral genetic diversification and range expansion within Northern America; efficient vector‑borne transmission in equids and cattle facilitated rapid local spread and supported limited overwintering between years.
Review: Decision: retain. Corrected continent/sub-region/country fields so this row now represents the well-documented 1995–1998 western US epizootic, with Mexico treated as the endemic viral source rather than a separate outbreak country; this aligns with UN subregion coding and the event description, which focuses on disease impact in US livestock. Classification as re-emergence driven by distinct New Jersey and Indiana lineages introduced from endemic areas is supported by phylogenetic work, but a specialist may wish to consider whether the 1997–1998 Indiana-serotype outbreaks should be summarized more explicitly or split into their own event if finer resolution is needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Vesicular stomatitis virus
EPP.common.name: VSV
Host: Horses and cattle (index premises in equids with cattle exposure)
Event.summary: In 2012, a vesicular stomatitis outbreak was detected in the southwestern United States, with vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus (VSNJV) identified on equine premises in New Mexico and a small number of additional livestock herds investigated in the region. Epidemiologic and phylogenetic analysis showed that the 2012 virus was most closely related to a lineage previously detected in Veracruz, Mexico in 2000, indicating a relatively recent introduction from endemic Mexican reservoirs rather than persistence of the 2004–2006 outbreak viruses. Following targeted quarantines, movement restrictions and biosecurity measures, the outbreak was contained to a limited number of premises and ended with the seasonal decline in vectors and strict surveillance to exclude foot‑and‑mouth disease and other vesicular infections.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction of VSNJV from endemic Mexican regions into US border states via movement of infected animals or insect vectors; heightened summer vector activity around irrigated pastures and riparian areas; and high livestock densities in affected counties. Internal mechanisms: genetic analysis demonstrated a distinct viral genotype, different from the 2004–2006 lineage yet related to Mexican 2000 isolates, indicating re-emergence through a new viral introduction and phylogeographically distinct lineage rather than simple reactivation of earlier US outbreak strains.
Review: Decision: review. Restricted geography to the United States only (Northern America/Northern America; United States [2012]) and removed Mexico as an outbreak country because the 2012 episode was confined to New Mexico and neighboring US areas, with Mexican 2000 isolates serving only as ancestral references. The event is correctly classified as re-emergence due to a distinct VSNJV genotype, but given its small scale relative to major US cycles and the large 2018 Ecuador outbreak, its inclusion among the top 10 highest-impact events warrants re-evaluation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Vesicular stomatitis virus
EPP.common.name: VSV
Host: Horses and cattle (mixed‑species outbreaks on farms in northeastern Brazil)
Event.summary: Between June and August 2013, vesicular stomatitis outbreaks occurred on multiple farms in Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte states in northeastern Brazil, affecting horses and cattle with vesicular lesions clinically indistinguishable from foot‑and‑mouth disease. Diagnostic workup confirmed vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus subtype 3 (VSIV‑3, Alagoas virus) as the cause, and molecular analyses indicated that the viruses formed a distinct clade relative to historical VSIV‑3 strains, representing renewed viral activity of this subtype in the region after a long quiet period. Control efforts focused on quarantine, clinical management and movement restrictions, and the wave of outbreaks subsided by late 2013 as vector populations declined and affected premises recovered.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: endemic circulation of vesicular stomatitis viruses in parts of Brazil, with climatic and ecological conditions in northeastern states favoring vector populations; close contact among horses and cattle on mixed farms; and limited prior exposure or vaccination against VSIV‑3 in equids and cattle. Internal mechanisms: re-emergence of the Alagoas VSIV‑3 subtype as a distinct lineage, with molecular data showing a separate clade associated with the 2013 outbreaks; vector-borne transmission by local insects (likely biting flies and midges) facilitated rapid spread between animals on affected properties.
Review: Decision: retain. Removed a secondary summary link (madbarn.com) in favor of the primary JVDI article and a Brazilian sero-epidemiologic study, which together provide stronger peer-reviewed evidence for the scale and genetic distinctness of the 2013 VSIV-3 Alagoas outbreaks. This event represents the documented re-emergence of an important Indiana subtype in Brazil after decades of sparse detection and is a key South American counterpart to the major US cycles.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Vesicular stomatitis virus
EPP.common.name: VSV
Host: Cattle, horses and one mule (mixed herds on several farms in Maranhão state)
Event.summary: In 2016, vesicular stomatitis outbreaks were reported on multiple cattle farms in Maranhão state in northeastern Brazil, where cattle, horses and a mule showed vesicular lesions, prompting investigation for foot‑and‑mouth disease. Laboratory testing confirmed infection with Alagoas vesiculovirus (VSAV, a VSIV subtype) closely related to, but genetically distinct from, viruses identified in the 2013 Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte outbreaks, indicating ongoing viral evolution and spread within northeastern Brazil. After implementation of on‑farm quarantines, movement restrictions and supportive care, clinical cases declined and the outbreak series ended as environmental conditions became less favorable for vector transmission.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: endemic VS circulation in northeastern Brazil; large cattle herds co‑grazed with equids; and environmental conditions (warm, humid climate with abundant insect vectors) that supported recurrent VSAV transmission. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses show that the 2016 VSAV strains in Maranhão formed a clade related to, but distinct from, the 2013 viruses, providing evidence of re-emergence via an evolving lineage; vector adaptation to local conditions and persistence in regional reservoirs likely facilitated multi‑year activity.
Review: Decision: review. This row accurately describes the genetically distinct VSAV lineage causing the 2016 Maranhão outbreaks and is well supported by molecular and clinical data, but the number of affected farms was modest compared with the 2018 Ecuador and major US cycles. Retain for now as a key example of South American re-emergence of the Alagoas subtype, but its priority relative to other medium-sized events should be reassessed if a strict cap of 10 highest-impact episodes is enforced.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Vesicular stomatitis virus
EPP.common.name: VSV
Host: Cattle primarily, with some equids implicated in endemic transmission foci
Event.summary: In 2018, Colombia’s veterinary authority (ICA) reported a marked increase in notifications of vesicular stomatitis (estomatitis vesicular) in cattle herds, with numerous foci concentrated in departments such as Santander, Norte de Santander, Cesar and Antioquia where the disease is endemic. This resurgence led to intensified vaccination recommendations and reinforced surveillance, as VS cases complicate differential diagnosis with foot‑and‑mouth disease in a country striving to maintain FMD‑free status with vaccination. The elevated incidence declined after targeted vaccination campaigns, improved reporting and seasonal changes reduced vector populations, although VS remains a common vesicular disease in Colombian cattle and occasional equids.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: endemic VSV circulation in Colombia combined with favorable climatic conditions for vectors in 2018; high cattle density with frequent animal movements between farms and grazing areas; and gaps in vaccination coverage contributing to a larger‑than‑usual outbreak year. Internal mechanisms: reports emphasize established VSIV/VSNJV circulation without clear evidence of a novel strain or major host shift; thus the 2018 surge is categorized as a re-occurrence driven mainly by environmental conditions, herd immunity gaps and control program performance rather than viral genetic innovation.
Review: Decision: review. The Colombian surge in 2018 is well documented by ICA as an unusually high notification year in endemic departments, justifying classification as a re-occurrence in South America. However, the number of affected herds and geographic impact are smaller than for Ecuador’s 2018 multi-hundred-outbreak epizootic, so this row should be revisited when ranking events by continental and global impact.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Vesicular stomatitis virus
EPP.common.name: VSV
Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds across coastal, Andean and Amazonian regions; other domestic species were not reported clinically affected)
Event.summary: In 2018, Ecuador experienced a very large vesicular stomatitis epizootic, with approximately 399 registered bovine outbreaks reported across most provinces over a short period, especially between September and November. Molecular analysis of vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus (VSNJV) and Indiana virus (VSIV) isolates showed that 2018 strains formed closely related clades distinct from, yet descended from, variants associated with a smaller 2004 Amazonian outbreak, indicating renewed epizootic activity arising from enzootic circulation. As climatic conditions shifted, vector pressure decreased and control measures such as movement restrictions and on-farm biosecurity were implemented, outbreak notifications declined and the widespread national wave subsided.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: favorable climatic conditions and abundant insect vectors in the Amazon, coastal lowlands and Andean highlands; high cattle densities and frequent movements of animals to auctions and between farms, particularly in coastal and highland regions; and long-term endemic circulation of VSV in Ecuador that provided viral reservoirs for rapid spread when environmental conditions were suitable. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses demonstrate that 2018 VSNJV and VSIV strains clustered in South American clades with two main Ecuadorian subclades (Amazonian and Andean/coastal), with close ancestry to 2004 Ecuadorian and Colombian variants, supporting classification as a major re-emergent epizootic driven by evolution and amplification of existing regional lineages rather than introduction of an entirely novel serotype.
Review: Decision: retain. Newly added row for the 2018 Ecuador outbreak, which involved about 399 recorded bovine outbreaks and nationwide spread over multiple ecological regions, clearly placing it among the most impactful VSV events in South America since 1990. Classified as re-emergence based on molecular evidence linking 2018 strains to earlier 2004 Ecuadorian and Colombian variants, with strong external drivers (vectors, climate, cattle trade) documented in primary sources; this event should be considered a core component of any top-10 VSV emergence list.

EPP.scientific.name: Vesicular stomatitis virus
EPP.common.name: VSV
Host: Horses and cattle (index and majority of premises equine, with many mixed equine–bovine herds; some small ruminants and camelids affected)
Event.summary: A large vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus (VSIV) outbreak began in June 2019 in the southwestern United States, with the first confirmed index premises in horses in Texas and New Mexico and rapid spread to Colorado and Wyoming, then further expansion to Oklahoma, Nebraska, Utah and Kansas over the season. By the end of 2019, approximately 1,144 VSV‑affected premises were identified in 111 counties across eight US states, representing the largest recorded VSIV incursion in recent decades and affecting primarily horses but also many cattle herds. The 2019 wave ended with the onset of winter and aggressive control measures, but evidence of overwintering and continued circulation in vectors and livestock set the stage for a follow‑on outbreak in 2020.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: incursion of VSIV from endemic areas into US border states; extensive vector habitat along rivers and irrigated lands in affected states; dense populations of horses and cattle on pasture during peak vector season; and livestock movements for shows, sales and grazing that carried virus between regions. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses of VSIV from the 2019 outbreak revealed low genetic diversity consistent with a single incursion followed by rapid expansion, and later work showed that the same lineage successfully overwintered, with 2020 sequences nested within 2019 viruses, demonstrating re-emergence through persistence and adaptation to the North American ecological context.
Review: Decision: retain. Updated geography to treat this as a United States–only event (Northern America/Northern America; United States [2019]), removing Mexico [2018] because Mexican strains are implicated as ancestral sources but official data show no comparably large Mexican outbreak in 2018–2019. With 1,144 affected premises across eight states, this VSIV incursion is one of the largest VSV outbreaks in at least 40 years and clearly merits inclusion as a major re-emergent episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Vesicular stomatitis virus
EPP.common.name: VSV
Host: Horses and cattle (numerous mixed‑species premises; some small ruminants)
Event.summary: Following the large 2019 incursion, vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus re-emerged in 2020 across parts of the central United States, with virus overwintering and causing new infections in horses and cattle from spring through late summer. The 2020 episode affected about 326 premises in 70 counties, with notable eastward spread into Kansas and Missouri for the first time in several decades, alongside continued cases in previously affected western states. Vector control, on‑farm biosecurity, quarantines and movement restrictions, combined with the seasonal decline in biting flies and midges, eventually curtailed transmission and the outbreak ended by late 2020, although the event highlighted the potential for VSIV to expand into new areas of the US livestock belt under favorable conditions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: overwintering of the 2019 VSIV lineage in the US, likely in local reservoirs or insect vectors; favorable climatic conditions in 2020 that supported high vector densities in both traditional western foci and more easterly states; and livestock movements that facilitated establishment of infection in Kansas and Missouri. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic and genomic analyses show 2020 viruses forming a monophyletic subset of 2019 sequences, consistent with re-emergence via persistence of the same lineage; viral traits supporting survival across seasons and efficient transmission by local insect vectors underpinned geographic range expansion into new parts of Northern America.
Review: Decision: retain. Corrected the countries list to "United States of America [2020]" and removed Mexico [2019] as well as state names (Kansas, Missouri) that had been incorrectly formatted as countries, while keeping the description of eastward spread within the US. This row appropriately captures the expansion year of the 2019 VSIV lineage, which overwintered and re-emerged to affect hundreds of premises and new US regions, and together with the 2019 incursion forms one of the most consequential modern VSV epizootic cycles.

EPP.scientific.name: Vesicular stomatitis virus
EPP.common.name: VSV
Host: Horses predominantly, with some cattle and a few non-domestic species (e.g. rhinoceros) affected on mixed or zoological premises
Event.summary: In May 2023, vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus (VSNJV) was confirmed on an equine premises in San Diego County, California, marking the first VS outbreak in that state since the early 1980s, and cases soon appeared in additional California counties as well as isolated premises in Nevada and Texas. Between May 2023 and January 2024, about 319 VSV‑affected premises were identified across 19 California counties plus one county in Nevada and two in Texas, with most clinical disease reported in horses but some cattle and zoo animals also affected, prompting extensive quarantines and movement restrictions. As vector activity diminished over winter and control measures (vector management, movement controls, heightened surveillance) took effect, new case reports ceased and the 2023–2024 outbreak was declared resolved.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely incursion of VSNJV from endemic areas via infected insect vectors into southern California, followed by local amplification under favorable climatic conditions that supported high densities of biting midges and black flies; high concentrations of horses at equine facilities and events in affected regions; and limited prior exposure to VSV in California, which had not seen an outbreak for decades. Internal mechanisms: virologic investigations during the outbreak detected VSNJV RNA in multiple vector species (including Culicoides midges and black flies) and indicated a relatively homogeneous viral lineage consistent with a single recent introduction that expanded within the western US; the ability of this lineage to exploit new ecological niches in California underlies its classification as a significant re-emergent epizootic in Northern America.
Review: Decision: retain. Newly added row summarizing the 2023–2024 US VSNJV outbreak, which involved roughly 319 affected premises across California, Nevada and Texas and represented the first vesicular stomatitis activity in California since the early 1980s. The event is treated as a US-only re-emergence with strong evidence for vector-borne introduction and spread, and its scale and geographic novelty justify inclusion among the highest-impact modern VSV emergence episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: WNV, West Nile encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (primary reported), with local Culex pipiens mosquitoes, urban birds and likely incidental equines contributing to transmission cycles
Event.summary: In summer–autumn 1996, West Nile virus re‑emerged in Romania, causing a large outbreak of neuroinvasive disease centred on Bucharest and the southern Danube plain after decades with little recognized activity in Eastern Europe. Intense transmission in urban Culex mosquitoes feeding on birds and humans led to several hundred confirmed neuroinvasive cases and multiple deaths before incidence declined with the end of the mosquito season. The outbreak subsided as temperatures fell and vector populations dropped, but it signalled renewed epidemic potential of WNV in Eastern Europe and prompted establishment of sustained human, mosquito and bird surveillance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Urban expansion with abundant breeding sites for Culex pipiens, warm summer conditions and limited prior surveillance or awareness facilitated intense local amplification in Bucharest and surrounding areas. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not support emergence of a novel lineage here; amplification of existing lineage 1 strains in dense urban bird–mosquito cycles produced a pronounced re‑occurrence of severe human disease in a previously affected subregion.
Review: review – Retain this event as one of the major modern WNV outbreaks; timing, geography and classification as re-occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence or re-emergence) are consistent with historical evidence. Updated source URLs to rely on WHO Disease Outbreak News and primary outbreak investigations (Tsai et al., Lancet; Savage et al., EID) instead of general Wikipedia pages; no other fields changed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: WNV, West Nile encephalitis virus
Host: Horses, livestock (cattle, small ruminants), wildlife (e.g. wild ungulates), humans (sporadic)
