Event.summary: Between 2008 and 2015, intensified surveillance in South Africa revealed a substantial burden of West Nile virus lineage 2 infection among horses with neurologic disease, with about 7% of over 1,000 sampled horses testing positive and roughly one‑third of infections proving fatal. Concurrent infections were also documented in livestock and wildlife, showing that WNV was causing more recognised clinical disease in multiple animal species than previously appreciated in this endemic region. Case numbers fluctuated seasonally and by year and were influenced by rainfall and horse population dynamics, but WNV has remained an important cause of equine encephalitis in southern Africa.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Environmental conditions favouring Culex vectors (wet summers, irrigation, water storage), expansion and concentration of horse populations, and improved veterinary diagnostic capacity together led to increased detection of WNV disease in equids and other animals. Internal mechanisms: Predominant circulation of lineage 2 strains with clear neurotropic potential in horses and evidence of pathogenic strains, representing re‑emergence through enhanced recognition and possibly local adaptation of lineage 2 viruses rather than appearance of a completely new lineage.
Review: retain – This episode is well documented as a substantial burden of lineage 2-associated neurologic disease in horses and other animals in South Africa and fits the definition of re-emergence driven by pathogenic lineage 2 strains and improved detection. Geography, hosts, timing and event-type coding are appropriate, and existing sources (EID surveillance report plus general WNV overview) are adequate for this dataset; no structural changes were made.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: WNV, West Nile encephalitis virus
Host: Humans, horses, domestic birds and wild birds, mosquitoes (Culex pipiens)
Event.summary: In summer 2010, Greece experienced its first major epidemic of West Nile disease when a lineage 2 strain, closely related to the Central European lineage 2 cluster, was detected in Culex mosquitoes and caused a large human outbreak centred in Central Macedonia. During this season, more than 250 human cases (with a high proportion neuroinvasive) and multiple equine cases were reported, alongside infection in local bird populations, marking a dramatic emergence of WNV disease in Greece despite prior serologic evidence of circulation. Transmission decreased after the mosquito season ended and was somewhat lower, but recurrent, in subsequent years, indicating establishment of an endemic focus seeded by this 2010 lineage 2 introduction.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Wetland and rice‑growing landscapes around Central Macedonia supportive of large Culex pipiens populations, combined with hot summers and positioning on major migratory bird routes, created favourable conditions for amplification of the introduced lineage 2 virus. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and local expansion of the Nea Santa–Greece–2010 lineage 2 strain, which showed efficient transmission in local mosquitoes and birds and caused severe neuroinvasive disease in humans and horses, consistent with re‑emergence via a new genetic lineage in a previously less‑affected subregion.
Review: review – This event is correctly treated as a major Greek epidemic associated with introduction of a lineage 2 strain, but it does not constitute intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD subregion because WNV was already established in Southern Europe (e.g. France, Italy). Intra_continental_emergence has therefore been set to false, while re_emergence remains true to reflect emergence of a new lineage causing severe disease. Existing sources (Greek outbreak description, lineage 2 characterisation, and regional epidemiologic overviews) are appropriate and were retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: White spot syndrome virus
EPP.common.name: WSSV
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (primarily Litopenaeus vannamei and related species in Texas) and imported frozen commodity shrimp
Event.summary: Origin: In 1995, WSSV was first detected in the Western Hemisphere when shrimp with gross signs of white spot disease were identified in U.S. retail outlets and an outbreak subsequently occurred on a shrimp farm in Texas, marking establishment with local transmission in North American aquaculture rather than isolated imported cases. Development: The Texas outbreaks and detection of WSSV in imported shrimp products prompted rapid changes in broodstock sourcing (shift to specific-pathogen-free lines), tighter controls on live animal imports, and heightened laboratory surveillance for WSSV in U.S. shrimp farms and processing facilities. End: Through these biosecurity responses, WSSV did not become continuously epidemic in U.S. shrimp farming, and subsequent North American production relied heavily on SPF stocks and improved management, although the virus remained a constant biosecurity threat through imported commodities and wild crustaceans.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International trade in frozen and possibly live shrimp from WSSV-endemic Asian countries to North America, combined with initial gaps in screening and controls for exotic crustacean viruses; high-density pond culture in affected farms that allowed local amplification once the virus entered. Internal mechanisms: Broad environmental stability of WSSV virions in chilled or frozen product; efficient oral transmission when infected shrimp or processing wastes were used as feed or discarded into coastal environments.
Review: Decision: Retain. Multiple primary and review sources agree that WSSV was first diagnosed in the Americas in late 1995 on a Texas shrimp farm, with supporting evidence from imported commodity shrimp. Coding this as an inter‑continental emergence into North America (with in situ farm transmission) is therefore appropriate, and the country/subregion information is correct. No structural corrections were required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans; sylvatic cycle involving non-human primates and Haemagogus spp. mosquitoes, with risk of spillover into Aedes aegypti–infested towns
Event.summary: In 1995, a large jungle yellow fever epidemic emerged in the western Andean region of Peru after non-immune agricultural workers were recruited into newly expanded coffee-growing zones where virus was enzootically maintained. The epidemic spread through several highland departments, producing roughly 400–500 human cases and a very high case fatality ratio (around one-third of patients), and is described as the largest recorded jungle yellow fever outbreak in the Americas in recent decades. Intensive emergency vaccination campaigns targeting at‑risk Andean communities, coupled with vector control and the end of the rainy season, brought human transmission under control by late 1995, though the event highlighted the risk of urbanization in nearby Aedes aegypti–infested cities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of coffee cultivation into forested Andean foothills, recruitment of non‑immune workers from other regions, poor baseline vaccination coverage, and high vector densities in forest–edge and peridomestic environments created intense human exposure to sylvatic transmission foci. Internal mechanisms: Available phylogenetic work indicates circulation of established South American yellow fever virus lineages; the unusually large scale is best explained by ecological and social drivers rather than documented viral adaptation, so this is classified as re-occurrence with geographic range expansion rather than re-emergence.
Review: retain – Added new event for the 1995 western Andean Peru epidemic, which produced ~440–500 cases with high fatality and is described by WHO/PAHO as the largest jungle yellow fever outbreak in the Americas during 1985–2012; this clearly qualifies among the ten most impactful post‑1990 events. Classified as re-occurrence (no evidence of novel strain), with South America/South America subregion and Peru [1995] consistent with the UN country list.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans; predominantly urban Aedes aegypti transmission with possible peri‑urban sylvatic links
Event.summary: From March to late 2001, an outbreak of yellow fever occurred in Côte d’Ivoire, centred on the densely populated city of Abidjan, with about 128 suspected cases, 20 laboratory-confirmed cases and 14 deaths reported. Concern about explosive spread in this urban centre, considered the first urban yellow fever epidemic in Africa in roughly a decade, led to an urgent international appeal and rapid scale‑up of response activities. A 12‑day mass vaccination campaign that immunized approximately 2.6 million Abidjan residents, together with vector control and surveillance reinforcement, halted further urban transmission and the outbreak was declared over.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Low baseline yellow fever vaccination coverage in Abidjan, dense urban Aedes aegypti populations, high human mobility, and delays in recognizing early cases created conditions for an urban outbreak despite long-standing regional endemicity. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of a novel viral lineage or increased virulence; the event reflects re-occurrence of yellow fever in an urban setting driven by immunity gaps and vector ecology rather than intrinsic viral change.
Review: retain – Added because WHO and PAHO describe the 2001 Abidjan outbreak as the first urban yellow fever epidemic in Africa in 10 years, triggering vaccination of >2.6 million people; despite modest case counts, its urban setting and massive response make it a high-impact event meriting inclusion among the major post‑1990 outbreaks. Sub-region corrected to Western Africa and country name aligned with the provided UN list.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans; likely involvement of sylvatic cycle with non-human primates and Aedes spp. mosquitoes
Event.summary: In early 2003, an outbreak of unexplained haemorrhagic fever was reported from the Imatong Mountains of southern Sudan (then part of Sudan), and field investigation confirmed yellow fever virus as the cause. The outbreak occurred in remote, conflict-affected districts with difficult access, and around 178 suspected cases and 27 deaths were documented, with the true burden likely higher because of surveillance gaps. Transmission declined after targeted outbreak response measures, including case management, vector control, and deployment of emergency vaccination in the affected localities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Population displacement and insecurity in southern Sudan, poor access to health services, low vaccination coverage, and favourable ecological conditions for Aedes vectors in forested highland areas enabled the reappearance of yellow fever. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses classified the viruses within an East African genotype that had circulated previously; no evidence of a novel strain or resistance was reported, so the outbreak is best viewed as a re-occurrence exploiting immunity and surveillance gaps.
Review: review – Retain as a well-documented Sudan outbreak with ~178 suspected cases and 27 deaths, but it is smaller than the subsequent 2005 South Kordofan and 2012 Darfur epidemics; if a strict ‘top 10’ is enforced, experts may ultimately drop this in favour of those larger Sudanese events. Sub-region has been corrected from “Eastern Africa” to “Northern Africa” to match the supplied UN classification for Sudan, and an additional peer‑reviewed source was added.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans; primarily sylvatic/intermediate cycle in rural and nomadic populations with Aedes spp. mosquitoes
Event.summary: Between September and December 2005, a large yellow fever epidemic occurred in South Kordofan State, Sudan, with over 600 suspected cases and around 180 deaths reported from multiple rural localities. The outbreak affected both settled communities and nomadic groups, in an area with limited health infrastructure and very low baseline vaccination coverage, and laboratory investigations also identified concurrent chikungunya virus circulation. A major emergency vaccination campaign supported by national authorities, WHO and partners, together with improved surveillance and the natural decline in vector densities, brought the outbreak under control by early 2006.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of competent vectors in rural and forest-edge environments, extensive movements of largely unvaccinated nomadic populations, weak surveillance and delayed laboratory confirmation, and limited access to clinical care created conditions for wide spread in South Kordofan. Internal mechanisms: Available reports describe circulation of endemic East African yellow fever virus genotypes rather than a new variant; the epidemic is best explained by re-occurrence driven by ecological and social factors, not documented viral change.
Review: retain – Added because Sudan’s 2005 South Kordofan epidemic (≈615 suspected cases and 183 deaths) is highlighted by WHO and EMRO as one of the largest yellow fever outbreaks in the Eastern Mediterranean Region in recent decades and clearly belongs among the top global post‑1990 events. Classified as re-occurrence in Northern Africa (Sudan), with no evidence for viral re-emergence in the sense of intrinsic pathogen change.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis
Host: Sheep (Ovis aries) transported from Inner Mongolia to Hunan Province
Event.summary: Origin: In 1994, an acute outbreak of yersiniosis occurred among a consignment of sheep transported from Inner Mongolia to Hunan Province in southern China, shortly after arrival at their destination. Development: Approximately 41% of the transported animals became clinically ill with acute systemic disease, and necropsy of affected sheep revealed multifocal lesions in skin, intestine, liver and lungs from which Yersinia enterocolitica biotype 3, a strain apparently distinct from previously reported ovine isolates in Europe and Oceania, was repeatedly cultured. End: The outbreak was limited to this transported group and resolved after the acute episode; the publication reports no further spread but emphasizes that the infection source remained undetermined and highlighted this event as a severe, unusual manifestation of ovine yersiniosis in China.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7953581/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers (external): Long-distance transport of sheep from Inner Mongolia to Hunan, associated crowding and stress, and movement into a different climatic region likely predisposed the flock to infection and severe clinical disease, although the original environmental or feed source of Y. enterocolitica was not identified. Internal mechanisms: All isolates from affected animals were identified as Y. enterocolitica biotype 3 and were described as apparently different from previously characterized ovine and caprine isolates in other countries, consistent with emergence of a distinct biotype with enhanced virulence for sheep in this setting.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7953581/))
Review: review – New high-impact ovine outbreak (China, 1994) added because it shows very high morbidity and mortality in sheep and involves a distinct biotype 3 strain; classified as re-emergence (strain/biotype change in a previously infected host system and subregion rather than first global emergence), with country and sub-region set according to the UNSD list and time span restricted to 1990+ as per protocol.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis
Host: Domestic South American camelids (alpacas, Vicugna pacos) in a commercial breeding herd
Event.summary: Origin: In autumn 2016, a commercial alpaca herd in Saskatchewan, Canada, experienced an abrupt onset of enterocolitis and sudden deaths among adults and crias, with an overall herd mortality of about 18.6%, prompting veterinary investigation. Development: Necropsy and laboratory testing of affected animals demonstrated Yersinia enterocolitica in multiple tissues and feces, and additional clinically affected alpacas were confirmed positive, establishing a herd-level outbreak of yersiniosis in a camelid species where only sporadic single-animal cases had previously been described in North America. End: Targeted antimicrobial treatment (oxytetracycline), supportive care, and farm biosecurity improvements were followed by cessation of new clinical cases, negative follow-up fecal cultures, and resolution of the outbreak, which was later reported as the first documented herd outbreak of yersiniosis in camelids in North America.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6625175/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers (external): Investigators noted multiple potential stressors and management-related risk factors, including overcrowding, suboptimal nutrition, and an abrupt drop in ambient temperature preceding the first deaths, which likely compromised immunity and facilitated expression of clinical yersiniosis in a naive alpaca herd. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain was confirmed as Y. enterocolitica but no novel biotype, resistance profile or clear intrinsic virulence change was reported; disease expression is therefore best explained by exposure of a susceptible, previously unexposed camelid population to an endemic pathogen under stressful environmental and husbandry conditions, rather than by documented genetic innovation of the bacterium.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6625175/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event is real and clearly among the most impactful animal yersiniosis outbreaks post‑1990, but the original classification as re-emergence is adjusted to re-occurrence because no novel biotype, host jump at species level, or other pathogen-level change was demonstrated; year field has been normalised to the yyyy-yyyy format and the countries field simplified to 'Canada [2016]' to match the event-sheet specification, and source URLs were pruned to retain the primary case report and one independent summary.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis
Host: Goats (Capra hircus) in a mixed-age meat goat herd (North West New South Wales)
Event.summary: Origin: Between December 2020 and February 2021, a mixed-age herd of approximately 260 goats in the Gunnedah district of North West New South Wales, Australia, developed unexplained ill thrift, rapid weight loss, submandibular and facial oedema, diarrhoea and deaths after owners initially attributed the problem to internal parasites. Development: Fourteen goats were affected and eight died over several weeks; necropsy of a severely affected doe showed ulcerative enterocolitis and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, and culture of ileal contents yielded a profuse growth of Yersinia enterocolitica, while parasitism, coccidiosis, Johne’s disease and enterotoxaemia were excluded. End: Following institution of nutritional supplementation (grain and lucerne hay) and treatment of clinically ill animals with oxytetracycline, clinical signs abated, submandibular oedema resolved and no further deaths occurred, leading investigators to classify this episode as a yersiniosis outbreak likely facilitated by concurrent summer rainfall, temperature fluctuations and unusually high rodent numbers on the farm.([dpi.nsw.gov.au](https://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0005/1321862/Animal-Health-Surveillance-Issue-2021-1.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers (external): The outbreak coincided with significant summer rainfall followed by a drop in ambient temperature and an exceptional local mouse plague, with rodents recognized as potential Yersinia carriers, as well as possible contribution from preceding parasite burdens and nutritional stress, all of which could have predisposed goats to infection. Internal mechanisms: The report did not identify a novel biotype or resistance phenotype; the episode is interpreted as re-occurrence of pathogenic Y. enterocolitica in a susceptible goat herd under environmentally and nutritionally stressful conditions rather than emergence of a new strain.([dpi.nsw.gov.au](https://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0005/1321862/Animal-Health-Surveillance-Issue-2021-1.pdf))
Review: review – Newly added event capturing a well-documented outbreak of Y. enterocolitica yersiniosis in a 260-head goat herd in New South Wales with 14 clinical cases and 8 deaths; classified as re-occurrence in a previously affected subregion (Oceania) driven by environmental and management stressors, with continent, sub-region, and country fields aligned to the UNSD-based Country sheet and the event year spanning 2020–2021 to reflect the documented December–February timeline.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: Plague bacillus
Host: Humans; commensal and wild rodents (sylvatic reservoirs); fleas (vectors).
Event.summary: In 1991 Namibia experienced a major bubonic plague epidemic in the north, notably in Ohangwena and neighbouring districts, with around 1,092 suspected human cases and 45 deaths following smaller outbreaks in 1989–1990. The outbreak spread across multiple rural communities as rodent die‑offs and high flea burdens around homes and grain stores facilitated rodent‑to‑human transmission until a national plague control programme with improved case detection, antibiotic treatment, and rodent and flea control was implemented. Over the following two to three years, reported human cases and deaths declined steeply and transmission was brought under control in the main epidemic focus, although natural Y. pestis foci persisted in local rodent populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High rodent densities around granaries and within poorly constructed houses, inadequate sanitation, cross‑border population movements, and limited prior surveillance in rural northern districts allowed rapid amplification of plague and delayed detection of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence for a novel Y. pestis strain; the epidemic reflects intense amplification and geographic spread of existing plague foci in local rodent reservoirs, with enhanced flea‑mediated transmission under favourable environmental and socio‑economic conditions.
Review: retain: Event is real, well documented and one of the largest single‑year national plague epidemics since 1990 (about 1,092 cases and 45 deaths), clearly within the global top‑10 by impact. Sub‑region (Southern Africa), country assignment and classification as re‑occurrence in an existing focus are all consistent with WHO data and the Namibia control programme evaluation; no structural changes were made to this row.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: Plague bacillus
Host: Humans; commensal rats (Rattus spp.) as primary reservoirs; fleas (Xenopsylla spp.) as vectors.
Event.summary: In late August 1994 India reported outbreaks of bubonic and pneumonic plague in several states after roughly 30 years without confirmed human cases, with WHO compiling about 876 cases and 54 deaths nationwide and other reports noting 693 serologically positive suspected cases and 56 deaths. The epidemic began in Beed district (Maharashtra) with bubonic disease and then spread to urban centres such as Surat (Gujarat), where overcrowding, poor sanitation, rat infestations and panic‑driven mass migration complicated control efforts and raised intense international concern about possible global spread. Rapid institution of antibiotic treatment, vector control, travel advisories, and strengthened surveillance halted transmission by mid‑October 1994; subsequent molecular work showed that the outbreak strains represented a distinct ribotype (designated S) of Y. pestis, underlining the episode as a modern urban re‑emergence of plague in India.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Deteriorating urban infrastructure, accumulation of garbage, proliferation of commensal rats in slums and unplanned housing, and severe crowding all facilitated rodent–flea–human transmission; mass movement of people out of affected cities in response to rumours and fear further disrupted control efforts and contributed to the economic and social impact. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing demonstrated that Y. pestis isolates from the 1994 outbreak belonged to a new ribotype (S), distinct from the historic Indian ribotype B, and that the same lineage was present in local rodents, fleas and patients, indicating clonal expansion of a distinct strain; this supports classification as re‑emergence driven in part by strain‑level genetic change, rather than a simple resurgence of an unchanged endemic lineage.
Review: review: Event is real and widely recognised as a major modern plague re‑emergence, with case and death estimates matching WHO and CDC summaries; it clearly belongs in the global top‑10 by impact because of both its size and its international public‑health consequences. The classification has been adjusted so that the event is coded as re‑emergence (true) but not re‑occurrence, in line with the instruction that categories are generally mutually exclusive and with evidence that the outbreak involved a distinct ribotype (S) of Y. pestis; external social and environmental drivers are still described in the mechanism field rather than encoded via a separate “re‑occurrence” flag. Source URLs have been expanded to include primary molecular and epidemiologic investigations of the 1994 Indian strains; a domain expert should review this balance between strain‑level novelty and long‑standing enzootic presence in India but the event’s inclusion is strongly supported.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: Plague bacillus
Host: Humans; wild rodents and other small mammals; fleas.
Event.summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has long been one of the world’s main plague foci, and in 2003 reported a particularly high burden with about 1,092 human cases and 68 deaths, mainly from rural highland zones of Ituri and adjacent areas in the northeast. This peak capped more than a decade of sustained transmission with recurrent outbreaks in conflict‑affected, impoverished communities where rodent control and access to health care were extremely limited. Intensified international support, targeted surveillance in natural foci, and expanded access to antibiotics and vector control gradually reduced—but did not eliminate—plague incidence in subsequent years, and DRC remained one of the leading contributors to global plague case counts through at least 2014.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Prolonged armed conflict, population displacement into rodent‑rich environments, food insecurity, poor housing, and severely weakened health services combined to increase human exposure to sylvatic rodent reservoirs and to delay recognition and treatment of plague cases; isolation of highland communities further hampered control. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate long‑established plague foci in north‑eastern DRC with sustained rodent–flea transmission rather than recently introduced or genetically novel strains; high transmission intensity and human vulnerability within these endemic systems explain the large multi‑year burden.
Review: retain: This row correctly captures one of the single largest country‑year plague burdens in the modern era (2003 DRC) and stands in for a broader high‑incidence period in north‑eastern DRC from the late 1990s through the early 2010s; it is clearly within the global top‑10 by impact. The sub‑region (Middle Africa), event type (re‑occurrence in a long‑known focus), and lack of intra‑/inter‑continental emergence are consistent with WHO and recent ecological analyses; no structural corrections to the row were required, though an additional reference on 2004–2014 DRC plague ecology has been added at the top‑level source list.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis pseudotuberculosis
Host: Farmed cervids (red deer, chital deer, elk, fallow deer and red deer–elk hybrids)
Event.summary: From January 1990 to December 1993, multiple outbreaks of acute diarrhea, sudden death, and wasting occurred in farmed deer herds on at least eight farms in Ontario, Canada, predominantly affecting recently weaned 4–6‑month‑old calves in autumn. Veterinary diagnostic laboratories confirmed Yersinia pseudotuberculosis (mainly serotype III) as the primary pathogen in 25 necropsied deer from several cervid species, with severe enteritis, mesenteric lymphadenitis, and high on‑farm mortality often following cold, wet snaps after milder weather. After recognition of yersiniosis as an emerging health problem in the expanding farmed cervid industry and implementation of management changes (stress reduction around weaning, improved nutrition, and prompt antimicrobial therapy), affected herds recovered and subsequent control programs focused on husbandry and vaccination.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/104063879500700112))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of a new farmed deer industry in Ontario with increasing herd size; management‑related stressors including recent weaning, high stocking density, transport, and adverse autumn weather (sudden cold snaps, often with rain) repeatedly precipitated disease; likely environmental build‑up and recirculation of Y. pseudotuberculosis on affected farms over several seasons. Internal mechanisms: All characterized isolates in this series were Y. pseudotuberculosis serotype III, a lineage already associated with enteric disease in ungulates; there is no evidence for a novel genotype, and the pattern is most consistent with stress‑triggered expression of disease from an established environmental and host reservoir rather than de novo evolution.
Review: review – Event is real and well documented in farmed cervids in Ontario, but the original classification as a first_detection event was incorrect because Y. pseudotuberculosis had been reported in deer and other livestock in North America and elsewhere before 1990 (e.g., fallow deer in Michigan, farmed deer in Australia and New Zealand).([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/104063879500700112)) The emergence type has been changed to re_occurrence (stress‑ and weather‑driven resurgence in a previously affected subregion), and the Countries field has been simplified to a single entry (Canada [1990]) consistent with the event‑year convention. Duplicate URLs in the source list were removed. Recommend expert review but retain this as a major multi‑farm cervid outbreak.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis pseudotuberculosis
Host: Captive ruminants in a wildlife park (multiple ungulate species)
Event.summary: In 1992, a wildlife park served by the Oklahoma Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory in the United States experienced an epizootic of acute, often fatal disease in several captive ruminants, which prompted necropsy and laboratory investigation. Microbiologic culture and histopathology confirmed Yersinia pseudotuberculosis infection in the affected ruminants, and an epornitic of Y. pseudotuberculosis infection was identified in the vicinity during the same period, indicating wider circulation of the pathogen in the local environment. The report emphasized the zoonotic risk to people in contact with infected animals and recommended strict hygiene precautions; the episode is presented as a discrete outbreak limited to that period.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1644638/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Mixed‑species captive ruminant collections at a wildlife park with shared feed and water sources and likely exposure to fecal contamination from wild rodents and birds would have facilitated fecal–oral transmission; the concurrent epornitic in the surrounding area suggests environmental contamination or a common‑source exposure outside the enclosures. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or host jump was described; the episode is consistent with stress‑precipitated yersiniosis caused by established pathogenic Y. pseudotuberculosis lineages in susceptible captive ruminants rather than de novo evolution, and is therefore interpreted here as a major re‑occurring outbreak in a previously affected host group.
Review: review – New event added to capture the widely cited 1992 epizootic of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis in captive ruminants in a wildlife park, which likely represents one of the more impactful post‑1990 outbreaks in ungulates. Location has been coded as United States of America based on the Oklahoma Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory affiliation in the original report; the exact state and species composition are not specified in the abstract and should be verified from the full article. Emergence type is coded as re_occurrence (no evidence of a new strain or continent/subregion jump). Recommend expert review and retention as a major ruminant outbreak if full‑text details confirm this interpretation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis pseudotuberculosis
Host: Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus) in a closed zoo colony
Event.summary: In June and July 2003, a closed colony of approximately 115 Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus) at the Rosamond Gifford Zoo in Syracuse, New York, experienced an outbreak of yersiniosis in which seven bats died over a six‑week period. Post‑mortem examination and bacteriology showed that about 70% of the colony had mesenteric lymphadenopathy, hepatic abscessation, and/or splenomegaly consistent with Yersinia pseudotuberculosis infection, and culture confirmed Y. pseudotuberculosis in many clinically affected and subclinically infected bats. Following recognition of the extent of infection, the colony was depopulated and the outbreak was highlighted as an important example of Y. pseudotuberculosis epizootics in captive bats and the need for rigorous hygiene, pest control, and surveillance because of the organism’s zoonotic potential.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19368235/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑density housing and long‑term confinement in an indoor bat colony, with chronic accumulation of fecal contamination and probable exposure to rodent or insect vectors, created conditions favorable for amplification and rapid within‑colony spread of Y. pseudotuberculosis; concomitant stressors in the captive environment (social hierarchy, handling, diet or microclimate) may have further reduced resistance. Internal mechanisms: Although no entirely novel genotype was reported, the outbreak strain produced widespread systemic disease with high lesion prevalence in a bat species not traditionally regarded as a primary host, illustrating the capacity of established Y. pseudotuberculosis lineages to exploit new ecological niches in stressed captive wildlife rather than representing a de novo evolutionary event.
Review: review – New event representing the well‑documented 2003 Yersinia pseudotuberculosis outbreak in a closed colony of Egyptian fruit bats at the Rosamond Gifford Zoo in Syracuse, New York. Year, magnitude (7 deaths over 6 weeks in a colony of ~115 bats), and lesion patterns are taken from Childs‑Sanford et al. (2009) and related summaries.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19368235/)) Classified as a high‑impact re_occurrence event in a captive wildlife host; recommend retention, with a human reviewer confirming species numbers and any additional management details from the full article.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis pseudotuberculosis
Host: Mixed zoo mammals and primates: addax (Addax nasomaculatus), agouti (Dasyprocta spp.), giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla), Arabian oryx (Oryx leucoryx), marmosets (Callithrix spp.), macaques (Macaca spp.)
Event.summary: Between February and April 2012, the National Zoo at the Ramat Gan Safari in central Israel experienced a multi‑species outbreak of acute enteric and systemic disease that caused the deaths of 15 animals including addax, Arabian oryx, agouti, a giant anteater, and several New World and Old World primates. Necropsy and laboratory investigations consistently isolated Yersinia pseudotuberculosis biovar 1, serotype O:1b, from intestines, mesenteric lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and other organs, with severe fibrino‑hemorrhagic enterocolitis and necrotizing lymphadenitis, and no other primary pathogen identified. Following diagnosis, the zoo implemented biosecurity measures and supportive treatment; the outbreak was temporally associated with an unusually cold, wet winter, and no further yersiniosis cases were reported from the facility in subsequent years.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/394106985_Outbreak_of_Yersinia_Pseudotuberculosis_in_a_Zoo_in_Israel))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Multi‑species husbandry in an open safari‑style ruminant yard with shared or adjacent enclosures created opportunities for fecal contamination of soil, feed, and water; the winter of 2012 in Israel was particularly cold and rainy, conditions known to favor Y. pseudotuberculosis persistence and trigger stress‑associated outbreaks. A nearby dump site attracting migratory birds was suggested as a possible source of introduction, and cross‑contamination from ruminant carcasses stored in a shared refrigerator likely spread infection to carnivores and primates.([ijvm.org.il](https://www.ijvm.org.il/sites/default/files/blum_sept_2023_internet.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain belonged to pathogenic biovar 1, serotype O:1b, and carried virulence genes inv and yadA, but did not represent a newly described genotype; disease reflects amplification of an existing zoonotic lineage in a stressed, susceptible zoo population rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: review – Event is strongly supported by Blum et al. (2023), which documents a 2012 multi‑species outbreak of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis at the Ramat Gan Safari.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/394106985_Outbreak_of_Yersinia_Pseudotuberculosis_in_a_Zoo_in_Israel)) Emergence type as re_occurrence in Western Asia is appropriate, as Y. pseudotuberculosis had previously been reported from Israeli cattle and primates; there is no evidence that this was a first_detection or continent‑level emergence. The Review field now notes the unusually cold, wet winter and likely role of carcass handling and a nearby dump as drivers, and adds the official journal PDF URL alongside the ResearchGate copy. Recommend retention with minor human verification of the country/subregion coding and species list.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis pseudotuberculosis
Host: Eurasian collared doves (Streptopelia decaocto) in a private aviary
Event.summary: In February 2015, a private aviary in California, United States, experienced sudden, high mortality in a small flock of adult Eurasian collared doves, with four of nine birds dying over a short period. Two carcasses submitted to the California Animal Health and Food Safety (CAHFS) Laboratory showed numerous pale yellow foci in liver and spleen, and histology confirmed acute, fatal septicemia with multifocal necrotizing hepatitis and splenitis caused by Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, which was isolated from multiple organs. After diagnosis, the outbreak was managed at the aviary level through removal of dead birds and husbandry changes, and no broader spread beyond this small collection was reported in the case series.([meridian.allenpress.com](https://meridian.allenpress.com/avian-diseases/article/60/1/82/209905/Yersinia-pseudotuberculosis-in-Eurasian-Collared))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑density captive housing of doves with shared food and water sources, potential contamination of feed or water by feces from reservoir species (wild birds or rodents), and possible recent introduction of an infected bird into a naïve flock likely contributed to rapid within‑aviary transmission. Internal mechanisms: The cases illustrate the ability of established Y. pseudotuberculosis lineages to cause acute septicemia and high mortality in naïve columbids; there is no evidence for a novel genotype or host species jump, so the episode is best interpreted as a re‑occurring outbreak from environmental or reservoir sources in a susceptible host group.
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects the 2015 private aviary outbreak in Eurasian collared doves in California described by Stoute et al. (2016), including flock size, mortality (4/9), pathology consistent with acute septicemia, and interpretation as a localized outbreak without wider spread.([meridian.allenpress.com](https://meridian.allenpress.com/avian-diseases/article/60/1/82/209905/Yersinia-pseudotuberculosis-in-Eurasian-Collared)) Emergence type as re_occurrence (not first_detection or inter‑continental) is appropriate because avian yersiniosis due to Y. pseudotuberculosis had been reported globally for decades. No corrections beyond minor wording have been made, and the event appears to be a valid, if relatively small, outbreak within the top‑10 set.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis pseudotuberculosis
Host: Captive rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) in a breeding or research colony
Event.summary: In 2016, a captive colony of 18 rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) in China experienced an outbreak of systemic disease in which six animals died, and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis serotype O:1a was identified as the causative agent. Standard bacteriologic, molecular, and serotyping methods confirmed the infection, and experimental infection of mice demonstrated the high pathogenicity of the outbreak strain, which carried multiple virulence genes and antimicrobial resistance determinants. This episode was notable as the first report of serotype O:1a infection in non‑human primates, and the authors concluded that this lineage represents a pathogen of concern for primate conservation and colony health.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27535288/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Close confinement of rhesus monkeys in a captive breeding or research facility with shared housing, feed, and water likely facilitated rapid transmission once Y. pseudotuberculosis was introduced, and stress associated with captivity, social hierarchy, and experimental or husbandry procedures may have predisposed some animals to severe disease. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain belonged to serotype O:1a, which had not previously been reported from non‑human primates, and demonstrated high virulence and antimicrobial resistance in experimental models, fulfilling the criteria for re_emergence driven by a new strain with altered pathogenic potential in an existing host system.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27535288/))
Review: review – New event added to represent the EcoHealth‑reported 2016 outbreak of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis serotype O:1a in captive rhesus monkeys in China, with 6 deaths among 18 animals and experimental confirmation of high virulence.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27535288/)) This is the first description of serotype O:1a in non‑human primates and therefore coded as re_emergence (novel strain in an existing host group) rather than simple re_occurrence. Country and subregion coding (China, Eastern Asia) are straightforward, but facility type (breeding vs research colony) is left generic because the abstract does not specify details; recommend human review of the full text to refine the host/facility description if needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis pseudotuberculosis
Host: Capybaras (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) kept in captivity at the Córdoba Zoo Conservation Center
Event.summary: In January 2020, the capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) group at the Córdoba Zoo Conservation Center in southern Spain experienced an outbreak of acute mortality in which five of seven animals (71% morbidity, 100% case fatality among affected) died within three days. Necropsy and histopathology revealed multifocal fibrinopurulent bronchopneumonia and generalized vascular lesions, and cultures from lung and other organs yielded Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, which was confirmed by PCR and MALDI‑TOF; two remaining adult males were treated prophylactically with marbofloxacin and survived. The authors described this as the first fatal outbreak of Y. pseudotuberculosis infection in zoo animals in Spain and stressed the potential implications for animal health, conservation of susceptible species, and public health.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0147957122000686))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Group housing of capybaras in an outdoor zoo enclosure with shared feed and water sources likely allowed fecal–oral transmission once Y. pseudotuberculosis was introduced, and environmental or climatic conditions in winter may have favored bacterial persistence and stress‑associated susceptibility. Potential sources include contamination of water or feed by wild rodents or birds, although the exact source was not identified. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak demonstrates high susceptibility of capybaras to systemic Y. pseudotuberculosis infection, with rapid progression and high fatality, and represents the first reported fatal Y. pseudotuberculosis outbreak in this host species and in Spanish zoo animals; this is therefore coded as re_emergence driven by host expansion to a new, highly susceptible rodent species in a captive conservation setting.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0147957122000686))
Review: review – New event added for the 2020 outbreak of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis in captive capybaras at the Córdoba Zoo Conservation Center in Spain, with 5 of 7 animals dying and confirmation by culture and molecular methods.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0147957122000686)) This is explicitly described as the first fatal Y. pseudotuberculosis outbreak in zoo animals in Spain and the first in capybaras, justifying classification as re_emergence via host expansion rather than simple re_occurrence. Continent, subregion, and country coding (Europe, Southern Europe, Spain) follow the UNSD scheme. Recommend human review to confirm that this event is among the top‑impact zoo outbreaks selected for the top‑10 list, but available data strongly support retention.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis pseudotuberculosis
Host: Captive parrots and passerine birds (e.g., eastern rosella Platycercus eximius, red‑rumped parrot Psephotus haematonotus) and other zoo birds in German collections
Event.summary: Around 2023, German zoos including the Zoological‑Botanical Garden Wilhelma in Stuttgart documented sudden deaths of psittacine birds such as an eastern rosella and a red‑rumped parrot, which died within a few days of onset with minimal premonitory signs. Post‑mortem examinations revealed granulomatous or necrotizing hepatitis, pneumonia, and enteritis, and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis was isolated from liver and other organs, fitting a pattern of high‑mortality avian yersiniosis previously reported in these collections; additional cases in other species were identified in retrospective and prospective surveillance between 2011 and 2024. The episode led to targeted fecal screening and environmental sampling in affected zoos, and during a one‑year monitoring period after the index cases, no further positive environmental samples were detected, indicating successful containment of that particular episode despite sporadic cases continuing over longer time scales.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11946000/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Outdoor mixed‑species aviary and zoo bird housing in temperate Central Europe exposes captive birds to wild birds and rodents that act as reservoirs, with seasonal factors (late autumn and winter) enhancing environmental survival of Y. pseudotuberculosis and physiological stress in birds; high stocking density and shared food and water sources facilitate fecal–oral transmission once introduced. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved established pathogenic Y. pseudotuberculosis lineages capable of causing septicemia in psittacines and other birds; no novel serotype or genotype was highlighted, so the episode most likely represents re_occurrence of a known zoo‑associated pathogen within susceptible aviary populations.
Review: retain – Event is consistent with the multi‑year dataset on Yersinia pseudotuberculosis infections in German zoo animals compiled by Hertwig et al., including sudden deaths in psittacine birds at Wilhelma and other facilities around 2023 and subsequent negative environmental surveillance.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11946000/)) Emergence type as re_occurrence (no new continent, subregion, or host species) appears appropriate, and continent/subregion/country coding matches the UNSD classification. No substantive corrections were required beyond aligning wording with the published study; retaining this event as one of the major recent avian outbreaks is justified.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Yersiniosis pseudotuberculosis
Host: Zoo aviary birds in central California: hooded pitta (Pitta sordida), beautiful fruit dove (Ptilinopus pulchellus), golden‑crested myna (Ampeliceps coronatus)
Event.summary: During winter and early spring 2025, a mixed‑species indoor aviary at a zoo in central California recorded the deaths of three exotic birds—a hooded pitta, a beautiful fruit dove, and a golden‑crested myna—over roughly three months, two of which showed only brief signs of respiratory distress, fluffed feathers, and lethargy before death. Necropsy and histopathology revealed necrotizing heterophilic and histiocytic hepatitis, splenitis, pneumonia, nephritis, myocarditis, and enteritis, and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis was consistently isolated and identified as the primary pathogen, whereas other organisms such as Streptococcus gallolyticus were considered opportunistic. Following confirmation, the zoo instituted an 11‑month quarantine of the aviary (20 March 2025 to 20 February 2026) and conducted an extensive field investigation of potential environmental sources; no new cases of yersiniosis were detected for over a year after the outbreak ended, and the episode was considered contained.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13096001/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Enclosed mixed‑species aviary with shared food and water sources and likely exposure to reservoir hosts such as wild birds and rodents created ideal conditions for fecal–oral transmission once Y. pseudotuberculosis was introduced; seasonal conditions during the cold, wet season may have favored bacterial persistence. A hooded pitta was suspected as a potential carrier bird based on epidemiologic investigation, and stress from captivity and interspecific interactions may have increased susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: A virulent Y. pseudotuberculosis lineage capable of causing systemic septicemia in multiple avian species was involved, but no novel genotype was reported; the outbreak demonstrates efficient spread and high pathogenicity of known Y. pseudotuberculosis strains in naïve zoo birds and is therefore classified as re_occurrence.
Review: retain – Event closely follows Resendiz‑Pozos et al. (2025), including the affected species, pathologic findings, outbreak timing, 11‑month quarantine period, and interpretation of the hooded pitta as a likely carrier.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13096001/)) Classification as a localized re_occurrence event in North America is appropriate; there is no evidence for a new strain or new continent/subregion, and the event clearly has substantial management impact for the zoo. No corrections beyond aligning URLs to the primary sources were needed, and the event should be retained as one of the major recent avian outbreaks.

EPP.scientific.name: Acanthospermum hispidum
EPP.common.name: hispid starbur, hispid starburr, bristly starbur
Host: Primarily associated with imported soybean and other grain commodities in port areas (Antwerpen and Gent), with plants establishing on unloading quays, near grain mills, grain dumps and other highly disturbed ruderal sites.
Event.summary: Between 1997 and 2005, Acanthospermum hispidum was repeatedly recorded for the first time in Belgium as an alien “grain adventive” emerging from imported soybean and other cereals in the major ports of Antwerpen and Gent. The weed established small, transient populations on unloading quays, grain dumps and other disturbed port substrates, but remained rare and reluctant to flower in the Belgian climate. By the mid‑2000s most occurrences were ephemeral and confined to port infrastructure, with no evidence that the species had become widely naturalized in surrounding agricultural land, though continued trade meant that new introductions remained possible.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International trade in contaminated grain (especially soybean) was the primary driver, with seeds arriving as contaminants in bulk commodities unloaded at the ports of Antwerpen and Gent; highly disturbed, open ruderal habitats on quays and grain dumps facilitated germination and short‑term establishment. Internal mechanisms: High propagule production (thousands of seeds per plant) and burr morphology enabling adhesion to materials and machinery aided local persistence in port environments, while broad ecological tolerance as a ruderal annual facilitated establishment in disturbed sites, although limited cold tolerance and daylength constraints likely restricted sustained reproduction in Western Europe.
Review: Review – Event retained as representing the first well-documented occurrence of A. hispidum in Europe as a grain-adventive weed in Belgian ports. Emergence-type coding has been corrected: ‘first_detection’ is set to No because global discovery predates this event by more than a century, ‘intra_continental_emergence’ is set to No, and ‘inter_continental_emergence’ is set to Yes to reflect first establishment on a new continent. Years, sub-region and country (Belgium [1997]) are consistent with the Belgian alien-flora account, and sources are appropriate (alienplantsbelgium for the event itself, POWO for corroborating distribution). Recommended for expert review mainly to confirm that no earlier pre‑1990 European records warrant redefining the timing of Europe’s inter-continental emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Acroptilon repens
EPP.common.name: hardheads, Russian knapweed, Turestan thistle
Host: Rangeland and pasture vegetation (native perennial grasses and forbs), alfalfa and other perennial forage crops, and weedy vegetation in irrigated cropland of the western United States
Event.summary: Around 1990, Russian knapweed infestations that had been present for decades in western U.S. rangelands began to expand rapidly, forming dense, nearly monospecific stands across large areas of semi‑arid grazing land and irrigated fields. By the late 1990s the species was estimated to infest roughly 557,000 ha in the western United States and was spreading at up to 14% per year in some regions, reaching about 1.2 million acres across 17 western states by 2000. As weed management programs, biological control initiatives and improved grazing and revegetation practices were implemented in the early 2000s, local populations were suppressed in some areas but the species remained a dominant, entrenched invader over much of its expanded range.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term overgrazing and soil disturbance in semi‑arid rangelands, expansion of irrigated agriculture and disturbed field margins, and widespread movement of contaminated hay, forage seed and soil facilitated rapid local and regional spread. Internal mechanisms: An extensive creeping rhizome system enabling vegetative spread, relatively low but sufficient seed production, and strong allelopathic effects that suppress neighboring plant germination and growth allowed Russian knapweed to displace native and desirable forage species and maintain dominance once established.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures a major 1990–2000 re‑occurrence episode in long‑invaded western U.S. rangelands, with acreage and spread rates supported by extension and research estimates.([extension.unr.edu](https://extension.unr.edu/publication.aspx?PubID=4109&utm_source=openai)) Geography, host system and emergence‑type coding (re‑occurrence only) are consistent with the definitions and the species’ much earlier arrival. I recommend keeping this row but noting that it forms part of a longer North American re‑occurrence episode that overlaps with Event 2; the two could be merged in a future revision to avoid double‑counting one broad invasion episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Acroptilon repens
EPP.common.name: hardheads, Russian knapweed, Turestan thistle
Host: Semi‑arid and arid rangelands, irrigated pastures, horticultural fields and roadsides in Argentina, affecting forage species and occasionally horses grazing heavily infested areas
Event.summary: Russian knapweed was introduced into Argentina around 1920–1930 with contaminated alfalfa seed and by the 1980s already infested roughly 2,000 ha in the Valle Inferior del Río Negro irrigation scheme, with surveys showing more than half of irrigated farms reporting the weed. From the 1990s onward, the species spread from these irrigated foci into surrounding semi‑arid and arid rangelands and along roadsides in several provinces, forming dense patches that reduced forage production and occasionally caused neurotoxic “chewing disease” in horses grazing heavily infested sites. Through the 2000s and early 2010s, national reviews and invasion‑risk assessments listed Rhaponticum/Acroptilon repens among the most important invasive plants of Argentina’s rangelands, prompting monitoring and management programs but without achieving broad‑scale containment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and degradation of rangelands, intensification of irrigated horticulture, road construction and vehicle‑mediated dispersal, and movement of contaminated hay and livestock between ranches facilitated spread of Russian knapweed from initial irrigated foci across Argentine drylands. Internal mechanisms: Very deep root systems and pronounced allelopathic effects help the species dominate in water‑limited environments, while tolerance of semi‑arid climates and the ability to regenerate from rhizome fragments allow it to persist under grazing and partial control efforts.
Review: review – This event represents one of the major global impacts of Russian knapweed and should be retained, but several details required correction. Historical work from the Valle Inferior del Río Negro shows introduction in about 1920–1930, substantial spread by the 1960s and around 2,000 ha affected by the mid‑1980s, so the weed was not merely “localized” by the mid‑1990s.([repositoriodigital.uns.edu.ar](https://repositoriodigital.uns.edu.ar/bitstream/123456789/4564/1/Gajardo%20Acroptilon%20repens.pdf)) I have adjusted the Event Year to 1990–2015 and the country‑specific date to “Argentina [1990]” to align the episode with the start of the analysis window while acknowledging earlier invasion history, and rewritten the summary to reflect pre‑1990 expansion and the post‑1990 spread into wider rangelands documented in national reviews and risk‑assessment studies.([ri.conicet.gov.ar](https://ri.conicet.gov.ar/handle/11336/12543?utm_source=openai)) Emergence type as re‑occurrence (not intra‑/inter‑continental, not first detection) remains appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Acroptilon repens
EPP.common.name: hardheads, Russian knapweed, Turestan thistle
Host: Cereal crops (especially wheat and other winter cereals), vineyards, horticultural crops, irrigation channels and drains, and pastures in southern and eastern Australia
Event.summary: By about 1990 Russian knapweed (creeping knapweed) was already present in parts of south‑eastern Australia but began to increase and spread within irrigated cropping regions and pastures, particularly in New South Wales and Victoria, where it invaded cereals, vineyards and horticultural crops. During the 1990s and 2000s it was detected and declared in additional Australian states, including South Australia, Western Australia and Queensland, and was recognized nationally as a serious invasive weed capable of reducing cereal yields by up to 80% and tainting flour and grain. Into the 2010s and up to 2020, strict biosecurity regulations, statewide eradication or containment programs, and farmer awareness campaigns have limited new incursions and aim to eradicate or contain remaining infestations, though scattered populations persist.

Review: review – The Australian episode is real and highly impactful, with national and state sources documenting widespread establishment in New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland and South Australia, recognition as a serious agricultural weed, and potential wheat yield losses of up to ~80%.([weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au](https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weed/CreepingKnapweed?utm_source=openai)) However, the original Countries field incorrectly treated Australian states (New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia, Queensland) as if they were separate countries, which violates the coding rules that restrict this field to UN‑recognized countries. I have corrected the Countries field to “Australia [1990]” and left the description of state‑level spread in the narrative summary instead. Because the species arrived in Australia well before 1990, this is appropriately coded as a re‑occurrence episode (not first detection, not inter‑continental emergence).([pir.sa.gov.au](https://www.pir.sa.gov.au/aghistory/natural_resources/weeds_pests_disease_management/overview_period_histories/science_to_the_rescue_19211970?utm_source=openai))

The study found that while many populations remained sensitive, a subset showed clear reductions in sensitivity, with relative resistance ratios up to about ninefold compared with the most sensitive population.
