Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expanding and often repeated use of glyphosate in southwestern Chinese agriculture, including non‑crop and pre‑plant applications, combined with movement of contaminated machinery or crop seed facilitating spread of tolerant or resistant biotypes. Internal mechanisms: the Guizhou study quantified resistance levels but did not characterise specific mechanisms; by analogy with other Chinese glyphosate‑resistant A. retroflexus populations, resistance is likely mediated by EPSPS target‑site changes and/or enhanced metabolism, contributing to a broader pattern of herbicide‑driven re‑emergence.
Review: review – Event retained and confined to southwestern China, with the time span 2021–2022 reflecting the survey and publication timeline. The original ChatGPT description slightly overstated mechanistic certainty; this has been softened to note that mechanisms were not determined in the Guizhou study and are inferred from other glyphosate‑resistant A. retroflexus populations in China.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Amaranthus retroflexus
EPP.common.name: red-root amaranth, redroot pigweed, careless weed, rough pigweed, redroot amaranth
Host: Sugar beet (CONVISO® SMART ALS herbicide‑tolerant system) and other ALS‑treated crops
Event.summary: In the early 2020s, growers using the CONVISO® SMART system (ALS herbicide‑tolerant sugar beet) in the Czech Republic reported poor control of Amaranthus retroflexus despite label‑rate applications of the ALS‑inhibiting mixture foramsulfuron + thiencarbazone‑methyl. Two A. retroflexus biotypes collected from these sugar beet fields were confirmed as highly resistant, with 12‑ to 351‑fold reduced sensitivity compared with a susceptible biotype and cross‑resistance to other ALS inhibitors such as imazamox and tribenuron‑methyl. Mechanistic work showed a Trp574Leu mutation in ALS and evidence that cytochrome P450‑mediated metabolism contributed to resistance in at least one biotype. By 2024 this resistance was recognised as an emerging threat for ALS‑based weed control in Czech sugar beet and potentially neighbouring regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid and extensive adoption of ALS‑tolerant sugar beet technologies and associated ALS‑inhibiting herbicides, together with widespread ALS‑inhibitor use in other crops, created high selection pressure on A. retroflexus populations in eastern and central Europe. Internal mechanisms: an ALS Trp574Leu target‑site mutation combined with enhanced metabolic detoxification in some biotypes conferred strong cross‑resistance to multiple ALS herbicides, constituting a textbook example of resistance‑mediated re‑emergence.
Review: review – Event retained; description now more closely aligned with the 2024 EWRS abstract and 2025 Weed Research article on ALS‑inhibitor resistance in A. retroflexus in CONVISO® SMART sugar beet. The 2021 start year is approximate, inferred from context that resistant biotypes were present before conference reporting. Classification as re‑emergence is appropriate because the species and ALS herbicides were already present in the region, and imported cases are not involved.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Amaranthus spinosus
EPP.common.name: pigweed, spiny amaranth
Host: Glyphosate‑resistant cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) and soybean (Glycine max) production systems in Mississippi row‑crop fields
Event.summary: In 2011, a grower in Lafayette County, Mississippi, reported spiny amaranth surviving labeled glyphosate applications in glyphosate‑resistant cotton fields where the species had long been present as a susceptible weed. Subsequent greenhouse and molecular studies conducted from 2011 to 2013 confirmed a strongly glyphosate‑resistant Amaranthus spinosus biotype whose resistance was conferred by high copy‑number amplification of the EPSPS gene identical to that in glyphosate‑resistant Palmer amaranth, indicating interspecific gene flow. Further work on the same hybrid lineage demonstrated ALS‑inhibitor resistance alleles originating from A. palmeri, creating multiple herbicide‑resistant spiny amaranth populations in cotton and soybean rotations and substantially increasing control costs and management complexity in affected Mississippi fields.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy and prolonged reliance on glyphosate in glyphosate‑resistant cotton and soybean systems, limited diversification of herbicide modes of action, and mixed infestations with glyphosate‑resistant Palmer amaranth (Amaranthus palmeri) produced strong selection pressure and frequent opportunities for interspecific hybridization. Internal mechanisms: Novel herbicide‑resistant biotypes arose via introgression from A. palmeri—amplified copies of the EPSPS gene conferring high‑level glyphosate resistance and ALS target‑site mutations conferring resistance to ALS‑inhibiting herbicides—resulting in multiple herbicide resistance in A. spinosus. This is a clear case of re‑emergence driven by genetic change (pesticide resistance and hybridization‑mediated gene transfer) in an already established weed species.
Review: retain: Event is well supported and represents one of the most impactful modern emergence episodes for this weed, documenting the first confirmed glyphosate‑resistant (and subsequently multiple herbicide‑resistant) A. spinosus populations in Mississippi cotton/soybean systems. Geography (USA – Mississippi, Northern America) and timing (grower observations in 2011, confirmation and characterization by 2013) are consistent with Nandula et al. 2014, later work on ALS resistance, and the International Herbicide‑Resistant Weed Database. Classification as re‑emergence only is appropriate: the species was long present in the region and the key novelty is the evolution and introgression of herbicide‑resistant biotypes. I have slightly broadened the host description to include soybean and updated the narrative and sources to reflect the later demonstration of ALS‑inhibitor resistance, but these changes do not alter event type; the row should be retained as a major re‑emergence episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Amaranthus spinosus
EPP.common.name: pigweed, spiny amaranth
Host: Weed of disturbed sites and cultivated areas (roadsides, public gardens, and cultivated land, including crop fields) in coastal Northern Tunisia
Event.summary: Between 2012 and 2016, Amaranthus spinosus was first detected and documented as a new alien species in Tunisia, where it had not previously been recorded despite being widespread elsewhere in tropical Africa and across the EPPO region. During botanical surveys, four populations were found in Bizerta, Bir Bouregba, Hammamet and Nabeul along roadsides, in public gardens and in cultivated areas, including one population covering about 25 m², indicating local establishment but still limited geographic extent. By 2018 the species was formally reported as a casual alien in Tunisia, with concerns that, if left unmanaged, it could spread further into agricultural systems and natural habitats as it has in other African countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance dispersal of contaminated seed or grain, movement via vehicles and agricultural machinery, and regional trade likely introduced A. spinosus into coastal Tunisia, where disturbed urban and peri‑urban habitats provided suitable establishment sites. Internal mechanisms: No new genotype was implicated; establishment relied on the general traits of A. spinosus as a prolific, disturbance‑adapted annual weed capable of producing very high seed numbers and exploiting open microsites in Mediterranean climates, allowing it to naturalize quickly once introduced.
Review: review: Corrected the type of emergence event. A. spinosus was already present elsewhere in the Northern Africa subregion (e.g. Egypt and Sudan, where it is treated as an introduced/naturalized species) prior to 2012, so the Tunisian record represents spread to a new country within an already invaded subregion, not introduction into a new subregion or continent. Accordingly, I changed first_detection from true to false and intra_continental_emergence from true to false, and set re_occurrence to true to reflect a new occurrence within a previously affected subregion driven by propagule pressure and human‑mediated dispersal. Continent, sub‑region, country, and time span (2012–2016) are consistent with the EPPO Reporting Service note and underlying floristic work. The event is retained because it documents a clearly dated, well‑described northward expansion at the Mediterranean margin, but it should be interpreted as a regional re‑occurrence rather than a continental/sub‑regional first emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Amaranthus spinosus
EPP.common.name: pigweed, spiny amaranth
Host: Weed in roadsides, pavements, ornamental tree nurseries, gardens and wastelands along Morocco’s Atlantic coastal zone; potential invader of agricultural fields and pastures
Event.summary: In 2021, field surveys along the Atlantic coastline of Morocco documented Amaranthus spinosus for the first time in the country, where it had not previously been part of the native or alien flora. The species was found at multiple localities (Mehdia, Sidi Boughaba, Rabat and Casablanca) in diverse disturbed habitats including roadsides, pavements, ornamental nurseries, gardens and wastelands, with population sizes ranging from a few individuals to over 1,000 plants, suggesting multiple introductions and rapid local spread. By 2023, EPPO reported these findings as a new record for Morocco and highlighted concern that, given the species’ behavior as a problematic weed in agricultural areas and pastures elsewhere, it could expand from coastal urban sites into cropland if not monitored and managed.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction via contaminated plant seed, grain, nursery stock and agricultural machinery, combined with high propagule pressure in trade hubs along the Atlantic coast and the availability of disturbed urban and peri‑urban habitats, enabled initial establishment in Morocco. Internal mechanisms: The species’ inherent traits—prolific seed production, effective dispersal by wind and water, tolerance of a wide range of soil and moisture conditions, and competitive ability in disturbed sites—facilitated rapid local population growth without evidence for a novel strain, representing geographic range expansion within Africa rather than a genetic shift.
Review: review: As with Tunisia, this event was originally labeled as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence, but Amaranthus spinosus was already established in the Northern Africa subregion (e.g. Egypt, and since 2012–2016 Tunisia) before its first national record in Morocco. Under the given definitions, spread to a new country within the same sub‑region should not be classified as intra‑continental emergence. I therefore set first_detection to false and intra_continental_emergence to false, and marked re_occurrence as true to indicate further spread and increased incidence within a previously affected subregion driven by human‑mediated dispersal and disturbed habitats. Continent, sub‑region, country and year (Morocco, Northern Africa, 2021) match the EPPO 2023/100 report and underlying Flora Mediterranea paper; the event is retained but flagged for review because it is a national first record rather than a sub‑regional first emergence, and current agronomic impacts remain mostly prospective.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia artemisiifolia
EPP.common.name: annual ragweed, common ragweed, ragweed, low ragweed, Roman wormwood, short ragweed, small ragweed
Host: Weed of annual crops (maize, soybean, peanut), orchards, plantations and disturbed non-crop habitats (roadsides, riverbanks) across northern and eastern China
Event.summary: Common ragweed, first recorded in China in 1935 near Hangzhou, remained relatively localized until the late 20th century, when populations began to expand rapidly in northern and eastern provinces after about 1990. During the 1990s and 2000s the species spread along transport corridors and agricultural frontiers, so that by around 2010–2020 it was recorded as naturalized in more than 20 provinces spanning northern, central, eastern and parts of southern China, with dense infestations in some croplands and river basins. Recent analyses show continuing spread and niche filling in cooler northern provinces and along the southern periphery of its stable range, accompanied by increasing concern for both crop losses and pollen allergies and prompting local management and biological control studies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid economic development in China with major increases in road and rail networks, long‑distance movement of contaminated grain and forage seed, large‑scale land‑use change and disturbance, and climate warming that created more suitable thermal regimes all facilitated the spread from initial bridgehead regions. Internal mechanisms: reciprocal transplant and common‑garden studies indicate rapid evolution of invasive traits (e.g. higher growth and reproductive allocation in Chinese populations compared with native US populations) and regional adaptation to local climates, consistent with novel trait evolution and inherent geographic range expansion; together these justify classification as both intra‑continental emergence into new Chinese subregions and re‑emergence linked to genetic and phenotypic shifts.
Review: retain – The chronology (localized presence after first record in 1935 followed by rapid post-1990 expansion into >20 provinces) and mechanisms (trade- and infrastructure-driven spread plus well-documented rapid evolution of invasive traits and climatic adaptation) are consistent with EPPO distribution data and recent Chinese ecological/genomic studies; classifying this as both intra-continental emergence and re-emergence is therefore appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia artemisiifolia
EPP.common.name: annual ragweed, common ragweed, ragweed, low ragweed, Roman wormwood, short ragweed, small ragweed
Host: Ruderal and agricultural weed of pastures, arable land, roadsides and urban wasteland, with pollen acting as a major aeroallergen for human populations in affected cities
Event.summary: Although common ragweed has been present and naturalized in South Africa since at least the late 19th century, it was not previously regarded as a major aeroallergen until Ambrosia pollen was first consistently detected by the South African Pollen Network from 2019 onwards at several monitoring sites. During 2019–2024, aerobiological and eDNA metabarcoding studies demonstrated recurring Ambrosia pollen seasons in cities such as Durban, Potchefstroom, Pretoria, Johannesburg and Kimberley, and documented baseline sensitization to Ambrosia allergens in South African patients, highlighting ragweed as an emerging contributor to late‑summer respiratory allergy. By 2024, ragweed pollen was recognised as a growing aeroallergen of concern in South Africa, prompting calls for its inclusion in diagnostic testing panels and for improved management of established ragweed populations in urban and agricultural landscapes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: long‑standing but previously overlooked naturalized populations of Ambrosia spp. in South Africa, combined with urban expansion, roadside disturbance and possibly favourable recent rainfall and temperature regimes, have increased the likelihood that ragweed reaches reproductive maturity and produces significant pollen near population centres; the establishment of a national pollen monitoring network since 2019 has also greatly improved detection and awareness of Ambrosia pollen. Internal mechanisms: no specific new African genotype has yet been identified; this episode is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence in a previously colonized subregion where external environmental change and improved monitoring have revealed a substantial aeroallergen burden rather than as a genetically driven re‑emergence.
Review: review – This new row has been added to capture the recent 2019–2024 recognition of common ragweed as a significant aeroallergen in South Africa, based on national pollen monitoring and sensitization data; it is classified as a re-occurrence in a subregion where the plant has been naturalized since the 19th century. The temporal bounds (2019–2024) are tied to the start of systematic pollen monitoring rather than to first botanical records, and some uncertainty remains about the exact onset and magnitude of health impacts, so the event should be retained but reviewed by a regional expert to refine dates and quantify burden.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia confertiflora
EPP.common.name: weakleaf bur ragweed, weakleaf burr ragweed, ragweed
Host: Ruderal and disturbed vegetation along roadsides, agricultural field edges and other open disturbed habitats
Event.summary: In 2023, Ambrosia confertiflora was documented for the first time as a naturalized alien in central Tunisia, marking the first well‑established Ambrosia species reported for the African vascular flora and the first known establishment of this species on the African continent. The plant was found forming small but established populations in several localities in central Tunisia, mainly in ruderal, disturbed habitats along roadsides and edges of cultivated fields, indicating local spread after an initially unnoticed introduction. At the time of reporting, populations remained geographically limited, but the authors highlighted a substantial risk of further expansion into disturbed and agricultural areas in North Africa if not managed early.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely accidental introduction via contaminated seed, fodder or grain trade from regions where Ambrosia confertiflora is established (e.g. the Americas or Western Asia), followed by establishment in road verges, waste places and agricultural margins that provide open, disturbed niches. Road construction, vehicle traffic and movement of soil along transportation corridors probably facilitated local dispersal of the burrs. Internal mechanisms: the same traits that promote invasiveness elsewhere—high reproductive output, buoyant and spiny achenes suited to animal and vehicle dispersal, vegetative regeneration from rootstocks, and tolerance of Mediterranean semi‑arid climates—underpin its initial geographic range expansion into North Africa; there is no specific evidence yet for novel genotypes, resistance or host shifts in Tunisian populations.
Review: review – Retain this event as the first confirmed inter‑continental emergence of Ambrosia confertiflora into Africa, documented by floristic work in central Tunisia and recognized as the first well‑established Ambrosia in the African vascular flora. Corrected misclassification of the “first_detection” flag (now false because global first detection of the species predates 1990 in its native range) so that the event is characterized solely as an inter‑continental emergence. The year 2023 is used as the detection/publication year; earlier unnoticed presence cannot be excluded but is not documented. Given that current populations are still geographically limited and impacts are mostly potential at this stage, the event is flagged for expert review in future updates (e.g. to adjust the date range or add further African countries if the species spreads), but it should be retained due to its high significance as the first continental establishment.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia grayi
EPP.common.name: woollyleaf bur ragweed (woollyleaf bursage, bur ragweed, lagoonweed, woollyleaf franseria, woollyleaf povertyweed)
Host: Field crops (wheat and dry beans), vineyards (grapes), peach and loquat orchards, and adjacent disturbed grassland/roadside vegetation near Shfeya Junction in northern Israel.
Event.summary: Ambrosia grayi, a perennial ragweed native to northern Mexico and the south‑central Great Plains of the USA, was first formally documented in Israel in June 2017, when a dense, spreading infestation was identified in vineyards, a peach orchard and adjacent cereal fields near the Shfeya agricultural school between Zikhron Ya’akov and Pardes Hanna. Over 2017–2024 the population persisted and expanded vegetatively within these cultivated fields, forming thousands of interconnected shoots over roughly 0.5–4 ha, prompting its categorization as an alien, quarantine weed and inclusion on the EPPO Alert List because of its potential to invade further agricultural land and contribute allergenic ragweed pollen. Intensive eradication efforts by Israel’s Plant Protection and Inspection Services and local land managers, including repeated herbicide treatments and delimiting a quarantine zone, have substantially reduced the infested area but have not yet achieved complete eradication by 2025, so the episode remains an ongoing, closely monitored inter‑continental introduction confined to a single focus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction into Israel was almost certainly unintentional, most likely via contaminated grain, animal feed, soil or machinery associated with agricultural trade, paralleling documented pathways for other alien Ambrosia species in the region. The infestation established in intensively managed agricultural landscapes (vineyards, orchards and arable fields) with repeated soil disturbance and irrigation, conditions that favor rhizomatous weeds and facilitate local spread along field margins, irrigation ditches and machinery tracks. Internal mechanisms: A. grayi reproduces vigorously via deep, long‑lived rhizomes capable of resprouting after drought and control measures, and can emerge across a broad range of temperatures (around 20/30 °C night/day) and soil moisture conditions, while producing a limited number of viable seeds that may aid occasional dispersal. This combination of clonal growth, stress tolerance and absence of specialized natural enemies in Israel underpins its ability to form dense colonies from a single introduction focus, although the small current range and aggressive eradication have so far constrained further expansion.
Review: retain – New inter‑continental emergence event added for introduction and establishment of Ambrosia grayi in Israel starting with formal detection in 2017. Supported by EPPO distribution and alert‑list records, Israeli botanical accounts (including the 2017 Kalanit article), and peer‑reviewed studies on distribution, allergenicity and weed biology; geographic fields (Asia, Western Asia, Israel) and event type (inter‑continental emergence only) are consistent with project definitions, and no evidence suggests additional multi‑country episodes that would warrant splitting this into multiple rows.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia tenuifolia
EPP.common.name: slimleaf bur ragweed, slimleaf burr ragweed, field ragweed
Host: Non‑crop ruderal vegetation and disturbed Mediterranean shrublands (roadsides, railways, waste ground) with occasional occurrence along agricultural field margins.
Event.summary: Seed of Ambrosia tenuifolia was probably introduced to Israel with contaminated grain or forage shipments from the Americas and the species was first documented as an adventive plant near Hadera and Ma’agan Michael on the Mediterranean coastal plain in 1991. During the 1990s–2010s, small perennial stands persisted along railways and roadsides and in other disturbed coastal sites, remaining much rarer than the invasive A. confertiflora and other ragweed species. By the late 2010s, A. tenuifolia was still confined to a few coastal localities but was recognized in floristic surveys and allergenicity studies as a naturalized perennial ragweed of limited distribution in Israel.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance introduction via contaminated seed or other traded plant material (grain, fodder) combined with high levels of disturbance along transport corridors (railways, roads) and around fishponds and feed centres, which favour establishment of ruderal weeds. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion facilitated by a perennial rhizomatous growth form, clonal spread via creeping roots, and tolerance of open, dry, disturbed Mediterranean habitats; local dispersal by seed and rhizome fragments allows maintenance of small but persistent colonies even though the species remains less invasive than other Ambrosia taxa in Israel.
Review: retain – Verified that A. tenuifolia was first recorded as an adventive plant in Israel in 1991 and that no earlier Asian records are known, so classification as a first detection for Western Asia and an inter‑continental emergence event is appropriate. Geographic fields (Asia / Western Asia / Israel) align with the UNSD scheme and sources consistently describe the taxon as a rare, localized perennial weed confined to a few coastal localities; no corrections to timing, geography or event type are required, and the cited floristic and allergenicity studies are relevant and sufficient for this event.

EPP.scientific.name: Anastrepha grandis
EPP.common.name: South American cucurbit fruit fly
Host: Wild cucurbit Fevillea cordifolia (only confirmed host in the infested area during this episode), with commercial cucurbit crops (melons, watermelons, pumpkins, squash, cucumbers) remaining officially free of infestation but at high risk and therefore subject to quarantine restrictions and intensive surveillance.
Event.summary: In early 2009, Anastrepha grandis was detected for the first time in Panama through the national fruit-fly surveillance network, with adults captured in sentinel traps in Darién Province and in eastern Panamá Province near the Colombian border, indicating recent spread from infested areas in northern South America. Emergency measures including internal quarantines, intensified trapping, insecticide bait-sprays, and extensive host-fruit sampling were implemented, and from 2009 through 2015 official trap data showed that A. grandis remained confined to a series of foci in eastern Panama while more than 12,000 kg of sampled cultivated cucurbit fruit from across the country remained free of larvae. In 2012 the wild cucurbit Fevillea cordifolia was confirmed as the sole reproductive host in the affected area, and by the mid‑2010s declining trap catches plus systems-approach agreements with trading partners allowed exports of melons and watermelons from pest-free western production zones to resume under strict surveillance, while the eastern infestation continued under official control with restricted distribution.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Natural spread from established populations in northern South America into the Darién–eastern Panamá corridor, facilitated by contiguous forested and riparian habitats and the presence of abundant wild host plants near the Panama–Colombia border; stringent internal quarantines prevented movement of cucurbit fruit from infested eastern zones into the main production areas to the west but required costly surveillance and trade negotiations. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive potential, multivoltinism and the ability to exploit Fevillea cordifolia as a wild host allowed establishment and persistence in humid lowland forest habitats; no evidence of novel strains or resistance was reported, so this episode is best interpreted as inherent geographic range expansion into a new sub-region of the continent rather than genetic change in the pest.
Review: review – Event correctly captures the major 2009 incursion of A. grandis into Panama and its status as the first confirmed establishment in the Central America sub-region, supported by NAPPO alerts, EPPO and IPPC/NPPO documentation. Corrections made: (1) reclassified the event from including 'first_detection = true' to 'first_detection = false' because first detection in the plant host system occurred in Brazil in the 19th century; this episode is a sub-continental range expansion, not the global first detection. (2) Refined the event-year span from '2009-2018' to '2009-2015' to align with official trap-capture data presented by the NPPO of Panama, which document positive captures through 2015 with subsequent years characterized by greatly reduced or zero captures in official traps but continued low-level presence on the wild host; the broader regulatory status (present, restricted, under official control) persists beyond 2015 but is better treated as the aftermath of this emergence. (3) Narrowed the host description from a broad list of cultivated cucurbits plus Fevillea cordifolia to emphasize F. cordifolia as the only confirmed reproductive host in Panama during this period, with commercial cucurbits treated as at-risk but not yet infested, in line with extensive negative fruit-sampling data. (4) Updated the driver description to focus on documented spread pathways (natural dispersal along riparian corridors and association with wild hosts) and removed speculative emphasis on movement of infested commercial cucurbit fruit within Panama, which existing surveys do not support. (5) Added the NAPPO Phytosanitary Alert System link as a primary event source and retained EPPO/IPP/MIDA and recent review articles as contextual sources; overall structure and classification as an intra-continental emergence with significant trade impact are retained but should be re-checked by a human reviewer given the interpretive choices about the event end-year and the continued low-level presence on wild hosts.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Anastrepha grandis
EPP.common.name: South American cucurbit fruit fly
Host: Field-grown cucurbit crops in São Paulo state, notably pumpkins and squash (Cucurbita maxima, Cucurbita moschata × C. maxima hybrids) in mixed cucurbit plantings.
Event.summary: Between late 2010 and early 2012, mixed cucurbit plantings at the APTA Regional experimental station in Monte Alegre do Sul (São Paulo state) experienced heavy natural infestation by Anastrepha grandis, with the pest attacking pumpkins and squash in a region where it was already known but usually maintained at lower levels. In the 2011 harvest, field monitoring and economic analysis documented severe yield losses, with moranga squash and a dry pumpkin type suffering approximately 46% and 16% fruit loss, respectively, due to larval damage and consequent unmarketability of infested fruits. In the 2011–2012 cropping season at the same site, following adjustments in cropping patterns and improved management, infestation intensity and associated losses declined markedly (to roughly 4.6–5.5%), demonstrating that local agronomic practices and control measures can strongly modulate the economic impact of this endemic pest.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Local agronomic conditions—including continuous or dense cucurbit cultivation, limited or poorly synchronized use of insecticidal and cultural controls, and favorable seasonal weather—likely allowed resident A. grandis populations to build up to damaging levels in Monte Alegre do Sul, while strong market demand for cucurbits sustained extensive host availability. Internal mechanisms: No evidence was reported of new strains, host shifts or resistance; the episode reflects the species’ inherent capacity for rapid population increase and multiple generations per year on preferred cucurbit hosts, so it is best interpreted as a re-occurrence driven by ecological and management factors rather than by evolutionary change.
Review: review – Event describes a well-documented local resurgence of A. grandis in cucurbit fields at Monte Alegre do Sul, São Paulo, with quantitative loss estimates (46% and 16% losses in 2011 and much lower losses in 2012) that make it one of the few episodes where economic impact has been rigorously measured. Classification as a re-occurrence (endemic pest flare-up) without intra- or inter-continental components, and without first-detection attributes, is appropriate because A. grandis was already long established in São Paulo and the episode did not involve new host species or genetic changes. Minor curation steps: (1) Confirmed that the field trials comprised two cropping periods (October 2010–March 2011 and September 2011–February 2012), so the year span '2010-2012' is acceptable but users should note that the major documented losses correspond to the 2011 and 2012 harvests. (2) Replaced aggregator links (manualzilla) with the original proceedings PDF (sicam.com.br/anais-i-sicam.pdf) for the economic-loss study and retained additional peer-reviewed sources on A. grandis biology and distribution as contextual references. No contradictions with current distribution or management knowledge were found, but the event remains flagged for review so that human curators can confirm that this localized episode is indeed among the top-impact events they wish to retain for this species.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis spiraecola
EPP.common.name: black bean aphid
Host: Citrus spp.; various native and introduced shrubs and trees in agroecosystems and disturbed habitats on multiple islands
Event.summary: In 1991, Aphis spiraecola was first recorded in the Galápagos Islands, where it was not part of the native insect fauna and is considered an introduced, established species. During the 1990s and 2000s it spread to several islands (including Española, Fernandina, Isabela, Santa Cruz and Santiago), colonising citrus, ornamentals and other shrubs in cultivated and disturbed habitats and becoming naturalised. It is now regarded as a potentially invasive but established component of the Galápagos arthropod fauna, and management focuses on general invasive-species quarantine and biosecurity rather than targeted eradication.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction to Galápagos was almost certainly accidental via infested nursery stock or other plant material imported from mainland South America or abroad, consistent with its general pathway as a contaminant on live plants. Internal mechanisms: Broad host range and rapid parthenogenetic reproduction under subtropical island climates allowed A. spiraecola to establish and spread across islands once introduced, without any special new strain being documented.
Review: review – Retain as an important island invasion. The event-type has been corrected from re-occurrence to intra-continental emergence, because this is the first establishment of A. spiraecola in a previously uninfested island system within the South America continent rather than a resurgence in a known subregion. Timing (first record 1991) and island distribution are well supported by the Galápagos Species Database and alien-insect surveys, but the exact host range in natural vegetation could be further verified.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis spiraecola
EPP.common.name: black bean aphid
Host: Citrus spp.; later also various native and ornamental hosts (e.g. Pittosporum coccineum, Artia balansae, Ixora cauliflora)
Event.summary: In 2004 Aphis spiraecola was first recorded from New Caledonia on citrus, marking its arrival in this Melanesian biodiversity hotspot where it had not previously been reported. Over the following years it was repeatedly found on citrus and then on several native and ornamental hosts, indicating establishment and spread beyond initial plantings. The species is now regarded as a polyphagous, cosmopolitan invasive aphid in New Caledonia, raising concern for citrus production and for the risk of transmitting plant viruses in a region with high endemic biodiversity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The introduction pathway was almost certainly infested citrus or ornamental nursery stock imported from other parts of Oceania or Asia, combined with intensive horticulture and initially limited surveillance for non‑regulated aphid species. Internal mechanisms: Polyphagy and ability to reproduce continuously under warm conditions support rapid population build‑up and persistence in New Caledonia’s subtropical climate, allowing A. spiraecola to colonise both cultivated and native hosts once present.
Review: review – Retain as a key island invasion in Oceania, but simplify emergence-type coding. The event clearly represents an intra-continental emergence into a new sub-region (Melanesia) within Oceania from established populations elsewhere; there is no evidence for novel strains or host shifts that would justify a re-emergence label, so the re-emergence flag has been set to false. First-record year (2004) and the host range are consistent with IRD reports and subsequent aphid-fauna surveys, but continued colonisation of additional native hosts should be monitored.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis spiraecola
EPP.common.name: black bean aphid
Host: Vegetable crops in smallholder and peri-urban systems (including Brassicaceae and other leafy and fruiting vegetables)
Event.summary: During vegetable agroecosystem surveys in Benin in the mid‑2000s, Aphis spiraecola was recorded for the first time in West Africa, expanding its known African range beyond earlier records from North and East/Southern Africa. Over subsequent seasons it was found across several agro‑ecological zones within Benin’s urban and peri‑urban vegetable production areas, contributing to mixed aphid complexes that damage cabbage and other vegetables and that can potentially vector plant viruses. The species is now considered part of the invasive aphid fauna of West African vegetable systems, and its management is usually embedded in broader IPM programmes targeting multiple aphid species.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and diversification of vegetable production, increased movement of planting material and produce within and into West Africa, and lack of specific quarantine attention to minor aphid species likely facilitated westward spread of A. spiraecola within Africa. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and polyphagy (ability to exploit many vegetable hosts and associated weeds) aided its establishment once it reached West African agroecosystems.
Review: review – Retain as the first well-documented West African emergence, but adjust the emergence-type. The event is best classified as intra-continental emergence into a new African sub-region (Western Africa), because A. spiraecola was already present in other African sub-regions; the previous re-emergence flag has been removed given the lack of evidence for new strains or resistance. The timing and interpretation as the first West African record are supported by Benin surveys and associated book chapters, though any earlier unpublished records from neighbouring countries should be checked.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis gossypii
EPP.common.name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) across the U.S. cotton belt, especially Texas High Plains and California’s San Joaquin Valley
Event.summary: Beginning with major outbreaks in West Texas in 1991 and followed by severe mid‑season infestations in California’s San Joaquin Valley in 1994–1995, Aphis gossypii escalated from a sporadic pest to a key annual pest of U.S. cotton. During 1991–1997, mid‑season aphid populations frequently reached damaging levels over large acreages, with the 1995 San Joaquin Valley outbreak alone causing an estimated 5–6% lint yield loss and widespread sticky‑cotton problems that triggered multiple insecticide applications and emergency management discussions. By the late 1990s, improved understanding of aphid ecology, greater use of selective insecticides, conservation of natural enemies and better integration of aphid thresholds into IPM programs reduced the frequency of extreme outbreaks, although A. gossypii has remained a major management concern in parts of the U.S. cotton belt.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive use of broad‑spectrum pyrethroids and other insecticides against lepidopteran and lygus pests disrupted natural enemies, while adoption of plant growth regulators and higher nitrogen fertilization created lush, favorable host plants; hot, dry summers in key regions further favored aphid population growth and honeydew accumulation. Internal mechanisms: Field studies from this period documented substantial resistance of A. gossypii to several organophosphates and pyrethroids in parts of the U.S., contributing to control failures and justifying classification as a resistance‑linked re‑emergence of a previously minor pest.
Review: review – new event capturing the early‑ to mid‑1990s transformation of A. gossypii from a sporadic to key pest in the U.S. cotton belt, especially the 1991 Texas and 1995 San Joaquin Valley outbreaks; classification as re‑emergence (insecticide resistance plus agronomic changes) and the 1991–1997 window are well supported by extension and conference reports, but a curator should confirm the precise years and magnitude of yield losses using U.S. cotton loss survey data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis gossypii
EPP.common.name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) in central Pakistan (Multan region)
Event.summary: Between 1997 and 2000, bioassay monitoring of Aphis gossypii populations collected from cotton fields around Multan in central Pakistan revealed extremely high resistance ratios to seven pyrethroid insecticides compared with a susceptible laboratory strain. These findings indicated that field populations had evolved strong multi‑pyrethroid resistance, consistent with field reports of poor aphid control despite repeated sprays and prompting recommendations to modify insecticide programs and introduce alternative chemistries. Subsequent studies on Pakistani cotton aphid populations confirmed complex cross‑resistance patterns across organophosphate and carbamate insecticides as well, shaping regional insecticide resistance management strategies even though precise yield losses attributable to this resistance episode were not always quantified.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive and repeated use of pyrethroids in Pakistani cotton, often in mixtures and without sufficient rotation among modes of action, created strong selection pressure on A. gossypii populations; large contiguous cotton areas and limited non‑chemical control options further favored spread of resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Laboratory studies documented very high resistance ratios to multiple pyrethroids and changes in detoxification enzyme activity consistent with metabolic resistance and potentially altered target sites, making this a clear example of resistance‑driven re‑emergence of a long‑established pest.
Review: retain – Pakistan cotton aphid pyrethroid resistance between 1997 and 2000 is well documented by quantitative bioassays and clearly represents a major resistance‑driven re‑emergence event; geography (Southern Asia, Pakistan) and classification as re‑emergence are appropriate, though regional yield impacts are inferred rather than always reported explicitly.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis gossypii
EPP.common.name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum), predominantly Bt cotton but also non‑Bt cotton in northern and central China
Event.summary: Around 1999, shortly after rapid adoption of Bt cotton in the Yellow River and Yangtze River cotton regions of China, Aphis gossypii and other sucking pests resurged as secondary pests in fields where broad‑spectrum insecticide sprays targeting bollworm had been reduced. Over roughly 1999–2004, county‑ and household‑level surveys and economic analyses documented increasing aphid and other secondary pest problems across multiple northern provinces, leading to renewed insecticide use and concerns that these outbreaks eroded some of the anticipated economic and environmental benefits of Bt cotton. By the mid‑2000s, adjustments in integrated pest management, including more selective sprays, conservation of natural enemies and revised planting patterns, moderated aphid pressure, although A. gossypii has remained an important recurrent pest in Chinese cotton systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread adoption of Bt cotton reduced the need for frequent broad‑spectrum insecticide sprays that had previously suppressed a complex of secondary pests; in this new environment, combined with favorable weather and abundant host plants in surrounding landscapes, A. gossypii populations were able to increase to damaging levels. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel aphid biotype was implicated in this resurgence; available data are consistent with a re‑occurrence driven primarily by external agronomic and ecological change rather than by clear genetic change in the aphid.
Review: retain – this Bt‑cotton secondary‑pest resurgence in northern/central China (1999–2004) is well supported by economic and ecological studies and is among the most impactful modern A. gossypii outbreaks; classification as re‑occurrence (external agronomic driver) and geography (Asia, Eastern Asia, China) match UNSD regions and the event definition.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis gossypii
EPP.common.name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) and, in some regions, nearby cucurbits and vegetables exposed to similar insecticide regimes in northern and eastern China
Event.summary: From the late 1990s into the early 2000s, field monitoring in Shandong and other key cotton‑producing provinces of China documented rapid increases in resistance of Aphis gossypii to several major insecticide groups, including pyrethroids (e.g. fenvalerate), organophosphates (e.g. omethoate, carbosulfan) and later neonicotinoids (imidacloprid, acetamiprid). Comparative bioassays using samples collected in 1985, 1999 and 2004 showed resistance ratios climbing to very high levels in multiple cotton regions, and subsequent work revealed widespread and heterogeneous imidacloprid resistance across China, contributing to control failures on cotton and some cucurbit crops and raising concern about the sustainability of conventional chemical control programs. In the following decade, resistance‑management recommendations and rotation with alternative modes of action were promoted, but high and spatially variable resistance to several insecticide classes has persisted in many Chinese A. gossypii populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term, intensive use of organophosphates, carbamates, pyrethroids and later neonicotinoids on cotton and surrounding vegetable crops, often with limited rotation among chemistries, imposed strong selection for resistance. Internal mechanisms: Field and laboratory studies documented high resistance ratios to multiple insecticide classes and identified both enhanced detoxification (e.g. elevated esterases and P450s) and target‑site modifications (including nicotinic acetylcholine receptor and acetylcholinesterase changes), fitting the definition of a re‑emergence event driven by evolved insecticide resistance.
Review: review – end year adjusted from 2007 to 2004 so that the event aligns with years when very high resistance levels were directly measured (1985 vs 1999 and 2004) in Chinese cotton fields; classification as resistance‑driven re‑emergence is sound, but a curator may wish to consider whether post‑2004 resistance dynamics should be summarized as a separate, later episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis gossypii
EPP.common.name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) in irrigated cotton systems of eastern Australia, mainly New South Wales and Queensland
Event.summary: In the mid‑2000s, Australian cotton fields began to show declining control of Aphis gossypii with neonicotinoid seed treatments and foliar sprays that had previously been highly effective. By about 2010–2011, detailed bioassays confirmed strong resistance to imidacloprid and other neonicotinoids in cotton aphid populations from several cotton valleys, marking the first well‑documented neonicotinoid‑resistant A. gossypii populations on the continent and causing serious management difficulties in some seasons. From 2011–2012 onwards, industry‑wide resistance‑management programs, including rotation away from neonicotinoids, more selective aphicides and strengthened IPM guidelines, were implemented to slow further resistance increase and to recover acceptable control levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy reliance on neonicotinoid seed treatments and foliar sprays in Australian cotton, together with the aphid’s rapid parthenogenetic reproduction and multiple generations per season, created intense selection pressure; regional agronomic practices limited opportunities for susceptible immigration. Internal mechanisms: Bioassays and molecular work showed high levels of resistance to thiamethoxam and other neonicotinoids, likely mediated by overexpression of detoxification enzymes and changes in nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunits, with cross‑resistance complicating management and necessitating formal resistance‑management strategies.
Review: retain – the Australian neonicotinoid resistance episode is well described and clearly among the most important resistance‑driven A. gossypii events globally; dates and geography are appropriate, though the precise onset (mid‑2000s) could be fine‑tuned by a curator using local monitoring records.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis gossypii
EPP.common.name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cucurbit crops (melon, watermelon, zucchini, squash and pumpkin) in open‑field and greenhouse systems in southeastern and eastern Spain
Event.summary: Cucurbit aphid‑borne yellows virus (CABYV) was first detected in 2004 in open‑field melon and zucchini crops in the Murcia region of Spain, where surveys already found high incidence of yellowing disease and Aphis gossypii as the dominant colonizing aphid. From 2004 through at least 2022, long‑term monitoring in major cucurbit‑growing areas (Murcia, Castilla‑La Mancha and Alicante) showed CABYV becoming the most prevalent virus in melon, squash, zucchini and watermelon, with incidences often exceeding 50–80% in symptomatic samples and frequent mixed infections with watermelon mosaic virus and other aphid‑borne viruses, leading to substantial yield and quality losses. By the early 2020s, CABYV remained widespread and difficult to control, and management focused on resistant or tolerant cultivars, cultural practices and vector management, but A. gossypii continued to drive recurrent, high‑impact virus–aphid outbreaks in Spanish cucurbit systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of cucurbit production in Mediterranean Spain, presence of multiple susceptible cucurbit hosts and weed reservoirs, and climatic conditions favorable to melon aphid population build‑up created conditions in which CABYV could become endemic; limitations of chemical vector control and increased organic production further complicated management. Internal mechanisms: No new aphid biotype has been implicated; the main biological factor is the inherent efficiency of A. gossypii (and to a lesser extent Myzus persicae) as a persistent vector of CABYV and other cucurbit viruses, so this episode is best described as a re‑occurrence of impact in a long‑established aphid–crop system rather than a genetically novel strain in the aphid.
Review: review – start year changed from 2011 to 2004 to reflect first detection and already high CABYV incidence in Murcia, and the event is now treated as a long linked episode of CABYV‑driven losses in Spanish cucurbits; classification as re‑occurrence (no new A. gossypii genotype) and geography (Southern Europe, Spain) are appropriate, but a curator may wish to refine quantitative estimates of yield loss.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis gossypii
EPP.common.name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) in the southeastern U.S. cotton belt (e.g. Alabama, Georgia, Florida, Louisiana and neighbouring states)
Event.summary: In 2017, cotton fields in coastal Alabama showing stunting, leaf rolling and blue‑green discoloration consistent with cotton blue disease were found to be infected with cotton leafroll dwarf virus (CLRDV), with abundant populations of Aphis gossypii present, marking the first confirmed CLRDV outbreak in U.S. cotton. Over the 2017–2019 seasons, CLRDV was detected across much of the southeastern and south‑central U.S. cotton belt, and in Alabama alone disease incidence of 3–30% in affected fields was estimated to have caused yield losses of about 560 kg/ha over roughly a quarter of the state’s cotton area in 2018, while surveys showed near‑100% infection in some sentinel plots even where symptoms were mild. By 2020, CLRDV had been confirmed in cotton in numerous states from Texas to Virginia, and although many U.S. cultivars proved tolerant and average regional yields remained acceptable, CLRDV and its efficient vector A. gossypii became a persistent concern, with management focusing on avoidance of highly susceptible varieties and improved understanding of vector ecology rather than on intensive aphid spraying, which has limited effect on this persistently transmitted virus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and rapid spread of CLRDV into an aphid‑rich, high‑value cotton production landscape created a new disease problem in a system where viral diseases of cotton had previously been negligible; widespread planting of cultivars of variable susceptibility and the presence of alternative host plants and aphid reservoirs favored virus establishment. Internal mechanisms: Aphis gossypii itself did not show evidence of new biotypes in this episode; instead, its existing capacity as the primary CLRDV vector in cotton, combined with persistent transmission biology, underpins the event, so it is best classified as a re‑occurrence of aphid impact mediated by a new virus rather than a re‑emergence caused by changes in the aphid.
Review: review – added to capture the major emergence of CLRDV in the U.S. cotton belt, where A. gossypii is the primary vector; geography (North America, Northern America, United States) and classification as a re‑occurrence (new virus in an established vector–host system) are appropriate, but exact yield loss estimates and the list of affected states should be rechecked against updated surveillance data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Didymella pinodes
EPP.common.name: pea foot rot fungus
Host: Field pea (Pisum sativum) in rainfed grain production systems
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through the mid‑2000s, ascochyta blight (black spot) dominated by Didymella pinodes became one of the most important constraints on field pea in southern and western Australia, with the pathogen present across virtually all pea-growing areas and causing frequent epidemics in seasons with cool, wet conditions. Meta‑analysis and field studies reported yield losses commonly around 10–25%, occasionally reaching 30–75% in severely affected crops, with national losses estimated at roughly AUD $20–25 million per year; these pressures led to development of tools such as the Blackspot Manager forecasting system, changes in rotations and sowing dates, and increased fungicide use, yet the disease has remained a major limitation on pea expansion.([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/8634086/ascochyta-blight-of-field-pea--pisum-sativum-?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of pea area into lower-rainfall and continuous-cropping zones; short or pea-on-pea rotations; retention of infected stubble that produces airborne ascospores; and seasons with prolonged cool, moist weather during early growth all favored intense epidemics and high carry‑over inoculum. Internal mechanisms: The pathogen’s hemibiotrophic lifestyle, prolific production of ascospores and pycnidiospores on residue and foliage, seedborne transmission, and the widespread use of cultivars lacking strong quantitative resistance underpinned a geographic and epidemic expansion of an already-adapted pathogen, without clear evidence of a single novel strain driving the outbreaks.
Review: Decision: review – This Australian episode clearly represents a high‑impact, multi‑year resurgence of D. pinodes in major pea areas and should remain among the top global events, but the original classification overstated internal evolutionary change. Re-emergence has been set from Yes to No because the literature attributes losses mainly to agronomic drivers (cropping intensity, rotation, environment, susceptible cultivars) and the polycyclic biology of an already established pathogen, without evidence for a distinct new strain or resistance-breaking genotype as the primary driver. All other geographic fields and sources are appropriate for this event.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Didymella pinodes
EPP.common.name: pea foot rot fungus
Host: Field pea (Pisum sativum) in Prairie grain systems
Event.summary: Over the 1990s and 2000s, Didymella pinodes became the most common and economically important member of the ascochyta blight complex on field pea across the Canadian Prairies, where pea acreage expanded from under 0.1 million ha in the 1970s to around 1–1.5 million ha. Surveys and yield‑loss studies showed chronic mycosphaerella blight with average yield losses near 10% and reported losses up to 30–80% in heavily infected crops or trials under cool, wet conditions, making ascochyta/Mycosphaerella blight the primary foliar disease of pea in western Canada and a major constraint on both yield and seed quality.([collectionscanada.gc.ca](https://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/obj/s4/f2/dsk2/ftp03/MQ37569.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of pea acreage in short rotations on the Prairies; use of cultivars bred mainly for resistance to Ascochyta pisi rather than D. pinodes; frequent cool, moist weather from late vegetative stages through pod fill; and widespread retention of infested residue and use of seed with low levels of ascochyta infection created persistent high inoculum pressure and favored severe epidemics. Internal mechanisms: D. pinodes’ superior competitive fitness within the ascochyta complex, ability to survive for years in seed and residue, and efficient splash‑ and wind‑dispersed sporulation allowed it to dominate disease complexes and drive recurrent yield loss, but available evidence points to gradual selection within a long‑present population rather than emergence of a single novel genotype.
Review: Decision: review – This event represents a major, well‑documented regional re‑occurrence of severe D. pinodes–driven mycosphaerella blight in a very large production area and should remain in the high‑impact set. However, re_emergence has been corrected from Yes to No, as available Canadian work attributes the increasing dominance of D. pinodes primarily to cropping patterns, seedborne inoculum and environmental conditions rather than to a clearly defined new strain or resistance-breaking pathotype. The country, subregion and continent fields are consistent with the Canadian Prairies focus, and event-specific sources were replaced with Canada-focused extension and research documents that better quantify local impact.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Didymella pinodes
EPP.common.name: pea foot rot fungus
Host: Field pea (Pisum sativum) in temperate Atlantic and northern French production regions
Event.summary: From roughly 1990 through the mid‑2000s, Mycosphaerella blight caused by Didymella pinodes was consistently identified as the most destructive foliar disease of pea in France, particularly in Atlantic and northern production areas with cool, wet springs. Field trials and modeling studies indicated that in about seven years out of ten, Mycosphaerella blight reduced yields by around 20% on average, with documented loss ranges up to 30–70% under highly conducive conditions, prompting widespread preventive fungicide programs and intensive research on disease–yield relationships and resistance but without eliminating the pathogen as a chronic constraint on pea.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229642943_A_simple_model_of_pea_Pisum_sativum_growth_affected_by_Mycosphaerella_pinodes?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large and relatively intensive pea acreage in short rotations with cereals, frequent conservation of infected pea debris, and humid temperate weather during stem elongation and flowering provided repeated opportunities for early infection and rapid canopy blighting; economic incentives favored systematic fungicide programs rather than major shifts away from pea. Internal mechanisms: D. pinodes’ ability to infect all aerial organs, produce abundant ascospores on senescent tissue, and cause substantial seed infection, combined with limited durable host resistance, maintained high pathogen pressure but there is no strong evidence that a discrete new genotype drove these French epidemics; this episode is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence in an established pathosystem.
Review: Decision: review – This new event has been added because French pea production is repeatedly cited as one of the systems most severely affected by D. pinodes, with long‑term average yield reductions of about 20% and higher losses in bad years, clearly placing it among the top global impact episodes. It is classified as a re-occurrence (chronic, climate‑ and management‑driven disease) with no evidence of a novel strain; geographic fields (Europe | Western Europe; France) match UNSD conventions. Sources focus on French yield‑loss quantification and population studies; this event should be retained after expert review of the chosen time window.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Didymella pinodes
EPP.common.name: pea foot rot fungus
Host: Field pea (Pisum sativum) in highland rainfed smallholder systems
Event.summary: Between the early 1990s and mid‑2010s, ascochyta blight of field pea, with Mycosphaerella/Didymella pinodes as the dominant pathogen, was repeatedly reported as one of the most widespread and destructive diseases of pea in the Ethiopian highlands, including Arsi, Bale and southern highland zones. Regional surveys and experiments indicate typical yield losses of 25–70%, with near‑total crop failure in susceptible landraces under persistently wet high‑altitude conditions, and more recent trials have shown grain yield more than doubling under intensive fungicide protection compared with unsprayed controls, underscoring the disease’s major impact on food security and income.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/350755059_Grain_Yield_and_Yield_Components_of_Field_Pea_Pisum_sativum_L_As_Influenced_by_Ascochyta_Blight_Mycosphaerella_pinodes_Disease_in_the_Highlands_of_Bale_Oromia?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and continued importance of field pea as a staple legume in highland Ethiopia; reliance on susceptible local landraces or only moderately resistant varieties; dense stands planted in cool, humid environments with long leaf‑wetness periods; and widespread use of farm‑saved seed carrying ascochyta infection all contributed to intense, recurrent epidemics. Internal mechanisms: D. pinodes is considered the main pathogen within the Ethiopian ascochyta complex and shows strong aggressiveness on pea, but available studies emphasize high inoculum pressure and environment rather than distinct new genotypes; the episode is therefore best categorized as severe re‑occurrence rather than emergence of a novel strain.
Review: Decision: review – This new African highlands event has been added because Ethiopian sources consistently rank D. pinodes–driven ascochyta blight as the most severe foliar disease of field pea, with large, quantified yield losses and widespread geographic extent, making it clearly among the most impactful modern episodes for this pathogen. It is classified as a re-occurrence (longstanding pathogen with repeated severe epidemics), with continent/subregion/country fields aligned to UNSD (Africa | Eastern Africa; Ethiopia). Given the societal importance of pea in Ethiopia, this event should be retained after further expert validation of severity estimates and time bounds.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Didymella pinodes
EPP.common.name: pea foot rot fungus
Host: Field pea (Pisum sativum) in humid eastern Chinese production (e.g. Zhejiang Province)
Event.summary: From the early 2000s through at least the mid‑2010s, repeated ascochyta blight epidemics affected field pea in humid eastern Chinese regions such as Zhejiang Province, where surveys of diseased crops at multiple locations recovered only Ascochyta/Didymella pinodes from 65 isolates, confirming it as the predominant causal agent. Chinese and global syntheses estimate typical yield losses of around 10–30% from ascochyta blight in China under conducive conditions, with greater reductions in susceptible cultivars, leading to recommendations for fungicide sprays and screening for improved resistance to manage this chronic, climate‑driven disease pressure.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27148177/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of pea cultivation in warm, humid monsoon climates with frequent rainfall during vegetative growth and flowering; dense canopies; and use of susceptible local varieties or breeding lines created environments highly favorable to D. pinodes infection and spread. Internal mechanisms: The surveys and pathogenicity tests demonstrate that D. pinodes is well adapted to these environments and dominant within the ascochyta complex, but they do not implicate a discrete novel genotype, so this episode is best interpreted as a significant regional re‑occurrence in an already globally distributed pathogen.
Review: Decision: review – This new event has been added to capture high, recurrent ascochyta blight pressure in humid eastern Chinese pea regions where surveys showed D. pinodes as the sole or dominant pathogen and reviews report substantial typical yield losses. It is classified as re-occurrence rather than emergence, because pea ascochyta blight and D. pinodes were known in China earlier, and no distinct new pathotype is described. Geography (Asia | Eastern Asia; China) follows UNSD; time bounds are approximate and should be validated against more detailed national data before final retention.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactericera cockerelli
EPP.common.name: potato/tomato psyllid
Host: Greenhouse and field tomato, capsicum, potato, tamarillo and other solanaceous crops
Event.summary: In the summer of 2005–2006, Bactericera cockerelli invaded New Zealand, with the first authenticated detections made in May–June 2006 in glasshouses and nearby outdoor crops around Auckland. Over the next three years the psyllid spread rapidly by natural dispersal and human-assisted movement of infested nursery plants, becoming established across much of the North Island and the northern South Island and infesting greenhouse and field solanaceous crops. By 2009 the species was widespread and regarded as a serious invasive pest, leading authorities to abandon eradication and focus on long‑term management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International trade and the movement of infested plant material or contaminated packaging most likely introduced the psyllid from the Americas into New Zealand; once introduced, a suitable temperate climate, extensive greenhouse production and widespread solanaceous hosts facilitated establishment and rapid spread. Internal mechanisms: No major intrinsic biological change relative to American populations has been documented; this event primarily reflects geographic range expansion into a previously pest‑free continent, enabled by the existing association between B. cockerelli and CLso and the psyllid’s strong dispersal capacity.
Review: retain (minor clean‑up). Event correctly captures the first establishment of B. cockerelli in New Zealand as an inter-continental emergence into Oceania, which has had major economic consequences. Sub-region and country fields match the UNSD scheme (Oceania | Australia and New Zealand; New Zealand [2006]). The main edit is removal of a duplicated NZPPS article in the source list; remaining sources (Teulon et al. on incursion and dispersal, EPPO distribution record, and New Zealand pest-management papers) provide strong documentation of timing, spread and impact.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactericera cockerelli
EPP.common.name: potato/tomato psyllid
Host: Potato (field crops), tamarillo, greenhouse tomato and capsicum
Event.summary: From 2008, soon after establishment of B. cockerelli, New Zealand growers and diagnosticians reported severe foliar symptoms and internal tuber discoloration in potatoes and other solanaceous crops resembling zebra chip. During 2008–2010, Candidatus Liberibacter solanacearum was detected in symptomatic potatoes, tamarillo and other hosts, confirming a new plant disease complex tightly associated with the invasive psyllid. By the early 2010s, zebra chip and related disorders transmitted by B. cockerelli were causing major yield and quality losses in potatoes and tamarillo, triggering substantial industry investment in research, surveillance and integrated management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid nationwide spread and high densities of the recently introduced psyllid in both greenhouse and field production systems, coupled with susceptible cultivars and initially limited awareness and control experience, allowed CLso to disseminate widely before effective management practices were in place. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of CLso haplotypes in New Zealand via B. cockerelli constituted a novel strain/genotype emergence event for the region; the combination of an efficient vector and a new phloem‑limited bacterium resulted in increased virulence/pathogenicity compared with prior psyllid feeding damage alone, and created a high-impact vector–pathogen complex in key solanaceous crops.
Review: retain. This event correctly distinguishes the emergence of CLso and zebra chip disease in New Zealand (a re-emergence of B. cockerelli’s impact via a new pathogen association) from the earlier vector incursion. Oceania and sub-region coding are correct, and classification as re-emergence without intra-/inter-continental emergence matches the definitions. Sources (JIPM biology/management paper, Plant Health Progress review, EPPO distribution, national factsheets) are appropriate and specific to this disease phase.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactericera cockerelli
EPP.common.name: potato/tomato psyllid
Host: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) in major processing and fresh-market production regions of Idaho, Oregon and Washington (Pacific Northwest)
Event.summary: Late in the 2011 growing season, zebra chip disease and its vector Bactericera cockerelli were detected for the first time in commercial potato fields in the Columbia Basin of Washington and Oregon, and in Idaho, a region that produces more than half of U.S. potatoes. During 2011–2012, outbreaks in these Pacific Northwest production areas led to widespread detection of CLso‑infected psyllids and tubers and triggered intensive insecticide programs to protect high‑value processing crops. By about 2013, regional monitoring networks and refined management practices had reduced zebra chip incidence to relatively low levels, but both the psyllid and CLso remained established, making the disease an ongoing threat in the Pacific Northwest.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance movement of infected psyllids and/or planting material from previously affected regions (e.g. Texas and other southwestern/central states), coupled with extensive, contiguous potato production in the Columbia Basin and favorable climatic conditions, allowed rapid establishment of the psyllid–CLso complex in the Pacific Northwest. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of CLso haplotypes A and B into potato‑associated B. cockerelli populations in the region created a new high‑impact disease system in an area that had not previously experienced zebra chip, representing a re-emergence of the psyllid’s impact in the same continental sub-region through arrival of the pathogen, rather than through genetic change in the vector itself.
Review: added – retain. EPP.scientific.name: Bactericera cockerelli
EPP.common.name: potato/tomato psyllid

Event.summary: From late 2017, Bactericera cockerelli was observed for the first time attacking potatoes in northern Ecuador, and subsequent surveys found the psyllid widely distributed on solanaceous crops in Andean provinces such as Carchi, Imbabura, Pichincha, Cotopaxi and Tungurahua. By around 2020, B. cockerelli and the associated phytoplasma/CLso complex were recognized as major constraints on potato and other solanaceous crops in the northern Andean corridor, prompting the development of national monitoring, identification manuals and integrated management strategies.

Under the provided UNSD scheme, Ecuador lies in the South America sub-region of the South America continent, whereas earlier occurrences of B. cockerelli were confined to the Central America sub-region; therefore, this is coded as an intra-continental emergence (new sub-region within the same continent) rather than an inter-continental event. Because the impact in Ecuador depends critically on the introduction of CLso and its interaction with the psyllid, re-emergence is also marked as true, consistent with how similar vector–pathogen transitions are treated for earlier events. EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera correcta
EPP.common.name: guava fruit fly
Host: Imported and locally grown tropical and subtropical fruits (e.g. guava, mango, citrus and other soft fruits) in urban and peri-urban settings

Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This event is retained as a major re-occurrence episode because it summarises a long series of guava fruit fly incursions into Florida that have required repeated regulatory responses and illustrate sustained invasion pressure, even though no establishment occurred. I extended the end year from 2013 to 2015 to include the Boynton Beach captures documented by FDACS, and clarified that the first inter-continental emergence into North America occurred earlier in California (1986), so this Florida sequence should not be coded as inter-continental emergence. Accordingly, I set inter_continental_emergence to 'false' and re_occurrence to 'true' only, consistent with APHIS and FDACS documentation that regard these records as transient incursions without establishment.

Event.summary: Following the first Western Hemisphere record of Bactrocera correcta in Garden Grove, Orange County, California, in August 1986, the species was repeatedly detected in California from the early 1990s through 2012, mainly in the greater Los Angeles–Orange County region and other urban fruit-growing areas. Despite frequent incursions, intensified trapping, male-annihilation treatments and host-fruit removal meant that each detected infestation was declared eradicated, and B. correcta is still considered absent from California, though it remains a key target of the state’s invasive fruit fly detection network.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large volumes of air travel and trade between California and tropical fruit-producing regions in Asia, including both legal and smuggled shipments of fresh fruit, create repeated opportunities for introduction; widespread backyard plantings of guava and other host trees in urban and suburban landscapes provide resources where introduced flies can survive long enough to be trapped. Strong regulatory frameworks and public concern in California lead to rapid, resource-intensive responses each time a fly is detected. Internal mechanisms: No evidence indicates new strains or altered virulence; the incursions are driven by repeated introduction pressure acting on a polyphagous, high-fecundity species whose biology supports transient establishment but which has so far been eradicated whenever detected.

EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Host: Mango, guava, lychee and other fleshy fruits and vegetables in backyard trees and orchards in southern Mauritius
Event.summary: On 5 June 1996, a single female oriental fruit fly was trapped near Camp Carol close to Mauritius’ international airport, and subsequent intensive trapping quickly revealed a localized but serious infestation in the south of the island, marking the first confirmed establishment of Bactrocera dorsalis in Africa.([b3.net.nz](https://b3.net.nz/gerda/refs/73.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Over 1996–1999, authorities implemented an island‑scale eradication campaign based on male annihilation and protein‑bait sprays, containing the population to roughly 150 km² and progressively driving trap catches to zero.([b3.net.nz](https://b3.net.nz/gerda/refs/73.pdf?utm_source=openai)) After more than two consecutive years without detections, Mauritius declared B. dorsalis eradicated in mid‑1999 and EPPO recorded the African introduction as successfully eliminated, although the episode highlighted the continent’s vulnerability to this species.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction was most likely via infested fruit or other plant material carried by air travellers or cargo from South or South‑East Asia into Mauritius, with detection aided by an existing area‑wide fruit fly monitoring network.([b3.net.nz](https://b3.net.nz/gerda/refs/73.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: High reproductive potential and broad host range allowed rapid build‑up after arrival, but the population remained geographically limited, enabling eradication using attractant‑based male annihilation and bait sprays before long‑distance secondary spread occurred.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added).
