This event was missing in the original file but is clearly one of the most important post‑1990 emergence events for B. dorsalis: it represents the first documented establishment of the species in Africa (Mauritius), followed by a textbook area‑wide eradication, and is widely cited in EPPO and Mauritian sources.([b3.net.nz](https://b3.net.nz/gerda/refs/73.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Classified as inter‑continental emergence (Asia→Africa) with first_detection and first_global_emergence set to No to respect the global‑scale definitions; sub‑region and country entries follow the UNSD list (Eastern Africa; Mauritius only). Flagged for awareness but not for further technical review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera zonata
EPP.common.name: peach fruit fly
Host: Guava (Psidium guajava), mango (Mangifera indica), stone fruits (Prunus spp.), fig (Ficus carica) and other orchard fruits
Event.summary: Bactrocera zonata was first recorded causing serious damage in Egypt in the early 1990s, with outbreaks reported from Kalubia and Fayoum governorates on guava and other fruits, representing the first major establishment of the species in continental North Africa. Over the mid‑ to late‑1990s the fly spread rapidly along the Nile valley and delta, reaching Alexandria, Giza and later Upper Egypt and desert oases, and quickly became one of the most injurious fruit flies in the country. By the early 2000s it was widespread and often dominant in orchards, displacing Mediterranean fruit fly in some areas and causing serious losses in mango and guava production despite large‑scale control programmes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely introductions via regional or international trade in infested fruit, combined with highly suitable irrigated horticultural systems in the Nile valley and delta, continuous host availability in mixed fruit orchards and limited early detection and control capacity. Internal mechanisms: strong competitive ability relative to Ceratitis capitata, broad host range and high reproductive potential enabling rapid geographic expansion and very high local population densities.
Review: retain – This is correctly characterized as a major intra-continental emergence event: it captures the first large-scale establishment of B. zonata in the Northern Africa subregion and its rapid spread and economic impact in Egypt. The 1993 start date reflects the onset of damaging outbreaks reported in national and regional literature, even though EPPO’s first official report dates from the late 1990s; no changes to geography or emergence-type classification are needed, but the slight uncertainty in the precise first-detection year is already reflected in the high-but-not-perfect confidence score.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera zonata
EPP.common.name: peach fruit fly
Host: Various fruit crops in southern Iran (including mango and other fleshy fruits)
Event.summary: In 2002 the Iranian NPPO officially confirmed the first presence of Bactrocera zonata in a limited area in southern Iran, indicating westward spread of the species from its long-established South Asian core range. Following initial detection, the pest remained restricted in distribution but required monitoring and control to protect local orchards, primarily in Fars and neighbouring provinces. Through the 2000s B. zonata persisted at low to moderate densities in southern Iran, periodically detected in surveys but not yet reported as widespread nationally, while nevertheless increasing the invasion pressure on adjacent countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction through movement of infested fruits from neighbouring countries on the Arabian Peninsula or from Pakistan and India; favourable warm climate in southern Iran and increasing regional horticultural trade. Internal mechanisms: strong dispersal capacity and broad host range, allowing B. zonata to establish in new agro‑ecosystems at the western edge of its native/South Asian range.
Review: review – Event retained as a significant westward extension of B. zonata within Asia, but emergence-type flags have been corrected: first_detection is set to No because the species was described and long known from South Asia well before 2002, and intra_continental_emergence is set to No because Iran lies in the Southern Asia subregion where B. zonata was already established (India, Pakistan, etc.). Under the project rules, spread to a new country within an already infested subregion should not be coded as intra-continental emergence; the event is therefore left untyped in the emergence-type columns and flagged for expert review regarding its relative importance compared to long-standing damage in neighbouring South Asian countries.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera zonata
EPP.common.name: peach fruit fly
Host: Mango, guava, banana, date palm, citrus and other fruit crops
Event.summary: Bactrocera zonata was first detected in Sudan in July 2011, when methyl‑eugenol traps in Wad Medani (Gezira state) captured the species in several orchards, signalling its arrival in mainland Eastern Africa. Subsequent monitoring from 2012 onward documented its presence not only in Wad Medani but also in Elkamlin and Singa, with the species becoming established and sometimes abundant in mango, guava and other fruit orchards while co‑occurring with B. dorsalis. By the mid‑2010s the fly was widespread in surveyed areas of Gezira and Sinnar states, infesting multiple host fruits and raising concern about severe economic losses and competitive displacement of other tephritid pests, although quantitative loss data remain limited.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: southward movement along trade and transport routes and possibly along the Nile corridor from already infested Egypt and Libya; expansion of irrigated fruit production in central Sudan; and limited early surveillance infrastructure. Internal mechanisms: strong competitive interactions with existing fruit flies (e.g. B. dorsalis), high reproductive rate and adaptation to hot, semi‑arid conditions, facilitating rapid establishment and local spread once introduced.
Review: review – This Sudan episode is clearly a major expansion of B. zonata onto the African mainland south of Egypt and Libya and should be retained. However, to align with the project definitions, first_detection has been set to No (global first detection occurred much earlier in Asia) and intra_continental_emergence to No because the Eastern Africa subregion already contained established populations in Mauritius and Réunion; Sudan represents spread to a new country within the same subregion, which should not be coded as intra-continental emergence. Given the continuing uncertainty about the scale of yield losses relative to other Bactrocera species, the event is flagged for further expert review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera zonata
EPP.common.name: peach fruit fly
Host: Various fruit trees in private gardens and public green areas (including citrus and other backyard fruits)
Event.summary: After an earlier border incursion in 2000–2001 that had been eradicated, Bactrocera zonata reappeared in Israel in 2014, when traps detected an outbreak in the metropolitan Tel‑Aviv area. The pest was found mainly in private gardens and public green spaces, prompting immediate official control measures including male‑annihilation techniques, mass trapping and insecticide sprays to prevent spread to commercial orchards. The outbreak was contained under official control, and later reports still categorized the species as present with few occurrences rather than widely established, highlighting the episode as a high‑profile but spatially limited re-introduction.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: re‑introduction via infested passenger fruit or regional trade from neighbouring infested areas (especially Egypt and other countries on the Arabian Peninsula); high host availability in urban and peri‑urban gardens around Tel‑Aviv. Internal mechanisms: high dispersal capacity and responsiveness to methyl‑eugenol lures allowing rapid local population build‑up but also facilitating detection; no clear evidence of novel strain or resistance, so this episode is treated as a re-occurrence driven mainly by renewed introduction and surveillance gaps rather than by evolutionary change.
Review: retain – This outbreak is correctly treated as a re-occurrence within the Western Asia subregion, following an earlier incursion eradicated in 2001, and it is important because it triggered intensive official control in an EPPO member country. Emergence-type coding (re_occurrence Yes; intra- and inter-continental No) is fully consistent with the project definitions and with EPPO’s description of the pest status as a localized outbreak under official control; no further corrections are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera zonata
EPP.common.name: peach fruit fly
Host: Citrus (e.g. sweet orange), pomegranate, pear, pummelo, stone fruits (apricot, peach) and other orchard fruits
Event.summary: Peach fruit fly was first intercepted in Iraq in 1972 in imported fruits from Bahrain but did not establish, and the country remained free of the pest for decades. In spring 2016 Bactrocera zonata was officially recorded from Wasit province, and subsequent pheromone trapping quickly detected the pest in several other provinces, with the species infesting citrus and other fruit orchards and marking the first confirmed establishment of B. zonata in Iraq. By the late 2010s and early 2020s the fly had become widespread in central and southern orchards, often reaching high densities, inflicting heavy economic losses and in some stone‑fruit systems outcompeting Mediterranean fruit fly.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: weak agricultural quarantine and ongoing import of citrus and other fruits from infested countries such as Iran, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Yemen; extensive mixed orchards of citrus and stone fruits in central and southern Iraq that provide continuous host availability; limited prior experience with this specific pest among growers and extension services. Internal mechanisms: high adaptability to local hosts and climate, high fecundity and rapid population growth, and strong competitive ability that allowed B. zonata to displace Ceratitis capitata in some orchards once established.
Review: review – The Iraqi establishment is retained as a major recent event because it represents rapid spread and high impact in previously pest-free central and southern orchards. To comply with the definitions, intra_continental_emergence has been changed to No because Western Asia was already infested through earlier invasions in Oman, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Israel, and re_occurrence/re_emergence have been set to No because the 1972 interception did not represent an established population and there is no clear evidence of evolutionary change driving the 2016 outbreak. The episode is therefore treated as a significant, but emergence-type-uncategorized, establishment within an already infested subregion and is flagged for further expert review of its relative ranking among global top-10 events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bemisia tabaci
EPP.common.name: sweetpotato whitefly
Host: cotton, melons, vegetables, ornamentals
Event.summary: Around 1990, a newly introduced MEAM1 (B) biotype of Bemisia tabaci began causing severe outbreaks in low desert cotton, melon and vegetable production areas of the southwestern United States, where earlier Bemisia populations had rarely required control. Outbreaks intensified in 1991 in southwestern Arizona and southern California and reached full outbreak status by 1992, becoming the most destructive pest force in the low Sonoran Desert agricultural system in decades. The crisis was gradually mitigated through the adoption of integrated pest management programs and new insecticides, which reduced populations and economic losses in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of irrigated desert agriculture, intensive use of broad-spectrum insecticides that disrupted natural enemies, and large-scale movement of infested ornamentals facilitated establishment and rapid spread of the invasive biotype. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (MEAM1/B biotype with greater fecundity and host range than indigenous Bemisia), enhanced transmission and colonization ability, and development of strong resistance to key insecticides, which together produced much higher population densities and crop damage than historic populations.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bemisia tabaci
EPP.common.name: sweetpotato whitefly
Host: greenhouse ornamentals and vegetables; some outdoor vegetables
Event.summary: In 2004, the MED (Q) biotype of Bemisia tabaci was first detected in the United States in greenhouse ornamentals, adding to already established MEAM1 populations. Over the following years MED spread within greenhouse production systems in several states, raising concern because of its high resistance to many insecticide classes and potential to move into field crops. Intensive surveys during the late 2000s documented its establishment in a range of ornamental and vegetable greenhouses, though sustained management and quarantine protocols limited large-scale outdoor establishment in many regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International trade in ornamental plants and protected-crop transplants introduced MED into U.S. greenhouse systems, where year‑round production and frequent insecticide applications provided strong selection pressure. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype (MED) with broad-spectrum insecticide resistance and high fitness under greenhouse conditions, leading to re-emergence of Bemisia problems even in systems that had adapted to MEAM1 management.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bemisia tabaci
EPP.common.name: sweetpotato whitefly
Host: cotton, vegetables, ornamentals
Event.summary: Between 2008 and 2010, monitoring in Israel showed substantial shifts in Bemisia tabaci biotype composition and resistance levels, with earlier MED (Q) populations in many regions being replaced or dominated by MEAM1 (B) by 2010. During this period, growers experienced severe control problems in cotton and vegetable systems due to resistance to several insecticide groups and changing responses to control programs. Adjustments in insecticide rotations, introduction of new modes of action and broader IPM strategies helped stabilize whitefly populations after 2010, although resistance and biotype shifts continued to pose challenges.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very intensive pesticide use in cotton and vegetable systems, regional selection pressure from repeated application of similar insecticide modes of action, and movement of infested planting material. Internal mechanisms: Rapid evolution of insecticide resistance within MED and MEAM1 populations, biotype replacement dynamics, and associated changes in virulence and fitness that drove re-emergence of severe Bemisia outbreaks despite ongoing management.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.), primarily winter wheat – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event.summary: Between 1993 and 1996, wheat powdery mildew populations of Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici in France developed multiple resistance to demethylation inhibitor (DMI) fungicides (e.g., triadimenol) and morpholines (e.g., fenpropimorph), after years of intensive use for mildew control. As these resistant populations increased in frequency, field efficacy of key fungicides declined markedly and farmers experienced recurrent mildew epidemics despite standard spray programs, forcing adjustments to fungicide mixtures and doses. By the late 1990s the episode stabilized as resistant phenotypes became widespread and management shifted toward diversified chemistries and integrated strategies, but the event marked a major re-emergence of wheat mildew damage under fungicide selection pressure in Western Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Heavy and repeated use of closely related DMI and morpholine fungicides on large wheat areas in France, combined with high disease pressure in intensive cereal systems, created strong selection for resistant mildew strains. Mild, humid seasons during some years favored epidemic development and large pathogen populations.
Internal mechanisms: Antifungal target-site and/or regulatory mutations leading to reduced sensitivity or resistance to DMIs and morpholines in B. graminis f. sp. tritici, followed by clonal amplification and dispersal of these resistant genotypes (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission of adapted clones).
Review: retain – Well-supported multiple-resistance episode in French wheat mildew (1993–1996) documented by Godet & Limpert and later reviews; timing, geography (France, Western Europe) and classification as re-emergence via fungicide resistance are appropriate, and sources are relevant to a major post-1990 Bgt event.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event.summary: In 1999–2000, surveys of wheat powdery mildew in three major production areas of Morocco showed that Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici populations had become highly complex and virulent, with rapidly increasing virulence to the widely deployed resistance gene Pm8 and many other Pm genes. As these virulent pathotypes spread across fields, cultivars relying on Pm8 and some other single resistance genes suffered significant mildew infection and yield risk, indicating a breakdown of formerly effective host resistance. By 2000 the Moroccan mildew population was dominated by pathotypes carrying multiple virulences, and breeders and agronomists had to reconsider resistance gene deployment strategies and fungicide use to manage this re-emergent disease pressure.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Extensive cultivation of wheat cultivars carrying Pm8 and related resistance genes over large areas, combined with favorable environmental conditions for mildew epidemics, promoted selection of complex virulence profiles. Regional wind patterns facilitated gene flow among populations.
Internal mechanisms: Rapid evolution and spread of B. graminis f. sp. tritici pathotypes with new virulence combinations, especially virulence to Pm8, leading to resistance breakdown (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: retain – Correctly represents the 1999–2000 virulence survey in Moroccan Bgt populations showing high virulence to Pm8 and complex virulence spectra; timing, country (Morocco, Northern Africa) and classification as re-emergence driven by virulence evolution are consistent with the Plant Disease report and subsequent summaries, so no structural changes are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), mainly soft red winter cultivars carrying Pm17 via the 1AL.1RS rye translocation – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, soft red winter wheat cultivars in the eastern and mid-Atlantic United States, such as ‘McCormick’, ‘Tribute’ and TAM 303, were widely deployed with the 1AL.1RS rye translocation carrying the powdery mildew resistance gene Pm17, providing strong protection against Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici. Within less than a decade, field observations from North Carolina and neighboring states documented severe powdery mildew on Pm17-bearing cultivars, and a 2009 Plant Disease note reported isolates virulent to Pm17 across multiple sites, indicating rapid breakdown of this resistance. Subsequent AvrPm17-based population genomic work showed that virulent AvrPm17 haplotypes were already present as standing variation in global Bgt populations before Pm17 deployment, explaining the swift re-emergence of mildew on Pm17 cultivars and prompting breeders to move toward gene pyramiding and alternative resistance sources.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Heavy reliance on a narrow set of soft red winter wheat cultivars carrying Pm17 in the eastern United States created strong selection pressure on Bgt; favorable climates for mildew in the mid-Atlantic region maintained large pathogen populations.
Internal mechanisms: Standing genetic variation at the avirulence gene AvrPm17, including ancient virulent haplotypes present before agricultural deployment of Pm17, enabled rapid selection of Pm17-virulent isolates once the gene was widely used (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence from standing variation; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity; Enhanced Transmission via wind-borne spores in dense wheat production zones).
Review: review – Original row incorrectly portrayed Pm17 breakdown as a Europe-wide event; literature shows that large-scale deployment and first documented breakdown of Pm17 occurred in the United States (soft red winter wheat in the mid-Atlantic), with virulent isolates reported from North Carolina by 2009 and virulent AvrPm17 haplotypes largely present beforehand. The event has been re-scoped to North America (USA), 2000–2009, as a re-emergence driven by selection on standing AvrPm17 variation rather than an intra-continental emergence in Europe. Human review should confirm the temporal bounds and whether this Pm17-specific episode is prioritized among the top ten global Bgt events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event.summary: From the 2008 growing season onward, wheat farmers and advisers in southern Brazil increasingly reported failure of triadimenol seed treatments to control powdery mildew, despite this DMI fungicide having provided effective protection for decades. Growth-chamber experiments reported in 2013 showed that Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici populations from affected fields exhibited greatly reduced sensitivity to triadimenol at recommended rates, with only modest reductions in incidence and severity compared with untreated controls, confirming a significant loss of fungicide efficacy. This resistance-driven re-emergence of wheat powdery mildew forced changes in fungicide recommendations, including reduced reliance on triadimenol seed treatments, greater use of alternative modes of action, and integration of varietal resistance and agronomic control in Brazilian wheat systems.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Nearly three decades of intensive use of triadimenol as a wheat seed treatment (and sometimes foliar applications) in southern Brazil, often without adequate resistance-management strategies, created sustained selection pressure on local Bgt populations; conducive climates in the region supported repeated mildew epidemics and large pathogen populations.
Internal mechanisms: Progressive reduction in triadimenol sensitivity in Bgt, likely involving mutations in the CYP51 target (and possibly other mechanisms), leading to a fungicide-resistant population and control failure (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission/Geographic Range Expansion of resistant phenotypes within Brazil).
Review: review – Host was corrected from barley (Bgh) to wheat (Bgt) and the episode re-dated from a single year (2013) to 2008–2013 to reflect field control failures noted from 2008 and experimental confirmation of reduced triadimenol sensitivity published in 2013. Inter-continental emergence has been reset to 'No' because this is resistance evolution within an established Bgt population in South America. The Tropical Plant Pathology short communication has been added as the primary event source; a curator may wish to verify impact metrics (area affected, yield loss) to confirm its ranking among the most impactful regional events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici (Pm8-carrying cultivars)
Event.summary: Between roughly 2011 and 2015, large-scale virulence surveys across major wheat-growing regions of China showed that Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici populations had very high virulence frequencies to the Pm8 resistance gene carried on the widely used 1BL.1RS rye translocation, often exceeding 50–70% of isolates in multiple provinces. As Pm8-virulent pathotypes became dominant, many Chinese wheat cultivars relying on Pm8 or Pm8-containing gene combinations suffered frequent and severe powdery mildew epidemics, despite earlier resistance, echoing patterns seen in Europe and Morocco. By the mid‑2010s, Pm8 was considered largely ineffective across key Chinese wheat production zones, and breeding and deployment strategies shifted toward alternative genes such as Pm21 and resistance gene pyramids to manage the renewed mildew threat.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Extremely widespread deployment of 1BL.1RS wheat cultivars carrying Pm8 across Chinese wheat regions, combined with favourable climates for mildew and large, genetically diverse Bgt populations, produced strong and sustained selection pressure for Pm8 virulence.
Internal mechanisms: Hypermutation and selection of virulent AvrPm8 alleles in Chinese Bgt populations, with virulent haplotypes rising to high frequency where Pm8 cultivars dominated, resulting in effective breakdown of Pm8-mediated resistance (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via avirulence-gene diversification; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: review – Newly added event to capture the large-scale breakdown of the Pm8 resistance gene in Chinese wheat from approximately 2011–2015, as evidenced by nationwide virulence surveys showing high Pm8 virulence frequencies and AvrPm8 hypermutation analyses that highlight particularly strong selection in China. Classified as re-emergence driven by avirulence-gene diversification under heavy Pm8 deployment. Exact start-year and regional coverage should be checked against detailed Chinese survey data, and the end date extended if more recent monitoring shows continued dominance of Pm8-virulent pathotypes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event.summary: Around the mid‑2010s, virulence surveys in Egypt showed that local Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici populations had high virulence frequencies to the widely used resistance gene Pm8 and complex virulence spectra against many other Pm genes, paralleling patterns previously seen in Europe and Morocco. As these virulent populations became dominant, several Egyptian wheat cultivars with Pm8 or similar resistance backgrounds suffered increased powdery mildew severity, and disease control shifted towards fungicide applications and the search for new resistance sources. By approximately 2017, Pm8 was no longer considered a reliable resistance source in Egypt, and breeding programs began diversifying resistance gene deployment to manage this re‑emergent threat.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Extensive cultivation of wheat cultivars sharing resistance genes already defeated by local mildew populations (especially Pm8), combined with conducive climatic conditions for mildew in Nile Delta and valley production systems, promoted expansion of virulent pathotypes.
Internal mechanisms: Accumulation and spread of complex virulence combinations in Egyptian B. graminis f. sp. tritici populations, including high virulence frequency to Pm8 and partial or full virulence to other Pm genes (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: retain – Event accurately summarizes Egyptian virulence surveys showing high frequencies of virulence to Pm8 and several other genes and recommending against further use of Pm8; timing in the mid‑2010s is broadly consistent with sampling years reported in the Plant Disease papers. It is correctly classified as re-emergence driven by virulence evolution in an existing Northern African Bgt population; if desired, a curator could refine the exact start and end years once detailed sampling dates are consulted.

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Barley (Hordeum vulgare) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. hordei
Event.summary: Between about 2015 and 2019, intensive surveys in southeastern and southwestern China documented high virulence variability and genetic diversity in Blumeria graminis f. sp. hordei populations, with frequent emergence of new virulences that rendered many barley resistance genes ineffective only a few years after cultivar release. As these diverse and rapidly evolving pathotypes spread across key barley-growing regions in Yunnan, Tibet and Zhejiang, powdery mildew epidemics became more common and severe on popular cultivars, threatening grain yield and malting quality and increasing dependence on fungicide sprays. By the end of this period, many previously effective barley resistance alleles in China were compromised, and breeding and management programs shifted towards stacking multiple resistance genes, monitoring virulence changes, and integrating fungicide and agronomic control measures.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: High-density barley cultivation, including malting barley, in subtropical and temperate regions of southeastern and southwestern China, combined with frequent mildew-conducive weather, produced large pathogen populations and strong selection on resistance genes deployed in relatively narrow genetic backgrounds.
Internal mechanisms: Rapid, recurrent appearance of new virulence combinations in B. graminis f. sp. hordei populations, leading to repeated breakdown of single resistance genes (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity; Enhanced Transmission via wind-dispersed spores across landscapes).
Review: review – Time span was adjusted from 2016–2020 to 2015–2019 to match the sampling period in the Plant Disease study on Bgh virulence variability in southeastern and southwestern China, and the country field standardized to 'China [2015]'. Intra-continental emergence has been reset to 'No' because this episode reflects rapid virulence diversification within regions where barley powdery mildew was already endemic; it fits the re-emergence category based on continual pathotype evolution. The event remains a major example of recurrent breakdown of barley resistance genes in China and merits inclusion among key post-1990 Bgh episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event.summary: Around 2016–2017, Australian monitoring programs for wheat powdery mildew detected the first cases of QoI (strobilurin) fungicide resistance in Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici, initially in southern and island regions such as Victoria and Tasmania, after many years of QoI use without confirmed resistance. Following these detections, growers and advisors reported reduced efficacy of strobilurin-based fungicides in some high-pressure seasons, and resistance management warnings were issued for wheat mildew in southern and western regions. By 2018, QoI-resistant mildew had become an established concern in parts of Australia, leading to recommendations for limiting QoI applications, using mixtures with other modes of action, and greater emphasis on varietal resistance and crop management.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Widespread and repeated use of QoI fungicides in Australian wheat production, often targeting multiple foliar diseases, created strong selection pressure; dense cereal acreage and suitable weather in southern and western regions favored large mildew populations.
Internal mechanisms: Emergence and selection of QoI-resistant B. graminis f. sp. tritici strains (involving the well-known G143A mutation in cytochrome b), with subsequent spread within Australian wheat regions (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Geographic Range Expansion of resistant phenotypes within the continent).
Review: review – Event reflects the first confirmed cases of QoI (Group 11) resistance in wheat powdery mildew in Australia (initially in Victoria and Tasmania, then other southern regions) reported from 2016 onward. The countries field has been simplified to the country-level 'Australia' (with state-level detail kept in the summary) to align with the country coding scheme, and inter-continental emergence has been reset to 'No' because the episode represents fungicide resistance evolution in an already established Bgt population. Sources from Curtin University, Grain Central and GRDC remain appropriate; a curator may wish to verify the full geographic spread and whether New Zealand experienced similar resistance during this period.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bradybaena similaris
EPP.common.name: Asian trampsnail
Host: Ornamental tropical plants and greenhouse vegetation (tropical rainforest eco-display)
Event.summary: Around 2002, Bradybaena similaris was first detected in the tropical greenhouse (Burgers’ Bush) of Burgers’ Zoo near Arnhem in the Netherlands, where it had established a self-sustaining population on ornamental plants and greenhouse structures. Over the subsequent years the population persisted and spread within the enclosed rainforest exhibit, leading to its formal documentation and identification as the Asian trampsnail in a 2009 taxonomic and ecological note that recognized the record as the first for Europe. The population has remained confined to greenhouse environments with ongoing local management, and there is no evidence to date of escape into outdoor Dutch ecosystems, so the event can be considered a contained but significant inter-continental introduction into the European horticultural production and display chain.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International trade in live plants and greenhouse stock introduced B. similaris inadvertently with potted tropical ornamentals; the warm, humid, predator-poor conditions of the covered rainforest exhibit favored survival and reproduction. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent), as traits enabling survival on a wide range of ornamental hosts and tolerance of greenhouse climates facilitated colonization of a previously unoccupied continent; enhanced transmission in dense plantings and sheltered microhabitats within the greenhouse likely supported high local population densities.
Review: Review – retain with correction. Confirmed that the Burgers’ Zoo population in Arnhem (Netherlands) represents the first published European record of Bradybaena similaris and a small but well-documented, self-sustaining introduction confined to a tropical greenhouse. Corrected event-type coding by setting first_detection = false, since global first detection in the plant host system predates 1900 and this event is specifically the first European occurrence; inter_continental_emergence = true is appropriate as this is the first established population on a new continent. Country and subregion (Netherlands in Western Europe) match UNSD classifications. Sources (de Winter et al. 2009 and EPPO distribution details) are appropriate and specific to this event. Recommended action: keep this as a major post‑1990 event, but human reviewer should verify that no earlier European establishment has been documented since the Basteria paper was published.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bradybaena similaris
EPP.common.name: Asian trampsnail
Host: Citrus budwood nurseries (young citrus plants under protected cultivation)
Event.summary: By 2020, Bradybaena similaris had become a consistently abundant pest in protected citrus bud nurseries in Santa Catarina State, Brazil, prompting a detailed study of its population dynamics to support control decisions. Weekly monitoring in a commercial budwood nursery showed high snail densities on plants and in soil traps during two main peaks (July–September and January–March), with overlapping generations and significant risk of feeding damage to young citrus tissues. Management efforts during and after this monitoring period focused on optimizing molluscicide timing and modifying cultural practices, reducing visible snail activity outside the key peak periods but not eliminating the species from the nursery environment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of protected citrus propagation systems with dense plantings, abundant leaf litter, and irrigation created favorable, stable microclimates that promote high B. similaris survival and reproduction; regional trade in budded plants likely aids its movement among nurseries. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, multivoltine life history, and broad environmental tolerance allow rapid build-up in protected environments; behavioral use of litter and irrigation structures for shelter increases persistence despite control measures.
Review: Review – retain with reclassification. Validated that B. similaris has been established in Brazil since the 19th century, and the 2020 study from Santa Catarina documents a high-density, economically relevant nursery pest situation rather than a new introduction or new host. Re-coded this event as re_occurrence = true and re_emergence = false to reflect resurgence and recognition as a serious pest in a protected citrus propagation system driven largely by external agronomic factors (use of covered nurseries, irrigation, and dense plantings), with no evidence of a novel strain, new host jump, or resistance evolution. Event year, location (Santa Catarina, Brazil), and host description are consistent with the Citrus Research & Technology paper; continent, subregion, and country naming accord with the UNSD scheme. Recommended action: keep as a major Brazilian outbreak episode, with classification change flagged for human review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bradybaena similaris
EPP.common.name: Asian trampsnail
Host: Vegetation along irrigation canals and adjacent cultivated fields (mixed crops)
Event.summary: In 2019, Bradybaena similaris was recorded for the first time in Bangladesh when populations were discovered along an irrigation canal next to cultivated fields in Kayangghat in the country’s east, a finding later detailed in a 2020 BioInvasions Records paper. The snails were found in moist, disturbed vegetation bordering agricultural land, indicating that the species had already established locally by the time of detection and likely arrived through regional trade or transport from neighboring countries such as India, where it was already present. After publication, the EPPO Global Database listed the species as present in Bangladesh with no further details, and while large agricultural outbreaks have not yet been reported, authorities and researchers have recommended vigilance because the species is a known cosmopolitan pest of fruits, vegetables, and ornamentals and may expand into irrigated cropping systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of goods, vehicles, and plant material from neighboring India and other South Asian trade partners likely introduced B. similaris to eastern Bangladesh; the presence of irrigated agriculture and permanent canal systems created humid microhabitats favorable for its establishment. Internal mechanisms: High dispersal potential via egg-laying on soil and plant debris and the ability to exploit disturbed, human-dominated habitats contribute to spread and establishment within Southern Asia, but there is no evidence of a novel strain or host shift in this event.
Review: Review – retain with reclassification. EPPO distribution details and the BioInvasions Records article confirm that 2019 was the first confirmed national record of B. similaris in Bangladesh, within a Southern Asian subregion where the species was already known (e.g., India, Nepal). Accordingly, this is not a global first detection and not a new subregional or continental emergence, but rather spread into a new country within a previously affected subregion. Re-coded as re_occurrence = true and re_emergence = false to reflect resurgence/expansion driven by trade and habitat conditions, without evidence of evolutionary change. Event year, locality (Kayangghat, east Bangladesh), and host context (canal-side vegetation adjacent to fields) align with the published record. Recommended action: keep as a key post‑2000 range-expansion event in Southern Asia, while noting that current agricultural impacts are more potential than realized and should be monitored.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bremia lactucae
EPP.common.name: lettuce downy mildew
Host: Lactuca sativa (cultivated lettuce)
Event.summary: In June 1994, typical downy mildew symptoms were first observed on lettuce in commercial production areas of Natal (now KwaZulu‑Natal), South Africa, with angular chlorotic lesions and abundant white sporulation on leaf undersides. Surveys across ten lettuce‑growing sites documented an average of about 50% infection and severe leaf necrosis, and the pathogen was isolated and confirmed microscopically and via pathogenicity tests as Bremia lactucae. The outbreak highlighted downy mildew as a new constraint on lettuce production in this Southern African subregion and led to implementation of fungicide programs and monitoring to limit subsequent epidemics.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion and intensification of lettuce cultivation in Natal created new habitat for B. lactucae; suitable cool, moist winter conditions favored epidemic development. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – establishment of B. lactucae in a previously unreported Southern African subregion, with strains able to exploit local climatic conditions and production practices.
Review: Decision: Review. Event year was narrowed from 1994–1996 to 1994–1994 because the APS Disease Note only documents the initial June 1994 outbreak in Natal; ongoing problems are plausible but not substantiated in that source. The 'first_detection' flag was set from Yes to No, as B. lactucae had been recognized on lettuce for decades and was already present elsewhere in Africa, whereas this episode fits the definition of intra‑continental emergence (first report in the Southern Africa sub‑region). Geography, host and mechanism now align well with the source, but the impact ranking as a top‑10 event should be confirmed by regional experts.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bremia lactucae
EPP.common.name: lettuce downy mildew
Host: Lactuca sativa (cultivated lettuce)
Event.summary: From 2003 onward, severe downy mildew outbreaks began to affect lettuce production in São Paulo state, Brazil, with increasing difficulty in disease control and major yield and quality losses in intensively managed areas. Race‑typing of Brazilian B. lactucae populations between 2003 and 2011 using the sextet code system identified a succession of local races (SPBl:01 through SPBl:06 and later types), several of which emerged after 2006 and were associated with repeated resistance breakdown and severe epidemics in commercial cultivars. Continued monitoring through 2010–2011 confirmed that these novel races had become established in São Paulo’s lettuce districts, prompting recommendations for new resistant varieties, diversified Dm‑gene deployment and improved fungicide strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid intensification of lettuce production in São Paulo, year‑round cropping and dense plantings increased inoculum pressure; reliance on a narrow set of resistance genes and fungicides favored selection of new virulent types. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – multiple new races (SPBl series) with distinct virulence profiles; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – successive races overcame Dm‑mediated resistance in widely grown cultivars; possible Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance due to repeated fungicide use.
Review: Decision: Retain. This event captures a prolonged and well‑documented period in which multiple local races (SPBl:01–06 and later) emerged and spread in São Paulo, causing serious control failures and prompting large breeding and management responses; this clearly ranks among the most impactful post‑1990 episodes for B. lactucae in South America. The timing, host, mechanisms and geographic focus agree with Brazilian monitoring studies; no structural changes are proposed, but future work could refine the end‑year if more recent São Paulo race data are incorporated.

EPP.scientific.name: Bremia lactucae
EPP.common.name: lettuce downy mildew
Host: Lactuca sativa (primarily coastal and desert lettuce production in California and Arizona)
Event.summary: Between 2015 and 2017, IBEB‑US monitoring in western US lettuce fields identified a group of Bremia lactucae isolates with a new virulence pattern that overcame several resistance genes used in commercial cultivars. Because this pattern was repeatedly recovered from different locations and seasons and persisted in the pathogen population, the consortium denominated it as race Bl:9US in 2018, extending the US race set beyond Bl:8US. Bl:9US contributed to renewed downy mildew problems in parts of coastal California and the desert production regions until cultivars with effective resistance and adjusted fungicide and hygiene programmes were adopted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive, year‑round lettuce production in the Salinas, coastal and desert valleys of California and Arizona, with high inoculum pressure and heavy use of race‑specific resistance and fungicides, favored selection of novel virulence types. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:9US represents a distinct virulence type stable over multiple years and locations; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – ability to infect cultivars carrying resistance to earlier US races (Bl:5–8US); Enhanced Transmission – persistence across major western‑US lettuce districts.
Review: Decision: Review. This new row was added to represent the emergence of race Bl:9US in the western United States, as described by the IBEB‑US press release and extension notes, which report repeated detections of the same virulence pattern in 2015–2017 followed by denomination in 2018. Because public sources provide limited quantitative yield‑loss estimates, the 2015–2018 window and qualitative impact assessment should be checked with regional specialists, but Bl:9US clearly marks an important race shift for US lettuce production. Classified as re‑emergence only, since it reflects a new virulent race in an established pathogen population.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bremia lactucae
EPP.common.name: lettuce downy mildew
Host: Lactuca sativa (western-US head, romaine and baby leaf lettuce)
Event.summary: From about 2022, IBEB‑US began to recover Bremia lactucae isolates with the IBEB‑D sextet code 45‑7‑2 from multiple western US lettuce districts, including locations in California and Arizona. Because isolates with this virulence profile were collected repeatedly over three years across several production areas, the representative isolate VP‑302 from San Benito County, California, was denominated on 1 July 2025 as the type isolate of the new race Bl:10US. Bl:10US was reported to overcome several commonly used resistance genes, including Dm25, Dm38 and Dm56, and was associated with renewed downy mildew pressure in some western‑US plantings until breeders and growers adjusted resistance packages and management practices.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: large‑scale, continuous lettuce production in California and Arizona using similar resistance backgrounds and intensive fungicide use has created strong selection pressure for new virulent Bremia races; regional movement of transplants and seed links different production valleys and facilitates spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:10US shows a distinct and stable virulence profile not represented by races Bl:5–9US; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – its documented ability to defeat multiple major resistance genes; Enhanced Transmission – repeated recovery across multiple western‑US locations over several years indicates competitive fitness within the local pathogen population.
Review: Decision: Review. This newly added row summarizes the emergence of race Bl:10US in the western United States, based on the 2025 IBEB‑US press release and supporting industry communication detailing repeated detections across California and Arizona over three years and the race’s ability to overcome key resistance genes such as Dm25, Dm38 and Dm56. Because Bl:10US has only recently been denominated, its full agronomic impact is still developing; the 2022–2025 window should therefore be treated as provisional and revisited as more field data become available. Classified as re‑emergence rather than geographic emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cacopsylla pyri
EPP.common.name: pear psyllid
Host: Pyrus communis (commercial European pear cultivars in intensive orchards, especially in northern Italy’s pear districts)
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through at least the mid‑2010s, Cacopsylla pyri remained the most economically important pest of pear in Italy’s main production regions, particularly in high-density orchards in Emilia‑Romagna and other northern districts, where repeated heavy infestations caused honeydew, sooty mould and fruit downgrading. Long-term reliance on organophosphate and pyrethroid insecticides contributed to resistance problems documented in European C. pyri populations, and after the banning of amitraz around 2005 Italian growers increasingly depended on abamectin, spirotetramat and other selective products alongside intensified monitoring and cultural measures. By the 2010s, integrated pest management strategies based on selective insecticides, conservation of natural enemies and host-plant resistance breeding reduced but did not eliminate pest pressure, and C. pyri continued to be the key pest and a major vector of pear decline phytoplasma in Italian pear orchards.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensification of pear production in northern Italy (large monoculture orchards, highly susceptible cultivars) and many years of frequent broad-spectrum insecticide applications created favourable conditions for C. pyri outbreaks and strong selection pressure on pest populations; regulatory withdrawal of older active ingredients (e.g. amitraz) further narrowed chemical options. Internal mechanisms: resistance to several organophosphate insecticides and pyrethroids has been demonstrated in European C. pyri, and Italian monitoring showed variation in susceptibility to abamectin and other compounds, consistent with ongoing selection for enhanced detoxification; the pest’s multivoltine life cycle, high fecundity and overwintering adults supported rapid responses to these pressures, making this a classic re‑emergence episode driven by evolved resistance and production intensification rather than by new geographic spread.
Review: Decision: retain. Corrected the 'countries' field to 'Italy [1990]' so that the bracketed year represents the approximate start of the re‑emergence episode in this country, consistent with the event-year range. The event summary and mechanism text were revised to match the literature more closely by emphasising strong resistance to organophosphates and pyrethroids and monitored variation (rather than confirmed high-level resistance) in abamectin susceptibility, and by framing this as a resistance-driven re‑emergence in long-infested Italian pear regions rather than as any form of geographic emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Cacopsylla pyri
EPP.common.name: pear psyllid
Host: Pyrus communis (commercial pear orchards, especially in Provence–Alpes–Côte d’Azur and other intensive pear regions)
Event.summary: From about 1990 through 2000, pear psylla populations in the main French pear-growing areas, particularly around Avignon in southeastern France, developed very high levels of resistance to key organophosphate insecticides such as azinphosmethyl and phosmet and reduced susceptibility to pyrethroids and amitraz, leading to repeated control failures and heavy larval infestations with honeydew and sooty mould. Detailed bioassays in the mid‑1990s documented resistance ratios of roughly 25–180-fold for several organophosphates and lower but significant resistance to pyrethroids and amitraz, prompting renewed efforts to redesign control programmes and to screen for psylla-resistant pear germplasm. By the early 2000s, greater use of mineral oils, more selective insecticides and integrated pest management helped to partially restore control, but C. pyri remained a major pest and resistant genotypes persisted in French pear orchards.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: decades of intensive pear production in France with repeated applications of organophosphate and pyrethroid insecticides, withdrawal of some older pesticide classes and high cosmetic standards for fruit created very strong selection pressure and high carrying capacity for C. pyri. Internal mechanisms: French laboratory and field studies demonstrated high resistance ratios to azinphosmethyl and other organophosphates, cross-resistance to phosmet and monocrotophos, and reduced sensitivity to pyrethroids and amitraz, associated with altered acetylcholinesterase and enhanced detoxifying enzymes (esterases and mixed-function oxidases); these evolved changes are characteristic of re‑emergence driven by insecticide resistance rather than any new geographic intrusion.
Review: Decision: retain. Added this event to capture the well-documented 1990s insecticide-resistance crisis in French C. pyri populations around Avignon and other pear regions, which produced very high organophosphate resistance ratios and widespread control failures and is therefore among the most impactful post‑1990 episodes for this pest. Classified as re‑emergence (internal change: evolution of resistance); no intra- or inter-continental emergence is involved. The time window 1990–2000 is an approximation covering the decade in which resistance was first quantified and widely recognised; more precise dating would require integrating detailed French resistance-monitoring datasets.

EPP.scientific.name: Cacopsylla pyri
EPP.common.name: pear psyllid
Host: Pyrus communis in commercial pear orchards
Event.summary: Between roughly 1990 and 2005, Cacopsylla pyri resurged as a major limiting factor in Bulgarian pear production, with growers reporting marked increases in pest abundance and damage compared with the previous two decades. Intensive spraying with non‑selective insecticides led to widespread resistance or reduced efficacy of organophosphates, pyrethroids and amitraz and to disruption of natural enemy complexes, allowing severe recurrent infestations characterised by heavy honeydew, sooty mould and yield downgrading. After amitraz was banned around 2005, abamectin became the primary control option and provided improved but still incomplete suppression, prompting recommendations for more selective insecticides and stronger emphasis on biological control and integrated pest management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: long-term frequent application of broad-spectrum insecticides in Bulgarian pear orchards increased carrying capacity for C. pyri by removing natural enemies and imposed strong selection pressure for resistance; structural factors (small orchards with limited adoption of integrated pest management) further constrained the feasibility of resistance-management strategies. Internal mechanisms: European and Bulgarian reports indicate cross-resistance in C. pyri to multiple organophosphates, pyrethroids and amitraz, together with high fecundity and many generations per year, which facilitated rapid increase and spread of resistant genotypes; these internal changes underpin the observed re‑emergence in impact without representing new geographic occurrence.
Review: Decision: retain. Updated the 'countries' field from a narrative phrase to 'Bulgaria [1990]' so that the bracketed value gives the approximate start of the resurgence episode in this country, consistent with the 1990–2005 event window. The summary and mechanism remain appropriate, reflecting Bulgarian and regional evidence of increased C. pyri damage and broad-spectrum insecticide resistance; classification as re‑emergence (driven by evolved resistance and natural-enemy disruption) is consistent with the event-type definitions and no intra- or inter-continental emergence is implied.

EPP.scientific.name: Cacopsylla pyri
EPP.common.name: pear psyllid
Host: Pyrus communis (commercial pear orchards in the Ebro Valley and southeastern Spain)
Event.summary: From roughly 2000 to the mid‑2010s, Cacopsylla pyri intensified as the key pest of pear orchards in Spain, particularly in the Ebro Valley (Lleida area) and in southeastern regions such as Murcia, where it caused repeated severe honeydew deposition, sooty mould, fruit russeting and downgrading. Growers relied heavily on insecticide control, yet field monitoring and bioassays revealed reduced susceptibility or resistance to pyrethroids such as cypermethrin and lower efficacy of amitraz and abamectin in some orchards, leading to control difficulties and concern about resistance evolution; at the same time, the pest was implicated in the epidemiology of pear decline and peach yellow leaf roll associated with 'Candidatus Phytoplasma pyri'. Over time, research on natural enemies, alternative chemistries and integrated pest management helped to stabilise pest pressure in some orchards, but C. pyri remained the principal pear pest in major Spanish pear-growing regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion and intensification of commercial pear orchards in northeast and southeast Spain, combined with long-term heavy use of a limited set of insecticides, created strong selection pressure on C. pyri and disrupted natural enemy complexes; regulatory restrictions on certain older active ingredients further constrained rotation options. Internal mechanisms: toxicity bioassays and biochemical studies on field populations from the Ebro Valley documented elevated esterase, glutathione S-transferase and cytochrome P450 reductase activities and higher LC50 values to cypermethrin, consistent with emerging metabolic resistance; these changes underpin the re‑emergence of the pest as a difficult-to-control problem rather than any new geographic incursion.
Review: Decision: retain. This event was added because multiple studies from Lleida and southeastern Spain show that C. pyri is the principal pear pest in major Spanish production areas, with documented control difficulties and evidence of reduced susceptibility or resistance to pyrethroids and other insecticides, making it one of the more impactful post‑1990 emergence/re‑emergence episodes for the species. It is appropriately classified as re‑emergence driven by evolving metabolic resistance and management changes, without any intra- or inter-continental emergence component. The 2000–2015 time window is approximate and reflects the period during which Spanish sources repeatedly report control problems and resistance concerns; more precise dating would require a consolidated review of Spanish monitoring data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chilo suppressalis
EPP.common.name: striped riceborer
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa; conventional irrigated rice systems in multiple provinces)
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, populations of Chilo suppressalis in China rebounded after a period of lower pest pressure and, by 1993, densities had increased markedly in major rice-growing regions, culminating in widespread outbreaks around 1996. The resurgence developed across large areas of the Yangtze River rice belt and other provinces, where both C. suppressalis and the yellow rice borer Scirpophaga incertulas caused heavy stem-borer damage, prompting renewed insecticide use and major yield-loss assessments. As management practices and planting structures were adjusted and new control tactics were introduced, these outbreak levels eventually declined in some areas, although the pest remained a key constraint on Chinese rice production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of hybrid rice, changes in planting dates and crop structure, and heavy reliance on broad-spectrum insecticides are cited as major factors behind the marked population increases and renewed outbreaks in Chinese rice fields in the early–mid 1990s. Internal mechanisms: No clear novel strain was implicated; the event is best characterized as a resurgence of established populations responding to agronomic and landscape changes rather than inherent biological innovation.
Review: Decision: retain. This row correctly captures the mid‑1990s resurgence of C. suppressalis in Chinese rice, as documented by Sheng et al. (2003) and later reviews, including timing (densities rising by 1993, major outbreaks and sustained high damage by 1996), geography (China/Eastern Asia), host (rice), and classification as a re-occurrence driven by agronomic change rather than by new genotypes. No structural corrections were required; minor narrative refinements could be made later but are not essential.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chilo suppressalis
EPP.common.name: striped riceborer
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa), especially high-yielding hybrid and “super rice” cultivars, with occasional use of maize, wheat and sugarcane as secondary or overwintering hosts in the landscape matrix
Event.summary: From the early 2000s through at least the mid‑2010s, Chilo suppressalis caused sustained, large-scale damage in Chinese hybrid and super-rice systems, representing one of the most impactful long-lasting emergence episodes for this pest. The event developed as super rice and intensified double-cropping systems expanded across the Yangtze basin and other regions, with national statistics indicating that C. suppressalis and allied borers damaged more than 14 million hectares of rice fields annually in China during much of this period, often requiring intensive insecticide use and additional IPM interventions. Expanded adoption of improved cultivation techniques, pheromone-based control and integrated management gradually reduced outbreak severity in some areas, though the pest remained entrenched and continues to pose a major production risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of high-yielding hybrid and super-rice cultivars, changes in planting density and sowing dates, longer growing seasons and stubble management practices created more favorable habitats and overwintering refuges; irrigation-based intensification and climate suitability maintained high population carrying capacity. Internal mechanisms: C. suppressalis biology (diapause capability, stem-boring habit, tolerance of wide temperature ranges) inherently supports persistence and geographic spread, but this episode is primarily driven by external agronomic drivers rather than documented new genotypes; it is therefore best categorized as a large-scale re-occurrence of an established pest.
Review: Decision: review. I corrected the geographic coding so that this event now refers only to Eastern Asia/China, and simplified the countries field from the vague “China [2000], multiple other Asian rice-growing countries” to “China [2000]”. The supporting literature (e.g., Sheng et al. 2003; Qu et al. 2011; recent resistance-monitoring syntheses) quantifies long-term damage and management responses specifically for China; similar chronic pressure elsewhere in Asia is real but less clearly documented as a distinct, linked 2000–2015 episode. Classification as a large-scale re-occurrence of an established pest remains appropriate, and the event is clearly among the top global episodes by area affected, but the revised row should be checked by a regional rice entomologist for temporal bounds and whether additional countries merit inclusion as a linked multi-country episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chilo suppressalis
EPP.common.name: striped riceborer
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in intensively treated paddy systems
Event.summary: Beginning around 2002, systematic resistance monitoring in eastern China showed that populations of Chilo suppressalis in key rice areas such as Lianyungang (Jiangsu) and Ruian (Zhejiang) were evolving resistance to multiple conventional insecticides. Over the subsequent decade, resistance ratios to several active ingredients (including organophosphates, carbamates, nereistoxin analogues and fiproles) increased significantly, reducing field efficacy and prompting changes in control recommendations and rotation strategies. By about 2011, monitoring data documented established, multi-insecticide-resistant field populations in several provinces, and management programs increasingly emphasized resistance management, IPM and alternative tools rather than sole reliance on broad-spectrum insecticides.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive and repeated use of the same insecticide classes in high-value rice regions, often on successive generations within the same season, created strong selection pressure; dense planting and high pest pressure further favored survival of resistant individuals. Internal mechanisms: Evolution and spread of metabolic and target-site resistance to multiple insecticide modes of action in field populations of C. suppressalis, documented through bioassays and resistance monitoring, constitutes a clear re-emergence of the pest via pesticide-resistance mechanisms rather than geographic invasion.
Review: Decision: review. The conceptualization of this event as a resistance-driven re-emergence of C. suppressalis in Chinese rice from 2002–2011 is well supported by long-term bioassay data (e.g., He et al. 2013 and related Chinese monitoring studies), and the emergence types (re-emergence=yes; re-occurrence=no) are correctly used. I simplified the countries field to “China [2002]” (localities such as Lianyungang and Ruian are more appropriate in the narrative) and replaced a diamide-focused review with more directly relevant multi-insecticide resistance sources. The time window and list of chemistries under selection should be rechecked by a resistance specialist, but the event is clearly among the globally important episodes given the breadth of compounds affected and the large rice area involved.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chilo suppressalis
EPP.common.name: striped riceborer
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in areas treated with diamide insecticides (chlorantraniliprole, flubendiamide and related compounds)
Event.summary: Around 2013, shortly after diamide insecticides had been widely adopted to control rice stem borers, resistance to chlorantraniliprole and related compounds was first detected in field populations of Chilo suppressalis in Hubei Province, China. Over the next several years, reports of reduced field efficacy and elevated resistance ratios emerged from other eastern and central Chinese provinces including Hunan, Zhejiang, Shandong and Jiangxi, indicating rapid spread or independent evolution of diamide resistance in multiple C. suppressalis populations. By approximately 2016, resistance levels in some populations (e.g., in Jiangxi) had increased markedly, and although control failure was not yet universal, the episode forced adjustments to treatment thresholds, rotation schemes and integration with nonchemical measures to sustain effective management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread, intensive use of diamide insecticides in Chinese rice production beginning in the late 2000s created strong selection for resistant phenotypes; high pest pressure and frequent applications magnified selection intensity. Internal mechanisms: Genetic changes in C. suppressalis conferring reduced susceptibility to diamides, including target-site ryanodine receptor mutations (e.g., G4910/4946E) and metabolic mechanisms documented in multiple field populations, represent a classic pesticide-resistance-driven re-emergence, with evidence of moderate but persistent resistance across several provinces over multiple years.
Review: Decision: review. The event correctly describes the first documented field resistance of C. suppressalis to diamide insecticides in China (initially in Hubei, then in other eastern/central provinces) and appropriately codes it as a re-emergence driven by pesticide resistance. I simplified the countries field to “China [2013]” and replaced a generic methods page with more specific monitoring and mechanism studies (e.g., Yao et al. 2017; Yao et al. 2016). The 2013–2016 window captures the initial emergence and rapid escalation of resistance; however, resistance has persisted and evolved further beyond 2016, so experts may wish to extend the end year or treat later intensification as a follow-on episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chilo suppressalis
EPP.common.name: striped riceborer
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in the irrigated paddies of the Ebro delta (Catalonia), with larvae also present in nearby wetland grasses
Event.summary: From roughly 1990 through the end of the decade, Chilo suppressalis remained the principal insect pest of rice in Spain’s Ebro delta, causing recurrent local outbreaks that prompted intensive insecticide use and stimulated the development of new control strategies. Drawing on detailed studies of the pest’s larval development and phenology in the delta, regional plant-protection services and collaborators tested and refined mass trapping with synthetic sex pheromones throughout the 1990s, culminating in large-scale deployment. By about 2000, control of C. suppressalis in the Ebro delta relied predominantly on pheromone-based mass trapping, which substantially reduced the number of insecticide applications and overall control costs while maintaining acceptable levels of crop protection, effectively marking the end of this high-pressure resurgence phase.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The Ebro delta comprises a large, continuous area of irrigated rice with favorable flooding regimes and abundant stubble, which historically supported high C. suppressalis populations; reliance on insecticides and lack of rotation further favored recurrent outbreaks. Regional investment in monitoring and in pheromone-based mass trapping was driven by the need to manage these chronic high populations more sustainably. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence that novel strains or resistance traits unique to the Ebro delta were responsible for the resurgence; the episode is best viewed as a re-occurrence of an established European population under conducive agronomic and landscape conditions, followed by successful suppression via behaviorally based control.
Review: Decision: review (new event added). This row has been added to capture a major 1990s re-occurrence episode in the Spanish Ebro delta, where C. suppressalis was the dominant rice pest and where large-scale pheromone-based mass trapping was developed and adopted around 2000. The timing (1990s development work, mass trapping as the main control from 2000 onward), geography (Spain/Southern Europe, specifically the Ebro delta) and classification as a re-occurrence of an already established European population are consistent with Spanish plant-protection bulletins and extension reports. Precise start and end years are approximate, and quantitative information on hectares affected and yield loss is limited in the accessible literature, so this event should be reviewed by regional experts, but its inclusion is justified as one of the largest post‑1990 European emergence episodes for this pest.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chrysodeixis includens
EPP.common.name: Soybean Looper Moth, soybean looper
Host: Soybean (Glycine max), cotton (Gossypium hirsutum and other cultivated cottons)
Event.summary: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, soybean looper populations in the southern United States surged in importance as a defoliating pest in soybean–cotton production systems, coinciding with intensive pyrethroid use. Field populations developed high levels of resistance to pyrethroid and other insecticide groups, leading to recurring late‑season outbreaks and control failures across the southern soybean belt. Management stabilized only after shifts in insecticide programs and integrated pest management tactics reduced reliance on single chemistries and incorporated additional control measures.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive and repeated use of pyrethroid and other broad‑spectrum insecticides in soybean–cotton rotations, large contiguous areas of susceptible crops, and favorable warm, humid conditions that supported multiple generations per year. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (evolution of high resistance to pyrethroids and other chemistries), with resistance maintaining large populations despite control pressure; this indirectly increased effective reproductive rate but there is no clear evidence of increased virulence per se.
Review: Review – Event correctly represents major pyrethroid‑resistance‑driven outbreaks of soybean looper in the southern United States; re_occurrence has been set to No and re_emergence kept as Yes so that emergence types remain mutually exclusive while emphasizing that the key internal change was insecticide resistance in an already established pest. The 1990–1995 window is broadly consistent with reports of high pyrethroid resistance from the late 1980s into the early 1990s but could be fine‑tuned by a US cotton–soybean resistance historian. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/267218002_Pyrethroid_Resistance_Levels_in_%27vo_Generations_of_Soybean_Looper_Lepidoptera_Noctuidae_on_Soybean_in_Mississippi_J?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chrysodeixis includens
EPP.common.name: Soybean Looper Moth, soybean looper
Host: Soybean (Glycine max) (primary), with spillover to cotton and other broadleaf crops in some areas
Event.summary: During the early 2000s, especially from the 2002–2003 soybean seasons onward, Chrysodeixis includens shifted from a historically secondary role to an emerging key pest of soybean across most major producing regions of Brazil. As soybean expanded rapidly into the Cerrado and other new frontiers and cropping systems intensified (no‑till and double‑cropping), repeated severe defoliation episodes were reported and control became increasingly reliant on foliar insecticides. By the late 2000s the species was widely recognized as a principal defoliator causing economically significant yield losses in Brazilian soybean, with its growing importance in neighboring Southern Cone countries setting the stage for later region‑wide outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of soybean into new frontiers (e.g. Brazilian Cerrado) with large, continuous monocultures; adoption of no‑till and double‑cropping systems increasing green cover and host availability year‑round; suppression of natural enemies and shifts in the pest complex associated with fungicide use and landscape simplification; climate variability (including El Niño–linked rainy seasons) favoring multiple pest generations. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within South America associated with adaptation to extensive soybean landscapes and strong migratory ability, but without clear evidence of a discrete new biotype driving the initial outbreaks.
Review: Review – Event retained but refocused on Brazil, with the start year changed from 2000 to 2002 and the country list narrowed to Brazil [2002] because multi‑source evidence indicates that widespread outbreaks transforming soybean looper from a secondary to a key soybean pest began in the 2002/03 seasons in Brazil, whereas comparable dominance in Argentina and Paraguay arose later and is captured in a separate Southern Cone event. Emergence type has been simplified to re_occurrence (re_emergence set to No) since the main drivers appear to be cropping‑system and landscape changes plus climatic suitability rather than a clearly delimited new strain. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0085562615001089?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chrysodeixis includens
EPP.common.name: Soybean Looper Moth, soybean looper
Host: Soybean (Glycine max)
Event.summary: Between roughly 2011 and 2016, large‑scale surveys across more than 35 million hectares of soybean in Brazil documented Chrysodeixis includens as the predominant lepidopteran pest in non‑Bt (glyphosate‑tolerant) soybean fields in virtually all major producing regions. These years were characterized by frequent and sometimes overlapping generations of soybean looper, high defoliation pressure and heavy dependence on foliar insecticide applications to prevent yield losses. The situation began to ease only with broader adoption of Bt soybean expressing Cry1Ac and better integration of IPM, which reduced defoliator pressure and insecticide use in some regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very large and expanding soybean area under non‑Bt cultivars, especially before and during early adoption of Bt soybean; landscape simplification around soy and favorable climatic conditions in Central–West and other regions leading to long favorable seasons; intense reliance on foliar insecticides for defoliator control. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced dispersal and recolonization capacity allowing C. includens to dominate regional soybean pest communities; possible fine‑scale variation in insecticide susceptibility, although high‑level field resistance to Cry1Ac was not yet detected in this period.
