Review: Review – Event retained as a distinct phase describing the 2011–2016 period when C. includens dominated non‑Bt soybean in Brazil and Cry1Ac soybean was widely evaluated; emergence type has been simplified to re_occurrence only (re_emergence set to No) because the main signal is a management‑ and landscape‑driven upsurge in an already widespread pest, while specific resistance evolution is handled in a separate insecticide‑resistance event. The cited large‑scale Cry1Ac and Bt/ conventional field surveys appropriately support the timing and scale. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4450/16/4/365?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Chrysodeixis includens
EPP.common.name: Soybean Looper Moth, soybean looper
Host: Soybean (Glycine max), cotton (Gossypium spp.)
Event.summary: From approximately 2013 onward, Brazilian populations of Chrysodeixis includens began to show clear, field‑evolved resistance to several chitin synthesis inhibitor (benzoylphenylurea) insecticides and variable susceptibility to other active ingredients used against soybean defoliators. As these chemistries lost efficacy in several regions, pest managers reported reduced control and higher survivorship of late‑instar larvae, forcing changes in spray programs and raising concern about resistance management in soybean and cotton. Over the latter 2010s, resistance monitoring and rotation strategies were introduced and, together with Bt crop deployment, helped limit but not eliminate resistance‑driven risk from this pest.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term, intensive use of benzoylphenylurea insect growth regulators and other insecticides in soybean and cotton landscapes, often with limited rotation of modes of action; high pest pressure and frequent applications in large contiguous production areas. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (field‑evolved resistance to chitin synthesis inhibitors such as teflubenzuron, novaluron and lufenuron, and documented variation in susceptibility to multiple insecticides); survival of resistant individuals enabling their disproportionate contribution to regional migratory populations.
Review: Retain – Event appropriately captures field‑evolved resistance of Brazilian soybean looper populations to benzoylphenylurea chitin‑synthesis‑inhibitor insecticides during the mid‑2010s, with classification as re_emergence (due to evolution of pesticide resistance) and other emergence types set to No in line with the scheme. Chemosphere and related resistance‑monitoring studies provide direct evidence of resistance levels, cross‑resistance patterns and approximate timing, and no higher‑impact insecticide‑resistance episode for this species in Brazil was identified that would supersede this one. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0261219425000286?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Chrysodeixis includens
EPP.common.name: Soybean Looper Moth, soybean looper
Host: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), soybean (Glycine max), common bean and other legumes (Phaseolus spp.), eggplant (Solanum melongena), sunflower (Helianthus annuus)
Event.summary: In Puerto Rico, Chrysodeixis includens has long been a severe pest of tomatoes, soybean and other broadleaf crops, with reports of up to 90% tomato fruit damage and complete defoliation in heavily infested fields. From around 2014, growers and resistance‑monitoring programs began reporting field failures and very high resistance ratios to key insecticides, particularly the diamide chlorantraniliprole, in soybean looper populations from Puerto Rican vegetable and seed‑production systems. By the late 2010s and early 2020s, bioassays and molecular work on the ryanodine receptor confirmed moderate to high diamide resistance, prompting recommendations for strict resistance‑management strategies and raising concern about potential spread of resistant migrants to the continental United States.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive, repeated use of diamide insecticides (e.g. chlorantraniliprole, flubendiamide) and other chemistries in year‑round vegetable and seed‑production systems in Puerto Rico; warm climate permitting multiple generations per year and continuous host availability; limited refuges from insecticide exposure. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (field‑evolved resistance to diamides and other insecticide classes, including evidence of moderate chlorantraniliprole resistance and associated ryanodine‑receptor changes, as well as likely metabolic resistance); survival and buildup of resistant genotypes in an already severe pest, with potential for long‑distance migration to other parts of the Americas.
Review: Review – New event added to represent the emergence of moderate to high resistance of Puerto Rican soybean looper populations to diamide insecticides during roughly 2014–2023 in a context where C. includens was already a long‑established, very damaging pest of tomato, soybean and other crops. Classified as re_emergence because the defining feature is evolution of insecticide resistance, not spread to a new region; the 2014 start date reflects IRAC and monitoring reports of field failures, while upper bounds are based on recent RyR‑focused molecular studies and bioassays. Given that Puerto Rico’s cropped area is smaller than that of Brazil or the US mid‑south but resistance there has clear regional implications via migration, human experts should confirm whether this episode should remain among the top ten emergence events for this species. ([cotton.org](https://www.cotton.org/beltwide/proceedings/2005-2022/data/conferences/2022/paper/21635.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Commelina communis
EPP.common.name: common dayflower, Asiatic dayflower
Host: Soybean (Glycine max), maize/corn (Zea mays), cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) and other row crops in glyphosate-resistant (Roundup Ready) production systems, especially in no-till or reduced-tillage fields of the Midwest, Midsouth and Southeast
Event.summary: After the introduction and rapid adoption of glyphosate-resistant (Roundup Ready) soybean in 1996 and subsequent glyphosate-based corn and cotton systems, Asiatic dayflower populations that had previously occurred at low densities in fields across parts of the US Midwest, Midsouth and Southeast began to increase and were first reported as troublesome weeds in no-till corn and soybean in the early 2000s. Through the 2000s, university weed science and extension reports from Iowa, Missouri and several other states documented Asiatic dayflower as a persistent broadleaf weed in glyphosate-resistant crops, characterized by extended emergence, survival of labeled glyphosate applications, and inclusion in regional lists of the most troublesome or hard-to-control soybean weeds. By the early–mid 2010s this weed shift had stabilized into a chronic management challenge in affected regions, with growers relying on diversified pre- and post-emergence herbicide programs and cultural practices to limit its impact on row-crop yields.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers (external): Rapid and widespread adoption of glyphosate-resistant soybean, corn and cotton from 1996 onward led to heavy reliance on glyphosate as the primary or sole post-emergence herbicide, reduced use of alternative herbicide modes of action, and increased use of no-till or reduced tillage. These management shifts created strong selection for weed species that are naturally tolerant of glyphosate and well adapted to minimally tilled, moist row-crop fields, allowing Asiatic dayflower to escape control and increase in density. Internal mechanisms: Commelina communis exhibits natural (inherent) tolerance to field rates of glyphosate, with partial survival at labeled doses and extended emergence that allows seedlings to escape the application window; there is no clear evidence of newly evolved glyphosate-resistant biotypes, and the event is best interpreted as a weed community shift driven by management rather than the appearance of a novel resistant strain. Life-history traits such as high seed production, prolonged emergence, and ability to root at stem nodes facilitate local population build-up and spread within affected production systems.
Review: review – Event is retained as a major emergence episode but reclassified from re_emergence to re_occurrence because current evidence indicates that C. communis in US glyphosate-resistant cropping systems is primarily exploiting pre-existing natural tolerance rather than a newly evolved herbicide-resistant biotype. Updated the mechanism_or_driver text to emphasize weed community shifts driven by glyphosate-dominated management and reduced tillage, and clarified that no intra- or inter-continental emergence is involved. Time span 1996–2015 is kept as an approximate period covering the main phase of weed shift and documentation, but the persistence of the problem beyond 2015 means dates should be treated as indicative and could be refined in a future pass.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Commelina communis
EPP.common.name: common dayflower, Asiatic dayflower
Host: Soybean (Glycine max) and maize/corn (Zea mays) in rainfed and irrigated summer cropping systems of northeastern China (especially Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning provinces)
Event.summary: From around the early 2000s, Asiatic dayflower populations in the major soybean- and corn-growing areas of northeastern China increased rapidly and became one of the three most troublesome weeds in soybean fields in this region, with dense infestations causing significant reductions in yield and quality. Surveys and genetic studies in Heilongjiang and neighboring provinces documented C. communis as the worst or dominant summer broadleaf weed in many fields, with long emergence periods, high seed production and poor control by the limited set of selective broadleaf herbicides available. By the late 2010s and early 2020s, prolonged and intensive use of atrazine and related herbicides had selected for C. communis populations with confirmed resistance to atrazine, and the species is now described as the dominant broadleaf weed in corn and soybean fields across northeastern China, with resistant biotypes and expanding distribution making management increasingly difficult through at least the mid‑2020s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers (external): Expansion and intensification of corn–soybean rotations in northeastern China, combined with widespread adoption of simplified herbicide programs and limited availability of effective selective broadleaf herbicides, created strong selection pressure favoring C. communis. Changes in farming systems (larger fields, reduced tillage and heavy reliance on a small number of herbicide modes of action, especially triazines) and climate conditions suitable for prolonged summer emergence further promoted its dominance. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – field and laboratory studies from northeastern China have demonstrated C. communis populations with resistance to atrazine, associated with psbA gene over-expression, enhanced detoxification and high antioxidant enzyme activity; this resistance allows survival and reproduction under herbicide regimes that previously suppressed the species. Geographic and numerical expansion within its native range is facilitated by traits such as extended emergence, prolific seed production and rapid vegetative growth that allow C. communis to outcompete crops under current management, turning a previously less significant native weed into a dominant, high-impact pest in regional corn and soybean production.
Review: review – New event added to capture the major emergence of Commelina communis as a dominant and, in part, atrazine-resistant weed in corn and soybean systems of northeastern China. Classified as re_emergence because the high impact is closely linked to herbicide-resistant and highly adapted field populations within a region where the species was already present, rather than to spread into new continents or subregions. Time span 2000–2025 is an approximate linked episode covering its recognition as a worst or most troublesome weed in Heilongjiang province, subsequent dominance across northeastern China, and documented evolution of atrazine-resistant biotypes; exact onset and end years could be refined with more detailed Chinese-language agronomic data in a future revision.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryphonectria parasitica
EPP.common.name: chestnut blight fungus
Host: Castanea sativa (European/sweet chestnut)
Event.summary: In 1992, chestnut blight caused by Cryphonectria parasitica was detected for the first time in Germany on sweet chestnut in south‑western localities of Baden‑Württemberg, extending the pathogen’s range from already affected Italian, French and Swiss chestnut regions into central Europe. Subsequent monitoring through the 1990s and 2000s showed a limited number of scattered foci but confirmed in situ establishment of the pathogen in German chestnut stands. Disease has persisted at low to moderate levels in these areas, prompting continued surveillance and quarantine measures but without the landscape‑scale forest losses observed earlier in southern Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance movement of infected nursery stock and other planting material within Europe, facilitated by regional trade in chestnut trees and insufficient early detection at import. Internal mechanisms: efficient local spread via rain‑dispersed conidia and airborne ascospores, and demonstrated adaptation of European C. parasitica populations to Castanea sativa, allowing successful colonization of more northerly German chestnut stands.
Review: review – Retain as a major post‑1990 event but reclassify as re_occurrence rather than intra‑continental emergence, because Western Europe (France, Switzerland, etc.) was already affected before 1990; updated source list to use Germany‑specific first‑report and review articles instead of less relevant UK/Swiss references.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cucumber mosaic virus
EPP.common.name: cucumber mosaic cucumovirus
Host: Solanum lycopersicum (tomato)
Event.summary: In the 1980s and early 1990s cucumber mosaic virus was a major constraint on field tomato production in parts of China, and field trials summarised around 1990–1991 reported that CMV infection could reduce total tomato yield by roughly 25–50%. In heavily affected areas, abundant aphid vectors, mixed vegetable cropping with many CMV reservoir hosts and the absence of resistant tomato cultivars led to widespread infection and substantial reductions in marketable fruit quality and quantity. Subsequent adoption of integrated management, including deployment of attenuated CMV strains and satellite RNAs for cross‑protection in some regions, together with vector control and cultural practices, reduced the frequency and severity of such large CMV epidemics in Chinese tomato production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High aphid pressure, dense and mixed plantings of CMV‑susceptible vegetables and weeds, and the lack of effective CMV‑resistant tomato cultivars created conditions for rapid CMV spread and high disease incidence in Chinese tomato fields. Internal mechanisms: Available syntheses do not identify a single new genotype as responsible; rather, existing CMV populations (sometimes supporting satellite RNAs) reached very high prevalence under favourable ecological conditions, so this episode is best interpreted as a severe re-occurrence of established CMV complexes in tomato rather than a distinct re-emergence driven by novel strains.
Review: review – New event added to represent CMV epidemics in Chinese tomato production where multiple syntheses report yield losses of roughly 25–50% of total yield attributable to CMV infection in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The 1990–1991 window is an operational approximation that captures the end of the eight‑year period of field trials reported by Tien and co‑workers while keeping within the 1990+ constraint; precise province‑level coverage and starting year could not be resolved from secondary sources. Classified as re-occurrence because CMV was already endemic in China and the published analyses attribute the impact mainly to high inoculum pressure and vector activity rather than clearly defined newly emerged CMV genotypes. A human curator should verify whether this Chinese episode should be retained among the top‑impact CMV events or further subdivided regionally.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cucumber mosaic virus
EPP.common.name: cucumber mosaic cucumovirus
Host: Cucumis melo (melon); Capsicum annuum (pepper)
Event.summary: In the mid‑1990s, CMV was one of the predominant viruses infecting field‑grown melon and pepper in Spain, with large surveys of the main melon‑growing regions in 1995–1996 showing CMV (alongside WMV‑2) as the most frequently detected virus in symptomatic plants. Experimental infections in central Spain demonstrated that early CMV infection before flowering could reduce melon yield by about 50% overall and by roughly 60% compared with healthy controls, and severe CMV epidemics in some pepper plantings were reported to cause yield losses approaching 80% in bad years. After these outbreaks, integrated management strategies—combining control of aphid vectors, barrier crops and physical protection, removal of infected plants and weeds, and in some cases the use of mild strains or satellite RNAs for cross‑protection—helped to reduce CMV incidence and mitigate the most extreme yield losses, although the virus has remained a recurrent problem in Mediterranean cucurbit and pepper systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive greenhouse and open‑field horticulture along the Spanish Mediterranean arc, high early‑season aphid densities, mixed cropping of solanaceous and cucurbit hosts near perennial weed reservoirs, and the lack of widely adopted CMV‑resistant cultivars combined to favour rapid CMV spread; early infection before flowering was especially damaging in melon. Internal mechanisms: The epidemics reflected high prevalence of existing CMV populations (often in mixed infections with other cucurbit viruses and sometimes associated with satellite RNAs) rather than a single clearly documented novel strain, so they are best classified as severe re-occurrence events in an already CMV‑endemic region rather than as re-emergence driven by strain innovation.
Review: review – Added to represent the mid‑1990s CMV epidemics in Spanish melon and pepper, which are documented by surveys and field experiments showing CMV as one of the most prevalent viruses in melon fields and yield reductions of up to ~60% in melon and ~80% in pepper under early, severe infection. The 1995–1997 window aligns with the main melon surveys (1995–1996) and the 1997 impact study; pepper losses from this period are captured via later syntheses that cite Avilla et al. and Luis‑Arteaga et al. Classified as re-occurrence because CMV was already widespread in Southern Europe and there is no strong evidence that a single new CMV genotype was the primary driver; instead the impact reflects high inoculum pressure, vector abundance and mixed infections. Human review is advised to decide whether to keep this as a single multi‑crop event or split into separate melon and pepper entries if finer granularity is desired.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Cucumber mosaic virus
EPP.common.name: cucumber mosaic cucumovirus
Host: Capsicum annuum (hot and sweet peppers)
Event.summary: In Korean pepper production, CMV pathotypes P0 and P1 had been endemic and highly damaging since the 1980s and 1990s, but their impact was reduced by widespread deployment of pepper cultivars carrying resistance effective against these pathotypes. From the early 2010s, and particularly after 2013, new CMV variants such as strain GTN and several related isolates were recovered from commercial pepper fields where they caused severe disease on cultivars previously resistant to P1, marking a resistance‑breaking re-emergence associated with renewed heavy losses in pepper production. Following these outbreaks, breeding efforts shifted toward broader‑spectrum resistance loci (e.g. cmr2) capable of controlling the new variants, and integrated aphid and crop management practices were emphasised to reduce CMV pressure in Korean pepper fields.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large areas of pepper grown as monocultures of CMV‑resistant cultivars imposed strong selection pressure on viral populations, while intensive production, overlapping cropping cycles and abundant aphid vectors promoted rapid spread once resistance‑breaking variants arose. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity were demonstrated, as resistance‑breaking variants such as CMV‑GTN carry nonsynonymous mutations in RNA1 encoding the 1a protein that allow infection of P1‑resistant cultivars, while maintaining high fitness in the field; these changes reflect adaptation to the host resistance background rather than geographic spread and underlie classification of this episode as a re-emergence event.
Review: review – Event retained as a key CMV re-emergence episode in pepper but the time window has been corrected from 2010–2013 to 2013–2016 to align with the documented isolation of the resistance‑breaking strain CMV‑GTN from pepper in 2013 and the collection of additional resistance‑breaking isolates from P1‑resistant cultivars in 2016, rather than implying emergence already by 2010. The geographic assignment (Eastern Asia, Republic of Korea) and classification as re-emergence driven by resistance‑breaking viral evolution in an already affected subregion remain appropriate. A human curator may wish to refine the end year further if more detailed epidemiological information on the dominance period of these variants becomes available, but the current adjustments improve consistency with the primary literature.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cucumber mosaic virus
EPP.common.name: cucumber mosaic cucumovirus
Host: Solanum lycopersicum (tomato)
Event.summary: During a survey in January 2006 near Salem in Tamil Nadu, South India, tomato fields showing severe mosaic, leaf puckering and stunting were found to have more than 70% of plants symptomatic, and laboratory testing identified the causal agent as cucumber mosaic virus subgroup II. This was the first report of subgroup II CMV infecting tomato in India, where previous tomato infections had been associated predominantly with subgroup I strains, and it demonstrated that subgroup II variants had established in open‑field tomato with conspicuous disease and yield reduction. The discovery prompted recommendations for improved seed and seedling health management, stronger aphid control and attention to CMV subgroup structure when breeding and screening for resistance in Indian tomato and other solanaceous crops.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of tomato cultivation in southern India, often with limited vector control and proximity to other CMV hosts, facilitated introduction and establishment of subgroup II CMV in tomato fields. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence at the country/host level is central, as this outbreak represents the first documented occurrence of CMV subgroup II infecting tomato in India, indicating either recent introduction of subgroup II strains or successful host shift of existing subgroup II variants; this change in subgroup composition constitutes a re-emergence of CMV disease in a known host and subregion driven by viral diversification with potential implications for symptom severity and resistance specificity.
Review: review – Retained as an important re-emergence event representing the first report of CMV subgroup II infecting tomato in India, with field incidence greater than 70% in surveyed sites. The event’s source URL has been corrected to the Plant Disease note by Sudhakar et al. (2006, PD‑90‑1457B), which directly documents this outbreak; the previously cited CSIRO Plant Disease Notes PDF (DN08013) actually describes CMV subgroup IB on periwinkle and only references the tomato report secondarily. Geographic assignment (Southern Asia, India) and classification as re-emergence driven by a shift in CMV subgroup composition in tomato are appropriate, although quantitative yield‑loss estimates remain limited and could be refined if more data emerge.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cucumber mosaic virus
EPP.common.name: cucumber mosaic cucumovirus
Host: Capsicum annuum (pepper); Solanum lycopersicum (tomato); Citrullus lanatus (watermelon)
Event.summary: In the mid‑ to late 2010s, surveys of vegetable fields at multiple locations in Nigeria found cucumber mosaic virus infecting pepper, tomato and watermelon with typical mosaic, leaf deformation and stunting symptoms that farmers associated with yield reductions in smallholder and commercial systems. Molecular analyses of isolates from these outbreaks showed that Nigerian CMV populations belonged to subgroup IB but were unusually diverse and included at least one recombinant RNA1 segment, indicating ongoing in situ evolution of CMV in Nigerian agroecosystems. As awareness of this diversity increased, recommendations emphasised integrated management—removal of infected plants and weed reservoirs, seed health measures and aphid control—to limit further spread of divergent and recombinant CMV strains in West African vegetable value chains.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of vegetable production, frequent movement of infected planting material, high densities of alternative weed hosts and abundant aphid vectors in tropical agroecosystems favoured repeated CMV infection, mixed infections and long‑term virus persistence in Nigeria. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via recombination and accumulation of genetic diversity within subgroup IB was documented, with one Nigerian isolate identified as a putative recombinant and population‑genetic analyses indicating high diversity and predominance of purifying selection; these processes underlie CMV re-emergence in the same subregion with altered strain composition and potentially modified host‑range and pathogenicity profiles.
Review: review – Kept as a re-emergence event highlighting the discovery of genetically diverse subgroup IB CMV populations and a putative recombinant isolate infecting pepper, tomato and watermelon in Nigeria, representing the first detailed molecular description of such populations from West Africa. However, the underlying study is primarily a genetic survey of 106 samples collected from 16 locations, and while symptomatic plants and potential yield impacts are described qualitatively, quantitative estimates of national‑scale production losses are lacking, so its rank among the very largest CMV emergence events is somewhat uncertain. The event years (2015–2019) and Nigeria [2015] start year are approximate, reflecting the likely sampling period and prior Nigerian CMV reports rather than explicit dates in the paper. Human review is advised to confirm whether this episode should be retained among the top‑impact events or reframed as a key evolutionary/virological milestone for CMV in West Africa.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Cucumber mosaic virus
EPP.common.name: cucumber mosaic cucumovirus
Host: Capsicum annuum (commercial pepper cultivars carrying cmr1 resistance)
Event.summary: In 2019–2020, growers in Antalya province, Türkiye, reported alarming CMV‑like symptoms on commercial pepper cultivars that carried the cmr1 allele conferring resistance to CMV pathotype P0, indicating breakdown of previously effective resistance. Field and greenhouse inoculation tests followed by complete genome sequencing confirmed that these plants were infected by a resistance‑breaking CMV‑P1 strain (rbCMV) capable of overcoming cmr1, and all tested resistant cultivars became systemically infected under experimental conditions. After this finding, local recommendations stressed the urgent need to deploy new resistance sources effective against CMV‑P1, alongside improved aphid management and sanitation, to restore control of CMV in Turkish pepper production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive cultivation of cmr1‑based resistant pepper varieties in Antalya created strong, long‑term selection favouring CMV variants able to evade this single dominant resistance gene, while high aphid populations and intensive protected and open‑field pepper production enabled rapid spread once resistance‑breaking strains arose. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity are clearly involved, as sequence comparisons showed SNP patterns characteristic of CMV‑P1 resistance‑breaking strains and all cmr1 cultivars tested developed systemic infection; this is a straightforward re-emergence event in which viral evolution overcame a major resistance gene rather than a geographic range expansion.
Review: retain – This event accurately describes the first report of CMV‑P1 resistance‑breaking strains infecting cmr1‑based resistant pepper cultivars in Antalya, Türkiye, during 2019–2020, as documented by Fidan et al. (2023). The geographic assignment (Western Asia, Türkiye), host specification (cmr1‑carrying Capsicum annuum cultivars) and classification as re-emergence driven by resistance‑breaking evolution in an already CMV‑endemic region are appropriate, and the Journal of Phytopathology article cited provides a suitable primary source. No changes to timing, geographic scope or emergence‑type classification are recommended, and this row can be retained as one of the major recent CMV resistance‑breaking episodes in pepper.

EPP.scientific.name: Cuscuta campestris
EPP.common.name: field dodder
Host: Vegetable crops including potato and other market‑garden species, together with numerous wild dicot hosts in field margins, forest edges and along streams
Event.summary: In 2010, Cuscuta campestris was observed for the first time in north‑west Tunisia (Mogods region), adding a new non‑chlorophyllous holoparasite to the country’s flora and to the North African weed flora. Over the following years, additional foci were documented in northern and central Tunisia, including a heavily infested potato and vegetable field near Boussalem by 2013, as well as infestations on numerous wild host species around field margins and forest edges. By the mid‑2010s, the species was recognised as an invasive alien with the potential to severely damage cultivated crops in affected areas and to spread further within Northern Africa if not contained.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction is most plausibly linked to contaminated crop seed or planting material entering vegetable‑growing areas, followed by local spread via agricultural machinery, movement of infested plant material and possibly water. Internal mechanisms: The same traits seen elsewhere—holoparasitic growth on many hosts, dense mats that smother vegetation and a persistent seed bank—allow rapid build‑up once established, so that even relatively small initial incursions can quickly become agronomically significant.
Review: review – Newly added event capturing the first confirmed records of C. campestris in Tunisia in 2010 and subsequent severe infestations of vegetable and potato fields and nearby wild vegetation by 2013, as documented by El Mokni et al. (2016); this is best classified as an intra‑continental emergence into the Northern Africa sub‑region rather than a global first emergence, but the full spatial extent and quantitative yield impacts still need further documentation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Dasineura gleditchiae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie du févier, honeylocust podgall midge
Host: Gleditsia triacanthos (honeylocust) in urban plantings and nurseries
Event.summary: Around 1992, characteristic pod galls of Dasineura gleditchiae were first observed on honeylocust street trees near Budapest, indicating introduction of the North American midge into Hungary. Over the following years the species spread to additional cities and regions, becoming widespread and common on honeylocust across the country by the late 1990s. The outbreak stabilized as an established urban pest, with damage mainly aesthetic and managed through pruning, monitoring and occasional insecticide use rather than eradication.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increased planting of thornless ornamental honeylocust cultivars in Hungarian cities and trade of nursery stock from already infested Western and Southern European sources facilitated introduction and rapid spread. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion (inherent) by a highly host‑specific, multivoltine gall midge well adapted to complete several generations per year on planted honeylocust under Central/Eastern European climatic conditions.
Review: Retain – Event correctly represents the first documented record of Dasineura gleditchiae in Eastern Europe (Hungary, near Budapest, 1992) and subsequent spread within the country. Continent, sub‑region, country and timing agree with EPPO and regional literature. Classification as an intra‑continental emergence (first occurrence in the Eastern Europe sub‑region) is appropriate; no changes were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Dasineura gleditchiae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie du févier, honeylocust podgall midge
Host: Gleditsia triacanthos in experimental orchards and urban plantings near Thessaloniki
Event.summary: In June 1995, Dasineura gleditchiae was first detected in Greece on honeylocust trees in experimental orchards near Thessaloniki, marking its arrival in Greek plantings within an already invaded Southern Europe. During the late 1990s the midge spread locally in northern Greek urban and roadside honeylocust, causing conspicuous galling and defoliation of new foliage on ornamental trees. The pest became established but remained mostly confined to planted honeylocust, with damage managed through monitoring and targeted treatments in high‑value plantings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction via international trade in ornamental honeylocust nursery stock into Greek experimental orchards and amenity plantings, together with increasing use of susceptible cultivars in urban greening. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion (inherent) by an invasive European population, with multiple generations per year enabling rapid build‑up on honeylocust under Mediterranean conditions.
Review: Review – Event is well supported as the first Greek record (1995) and a clear example of spread into the eastern Mediterranean part of Southern Europe. However, Southern Europe already harboured D. gleditchiae (Italy, 1980), so this is not an intra‑continental emergence into a new sub‑region. I changed 'intra_continental_emergence' from 'true' to 'false' and left other emergence‑type flags 'false'. Recommended to retain with the updated classification.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Dasineura gleditchiae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie du févier, honeylocust podgall midge
Host: Gleditsia triacanthos in parks and recreation areas of Ankara
Event.summary: In 2005, Dasineura gleditchiae was first recorded in Türkiye on honeylocust trees in parks and recreation areas of Ankara, representing the first confirmed occurrence of the species in Asia. Following its discovery, the midge was found more widely on ornamental honeylocust in urban greenery in and around Ankara, indicating successful establishment in Western Asia. The pest has since persisted as an invasive gall‑forming insect on honeylocust in Türkiye, with management focused on monitoring and localized treatments rather than large‑scale eradication.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction with imported honeylocust planting material from infested European nurseries into Ankara’s urban parks and roadside plantings, and the popularity of honeylocust as an ornamental tree in Turkish cities. Internal mechanisms: inter‑continental geographic range expansion (inherent) into climatically suitable Western Asia, supported by the midge’s multivoltine life cycle and its ability to overwinter in soil near host trees.
Review: Retain – Bayram et al. (2005) and EPPO clearly document the 2005 finding on honeylocust in Ankara as both the first Turkish and first Asian record. Continent/sub‑region assignment, timing and narrative are appropriate, and classification as an inter‑continental emergence is correct. No changes were needed; this is one of the key global emergence events for the species.

EPP.scientific.name: Dasineura gleditchiae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie du févier, honeylocust podgall midge
Host: Gleditsia triacanthos ornamental trees in Alnarp, Lund and Malmö
Event.summary: Dasineura gleditchiae was first observed in Sweden in 2007 on honeylocust trees at Alnarp, and by 2008 it had also been found in Lund and Malmö, marking its arrival in the Scandinavian part of Northern Europe. During 2008, pheromone trapping and visual surveys showed established but relatively low‑density populations, with visible galling and premature leaf drop on affected honeylocust trees. The midge has persisted in southern Sweden as an invasive but locally managed pest, with monitoring via sex‑pheromone traps and an emphasis on maintaining tree health rather than intensive chemical control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: northward spread facilitated by trade in ornamental honeylocust between continental Europe and Scandinavian nurseries and by planting of honeylocust in university campuses and urban parks in southern Sweden. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion (inherent) into cooler northern climates, coupled with efficient mate‑finding mediated by sex pheromones, which has been exploited for monitoring.
Review: Review – Molnár et al. (2009) confirm first observations in Alnarp in 2007 and additional sites in 2008, so the timing and geography are sound. Northern Europe already had D. gleditchiae (United Kingdom from 1983 and Denmark from 2006), so this episode is not an intra‑continental emergence into a new sub‑region. I therefore set 'intra_continental_emergence' from 'true' to 'false'; all other fields were left unchanged. Recommended to retain as the key event marking spread into Scandinavia.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Dasineura gleditchiae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie du févier, honeylocust podgall midge
Host: Gleditsia triacanthos in nurseries and urban plantings
Event.summary: In May 2010, Dasineura gleditchiae was reported as a new invasive species in Slovenia after being detected on honeylocust in Ljubljana, its surroundings and in Maribor, where attacks on ornamental trees were described as strong. Over the early 2010s it became more widely observed in Slovenian urban greenery and in nurseries, with pod galls affecting the appearance and growth of young honeylocust foliage. The species is now included among Slovenia’s alien Diptera, and management consists mainly of monitoring nursery stock and applying localized control where high‑value trees are heavily infested.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction with imported honeylocust nursery plants from infested neighbouring countries and ongoing intra‑European ornamental plant trade. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion (inherent) and efficient colonization of new plantings, aided by multiple annual generations and high host specificity to honeylocust.
Review: Review – Jurc & Jurc (2010) document a strong attack on honeylocust in Ljubljana and Maribor in 2010, so the event year and location are appropriate. Because Southern Europe was already affected (Italy, Greece, Spain, Serbia, Croatia, Bulgaria), this is not an intra‑continental emergence into a new sub‑region; I changed 'intra_continental_emergence' from 'true' to 'false'. The event still represents an important national invasion with notable local impact and should be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Dasineura gleditchiae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie du févier, honeylocust podgall midge
Host: Gleditsia triacanthos in urban plantings, roadside trees, shelterbelts and forest belts (Donetsk, Zaporizhzhya and Kyiv regions)
Event.summary: In 2014, Dasineura gleditchiae was recorded for the first time in Ukraine, with massive damage to honeylocust trees documented in June–August in the industrial cities of Avdiivka and Donetsk, where galls were present on virtually all examined trees. In the same year the midge was also found in protective forest belts in Donetsk Region, in the Zaporizhzhya Region near the "Kamyani Mogyly" Reserve, and on ornamental honeylocust in Kyiv, indicating rapid spread across eastern and central parts of the country. The outbreak marked fast establishment of the species in urban plantings and shelterbelts; subsequent observations suggest that D. gleditchiae is now widespread wherever honeylocust is grown in Ukraine, but no targeted eradication has been attempted beyond general monitoring.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction of D. gleditchiae into Ukraine via movement of infested honeylocust planting stock and ornamental trees from already invaded Central and Eastern European countries, combined with extensive use of Gleditsia triacanthos in urban landscaping and shelterbelts in industrial regions. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion (inherent) of a monophagous, multivoltine gall midge capable of causing heavy galling and partial defoliation on honeylocust across a broad climatic gradient, leading to a regional outbreak once established.
Review: Add – This event was missing from the original dataset but 2014 surveys in Ukraine documented the first national record together with massive damage and wide distribution across eastern and central regions, making it one of the most impactful emergence episodes for this species. A new row has therefore been added with year 2014, Eastern Europe/Ukraine geography and an outbreak‑focused summary. It is classified as 're_occurrence' at the Eastern Europe sub‑region level because the species was already present in other Eastern European countries (e.g. Hungary, Poland, Slovakia, Czech Republic, Krasnodar Region of Russia) by this time. Recommended to retain as part of any top‑ten set of emergence events.

EPP.scientific.name: Dasineura gleditchiae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie du févier, honeylocust podgall midge
Host: Gleditsia triacanthos in urban and roadside plantings and forest shelterbelts (north‑eastern and south‑eastern Romania)
Event.summary: On 3 August 2016, Dasineura gleditchiae was first confirmed in Romania when pod‑like galls were found on honeylocust in Dumbrava, Bacău County, in the north‑eastern region of Moldova. Surveys in 2016–2017 then recorded the midge on honeylocust at more than 20 additional localities across almost all counties of north‑eastern Romania, mostly on isolated trees, urban park plantings and shelterbelts, with generally low to moderate attack frequencies but occasional sites showing up to about 60% of trees or leaves galled. Subsequent work on invasive forest insects documented the species also in southern and south‑eastern Romania, indicating that by the late 2010s D. gleditchiae had become widely established nationally; management focuses on surveillance and, where necessary, silvicultural or chemical measures in high‑value stands.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: spread from neighbouring infested countries (notably Hungary and other Central/Eastern European states) via regional plant trade and movement of ornamental and forestry planting stock, alongside increased planting of honeylocust in Romanian towns and shelterbelts. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion (inherent) and efficient colonization of new hosts across a range of temperate to continental climates, without evidence that novel genotypes or increased virulence were required for establishment.
Review: Review – The original row mis‑dated the first Romanian record to 2011 and treated the episode as an intra‑continental emergence. National survey data show that D. gleditchiae was first detected on 3 August 2016 in Bacău County, with many further localities recorded in 2016–2017 in north‑eastern Romania and later observations from southern and south‑eastern regions. I therefore changed the event year to '2016‑2018', corrected the country tag to 'Romania [2016]', rewrote the event summary to match the Romanian data, and set 'intra_continental_emergence' to 'false' and 're_occurrence' to 'true' because Eastern Europe already had the species but this represents a major resurgence and spread within the sub‑region. Recommended to retain, but flagged for review of the revised timing and scope.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Dasineura gleditchiae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie du févier, honeylocust podgall midge
Host: Gleditsia triacanthos ornamental trees
Event.summary: In 2017, the Honeylocust Podgall Midge (Dasineura gleditchiae) was reported as new to Ireland in the Irish Naturalists’ Journal, confirming its arrival in the island’s honeylocust plantings. The detection came from infested ornamental honeylocust with characteristic pod galls, indicating that the species had successfully established a reproducing population. Since its first record, the midge has been incorporated into Irish biodiversity and pest recording schemes, with ongoing surveillance but no indication of large‑scale tree mortality.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction via importation of infested nursery stock or ornamental honeylocust trees from Britain or continental Europe, reflecting strong horticultural trade links. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion (inherent) from existing European populations, taking advantage of suitable host trees and mild coastal climates in parts of Ireland.
Review: Review – The event correctly captures the first Irish record of D. gleditchiae around 2017 and its establishment on ornamental honeylocust, as reported in the Irish Naturalists’ Journal. Because Northern Europe already contained established populations (United Kingdom, Denmark, Sweden), this is not an intra‑continental emergence, so I changed 'intra_continental_emergence' from 'true' to 'false'. This is a relatively small, largely ornamental‑tree event but it does add a new country; it can be retained, noting that it may fall below a strict top‑ten impact threshold if further pruning is required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Dialeurodes citri
EPP.common.name: citrus whitefly
Host: Citrus spp. (lemon and other citrus in commercial orchards, nurseries and residential plantings; additional ornamental hosts such as Ficus, Coffea, Gardenia, Punica and others were also noted in surveys).
Event.summary: In February 2023, Dialeurodes citri was identified for the first time in New Caledonia, on lemon trees in a residential area of Nouméa, marking the first confirmed establishment of citrus whitefly in an UNSD Oceania country. Follow‑up surveys by the New Caledonian NPPO found the pest present in multiple areas, including nurseries and citrus orchards, and its status was soon updated to ‘Present: widely distributed’ within the territory. During 2023–2025, no major citrus production losses were yet reported, but the incursion represents a significant new geographic foothold in Oceania and prompted increased surveillance and consideration of regulatory and biological control options.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Human‑mediated movement of infested plant material (especially citrus nursery stock and ornamental hosts) into New Caledonia via regional and international trade is the most plausible introduction pathway. The island’s warm, humid subtropical climate and widespread cultivation of citrus and ornamental hosts provided suitable conditions for establishment and rapid local spread once the pest arrived. Internal mechanisms: Primarily inherent geographic range expansion of an already polyphagous, climate‑tolerant whitefly; there is no evidence that novel biotypes, insecticide resistance, or increased virulence played a specific role in this event.
Review: review – Newly added major event: first documented establishment of Dialeurodes citri in New Caledonia (Oceania) in 2023, supported by the New Caledonia NPPO/IPPC pest report and EPPO’s subsequent inclusion of New Caledonia in the species’ distribution. Classified as an inter‑continental emergence into the Oceania continent under the UNSD scheme used in this project. While the geographic and regulatory evidence is strong, finer details on area affected, longer‑term production impacts and any subsequent management campaigns should be confirmed or updated by subject‑matter experts before finalizing the ranking of this event among the species’ top emergence episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Diaphorina citri
EPP.common.name: Asian citrus psyllid
Host: Sweet orange and other citrus spp.
Event.summary: In 1997, Diaphorina citri was detected for the first time in southeastern Iran near the Pakistan border, in association with trees later confirmed to be infected with huanglongbing (HLB), marking the onset of a serious citrus disease complex in the country. Over the subsequent decade the psyllid and HLB spread within key citrus areas of southeastern Iran, causing increasing tree decline and yield loss. The event stabilized only after intensified surveillance, tree removal, and vector management programs slowed further spread, though the pest and disease remained established.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement of infected plant material and natural spread from neighboring Pakistan and other Asian foci, combined with expansion of susceptible citrus plantings in southeastern Iran, facilitated establishment. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion/spillover of the Asian HLB pathosystem into Iranian orchards, geographic range expansion of established D. citri populations into new climatic zones in Western Asia, and enhanced transmission efficiency due to the close association between the psyllid and infected citrus trees.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Diaphorina citri
EPP.common.name: Asian citrus psyllid
Host: Backyard and commercial citrus (sweet orange, grapefruit, mandarin) and ornamental Murraya paniculata
Event.summary: In June 1998, Diaphorina citri was detected for the first time in the United States on orange jasmine hedges and dooryard citrus in Palm Beach County, Florida, establishing the pest on a new continent and raising concern about future citrus greening. Over the next several years the psyllid spread rapidly across most citrus‑producing counties in Florida, and after huanglongbing was detected in 2005 it became the primary vector driving near‑statewide infection and dramatic declines in citrus yield and tree health. By the mid‑2010s, D. citri and HLB were entrenched throughout Florida, forcing a long‑term shift toward intensive vector control, tree removal, and replanting strategies with major economic losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction likely via human‑mediated movement of infested ornamental Murraya plants, followed by rapid regional spread aided by dense commercial citrus plantings, mild subtropical climate, and long periods of leaf flushing; industry structure and initial regulatory delays allowed the pest to build large populations before greening was detected. Internal mechanisms: Highly efficient acquisition and transmission of Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus by D. citri, high fecundity and multiple overlapping generations, and adaptation to Florida’s climate led to enhanced transmission and severe re‑emergence of the HLB pathosystem on a new continent.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Diuraphis noxia
EPP.common.name: Russian wheat aphid
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event.summary: Introduced into the United States in 1986, Russian wheat aphid spread rapidly through the western Great Plains and by the 1991–1992 seasons caused its most damaging outbreak phase, infesting millions of acres of winter wheat and barley across 17 western states. Economic assessments for 1987–1993 attribute several hundred million to nearly US$900 million in direct and indirect losses to RWA in the western USA, with 1991–1992 among the peak years for infested acreage and yield loss. In the mid‑1990s, a combination of intensive insecticide use, biological control introductions and especially the deployment of resistant cultivars carrying gene Dn4 reduced average losses and shifted the pest from crisis level to a manageable but still important constraint.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very large contiguous areas of susceptible dryland winter wheat and barley, favorable cool and dry conditions in several early 1990s seasons, and the initial lack of resistant cultivars or effective natural enemies allowed extremely high aphid densities and widespread crop losses during 1991–1992. Internal mechanisms: The invasive North American RWA population showed high reproductive rates and good cold tolerance but was not yet differentiated into multiple virulent biotypes; this episode is therefore interpreted as a major re‑occurrence (dramatic increase in incidence and impact) in a previously invaded sub‑region rather than as re‑emergence driven by new strain evolution.
Review: retain (newly added) – This event was missing from the original list but is clearly among the top global post‑1990 emergence episodes for RWA, with very large infested areas and economic losses in the western United States during 1991–1992. Classified as re‑occurrence because it represents the peak of a multi‑year invasion in a sub‑region where the species was already established and there is no evidence that a novel biotype was responsible.

EPP.scientific.name: Diuraphis noxia
EPP.common.name: Russian wheat aphid
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare), oats (Avena sativa), rye (Secale cereale)
Event.summary: Following its first South American record in Chile in 1987–1988, Russian wheat aphid was detected in Argentina in 1991 at Malargüe, Mendoza, and soon after in wheat fields in Buenos Aires province, marking its spread into one of the continent’s major wheat belts. Through the mid‑1990s the pest became established across key cereal‑growing regions such as Bahía Blanca, with high local aphid densities, characteristic foliar streaking and rolling, and documented economic importance for bread wheat and malting barley production. By the late 1990s, RWA was widely distributed in Argentina’s wheat region, and management had shifted from detection and containment to ongoing integrated control based on monitoring, selective insecticides and the gradual development of resistant or tolerant cereal germplasm.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Human‑mediated movement of infested plant material and wind‑borne spread from Chile into neighboring Argentine cereal areas, combined with extensive areas of susceptible wheat and barley in dry, sunny climates, facilitated rapid establishment and regional spread. Internal mechanisms: The invasive South American populations possessed the species’ inherent capacity for parthenogenetic reproduction, high intrinsic growth rates and adaptation to dryland cereals; early Argentine work did not document distinct virulence biotypes, so this episode is interpreted primarily as a major geographic range expansion within an already invaded continental sub‑region.
Review: review – Retain as a major South American emergence event, since RWA became an economically important pest in Argentina’s main wheat region from 1991 onward. Corrected misclassification by setting intra‑continental emergence to No, because RWA was already present in the same UNSD sub‑region (“South America”) via Chile prior to 1990; spread into Argentina represents country‑level expansion within an existing sub‑region rather than first occurrence in a new sub‑region. Countries field was simplified to the country‑level with provinces described in the summary, and a key Argentine field study (SciELO article from Bahía Blanca) was added as a more directly relevant source.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Diuraphis noxia
EPP.common.name: Russian wheat aphid
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event.summary: After its initial emergence as a major pest in South African wheat in 1978, Russian wheat aphid remained entrenched, and by 1993 the country experienced one of its largest recorded outbreak seasons in the summer‑rainfall dryland wheat and barley areas. National estimates indicate that in 1993 large areas of dryland wheat suffered substantial yield reductions and that cumulative direct losses from the late 1980s through 1993 were on the order of tens of millions of South African rand. Intensified chemical control, gradual adoption of RWA‑resistant wheat cultivars and improved agronomic practices helped to bring infestations back to more manageable levels in subsequent seasons, though the pest continued to be a key constraint in susceptible cultivars.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive planting of susceptible wheat cultivars, favorable cool and dry conditions for aphid population build‑up, and limited early‑season control allowed very high aphid densities during the 1993 season, translating into large national yield and monetary losses. Internal mechanisms: No distinct new biotype was associated with this particular year; the outbreak reflects the invasive South African population’s ability to reach economic thresholds rapidly under conducive environmental conditions, so it is classified as a severe re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.
Review: retain – Event corresponds to a well‑documented peak outbreak year in South Africa with large national yield and economic losses. Classification as re‑occurrence (no new biotype, dramatic resurgence in an already affected sub‑region driven by weather and cropping patterns) is consistent with definitions. No structural corrections were needed beyond clarifying the nature of the losses in the summary.

EPP.scientific.name: Diuraphis noxia
EPP.common.name: Russian wheat aphid
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event.summary: From the mid‑2000s, South African researchers documented the appearance of new Russian wheat aphid biotypes able to damage cultivars previously considered resistant, beginning with RWASA2 in 2005 and followed by RWASA3 (2009) and RWASA4 (2011). These biotypes progressively overcame combinations of Dn1, Dn2, Dn3, Dn4 and other resistance genes deployed in commercial wheat, and during seasons such as 2005–2006 growers reported severe damage and significant localized yield losses even in fields planted to resistant cultivars. In response, wheat breeding programs intensified efforts to pyramid multiple resistance genes and to identify new sources of resistance, while integrated pest management recommendations were updated; although some control was regained, the durability and cost of resistance‑based management were substantially affected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term, large‑scale planting of cultivars with similar RWA resistance backgrounds, combined with continued high pest pressure in South Africa’s summer‑rainfall wheat areas, imposed strong selection for resistance‑breaking aphid genotypes. Internal mechanisms: Successive Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence events (RWASA2–RWASA4) with increased virulence to multiple Dn genes underpin this re‑emergence, with South African populations showing biotypic and genetic differentiation relative to earlier invasive populations; this episode thus represents re‑emergence due to genetic adaptation to resistant hosts rather than simple resurgence of existing biotypes.
Review: review – Retain as a major re‑emergence episode in South Africa linked to successive resistance‑breaking biotypes, but extend the event period from 2005–2010 to 2005–2011 to encompass the first reports of RWASA4. Classification as re‑emergence is appropriate and was left unchanged; other emergence‑type flags remain No because the episode does not involve spread to a new continent or UNSD sub‑region. A South African extension article specifying years of detection for RWASA1–RWASA4 has been incorporated as a more precise source.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Diuraphis noxia
EPP.common.name: Russian wheat aphid
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare)
Event.summary: Around 2018, a highly virulent South African Russian wheat aphid biotype, later designated RWASA5, was first detected on multiple wheat fields in the Free State province and shown to overcome all known resistance genes present in commercial cultivars. By the early 2020s, RWASA5 had spread within major wheat‑growing areas of South Africa, and extension bulletins highlighted the absence of effective resistant cultivars, the potential for substantial yield losses in both wheat and barley, and concern about possible spread into neighboring Southern African countries. Management responses have focused on intensified monitoring for RWASA5, accelerated breeding to identify new resistance sources effective against this biotype, and integrated chemical and agronomic strategies to limit damage while longer‑term genetic solutions are developed.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued large‑scale planting of cultivars carrying a limited set of resistance genes and the presence of multiple earlier South African biotypes provided strong selection pressure for an even more virulent biotype, while regional trade in seed and grain and movement of infested plant material increase the risk of further spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity are central, as RWASA5 can damage plants carrying resistance genes that were effective against RWASA1–RWASA4, representing a clear re‑emergence driven by further biotypic evolution within South African RWA populations.
Review: review – Event is retained as a major recent re‑emergence episode because RWASA5 poses a serious threat to South African wheat and barley production. The start year has been corrected from 2015 to 2018 to align with reports of the first field detections and early distribution surveys, and the countries field has been restricted to South Africa, as neighboring states are currently described mainly as at risk rather than confirmed RWASA5 foci in available sources. Classification as re‑emergence remains appropriate, driven by a newly recognized, highly virulent biotype; new South African research articles and extension pieces documenting RWASA5 were added to strengthen sourcing.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine indica
EPP.common.name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Host: Vegetables, fruit orchards (including citrus and other tree fruits), oil palm plantations, other plantation and field crops
Event.summary: In 1990, Malaysian vegetable systems reported Eleusine indica biotypes resistant to the ACCase-inhibiting herbicides fluazifop and propaquizafop and to the PSI inhibitor paraquat, marking the start of a herbicide‑resistance problem in this weed in the country. Over the 1990s, resistant goosegrass spread across vegetable and plantation systems, and in 1997 a Teluk Intan fruit orchard reported severe control failure of glyphosate, with field and follow‑up trials confirming an 8–12‑fold glyphosate‑resistant biotype – the first such case globally in this species. Through the 2000s–2020s, repeated herbicide selection across oil palm, orchards and other crops led to multiple resistance to ACCase inhibitors, glyphosate, glufosinate, PS II inhibitors and oxidative phosphorylation uncouplers, making E. indica one of Malaysia’s most complex herbicide‑resistant weeds and a persistent management challenge.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive year‑round vegetable and plantation production with heavy reliance on a small set of post‑emergence herbicides (paraquat, fluazifop, glyphosate and others); limited rotation of modes of action; labour constraints favouring chemical over manual control; expansion of perennial crops (e.g. oil palm, fruit trees) where goosegrass thrives in inter‑rows. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via multiple target‑site mutations in ACCase (e.g. Trp‑2027‑Cys and other substitutions) and EPSPS (e.g. Pro106 substitutions and, in some populations, double EPSPS mutations), EPSPS overexpression and amplification, and non‑target‑site mechanisms; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through prolific seed production and seed dispersal in plantation landscapes; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within Malaysian agro‑ecosystems as resistant biotypes colonized diverse crops and plantation environments.
Review: Decision: retain – Key Malaysian herbicide-resistance milestones (ACCase and paraquat resistance in vegetables around 1990; first glyphosate-resistant biotype from a Teluk Intan orchard in 1997; subsequent evolution of multiple resistance including EPSPS double mutations) are supported by FAO, weedscience.org and mechanistic studies. No changes were made to geography, years or event typing; classification as re-emergence (novel resistant biotypes of an established weed) is appropriate and the event clearly ranks among the largest global Eleusine indica emergence episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine indica
EPP.common.name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Host: Coffee plantations (central coffee zone), rice, herbicide-resistant maize and cotton rotations
Event.summary: In 2006, studies in Colombia’s central coffee zone documented Eleusine indica populations with reduced susceptibility to glyphosate in coffee plantations, signaling the emergence of resistance in a key perennial crop system. During the late 2000s–2010s, goosegrass control problems spread into rice and rotations with herbicide‑resistant maize and cotton, where glyphosate and paraquat were used intensively before and after crop establishment. By around 2016–2021, detailed dose–response and physiological studies confirmed high‑level resistance to both glyphosate and paraquat in goosegrass from central Colombia, with resistance factors up to about 10 for glyphosate and 7 for paraquat, making this the first confirmed multiple resistance (EPSPS + PSI) case for E. indica in the country and a serious threat to rice and HR‑crop productivity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive use of glyphosate in coffee, HR maize and HR cotton systems and paraquat for burndown in rice rotations; limited diversification of weed control tactics; increased technification and large‑scale monocropping of rice and HR crops. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence involving EPSPS target‑site mutations and/or overexpression, together with mechanisms conferring paraquat resistance (reduced uptake/translocation and altered oxidative stress responses), leading to multiple resistance to EPSPS and PSI inhibitors; Enhanced Transmission via prolific seed production and spread along mechanized production corridors.
Review: Decision: retain – Weedscience.org and Cenicafé reports confirm glyphosate-resistant goosegrass in Colombian coffee from 2006 and later glyphosate+paraquat multiple resistance in maize/rice systems, matching the stated timing, crops and mechanisms. The event is correctly framed as a national, multi‑crop re-emergence driven by resistance evolution rather than geographic spread; no structural corrections were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine indica
EPP.common.name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Host: Soybean, maize (corn), cotton and other grain/row crops
Event.summary: From the mid‑2000s, Eleusine indica populations began to increase sharply in Brazilian soybean, maize and cotton fields under glyphosate‑based conservation tillage, initially as a troublesome but controllable grass weed. Over the 2010s, repeated glyphosate use in glyphosate‑resistant crop systems and heavy reliance on ACCase herbicides selected glyphosate‑ and ACCase‑resistant goosegrass across major producing regions, with resistant populations documented and spreading in South, Southeast and Central‑West Brazil. By the early–mid 2020s, reviews identified goosegrass as Brazil’s most troublesome weed in grain systems, infesting over 60% of grain‑producing areas and capable of reducing yields by more than 50% if uncontrolled, with multiple resistance to glyphosate and ACCase inhibitors now common.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Massive expansion of glyphosate‑resistant soybean, maize and cotton; widespread adoption of no‑till systems with glyphosate‑dominated weed control; limited rotation of herbicide modes of action; high cropping intensity and reduced tillage favouring E. indica establishment; economic incentives for low‑labour chemical control. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via EPSPS target‑site mutations, EPSPS gene amplification/overexpression, and ACCase target‑site mutations; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as highly adapted resistant biotypes expanded from local foci to dominate grain production landscapes.
Review: Decision: retain – Recent Brazilian syntheses document Eleusine indica infesting more than 60% of national grain area with potential yield losses >50% and multiple resistance to glyphosate and ACCase inhibitors, supporting this as one of the largest global emergence events. The timing (mid‑2000s onset with strong escalation through the 2010s–2020s), geography (Brazil, South America) and classification as re-emergence via resistance evolution are appropriate; no corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine tristachya
EPP.common.name: threespike goosegrass
Host: Urban lawns, road verges and other disturbed ruderal sites in the Lyon agglomeration, with limited potential spillover into nearby gardens and field margins
Event.summary: In 1995, Eleusine tristachya was first noticed in the Lyon agglomeration of eastern France on a roadside embankment at Chaponost and at a few additional disturbed urban sites, extending its known French range from earlier records confined to the south‑west Atlantic coast.([persee.fr](https://www.persee.fr/doc/linly_0366-1326_2007_num_76_2_13647)) Subsequent botanical surveys through the late 1990s and early 2000s recorded a small but increasing number of local populations around Lyon, indicating successful establishment in urban ruderal habitats while remaining much less expansive than the congener E. indica.([persee.fr](https://www.persee.fr/doc/linly_0366-1326_2007_num_76_2_13647)) By the mid‑2000s the species was regarded as locally naturalised in parts of Lyon but still rare in France overall, with spread largely limited to dry, disturbed sites along roads and in built‑up areas.([biblio.cbnpmp.fr](https://biblio.cbnpmp.fr/doc_num.php?explnum_id=7985))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion along transport corridors and in urban disturbed habitats in southern and eastern France, facilitated by vehicle traffic, movements of soil and construction materials, and warm, dry microclimates along roads and railways that mimic the species’ subtropical native conditions.([persee.fr](https://www.persee.fr/doc/linly_0366-1326_2007_num_76_2_13647)) Internal mechanisms: No specific genetic or physiological novelty has been reported for French populations; floristic treatments regard them as similar to South American material, so this episode is best interpreted as geographic range expansion of pre‑existing genotypes rather than evolution of new biotypes.([powo.science.kew.org](https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A30127333-2))
Review: Review – Reclassified this episode as a re‑occurrence rather than intra‑continental emergence. Eleusine tristachya was already recorded in south‑west France well before 1995, so the Lyon discovery represents a local resurgence within the same UNSD sub‑region (Western Europe), not colonisation of a new European sub‑region.([persee.fr](https://www.persee.fr/doc/linly_0366-1326_2007_num_76_2_13647)) The event is retained as one of the few well‑documented post‑1990 expansions in Europe, but its impact is modest (small ruderal populations with little documented crop damage), so it may be dropped if a stricter top‑10‑by‑impact filter is later applied.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine tristachya
EPP.common.name: threespike goosegrass
Host: Field margins, waste ground and cropped fields in Kanagawa Prefecture receiving cattle‑manure amendments (including vegetable and arable land adjacent to cattle feedlots)
Event.summary: In 1998, Eleusine tristachya was collected for the first time in Japan in Kanagawa Prefecture, growing along fields fertilised with cattle manure near a feedlot, and Koba & Matsumoto (2003) described it as a newly naturalised alien grass.([nh.kanagawa-museum.jp](https://nh.kanagawa-museum.jp/assets/icp/contents/1600215407483/simple/Bull32.pdf)) Subsequent observations at and near the original sites showed that populations persisted and set seed over multiple years, indicating successful establishment in disturbed agricultural margins and waste ground. Japanese naturalised‑plant lists compiled in the 2000s then treated E. tristachya as a casual to naturalised exotic with a restricted distribution, completing an inter‑continental colonisation from South America to eastern Asia while the species remained a minor weed.([rib.okayama-u.ac.jp](https://www.rib.okayama-u.ac.jp/wild/kika_table.htm))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction as a contaminant of cattle feed or forage imported from regions where Eleusine tristachya is common, with subsequent spread via manure application to fields; establishment was facilitated by disturbed, well‑drained soils in peri‑urban agriculture and transport of contaminated soil or machinery.([nh.kanagawa-museum.jp](https://nh.kanagawa-museum.jp/assets/icp/contents/1600215407483/simple/Bull32.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: No herbicide resistance, host shift or other specific evolutionary changes have been documented in Japanese populations; establishment appears driven primarily by propagule pressure and environmental suitability rather than novel biotypes.([powo.science.kew.org](https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A30127333-2))
Review: Retain – Evidence from Koba & Matsumoto (2003) clearly documents Eleusine tristachya as newly naturalised in Japan from collections in 1998 near manure‑amended fields, with no prior Japanese records.([nh.kanagawa-museum.jp](https://nh.kanagawa-museum.jp/assets/icp/contents/1600215407483/simple/Bull32.pdf)) At the time of that work the species was known to be naturalised in North America and Africa but not in Asia, and later databases list only Japan and the Caucasus as Asian regions of naturalisation.([powo.science.kew.org](https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A30127333-2)) Given the lack of older, well‑dated Caucasus records, classifying this as an inter‑continental emergence into Asia is reasonable, though future herbarium studies could refine which Asian region holds the true earliest record.

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine tristachya
EPP.common.name: threespike goosegrass
Host: Perennial tree and vine crops (especially almond, walnut and prune orchards) and adjacent non‑crop ground in California’s Central Valley and other warm regions of the western United States
Event.summary: Although threespike goosegrass has been present in California since at least 1967,([wcngg.com](https://wcngg.com/2019/09/01/threespike-goosegrass-presents-orchard-challenges/)) it was only from the late 2000s and early 2010s that growers and weed scientists began reporting it as a serious problem in tree‑nut orchards of the Central Valley. Extension blogs and trade articles from the 2010s describe rapidly expanding, dense patches in almond, walnut and prune orchards, where the low, tufted growth interferes with irrigation and mechanical nut harvest and proves difficult to control with standard glyphosate‑based programmes.([ucanr.edu](https://ucanr.edu/blog/uc-weed-science-weed-control-management-ecology-and-minutia/article/tale-two-goosegrasses)) Herbicide trials conducted between 2016 and 2019 at multiple orchard sites confirmed the species’ poor response to glyphosate alone and evaluated alternative pre‑emergence and post‑emergence herbicide combinations, leading to updated management recommendations and underscoring a sustained resurgence of Eleusine tristachya as a key orchard weed through at least 2023.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/675acd4e0ce2cede71d18f38))
