Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of California tree‑nut acreage and a shift toward glyphosate‑based, reduced‑tillage orchard‑floor management created wide strips of disturbed, irrigated ground in which tufted, warm‑season grasses such as threespike goosegrass can thrive; repeated glyphosate use, limited mechanical disturbance and traffic along tree rows facilitated the build‑up and spread of dense clumps.([ucanr.edu](https://ucanr.edu/blog/uc-weed-science-weed-control-management-ecology-and-minutia/article/tale-two-goosegrasses)) Internal mechanisms: Greenhouse dose–response work and field trials show that established E. tristachya plants survive very high glyphosate rates and often resume growth, indicating strong innate or slowly selected tolerance, but there is still no published molecular evidence for specific target‑site or metabolic resistance mutations in this species; the episode is therefore best interpreted as a re‑occurrence driven by management practices and physiological tolerance rather than a clearly defined new resistant biotype.([ucanr.edu](https://ucanr.edu/blog/uc-weed-science-weed-control-management-ecology-and-minutia/article/tale-two-goosegrasses))
Review: Review – Updated the event period from 2010–2020 to 2010–2023 to reflect the continued importance of threespike goosegrass in California nut orchards and recently published herbicide‑trial data.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/675acd4e0ce2cede71d18f38)) Reinterpreted the episode as a management‑driven resurgence within an area where the species has been present since at least 1967, keeping the classification as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence, because field and greenhouse studies show strong tolerance and poor control with glyphosate but do not yet document a specific resistance mutation.([ucanr.edu](https://ucanr.edu/blog/uc-weed-science-weed-control-management-ecology-and-minutia/article/tale-two-goosegrasses)) Source URLs were adjusted to emphasise orchard‑specific extension and peer‑reviewed literature (UCANR blog, West Coast Nut article, HortTechnology trials, Calflora distribution) and to drop a mechanistic paper on glyphosate resistance in Eleusine indica that did not provide primary data on E. tristachya.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Elsinoë fawcettii
EPP.common.name: citrus scab fungus
Host: Citrus spp. (mainly lemons and other susceptible citrus in commercial orchards)
Event.summary: In October 1999, citrus orchards in New Zealand were found to harbour Elsinoë fawcettii populations resistant to the systemic benzimidazole fungicide benomyl, confirming active citrus scab in the country and reduced efficacy of a key control product. Over the following seasons around 2000–2001, surveys and research showed benomyl‑resistant strains becoming prevalent in affected orchards, complicating management of scab on lemons and other susceptible citrus. Growers responded by shifting to alternative fungicides and integrated control strategies, stabilising disease losses but with higher management costs and the need for resistance‑management programmes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive use of benzimidazole fungicides in New Zealand citrus orchards selected for resistant E. fawcettii populations; humid coastal climates favoured repeated infection cycles. Internal mechanisms: Antifungal resistance (development of benomyl-resistant strains); possible associated shifts in pathogen population structure under fungicide selection pressure.
Review: Decision: Retain. Evidence from the EPPO Reporting Service 2002/107 and the EPPO Global Database confirms that benomyl resistance in Elsinoë fawcettii was first observed in New Zealand citrus orchards in October 1999 and that this followed earlier establishment of the pathogen in the country. The event is correctly classified as re‑emergence because it reflects the evolution of fungicide resistance (an internal change in the pathogen) in an already affected subregion, not a new geographic occurrence. Geographic fields (continent: Oceania; sub-region: Australia and New Zealand; country: New Zealand) are consistent with UNSD groupings, and the selected sources are appropriate and specific to this resistance episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Wheat (Triticum aestivum), mainly intensively managed winter wheat
Event.summary: From the late 1970s through the 1980s, wheat powdery mildew in China expanded from a largely local problem in the Yangtze River basin to a much wider distribution as wheat production intensified and semi-dwarf, high-yielding cultivars replaced traditional landraces. In 1990 and 1991, favourable weather, high planting densities, heavy nitrogen use and expanded irrigated area triggered a nationwide crisis in which powdery mildew epidemics affected wheat in roughly two dozen provinces, with tens of millions of hectares exposed and several million tonnes of grain lost each year. Following emergency fungicide use, adjustments in agronomic practices and greater attention to resistance breeding, national epidemic intensity declined somewhat after the early 1990s, although powdery mildew has remained one of the most important foliar diseases of Chinese wheat.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of wheat production in China, including increased plant population densities, higher nitrogen fertilizer inputs, expansion of irrigated area in northern regions and widespread adoption of high-yielding, semi-dwarf cultivars, created dense, humid canopies highly favourable for powdery mildew epidemics; conducive weather in 1990–1991 allowed the pathogen to spread across most wheat-growing provinces. Internal mechanisms: No single new strain is highlighted; the event is best interpreted as a re-occurrence driven mainly by cropping-system and climatic factors acting on existing B. graminis f. sp. tritici populations, although local adaptation of mildew populations to modern cultivars likely contributed.
Review: review – New event added. Large-scale wheat powdery mildew epidemics in China in 1990–1991, affecting about two dozen provinces and many millions of hectares with multi-million-tonne yield losses, clearly qualify among the most impactful modern events for B. graminis. Classified as re-occurrence (disease resurgence in an already affected region driven mainly by intensification and weather) rather than first detection or inter-/intra-continental emergence. Geography (Asia/Eastern Asia, China) and timing (1990–1991) are based on national surveys and review articles; specific provincial breakdowns are not listed and could be refined by a human reviewer.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia davidii
EPP.common.name: David's spurge; toothed spurge
Host: Maize and sunflower (primary), other arable crops
Event.summary: In 2007, dense populations of E. davidii were first recorded in arable fields in the Vojvodina region of northern Serbia, between the villages of Aleksa Šantić, Pačir and Đurđin, marking the species’ emergence within the southern Pannonian cropping region. Over the following six years the weed spread and formed increasingly dense patches in maize and sunflower fields, with infested areas expanding from about 3 ha to 7 ha in the monitored blocks and observational reports of sunflower crops suffering reduced plant and head size and up to 300 ha being taken out of sunflower production in favour of less valuable crops. By around 2014, despite trials with various herbicide treatments (notably high‑rate glyphosate) the species was recognised as a significant invasive agricultural weed in Serbia, with ongoing monitoring and management experiments recommended.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction via contaminated grain or seed (likely from other infested European areas) combined with intensive maize and sunflower cultivation in Vojvodina and limited crop rotation options that allowed rapid build‑up in specific fields; mechanical operations and local seed movement facilitated spread between neighbouring farms. Internal mechanisms: high seed production and a persistent seed bank that make eradication difficult once established, and strong competitive ability in row crops leading to economically significant yield impacts (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: Review – Retain this event as a major high‑impact outbreak in Serbia but change the event type from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence. The Southern Europe sub‑region was already invaded by E. davidii through its earlier establishment in northern Italy; Serbian crop‑field infestations therefore represent a resurgence and spread within an already affected sub‑region, not the first intra‑continental emergence into a new sub‑region. The magnitude of impact (sunflower taken out of production on hundreds of hectares) justifies keeping this as a separate key event.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia graminea
EPP.common.name: grassleaf spurge
Host: Ruderal herbaceous vegetation along a country road near Palermo (Sicily), within a matrix of native and other alien species.([herbmedit.org](https://herbmedit.org/storage/1158/FL26_025-030.pdf))
Event.summary: In December 2015 a considerable population (~300 individuals over ~150 m² with ~20% cover) of grassleaf spurge was discovered along a roadside at Boccadifalco near Palermo, Sicily, representing the first record for Italy and for Europe. The population was well established and reproducing sexually, indicating naturalization at the site by the time it was described in 2016. The authors inferred accidental introduction, probably via nearby garden centers and escaped container plants, and recommended ongoing monitoring because of the species’ invasive behavior elsewhere; no subsequent eradication has yet been reported.([herbmedit.org](https://herbmedit.org/storage/1158/FL26_025-030.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: accidental escape from ornamental or nursery stock at a nearby garden center, with roadside disturbance providing ideal habitat for establishment and spread. Internal mechanisms: high seed production, effective local dispersal and ability to dominate ruderal herb communities facilitate naturalization; the event also reflects the species’ capacity for long-distance dispersal and climatic tolerance of Mediterranean conditions.([herbmedit.org](https://herbmedit.org/storage/1158/FL26_025-030.pdf))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia graminea
EPP.common.name: grassleaf spurge
Host: Weed of roadsides, campus grounds and botanic garden surroundings in lowland urban Java.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/334030263_REKAMAN_BARU_Euphorbia_graminea_Jacq_DAN_E_hyssopifolia_L_Euphorbiaceae_DI_PULAU_JAWA))
Event.summary: Exploratory surveys in 2019 around Bogor (IPB campus, Cibinong and Bogor Botanic Garden) recorded grassleaf spurge populations that had not been included in Flora of Java, leading to its publication that year as a new record for the island. The species was observed as an alien weedy herb along roads and in disturbed urban green spaces, indicating recent introduction and local spread on Java. The authors interpreted the finding as evidence that Java’s flora is still accumulating alien weeds and emphasized the need to update regional floras, while long‑term invasion impacts remain under study.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/334030263_REKAMAN_BARU_Euphorbia_graminea_Jacq_DAN_E_hyssopifolia_L_Euphorbiaceae_DI_PULAU_JAWA))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction via horticultural or academic plant exchanges associated with major research institutions and botanic gardens in Bogor, combined with urban disturbance and transport corridors that favour establishment of alien weeds. Internal mechanisms: generalist ruderal life history and efficient seed dispersal allow rapid colonization of new tropical lowland environments without any identified novel strain.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/334030263_REKAMAN_BARU_Euphorbia_graminea_Jacq_DAN_E_hyssopifolia_L_Euphorbiaceae_DI_PULAU_JAWA))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia serpens
EPP.common.name: matted sandmat, creeping spurge, round-leafed spurge
Host: Weed in irrigated flower beds, domestic and non‑domestic gardens, lawns, coastal rocky sites and roadsides in western Cyprus (anthropogenic and ruderal plant communities rather than a specific crop host)
Event.summary: In 2010, Euphorbia serpens was first documented for the flora of Cyprus from flower beds near Pissouri Beach and additional coastal localities, indicating its recent arrival as an alien garden and roadside weed in Western Asia. Subsequent records during the 2010s confirmed scattered but persistent populations in irrigated gardens, parks, coastal rocky habitats and roadside verges, where it behaved as a low-impact naturalized groundcover. By around 2020, Cypriot floristic syntheses and the national alien-species database classified E. serpens as a naturalized, non‑invasive alien weed with no evidence of major spread into semi‑natural habitats or significant economic damage.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction is attributed to the horticultural and landscaping trade, likely via contaminated soil or planting material associated with ornamental plantings and tourist infrastructure, combined with irrigation and disturbance in coastal gardens, parks and roadsides that provide suitable establishment sites. Internal mechanisms: The species’ prostrate, mat-forming growth, prolific seed production, ability to root at stem nodes and tolerance of trampling and dry, disturbed soils facilitate local establishment and geographic range expansion in anthropogenic habitats, without any evidence of novel genotypes, increased invasiveness or herbicide resistance specifically associated with Cyprus populations.
Review: review – Retain this as a well-documented, clearly dated first national record and small-scale naturalization event in Cyprus. Corrected misclassified emergence types by setting both 'first_detection' and 're_occurrence' to false, because the species was already known from the plant host system globally and from the Western Asia subregion (e.g. Iran, Turkey) before 2010, and new-country spread within an already colonized subregion should not be coded as first detection or re-occurrence. Pruned event-level sources to focus on the Cyprus-specific floristic references and the EPPO overview; broader range databases remain at profile level. Recommended for expert review mainly to confirm its relative importance among other small post-1990 introduction events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia serpens
EPP.common.name: matted sandmat, creeping spurge, round-leafed spurge
Host: Weed in lawns, garden beds and ruderal patches in fields and gardens of the University of Baghdad (Al‑Jadriyah campus), Baghdad city (urban anthropogenic habitats rather than a specific crop host)
Event.summary: During the 2021–2022 growing seasons, Euphorbia serpens was discovered during botanical field surveys in fields and gardens on the University of Baghdad’s Al‑Jadriyah campus, and was formally published in 2022 as a new record for the Iraqi flora. The species was observed forming small population groups in disturbed campus habitats, confirming its establishment as a casual to locally naturalized weed in urban Baghdad. By the mid‑2020s there were still no reports of major agronomic losses or large-scale spread beyond such urban greenspaces in Iraq.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The most plausible pathway is accidental introduction via regional trade and transport of ornamental plants, potting soil or other plant material to university gardens and nearby urban plantings, combined with expansion of irrigated lawns and disturbed ruderal patches that provide microsites for establishment. Internal mechanisms: As elsewhere, E. serpens' annual life cycle, prolific seed set, tolerance of heat and drought, rooting at stem nodes and C4 photosynthesis support rapid colonization of disturbed, well‑drained soils, enabling geographic range expansion within Western Asia; there is no evidence of novel strain emergence or herbicide resistance specifically associated with the Iraqi populations.
Review: review – Retain as the first documented national record for Iraq, but correct and flag for review. Updated the event year to '2021-2022' to match the primary paper, which reports collections during two growing seasons 2021–2022 with publication in 2022, rather than the broader and partly speculative '2020-2022' span. Adjusted the habitat/host description to reflect that records come from university fields and gardens in Baghdad rather than generalized 'agricultural surroundings'. Set 'first_detection' and 're_occurrence' to false, since this is neither the first detection in the plant host system globally nor a resurgence in a previously known Iraqi subregion. Pruned event-level sources to the dedicated Iraqi floristic paper plus EPPO for general context, removing a second article that focuses on Euphorbia maculata rather than E. serpens.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia serpens
EPP.common.name: matted sandmat, creeping spurge, round-leafed spurge
Host: Casual weed in ornamental planters, pavement and sidewalk cracks, and an abandoned citrus grove in urban and peri‑urban sites around Reggio Calabria (Southern Italy), associated with mixed ruderal and ornamental vegetation rather than specific crops.
Event.summary: In late summer and autumn 2022, Euphorbia serpens subsp. serpens was reported as a casual alien for Calabria and continental Southern Italy, based on several small populations found in planters, sidewalk and pavement cracks, and an abandoned citrus grove in the Reggio Calabria area. These records extended the known Italian range of the species, which had already been documented as a casual or naturalized alien in other regions (e.g. central and northern Italy and Sicily), but in Calabria it remained confined to highly disturbed urban and peri‑urban habitats. As of the early 2020s, there was no evidence of spread into cropland or semi‑natural habitats, nor of any notable economic impact in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction to Calabria is most likely linked to the movement of ornamental plants and associated soil or substrates, as well as other horticultural and urban trade flows within Italy and the wider Mediterranean region. Urbanization, road and pavement construction, and abandonment of small orchards and citrus groves create disturbed, open habitats in which the species can establish. Internal mechanisms: The plant’s mat-forming habit, C4 photosynthesis, tolerance of periodically dry, nutrient‑poor substrates, and high seed production promote persistence in cracks, planters and ruderal sites, supporting local range expansion in disturbed Mediterranean environments, but there is no current evidence of increased invasiveness, new genotypes or resistance traits in the Calabrian populations compared with previously established European populations.
Review: review – Retain only as a minor, well-documented regional extension of the species’ European range, but note that major corrections were necessary. The original entry incorrectly dated the Calabrian record to '2015–2021' and implied long-standing presence along riverbanks and agricultural margins; these have been corrected to a first record in 2022 confined to planters, sidewalk and pavement cracks, and an abandoned citrus grove in Reggio Calabria, as reported in Musarella et al. ("New Alien Plant Taxa for Italy and Europe: An Update"). Emergence-type flags have been set to false for all categories because this event does not represent first detection in the plant host system, nor a new continent or subregion, nor a documented resurgence. Event-level sources were narrowed to the primary Italian update paper; earlier Italian Notulae documenting E. serpens in other regions remain relevant at the profile level. Given that this is a small-scale regional record within a country where the species was already present, human reviewers may wish to reassess whether this event merits inclusion among the limited set of emergence events for this low-impact weed, or whether a more agronomically significant episode should be substituted.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Frankliniella occidentalis
EPP.common.name: western flower thrips
Host: Mixed ornamentals and cut flowers (glasshouse and nursery crops), vegetables and seed crops (e.g. lettuce, pepper, tomato) and later field crops affected via Tomato spotted wilt virus
Event.summary: In May 1993, western flower thrips was first detected on ornamentals near Perth in Western Australia, marking its introduction into the Australian portion of the Australia–New Zealand subregion. During the mid‑ to late 1990s the pest spread to other Australian states and became established in greenhouse ornamentals and vegetables and in some outdoor horticultural crops. Its arrival coincided with, and contributed to, severe TSWV outbreaks in vegetables and ornamentals in eastern and south‑eastern Australia, where it displaced or supplemented native thrips as a vector and necessitated major changes in virus and thrips management.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/FRANOC/reporting))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: imports of infested cut flowers and ornamental plant material, particularly into Western Australia; protected cropping systems that provided suitable year‑round habitat; and increasing areas of intensive horticulture in coastal and irrigated regions. Internal mechanisms: invasion by insecticide‑resistant greenhouse lineages of F. occidentalis; high fecundity and polyphagy facilitating rapid establishment on many hosts; and its superior efficiency as a vector of TSWV relative to native thrips, which led to large disease outbreaks in susceptible crops.([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1111/1744-7917.12721))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Kept as a major emergence event for Australia but with corrected classification: inter‑continental emergence is set to “No”, because Frankliniella occidentalis (or a closely related taxon) was already present in New Zealand by the 1980s, so the Australian incursion represents spread within the Australia–New Zealand subregion rather than the first occurrence in Oceania. The event is instead treated as re‑emergence of an invasive, insecticide‑resistant strain in a subregion where related lineages were already present. Host range and linkage to TSWV epidemics are supported but could be further refined by an Australian specialist.

EPP.scientific.name: Frankliniella occidentalis
EPP.common.name: western flower thrips
Host: Ornamental and cut‑flower crops (Alstroemeria, Gypsophila and other ornamentals in nurseries and botanical gardens)
Event.summary: In 1996 surveys of nurseries and botanical gardens in Sri Lanka detected western flower thrips on Alstroemeria and Gypsophila, representing the first report of the species in the country and, as far as current evidence indicates, the first occurrence in the Southern Asia subregion. Over the late 1990s it became established in multiple ornamental and cut‑flower nurseries, reflecting local spread in protected cultivation, and raised concerns about possible future spillover into vegetable and other horticultural crops in Sri Lanka and neighbouring countries.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3692))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: importation of infested ornamental planting material and cut flowers from regions where F. occidentalis was already invasive; concentration of susceptible hosts in protected nurseries and botanical gardens; and initially limited awareness and surveillance for exotic thrips. Internal mechanisms: high reproductive rate on ornamental hosts; polyphagy enabling persistence on diverse nursery plants; and efficient short‑distance dispersal within and between greenhouses.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3692))
Review: Decision: RETAIN. This event corresponds well to the documented first report of F. occidentalis in Sri Lanka and likely the first incursion into the Southern Asia subregion. Classification as first detection and intra‑continental emergence (new Asian subregion, given earlier records in Western and Eastern Asia) is appropriate, and no clear higher‑impact event in Southern Asia before India’s incursion has been identified. Laboratory bioassays on larvae and adults collected from these fields confirmed strong resistance to several pyrethroids, and by 1997 resistant moths were detected at additional South Carolina locations, indicating local spread of resistant populations. Changes in insecticide programmes and the subsequent adoption of Bt cotton reduced the frequency of catastrophic control failures, but pyrethroid‑resistant H. zea persisted as an important management problem in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive and repeated use of pyrethroid insecticides in cotton in the southeastern United States created strong selection pressure, while large contiguous cotton acreage and favourable climate supported high population densities and rapid selection. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of resistance to multiple pyrethroid active ingredients (e.g. cyhalothrin, cypermethrin, permethrin), with resistance to cyhalothrin expressed as an incompletely dominant trait; inherent high dispersal capacity and multiple generations per year facilitated spread of resistant alleles within the cotton belt.

Type‑of‑emergence classification has been corrected to treat this as re‑emergence only (re_emergence = true; re_occurrence = false), because the resurgence is clearly linked to genetic changes in the pest rather than purely external factors. Geographic fields (North America / Northern America / United States of America) conform to the UNSD scheme and match the locations reported in Brown et al. (1998) and subsequent resistance monitoring. Sources are appropriate and specific to this episode; row should be retained with this corrected classification.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261219498000386?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Helicoverpa zea
EPP.common.name: bollworm, corn earworm, tomato fruitworm, noctuelle de la tomate, "ver de lépi du maïs"
Host: Bt cotton producing Cry1Ac (single‑toxin Bollgard) and, later, two‑toxin cotton (Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab or Cry1Ac + Cry1F) targeting heliothine pests, with H. zea as a primary pest in the southeastern and mid‑south cotton belt.
Event.summary: After the commercialization of Bt cotton (Cry1Ac) in 1996, H. zea populations in the southeastern and mid‑south United States were exposed across millions of hectares with only moderate toxin dose and limited non‑Bt refuge. Around 2002–2004, resistance monitoring began to detect decreased susceptibility to Cry1Ac and later cross‑resistance to Cry2Ab in several cotton‑belt states, and by the late 2000s some fields experienced unexpected boll damage on Bt cotton and required supplemental insecticide sprays. With broader deployment of pyramided two‑toxin cultivars and adjustments in scouting and spray thresholds, regional crop failure was avoided, but Cry1Ac/Cry2Ab resistance alleles became established in H. zea populations and laid the groundwork for more widespread Cry1/Cry2 resistance problems in the following decade.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive, long‑term planting of single‑toxin Cry1Ac Bt cotton, followed by rapid adoption of two‑toxin Bt cotton, in the southeastern and mid‑south United States; overlapping exposure to related Cry1 toxins in Bt maize; declining availability and/or use of structured non‑Bt refuges; and favourable climate allowing multiple H. zea generations per year. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – field‑evolved resistance to Cry1Ac and partial cross‑resistance to Cry2Ab, documented by increased survival at diagnostic toxin concentrations and elevated resistance ratios in bioassays; inherent high mobility and multivoltinism of H. zea facilitated spread of resistant genotypes within the existing North American range.
Review: review – Event retained as a major re‑emergence episode capturing the first broadly documented field‑evolved resistance of H. zea to Cry1Ac (and associated cross‑resistance to Cry2Ab) in U.S. Bt cotton. The year range has been adjusted from 2003–2008 to 2002–2010 to reflect evidence that resistance was first detected about six years after Bt cotton commercialization and that increased sprays against H. zea on Bt cotton became apparent by 2009–2011. Geographic information has been simplified to the country level (United States of America [2002]) in line with the UNSD country list, with affected southeastern and mid‑south cotton states now described in the event summary rather than in the 'countries' field. Type‑of‑emergence coding has been corrected to re‑emergence only (re_emergence = true; re_occurrence = false), as this resurgence is primarily driven by genetic adaptation to Bt toxins rather than external factors alone. Because the magnitude and timing of field impact have been debated in the resistance‑management literature, this row is flagged for expert review but should remain in the top‑impact set.([food.ec.europa.eu](https://food.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2018-10/gmo_rep-stud_mon-810_report-2017_ref-043.pdf))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Helicoverpa zea

Host: Bt maize (including sweet corn and field corn) expressing Cry1Ab, Cry1A.105 and/or Cry2Ab2, and pyramided Bt cotton (Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab, Cry1Ac + Cry1F) grown across the eastern and southern United States.
Event.summary: From around 2010, growers and researchers in the eastern and southern United States began reporting unexpected injury by H. zea on Bt sweet corn and Bt field corn expressing Cry1 and Cry2 toxins, suggesting reduced field performance of these events. Sentinel sweet corn trials in Maryland and later detailed studies in northeast Louisiana documented field‑evolved resistance of H. zea to pyramided Cry1A.105/Cry2Ab2 maize, with significant ear damage and larval survival on hybrids that had previously provided high levels of control. This resistance episode increased reliance on foliar insecticides, reduced yield protection in some Bt maize and cotton hybrids, and prompted regulatory and research responses aimed at revising resistance‑management strategies and shifting toward traits that included Vip3A.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High adoption and long‑term use of Bt maize and cotton producing Cry1 and Cry2 toxins across the southern and eastern United States; landscape‑scale mosaics of Bt crops exposing H. zea to similar toxins on multiple host plants; and variability in refuge implementation. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of resistance to Cry1A and Cry2A proteins in H. zea, confirmed by elevated survival in diet and plant bioassays on pyramided maize and cotton; inherent mobility, polyphagy and multiple generations per year facilitated rapid selection and spread of resistant genotypes within existing production areas.
Review: review – Event appropriately describes the first clearly documented field‑evolved resistance of H. zea to pyramided Cry1A.105/Cry2Ab2 maize (and related Bt sweet corn) in the eastern and southern United States, supported by Maryland sentinel‑plot data and northeast Louisiana field trials, and captures its agronomic impacts. The 'countries' field has been standardised to 'United States of America [2010]' to conform with the UNSD country list; specific states and regions are now described in the event summary rather than embedded in the country string. Type‑of‑emergence coding is corrected to re‑emergence only (re_emergence = true; re_occurrence = false), as the event reflects genetic adaptation (Bt resistance) within an existing range rather than a simple external re‑occurrence. Wording in the mechanism section has been clarified so that spread of resistant genotypes is described as occurring within the existing North American range rather than implying colonisation of new geographic regions. This remains one of the most important Bt‑resistance events for H. zea and should be retained.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28036388/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Helicoverpa zea
EPP.common.name: bollworm, corn earworm, tomato fruitworm, noctuelle de la tomate, "ver de lépi du maïs"
Host: Pyramided Bt cotton (dual‑gene and triple‑gene varieties such as Cry1Ac + Cry1F, Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab, and Cry1Ac + Cry1F + Vip3A) and Bt corn (including events expressing Cry1Ab, Cry1Fa, Cry1A.105, Cry2Ab2 and Vip3Aa) grown across major cotton and maize production areas of the southeastern and south‑central United States.
Event.summary: From about 2016 onward, large‑scale monitoring across the southeastern United States documented that many Helicoverpa zea populations had developed widespread practical resistance to Cry1 and Cry2 proteins in both Bt cotton and Bt corn, with frequent unexpected boll and ear damage despite use of pyramided traits. Multi‑state surveys during 2016–2019 showed high survival of field‑collected H. zea on diagnostic concentrations of Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab2 and correlated increases in injury to Bt crops, leading growers to rely again on multiple foliar insecticide sprays and raising serious concerns over the durability of existing Bt technologies. By 2020–2021, field trials and resistance monitoring indicated that triple‑gene cotton including Vip3Aa still provided effective control, but resistance allele frequencies to Cry1 and especially Cry2 were high and early warning signs for Vip3Aa resistance were emerging, prompting recommendations to adjust deployment strategies and resistance‑management plans to preserve Vip3A efficacy.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued intensive cultivation of Bt corn and cotton over large contiguous areas of the southern United States; widespread planting of pyramided Cry1/Cry2 traits with relatively few non‑Bt host refuges; and cropping patterns that maintain high densities of H. zea across seasons. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – widespread practical resistance to Cry1Ac, Cry1Ab, Cry1A.105, Cry1Fa and Cry2Ab2 documented through diet and plant bioassays, with high resistance ratios and high frequencies of resistance alleles; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – genomic and phenotypic evidence of resistant genotypes associated with Cry1Ac/Cry2Ab resistance; inherent life‑history traits (high mobility, polyphagy and multiple generations per year) allowed resistant genotypes to persist and spread within the existing North American range, while susceptibility to Vip3Aa was still generally high but threatened by detectable resistance alleles in some Texas and southeastern populations.
Review: review – This row summarises the broad, multi‑state phase (approximately 2016–2021) in which practical resistance of H. zea to Cry1 and Cry2 proteins in Bt cotton and Bt corn became widespread across the southeastern and south‑central United States, as documented by multi‑state bioassays, field injury data and increased use of foliar insecticides. The 'countries' field has been standardised to 'United States of America [2016]' to match the UNSD country list, with affected states now described in the narrative fields. Type‑of‑emergence coding has been corrected so that the episode is classified solely as re‑emergence (re_emergence = true; re_occurrence = false), reflecting that the resurgence is driven primarily by resistance evolution rather than external factors alone. Sources (regional resistance surveys, Vip3Aa resistance‑allele studies and USDA ARS field efficacy work) are appropriate and up‑to‑date for this episode, but the row is flagged for expert review as new data on Vip3Aa field performance and resistance may justify further subdivision or extension of the event period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10058025/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Hemileia vastatrix
EPP.common.name: coffee rust fungus
Host: Coffea arabica in mostly older shade and sun coffee plantations at mid-elevations
Event.summary: Between 2002 and 2003, El Salvador experienced a nationally significant coffee leaf rust epidemic as Hemileia vastatrix caused unusually heavy defoliation in many aging, rust-susceptible Coffea arabica plantations at low and mid elevations, against a backdrop of record-low international coffee prices and structural overproduction that had already weakened farm finances. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) As fungicide use, fertilization and renovation were cut back, rust incidence and severity rose sharply and contributed to marked drops in national coffee output and export revenue compared with the 1990s, prompting concern over the long‑term viability of the sector and early policy discussions on renovation and diversification. ([ipsnews.net](https://www.ipsnews.net/2002/07/coffee-central-america-el-salvador-bears-brunt-of-severe-crisis/?utm_source=openai)) In subsequent years, production partially stabilized at a lower level, but many highly affected farms were not fully rehabilitated, and this episode highlighted vulnerabilities in El Salvador’s coffee sector that later exacerbated the impacts of the 2012–2013 regional Big Rust epidemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers (external): The epidemic coincided with a period of global coffee overproduction and historically low prices around 2000, which sharply reduced profitability and led many Salvadoran growers to delay pruning and renovation, reduce fertilizer inputs, and apply fewer or no fungicide sprays, leaving dense, old stands of rust-susceptible arabica varieties with high inoculum levels. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) Favourable weather for rust infection—frequent rains and prolonged leaf wetness at key times in the 2002–2003 seasons—further accelerated epidemic development. Internal mechanisms: Available accounts attribute the outbreak mainly to management and climatic factors rather than the emergence of a clearly novel hyper‑virulent race; the episode is therefore interpreted here as a re‑occurrence of established rust populations under conditions of economic stress and conducive climate, not a re‑emergence driven by pathogen genetic change.
Review: Decision: review. This new row has been added to represent the 2002–2003 El Salvador coffee leaf rust epidemic, which multiple regional syntheses identify as one of the few clearly documented severe national CLR outbreaks in Mesoamerica prior to the 2008–2013 Big Rust wave and link to the early‑2000s coffee price collapse and under‑investment in crop management. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) Classification as a re-occurrence (rather than re-emergence) reflects the absence of evidence for a single novel virulent rust race driving the event. Because quantitative loss estimates vary and the relative contribution of rust versus market forces is still debated, this row should be retained but reviewed by a coffee‑rust specialist to confirm that it meets the project’s impact threshold for inclusion among the largest post‑1990 emergence events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera glycines
EPP.common.name: soybean cyst nematode
Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event.summary: During the 1991/1992 soybean season, soybean cyst nematode (SCN) was first detected in Brazil in commercial fields in the Cerrado, including areas near Nova Ponte (Minas Gerais), Chapadão do Céu (Goiás), Campo Verde (Mato Grosso) and Chapadão do Sul (Mato Grosso do Sul), after growers reported patches of stunted, yellow soybeans. Surveys through the mid‑1990s revealed additional infested fields across central Cerrado states and later into southern production areas such as Paraná, São Paulo and Rio Grande do Sul, indicating that SCN was already widely established and spreading under intensive soybean monoculture. By the late 1990s the nematode was recognized as a major constraint on Brazilian soybean production, affecting millions of hectares and prompting national recommendations for crop rotation, resistant cultivars and strict hygiene, although eradication proved impossible and SCN remains entrenched with highly variable field‑level densities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of soybean monoculture into the Brazilian Cerrado, widespread use of continuous soybean or short rotations, and frequent movement of contaminated soil on machinery, trucks and seed lots allowed SCN to invade and spread among newly opened production frontiers. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity and multiple generations per season, combined with long‑term survival of eggs within durable cysts and efficient root invasion, enabled rapid population build‑up and persistence once fields were infested, facilitating geographic range expansion within the South America subregion.
Review: Review: Retain as a major South American emergence event. Adjusted event year from 1991–1992 to 1991–1997 to reflect multi‑year spread documented by Embrapa surveys and the 1993 Plant Disease report; kept the event classified as re_occurrence (South America’s first SCN record was Colombia 1983, so Brazil is not a continental or subregional first). Continent, subregion and country coding are correct, and the mechanism description appropriately emphasizes Cerrado soybean expansion and soil movement. Sources were focused on Embrapa Ageitec, early Brazilian survey publications and EPPO distribution data; no further structural changes recommended, but timing and impact estimates could be refined with additional Brazilian loss data.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera glycines
EPP.common.name: soybean cyst nematode
Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event.summary: During the 1997/1998 season, soybean cyst nematode was detected for the first time in Argentina in the core soybean‑growing region (“región núcleo sojera”) of Córdoba and Santa Fe, where patches of stunted, chlorotic soybeans prompted nematological analyses confirming Heterodera glycines. Over the following decade, surveys and diagnostic work documented SCN in additional Pampas and north‑western provinces such as Tucumán, Salta and Santiago del Estero, with moderate to high egg and cyst densities in many fields and increasing recognition that the nematode had become one of the most important soybean parasites in the country. By around 2008 SCN was considered widely but heterogeneously distributed across Argentina’s main soybean zones, stimulating breeding programs for resistant cultivars, regional guidelines on rotation and sanitation, and ongoing monitoring of local HG types, even though national‑scale yield‑loss estimates remain limited.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of soybean acreage in the Pampas and Northwest, widespread adoption of no‑till systems, and intensive movement of seed, soil and machinery among farms and across borders with already infested neighbours (especially Brazil and Paraguay) facilitated SCN introduction and subsequent field‑to‑field spread. Internal mechanisms: The nematode’s high reproductive potential, capacity for several generations per season, long‑term egg survival in cysts and ability to exploit susceptible local cultivars allowed small initial foci to expand into a widely distributed, economically important pest within little more than a decade.
Review: Review: New event added to capture the first detection (1997/1998) and rapid spread of SCN in the Argentine soybean belt, which national reviews identify as one of the most important regional emergence episodes. Classified as re_occurrence within the South America subregion because the first continental record was Colombia 1983 and Brazil was already infested; no first_detection or inter‑/intra‑continental flags are used. The 1997–2008 time window follows Argentine extension literature that dates first detection to the 1997/1998 campaign and notes that SCN emerged over the subsequent decade as a key soybean pathogen. Sources include EPPO distribution data, the Doucet et al. book chapter on SCN in Argentina and recent EEAOC publications; exact timing of spread into each province and quantitative loss estimates should be refined in future expert review.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera glycines
EPP.common.name: soybean cyst nematode
Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event.summary: In summer 2000, soybean cyst nematode was detected for the first time in Europe when three commercial soybean fields near Pavia in Lombardia, northern Italy, with long‑standing yellow‑dwarf symptoms were found to harbour dense, reproducing populations of Heterodera glycines. For more than a decade the pest remained confined to a few known sites under official control, but new isolated outbreaks were reported in a soybean field in Veneto in 2018 and in Friuli Venezia Giulia in 2020, confirming establishment at multiple locations in northern Italy. Up to 2020 SCN had not been reported from other European countries and remained present in Italy with restricted distribution, but its detection in several northern regions demonstrated that it can survive and reproduce under temperate European conditions and justified its continued listing as an EPPO A2 quarantine pest.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infested soil or seed lots into northern Italian soybean areas, probably via trade or movement of contaminated machinery from already infested regions, combined with susceptible cultivars and intensive local soybean production, created conditions for establishment once the nematode arrived. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive capacity, survival of eggs in resilient cysts and the ability to complete multiple generations per year in temperate climates facilitated establishment and persistence in a new continent, representing geographic range expansion from Asia and the Americas into Europe.
Review: Review: Retain as the key inter‑continental emergence event for Europe, but corrected classification by setting first_detection=No (global first detection occurred in Japan in the early 20th century) and leaving only inter_continental_emergence=Yes. Verified first Italian records near Pavia in 2000 and subsequent, still limited finds in Veneto (2018) and Friuli Venezia Giulia (2020) from the EPPO Global Database and the original Italian report; the 2000–2020 period and Southern Europe subregion coding are appropriate. Sources have been focused on EPPO reporting articles and the Manachini (2000) paper, which together provide a good description of origin, spread and regulatory context; further European surveys should be consulted periodically to confirm that no additional countries have become infested.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera glycines
EPP.common.name: soybean cyst nematode
Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event.summary: In the 2002/2003 season, soybean cyst nematode was reported for the first time in Paraguay from a soybean field in the Caaguazú region, extending SCN occurrence across the South American soybean belt. Follow‑up surveys between 2004 and 2006 documented the nematode in numerous fields across key soybean‑producing departments such as Alto Paraná, Canindeyú and Caaguazú, with patches of stunted, yellow plants and moderate to high cyst densities indicating local yield losses. By the late 2000s Paraguay considered SCN present with restricted distribution, and national recommendations focused on crop rotation, use of resistant cultivars and hygiene measures to slow further spread from infested zones.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera glycines
EPP.common.name: soybean cyst nematode
Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event.summary: In 2018, Chile’s agricultural and livestock service (SAG) confirmed the first detection of soybean cyst nematode in the country following a phytosanitary complaint from soybean crops, identifying localized foci of infestation in Glycine max fields. Subsequent inspections indicated that infestations were limited to a small number of sites, and SCN was classified as a quarantine organism under official control, with emergency measures imposed on movement of soil, machinery and seed from affected areas. Up to about 2021, SCN in Chile remained recorded only from restricted locations and was considered transient and under eradication or containment, with no evidence of widespread establishment, but the detection highlighted the ongoing risk of introductions via trade and regional seed movement from heavily infested neighbouring countries.

EPP.scientific.name: Hordeum jubatum
EPP.common.name: foxtail barley
Host: Steppe grasslands, hayfields, pastures and ruderal sites in the South Urals and adjacent parts of European Russia (especially the Republic of Bashkortostan and neighboring regions)
Event.summary: Foxtail barley, first recorded as an adventive in Bashkortostan in the mid‑1980s, expanded markedly in the South Urals and Cis‑Urals, and from about 2010 onward began forming dense, often monodominant stands in disturbed steppe grasslands, village pastures, lakeshores and ruderal habitats. Detailed phytosociological work in the 2010s described new plant communities dominated by H. jubatum (e.g. the association Polygono avicularis–Hordeetum jubati) and documented its inclusion in regional black lists and Black Books as an invasive ‘transformer’ species with an invasion area exceeding 500 ha in Bashkortostan alone.([binran.ru](https://www.binran.ru/files/journals/VegRus/2016_28/VEG_RUS_Abramova_Golovanov_2016_28.pdf)) By the late 2010s the species had become a regular and locally abundant component of semi‑natural grasslands and ruderal sites in the South Urals and Trans‑Urals, with authors projecting continued northward and westward spread within Eastern Europe from these outbreak foci.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction through ornamental plantings in settlements and repeated propagule inputs along major transport corridors (highways and railways) acted together with overgrazing, agricultural abandonment and salinization to create open, disturbed niches in steppe pastures, hayfields and lakeside meadows that favored establishment and dominance of H. jubatum.([binran.ru](https://www.binran.ru/files/journals/VegRus/2016_28/VEG_RUS_Abramova_Golovanov_2016_28.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: High tolerance of salinity and drought, a short vegetation period, prolific seed production and efficient dispersal of awned spikelets by wind and along hardened surfaces allowed rapid colonization and formation of monodominant stands in halophytic and steppe vegetation (Geographic Range Expansion – inherent; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: Review: Retain this event; it is well supported as a major post‑1990 invasion focus in the South Urals and Cis‑Urals, but it has been re‑documented here with tighter linkage to primary Russian sources. The event type re‑occurrence (Yes) is appropriate because H. jubatum was already present in the Eastern Europe sub‑region before 1990, and the 2010–2020 episode reflects a sharp increase in abundance and impact driven by external factors (land use, transport, salinization) rather than a documented new genotype, so re‑emergence was kept as No.([binran.ru](https://www.binran.ru/files/journals/VegRus/2016_28/VEG_RUS_Abramova_Golovanov_2016_28.pdf)) The event summary and mechanism sections were expanded to incorporate quantitative information on invasion area, community types and black‑list status from Abramova & Golovanov and subsequent reports, and key URLs for those works and the national Top‑100 IAS assessments were added to the event’s sources. Flagged for expert review mainly to confirm the chosen 2010 start year and whether any later (>2020) escalation in extent or impact within the same sub‑region should be captured in an extended time window.

EPP.scientific.name: Hordeum jubatum
EPP.common.name: foxtail barley
Host: Creeping red fescue (Festuca rubra) seed fields and associated grasslands in Alberta, Canada
Event.summary: In 2022, a foxtail barley population infesting creeping red fescue fields in Alberta was confirmed to have evolved resistance to Group 1 (ACCase‑inhibiting) herbicides, representing the first documented case of herbicide‑resistant H. jubatum in the International Herbicide‑Resistant Weed Database.([weedscience.org](https://weedscience.org/Pages/Case.aspx?ResistID=25263)) This biotype survived quizalofop‑ethyl at rates that normally control susceptible foxtail barley, indicating a shift in the species’ response to a key class of grass herbicides used in perennial grass seed production. From 2022 through at least 2023 the resistant population persisted in the affected fields, raising concerns about the potential spread of resistant seed and the loss of an important herbicide mode of action for managing foxtail barley in fescue and other perennial grass systems in Western Canada.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term and repeated use of Group 1 (ACCase‑inhibiting) herbicides in creeping red fescue and other grass‑based systems in the region likely imposed strong selection pressure favoring resistant foxtail barley biotypes, in the context of reduced tillage and limited alternative control options.([weedscience.org](https://weedscience.org/Pages/Case.aspx?ResistID=25263)) Internal mechanisms: Evolution of herbicide resistance (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance) in foxtail barley—documented as resistance to quizalofop‑ethyl and potentially other Group 1 herbicides—constitutes a genetic change that increases survival under herbicide treatment, fitting the definition of re‑emergence; additional mechanisms of spread (wind‑dispersed awned seeds, movement with harvested seed or machinery) may facilitate wider geographic expansion of this resistant biotype in coming years.
Review: Review: New event added as a re‑emergence episode to capture the first documented evolution of Group 1 (ACCase‑inhibitor) herbicide resistance in foxtail barley, which represents a qualitatively new management challenge even though the current confirmed distribution is limited to Alberta creeping red fescue fields.([weedscience.org](https://weedscience.org/Pages/Case.aspx?ResistID=25263)) Classified as re‑emergence (Yes) because a heritable change in the EPP (herbicide resistance) is directly implicated, while other emergence types remain No given that the species was long established in the Northern America sub‑region. The event window (2022–2025) reflects the first year of confirmed resistance and the current period of observation in the database; recommend expert review to assess whether this resistance case is sufficiently widespread and impactful to remain among the top 10 emergence events for the species as more data become available, and to consider integration with broader Canadian weed‑resistance datasets.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Liriomyza huidobrensis
EPP.common.name: pea leafminer
Host: Greenhouse ornamentals and a variety of vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, celery, crucifers, cucumbers and onions grown under glass in Ontario and nearby regions, with some spillover into adjacent field crops
Event.summary: In 1998, Liriomyza huidobrensis was first discovered in Canada in an ornamental flower greenhouse near Kettleby, Ontario, likely introduced on infested plant material imported from Costa Rica. During the following several years it reached outbreak levels in multiple Canadian greenhouses and in nearby field vegetable crops in the Holland Marsh region, damaging a broad range of vegetable and ornamental hosts and leading to substantial control costs and crop losses. By the early 2000s, implementation of biological control with parasitoids and improved IPM strategies reduced populations, and L. huidobrensis became a managed but persistent greenhouse pest in Canada.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Commercial importation of infested ornamental plant material from Central America introduced the pest into Canadian greenhouses; year-round greenhouse production and intensive insecticide use favored rapid population increases and spillover into nearby field crops. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive potential, polyphagy and likely insecticide resistance facilitated establishment and made eradication infeasible, resulting in long-term persistence at lower, managed densities.
Review: review: Retain this as the principal North-American event but adjust the emergence typing to inter-continental emergence only (first established populations of L. huidobrensis in North America), removing intra-continental emergence, and emphasize that the main impacts were in Ontario greenhouses and adjacent muck-vegetable fields; a reviewer may wish to confirm that no other large post-1990 outbreaks of true L. huidobrensis (distinct from L. langei) elsewhere in North America justify a separate row.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Liriomyza huidobrensis
EPP.common.name: pea leafminer
Host: Field and protected vegetables (lettuce, Asian greens, beans, celery, brassicas, alliums), ornamentals and weeds in the Sydney Basin, southern Queensland and subsequently parts of Victoria and other affected Australian regions
Event.summary: In October 2020, Liriomyza huidobrensis was detected causing damage on field-grown vegetables in the Sydney Basin of New South Wales, marking the first established populations of this species on the Australian mainland; delimiting surveys soon found it widely present in the Sydney region and at sites in southern Queensland. Over the next few years the pest spread within affected states and was later confirmed in Victoria, where it attacked a broad range of vegetable and ornamental hosts and triggered an emergency biosecurity response. When eradication was judged infeasible, Australia shifted to long-term management and containment, and L. huidobrensis is now considered established but under official control, with substantial ongoing implications for vegetable and nursery production and interstate trade.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction on infested propagation material or produce from overseas (likely from already infested regions in Asia or the Americas), combined with dense vegetable and ornamental production near major ports and favorable temperate climates, facilitated establishment and spread; intense chemical control in response to the incursion has potential to disrupt local natural enemies. Internal mechanisms: High polyphagy, rapid life cycle and pre-existing insecticide resistance in introduced lineages favor persistence and make eradication difficult once multiple foci have been established.
Review: review: Newly added event representing the first established populations of L. huidobrensis in mainland Australia (Sydney Basin and southern Queensland, later parts of Victoria), which is a major recent development; it is coded as intra-continental emergence within Oceania because Guam already held established populations earlier, and the window 2020–2025 is used to cover the initial detection and rapid spread; a specialist should verify the current geographic extent (including any confirmed occurrences in other Australian states or territories) and whether additional Oceanian territories should be explicitly mentioned.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Liriomyza sativae
EPP.common.name: vegetable leafminer, mineuse maraichère
Host: Vegetable crops and legumes including tomato, cucumber, beans and other open‑field and greenhouse vegetables
Event.summary: In October 1993, Liriomyza sativae was first recorded on Hainan Island in China, marking its initial confirmed establishment in Eastern Asia and the start of a rapid invasion of the country’s vegetable production areas. Over the following decade the pest spread northwards and westwards through most provinces, and by about 2005 it had colonised the vast majority of China’s vegetable‑growing regions, affecting more than a million hectares and becoming one of the dominant leafminer species on tomato, cucumber, beans and other horticultural crops. After this explosive spread, L. sativae became entrenched, and management shifted from emergency responses towards long‑term integrated control, including heavy insecticide use (which selected for resistance) and increasing reliance on parasitoid wasps and other biological‑control tactics, with later community shifts in some crops as L. trifolii displaced L. sativae in parts of southern China.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of open‑field and protected vegetable production in subtropical and warm‑temperate China; intensive movement of infested seedlings and fresh produce within the country; and introduction of the pest from earlier invaded regions (likely via plant material from the Americas and/or Arabian Peninsula). Internal mechanisms: high fecundity and short generation time enabling fast population build‑up; broad host range across key vegetable families (Solanaceae, Fabaceae, Cucurbitaceae); thermophilic biology allowing establishment from tropical Hainan into warmer temperate areas; and strong selection for insecticide resistance under frequent insecticide applications, which exacerbated outbreaks and allowed L. sativae to dominate many systems in the first decade after invasion.
Review: review – Retain as one of the largest global emergence events, but clarify that this represents first large‑scale establishment in Eastern Asia rather than the first occurrence in Asia overall (which was in Oman in 1990). Sub‑regions were restricted to ‘Eastern Asia’ (Southern Asia was removed because no specific countries from that sub‑region are part of this linked episode), and emergence‑type coding was corrected to intra‑continental emergence only (no inter‑continental flag, and no first_detection flag, since Asia already had records from Oman/Yemen). The event summary and impact description are consistent with invasion histories reported in Chinese entomological studies and recent genomic work, but a specialist should confirm whether the 1993–2005 window best captures the main high‑impact phase.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Liriomyza sativae
EPP.common.name: vegetable leafminer, mineuse maraichère
Host: Commercial tomato, beans, eggplant and other greenhouse and field vegetables
Event.summary: In 1999–2000, Liriomyza sativae was newly recorded in Japan on tomato and other vegetables, invading protected and open‑field systems where the invasive L. trifolii and the native L. bryoniae were already present. Within only a few years the species spread widely through Japanese vegetable production regions, and in many crops it became the predominant leafminer, displacing L. trifolii on some hosts and causing substantial damage that prompted intensified control efforts. After this rapid establishment and community shift, Japanese growers and regulators increasingly adopted more targeted insecticide programmes and biological control, yet L. sativae has remained a key component of the national leafminer complex.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction on infested ornamentals and vegetable seedlings imported from other invaded regions (likely Asia or the Pacific) and rapid dissemination via domestic plant‑trade networks, combined with intensive greenhouse and high‑value vegetable production that provided abundant hosts and frequent insecticide applications. Internal mechanisms: competitive advantages over L. trifolii under Japanese cropping and insecticide regimes, including differential susceptibility to commonly used insecticides and possible interspecific interactions, which facilitated displacement; strong adaptation to protected‑cultivation environments; and high reproductive success on tomato, cucumber and beans, leading to fast population growth and dominance in many vegetable systems.
Review: review – Event retained as a major intra‑continental emergence into Japan with substantial impacts on greenhouse and field vegetables, but emergence‑type coding has been adjusted: re_emergence has been set to ‘No’ because Japan had no prior established L. sativae populations in this sub‑region, and first_detection has been set to ‘No’ to avoid conflating global first description with country‑level first reports. The summary was lightly edited to emphasise the role of species displacement and interaction with L. trifolii. Overall structure and timing are well supported by Japanese sources and regional invasion analyses, but the balance between displacement and coexistence could benefit from specialist review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Liriomyza trifolii
EPP.common.name: celery leafminer
Host: Open-field vegetable crops including beans, tomato, pepper, melon, cucumber, pumpkin, lettuce, cabbage and onion
Event.summary: In 1991, Liriomyza trifolii was reported for the first time from Tonga, adding Polynesian vegetable systems to a Pacific distribution that already included Guam and other Micronesian islands. The fly quickly reached damaging levels on a wide range of vegetables, with serpentine leaf mines reducing photosynthetic area and marketability and prompting concern among growers. The pest subsequently became established as part of the endemic leafminer complex in Tonga, managed mainly with insecticides and limited cultural measures rather than eradicated.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-5390))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increasing inter-island trade in fresh vegetables and planting material from previously infested Pacific islands, combined with growth of intensive smallholder vegetable production, facilitated the jump from Micronesia to Polynesia. Internal mechanisms: Broad host range and good adaptation to tropical climates supported successful establishment in Tonga; no specific evidence of novel resistance or strains has been reported for this event.
Review: retain – Event is well supported by EPPO Reporting Service 1991/14 as the first confirmed record in Tonga and effectively marks intra‑continental emergence into the Polynesia subregion; no major corrections were needed beyond re‑checking the subregion and impact description.

EPP.scientific.name: Liriomyza trifolii
EPP.common.name: celery leafminer
Host: Faba bean (Vicia faba) in irrigated field systems (New Halfa scheme)
Event.summary: In the mid‑1990s, field studies on sowing dates of faba bean in the New Halfa irrigation scheme in Sudan documented heavy infestations by Liriomyza trifolii, representing the first detailed record of this pest from the country. By that time, L. trifolii was already widespread in other parts of Africa, but its recognition as a serious faba bean pest in Sudan raised concern about potential yield losses and appropriate planting strategies. Subsequent work treated the leafminer as an established component of the pest complex in irrigated legume systems in Sudan rather than an eradication target.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3890))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of irrigated faba bean and movement of infested seed or plant material from other African countries where L. trifolii was already present likely introduced the pest into the New Halfa scheme. Internal mechanisms: Generalist feeding on legumes and tolerance of semi‑arid irrigated environments underpinned establishment; no specific resistant strain or novel genotype has been implicated in this local emergence.
Review: review – Corrected the UN subregion from “Eastern Africa” to “Northern Africa” in line with the country list, and removed both “first_detection” and “intra_continental_emergence” flags because L. trifolii was already present in multiple African subregions including North Africa (e.g. Tunisia 1992) before this record; event is now treated as a country‑level emergence with moderate impact whose ranking among the top 10 African events should be reassessed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Liriomyza trifolii
EPP.common.name: celery leafminer
Host: Various vegetable crops and ornamentals (e.g. tomato and other greenhouse and field vegetables; ornamental plants)
Event.summary: Between July 1995 and September 1996, a national survey of agromyzid leafminers in Jordan identified Liriomyza trifolii, together with L. huidobrensis and L. sativae, for the first time in the country on vegetables, ornamentals and weeds. The species was found at multiple locations, showing that it had already become established and was contributing to leafminer damage in commercial fields and greenhouses. Since then, L. trifolii has remained present in Jordan as part of the regional leafminer complex managed within broader IPM and quarantine frameworks, without any attempt at eradication.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-2274))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of infested seedlings, cuttings and vegetables from neighbouring Mediterranean and Near Eastern countries where L. trifolii was already present, along with intensification of irrigated and protected vegetable production, favoured establishment in Jordan. Internal mechanisms: Polyphagy and adaptation to warm, semi‑arid climates facilitated establishment, but there is no clear evidence of a novel strain or major resistance change specific to this episode.
Review: review – Maintained the event as Jordan’s first country record but removed the “first_detection” and “intra_continental_emergence” flags because L. trifolii was already present in the same UN subregion (Western Asia) in Israel and Lebanon before 1990; this is now treated as a within‑subregion spread event of moderate, regionally focused impact.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Manduca sexta
EPP.common.name: Carolina Sphinx, Tobacco Hornworm
Host: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) in university glasshouse trials
Event.summary: In 2003, larvae of Manduca sexta were discovered causing defoliation on tomato trial plants in two glasshouses at Humboldt University in Berlin, Germany, representing an accidental introduction of this American solanaceous pest into Europe. The infestation was traced to adults that most likely escaped from a nearby research rearing facility where M. sexta was maintained, and their progeny developed on tomato plants under protected cultivation before being detected. All larvae were removed and the crop was chemically treated; follow-up inspections found no additional specimens, and German authorities and EPPO subsequently classified the incursion as eradicated and the species as absent from Germany and the wider EPPO region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Human-mediated escape of adult Manduca sexta from a nearby laboratory/rearing facility into adjacent tomato glasshouses, combined with the presence of suitable host plants and favorable protected-climate conditions that allowed temporary local reproduction. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel strains, resistance, or host shifts in this episode; the event reflects a short-lived anthropogenic geographic range jump into a new continent rather than evolutionary change in the pest.
Review: retain – This row accurately captures the only well-documented inter-continental incursion of Manduca sexta: a 2003 tomato glasshouse outbreak in Berlin, Germany, with larvae feeding on tomatoes, eradication by removal and chemical treatment, and subsequent official status as “absent, single occurrence, eradicated.” Continent (Europe), subregion (Western Europe), and country (Germany [2003]) are consistent with the UNSD scheme and EPPO reporting. Classification as inter-continental emergence is appropriate because there was local reproduction and feeding on host plants in a new continent, not merely detection of imported material with no in situ development. No evidence was found for other larger emergence events (e.g. establishment in Europe, Africa, or Asia) between 1990 and 2025, and the cited EPPO reporting article plus the German and English Julius Kühn-Institut express PRAs are the most relevant primary sources for this event, so the event is retained without modification.

EPP.scientific.name: Neofabraea perennans
EPP.common.name: perennial canker of apple
Host: Apple trees (Malus domestica) – trunk and branch cankers (perennial canker) and associated bull’s‑eye rot of fruit in Washington State orchards
Event.summary: Around 1990–1995, perennial canker and associated bull’s‑eye rot caused by Neofabraea perennans were documented as serious problems in apple orchards in eastern Washington State, USA, with trunk and limb cankers plus latent fruit infections leading to substantial tree decline and postharvest losses. Studies conducted in 1987–1990 showed abundant conidial production on cankers during cool, wet periods and highlighted high infection risk around winter pruning, consistent with the heavy disease pressure seen in the early 1990s. Improved pruning sanitation, removal of cankered wood, and adjustments to irrigation and fungicide programs subsequently reduced inoculum levels and limited further spread within affected orchards.([apsnet.org](https://www.apsnet.org/publications/plantdisease/backissues/Documents/1992Articles/PlantDisease76n11_1109.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Shift to high‑density plantings on dwarf rootstocks, use of overhead irrigation, and longer cold‑storage periods favored canker development and latent fruit infections; limited awareness of Neofabraea canker epidemiology delayed effective management. Internal mechanisms: No clear novel genotype was described; impact appears mainly linked to enhanced transmission and perennation via abundant sporulation on cankers and infected fruit, increasing inoculum pressure in intensively managed orchards.
Review: retain – Evidence from Grove (1992) shows that perennial canker and bull’s‑eye rot caused by N. perennans were chronic and economically important in eastern Washington through 1987–1990, with severe bull’s‑eye rot outbreaks in the mid‑1980s; treating the early 1990s as a major re‑occurrence episode in the same subregion is consistent with the dataset scope. Geography and event‑type coding (re‑occurrence only) match the definitions, and the sources used are appropriate.([apsnet.org](https://www.apsnet.org/publications/plantdisease/backissues/Documents/1992Articles/PlantDisease76n11_1109.pdf))

EPP.scientific.name: Neofabraea perennans
EPP.common.name: perennial canker of apple
Host: Apple fruit (Malus domestica) in commercial orchards and long‑term storage in southern Brazil (Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul)
Event.summary: In the 1995–1996 seasons, bull’s‑eye rot was first reported in commercial apple orchards in southern Brazil and the causal agent was identified as Neofabraea perennans, leading to serious postharvest losses on ‘Fuji’ and other cultivars during long‑term cold storage and marking the first establishment of this pathogen on apples in South America. Through the late 1990s and early 2000s the disease became widespread in the main production areas of Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul, with lesions appearing after several months in storage and causing high cull rates in export lots. Later taxonomic studies showed that many Brazilian bull’s‑eye rot epidemics were actually caused by newly described Neofabraea species (N. brasiliensis and N. actinidiae), but historical reports and extension bulletins confirm that N. perennans was present and initially regarded as the main etiological agent in this period.([educapes.capes.gov.br](https://educapes.capes.gov.br/handle/capes/901976?mode=full))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive apple production and long‑term controlled‑atmosphere storage in southern Brazil, combined with movement of nursery stock and fruit from temperate production regions, facilitated introduction and establishment of Neofabraea spp. Internal mechanisms: Initial outbreaks were driven by latent infection biology and efficient survival on pruning wounds and fruit rather than documented novel genotypes; later work showed diversification into regionally adapted species (N. brasiliensis, N. actinidiae), indicating ongoing evolutionary adaptation of the Neofabraea complex to Brazilian environments.
Review: review – Retain the event but with corrected timing: Brazilian sources consistently state that bull’s‑eye rot on apples was first observed and attributed to N. perennans in the 1995–1996 seasons, so the event year has been updated from 1996–2002 to 1995–2002 and the country tag to “Brazil [1995]”.([educapes.capes.gov.br](https://educapes.capes.gov.br/handle/capes/901976?mode=full)) Classification as an inter‑continental emergence (first establishment of N. perennans on apples in South America with substantial storage losses) is appropriate. However, later work shows that other Neofabraea spp. now dominate Brazilian bull’s‑eye rot, so the share of impact attributable specifically to N. perennans is uncertain and should be reviewed by subject‑matter experts.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Neofabraea perennans
EPP.common.name: perennial canker of apple
Host: Pear (Pyrus communis, mainly ‘Packham’s Triumph’) and other pome fruit in Western Cape orchards and storage
Event.summary: From around 2012 to 2015, bull’s‑eye rot (lenticel decay) began to be recognised as a postharvest problem on ‘Packham’s Triumph’ and other pears in the Western Cape of South Africa. A dedicated MSc study and industry surveys detected Neofabraea alba as the main causal agent on apples but also recorded conidia of Neofabraea perennans and N. kienholzii on pear and apple fruit, and identified N. perennans on Packham’s Triumph pears, representing the first reports of this species on pome fruit in South Africa and, by extension, in Africa. Although N. perennans was not the dominant species in the complex, the finding triggered further surveys and incorporation of Neofabraea lenticel decay into postharvest risk assessments and control programmes for export pears.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/fr/records/6a32c781c5555e957fa7d328))
