Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of Neofabraea spp. (including N. perennans) with infected nursery stock or fruit into Western Cape orchards, combined with cool, wet winters and increasing use of long‑term cold storage for export pears, favoured expression of latent infections. Internal mechanisms: This episode mainly reflects geographic range expansion of existing lineages into a new continent rather than documented novel genotypes; the strong capacity of Neofabraea spp. for latent lenticel infection and survival during storage underpins their impact.
Review: review – Retain as the first confirmed record of N. perennans on pome fruit in Africa, but correct the timing and event‑type coding. Published MSc work and industry reports indicate that N. perennans and N. kienholzii were first detected on pears and apples in the Western Cape around 2012–2013, not as early as 2008, so the event window has been updated to 2012–2015 and the country tag to “South Africa [2012]”.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/fr/records/6a32c781c5555e957fa7d328)) Re‑emergence has been set to No because this is a first detection on the continent rather than a resurgence driven by genetic change; inter‑continental emergence remains Yes. The summary and sources have been revised to clarify that N. alba is the predominant species and N. perennans occurs at low frequency, so the quantitative impact attributable to N. perennans should be further assessed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Neofabraea perennans
EPP.common.name: perennial canker of apple
Host: Apple fruit (Malus domestica) in commercial orchards and cold storage in Poland
Event.summary: From around 2010 to 2015, bull’s‑eye rot caused increasing postharvest losses in stored apples in Poland, and a survey of fruit from major production regions identified three Neofabraea species—N. alba, N. perennans and N. kienholzii—with N. alba dominant and N. perennans present in a minority of samples. The disease manifested after long‑term cold storage, when apparently healthy fruit at harvest developed characteristic sunken, brown, bull’s‑eye lesions, leading to substantial culling of susceptible cultivars. The work confirmed that Neofabraea spp., including N. perennans which had already been reported in Poland in the 1960s, are important components of the postharvest rot complex, and it supported the adoption of molecular diagnostics, revised fungicide programmes and improved orchard sanitation and storage practices to limit future outbreaks.([bsppjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://bsppjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ppa.12449))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased use of long‑term controlled‑atmosphere storage, widespread planting of susceptible cultivars and changes in permitted postharvest fungicides likely favoured Neofabraea spp. over other storage pathogens. Internal mechanisms: The Polish study did not demonstrate specific novel genotypes or resistance traits in N. perennans; the pattern is more consistent with re‑occurrence driven by management and storage conditions than with documented re‑emergence due to evolutionary change.
Review: review – Keep the event but re‑interpret its type. Molecular work from Poland shows that N. perennans was already reported there in the 1960s and that N. alba is the dominant species in recent outbreaks, with N. perennans recovered from only about 5% of symptomatic apples.([bsppjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://bsppjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ppa.12449)) Accordingly, the event has been recoded from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence (no evidence of new N. perennans genotypes) in a previously affected subregion. Because the quantitative contribution of N. perennans to losses is modest relative to N. alba, the importance of this event for this specific EPP should be reviewed before final inclusion among the top global events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Neofabraea perennans
EPP.common.name: perennial canker of apple
Host: Apple trees and fruit (Malus domestica) – cankers and bull’s‑eye rot in the U.S. Pacific Northwest
Event.summary: Between about 2012 and 2018, growers in the U.S. Pacific Northwest reported renewed problems with perennial canker of apple trees and bull’s‑eye rot of stored fruit, and field studies showed Neofabraea perennans and N. kienholzii to be the main species associated with cankers and fruit decay. Experiments in commercial orchards during 2012–2014 quantified infection timing and showed that fruit infections initiated near harvest could lead to substantial losses after several months in cold storage, while complementary work on twig inoculations clarified when cankers develop most readily. These findings, together with fungicide‑efficacy trials, underpinned adjustments in pruning timing, wound protection, and integrated pre‑ and postharvest fungicide programmes that allowed the industry to reduce disease severity to more manageable levels.([rex.libraries.wsu.edu](https://rex.libraries.wsu.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/Timing-of-Perennial-Canker-Development-in/99900547488001842))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Aging high‑density orchards with accumulated inoculum in cankers, restrictions or shifts in available fungicides, and continued reliance on long storage periods increased the relative importance of Neofabraea perennans and related species. Internal mechanisms: The renewed impact reflects efficient latent infection and sporulation under cool, wet conditions; available data do not yet demonstrate stable fungicide resistance or distinct new genotypes of N. perennans, so this episode is best interpreted as re‑occurrence driven mainly by management and climatic factors.
Review: review – Retain as a major recent episode but adjust the event type. Plant Disease articles on infection timing, canker development and fungicide efficacy document a pronounced resurgence of N. perennans‑associated cankers and bull’s‑eye rot in Pacific Northwest apples from 2012 onward, with substantial research and management responses.([rex.libraries.wsu.edu](https://rex.libraries.wsu.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/Timing-of-Perennial-Canker-Development-in/99900547488001842)) However, they do not present clear evidence of novel N. perennans genotypes or stable fungicide resistance, so re‑emergence has been set to No and the event is classified as a re‑occurrence driven largely by orchard structure, fungicide programmes and storage practices.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Neofabraea perennans
EPP.common.name: perennial canker of apple
Host: Apple fruit (Malus domestica; e.g. ‘Fuji’, ‘Granny Smith’, ‘Cripps Pink’) in Chilean export orchards and cold storage
Event.summary: In 2017–2018, apple lots from Chile stored for export began to show typical bull’s‑eye rot symptoms, and isolation plus multilocus sequencing confirmed Neofabraea perennans as the causal agent, leading to a 2020 disease note reporting the first occurrence of this species causing bull’s‑eye rot of apple in Chile. The disease became evident after extended cold storage, with slightly sunken, circular brown lesions developing on fruit from some orchards and raising concern about postharvest quality for distant markets. Following confirmation of N. perennans, Chilean producers and advisors strengthened orchard sanitation, adjusted fungicide applications around infection periods and implemented stricter storage and fruit‑selection practices to limit spread and economic impact, while continuing to manage N. alba, the previously recognised bull’s‑eye rot pathogen in the country.([apsjournals.apsnet.org](https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PDIS-12-19-2561-PDN))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased volume of long‑stored export apples from cool, wet production zones in Chile, combined with regional and international movement of planting material and fruit, likely facilitated introduction and establishment of N. perennans. Internal mechanisms: The pathogen’s inherent ability for latent infection and survival during long cold storage underpins its success; there is no direct evidence of a novel Chile‑specific genotype, but its appearance in a previously N. perennans‑free South American country suggests geographic range expansion of existing lineages adapted to intensive storage systems.
Review: review – Retain as a well‑documented national emergence but correct the event‑type coding and sources. A 2020 Plant Disease note demonstrates that N. perennans was newly detected causing bull’s‑eye rot of apple in Chile in 2017–2018; earlier Chilean work had only found N. alba as the bull’s‑eye rot pathogen.([apsjournals.apsnet.org](https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PDIS-12-19-2561-PDN)) Because N. perennans was already present in Brazil, this Chilean outbreak does not represent inter‑continental emergence, and there is no evidence for genetic change in the pathogen, so re‑emergence has been set to No and all emergence‑type flags are left as No. The Brazilian thesis has been removed from the event‑level sources and replaced with the earlier Chilean characterization paper as more relevant context for the local species shift.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Ophiomyia phaseoli
EPP.common.name: bean fly
Host: Black gram (Vigna mungo) grown as a rabi crop in the southern zone of Andhra Pradesh, India
Event.summary: During the 2018–2019 rabi season in the southern zone of Andhra Pradesh, India, field trials and observations reported exceptionally high infestation of black gram by the stem fly Ophiomyia phaseoli, with average plant infestation exceeding 40% in the latest sowing dates and plot-level incidence reaching up to 100% in some observation periods. This episode led the authors to describe O. phaseoli as having attained major pest status on black gram in this region for the first time, with severe tunnelling and basal stem damage in young plants threatening yields across an important production area. Subsequent pest and breeding reviews on black gram have cited stem fly (O. phaseoli) as a recently emerging or resurging internal feeder in Andhra Pradesh, although detailed multi-year regional impact data beyond the 2018–2019 season are still limited.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased cultivation of black gram as a rabi crop in rice fallows in southern Andhra Pradesh, together with periods of high maximum temperatures (around 36–38 °C) and declining relative humidity during late February–March, created highly favourable conditions for rapid build-up and survival of Ophiomyia phaseoli populations. Additional contributing factors likely include limited adoption of targeted stem-fly management, cropping calendars that expose seedlings during peak favourable weather, and possibly changes in insecticide use patterns that did not effectively target stem fly. Internal mechanisms: no evidence has been presented for novel strains, pesticide resistance or host shifts in this episode; the event is therefore interpreted as a climate- and management-driven resurgence of an existing pest within a previously affected subregion rather than a re-emergence driven by evolutionary change in the fly.
Review: retain – This new row has been added to capture the 2018–2019 episode in which Ophiomyia phaseoli reached major pest status on black gram in the southern zone of Andhra Pradesh, India. It is classified as a re-occurrence event (re_occurrence = true; re_emergence = false) within Southern Asia because O. phaseoli has long been present on black gram and other pulses in South Asia, and the episode represents a documented surge in pest importance in a major production zone, driven by weather and management conditions rather than first establishment in the subregion or demonstrable genetic change. The event fits the project’s emphasis on high-impact post‑1990 emergence episodes (very high local infestation levels in a large cropping area and subsequent recognition as an “emerging pest” in the regional literature), although the exact spatial extent and aggregate yield loss remain to be quantified. Recommended decision: retain as one of the principal post‑2005 emergence events for O. phaseoli, with a note that future updates should revisit its ranking if more quantitative impact data become available.

EPP.scientific.name: Panicum dichotomiflorum
EPP.common.name: western witchgrass, fall panicum, fall panicgrass, fall panic
Host: Sweet corn (Zea mays var. saccharata) and other maize production systems in the U.S. Midwest
Event.summary: In 2019, a sweet-corn grower in Wisconsin (USA) reported fall panicum escapes following applications of the ALS-inhibiting herbicide nicosulfuron, prompting collection of seed from surviving plants and formal resistance testing. Greenhouse and molecular studies published in 2022 demonstrated high-level resistance to nicosulfuron (with plants surviving multiple times the labelled rate) and identified an Asp‑376‑Glu substitution in one copy of the ALS gene, confirming the first documented case of herbicide resistance in fall panicum in the United States. Although currently known from a limited number of Midwestern sweet-corn fields, this resistant biotype has re‑emerged as a management concern in systems previously relying on nicosulfuron, and extension bulletins now recommend alternative herbicide programmes and integrated management to prevent wider spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy and repeated reliance on nicosulfuron as the main post‑emergence grass herbicide in sweet-corn production, combined with limited non-ALS herbicide options and reduced tillage, created strong selection pressure on fall panicum populations in affected fields. Internal mechanisms: Target-site resistance evolved via an ALS gene mutation (Asp‑376‑Glu) in at least one gene copy, conferring high-level resistance to nicosulfuron; this clear evolutionary change in the weed’s herbicide sensitivity constitutes a classic re‑emergence event driven by internal mechanisms and requiring substantial adaptation of management practices.
Review: Decision: review. This newly added event is strongly supported by peer‑reviewed experimental work and extension reports confirming ALS target‑site resistance in a Wisconsin fall panicum population, and it is notable as the first herbicide‑resistant fall panicum case reported in the United States. It is appropriately classified as a re‑emergence (internal evolutionary change) within the native North American range, but the temporal bounds (2019–2022), the restriction to U.S. Midwest sweet-corn systems, and the judgement that this episode is among the globally most impactful events for this species should be validated against any future data on the geographic spread and agronomic significance of this resistant biotype.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (rural and forest-fringe populations, including migrant workers in Amazonian departments)
Event.summary: In 1995, Peru experienced a major resurgence of jungle yellow fever, with outbreaks reported from at least seven Amazonian and Andean-foothill departments and on the order of 470–500 reported human cases and an estimated case-fatality of around 40%. The epidemic was concentrated among unvaccinated agricultural workers, loggers and other migrants entering forested areas, and it strained regional health services as cases were referred to departmental hospitals from remote zones. National authorities, PAHO and partners responded with intensified surveillance, health education and targeted vaccination in affected departments, and incidence declined after 1995, although Peru has continued to report smaller numbers of sylvatic yellow fever cases in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid colonization of Amazonian forests and foothills (road building, logging, agriculture, hydrocarbon exploration) brought large numbers of non-immune workers into enzootic yellow fever foci with abundant Haemagogus/Sabethes vectors and non-human primate reservoirs; routine vaccination coverage in these populations was very low. Internal mechanisms: Available virological work indicates circulation of South American genotype II viruses endemic to Peru rather than a fundamentally novel strain; the outbreak mainly reflects intense amplification of existing enzootic virus in newly exposed human populations (re-occurrence) rather than true re-emergence driven by viral evolution.
Review: Review: Newly added event. This 1995 jungle yellow fever epidemic in Peru, with roughly 470–500 reported cases and high case fatality across at least seven departments, is widely cited as one of the largest yellow fever outbreaks in the Americas since the 1950s and clearly belongs among the top post‑1990 events. Classified as re-occurrence in the South America subregion because the virus and transmission cycle were long established there and no strong evidence points to a distinct new genotype or host shift driving the epidemic. Case counts vary somewhat across sources; values in the summary are given as rounded ranges and should be checked against national surveillance or PAHO country profiles before finalization.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (rural populations in Mamou, Labé, Kankan and surrounding areas)
Event.summary: In September 2000, a large yellow fever epidemic erupted in Guinea, affecting mainly inland prefectures such as Mamou, Labé and Kankan and causing hundreds of suspected cases in rural communities. Between early September 2000 and early January 2001, authorities reported around 688 suspected cases and 225 deaths, and Médecins Sans Frontières and partners launched mass vaccination despite a global vaccine shortage. Transmission declined after emergency vaccination campaigns and vector control, and the epidemic was brought under control by early 2001, though Guinea remained recognized as an at‑risk country for future outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High proportions of unvaccinated populations due to gaps in routine immunization, ecological suitability for sylvatic transmission, and limited vaccine stocks that delayed mass campaigns; population movements and seasonal climatic conditions likely enhanced vector abundance. Internal mechanisms: Evidence suggests continued circulation of endemic West African YFV lineages rather than a distinct novel genotype; the main mechanism was resurgence of transmission in an under-immunized population, not major viral evolution.
Review: Retain: This was a large, high-fatality epidemic (≈688 suspected cases, 225 deaths) in a West African country with documented historical transmission. Classification as re-occurrence in Western Africa is appropriate; no evidence supports intra- or inter-continental emergence or a novel viral genotype. Source set (Lancet letter, MSF operational reports) is appropriate and focused on this event.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (urban and peri-urban residents of Abidjan and other affected areas)
Event.summary: From March to December 2001, Côte d’Ivoire experienced a major yellow fever outbreak that began in the western town of Duékoué and progressed eastwards to Abidjan, ultimately causing about 280 reported cases (32 laboratory-confirmed) and six deaths across 11 of 62 health districts, with many cases in large urban centers including Abidjan. The epidemic spread along transport corridors into densely populated neighborhoods with heavy Aedes aegypti infestation, raising concern about explosive urban transmission and prompting international alarm. A large-scale emergency vaccination campaign that immunized more than 3.7 million people in Abidjan and other affected districts, combined with vector control and strengthened surveillance, curtailed urban transmission and the outbreak was declared over by late 2001.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High population density in Abidjan, abundant urban Aedes aegypti breeding sites, and immunity gaps due to limited prior vaccination in affected districts, combined with introduction of virus from sylvatic or rural foci into an urban setting with intense human–mosquito contact. Internal mechanisms: Available data indicate circulation of known West African YFV lineages rather than a novel genotype; the key internal factor was efficient urban transmission by Aedes aegypti in a largely susceptible urban population rather than genetic change.
Review: Review: Event is correctly identified as an important urban yellow fever epidemic in Western Africa, but the original summary understated case numbers and deaths. Updated the event_summary to reflect published estimates (~280 reported cases, 32 confirmed, 6 deaths, 3.7 million people vaccinated) and to clarify that spread began in Duékoué and moved east to Abidjan. Classification as re-occurrence in a historically endemic West African subregion is appropriate; no intra- or inter-continental emergence is involved. Sources are now clearly anchored in Med Trop and WHO documentation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (rural populations and displaced persons in what is now South Sudan, especially Eastern Equatoria and surrounding areas)
Event.summary: In 2003, a large yellow fever outbreak was detected in the Imatong Mountains and surrounding areas of what was then southern Sudan (now South Sudan’s Eastern Equatoria), representing the first major confirmed yellow fever epidemic in East Africa since the 1960s despite earlier serologic evidence of virus circulation. The outbreak progressed in rural and semi-rural communities with numerous suspected and laboratory-confirmed cases and substantial mortality before it was fully recognized. Following case confirmation, national authorities, WHO and partners undertook reactive vaccination and strengthened surveillance, and transmission waned as the dry season progressed and control measures took effect.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-term low-level sylvatic circulation in East Africa combined with humanitarian crisis conditions, displacement and limited health services in conflict-affected southern Sudan, which allowed extensive human–vector contact and delayed detection. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses indicate involvement of known East African YFV lineages without compelling evidence of a novel, more virulent genotype; the event mainly reflects ecological spillover and expansion into susceptible human populations within an already affected subregion (re-occurrence), not appearance in a new UNSD subregion.
Review: Review: Geographic coding has been aligned with the Country sheet by listing the country as South Sudan [2003] (the outbreak area corresponds to territory that is now South Sudan), while keeping the subregion as Eastern Africa. Previously labelled as intra-continental emergence; this is incorrect because yellow fever had already been documented in the Eastern Africa subregion (e.g. earlier Sudan and Ethiopia epidemics). Re-classified intra_continental_emergence from Yes to No and re_occurrence from No to Yes. Sources (EID article and related CDC report) appropriately describe both the size and East African context of this outbreak.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (urban and peri-urban residents, particularly around Asunción)
Event.summary: In early 2008, Paraguay reported its first yellow fever cases since the 1970s, with confirmed and suspected cases initially identified in rural San Pedro Department and then in urban and peri-urban areas around Asunción, including several fatalities. Although the number of confirmed human cases remained relatively small (on the order of two dozen), the detection of probable urban transmission near the capital in a largely unvaccinated population triggered major regional concern and an urgent appeal for vaccine supplies. Intensive mass vaccination campaigns, supported by PAHO/WHO and neighboring countries and reaching more than a million people, along with vector control, halted transmission within months and no large subsequent outbreaks have been reported in Paraguay since.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reintroduction of sylvatic YFV or infected vectors into an urbanized, highly susceptible population with minimal routine vaccination, coupled with abundant Aedes aegypti breeding sites in and around Asunción; delays and uncertainty in early recognition contributed to heightened risk. Internal mechanisms: The event reflects resurgence of long-established South American YFV rather than a new strain; no clear evidence indicates that viral genetic changes drove increased virulence or transmissibility in Paraguay. The global impact derived largely from the potential for urban spread and the stress on vaccine stockpiles, rather than absolute case counts.
Review: Retain: Although numerically smaller than some African epidemics, this episode was the first recognized urban yellow fever outbreak in the Americas in decades and led to emergency vaccination of over a million people and serious concern about potential international spread. Classification as re-occurrence in the South America subregion is appropriate. Source set (PAHO/WHO, PHAC, PLoS NTD analysis) adequately documents both the modest case count and the large-scale response.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (rural populations in northern Uganda districts)
Event.summary: Between October 2010 and January 2011, northern Uganda experienced a sizeable yellow fever outbreak with 181 suspected cases and 45 deaths, characterized by fever and hemorrhagic signs and notable case-fatality. The epidemic evolved across multiple districts among rural populations engaged in farming and forest or swamp-related activities, reflecting intense exposure to sylvatic vectors and primate reservoirs. Following confirmation, Uganda and partners launched reactive vaccination campaigns, strengthened surveillance, and implemented vector control, and the outbreak subsided by early 2011, though Uganda has since remained a high-risk country with additional outbreaks in 2016, 2019 and 2020.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large pockets of unvaccinated adults and children in high-risk ecological zones, occupational exposure in forest and swamp farming areas with non-human primates present, and limited routine vaccination before the outbreak; seasonal rainfall patterns likely favored vector proliferation. Internal mechanisms: Molecular and epidemiologic data suggest typical East African YFV strains closely related to earlier regional viruses; the main mechanism was resurgence of endemic virus in susceptible human populations (re-occurrence) rather than emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: Retain: This was the largest documented yellow fever outbreak in Uganda and an important example of East African resurgence within an already affected subregion. Classification as re-occurrence in Eastern Africa is appropriate, and the case and death counts have been aligned with the primary investigation (181 suspected cases, 45 deaths). Sources (IJID article and WHO DON) are appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (rural communities, displaced populations and traditional miners across the Darfur states)
Event.summary: From September 2012 to early 2013, a massive yellow fever outbreak struck Sudan’s Darfur region, with approximately 847–849 suspected cases and 171 deaths reported across all five Darfur states, making it the largest yellow fever epidemic in Africa in at least two decades. The outbreak began in remote mining and rural areas of Central Darfur and spread to dozens of localities, including camps for internally displaced persons, before being recognized and laboratory-confirmed. A large emergency vaccination campaign, coordinated by Sudan’s Federal Ministry of Health, WHO and partners and ultimately targeting several million people, along with intensified surveillance and vector control, progressively reduced transmission, and no new cases were reported after early 2013.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Protracted conflict and population displacement in Darfur created crowded, poorly serviced settlements with limited access to routine vaccination, while traditional gold mining and other outdoor occupations brought non-immune adults into high-contact environments with Aedes vectors; delays in recognition and limited early laboratory capacity allowed the outbreak to grow before control measures were deployed. Internal mechanisms: Molecular work links the outbreak virus to contemporary East African YFV lineages (including links to Uganda 2010) rather than a novel genotype; the epidemic is best characterized as a major re-occurrence of yellow fever in Sudan driven by ecological and programmatic factors, not by fundamental viral change.
Review: Review: Newly added event. The 2012–2013 Darfur epidemic, with ≈847–849 suspected cases and 171 deaths across all Darfur states, is widely recognized as the largest African yellow fever outbreak in at least 20 years and clearly merits inclusion among the top post‑1990 events. Coded under Sudan in the Northern Africa subregion, consistent with the Country sheet. Classified as re-occurrence because Sudan had experienced earlier yellow fever outbreaks and available phylogenetic data indicate reintroduction/expansion of existing East African lineages rather than a new genotype or continental spread. Case numbers and timeline are well supported by WHO, NEJM and national/IFRC reports but should be cross-checked with final national surveillance data for exact totals.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (mainly rural and peri-urban residents in Southeast and South regions) and non-human primates (multiple Neotropical monkey species)
Event.summary: From late 2016 through 2019, Brazil experienced the largest sylvatic yellow fever epidemic in roughly 70 years, beginning in the Midwest/North regions and rapidly spreading into previously low-risk Southeast states (Minas Gerais, Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo) and later parts of the South, causing more than 2,000 confirmed human cases and hundreds of deaths, as well as extensive epizootics in howler and other monkeys. The epidemic developed as virus lineages moved along forest corridors into densely populated regions with substantial immunity gaps among adults and intense epizootics in non-human primates, with multiple clusters of infections in forest-fringe communities and travelers and numerous exported cases to neighboring countries and Europe. Large-scale emergency vaccination campaigns, expansion of routine immunization to new regions, and improved surveillance progressively reduced cases, and human transmission declined markedly after 2018–2019, though YFV persists enzootically in Brazil.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of human settlement and agriculture into Atlantic Forest and Cerrado biomes; high densities of susceptible non-human primates and Haemagogus/Sabethes mosquito vectors in forested areas; large unvaccinated adult populations in Southeast and South Brazil due to prior classification of these areas as low-risk; domestic and international travel that exported cases. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses identified a distinct lineage (BR-YFV_2016/18) with an inferred most recent common ancestor around 2015, representing geographic expansion of existing Amazonian lineages; while definitive increases in virulence have not been proven, the successful invasion of previously low-risk ecological zones and intense epizootics support classification as re-emergence driven in part by viral lineage dynamics (“geographic range expansion (inherent)”) rather than simple re-occurrence.
Review: Review: The event remains one of the most impactful post-1990 yellow fever epidemics, with >2,000 confirmed human cases and very large epizootics and geographic spread into densely populated Southeast and South Brazil. However, labelling it as intra-continental emergence is not consistent with the UNSD subregion definition, because transmission remained within the long-affected South America subregion. Intra_continental_emergence has therefore been set to No, while re_emergence remains Yes to reflect the emergence and spread of a distinct viral lineage into new ecological zones within Brazil. Source set is appropriate (Viruses, PLoS NTDs, Scientific Reports, WHO DON).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (rural and peri-urban populations across multiple Nigerian states)
Event.summary: In 2017, Nigeria confirmed its first yellow fever cases in over two decades, starting with an outbreak in Ifelodun LGA, Kwara State, and then reporting widespread suspected and confirmed cases across many states through 2018–2019. The outbreak developed into a nationwide resurgence, with thousands of suspected cases reported and multiple confirmed clusters, particularly during late 2018, highlighting large immunity gaps despite prior vaccination campaigns. Multi-phase reactive and preventive mass vaccination campaigns, coordinated by Nigeria’s Centre for Disease Control, WHO, and partners under the EYE strategy, along with enhanced surveillance and risk communication, progressively reduced transmission, though sporadic outbreaks and clusters have continued in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Declining or incomplete yellow fever vaccination coverage in many Nigerian states, rapid urbanization with Aedes aegypti proliferation, and limitations in surveillance and laboratory capacity that delayed early confirmation and response; population mobility across states facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: Available analyses attribute the resurgence to existing West African YFV lineages in under-immunized populations rather than emergence of a new resistant or more virulent strain; the event is best characterized as re-occurrence driven by external factors such as immunity gaps and health system constraints.
Review: Retain: This multi-year resurgence involved large numbers of suspected cases across many Nigerian states and is clearly among the most consequential recent yellow fever events in West Africa. Classification as re-occurrence in Western Africa is appropriate; historical data show extensive prior transmission in Nigeria, and there is no indication of a fundamentally new viral genotype. Sources (IJID article, BMC Infectious Diseases review, Africa Check/WHO data) are appropriate for magnitude and drivers.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
EPP.common.name: Zika virus
Host: Humans (general population)
Event.summary: In early 2007, clinicians on the Yap Islands in the Federated States of Micronesia noted an outbreak of rash, conjunctivitis and arthralgia initially suspected to be dengue, but laboratory testing identified Zika virus as the cause, marking the first recognized large outbreak of Zika fever and the first documented transmission outside Africa and Asia. The outbreak spread widely in the small island population, with 49 confirmed and 59 probable cases and serologic evidence that roughly three-quarters of residents were infected. Transmission declined over subsequent months as the susceptible population was exhausted and vector control and community protection measures were implemented, with no further large outbreaks reported there afterward.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of Zika virus via travel from endemic regions in Asia into an immunologically naïve island population with abundant Aedes mosquitoes and limited prior arboviral immunity; small, highly connected communities that facilitated rapid person–mosquito–person transmission. Internal mechanisms: Efficient transmission in dense Aedes populations and a high proportion of asymptomatic infections facilitating silent spread; geographic range expansion inherent to the virus as it moved from Asia to Micronesia, representing an inter-continental jump.
Review: retain – Event is real, correctly dated and clearly among the major emergence episodes (first large outbreak and first spread outside Africa/Asia). Country name was standardized to match the Country sheet (“Micronesia (Federated States of)”), but classification as an inter-continental emergence remains appropriate and no substantive issues were identified.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
EPP.common.name: Zika virus
Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women and fetuses/newborns possibly affected)
Event.summary: In 2007, during a large outbreak of febrile illness in Libreville and northern Gabon initially attributed mainly to chikungunya and dengue, virologic investigations detected Zika virus in Aedes albopictus mosquito pools and retrospectively in human samples, revealing substantial but previously unrecognized Zika circulation as part of the mixed arboviral epidemic. Subsequent analyses suggested that many thousands of people may have been infected with Zika virus alongside chikungunya and dengue, and later work raised the possibility of an associated rise in microcephaly and other adverse pregnancy outcomes during that period. As the rainy season ended and vector densities fell, reported febrile cases diminished and the outbreak subsided within several months, but the true burden and congenital impact of the Zika component likely remained underestimated.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Recent invasion and rapid spread of Aedes albopictus in urban Gabon, high vector densities during the rainy season, co-circulation of chikungunya and dengue viruses that complicated diagnosis, and limited arboviral surveillance capacity leading to under-recognition of Zika infections. Internal mechanisms: Apparent adaptation of Zika virus to Aedes albopictus as an efficient urban vector, enabling large-scale transmission in a previously low-recognition setting and representing a notable re-emergence of Zika in Central Africa.
Review: review – This major Central African outbreak, with strong entomological and retrospective evidence for extensive Zika transmission and probable microcephaly impact in Gabon in 2007, was missing and has been added as a re-emergence event in Middle Africa. Classification as re-emergence (rather than intra- or inter-continental emergence) reflects long-standing Zika presence in Africa but a dramatic resurgence linked to a new predominant vector (Aedes albopictus); wording and scale should be checked against any additional outbreak reconstructions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
EPP.common.name: Zika virus
Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women; fetuses/newborns)
Event.summary: In October–November 2015, Cabo Verde reported its first epidemic of Zika virus infection, with rapid spread across the archipelago and over 7,500 suspected cases recorded in the 2015–2016 season. During the outbreak, at least 18 microcephaly cases and additional suspected congenital Zika syndrome outcomes were identified, representing the first large African outbreak associated with congenital malformations and molecularly linked to an imported Asian-lineage virus closely related to strains circulating in Brazil. Transmission subsided by mid‑2016 as the outbreak burned through the susceptible population and intensive vector-control activities, pregnancy surveillance and public health messaging were implemented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of the Asian/American lineage of Zika virus from Brazil into Cabo Verde via air travel; presence of abundant Aedes mosquitoes and suitable climate in a largely Zika-naïve island population; limitations in sustained vector control and water/sanitation infrastructure; increased movement between Brazil and Lusophone West Africa. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a novel strain/genotype (Asian lineage) into the region with demonstrated teratogenic potential; geographic range expansion within Africa beyond historical African-lineage foci; high susceptibility of the local population allowing a large outbreak and clear detection of congenital Zika syndrome.
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects the size and significance of the Cabo Verde outbreak (first large African epidemic with clearly documented congenital Zika syndrome caused by the Asian lineage). Geographic coding (Western Africa, Cabo Verde) and classification as a re-emergence driven by introduction of a new lineage and new clinical phenotype are appropriate; no major corrections needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
EPP.common.name: Zika virus
Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women; fetuses/newborns)
Event.summary: In 2016, Zika virus infection was confirmed in a resident of Angola and in a traveller returning from Angola to Europe, signalling previously unrecognized transmission of the Asian lineage of the virus in the country. Subsequent investigations and genomic analyses indicated that Zika was likely introduced from Brazil sometime between mid‑2015 and mid‑2016, and by 2017 Angola reported clusters of microcephaly in newborns consistent with congenital Zika syndrome. By late 2017, available data suggested that the outbreak had diminished, likely due to a combination of immunity build-up and vector control, though surveillance gaps meant the full size and duration of the epidemic were probably underestimated.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Travel links and migration between Brazil and Angola, including historical Lusophone connections, allowing trans-Atlantic introduction of the Asian lineage; high Aedes mosquito densities in urban Angolan settings with limited vector-control infrastructure; under-resourced surveillance that delayed detection and response. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of the Asian/American lineage into this subregion (replacing silent circulation of African lineages) with strong teratogenic potential; geographic range expansion within Africa; possible silent circulation before overt recognition via congenital cases, reflecting a high proportion of asymptomatic adult infections.
Review: retain – Event appropriately summarizes the Angola emergence of the Asian lineage with associated congenital Zika syndrome and treats it as a re-emergence in a continent where Zika was already endemic. Geographic assignment to Middle Africa and Angola is consistent with the Country sheet, and no clear misclassification or non-major status issues were found.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
EPP.common.name: Zika virus
Host: Humans (general population, including migrant workers and residents in urban clusters)
Event.summary: In 2016, after detecting an imported Zika case and genetically characterizing the virus, Singapore reported its first locally acquired Zika infections, with rapid emergence of large urban clusters in residential and industrial areas such as Aljunied Crescent and Sims Drive. Hundreds of autochthonous cases were identified over the following months despite intensive vector-control efforts, representing one of the most substantial documented Zika outbreaks in South‑eastern Asia’s urban settings, though no associated microcephaly or Guillain–Barré syndrome clusters were confirmed. By late 2016, case numbers had declined substantially as vector-control campaigns, heightened community awareness and seasonal changes reduced transmission, and no similar-scale outbreaks have been reported in Singapore since.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of Zika virus into a densely populated, highly urbanized city-state with widespread Aedes aegypti despite long-standing dengue control; intense human mobility within and between residential and workplace areas facilitating mosquito-mediated spread; challenges in fully suppressing vector breeding in construction sites and older housing estates. Internal mechanisms: Efficient transmission by Asian-lineage Zika viruses already adapted to urban Aedes aegypti; high asymptomatic fraction that allowed cryptic spread before outbreak recognition, though severe congenital outcomes were not documented in this event.
Review: retain – Event is well-supported and clearly one of the larger and better-characterized urban Zika outbreaks in South‑eastern Asia, with correct geographic coding (Asia, South-eastern Asia, Singapore) and classification as a re-occurrence in a region with long-standing Zika circulation but renewed, intensified transmission in 2016.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
EPP.common.name: Zika virus
Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women; fetuses/newborns)
Event.summary: From early 2016, Thailand expanded nationwide Zika surveillance and rapidly confirmed locally acquired infections in multiple provinces, revealing that Zika had been silently circulating and was now causing noticeable outbreaks. Over 2016–2017, national data documented more than a thousand laboratory-confirmed infections distributed across at least 16 provinces, along with a small number of pregnancies and congenital anomalies temporally associated with maternal Zika infection. By 2018, reported case numbers had fallen as awareness, targeted vector control and routine surveillance improved, and Zika was recognized as an endemic but generally low-incidence arboviral infection in Thailand rather than a one-off explosive epidemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Longstanding presence of competent Aedes mosquitoes in Thailand, high background dengue transmission, favourable tropical climate, dense human populations and increased clinical and laboratory surveillance that improved detection of Zika from 2016 onward. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of Asian-lineage Zika virus without clear evidence of major new genetic changes, consistent with a re-occurrence driven primarily by environmental and surveillance factors rather than viral evolution.
Review: review – This substantial 2016–2017 outbreak in Thailand, with over a thousand confirmed infections and documented pregnancy exposures, was missing and has been added as a re-occurrence event in South‑eastern Asia. Classification as re-occurrence (rather than first detection or re-emergence) reflects evidence of earlier Zika circulation in Thailand and the absence of a clearly novel viral lineage; the summary and scale should be cross-checked against national surveillance reports for final inclusion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
EPP.common.name: Zika virus
Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women)
Event.summary: After three autochthonous Zika cases were identified in Gujarat and one in Tamil Nadu during 2016–2017, India detected a much larger outbreak beginning in September 2018 in Jaipur, Rajasthan, followed by confirmed local transmission in parts of Madhya Pradesh. By late 2018, national and WHO reports documented at least 159 confirmed cases in Rajasthan and over 120 in Madhya Pradesh, including many pregnant women, prompting extensive vector control, household screening and intensified surveillance. These outbreaks were contained over several months without documented clusters of microcephaly or Guillain–Barré syndrome, but subsequent years saw additional, smaller Zika clusters in other Indian states, indicating ongoing low-level circulation in Southern Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread presence of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus in Indian urban and peri-urban settings, high human population density, climatic conditions suitable for arbovirus transmission, and increased clinical and laboratory surveillance following the Americas epidemic that enabled recognition of the 2018 outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of South-East Asian lineage Zika virus without clear evidence of novel genotype or major virulence change, suggesting that these events represent a re-occurrence of an established regional pathogen in a large, previously under-recognized national setting.
Review: review – India’s 2018 outbreaks in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh represent the country’s first large, well-documented Zika epidemics (hundreds of confirmed cases) and clearly belong among the major global emergence events. This row has been added as a re-occurrence in Southern Asia, given longstanding regional Zika evidence; country and year coding follow the Country sheet conventions and states are described in the narrative rather than in the country field.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
EPP.common.name: Zika virus
Host: Humans (general population in affected neighbourhood)
Event.summary: In the summer of 2019, health authorities in the Var department in southern France detected a cluster of three Zika virus infections in residents with no travel history, indicating local mosquito-borne transmission in a neighbourhood of Hyères. Epidemiologic investigations and viral genetic analyses pointed to introduction of an Asian-lineage virus, probably from a traveller returning from a Zika-affected area in South-East Asia, and confirmed this as the first recognized local vector-borne Zika transmission in Europe. Intensive vector control around the cases and the onset of cooler weather were followed by no additional autochthonous cases, and the event remained a short-lived, geographically limited emergence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Presence and seasonal abundance of Aedes albopictus in southern France, international travel from Zika-affected regions, and conducive summer climatic conditions that allowed a brief transmission chain in a small urban area. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of Asian-lineage Zika virus capable of being transmitted by European Aedes albopictus; no evidence of large-scale adaptation, but demonstration that local vectors can support short chains of transmission under favourable conditions, marking an inter-continental emergence into Europe.
Review: review – This small but epidemiologically important cluster in southern France constitutes the first documented local mosquito-borne Zika transmission in Europe and thus an inter-continental emergence event despite the very low case count. The row has been added with Europe/Western Europe/France coding and inter-continental emergence marked as “Yes”; outbreak size and timing are consistent with WHO and ECDC reports but should be rechecked when integrating with other European arbovirus emergence records.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (local residents and visitors to Madeira Island)
Event.summary: In October 2012, Portugal reported the first autochthonous dengue cases on Madeira Island, marking the first sustained dengue epidemic in Europe since the 1920s, with over 1,000 confirmed and more than 2,000 probable infections and numerous cases exported to mainland Europe. The outbreak was caused by DENV‑1 closely related to strains circulating in Venezuela and Brazil, likely introduced by travelers into a naive population with abundant Aedes aegypti. Intensive vector control, seasonal decline in mosquito populations, and public health measures led authorities to declare the outbreak over in early 2013.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of DENV‑1 via infected travelers from South America; dense local Aedes aegypti populations; favorable climate and urban conditions; immunologically naive human population; high tourist traffic facilitating both importation and exportation. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion supported by an established competent vector; virus belonged to known DENV‑1 lineages without evidence of dramatically increased virulence; this represents re‑occurrence of dengue epidemic activity in Europe after a long hiatus.
Review: Retained and reclassified: inter_continental_emergence is set to false and re_occurrence to true. Madeira 2012 is well documented as the first large dengue epidemic in Europe since the inter‑war period, with >2,000 local cases, but dengue transmission had already occurred historically on the continent (including the major Greece epidemic in 1927–1928). It therefore represents a major regional re‑occurrence in a previously dengue‑silent setting rather than a first occurrence on a new continent.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Countries: United States of America (Florida – Key West/Monroe County) [2009]
Host: Humans (residents and visitors in Key West, Florida)
Event.summary: In mid‑2009, dengue virus type 1 was identified in a visitor and subsequently in residents of Key West, Florida, and serosurveys showed 3–5% of Old Town residents had recent infection, confirming local transmission after decades without endemic dengue in the continental United States. Additional locally acquired cases occurred in Key West and other Florida counties in 2010–2011, with DENV‑1 detected in local Aedes aegypti populations and a distinct Key West viral sub‑lineage related to Central American strains. Aggressive vector control, public awareness campaigns, and seasonal decline in mosquito abundance curtailed transmission and prevented long‑term establishment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Travel‑related introduction from the Caribbean/Central America, abundant Aedes aegypti in subtropical South Florida, high human–mosquito contact, and limited population immunity after a long dengue‑free period; urban environments with water‑holding containers supported breeding. Internal mechanisms: Local diversification of a DENV‑1 lineage (Key West sub‑lineage), but no clear evidence of increased virulence; the episode is best viewed as re‑occurrence of dengue transmission in a historically affected region rather than a novel inter‑continental emergence.
Review: Retained but corrected: inter_continental_emergence has been reset to false and re_occurrence kept as true. Dengue has a long history in the Americas, and autochthonous transmission in the United States occurred earlier in the 20th century and again in Texas and Hawaii before 2009, so Key West does not represent first occurrence on a new continent. It is, however, an important re‑establishment of local transmission in the continental USA after several dengue‑free decades, and is appropriate to retain as a major re‑occurrence.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (primarily urban residents in Lahore and Punjab Province)
Event.summary: In 2011, Pakistan experienced its largest recorded dengue outbreak, centered in Lahore in Punjab Province, with approximately 22,000 reported cases and more than 300 deaths, far exceeding prior years’ activity. Co‑circulation of multiple serotypes (notably DENV‑2 and DENV‑3), intense urban crowding, inadequate vector control, and monsoon‑related breeding sites fueled rapid expansion of cases within Lahore and neighboring districts. Emergency vector control campaigns, clinical management improvements, and the end of the monsoon season gradually reduced transmission, though dengue has remained endemic with recurrent outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid urbanization and high population density, inadequate water and waste management enabling Aedes breeding, heavy monsoon rains, and limited sustained vector control; delayed recognition and health‑system overload contributed to high case fatality. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies show circulation of DENV‑2 cosmopolitan genotype related to strains already present in Pakistan, without strong evidence of a fundamentally novel viral lineage; increased severity largely reflects hyperendemic circulation and secondary infections rather than a new strain, so the event is best characterized as a major re‑occurrence in a long‑endemic setting.
Review: Retained but reclassified from re_emergence to re_occurrence only. Phylogenetic work on the 2011 Lahore epidemic indicates that the outbreak strains belonged to locally evolved DENV‑2 cosmopolitan genotype rather than a clearly new, more virulent variant, and key drivers were external (urban crowding, monsoon rains, limited control). This fits the definition of re‑occurrence (resurgence due to external factors) better than re‑emergence (which requires clear changes in the pathogen such as a new strain, host jump or resistance).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (local residents and domestic travelers, mainly exposed in urban parks)
Event.summary: In August 2014, Japan reported its first autochthonous dengue case since 1945 in a patient infected in Tokyo’s Yoyogi Park, and by late October a total of about 160 locally acquired cases with no overseas travel history were confirmed around several Tokyo parks. Molecular analysis showed DENV‑1 closely related among cases, indicating a single introduction likely from an imported case and subsequent propagation by local Aedes albopictus populations in popular urban recreational areas. Closure and insecticide treatment of affected parks, public advisories, and the onset of cooler weather ended local transmission by late 2014, and dengue has not become endemic in Japan.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of DENV‑1 by an infected traveler, dense Aedes albopictus populations in urban green spaces, high human visitation to parks, and summer temperatures permitting efficient transmission in a largely non‑immune population. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of markedly novel viral traits; the outbreak mainly illustrates how a single introduction can trigger transient re‑occurrence where competent vectors and favorable climate coexist.
Review: Retained without changes in emergence typing. Japan had sizeable dengue outbreaks in the 1940s, so the 2014 Yoyogi Park cluster is correctly captured as re_occurrence driven by travel‑related introduction, established Aedes albopictus and favorable summer conditions, with no clear viral innovation. It is a relatively small outbreak in absolute numbers but is an important indicator of dengue’s capacity to re‑appear in temperate East Asia.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (urban and peri‑urban populations across multiple Indian states)
Event.summary: In 2015, India experienced one of its worst dengue years in decades, with national surveillance indicating that reported dengue cases roughly doubled compared with 2014, exceeding about 80,000–100,000 suspected or confirmed cases and causing substantial mortality, particularly in Delhi and other large cities. Hyperendemic circulation of multiple serotypes, rapid unplanned urbanization, and water storage practices facilitated high Aedes aegypti densities and explosive transmission across many states. Intensified vector control campaigns, public education, and improved clinical management reduced case fatality and led to the typical seasonal decline in transmission toward the end of the year, though dengue has remained hyperendemic with recurrent large outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Urban crowding, poor water and waste infrastructure, favorable monsoon seasons, and limited sustained vector control; large susceptible cohorts accumulated between epidemic waves; health‑system strain may have delayed effective responses in some areas. Internal mechanisms: Hyperendemic co‑circulation of multiple DENV serotypes raises risk of severe disease through secondary infection; however, no single novel genotype has been clearly implicated, so the event is best viewed as a major re‑occurrence in a long‑endemic setting.
Review: Retained as a re_occurrence event. India has had dengue transmission for many decades, and 2015 is well documented as a year when nationally reported case counts roughly doubled relative to 2014, with major urban outbreaks. No strong evidence for viral novelty has been presented, so re_emergence is not appropriate. From a global top‑10 perspective this event is somewhat less exceptional than Sri Lanka 2017 or the 2019 and 2024 Americas epidemics, but it remains one of the largest recorded Indian dengue seasons and is reasonable to keep.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (children and adults nationwide, with high incidence in several regions)
Event.summary: In 2019, the Philippines experienced a massive dengue epidemic, with over 146,000 cases and more than 600 deaths reported by late July, prompting the Department of Health to declare first a National Dengue Alert and then a National Dengue Epidemic in August. Cases surged across multiple regions, driven by intense Aedes aegypti infestation, favorable weather, waning population immunity, and health‑system challenges following controversy surrounding a prior dengue vaccination program. Expanded community clean‑up campaigns, enhanced surveillance, and strengthened clinical management reduced mortality and, together with seasonal changes, led to declining case numbers later in the year.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climatic conditions conducive to mosquito proliferation, high household water storage and waste, rapid urbanization, and reduced trust in some public‑health interventions; large susceptible cohorts after previous inter‑epidemic periods. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of multiple serotypes typical for hyperendemic settings; no clearly novel strain was identified as the main driver, so this represents a severe re‑occurrence in an endemic country.
Review: Retained as a major re_occurrence: national authorities declared a dengue epidemic in 2019 after an unusually large surge in cases and deaths, and the event is well documented. No evidence supports first/global emergence, inter‑continental or intra‑continental emergence, or pathogen‑level changes, so the current categorization is appropriate. If the dengue dataset ultimately has to be reduced to 10 events, this could be weighed against other very large Asian epidemics (e.g. Sri Lanka 2017, Bangladesh 2019) for prioritization.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (especially residents of Dhaka and other major cities)
Event.summary: Beginning in April 2019, Bangladesh experienced its largest dengue outbreak on record, with national data indicating over 100,000 confirmed cases and dozens of deaths by the end of the year, more than doubling prior peaks since dengue was first recognized in the country in 2000. The epidemic was initially concentrated in Dhaka, one of the world’s most densely populated megacities, before spreading to all 64 districts as population movements during religious holidays redistributed infected individuals and vectors. Emergency vector control, risk communication, and improved hospital triage and management helped reduce the case‑fatality rate, and case numbers declined with the end of the monsoon season though dengue has since remained a recurrent national threat.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extreme population density and informal housing in Dhaka, inadequate water and waste infrastructure generating abundant Aedes breeding sites, heavy monsoon rains, and inter‑district human movement during holidays; limitations in sustained vector control and urban planning. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of several DENV serotypes and potential shifts in serotype predominance contributed to severe disease risk, but no specific new genotype is clearly established as causal; the event is best characterized as a major re‑occurrence in an increasingly endemic setting.
Review: Retained as a major re_occurrence event. The 2019 Bangladesh epidemic is well documented as the largest since dengue was first recognized nationally in 2000, with >100,000 cases and nationwide spread. Available data implicate external drivers (urban crowding, monsoon rains, health‑system capacity) and shifting serotype predominance, but do not demonstrate a fundamentally novel viral strain, so re_emergence is not indicated.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (residents of multiple islands including Santiago, Maio, Fogo and Brava)
Event.summary: From late September 2009, Cabo Verde reported its first known dengue epidemic, with thousands of suspected cases across the southern islands of Santiago, Maio, Fogo and Brava; by November, national and partner reports indicated more than 13,000–20,000 suspected infections and several deaths, making it at the time the largest recorded dengue outbreak in Africa. The epidemic, caused by DENV‑3 likely introduced from the Americas, spread rapidly through densely populated urban neighborhoods with abundant Aedes aegypti breeding sites and a largely dengue‑naive human population. Intensive emergency vector control, community clean‑up campaigns, clinical support and seasonal declines in mosquito density reduced transmission, and incidence fell sharply in early 2010, although Cabo Verde and the wider West African region have continued to report dengue activity thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of DENV‑3 via infected travelers (probably from Latin America), high densities of Aedes aegypti in urban areas, water storage and waste management practices favoring breeding, and a largely immunologically naive population in Cabo Verde; limited prior experience with dengue diagnosis and control delayed early recognition. Internal mechanisms: Virus belonged to known DENV‑3 lineages without evidence of unique resistance or virulence traits; the outbreak represents a dramatic re‑occurrence of dengue in the West African subregion, where dengue had been documented in countries such as Nigeria and Senegal decades earlier, rather than first emergence on the continent.
Review: Newly added and should be retained. WHO and MSF describe the 2009–2010 Cabo Verde epidemic as the country’s first dengue outbreak and, at the time, the largest recorded dengue epidemic in Africa, with >13,000–20,000 suspected cases. Because dengue virus had already been isolated from humans in West African countries such as Nigeria and Senegal in the 1960s–1970s, this is best classified as a major re_occurrence in a previously affected subregion, not as intra‑continental or inter‑continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (urban residents of Guangzhou and surrounding districts)
Event.summary: In 2014, Guangzhou in Guangdong Province experienced the largest recorded dengue outbreak in mainland China, with around 37,000–38,000 laboratory‑confirmed indigenous cases and several deaths, accounting for the great majority of dengue cases in China that year. After an imported index case in June, transmission expanded explosively during the hot, humid summer and early autumn, driven by very high densities of Aedes albopictus, high human–mosquito contact in crowded urban neighborhoods and widespread unprotected water containers. Intensive emergency vector control, community mobilization and the onset of cooler weather in late autumn curtailed transmission, but Guangzhou has remained the primary epicenter for recurrent dengue activity in China.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid urbanization, high population density, favorable climatic conditions for Aedes albopictus, abundant artificial containers and limited early vector control, together with repeated viral importations from dengue‑endemic areas in Southeast Asia. Internal mechanisms: Molecular investigations indicated circulation of DENV‑1 and DENV‑2 lineages closely related to strains from Southeast Asia, without evidence of a uniquely new genotype; the event therefore represents an extreme re_occurrence in a region where dengue had been present since the 1970s, not a new continental or subcontinental emergence.
Review: Newly added and appropriate to retain as a major event. Multiple epidemiological analyses describe the 2014 Guangzhou outbreak as the largest dengue epidemic ever recorded in mainland China, with >37,000 indigenous cases and strong concentration of national burden in one metropolitan area. Dengue was already recognized in southern China, so classification as re_occurrence (without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or re_emergence) is consistent with the framework.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (nationwide, with highest incidence in Colombo and the Western Province)
Event.summary: In 2017, Sri Lanka experienced its largest dengue epidemic since national notification began, reporting about 186,000 suspected cases and more than 400 dengue‑related deaths nationwide, with a marked concentration in the densely populated Western Province around Colombo. Following heavy rains and flooding that created extensive Aedes breeding sites, a shift from predominant DENV‑1 to a cosmopolitan DENV‑2 genotype associated with more severe disease coincided with explosive spread among older school‑age children and young adults and substantial strain on hospital capacity. Large‑scale vector control campaigns, triage and clinical management improvements, and the end of the southwest monsoon season led to a gradual decline in cases later in 2017, but dengue has remained a major recurrent public‑health threat.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intense monsoon rains and flooding, high urban population density (especially in Colombo), suboptimal solid‑waste and water management, and limited sustained vector‑control capacity created ideal conditions for Aedes proliferation; health‑system crowding and delayed care seeking increased severity and mortality. Internal mechanisms: Virological investigations show a replacement of DENV‑1 by a cosmopolitan DENV‑2 genotype temporally associated with increased incidence and more severe disease, consistent with re_emergence driven by serotype/genotype change superimposed on an already endemic setting; this justifies coding both re_occurrence and re_emergence, as allowed by the framework.
Review: Newly added and strongly recommended for inclusion. WHO and peer‑reviewed analyses concur that 2017 was Sri Lanka’s largest dengue epidemic on record, with ~186,000 suspected cases and >400 deaths, and that a shift to DENV‑2 cosmopolitan genotype was temporally associated with the unprecedented severity. This fits both re_occurrence (major resurgence in a known endemic subregion) and re_emergence (pathogen‑level change in circulating serotype/genotype), which are allowed to co‑occur under the project’s rules.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Plasmodium spp.
EPP.common.name: malaria parasites
Host: Humans (zoonotic Plasmodium knowlesi infections from macaque reservoirs via Anopheles mosquitoes)
Event.summary: Between roughly 1998 and 2002, investigators in Kapit Division, Sarawak (Malaysian Borneo) documented a large cluster of human malaria cases initially diagnosed as Plasmodium malariae but subsequently confirmed by PCR, in 2004, to be Plasmodium knowlesi, revealing frequent naturally acquired zoonotic infections in humans in this forested region. This discovery showed that what had been considered rare simian malaria spillover was in fact a substantial and ongoing transmission cycle involving macaque reservoirs and Anopheles leucosphyrus‑group vectors, and subsequent surveillance identified many additional human P. knowlesi cases in other parts of Malaysian Borneo and Peninsular Malaysia. Control efforts have therefore focused on improving molecular species diagnosis, clinical management of knowlesi malaria and targeted vector control near forest–fringe communities, but because of the persistent macaque reservoir, human P. knowlesi infections have continued to occur rather than being eliminated.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Deforestation, agricultural expansion, road building and human settlement in interior Sarawak increased human exposure to forest‑dwelling macaques and competent Anopheles vectors, while the introduction of species‑specific PCR assays allowed accurate differentiation of P. knowlesi from morphologically similar P. malariae that had previously masked its true incidence. Internal mechanisms: The event primarily reflects recognition and amplification of an existing zoonotic transmission cycle, rather than emergence of a clearly novel parasite genotype; it is therefore best treated as a re-occurrence driven by ecological change and improved detection, with host expansion (spillover into humans) occurring at clinically important incidence but likely predating the 1990s.
Review: review – retain event but reclassified and re-dated. Changes made: (1) Event years adjusted from 2000–2004 to 1998–2002 to align with the surveillance period underlying the 2004 Lancet description of the Kapit Division focus. (2) 'First detection' set to No because Plasmodium spp. were detected in humans long before 1990 and a naturally acquired human P. knowlesi infection was documented in 1965; this episode is the first recognition of a large zoonotic focus, not the first global detection. (3) Event type changed from re-emergence to re-occurrence, reflecting that current evidence points to ecological change and improved diagnostics rather than a clearly novel parasite genotype; host expansion is recognized but may have pre-dated the 1990s. Geography (Malaysia, South-eastern Asia) and sources are appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Shigella spp.
EPP.common.name: Shigellosis
Host: Humans (predominantly men who have sex with men in Victoria; some women and non‑MSM men)
Event.summary: Between February 2018 and May 2019, the Australian state of Victoria detected 184 cases of extensively drug-resistant Shigella sonnei, largely among men who have sex with men, alongside broader co-circulation of multidrug-resistant Shigella in MSM across Australia. Genomic analyses linked the outbreak to global MSM-associated resistant lineages and demonstrated resistance to most key oral antimicrobials, complicating treatment. Following intensified surveillance, clinician alerts and sexual health messaging, case numbers in this XDR cluster declined, although multidrug-resistant Shigella continued to circulate in Australian MSM networks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International travel and sexual networking between Australian MSM and counterparts in Europe and Asia; dense urban sexual networks; prior antibiotic exposure in affected populations; limited early awareness of XDR Shigella risks. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (XDR profile including resistance to ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, and other first‑line agents); Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (XDR S. sonnei lineage closely related to global MSM-associated clones); Enhanced Transmission (efficient sexual transmission at a very low infectious dose).
Review: review – Event retained as a major XDR episode in Oceania, but 'inter_continental_emergence' has been changed from 'Yes' to 'No'. Extensively drug-resistant S. sonnei in Australian MSM represents re-emergence of Shigella with a markedly expanded resistance profile in a continent where shigellosis has long been endemic; per the definitions, this should be coded as re-emergence due to novel resistance, not as inter-continental emergence of the pathogen. Other fields and sources (NEJM correspondence, CID analysis, NSW alert) are appropriate and unchanged.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Giardia intestinalis
EPP.common.name: Giardia lamblia, Lamblia intestinalis
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From January to April 1990, the neighbouring communities of Creston and Erickson in British Columbia, Canada, experienced a large community outbreak of giardiasis linked to an unfiltered, unchlorinated surface water supply. Public health investigation documented 124 laboratory-confirmed cases among residents and associated the outbreak with beavers excreting large numbers of Giardia cysts into the municipal source water. Following issuance of boil-water advice and subsequent improvements to water treatment and source protection, case numbers declined and the outbreak ended.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reliance on unfiltered, unchlorinated surface water for municipal supply; high densities of Giardia-infected beavers in the catchment; inadequate source protection and treatment allowed substantial cyst loads to reach consumers. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a novel strain or altered virulence; the event reflects re-occurrence of an established parasite driven by environmental contamination and infrastructure deficiencies rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Review – Added new event. Well-documented 1990 Creston & Erickson drinking-water outbreak with 124 laboratory-confirmed cases and clear linkage to untreated surface water and beaver contamination, meeting the definition of a major post-1990 re-occurrence event in North America. Classified as re-occurrence (not re-emergence) because no novel genotype or host shift was implicated. Geography (Northern America, Canada) and timing (Jan–Apr 1990) taken from Health Canada Appendix B; further detail from Isaac‑Renton et al. is not directly accessible in this environment and should be checked, but overall event characterization is robust. Retain as a major Canadian reference outbreak; flagged for expert review of its relative ranking among the global top 10 by case count.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Giardia intestinalis
EPP.common.name: Giardia lamblia, Lamblia intestinalis
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From February to May 1994, residents of Temagami, a small community in northeastern Ontario, Canada, experienced a marked increase in gastrointestinal illness that was traced to the municipal surface-water supply. Investigation identified 26 laboratory-confirmed giardiasis cases and an estimated 160–330 clinical cases linked to consumption of unboiled tap water from a poorly protected and inadequately treated lake source, leading to a boil-water advisory and intensified parasitological monitoring. Once boil-water recommendations were implemented and filtration and chlorination performance improved, case numbers declined and the outbreak was declared over later in 1994.
