Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Contamination of a small community surface-water supply by human sewage during a premature winter thaw and by beavers, together with poor filtration performance and inadequate chlorine disinfection, resulted in significant Giardia contamination of finished water and delayed recognition of the problem. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype or change in virulence was documented; the outbreak represents re-occurrence of endemic Giardia transmission amplified by infrastructure and operational failures rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Review – Original event is real and correctly located but required reclassification and clarification. (1) Re-emergence has been set to "No": available descriptions treat this as a classic water-treatment failure in a community where Giardia was already known, with no clear evidence that a novel strain, host shift, or resistance mechanism drove the outbreak; thus it fits the definition of re-occurrence only.([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/environmental-workplace-health/reports-publications/water-quality/enteric-protozoa-giardia-cryptosporidium.html)) (2) Case counts and drivers (26 laboratory-confirmed, 160–330 clinical cases; sewage and beaver contamination; inadequate filtration and chlorination) have been aligned with Health Canada Appendix B, which is the most authoritative concise source for this outbreak.([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/environmental-workplace-health/reports-publications/water-quality/enteric-protozoa-giardia-cryptosporidium.html)) (3) Two PubMed citations could not be directly verified here because of access restrictions but likely correspond to Canadian waterborne protozoan outbreak investigations; they are left in place and flagged for curator verification, while the Health Canada guideline and the Clinical Microbiology Reviews article are treated as the primary sources.([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/environmental-workplace-health/reports-publications/water-quality/enteric-protozoa-giardia-cryptosporidium.html)) Given its moderate size relative to several much larger post-1990 outbreaks (e.g. Montgomery County, New York; Bergen, Norway; Sant’Agata Bolognese, Italy), this event may fall below a strict global top‑10 threshold and is therefore flagged for review rather than automatic retention.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Giardia intestinalis
EPP.common.name: Giardia lamblia, Lamblia intestinalis
Countries: United States of America [2003] (membership country club in a suburb of Boston, Massachusetts)
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In June 2003, a membership country club in a Boston-area suburb reported clusters of giardiasis among children and family members who had used the club’s swimming facilities. A detailed investigation documented a prolonged outbreak that began with exposure to an inadequately chlorinated children’s pool and then continued for several months via household and community person-to-person transmission, ultimately involving 149 epidemiologically linked cases (97 laboratory-confirmed).([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/44976C514341F576ECF16B0990C80E5F/S0950268805005832a.pdf/prolonged_outbreak_of_giardiasis_with_two_modes_of_transmission.pdf)) Closure of the pools, correction of pool operation and disinfection practices, and public health messaging on hygiene eventually curtailed transmission, and the outbreak waned by late 2003.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Inadequate pool maintenance and suboptimal chlorination of a heavily used children’s pool, including documented fecal accidents and poor response, created conditions for Giardia contamination of recreational water; high bather loads of diaper-aged children and delayed recognition of parasite etiology amplified the outbreak and enabled spread into households and the wider community.([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/44976C514341F576ECF16B0990C80E5F/S0950268805005832a.pdf/prolonged_outbreak_of_giardiasis_with_two_modes_of_transmission.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: No novel assemblage or increased virulence was reported; this is a classic multi-mode re-occurrence event (recreational water followed by person-to-person transmission) driven by behavioural and operational factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Event is well described and represents a sizeable (149-case) and epidemiologically important outbreak with combined recreational-water and person-to-person transmission in a high‑income setting.([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/44976C514341F576ECF16B0990C80E5F/S0950268805005832a.pdf/prolonged_outbreak_of_giardiasis_with_two_modes_of_transmission.pdf)) Classification as re-occurrence (with no intra- or inter-continental emergence) is appropriate, and the geographic coding (Northern America, USA) is correct. While not as large as the Montgomery County or Bergen outbreaks, it is among the larger documented community giardiasis outbreaks in the 1990–2010 period and illustrates an important transmission route (children’s pools). Recommended to retain, but its inclusion in a strict "top 10 by case count" set should be revisited once all candidate outbreaks are tabulated.

EPP.scientific.name: Giardia intestinalis
EPP.common.name: Giardia lamblia, Lamblia intestinalis
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In autumn 2004, clinicians in Bergen, Norway, noted an unusual rise in giardiasis among residents with no recent travel, in a city where the disease had been considered mainly imported. Investigation revealed a large community-wide outbreak caused by contamination of the Svartediket municipal surface-water reservoir, resulting in about 1,268 laboratory-confirmed cases and an estimated ~2,500 persons treated for giardiasis, with later studies suggesting that roughly 5,000 people experienced related illness.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1524744/?utm_source=openai)) After the contaminated reservoir was removed from service, water treatment was upgraded, and boil-water and hygiene advice issued, new case numbers declined over winter 2004–2005, though many patients experienced prolonged post-infectious gastrointestinal sequelae.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy rainfall and runoff with sewage or fecal contamination of a surface-water reservoir, combined with deficiencies in filtration and disinfection and delayed suspicion of giardiasis in a low-endemic urban population, allowed extensive contamination of the municipal water supply and widespread exposure.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1524744/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Genotyping showed Giardia assemblage B predominated, but there is no convincing evidence of a fundamentally novel or more virulent strain; the scale of the outbreak is best explained by water-treatment vulnerabilities and delayed detection, so it is classified as a large re-occurrence of an established parasite rather than a re-emergence driven by evolutionary change.
Review: Retain – This outbreak is clearly one of the largest documented giardiasis outbreaks worldwide in the 1990–2025 window, with >1,200 laboratory-confirmed cases and several thousand persons treated or ill, and has been extensively characterized in the literature.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1524744/?utm_source=openai)) Geographic and temporal coding (Europe, Northern Europe, Norway; 2004 start) are correct; the summary appropriately notes that cases and control measures extended into early 2005 but, per the event-specification rules, this can remain coded by start year. Classification as re-occurrence only is appropriate, as Giardia was long present in Europe and no new host system or genotype-driven change was central to the event. Strongly recommended to retain as a benchmark high-impact emergence episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Host: Humans (adolescent boarding-school students)
Event.summary: In September–October 2002, staff at a boarding school in İzmir, western Türkiye, observed a surge of mildly symptomatic students with cervical lymphadenopathy and low-grade fever, prompting serologic screening for toxoplasmosis. All 171 evaluated students were positive for T. gondii IgG and IgM, and of 43 tested for IgG avidity, 40 (93%) had low-avidity antibodies, indicating recent primary infection and making this one of the largest single-institution outbreaks described. No specific food or water vehicle was identified; instead, the outbreak was attributed to rapid spread in a closed community, likely through environmental exposure to oocysts from cats kept on or near the school grounds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Crowded dormitory living with shared facilities, presence of cats and cat litter on campus, and limited environmental hygiene created opportunities for common-source or repeated oocyst exposure through contaminated soil, dust, or surfaces. Internal mechanisms: Conventional oocyst-borne transmission without demonstration of a novel genotype or increased parasite virulence; this event is best categorized as re-occurrence in a setting with dense susceptible hosts and high environmental contamination.
Review: Retain (added). This large school-based outbreak (171 recent infections) was missing from the original dataset despite being explicitly identified as “the largest recent outbreak of toxoplasmosis” in its primary report and included in the CDC systematic review of outbreaks. Asia/Western Asia/ Türkiye coding aligns with UNSD regions, and classification as re-occurrence (environmental oocyst exposure in a previously endemic country) is consistent with available evidence. Event and mechanism summaries and source URLs were added and should be kept; the event clearly belongs in any top‑10 list by case count.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Countries: Brazil [2004] (Pará State; Monte Dourado District, Almeirim)
Host: Humans (residents of a semi-isolated company town)
Event.summary: In 2004, health services in the Monte Dourado District of Almeirim, northern Brazil, responded to an increase in febrile lymphadenopathic illness and conducted a community investigation. Of 186 residents and close contacts tested, 40 (21.5%) had serologic profiles consistent with acute or recent toxoplasmosis, and epidemiologic findings pointed toward local environmental exposure in a town with a high domestic cat population rather than contamination of the treated municipal water system. Clinical management focused on treating symptomatic individuals and providing health education; the outbreak waned once suspected environmental sources were mitigated.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High density of domestic/peridomestic cats, poor disposal of cat feces, and inadequate sanitation in a small Amazonian company town facilitated contamination of soil and possibly food with oocysts, with many residents sharing similar environmental exposures. Internal mechanisms: Typical oocyst-borne transmission via contaminated soil, dust, or food, without documented emergence of a new genotype or intrinsic change in virulence; this is best classified as re-occurrence driven by environmental and infrastructural conditions.
Review: Retain. This community outbreak (40 acute/recent infections) is among the larger post‑1990 events, especially in the Brazilian Amazon, and is specifically tabulated in the CDC outbreak review. Geographic coding is correct. The main correction made is to emphasize that the municipal water system was considered unlikely to be the source, with soil/food exposure from numerous cats favored; the previous text implying a probable water source has been softened accordingly. Classification as re-occurrence remains appropriate. Flagged for review due to this clarified transmission narrative.
