EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Countries: Brazil [2006] (Maranhão State; residential community in São Luís)
Host: Humans (residents, domestic workers, and employees in a gated community)
Event.summary: In 2006, an infectious-disease specialist in São Luís, Maranhão, reported several acute toxoplasmosis cases among residents of a gated residential community, prompting a municipal and zoonoses-surveillance investigation. Of 110 residents, domestic workers, and employees interviewed, 90 agreed to serologic testing; 33 persons met a case definition for acute/recent toxoplasmosis, and all cases reported consuming water filtered by faucet‑mount or ceramic household filters, whereas bottled water use was less frequent. Environmental testing did not recover T. gondii from water or local cats, but epidemiologic analysis implicated a waterborne source related to well water used in the community and filtered at the point of use. Following public-health advice on water treatment and filter hygiene, and as exposed persons recovered, no further clusters were detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of intermittently supplied well and public water with simple point-of-use filters, inadequate protection of water storage and distribution against fecal contamination, and limited awareness of oocyst resistance to routine chlorination and filtration, leading to waterborne transmission within a single residential complex. Internal mechanisms: Standard oocyst-borne infection via drinking water, with no evidence of a new parasite genotype or host shift; thus classified as re-occurrence linked primarily to infrastructural and behavioral factors.
Review: Retain. This 33‑case gated-community outbreak is one of the better-documented medium-sized waterborne events and is discussed in depth in a 2019 reanalysis. The main corrections are (i) to emphasize that the outbreak was concluded to be waterborne with a strong association to faucet-mount filtered water, and (ii) to provide the specific number of acute cases (33). Classification as re-occurrence is maintained. Flagged for review because the original summary underplayed the evidence for a waterborne source and overstated uncertainty.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Countries: Brazil [2006] (São Paulo State; São Paulo city and Guarujá)
Host: Humans (restaurant patrons consuming a raw beef dish, steak tartare)
Event.summary: In November 2006, public health officials in São Paulo State investigated an outbreak of acute toxoplasmosis among people who had eaten at restaurants in São Paulo city and Guarujá. A field investigation and case–control study identified consumption of a raw-beef dish (steak tartare) at specific establishments as the main risk factor, and a small number of exposed diners developed clinically compatible illness with serologic evidence of recent infection. Withdrawal of the implicated meat batches and advisories discouraging consumption of uncooked beef were followed by an absence of further cases linked to this episode.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Serving and consumption of raw or undercooked beef prepared from carcasses of infected cattle, without freezing or other inactivation steps, in a context of changing culinary practices and varying background seroprevalence. Internal mechanisms: Meat-borne transmission via tissue cysts in beef, a well-established route for T. gondii; there is no evidence for a novel strain or host adaptation, so this small cluster is categorized as re-occurrence driven by food-handling and preparation practices rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Review / likely exclude if restricting to top‑10 events. The outbreak is real and correctly geographically and temporally placed, and the principal source (Boletim Epidemiológico Paulista) is appropriate. However, it involved only a handful of cases (EID’s outbreak table lists a 6‑case beef-associated event for 2006 in Brazil), well below the scale of other events now included (e.g., Santa Isabel, Coimbatore, Izmir, açaí-related outbreaks). The key correction is reclassifying it from re-emergence to re-occurrence, because there is no evidence of parasite change—only meat-borne transmission via an already known route. Recommended: keep only if smaller foodborne clusters are desired for transmission-pattern illustration; otherwise mark for exclusion in a strictly “largest-impact outbreaks” list.
Review.Comment: We do not restrict to only top-10 events

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Countries: Brazil [2009] (São Paulo State; large industrial plant)
Host: Humans (industrial-plant employees consuming cafeteria meals)
Event.summary: In 2009, an industrial plant in São Paulo State with roughly 2,300 employees reported a cluster of workers with acute febrile illness compatible with toxoplasmosis. Investigation identified nine symptomatic and three asymptomatic employees with recent T. gondii infection (11 acute infections total) and used a case–control design to compare food and water exposures among 11 cases and 20 seronegative controls. Only consumption of green leafy vegetables from the factory cafeteria was significantly associated with illness, suggesting contamination of fresh produce by oocysts during production or handling. After reinforcing produce washing practices and reviewing supplier hygiene, no further clusters attributable to the cafeteria were observed.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Mass catering using raw green vegetables that had likely been contaminated with oocysts via irrigation water, soil, or handling, in the absence of adequate washing and sanitation procedures, allowed a small but clear foodborne outbreak in a large workforce. Internal mechanisms: Oocyst-borne transmission on fresh produce, highlighting an under-recognized food vehicle for toxoplasmosis; there is no evidence of a new genotype or altered virulence, so this is classified as re-occurrence driven by food-safety lapses.
Review: Review / likely exclude if restricting to top‑10 events. Corrections made: (i) clarified the year as 2009 (not “~2010”), in line with the primary case–control report and the CDC outbreak review; (ii) corrected the scale to 11 acute infections (rather than implying that “many” of the 2,300 workers became ill); and (iii) reclassified the event from re-emergence to re-occurrence, as the outbreak reflects a known route (oocyst-contaminated vegetables) without demonstrated parasite change. The outbreak is epidemiologically important for highlighting vegetable-borne transmission but is small in absolute impact relative to the major events now included.
Review.Comment: We do not restrict to only top-10 events

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Host: Humans (family and close contacts sharing a lamb meal)
Event.summary: In November 2010, public health authorities in Aveyron, southern France, investigated a cluster of acute toxoplasmosis among persons who had shared a family meal. Several attendees developed febrile lymphadenitis and serologic evidence of recent infection, and the common exposure identified was a single meal featuring undercooked lamb. No further spread beyond the exposed group occurred, and control actions focused on clinical follow-up—particularly of women of childbearing age—and reinforcing advice on thoroughly cooking lamb and other meats.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cultural preference for rare or undercooked lamb and entry of infected small-ruminant meat into the food chain, combined with a population in which baseline immunity to T. gondii may be declining. Internal mechanisms: Conventional meat-borne transmission via tissue cysts in lamb, with no evidence of a novel genotype or shift in virulence; appropriately classified as a localized re-occurrence driven by food-preparation practices.
Review: Review / likely exclude if restricting to top‑10 events. This small family/meal-associated outbreak is correctly located and classified and uses high-quality national surveillance and peer‑reviewed sources. However, the number of affected persons is low compared with large Brazilian and Asian outbreaks and even some medium-sized waterborne events; it is not among the ten largest post‑1990 events by case count or geographic scope. Recommended: retain only if the dataset aims to illustrate diverse meat-borne scenarios; otherwise mark for exclusion in a strictly impact-focused list.
Review.Comment: We do not restrict to only top-10 events

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Countries: Brazil [2011] (Rondônia State; Ji-Paraná, Ouro Preto do Oeste, Jaru)
Host: Humans (municipal residents consuming açaí juice)
Event.summary: In 2011, Brazil’s Ministry of Health investigated a large outbreak of acute toxoplasmosis in three municipalities of Rondônia State—Ji‑Paraná, Ouro Preto do Oeste, and Jaru—after numerous residents presented with febrile lymphadenopathy. The investigation documented at least 141 persons with clinical and serologic profiles compatible with recent T. gondii infection, making it one of the largest non‑waterborne outbreaks recorded. Epidemiologic analysis implicated consumption of açaí juice prepared from pulp acquired outside the local production season as the common exposure, suggesting contamination with oocysts during harvesting or processing in endemic forest areas. Public health responses included enhanced surveillance, guidance to açaí vendors on hygienic processing, and community education, after which new cases declined.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High consumption of raw açaí juice, sourcing of fruit from external producers during a period when local production was minimal, and insufficient sanitary controls in harvesting and pulping created conditions for contamination of açaí with T. gondii oocysts. Internal mechanisms: Typical oocyst-borne transmission via fruit beverages in a highly endemic Amazonian setting; no specific novel genotype was characterized in this investigation, so this event is considered a large-scale re-occurrence rather than confirmed re-emergence.
Review: Retain (added). This ≈141‑case multi-municipality outbreak linked to açaí consumption is described in detail in Brazilian public-health literature and highlighted in the CDC review as an example of large oocyst-borne outbreaks outside water systems. It was missing from the original dataset despite clearly ranking among the largest recent outbreaks by case count. Geography (South America | South America | Brazil, with Rondônia municipalities) and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate. Flagged for review primarily because detailed Ministry of Health bulletins were not directly accessed; if those are later obtained, case numbers and municipal breakdowns can be refined.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Countries: Brazil [2013] (Pará State; Ponta de Pedras, Marajó archipelago)
Host: Humans (municipality residents consuming açaí juice)
Event.summary: In May 2013, clinicians and the municipal health service in Ponta de Pedras, in Pará State’s Marajó archipelago, noted several patients with febrile lymphadenopathy whose serology indicated acute toxoplasmosis, raising suspicion of an outbreak. A field investigation evaluated 270 residents and identified 73 individuals with clinical and laboratory profiles consistent with recent T. gondii infection; geospatial analysis showed strong clustering around three main points of sale for açaí juice. Consumption of açaí was the only exposure strongly associated with illness, and contamination of the juice with oocysts during fruit handling and pulping was considered the most plausible source. After intensified hygiene measures at açaí production sites and public education, incident cases subsided.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional consumption of raw açaí juice, use of processing practices that allow contamination of fruit with oocysts from cats or wild felids, and high demand during a period when fruit may have been sourced from areas with intense environmental contamination. Internal mechanisms: Oocyst-borne transmission via açaí beverages, in line with an emerging pattern of Amazonian foodborne outbreaks; no confirmed novel genotype was reported in this specific outbreak, so it is treated as re-occurrence.
Review: Retain (added). This well-documented 73‑case outbreak, confirmed serologically and analyzed with geo-statistical methods, is explicitly featured in the CDC outbreak review as a representative example of açaí-associated toxoplasmosis. It clearly falls within the top tier of events by case count and public-health attention. Geography (Brazil, Pará, Marajó archipelago) and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate. Sources from the Pan-Amazonian Journal of Health and the CDC review are relevant and should be kept.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Countries: Brazil [2018] (Rio Grande do Sul State; Santa Maria)
Host: Humans (citywide population, including many pregnant women and newborns)
Event.summary: In early 2018, Santa Maria, a city in Rio Grande do Sul, experienced a rapidly growing number of residents with febrile illness, lymphadenopathy, and serologic evidence of acute toxoplasmosis. By mid‑2018, state and municipal bulletins reported over 800 laboratory-confirmed recent infections and more than a thousand notifications overall, with hundreds of suspected or confirmed gestational cases and numerous congenitally infected newborns; the event has been described as the largest recorded outbreak of human toxoplasmosis. Intensive investigation suggested contamination of widely consumed food or water, and multiple studies isolated and genotyped T. gondii from human placentas, amniotic fluid, and animal sources, identifying highly virulent strains associated with severe fetal outcomes. Public health actions included mandatory notification of gestational and congenital toxoplasmosis, expanded prenatal screening and treatment, targeted environmental and food investigations, and extensive risk-communication campaigns.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High background environmental contamination with oocysts, dense domestic cat populations, complex food supply chains, and previously incomplete prenatal screening programs, in combination with one or more contaminated citywide food or water vehicles, enabled extensive exposure of reproductive-age women and the general population. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of highly virulent, atypical T. gondii genotypes in southern Brazil, demonstrated by isolation and genetic characterization from placental tissue and other specimens, with strong association to severe congenital disease and fetal demise—an archetypal re-emergence episode driven by genotype and virulence in a large urban population.
Review: Retain. The Santa Maria outbreak is widely recognized as the largest documented human toxoplasmosis outbreak, with several hundred to >800 confirmed acute cases and major gestational and congenital impact, and is therefore unquestionably among the top events by impact. Classification as re-emergence is appropriate given repeated isolation of atypical, highly virulent genotypes from human placentas and strong associations with severe fetal disease. Geography and timelines are correct; additional Brazilian state and municipal bulletins have been implicitly incorporated to refine case numbers but not individually listed as URLs to avoid redundancy. No structural corrections beyond clarifying approximate confirmed case counts and emphasizing its scale were necessary.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Escherichia coli
Countries: United States of America [1992] (California, Idaho, Nevada, Washington)
Host: Humans (primarily children and young people consuming undercooked ground beef)
Event.summary: In late 1992 and early 1993, a multistate outbreak of Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli O157:H7 infections occurred among customers of the Jack in the Box fast-food chain in four western U.S. states, after contaminated ground beef hamburgers were undercooked and widely served. Publicity and active case finding identified about 732 illnesses, many with bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome, and four children died as the outbreak spread across the restaurant network. The outbreak ended after a large recall of beef lots, restaurant closures, and new cooking and inspection standards were implemented, and it catalyzed major reforms in U.S. meat safety regulation and E. coli surveillance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Industrially produced ground beef patties distributed across a large fast-food chain; inadequate cooking temperatures and food-safety controls; delayed recognition of STEC as a major foodborne threat. Internal mechanisms: no clearly novel genotype described, but the outbreak highlighted high virulence of E. coli O157:H7 and its propensity to cause HUS in children.
Review: retain – Outbreak is well documented as the 1992–1993 Jack in the Box multistate E. coli O157:H7 event (~732 cases, 4 deaths in WA, CA, ID, NV). Geography, timing, classification as a re‑occurrence (no new region or strain), and the chosen CDC/EID sources are appropriate, and this clearly ranks among the most impactful global STEC outbreaks. No changes made.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Escherichia coli
Countries: Japan [1996] (Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture; other clusters in Japan)
Host: Humans (schoolchildren and factory workers consuming contaminated radish sprouts and school lunches)
Event.summary: In summer 1996, Japan experienced a massive series of outbreaks of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7 infections, most prominently in Sakai City, Osaka, where contaminated white radish sprouts served in school lunches caused acute gastroenteritis in thousands of elementary school children and at least three deaths. Additional linked clusters, including an outbreak among factory workers in Kyoto, were traced to radish sprouts from the same grower, with an estimated total of around 8,000–10,000 associated cases nationally. The epidemic was controlled after withdrawal of implicated sprouts, suspension of school lunches, and strengthened hygiene and sprout-production controls.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Centralized preparation and distribution of school lunches; burgeoning sprout consumption; inadequate disinfection of seeds and sprout-growing water; possible contamination from livestock manure. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak involved highly virulent E. coli O157:H7 strains associated with a high risk of HUS but not clearly a new serotype; enhanced transmission was primarily due to food-distribution practices rather than a novel genotype.
Review: retain – Correctly captures the 1996 Sakai City and related Japanese O157:H7 outbreaks linked to radish sprouts, which remain the largest STEC O157 outbreaks ever recorded. Case numbers, setting (school lunches and factory cafeteria), geography (Japan/Eastern Asia), classification as re‑occurrence, and the technical sources used are appropriate. No structural changes needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Escherichia coli
Host: Humans (residents using contaminated municipal drinking water)
Event.summary: In May 2000, the municipal drinking water supply of Walkerton, Ontario became contaminated with Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Campylobacter jejuni after heavy rainfall washed cattle manure into inadequately chlorinated wells, leading to Canada’s worst recorded E. coli outbreak. Approximately 2,300 of the town’s 5,000 residents developed gastroenteritis, dozens developed hemolytic uremic syndrome, and six to seven deaths were ultimately attributed to the outbreak. Following identification of the contaminated wells, boil-water advisories, and a major overhaul of the town’s water management and provincial oversight, the outbreak subsided and triggered sweeping reviews of drinking-water safety across Canada.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Inadequate chlorination and monitoring of municipal groundwater; proximity of cattle operations and manure application to wellheads; heavy rainfall events facilitating fecal contamination of aquifers; weaknesses in regulatory oversight and reporting. Internal mechanisms: typical E. coli O157:H7 virulence profile with high potential for HUS; no specific novel genotype or resistance reported, so resurgence was driven primarily by infrastructure, environmental, and governance failures rather than microbial change.
Review: review – Major waterborne O157:H7/Campylobacter outbreak is accurately described and appropriately classified as a re‑occurrence in an already affected region. I removed a non-authoritative Reddit link from source_urls and retained official and investigative sources (Walkerton inquiry report, WHO, etc.). Otherwise, geography, timing and impact are correct and this remains one of the most consequential STEC outbreaks globally.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Escherichia coli
Host: Humans (patrons of a buffet-style restaurant consuming multiple contaminated foods)
Event.summary: In August 2008, public health officials in northeastern Oklahoma identified an unusual cluster of bloody diarrhoea and hemolytic uremic syndrome in patrons of the Country Cottage buffet restaurant in Locust Grove and confirmed Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli O111:NM infection. Active case finding documented about 341 outbreak-related illnesses, more than 70 hospitalizations, 26 HUS cases and one death, making this the largest recorded STEC O111 outbreak in the United States and a key event in recognizing the severity of non-O157 STEC. The outbreak subsided after the restaurant voluntarily closed, environmental and food investigations were conducted, and guidance and surveillance for non-O157 STEC were strengthened, although a single contaminated food vehicle was never definitively identified.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Buffet-style restaurant service with many shared, ready-to-eat dishes; probable cross-contamination of multiple foods and food-contact surfaces; delayed routine testing and recognition of non-O157 STEC; and heavy customer traffic from a wide catchment area. Internal mechanisms: infection with a virulent STEC O111:NM strain capable of causing HUS in adults and children but not clearly a novel genotype; the magnitude and severity mainly reflected amplification of an established non-O157 STEC serogroup in a high-risk food-service setting.
Review: retain – Newly added high-impact event: the 2008 Oklahoma STEC O111:NM outbreak associated with the Country Cottage restaurant (~341 illnesses, >70 hospitalizations, 26 HUS cases, 1 death), which is consistently described as the largest documented non‑O157 STEC outbreak in the U.S. Classification as a major re‑occurrence (non‑O157 STEC already present in North America) is appropriate; geography, timing and burden are supported by state health department reports and peer‑reviewed analyses.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: West Nile virus
Countries: Russian Federation [1999] (Volgograd Oblast; Astrakhan Oblast; Rostov Oblast)
Host: Humans (primarily adults in urban and rural communities of Volgograd, Astrakhan and Rostov regions)
Event.summary: During the summer of 1999, a large outbreak of West Nile fever and neuroinvasive disease occurred in southern European Russia, centered on the Volgograd Region with extension into neighboring Astrakhan and Rostov oblasts. From late July to early October, several hundred clinically compatible human cases were hospitalized (estimates around 800), including 84 meningoencephalitis cases with about 40 deaths, making this one of the largest recognized West Nile outbreaks in Europe and the Mediterranean to that time. Human transmission declined with the onset of cooler weather and intensified mosquito control, but subsequent surveillance documented continued endemic WNV circulation and recurrent seasonal cases in these regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: hot summer conditions along the lower Volga, extensive floodplains and irrigation systems, and high densities of Culex pipiens and related mosquito vectors feeding on local and migratory birds created favorable conditions for intense amplification; low population immunity after a long inter‑epidemic period increased the pool of susceptible adults. Internal mechanisms: outbreak viruses belonged to WNV lineage 1 and were closely related to strains circulating in Romania and the eastern Mediterranean, without strong evidence of a novel, more virulent genotype; the event is therefore best interpreted as a major re-occurrence in an already endemic region driven mainly by climatic and ecological factors rather than by documented viral innovation.
Review: review: New event added for the 1999 Volgograd–Astrakhan–Rostov outbreak in the Russian Federation, which multiple reviews and WHO documents identify as one of the largest global West Nile outbreaks (hundreds of cases and ~40 deaths). Classified as re-occurrence in Eastern Europe (no new continent or clearly novel lineage), with timing and geography aligned to primary outbreak reports; recommended to retain as a major event.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Deltainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza D virus
Countries: Italy [2005] (regions of Tuscany and Apulia; general adult population, archived sera)
Host: Humans (general adult population – residual serum samples from Tuscany and Apulia)
Event.summary: From 2005 through 2017, random adult serum samples from Tuscany and Apulia contained IDV‑specific antibodies every year, with low baseline seroprevalence (~5–10%) in 2005–2007 rising sharply to 30–45% in 2008–2010 and again in 2013–2014 and 2016, indicating substantial and recurrent human exposure well before and after the formal discovery of IDV in swine. Seroprevalence peaks closely followed documented IDV outbreaks in cattle and pigs in Italy and neighboring countries, suggesting repeated spillover waves rather than sustained human‑to‑human transmission. By 2017, seroprevalence had fallen from peak levels but remained above the 2005 baseline, implying ongoing low‑level zoonotic exposure without any recognized, IDV‑attributable human epidemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and geographic expansion of cattle and swine production in northern and southern Italy, frequent animal movements, and bovine respiratory disease outbreaks created sustained opportunities for zoonotic exposure at the human–livestock interface; human antibody peaks lagged behind livestock epidemics by roughly one year, consistent with spillover driven by animal infection dynamics. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – co‑circulation of multiple antigenic lineages (e.g. D/OK‑like and D/660‑like viruses) in European cattle; Host Expansion (Spillover) – repeated infections of nearby humans; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – efficient replication of IDV in human airway epithelial cells and in ferret respiratory tracts suggests high compatibility with mammalian airways even though sustained human transmission has not yet been demonstrated.
Review: Review – Reclassified this Italian multi‑year episode as the earliest robust human evidence of IDV (first_detection = Yes) and extended the time span from 2005–2014 to 2005–2017 to match the underlying serosurvey. Removed previous labels of inter‑continental emergence and re‑emergence, which were inconsistent with it being the global first detection and with limited evidence for virus‑intrinsic change in this period. This event now anchors the top‑level first_emergence_time/place fields and should be re‑checked by a subject‑matter expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Deltainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza D virus
Countries: United States of America [2016] (north‑central Florida; cattle‑exposed adults and non‑exposed controls)
Host: Humans (adult dairy and beef cattle workers; small comparison group of non‑cattle‑exposed adults)
Event.summary: In a cross‑sectional serologic study published in 2016, serum from 35 cattle‑exposed adults and 11 non‑exposed adults in north‑central Florida was tested for IDV antibodies, revealing extremely high seroprevalence among cattle workers (91% by HI and 97% by microneutralization) and much lower seropositivity (18%) among controls, consistent with intense occupational exposure. The study was motivated by growing evidence of widespread IDV circulation in U.S. cattle and the earlier 1.3% seroprevalence estimate in the general population, and it demonstrated that frequent, mostly subclinical infections were occurring in a well‑defined worker population. The episode ended without identification of any IDV‑specific clinical outbreak, but it established cattle workers as a key risk group and prompted calls for more systematic occupational surveillance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large‑scale dairy and beef operations in Florida with high animal densities, prolonged close human–cattle contact, and minimal respiratory protection created repeated opportunities for IDV exposure; the absence of targeted occupational surveillance before IDV’s discovery meant such infections went unrecognized. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – repeated zoonotic infections of cattle workers, as indicated by near‑universal neutralizing antibodies; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – established IDV lineages circulating in U.S. cattle herds by the mid‑2010s, maintaining a high environmental viral load in workplace settings.
Review: Review – Corrected the event type from re_emergence to re_occurrence because this represents resurgence of infection in the same sub‑region (Northern America) linked to occupational exposure and livestock management, without clear evidence of major viral genetic change. Adjusted the year from 2011–2012 to a single year (2016) aligned with the publication and contemporaneous cattle data, noting that the exact sampling year is not reported and should be verified in the full article. Countries/sub‑regions remain accurate (Florida, United States; Northern America).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Deltainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza D virus
Countries: Malaysia [2017] (Sarawak – Sibu and Kapit divisions; swine farms, abattoirs and live‑animal markets)
Host: Humans (swine farm, abattoir and live‑animal market workers; at least one worker with IDV‑positive nasal wash)
Event.summary: During June–July 2017, a One Health surveillance study at the human–pig interface in Sarawak, Malaysia, collected nasal washes from 78 workers at pig farms, abattoirs and live‑animal markets, alongside animal and environmental samples. Among these workers, influenza D virus RNA was detected by rRT‑PCR in one nasal wash (1.3%), alongside detections of other respiratory and enteric swine viruses, providing the first molecular evidence of IDV infection in a human in Asia. No symptomatic outbreak was associated with this isolated detection, and follow‑up sampling was not performed, so the episode is interpreted as a sporadic zoonotic spillover event documenting that IDV can infect swine‑exposed workers in South‑eastern Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense pig production in Sarawak, frequent close contact between humans and pigs in farms, abattoirs and wet markets, and limited consistent use of respiratory personal protective equipment facilitated occasional aerosol or contact exposure to multiple swine viruses, including IDV. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – zoonotic transmission from infected pigs or contaminated aerosols to at least one human worker; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – IDV’s ability to persist in bioaerosols and infect diverse mammalian hosts, together with experimental evidence of efficient replication in human airway cells and ferrets, underpins concern that such sporadic infections might presage broader adaptation.
Review: Review – Added this previously omitted event to capture the first molecular (PCR) detection of IDV in a human in Asia, as reported from Sarawak, Malaysia, in 2017; classified it as an inter‑continental emergence because it represents the earliest documented occurrence of human IDV infection on the Asian continent. Countries and sub‑region (Malaysia; South‑eastern Asia) were derived from the study sites (Sibu and Kapit). This event should be retained but flagged for expert review regarding its relative importance versus larger Asian seroprevalence studies.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Deltainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza D virus
Countries: United States of America [2019] (Western and Southwestern United States; five large‑herd dairy operations)
Host: Humans (dairy cattle workers in large‑herd operations; nearby community members involved in related surveillance)
Event.summary: Between May 2019 and January 2020, a NIOSH‑funded prospective study followed 31 workers at five large‑herd dairy operations in two U.S. states, collecting paired pre‑ and post‑shift nasal washes and personal bioaerosol samples over one to five consecutive workdays. IDV RNA was detected in nasal washes from 21 workers (67.7%) at least once and in 29.3% of all nasal‑wash specimens, with transient carriage patterns and no clear association with respiratory symptoms, demonstrating frequent, mostly asymptomatic nasal carriage of IDV among dairy workers across multiple facilities. The episode concluded without evidence of sustained human‑to‑human transmission, but it confirmed chronic occupational exposure and helped frame IDV as an under‑recognized hazard in industrial dairy environments.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Industrialization of U.S. dairy production with very large herds, high animal stocking densities, and open facilities that facilitate aerosolized virus exposure; lack of IDV‑specific surveillance before this study meant that such exposures were previously invisible; targeted occupational health research and molecular diagnostics enabled detection of transient infections. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – repeated infection of cattle workers as incidental hosts; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – IDV’s ability to persist in aerosols and efficiently infect mammalian airways, including humans and ferrets, supports frequent acquisition and short‑term carriage; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – widespread circulation of multiple IDV lineages in U.S. cattle herds maintained a high force of infection at the human–animal interface.
Review: Review – Corrected the event years from 2018–2021 to 2019–2020 based on the study’s recruitment period (May 2019–January 2020) and removed an unrelated NIOSH annual report (cdc/101894) from the event‑level sources. Reclassified the event from re_emergence to re_occurrence because it represents repeated exposure and transient infection in the same sub‑region, driven by dairy production practices, without clear evidence of novel viral genotypes emerging in this setting. Countries and sub‑region (United States; Northern America) remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Deltainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza D virus
Countries: China [2020] (Northeast China – urban and rural general population; outpatients with acute respiratory symptoms)
Host: Humans (general population in Northeast China; individuals with acute respiratory symptoms; subset with agricultural or animal‑contact backgrounds)
Event.summary: Serologic surveillance in Northeast China using sera collected between 2020 and 2024 found very high IDV seropositivity in the general population (73.37%, 449/612) and even higher rates among patients with respiratory symptoms (96.67%, 58/60), while experimental infection studies showed that a contemporary cattle‑derived strain (D/HY11) replicated efficiently and transmitted via airborne routes between ferrets. These findings, combined with nationwide surveys showing IDV RNA in cattle across at least 13 of 16 sampled provinces and >90% IDV seroprevalence in cattle, indicate that IDV lineages, particularly those related to the D/Yama2019 lineage, are now widely established in Chinese livestock and have spilled over extensively into humans in Northeast China. By 2024, IDV exposure in this region appeared widespread and largely silent, without a clearly defined large clinical outbreak but with serologic and experimental evidence suggesting that some strains may have acquired the capacity for efficient mammal‑to‑mammal, and potentially human‑to‑human, transmission.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High national IDV prevalence in cattle and documented circulation of multiple lineages (including D/Yama2019‑like and D/660‑like viruses) across at least 16 provinces, long‑distance movement and trade of cattle, and dense human–animal interfaces in Northeast China created persistent opportunities for zoonotic exposure; increased research interest after isolation of live IDV from Chinese cattle prompted focused human serosurveys. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – characterization of the D/HY11 strain with enhanced polymerase activity and association with the D/Yama2019 lineage; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – experimental demonstration of efficient airborne transmission of D/HY11 between ferrets, together with very high human antibody titers, suggests improved adaptation for mammalian respiratory spread; Host Expansion (Spillover) – extensive serologic evidence of infection in both rural and urban residents with and without direct cattle contact; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – establishment and diversification of IDV lineages throughout East Asia underpins the broad geographic extent of human exposure documented in this episode.
Review: Review – Reclassified this event from inter_continental_emergence to intra_continental_emergence plus re_emergence because IDV had already been detected in a human in Asia (Malaysia, 2017) and because the Northeast China findings reflect spread into a new Asian sub‑region (Eastern Asia) combined with evidence of a newly dominant lineage (D/Yama2019‑like, including D/HY11) with enhanced airborne transmissibility in ferrets. Confirmed the 2020–2024 serologic surveillance window from the article abstract and related news coverage. Countries and sub‑region (China; Eastern Asia) are correct, but the contribution of human‑to‑human versus repeated animal‑to‑human transmission remains uncertain and should be interpreted cautiously.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Host: Humans exposed through handling and consuming meat from infected livestock (pastoralist communities)
Event.summary: In 2000, a large anthrax outbreak occurred among pastoralist communities in Ethiopia’s Afar Region after livestock died suddenly and were slaughtered or consumed, leading to hundreds of suspected human cases, many with gastrointestinal and cutaneous disease. The outbreak expanded rapidly in communities with close contact to sick animals and carcasses, reflecting high livestock incidence and limited veterinary control. The episode subsided after recognition of the problem, cessation of consumption of suspect meat, and local public‑health and veterinary response, but anthrax remained endemic in the area.([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK310487/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Endemic environmental foci of B. anthracis spores in grazing areas; high livestock burden and lack of routine vaccination; food insecurity and cultural practices of butchering and consuming animals that die suddenly; limited access to veterinary and human health services.
Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a novel strain; outbreak represents high exposure to existing environmental strains rather than genetic change.
Review: retain – Large suspected human anthrax outbreak in Afar Region with hundreds of cases and fatalities is well documented by WHO and later Ethiopian One Health analyses; classification as re‑occurrence (endemic anthrax with heightened exposure) and Africa/Eastern Africa/Ethiopia geography are correct, so no structural changes were made to this row.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11020881/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Countries: Zambia [2011] (Chama District, Luangwa Valley game management area along the South Luangwa River)
Host: Humans in rural communities exposed by butchering, carrying, preparing and consuming meat from hippopotamuses and other wildlife that died of anthrax
Event.summary: In August–September 2011, a major anthrax outbreak occurred among rural communities in the Chama District of northeastern Zambia after at least 81–85 hippopotamuses in a South Luangwa River game management area died of suspected anthrax and were butchered for food, resulting in approximately 511–521 suspected human cases and 5 deaths. Most patients developed cutaneous lesions, sometimes with gastrointestinal symptoms, after handling or eating meat from dead hippopotamuses, with illness concentrated in households experiencing chronic food shortages despite public‑health warnings to avoid the carcasses. Joint investigations by Zambian health authorities and international partners, coupled with health education, restriction of access to carcasses and antibiotic treatment of cases, were followed by a decline in new illnesses as contaminated meat sources were exhausted and the outbreak subsided.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/9/16-1597_article))
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Severe drought and delayed rainy season in 2011 leading to crop failure, food insecurity and reliance on bushmeat; mass mortality of hippopotamuses from anthrax in a game management area with limited carcass disposal; close proximity of wildlife carcasses to villages, combined with poverty and limited veterinary and public‑health infrastructure.
Internal mechanisms: Reactivation of endemic environmental foci of B. anthracis in the Luangwa Valley; available data do not indicate a novel genotype—human infections reflected intense exposure to spores from infected wildlife rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – Newly added event. The 2011 Luangwa Valley/Chama District outbreak in Zambia, with ≈511–521 suspected human cases and 5 deaths linked to mass hippopotamus mortality, is one of the largest well‑documented human anthrax outbreaks post‑1990 and was missing from the original dataset. It is correctly placed in Eastern Africa (Zambia) and coded as re‑occurrence from an endemic wildlife focus driven by drought and food insecurity; sources include detailed EID field investigation and supporting veterinary/clinical reports.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/23/9/16-1597_article))

EPP.scientific.name: Bacillus anthracis
EPP.common.name: anthrax bacterium
Countries: Russian Federation [2016] (Yamal‑Nenets Autonomous Okrug, Yamal Peninsula)
Host: Humans (Nenets reindeer herders and local residents) exposed through contact with or consumption of infected reindeer and environmental contamination
Event.summary: In July–August 2016, a major anthrax epizootic occurred in reindeer on the Yamal Peninsula in northwest Siberia, killing over 2,300–2,650 animals and leading to approximately 36 confirmed human cases and at least one child’s death among Nenets herders. Human cases arose after close contact with sick or dead reindeer and possibly consumption of contaminated meat, with dozens of people hospitalized and large numbers evacuated or quarantined. Emergency mass vaccination of reindeer, large‑scale culling, carcass disposal and decontamination of burial sites, along with medical treatment and prophylaxis for exposed people, curtailed the outbreak by late summer, though it highlighted the potential for climate‑driven re‑activation of old anthrax foci in permafrost regions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8264129/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Unusually warm summer temperatures and permafrost thaw that likely exposed historic anthrax burial sites or carcasses, releasing long‑dormant spores; dense reindeer herds and traditional herding practices that facilitated rapid animal‑to‑animal and animal‑to‑human exposure; remoteness of the region complicating rapid veterinary and medical response.
Internal mechanisms: Resurgence from long‑term environmental spore survival rather than a novel genotype; the key mechanism is climatic/environmental change enabling geographic range re‑expansion from old foci (geographic range expansion inherent to existing strains).
Review: retain – 2016 Yamal Peninsula outbreak (≈2,650 infected reindeer with ~2,350 deaths and 36 human cases, one fatal) is correctly located in Eastern Europe (Russian Federation) and coded as re‑occurrence driven by permafrost thaw and a lapse in reindeer vaccination; there is no evidence of a novel strain, so re‑emergence remains No. Event summary and mechanisms are consistent with detailed veterinary and climatic analyses of the outbreak.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8264129/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Lyssavirus rabies
EPP.common.name: Rabies virus
Countries: Peru [1990] (Amazonian departments, especially Loreto; multiple remote riverine and indigenous communities)
Host: Humans (bitten by common vampire bats, Desmodus rotundus)
Event.summary: From 1990 through about 2010, remote communities in the Peruvian Amazon experienced recurrent vampire bat–mediated human rabies outbreaks. An early outbreak in two jungle villages in 1990 caused roughly 29 fatal human cases following bat bites, and further clusters were reported in Loreto and neighboring departments in the mid‑1990s and 2000s. Between 1996 and 2010, around four‑fifths of Peru’s reported human rabies cases were attributed to vampire bat exposure, prompting repeated emergency vaccination campaigns, intensified surveillance and health education that reduced, but did not eliminate, these outbreaks in vulnerable riverine and indigenous populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Deforestation, settlement expansion and livestock introduction in the Amazon increased contact between humans, domestic animals and vampire bats; many affected communities had open-walled housing that allowed bats to feed on sleeping people, very limited access to health facilities and post‑exposure prophylaxis (PEP), and low awareness that small bat bites could be fatal. Internal mechanisms: Maintenance of rabies virus in dense Desmodus rotundus colonies with periodic spillover into humans; available data show bat-associated variants typical for the region without evidence of a novel lineage or changed virulence, so the episode is best characterized as a re‑occurrence driven by ecological and health‑system factors rather than viral evolution.
Review: Review – Retained as a major bat‑mediated human rabies episode, but corrected: (i) event period extended from 1995–2010 to 1990–2010 to include the well-documented 1990 outbreak with ~29 deaths in two Amazonian villages, and countries field updated to Peru [1990]; (ii) type reclassified from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence, because sources describe repeated spillover of long‑established vampire‑bat rabies variants driven by ecological and health‑system changes, without evidence of a novel strain or virus‑level host adaptation. Generic Wikipedia citation removed at event level in favor of primary epidemiologic reports; recommend expert review of final wording but clear basis to keep this as one of the largest post‑1990 human rabies emergence episodes in South America.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lyssavirus rabies
EPP.common.name: Rabies virus
Countries: Indonesia [1997] (initially Flores Island in East Nusa Tenggara, later spread to other islands including Lembata and Ambon/ Maluku)
Host: Humans (exposed via domestic dogs in previously rabies‑free island populations)
Event.summary: In 1997, dog-mediated rabies was introduced for the first time into previously rabies‑free Flores Island (East Nusa Tenggara), likely via an infected dog imported by boat from Sulawesi, with the first human rabies death recorded in March 1998. Over 1998–2002, a severe island-wide epidemic spread across Flores and neighboring islands such as Lembata, causing at least 113 human deaths on Flores alone and thousands of canine cases, while control efforts relied on dog culling and patchy vaccination in resource‑limited settings. By 2003, related canine rabies virus lineages had been introduced into other eastern Indonesian islands, including Ambon in Maluku where more than 20 additional human rabies deaths were recorded, before intensified mass dog vaccination and strengthened surveillance gradually reduced, but did not eliminate, rabies across East Nusa Tenggara.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Human-mediated movement of infected dogs by boat from endemic Sulawesi into naïve island dog populations; large numbers of free‑roaming owned and community dogs that play important cultural and economic roles; shortage of trained vaccinators and limited cold‑chain; initial reliance on culling rather than systematic mass vaccination; low awareness of rabies risk and constrained access to timely PEP for bite victims. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of existing canine rabies virus lineages from mainland/large islands into new islands; molecular studies link Flores and Ambon viruses to Sulawesi origins, with no evidence of markedly increased virulence – high human impact primarily reflects intense dog–human contact in wholly susceptible island communities.
Review: Review – New event added to capture a major emergence episode omitted from the original profile: the introduction and explosive spread of dog-mediated rabies on previously rabies‑free Flores and neighboring eastern Indonesian islands, causing ≥113 human deaths on Flores alone and >20 on Ambon, with about 216 human deaths reported in East Nusa Tenggara from 1997–2011. Sources consistently describe introduction from Sulawesi and subsequent multi‑year island epidemics, making this clearly one of the largest post‑1990 human rabies events. Classified as re‑occurrence in South‑eastern Asia (rabies long present in the sub‑region) rather than intra‑continental emergence, because the UNSD sub‑region is unchanged; recommended for retention but flagged for expert review of exact temporal bounds (1997–2003 used here to cover the main epidemic phase).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lyssavirus rabies
EPP.common.name: Rabies virus
Countries: Brazil [2004] (remote rural municipalities in Pará and Maranhão states, including Portel, Viseu, Augusto Corrêa and affected communities in Maranhão)
Host: Humans (bitten by vampire bats, mainly Desmodus rotundus)
Event.summary: In 2004–2005, northern Brazil experienced large clusters of bat-transmitted human rabies in remote Amazonian and coastal communities. In 2004, 21 persons died of paralytic rabies in Portel and Viseu municipalities in Pará State after nocturnal vampire bat attacks, and in 2005 a further series of outbreaks caused at least 41 additional human cases in Augusto Corrêa (Pará) and several municipalities in neighboring Maranhão State. These events, representing most of the bat-transmitted human rabies cases reported in Latin America during this period, prompted emergency mass vaccination of exposed populations, intensified livestock vaccination and bat control, and detailed virologic investigations that confirmed Desmodus rotundus–associated rabies virus variants as the cause.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Poor, sparsely served rural communities with open or partially enclosed houses that facilitated nightly bat feeding on humans; expansion of cattle ranching and land‑use change creating abundant food sources for vampire bats; limited access to prompt human PEP and weak routine surveillance, so outbreaks were recognized only after multiple deaths. Internal mechanisms: Maintenance of established D. rotundus rabies virus variants in bat colonies with high bite rates on humans and livestock; antigenic and phylogenetic analyses show these strains cluster with typical vampire bat variants rather than representing a novel lineage, so the episode is best characterized as a major re‑occurrence of bat‑mediated rabies in humans driven by ecological and health‑system factors.
Review: Review – New event added to address a conspicuous omission: the well-documented bat‑transmitted human rabies outbreaks in Pará and Maranhão, Brazil, in 2004–2005, which caused 21 deaths in Portel and Viseu in 2004 and contributed to at least 62 human cases linked to vampire bats in Brazil over 2004–2005. Multiple peer‑reviewed sources agree on the magnitude and bat origin of these outbreaks, and they are widely cited as emblematic of emerging vampire bat–mediated rabies in Latin America. Classified as re‑occurrence in South America, since rabies was long present in the region; recommended for retention as one of the largest modern human rabies emergence episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lyssavirus rabies
EPP.common.name: Rabies virus
Countries: China [2004] (notably spread from long‑affected southern provinces into central and northern provinces including Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Beijing)
Host: Humans (exposed primarily via domestic dogs)
Event.summary: From about 2004 onward, human rabies in China showed marked spatial expansion from historically high‑incidence southern provinces into central and northern provinces that had previously reported few or no cases, even as national totals peaked in 2006–2007. New foci of human cases appeared in northern provinces such as Shanxi, Inner Mongolia and Beijing, where relative increases in reported incidence were large despite lower absolute case numbers compared with the south. After 2008, enhanced control efforts and dog vaccination reduced incidence in most southern hotspots, but several of the newer northern foci continued to report sustained or increasing human rabies for several years before gradually declining.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of infected dogs and humans along expanding road and transport networks; urbanization and peri‑urban sprawl creating new interfaces between rural dog populations and previously low‑exposure human communities; uneven implementation of dog vaccination and stray dog control; limited bite management and PEP capacity in newly affected northern provinces. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of established dog‑mediated rabies virus lineages into climatically and ecologically suitable but previously low‑incidence areas, facilitated by dog movement and demographic turnover rather than major viral genetic change; local effective reproductive numbers rose where dog vaccination coverage remained low and dog densities high.
Review: Review – Retained as a distinct event describing the documented south‑to‑north geographic expansion of China’s epidemic, but corrected a misclassification: intra‑continental emergence has been set to No because the spread occurred entirely within the same UNSD sub‑region (Eastern Asia) and within a single country, which the protocol states should not be coded as intra‑continental emergence. Re‑occurrence remains Yes to capture the resurgence and spatial spread of established dog‑mediated rabies lineages. Consider merging analytically with the 1996–2007 China epidemic wave if future work aims to minimize splitting of closely linked episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lyssavirus rabies
EPP.common.name: Rabies virus
Countries: Viet Nam [2006] (central coastal provinces; case series includes fatal cases from Khanh Hoa and neighboring provinces)
Host: Humans (primarily dog‑mediated exposure)
Event.summary: In the mid‑2000s, central coastal Viet Nam experienced an increase in reported human rabies deaths compared with the early 2000s, with national surveillance indicating that fatal human cases in several coastal provinces rose roughly 1.5–2‑fold in 2006–2007. By 2008, a documented case series from one central coastal referral hospital described 12 laboratory‑ or clinically confirmed fatal rabies patients over a relatively short period, highlighting a localized resurgence in an area with under‑recognized endemic dog rabies. Strengthening of public health messaging, dog vaccination and access to PEP in the affected provinces contributed to reduced human case numbers after this localized peak, even though dog‑mediated rabies remained endemic nationally.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of free‑roaming and poorly vaccinated dogs in central coastal provinces; low awareness of the need for immediate wound washing and timely, complete PEP after dog bites; financial and geographic barriers to completing full PEP regimens; under‑resourced rabies surveillance prior to the mid‑2000s leading to delayed recognition of rising incidence. Internal mechanisms: Resurgence of established dog‑mediated rabies virus lineages rather than emergence of a novel variant; available evidence does not implicate increased virulence, with risk driven mainly by higher exposure pressure and incomplete prophylaxis coverage.
Review: Review – Event corresponds to a documented, though relatively localized, increase in human rabies deaths in Viet Nam’s central coastal region around 2006–2008, supported by a detailed case series and regional reviews. Geographic coding (Asia/South‑eastern Asia; Viet Nam) and classification as re‑occurrence without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence are appropriate, because canine rabies had long been endemic in the country. The absolute number of deaths is modest compared with other episodes in this profile; compilers may choose to retain this as an illustrative localized resurgence or exclude it if a stricter “top 10 by global impact” filter is enforced. Flagged for review on those grounds, but no factual corrections were required.
Review.Comment: Not top 10

EPP.scientific.name: Lyssavirus rabies
EPP.common.name: Rabies virus
Host: Humans (exposed via domestic dogs; limited role of other mammals)
Event.summary: In late 2008, Bali, previously considered free of dog‑mediated rabies, detected its first human rabies fatality after rabid dogs were introduced from other Indonesian islands, marking the start of a large island‑wide epidemic in dogs and humans. Through 2009–2010, dog rabies spread rapidly from initial foci in the Bukit Peninsula and Denpasar to all nine regencies, and human deaths accumulated, with about 90–100 recorded fatalities in the first three years and more than 150 deaths reported by the mid‑2010s. Beginning in late 2010 and 2011, intensive island‑wide mass dog vaccination campaigns, improved dog population management and expanded access to human PEP sharply reduced human rabies deaths, although canine rabies became endemic and sporadic human cases have continued beyond 2011.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of an infected dog (likely via fishermen or informal inter‑island dog movements from endemic provinces such as Sulawesi or Flores) into a naïve island dog population; very high densities of free‑roaming owned and community dogs closely associated with humans; initial control measures that relied heavily on localized culling and incomplete vaccination, with limited early public awareness and delayed access to PEP for many bite victims; strong tourism-related concerns once the outbreak became widely known. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of an established Indonesian dog‑mediated rabies virus lineage into a previously rabies‑free island; phylogenetic work supports one main introduction followed by rapid local spread rather than evolution of a novel viral strain. Enhanced transmission reflects demographic and behavioral factors (large susceptible dog population, free roaming, high dog–human contact) rather than demonstrable increases in viral virulence.
Review: Review – Retained as a key emergence episode but corrected the type-of-emergence coding: intra‑continental emergence has been set to No and re‑occurrence to Yes, because dog-mediated rabies was long established elsewhere in South‑eastern Asia and the event represents introduction into a previously rabies‑free island within the same UNSD sub‑region, not first confirmation of the virus in a new sub‑region or continent. Sources from WHO, FAO, and peer‑reviewed studies consistently describe Bali as historically rabies‑free until 2008 and report ≥150 human deaths over the first several years, confirming that this remains one of the most impactful modern human rabies events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lyssavirus rabies
EPP.common.name: Rabies virus
Countries: Indonesia [2015] (West Kalimantan province; multiple affected regencies including Kapuas Hulu, Kubu Raya, Mempawah, North Kayong and others)
Host: Humans (exposed via domestic and free‑roaming dogs)
Event.summary: From about 2015 onward, West Kalimantan province on the Indonesian portion of Borneo experienced a substantial dog‑mediated rabies outbreak affecting multiple regencies that had previously reported little or no recent human rabies. Provincial authorities reported increasing numbers of canine and human cases across at least eight regencies, with local media and official summaries indicating that around 21 people had died of rabies by mid‑2017. The outbreak spurred emergency vaccination of dogs, public education campaigns and increased allocation of national funds for rabies control, but persistent transmission in dogs and ongoing human exposures kept the province on high alert and created a risk of cross‑border spread to neighboring Sarawak in Malaysia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Low baseline dog vaccination coverage (reported at roughly half the dog population), substantial numbers of free‑roaming owned and stray dogs, unregulated dog trade between regencies, and limited awareness and PEP access in rural communities contributed to rapid amplification once rabies was introduced or re‑introduced. Internal mechanisms: Expansion and re‑establishment of existing canine rabies virus lineages within West Kalimantan; available information points to human-mediated dog movements, rather than viral change, as the key factor in spread. The outbreak is epidemiologically linked to subsequent rabies emergence across the border in Sarawak but itself represents a re‑occurrence in a sub‑region where canine rabies was already recognized.
Review: Review – New event added to reflect a sizable and epidemiologically important dog‑mediated rabies outbreak in West Kalimantan that was not captured in the original profile but is cited as the likely source of the subsequent Sarawak outbreak. Available governmental and media sources report at least 21 human deaths in the province since 2015 and extensive canine transmission. Classified conservatively as re‑occurrence in South‑eastern Asia (rabies long present regionally) rather than intra‑continental emergence, because it does not involve a new UNSD sub‑region or continent. Evidence base relies partly on grey literature and secondary summaries, so this row is flagged for expert review of dates and death counts, but inclusion is warranted given its scale and its role in cross‑border spread.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lyssavirus rabies
EPP.common.name: Rabies virus
Countries: Malaysia [2017] (Sarawak state; divisions including Serian, Kuching, Sibu, Betong, Kapit, Samarahan, Sarikei, Sri Aman and Miri)
Host: Humans (exposed via domestic and stray dogs)
Event.summary: In July 2017, Sarawak state in Malaysia reported its first locally acquired human rabies deaths in nearly two decades, following introduction of canine rabies from neighboring West Kalimantan in Indonesia, and a state‑wide rabies outbreak was declared. Over the next several years, rabies spread from initial foci in Serian Division to most of Sarawak’s divisions, with 49 confirmed human cases and 44 deaths recorded by December 2022, alongside widespread infection in dogs. The state and federal governments mounted large‑scale responses, including declaration of a Level‑2 disaster, mass dog vaccination campaigns, movement controls and culling of stray dogs, establishment of bite clinics and expanded PEP provision, as well as creation of an immune belt along the border with Indonesia, which progressively reduced but has not yet eliminated human rabies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement of infected dogs from West Kalimantan into a state that had been free of dog-mediated human rabies for many years; substantial numbers of unvaccinated owned and free‑roaming dogs; delayed presentation of bite victims to health services despite intensive public messaging; and limited initial capacity for rapid diagnosis and coordinated One Health response. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and re‑establishment of existing canine rabies virus lineages on Borneo; molecular and epidemiologic data implicate origin from Indonesian foci rather than a novel variant. The episode is therefore best characterized as a major re‑occurrence of canine and human rabies in South‑eastern Asia, not an inter‑continental emergence.
Review: Review – New event added to represent the large, well‑documented rabies outbreak in Sarawak, Malaysia, from 2017 onwards, during which 49 human cases and 44 deaths were reported by late 2022 after decades without locally acquired human rabies. This outbreak is widely recognized in national and international reports and is epidemiologically linked to incursions from West Kalimantan. Classified as re‑occurrence (rabies long endemic in South‑eastern Asia) and not inter‑continental emergence, consistent with the protocol that imported or cross‑border spread within a continent should not be coded as inter‑continental. Recommended for retention as one of the most consequential recent human rabies emergence events and for detailed expert review of evolving case counts beyond 2022.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Acinetobacter baumannii
EPP.common.name: Acinetobacter baumannii infection
Countries: United States of America [1999] (citywide outbreak across 15 hospitals in Brooklyn, New York)
Host: Humans (hospitalized patients, predominantly ICU, with nosocomial A. baumannii infection or colonization)

EPP.scientific.name: Naegleria fowleri
EPP.common.name: primary amebic meningoencephalitis
Countries: Guadeloupe [2008] (Dolé geothermal baths, French West Indies)
Host: Humans (9‑year‑old child bathing and diving in geothermal pool)
Event.summary: In 2008, a previously healthy 9‑year‑old boy in Guadeloupe, French West Indies, developed rapidly fatal primary amebic meningoencephalitis after swimming and diving in a popular geothermal bath at Dolé; laboratory testing confirmed Naegleria fowleri infection. The case represented both the first documented PAM case in Guadeloupe and the first recognized N. fowleri–associated death in the Caribbean subregion of the Americas, prompting concern about geothermal recreational waters as a new regional risk setting. Subsequent surveys of geothermal baths in Guadeloupe repeatedly detected N. fowleri and led to implementation of regular monitoring, risk communication, and engineering controls, after which no further large clusters were reported, though sporadic risk persists.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of untreated or minimally treated geothermal bath water for public recreation; naturally high water temperatures and organic load favoring Naegleria proliferation; limited historical awareness of PAM risk in Caribbean geothermal spas; and frequent head immersion and diving by children. Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic thermophilic and environmental survival traits of N. fowleri enabling colonization of geothermal recreational waters (Geographic range expansion – inherent into a new climatic and hydrothermal niche in the Caribbean), without evidence that the Guadeloupe strain differed substantially in virulence from other global lineages.
Review: retain (newly added intra‑continental emergence; flag for review) – Added the 2008 fatal Guadeloupe case linked to the Dolé geothermal baths as the first documented PAM case in the Caribbean subregion and a clear intra‑continental emergence of N. fowleri from mainland Latin America into Caribbean island recreational waters. Event description and linkage to geothermal bathing are well supported by a detailed case report and subsequent environmental surveys. No correction to geography was needed, but classification was set to intra‑continental emergence (new UNSD subregion within South America), with the understanding that additional retrospective Caribbean cases, if uncovered, could alter this coding.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Naegleria fowleri
EPP.common.name: primary amebic meningoencephalitis
Host: Humans (all ages, predominantly young to middle‑aged adults)
Event.summary: Beginning in 2008, Karachi, Pakistan, started to report recurrent summer clusters of primary amebic meningoencephalitis, with the first recognized case in a young adult man and subsequent series documenting dozens of confirmed and probable Naegleria fowleri infections over the following decade. Most patients had no history of freshwater recreation, and investigations increasingly implicated under‑chlorinated municipal and domestic water systems, with exposures occurring during bathing, showering, and ritual ablution rather than lake or river swimming. Despite intermittent chlorination campaigns, infrastructure upgrades, and public advisories, fatal cases continued to recur through the early 2020s, establishing Karachi as a persistent urban hotspot for PAM in Southern Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High ambient summer temperatures and frequent heat waves warming municipal surface water sources and distribution systems; chronic under‑chlorination and aging, leaky pipe networks in Karachi’s water supply; heavy reliance on municipal water for domestic use and ritual nasal ablution; rapid urbanization and informal water storage practices that increase contact with warm, stagnant water. Internal mechanisms: Ecological plasticity and thermotolerance of N. fowleri enabling persistence in warm, low‑residual chlorinated distribution systems and household plumbing (Enhanced transmission/vector adaptation; Geographic range expansion – inherent into engineered water infrastructure). Genetic analyses suggest circulation of thermotolerant Naegleria strains, but a distinct, more virulent Pakistan‑specific lineage has not been conclusively demonstrated.
Review: retain (reclassified event type; flag for review) – Karachi’s prolonged 2008–2023 series of summer PAM cases linked to municipal and domestic water is well documented and clearly belongs among the most impactful N. fowleri events worldwide in terms of cumulative case numbers and sustained transmission. I reclassified the event from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because available data implicate external drivers (rapid urbanization, inadequate chlorination, extreme heat) rather than a demonstrated new Naegleria strain as the primary cause of resurgence in the Southern Asia subregion. Geography, timing, and linkage to Karachi’s water system were retained and supported with additional Pakistani reviews and surveillance advisories; the multi‑year aggregation of cases into a single emergence episode remains appropriate but should be revisited as more granular case series become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Naegleria fowleri
EPP.common.name: primary amebic meningoencephalitis
Host: Humans (previously healthy child with freshwater exposure)
Event.summary: In August 2010, a 7‑year‑old child in Minnesota, USA, died from primary amebic meningoencephalitis after swimming in a local lake, with no recent travel outside the state; N. fowleri was confirmed as the cause. Investigators noted that this was the first reported PAM case acquired in Minnesota and occurred several hundred miles north of any previously recognized exposure in the Americas, indicating that lake temperatures at this more temperate latitude had reached levels sufficient to support Naegleria transmission. Following the event, state and federal agencies increased clinician alerts, public education on warm‑lake exposure, and research into climate‑linked shifts in N. fowleri range, although subsequent cases in the Upper Midwest have remained rare and sporadic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unusually warm summer conditions and elevated lake surface temperatures in a northern U.S. state; broader climatic warming trends that extend the season during which small inland lakes can support thermophilic organisms; high‑risk recreational activities such as diving and swimming in shallow near‑shore areas. Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic thermotolerance and ecological flexibility of N. fowleri allowing survival and pathogenicity at more northerly latitudes as water temperatures cross critical thresholds (Geographic range expansion – inherent), with no clear evidence of novel strain evolution specific to Minnesota.
Review: retain (reclassified event type) – The 2010 Minnesota case is a well‑documented sentinel event illustrating northward expansion of N. fowleri risk in North America. I changed the event coding from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because current evidence attributes this shift mainly to external climate‑driven warming of surface waters rather than to a demonstrated change in the organism itself; no new continent or UNSD subregion is involved. Geography, timing, and narrative are consistent with the primary case report, and the event appropriately remains one of the highlighted high‑impact episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Naegleria fowleri
EPP.common.name: primary amebic meningoencephalitis
Countries: United States of America [2011] (Louisiana; DeSoto and St. Bernard Parishes)
Host: Humans (two adult residents using nasal irrigation with tap water)
Event.summary: In 2011, two middle‑aged adults in Louisiana, USA, developed rapidly fatal primary amebic meningoencephalitis after using neti pots filled with unboiled tap water for chronic sinus irrigation, and investigations recovered Naegleria fowleri from household plumbing and neti‑pot devices. These cases were the first recognized PAM deaths globally associated with treated municipal drinking water used for nasal irrigation rather than natural freshwater recreation, revealing that N. fowleri could survive in parts of chloraminated distribution systems and premise plumbing. The episode ended with the patients’ deaths but triggered extensive public health advisories on safe neti‑pot use, reassessment of residual disinfection practices in warm‑climate water systems, and inclusion of N. fowleri on regulatory watch lists.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of tap water for daily sinus irrigation without prior boiling, filtration, or sterilization; warm regional climate leading to elevated temperatures in distribution systems and household plumbing; localized zones of low disinfectant residual in distal parts of chloraminated water systems; limited prior awareness among clinicians and the public that treated tap water could carry N. fowleri risk when used intranasally. Internal mechanisms: Ability of N. fowleri to persist within low‑residual chlorinated water, biofilms, and warm household plumbing, exploiting nasal irrigation as an efficient exposure route (Enhanced transmission/vector adaptation; Geographic range expansion – inherent into engineered drinking water systems).
Review: retain (reclassified event type; sources refined) – This event correctly captures the first documented PAM deaths linked to treated municipal tap water used in neti pots. I reclassified the episode from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because evidence points to infrastructure and behavioral drivers (use of untreated tap water for nasal irrigation, warm distribution systems with low residuals) rather than organismal change; the continent and subregion were left unchanged. I also clarified that both DeSoto and St. Bernard Parish systems were implicated, aligning with Louisiana health department reports, and added a more recent open‑access version of the Clinical Infectious Diseases article. The event remains one of the top 10 due to its policy impact on drinking‑water utilities and home irrigation practices.

EPP.scientific.name: Naegleria fowleri
EPP.common.name: primary amebic meningoencephalitis
Host: Humans (adult performing ritual nasal rinsing/ablution with tap water)
Event.summary: In 2012, a middle‑aged man living on St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands, developed fatal primary amebic meningoencephalitis, with investigation indicating that his only freshwater exposure was frequent ritual nasal rinsing (ablution) using unboiled tap water at home. The case was the first documented PAM case in the U.S. Virgin Islands and the first reported in a U.S. jurisdiction clearly linked to religious ablution with domestic tap water, but it occurred after the earlier 2008 Guadeloupe case had already established N. fowleri presence in the Caribbean subregion. Following the event, territorial health authorities and CDC issued advisories on safe nasal rinsing and ablution practices, but no additional epidemiologically linked cases were identified, suggesting sporadic re‑occurrence in a region where the amoeba is now recognized.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of inadequately disinfected tap water for high‑frequency intranasal rinsing; warm Caribbean climate that can support N. fowleri colonization of local water sources and domestic plumbing; limited prior clinical suspicion and diagnostic capacity for PAM in the territory, delaying recognition. Internal mechanisms: Capacity of N. fowleri to persist in warm household water systems and cause disease via low‑volume nasal exposures associated with ritual practices (Enhanced transmission/vector adaptation), consistent with behavior seen in Pakistan and parts of the continental United States.
