Review: retain (corrected emergence type and narrative; flag for review) – The U.S. Virgin Islands ablution‑associated case is real and epidemiologically important as a first for that territory, but earlier 2008 Guadeloupe reports mean it cannot be treated as the first Caribbean occurrence. I reclassified the event from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence within the Caribbean subregion and revised the summary to acknowledge the prior Guadeloupe case. Geographic coding (continent South America, subregion Caribbean) remains consistent with the project’s country sheet. Because detailed environmental sampling results from St. Thomas are limited in the public record, the event should be kept but flagged for further expert review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Naegleria fowleri
EPP.common.name: primary amebic meningoencephalitis
Countries: United States of America [2013] (Louisiana; St. Bernard Parish and a second colonized system)
Host: Humans (primarily a fatal pediatric case; environmental detection in treated‑water consumers)
Event.summary: In 2013, a child who had played on a home slip‑and‑slide supplied by a public drinking water system in St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana, died of primary amebic meningoencephalitis, and investigations found Naegleria fowleri in tap water samples from the treated distribution system. Subsequent sampling in 2013–2014 demonstrated colonization of two Louisiana treated drinking water systems by N. fowleri, leading authorities to carry out aggressive system‑wide hyperchlorination, flushing, and infrastructure assessments to eradicate the amoeba. No additional PAM cases were confirmed from those specific systems after remediation, but the episode fundamentally changed guidance for warm‑climate utilities on maintaining higher disinfectant residuals and monitoring for free‑living amoebae in distribution networks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High summertime temperatures within drinking water distribution systems and premise plumbing; aging, complex pipe networks with low‑flow zones where disinfectant residuals were undetectable; recreational use of outdoor hoses and splash equipment that delivered warm, stagnant tap water directly to children’s faces and noses. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrated ability of N. fowleri to colonize and persist in treated drinking water systems and associated biofilms at residual disinfectant levels previously considered adequate (Enhanced transmission/vector adaptation; Geographic range expansion – inherent into engineered drinking water infrastructure).
Review: retain (reclassified event type) – This event accurately summarizes the first confirmed association of a U.S. PAM death with culturable N. fowleri in a treated public water system and the subsequent discovery of amoeba colonization in two Louisiana systems. I changed the coding from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence, treating the episode as a notable resurgence of PAM in an already affected subregion driven by water‑system conditions, not by proven pathogen evolution. The temporal span (2013–2014) and geography match the primary environmental and remediation reports. Because this event underpins modern drinking‑water guidance, it remains appropriately included among the top 10 emergence episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Naegleria fowleri
EPP.common.name: primary amebic meningoencephalitis
Countries: Argentina [2017] (Buenos Aires Province; Junín/General Arenales area)
Host: Humans (8‑year‑old child with freshwater exposure in a lagoon)
Event.summary: In February 2017, Argentina reported its first laboratory‑confirmed human case of primary amebic meningoencephalitis due to Naegleria fowleri in an 8‑year‑old boy from General Arenales, Buenos Aires Province, who had recently bathed in a eutrophic lagoon near Vedia and died within days of symptom onset. The diagnosis was established by microscopic and molecular detection of N. fowleri in clinical samples and confirmed by isolation of the amoeba from the implicated lagoon, demonstrating local environmental contamination. Although N. fowleri had long been recognized in other South American countries such as Venezuela and Brazil, this highly publicized Argentine case expanded documented human disease occurrence within the South America subregion and prompted national alerts, environmental investigations, and greater clinical awareness, but no large domestic outbreak has been reported since.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Recreational exposure to warm, nutrient‑rich freshwater in a temperate South American setting during hot weather; likely long‑standing under‑recognition of PAM in Argentina due to limited suspicion and diagnostic testing, leading to historical misclassification of compatible encephalitis cases. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrated ability of N. fowleri to cause disease in southern South American latitudes when environmental conditions (summer temperatures, organic load) favor proliferation (Geographic range expansion – inherent within the continent), though current data do not distinguish whether the Argentine isolate represents a novel lineage versus an established Latin American genotype.
Review: retain (corrected emergence type and sources; flag for review) – The 2017 Argentine case is well supported as the country’s first documented PAM due to N. fowleri, but global first detection occurred decades earlier, so I set first_detection to false and coded the episode as re‑occurrence within the South America subregion. I removed generic or unrelated citations and replaced them with Argentina‑specific case reports and public‑health summaries that directly describe the Junín/General Arenales case and environmental confirmation from the lagoon. Because Latin America already had multiple PAM reports (e.g., Venezuela, Brazil, Peru) prior to 2017, the event is important mainly as a country‑level expansion within an already affected subregion, and this context is now reflected in the summary.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Naegleria fowleri
EPP.common.name: primary amebic meningoencephalitis
Host: Humans (adult woman using an indoor surfing facility)
Event.summary: In July 2023, a 30‑year‑old woman in northern Taiwan developed rapidly progressive primary amebic meningoencephalitis after visiting an indoor surfing center, and Naegleria fowleri was identified by next‑generation sequencing and confirmatory testing of cerebrospinal fluid. An environmental investigation of the facility found one qPCR‑positive water sample in stagnant water beneath a basement ladder, while the main pools and surf reservoirs were negative, indicating focal colonization in warm, poorly disinfected areas connected to the surf system. This case represented Taiwan’s first recognized PAM due to N. fowleri and one of the first well‑documented infections linked to an indoor artificial surfing venue, prompting facility closure, engineering and disinfection upgrades, and strengthened surveillance for free‑living amoebae in engineered recreational waters.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Warm indoor recreational water facility with complex plumbing where some components received little or no disinfectant; intense surfing activity producing water aerosolization and forceful nasal exposure; incomplete regulatory oversight and monitoring for free‑living amoebae in indoor surf and spa centers. Internal mechanisms: Ability of N. fowleri to persist in small pockets of stagnant, under‑chlorinated water within an engineered recreational system and cause infection following high‑energy water contact (Enhanced transmission/vector adaptation; Geographic range expansion – inherent into novel indoor surfing environments), consistent with earlier reports from other artificial water venues.
Review: retain (newly added engineered‑water event; flag for review) – Added Taiwan’s 2023 indoor surfing‑center case as a high‑impact example of N. fowleri emergence in a novel engineered recreational environment and the country’s first recognized PAM case. Classified as re‑occurrence within Eastern Asia rather than as intra‑continental emergence because prior PAM cases were already reported from China and Japan. The summary and mechanisms closely follow the Emerging Infectious Diseases report and associated CDC materials. Further national surveillance data may refine whether additional, undetected cases or environmental positives warrant expanding this into a longer multi‑year episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Naegleria fowleri
EPP.common.name: primary amebic meningoencephalitis
Countries: India [2024] (Kerala state; mainly northern coastal and riverine districts)
Host: Humans (children and adults across a broad age range)
Event.summary: From mid‑2024 and especially during 2025, the Indian state of Kerala experienced an unprecedented surge in reported amoebic meningoencephalitis cases, with national and state sources citing roughly 60–70 primary amebic meningoencephalitis cases and about 19 deaths in 2025 alone and larger series of Naegleria fowleri meningoencephalitis patients under systematic study. Many patients had histories of swimming or bathing in warm ponds, rivers, or poorly maintained pools, and a smaller subset had exposures to domestic water or splash pads. Enhanced surveillance after a 2024 technical alert led to routine testing of cerebrospinal fluid for free‑living amoebae in acute encephalitis cases, revealing a concentration of N. fowleri infections in several northern coastal districts and making the 2024–2025 Kerala episode the largest documented PAM outbreak‑like occurrence worldwide to date. Intensive public health messaging, environmental investigations of water bodies, and standardized treatment protocols were implemented, and while sporadic cases continued, incidence appeared to decline somewhat after peak 2025 activity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Tropical monsoon climate with persistently high temperatures favoring warm, stagnant freshwater bodies; widespread recreational and domestic use of unchlorinated ponds, canals, and poorly maintained pools; variable water and sanitation infrastructure; and greatly intensified surveillance that reclassified previously unexplained encephalitis deaths as free‑living amoebic infections, including N. fowleri. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel Naegleria strain has yet been conclusively identified, but the organism’s thermophilic ecology and tolerance for nutrient‑rich, low‑disinfectant waters enable expansion into heavily used rural and peri‑urban freshwater bodies under warming climate conditions (Geographic range expansion – inherent), with case concentrations driven mainly by exposure opportunities and diagnostic intensity.
Review: retain (new large outbreak; flag for detailed specialist review) – Added the 2024–2025 Kerala episode as a major re‑occurrence event in Southern Asia, given multiple governmental and journal sources describing dozens of Naegleria fowleri meningoencephalitis cases and nearly twenty deaths, and at least one large clinical series indicating about 200 laboratory‑confirmed N. fowleri cases during the 2025 outbreak. I coded the event as re‑occurrence, since N. fowleri and sporadic PAM cases were already known in India, and current reports emphasize climatic conditions, water use, and enhanced surveillance rather than clear organismal change. However, early media coverage and some epidemiologic summaries conflated Naegleria infections with other free‑living amoebic encephalitides, and detailed strain‑level data are still emerging, so this event should be carefully re‑evaluated by subject‑matter experts as more peer‑reviewed analyses become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Listeria monocytogenes
EPP.common.name: listeriosis
Countries: South Africa [2017] (implicated ready‑to‑eat processed meats also exported widely within Southern and Eastern Africa, but confirmed human outbreak largely confined to South Africa)
Host: Humans nationwide, including many neonates and pregnant women, infected after consuming contaminated ready‑to‑eat processed meat products (‘polony’ and related sausages)
Event.summary: From early 2017, South Africa observed rising invasive listeriosis incidence, especially among neonates, and in December 2017 the Minister of Health formally declared a national outbreak. Epidemiologic investigations, supported by whole‑genome sequencing, linked 1,060 laboratory‑confirmed cases and about 216 deaths between January 2017 and July 2018 to a single L. monocytogenes sequence type 6 (ST6) clone contaminating ready‑to‑eat processed meat (polony) produced at an Enterprise Foods factory in Polokwane; related products were widely distributed domestically and exported to multiple African countries. A nationwide recall of all implicated processed meats, closure and decontamination of the plant, and strengthened food‑safety regulations led to a steep fall in new cases, and the outbreak was officially declared over in September 2018.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent contamination of a large industrial processed‑meat facility, high consumption of affordable ready‑to‑eat polony among low‑income populations, limited routine environmental testing in factories before the outbreak, and extensive regional trade in processed meats. Internal mechanisms: dominance of a single hyperinvasive ST6 clone associated with high attack rates and severe disease, indicating clonal expansion of a particularly fit genotype; this fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by changes in the EPP (novel strain/genotype and enhanced transmission in processed‑meat environments).
Review: review – Re‑occurrence flag was changed to ‘false’ and re‑emergence left ‘true’ to align with definitions: this unprecedented outbreak was driven by expansion of a hypervirulent ST6 lineage in an already affected sub‑region, representing re‑emergence due to pathogen change rather than simple resurgence under unchanged conditions. Geography, timeline and magnitudes (1,060 cases, ~216 deaths; polony plant in Polokwane with exports to other African countries) match NICD, WHO and comparative analyses. Clearly one of the highest‑impact listeriosis events globally and should be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: yersiniosis
Countries: India [1996] (North Arcot District, Tamil Nadu – village feast)
Host: Humans (adults and children attending a village feast)
Event.summary: On 29 September 1996, 48 villagers in North Arcot District, Tamil Nadu shared a vegetarian feast that included rice dishes and buttermilk; within about 16 hours on average, 25 participants (52%) developed acute diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, vomiting and fever, and seven required hospital care. Investigators cultured toxigenic Yersinia enterocolitica serotype O:3 biotype 4 from one patient’s stool and from the borewell water used to dilute the buttermilk, and illness was strongly associated with buttermilk consumption. After the contaminated borewell was withdrawn from use and safe water and food-hygiene practices were reinforced, no additional outbreak-related cases were detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Use of inadequately protected borewell water to dilute buttermilk for a mass community meal, probable faecal contamination of the well (likely from nearby livestock), and lack of routine outbreak investigation and water-quality monitoring. Internal mechanisms: a heat-stable enterotoxin–producing Y. enterocolitica O:3/biotype 4 strain able to proliferate in buttermilk at refrigeration and ambient temperatures; however, this bioserotype was already recognised in India and elsewhere, with no evidence for new virulence traits or resistance, so the event represents re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: Retain: Newly added as the first well-documented foodborne Y. enterocolitica outbreak in India (25 cases, seven hospitalisations). Classified as re-occurrence in a country where the pathogen was already known from sporadic cases; geography, case counts and vehicle match the Indian Journal of Medical Research report.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: yersiniosis
Host: Humans (children and adults)
Event.summary: In mid-December 2003, an outbreak of Yersinia enterocolitica 4/O:3 infection was detected in the coastal city of Kotka, Finland, when several patients presented with severe abdominal pain and fever, with some undergoing appendectomy before yersiniosis was recognised. Approximately 30 persons were affected, and 12 culture-confirmed isolates of Y. enterocolitica 4/O:3 showed a characteristic multidrug-resistant phenotype and clustered by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis and multilocus variable-number tandem-repeat analysis, distinguishing them from sporadic background strains. After investigation and control measures targeting the suspected local food vehicle and improvements in hygiene, reported cases declined and the outbreak ended in early 2004.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Local contamination of a shared food or water source in Kotka (likely a pork or fresh-produce item, though the precise vehicle was not definitively identified) and winter consumption patterns that favoured exposure among families. Internal mechanisms: circulation of a multidrug-resistant Y. enterocolitica 4/O:3 strain with a distinct PFGE/MLVA profile compared to sporadic isolates, consistent with re-emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance and clonal expansion rather than geographical spread to a new region.
Review: Retain: One of the few well-described European Y. enterocolitica outbreaks post-1990 (≈30 cases, 12 confirmed) and notable for a distinct multidrug-resistant 4/O:3 clone. Classification as re-emergence is justified by the resistance profile and clonal signature; inter-/intra-continental flags correctly remain negative. Sources (Finnish national surveillance report and BMC Microbiology paper) are appropriate and specific to the event.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: yersiniosis
Host: Humans (nursery school children, mainly 3–6 years old)
Event.summary: In late July 2004, a nursery school in Nara Prefecture reported multiple children with abrupt high fever, intense right lower abdominal pain and, in some cases, diarrhoea, prompting an investigation by local health authorities. Among 182 enrolled children, roughly 40 met the clinical case definition (≈36–42 symptomatic), and Yersinia enterocolitica serotype O8 biotype 1B—a highly pathogenic bioserotype rarely seen in Japan—was isolated from 16 symptomatic children, from a mixed apple salad served at lunch on 23 July, and from a composite sample of its raw ingredients. School meals were temporarily halted, the kitchen and equipment were disinfected, remaining ingredients were discarded and food-handling practices were reinforced; no additional cases occurred after these measures and the outbreak was declared over.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Preparation and serving of a mixed apple salad (apple, cucumber, potato, carrot, ham and mayonnaise) in a nursery-school kitchen with insufficient controls against contamination, exposing a highly susceptible population of young children, and limited early awareness of Y. enterocolitica as a cause of paediatric pseudoappendicitis. Internal mechanisms: involvement of Y. enterocolitica serotype O8 biotype 1B carrying yst, ail and virF virulence genes—more virulent and less common than the usual O:3 strains in Japan—which supports classification as re-emergence of a particularly pathogenic lineage rather than simple re-occurrence of endemic strains.
Review: Retain: Newly added and clearly among the most impactful post-1990 Y. enterocolitica outbreaks (≈40 paediatric cases, 13 hospitalisations) and the first documented O8 biotype 1B food-poisoning outbreak in Japan. Classified as re-emergence owing to the unusually virulent O8/1B bioserotype; inter-/intra-continental flags correctly remain negative. Sources are strong and event-specific (Jpn J Infect Dis case report plus national hazard database entry).

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: yersiniosis
Countries: Norway [2005] (two neighbouring counties in southern Norway)
Host: Humans (primarily older adults, one child)
Event.summary: Between December 21, 2005 and February 6, 2006, Norway’s National Reference Laboratory identified 11 cases of Yersinia enterocolitica serogroup O:9 biotype 2 infection in residents of two neighbouring counties, far exceeding the expected incidence for this serogroup. A case–control study linked illness to consumption of a ready-to-eat Christmas pork product (spiced headcheese, “julesylte”) manufactured at a single facility; most cases were elderly, four required hospitalisation and two died, and several reported prolonged symptoms or reactive arthritis. Following withdrawal of the implicated product lot, improvements in production hygiene and public risk communication, no further outbreak-related O:9 cases were reported from the affected counties.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Seasonal production and high winter consumption of a vacuum-packed ready-to-eat pork product distributed regionally, combined with the ability of Y. enterocolitica to grow at refrigeration temperatures and gaps in hygienic control late in the processing chain. Internal mechanisms: emergence of an outbreak-associated O:9 clone in a setting where O:9 infections had been rare, with severe disease and mortality in vulnerable older adults; this shift in dominant serogroup and clinical impact is consistent with functional re-emergence of a distinct pathogenic lineage rather than mere fluctuation in incidence.
Review: Retain: Moderate-sized but high-severity outbreak (11 cases, two deaths) that played an important role in highlighting ready-to-eat processed pork as a vehicle for Y. enterocolitica O:9 in Scandinavia. Classification as re-emergence is reasonable given the rare serogroup and severe outcomes; treating this as inter- or intra-continental emergence would be incorrect because human Y. enterocolitica was already established in Norway.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: yersiniosis
Host: Humans (adolescents and adults)
Event.summary: In early 2011, Norway’s reference laboratory detected a cluster of Yersinia enterocolitica O:9 isolates sharing an identical, previously unseen multilocus variable-number tandem-repeat analysis (MLVA) profile, prompting a nationwide investigation. Ultimately 21 laboratory-confirmed cases were identified across 10 municipalities; a matched case–control study implicated a particular brand of ready-to-eat mixed salad, and traceback pointed to imported radicchio rosso as the most likely contaminated ingredient. After voluntary withdrawal of all salad mixes containing radicchio rosso from the Norwegian market, no additional outbreak-strain infections were reported and the outbreak was declared over.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Globalised supply chains for fresh leafy vegetables, centralised industrial washing and packing of mixed salads, and extended cold storage that allowed psychrotrophic Y. enterocolitica to persist and reach consumers. Internal mechanisms: emergence or introduction of a Y. enterocolitica O:9 strain with a unique MLVA profile not previously recorded in Norway, demonstrating clonal expansion via a novel fresh-produce vehicle; this fits the definition of re-emergence rather than first or inter-continental emergence.
Review: Retain: Well-characterised 21-case outbreak that was the first clearly documented Y. enterocolitica outbreak associated with bagged salad mix and a distinct O:9 MLVA profile. Classification as re-emergence (new clone and vehicle within an endemic country) is appropriate; no changes to geography or timing are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: yersiniosis
Countries: United States of America [2011] (southwestern Pennsylvania – Allegheny and surrounding counties)
Host: Humans (children and adults)
Event.summary: Between March 24 and August 5, 2011, surveillance in four counties of southwestern Pennsylvania detected an unusual increase in Yersinia enterocolitica infections: 22 residents met the definition for culture-confirmed yersiniosis, compared with only three to five cases over comparable periods in previous years. Sixteen patients reported consuming pasteurised milk or ice cream from a single small dairy (Dairy A), and Y. enterocolitica with an indistinguishable pulsed-field gel electrophoresis pattern was isolated from unopened ice cream and homemade yogurt prepared from Dairy A milk. After Dairy A voluntarily halted production, recalled products and corrected deficiencies in post-pasteurisation handling, no further outbreak-associated Yersinia cases were identified.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Inadequate pasteurisation and post-pasteurisation hygiene at a farm-based dairy using reusable glass bottles, combined with wide household distribution of its milk and ice cream and the pathogen’s ability to grow at refrigeration temperatures. Internal mechanisms: survival and growth of pathogenic Y. enterocolitica in dairy matrices; no evidence that the outbreak strain was unusually virulent or resistant compared with other O:9 lineages, so the event is best classified as re-occurrence driven by process failures rather than re-emergence.
Review: Retain: Substantial dairy-associated outbreak (22 confirmed cases, seven hospitalisations, three ICU admissions) with clear implications for pasteurised-milk safety. Event summary has been updated to reflect the full 22-case outbreak described in the detailed epidemiologic study rather than only the initial 16 cases in the MMWR "Notes from the Field". Reclassified to re-occurrence, as drivers were pasteurisation and hygiene failures, not documented organismal change.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: yersiniosis
Countries: Japan [2012] (Nagano Prefecture – mountain hotel used for high-school trip)
Host: Humans (high-school students and two accompanying staff)
Event.summary: In August 2012, a Tokyo high school group staying at a mountain hotel in central Japan experienced an outbreak of gastroenteritis: 39 of the 41 guests (37 students and 2 staff) developed abdominal pain, diarrhoea and fever. Yersinia enterocolitica serogroup O:8 was isolated from 18 of 28 stool specimens, but despite extensive testing the pathogen was not recovered from specific menu items or the hotel environment, so the precise contaminated food vehicle remained undetermined. After the hotel suspended food service, implemented hygiene improvements and cooperated with the investigation, the outbreak ended and no further associated cases were reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Mass catering of multiple meals to a large group at a mountain hotel with limited kitchen infrastructure, potential cross-contamination among foods prepared for consecutive meals and inadequate temperature control of perishable ingredients. Internal mechanisms: infection with pathogenic O:8 strains of a lineage already established in Japan; no evidence of novel virulence markers or resistance compared with prior O:8 outbreaks, so the event is best viewed as a high-impact re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: Retain: Newly added large O:8 outbreak (39 cases) investigated by the Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Public Health and listed in national food-poisoning statistics. Classification as re-occurrence is appropriate because it reflects spread of an already established O:8 lineage via mass catering; geography, serogroup and case numbers are internally consistent across Japanese sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: yersiniosis
Countries: Japan [2012] (Morioka City, Iwate Prefecture – ryokan hosting seven primary schools)
Host: Humans (primary-school children and accompanying adults)
Event.summary: On 6 September 2012, an outbreak of acute febrile gastroenteritis occurred among seven primary-school groups from Miyagi, Aomori and Iwate Prefectures that had stayed at the same ryokan (traditional inn) in Morioka City, Iwate. Of 261 pupils and staff who ate the inn’s meals, 92 developed fever, abdominal pain, malaise and diarrhoea, making this the first recorded Yersinia enterocolitica food-poisoning incident in the prefecture. Because stool samples were collected late in convalescence, Y. enterocolitica serogroup O:8 was eventually isolated only from three symptomatic pupils using prolonged low-temperature enrichment, but the epidemiologic link to the inn’s catering was clear. The ryokan suspended meal service, thoroughly cleaned and disinfected its kitchen and revised its food-safety procedures; no additional related yersiniosis cases were detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large-scale preparation and serving of multiple meals to school groups in a single kitchen, likely contamination of one or more menu items with Y. enterocolitica O:8, and the organism’s ability to survive and possibly multiply during refrigeration, allowing exposure across several days and school cohorts. Internal mechanisms: involvement of pathogenic O:8 strains with typical virulence determinants; there is no evidence that a new serovar or resistance phenotype emerged, so the event is best classified as re-occurrence within an endemic setting.
Review: Retain: Added as one of the largest post-1990 Y. enterocolitica outbreaks globally (92 symptomatic cases among 261 exposed), and the first recognised O:8 food-poisoning event in Iwate Prefecture. Treated as a single temporally and epidemiologically linked episode; classified as re-occurrence. Geographic fields (Asia/Eastern Asia/Japan) and the multi-prefecture school involvement via a single ryokan are now explicitly captured.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: yersiniosis
Host: Humans (students living in a dormitory and kitchen staff)
Event.summary: In April 2013, a student dormitory in Tokyo reported a cluster of acute diarrhoea and fever among residents; investigation identified 52 affected students. Yersinia enterocolitica serogroup O:8 was isolated from 21 students and three kitchen workers, and intensive microbiological testing of stored foods, including prolonged cold enrichment with immunomagnetic bead concentration, eventually yielded O:8 with the same characteristics from a fresh vegetable salad served in the dormitory cafeteria. Following withdrawal of the implicated salad, reinforcement of kitchen hygiene and monitoring of food handling, the outbreak subsided and no further Yersinia infections linked to the dormitory kitchen were reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Centralised preparation of large batches of minimally processed vegetable salad for dormitory meals, contamination of raw produce or salad during preparation, and refrigeration practices that allowed psychrotrophic Y. enterocolitica to persist in ready-to-eat salads. Internal mechanisms: pathogenic O:8 strains of an established lineage capable of colonising raw vegetables; no indication of novel virulence or resistance beyond what had been observed in earlier O:8 outbreaks, so this event is classified as re-occurrence.
Review: Retain: Newly added large fresh-vegetable–associated outbreak (52 dormitory residents and staff) that, together with the Norwegian salad outbreaks, illustrates the growing importance of produce vehicles for Y. enterocolitica. Classified as re-occurrence; geography, case counts and vehicle are well supported by the Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Public Health publication and national summaries.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
EPP.common.name: yersiniosis
Countries: Norway [2014] (four military bases in northern Norway; civilian cases from several counties)
Host: Humans (military recruits and staff, plus civilian population)
Event.summary: In May 2014, a gastrointestinal illness cluster due to Yersinia enterocolitica O:9 was reported from a military base in northern Norway, coinciding with an increase in Yersinia notifications among civilians in the national surveillance system. A national investigation ultimately identified 133 laboratory-confirmed cases with a shared, previously unrecorded MLVA profile (5-6-9-8-9-9), including 117 cases linked to four military bases supplied by common catering contractors and 16 civilian cases from geographically dispersed counties; mixed salad (containing iceberg lettuce and radicchio rosso from a common supplier) was identified as the most likely vehicle. After contaminated salad components were withdrawn from military catering and restaurant menus and the upstream supply of radicchio rosso was addressed, case counts declined and the prolonged outbreak was brought under control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Centralised catering systems in the Norwegian Armed Forces and civilian cafeterias that widely distributed a contaminated mixed-salad component sourced from a common supplier, coupled with long shelf-life and refrigerated storage of chicory products (radicchio rosso) that favour survival of Y. enterocolitica. Internal mechanisms: clonal expansion of a specific O:9 strain defined by a distinctive MLVA profile not previously seen in Norway, demonstrating re-emergence of a particular genotype within an existing endemic range via a fresh-produce vehicle rather than spread to a new continent.
Review: Retain: The largest documented Y. enterocolitica outbreak in the post-1990 period (133 confirmed cases, predominantly among military recruits) and a key example of national dissemination through centrally sourced mixed salads. Classification as re-emergence of a distinct O:9 clone via food-system changes is appropriate; this event should definitely be retained among the top-impact outbreaks.

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Host: Humans—neutropenic leukemia patients in a temporary hematology ward during hospital renovations
Event.summary: In 1995, Hospital Central de Asturias in Oviedo, Spain, experienced a nosocomial outbreak in which four neutropenic leukemia patients housed in a temporary hematology unit during major renovations developed fatal disseminated Scedosporium (Lomentospora) prolificans infection over about one month, representing one of the first clearly documented hospital outbreaks of this mold. All four patients had fungemia with widespread angioinvasive hyphae and conidia at autopsy, and in vitro testing showed uniformly high MICs to amphotericin B, azoles and flucytosine, with no survivors despite aggressive therapy. After the cluster was recognized, the two affected rooms were closed and infection‑control interventions implemented, and no further linked cases occurred in that ward, indicating a renovation‑associated re‑occurrence of L. prolificans in a previously affected European subregion.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Major construction and renovation activities around the hematology service likely increased airborne dust and fungal spores; relocation of profoundly neutropenic patients to a temporary unit without optimal protective air‑handling facilitated opportunistic acquisition. Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic multidrug resistance (high MICs to amphotericin B and azoles) and strong angioinvasiveness produced rapidly fatal disseminated disease once spores were inhaled by neutropenic hosts.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Reclassified the event type from “re_emergence” to “re_occurrence” because the cluster occurred in a subregion (Southern Europe/Spain) where L. prolificans was already established from earlier deep infection cases, and the main drivers were external (renovation and suboptimal protective environment) rather than documented changes in the pathogen.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8586719/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Explicitly added location details (“Oviedo, Hospital Central de Asturias”) and clarified that this is a nosocomial construction‑associated outbreak rather than a new continental spread. Geography, timing and host description remain consistent with the primary J Clin Microbiol report. Flagged for review only to confirm alignment with the project’s operational definitions for re‑occurrence vs re‑emergence; the outbreak itself is well‑documented and should be kept.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Countries: Australia [1999] (single university hospital, New South Wales)
Host: Humans—immunocompromised adults including hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, patients with hematologic malignancies, solid organ transplants, HIV infection, and chronic lung disease; a minority of trauma-associated soft tissue infections
Event.summary: From late 1999 through 2003, a large Australian university hospital documented the first local detections and invasive case series of Lomentospora (Scedosporium) prolificans, reporting eight patients with invasive L. prolificans infection within a broader 6.5‑year study of scedosporiosis. The fungus was first recognized in this center in December 1999, after which multiple invasive cases occurred—including pneumonia, disseminated fungemia and deep tissue disease—mainly in severely immunocompromised patients such as HSCT recipients, cancer patients and those with advanced HIV, with high mortality despite therapy. Isolation data showed that L. prolificans rapidly became the more invasive of the two main Scedosporium species at the hospital, with two temporal clusters of isolates coinciding with major construction work, thereby marking the inter‑continental emergence and establishment of this mold as a clinically important pathogen in Australasia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of transplant, oncology and HIV care in Australian tertiary hospitals created sizable populations of severely immunocompromised patients; hospital construction works with deep excavation were temporally associated with peaks in L. prolificans isolation, suggesting increased airborne exposure.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2828065/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Compared with S. apiospermum, L. prolificans showed a higher propensity for invasive rather than colonizing infection and broad antifungal resistance, allowing it to exploit these high‑risk hosts and outcompete more susceptible molds in this setting.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Adjusted event_year from “1997–2003” to “1999–2003” and the country‑year tag from “Australia [1997]” to “Australia [1999]”, because the primary epidemiological study shows that S. prolificans was first detected at this hospital in December 1999, with subsequent invasive cases occurring thereafter; 1997–1998 belonged to the baseline Scedosporium apiospermum period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2828065/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Clarified that this episode is best classified as an inter‑continental emergence into Oceania (first documented regional series) rather than a re‑emergence, so ‘first_detection’ was set to false (global first occurred in 1984) and ‘re_occurrence’/‘re_emergence’ were set to false. The summary and mechanisms were reworded to align closely with the Australian data (including construction-associated clusters) without overstating case numbers. Flagged for review to confirm that the time window used for the “event” matches how the project wants to aggregate the early Australian emergence signal, but the underlying episode is robust and should be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Host: Humans—primarily adults with hematologic malignancies who developed bloodstream infection (fungemia), plus occasional other immunocompromised hosts
Event.summary: Between 2000 and 2019, state-wide surveillance in Queensland, Australia, identified 22 incident episodes of bloodstream infection due to Scedosporium species and Lomentospora prolificans among 21 residents, 18 of which were caused by L. prolificans, documenting a rare but highly lethal pattern of fungemia in patients with hematologic malignancy. Nearly all patients had profound neutropenia during intensive chemotherapy or HSCT and deteriorated quickly after first positive blood cultures, with all patients with hematologic malignancy dying within a year and a median time to death of around 9 days despite antifungal therapy. This prolonged surveillance period demonstrates the recurrent re‑occurrence of L. prolificans fungemia as a uniformly or near‑uniformly fatal complication in Queensland leukemia care, reinforcing the species’ status as a critical threat in high‑risk hematology populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Centralization of hematology and HSCT services in Queensland created a repeated, well‑defined cohort of profoundly neutropenic patients exposed to environmental molds; statewide laboratory surveillance improved recognition of rare mold fungemias. Internal mechanisms: L. prolificans’ intrinsic multidrug resistance and strong angioinvasiveness confer a uniquely poor prognosis for bloodstream infection, with virtually no survivors among patients with hematologic malignancy in this series, suggesting that even modern combination antifungal regimens rarely alter the course without rapid immune recovery.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37599232/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Clarified that this event is a long-term population‑based surveillance signal from Queensland, not a discrete short outbreak, and that 22 bloodstream infection episodes (18 L. prolificans) were identified over 20 years.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37599232/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Reclassified the event from ‘re_emergence’ to ‘re_occurrence’, as there is no evidence that pathogen evolution (new strain or host jump) drove this pattern; instead, it reflects the recurrent appearance of L. prolificans fungemia in an already endemic Australian setting driven by external factors (hematology service organization, patient mix, and surveillance). No geographic corrections were required. Flagged for review mainly to confirm that treating this entire 20‑year surveillance period as one aggregated “event” fits the project’s approach to temporally extended episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Countries: Spain [2001] (La Coruña, Complexo Hospitalario Juan Canalejo)
Host: Humans—adult inpatients with acute non‑lymphocytic leukemia in a hematology isolation unit
Event.summary: In the period leading up to a 2001 report, a hematology unit at Complexo Hospitalario Juan Canalejo in La Coruña, Spain, experienced an airborne nosocomial outbreak in which six inpatients with acute non‑lymphocytic leukemia developed invasive Scedosporium (Lomentospora) prolificans infection, all of whom died despite antifungal therapy. Phenotypic and genotypic analysis showed that isolates from patients and from the air of the isolation rooms were indistinguishable, indicating that a single clonal strain disseminated via the ward air, and implementation of intensified airborne infection‑control measures led to cessation of new cases. This outbreak represents a major re‑occurrence of L. prolificans disease in Southern Europe, demonstrating that the fungus can cause lethal, air‑transmitted epidemics in specialized hematology units.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Care of severely immunosuppressed leukemia patients in an isolation unit with inadequate control of airborne fungal contamination; likely environmental amplification of a single L. prolificans strain in or near the ward air‑handling or building fabric.([pascal-francis.inist.fr](https://pascal-francis.inist.fr/vibad/index.php?action=getRecordDetail&idt=972649&utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic multidrug resistance and high virulence allowed the clonal strain to cause invasive infection and death in all six affected patients once inhaled, underscoring the pathogen’s capacity for point‑source airborne outbreaks in vulnerable hospital populations.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Substantially revised this row, which previously described an imprecise “around 1997” Spanish outbreak with multiple genotypes; it is now aligned with the well‑documented airborne outbreak described by Guerrero et al. in La Coruña, Spain, involving six acute non‑lymphocytic leukemia patients with invasive infection and 100% mortality.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11418156/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Updated event_year to 2001 (matching the outbreak report) and countries field to specify La Coruña and the Complexo Hospitalario Juan Canalejo, and corrected the molecular description: genotyping showed a single clonal strain shared between clinical and air isolates, not multiple unrelated genotypes. (iii) Reclassified the event as ‘re_occurrence’ only (Southern Europe was already affected by earlier Spanish cases), removing erroneous ‘re_emergence’ and any implication that this was a new continental introduction. Flagged for review because this row has been materially reinterpreted; however, the updated version clearly corresponds to a major, well‑sourced outbreak that should be kept as one of the highest‑impact events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Host: Humans—diverse immunocompromised patients, predominantly with acute leukemias and other hematologic malignancies, and recipients of solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplants
Event.summary: From 2005 to 2021, an Australian multicenter retrospective cohort of non‑Aspergillus mold infections documented 61 proven or probable invasive episodes due to Scedosporium/Lomentospora species, of which 37 (about 61%) were attributable to Lomentospora prolificans, confirming it as a leading non‑Aspergillus mold pathogen nationally. Patients frequently had acute leukemia or had undergone hematopoietic stem cell or solid‑organ transplantation, and nearly half of L. prolificans infections were disseminated, with high early and late all‑cause mortality despite combination antifungal therapy and aggressive supportive care. This prolonged observational period reflects a sustained re‑occurrence and consolidation of L. prolificans as a major opportunistic fungus in Australian tertiary centers, contributing to its inclusion on global fungal priority‑pathogen lists and stimulating interest in novel antifungal agents and combination regimens for lomentosporiosis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Ongoing growth and specialization of transplant and cancer services in Australia, with increasingly intensive immunosuppressive regimens and high‑risk hematology and HSCT populations; widespread use of mold‑active prophylaxis that may selectively suppress susceptible molds and leave niches for intrinsically resistant species such as L. prolificans. Internal mechanisms: Intrinsic or high‑level resistance to nearly all licensed antifungals and a marked propensity for angioinvasion and dissemination underpin the very poor outcomes, and the apparent persistence of high case‑fatality over the 16‑year period suggests that any adaptive changes are outweighed by the fungus’s baseline virulence and resistance profile.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36861090/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Clarified that the 61 invasive episodes and 37 L. prolificans cases come from a formal multicenter retrospective cohort running 2005–2021, not a single‑center outbreak, and checked that timing, case numbers and underlying conditions match the Open Forum Infectious Diseases report.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36861090/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Reclassified the event as ‘re_occurrence’ rather than ‘re_emergence’, because it represents continuing and expanding incidence in a continent where L. prolificans was already established by the early 2000s; there is no specific evidence for a new strain or host jump driving the increase. (iii) Updated the WHO fungal priority‑pathogen list URL to the current version for supporting context on the species’ recognized importance. Flagged for review to ensure the long time span and aggregation of diverse centers are acceptable as a single high‑impact event, but the data are strong and this episode clearly merits retention.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Countries: Japan [2011] (multiple centers; including Kobe and other tertiary hospitals)
Host: Humans—immunocompromised adults, mainly with acute myeloid leukemia and other hematologic malignancies; cases included infective endocarditis, disseminated infection, and severe ocular or CNS disease
Event.summary: Starting in 2011, Japanese centers began reporting invasive Scedosporium/Lomentospora prolificans infections, including fungemia, infective endocarditis, ocular involvement and disseminated disease in patients with acute myeloid leukemia and other hematologic malignancies, marking the establishment of this pathogen in Japanese hematology and transplant practice. A 2015 endocarditis case report noted that the geographic distribution of S. prolificans infections had historically been limited to Australia, the United States and southern Europe, and that the first Japanese case had only been reported in 2011, with four cases recognized up to that time and a perceived increase in disseminated infections.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25630434/?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent reports described additional invasive and disseminated lomentosporiosis in Japanese patients, indicating a growing, though still uncommon, presence of this intrinsically resistant mold in Eastern Asian hospitals.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of high‑risk hematology and transplant programs in Japan and heightened awareness of non‑Aspergillus molds, together with improved fungal culture and species‑level identification, allowed recognition of a pathogen previously thought to be confined mainly to Spain, Australia and the southern United States. Internal mechanisms: The same intrinsic antifungal resistance and virulence profile seen elsewhere enabled L. prolificans to cause lethal disseminated disease in Japanese leukemia and transplant patients once introduced, but there is no evidence that Asian strains are biologically distinct; the emergence signal appears driven by host and healthcare‑system factors rather than major pathogen evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Removed incorrect flags for ‘first_detection’ and ‘inter_continental_emergence’, because earlier Korean cases (2004–2005) already document L. prolificans infection in Asia; this Japanese cluster is better interpreted as re‑occurrence within an already affected subregion.([acm.or.kr](https://www.acm.or.kr/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/ACM-0802-15.pdf)) (ii) Removed the ‘intra_continental_emergence’ flag, as both Korea and Japan fall within the same UNSD Eastern Asia subregion, and the guidance specifies that spread to a new country within a subregion should generally be treated as re‑emergence or re‑occurrence rather than intra‑continental emergence. (iii) Tightened the event description to emphasize that published Japanese cases up to 2015 were still few (around four at the time of the key endocarditis report) but signaled a new, ongoing presence in Japanese hematology/transplant centers. Flagged for review to confirm the choice to represent Japan’s emergence as a separate high‑impact event in addition to the Korean continental‑first episode; from an epidemiological perspective, this is justified by the different healthcare systems and the clustering of severe invasive cases.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Countries: Australia [2015] (Western Australia, Perth—Fiona Stanley Hospital haematology unit)
Host: Humans—inpatients in a high‑risk haematology unit with hematologic disease and severe immunosuppression, including stem cell transplant recipients
Event.summary: Over an approximately eight‑month period spanning 2015–2016, a haematology unit at Fiona Stanley Hospital in Perth, Western Australia, recorded a concerning cluster of four invasive Lomentospora prolificans infections in intensively treated patients, prompting a detailed outbreak investigation with whole‑genome sequencing. All four patients had severe underlying haematologic disease and profound immunosuppression, and developed invasive lomentosporiosis—including disseminated infection—with high morbidity and mortality owing to intrinsic antifungal resistance. Whole‑genome sequencing of clinical isolates from the cluster, together with two contemporaneous isolates from another hospital, demonstrated that the strains were genetically diverse (differing by >10,000 SNPs), arguing against a single point‑source clone and instead suggesting repeated environmental acquisition of L. prolificans by extremely vulnerable patients; after enhanced environmental assessment and strengthened infection‑control measures, no further temporal cluster was observed.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Concentration of profoundly immunocompromised haematology and HSCT patients in a single ward in a region where L. prolificans is environmentally prevalent (Australian urban and semi‑arid settings), combined with possible micro‑environmental contamination in hospital spaces and air during a period of intense building activity in the broader healthcare system.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7248584/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: A polyclonal set of intrinsically antifungal‑resistant strains capable of angioinvasion and dissemination repeatedly infected this ultra‑high‑risk population; genomic diversity implies that infection prevention must address broad environmental exposure rather than a single outbreak clone.
Review: Decision: retain. Changes made: (i) Confirmed that the cluster comprised four invasive L. prolificans infections over eight months in a haematology unit and that whole‑genome sequencing demonstrated polyclonality, not a single outbreak strain, which is now explicitly stated in the summary.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7248584/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Reaffirmed classification as a re‑occurrence event in an already endemic Australian setting rather than inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence. (iii) Left geography and timeframe unchanged, as they are consistent with the published Medical Mycology Case Reports study. Flagged for review only in the sense that, if a strict 10‑event cap is later enforced, project leads may wish to weigh this four‑case hospital cluster against single‑case but continent‑first events; scientifically, it is one of the better‑documented outbreaks and merits retention.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Host: Humans—adult patient after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo‑HSCT) for acute myeloid leukemia
Event.summary: In 2016, a hematology team in Osaka, Japan, reported a fatal case of fungal meningitis caused by Lomentospora prolificans shortly after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukemia, described as the first documented instance of L. prolificans meningitis after allo‑HSCT. The patient developed central nervous system symptoms and imaging findings consistent with meningitis in the setting of profound post‑transplant immunosuppression, and despite systemic antifungal therapy, clinical status deteriorated and the patient died, underscoring the extremely poor prognosis of CNS lomentosporiosis. This case expanded the recognized clinical spectrum of L. prolificans in Eastern Asia to include HSCT‑associated CNS disease and highlighted diagnostic challenges when a very rare mold is responsible for post‑transplant meningitis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Highly immunosuppressive allo‑HSCT conditioning and post‑transplant regimens in a healthcare environment where L. prolificans had recently emerged, coupled with diagnostic delay due to the rarity of this pathogen in CNS infections.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27258644/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The species’ ability to invade CNS tissues under conditions of profound immunosuppression and its intrinsic resistance to most antifungals permitted rapid progression despite treatment, illustrating how even sporadic cases can be almost uniformly fatal without early recognition and immune recovery.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: (i) This is a well‑documented and clinically important case—the first reported L. prolificans meningitis after allo‑HSCT—but it involves a single patient in a subregion (Eastern Asia/Japan) where the pathogen was already established, so its impact is more in expanding clinical phenotype than in geographic spread or case numbers.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27258644/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Event‑type flags were simplified to ‘re_occurrence’ only, removing earlier ‘re_emergence’ and inter‑/intra‑continental flags since there is no clear evidence of pathogen evolution and the case does not represent a new region. (iii) If a strict limit of 10 highest‑impact events is applied, this single‑case HSCT meningitis episode may be a candidate for exclusion in favor of continent‑first or larger multicase episodes (e.g., South American emergence or additional European clusters). For now it is retained as it illustrates the extreme severity of CNS lomentosporiosis, but it is flagged for strategic review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Countries: China [2019] (tertiary center caring for HSCT recipients)
Host: Humans—young adult with acute myeloid leukemia after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with chronic graft‑versus‑host disease
Event.summary: In 2019–2020, a tertiary hospital in China reported a case of pulmonary Lomentospora prolificans infection in a 27‑year‑old man with acute myeloid leukemia following allo‑HSCT and severe chronic graft‑versus‑host disease, described as the first successfully treated post‑HSCT L. prolificans infection in the country. The patient developed pulmonary lomentosporiosis while receiving intense immunosuppression; combination therapy with voriconazole and terbinafine, alongside careful adjustment of immunosuppressive drugs, led to sustained clinical and radiologic remission—an exceptional outcome for this pathogen given its usual high mortality. Accompanying literature review suggested that L. prolificans infections were increasingly recognized in HSCT recipients worldwide but outcomes remained poor, making this Chinese case notable both as a first national report and as a rare therapeutic success.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of HSCT programs and intensive leukemia care in China, leading to more patients at risk for rare molds, and improved mycological diagnostics enabling species‑level identification of L. prolificans.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12297014/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: While intrinsic multidrug resistance constrained treatment options, partial susceptibility to voriconazole and terbinafine allowed for a synergistic combination regimen in this case, and some immune recovery likely contributed to successful control, illustrating that early aggressive multi‑agent therapy can occasionally overcome the fungus’s high virulence.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: (i) This event is accurately described as the first successfully treated post‑HSCT L. prolificans infection reported from China and reflects growing recognition of the pathogen in Eastern Asia; however, it is a single case in a subregion where L. prolificans was already present (Korea and Japan), so its impact is more clinical (treatment breakthrough) than epidemiological.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12297014/?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Event‑type flags were simplified to ‘re_occurrence’ only; earlier ‘first_detection’ and continental emergence flags were removed to align with definitions that reserve inter‑continental emergence for first presence in a continent (which is already captured by the earlier Korean episode). (iii) Because the project prioritizes the ten most impactful emergence events by case numbers and spread, this case may be considered for exclusion in a stricter pruning step, but it is currently retained as a high‑value example of successful therapy in a setting of growing regional incidence. Flagged for review with that caveat.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Falciformispora senegalensis
EPP.common.name: Eumycetoma (black-grain eumycetoma due to Falciformispora senegalensis)
Countries: India [1991] (Tamil Nadu, Madras region; first culture-confirmed isolation in India)
Host: Humans (subcutaneous black-grain eumycetoma)
Event.summary: In 1991, a histopathology and mycology review of 210 mycetoma biopsies from Tamil Nadu, India, reported isolation of Leptosphaeria species, including Leptosphaeria senegalensis (now Falciformispora senegalensis), in pure culture from several autochthonous black-grain eumycetoma cases, representing the first culture-confirmed documentation of this typically West African agent in India. The isolates occurred as a very small fraction of a much larger mycetoma burden dominated by Madurella mycetomatis, Actinomadura madurae and other agents, indicating that F. senegalensis was present at low endemic frequency rather than driving a noticeable increase in overall case numbers. Following this report, subsequent reviews and regional syntheses have continued to list F. senegalensis as an occasional eumycetoma cause in India, but without identifying any subsequent spikes in incidence or discrete outbreak clusters attributable specifically to this species.
Mechanism.or.driver: External drivers: most likely long-standing but previously unrecognized environmental presence of F. senegalensis in dry tropical soils and thorny vegetation in parts of Southern India, with traumatic inoculation during agricultural work analogous to West African settings, combined with improved culture and histopathology that enabled species-level identification in the 1991 review. Internal mechanisms: no evidence for a novel genotype, increased virulence, host jump or enhanced transmissibility; the event appears to reflect diagnostic detection of a rare, pre-existing agent rather than true biological emergence or range expansion during the study period.
Review: review – New event added to capture the first culture-confirmed detection of Leptosphaeria senegalensis (now Falciformispora senegalensis) in India, based on Venugopal 1991 and later textbook summaries that list West Africa and India as the main regions where this species causes mycetoma.([ijdvl.com](https://ijdvl.com/prevalence-of-mycetomas-in-madras/)) The event is interpreted as an inter-continental emergence with in situ transmission in Southern Asia, but the underlying biopsies span an undefined period prior to 1991 and species-level identification historically suffered from misclassification, so the exact timing and magnitude of any true geographic spread remain uncertain. Retain this event for geographic-range context but flag for expert review of whether it should be considered a discrete emergence episode under the project’s strict criteria or treated purely as improved detection of long-standing background infections.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Ehrlichia sp.
EPP.common.name: ehrlichiosis
Countries: United States of America [1994] (Minnesota, Wisconsin, New York)
Host: Humans (patients with febrile illness and cytopenias following Ixodes tick bites)
Event.summary: In 1994, a new form of granulocyte‑tropic ehrlichial infection was recognized in patients from Minnesota and Wisconsin who presented with acute febrile illness, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia after tick bites, and whose blood smears and serology showed morulae in neutrophils and reactivity to a granulocytic Ehrlichia‑like agent. By 1995, additional cases were reported from New York and other states, defining human granulocytic ehrlichiosis (HGE) as a distinct clinical entity transmitted by Ixodes scapularis in the upper Midwest and northeastern United States. Subsequent molecular work demonstrated that the agent was closely related to, and ultimately reclassified as, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, but the 1990s emergence literature consistently treated it within the Ehrlichia complex and established granulocytic ehrlichiosis as a major tick‑borne zoonosis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of white‑tailed deer and small mammal hosts together with expanding Ixodes scapularis populations in the upper Midwest and northeastern United States increased opportunities for human exposure to granulocytic Ehrlichia‑like pathogens in Lyme borreliosis–endemic areas. Internal mechanisms: Recognition of a distinct granulocyte‑tropic lineage within the broader Ehrlichia/Anaplasma complex represented novel strain/genotype emergence causing human disease in a region where monocytotropic ehrlichiosis was already present, with ecological conditions favoring establishment in Ixodes–rodent–deer cycles.
Review: Decision: review. The event (1994–1997 recognition of human granulocytic ehrlichiosis in the upper Midwest and New York) is real and highly impactful, but the etiologic agent is now classified as Anaplasma phagocytophilum rather than an Ehrlichia species. I therefore turned off the first_global_emergence and first_detection flags and reclassified this as a re_emergence event (novel granulocyte‑tropic lineage within the ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis complex in a subregion where E. chaffeensis had already emerged). Curators should decide whether this episode should instead be moved to a dedicated Anaplasma phagocytophilum event sheet to avoid double counting.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus chapareense
EPP.common.name: Chapare virus
Countries: Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2019] (Caranavi and other municipalities in La Paz Department)
Host: Humans (rural residents and healthcare workers in La Paz Department)
Event.summary: In 2019, Chapare virus re-emerged in rural areas of La Paz Department, Bolivia, with an outbreak centered in Caranavi that resulted in nine confirmed cases and four deaths, including infections in healthcare workers providing care to index patients. The outbreak demonstrated person-to-person transmission in healthcare settings and was associated with a Chapare virus strain genetically distinct from the 2003 Cochabamba strain, marking the first recognized spread of the virus into La Paz Department. Intensive epidemiologic investigation, infection-prevention measures, and rodent-focused environmental interventions halted further transmission, and no additional outbreak-related cases were reported after 2019.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rural agricultural livelihoods with heavy rodent exposure, suboptimal housing and storage conditions promoting rodent infestation, and limited early recognition of Chapare hemorrhagic fever in health facilities contributed to zoonotic introduction and nosocomial spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence, with sequencing confirming a Chapare virus strain different from the 2003 strain; Enhanced Transmission in the sense of demonstrated efficient human-to-human transmission via contact with blood and body fluids in healthcare settings; possible Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within Bolivia, enabling persistence in rodent populations of La Paz Department.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2019 Caranavi/La Paz outbreak with nine cases (four deaths) and documented nosocomial person‑to‑person transmission is consistently reported by NEJM, PAHO, Canada’s pathogen datasheet, CDC and WHO as the major modern Chapare event, and the description here (size, locations, involvement of healthcare workers, and genetic distinctness from 2003) matches those sources.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10245337/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re_emergence (new genotype and changed transmission pattern in a previously affected country and sub-region) without intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate and consistent with the event definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus chapareense
EPP.common.name: Chapare virus
Countries: Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2021] (rural municipalities in northern La Paz Department)
Host: Humans (rural residents in northern La Paz Department)
Event.summary: In 2021, a third documented Chapare hemorrhagic fever outbreak occurred in La Paz Department, Bolivia, involving three laboratory-confirmed human cases and two deaths in rural communities within the known at-risk zone of northern La Paz. This episode took place in the same broad ecological setting previously affected in 2019, indicating ongoing local zoonotic transmission from infected rodents rather than expansion to new regions or continents. The outbreak was contained through enhanced surveillance, clinical management, and community-level rodent control and public health messaging, with no evidence of sustained chains of human-to-human transmission.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent ecological suitability for the rodent reservoir in rural northern La Paz, including jungle corridors with agricultural settlements, poor-quality housing, and ongoing rodent infestation in and around homes, underpinned repeated zoonotic spillover events. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence driven primarily by continued zoonotic transmission from the established reservoir rather than clear evidence of new viral genotypes or major changes in virulence; any human-to-human spread appears limited, without indications of substantially enhanced transmissibility compared with earlier events.
Review: Decision: retain. WHO’s 2025 Disease Outbreak News and subsequent reviews describe a third Chapare outbreak in 2021 in La Paz Department with three confirmed cases and two deaths, matching the case numbers and geography used here.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2025-DON553)) Detailed locality and driver information are necessarily more generic and largely inferred from descriptions of the established risk corridor (Caranavi–Teoponte–Palos Blancos), but remain consistent with the known ecology of the reservoir and with PAHO/WHO risk communication for rodent‑borne diseases in northern La Paz.([paho.org](https://www.paho.org/es/noticias/17-10-2022-pobladores-municipios-norte-paz-son-sensibilizados-capacitados-para-prevenir?utm_source=openai)) Event-type coding as re_occurrence (no new continent or UN sub‑region, and no documented novel genotype) is appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus chapareense
EPP.common.name: Chapare virus
Countries: Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2024] (northern La Paz Department – Teoponte/Muñecas–Alcoche area)
Host: Humans (25-year-old man from northern La Paz Department)
Event.summary: In June 2024, Bolivia’s Ministry of Health confirmed a single laboratory-positive arenavirus infection attributed to Chapare virus in a 25-year-old man from the tropical north of La Paz Department, after field teams documented rodent exposure in rural communities such as Muñecas and Alcoche in Teoponte municipality. The patient was transferred to a referral hospital in El Alto and initially showed clinical improvement under intensive supportive care, but later developed severe pulmonary and neurologic complications and died in early August 2024; epidemiologic follow-up reported that 59 close contacts all tested negative for Chapare hemorrhagic fever. Health authorities delimited the affected area, implemented rodent-control and environmental sanitation measures, and provided additional training on Chapare hemorrhagic fever management in Caranavi and Teoponte, and no further confirmed human cases were reported in 2024, so this was treated as a localized zoonotic spillover event.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rural agricultural settlements in northern La Paz with substantial infestation by the wild rodent Oligoryzomys microtis, substandard housing, and human encroachment into forest habitat likely enabled this spillover; the case was detected in the context of strengthened surveillance and rodent-borne disease control efforts in the Caranavi–Teoponte corridor. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence driven by continued zoonotic transmission of an established Chapare virus lineage within Bolivia, with no current evidence of major genetic change or markedly increased human-to-human transmissibility in this event.
Review: Decision: review (corrected). The original row misattributed the December 19, 2024 adult male case described by WHO as part of the 2025 outbreak, and instead used that description for the 2024 event. I replaced the event_summary, host description and drivers with details from Bolivian Ministry of Health and SEDES La Paz communications, which document a distinct mid‑2024 Chapare hemorrhagic fever case in a 25‑year‑old man from Teoponte (northern La Paz), with 59 contacts tested and no secondary cases, and subsequent death from pulmonary complications.([minsalud.gob.bo](https://www.minsalud.gob.bo/8179-ministerio-de-salud-realizara-estudios-para-control-de-arenavirus-en-el-norte-paceno-y-descarta-caso-sospechoso-del-hospital-de-clinicas)) Event-type coding as re_occurrence in an already affected sub-region remains appropriate, and continent/sub-region/country fields are unchanged; I also updated source_urls to include the Bolivian primary reports and the June 2024 UK emerging infections summary as the most direct documentation for this outbreak.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus chapareense
EPP.common.name: Chapare virus
Countries: Bolivia (Plurinational State of) [2024] (rural municipalities in northern La Paz Department, including Bajo Inicua, Palos Blancos)
Host: Humans (adult male farmer and 7-year-old girl from rural northern La Paz Department)
Event.summary: In late 2024 and early 2025, the fifth documented Chapare hemorrhagic fever outbreak in Bolivia occurred in the established risk corridor of northern La Paz Department and consisted of two confirmed human cases. The first patient, an adult male farmer aged about 50–60 years from a rural municipality in La Paz Department, developed fever, myalgia, arthralgia and gingival bleeding on 19 December 2024, was hospitalized on 24 December, and died on 30 December; Chapare virus infection was confirmed by real-time RT-PCR on a blood sample collected before death, and field investigation found intense rodent infestation in and around his wooden, dirt-floored home. A second laboratory-confirmed case was reported on 22 January 2025 in a 7-year-old girl from the indigenous Chimán community of Bajo Inicua in Palos Blancos municipality, whose symptoms began around 14 January; she required intensive care at Hospital del Norte but recovered, and comprehensive contact tracing, testing and rodent-control campaigns around both households found no further human cases, so authorities considered this a self-limited episode of repeated zoonotic spillover without sustained human-to-human transmission.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Marked peri-domestic rodent infestation around smallholder farms in northern La Paz, wooden and metal housing with dirt floors, agricultural work that disturbs rodent burrows, and limited early recognition of Chapare hemorrhagic fever in remote facilities contributed to repeated zoonotic introductions; strengthened community surveillance and awareness allowed relatively rapid isolation and management once cases were suspected. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence driven by ongoing circulation of Chapare virus in local rodent reservoirs, with no current evidence of new viral genotypes or markedly increased virulence compared with the 2019 strain; human-to-human transmission was not documented in either 2025 case, in contrast to the nosocomial spread seen in 2019.
Review: Decision: review (corrected). The original 2025 row conflated the December 19, 2024 adult male case with later sporadic cases and described that index case under the 2024 event as well, effectively double-counting it; it also did not clearly distinguish the mid‑2024 outbreak from the fifth outbreak spanning December 2024–January 2025. I have redefined this row to represent the fifth outbreak as described by WHO—beginning with the adult male farmer whose illness started on 19 December 2024 and was notified to WHO in early January 2025—and added the second confirmed 2025 case in a 7‑year‑old girl from Bajo Inicua, Palos Blancos, as documented by SEDES La Paz and a 2025 national case-series.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2025-DON553)) The year field is updated to 2024–2025 to reflect the cross-year onset and resolution, countries/host fields were corrected to emphasize northern La Paz municipalities, event_summary and drivers were rewritten to avoid overlap with the distinct 2024 Teoponte case, and confidence was increased to 0.9 given multiple convergent official and peer-reviewed sources; event-type classification as re_occurrence (no new continent or UN sub-region and no clear evidence of a novel genotype) remains appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia mayonii
EPP.common.name: Lyme disease (caused by Borrelia mayonii)
Host: Humans (patients with Lyme-like illness); Ixodes scapularis ticks; small mammal reservoirs (e.g., Peromyscus spp.) in endemic Minnesota and Wisconsin foci
Event.summary: This event began in 2013 when a Minnesota resident with Lyme-like illness was found to be infected with an atypical Borrelia that was subsequently detected in additional patients from Minnesota and Wisconsin and in Ixodes scapularis ticks collected in both states.
