Over 2013–2014, retrospective molecular analyses of more than 100,000 Lyme diagnostic specimens and targeted tick testing identified six human infections and a measurable, though low, prevalence of this novel Borrelia in blacklegged ticks in the Upper Midwest, leading to its formal description as Borrelia mayonii and recognition in 2016 as a new cause of Lyme disease. The episode concluded as the pathogen was incorporated into routine diagnostic algorithms and surveillance definitions, with only sporadic human cases reported thereafter and no evidence of large outbreaks, but with establishment of an endemic zoonotic cycle in parts of Minnesota and Wisconsin.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensified molecular surveillance and PCR-based genotyping of Lyme disease specimens at reference laboratories (Mayo Clinic and CDC) allowed discrimination of atypical oppA1 gene sequences from Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto; concurrent expansion and densification of Ixodes scapularis populations in Minnesota and Wisconsin, linked to land-use change (reforestation, suburbanization) and a warming climate, increased human–tick contact in the Upper Midwest. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel Lyme borreliosis genospecies within the B. burgdorferi sensu lato complex (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence), characterized by higher spirochetemia and more diffuse rash and systemic symptoms than typical B. burgdorferi infection, which may facilitate detection via blood PCR and potentially alter transmission dynamics (Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: retain: Event appropriately captures the discovery and early characterization of Borrelia mayonii as a human Lyme disease agent in Minnesota and Wisconsin during 2013–2016, with correct timing, geography (Upper Midwest, United States), and event-type classification as both first global emergence and first detection in the human host system; no corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia mayonii
EPP.common.name: Lyme disease (caused by Borrelia mayonii)
Host: Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes angustus ticks; small mammal reservoirs (rodents); no confirmed human clinical cases as of 2019
Event.summary: Following its recognition in the Upper Midwest of the United States, Borrelia mayonii or B. mayonii-like organisms were detected in the mid‑2010s in Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes angustus ticks and wild animal hosts in Ontario and British Columbia, marking spread of the enzootic cycle into Canadian foci without confirmed human illness. Through 2014–2019, national tick-borne disease assessments in Canada documented B. mayonii/B. mayonii-like detections in ticks and wildlife from these provinces while human Lyme disease remained dominated by Borrelia burgdorferi, suggesting silent geographic expansion of the novel genospecies. The episode is characterized as an ecological range expansion rather than a discrete outbreak, ending with B. mayonii recognized as present but rare in Canadian tick populations and as a potential future threat for human Lyme disease in Canada.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: northward and westward expansion of Ixodes scapularis and related tick species into higher-latitude and coastal regions of Canada due to climate warming, changing host distributions (e.g., deer and small mammals), and landscape changes that favor forested edge habitats; enhanced national tick and wildlife surveillance programs increased sensitivity for detecting rare pathogens. Internal mechanisms: no specific genetic or phenotypic changes in B. mayonii have been demonstrated for these Canadian detections; they are best interpreted as low-prevalence geographic range expansion of existing B. mayonii/B. mayonii-like lineages into new tick populations and ecozones, facilitated primarily by climate- and host-driven processes rather than documented novel adaptation.
Review: review: Event is retained as it reflects documented detection of Borrelia mayonii/B. mayonii-like organisms in ticks and wildlife in Ontario and British Columbia beginning around 2014, but the type-of-emergence classification has been corrected from re-emergence to re-occurrence because this represents geographic spread within the same UN subregion (Northern America) driven mainly by climate- and host-mediated tick range expansion rather than demonstrated pathogen-level change; an obsolete CDC PRCATS URL (404) was removed from the source list, and the mechanism/driver text was edited to avoid speculative claims about specific adaptive changes in the bacterium.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia mayonii
EPP.common.name: Lyme disease (caused by Borrelia mayonii)
Countries: United States of America [2025] (New York – Herkimer County)
Host: Humans (autochthonous Lyme disease case); Ixodes scapularis ticks as presumed local vector
Event.summary: In July 2025, an adult resident of Herkimer County, New York, who had not traveled outside the state, was found by a commercial laboratory to be PCR‑positive for Borrelia mayonii, prompting investigation by the New York State Department of Health and CDC, and representing the first reported autochthonous human B. mayonii infection outside Minnesota and Wisconsin. Public health follow‑up confirmed absence of travel, transplant, or transfusion exposures and identified likely local tick exposure in upstate New York, indicating that B. mayonii had expanded beyond its previously recognized Upper Midwestern human range. The episode concluded as a single, severe but self‑limited Lyme disease case, with no identified secondary human transmission, but it led to heightened clinician awareness, inclusion of B. mayonii in regional Lyme diagnostics, and consideration of the pathogen in future tick and wildlife surveillance in the northeastern United States.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: ongoing expansion and high density of Ixodes scapularis populations and Lyme disease risk in the northeastern United States, driven by reforestation, abundant deer and small mammal hosts, and climatic conditions favoring tick survival; increased clinician and laboratory awareness of B. mayonii and use of PCR assays capable of discriminating it from B. burgdorferi facilitated detection, together with targeted tick surveillance around the patient’s residence. Internal mechanisms: no specific genetic or phenotypic changes have yet been demonstrated for New York B. mayonii isolates; this episode is best interpreted as geographic range expansion of previously recognized Upper Midwestern B. mayonii lineages into northeastern tick populations rather than emergence of a novel, more virulent strain.
Review: review: Event is retained and reflects the first documented locally acquired human Borrelia mayonii infection and associated tick detections in New York State in 2025, but the type-of-emergence classification has been revised from re-emergence to re-occurrence because the episode represents spread within the same UN subregion (Northern America) without evidence for new host range or virulence traits; the host description was corrected for a typographical error ('autochthonous'), and the mechanism/driver narrative was adjusted to remove unsupported suggestions of increased virulence and to emphasize vector ecology, land-use/climate drivers, and enhanced surveillance as the primary explanatory factors.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia psittaci
EPP.common.name: psittacosis
Countries: United States of America [1995] (Georgia; Florida bird distributor)
Host: Humans in households that purchased infected pet birds (parakeets, cockatiels, finches and other small birds) from Atlanta‑area pet stores supplied by a single Florida distributor
Event.summary: In August 1995, a veterinarian in Georgia reported a dead pet bird with avian chlamydiosis, and tracing showed that more than 700 birds from a Florida distributor had been shipped to nine Atlanta‑area pet stores, after which several recent purchasers developed febrile respiratory illness. Follow‑up of 114 exposed households identified 46 persons among 428 exposed who met a clinical definition for psittacosis, and epidemiologic investigation plus serology confirmed a large outbreak linked to recently purchased psittacine and passerine birds from the infected shipment. Removal or treatment of infected birds, quarantine and record‑keeping measures under the Georgia Bird Dealer Licensing Act, and public health advisories to clinicians and bird owners were implemented, after which no additional outbreak‑related human cases were detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: large‑scale interstate trade in mixed‑species pet birds with minimal quarantine, limited infection control and record‑keeping in retail pet shops, and intense household contact with stressed, shedding birds shortly after transport. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel C. psittaci genotype or resistance phenotype was reported; the outbreak reflects amplification of endemic strains in commercial bird supply chains rather than evolutionary change in the pathogen.
Review: review – Added as a major 1995 U.S. household outbreak, with 46 clinically defined psittacosis cases among 428 exposed persons linked to a shipment of >700 infected pet birds sold through nine Atlanta‑area pet shops. This event clearly ranks among the most impactful modern psittacosis outbreaks by case count and is well documented in primary sources; it is appropriately classified as re‑occurrence in Northern America. Final subdivision of cases into confirmed versus probable, and any small discrepancies in the exact number of affected households, should be checked against Moroney et al. (1998) and the Georgia Epidemiology Report when constructing the Excel table.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia psittaci
EPP.common.name: psittacosis
Host: Humans (poultry slaughter‑plant workers) exposed to infected chickens and contaminated aerosols on processing lines
Event.summary: During August–September 2018, clusters of severe respiratory illness and pneumonia among workers at two large chicken slaughter plants in Virginia and Georgia led to investigation by state health departments and CDC, ultimately identifying 82 employees who met a probable or confirmed psittacosis case definition, including 13 with C. psittaci infection confirmed by real‑time PCR. Most confirmed cases had radiologically verified pneumonia, high hospitalisation rates, and a small number required intensive care, and the outbreak was linked to intense exposure to infected chickens and aerosols generated during evisceration and further processing on fast, crowded production lines supplied by shared source farms. After plant‑level interventions—including temporary line slow‑downs, improved ventilation and sanitation, enhanced respiratory protection and clinical evaluation for workers, and sustained public‑health follow‑up—no further outbreak‑related cases were detected and national psittacosis surveillance in the United States returned to baseline levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive industrial poultry production with high bird throughput, close worker proximity to infected carcasses and contaminated aerosols, suboptimal respiratory protection and diagnostic suspicion before the outbreak was recognised, and structural factors that favoured rapid within‑plant amplification once C. psittaci entered the production system. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype or resistance pattern was reported; molecular and epidemiologic data support classification as a large occupational re‑occurrence in a long‑recognised risk setting rather than emergence of a new strain.
Review: review – The event row has been updated to reflect that this was the largest U.S. psittacosis outbreak in three decades, with 82 workers meeting probable/confirmed case definitions and 13 PCR‑confirmed infections across two poultry plants in Virginia and Georgia, as documented in both the Emerging Infectious Diseases article and a subsequent MMWR analysis. Country and subregion coding (United States, Northern America) and classification as a re‑occurrence are correct. Because the original summary understated the outbreak size, the revised text and numbers should be carefully aligned with CDC reports when finalising the Excel dataset.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia psittaci
EPP.common.name: psittacosis
Host: Humans (duck slaughter‑ and processing‑plant workers and several close contacts) with severe community‑acquired pneumonia, including multiple human‑to‑human transmission chains
Event.summary: In December 2020, a hospital in Shandong Province, China, notified authorities of a cluster of severe community‑acquired pneumonia among workers from a duck slaughter and processing plant and some of their close contacts, and metagenomic next‑generation sequencing together with PCR identified Chlamydia psittaci as the causative agent. Detailed field investigation documented 22 laboratory‑confirmed human cases, eight of whom developed severe pneumonia and one of whom died, with evidence of multiple person‑to‑person transmission chains in addition to intense primary exposure to infected ducks and contaminated aerosols in crowded indoor processing areas. After closure of the implicated plant, antibiotic treatment and quarantine of exposed workers and close contacts, and strengthened surveillance in the region, no further transmission was detected and the outbreak was considered contained.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: large‑scale intensive duck production with high bacterial loads on carcasses, inadequate early respiratory protection, crowded indoor workstations enabling both zoonotic exposure and spread between workers, and delayed recognition of psittacosis as an etiology of severe pneumonia. Internal mechanisms: outbreak investigations showed the same C. psittaci genotype infecting multiple patients but did not conclusively demonstrate novel virulence determinants; the efficient human‑to‑human spread observed under very high‑exposure conditions suggests enhanced transmission potential yet, at present, is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence within an existing zoonotic system rather than a distinct re‑emergent lineage.
Review: review – New large 2020 outbreak in Shandong Province, China (22 confirmed cases, eight severe, one death, with well‑documented person‑to‑person transmission among duck‑plant workers and their contacts) added as one of the most impactful recent psittacosis episodes. Coding as Eastern Asia (China) and classification as re‑occurrence in a region with pre‑existing C. psittaci circulation are appropriate. Because numerical and some clinical details are synthesised from several English‑language summaries of the original Chinese investigations, national experts should confirm final case counts, case definitions and inferred transmission chains before the event is locked into the Excel dataset.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia psittaci
EPP.common.name: psittacosis
Countries: Argentina [2024] (Buenos Aires Province; Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area)
Host: Humans with severe community‑acquired atypical pneumonia, many ultimately diagnosed with psittacosis and some with known or suspected contact with psittacine birds in urban and peri‑urban settings
Event.summary: In March–April 2024, Argentina’s Ministry of Health, through severe acute pneumonia surveillance and intensive‑care networks, detected an increase in severe atypical pneumonia cases in the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area and other parts of Buenos Aires Province, and enhanced etiologic investigation revealed an excess of psittacosis diagnoses within this group. National and provincial reports indicated roughly 60 suspected psittacosis cases, around 20 of which were laboratory‑confirmed C. psittaci infections, many in patients with no immediately obvious pet‑bird exposure although background information highlighted ongoing illegal trade and ownership of parrots and other captive birds and prior localised psittacosis clusters in the country. The episode led to epidemiologic alerts, clinical guidance to consider psittacosis in severe community‑acquired pneumonia, and public messaging on avoiding illegal bird trade and practising safe bird handling; as targeted control measures were implemented and winter progressed, case numbers declined and the event was assessed as a limited urban re‑occurrence rather than sustained widespread transmission.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increased recognition and systematic investigation of severe community‑acquired pneumonia within sentinel hospitals, in the context of urban and peri‑urban exposure to parrots and other birds (including through illegal wildlife trade and informal keeping), together with social and economic conditions that favour crowded bird‑keeping and limited veterinary oversight. Internal mechanisms: available reports do not implicate a novel genotype or clear change in virulence; the pattern is most consistent with a surveillance‑ and exposure‑driven resurgence of an endemic zoonosis rather than genetic re‑emergence.
Review: review – Retained as a recent, nationally recognised increase in psittacosis cases associated with investigations of severe atypical pneumonia in Buenos Aires Province, with around 60 suspected and approximately 20 laboratory‑confirmed infections according to official Argentine bulletins and contemporaneous reviews. Continent, subregion and country coding (Argentina, South America) and classification as a re‑occurrence fit the historical presence of psittacosis in the region. Because data are still evolving and detailed outbreak analyses are being published, final case counts, geographic spread within Argentina and degree of bird‑exposure documentation should be re‑checked against the most recent national epidemiologic reports before finalising the Excel event row.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
EPP.common.name: diphtheria
Countries: Bangladesh [2017] (Cox’s Bazar district, especially Rohingya refugee camps and nearby host communities)
Host: Humans (predominantly Rohingya refugees, mainly children and adolescents; some cases among Bangladeshi hosts)
Event.summary: Following the mass influx of Rohingya refugees from Myanmar into Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, in August 2017, a large diphtheria outbreak was first detected in November 2017 in overcrowded refugee camps. The epidemic spread rapidly through 2017–2018, ultimately generating approximately 8,400 suspected cases among the Rohingya population and lasting for over two years, with children and adolescents most affected and substantial morbidity but relatively low overall case‑fatality due to intensified clinical care and antitoxin use. Multiple rounds of mass vaccination, expansion of treatment centers, and strengthening of surveillance gradually brought the outbreak under control by 2019, though sporadic cases and ongoing vulnerability persisted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extreme overcrowding, poor sanitation, limited initial access to health care, low or uncertain prior vaccination coverage among Rohingya refugees, and the stress of forced displacement created ideal conditions for explosive transmission. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain or resistance pattern was highlighted; the outbreak mainly reflects intense spread in a highly susceptible displaced population, i.e., re‑occurrence facilitated by social and environmental drivers rather than genetic change.
Review: retain – Correctly identifies one of the three largest modern outbreaks (≈8,400 cases) and appropriately classifies it as re‑occurrence driven by extreme crowding and low prior coverage in a refugee setting. Geography, years, and sources are appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
EPP.common.name: diphtheria
Host: Humans (children and adolescents, with some adults)
Event.summary: In October 2017, amid protracted armed conflict and health‑system collapse, Yemen’s Ministry of Health and WHO announced a diphtheria outbreak after clusters were reported from Ibb governorate. Over 2017–2019, the outbreak spread to most districts in 23 of Yemen’s governorates, with several thousand suspected cases and hundreds of deaths recorded, making it one of the largest modern diphtheria emergencies in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. Large‑scale emergency vaccination campaigns, deployment of antitoxin and antibiotics, and international support reduced incidence in later years, but continuing conflict and service disruptions mean that diphtheria transmission remains an ongoing risk rather than a clearly ended episode.
