Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Seasonal sand fly abundance and human exposure in rural/suburban environments, with summer climatic conditions (warm temperatures and higher humidity at dusk/night) favoring intense Phlebotomus activity; increased clinical and laboratory surveillance for viral CNS infections enhanced recognition of TOSV. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of a novel strain; the event reflects amplification of endemic transmission in existing natural foci rather than documented viral evolutionary change.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: eastern equine encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (severe neuroinvasive disease/encephalitis)
Event.summary: Between 1990 and 1992, Massachusetts experienced a renewed episode of human eastern equine encephalitis (EEE), with four confirmed cases and one death after several quieter years, indicating cyclical resurgence in long‑established foci. The episode developed alongside intense equine and mosquito activity in freshwater swamp habitats of southeastern Massachusetts, prompting strengthened arboviral surveillance and targeted mosquito control. Human activity then subsided in the mid‑1990s, with only sporadic cases in the wider region until the next major multi‑year cycle in the mid‑2000s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing EEEV foci in freshwater swamp habitats of southeastern New England; favorable hydrological and climatic conditions that increased populations of the ornithophilic vector Culiseta melanura and bridge vectors; human residence and recreation near wetland margins. Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence of a novel lineage or major viral change; this episode reflects cyclical amplification within established enzootic foci leading to spillover into humans (re-occurrence rather than re-emergence).
Review: retain – Massachusetts surveillance tables document four human EEE cases and one death during 1990–1992, with activity confined to long‑known foci; classification as re-occurrence, and the geography, hosts, and timing, are consistent with available data, so no structural changes were made.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: eastern equine encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (encephalitis and febrile illness), Equines
Event.summary: In 2010, an outbreak of encephalitis was recognized in eastern Panama (Darién and neighboring provinces), where multiple hospitalized patients were found to have laboratory‑confirmed EEEV infection, including at least seven confirmed human cases, one co‑infected with Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, and one suspected fatal case. The event developed concurrently with equine encephalitis cases and widespread EEEV detection in local mosquito and equine populations, representing the first documented human EEE outbreak in Central America against a background of previously rare, sporadic human infections elsewhere in Latin America. The outbreak ended after intensified surveillance, vector control and the seasonal decline in mosquito populations, with no evidence of sustained large‑scale human transmission in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of agriculture and human settlements into rainforest and swamp habitats in eastern Panama; high densities of competent mosquito vectors and susceptible equine populations; limited prior human immunity; intensified case finding once the outbreak was recognized. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses indicate that the outbreak involved a North American–like EEEV lineage introduced into a region previously dominated by largely equine, low‑virulence South American strains, increasing neurovirulence in humans and extending pathogenic Group I virus into Central America; this represents intra-continental emergence of a more virulent lineage rather than re-emergence in a previously human-affected subregion.
Review: review – The 2010 Panama outbreak with ≥7 lab-confirmed human cases is well documented and clearly constitutes the first recognized human EEE outbreak in Central America. I set intra_continental_emergence=Yes and re_emergence=No to align with the definitions (new subregion within the Americas, but no prior human cases there), and clarified the mechanism text to describe introduction of a more neurovirulent North American–like lineage without labeling the event as "re-emergence." This episode remains one of the most important post‑1990 EEEV human emergences because of both outbreak size and geographic significance.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: eastern equine encephalitis virus
Countries: United States of America [2012] (Massachusetts, Vermont, Florida, North Carolina, Georgia, Virginia)
Host: Humans (neuroinvasive EEE disease)
Event.summary: In 2012, the United States experienced a notable multi‑state EEE season in which 15 neuroinvasive human cases were reported from six states, including seven in Massachusetts, two in Vermont, two in Florida, and single cases in Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia, representing the highest national total since 2005. The outbreak developed alongside widespread arboviral activity, including a large West Nile virus epidemic, with intensive mosquito surveillance documenting high EEEV infection rates in bridge vectors and multiple equine and wildlife infections. Human EEE case counts decreased in subsequent years, but this season reinforced the pattern of episodic, regionally extensive amplification across both northeastern and southeastern endemic foci.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Favorable summer weather patterns (warm temperatures and substantial rainfall) that increased mosquito abundance and extended the transmission season; high densities of avian reservoir hosts; extensive freshwater swamp habitats in affected states; and intensified testing and reporting during the concurrent West Nile virus epidemic. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of established North American Group I EEEV lineages without clear evidence of a novel strain; the spike in cases is best attributed to ecological and climatic amplification (re-occurrence) rather than major viral evolution.
Review: retain – CDC’s 2012 arboviral surveillance report confirms 15 EEEV neuroinvasive cases from Massachusetts, North Carolina, Vermont, Florida, Georgia and Virginia, matching the states and magnitude described here. The episode fits the definition of re-occurrence within existing North American foci, and no geographic or timing corrections were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: eastern equine encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (neuroinvasive encephalitis)
Event.summary: In 2014, Maine confirmed its first‑ever human case of neuroinvasive EEE in a York County adult who required hospitalization, marking a significant northward extension of recognized human risk along the U.S. Atlantic coast. Human EEE activity continued into 2015, when state surveillance documented another neuroinvasive case in a Maine resident that resulted in the state’s first recorded EEE-related death, alongside continued detection of EEEV in mosquitoes and animals. After 2015, no human cases were reported in Maine for several years, but the virus persisted in local enzootic cycles with periodic detection in mosquitoes, birds and horses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Progressive spread of EEEV‑infected birds and mosquitoes into more northerly wetlands in Maine; regional climate trends increasing summer temperatures and lengthening mosquito seasons; expansion of human residences and recreational use near swamp habitats; and enhanced testing prompted by earlier equine and wildlife outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Evidence from serologic and entomological studies suggests geographic range expansion of existing Group I EEEV strains into newly suitable northern habitats, representing re-emergence via inherent geographic adaptation into a new state-level focus within an already affected subregion.
Review: review – Maine CDC surveillance reports and contemporaneous news articles corroborate a first human EEE case in 2014 and a second, fatal case in 2015, confirming Maine as a new northern focus. I replaced a dead Maine Public link with working Bangor Daily News, Portland Press Herald, and Maine CDC epidemiology URLs; the timing, geography and classification as re-emergence (northward geographic adaptation into a new state) are otherwise accurate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: eastern equine encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (neuroinvasive disease), Equines
Event.summary: In the summer of 2016, Canada reported its first documented human case of mosquito‑borne EEEV infection in a resident of southwestern Ontario, a region where EEEV had previously been detected primarily in horses and mosquitoes. The case was identified through enhanced arboviral diagnostic capacity and occurred against a backdrop of sporadic equine EEE and expanding vector surveillance in Ontario and neighboring provinces. No sustained series of human cases followed immediately, but subsequent reports from Ontario and other parts of eastern Canada have documented occasional equine and very rare human infections, confirming that EEEV has extended its human disease range into Canada.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Northward expansion of competent mosquito vectors and EEEV‑infected birds into the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence region, plausibly influenced by climate warming and landscape changes; increased equine and wildlife surveillance improving early warning; greater clinician awareness and testing for rare arboviral encephalitides. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of North American Group I EEEV into Canadian ecosystems, with geographic range expansion and local adaptation allowing overwintering and transmission in more northerly climates—classified here as re-emergence into a previously unaffected national population within the same continental subregion.
Review: retain – PHAC’s 2016 mosquito-borne disease report explicitly notes the first human EEE case in Canada in an Ontario resident, and later reviews corroborate this as a climate-linked northward expansion. Treating this as a re-emergence (range expansion into a new national population within Northern America) without intra- or inter-continental emergence is consistent with the project definitions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: eastern equine encephalitis virus
Countries: United States of America [2019] (Alabama, Connecticut, Georgia, Indiana, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Tennessee)
Host: Humans (neuroinvasive disease/encephalitis)
Event.summary: In 2019, the United States experienced the largest recorded EEE outbreak in the modern surveillance era, with 38 neuroinvasive human cases and 19 deaths reported across 10 states, heavily concentrated in Massachusetts and Michigan but also affecting several other New England, Mid‑Atlantic and Midwestern states. The outbreak developed following intense EEEV activity in mosquito pools and equines, with some states documenting more EEEV‑positive mosquitoes and higher human case counts than in any previous year, prompting aggressive vector control, public advisories and outdoor-activity restrictions. Human case numbers declined sharply in 2020 and subsequent years, but the 2019 season highlighted the potential for rare yet severe spikes in EEE incidence and contributed to renewed calls for strengthened arboviral preparedness and vaccine development.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Exceptionally favorable weather patterns (wet spring and warm summer) that increased larval habitats and adult mosquito abundance; high densities of avian reservoir hosts and bridge vectors in endemic swamp complexes; human exposure through outdoor recreation and residence near wetlands; heightened surveillance and diagnostic testing that improved case detection. Internal mechanisms: Available molecular data indicate that the outbreak involved circulating North American Group I strains without clear evidence of a novel genotype or marked change in virulence; thus, the event is best explained as a very large re-occurrence driven by environmental and ecological amplification, though the frequency of such high‑intensity years may be increasing with ongoing climate and land‑use change.
Review: retain – Multiple CDC and state sources confirm 38 neuroinvasive cases across the listed 10 states in 2019 and identify this as the largest annual EEEV case count in decades. The event summary and mechanisms are consistent with these reports, and coding it as a large re-occurrence within existing North American foci (rather than re-emergence or inter-continental spread) fits the project’s criteria.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: eastern equine encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (neuroinvasive disease), Equines, Mosquitoes
Event.summary: In 2023 and 2024, Vermont documented a marked increase in EEEV activity after several quiet years, with enhanced surveillance detecting multiple EEEV‑positive mosquito pools and several fatal equine cases in northern Vermont during this two‑year period. In 2024, two adult men from the same northwestern county developed neuroinvasive EEE, representing the first human cases in the state since the initial pair reported in 2012 and underscoring the persistence and intermittent amplification of local enzootic cycles. Nationally, 16 neuroinvasive EEE cases were reported across eight U.S. states in 2024, with Vermont’s two cases occurring alongside cases in Massachusetts, New Hampshire and several other states, highlighting a broader regional resurgence during that season.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Recurrent favorable climatic conditions and wetland hydrology in northern Vermont that supported high vector densities; increased mosquito and equine surveillance and diagnostic testing revealing wider geographic virus activity than previously recognized; expansion of equine populations with variable vaccine coverage and human outdoor exposure near swamp habitats. Internal mechanisms: Sustained establishment of North American Group I EEEV in Vermont since its first detection in 2011–2012, with periodic ecological amplification in this relatively new endemic focus; available data support classification as re-occurrence driven mainly by environmental and surveillance factors rather than emergence of a distinct new viral lineage.
Review: review – Vermont and CDC reports confirm renewed EEEV activity, with three equine cases in 2023–2024 and two human neuroinvasive cases in 2024 after a 12‑year gap. I corrected the countries field so Vermont is linked to this episode starting in 2023 (removing the erroneous [2012]) and set re_emergence to No, because current evidence points to ecological re-occurrence in an established focus without a new viral lineage. The summary now explicitly situates Vermont’s experience within the larger 2024 U.S. season of 16 neuroinvasive EEE cases.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus granulosus
EPP.common.name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Countries: Peru [1991] (especially Junín Department and other central Andean highlands)
Host: Humans in rural Andean communities (sheep‑ and camelid‑raising areas)
Event.summary: Hospital‑based surveillance in the central Andean department of Junín, Peru, recorded about 1,100 surgically treated human cystic echinococcosis cases between 1991 and 2002, confirming a long‑standing but very high endemic burden in highland sheep‑ and camelid‑raising communities. Subsequent community ultrasound surveys and national analyses in the late 2000s and early 2010s found annual incidence around 10 cases per 100,000 population in highly endemic regions and point prevalences of roughly 5–10% in some pastoral communities. By the mid‑2010s, cystic echinococcosis remained an important public‑health and economic problem in several Peruvian Andean departments, with improved imaging and reporting contributing to higher detection of cases compared with earlier decades.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent infection of dogs through access to infected sheep and camelid offal, backyard and informal slaughter with poor offal disposal, limited routine dog deworming and socio‑economic conditions favouring close human–dog contact sustained high transmission; expansion of ultrasound and CT imaging and referral to central hospitals also increased case detection. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel E. granulosus genotype has been implicated; the high burden is consistent with intense transmission of established sheep strains in a favourable ecological and husbandry context rather than parasite evolution.
Review: review – Event retained as representing one of the world’s highest‑burden CE foci, but re_occurrence was changed from Yes to No because the Peruvian central Andes have been highly endemic for many decades and available data describe persistent high prevalence with better diagnosis, not a resurgence after prior control or absence. The summary was rephrased to emphasise chronic endemicity, and in‑line web citations were removed; no changes were made to geography or host classification.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus granulosus
EPP.common.name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Host: Humans in pastoral and agro‑pastoral communities (notably Uyghur and other ethnic groups in north‑west China)
Event.summary: In north‑west China, large community ultrasound screening campaigns and hospital data in the mid‑1990s documented extremely high burdens of human cystic echinococcosis in counties of Xinjiang, Gansu and neighbouring provinces, with surgical incidence reported as high as 43–80 cases per 100,000 in some areas and more than 21,000 hydatid surgeries recorded in Xinjiang alone by 1995. Follow‑up community surveys in Hoboksar County, Xinjiang from 2005 to 2008 showed persistent high prevalence and frequent reinfection despite treatment, indicating sustained intense transmission over more than a decade. WHO and Chinese technical reports estimated that by the early 2000s China harboured several hundred thousand human CE cases, making western China one of the world’s largest single‑country foci of cystic echinococcosis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: In endemic areas of Xinjiang, Gansu, Qinghai and adjacent provinces, traditional pastoral and agro‑pastoral systems with large dog populations, home slaughter of sheep and other livestock, use of dogs to guard herds and poor offal disposal created highly efficient dog–livestock cycles, while remoteness and limited access to health care delayed diagnosis and treatment. Internal mechanisms: Transmission is dominated by the globally common E. granulosus sensu stricto (G1) sheep strain; available evidence does not implicate any novel genotype or intrinsic change in the parasite, and the enormous burden is attributed to ecological and husbandry factors rather than parasite evolution.
Review: review – Event retained as a major high‑burden focus, but re_occurrence was set from Yes to No because western China has been hyperendemic for CE since well before 1990 and available data describe long‑standing high incidence documented by ultrasound surveys and surgical series, not a resurgence after previous control. The summary now relies on quantitative estimates from WHO/Chinese reports, and in‑line web citations were removed; geography and host system are unchanged.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus granulosus
EPP.common.name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Countries: Argentina [1997] (Rio Negro Province and neighbouring Patagonian provinces)
Host: Humans in rural and peri‑urban sheep‑raising communities of Patagonian Argentina
Event.summary: In Rio Negro Province in Argentine Patagonia, community ultrasound surveys in the mid‑1980s found cystic echinococcosis prevalence of about 5–6% among schoolchildren aged 6–14 years, prompting the establishment of a provincial hydatidosis control programme based on dog deworming, health education and ultrasound screening. From 1997 onwards the programme implemented annual ultrasound examinations of at‑risk schoolchildren and shepherds, and over 1997–2014 tens of thousands of people were screened, yet repeated community studies in small towns such as Ingeniero Jacobacci, Ñorquinco and Ramos Mexia still documented adult abdominal CE prevalences of roughly 4–7% and a substantial proportion of active cysts. Economic analyses estimated that human and livestock CE together caused large annual losses to the provincial health and agricultural sectors even as paediatric incidence declined, making Rio Negro one of the best‑documented but still heavily affected CE hotspots worldwide and an influential One Health control model.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive sheep farming with transhumant flocks, home slaughter and informal meat inspection, widespread dog ownership and feeding of raw infected offal, and historically limited access to diagnostic imaging in remote Patagonian communities created efficient dog–sheep–human transmission cycles; sustained provincial control activities (public education, dog deworming, ultrasound screening and deployment of the EG95 sheep vaccine) have reduced but not eliminated these risks. Internal mechanisms: Parasite populations are dominated by common E. granulosus sensu stricto sheep strains; there is no evidence that parasite evolution, rather than transmission intensity and the difficulty of maintaining long‑term control, explains the persistent human burden.
Review: review – Added as a new event because Rio Negro and neighbouring Patagonian provinces combine very high historical CE prevalence with sustained, well‑documented human and livestock economic losses and a long‑running integrated control programme; WHO and multiple reviews consistently cite this region alongside Peru, Central Asia, China and East Africa as among the highest‑burden CE areas globally. Classified without a specific emergence type because the event reflects chronic hyperendemicity under partial control rather than re‑emergence or spread into new regions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus granulosus
EPP.common.name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Host: Humans (with parallel infections in sheep and dogs in Magallanes)
Event.summary: In the Magallanes Region of southern Chile, a long‑running hydatidosis control programme that began in 1979 and markedly reduced infection in humans, sheep and dogs was terminated in 2004 after apparent success. In the years after the final mass praziquantel dosing of rural dogs, surveillance data showed a re‑emergence of Echinococcus granulosus infections in sheep and dogs and a parallel rise in human cystic echinococcosis incidence through at least 2021, reversing much of the progress achieved by the programme. The Magallanes experience is widely cited as a cautionary example that stopping dog deworming and surveillance too early can allow hydatidosis to bounce back in previously controlled areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The proximate driver was termination of a successful regional control programme (regular dog deworming, meat inspection and public education) in 2004, which allowed dog infection to rise again as dogs regained access to infected livestock offal; persistent pastoral practices meant the ecological context for transmission remained intact, so human exposure quickly increased once control pressure was removed. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence for new genotypes or increased parasite virulence; this event exemplifies re‑occurrence driven by withdrawal of control measures rather than biological change in E. granulosus.
Review: retain – Event appropriately captures a well‑documented regional re‑occurrence of CE in the Magallanes Region following termination of a successful dog‑deworming and surveillance programme; classification as re_occurrence (without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or re_emergence) is consistent with the definitions. Minor editorial changes (removal of in‑line citations, clearer wording) do not affect the epidemiological content, so the event is retained as one of the key global examples of control programme failure leading to resurgence.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis (human infection with Trichinella spp.)
Host: Humans; wild boar and domestic pigs (Sus scrofa) as source animals
Event.summary: During 1994–1995, an outbreak of trichinellosis in Chumphon Province, southern Thailand infected 59 people, one of whom died, after communal meals that included undercooked wild pig and pork; muscle biopsy and serology identified the agent as the non‑encapsulated species Trichinella pseudospiralis. This was the first recognised human outbreak caused by T. pseudospiralis and highlighted that non‑encapsulated Trichinella species circulating in wildlife and domestic reservoirs in Southeast Asia could spill over into humans via traditional dishes made with raw or lightly cooked meat. The outbreak was controlled by clinical management of cases, tracing and removing contaminated meat, and intensifying education on proper cooking of pork and wild game.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rural and peri‑rural dietary practices involving consumption of raw or undercooked wild pig and pork, small‑scale pig production with weak veterinary inspection, and close ecological contact between domestic pigs and wildlife reservoirs harbouring non‑encapsulated Trichinella. Internal mechanisms: emergence of T. pseudospiralis as a recognised human pathogen in the region (a non‑encapsulated species with a broader host range, including birds, and different muscle pathology from T. spiralis), representing a re‑emergence event defined by a biologically distinct species infiltrating existing domestic and sylvatic cycles rather than purely by increased exposure to classic T. spiralis.
Review: retain – Corrected the year from 1998 to 1994–1995 and specified the location in Chumphon Province, based on the original clinical description of an outbreak affecting 59 people, including one death, which is cited as the first human outbreak caused by Trichinella pseudospiralis.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9455518/?utm_source=openai)) The event is appropriately coded as re‑emergence (novel non‑encapsulated species in humans) rather than first detection of Trichinella overall; Peromyscus‑focused and unrelated background URLs have been removed and replaced with a Thailand‑specific epidemiologic review as a more relevant source.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis (human infection with Trichinella spp.)
Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as main source animals
Event.summary: In 1995, a large village‑wide outbreak of trichinellosis occurred in southern Lebanon after residents consumed home‑prepared pork products contaminated with Trichinella spiralis, leading to dozens of clinically and serologically confirmed cases. The outbreak struck a predominantly Christian rural community where pig keeping and pork consumption occur, and investigations linked illness to meat from locally slaughtered pigs rather than imported products. Control actions included culling of infected pigs, advising against further consumption of the implicated pork, treatment of cases and health education, after which no additional cases were reported from this episode.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: small‑scale, home slaughtering of pigs without veterinary inspection, production and consumption of inadequately cooked pork sausages in a resource‑limited rural setting, and limited awareness of trichinellosis and diagnostic capacity, which together led to a high attack rate once contaminated pork entered the local food chain. Internal mechanisms: infections were attributed to classic T. spiralis with no evidence of new lineages or resistance; this is thus a re‑occurrence of a known zoonosis in a vulnerable community on the eastern Mediterranean fringe, driven by husbandry and culinary practices rather than biological evolution of the parasite.
Review: review – The Lebanese village outbreak is real and correctly located in Western Asia, and it is epidemiologically notable because trichinellosis in the Eastern Mediterranean has been documented mainly among Christian communities consuming pork or wild boar.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2809009/?utm_source=openai)) However, available data suggest a moderate outbreak size compared with the very large multi‑year waves in Romania, Bulgaria, Argentina and the 2005 Laos outbreak now included here. Consider retaining this event for regional representativeness or first‑in‑region context, but it likely falls below the global top‑10 in terms of total cases and should be revisited during final prioritisation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis (human infection with Trichinella spp.)
Countries: Lao People’s Democratic Republic [2005] (Udomxay Province, northern Laos)
Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as the principal source animals, with evidence of infection in local swine herds and likely involvement of village‑raised pigs
Event.summary: In 2005, a major outbreak of trichinellosis occurred in Udomxay Province in northern Laos after funeral and wedding ceremonies at which villagers consumed raw or fermented pork, with an estimated ≥650 people affected and more than 600 probable cases identified over the following year; no deaths were reported but many patients required hospital care. Serologic testing of suspected cases showed a high proportion with anti‑Trichinella antibodies, and muscle larvae of Trichinella spiralis were detected in at least one local pig not directly linked to the ceremonies, indicating established transmission in the local pig population. The outbreak revealed that trichinellosis was likely highly endemic yet under‑recognised in northern Laos and prompted calls for improved veterinary control and consumer education.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: free‑roaming smallholder pig husbandry with pigs accessing potentially infected carcasses or waste, cultural practices of sharing raw or fermented pork at communal ceremonies, low access to veterinary inspection and diagnostic services, and limited awareness of trichinellosis among health workers and communities, all of which allowed a large common‑source outbreak once heavily infected pork entered village feasts. Internal mechanisms: the causative species was identified as T. spiralis, with no evidence of new strains or resistance; the event is therefore best seen as a dramatic re‑occurrence in a setting where the parasite had likely long circulated undetected, brought to light by heightened clinical and serologic investigation.
Review: retain – Added this Laos episode because outbreak investigations estimated at least ~650 human trichinellosis cases in Udomxay in 2005, making it the largest documented outbreak in Southeast Asia and one of the major post‑1990 events globally; the outbreak also revealed previously unrecognised endemicity in northern Laos.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7611085/?utm_source=openai)) Coded as re‑occurrence in South‑eastern Asia (long‑standing but under‑detected circulation) rather than first detection; country name and sub‑region follow the UNSD list.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis (human infection with Trichinella spp.)
Countries: China [2006] (Yunnan Province; imported pork from Laos)
Host: Humans; pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as principal source animals via imported pork
Event.summary: In December 2006, Yunnan Province in southwestern China recorded an outbreak of 49 human trichinellosis cases linked to pork imported from neighbouring Laos, which was identified as the first documented imported trichinellosis outbreak in China. Clusters of patients developed febrile myalgia and eosinophilia after shared meals containing undercooked pork, and investigations confirmed Trichinella larvae in leftover meat, while tracing showed that the meat had been brought in informally from across the Lao border. The outbreak subsided after remaining suspect meat was withdrawn, affected patients were treated and cross‑border trade in uninspected pork was more closely scrutinised.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: informal cross‑border trade in inadequately inspected pork from Laos into Yunnan, absence of systematic Trichinella testing for such imported meat, and culinary practices in rural communities that favour raw or lightly cooked pork, all of which enabled introduction of heavily infected meat into a consumer population with limited risk awareness. Internal mechanisms: available data do not indicate a novel genotype or altered virulence; the episode is best interpreted as a geographic re‑occurrence of classic T. spiralis infection associated with regional pork trade rather than a biologically driven re‑emergence.
Review: review – Corrected the geographic coding by treating this as an outbreak in China (Yunnan) linked to imported pork from Laos, and therefore listing only China in the country field and restricting the sub‑region to Eastern Asia; Laos is better handled as the source of meat and now has its own major 2005 outbreak event.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21324302/?utm_source=openai)) The event remains coded as a notable re‑occurrence and the first recorded imported trichinellosis outbreak in China, but its case count (49) is modest compared with the new large multi‑year waves; retain or down‑select depending on how strictly the top‑10 criterion is enforced.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis (human infection with Trichinella spp.)
Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as source animals
Event.summary: In 2009, Lanping County in Yunnan Province, China, experienced a trichinellosis outbreak in which many residents developed fever, myalgia and eosinophilia after communal meals involving raw or undercooked pork, with laboratory confirmation of Trichinella infection in human sera and pork samples. The event formed part of a series of outbreaks reported from southwestern China in the 2000s, underscoring the persistently high burden of trichinellosis in Yunnan and surrounding areas where consumption of traditional raw pork dishes and backyard pig production remain common. Intensive case finding, antiparasitic treatment, health education and local improvements in meat inspection and pig‑rearing practices eventually halted transmission in the affected communities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: subsistence‑level pig production with inadequate housing and feeding, slaughter and distribution of pork outside formal inspection systems, and cultural traditions in parts of Yunnan for eating raw or lightly cooked pork during festivals and communal events, all of which repeatedly introduce infected pork into the human food chain. Internal mechanisms: available reports do not demonstrate a novel lineage or resistance phenotype; this outbreak is representative of ongoing re‑occurrence in an endemic focus driven mainly by food‑production and cultural factors.
Review: review – This Yunnan outbreak is consistent with Chinese national summaries that document multiple outbreaks (15 outbreaks, 1,387 cases and 4 deaths in southwestern provinces during 2004–2009), but the available literature suggests that it was one of several medium‑sized outbreaks rather than uniquely large.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21324302/?utm_source=openai)) Recommend keeping it as a representative example of the sustained high burden in Yunnan, but its relative impact should be reassessed against larger national or regional episodes when enforcing a strict top‑10 list.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis (human infection with Trichinella spp.)
Countries: Argentina [2010] (Pueblo General Belgrano and Gualeguaychú, Entre Ríos Province)
Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) and possibly other local domestic animals as sources
Event.summary: In July–August 2010, an outbreak of human trichinellosis occurred in the village of Pueblo General Belgrano and the nearby city of Gualeguaychú in Entre Ríos Province, Argentina, affecting 64 individuals after consumption of locally produced pork products from pigs slaughtered outside official inspection. The area had previously been regarded as free of Trichinella for more than 20 years, but outbreak investigations showed both human infections and the presence of Trichinella spiralis larvae in pigs and game animals, indicating an established local transmission cycle. Control measures included recall of implicated pork, testing and culling of infected animals, strengthened surveillance and intensive public education, which curtailed further human cases and highlighted the need not to assume absence of risk in nominally ‘Trichinella‑free’ zones.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of small‑scale pig and game‑animal production with inadequate biosecurity and meat inspection in a region considered low‑risk, informal marketing and home processing of pork products, and consumption of undercooked or poorly cured sausages. Internal mechanisms: molecular typing confirmed T. spiralis, a long‑established species in Argentina, without evidence of novel traits; the event is therefore interpreted as a re‑occurrence in a previously quiescent local focus driven by surveillance gaps and food‑safety practices, rather than parasite evolution.
Review: review – The Entre Ríos outbreak (64 confirmed cases) is accurately described and important because it revealed established transmission in a province officially considered Trichinella‑free, but it is smaller than the newly added national‑scale Argentine caseload (5,217 cases in 1990–1999).([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S030440171400003X)) Retain it as a key local re‑occurrence illustrating hidden foci, but consider whether it should remain in a strict top‑10 list now that major multi‑year episodes have been added.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis (human infection with Trichinella spp.)
Host: Humans; domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) and wild boar (Sus scrofa) as sources
Event.summary: In 2013, Lancang County in Yunnan Province, China, experienced another substantial trichinellosis outbreak associated with consumption of undercooked pork and possibly wild boar meat at communal events, with dozens of symptomatic cases presenting with myalgia, fever and eosinophilia. Trichinella infection was confirmed in human sera and in leftover meat, reinforcing evidence of persistent intense transmission in this region of southwestern China where domestic and sylvatic cycles overlap. Local authorities intensified surveillance, enforced meat inspection standards and issued risk‑communication campaigns about safe preparation of pork and game, bringing the outbreak under control but not eliminating the underlying endemic risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: continued high‑risk food practices involving raw or undercooked pork and wild boar, extensive overlap between domestic pig herds and wildlife reservoirs, and incomplete coverage of veterinary inspection in rural and mountainous areas, permitting heavily infected meat to reach consumers during festivals and communal meals. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel genotype or resistance phenotype has been described for this outbreak; it is another example of repeated re‑occurrence in a persistent endemic focus shaped by social and husbandry factors.
Review: review – This event is consistent with Chinese summaries that describe multiple outbreaks in Yunnan during the 2000s and early 2010s, but available data do not indicate that the Lancang outbreak was uniquely large relative to other Chinese clusters or to the newly added Romanian, Bulgarian, Argentine and Laotian waves.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21324302/?utm_source=openai)) It should be retained as an illustrative example of ongoing intense transmission in southwestern China, but its inclusion in a strict top‑10 list should be revisited.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alcelaphine gammaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Bali cattle in smallholder mixed farms; nearby sheep and goats as OvHV‑2 reservoirs
Event.summary: In 2016, veterinary services investigated reports of sudden deaths among Bali cattle in Musi Rawas District, South Sumatra, Indonesia, where affected animals showed fever, ocular and nasal discharge and erosive oral lesions consistent with malignant catarrhal fever. Field epidemiology linked the outbreak to close proximity of susceptible Bali cattle to small ruminants, and laboratory testing implicated OvHV‑2 infection, with multiple cattle in affected villages dying over a short period. Control efforts focused on movement restrictions, advising farmers to separate Bali cattle from lambing sheep and goats, and local awareness campaigns, although technical reports note that sporadic MCF cases continue to be reported from other Indonesian provinces.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of mixed smallholder systems in South Sumatra where Bali cattle are kept in close proximity to growing populations of sheep and goats, often with free‑range management and minimal biosecurity, together with low farmer awareness of MCF and the risk posed by lambing sheep. Internal mechanisms: High inherent susceptibility of Bali cattle to SA‑MCF caused by OvHV‑2 circulating in Indonesian sheep, with high viral load in lambs and intense close contact driving localized outbreaks with high case fatality; no evidence has been published for emergence of new OvHV‑2 genotypes in this setting.
Review: Review: Outbreak reports and provincial risk‑management documents support a 2016 SA‑MCF episode in Bali cattle in Musi Rawas (South Sumatra), but detailed numbers of affected and dead animals in English are limited. Geographic coding (Asia → South‑eastern Asia → Indonesia) and classification as a re‑occurrence in an already endemic country are appropriate. Recommend a native‑language reviewer confirm herd sizes and mortality to judge whether this episode ranks among Indonesia’s largest documented MCF outbreaks and should be retained in a strict top‑10 list.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alcelaphine gammaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Malignant catarrhal fever virus, MCF virus
Host: Bali cattle on smallholder farms; nearby lambing sheep as OvHV‑2 reservoir
Event.summary: Between January and September 2016, an outbreak of malignant catarrhal fever was documented in 231 Bali cattle on Lombok Island, West Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia. Twenty cattle died during the episode, 16 of which showed classical clinical signs including high fever, corneal opacity, mucopurulent nasal discharge, hypersalivation, enlarged superficial lymph nodes and characteristic necrotizing vasculitis on histopathology; nested PCR detected OvHV‑2 in peripheral blood leukocytes of surviving clinically affected cattle and in nasal, ocular and vaginal swabs from nearby adult sheep. The outbreak waned after the deaths and emergency culling, and control recommendations emphasized separating Bali cattle from lambing sheep and improving farmer awareness, with subsequent reports recognizing MCF as an endemic threat to Bali cattle in multiple Indonesian provinces.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of mixed sheep–Bali cattle systems on Lombok with minimal separation between species, particularly during lambing, combined with relatively high stocking densities and housing that facilitated aerosol spread of ovine nasal secretions to cattle. Internal mechanisms: Established OvHV‑2 infection in Indonesian sheep spilling over into highly susceptible Bali cattle, producing high case fatality without clear evidence of a novel genotype; the outbreak’s severity reflects the inherent susceptibility of Bali cattle and management factors rather than recent viral evolution.
Review: Review: Corrected a major dating error. The cited Jurnal Veteriner paper clearly documents a Bali cattle MCF outbreak on Lombok Island occurring from January to September 2016 with 20 deaths among 231 cattle, not an early‑2000s event; the Event Year has been updated to '2016' and the country annotation revised to 'Indonesia [2016] (Lombok Island, West Nusa Tenggara)'. Confidence has been raised to reflect the strong primary data. Classification as a re‑occurrence of SA‑MCF in an already endemic Indonesian context remains appropriate. Recommended for curator verification of mortality figures and confirmation that this outbreak is among the country’s largest documented MCF episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Anaplasma marginale
EPP.common.name: Bovine anaplasmosis
Host: Beef cattle (mixed-age herd of 75 animals)
Event.summary: In late summer–early autumn 2009, a 75-head beef herd in northern Hungary developed an outbreak of bovine anaplasmosis in which Anaplasma marginale was first recognized in blood smears of 51 cattle and 5 animals showed acute clinical disease with lethargy, ruminal atony, anemia and organ pathology; 2 cows died within three days, and PCR showed at least 92% of animals were bacteraemic. Molecular typing of the msp4 gene revealed three previously undescribed A. marginale genotypes circulating in the herd and in Dermacentor reticulatus and Ixodes ricinus ticks, alongside concurrent infection with haemotropic mycoplasmas (“Candidatus Mycoplasma haemobos” and Mycoplasma wenyonii). Control measures focused on oxytetracycline treatment and tick removal, and the outbreak highlighted destabilisation of an endemic but subclinical situation by introduction of naïve cattle and novel A. marginale variants.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Frequent introduction of newly purchased, naïve cattle into an area with established but subclinical A. marginale circulation disrupted endemic stability, while heavy tick infestation (especially D. reticulatus) facilitated rapid spread within the herd. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of several new A. marginale msp4 genotypes in the herd, together with widespread co-infection by haemotropic mycoplasmas, likely increased pathogenicity and contributed to the fatal clinical presentation, meeting the definition of re-emergence driven by pathogen genetic change and co-infection.
Review: Review: New event added because the 2009 northern Hungary outbreak is a well-characterised, high-prevalence (≈92% of 75 cattle) and partially fatal episode associated with novel A. marginale genotypes and concurrent haemoplasmosis, and is repeatedly cited as a key European emergence event. Classified as re-emergence (novel strain/genotype emergence in an already affected sub-region) rather than intra-continental emergence, since A. marginale was already endemic in Eastern Europe. Recommend retaining as one of the top global emergence/re-emergence events, but final inclusion should be confirmed by comparing its impact against other large Latin American or African outbreaks not individually documented here.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Anaplasma marginale
EPP.common.name: Bovine anaplasmosis
Host: Dairy cattle (≈680 lactating Holstein cows)
Event.summary: In 2010, a large confinement dairy herd in northern Iowa (≈680 lactating Holstein cows) experienced a clinically recognized outbreak of bovine anaplasmosis, with many adult cows developing fever, anemia, weight loss and decreased milk production, prompting culling or death in a notable proportion of affected animals. Serologic follow-up in 2011 showed about 38% of cows seropositive for A. marginale, while roughly two-thirds of the herd remained susceptible, indicating substantial within-herd spread during the outbreak. Epidemiologic investigation implicated both tick exposure and iatrogenic mechanical transmission through reuse of needles and multi-dose oxytocin vials, and subsequent management changes (eliminating needle sharing, improved biosecurity and vector control) reduced clinical cases, although previously infected cows had persistently reduced milk yields in subsequent lactations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density confinement management, reuse of blood-contaminated needles and injection equipment, and presence of competent tick vectors in a region where bovine anaplasmosis had historically been considered of lower concern led to efficient within-herd spread among adult cows. Internal mechanisms: No novel A. marginale genotypes were implicated; the outbreak’s impact derived mainly from high force of infection in immunologically naïve adult animals, resulting in severe clinical disease and long-term subclinical carrier states with measurable production losses.
Review: Retain: Large, well-documented within-herd outbreak in a >600-cow U.S. dairy with clear evidence of economic impact (sustained milk loss) and mixed tick/iatrogenic transmission, consistent with a major re-occurrence event in a partially naïve herd in an endemic country. Geographic (Northern America) and temporal information match the primary sources, and the event is reasonably among the most impactful post‑1990 emergence episodes for this pathogen in North America.

EPP.scientific.name: Anaplasma marginale
EPP.common.name: Bovine anaplasmosis
Host: Dairy cattle (adult mixed-age cows)
Event.summary: In 2013, the long-established San Miguel dairy farm in the municipality of Nariño, highland southern Colombia, reported its first-ever acute outbreak of bovine anaplasmosis after more than 50 years of cattle production without known cases, with 37 clinical cases and 6 deaths among predominantly high-producing adult cows. During the critical phase, affected animals showed fever, marked drops in milk yield, anorexia, emaciation, abortions and sudden deaths, and blood smears confirmed A. marginale with severe hemolytic anemia. Intensive treatment and improved vector control eventually halted the outbreak, but high abortion rates and abrupt cessation of milk production in surviving cows produced major economic losses and were interpreted locally as evidence of tick-borne disease expansion into previously cooler Andean zones.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional climate change and variability in the tropical Andes likely facilitated altitudinal expansion of tick vectors and A. marginale into historically cool, highland areas, and decades without exposure left the herd immunologically naïve. Internal mechanisms: No new A. marginale genotype was described; the event is better explained as geographic range expansion and exposure of adult naïve cattle, fitting the definition of re-occurrence driven by external climatic and management factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain: Case report clearly documents a sizeable acute outbreak with deaths, abortions and major production loss in a historically anaplasmosis-free Andean dairy area, aligning with a re-occurrence/range-expansion event in South America. Country, sub-region and timing are correct, and the event is among the relatively few well-quantified, high-impact emergence episodes in Latin American highlands since 1990.

EPP.scientific.name: Anaplasma marginale
EPP.common.name: Bovine anaplasmosis
Host: Lactating dairy cattle (local dairy herd)
Event.summary: In March and again in September 2015, a dairy herd in Kırklareli Province in the Thrace region of Türkiye experienced an outbreak of bovine anaplasmosis in which 30 lactating cows developed fever, anemia, reduced milk yield, anorexia and respiratory distress, and A. marginale infection was confirmed by PCR. Genotyping of the major surface protein genes revealed several novel msp1a genotypes of A. marginale in the herd, and examination of placental tissues provided evidence of transplacental transmission to calves. After targeted therapy and reinforced tick control and herd management, clinical cases resolved, but the presence of highly pathogenic variants and vertical transmission indicated a worrisome re-emergence pattern with significant production losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional abundance of competent ticks and possible introduction of infected animals or ticks into the herd likely seeded new A. marginale variants into adult dairy cows with limited prior immunity. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of novel A. marginale msp1a genotypes associated with severe clinical disease and probable placental (vertical) transmission demonstrates pathogen evolution toward enhanced pathogenicity and transmission, justifying classification as re-emergence with internal genetic change rather than simple re-occurrence.
Review: Retain: Strongly supported by peer-reviewed data as an outbreak with novel genotypes and evidence of vertical transmission in a dairy herd, exemplifying re-emergence via pathogen genetic diversification in Western Asia. Country, sub-region and timing are appropriate under the UN classification used in the Country sheet (Türkiye in Western Asia). No corrections required beyond pruning less directly relevant secondary citations.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Anaplasma marginale
EPP.common.name: Bovine anaplasmosis
Countries: Croatia [2018] (Glina area and a second continental herd)
Host: Beef cattle (Simmental cows and other local breeds)
Event.summary: From June to July 2018, a beef herd of about 50 Simmental cows near Glina in continental Croatia had an outbreak in which five adult cows died acutely with fever, anemia and icterus; spleen imprints and PCR confirmed A. marginale infection, representing the first indigenous lethal bovine anaplasmosis reported in Croatian cattle. A contemporaneous outbreak in another Croatian herd involved three cows that died from co-infection with A. bovis and Theileria orientalis, further demonstrating establishment of multiple tick-borne haemoparasites in local cattle. Following recognition of these outbreaks, Croatian veterinarians updated differential diagnoses and implemented stricter tick control and management practices to prevent additional lethal episodes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increasing presence of competent ticks (e.g. Dermacentor reticulatus) in continental Croatia and extensive pasture grazing promoted exposure of older, naïve cattle to A. marginale and other tick-borne agents; limited prior clinical recognition delayed diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: No unique Croatian A. marginale lineage was reported; severe outcomes likely reflected infection of older animals and synergistic effects of co-infections (particularly A. bovis and T. orientalis) rather than clear pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain: The Croatian outbreaks provided the first reports of indigenous lethal bovine anaplasmosis in that country and signalled establishment of A. marginale and other tick-borne haemoparasites in continental Southern Europe. Sub-region and country assignments are correct, and classifying this as re-occurrence (rather than intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because A. marginale had long been present in other Southern European countries. No structural corrections required.

EPP.scientific.name: Anaplasma marginale
EPP.common.name: Bovine anaplasmosis
Countries: Poland [2021] (Białowieża Primeval Forest and Knyszyńska Forest)
Host: European bison (Bison bonasus), with potential spillover relevance for cattle
Event.summary: In 2021, blood samples from free-ranging European bison in north-eastern Poland (Białowieża Primeval Forest and Knyszyńska Forest) were found by PCR and sequencing of the msp4 gene to be infected with Anaplasma marginale, marking the first confirmed occurrence of this pathogen in Poland, the first report in European bison, and the northernmost confirmed A. marginale record in Europe. Prevalence of A. marginale in sampled bison was about 17.8%, and phylogenetic analysis showed that the genotypes clustered with A. marginale strains from cattle in Hungary, Africa and Russia rather than with North or South American strains. Although no mass mortality event was described, the discovery revealed an autochthonous A. marginale cycle in a strictly protected wild bovid population and raised concern that bison could act as reservoirs posing spillover risk to sympatric cattle as the pathogen expands its range northward.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Northward expansion of competent tick vectors (e.g. Dermacentor reticulatus) and increasing spatial overlap between recovering European bison populations and cattle grazing areas in north-eastern Poland likely facilitated spillover and maintenance of A. marginale. Climate warming and land-use changes in Eastern Europe may be contributing to northward extension of both tick and pathogen ranges. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion from cattle into European bison represents re-emergence in a new wild host species within an already affected sub-region; phylogenetic evidence suggests recent cross-species transmission of cattle-like A. marginale genotypes rather than a long-standing, bison-adapted lineage.
Review: Review: Event year corrected from 2025 (publication year) to 2021 (sample collection year) based on the Parasites & Vectors article, and the country bracket updated accordingly. The event is appropriately classified as re-emergence via host expansion in Eastern Europe rather than intra-continental emergence, because A. marginale was previously established in neighboring Hungary. Two less relevant citations (a general South African A. marginale/A. centrale review and a paper on A. phagocytophilum in bison) have been removed from the event-level Source URLs to focus on the primary bison report and its bibliographic index. Recommended for retention as an important host-expansion event, but not a mass-mortality outbreak.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Babesia bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine babesiosis
Countries: Brazil [2007] (Rio Grande do Sul state, Picada Café municipality)
Host: Beef heifers (Bos taurus / crossbred) recently introduced to endemic tick areas; Rhipicephalus microplus as vector
Event.summary: In April 2007, a severe cerebral babesiosis outbreak caused by Babesia bovis occurred in a herd of 55 heifers recently brought onto a farm in Picada Café, Rio Grande do Sul, an area where bovine babesiosis is endemic.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29)) Within five days, 28 animals (50.9%) died after acute fever, neurological signs, anemia and red‑coloured urine, and necropsy showed characteristic cherry‑pink discoloration of the gray matter of the brain with capillaries heavily congested by B. bovis‑infected erythrocytes.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29)) Treatment of remaining cattle with imidocarb dipropionate, together with tick control and management changes, prevented further deaths during at least two months of follow‑up, after which surviving animals were sent to slaughter.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of immunologically naïve heifers into an area with heavy R. microplus infestation, along with management and environmental conditions favouring intense tick challenge, likely precipitated this high‑mortality cluster of cerebral babesiosis in an otherwise endemic region.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29)) Internal mechanisms: The pathology and clinical pattern are consistent with typical highly virulent B. bovis strains that sequester in cerebral capillaries; no evidence was presented for a novel genotype or drug‑resistant phenotype, so this episode is best interpreted as a severe re‑occurrence in an endemic area rather than a genetically driven re‑emergence.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29))
Review: This row describes a well‑documented but highly localised outbreak confined to a single herd (28 deaths among 55 heifers over five days) in an area where Babesia bovis is already endemic.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122436/records/67598357c7a957febdf9fe29)) While clinically severe, its geographic scale and duration are small relative to continent‑wide spread or multi‑country emergence events; accordingly, it is unlikely to be among the ten most impactful global emergence episodes for B. bovis. Recommended decision: exclude from the final prioritised top‑ten event list, but retain the row in the working dataset as an example of severe re‑occurrence in an endemic South American setting and as a reference for cerebral babesiosis case descriptions.
Review.Comment: we still keep althought it might not be the top 10 most impactful event

EPP.scientific.name: Babesia bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine babesiosis
Host: Indigenous and improved cattle breeds in smallholder and pastoral systems along the Kenyan coast; R. microplus and other ticks as vectors
Event.summary: Between roughly 2013 and 2020, cross‑sectional molecular surveys of 506 cattle in Kwale County on the Kenyan coast detected Babesia bovis DNA in 17.2% of animals, providing the first detailed evidence that this highly pathogenic species is present at substantial levels in Kenyan herds where bovine babesiosis had previously been attributed mainly to B. bigemina.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai)) The study showed marked spatial variation in infection prevalence across sub‑counties and coincided with recent records of the invasive tick Rhipicephalus microplus in the same region, raising concerns that babesiosis risk could increase along this busy livestock trade corridor linking Kenya and Tanzania.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai)) Although most sampled cattle were clinically normal when bled, the authors warned that high underlying infection pressure could precipitate severe B. bovis outbreaks in susceptible herds and called for stronger surveillance and tick‑control programmes.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and spread of R. microplus into coastal Kenya via cross‑border movements of infested cattle, combined with expanding smallholder and commercial cattle production in humid coastal environments favourable for ticks, have increased opportunities for B. bovis transmission where earlier tick communities limited its impact.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Current evidence suggests geographic range expansion and enhanced transmission mediated by an invasive vector rather than a novel parasite strain; nevertheless, continuing evolution and local adaptation of B. bovis populations in East Africa remain possible and justify continued molecular surveillance.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain as a significant detection/re‑occurrence event but correct the event typing. The Parasites & Vectors study reports that Babesia bovis DNA had already been detected in Kenyan cattle before this survey and describes it as the first detailed report of a substantial level of occurrence, not the first detection in the host system; the 'first_detection' field has therefore been set to No.([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13071-022-05279-7?utm_source=openai)) Because B. bovis was documented in other parts of Eastern Africa, including Tanzania and the islands of Pemba and Unguja, well before 1990, this episode does not qualify as intra‑continental emergence at the UNSD sub‑region scale; that flag has been set to No and the event reclassified as a re‑occurrence linked to the recent invasion of R. microplus and changing tick ecology in coastal Kenya.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1702568/?utm_source=openai)) Event‑level source URLs have been focused on the Kenyan molecular survey and African tick‑range/epidemiology reviews; non‑specific references such as generic Wikipedia tick pages have been removed from this row.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bluetongue virus
EPP.common.name: BTV
Host: Primarily domestic sheep in southern India; goats and cattle infected but with much lower apparent clinical impact
Event.summary: In 1997, severe bluetongue outbreaks due to multiple serotypes (notably BTV‑1, ‑2 and ‑23) erupted among sheep flocks across Tamil Nadu, a state where the virus had been endemic since the 1980s, leading to rapid spread through densely stocked, largely unvaccinated rural flocks. Through 1997–1998 the epizootic caused extensive morbidity and exceptionally high mortality in small ruminants, with more than 300,000 sheep deaths reported by state authorities, before natural immunity, ad‑hoc movement controls and early vaccination efforts gradually reduced transmission. After 1998, bluetongue became an entrenched seasonal problem in southern India with recurrent but generally less catastrophic outbreaks, and efforts shifted toward development and deployment of multivalent inactivated vaccines tailored to the serotypes circulating in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Endemic presence of BTV in southern India combined with high densities of susceptible indigenous and crossbred sheep, communal grazing, and abundant Culicoides vector populations during monsoon and post‑monsoon periods; limited early vaccination and reliance on clinical recognition favoured rapid amplification once climatic conditions triggered vector population booms. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of several virulent serotypes (including BTV‑1, ‑2 and ‑23) in largely naïve flocks, but no clear evidence that a fundamentally new genotype or host shift was responsible; this episode is best interpreted as a dramatic climatic and management‑driven re‑occurrence of an established pathogen rather than a true genetic re‑emergence.
Review: Decision: retain. Reasoning: Added as a new event because the 1997–1998 Tamil Nadu epidemic caused >300,000 sheep deaths and is clearly among the most impactful bluetongue episodes globally since 1990, yet was missing from the original dataset. Classified as re‑occurrence (not intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or re‑emergence) because BTV had been endemic in India since the 1960s and there is no strong evidence that a novel strain or host shift, rather than climatic and husbandry factors, drove this severe wave. Country and timing are constrained to Tamil Nadu, India [1997], based on state‑level reports; broader Indian endemicity is not treated as separate events. This row should be reviewed by an expert familiar with Indian field data to validate impact estimates and confirm that no even larger Indian outbreak after 1990 has been overlooked.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia spp.
EPP.common.name: Lyme borreliosis
Countries: Brazil [1992] (initially São Paulo state, then additional autochthonous foci in Rio de Janeiro and other southeastern, central-western, southern and Amazonian regions)
Host: Humans, with evidence of infection or exposure in horses, dogs and cattle; transmitted mainly by Amblyomma and Rhipicephalus ticks rather than Ixodes, with Borrelia burgdorferi-like organisms associated with Baggio–Yoshinari syndrome (Brazilian Lyme-like borreliosis).
Event.summary: In 1992, Brazil reported the first locally acquired Lyme-like borreliosis cases in siblings from Cotia (São Paulo state) who developed erythema migrans, flu-like illness and arthritis after tick bites, with positive serology for Borrelia burgdorferi, marking the first recognized autochthonous Borrelia-associated borreliosis in South America. Through the 1990s and 2000s, additional human cases with similar clinical pictures were identified in multiple Brazilian regions and the syndrome was formally described and renamed Baggio–Yoshinari syndrome, while surveys detected Borrelia DNA or serologic evidence of exposure in horses, dogs and cattle in endemic areas, indicating a broader zoonotic cycle. By around 2015, Brazilian borreliosis/Baggio–Yoshinari syndrome was recognized as a controversial but persistent emerging tick-borne zoonosis distinct from classical Northern Hemisphere Lyme borreliosis, with endemic foci in several states and ongoing debate over the etiologic agent and case definitions rather than a clearly resolved outbreak end.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of human activity into tick-infested rural and peri-urban environments in southeastern and other regions of Brazil; high contact between humans, dogs, horses and cattle and Amblyomma and Rhipicephalus ticks in pasture and forest-edge settings; and limited early clinical awareness and diagnostic tools resulting in under-recognition and delayed control. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and possible novel strain/genotype emergence, with evidence that Brazilian cases involve Borrelia burgdorferi-like spirochetes adapted to non-Ixodes hard ticks and possibly altered morphologic or antigenic features; enhanced transmission via abundant non-Ixodes vectors; and potential geographic range expansion within Brazil as ticks and reservoir hosts occupy varied ecosystems. The syndrome is often considered distinct from classic Lyme borreliosis, but is treated here as an inter-continental emergence of Borrelia-associated Lyme-like borreliosis in a new ecological and vector context in South America.
Review: review – This row is retained as the first clearly described autochthonous Lyme-like borreliosis/Baggio–Yoshinari syndrome event in South America, with documented human disease and evidence of exposure in horses, dogs and cattle, and it is appropriately coded as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence because it marks the first recognized occurrence of a Borrelia-associated Lyme-like zoonosis on this continent. The time span, country attribution (Brazil), and host description are consistent with clinical series and reviews, and there is no indication that this is a spurious or minor event relative to other first-detection episodes. However, there is substantial ongoing debate over whether the Brazilian agent(s) should be regarded as classical Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato or a distinct Borrelia entity, and case numbers remain much lower than in North America and Europe; for these reasons, I recommend keeping the event but flagging it for review when harmonizing taxonomy and inclusion criteria across EPPs.
