EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter fetus
EPP.common.name: Bovine genital campylobacteriosis
Host: Dairy cows in herds using natural service in the state of Pernambuco, Brazil
Event.summary: In 2013, a PCR‑based prevalence study of bovine genital campylobacteriosis and bovine trichomonosis in the state of Pernambuco, northeastern Brazil, analysed cervico‑vaginal mucus from 383 dairy cows in 21 herds. Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis DNA was detected in 1.8% of cows, and at least one positive cow was found in 28.6% of herds, while Tritrichomonas foetus DNA was identified in about one‑third of cows and over 90% of herds, confirming venereal pathogens as important contributors to reproductive inefficiency in the region. Herds larger than 100 animals and reliance on natural breeding were identified as significant risk factors for BGC, leading to recommendations for improved biosecurity, greater use of artificial insemination and, where feasible, testing and culling of bulls to mitigate venereal disease‑related production losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive and semi‑intensive dairy systems in Pernambuco that rely on natural mating, large herd size, limited veterinary infrastructure and diagnostic capacity, and frequent mixing of animals all favoured the maintenance and spread of Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis and Tritrichomonas foetus; the absence of systematic venereal disease control programmes meant infections remained largely unrecognised until targeted surveys were undertaken. Internal mechanisms: this episode reflects endemic persistence of established C. fetus subsp. venerealis lineages, with improved molecular diagnostics (PCR) revealing infections that may have been under‑detected by earlier methods, rather than emergence of novel genetic variants.
Review: Decision: Review. The underlying event corresponds to the 2013 PCR‑based study of bovine genital campylobacteriosis and trichomonosis in dairy cows from 21 herds in Pernambuco, Brazil, but the original row mis‑stated several details. I changed the Event Year from 2015 to 2013 to reflect the sampling period rather than the publication date and corrected the host description from 'breeding bulls and cattle herds' to 'dairy cows in herds using natural service', because only cervico‑vaginal mucus from cows was sampled. The event summary was re‑written to report the published prevalences (≈1.8% of cows PCR‑positive for C. fetus subsp. venerealis and 28.6% of herds with at least one positive cow) and to clarify that herd size >100 and natural breeding were risk factors. Coding as re‑occurrence remains appropriate given Brazil’s long history of BGC; there is no evidence of new introduction or novel strain emergence. The source list was streamlined to focus on the primary Pernambuco paper plus the regional South America review that contextualises these findings.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Campylobacter fetus
EPP.common.name: Bovine genital campylobacteriosis
Host: Breeding bulls in beef and dual‑purpose herds in central Tamaulipas, Mexico
Event.summary: In 2022 (published 2023), a study of breeding bulls in the central zone of Tamaulipas, Mexico, examined semen and preputial samples and detected Campylobacter fetus, including Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis associated with bovine genital campylobacteriosis, by PCR and sequencing, documenting affected herds with reproductive problems. The authors emphasised that this represented the first report of C. fetus subsp. venerealis in Mexico confirmed by molecular methods and argued that venereal campylobacteriosis had likely been an unrecognised contributor to infertility and early embryonic loss in local cattle for some time. The work spurred calls for broader surveillance, routine testing of breeding bulls and strengthened control measures to prevent further spread and to improve reproductive outcomes in Mexican cattle systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: reliance on natural mating in many Mexican beef and dual‑purpose herds, limited routine pre‑breeding testing of bulls for venereal pathogens, low awareness of bovine genital campylobacteriosis among producers and veterinarians, and historically scarce access to molecular diagnostics allowed long‑standing but largely undetected circulation of Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis. Increasing availability of PCR‑based tests triggered recognition of infections in regions such as Tamaulipas. Internal mechanisms: this episode primarily reflects improved molecular detection of an established pathogen in Mexican herds, rather than emergence of a novel strain, with venereal transmission and chronic colonisation of the bull genital tract underpinning reproductive losses before laboratory confirmation.
Review: Decision: Review. The 2023 SciELO study from central Tamaulipas does provide the first molecular confirmation of Campylobacter fetus (including C. fetus subsp. venerealis) in Mexican breeding bulls and supports the view that BGC has been under‑diagnosed in this region. However, bovine genital campylobacteriosis was already documented in Mexico long before this work, for example a 1975 bacteriological investigation of bovine genital vibriosis in Sonora beef herds and later sero‑epidemiological studies in tropical Mexican cattle, so this episode cannot be considered the first detection of the pathogen in the country. I therefore set first_detection to No and interpret the event as a re‑occurrence / re‑documentation of an endemic infection revealed by improved molecular diagnostics. The summary was adjusted to emphasise that the study reports the first PCR‑based confirmation in Mexico rather than true first occurrence. The source URLs were updated to include both the recent Tamaulipas molecular study and an earlier Mexican bacteriological report to substantiate this reinterpretation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Caprine arthritis encephalitis virus
EPP.common.name: CAEV, Small ruminant lentivirus
Countries: Japan [2002] (Nagano Prefecture index farm; national surveys [2002-2004])
Host: Domestic goats (dairy and meat breeds)
Event.summary: In 2002, caprine arthritis/encephalitis was detected for the first time in Japan in a large dairy goat herd in Nagano Prefecture, where numerous goats showed carpal arthritis and occasional pneumonia and CAEV infection was confirmed by histopathology, serology and virus isolation. Subsequent national surveillance from 2002 to 2004 found about one-fifth of 3,102 tested goats seropositive, indicating that the virus had already spread beyond the index herd and was present at low-to-moderate prevalence in multiple Japanese herds. Control on the affected farm and nationally relied on testing and culling or segregation of positives, kid-rearing and colostrum management, and movement restrictions, which reduced prevalence substantially but did not completely eradicate CAEV from Japan.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected breeding stock into what had been assumed to be a CAE‑free national herd, probably via international trade in high-yield dairy goats, combined with intensification in a few large herds that facilitated close contact, shared milking equipment and kid-rearing practices favouring lactogenic transmission. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was reported; persistence of infection and efficient milk‑borne and horizontal transmission typical of CAEV enabled several years of silent spread in Japan before the first clinical outbreak was recognised.
Review: retain – corrected the emergence-type classification: intra_continental_emergence was set from true to false because CAEV had already been present in the same UN subregion (Eastern Asia) in China since 1988, so Japan represents spread to a new country within an already affected subregion rather than a new subregion. Marked this instead as a major regional re_occurrence (true) reflecting renewed detection and substantial prevalence in Eastern Asia. Slightly broadened the year range to 2002–2004 to align with the documented outbreak and early national surveys, but left geography and impact description unchanged; event is clearly among the major post‑1990 CAEV episodes and should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Caprine arthritis encephalitis virus
EPP.common.name: CAEV, Small ruminant lentivirus
Countries: Thailand [2011] (Ratchaburi, Phetchaburi, Kanchanaburi provinces – western Thailand)
Host: Domestic goats (smallholder and commercial herds)
Event.summary: In 2011, a cross‑sectional serological survey in the western part of Thailand (Ratchaburi, Phetchaburi and Kanchanaburi provinces) revealed that CAEV antibodies were present in goats, with an individual‑animal seroprevalence of about 5–6% and higher herd-level prevalence, providing one of the first clear demonstrations that CAEV was circulating in Thai goat populations. The study identified older age, larger herd size and introduction of new goats as significant risk factors for seropositivity, indicating ongoing transmission dynamics within and between herds in these western border provinces. Awareness of CAEV in Thailand increased following these findings, and recommendations were made for improved movement control, testing of new stock, and enhanced kid‑rearing management to curb further spread; however, subsequent national surveys still detect SRLV infection, showing that CAEV remains endemic at low to moderate levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of goat production and cross‑border trade of animals in western Thailand; herd expansion via purchase of replacement stock from multiple sources was statistically associated with infection. Internal mechanisms: Standard CAEV/SRLV biology – lifelong persistent infection, late seroconversion and efficient lactogenic and horizontal transmission – contributed to under‑recognition and ongoing endemic circulation rather than any novel genotype or virulence shift.
Review: review/exclude – this survey is an important early documentation of CAEV in Thai goats but is smaller in scale and shows lower prevalence than several other events now included (e.g. Taiwan and the Philippines). It has been reclassified as a regional re_occurrence within South‑eastern Asia (Malaysia already documents first introduction to the subregion), which is appropriate. If the dataset must be limited strictly to the ten most impactful post‑1990 CAEV emergence events, this Thai episode is a candidate for exclusion in favour of higher-prevalence or broader national studies; otherwise it can be retained as a secondary regional event.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: EEEV, EEE virus
Countries: United States of America [2003] (multiple southeastern and Gulf Coast states including Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi and others)
Host: Horses; other equids; occasionally ratites and gamebirds on affected farms
Event.summary: In 2003, the United States experienced an exceptionally large multi‑state epizootic of Eastern equine encephalitis, with national surveillance recording roughly 700 equine cases across many states and particularly heavy burdens in Florida, Georgia and South Carolina, where dozens to over a hundred horses died despite available vaccination. At the same time, 14 human neuroinvasive EEE cases were reported from eight states, the highest annual human total since systematic surveillance began, underscoring the public‑health significance of the equine outbreaks. Transmission subsided with the end of the mosquito season, but the scale of equine and human disease prompted renewed emphasis on routine equine vaccination, mosquito‑control programs and swamp‑habitat risk communication throughout the southeastern and Gulf Coast regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing enzootic circulation of EEEV in bird–mosquito cycles in Atlantic and Gulf Coast hardwood swamps, combined with favorable spring and summer precipitation, high mosquito abundance and low or inconsistent vaccination coverage of horses in some southeastern states, likely allowed intense amplification and widespread spillover into equids and occasionally humans in 2003. Internal mechanisms: Available genetic and epidemiologic analyses attribute the outbreak to endemic North American EEEV lineages rather than to a novel strain, so this episode is best interpreted as a large‑scale incidence re‑occurrence driven by environmental conditions, vector dynamics and gaps in equine immunity rather than viral evolutionary change.
Review: review – New event added because USDA national surveillance documents 712 equine EEE cases in 2003 (the highest annual U.S. equine total in the 2003–2012 series) and CDC reports 14 human cases that year, making this clearly one of the most impactful modern epizootics; coded as a large re‑occurrence in existing southeastern and Gulf Coast foci, with no evidence for a novel strain. Geographic scope is summarized at the country/region level rather than listing all affected states and should be checked by a subject‑matter expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: EEEV, EEE virus
Countries: United States of America [2009] (Maine – York, Cumberland, Waldo, Kennebec, Penobscot counties)
Host: Horses; domestic gamebirds (pheasants and other gallinaceous birds); a llama on one affected premises
Event.summary: In summer 2009, eastern equine encephalitis virus activity in Maine intensified from prior sporadic detections to a large, geographically dispersed epizootic, with horses and farmed gamebirds dying in at least five counties across southern and central Maine. State surveillance and veterinary reports documented about 15 laboratory‑confirmed equine cases, several pheasant flock die‑offs and infection in a llama between July and October, representing a marked northward extension of recognized EEEV activity within New England. Transmission waned as the mosquito season ended, but authorities issued strong guidance on routine equine vaccination, expanded vector surveillance and, in some areas, aerial spraying because of the risk of recurrent transmission in the newly affected parts of the state.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unusually favorable climatic conditions for mosquito vectors (notably Culiseta melanura and mammal‑biting bridge vectors), abundant freshwater swamp habitat and low or incomplete vaccination coverage in horses and gamebirds likely enabled intense amplification in avian reservoirs and spillover into equids across a broader area of Maine than previously affected. Internal mechanisms: No clearly novel viral strain was identified; the episode is best interpreted as geographic and incidence re‑occurrence at the northern fringe of the established North American EEEV range, driven by environmental and host‑immunity factors rather than viral genetic change.
Review: retain – Event accurately captures the well‑documented 2009 Maine epizootic, including approximate equine case counts, affected counties and involvement of farmed gamebirds; geography and classification as a re‑occurrence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) are consistent with prior low‑level EEEV detections in Maine and with the project rule that spread to a new state within the same subregion is not coded as intra‑continental emergence. No changes beyond minor wording clarifications were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: EEEV, EEE virus
Countries: Panama [2010] (Darién, Panamá, Colón provinces, with additional scattered equine cases in Coclé and Veraguas)
Host: Horses and other equids; humans (linked but dead-end hosts)
Event.summary: From May to August 2010, a large outbreak of viral encephalitis occurred in eastern Panama, where 161 horses with acute febrile or neurologic illness consistent with Eastern or Venezuelan equine encephalitis were identified across Darién, Panamá and Colón provinces, and laboratory testing confirmed multiple equine and human infections with South American lineages of Eastern equine encephalitis virus, now classified as Madariaga virus, as well as mixed Madariaga/Venezuelan equine encephalitis infections. The episode represented an unusually intense cluster of equine disease in a region with long‑standing enzootic alphavirus circulation but historically sparse recognition of human EEE‑like illness and was the first well‑documented human outbreak attributed to Madariaga virus in Latin America. Transmission declined after vector control measures, public health alerts and seasonal reduction in mosquito activity, but subsequent studies documented ongoing enzootic circulation of Madariaga/EEEV in wildlife and vectors and highlighted its potential to cause recurrent equine and human encephalitis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Pre‑existing enzootic circulation of Madariaga virus (formerly South American EEEV lineages) and Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus in humid tropical forest and wetland habitats, combined with climatic and land‑use conditions that favored high mosquito abundance and close contact between horses, humans and vector habitats, likely facilitated amplification and widespread spillover into equids and people. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses implicated South American EEEV/Madariaga virus lineages capable of causing severe neurologic disease in both horses and humans, and the 2010 outbreak coincided with recognition of Madariaga virus as a distinct species causing human encephalitis; this episode is therefore best interpreted as a re‑emergence of a virulent lineage with broadened recognized host and clinical impact, rather than simple incidence re‑occurrence of long‑known equine disease.
Review: review – Event retained but clarified to note that the outbreak was caused by South American EEEV lineages now classified as Madariaga virus, and the type coding was adjusted so that only re_emergence is marked "true" (re_occurrence set to "false") in line with the project rule that event‑type categories are generally mutually exclusive except where re‑emergence co‑occurs with intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence. A separate Madariaga‑virus EPP, if defined, might ultimately be a more appropriate home for this event, so taxonomic treatment should be confirmed by the project team.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: EEEV, EEE virus
Countries: United States of America [2012] (multiple southeastern, Gulf Coast and northeastern states, including Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Florida, North Carolina, South Carolina, Massachusetts, Vermont, New Hampshire and others)
Host: Horses; other equids; humans (linked but dead-end hosts)
Event.summary: In 2012, the United States experienced another large EEE epizootic, with USDA surveillance documenting 209 equine cases in 19 states, heavily concentrated in Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina and Florida but also including several cases in New England states such as Massachusetts, Vermont and New Hampshire. In the same year, CDC recorded 15 human neuroinvasive EEE cases nationwide, seven of them in Massachusetts and two in Vermont, reinforcing the strong linkage between intense equine activity and sporadic severe human disease. By late autumn, transmission declined with cooler weather and intensified mosquito‑control efforts, yet the 2012 season was recognized as one of the largest modern EEE years in terms of combined equine and human impact, prompting calls for sustained vaccination coverage of horses in high‑risk southeastern and Atlantic coastal regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive wetland habitat along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, favorable rainfall patterns during the spring and summer of 2012, high densities of competent mosquito vectors and gaps in equine vaccination coverage in parts of the Southeast and Gulf Coast states likely drove high levels of EEEV amplification in bird reservoirs and spillover into horses and, less frequently, humans. Internal mechanisms: Surveillance and phylogenetic studies attribute the 2012 outbreaks to endemic North American EEEV lineages without evidence of a new variant associated with increased virulence or transmissibility, so the episode is classified as a major re‑occurrence in existing enzootic foci rather than as genetic re‑emergence.
Review: review – New event added because USDA summaries show 209 equine EEE cases across 19 U.S. states in 2012 and CDC reports 15 human neuroinvasive cases (the second‑highest yearly human total after 2019), making this one of the most impactful post‑2000 seasons; coded as a large re‑occurrence in established U.S. foci. Geographic description is kept at country/region level, and a subject‑matter expert may wish to refine which states are highlighted or whether 2012 should be merged with adjacent high‑activity years into a broader episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus eastern
EPP.common.name: EEEV, EEE virus
Countries: United States of America [2019] (multiple states including Massachusetts, Michigan, Connecticut, New Jersey, Rhode Island, New York, Indiana and numerous southeastern and Gulf Coast states with equine cases)
Host: Horses; other domestic animals (e.g., llamas, gamebirds); humans (linked but dead-end hosts)
Event.summary: During the 2019 transmission season, the United States experienced a pronounced multi‑state resurgence of Eastern equine encephalitis virus, with 38 human disease cases (15 deaths) reported from 10 states and USDA documenting 184 equine cases in 24 states, making it the largest modern human outbreak and a major equine epizootic. Human cases clustered in New England and the upper Midwest, while equine disease was widespread in the Northeast, Great Lakes region and parts of the Southeast, often in unvaccinated or undervaccinated horses, and vector surveillance showed unusually high EEEV infection rates in Culiseta melanura and bridge‑vector mosquitoes in hardwood swamp habitats. Transmission fell sharply as cooler weather arrived and targeted mosquito‑control operations were implemented, but the season was widely recognized as a record‑breaking EEEV year and spurred renewed emphasis on equine vaccination, integrated mosquito management and improved clinical awareness of EEE in endemic regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Exceptional seasonal mosquito abundance and high infection rates in enzootic (Culiseta melanura) and mammal‑biting bridge vector species, influenced by antecedent precipitation and warm summer conditions, created intense enzootic amplification and frequent spillover into horses and humans; in several affected areas, residential and equine development near swamp habitats and incomplete equine vaccination coverage further elevated risk. Internal mechanisms: Genomic and phylogenetic analyses indicate circulation of typical North American EEEV lineage I variants without evidence of a novel, more virulent strain, so the 2019 season is interpreted as a major re‑occurrence driven primarily by environmental conditions, vector dynamics and host immunity/vaccination patterns rather than by viral evolution.
Review: review – Event retained but updated to reflect final national counts of 38 human cases (15 deaths) and 184 equine cases across 24 states, based on USDA equine surveillance and CDC/NEJM reports; earlier wording that cited 34 human cases from a preliminary MMWR has been corrected. Classification as a large re‑occurrence (rather than re‑emergence) remains appropriate because available genomic analyses do not implicate a novel strain.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus multilocularis
EPP.common.name: Alveolar echinococcosis
Countries: Japan [1990] (Hokkaido – Rebun Island and eastern Hokkaido; occasional spillover to pigs and dogs on Honshu)
Host: Humans; red foxes (Ezo red fox, Vulpes vulpes schrencki); domestic dogs and cats; gray‑backed voles and other small rodents; pigs (as intermediate hosts)
Event.summary: By the late 20th century, a long‑standing focus of alveolar echinococcosis in Hokkaido, Japan, centred on Rebun Island and eastern Hokkaido, had evolved into a major endemic area, with several hundred cumulative human cases and widespread infection in foxes and voles. From 1999 to 2018, Japan’s national surveillance system recorded 425 human echinococcosis notifications, about 400 of them alveolar echinococcosis and over 95% from Hokkaido, corresponding to roughly a dozen or more new AE patients each year. Despite intensive control measures, including baiting programmes to deworm wild foxes, routine praziquantel treatment of dogs and public health campaigns, Hokkaido remained a persistent high‑burden focus by 2018, with continuing human and canine cases and concern about spread to Honshu and other islands.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Historical anthropogenic translocations of infected foxes to Hokkaido followed by decades of ecological change, including dense fox and vole populations, have sustained intense transmission; modern land use, urban expansion and tourism increased human exposure to contaminated environments. National legislation making echinococcosis notifiable in 1999 and improved imaging and serology greatly increased case detection, revealing the true scale of the problem. Internal mechanisms: Available molecular data indicate that the parasite population in Hokkaido derives from introductions of existing northern haplotypes rather than a newly evolved strain; the key processes are ecological and anthropogenic spread rather than major changes in virulence.
Review: Decision: review – This new event was added because Hokkaido is one of the largest long‑term AE foci outside China. National surveillance (1999–2018) reports 425 human echinococcosis cases, of which 400 are AE and >95% from Hokkaido, with mean annual notifications on the order of 20 cases.([id-info.jihs.go.jp](https://id-info.jihs.go.jp/niid/en/iasr/8695-469te.html)) Fox infection prevalences around 50% and a long history of human cases since 1937 are documented in Japanese mammalogy and NIID reviews.([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/mammalstudy/30/Supplement/30_Supplement_S101/_article/-char/en?utm_source=openai)) This magnitude makes Hokkaido comparable in impact to the better‑documented European and Central Asian foci and clearly among the top 10 global AE events. The event is coded as re‑occurrence rather than first detection because both human disease and wildlife cycles long predate 1990; recent decades represent continued high incidence under modern surveillance and control. Further refinement of the start and end years (e.g. distinguishing Rebun vs. mainland Hokkaido phases) could be done if more granular Japanese data are used.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus multilocularis
EPP.common.name: Alveolar echinococcosis
Countries: China [1991] (Gansu, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, Qinghai, Sichuan, Tibet Autonomous Region, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region)
Host: Humans; domestic dogs; foxes; small rodents (e.g. Microtus, Cricetulus, Eospalax spp.)
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, mass ultrasound and serological surveys in rural south Gansu revealed a very large, previously under‑recognized focus of human alveolar echinococcosis in central China, with about 5% of residents in some communes affected, after scattered clinical case reports from the 1960s–1980s. Subsequent field surveys through the 1990s and early 2000s documented extremely high prevalences across multiple western provinces on and around the Tibetan Plateau, with dogs, foxes and small rodents sustaining intense transmission in poor upland farming and herding communities. By the mid‑2000s, these Chinese plateau regions were recognized as accounting for more than 90% of an estimated ~18,000 new AE cases per year globally, making them the dominant global hotspot of the disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional pastoral/agropastoral livelihoods on the Tibetan Plateau with large dog populations, free‑roaming owned dogs, close human–dog contact, high densities of arvicoline rodents in upland grasslands, and limited access to veterinary care and anthelminthics created ideal conditions for intense parasite cycling and human exposure. Deforestation, land‑use change and poverty exacerbated exposure risks, while the introduction of mass ultrasound screening revealed many previously undiagnosed chronic infections. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain has been clearly implicated; instead, the parasite’s ecological adaptation to plateau ecosystems, combined with demographic and behavioural factors, underpinned sustained high transmission, representing amplification and geographic consolidation in human populations rather than a distinct genotype‑driven shift.
Review: Decision: review – The event (large plateau focus in China) is clearly one of the largest global AE episodes and should be retained, but the event‑type coding was incorrect. China had published AE case series since at least the 1960s, and the Gansu focus itself was first documented in 1991–1992 mass ultrasound surveys and follow‑up work rather than being the first detection of AE in the country or in Eastern Asia.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/014067369292693A?utm_source=openai)) Therefore the ‘first_detection’ flag was set to No and the event re‑classified as re‑occurrence, reflecting a dramatic increase in recognized incidence and visibility in a previously known subregion driven by environmental and social changes plus improved case finding. ‘Intra‑continental emergence’ was set to No to avoid conflating this intensification within Eastern Asia with true spread to new Asian sub‑regions (which is better captured in the Kyrgyzstan event). Sources were also refined to focus on the original Lancet description of the Gansu focus, subsequent ecological work, China‑wide prevalence meta‑analysis and the global burden estimates that underpin the statement that China accounts for >90% of new AE cases.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pntd.0000722))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus multilocularis
EPP.common.name: Alveolar echinococcosis
Countries: China [2004] (Gansu, Ningxia, Qinghai, Sichuan, Tibet Autonomous Region, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, Inner Mongolia)
Host: Humans; domestic dogs; foxes; small rodents; livestock (economic impact through dog–livestock interface rather than direct infection)
Event.summary: Building on earlier recognition of large foci in the 1990s, nationwide echinococcosis surveillance and control programmes in China from 2004 onwards revealed sustained, very high burdens of alveolar echinococcosis across Tibetan Plateau provinces, with repeated county‑level surveys showing some of the highest prevalences and incidence rates in the world. Over 2004–2022, tens of thousands of echinococcosis cases were recorded nationally, with AE accounting for a substantial share of the disease burden and disability in plateau counties, and new foci documented in areas such as parts of Inner Mongolia and western Gansu. Despite gradual scale‑up of dog deworming, fox and dog management and health education, AE remained entrenched, though some local reductions in prevalence were observed toward the end of this period.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing pastoral systems with large free‑roaming dog populations, high small‑mammal densities in high‑altitude grasslands, climate conditions favouring egg survival, and persistent poverty and limited access to healthcare allowed AE transmission to remain intense despite control efforts. Expansion of national programmes for ultrasound screening and control improved detection and treatment coverage, changing the apparent incidence and burden over time. Internal mechanisms: Continued high transmission is largely ecological and behavioural rather than driven by identifiable novel genotypes; survival analyses and burden estimates indicate chronic, entrenched endemicity rather than a short‑term outbreak, although local micro‑evolutionary changes in parasite populations cannot be excluded.
Review: Decision: review – This row usefully summarises the long period of very high AE burden under national surveillance and control in China after 2004 and should be kept, but it does not fit neatly into any single emergence‑type category. The original coding as ‘re_occurrence’ implied a resurgence after prior decline, whereas available data suggest persistent hyperendemicity punctuated by improved case finding and gradual, spatially heterogeneous effects of control measures.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7362549/?utm_source=openai)) Accordingly, all six emergence‑type flags have been set to No and the episode is framed as a continuation and national scaling‑up of the plateau hotspot first highlighted in the early 1990s (now captured in the 1991–2005 event). Experts may wish ultimately to merge these two Chinese rows into a single long episode, or to split them into more precise phases (e.g. pre‑ and post‑national control programme) if detailed Chinese surveillance data are to hand; this is why the row is flagged for review rather than retain.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus multilocularis
EPP.common.name: Alveolar echinococcosis
Countries: Canada [2009] (British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, southern Ontario)
Host: Coyotes; red foxes; domestic dogs; humans; small rodents
Event.summary: Although Echinococcus multilocularis has been present in North American wildlife since the mid‑20th century, from 2009 a European‑type strain was identified in a dog in British Columbia with no travel history outside the province and subsequently in urban coyotes and dogs in western Canada, indicating recent introduction and establishment of a more pathogenic lineage. By the early 2010s, high prevalences were documented in urban coyotes around Calgary, Alberta, and autochthonous human alveolar echinococcosis cases began to be recognized in western Canada, a condition previously almost unheard of there. Over the following decade, further human cases and widespread wildlife infection suggested an emerging public health concern linked to this introduced strain in prairie and urban ecosystems in several western and central provinces.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International movement of dogs (e.g. importation or rescue of infected dogs from endemic European regions) is thought to have introduced the European strain into western Canada, where expanding urban coyote and dog populations and close human–pet contact facilitated establishment and spillover to humans. Urban growth and green space expansion increased overlap between humans, coyotes, dogs and rodent intermediate hosts, while limited awareness of AE delayed diagnosis and reporting. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of European‑type genotypes with higher propensity to cause disease in dogs and humans, and apparent competitive displacement of some native North American strains, represents re‑emergence driven by parasite genetic change superimposed on a pre‑existing wildlife transmission system.
Review: Decision: review – The introduction and spread of European‑type E. multilocularis lineages in western Canada, with emerging human AE in Alberta and neighbouring provinces, is a key modern event and should be retained, but the original classification as ‘inter‑continental emergence’ was incorrect because E. multilocularis has been endemic in North American wildlife (e.g. Arctic foxes, coyotes) since at least the mid‑20th century.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pntd.0000722)) The event better fits the definition of re‑emergence, driven by internal change (introduction of more pathogenic genotypes) on top of an existing host–parasite system, so only ‘re_emergence’ is set to Yes. The countries list has been restricted to Canada, where the European‑type strain and most documented human cases are clearly established; evidence for similar genotypes in the USA is emerging but largely post‑2020 and beyond the temporal scope of this event.([canada.ca](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/reports-publications/canada-communicable-disease-report-ccdr/monthly-issue/2024-50/issue-9-september-2024/human-echinococcosis-incidence-2000-2020.html?utm_source=openai)) Because strain attribution and spatial spread in North America are evolving rapidly, this row should be revisited as new genomic and surveillance data accumulate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Equid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: EHV-1, Equine herpesvirus 1
Countries: United States of America [2003] (University of Findlay English Equestrian Center, Ohio)
Host: Horses in a university English riding / equestrian program (mixed breeds; school and show horses)
Event.summary: In January 2003, an outbreak of EHV-1 at the University of Findlay’s English equestrian center in Ohio affected most of the 135 horses on the premises: 117 developed clinical signs of infection and 46 showed neurologic deficits consistent with equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy (EHM), with 12 horses ultimately dying or being euthanized. The disease began with fever and respiratory signs before progressing to ataxia, weakness, and recumbency in a subset of mainly older horses, leading the university to suspend riding classes and competitions for several months while strict isolation, movement controls, and intensive nursing care were implemented. Over subsequent weeks, no new neurologic cases occurred, surviving horses gradually recovered, and the facility was able to reopen under enhanced biosecurity and revised vaccination and entry policies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high-density housing of school and show horses, frequent movement between barns and arenas, and intensive training of older, highly used equids promoted rapid virus transmission once introduced, while continual horse turnover complicated early control. Internal mechanisms: Molecular and epidemiologic work on this outbreak linked severe neurologic disease to infection with neuropathogenic EHV-1 strains harboring the ORF30 D752 (G2254) variant, and risk-factor analysis identified older age and high peak fever as strong predictors for EHM, supporting classification as a re-emergence event driven by strain virulence interacting with host factors.
Review: Retain – The original row mis-identified this outbreak as occurring at a California racetrack; it actually took place at the University of Findlay English equestrian center in Ohio, where 117/135 horses became ill, 46 developed neurologic signs, and 12 died. I corrected the location, host description, and narrative using Henninger et al. (2007) and contemporaneous reports, and kept the classification as re-emergence because the event involved a neuropathogenic EHV-1 variant causing unusually high neurologic morbidity and mortality. This is clearly one of the largest and most influential EHV-1/EHM outbreaks in the post‑1990 period and should be retained as a top‑tier event.

EPP.scientific.name: Equid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: EHV-1, Equine herpesvirus 1
Countries: United States of America [2006] (clusters at Florida showgrounds and racetracks, Kentucky racetracks, Maryland tracks including Pimlico and Bowie)
Host: Horses at Thoroughbred racetracks and high-level show / training facilities
Event.summary: From late 2006 into early 2007, multiple EHV-1 outbreaks with neurologic cases occurred at major U.S. equine venues, including a highly publicized episode at Pimlico Race Course in Maryland and contemporaneous outbreaks at Florida showgrounds and Kentucky tracks. At Pimlico, several barns were quarantined for weeks, at least three horses were euthanized, and movement of racehorses into and out of Maryland was heavily restricted, while related concerns at Bowie and other training centers further disrupted the Mid-Atlantic racing circuit. Similar EHM events at Florida training and show facilities and at Kentucky racetracks triggered quarantines, race cancellations, and widespread interstate movement controls, and collectively these clustered outbreaks prompted USDA to classify neurologic EHV-1/EHM as an emerging equine disease and spurred development of national guidance on outbreak management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Concentration of large numbers of race and show horses at racetracks and winter show circuits, frequent interstate transport, and shared stabling / training environments allowed rapid dissemination of EHV-1 once infected horses were introduced. Internal mechanisms: Many neurologic cases were associated with neuropathogenic ORF30 D752 EHV-1 strains, and high viral loads in blood and nasal secretions in some horses, combined with host factors such as age and intense training stress, contributed to severe EHM expression and the perception of a newly emerging neurologic form of EHV-1.
Review: Retain – This row reasonably summarizes the 2006–2007 cluster of neurologic EHV-1 outbreaks at Florida show facilities and Mid‑Atlantic/Kentucky racetracks (notably Pimlico and associated tracks) and correctly treats them as a major re-emergence of neuropathogenic EHV‑1 rather than first emergence. Geographic attribution to the United States with specification of affected tracks is appropriate, and the time window 2006–2007 matches regulatory reports. I recommend retaining this as a single linked episode representing the mid‑2000s racetrack/showground EHM cluster; no structural changes are required, though additional primary sources (state veterinary and USDA reports) could be added if more detail is desired.

EPP.scientific.name: Equid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: EHV-1, Equine herpesvirus 1
Countries: Germany [2009] (mixed riding and breeding facility in southern Germany)
Host: Horses at a mixed riding and breeding farm (pregnant mares, youngstock and sport horses)
Event.summary: In early 2009, a riding and breeding facility in southern Germany experienced a severe EHV-1 outbreak that began with an index abortion and rapidly progressed to multiple additional abortions, febrile illness in many horses, and a cluster of equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy (EHM) cases. Neurologic horses showed ataxia, weakness, and urinary dysfunction, but with intensive care all survived, while pregnant mares suffered repeated late-term losses over several weeks. Implementation of strict isolation of febrile and neurologic horses, separation of pregnant mares, enhanced temperature monitoring, and stable-level biosecurity measures eventually halted new cases and prevented wider spread beyond the farm, although the episode highlighted the potential for EHV-1 to cause concurrent abortion storms and neurologic disease on a single premises.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High intra-farm contact rates, shared housing of pregnant mares and performance horses, and delayed recognition of early febrile cases facilitated within-farm transmission after introduction or reactivation of EHV-1. Internal mechanisms: Virologic work identified a neuropathogenic EHV-1 strain and emphasized the role of ORF30 polymorphism and endothelial tropism in the pathogenesis of both abortion and neurologic disease, making this a clear example of re-emergence driven by strain characteristics within an already endemic region.
Review: Retain – This event corresponds closely to a well-described 2009 German farm outbreak with combined abortions and EHM, and the location, hosts, and clinical pattern in the row match the primary literature. Classifying it as re-emergence (neuropathogenic strain causing unusually severe disease on a premises where EHV‑1 was already present) rather than first emergence or intra-/inter-continental spread is appropriate. I recommend retaining this as one of the larger European EHV‑1 outbreaks in the period.

EPP.scientific.name: Equid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: EHV-1, Equine herpesvirus 1
Countries: United States of America [2012] (Hawthorne Race Course, Illinois)
Host: Thoroughbred racehorses at Hawthorne Race Course
Event.summary: Beginning in October 2012, Hawthorne Race Course near Chicago, Illinois, experienced an outbreak of neurologic EHV-1 in backstretch horses, with multiple animals developing fever that progressed to ataxia and recumbency and at least six to seven fatalities over the course of the event. The Illinois Department of Agriculture imposed a prolonged quarantine of the track, racing officials dropped at least seven race days, and other jurisdictions temporarily restricted entry of Illinois-based racehorses, generating substantial economic losses and logistical disruption. After several weeks of strict isolation of affected barns, enhanced monitoring, and no new neurologic cases, quarantine was lifted, but the event prompted long-term regulatory changes including specific EHV-1 vaccination and entry requirements for horses racing at Illinois tracks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density stabling and continual movement of racehorses into and out of Hawthorne, together with the financial pressure to maintain racing, initially hampered rapid control and facilitated EHV-1 transmission once an infected horse was present. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved the neurologic form of EHV‑1 (EHM) and likely neuropathogenic genotypes, illustrating how racetrack management conditions can amplify an otherwise endemic virus into a high-impact neurologic outbreak, justifying its classification as re-emergence.
Review: Retain – The Hawthorne 2012 outbreak is correctly located and characterized as a neurologic EHV‑1 event with multiple deaths and substantial economic impact. The sources cited specifically describe this outbreak, and classifying it as re-emergence (severe clinical expression of an endemic virus in a racetrack environment) is appropriate. I recommend keeping this as one of the larger racetrack EHM events in the dataset.

EPP.scientific.name: Equid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: EHV-1, Equine herpesvirus 1
Countries: United States of America [2016] (Sunland Park Racetrack, New Mexico)
Host: Thoroughbred and Quarter Horse racehorses at Sunland Park Racetrack
Event.summary: In early 2016, an EHV-1 outbreak at Sunland Park Racetrack in New Mexico resulted in dozens of confirmed infections, multiple neurologic EHM cases, and quarantine of roughly 3,000 horses at Sunland Park and connected facilities. Racing was suspended for 19 days, the Grade III Sunland Derby and Sunland Park Oaks were cancelled, and approximately 72 races with several million dollars in purses were lost while regulators and track management implemented stringent testing and movement controls. With sustained quarantine, isolation of affected barns, and progressive decline in new cases, the outbreak was brought under control and restrictions were gradually lifted, and the episode became a key case study in large-scale racetrack EHV‑1 risk and economic impact.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very large numbers of racehorses housed in close quarters, frequent movement between barns and training centers, and intense racing schedules created ideal conditions for rapid amplification of EHV‑1 once introduced, with substantial economic incentives initially favoring continued operations. Internal mechanisms: The occurrence of neurologic EHM cases in a partially immune population suggests involvement of neuropathogenic EHV‑1 variants and high within-barn viral loads; the outbreak is best interpreted as re-emergence of severe EHV‑1 disease in a racetrack setting rather than a new geographical introduction.
Review: Retain – This row accurately summarizes the 2016 Sunland Park EHV‑1 outbreak, including the scale of quarantine and cancellation of the Sunland Derby and Oaks, and correctly codes it as re-emergence in an endemic region. I adjusted the summary to emphasize the approximate number of horses under quarantine and the documented racing and economic impacts based on New Mexico Livestock Board and racing-industry reports. This remains one of the more impactful racetrack-associated EHV‑1 events and should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Equid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: EHV-1, Equine herpesvirus 1
Countries: United States of America [2024] (aged working equids at a horseback riding operation in the Sierra Nevada Mountains, California)
Host: Aged working horses and one mule (trail and ranch-type equids in a single closed operation)
Event.summary: In the summer of 2024, an outbreak of EHV-1 myeloencephalopathy was documented in a population of 33 aged working equids at a horseback riding operation in the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California, with 18 animals developing clinical disease. Fourteen horses developed neurologic signs consistent with EHM (ataxia, weakness, urinary incontinence, recumbency), and several others exhibited only fever and respiratory signs; six neurologic horses were euthanized due to severity of deficits. Strict on-farm quarantine, supportive treatment (including antivirals, anti-inflammatories, and anticoagulants), and monitoring of all exposed equids led to a gradual decline in new cases, and by about three weeks after onset, viral shedding had ceased and surviving horses stabilized, though some retained long-term neurologic deficits.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: An older equid population with waning immunity, chronic work-related stress, and close contact in a single operation created conditions for efficient spread once EHV‑1 was introduced or reactivated, while limited resources constrained options for referral or extensive isolation facilities. Internal mechanisms: Quantitative PCR documented high viral loads in blood and nasal secretions in many clinically affected animals, and all typed isolates were of the non-neuropathogenic N752 genotype, illustrating that EHM can arise in older horses even without the classic neuropathogenic marker and supporting classification as re-emergence driven by host and viral-load factors rather than expansion into new areas or hosts.
Review: Review – The original row incorrectly placed this outbreak in Nevada and implied an uncertain 2023–2024 time span; I corrected the location to a horseback riding operation in the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California and the year to 2024, and updated the host description and case numbers to match the Viruses case report. Classification as re-emergence (unusually severe EHM in a closed, aged herd within an endemic region) remains appropriate. Scientifically this is a valuable illustration of EHM in older working equids, but in terms of absolute scale it is smaller than major multi-state or multi-country events; I therefore recommend flagging it as below the top tier of impact and potentially excluding it if a strict "10 largest events" filter is enforced, while retaining it for now as a well-documented local outbreak.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Equid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: EHV-1, Equine herpesvirus 1
Countries: United States of America [2022] (Desert International Horse Park, Thermal, California, with linked cases and quarantines across multiple California counties and western states)
Host: Show-jumping and hunter/jumper sport horses at a multi-week winter circuit
Event.summary: In February 2022, Desert International Horse Park (DIHP) in Thermal, California, reported an outbreak of EHV-1 during its multi-week Desert Circuit, with an initial neurologic EHM case confirmed on-site and subsequent detection of additional febrile and neurologic horses. Over the following weeks, at least a dozen confirmed EHV-1 cases (including several EHM) were identified at the venue, one horse was euthanized, and show management ultimately cancelled the remaining Desert Circuit weeks and Desert Dressage IV to limit spread. Horses that had competed at DIHP seeded secondary cases at other California shows and training barns, leading to a multi-county outbreak, extensive quarantines, and heightened surveillance; by late March, after nearly six weeks of movement controls, temperature monitoring, and targeted testing, California authorities began lifting quarantines and the outbreak was considered contained.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large numbers of high-value show horses from many states stabled in close quarters for a prolonged winter circuit, together with early horse movement off-site before full recognition of the outbreak, facilitated regional dissemination of EHV-1. Internal mechanisms: Investigations showed that both neuropathogenic and non-neuropathogenic EHV‑1 genotypes could be associated with EHM, and risk-factor analyses identified older age and certain management practices (e.g., discipline, housing patterns) as contributors to infection and neurologic disease, supporting interpretation of this episode as a major re-emergence event in a dense sport-horse network.
Review: Review – The previous row conflated this outbreak with speculative, later "recurrent" events and labeled the period 2021–2025; I have restricted the event to the well-documented 2022 DIHP Desert Circuit outbreak and updated the narrative to align with peer-reviewed analyses and official reports. Location (Thermal, California) and the multi-county nature of the episode are now explicitly described, and sources have been changed to DIHP- and California-specific outbreak reports and epidemiologic studies rather than to the separate 2025 Pusterla et al. management case, which describes a smaller, distinct outbreak at a multi-week event. Classification as re-emergence (severe disease expression in an endemic region with high sport-horse mobility) remains appropriate. Recommended status: retain as a major sport-horse EHV‑1 event.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Equid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: EHV-1, Equine herpesvirus 1
Countries: United States of America [2025] (multi-state outbreak originating at the WPRA World Finals and Elite Barrel Race, Waco, Texas; cases reported in Texas, Oklahoma, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, Washington, South Dakota, Louisiana and other states)
Host: Barrel racing and rodeo horses attending the WPRA World Finals and Elite Barrel Race, plus secondary cases in exposed performance and ranch horses across multiple states
Event.summary: In November 2025, an outbreak of EHV-1 and equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy (EHM) began among horses competing at the Women’s Professional Rodeo Association (WPRA) World Finals and Elite Barrel Race in Waco, Texas, and rapidly expanded as exposed horses returned home. By late November, official and industry summaries reported at least 50 confirmed EHV-1–positive horses, including around 28 with neurologic EHM, and more than 150 exposed horses distributed across multiple U.S. states, with numerous deaths reported by treating clinics. State animal health agencies and the Equine Disease Communication Center issued urgent advisories, many barrel races and rodeo events were cancelled or postponed, and multiple states imposed new testing and entry requirements for horses returning from Texas and Oklahoma. Intensive quarantine, contact tracing, and public outreach over subsequent weeks gradually reduced new case reports, but the episode underscored the vulnerability of large rodeo and barrel-racing circuits to widespread dissemination of endemic EHV‑1.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A very large, multi-day barrel racing and rodeo event with extensive interstate participation, shared stabling, and frequent horse movement between events allowed rapid amplification and long-distance dissemination of EHV‑1 from a single venue. Subsequent long-haul transport of exposed horses into diverse boarding, training, and competition environments, sometimes before clinical signs were recognized, further widened the outbreak footprint, while the economic and competitive pressures of high‑stakes events initially impeded rapid containment. Internal mechanisms: Early reports describe the strain as clinically aggressive with a high proportion of neurologic cases, but definitive genomic characterization is still limited; in the absence of clear evidence for a novel genotype, the episode is best treated as a large re-occurrence of severe disease caused by endemic EHV-1 under high-risk management and movement conditions rather than a true viral re-emergence in a new host or region.
Review: Added – The original dataset omitted the large 2025 multi-state EHV‑1/EHM outbreak linked to the WPRA World Finals and Elite Barrel Race in Waco, Texas, despite its clear importance: at least 50 confirmed positive horses (roughly half with neurologic EHM) and more than 150 exposed animals across numerous U.S. states, with multiple deaths and widespread event cancellations. I created a new row to capture this episode, coded it as a re-occurrence (large-scale resurgence of endemic virus driven by event structure and horse movements) rather than first emergence, and drew on EDCC alerts, extension summaries and state/regional advisories for dates and approximate scale. This outbreak is comparable in impact to the 2011 Ogden and 2021 Valencia events and should be retained among the major post‑1990 EHV‑1 events.

EPP.scientific.name: Equid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: EHV-1, Equine herpesvirus 1
Host: Polo horses (Thoroughbred–Criollo crosses and related sport-horse types) in a large Chilean polo operation
Event.summary: In early 2025, Chile reported its first documented outbreak of equine herpes myeloencephalopathy in a large polo-horse operation housing more than 500 horses, where EHV-1 infection had previously been associated only with respiratory disease and abortion. During the outbreak, numerous horses developed fever and respiratory signs and a subset progressed to neurologic deficits such as hindlimb ataxia, weakness and urinary incontinence, prompting notification of the national animal-health authority and the implementation of strict on-farm quarantine, movement restrictions, and enhanced hygiene measures. Over several weeks, targeted isolation of clinical cases, temperature monitoring, and restricted horse movement gradually reduced transmission; by the end of the official quarantine period in April 2025 no new cases were detected, although a minority of affected horses retained residual neurologic deficits.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density stabling, intense training and competition of polo horses, and frequent within-operation mixing likely facilitated rapid EHV‑1 transmission once a neurologically virulent strain or reactivated infection entered the herd; increased clinical and laboratory surveillance following recognition of neurologic signs enabled the first formal identification and reporting of EHM in Chile. Internal mechanisms: This outbreak represents re-emergence of EHV‑1 with a new clinical phenotype (EHM) in a country where the virus was already endemic for respiratory and reproductive disease, reflecting the role of neuropathogenic or high‑viremia infections in shifting disease expression toward neurologic involvement among adult performance horses under stress.
Review: Retain – This row aligns closely with the published case report describing the first recognized EHM outbreak in Chile, including host type (polo horses), the large operation size, the onset and end of quarantine, and the classification of EHM as a new clinical manifestation of an already endemic EHV‑1. Coding this as re-emergence (new disease expression in an existing host population and region) rather than first detection of the virus itself is appropriate. Given its status as the first reported EHM outbreak in Chile and a significant regional event, this row should be retained among the major emergence events.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine arteritis virus
EPP.common.name: EAV, Equine arterivirus
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2004] (index stallion infected during transport from the Netherlands, Kingdom of the [2004])
Host: Imported stallion and in‑contact horses in Great Britain (non‑Thoroughbred; Dutch stallion and associated consignment)
Event.summary: In 2004, the United Kingdom reported a new occurrence of equine viral arteritis, classified by the World Organisation for Animal Health as a re‑occurrence of a previously listed infection in a country that had been free since the 1993 outbreak. During transport from the Netherlands to Great Britain, a Dutch stallion that was subsequently confirmed as an EAV carrier shared transport with other horses, and an outbreak involving 18 equines (one clinical case and 17 in‑contacts) was detected, with most infections subclinical and no deaths reported. National veterinary authorities imposed investigation, movement restrictions, and testing around the affected premises, and the incident was rapidly contained, reinforcing UK controls on imported stallions and semen.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement of a carrier stallion within the European single market, shared transport conditions, and absence of stringent pre‑movement EVA testing for stallions at that time allowed re-introduction of EAV into previously free UK premises. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – venereal exposure and close-contact respiratory transmission from a persistently infected carrier stallion led to infection of in‑contact horses; this represents a regulatory and surveillance‑driven re-occurrence of known EAV lineages rather than the emergence of a new viral genotype.
Review: retain – Well supported by OIE/WOAH notification as a limited but policy‑relevant re-occurrence in a country that had been EVA-free since 1993. No changes to type classification were needed; row retained as a smaller but still notable re-introduction event within Europe.
