EPP.scientific.name: Equine arteritis virus
EPP.common.name: EAV, Equine arterivirus
Countries: France [2007] (mainly Normandy and other western departments)
Host: Breeding and sport horses on multiple premises in Normandy and western France (various draught, warmblood and sport‑horse types)
Event.summary: In summer 2007, France experienced its first major recorded occurrence of equine viral arteritis when a virulent EAV strain emerged in Normandy, causing clinical EVA with abortions, neonatal deaths and occasional adult mortality in affected foals and horses. The epidemic spread through the breeding season to at least 18–30 premises in five western departments, with index, primary and secondary premises linked through movements of stallions, mares and shipped semen, and more than 200 horses affected overall. Intensive surveillance, use of real‑time RT‑PCR for rapid diagnosis, movement restrictions, and targeted control measures in breeding stallions and mares brought the epidemic under control by late summer, although less pathogenic EAV strains and sporadic cases continued to be detected in France thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density breeding activity and frequent movements of stallions and mares within Normandy and neighbouring western regions, limited pre‑existing EVA vaccination in French breeding populations, and intensive use of shipped semen and competition horses created a highly connected network that facilitated rapid farm‑to‑farm spread; the outbreak also prompted heightened regulatory and industry responses. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – virological studies demonstrated that the epidemic was driven by an emergent EAV variant arising from a persistently infected carrier stallion, distinct from previously circulating low‑pathogenic French strains; Enhanced Transmission – this variant showed high clinical impact with abortions and foal deaths and efficient spread in both breeding and sport‑horse populations; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – swift dissemination within western France from a single carrier‑stallion source.
Review: retain – The 2007 Normandy epidemic is clearly one of the largest and best documented EVA outbreaks in Europe, with >200 affected horses, multiple premises, foal deaths and abortions, and demonstration of a novel outbreak strain. Existing classification as a re-emergence linked to a new variant is consistent with the literature; only minor wording changes were made to align case numbers and affected departments with primary sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine arteritis virus
EPP.common.name: EAV, Equine arterivirus
Countries: Argentina [2010] (San Antonio de Areco, Buenos Aires Province)
Host: Thoroughbred breeding mares and foals on a Thoroughbred stud farm in San Antonio de Areco, together with related sport-horse mares inseminated with imported frozen semen
Event.summary: In March 2010, Argentina experienced its first reported clinical outbreak of equine viral arteritis when an abortion storm associated with EAV infection occurred on a Thoroughbred breeding farm in San Antonio de Areco, Buenos Aires Province. Abortions and reproductive losses were detected in Thoroughbred mares after they had been mixed with showjumping mares that had recently been inseminated with frozen semen imported from the Netherlands, and EAV was isolated from semen straws and fetal or placental material; epidemiologic investigation and genetic analysis later confirmed that the outbreak strain (GLD-LP-ARG) belonged to the European EU-1 group. In response, the national veterinary authority (SENASA) imposed temporary restrictions on horse movements in Buenos Aires Province, expanded testing of stallions and semen, and strengthened the national EVA surveillance and control programme, after which the outbreak was contained and no wider dissemination into other regions of Argentina was documented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A largely EAV-naïve national horse population with very low background seroprevalence, combined with the importation and use of infected frozen semen from a European carrier stallion, provided the conditions for an abortion outbreak in highly valuable Thoroughbred breeding stock; the lack of permitted EVA vaccination in Argentina at that time and extensive mixing of Thoroughbred and sport-horse mares on the affected premises further increased vulnerability. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Introduction – molecular characterisation showed that the outbreak was caused by a European-type EU‑1 strain closely related to certain Belgian and previously isolated Argentinean strains, representing re-emergence of EAV disease in Argentina through introduction and amplification of a virulent genotype; Enhanced Transmission – the ability of the imported strain to cause abortions and limited lateral spread among mares and foals underscores its pathogenicity in an otherwise naïve population.
Review: retain – This 2010 abortion outbreak, with provincial movement restrictions and the first documented clinical EVA in Argentina, is consistently highlighted in international reviews as a major recent EVA event and is likely one of the top 10 globally by impact since 1990. New row added and classified as a re-emergence driven by introduction of a European EU‑1 strain into a largely naïve South American horse population; not coded as inter-continental emergence because EAV had been present serologically and virologically in Argentina prior to 2010.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Equine arteritis virus
EPP.common.name: EAV, Equine arterivirus
Host: Breeding horses on stud farms in south‑eastern France (including foals and mares)
Event.summary: In 2011, several years after the major 2007 Normandy epidemic, a localized outbreak of equine viral arteritis was detected in south‑eastern France, with clinical EVA reported on at least one stud farm, including abortion and the death of a foal. Case numbers and geographical spread were modest compared with 2007, but the episode confirmed that EAV continued to circulate at low levels in French breeding populations outside Normandy. Rapid diagnosis, tracing of exposed animals, and reinforcement of existing surveillance and biosecurity protocols in breeding stallions and mares limited the outbreak, and France has since reported sporadic EVA cases and small clusters but no epidemic on the scale of 2007.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Residual EAV circulation in regional breeding populations and movement of subclinically infected horses or semen into south‑eastern holdings enabled re-occurrence; uneven vaccination uptake and lower surveillance intensity outside core breeding regions may have contributed. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence driven by persistence of existing French EAV lineages rather than emergence of a novel genotype; Enhanced Transmission – local horse‑to‑horse contact and breeding activity sustained a small outbreak that was rapidly halted once detected.
Review: retain – A modest but well-documented re-occurrence confirming ongoing low-level EAV circulation in France with abortion and a foal death. Kept because, once higher-impact events are included, there is still room within the approximate top 10 for a representative smaller re-occurrence; type classification as re-occurrence without emergence was confirmed, and no major corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Gyrodactylus salaris
EPP.common.name: Gyrodactylosis
Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) parr in the River Batnfjordselva
Event.summary: From 1991 to 1994, intensive field studies in the Norwegian river Batnfjordselva documented extremely high burdens of Gyrodactylus salaris on multiple year classes of Atlantic salmon parr, with prevalence close to 100% and seasonal median parasite loads often reaching several hundred to over a thousand worms per fish, contributing to severe juvenile mortality and collapse of the local wild salmon stock. The river had been infected since around 1980 following introduction of infected hatchery smolts, and by the early 1990s the epizootic represented a mature, high‑impact phase of the wider Norwegian G. salaris epidemic. Infection pressures only began to decline after subsequent eradication attempts, including rotenone and later aluminium‑based treatments, as part of Norway’s broader eradication programme for the Driva infection region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Human‑mediated introduction of G. salaris via stocking of infected salmon juveniles from Norwegian hatcheries seeded the Batnfjordselva infection in the early 1980s; continued use of the river for angling and salmon management, together with cold freshwater conditions supporting high host densities, facilitated sustained transmission and heavy parasite burdens. Internal mechanisms: The event mainly reflects the high intrinsic virulence and reproductive potential of the Atlantic Norwegian G. salaris lineages on naïve Atlantic salmon hosts—parasites reproduced explosively on parr skin and fins, with no evidence that a novel genotype arose during this period; host immunity and density‑dependent processes, rather than parasite evolution, eventually limited parasite numbers locally.
Review: retain – This row correctly describes a major early‑1990s high‑burden epizootic in Batnfjordselva: timing (1991–1994), location (Norway, Northern Europe), host, and the classification as re‑occurrence in a river infected since ~1980 are consistent with Appleby & Mo’s population‑dynamics work and Norwegian management reports. No changes to geography, timing, or event‑type flags were needed; only additional supporting references were added for context.

EPP.scientific.name: Gyrodactylus salaris
EPP.common.name: Gyrodactylosis
Countries: Norway [1996] (Lærdalselva and Rauma river systems, Sognefjord region, western Norway)
Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) and sea trout (Salmo trutta) in Lærdalselva and Rauma river systems
Event.summary: In autumn 1996, Gyrodactylus salaris was first detected on Atlantic salmon parr in Lærdalselva and in the Rauma system, marking spread of the parasite into a previously uninfected, highly valued wild‑salmon region on Norway’s west coast and triggering a major crisis for one of the country’s flagship salmon fisheries. Lærdalselva was treated with rotenone in 1997 in an attempt to eradicate G. salaris, but the parasite reappeared by 1999 and persisted at damaging levels through the early 2000s, causing severe declines in wild salmon and necessitating prolonged restrictions on angling. This pre‑2005 phase set the stage for more radical eradication strategies using aluminium‑based treatments later in the decade and cemented Lærdalselva and Rauma as focal points in Norway’s national action plan against G. salaris.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Anthropogenic translocation of infected salmon or rainbow trout from already infected facilities or rivers, combined with intensive fishery use and river regulation in the Sognefjord region, most likely introduced G. salaris into Lærdalselva and Rauma; stocking and movement of fish within and among rivers increased host contact rates and amplified spread. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was driven by the high virulence of established G. salaris lineages on naïve Atlantic salmon in these western rivers rather than by a clearly novel genotype; failure of the initial rotenone eradication attempt is attributed to limitations of coverage and refugia for hosts and parasites, not demonstrable evolutionary change in the parasite.
Review: review – The original row mixed the early detection/rotenone phase with later aluminium treatments and incorrectly flagged the episode as both intra‑continental emergence and re‑occurrence. I have (i) adjusted the event years to 1996–2004 so this row covers the initial detection in Lærdalselva/Rauma and the 1997 rotenone phase up to just before large‑scale aluminium treatments began in 2005, (ii) changed intra_continental_emergence from Yes to No because spread occurred within the same UN sub‑region (Northern Europe), and (iii) retained re_occurrence as Yes, reflecting renewed high incidence of G. salaris within a sub‑region where the parasite was already known (Baltic area and other Norwegian rivers). A Store norske leksikon entry for Lærdalselvi was added as a more authoritative narrative source. Please review this split together with the 2005–2017 Lærdalselva eradication event to ensure it matches your preferred episode structure.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Gyrodactylus salaris
EPP.common.name: Gyrodactylosis
Countries: Finland [1984] (multiple salmon-smolt farms in northern Finland)
Host: Baltic Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in hatchery and smolt-production farms
Event.summary: From 1984 through 1993, long‑term monitoring of several salmon smolt farms in northern Finland documented persistent but generally low to moderate prevalence of Gyrodactylus salaris on Baltic Atlantic salmon stocks, with infections recurring over 6–7 years at some facilities without causing catastrophic mortality. The parasite, already endemic in Baltic salmon elsewhere, became established in roughly 40% of surveyed Finnish salmonid farms and provided a key case study of how relatively resistant Baltic salmon can carry G. salaris with sublethal effects. By the early 1990s, Finnish authorities used these data to strengthen surveillance and movement controls to prevent spillover from farms into wild Atlantic salmon rivers shared with Sweden and Russia and to limit the risk of exporting infection to more susceptible Atlantic populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Transfers of salmon broodstock and smolts among Finnish farms and from the wider Baltic basin, together with farm‑level management factors such as changes in water intakes, occasional holding of wild fish and movements of fish between units, allowed repeated introduction and persistence of G. salaris across multiple facilities. Internal mechanisms: The episode primarily reflects the partial resistance of Baltic salmon to G. salaris—parasite burdens increased on older year classes and before stocking but seldom reached levels associated with mass mortality, in contrast to the explosive growth and severe disease observed on East‑Atlantic salmon stocks in Norway and the White Sea.
Review: review – The event is real and provides one of the main long‑term data sets on G. salaris in Baltic salmon farms, but the original classification as both first_detection and intra‑continental emergence was not consistent with the definitions: the parasite was first described on Baltic salmon in Sweden in the early 1950s and was already present in the same UN sub‑region (Northern Europe). I have therefore set first_detection and intra_continental_emergence to No and flagged re_occurrence as Yes to reflect renewed establishment and increased incidence within a sub‑region where G. salaris was already known. The time span (1984–1993) slightly predates 1990 but is retained because the episode extends into the 1990s and is likely still among the ~10 most important events for this EPP; if strict adherence to a 1990 start is required, this row should be truncated to 1990–1993 or excluded.
Review.Comment: Accept after correction

EPP.scientific.name: Gyrodactylus salaris
EPP.common.name: Gyrodactylosis
Countries: Russian Federation [1992] (Keret River, Republic of Karelia, White Sea basin)
Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) parr and smolts in the Keret River (White Sea drainage)
Event.summary: In 1992, Gyrodactylus salaris was first recorded on juvenile Atlantic salmon in the Keret River in the White Sea basin of Russian Karelia, a region that had previously lacked this parasite on anadromous salmon. Within about four years the infestation spread throughout the river system and some tributaries reached 100% prevalence and very high intensities, leading to an estimated 25–200‑fold reduction in salmon parr densities and a comparable collapse of the adult salmon stock. After this acute epizootic phase, parasite abundance and host densities fluctuated, with G. salaris sometimes undetectable in particular years but persisting as a chronic threat, and Russian authorities initiated long‑term monitoring and risk‑mitigation measures for White Sea and Barents Sea rivers.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The Keret outbreak was strongly linked to anthropogenic transfer of infected juvenile salmon from the Vyg hatchery and Lake Onega in the Baltic basin into the Keret catchment during the late 1980s, using shared transport equipment (e.g. canvas bags) and lacking adequate biosecurity, which introduced a virulent Baltic strain into a naïve White Sea salmon population. Internal mechanisms: The imported G. salaris lineage, well adapted to Baltic salmon, proved highly pathogenic to Keret’s East‑Atlantic salmon; rapid parasite reproduction on juvenile salmon skin and fins produced extreme burdens, overwhelming host immune responses and causing mass mortality, with no evidence that additional novel genotypes beyond this introduced strain were needed to drive the epidemic.
Review: retain – This high‑impact White Sea epidemic, omitted in the original file, clearly belongs among the most important global emergence events for G. salaris: it was the first pathogenic outbreak in a Russian Atlantic‑salmon river, with 25–200‑fold reductions in parr and adult stocks linked to anthropogenic introduction of a Baltic strain. The Keret River lies in Eastern Europe, a sub‑region where G. salaris was already present in Baltic drainages, so I classified the episode as re_occurrence (dramatic incidence increase within a known sub‑region) rather than first_detection or intra‑continental emergence. New, well‑documented Russian and NASCO sources were added; this row should be retained and used to represent the White Sea component of the G. salaris range expansion.

EPP.scientific.name: Gyrodactylus salaris
EPP.common.name: Gyrodactylosis
Countries: Sweden [1989] (Atlantic-draining west-coast rivers including Säveån, Ätran system, Fylleån, Nissan, Viskan, Rönne å and other salmon rivers south of Anråse å, plus Munkedalsälven [2025])
Host: Wild Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) parr and smolts in multiple Swedish west-coast rivers; occasionally farmed salmon and rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) as carriers
Event.summary: Beginning with first detection of Gyrodactylus salaris on wild Atlantic salmon in Säveån (Göta älv system) in 1989, the parasite spread during the 1990s and 2000s to most Swedish Atlantic‑draining west‑coast salmon rivers south of Anråse å, with detections in at least twenty rivers and tributaries including Ätran, Fylleån, Nissan, Viskan and Rönne å, and into some fish farms. A national monitoring programme established from 2001 onward has shown that while G. salaris can reach high burdens on individual fish and negative trends in juvenile salmon densities have occurred in several rivers, overall population‑level effects have generally been much less severe than in Norwegian rivers, likely reflecting differences in host susceptibility and environmental conditions. In 2025, the parasite was confirmed for the first time in Munkedalsälven, a tributary of Örekilsälven north of Göta älv, indicating northward extension of the west‑coast infection zone and reinforcing Swedish concerns about ongoing risk to remaining uninfected stocks and to neighbouring Norwegian rivers.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Multiple introductions from infected Baltic salmon and rainbow trout farms, including stocking of smolts and escapes or transfers of farmed fish, together with movements of fishing gear and boats without proper disinfection, are considered the main sources of G. salaris into Swedish Atlantic‑draining rivers; the parasite cannot easily cross high‑salinity coastal stretches unaided. Internal mechanisms: Several mitochondrial haplotypes of G. salaris have been detected on the Swedish west coast, indicating multiple introduction events, but there is no clear evidence of novel, more virulent strains compared with other Baltic‑derived lineages; instead, host–parasite interactions and local environmental factors modulate disease impact, with west‑coast salmon appearing more susceptible than Baltic salmon yet less catastrophically affected than Norwegian Atlantic salmon.
Review: retain – This new row has been added to cover the long‑running emergence of G. salaris in Swedish Atlantic‑draining west‑coast rivers, which was entirely missing from the original dataset despite being a key range‑expansion event highlighted by NASCO and Swedish authorities. I have set the event years to 1990–2025 (noting first detection in 1989 in Säveån) to comply as far as possible with the 1990 cut‑off while capturing subsequent spread to many rivers and the important 2025 detection in Munkedalsälven. Because G. salaris was already endemic in the Baltic part of the same UN sub‑region (Northern Europe), the episode is classified as re_occurrence rather than intra‑continental emergence or first_detection. High‑quality Swedish and NASCO sources documenting detection years, monitoring results and impact were added; this row should be retained as one of the major emergence events for this EPP.

EPP.scientific.name: Gyrodactylus salaris
EPP.common.name: Gyrodactylosis
Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) and sea trout (Salmo trutta) in Lærdalselva
Event.summary: Following the failure of the 1997 rotenone treatment to eradicate Gyrodactylus salaris from Lærdalselva, Norwegian authorities launched full‑scale chemical eradication trials using acidified aluminium sulphate (AlS) in 2005–2006, dosing the main river stem and major tributaries and sacrificing large numbers of salmon and sea trout in the process. Initial monitoring after the 2005–2006 treatments showed a sharp decline in G. salaris, but low‑level survival and reinfestation led to further Al‑based and supplementary rotenone treatments in 2008 and again in 2011–2012, while angling closures and strict biosecurity remained in place. After extensive post‑treatment surveillance, Lærdalselva was finally declared free of G. salaris from 2017 onwards, making this prolonged eradication phase one of the most technically challenging and costly, but ultimately successful, control campaigns for the parasite in a major Norwegian salmon river.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Strong economic and cultural value of the Lærdalselva salmon fishery and the need to prevent spread of G. salaris within the Sognefjord region prompted development and large‑scale deployment of novel aluminium‑based eradication methods, supported by national funding and regulatory approvals; hydraulic regulation and complex side channels made complete coverage difficult and required repeated campaigns. Internal mechanisms: The eradication phase targeted the same highly virulent G. salaris strain introduced in the 1990s, but the parasite’s ability to persist at low densities in refugia and possibly on non‑salmonid hosts allowed re‑establishment after initial treatments; the episode illustrates resilience of the parasite’s direct life cycle under intense control pressure rather than evolution of new genotypes.
Review: review – The original 2005–2007 Lærdalselva eradication row accurately captured the early aluminium treatments but truncated the episode before the additional 2008 and 2011–2012 treatments and the eventual declaration of freedom in 2017, effectively under‑representing the duration and impact of this eradication phase. I have therefore extended the event years to 2005–2017 and updated the summary to include later treatments and the 2017 ‘friskmelding’, while keeping the classification as re_occurrence (continued presence of the same introduced strain in a known sub‑region) consistent with Norwegian sources. More detailed Norwegian technical reports and SNL’s Lærdalselvi entry were added or emphasised as primary references. Please check that this extended time span fits your event‑selection rules; if you prefer shorter, more discrete interventions, the episode could be split differently.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Gyrodactylus salaris
EPP.common.name: Gyrodactylosis
Host: Arctic char (Salvelinus alpinus) – anadromous and resident forms; sympatric Atlantic salmon and rainbow trout as comparators
Event.summary: Around 2006–2007, molecular and morphometric analyses demonstrated that Gyrodactylus salaris infecting anadromous Arctic char in the River Signaldalselva in northern Norway and resident Arctic char in Lake Pålsbufjorden in southern Norway were true G. salaris, confirming the first viable wild populations of this parasite on a host species in the absence of Atlantic salmon. Parasites on Signaldalselva char shared mitochondrial haplotypes with those on sympatric Atlantic salmon, while the Pålsbufjorden parasites carried a haplotype previously associated with rainbow trout, indicating at least two independent host‑switch events within Norway. Recognition of Arctic char as a competent reservoir host raised concerns that G. salaris could persist and spread even where salmon are absent or eradicated, complicating eradication strategies and requiring expanded surveillance and risk assessments for non‑salmon hosts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Human‑mediated introductions of G. salaris via stocking of salmon and rainbow trout and movements of equipment likely seeded infections into Signaldalselva and the upstream Lake Pålsbufjorden system, where hydroelectric development and multi‑species fisheries brought char into repeated contact with infected salmonids. Internal mechanisms: Clear host expansion and lineage diversification were documented—G. salaris on Arctic char exhibited mitochondrial haplotypes and subtle morphometrics distinct from some salmon‑associated strains, yet maintained reproductive success and transmission; this expansion of the host range and creation of new wild reservoirs justifies classification as re‑emergence driven by host expansion and enhanced transmission potential.
Review: retain – This event accurately summarizes the 2006–2007 demonstration that Arctic char can serve as a competent wild host and reservoir for G. salaris in Signaldalselva and Lake Pålsbufjorden, based on robust molecular and morphometric evidence. The classification as re_emergence (driven by host expansion and new reservoir formation within an already affected sub‑region) is appropriate, and the geography, timing and host description match the primary Parasitology paper and related Norwegian reports; no corrections beyond minor wording clarifications were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Gyrodactylus salaris
EPP.common.name: Gyrodactylosis
Countries: Norway [2014] (remaining infection regions with multiple infected rivers in central, western and south-eastern Norway)
Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) populations in numerous Norwegian rivers; other salmonids (brown trout, Arctic char, rainbow trout) acting as carriers or secondary hosts
Event.summary: Between roughly 2014 and 2020, Norway implemented an updated national eradication programme for Gyrodactylus salaris under a formal action plan and EEA‑approved national measures, targeting residual infection regions such as Rana, Vefsn, Skibotn, Steinkjer, Driva and Drammenselva while many previously treated rivers were being declared parasite‑free. During this period, G. salaris had historically been detected in over 50 Norwegian rivers, but coordinated chemical treatments (mainly rotenone and aluminium‑based methods), stricter movement controls and enhanced diagnostics progressively reduced the number of actively infected rivers to fewer than ten, concentrated in a few infection regions. The episode culminated in substantial progress towards the national goal of eradicating pathogenic G. salaris strains from all Norwegian rivers and farms, while also documenting continued re‑occurrence in a small subset of rivers where eradication had not yet succeeded, setting up final eradication campaigns in the 2020s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Strong policy and economic incentives to restore wild Atlantic salmon stocks and protect angling tourism, coupled with evolving European fish‑health regulations and EFTA Surveillance Authority approvals, underpinned Norway’s intensified national eradication plan, which used integrated piscicide and aluminium treatments, zoning and long‑term surveillance. External drivers included improved availability of piscicides, development of aluminium‑based methods, and advances in diagnostic tools (microscopy, molecular assays, eDNA), enabling more targeted interventions. Internal mechanisms: Persistent low‑level G. salaris infection in some rivers appears to reflect the parasite’s capacity to survive in refugia and exploit multiple salmonid hosts within complex catchments rather than emergence of new genotypes, so the episode is best treated as re_occurrence in a shrinking set of infection foci under sustained control pressure.
Review: retain – This row provides a reasonable synthesis of the 2014–2020 national eradication programme and its impact on the number of infected Norwegian rivers, consistent with Mo (2024), the Norwegian Fish Health Reports and the EFTA Surveillance Authority decision approving updated measures. Classification as re_occurrence (persistence and local resurgence within a long‑affected sub‑region) rather than inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence is appropriate, and the geographic scope (Norway, Northern Europe) matches the country sheet. No structural changes were necessary; I only tightened the linkage to key official sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Gyrodactylus salaris
EPP.common.name: Gyrodactylosis
Countries: Norway [2022] (Driva infection region: Rivers Driva, Litldalselva, Usma, Batnfjordselva and Gylelva, Møre og Romsdal)
Host: Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) and other salmonids in the Driva infection-region river systems
Event.summary: From 2022 to 2024, Norway carried out an intensive, multi‑river eradication campaign against Gyrodactylus salaris in the Driva infection region, treating the rivers Driva, Litldalselva, Usma, Batnfjordselva and, following a 2023 detection, Gylelva with a combination of rotenone and chlorine. The operations required complex logistics to ensure that all salmonid hosts and parasite refugia throughout these interconnected catchments were exposed to lethal concentrations, while parallel environmental monitoring and eDNA surveys documented treatment efficacy and the absence of surviving parasite populations. By 2024, Norwegian authorities reported completion of the chemical treatments with no subsequent detections of G. salaris in 2023–2024 sampling, and a formal post‑treatment surveillance (friskmeldings) programme starting in 2025, marking one of the final and most challenging steps toward eradicating G. salaris from all Norwegian wild salmon rivers.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing recognition of the ecological and economic value of Driva‑region salmon stocks and Norway’s national and international commitments to eradicate G. salaris led to major investments in this final eradication phase, implemented through a multi‑agency partnership involving the Environment Agency, Food Safety Authority, regional governors, Norwegian Veterinary Institute, NINA and NIVA. Internal mechanisms: As in other Norwegian rivers, the campaign targeted established high‑virulence G. salaris lineages that had persisted since the 1980s; the key biological challenge was eliminating parasites surviving in refugia or on non‑target hosts within a cold, complex river network, rather than coping with newly evolved strains, justifying classification as re_occurrence under intense control rather than re‑emergence.
Review: retain – This event is a well-documented, recent large‑scale eradication campaign in the Driva infection region and clearly among the most consequential late‑phase episodes for G. salaris in Norway. The timing (2022–2024), river list and description of combined rotenone and chlorine treatments align with Veterinary Institute reports and regional management documents, and classification as re_occurrence (removal of a long‑standing infection focus rather than new emergence) is appropriate. No corrections were required beyond minor wording changes and adding the newly published 2026 summary report as a key source.

EPP.scientific.name: Histoplasma farciminosum
EPP.common.name: Cryptococcus farciminosus, Zymonema farciminosum
Countries: Ethiopia [1999] (Debre Zeit, Mojo, Nazareth, Bako, Ejaji and 28 additional cart‑horse and cart‑mule towns)
Host: Equids – primarily carthorses and cart‑mules used for urban and peri‑urban transport
Event.summary: From December 1999 to January 2001, a cross‑sectional study of 2,907 carthorses in Debre Zeit, Mojo and Nazareth in central Ethiopia found Histoplasma farciminosum infection in 26.2% of animals, demonstrating rampant endemic epizootic lymphangitis in key cart‑horse towns.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12441683/?utm_source=openai)) Between November 2002 and April 2003, 21% of 309 cart‑mules in Bako and Ejaji in western Ethiopia were affected, and between January 2003 and June 2004 a survey of 19,082 carthorses in 28 towns recorded 18.8% prevalence, with highest burdens in warm, humid mid‑altitude towns and in larger horse populations.([colab.ws](https://colab.ws/articles/10.1016%2Fj.prevetmed.2004.09.008?utm_source=openai)) Taken together, these linked investigations (1999–2004) confirmed that epizootic lymphangitis had re‑occurred as one of the most important constraints on working equids across much of Ethiopia, without any coordinated national control effort.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of urban and peri‑urban cart‑horse and cart‑mule transport, concentration of equids at parking stations and markets, poor harness design causing chronic skin trauma at the chest, neck and limbs, limited owner awareness and access to antifungal treatment, and climatic suitability (warm, humid mid‑altitude towns) that favours survival of Histoplasma capsulatum var. farciminosum.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12441683/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: field and phylogenetic studies to date have not identified a novel epizootic lineage during this period; disease resurgence is best explained by increased transmission opportunities and work‑related skin injury, so the event is classified as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9330904/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event retained but the time span has been adjusted from “2002–2005” to “1999–2004” to reflect the actual periods of the major Ethiopian prevalence studies (2,907 carthorses in three central towns in 1999–2001; 309 cart‑mules in Bako/Ejaji in 2002–2003; 19,082 carthorses in 28 towns in 2003–2004).([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12441683/?utm_source=openai)) Countries and sub‑region are correctly coded as Ethiopia, Eastern Africa; event type is appropriately coded as re‑occurrence (no evidence for new continent or sub‑region invasion or for emergence of a new strain). Sources have been updated to include the 2002 Journal of Veterinary Science study and to remove inline URLs from the Countries field; a human reviewer should confirm that merging these linked surveys into a single 1999–2004 episode matches the project’s outbreak‑episode criteria.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Histoplasma farciminosum
EPP.common.name: Cryptococcus farciminosus, Zymonema farciminosum
Countries: Ethiopia [2010] (Bahir Dar, Amhara Region – cart‑mule population)
Host: Equids – primarily cart‑mules, with related burden in local cart‑horses
Event.summary: Baseline screening in 2010 of 430 cart‑mules in Bahir Dar, a major lake‑side city in Amhara Region, found epizootic lymphangitis prevalence of 23.9%, confirming a heavy local burden of chronic, debilitating disease similar to that seen in other Ethiopian towns.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8632952/?utm_source=openai)) From 2010 to 2017, an integrated community‑based control programme led by The Donkey Sanctuary and partners introduced improved diagnosis and treatment, owner education, better harnesses and carts, and euthanasia of advanced cases, with annual cross‑sectional surveys documenting a decline in prevalence to around 5–6%, a transient rise to 10% in 2016, and 5.9% (58/981) in 2017.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8632952/?utm_source=openai)) Despite substantial reductions in clinical case burden and improved welfare, epizootic lymphangitis remained endemic in Bahir Dar at the end of the programme.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: before intervention, high prevalence was linked to poorly fitting harnesses and carts that produced chronic harness wounds, overcrowded working and stabling conditions, and limited access to effective antifungal therapy, all of which prolonged infectiousness and favoured mechanical transmission by biting flies and contaminated equipment.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8632952/?utm_source=openai)) The control programme demonstrated that improving harness design, clinical management, owner awareness and municipal regulation can markedly reduce transmission in an endemic focus, but that underlying environmental suitability and reliance on working equids continue to sustain low‑level circulation. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype or change in virulence was identified during this period, so the episode is coded as re‑occurrence rather than re‑emergence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9330904/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event retained with minor corrections: Countries field simplified to “Ethiopia [2010] (Bahir Dar, Amhara Region)” and inline URLs removed; classification as re‑occurrence (with all other emergence‑type flags set to No) is consistent with the description of a long‑standing endemic focus experiencing control‑driven changes in prevalence rather than spread to a new continent/sub‑region or emergence of a new strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8632952/?utm_source=openai)) Source list appropriately emphasises the Frontiers 2021 community‑based intervention paper and supporting local prevalence studies; a human reviewer should confirm that treating the entire 2010–2017 control period as a single episode meets the project’s temporal‑linkage rules.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Histoplasma farciminosum
EPP.common.name: Cryptococcus farciminosus, Zymonema farciminosum
Countries: Ethiopia [2018] (17 cart‑horse towns across multiple regions including Kombolcha, Gondar and Debre Birhan)
Host: Equids – carthorses
Event.summary: Between October 2018 and June 2019, a cross‑sectional survey of 4,162 carthorses in 17 Ethiopian towns found an overall epizootic lymphangitis prevalence of 16.67% (95% CI 15.6–17.8) and detected disease in 16 of the 17 towns, with town‑level prevalences up to 33.3% at Kombolcha.([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2021.762937/full)) This large, multi‑site study confirmed that, more than a decade after earlier nationwide surveys and despite local control efforts, epizootic lymphangitis remained widely endemic in the cart‑horse sector across diverse climatic zones in Ethiopia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: logistic‑regression analyses indicated higher epizootic lymphangitis prevalence in warmer, more humid mid‑altitude towns and in areas with larger carthorse populations, supporting the role of climate suitability, urban aggregation of working equids, and associated harness‑related skin trauma as key external risk factors.([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2021.762937/full)) Limited access to affordable antifungal treatment and weak surveillance further allow chronic cases to persist and spread infection. Internal mechanisms: molecular studies of Ethiopian Histoplasma capsulatum var. farciminosum isolates show a relatively conserved equine‑associated lineage without evidence of a newly emerged hypervirulent strain during this period, so this episode is best classified as re‑occurrence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9330904/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – New event added to capture the large 2018–2019 multi‑town survey of 4,162 carthorses in 17 Ethiopian towns, which is among the largest post‑1990 datasets on epizootic lymphangitis and demonstrates widespread endemic re‑occurrence across the country.([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2021.762937/full)) Event is coded as re‑occurrence (all other emergence‑type flags No) because the pathogen and affected host system were long‑established in Ethiopia and no new continent or UN sub‑region was involved. Countries and sub‑region are coded as Ethiopia, Eastern Africa; a human reviewer should confirm that treating this survey as a distinct emergence episode, separate from earlier 1999–2004 studies and the 2010–2017 Bahir Dar control period, aligns with the project’s episode‑definition guidelines.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Iltovirus gallid2
EPP.common.name: Gallid alphaherpesvirus 1, ILT virus
Countries: Namibia [2018] (commercial farms near Windhoek and one farm in northern Namibia – three linked outbreaks)
Host: Domestic chickens (commercial layers and broilers)
Event.summary: Between July and August 2018, two ILT outbreaks near Windhoek, Namibia, caused the death of over 116,000 commercial layers and broilers on two farms; a third outbreak in September 2018 occurred roughly 800 km to the north in a smaller broiler flock.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) Affected flocks exhibited severe respiratory distress, 23–70% reported mortality, and marked drops in egg production on the layer farm, with necropsy revealing classic fibrinous and haemorrhagic laryngotracheitis.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) Molecular analysis showed that outbreak viruses were essentially identical to the Nobilis ILT live vaccine strain, indicating reversion to virulence and spread of a vaccine‑derived virus.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) Despite movement bans, illegal transport of birds and likely airborne spread between nearby farms contributed to wider dissemination; by late 2018 over 200,000 chickens had been lost, before improved vaccination practices and enforcement of movement controls brought the epizootic under control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Incorrect administration of live Nobilis ILT vaccine (aerosol spray instead of eye‑drop), unavailability of registered vaccine locally leading to probable off‑label sourcing, illegal movement of birds despite movement bans, shared worker housing, and windy seasonal conditions all contributed to vaccine‑virus spread between farms separated by up to 800 km.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) Internal mechanisms: Molecular epidemiology demonstrated that the outbreaks were caused by a reverted‑to‑virulence vaccine strain genetically indistinguishable from Nobilis ILT, exemplifying how live attenuated vaccines can re‑emerge as field pathogens when misused, but representing the first documented ILT outbreaks in southern Africa rather than a new genotype at global scale.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content))
Review: Decision: review. Reason: This high‑mortality Namibian episode (>116,000 birds dead and >200,000 birds lost overall; first documented ILT outbreaks in southern Africa) was missing from the original dataset and clearly qualifies among the most impactful modern ILT events.([repository.unam.edu.na](https://repository.unam.edu.na/server/api/core/bitstreams/5a9fea7d-b0b1-404e-9046-0516b3aa3f84/content)) It has been added and classified as intra‑continental emergence (new subregion within Africa) driven by vaccine‑strain reversion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Iltovirus gallid2
EPP.common.name: Gallid alphaherpesvirus 1, ILT virus
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2021] (Northern Ireland – mainly Armagh and Tyrone counties near Dungannon; ~19 affected flocks)
Host: Domestic chickens (mostly commercial poultry flocks of varying production types; some small flocks)
Event.summary: From early May 2021, Northern Ireland experienced a notable ILT outbreak centred around the Dungannon area, with 17–19 poultry flocks (mostly commercial) reported infected and roughly 250,000 birds estimated to have been affected.([fbcc.ca](https://www.fbcc.ca/file.aspx?id=9be515c1-49ba-466c-bacb-504e0d19812f)) Clinical signs were mainly respiratory, with generally low mortality but significant temporary production losses in recovering birds; ILT was already considered endemic in the region but had not caused a major commercial‑sector outbreak for nearly a decade.([daera-ni.gov.uk](https://www.daera-ni.gov.uk/articles/infectious-laryngotracheitis-ilt?utm_source=openai)) DAERA treated ILT as a production disease rather than imposing compulsory culling, instead emphasising strict farm biosecurity, careful handling and storage of litter, and targeted vaccination; by mid‑June 2021, the rate of new case reports had slowed and the outbreak was regarded as stabilising.([farmersjournal.ie](https://www.farmersjournal.ie/news/news/poultry-industry-getting-on-top-of-ilt-629101))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: ILTV is endemic in Northern Ireland, and officials believe initial spread in 2021 likely involved wind‑borne transmission between closely sited poultry houses, followed by further dissemination via contaminated litter and farm traffic in a dense poultry region.([farmersjournal.ie](https://www.farmersjournal.ie/news/news/poultry-industry-getting-on-top-of-ilt-629101)) Internal mechanisms: No evidence has been published of a novel genotype; available information suggests re-occurrence of existing ILTV lineages in commercial flocks that had previously been protected primarily through biosecurity and controlled vaccine use.
Review: Decision: review. Reason: This Northern Ireland episode, affecting nearly 250,000 birds across ~19 flocks, is one of the larger recent European ILT events and was missing from the original dataset.([fbcc.ca](https://www.fbcc.ca/file.aspx?id=9be515c1-49ba-466c-bacb-504e0d19812f)) A new row has been added and classified as re-occurrence in an already endemic Northern European region; geography and scale are based on DAERA and independent surveillance summaries.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Countries: United States of America [2002] (Virginia, West Virginia, North Carolina)
Host: Commercial turkeys and chickens (broilers and layers) in the Shenandoah Valley and adjacent regions; LPAI H7N2 subtype.
Event.summary: In March 2002, an outbreak of low pathogenic H7N2 avian influenza was detected among commercial turkey and chicken operations in Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley, signalling a major regional epizootic rather than sporadic LPAI detections. Over roughly four months, the virus spread to nearly 200 affected flocks in Virginia, West Virginia and North Carolina, prompting large-scale depopulation, movement controls and intensive surveillance. By mid-2002, stamping‑out of about 4.7 million birds, carcass disposal, disinfection, and surveillance activities brought the outbreak under control, and virus circulation was no longer detected in commercial operations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High poultry density in the Shenandoah Valley, frequent movement of live birds and shared equipment between premises, and delayed initial detection allowed extensive farm-to-farm spread before full control measures were implemented; logistical challenges with rapid depopulation and carcass disposal further complicated the response. Internal mechanisms: no clearly novel genotype was implicated; the episode represents a major re-occurrence and amplification of an H7N2 lineage already circulating in the eastern United States, driven more by management and trade networks than by marked viral change.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/104063870701900401))
Review: Retain. The 2002 Shenandoah Valley H7N2 LPAI outbreak is correctly described as a large regional re-occurrence of an existing lineage with ~4.7 million birds depopulated and nearly 200 infected premises, and the geography (USA/Northern America) matches the UNSD scheme.([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/104063870701900401)) Classification as re-occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental spread) aligns with project definitions.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Countries: China [2013] (initially Shanghai and neighbouring eastern provinces, then multiple eastern and southern provinces over successive waves).
Host: Primarily chickens (especially in live poultry markets), also other domestic poultry species; H7N9 LPAI virus in birds, with later emergence of H7N9 HPAI in poultry.
Event.summary: In March 2013, China reported the first human infections with a novel H7N9 avian influenza virus, and within days low pathogenic H7N9 was detected in chickens and environmental samples from live poultry markets in Shanghai and nearby provinces, revealing widespread silent circulation in poultry. Over multiple epidemic waves from 2013 to about 2017, H7N9 LPAI circulated in poultry across many eastern Chinese provinces, driving major live poultry market closures, mass culling and restructuring of the live poultry supply chain, and later gave rise to highly pathogenic H7N9 variants in poultry. After aggressive interventions including large-scale vaccination of poultry and permanent or prolonged closure of many live bird markets, reported H7N9 detections in poultry and humans declined sharply by the late 2010s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive live poultry market networks in eastern China, mixing of birds from many sources, high human–poultry contact, and complex poultry value chains allowed a newly reassorted H7N9 LPAI virus to spread widely before detection; subsequent control relied on large-scale market closures, culling and changes in marketing practices. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel reassortant H7N9 virus derived from multiple avian influenza lineages, exhibiting efficient replication in chickens with minimal clinical signs, enhanced zoonotic potential, and later mutations that converted some lineages to HPAI, which together constitute a major re-emergence event driven by viral evolution and enhanced transmission in an existing LPAI ecosystem.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6652192/))
Review: Retain with corrections. The description of timing, geography, and control measures for the H7N9 LPAI/HPAI episode in China is accurate and well sourced.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6652192/)) However, the event was originally coded as "first_detection" and "intra-continental emergence"; because H7N9 viruses existed before 2013 and LPAI influenza A was long established in East Asia, the 2013 episode is better classified as re-emergence of a novel reassortant lineage rather than as global first detection or intra-continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Jaagsiekte sheep retrovirus
EPP.common.name: JSRV, Sheep pulmonary adenocarcinoma virus
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event.summary: Origin: In the early 2010s, a severe episode of ovine pulmonary adenocarcinoma was recognized in sheep flocks in Shandong Province, China, where OPA had been reported historically but rarely characterized with modern virology. Development: Clinical, pathological, and RT‑PCR investigations confirmed numerous cases caused by exogenous JSRV, with phylogenetic analysis linking the Shandong strain closely to a Kenyan JSRV isolate and indicating widespread infection within affected flocks. End: The outbreak subsided only after heavily affected animals were removed and diagnosis clarified, but the study emphasized that JSRV‑associated OPA remains endemic and economically important in Chinese sheep production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑density sheep production, close housing, and movement of infected but subclinically affected animals facilitated flock‑level spread before recognition. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or clear virulence shift was reported; the outbreak reflected efficient transmission and long incubation of endemic exogenous JSRV rather than emergence of a distinct genotype.
Review: retain – Well‑documented severe OPA outbreak in Shandong, China, with molecular characterization and clear production impact. OPA was first reported in China in the 1950s, so classification as re_occurrence (not first_detection) is appropriate, and the Asia/Eastern Asia/China coding is consistent with the UNSD scheme. No changes made beyond confirming that this episode merits inclusion as one of the major post‑1990 outbreak‑scale events.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3909617/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Jaagsiekte sheep retrovirus
EPP.common.name: JSRV, Sheep pulmonary adenocarcinoma virus
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event.summary: Origin: Although OPA had been clinically suspected and is a notifiable disease in Ireland, its causative virus had not previously been confirmed, and an abattoir survey of adult sheep lungs was undertaken in the mid‑2010s. Development: Using gross examination, histopathology, JSRV‑specific RT‑PCR, and immunohistochemistry, researchers documented multiple OPA cases and, for the first time in Ireland, molecularly confirmed JSRV infection in affected sheep, enabling preliminary estimates of national prevalence and distribution. End: The study concluded that JSRV‑associated OPA was present but underdiagnosed in Ireland and recommended improved surveillance and control measures, marking a key diagnostic emergence event within the Irish sheep industry rather than a new introduction of the virus globally.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Enhanced abattoir surveillance combined with modern molecular methods revealed existing infection rather than a sudden biological change; movement of breeding sheep within and into Ireland likely sustained low‑level circulation. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain, resistance, or virulence change was identified; the primary mechanism was improved detection of endemic exogenous JSRV.
Review: retain – Lee et al. (2017) explicitly frame this as the first PCR confirmation of JSRV in Ireland and provide a national abattoir prevalence estimate, so classification as first_detection in this country is appropriate. The event is epidemiologically important despite modest case numbers and fits the brief to include major diagnostic emergence events. Geographic coding (Europe, Northern Europe, Ireland) is correct and source selection is appropriate.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5735933/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Maedi-visna virus
EPP.common.name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Countries: India [2016] (Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh; abattoirs in northern India)
Host: Sheep (slaughtered and farmed) and goats (serology in mixed small‑ruminant flocks)
Event.summary: Around 2016, investigators in Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh, reported ELISA evidence of Maedi–Visna and caprine arthritis–encephalitis virus antibodies in sheep and goats, giving the first published indication of SRLV circulation in that region of India.([ndpublisher.in](https://ndpublisher.in/admin/issues/JARV6N13.pdf)) In 2017, a pathology study on 888 slaughtered sheep from Indian abattoirs identified lungs with lesions consistent with maedi and confirmed MVV proviral DNA by PCR in a subset, which the authors described as probably the first molecular confirmation of maedi‑visna infection in India.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29263606/)) Subsequent work from the same group has demonstrated MVV nucleic acid and antigen in various tissues of spontaneously affected sheep and goats, indicating that SRLV infection is established in parts of the Indian small‑ruminant population, although national prevalence and economic impact remain poorly quantified.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11327649/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of sheep and goat production in some Indian states, together with movement or importation of exotic and crossbred animals for genetic improvement, likely introduced MVV and related SRLVs into previously unrecognised foci; limited prior surveillance meant that infection could circulate silently for years before serological and molecular tools were applied.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29263606/)) Internal mechanisms: Early reports have not identified a unique Indian lineage associated with changed virulence; observed lesions and tropism match typical SRLV infections. Long incubation periods, multisystemic pathology and variable antibody responses complicate diagnosis and control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11327649/))
Review: Decision: review. Updates: (i) changed first_detection from Yes to No, since MVV was globally recognised long before and there is evidence of SRLV infection in other Southern Asian countries (e.g. Iran) before 2016; (ii) set re_occurrence to Yes, interpreting this as emergence of MVV/SRLVs in a new country within a continent and sub‑region where they were already present; and (iii) clarified that 2017 represents the first molecular confirmation in India rather than necessarily the first true presence. The event is important for documenting the entry of MVV into Indian small‑ruminant populations, but final weighting among the ‘top 10’ should be checked against any future evidence of larger, multi‑flock outbreaks in the region.

EPP.scientific.name: Maedi-visna virus
EPP.common.name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Countries: Brazil [2018] (Rio Grande do Sul, Salvador do Sul municipality)
Host: Sheep (Texel flock, southern Brazil)
Event.summary: In January 2018, a closed flock of 96 Texel ewes in Salvador do Sul, Rio Grande do Sul, developed an outbreak of respiratory and neurological disease; 14 animals showed clinical signs such as weight loss, dyspnoea and hindlimb ataxia and 14.5% of the flock were seropositive for MVV.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9433499/)) Histopathology and PCR confirmed concurrent maedi (lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia) and visna (encephalitis), and the authors reported this as the first well‑documented outbreak of clinical visna‑maedi disease in a Brazilian sheep flock.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9433499/)) All seropositive sheep were eventually culled, representing a major loss for the pedigree meat flock and illustrating the potential for severe disease expression where MVV enters a naïve, intensively managed system.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9433499/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The flock had acquired replacement ewes from multiple external sources without MVV testing and used artificial insemination with semen of uncertain lentiviral status; combined with semi‑intensive management (indoor housing at night, high stocking density), these practices facilitated efficient within‑flock spread once MVV was introduced.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9433499/)) Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was identified; the episode shows how typical SRLV strains can cause overt maedi and visna when introduced into large, genetically susceptible and previously unexposed flocks, with chronic infection and high contact rates leading to cumulative pathology and production loss.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9433499/))
Review: Decision: review. Correction: reclassified this episode from re_emergence to re_occurrence, because the clinical outbreak involved typical MVV strains in an already infected country and there is no evidence for a new genotype, host switch or change in intrinsic viral properties; the severe expression is best explained by introduction into a naïve, intensively housed Texel flock. The event is flock‑scale (≈100 animals) but is notable as the first fully documented clinical visna–maedi outbreak in Brazil and helps to illustrate the production impact of MVV in South American systems; it should likely be retained but may be ranked slightly below the very largest multi‑flock events (e.g. Ethiopia and Norway) when enforcing a strict top‑10 cut‑off.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Maedi-visna virus
EPP.common.name: MVV, Small ruminant lentivirus, Ovine progressive pneumonia virus
Host: Sheep (commercial and breeding flocks in Trøndelag)
Event.summary: In 2019, the Norwegian SRLV surveillance programme detected a new case of maedi in a sheep flock in Trøndelag county after more than a decade without detected cases.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf)) Tracing of animal movements and intensive regional screening in northern Trøndelag led to the identification of an outbreak cluster; surveillance reports and subsequent analyses describe nine initially recognised infected flocks, with extended investigations revealing well over a hundred infected flocks overall and necessitating culling of thousands of sheep.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf)) By 2020, aggressive test‑and‑cull measures, movement controls and targeted surveillance had again reduced apparent prevalence to very low levels, but the outbreak underscored the diagnostic challenges of eliminating SRLVs and the risk of re‑introduction even in countries with long‑standing control programmes.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The 2019–2020 outbreak appears to have stemmed from undetected introduction of MVV‑infected animals into a regional breeding network with extensive movement of rams and ewes between flocks, coupled with earlier surveillance strategies that focused on specific flock types and may have allowed infection to persist unrecognised in other holdings.([vetinst.no](https://www.vetinst.no/_/attachment/inline/70d0e11c-6735-47b1-a443-c2eb90d8ba38%3A50b8e63ed712bf20292cc9de8d5cb67782bee6cb/2021_17_OK_SRLV%20in%20sheep%20and%20goats%20in%20Norway%202020.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate emergence of a novel, more virulent MVV strain; instead, the outbreak is consistent with the known epidemiology of SRLVs—long incubation, intermittent seropositivity and focal high within‑flock prevalence—interacting with imperfectly sensitive serological tests and incomplete coverage of prior surveillance.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11225221/))
Review: Decision: review. New event added. Rationale: more recent Norwegian reports and outbreak analyses show that the 2019–2020 Trøndelag episode involved a substantial number of infected flocks (on the order of 100–200) and culling of thousands of sheep, clearly marking it as one of the most impactful modern MVV re‑occurrence events. I therefore added a dedicated row rather than subsuming it under the earlier 2002–2005 outbreak. The event is coded as re_occurrence, with no evidence for a new strain or inter‑continental introduction. Precise numbers of infected flocks (e.g. the figure of 179 reported in at least one analysis) should be verified and harmonised across the dataset by a Nordic expert.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine tuberculosis, bTB
Countries: Canada [1992] (Manitoba – Riding Mountain National Park ecosystem)
Host: Elk (Cervus elaphus manitobensis); cattle (Bos taurus); white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus)
Event.summary: In 1992, the first case of bovine tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium bovis was confirmed in a free-ranging bull elk shot near Rossburn, Manitoba, representing the first reported infection in wild elk in North America and linking wildlife to a nearby infected cattle herd.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC539224/?utm_source=openai)) Through the 1990s and early 2000s, additional infected elk and at least 11 infected cattle herds were detected around Riding Mountain National Park, leading authorities to designate a Riding Mountain TB Eradication Area and implement intensive surveillance and control measures for both wildlife and livestock.([digitalcommons.unl.edu](https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/michbovinetb/49/?utm_source=openai)) By about 2010, prevalence in elk and deer had declined and no new cattle outbreaks were detected for several years, but the area continued to be managed as one of Canada’s last wildlife-associated M. bovis foci because of persistent low‑level infection in elk.([gov.mb.ca](https://gov.mb.ca/agriculture/animal-health-and-welfare/animal-health/bovine-tuberculosis.fr.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High local elk densities, supplemental winter feeding practices that concentrated elk and cattle on shared hay bales, and overlap between elk wintering grounds and cattle pastures facilitated indirect transmission at feeding sites, while initial lack of targeted wildlife surveillance delayed recognition of elk as a reservoir.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC539224/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) with establishment of free-ranging Manitoban elk as a wildlife maintenance host for M. bovis, sustained elk‑to‑elk transmission in a relatively sedentary subpopulation, and spillback to cattle and occasionally to white‑tailed deer, consistent with a re-emergence event driven by a new multi‑host reservoir rather than by a novel bacterial lineage.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC539224/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Added as a major wildlife host-expansion event: the Riding Mountain National Park elk–cattle system is one of the few documented free-ranging M. bovis wildlife reservoirs in Canada, with repeated cattle outbreaks and a long-running eradication programme, and is widely recognized in the global wildlife TB literature.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC539224/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-emergence (new elk maintenance host within an already endemic region) and North America/Northern America/Canada geographic coding are appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine tuberculosis, bTB
Host: White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus); cattle (Bos taurus); humans (spillover)
Event.summary: In 1994, Mycobacterium bovis was identified in a hunter-harvested free-ranging white-tailed deer in northeastern Michigan, marking the beginning of a recognized wildlife epidemic in cervids in North America.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/13838035_Bovine_Tuberculosis_in_Free-Ranging_White-Tailed_Deer_From_Michigan?utm_source=openai)) Over the subsequent decade, bovine TB became endemic in the local deer population, with repeated spillback infections in nearby cattle herds and documented zoonotic cases in humans with exposure to deer or unpasteurized products.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2570927/?utm_source=openai)) By around 2007, intensive management (deer population reduction, feeding restrictions, cattle surveillance) reduced but did not eliminate transmission, leaving a persistent deer reservoir that continues to threaten cattle herds.([michigan.gov](https://www.michigan.gov/en/emergingdiseases/home/bovine-tuberculosis?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High deer densities, supplemental feeding and baiting practices that aggregated deer, close proximity of cattle farms to deer habitat, and historical under-recognition of TB in wildlife allowed M. bovis to establish in free-ranging deer.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/13838035_Bovine_Tuberculosis_in_Free-Ranging_White-Tailed_Deer_From_Michigan?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) with establishment of white-tailed deer as a new wildlife maintenance host; Enhanced Transmission via dense winter feeding aggregations; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of deer-associated strains within northeastern Michigan; and intrinsic pyrazinamide resistance of M. bovis complicating treatment in spillover human cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2570927/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This is the archetypal North American wildlife host-expansion event: Michigan’s endemic white‑tailed deer reservoir with recurrent cattle and human cases is clearly one of the highest‑impact M. bovis episodes globally since 1990.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/13838035_Bovine_Tuberculosis_in_Free-Ranging_White-Tailed_Deer_From_Michigan?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-emergence (new maintenance host), with North America/Northern America/USA (Michigan) geographic coding, is appropriate; no changes made.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium bovis
EPP.common.name: Bovine tuberculosis, bTB
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2002] (England, Wales, Northern Ireland)
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus); humans (zoonotic TB due to M. bovis)
Event.summary: Between 2002 and 2014, surveillance in England, Wales and Northern Ireland recorded a small but statistically significant increase in human tuberculosis cases caused by Mycobacterium bovis amid a background of rising bovine TB in cattle.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai)) During this period, most human M. bovis patients had exposures such as contact with TB‑affected cattle or consumption of unpasteurized dairy products, highlighting ongoing zoonotic risk despite historical declines after pasteurization and cattle control.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai)) By 2014, overall human M. bovis incidence remained low but stable, with public health guidance emphasizing continued control of bovine TB in cattle and risk‑based messaging to farmers, veterinarians, and consumers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Re-occurrence of bovine TB in cattle herds in high‑incidence regions, occupational and food‑borne exposures (raw milk, contact with infected livestock or wildlife), and travel or migration leading to exposure in high‑incidence rural areas were key external drivers of zoonotic cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: No major novel genotype or increased virulence was identified in human M. bovis isolates; the increase reflects spillover from expanding or persistent animal reservoirs that themselves were sustained by wildlife–livestock transmission cycles, so this episode is best classified as re-occurrence linked to broader bovine TB dynamics.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Geographic coding has been corrected to remove the Republic of Ireland, because the underlying surveillance study and notification data cover only England, Wales and Northern Ireland.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5382737/?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (low but increasing zoonotic cases reflecting spillover from resurgent animal reservoirs) is appropriate, but the overall human case numbers are modest relative to the major animal and wildlife events; recommend retaining the row to document the zoonotic dimension while flagging it for expert review of whether it should rank among the top 10 emergence events for this host system.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae
EPP.common.name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Wild Tibetan antelope (Pantholops hodgsonii)
Event.summary: In 2012, a fatal pneumonia outbreak occurred in endangered Tibetan antelope on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau in China, and microbiological and molecular investigations identified Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae as the causative agent, establishing CCPP in this wild species for the first time. The outbreak caused notable mortality in antelope herds that share pastures with domestic goats and sheep, indicating a wildlife–livestock interface source and revealing a new, highly susceptible wild host in this high‑altitude ecosystem. Following recognition of the etiologic agent, Chinese authorities and researchers increased surveillance in both wildlife and small ruminants in the region; no similarly large CCPP outbreaks have since been reported in Tibetan antelope, though the species remains at risk due to ongoing contact with infected domestic goats. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3840868/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increasing overlap of domestic goat and sheep grazing with Tibetan antelope ranges on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, combined with transhumant movements and minimal separation between livestock and wildlife, created opportunities for pathogen spillover into this endangered antelope. Internal mechanisms: This event exemplifies host expansion of Mccp from domestic goats into a novel wild antelope species, demonstrating that existing strains can cross species barriers and cause severe disease without clear evidence of major genetic change, and is therefore coded as re-emergence driven by host expansion and enhanced transmission at a wildlife–livestock interface. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3840868/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event correctly summarises the first documented CCPP outbreak in Tibetan antelope on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (China, 2012), with appropriate emphasis on wildlife–livestock interface and host-range expansion. Geography (Asia; Eastern Asia; China), timing, host description and classification as re-emergence (host expansion) match the primary EID report and subsequent reviews, and no substantial corrections are required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae
EPP.common.name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Domestic goats (Capra hircus) in a large commercial herd (~2,000 head)
Event.summary: In August 2021, a large herd of approximately 2,000 goats near Tehran, Iran, experienced a severe outbreak of respiratory disease with pleuropneumonia; clinical investigation recorded substantial morbidity and a high case fatality rate among affected goats, and PCR on lung samples confirmed Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae as the cause. This outbreak provided the first detailed, peer‑reviewed description of a CCPP outbreak in Iran with laboratory confirmation of Mccp, complementing earlier OIE reports of CCPP without etiologic confirmation in 2006–2007. The disease spread rapidly through the herd before diagnosis, causing major losses, but was brought under control through whole‑herd antibiotic treatment followed by vaccination with an inactivated Pulmovac‑In Mccp vaccine, after which no further severe CCPP episodes were reported in this herd in the short term. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10003596/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A history of malnutrition and heat stress in the preceding two months likely reduced herd immunity, while dense stocking and internal movement of animals facilitated rapid aerosol spread once CCPP was introduced; initial lack of specific vaccination against CCPP and delayed laboratory confirmation also contributed to the severity. Internal mechanisms: Pathology and clinical course were typical of virulent Mccp infection, with no evidence of a novel genotype; this represents re-occurrence of endemic disease in a susceptible large herd, with severity shaped largely by management and environmental stressors rather than by new pathogen traits. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10003596/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This event summarises the 2021 Tehran-region herd outbreak described by Abdollahi et al. 2023, correctly highlighting it as the first peer-reviewed, Mccp-confirmed CCPP outbreak report from Iran while acknowledging earlier OIE-notified epizootics. Classification as re-occurrence (in a country and sub-region known to be affected) without intra-/inter-continental emergence is appropriate; detailed morbidity and case-fatality figures should still be checked directly against the article before final publication.
