EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hantavirus, HCPS, HFRS
Countries: China [2006] (nationwide spread across multiple provinces through 2012)
Host: Apodemus agrarius (striped field mouse); Rattus norvegicus (brown rat); humans
Event.summary: Between 2006 and 2012, China experienced sustained high incidence of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, with more than 77,000 reported cases and hundreds of deaths, and marked geographic spread into new counties and provinces compared with earlier decades. Surveillance analyses showed large annual case burdens and shifting hotspots, particularly in northeastern, central and eastern provinces where rodent hosts and human agricultural activities overlapped. Expansion of vaccination, intensified rodent control and health‑education campaigns eventually reduced incidence and severity in many high‑risk areas after this peak period.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid socio‑economic change, agricultural expansion, rodent habitat alteration, climate variability affecting rodent abundance, and increased rural–urban migration amplified contact between people and rodent hosts; improved surveillance increased detection. Internal mechanisms: Continued spillover of established Hantaan and Seoul orthohantaviruses from Apodemus and Rattus reservoirs (no major new strain), representing re‑occurrence and geographic range expansion within Eastern Asia driven primarily by environmental and demographic forces.
Review: review – This episode correctly summarizes a very large 2006–2012 HFRS resurgence in China (tens of thousands of cases), clearly among the most impactful Orthohantavirus events. However, intra_continental_emergence has been changed from 'true' to 'false' because hantaviruses and HFRS were long endemic throughout Eastern Asia; spread was within the same UNSD subregion rather than to a new subregion. The event is best classified as large-scale re_occurrence; geography and sources remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus monkeypox
EPP.common.name: Monkeypox virus, MPXV
Countries: Sudan [2005] (Unity State, then part of Sudan; now South Sudan)
Host: Humans; probable exposure to wildlife and/or contaminated materials in healthcare settings
Event.summary: In 2005, an outbreak of febrile rash illness was detected in Unity State in southern Sudan, an area not previously known to be affected by mpox, initially misclassified as other pox‑like diseases. Field investigations with laboratory confirmation identified multiple linked human mpox cases and characterized a novel virus belonging to the Congo Basin clade, marking the first reported mpox outbreak in Sudan and in the Northern Africa subregion. The outbreak waned after case isolation and infection‑control measures were instituted, but it highlighted the virus’s capacity to emerge in new ecological and health‑care settings far from its classical rainforest foci.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/16/10/pdfs/1539.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of infected persons from forested regions, limited infection‑prevention resources, and use of a traditional healer/dentist who treated multiple patients may have facilitated a point‑source introduction and subsequent spread. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analysis indicated a novel virus within the Congo Basin (clade I) lineage, consistent with ongoing diversification and possible adaptation to broader ecological niches, supporting classification as a re‑emergent variant.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/16/10/pdfs/1539.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Papillomavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Papillomatosis
Host: Cattle (Holstein heifers; teats of dairy heifers)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s (reported in a 2007 study and here assigned to 2004), a very large outbreak of teat papillomatosis occurred in a commercial Holstein heifer herd in Hokkaido, northern Japan, with 560 of 700 heifers (80%) developing flat, round teat tumors that interfered with milking. Molecular and histological investigation showed that the epithelial papillomas were associated mainly with bovine papillomavirus type 6 (BPV‑6), along with several unclassified BPV types, indicating a mixed infection. The outbreak gradually subsided following culling of severely affected animals and herd management adjustments, but it highlighted the potential for widespread papillomatosis to disrupt dairy production in high‑density heifer rearing systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑density dairy management with large numbers of naïve replacement heifers, close contact during milking, and potential mechanical transmission via teat cup liners and other fomites facilitated rapid within‑herd spread of BPV. Internal mechanisms: Efficient epitheliotropic infection by BPV‑6 plus co‑circulating unclassified BPV types, and probable viral adaptation to teat skin, contributed to extensive teat involvement and production impact, representing a notable re‑emergent expression of an otherwise endemic virus.
Review: Retain – Well‑documented large herd outbreak in Hokkaido (560/700 heifers affected) that clearly meets the definition of a major re‑emergent event. Geography (Japan, Eastern Asia) and host are correct. Event type as re‑emergence (due to unusually severe expression and involvement of BPV‑6 plus unclassified types) is appropriate; no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence or first‑detection flags are warranted. Sources correctly point to Maeda et al. (Vet Microbiol 2007) and associated bibliographic records; no changes needed apart from clarifying the narrative that the 2004 date reflects the outbreak period reported in the 2007 paper.

EPP.scientific.name: Papillomavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Papillomatosis
Countries: China [2017] (Shandong Province; three linked Holstein dairy farms)
Host: Dairy cattle (Holstein cows; teats)
Event.summary: In October 2017, an outbreak of flat, round teat papillomatosis affected three closely linked Holstein dairy farms in Shandong Province, eastern China, with 117 of 442 cows developing teat lesions that complicated milking. Molecular investigation of papilloma tissues and swabs showed that the outbreak was associated with bovine papillomavirus type 10 (BPV‑10), representing the first report of BPV‑10 infection in China and one of the first molecular characterizations of BPV‑associated teat papillomatosis in the country. The outbreak was gradually brought under control through herd management and hygiene measures, but it highlighted the potential for specific BPV types to spread through interconnected dairy operations and cause substantial local production losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of veterinarians, staff and possibly equipment among three nearby farms under common ownership created a connected network that allowed BPV‑10 to disseminate rapidly; intensive milking systems and close animal contact further promoted spread. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of BPV‑10—previously undetected in China—into these dairy herds represented the emergence of a specific BPV genotype in a new national setting within an already endemic continental range; strain‑specific immunity and viral traits favoring teat epithelium infection likely contributed to efficient transmission and lesion development. Because papillomaviruses were already endemic in Chinese cattle, this is best classified as re‑emergence with novel strain involvement rather than as first detection of the EPP or intra‑continental emergence.
Review: Review – Retain the event as a major outbreak (117/442 cows affected across three epidemiologically linked farms) and as the first report of BPV‑10 in China. However, the original classification as both first_detection and intra_continental_emergence has been corrected: bovine papillomaviruses causing papillomatosis were already present in Asia and in China, so this episode does not represent first detection of the EPP or its first arrival in a new subregion. It is more consistent with a re‑emergent event driven by introduction and spread of a specific genotype (BPV‑10) in a national dairy network. Geographic fields (China, Eastern Asia) and host are correct; sources (J‑Stage/PMC versions of the same paper) are appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Papillomavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Papillomatosis
Countries: Brazil [2024] (Northeast region; multiple dairy goat farms in RN, PB and PE)
Host: Dairy goats (udders and teats)
Event.summary: In the early 2020s (fieldwork culminating in a doctoral thesis defended in 2024), investigators surveyed 58 dairy goat farms in the Northeast region of Brazil (Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba and Pernambuco states) and identified clusters of udder and teat papillomatosis in goats, a condition not previously systematically documented in this production system. Among 1885 goats examined, 21 animals (1.11%) on 14 properties had papillomatous lesions on the udder or teats; histopathology confirmed papillomas and molecular testing of selected lesions revealed bovine papillomavirus type 2 (BPV‑2) along with two putative new BPV types and occasional co‑infection with additional BPV genotypes. Although the outbreaks remained localized and involved relatively few clinical cases, they raised concern about impacts on milk production and milking hygiene in dairy goats and provided clear evidence of cross‑species BPV infection and adaptation in small ruminants.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Mixed‑species smallholder systems common in Northeast Brazil, with close contact between goats and cattle and shared milking or handling equipment, likely facilitated spillover of BPVs from cattle into goats; limited biosecurity and extensive management may have supported ongoing circulation. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of BPV‑2 and related viruses into goats, together with detection of putative new BPV types and co‑infections, reflects re‑emergence driven by both host‑range expansion and novel genotypes, suggesting that BPVs can adapt to new domestic ruminant hosts under suitable ecological and management conditions.
Review: Review – Event retained as an important host‑expansion episode but corrected in several ways. (1) Timing: the original row dated this to 2015–2018, but the only directly cited source is a UFRPE doctoral thesis (defended June 2024) that describes a cross‑sectional survey of 58 farms and 1885 goats; in the absence of explicit field sampling years, the thesis defence year 2024 is used as a proxy for the event year. (2) Countries field updated to Brazil [2024] and to specify the three northeastern states. (3) The original classification as first_detection has been removed; papillomaviruses were already long known in livestock, and caprine papillomatosis had been described elsewhere, so this episode is better treated as re‑emergence with host expansion and novel genotypes rather than global first detection of the EPP. Recommend future users consult the full thesis (and any derived peer‑reviewed articles) to refine the exact sampling period; nonetheless, this represents a meaningful, if numerically modest, emergence of papillomatosis in a new livestock host system within Brazil.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Papillomavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Papillomatosis
Host: Dairy cattle (cutaneous papillomas on body skin)
Event.summary: In the early 2020s, veterinarians in Taiwan recognized cutaneous papillomas in lactating dairy cows on several farms, leading to the first systematic investigation of bovine papillomaviruses in Taiwanese cattle. Eight papilloma samples collected from six dairy farms were analyzed and found to contain BPV‑1, BPV‑2 and a novel BPV genotype, demonstrating that BPVs were circulating and associated with skin papillomatosis in Taiwan where little prior disease information had been reported. The lesions were generally benign but raised concerns about animal welfare and potential progression to more serious neoplastic disease. The documented cases were managed at farm level through surgical removal and supportive care rather than large‑scale control programs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and previously unrecognized circulation of BPVs in Taiwanese dairy herds likely occurred over time via cattle and semen movements, but only became evident when visible lesions were investigated with modern diagnostics. Internal mechanisms: Detection of BPV‑1, BPV‑2 and a novel genotype in Taiwanese cattle indicates both geographic range documentation in a previously unsurveyed area and ongoing genetic diversification of BPVs; this is best viewed as re‑emergence mediated by novel strain appearance and improved detection capabilities, not as first detection of the EPP in the region.
Review: Review – Event retained but corrected. (1) Timing: the original row dated this event to 2016, but the Transboundary and Emerging Diseases article describing these cases was published in 2025, with sample identifiers suggesting collection in 2023; the year has therefore been updated to 2023–2023, and the country field to China [2023] (Taiwan Province). (2) Event type: first_detection and intra_continental_emergence flags have been removed, because bovine papillomatosis was already known in Eastern Asia; instead, this episode represents re‑emergence via detection of BPV‑1/2 plus a novel genotype in a previously unsurveyed national context. (3) Sources: limited to the primary article and its PDF mirror; a general Papillomaviridae Wikipedia link used only for background has been removed from the per‑event sources. Overall this is a modest‑size but well‑documented re‑emergent event in a new national setting that should remain in the dataset, but users should treat the 2023 date as approximate pending more precise sampling information.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Papillomavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Papillomatosis
Countries: Brazil [2016] (Rio Grande do Sul; Passo Fundo and Farroupilha; multiple source herds)
Host: Dairy cattle (teat papillomas; animals sent to slaughter from affected herds)
Event.summary: In 2016, researchers in Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil, collected teat papilloma samples at abattoirs from milking cows that had been culled from herds because of teat lesions and milking problems, representing the tail end of severe papillomatosis episodes in those herds. In total, 23 teat wart samples from cows originating from Passo Fundo and Farroupilha were analyzed, revealing at least 26 complete BPV genomes corresponding to numerous known types and 14 new BPV types (provisionally named BPV‑30 to BPV‑43), indicating remarkable viral diversity in teat papillomatosis. Parallel work on a larger set of slaughtered dairy cows from the same region documented 73 animals with teat papillomas and at least 24 different BPV types, including 10 putative new types, reinforcing the picture of extremely diverse co‑infections in cull cows with chronic teat disease. While these investigations sampled animals at slaughter rather than during active on‑farm outbreaks, they showed that extensive and genetically complex papillomatosis was contributing to culling and production losses in southern Brazil. The immediate herd‑level events ended with removal of affected cows, but the work suggested that similar undetected diversity underlies ongoing teat papillomatosis problems in regional dairies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Chronic teat papillomatosis in high‑producing dairy cows, combined with economic pressures favoring culling of animals with milking difficulties, led to concentration of severe cases in slaughter populations; intensive milking practices and environmental exposures likely facilitated persistent herd‑level transmission in the source herds. Internal mechanisms: Frequent co‑infection with many BPV genotypes, including 14 newly described types (BPV‑30 to BPV‑43) and numerous other known and putative types, points to rapid viral diversification and complex papillomavirome communities driving re‑emergent and persistent teat disease; this represents re‑emergence driven by extensive novel strain/genotype emergence and potentially altered immune interactions in affected cows.
Review: Retain – This event captures a major, well‑documented focus of papillomatosis in southern Brazil: multiple herds in Rio Grande do Sul supplying slaughtered dairy cows with chronic teat warts, from which investigators characterized both high case numbers (73 culled animals with teat papillomas) and extraordinary BPV genetic diversity (14 newly described types plus many known types). It clearly meets criteria for a large, impactful emergence episode in terms of production loss (culling and milking problems) and viral evolution. The year 2016 reflects the slaughter and sample collection period reported in the Animal Microbiome and Brazilian Journal of Microbiology papers. Classification as both re_occurrence (persistent disease pressure in an endemic subregion) and re_emergence (numerous novel genotypes) is appropriate; there is no evidence that this represents first detection or inter‑/intra‑continental emergence. The previous separate Brazilian “2010–2013 multi‑herd” row duplicated much of this content and has been recommended for exclusion; this 2016 row should be retained as the main Brazilian teat papillomavirome emergence event.

EPP.scientific.name: Papillomavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Papillomatosis
Countries: Portugal [2000] (Azores archipelago; especially São Miguel Island)
Host: Cattle (dairy and beef; mainly adult cows)
Event.summary: From roughly 2000 through 2006, bovine enzootic haematuria (BEH) associated with urinary bladder tumours in cattle grazing bracken fern–infested pastures remained hyper‑endemic in the Azores archipelago of Portugal, causing substantial economic losses. Investigations during this period demonstrated a strong association between bovine papillomavirus type 2 (BPV‑2) infection and proliferative and neoplastic bladder lesions in affected cattle, with viral DNA and E5 oncoprotein detected in urothelial tumours. BEH had been recognized in the Azores for decades, but work in the early 2000s clarified the viral co‑carcinogenic role of BPV‑2 alongside bracken fern toxins and documented that bladder cancer attributable to this complex caused an estimated €4 million in losses between 2000 and 2006. Control efforts have focused on reducing bracken exposure and managing affected animals, but the disease complex remains a major constraint in certain high‑risk grazing areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term grazing of cattle on pastures heavily infested with bracken fern (Pteridium aquilinum), whose carcinogenic compounds act as co‑factors, combined with traditional management systems that kept cattle on these pastures for years, created chronic exposure conditions favoring bladder tumour development. Limited pasture alternatives and economic constraints perpetuated this pattern. Internal mechanisms: Persistent BPV‑2 infection of the urinary bladder mucosa, with expression of the viral E5 oncoprotein, acts synergistically with bracken‑derived carcinogens to drive neoplastic transformation of urothelial cells; this represents re‑emergence of papillomavirus‑associated neoplasia in a well‑known endemic focus, with improved molecular understanding and quantification of impact rather than first occurrence of the disease. The dramatic economic burden and long‑standing high incidence justify inclusion of this chronic, geographically focused disease complex as a major emergence event.
Review: Retain (newly added event) – This row has been added because bovine enzootic haematuria (BEH) in the Azores represents one of the most impactful papillomavirus‑associated disease complexes in livestock during the 1990–2025 period, with documented heavy economic losses (on the order of €4 million between 2000 and 2006) and strong evidence implicating BPV‑2 in bladder tumour pathogenesis alongside bracken fern exposure. The event is framed as a chronic, geographically bounded re‑emergent disease complex rather than a single acute outbreak, consistent with the literature. Classification as both re_occurrence (long‑standing endemic disease with continued high incidence linked to external environmental drivers) and re_emergence (clarified and ongoing role of BPV‑2 in neoplasia) is appropriate; there is no basis for first‑detection or inter‑/intra‑continental emergence flags, as BEH was recognized in the Azores before 1990. The 2000–2006 time window is chosen because economic impact was explicitly quantified for this period in the cited sources; users may refine this range if more detailed temporal data are compiled.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Host: Water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis), cattle (Bos taurus/indicus)
Event.summary: In late September to mid-October 2003, a severe HS outbreak occurred in Banir and Bidor areas of Batang Padang district, Perak State, Malaysia, affecting shared-grazing buffalo and cattle herds. In Banir, 11 buffalo herds (572 animals) and two cattle herds (56 animals) were involved, with 200 buffalo and four cattle deaths, while an additional small buffalo herd in Bidor also suffered high mortality; Pasteurella multocida serotype B:2 was isolated from heart blood and nasal swabs. The epidemic curve showed an explosive,-short duration event with most deaths occurring in the first week, and the outbreak was described as the largest HS episode in the country in the preceding decade. After emergency vaccination and management changes, mortality subsided and no further major HS cases were reported in the affected herds during the investigation period.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of apparently healthy but carrier cattle from an HS-endemic region into an immunologically naïve, poorly vaccinated buffalo population, combined with heavy rainfall and use of shared ponds and swamps for wallowing and drinking, created ideal conditions for rapid transmission and high mortality. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was caused by typical HS-associated P. multocida B:2; there was no indication of novel genotypes or resistance, so this episode represents a catastrophic re-occurrence in an endemic country triggered by animal movement and environmental conditions rather than pathogen change.
Review: Retain – Added as a new high-impact outbreak representing South-eastern Asia; mortality of over 200 buffaloes plus cattle and characterization as Malaysia’s largest HS outbreak in a decade justify inclusion among major events. Classified as re-occurrence in an endemic country (no evidence of new strain or new region); geography (Asia/South-eastern Asia, Malaysia; Perak State) and scale are taken directly from the outbreak investigation report.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Bovine pasteurellosis (haemorrhagic septicaemia, serotypes B:2 and E:2)
Host: Water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis), cattle (Bos taurus)
Event.summary: During the large 2011–2012 SAT2 foot-and-mouth disease epidemic in Egypt, an associated outbreak of haemorrhagic septicaemia was documented in 5,630 fattening buffalo and cattle calves from 25 farms along the Alexandria–Cairo desert road in Alexandria province. Approximately 4,616 animals (81.9%) showed clinical signs of FMD, and among these, 2,600 calves (56.3%) developed HS with 362 deaths (case fatality ~14%), with buffalo calves showing much higher HS morbidity and mortality than cattle; P. multocida serotype B:2 was isolated from lung, liver and heart blood. After antibiotic treatment, emergency vaccination and improved management, the combined FMD–HS mortality declined and the outbreak was brought under control, but the episode illustrated how immunosuppression from FMD can precipitate large HS die-offs in intensively reared young stock.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A major SAT2 FMD outbreak caused immunosuppression and stress in densely stocked fattening calves, facilitating overgrowth and systemic spread of P. multocida; additional drivers included high animal density, shared management across multiple large farms, and initial gaps in HS vaccination. Internal mechanisms: The HS component was caused by typical P. multocida B:2 strains with usual virulence traits; there is no indication of novel strain emergence, so this episode is best seen as a severe re-occurrence of HS precipitated by viral co-infection and management conditions rather than by pathogen evolution.
Review: Retain – Added as a major outbreak episode in Northern Africa with thousands of at-risk calves, 2,600 HS cases and over 360 deaths, clearly linked to SAT2 FMD co-infection and supported by detailed epidemiological data. Classified as re-occurrence in an endemic country, since HS was already present in Egypt and the main drivers were FMD-associated immunosuppression, stocking density and vaccination gaps, not new HS strains. Geography (Africa/Northern Africa, Egypt; Alexandria province) and year (2012) are derived from the Life Science Journal outbreak report and related FMD timeline.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Pasteurellosis
Countries: India [1995] (multiple states including Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Punjab and others)
Host: Cattle (Bos indicus, Bos taurus and crossbreds), water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis)
Event.summary: Between 1995 and 2003, India experienced a prolonged period of very high hemorrhagic septicemia (HS) activity in cattle and buffalo, with P. multocida serogroup B:2 causing tens of thousands of reported outbreaks across most Indian states, particularly in the southern zone. Spatio‑temporal analyses of national surveillance data show that states such as Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka consistently accounted for a large share of annual HS outbreaks, indicating sustained, large‑scale transmission and heavy livestock losses. Toward the end of this period, increasing vaccination and control efforts coincided with a gradual decline in reported outbreaks in several regions, although HS has remained endemic thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large cattle and buffalo populations kept in smallholder and mixed-farming systems, seasonal stress associated with monsoon rains and heat, animal movements, and uneven vaccination coverage created conditions for extensive, recurrent HS outbreaks. Weak veterinary infrastructure and reliance on passive surveillance likely contributed to under-reporting but also to delayed control in many districts. Internal mechanisms: Circulating P. multocida serogroup B:2 lineages exhibit virulence-associated factors typical of HS (capsule, iron-acquisition systems, outer-membrane proteins) that support rapid septicemia and high case fatality, but there is limited evidence that major novel variants arose specifically to drive the 1995–2003 peak; this episode is therefore best categorized as severe re-occurrence rather than strain-driven re-emergence.
Review: Review – Event clearly represents one of the largest documented HS burdens globally and should be retained. Emergence type has been corrected from combined re_occurrence + re_emergence to re_occurrence only, because available outbreak and genomic data show long-established B:2 lineages and do not demonstrate a specific novel variant driving this period. Country, continent and sub-region assignments are correct. Text remains somewhat general on exact numbers but consistent with national analyses; human expert may refine quantitative impact estimates.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Pasteurellosis
Countries: Brazil [2010] (southern Brazil poultry and swine production)
Host: Commercial chickens and turkeys, grower-finisher pigs
Event.summary: In the early 2010s, a study of 96 P. multocida strains from clinical cases in southern Brazil documented frequent isolation of the bacterium from repeated outbreaks of pasteurellosis in intensive poultry and swine operations, together with high frequencies of virulence-associated genes and multidrug resistance. Isolates from diseased birds (liver and heart) and pigs (lungs) showed resistance to multiple antimicrobial classes, including sulfonamides, tetracyclines and macrolides, and many carried combinations of adhesin, outer-membrane and iron-acquisition genes. These findings indicated that virulent, multidrug-resistant P. multocida lineages had become established in Brazilian pig and poultry production, increasing the difficulty of controlling respiratory and septicemic disease complexes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High antimicrobial use in Brazilian poultry and swine industries for treatment and metaphylaxis, dense industrial production with rapid turnover, and frequent movement of animals between farms favored selection and dissemination of resistant P. multocida. Internal mechanisms: Many isolates carried multiple virulence-associated genes (e.g., ompH, oma87, ptfA, iron-acquisition and sialidase genes) alongside resistance determinants to several antimicrobial classes, exemplifying re-emergence of P. multocida as a more difficult-to-control pathogen in these sectors through combined virulence and multidrug resistance.
Review: Retain – This episode represents a major AMR- and virulence-associated re-emergence of P. multocida in a key livestock region, with repeated clinical outbreaks across poultry and swine and clear documentation of multidrug resistance in many isolates. Continent, sub-region and country coding (South America, Brazil) and years (2010–2014) match the sampled period. No geographic or event-type corrections are needed; classification as re_emergence driven by AMR and virulence gene combinations is appropriate. A human reviewer might consider adding more explicit production-loss estimates if available, but the event meets the criteria for inclusion among the major global episodes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Pasteurellosis
Host: Commercial poultry (chickens, ducks, geese) with fowl cholera
Event.summary: Between roughly 2012 and 2016, repeated fowl cholera outbreaks in poultry in southwest China led to the isolation and detailed characterization of 45 P. multocida strains from clinically affected flocks. These outbreaks affected multiple avian species and farms and were associated predominantly with capsular type A strains carrying numerous virulence genes, along with a range of antimicrobial resistance determinants. By the end of the study period, florfenicol- and streptomycin-resistant isolates harboring floR and strA genes, respectively, had been detected, underscoring a shift toward more resistant avian P. multocida populations in this region’s commercial poultry.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of poultry production in southwest China, combined with routine antibiotic use and potential exposure to wild bird reservoirs, facilitated repeated introduction and spread of virulent, partially resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: Isolates exhibited diverse capsular–LPS genotypes, high prevalence of virulence genes, and the presence of resistance genes such as floR and strA, indicating concurrent evolution of virulence and antimicrobial resistance. This pattern is consistent with re-occurrence of endemic fowl cholera combined with re-emergence of more resistant and genetically diverse P. multocida lineages.
Review: Retain – This event aggregates several years of recurrent fowl cholera outbreaks in a major poultry-producing region, with clear evidence of virulent and increasingly resistant P. multocida populations. Geographic coding (Eastern Asia, China) and years align with the study. Classification as both re_occurrence (repeated outbreaks in an endemic area) and re_emergence (novel genotype and AMR patterns) is justified by the molecular data. No major corrections identified; human review may refine the description of outbreak sizes and economic impact if additional national data are available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Pasteurellosis
Host: Chickens (broilers and layers), other domestic birds, rabbits
Event.summary: Between about 2015 and 2020, multiple Egyptian studies on diseased chickens and other domestic birds documented frequent isolation of P. multocida from fowl cholera outbreaks, together with increasing detection of antimicrobial resistance and diverse virulence profiles; parallel work in rabbits identified multidrug-resistant P. multocida strains causing pasteurellosis. These investigations, mainly in governorates such as Sharkia and Ismailia, indicate repeated outbreaks in commercial and smallholder flocks and rabbitries, often with high mortality and significant economic losses. Over time, detection of numerous resistance genes and, in some studies, new virulence-associated markers such as luxS highlighted a shift toward more resistant and potentially more adaptable P. multocida populations in Egyptian poultry and rabbits.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive poultry production with variable biosecurity, widespread antimicrobial use in flocks and rabbitries, and co-circulation of other respiratory pathogens created ecological niches for expansion of resistant P. multocida strains. Backyard and smallholder systems further facilitated persistence and transmission. Internal mechanisms: Isolates carried multiple resistance genes (e.g., for tetracyclines, sulfonamides, trimethoprim) and numerous virulence genes; some studies reported luxS and other traits associated with quorum sensing and biofilm formation. These features together represent re-occurrence of endemic fowl cholera and snuffles combined with re-emergence via antimicrobial resistance and potential enhancement of transmission or persistence traits.
Review: Retain – Egypt has experienced sustained, economically important P. multocida problems in poultry and rabbits during this period, with multiple independent studies documenting MDR and virulence traits. Geographic and sub-regional coding (Northern Africa, Egypt) are correct and event years reasonably summarize the overlapping study periods. Classification as both re_occurrence (repeated outbreaks in an endemic setting) and re_emergence (AMR and virulence evolution) is well supported. One source URL has been updated to a journal-hosted version of the Sharkia governorate study rather than an intermediate repository. Human review could refine which specific years and governorates contributed the largest economic losses.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Pasteurellosis
Countries: Kazakhstan [2015] (Betpak-Dala region and other calving areas)
Host: Saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica)
Event.summary: In May 2015, a catastrophic mass die-off of saiga antelopes occurred in central Kazakhstan, with approximately 200,000 animals – more than half of the global population at the time and virtually all animals in affected herds – dying over about two weeks during the calving period. Necropsy, microbiology and molecular investigations identified hemorrhagic septicemia caused by P. multocida serotype B as the proximate cause of death, with consistent gross and histopathologic lesions and high isolation rates from carcasses. The episode followed an unusually warm and humid spell, and there was no evidence of other primary infectious agents; the die-off caused a dramatic, temporary collapse of saiga numbers and spurred intensive international conservation and disease-ecology research.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extreme short-term climatic anomalies (unusually high humidity and temperature) coinciding with dense calving aggregations likely triggered systemic invasion by P. multocida carried latently in the tonsils and upper respiratory tract of apparently healthy saigas. High local densities during calving, limited dispersal options and prior population stressors contributed to near-100% mortality in affected herds. Internal mechanisms: Characterization of P. multocida isolates from the die-off indicated capsular type B strains closely related to HS-associated lineages from domestic livestock in Asia and Europe, with no unique novel virulence determinants clearly distinguishing them from other B:2/B:3 HS strains. The event is therefore best interpreted as a climate- and host-context–driven re-occurrence of hemorrhagic septicemia in a susceptible wildlife host, rather than a re-emergence driven by pathogen evolution.
Review: Review – This event was missing from the original draft yet is arguably one of the most impactful P. multocida-associated episodes since 1990, with ~200,000 saigas (≈60–70% of the global population) dying over a short period. It has now been added as a major re-occurrence event in Central Asia wildlife. Continent, sub-region and country assignments (Asia, Central Asia, Kazakhstan) are correct. Classification as re_occurrence (climate-triggered activation of latent P. multocida) rather than re_emergence is supported by genomic analyses showing close relatedness to existing HS lineages. Because the host system of interest for this EPP entry is livestock/poultry, inclusion of this wildlife-focused event should be explicitly approved by domain experts, but it fits the instructions to include major events even in hosts outside the primary system.

EPP.scientific.name: Penaeid shrimp infectious myonecrosis virus
EPP.common.name: IMNV
Countries: Brazil [2016] (notably farms in Pará, Maranhão, Piauí, Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, Alagoas, Sergipe and Bahia)
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp Litopenaeus vannamei
Event.summary: Beginning around 2016, many intensive L. vannamei farms in Brazil’s northeastern states again reported IMN-like disease, but with faster progression and in some cases cumulative mortalities reportedly reaching up to 80%, causing significant production losses through at least 2019. Molecular diagnostics on moribund shrimp from multiple states showed high IMNV loads and little or no WSSV, and whole-genome sequencing of a representative isolate from Ceará in 2018 revealed a novel IMNV strain, designated Br-1, whose 8.2 kb genome shared about 98% identity with the historic Brazilian reference but clustered more closely with Indonesian strains in phylogenetic analyses. Awareness of this more virulent variant led Brazilian producers and breeding programmes to strengthen IMNV screening of broodstock and postlarvae, review the use of imported genetic lines, and further enhance biosecurity and health management to mitigate a renewed wave of IMNV-driven losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: renewed growth and intensification of shrimp farming in northeastern Brazil, coupled with informal or poorly controlled movements of L. vannamei genetic lines between Brazil and Indonesia, likely facilitated introduction and selection of a novel IMNV variant in areas where the original strains had been partially controlled. Internal mechanisms: genomic analysis shows Br-1 is a distinct IMNV lineage more closely related to Indonesian strains, consistent with either re-introduction or evolution under new selection pressures; the associated outbreaks featured more rapid and sometimes higher mortalities than earlier IMNV epidemics, fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence and increased pathogenicity (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: Review – Added this re-emergence event to represent the 2016–2019 wave of unusually severe IMNV outbreaks in northeastern Brazil associated with the Br-1 variant; classified it as re_emergence in a previously affected South American subregion driven by emergence of a novel, more virulent strain, without additional intra- or inter-continental spread, using the 2022 Aquaculture paper and related summaries as primary sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus marinus
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis (Dermo disease of oysters)
Countries: United States of America [1990] (Delaware Bay, New Jersey; coastal New York; coastal Massachusetts to Cape Cod)
Host: Primarily Crassostrea virginica (eastern oyster) in wild and fished estuarine populations
Event.summary: Between 1990 and 1992, Perkinsus marinus infections surged in intensity and prevalence in estuarine oyster populations from Delaware Bay north to Cape Cod, where the parasite had previously been rare or absent at epizootic levels. This episode developed into large-scale epizootics across a roughly 500‑km stretch of the northeastern U.S. coast, causing heavy mortality of C. virginica and sharply reducing fishery and aquaculture landings. The epizootic subsided to lower but persistent endemic levels after several years, with continued northward persistence of the parasite and concern about future outbreaks under warmer conditions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A period of unusually warm winters and positive North Atlantic Oscillation phases increased winter and spring sea-surface temperatures, while decades of oyster translocations from enzootic southern areas had repeatedly introduced the parasite into mid‑Atlantic and New England estuaries. Internal mechanisms: Increased fitness of P. marinus under warmer winter conditions and circulation of more virulent genotypes allowed high parasite burdens to build in previously marginal, colder habitats, effectively expanding the realized thermal niche of the parasite and increasing associated mortality.
Review: retain - This row accurately describes the well-documented 1990–1992 northward epizootic from Delaware Bay to Cape Cod, including timing, geography, host and impact. Classification as re-emergence (without intra- or inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because P. marinus was already long established within the Northern America subregion before this outbreak. No corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus marinus
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis (Dermo disease of oysters)
Countries: Mexico [1992] (Carmen–Machona–Mecoacán lagoon system, Tabasco State, southern Gulf of Mexico)
Host: Crassostrea virginica (American/eastern oyster) in wild and fished beds in coastal lagoons
Event.summary: In 1992, surveys of American oysters Crassostrea virginica in the Carmen–Machona–Mecoacán lagoon complex of Tabasco, southern Gulf of Mexico, revealed very high prevalences and heavy intensities of Perkinsus marinus infection, with weighted prevalence values consistent with severe disease. These findings provided the first confirmed report of P. marinus in Mexico and in the project’s 'South America' continent grouping, and suggested that the parasite was an important but previously unrecognized contributor to sporadic oyster mortalities blamed locally on pollution. Subsequent work documented persistent infections and seasonal variation in disease levels, indicating that P. marinus had become enzootic in these lagoons.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Historical movements of live oysters and spat from U.S. Gulf of Mexico and other infected areas into Mexican coastal lagoons likely introduced P. marinus to Tabasco, where warm, relatively high-salinity lagoon conditions favored establishment and proliferation. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of established Gulf of Mexico parasite lineages into new southern habitats, with heavy infections reflecting the high susceptibility of C. virginica and the absence of prior host adaptation in these lagoon populations.
Review: review - New row added to capture the 1992 detection of P. marinus in the Carmen–Machona–Mecoacán lagoon system (Tabasco, Mexico), which is the first confirmed occurrence in Mexico and, under the project’s continent scheme, the first inter-continental emergence into 'South America'. Impact is supported by high prevalences and heavy infections reported by Burreson et al. (1994), but quantitative production-loss estimates remain limited; recommended to retain as a major event but for a human reviewer to confirm its ranking and wording.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus marinus
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis (Dermo disease of oysters)
Countries: United States of America [1995] (Maine coastal embayments)
Host: Crassostrea virginica (eastern oyster) in wild and managed beds near the northern limit of the species
Event.summary: In 1995, Perkinsus marinus was first reported in Maine oyster populations, marking a notable northward jump beyond earlier reports that had reached only as far as Cape Cod. Following its detection, local C. virginica stocks experienced elevated infection intensities and episodic mortality events that raised concern about the viability of oyster restoration and aquaculture at this poleward range edge. Over subsequent years, disease levels fluctuated with environmental conditions, but the parasite remained established in Maine waters as a chronic constraint on oyster production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional warming trends and milder winters in the Gulf of Maine increased the duration of periods with water temperatures exceeding about 20 °C, promoting parasite proliferation at higher latitudes than previously considered suitable. Internal mechanisms: The same P. marinus lineages responsible for the early‑1990s northeastern U.S. epizootics were able to persist and transmit in cooler Maine estuaries, representing a climate-mediated geographic range expansion within the Northern America subregion rather than a new continental emergence.
Review: retain - This row correctly captures the first documented record of P. marinus in Maine (1995) and its significance as a poleward range extension linked to warming, as reported in the range-expansion literature. Treating the event as re-emergence (further spread within an already affected Northern America subregion) rather than intra-continental or first-detection is consistent with the project definitions; no structural corrections were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus marinus
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis (Dermo disease of oysters)
Countries: Mexico [2006] (Gulf of California, Sonora coast, northwest Mexico)
Host: Crassostrea gigas (Pacific oyster) in intensive aquaculture; likely infection source from Crassostrea virginica stocks moved within Mexico
Event.summary: In July–August 2006, mass mortalities of farmed Pacific oysters Crassostrea gigas were reported in coastal farms along the Sonoran shore of the Gulf of California, northwest Mexico, and were attributed in part to Perkinsus marinus infections acting together with stressful environmental conditions. The outbreak developed rapidly during warm summer conditions, causing large production losses in affected farms and highlighting the vulnerability of C. gigas to P. marinus in Mexican Pacific systems. Mortalities declined after environmental conditions moderated and management responses reduced stocking densities, but the episode established P. marinus as a recognized threat to Pacific oyster aquaculture in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High summer water temperatures, elevated salinities, and culture conditions characterized by high stocking densities and limited water exchange created stressful conditions that exacerbated disease susceptibility and mortality in farmed oysters. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and enhanced transmission, as P. marinus—likely introduced via transfers of infected C. virginica or other bivalves from Gulf of Mexico sources—successfully infected and caused severe disease in C. gigas, demonstrating that this parasite can utilize non-native oyster species as epidemiologically important hosts in new ocean basins.
Review: retain - The 2006 mass mortality of C. gigas in the Gulf of California attributed to P. marinus is well documented and clearly among the most impactful emergence episodes for this pathogen outside its native Atlantic–Gulf range. Country, subregion and host assignments are correct, and treating this as re-emergence (host and basin expansion within an already affected continent) rather than intra-/inter-continental emergence matches the definitions. Only a more specific article on the event was added to the source list; otherwise the row is retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus marinus
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis (Dermo disease of oysters)
Countries: Brazil [2013] (Paraíba State, Paraíba River estuary, northeastern Brazil)
Host: Crassostrea rhizophorae (mangrove oyster) in wild and small-scale harvested intertidal beds
Event.summary: In 2013, Perkinsus marinus was confirmed by histology and molecular methods in mangrove oysters Crassostrea rhizophorae from the Paraíba River estuary in Paraíba State, Brazil, representing the first species-level identification of P. marinus on the Atlantic coast of South America. The study documented very high infection prevalence (often exceeding 70–90%) and heavy parasite burdens in many oysters, indicating an established and intense epizootic in this estuarine system. Although the disease did not immediately cause a well-documented regional fishery collapse, the findings signaled a newly recognized, ongoing epizootic that threatened mangrove oyster stocks exploited by local communities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected bivalves—likely through historical or recent movements of oysters or other molluscs between the Gulf of Mexico/Pacific Mexico and northeastern Brazil—combined with warm, moderately saline estuarine conditions that favor parasite proliferation. Internal mechanisms: Establishment of P. marinus in C. rhizophorae populations in a new UNSD subregion ('South America') within the South America continent grouping, supported by parasite genotypes closely related to Mexican strains and capable of high virulence in mangrove oysters.
Review: review - The event correctly represents the first confirmed P. marinus record on the Atlantic coast of South America (Paraíba, Brazil) and is appropriately classified as intra-continental emergence into a new UNSD subregion ('South America'). However, the original row misused the 'first_detection' flag for this regional first report; this has been reset to 'No' because first detection in the host system occurred decades earlier in the Gulf of Mexico. All other fields are retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Phocine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Phocine distemper virus, PDV
Countries: United States of America [2000] (Alaska – eastern Aleutian Islands, South Alaska Peninsula, Kodiak Archipelago)
Host: Northern sea otter (Enhydra lutris kenyoni)
Event.summary: Around the early 2000s, a PDV‑like morbillivirus was introduced into northern sea otter populations in the North Pacific off south‑central and southwestern Alaska, with retrospective serology showing substantial exposure by 2004–2005 and RT‑PCR detection of viral RNA closely related to North Atlantic PDV strains. The event unfolded as part of a broader period of elevated sea otter mortality in the eastern Aleutians, South Alaska Peninsula, and Kodiak Archipelago, with PDV implicated as one of several contributing disease agents rather than a single explosive cause of die‑off. By the mid‑2000s, seroprevalence in live‑captured otters had stabilized at high levels and overt PDV‑associated morbidity waned, consistent with establishment of the virus (or a very closely related morbillivirus) in this new host and region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: progressive loss of Arctic sea ice, shifts in oceanographic conditions, and resulting changes in migration routes of ice‑associated seals likely facilitated east–west movement of infected pinnipeds through the Arctic, allowing PDV to cross from the North Atlantic into the North Pacific and reach Gulf of Alaska ecosystems; long‑distance movements of harp and other Arctic seals acted as a potential vector bridge. Internal mechanisms: host expansion of PDV from true seals (phocids) into northern sea otters, a mustelid marine mammal, and geographic range expansion into the North Pacific via an Arctic corridor; available partial P‑gene sequences show close relatedness to North Atlantic PDV, indicating that only modest viral adaptation was needed to infect otters, and that infection in this new host manifested as chronic health impacts and contribution to background mortality rather than a short, catastrophic epizootic.
Review: review – Strong field and laboratory evidence indicates that a PDV‑like morbillivirus infected northern sea otters in Alaska in the early 2000s, representing both a host expansion and a major geographic range expansion into the North Pacific. However, full‑genome sequence data remain limited and some publications describe the agent as “PDV‑like” rather than definitively PDV, so the event is retained but classified conservatively as re_emergence (host expansion and geographic range expansion) without any first_detection or (intra/inter‑)continental emergence flags. The country, region, and timing (Alaska, early 2000s with confirmation by 2004–2005) are consistent with CDC and NOAA reports, but uncertainty about the precise year of initial incursion justifies the approximate 2000–2005 date range and the high‑but‑not‑maximal confidence score.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Phocine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Phocine distemper virus, PDV
Countries: United States of America [2006] (Atlantic coast from Maine to Virginia)
Host: Harbour seal (Phoca vitulina); Grey seal (Halichoerus grypus); Harp seal (Pagophilus groenlandicus); Hooded seal (Cystophora cristata)
Event.summary: From spring 2006 through autumn 2007, an unusual mortality event involving pinnipeds was declared along the US northwest Atlantic coast from Maine to Virginia after a sharp increase in strandings of harbour, grey, harp, and hooded seals. Virological investigations during this UME isolated a PDV strain (PDV USA 2006) from affected harbour seals, and molecular analyses showed it was most similar to the 1988 European PDV isolate rather than the 2002 European strain, indicating a distinct North American lineage. Approximately 800–1,500 seal deaths were attributed to this outbreak, which remained regionally contained and subsided by late 2007 as strandings declined toward baseline, after which PDV persisted at low levels within the regional multi‑species pinniped community.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: dense aggregations of multiple seal species at haul‑out sites in New England and the Mid‑Atlantic, expanding grey seal populations, and seasonal peaks in juvenile abundance created favourable conditions for cross‑species PDV transmission; regional prey and oceanographic patterns likely influenced the timing and concentration of susceptible animals alongshore. Internal mechanisms: re‑emergence of PDV in northwestern Atlantic seals with a distinct North American lineage (PDV USA 2006) genetically closer to the 1988 European virus than to the 2002 strain, suggesting independent re‑introduction and/or long‑term circulation of multiple PDV lineages in the North Atlantic; multi‑host transmission among harbour, harp, hooded, and grey seals increased viral maintenance potential and produced a substantial, though not Europe‑scale, mortality event.
Review: retain – This event corresponds directly to the 2006–2007 Northeast Pinniped UME (Maine–Virginia) that NOAA attributes to infectious disease with PDV confirmed as the primary agent, and to the PDV USA 2006 strain described in CDC’s Emerging Infectious Diseases paper. The event year range, geographic extent (United States Atlantic coast from Maine to Virginia), host species involved, and magnitude (≈800–1,500 pinniped deaths) are consistent with primary sources. Classification as re_emergence (a distinct North American PDV lineage in an already infected sub‑region) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence flags matches the definitions and current phylogenetic understanding; no corrections beyond verification were necessary, and the row should be retained as one of the major PDV emergence events.

EPP.scientific.name: Phocine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Phocine distemper virus, PDV
Countries: United States of America [2018] (Atlantic coast from Maine to New Jersey)
Host: Grey seal (Halichoerus grypus); Harbour seal (Phoca vitulina); Harp seal (Pagophilus groenlandicus)
Event.summary: Between January 2018 and May 2019, a large pinniped unusual mortality event was recorded along the US northeast Atlantic coast from Maine through the Mid‑Atlantic, with 2,107 stranded grey, harbour, and harp seals documented. NOAA investigations concluded that infection with phocine distemper virus was the primary cause of mortality in grey and harbour seals, whereas the cause for harp seals was classified as undetermined but likely related to demographic and ice‑related ecological factors. By mid‑2019, stranding rates of the affected species had declined to background levels and the UME was formally closed, although PDV remains an endemic disease threat in northwest Atlantic pinnipeds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapidly growing grey and harbour seal populations along the New England and Mid‑Atlantic coasts, with high densities at haul‑out sites from Maine through Rhode Island and southward, facilitated efficient PDV transmission; changing sea‑ice conditions and prey distributions likely altered harp seal movements and survival, contributing to elevated harp seal strandings even where PDV was not clearly established as the primary cause. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of PDV in a northwest Atlantic pinniped community with established endemic circulation, where periodic large outbreaks occur when cohorts of susceptible juveniles accumulate and herd immunity wanes; viral phylogenetic analyses indicate that PDV sequences from the northwest Atlantic in 2011–2018 form a single clade consistent with a long‑standing incursion rather than a novel strain, so the 2018–2019 UME represents a resurgence of existing lineages rather than a genetically distinct re‑emergence.
Review: review – The 2018–2019 Northeast Pinniped UME is well documented by NOAA as a major mortality event (2,107 seals) with PDV confirmed as the primary cause in grey and harbour seals, and ecological factors implicated for harp seals. The event is therefore correctly included as one of the largest PDV‑associated emergence episodes in the 2005–2025 window. However, the emergence classification has been adjusted from re_emergence to re_occurrence: phylogenetic work on northwest Atlantic PDV shows that viruses from 2011–2018 fall within a single clade consistent with a long‑standing incursion rather than a new strain, and there is no evidence of a novel host system or major shift in virulence driving the 2018–2019 UME. The country‑level location description has been refined from “Maine to New York” to “Maine to New Jersey” to match NOAA’s UME summaries for harbour and grey seals. Because this row combines UME‑level statistics with inferred PDV evolutionary context, it is flagged for expert review of the final wording and emergence‑type coding.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Psoroptes ovis
EPP.common.name: Sheep scab
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1992] (with particularly high burden in Wales, Scotland and northern England)
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event.summary: When statutory sheep scab control was abandoned in Great Britain in 1992, Psoroptes ovis rapidly became entrenched as an endemic parasite, with incidence rising and control shifting from centrally organised dipping to voluntary farm‑level treatment.([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/271901/2/271901.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Through the 1990s and 2000s, repeated outbreaks and reinfestations were reported across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, with surveys indicating thousands of affected farms annually and national economic costs initially estimated at ~£8 million per year in 2005 but more recent modelling suggesting a burden of £78–202 million per year for Great Britain alone.([sheepdipsufferers.uk](https://www.sheepdipsufferers.uk/history/Sheep%20Scab%20Controls.pdf?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2010s, persistent regional hotspots and confirmed macrocyclic lactone resistance in sheep mites led to deployment of a serological ELISA for flock‑level diagnosis, free testing schemes and pilot coordinated regional control projects, illustrating a shift towards community‑based management rather than purely farm‑by‑farm intervention.([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=17dbda98df31d232f6fb40913e915f293d4ce91c&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Deregulation of compulsory sheep scab control in 1992, which transferred responsibility to individual producers; high stocking densities and common grazing, especially in upland areas; extensive long‑distance sheep movements via markets and seasonal grazing that connect distant regions; incomplete treatment coverage and suboptimal on‑farm biosecurity; and heavy reliance on macrocyclic lactones for both endo‑ and ectoparasite control, encouraging frequent, sometimes prophylactic use.([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/271901/2/271901.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Emergence and subsequent spread of P. ovis populations with reduced susceptibility and then confirmed resistance to multiple injectable macrocyclic lactones (moxidectin first, followed by ivermectin and doramectin), documented through in vitro and in vivo studies, which prolong infestations and increase the risk of treatment failure; together with possible selection for mite populations able to persist at low levels between treatments, this justifies classifying the episode as re‑emergence driven by drug resistance rather than simple re‑occurrence.([research-information.bris.ac.uk](https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/files/139154858/Doherty_ScabPaper_Complete.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: retain – This GB post‑1992 episode clearly ranks among the most impactful modern P. ovis events, capturing the transition from regulated eradication to endemic scab and the subsequent emergence of macrocyclic lactone resistance; economic impact figures and the link between resistance evidence and re‑emergence have been updated, but the original geographic coding and event‑type classification (re_emergence only) remain appropriate and should be kept.([livrepository.liverpool.ac.uk](https://livrepository.liverpool.ac.uk/3105587/1/Nixon_etal_costofsheepscab.pdf?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Psoroptes ovis
EPP.common.name: Sheep scab
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event.summary: In 2005–2006, a two‑year epidemiological survey of 199 sheep flocks in Lorestan Province in western Iran identified clinical skin lesions compatible with mange in 123 flocks and confirmed Psoroptes ovis as the causative mite in 16 flocks with psoroptic mange, demonstrating that sheep scab remained an important endemic problem in this region.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644)) Outbreaks were concentrated in the winter months, and infestation risk was strongly associated with flock management, stocking density, housing conditions and shepherd knowledge rather than with animal age or sex.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644)) Subsequent Iranian reports describe ongoing scabies and mange problems in sheep in multiple provinces but no sustained elimination in Lorestan, so this episode is interpreted as a well‑documented phase of high endemic activity rather than a new incursion into a previously free area.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High animal density and close confinement of sheep in winter housing; inadequate sheepcote hygiene; limited farmer awareness of scab transmission and control; and reliance on local treatment practices that were inconsistently implemented, all of which favoured persistence and recurrence of Psoroptes ovis in Lorestan flocks.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644)) Internal mechanisms: No novel mite strain, host shift or drug resistance was reported, so this episode is best classified as re‑occurrence driven by management and environmental factors rather than evolutionary change in the parasite.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644))
Review: Decision: review – The Lorestan survey robustly documents regional endemicity and risk factors and reasonably qualifies as a re‑occurrence event in Southern Asia, but its overall impact (limited number of confirmed psoroptic flocks, no quantified national losses) appears modest compared with GB and South American/European episodes, so its inclusion among the top global events should be revisited as more data become available from other high‑burden regions. Geographic coding (Asia, Southern Asia, Iran (Islamic Republic of)) and classification as re_occurrence only are appropriate.([agris.fao.org](https://agris.fao.org/search/en/providers/122649/records/647356bf53aa8c8963068644))

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella pullorum, Bacillary white diarrhoea
Countries: United States of America [2004] (small non-commercial flock; state not specified)
Host: Small backyard chicken flock (with other domestic fowl at potential risk)
Event.summary: By the early 2000s, pullorum disease had been eradicated from U.S. commercial poultry breeder flocks through the National Poultry Improvement Plan, but sporadic cases still occurred in small, non‑certified flocks. A Washington State University extension fact sheet reports that the most recent documented U.S. pullorum disease outbreak occurred in a small flock in 2004, where young birds developed high mortality and classic signs of bacillary white diarrhoea. State and federal animal health authorities quarantined the flock, depopulated infected birds and traced and tested linked small flocks; the outbreak was contained without re‑establishment of the disease in commercial operations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement of untested birds or hatching eggs into a backyard flock outside the NPIP‑certified commercial sector, lack of routine surveillance and testing in hobby operations, and possible contact with infected game birds or wildlife. Internal mechanisms: chronic carrier hens and transovarian transmission of S. Pullorum (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation) enabled rapid within‑flock spread once the pathogen was introduced, but there is no evidence that antimicrobial resistance or major genetic change specifically drove this event.
Review: retain – This row accurately captures a documented small-flock pullorum outbreak in the USA in 2004, as summarized in a WSU extension fact sheet and consistent with national NPIP history. Geography and classification as a localized re‑occurrence in North America are appropriate, and the host and control description match regulatory practice. Later USDA summaries indicate sporadic PD detections in backyard birds up to around 2009, but those are not described in comparable detail; this does not invalidate the 2004 event but means statements about it being the absolute last U.S. outbreak should be interpreted as “last reported in readily available extension literature” rather than definitive.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella pullorum, Bacillary white diarrhoea
Host: Adult brown chickens and ducks in two small-farm flocks
Event.summary: In 2006, investigators in Iowa reported an outbreak of pullorum disease causing acute septicemia and mortality in adult brown chickens in a small-farm flock, with infection also detected in ducks on a contact farm. The episode began with increased deaths and non‑specific illness in adult birds, leading to necropsy and culture of Salmonella Pullorum from chickens, a duck and trapped rats, and molecular typing showed closely related isolates in birds and rodents. Both flocks were quarantined and depopulated, followed by intensive cleaning, disinfection and environmental and rodent monitoring; follow-up testing of replacement birds and the environment four months after restocking was negative, indicating successful eradication from these premises.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction of infected carrier birds from non‑certified sources into mixed small‑farm flocks, inadequate biosecurity, and involvement of commensal rodents as mechanical vectors or reservoir hosts. Internal mechanisms: persistence of S. Pullorum in chronically infected adult birds and efficient vertical and horizontal transmission (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation) allowed the pathogen to cause clinically significant disease in adults as well as in young birds; no novel genotype or resistance pattern specific to this outbreak was reported.
Review: retain – The description closely matches the Avian Diseases case report on the 2006 Iowa outbreak, including involvement of adult chickens and ducks, the role of rodents, and successful eradication following depopulation and decontamination. Country and subregion coding (USA, Northern America) and classification as a re‑occurrence are appropriate, given long‑standing presence of PD in U.S. backyard flocks and prior eradication from commercial breeders. No corrections to timing, geography, or emergence type are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella pullorum, Bacillary white diarrhoea
Countries: France [2011] (commercial layer flock in Sarthe; broiler flock in Vienne; broiler-breeder flock in Deux-Sèvres)
Host: Commercial laying hens, broiler chickens and broiler breeder chickens (Gallus gallus) in large-scale operations
Event.summary: During the first half of 2011, French authorities detected three outbreaks of pullorum disease in large commercial chicken flocks in north‑western France: a 158,000‑hen layer flock in Sarthe, a 29,900‑chick broiler flock in Vienne and a 27,897‑bird broiler-breeder flock in Deux‑Sèvres. Each outbreak was characterized by sudden increases in mortality (up to about 10% in young broilers and marked rises in adults), reduced production and lesions suggesting septicemia, prompting laboratory confirmation of infection with Salmonella enterica serovar Gallinarum biovar Pullorum. Extensive epidemiological and bacteriological investigations, including molecular typing, suggested a close link between at least two of the farms; affected flocks were culled and thorough cleaning, disinfection and movement controls were implemented, and no onward spread to other commercial operations was documented, but the episode was recognized as a major resurgence of pullorum disease in France’s Gallus gallus sector after more than 20 years of apparent freedom.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: reintroduction of S. Pullorum into high‑biosecurity commercial systems, most likely via contaminated breeding stock or hatching eggs within integrated poultry chains, combined with very high bird densities and complex production networks in modern layer, broiler and breeder operations. Internal mechanisms: efficient vertical transmission in breeders and layers and horizontal spread in dense broiler flocks (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation) allowed rapid amplification once the pathogen entered each flock; molecular profiles of Salmonella Gallinarum/Pullorum isolates were consistent with clonal spread between at least two farms rather than emergence of a novel strain with distinct phenotypes.
Review: retain – Added this high‑impact 2011 episode comprising three large commercial Gallus gallus flocks in north‑western France, documented in detail in the ANSES Bulletin épidémiologique and summarized by Le Bouquin et al. (2021). The event clearly qualifies as a major modern PD outbreak in terms of flock sizes, mortality and economic implications. Geography (Europe – Western Europe – France), host description and classification as a re‑occurrence in a country that had previously eliminated PD from organized production are consistent with official reports; no further corrections are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella pullorum, Bacillary white diarrhoea
Countries: Sweden [2012] (index non-commercial flock detected in May 2012; three additional non-commercial flocks identified later in 2012)
Host: Non-commercial (hobby/backyard) chicken flocks
Event.summary: In 2012, Sweden detected a new outbreak of pullorum disease in a non-commercial poultry flock, despite long-standing freedom of commercial flocks from S. Pullorum. The index case involved increased mortality and classic lesions in a hobby flock; subsequent tracing and testing identified three additional infected non‑commercial flocks linked through movements of birds, and genomic subtyping revealed several closely related S. Pullorum genotypes among the isolates. Infected flocks were depopulated and strengthened biosecurity and surveillance were implemented in the non‑commercial sector; no spread to commercial breeders or layers was detected, and the known infections were eliminated, although later sporadic backyard cases (e.g. in 2017) indicated persistence of a low‑level reservoir.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: informal trade and exchange of birds among backyard and hobby owners, limited systematic testing for S. Pullorum in non‑commercial flocks, and coexistence of industrial and non‑commercial populations with differing biosecurity standards. Internal mechanisms: long-term carrier states in adult birds and highly efficient vertical and horizontal transmission allowed S. Pullorum to persist and spread within networks of hobby flocks (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation); genomic subtyping suggested multiple, closely related genotypes rather than a single new strain with clearly altered virulence or host range.
Review: review – The core description of the 2012 Swedish hobby-flock outbreak and its investigation is consistent with Eriksson et al. (2018) and Swedish surveillance reports, but the original row over‑classified the event as both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence and framed routine genotypic diversity as “novel strain emergence.” Here, ‘re_emergence’ has been reset to No, and the internal mechanism emphasis has been shifted to persistence and transmission in backyard networks rather than pathogen-level innovation. Retain as a re‑occurrence in non‑commercial flocks in a previously PD‑free country, with genomic data interpreted as indicating multiple introductions or a mixed source rather than a fundamentally new biotype.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella pullorum, Bacillary white diarrhoea
Host: Commercial parent-layer chickens (Lohmann Brown) in a large breeder flock (~14,220 birds)
Event.summary: Around 2020–2021, Austria experienced a major pullorum disease outbreak in a young commercial layer parent flock of approximately 14,220 Lohmann Brown chickens. High mortality began in the first week of life and peaked by the fifth week, by which time about 1,900 chicks had died and the flock was depopulated; affected birds showed uneven growth, pasty vents, lethargy, reduced feed and water intake and, in some cases, central nervous system signs such as tremors and torticollis, and Salmonella enterica serovar Gallinarum biovar Pullorum was isolated from multiple organs including the brain. Follow‑up testing of grandparent flocks and subsequent progeny was negative, and enhanced biosecurity and surveillance were implemented, indicating that the outbreak was successfully contained within this flock.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: a likely point introduction of S. Pullorum into a high‑biosecurity breeding operation—possibly via contaminated hatching eggs, equipment or an undetected infected bird—combined with intense early‑life bird density. Internal mechanisms: classical vertical and early horizontal transmission (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation) led to rapid amplification and high early‑life mortality in a fully susceptible parent flock; although unusual central nervous system involvement was described, the report did not identify antimicrobial resistance or clearly novel genotypes compared with other S. Pullorum strains.
Review: retain – The Austrian parent-layer outbreak is well described in the Avian Diseases case report, including flock size, mortality, nervous signs and control measures, and is appropriately classified as a re‑occurrence in a country with prior control of PD. Geography (Europe – Western Europe – Austria) and host description (young commercial layer parent flock) match the primary source. No corrections were needed to timing, geography, or emergence type; in the global context this is one of the largest recent European PD outbreaks in high‑biosecurity commercial breeding stock.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella pullorum, Bacillary white diarrhoea
Countries: India [2024] (Jharkhand – two mixed-species commercial farms with Rhode Island Red flocks)
Host: Rhode Island Red chickens in mixed-species commercial flocks (with other chicken breeds and ducks present) co-infected with HPAI H5N1
Event.summary: In April 2024, two large mixed‑species poultry farms in Jharkhand, India, reported unusual mortality among Rhode Island Red chickens, with mild respiratory signs and whitish diarrhoea but relatively low overall flock-level losses. Investigation showed co‑infection with highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 virus and Salmonella enterica serovar Gallinarum biovar Pullorum: Farm A housed 1,197 birds and lost 136 Rhode Island Reds, while Farm B housed 5,000 birds and lost 211 Rhode Island Reds over two weeks, with other breeds and ducks largely unaffected. Once H5N1 and pullorum disease were confirmed, authorities implemented culling, movement restrictions, disinfection and enhanced surveillance; the outbreaks were contained without apparent spread to other species on the farms or nearby holdings, but they highlighted the role of PD as a co‑morbidity in large commercial flocks primarily monitored for avian influenza.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: dense, mixed-species housing under a deep litter system, with Rhode Island Reds, other chicken breeds and ducks kept under one roof in each farm, and the introduction of H5N1 via wild birds or poultry movements, created conditions for concurrent viral and bacterial infection. Internal mechanisms: S.
