Pullorum’s capacity for vertical and horizontal transmission and for persistence in adult carriers (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation) likely contributed to background infection in Rhode Island Reds; in this case, co‑infection with H5N1 appears to have modulated clinical expression, producing a relatively low overall mortality rate despite infection with a highly pathogenic influenza strain.
Review: retain – Added a 2024 co-infection event in Jharkhand, India, documented in detail in a 2025 Discover Viruses case study, in which large mixed flocks experienced simultaneous H5N1 HPAI and Salmonella Pullorum infection with modest but notable mortality confined to Rhode Island Reds. The flock sizes, regulatory response and unusual co‑infection context make this a relevant modern PD event. It is classified as a re‑occurrence within Southern Asia, with no evidence that novel S. Pullorum genotypes were responsible; the main drivers were high-density mixed-species housing and introduction of H5N1, with PD acting as a significant bacterial co‑pathogen.

EPP.scientific.name: Sarcoptes scabiei
EPP.common.name: Scabies, Sarcoptic mange
Host: Wild caprine ungulates, primarily Iberian ibex (Capra pyrenaica hispanica)
Event.summary: In 1992, sarcoptic mange was recognized as an epizootic in the Iberian ibex population of the Sierra Nevada Natural Park in southern Spain, with Sarcoptes scabiei confirmed from skin scrapings and mange prevalence averaging over 20% across 1992–1996 and reaching almost 45% in a core focus area. During this period the disease spread spatially within the park, with highest prevalence and mortality in a western focus but without complete collapse of the overall ibex population, which continued to increase in density. By the late 1990s the outbreak transitioned toward endemic circulation with fluctuating prevalence modulated by climate and host demography, and later work documented partial host resistance and generally lower mange prevalence into the 2000s and 2010s.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: High ibex density within a protected mountain habitat, overlap and potential contact with domestic small ruminants in surrounding areas, and climatic conditions (cooler, wetter months) that favored mite survival and transmission have been implicated in sustaining the epizootic and shaping its seasonality. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and epidemiologic work in Iberian wild ruminants supports introduction of a host‑taxon–adapted Sarcoptes scabiei strain from domestic goats or sheep and its establishment in Iberian ibex, consistent with re‑emergence driven primarily by host expansion (spillover from domestic small ruminants) and geographic range expansion of an existing strain within southern Spain.
Internal mechanism tags: Host Expansion (Spillover from domestic goats/sheep to Iberian ibex); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within Southern Europe).
Review: retain – Well‑documented mange epizootic in Sierra Nevada Iberian ibex from 1992–1996 with 20–45% prevalence and clear spatial spread, matching Pérez et al. 1997 and subsequent ibex disease syntheses. Timing, geography (Spain, Southern Europe), and classification as re‑emergence (spillover of a goat‑derived strain into a wild ibex population within an already affected subregion) are consistent with primary literature. Earlier, more catastrophic Iberian ibex outbreaks in Cazorla (1987–1991, >90% mortality) are correctly omitted here because their onset precedes the 1990 cutoff. No changes to event fields recommended; mechanism text already emphasizes domestic‑origin strain and host expansion, which aligns with current evidence, though detailed strain pathogenicity remains an active research topic.

EPP.scientific.name: Sarcoptes scabiei
EPP.common.name: Scabies, Sarcoptic mange
Host: Non-native Barbary sheep (Ammotragus lervia) introduced to Spain
Event.summary: Between 1991 and 1995, a severe sarcoptic mange epizootic affected the introduced Barbary sheep population in Sierra Espuña Regional Park, southeastern Spain, with Sarcoptes scabiei confirmed in affected animals. Over the course of the outbreak, population monitoring documented an approximately 86% decline in Barbary sheep numbers, transforming a previously overabundant exotic ungulate population into a small remnant. Following intensive management and natural fade‑out of the epizootic, the surviving population remained at much lower density, and mange became enzootic at low levels rather than continuing as a high‑mortality wave.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: The Barbary sheep population in Sierra Espuña had been introduced and allowed to increase to high densities in a relatively small protected area, facilitating rapid transmission once sarcoptic mange was introduced; contact with domestic small ruminants or other sympatric ungulates is considered a likely source of introduction, and rugged terrain made carcass removal and other interventions difficult. Internal mechanisms: The event represents establishment of Sarcoptes scabiei in a non‑native wild Caprinae host within the Iberian Peninsula, probably via spillover of a host‑taxon–adapted strain from domestic or other wild ruminants, consistent with re‑emergence driven by host expansion and geographic range expansion of an existing mite lineage.
Internal mechanism tags: Host Expansion (Spillover into non‑native Barbary sheep); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within Southern Europe).
Review: review – Added as a missing major event: the 1991–1995 sarcoptic mange epizootic in non‑native Barbary sheep (arruí) in Sierra Espuña Regional Park, Spain, which caused an ≈86% population decrease and is repeatedly cited as a high‑impact example in later mange literature. Years, host, location and impact are based on the Journal of Wildlife Diseases paper and the associated University of Murcia thesis, with additional confirmation from Ferreyra et al. 2022 referencing this outbreak. Classified as re‑emergence (spillover and establishment of Sarcoptes in a new wild host population within an already affected subregion), not intra‑continental emergence, because Sarcoptes was already established in Iberian wildlife. Recommend expert review of the summarized drivers and internal mechanism tags, but inclusion of this event among the top‑impact epizootics is well supported.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Sarcoptes scabiei
EPP.common.name: Scabies, Sarcoptic mange
Host: Cantabrian chamois (Rupicapra pyrenaica parva) with spillover to other wild ungulates (e.g., red deer, roe deer, mouflon)
Event.summary: In May 1993, an epizootic of sarcoptic mange caused by Sarcoptes scabiei was first detected in Cantabrian chamois in the Cantabrian Mountains of northwestern Spain, where mange had not previously been reported in this wild caprine. Over the mid‑1990s and 2000s, the disease front spread progressively eastwards across the range at an estimated 2.6–4 km per year, causing marked local population declines and high mortality in affected chamois units and also infecting sympatric wild cervids and other ungulates. By around 2008, the main epidemic wave had traversed most of the chamois range and transitioned into lower‑level endemic circulation with sporadic mortality, leaving long‑term effects on population structure and demography in affected areas.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Close contact between wild caprines and domestic goats and sheep grazing on mountain pastures is strongly implicated as the original source of S. scabiei, while protected‑area management and increasing wild ungulate densities facilitated sustained transmission; the metapopulation structure of chamois along a linear mountain chain shaped the speed and pattern of spread. Internal mechanisms: Molecular work indicates host‑taxon–derived mite strains with high pathogenicity in naive chamois, representing a host‑adapted strain spilling over from domestic small ruminants and establishing persistent transmission in wild populations, consistent with re‑emergence via host expansion and geographic range expansion within Southern Europe.
Internal mechanism tags: Host Expansion (Spillover from domestic goats/sheep to wild chamois); Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (host‑taxon–specific variant in Cantabrian chamois); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within Southern Europe).
Review: retain – Major long‑duration mange epizootic in Cantabrian chamois beginning in 1993 with eastward spread over ~15 years and substantial local population impacts, as described by Fernández‑Morán et al. and summarized in later reviews and the Cantabrian chamois species account. Years, host, and geography (Spain, Southern Europe) are correct, and the epidemic wave classification as re‑emergence (domestic goat/sheep–derived strain establishing in a new wild caprine population) matches microsatellite evidence that links these outbreaks to small‑ruminant sources. No corrections to emergence‑type flags are needed; intra‑continental emergence is not triggered because the event remains within the Southern Europe subregion. The Wikipedia URL is secondary but accurate; primary scientific articles already provide the core documentation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Sarcoptes scabiei
EPP.common.name: Scabies, Sarcoptic mange
Countries: Australia [2010] (Narawntapu National Park, central north Tasmania)
Host: Common wombat / bare-nosed wombat (Vombatus ursinus), primarily Tasmanian subspecies, with mange also affecting other common wombat populations in south‑eastern Australia
Event.summary: Around 2010, a severe outbreak of sarcoptic mange emerged in the common wombat population of Narawntapu National Park in central north Tasmania, a site previously known for high wombat density but within a region where mange had already been present historically. From 2010 to 2016, systematic spotlight and monitoring surveys documented a catastrophic 94% decline in the resident wombat population attributable to mange, making this event one of the most extreme local impacts recorded for the species. By 2016 wombat numbers in Narawntapu had effectively collapsed, while wombat populations elsewhere in Tasmania were generally stable or increasing, and the outbreak prompted ongoing research and trials of novel single‑dose mange treatments and management strategies to prevent similar localized crashes.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Historical introduction of S. scabiei to Australia with European settlers and domestic animals in the 19th century, combined with high local wombat density in improved pasture landscapes around Narawntapu, limited effective treatment options, and landscape features that promoted local host aggregation, created conditions for intense, localized transmission. Internal mechanisms: The Narawntapu event reflects a severe resurgence of an established human/domestic‑origin Sarcoptes strain in wombats rather than emergence of a novel genotype or new host association; efficient transmission through shared burrows and high contact rates drove a travelling epidemic wave and extreme local mortality, without evidence to date of major new parasite adaptations.
Internal mechanism tags: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (burrow sharing, high host density); Geographic Range Expansion (fine‑scale within Tasmania).
Review: review – The Narawntapu outbreak is correctly identified as an exceptionally severe mange episode in common wombats, with a 94% local population decline between 2010 and 2016 documented by Tasmanian monitoring programs and Martin et al. (2018). However, Sarcoptes scabiei has been present in wombats and other Australian mammals for over a century, and wombat mange was already widespread in south‑eastern Australia; this event is therefore best interpreted as a dramatic re‑occurrence in an already affected host and subregion, not as re‑emergence driven by a new strain or host expansion. Re‑emergence has been set to "No" and re‑occurrence to "Yes", and the mechanism text has been adjusted to emphasize external drivers (host density, land use, limited treatment) and intense local transmission of an established strain rather than novel host adaptation. Recommend expert review of the precise end year (2016 captures the documented crash, though lower‑level persistence likely continues) and of any future evidence for parasite evolution in wombats.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Sarcoptes scabiei
EPP.common.name: Scabies, Sarcoptic mange
Countries: Argentina [2014] (San Guillermo National Park and Biosphere Reserve, San Juan Province)
Host: Wild South American camelids: vicuña (Vicugna vicugna) and guanaco (Lama guanicoe); probable source in domestic llamas (Lama glama) introduced near the park
Event.summary: In 2014, sarcoptic mange caused by Sarcoptes scabiei was first diagnosed in vicuñas and guanacos in San Guillermo National Park, Argentina, a protected area that previously supported one of the country’s largest sympatric wild camelid populations and had no recorded mange outbreaks in native camelids for at least five decades. Between 2014 and intensive surveys in 2017–2019, the outbreak expanded rapidly, with transect data showing 68% and 77% short‑term declines in vicuña and guanaco densities between 2017 and 2018 and an overall 95–98% decline in abundance relative to pre‑outbreak levels; by April 2019, surveys recorded no living vicuñas or guanacos along park transects, indicating near‑extirpation. Genetic data on mites and the timing and location of infected domestic llamas point to recently introduced llamas as the most likely source, and by the end of the study period the park’s wild camelid populations remained functionally collapsed with uncertain prospects for natural recovery.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: A provincial livestock incentive program introduced domestic llamas into areas adjacent to San Guillermo Biosphere Reserve from 2009 onward, some reportedly affected by mange; spatial and temporal overlap between infected llamas and wild camelids, the absence of prior mange in local livestock and wild camelids for decades, and small, isolated wild populations created ideal conditions for a severe spillover event and rapid, density‑dependent transmission. Internal mechanisms: Multilocus genotyping of mites from vicuñas and guanacos supports a recent, exogenous introduction of Sarcoptes scabiei with limited time for co‑evolution, representing host expansion from domestic llamas into previously naive wild camelids and resulting in an aggressive, high‑mortality epizootic—i.e. re‑emergence driven by host expansion and novel strain/genotype introduction within South America.
Internal mechanism tags: Host Expansion (Spillover from domestic llamas to wild vicuñas and guanacos); Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (recent introduction into the wild camelid community); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within South America).
Review: retain – One of the most extreme documented Sarcoptes outbreaks in wild mammals, with PLOS ONE and associated reports showing 68–77% short‑term density declines and 95–98% overall reductions in vicuña and guanaco abundance, culminating in near‑absence of live animals on 2019 transects in San Guillermo. The 2014–2019 window correctly brackets first detection and the last intensive surveys; host species, location (Argentina, South America) and linkage to recently introduced domestic llamas as the likely source are well supported by genetic and epidemiologic analyses. Classification as re‑emergence (host expansion and novel introduction of mites into previously mange‑free wild camelids in this area) is appropriate. No changes to event fields or URL set recommended.

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria equi
EPP.common.name: Equine babesiosis, Piroplasmosis
Countries: United States of America [2008] (Florida – multiple premises linked to unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing)
Host: Horses (Equus caballus) on unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing premises and associated farms in Florida
Event.summary: In August 2008 a 7‑year‑old Quarter Horse gelding in Florida developed fever, anemia and dark urine and was diagnosed with equine piroplasmosis due to Theileria equi, triggering a foreign animal disease investigation in a country declared EP‑free since 1988. Testing of roughly 200–210 horses on about 25 epidemiologically linked premises identified 20 T. equi–infected horses on seven unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing farms, most of which were clinically inapparent carriers but all of which posed a regulatory and trade concern. Affected premises were quarantined, infected horses were euthanised or removed from the state, and with intensive tracing, testing and tick surveillance, authorities reported eradication of this outbreak from Florida by early 2009.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of chronically infected horses (likely imported from endemic areas such as Mexico) into Florida’s unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing circuit, combined with extensive iatrogenic blood‑borne transmission through practices such as blood‑doping, reuse of needles and syringes, and sharing of multidose drug vials, allowed T. equi to spread despite the absence of demonstrated local tick vectors. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a novel strain or increased virulence; the event reflects efficient mechanical transmission from long‑term carrier horses in a high‑risk management system rather than evolutionary change in the parasite.
Review: review – Event correctly represents the 2008 Florida re‑emergence of T. equi in an officially EP‑free United States and is among the largest recent outbreaks, so it should be retained. I corrected the description of scale to match regulatory and case‑report data (≈20 infected horses, seven epidemiologically linked premises, ~200–210 horses tested) and clarified that this was a re-occurrence in a previously endemic subregion rather than intra- or inter-continental emergence. Source list was kept but augmented with a primary outbreak description and USDA reporting documents; classification as re-occurrence with no re-emergence (no clear pathogen change) remains appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria equi
EPP.common.name: Equine babesiosis, Piroplasmosis
Countries: United States of America [2009] (Jackson County, Missouri)
Host: Horses, ponies and mules on a boarding stable in Jackson County, Missouri (index 7‑year‑old Quarter Horse gelding plus six additional equids)
Event.summary: In early June 2009 a 7‑year‑old Quarter Horse gelding from a stable in Jackson County, Missouri was hospitalized in Kansas with acute fever, jaundice and anemia, and laboratory testing at the National Veterinary Services Laboratories confirmed Theileria equi infection, initiating a foreign animal disease investigation in another U.S. state previously regarded as EP‑free. Quarantine and testing of 63 equids (horses, ponies and mules) on the premises identified six additional T. equi–positive animals, for a total of seven infected equids, while intensive examination of the animals and premises found no competent tick vectors, pointing instead to blood‑borne spread via shared needles or other contaminated injection equipment. Positive horses were euthanised or otherwise removed under a stamping‑out policy, the premises remained under quarantine until repeat testing of remaining animals was negative, and the outbreak was declared resolved with no evidence of further local or interstate transmission.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of a T. equi–infected horse of uncertain origin onto a Missouri boarding stable, together with unsafe parenteral medication practices (reuse of needles, syringes or multidose vials), created an opportunity for iatrogenic blood‑borne transmission in an area lacking established EP vector ticks. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of a novel or more virulent T. equi strain; the event is best explained by amplification of a chronically infected carrier horse through mechanical transmission, similar in mechanism to the 2008 Florida outbreak, and therefore reflects re-occurrence rather than pathogen re-emergence.
Review: review – This Missouri 2009 outbreak (seven T. equi–positive equids on a single premises, mechanical transmission suspected) was entirely missing from the original dataset but is clearly highlighted in OIE-linked reports and U.S./UK summaries as one of the key EP re-emergence events between the Florida 2008 and Texas 2009 episodes. I added it as a separate re-occurrence event for Northern America, using official surveillance summaries and veterinary reports for timing, case numbers and transmission route, and classified it as re-occurrence without intra- or inter-continental emergence. Because it is newly added and partly overlaps in timeframe with other U.S. events, it should be reviewed by a domain expert for consistency of case counting and episode delineation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria equi
EPP.common.name: Equine babesiosis, Piroplasmosis
Countries: United States of America [2009] (large ranch in south Texas)
Host: Horses (primarily Quarter Horses and other equids) on a large ranch in south Texas
Event.summary: In October 2009 a ranch horse in south Texas was diagnosed with equine piroplasmosis due to Theileria equi, revealing widespread infection on a large ranch in a country officially declared EP‑free since 1988. Serologic screening of approximately 2,500 horses linked to the ranch identified about 292 of 360 horses on the index ranch, and more than 400 horses in total, as T. equi–infected, and field plus experimental work demonstrated efficient tick‑borne transmission, particularly by the cayenne tick Amblyomma cajennense (now A. mixtum) and the American dog tick Dermacentor variabilis, with horse movements between the Texas ranch and an EP‑endemic sister ranch in Brazil considered the most likely source. The outbreak was gradually controlled and T. equi eradicated from the ranch through long‑term quarantine, aggressive acaricide‑based tick control, culling or supervised imidocarb treatment of 160+ infected horses, and extensive tracing and testing of horses sold from the premises, with no further ranch‑linked tick-borne transmission detected after completion of the control program.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term movement of chronically infected horses between an EP‑endemic sister ranch in Brazil and the south‑Texas ranch, combined with suitable tick habitat and limited initial tick control, allowed establishment of local vector‑borne transmission in a region that previously had eliminated EP. Increased interstate and international trade in high‑value horses, and gaps in pre‑movement EP testing at the time, further contributed to the extensive spread among ranch horses. Internal mechanisms: Experimental work during this event showed that Amblyomma cajennense and Dermacentor variabilis were competent vectors for T. equi in this setting, broadening the recognized vector range (enhanced transmission/vector adaptation at the system level), but there is no clear evidence that the parasite itself evolved increased virulence or altered host range in this outbreak.
Review: retain – This record accurately captures the large 2009 south‑Texas ranch outbreak, including order‑of‑magnitude case numbers (≈292/360 horses on the index ranch, >400 infected overall), the key tick vectors (Amblyomma cajennense/A. mixtum and Dermacentor variabilis), and the linkage to a Brazilian sister ranch. Geographic fields (Northern America, United States, south Texas) and classification as a re-occurrence in a previously endemic subregion (not a new continental or subregional emergence) are appropriate. No substantive changes were required beyond minor wording harmonization, but a human reviewer may wish to confirm whether they prefer Texas ranch–associated infections detected off‑ranch be counted within this event or within the broader multi‑state episode below.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria equi
EPP.common.name: Equine babesiosis, Piroplasmosis
Countries: United States of America [2009] (multiple states; at least 16 states detecting infected horses)
Host: Horses, especially Quarter Horse racehorses involved in sanctioned and unsanctioned racing across multiple U.S. states
Event.summary: From early 2009 through late 2010, expanded surveillance following the Florida and Texas equine piroplasmosis events identified hundreds of additional T. equi– and Babesia caballi–infected horses across at least 16 U.S. states, with about 540+ positives reported in federal risk assessments and committee reports. Many of these horses were apparently healthy Quarter Horse racehorses and other performance horses, and epidemiologic investigations linked a substantial proportion of the multi‑state cluster to unsanctioned Quarter Horse racing circuits, extensive interstate movement, and iatrogenic blood‑borne transmission via shared needles, illicit blood‑doping and contaminated multidose vials. The cluster led to new EP testing requirements at some racetracks, long‑term quarantine and supervised treatment programs for infected horses, and targeted outreach to racing sectors, after which the number of newly detected positives associated with these pathways declined markedly, although sporadic EP cases continue to be detected in the U.S.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑volume movement of racehorses between states and across the Mexican border, coupled with high‑risk husbandry practices (blood‑doping, reuse of needles and IV equipment, and possible informal blood transfusions) created multiple mechanical transmission routes that bypassed the need for tick vectors; prior to 2009, limited routine EP testing in racing sectors allowed accumulation and silent spread of carrier horses. Internal mechanisms: Genotyping studies suggest a limited number of T. equi introduction sources rather than widespread parasite diversification, and there is no evidence of increased intrinsic virulence; the primary mechanism is efficient human‑mediated blood‑borne spread in mobile, high‑density equine populations, representing a large-scale re-occurrence rather than evolutionary re-emergence.
Review: retain – This entry appropriately treats the 2009–2010 multi‑state U.S. detection of ≈500+ EP‑positive horses (largely linked to racing circuits and iatrogenic transmission) as a single, epidemiologically related re-occurrence episode, in line with USDA pathway assessments and subsequent reviews. The impact is large (hundreds of infected horses across ≥16 states) and clearly within the top tier of global T. equi emergence events, so it should be retained. No corrections were needed to geography or event‑type coding; a note of caution is that some horse counts in federal summaries may overlap with those from the Texas ranch outbreak, so final quantitative impact comparisons should recognise this potential double counting.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria equi
EPP.common.name: Equine babesiosis, Piroplasmosis
Countries: Ireland [2009] (County Meath – Thoroughbred racing stable near Dunshaughlin)
Host: Thoroughbred racehorses and a pony at a racing stable in County Meath, Ireland
Event.summary: In June 2009 several Thoroughbred racehorses at a yard near Dunshaughlin, County Meath, developed fever, anemia and poor performance, and laboratory investigation confirmed equine piroplasmosis due to Theileria equi, constituting the first officially reported EP outbreak in Ireland. Subsequent testing of 60 equids on the premises (59 racehorses and one pony) found 28 animals positive by serology and/or PCR, prompting quarantine of the yard, movement restrictions, and tracing of recent horse movements, although no competent EP vector ticks were identified and there was no evidence of wider geographic spread. After infected horses were managed under strict biosecurity and no additional foci were detected, Ireland continued to be regarded as EP‑free, and the event was closed as a limited import‑associated incursion highlighting the vulnerability of EP‑free regions to introduction via international horse movement and local iatrogenic spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of one or more T. equi–infected horses or contaminated blood products from endemic regions into a high‑density racing yard, along with close contact and potential reuse of needles or other equipment among valuable Thoroughbreds, likely enabled limited local mechanical transmission in a country with few or no established EP tick vectors. Internal mechanisms: There is no indication of a novel strain or altered parasite behaviour; the event is best interpreted as first detection and intra‑continental emergence of T. equi in Ireland driven by horse movements and management practices rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – The original row correctly identified Ireland 2009 as a first detection and intra-continental emergence event but substantially underestimated its scale (describing only three clinically ill horses). I updated the event summary and impact to reflect official reports indicating 28 of 60 horses on the premises tested positive, and clarified that competent vector ticks were not demonstrated and spread was likely mechanical and limited to the yard. I added a more detailed event report from The Horse and a peer‑reviewed retrospective analysis as key sources; because I changed numerical impact and interpretation of transmission mode, this row should be reviewed, but it clearly remains one of the most important recent European emergence events and should be retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria equi
EPP.common.name: Equine babesiosis, Piroplasmosis
Host: Horses of various breeds in the south‑west of the Netherlands, including two with autochthonous clinical Theileria equi infection and additional subclinical indigenous cases
Event.summary: Between May and September 2010 a cross‑sectional survey of 300 randomly selected horses in the south‑west of the Netherlands, initiated after detection of an apparently indigenous Babesia caballi case, identified low‑level exposure to equine piroplasms and four horses considered truly indigenous infections, including two with clinical Theileria equi infection and two additional subclinical carriers. These affected horses had no history of travel outside the Netherlands and grazed in areas where the tick vector Dermacentor reticulatus had recently established, providing the first evidence of autochthonous T. equi transmission in a country previously regarded as non‑endemic. Follow‑up surveillance of horses and expanding D. reticulatus populations indicated that T. equi prevalence remained low and focal, and the Netherlands continues to be considered non‑endemic with only sporadic locally acquired cases associated with newly suitable tick habitats.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: North‑westward expansion and establishment of Dermacentor reticulatus tick populations in the Netherlands from the mid‑2000s, likely driven by climate and land‑use changes, increased the ecological suitability for EP transmission, while the importation or movement of infected equids from endemic European regions seeded T. equi into these new vector‑supported environments. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence for a novel T. equi strain in this event; emergence is best explained by geographic range expansion of competent tick vectors (geographic range expansion of the transmission system) combined with horse movements, enabling local autochthonous transmission in an area previously free of indigenous EP.
Review: review – The original row correctly captured the nature of the Dutch event (first autochthonous clinical T. equi infections associated with recently established Dermacentor reticulatus populations) but mis‑dated it to 2012, the publication year of the key study, rather than 2010 when the horses were sampled and cases occurred. I changed the event year to 2010–2010 and updated the country field accordingly, and slightly rephrased the summary to match the Vet Parasitol paper (four truly indigenous cases, two clinical T. equi infections). Source URLs already pointed to the primary study and relevant European reviews and were therefore retained; because timing and impact details were adjusted, this event is flagged for review but clearly remains among the major European emergence events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria equi
EPP.common.name: Equine babesiosis, Piroplasmosis
Countries: Austria [2020] (eastern Austria – Güssing/Burgenland farm with 18 resident horses)
Host: Domestic horses on a single farm in eastern Austria, including a pregnant Austrian Warmblood mare, her foal and multiple subclinical T. equi–infected pasturemates
Event.summary: In 2020 a 23‑year‑old pregnant Austrian Warmblood mare from a pasture near Güssing in Burgenland, eastern Austria, was admitted with fever, anemia and icterus, and subsequent microscopy, PCR and sequencing confirmed Theileria equi infection despite the mare never having left Austria, constituting the first documented autochthonous equine piroplasmosis case in the country. Follow‑up investigations of the same farm over the next two years sampled 18 resident horses and local ticks, revealing that initially two horses showed clinical disease while 12 of the remaining 16 were subclinically infected, and by the second year a total of 16 of 18 horses had evidence of T. equi infection, with multiple questing ticks (Dermacentor reticulatus, Ixodes ricinus and Haemaphysalis concinna) also PCR‑positive for the same T. equi genotype E. Quarantine, tick control and management changes limited further clinical cases but the persistence of infected horses and infected ticks on the premises indicated establishment of a local transmission focus in Austria, raising concern that T. equi could become endemic in suitable parts of the country.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of T. equi into an Austrian farm via movement of infected horses from neighbouring endemic regions (notably an imported Hungarian horse sharing pasture with the index mare) into an area where several tick species, including Dermacentor reticulatus, had recently expanded their range created conditions for local transmission; climate‑driven shifts and changes in land use likely facilitated this vector expansion. Internal mechanisms: Sequencing showed that all equine and tick isolates belonged to T. equi genotype E, with no evidence of a novel highly virulent lineage; the emergence reflects geographic and ecological expansion of the parasite–vector system into a previously non‑endemic country combined with the long carrier state in horses, rather than intrinsic changes in parasite virulence or host range.
Review: review – This significant recent emergence episode in Austria was absent from the original dataset but clearly belongs among the top T. equi events because it documents both the first autochthonous clinical case and a two‑year farm‑level study in which 16 of 18 horses and multiple tick species were infected in a previously non‑endemic country. I added a new event row starting in 2020 and extending through the two‑year follow-up (2020–2022), classified as first detection and intra-continental emergence in Western Europe, with drivers focused on importation of infected horses and northward expansion of Dermacentor and other ticks. Because this is a newly added and complex episode, it should be reviewed by a subject‑matter expert, but its inclusion materially improves coverage of recent European emergence linked to vector range expansion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria spp.
EPP.common.name: Theileriosis
Countries: Australia [2006] (initially coastal New South Wales; spread to Queensland, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia)
Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds)
Event.summary: From 2006 onward, cattle in coastal New South Wales, Australia, began experiencing outbreaks of severe haemolytic anaemia and mortality linked to virulent genotypes of Theileria orientalis, particularly Ikeda and Chitose, in herds previously considered affected only by benign T. orientalis. Over the subsequent decade, hundreds of clinical outbreaks of bovine anaemia associated with T. orientalis were reported along the eastern seaboard and into South Australia and Western Australia, with substantial production losses in both dairy and beef systems and widespread detection of pathogenic genotypes in cattle and Haemaphysalis longicornis ticks. Although the spatial spread of Ikeda into new areas largely stabilised after about 2015, clinical cases continued within the endemic zone through at least 2022, managed via improved diagnostics, tick‑control and herd management but with oriental theileriosis now recognised as a major endemic constraint.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expanded movement and trading of cattle within eastern and southern Australia, including movement of infected breeder stock between tick‑free and tick‑endemic areas; widespread presence of H. longicornis and other Haemaphysalis ticks in coastal and temperate regions; intensification of grazing systems and climatic conditions favourable to ticks. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and introduction of the virulent Ikeda genotype (often with co‑infection by Chitose and other types) into herds historically exposed only to benign T. orientalis strains (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence), with higher parasitaemia and anaemia and apparent fitness advantages that facilitated rapid spread and establishment (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: review – Major emergence of pathogenic T. orientalis Ikeda in Australia with hundreds of outbreaks and sustained impact; event period extended from 2006–2014 to 2006–2022 to reflect continued clinical activity. Inter-continental emergence was set to No because T. orientalis was already present in Oceania; under the project rules, genotype-level novelty is captured as re-emergence, not inter-continental emergence. Recommended to retain as one of the largest events, but classification and time window should be checked by a domain expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria spp.
EPP.common.name: Theileriosis
Countries: New Zealand [2012] (Northland, Waikato and wider upper North Island)
Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds)
Event.summary: In August 2012, index cases of severe anaemia and mortality due to Theileria orientalis Ikeda type were identified on dairy farms in Kamo (Northland) and Reporoa (Waikato) in New Zealand, where only benign T. orientalis types had previously been recognised. During 2012–2013 the epidemic of Theileria‑associated bovine anaemia (TABA) spread rapidly across the upper North Island, and by August 2014 at least 633 infected herds had been reported, with substantial economic losses from deaths, production drops and movement restrictions. After 2014, the disease was managed through enhanced surveillance (Ikeda declared a new‑to‑New‑Zealand organism in 2012), rollout of rapid qPCR diagnostics, tick‑control measures, movement management and farmer awareness, leading to a decline in new severe outbreaks even as Ikeda became established in cattle and Haemaphysalis longicornis populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of T. orientalis Ikeda into New Zealand, likely via imported cattle or biological material from endemic countries; established populations of H. longicornis ticks in North Island regions that enabled rapid local transmission; routine seasonal movements of pregnant and lactating cows between Northland, Waikato and other areas that disseminated infection; high within‑herd tick burdens on pasture in suitable climatic zones. Internal mechanisms: A virulent Ikeda genotype entering a cattle population previously infected mainly with benign Chitose and Buffeli types (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence), capable of causing high parasitaemia and severe anaemia; efficient transmission by a competent vector already adapted to local environments (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation), resulting in fast geographic spread within the country.
Review: review – Large, well-documented epidemic of T. orientalis Ikeda in New Zealand with >600 affected herds and major economic impact; clearly qualifies as a top emergence event. Reclassified as re-emergence (novel pathogenic genotype in a host system where T. orientalis was already present) rather than a mixed re-occurrence/re-emergence event, in line with the project rule that strain-level novelty should be captured as re-emergence, not intra/inter-continental emergence. Recommended to retain with this corrected classification.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria spp.
EPP.common.name: Theileriosis
Countries: China [2020] (Hebei Province, Zhangjiakou, confined dairy cattle)
Host: Cattle (confined dairy herds)
Event.summary: In June 2020, a confined dairy herd in Zhangjiakou, Hebei Province, China experienced an outbreak of piroplasmosis‑like illness with anaemia and deaths in adult cows, and laboratory investigation showed that two‑thirds of sampled animals were infected with Theileria orientalis. Molecular characterisation of the major piroplasm surface protein (MPSP) and 18S rRNA genes demonstrated the presence of both Chitose (type 1) and Ikeda (type 2) genotypes, and experimental infection indicated that Ikeda was the predominant and pathogenic type responsible for disease, representing one of the first clearly documented clinical outbreaks of Ikeda‑associated oriental theileriosis in Chinese dairy cattle. The episode raised awareness that pathogenic T. orientalis genotypes, previously regarded as mostly benign in China, can cause severe disease in intensive dairy systems and highlighted the need for improved surveillance, tick control and biosecurity in rapidly modernising herds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and confinement of dairy production in Hebei with high animal densities and introduction of high‑producing but more susceptible cattle; exposure of naive or partially immune animals to infected ticks or iatrogenic transmission within the herd; limited prior recognition of T. orientalis Ikeda as a cause of serious disease in Chinese cattle, which may have delayed control responses. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and predominance of the virulent Ikeda genotype in an affected herd (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity), with high within‑herd infection prevalence and mortality in clinically affected animals, consistent with patterns seen in Australasia and New Zealand.
Review: review – Newly added event describing a high-mortality outbreak of T. orientalis Ikeda in confined dairy cattle in Hebei, China, which is among the clearest examples of clinical Ikeda emergence in Eastern Asia. Classified as re-emergence because T. orientalis (including Ikeda) had been detected previously in China, but this was one of the first large, well-characterised clinical outbreaks in intensive dairy cattle. Recommended to retain, with timing and herd-scale impact (number of deaths) to be confirmed from the full Chinese-language and supplementary materials.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas foetus
EPP.common.name: Bovine trichomoniasis, Tritrichomonas foetus
Countries: United States of America [1990] (California beef herds)
Host: Beef cattle (bulls and breeding cows) under natural service systems
Event.summary: In 1990, a random survey of California cow–calf beef herds found that about 15.8% of herds had at least one bull infected with Tritrichomonas foetus, confirming substantial ongoing bovine trichomoniasis in western US beef operations and quantifying its prevalence at the herd level. The survey showed that infection was widespread yet clinically unapparent in bulls, with impacts expressed as reduced pregnancy rates and extended calving seasons in naturally serviced herds. These findings underpinned subsequent regulatory attention and testing requirements in several western states, although trichomoniasis has persisted as a chronic reproductive constraint in extensive beef systems relying on natural service.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive cow–calf operations depending on natural service, commingling of multiple herds on shared rangeland, and lack of routine trichomoniasis testing for breeding bulls allowed persistent transmission; low producer awareness meant infection was often only suspected after marked reproductive loss. Internal mechanisms: typical bovine T. foetus biology—lifelong asymptomatic colonisation of the preputial mucosa in older bulls and highly efficient venereal transmission—supports stable endemicity in herds using natural mating.
Review: Retain – Verified via state veterinary sources and reviews that a 1990 California survey found ~15.8% of beef herds with at least one infected bull and that T. foetus was long‑established in North America; geography, timing and classification as re‑occurrence (endemic disease documented with renewed attention) are appropriate, and sources are relevant to this event.([cdfa.ca.gov](https://www.cdfa.ca.gov/ahfss/Animal_Health/trich_Q_and_A.html?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma brucei
EPP.common.name: Nagana, Animal African trypanosomiasis, AAT
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus/Bos indicus); wildlife (especially African buffalo and other game) as important reservoir hosts, though the documented production impact was on cattle mortality.
Event.summary: In 1990 a severe outbreak of African animal trypanosomosis (nagana) occurred in the tsetse‑infested areas of north‑eastern KwaZulu‑Natal, South Africa, where tsetse and AAT had long been present but livestock case numbers had been relatively low in preceding years. During a major drought, high tsetse densities and limited grazing drove cattle into heavily infested thickets, leading to an explosive epidemic in which about 10,000 cattle died and over 100,000 were treated with trypanocides under an emergency control programme. Integrated measures based on mass chemotherapy and intensive dipping with pyrethroid insecticides reduced tsetse challenge and infection prevalence over subsequent years, although low‑level endemicity and periodic local flare‑ups have persisted in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Severe drought and land‑use changes in north‑eastern KwaZulu‑Natal in the late 1980s forced communal and commercial cattle herds into dense thicket habitats with high densities of Glossina austeni and G. brevipalpis, while gaps or changes in vector control allowed tsetse populations to rebound and contact rates with cattle to increase. Internal mechanisms: Parasitological and molecular surveys indicate that infections in cattle in this focus are dominated by T. congolense, with T. brucei not consistently detected and no specific novel genotypes reported; the outbreak is therefore best interpreted as a classic re‑occurrence of endemic AAT driven by ecological and control‑system changes rather than by documented evolutionary change in the parasites.
Review: review – retain; major AAT outbreak with ~10,000 cattle deaths and >100,000 treatments in north‑eastern KwaZulu‑Natal is well documented and clearly among the most impactful post‑1990 episodes. Narrative was adjusted to emphasise that cattle infections in this focus are dominated by T. congolense (T. brucei is not consistently detected), treating the event as part of the multi‑species AAT complex under this EPP rather than implying strong T. brucei involvement. Classification as re‑occurrence and the geographic coding (Southern Africa, South Africa) are consistent with project definitions and should be kept, but the updated wording and cross‑species framing merit human review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma brucei
EPP.common.name: Nagana, Animal African trypanosomiasis, AAT
Host: Cattle (village and transhumant herds)
Event.summary: Between the late 1990s and early 2000s, village cattle in Kénédougou Province, south‑western Burkina Faso, experienced persistent, high burdens of African animal trypanosomosis despite intensive chemoprophylaxis and treatment campaigns, indicating a major episode of control failure. Field studies using parasitological, mouse‑based and PCR methods in multiple villages showed widespread infections with T. congolense and T. vivax, with T. brucei‑group trypanosomes also detected, and many cattle relapsed after treatment with isometamidium chloride or diminazene aceturate, demonstrating multi‑drug resistance. Over this period, cattle condition and productivity deteriorated and routine chemotherapy became increasingly ineffective, and the episode ended only when resistance was recognised and control strategies (including drug‑use policies and vector control) were revised, although resistant strains remained entrenched in the area.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy reliance on chemotherapy in the Kénédougou cattle corridor, with frequent, sometimes farmer‑administered dosing and limited veterinary oversight, created strong selection pressure for drug‑resistant trypanosomes; continued high tsetse challenge and movement of cattle between villages maintained intense transmission. Internal mechanisms: Multiple studies using the standard mouse test and PCR confirmed the emergence and spread of trypanocidal‑drug‑resistant trypanosome populations (primarily T. congolense, with T. vivax and some T. brucei‑group parasites) resistant to both isometamidium and diminazene, a clear example of re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance rather than environmental change alone.
Review: retain – Kénédougou is one of the best‑documented foci of multi‑drug‑resistant AAT, with field and laboratory evidence of widespread resistance to both isometamidium and diminazene and clear production impacts across many villages. Geographic coding (Western Africa, Burkina Faso) and classification as re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance align with the project’s definitions. No structural changes were needed beyond adding the core field‑study PubMed citation; event should be kept as one of the key post‑1990 AAT emergence episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma brucei
EPP.common.name: Nagana, Animal African trypanosomiasis, AAT
Countries: Uganda [2000] (central and south‑eastern cattle corridor; districts including Kaberamaido, Soroti and neighbouring areas)
Host: Cattle (Bos indicus‑dominant mixed herds) and other livestock (goats, sheep) in the cattle corridor
Event.summary: During the early 2000s, Uganda’s central and south‑eastern cattle corridor experienced a marked increase in African animal trypanosomosis, with districts such as Kaberamaido declaring emergency situations: surveys found around 9–10% of screened cattle infected in some subcounties, and many animals showed severe clinical disease. National assessments around this time estimated that approximately 100,000 cattle were dying annually from nagana in the wider cattle corridor, coinciding with overlapping epidemics of human T. brucei rhodesiense sleeping sickness in the same region. In response, Uganda and partners mobilized substantial funding (about US$9.8 million from the African Development Bank in 2008) and implemented intensified tsetse control, livestock treatment and community‑based surveillance, which gradually reduced mortality and prevalence, though nagana remained a chronic constraint on livestock production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased cattle movements along the cattle corridor, restocking initiatives into endemic sleeping‑sickness areas, high densities of tsetse flies in riverine and bush habitats, and under‑resourced veterinary and vector‑control services all contributed to the resurgence of AAT. The overlap of zoonotic T. b. rhodesiense foci in livestock and humans further complicated control and likely increased awareness and reporting. Internal mechanisms: There is no clear evidence that novel animal‑infective T. brucei strains or other genetic shifts were responsible for this resurgence; instead, the episode reflects re‑occurrence driven mainly by ecological and socio‑economic factors (livestock movement, weak control systems) and possible but poorly quantified drug resistance.
Review: retain – this row captures the widely recognised early‑2000s resurgence of nagana (and overlapping rhodesiense sleeping sickness) along Uganda’s cattle corridor, with credible though approximate estimates of ~100,000 cattle deaths per year and major external funding for control. Time bounds (2000–2005) are necessarily approximate but broadly consistent with reported emergencies in Kaberamaido and the subsequent AfDB‑funded control project. Classification as re‑occurrence (rather than emergence or re‑emergence) appropriately reflects the dominant role of livestock movement and control‑system weaknesses rather than confirmed parasite change; no corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma brucei
EPP.common.name: Nagana, Animal African trypanosomiasis, AAT
Countries: Ethiopia [2001] (western Ethiopia—Ghibe Valley, Metekel, Upper Didessa, FITCA project areas)
Host: Cattle (smallholder and project herds in tsetse‑infested zones)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, several western Ethiopian tsetse‑infested zones (including the Ghibe Valley, Metekel and Upper Didessa) recorded persistently high prevalence of bovine trypanosomosis despite long‑standing control efforts, marking a significant resurgence of nagana. Field trials and follow‑up studies in cattle under natural challenge showed frequent relapse infections with T. congolense and, to a lesser extent, T. brucei‑group parasites after treatment with isometamidium and diminazene, and earlier work in Ghibe had already demonstrated triple resistance to diminazene, isometamidium and homidium. Meta‑analyses of Ethiopian data report prevalences exceeding 10% in some late 1990s–early 2000s studies in these areas. Continued poor treatment responses and sustained transmission signalled a shift from manageable endemicity to a difficult‑to‑control, high‑impact situation, which gradually improved only as vector control and drug‑use policies were adjusted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of cattle production into high‑challenge tsetse habitats, limited availability of alternative control methods, heavy reliance on a small set of trypanocides obtained from both formal and informal markets, and often suboptimal dosing practices fostered conditions for drug resistance and persistent transmission. Internal mechanisms: Multiple studies from the FITCA project and related research documented reduced efficacy and laboratory‑confirmed resistance of circulating trypanosome populations (especially T. congolense) to isometamidium and diminazene; together with earlier evidence of triple‑drug‑resistant T. congolense in Ghibe, this constitutes a clear re‑emergence event characterised by antimicrobial resistance and increased persistence of infections rather than simple ecological re‑occurrence.
Review: retain – this row consolidates well‑documented evidence of multi‑drug‑resistant AAT in western Ethiopia (Ghibe, Metekel, Upper Didessa) in the late 1990s–early 2000s. The geographic coding (Eastern Africa, Ethiopia) and classification as re‑emergence driven by confirmed resistance to isometamidium and diminazene are consistent with the event definition. Although burden estimates are indirect (prevalence data and reports of repeated relapse), this focus is widely cited as a major AAT problem area and plausibly belongs among the top post‑1990 events; no changes to coding were necessary.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma brucei
EPP.common.name: Nagana, Animal African trypanosomiasis, AAT
Countries: Sudan [2010] (Blue Nile State, Kurmuk District; cattle infected after grazing in neighbouring Ethiopian tsetse‑infested areas)
Host: Cattle (Kenana and Fulani breeds)
Event.summary: In June 2010 an acute outbreak of bovine trypanosomiasis occurred in Kurmuk District of Blue Nile State, south‑eastern Sudan, involving indigenous Kenana and Fulani cattle that had crossed the border to graze in Ethiopia’s tsetse‑infested belt and then returned to Sudan. The outbreak was characterized by high morbidity and mixed infections with up to four Trypanosoma species (including T. vivax, T. congolense, T. brucei‑group parasites and T. simiae) in affected cattle, leading to substantial production losses and prompting urgent veterinary investigation and laboratory confirmation. Control efforts focusing on treatment of infected herds, improved management of cross‑border grazing and targeted vector control gradually reduced case numbers, and the outbreak subsided as cattle movements and grazing patterns were modified and trypanocidal treatments were applied more systematically.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Seasonal transboundary movement of cattle from relatively lower‑risk Sudanese areas into high‑challenge Ethiopian tsetse belts exposed naïve or partially protected animals to intense infection pressure, and returning animals carried parasites back into Blue Nile State; limited veterinary infrastructure and surveillance capacity in this remote border area delayed recognition and response. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak was attributed to the introduction of different parasite variants via cross‑border movement, but no specific novel genotype or resistance mechanism was conclusively identified, so this event is best viewed as a re‑occurrence driven by livestock movements and high tsetse challenge rather than by documented genetic change in the trypanosomes.
Review: review – retain but with corrected geography. The 2010 Kurmuk outbreak is clearly centred in Blue Nile State, Sudan, with Ethiopian tsetse belts acting as an exposure source during seasonal grazing; accordingly, the event is now coded to Northern Africa/Sudan only, with Ethiopia mentioned in the narrative rather than as a second affected country/sub‑region. Classification as re‑occurrence (acute outbreak in a known tsetse‑trypanosomosis setting) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence remains consistent with the definitions. Human review is recommended to confirm that limiting the formal country list to Sudan matches how other cross‑border episodes are treated in the wider dataset.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma brucei
EPP.common.name: Nagana, Animal African trypanosomiasis, AAT
Countries: Uganda [2010] (Karamoja region; Moroto, Kotido, Nakapiripirit and neighbouring districts)
Host: Cattle and donkeys (primary documented hosts), with probable involvement of goats and sheep in pastoral systems
Event.summary: From around 2010 onwards, the semi‑arid Karamoja region in north‑eastern Uganda, historically underserved and long considered peripheral in AAT control planning, experienced growing burdens of African animal trypanosomosis that significantly constrained pastoral livelihoods. Detailed surveys documented appreciable prevalence of trypanosome infections in cattle and donkeys and widespread reports from pastoral households of substantial cattle losses, poor traction, low milk yields and herd depletion, leading national authorities to list AAT among the top livestock health constraints in Karamoja. By the mid‑2010s the Ugandan government launched an emergency cattle treatment and tsetse control project in Karamoja, after which prevalence declined in targeted areas but the region remained classified as a priority focus for AAT control rather than a low‑risk zone.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and concentration of cattle herds around limited water sources, vegetation changes, chronic insecurity and remoteness that limited access to veterinary services, and under‑investment in tsetse control likely increased local Glossina abundance and contact rates, while increasing connectivity with higher‑risk neighbouring areas may have introduced more infected animals. Internal mechanisms: Available reports emphasise environmental, management and service‑delivery drivers rather than specific novel strains or resistance; thus the episode is interpreted primarily as a re‑occurrence and intensification of AAT within an under‑served part of the Eastern Africa sub‑region rather than as an intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence driven by parasite change, although unquantified drug resistance may contribute to persistence.
Review: review – retain but reclassified. Under the project’s rules, intra‑continental emergence refers to first spread into a new UNSD sub‑region; Karamoja lies within the already endemic Eastern Africa sub‑region (Uganda), and published work describes a neglected, high‑burden focus rather than first appearance on a new continent or in a new sub‑region. Accordingly, intra_continental_emergence has been set to “no” and re_occurrence to “yes”. This still recognises Karamoja as a major 2010s AAT constraint but frames it as a resurgence in an under‑served area rather than a distinct continental emergence; human review is advised to confirm that this interpretation is applied consistently across the dataset.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma evansi
EPP.common.name: TEVA
Host: Horses (working/ranch horses; outbreak on a large beef-cattle ranch)
Event.summary: In 1994–1995, surra due to Trypanosoma evansi caused a severe outbreak among ranch horses in the Pantanal Mato-Grossense wetlands of Brazil, with one herd losing 48 of 95 horses (51% mortality) and at least one neighboring ranch reporting similarly catastrophic losses. Epidemiological and serological investigations showed that T. evansi had been (re)introduced into the southern Pantanal in the early 1990s after an apparent absence from local horse populations, and that infection was now maintained by a multi-host system involving horses, dogs and wild reservoirs such as coatis and capybaras under very high tabanid-fly challenge. Over subsequent years, recurrent surra outbreaks and endemic transmission in the Pantanal became recognized as a major constraint on equine health and on cattle ranching operations that depend on horse traction, with modeling studies later estimating thousands of horse deaths and multi-million dollar annual losses if the disease is left uncontrolled.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Seasonal flooding in the Pantanal concentrates domestic livestock and wildlife on small areas of dry land during the wet season, greatly increasing contact rates and exposure to biting flies; intensive cattle marketing with long-distance, on-foot movements of large cattle lots and their working horses promotes spread of infected animals between ranches; limited access to timely diagnosis and effective trypanocides, combined with the high working and cultural value of horses, amplifies the perceived impact when outbreaks occur. Internal mechanisms: Isolates from Pantanal outbreaks show typical Trypanosoma evansi morphology and isoenzyme patterns without evidence of a novel strain; the outbreak is best interpreted as re-introduction and amplification of an existing South American lineage (re-occurrence) driven by ecological conditions, husbandry practices and vector abundance rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Review – Newly added event. Strongly supported by Silva et al. (1995) and subsequent FAO/EMBRAPA work showing >50% horse mortality in an affected herd and recurrent outbreaks causing several hundred equine deaths annually, plus modeled annual losses of ~US$2.4 million in the Pantanal horse population.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8644453/?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence within the South America subregion (not intra-/inter-continental emergence) because T. evansi was already long-established elsewhere in South America.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma evansi
EPP.common.name: TEVA
Countries: Spain [1997] (Canary Islands – especially Gran Canaria, later other islands)
Host: Dromedary camels (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: In 1997–1998, Trypanosoma evansi was detected for the first time in Spain and in Europe when a dromedary camel imported from Mauritania to Gran Canaria showed chronic surra and parasitaemia; subsequent surveys during 1997–1999 found seroprevalence around 6–9% in camels across multiple Canary Islands, confirming local establishment rather than a single imported case. Follow-up control programmes with treatment of parasitologically and/or serologically positive camels reduced prevalence but did not completely clear infection, leaving a persistent focus on two Gran Canaria farms. Over the following decade the Canary Islands remained the only endemic European focus, with sporadic clinical cases but ongoing surveillance due to the risk of onward spread via camel movements.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected camels from enzootic North African countries (e.g. Mauritania, Morocco) into the Canary Islands with inadequate pre-import trypanosomosis testing; high densities of mechanical vectors (Stomoxys calcitrans and possibly tabanids) in camel farms favoured local transmission; limited awareness of surra risk and historical EU trade rules that did not list T. evansi infection in camels allowed entry and establishment. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a distinct genotype relative to North African strains; emergence here is best explained by geographic range expansion via livestock movement, ecological suitability for mechanical vectors and high local camel density, rather than parasite change.
Review: Review – Keep as major event (first established T. evansi focus in Europe), but event types have been corrected. Set first_detection='No' because global first detection in animals occurred in India in the 1880s, and retained inter_continental_emergence='Yes' to reflect the first occurrence with local transmission in the European continent. Sub-region (Southern Europe) and country coding (Spain [1997], Canary Islands) are consistent with the UNSD scheme, and sources now emphasise primary Canary Islands seroprevalence and control studies.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11018734/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma evansi
EPP.common.name: TEVA
Countries: Thailand [2000] (Khon Kaen Province, equine breeding farm)
Host: Horses; mules
Event.summary: During June–July 2000, a severe surra outbreak occurred on an equine breeding farm in Khon Kaen Province in north‑east Thailand, where Trypanosoma evansi was confirmed parasitologically in surviving animals. About 40% (19/47) of horses and 10% (1/10) of mules were suspected to have died from surra, and 42% of pregnant mares aborted or produced stillborn foals. Remaining horses and mules were treated with diminazene aceturate and followed for several weeks with parasitological tests, haematocrit and serology, which documented clearance of detectable parasitaemia after treatment but also highlighted drug toxicity and the scale of production losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The outbreak occurred on a farm in an area where surra is endemic in cattle and buffaloes, and is consistent with spillover and amplification when large numbers of equids are kept together under high biting-fly pressure; shared grazing and watering with other livestock, plus seasonal abundance of tabanid and stable flies, likely promoted intense mechanical transmission. External drivers include limited availability of trypanocides (diminazene as the only registered product at that time) and potential underestimation of equine surra risk in local health planning. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was reported; the event reflects re-occurrence and intensification of an existing endemic parasite in the South‑eastern Asia subregion, rather than evolutionary change.
Review: Review – Newly added as a high-impact re-occurrence event. The Khon Kaen breeding-farm outbreak caused ~40% mortality in horses and very high abortion/stillbirth rates in mares, and is widely cited as a key example of severe equine surra in South‑east Asia.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304401702003047?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence in an already endemic South‑eastern Asia subregion, not as intra-/inter‑continental emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma evansi
EPP.common.name: TEVA
Countries: Philippines [2002] (southern Philippines, multiple villages in Mindanao/Agusan del Sur)
Host: Water buffalo (carabao); cattle (minor); other village livestock
Event.summary: Between 2002 and 2006, cross-sectional surveys in 71 villages in southern Philippines identified a substantial burden of Trypanosoma evansi infection in 1,732 water buffaloes, with seroprevalence reaching 13–100% in high‑risk areas and strong associations with poor reproductive performance and mortality. The work revealed that surra had been causing major but under-recognized production losses in buffalo-dependent smallholder systems in Mindanao. Subsequent modeling showed that a typical village herd under moderate to severe surra could lose the equivalent of tens to hundreds of thousands of US dollars annually through mortality, reduced calving and the need to import replacement animals, prompting the disease’s recognition as the country’s second most important livestock disease and informing national control strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Traditional free-grazing and communal watering of buffaloes and cattle in lowland agro-ecosystems, high densities of biting flies during the wet season, and socio-economic constraints limiting access to veterinary services and trypanocides all favoured persistent transmission and recurrent outbreaks; long-distance movements of animals for draught and breeding likely helped maintain high-force-of-infection foci. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain was highlighted; the episode represents re-occurrence and intensification of long-established surra in the South‑eastern Asia subregion due to management and environmental drivers, rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – This event is well supported by large cross-sectional datasets and economic modeling showing very high seroprevalence and major impacts on buffalo population dynamics and village economies in Mindanao.([researchportal.murdoch.edu.au](https://researchportal.murdoch.edu.au/esplorows/assetMapper?instCode=61MUN_INST&path=https%3A%2F%2Fresearchrepository.murdoch.edu.au%2F3407&utm_source=openai)) Classification as a major re-occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence) in South‑eastern Asia is appropriate and has been left unchanged.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma evansi
EPP.common.name: TEVA
Countries: Israel [2006] (southern Dead Sea area, desert farm)
Host: Dromedary camels; horses; donkeys
Event.summary: In September 2006, the first clinical cases of surra in Israel were diagnosed on a secluded desert farm in the southern Dead Sea area when a chronically wasted camel and, two months later, a mare showed high trypanosome parasitaemia and neurological signs, with fatal outcomes despite treatment. Over the next two years, a longitudinal study of the farm documented Trypanosoma evansi infection in 8 of 10 camels, 3 of 7 horses and 6 of 13 donkeys, with several animals acting as asymptomatic carriers detected by PCR and reverse dot-blot assays. The outbreak, recognized as the first reported T. evansi outbreak in domestic animals in Israel, led to intensive monitoring, treatment with melarsenoxide cysteamine and heightened awareness of surra risk in the Middle East.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The affected farm kept mixed equid and camel herds in an arid area where T. evansi is known from neighboring countries (e.g. Jordan); introduction of infected animals or contact with infected camels from the wider region combined with local mechanical vectors (tabanid flies) likely initiated the outbreak, which then persisted because of carrier animals and limited prior experience with surra diagnosis and treatment. Internal mechanisms: No novel parasite genotype was implicated; the episode is best interpreted as a notable re-occurrence of T. evansi within the Western Asia subregion, manifesting as the first recognized multi-species farm outbreak in Israel rather than a genuine inter-continental or subregional emergence.
Review: Review – Newly added event. The Israeli Dead Sea farm outbreak is well documented as the first recognized multi-species T. evansi outbreak in domestic animals in Israel, with high infection prevalence in camels, horses and donkeys.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20926194/?utm_source=openai)) It is coded as re-occurrence within Western Asia because T. evansi had already been reported in neighbouring Middle Eastern countries, so this is not an intra-/inter-continental emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma evansi
EPP.common.name: TEVA
Host: Dromedary camels; co-located sheep (ovine exposure, limited infection)
Event.summary: In July 2006, five camels were imported from the endemic Canary Islands to a mixed camel–sheep farm in Aveyron, southern France; by October one imported camel died with trypanosomes observed in blood smears, marking the first outbreak of Trypanosoma evansi in metropolitan France. Further testing revealed infection in five camels (both imported and locally born) and serological evidence of exposure in some neighboring sheep, indicating local mechanical transmission rather than mere importation. Infected camels were treated with melarsomine, and follow-up parasitological and serological monitoring over subsequent months showed clearance of detectable infection and no spread beyond the index farm.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Legal importation of camels from an endemic region (Canary Islands) into continental Europe without mandatory surra screening; abundant tabanid horseflies and stable flies (Stomoxys calcitrans) on the farm during summer facilitated mechanical transmission between camels and possibly sheep; lack of recognition of T. evansi as an EU trade-relevant pathogen at the time delayed specific preventive surveillance. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain was implicated; outbreak dynamics primarily reflect introduction of heavily infected camels from a nearby endemic focus (Canary Islands) and efficient vector-mediated spread in a naïve host population, i.e. geographic range expansion within Europe rather than parasite change.
Review: Review – Recommended to retain as a key intra-continental emergence event (first autochthonous outbreak in Western Europe), but the emergence coding has been clarified: first_detection is now 'No' (global first detection occurred in the 19th century) while intra_continental_emergence remains 'Yes' for spread from the Southern European Canary Islands focus into Western Europe with local transmission. A duplicate ELISA follow-up article URL was removed, and an EFSA/WOAH risk assessment retained as a regional context source.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18540034/?utm_source=openai))
