EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera carambolae
EPP.common.name: carambola fruit fly
Host: Primarily carambola (Averrhoa carambola) and other tropical fruit trees including rose apple (Syzygium samarangense), guava (Psidium guajava) and mango (Mangifera indica) in backyard and orchard plantings
Event.summary: In 1994, Bactrocera carambolae was first reported causing serious damage to carambola and other fruit trees in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands of India, marking the species’ first confirmed occurrence in the Southern Asia subregion and leading to its designation as a quarantine pest for mainland India. During the late 1990s and 2000s, the fly became established across several islands, infesting backyard and commercial plantings of carambola, rose apple, guava and mango and prompting repeated warnings about the risk of spread to continental India via passenger baggage and unregulated fruit trade. Up to at least the mid‑2020s, B. carambolae remains confined to the Andaman–Nicobar archipelago but is subject to ongoing surveillance and phytosanitary risk assessments aimed at preventing its escape to the Indian mainland and beyond.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction is attributed to the movement of infested fruits or planting material from Southeast Asian source areas to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands via shipping and air travel, combined with limited quarantine controls between the islands and mainland India; continued human transport of fresh fruit within the archipelago maintains a high risk of local spread. Internal mechanisms: the fly’s polyphagy on common tropical fruit hosts, high reproductive potential and good adult dispersal, together with the warm, humid island climate, favour persistent high‑density populations once established.
Review: review – added new intra‑continental emergence event for India [1994] (Andaman and Nicobar Islands), reflecting the first confirmed occurrence of Bactrocera carambolae in the Southern Asia subregion and its recognition as a serious pest and quarantine threat for mainland India; timing, location and host range are based on Indian fruit‑fly catalogues, regional pest accounts and EPPO distribution data. Emergence‑type coding has been set to 'intra_continental_emergence = Yes' and other types 'No' to reflect expansion from the species’ native South‑East Asian range into a new Asian UNSD subregion. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/241723285_Catalogue_of_Indian_fruit_flies_Diptera_Tephritidae?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera carambolae
EPP.common.name: carambola fruit fly
Host: A wide range of tropical fruits including carambola, guava, citrus, mango and other commercial and backyard fruit species
Event.summary: In March 1996, Bactrocera carambolae was first detected in Brazil at Oiapoque in the state of Amapá on the border with French Guiana, representing the pest’s entry into one of South America’s largest fruit‑producing countries and triggering the establishment of a national eradication and containment programme. Over subsequent years, despite continuous trapping and control, the fly established and spread within northern Amapá and later into Roraima and northern Pará, maintaining localized populations that periodically reached high densities in host fruits and posed a persistent threat of southward spread into major commercial fruit regions, prompting the maintenance of around 10,000 Jackson and McPhail traps and intensive male‑annihilation, bait spraying and fruit‑destruction measures. Up to at least the mid‑2020s, B. carambolae remains confined to northern Brazil but not eradicated, and the Brazil MAPA sub‑programme continues long‑term containment and suppression operations to protect national fruit production and export markets.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Initial introduction is attributed to small‑scale trade and passenger movement of infested fruits from Southeast Asia via already infested Suriname and French Guiana, combined with porous land borders and high local fruit availability in northern Brazil; continued risk of spread is linked to movement of fruits along road and river corridors, as well as climatic suitability of much of Brazil for establishment. Internal mechanisms: High polyphagy, strong dispersal and reproductive capacity, and climatic tolerance to humid tropical conditions underpin successful establishment and range expansion in Amapá, Roraima and northern Pará; ecological niche modelling indicates large areas of Brazil are inherently suitable for the species’ survival and further expansion in the absence of intensive control.
Review: retain – event provides an integrated account of Brazil’s long‑running eradication and containment programme from the first detection at Oiapoque (Amapá) in 1996 through continuing restricted distribution in Amapá, Roraima and parts of Pará, consistent with EPPO, MAPA and recent ecological studies; the statement that B. carambolae remains confined to northern Brazil is still valid even though quarantine areas now also include several municipalities in Amazonas. No changes were made to dates, geography or emergence‑type flags. ([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/BCTRCB/distribution/BR?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera carambolae
EPP.common.name: carambola fruit fly
Countries: Brazil [2014] (Pará – Marajó Archipelago: Portel, Curralinho, Gurupá, Breves)
Host: Backyard and commercial plantings of guava (Psidium guajava), carambola (Averrhoa carambola), acerola/West Indian cherry (Malpighia emarginata), mango (Mangifera indica) and other tropical fruits in riverine communities of the Marajó Archipelago
Event.summary: In early 2014, Bactrocera carambolae was detected for the first time in the municipalities of Portel and Curralinho in the Marajó Archipelago of Pará state, Brazil, more than 500 km south of the long‑standing infested focus in Amapá, signalling a serious jump in the pest’s range along Amazon river transport routes. Over 2014–2015, intensive delimiting trapping documented hundreds of adult flies in several Marajó municipalities, and federal and state authorities implemented an emergency eradication programme combining male‑annihilation technique, protein‑bait sprays, host‑fruit collection and destruction, quarantine restrictions on fruit movement and extensive public awareness campaigns. By 2015–2017, trap catches had fallen to zero and subsequent surveys supported formal declaration of eradication of B. carambolae from the affected areas of Pará, although phytosanitary education and surveillance along river routes from Amapá continue to prevent re‑infestation.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The Marajó outbreak is attributed to the movement of infested fruit and river‑borne trade from infested areas of Amapá into the lower Amazon region, facilitated by intense boat traffic and consumption of fresh fruit during river journeys; socio‑economic reliance on informal fruit markets complicated early containment. Internal mechanisms: the fly’s ability to exploit a wide range of common backyard hosts, high reproductive rate and suitable humid tropical conditions in the archipelago favoured rapid build‑up of populations once introduced, while its strong response to methyl eugenol lures allowed effective trapping as part of the eradication campaign.
Review: review – new event added to represent the major 2014–2017 outbreak and subsequent eradication of Bactrocera carambolae in the Marajó Archipelago of Pará, Brazil, which involved large trap catches, intensive area‑wide control measures and formal declaration of eradication; this episode is epidemiologically linked to but spatially distinct from the long‑standing focus in Amapá and is therefore treated as a separate high‑impact event. Emergence‑type flags remain 'No' because the pest was already established in the South America subregion and this represents a range jump and local outbreak rather than first introduction or re‑emergence after regional disappearance. ([taylorfrancis.com](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/oa-edit/10.1201/9780429355738-29/eradication-outbreak-bactrocera-carambolae-carambola-fruit-fly-marajo-archipelago-state-para-brazil-maria-julia-godoy-wilda-pinto-clara-brand%C3%A3o-cl%C3%B3vis-vasconcelos-jos%C3%A9-pires?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Countries: French Polynesia [1996] (initially Tahiti and nearby Society Islands; later Austral and Marquesas archipelagos)
Host: Mango, guava, carambola and many other tropical fruits in smallholder and backyard plantings across French Polynesia
Event.summary: In July 1996, Bactrocera dorsalis was first detected on Tahiti in French Polynesia, adding a fourth highly damaging invasive Bactrocera species to an already pest‑rich fruit fly fauna.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553587/?utm_source=openai)) Over the following decade it spread from the Society Islands to other archipelagos (including the Australs and, later, the Marquesas), rapidly becoming the dominant fruit fly and causing heavy infestations of mango, guava and other fruits.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553587/?utm_source=openai)) From 2002 onward, large‑scale classical biological control with the parasitoid Fopius arisanus and other measures substantially suppressed B. dorsalis populations and reduced damage, though the species remains established and under ongoing management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensifying air and sea links and movement of infested fruit between Pacific islands, probably from Hawaii, introduced B. dorsalis into Tahiti and then facilitated its spread to other archipelagos; limited pre‑existing surveillance in remote islands delayed detection beyond Tahiti.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4553587/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: High reproductive rate, strong flight capacity and broad host range allowed B. dorsalis to rapidly dominate island fruit fly communities where other polyphagous species were already present, leading to ecological displacement and severe farmer losses until successful parasitoid‑based biological control was deployed.
Review: Decision: retain. The French Polynesia invasion is well‑documented, clearly post‑1990, and among the more consequential island invasions (large geographic spread within the territory and major changes in fruit fly communities). Classification as intra‑continental emergence (Oceania already had B. dorsalis in Micronesia and Hawaii before 1996) with other emergence‑type flags set to No is appropriate. Minor edits were made to the countries field to align with the UNSD country list (using French Polynesia as the country and archipelagos as sub‑national detail) and to clarify the invasion timeline; sources remain appropriate and no major additional events in Polynesia warrant a separate row.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Countries: United States of America [2015] (Florida, Miami-Dade County – Redland agricultural area)
Host: Avocado, citrus, guava, mango, papaya, tropical vegetables and other hosts in the Redland production area and surrounding residential plantings
Event.summary: In late August 2015, oriental fruit fly adults were detected in traps in the Redland agricultural area of Miami‑Dade County, triggering declaration of a major OFF outbreak and the establishment of a federal quarantine of about 98.6 square miles.([content.govdelivery.com](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USDAAPHIS/bulletins/127b5f3?utm_source=openai)) By November 10, 2015, 157 adult flies and one larval infestation site had been confirmed, leading to intensive eradication measures including male annihilation, protein‑bait sprays, host removal and movement controls that significantly disrupted harvest and marketing of tropical fruits; affected producers later received more than US$1.6 million in compensation.([blogs.ifas.ufl.edu](https://blogs.ifas.ufl.edu/miamidadeco/2015/09/29/oriental-fruit-fly-quarantine-expanded-in-miami-dade-as-092815/?utm_source=openai)) After three fly‑free life cycles, APHIS and Florida authorities declared eradication and removed the quarantine on 13 February 2016, ending this re‑occurrence episode in a state that has seen multiple past OFF incursions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: One or more introductions of infested fruit or plant material from regions where B. dorsalis is established (Asia, Pacific or Africa), coupled with a highly suitable subtropical climate and dense plantings of preferred hosts in Miami‑Dade, enabled temporary establishment and rapid population increase.([ask.ifas.ufl.edu](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN240?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The fly’s inherent traits—high fecundity, broad host range and strong dispersal—allowed it to quickly reach outbreak densities once introduced, necessitating an intensive, area‑wide eradication response using attractant‑based trapping, sterile male releases and chemical and cultural control.
Review: Decision: retain. This Florida outbreak is one of the most impactful recent B. dorsalis incursions in North America, with a large quarantine area and documented economic compensation, and it fits the definition of a re‑occurrence (previous OFF incursions in Florida, no evidence of novel strain or host jump). Minor numerical details in the original summary (fly counts and quarantine size) were tightened using APHIS and NAPPO reports,([content.govdelivery.com](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USDAAPHIS/bulletins/127b5f3?utm_source=openai)) but the overall structure and emergence classification (re_occurrence = Yes; others No) are sound. No issues with country or sub‑region coding were found.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Countries: United States of America [2023] (California: Redlands area of San Bernardino and Riverside Counties; concurrent OFF quarantines in parts of Sacramento, Contra Costa and Santa Clara Counties)
Host: Citrus, avocado, grapes, stone fruits, figs, peppers, tomatoes and other fruit and vegetable hosts in commercial orchards and backyard trees within quarantined urban and peri‑urban areas of California
Event.summary: In 2023, California detected unusually large numbers of oriental fruit flies, with a particularly severe outbreak centred on Redlands in San Bernardino and Riverside Counties where an OFF quarantine established on 27 September 2023 was repeatedly expanded to cover about 553 square miles and roughly 6,500 acres of commercial production.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news/program-update/aphis-expands-oriental-fruit-fly-quarantine-san-bernardino-riverside-counties?utm_source=openai)) At the same time, additional OFF quarantines were declared in portions of Sacramento, Contra Costa and Santa Clara Counties, leading state authorities to describe the situation as the largest fruit fly infestation in California’s history and prompting substantial federal emergency funding.([universityofcalifornia.edu](https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/one-worlds-worst-pests-attacks-california?utm_source=openai)) Through 2024, APHIS and CDFA implemented intensive trapping, male‑annihilation, bait sprays and public outreach; by mid‑2024 the Sacramento and Santa Clara quarantines had been lifted following eradication, while work continued in remaining regulated areas as part of an expanded, statewide exotic fruit fly response.([wga.com](https://www.wga.com/news/cdfa-lifts-oriental-fruit-fly-quarantine-in-sacramento-county/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A combination of increased volumes of imported and passenger‑carried fresh produce, frequent movement of home‑grown fruit within California, and warm conditions conducive to overwintering contributed to multiple introductions and unusually sustained OFF populations in 2023–2024.([ask.ifas.ufl.edu](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN240?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The species’ high fecundity, multivoltine life cycle and ability to exploit a wide host range in suburban and commercial plantings allowed rapid population build‑up once introduced, so that several separate but temporally overlapping outbreaks required large, coordinated state‑ and federal‑level eradication campaigns; these characteristics underpin classification as a major re‑occurrence rather than a new intra‑continental emergence.
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). This large, multi‑county California outbreak was absent from the original dataset but clearly meets the criteria for a top‑impact emergence event: extensive quarantined area (hundreds of square miles), multiple commercial cropping systems affected, and substantial emergency funding and regulatory impact.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news/program-update/aphis-expands-oriental-fruit-fly-quarantine-san-bernardino-riverside-counties?utm_source=openai)) It is coded as a re‑occurrence because California has experienced repeated OFF incursions since the 1960s, with no evidence that the 2023–2024 episode involved a fundamentally new strain or host jump. The countries, sub‑region and dates were cross‑checked against APHIS and CDFA reports; future expert review may wish to decide whether to split Redlands and the northern California quarantines into separate rows, but they are treated here as a single temporally linked episode for parsimony.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cenchrus spinifex
EPP.common.name: field sandbur, coast sandspur, sandbur, southern sandbur, spiny burrgrass
Countries: China [2008] (Inner Mongolia – Tongliao and Chifeng in Horqin Sandy Land; neighboring parts of Liaoning and Jilin provinces)
Host: Natural and semi-natural sandy grasslands and pastures of the Horqin Sandy Land and surrounding rangelands; field margins, roadsides and disturbed sandy sites; dryland crops such as maize, sorghum, soybean and other field crops in infested zones; indirect impacts on grazing livestock via reduced forage quality and injurious burrs.
Event.summary: Cenchrus spinifex (少花蒺藜草, treated historically as C. pauciflorus/C. incertus) was first recorded in Horqin district of northern China in 1983 and was recognized as a harmful weed in Liaoning by the mid‑1990s, but from 2008 onward systematic surveys in Tongliao and adjacent parts of Inner Mongolia documented a rapid increase in its abundance and area.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10618509/?utm_source=openai)) Between 2008 and 2017 fixed monitoring plots showed steadily rising cover and seed bank densities, and by 2016 the Tongliao region accounted for nearly 80% of the national area infested, with large monodominant stands in Horqin sandy grassland and extensive occurrence along roadsides, crop fields and village margins.([journal30.magtechjournal.com](https://journal30.magtechjournal.com/bfnyxb/CN/10.3969/j.issn.2096-1197.2018.05.17)) Provincial early‑warning and control programs (manual removal, herbicides and monitoring) were launched in Liaoning and Inner Mongolia, but the species remained widely established by the late 2010s and continues to spread within northeastern China.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The invasion in Horqin and surrounding areas has been promoted by extensive overgrazing, cultivation and other land‑use changes that leave large areas of bare, sandy soil, together with road construction and transport of soil, fodder and contaminated seed that facilitate long‑distance dispersal of burrs.([cjae.net](https://www.cjae.net/CN/10.13287/j.1001-9332.201705.040)) Semi‑arid temperate monsoon climate with variable rainfall favors opportunistic establishment in degraded grasslands. Internal mechanisms: C. spinifex produces large numbers of barbed burrs, forms a persistent soil seed bank with heteromorphic seeds differing in dormancy and germination, tolerates drought and low fertility, and strongly alters soil nitrogen pools and microbial communities in invaded sandy grasslands, enabling formation of pure stands and competitive exclusion of native forage species.([cjae.net](https://www.cjae.net/CN/10.13287/j.1001-9332.201705.040))
Review: review – Retain this as a major post‑1990 event capturing the rapid expansion and dominance of C. spinifex in Horqin and northeastern China, but reclassify it from inter‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence because the species was first found in Horqin in 1983 and documented as harmful in Liaoning by 1995 (pre‑1990 for first emergence on the continent).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10618509/?utm_source=openai)) Geography (Asia, Eastern Asia, China) and host description are appropriate, and sources are relevant Chinese scientific and government reports; dates remain approximate and should be checked against additional Chinese floristic records.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Choristoneura rosaceana
EPP.common.name: oblique banded leafroller
Host: Apples (Malus domestica) and pears (Pyrus communis) in commercial orchards
Event.summary: From about 1993, populations of Choristoneura rosaceana in southern Ontario apple and pear orchards began showing frequent control failures with standard organophosphate programs, prompting targeted resistance surveys. Over the mid‑ to late‑1990s, laboratory and field assays demonstrated widespread organophosphate resistance and cross‑resistance to other insecticides across multiple Ontario production areas, and growers reported persistent leafroller damage despite repeated sprays. By the end of the decade, management programs were being redesigned around resistance‑management principles, alternative chemistries, and integrated pest management to restore control and reduce selection pressure on resistant populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-term intensive use of organophosphate insecticides in apple and pear orchards, limited rotation of modes of action, and reliance on calendar sprays created strong selection pressure for resistant C. rosaceana populations; high host availability in large contiguous orchard landscapes facilitated persistence of resistant genotypes. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – biochemical and physiological mechanisms of resistance to organophosphorus insecticides were documented in field populations from southern Ontario, with associated cross‑resistance to some other products; increased virulence is not implicated, but resistance increased effective pest pressure by undermining previously effective control programs.
Review: Retain: Well documented, large-scale resistance-driven re-emergence affecting major southern Ontario apple and pear regions in the 1990s; geography, timing, host range, and classification as re-emergence (via insecticide resistance) are appropriate. No corrections required, but timing remains approximate to the main survey years.

EPP.scientific.name: Choristoneura rosaceana
EPP.common.name: oblique banded leafroller
Countries: United States of America [2000] (Washington – Columbia Basin, Wenatchee Valley, Yakima and Snake River areas; Oregon [early 2000s] – Milton-Freewater apple region)
Host: Apples (Malus domestica) in commercial orchards
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, Washington State and adjacent Oregon apple orchards experienced persistent oblique banded leafroller infestations despite standard insecticide programs, raising concern about emerging resistance. Field collections from numerous orchards across central Washington and nearby Oregon revealed markedly reduced susceptibility to several commonly used insecticides and documented resistance and cross‑resistance patterns across the region, confirming that resistant populations had spread in key production zones. By around 2006, regional management recommendations shifted toward rotation of chemistries, incorporation of mating disruption, and broader IPM tactics to mitigate resistance and restore acceptable control levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Decades of intensive, often prophylactic insecticide use against multiple apple pests, combined with large, high‑value orchards that favored repeated sprays, created strong regional selection for resistant C. rosaceana; coordinated area‑wide resistance management was initially limited, allowing resistant populations to persist and spread locally. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – documented resistance and cross‑resistance in obliquebanded leafroller populations to organophosphates and other insecticides in Washington apples; although transmission biology was unchanged, resistant populations had higher survival under spray regimes, effectively increasing pest pressure and damage potential.
Review: Retain: Supported by detailed resistance studies and regional extension reports showing widespread control failures and cross-resistance in Washington and adjacent Oregon orchards in the early 2000s. Geography, timing and classification as re-emergence driven by insecticide resistance are appropriate; no corrections made, but exact end year (2006) remains an informed approximation based on study and recommendation timelines.

EPP.scientific.name: Choristoneura rosaceana
EPP.common.name: oblique banded leafroller
Continent: South America (including Central America and the Caribbean)
Host: Wild and cultivated rosaceous and broadleaf hosts (including wild apples and ornamental/broadleaf trees)
Event.summary: Around 2004, a comprehensive survey of Lepidoptera on the Baja California peninsula documented Choristoneura rosaceana in northern Mexico, representing the first confirmed records of the species in the country and extending its known range southward from the USA. During this period the moth was detected on native and cultivated hosts in lowland habitats, indicating that viable populations were established beyond the previously recognized US–Canada range. The species has since been considered part of the native North American fauna extending into northern Mexico, with phytosanitary concern focused on preventing further movement into new continents or regions via plants for planting.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely gradual natural range extension and/or previously undocumented occurrence associated with continuous temperate habitats from the south-western United States into northern Mexico; increased entomological sampling intensity and taxonomic work in Baja California enabled detection. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the species’ broad host range and adaptability to diverse temperate and semi‑arid habitats facilitate persistence in northern Mexico; no specific genetic novelty is documented, but inherent ecological flexibility supports southward range continuity.
Review: Review: This event correctly captures the first confirmed records of C. rosaceana in Mexico (Baja California) and the associated southward range extension from the USA, and it is reasonable to treat it as an inter-continental emergence under the project’s scheme because it represents establishment in the 'South America (including Central America and the Caribbean)' region. However, first_detection has been set to No, since global first detection in the plant host system occurred much earlier in Canada/USA; the original classification conflated first records for Mexico with global first detection. The country description was also refined to refer specifically to the Baja California peninsula. Recommended for expert review to confirm that, despite limited quantified damage data, this range-extension event merits inclusion among the main post-1990 emergence events for this species.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Choristoneura rosaceana
EPP.common.name: oblique banded leafroller
Continent: South America (including Central America and the Caribbean)
Host: Apples (Malus domestica) in commercial orchards
Event.summary: In 2011, Choristoneura rosaceana was reported for the first time as a pest of apples in the Ejido Vista Hermosa near Ciudad Cuauhtémoc, Chihuahua, marking its emergence as a new economic pest in northern Mexico’s highland apple belt. Surveys in infested orchards found larvae feeding in rolled leaves and on fruit clusters, with visible damage to developing apples, indicating that the moth had successfully colonized commercial apple production and could reach damaging densities under local conditions. Subsequent recommendations emphasized monitoring and adoption of management tactics based on experience from US and Canadian orchards to prevent the pest from becoming a chronic, high‑impact problem in Mexican apple regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive apple production in northern Mexico, movement of infested planting material or host plants from already infested North American regions, and relatively limited prior monitoring for this specific tortricid likely facilitated unnoticed establishment in Chihuahua orchards. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) – although the moth already attacked apples elsewhere in North America, this event represents its establishment as an apple pest in a new production region; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – natural or human‑assisted spread from existing populations in northern Mexico or the south-western USA into the Chihuahua highlands contributed to this emergence.
Review: Retain: Accurately reflects the first report of C. rosaceana damaging apples in the Ciudad Cuauhtémoc region of Chihuahua and its emergence as a new economic pest in Mexico’s main apple-growing state. Classification as re-emergence (host expansion and range consolidation within an already infested subregion) is consistent with prior records from northern Mexico; geographic and temporal details match the primary source, so no corrections are proposed.

EPP.scientific.name: Coccus pseudomagnoliarum
EPP.common.name: citricola scale
Countries: Cyprus [2005] (Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus citrus-growing areas)
Host: Citrus spp. (commercial citrus orchards and associated host plants in Northern Cyprus).
Event.summary: Between 2005 and 2007, a survey of scale insects in cultivated and non‑cultivated areas of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus recorded Coccus pseudomagnoliarum for the first time as part of the island’s Coccoidea fauna. During the survey, citricola scale was found on citrus and other host plants, and its presence was significant enough that the authors listed it among new country records and noted post‑harvest increases in populations alongside other soft scales. By the end of the survey period, citricola scale had become established in Northern Cyprus citrus ecosystems, although it was not yet highlighted as the dominant citrus pest due to the presence of other major scale species and their natural enemies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely drivers include regional trade and movement of infested citrus nursery stock or plant material between Türkiye and Northern Cyprus, which share close economic and logistical links in the eastern Mediterranean. Climatic suitability of coastal Northern Cyprus for subtropical soft scales and increasing intensity of citrus cultivation provided favorable conditions for establishment following introduction. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype or resistance mechanism was described for the Northern Cyprus populations; the event is best interpreted as geographic spread and re-occurrence of an already widespread Mediterranean/West Asian pest in a new territory within the same subregion.
Review: Review – Event is a valid new-country record for C. pseudomagnoliarum in Northern Cyprus based on 2005–2007 surveys, but the emergence type has been corrected. Because the species had been established in the Western Asia subregion (e.g. Türkiye, Israel) for decades, this occurrence represents spread within an already affected subregion rather than a host-system-level first detection. 'first_detection' has therefore been set to false and 're_occurrence' set to true. Geographic assignment (Asia | Western Asia; country = Cyprus with specification of Northern Cyprus citrus areas) and timing (2005–2007 survey window) are retained. Impact appears limited (low densities, not a dominant citrus pest), so this event may be deprioritized if later evidence identifies additional, more damaging post‑1990 events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Coccus pseudomagnoliarum
EPP.common.name: citricola scale
Countries: Spain [2006] (Comunidad Valenciana: interior citrus-growing districts around Serra and other inland Valencia province orchards)
Host: Citrus spp. (mainly sweet orange and other commercial citrus varieties in interior Valencia citrus orchards).
Event.summary: In 2006, the regional citrus phytosanitary surveillance program of the Comunidad Valenciana (Spain) detected Coccus pseudomagnoliarum for the first time in a citrus plot near Serra (Valencia), an area where this soft scale had not previously been recorded. Follow-up surveys during 2006–2008 showed that citricola scale was already widely distributed in many interior citrus-growing districts of Valencia province, although typically at moderate densities that rarely reached severe pest status. The species was therefore recognized as a 'new pest' in Valencian citrus, prompting detailed studies of its parasitoid complex and management, and its presence has since been incorporated into Mediterranean citrus IPM programs even though it remains generally less damaging than other key citrus pests in Spain.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction is most plausibly linked to movement of infested citrus plant material or propagative stock within the Mediterranean citrus trade, from regions such as Italy, Greece or California where the pest was already established, into the interior citrus districts of Valencia. The large area under citrus, relatively warm inland climate, and reduced use of broad-spectrum insecticides under Spanish citrus IPM programs created conditions that allowed citricola scale to establish and spread undetected for several years before formal detection. Internal mechanisms: No evidence has been presented for novel strains, resistance traits, or host shifts specific to Spanish populations; the event is best interpreted as geographic spread and re-occurrence within the already affected Southern Europe subregion.
Review: Retain – New event added to capture the introduction and spread of C. pseudomagnoliarum in the Valencian citrus industry, first detected in 2006 by the regional citrus surveillance program and subsequently found widely distributed in interior Valencia orchards. Classified as re-occurrence because the species had long been established in the Southern Europe subregion (Italy, Greece, Turkey), so this is spread to a new country within an existing subregion rather than intra- or inter-continental emergence or a global first detection. Sources consistently describe substantial concern, extensive monitoring and biological-control work but generally low–moderate infestation levels; given the importance of Valencia as a major citrus-producing area, this is considered one of the key post‑1990 emergence events.

EPP.scientific.name: Coccus pseudomagnoliarum
EPP.common.name: citricola scale
Countries: Tunisia [2008] (Cap Bon citrus region and later other northern citrus-growing areas including Nabeul, Béja, Jendouba and Zaghouan districts)
Host: Citrus spp. (oranges, mandarins, lemons and other commercial citrus in Cap Bon and north-eastern Tunisian orchards).
Event.summary: During surveys of citrus orchards in the Cap Bon region of Tunisia reported in 2008, Coccus pseudomagnoliarum was recorded for the first time as part of the Tunisian Coccoidea fauna, representing a new country record and, based on available literature, the first confirmed occurrence of this species in Africa. Subsequent faunistic work and national-scale surveys up to about 2011 documented citricola scale on citrus in additional northern Tunisian citrus regions, typically at low densities and in association with other scale insects such as Aonidiella aurantii and Saissetia oleae. Although citricola scale has not yet been identified as a major cause of yield loss in Tunisia, its establishment signifies an expansion of the pest’s range into North African citrus ecosystems, where it now forms part of a diverse alien scale insect complex.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The most likely pathway is trade and movement of infested citrus plant material (nursery stock, budwood or ornamental hosts) from Mediterranean countries where C. pseudomagnoliarum was already present (e.g. Italy, Greece, Spain, Turkey) into Tunisian citrus regions. Climatic similarity between Cap Bon and other Mediterranean citrus zones, combined with high citrus planting density and historical under-appreciation of soft scale diversity, facilitated establishment and spread before detection. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of novel strains, host shifts or resistance traits associated specifically with Tunisian populations; the event is best interpreted as inter-continental emergence due to geographic range expansion into Africa without documented intrinsic changes in the pest.
Review: Retain – New event added and classified as an inter-continental emergence, representing the first confirmed establishment of C. pseudomagnoliarum in Africa (Tunisia). Jendoubi et al. (2008) and later surveys document the species as a new record in Cap Bon citrus orchards and subsequently in other northern regions, with faunistic overviews confirming its inclusion among Tunisian citrus scale insects. Although current impact appears modest (low relative abundance and no major yield losses reported), the crossing into a new continent and a significant citrus-producing country warrants treating this as one of the major post‑1990 emergence events.

EPP.scientific.name: Coccus pseudomagnoliarum
EPP.common.name: citricola scale
Countries: Syrian Arab Republic [2010] (Lattakia Governorate: Al-Ramma, Ein Al-Arus, Hmaimim, Albassa and nearby untreated citrus orchards)
Host: Citrus spp. in untreated citrus orchards of Lattakia Governorate.
Event.summary: Around 2010, Coccus pseudomagnoliarum was reported as 'recently found' in Syria and recognized as a potential insect pest of citrus, with surveys in 2010–2011 documenting its presence on citrus trees in several districts of Lattakia Governorate. In untreated orchards, citricola scale caused economic damage primarily through heavy honeydew excretion and subsequent development of black sooty mold on leaves and fruit, reducing photosynthesis and marketability. During this period, researchers also characterized a diverse complex of parasitoids and predators associated with the scale, reflecting growing concern about its status in Syrian citrus production and the need for integrated management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction into Syrian citrus is most plausibly linked to regional movement of infested citrus planting material or fruit from neighboring Eastern Mediterranean countries (e.g. Türkiye, Lebanon) where C. pseudomagnoliarum was already present, coupled with favorable coastal climate and limited prior exposure of local natural enemy complexes to this specific pest. Economic and logistical constraints on pesticide use in some orchards may also have facilitated local population build-up. Internal mechanisms: Published studies emphasize phenology and natural enemies rather than intrinsic changes in the pest; there is no current evidence that Syrian populations possess unique resistance traits or host shifts, so the event is interpreted as re-occurrence and spread within the existing Western Asia subregion.
Review: Retain – New event added to describe the recent establishment and local build‑up of C. pseudomagnoliarum on citrus in Lattakia, Syria (2010–2011), which surveys characterize as a recently found pest causing economic damage via honeydew and sooty mold. Because the species had long been present in other Western Asia citrus regions (e.g. Türkiye, Israel), this is classified as re-occurrence (spread and resurgence within the same subregion) rather than inter- or intra-continental emergence or a global first detection. The event has moderate economic significance and substantial biological-control interest, justifying its inclusion among the limited number of post‑1990 emergence events for this pest.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinochloa crus-galli
EPP.common.name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: United States of America [1990] (Arkansas rice-growing regions)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in flooded rice production systems
Event.summary: In 1990, propanil-resistant barnyardgrass (Echinochloa crus-galli) was first documented in Arkansas rice fields, following decades of intensive propanil use as the primary post-emergence grass herbicide, and resistant populations spread rapidly within major rice counties over the early 1990s, causing severe control failures and yield losses; the event stabilized only after growers began diversifying herbicide programs and integrating additional pre-emergence products and cultural tactics.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Heavy, recurrent use of propanil in monoculture rice with limited herbicide rotation; expansion of high-input flooded rice acreage; limited non-chemical weed management.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of propanil-resistant E. crus-galli biotypes under strong selection pressure; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – not vector-based, but agronomic practices (continuous rice, flooding) favored rapid population build-up and seedbank enrichment of resistant plants.
Review: retain - This row correctly describes the first confirmation and rapid spread of propanil-resistant barnyardgrass in Arkansas rice, a globally important emergence event. I left the temporal and geographic framing unchanged but replaced the generic Wikipedia source with primary literature documenting 1990 confirmation and statewide spread (Carey et al. 1995; subsequent mechanism work). Classification as re-emergence only (no intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because the species was already long established in North America.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinochloa crus-galli
EPP.common.name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: United States of America [1998] (quinclorac-resistant barnyardgrass first confirmed in Louisiana; multiple resistance to propanil and quinclorac confirmed in Arkansas [1999] with spread to additional southern rice-producing states by the early 2000s)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in flooded and semi-flooded systems
Event.summary: In 1998 quinclorac-resistant E. crus-galli was documented in Louisiana rice fields, and by 1999 Arkansas confirmed barnyardgrass biotypes with resistance to both propanil and quinclorac, marking the first major multiple-herbicide-resistant grass problem in U.S. rice; resistant populations spread across additional rice-growing states by the early 2000s, undermining the two main post-emergence herbicides and forcing costly, complex control programs; the episode has persisted with chronic management difficulties, though diversified herbicide mixtures and rotation have partially contained further spread.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Sequential and frequent use of propanil and quinclorac in the same rice fields; limited crop rotation; economic pressure to rely on chemical control.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – independent evolution and subsequent spread of quinclorac resistance, followed by multiple resistance to both propanil and quinclorac in some biotypes; Enhanced Transmission – prolific seed production and dispersal via machinery and irrigation water facilitated rapid regional spread of resistant populations.
Review: review - Retain as a major event, but I broadened the time window to 1998–2003 to cover confirmation and early spread of quinclorac and multiple resistance, and simplified the country field to avoid unsupported state-level dating for Texas and Missouri. Louisiana 1998 quinclorac resistance and Arkansas 1999 propanil+quinclorac multiple resistance are well documented by weedscience.org and Weed Technology articles. The original use of the intra-continental emergence flag was incorrect for a resistance trait and has been set to re-emergence only, in line with the definitions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinochloa crus-galli
EPP.common.name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: Italy [2000] (Po Valley rice-growing regions, especially Lombardy and Piedmont)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in flooded and water‑seeded rice systems
Event.summary: From about 2000 onwards, northern Italian rice growers in the Po Valley began reporting barnyardgrass escapes after treatments with propanil and newer ALS‑inhibiting herbicides, and surveys over the 2000s confirmed multiple E. crus-galli populations with high resistance to azimsulfuron, imazamox, penoxsulam and other ALS inhibitors, with several populations also showing cross‑resistance to the ACCase inhibitor profoxydim; by roughly 2011, ALS and ALS+ACCase multiple-resistant barnyardgrass had become widespread in Italian rice fields, seriously reducing the effectiveness of the main post‑emergence herbicides and prompting recommendations for integrated weed management and rotation of herbicide modes of action.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Long‑term reliance on a narrow suite of ALS‑ and ACCase‑inhibiting herbicides in intensive rice monoculture in the Po Valley; limited crop rotation and non‑chemical weed control.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – target‑site ALS mutations (e.g. Trp574Leu and other substitutions) and, in some populations, ACCase target‑site changes conferring high‑level cross‑resistance to multiple ALS chemistries and low‑ to moderate‑level resistance to profoxydim; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – resistant genotypes becoming dominant within Italian rice agroecosystems and replacing susceptible barnyardgrass populations.
Review: retain - New row added: multi‑herbicide‑resistant barnyardgrass in Italian rice (ALS and ACCase resistance) is clearly one of the globally important emergence episodes, with numerous resistant populations across the main Po Valley rice area and documented cross‑ and multiple resistance patterns. Dates and modes of action are aligned with the Italian cases in the International Herbicide-Resistant Weed Database and detailed ALS/ACCase target‑site studies; the event is classified purely as re‑emergence (evolution of resistant biotypes) rather than spatial emergence of the species.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinochloa crus-galli
EPP.common.name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: United States of America [2000] (especially Arkansas rice region, with spread to neighboring rice-producing states)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in flooded and furrow-irrigated systems
Event.summary: From the early 2000s through the 2020s, Arkansas and neighboring U.S. rice states experienced a sustained escalation of herbicide-resistant barnyardgrass problems, with populations evolving resistance to ALS inhibitors, ACCase inhibitors, propanil, quinclorac, clomazone and newer auxin herbicides, leading to complex multi-resistant biotypes that became the most troublesome weed in Arkansas rice and significantly increased weed management costs; surveys in the 2010s and early 2020s documented widespread producer concern, higher herbicide inputs and greater reliance on integrated management, while new herbicides such as tetflupyrolimet were explicitly developed and tested to help manage these resistant populations.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Long-term reliance on a narrow set of herbicide modes of action in rice; development of furrow‑irrigated and high-yield rice systems favoring barnyardgrass; limited adoption initially of non-chemical weed control; economic pressure to maintain high yields.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – sequential evolution and stacking of resistance to multiple herbicide classes (ALS, ACCase, synthetic auxins, propanil, others) in E. crus-galli; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity (operational) – resistant biotypes able to survive most standard programs and cause higher competitive yield loss; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – spread of multi-resistant genotypes across much of the Arkansas rice area and into neighboring states.
Review: review - This event is retained as a major, long‑running episode describing the accumulation of multiple resistance mechanisms in U.S. rice barnyardgrass. I corrected the emergence-type flags by removing intra-continental emergence and re-occurrence so that the event is classified solely as re‑emergence (sequential evolution of new resistance traits in an already widespread weed), consistent with the definitions. The time window and narrative match survey and research data on multi-resistant barnyardgrass in Arkansas rice.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinochloa crus-galli
EPP.common.name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: Brazil [2003] (especially Rio Grande do Sul and other southern rice regions)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa), mainly direct-seeded irrigated rice with Clearfield (imidazolinone-tolerant) cultivars
Event.summary: During the 2000s, the rapid adoption of imidazolinone-tolerant (Clearfield-type) rice in southern Brazil led to intensive use of imidazolinone herbicides and selection of E. crus-galli populations with resistance to imidazolinones and often quinclorac, with surveys by 2009–2012 estimating that a very high proportion of barnyardgrass accessions in some rice areas carried imidazolinone resistance and caused major yield and quality losses; by the early 2010s this resistance had spread across much of the southern rice belt, and integrated programs combining clomazone and alternative post-emergence herbicides plus crop rotation were promoted to curb further expansion.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Large-scale deployment of imidazolinone-resistant rice technology; repeated, often exclusive use of imidazolinone herbicides in direct-seeded rice; economic incentives for simplified chemical-based weed management.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – ALS target-site mutations and non–target-site enhanced metabolism conferring resistance to imidazolinones and in some populations to quinclorac; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – resistant genotypes became dominant within rice agroecosystems throughout southern Brazil, replacing susceptible barnyardgrass populations.
Review: retain - This Clearfield-based Brazilian episode is a high-impact, multi‑resistance event in a million‑hectare rice region and should clearly remain among the top 10. I only standardised the emergence classification to re‑emergence (evolution of imidazolinone and quinclorac resistance) and tightened the country/year wording to reflect introduction of Clearfield rice in 2003 and high resistance frequencies by 2009–2012, as reported in Brazilian surveys.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinochloa crus-galli
EPP.common.name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: Republic of Korea [2008] (direct-seeded rice areas in Taean, Gimje and other mid-west regions)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in direct-seeded and puddled rice systems
Event.summary: Around 2008, South Korean rice farmers began to experience frequent failures of ALS- and ACCase-inhibiting herbicides on barnyardgrass, and resistance surveys conducted in 2012 across 155 E. crus-galli var. crus-galli accessions from Taean, Gimje and other mid-west rice areas showed that 42 accessions were resistant to at least one ALS or ACCase inhibitor and 10 accessions carried multiple resistance to both modes of action; these multi-resistant populations, recorded in the International Herbicide-Resistant Weed Database as the first multiple-resistant barnyardgrass in Korea, rapidly reduced the efficacy of the dominant post-emergence herbicides and forced adoption of more complex mixtures, rotation of modes of action and integrated management in Korean rice systems.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Long-term, repeated use of ALS- and ACCase-inhibiting herbicides in direct-seeded rice with limited rotation of chemistries; high selection pressure from simplified weed-control programs.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – cross- and multiple resistance to several sulfonylurea and imidazolinone ALS inhibitors and to ACCase inhibitors such as cyhalofop-butyl, fenoxaprop-ethyl and metamifop, associated with target-site changes and likely enhanced metabolism; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – resistant biotypes detected across multiple key rice districts in mid-western Korea.
Review: retain - New row added: multiple resistance to ALS and ACCase herbicides in South Korean barnyardgrass is a major, well-documented episode (42 of 155 accessions resistant and 10 showing multiple resistance in nationwide surveys) and is clearly among the top global emergence events for this weed. The event is classified as re‑emergence of resistant biotypes; continent and subregion fields follow UN definitions (Asia/Eastern Asia).

EPP.scientific.name: Echinochloa crus-galli
EPP.common.name: cockspur, Japanese millet, watergrass, barnyardgrass, barnyard grass, large barnyard grass
Countries: Uruguay [2013] (major irrigated rice regions in eastern and northern Uruguay)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in direct dry-seeded rice systems
Event.summary: From about 2013 onward, Uruguayan rice growers began to experience recurrent barnyardgrass control failures, and more than 40 E. crus-galli biotypes collected between roughly 2013 and 2015 from rice regions across the country were later shown to include numerous populations resistant to quinclorac, imazapyr + imazapic, penoxsulam and, in some cases, propanil; the 2019 national report confirmed herbicide-resistant barnyardgrass for the first time in Uruguay and highlighted that quinclorac-resistant biotypes were widespread across rice areas, reducing herbicide options and prompting calls to redesign production systems around more diverse cultural and chemical weed management.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Long-standing reliance on a small set of herbicides (especially quinclorac and imidazolinone mixtures) for barnyardgrass control in direct dry-seeded rice; limited adoption of non-chemical weed control at landscape scale; regional spread risk from neighboring resistance hotspots in South America.
Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of barnyardgrass biotypes with resistance to quinclorac, imazapyr + imazapic, penoxsulam and sometimes propanil, with several biotypes showing multiple resistance; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – establishment and early spread of resistant E. crus-galli biotypes throughout Uruguay’s rice agroecosystems.
Review: retain - Uruguay’s first confirmation of herbicide-resistant barnyardgrass involved multiple modes of action and biotypes distributed across essentially all national rice regions, threatening a major export crop. I corrected the event start year to 2013 (in line with weedscience.org entries for quinclorac and imazapic/imazapyr resistance) and reclassified it as re‑emergence (new resistant biotypes of a long-established weed) rather than first detection or intra-continental emergence. Given the national scale and multiple resistance, I recommend retaining this as one of the top 10 events.

EPP.scientific.name: Eriosoma lanigerum
EPP.common.name: woolly apple aphid
Host: Malus domestica (apple)
Event.summary: In 2019, a targeted survey of apple orchards at Fushoushan farm in central Taiwan detected woolly apple aphid for the first time in the country, representing a new incursion into Taiwanese pome‑fruit production. The survey examined 12,082 apple trees between June 24 and July 5, 2019, finding 2,531 trees colonized by WAA, an orchard-level infestation rate of about 21%, with colonies showing an aggregated spatial pattern concentrated in higher‑elevation blocks. Following this discovery, researchers modelled the potential suitable distribution of the pest across Taiwan’s highland apple areas and recommended urgent control measures at Fushoushan plus intensified surveillance in nearby mountain farming zones to prevent further spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via movement of infested plant material or nursery stock into Taiwan’s high-elevation apple orchards, combined with climatic suitability of cool mountainous areas; the pest was treated as a quarantine organism due to its absence from Taiwan prior to this detection. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – intrinsic capacity of WAA to colonize new apple-growing regions with climates similar to existing infested areas; no evidence yet for novel strain, host expansion beyond apple, or changed virulence, so emergence is best interpreted as range expansion rather than genetic innovation.
Review: retain – The 2019 Fushoushan farm survey is clearly documented as the first record of woolly apple aphid in Taiwan, with quantified infestation (about 21% of 12,082 trees) and spatial analyses. Continent and sub-region (Asia – Eastern Asia) and the use of “Taiwan [2019]” as the country are geographically correct. Because WAA was already established elsewhere in Eastern Asia (e.g. China, Japan), the event is rightly not coded as first/global emergence, first detection (global) or intra-/inter-continental emergence. No field values were changed.

EPP.scientific.name: Eriosoma lanigerum
EPP.common.name: woolly apple aphid
Countries: Belgium [2010] (Sint-Truiden region, representing Western European apple-growing areas with similar resurgence)
Host: Malus domestica (apple)
Event.summary: From roughly 2000 onwards, regulatory withdrawal and restricted use of broad-spectrum insecticides in European apple orchards, coupled with increased reliance on selective crop protection products and biological control, allowed woolly apple aphid populations to rebound in many Western European production regions. In Belgium’s Sint-Truiden apple belt, a decade of detailed field monitoring from 2010–2020 documented recurrent high WAA pressure on trees and roots, prompting development of a knowledge-based decision support system to time interventions while conserving the parasitoid Aphelinus mali. Similar experiences reported from other Western European apple-growing areas led to renewed focus on WAA monitoring, trunk-targeted spray technologies and organic-compatible tactics, indicating a sustained resurgence phase rather than isolated minor outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: European policy-driven withdrawal and restriction of organophosphate and other broad-spectrum insecticides, adoption of integrated and organic production schemes, and milder winters that improve overwinter survival of WAA colonies; orchard intensification in key apple belts such as Sint-Truiden. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation and Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) at orchard scale – dense wax-protected aerial colonies and hidden root colonies make WAA less susceptible to newer chemistries and allow rapid recolonization once broad-spectrum suppression is removed; no clearly documented novel biotype has been linked specifically to this Western European resurgence.
Review: review – New event added to capture the well-documented resurgence of woolly apple aphid as one of the most serious apple pests in Western Europe following withdrawal and restriction of broad-spectrum insecticides, with intensive monitoring in Belgian orchards during 2010–2020. Classified as re-occurrence in a previously infested sub-region because the increase is driven by changes in pesticide policy, production systems and climate, not by a clearly identified new WAA strain. Time window (2010–2020), continent/sub-region (Europe – Western Europe) and the use of Belgium as the focal country are well supported but should be checked by experts for potential refinement of the country list and exact outbreak period.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus
EPP.common.name: rice water weevil
Countries: China [1988] (first detected in Tanghai County, Hebei; by 2003 present in at least 11 provinces and the municipalities of Beijing and Tianjin)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) and wild Poaceae/Cyperaceae in and around irrigated rice fields
Event.summary: After first detection of Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus in Tanghai County, Hebei Province, China in 1988, parthenogenetic populations rapidly established in irrigated rice on the northeast coast. Through the 1990s and early 2000s the weevil expanded southwards and inland along irrigation networks and rice belts so that by late 2003 it infested more than 400,000 ha of rice across 11 provinces plus the municipalities of Beijing and Tianjin, with local yield losses of 10–80% in severely affected paddies. By the early 2000s the invasion front had approached climatic limits in northern and western China, and national surveillance, quarantine and integrated chemical and agronomic control programmes were intensified to manage this now widely established invasive pest.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement of infested rice seedlings, straw and other plant material; dense irrigated rice monocultures interconnected by canals and rivers; expansion of high-yielding rice production into suitable temperate areas; and incomplete quarantine enforcement facilitated spread from the initial coastal focus. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (invasive parthenogenetic California-derived lineage distinct from native bisexual U.S. populations), Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (strong flight and effective use of irrigation infrastructure for dispersal), and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent physiological tolerance allowing colonization of cooler, more northerly rice-growing zones within Eastern Asia).
Review: review – Retain this as one of the major post‑1990 emergence events because it represents the large invasive outbreak in mainland China, but corrected the emergence‑type classification: intra_continental_emergence is set to No (the spread occurred within the already infested Eastern Asia subregion, not into a new UN subregion) and re_emergence is kept as Yes to reflect a dramatic increase in incidence in an already affected subregion driven by the parthenogenetic invasive lineage. The description of invaded area and impact was aligned with Chen et al. 2005 and EPPO RS 2006/062 (≈11 provinces plus Beijing and Tianjin by 2003); a human review is recommended to confirm the choice of re_emergence (rather than re_occurrence) at subregional scale.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus
EPP.common.name: rice water weevil
Countries: Italy [2004] (initial foci in Lombardia, then spread across Piemonte; later new foci in Emilia-Romagna and Veneto)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) and associated wild grasses and sedges (Poaceae, Cyperaceae) in and around paddy fields
Event.summary: In 2004, parthenogenetic females of Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus were first detected in rice-growing areas of western Lombardia (Abbiategrasso and Vigevano) in Northern Italy, constituting the first record for both Italy and Europe. Over the following decade the pest invaded the entire rice-growing area of Piemonte and Lombardia and, by 2013–2014, new foci were discovered near Ferrara in Emilia-Romagna and near Verona in Veneto, several hundred kilometres from the original outbreak. By 2014 the weevil was firmly established across Northern Italy’s main rice belt, though reported economic losses remained generally localized and modest due to intensive monitoring and chemical and agronomic management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely transcontinental introduction via infested plant material or straw, probably from North America or already invaded parts of Asia, with the first established Italian foci occurring close to major trade and air-transport hubs in the Milan area; subsequent spread facilitated by the fragmented but extensive network of rice paddies and waterways, and by movement of rice straw, machinery and soil between farms. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence at continental scale (establishment of the invasive parthenogenetic lineage in Europe), Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (adult dispersal by flight and use of semi-aquatic habitats), and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent traits enabling survival and reproduction in temperate European rice agroecosystems).
Review: review – This event correctly represents the first introduction and spread of L. oryzophilus in Europe, but the emergence‑type flags have been adjusted: first_detection is set to No because the first description of the species as a rice pest dates to the 1880s in the United States, and re_emergence is set to No because this is a true first establishment event for Europe. Inter_continental_emergence remains Yes to capture the first occurrence on a new continent. EPPO RS 2005/005, RS 2015/073 and Lupi et al. 2015 support the timing, regional spread and generally modest economic impact; the row should be retained with these corrected classifications.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus
EPP.common.name: rice water weevil
Countries: France [2014] (initial finds in two rice plots in eastern France, later confirmed in Bouches-du-Rhône/Camargue and other Camargue rice areas)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in Camargue and other French rice-growing areas; associated wild grasses and sedges (Poaceae, Cyperaceae) in irrigation and field margins
Event.summary: In 2014, Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus was first notified from France when adults were detected in two rice plots in the eastern part of the country and soon after confirmed in the main Mediterranean rice area of Camargue (Bouches-du-Rhône), indicating a secondary introduction from already infested regions. Over the next several seasons the weevil spread through many Camargue paddies and additional rice parcels, with French monitoring reports noting an increasing number of infested fields and concern about potential yield losses where control was not applied. By 2021, the NPPO of France considered the species present and widespread in national rice-growing areas, and management relied on targeted insecticide treatments, agronomic measures and continued surveillance to protect previously pest-free zones and track economic impact.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Secondary introduction from other invaded European regions (particularly Italy and possibly Spain) via movement of infested rice plants or straw, shared harvesting machinery, and regional trade in rice seed and by-products; the dense, irrigated rice landscape of the Camargue provides highly suitable habitat and hydrological connectivity that facilitates local spread. Internal mechanisms: Establishment of the invasive parthenogenetic lineage already present in other parts of Europe, with Geographic Range Expansion (inherent cold and heat tolerance) enabling colonization of Mediterranean Western Europe; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation via strong adult dispersal and exploitation of irrigation canals and adjacent wild hosts.
Review: review – This row has been added to capture a major emergence event that was previously omitted: first detection in France in 2014 followed by spread leading to a current official status of “present, widespread” in national rice-growing areas. It is classified as intra_continental_emergence (first establishment in the Western Europe subregion of an invasive lineage already present in Southern Europe). The timing and distribution are supported by the EU 2014 harmful organisms report, EPPO distribution details for France and Ferrand (2017); the event should be treated as one of the top global emergence events for this pest, but the narrative and time window (2014–2021) should be checked and refined by a domain expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus
EPP.common.name: rice water weevil
Countries: Greece [2016] (Central Macedonia, Axios river delta near Thessaloniki)
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in deltaic paddy fields, with likely use of associated wild grasses and sedges as ancillary hosts
Event.summary: In July–August 2016, during mosquito surveillance in rice fields in the Axios river delta of Central Macedonia, Greece, adult Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus were collected and identified morphologically and by COI DNA barcoding, marking the first record of the species in Greece and the Balkans. This finding showed that the European invasion, previously centred in Italy, had expanded eastwards within Southern Europe into a new rice-producing country, although at that time no severe economic damage had yet been documented in Greek paddies. Following confirmation, Greek authorities and researchers initiated further surveys around the Axios delta to delimit the infestation, investigate likely introduction routes and assess potential agronomic impacts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Secondary spread within Europe, most likely via trade and movement of contaminated plant material, rice straw or machinery from already infested areas (e.g. Italy), combined with the availability of large areas of flooded rice and interconnected water networks in the Axios delta that favour establishment and local dispersal. Internal mechanisms: Continued exploitation of the invasive parthenogenetic lineage without evidence of new genotypes, Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation (effective dispersal in irrigated Mediterranean deltas), and Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) as the species occupies additional parts of the Southern Europe rice belt.
Review: review – This event remains important as it documents expansion of the European invasion into the Balkans, but its categorization and sources have been updated. Intra_continental_emergence is set to No because the spread is to a new country within the already affected Southern Europe subregion rather than to a new UN subregion, and re_occurrence is set to Yes to reflect renewed occurrence and increased regional incidence within an already infested subregion driven mainly by trade and irrigation networks rather than further genetic change. The source list has been focused on EPPO RS 2017/162 and Giantsis et al. 2017, removing a largely irrelevant U.S. agronomic study; human review is advised to confirm the choice of re_occurrence and the spatial scale at which it is applied.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus
EPP.common.name: rice water weevil
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) in Ebro Delta paddies; detection also via DNA metabarcoding of insectivorous bat (Pipistrellus pygmaeus) faeces
Event.summary: In August 2018, adults of Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus were collected from rice crops at several localities in the Ebro Delta in Catalonia, Spain, and later confirmed taxonomically, representing the first record of the species in the Iberian Peninsula.
