EPP.scientific.name: Obolodiplosis robiniae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) in urban/amenity plantings, Vancouver Island, British Columbia
Event.summary: In 1999, Obolodiplosis robiniae was reported from Victoria on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, marking its spread within North America from its native eastern U.S. range to western Canada. The midge established on ornamental and planted black locust trees in urban areas, where conspicuous marginal leaf-roll galls were observed. The event represented westward geographic expansion within the continent rather than a new host association, and the pest has since persisted locally without evidence of continent-wide outbreaks comparable to those later seen in Eurasia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement of infested nursery stock or ornamental black locust saplings across North America, combined with widespread planting of Robinia pseudoacacia in western Canadian cities, likely enabled colonization of Vancouver Island. Internal mechanisms: The species’ multivoltine life cycle and high fecundity, together with the high suitability of black locust foliage, supported establishment but no specific novel strain or resistance trait was reported in this event.
Review: Decision: retain. The 1999 detection on Victoria, Vancouver Island, is documented in European invasion syntheses and Csóka (2006) as an early extra-native-range record within North America, and there is no evidence of earlier western Canadian establishment. Classification as a minor within-continent range expansion (no intra- or inter-continental emergence flag under the UNSD subregion scheme) is appropriate, and although impact was limited compared with later Eurasian and New Zealand invasions, this stepping-stone event is retained because the total number of major episodes for this species is below ten.

EPP.scientific.name: Obolodiplosis robiniae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Countries: China [2004] (initially Hebei Province, later many northern and eastern provinces)
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia plantations, shelterbelts and urban trees in northern and eastern China
Event.summary: In 2004 Obolodiplosis robiniae was first recorded in China from Qinhuangdao City in Hebei Province, and in subsequent years it spread rapidly across northern and eastern Chinese regions where black locust is widely planted. During the late 2000s and early 2010s, high infestation levels were documented in shelterbelts, plantations and urban trees, with multiple generations per season causing repeated galling and, in heavy outbreaks, partial defoliation and growth reduction. As the midge became established throughout much of the Chinese range of black locust, it transitioned from an emerging invader to a chronic foliar pest whose impact varied among regions and years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The Chinese outbreak was facilitated by extensive, often monocultural plantings of Robinia pseudoacacia for afforestation, sand stabilization and urban greening, which created continuous host corridors; long-distance movement of infested plants and nursery stock between provinces further accelerated spread. Internal mechanisms: Population genetic analyses indicate relatively high genetic diversity in Chinese O. robiniae populations, consistent with multiple introductions and/or large founding populations, which may have enhanced adaptive potential and colonization success; life‑history traits such as multivoltinism and efficient exploitation of young leaves supported repeated, high‑density infestations once the species was established.
Review: Decision: retain. This event accurately summarizes the first discovery of O. robiniae in China in 2004 (Qinhuangdao, Hebei) and the subsequent decade of rapid spread and frequent heavy infestations across northern and eastern China, as described by Yang et al. 2006 and Du et al. 2020, and appropriately treats it as a major re-occurrence episode within Eastern Asia following the earlier 2002 East Asian introduction. No corrections to geography, timing or emergence-type flags are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Obolodiplosis robiniae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Countries: New Zealand [2009] (Auckland, then Bay of Plenty, Hawke’s Bay, Northland, Taupo, Waikato, Wairarapa, Wellington, Canterbury and other regions)
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia in parks, shelterbelts and amenity plantings across New Zealand
Event.summary: In early 2009 the New Zealand biosecurity surveillance system detected Obolodiplosis robiniae for the first time, with samples from black locust trees collected at high‑risk sites and confirmed as the North American gall midge, representing its arrival in Australasia. Over the following decade the species spread widely through much of New Zealand, with distribution records from Auckland, Bay of Plenty, Hawke’s Bay, Northland, Taupo, Waikato, Wairarapa, Wellington, Canterbury and other regions, where repeated galling of Robinia foliage was observed. By the early 2020s the pest was considered established nationwide, causing recurring cosmetic damage and some defoliation on black locust, though impacts on native flora were judged low and management focused mainly on monitoring rather than eradication.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction was most likely via infested ornamental or forestry plant material of Robinia pseudoacacia imported from regions where O. robiniae was already established (Asia or Europe), with subsequent within‑country spread along human transport corridors and through local planting and movement of black locust. Internal mechanisms: The midge’s strict association with Robinia pseudoacacia, combined with its ability to complete several generations per year under New Zealand conditions, promoted establishment; later reports of heavy parasitism by a previously unrecognized parasitoid wasp suggest that natural enemy recruitment may begin to moderate populations, although this did not influence the initial establishment phase.
Review: Decision: retain. The 2009 detection and subsequent spread of O. robiniae across New Zealand are well supported by national surveillance reports (Biosecurity 92, Forest Health News 195; MPI Surveillance 48(3) 2021) and comparative invasion analyses, and correctly represent the first established populations in Oceania. Classification as an inter-continental emergence into a new continent, with modest but persistent impacts on ornamental black locust, is appropriate and no corrections are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus C
EPP.common.name: Poliovirus (poliovirus 1; poliovirus 2; poliovirus 3)
Sub.regions: Western Africa; Middle Africa; Eastern Africa; Northern Africa; Western Asia; Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia
Host: Humans, predominantly children under 5 years
Event.summary: In 2003, several northern Nigerian states suspended oral polio vaccine campaigns after rumors and political/religious opposition, rapidly creating large cohorts of unvaccinated children and fueling explosive resurgence of wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) in Nigeria. Over 2003–2006, genetically related WPV1 spread from northern Nigeria through much of West and Central Africa and onwards to the Horn of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, and parts of South and South‑East Asia, re‑infecting at least 20 previously polio‑free countries—including large outbreaks in Sudan, Yemen (~478 cases) and Indonesia (~305 cases)—and accounting for more than half of global polio cases in 2005.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/preview/MMWRhtml/mm5506a1.htm?utm_source=openai)) Intensified synchronized SIAs with monovalent OPV1, engagement of traditional and religious leaders, and improved surveillance progressively interrupted these importation‑related outbreaks by about 2006, although further waves of spread from Nigeria continued later in the decade.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/preview/MMWRhtml/mm5506a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Suspension of vaccination in parts of northern Nigeria due to mistrust of government and international agencies and rumors of vaccine contamination, combined with weak routine immunization, high population mobility, and conflict-affected or remote communities across West and Central Africa, created extensive immunity gaps and enabled long-distance spread of imported virus.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1831725/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved typical WPV1 genotypes exported from endemic northern Nigeria without evidence of major antigenic novelty; resurgence reflects amplification and geographic spread of existing wild virus driven by social, political and programmatic failures, fitting the re-occurrence category rather than re-emergence.
Review: retain – This is correctly one of the most impactful post‑1990 polio events (over 1,000 importation-related cases across ≥20 countries). Countries list has been amended to include Nepal [2005] to justify inclusion of the Southern Asia subregion and better reflect WHO reports of importations into Nepal, and vague 'other affected countries in West and Central Africa' is retained to cover the full set of re‑infected states.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/preview/MMWRhtml/mm5506a1.htm?utm_source=openai)) Event type remains re-occurrence (wild virus re‑introduced into previously polio-free areas due to immunity gaps) and not inter-continental emergence, since poliovirus was historically present on all affected continents. Wikipedia links used previously have been replaced at event level by WHO and CDC primary sources focused on this outbreak; recommend retaining Wikipedia only as a contextual background source at most.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWR/preview/MMWRhtml/mm5506a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Sub.regions: Western Africa; Middle Africa; Eastern Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Humans, predominantly children in under-immunized communities across multiple African countries
Event.summary: From about 2017 onward, numerous genetically independent outbreaks of circulating vaccine‑derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) emerged or expanded across West, Central, East and parts of Southern Africa, collectively accounting for the majority of global cVDPV2 emergences, outbreaks and virus detections after the global withdrawal of OPV2.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6855511/?utm_source=openai)) These lineages, many arising in countries such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Nigeria, Somalia, Ethiopia, Angola and the Central African Republic, spread widely across borders to affect >20 African countries and produced hundreds of paralytic cases during 2018–2023, particularly in chronically underserved, conflict‑affected or nomadic populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6855511/?utm_source=openai)) The Global Polio Eradication Initiative mounted a continent‑wide response involving repeated outbreak assessments, large-scale use of monovalent OPV2 and, from 2021, novel OPV2 (nOPV2), along with intensified AFP and environmental surveillance; many outbreak lineages were closed by 2020–2023, but new emergences continued to appear, keeping cVDPV2 a major threat.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/circulating-vaccine-derived-poliovirus-type-2-global-update?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing weaknesses in routine immunization, fragile and conflict‑affected health systems, high population mobility (including in the Lake Chad basin and Horn of Africa), and logistical challenges in rapidly responding to multiple simultaneous outbreaks created conditions in which residual Sabin 2 and outbreak response use of mOPV2 could repeatedly seed new cVDPV2 lineages.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10354706/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Dozens of independent cVDPV2 emergences, each showing substantial VP1 divergence from Sabin 2 and restored neurovirulence, represent repeated novel strain/genotype emergence events; some lineages show evidence of enhanced fitness in low‑immunity populations, driving extensive geographic range expansion across multiple African subregions.
Review: retain – This aggregated event appropriately captures the highly impactful, multi‑country wave of post‑switch African cVDPV2 outbreaks that together account for the majority of global cVDPV2 burden since 2017, and is clearly among the top post‑1990 poliovirus emergence episodes by both case count and geographic spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6855511/?utm_source=openai)) Event year has been adjusted from 2018–2023 to 2017–2023 to reflect early post‑switch cVDPV2 emergence and spread in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and neighboring countries; countries list remains illustrative rather than exhaustive, consistent with WHO summaries. Classification as re-emergence driven by multiple novel vaccine‑derived lineages is appropriate.

Continent: Africa; Europe; North America; South America; Asia; Oceania

Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2022]
Host: Humans (predominantly adults, especially gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men; occasional infections in women and children)
Event.summary: In May 2022, the United Kingdom reported a cluster of mpox cases without clear links to endemic regions, soon followed by multiple cases across Europe and North America, marking the start of the first large, multi-country mpox outbreak in non-endemic countries driven by sustained human-to-human transmission. Over 2022–2023 the clade IIb lineage linked to Nigeria spread through interconnected sexual networks, predominantly among men who have sex with men, causing tens of thousands of confirmed cases and hundreds of deaths worldwide, with the Americas and Europe initially most affected and later notable transmission also in other WHO regions. Intensive public health measures—including case isolation, contact tracing, risk communication targeting high‑risk sexual networks, and large-scale use of third‑generation smallpox/mpox vaccines and antivirals—led to a sharp decline in incidence by late 2022–2023, though low-level transmission persisted in several regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: dense international travel and social/sexual networks, particularly among MSM communities; overlapping HIV and STI epidemics; reduced orthopoxvirus immunity in the global population; and surveillance systems pre-focused on COVID-19 leading to some delays in early recognition. Internal mechanisms: emergence and dissemination of clade IIb mpox virus with genetic changes associated with accelerated mutation (e.g. APOBEC editing) and apparent adaptation for efficient human-to-human (especially sexual) transmission, representing a clear re‑emergence with a novel genotype and enhanced transmission compared with historically sporadic zoonotic outbreaks; this outbreak also entailed both inter-continental spread into previously unaffected continents (e.g. South America, parts of Oceania) and intra-continental spread into new subregions.
Review: review – Retained classification of this unprecedented multi-country outbreak as both inter-continental and intra-continental emergence plus re-emergence driven by clade IIb adaptation, but set re_occurrence from true to false to comply with the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra-/inter-continental emergence; geography, scale, timing and mechanisms are consistent with WHO and CDC summaries, though case and country counts are necessarily summarized rather than exhaustive.

Event.summary: In the early 1990s, clusters of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), resistant at least to isoniazid and rifampicin, were reported in New York City and other urban centers, particularly among HIV-infected patients. From about 1991 to 1995, nosocomial and prison outbreaks with high case‑fatality rates revealed that MDR-TB had become a major public health threat in the United States and several Western European countries. Intensified infection control in hospitals and prisons, improved TB/HIV management, and implementation of directly observed therapy (DOTS) subsequently contained these MDR outbreaks in many high-income settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Overcrowded hospitals and correctional facilities, inadequate TB treatment regimens, poor adherence, and co‑location of patients with HIV created conditions for selection and transmission of drug-resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: accumulation of resistance mutations to first‑line drugs, giving rise to MDR-TB with increased fitness under widespread antibiotic pressure and enabling sustained person‑to‑person transmission in congregate settings.

Time window and locations match published outbreak reports; no structural changes required.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Tuberculosis
Host: Humans, including general population, prisoners, and people living with HIV
Event.summary: After the dissolution of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s, tuberculosis incidence and mortality rose sharply in many Eastern European and Central Asian countries, reversing previous declines. Between roughly 1991 and 2005, severe epidemics of TB and MDR-TB emerged in the Russian Federation, Ukraine, Moldova, and Central Asian republics, fuelled by deteriorating health systems and explosive transmission in prisons. By the early 2000s, this region accounted for a large share of the world’s MDR and XDR-TB burden, and international programmes focused on scaling up DOTS-Plus and prison TB control to gradually stabilize the situation.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Socioeconomic crisis, underfunded and fragmented TB services, irregular drug supply, and overcrowded prisons allowed incomplete or inappropriate treatment and extensive transmission; rising HIV prevalence in some areas further increased susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: independent evolution and spread of MDR and later XDR M. tuberculosis lineages (e.g., Ural and Beijing families) through stepwise accumulation of resistance mutations under intense selection pressure, with some strains later shown to expand clonally across Eastern Europe.
Review: review – Corrected misclassification of this episode as an intra-continental emergence event. TB was long established in Eastern Europe and Central Asia; the period 1991–2005 reflects resurgence and spread of MDR/XDR strains in an existing endemic area, which fits the project definition of re-emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance rather than first presence in a new sub-region. Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false and retained re_emergence = true; years, regions and countries remain appropriate but should be checked by a human reviewer for final confirmation.

Event.summary: From 1990 to about 2005, tuberculosis incidence in sub‑Saharan Africa more than doubled, in stark contrast to stable or declining trends elsewhere. As generalized HIV epidemics expanded through the 1990s, countries such as South Africa and its neighbours experienced explosive growth in HIV‑associated TB, with millions of co‑infected individuals and overwhelmed TB programmes. By the mid‑2000s, regional and global initiatives to scale up antiretroviral therapy, improve TB/HIV collaborative activities, and strengthen DOTS began to slow and then partially reverse the rise in incidence, though TB burden remained extremely high.

Internal mechanisms: mainly increased reactivation and transmission of existing strains in highly immunocompromised populations, with drug‑resistant TB emerging later as a compounding problem but not the initial primary driver of this regional resurgence.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Tuberculosis
Host: Humans, including general adult population, prisoners, and people living with HIV
Event.summary: During the 2010–2020 period, the WHO European Region, particularly Eastern Europe and parts of Central Asia, remained the world’s epicentre of MDR and XDR-TB, with drug‑resistant TB notification and treatment success indicators significantly worse than global averages. Countries such as the Russian Federation, Ukraine, and Moldova reported very high proportions of MDR among new and previously treated TB cases, alongside rising HIV/TB co‑infection in some settings. Intensified international and national efforts to scale up rapid molecular diagnostics, patient‑centred MDR regimens, and prison TB control aimed to curb ongoing transmission and improve outcomes, but MDR/XDR-TB continued to pose a major regional threat into the late 2010s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Legacy of earlier health‑system collapse and prison epidemics, persistent gaps in adherence support and infection control, and in some countries the growing HIV epidemic sustained high levels of transmission of resistant strains. Internal mechanisms: established MDR and pre‑XDR/XDR lineages with accumulated resistance mutations maintained transmission across communities and prisons, with genomic studies (e.g., Ural/4.2 in Moldova) demonstrating clonal expansion and cross‑border spread within Eastern Europe.
Review: review – Changed intra_continental_emergence from true to false. This event reflects persistence and further expansion of MDR/XDR-TB within Eastern Europe and Central Asia, regions where TB was already endemic and MDR had emerged in the 1990s; under the project definitions, it is more accurately classified purely as re-emergence driven by established resistant lineages rather than as intra-continental emergence. Time window (2010–2020) and geographic focus on Eastern Europe and Central Asia are consistent with WHO/Europe descriptions and should be retained after review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Humans in all age groups, especially in high‑burden countries with disrupted health systems during the COVID‑19 pandemic
Event.summary: In 2020, the COVID‑19 pandemic severely disrupted TB services worldwide, leading to sharp reductions in TB case notifications and delays in diagnosis and treatment. By 2020–2021, WHO estimated that TB deaths had increased for the first time in more than a decade and that the world was off track for End TB targets because of COVID‑19‑related disruptions. As countries adapted TB services, deployed catch‑up campaigns, and integrated TB and COVID‑19 responses, some recovery in notifications occurred by 2022, but global TB incidence and mortality remained above pre‑pandemic trajectories.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Health‑system overload, lockdowns, reduced access to clinics, diversion of diagnostic resources (e.g., GeneXpert machines) to COVID‑19 testing, and economic hardship reduced TB case finding, treatment initiation, and adherence, causing more advanced disease and ongoing community transmission. Internal mechanisms: no novel TB strain was responsible; rather, existing drug‑susceptible and drug‑resistant lineages resurged due to service disruptions and social conditions that temporarily reversed previous gains in TB control.
Review: review – Replaced the non-standard continent value "Global" with the full list of continents (Africa; Asia; Europe; North America; South America; Oceania) and explicitly listed all inhabited UN sub-regions in the sub_regions field to match the project’s geographic conventions. Updated the countries field to name key high TB-burden countries that contributed substantially to the pandemic-related setback (India, Indonesia, China, the Philippines, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nigeria, South Africa, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia) while still noting global involvement. Event remains correctly coded as a re-occurrence episode driven by external COVID-19 disruptions, with no intra- or inter-continental emergence; should be retained after review.

Countries: Multiple EU/EEA member states with sustained increases, notably France [2008]
Host: Humans (sexually active population in EU/EEA, including both MSM and heterosexual men and women)
Event.summary: From around 2008, EU/EEA surveillance began to record renewed increases in gonorrhoea notifications in many Western and Northern European countries after previous declines, with France and Portugal experiencing roughly six‑fold rises and Denmark and Ireland more than tripling reported cases by 2017. Through the 2010s, diagnoses rose across most EU/EEA states, driven by high rates among MSM but also marked increases among young heterosexual men and women, leading to more than 89 000 confirmed cases in 2017 and around 118 000 cases in 2019, the highest annual total recorded since EU‑level STI surveillance began. This multi‑country resurgence prompted intensified testing, partner notification and prevention campaigns as well as ongoing updates to European and national STI strategies, but incidence remained high until temporarily disrupted by COVID‑19–related changes in sexual behaviour and service access in 2020.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Behavioural changes including increases in partner numbers, condomless sex and use of geospatial networking apps; reduced fear of HIV due to effective antiretroviral therapy and wider availability of PrEP; high background prevalence of bacterial STIs in core networks; expanded use of highly sensitive nucleic acid amplification tests and dual chlamydia/gonorrhoea testing, which increased case detection; strengthened EU/EEA surveillance improving ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of multiple N. gonorrhoeae lineages, many with resistance to older antibiotics; however, no single novel strain or resistance mechanism uniquely defines this resurgence, so it is best characterised as a behaviour- and system-driven re-occurrence.
Review: Review – Added as a new high-impact event to capture the large, multi-country resurgence of gonorrhoea incidence across the EU/EEA culminating in record notifications in 2017–2019. Classified as re-occurrence (behavioural and system drivers, without a single defining novel strain) and linked to specific EU/EEA reports; should be retained among the top events, but details (country list and exact start year) may warrant further refinement with full access to surveillance datasets.

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
EPP.common.name: gonoccocus
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Australia and New Zealand; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Northern America
Host: Humans (urogenital and pharyngeal infections in heterosexual and MSM populations)
Event.summary: In January 2015, Japan identified Neisseria gonorrhoeae strain FC428, carrying mosaic penA-60.001 and showing ceftriaxone resistance and multidrug resistance while retaining good biological fitness. Over 2016–2018, closely related FC428‑like isolates were reported from China, Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, Ireland and the United Kingdom, often with epidemiological links to travel in the Asia‑Pacific region and occasional evidence of limited local onward transmission. By the early 2020s, surveillance data documented continued detection of FC428‑like strains across the Asia‑Pacific and sporadically in Europe and Northern America, prompting international alerts and efforts to enhance genomic surveillance and resistance‑guided therapy.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Global dependence on ceftriaxone as the last reliable monotherapy for gonorrhoea; extensive cephalosporin and quinolone use at population level; high volumes of travel between East/South‑East Asia and Europe/Oceania/Northern America, particularly among sexually active adults; limited routine genomic surveillance delaying recognition of a single, fit international clone. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of the mosaic penA-60.001 allele and additional chromosomal changes conferring ceftriaxone and cefixime resistance while maintaining high fitness; combination of resistance to multiple older drugs (penicillin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline) generating an extensively drug‑resistant phenotype; clonal expansion and international spread of FC428 and FC428‑like strains through interconnected sexual networks.
Review: Review – This event correctly captures the emergence and international dissemination of the FC428 clone and related ceftriaxone-resistant lineages and appropriately classifies them as re-emergence via a novel resistance genotype. Removed intra- and inter-continental emergence flags to align with the definition that geographic spread of resistant variants of an already global species should be coded as re-emergence rather than new continental emergence.

EPP.common.name: Escherichia coli
Host: Humans (primarily adults consuming fenugreek or mixed sprouts)
Event.summary: Between May and July 2011, an explosive outbreak of enteroaggregative Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli O104:H4 infections occurred in northern Germany, with smaller associated clusters in France and a few other European countries, following consumption of contaminated fenugreek and mixed sprouts. Germany ultimately reported around 3,950 cases, including about 800 hemolytic uremic syndrome cases and 53 deaths, making this one of the largest and deadliest STEC outbreaks ever recorded. Event.summary: Beginning around 1990, a multidrug‑resistant clone of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium, definitive phage type 104 (DT104) with ACSSuT resistance, expanded rapidly in food‑animal populations and humans in the United Kingdom and other parts of Western and Northern Europe. During the mid‑1990s, surveillance in the United States and Canada documented a steep rise in Typhimurium isolates showing the characteristic five‑drug resistance pattern, with phage typing confirming DT104 or closely related types, indicating international spread of this epidemic clone. By the early 2000s, DT104 had become established across multiple livestock sectors and food chains in Europe and North America, accounting for a substantial proportion of human salmonellosis cases and raising major concerns about treatment failure and further resistance acquisition.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive livestock production with heavy use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics in cattle, pigs and poultry created strong selection pressure for multiresistant Salmonella strains; regional and international trade in animals and animal products facilitated dissemination of contaminated herds, flocks and meat. Event.summary: In November 2016, health authorities in Sindh Province, Pakistan, detected an outbreak of extensively drug‑resistant (XDR) Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi causing typhoid fever, initially centered in Hyderabad and later spreading to Karachi and other districts. Between 2016 and late 2018, over 5,000 XDR typhoid cases were laboratory‑confirmed among more than 8,000 typhoid cases in Sindh, with the outbreak strain resistant to first‑line drugs, fluoroquinolones and third‑generation cephalosporins and susceptible only to azithromycin and carbapenems; travel‑associated cases were subsequently reported in several high‑income countries but did not lead to sustained local transmission. While incidence has fluctuated and typhoid conjugate vaccine campaigns have been rolled out in Pakistan, XDR S. Typhi continues to circulate, posing ongoing treatment challenges and risk of wider regional or global spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy prior use and misuse of antibiotics in Pakistan, limited water and sanitation infrastructure, densely populated urban areas, and under‑resourced surveillance created an environment in which a highly resistant typhoid clone could emerge and disseminate; internal and international travel then exported cases abroad. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – evolution of an H58 S. Typhi clone harboring a promiscuous plasmid conferring resistance to fluoroquinolones and third‑generation cephalosporins; Antimicrobial Resistance – progression to an extensively drug‑resistant phenotype with very limited remaining oral treatment options; Enhanced Transmission – clonal expansion of this XDR lineage within endemic typhoid networks.

Event.summary: Following the near‑absence of RSV in 2020–2021, many countries experienced unusually timed and often sizeable RSV resurgences beginning in spring or summer 2021, including large outbreaks in the United States, Brazil, Chile, multiple European states, Israel, South Africa, Japan, the Republic of Korea and Australia. These epidemics frequently peaked months earlier than traditional autumn–winter seasons, produced high paediatric hospitalization rates (sometimes exceeding prior off‑season baselines), and involved a broader age range of susceptible children, including older infants and toddlers who had not been infected during 2020. Through late 2021 and early 2022, RSV activity in many regions gradually shifted back toward more typical calendar timing, but incidence remained elevated compared with immediate pre‑pandemic seasons. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7214a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Relaxation of COVID‑19 NPIs, reopening of schools and childcare, and resumption of domestic and international travel markedly increased contact rates among children and families, while one to two unexposed birth cohorts (“immunity debt”) accumulated during the suppression period, amplifying epidemic size. Health systems in several countries were still coping with COVID‑19 waves, compounding the impact of RSV resurgences. Internal mechanisms: Genetic data indicate continued dominance of ON1 and BA9 lineages, with no single novel variant clearly linked to these resurgences, so the episode is best interpreted as re‑occurrence driven by host and behavioural factors rather than viral change. Event.summary: From the mid‑1990s, Balamuthia mandrillaris was increasingly recognized as a cause of fatal meningoencephalitis in Latin America, with a 4‑case Mexican series published in 1997 and additional cases described from Peru, Argentina, Brazil and Venezuela. By the mid‑2000s, Central and South America together accounted for a substantial fraction of globally reported Balamuthia infections, firmly establishing the pathogen in a second continent beyond its original recognition in North America.

EPP.scientific.name: Balamuthia mandrillaris
EPP.common.name: granulomatous amebic encephalitis
Sub.regions: Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Humans, including children and adults, generally previously healthy or with limited immunosuppression, presenting with encephalitis sometimes initially suspected to be brain tumors.
Event.summary: In 1998, a fatal case of amebic encephalitis in a 3‑year‑old child in Czechia was identified as Balamuthia mandrillaris, representing the first documented human infection in Europe. In the early 2000s, the first UK case was confirmed by post‑mortem culture, and in 2001 Portugal reported its first fatal Balamuthia encephalitis case initially misdiagnosed as a brain tumor, bringing the total to only a handful of European patients. Over subsequent years, a few additional isolated European cases were reported as specialist centers adopted immunofluorescence and PCR for diagnosis, demonstrating that Balamuthia could cause severe disease in Europe but that incidence remained extremely low and outcomes were usually fatal.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased neuropathology and molecular diagnostic capacity in European referral centers allowed recognition of Balamuthia among patients with idiopathic brain lesions, but there is no evidence of local outbreaks; cases remained sporadic. Internal mechanisms: No distinct European lineage has been described; emergence in Europe is best explained by global environmental distribution of the amoeba with rare spillover from soil exposure to humans, rather than human‑to‑human spread or strain‑specific changes.
Review: review – Retain as the inter‑continental emergence into Europe, but correct the original misstatement that the first European case occurred in the UK. Primary sources show the first confirmed human case was a Czech child in 1998, followed by UK and Portuguese cases in the early 2000s. Sub‑regions have been narrowed to Eastern, Northern and Southern Europe to match documented human cases during this period, and Turkey has been removed from the narrative because it is classified as Western Asia in the UNSD scheme, not Europe.

EPP.scientific.name: Balamuthia mandrillaris
EPP.common.name: granulomatous amebic encephalitis
Sub.regions: South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Eastern Asia
Host: Humans, including children and adults, often with chronic facial or limb skin lesions or sinus involvement preceding CNS disease.
Event.summary: From the mid‑1990s onward, Balamuthia mandrillaris infections were reported from several parts of Asia, including Japan and India, indicating that the pathogen was present in both temperate and tropical Asian environments. In 2002, China documented its earliest known Balamuthia infection, and in 2004 Thailand reported the first recognized Southeast Asian case, followed by additional sporadic cases over the remainder of the decade. By around 2010, Balamuthia had been recognized across multiple Asian subregions, though reports remained sporadic and case‑fatality rates exceeded 90%.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of advanced neuroimaging, neurosurgery, histopathology and molecular diagnostics in large Asian referral hospitals enabled recognition of Balamuthia among patients with previously unexplained brain lesions or chronic granulomatous skin disease; widespread environmental contact with soil and dust in agricultural and peri‑urban settings likely provided exposure opportunities. Internal mechanisms: No consistent evidence supports a distinct Asian lineage or novel virulence trait; the pattern is compatible with long‑standing environmental presence and rare opportunistic human infection that became visible as diagnostic capacity improved, i.e. documentation of geographic range rather than de novo evolutionary expansion.
Review: review – This remains the appropriate inter‑continental emergence episode for Asia, but the original row placed the first Thai case around 2001–2002 and implied Asian cases started only in the early 2000s. Published reports show that Japan and India had cases by the mid‑to‑late 1990s and that the first clearly documented Southeast Asian case from Thailand was in 2004. The event window has been widened to 1993–2010 (matching CDC’s statement that Asian cases have been reported since 1993), country annotations have been adjusted accordingly, and the inter‑continental emergence classification remains justified.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Enterococcus faecium
EPP.common.name: Enterococcus faecium infection
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Humans (hospital inpatients with bloodstream infections; adults and elderly predominating)
Event.summary: From 2012 to 2018, the European Union/European Economic Area experienced a pronounced increase in vancomycin‑resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) among blood culture isolates reported to the European Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network, with the population‑weighted mean proportion of VREfm rising from about 8% to around 19% and high levels reported in many countries across all European regions. The event reflects a continent‑wide expansion of hospital‑adapted VREfm lineages that built on earlier sporadic outbreaks and spread through referral networks, leading to a growing burden of nosocomial bloodstream infections. After 2018, VREfm proportions remained high in many countries, prompting intensified infection‑prevention and antimicrobial‑stewardship efforts, but sustained control remains challenging.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high and often inappropriate use of broad‑spectrum antibiotics (including cephalosporins, carbapenems and glycopeptides), increasing numbers of immunocompromised patients and complex medical interventions, and variable implementation of infection‑prevention and control programs across Europe contributed to rising colonization pressure and transmission in hospitals. Internal mechanisms: expansion and diversification of hospital‑adapted E. faecium clonal complex 17/A1 and related lineages (including ST80, ST117, ST78 and others) carrying vanA or vanB determinants and multiple additional resistance and virulence genes, leading to a marked re‑emergence of VREfm bloodstream infections across multiple European sub‑regions (Re‑emergence; Antimicrobial Resistance; Enhanced Transmission; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence).
Review: retain – Newly added event capturing the EU/EEA‑wide surge in vancomycin‑resistant Enterococcus faecium bloodstream infections between 2012 and 2018, documented by EARS‑Net analyses. Classified as re‑emergence (large increase in incidence associated with expansion of hospital‑adapted VREfm lineages) without additional intra‑/inter‑continental flags. This episode involves tens of thousands of bloodstream infections across multiple European sub‑regions and should be included among the most impactful global emergence events for this EPP.

Host: Humans (immunocompromised and immunocompetent patients with tick exposure in Western and Northern Europe)

Together, these reports demonstrated that B. miyamotoi was widely established in Ixodes ricinus across Europe and capable of causing both acute febrile illness and meningoencephalitis in immunocompromised and immunocompetent persons, leading several centers to add B. miyamotoi testing to diagnostic algorithms for tick-associated fever and neuroborreliosis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7059645/?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans (mainly children and adolescents)
Event.summary: From 2011 onward, East Java Province, Indonesia, experienced repeated diphtheria outbreaks, leading to its declaration as an outbreak area as case numbers and mortality climbed sharply in 2011–2012. EPP.scientific.name: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
EPP.common.name: diphtheria
Host: Humans (mostly children and adolescents)
Event.summary: Beginning in late 2014, Haiti reported renewed diphtheria transmission after years of very low incidence, with continuous suspected and confirmed cases recorded each year through at least 2020–2021. Over 2014–2021, Haiti documented roughly one thousand or more suspected cases and well over one hundred deaths, with multiple peaks and spread across several departments, signaling a prolonged nationwide re‑occurrence. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain, resistance, or virulence increase has been highlighted; the event reflects re‑occurrence in a setting where diphtheria was once largely controlled but resurged due to external drivers.
Review: retain – Haiti’s prolonged national outbreak (≈1,000+ suspected cases and high mortality) is among the larger modern diphtheria resurgences in the Americas; continents/sub‑regions and event‑type classification as re‑occurrence are appropriate. Minor numerical differences across PAHO reports are within expected uncertainty and do not require restructuring.

EPP.scientific.name: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
EPP.common.name: diphtheria
Host: Humans (primarily children and adolescents, with increasing share of older age groups)
Event.summary: Throughout 2000–2017, India and some neighboring South‑East Asian countries maintained the highest global diphtheria case counts, with India alone accounting for the majority of reported cases worldwide each year and periods of increased incidence after 2010. Within India, surveillance analyses documented persistent endemic transmission with recurrent local outbreaks and a gradual shift toward older children and adults among reported cases. Intensification of routine immunization, supplemental activities, and discussions about life‑course booster strategies have been ongoing to address this chronic high‑burden situation, though diphtheria remains entrenched in several Indian states.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large population size, heterogeneous and often suboptimal DTP coverage in some states, socio‑economic disparities, and insufficient adolescent/adult booster policies sustain a large pool of susceptible individuals and recurrent outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence emphasizes immunity gaps and age‑shifts rather than a single novel strain or resistance pattern; this period is best considered a long‑running re‑occurrence and concentration of endemic disease rather than re‑emergence driven by a discrete pathogen change.
Review: review – Appropriately highlights India’s dominant contribution to global diphtheria incidence since 2000, but re_emergence has been set to 'false' because the sustained high burden and age‑shift are better explained by persistent immunity gaps and booster‑dose weaknesses than by clearly documented strain‑level changes. EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus louisense
EPP.common.name: St. Louis encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (encephalitis and febrile neurologic disease), Culex mosquitoes, urban and peri‑urban birds (e.g., pigeons, sparrows, domestic fowl)
Event.summary: Between 2010 and 2011, Argentina experienced a series of Saint Louis encephalitis outbreaks beyond Córdoba and Paraná, including confirmed clusters in Buenos Aires Province and the Andean province of San Juan, demonstrating multi‑provincial re‑emergence of SLEV as a human neurologic pathogen. In 2010, SLEV cases were detected in Buenos Aires and other central provinces during the warm season, and in early 2011 at least seven human cases were confirmed in San Juan, prompting provincial alerts and intensified vector‑control recommendations. Coordinated national and provincial mosquito‑control campaigns, public communication on personal protection, and seasonal declines in mosquito populations curtailed these outbreaks, but subsequent serologic and entomologic work indicated continued low‑level viral circulation in central Argentina.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued regional circulation of genotype III SLEV in birds and mosquitoes from earlier central‑Argentina outbreaks, urbanization, and climatic conditions favorable to Culex vectors promoted spread into densely populated Buenos Aires and more arid San Juan; human travel and movement of birds likely facilitated seeding of new foci. Internal mechanisms: The same re‑emergent genotype III lineage, associated with higher virulence, underpinned these outbreaks, representing ongoing geographic range expansion and repeated re‑emergence of a more pathogenic strain across multiple Argentine provinces rather than independent emergence of novel genotypes in each locality.
Review: retain – the 2010–2011 multi‑provincial Argentine outbreaks (Buenos Aires and San Juan) are correctly represented as linked re‑emergence of genotype III within Argentina, with appropriate timing, geography, and event‑type coding; sources from PAHO, national press, and CDC syntheses adequately support inclusion as one of the major SLEV emergence episodes since 1990.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus louisense
EPP.common.name: St. Louis encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (sporadic neuroinvasive cases including a fatal Kern County case), Culex tarsalis and Culex quinquefasciatus mosquitoes, wild and sentinel birds (e.g., house finches, house sparrows, chickens)
Event.summary: After an 11‑year apparent absence of detectable activity, St. Louis encephalitis virus reappeared in California in 2015, with SLEV‑positive mosquito pools and sentinel chicken seroconversions first detected in Riverside County’s Coachella Valley, concurrent with the Arizona outbreak and accompanied by detections in neighboring Nevada. Over 2015–2020, SLEV spread northward within California, with repeated detections in mosquitoes and sentinel chickens and sporadic human cases, including a fatal neuroinvasive infection in Kern County in 2016. Sustained vector surveillance, targeted larval and adult mosquito control, and public communication about personal protection limited human disease to relatively small numbers each year, although enzootic transmission of the introduced genotype III lineage became established across much of southern and central California.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive irrigated agriculture and urban water management in California’s Central Valley and southern deserts provided ideal habitats for Culex tarsalis and Cx. quinquefasciatus, while high densities of susceptible passerine birds supported enzootic amplification; long‑term surveillance focused on West Nile virus may initially have reduced sensitivity to SLEV reintroduction. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed that all post‑2015 California SLEV isolates belonged to genotype III, closely related to 2005 Córdoba and 2014 Argentine mosquito isolates and to Arizona 2015 outbreak viruses, indicating re‑emergence via introduction of a South American genotype with traits supporting efficient transmission and long‑distance dispersal in western US ecosystems.
Review: retain – the 2015–2020 California (and associated Nevada) re‑emergence episode is correctly described as re‑introduction and sustained circulation of genotype III SLEV after extirpation from the state, with accurate timing, geography, and emphasis on the 2016 fatal Kern County case; classification solely as re‑emergence, without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus louisense
EPP.common.name: St. Louis encephalitis virus
Host: Primarily birds (wild passerines and sentinel chickens) and Culex mosquitoes, with scattered human neuroinvasive cases documented in some western states
Event.summary: Following its identification as the cause of a 2015 outbreak in Maricopa County, Arizona, a South American‑derived genotype III St. Louis encephalitis virus lineage spread across the western United States between 2015 and 2018, with first detections in mosquito pools in southeastern California and southern Nevada in 2015 and subsequent spread into central California, Texas, Idaho, and Oregon. By 2018, molecular and surveillance data indicated that the introduced genotype III lineage had established persistent transmission across much of the arid and semi‑arid western US, after which its geographic range appeared to stabilize under ongoing vector‑control and arbovirus‑surveillance programs.

Internal mechanisms: Phylogeographic analyses demonstrated that all western US post‑2015 SLEV genomes clustered within the Argentine‑derived genotype III lineage introduced into Arizona, with rapid radiation into multiple clades and three main dispersal routes (Arizona to southern California, to central California, and to regions east of the Sierra Nevada), consistent with a successful, more fit genotype undergoing geographic range expansion and enhanced transmission in new ecological settings.

EPP.scientific.name: Rotavirus spp.

Continent: Asia; Europe; South America; Northern America; Africa; Oceania
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Northern Europe; Western Europe; South America; Eastern Africa; Western Africa; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans (primarily infants and young children)
Event.summary: From the mid‑1990s to early 2000s, previously rare serotype G9 rotaviruses (most often G9P[8]) expanded rapidly from initial detections in Bangladesh and India to become a major cause of pediatric gastroenteritis across Asia, the Americas, Europe, Africa and Australia. Surveillance sites reported seasons in which G9P[8] composed 70–90% of rotavirus infections and caused large outbreaks, such as the 2001 G9P[8] epidemic across central and northern Australia. By the mid‑2000s, G9 was recognised as the fifth globally common human rotavirus genotype, after which its prevalence began to oscillate as other genotypes and vaccines altered strain ecology.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High background transmission in largely unvaccinated child populations, extensive international travel and migration, and limited prior population immunity to G9 facilitated rapid multi‑continental spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence through frequent reassortment among human Wa‑like strains (and occasional animal contributions) generated successful G9P[8] lineages, enabling re‑emergence of a once‑rare serotype as a globally dominant genotype.
Review: review: Retain this event as one of the most impactful genotype-level emergences. Corrected emergence-type classification (now only re_emergence, not intra-/inter-continental, in line with the rule that new serotypes of an established EPP are not inter- or intra-continental events). Updated continents/subregions to include Oceania and South-eastern Asia and expanded the country list (adding Bangladesh, Thailand, Australia and approximate first-detection years) based on multi-country G9 reports.

EPP.common.name: Taura syndrome virus, TSV
Sub.regions: South America; Central America; Caribbean; Northern America
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp, predominantly L. vannamei (with involvement of other cultured penaeid species in affected farms)
Event.summary: Beginning in 1993, soon after its emergence in Ecuador, TSV‑associated Taura syndrome spread south to Peru and, from 1994, to Colombia, Brazil and the Pacific and Caribbean coasts of Central America, causing severe mortality in juvenile L. vannamei. By 1994–1995 the virus had reached Hawaii and coastal farms in Florida and Texas in the United States, and by 1995–1996 it had extended to Mexico and Belize, with further spread to virtually all major shrimp‑growing regions of the Americas by 1997. Cumulative industry losses during this American panzootic are estimated in the order of US$1–2 billion, and by the late 1990s TSV was widely endemic throughout the American shrimp‑farming belt.

Internal mechanisms: TSV’s efficient oral and horizontal transmission, high viral loads in clinically and subclinically infected shrimp, and environmental stability in pond systems facilitated explosive epizootics as the virus entered immunologically naïve farm populations across multiple countries.
Review: Review (classification and geography corrected). Simplified the Continent field to South America; Northern America and standardised the Countries list to recognised country names, removing state‑level labels (e.g. “USA – Hawaii”) that are not in the Country sheet. Corrected Colombia’s first‑report year from 1993 to 1994 and aligned the overall spread sequence with FAO/OIE timelines. Set inter_continental_emergence = Yes and intra_continental_emergence = No, because this linked panzootic includes first establishment in a new continent (Northern America); under the project rules, intra‑continental and inter‑continental categories should not co‑occur for the same linked episode. EPP.scientific.name: Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis
EPP.common.name: Xenohaliotis californiensis
Sub.regions: South America; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Western Asia
Host: Primarily farmed red abalone (Haliotis rufescens), with subsequent detections in other cultured abalones including European abalone (Haliotis tuberculata) and Asian species such as Haliotis discus discus
Event.summary: Beginning around the early 2000s, withering syndrome associated with Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis was introduced, largely via trade in infected Californian red abalone seed and broodstock, into overseas abalone aquaculture operations in Chile, several European countries (Iceland, Ireland, Spain, France) and parts of Asia (China, Chinese Taipei, Japan, Thailand, Israel). As the international abalone industry expanded, the pathogen was detected in cultured Haliotis rufescens in Chile and subsequently in European and Asian abalone species, with official notifications including a 2004 report from Iceland, a 2004 report of infection in Haliotis tuberculata in Spain, and a 2006 OIE report from Irish farms, followed by additional detections in France and multiple Asian hatcheries. Over the following decade and a half, affected countries implemented surveillance, movement controls, and husbandry changes to limit spread, and many farms adopted selective breeding, antibiotic treatments and improved biosecurity to manage the disease and maintain production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid globalization of abalone aquaculture and trade in live seed and broodstock from California facilitated long‑distance translocation of Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis to South America (notably Chile), Europe (including Iceland, Ireland, Spain and France) and Asia (China, Chinese Taipei, Japan, Thailand and Israel); limited early awareness and diagnostic capacity in importing regions delayed detection; intensive culture conditions in new environments promoted establishment. Internal mechanisms: The pathogen’s ability to infect multiple Haliotis species, survive transport with infected hosts, and persist in culture systems under a range of temperatures enabled successful colonization of new geographic regions and host species; in some European stocks of Haliotis tuberculata and cultured red abalones, infection dynamics and susceptibility patterns indicate host expansion and strain adaptation consistent with re‑emergence in novel host–environment combinations.
Review: Review – Retained as a single linked international aquaculture emergence episode capturing long‑distance spread of the pathogen via trade in Californian red abalone seed and broodstock. Sub_regions and country coding were expanded so that Chile (South America), Iceland and Ireland (Northern Europe), Spain and France (Southern and Western Europe), and China, Chinese Taipei, Japan, Thailand and Israel (Eastern, South‑eastern and Western Asia) are explicitly represented, and bracketed first‑detection years were added where supported by OIE notifications or primary reports (notably Iceland 2004, Spain 2004, Ireland 2006). EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: HPAI in wild birds
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; Central Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Africa; Western Africa; Middle Africa
Host: Migratory and resident wild waterfowl (e.g. bar‑headed geese, ducks, swans), gulls, grebes and a range of other wild bird species using Central Asian and Eurasian flyways
Event.summary: In spring 2005, a massive die‑off of more than 6,000 migratory waterbirds at Qinghai Lake in China revealed a novel H5N1 clade 2.2 virus causing high mortality in wild geese, gulls and other species, the first large‑scale HPAI epizootic in free‑living migratory waterfowl. During late 2005 and 2006, viruses closely related to the Qinghai lineage spread westward with migration along the Central Asian and Black Sea–Mediterranean flyways, seeding outbreaks and die‑offs in wild birds across Russia, Mongolia, Kazakhstan, the Middle East and Europe, and then in multiple African countries. By 2007 the initial wave had subsided, with H5N1 circulation shifting increasingly into poultry in many affected regions, though sporadic wild‑bird outbreaks continued along flyways.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance migration of infected waterfowl from Qinghai and other breeding areas, overlap between wild‑bird staging sites and backyard or commercial poultry, and insufficient biosecurity in Eurasian and African poultry systems enabled rapid inter‑continental spread. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of the Qinghai‑lineage clade 2.2 H5N1 with high virulence in waterfowl and efficient shedding supported both severe disease in wild birds and carriage over long migratory distances, representing geographic range expansion facilitated by viral traits and host ecology.
Review: review – Retain as the key 2005–2007 Qinghai‑lineage wave that first spread HPAI H5N1 via migratory wild birds from Asia to Europe and Africa. Host: Migratory and resident wild waterfowl (e.g. bar‑headed geese, ducks, swans), gulls, grebes and a range of other wild bird species using Central Asian and Eurasian flyways
Event.summary: In spring 2005, a massive die‑off of more than 6,000 migratory waterbirds at Qinghai Lake in China revealed a novel H5N1 clade 2.2 virus causing high mortality in wild geese, gulls and other species, the first large‑scale HPAI epizootic in free‑living migratory waterfowl. During late 2005 and 2006, viruses closely related to the Qinghai lineage spread westward with migration along the Central Asian and Black Sea–Mediterranean flyways, seeding outbreaks and die‑offs in wild birds across Russia, Mongolia, Kazakhstan, the Middle East and Europe, and then in multiple African countries. By 2007 the initial wave had subsided, with H5N1 circulation shifting increasingly into poultry in many affected regions, though sporadic wild‑bird outbreaks continued along flyways.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance migration of infected waterfowl from Qinghai and other breeding areas, overlap between wild‑bird staging sites and backyard or commercial poultry, and insufficient biosecurity in Eurasian and African poultry systems enabled rapid inter‑continental spread. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of the Qinghai‑lineage clade 2.2 H5N1 with high virulence in waterfowl and efficient shedding supported both severe disease in wild birds and carriage over long migratory distances, representing geographic range expansion facilitated by viral traits and host ecology.
Review: review – Retain as the key 2005–2007 Qinghai‑lineage wave that first spread HPAI H5N1 via migratory wild birds from Asia to Europe and Africa. Corrected event‑type flags so only 'inter_continental_emergence' is true (previously both 'intra_continental_emergence' and 'inter_continental_emergence' were true, which conflicts with the rule that only re‑emergence may co‑occur). Updated sub_regions to add Western Europe and Middle Africa (to reflect Germany, France and Cameroon) and removed Eastern Africa, for which no specific wild‑bird countries are listed in this row. Country list and narrative remain broadly consistent with the literature on the 2005–2007 wave.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: HPAI in wild birds
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; Central Asia; South-eastern Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa; Eastern Africa
Host: A wide range of wild birds including waterfowl, gulls, terns, geese, cranes and especially seabirds (gannets, skuas, cormorants), with frequent spillover into domestic poultry and wild and captive mammals
Event.summary: Around 2020, clade 2.3.4.4b H5Nx viruses, including H5N8 that subsequently reassorted into H5N1, began causing large‑scale outbreaks and mortality in wild birds across Asia, Europe and Africa, with wild birds increasingly acting as a long‑term maintenance host. Through 2021–2023, H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b produced the largest recorded HPAI epizootics in Europe and many parts of Eurasia and Africa, with year‑round circulation, repeated waves, and unprecedented die‑offs in colonial seabirds and other wild species, alongside massive poultry losses. Despite control in poultry sectors and seasonal declines after peaks, the virus has persisted in wild‑bird populations with continued recrudescence each migration season.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense poultry production intertwined with wetland and coastal habitats, ongoing poultry–wild bird interfaces, and large‑scale wild‑bird migrations across Eurasian and African flyways drove rapid geographic expansion and repeated reseeding. Internal mechanisms: Evolution of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 with a wild‑bird‑adapted neuraminidase gene, reassortment with local low‑pathogenic avian influenza viruses, increased virulence and broader host range (especially seabirds and some mammals), and enhanced capacity for year‑round persistence in wild‑bird communities underpinned the re‑emergence and panzootic behavior.
Review: review – Retain as the main 2020–2023 clade 2.3.4.4b panzootic wave across Asia, Europe and Africa. Adjusted event‑type classification so that this episode is treated as an 'intra_continental_emergence' (reflecting first establishment of HPAI H5N1 in some African sub‑regions such as Southern Africa) combined with 're_emergence' (novel genotype and altered host range), and set 're_occurrence' to false. Years are kept as 2020–2023 to capture the period of most explosive spread and unprecedented wild‑bird mortality, even though lower‑level circulation has continued beyond 2023.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; Central Asia; South-eastern Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa; Eastern Africa
Host: A wide range of wild birds including waterfowl, gulls, terns, geese, cranes and especially seabirds (gannets, skuas, cormorants), with frequent spillover into domestic poultry and wild and captive mammals
Event.summary: Around 2020, clade 2.3.4.4b H5Nx viruses, including H5N8 that subsequently reassorted into H5N1, began causing large‑scale outbreaks and mortality in wild birds across Asia, Europe and Africa, with wild birds increasingly acting as a long‑term maintenance host. Through 2021–2023, H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b produced the largest recorded HPAI epizootics in Europe and many parts of Eurasia and Africa, with year‑round circulation, repeated waves, and unprecedented die‑offs in colonial seabirds and other wild species, alongside massive poultry losses. Despite control in poultry sectors and seasonal declines after peaks, the virus has persisted in wild‑bird populations with continued recrudescence each migration season.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense poultry production intertwined with wetland and coastal habitats, ongoing poultry–wild bird interfaces, and large‑scale wild‑bird migrations across Eurasian and African flyways drove rapid geographic expansion and repeated reseeding. Internal mechanisms: Evolution of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 with a wild‑bird‑adapted neuraminidase gene, reassortment with local low‑pathogenic avian influenza viruses, increased virulence and broader host range (especially seabirds and some mammals), and enhanced capacity for year‑round persistence in wild‑bird communities underpinned the re‑emergence and panzootic behavior.
Review: review – Retain as the main 2020–2023 clade 2.3.4.4b panzootic wave across Asia, Europe and Africa. Adjusted event‑type classification so that this episode is treated as an 'intra_continental_emergence' (reflecting first establishment of HPAI H5N1 in some African sub‑regions such as Southern Africa) combined with 're_emergence' (novel genotype and altered host range), and set 're_occurrence' to false. Years are kept as 2020–2023 to capture the period of most explosive spread and unprecedented wild‑bird mortality, even though lower‑level circulation has continued beyond 2023.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: HPAI in wild birds
Sub.regions: Northern America; Caribbean; Central America; South America
Host: Wild waterfowl, shorebirds and especially marine and coastal birds (pelicans, boobies, cormorants, gulls, terns), with extensive spillover into sea lions and other mammals; concurrent outbreaks in domestic and backyard poultry
Event.summary: In late 2021, clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 of Eurasian origin was first detected in wild birds and poultry in Newfoundland, Canada, signifying a transatlantic introduction from Northwest Europe via migratory seabirds and waterfowl. During 2022–2023 the virus spread widely through wild birds across Canada and the United States, then moved south along flyways into Mexico, Central America and eventually much of South America, where it caused catastrophic mortality in coastal seabirds and pinnipeds and extensive poultry outbreaks. Although control measures reduced poultry impacts in some areas, H5N1 has remained established in wild‑bird populations throughout the Americas, sustaining recurrent waves of infection.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Transatlantic dispersal by migratory seabirds and waterfowl from Europe to Atlantic Canada, followed by spread along North, Central and South American migratory flyways, high‑density seabird colonies, and close contact between wild coastal birds and backyard or commercial poultry underpinned continent‑wide dissemination. Internal mechanisms: Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 demonstrated enhanced capacity for long‑distance transmission and adaptation to a broad range of wild‑bird and mammalian hosts, with reassortant Eurasian–North American genotypes in the Americas and increased neurotropism and virulence contributing to very high mortality in seabirds and marine mammals.
Review: review – Retain as the principal clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 wave in the Americas. Updated the country list to add Paraguay and the UK overseas territories Falkland Islands (Malvinas) and South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, which experienced major seabird and marine‑mammal mortality, and kept a generic 'other affected countries' clause for remaining states. Re‑classified the event as 'inter_continental_emergence' plus 're_emergence': this wave represented the first incursion of the EPP into South America (including Central America and the Caribbean) while also constituting a genotype‑driven re‑emergence in North America, where HPAI H5 had already appeared in wild birds in 2014–2015. 'Intra_continental_emergence' was set to false to avoid double‑counting.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Host: Wild waterfowl, shorebirds and especially marine and coastal birds (pelicans, boobies, cormorants, gulls, terns), with extensive spillover into sea lions and other mammals; concurrent outbreaks in domestic and backyard poultry
Event.summary: In late 2021, clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 of Eurasian origin was first detected in wild birds and poultry in Newfoundland, Canada, signifying a transatlantic introduction from Northwest Europe via migratory seabirds and waterfowl. During 2022–2023 the virus spread widely through wild birds across Canada and the United States, then moved south along flyways into Mexico, Central America and eventually much of South America, where it caused catastrophic mortality in coastal seabirds and pinnipeds and extensive poultry outbreaks. Although control measures reduced poultry impacts in some areas, H5N1 has remained established in wild‑bird populations throughout the Americas, sustaining recurrent waves of infection.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Transatlantic dispersal by migratory seabirds and waterfowl from Europe to Atlantic Canada, followed by spread along North, Central and South American migratory flyways, high‑density seabird colonies, and close contact between wild coastal birds and backyard or commercial poultry underpinned continent‑wide dissemination. Internal mechanisms: Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 demonstrated enhanced capacity for long‑distance transmission and adaptation to a broad range of wild‑bird and mammalian hosts, with reassortant Eurasian–North American genotypes in the Americas and increased neurotropism and virulence contributing to very high mortality in seabirds and marine mammals.
Review: review – Retain as the principal clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 wave in the Americas. Updated the country list to add Paraguay and the UK overseas territories Falkland Islands (Malvinas) and South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, which experienced major seabird and marine‑mammal mortality, and kept a generic 'other affected countries' clause for remaining states. Re‑classified the event as 'inter_continental_emergence' plus 're_emergence': this wave represented the first incursion of the EPP into South America (including Central America and the Caribbean) while also constituting a genotype‑driven re‑emergence in North America, where HPAI H5 had already appeared in wild birds in 2014–2015. 'Intra_continental_emergence' was set to false to avoid double‑counting.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Host: Primarily chickens (commercial broilers, layers, breeders and backyard flocks), with detections also in live bird markets; LPAI H9N2 viruses related to G1-lineage strains.
Event.summary: In 2006, H9N2 low pathogenic avian influenza was first detected in domestic poultry in Bangladesh, marking the introduction of this subtype into a densely populated poultry system in Southern Asia. Over the following years, H9N2 spread widely through commercial and backyard flocks and became endemic, with repeated respiratory disease outbreaks and production losses, especially in broiler and layer chickens and in urban live bird markets. By the early 2010s, phylogenetic analyses showed a relatively homogeneous endemic H9N2 genotype of Pakistani and Middle Eastern origin circulating throughout Bangladesh, prompting intensified surveillance and control efforts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of Bangladesh’s poultry sector, high bird densities, poor biosecurity in backyard flocks and live bird markets, and extensive live-bird movement within the country facilitated establishment and onward spread of the introduced H9N2 lineage. Internal mechanisms: introduction and subsequent local evolution of a G1-lineage H9N2 genotype carrying multiple gene segments from Pakistani H7N3 and other H9N2 viruses, with molecular markers associated with mammalian adaptation and efficient replication in chickens, underpinning re-emergence as a dominant endemic LPAI subtype.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12123974/))
Review: Retain with corrections. Evidence confirms first detection of H9N2 in Bangladeshi poultry in 2006 and subsequent endemic circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12123974/)) However, per the event-type definitions, this episode should not be coded as "first_detection" (LPAI and H9N2 were already known globally) nor as intra-continental emergence (Bangladesh is in the same UNSD subregion as Pakistan, where H9N2 had circulated since 1998). The event is now coded solely as re-emergence driven by introduction and evolution of a new lineage in an already affected subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Dogs (companion animals); wildlife reservoirs such as rodents and hedgehogs; livestock (pigs, horses, cattle) as maintenance hosts for some serovars
Event.summary: From the mid-1990s onward, multiple European countries reported a re-emergence of canine leptospirosis, with increasing clinical cases and a shift in predominant serovars away from the classical Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae toward Grippotyphosa, Bratislava, Pomona and others maintained in wildlife and livestock reservoirs. This trend was documented across Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe as serosurveys in dogs and wildlife and case series highlighted rising exposure to these non-classical serovars and concerns that older bivalent vaccines no longer provided adequate coverage. Progressive roll-out of multivalent canine leptospirosis vaccines and adjustments in vaccination policies followed, reducing severe disease risk in some regions but leaving infection widely established in dogs and wildlife.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased contact between dogs and wildlife (especially rodents and hedgehogs) in urban and peri-urban environments, pet travel and trade within Europe, and incomplete vaccine coverage against the newly important serovars all contributed to the resurgence. Internal mechanisms: The growing importance of non-classical pathogenic serovars such as Grippotyphosa and Bratislava in canine infections represents a shift in serovar ecology and effective host expansion within dog populations, fitting the definition of re-emergence driven by changes in the pathogen repertoire rather than simple environmental fluctuation.
Review: Review – Intra-continental emergence was set to “Yes” in the original file, but available evidence shows longstanding leptospirosis across European subregions; the 1995–2015 pattern is best characterized as re-emergence with changing dominant serovars rather than first introduction into new subregions. The intra_continental_emergence flag has therefore been changed to false, with re_emergence kept as true; otherwise, geography and description are appropriate. Recommended status: retain as a major animal-health re-emergence episode but flagged for expert confirmation of the selected timeframe.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Sub.regions: Eastern Europe; Western Asia; Central Asia
Host: Domestic cattle
Event.summary: Following the 2015 incursion into south‑eastern Europe, LSDV extended its range north and east between 2016 and 2019 into the Caucasus, southern Russia and Kazakhstan, establishing endemic foci beyond the Balkans. Initial outbreaks appeared in the Caucasus republics and southern Russia, with further spread into Kazakhstan and neighboring areas in subsequent years. By around 2019, sustained vaccination and control campaigns had reduced reported outbreak numbers in many of these newly affected territories, although the virus became entrenched in some border regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Progressive spread along cattle movement routes and contiguous grazing areas from the Balkans and Türkiye into the Caucasus and Central Asia, aided by suitable climatic conditions for vector flies over extended summers. Limited early vaccination coverage and challenges in coordinating control across multiple jurisdictions facilitated continued expansion. Internal mechanisms: Viruses in this wave were closely related to earlier European/Middle Eastern field strains; geographic range expansion was driven mainly by host and vector ecology and movement patterns rather than clearly defined novel viral adaptations.
Review: retain – This row appropriately represents the onward spread from the Balkans into the Caucasus, southern Russia and Kazakhstan as intra-continental emergence within Europe and Asia, supported by EFSA/WOAH data and genomic studies showing close relatedness to earlier Balkan/Middle Eastern field strains. No corrections to geography or emergence type were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus monkeypox
EPP.common.name: Monkeypox virus, MPXV
Host: Humans; suspected exposure to small mammals (rodents) and possibly other wildlife reservoirs
