EPP.common.name: Paramyxovirosis
Host: Sheep; goats; various wild small ruminants in affected regions
Event.summary: In November–December 2013, China reported new PPR outbreaks in Huocheng County of Xinjiang after several quiet years following the 2007 Tibetan outbreaks, marking re-emergence of the virus and signaling a fresh introduction into northwestern border areas. Large-scale vaccination campaigns, culling in outbreak foci, and strengthened movement controls gradually contained the epidemic by mid-2014, although PPRV has continued to pose a risk of further spread within China and to neighboring countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement and trade of small ruminants across China’s western and northern borders and between provinces; dense sheep and goat populations (over 300 million animals) with limited prior PPR immunity outside earlier Tibetan foci; gaps in routine vaccination and surveillance that allowed undetected spread before recognition. Internal mechanisms: Rapid geographic range expansion of lineage IV PPRV across Eastern Asia following a likely single introduction around mid‑2013, as inferred from full-genome phylogenetics; high transmissibility and adaptation to sheep and goats facilitated extensive spread, with viruses from multiple provinces forming a closely related genetic cluster indicative of a recent common ancestor.

EPP.scientific.name: Poxvirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Pox viruses infection
Sub.regions: Southern Asia; Central Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Europe; Northern Africa; Eastern Africa
Host: Sheep; goats
Event.summary: From about 2005 to 2022 sheep and goat pox viruses caused recurrent and sometimes expanding waves of outbreaks across Africa and Asia, with occasional incursions into previously disease-free areas of Central Asia and Eastern Europe, such as Kazakhstan and parts of the Russian Federation. Individual country epizootics were often intense, involving thousands of outbreaks and major production and trade losses, but collectively they formed a pattern of persistent endemicity with periodic geographic expansion into new administrative regions and some new countries. Continued use of capripox vaccines, improved surveillance and targeted control campaigns have helped limit spread in some regions, but sheep and goat pox remain among the most important transboundary small-ruminant diseases in Afro‑Eurasia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expanding small-ruminant populations in low- and middle‑income countries; increased live animal trade and transboundary movement; low vaccination coverage and uneven veterinary infrastructure; socio-economic factors (e.g. conflict, poverty) reducing capacity for routine control; environmental conditions that facilitate congregation and long-distance movement of animals. Internal mechanisms: Predominantly geographic range expansion (inherent) of existing capripoxvirus lineages into new districts and some new countries; although genetic diversity exists, no single novel global lineage has been shown to drive this 18‑year pattern, so it is best described as repeated intra-continental emergence episodes rather than a discrete novel-genotype event.
Review: Review – Retained as a single high-level episode summarising major sheep and goat pox activity and geographic spread since 2005, but the event-type flags were adjusted: intra-continental emergence remains “Yes” to reflect spread into new subregions (e.g. Central Asia, Eastern Europe), while re-occurrence was set to “No” to comply with the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra- or inter-continental emergence. Country list still mixes historical first-detection years (e.g. Kazakhstan [1993]) with the 2005–2022 focus period and should be interpreted as indicative; consider refining these years in a future pass.

EPP.common.name: Pox viruses infection
Host: Cattle; occasional water buffalo
Event.summary: After initial transcontinental introduction of lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) from Africa into Israel in the late 1980s, the disease re‑emerged strongly from 2012, with outbreaks in Israel and neighbouring Middle Eastern countries indicating sustained establishment in western Asia. From 2013 to 2015 the disease spread widely through Türkiye, Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq and adjacent states, causing substantial cattle production losses and prompting emergency vaccination and movement restrictions. By around 2015 improved vaccination coverage and surveillance began to reduce the frequency of large epidemics in some western Asian countries, although the virus persisted endemically and served as a source for onward spread into Europe and further into Asia.

Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of LSDV within Western Asia from earlier foci in Israel and Egypt, followed by establishment in local vector–host systems; no specific novel genotype has been consistently linked to this regional wave, so changes are best characterised as range expansion and re-occurrence rather than major viral innovation.

EPP.scientific.name: Taylorella equigenitalis
EPP.common.name: CEM organism
Host: Horses (stallions, mares, one gelding; multiple breeds)
Event.summary: In December 2008, a Quarter Horse stallion in Kentucky tested culture‑positive for Taylorella equigenitalis during semen‑export testing, triggering investigation of what became the largest recorded contagious equine metritis outbreak in the United States. From late 2008 through 2010, federal and state authorities traced and tested roughly 1,000 exposed horses in 48 states, ultimately confirming 22 infected stallions, one gelding and five mares as T. equigenitalis‑positive carriers, all epidemiologically linked to a Fjord stallion imported from Europe in 2000. After extensive quarantine, standardized genital treatment and repeated negative testing of all infected and exposed animals, the outbreak was declared eradicated and the U.S. again considered CEM‑free, although the event highlighted the vulnerability of artificial insemination networks to silent dissemination from a single carrier horse.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread use of artificial insemination and shipped cooled semen, together with lapses in hygiene and incomplete screening of breeding stallions, enabled a single imported carrier stallion to disseminate Taylorella equigenitalis widely via semen distribution and shared handling equipment. Internal mechanisms: Persistence of T. equigenitalis in asymptomatic stallions and some mares, efficient venereal transmission and the organism's ability to survive in semen and on breeding equipment underpinned the large geographic footprint of the outbreak; molecular typing showed that U.S. isolates from this incident were closely related but did not identify a uniquely more virulent or resistant strain.
Review: retain – This multi‑state U.S. outbreak is clearly one of the most impactful modern CEM events, with detailed peer‑reviewed documentation of case numbers, geographic spread and control measures. The existing event narrative correctly reflects the scale (about 1,000 exposed horses across 48 states with 28 culture‑positive animals) and its classification as a major re‑occurrence rather than a new continental emergence. I retained the event as written, keeping the key Preventive Veterinary Medicine investigation, the Equine Veterinary Journal review and official U.S. extension materials as primary sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Taylorella equigenitalis
EPP.common.name: CEM organism
Host: Horses (domestic ponies, riding horses and draft horses; predominantly geldings with some stallions and mares)
Event.summary: In May 2024, the U.S. National Veterinary Services Laboratories confirmed Taylorella equigenitalis infection in an 11‑year‑old pony mare and subsequently in pony stallions on a farm in Orange County, Florida, revealing the first U.S. detection of CEM since the 2008–2010 outbreak and an infection that retrospective tracing showed had been present on the index farm since at least 2017. Intensive testing through late 2024 and early 2025 identified a total of 53 T. equigenitalis‑positive horses, including ponies, riding horses and draft horses, with 41 cases on the index farm and additional positive geldings on multiple trace‑out premises in Florida, Iowa, Maine, Maryland, North Carolina and South Carolina, while exposed horses in several other states were quarantined and tested. All infected and exposed horses were placed under regulatory quarantine, treated with standard genital cleansing and antimicrobial protocols and repeatedly re‑tested; by April 2025 most positive animals had cleared infection and further tracing was ongoing, but the outbreak appeared to be confined to a defined network linked to the original Florida premises.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term undetected carriage of T. equigenitalis in geldings and stallions on a Florida farm, combined with shared semen‑collection and sheath‑cleaning equipment, movement of horses off the property over several years and limited suspicion of CEM in non‑breeding geldings, allowed the organism to circulate silently from at least 2017 until detected in 2024. EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Western Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Primarily mango and other tropical fruits (mango, citrus, guava, papaya) in smallholder and commercial orchards, but also a wide range of cultivated and wild fruit hosts across African agroecosystems
Event.summary: In 2003 routine field surveys on the Kenyan coast detected an unknown Bactrocera of Asian origin that was later described as Bactrocera invadens and is now synonymized with B. dorsalis, marking the first major establishment of this species complex on the African mainland following the earlier but eradicated Mauritius incursion. Within just a few years the fly spread rapidly through East Africa and into West, Central and eventually Southern Africa as well as archipelagos such as the Comoros, Mayotte, Madagascar and, after earlier eradication, back into Mauritius, being recorded from more than 30–40 African countries by the early 2010s. Across much of sub‑Saharan Africa B. dorsalis quickly became the dominant fruit fly of mango and many other hosts, causing substantial yield and quality losses, market rejections and new phytosanitary barriers, so that by around 2015 it was widely regarded as a permanent, high‑impact pest and management focus shifted from eradication to long‑term integrated control and quarantine.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Transcontinental introduction from Asia, likely via infested fruit from the Indian subcontinent, initiated the Kenyan coastal outbreak, and subsequent rapid spread across Africa was facilitated by extensive regional trade in fresh fruit, weak internal quarantine, year‑round availability of highly suitable hosts (mango, guava, citrus, papaya) and broadly suitable tropical to subtropical climates. Internal mechanisms: The invading populations shared typical B. dorsalis traits of very high fecundity, strong flight and polyphagy; genetic studies show limited differentiation and signatures of recent demographic expansion, indicating one or few founding events followed by rapid range expansion and high gene flow across Africa. Compared with pre‑invasion fruit fly complexes dominated by Ceratitis spp., the arrival of this invasive B. dorsalis lineage represented a major re‑emergence of fruit fly damage driven by biological invasion and, after the earlier Mauritius episode, constitutes a continent‑wide intra‑continental emergence into new African subregions.
Review: retain (modified): This event is correctly among the largest global emergence events for B. dorsalis, but the original entry mis‑classified it as the inter‑continental emergence and understated the prior African incursion in Mauritius. The event has been reclassified as a major intra‑continental emergence and re‑emergence within Africa following the earlier 1996–1999 Mauritius episode, sub_regions have been simplified to the four relevant UNSD African subregions, and countries have been expanded and annotated with example first‑record years using EPPO and regional syntheses. The narrative has been updated to acknowledge the Mauritius precedent and the role of both mainland and island invasions; sources remain appropriate and highly relevant. Flag for review to confirm the chosen 2003–2015 temporal window and country list capture the most impactful phase.

EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Host: Papaya/papaw, mango, citrus, coffee berries, guava, tomato and many other tropical and subtropical fruits (≥35 host species recorded during surveys)
Event.summary: In the mid‑1990s, Bactrocera dorsalis (then known as papaya fruit fly B. papayae, now a synonym) moved from Papua New Guinea into Australia’s Torres Strait Islands and in October 1995 was detected infesting papaya near Cairns, marking the first major incursion of Oriental fruit fly into mainland Australia. The outbreak rapidly spread across a quarantine area of approximately 78,000 km² in north Queensland, where the fly bred in at least 35 fruit and vegetable species and threatened key tropical fruit industries. A national eradication campaign based on male annihilation, protein bait spraying and strict quarantine was implemented from late 1995 and, after four years of intensive operations, the pest was declared eradicated from mainland Australia in 1999, at a program cost of roughly AU$34 million and an estimated total industry impact of around AU$100 million.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high propagule pressure from neighbouring infested regions (Papua New Guinea and Torres Strait), movement of infested fruit and limited early surveillance at the time, combined with favourable wet-tropics climate and dense plantings of susceptible hosts around Cairns. Internal mechanisms: broad host range, high reproductive rate and capacity to exploit both rainforest and cultivated habitats facilitated rapid build‑up from small founding populations; however, no specific resistance or novel strain was implicated, and the population was successfully eradicated using area‑wide male annihilation and bait control once detected. (Supported by Queensland government summaries and detailed analyses of the papaya fruit fly eradication campaign.)
Review: review – New event added to capture the major papaya fruit fly/Oriental fruit fly incursion in north Queensland, which was one of the largest OFF eradication campaigns globally in both area and cost. Classified as intra-continental emergence because it represents the first confirmed occurrence of B. dorsalis sensu lato in the UN sub-region ‘Australia and New Zealand’ within Oceania, after earlier establishment in other Pacific sub-regions. Years, geography and impact metrics are well supported by Queensland government sources and eradication-campaign reports, but precise timing of initial island detections and full host lists could be further cross-checked against NAQS and QDPI technical reports.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera tryoni
EPP.common.name: Queensland fruit fly
Countries: Australia (Tasmania – north‑west and northern regions including Spreyton/Devonport [2018] and George Town [2018]
Host: Commercial and backyard host fruits (including pome and stone fruits and some vegetable hosts) in northern Tasmania horticultural districts and on Flinders Island
Event.summary: In January 2018, Queensland fruit fly larvae were detected in apricots from backyard trees on Flinders Island and at Spreyton near Devonport in north‑west Tasmania, triggering declaration of control zones in a state that had long been recognised as fruit‑fly‑free. Subsequent detections extended regulated areas to additional northern sites such as George Town, and the series of incursions prompted Tasmania’s largest single biosecurity response on record, including intensive trapping, baiting, fruit stripping, on‑farm hygiene measures and the establishment of contract fumigation and treatment capacity, with substantial compliance and export costs for growers. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, short generation time and ability to exploit many ornamental and fruit hosts; capacity for geographic range expansion into warm temperate zones; initial lack of effective native natural enemies prior to deliberate introduction of parasitoids such as Anagyrus kamali and Gyranusoidea indica and predators such as Cryptolaemus montrouzieri.
Review: review – Event is real and among the most important emergence episodes because it marks the establishment and subsequent containment of M. hirsutus on the continental United States. However, it was misclassified as an inter‑continental emergence in the original file: North America was already colonised in 1983–1984 via Hawaii, so spread to California and Florida in 1999–2002 represents a major re‑occurrence within an already infested continent rather than the first continental record.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6359081/?utm_source=openai)) Sub‑regions have been restricted to Northern America and Mexico/Central American countries were removed from this row to avoid mixing two continents and double‑counting spread already covered under the Caribbean–Central America episode. Recommended action: retain as a major event but keep flagged for expert review of the exact list of affected U.S. states and the end date of the episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Maconellicoccus hirsutus
EPP.common.name: hibiscus mealybug
Host: Fruit crops (e.g. soursop, citrus, carambola, grapevine and other fruit trees), ornamentals (especially Hibiscus) and various spontaneous hosts in and around orchards, vineyards and urban plantings
Event.summary: In 2010, hibiscus mealybug was recorded for the first time in Brazil in the northern state of Roraima on hibiscus and several other hosts, representing a southward extension from previously infested parts of northern South America. Over the following few years the pest spread rapidly within Brazil, being found by 2012 in Espírito Santo in the south‑east and subsequently in multiple northern, north‑eastern, central‑western and southern states, where it attacked a broad range of fruit and ornamental hosts and triggered concern about impacts on crops such as cocoa and grapevine. By about 2014, the species was established in at least 11 Brazilian states, and research and extension focused on documenting its host range, natural enemies and suitable integrated management options.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PHENHI/distribution/BR_rr?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Internal Brazilian movement of infested planting material (especially ornamentals and fruit trees) from the initial focus in Roraima; expansion of perennial crop and ornamental plantings across climatic zones favourable for mealybug development; limited early awareness and surveillance, which allowed populations to build up before detection in new regions. Internal mechanisms: Strong capacity for geographic range expansion across tropical and subtropical climates; polyphagy on numerous cultivated and wild hosts; effective local dispersal via crawlers and human‑assisted movement on nursery stock, enabling rapid colonisation of distant production regions once introduced.
Review: review – This is a genuine, high‑impact expansion episode in Brazil and should be retained, but several corrections were necessary. Evidence from EPPO RS 2013/009 and Brazilian studies shows that the first record in Brazil was in Roraima in 2010, not São Paulo, and that subsequent spread involved many states including Espírito Santo and several in the north‑east, central‑west and south.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PHENHI/distribution/BR_rr?utm_source=openai)) The original classification as an intra‑continental emergence has been changed to re‑occurrence, because South America (including the ‘South America’ UN sub‑region) was already infested (e.g. Guyana, French Guiana, Venezuela, Suriname) before 2010; Brazil represents further spread within an already affected sub‑region, driven by trade and internal plant movement rather than a first occurrence on a new continent or sub‑region. Recommended action: retain but have a regional expert review the precise list of Brazilian states and the chosen end year for the episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Tuberculosis
Host: Humans, especially people living with HIV attending rural hospitals in KwaZulu-Natal
Event.summary: In 2005–2006, an outbreak of extensively drug‑resistant tuberculosis (XDR‑TB) was identified around the Church of Scotland Hospital in Tugela Ferry, KwaZulu‑Natal, with extremely high mortality among HIV‑infected patients. During 2005–2007, South African surveillance revealed that thousands of TB cases in KwaZulu‑Natal were multidrug resistant, and a significant fraction met criteria for XDR-TB, signaling that highly resistant strains were already transmitting widely. Over the following years, this Tugela Ferry XDR‑TB cluster became emblematic of drug‑resistant TB in southern Africa, and international reports documented spread of epidemiologically linked MDR/XDR cases to other countries, prompting intensive infection‑control efforts, treatment program expansion, and research into shorter MDR/XDR regimens.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High HIV prevalence, overcrowded hospital wards, delayed diagnosis, and limited drug‑susceptibility testing allowed undetected MDR cases to evolve further resistance and spread in health‑care settings; weaknesses in second‑line drug management also contributed. Internal mechanisms: stepwise accumulation of resistance mutations to first‑ and second‑line TB drugs produced XDR-TB strains with high-level resistance; despite some fitness costs, these strains transmitted efficiently among severely immunocompromised patients, representing a clear example of re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance and enhanced transmission in a specific context.
Review: review – Narrowed the countries field to "South Africa [2005], especially KwaZulu-Natal Province (Tugela Ferry)" and removed the vague phrase about "later detection of linked cases outside South Africa" to avoid implying a separate inter-continental emergence episode; imported cases elsewhere are better treated as part of the same linked outbreak, consistent with the project rules. Event remains correctly coded as re-emergence driven by XDR-TB and should be retained after review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Tuberculosis
Host: Humans, including smear-positive pulmonary TB patients and previously treated cases
Event.summary: Around 2000, nationwide epidemiologic surveys and WHO analyses highlighted China as a country with a very large burden of MDR-TB, despite an overall decline in TB incidence. During the 2000s and early 2010s, surveys estimated that roughly one‑third of the world’s MDR‑TB cases resided in China, far exceeding its share of total global TB burden, indicating extensive resistance evolution and transmission. Implementation and scale‑up of DOTS and later MDR-TB programmes across China gradually improved detection and treatment, contributing to subsequent declines in TB incidence and better control of drug‑resistant disease, although absolute numbers remained high.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Historical use of non‑standard TB regimens, treatment interruptions, and health‑system gaps, especially among previously treated patients, selected for MDR strains; rapid urbanization and migration facilitated transmission. Internal mechanisms: evolution and regional spread of drug‑resistant M. tuberculosis lineages (notably Beijing genotype strains) with mutations conferring resistance to isoniazid, rifampicin and other drugs, some of which showed good transmission fitness under programmatic conditions.
Review: review – Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false. The emergence here is of widespread MDR-TB within China, not first presence of M. tuberculosis in a new Asian sub-region; under the project definitions, this is a classic re-emergence event driven by resistance evolution rather than intra-continental emergence. Re-emergence coding, geography and time frame are otherwise appropriate; event should be retained after review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
EPP.common.name: Tuberculosis
Host: Humans, especially urban TB patients and those previously treated for TB
Event.summary: By the mid‑2000s, India began reporting growing numbers of MDR-TB cases, initially concentrated in large cities and among previously treated patients, signaling a shift from sporadic resistance to a large‑scale MDR epidemic. Between about 2005 and 2015, the country’s MDR/RR‑TB burden increased to become one of the highest in the world, with India ultimately ranked among the top global contributors to MDR-TB incidence in WHO reports. Expansion of the Revised National TB Control Programme, introduction of programmatic MDR‑TB treatment, and rollout of rapid molecular testing subsequently improved detection and management, though the absolute burden of drug‑resistant TB remained substantial.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High background TB incidence, widespread use of private‑sector and often inappropriate TB treatment regimens, treatment default, and delayed diagnosis created strong selection for resistance and ongoing transmission in densely populated settings. Internal mechanisms: emergence and clonal spread of MDR M. tuberculosis strains through accumulation of resistance mutations under widespread, sometimes unsupervised, antibiotic exposure, with some lineages maintaining sufficient fitness for sustained community transmission.
Review: review – Corrected intra_continental_emergence from true to false. India’s episode represents large-scale re-emergence of TB in drug-resistant form within an already endemic country and region, driven by resistance evolution and treatment/system failures, not first establishment in a new Asian sub-region. Re-emergence coding and focus on India as a top global MDR/RR-TB contributor remain appropriate; event should be retained after human verification of the chosen 2005–2015 window.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Balamuthia mandrillaris
EPP.common.name: granulomatous amebic encephalitis
Host: Humans of all ages, including children and older adults; both cutaneous balamuthiasis and CNS disease (encephalitis and encephalomyelitis) have been described.
Event.summary: China’s earliest reported Balamuthia mandrillaris case had onset in 2002, but cases remained poorly recognized until systematic reviews revealed a growing series of infections over the following two decades. Between 2002 and September 2025, at least 66 confirmed Balamuthia infections were reported in China, with patients drawn from multiple provinces and many diagnosed using metagenomic next‑generation sequencing or species‑specific PCR. Despite occasional therapeutic successes, most Chinese patients died, and by the 2020s Balamuthia was increasingly recognized domestically as a rare but serious cause of granulomatous encephalitis and cutaneous disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of tertiary‑care capacity and of advanced diagnostic tools (particularly metagenomic next‑generation sequencing of cerebrospinal fluid and tissue, and wider availability of species‑specific PCR) enabled recognition of Balamuthia in patients who previously would have been labeled as having idiopathic encephalitis or brain tumors; increasing publication of case reports in Chinese and English amplified awareness. Internal mechanisms: Current data do not implicate a distinct, more virulent Chinese lineage; this episode is best interpreted as intra‑continental emergence of recognized disease into Eastern Asia, driven by diagnostics and reporting rather than newly evolved transmissibility or virulence.
Review: review – China clearly represents one of the largest national clusters (66 confirmed cases with onset from 2002 through 2025), supported by the recent Emerging Infectious Diseases review. However, the original row incorrectly marked this as both intra‑continental emergence and re‑occurrence; by definition re‑occurrence cannot co‑occur with intra‑/inter‑continental emergence and implies resurgence within a previously known subregion. The curated row treats China as an intra‑continental emergence episode within Asia, without tagging it as re‑occurrence; dates and case counts have been cross‑checked against the 2026 EID synthesis.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Balamuthia mandrillaris
EPP.common.name: granulomatous amebic encephalitis
Host: Humans, including children and adults, some of whom survived after aggressive combination antimicrobial therapy and, in selected cases, neurosurgical excision.
Event.summary: In 1997, clinicians in South Australia reported a fatal case of granulomatous amoebic encephalitis caused by Balamuthia mandrillaris, establishing the first documented human infection in Oceania. Over the following decade, additional Australian cases were identified, including a brain abscess successfully treated by complete surgical excision and prolonged multidrug therapy reported around 2010 and further encephalitis cases from Western Australia described in detailed neuropathological case reports. By the mid‑2010s, Australia had contributed several human cases, including rare survivors, demonstrating that Balamuthia is present in Australian soil and capable of causing severe CNS disease, even though reported incidence remained extremely low.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑level neurosurgical, radiologic and neuropathologic capacity in Australian tertiary hospitals enabled recognition of Balamuthia brain lesions and, in selected cases, allowed surgical management that contributed to survival; improved awareness and access to PCR and immunohistochemistry through collaboration with international reference laboratories facilitated species‑level diagnosis. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not suggest a unique Australian strain; rather, cases illustrate that early diagnosis, surgical debulking and multidrug regimens can occasionally overcome the organism’s intrinsic high virulence, while the underlying environmental distribution appears similar to that in other warm regions.
Review: review – The original row correctly identified Australia as the site of Oceania’s emergence but treated a 2010 successfully treated brain abscess case as if it were the first local human infection. Earlier literature documents a fatal Balamuthia GAE case in South Australia in 1997, which is the continent’s first recognized human case. The event window has been extended back to 1997, the summary updated to include the earlier fatal case alongside later survivors, and the inter‑continental emergence classification retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus kyasanurense
EPP.common.name: Kyasanur Forest disease virus
Host: Humans (cashew plantation workers, forest‑going villagers); associated monkey die‑offs and infected ticks
Event.summary: KFDV was first detected in Goa in 2015 during an outbreak in Pali village, Sattari taluka, with around 36 human cases and evidence of local tick and monkey infection, indicating in situ transmission rather than importation alone.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6938374/)) Over 2015–2018, KFD cases spread to multiple forest‑fringe villages in North Goa, with annual confirmed human cases peaking at approximately 284 in 2016 and continued transmission through 2017–2018 despite vaccination campaigns.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7187534/)) Strengthened surveillance, large‑scale vaccination of high‑risk communities, and public‑health interventions eventually reduced the number of affected villages and case counts after 2018, though KFD remains a recognized zoonotic risk in the state.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7187534/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement of infected ticks and migrant cashew plantation workers along contiguous Western Ghats forests from Karnataka into Goa, high occupational exposure in plantations and forest‑edge settlements, and initial absence of vaccination or recognition of KFD in Goa’s health system.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/kyasanur-forest-disease)) Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of endemic KFDV lineages into a new state, supported by phylogeographic reconstructions showing spread along the Ghats; no strong evidence for a novel genotype uniquely associated with Goa, so this is classified as First detection and Re‑emergence in Goa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7005018/))
Review: review – The description of the 2015–2018 Goa episode (index village Pali in Sattari taluka, 36 confirmed cases in 2015, peak of 284 cases in 2016 and continued spread to other villages) matches state surveillance data and detailed geospatial analyses, and this clearly ranks among the most impactful KFD events by case burden and geographic spread.([monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk](https://monkeyfeverrisk.ceh.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-05/Operational-Manual-Kyasanur-Forest-Disease-DHFWS-2020-compressed.pdf?utm_source=openai))  I corrected the event‑type classification by setting first_detection to false, because the first detection of KFDV in humans globally occurred in Karnataka in 1957; within the agreed framework, spread to Goa is best captured as re_emergence (range expansion within Southern Asia) rather than a new host‑system detection. All other fields and sources remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus cacheense
EPP.common.name: Cache Valley virus
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) – general urban and peri-urban residents sampled in serosurveys
Event.summary: Between 2004 and 2005, investigators conducted reduction neutralization tests on human sera from Córdoba City and the nearby suburban towns of Jesús María and Colonia Caroya in central Argentina and found roughly 6–8% of samples with neutralizing antibodies to CVV. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18930511/?utm_source=openai)) These results provided the first documented evidence that people in South America had been infected with CVV or a closely related orthobunyavirus, expanding the recognized continental range of human infection beyond North America. No discrete clinical outbreak was linked to these infections, so this episode represents sero‑epidemiologic detection of past transmission rather than an identified epidemic of symptomatic disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing or expanding circulation of CVV‑like orthobunyaviruses and competent mosquito vectors in temperate regions of central Argentina, combined with focused serologic surveys, enabled recognition of prior human exposure. Internal mechanisms: Serologic cross‑reactivity within the Bunyamwera/Orthobunyavirus group complicates precise attribution to CVV, but there is no clear evidence for a novel genotype or host shift; the event reflects geographic range recognition of existing virus circulation rather than intrinsic viral adaptation.
Review: Decision: review. The event correctly summarizes Tauro et al. 2009 and appropriately treats the finding as evidence of human CVV infection in Argentina, but the event-type coding has been corrected: first_detection is now set to false and inter_continental_emergence to true so that this episode is interpreted as first recognized occurrence in a new continent rather than a second global first_detection, in line with the largely mutually exclusive event-type definitions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bandavirus heartlandense
EPP.common.name: Heartland virus
Host: Humans (confirmed cases in Missouri, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Georgia, and Kentucky) and wildlife (white-tailed deer, raccoons, coyotes, moose, and other mammals as amplification or sentinel hosts)
Event.summary: Between 2009 and 2014, after the Missouri index cases, Heartland virus was detected in additional human patients in Missouri and sporadic patients in other midwestern and southern states including Oklahoma, Tennessee, Georgia, and Kentucky, while concurrent wildlife serosurveys documented HRTV-neutralizing antibodies in vertebrate hosts across 13 central and eastern US states, revealing a much wider enzootic range than initially suspected. During the same period, intensive tick sampling found HRTV-infected lone star ticks on case-patient farms and nearby conservation areas in Missouri and Kansas, indicating that the virus can overwinter and persist locally where competent vectors and vertebrate hosts are abundant. By the end of this episode, Heartland virus had transitioned from a localized curiosity to a recognized, albeit rare, zoonotic threat distributed broadly across much of the lone star tick’s range, leading to continued but low-level case detection rather than a discrete outbreak termination.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: broad geographic distribution and increasing abundance of lone star ticks across the central and eastern United States; high densities of white-tailed deer and other wildlife supporting large tick populations; land-use changes and suburbanization that bring humans, deer, and ticks into closer contact; and expanded targeted surveillance and serologic surveys in wildlife and humans that revealed previously unrecognized foci. Internal mechanisms: ecological and host–vector adaptation likely underlie the virus’s ability to persist across diverse habitats, but there is no clear evidence of novel strains emerging during this period; geographic range expansion appears primarily vector- and habitat-driven rather than due to a new genotype, so this is treated as re-occurrence within a previously under-recognized but existing range.
Review: review – updated the list of affected US states and timing in the countries and event_summary fields using wildlife serosurveys and synthetic reviews; removed the earlier, unsupported implication that Oklahoma’s first cases dated specifically to 2012 and now describe Oklahoma and other states as having sporadic human cases by 2014; overall classification as a multi-state re-occurrence driven by vector and host ecology remains appropriate, but per-state first-year annotations should be checked by a domain expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bandavirus heartlandense
EPP.common.name: Heartland virus
Host: Humans (adult patients with tick exposure, including severe and one fatal case)
Event.summary: Beginning in 2012, enhanced surveillance in Missouri hospitals, guided by CDC and state health authorities, identified additional Heartland virus disease cases beyond the two 2009 index patients, establishing the virus as a recurrent cause of severe febrile illness in the region rather than a one-off event. In 2013, a severely ill 80-year-old man from central Tennessee with extensive outdoor exposure was diagnosed posthumously with Heartland virus infection, representing both geographic spread of recognized human disease into the south-central United States and the first clearly documented Heartland virus–associated death. This multi-year episode ended without sustained community-wide outbreaks but solidified Heartland virus disease as a recognized, potentially fatal tick-borne infection in multiple US states and prompted more systematic tick and wildlife investigations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increased clinician awareness and targeted surveillance protocols for ehrlichiosis-like illness with negative routine tests; ongoing high exposure to lone star ticks in rural Missouri and Tennessee; probable underrecognition before diagnostic assays became available. Internal mechanisms: no specific new strain linked to this period; the notable outcomes (including the Tennessee fatality) largely reflect host factors (advanced age, comorbidities) and heavy exposure rather than documented changes in viral virulence, so this is categorized as re-occurrence related to detection and spread within an existing ecological niche.
Review: retain – event accurately summarizes the 2012–2013 cluster of six additional cases in Missouri and Tennessee, including the first clearly documented fatal case, and appropriately codes this period as re-occurrence within an already affected subregion; no corrections required.

EPP.scientific.name: Bandavirus heartlandense
EPP.common.name: Heartland virus
Host: Humans (at least two confirmed cases in Illinois) and ticks (Amblyomma americanum with HRTV RNA detected at multiple sites)
Event.summary: In 2018, Heartland virus infection was confirmed in two human patients from Illinois, accompanied by laboratory confirmation of HRTV in pools of adult lone star ticks collected at two locations separated by hundreds of kilometers, demonstrating established transmission within the state. Continued tick surveillance through 2019 found additional HRTV-positive tick pools and showed that ecologically suitable habitat for lone star ticks—and thus potential HRTV transmission—extends across much of Illinois. This episode ended without documented large human clusters but shifted Illinois from a predicted risk area to a confirmed site of human disease and enzootic circulation, informing public health messaging about tick-bite prevention in the Midwest.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: northward and westward expansion of lone star tick populations into Illinois, likely influenced by climate warming, changes in host (especially deer) distributions, and landscape fragmentation; increasing outdoor recreation and residential development in tick habitat. Internal mechanisms: inherent capacity of Heartland virus to be maintained in lone star tick populations and local wildlife, enabling establishment in newly colonized tick habitats; no specific novel strain was implicated, so this represents geographic range expansion driven largely by vector ecology rather than viral mutation.
Review: review – corrected the event summary to note that two human Heartland virus cases were identified in Illinois in 2018, consistent with the primary field investigation; classification as a re-occurrence driven by lone star tick expansion within the existing US range remains appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bandavirus heartlandense
EPP.common.name: Heartland virus
Host: Humans (primarily older adults with outdoor exposure, including severe and fatal cases)
Event.summary: Around 2019, Heartland virus disease was identified in an elderly patient in rural North Carolina who initially was suspected of having ehrlichiosis, highlighting that HRTV had become an underrecognized cause of severe tick-borne illness in the southeastern United States. Over the subsequent years, additional sporadic human cases were documented in eastern and northeastern states, and by late 2022 CDC summaries reported more than 60 confirmed infections from at least 14 states, with virologic and serologic studies detecting Heartland virus in ticks and wildlife in areas such as New York and Georgia, reflecting both gradual geographic spread and improved clinical recognition. In 2023, a fatal Heartland virus case acquired in the Maryland–Virginia region was described in detail, and subsequent updates through 2026 now list more than 80 human cases across 15 states, so public health responses have focused on clinician education and tick-bite prevention across the eastern, southeastern, and south-central United States rather than classical outbreak containment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: continued expansion and high densities of lone star ticks into the Mid-Atlantic and parts of the Northeast; increased clinical suspicion and testing for Heartland virus in patients with ehrlichiosis-like illness who test negative for common agents; aging populations with comorbidities who are more susceptible to severe outcomes; and recreational and residential use of wooded and edge habitats that sustain ticks and deer. Internal mechanisms: no distinct new genotype has been tied to these recent cases; severe and fatal outcomes, including the Mid-Atlantic death, appear linked mainly to host vulnerability and heavy tick exposure rather than clear increases in inherent viral virulence, so the pattern is best categorized as re-occurrence with geographic range expansion mediated by vector ecology.
Review: review – corrected the countries field and narrative to remove an unsupported implication that West Virginia had reported human cases by 2022 and to align state counts with CDC maps and recent case reports; event appropriately captures late-2010s to early-2020s geographic expansion, but precise first-case years for some states remain uncertain and should be checked in future updates.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Duck herpesvirus 1, Duck plague virus
Host: Commercial domestic ducks (meat and/or layer flocks) on three intensive farms
Event.summary: From February to June 2018, natural outbreaks of duck plague were reported on three commercial duck farms in Netrokona, Mymensingh and Nilphamari districts of Bangladesh, causing substantial mortality in flocks that had received duck plague vaccination; duck viral enteritis virus was confirmed by virus isolation and PCR targeting the DNA polymerase gene.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density commercial production, incomplete or suboptimal vaccination schedules, and likely exposure to contaminated surface waters or contact with infected scavenging ducks or wild waterfowl favored virus introduction and amplification on individual farms. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the 2018 isolates were almost identical to previously reported Bangladeshi, Vietnamese and Chinese duck plague viruses, indicating re-occurrence of an established virulent lineage rather than the emergence of a novel genotype.
Review: retain – Well-supported, multi-farm outbreak with virologic confirmation and phylogenetic data linking Bangladeshi field strains to broader Asian lineages; classification as re-occurrence in Southern Asia/Bangladesh is appropriate. While smaller in scope than the Haor episode, its clear documentation and demonstration of vaccine-breakthrough infections justify keeping it among the higher-impact modern events.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic haematopoietic necrosis virus
EPP.common.name: EHNV
Host: Wild European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis) as the confirmed host; co‑occurring native species such as Macquarie perch (Macquaria australasica) were shown experimentally to be highly susceptible and were almost certainly exposed in some affected impoundments, but clinical EHN has not been definitively documented in native fish during this episode.([ewater.org.au](https://ewater.org.au/archive/crcfe/freshwater/publications.nsf/3eb684c73f8449acca256f1200284afb/9ffa733471131b0aca25725f00244a04/%24FILE/Macq%20Perch%20reintrod%20Qbyn%20R%20-%20Web%202006.pdf))
Event.summary: From 1990 to 1994, EHNV caused recurrent mass mortality events in wild redfin perch across several impoundments in the upper Murrumbidgee River catchment, including Burrinjuck Dam, Lake Burley Griffin, Lake Ginninderra and Googong Reservoir, representing a major wave of spread north from the original Victorian focus into the Canberra region.([ewater.org.au](https://ewater.org.au/archive/crcfe/freshwater/publications.nsf/3eb684c73f8449acca256f1200284afb/9ffa733471131b0aca25725f00244a04/%24FILE/Macq%20Perch%20reintrod%20Qbyn%20R%20-%20Web%202006.pdf)) These outbreaks produced sudden die‑offs dominated by juvenile redfin but also occasionally affecting adults, and coincided with areas holding threatened native species such as Macquarie perch, which were likely exposed to the virus. Following this wave, EHNV became established as an endemic pathogen in redfin populations of the upper Murrumbidgee system, with later surveillance detecting the virus at low prevalence even as overt epizootics became less frequent.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Equine arteritis virus
EPP.common.name: EAV, Equine arterivirus
Host: Thoroughbred racehorses on the Arlington Park racetrack in Illinois and subsequently at other linked racetracks in Kentucky, Iowa and Nebraska
Event.summary: In the summer of 1993, a large epizootic of equine viral arteritis occurred over roughly eight weeks among Thoroughbred racehorses at Arlington Park racetrack in Illinois, with more than 200 horses developing clinical illness characterized by fever, respiratory signs, edema and urticaria. Infected horses subsequently moved to other racetracks, and related EVA cases were reported at Churchill Downs (Kentucky), Prairie Meadows (Iowa) and Ak‑Sar‑Ben (Nebraska), disrupting race meetings and training schedules across several US states. Track‑level movement controls, enhanced biosecurity, and natural resolution of clinical cases brought the multi‑track outbreak under control, after which EVA remained sporadic in US racehorses until larger Quarter Horse breeding‑farm outbreaks later in the 2000s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of incubating or subclinically infected racehorses between racetracks in the Midwestern racing circuit, combined with dense stabling, shared airspace and equipment, and lack of routine EVA vaccination in Thoroughbreds, created ideal conditions for intense respiratory spread and rapid dissemination along the racing network. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – efficient droplet and aerosol transmission of an existing EAV lineage in confined stabling; no clear evidence for a novel genotype, so this episode is best interpreted as a major re-occurrence driven mainly by horse movements and management factors rather than viral change.
Review: retain – This multi-track epizootic (>200 clinical cases across several US racetracks) is consistently cited as a major EVA event. Countries field updated to reflect spread from Illinois to additional US states, and the event summary expanded beyond a single racetrack; classification as a national re-occurrence without intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine arteritis virus
EPP.common.name: EAV, Equine arterivirus
Host: Quarter Horse breeding stock (stallions, mares and foals) on multiple breeding farms in several US states
Event.summary: From late 2005 through 2007, equine viral arteritis emerged as a major problem in the American Quarter Horse breeding industry when EVA was first recognized on a large breeding farm in New Mexico, where early pregnancy losses and abortions were traced to EAV infection. During 2006–2007, the outbreak expanded into a multi‑state occurrence, with EVA confirmed on premises in at least six US states (including Kansas, Montana, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Utah and Alabama) and additional respiratory disease, abortions, neonatal pneumonia and foal deaths, largely linked to movements and semen of infected Quarter Horse stallions. Quarantine of affected premises, extensive testing of stallions and mares, restrictions on shipment of semen, and increased vaccination and biosecurity measures gradually controlled the outbreak by 2007, but it caused substantial economic disruption and cemented EAV’s status as an important emerging reproductive pathogen in the US Quarter Horse sector.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive interstate trade in breeding stallions and cooled-shipped semen within the Quarter Horse industry, concentration of large numbers of pregnant mares on a few breeding farms, and historically low EVA vaccination coverage in Quarter Horses enabled rapid venereal and respiratory spread across multiple states; export and competition restrictions for affected horses amplified the economic impact. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – molecular epidemiology showed that the multi‑state outbreak was driven by a distinct EAV strain with characteristic insertions in nsp2 and ORF3 shared among isolates from several western and midwestern states; Enhanced Transmission – the carrier‑stallion state and efficient venereal transmission via semen were central to persistence and dissemination; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – rapid spread of this variant across a wide geographic area of the US within a single subregion.
Review: retain – This multi‑state Quarter Horse outbreak is universally described as one of the most significant EVA events since the 1984 Kentucky epidemic, with abortions, foal deaths, and widespread trade disruption. Minor edits were made to clarify that additional states beyond those listed were affected; type classification as a re-emergence driven by a distinct outbreak strain remains appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: RHD virus, RHDV (RHDV1/GI.1 and RHDV2/GI.2)
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Host: Domestic and wild European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus); some hare species (Lepus spp., including Sardinian Cape hare)
Event.summary: In 2010, a novel pathogenic lagovirus with distinct antigenic and genetic characteristics, later designated RHDV2 or Lagovirus europaeus/GI.2, was identified in domestic and wild rabbits in north‑western France, including cases in previously vaccinated and younger animals. Over the next several years, RHDV2 spread rapidly across continental Europe and nearby islands—including Spain, Portugal, Italy, the Netherlands, the UK and Ireland—often replacing classical RHDV1 as the dominant circulating strain. By around 2014, RHDV2 had become enzootic in much of Western and Southern Europe, with recurrent outbreaks in wild and domestic lagomorphs and initial documented spillover into hares.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive movement of domestic rabbits and rabbit products across Europe, high densities of wild European rabbits, and widespread vaccination programs targeting only RHDV1 which provided limited cross‑protection to RHDV2. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a recombinant GI.2 genotype with a distinct antigenic profile, broader age susceptibility (including young rabbits), partial escape from existing RHDV1 immunity and vaccines, and enhanced fitness relative to classical strains, resulting in rapid replacement of GI.1 and clear re‑emergence mediated by novel strain/genotype emergence and host expansion.
Review: review – Retain as the foundational global event for RHDV2 emergence but adjust classification. This episode represents (i) first detection of GI.2/RHDV2 globally and (ii) re‑emergence of the EPP in Europe driven by a novel genotype with altered antigenicity and host range. However, per project definitions, it should not be classified as intra‑continental emergence because RHDV (the EPP) was already widespread in all the affected European sub‑regions; spread of a new serotype within an already infected continent is to be treated as re‑emergence. Accordingly, intra_continental_emergence has been set to "false" while first_detection and re_emergence remain "true".
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Primarily mango (Mangifera indica) and other tropical fruits such as guava (Psidium guajava), Citrus spp., papaya (Carica papaya), as well as various wild fruits; later also recorded on numerous cultivated and wild hosts across sub‑Saharan Africa.
Event.summary: In 2003, a new invasive fruit fly in the B. dorsalis complex (later synonymized with B. dorsalis and described as B. invadens) was first detected in coastal Kenya and almost simultaneously in Tanzania, marking the beginning of a rapid invasion across sub‑Saharan Africa. Within a few years the species spread through East, Central and West Africa, reaching at least 11 countries by 2005 and ultimately most mango‑producing regions of sub‑Saharan Africa, where it became the dominant fruit fly on mango, seriously damaging fruit production and disrupting export markets. By the mid‑2010s, B. dorsalis was established across much of sub‑Saharan Africa, with ongoing management relying on lure‑and‑kill, protein baiting and biological control, but with persistent high impacts on smallholder and commercial orchards.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance dispersal via trade and informal movement of infested mango and other host fruits within and between African countries; rapid expansion of mango cultivation and marketing; weak cross‑border phytosanitary controls; favorable tropical and subtropical climates. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, strong attraction to methyl eugenol facilitating mate finding, broad host range, and competitive superiority over native tephritids (e.g. Ceratitis cosyra), enabling displacement of resident species and geographical range expansion across multiple African sub‑regions.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

Host: Primarily mango (Mangifera indica) and other tropical fruits such as guava (Psidium guajava), Citrus spp., papaya (Carica papaya), as well as various wild fruits; later also recorded on numerous cultivated and wild hosts across sub‑Saharan Africa.
Event.summary: In 2003, a new invasive fruit fly in the B. dorsalis complex (later synonymized with B. dorsalis and described as B. invadens) was first detected in coastal Kenya and almost simultaneously in Tanzania, marking the beginning of a rapid invasion across sub‑Saharan Africa. Within a few years the species spread through East, Central and West Africa, reaching at least 11 countries by 2005 and ultimately most mango‑producing regions of sub‑Saharan Africa, where it became the dominant fruit fly on mango, seriously damaging fruit production and disrupting export markets. By the mid‑2010s, B. dorsalis was established across much of sub‑Saharan Africa, with ongoing management relying on lure‑and‑kill, protein baiting and biological control, but with persistent high impacts on smallholder and commercial orchards.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance dispersal via trade and informal movement of infested mango and other host fruits within and between African countries; rapid expansion of mango cultivation and marketing; weak cross‑border phytosanitary controls; favorable tropical and subtropical climates. Internal mechanisms: High fecundity, strong attraction to methyl eugenol facilitating mate finding, broad host range, and competitive superiority over native tephritids (e.g. Ceratitis cosyra), enabling displacement of resident species and geographical range expansion across multiple African sub‑regions.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Host: Urban and backyard fruit trees and vegetable crops (e.g. citrus, tropical fruits) in affected neighbourhoods and nearby smallholder plantings
Event.summary: Beginning in 1999, Florida recorded repeated detections of Bactrocera dorsalis in urban and suburban areas, usually as single or few flies in traps around Tampa, Orlando and other central Florida locations, each triggering delimitation surveys and local treatments. In 2015, a much larger outbreak occurred in southern Miami‑Dade County, where 140 adult flies, 18 mated females and 8 larvae were detected in the Redland agricultural area and nearby suburbs, indicating an actively breeding population that prompted a major eradication program costing several million US dollars. By 2016–2018, eradication efforts had succeeded in removing the outbreak and the pest is still officially considered absent from mainland Florida, but sporadic new detections continue to occur and require rapid response to protect the state’s fruit industries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: repeated introductions via infested fruit carried in passenger baggage or commercial shipments from infested regions (Asia, Hawaii, Africa); year‑round availability of suitable hosts in subtropical south Florida; and high human population density and travel volumes that increase introduction pressure. Internal mechanisms: high dispersal and reproductive capacity allow small founder populations to reach detectable levels quickly, as illustrated by the 2015 Redland focus, but there is no evidence of resistance or unusually adapted genotypes; outbreaks have remained transient because of aggressive trap-based detection, insecticide baiting and other eradication measures rather than intrinsic limitations of the pest. (Based primarily on Florida and federal regulatory reports and the American Entomologist review of Bactrocera spp. detections in Florida.)
Review: review – Event retained as a major high-cost re-occurrence episode in Northern America but reclassified: inter_continental_emergence was set to No because B. dorsalis has been present in the USA (Hawaii) since the 1940s and was first detected in Florida in 1964; the 1999–2018 detections represent repeated incursions and a significant 2015–2016 outbreak in a previously known sub-region. Re_occurrence remains Yes to reflect repeated reappearance driven by introduction pressure rather than evolutionary change. Timeline, trap counts and cost estimates are consistent with the American Entomologist review and Florida regulatory documents, but detailed cost figures and the formal end-date of eradication should be checked against primary FDACS/USDA reports.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera tryoni
EPP.common.name: Queensland fruit fly
Countries: Australia (South Australia – Riverland pest-free area: Loxton [2014]
Host: Commercial and backyard fruit crops, mainly Citrus spp. and Prunus spp. (stone fruit) in the Riverland horticultural region
Event.summary: In January 2014, after more than two decades without fruit fly, two Queensland fruit fly outbreaks were declared in South Australia’s Riverland pest‑free area at Loxton and nearby Pyap following the detection of 11 male flies in traps within a fortnight, triggering quarantine and emergency response plans. Intensive baiting, hygiene measures and movement controls were imposed around 1.5 km outbreak zones and 15 km restricted areas, disrupting local marketing and requiring cold treatment or fumigation of fruit but successfully containing the pest. After approximately 12 weeks without further detections, authorities declared the Loxton and Pyap outbreaks eradicated in April 2014 and the Riverland regained its fruit‑fly‑free status.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance human-mediated movement of infested host fruit from endemic eastern Australian states into South Australia, breaching quarantine restrictions, is cited as the likely source of the outbreaks; high host availability in the irrigated Riverland citrus and stone-fruit production systems allowed rapid local build-up until emergency measures were implemented. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of novel genotypes, resistance or host range shifts was reported; the event reflects re-occurrence of an existing pest facilitated by trade and travel rather than evolutionary change.
Review: retain – Well-documented major outbreak in the Riverland Pest Free Area in 2014; locations, timing and quarantine measures are consistent with ABC and PIRSA sources, and classification as re‑occurrence (without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) correctly reflects that Qfly was already established elsewhere in the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region and no evolutionary change was involved.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera tryoni
EPP.common.name: Queensland fruit fly
Countries: Australia (South Australia – Riverland pest-free area: Renmark [2021]
Host: Intensive commercial horticultural crops in the Riverland including citrus, table grapes, and stone fruits, as well as backyard host trees in towns and settlements across the pest-free area
Event.summary: Beginning in late 2020 and early 2021, multiple Queensland fruit fly outbreaks were detected across South Australia’s Riverland pest‑free area, with early clusters around Monash, Glossop and Renmark rapidly followed by further detections in many towns, leading to loss of formal pest‑free status and extensive quarantine zones. Over 2021–2024, the number of declared outbreaks in the Riverland grew to more than 50, with severe impacts on growers who faced movement restrictions, additional cold treatment costs, market disruptions and labour-intensive on‑farm hygiene measures; the state mounted a large emergency response including area‑wide baiting, fruit stripping and mass release of millions of sterile flies. As of 2025–2026 the Riverland remains under active eradication, with numerous outbreak areas still in force and projected end dates in late 2026, and full reinstatement of pest‑free status pending successful completion of eradication and recognition by trading partners.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: This prolonged resurgence reflects repeated human‑mediated introductions of infested fruit from endemic eastern mainland states, high host density and continuous fruiting in irrigated Riverland production systems, and possibly warmer conditions and extreme weather (including regional droughts and subsequent wet years) that favoured survival and spread; lapses or challenges in enforcing quarantine restrictions between states and within South Australia also contributed, as acknowledged by government reviews. Internal mechanisms: Available reports emphasize demographic expansion of existing eastern Australian populations rather than emergence of a distinct strain; genetic analyses of incursions into South Australia and Tasmania indicate source populations from east‑coast Australia without clear adaptive novelties, so the episode is best classified as re-occurrence driven by external drivers and repeated introductions rather than evolutionary re-emergence.
Review: retain – Multi‑year series of more than 50 Qfly outbreaks across South Australia’s Riverland Pest Free Area since late 2020/early 2021, with large SIT programs and major market impacts; locations, timing and impacts are supported by PIRSA and ABC sources. Classification as re‑occurrence (without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) is appropriate, as the episode represents resurgence and repeated re‑introduction of an existing pest into a known sub‑region rather than expansion to a new continent or UN sub‑region.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryphonectria parasitica
EPP.common.name: chestnut blight fungus
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland – England (Warwickshire [2011]
Host: Castanea sativa (European/sweet chestnut)
Event.summary: At the end of 2011, inspections of a five‑year‑old sweet chestnut nut‑production plantation near Leamington Spa (Warwickshire) revealed numerous trees with cankers and dieback, and laboratory testing confirmed Cryphonectria parasitica, marking the first detection of chestnut blight in the United Kingdom and in the Northern Europe subregion. Shortly afterwards, a second outbreak was found on a smaller plantation in East Sussex supplied from the same continental nursery source, and intensive surveys in 2011–2012 identified additional infected young chestnut trees linked to this planting material, although infections remained confined to recently planted stock. All known infected trees at these early sites were felled, uprooted and burnt, surrounding areas were surveyed within 3‑km radii, and strict movement controls for chestnut plants were implemented, leading to an apparent short‑term eradication of these initial outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction via international trade in infected nursery stock from mainland Europe, with several English sites traced back to a single French nursery; planting of many susceptible young chestnut saplings for nut production created concentrated host resources in previously disease‑free areas. Internal mechanisms: aggressive European C. parasitica strains capable of rapid canker formation and dieback on C. sativa, but the early foci were limited in extent and amenable to eradication because the pathogen had not yet established widely in surrounding woodland or older trees.
Review: review – Retain as the first established occurrence of chestnut blight in Northern Europe, i.e. a valid intra‑continental emergence event; restricted the list of affected counties in the “countries” field to Warwickshire and East Sussex to match EPPO first‑report information and avoid including later detections that belong to the 2016–2020 re‑occurrence episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Diaphorina citri
EPP.common.name: Asian citrus psyllid
Countries: United States of America – Florida [2005] and later detections in other southeastern states (e.g. Louisiana [2008]
Host: Commercial and backyard citrus (sweet orange, grapefruit, mandarin)
Event.summary: In 2005, huanglongbing was confirmed for the first time in Florida citrus groves that had already been colonized by Diaphorina citri since 1998, initiating one of the most severe citrus disease epidemics recorded in the United States. Within about three years HLB, vectored by abundant D. citri populations, had spread to the majority of commercial citrus farms in Florida, causing rapid tree decline, reduced fruit quality, and sharp drops in statewide orange production. Through the early to mid‑2010s, continued spread to additional southeastern states and chronic tree losses in Florida led to sustained economic damage, large‑scale tree removal, and major shifts in grove management and planting decisions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High density of susceptible citrus plantings, year‑round suitable climate, and widespread presence of D. citri created ideal conditions for HLB introduction and explosive spread; movement of infected nursery trees and lack of early detection further accelerated the epidemic. Internal mechanisms: Highly efficient acquisition and transmission of CLas by D. citri, coupled with the pathogen’s systemic, incurable infection of trees and absence of resistant commercial cultivars, drove a severe re‑emergence of citrus decline in regions where the vector had already been established.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera glycines
EPP.common.name: soybean cyst nematode
Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event.summary: Although soybean cyst nematode had long been known from temperate northeastern and northern China, in 2008 it was detected for the first time on soybean in Zhejiang province in subtropical eastern China, marking a southward extension beyond its traditional cool‑climate range. Over the following decade, first‑report disease notes documented SCN for the first time on soybean in several additional southern and western provinces (Guangxi, Guizhou, Jiangxi) and, by around 2018, EPPO and Chinese sources reported it from further provinces including Beijing, Shanghai, Sichuan and Yunnan, showing that the nematode had spread widely into warm, high‑yield soybean areas. This internal range expansion increased the area of Chinese soybean production at risk from SCN and prompted intensified surveys, breeding of locally adapted resistant cultivars and integrated management recommendations aimed at limiting further spread and virulence evolution.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Southward and westward expansion of soybean cultivation in China, increased movement of infested seed and soil between provinces, and changes in climate and cropping systems that favoured soybean in warmer regions facilitated the spread of SCN into new agroecological zones. Internal mechanisms: Adaptation of SCN populations to warmer, subtropical conditions, high reproductive capacity, multiple generations per season and long‑term egg survival in cysts underpinned inherent geographic range expansion within Asia and justified classifying this episode as re‑emergence rather than simple redistribution within already infested provinces.
Review: Review: Retain as a major Asian re‑emergence episode but corrected event typing and host information. Set intra_continental_emergence=No because all listed detections occur within the existing Eastern Asia subregion (China), so the event reflects expansion within a subregion already known to be infested, and retained re_emergence=Yes to capture the clear southward/westward range expansion into new agroecological zones. Simplified the host list to soybean only, because tobacco infestations and the newly described tobacco‑parasitizing subspecies fall outside the defined outbreak period. Province‑level years are inferred from first‑report publications and EPPO summaries and appear reasonable but remain approximate; they are flagged for further checking against Chinese national records.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio cholerae
EPP.common.name: Cholera bacterium
Sub.regions: South America; Central America; Northern America
Host: Humans (general population in coastal and inland communities, including urban poor)
Event.summary: The event began in January 1991 with explosive cholera outbreaks due to Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor Inaba in coastal Peru, rapidly affecting major urban centres and riverine communities across the country. Within months, the same seventh‑pandemic strain spread via travel, trade, and contaminated water along Pacific and inland corridors across most Andean and many Central American countries, later reaching Mexico and causing limited autochthonous transmission along the United States Gulf Coast, ultimately resulting in over one million reported cases and nearly 10,000 deaths by 1994. Intensified water and sanitation interventions, food safety measures, and public health campaigns gradually reduced transmission, and by the late 1990s cholera had receded to sporadic or focal incidence in most of Latin America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Re‑introduction of seventh‑pandemic El Tor V. cholerae O1 into a hemisphere that had been free of epidemic cholera for roughly a century; heavy reliance on untreated surface and municipal water; rapid urbanization and growth of peri‑urban slums; regional food trade, coastal shipping, and river transport; climatic variability (including El Niño events) affecting coastal ecology. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence in the regional context (introduction and dominance of seventh‑pandemic El Tor lineage over any residual classical strains); Enhanced Transmission linked to the strain’s environmental persistence and high proportion of asymptomatic infections, facilitating sustained water‑ and food‑borne spread over a vast geographic area.
Review: retain – Major, well‑documented event with >1 million cases in the Americas. Corrected geography: continent now includes both South America and North America, sub‑regions restricted to South America, Central America and Northern America, and Uruguay and the Caribbean islands removed because they reported no cholera cases during this wave.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0020245299800025?utm_source=openai)) Event type adjusted from “inter‑continental emergence + re‑emergence” to “re‑emergence only”, in line with the rule that inter‑continental emergence should not be used when the organism is historically established on the continent and the apparent novelty is at strain level. Sources updated to emphasize PAHO/WHO and CDC MMWR over secondary summaries.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio cholerae
EPP.common.name: Cholera bacterium
Countries: Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo) – Goma and surrounding refugee camps [1994]
Host: Humans (Rwandan refugees in emergency camps, local host populations)
Event.summary: Following the 1994 Rwandan genocide, around a million predominantly Hutu refugees crossed into Zaire and Burundi, rapidly forming overcrowded camps around Goma and in northern Burundi with virtually no safe water or sanitation. Within days, explosive outbreaks of acute watery diarrhoea due largely to Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor and Shigella dysenteriae type 1 caused extremely high mortality, with crude death rates in some camps reaching tens of deaths per 10,000 persons per day and an estimated 12,000 or more cholera deaths in a few weeks. Massive international deployment of emergency water and sanitation interventions, rehydration therapy, and re‑organization of camp layouts gradually reduced cholera transmission over subsequent weeks, though the crisis left a large burden of mortality and became a paradigmatic example of cholera risk in mass displacement settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Sudden mass displacement of hundreds of thousands of people into densely packed camps; collapse of water, sanitation and health services; use of highly contaminated surface waters from Lake Kivu and nearby streams; severe malnutrition and co‑infections; insecurity and logistical constraints hampering aid delivery. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a novel strain or altered pathogen biology; the event represents re‑occurrence of existing seventh‑pandemic El Tor in an extreme humanitarian emergency.
Review: retain – Event is real and remains one of the most consequential cholera emergencies of the 1990s in terms of mortality among a concentrated population. Countries list has been narrowed to Zaire/DRC and Burundi, removing Rwanda which did not experience a comparably large in‑country epidemic during this episode; the main outbreaks were in refugee camps located in Zaire and Burundi.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673695903380?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re‑occurrence (no strain change, in a historically affected region) is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio cholerae
EPP.common.name: Cholera bacterium
Host: Humans (urban and peri‑urban communities, including informal settlements, and populations along river and road corridors)
Event.summary: The outbreak started in February 2006 in the Boa Vista neighbourhood of Luanda, Angola, and was rapidly recognized as a major cholera epidemic fuelled by grossly contaminated drinking‑water and inadequate sanitation in rapidly growing informal settlements. EPP.common.name: Cholera bacterium
Host: Humans (urban and rural populations; particularly high impact in densely populated high‑density suburbs and informal settlements)
Event.summary: Cholera re‑emerged in August 2008 in Chitungwiza and high‑density suburbs of Harare, Zimbabwe, against a backdrop of economic collapse, water system failure, and health‑system breakdown.
