EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio cholerae
EPP.common.name: Cholera bacterium
Host: Humans (rural riverine communities and urban/slum populations in Haiti and the Dominican Republic, with smaller outbreaks in Cuba and Mexico)
Event.summary: In October 2010, months after Haiti’s devastating earthquake, cholera was introduced into the Artibonite River region—molecular and epidemiologic evidence later tracing the outbreak strain to South Asia—and rapidly spread through river systems and informal urban settlements with poor WASH infrastructure. Over subsequent years, Haiti experienced persistent transmission and multiple epidemic waves, accounting for more than half of the world’s reported cholera cases in 2010–2011 and ultimately causing over 812,000 reported cases and at least 9,600 deaths, with sustained transmission and spillover to the Dominican Republic and smaller linked outbreaks in Cuba and Mexico. Intensified investments in water and sanitation, large‑scale oral cholera vaccination campaigns, and strengthened surveillance progressively reduced incidence, and by early 2019 Haiti reported its last confirmed case in this epidemic, allowing the country to be considered cholera‑free for more than a year by 2020, although a new outbreak began in 2022 outside this event window.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Post‑earthquake collapse and chronic weakness of water and sanitation infrastructure; contamination of the Artibonite River and irrigation canals; population displacement into camps and informal settlements; limited access to timely rehydration and health care; delayed recognition of cholera in a country that had not reported it for over a century. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence in the Hispaniola context through introduction of a South Asian seventh‑pandemic El Tor O1 Ogawa lineage with hybrid classical/El Tor traits, to an immunologically naïve population; Enhanced Transmission via prolonged environmental persistence in rivers and estuaries, facilitating spread to neighbouring Caribbean settings and Mexico.
Review: retain – This epidemic is unequivocally one of the largest cholera outbreaks ever recorded in a single country and had substantial regional spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7774537/?utm_source=openai)) Event type has been corrected from ‘intra‑continental emergence + re‑occurrence + re‑emergence’ to ‘re‑emergence only’, since cholera was historically present in the Americas and the novelty was the introduction of a new seventh‑pandemic lineage into a long‑cholera‑free region.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5948a4.htm?utm_source=openai)) Countries list and sub‑regions have been made explicit by adding Cuba and Mexico, for which small but genuine local outbreaks caused by the Haitian‑related strain were documented, while limiting the geography to settings with in‑country transmission (imported‑only cases elsewhere are referenced in the summary but not coded as part of the event).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3933092/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus C
EPP.common.name: Poliovirus (poliovirus 1; poliovirus 2; poliovirus 3)
Host: Humans, primarily under-immunized children under 5 years (with some older children/adolescents)
Event.summary: After the Americas were certified polio-free in 1994, pockets of very low oral polio vaccine (OPV) coverage in poor communities on Hispaniola allowed a Sabin type 1 vaccine strain introduced around 1998–1999 to circulate silently and diverge genetically. Between July 2000 and September 2001, 21 confirmed paralytic poliomyelitis cases (and additional compatible cases) occurred in Haiti and the Dominican Republic, caused by a vaccine-derived poliovirus type 1 that had regained neurovirulence and spread efficiently via the fecal–oral route in under-immunized neighborhoods. Intensified investigation, high‑coverage mop‑up OPV campaigns, and strengthened AFP surveillance stopped circulation by mid‑2001, and no further cVDPV1 transmission was detected in the Americas, though the event highlighted the risk of vaccine-derived outbreaks where coverage is low.([jamanetwork.com](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/articlepdf/194465/jwr1212-1-1.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Localized very low routine OPV coverage, absence of recent national immunization days, poverty, crowding, and poor sanitation in affected communities on Hispaniola permitted long-term person‑to‑person circulation of vaccine virus. Internal mechanisms: A Sabin 1 OPV strain acquired ~3% VP1 nucleotide divergence and recombined with other Enterovirus C genomes, regaining wild‑like neurovirulence and transmissibility; this constitutes the first recognized emergence of circulating vaccine‑derived poliovirus type 1 (cVDPV1) and a clear example of novel strain/genotype emergence from a vaccine strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2570794/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Major cVDPV1 outbreak (21 confirmed paralytic cases, first recognized circulating vaccine-derived outbreak globally) that was missing from the original dataset; added as a dedicated event row with correct years, continent (South America), subregion (Caribbean), countries (Dominican Republic and Haiti), and classification as re-emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence from OPV; sources updated to primary CDC and peer‑reviewed descriptions.([jamanetwork.com](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/articlepdf/194465/jwr1212-1-1.pdf?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus C
EPP.common.name: Poliovirus (poliovirus 1; poliovirus 2; poliovirus 3)
Host: Humans, predominantly children but also adolescents and young adults
Event.summary: In early 2010, after more than a decade without indigenous polio and eight years after the WHO European Region was certified polio‑free, Tajikistan detected a large outbreak of wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) traced phylogenetically to importation from northern India in late 2009, ultimately confirming about 460 laboratory‑proven paralytic cases and additional compatible cases.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24576474/?utm_source=openai)) During 2010 the same outbreak strain spread into neighboring Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan and into the Russian Federation’s North Caucasus region, affecting mainly un- or under‑vaccinated children and young adults and revealing substantial immunity gaps despite prior polio‑free certification.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5943a1.htm?utm_source=openai)) Aggressive outbreak response with multiple rounds of monovalent OPV1 and intensified AFP surveillance interrupted transmission in Tajikistan by mid‑2010 and in the wider region by early 2011, allowing the European Region to maintain its polio‑free status.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5943a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Declining or heterogeneous population immunity after years without cases, gaps in adult vaccination, high rates of labor migration and travel between India and Central Asia, and initial delays in outbreak recognition permitted a single importation to generate a large multi-country outbreak.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24576474/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The virus was a typical WPV1 lineage imported from India, without evidence of unusual virulence or novel antigenic properties; resurgence reflects re-occurrence of wild virus in previously polio‑free areas driven by immunity gaps rather than viral evolution.
Review: retain – Correctly captured as one of the largest post‑1990 WPV1 outbreaks outside the traditional endemic zone (≈463 confirmed cases). Countries list has been corrected to remove Uzbekistan, which did not confirm indigenous cases (only possible undetected transmission inferred from one exported case to Russia); subregions and continents remain accurate.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2010_11_13-en?utm_source=openai)) Classification as re-occurrence (wild virus return to a previously polio‑free region due to immunity gaps) without inter‑continental emergence is consistent with project definitions. Sources are appropriate WHO and CDC outbreak reports and epidemiologic analyses; recommend no further changes beyond this geographic correction.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus C
EPP.common.name: Poliovirus (poliovirus 1; poliovirus 2; poliovirus 3)
Host: Humans, predominantly inadequately immunized adolescents and young adults
Event.summary: Following re-establishment of wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) transmission in Angola and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) from 2006 onward, virus spread north into the Republic of the Congo and, in late 2010, triggered an explosive outbreak centered in the coastal city of Pointe‑Noire after a decade without detected polio there.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4156724/?utm_source=openai)) Between September 2010 and February 2011, at least 445 confirmed paralytic cases and 179 related deaths were reported—mostly in young adults with low lifetime exposure to OPV—giving an unusually high case‑fatality ratio of about 40–47% and overwhelming intensive care capacity.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4156724/?utm_source=openai)) Intensive multi‑round immunization campaigns with monovalent OPV1 targeting the entire population, combined with strengthened surveillance and cross‑border coordination with Angola and DRC, brought the outbreak under control by early 2011, with no further cases linked to this lineage after January 2011.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/8/11-0195_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A decade without local wild poliovirus circulation, low adult vaccination coverage, and weak health systems in parts of central Africa created a large susceptible adult cohort; crowded urban living conditions and delayed recognition of early cases in Pointe‑Noire facilitated rapid spread and high mortality.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/17/8/11-0195_article?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Outbreak viruses were WPV1 genetically related to strains circulating in Angola and DRC, with some studies suggesting relative resistance to neutralization by vaccine‑induced sera but no clear evidence of a fundamentally novel serotype or vaccine‑escape phenotype; overall this is best categorized as a severe re-occurrence of wild virus in a previously polio‑free country, not as re-emergence via new genotype.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4156724/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Added as a missing high-impact event: the 2010–2011 Republic of the Congo WPV1 outbreak is one of the largest and deadliest post‑1990 polio outbreaks (≈445 cases, ~179 deaths, unusually high adult case‑fatality), and was not represented in the original dataset.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4156724/?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence because it reflects re‑introduction of wild virus into a previously polio‑free setting with large immunity gaps, without clear evidence of stable, fundamentally novel viral properties that would warrant re‑emergence classification.

Review: retain – This lineage represents the first documented instance of sustained cVDPV2 transmission detected in high‑income, long‑polio‑free settings in Europe and North America and therefore has high strategic importance despite relatively few paralytic cases.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2022-DON408?utm_source=openai)) Event-type coding has been corrected: inter_continental_emergence is now set to “false” because the poliovirus EPP has long been present on all affected continents; instead the event is treated as re-emergence of poliovirus transmission from a vaccine-derived lineage in previously polio‑free regions. EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In December 2013, autochthonous chikungunya transmission was first reported in the Western Hemisphere on the island of Saint Martin/Sint Maarten, where an Asian‑lineage virus caused locally acquired cases in residents without travel history. Over 2013–2014 the virus spread explosively throughout the Caribbean, with PAHO and CARPHA reporting several hundred thousand suspected and confirmed cases and some territories (e.g. Dominican Republic) recording hundreds of thousands of infections. By late 2014 transmission had declined in many islands, but the epidemic established chikungunya as an endemic arbovirus in the Caribbean basin and marked the first inter‑continental emergence of the virus into the Americas.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5137246/?utm_source=openai))

Seasonal conditions favorable for dengue transmission similarly promoted Aedes proliferation and chikungunya spread. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic was driven by an Asian‑lineage virus already well adapted to transmission by Aedes aegypti, without evidence of a major new mutation; the key mechanism was geographic range expansion with efficient transmission in permissive vector and host populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4624217/?utm_source=openai))

The previous use of “first_detection” for this regional introduction was removed to avoid confusion with global first detection in humans (1950s East Africa). Geography (Caribbean subregion under the South America continent code) and timing are consistent with PAHO/ECDC documentation.

Event.summary: Following the 2013–2014 Caribbean introduction, chikungunya reached mainland South America in early 2014, with French Guiana reporting imported and then locally acquired cases and an estimated >16,000 clinical cases in Cayenne and surroundings. EPP.common.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In May 2016, Kenyan authorities reported a chikungunya outbreak in Mandera East sub‑county near the Somalia border, in a population that had not experienced major transmission since the mid‑2000s Indian Ocean wave. By late June, about 1,800 cases had been line‑listed, and WHO and national sources estimated that up to 80% of Mandera’s residents and roughly half of health‑care workers may have been affected, with linked cases reported across the border in Bula Hawa, Somalia. Transmission subsided later in 2016 after cross‑border coordination, vector control and community interventions were implemented, but the outbreak underscored the potential for large epidemics in East African border towns.([afro.who.int](https://www.afro.who.int/news/chikungunya-kenya?utm_source=openai))

Cross‑border population movement between Somalia and Kenya facilitated virus circulation and complicated response operations. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses showed circulation of an ECSA lineage virus carrying additional mutations (e.g. E1:K211E, E2:V264A) associated with enhanced fitness in Aedes vectors, supporting classification of this episode as viral re‑emergence driven partly by genetic adaptation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6493958/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event kept as an illustrative example of high‑attack‑rate re‑emergence in East Africa and of an adapted ECSA lineage but categorized solely as re‑emergence; an earlier “re‑occurrence” flag was removed to avoid overlapping categories. Country list clarified to name Somalia explicitly rather than “Somalia (border communities)”. Case estimates and attack rates rely on WHO AFRO and genomic/epidemiologic studies.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: plague bacillus
Host: Humans (predominantly bubonic plague, with occasional septicemic and pneumonic cases) in rural highland villages of Lushoto district and other foci in northern and central United Republic of Tanzania; reservoirs mainly commensal and wild rodents with flea vectors.
Event.summary: After sporadic plague activity in the early 20th century, human plague re‑intensified in Tanzania from 1980, with Lushoto district becoming a highly active focus; between 1980 and 1996 more than 6,500 human cases and ≈530 deaths were recorded, with major peaks after 1990. From 1990–1997, national surveillance reported repeated large waves, including 364 cases in 1990, 1,293 in 1991, and 444–947 cases annually between 1994 and 1996, largely concentrated in Lushoto and neighbouring highland districts. Through the late 1990s, strengthened surveillance, improved rodent and flea control, and better access to antibiotics gradually reduced annual case numbers, though plague has persisted at lower incidence in a small number of endemic villages.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: subsistence agriculture and food storage practices that attract rodents into mud‑and‑thatch housing; high household and peridomestic rodent densities in cool, humid highland environments; poverty, limited health infrastructure and delayed care‑seeking that allowed localised outbreaks to grow before control measures were deployed; land‑use and climate variability influencing rodent and flea population dynamics. Internal mechanisms: re‑activation and sustained transmission in long‑established natural foci of Y. pestis in Tanzanian highlands with classic flea‑borne transmission; available data do not indicate emergence of a novel genotype, host jump or antimicrobial resistance during this period, so the pattern is best classified as large‑scale re‑occurrence rather than evolutionary re‑emergence.
Review: retain – Added as a major omission: WHO regional summaries and Tanzanian field studies indicate >6,000 human cases and several hundred deaths in Lushoto and other foci between 1980 and 1996, with peaks of 1,293 cases in 1991 and >800 cases in several mid‑1990s years, making this one of the largest modern plague episodes globally.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0001706X9700096X?utm_source=openai)) Classified as re-occurrence (not re-emergence) because there is no evidence for a new strain, host jump, or resistance; changes are driven by social, ecological and climatic factors. Spatial resolution is national/highland rather than village‑level, so confidence set to 0.8.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: plague bacillus
Host: Humans (predominantly bubonic plague) in the coastal city of Mahajanga and surrounding urban/peri‑urban neighbourhoods, with Rattus rattus and the Asian house shrew (Suncus murinus) as key reservoirs and Xenopsylla cheopis and other fleas as vectors.

Intensive rodent and flea control, antibiotic treatment, and improved urban sanitation suppressed transmission, and after 1999 human plague again retreated mainly to the highland foci, although coastal rodent and shrew reservoirs persisted.

Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion from highland to coastal urban environments and establishment of a novel coastal reservoir community in which the Asian house shrew S. murinus became a major maintenance host, alongside R. rattus, while efficient flea vectors sustained intense human exposure; emergence of new Y. pestis ribotypes in Madagascar and the first naturally occurring multidrug‑resistant strain were documented during the 1990s, although not restricted to Mahajanga.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/4/1/98-0114_article))

EPP.common.name: plague bacillus
Host: Humans (mainly bubonic plague, with sporadic septicemic and secondary pneumonic cases) in rural Andean and adjacent coastal districts of the northern departments of Cajamarca, La Libertad, Lambayeque and Piura.
Event.summary: In October 1992, after many years with only scattered cases, bubonic plague re‑emerged in northern Peru, first in highland districts and then across parts of Cajamarca, La Libertad, Lambayeque and Piura, causing 120 reported human cases that year. National data compiled by WHO show a major escalation in 1993 with 611 cases and 31 deaths, followed by a further 420 cases and 19 deaths in 1994, making this the largest modern plague epidemic in the Americas. Intense control efforts—mass chemoprophylaxis for contacts, community flea control, rodent reduction campaigns and environmental sanitation—gradually reduced incidence after 1994, and by the late 1990s only smaller clusters persisted in the same rural foci.

Internal mechanisms: re‑amplification of entrenched Y. pestis foci with classic flea‑borne transmission to humans; available evidence from Peruvian and WHO reports does not indicate a novel genotype, host jump or resistance phenotype, so this multi‑year epidemic is best classified as a large-scale re-occurrence in previously affected subregions.

EPP.scientific.name: Shigella spp.
EPP.common.name: Shigellosis
Host: Humans (refugees and internally displaced persons, especially children)
Event.summary: Beginning in late 1993, large epidemics of bloody diarrhoea due to Shigella dysenteriae type 1 struck refugee and displaced-person camps in Central Africa, first in Nzangwa camp in Rwanda and then in camps in Tanzania and eastern Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo). Over 1993–1995, at least 11 major Sd1 epidemics occurred in camps in Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania and Zaire, with attack rates often exceeding 10–30% and camp-level case-fatality ratios up to around 9%, contributing substantially to excess mortality during the Great Lakes refugee crisis. The epidemics gradually declined as safe water supplies, sanitation, effective antimicrobials and better camp management were put in place, but they highlighted the devastating potential of multidrug-resistant Sd1 in crowded humanitarian settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Armed conflict and genocide in Rwanda and neighbouring countries causing massive population displacement into overcrowded, poorly serviced refugee camps; extremely limited clean water (initially often <1–3 L per person per day), inadequate sanitation, and shortfalls in clinical care; large-scale cross-border movements facilitating regional spread. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (multiply drug-resistant Sd1 strains with resistance to first-line agents such as ampicillin and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, often with reduced susceptibility to nalidixic acid); Enhanced Transmission (very low infectious dose of Sd1 combined with high faecal–oral exposure in camp conditions, enabling explosive camp-wide outbreaks).
Review: review – New event added to capture the 1993–1995 Shigella dysenteriae type 1 epidemics in refugee settings in Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania and Zaire/DRC, which had very high attack rates and contributed substantially to excess mortality in the Great Lakes refugee crisis. Classified as re-emergence of multidrug-resistant Sd1 in already affected African subregions, not as inter-/intra-continental emergence. Countries and dates are synthesised from Médecins Sans Frontières/WHO analyses and MMWR refugee surveillance; please verify the exact camp and country list for inclusion in a top‑10 event set.

EPP.scientific.name: Shigella spp.
EPP.common.name: Shigellosis
Host: Humans (primarily men who have sex with men; some travel-associated and foodborne cases)
Event.summary: From 2001, when Berlin reported a cluster of sexually transmitted Shigella sonnei infections among men who have sex with men, through at least 2015, several northern and western European countries documented intensifying shigellosis epidemics linked to MSM sexual networks. Early outbreaks in Berlin and later in London during 2004–2005 were followed by recurrent clusters in other cities in the United Kingdom, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, France and Germany, involving both Shigella flexneri and S. sonnei. Over this period, sexually transmitted shigellosis in MSM shifted from sporadic reports to a recurring and expanding problem, with fluctuating but persistent domestic transmission and growing recognition in European surveillance data.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increasing high-risk sexual practices and dense, interconnected MSM sexual networks across major European cities; international travel and mixing at sex venues and events; limited awareness of enteric pathogens as sexually transmitted infections. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission (adaptation of existing Shigella lineages to efficient faecal–oral transmission within MSM networks, including prolonged shedding and asymptomatic carriage); in some lineages, Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (emergence of multidrug-resistance plasmids shared between MSM-associated S. flexneri and S. sonnei strains).

Sub.regions: Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans (travellers returning from South Asia and local community cases in high-income countries)
Event.summary: From the early 2010s, the fluoroquinolone-resistant Shigella sonnei clone that had originated in South Asia was increasingly detected in travellers returning to Europe, North America and Australia, and then in domestically acquired infections. Over several years, this clone established sustained local transmission in multiple high-income countries, shifting shigellosis epidemiology from predominantly imported, fluoroquinolone-susceptible infections towards domestically acquired, fluoroquinolone-resistant disease. By around 2016, this lineage had disseminated across several continents and contributed substantially to the global burden of drug-resistant shigellosis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-volume international travel and migration linking South Asia with Europe, North America and Australia; empirical use of fluoroquinolones for diarrhoea in travellers and destination countries; sanitation gaps in some receiving communities and institutions. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (single successful fluoroquinolone-resistant S. sonnei clone within lineage III); Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (stable high-level fluoroquinolone resistance); Enhanced Transmission (clone maintains sufficient fitness to spread widely despite resistance-associated mutations).
Review: review – Event retained as a key global episode, but corrected in three ways: (i) continent list now uses 'North America' (not 'Northern America') to align with the specified continent categories; (ii) 'Southern Europe' has been added to sub_regions because Spain and Italy are explicitly included among affected countries; (iii) 'inter_continental_emergence' has been changed from 'Yes' to 'No', leaving 're_emergence' = 'Yes', since this episode reflects global dissemination of a resistant S. sonnei clone into continents where Shigella was already long established, which per the protocol is re-emergence via a novel resistant lineage, not inter-continental emergence of the pathogen itself.

EPP.scientific.name: Shigella spp.
EPP.common.name: Shigellosis
Host: Humans (children and adults; travellers and domestically infected persons)
Event.summary: From May 2014 to February 2015, the United States experienced a multistate outbreak of ciprofloxacin-resistant Shigella sonnei, with 243 laboratory-confirmed cases reported from 32 states and Puerto Rico, many initially linked to international travel. The outbreak strain subsequently spread domestically, including a large cluster in San Francisco and additional cases among men who have sex with men and homeless populations. By mid‑2015, investigations had documented several S. sonnei isolates meeting criteria for extensively drug-resistant shigellosis, highlighting a major re-emergence of highly resistant Shigella in North America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International travel from regions with endemic fluoroquinolone-resistant S. sonnei (particularly South and South‑East Asia); crowded or marginal living conditions (e.g. shelters, encampments) facilitating faecal–oral transmission; sexual networks among MSM; widespread empirical use of fluoroquinolones and azithromycin. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (combined resistance to ampicillin, trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, fluoroquinolones and decreased susceptibility to azithromycin, with some XDR isolates); Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (importation of the South Asian fluoroquinolone-resistant clone with subsequent acquisition of macrolide-resistance determinants).
Review: review – Event retained as a major North American episode, but 're_occurrence' has been changed from 'Yes' to 'No', leaving 're_emergence' = 'Yes'. This outbreak is best characterised as re-emergence driven by importation and spread of a multidrug-resistant, often fluoroquinolone-resistant S. sonnei clone, rather than simple recurrence of incidence due purely to external drivers. Timeline, affected areas and resistance profile match CDC MMWR and press-release descriptions; no changes were made to geography or sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Shigella spp.
EPP.common.name: Shigellosis
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2020]
Host: Humans (predominantly gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men; also some children and travellers)
Event.summary: From 2020 onward, surveillance in the EU/EEA has documented sustained and growing circulation of multiple multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant Shigella sonnei and Shigella flexneri clusters, especially among men who have sex with men, with more than 2,300 MDR/XDR infections reported since 2023 across at least 14 countries. These clusters build on earlier MSM-associated epidemics but involve more complex resistance profiles and several distinct genetic lineages distributed widely across Europe. By 2025, MDR/XDR Shigella had become a significant and recurrent challenge for European sexual health and infectious disease services, with sporadic spillover to non‑MSM populations and children.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent high-density MSM sexual networks across Europe; increased international travel and mixing at events after relaxation of COVID‑19 restrictions; ongoing antibiotic use in affected populations; disruptions in sexual health services and healthcare access during and after the COVID‑19 pandemic. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance (co-circulation of multiple MDR and XDR S. sonnei and S. flexneri clusters); Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (at least seven distinct MDR/XDR genetic clusters in MSM); Enhanced Transmission (efficient person-to-person spread at very low infectious dose in high-contact sexual and household networks).
Review: review – Event retained to summarise the broader 2020–2025 MDR/XDR Shigella situation in the EU/EEA, but classification has been adjusted: 're_occurrence' and 'intra_continental_emergence' are now set to 'No', leaving 're_emergence' = 'Yes'. Multiple novel MDR/XDR genetic clusters expanding within existing European MSM and community networks fit the definition of re-emergence driven by resistance and strain diversification, rather than simple recurrence or first detection in new European subregions. Note that this row partially overlaps the more sharply defined 2021–2022 XDR S. sonnei MSM outbreak; in future curation, consider whether to merge these into a single 2020–2025 MDR/XDR event with 2021–2022 as peak years. Sources (recent ECDC news and reports) support the timing, multi-country spread and case counts.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.common.name: Influenza A virus
Host: Humans (severe pneumonia, mostly in children and young adults) with concurrent massive outbreaks in domestic poultry

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza A virus
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Western Asia; Northern Africa; Eastern Africa; Western Africa
Host: Humans with severe zoonotic infection (especially children), against a backdrop of extensive poultry and wild‑bird outbreaks
Event.summary: From 2005 to 2007, new clades of H5N1 (including clade 2.2) spread westward from East and South‑East Asia via migratory birds and poultry trade, causing large outbreaks in poultry and wild birds across parts of Asia and Africa and leading to the first human cases in Turkey and several neighbouring countries. Within months, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Egypt, Djibouti and Nigeria all reported laboratory‑confirmed human H5N1 infections alongside major poultry epizootics, while Viet Nam, Thailand, Indonesia, China, Cambodia and Lao People’s Democratic Republic continued to report severe zoonotic cases. Intensified animal and human surveillance, mass poultry culling, and public‑health messaging eventually reduced human spillover, but H5N1 became endemic in poultry in several affected countries, particularly parts of Egypt and Indonesia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance migratory bird flyways, regional and international poultry trade, and inadequate farm biosecurity enabled trans‑continental spread from East and South‑East Asia into Western Asia and Africa; rural poverty and reliance on backyard poultry increased close human–bird contact. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (e.g. clade 2.2 and related lineages) with improved environmental stability and fitness in wild and domestic birds; geographic range expansion (inherent) into new ecological zones; continued host expansion to humans with very high observed case fatality.
Review: review – adjusted geography and emergence classification. Europe was removed from 'continent' and European countries without human H5N1 cases (Romania, Ukraine, Croatia) were removed from 'countries', because those countries experienced only avian outbreaks during 2005–2007. Country start years were corrected (e.g. Lao People’s Democratic Republic [2007] and Nigeria [2007]) to match WHO case tables. 'Intra_continental_emergence' and 'inter_continental_emergence' were set from Yes to No and 're_emergence' kept as Yes, since influenza A was already present on all affected continents and this wave reflects spread of a new H5N1 clade rather than first presence of the EPP in new continents.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Event.summary: In March–April 2012, a cluster of 13 cases of severe pneumonia among healthcare workers and patients at a hospital in Zarqa, Jordan, including two fatalities, was investigated and later retrospectively confirmed by serology and RT‑PCR as infection with a previously unrecognized coronavirus, now known as MERS‑CoV. In June 2012, a 60‑year‑old man from Saudi Arabia who developed acute pneumonia and renal failure and was treated in Jeddah had a novel betacoronavirus isolated from respiratory samples, providing the first virological characterization of MERS‑CoV. Following these detections, additional sporadic and small cluster cases were identified in Saudi Arabia and Jordan as awareness and diagnostic capacity increased, marking the global first emergence and first detection of MERS‑CoV infection in humans.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: zoonotic spillover from infected dromedary camels in the Arabian Peninsula, with close human–camel contact in farm and market settings, and limited early infection prevention and control (IPC) measures in hospitals that allowed intra‑facility transmission. Internal mechanisms: host expansion of a bat‑related merbecovirus lineage into dromedary camels and then humans; viral traits enabling infection of the lower respiratory tract and efficient person‑to‑person transmission in close‑contact healthcare settings, while maintaining a basic reproduction number near or below 1 in the community.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the first recognized human MERS‑CoV cluster in Zarqa, Jordan, and the index virologically characterized Saudi case in 2012; timing, countries (Jordan, Saudi Arabia), subregion (Asia – Western Asia) and classification as first_global_emergence and first_detection are consistent with primary WHO, CDC and NEJM sources, so no structural changes were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus
Host: Humans (camel workers, household contacts, healthcare workers and patients); reservoir dromedary camels
Event.summary: From early 2013 through mid‑2014, Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates documented 65 laboratory‑confirmed human MERS‑CoV infections, many occurring in defined clusters linked to healthcare facilities, households and dromedary camel holdings, while additional primary and secondary cases were detected in neighboring Gulf states including Qatar, Oman and Saudi Arabia. The episode was characterized by repeated introductions from infected camels into humans, followed by limited human‑to‑human transmission in hospitals and family settings across multiple countries within Western Asia, contributing substantially to the regional rise in MERS cases in 2013–2014. Intensified surveillance, improved IPC in healthcare settings and targeted control measures in camel farms and markets gradually reduced the frequency and size of clusters by mid‑2014.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: close occupational and cultural contact with infected dromedary camels (farms, racing, markets), high utilization of tertiary care facilities, and expanded case finding through enhanced surveillance all contributed to increased detection and healthcare‑associated amplification across the Arabian Peninsula. Internal mechanisms: widespread camel reservoir infection with MERS‑CoV strains capable of zoonotic spillover and efficient transmission in healthcare and household settings, though transmission chains in the wider community typically remained short.
Review: review – Removed intra_continental_emergence and re_emergence flags and set re_occurrence=true to better reflect that this multi‑country Gulf episode was a major resurgence and geographic broadening of MERS within the already affected Western Asia subregion, driven by zoonotic exposure and healthcare‑associated spread rather than the virus entering a new UNSD subregion or acquiring clearly enhanced virulence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.common.name: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus
Sub.regions: Europe – Western Europe; Europe – Northern Europe; Europe – Southern Europe; Africa – Northern Africa; Asia – Western Asia
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2012]
Host: Humans (travellers returning from the Middle East, family contacts, limited hospital contacts)
Event.summary: Beginning with imported cases to the United Kingdom and Germany in 2012 and accelerating over 2013–2014, several European and North African countries detected their first MERS‑CoV infections in travellers recently returned from the Arabian Peninsula, including the UK, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Austria, Greece, Türkiye, Tunisia, Algeria and Egypt. In a subset of these introductions, such as the UK family cluster, a French nosocomial transmission to a hospital roommate and a Tunisian family cluster, limited secondary spread occurred in households or healthcare settings, but transmission chains remained short and were rapidly contained. By 2015, Europe and North Africa together had reported only a few dozen cases and single‑digit deaths, and strengthened surveillance and IPC in receiving countries prevented any large‑scale outbreaks despite ongoing importation risk linked to travel and medical evacuation from the Middle East.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increasing international travel, labour migration and medical evacuation between the Arabian Peninsula and Europe/North Africa, combined with heightened clinical awareness and improved diagnostic capacity, led to detection of imported MERS cases and small secondary clusters. Internal mechanisms: the same Arabian Peninsula–derived MERS‑CoV lineages retained the capacity for human infection and limited person‑to‑person transmission in close‑contact settings, but there was no evidence of adaptation for sustained community transmission in Europe or North Africa during this period.
Review: review – Updated the event year to 2012-2015 to match the first imported cases to the UK and Germany in 2012, corrected the geography to include Europe, Africa and Asia (for Türkiye) while removing the unsupported 'Europe – Eastern Europe' subregion, and reset first_detection to false while retaining inter_continental_emergence=true to reflect that this episode represents the first documented in situ transmission of MERS‑CoV in new continents (Europe and Africa) through small household and healthcare clusters.

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus
Host: Humans (hospital patients, visitors, healthcare workers, household contacts)
Event.summary: On 20 May 2015, the Republic of Korea reported its first laboratory‑confirmed MERS‑CoV case in a traveller recently returned from Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, who became the index patient for a large nosocomial outbreak. Over the following weeks, healthcare‑associated transmission in multiple hospitals generated 186 confirmed cases and 38 deaths in Korea, with one infected contact travelling to China and becoming that country’s first MERS case, making this the largest MERS outbreak outside the Middle East. Aggressive public health measures, including rapid case isolation, closure or restriction of affected hospitals, extensive contact tracing and quarantine of more than 16,000 contacts, eventually interrupted transmission, with the last case confirmed in early July 2015 and no further major outbreaks reported in Eastern Asia thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: delayed recognition of MERS in the index traveller, repeated healthcare‑seeking at multiple facilities, crowded emergency rooms and multi‑bed rooms, and gaps in early IPC allowed extensive hospital‑to‑hospital spread; high domestic mobility and international air travel facilitated introduction and limited exportation of cases. EPP.scientific.name: Aspergillus fumigatus
EPP.common.name: aspergillosis
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Humans (clinical invasive and chronic pulmonary aspergillosis) with linked environmental reservoirs in agricultural soils and compost
Event.summary: Following the Dutch discovery of TR34/L98H pan‑azole–resistant A. fumigatus in the late 1990s, similar resistant isolates were increasingly reported from patients and environmental samples across multiple European countries from the early 2000s onward. Updated the event years to 1998–2015 and adjusted the Netherlands country start year to 1998, consistent with the first documented TR34/L98H isolates outside the original Dutch focus. EPP.common.name: aspergillosis
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Humans (clinical invasive and chronic pulmonary aspergillosis) with linked environmental reservoirs in agricultural soils and compost
Event.summary: Following the Dutch discovery of TR34/L98H pan‑azole–resistant A. fumigatus in the late 1990s, similar resistant isolates were increasingly reported from patients and environmental samples across multiple European countries from the early 2000s onward. Between roughly 1998 and 2015, surveillance studies and case series documented rapid expansion of TR34/L98H and later TR46/Y121F/T289A genotypes in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Denmark, Spain, Italy, Belgium, Norway, Austria and other countries, with resistance prevalences exceeding 10% in some centers and clear associations with breakthrough invasive aspergillosis on voriconazole therapy. By the mid-2010s, azole-resistant A. fumigatus was established across several European subregions, prompting an ECDC risk assessment, multicountry surveillance, and guideline recommendations to avoid azole monotherapy in high-resistance settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Europe-wide use of agricultural DMI triazole fungicides on cereals, ornamentals, and other crops created multiple environmental hotspots (compost, flower fields, greenhouses) where resistant A. fumigatus could evolve and persist; cross-border movement of plant material, compost, and air dispersal of conidia facilitated regional spread of successful resistant clones; high clinical use of triazoles for prophylaxis and treatment in oncology and transplant programs increased the selective advantage of resistant isolates once established. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via expansion of TR34/L98H and TR46/Y121F/T289A cyp51A promoter-repeat plus point-mutation genotypes conferring pan-azole or multi-azole resistance; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence of clonally related, environmentally selected lineages able to infect azole-naïve patients; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation in the sense that these resistant genotypes showed no obvious fitness cost and dispersed efficiently via airborne conidia across farms and urban environments.
Review: review – Retain this as a major event describing pan-European spread of environmentally selected azole-resistant A. fumigatus, but correct its interpretation. Updated the event years to 1998–2015 and adjusted the Netherlands country start year to 1998, consistent with the first documented TR34/L98H isolates outside the original Dutch focus. Removed the intra-continental emergence label, because per protocol new resistance genotypes in a species long present in Europe should be classified as re-emergence rather than intra-continental emergence of the EPP. EPP.scientific.name: Aspergillus fumigatus
EPP.common.name: aspergillosis
Host: Humans with invasive aspergillosis in the United States; environmental A. fumigatus in agricultural fields and flower production systems in Colombia and the USA
Event.summary: Retrospective and prospective surveillance of more than 1,000 U.S. clinical A. fumigatus isolates from 2011–2013 initially suggested an absence of TR34/L98H or TR46/Y121F/T289A genotypes, but re-examination identified the first U.S. clinical isolates carrying these tandem-repeat cyp51A mutations from patients sampled as early as 2008. In subsequent years, additional U.S. cases were reported and, by 2017, environmental sampling of azole-treated peanut fields in the southeastern USA recovered TR34/L98H isolates, confirming a local environmental source. Around the same period, intensive sampling of flower fields in Colombia yielded the first environmental TR34/L98H, TR46/Y121F/T289A, and TR53 azole‑resistant A. fumigatus isolates described in South America, establishing that environmentally selected multi-azole–resistant genotypes had spread into agricultural and clinical settings in both North and South America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Agricultural use of triazole fungicides (e.g., tebuconazole, propiconazole and related DMIs) in U.S. peanut production and Colombian flower cultivation created strong local selection pressure for azole-resistant A. fumigatus in crop debris and soils; international trade in plant material, bulbs, and compost likely facilitated long-distance dispersal of resistant clones; in North America, increasing clinical use of voriconazole and other triazoles for prophylaxis and treatment of aspergillosis amplified the clinical impact of resistant infections once strains were introduced. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via TR34/L98H, TR46/Y121F/T289A, and TR53 cyp51A promoter-repeat and coding mutations producing high-level multi-triazole resistance; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence of resistant environmental genotypes related to European and Asian TR34/L98H lineages but showing local diversification; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) across continents as these clones established in new agro-ecosystems and began causing human disease.
Review: review – Retain this as a major event covering the first documented entry and establishment of environmentally selected azole-resistant A. fumigatus in the Americas, but correct its classification and timing. Changed the event years to 2008–2017 and the U.S. country tag to [2008] to reflect the earliest known TR34/TR46 clinical isolates, while keeping 2017 for the first environmental detections in U.S. peanut fields and Colombian flower farms. Set inter-continental emergence to “false” because the EPP species was long present in both continents and this episode concerns resistant genotypes (re-emergence). The cited MMWR report, JCM first-detection paper, and environmental JAC articles appropriately document the clinical and environmental components of this event.

EPP.scientific.name: Aspergillus fumigatus
EPP.common.name: aspergillosis
Host: Humans with severe influenza A (including 2009 pandemic H1N1) or seasonal influenza admitted to intensive care units, many without classical immunocompromising conditions
Event.summary: During and after the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic, intensive care units in the Netherlands and Belgium noted unexpectedly frequent and often fatal invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in patients with severe influenza, including many who lacked classical EORTC host risk factors. Retrospective and then prospective multicenter cohort studies across the 2009–2016 influenza seasons showed that roughly 14–20% of mechanically ventilated ICU influenza patients developed influenza-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (IAPA), with substantially higher mortality than matched influenza patients without aspergillosis. This led to recognition of IAPA as a severe viral–fungal syndrome in a broader ICU population, and to changes in diagnostic and empirical antifungal strategies during influenza seasons, although the phenomenon represents a recurring complication rather than a self-limited outbreak.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The 2009 H1N1 pandemic and subsequent severe influenza seasons produced large numbers of critically ill, mechanically ventilated ICU patients with diffuse lung damage; frequent use of systemic corticosteroids and other immunomodulatory therapies in severe influenza further impaired antifungal defenses; high ICU occupancy and aerosol-generating procedures increased exposure to airborne Aspergillus conidia. Internal mechanisms: No specific new A. fumigatus genotype has been implicated; rather, severe viral lung injury and dysregulated host immune responses created a new high-risk clinical niche in which typical A. fumigatus strains could more easily invade lung tissue, effectively expanding the at-risk host group without clear evidence of fungal adaptation.
Review: review – Retain this event as a major, well-documented shift in aspergillosis epidemiology in European ICUs, but adjust its type classification and sources. Reclassified the episode as re-occurrence (driven primarily by external factors: influenza epidemics, lung injury, corticosteroid use) rather than re-emergence, because there is no evidence of a genetically altered A. fumigatus strain. The geographical focus on the Netherlands and Belgium and the 2009–2016 timeframe matches the seminal cohort data, though IAPA has since been reported more widely. Replaced the general Wikipedia link with the ECDC rapid risk assessment on influenza-associated invasive aspergillosis, which is more appropriate as an event-level source; this event should remain flagged for expert review as understanding of IAPA continues to evolve.

EPP.scientific.name: Aspergillus fumigatus
EPP.common.name: aspergillosis
Continent: Europe; Asia; North America; South America; Africa; Oceania
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Asia; Western Asia; Southern Asia; Northern America; South America; Northern Africa; Southern Africa; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans with severe COVID-19 (SARS‑CoV‑2 pneumonia) in intensive care units, typically mechanically ventilated and often receiving corticosteroids or other immunomodulators
Event.summary: With the onset of the COVID‑19 pandemic in early 2020, ICUs in Europe and Asia rapidly began reporting invasive pulmonary aspergillosis complicating severe SARS‑CoV‑2 pneumonia, and the term COVID‑19–associated pulmonary aspergillosis (CAPA) was introduced. Between March and August 2020, an international registry and literature review identified at least 186 CAPA cases across 17 countries, with ICU-level cumulative incidences ranging from about 1% to nearly 40% depending on case definitions and diagnostic intensity, and subsequent cohorts from Europe, Asia, the Americas, Africa, and Australia confirmed substantial CAPA burdens with high mortality. By 2021–2022, CAPA was widely recognized as a major fungal complication of severe COVID‑19 requiring targeted screening and updated diagnostic criteria in high-risk ICU patients, although incidence has varied over time with changes in SARS‑CoV‑2 variants, corticosteroid regimens, ventilation practices, and vaccination rather than following a single outbreak curve.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The global COVID‑19 pandemic generated unprecedented numbers of patients with extensive viral lung injury, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and ICU stays; widespread use of systemic corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) and other immunomodulators (e.g., IL‑6 inhibitors) further impaired antifungal immunity; overwhelmed ICUs and altered infection-prevention practices may have increased exposure to Aspergillus spores. Internal mechanisms: No specific new A. fumigatus lineage has been consistently associated with CAPA; instead, the combination of severe viral pneumonia, dysregulated host immune responses, and iatrogenic immunosuppression has created a new, very large high-risk host group in which typical A. fumigatus strains can cause invasive disease, making this a syndromic and host-population expansion rather than a genetically driven fungal change.
Review: review – Retain CAPA as a major global emergence event for aspergillosis during the COVID‑19 pandemic, but adjust classification, geography, and sources. Reclassified it as re-occurrence, because increased incidence is driven mainly by the external shock of SARS‑CoV‑2, corticosteroid and immunomodulator use, and ICU pressures, with no consistent evidence of a new A. fumigatus genotype. Added Oceania (Australia and New Zealand) and Australia [2020] to the geography based on published case reports, and broadened the source list to include the ECMM/ISHAM consensus criteria and key systematic reviews alongside the initial EID registry paper. Precise country lists remain illustrative rather than exhaustive and should be revisited as CAPA data continue to accumulate.

EPP.scientific.name: Aspergillus fumigatus
EPP.common.name: aspergillosis
Host: Humans with invasive or chronic pulmonary aspergillosis; environmental A. fumigatus in agricultural soils, compost, and urban environments in Iran and China
Event.summary: During 2003–2009, clinical surveillance in Iran identified azole-resistant A. fumigatus in approximately 3% of patient isolates, with the earliest TR34/L98H-positive isolate recovered in 2005 and additional resistant strains found in both clinical and environmental samples, indicating an environmental origin. In parallel, global surveillance in 2008–2009 and subsequent multicenter studies in China documented clinical and environmental A. fumigatus isolates harboring TR34/L98H and TR34/L98H/S297T/F495I mutations across multiple provinces, with clinical resistance prevalences around 2–3% and environmental hot spots in intensively fungicide-treated areas. By around 2015, these findings established the Middle East (notably Iran) and East Asia (notably China) as important additional regional reservoirs of environmentally selected azole-resistant A. fumigatus, contributing to the global dissemination of TR34/L98H-lineage resistance beyond Europe and India.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heavy and often repeated use of DMI azole fungicides in cereal, greenhouse vegetable, and ornamental crop production in Iran and China created strong selection pressure for azole-resistant A. fumigatus in soils, compost, and plant waste; rapid urbanization and construction, together with increased use of azoles in material preservation, may have further expanded environmental niches; limited routine susceptibility testing in many hospitals delayed recognition of resistance. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via TR34/L98H and composite TR34/L98H/S297T/F495I cyp51A promoter-repeat and coding mutations conferring high-level resistance to multiple medical azoles and many agricultural azoles; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence with both globally distributed TR34/L98H clones and regionally distinctive TR34/L98H/S297T/F495I variants; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as these resistant lineages became established in human disease and diverse environments across western and eastern Asia.
Review: review – This row has been added as a missing major emergence event to capture the documented rise of environmentally selected azole-resistant A. fumigatus in Iran and China, which together represent significant regional reservoirs beyond Europe and India. Classified as re-emergence because it reflects the spread of resistant genotypes (TR34/L98H and TR34/L98H/S297T/F495I) in regions where the species has long been present, rather than first detection of the EPP. The 2005–2015 window is anchored in the first Iranian TR34/L98H isolate (2005) and the 2008–2009 global surveillance and subsequent multicenter Chinese studies; precise country-specific start and end years may warrant fine-tuning as more longitudinal data emerge.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida albicans
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa
Host: Humans (people living with HIV/AIDS with advanced immunosuppression)
Event.summary: From about 1990 through the mid‑2000s, as the HIV pandemic expanded and many patients progressed to advanced immunosuppression, oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis due to Candida albicans became one of the most frequent opportunistic infections, affecting an estimated 80–90% of HIV‑infected individuals at some point in their disease course in many high‑burden African settings.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3218701/?utm_source=openai)) Throughout the 1990s and early 2000s, clinics and hospitals in Eastern, Southern, and Western Africa reported very high caseloads of recurrent thrush and dysphagia requiring repeated azole therapy, creating a substantial clinical and healthcare burden.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2843789/?utm_source=openai)) With the scale‑up of effective antiretroviral therapy around 2000–2005, rates of mucosal candidiasis declined sharply in patients achieving viral suppression but remained high in areas with limited ART access or poor adherence, so the problem became more localized rather than fully resolved.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9684632/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Global spread of HIV with large numbers of severely immunocompromised adults and children; delayed rollout and uneven coverage of effective antiretroviral therapy; malnutrition and co‑morbid infections; widespread but often intermittent use of fluconazole and other azoles for treatment and prophylaxis of recurrent mucosal candidiasis. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/host adaptation of C. albicans as an opportunistic pathogen in severely immunosuppressed hosts; later in the period, selection for azole‑resistant C. albicans and increased prominence of intrinsically less susceptible non‑albicans Candida species in some cohorts, setting the stage for subsequent resistance‑focused emergence events.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3218701/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Review – New high‑impact event added to capture the extremely common HIV‑associated oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis epidemic (tens of millions of cases) that was previously omitted. Time window (1990–2005) and representative African countries are approximate and focus on high‑burden regions rather than an exhaustive global list, so this row should be retained but checked by a human curator for geographic scope and country listing.

EPP.scientific.name: Candida tropicalis
EPP.common.name: candidiasis
Host: Hospitalized adults and children with Candida bloodstream infection in tertiary‑care hospitals (Brazilian sentinel network and Latin America Invasive Mycosis Network)
Event.summary: From March 2003 through December 2004, a nationwide sentinel surveillance study in 11 tertiary hospitals in nine Brazilian cities identified 712 candidemia cases with an incidence of 2.49 episodes per 1,000 admissions—2–15 times higher than many Northern Hemisphere series—with C. tropicalis the second most common species (20.9%) and a 30‑day mortality of 54%.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/1594610/?utm_source=openai)) Building on these findings, the Latin America Invasive Mycosis Network conducted a 24‑month prospective laboratory‑based survey between November 2008 and October 2010 in 21 hospitals across Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Honduras and Venezuela, documenting 672 candidemia episodes (overall incidence 1.18/1,000 admissions) in which C. tropicalis accounted for 17.6% of bloodstream infections, particularly among adults, with 30‑day survival around 59%.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0059373&type=printable)) Together, these linked surveys revealed a persistently high regional burden of candidemia in Latin American tertiary hospitals where C. tropicalis is a leading non‑albicans pathogen, prompting region‑specific treatment and prevention recommendations despite generally low azole resistance during this period.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high utilization of intensive care, central venous catheters, broad‑spectrum antibiotics, abdominal surgery and oncologic care in resource‑constrained Latin American public hospitals, combined with delays in blood culture diagnosis and limited early access to echinocandins, contributed to high candidemia incidence and mortality.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/1594610/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: during 2003–2010 most C. tropicalis isolates remained susceptible to fluconazole and other triazoles, with only sporadic decreased susceptibility, so this episode reflects a re‑occurrence and consolidation of C. tropicalis as a major bloodstream pathogen driven primarily by host and healthcare‑system factors rather than by a distinct resistant clonal lineage.

EPP.scientific.name: Toxoplasma gondii
EPP.common.name: toxoplasmosis parasite
Countries: United States of America [2017] (Midwestern hunting retreat area)
Host: Humans (deer hunters and family members consuming undercooked white-tailed deer meat)
Event.summary: In November–December 2017, a group of hunters attending a deer-hunting retreat in the Midwestern United States consumed freshly prepared venison that was served rare; eight of ten attendees developed febrile illness with headache and myalgia, and all eight had serologic evidence of recently acquired T. gondii infection. In 2018, public health authorities in Quebec investigated several returning hunters with similar syndromes, ultimately linking their illnesses to consumption of undercooked venison from white‑tailed deer hunted in the same region and season. The outbreak underscored the risk posed by North American wildlife strains and the importance of thoroughly cooking wild game meat; communication campaigns and hunter-targeted guidance followed, and no further cases associated with this particular retreat were reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cultural practices of consuming freshly hunted deer meat rare or undercooked at hunting retreats, limited awareness of toxoplasmosis risk from venison, and circulation of T. gondii in white‑tailed deer populations. Internal mechanisms: Meat-borne infection with wildlife-associated T. gondii haplotypes common in North American cervids, causing sometimes severe but self-limited disease in immunocompetent adults; available data do not establish recent parasite evolution, so the event is best characterized as a notable re-occurrence highlighting a wildlife transmission cycle rather than confirmed re-emergence.
Review: Review / likely exclude if restricting to top‑10 events. This venison-associated outbreak is well documented and important for demonstrating the role of North American wildlife strains and hunting practices, but it involved only eight confirmed acute cases and is therefore small relative to the largest outbreaks. The main correction is to reclassify it from re-emergence to re-occurrence, since haplogroup 12 and other wildlife genotypes pre‑dated this event and there is no clear evidence of a new host jump or novel strain emerging at this time. Retain only if the dataset aims to capture illustrative wildlife/meat-borne clusters; otherwise consider exclusion.
Review.Comment: We do not restrict to only top-10 events

EPP.scientific.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
EPP.common.name: gonoccocus
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans (urogenital and pharyngeal gonorrhoea)
Event.summary: In 2009, Kyoto, Japan reported strain H041, the first Neisseria gonorrhoeae isolate with high‑level ceftriaxone resistance, signalling that the last widely used monotherapy option was at risk. Between 2010 and 2014, additional ceftriaxone‑resistant isolates including F89 in France and Spain, A8806 in Australia and GU140106 in Japan were identified, often linked to international travel but causing only limited local transmission. These sporadic but worrisome strains demonstrated that ceftriaxone resistance could arise in multiple lineages, prompting more intensive surveillance, greater reliance on dual therapy and discussion of higher‑dose cephalosporin regimens.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive global reliance on third‑generation cephalosporins—especially cefixime and ceftriaxone—as last‑line empiric gonorrhoea therapy; incomplete surveillance in many countries allowing sporadic resistant strains to emerge before detection; continued high burden of untreated or partially treated infections. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition of mosaic penA alleles (including penA-34-like and related forms) and other chromosomal changes reducing affinity of penicillin‑binding protein 2 for cephalosporins; concurrent accumulation of additional resistance determinants (e.g. penicillinase, fluoroquinolone resistance), producing multidrug‑resistant phenotypes; biological fitness sufficient for sporadic spread but generally limited compared with fully susceptible strains, which helped prevent global establishment of these early clones.
Review: Review – Correctly identifies the early sporadic ceftriaxone-resistant strains (H041, F89, A8806 and GU140106) as a major re-emergence episode threatening last-line therapy. Updated the time span to 2009–2014 and removed intra- and inter-continental emergence flags, since these resistance phenotypes represent new strains of an already globally distributed pathogen rather than first presence of the species on new continents.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: Nipah henipavirus, Nipah virus
Host: Humans (pig farmers, abattoir workers), pigs (amplifying host); Pteropus fruit bats (reservoir, implicated epidemiologically)
Event.summary: From September 1998, a new syndrome of encephalitis and respiratory disease emerged among pig farmers in Perak and later in major pig‑farming districts of Negeri Sembilan and Selangor, Malaysia, and was traced to a novel bat‑borne paramyxovirus that had spilled over into intensively raised pigs. Movement of infected pigs disseminated infection between farms and across the border to abattoir workers in Singapore, ultimately causing roughly 265–276 human cases and more than 100 deaths. The outbreak was halted by mass culling of pigs, closure of affected farms, and strict movement restrictions, after which no further large pig‑associated human Nipah outbreaks occurred in Malaysia or Singapore.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid intensification and high density of commercial pig production, planting of fruit trees near pig sheds, and frequent movement of live pigs between farms and to Singapore abattoirs allowed repeated contact between Pteropus fruit bats, pigs, and humans. Internal mechanisms: host expansion from bats to pigs and humans, high viral shedding in pig respiratory secretions, and Nipah virus’s strong neurotropic and pneumotropic properties enabled efficient pig‑to‑human transmission and severe disease in humans.
Review: retain – correctly describes the first recognized human Nipah virus outbreak in Malaysia and linked cases in Singapore, with appropriate geography, timing, event typing (first/global emergence and first detection), and high‑quality primary sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Escherichia coli
Host: Humans (consumers of prepackaged fresh spinach)
Event.summary: From late August to early October 2006, a large North American outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 infections was linked to prepackaged fresh spinach grown in California and distributed widely across the United States and parts of Canada. By early October, U.S. authorities reported roughly 199 confirmed cases from 26–27 states, with at least three deaths and dozens of hemolytic uremic syndrome cases, and a small number of related illnesses were reported in Ontario. The outbreak ended after nationwide recalls of spinach, consumer advisories, and subsequent changes in leafy-green safety practices, including the establishment of the California Leafy Greens Marketing Agreement.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large-scale cultivation and centralized processing of leafy greens; likely fecal contamination of fields or processing water from nearby livestock or wildlife; widespread distribution of bagged spinach enabling rapid multi-state spread. Internal mechanisms: typical highly virulent O157:H7 with strong association with HUS; no documented novel strain emergence, but the event underscored STEC’s capacity for severe disease from minimally processed produce.
Review: retain – Correctly describes the 2006 spinach-associated O157:H7 outbreak (≈199 U.S. cases, 3 deaths, plus a Canadian case) and its regulatory impact on leafy-green safety. Geography (U.S. and Ontario), timing, and classification as a re‑occurrence driven by produce-contamination pathways are appropriate, and the CDC/MMWR sources are suitable. No further changes recommended.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Escherichia coli
Host: Humans (primarily young children with HUS after STEC O26:H11 infection; one travel-related case in Italy)
Event.summary: In early 2016, Romania detected an unusual rise in hemolytic uremic syndrome among infants and young children, and investigations confirmed a community-wide outbreak caused mainly by Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli O26:H11, with around 30–32 pediatric HUS cases and at least three deaths. Epidemiologic studies suggested a link to dairy products from a local Romanian producer, and a related HUS case in Italy was traced to cheese imported from Romania, indicating limited cross-border spread. The outbreak subsided after recall of suspect dairy products, enhanced hygiene measures at implicated facilities, and heightened surveillance, though STEC O26 continued to circulate sporadically in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Possible contamination within small-scale dairy processing and distribution; insufficient pasteurization or post-processing hygiene; limited routine STEC testing in dairy supply chains; high exposure of infants and toddlers to locally produced dairy foods. Internal mechanisms: dominance of STEC O26:H11 ST21 lineage strains carrying virulence genes associated with severe pediatric HUS (novel or newly recognized high-risk clone in the regional context), consistent with a re‑emergence event driven by strain characteristics.
Review: retain – Correctly captures the 2016 multi-country O26:H11 HUS outbreak centered in Romania with a linked case in Italy. Geography (Eastern and Southern Europe), case numbers, dairy linkage and molecular characterization of the ST21 clone match ECDC/EFSA and Eurosurveillance descriptions. Classification as a re‑emergence (due to a particularly virulent regional O26 lineage rather than simply increased exposure) is defensible. No major corrections required.

Event.summary: In 2014, a large multinational outbreak of Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis phage type 14b infections occurred in Europe, first detected in the United Kingdom and Germany and then recognized in Austria, France and Luxembourg. After contaminated flocks were culled or controlled and implicated egg batches were withdrawn, case numbers declined and the outbreak was considered over later that year.

Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain did not represent a fundamentally new serovar but rather a successful epidemic clone of S. Enteritidis; its impact derived mainly from food‑chain amplification and possible adaptations for persistence in poultry environments (Enhanced Transmission via the poultry‑egg pathway).

Enteritidis was already well established across Europe and this episode represents a sizeable but classical egg‑associated outbreak rather than first occurrence in a new European sub‑region.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/joint-ecdc-efsa-rapid-outbreak-assessment-multi-country-outbreak-salmonella?utm_source=openai)) Event scale (>350 confirmed cases and multiple affected countries) justifies inclusion as a major European episode, but compared with very large outbreaks such as the 1994 Schwan’s ice‑cream outbreak or the prolonged multi‑country Polish‑egg‑linked epidemic, it is somewhat smaller; users enforcing a strict global top‑ten list might consider it a candidate for replacement. EPP.common.name: pneumococcal disease
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe

Event.summary: From the mid‑1990s through the 2000s, several Western and Southern European countries recorded increasing incidence of IPD due to non‑PCV7 serotypes, notably serotype 19A, even before widespread PCV7 use. After PCV7 introduction (2001 onward, with national implementation between roughly 2002 and 2006), surveillance in Spain, Belgium, France, England and Wales, and later Norway showed accelerated rises in 19A IPD, particularly in children, with doubling or more of incidence in some age groups by the mid‑2000s. As higher‑valent vaccines (PCV10/PCV13) were rolled out from 2009–2011, 19A disease burden declined, though country‑specific patterns varied and some additional non‑PCV13 serotypes began to increase. ([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/16/9/10-0102?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Progressive uptake of PCV7 and heterogeneous vaccine schedules across Europe altered serotype ecology, while ongoing macrolide and beta‑lactam consumption exerted selection pressure favoring resistant replacement serotypes. Internal mechanisms: Capsular switching, novel strain/genotype emergence, and clonal expansion of serotype 19A and other non‑vaccine serotypes—often with significant antimicrobial resistance—under vaccine and antibiotic selection drove re‑emergent IPD through serotype and lineage shifts rather than introduction into naïve regions.
Review: review – standardized the country name to the UN form 'United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland' (the underlying data come from England and Wales) but otherwise retained the 1996–2010 multi‑country European serotype 19A replacement episode; evidence base, geographic scope, and classification as re-emergence driven by serotype/genotype shifts under vaccine and antibiotic pressure are appropriate.

Large epidemics were reported in South Africa, Angola, Namibia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and many other countries, with about 83,000 reported cases in 2009 and roughly 170,000 in 2010 region‑wide. Intensified supplemental immunization activities and renewed political commitment subsequently reduced incidence, but the episode demonstrated the fragility of gains and the potential for rapid measles resurgence when coverage goals are not sustained.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: suboptimal routine MCV1 coverage and incomplete or delayed follow‑up campaigns across many African countries created large susceptible cohorts, compounded by health‑system challenges and funding gaps. Event.summary: In December 2014, a measles outbreak linked to Disneyland Resort in California began after an infected traveler exposed visitors at the parks, leading to chains of transmission in several U.S. states and onward spread to Mexico and Canada. By February–April 2015, about 125 U.S. cases across multiple states were epidemiologically linked to the Disneyland exposure, and additional clusters occurred in Quebec, Canada, while concurrent importations from the large Philippines outbreak seeded other North American outbreaks. The episode ended by mid‑2015 after aggressive case finding, isolation and vaccination activities, but it highlighted vulnerabilities in measles‑eliminated settings where pockets of undervaccination persist and theme-park or travel hubs can amplify imported cases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: international travel from regions with large measles outbreaks (notably the Philippines), clusters of unvaccinated or under‑vaccinated individuals (including vaccine‑hesitant communities), and crowded theme‑park settings that facilitated exposure. Internal mechanisms: the outbreak was caused by measles genotype B3, already widely circulating globally; re-occurrence in elimination settings was driven by human mobility and vaccination gaps, not novel viral traits.
Review: Decision: review (borderline for "top 10"; emergence classification corrected). Changes made: (1) Continent/sub-region and country fields were narrowed to North America and South America (via Mexico classified under Central America) with listed countries United States, Canada and Mexico; Brazil and a generic "other affected countries" phrase were removed because available CDC/WHO reports link the Disneyland-associated chains specifically to the U.S., Canada and Mexico, not to large outbreaks in Brazil, which were epidemiologically distinct.
