EPP.common.name: Measles morbillivirus
Host: Humans (primarily unvaccinated children and members of tight‑knit religious communities, plus travelers)
Event.summary: From late 2018 through 2019, the United States experienced its largest measles resurgence since 1992, with 1,249 confirmed cases and 22 outbreaks nationwide despite having eliminated endemic measles in 2000. The majority of cases were concentrated in long‑duration outbreaks in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York City and Rockland County, seeded by imported cases and amplified by low vaccination coverage, with smaller clusters across multiple states and some spillover into Canada. These outbreaks temporarily threatened the country’s elimination status but were brought under control just before a full year of continuous transmission elapsed, following intensive vaccination campaigns, emergency public‑health orders and community engagement efforts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: under‑vaccination and vaccine refusal in specific close‑knit communities, high population density and close social networks, frequent international travel importing virus from endemic regions (notably Israel, Ukraine and the Philippines), and sometimes delayed vaccination of infants. Internal mechanisms: circulating measles genotypes (mainly D8, with some B3) were not new to the U.S.; the episode is best classified as re-occurrence in an elimination setting due to local immunity gaps rather than viral evolution, though high intrinsic transmissibility meant relatively small drops in coverage yielded large outbreaks.
Review: Decision: review (high policy importance but modest burden relative to other events). No structural field changes were made: geography, timing, host, and emergence classification (re_occurrence only) align with CDC’s national update on the 2019 outbreaks and the definition of re-occurrence in a previously affected sub-region. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/68/wr/mm6840e2.htm)) However, with 1,249 U.S. cases and no reported deaths, the quantitative burden is far smaller than for African, European, or Philippine outbreaks listed here. Its inclusion is justified by its near‑loss of U.S. elimination status and the global attention it received, but if the dataset must strictly contain the ten largest events by cases/deaths, this row should be reconsidered for exclusion or treated as a secondary elimination-setting case study rather than a core top‑10 burden event.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia burgdorferi
EPP.common.name: Lyme disease
Host: Humans
Event.summary: By the early 1990s, Lyme borreliosis had become highly endemic in parts of central Europe, with particularly high incidence documented in countries such as Slovenia, Austria, southern Germany, Switzerland and the Czech Republic. Through the 1990s and 2000s, these foci experienced sustained high annual incidence, in some areas exceeding 100 cases per 100,000 inhabitants, with clinical manifestations including erythema migrans, neuroborreliosis and Lyme arthritis. By around 2010, incidence in many central European regions had stabilized at high levels as awareness, diagnostics and preventive measures improved, while the pathogen remained firmly entrenched in local Ixodes ricinus–rodent cycles.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive forest cover and high human use of forested, agricultural and peri‑urban recreational areas; large populations of rodent reservoirs and wild ungulates; and greater clinical recognition and reporting after the identification of B. burgdorferi sensu lato in Europe. Internal mechanisms: maintenance of diverse B. afzelii, B. garinii and other genospecies adapted to local hosts and vectors; increases are best explained by ecological and sociobehavioral factors (re‑occurrence) rather than emergence of a single new strain.
Review: review – The event period was extended to 1990–2010 (from 1990–2000) to reflect persistently high Lyme borreliosis incidence in core central European countries into the 2000s, and Czechia was added to the country list to better match surveillance and review data identifying Austria, Czechia, Germany, Slovenia and Switzerland as central high‑incidence areas. The event remains correctly classified as a re‑occurrence episode spanning Southern and Western Europe, but dates and country coverage should be checked against country‑level datasets.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia burgdorferi
EPP.common.name: Lyme disease
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From the early 1990s, northern European countries with extensive boreal and mixed forests, including Sweden, Finland and Norway as well as the Baltic states, reported substantial and in some areas increasing Lyme borreliosis incidence, paralleling but distinct from long‑standing tick‑borne encephalitis foci. By the 1990s and 2000s, parts of Scandinavia and the Baltic region had some of the highest recorded national or subnational Lyme incidence in Europe, with localized rates often exceeding 100 cases per 100,000 inhabitants, and a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations from erythema migrans to neuroborreliosis. By around 2010, Lyme disease was firmly established as a common tick‑borne infection across much of Northern Europe, with some regional stabilization as preventive measures and public awareness improved.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high densities of Ixodes ricinus in forested, coastal and island habitats; high recreational and occupational exposure in outdoor environments; and, in some areas, climate‑related shifts that supported longer tick activity seasons and northward/altitudinal expansion of risk. Internal mechanisms: maintenance and local adaptation of B. afzelii, B. garinii and related genospecies within rodent and bird reservoirs; changes are best characterized as re‑occurrence linked to environmental and behavioral factors rather than emergence of a distinct new strain or host jump.
Review: review – Norway was added to the country list to better reflect high Lyme borreliosis incidence reported from parts of the Scandinavian region alongside Sweden and Finland, while Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are retained to represent the high‑incidence Baltic states. The 1990–2010 period, Northern Europe sub‑region and re‑occurrence classification remain appropriate for this large, long‑running regional episode, but exact start years by country are approximate and should be validated against national surveillance data.

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia burgdorferi
EPP.common.name: Lyme disease
Host: Humans
Event.summary: From the late 1980s and early 1990s, Lyme borreliosis began to be recognized along the Mediterranean coast of North Africa and the Indian Ocean coast of East Africa, with clusters of erythema migrans and compatible Lyme cases reported in Tunisia and Egypt and a probable autochthonous human case documented in Mozambique in 1993. Through the 1990s and 2000s, studies detected Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato (notably B. lusitaniae, B. garinii and B. burgdorferi sensu stricto) in Ixodes and Hyalomma ticks, lizards, rodents and livestock in Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, Egypt, Kenya, the United Republic of Tanzania and Mozambique, accompanied by sporadic human cases with erythema migrans, neuroborreliosis or positive serology, although overall human incidence remained very low. By around 2020, Lyme borreliosis was still non‑endemic but established as an emerging tick‑borne zoonosis in selected coastal zones of North and East Africa, raising concern that climate change, migratory birds and changing tick vectors could facilitate further spread in coming decades.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: long‑distance movement of Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato into Africa via migratory birds carrying Ixodes and Hyalomma ticks from Europe; suitable humid Mediterranean and coastal climates in North and East Africa that allow survival of these vectors; movements of livestock, dogs and horses that help disseminate infected ticks; and limited awareness and diagnostic capacity that likely result in under‑recognition of human cases. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of Lyme group borreliae into new vertebrate reservoirs (including lizards) and probable adaptation to Hyalomma ticks as vectors in some settings, enabling sporadic autochthonous human transmission and constituting an inter‑continental emergence of the Lyme borreliosis system into African ecosystems.
Review: review – New row added to capture the inter‑continental emergence of Lyme borreliosis in Africa from the early 1990s onward, including documented autochthonous human cases in Tunisia, Egypt, Mozambique, Kenya and the United Republic of Tanzania and widespread detection of Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato in ticks and animal reservoirs along the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean coasts. Because case numbers are still low, some reports rely mainly on serology and molecular characterization is incomplete, this event is classified as an inter‑continental emergence episode of modest current burden and should be reviewed carefully by regional experts for confirmation of country start years and the strength of evidence for human infection.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: West Nile virus
Host: Humans (United States and multiple Canadian provinces)
Event.summary: In 2003, West Nile virus caused a second consecutive large epidemic across North America, consolidating its spread into western U.S. states and Canadian provinces after initial detections earlier in the decade. U.S. surveillance recorded roughly 9,000 human cases when confirmed and probable reports are combined, and Canada documented about 1,482 human cases and 24 deaths, indicating intense circulation in the Prairie provinces and parts of central Canada. EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: West Nile virus
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe; Western Asia
Host: Humans (multiple EU/EEA and neighbouring countries across southern, eastern and parts of western Europe and adjacent Western Asia)
Event.summary: During the 2018 transmission season, Europe and neighbouring Western Asian countries experienced their largest recorded West Nile virus epidemic, with an unusually early start and widespread human cases across southern, eastern and parts of western Europe. EU/EEA surveillance documented 1,605 locally acquired human infections in 11 Member States, while a total of about 2,083 autochthonous human cases and 181 deaths were reported across 15 European and neighbouring countries including Italy, Serbia, Greece, Romania, Hungary, Israel and others, with many regions reporting cases for the first time or at record levels. Transmission gradually declined by late autumn, but the event marked a step‑change in WNV epidemiology in Europe, with sustained endemo‑epidemic circulation in several foci thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: exceptionally warm spring and summer temperatures in 2018 shortened the extrinsic incubation period of WNV in mosquitoes, boosted Culex population growth and likely increased viral replication and transmission in bird reservoirs; climatic anomalies, changes in land use (e.g. irrigated agriculture, wetlands), and human outdoor activities intensified exposure, and blood‑safety measures had to be rapidly scaled up. Internal mechanisms: multiple introductions and widespread circulation of WNV lineages 1 and especially 2, already established in Greece and central–eastern Europe, suggest ongoing viral evolution and adaptation to European vectors and hosts; these internal changes, together with climatic drivers, underpin classification as a re-emergence accompanied by intra-continental emergence into new subregions (including first or unusually intense transmission in several countries).
Review: review: Updated geography so this multi-country epidemic now lists the principal affected countries individually and recognises that some (Israel, Türkiye, Cyprus) are in Asia/Western Asia by setting continent = "Europe; Asia" and sub_regions = "Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe; Western Asia". Corrected the country name Turkey→Türkiye and removed the vague "other neighbouring countries" wording. Classification as a large re-emergence with intra-continental emergence into new subregions is well supported; event should be retained as Europe’s largest WNV epidemic but has been flagged for review because of these geographic refinements.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: West Nile virus
Countries: United States of America [2021] – Arizona (Maricopa, Pinal, Pima counties) [2021]
Host: Humans (primarily residents of Maricopa County and neighbouring counties in Arizona, plus smaller numbers elsewhere in the U.S.)
Event.summary: In 2021, the United States experienced a substantial West Nile virus season with an unprecedented focal outbreak in Maricopa County, Arizona, more than two decades after the virus became endemic. Internal mechanisms: investigations did not identify a fundamentally new viral lineage compared with prior Arizona strains; the outbreak appears driven primarily by climatic and ecological amplification in an already endemic area, consistent with re-occurrence rather than re-emergence, although ongoing local viral evolution and possible vector adaptation may have contributed to enhanced transmission efficiency.
Review: retain: The 2021 Maricopa County-focused outbreak (≈1,487 local cases, 101 deaths, within a U.S. total of ~2,445 cases) is well documented and represents one of the largest and most intense focal WNV outbreaks in an already endemic setting; geography and coding as re-occurrence without intra-/inter-continental emergence are appropriate, and no structural corrections were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Betainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza B virus
Continent: Asia; Europe; North America; South America; Africa; Oceania
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern America; South America; Southern Africa; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans (all ages; notable burden in children and adolescents)
Event.summary: After being largely restricted to eastern Asia throughout the 1990s, B/Victoria/2/87-lineage influenza B viruses re-emerged around 2000 in East Asia and then spread globally.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5038a2.htm?utm_source=openai)) During the 2000–2001 and especially 2001–2002 seasons, B/Victoria variants seeded seasonal epidemics in North America, Europe, South America, Oceania and parts of Africa, displacing B/Yamagata viruses in many countries and causing sizeable outbreaks in populations—particularly children—that had little prior exposure to this lineage.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmWR/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5123a3.htm)) The episode concluded with inclusion of a B/Victoria-lineage virus (B/Hong Kong/330/01-like) in the 2002–2003 vaccine and long-term establishment of global co-circulation of the Victoria and Yamagata lineages.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The concentration of B/Victoria viruses in East Asia during the 1990s created large susceptible cohorts elsewhere; increasing international air travel, especially between Asia and other continents, enabled rapid seeding of the lineage into North America, Europe, South America, Oceania and parts of Africa just as vaccine formulations still targeted B/Yamagata-lineage viruses, generating substantial lineage-level mismatch.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmWR/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5123a3.htm)) Internal mechanisms: Antigenic drift within the B/Victoria lineage and reassortment with B/Yamagata-derived gene segments produced variants with reduced cross-reactivity to B/Yamagata-based vaccines and good fitness across climates, facilitating geographic range expansion and long-term re-establishment of this lineage in global circulation.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0042682202917198?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review – corrected continents to include Africa, added Southern Africa and representative South-East Asian and African countries (Singapore, Malaysia, South Africa) based on surveillance reports, and reclassified the event as a lineage-level re-emergence rather than an inter‑continental emergence of influenza B (which was already globally established). Country-year annotations remain approximate and should be cross-checked against detailed national data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Betainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza B virus
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans, with continued susceptibility in children but markedly reduced overall influenza activity in 2020–2021
Event.summary: Following the onset of the COVID‑19 pandemic in early 2020, global influenza activity collapsed, but among the few influenza B detections almost all were B/Victoria-lineage and virological surveillance recorded no confirmed naturally occurring B/Yamagata-lineage viruses after March 2020.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7976381/?utm_source=openai)) During the 2020–2021 and 2021–2022 seasons, countries in East Asia, Europe, North America and Oceania that did observe influenza circulation reported overwhelming dominance of B/Victoria, while B/Yamagata remained undetected despite continued typing and sequencing.([who.int](https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/influenza-update-n-381?utm_source=openai)) By 2023–2024, WHO and national advisory bodies concluded that inclusion of a B/Yamagata antigen in seasonal vaccines was no longer warranted and recommended a transition back to trivalent vaccines containing only a B/Victoria component, marking a major reconfiguration of global influenza B ecology.([cdn.who.int](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/influenza/who-influenza-recommendations/vcm-southern-hemisphere-recommendation-2024/202309_recommendation.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=2c2cbebd_7&utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Non-pharmaceutical interventions against COVID‑19 (travel restrictions, masking, school closures and distancing) dramatically reduced influenza transmission worldwide and disrupted the usual reseeding of influenza lineages between hemispheres; differences in local timing and stringency of these measures, along with prior immunity and vaccine use, appear to have favored persistence and reintroduction of B/Victoria viruses while pushing B/Yamagata to extremely low, and possibly zero, effective circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7976381/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Pre‑existing antigenic properties and fitness of contemporary B/Victoria clades, together with B/Yamagata’s tendency to infect older age groups and its relatively antigenically stable vaccine strain, may have interacted with pandemic-era behavior changes to produce the first documented disappearance of an influenza B lineage in the genomic surveillance era, effectively re‑establishing a single-lineage influenza B population dominated by B/Victoria.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12325168/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review – updated sub-regions to remove unsupported 'South-eastern Asia' (no specific countries listed) and reclassified the episode as re-emergence, reflecting the lineage-level restructuring of influenza B (apparent disappearance of B/Yamagata and dominance of B/Victoria) rather than a simple re-occurrence of typical seasonal activity; descriptions now align more closely with WHO and national vaccine‑composition recommendations.

EPP.scientific.name: Deltainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Influenza D virus
Host: Humans (general adult population – residual sera from blood donors and other clinical collections)
Event.summary: In 2011, a serologic survey of 316 human serum samples from the general population in the United States and Canada detected IDV hemagglutination‑inhibition antibodies in 1.3% of individuals, providing the first widely publicized indication that humans in North America had been exposed to influenza D virus. This low but measurable seroprevalence, identified after IDV had been isolated from swine and cattle, showed that zoonotic exposure was not confined to Italy and suggested that IDV or closely related viruses were already circulating silently in North American livestock and occasionally infecting humans. No discrete human outbreak or characteristic clinical syndrome could be linked to these serologic findings, and the episode is best interpreted as a baseline documentation of low‑level, previously unrecognized exposure.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Heightened interest in IDV following its 2011 isolation from pigs in Oklahoma and subsequent recognition of cattle as the primary reservoir prompted retrospective testing of available human sera from North America; extensive livestock movements and high cattle densities in U.S. and Canadian feedlot systems likely created undetected opportunities for past spillover. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – recognition of IDV as a distinct influenza species with antigenic properties separable from influenza C enabled specific serologic assays; Host Expansion (Spillover) – rare zoonotic infections from cattle or swine into humans inferred from low‑titer antibodies in a small fraction of the sampled general population.
Review: Review – Changed this event from first_global_emergence/first_detection to an inter‑continental emergence in North America, because archived Italian sera show earlier human IDV exposure from 2005 onward. Clarified that only 4 of 316 samples (1.3%) were positive and that these data reflect low‑level background exposure rather than a large clinical outbreak. Country and sub‑region assignments (United States, Canada; Northern America) are correct; event retained but downgraded in hierarchical importance relative to the Italian event.

Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; South America; Northern America
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2016]
Host: Humans, predominantly men who have sex with men (MSM), with some spread to other adults
Event.summary: Between mid-2016 and 2018, an unusual wave of hepatitis A outbreaks occurred across at least 22 EU/EEA countries and extended into the Americas, disproportionately affecting men who have sex with men (MSM), with over 4,400 outbreak-confirmed cases reported in Europe alone and hundreds of related cases in Chile, Argentina, Brazil, the United States and Canada. The outbreaks began with clusters at MSM social venues and events in Western Europe and spread through sexual networks and international travel, with molecular typing showing three closely related HAV genotype IA strains (VRD_521_2016, RIVM-HAV16-090 and V16_25801) shared between European and American MSM outbreaks. Intensified vaccination campaigns targeting MSM, sexual health messaging, and depletion of susceptibles gradually reduced transmission by 2018, though some countries in Latin America continued to report MSM-associated clusters into 2019.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High susceptibility among adult MSM in low- or medium-endemicity countries due to limited prior natural infection and incomplete vaccination coverage; dense sexual networks and large MSM gatherings (e.g. Pride events); international travel connecting European and American MSM communities; global HAV vaccine shortages that hampered rapid scale-up of targeted immunisation. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of specific HAV genotype IA strains capable of efficient person-to-person transmission via sexual and close contact routes, but without clear evidence of fundamentally increased virulence; overall pattern is best characterized as behavioral and immunity-pattern-driven re-occurrence rather than emergence of a new viral lineage.
Review: review – This represents a major, well-documented global outbreak wave among MSM (≈4,475 outbreak-confirmed cases in 22 EU/EEA countries plus large MSM-associated epidemics in Chile and other American countries) and clearly belongs among the highest-impact events. Classification as re-occurrence (rather than inter-continental emergence or re-emergence) is appropriate, since HAV was long established in all affected regions and no fundamentally new genotype emerged. However, the countries column uses a placeholder (“other EU/EEA countries”) and mixes European and American MSM clusters that are epidemiologically linked but sometimes treated as separate sub-episodes; there is also potential overlap with the Latin America MSM 2017–2019 event row. Recommend: (i) replacing the placeholder with the explicit 22 EU/EEA country list from ECDC; and (ii) agreeing at dataset level whether all MSM outbreaks linked to the three IA strains (Europe + Americas) should be merged into one global MSM episode (2016–2019) or kept as regional sub-events to avoid double counting. Event.summary: Between 2002 and 2004, multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter calcoaceticus–baumannii complex emerged as a major cause of bloodstream and wound infections among U.S. and coalition military personnel injured in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Kuwait, with 102 A. baumannii bloodstream infections identified in military treatment facilities and numerous additional extremity and wound infections reported. Molecular investigations suggested environmental and nosocomial acquisition of highly resistant clones in field hospitals and during aeromedical evacuation, followed by transmission in tertiary care hospitals in Germany and the United States. The outbreak was eventually mitigated through strengthened infection control, environmental decontamination, and changes in antibiotic use, but it highlighted the capacity of MDR A. baumannii to exploit war-related medical care networks for rapid multinational dissemination and led to the colloquial label “Iraqibacter.”

EPP.common.name: Pertussis, whooping cough
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Humans across age groups in countries using acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines
Event.summary: Beginning in the late 1990s, serial collections of Bordetella pertussis isolates from multiple European countries started to reveal rare strains that no longer expressed the vaccine antigen pertactin, first detected in Sweden and later in France and the Netherlands. Through the 2000s and early 2010s, the proportion of pertactin‑deficient isolates rose steadily in France, Norway, Sweden, Italy, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, reaching around one quarter of all tested isolates overall and more than half in some countries by 2012–2015, while pertussis incidence remained cyclically elevated. By the mid‑2010s, pertactin‑negative, often ptxP3‑lineage strains had become established components of national B. pertussis populations across Western, Northern and Southern Europe, with no sharp end point but clear stabilisation of these vaccine‑escape variants at high frequency.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and high uptake of pertactin‑containing acellular pertussis vaccines created strong selection pressure favouring strains that could evade pertactin‑targeted antibodies, and sustained transmission in partially immune populations allowed such variants to spread between countries on normal travel and contact networks. Internal mechanisms: Multiple independent disruptive mutations in the prn gene (insertions, deletions and nonsense mutations) arose on successful ptxP3 genetic backgrounds and were repeatedly selected, leading to convergent loss of pertactin expression in diverse lineages; this pattern of antigen‑specific vaccine‑driven evolution and regional range expansion of pertactin‑deficient clones is characteristic of re_emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence rather than geographic introduction of the pathogen itself.

EPP.scientific.name: Bordetella pertussis
EPP.common.name: Pertussis, whooping cough
Host: Humans, with highest burden in infants and young children but many cases in older children and adults
Event.summary: From 2008, Australia entered its largest recorded pertussis epidemic since national surveillance began, with notifications climbing sharply and peaking at nearly 40,000 cases in 2011, contributing to more than 140,000 reports between 2008 and 2012 and substantial infant hospitalisations. In nearby New Zealand, a linked regional resurgence began in August 2011 and lasted until December 2013, generating over 10,000 notifications, around 560 hospitalisations and three deaths in unimmunised young children, with incidence highest in deprived communities. Following intensified control efforts, including cocooning strategies, promotion of adolescent and adult boosters, and, in New Zealand, introduction and later optimisation of maternal vaccination, notifications gradually decreased by 2013–2014, though pertussis has remained cyclic and endemic in both countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: In both Australia and New Zealand, widespread use of acellular pertussis vaccines with relatively rapid waning of protection, together with several years since the previous large wave, allowed build‑up of susceptible older children and adults who then transmitted infection to very young infants; improved PCR diagnostics and clinician awareness further amplified detected incidence. Internal mechanisms: Genotyping of Australian isolates during the epidemic documented rapid expansion of ptxP3, prn2 and pertactin‑deficient lineages, mirroring global vaccine‑driven evolution, and similar ptxP3/pertactin‑variant profiles were seen in New Zealand; the rise of these fitter genotypes in highly vaccinated populations supports classification as re_emergence driven by antigenic evolution, superimposed on expected multi‑year epidemic cycling.
Review: review – Retain as a major Oceania epidemic episode, but the event year has been extended from 2008–2012 to 2008–2013 to capture the full New Zealand outbreak period (August 2011–December 2013). Emergence‑type coding has been adjusted so that only re_emergence is “true” (re_occurrence set to “false”), reflecting strong evidence for vaccine‑driven expansion of ptxP3 and pertactin‑deficient lineages alongside external drivers such as waning aP immunity and improved diagnostics.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia trachomatis
EPP.common.name: Chlamydia
Sub.regions: Europe | Western Europe; Europe | Northern Europe; Europe | Southern Europe; Europe | Eastern Europe; Northern America | Northern America; Oceania | Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans – primarily men who have sex with men (MSM), with occasional bisexual men; infection type mainly anorectal and inguinal lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) due to C. trachomatis serovar L2b.
Event.summary: Around 2003, public health authorities in the Netherlands detected an unusual cluster of severe proctitis among men who have sex with men, which was confirmed as lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by a C. trachomatis serovar L2b strain that previously had been rarely recognized in industrialized countries. Subsequent enhanced surveillance and molecular typing showed rapid expansion of this L2b epidemic among MSM across multiple Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern European countries and then to North America and Australia over the mid‑2000s, with hundreds to thousands of anorectal LGV cases reported in large urban sexual health clinics. The outbreak was gradually brought under better control after targeted awareness campaigns, improved diagnostic testing for rectal chlamydia in MSM, and guideline‑based doxycycline treatment of LGV cases and contacts, though L2b‑LGV remains an established STI among MSM in many affected countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The resurgence was linked to dense international sexual networks among MSM, high‑risk sexual practices (e.g. unprotected receptive anal intercourse, group sex, use of sex venues), overlapping HIV and STI epidemics, and increased travel between major cities in Europe, North America, and Australia, which facilitated long‑distance spread of an LGV strain that had previously been rare in these populations. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses identified a distinct L2b variant of C. trachomatis responsible for nearly all investigated LGV cases in MSM during this epidemic, indicating Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence combined with Enhanced Transmission within specific sexual networks rather than introduction of an entirely new species to these regions.
Review: Decision: review. The LGV L2b epidemic among MSM in Europe, North America and Australia is correctly identified as a major, epidemiologically linked re‑emergence episode of C. trachomatis. However, the event was misclassified as an inter‑continental emergence, which conflicts with the instructions that new serotypes/manifestations of an already‑endemic EPP in a continent should be treated as re‑emergence rather than inter‑continental emergence. I changed inter_continental_emergence from true to false and retained re_emergence = true to reflect a novel epidemic strain expanding within existing C. trachomatis–endemic regions. I also corrected the country name to “Netherlands (Kingdom of the)” to match the Country sheet. The listed countries and sub‑regions (including Poland as Eastern Europe) and approximate timing are supported by multi‑country LGV reviews and outbreak summaries and are appropriate to retain; no additional LGV‑related emergence events of greater impact were identified that would displace this episode from a top‑10 list for this EPP.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia trachomatis
EPP.common.name: Chlamydia
Sub.regions: Europe | Northern Europe; Europe | Western Europe
Host: Humans – sexually active adolescents and adults with genital chlamydia infections detected in routine screening and diagnostic programmes.
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, Sweden observed unexpected declines in reported Chlamydia trachomatis cases in some counties despite stable or rising test volumes, prompting investigation into potential diagnostic problems. In 2006, investigators discovered a new C. trachomatis variant (nvCT) with a 377‑bp deletion in the cryptic plasmid that removed the single NAAT target sequence used by Abbott m2000 and Roche Amplicor/TaqMan assays, allowing the strain to spread largely undetected for several years and to reach high prevalence in counties using these tests, while remaining detectable in counties and countries using alternative assays. After recognition of nvCT, Sweden and a few other European countries where sporadic nvCT cases were identified rapidly updated NAATs to include additional targets, undertook recall testing and partner notification, and by the late 2000s the proportion of nvCT among all chlamydia diagnoses in Sweden declined substantially as the diagnostic escape advantage was removed, with only limited transmission documented in Norway, Denmark, Ireland and France.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The emergence was facilitated by widespread use of single‑target nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) in routine chlamydia screening, creating strong diagnostic selection pressure in regions relying on Abbott and Roche assays that failed to detect the new variant; high screening coverage and sexual network connectivity in Sweden further supported rapid dissemination. Internal mechanisms: The nvCT strain carried a 377‑bp deletion in the plasmid region targeted by these NAATs, representing Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence with Diagnostic Escape, leading to apparent drops in case notifications and substantial under‑diagnosis until multi‑target assays and specific nvCT tests were introduced, after which its fitness advantage waned and its prevalence began to fall.
Review: Decision: review. The Swedish nvCT diagnostic‑escape episode is correctly included as a major re‑emergence event driven by a novel plasmid deletion variant and by NAAT testing practices, and classification as re_emergence (with all other emergence‑type flags set to false) is appropriate. However, the original row overstated the geographic extent and timing of nvCT spread outside Sweden by listing the United Kingdom and unspecified “other European countries” and by implying broader circulation. Based on national investigations and a Europe‑wide survey, there is strong evidence that nvCT transmission remained largely confined to Sweden, with only small numbers of confirmed cases in Norway, Denmark, Ireland and France, and no confirmed circulation in the UK. I therefore (i) removed the United Kingdom and the vague “other European countries with sporadic detections” from the country list; (ii) restricted countries to Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Ireland and France with starting years aligned to documented detections (Sweden 2002–2006 period of undetected spread; other countries 2007); and (iii) removed “Europe | Southern Europe” from sub_regions, as no Southern European country with nvCT circulation is well‑documented. Event years (2002–2009), host description and mechanism/driver text remain valid. Given these corrections, the event should be retained but flagged for expert review of the exact end year and any very small additional national clusters that do not substantially change its impact ranking.

EPP.scientific.name: Haemophilus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Haemophilus influenzae infection
Countries: Canada [2000] (Northern Canada, including Arctic and sub‑Arctic regions)
Host: Humans (disproportionately Indigenous children in Arctic and sub‑Arctic communities)
Event.summary: From 2000 through at least 2010, invasive Haemophilus influenzae serotype a (Hia) emerged as a major cause of invasive disease in the North American Arctic, where Hib had previously predominated before vaccination. Surveillance in Alaska and northern Canada documented that non‑b serotypes, especially Hia, rapidly increased to comprise most invasive H. influenzae cases and reached very high incidence levels in Indigenous children, in some northern regions approaching or exceeding historical Hib rates. The episode persisted over the decade, with ongoing high incidence but gradual strengthening of surveillance, clinical management and discussion of dedicated Hia vaccines rather than a clearly demarcated epidemic end.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High underlying burden of social and environmental risk factors in Indigenous Arctic communities (crowded housing, smoking exposure, limited healthcare access), combined with elimination of Hib by vaccination, likely created an ecological niche for non‑b serotypes. Internal mechanisms: Serotype replacement and expansion of particularly fit Hia lineages with high invasiveness; this represents a serotype shift and increased virulence or transmissibility of Hia in this setting, fitting the definition of re‑emergence driven by pathogen characteristics rather than spread into a truly new sub‑region.
Review: Review – The North American Arctic Hia episode is well supported by population-based incidence data and clearly qualifies as a major re-emergence event with serotype replacement and high disease burden in Indigenous children. However, the original classification as an intra-continental emergence has been corrected to re-emergence only, because H. influenzae (and probably Hia at low levels) was already present in Northern America and the episode reflects a serotype shift with increased incidence, not first presence in a new UN sub-region. No changes were needed to timing or geography, but the event is flagged for review due to this reclassification.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyclospora cayetanensis
EPP.common.name: cyclosporiasis
Host: Humans (consumers of Fresh Express bagged salad mixes and other fresh produce in the United States and Canada)
Event.summary: From May through September 2020, a major North American cyclosporiasis episode occurred in the context of substantial seasonal case numbers. In the United States, at least 641 laboratory-confirmed illnesses and 37 hospitalizations in multiple Midwestern and neighboring states were linked to bagged garden salad mixes containing iceberg lettuce, red cabbage and carrots produced by Fresh Express at a facility in Illinois and sold under several brand names at large retail chains. Environmental sampling detected Cyclospora in an irrigation canal near a farm suspected of supplying red cabbage for the mixes. Canada concurrently reported 370 confirmed cyclosporiasis cases across six provinces and territories; some of these illnesses were associated with recalled Fresh Express salads, while others were linked to fresh herbs such as cilantro and parsley or had no identified vehicle. Extensive recalls of Fresh Express salad products, adjustments in sourcing and processing, and the close of the growing season were followed by a decline in new case reports.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Centralized production and interstate/international distribution of bagged salad mixes from a single processing facility serving both U.S. and Canadian markets; contamination of surface or irrigation water used on leafy greens; the resilience of Cyclospora oocysts to standard produce washing and processing steps; and seasonal climatic conditions favorable to parasite survival and sporulation in source fields. Internal mechanisms: No strong evidence for novel parasite strains or increased virulence; outbreak dynamics primarily reflect contamination of salad ingredients and agricultural water. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence driven by environmental contamination and industrial-scale processing and distribution, with enhanced effective transmission through widely distributed bagged salads that combined ingredients from multiple fields and farms.
Review: retain: This row correctly represents the 2020 North American episode linked to Fresh Express bagged salads and contemporaneous Canadian cases. I clarified that Canadian illnesses comprised both salad-associated and herb-associated cases and limited the geography to Northern America (United States and Canada). Classification as re_occurrence is appropriate because similar large produce-associated outbreaks had occurred repeatedly in the preceding decade. Given its substantial binational case burden and strong documentation, this event should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas vaginalis
EPP.common.name: Trichomoniasis
Host: Humans (adult women and men; predominantly women attending STI/vaginitis clinics)
Event.summary: During the 1990s, clinicians in the United States and Canada increasingly reported sporadic cases of vaginal trichomoniasis that failed standard single- or short-course oral metronidazole therapy, and laboratory testing of isolates from many U.S. states and Canadian sites confirmed reduced susceptibility or resistance to metronidazole.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/153/5/948/927091?utm_source=openai)) Building on earlier case series from the mid‑1980s, research through the decade—including a 1999 New England Journal of Medicine report—characterized metronidazole‑resistant vaginal trichomoniasis as an emerging therapeutic problem rather than an isolated curiosity.([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM199907223410417?utm_source=openai)) By the end of the 1990s, high‑dose or prolonged nitroimidazole regimens, tinidazole, and topical agents were being used for a small but clinically important subset of women with persistent infection, and expert reviews began to frame nitroimidazole‑resistant T. vaginalis as a re‑emerging treatment challenge in Northern America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Widespread use of single-dose or short-course metronidazole for trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis created strong selection pressure; incomplete partner treatment and reinfection also contributed to persistent infections that were heavily exposed to nitroimidazoles. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial resistance – clinical and in vitro metronidazole resistance associated with altered parasite redox metabolism and reduced drug activation (nitroimidazole resistance); molecular studies show diverse resistant genotypes, suggesting multiple evolutionary events rather than a single clone.
Review: review – Event concept (emergence and recognition of nitroimidazole-resistant T. vaginalis in Northern America) is well supported by case series and expert reviews and should be retained as one of the key high‑impact episodes. The event summary was revised to (a) describe resistance cases as rare but increasingly recognized, rather than implying large clustered outbreaks, and (b) attribute framing of resistance as an emerging problem mainly to clinical experts and literature (e.g. JID 1986 series and the 1999 NEJM report) rather than formal public-health authorities. No changes were made to geography, timing, or emergence-type classification (re‑emergence due to antimicrobial resistance).

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas vaginalis
EPP.common.name: Trichomoniasis
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa
Host: Humans (sexually active women and men in the general population and high‑risk groups)
Event.summary: From 1990 through roughly 2010, trichomoniasis remained highly prevalent across many parts of sub-Saharan Africa, with community- and clinic-based studies in Rakai District (Uganda), Zimbabwe, South Africa, Malawi, Tanzania, Zambia, Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of the Congo typically finding T. vaginalis infection in roughly one quarter to one third of sexually active women, and even higher levels in some high‑risk groups.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10195051/?utm_source=openai)) As large generalized heterosexual HIV epidemics expanded during the 1990s and early 2000s, longitudinal and case–control studies in Uganda, Zimbabwe, South Africa and other settings showed that T. vaginalis infection approximately doubled the risk of HIV acquisition in women, magnifying the public health impact of this otherwise often-neglected STI.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18275275/?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2000s, intensified HIV prevention and STI control programs in several African countries were incorporating syndromic management and, in some programs, specific screening for trichomoniasis, yet the parasite remained endemic at high levels in many subregions and continued to act as an important cofactor in HIV transmission.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Explosive heterosexual HIV epidemics with overlapping sexual networks; limited access to quality STI diagnosis and treatment; high background prevalence of other STIs; gender and socioeconomic factors constraining women’s ability to negotiate condom use; and health‑system weaknesses in laboratory capacity, surveillance, and routine screening. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain or resistance mechanism is clearly linked to this pattern; the episode represents sustained high transmission in widely infected sexual networks rather than biologically distinct re‑emergent variants. The main mechanistic role is that existing T. vaginalis infections increase genital inflammation and susceptibility to HIV, thereby amplifying HIV transmission.
Review: review – Event appropriately captures the very high burden of trichomoniasis and its role as an HIV cofactor across sub-Saharan Africa and should be retained as one of the main high‑impact episodes. However, several corrections were made: (a) the statement that prevalence reached “up to half of women” in Rakai, Uganda, was inaccurate (Rakai surveys report ~24–31% T. vaginalis in women, with ~50% referring to bacterial vaginosis) and has been revised to describe more realistic ranges based on population-based and clinic-based studies; (b) the country list was expanded to include explicit examples from Eastern, Southern, Western, and Middle Africa (Malawi, Zambia, Nigeria, Democratic Republic of the Congo) consistent with published prevalence data; and (c) the emergence-type flag re_occurrence was changed from Yes to No, because available evidence indicates long-standing high prevalence rather than a clearly documented post‑1990 resurgence in incidence. The episode is now treated as a chronic high-burden pattern without a specific emergence-type label and is flagged for expert review of the chosen representation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Event.summary: During the 1990s, gambiense human African trypanosomiasis resurged dramatically in conflict‑affected parts of Central Africa, with the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) at the epicentre and substantial transmission in Angola, Central African Republic and (South) Sudan, plus foci in northern Uganda.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3310607/?utm_source=openai))  Reported global HAT cases peaked at around 40,000 in 1998, two‑thirds of them in DRC (26,318 detected cases that year), before intensified screening and treatment campaigns from 2000 onwards began to reverse the trend.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3310607/?utm_source=openai))  Between about 2000 and 2003, large‑scale mobile screening and renewed investment in national control programmes reduced DRC’s detected HAT cases from ~26,000 to ~11,000 per year and initiated a sustained continental decline in gambiense HAT incidence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Prolonged civil wars and political instability in DRC, Angola and southern Sudan in the 1980s–1990s disrupted health systems, halted vector control and active screening, and displaced populations into highly tsetse‑infested areas, allowing intense transmission and late presentation with advanced disease.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3375795/?utm_source=openai))  Funding shortages and the collapse or decentralization of dedicated HAT programmes further reduced case detection until new public–private and WHO partnerships restored drug supply and control operations in the early 2000s.([who.int](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-TRS-881?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: Available evidence points to resurgence driven mainly by increased human–vector contact and programmatic failure rather than emergence of novel, more virulent T. brucei gambiense strains (no consistent genotype shift has been linked to the 1990s epidemic).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4130665/?utm_source=openai))

Event.summary: From the late 1990s onward, Europe experienced a marked emergence of Chagas disease as millions of migrants from endemic Latin American countries settled primarily in Spain, Italy, France, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Portugal, Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands, bringing an estimated 68,000–122,000 chronic T. cruzi infections by 2009.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21944556/?utm_source=openai))  Initially, Chagas was almost entirely unrecognized and under‑diagnosed, but during 1999–2013, accumulating reports of transfusion‑, transplant‑ and congenitally acquired cases led several countries to implement systematic or targeted screening of at‑risk blood donors and, in some settings, pregnant women (UK 1999; Spain 2005; France and Sweden 2009; Switzerland 2012; Belgium 2013), while others introduced donor deferral policies.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0953620517301772?utm_source=openai))  By 2013, Chagas disease had become a recognized public‑health concern in parts of Southern and Western Europe, with thousands of diagnosed cases but a large, mostly undetected reservoir of chronic infection in migrant communities and ongoing non‑vector local transmission via blood, organ transplantation and vertical routes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensified economic migration from endemic Latin America to Southern and Western Europe since the 1990s created sizeable populations of chronically infected yet often asymptomatic migrants, many of reproductive age, in health systems unfamiliar with Chagas disease.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0953620517301772?utm_source=openai))  Modern transfusion and transplant networks, combined with the absence of routine T. cruzi screening in blood banks until 1999–2013, enabled in situ transmission to European recipients, and unrecognized infection in pregnant women led to congenital cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4214631/?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of a new parasite genotype adapted to Europe; instead, multiple Latin American strains were imported, and emergence is driven by host‑population movements and health‑system gaps rather than evolutionary change in T. cruzi.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10747626/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – The described emergence of Chagas disease in Europe is real and highly impactful, with strong support for substantial chronic infection burdens and documented transfusion and congenital transmission in multiple countries. The time span 1999–2013 aligns with the roll‑out of blood‑donor screening and initial policy responses in the UK, Spain, France, Sweden, Switzerland and Belgium, and the sub‑region and country lists are appropriate. However, the original row incorrectly set both inter‑continental emergence and re‑emergence to “Yes”. Under the project definitions, Europe represents a new continent for human T. cruzi transmission, so inter‑continental emergence should be “Yes”, but re‑emergence should be “No” because there was no prior established Chagas presence in this region. This classification has been corrected accordingly; users should review and confirm.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma spp.
EPP.common.name: Trypanosomiasis
Host: Humans (acute orally acquired T. cruzi infection in family and school clusters); triatomine bugs and wild/peridomestic mammalian reservoirs contaminating food (e.g. opossums, other sylvatic mammals)
Event.summary: Beginning around 2000, Brazil’s Amazon region and later parts of Venezuela and Colombia saw a sharp increase in outbreaks of acute Chagas disease transmitted orally through contaminated foods and beverages, especially unpasteurized açaí and other fruit juices. In Brazil, surveillance data indicate that from 2000 to 2010 more than 1,000 acute cases occurred in 138 outbreaks, about 71% attributed to orally transmitted epidemics, predominantly in northern states such as Pará and Amapá.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/35f3/549a561b5673258de8fb7b3e21fc5ea0cb7a.pdf))  In Venezuela, the first large recognized urban food‑borne outbreak occurred at a school in Caracas in 2007, infecting 103 of roughly 1,000 exposed children and adults, followed by additional school and family clusters (e.g. Chichiriviche de la Costa in 2009), with at least 249 oral‑transmission cases reported nationally by 2015.([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=6b81f946d6362f3da7750b2bf9b0f78c4159d5b5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))  Colombia documented dozens of family‑type oral outbreaks over this period—64 outbreaks and 302 affected individuals by 2023, with a case‑fatality rate around 11% and notable events such as the 2014 Paz de Ariporo outbreak with 41 cases—making oral transmission a major cause of acute Chagas disease in the Orinoco and Andean regions as well.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11262278/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of regional and extra‑regional demand for açaí and other fresh juices led to expanded harvesting and artisanal processing in sylvatic or peri‑urban settings where infected triatomines and marsupials (e.g. Didelphis spp.) are common, often without adequate washing, pasteurization or vector exclusion, facilitating contamination of juice and pulp with infected insects or their feces.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/35f3/549a561b5673258de8fb7b3e21fc5ea0cb7a.pdf))  Seasonal peaks in fruit harvest (e.g. November–January for açaí) coincide with warmer, wetter conditions that enhance triatomine activity and allow T. cruzi to remain viable for hours to days in moist foods, promoting micro‑epidemics with high attack rates among households, schoolchildren and workers sharing contaminated drinks.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/35f3/549a561b5673258de8fb7b3e21fc5ea0cb7a.pdf))  Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing shows that specific T. cruzi discrete typing units (notably TcI and TcIV) are repeatedly associated with oral outbreaks, but there is no single novel lineage; the key change is the epidemiologic route—large inocula delivered to the oral mucosa or gastrointestinal tract—which is linked to more severe myocarditis and higher acute mortality than typical vector‑borne infection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9113729/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – This new row has been added because large food‑borne outbreaks of acute Chagas disease in Brazil, Venezuela and Colombia since about 2000 clearly qualify among the most impactful post‑1990 events for human trypanosomiasis, with >1,000 Brazilian cases in 138 outbreaks between 2000–2010, at least 249 oral cases reported in Venezuela by 2015, and 64 documented outbreaks affecting 302 people in Colombia by 2023, many with high case‑fatality. These episodes occur within long‑endemic South American sub‑regions and reflect a dramatic resurgence and shift in transmission route rather than spread to a new continent or UNSD sub‑region, so they are classified as re‑occurrence only. The temporal window (2000–2015) and country list focus on the period and locations where outbreak incidence and impact were highest; users may wish to refine the end date or extend the episode forward if acute oral outbreaks continue at similar scale after 2015.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterococcus faecium
EPP.common.name: Enterococcus faecium infection
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1990]
Host: Humans (hospital inpatients; bloodstream and other invasive infections)
Event.summary: During the 1990s and early 2000s, vancomycin‑resistant E. faecium that had first appeared in British and other European hospitals in the late 1980s spread widely across Western and later Eastern Europe, leading to increasing proportions of E. faecium blood isolates resistant to vancomycin. Surveillance data from the European Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System (EARSS) documented steep rises in VREfm bloodstream infections in multiple countries, with particularly high prevalence in Greece, Ireland, Portugal and the UK by the early 2000s. By around 2002, clonal complex 17 (CC17)/A1 hospital‑adapted VREfm lineages were established and disseminating between hospitals across Europe, and control efforts focused on improving infection prevention and hospital antibiotic stewardship.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: widespread hospital use of glycopeptides and broad‑spectrum cephalosporins, poor early infection‑control practices, and widespread agricultural use of the glycopeptide avoparcin in food animals contributing to a community reservoir all promoted selection and dissemination. Internal mechanisms: emergence and expansion of hospital‑adapted E. faecium clonal complex 17 (A1 group) carrying vanA/vanB determinants and multiple additional resistance and virulence genes, enabling survival under high antibiotic pressure and enhanced ability to colonize and transmit in hospital settings (Re‑emergence; Antimicrobial Resistance; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity; Enhanced Transmission; Geographic Range Expansion – inherent).
Review: retain – Event appropriately summarizes the spread and establishment of hospital‑adapted VREfm (CC17/A1) across multiple European sub‑regions in the 1990s–early 2000s. Geography matches UN sub‑regions, and classification as intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence is consistent with the definitions. Sources are relevant and event impact is clearly among the largest for this EPP.

Event.summary: By the late 1980s and 1990s, MRSA had become highly prevalent in large tertiary hospitals in Japan and several other East Asian countries, and in 1996–1997 Japan reported the first clinical isolates of S. aureus with reduced susceptibility to vancomycin (hVISA/VISA), signalling a major escalation in resistance. During the late 1990s and 2000s, MRSA became endemic in many Asian hospitals and spread into community hospitals, while community-associated MRSA clones—especially ST59 (Taiwan/Asia-Pacific clone) and ST30—emerged as important causes of skin, soft tissue and invasive infections in Taiwan, parts of China and other Asian settings and increasingly spilled back into healthcare facilities. Into the 2000s, VISA and heterogeneous VISA phenotypes were documented at low but concerning prevalence in several Asian countries, prompting revisions of vancomycin breakpoints and the gradual introduction of stricter infection-control and antibiotic stewardship programmes, which stabilized but did not eliminate the regional MRSA burden.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: heavy and sometimes unregulated antibiotic use in hospitals and communities across much of Asia, high patient density and overcrowded healthcare facilities, widespread use of invasive devices, and variable infection-prevention infrastructure. Internal mechanisms: accumulation of multidrug resistance in long-established hospital MRSA lineages (e.g., ST239, ST5), stepwise mutations and cell-wall changes leading to VISA/hVISA phenotypes, and emergence of virulent CA-MRSA clones such as ST59 and ST30 that expanded in the community and increasingly contributed to hospital infections—collectively representing novel strain/genotype emergence, antimicrobial resistance escalation and enhanced transmission.

Internal mechanisms: introduction and clonal expansion of CA‑MRSA lineages (ST30 and USA300‑Latin American variant) carrying PVL and other virulence factors, representing novel strain/genotype emergence, increased virulence/pathogenicity, and enhanced community transmission; diversification and adaptation of these clones within the region over time.

Event.summary: In 2003, a novel MRSA clone associated with pigs and cattle (sequence type ST398) was first identified in a human in the Netherlands, representing the emergence of livestock-associated MRSA (LA‑MRSA) as a new ecological form of S. aureus. Between 2003 and around 2010, LA‑MRSA ST398 spread widely in pig‑ and veal‑producing regions of the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium and neighboring countries, leading to high carriage rates among farmers, veterinarians and slaughterhouse workers, with occasional infections in exposed persons and limited community spread. By the early to mid‑2010s, ST398 and related LA‑MRSA lineages were detected across much of Western and parts of Northern and Southern Europe, prompting changes in MRSA surveillance and infection-control policies focused on livestock contact as a specific risk factor.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive pig and veal calf production with high-density animal husbandry, frequent use of antimicrobials in livestock, close occupational contact between humans and colonized animals, and movement of animals within European trade networks. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a livestock-adapted MRSA lineage (ST398) with ability to colonize multiple animal hosts and spill back into humans, representing novel strain/genotype emergence, antimicrobial resistance selection in livestock, host expansion (spillover from animals to humans), and geographic range expansion within Europe.
Review: retain – Livestock-associated MRSA ST398 emergence in Dutch pig and veal production and subsequent spread to humans across several European countries is well documented and represents a distinct ecological expansion of S. aureus. Event years (2003–2015), subregions and countries are in line with surveillance and outbreak reports, and classification as re_emergence (novel livestock-adapted lineage spilling back into humans) without inter-continental flags is appropriate.

Event.summary: By 2005, MRSA had become a leading cause of healthcare-associated bloodstream infections in the United States, with data from CDC’s Emerging Infections Program showing high incidence of invasive MRSA across multiple surveillance sites amid ongoing circulation of both traditional hospital clones and newer strains like USA300. During 2005–2011, invasive MRSA incidence remained high but began to decline in many hospitals as infection-control interventions (central line bundles, decolonization, hand hygiene) expanded, even as USA300 and other CA‑MRSA lineages moved into healthcare settings and contributed to hospital-onset disease. Internal mechanisms: coexistence and partial replacement of older multidrug-resistant hospital MRSA clones by USA300 and other strains able to thrive in both community and hospital environments, reflecting novel strain/genotype emergence, enhanced transmission, and in some cases increased virulence/pathogenicity, which together produced a resurgence and then partial decline (re-emergence) of invasive MRSA.
Review: review – This episode captures the period when invasive MRSA bloodstream infections were at high incidence in the United States and then declined substantially with intensified infection-prevention programs, while community-onset invasive disease remained a major problem. The re_occurrence flag has been set to “No” because the pattern is dominated by the expansion and hospital penetration of new clones such as USA300 (an internal evolutionary change) rather than by purely external drivers in a previously quiescent subregion; re_emergence remains “Yes”. EPP.scientific.name: Caliciviridae
EPP.common.name: norovirus
Sub.regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Host: humans (all ages; high proportions of outbreaks in institutional settings such as hospitals, nursing homes and cruise ships)
Event.summary: In 1995–1996 a new GII.4 strain, US95/96, became the predominant cause of norovirus outbreaks in the United States and the Netherlands, responsible for roughly half to four‑fifths of all typed outbreaks and marking the first clearly recognized global pandemic wave of GII.4 norovirus. In subsequent months and years, closely related US95/96‑like viruses seeded widespread epidemics across North America, Europe and parts of Australasia, with repeated institutional and community outbreaks. As population immunity accumulated and newer GII.4 variants arose, US95/96 activity waned by the early 2000s and was displaced by later pandemic variants such as Farmington Hills 2002 and Hunter 2004.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expanding molecular surveillance in the mid‑1990s improved recognition of norovirus and linked geographically separated outbreaks, while increasing international travel and institutional crowding (e.g. long‑term care, cruise ships) facilitated rapid dissemination of a highly contagious virus with a very low infectious dose. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (US95/96 GII.4 variant with antigenic properties that allowed escape from existing herd immunity); Enhanced Transmission (GII.4 lineage shows higher transmissibility and broader binding to host histo‑blood‑group antigens than many other genotypes).
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event correctly captures the first recognized GII.4 pandemic wave (US95/96) and its major early-affected countries; classification as re-emergence (strain-driven resurgence in an already endemic virus) and not first detection or inter-/intra-continental emergence is appropriate. Literature also documents US95/96 outbreaks in additional countries and continents (e.g. Brazil, China, Germany), but given the impracticality of listing every affected country and the stated approach of using illustrative high‑impact locations, the current geographic scope is acceptable; no field changes made, but future expansion of country lists could be considered if finer regional detail is needed.

Event.summary: In early 2004 surveillance in New South Wales, Australia, detected a marked rise in norovirus GII.4 activity dominated by a novel variant, later termed Hunter 2004, which rapidly became the main cause of institutional outbreaks in nursing homes and hospitals. During late 2004–2005 the Hunter virus was identified as the etiologic agent in hundreds of outbreaks and large epidemics in the Netherlands, Japan, Taiwan and other parts of Europe and Asia, indicating a new globally disseminated GII.4 pandemic wave. As with earlier GII.4 variants, Hunter circulation declined over the following seasons as it was displaced by still newer GII.4 strains, notably the 2006 Minerva/Den Haag variants that underpinned the 2006–2007 pandemic wave.

Rationale: New event added to capture the Hunter 2004 GII.4 variant, which is consistently identified in primary literature and reviews as one of the six major pandemic norovirus GII.4 variants and is clearly among the largest post-1990 emergence events. By 2012, however, the New Orleans variant was itself overtaken in many regions by the emergent GII.4 Sydney 2012 strain, and New Orleans circulation dropped to lower, sporadic levels.

Event.summary: In 2012 global norovirus surveillance detected a novel GII.4 variant, Sydney 2012, first identified in Australia in March 2012 and associated with rapidly increasing outbreaks; by late 2012 it had been confirmed on multiple continents and was replacing New Orleans 2009. During the 2012–2013 winter season, Sydney 2012 became the predominant outbreak strain in many countries including Australia, New Zealand, the United States, several European nations and parts of Asia and Latin America, and was linked to increased norovirus activity in some settings. By about 2014 its dominance began to decline as non‑GII.4 genotypes (e.g. GII.17, GII.P16‑GII.2) started to emerge regionally, although Sydney 2012 continued to circulate at lower levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High baseline global burden of norovirus, winter seasonality in temperate regions, and extensive international travel allowed the Sydney 2012 variant to spread almost simultaneously across continents, while institutional and food‑service outbreaks amplified local transmission. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (GII.4 Sydney 2012, phylogenetically distinct from Apeldoorn 2007 and New Orleans 2009); Escape from Herd Immunity and Enhanced Transmission (mutations in surface‑exposed P2 epitopes and HBGA‑binding interfaces correlate with antigenic changes and epidemiologic evidence of immune escape, enabling this variant to cause a new pandemic wave).
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Event correctly identifies GII.4 Sydney 2012 as a major pandemic variant and captures its rapid global replacement of New Orleans 2009. However, the original version omitted Africa and underrepresented South and South‑East Asia despite clear evidence of Sydney 2012 predominance in South Africa, Bangladesh and Thailand; continents, subregions and countries have been expanded accordingly, and Bangladesh, Thailand and South Africa were added with approximate start years based on outbreak and surveillance reports. Because some country start years are inferred at annual resolution and additional affected countries are not listed exhaustively, this row should be reviewed against detailed national data before finalization.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: tick-borne encephalitis (tick-borne encephalitis virus, European/Siberian/Far Eastern subtypes)
Host: Humans (mainly unvaccinated rural and peri-urban residents, forestry and agricultural workers, and people engaging in outdoor activities)
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia experienced one of the most dramatic upsurges of tick-borne encephalitis in Europe, with incidence in Latvia averaging nearly 28 cases per 100,000 during 1990–1999 and sharp increases also seen in Estonia and Lithuania compared with the 1970s–1980s. This resurgence developed as these newly independent Baltic states underwent rapid socio‑economic and land‑use changes that increased human exposure to infected Ixodes ticks, with particularly high incidence in forested rural counties. Toward the late 1990s local control measures, changing economic conditions, and in some areas improved vaccination coverage contributed to a decline from the mid-1990s peak, although incidence remained above pre‑1990 levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Post‑communist socio‑economic transition (increased unemployment, subsistence activities, forest use and recreation), changes in agricultural practices and land abandonment leading to more suitable tick habitat, and incomplete or disrupted vaccination programs increased human contact with infected ticks and susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel viral lineage was identified as the primary cause; the upsurge is best explained as a re-occurrence driven by external socio‑economic factors acting on existing endemic foci rather than intrinsic viral change.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1876807/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This is a well-documented major 1990s upsurge in TBE incidence in the Baltic States, with some of the highest rates in Europe and clear socio‑economic drivers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1876807/?utm_source=openai)) Sub-region label corrected from "Northern Europe; Eastern Europe" to "Northern Europe" only, because Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are all classified as Northern Europe in the UNSD scheme used by the Country sheet. EPP.scientific.name: Streptococcus agalactiae
EPP.common.name: Group B Streptococci
Host: Humans – adults and neonates; aquaculture fish (tilapia and other freshwater fish) serving as reservoirs for human infection
Event.summary: Retrospective genomic and surveillance work shows that from the early–mid 1990s onward, a hypervirulent serotype III sequence type 283 (ST283) clone of Streptococcus agalactiae caused invasive disease in adults in Hong Kong and Singapore and was later found in invasive collections from Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Thailand and Viet Nam, as well as in diseased tilapia and other freshwater fish across the region. During the 2000s and 2010s, ST283 became the dominant cause of invasive GBS in some hospital series from Laos and Thailand and was widely detected in human invasive disease and farmed tilapia in Singapore, Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Thailand, Viet Nam and Malaysia. By around 2017, ST283 had established itself as a widespread regional lineage with bidirectional transmission between humans and aquaculture fish, recognized as a distinct, hypervirulent clone with major public health and aquaculture impacts in South-eastern and Eastern Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid growth of freshwater fish aquaculture and high per‑capita fish consumption in Southeast Asia; preparation and consumption of raw or undercooked freshwater fish dishes; warm tropical temperatures favoring bacterial survival in aquatic environments; regional trade in live and chilled fish facilitating dissemination. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a genetically distinct hypervirulent clone (ST283, clonal complex 283) with traits supporting invasion and survival in both humans and fish; acquisition of resistance determinants such as tet(M) on mobile genetic elements aiding persistence under antibiotic exposure in both human medicine and aquaculture; host expansion between humans and fish and possible enhanced transmission via adaptation to aquatic and human gastrointestinal niches (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion/Spillover; Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion – inherent adaptation to regional aquatic–human interfaces).
Review: review – Event correctly highlights the emergence and regional spread of the hypervirulent ST283 clone in humans and fish across South-eastern and Eastern Asia and is clearly among the most impactful GBS emergence events. However, several corrections were needed: (1) start year adjusted from 1995 to 1993 to reflect earliest documented invasive ST283 disease in Hong Kong, while still capturing mid‑1990s first human cases in Singapore and Hong Kong; (2) Hong Kong entry standardized to “China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region” and first-detection year corrected from 2010 to 1993–1995 based on the 1993–2012 invasive series; (3) country list refined to Singapore, Hong Kong SAR, Malaysia, Lao PDR, Thailand and Viet Nam with approximate first-detection years drawn from invasive collections and fish outbreaks, and Myanmar was removed because only sparse, later reports exist and its contribution to this 1993–2017 regional emergence episode is uncertain; (4) “Western Asia” removed from sub_regions, as available data show ST283/CC283 is essentially confined to Asia with only very rare detections in Europe and no clear large-scale Western Asian emergence during this period; and (5) event type updated by switching intra_continental_emergence from Yes to No, keeping re_emergence as Yes, because the EPP (S. agalactiae in humans) was already established in these Asian subregions and this episode reflects re-emergence via a novel hypervirulent clone rather than first establishment of the species. An additional key source (Hong Kong 1993–2012 ST283 series) was added to the URL list to support the corrected Hong Kong dates and burden.
