EPP.scientific.name: Treponema pallidum
EPP.common.name: Syphilis
Host: Humans (general sexually active population, with high incidence in sex workers, clients, and people who inject drugs)
Event.summary: After relatively low syphilis rates in the 1980s, the early 1990s saw a dramatic resurgence of infectious syphilis across the Newly Independent States of the former Soviet Union, with reported incidence in Russia increasing roughly 50-fold by 1997 compared with 1990. The epidemic expanded rapidly through the mid‑1990s, fueled by rising sex work, injecting drug use, and social disruption, and spread widely across Eastern European successor states including Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, the Republic of Moldova and the Baltic countries. Toward the late 1990s incidence began to plateau and then decline in several countries, though levels remained well above those of Western Europe and left a legacy of elevated STI and HIV risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Profound socio-economic upheaval following the collapse of the Soviet Union (unemployment, migration, weakening public health systems), rapid expansion of commercial sex, and increasing injecting drug use created dense sexual and injecting networks with limited access to condoms and STI care; reductions in organized STI control programs and stock-outs of diagnostics and treatment further weakened control. Internal mechanisms: No specific new Treponema pallidum genotype was identified as causal; the event is best understood as a resurgence of existing strains under changed social and health-system conditions (re-occurrence).
Review: review – Retain as one of the largest modern syphilis emergence events, but sub-region and country coding have been corrected: Baltic countries are now listed individually (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) and assigned to Northern Europe, while the event scope is restricted to Eastern European and Baltic successor states rather than all of Central Asia. Text of the event summary was adjusted to match this geographic scope. Host: Humans, predominantly men who have sex with men (MSM), including many living with HIV; smaller contributions from heterosexual transmission and congenital cases
Event.summary: After historically low syphilis incidence in Western and Northern Europe in the mid‑1990s, outbreaks of infectious syphilis were reported from 1997 onward, initially in UK cities and soon in Ireland, the Netherlands, France, Norway and other EU/EEA countries, largely concentrated among MSM. Through the 2000s and 2010s, case notifications rose steadily in many Western and Central European states, with particularly sharp increases among MSM and in urban centers, reversing previous declines. By around 2020, several European countries were reporting their highest syphilis rates in decades, with continued concentration in MSM and emerging concerns about congenital and heterosexual transmission.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Behavioral changes in MSM populations after the advent of effective antiretroviral therapy for HIV (reduced fear of HIV, more condomless sex, higher partner numbers), internet and app-facilitated partner finding, chemsex practices, and sexual mixing within dense urban networks; reduced intensity of classic STI control programs and stigma or barriers limiting access to testing and treatment for MSM and migrants. Internal mechanisms: No dominant new T. pallidum strain has been shown to drive this resurgence; available data suggest circulation of multiple lineages, so this event is best classified as re-occurrence driven by social and behavioral factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review – Retain as a major event describing the MSM-focused resurgence in Western/Northern/Southern Europe, but the type-of-emergence coding has been corrected: intra_continental_emergence has been set to false so that this episode is treated purely as re-occurrence (syphilis was not new to these sub-regions). Countries are broadly correct but include a non-specific "other EU/EEA countries" category; a human reviewer may wish to expand this list for more granular country coverage.

Event.summary: After syphilis rates in the United States fell to historic lows around 2000 and near-elimination was considered achievable, cases began increasing again in the early 2000s, initially largely among MSM in major cities. Through the 2010s, reported primary and secondary syphilis rates rose steadily, with MSM continuing to bear the highest burden but incidence also rising in heterosexual men and women, including those who inject drugs. By the early 2020s, the United States and, to a lesser extent, Canada were experiencing a broad syphilis epidemic across many demographic groups, setting the stage for explosive growth in congenital syphilis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Changing sexual behaviors related to HIV treatment optimism and decreased perceived HIV risk, increased partner concurrency and network connectivity among MSM, use of digital platforms for partner seeking, ongoing substance use and structural vulnerabilities (homelessness, incarceration), and erosion or underfunding of STI control programs. Macrolide-resistant strains became more common during this period but played a relatively modest role in overall incidence trends.

EPP.scientific.name: Histoplasma spp.
EPP.common.name: histoplasmosis
Host: Humans living with HIV, especially with advanced HIV disease (AIDS)
Event.summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, disseminated histoplasmosis emerged as a leading AIDS-defining opportunistic infection and cause of death among people with advanced HIV in several Latin American settings, notably French Guiana and likely other South and Central American countries. Longitudinal cohorts from French Guiana documented hundreds of microbiologically proven disseminated cases from the early 1990s through the 2010s, with incidence rates up to 15 cases per 1,000 person‑years in HIV cohorts and case‑fatality comparable to or exceeding tuberculosis when diagnosis was delayed. Modelling and multicountry data later showed that, by around 2012, HIV-associated histoplasmosis incidence and deaths in Latin America rivalled or exceeded those due to tuberculosis in people living with HIV, cementing its role as a major, previously neglected killer in this region.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6958354/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The HIV epidemic created large populations of profoundly immunosuppressed individuals in endemic Histoplasma regions of Latin America, dramatically increasing the probability of progression from latent or subclinical infection to disseminated disease. Health-system factors—limited awareness, misdiagnosis as tuberculosis, and poor access to rapid antigen testing and effective antifungals—contributed heavily to high mortality, making histoplasmosis a neglected opportunistic infection. External social drivers included poverty, delayed HIV testing, and late presentation to care. Internal mechanisms: No single new fungal genotype is implicated; rather, established Histoplasma lineages caused severe disease in immunocompromised hosts, demonstrating host-population expansion (high-risk HIV group) and clinical re-expression of an old pathogen under new immunologic conditions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10687118/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.common.name: histoplasmosis
Sub.regions: Western Africa; Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Humans, predominantly people with advanced HIV disease and patients misdiagnosed with tuberculosis
Event.summary: Although histoplasmosis has long been present in Africa, from about the mid‑2010s onward new studies and reviews highlighted it as an emerging or neglected disease, particularly among people with advanced HIV. EPP.scientific.name: Cryptococcus gattii
EPP.common.name: cryptococcosis
Host: Humans (mainly immunocompetent or mildly immunocompromised adults); also domestic animals and wildlife (part of the same environmental focus but not the primary focus of this human event sheet)
Event.summary: In 1999, Cryptococcus gattii emerged as a cause of cryptococcosis on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada, in a previously non‑endemic, temperate coastal forest environment, with the earliest recognized human and animal cases traced to that year and environmental isolation from trees and soil confirming local reservoirs. Over 1999–2007 more than 200 human cases were reported in British Columbia, with spread from Vancouver Island to mainland British Columbia and additional cases in residents and travelers exposed in the outbreak area, establishing a new temperate, coastal focus of disease distinct from earlier tropical and subtropical endemic zones.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/cmr.00126-13)) By the early 2010s, incidence in British Columbia had declined from its peak but C. gattii VGII lineages remained established in the environment, with continued sporadic human and animal cases in the broader Pacific Northwest region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely long‑distance dispersal of C. gattii VGII lineages (probably originating from South America or Australia) via movement of contaminated plant material, timber, soil, animals or shipping routes into coastal British Columbia, where mild, wet winters and dry summers, together with specific tree species and forestry/land‑use practices, favored establishment and aerosolization of infectious propagules.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23940707/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion into a novel temperate ecological niche; emergence and clonal expansion of hypervirulent VGIIa (and related VGII) genotypes capable of infecting predominantly immunocompetent hosts; and evidence of enhanced virulence/pathogenicity and efficient environmental persistence compared with many historical tropical strains.
Review: retain – The Vancouver Island/British Columbia episode is correctly captured as a major high‑incidence emergence in a new temperate niche and is among the largest global C. gattii events. However, inter_continental_emergence has been changed from Yes to No because C. gattii had already been documented clinically and environmentally in North America (southern California and the southeastern United States) well before 1999, so this episode represents a large regional re‑emergence and climatic range expansion within an already affected continent rather than first introduction.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/24/11/18-0975)) Countries, years and summary text remain consistent with major epidemiologic descriptions of the Vancouver Island and mainland British Columbia outbreak, so no further structural changes are recommended.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptococcus gattii
EPP.common.name: cryptococcosis
Host: Humans (sporadic autochthonous cases, including immunocompetent adults) with linked environmental reservoirs identified in eucalyptus and carob trees and in forest habitats; additional cases in animals and travelers are epidemiologically linked but not the primary focus here.
Event.summary: From the late 1990s onward, autochthonous C. gattii infections were documented in Mediterranean Europe, including clinical cases in Italy and Spain and associated environmental isolates from Eucalyptus camaldulensis and carob trees near patients’ residences, confirming that parts of Southern Europe harbored endemic foci rather than only imported infections.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3471617/?utm_source=openai)) Around 2010–2012, environmental sampling in the Netherlands identified C. gattii in a forested area and linked it to a local human case, extending the known ecological range of the species into temperate Northern Europe and demonstrating that suitable niches exist beyond the Mediterranean climate zone.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/18/1/11-1190_article?utm_source=openai)) By the early 2010s, Europe was recognized as having both endemic Mediterranean clusters (largely AFLP4/VGI) and emergent temperate foci of C. gattii, with overall human case numbers still low but increasingly understood as a mix of locally acquired and travel‑related infections and reactivation of dormant infections acquired outside Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Mediterranean and some temperate European climates, together with widespread planting of susceptible tree species (e.g. Eucalyptus, carob), appear to support environmental persistence of C. gattii, and international movement of trees, plant material and travelers from endemic tropical regions likely introduced and redistributed genotypes within Europe.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3471617/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion into new European subregions (Northern Europe) and climatic zones; local adaptation of predominant European AFLP4/VGI genotypes to Mediterranean and temperate tree hosts and environments; and a combination of reactivation of long‑dormant infections and in situ environmental transmission, consistent with re‑emergence driven by both host factors and pathogen ecology.
Review: review – The European episode is correctly identified as an important mix of autochthonous and travel‑related C. gattii infections with clear evidence of endemic Mediterranean foci and a newly recognized temperate niche in the Netherlands, and thus merits inclusion as one of the major global emergence/re‑emergence events.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3471617/?utm_source=openai)) To comply better with the country‑format guidance, the countries field has been updated from vague labels ("mid‑2000s", "2000s", "2010–2012") to approximate start years based on the first documented autochthonous clinical or environmental reports in each country (Italy [1997], Spain [2003], Netherlands [2010]); these dates should be treated as indicative rather than exact and therefore warrant a review flag. The dual classification as intra_continental_emergence = Yes (expansion into Northern Europe) and re_emergence = Yes (increased recognition and local adaptation of existing genotypes within Europe) is appropriate and has been retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptococcus neoformans
EPP.common.name: cryptococcosis
Continent: Africa; Asia; South America; Oceania; Europe; North America
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa; Western Africa; Northern Africa (limited data); Southern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Caribbean; South America; Australia and New Zealand; selected high-burden subregions in Europe and North America
Host: Humans (overwhelmingly people living with HIV with CD4 <100 cells/µL; smaller share in other immunosuppressed groups)
Event.summary: A 2017 global burden analysis estimated that in 2014 about 278,000 people with advanced HIV infection were cryptococcal-antigen positive and there were approximately 223,100 incident cases of HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, leading to an estimated 181,100 deaths worldwide that year; roughly 135,900 deaths (75%) occurred in sub-Saharan Africa. Despite substantial ART expansion and some decline in incidence compared with estimates based on 2006 data, cryptococcal meningitis remained a major cause of AIDS-related mortality globally in 2014, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia and Latin America. Subsequent years have seen gradual reductions in incidence where ART coverage, CrAg screening, and improved induction regimens expanded, but high mortality and substantial burden persisted in many low-resource settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent gaps in early HIV diagnosis and ART initiation, continued high prevalence of advanced HIV disease, lack of routine CrAg screening in many countries, shortages of amphotericin B and especially flucytosine, and limited capacity for intensive supportive care sustained a very high global burden in 2014. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel fungal strain is required to explain the burden; the pattern is driven by opportunistic infection of severely immunocompromised hosts by globally endemic C. neoformans. The classification as re-occurrence reflects sustained high incidence and mortality relative to pre-HIV eras, driven primarily by external host and health-system factors.
Review: review: This event correctly represents the 2014 global burden episode described by Rajasingham et al., which estimated 223,100 incident cases of HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis and 181,100 deaths worldwide, with ~75% of deaths in sub-Saharan Africa.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28483415/?utm_source=openai)) Corrections focused on the Countries field: generic phrases such as “Sub-Saharan African countries (e.g. …)” were replaced with an explicit list of exemplar high-burden countries (South Africa, Nigeria, Uganda, etc.) plus an “other high-burden countries” clause, and each listed country was assigned the event year 2014. Geography (all inhabited continents) and classification as a large re-occurrence episode remain appropriate. Flagged for review mainly to confirm whether any additional high-burden countries should be named explicitly, given space constraints.

EPP.scientific.name: Lomentospora prolificans
EPP.common.name: lomentosporiosis
Countries: Republic of Korea [2004] (trauma‑associated knee and bone infection)
Host: Humans—one immunocompetent child with post‑traumatic osteoarticular infection and one adult with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia and profound chemotherapy‑induced neutropenia
Event.summary: In 2004–2005, clinicians in South Korea reported the earliest confirmed human infections with Scedosporium (Lomentospora) prolificans from Asia: first, a 10‑year‑old immunocompetent boy who developed neglected bone and joint infection of the knee after laceration by a broken flowerpot, and then a 45‑year‑old woman with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia who developed fulminant S. prolificans fungemia during salvage chemotherapy and died within a day of starting amphotericin B. The orthopedic case established that this soil‑associated mold could cause musculoskeletal infection following traumatic inoculation in an Asian setting, while the subsequent Korean fungemia report explicitly noted that no bloodstream isolates of S. prolificans had previously been described in Korea or elsewhere in Asia. Together, these cases mark the inter‑continental emergence of L. prolificans in Eastern Asia and showed that both immunocompetent trauma patients and profoundly neutropenic leukemia patients in the region were at risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Environmental exposure to contaminated soil or potted‑plant material in the community (flowerpot injury in the child) and increasing use of intensive chemotherapy for acute leukemia in Korean tertiary centers producing profound neutropenia (adult fungemia case).([jkoa.org](https://jkoa.org/pdf/10.4055/jkoa.2004.39.4.426?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The fungus’ ability to establish chronic osteoarticular infection in an otherwise healthy host, its intrinsic resistance to standard antifungals, and its high virulence in neutropenic hosts (with rapid progression to fatal sepsis) allowed these early Asian cases to occur despite empiric antibacterial and antifungal treatment, signaling that once introduced, L. prolificans could behave similarly to patterns seen in Spain and Australia.
Review: Decision: retain. New event added. Rationale and changes: (i) This row is newly introduced to capture Asia’s true early emergence signal, drawing on a 2004 Korean case of post‑traumatic knee bone/joint infection and a 2005 Korean case of fatal fungemia in a relapsed AML patient. The 2005 report explicitly states that S. prolificans fungemia had not previously been reported in Korea or Asia, indicating that these closely spaced cases represent the first recognized human infections by this species in the region.([jkoa.org](https://jkoa.org/pdf/10.4055/jkoa.2004.39.4.426?utm_source=openai)) (ii) Classified as ‘inter_continental_emergence’ for Asia, with ‘first_detection’ kept false at the global level (global first was in Minnesota in 1984). (iii) Countries and subregion were set according to the UNSD list (Republic of Korea, Eastern Asia). (iv) The event is temporally modest (two cases) but high‑impact for this rare EPP due to being the first confirmed Asian infections and illustrating both trauma‑associated disease and rapidly fatal disseminated infection. Flagged for review to confirm acceptance as one of the top global emergence events; if a strict cap of 10 events is enforced, this would still warrant inclusion given its continental significance.

EPP.scientific.name: Fusarium spp.
EPP.common.name: fusariosis
Host: Humans (medical tourists and local patients receiving cosmetic surgery under epidural anesthesia in Matamoros and subsequent care in Mexico or the United States)
Event.summary: In early 2023, health authorities in Texas were notified of severe meningitis cases among US residents who had recently traveled to Matamoros, Tamaulipas, Mexico, for cosmetic procedures performed under epidural anesthesia, prompting a binational investigation. Public health agencies in Mexico and the United States ultimately identified hundreds of potentially exposed patients linked to two clinics (Clinica K‑3 and River Side Surgical Center) and documented at least two dozen confirmed and probable fungal meningitis cases among US residents plus additional affected patients in Mexico, with Fusarium solani species complex DNA detected in cerebrospinal fluid and a highly resistant F. solani strain isolated from at least one patient; about half of the confirmed and probable US cases died. Closure of the implicated clinics, international notification and screening of exposed individuals, and aggressive combination antifungal therapy and long‑term follow‑up led to progressive containment of the outbreak, though many patients experienced prolonged illness, neurovascular complications and significant morbidity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unsafe injection practices or contaminated anesthetic or related materials used for epidural anesthesia in high‑volume cosmetic surgery clinics that catered to international medical tourists created a direct route for Fusarium inoculation into the central nervous system, while cross‑border travel and delayed recognition of fungal meningitis facilitated a multinational outbreak spanning patients in Mexico and multiple US states. Internal mechanisms: The Fusarium solani complex isolates involved demonstrated high antifungal minimum inhibitory concentrations, consistent with substantial intrinsic resistance that complicated treatment, but current evidence points to contaminated procedures and direct CNS exposure rather than a fundamentally new, more transmissible or virulent Fusarium genotype; cases detected in the United States and any other countries are epidemiologically part of the same Matamoros‑centred healthcare‑associated episode and do not constitute separate inter‑continental emergence events.

Event.summary: In 2006, a substantial meningitis outbreak due to serogroup X Neisseria meningitidis ST‑181 occurred in south‑western Niger, where serogroup A had previously dominated, with over 550 confirmed cases in Niamey and surrounding areas. Over 2006–2010, serogroup X ST‑181 lineages spread to additional meningitis‑belt countries including Burkina Faso and Togo, while a distinct ST‑5403 serogroup X lineage caused outbreaks in northeastern Uganda and parts of Kenya, making X a significant contributor to the regional meningitis burden in some years. These epidemics declined seasonally and following reactive A/C vaccination campaigns (which did not cover X) and the buildup of natural immunity, but serogroup X persisted at low levels without a specific vaccine, contributing to concern about multivalent conjugate vaccine needs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Low baseline population immunity to serogroup X, climatic and ecological conditions of the meningitis belt, and limited vaccine formulations that did not include X allowed this serogroup to exploit ecological space as serogroup A dynamics changed. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and geographic expansion of epidemic‑prone serogroup X lineages (ST‑181 in West Africa and ST‑5403 in East Africa) represent strain‑specific re-emergence of N. meningitidis with novel serogroup patterns and geographic range expansion within Africa.
Review: review – Retain as a major serogroup X episode but correct emergence typing. Because meningococci were already widely established across these African sub‑regions, and the event reflects the rise of serogroup X lineages in areas where other serogroups had long circulated, it should not be marked as intra‑continental emergence. I set intra_continental_emergence to false and kept re_emergence as true, in line with the instruction that new serogroups/strains in previously affected subregions be treated as re‑emergence rather than intra‑continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Ehrlichia sp.
EPP.common.name: ehrlichiosis
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Humans (adult and pediatric patients with tick-associated febrile illness in Lyme borreliosis–endemic areas)
Event.summary: In 1996–1997, clinicians in Slovenia reported the first molecularly confirmed human cases of granulocytic ehrlichiosis in Europe, with several adult and pediatric patients presenting with acute febrile illness, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia after Ixodes tick bites in Lyme borreliosis–endemic areas. Shortly thereafter, additional cases were described from western Europe, including the Netherlands, showing that a granulocytic Ehrlichia‑like agent (subsequently recognized as Anaplasma phagocytophilum) was causing human disease on the continent. Over the following years, further autochthonous cases were confirmed in multiple European countries, establishing granulocytic ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis as an emerging tick‑borne infection in central and western Europe rather than a problem confined to North America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Shared Ixodes ricinus tick vectors and reservoir hosts with Lyme borreliosis in central and western Europe provided ecological conditions favoring maintenance and spillover of granulocytic Ehrlichia/Anaplasma lineages; increased awareness in Lyme‑endemic regions led to targeted testing of atypical febrile illnesses after tick bites. Internal mechanisms: The same or closely related granulocytic lineages identified in North America appear to have been present in European Ixodes populations for some time, so this episode reflects inter‑continental recognition of an already widespread agent rather than de novo evolution in Europe.
Review: Decision: review. This episode accurately captures the first confirmed human granulocytic ehrlichiosis cases in Europe and the initial recognition that this disease (now classified as human granulocytic anaplasmosis) occurs on a second continent. I turned off the first_detection flag so that the row now represents inter-continental emergence rather than a second global “first detection” event. Because the etiologic agent is Anaplasma phagocytophilum and not a current Ehrlichia species, curators should consider whether to retain this event under the Ehrlichia sp. EPP or migrate it to an Anaplasma phagocytophilum sheet; the sub-region list (Southern, Western, and possibly Eastern Europe) may also be broader than what is documented for 1996–1997 and merits expert checking.

EPP.scientific.name: Ehrlichia sp.
EPP.common.name: ehrlichiosis
Host: Humans (an adult patient with tick-associated febrile illness), domestic goats (index animal host)
Event.summary: In the mid‑2000s, a previously undescribed Ehrlichia species closely related to E. ruminantium was identified in a goat experimentally exposed to Amblyomma americanum ticks from Panola Mountain State Park, Georgia, and later termed the Panola Mountain Ehrlichia. EPP.scientific.name: Ehrlichia sp.
EPP.common.name: ehrlichiosis
Countries: United States of America – southeastern, south‑central, and mid‑Atlantic states [2008]
Host: Humans (nationally reported cases of E. chaffeensis and E. ewingii ehrlichiosis)
Event.summary: From 2008 to 2012, US national surveillance documented a marked increase in reported cases and incidence of ehrlichiosis due to E. chaffeensis and E. ewingii, with over 1,500 E. chaffeensis infections reported in 2013 and incidence highest in the southeastern, south‑central and mid‑Atlantic regions but with an increasing number of cases identified in parts of the Midwest. EPP.scientific.name: Mammarenavirus lujoense
EPP.common.name: Lujo virus
Host: Humans (index case in Zambia and healthcare workers in South Africa)
Event.summary: Origin: In early September 2008, a female office worker living near Lusaka, Zambia developed an acute febrile illness that rapidly progressed to severe viral hemorrhagic fever; she was airlifted to Johannesburg, South Africa for treatment, where she later died. Development: Over subsequent weeks, four secondary nosocomial cases occurred—a Zambian paramedic involved in her evacuation and three South African healthcare or hospital workers—after unprotected exposure to the index patient’s blood and body fluids, creating a cluster of five epidemiologically linked cases with an approximately 80% case‑fatality rate and triggering intensive outbreak investigation and infection‑control measures. End: Following recognition of a probable viral hemorrhagic fever, barrier nursing, strict infection‑prevention and control practices, contact tracing, and isolation were implemented in Johannesburg, and no further cases occurred beyond the initial five; no additional human infections have been confirmed since this outbreak.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Zoonotic spillover from an as‑yet‑unidentified rodent reservoir in or near Lusaka, Zambia, followed by international medical evacuation of an undiagnosed severe febrile illness and initially inadequate infection‑prevention and control in the receiving hospital, which enabled limited nosocomial human‑to‑human transmission in Johannesburg. Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) from a rodent‑borne Old World arenavirus into humans, with documented person‑to‑person transmission via direct contact with blood and other body fluids in healthcare settings; there is no evidence to date of broader viral adaptation, sustained community transmission, or inherent geographic range expansion beyond this single, highly contained outbreak.
Review: review – Retain this event as the sole major emergence episode for Lujo virus (the 2008 Zambia/South Africa outbreak), which is well supported by primary literature and public‑health agency reports. Corrections applied: (1) event‑type coding adjusted to keep categories mutually exclusive for this single linked outbreak, setting first_global_emergence = Yes while changing first_detection from Yes to No and intra_continental_emergence from Yes to No, because all cases form one cross‑border nosocomial episode initiated by medical evacuation rather than independent emergence in a new sub‑region; (2) mechanism/driver text revised to remove unsupported reference to “Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)” and to emphasize zoonotic spillover plus limited nosocomial spread; (3) added the PLOS Pathogens genetic‑detection paper as a primary description of the same 2008 outbreak to both event‑level and profile‑level source lists. A human reviewer should confirm agreement with this coding choice (first/global emergence only) but no additional events appear to be missing or spurious for this EPP.

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
EPP.common.name: melioidosis
Host: Humans (three adults with risk factors) and livestock (two animal cases)
Event.summary: Between 2018 and 2021, Southern Africa documented an emergence cluster of three human and two animal melioidosis cases in South Africa and Namibia, with whole‑genome sequencing showing substantial diversity among B. pseudomallei isolates and supporting long‑term regional persistence. The episode unfolded as sporadic but clinically severe infections in persons with diabetes and other risk factors and in livestock, all initially unexpected because melioidosis had not previously been recognized in Southern Africa. Following these detections, the event stabilized into sporadic recognized cases with calls for enhanced environmental sampling and improved diagnostic capacity rather than a continuous high‑incidence outbreak.

Prior African human cases and environmental detections were in other sub-regions (principally Eastern and Western Africa), whereas these are the first confirmed human and ovine cases from Southern Africa (South Africa and Namibia), representing spread into a new UN African sub-region. EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia psittaci
EPP.common.name: psittacosis
Host: Humans with psittacosis, most with pneumonia, exposed mainly to wild birds and pet birds in community settings across multiple European countries
Event.summary: From early 2023 through at least February 2024, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands reported through the EU Early Warning and Response System an unusual and unexpected increase in human psittacosis cases, with numbers rising sharply from November–December 2023 and five deaths recorded, prompting a WHO Disease Outbreak News notification. National investigations found that most affected patients had recent exposure to wild or domestic birds (often via garden bird feeders or hobby poultry) rather than to each other, and no common cross‑border point source or evidence of sustained human‑to‑human transmission or spread beyond Europe was identified, although many cases required hospitalisation for pneumonia. By late winter 2024, reported case numbers began to decline, and WHO and EU agencies assessed the overall public‑health risk as low while recommending continued surveillance, veterinary investigations in wild and domestic birds, and targeted risk communication on zoonotic transmission routes and timely antibiotic treatment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increased seasonal exposure to infected wild and domestic birds across several Northern and Western European countries, including heavy use of garden bird feeders, possible underlying changes in avian population dynamics and infection prevalence, and enhanced clinical awareness and molecular testing once the multi‑country signal was detected; improvements in surveillance sensitivity may have amplified the apparent increase. Internal mechanisms: no specific novel C. psittaci variant has been implicated, and available evidence favours interpretation of this event as a regional re‑occurrence of psittacosis amplified by environmental and surveillance factors rather than emergence of a fundamentally new strain.
Review: retain – This multi‑country 2023–2024 European event is correctly represented as a substantial regional re‑occurrence involving at least five EU/EEA countries, with over a hundred reported cases and five deaths, and no evidence of sustained inter‑continental spread or primarily human‑to‑human transmission. Country list, subregions (Northern and Western Europe) and timing are consistent with WHO’s Disease Outbreak News and EU threat assessments, and the emergence‑type classification (re‑occurrence only) matches the definitions. Existing sources adequately document the event, so no further structural corrections are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridium botulinum
EPP.common.name: Botulism
Host: Humans (adult consumers in the United States and Canada drinking commercially produced refrigerated carrot juice)
Event.summary: In September–October 2006, an international outbreak of severe foodborne botulism was identified in the United States (Georgia, Florida) and Canada among adults who drank a commercially produced, pasteurized carrot juice that was inadequately refrigerated after purchase. Investigations confirmed botulinum neurotoxin type A in leftover juice and linked at least six severe cases—four in the United States and two in Canada, several requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation—to consumption of juice from specific lots, prompting recalls and consumer warnings in both countries. EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus kyasanurense
EPP.common.name: Alkhurma virus
Countries: Egypt [2010] (southern Egypt near the Red Sea/Sudan border)
Host: Humans (Italian travelers exposed in southern Egypt, likely via tick bites or contact with camels); camels and local ticks in southern Egypt are implicated as part of the zoonotic cycle based on exposure histories and phylogenetic similarity to Saudi strains.
Event.summary: In early 2010, two Italian tourists developed acute febrile illness with thrombocytopenia and other systemic signs shortly after returning from travel in southern Egypt near the Sudan border, where they had close contact with camels and likely exposure to ticks, and were hospitalized in Italy with fever of unknown origin. Molecular testing of acute‑phase sera identified Alkhurma hemorrhagic fever virus RNA, and sequencing of viral envelope gene fragments showed close clustering with Saudi AHFV strains, providing the first laboratory confirmation that AHFV was circulating in humans outside Saudi Arabia and indicating a transmission focus in southern Egypt on the African continent. Both illnesses resolved with supportive care in Italy and no secondary transmission occurred there, but this episode marked the first recognized human AHFV infections acquired in Africa and prompted calls for targeted ecological and serologic studies in Egypt and neighboring countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of camel‑based tourism and travel in southern Egypt created new interfaces between international travelers and local camel/tick enzootic cycles, facilitating unnoticed exposure to infected Ornithodoros or other ticks in desert and oasis environments; regional movement of livestock and camels between the Arabian Peninsula and northeast Africa may have contributed to the introduction or maintenance of AHFV in Egypt. Internal mechanisms: Egyptian traveler-derived sequences showed low genetic distance from Saudi AHFV isolates, suggesting recent divergence and limited microevolution rather than a distinct African lineage; the main biological process is host expansion/spillover from an established camel/tick cycle into naive human travelers rather than altered viral virulence or transmissibility.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Retained the event as the first documented human infections acquired in Africa and appropriately classified it as inter‑continental emergence because exposure and infection occurred in Egypt, but corrected the first_detection flag to false since first detection of AHFV in humans occurred in Saudi Arabia in the mid‑1990s; country listing was also clarified to distinguish infection location (Egypt) from place of diagnosis (Italy, imported cases only).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus kyasanurense
EPP.common.name: Alkhurma virus
Host: Humans (Italian traveler infected after a camel tour in southern Egypt); camels and local ticks along Red Sea desert routes likely involved as reservoir/vector system.
Event.summary: In 2013, an Italian woman who had traveled across southern Egypt from the Red Sea coast toward the Sudan border, including participation in a camel tour, developed high fever, malaise and later severe muscular weakness and rhabdomyolysis within days of returning to Italy. Diagnostic work‑up identified Alkhurma hemorrhagic fever virus infection by molecular methods, representing a further documented AHFV infection acquired in Egypt and expanding the recognized clinical spectrum of disease to include prominent myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. The patient recovered after intensive supportive treatment without onward transmission in Italy, but this case confirmed ongoing AHFV circulation in southern Egypt several years after the 2010 traveler cases and underscored the need for heightened awareness among clinicians seeing returning travelers from camel‑ and tick‑exposed areas of northeastern Africa.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued development of desert and camel‑based tourism in southern Egypt sustained opportunities for high‑risk tick exposure among travelers, while limited local surveillance meant that endemic AHFV circulation could persist largely undetected in resident populations; cross‑border movements of camels and pastoral communities between Egypt and Sudan likely support a broader regional focus. Internal mechanisms: Viral sequencing in traveler‑associated cases has consistently shown close relatedness to Saudi AHFV strains with minimal divergence, indicating that this recurrence in Egypt reflects a stable, established lineage rather than a newly evolved variant; the event is thus categorized as re‑occurrence driven by persistent enzootic transmission and human behavior rather than by major intrinsic viral change.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: Event corresponds to a well‑documented imported case of AHFV in an Italian traveler with exposure in southern Egypt, correctly located in Africa | Northern Africa and classified as re‑occurrence in the same African focus first identified in 2010; although numerically small, it is one of very few known non‑Saudi human infections and is appropriately included among the major emergence events.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus powassanense
EPP.common.name: Powassan/Deer tick virus
Host: Humans; ticks (primarily Ixodes cookei, with emerging involvement of Ixodes scapularis); small mammals (woodchucks, squirrels, other rodents as reservoirs)
Event.summary: After several decades with only sporadic reports, Powassan virus reappeared in the northeastern United States when a neuroinvasive case was reported in Massachusetts in 1994, followed by a four‑case outbreak of Powassan encephalitis in Maine and Vermont during 1999–2001 that represented the first recognized cases in those states and the first U.S. cases since 1994. These cases marked renewed recognition of endemic foci in New England, with enhanced surveillance and serologic testing revealing that the virus had been circulating more widely than previously appreciated. The episode ended as incident cases again became rare after 2001, but it set the stage for subsequent expansion and increasing detection of lineage II (deer tick virus) in the same broader region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increased clinical awareness and use of flavivirus serology in patients with encephalitis; expanding populations of ticks and wildlife hosts in New England due to land‑use change, reforestation, and growing deer populations; overlap with emerging Lyme disease ecology. Internal mechanisms: emergence and recognition of Powassan lineage II (deer tick virus) in Ixodes scapularis ticks in the northeastern U.S., representing a novel genotype associated with more efficient human exposure via a common human‑biting tick (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Host Expansion (Spillover); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).
Review: review – Event is real and represents the key New England re‑emergence episode (Massachusetts 1994 case and the 1999–2001 Maine/Vermont outbreak). Updated the countries field to give state‑specific start years (Massachusetts [1994]; Maine, Vermont [1999–2001]) and left the event year span at 1994–2001 to cover this linked regional episode. Event type was restricted to re_emergence (re_occurrence kept at No) to comply with the project rule that categories are mutually exclusive except where re_emergence co‑occurs with inter/intra‑continental emergence. Added the CDC MMWR outbreak report as a primary source; recommend expert review of the chosen temporal grouping (single event versus splitting 1994 and 1999–2001) but keep the event as one of the major Powassan episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus usutuense
EPP.common.name: Usutu virus
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Humans (mix of neuroinvasive disease, febrile illness, and asymptomatic blood donors)
Event.summary: In 2018, Europe experienced a marked amplification of Usutu virus activity, with human infections documented in several countries including Italy, the Netherlands, Croatia, Hungary and Czechia, making this the largest recognized multi‑country episode of human Usutu infection to date. In northern Italy, eight cases (one neuroinvasive, six febrile and one viremic blood donor) were identified through targeted diagnostics and blood‑donor screening; Croatia detected three additional neuroinvasive cases during a large West Nile virus outbreak; Hungary confirmed its first human Usutu infection in a patient with aseptic meningitis; and the Netherlands identified seven RNA‑positive blood donors during West Nile virus screening. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31771697/?utm_source=openai)) This episode coincided with exceptional epizootic transmission and large‑scale bird mortality across central and western Europe, and after 2018 human detections continued at lower but persistent levels, reflecting established enzootic circulation and ongoing, though still relatively rare, human spillover events.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Exceptionally warm summer conditions in 2018 that enhanced Culex mosquito abundance and competence, synchronized epizootics in wild and captive birds across much of Europe, and widespread blood‑donor NAT screening for arboviruses that increased detection sensitivity; land‑use factors (urban green spaces, river valleys, irrigated agriculture) and overlapping West Nile virus surveillance also contributed to increased ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: Circulation of multiple European Usutu virus lineages (notably Europe 2 and Europe 1) with demonstrated capacity for geographic expansion and overwintering in local mosquito populations supported broad range expansion within Europe, while lineage‑specific differences in neurovirulence (for example, Europe 2 strains over‑represented among severe infections in Italy, Croatia, Hungary and Czechia) likely contributed to the observed spectrum of neuroinvasive disease.
Review: review – event retained as the principal 2018 multi‑country amplification episode but edited to align with the documented pattern of human infections. Countries now listed (Italy, Netherlands, Croatia, Hungary, Czechia) all have confirmed 2018 human cases, while Belgium, Germany and France were removed because, to date, Belgium has only animal infections and German (2012, 2016) and French (2016) human cases occurred in earlier years. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10436690/?utm_source=openai)) Sub‑regions were corrected to Southern, Western and Eastern Europe, and the episode is now classified as both intra‑continental emergence (first confirmed human infections in Eastern Europe – Hungary and Czechia) and re‑emergence within already affected southern and western sub‑regions. Source URLs were replaced with primary reports on 2018 human cases (Italy, Croatia, Hungary, Czechia, Netherlands) and the ECDC EU/EEA synthesis.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Rubivirus rubellae
EPP.common.name: Rubella virus
Host: Humans (primarily unvaccinated children and young adults in orthodox Protestant communities; pregnant women; infants with CRS)
Event.summary: Beginning in September 2004, a large rubella outbreak occurred in an under‑vaccinated orthodox Protestant population in the Netherlands’ Bible Belt, resulting in 300–400 reported cases and at least 11 infants with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) following infection of pregnant women. Transmission in both countries declined by late 2005 after intensified case finding, isolation, and targeted vaccination in the affected communities, but the episode highlighted how clustered vaccine refusal and introduction of a new rubella virus genotype could generate substantial CRS burden and cross‑Atlantic spread even in regions close to elimination.

Internal mechanisms: Introduction and sustained circulation of a distinct rubella virus genotype not previously documented in this community or in Canada, which spread between the Netherlands and Ontario; although no major change in virulence was demonstrated, the genotype introduction and associated CRS burden justify classifying this as a re‑emergence event rather than simple re‑occurrence.

Rationale: This previously missing event represents a major elimination-era outbreak with high CRS burden in the Netherlands and a sizable linked outbreak in Ontario, Canada, all within a well-defined under-vaccinated religious network; it is widely cited as a key example of clustered susceptibility and international spread. EPP.scientific.name: Morganella spp.
EPP.common.name: Morganella infection
Continent: Asia; Europe; Africa; North America; Oceania
Sub.regions: Southern Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Eastern Africa; Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Hospitalized human patients (mixed adult populations, mainly with prior healthcare exposure or recent medical care in the Indian subcontinent) infected or colonized with NDM‑producing Enterobacteriaceae, including occasional Morganella morganii isolates
Event.summary: From 2008 onward, New Delhi metallo‑β‑lactamase‑1 (NDM‑1) was first recognized in carbapenem‑resistant Enterobacteriaceae in patients linked to healthcare in the Indian subcontinent, and early collections of NDM‑1 producers already included a Morganella morganii isolate among predominantly Klebsiella and Escherichia coli strains. Over 2008–2010, NDM‑1‑producing Enterobacteriaceae spread rapidly from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh to hospitals in the United Kingdom and other European centers via travelers and medical tourists, with Morganella occasionally identified among colonizing or infecting species. By roughly 2010–2012, NDM‑positive Enterobacteriaceae carrying blaNDM‑1 (and related NDM variants) had been reported from health‑care settings across multiple continents—including Western Asia, East and South‑East Asia, Northern Europe, Northern America, Eastern Africa and Oceania—establishing the potential for Morganella to participate in globally disseminated, carbapenem‑resistant Enterobacterales lineages.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: growth of high‑intensity tertiary care and medical tourism in the Indian subcontinent; extensive broad‑spectrum antibiotic use in hospitals; widespread carriage of blaNDM‑bearing plasmids in Enterobacteriaceae; international travel and cross‑border patient transfers facilitating export of NDM‑producing strains to Europe, North America, Africa and Oceania. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – acquisition of blaNDM genes on promiscuous plasmids by Morganella morganii; Antimicrobial Resistance – emergence of high‑level carbapenem resistance mediated by NDM; Enhanced Transmission – efficient horizontal transfer of NDM plasmids across diverse Enterobacterales in healthcare environments, allowing Morganella to join multispecies AMR clones; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – no change in the organism’s ecological niche is proven, but plasmid‑mediated carbapenem resistance allowed survival under intense carbapenem selection pressures worldwide.
Review: review: Event retained but reinterpreted as a re-emergence episode driven by acquisition of NDM-type carbapenemases in Morganella rather than as first detection or true inter-continental emergence of the organism itself. Corrected type-of-emergence coding by setting first_detection and inter_continental_emergence to No and re_emergence to Yes, consistent with the project’s guidance that new resistance determinants should not be classified as inter-/intra-continental emergence of the EPP. Sub-region list was cleaned to remove the non-standard entry “Northern Europe (Nordic countries)”; the countries list was pruned to drop “Nordic countries (unspecified)” and “Taiwan, Province of China”, which lacked specific Morganella data in the cited sources. Country-specific years remain approximate for some sites (e.g. “2010s”) and should be refined if more detailed Morganella-focused NDM surveillance data become available.

EPP.scientific.name: Proteus spp.
EPP.common.name: Proteus infection
Host: Humans (hospitalized, long‑term‑care, and some community patients with urinary tract and other infections caused by CMY‑type AmpC-producing Proteus mirabilis)
Event.summary: Between 1999 and 2008, a multidrug‑resistant Proteus mirabilis clone carrying chromosomal CMY‑type AmpC β‑lactamases of Citrobacter freundii origin (notably CMY‑16 and related variants) emerged and spread across multiple European countries, with earliest detections in Poland in 1999 and subsequent expansion to northern Italy and Greece from 2003 onwards. A focused investigation at an Italian hospital in Varese from 2004–2006 found that 43 of 2,070 P. mirabilis clinical isolates (prevalence rising from 0.3% to 4.6%) produced acquired AmpC‑type cephalosporinases, all harboring CMY‑16 and showing clonal relatedness, and similar CMY‑type chromosomal cephalosporinases were documented in Poland and Greece. Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Sustained use of third‑generation cephalosporins and other broad‑spectrum β‑lactams in European hospitals and long‑term‑care facilities favored selection and maintenance of AmpC‑producing Proteus mirabilis; high antibiotic pressure in elderly and chronically ill patient populations provided a niche for establishment of multidrug‑resistant clones. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – acquisition of blaCMY‑type AmpC genes (especially CMY‑16) from Citrobacter freundii via ISEcp1-associated transposition modules (Tn6093), followed by stable chromosomal integration and clonal expansion; Antimicrobial Resistance – AmpC production conferred high‑level resistance to most penicillins and expanded‑spectrum cephalosporins and reduced susceptibility to β‑lactam/β‑lactamase inhibitor combinations; Enhanced Transmission – a successful CMY‑16‑producing P. mirabilis clone disseminated across multiple hospitals and countries in Europe.
Review: Review – New event added to capture the Europe‑wide clonal spread of CMY‑type AmpC-producing P. mirabilis (especially CMY‑16) documented between 1999 and 2008 in Poland, Italy and Greece, and associated with a substantial, measurable increase in cephalosporin resistance prevalence and dozens of clinical infections. EPP.scientific.name: Simplexvirus spp.
EPP.common.name: herpes simplex virus 1; herpes simplex virus 2
Host: Humans (sexually active adolescents and adults, predominantly 15–49 years)
Event.summary: From roughly 1990 to 2010, genital herpes due to HSV-2 remained a major hidden epidemic in the United States and Canada. National estimates suggest that about 45 million Americans were already HSV-2-seropositive in the early 1990s, and modelling indicates roughly 1.6 million new HSV-2 infections in 2000 alone, with about 640,000 of these in 15–24-year-olds. Although U.S. HSV-2 seroprevalence among adults aged 14–49 years declined modestly from around 21% in 1988–1994 to about 15–16% by 2007–2010, the absolute number of infected adults and annual incident infections remained very high, concentrated in adolescents and young adults. By the late 2000s HSV-2 genital herpes was still one of the most common sexually transmitted infections in Northern America, with the vast majority of infected people unaware of their status and driving ongoing transmission.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High levels of sexual risk behaviour (multiple partners, inconsistent condom use), urbanization, and overlapping HIV/STI epidemics during the 1970s–1990s created and then sustained a large pool of HSV-2-infected adults; persistent underdiagnosis and lack of routine screening meant that most infections were asymptomatic or unrecognized, facilitating silent spread. Internal mechanisms: No major new HSV-2 genotypes were implicated; this episode reflects persistence of high transmission in established sexual networks driven by external social and behavioural factors rather than virologic change, so it is best characterised as re-occurrence in an already endemic setting.
Review: review - Retain as a major regional burden episode for genital HSV-2 in Northern America. The event summary was revised to clarify that HSV-2 seroprevalence in the U.S. plateaued or modestly declined between 1990 and 2010 rather than continuously increasing, while still involving tens of millions of prevalent infections and roughly 1.6 million new infections in 2000 based on modelling. No changes were needed to geography or event-type classification (re-occurrence driven by external behavioural factors). Source set is appropriate and was left unchanged.

Event.summary: Between the early 1990s and about 2010, industrialized countries in Northern and Western Europe, Northern America, and Australasia documented a marked epidemiological shift, with HSV-1 causing an increasing proportion of first-episode genital herpes in young adults. Clinic and surveillance data from settings such as the United Kingdom, the United States, the Nordic countries, and Australia/New Zealand showed the share of genital herpes due to HSV-1 rising from a minority of cases in the 1970s–1980s to 20–50% or more of first-episode genital herpes by the mid-1990s and 2000s, and exceeding 50% in some younger cohorts by the 2000s. By the end of the period, genital HSV-1 had become a leading cause of new genital herpes episodes in younger age groups in several high-income countries, while HSV-2 remained dominant among older adults.

Internal mechanisms: No major novel HSV-1 strains were implicated; instead, the same virus shifted anatomic niche from predominantly oral to increasingly genital infection (a change in clinical and epidemiologic manifestation rather than host species). In line with the project guidance that new manifestations in an already affected host system should be treated as re-emergence rather than intra- or inter-continental emergence, this episode is classified as re-emergence within existing subregions.

Event.summary: From 1990 through at least 2016, countries across Eastern, Southern, Western and parts of Middle Africa experienced extremely high HSV-2 prevalence and genital ulcer disease burden, particularly among women of reproductive age. Regional modelling suggests that around one-third of adults aged 15–49 years in the WHO African Region—rising to about half of women aged 25–34 years—were living with HSV-2 infection by 2012–2016, with HSV-2 accounting for the majority of genital ulcer disease in many populations. In 2016 an estimated 420,000 of 1.4 million sexually acquired HIV infections worldwide were attributable to HSV-2 infection, with the largest share and highest population-attributable fraction in Africa, highlighting HSV-2 as a key cofactor sustaining the region’s generalised HIV epidemics.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of heterosexual HIV epidemics, high rates of partner change in some sexual networks, limited access to condoms and STI care, gender inequality, and structural factors such as poverty and urbanisation created conditions in which HSV-2 spread widely and remained largely untreated. The biological synergy between HSV-2 and HIV—HSV-2 ulcers increasing HIV acquisition and transmission risk and HIV-related immunosuppression enhancing HSV reactivation—further amplified both epidemics. Internal mechanisms: No specific new HSV-2 lineage has been implicated; rather, long-established HSV-2 strains caused frequent genital ulcer disease in the context of overlapping HIV infection, so this is classified as a large regional re-occurrence of an endemic pathogen driven by external social and epidemiological factors.

Event.summary: From 1990 through 2021, global burden assessments documented a large and growing absolute number of genital herpes cases worldwide. Global Burden of Disease estimates indicate that incident genital herpes cases among people aged 15–49 years increased by about 52% over this period, from roughly 23.6 million new cases in 1990 to about 35.8 million in 2021, while the global incidence rate remained relatively stable (around 0.9% per year). By 2012–2016, approximately two-thirds of the world’s population under age 50 had HSV-1 infection and about 11–13% of individuals aged 15–49 years had HSV-2 infection, corresponding to more than half a billion people with genital HSV infection and tens of millions of new genital herpes episodes annually. By 2021, genital herpes remained one of the most prevalent STIs worldwide, with especially high HSV-2 prevalence and genital ulcer disease burden in sub-Saharan Africa and persistently high or increasing incidence in regions such as South Asia, Southern sub-Saharan Africa, and Central Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent high-risk sexual transmission dynamics (including inconsistent condom use, multiple partners, and overlapping HIV/STI epidemics), demographic growth in low- and middle-income countries, limited access to STI prevention and clinical services, and lack of vaccines or population-level HSV control programmes have maintained or increased the global burden; in some high-income regions, delayed HSV-1 acquisition in childhood and changes in sexual practices also contribute to genital HSV-1. Internal mechanisms: No single novel HSV lineage has been shown to drive global expansion; instead, the episode reflects sustained transmission of long-established HSV-1 and HSV-2 strains across diverse settings. It is therefore categorised as a large-scale re-occurrence (persistence and expansion of absolute case numbers and stable or rising incidence in several regions) of an endemic infection rather than new emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
EPP.common.name: Oropouche virus
Host: Humans (urban and rural populations across Amazonian and non‑Amazonian regions of Brazil and Peru, Andean and coastal areas of Bolivia, Colombia and Ecuador, and Caribbean/Central American populations in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Panama and Guyana)
Event.summary: Beginning in late 2023 and accelerating through 2024, Brazil and Peru experienced an unprecedented surge of Oropouche fever cases, with Brazil alone reporting nearly 6,000 RT‑PCR–confirmed cases by March 2024 and >9,500 by November 2024 across at least 22 states, including many non‑Amazonian areas, while Peru reported hundreds of cases in multiple departments. During 2024, locally acquired Oropouche virus disease was confirmed for the first time or at expanded scale in several additional countries and territories—Bolivia, Colombia, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Guyana and Panama—leading PAHO and WHO to estimate >10,000 confirmed cases and to document the first deaths and suspected congenital infections associated with Oropouche virus. EPP.scientific.name: Bandavirus dabieense
EPP.common.name: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus; SFTSV
Host: Humans (adult and pediatric patients with acute febrile illness and thrombocytopenia; several with SFTSV–scrub typhus co-infection; likely tick exposure in rural areas)
Event.summary: In 2017, clinicians at Hue University Hospital in central Viet Nam retrospectively analysed stored serum from patients with acute fever and thrombocytopenia and detected SFTSV RNA in two patients without travel history to known endemic countries, confirming the first recognised autochthonous human SFTS infections in South‑eastern Asia. During 2018–2019, molecular testing of 152 suspected scrub typhus patients in Sagaing and Magway Regions of Myanmar identified SFTSV RNA in five co‑infected patients, whose viral S‑segment sequences closely resembled Vietnamese strains, indicating that SFTSV was also transmitting locally in neighbouring Myanmar. Together these findings show that by 2017–2018 SFTSV had expanded from East Asia into the South‑eastern Asia subregion, although only small numbers of sporadic human cases were recognised clinically in this early emergence phase.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: under‑recognised tick exposure among rural residents in central Viet Nam and northern Myanmar, limited initial diagnostic capacity for SFTSV in South‑eastern Asia, and ecological suitability of local hard-tick species and vertebrate hosts. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of SFTSV from East Asia into a new UNSD subregion (South‑eastern Asia), likely via movement of infected ticks on livestock or wildlife; phylogenetic analyses indicate that Vietnamese and Myanmar strains are closely related to East Asian lineages and to each other, consistent with recent introductions and early local establishment rather than long-term cryptic circulation.
Review: review – expanded this event to represent a linked South‑eastern Asia emergence episode spanning Viet Nam (2017) and Myanmar (2018); corrected the year span and country list, updated the event summary to include Myanmar’s RT‑PCR–confirmed co-infections, and added key primary sources (Myanmar EID report and Japanese risk assessment). Coding as intra‑continental emergence (new UNSD subregion within Asia) is appropriate but should be revisited as regional data accumulate.

Host: Humans (general population; blood donors; individuals with suspected CNS infection)
Event.summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, sero-epidemiological surveys across nine Spanish regions revealed widespread exposure to Toscana virus, with around 26% seroprevalence in a random cohort of individuals without reported meningitis or febrile illness, indicating substantial silent circulation. Subsequent studies in Murcia and Madrid (2007, 2018–2019) confirmed high and sometimes increasing TOSV antibody prevalence in blood donors, alongside documented neuroinvasive cases, highlighting an entrenched but previously underrecognized public health burden. Transmission continues to recur seasonally in Mediterranean Spain, with no clear end to virus circulation but improved awareness and diagnostic capacity in recent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-standing presence of competent sand fly vectors in Mediterranean Spain, outdoor occupational and recreational exposure, and underdiagnosed arboviral CNS infections that were gradually recognized as diagnostic algorithms expanded. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel genotype identified as responsible for emergence; the apparent rise is primarily due to improved detection of an endemic virus rather than a documented shift in virulence or host range.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (mostly children under 5 years with HFMD and severe neurologic or cardiopulmonary complications; EV-A71 responsible for most fatal cases)
Event.summary: Beginning in spring 2008, mainland China reported large HFMD outbreaks due largely to EV-A71, prompting HFMD to become a nationally notifiable disease and revealing millions of pediatric infections and thousands of deaths over subsequent years. Between 2008 and 2012 alone, the national surveillance system recorded over 7.2 million probable HFMD cases and at least 2,457 deaths, with further data to 2014 indicating more than 10.7 million reported cases and over 3,000 deaths, over 90% of laboratory-confirmed fatal cases attributed to EV-A71 subgenogroup C4a. The epidemic pattern evolved into intense annual and sometimes multi-peak seasons that gradually decreased in mortality following strengthened clinical management, public health measures, and later the introduction of EV-A71 vaccines, but EV-A71 remained an important cause of severe and fatal HFMD in China into the 2010s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid economic development with high urban density, extensive internal migration, and expansion of daycare and kindergartens increased child-to-child contact; variable access to early care and delayed recognition of severe HFMD in rural areas raised mortality risks; climatic conditions favored seasonal enterovirus peaks. Internal mechanisms: dominance of EV-A71 subgenogroup C4a and related C4 lineages, characterized by efficient person-to-person transmission and marked neurovirulence, reflects novel strain/genotype emergence and enhanced transmission coupled with increased virulence/pathogenicity; available phylogenetic data suggest broader geographic range expansion (inherent) as these C4a lineages spread nationally across diverse climates and into Hong Kong and Macao.
Review: Decision: retain with minor geographic correction. Updated the countries field from 'China, Macao Special Administrative Region [2010]' to '[2008]' because Macao reported EV-A71 infection and HFMD activity in 2008 in parallel with the wider regional wave, and Hong Kong also had recurrent EV-A71 activity in the 2000s before the large 2008 epidemic year. Aggregating mainland China together with Hong Kong and Macao over 2008–2014 is appropriate because all three jurisdictions experienced continuous or near-continuous annual HFMD seasons dominated by EV-A71 C4a, and national/supranational surveillance treats them as part of one prolonged epidemic period. Classification as re-emergence (and re-occurrence) without inter-/intra-continental emergence remains correct, since EV-A71 had been isolated in China since the late 1980s.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus A
EPP.common.name: enterovirus A71
Host: Humans (children with severe neurologic conditions including encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, and other CNS syndromes associated with EV-A71)
Event.summary: In 2016–2017, France reported an upsurge of severe pediatric neurologic disease associated with EV-A71 infection, temporally linked to the spread of the multirecombinant EV-A71 C1v2015 lineage that had emerged in Germany in 2015 and was concurrently causing outbreaks in Spain and other European countries. During May–October 2016, French surveillance documented 59 severe pediatric enterovirus cases, about half due to EV-A71, many presenting with brainstem encephalitis or acute flaccid paralysis, and molecular sequencing confirmed most belonged to the C1-variant lineage; sporadic cases continued into 2017. Similar C1v2015 viruses were detected in Germany in 2015 and the Netherlands in 2016 in association with neurologic disease. The outbreak subsided after the enterovirus season and heightened infection control and surveillance, but it marked a continent-wide re-emergence of EV-A71 as a neurologic pathogen in Western Europe driven by a newly introduced recombinant lineage.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: pan-European movement of people and viruses, coupled with historically low EV-A71 incidence and immunity in Europe, enabled efficient spread of the imported C1v2015 lineage; improved surveillance for non-polio enteroviruses and neurologic disease increased case ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: the C1v2015 lineage shows clear evidence of recombination across multiple genomic regions and is associated with disproportionate neurologic disease, indicating novel strain/genotype emergence, enhanced transmission and increased virulence/pathogenicity; its spread from initial detection in Germany to France, Spain, the Netherlands and other countries illustrates continental-scale range expansion and re-emergence.
Review: Decision: retain with corrected emergence typing and clarification of linkage to the broader C1v2015 episode. Removed inter_continental_emergence and intra_continental_emergence flags because EV-A71 had been documented previously in all included countries (Germany, France and the Netherlands) and more broadly across Europe, so this wave does not represent first presence in a new continent or sub-region. Instead, the 2015–2017 activity reflects re-emergence of a multirecombinant C1 lineage that produced an unusual burden of neurologic disease. The time window and country list appropriately summarise the upsurge of severe EV-A71 C1v2015-associated cases in these Western European countries; together with the Spain 2016 row, this row describes a single pan-European C1v2015-linked emergence episode that could be merged into one multi-country event in later harmonisation.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus B
EPP.common.name: enterovirus infection
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Humans (predominantly children and adolescents with aseptic meningitis)
Event.summary: During 2017–2018, Europe experienced a large upsurge of echovirus 30 infections with numerous meningitis outbreaks reported in multiple countries including Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and Bulgaria. Surveillance data showed that E30 accounted for a high proportion of typed enterovirus meningitis cases and that positivity sharply increased compared with 2015–2017, indicating a pan‑European wave. The wave declined after 2018 as population immunity to the circulating clades increased and routine public health measures contained localized outbreaks, though E30 persists as a leading meningitis‑associated Enterovirus B type.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/27/6/20-3096_article?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: synchronized seasonal enterovirus transmission across Europe, travel‑related seeding among countries, and high susceptibility among children and adolescents to the emergent E30 clades. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and clade replacement (new E30 clades within genogroup II identified across Europe), enhanced transmission of these clades relative to preceding ones, and geographic range expansion within Europe (intra‑continental emergence into Eastern Europe, including Bulgaria, from Western/Northern European sources).([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/27/6/20-3096_article?utm_source=openai))

Host: Humans (primarily neonates in the first week of life; mothers with peripartum enterovirus infection)
Event.summary: Beginning in mid‑2022, France detected an unusual rise in severe neonatal infections due to a new echovirus 11 variant, with at least nine neonates hospitalized for sepsis‑like illness and hepatitis between July 2022 and April 2023, seven of whom died. By mid‑2023, additional severe neonatal E11 cases were reported from several EU/EEA countries including France, Croatia, Sweden, Spain, Italy, and the United Kingdom, prompting European and WHO alerts about a multi‑country event. The outbreak has persisted with fluctuating intensity, though increased clinical awareness, perinatal testing, and infection‑prevention measures in maternity and neonatal units aim to limit further severe neonatal cases.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10236930/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: vertical and peripartum transmission from pregnant women with unrecognized enterovirus infection, high susceptibility and lack of immunity in neonates, and routine obstetric and neonatal care settings that may facilitate close contact and early transmission. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of a new echovirus 11 variant associated with severe hepatitis and high case‑fatality in neonates; genomic studies indicate a distinct recombinant variant with apparent increased virulence/pathogenicity and possibly enhanced transmission in the perinatal setting. The multi‑country spread within Europe reflects both intra‑continental emergence of this variant and re‑emergence in subregions with prior E11 circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10236930/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.common.name: enterovirus D68
Sub.regions: Asia: South-eastern Asia, Eastern Asia; Europe: Western Europe; North America: Northern America
Host: Humans (primarily children with severe acute respiratory infections and pneumonia)
Event.summary:
From late 2008, clusters of severe lower respiratory tract infection and pneumonia in hospitalized children in the Eastern Visayas region of the Philippines were linked to EV-D68, marking the first clearly recognized multi-patient outbreaks of this serotype.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6038a1.htm))
During 2009–2010, additional clusters of acute respiratory illness caused by EV-D68 were reported in Japan, the Netherlands and several U.S. states (Georgia, Pennsylvania, Arizona), showing that the virus had shifted from sporadic detection to widespread regional outbreaks across three continents.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6038a1.htm))
By 2010, these temporally related outbreaks had subsided, but they revealed a re-emerging pathogen with the capacity for broader transmission and severe pediatric respiratory disease, setting the stage for larger epidemics later in the decade.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: increased use of molecular diagnostics and multi-pathogen respiratory panels enabled detection of EV-D68 that would previously have been misclassified as rhinovirus; sentinel and hospital-based surveillance in the Philippines, Japan, the Netherlands and U.S. sites highlighted an apparent rise in severe wheezing, pneumonia and asthma exacerbations linked to this virus.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/MMWr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6038a1.htm))
Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses from Asia, Europe and North America show emergence and spread of novel EV-D68 lineages (early clades A and B) with changes in capsid and receptor-binding regions thought to favor respiratory tropism and more efficient transmission, consistent with novel strain/genotype emergence and early geographic range expansion of fitter variants.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7171721/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Event corresponds to the six early multi-country clusters of EV-D68 respiratory illness described by CDC for 2008–2010 and is among the key pre‑2014 emergence episodes. The countries list has been corrected to remove New York (not part of the 2008–2010 clusters) and to drop the separate China [2006–2008] entry, which referred to sporadic circulation outside this episode and predates the 2008 start year; retained Philippines, Japan, the Netherlands and the U.S. states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Arizona with timing aligned to the MMWR description.
