EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus D
EPP.common.name: enterovirus D68
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Humans (children and adolescents with severe respiratory illness and acute flaccid myelitis; some adults)
Event.summary:
Following the 2014 North American epidemic, several European countries documented increased EV-D68 detections in children hospitalized with severe respiratory disease, including Norway where about 11% of pediatric respiratory samples in one hospital were EV-D68-positive and two children developed severe AFM.([ecdc.europa.eu](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/publications-data/rapid-risk-assessment-enterovirus-68-detected-usa-canada-and-europe-second-update?utm_source=openai))
During late 2014 and through 2015, France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden and Italy (along with Denmark and Germany reporting clusters of respiratory illness) all recorded EV-D68 circulation with smaller respiratory outbreaks and sporadic but severe neurologic cases, including the first recognized EV-D68–associated AFM clusters in Europe.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/microbiolspec.ei10-0018-2016?utm_source=openai))
By late 2015, European EV-D68 activity declined seasonally, but the region had transitioned from sporadic detections to a recognized pattern of EV-D68 outbreaks with associated AFM, preparing the ground for the larger pan-European AFM wave documented in 2016.

The countries list has been expanded to include Denmark [2014] and Germany [2014], which reported EV‑D68 respiratory clusters during the same wave, while keeping Norway, the Netherlands, France, the United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden and Italy; sub‑regions and classification as re‑emergence remain appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus D
EPP.common.name: enterovirus D68
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Humans (primarily children with acute flaccid myelitis and preceding respiratory illness)
Event.summary:
In early 2016, European clinicians and laboratories reporting through ENPEN and ECDC noted increasing EV-D68 circulation in pediatric respiratory samples, particularly in northern and western Europe, following smaller waves in 2014–2015.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5718392/?utm_source=openai))
Between March and October 2016, a coordinated European case series identified 29 laboratory-confirmed EV-D68–associated AFM cases across 12 countries (including France, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Norway, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands) among more than 16,000 respiratory specimens screened, representing a >10-fold rise over 2014 and confirming a continent-wide AFM wave temporally linked to EV-D68 clade B3 circulation.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6296836/?utm_source=openai))
As EV-D68 detections and AFM cases declined with the end of the 2016 enterovirus season, Europe established AFM working groups and highlighted the need for formal AFM surveillance, recognizing EV-D68 as a recurrent neurotropic outbreak pathogen.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: accumulation of a cohort of young children without prior exposure to newly circulating EV-D68 lineages after the 2014 wave; school- and daycare-based transmission during late summer and autumn; and enhanced case-finding via AFP/AFM surveillance and pan-European laboratory collaboration (ENPEN, ECDC), which increased ascertainment of both EV-D68 infection and AFM.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5718392/?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses showed dominance of subclade B3 viruses across Europe in 2016, distinct from the B1/B2 strains prominent in 2014; these B3 strains display amino acid substitutions in capsid proteins and other regions associated with increased neurotropism and replication in neuronal tissue, constituting novel strain/genotype emergence with increased virulence/pathogenicity and enhanced transmission in pediatric populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6296836/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the 2016 pan‑European AFM wave with 29 confirmed EV‑D68–associated cases in 12 countries and dominance of subclade B3; continent, sub‑regions, and re‑emergence classification are consistent with the case‑series data, and the generic reference to “other European countries participating in ENPEN” is acceptable given incomplete country-level reporting.

Event.summary:
In 2016, within the framework of poliomyelitis acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance in West Africa, investigators retrospectively tested stool specimens from children with AFP and identified EV-D68 RNA and subclade B3 sequences in several cases from countries including Guinea (Guinea-Conakry), Senegal and Niger.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7454047/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus D
EPP.common.name: enterovirus D68
Sub.regions: Northern America; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans (primarily children with severe respiratory illness and AFM)
Event.summary:
After a relatively quiet EV-D68/AFM year in 2017, surveillance in the United States recorded a sharp rise in AFM cases in 2018 (about 238 confirmed AFM cases nationwide) temporally associated with renewed EV-D68 circulation in late summer and autumn, following the now-characteristic biennial pattern first observed after 2014.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/68/wr/mm6812a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Parallel increases in EV-D68 detections and AFM cases were documented across Europe in 2018, with ENPEN data showing that 2016, 2018 and later 2022 accounted for the majority of European AFM cases, and additional AFM cases with EV-D68 infection were recognized in Australia and New Zealand using AFP surveillance systems.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12124111/?utm_source=openai))
The 2018 wave subsided by winter, but it established EV-D68-associated AFM as a recurring global phenomenon with large peaks approximately every two years, aligning with shifts in population immunity and viral genetic evolution.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: accumulation of a birth cohort of young children lacking immunity to circulating EV-D68 clades following the 2016 wave; normal resumption of school and social mixing after the 2016 season; and increased awareness plus standardized case definitions for AFM leading to improved reporting.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/68/wr/mm6812a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: ongoing evolution within B3 and related clades, with evidence of antigenic drift and changing neutralization profiles, likely allowed escape from existing population antibodies and supported repeated large waves; combined with established neurotropic determinants, this produced re-emergence characterized by increased virulence/pathogenicity (AFM) and enhanced transmission on a biennial timescale.([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/mra.00388-19?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event appropriately aggregates the substantial 2018 EV‑D68/AFM wave across the United States, Canada, multiple European countries and Australia/New Zealand, with case numbers and the biennial pattern consistent with NVSN and AFM surveillance data; no structural corrections to geography, timing or emergence type were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus D
EPP.common.name: enterovirus D68
Sub.regions: Northern America; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Humans (children and adolescents with acute respiratory illness, asthma exacerbations, and occasional neurologic disease)
Event.summary:
After non-pharmaceutical interventions for COVID-19 dramatically reduced circulation of many respiratory viruses, including EV-D68, in 2020–2021, U.S. surveillance detected a substantial increase in EV-D68-positive respiratory specimens and pediatric emergency visits for acute respiratory illness and asthma/reactive airway disease during July–September 2022, indicating a large nationwide EV-D68 respiratory outbreak.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/mm7047a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
In the same year, Finland reported a notable EV-D68 outbreak with at least 56 hospitalized children with respiratory illness and one case of encephalitis, and ENPEN data showed that European AFM cases again clustered in EV-D68 circulation years (2016, 2018, 2022), though the 2022 AFM peak appeared lower than expected, possibly due to interference from other respiratory viruses or partial population immunity.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/29/6/22-1795_article?utm_source=openai))
By late 2022 the EV-D68 wave receded, but its timing after a skipped 2020 peak underscored how changes in contact patterns and competing respiratory viruses can modulate the biennial pattern of EV-D68 re-emergence, while the virus remains capable of causing sizeable respiratory outbreaks and sporadic neurologic disease.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: relaxation of COVID-19 mitigation measures restored typical contact patterns in schools and communities, allowing re-expansion of EV-D68; an immunity gap may have developed in children who missed exposure during 2020–2021; and concurrent circulation of SARS-CoV-2, RSV and other enteroviruses might have shaped both susceptibility and clinical expression, potentially blunting AFM incidence despite high respiratory circulation.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/mm7047a1.htm?utm_source=openai))
Internal mechanisms: 2022 viruses belonged to contemporary EV-D68 clades (including B3 and newer lineages) that have diversified antigenically since 2014, suggesting continued evolution under immune pressure with preserved or modestly enhanced transmissibility in the respiratory tract; however, AFM associations appeared weaker, raising the possibility that specific genetic determinants of neurovirulence, host immunity, or viral interference modulated clinical outcomes in this re-emergence wave.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/ofid/article/doi/10.1093/ofid/ofad500.950/7448594?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects the large 2022 EV‑D68 respiratory surge in the United States and Finland (and other European countries) after COVID‑19 mitigation was relaxed, including the notable decoupling between high respiratory circulation and relatively modest AFM counts; geography, timing, and classification as re‑emergence are consistent with available surveillance reports, so only editorial wording changes, not structural corrections, would be needed if further refinement were desired.

EPP.scientific.name: Rhinovirus C
EPP.common.name: common cold
Continent: North America; Africa; Asia; Europe; Oceania
Sub.regions: Northern America; Western Africa; Southern Africa; Southern Asia; Eastern Asia; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans (infants, children, and adults with influenza-like illness, acute respiratory infections, and lower respiratory tract infections in hospital- and community-based surveillance)
Event.summary: Between roughly 2003 and 2007, a genetically distinct rhinovirus clade later designated HRV-C was identified through MassTag multiplex PCR, pan-viral microarrays, and VP4/VP2 or VP1 sequencing in respiratory samples from patients with influenza-like illness in New York State, infants with bronchiolitis in Queensland, Australia, and then in children and adults with acute respiratory disease in South Africa, Côte d’Ivoire, Nepal, India, Western Australia, Denmark, Spain, Hong Kong, Germany, and California. These investigations showed that viruses in this novel clade were associated with community outbreaks of acute respiratory illness and with severe lower respiratory tract infections and respiratory distress in infants and young children across Africa, Asia, Europe, Oceania, and North America. By 2007, phylogenetic and molecular-clock analyses indicated that this clade was as diverse and long-established as HRV-A and HRV-B and had likely circulated in humans for at least several hundred years, shifting the interpretation of HRV-C from a newly emerged pathogen to a long-endemic virus newly detected by advanced molecular diagnostics.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Deployment of broad-range molecular assays (MassTag PCR, multiplex PCR, microarrays) in respiratory virus surveillance and outbreak investigations enabled sensitive detection and typing of unculturable or previously untyped rhinoviruses, and coordinated sample sharing between laboratories in North America, Africa, Asia, Europe, and Oceania provided geographically diverse material. Host: Humans (hospitalized children with rotavirus gastroenteritis)
Event.summary: Around 2012, unusual G1P[8] rotavirus A strains possessing a DS‑1‑like genomic backbone rather than the typical Wa‑like constellation were recognised during outbreaks in Japan and then in hospitalised children in Viet Nam and Thailand. Shortly thereafter, similar DS‑1‑like G1P[8] strains rose to predominance among hospitalised children in Malawi soon after Rotarix introduction and were detected in Brazil and in archived pre‑vaccine samples from South Africa, indicating broader circulation. By the mid‑2010s these atypical G1P[8] reassortants had become an important but transient component of the global rotavirus strain pool, later declining as other genotypes and lineages gained prominence.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High background transmission, frequent mixed infections and, in some settings, the altered post‑vaccine immune landscape facilitated the emergence and spread of DS‑1‑like G1P[8] strains, although vaccine effectiveness against them remained high. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence via reassortment—whole‑genome sequencing showed that these viruses combined G1 and P[8] outer capsid genes with DS‑1‑like internal genes, often derived from locally circulating G2P[4] or other DS‑1‑like strains, representing a major genomic shift (re_emergence) without clear evidence of vaccine escape.
Review: review: Retain as a key genotype-level re_emergence event. Corrected emergence-type classification to remove intra- and inter-continental flags (new genomic constellation within an already cosmopolitan species) and expanded the country list to include Japan, Thailand and Brazil, with South Africa explicitly noted as pre-vaccine detection in archived samples, in line with multiple genomic and outbreak reports.

Event.summary: From 2004 to 2006, the northeastern United States, especially Massachusetts and New Hampshire, experienced an amplified EEE cycle that peaked in 2005, when New Hampshire reported seven locally acquired human cases and national totals reached about 21 cases, the highest annual count since national surveillance began. The outbreak developed as widespread EEEV activity was detected in mosquitoes, birds and equines across New England and parts of the Gulf Coast, leading to multiple human encephalitis cases and deaths. Transmission waned after 2006, but this episode established the modern pattern of episodic, regionally extensive human EEE outbreaks in the United States.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Above‑average rainfall and warm summer conditions that enhanced larval habitats; extensive hardwood swamp ecosystems sustaining large Culiseta melanura populations; residential development and outdoor activity near swamp margins; improved clinical recognition and laboratory testing. No evidence for a novel viral lineage; treating this as a large re-occurrence in long‑affected areas is appropriate, and country/subregion fields are correct.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus sindbis
EPP.common.name: Sindbis virus
Host: Humans (Pogosta disease in Finland, Ockelbo disease in Sweden, Karelian fever in north‑west Russian Federation); associated wild birds and ornithophilic mosquitoes (enzootic cycle)
Event.summary: In late summer and autumn 1995, Finland experienced its largest recorded epidemic of Pogosta disease, with more than 1,300 serodiagnosed Sindbis virus infections concentrated in eastern and central regions but with cases reported across much of the country; contemporaneous increases in clinically similar Ockelbo disease and Karelian fever were noted in neighbouring Sweden and Russian Karelia, indicating a broader Fennoscandian outbreak. The epidemic followed the characteristic roughly seven‑year cyclic pattern of SINV activity in the region, with incidence peaking in highly endemic lake‑forest districts before declining over subsequent seasons as population immunity rose and vector densities fell. Transmission ended with the winter collapse of mosquito populations, after which SINV persisted at low levels in local bird–mosquito cycles during inter‑epidemic years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: cyclic build‑up of susceptible human populations between major outbreak years; favourable weather in preceding seasons (warm, wet summers) that supported high densities of ornithophilic mosquitoes; high abundance of grouse and other reservoir birds in forested lake districts; outdoor recreational and subsistence activities (e.g. berry and mushroom picking) that increased human exposure to mosquitoes. Internal mechanisms: circulation of endemic European SINV genotype I without clear evidence of major new variants or expanded host range; the 1995 resurgence is best explained by ecological and climatic forcing superimposed on partial human immunity rather than by viral evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: 1995 is consistently documented as the largest Pogosta/Ockelbo/Karelian fever outbreak (>1,300 confirmed cases in Finland) with concurrent activity in Sweden and Russian Karelia; geography, timing and classification as a re-occurrence in an established endemic focus are well supported by national surveillance and outbreak investigations, and no major corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus sindbis
EPP.common.name: Sindbis virus
Host: Humans; migratory and resident birds (especially grouse); ornithophilic mosquitoes (e.g. Culex, Ochlerotatus spp.)
Event.summary: In 2002, a major Sindbis virus epidemic struck Finland, producing approximately 600 serologically confirmed Pogosta disease cases nationwide with particularly high incidence (around 81 per 100,000) in the highly endemic North Karelia region and additional clusters in other eastern and central districts, while contemporaneous outbreaks of related Ockelbo and Karelian fever syndromes occurred in adjacent parts of Sweden and Russian Karelia. The outbreak developed over summer and early autumn following a build‑up of vector and bird reservoir populations and was accompanied by serological evidence of intense SINV circulation in both resident and migratory birds. Transmission subsided with the onset of colder weather and mosquito die‑off, after which case numbers returned to baseline, although chronic arthralgia persisted in a substantial subset of patients and SINV continued to circulate at low levels in bird–mosquito cycles.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: warm, wet conditions in preceding seasons that boosted mosquito populations; high densities of tetraonid birds (black grouse, capercaillie) acting as amplifying hosts; human outdoor activities in forested lake areas, such as berry and mushroom picking and fishing, increasing exposure to mosquitoes. Internal mechanisms: continued circulation of SINV genotype I without strong evidence for a more virulent novel strain; the epidemic pattern largely reflects ecological amplification and periodic depletion and replenishment of human immunity rather than fundamental change in viral biology, although this outbreak also yielded the first human SINV isolates from Europe and confirmed SINV as the aetiologic agent of Pogosta disease.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2002 Finnish-led Fennoscandian outbreak is the second-largest recorded SINV epidemic (~600 cases in Finland) and a key event in which SINV was first isolated from European patients; the geography and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate. The event description was retained but the Wikipedia citation was replaced with primary outbreak reports and analytic studies, and the role of this outbreak in yielding the first European human isolates was clarified.

EPP.common.name: Sindbis virus
Host: Humans; wild birds; mosquitoes

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus sindbis
EPP.common.name: Sindbis virus
Host: Humans; wild birds; mosquitoes
Event.summary: In 2012, Finland experienced another sizeable Pogosta disease epidemic with 189 Sindbis virus infections recorded in the National Infectious Diseases Register, making it the largest Finnish outbreak since 2002; smaller contemporaneous increases in Ockelbo disease were noted in parts of Sweden. The outbreak began in late summer, with cases concentrated in traditional endemic eastern districts but also affecting additional areas, while virological work demonstrated multiple divergent but genotype I SINV strains circulating in humans and mosquitoes. As usual, human incidence declined sharply with the end of the mosquito season, leaving a new cohort of individuals with long‑lasting arthralgia and contributing to accumulated population immunity that reduced incidence in subsequent years until the very large resurgence in 2021.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: favourable climatic conditions for mosquitoes in 2012 and high densities of avian reservoirs in endemic forest–lake landscapes; outdoor recreational exposure and limited use of personal protection in affected communities; sensitive surveillance via mandatory notification and serological testing in Finland. Internal mechanisms: genomic analyses of isolates from the 2012 outbreak revealed co‑circulation of several divergent but typical SINV genotype I lineages, implying multiple introductions or long‑standing micro‑foci rather than a single novel variant; disease resurgence is therefore best classified as ecological re-occurrence rather than re-emergence through major viral evolution.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: The 2012 Finnish outbreak (189 reported cases) is well documented and clearly among the largest post-1990 SINV epidemics; including Sweden reflects modest concurrent activity there. Geography and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate, and the source set (outbreak report plus ecological analyses) is relevant.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (predominantly adults co-infected with HIV: visceral leishmaniasis caused mainly by Leishmania infantum)
Event.summary: Beginning around 1990, southern European countries with long-standing zoonotic L. infantum transmission experienced a sharp rise in visceral leishmaniasis among people living with HIV, as HIV-related immunosuppression exposed latent infections and increased progression from subclinical to clinical disease. Over the 1990–2001 period, more than 1,600 Leishmania/HIV co-infections were notified from Spain, Italy, France and Portugal, concentrated among people who inject drugs and other high-risk groups, before widespread antiretroviral therapy and improved HIV control gradually reduced incidence. As antiretroviral therapy coverage expanded in the late 1990s and early 2000s and harm-reduction measures improved, the incidence of new co-infection cases declined, though sporadic co-infections continued to be reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The HIV pandemic in Western and Southern Europe created large populations of severely immunocompromised adults, especially among people who inject drugs, in areas where zoonotic L. infantum was already endemic in dogs and sandfly vectors; poverty, marginalization and urban crowding in some neighborhoods increased vector exposure. Internal mechanisms: Increased clinical expression of existing infections under immunosuppression rather than a novel parasite strain; no strong evidence of major parasite change, so this is best characterized as a resurgence triggered by host-population and health-system changes rather than intrinsic parasite evolution.
Review: Retain – Correctly captures the well-documented 1990s Leishmania/HIV co-infection epidemic in Spain, Italy, France and Portugal, including scale (~1,600+ co-infections) and decline after HAART. Countries and sub-regions are consistent with UNSD classification, and classification as re-occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because the increase reflects HIV-driven susceptibility in an already endemic focus rather than spread to new regions or parasite change. No structural changes made.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (anthroponotic visceral leishmaniasis, “kala-azar”, caused by Leishmania donovani)
Event.summary: During the 1990s and early 2000s, the contiguous visceral leishmaniasis focus spanning northeastern India (especially Bihar), central and western Bangladesh and southeastern Nepal experienced recurrent large epidemics, with Bihar alone estimated to have ≈250,000 cases in 1991 and realistic annual incidences of roughly 250,000 cases in India, 40,000 in Bangladesh and 3,000 in Nepal—about 60% of the global VL burden. Widespread failure of pentavalent antimonials in North Bihar, interrupted and patchy indoor residual spraying, and entrenched poverty, malnutrition and crowded rural housing allowed sustained high transmission and repeated peaks up to the early 2000s. In 2005 the three governments, in partnership with WHO, launched a regional kala-azar elimination programme, and by 2014 reported cases in Bangladesh, India and Nepal had fallen by about 75% compared with 2005, although residual hotspots, post–kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis and HIV co-infection continued to threaten elimination goals.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large impoverished rural populations living in densely packed, poorly constructed houses; reduced or poorly targeted vector control after the malaria eradication era; weak health systems and delayed diagnosis; and high human mobility across porous borders contributed to intense and sustained VL transmission. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of high-level resistance to pentavalent antimonials in L. donovani in Bihar and neighboring areas, together with chronic human reservoirs such as post–kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis cases, represent parasite-level changes that helped maintain or resurge transmission, justifying classification as re-emergence rather than simple re-occurrence.
Review: Review – New multi-country event added to represent the very high-burden visceral leishmaniasis epidemics and subsequent elimination programme in India, Bangladesh and Nepal, which together accounted for ≈60% of global VL and included epidemic peaks of ≈250,000 cases in Bihar alone. Classified as re-emergence because sustained high incidence was closely linked to widespread antimonial drug resistance and long-lived human reservoirs, not to spread into a new sub-region or host system. Time window 1990–2014 approximates the late-20th‐century epidemic wave and the period up to the first major regional declines under the kala-azar elimination programme; exact start and end years may be refined using national programme data.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
Host: Humans (primarily cutaneous leishmaniasis due to Leishmania tropica and L. major, with cases largely among Syrian civilians and refugees)
Event.summary: With the onset of the Syrian civil war around 2011, long-endemic cutaneous leishmaniasis in Syrian cities such as Aleppo and Homs surged dramatically as vector control and health services collapsed, leading to very high local incidence. From 2012 onward, large numbers of Syrian refugees carrying CL lesions were identified in Lebanon, Jordan and Türkiye, with Lebanon alone reporting more than 1,200 CL cases in 2012, almost all among refugees, and smaller numbers of locally acquired infections documented in host communities. Over the mid‑2010s, as conflict dynamics shifted and some control measures were introduced in refugee camps and host countries, reported cases in Lebanon and Jordan gradually declined, though the disease remained entrenched in parts of Syria and continued to pose a risk in overcrowded, under-served refugee settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Armed conflict, mass displacement, overcrowded refugee camps, breakdown of vector control and primary healthcare, and poor housing and sanitation in both war-affected Syrian neighborhoods and refugee settlements greatly increased human exposure to sandfly vectors and impeded timely diagnosis and treatment. Internal mechanisms: The episode reflects amplification and geographic redistribution of existing L. tropica and L. major transmission cycles rather than a newly evolved parasite genotype; key mechanisms are enhanced transmission via socio-environmental change and movement of infected hosts across borders, not intrinsic changes in virulence or tropism.
Review: Review – Countries and timing have been slightly corrected by changing Jordan’s start year from 2010 to 2012, in line with data showing that the marked increase in CL associated with Syrian refugees in Jordan occurred after the war began and refugees arrived in substantial numbers; Lebanon and Türkiye remain at 2012 consistent with outbreak reports. Classification as re-occurrence (rather than inter-continental emergence) is appropriate because almost all cases were acquired within Western Asia and many were imported from Syria into neighboring countries, with only limited local transmission. This row should be rechecked against national surveillance time series, but the overall framing of a war- and displacement-driven CL resurgence is sound.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus granulosus
EPP.common.name: cystic echinococcosis (hydatidosis; E. granulosus sensu lato)
Host: Humans (primarily rural pastoral communities in Central Asian republics)
Event.summary: Following independence of the Central Asian republics, Global Burden of Disease estimates and national surveillance data show that cystic echinococcosis incidence rose across Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan from the early 1990s, with particularly steep increases around 2000–2004. Over 1990–2019 these countries recorded some of the highest age‑standardised CE incidence rates worldwide, with ASIRs exceeding 120 per 100,000 in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, making CE one of the most prominent zoonotic neglected tropical diseases in the region. Although mortality and disability‑adjusted life years began to fall modestly after the mid‑2000s and some countries have seen partial control, incidence has remained elevated into the 2010s, consistent with a long‑lasting regional epidemic rather than isolated national outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Region‑wide socio‑economic transition after the Soviet collapse led to reduced funding for public and veterinary health services, weakened meat inspection and dog control, privatisation and informal home slaughter of livestock, and increases in unregulated dog ownership, collectively increasing human exposure to E. granulosus eggs in Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate emergence of new parasite genotypes or increased virulence in this region; the pattern is best explained by geographic and intensity expansion of long‑established dog–livestock transmission cycles under changed husbandry and control conditions.

Mechanism/driver text was clarified to reflect region‑wide breakdown of veterinary and meat‑inspection systems, and in‑line web citations were removed.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio parahaemolyticus
Host: Humans (hospitalized diarrhea/gastroenteritis patients)
Event.summary: In 1996, a large outbreak of acute watery diarrhea in Calcutta, India was linked to a single highly virulent Vibrio parahaemolyticus serotype O3:K6 that had not previously been detected in routine surveillance. Active and retrospective investigations in 1996–1997 showed the same O3:K6 clone causing hospital outbreaks in neighboring Bangladesh and among travelers arriving in Japan, revealing the emergence of the first known pandemic lineage of V. parahaemolyticus. This initial wave established O3:K6 as a dominant cause of V. parahaemolyticus gastroenteritis in parts of South and East Asia and set the stage for rapid regional and global spread in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased seafood consumption and distribution in rapidly urbanizing Asian coastal cities, coupled with warm coastal waters favoring Vibrio growth, facilitated amplification and spread of the new clone. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of the O3:K6 clonal complex with tdh+, trh−, toxRS/new and ORF8 markers and multiple genomic islands, associated with increased virulence and epidemic potential; enhanced transmission via high bacterial loads in shellfish and efficient fecal–oral spread among exposed populations.
Review: review – Retained as the first major emergence of the pandemic O3:K6 clonal complex, but the start year has been corrected to 1996 (not 1995) and the country list restricted to India, Bangladesh and Japan where early in situ transmission is well documented; emergence type has been changed from 'first/global emergence' and 'intra-continental emergence' to 're-emergence' only, because V. parahaemolyticus had been recognized in Asian humans since the 1950s and project guidance specifies that new serotypes or clones should be treated as re-emergence rather than first or intra-continental emergence when the species is already established.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio parahaemolyticus
Sub.regions: Southern Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia
Host: Humans (seafood-associated gastroenteritis cases and outbreaks)
Event.summary: Following its initial recognition in India, the pandemic O3:K6 clonal complex spread widely between 1996 and 1999, with surveillance documenting rapidly increasing proportions of Vibrio parahaemolyticus diarrhea cases due to O3:K6 and related serovariants in multiple South, Southeast, and East Asian countries. The clone became established in coastal seafood and human populations around the Bay of Bengal, South China Sea, and western Pacific, displacing diverse pre-existing serotypes as the leading cause of V. parahaemolyticus gastroenteritis. By the late 1990s this Asian expansion had stabilized into seasonal but recurrent outbreaks driven by warm-water shellfish exposure, forming the epidemiologic foundation of the subsequent global pandemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensified regional trade and movement of seafood, human travel, and possibly ballast water exchange allowed rapid dissemination of the pandemic lineage throughout Asian coastal waters; warm seasonal sea-surface temperatures and high shellfish harvesting and raw consumption amplified exposure. Internal mechanisms: Pandemic O3:K6 lineage and its serovariants exhibited a clonal genotype with virulence-associated genes and pathogenicity islands that increased virulence and fitness, enabling geographic range expansion and dominance over local strains.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio parahaemolyticus
Host: Humans (illnesses after raw oyster consumption)
Event.summary: In the summer of 1997, the first oyster-associated outbreak of Vibrio parahaemolyticus recognized under the U.S. National Shellfish Sanitation Program occurred in the Pacific Northwest, with 209 culture-confirmed cases reported in U.S. Pacific states and Canada after consumption of raw oysters harvested from regional beds. The outbreak, along with other contemporaneous oyster-associated clusters, marked a sharp increase in recognized V. parahaemolyticus illness in North America compared with previous sporadic reports. Following targeted control measures and changes in harvest practices, including closure of implicated harvest areas, cases from the implicated beds declined, although V. parahaemolyticus continued to cause seasonal outbreaks in U.S. coastal waters.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High summer seawater temperatures in Pacific Northwest estuaries, increased raw oyster consumption, and limited prior regulatory focus on V. parahaemolyticus levels in shellfish beds facilitated this large outbreak. Internal mechanisms: No single novel genotype dominated; rather, elevated environmental Vibrio loads in oysters and existing pathogenic strains led to enhanced exposure and disease, representing a re-occurrence driven mainly by environmental favorability rather than a new strain.
Review: retain – The 1997 Pacific Northwest raw-oyster outbreak (209 culture-confirmed cases across multiple U.S. Pacific states and British Columbia) is well documented and correctly classified as a major re-occurrence driven by anomalously warm coastal waters and high oyster consumption, with no evidence that a novel strain or new geographic sub-region is involved.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio parahaemolyticus
Host: Humans (seafood-associated diarrhea in coastal cities including Antofagasta and Puerto Montt)
Event.summary: Chile first documented Vibrio parahaemolyticus diarrhea outbreaks due to pandemic-lineage strains in the northern city of Antofagasta in 1998, and beginning in 2004–2005 large epidemics emerged in southern Chile around Puerto Montt and Región de los Lagos, where most of the country’s seafood is produced. Outbreaks that began in 2004 peaked in the summer of 2005 with approximately 3,600 clinical cases in Puerto Montt alone and more than 10,000 V. parahaemolyticus infections reported across southern and central Chile that season, all largely associated with the O3:K6 pandemic clone or closely related variants. Subsequent seasons saw continued but fluctuating summer outbreaks, with later molecular work documenting replacement of the original O3:K6 pandemic strain by new serotypes such as O3:K59, indicating ongoing evolution within the regional V. parahaemolyticus population.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of shellfish aquaculture and harvesting in southern Chile, high domestic consumption of raw or lightly cooked seafood, and favorable summer sea-surface warming in the Humboldt upwelling system facilitated explosive amplification and transmission; global shipping and seafood trade likely introduced the pandemic clone from Asia or North America. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of the pandemic O3:K6 complex into Chile and subsequent local diversification into new serotypes (e.g., O4:K12, O3:K59) that maintained key pandemic virulence markers illustrate both adaptation to local host–environment conditions and continuing re-emergence via novel genotypes.
Review: review – This row aggregates the Chilean experience with pandemic V. parahaemolyticus (≈300 cases in Antofagasta in 1998 and ≈10,000 cases nationwide during the 2004–2005 southern Chile epidemics) and clearly represents one of the highest-impact events globally; however, because pandemic strains had already reached South America (Peru and northern Chile) before the 2004–2005 southern outbreaks, the event has been reclassified from 'inter-continental + intra-continental emergence' to 're-emergence' only, with mechanism wording adjusted accordingly; if a strict global top-10 by impact is enforced, this event should definitely be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio parahaemolyticus
Host: Humans (seafood-associated diarrhea in coastal regions)
Event.summary: By the early 2000s, pandemic Vibrio parahaemolyticus O3:K6 strains had been detected in Europe, with clinical cases linked to seafood consumption reported in France from 1997 onwards and an oyster-associated outbreak in Spain in 2004, followed by the detection of pandemic-marker strains in Italian coastal waters in 2007. A 2005 report from France documented that O3:K6 isolates from French patients carried the pandemic toxRS/new and ORF8 markers and were closely related to the Asian and American pandemic strains, demonstrating that the clone had reached European coastal ecosystems. Following these introductions, sporadic and small-cluster outbreaks of vibriosis associated with local shellfish and imported seafood occurred in western and southern Europe, particularly during warm summers, but were generally contained with improved surveillance and food safety measures.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of contaminated seafood and transoceanic shipping and ballast water likely introduced the pandemic clone into European waters; warming of coastal seas, especially during anomalously hot summers, increased environmental suitability for Vibrio proliferation and human exposure via local shellfish. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence of the O3:K6 pandemic clonal complex with characteristic virulence genes in European human and environmental reservoirs, followed by limited local adaptation of strains carrying pandemic genetic markers in marine environments.
Review: review – Evidence from French and Spanish clinical series and Italian environmental surveys confirms that pandemic O3:K6-like strains reached European patients and coastal waters by the early 2000s; the country years have been corrected to France [1997] (first documented O3:K6 cases), Spain [2004] (first O3:K6-associated outbreak) and Italy [2007] (pandemic-marker strains in seawater and plankton), and the episode is now coded as re-emergence of a pandemic clone in a region where V. parahaemolyticus was already known, rather than as inter- or intra-continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Vibrio parahaemolyticus
Host: Humans (consumers of raw oysters and clams from U.S. Pacific Northwest and British Columbia)
Event.summary: From May 20 to July 31, 2006, health departments in New York City, New York State, Oregon and Washington reported 177 Vibrio parahaemolyticus infections, of which 72 were laboratory-confirmed and 105 were epidemiologically linked probable cases, associated with consumption of raw oysters and clams harvested from coastal waters of Washington State and British Columbia. The incidence far exceeded baseline levels, with the number of confirmed cases in these jurisdictions alone surpassing the typical total for the entire United States during the same months in previous years, and traceback investigations implicated multiple harvest areas supplying shellfish to restaurants, seafood markets and recreational harvesters nationwide. After closure of at least eight implicated harvest areas in Washington, recalls of oysters from affected beds, and intensified advisories about cooking shellfish, reported cases declined, although sporadic Vibrio parahaemolyticus infections in the Pacific Northwest have continued to occur in warm summers.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Elevated summer sea-surface temperatures in U.S. Pacific Northwest and adjacent British Columbia waters, delays in refrigeration after harvest, and wide distribution of raw shellfish through commercial and recreational channels allowed low-level environmental Vibrio parahaemolyticus contamination to amplify to infectious doses and cause widespread illness; under-ascertainment suggests the true number of cases was many times higher than those reported. Internal mechanisms: The majority of isolates were serotype O4:K12 and tdh-positive but unrelated to the O3:K6 pandemic clone, indicating that this episode reflects re-occurrence of existing pathogenic lineages under favorable environmental and handling conditions rather than emergence of a new genotype.
Review: review – This previously missing multistate outbreak (177 reported cases across New York City, New York State, Oregon and Washington) has been added because it is one of the largest documented Vibrio parahaemolyticus outbreaks in North America after the 1997–1998 events and is explicitly highlighted in CDC and climate-risk reviews; it is classified as re-occurrence driven by warm seawater, handling and distribution practices, as the dominant O4:K12 serotype was not a novel pandemic clone.

EPP.common.name: AHPND
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei and Penaeus monodon)
Event.summary: From about 2010, AHPND spread southward from China into Viet Nam, initially causing severe early‑stage mortalities in intensive whiteleg shrimp farms of the Mekong Delta and prompting an FAO emergency mission. By 2011–2012 the disease had extended through much of South‑eastern Asia, with major industry crises in Malaysia and Thailand involving repeated crop failures, farm closures and sharp national production declines; it was subsequently confirmed in the Philippines by 2015 and in Bangladesh by around 2017, marking incursion into Southern Asia. As countries rolled out better diagnostics, biosecurity, pond management and stocking strategies, epidemic‑scale losses were partly reduced, but AHPND remains an important endemic constraint with periodic regional flare‑ups.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intra‑Asian movement of infected postlarvae and broodstock through shared hatchery networks and informal transboundary trade, combined with high‑density monoculture of L. vannamei, suboptimal pond conditions and co‑occurring stressors (e.g. EHP, poor water quality), created ideal conditions for rapid spread and explosive outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: closely related pirABvp‑positive V. parahaemolyticus lineages were found across Viet Nam, Malaysia and Thailand, indicating dissemination of a few epidemic plasmid‑bearing clones; subsequent detection of AHPND‑causing Vibrio species beyond V. parahaemolyticus (e.g. V. campbellii, V. harveyi) reflects horizontal transfer of the virulence plasmid within regional Vibrio communities (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)). Some isolates also carry multiple antimicrobial‑resistance genes, potentially favoring persistence under antibiotic use (Antimicrobial Resistance).
Review: Retain – This row appropriately summarizes the large intra‑continental spread of AHPND from China into key shrimp‑producing countries in South‑eastern and Southern Asia (Viet Nam 2010, Malaysia 2011, Thailand 2012, Philippines 2015, Bangladesh ~2017) and is well supported by FAO/MARD reports and subsequent reviews.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0145305X25001338))  The classification as a single intra‑continental emergence episode, rather than separate events for each country, is consistent with the project rule to merge epidemiologically linked regional epidemics, so no structural changes are recommended.

EPP.scientific.name: African horse sickness virus
EPP.common.name: AHSV
Host: Horses; mules; donkeys; zebras (index introduction via imported zebras)
Event.summary: After African horse sickness virus serotype 4 was introduced into a safari park near Madrid in 1987, probably via subclinically infected zebras imported from Namibia, the virus caused a multi-year epizootic in Iberia and the western Mediterranean. Large outbreaks occurred in southern Spain in 1988–1990 and spread to southern Portugal and northern Morocco in 1989, resulting in several hundred equine deaths and mass vaccination of more than 200,000 equids; Morocco continued to report cases until 1991. Intensive stamping-out, vaccination, movement restrictions and vector control ultimately led to official declaration of freedom from AHS in Spain and Portugal in 1991, ending the last recorded European AHS epizootic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance movement of wild equids (particularly asymptomatically infected zebras from southern Africa), high densities of susceptible horses in southern Spain and Portugal, favourable climatic conditions for Culicoides vectors, and incomplete early vaccination coverage permitted AHSV-4 to overwinter and spread between Spain, Portugal and Morocco. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not indicate that the AHSV-4 strain involved was novel or unusually virulent compared with southern African strains; the episode is best interpreted as geographic re-introduction and amplification of an endemic African serotype into previously affected European and North African regions rather than evolution of a new viral variant.
Review: review – Retained as one of the major post-1990 AHS emergence episodes, but corrected the time span to 1987–1991 (to reflect the full Iberian/North African epizootic), simplified country annotations to first involvement years only, removed Algeria because primary OIE, EU and Spanish sources consistently list Spain, Portugal and Morocco but not Algeria for the 1987–1991 serotype 4 outbreak, and reclassified the event from inter-continental emergence to re-occurrence since AHS had already occurred in Europe and North Africa during the 1965–1966 serotype 9 epizootic.

EPP.scientific.name: African horse sickness virus
EPP.common.name: AHSV
Host: Horses; other domestic equids
Event.summary: In 2011, southern Africa experienced a particularly severe African horse sickness season: SADC regional data record 720 outbreaks, 1,302 cases and 525 deaths across South Africa (675 outbreaks, 1,183 cases, 477 deaths), Namibia (44 outbreaks, 112 cases, 45 deaths) and Eswatini (1 outbreak, 7 cases, 3 deaths), the highest burden reported since systematic electronic recording began. Within this broader epizootic, an outbreak of AHSV-1 occurred in the African horse sickness controlled area of Western Cape Province in South Africa, centred on Mamre in the surveillance and free zones, with 73 laboratory-confirmed cases and about 70 deaths, leading to strict movement bans and a temporary suspension of horse exports. Following intensive vector control, quarantine, movement restrictions and blanket vaccination, cases in the controlled area ceased by May 2011 and regional outbreak numbers declined later that year, although AHS remains endemic in much of southern Africa.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Above-average rainfall and temperatures in early 2011, together with endemic AHS and extensive horse movements within southern Africa, were associated with a marked regional increase in outbreaks; the Mamre cluster most likely arose from movement of infected horses into the Western Cape controlled area. Internal mechanisms: Whole-genome analyses showed that the AHSV-1 strains responsible for the 2004 and 2011 Western Cape controlled-area outbreaks were reassortants derived from live-attenuated vaccine viruses that had reverted to virulence, so the controlled-area component of the 2011 epizootic is a clear example of re-emergence via vaccine-derived viral evolution, whereas the wider regional peak reflects re-occurrence of endemic strains under favourable climatic conditions.
Review: review – Event retained but outbreak statistics were corrected to use SADC regional figures (720 outbreaks, 1,302 cases, 525 deaths across South Africa, Namibia and Eswatini in 2011) rather than South Africa-only counts, and the description was clarified to distinguish the vaccine-derived AHSV-1 outbreak in the Western Cape controlled area from the broader climate-driven regional epizootic; classification as both re-occurrence (regional upsurge) and re-emergence (vaccine-derived strains in the controlled area) is supported by surveillance and genomic data.

EPP.scientific.name: African horse sickness virus
EPP.common.name: AHSV
Host: Horses (working and riding horses; donkeys may also have been exposed)
Event.summary: In 2019, African horse sickness reappeared prominently in Central Africa, with severe outbreaks reported in both Cameroon and Chad after decades without officially recognised clinical epizootics in the region. In Chad, veterinary reviews based on WOAH notifications describe 376 reported equine cases with more than 85% case-fatality, implying over 300 horse deaths, while veterinary services in Cameroon notified an epidemic of AHS in horses for the first time and undertook reactive investigations and control. The outbreaks mainly affected horses in savannah and Sahelian areas where they are essential for transport and draught, prompting emergency vaccination, restrictions on horse movements and vector control; reported clinical activity declined after 2019, although serological surveys indicate that AHSV continues to circulate in parts of Cameroon.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance trade and informal movement of horses between West and Central African countries where AHS is endemic, together with favourable environmental conditions for Culicoides vectors in riverine, irrigated and peri-urban zones, probably introduced and amplified AHSV in largely unvaccinated horse populations in Cameroon and Chad; limited veterinary infrastructure and delayed recognition likely contributed to the high apparent mortality. Internal mechanisms: Historical serological evidence shows that AHSV serotype 9 circulated in Central Africa (including Cameroon and Chad) decades earlier, and recent reviews suggest that additional serotypes (2, 4, 6, 7, 8) are now present in the region, but detailed molecular data for the 2019 viruses are still sparse; the episode is therefore conservatively classified as a high-impact re-occurrence of AHS pending more comprehensive genotypic characterisation.
Review: retain – New row added to represent the 2019 Central African outbreaks in Cameroon and Chad, which together involved at least 376 reported cases in Chad with >85% mortality and an officially recognised epidemic in Cameroon; classified as re-occurrence rather than intra-continental emergence because AHSV (particularly serotype 9) had already been documented serologically and virologically in Central African countries, including Cameroon and Chad, since the 1960s, although the apparent recent involvement of additional serotypes suggests ongoing viral diversification that merits continued monitoring.

EPP.scientific.name: African swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: ASFV
Host: Domestic pigs
Event.summary: In April 1996, African swine fever was reported for the first time in Côte d’Ivoire, where outbreaks around Abidjan rapidly devastated a previously expanding commercial and smallholder pig sector and triggered large-scale culling. Over 1997–2002, the same West African lineage ASF virus spread along coastal trade routes to Benin, Togo, Nigeria, Ghana and later Burkina Faso, causing near‑total loss of pigs in many affected areas and severe socio‑economic impacts on smallholders reliant on free‑ranging pigs. Intensive stamping‑out and movement controls eliminated ASF from Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana within a few years, but the virus became endemic in parts of the wider Western Africa region and permanently altered pig production and marketing systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid growth of pig production in West African coastal countries, dominated by low‑biosecurity free‑range and backyard systems; informal cross‑border trade in live pigs and pork; swill feeding of uncooked waste; limited veterinary capacity and compensation, leading to under‑reporting and illegal sale of sick animals. Internal mechanisms: introduction and regional dissemination of genotype I viruses belonging to the West African lineage, maintained entirely in domestic pig cycles without a sylvatic reservoir, allowing sustained circulation and large‑scale geographic expansion within Western Africa without the involvement of new genotypes or resistance traits.
Review: retain – Added because the 1996–2002 West Africa epidemic in Côte d’Ivoire, Benin, Togo, Nigeria, Ghana and Burkina Faso is widely recognised as one of the most consequential ASF epizootics since 1990, with very high pig mortality and major livelihood impacts, and was missing from the original dataset. Classified as re‑occurrence within the Western Africa subregion (not intra‑continental emergence), since ASF was already present in parts of Western Africa (e.g. Senegal, Cape Verde) before 1996; countries and timing follow FAO and Brown et al. (2018).

EPP.scientific.name: African swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: ASFV
Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar
Event.summary: In spring 2007, African swine fever appeared for the first time in the Caucasus, with an explosive outbreak in domestic pigs across most districts of Georgia that was traced to contaminated pork waste from ships and rapidly confirmed virologically. Over late 2007–2008 the same genotype II virus spread into Armenia, Azerbaijan and the Russian Federation (Chechnya and other regions), establishing infection in both backyard pigs and wild boar and extending beyond the Caucasus into key Russian pig‑producing regions. The virus was not eradicated and became entrenched in parts of the domestic pig and wild boar populations, seeding subsequent spread north and west into Eastern Europe and eastwards deeper into Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction via contaminated pork or ship waste at a Black Sea port, low farm biosecurity, widespread backyard pig keeping, swill feeding, and uncontrolled movements of pigs and pork; later spread was aided by movement of animals and pork along trade routes and by wild boar movements. Internal mechanisms: introduction and establishment of a highly virulent genotype II strain with efficient transmission in domestic pigs and wild boar facilitated geographic range expansion from Africa and Europe into Asia under the UNSD classification, and re‑establishment of ASF in Eastern Europe after prior eradication.
Review: retain – Confirmed as a key high‑impact emergence event: the introduction of genotype II ASFV into the Caucasus and, under the UNSD scheme, the first occurrence of ASF in Asia, as well as re‑establishment in Eastern Europe. Corrected the event type by setting 'first_detection' to No (because global first detection occurred many decades earlier) and retaining 'inter_continental_emergence' = Yes to reflect the first occurrence of ASF in the Asian continent in this classification. Countries, years and hosts are appropriate and supported by primary literature and WOAH/FAO reports.

EPP.scientific.name: African swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: ASFV
Host: Wild boar; domestic pigs
Event.summary: In early 2014, African swine fever was detected for the first time in the European Union in wild boar and backyard pigs in Lithuania and almost simultaneously in eastern Poland, following earlier spread through Belarus and western Russia in 2013. Infection rapidly became established in wild boar populations in the Baltic states and eastern Poland, with a slowly expanding front and repeated spillover to domestic pigs, causing numerous outbreaks in backyard and some commercial farms despite intensive control efforts. By 2018, much of Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and eastern Poland was affected, and ASF had become endemic in local wild boar populations with recurrent outbreaks in pigs, rather than being eliminated.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement of infected wild boar across borders, human‑mediated long‑distance jumps via transport of contaminated pork products and fomites, low biosecurity in backyard farms, and difficulties in controlling infection in free‑ranging wild boar. Internal mechanisms: efficient transmission of the same highly virulent genotype II strain in wild boar and pigs supported sustained wildlife reservoirs and geographic range expansion within Eastern and Northern Europe, including first establishment in the Northern Europe subregion.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the first introduction and establishment of genotype II ASFV in EU member states (Baltic countries and eastern Poland) and its spread into the Northern Europe subregion. Corrected the emergence‑type coding by setting 'first_detection' to No (not a global first detection) and removing 're_occurrence', leaving 'intra_continental_emergence' = Yes to reflect spread from already affected Eastern Europe into the previously ASF‑free Northern Europe subregion. Simplified the Belarus entry to 'Belarus [2013]' while still acknowledging its epidemiological linkage.

EPP.scientific.name: African swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: ASFV
Host: Domestic pigs; wild boar
Event.summary: In July 2017, Romania detected its first African swine fever outbreaks in backyard pigs near the Ukrainian and Hungarian borders, followed by rapid spread during 2018 that produced a nationwide epidemic with thousands of outbreaks and large‑scale culling in both backyard and commercial herds. Around the same time, focal introductions of ASFV genotype II occurred in Czechia (2017), Hungary (2018), Bulgaria (2018), Slovakia (2019), the Republic of Moldova (2016) and Serbia (2019), typically beginning in wild boar with occasional spillover to domestic pigs. By 2020, many Central and South‑Eastern European countries had experienced repeated outbreaks, with some (e.g. Czechia) achieving eradication from wild boar while others, notably Romania, continued to report intense circulation and heavy production losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement of infected pigs and pork from earlier affected Eastern European areas, poor biosecurity and backyard production in Romania and parts of the Balkans, swill feeding, informal trade, and human‑mediated long‑distance movement of contaminated materials leading to focal introductions in naïve wild boar populations. Internal mechanisms: continued circulation of genotype II with high virulence and environmental stability, facilitating persistence in carcasses and wild boar populations and enabling further geographic spread and resurgence within already affected Eastern and Southern Europe subregions.
Review: retain – Verified as a major high‑impact episode dominated by the very large Romanian epidemic and repeated outbreaks in several Central and South‑Eastern European countries. Corrected the emergence‑type coding from 'first_detection' + intra‑continental emergence + re‑occurrence to re‑occurrence only, because all affected countries lie within subregions (Eastern and Southern Europe) where ASF was already present after 2007; spread here represents expansion and resurgence within existing subregions rather than first occurrence in a new subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: African swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: ASFV
Host: Domestic pigs; free‑ranging village pigs
Event.summary: In July 2021, Dominican authorities confirmed African swine fever in domestic pigs after laboratory testing, representing the re‑appearance of ASF in the Americas and in Hispaniola roughly four decades after the 1970s–1980s Caribbean epizootic; widespread culling and movement controls were implemented to limit spread. Through 2022–2025, ASF continued to pose a major threat to Caribbean pig production and to the biosecurity of continental North and South America, prompting intensive regional surveillance and preparedness measures and substantial losses in parts of the Dominican and Haitian swine sectors.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: re‑introduction via infected pork products or live pigs, possibly related to trade or traveller‑carried meat from ASF‑affected regions; widespread low‑biosecurity backyard pig systems; free‑ranging pigs scavenging waste; and limited veterinary capacity and compensation mechanisms. Internal mechanisms: circulation of highly virulent genotype II ASFV similar to contemporary Eurasian strains, enabling rapid local spread. From a continental perspective this episode is best characterized as a geographic re‑occurrence in the Caribbean subregion of the Americas, rather than a new inter‑continental emergence or viral re‑emergence driven by evolutionary change.

EPP.scientific.name: Aparavirus tauraense
EPP.common.name: Taura syndrome virus, TSV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (L. vannamei) in imported and locally cultured stocks
Event.summary: Around 1999 TSV was first detected in Taiwan Province of China in L. vannamei broodstock imported from Central/South America, with multiple outbreaks reported to the OIE during 1999–2001 and hundreds of thousands of affected shrimp and substantial mortalities. In 1999–2000 the virus was also confirmed in Mainland China as L. vannamei and its pathogens were introduced with imported broodstock and postlarvae, leading to disease outbreaks in coastal farms and rapid recognition of TSV as a new, serious threat to East Asian shrimp aquaculture. By the early 2000s TSV had become established in affected Taiwanese and Chinese farming regions, with recurrent local epizootics and incorporation into regional surveillance and control programmes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: inter‑continental transfer of L. vannamei broodstock and postlarvae from the Americas into Taiwanese and Chinese hatcheries and grow‑out farms without adequate TSV screening or quarantine was the primary driver of spread; rapid scaling‑up of L. vannamei culture in Taiwan and coastal China created dense, susceptible farm populations. Internal mechanisms: high viral loads in subclinically infected broodstock, vertical and early‑life transmission to progeny, and efficient horizontal spread in ponds allowed TSV to establish quickly in newly stocked farms once introduced.
Review: Retain (minor standardisation). Updated country names to match the Country sheet (Taiwan Province of China; China) and kept the 1999–2001 timeframe, which is well supported by OIE case reports and FAO documentation. Classification as an inter‑continental emergence from the Americas to Asia is appropriate, and there is strong evidence for major production losses, so this remains one of the top impact events.

EPP.scientific.name: Aparavirus tauraense
EPP.common.name: Taura syndrome virus, TSV
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp, especially L. vannamei (with involvement of other cultured species where co‑cultured)
Event.summary: Following its establishment in Taiwan and coastal China, TSV was detected in Indonesia in 2002 soon after the official introduction and rapid expansion of L. vannamei culture, and in Thailand around 2003 as farmers shifted from P. monodon to L. vannamei. By about 2004, TSV had been reported from additional coastal provinces in China and from farms in the Republic of Korea, Myanmar and Viet Nam, where it contributed to high disease losses as the virus entered naïve shrimp‑farming areas. Over subsequent years, TSV became endemic in many East and South‑East Asian shrimp‑farming zones, co‑circulating with other major viral pathogens such as white spot syndrome virus (WSSV).
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intra‑Asian movement and trade of live L. vannamei postlarvae and broodstock, often sourced from previously infected regions within Asia, combined with rapid regional expansion and intensification of shrimp farming, drove TSV spread to new Asian subregions; limited biosecurity, water exchange among farms, and co‑culture or sequential culture of different penaeid species facilitated virus maintenance and spread. Internal mechanisms: TSV’s ability to infect multiple penaeid hosts and its efficient horizontal transmission allowed rapid establishment and persistence in new Asian production systems once introduced.
Review: Review (approximate timing). This event appropriately captures intra‑continental expansion of TSV within Asia from its initial foci in Taiwan/China to Indonesia, Thailand, Korea, Myanmar and Viet Nam and is clearly among the major impact events. Countries and sub‑regions have been standardised to the UNSD list. However, the specific year assignments for Myanmar and Viet Nam are approximate (sources document that TSV was endemic in these countries by 2004 rather than giving exact first‑detection years), so the event is flagged for expert review of country‑specific start years while being retained as a major Asian spread episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Chickens (broilers and pullets; commercial layer and broiler operations)
Event.summary: During the 1990s, very virulent infectious bursal disease virus (vvIBDV), first recognized in Europe in the late 1980s, caused a continent-wide wave of severe Gumboro disease outbreaks, beginning in Benelux countries and rapidly involving major poultry producers across Western and Northern Europe. The epizootic led to high flock mortality and heavy production losses, exemplified by a 1998 Danish episode affecting 36 broiler farms and causing the loss of over 200,000 broilers, while similar patterns of mortality and immunosuppression were reported in multiple European states. Improved vaccination strategies, biosecurity, and adaptation of control programs to vvIBDV pathotypes gradually reduced overt mortality by the late 1990s, though vvIBDV became enzootic in many European poultry sectors.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and geographic concentration of broiler and layer production, dense poultry populations with high farm connectivity, and movement of live birds and hatching eggs facilitated rapid dissemination of vvIBDV between European countries; gaps in existing vaccination programs, designed for classical strains, left flocks vulnerable. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of very virulent serotype 1 strains with increased virulence (increased virulence/pathogenicity) and enhanced capacity to cause high mortality and severe bursal damage; antigenic differences from classical and U.S. variant strains reduced protection from existing vaccines and favored geographic range expansion within Europe (geographic range expansion, inherent).
Review: review: Retain this event as the major vvIBDV epizootic in Europe, but change 'intra_continental_emergence' from Yes to No because vvIBDV arose within an already endemic IBDV population and, per the project rules, new pathotypes should be treated as re-emergence rather than intra-continental emergence. Geography, timing and impact are well supported by European reviews and outbreak reports, but the revised classification should be quality-checked.

EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Host: Chickens (backyard and commercial flocks)
Event.summary: The first recognized infectious bursal disease outbreaks in Bangladesh were reported at the end of 1992, coinciding with reports of severe Gumboro disease in neighboring South Asian countries and marking the southward spread of vvIBDV within Asia into high-density poultry systems of the subcontinent. Through the 1990s, repeated, large-scale outbreaks with high mortality and marked bursal pathology occurred in broiler and layer flocks across Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, causing heavy production losses and predisposing birds to secondary infections. By around 2000, IBDV—often in very virulent form—was firmly established in South Asian poultry; improved vaccines and control programs subsequently mitigated but did not eliminate recurrent disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of commercial poultry production in South Asia, movement of day-old chicks and hatching eggs, and limited early diagnostic and surveillance capacity supported the introduction and spread of vvIBDV into Bangladesh and neighboring countries; concurrent endemic diseases amplified the impact of IBDV-induced immunosuppression. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and regional expansion of vvIBDV strains closely related to European/Asian very virulent lineages (novel strain/genotype emergence relative to previously circulating or undetected IBDV) with high virulence and strong B-cell tropism (increased virulence/pathogenicity), combined with selection for variants able to escape partial vaccine immunity (antigenic diversification facilitating re-emergence).
Review: review: This South Asian wave of severe IBD (vvIBDV) should be kept as one of the major emergence events, but 'intra_continental_emergence' was set to No because the virus species was already endemic in the region and the new pathotype represents re-emergence rather than spread of a previously absent EPP. Otherwise, the timing (Bangladesh first recognized in 1992 with spread across India and Pakistan in the 1990s) and the listed countries align with primary reports and reviews.

EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Host: Chickens (broilers and layers, often subclinically affected)
Event.summary: From the mid‑2010s, a novel variant IBDV genotype (nvIBDV, classified as A2dB1b) emerged in China and subsequently spread through East and parts of Southeast Asia, generating a large-scale epidemic characterized largely by subclinical infections with severe bursal atrophy and immunosuppression rather than classic high-mortality Gumboro disease. Over this period, nvIBDV became widespread in Chinese broiler and layer flocks and was detected in other countries such as Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Malaysia, undermining vaccine programs targeting classical and vvIBDV strains and contributing to increased susceptibility to other poultry pathogens. Adjustments to vaccination strategies, including development and deployment of variant-adapted vaccines and improved monitoring, have begun to address this challenge, but nvIBDV remains an important, immunosuppressive re-emergent form of the virus in Asian poultry systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High vaccine pressure against classical and vvIBDV phenotypes, dense poultry production, and extensive movement of birds and products across East and Southeast Asia promoted emergence and spread of variants better adapted to partially immune flocks; intensive production favored viruses that cause subclinical yet immunosuppressive infection. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of the novel variant genotype A2dB1b with distinct VP2 antigenic properties and altered pathogenic profile (novel strain/genotype emergence), associated with strong bursal atrophy but often reduced overt mortality; partial escape from existing vaccine-induced immunity (antigenic variation/functional vaccine escape) allowed successful regional expansion (enhanced transmission/geographic range expansion).
Review: review: Retain this event as the major emergence of the Chinese novel variant nvIBDV (A2dB1b) and its subsequent spread in East and South‑eastern Asia, but update the period to 2015–2022 to match analyses showing reappearance of variants as novel strains in the mid‑2010s and their rapid expansion thereafter. EPP.scientific.name: Avibirnavirus gallinae
EPP.common.name: IBDV, Gumboro disease virus
Host: Chickens (commercial broilers and layers)
Event.summary: From the early 2020s, molecular surveillance revealed rapid spread of the novel variant IBDV genotype A2dB1b from its origin in East Asia into the Near East and North Africa, with first detections in Jordan and Lebanon in late 2023, followed by rapid establishment in the United Arab Emirates and evidence of related nvIBDV strains in Iraq. In parallel, Egypt reported nvIBDV A2dB1b in poultry flocks alongside existing vvIBDV strains, indicating further geographic expansion and leading to outbreaks characterized mainly by subclinical infection, bursal atrophy, and immunosuppression rather than high mortality. Ongoing circulation of these variants in the Middle East and North Africa has complicated control strategies based on classical and vvIBDV vaccines and raised concern about their long-term impact on vaccine performance and poultry health.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Trade in live birds and hatching eggs and regional integration of poultry supply chains between Asia, the Near East, and North Africa facilitated long-distance movement of nvIBDV; limited early awareness and diagnostic targeting of this genotype allowed silent spread before it was molecularly characterized. Internal mechanisms: The A2dB1b genotype possesses distinct VP2 antigenic signatures and is adapted to infect partially immune flocks previously vaccinated against classical and vvIBDV (novel strain/genotype emergence and vaccine escape), with a tendency toward subclinical yet strongly immunosuppressive disease (increased pathogenicity in terms of immune dysfunction rather than overt mortality), enabling re-emergence in regions where IBDV was already endemic and geographic expansion across Western Asia and into North Africa.
Review: review: This event is retained as the spread of nvIBDV A2dB1b into the Near East and North Africa, but the dates and geography were corrected using recent molecular surveillance: the wave now spans roughly 2021–2025, with nvIBDV first detected in Egypt around 2021–2023 and then in Jordan, Lebanon and the UAE from late 2023 onward, and Iraq added based on A2dB1b-classified sequences; Oman and Qatar were removed because current data primarily show other genotypes there. 'First_detection', 'intra_continental_emergence' and 'inter_continental_emergence' were all set to No so the episode is treated strictly as re-emergence of a new genotype in continents where IBDV was long established; the sources now cleanly support these corrections and should be reviewed by a domain expert for final confirmation.

EPP.scientific.name: BSE prion
EPP.common.name: Mad cow disease, BSE
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event.summary: From 1989 through the early 1990s, BSE was detected for the first time in native-born cattle in several European countries outside the UK, beginning with Ireland in 1989 and followed by Switzerland and Portugal in 1990, France in 1991, and Italy in 1994. These detections, often in animals born and reared locally, were epidemiologically linked to earlier imports of contaminated MBM or live cattle from the UK, showing that the UK feed-borne epidemic had seeded infection into multiple European herds. Subsequent adoption of ruminant-to-ruminant feed bans and intensified surveillance across these countries gradually curbed incidence, though additional cases continued to arise for years from already-exposed birth cohorts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of MBM and live cattle from the UK during the 1980s before BSE risk was fully recognised; lack of early risk communication and harmonised feed controls in importing states; delays and inconsistencies in implementing effective ruminant protein bans at the European level. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of the classical BSE strain into new European subregions via contaminated feed chains; prolonged incubation periods that allowed infected cohorts to move through trade networks before clinical disease appeared.
Review: retain – This row correctly captures the first indigenous BSE detections in key European countries outside the UK and is now aligned with FAO/EFSA tables: Ireland 1989, Switzerland 1990, Portugal 1990, France 1991, and Italy 1994. Countries whose first cases occurred later (Denmark, Germany, Spain, Belgium, Netherlands) have been removed from this row to avoid incorrect early-1990s dating and are instead represented in the later EU-wide 2000–2001 crisis event. The event year range has been adjusted from 1990–1994 to 1989–1994 to match the first Irish cases that were already cited in the original row. Type classification as intra-continental emergence and first detection (for these countries) is appropriate; no inter-continental or re-emergence flags are warranted.

EPP.common.name: Bovine babesiosis
