EPP.scientific.name: Babesia spp.
EPP.common.name: Babesiosis
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Host: Dogs (including fighting breeds and imported dogs)
Event.summary: In 2003, a dog in Spain with clinical babesiosis was confirmed by molecular testing to be infected with Babesia gibsoni, providing the first PCR-verified record of this predominantly Asian small Babesia species in a European dog. Over the 2000s and early 2010s, additional B. gibsoni infections were identified in dogs in Germany, the United Kingdom and other European countries, often in American Pit Bull Terriers, American Staffordshire Terriers or other fighting breeds, some of which had links to imported dogs or organized dog fighting. Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International movement and trade of dogs, particularly importation of fighting breeds from B. gibsoni-endemic regions in Asia and North America, and contact during dog fighting or other close-contact activities facilitated introduction and localized spread; increasing use of molecular diagnostics allowed differentiation of B. gibsoni from other small piroplasms. Internal mechanisms: Persistence of B. gibsoni in chronically infected carrier dogs and efficient non-tick transmission via blood exposure (bites, transfusions) enabled establishment in new canine populations despite the apparent absence of its primary tick vector in much of Europe; no clearly novel parasite lineage was implicated, so the event is best interpreted as inter-continental geographic spread of an existing lineage rather than true re-emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis
EPP.common.name: Bd
Host: High-Andean stream-breeding frogs, especially harlequin toads (Atelopus spp.), Telmatobius water frogs (Telmatobius spp.), and other montane anurans
Event.summary: From roughly 1990 onward, herpetological surveys across the northern and central Andes documented abrupt disappearances and mass mortalities of high-elevation frogs—particularly Atelopus harlequin toads and Telmatobius water frogs—in montane forests and páramo of Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela, Peru and Bolivia, with retrospective histology and molecular screening later confirming widespread Bd infection at many decline sites. Through the 1990s and 2000s, Bd spread along the main Andean cordilleras, producing epidemic waves and high infection prevalence that coincided with catastrophic losses of local amphibian communities and presumed extinctions of dozens of narrow-ranged species. By around 2010, the initial epidemic fronts had passed, Bd had become enzootic across much of the tropical Andes, and some species persisted or were rediscovered at low abundance while many others remained missing, leaving a long-term legacy of reduced diversity in high-elevation amphibian assemblages.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction and regional spread of Bd via amphibian trade and other human-assisted movements of animals and fomites, coupled with cool, moist high-Andean climates and dense stream-breeding assemblages that favored sustained transmission; climatic variability and warming-related changes to glacial and hydrological regimes may have further stressed host populations and modulated epidemic timing. Internal mechanisms: Invasion and dominance of highly virulent BdGPL or closely related lineages with efficient transmission in cold montane streams drove classic invasion waves and epizootics in naïve Atelopus and Telmatobius populations that showed limited innate resistance, producing rapid population crashes, local extirpations and numerous suspected species-level extinctions across the Andean region.
Review: review – New event added to capture the large, well-documented Bd-associated declines and extinctions of high-Andean Atelopus and Telmatobius species across Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela, Peru and Bolivia from the early 1990s through about 2010. Classified as re-emergence (not first or inter-continental emergence) because Bd was already present in South America before 1990, but epidemic dynamics and likely BdGPL introduction led to a step change in incidence and impact. Years and country onset dates are approximate mid-points constrained by the post-1990 rule and multiple regional syntheses, and should be checked by a subject-matter expert.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis
EPP.common.name: Bd
Host: Neotropical stream and montane frogs (e.g., Atelopus spp., Craugastor spp., other anurans)
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, unexplained crashes of stream-breeding frogs began in highland Costa Rica, with Bd-associated chytridiomycosis later confirmed as the cause of mass mortalities and severe declines. By the late 1990s and early 2000s, a west-to-east wave of Bd spread across western and central Panama, driving synchronous collapses and local extinctions of multiple amphibian assemblages as the pathogen invaded previously unexposed drainages, exemplified by the El Copé and Fortuna outbreaks. After about 2004 the initial epizootic front had passed through most monitored sites, leaving many species extirpated or at very low abundance, with Bd becoming enzootic in remaining populations and amphibian communities reorganized around more tolerant species.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of amphibians (including regional and international trade and translocation), high connectivity of montane stream habitats, and cool, moist cloud-forest climates promoted spread of Bd along the Central American cordilleras; climatic variability may have further influenced host susceptibility and epidemic timing. Internal mechanisms: Expansion of highly virulent BdGPL lineages into dense, species-rich stream frog communities produced classic invasion fronts and severe disease-driven declines and extinctions, with susceptible genera such as Atelopus and Craugastor collapsing rapidly after Bd arrival.
Review: review – Retain this as a major Lower Central American epizootic affecting Costa Rica and Panama, with continent/sub-region coding and timing consistent with USGS, EID and PNAS studies, but set 're_occurrence' to false so that the episode is classified solely as a lineage-driven re-emergence in a region where Bd was already present historically. No changes were made to geography, years or sources, but the dual labelling as both re-occurrence and re-emergence has been corrected to align with the intended mutual exclusivity of these categories.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis
EPP.common.name: Bd
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Host: European midwife toad (Alytes obstetricans), fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra), and other European amphibians
Event.summary: Beginning in 1997, mass mortality events of common midwife toads in Peñalara Natural Park in central Spain were documented and chytridiomycosis confirmed as the cause, marking the first recognized Bd-driven declines in wild European amphibians. Between the late 1990s and early 2000s, surveys and diagnostics revealed Bd infections and associated declines in Spain and Portugal and then in Italy, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, indicating spread and establishment of Bd across Southern, Western and Northern Europe from initial Iberian foci and introductions via captive and invasive amphibians. By around 2004, Bd had become established in multiple European amphibian communities, with ongoing localized die-offs and long-term population effects, particularly in high-elevation or pond-breeding species such as Alytes obstetricans and Salamandra salamandra.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of Bd to Europe via international amphibian trade (e.g., pet, zoo and laboratory animals, including invasive North American bullfrogs and African clawed frogs) followed by spread through translocation of animals and contaminated equipment, plus high host densities in ponds and alpine sites that facilitated local transmission. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and expansion of virulent BdGPL genotypes into naïve European host assemblages led to severe disease outbreaks in some species, while variation in host susceptibility and the presence of multiple Bd lineages contributed to heterogeneous impacts across countries and sites.
Review: review – Corrected country-specific first-detection years using Duffus & Cunningham (2010): Spain [1997], Switzerland [1998], Italy [2003], Portugal [2003] and United Kingdom [2004], and expanded the sub_regions field to 'Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe' to match the UN geoscheme for the listed countries. Reclassified the episode solely as an inter-continental emergence into Europe (removing intra-continental and re-emergence labels) because it represents the first confirmed establishment of Bd in wild European amphibians, while subsequent spread within Europe can be treated as part of the same linked episode. Retain as one of the major Bd emergence events.

Host: European midwife toad (Alytes obstetricans), fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra), and other European amphibians
Event.summary: Beginning in 1997, mass mortality events of common midwife toads in Peñalara Natural Park in central Spain were documented and chytridiomycosis confirmed as the cause, marking the first recognized Bd-driven declines in wild European amphibians. Between the late 1990s and early 2000s, surveys and diagnostics revealed Bd infections and associated declines in Spain and Portugal and then in Italy, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, indicating spread and establishment of Bd across Southern, Western and Northern Europe from initial Iberian foci and introductions via captive and invasive amphibians. By around 2004, Bd had become established in multiple European amphibian communities, with ongoing localized die-offs and long-term population effects, particularly in high-elevation or pond-breeding species such as Alytes obstetricans and Salamandra salamandra.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of Bd to Europe via international amphibian trade (e.g., pet, zoo and laboratory animals, including invasive North American bullfrogs and African clawed frogs) followed by spread through translocation of animals and contaminated equipment, plus high host densities in ponds and alpine sites that facilitated local transmission. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and expansion of virulent BdGPL genotypes into naïve European host assemblages led to severe disease outbreaks in some species, while variation in host susceptibility and the presence of multiple Bd lineages contributed to heterogeneous impacts across countries and sites.

Retain as one of the major Bd emergence events.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis
EPP.common.name: Bd
Host: Mountain chicken frog (Leptodactylus fallax) and sympatric amphibians
Event.summary: In 2002, reports from Dominica described sudden mass mortalities of the mountain chicken frog, and investigations confirmed Bd infection and chytridiomycosis as the cause of catastrophic declines that reduced populations by more than 85% in less than two years. After the Dominica crash, the remaining stronghold of the species on Montserrat was initially disease-free, but Bd was detected there in 2009, followed by a rapid wave of mortality and near-extirpation similar to that seen on Dominica. By around 2010, wild mountain chicken populations on both islands had been reduced to tiny remnants or functionally extirpated, with the species surviving mainly in captive assurance colonies while Bd remained established in local amphibian communities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction of Bd to the Lesser Antilles via regional or international movement of infected amphibians (including invasive tree frogs) or contaminated fomites, with small, insular ranges and limited refugia greatly increasing the vulnerability of island populations. Internal mechanisms: Highly virulent BdGPL strains caused intense epizootics with extremely high case fatality in Leptodactylus fallax, a highly susceptible host, driving rapid range collapses; high transmission in moist island habitats and limited genetic resilience in small, fragmented populations amplified the impact.
Review: review – Retain this as a major, well-documented Bd-driven collapse of an endemic Caribbean species, with continent/sub-region coding and timing (Dominica 2002; Montserrat 2009) supported by primary literature and conservation reports. 'Re_emergence' has been set to false because there is no evidence of earlier Bd presence in the Lesser Antilles; the episode is best characterized as an intra-continental emergence into a new sub-region (Caribbean) within the South America continent definition used by the project.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans
EPP.common.name: Bsal
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Captive collections of salamanders and newts (multiple urodele species, including European and Asian taxa) in Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom
Event.summary: Beginning in the early 2010s, Bsal was detected in captive salamander collections in Germany, initially associated with mass mortality of fire salamanders, and shortly thereafter in additional collections in the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. Epidemiological tracing showed that many affected private and zoological collections had imported salamanders from continental Europe and Asia, with Bsal infection often present in multiple species and sometimes causing clinical disease and die‑offs, while other taxa carried infections subclinically. These findings revealed that captive populations across several European subregions served as reservoirs and amplification hosts for Bsal and highlighted ongoing risk of repeated spillover into wild populations and long‑distance dissemination via the pet and zoo trade.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International pet, zoo, and hobbyist trade moving live salamanders among Asia and multiple European countries, inadequate quarantine and pathogen screening of imported animals, and dense mixed‑species housing in private and institutional collections all facilitated establishment and spread of Bsal in captivity. Internal mechanisms: Broad host range among urodeles, the capacity for subclinical persistent infections in some Asian and European species, and efficient transmission in high‑density captive environments led to recurrent outbreaks and made captive collections important reservoirs and bridge populations for Bsal, enabling repeated introductions into new regions and host communities.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections and additions: (1) The original row only listed Germany and the UK and labeled the event as intra-continental emergence + re-emergence. EFSA and subsequent summaries show that major Bsal-positive captive collections with associated mortality were documented in Germany, the Netherlands, Spain and the UK by 2017, with additional asymptomatic infection documented in Swedish collections and evidence of infection in at least one Belgian collection. Countries and subregions have therefore been expanded to include Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom, and the sub_regions field updated to "Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe." Country start years are approximate mid‑2010s values reflecting earliest published detections and should be refined in any future update. (2) Under the project’s rules, intra-continental emergence is reserved for first occurrence in a new UNSD subregion in the wild; here, the same pathogen is appearing in captive populations across subregions that are already affected (or at risk) via trade. This event is therefore better treated as `re_emergence = TRUE` (expansion into new host communities and captive reservoirs) and `intra_continental_emergence = FALSE`. (3) Because multiple new countries and a type reclassification were introduced based on synthesis of several sources, this row is flagged for further expert review, but it should be retained as one of the major Bsal events given its role in amplifying and moving the pathogen across Europe.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans
EPP.common.name: Bsal
Host: Wild Asian salamanders and toads (multiple urodele species in Thailand, Viet Nam, Japan, China, Taiwan; a small‑webbed fire‑bellied toad, Bombina microdeladigitora, in Viet Nam and traded individuals; and occasionally imported amphibians in or via Hong Kong)
Event.summary: Through retrospective and prospective surveys published from 2013 onward, Bsal DNA was detected in wild salamanders in Thailand, Viet Nam, and Japan without obvious associated mass mortality, leading to the hypothesis that East and South‑eastern Asia represent the pathogen’s endemic range. Subsequent broader screening demonstrated Bsal infection in additional wild urodele species in Viet Nam and China, in a small‑webbed fire‑bellied toad (Bombina microdeladigitora) in Viet Nam and the trade, and in some amphibians in Taiwan and Hong Kong, again largely without severe disease, indicating long‑term coexistence between local hosts and the fungus. By about 2020, these findings had firmly established East/South‑eastern Asia as a major reservoir region for Bsal, with numerous wild host species carrying the pathogen at low apparent impact but constituting a continuing source for global spread via trade.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing natural presence of Bsal in East/South‑eastern Asian amphibian communities combined with rapidly expanding regional and international trade in wild‑caught and farmed salamanders and other amphibians, particularly from China and Viet Nam, has created conditions for intercontinental dissemination of the pathogen. Internal mechanisms: Co‑evolution of Bsal with Asian host lineages has produced many tolerant or reservoir hosts capable of harboring infection with minimal clinical disease, supporting persistent environmental circulation and wide geographic spread while maintaining overall low‑level prevalence in source populations. This reservoir dynamics underpins Bsal introductions to Europe and other regions via the amphibian trade.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections: (1) The original row labeled this Asian reservoir event as `first_detection = TRUE`, which conflicts with the Netherlands outbreak being the global first description and detection of Bsal. To avoid multiple first-detection events, `first_detection` has been set to FALSE here. (2) Instead, this episode is classified as `inter_continental_emergence = TRUE`, representing the first *documented* occurrence of Bsal in Asia as a continent following its initial description from Europe, and the subsequent recognition of East/South‑eastern Asia as the main natural reservoir. Although phylogenetic evidence indicates a long evolutionary history of Bsal in Asia, the project’s operational definitions are based on detection and documentation rather than inferred ancient presence. (3) Countries, subregions, and the broad 2013–2020 time range remain appropriate for an aggregated, linked episode of detections across multiple Asian countries in wild populations and traded animals, but the confidence score is kept at 0.85 to reflect residual uncertainty in exact first‑detection years per country. The event is retained because recognizing the Asian reservoir is essential for understanding the global emergence and trade‑driven risk profile of Bsal, but it is flagged for expert review due to the change in emergence-type classification and the conceptual nuance around endemicity vs. emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Betaarterivirus suid 1
EPP.common.name: PRRSV, Blue-ear pig disease
Sub.regions: Asia | Eastern Asia; Asia | South-eastern Asia
Host: Domestic pigs (breeding and grower-finisher herds) in commercial and smallholder systems
Event.summary: Following its emergence in China in 2006, highly pathogenic PRRSV-2 spread into neighbouring East and South‑East Asian countries beginning around 2007, with early severe outbreaks reported in Viet Nam and subsequently in other Indochina countries. Between 2007 and 2011 multiple countries in the Greater Mekong and broader South‑East Asian region—including Viet Nam, Lao PDR, Cambodia and Thailand—experienced large HP‑PRRSV epidemics with high pig mortality, substantial numbers of outbreaks (e.g. over 500 outbreaks in Viet Nam in 2010) and major economic losses. After these epidemic waves, HP‑PRRSV became entrenched in regional pig populations, with continued circulation and localized outbreaks reported in several South‑East Asian countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intense regional trade and movement of pigs and pig products among China and South‑East Asian countries, informal cross‑border movements, rapid growth of pig production in the Mekong region, and gaps in veterinary services and biosecurity facilitated geographic spread. Internal mechanisms: dissemination of the Chinese HP‑PRRSV-2 lineage into new sub‑regions represented geographic range expansion of this highly virulent variant, with phylogenetic studies indicating multiple introductions and subsequent diversification into distinct HP‑PRRSV clades in Thailand, Lao PDR, Cambodia and Viet Nam; these changes reflect both enhanced transmission and ongoing viral evolution within an already highly pathogenic background. Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2020]
Host: Companion animals (dogs, cats) living in households of human COVID-19 cases
Event.summary: In early 2020, SARS-CoV-2 was first detected in a pet dog belonging to a COVID-19 patient in Hong Kong, with viral RNA repeatedly detected from nasal and oral swabs, followed shortly by detection in a second dog in Hong Kong and then companion cats and dogs in other countries. Over the course of 2020, sporadic infections were confirmed in pets in North America and Europe, nearly all linked epidemiologically to close contact with infected owners and generally causing mild or no clinical signs. These pet infections remained incidental spillover events with no evidence of sustained pet-to-human transmission, and control consisted primarily of guidance on hygiene and quarantine of animals from infected households rather than mass depopulation.

Internal mechanisms: host expansion of a human-adapted virus into susceptible carnivores (dogs, cats) via shared ACE2 receptor compatibility; no clear evidence that these early pet infections involved distinct variants with increased virulence or transmission in animals. The main mechanism was repeated human-to-animal spillover without onward spread between animal populations.
Review: review – retain this event as the first documented natural infection of SARS-CoV-2 in the animal host system (pets) and hence the global first_detection/first_global_emergence entry. Event.summary: In April 2020, lions and tigers at the Bronx Zoo in New York became the first zoo animals reported with natural SARS-CoV-2 infection, showing respiratory signs after exposure to an infected keeper and testing positive for the virus, and similar cases in zoo felids were soon reported in other US facilities and in Europe. Over 2020–2022, additional outbreaks occurred in captive lions, tigers, pumas, snow leopards and other carnivores, as well as in gorillas in several zoos, with most animals experiencing mild to moderate respiratory illness but some felids suffering severe or fatal disease, and keepers often identified as the likely source. These outbreaks were managed through enhanced infection control for staff, temporary closure or distancing measures for visitors, and vaccination of susceptible zoo species where veterinary vaccines became available, and no long-term zoo-based reservoirs have been documented though repeated re-introductions from humans continued through successive waves of human infection.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: close, prolonged contact between infected zookeepers and susceptible zoo species, high visitor traffic before implementation of strict biosecurity, and the global spread of SARS-CoV-2 variants that increased the chance of introduction into zoos. Internal mechanisms: host expansion into diverse carnivores and great apes with high ACE2 receptor compatibility; in some zoos evidence of animal-to-animal transmission within enclosures; but overall infections reflected repeated re-introduction of human-circulating variants rather than long-term independent viral evolution in zoo populations.
Review: review – retain as a single multi-continent episode of repeated zoo-animal infections with clear animal health and One Health relevance. Emergence-type coding has been revised: inter_continental_emergence and re_occurrence are now set to 'No', with only re_emergence='Yes'. These episodes reflect repeated reverse-zoonotic introductions and limited within-zoo spread in highly susceptible species on continents where animal infections were already established; re_occurrence cannot span multiple subregions or co-occur with inter-/intra-continental emergence under the project definitions.

Host: Zoo and aquarium animals including large felids (tigers, lions, pumas, snow leopards), other carnivores, and great apes (gorillas) in captivity
Event.summary: In April 2020, lions and tigers at the Bronx Zoo in New York became the first zoo animals reported with natural SARS-CoV-2 infection, showing respiratory signs after exposure to an infected keeper and testing positive for the virus, and similar cases in zoo felids were soon reported in other US facilities and in Europe. Over 2020–2022, additional outbreaks occurred in captive lions, tigers, pumas, snow leopards and other carnivores, as well as in gorillas in several zoos, with most animals experiencing mild to moderate respiratory illness but some felids suffering severe or fatal disease, and keepers often identified as the likely source. These outbreaks were managed through enhanced infection control for staff, temporary closure or distancing measures for visitors, and vaccination of susceptible zoo species where veterinary vaccines became available, and no long-term zoo-based reservoirs have been documented though repeated re-introductions from humans continued through successive waves of human infection.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: close, prolonged contact between infected zookeepers and susceptible zoo species, high visitor traffic before implementation of strict biosecurity, and the global spread of SARS-CoV-2 variants that increased the chance of introduction into zoos. Internal mechanisms: host expansion into diverse carnivores and great apes with high ACE2 receptor compatibility; in some zoos evidence of animal-to-animal transmission within enclosures; but overall infections reflected repeated re-introduction of human-circulating variants rather than long-term independent viral evolution in zoo populations.
Review: review – retain as a single multi-continent episode of repeated zoo-animal infections with clear animal health and One Health relevance. Emergence-type coding has been revised: inter_continental_emergence and re_occurrence are now set to 'No', with only re_emergence='Yes'. These episodes reflect repeated reverse-zoonotic introductions and limited within-zoo spread in highly susceptible species on continents where animal infections were already established; re_occurrence cannot span multiple subregions or co-occur with inter-/intra-continental emergence under the project definitions.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus pandemicum
EPP.common.name: SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19 virus
Host: Free-ranging white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) and, to a lesser extent, other cervids in the wild
Event.summary: In 2020, experimental infections showed that white-tailed deer were highly susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 and capable of deer-to-deer transmission, prompting wildlife surveillance in the United States that soon detected widespread natural infection and antibodies in free-ranging deer across multiple states, with some populations showing very high seroprevalence. By late 2021 and 2022, US nationwide surveys found evidence of prior infection in large proportions of sampled deer across most of their range, while Canada reported its first detections in free-ranging deer in Quebec and Ontario in late 2021, confirming establishment of a wildlife reservoir in Northern America. Viral sequencing revealed that deer populations harbored multiple human-like variants and, in some locations, distinct deer-associated lineages persisting over time, raising concern that deer could serve as a long-term reservoir from which divergent viruses might spill back into humans or other wildlife even as human infections decline.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive spatial overlap between dense deer populations and humans in suburban and rural landscapes, including deer habituation to human-dominated environments, anthropogenic feeding, and hunting practices, all facilitating repeated human-to-deer spillover; limited initial awareness and surveillance delayed recognition of the scale of infection. Internal mechanisms: host expansion into a highly susceptible cervid species with efficient deer-to-deer transmission and capacity for sustained transmission cycles; geographic range expansion across much of the North American deer range; and, in some locales, emergence of deer-associated viral lineages and documented deer-to-human transmission events, suggesting within-deer adaptation and potential increased fitness in this host.
Review: review – retain as a major emergence event marking establishment of SARS-CoV-2 in a free-ranging wildlife reservoir (white-tailed deer) in North America. Emergence coding has been simplified by setting re_occurrence to 'No' and keeping re_emergence='Yes', reflecting that the key feature is host expansion, sustained transmission and viral evolution in a new wildlife host within an already affected subregion, driven by internal viral adaptation rather than purely external drivers of resurgence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bonamia exitiosa
EPP.common.name: Bonamiosis
Countries: United States of America – North Carolina [2003]
Host: Asian Suminoe oyster Crassostrea ariakensis (triploid experimental and candidate aquaculture stocks) with the native crested oyster Ostrea equestris/Ostrea stentina acting as a local reservoir host in parts of the southeastern USA
Event.summary: Beginning in 2003, a Bonamia parasite later confirmed as Bonamia exitiosa was detected in non‑native Suminoe oysters Crassostrea ariakensis deployed to Bogue Sound, North Carolina, where infections reached high prevalence and caused mortality exceeding 80–100% in small oysters, effectively halting prospects for commercial introduction of the species. Follow‑up field deployments in 2005 in Bogue and Masonboro Sounds showed strong seasonality, with heavy Bonamia infection and high mortality in warm, euhaline summer conditions and little or no infection in cooler seasons, while concurrent surveys documented infection of the native crested oyster Ostrea equestris in the same area. By 2007, a genetically matching B. exitiosa strain was also detected in C. ariakensis and C. virginica exposed to ambient Atlantic waters of the Indian River Lagoon, Florida, confirming establishment of this Southern Hemisphere parasite on the Atlantic coast of Northern America and highlighting its capacity to infect multiple oyster hosts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction is strongly suspected to have been shipping‑mediated, with C. ariakensis and/or associated biota in port areas near Morehead City, North Carolina, providing an entry point from Southern Hemisphere B. exitiosa lineages, after which warm, high‑salinity estuarine conditions favored parasite transmission. Intensive experimental deployments of dense C. ariakensis cohorts in Bonamia‑enzootic waters amplified transmission and revealed the parasite’s impact, while the presence of infected native Ostrea equestris indicates a local reservoir that could sustain B. exitiosa independent of the introduced host. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses of SSU and ITS rDNA group the North Carolina and Florida Bonamia isolates with B. exitiosa from New Zealand, Argentina and Australia, indicating geographic range expansion of this species into a new continent and host genus (Crassostrea) rather than emergence of a distinct taxon; the severe mortality observed in small C. ariakensis cohorts reflects high susceptibility of this host under suitable environmental conditions.
Review: review – New event added to capture the well‑documented epizootic of B. exitiosa in experimentally deployed Crassostrea ariakensis and associated reservoir hosts in North Carolina and Florida, which produced very high mortalities and represents the first established occurrence of B. exitiosa on the North American continent; coded as inter‑continental emergence (not first global emergence) with no re‑emergence flag, and limited to the USA (North Carolina, Florida). Classification as B. exitiosa rather than an unnamed Bonamia sp. follows later molecular work and international fact sheets that place these isolates within the B. exitiosa clade.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/5397965_Strong_seasonality_of_Bonamia_sp_infection_and_induced_Crassostrea_ariakensis_mortality_in_Bogue_and_Masonboro_Sounds_North_Carolina_USA))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bonamia exitiosa
EPP.common.name: Bonamiosis
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Host: European flat oyster Ostrea edulis (mainly wild beds and culture sites), with Bonamia exitiosa also associated with dwarf oyster Ostrea stentina as a reservoir in parts of the Mediterranean
Event.summary: In 2006, Bonamia exitiosa was first confirmed by histology and rDNA sequencing in European flat oysters Ostrea edulis from culture in the Ría de Arousa, Galicia (Spain), representing the first report of this Southern Hemisphere parasite in European waters and often co‑infecting oysters already affected by Bonamia ostreae. Over the following decade, B. exitiosa was detected at generally low to moderate prevalence in O. edulis from multiple European regions, including natural beds in the Manfredonia Gulf (Adriatic Italy), cultured stocks on the Spanish Mediterranean coast (Ebro Delta and other sites), flat‑oyster populations along the French Mediterranean, and later in southern Portugal and in Mali Ston Bay, Croatia, with occasional co‑occurrence in reservoir oysters such as O. stentina. In the United Kingdom, B. exitiosa was first reported in River Fal (Cornwall) in 2010–2011 and later detected ephemerally in adult and larval O. edulis from restoration and fishery sites in the Solent between 2015 and 2019, with subsequent surveys becoming negative; throughout Europe, infections have so far involved small proportions of sampled oysters and no large‑scale mortality events have been attributed solely to B. exitiosa, though concern persists about additive impacts alongside B. ostreae.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance human‑mediated movements of oysters and associated fouling/ballast, including transfers of O. edulis for aquaculture and restoration and potential reservoir hosts such as O. stentina and Pacific oysters Crassostrea gigas, are strongly implicated in introducing B. exitiosa from the Southern Hemisphere into multiple European coastal systems and in subsequent secondary spread within the Mediterranean and NE Atlantic. Internal mechanisms: European detections largely involve B. exitiosa lineages closely related (≈99% SSU rDNA similarity) to Southern Hemisphere strains, indicating geographic range expansion of existing genotypes rather than a novel species; co‑infection with B. ostreae, possible larval infection, and the presence of reservoir hosts may enhance transmission opportunities but have not yet been linked to altered virulence or dramatic, B. exitiosa‑driven mass mortalities.
Review: review – Years updated from 2007–2019 to 2006–2020 to reflect evidence that the first European detection occurred in Galicia in 2006 and that confirmed infections continued at least to 2020 in Croatia; country list expanded to include Portugal (Algarve) and clarified that UK detections encompass both the initial River Fal (Cornwall) outbreak and later ephemeral Solent detections. Inter‑continental emergence coding is appropriate because this is the first established occurrence of B. exitiosa in Europe, while re‑emergence is left ‘No’ given the absence of clear evidence for major parasite change driving these low‑prevalence detections; additional event‑level sources have been added for Spanish Mediterranean, Portuguese and UK outbreaks and an official UK factsheet.([ices.dk](https://www.ices.dk/sites/pub/CM%20Doccuments/CM-2010/ACOM/ACOM2910.pdf?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Burkholderia mallei
EPP.common.name: Malleus (glanders)
Host: Working equids (horses, donkeys, mules)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, a cross-sectional serosurvey of nearly 1,000 working equids in central Ethiopia found approximately 3–4% seropositive for glanders using complement fixation and Western blot, demonstrating previously unrecognized but widespread infection in an area thought to be largely free of the disease. These findings revealed endemic foci of glanders in Eastern Africa and prompted increased attention to equine health surveillance, although resource constraints have limited comprehensive eradication efforts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High reliance on working equids for transport and draught power, congregation of animals at markets and watering points, low biosecurity, and limited access to veterinary services favoured silent persistence of B. mallei infection in Eastern Africa. Cross-border movements of animals and trade in equids from endemic parts of Asia or the Middle East may have contributed to historical introduction, but the modern event largely reflects recognition of long-standing infection rather than a discrete introduction. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of new strains, resistance, or altered virulence was reported; hence the event is best interpreted as re-occurrence of a long-established pathogen in a previously affected continent, newly documented through improved serological surveys.
Review: review – Added new event to capture a major, previously omitted modern focus of glanders. This row summarises serological evidence for endemic infection in working equids in central Ethiopia (≈3–4% seropositive) and official WOAH notifications from Eritrea and Ethiopia around 2010–2011, which collectively represent the main documented re-occurrence of B. mallei in Eastern Africa. Event.summary: After approval of fluoroquinolone (e.g. enrofloxacin) use in food animals in several European countries around 1990, fluoroquinolone‑resistant Campylobacter jejuni rapidly emerged in poultry and other livestock, with high proportions of resistant isolates in Spain, the Netherlands and other countries documented within a few years. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via point mutations in the gyrA gene and related mechanisms conferring fluoroquinolone resistance; Enhanced Transmission within poultry flocks and along slaughter/processing chains; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of resistant lineages across European livestock and food‑trade networks.

EPP.scientific.name: Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei

Event.summary: In January–February 1993, a severe epizootic of necrotising hepatopancreatitis appeared in penaeid shrimp farms in the Tumbes region of north‑western Peru and adjacent farms in Ecuador, marking the first major spread of the Texas NHP agent beyond North America and its arrival in South America.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0044848694903298?utm_source=openai)) The outbreak rapidly affected numerous commercial ponds stocked with L. vannamei, with histology and TEM revealing massive intracellular infections of hepatopancreatic epithelium by a pleomorphic Gram‑negative bacterium closely resembling the Texas NHP agent and causing up to 90–95% mortality and severe production collapse.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0044848694903298?utm_source=openai)) By June 1993 nearly half of Peru’s 44 active shrimp farms in the affected area were forced to close or suspend operations, and control relied on pond fallowing, improved water management and biosecurity to limit further spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of L. vannamei farming in Peru and Ecuador using stock movements and shared water sources likely introduced the NHP bacterium from Texas into new farms; high ambient temperatures and high salinity in the Tumbes region favoured rapid amplification and farm‑to‑farm spread.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0044848694903298?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The etiologic agent showed close genetic and morphological similarity to the Texas NHP bacterium, later classified as Candidatus Hepatobacter penaei, indicating geographic range expansion of an existing highly virulent strain rather than a novel variant.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568585/?utm_source=openai))
Review: RETAIN. The 1993 Peru/Ecuador outbreak is well documented as a severe epizootic with very high mortalities and closure of roughly half of Peru’s active shrimp farms, and is widely recognised as the first confirmed spread of NHP from Texas to the South American continent.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0044848694903298?utm_source=openai)) Classifying this event as an inter‑continental emergence (North America to South America) is appropriate; Peru and Ecuador with 1993 onset years correctly capture the main affected countries, and the chosen Aquaculture and molecular papers are the most relevant sources for this episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Canine morbillivirus
EPP.common.name: Canine distemper virus, CDV
Host: African lion (Panthera leo); domestic dog (Canis lupus familiaris) as source reservoir; other sympatric carnivores (e.g. hyenas, jackals) involved in transmission
Event.summary: In early 1994, a morbillivirus closely related to canine distemper virus spilled over from infected domestic dogs into the lion population of Serengeti National Park and adjacent Maasai Mara, initiating an explosive epidemic. The outbreak rapidly spread through the high‑density lion population, killing roughly one‑third of Serengeti lions and causing marked neurological signs and pneumonia, with domestic dogs to the west of the park identified as the most likely infection source. The epidemic waned as susceptible lion numbers were depleted and herd immunity rose, leaving CDV established in the broader carnivore community with recurrent but less catastrophic circulation thereafter.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑density, poorly vaccinated domestic dog populations surrounding the protected area created a large, persistent reservoir of CDV; close spatial overlap and occasional contact between dogs and wildlife at park edges facilitated repeated spillover; climatic extremes and associated tick‑borne co‑infections (e.g. Babesia) amplified case fatality in lions. Internal mechanisms: Highly transmissible CDV lineages already circulating in regional dogs and wild canids spilled over into immunologically naïve lions; co‑infection with hemoparasites increased apparent virulence and mortality, but viral genetics were consistent with a local dog‑origin lineage rather than a completely novel genotype, in line with classification as re‑emergence rather than first emergence.
Review: review - Retain as a top-impact wildlife CDV emergence event. Corrected the event year from '1993-1994' to '1994' and aligned country-specific years for Tanzania and Kenya to 1994 because primary descriptions date the lion epidemic to early 1994 with no clear evidence for 1993 case onset; Maasai Mara involvement is contemporaneous. Event type (re_emergence due to spillover into naïve lions) and geographic coding (Africa | Eastern Africa; Tanzania, Kenya) are otherwise consistent with the literature.

EPP.scientific.name: Carp edema virus

Host: Ornamental koi carp; farmed and wild or stocked common carp
Event.summary: In autumn 2013, the first Dutch cases of koi sleepy disease due to CEV were confirmed in koi, signalling spread of the virus into Western Europe beyond the UK. EPP.scientific.name: Chelonid fibropapilloma-associated herpesvirus
EPP.common.name: FP-associated herpesvirus, CFPHV
Host: Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas)
Event.summary: Between 1998 and 2006, monitoring of foraging green turtles in Corisco Bay on the border of Equatorial Guinea and Gabon documented FP prevalences averaging around 17%, providing the first histopathologically confirmed FP hotspot in Central/West Africa and overturning the previous assumption that the region was FP‑free. By 2005, FP‑like tumors were observed on green turtles off the Republic of the Congo, and by the early 2010s, histological and virological work from Príncipe Island in Sao Tome and Principe confirmed ChHV5‑associated fibropapillomas there. Further surveys and case reports across the 2010s documented FP and/or ChHV5‑positive turtles in Ghana, Guinea‑Bissau, and Mauritania, indicating that clinically apparent FP had spread along much of the Gulf of Guinea coastline. Although reported prevalences generally remained lower than in Hawaii or Florida, this series of detections marks the establishment of FP across multiple Atlantic African foraging grounds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The Gulf of Guinea is undergoing rapid coastal development associated with oil and gas extraction, port expansion, urbanization and artisanal fisheries, all of which can alter water quality and increase turtle exposure to pollutants and eutrophication—conditions similar to FP hotspots elsewhere. Internal mechanisms: Histopathology and PCR from Príncipe Island and other sites confirmed classic FP lesions and ChHV5 infection, and global phylogeographic analyses of CFPHV show African haplotypes clustering with those from other Atlantic basins, suggesting that FP in Atlantic Africa reflects geographic expansion and local expression of an existing herpesvirus lineage rather than the emergence of a novel strain.
Review: retain – This event correctly identifies the first confirmed establishment and subsequent spread of FP in Atlantic Africa, which represents the first inter‑continental emergence of FP into the African continent. Event type has been reclassified from intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence to inter‑continental emergence only, aligning with the definition of a first occurrence in a new continent. Countries were expanded to include Guinea‑Bissau and Mauritania based on later surveys documenting FP and/or ChHV5 there. Flagged for review to refine timing for West African sites as more precise dates become available.

EPP.scientific.name: Chlamydia abortus
EPP.common.name: Enzootic abortion, EAE, Ovine enzootic abortion
Host: Goats (primary affected herds in Argentina and Chile); cattle (bovine abortions in La Pampa, Argentina)
Event.summary: In 2012, during the spring kidding season, a commercial goat herd in Mendoza Province, Argentina (400 criollo does) experienced a six‑week episode in which about 70 does aborted late‑term fetuses or delivered weak kids, prompting detailed pathological and laboratory investigation. Histopathology, immunohistochemistry and PCR on placental tissue confirmed Chlamydia abortus as the etiologic agent, while contemporaneous diagnostic work in Argentina detected C. abortus DNA in bovine reproductive losses in La Pampa and Chilean SAG laboratories documented multiple caprine abortion foci in the Metropolitan, Biobío and Atacama regions with real‑time PCR confirmation of C. abortus, together constituting the first laboratory‑confirmed C. abortus abortion outbreaks in Chile and Argentina within a continent where serologic evidence and isolated reports from Brazil and Uruguay had already suggested prior circulation. The affected herds controlled the outbreaks through improved hygiene at kidding/lambing, culling or segregation of aborting animals and broader awareness and testing, leading to a return toward baseline abortion rates while establishing C. abortus as a recognised cause of small‑ruminant and bovine abortion in southern South America rather than a new continental incursion.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion and partial intensification of small‑ruminant and cattle production in southern South America; increased movements of animals between regions and countries; and, critically, the progressive introduction of modern laboratory diagnostics (ELISA, PCR, real‑time PCR) in Argentina and Chile that enabled recognition of C. abortus in abortion material where it had previously gone undetected. Internal mechanisms: no novel genotype or resistance phenotype was reported; phylogenetic analysis showed close homology with existing ovine and caprine strains from Europe and China, consistent with long‑standing but previously under‑diagnosed presence followed by geographic range expansion and local amplification within the already infected South America sub‑region; this episode is therefore best classified as a regional re‑occurrence and recognition event, not a true inter‑continental emergence or global first detection.
Review: Decision: review (retain with corrected classification and sources). Changes made: (1) Removed the earlier claim that this episode represents inter‑continental emergence or a global first detection of C. abortus in South America; serologic and molecular data from Brazil and other countries show the pathogen was present in the region before 2012, so this outbreak is re‑classified as a re‑occurrence within the South America sub‑region.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/scielo.php?lng=en&pid=S0100-736X2012001100002&script=sci_arttext&tlng=en&utm_source=openai)) (2) Set first_detection and inter_continental_emergence to "No" and re_occurrence to "Yes" to align with the definitions, because the episode reflects recognition and spread in new countries (Argentina and Chile) within an already infected sub‑region rather than the first presence on the continent. (3) Clarified in the event summary that Chilean multi‑herd caprine abortion outbreaks with PCR‑confirmed C. abortus in 2012 are documented by SAG’s BVO report and that bovine reproductive losses in La Pampa, Argentina, also involved C. abortus.([sedici.unlp.edu.ar](https://sedici.unlp.edu.ar/bitstream/handle/10915/107832/Documento_completo.pdf?sequence=1)) (4) Added the SAG BVO 2014 document as a key source for the Chilean component of the event and retained the Argentinian caprine outbreak and La Pampa bovine abortion articles; these are more specific than the generic background review previously used. EPP.scientific.name: Chrysomya bezziana
EPP.common.name: Old world screwworm myiasis
Host: Sheep; goats; cattle; camels; humans (sporadic wound myiasis)
Event.summary: The event began when Old World screwworm myiasis due to Chrysomya bezziana was reported as an outbreak in livestock in Khuzestan Province, southern Iran, in spring 1995, and then appeared suddenly in the Mesopotamia valley of Iraq in September 1996, likely introduced or amplified via movement of infested sheep and goats in a period of trade disruption and constrained veterinary services. Within 1996–1997 the infestation spread along the Tigris–Euphrates system and across at least 13 Iraqi governorates, generating an estimated 54,000–60,000 myiasis cases in livestock with multi‑million‑dollar losses, while contemporaneous infestations were documented in Bahrain (mid‑1990s), Kuwait, Iran, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia from the late 1990s, predominantly affecting small ruminants. From the late 1990s to early 2000s, a regional emergency program led by AOAD, FAO, IAEA and partners implemented intensive surveillance, wound treatment, and feasibility work on sterile insect technique, after which reported case numbers declined and the epidemic wave subsided, leaving C. bezziana established but under better control in Gulf livestock populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of sheep and goats with frequent tail‑docking and other husbandry practices that create wounds, coupled with limited access to veterinary care and insecticides under economic sanctions and regional instability, created abundant oviposition sites and delayed treatment; movement of infested livestock among Gulf states facilitated transboundary spread along trade routes and river valleys, while climate in the Mesopotamia valley and Gulf lowlands provided optimal warm, humid conditions for screwworm development. Internal mechanisms: No single novel strain is clearly implicated, but genetic studies reveal structured haplotypes in Middle Eastern C. bezziana populations consistent with geographic range expansion from existing endemic foci; the outbreak reflects the species’ inherent high reproductive capacity, strong flight dispersal, and biological traits favoring geographic range expansion and efficient transmission in dense small‑ruminant systems rather than a major shift in virulence or host range.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the large mid‑1990s invasion of Iraq and regional Gulf outbreaks as a single epidemiologically linked wave across Western and Southern Asia. However, based on FAO and WOAH summaries, these infestations occurred in a subregion (Gulf / Western Asia) where C. bezziana was already present before 1990, and available studies do not demonstrate a novel strain or host shift; therefore the emergence type has been adjusted from re_emergence to re_occurrence, with intra‑ and inter‑continental emergence kept as “No”. Country lists and approximate country‑specific start years (Iran 1995; Iraq 1996; Gulf states late 1990s) are broadly consistent with regional syntheses but should be cross‑checked against primary national reports (e.g. for Oman, which may also have been substantially affected) if more granular dating is required.

EPP.scientific.name: Classical swine fever virus
EPP.common.name: Hog cholera virus, CSFV
Host: Domestic pigs (commercial and backyard); wild or free‑ranging pigs in some areas
Event.summary: Although Brazil had achieved CSF‑free status in its main commercial swine‑producing regions, from August 2018 classical swine fever re‑emerged in the non‑free Northeast zone, with the first outbreak detected in Forquilha municipality (Ceará). Over 2018–2019, a total of about 68 CSF outbreaks with thousands of cases were reported across dozens of municipalities, predominantly in Ceará and Piauí, with additional outbreaks in Alagoas, largely affecting smallholder and backyard systems but posing a risk to the national industry. Intensified surveillance, zoning to protect the free area, and, more recently, targeted vaccination campaigns in the non‑free Northeast progressively reduced outbreak numbers by 2020 and initiated a long‑term eradication effort for this region.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Concentration of low‑biosecurity backyard and smallholder pig systems in the Northeast, with frequent animal movements and informal trade; feeding of swill and limited access to veterinary services; socio‑economic constraints that hampered rapid detection and response; strong trade connections between non‑free and CSF‑free zones necessitating strict zoning. Internal mechanisms: Phylodynamic analyses indicate a long‑standing CSFV subgenotype 1.5 lineage circulating and evolving in Northeast Brazil, so the 2018–2020 surge reflected amplification and spatial expansion of an endemic lineage under suboptimal control rather than appearance of a completely new strain.
Internal mechanisms coded: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) within Brazil’s Northeast; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation through adaptation to backyard and smallholder systems.
Review: retain (with mechanism and country-field correction) – the 2018–2020 CSF outbreaks in Brazil’s non-free Northeast zone (mainly Ceará, Piauí and Alagoas) involved dozens of outbreaks and thousands of pigs and were highly significant because of the risk to Brazil’s large CSF-free export regions. Countries have been standardised to 'Brazil [2018]; Brazil [2019]' and internal mechanisms recoded to reflect amplification of an endemic 1.5 lineage (re-occurrence) rather than de novo strain emergence; otherwise the event is appropriately characterised and clearly merits inclusion among major CSF emergence events.

EPP.scientific.name: Covert mortality nodavirus
EPP.common.name: CMNV
Host: Farmed Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei), other penaeid shrimp and, in some systems, farmed freshwater prawn (Macrobrachium rosenbergii).
Event.summary: From around 2014, CMNV was detected by molecular assays in shrimp-farming systems in several Asian countries outside China, including Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Viet Nam and India, often in ponds experiencing chronic mortalities or running mortality syndrome not fully explained by other agents. Subsequent surveys showed CMNV-positive shrimp and pond-associated crustaceans in multiple coastal farming regions within these countries, indicating that the virus had established local transmission cycles with ongoing low to moderate mortality and growth retardation in affected crops. By the late 2010s, VCMD/CMNV was recognized in regional disease cards, biosecurity manuals and risk assessments as an important emerging viral threat to shrimp and freshwater prawn aquaculture across South-eastern and Southern Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Transboundary movement of live shrimp and prawn broodstock and postlarvae from China and other sources, often with limited CMNV-specific screening, likely introduced the virus into hatcheries and farms in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Viet Nam and India; regional trade in live crustaceans, shared coastal water bodies and limited farm-level biosecurity facilitated subsequent spread within and between national industries; co-occurrence with other major shrimp diseases (e.g. AHPND, WSSV) complicated attribution and delayed targeted management. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) – the ability of CMNV to persist in multiple crustacean hosts and environmental matrices allowed successful establishment in new tropical farming environments across South and South‑east Asia; host expansion – detection in farmed Macrobrachium rosenbergii and diverse crustaceans broadened the susceptible host community, reinforcing persistence; enhanced transmission – chronic, often subclinical infections in broodstock and postlarval supply chains enabled silent dissemination prior to overt disease expression.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Changes made: (1) Added Indonesia to the list of affected countries based on epidemiological summaries indicating CMD/VCMD problems and CMNV-positive ponds in Thailand, Indonesia, India and Ecuador, and on later genomic work noting CMNV detections in Thailand, India, Malaysia, Viet Nam and other countries since 2014. (2) Reformatted the Countries field to include approximate country-specific start years in square brackets (all set to 2014, reflecting that regional reports describe CMNV as present in these countries “since 2014” rather than providing exact first-detection years), in line with the requested convention for multi-country linked episodes. (3) Replaced an inaccessible training-manual link with more robust sources (Virus Research genomic characterization article, RT-LAMP diagnostic paper, NACA disease card, and Australian prawn import risk assessment) that collectively document spread to these Asian countries and recognition as an emerging regional disease. Rationale for review: first-detection years for individual countries are approximate and would benefit from confirmation against national reports; the assumption that these national outbreaks form a single intra-continental emergence episode driven by shared broodstock trade should also be validated.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Cyvirus cyprinidallo3
EPP.common.name: Koi herpesvirus (KHV)
Sub.regions: Europe – Western Europe; Europe – Northern Europe; Europe – Southern Europe; Europe – Eastern Europe
Host: Primarily ornamental koi carp and farmed common carp in ponds and aquaculture facilities; occasional infections in feral or wild carp noted later in the period
Event.summary: After the initial recognition of koi herpesvirus disease in the late 1990s, from 1999 onward CyHV‑3 was detected in rapid succession in many Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern European countries, causing high mortalities in koi collections and substantial losses in carp farms. National and international surveillance summarized by an early European workshop documented first detections and repeated outbreaks in Belgium, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Denmark, France, Austria, Switzerland, Italy, Luxembourg and Poland between 1999 and 2004, often linked to imports of infected koi. Emergency measures such as movement restrictions, culling of affected stocks and improved diagnostics reduced epidemic peaks in some areas, but the virus became established and now recurs sporadically in carp populations across Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intra‑European trade in ornamental koi and carp (including koi shows and private pond stocking), expanding and intensifying carp aquaculture, and initially limited diagnostics and non‑notifiable status that allowed the virus to spread undetected. Internal mechanisms: efficient CyHV‑3 transmission in dense culture systems and latent infection in asymptomatic carrier carp, enabling spread through apparently healthy fish into new countries and subregions; no distinct novel strain is implicated beyond the original emergent CyHV‑3 lineages circulating in Europe.
Review: review – Retain as a major intra‑European emergence episode but correct geography and country details: removed Germany (initial 1997 outbreaks are captured in the global first‑emergence event) and Czechia (no confirmed KHV outbreaks reported in this period), added Eastern Europe to subregions to reflect Poland, standardized country names (United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Luxembourg) and checked first‑outbreak years against the Haenen et al. 2004/Pokorová 2005 country table.

EPP.scientific.name: Decapod iridescent virus 1
EPP.common.name: Shrimp hemocyte iridescent virus
Host: Wild and captured black tiger shrimp (Penaeus monodon) from the northeastern Indian Ocean used as broodstock in Thailand; regional shrimp stocks and farms in Viet Nam where DIV1 was reported or strongly suspected in association with farmed shrimp
Event.summary: By 2018–2019, DIV1 DNA was detected by PCR in wild black tiger shrimp captured in the northeastern Indian Ocean and landed in Thailand for use as broodstock, representing the first confirmed presence of the virus in wild penaeid shrimp outside Chinese coastal waters. In 2020, regional authorities and international risk assessments reported that disease caused by DIV1 had been identified in farmed shrimp in Viet Nam, although detailed outbreak descriptions remained limited and national information campaigns emphasized prevention and border controls. These findings marked the first recognized spread of DIV1 into South-eastern Asian production and broodstock supply chains, prompting heightened controls on illegal cross‑border shrimp movements, targeted laboratory testing of wild-caught broodstock and imports, and inclusion of DIV1 among priority emerging diseases in regional surveillance plans.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: regional trade in live shrimp broodstock and postlarvae; capture of wild P. monodon for broodstock in ocean areas linked to Chinese waters; possible natural dispersal of infected wild shrimp along Indian Ocean and Andaman Sea currents; and initially limited screening for DIV1 in wild and farmed stocks in South-eastern Asia. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) of an established East Asian DIV1 lineage into wild P. monodon populations and, based on official risk assessments, into some farmed shrimp in Viet Nam, without evidence of a distinct new strain; infections in wild shrimp were often subclinical but created a reservoir that increased the risk of farm‑level outbreaks in the region.
Review: review – The original row correctly identified detection of DIV1 DNA in wild P. monodon from the northeastern Indian Ocean and the importance of this for regional spread but mis-specified timing (as 2020–2021) and treated the whole episode as a “first_detection” event. The year has been adjusted to 2018–2020, with Thailand [2018] for wild-caught broodstock and Viet Nam [2020] reflecting the timing used in the USDA APHIS risk assessment. The first_detection flag has been set to false and Intra-continental Emergence retained, because global first emergence occurred in China. Evidence for confirmed farm-level disease in Viet Nam remains limited and partly based on official assessments rather than detailed outbreak reports; therefore, the event is retained but flagged for review as new Vietnamese surveillance data become available.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus multilocularis
EPP.common.name: Alveolar echinococcosis
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Red foxes (Vulpes vulpes); voles and other small rodents; humans (sporadic and emerging cases in newly affected countries)
Event.summary: During the 1990s and early 2000s, Echinococcus multilocularis expanded its known range in European fox populations from four core endemic countries (Austria, France, Germany, Switzerland) to at least eight additional central, western, northern and southern European countries, with first records in foxes in Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, Italy and several central‑eastern states. As surveillance of red foxes and small mammals intensified, more newly infected areas were documented and occasional human cases began to be recognized in some of these countries. By the early 2000s, ecological and surveillance data confirmed that the parasite’s geographic range in Europe was far wider than previously thought, establishing new endemic foci across western and central Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large increases in red fox populations across Europe driven by oral rabies vaccination, hunting changes and urbanization, combined with high rodent densities in agricultural and peri‑urban landscapes, allowed the parasite to spread along expanding fox ranges and colonize new territories. Intensified wildlife surveillance and improved diagnostic tools (necropsy, copro‑PCR) increased detection probability and helped map the expanding range. Internal mechanisms: This episode reflects geographic range expansion of existing sylvatic cycles rather than a clearly distinct strain, although local adaptation of the parasite to new ecological settings likely supported establishment.
Review: Decision: review – Event is real and high‑impact, but several geographic details needed correction. (1) Sub‑regions expanded to include Northern and Southern Europe because Denmark and Italy are affected as documented in Oksanen et al. 2016 and subsequent Italian fox studies.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Event window extended to 1990–2002 so that Italy’s first fox detections in the early 2000s fall within the episode, consistent with Manfredi et al. and later confirmations from Alto Adige.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7789758/?utm_source=openai)) (3) Country list edited to remove non‑standard tags like “[historic]” and to reduce spurious precision (e.g. “Belgium [1991]”→“Belgium [1990s]”; “Netherlands [1996]”→“Netherlands [1998]” to match first published Dutch fox detections).([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304401798002635?utm_source=openai)) Event type kept as intra‑continental emergence only, which matches spread to multiple new European sub‑regions; no re‑occurrence flag is used because these are genuinely new endemic areas rather than resurgence in previously endemic ones. Because of these adjustments and remaining approximate dating for some central‑eastern countries, this row should be checked against national fox surveillance summaries before final use.
