Host: Red foxes (Vulpes vulpes); voles and other small rodents; humans (sporadic and emerging cases in newly affected countries)
Event.summary: During the 1990s and early 2000s, Echinococcus multilocularis expanded its known range in European fox populations from four core endemic countries (Austria, France, Germany, Switzerland) to at least eight additional central, western, northern and southern European countries, with first records in foxes in Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, Italy and several central‑eastern states. As surveillance of red foxes and small mammals intensified, more newly infected areas were documented and occasional human cases began to be recognized in some of these countries. By the early 2000s, ecological and surveillance data confirmed that the parasite’s geographic range in Europe was far wider than previously thought, establishing new endemic foci across western and central Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large increases in red fox populations across Europe driven by oral rabies vaccination, hunting changes and urbanization, combined with high rodent densities in agricultural and peri‑urban landscapes, allowed the parasite to spread along expanding fox ranges and colonize new territories. Intensified wildlife surveillance and improved diagnostic tools (necropsy, copro‑PCR) increased detection probability and helped map the expanding range. Internal mechanisms: This episode reflects geographic range expansion of existing sylvatic cycles rather than a clearly distinct strain, although local adaptation of the parasite to new ecological settings likely supported establishment.
Review: Decision: review – Event is real and high‑impact, but several geographic details needed correction. (1) Sub‑regions expanded to include Northern and Southern Europe because Denmark and Italy are affected as documented in Oksanen et al. 2016 and subsequent Italian fox studies.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Event window extended to 1990–2002 so that Italy’s first fox detections in the early 2000s fall within the episode, consistent with Manfredi et al. and later confirmations from Alto Adige.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7789758/?utm_source=openai)) (3) Country list edited to remove non‑standard tags like “[historic]” and to reduce spurious precision (e.g. “Belgium [1991]”→“Belgium [1990s]”; “Netherlands [1996]”→“Netherlands [1998]” to match first published Dutch fox detections).([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304401798002635?utm_source=openai)) Event type kept as intra‑continental emergence only, which matches spread to multiple new European sub‑regions; no re‑occurrence flag is used because these are genuinely new endemic areas rather than resurgence in previously endemic ones. Because of these adjustments and remaining approximate dating for some central‑eastern countries, this row should be checked against national fox surveillance summaries before final use.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus multilocularis
EPP.common.name: Alveolar echinococcosis
Host: Humans; red foxes; domestic dogs
Event.summary: In core endemic Alpine regions of Switzerland, Germany, France and Austria, human alveolar echinococcosis incidence rose in the late 1990s and early 2000s, with Switzerland documenting a statistically significant increase in annual incidence from about 0.10 to 0.26 per 100,000 population between 1993–2000 and 2001–2005. Parallel data showed increasing prevalence of Echinococcus multilocularis in foxes, including the establishment of dense, infected urban fox populations in German and Swiss cities. By the mid‑2000s, these countries reported growing numbers of human AE cases linked to peri‑urban or rural residence, leading to heightened concern and sustained clinical and veterinary surveillance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rabies control and hunting changes allowed fox populations to grow and colonize peri‑urban and urban areas, increasing proximity between infected foxes, domestic dogs and humans. Urban green spaces and peri‑urban farmland supported high rodent and fox densities, while lifestyle patterns involving outdoor recreation and gardening increased exposure to contaminated environments. Improvements in imaging and serology increased case detection but do not fully explain the observed incidence rises. Internal mechanisms: The main mechanism appears to be enhanced transmission via expanding and urbanizing fox and dog populations rather than clearly documented increases in parasite virulence or new genotypes.
Review: Decision: retain – This event correctly describes the well‑documented increase in human AE incidence in the historic Alpine core (Switzerland, southern Germany, eastern France, western Austria) around 2001–2005, driven by fox population growth and urbanization.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/13/6/06-1074_article?utm_source=openai)) The geographic scope, timing and mechanism are well supported by Swiss registry analyses and European reviews, and the event‑type classification as re‑occurrence (resurgence in a long‑established endemic area driven by external ecological change) is appropriate and mutually exclusive of intra‑/inter‑continental categories. No structural changes were necessary beyond minor source consolidation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hydatidosis, Hydatid disease
Host: Red foxes and raccoon dogs (definitive hosts); small mammals (intermediate hosts); domestic dogs (occasional definitive host); humans (accidental intermediate host, clinical AE)
Event.summary: From the late 1990s onward, Baltic and eastern‑central European countries recorded large new foci of Echinococcus multilocularis infection in foxes and raccoon dogs, accompanied by rising numbers of human AE cases, representing a major northward and eastward expansion from the classic endemic core in France, Germany, Switzerland and Austria. Lithuania diagnosed 96 human AE cases between 1997 and 2008 alongside very high fox infection intensities, while Poland documented over 120 human AE cases from 1990–2011 with a marked rise during 2000–2009 and clustering in the north‑east bordering Lithuania; similar first or early autochthonous human AE cases were reported in Latvia, Estonia, Belarus, Hungary and Romania during the 2000s. By around 2010, AE was recognized as emerging across large parts of the Baltic and eastern‑central Europe, with sustained fox infection and continuing human case detection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and urbanization of red fox populations following rabies vaccination campaigns, landscape changes increasing rodent intermediate hosts, expanding raccoon dog populations, and improved imaging/serology together created new and denser E. multilocularis transmission cycles and increased detection of human AE.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5039905/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion of E. multilocularis within Europe, with high worm burdens in foxes indicating enhanced transmission; at continental scale, spread is best explained by wildlife ecology and control of rabies rather than emergence of a single novel strain.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This episode represents a major intra‑European expansion of AE into the Baltic and eastern‑central European countries and is clearly among the largest post‑1990 emergence events. I corrected the emergence‑type classification: first_detection was set to “Yes” in the draft but should be “No” at the global host‑system scale, and there is no strong evidence that parasite evolution (as opposed to wildlife ecology and rabies control) is the primary driver, so re_emergence was changed to “No.” Intra‑continental emergence remains “Yes” because transmission was newly documented in UNSD subregions (Northern Europe – Baltics; Eastern Europe) beyond the pre‑1990 Alpine core. I also recommend removing the general Echinococcosis Wikipedia link in favour of more specific peer‑reviewed sources and have added a key EU‑wide systematic review of E. multilocularis distribution in wildlife as a more relevant source.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hydatidosis, Hydatid disease
Countries: China – nine western endemic provinces/autonomous regions (Xinjiang, Sichuan, Qinghai, Gansu, Ningxia, Tibet, Inner Mongolia, Yunnan, Shaanxi) [2004]
Host: Dogs and other canids (definitive hosts); livestock (sheep, goats, cattle, yaks) and small mammals (intermediate hosts); humans (accidental intermediate host, notifiable cases)
Event.summary: Following the introduction of nationwide notifiable disease reporting and echinococcosis surveillance in China in 2004, a sustained high burden of both CE and AE was documented through 2020, with more than 66,000 reported cases concentrated in nine western endemic provinces/autonomous regions and additional sporadic cases reported from non‑endemic provinces. Annual case numbers remained substantial throughout this period, with the Tibetan Plateau and adjacent highland areas consistently showing the highest notification rates and prevalence, while routine reporting newly delineated risk in many counties and identified occasional locally acquired infections in previously non‑endemic provincial‑level units. Despite stepped‑up control efforts (dog deworming, health education, improved slaughter hygiene), transmission persisted in core pastoral areas into the late 2010s.([jsczz.cn](https://www.jsczz.cn/EN/10.12140/j.issn.1000-7423.2022.04.009?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Systematic surveillance primarily revealed the scale and geography of a long‑standing problem, but also highlighted continuing drivers including extensive dog ownership, low deworming coverage, pastoral production systems, wildlife reservoirs, environmental contamination, and migration of people and livestock from endemic to non‑endemic provinces.([jsczz.cn](https://www.jsczz.cn/EN/10.12140/j.issn.1000-7423.2022.04.009?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Largely persistence and gradual geographic range expansion of existing parasite populations within suitable ecological zones; no convincing evidence that emergence of new genotypes at the country scale is the primary driver of the post‑2004 burden.
Review: Decision: REVIEW. This nationwide Chinese episode is high‑impact and should be retained, but it is best interpreted as re‑occurrence of a known endemic problem under modern surveillance rather than intra‑continental emergence. I therefore set intra_continental_emergence to “No” and kept re_occurrence as “Yes.” The event appropriately captures recognition of the true scale of burden (66,000+ reported cases 2004–2020 and many more likely unreported) in the nine endemic western provinces plus sporadic cases elsewhere, consistent with national surveillance analyses. The geography (China, Eastern Asia) and years are appropriate, and the source set (endemic status paper plus national burden analyses) is suitable for this event type.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Echinococcus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hydatidosis, Hydatid disease
Host: Wild canids (coyotes, foxes) as definitive hosts; domestic dogs (definitive host with severe clinical AE); small mammals (intermediate hosts); zoo primates and other captive mammals (aberrant intermediate hosts); humans (locally acquired AE cases)
Event.summary: From 2009 onward, Echinococcus multilocularis exhibiting European‑type genotypes was detected in dogs and wild canids in western and central Canada, including British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and later Ontario, extending well beyond the historically recognized Arctic and north‑central endemic zones. Molecular studies of a 2009 dog case in British Columbia showed the parasite to be closely related to European strains rather than traditional North American lineages, and subsequent surveys found increasing E. multilocularis prevalence in urban coyotes around Calgary and other cities, along with a growing number of severe canine AE cases and at least several locally acquired human AE cases in Alberta and sporadic locally acquired infections in the United States.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3358155/?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2010s, Canadian experts characterized E. multilocularis, particularly introduced European‑type strains, as an emerging and costly zoonotic problem in North America with expanding geographic range and host spectrum.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International and interprovincial dog movements (including imported dogs from Europe and endemic regions without mandatory Echinococcus testing or treatment), urban expansion into wildlife habitats, increasing and urbanizing coyote and fox populations, and low awareness and deworming coverage in dogs facilitated introduction and establishment of European‑type E. multilocularis in new regions.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1471492212000517?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Introduction and establishment of more pathogenic or highly zoonotic European‑type haplotypes into North America, followed by geographic range expansion and enhanced transmission in urban and peri‑urban canid–rodent cycles; this represents strain‑level re‑emergence of AE risk in regions where the species was previously absent or rare, rather than first continental introduction of E. multilocularis itself.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (borderline for inclusion). This event describes the strain‑level invasion of European‑type E. multilocularis into western and central Canada (and, to a lesser extent so far, parts of the USA). I corrected the emergence‑type classification: North America has long been endemic for E. multilocularis, so this is not an inter‑continental or intra‑continental emergence at the species level, nor a first_detection event globally. Instead, it is best treated as re‑emergence driven by introduction of more zoonotic European haplotypes and their establishment in new urban and peri‑urban canid–rodent cycles; accordingly, only re_emergence is set to “Yes.” I also refined the country list to focus on provinces and states where European‑type strains and locally acquired AE have been documented. Although the absolute number of human cases remains small compared with China, Central Asia or South America, the combination of novel genotype introduction, wide geographic spread in wildlife and dogs, and high per‑case costs gives this event strategic importance; whether it should remain among the top 10 highest‑impact events depends on how strictly impact is defined (current DALYs vs future risk), so it is flagged for further expert review rather than automatic exclusion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterocytozoon hepatopenaei
EPP.common.name: EHP
Host: Primarily Penaeus (Litopenaeus) vannamei (whiteleg shrimp), also Penaeus monodon in parts of the region
Event.summary: From 2010 onward, shrimp farms in Viet Nam and later in other South‑eastern Asian countries began reporting slow growth, size variation and white feces in P. monodon and especially P. vannamei, with histology, PCR and in situ hybridization confirming EHP as a key pathogen associated with these syndromes.([ouci.dntb.gov.ua](https://ouci.dntb.gov.ua/en/works/4aBVkKz5/?utm_source=openai)) By the mid‑2010s EHP was widely detected in shrimp farms across Viet Nam, Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia—Indonesia and Malaysia reporting confirmed farm outbreaks by 2016—contributing to chronic production losses and complex disease situations involving co‑infections such as AHPND.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27530403/?utm_source=openai)) Control efforts across the subregion emphasized improved pond preparation, biosecurity, screening of broodstock and postlarvae, and better management of co‑infections, but EHP remained highly prevalent and entrenched in shrimp‑farming areas of South‑eastern Asia.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive regional trade and movement of live shrimp (broodstock and postlarvae) between farms and countries, high farm densities along shared coastlines, shared water sources and equipment, and inadequate pond disinfection between cycles facilitated transboundary spread and persistence of EHP throughout South‑eastern Asia. Internal mechanisms: high environmental resilience of spores, efficient horizontal transmission via ingestion of contaminated feces and detritus, and probable vertical transmission from broodstock to larvae demonstrated experimentally, together with widespread adoption of P. vannamei, allowed the parasite to maintain high prevalence in the region.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5216530/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – Extended this linked South‑eastern Asia episode to 2010–2016 and updated country onsets to Viet Nam [2010] and Indonesia and Malaysia [2016], reflecting the timing of first peer‑reviewed reports and regional summaries. Retained the 're_occurrence' label because this represents intensification and geographic widening of EHP within an already affected sub‑region, not spread to a new UNSD sub‑region, and kept 'intra_continental_emergence' and 're_emergence' as 'No'. Event is broadly well supported but should be re‑checked for whether additional SE Asian countries (e.g. Philippines, Brunei) warrant explicit inclusion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus suid 1
EPP.common.name: Swine vesicular disease virus, SVDV
Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event.summary: After a period of low SVD activity in Europe, a new antigenic–genetic SVDV variant (the fourth European lineage) became established in Italy and was first recognized in both Italy and the Netherlands in 1992. Over the next few years, movement of infected pigs and contaminated vehicles seeded linked outbreaks in other Western and Southern European countries, including Belgium and Spain in 1993 and Portugal in 1995, prompting EU‑wide control measures and trade restrictions. Through aggressive stamping‑out, movement controls and intensified serological surveillance, these Western European outbreaks were eliminated by the mid‑1990s, leaving Italy as the main remaining reservoir of the new lineage.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of intra‑European trade in live pigs and pig products, movements of infected animals from Italy and possibly from Far‑Eastern source regions, and contaminated trucks and equipment facilitated spread into high‑density pig areas in the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain and Portugal; detection was hampered by the clinical similarity of SVD to other vesicular diseases. Internal mechanisms: molecular and antigenic studies show that this wave was driven by a distinct fourth antigenic–genetic variant of SVDV derived from earlier strains, consistent with viral evolution and selection facilitating renewed spread in European pig populations (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Enhanced transmission in intensive pig systems; Geographic range expansion within Europe).
Review: review – Corrected the event window to 1992–1995 (reflecting that the fourth antigenic SVDV variant was first reported in Italy and the Netherlands in 1992), and added Portugal [1995] as an affected country in this wave based on EU, WOAH/OIE and review data. Also removed a duplicate ScienceDirect URL and added more specific outbreak documentation (EU decision on Dutch outbreaks; OIE reports for Spain and Belgium). Classification as a re-emergence driven by a novel European lineage remains appropriate and is retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus suid 1
EPP.common.name: Swine vesicular disease virus, SVDV
Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event.summary: Following the 2006–2007 epidemic in northern Italy, SVDV continued to circulate at low levels in a few regions of Italy, causing sporadic outbreaks detected through the strengthened national surveillance and eradication programme. Between 2008 and 2015, these residual foci were repeatedly re‑ignited by illegal or poorly controlled pig movements, insufficient farm biosecurity and environmental persistence of the virus, prompting EU measures specifically targeting SVD in Italy and progressive enlargement of control zones. Implementation of enhanced surveillance, trace‑back and strict movement controls ultimately led to the last recorded clinical outbreak in Calabria in 2015, after which only seropositive pigs were detected (until 2017), and SVDV was subsequently declared eradicated from Italy and, by extension, from domestic pigs globally.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: continued movement of pigs from non‑compliant or illegal holdings, vehicles contaminated with manure or pork products, and the virus’s marked environmental stability allowed sporadic re‑introductions into Italian farms despite control programmes; policy tools such as EU Decision 2005/779/EC and intensified national measures were required to progressively close these gaps. Internal mechanisms: no fundamentally new genotypes were identified in this late phase; rather, persistence of existing Italian lineages and their ability to survive in the environment and in pork products underpinned recurrent flare‑ups (Re-occurrence driven by external factors and environmental persistence; geographic spread remained confined to already affected Italian subregions).

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: EHDV
Host: Cattle (mainly), with likely infection of wild ruminants
Event.summary: In 2020, EHDV re‑emerged in the eastern Mediterranean with outbreaks in cattle in Türkiye and several North African countries attributed primarily to EHDV‑6, after a period of apparent low‑level circulation following the mid‑2000s Maghreb epizootics.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10224379/?utm_source=openai)) Disease episodes presented with bluetongue‑like signs in cattle and were confirmed by molecular testing, indicating renewed regional spread of EHDV‑6 in the Mediterranean basin.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10224379/?utm_source=openai)) Transmission declined after the 2020 vector season, but this resurgence set the stage for subsequent introduction and spread of EHDV‑8 in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: ongoing climate warming in the Mediterranean ‘hotspot’ increasing vector seasons and high‑altitude suitability for Culicoides; animal movements between North African and Near‑Eastern countries; limited targeted surveillance for EHDV allowing silent spread. Internal mechanisms: re‑emergence of EHDV‑6 lineages with demonstrated cattle pathogenicity; geographic range re‑expansion within Western Asia and Northern Africa from previously established foci.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10224379/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: EHDV
Sub.regions: Northern Africa; Southern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Cattle (primary); wild red and fallow deer; sheep (subclinical and occasional clinical infections)
Event.summary: Building on the 2021 Tunisian outbreak, EHDV‑8 spread westward across North Africa in 2022 and then crossed the Mediterranean to Europe, with first European detections in cattle in Sicily and Sardinia (Italy) in October 2022 and in Andalusia (Spain) in November 2022.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37081599/?utm_source=openai)) The virus subsequently expanded during the 2022–2023 seasons to affect large areas of southern Spain, Portugal and southern France, as well as additional parts of Italy, causing thousands of cattle outbreaks and confirmed infections in wild cervids and, later, some sheep.([veterinariaitaliana.izs.it](https://veterinariaitaliana.izs.it/index.php/VetIt/article/view/3793?utm_source=openai)) By late 2023 the initial wave of transmission had slowed with winter vector decline, but EHDV‑8 had become established in both North Africa and southern Europe, fundamentally changing the regional orbivirus landscape.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12341390/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: climate warming and extended warm seasons in the Mediterranean ‘hotspot’ enhancing Culicoides survival and competence; strong north–south livestock trade and probable wind‑borne carriage of infected midges from North Africa to southern Europe; high densities of susceptible cattle and wild cervids in affected regions. Internal mechanisms: novel strain/genotype emergence and geographic range expansion—EHDV‑8 lineage originating in Tunisia with near‑identical genomes in North African and European isolates; efficient transmission via European Culicoides species; host expansion with significant clinical disease documented in cattle and wild red deer, and confirmed infections in sheep.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12341390/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review. Changes made: (i) Set first_detection from true to false, because EHDV was already known globally in ruminants; this event represents the first detection in Europe, which is captured via the inter‑continental emergence flag. (ii) Set intra_continental_emergence from true to false to avoid co‑classification, in line with guidance that emergence types are generally mutually exclusive and that this episode’s defining feature is first occurrence of EHDV in a new continent (Europe). (iii) Set re_emergence from true to false, as Southern and Western Europe were previously free of EHDV; the event is better characterized as de novo inter‑continental emergence of an existing lineage rather than re‑emergence in a previously affected subregion.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37081599/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.common.name: EHDV
Host: Cattle; wild red and fallow deer; sheep (documented infections)
Event.summary: In 2023, following initial detections in late 2022, EHDV‑8 caused explosive expansion within the Iberian Peninsula and parts of France and Italy, with Spain alone reporting over 3,000 EHD outbreaks within two months of intense transmission.([assets.publishing.service.gov.uk](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/66cdc8160671fa213911b341/14_August_2024_Epizootic_Haemorrhagic_Disease_in_Europe.pdf?utm_source=openai)) The virus spread northward and westward within Spain and into Portugal and southwestern France, and further cases were recorded in domestic cattle and wild deer populations in Sardinia and mainland Italy, with occasional infections documented in sheep.([veterinariaitaliana.izs.it](https://veterinariaitaliana.izs.it/index.php/VetIt/article/view/3793?utm_source=openai)) As temperatures dropped and control measures were implemented, the number of new outbreaks decreased into 2024, though surveillance indicated overwintering of the virus in parts of southern Europe and the need for continued vector and movement controls.([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/epizootic-haemorrhagic-disease-in-europe/28-november-2023-epizootic-haemorrhagic-disease-in-europe?utm_source=openai))

Internal mechanisms: ongoing geographic range expansion and establishment of EHDV‑8 as an endemic orbivirus in southern Europe; likely adaptation to local Culicoides species enhancing transmission efficiency; broader host involvement including wild cervids and sheep, indicating altered host range compared with earlier EHDV lineages.([veterinariaitaliana.izs.it](https://veterinariaitaliana.izs.it/index.php/VetIt/article/view/3793?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus
EPP.common.name: Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD)
Host: Cattle (dairy and beef herds)
Event.summary: In 2006, severe bluetongue‑like disease with fever, facial edema, oral lesions and production losses was reported in cattle herds across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, where EHDV infection had not previously been recognized as a cause of clinical disease in domestic ruminants. Molecular characterization showed that these outbreaks were caused by epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus serotype 6 (EHDV‑6), closely related to the 318 strain, and that the North African viruses formed a distinct cluster associated with pathogenicity in cattle. Following the 2006 vector season the acute epizootics waned, but EHDV‑6 established in the Maghreb, with subsequent serologic and virologic detections indicating continued circulation in regional ruminant populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Wind‑borne movement of infected Culicoides midges from endemic areas, coupled with local animal movements and climatic conditions in 2006 favorable to vector proliferation and survival across the Maghreb. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and geographic range expansion of a pathogenic EHDV‑6 lineage into North African cattle populations, with strain‑specific traits associated with clinical disease in bovines and subsequent regional persistence.
Review: Retain – event is well documented as the first major EHDV‑6 incursion into the Maghreb with substantial cattle morbidity and economic losses; continent, sub‑region, countries and 2006 timing align with OIE and peer‑reviewed sources. No changes to classification were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Verotoxigenic E. coli, STEC
Host: Humans (residents and refugees) exposed via beef and contaminated surface water; cattle as asymptomatic reservoir shedding O157 into dung and water
Event.summary: In late 1992, during a severe drought in Eswatini and neighbouring areas of South Africa, a massive outbreak of diarrhoeal disease occurred, initially characterised by bloody diarrhoea consistent with E. coli O157 infection and later complicated by cholera. Investigations identified E. coli O157 from human stools, surface and drinking water, sewage, cooked maize, and from cattle dung on affected sugar plantations and nearby communities, implicating stressed cattle herds and contaminated water as key sources. The episode, which likely involved tens of thousands of human infections, represented the first well-documented large outbreak of O157 in Africa and highlighted cattle as a central reservoir in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Prolonged drought forced cattle to graze around dwindling surface waters, increasing faecal contamination of rivers and waterholes that were then used for drinking and cooking; bans on cattle imports and economic pressures led to slaughter and consumption of distressed or dead animals, while abattoir hygiene was poor. These environmental and management conditions greatly amplified O157 contamination of beef and water supplies. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak strain (O157:NM with stx1 and stx2) showed no unique virulence features compared with other O157:H7 lineages; the event reflects geographic spread and intense exposure in a new continent rather than novel strain evolution.
Review: retain – Added as a key inter_continental_emergence event. The 1992 Eswatini/South Africa epidemic is widely regarded as the first major, well-characterised O157 outbreak in Africa and provides direct evidence of E. coli O157 in cattle dung and surface waters in the region. I classified it as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence (for Africa) and did not use intra-continental or re-emergence flags, because the main importance is appearance of STEC O157 in a new continent’s human and cattle populations on a large scale. Source is the detailed Emerging Infectious Diseases investigation.

EPP.scientific.name: Escherichia coli
EPP.common.name: Verotoxigenic E. coli, STEC
Host: Cattle (beef and dairy; healthy carriers), beef and dairy products; pediatric human cases linked to bovine and food isolates
Event.summary: In 1994, a survey of healthy cattle in Galicia, Spain, showed verotoxin-producing E. coli on most farms and confirmed that a diversity of VTEC serogroups, including O157:H7 and O26:H11, circulated widely in regional herds. A few years later, a one‑year prospective study in central France (1997–1998) concurrently examined cattle feces, beef, cheese and hospitalized children, finding high prevalence of stx-positive cattle and food samples and directly linking bovine and food isolates to pediatric STEC infections. Together, these studies marked the first comprehensive documentation that cattle and beef/dairy products in southern and western Europe formed an important reservoir–exposure pathway for STEC, reshaping regional risk assessments.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growth and regional concentration of beef and dairy industries in Iberia and France, combined with intensified microbiological surveillance of slaughter cattle, carcasses and foods, revealed widespread contamination that had previously gone undetected. Internal mechanisms: Persistence and diversification of STEC serotypes in European cattle populations, including both O157 and multiple non‑O157 groups, with demonstrated spillover to children via contaminated beef and dairy products; no single novel strain dominates, so the significance lies in geographic range expansion and recognition of the reservoir.
Review: review – Corrected the timing and geography: Spain is now coded as Spain [1994] based on Blanco et al. (Epidemiol Infect, cattle sampled February–July 1994), and France as France [1997] reflecting the 1997–1998 prospective study in Clermont-Ferrand (J Clin Microbiol 38:1023–1031). Event year was updated to 1994–1998 accordingly. I retained first_detection and intra_continental_emergence, interpreting this as first comprehensive documentation of bovine and food STEC reservoirs in Spain and central France within an already affected European continent. The previous citation to the Japanese cattle study was replaced with the Spain cattle paper to better match the described event.

EPP.scientific.name: Fascioloides magna
EPP.common.name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Wild cervids (primarily red deer Cervus elaphus and fallow deer Dama dama); occasional roe deer and mouflon
Event.summary: From the late 1980s onward, fascioloidosis outbreaks were recognised in cervids of the Danube floodplain forests, first in red deer in south‑western Slovakia and shortly afterwards in north‑western Hungary, signalling the formation of a new central European natural focus. During the 1990s and early 2000s the parasite spread along the Danube into floodplain and adjacent forests of eastern Austria, Croatia’s Baranja region and, by around 2007, northern Serbia near the Danube–Sava confluence, with very high prevalences and heavy liver pathology in local red and fallow deer. By the mid‑2000s the Danube floodplain forests had become a persistent multinational natural focus of F. magna, raising concern about long‑term effects on cervid populations and the risk of spillover to livestock.

EPP.scientific.name: Foot-and-mouth disease virus

Host: Cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, and other cloven‑hoofed livestock
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through 2001, a single genetic lineage of FMDV serotype O (topotype ME‑SA, PanAsia strain) that emerged in northern India expanded its range, first spreading across South Asia and the Middle East and then into East Asia, the Russian Federation, and parts of Africa. Control relied on rapid slaughter policies, emergency vaccination in some settings, strict movement controls, and coordinated international surveillance, after which the pandemic wave subsided although related ME‑SA lineages remain endemic in parts of Asia and the Middle East.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and globalization of livestock production and trade; long‑distance movement of live animals and animal products across Asia, the Middle East, and into Europe; porous borders and informal trade networks; limitations in regional vaccination coverage and strain matching at the time of spread. Event.summary: Beginning in 2013, FMDV serotype O, topotype ME-SA, lineage Ind‑2001d was detected in Libya after emerging from the Indian subcontinent and Middle East; over the following two years closely related viruses spread westward across the Maghreb. Over the 2000s and early to mid‑2010s, GI‑23 variants spread widely through Middle Eastern poultry industries, becoming a major cause of infectious bronchitis in Israel, Iran, Jordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and neighbouring Western Asian countries and accounting for a substantial fraction of clinical IB cases in regional surveillance. By around 2016, GI‑23 was firmly entrenched across much of the Middle East, co‑circulating with Mass‑like, 4/91‑like and other genotypes and continuing to cause recurrent outbreaks and vaccine failures.

EPP.common.name: IBV, Infectious bronchitis virus
Host: Commercial broiler and layer chickens
Event.summary: From about 2009, infectious bronchitis viruses of the GI‑16 lineage (Q1/624I‑like), originally detected in China in the mid‑1990s and already circulating in parts of Asia and Europe, were introduced into major South American poultry‑producing countries such as Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, where they were associated with respiratory and nephropathogenic disease and production drops in commercial flocks. Over the 2010s, GI‑16/Q1 spread widely through additional countries including Chile, Colombia and Peru, becoming one of the predominant field genotypes in several regions and contributing to numerous clinical IB outbreaks and the emergence of recombinant viruses with indigenous South American lineages such as GI‑11. By around 2020, GI‑16 was firmly established across much of South America, co‑circulating with Mass‑type and other variants and prompting adjustments to vaccination strategies and ongoing molecular surveillance to manage its impact.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected breeding stock, hatching eggs or contaminated equipment from Eurasian sources into a largely naïve South American GI‑16 niche, combined with rapid growth and concentration of the regional broiler and layer industries, facilitated continent‑wide dissemination; reliance on vaccines tailored to other genotypes (Mass‑, 4/91‑ or local variant‑based) led to gaps in protection. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Geographic Range Expansion – the GI‑16 (Q1/624I‑like) lineage, already established in Asia, expanded into South America and became one of its dominant genotypes; Recombination between GI‑16 and endemic South American lineages (e.g. GI‑11) generated additional genetic diversity; Antigenic differences from commonly used vaccines contributed to vaccine‑escape–type re‑emergence.
Review: Added event. Phylodynamic analyses identify GI‑16 (Q1/624I‑like) as one of the globally important IBV lineages and show a marked increase in its population size and geographic spread following its introduction into South America around 2005–2010, with reports from Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Colombia and Peru. This South American wave was missing from the original dataset despite its large regional impact, so it has been added and coded as re‑emergence of IBV due to a newly introduced lineage rather than as inter‑continental emergence of the species. Country start years are approximate, derived from first reports and molecular dating, and should be checked in future expert review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI)
Host: Backyard and commercial chickens, ducks, geese and other domestic poultry
Event.summary: From late 2003, a highly pathogenic H5N1 goose/Guangdong lineage expanded from East Asia into multiple South-East Asian countries, first causing large poultry outbreaks in the Republic of Korea and Viet Nam. By early 2004, the virus had spread across much of East and South-East Asia, including Japan, Thailand, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Indonesia, China and Malaysia, resulting in severe poultry losses and the culling or death of tens of millions of birds. Aggressive stamping out, movement controls and, in some settings, vaccination gradually contained the first wave by mid‑2004, though the virus became entrenched in some domestic duck and backyard poultry systems and re-emerged in later years.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2004_01_24-en?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid growth of intensive poultry production and regional trade; widespread backyard flocks with poor biosecurity; live bird markets facilitating mixing of species and onward spread; movement of fighting cocks and other high-value birds. Internal mechanisms: emergence and expansion of a highly virulent H5N1 genotype with broad host range; enhanced transmission in ducks enabling silent spread; geographic range expansion driven by virus traits allowing persistence in diverse agro-ecological settings.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1748232/?utm_source=openai))

Event.summary: Beginning in 2005, clade 2.2 H5N1 viruses associated with a major die‑off at Qinghai Lake in China spread westward via migratory birds and poultry trade into central Asia, Russia and Eastern Europe. Coordinated culling, movement controls and surveillance reduced epidemic activity after 2007, but H5N1 remained endemic in several poultry systems and continued to cause sporadic outbreaks.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4059878/?utm_source=openai))

Event.summary: During 2007–2008, China experienced a serious epizootic of equine influenza H3N8, with outbreaks reported in multiple provinces and affecting both horses and donkeys, including high-morbidity respiratory disease in working donkeys in Xinjiang. The virus spread widely across equine populations over several months, and genomic analyses showed that it represented a major new wave of equine influenza activity in China, with Florida clade 2 viruses related to contemporary strains circulating in Central Asia and Europe. Control efforts, including movement restrictions, improved surveillance and vaccination, reduced disease incidence by 2008, although Florida clade 2 EIV has since remained endemic in Chinese equine populations.

EPP.common.name: Equine influenza virus, EIV
Host: Horses (racing, sport, and working horses)
Event.summary: In 2018, South America experienced a major resurgence of equine influenza H3N8, with large outbreaks reported in Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Colombia, Ecuador and parts of Brazil, often in horses that had been vaccinated following the 2012 event. The virus spread between countries via frequent cross‑border movement of racehorses and sport horses, leading to high clinical attack rates and, in some areas, higher severity of disease than observed in 2012, with substantial disruption of equestrian activities and economic losses. The outbreak diminished towards the end of 2018 as emergency vaccination, strengthened biosecurity and natural immunity reduced the susceptible population, but Florida clade 1 viruses remained endemic in the region.

Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses indicate that the 2018 outbreak strains were closely related to contemporary Florida clade 1 viruses circulating globally, showing antigenic differences from existing vaccine strains and contributing to vaccine breakthrough; higher measured molecular prevalence and clinical severity in some studies suggest increased fitness and possibly enhanced transmissibility compared with the 2012 strains.
Review: review – Kept South America as the sole sub-region but changed the emergence classification to re-emergence rather than intra-continental emergence, reflecting resurgence of Florida clade 1 viruses in a long-affected region with further antigenic drift and vaccine mismatch. The listed countries align with regional reviews and national reports, but the exact extent and onset of infection in Colombia and Ecuador should be verified against OIE/WOAH data if more granular dating is required.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Equine influenza virus, EIV
Host: Horses and donkeys (including working equids, polo and ceremonial horses)
Event.summary: From late 2018 into 2019, a broad wave of equine respiratory disease associated with H3N8 equine influenza swept across West and parts of Central Africa, with first large outbreaks confirmed in Nigeria and subsequent spread or contemporaneous outbreaks reported in at least eight other countries, including Burkina Faso, Chad, Cameroon, The Gambia, Ghana, Mali, Niger and Senegal. The epizootic caused high morbidity and substantial mortality among working horses and donkeys that are critical for transport and agriculture, as well as in polo and ceremonial horses, with regional reports estimating that more than sixty thousand equids died during this period. Over time, as the wave passed, some countries reported declining case numbers, but the event highlighted the vulnerability of African equine populations and prompted calls for improved surveillance, vaccination and regional coordination to prevent future large-scale epidemics.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive cross-border movement and trade of horses and donkeys in the Sahel for work, cultural festivals and security forces, combined with limited prior vaccination, weak veterinary infrastructure in some regions and late laboratory confirmation, enabled rapid transboundary spread; environmental stresses and concurrent diseases likely exacerbated mortality. Internal mechanisms: molecular characterization showed that Florida clade 1 H3N8 viruses were newly introduced to West and Central Africa and then spread between countries, representing a major re-emergence of EI in Africa and illustrating geographical range expansion of this clade; very high impact in naïve, often undernourished working equids reflects both antigenic novelty relative to any prior exposure and increased susceptibility of the host population.
Review: review – Sub-regions were corrected to Western Africa and Middle Africa, removing unsupported references to Eastern and Northern Africa for this specific wave. The episode is re-classified as re-emergence of EI in a previously affected continent driven by a new Florida clade 1 incursion, rather than intra-continental emergence. The list of countries follows FAO and OIE-linked syntheses, but attribution of all reported ≈66,000 equid deaths solely to equine influenza is uncertain (African horse sickness and strangles also contributed), and confirmation of EI involvement in Ghana and The Gambia in particular should be revisited against primary outbreak and diagnostic data.

Event.summary: From late 2018 into 2019, a broad wave of equine respiratory disease associated with H3N8 equine influenza swept across West and parts of Central Africa, with first large outbreaks confirmed in Nigeria and subsequent spread or contemporaneous outbreaks reported in at least eight other countries, including Burkina Faso, Chad, Cameroon, The Gambia, Ghana, Mali, Niger and Senegal. The epizootic caused high morbidity and substantial mortality among working horses and donkeys that are critical for transport and agriculture, as well as in polo and ceremonial horses, with regional reports estimating that more than sixty thousand equids died during this period. Over time, as the wave passed, some countries reported declining case numbers, but the event highlighted the vulnerability of African equine populations and prompted calls for improved surveillance, vaccination and regional coordination to prevent future large-scale epidemics.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive cross-border movement and trade of horses and donkeys in the Sahel for work, cultural festivals and security forces, combined with limited prior vaccination, weak veterinary infrastructure in some regions and late laboratory confirmation, enabled rapid transboundary spread; environmental stresses and concurrent diseases likely exacerbated mortality. Internal mechanisms: molecular characterization showed that Florida clade 1 H3N8 viruses were newly introduced to West and Central Africa and then spread between countries, representing a major re-emergence of EI in Africa and illustrating geographical range expansion of this clade; very high impact in naïve, often undernourished working equids reflects both antigenic novelty relative to any prior exposure and increased susceptibility of the host population.
Review: review – Sub-regions were corrected to Western Africa and Middle Africa, removing unsupported references to Eastern and Northern Africa for this specific wave. The episode is re-classified as re-emergence of EI in a previously affected continent driven by a new Florida clade 1 incursion, rather than intra-continental emergence. The list of countries follows FAO and OIE-linked syntheses, but attribution of all reported ≈66,000 equid deaths solely to equine influenza is uncertain (African horse sickness and strangles also contributed), and confirmation of EI involvement in Ghana and The Gambia in particular should be revisited against primary outbreak and diagnostic data.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: HPAI in wild birds
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Northern America
Host: Wild migratory waterfowl (ducks, geese, swans), wild shorebirds and raptors, alongside spillover into domestic poultry
Event.summary: In early 2014, a novel clade 2.3.4.4 H5N8 virus emerged in South Korean poultry and wild waterfowl, then spread in wild birds across East Asia and into Russia during the same year. By late 2014 and early 2015, related H5N8 viruses and reassortant H5N2/H5N1 viruses were detected in wild birds and poultry across Europe and along the Pacific and Central flyways of North America, indicating inter‑continental spread via migratory waterfowl. Intensive control measures and seasonal migration patterns led to a sharp decline in detections in wild birds after mid‑2015, though the clade 2.3.4.4 lineage persisted and set the stage for later waves.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑density poultry production in East Asia, shared wetlands and rice paddies used by domestic ducks and wild waterfowl, and autumn and spring migration across Eurasia and the Bering Strait facilitated spread into Europe and North America. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of clade 2.3.4.4 H5Nx (H5N8, H5N2, H5N6) represented a major novel‑genotype event with reassortment between goose/Guangdong‑lineage H5 and multiple neuraminidase and internal gene constellations, coupled with relatively low clinical severity in some wild ducks that enabled silent carriage and efficient long‑distance transmission.
Review: review – Retain as the first major clade 2.3.4.4 H5N8/H5Nx epizootic in wild birds that introduced the EPP into North American wild birds. Adjusted event‑type flags so that 'inter_continental_emergence' and 're_emergence' are true, while 'intra_continental_emergence' and 're_occurrence' are set to false (this wave reflects inter‑continental spread to a new wild‑bird continent plus re‑emergence via a novel genotype, rather than a simple resurgence in previously affected sub‑regions). Removed 'South‑eastern Asia' from the sub_regions list because the main documented wild‑bird H5N8 activity in 2014–2015 was in East Asia, Europe and North America, and no South‑eastern Asian countries are specified in this row.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Event.summary: In October 2025, HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b was first confirmed on Australia’s sub‑Antarctic external territory of Heard Island and McDonald Islands, causing mass mortality in gentoo penguins, southern elephant seals and other wildlife and marking the first detection of this global H5 lineage in the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region. Genetic and epidemiologic investigations indicated introduction from the South American–sub‑Antarctic circulation zone via migratory seabirds, with subsequent spread among seabirds and marine mammals on the islands through 2025–2026. In June–July 2026, the same clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus was detected in wild seabirds along the coasts of mainland Australia and in a migratory seabird in New Zealand, prompting intensive surveillance, strict poultry biosecurity and wildlife protection measures; the epizootic in Oceania remains ongoing with concern about further establishment in wild‑bird populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction is strongly supported to have occurred via long‑distance migratory seabirds moving between heavily affected South American and sub‑Antarctic colonies and the Heard Island region, with onward dispersal along Southern Ocean flyways to Australian and New Zealand waters; dense colonial breeding of seabirds and haul‑out aggregations of marine mammals facilitated intense local transmission. Internal mechanisms: The same clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 lineage that has shown broad host range and high virulence in seabirds and marine mammals elsewhere appears capable of establishing in sub‑Antarctic and Australasian wild‑bird communities, representing an inter‑continental geographic range expansion of a highly adapted panzootic virus into a previously unaffected continent.
Review: review – Retain as the Oceania incursion event but broaden its scope and timing. Updated the start year to 2025 and added Heard Island and McDonald Islands as the first detection site in the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region, based on Australian government and Antarctic program reports of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 causing multi‑species mortality there in late 2025–early 2026. Added New Zealand [2026] to the country list to reflect the first confirmed detection of the same strain in a migratory seabird. Re‑classified the event solely as 'inter_continental_emergence' (first occurrence of the EPP in Oceania wild birds) and set 'first_detection' to false to avoid duplicating the global first‑emergence classification assigned to the 2002 Hong Kong event. Replaced the previous Reddit citation with official government and research sources documenting the Heard Island outbreak and the first Australian and New Zealand detections.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Host: Chickens (broilers and layers), quail and other domestic poultry species in southern and eastern China live poultry markets; predominantly H9N2 LPAI viruses (BJ94-, G1- and G9-like genotypes).
Event.summary: In 1992, low pathogenic H9N2 avian influenza viruses were first isolated from chickens in Guangdong Province, southern China, signalling the emergence of a new poultry-adapted lineage in East Asia. Through the mid-1990s, related BJ94-, G1- and G9-like H9N2 genotypes became established in chickens and quail in live poultry markets in southern China and Hong Kong, and by 1998–1999 H9N2 viruses accounted for the great majority of influenza isolates from Chinese chickens as the subtype spread to most provinces. As the virus became endemic, large-scale vaccination programmes and market interventions were introduced around 1999–2000, reducing explosive outbreaks but not eliminating circulation, and H9N2 has since remained the dominant low-pathogenic influenza subtype in Chinese poultry.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of China’s poultry industry, dense networks of live poultry markets where birds from many farms and species were commingled, and long-distance movement of live birds allowed H9N2 viruses introduced in the early 1990s to spread quickly across eastern and southern China and persist at high prevalence in chickens and minor poultry. Internal mechanisms: evolution of poultry-adapted BJ94-, G1- and G9-like H9N2 genotypes with HA and NA changes that enhanced replication and transmission in chickens, broadened host range to multiple domestic species, and enabled the viruses to donate internal genes to other zoonotic lineages such as H5N1 and H7N9, exemplifying re-emergence driven by viral adaptation rather than simple geographic spread.
Review: Retain (added new event). This large-scale emergence of H9N2 LPAI in Chinese poultry in the 1990s is very well documented and clearly among the most impactful LPAI episodes globally, with H9N2 becoming the predominant influenza subtype in Chinese chickens and a major gene donor for later zoonotic strains.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/proteincell/article/6/1/18/6803253)) It was missing from the original dataset and has been added as a re-emergence event (new poultry-adapted genotypes in a region where LPAI already circulated).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Host: Commercial and backyard chickens (broilers, layers, breeders), turkeys and quail; primarily G1-lineage H9N2 LPAI viruses.
Event.summary: Around 1998, H9N2 low pathogenic avian influenza viruses were first detected in chickens in Saudi Arabia and Iran, marking the introduction and establishment of G1-lineage H9N2 into poultry flocks in the Middle East. Over the late 1990s and early 2000s, related H9N2 viruses became enzootic in commercial and backyard poultry in Gulf and Levant countries including the United Arab Emirates, Israel and Jordan, causing repeated respiratory disease outbreaks, drops in egg production and increased mortality in the presence of co-infections. By the mid-2000s, vaccination programmes were widely adopted but H9N2 remained endemic across much of Western Asia, with distinct regional genetic lineages established in different countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of poultry production in the Middle East, high volumes of regional and international trade in live birds and hatching eggs from Asia, and suboptimal farm and market biosecurity allowed G1-lineage H9N2 introduced from southern China to spread and become endemic across multiple Middle Eastern countries. Internal mechanisms: emergence and regional diversification of poultry-adapted G1-lineage H9N2 genotypes with molecular markers of mammalian adaptation and efficient replication in chickens, representing re-emergence of LPAI in the region through introduction and evolution of a new lineage rather than simple spread of existing local LPAI strains.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9148743/))
Review: Retain with corrections. Iran was previously listed under Western Asia only, which conflicts with the UNSD classification (Southern Asia); sub_regions has been updated to "Western Asia; Southern Asia" and the countries field now lists specific countries with documented first H9N2 detections and approximate start years (Saudi Arabia, Iran, UAE, Israel, Jordan) instead of a vague "other Gulf and Levant countries".([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9148743/)) The event is reclassified as re-emergence only: per project rules, spread of a new H9N2 lineage within Asia into regions where LPAI was already present should not be coded as intra-continental emergence. First_detection remains No because H9N2 and LPAI influenza A were detected in poultry well before 1998 in other continents.

EPP.scientific.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
EPP.common.name: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI; multiple subtypes)
Host: Backyard and small-scale commercial chickens (layers and broilers) and other domestic poultry in West Africa; G1-lineage H9N2 LPAI viruses, with reports of increased pathogenicity in some flocks.
Event.summary: In 2017, G1-lineage H9N2 low pathogenic avian influenza virus was first reported in poultry in Burkina Faso and soon afterwards in Ghana, signalling spread of this lineage from North Africa and the Middle East into West African poultry populations. Over the subsequent years, H9N2 detections became more frequent in backyard and commercial poultry in Ghana, Benin, Togo, Nigeria and Senegal, with outbreaks associated with respiratory disease, production drops and occasional higher mortality in some flocks. Control efforts including culling, movement restrictions and heightened surveillance were implemented during outbreaks, but H9N2 has continued to circulate at low to moderate levels in West African poultry, and more recently human H9N2 infections have been reported in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of H9N2 via regional poultry trade and informal movements of live birds and hatching eggs from North Africa and the Middle East, combined with widespread backyard farming and open live bird markets with low biosecurity, promoted establishment and spread of the virus in West Africa. Internal mechanisms: introduction of a G1-lineage H9N2 genotype closely related to viruses from Morocco and the United Arab Emirates, followed by local diversification and adaptation to chickens, with molecular markers favouring mammalian receptor binding; the appearance of a human H9N2 infection in Ghana and later in Senegal underscores re-emergence driven by viral adaptation and geographic range expansion within Africa.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/50213/cdc_50213_DS1.pdf))
Review: Retain with corrections. West African H9N2 emergence is a major geographic expansion of the G1 lineage and is well documented beginning with Burkina Faso in 2017 and subsequent detections in Ghana, Benin, Togo, Nigeria and Senegal.([stacks.cdc.gov](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/50213/cdc_50213_DS1.pdf)) The original row mentioned only Ghana and treated the event as "first_detection" and "intra-continental emergence"; the countries field has been expanded to include other affected West African states with approximate first-detection years, and, following the project rules for new serotypes in regions where LPAI is already established, the event is now coded purely as re-emergence rather than first or intra-continental emergence.

EPP.common.name: Swine influenza virus, SIV
Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2001]
Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus)
Event.summary: From the early 1990s, surveillance in southern and eastern China identified avian-origin H1N1 influenza A viruses in pigs that clustered phylogenetically with the Eurasian avian-like swine H1N1 lineage, indicating independent introductions of avian H1N1 into Asian pig populations. By roughly 2005, EA H1N1 had largely replaced classical H1N1 as the dominant H1 lineage in many Chinese pig populations, establishing an endemic reservoir that subsequently reassorted with triple-reassortant and 2009 pandemic H1N1 viruses and contributed key gene segments to later globally important swine influenza genotypes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion and intensification of pig production in China and neighbouring regions, frequent movement of pigs between farms and through live markets, and close proximity of pigs to domestic poultry and wild birds created sustained opportunities for avian H1N1 viruses to spill over and become established in swine herds. Multiple virologic and phylogenetic studies document avian-origin European-lineage H1N1 viruses entering Chinese pigs in the early 1990s and forming an Asian EA sublineage, detection of EA H1N1 in pigs in Hong Kong SAR and Thailand by about 2001, and progressive replacement of classical H1N1 by EA H1N1 as the predominant H1 lineage in Chinese swine herds by around 2005.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC190877/?utm_source=openai)) This episode is widely regarded as a key shift in the global SIV gene pool and an important precursor to both the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus and later G4 EA H1N1 genotypes, so it qualifies as one of the top emergence events. I coded it as re-emergence (new strain and bird-to-pig host expansion within an already SIV-endemic region) with no first- or inter-continental emergence flags, and restricted the explicit country list to China (including Hong Kong SAR) and Thailand where early establishment is best documented. Host: Domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), with occasional spillover to turkeys and other poultry
Event.summary: In 1998, outbreaks of influenza-like illness in U.S. pig herds revealed the sudden emergence of a novel H3N2 swine influenza virus containing the so‑called triple reassortant internal gene (TRIG) cassette, with genes derived from human H3N2, classical swine H1N1 and North American avian influenza viruses; these viruses rapidly caused widespread disease in multiple U.S. states. During the following years, the TRIG internal gene constellation became established across U.S. swine populations and reassorted further with classical swine H1N1 to generate additional H1N2 and H1N1 variants, while similar triple-reassortant H3N2 viruses were detected in Canadian pigs by 2005, indicating regional spread within northern North America. By the mid‑2000s, triple‑reassortant lineage viruses (trH3N2, trH1N2 and trH1N1) had become dominant in North American swine, replacing classical H1N1 as the sole major lineage and establishing a genetically diverse, enzootic swine influenza ecosystem that persists and continues to generate novel reassortants.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density, multi-site pig production and frequent movement of weaned pigs between breeding and finishing units favoured rapid spread of the new TRIG lineage across North American herds; close contact between pigs and humans and between pig and poultry operations created repeated opportunities for multi-host infection and reassortment. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence through complex reassortment among human H3N2, classical swine H1N1 and avian influenza viruses produced the triple‑reassortant internal gene (TRIG) cassette, which conferred high fitness in pigs and subsequently seeded reassortant H1 and H3 subtypes; this represents re-emergence through genetic innovation, geographic range expansion of the TRIG lineage within North America, and enhanced transmission potential in pig populations.
Review: Retain. The emergence of triple-reassortant H3N2 viruses with the TRIG internal gene cassette in U.S. pigs in 1998 and their rapid establishment and diversification across North American swine, including detection in Canadian pigs by 2005, is extensively documented and widely recognised as one of the most important modern SIV emergence events.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0168170200001544?utm_source=openai)) The geographic scope (United States and Canada), approximate year range (1998–2005), host description and classification as re-emergence (novel reassortant genotype in an already SIV-endemic region) are all consistent with published evidence and with the project’s rule to treat genotype shifts, rather than the long-standing presence of influenza A in pigs, as re-emergence. The event’s sources are highly relevant primary virologic studies; no corrections were required, and this row should be retained as is.

Event.summary: In 2009, the novel pandemic H1N1 (H1N1pdm09) influenza A virus, a complex reassortant derived partly from North American triple‑reassortant swine viruses and Eurasian avian-like swine viruses, spilled over from swine into humans in Mexico and the United States and rapidly spread worldwide in humans; soon after, reverse zoonotic transmission from infected people led to introduction of H1N1pdm09 into domestic pig herds in multiple countries on six continents. From 2009 to roughly 2013, H1N1pdm09 viruses were repeatedly introduced into swine populations in the Americas, Europe, Asia, Oceania and Africa, where they established sustained pig-to-pig transmission and reassorted extensively with locally endemic SIV lineages, as documented in countries such as Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Colombia, Australia, Finland and Cameroon, and later detected in African pigs in Cameroon, Kenya, Nigeria and other countries. By the mid‑2010s, H1N1pdm09-derived gene segments had become entrenched in the global swine influenza gene pool, with numerous reassortant genotypes co-circulating in pigs across six continents and contributing to sustained endemic respiratory disease and an expanded reservoir of zoonotic viruses with pandemic potential.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus japonicum
EPP.common.name: JEV
Host: Domestic pigs; feral pigs; waterbirds; Culex mosquitoes; (humans as spillover hosts)
Event.summary: In 1995, Japanese encephalitis virus was detected for the first time in recognized natural transmission cycles in the Australasian region during an outbreak centered on Badu Island in the Torres Strait, where three human cases (two fatal) occurred and JEV infection was demonstrated in local pigs and mosquitoes, indicating establishment of a transmission cycle in domestic swine and wildlife. Subsequent investigations showed active JEV circulation in southern Papua New Guinea, with virus isolated from Culex mosquitoes and serologic evidence in humans and pigs during the late 1980s–1990s, likely serving as the source, and by 1997–1998 JEV was isolated from mosquitoes in Western Province PNG and from pig blood and mosquitoes in the Torres Strait, confirming an epizootic/enzootic focus spanning PNG and northern Australia. By 1998, virus activity had extended to mainland northern Australia (Cape York Peninsula), after which enhanced surveillance and vector control reduced detectable circulation, although low‑level activity persisted in the Torres Strait in later years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Strong cyclonic weather systems and prevailing winds in the Gulf of Carpentaria likely transported infected Culex mosquitoes from high‑transmission foci in southern Papua New Guinea into the Torres Strait and Cape York; the co‑location of piggeries, waterbird habitat, and rice or wetland environments provided ideal conditions for sustained transmission. Intensified regional travel and trade may also have facilitated movement of infected vectors or birds. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was implicated; instead, existing Asian JEV lineages expanded their geographic range into a previously non‑endemic continent (Oceania), representing geographic range expansion enabled by suitable vectors and amplifying hosts rather than intrinsic viral change.
Review: retain – This is the well-documented first establishment of JEV transmission in Oceania, covering the 1995 Torres Strait outbreak and subsequent spread to Cape York. Continent, subregions (Australia and New Zealand; Melanesia) and country assignments (Australia, Papua New Guinea) match the UNSD scheme and the literature. Coding as an inter‑continental emergence (new continent, with in situ pig–mosquito cycles) without first/global emergence or re‑emergence flags is appropriate; while 1995 and 1998 may represent separate incursions, treating 1995–1998 as a single linked early Australasian episode is defensible and does not misclassify the event type.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus japonicum
EPP.common.name: JEV
Host: Domestic pigs; waterbirds; Culex mosquitoes; (humans as spillover hosts)
Event.summary: In 2005, a very large Japanese encephalitis outbreak occurred in northern India (notably Uttar Pradesh) and adjoining districts of Nepal, where several thousand suspected human cases and more than a thousand deaths were reported in areas with extensive pig farming and rice cultivation. The episode built on long‑standing endemic circulation but represented a major resurgence, with pigs and waterbirds serving as key amplifying hosts sustaining high mosquito infection rates in rural communities. After emergency vector control and rollout of human vaccination campaigns, along with seasonal decline in mosquito populations, the outbreak subsided, although JE remained endemic in pigs and humans in the affected Terai and Gangetic plain districts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of unvaccinated children, extensive irrigated rice cultivation favoring Culex breeding, close proximity of pigs to human dwellings, monsoon‑related increases in vector populations, and limited initial vaccination coverage contributed to explosive amplification from the usual pig–bird reservoirs into humans. Internal mechanisms: No clearly novel genotype was uniquely implicated in this particular year; the event is best interpreted as a dramatic re‑occurrence driven mainly by environmental and socio‑economic factors that intensified transmission in an already endemic pig–mosquito–human system.
Review: retain – The 2005 epidemic in Uttar Pradesh and neighboring Nepal is widely recognized as one of the largest recent JE outbreaks by human cases and deaths, occurring in a long‑endemic Southern Asian focus with intensive pig and rice production. Geography (Southern Asia; India and Nepal) and classification as re‑occurrence (resurgence in a known subregion driven by external factors rather than a new genotype or new region) are consistent with the definitions, and no more impactful post‑1990 JE outbreak in this region has been omitted that would supersede it.

EPP.scientific.name: Lagovirus europaeus
EPP.common.name: EBHSV (European brown hare syndrome virus) / RHDV2 (GI.2)
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe
Host: Domestic and wild European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Event.summary: In 2010, a new pathogenic lagovirus variant, later designated Lagovirus europaeus GI.2 (RHDV2), was first identified during rabbit haemorrhagic disease outbreaks in domestic rabbits in France, where it caused high mortality despite vaccination against classical RHDV. Over 2011–2013 the virus spread explosively through Iberia (Spain, Portugal), Italy, the Netherlands, the UK, and other European countries, and by 2013–2014 it had reached several Atlantic islands including the Azores and Canary Islands, causing large die-offs in both farmed and wild rabbits. By about 2014–2015, RHDV2 had become widely established across Europe and many island systems, partially or fully replacing classical RHDV (GI.1) as the dominant cause of rabbit haemorrhagic disease.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive rabbit production and trade, movement of live rabbits and rabbit products, high hunting and translocation pressure in wild rabbit populations, and dense, interconnected European rabbit metapopulations facilitated rapid geographic spread on the continent and to offshore islands. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel genotype (GI.2/RHDV2) with distinct antigenic properties and partial vaccine escape relative to GI.1, increased ability to infect younger rabbits, and evidence of recombination with non-pathogenic lagoviruses likely enhanced its fitness and allowed it to outcompete endemic GI.1 strains. Mechanisms include novel strain/genotype emergence, enhanced transmission, and geographic range expansion inherent to the lineage.
Review: review – Corrected event-type coding so this early multi-country European wave of GI.2/RHDV2 is treated solely as re-emergence of Lagovirus europaeus driven by a new genotype, rather than as first/global emergence, first detection and intra-continental emergence. Geography (France, Iberia, Italy, the Netherlands, UK and Atlantic islands) and the 2010–2015 time window remain appropriate for one of the most impactful global events, but a human reviewer may wish to verify whether any additional highly affected European countries should be named explicitly.

EPP.scientific.name: Leptospira interrogans
EPP.common.name: Leptospirosis
Host: Dogs (companion animals); urban wildlife reservoirs including raccoons, skunks and rodents; incidentally humans
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through the early 2000s, North America saw a marked resurgence of canine leptospirosis, with increasing case series and serosurveys documenting rising prevalence in dogs in the United States and Canada and a shift from traditional vaccine-covered serovars Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae to emerging serovars such as Autumnalis, Grippotyphosa, Pomona and Bratislava. The problem became particularly evident by the late 1990s and early 2000s in regions such as Ontario and across the US, where the proportion of positive canine microscopic agglutination tests increased and disease clustered in urban and peri-urban areas with abundant raccoon and rodent populations. Expanded vaccination that incorporated additional serovars and increased awareness among veterinarians helped to reduce severe disease in some areas, but canine leptospirosis has remained an important re-emerging zoonosis in North America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Urbanization and expansion of suburbs into wildlife habitats increased contact between dogs and reservoir hosts such as raccoons and rodents; changes in pet management (e.g. more outdoor access) and lagging updates to vaccines left many dogs susceptible. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence was closely associated with a shift in dominant infecting serovars in dogs toward Pomona, Grippotyphosa, Bratislava and Autumnalis, reducing protection from older bivalent vaccines and representing both novel strain/genotype prominence and effective host expansion within dog populations, which justifies classification as re-emergence.
Review: Retain – The multi-country, multi-year resurgence of canine leptospirosis with a clear shift to non-classical serovars in the US and Canada is a major animal-health emergence event and fits the definition of re-emergence due to changes in circulating genotypes and host ecology. Geography, timeframe and sources are appropriate; no classification changes were needed beyond text clean-up.
