EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Host: Domestic cattle; water buffalo locally
Event.summary: In August 2015, LSDV was first detected in the European Union in cattle in northern Greece near the Turkish border, marking the first recognized establishment of the virus on the European continent. During 2015–2017, the virus spread extensively through Greece and into multiple Balkan countries, with thousands of outbreaks reported and severe trade and production impacts. A coordinated mass vaccination campaign and movement controls across the Balkans and EU member states led to a sharp decline in outbreaks after 2017, with most affected countries regaining disease‑free status in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction from the infected Middle East/Türkiye region, likely via wind‑borne or mechanically transported vectors and/or short‑distance animal movements, followed by regional spread under favorable climatic conditions for vector flies and ticks. Substantial movements of cattle among Balkan states and to EU markets amplified dissemination before control measures were harmonized. Internal mechanisms: Viruses belonged to the classical field strain lineage; no major genetic shifts were necessary for establishment, but the virus showed efficient transmission by local vector species, highlighting vector‑adaptation compatibility with European climates.
Review: review – Retained as the first confirmed inter-continental emergence of LSDV into Europe, but the continent and sub-region fields were corrected from “Europe; Asia / Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Asia” to “Europe / Southern Europe; Eastern Europe” because the outbreaks listed here occurred only in European territories (Balkans, European Thrace, European Russia). Emergence-type coding as inter-continental emergence (first occurrence in Europe) is consistent with EFSA and WOAH timelines.

Event.summary: In 2022, South Asia experienced an exceptionally severe LSD epidemic, with India reporting widespread outbreaks across many states and the death of tens of thousands of cattle within a few months, alongside major production losses. Neighboring Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh also recorded large numbers of cases, often in regions that had seen only limited disease in earlier years. Accelerated rollout of homologous and heterologous LSD vaccines, stricter movement controls and heightened farmer awareness gradually brought the large 2022 wave under better control by early 2023, though the virus is now entrenched in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High baseline prevalence following initial introduction in 2019–2021, intense livestock movement after easing of COVID‑19 disruptions, and warm, humid conditions that favored vector proliferation combined to trigger a large secondary epidemic wave. Gaps in early vaccination coverage and cold‑chain/logistics issues further allowed explosive spread. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses from India indicated that 2022 outbreak strains were distinct from earlier 2019 isolates and represented a separate genetic lineage circulating under vaccine and immune pressure, consistent with Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; reports of more severe disease in some areas support classification as viral re‑emergence rather than simple re‑occurrence.
Review: review – This severe South Asian wave is retained as a major re-emergence episode, but the emergence coding was adjusted so only ‘re_emergence’ is true (re_occurrence was set to false) to respect the guideline that event types are generally mutually exclusive, with re-emergence reserved for episodes involving clear viral genetic change. Genomic work from India demonstrates that 2022 strains form a distinct lineage from 2019 isolates under vaccine/immune pressure, justifying re-emergence classification.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Host: Domestic cattle
Event.summary: After several years without EU cases following successful control of the Balkan outbreaks, LSDV reappeared in 2025 with a first case reported in Sardinia (Italy), followed shortly by outbreaks on mainland Italy, a major epizootic in France beginning in summer 2025, and detections in Spain later that year. The French outbreak caused significant trade disruptions and required large‑scale vaccination, movement restrictions and emergency response measures over roughly eight months. By early 2026, French authorities reported that the national crisis was largely under control and remaining regulated zones were being lifted, although surveillance and vaccination remained in place to prevent renewed spread in Western Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Reintroduction of LSDV into previously free parts of Western and Southern Europe likely occurred via importation of infected animals or vectors, possibly linked to trade or movement of cattle or vector‑carrying goods under climatic conditions that allowed vector activity well into autumn. High cattle densities, intense trade within the EU and initial gaps in immunity in Western European herds facilitated rapid spread before emergency vaccination scaled up. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence suggests involvement of strains related to recombinant and field lineages circulating in Asia and eastern Europe; the event is best characterized as re‑emergence in a previously cleared region and intra‑continental emergence into new European subregions, with viral traits sufficient for efficient transmission via European vector species but without clear proof of substantially increased virulence.
Review: review – Retained as a major re-emergence and intra-continental emergence event in Western and Southern Europe (Italy, France, Spain) starting in mid‑2025, consistent with WOAH and EU/Swiss summaries. The source list was revised to prioritise WOAH, EFSA, EU and UK official outbreak assessments plus detailed French press reports, and to remove reliance on Wikipedia for this recent episode. Emergence typing as both intra-continental emergence (new European subregions) and re-emergence (return to a previously cleared continent) is justified.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: MERS-CoV, Betacoronavirus 1
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: Archived sera from dromedary camels in Somalia, Sudan and Kenya collected in the early 1980s and 1990s showed about 81% MERS-CoV–neutralizing antibody seropositivity, indicating intense, long-term endemic circulation in Eastern Africa; similar high seroprevalence was later documented in camels from Ethiopia.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4257824/)) During 2009–2013, additional surveys in Kenyan herds confirmed that high seroprevalence persisted in both nomadic and farmed camels, suggesting sustained transmission.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/20/8/14-0596_article)) The event remains ongoing, with Eastern Africa recognized as a major endemic reservoir for camel MERS-CoV.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High camel densities, nomadic and transboundary trade systems in the Greater Horn of Africa facilitated frequent mixing of herds and sustained virus circulation across national borders.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4257824/)) Internal mechanisms: Stable adaptation of MERS-CoV to dromedaries with efficient respiratory shedding in juveniles maintained viral circulation without causing noticeable disease, allowing unrecognized persistence for decades (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation).([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/21/7/pdfs/15-0070.pdf))
Review: review – This event correctly highlights Eastern Africa as a long-term endemic reservoir and should be retained, but two corrections were needed. (1) Somalia and Sudan were removed from the country list because all published sera from these countries with MERS-CoV antibodies were collected in 1983–1984 (pre-1990) and thus are now represented only in the first_emergence_time/background, not as ≥1990 event entries. The remaining countries, Kenya [1992] and Ethiopia [2011], match the earliest post‑1990 camel serologic evidence. (2) intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence have been set to No: Eastern Africa is the original known subregion for camel MERS-CoV, and these data represent long-standing endemicity rather than spread to a new subregion or a resurgence driven by external factors.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: MERS-CoV, Betacoronavirus 1
Sub.regions: Northern Africa; Western Africa; Eastern Africa
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: Serologic surveys of camel sera collected between 2009 and 2011 in Tunisia (North Africa), Nigeria (West Africa) and Ethiopia (East Africa) revealed widespread antibodies to MERS-CoV or a closely related virus, demonstrating that infection was not confined to the Horn of Africa but extended across multiple African subregions.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4111168/)) These findings extended the recognized endemic range of camel MERS-CoV throughout North, West and East Africa.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6518605/)) The event reflects long-standing, rather than newly introduced, circulation but marks the first documentation of infection in these subregions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional camel trade networks connecting Eastern Africa with North and West Africa, and movements for slaughter and pastoralism, likely allowed long-term spread and homogenization of MERS-CoV across the continent.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6518605/)) Internal mechanisms: No clear evidence for major viral change in this period; the event mainly represents improved serologic surveillance uncovering pre-existing endemic infection (no specific internal mechanism identified beyond existing host adaptation).
Review: review – This multi-country survey is an appropriate intra-continental emergence event, documenting first evidence from North and West Africa as well as additional data from East Africa, and should be retained. However, Nigeria’s start year has been corrected from 2009 to 2010 to align with the reported sampling period (2010–2011) in the African geographic-distribution serosurvey. No other changes to classification, geography, timing, or sources are required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
EPP.common.name: MERS-CoV, Betacoronavirus 1
Sub.regions: Northern Africa; Western Africa; Eastern Africa
Host: Dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius)
Event.summary: From about 2010 onwards, large-scale serologic and virologic surveys across North, West and East Africa identified very high MERS-CoV seroprevalence and, in some countries, viral RNA and full genomes in dromedary camels in Egypt, Tunisia, Senegal, Uganda, Burkina Faso, Morocco and Nigeria, confirming continental-scale endemicity.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/)) Genetic analyses showed that many African camel viruses formed a distinct clade C, differentiating them from Arabian clade B strains.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/)) The event is ongoing, with African clade C viruses continuing to circulate in camel populations without recognized large human outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of virologic surveillance in camels, combined with long-standing cross-border trade and movement of live animals from East and West Africa to North Africa and the Middle East, revealed and may have facilitated dispersion of distinct viral lineages.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6518605/)) Internal mechanisms: Emergence and maintenance of African clade C lineages (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence) and their adaptation to local camel populations, with genetic divergence from clade B viruses circulating in Arabia, represent viral evolution associated with this re-emergence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6723520/))
Review: review – This event captures the large-scale, multi-country African surveys and the genetic definition of African clade C viruses and should be retained. Two adjustments were made. (1) intra_continental_emergence has been set to No because North, West and East Africa were already known to harbor infected camels from earlier (2009–2011) work; this episode reflects intensified sampling and genomic characterization rather than first spread to new African subregions. (2) Nigeria’s start year was aligned to 2010 to reflect earlier serologic evidence, though the main clade C sequencing work dates from 2013 onward. Re_emergence=Yes remains appropriate as this event is driven by the recognition of distinct viral lineages with sequence-level changes (novel strain/genotype emergence).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Cattle (and some domestic buffalo) in eastern Türkiye, northern Iraq and north‑western Iran
Event.summary: In September 1991, Türkiye experienced a major rinderpest outbreak, its first since 1971, with rapid spread through eastern provinces: 516 herds in 44 localities were affected within two months, leading to about 2,700 cattle deaths, 12,000 animals slaughtered and emergency vaccination of roughly 12.5 million cattle. Intensive control measures eliminated clinical disease within four months. In March–April 1994, new outbreaks occurred in eastern Türkiye, northern Iraq and north‑western Iran, consistent with an endemic focus in Kurdish border areas fed by animal movements from more easterly endemic zones. Coordinated emergency vaccination and culling again contained the epizootic, and no further rinderpest has been reported from these countries since the mid‑1990s.

The need for rapid, large‑scale vaccination campaigns illustrates how declines in routine immunity can permit explosive re-occurrence once the virus is re‑seeded. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses linked these viruses to known Asiatic lineages, and there is no clear evidence of a novel genotype, altered virulence or host expansion; the events represent major re-occurrence of existing strains under conditions of weakened control.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Cattle and other domestic bovines (with some involvement of small ruminants and camels in parts of the Arabian Peninsula)
Event.summary: In the early to mid‑1990s, rinderpest caused a series of outbreaks on the Arabian Peninsula following introduction from endemic foci to the north. Oman reported a large epidemic in 1992 with well over 100 outbreaks, and rinderpest continued to be detected there until the mid‑1990s. Related incursions affected cattle in Saudi Arabia, and rinderpest remained present in hill cattle in Yemen until at least 1995 despite annual vaccination campaigns, with additional outbreaks reported in the United Arab Emirates in the mid‑1990s. Coordinated regional efforts under the West Asian Rinderpest Eradication Campaign (WAREC) and GREP, including intensified vaccination, movement control and improved surveillance, progressively eliminated these foci, so that by the late 1990s rinderpest was believed to persist only in Yemen.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing trade and movement of live cattle and other livestock from endemic areas in South and West Asia into Gulf states, combined with incomplete routine vaccination and weaknesses in border control, allowed repeated re-introduction of rinderpest. The early 1990s regional instability following the Gulf War likely exacerbated gaps in veterinary services. In Yemen, difficult terrain and dispersed hill cattle systems impeded high vaccine coverage, favouring endemic persistence until targeted campaigns closed remaining immunity gaps. Internal mechanisms: There is no indication that these outbreaks were driven by a novel strain or altered virulence; they are best interpreted as re-occurrence of known Asiatic lineages in a high‑risk trade hub.
Review: review – This multi‑country Arabian Peninsula focus, including a large epidemic in Oman and persistent endemic infection in Yemen with additional outbreaks in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, was absent from the original dataset but is clearly highlighted in FAO/OIE sources as one of the remaining rinderpest reservoirs in the mid‑1990s. A new row has been added with approximate year ranges and country‑specific last-report dates based primarily on regional summaries and OIE workshop data. Because detailed national outbreak timelines are heterogeneous and not always fully accessible, this event is flagged for human review to confirm the per‑country start years and relative weighting of Oman versus Yemen.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus pecoris
EPP.common.name: Rinderpest virus, Rinderpest morbillivirus
Host: Cattle and domestic buffalo in pastoral systems, and wild African buffalo and other susceptible wildlife in the Somali pastoral ecosystem
Event.summary: From the mid‑1990s, a mild lineage‑2 rinderpest virus persisted in the Somali pastoral ecosystem spanning north‑eastern Kenya, south‑eastern Ethiopia and southern Somalia, representing the last enzootic focus of rinderpest worldwide. The virus caused only low‑grade or inapparent disease in cattle but was associated with severe mortality in wildlife, being detected in Tsavo East National Park (Kenya) in 1994–1995 and in Nairobi National Park in 1996, and later in African buffalo in Meru National Park in 2001, the final confirmed natural infection globally. Despite sporadic reports of “mild rinderpest” in cattle up to the early 2000s, intensive participatory surveillance and wildlife monitoring after 2001 failed to detect further virus circulation, supporting eventual global eradication.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Highly mobile Somali pastoralist systems, cross‑border livestock movements, and chronic insecurity hindered conventional surveillance and mass vaccination, allowing a virus causing mostly mild disease in cattle to circulate cryptically at the livestock–wildlife interface. Gaps in vaccination left cohorts of young cattle and wildlife susceptible while older animals remained partially immune, favouring maintenance of low‑level transmission. Internal mechanisms: The virus in this focus belonged to African lineage 2 and showed an unusually mild clinical phenotype in cattle yet retained the capacity to cause severe disease in certain wild artiodactyls. Its distinct genotype and attenuated presentation, which enabled long‑term, largely inapparent persistence, justify classification of this episode as re-emergence driven by viral lineage characteristics, rather than simple re-occurrence of classic rinderpest.
Review: review – The time span has been adjusted from 1993–2001 to 1994–2001 to align with FAO EMPRES reports that first recognized mild lineage‑2 rinderpest in Tsavo East National Park in 1994, with subsequent detections in Nairobi and Meru National Parks, and no confirmed virus after 2001. Country‑specific start years have been updated (Kenya [1994–2001], Somalia [1994], Ethiopia [1996]) based on descriptions of spread from the Kenya–Somalia border and later suspicion in southern Ethiopia. Generalist sources (Wikipedia and a broad ScienceDirect topic page) were replaced with more focused FAO bulletins and peer‑reviewed articles. Because precise timing of first infection in each country is still approximate, this row is flagged for human review, but the classification as re-emergence linked to lineage‑2 virus is well supported.

EPP.scientific.name: Multiple pathogens
EPP.common.name: B virus, SFV, NHP-associated zoonoses
Host: Humans occupationally exposed to captive non-human primates (laboratory workers, animal caretakers, zoo personnel) in primate research centers and zoos
Event.summary: From 1995 through around 2000, serologic and molecular studies in cohorts of primate facility and zoo workers in North America and Europe provided the first clear, reproducible evidence that simian foamy viruses (SFV) had zoonotically infected humans, with multiple laboratory and animal‑house staff testing positive for persistent SFV infection. Initial reports of three infected laboratory or monkey-house personnel were followed by CDC-linked surveillance in U.S. and Canadian primate centers and a Lancet report of infected North American zoo keepers, documenting that roughly 1–5% of heavily exposed workers could become SFV infected. No disease clusters or human-to-human transmission were observed, but these findings firmly established SFV as a common occupational NHP zoonosis and led to long‑term follow‑up of infected workers and strengthened biosafety guidance in primate facilities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of large primate research colonies and zoos, with frequent bites, scratches, mucosal splashes and contact with saliva and blood, created sustained opportunities for SFV spillover into humans; limited early awareness and inconsistent use of personal protective equipment contributed to risk. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of highly prevalent, saliva-borne SFV from chimpanzees, baboons, macaques and other NHPs into humans, with viral properties favoring lifelong integration of proviral DNA but not efficient human-to-human transmission; no consistent evidence of increased virulence was found in infected workers.
Review: review – Updated the year to 1995–2000 to reflect the initial Schweizer et al. 1995 report and subsequent CDC cohort and zoo keeper studies; clarified that infections occurred in the United States, Canada, and at least one European facility (here represented by Germany). Removed vague phrasing about “likely additional industrialized countries” and specified countries with documented infections. Kept the classification as first_detection (first clear evidence of SFV infection in humans) and set other emergence-type flags to No. Human expert should confirm whether to further disaggregate North American and European sub-episodes or retain this as a single occupational SFV-recognition phase.

Host: Humans (monkey temple workers, local residents, pet owners, urban residents, and some tourists) exposed to free-ranging macaques; source hosts were mainly Macaca fascicularis, Macaca mulatta, Macaca assamensis, and other macaque species

EPP.scientific.name: Multiple pathogens
EPP.common.name: B virus, SFV, NHP-associated zoonoses
Host: Humans (bushmeat hunters, women involved in hunting and butchering, and other rural residents) exposed to wild non-human primates; source hosts included mandrills and several monkey species
Event.summary: Between roughly 2010 and 2013, expanded field investigations in Gabon and the Democratic Republic of the Congo documented additional naturally acquired SFV infections in hunters and rural residents, including several women infected by viruses from different monkey species, thereby broadening the demographic and host-range context of African SFV zoonoses beyond the earlier Cameroon cohorts. Detailed molecular studies showed that each human infection was closely related to SFV strains circulating in local non-human primate populations and that multiple distinct genotypes from mandrills and monkeys had independently crossed into humans. No evidence of onward human-to-human transmission or consistent clinical disease was found, but these results consolidated the view of Central African forests as a persistent source of genetically diverse SFV spillover and supported ongoing programs to monitor NHP-borne retroviruses and counsel high-risk groups about safe hunting and handling practices.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued reliance on bushmeat, expansion and professionalization of bushmeat trade networks, and evolving gender roles in hunting and butchering in Central Africa maintained or increased high-risk human contact with NHP blood and saliva; weak clinical and virologic surveillance systems meant asymptomatic infections were rarely recognized outside targeted studies. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergent host expansion (spillover) of diverse SFV genotypes from multiple monkey and mandrill species to humans within a subregion where SFV zoonoses were already known, with evidence of multiple independent cross-species transmission events; viral evolution reflected high genetic diversity in reservoir hosts but did not indicate enhanced human pathogenicity or transmissibility.
Review: review – Left geography unchanged (Middle Africa: Gabon and DRC) but changed emergence typing from intra-continental emergence plus re-emergence to re_emergence only. Because SFV spillover to humans had already been documented in the same subregion (Cameroon), these new infections represent additional, genetically diverse spillover events rather than spread into a new subregion of Africa. Event remains important as it documents broader host and demographic range for African SFV zoonoses.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis
EPP.common.name: MAP, Johne's disease
Host: Dairy cattle (Bos taurus)
Event.summary: In 1998, a national survey in the Netherlands estimated that 31–71% of dairy herds were infected with MAP (true animal‑level prevalence approximately 2.7–6.9%), highlighting Johne’s disease as a widespread endemic infection in one of Europe’s most intensive dairy industries. Around 2000, similar surveillance in Denmark reported an estimated 8.8% of dairy cows testing positive in a milk‑ELISA survey, confirming that MAP was an important, though variably distributed, production disease in Northern European dairy systems. These findings made clear that Johne’s disease was a large‑scale problem in high‑intensity European dairy sectors and spurred or reinforced national and regional control efforts in several countries, including herd‑assurance schemes, risk‑based testing, and integration of Johne’s control into broader bovine health programmes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑standing MAP infection in intensive dairy systems in the Netherlands and Denmark, combined with improved diagnostic tests (ELISA, culture) and structured national surveys, converted largely hidden endemic infection into a recognised large‑scale health and economic issue; intra‑EU cattle trade also contributed to cross‑border dissemination. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain is reported in these surveys; the episode represents enhanced detection and documentation of widespread endemic MAP leading to coordinated control efforts, rather than a discrete genetic or virulence shift.
Review: Decision: retain. Rationale: This row appropriately summarises the first robust national‑scale evidence of high MAP prevalence in intensive European dairy herds (Netherlands and Denmark) and the role of these surveys in catalysing or reinforcing control efforts. The time span (1998–2000) aligns with the key survey dates. Geographic coding (Europe; Western Europe for the Netherlands and Northern Europe for Denmark) and classification as re‑occurrence (recognition and response to high endemic prevalence) are consistent with definitions. Sources (Irish prevalence paper for comparative European data, USDA Johne’s 2002 report summarising Danish data, and the 48‑country control review) are relevant; no major corrections are needed, though human experts may wish to consider whether subsequent major expansions of European programmes (e.g. in Germany or the UK) warrant additional separate events.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae
EPP.common.name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Western Asia; Central Asia
Host: Domestic goats (Capra hircus)
Event.summary: In 2009, several countries reported sizeable contagious caprine pleuropneumonia outbreaks, including 10 outbreaks in Tanzania (≈200 goats affected), 12 outbreaks in Yemen (≈800 goats affected), the first recorded CCPP outbreak in previously free Mauritius (≈300 goats affected), and four outbreaks in Tajikistan involving 166 goats. In Tajikistan, field and laboratory investigations confirmed CCPP for the first time, marking extension of the disease into Central Asia, while the Tanzania and Yemen outbreaks reflected ongoing endemic circulation in Eastern Africa and Western Asia. In Mauritius, introduction of infected goats from the African mainland led to establishment of CCPP and prompted serological surveys, movement controls and vaccination to prevent long‑term persistence on the island. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6830973/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Transboundary movement and trade of goats between endemic East African and Middle Eastern areas and newly affected territories (Central Asia and an Indian Ocean island state), together with inadequate biosecurity and limited or absent vaccination against CCPP, enabled long‑distance jumps and establishment of infection in Tajikistan and Mauritius while fuelling outbreaks in Tanzania and Yemen. Internal mechanisms: Strain-typing from this period reveals regionally distinct African and Asian clusters of Mccp but does not indicate emergence of a single novel pandemic lineage; the episode is best explained by dissemination of existing strains along trade networks and into new ecological and political settings rather than by major changes in virulence or host range. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6830973/?utm_source=openai))
Review: review – This event captures a documented 2009 multi-country wave with first confirmed CCPP in Tajikistan and Mauritius and substantial outbreaks in Tanzania and Yemen; the countries, timing and approximate outbreak sizes are consistent with Yatoo et al. 2019, EFSA/OIE summaries and primary reports. To comply with the project’s definitions, emergence-type coding has been adjusted so that only intra-continental emergence is marked yes, reflecting first entry into the Central Asia sub-region via Tajikistan; re-occurrence is set to no, because re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra-/inter-continental emergence at row level even though the episode also includes flare-ups in endemic sub-regions. Sub-regions have been standardised to the UNSD names (Eastern Africa; Western Asia; Central Asia), and the source list has been curated to remove an irrelevant science.gov link and a Tibetan antelope paper and to add targeted sources for the Mauritius and Tajikistan components.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae
EPP.common.name: Mccp (agent of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, CCPP)
Host: Domestic goats (Capra hircus)
Event.summary: In 2013, four Eastern African countries—Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia and Tanzania—reported a major regional wave of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, with AU‑IBAR data indicating 152 epidemiological units affected, over 556,000 susceptible goats at risk, 4,171 clinical cases and 672 recorded deaths, concentrated particularly in Ethiopia and Somalia. The outbreaks were widely distributed within these countries, confirming Eastern Africa as a hotspot of CCPP endemicity and illustrating substantial year‑to‑year fluctuation in incidence. Control responses included targeted vaccination, movement controls and enhanced laboratory confirmation, although under‑reporting and misclassification with other small‑ruminant respiratory diseases remained concerns. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6636563/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense goat populations, frequent transboundary movements across porous borders, seasonal aggregation at water and grazing points, and limited systematic vaccination programs favoured resurgence of CCPP, with climatic variability and pastoral mobility likely influencing the 2013 peak in reported outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: There is no strong evidence that the 2013 wave was driven by a new strain; instead, it reflects re-occurrence of endemic Mccp lineages under favourable transmission conditions, illustrating how external drivers (animal movement, climate, gaps in control) can generate large multi-country flare-ups without major evolutionary change. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6830973/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This row appropriately describes a large 2013 Eastern Africa CCPP wave documented in AU‑IBAR’s Pan African Animal Resources Yearbook and subsequent Ethiopian epidemiological studies, with plausible quantitative figures and correct geography (Africa; Eastern Africa; Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, Tanzania). Classification as re-occurrence (endemic re-surge within an already affected sub-region) with no intra-/inter-continental emergence is consistent with the event definition, and no major corrections beyond routine numerical cross-checking are needed.

Event.summary: In 2013, four Eastern African countries—Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia and Tanzania—reported a major regional wave of contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, with AU‑IBAR data indicating 152 epidemiological units affected, over 556,000 susceptible goats at risk, 4,171 clinical cases and 672 recorded deaths, concentrated particularly in Ethiopia and Somalia. The outbreaks were widely distributed within these countries, confirming Eastern Africa as a hotspot of CCPP endemicity and illustrating substantial year‑to‑year fluctuation in incidence. Control responses included targeted vaccination, movement controls and enhanced laboratory confirmation, although under‑reporting and misclassification with other small‑ruminant respiratory diseases remained concerns. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6636563/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense goat populations, frequent transboundary movements across porous borders, seasonal aggregation at water and grazing points, and limited systematic vaccination programs favoured resurgence of CCPP, with climatic variability and pastoral mobility likely influencing the 2013 peak in reported outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: There is no strong evidence that the 2013 wave was driven by a new strain; instead, it reflects re-occurrence of endemic Mccp lineages under favourable transmission conditions, illustrating how external drivers (animal movement, climate, gaps in control) can generate large multi-country flare-ups without major evolutionary change. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6830973/?utm_source=openai))
Review: retain – This row appropriately describes a large 2013 Eastern Africa CCPP wave documented in AU‑IBAR’s Pan African Animal Resources Yearbook and subsequent Ethiopian epidemiological studies, with plausible quantitative figures and correct geography (Africa; Eastern Africa; Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, Tanzania). Classification as re-occurrence (endemic re-surge within an already affected sub-region) with no intra-/inter-continental emergence is consistent with the event definition, and no major corrections beyond routine numerical cross-checking are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma gallisepticum
EPP.common.name: MG
Host: House finch (Haemorhous mexicanus), American goldfinch (Spinus tristis) and other wild passerine species
Event.summary: In the winter of 1993–1994, house finches with severe conjunctivitis were first observed at bird feeders in the Washington, D.C.–mid‑Atlantic region of the eastern United States, and a novel strain of Mycoplasma gallisepticum was isolated from affected birds, representing the first recognized involvement of this poultry pathogen in wild songbirds. Over the next three years, mycoplasmal conjunctivitis spread rapidly through the introduced eastern range of house finches, with citizen‑science surveillance documenting a sharp rise in disease reports and high prevalences across much of the eastern United States and into eastern Canada by the mid‑ to late‑1990s, and by late 1995 the outbreak also involved American goldfinches and other passerines, accompanied by marked declines in local house finch abundance. The initial epidemic wave peaked within a few years, after which disease incidence declined from early epidemic highs as some host populations crashed and infection transitioned toward an endemic pattern with ongoing but fluctuating transmission in eastern North America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities and frequent aggregation of house finches and other passerines at backyard bird feeders in suburban and urban landscapes facilitated efficient transmission and allowed continent‑scale surveillance of spread; the house finch is an introduced species in eastern North America with relatively low genetic diversity and no prior exposure to MG, likely increasing susceptibility; long‑distance movements and dispersal of finches helped propagate the epidemic front across the eastern range. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover of a poultry‑adapted pathogen into a novel wild passerine host community), emergence of a genetically distinct house‑finch‑associated MG clade (novel strain/genotype emergence) that produced severe conjunctivitis and high early mortality, and traits favoring efficient conjunctival and respiratory transmission that allowed rapid establishment and spread in dense feeder‑aggregated populations.
Review: review — MG was already a well‑known poultry pathogen in this host system long before 1990, so this event is not a first detection at the host‑system level. Reclassified the event type from first_detection=true to first_detection=false and re_emergence=true to reflect a major host shift and emergence of a novel finch‑adapted MG lineage within a subregion where MG was previously present in domestic poultry. Corrected the Canadian introduction year from 1996 to 1995 based on early outbreak reports indicating that mycoplasmal conjunctivitis was widespread in the eastern United States and Canada and had spread to American goldfinches by late 1995.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/3/1/97-0110_article?utm_source=openai)) This event clearly ranks among the most impactful MG emergence episodes (large geographic extent, severe population declines in house finches) and should be retained after quality control.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma gallisepticum
EPP.common.name: MG
Host: House finch (Haemorhous mexicanus) and other wild passerines
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, surveillance data and field observations indicated that the house‑finch‑associated Mycoplasma gallisepticum strain, initially confined to the introduced eastern range of the species, had crossed the central North American barrier posed by the Rocky Mountains and begun infecting house finches in the native western range, with first detections in the Rocky Mountain region (e.g. Montana) in 2002. Over the subsequent several years, mycoplasmal conjunctivitis became established in western house finch populations and was documented in multiple western U.S. states and western Canadian provinces, including British Columbia by the mid‑2000s, marking a major geographic extension of the wildlife reservoir within the same UN subregion. By around 2010, MG‑associated conjunctivitis was recognized as occurring annually in house finches across most of the continental United States and parts of southern Canada, with disease dynamics shifting toward a background endemic presence punctuated by local flare‑ups rather than a single synchronized epidemic front.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Natural dispersal and migration of house finches, including movements across and along the Rocky Mountains and across the northern Great Plains, facilitated westward spread; backyard feeding and urban/suburban aggregation in western North America created similar high‑contact environments that had supported epidemics in the east; lack of MG‑specific management in wild bird populations allowed unimpeded geographical expansion and establishment in new western populations. Internal mechanisms: The same poultry‑derived MG lineage that had adapted to house finches in the east retained sufficient fitness to survive in new climatic and ecological conditions in western North America (geographic range expansion) and showed evidence of evolutionary change in virulence during spread, with some western isolates exhibiting altered pathogenicity; its efficient conjunctival and respiratory transmission supported establishment in naïve western finch populations and occasional spillover to other passerines, representing a spatial re‑emergence and further geographic range expansion of an already emergent wildlife pathogen rather than appearance of a completely novel strain.
Review: review — The original row correctly identified the westward spread of house‑finch‑associated MG across North America as a major emergence episode but misclassified the event type and under‑reported Canadian involvement. Reclassified the event as re_emergence (re_occurrence=false, re_emergence=true), because MG had not disappeared from the Northern America subregion between 1994 and 2002; this episode reflects spatial expansion of the same emergent lineage rather than a simple resurgence after control. Updated the countries field to "United States of America [2002]; Canada [2004]" to reflect first detections in the Rocky Mountain region in 2002 and documentation of MG conjunctivitis in western Canadian house finches (e.g. British Columbia) by the mid‑2000s.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225627780_Dynamics_of_Mycoplasmal_Conjunctivitis_in_the_Native_and_Introduced_Range_of_the_Host?utm_source=openai)) Source list was adjusted to emphasize studies and summaries that explicitly describe continent‑scale spread and occurrences in Canada and the western United States; this event should be retained but flagged for expert review of the exact start/end years and provincial timing.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma mycoides subsp. mycoides
EPP.common.name: MmmSC
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus, Bos indicus and crossbred beef and dairy cattle in pastoral and agropastoral systems)
Event.summary: From about 1990, CBPP re‑emerged explosively in East and parts of Southern Africa, with infection moving from long‑standing foci in Angola, Sudan and the Horn via Uganda and Kenya into northern Tanzania (Ngorongoro, Arusha Region) and then into Kagera on the Uganda border. Over roughly 1990–2003, linked epidemics spread through much of Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda, Burundi, the Ituri region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Namibia, Zambia and Botswana, reinvading countries that had been free for decades and greatly expanding the geographic range of a largely homogeneous African epidemic lineage. By the early 2000s, coordinated regional vaccination, movement control and stamping‑out campaigns had reduced outbreak numbers, but CBPP remained entrenched and endemic in many of these subregions and continued to threaten neighboring free areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: FAO and WOAH analyses attribute the 1990s–early 2000s CBPP resurgence in Africa to weakened veterinary services and vaccination programs during economic crises and conflict, coupled with extensive formal and informal cattle movements along trade and transhumance routes that carried infection from long‑standing endemic foci in Angola and the Horn into previously free countries such as Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Zambia and Botswana. Dense pastoral networks, porous borders, and inadequate quarantine and surveillance allowed the disease to spread widely across Eastern, Middle and Southern Africa, with economic losses for Africa as a whole estimated in the billions of US dollars and hundreds of thousands of cattle deaths in Tanzania alone during 1990–2003. Internal mechanisms: Molecular typing shows that most 1990s outbreaks in East and Southern Africa were caused by closely related MmmSC strains, including a distinct African/“southern African” lineage and, in Botswana, a novel biotype with phenotypic differences from classical strains, consistent with clonal expansion of established African lineages and, in some areas, emergence of new biotypes. This episode thus represents both intra‑continental emergence into new subregions and re‑emergence driven by pathogen lineage expansion and chronic carrier states rather than by a completely new species or host jump.
Review: REVIEW – Retain this row as the major 1990–2003 regional CBPP wave in East/Middle/Southern Africa, which is well documented as re‑invading many previously free countries and causing very large losses (e.g. Tanzanian losses alone estimated at ~350,000 cattle deaths and >US$40 million). Corrected the list of countries to remove Angola as a purely pre‑1990 endemic source and to add Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Ituri) in line with FAO descriptions of newly infected/re‑invaded areas in the 1990s. Kept classification as intra‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence, as the episode involved spread of established African lineages and at least one novel biotype into new subregions and countries, rather than a first detection on the continent.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Mycoplasma mycoides subsp. mycoides
EPP.common.name: MmmSC
Host: Cattle in pastoral and agropastoral systems in northern, western and central Tanzania
Event.summary: After Tanzania had eradicated CBPP and been considered free since the 1960s, the disease was re‑introduced in June 1990 into Ngorongoro District (Arusha Region) via transboundary cattle movements from northern Kenya, followed by a separate outbreak in Kagera Region in 1991–1992 linked to southern Uganda. Through the 1990s CBPP spread widely within Tanzania, with official records indicating more than 160 outbreaks and several thousand cases and deaths by about 2001, heavily affecting pastoral and mixed crop–livestock communities. Intensive national control efforts combining vaccination, movement control and surveillance gradually reduced outbreak numbers in the early 2000s, although abattoir and serological surveys showed that CBPP remained widespread and endemic in many regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement of infected and carrier cattle from endemic areas in Kenya and Uganda into northern Tanzania initiated the re‑introduction, and internal cattle trade and seasonal transhumance then disseminated infection into western and central regions. EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus piscine
EPP.common.name: Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus, VHSV
Host: Farmed turbot (Scophthalmus maximus) in land‑based and tank‑based marine aquaculture facilities in Germany, on the Scottish island of Gigha, and at commercial farms in southwest Ireland; associated wild marine fish in adjacent North Sea and northeast Atlantic waters.
Event.summary: In 1991, VHSV was identified as the cause of a severe disease episode in farmed turbot in Germany, representing one of the first natural VHS outbreaks in a high‑value marine flatfish. Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Rapid development and intensification of turbot aquaculture in northern Europe, using raw seawater supplies in regions where VHSV was already present in wild marine fishes, provided large populations of susceptible, high‑value hosts with limited initial biosecurity. Movements of fish, equipment and seawater between facilities and hatcheries likely facilitated regional spread once virus entered captivity. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of marine genotype III VHSV from wild fish into turbot, a species shown experimentally to be highly susceptible; enhanced transmission and amplification in dense tank systems; and the emergence and farm‑level dominance of a turbot‑adapted strain such as UK‑860/94 associated with higher virulence in turbot than historical freshwater trout isolates.
Sources emphasize the German 1991 and Scottish 1994 farm outbreaks, subsequent reports from Ireland, and the role of genotype III in turbot mariculture.

Classified as re‑emergence (host expansion of genotype III within an already affected European region) rather than intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, consistent with the long‑standing presence of VHSV in European trout aquaculture and marine fish. EPP.scientific.name: Novirhabdovirus piscine
EPP.common.name: Viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus, VHSV
Host: Wild marine fish (e.g. herring, cod, whiting, turbot and other demersal species) in the Baltic Sea, Kattegat, Skagerrak, North Sea and adjacent North Atlantic coastal waters; incidental spillover into nearby marine aquaculture sites.
Event.summary: By the late 1990s, coordinated surveys in the Baltic Sea, Kattegat, Skagerrak and North Sea documented widespread infection of wild marine fishes with VHSV, and from around 1998 several mass‑mortality or high‑prevalence events in multiple species were attributed to marine VHS‑like viruses. As surveillance expanded, multiple marine genotypes (notably I and II) were detected in diverse species and locations around the Baltic and North Sea, demonstrating that VHSV had established a substantial and genetically structured marine reservoir beyond its traditional association with freshwater rainbow trout farms. Although acute mass‑mortality episodes subsequently decreased in frequency, marine VHSV has remained enzootic in these European shelf seas and continues to pose a risk of spillover into susceptible marine aquaculture species such as turbot and sea‑farmed rainbow trout.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term anthropogenic changes in the Baltic and North Sea, including eutrophication, altered food webs and intensive fishing, likely reshaped host population structure and stress levels in ways that favored VHSV transmission and persistence; international movements of fish and eggs for aquaculture and stocking may also have helped redistribute viral genotypes. Internal mechanisms: Geographic and ecological niche expansion of genotypes I and II from freshwater rainbow trout aquaculture into a wide array of wild marine fish species; diversification of marine VHSV lineages and population structure as shown by nucleoprotein and glycoprotein gene analyses; and efficient transmission linked to dense schooling behavior and overlapping spawning aggregations of susceptible pelagic and demersal fishes.
Review: retain: This event appropriately summarizes the late‑1990s recognition of a broad marine VHSV reservoir in wild fish across the Baltic, Kattegat, Skagerrak and North Sea, which had important implications for European aquaculture and fisheries risk. Countries and subregions listed match those most intensively surveyed, and classification as re‑emergence (rather than intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence) is consistent with VHSV’s long history in European trout farming and earlier sporadic marine detections. Start–end years (1998–2000) should be regarded as an approximate window centered on the main survey and mass‑mortality period and could be fine‑tuned with more detailed national survey timelines if needed.

EPP.common.name: Snake fungal disease
Host: Multiple wild snake species across the continental United States (58 species tested) and native snakes in Puerto Rico on U.S. military lands
Event.summary: From roughly 2013 onward, coordinated surveillance across 56 U.S. Department of Defense installations tested 657 snakes representing 58 species for Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola and documented widespread infection and ophidiomycosis across much of the eastern, midwestern, and newly the western United States, as well as on military lands in Puerto Rico. Event.summary: Around 2013, South Africa experienced a new wave of Newcastle disease outbreaks caused by genotype VIIh viruses that replaced earlier circulating genotypes (VIII, VIIb, VIId), initially detected in KwaZulu-Natal and subsequently spreading to other provinces.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6238702/?utm_source=openai)) By late 2013 the same genotype VIIh strain had been confirmed in neighbouring Zimbabwe, indicating rapid regional dissemination and causing substantial losses in commercial and smallholder poultry.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/tbed.12771?utm_source=openai)) Over the following two years, strengthened vaccination programmes and movement controls reduced outbreak frequency, but genotype VIIh became established as the dominant virulent NDV lineage in the subregion.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6238702/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross-border movement of poultry and informal trade in live birds, together with gaps in vaccination coverage and biosecurity in both commercial and smallholder sectors, facilitated regional dissemination of the newly introduced genotype VIIh virus.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/tbed.12771?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Re‑emergence linked to a novel genotype (VIIh) with high virulence that replaced prior endemic genotypes and expanded geographically within Southern Africa, illustrating genotype turnover and ongoing viral evolution in the region.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/tbed.12771?utm_source=openai))
Review: Retain – This event accurately captures the introduction and spread of genotype VIIh Newcastle disease virus in South Africa and Zimbabwe from 2013 onward, including its displacement of earlier genotypes and regional spread. The geographic scope, timing and classification as re-emergence driven by a novel genotype are consistent with detailed South African and broader African molecular epidemiology studies.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus schmallenbergense
EPP.common.name: Schmallenberg virus, SBV
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Domestic ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats); wild ruminants including cervids (e.g. red deer, roe deer) and European bison in affected regions
Event.summary: Origin: Between August and October 2011, a previously unknown orthobunyavirus was detected in dairy cattle with fever, diarrhoea and acute milk drop in North Rhine‑Westphalia (Germany) and across the Netherlands, and was identified and named Schmallenberg virus after the town where the index samples originated. Development: Over the 2011 and 2012 Culicoides midge seasons, SBV spread explosively across western and northern Europe and then into southern and parts of eastern Europe, with more than 5,700 infected farms officially reported by August 1, 2012 and high national‑level seroprevalence by 2013, causing tens of thousands of congenital malformations, abortions and stillbirths in calves, lambs and goat kids as naïve pregnant animals were infected in mid‑gestation. Ending: By 2013–2014, very high within‑herd and regional seroprevalence, together with the seasonal nature of the midge vectors, led to a marked decline in new clinical cases and a transition from epidemic spread to low‑level endemic circulation and sporadic congenital disease in previously unexposed or replacement stock.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive populations of competent Culicoides biting midges across northern and central Europe, favourable summer–autumn climatic conditions for vector survival and long‑distance windborne dispersal, high densities and connectivity of cattle and small‑ruminant herds, and a wholly naïve European ruminant population to Simbu‑group viruses collectively enabled rapid continental spread once SBV was introduced. Enhanced veterinary surveillance following the 2006–2008 bluetongue serotype 8 epidemic aided early detection and case documentation. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses indicate SBV is a novel or recently derived Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyavirus, likely arising via reassortment, representing a novel strain/genotype; its efficient replication in Culicoides vectors and ruminant hosts, and strong transplacental tropism leading to arthrogryposis–hydranencephaly syndrome in fetuses, underpinned its high apparent impact in immunologically naïve European herds, although virulence appeared relatively stable throughout this initial epidemic wave.
Review: Review – Retain as the foundational global emergence/European epidemic event, but country‑specific first‑detection years were corrected for France, the United Kingdom and Denmark (now starting in 2012 based on national reports), and the intra‑continental emergence flag was set to “false” to keep event‑type categories mutually exclusive, leaving this row classified primarily as first global emergence/first detection. Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Domestic ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats); wild ruminants including cervids (e.g. red deer, roe deer) and European bison in affected regions
Event.summary: Origin: Between August and October 2011, a previously unknown orthobunyavirus was detected in dairy cattle with fever, diarrhoea and acute milk drop in North Rhine‑Westphalia (Germany) and across the Netherlands, and was identified and named Schmallenberg virus after the town where the index samples originated. Development: Over the 2011 and 2012 Culicoides midge seasons, SBV spread explosively across western and northern Europe and then into southern and parts of eastern Europe, with more than 5,700 infected farms officially reported by August 1, 2012 and high national‑level seroprevalence by 2013, causing tens of thousands of congenital malformations, abortions and stillbirths in calves, lambs and goat kids as naïve pregnant animals were infected in mid‑gestation. Ending: By 2013–2014, very high within‑herd and regional seroprevalence, together with the seasonal nature of the midge vectors, led to a marked decline in new clinical cases and a transition from epidemic spread to low‑level endemic circulation and sporadic congenital disease in previously unexposed or replacement stock.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive populations of competent Culicoides biting midges across northern and central Europe, favourable summer–autumn climatic conditions for vector survival and long‑distance windborne dispersal, high densities and connectivity of cattle and small‑ruminant herds, and a wholly naïve European ruminant population to Simbu‑group viruses collectively enabled rapid continental spread once SBV was introduced. Enhanced veterinary surveillance following the 2006–2008 bluetongue serotype 8 epidemic aided early detection and case documentation. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses indicate SBV is a novel or recently derived Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyavirus, likely arising via reassortment, representing a novel strain/genotype; its efficient replication in Culicoides vectors and ruminant hosts, and strong transplacental tropism leading to arthrogryposis–hydranencephaly syndrome in fetuses, underpinned its high apparent impact in immunologically naïve European herds, although virulence appeared relatively stable throughout this initial epidemic wave.
Review: Review – Retain as the foundational global emergence/European epidemic event, but country‑specific first‑detection years were corrected for France, the United Kingdom and Denmark (now starting in 2012 based on national reports), and the intra‑continental emergence flag was set to “false” to keep event‑type categories mutually exclusive, leaving this row classified primarily as first global emergence/first detection. Sources are appropriate EFSA/EID/ANSES syntheses plus national summaries; Wikipedia links are treated as supplementary only.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoebolavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Ebola virus, EBOV
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event.summary: From late 2001 to 2003, several linked Ebola virus disease outbreaks due to Zaire ebolavirus occurred in forested border areas of northeastern Gabon and northwestern Republic of the Congo following presumed wildlife exposure. Transmission repeatedly spread from hunters and carcass handlers into villages on both sides of the border, resulting in roughly 300 reported cases and high case fatality, with outbreaks responding slowly to control because of remoteness and community mistrust. By the end of 2003, intensive surveillance, safe burials, and movement controls curtailed cross‑border chains of transmission and these outbreaks subsided.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-risk contact with infected great apes or other wildlife, cross-border movement in remote forest regions, limited access to healthcare, and delayed outbreak recognition fostered repeated spillover and community spread. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence suggests circulation of Central African Zaire ebolavirus lineages without clearly documented novel genotypes driving the outbreak; thus this is treated primarily as re-occurrence in a known ecological focus.

EPP.common.name: Ebola virus, EBOV
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event.summary: In 2012, Uganda experienced multiple Ebola virus disease outbreaks, including Sudan virus disease in Kibaale District and a separate outbreak later in the year, while Democratic Republic of the Congo reported a contemporaneous Zaire ebolavirus outbreak in Orientale Province. These outbreaks involved dozens of cases each, with transmission driven by close contact and limited infection prevention, but were detected and responded to more quickly than earlier events. By late 2012, strengthened surveillance, case isolation, and safe burials in both countries halted transmission and the outbreaks were declared over.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Recurrent zoonotic spillover in forested rural areas, ongoing weaknesses in infection prevention and early case recognition, and intense caregiving and funeral contact sustained localized epidemics. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses showed circulation of previously known Sudan virus and Zaire ebolavirus lineages rather than a clearly novel variant; these events are thus treated as re-occurrence in previously affected subregions.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoebolavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Ebola virus, EBOV
Sub.regions: Western Africa; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe; Northern America
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens)
Event.summary: In December 2013, Ebola virus disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus emerged in southeastern Guinea, marking the first known Ebola outbreak in West Africa and likely originating from a zoonotic spillover in a village near forested areas. Through the first half of 2014, undetected transmission and highly connected population movements allowed the virus to spread widely within Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone and then to additional African countries and, via travel, to Europe and North America, culminating in more than 28,000 reported cases and over 11,000 deaths, the largest Ebola epidemic on record. By early 2016, after massive international response, improved case management, safe burials, and community engagement, all known chains of transmission in West Africa and secondary affected countries were interrupted and the epidemic was declared over, though surveillance continued for flare‑ups.([who.int](https://www.who.int/emergencies/situations/ebola-outbreak-2014-2016-West-Africa?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely bat‑to‑human spillover in a remote village, rapid urbanization, porous borders, traditional burial practices, weak health systems, delayed recognition, and intense regional and international mobility all contributed to explosive spread; later, international deployment of resources, novel vaccines, and community-based interventions helped suppress transmission. Internal mechanisms: Genetic studies documented adaptive mutations during prolonged human transmission, but the core driver was geographic range expansion of Zaire ebolavirus into a new UNSD subregion (Western Africa) and new continents with in situ transmission (Europe, North America), so this event is classified as both intra-continental and inter-continental emergence and as re-emergence of an existing virus in new ecological and social settings.

EPP.common.name: Ebola virus, Marburg virus
Host: Humans; frequent contact with infected great-ape and other wildlife carcasses (gorillas and chimpanzees) implicated in spillover
Event.summary: From October 2001 through December 2003, a series of linked outbreaks of Ebola virus disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus occurred in forested border areas of northeastern Gabon (Ogooué-Ivindo Province) and northwestern Republic of the Congo (Cuvette-Ouest Region). Together these outbreaks caused roughly 300 human cases and more than 250 deaths, often following handling of carcasses of gorillas and chimpanzees and subsequent amplification through household caregiving and funerals. An intensive international response, including surveillance for wildlife die-offs, isolation of patients, safe burials, and community engagement, progressively interrupted transmission in both countries, and the last outbreak was declared over by late 2003.

Internal mechanisms: Genetic and epidemiologic analyses indicate multiple independent introductions of Zaire ebolavirus rather than a single expanding transmission chain, and there is no clear evidence for major new viral traits; this episode is therefore best classified as a severe re-occurrence within an already affected subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoebolavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Ebola virus, Marburg virus
Host: Humans; likely spillover from bats (wildlife reservoir not fully confirmed)
Event.summary: In late 2013, Zaire ebolavirus spilled over into humans in rural southeastern Guinea, initiating the first known Ebola outbreak in the Western Africa subregion and rapidly spreading to Liberia and Sierra Leone. Through 2014–2015 the epidemic expanded into dense urban settings and across borders, ultimately causing about 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, with limited secondary transmission in Nigeria, Mali, and single imported cases in Senegal and outside Africa. Aggressive international response, improved case isolation, safe burials, and deployment of experimental vaccines and therapeutics progressively reduced transmission, and WHO declared the end of the West Africa Ebola epidemic in 2016, with flare-ups linked to viral persistence in survivors.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High baseline mobility across porous borders, care-seeking and funerary practices involving direct contact with bodies, weak health systems overwhelmed by the scale of transmission, delayed recognition of Ebola in a region without prior history, and dense urban transmission corridors all amplified spread. Internal mechanisms: Not primarily associated with a radically novel strain, but high viral load and efficient human-to-human transmission of Zaire ebolavirus, combined with documented long-term viral persistence in immune-privileged sites of survivors that caused late flare-ups, contributed to the epidemic’s scale.
Review: retain – The 2013–2016 West Africa epidemic is correctly represented as the largest Ebola outbreak in history and an intra-continental emergence into the Western Africa subregion, where sustained human transmission had not previously been documented. Event.summary: In August 2018, Zaire ebolavirus was confirmed in North Kivu Province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, marking the country’s tenth recorded Ebola outbreak and the first in this conflict-affected region. The epidemic persisted for nearly two years, causing roughly 3,470 cases and 2,287 deaths across North Kivu, Ituri, and South Kivu provinces and spilling over briefly into neighboring Uganda, where a few family-cluster cases were detected. Massive ring-vaccination campaigns with rVSV‑ZEBOV‑GP, enhanced surveillance, and eventually improved security coordination enabled control, and the outbreak was declared over in June 2020.

Internal mechanisms: The outbreak involved Zaire ebolavirus strains similar to earlier Central African lineages without evidence of major new virulence traits; its scale was driven more by context than by viral novelty, although survivor persistence and rare reintroductions likely contributed to prolonged transmission.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthohantavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Hantavirus, HCPS, HFRS
Host: Oligoryzomys spp. and other sigmodontine rodents; humans
Event.summary: Following recognition of HPS in the United States, similar severe respiratory illnesses were retrospectively and prospectively identified in Brazil in 1993 and then in Argentina and Chile from 1995 onward, with laboratory confirmation of hantavirus infection and description of distinct South American virus lineages such as Andes and Juquitiba viruses. By the mid‑1990s, confirmed HPS cases had been reported in multiple Southern Cone countries, establishing South America as an additional focus of New World hantavirus disease with increasing annual case counts. National surveillance systems and rodent studies were expanded, and HPS incidence stabilized at lower levels after initial emergence but has persisted as an endemic–epidemic zoonosis in several South American countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Improved clinical awareness post‑1993, expansion of diagnostic capacity, and land‑use change in rural/agro‑forestry areas increased recognition and true exposure to sigmodontine rodent hosts. Internal mechanisms: Long‑standing but previously undetected circulation of multiple South American orthohantaviruses (e.g., Andes, Laguna Negra, Juquitiba and related strains) with inherent capacity to cause HPS; the event represents first detection of these lineages in humans on a new continent rather than de novo viral evolution.
Review: review – Event correctly captures early emergence of HPS in the Southern Cone, but country-specific onset years have been corrected to Brazil [1993], Argentina [1995], Chile [1995], Paraguay [1995], and Uruguay [1997] based on PAHO and national reports. Classification as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence for South America remains appropriate, and the episode is clearly among the most impactful Orthohantavirus emergences; retain after these geographic corrections.

Host: Rattus norvegicus (pet and breeder rats); humans
Event.summary: Beginning in late 2016 and recognized in early 2017, health authorities in the United States detected Seoul virus infections among workers at home‑based rat‑breeding facilities in Wisconsin and Illinois, with subsequent tracing revealing additional human cases and many infected pet rats across multiple U.S. states. The investigation ultimately identified dozens of facilities in at least 15 U.S. states and Canada linked by rat movements, and multiple confirmed human HFRS cases, representing the first documented outbreak of Seoul virus associated with pet rats in North America. Quarantine, culling of infected rat colonies, trade restrictions and public guidance for rat owners were implemented and gradually stopped further human cases linked to the affected ratteries, though low‑level Seoul virus circulation in wild rats persists.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of the “fancy rat” hobby, interstate and cross‑border trade of live rats, limited biosecurity in small‑scale ratteries, and lack of prior awareness of Seoul virus risk in pet rats allowed widespread dissemination before detection. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and efficient transmission of Seoul orthohantavirus within dense pet‑rat breeding networks (host‑system expansion) constituted a significant re‑emergence in North America, with phylogenetic analyses linking U.S. pet‑rat strains to European Seoul virus lineages introduced via international trade.
Review: retain – The 2016–2017 Seoul virus outbreak in pet rats across the United States and Canada, with 17 confirmed human infections and 31 facilities identified as infected, is the first recognized large pet-rat-associated Seoul virus outbreak in North America and illustrates international host-system expansion. Intra_continental_emergence has been changed from 'true' to 'false' because Orthohantavirus (including Seoul virus in wild rats) was already present in Northern America; the event is best coded as re_emergence due to spread in a new managed host network. Despite modest case numbers, its cross-border scope and novelty justify retaining it.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthopoxvirus monkeypox
EPP.common.name: Monkeypox virus, MPXV
Host: Humans; pet prairie dogs (Cynomys spp.); imported African rodents (Gambian pouched rats, dormice, rope squirrels and other small mammals)
Event.summary: In April 2003, a shipment of approximately 800 small mammals, including African rodents infected with mpox virus, was imported from Ghana into Texas and subsequently distributed to a Midwestern animal vendor where they were housed with prairie dogs. Starting in May 2003, human mpox cases appeared in several US states among people who had contact with infected pet prairie dogs, leading to 70‑plus suspected and 35–37 laboratory‑confirmed human infections, the first recognized human mpox outbreak in the Western Hemisphere. The outbreak was controlled by June 2003 through federal and state bans on import and movement of implicated species, quarantine and euthanasia of exposed animals, and intensive contact tracing, with no further onward transmission detected.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mpox/outbreaks/past-us-cases/index.html?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International wildlife trade in exotic pets enabled long‑distance movement of infected African rodents from Ghana to US distributors, mixing with prairie dogs that became secondary amplifying hosts, and close human–pet contact facilitated zoonotic transmission. Internal mechanisms: No major novel strain change was identified; the outbreak was caused by a West African clade (clade II) virus whose pathogenicity was already established, with the main novelty being the new ecological bridge into North American rodents and humans.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5227a5.htm?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Paramyxovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Paramyxovirosis
Host: African lions (Panthera leo; primary affected wildlife host); domestic dogs (maintenance reservoir); spotted hyenas, bat-eared foxes and other wild carnivores (spillover hosts)
Event.summary: In late 1993–early 1994, a morbillivirus closely related to canine distemper virus spilled over from large domestic dog populations surrounding Serengeti National Park in northern Tanzania into lions, causing sudden-onset neurologic disease and pneumonia. Over subsequent months, approximately 85% of Serengeti lions seroconverted and about one-third of the population died, while the epidemic spread northward into Maasai Mara lions in Kenya and affected other carnivores such as hyenas and bat‑eared foxes. As herd immunity built up in lions and dog vaccination began in surrounding communities, case numbers declined and the outbreak burned out by late 1994, although CDV has continued to circulate endemically at lower impact in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density, largely unvaccinated domestic dog populations around the Serengeti–Mara ecosystem provided a persistent CDV reservoir; close spatial overlap of dogs and wild carnivores at livestock/wildlife interfaces facilitated cross-species transmission; severe drought and heavy tick infestations increased Babesia co-infections in lions, greatly amplifying mortality. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and enhanced pathogenicity of canine distemper virus in non-canid carnivores, with unusually high mortality in lions and other species; efficient lion-to-lion transmission once established in prides, leading to rapid spread through an otherwise CDV-naïve lion metapopulation.
Review: retain – Added as a missing major paramyxovirus event. The 1993–1994 canine distemper epidemic in Serengeti–Mara lions caused ~30% lion mortality with >80% seroprevalence and affected multiple carnivore species, clearly ranking among the most impactful wildlife morbillivirus events. Classified as re-emergence (not intra-/inter-continental emergence) because CDV was long present in domestic dogs in East Africa; this outbreak reflects dramatic host expansion and increased virulence in wildlife within an already affected subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Paramyxovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Paramyxovirosis
Host: Domestic pigs (primary amplifying host); humans (spillover); dogs (incidental spillover); fruit bats (Pteropus spp., reservoir)
Event.summary: Between late 1998 and mid-1999, a novel paramyxovirus (Nipah virus) caused severe respiratory and neurologic disease in pigs on farms in peninsular Malaysia, with at least 265 associated human encephalitis cases and over 100 deaths among pig farmers and abattoir workers, and 11 additional human cases linked to imported pigs in Singapore. The outbreak spread from initial foci in Perak through movement of infected pigs to large commercial farms in Negeri Sembilan and to abattoirs in Singapore, prompting intensive investigations that identified a new henipavirus closely related to Hendra virus. Drastic control measures, including culling of around one million pigs and bans on pig movement, ultimately stopped transmission in pigs and ended human cases by mid-1999.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Deforestation and agricultural expansion in peninsular Malaysia pushed fruit-bat reservoirs into closer contact with intensive pig production systems; large-scale, high-density pig farming with frequent animal movements facilitated rapid farm-to-farm and cross-border spread; initial misdiagnosis as Japanese encephalitis delayed targeted control. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a bat-borne henipavirus to pigs and then to humans, with highly efficient pig‑to‑pig respiratory transmission and high viral loads in respiratory secretions; geographic range expansion from localized bat reservoirs into intensive pig belts through livestock movements.
Review: retain – This is correctly identified as the first global emergence and detection of Nipah virus, with accurate description of pig and human case numbers, geographic spread within Malaysia and into Singapore, and control measures (mass pig culling and movement bans). Event classification focuses on virus-level emergence (henipavirus) rather than the broader paramyxovirus family, which is reasonable for this EPP entry. Sources (CDC MMWR, WHO, peer‑reviewed articles) are appropriate and more informative than general summaries.
