EPP.scientific.name: Paramyxovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Paramyxovirosis
Host: Harbour seals (Phoca vitulina; primary affected host); grey seals (Halichoerus grypus; some cases)
Event.summary: In May 2002, unusually high mortality among harbour seals was first detected around the Danish island of Anholt in the Kattegat, marking the start of a second major phocine distemper virus (PDV) epizootic in northwestern Europe following the 1988 outbreak. Over roughly nine months, the infection spread through seal colonies along the North Sea and Baltic coasts of Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, the United Kingdom and Ireland, killing an estimated 21,700–30,000 seals, or about half of the North Sea harbour seal population. As population immunity increased and the seasonal pupping period ended, new cases declined and the epidemic subsided by late 2002, leaving long-lasting demographic impacts on many regional seal populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A large, immunologically naïve generation of harbour seals born since the 1988 epizootic, high seal densities at haul-out sites in the Wadden Sea and other coastal areas, and seasonal movements and mixing of colonies facilitated rapid virus spread; migrating Arctic or sub-Arctic seals have been hypothesized as carriers introducing PDV into North Sea populations. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence of PDV in an already affected seal metapopulation, with efficient seal‑to‑seal transmission and high case-fatality leading to catastrophic mortality; no major genomic shift compared with the 1988 virus, but waning population immunity created conditions for a second large-scale outbreak.
Review: retain – Added as a missing event. The 2002 phocine distemper virus epizootic killed roughly 20,000–30,000 harbour seals (≈50% of the North Sea population) across multiple Northern and Western European countries, clearly placing it among the most impactful animal paramyxovirus events since 1990. Classified as re-occurrence (second major PDV epizootic in the same subregions, with no evidence of a fundamentally novel strain) and not as inter-continental emergence; subregions and affected countries have been expanded and corrected using CDC EID and other primary sources.

Host: Farmed Litopenaeus vannamei in land-based recirculating aquaculture and biosecure facilities in North America, with linked detections in imported stocks in the United Kingdom
Event.summary: After more than two decades without reports from U.S. shrimp farms, IHHNV was again detected in 2019 in specific‑pathogen‑free L. vannamei cultured in fully contained systems in New Mexico, California, Texas and Florida, with whole‑genome sequencing of Texas and Florida isolates showing they were infectious type 2 lineages nearly identical to an Ecuadorian strain. Immediate notifications to WOAH in 2019–2020 also documented first occurrences of IHHNV in four Canadian indoor L. vannamei facilities and at two sites in the United Kingdom (an experimental facility with high mortality in imported shrimp and a commercial facility receiving apparently healthy but infected post‑larvae), all epidemiologically linked to movements of live shrimp from the Americas. Although large‑scale mortalities were not reported in most affected North American farms, the episode demonstrated renewed transboundary spread of infectious IHHNV into high‑biosecurity systems, prompted quarantines and depopulation of affected units, and raised concern about chronic growth impacts and potential spillover to additional facilities or wild shrimp.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: international trade in live L. vannamei broodstock and post‑larvae between Ecuador, the United States and other countries; gaps in pre‑movement viral screening and certification that allowed IHHNV‑positive lines to be designated as specific‑pathogen‑free; and ongoing expansion of high‑density, land‑based shrimp culture in North America and Europe that creates new opportunities for pathogen introduction. Internal mechanisms: introduction of an infectious type 2 IHHNV lineage capable of persistent, often subclinical infection in L. vannamei; high genetic similarity between U.S. isolates and the Ecuador strain, implying a recent common source; and the virus’s ability to cause measurable reductions in growth and survival even in tolerant lines when viral loads in post‑larvae are high, as illustrated by experimental work estimating substantial per‑hectare economic losses at high infection intensities.
Review: Retain – This is a major recent re‑emergence episode in which an infectious type 2 IHHNV lineage linked to Ecuador was detected in multiple U.S. states and, via live‑shrimp movements, in Canada and the United Kingdom, triggering international notifications, quarantine and depopulation measures. I expanded the geographic and temporal scope to align with WOAH and USDA reporting (New Mexico and California as well as Texas and Florida; Canada and UK detections in 2019) and reworded the countries field accordingly. In line with the project’s rules and the Ebola example, I did not classify this as an inter‑continental emergence event for Europe, because the UK detections occurred in closed facilities with no documented onward establishment; instead, I treat them as part of a linked transboundary re‑emergence centered on North America. The original 'intra_continental_emergence' and 're_occurrence' flags were removed and the event is now coded purely as re‑emergence, reflecting introduction of a new infectious lineage into a previously infected continent with clear implications for modern high‑biosecurity production systems.

EPP.scientific.name: Penstylhamaparvovirus decapod1
EPP.common.name: PstDV1, IHHNV
Host: Wild and broodstock Penaeus monodon (black tiger shrimp)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, molecular studies of wild and broodstock Penaeus monodon from Madagascar, Mauritius, Mozambique and Tanzania identified IHHNV‑related DNA sequences integrated into the shrimp genome, representing genotypes 3 and 4 (Type A and Type B) that are distinct from the infectious IHHNV genotypes circulating in the Americas and much of Asia. These integrated endogenous viral elements (EVEs) did not produce clinical disease or transmissible infection in experimental bioassays, but their discovery demonstrated long‑standing historical exposure of African tiger shrimp lineages to IHHNV‑like viruses and revealed a major source of false positives for standard PCR assays designed to detect infectious IHHNV. The findings led to refinement of diagnostic methods and to guidance aimed at avoiding unwarranted trade restrictions on African P. monodon broodstock based solely on EVE-positive PCR results.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increased genetic and virological surveillance of wild P. monodon stocks for aquaculture broodstock sourcing and international trade; global concern over shrimp viral diseases triggering more intensive pathogen screening. Internal mechanisms: presence of ancient, non‑infectious IHHNV‑related EVEs (genotypes 3 and 4) integrated into the genomes of African P. monodon populations, which complicate molecular diagnosis of infectious IHHNV and required the development of discriminating PCR assays that can distinguish EVEs from active viral infection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3550757/))
Review: Decision: review. This row correctly describes the discovery of non-infectious IHHNV-related endogenous viral elements in African P. monodon but the original classification as inter-continental emergence and first detection of infectious IHHNV was misleading; all emergence-type flags have been set to No to avoid implying introduction or resurgence of infectious virus.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3550757/)) Because these EVEs have no demonstrated direct disease or production impact, but do have important diagnostic and trade implications, this episode sits at the margin of the project’s emergence-event definition and should be reviewed by domain experts to decide whether to retain it as one of the top events or treat it only as contextual information.

EPP.scientific.name: Penstylhamaparvovirus decapod1
EPP.common.name: PstDV1, IHHNV
Host: Farmed Penaeus vannamei (Pacific white shrimp) in indoor and outdoor aquaculture facilities
Event.summary: In 2019, IHHNV reappeared in North American shrimp aquaculture after a long absence from US farms and was reported for the first time from Canada and from Europe (United Kingdom), in a set of epidemiologically linked events associated with international trade in post‑larval P. vannamei. The United States reported two disease events in indoor facilities: a recurrence of IHHNV infection in New Mexico with subsequent movement of infected shrimp to a facility in California, and the first reported occurrences in Texas and Florida aquaculture facilities, prompting quarantine and depopulation of affected tanks. In the same year, Canada reported its first occurrence of IHHNV in four of its five indoor P. vannamei culture premises, traced to importation of infected post‑larvae from a common overseas supplier, and the United Kingdom reported its first detections in an experimental facility and a commercial aquaculture site, both linked to imported shrimp from an IHHNV‑positive source. These detections highlighted ongoing risks of long‑distance spread of IHHNV through international trade in ostensibly SPF post‑larvae and led to strengthened import controls, surveillance and on‑farm biosecurity in the affected countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: globalization of shrimp broodstock and post‑larval trade; reliance on indoor or recirculating aquaculture systems sourcing stock from international hatcheries; incomplete or inconsistent pathogen screening in export chains; and high animal movements between facilities within and across countries. Internal mechanisms: inter‑continental emergence of infectious IHHNV into Europe (first confirmed detection in the United Kingdom) and renewed establishment in previously affected North American production systems, with predominantly chronic infection phenotypes in P. vannamei causing reduced growth and economic losses rather than dramatic acute mortality.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/ihhnv-pathways-assessment.pdf))
Review: Decision: retain. Cleaned the country list to include only the three countries for which immediate notifications of cultured-shrimp IHHNV events were reported to WOAH in 2019 (United States, Canada, United Kingdom) and removed Mexico and the subnational entry “Texas, Florida aquaculture facilities”, which are either endemic-background or subnational and therefore inappropriate in the Countries field.([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/ihhnv-pathways-assessment.pdf)) Reclassified the emergence types so that this episode is treated primarily as an inter-continental emergence into Europe (first detection in the UK) plus a recurrence in North American facilities described in the narrative, but without tagging re_occurrence or re_emergence at the row level to avoid violating the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with inter-continental emergence in a single event row.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus marinus
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis (Dermo disease of oysters)
Countries: Mexico [2006] (Nayarit, Pacific coast lagoons including Boca de Camichín and Pozo Chino)
Host: Crassostrea corteziensis (native Cortez oyster, farmed and wild) and Saccostrea palmula (native rock oyster) on the Pacific coast of Mexico
Event.summary: Beginning in late 2006, Perkinsus marinus was detected in cultured populations of the native oyster Crassostrea corteziensis in Nayarit State on Mexico’s Pacific coast, marking establishment of the parasite in this native host and ocean basin. Over the subsequent years, surveys showed low to moderate prevalence infections in C. corteziensis in Nayarit and, by around 2010, in native rock oysters Saccostrea palmula across multiple coastal lagoons in Sinaloa, generally without dramatic mass mortalities but with evidence of sublethal effects. By the mid‑2010s, P. marinus was recognized as widely but patchily distributed in native oyster assemblages along sections of the Mexican Pacific, prompting concern about its longer-term impact on native oyster resources and aquaculture.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Historical and ongoing movements of live oysters and other bivalves from the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic coast for aquaculture and restoration are strongly implicated as the source of P. marinus introductions to Pacific lagoons, with local environmental conditions (warm temperatures, moderate to high salinity) supporting parasite establishment. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and geographic range expansion, as P. marinus successfully colonized new native hosts (C. corteziensis and S. palmula) and ecosystems on the Pacific side, aided by parasite genotypes closely related to U.S. Atlantic and Gulf strains that tolerate regional temperature–salinity regimes.
Review: review - Start year and within-country timing were corrected to reflect evidence that P. marinus was first detected in C. corteziensis in Nayarit in 2006 and subsequently in S. palmula in Sinaloa around 2010, based on Cáceres-Martínez et al. (2008, 2012, 2016) and related work. The event is retained as a single, linked re-emergence episode representing sustained host and geographic expansion within the Mexican Pacific, still not qualifying as intra-continental emergence because it remains within the existing 'Central America' subregion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus marinus
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis (Dermo disease of oysters)
Countries: Brazil [2014] (Rio São Francisco estuary, Sergipe State)
Host: Crassostrea gasar (= C. brasiliana; native mangrove/estuarine oyster) and Crassostrea rhizophorae in northeastern Brazil
Event.summary: Following the 2013 confirmation in Paraíba, subsequent studies in 2014–2015 documented Perkinsus marinus infecting native oysters Crassostrea gasar and C. rhizophorae in additional northeastern Brazilian estuaries, including the Rio São Francisco estuary in Sergipe State and the Mamanguape estuary in Paraíba. These surveys showed moderate to high infection prevalences, evidence of tissue damage, and concern about sublethal and lethal impacts on both wild and cultured oysters. Over the next several years, the parasite became recognized as widely distributed among northeastern Brazilian estuaries and capable of infecting multiple native oyster hosts, indicating an expanding and consolidating regional epizootic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued spread of P. marinus within interconnected coastal systems of northeastern Brazil, facilitated by natural dispersal of infective stages via currents, as well as local trade and movement of oysters for consumption and culture, in estuarine conditions favorable to parasite survival. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence through host expansion and increasing strain diversity, as P. marinus established in C. gasar—an important native cultured species—while maintaining high prevalence in C. rhizophorae, thereby enlarging the parasite’s host and ecological niche in the South Atlantic.
Review: review - This row appropriately summarizes the post-2013 spread of P. marinus to C. gasar and additional estuaries in northeastern Brazil and is best viewed as a re-emergence episode driven by host expansion and geographic consolidation within the same UNSD subregion ('South America'). The original classification incorrectly set 'intra_continental_emergence' to 'Yes' even though the parasite was already present in the same subregion; this has been changed to 'No' while retaining 're_emergence' as 'Yes'.

Host: Crassostrea virginica (eastern/American oyster) in wild and cultured populations at and beyond the historical northern range of the species

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus olseni
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis
Host: Manila clam Ruditapes philippinarum (wild and cultured)
Event.summary: From the mid‑1990s, high prevalences of Perkinsus olseni were documented in Manila clam beds in Japan and on the west coast of Korea, coinciding with marked declines in clam production and recurrent summer mortality episodes. The parasite became established with infection prevalences often approaching 100% and high infection intensities in many intertidal flats, contributing to density‑dependent growth reduction and mortality in heavily exploited or farmed beds. Through the early 2000s, these infections remained endemic with recurrent mortality peaks but did not lead to complete stock collapse everywhere due to ongoing recruitment, translocations and local management interventions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of Manila clam aquaculture and maintenance of very high natural densities in intertidal mudflats, combined with warming summer temperatures, eutrophication and occasional hypoxia, increased host stress and facilitated parasite transmission and persistence. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and establishment of P. olseni in East Asian Manila clam metapopulations, together with its high tolerance of warm, low‑oxygen conditions and ability to reach very high tissue burdens, drove a major re‑emergence of disease expression in this host, even though the parasite species was already known from other regions and hosts.
Review: review – Retain this as a major East Asian emergence episode, but I corrected the country‑specific start years to Japan [1998] and Republic of Korea [1997] based on Hamaguchi et al. 1998 and Choi & Park 1997, and recoded the event as re‑emergence only (host/geographic expansion and entrenched high‑intensity infection) instead of both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence, to keep emergence categories mutually exclusive as specified.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus olseni
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis
Host: Manila clam Ruditapes philippinarum; carpet shell clam Ruditapes decussatus
Event.summary: In the mid‑1990s, perkinsosis caused by Perkinsus olseni (then often termed P. atlanticus) was linked to severe mortality episodes in Manila and carpet shell clams in estuaries of Portugal and Spain, building on earlier outbreaks and causing substantial production losses. Through the late 1990s the parasite became widespread along Iberian Atlantic coasts and was also detected along the French Atlantic coast, sometimes with infection prevalences near 100% in affected beds. Mortalities abated somewhat after initial peaks but the parasite remained entrenched as an endemic, production‑limiting pathogen in European clam aquaculture and wild fisheries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Co‑introduction and large‑scale translocation of Manila clams for aquaculture in Europe from the 1970s onwards, together with eutrophication and warming coastal waters, facilitated establishment and spread of P. olseni between estuaries. Internal mechanisms: The parasite’s broad host range allowed spillover from introduced Manila clams to native Ruditapes decussatus and other venerids, and its capacity for very high proliferation in gill and digestive tissues impaired filtration, growth and condition, driving a re‑emergence of high‑impact disease in clam fisheries despite earlier recognition of the parasite in the region.
Review: review – Event is real and clearly among the highest‑impact global outbreaks (Portugal, Spain, France), but I recoded it as re‑emergence only. Earlier work (e.g. Azevedo 1989) shows that severe mortalities in R. decussatus began in the 1980s, so the 1994–2000 period represents continued and expanded epizootics rather than a simple re‑occurrence driven purely by external factors; host expansion from introduced Manila clams and sustained high parasite loads justify re‑emergence as the primary category.

EPP.scientific.name: Perkinsus olseni
EPP.common.name: Perkinsosis
Host: Mediterranean mussel Mytilus galloprovincialis (farmed and wild)
Event.summary: During routine monitoring of Mediterranean mussel farms and natural banks in Campania (Italy) from 2019 onward, histology and molecular diagnostics first revealed Perkinsus olseni infections in Mytilus galloprovincialis, a host not previously reported for this parasite in Europe. In parallel, mussel mortality events in Catalonia (Spain) in 2020 were associated with similar Perkinsus infections, with prevalence up to about 20% at some sites and inflammatory lesions in digestive and gonadal tissues. By 2021, P. olseni had been confirmed as an emerging pathogen of Mediterranean mussels in both countries, raising concern for mussel aquaculture and prompting recommendations for broader surveillance of cross‑species transmission from clams to mussels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive bivalve aquaculture with co‑cultured clams and mussels, movements of seed and market shellfish, and regional hydrodynamics likely facilitated spillover of P. olseni from heavily infected clam populations into mussel stocks; ongoing warming and environmental stress may have enhanced disease expression and host susceptibility. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion of a generalist parasite to M. galloprovincialis, with molecular analyses indicating distinct haplotypes in mussels compared to classic European clam isolates, represents a re‑emergence driven by cross‑species transmission and possible intraspecific genetic diversification toward a new host.
Review: review – This recent mussel event is well-supported by Carella et al. 2023 and clearly constitutes a host‑expansion episode with potential production impacts. I recoded emergence types by removing first_detection (which should apply at host‑system scale, not to individual new host species) and retaining re‑emergence to reflect cross‑species transmission of an established parasite within the same European subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Phlebovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Bunyaviridae (Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyaviruses affecting animals: Schmallenberg virus, Akabane virus, Cache Valley virus)
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Domestic ruminants (primarily cattle, sheep and goats)
Event.summary: In late summer and autumn 2011, dairy cattle in western Germany and the Netherlands developed a new febrile syndrome with milk drop and diarrhea, from which a novel Simbu‑serogroup orthobunyavirus—Schmallenberg virus (SBV)—was identified, marking the first known member of this virus group to cause disease in European ruminants. Over winter 2011–2012 and into 2013, SBV spread rapidly across western, northern and southern Europe via Culicoides midges, with malformed lambs, kids and calves reported in many countries as in utero infections during the 2011 vector season translated into congenital arthrogryposis, hydranencephaly, stillbirths and neonatal mortality, and tens of thousands of holdings ultimately reporting cases. After this epidemic phase, the virus transitioned to low‑level endemic circulation with occasional localized outbreaks, as high seroprevalence, changes in breeding management and, in some countries, voluntary vaccination limited the scale of subsequent waves.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of a novel Simbu‑serogroup virus into a naïve European ruminant population—originating likely from endemic regions in Africa or Asia through movement of infected vectors or animals—followed by efficient onward transmission by abundant Culicoides biting midges whose activity was favored by temperate climatic conditions; dense, seasonally breeding sheep and goat populations, and autumn pregnancies that coincided with peak vector activity, amplified the impact through synchronized congenital disease. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (SBV as a previously undescribed orthobunyavirus, probably a reassortant between Sathuperi‑ and Shamonda‑like viruses) conferring effective replication in European Culicoides species and high fetal neurotropism, enabling rapid geographic range expansion and high levels of congenital disease in susceptible herds and flocks.
Review: Decision: review. This event correctly captures the major 2011–2013 SBV epidemic in European ruminants and its classification as an inter‑continental emergence of Simbu‑group viruses into Europe is appropriate.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167587714000828?utm_source=openai)) However, the earlier version mis‑labelled it as first_global_emergence and first_detection, which properly refer to the 1970s Akabane emergence in Japan for this grouped EPP; these flags have been set to false. The list of affected countries was expanded to include Ireland, Norway and Estonia, based on national reports and EFSA/ECDC syntheses, though some country‑specific start years (2012–2013) are approximate and should be validated against EFSA datasets.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.common.name: Phocine distemper virus, PDV
Host: Harbour seal (Phoca vitulina); Grey seal (Halichoerus grypus)

By late 2002 and early 2003, mortality had fallen back to near‑baseline levels as the susceptible pool was depleted and herd immunity increased, leaving heavily reduced but recovering harbour seal populations across the North Sea–Kattegat–Skagerrak system, with grey seals widely exposed but much less affected clinically.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: high densities of harbour seals at coastal haul‑out sites, seasonal aggregation during moulting and breeding, and strong connectivity among colonies in the Wadden Sea, Kattegat–Skagerrak, North Sea, and parts of the southern Baltic facilitated rapid regional spread; possible re‑introduction from Arctic harp or ringed seal reservoirs or via long‑range movements of grey seals, combined with environmental stressors such as contaminants and prey shifts, may have increased susceptibility. EPP.scientific.name: Porcine circovirus 2
EPP.common.name: Porcine circovirus-associated disease, PCVAD
Host: Domestic pigs in commercial herds, including large integrated systems in China and neighboring East Asian countries
Event.summary: Around 2000, China reported its first PMWS cases linked to PCV2, followed by a major expansion of PCV2 infection and PCVAD outbreaks across coastal and central provinces by 2002–2003, with high seroprevalence in post‑weaning and grower pigs and heavy economic losses. During this period, PCV2‑associated disease was also documented in other East Asian countries such as Korea and Japan, indicating rapid regional establishment after initial incursions from North America/Europe. By the mid‑2000s, PMWS/PCVAD had become one of the most significant viral diseases of pigs in China and East Asia, prompting widespread diagnostic and control efforts and setting the stage for later genotype shifts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification and expansion of pig production in China and neighboring countries, high farm densities, and extensive movements of pigs and pig products (including genetic stock importation from Europe and North America) facilitated PCV2 establishment; limited early awareness and absence of vaccines allowed large outbreaks before control measures were developed. Internal mechanisms: Introduction and local evolution of multiple PCV2 genotypes (initially PCV2a, then PCV2b) with high prevalence and frequent co‑infections (PRRSV, CSFV and others) that enhanced disease severity; genomic studies indicate widespread circulation and diversification of PCV2 in China from 2000 onward, which underpinned later shifts toward more fit genotypes such as PCV2d.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections made: (1) Event Year adjusted from “2000-2003” to “1999-2003” so that the episode now includes the first published PMWS/PCV2 detections in Japan and the Republic of Korea in 1999, while still covering the early‑2000s expansion and major outbreaks in China and Viet Nam; (2) an additional primary source documenting the first PMWS‑associated PCV2 detection in Japan was added to the Source URLs. Continent and sub‑region labels and classification as an inter‑continental emergence event for Asia remain appropriate.

EPP.common.name: Porcine circovirus-associated disease, PCVAD
Sub.regions: Northern America; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Host: Domestic pigs in intensive swine production systems in North America and Western/Northern Europe
Event.summary: Between approximately 2003 and 2007, many pig‑producing regions in North America and Western/Northern Europe reported a wave of severe PCVAD outbreaks, with sharp increases in diagnostic submissions and field reports linking high nursery and grow‑finish mortality to PCV2, often of the emerging PCV2b genotype. In the United States and Canada, these outbreaks were characterized by high case fatality, extensive co‑infection with PRRSV and other respiratory pathogens, and substantial economic losses, while in Europe, similar increases in PMWS/PCVAD incidence were observed in France, the Netherlands, and the UK despite previous experience with PMWS. The wave of severe disease largely subsided after 2006–2007, coinciding with rapid rollout of effective PCV2 vaccines in major pig markets and widespread incorporation of vaccination into routine herd health programs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High global pig densities, intensive production practices, extensive movement of animals within continents, and frequent co‑infection with PRRSV and other pathogens created conditions for widespread expression of severe PCVAD; economic pressures and management changes (e.g., all‑in/all‑out, larger batch sizes) increased immunological stress and pathogen mixing. Internal mechanisms: Increasing dominance of PCV2b over PCV2a in North America and Europe, along with high viral loads and strong immunostimulation, contributed to more frequent and severe PCVAD episodes; although the primary internal mechanism was genotype replacement rather than a single novel strain, the resulting disease surge represents a major re‑occurrence and re‑emergence of PCVAD in already affected subregions, mitigated only after vaccination dramatically reduced clinical cases.
Review: Decision: review. Corrections made: (1) set Intra-continental emergence to “No”, because all listed sub-regions (Northern America; Western/Northern Europe) were already affected by PCVAD in earlier events and this represents a severe resurgence rather than first occurrence in a new sub-region; (2) set Re-emergence to “Yes” to reflect the global genotype shift from PCV2a to PCV2b associated with increased disease impact; (3) expanded the Event Year from “2005-2007” to “2003-2007” to encompass early PCV2b-associated surges in Europe as well as the 2004–2007 peak in North America; and (4) adjusted country-specific start years for the United States and Canada to 2004 so they fall within the revised event window. Event.summary: Beginning in late 2007, Thailand reported large PEDV outbreaks starting in Nakhon Pathom province and rapidly spreading to multiple provinces and swine farms nationwide. EPP.scientific.name: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus
EPP.common.name: PEDV, Alphacoronavirus 1
Host: Domestic pigs of all ages, with very high mortality in neonatal suckling piglets
Event.summary: From October 2010, China experienced a large-scale PED epizootic in which severe diarrhea with 80–100% mortality in suckling piglets spread rapidly among previously vaccinated sow herds in multiple southern and eastern provinces. During 2010–2012, genetically related PEDV variants displaced classical strains and caused repeated farm-level outbreaks despite routine use of CV777-based vaccines, leading to major piglet losses and economic damage to the Chinese swine industry. Outbreak intensity gradually declined as updated control measures and partial population immunity developed, although the new variant lineage became endemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density industrial pig production, extensive inter-provincial pig and piglet movements, and inadequate farm biosecurity allowed rapid geographic expansion; reliance on vaccines based on classical CV777 strains created strong selection for immune-escape variants. Internal mechanisms: Emergence of highly virulent GII variant strains with substantial spike-gene divergence from CV777 (reducing neutralization), increased intestinal tropism and high viral loads in the small intestine produced increased virulence and vaccine breakthrough, representing classic novel strain emergence with increased pathogenicity.
Review: retain - This is one of the highest-impact PEDV events globally and is accurately described as a re-emergence episode in China driven by highly virulent GII variants that broke through CV777-based vaccination. Geography, timing and mechanisms are well-supported by multiple primary EID reports and later molecular-epidemiology reviews; no structural corrections needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus
EPP.common.name: PEDV, Alphacoronavirus 1
Sub.regions: Northern America; Central America; Caribbean; South America
Host: Domestic pigs in all commercial sectors, particularly neonatal piglets in sow farms
Event.summary: In April–May 2013, highly virulent PEDV was first detected in the United States, where it rapidly spread to swine farms in dozens of states within months, causing very high morbidity and up to 95% mortality in suckling piglets and an estimated loss of more than seven million piglets during the first year. During late 2013 and 2014, the same Asian-like lineage was reported with in situ transmission in Mexico, Peru, the Dominican Republic, Canada, Colombia and Ecuador, establishing PEDV across much of North, Central and South America. Intensive control efforts, including enhanced biosecurity, transport and rendering/feed-chain sanitation, and sow exposure or vaccination, eventually reduced outbreak frequency, but PEDV became enzootic at lower levels throughout the Americas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of an Asian-derived, high-virulence PEDV GII lineage into a largely naïve Western Hemisphere pig population; extensive movements of pigs, piglets and contaminated transport vehicles; shared slaughter and rendering networks; and possible contamination of feed ingredients collectively drove rapid cross-border dissemination. Internal mechanisms: The invading strains belonged to genetically distinct, highly pathogenic GII lineages with spike-gene changes associated with enhanced virulence and efficient replication; in the absence of pre-existing population immunity, this produced explosive epidemics and very high piglet mortality across multiple American countries.
Review: review - Event retained as a major global episode but expanded from a North American focus (USA, Canada, Mexico) to cover the documented 2013–2014 inter-continental introduction of PEDV into the wider Americas (adding Peru, Dominican Republic, Colombia, Ecuador) and corrected continent/sub-region coding accordingly. The event type was adjusted so it is classified purely as inter-continental emergence (not first detection at the host-system level, which occurred decades earlier in Europe). Source list was strengthened by adding detailed Canadian and Mexican outbreak reports and the Lv et al. 2016 review while dropping reliance on Wikipedia; exact national start months and loss estimates remain approximate and warrant further checking.

Event.summary: After earlier PEDV activity in the 1990s and 2000s, Eastern Asia experienced a major re-emergence of highly virulent GII PEDV from late 2013 onward. South Korea reported widespread PED outbreaks in late 2013–2014, while Japan, after several quiet years, saw a large-scale epidemic beginning in late 2013 that spread to most prefectures by 2014 and continued with substantial herd-level losses into 2016, with hundreds of thousands of pigs estimated to have died. Internal mechanisms: Outbreak viruses clustered within highly virulent GIIa lineages and showed near-identity in the spike gene to North American epidemic strains but clear divergence from historical local PEDV, consistent with re-emergence driven by new, more virulent and transmissible genotypes that partially escaped existing vaccine-derived immunity.

EPP.scientific.name: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus
EPP.common.name: PEDV, Alphacoronavirus 1
Host: Domestic pigs on commercial and smallholder farms, with highest mortality in neonatal and suckling piglets
Event.summary: From 2013, South-eastern Asia experienced new high-virulence PEDV outbreaks associated with GII variants closely related to recent Chinese strains. In Viet Nam, genotype IIb PEDV was detected in multiple herds in 2013 and recurred over subsequent years, while in 2014–2015 the swine industry in the Philippines suddenly suffered large PED outbreaks characterized by severe watery diarrhea and near-100% mortality in suckling piglets on many affected farms. These episodes caused marked piglet losses and production disruptions in both countries, and PEDV remained enzootic with intermittent severe flare-ups despite increasing awareness and control efforts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of pig production in Viet Nam and the Philippines, high densities of pigs around urban and peri-urban areas, extensive movement of pigs and feed ingredients within and between countries, and limited early biosecurity and vaccine coverage favored introduction and onward spread of Chinese-origin PEDV. Internal mechanisms: The Vietnamese and Philippine outbreaks were caused by GIIb/GIIa variants with spike-gene changes linked to high virulence and close genetic relatedness to recent Chinese field strains, indicating re-emergence driven by novel, more pathogenic genotypes rather than persistence of older classical CV777-like viruses.
Review: review - New row added to capture major 2013–2015 re-emergence of high-virulence PEDV in South-eastern Asia, particularly genotype IIb/IIa outbreaks in Viet Nam and the large 2014–2015 epidemic in the Philippines with very high piglet mortality. These outbreaks are clearly among the more impactful regional episodes yet were missing from the original list; classification as re-emergence (not first detection or inter-/intra-continental emergence) is consistent with earlier PEDV presence in the region. National data could further refine the duration and relative impact in each country.

EPP.scientific.name: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus
EPP.common.name: PEDV, Alphacoronavirus 1
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Domestic pigs on breeding, farrow-to-finish and fattening farms
Event.summary: In 2014, Europe saw re-emergence of PEDV when epidemic diarrhea was reported on German pig farms, including a large 1,200-head fattening operation in southern Germany, followed by outbreaks in sow and farrow-to-finish herds. Over 2014–2016, closely related S-INDEL PEDV strains, genetically akin to the U.S. OH851 variant, were detected in the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Austria, Italy, Portugal, Slovenia and several Central and Eastern European countries including Czechia, Hungary and Ukraine, causing variable but sometimes high piglet mortality and widespread herd infection. By 2016, reported outbreaks had decreased, but PEDV persisted at low levels in parts of Europe, raising concern about ongoing viral evolution and sporadic severe episodes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long gaps without significant PEDV activity left many European herds immunologically naïve, while intense intra-European pig movements, shared transport networks, and initial lack of awareness created favorable conditions for dissemination of reintroduced strains. Internal mechanisms: Molecular studies showed that most 2014–2016 European strains formed a relatively homogeneous S-INDEL cluster related to, but distinct from, U.S. high-virulence strains, suggesting one or a few recent introductions followed by regional evolution with generally reduced but still variable virulence; in Ukraine, more virulent GIIa US-like viruses were also detected, illustrating co-circulation of different re-emergent genotypes.
Review: review - Event retained as the principal 2014–2016 European re-emergence but the country list was expanded (adding Netherlands, Austria and Slovenia) and some start years were corrected (for example Ukraine to 2014 and Belgium to 2015) based on comprehensive European reviews. Classification as re-emergence (rather than inter- or intra-continental emergence) remains appropriate because PEDV was already present in Europe. Given reliance on regional syntheses for some dates, country-specific onset years should be double-checked against national outbreak reports.

EPP.scientific.name: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus
EPP.common.name: PEDV, Alphacoronavirus 1
Host: Domestic pigs in industrial systems, particularly neonatal piglets despite prior vaccination
Event.summary: Following the large 2010–2012 PED epizootic, China continued to experience recurrent PEDV outbreaks from 2017 onward, with episodes of severe diarrhea and high piglet mortality reported on vaccinated farms across multiple provinces. During this period, genomic surveillance documented ongoing diversification of variant GII strains, with emergence of subgroup lineages such as GII-a (e.g. strain HM2017) showing high virulence in experimental infections. These recurrent outbreaks gradually declined in some regions as biosecurity and updated vaccine strategies improved, but PEDV remained an important endemic and periodically epidemic pathogen in Chinese pig production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent high-density industrial pig production, incomplete vaccine coverage, and continued long-distance movement of pigs and piglets sustained viral circulation and periodic re-introduction into susceptible herds. Internal mechanisms: Continued evolution of GII PEDV variants, including accumulation of mutations and recombination in the spike gene, produced sub-lineages with maintained or increased virulence and partial immune escape from existing CV777-based and early variant vaccines, exemplifying re-emergence driven by novel strain/genotype emergence and possible enhanced transmission.
Review: retain - This row appropriately captures the post-2016 pattern of recurrent, variant-driven PEDV outbreaks in China as a re-emergence episode with ongoing diversification of GII sub-lineages. Geography, time span and mechanisms are consistent with recent molecular-epidemiology reviews; detailed quantification of impact varies between sources but the episode clearly ranks among the major recent events, so no structural changes are recommended.

EPP.common.name: Pox viruses infection

Internal mechanisms: Host Expansion (Spillover) of monkeypox virus from endemic African rodent reservoirs to prairie dogs; Enhanced Transmission through high-density housing and close contact, although no clear adaptive mutations were documented; Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) across continents via trade rather than natural dispersal.
Review: Retain – Accurately describes the 2003 U.S. monkeypox epizootic with appropriate classification as first detection and inter-continental emergence (established transmission among imported/exotic rodents in North America, not just single imported cases). No changes needed.

Host: Cattle (Bos taurus, Bos indicus and crossbreds); water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis, limited)
Event.summary: In August 2015 lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) was confirmed for the first time in the European Union in cattle herds in Evros, northern Greece, following progressive northward spread from endemic foci in Africa and the Middle East. During 2016 the disease spread rapidly across the Balkans, affecting Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Serbia, Albania and Montenegro and causing thousands of outbreaks, production losses and extensive trade restrictions. Mass vaccination campaigns using live homologous capripox vaccines and movement controls from 2015–2017 progressively contained the disease, and by 2018 the Balkans were considered free of active LSDV transmission although the virus remained endemic in parts of Africa and Asia.

Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of LSDV from Africa–Middle East into the European continent; available genomic data indicate that the viruses in south‑eastern Europe were closely related to Middle Eastern field strains without major adaptive change.

Host: African lions (Panthera leo) – free-ranging populations in Serengeti ecosystem (Tanzania/Kenya) and in Kruger and Etosha National Parks (South Africa, Namibia)([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/237001/))
Event.summary: From the late 1980s into the 1990s, serosurveys of free-ranging African lions in East Africa (Serengeti ecosystem) and Southern Africa (Kruger and Etosha National Parks) revealed very high prevalences (often >70–90%) of antibodies and lentiviruses closely related to FIV, indicating that lion-specific FIV-like viruses (FIVple) were endemic across multiple lion populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/237001/)) Through the 1990s and early 2000s, follow-up epidemiologic and molecular studies confirmed widespread infection and multiple divergent FIVple subtypes, documenting natural history and patterns of multiple infection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC371036/)) The episode continued as an essentially stable, enzootic infection without clear mass die-offs, but raised conservation concerns regarding potential long‑term health impacts and risks of moving infected lions into naïve populations.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8877134/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-standing, high-density lion populations with frequent aggressive contact (fighting, biting) that facilitate efficient lentiviral transmission; translocation and management of lions between reserves with limited prior virological screening, raising concern over virus introduction into naïve populations.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8877134/)) Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and long-term adaptation of FIV-like lentiviruses to lions, yielding lion-specific FIVple strains; novel strain/genotype emergence (multiple distinct FIVple subtypes and co-infections in individual lions), and possible increased virulence/pathogenicity relative to domestic cat FIV, as suggested by immunopathologic changes in some lion populations.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/237001/))

Corrected emergence classification: SIV/FIV were already known in African primates and domestic cats before FIVple was characterized in lions, so this episode is not the first detection of the EPP in the animal host system nor clearly an intra-continental emergence into a new African sub-region. Instead it represents recognition of a long-established, host-adapted FIV lineage and associated novel clades in lions. I therefore set first_detection=No and intra_continental_emergence=No, and kept re_emergence=Yes to capture host expansion/novel genotype emergence. Geography, timing and sources remain appropriate but the row should be reviewed as part of a linked long-term enzootic rather than a short outbreak.

Event.summary: In the early 1990s, retrospective testing and prospective serosurveys in eastern Australia demonstrated that FIV had been present in domestic cats since at least the 1970s and had become widely established by the 1990s, with reported seroprevalence ranging from about 4% to over 30% in some populations of adult cats.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822633/)) Through the mid‑1990s, additional surveys in Australia and subsequently New Zealand documented FIV across pet, stray and feral cat populations, confirming that the virus was firmly endemic in Oceania and associated with outdoor access and fighting behavior.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822633/)) By the late 1990s, FIV was recognized as a major chronic infection of cats in the region and became an important consideration for vaccination, testing policies and cat population management.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12509431/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growth of outdoor and feral cat populations, high densities in urban and peri‑urban areas, and frequent bite-related contact promoted efficient horizontal transmission; limited early awareness and absence of control programs enabled silent spread.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822633/)) Internal mechanisms: FIV exhibits relatively low virulence and chronic infection with prolonged asymptomatic carriage, facilitating long-term survival and onward transmission; genetic subtypes (notably subtype A in Australia) demonstrate geographic structuring but no evidence of sudden virulence shifts during this emergence period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10822633/))
Review: Decision: retain. FIV-Fca was first isolated in California in 1986, so this episode is not the global first detection of the EPP but rather its establishment in a new continent. I therefore set first_detection=No and retained inter_continental_emergence=Yes to reflect the spread and endemic establishment of FIV in domestic cats in Oceania. Timing (early–mid 1990s) and geography (Australia and New Zealand) are consistent with published seroprevalence and molecular data, though the exact start year is approximate and should be treated as such.

EPP.scientific.name: Primate lentivirus
EPP.common.name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Domestic cats (Felis catus) – owned, stray and shelter cats in urban areas of Brazil and Argentina([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3347033/))
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, FIV was first recognized in domestic cats in South America, with reports from Brazil in 1993 and Argentina in 1994 documenting FIV-seropositive pets in major urban centers.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3347033/)) During the 1990s and 2000s, multiple studies across Brazilian states and Buenos Aires showed FIV seroprevalence typically between about 3% and 20% in tested cats, with some clinic-based series reporting even higher proportions in sick, free-roaming males.([scielo.br](https://www.scielo.br/j/cr/a/TWNSRzyDGTmDncgxDY4wj8M/?lang=en)) By around 2010, FIV was considered established in domestic cat populations throughout much of Brazil and parts of Argentina, making South America a fully involved continent in the global burden of feline lentiviral infection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3347033/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and dissemination of infected domestic cats within and between South American cities, combined with large populations of intact, free-roaming males, low neutering rates, and high levels of outdoor access, promoted efficient bite-associated transmission; limited early awareness and testing meant that infection could spread widely before being recognized.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3347033/)) Internal mechanisms: As elsewhere, chronic, often subclinical FIV-Fca infection with long infectious lifespans and multiple circulating subtypes supported persistence within cat populations, but there is no evidence of a major virulence shift unique to South America during this period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12509431/))
Review: Decision: retain (newly added). This row was added because FIV infection in domestic cats in South America, first recognized in Brazil (1993) and Argentina (1994), represents a clear inter-continental emergence event after 1990 and involves large numbers of cats with substantial reported seroprevalence.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3347033/?utm_source=openai)) The event is classified as inter_continental_emergence=Yes (spread of FIV-Fca into a previously unaffected continent) with first_detection=No (global first detection occurred in North America in 1986). Years and country start dates follow the earliest published reports but are still approximate and should be reviewed against any additional national data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Primate lentivirus
EPP.common.name: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
Host: Western lowland gorillas (Gorilla gorilla gorilla) and other gorillas in southwestern Cameroon and neighboring regions([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nri1992))
Event.summary: In 2006, researchers reported for the first time an HIV‑1–like virus in wild gorillas, identifying simian immunodeficiency virus from gorillas (SIVgor) in fecal samples from western lowland gorillas in southwestern Cameroon.([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nri1992)) Subsequent surveys during the late 2000s expanded sampling across multiple gorilla groups in Cameroon and neighboring countries, revealing additional SIVgor‑infected individuals and establishing that gorillas host a distinct SIV lineage most closely related to HIV‑1 group O.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3234451/)) By around 2010, molecular analyses indicated that SIVgor arose from a cross‑species transmission of SIVcpz from sympatric chimpanzees into gorillas, providing a likely primate source for HIV‑1 group O and refining our understanding of primate lentivirus evolution.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3234451/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Ecological overlap between chimpanzee and gorilla populations in Central African forests, including shared habitats and potential for interspecies aggression or scavenging, facilitated spillover of SIVcpz into gorillas; human bushmeat hunting and field surveys provided the samples enabling detection.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3234451/)) Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover of SIVcpz into gorillas) with establishment of a novel, gorilla-adapted lentivirus lineage (SIVgor); novel strain/genotype emergence through recombination and adaptation; potential differences in pathogenicity relative to SIVcpz remain under study.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3234451/))
Review: Decision: retain with corrections. Discovery of SIVgor in wild gorillas in southwestern Cameroon in 2006 is the first documented detection of this lentivirus lineage in gorillas and an important link to HIV‑1 group O, justifying first_detection=Yes.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3234451/?utm_source=openai)) However, SIVs were already known from Central African primates, and all sampled sites (Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon) fall in the UN “Middle Africa” sub-region, so intra_continental_emergence was set to No and the sub_regions field corrected to “Middle Africa” only. I also set re_emergence=No because available data indicate long-standing host adaptation rather than a recent viral change or resurgence.

EPP.scientific.name: Proboscivirus elephantid1
EPP.common.name: Elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus
Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – captive, orphan and free-ranging wild calves and juveniles
Event.summary: EEHV hemorrhagic disease was first recognized in India in 1997, with isolated fatal cases in young captive elephants later confirmed retrospectively by PCR, and by the early 2010s multiple investigations documented clusters of EEHV1-associated hemorrhagic deaths in both captive and wild calves in southern India. Studies from Kerala and neighboring states between roughly 2011 and 2017 identified at least 20 PCR-confirmed EEHV infections, including numerous fatal cases in wild and orphan calves and subclinical infections in adults, alongside later cases in Assam and other regions. By the late 2010s, Indian authorities reported dozens of EEHV-HD deaths nationwide, including a 2019 cluster of four calf deaths in Nandankanan Zoo and an additional wild calf in Odisha, establishing EEHV-HD as a substantial emerging threat to the country’s endangered Asian elephant population.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of wildlife veterinary capacity, necropsy programs, and PCR laboratories in Indian states such as Kerala and Assam greatly increased case detection; increasing habitat fragmentation and human–elephant interactions may have altered herd structure and calf stress, although direct causal evidence remains limited. Internal mechanisms: Indian cases are dominated by virulent EEHV1A (with additional EEHV1B and EEHV4 detections), and sequencing of more than 20 lethal cases has revealed a wide diversity of EEHV1A/1B lineages similar in range to those found in Europe and North America, supporting long-standing endemicity; the shift from rare recognized cases in the late 1990s to frequent confirmed cases in the 2010s reflects a combination of high underlying disease burden and improved molecular diagnostics, consistent with re-emergence driven by both viral diversity and changing surveillance.
Review:
RETAIN – This multi-year episode appropriately summarizes India’s emergence and subsequent high burden of EEHV-HD, including early recognition in 1997, extensive molecular documentation of lethal and subclinical cases, and major clusters such as the 2019 Nandankanan/Odisha events. Coding as intra_continental_emergence (new Asian sub-region: Southern Asia) and re_emergence (diverse local genotypes, broader host range including wild calves) is justified and consistent with the definitions.
No corrections to country, sub-region, or event-type coding were necessary. Additional primary Indian references (e.g., extended genotypic evaluation and Assam case series) could be cited for even greater detail but are not essential for this high-level event row.

EPP.scientific.name: Proboscivirus elephantid1
EPP.common.name: Elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus
Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – captive calves and juveniles
Event.summary: Beginning in 2006, Thailand reported its first PCR-confirmed EEHV cases in captive Asian elephant calves, and over 2006–2019 a growing number of fatal hemorrhagic disease episodes were documented across camps and zoos throughout the country. Survival analyses and national case series identified at least several dozen confirmed EEHV-HD cases, with EEHV1A and EEHV1B predominant and EEHV4 also detected, alongside evidence of subclinical shedding in adults. By the late 2010s, Thai veterinary authorities recognized EEHV-HD as a leading cause of death in young elephants under human care, prompting establishment of a national EEHV task force, coordinated surveillance, and standardized treatment protocols.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid growth of the captive elephant tourism sector increased the number of susceptible juveniles and facilitated close clinical monitoring, while establishment of national diagnostic laboratories and training in EEHV PCR significantly improved case ascertainment. Internal mechanisms: genetic analyses revealed multiple EEHV1 lineages and recognition of EEHV4 in Thai elephants, indicating ongoing diversification and highlighting that several EEHV subtypes can cause lethal disease; widespread subclinical infections in adults, documented by trunk swabs and serology, support a model of endemic latent infection with occasional high‑load primary infections in vulnerable calves driving re-emergence.
Review:
REVIEW – Thailand’s EEHV-HD burden is substantial and clearly belongs among the most impactful events, but the original classification marked this as intra_continental_emergence even though Thailand lies in the same UN sub-region (South-eastern Asia) as the earlier Cambodian case.
Change made: intra_continental_emergence reset to false because South-eastern Asia was already affected by EEHV-HD by 2004; the event is retained as re_emergence to reflect recognition of multiple viral subtypes and the sharp rise in diagnosed cases. Country and temporal span (2006–2019) are appropriate given national datasets; URLs are targeted Thai case-series and overviews.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Proboscivirus elephantid1
EPP.common.name: Elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Northern America
Host: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) – primarily captive calves and juveniles; occasional young adults
Event.summary: From 1990 through at least 2020, Europe and North America experienced a sustained accumulation of EEHV hemorrhagic disease cases, with retrospective and prospective studies documenting more than 60 confirmed fatal EEHV1/4/5 cases in young Asian elephants in zoos and circuses across these regions and numerous survivors following intensive antiviral and supportive therapy. Reviews of 27 European EEHV-HD fatalities and multiple North American case series showed that EEHV-HD had become the single largest cause of death in juvenile Asian elephants under human care in both continents. By the late 2010s, coordinated workshops, surveillance programs, and research collaborations recognized EEHV as a chronic, recurrent threat to ex situ Asian elephant populations rather than an isolated outbreak phenomenon.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: demographic shifts in zoo elephant populations (more calves surviving to the susceptible 1–8 year age window), changes in husbandry, and systematic adoption of PCR surveillance all increased recognition of EEHV-HD; international collaboration through EEHV advisory groups and workshops improved reporting and standardized case definitions. Internal mechanisms: co-circulation of multiple highly virulent EEHV1A/1B, EEHV4, and EEHV5 genotypes with latent infection in adults and intermittent shedding contributed to ongoing transmission; European analyses suggest possible roles for host genetics and zoo-associated management factors in mortality risk, indicating that both viral evolution and host/population factors underlie the sustained re-occurrence and re-emergence of disease.
Review:
RETAIN – This long-term Europe–North America episode appropriately synthesizes three decades of recurrent EEHV-HD, during which the virus became the leading cause of juvenile Asian elephant mortality in these regions. Coding as both re_occurrence (driven by demographic and management factors) and re_emergence (due to diversification and recognition of additional genotypes EEHV4 and EEHV5) is defensible, given the mixed external and internal drivers.
No changes to timing, geography, or event-type classification were necessary, although users should note that the U.S. country tag references archival cases dating back to the late 1980s within an event window starting in 1990. The cited European impact and prevalence studies are highly relevant for this aggregate event.

EPP.scientific.name: Pseudogymnoascus destructans
EPP.common.name: White-nose syndrome fungus, Pd
Host: Multiple species of hibernating insectivorous bats, including Myotis lucifugus, Myotis sodalis, Myotis septentrionalis, Perimyotis subflavus, Eptesicus fuscus and others
Event.summary: The event began in the winter of 2006–2007, when bats in a commercial cave near Albany, New York, USA, were first photographed with characteristic white fungal growth and then found dead in large numbers, marking the first recognized occurrence of white-nose syndrome and Pseudogymnoascus destructans in North America. Over the subsequent winters to about 2012, the fungus spread rapidly through hibernacula in eastern and central United States and into eastern Canada (first confirmed in Quebec and Ontario in 2010), causing catastrophic declines of several bat species and an estimated 5.7–6.7 million bat deaths across at least 16 U.S. states and four Canadian provinces. By around 2012 the disease had become entrenched throughout much of eastern North America, with some local populations functionally extirpated and mortality rates falling mainly because susceptible bats had already been largely eliminated rather than because the outbreak ended.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of an exotic, psychrophilic cave fungus from Eurasia into North American hibernacula, most likely via human-mediated movement (e.g. contaminated clothing or equipment) to a hub cave near New York; high connectivity among bat hibernation sites through seasonal movements and swarming behavior; and suitable cold, humid microclimates in mines and caves that favor persistent environmental contamination and repeated exposure. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission and environmental persistence of Pd on bat skin and cave substrates, allowing efficient spread among densely clustered, hibernating bats; geographic range expansion enabled by the fungus’s tolerance of cold subterranean environments throughout eastern North America; and extreme host naivete in North American bat species, which lacked evolved tolerance to infection and therefore experienced very high mortality compared with Eurasian bats.
Review: review: Retain this as the primary major emergence event for Pd because it captures the introduction into a new continent (North America) and the associated mass mortality (~5.7–6.7 million bats by 2012 across at least 16 U.S. states and four Canadian provinces).([fws.gov](https://www.fws.gov/story/2012-01/north-american-bat-death-toll-exceeds-55-million-white-nose-syndrome)) Classification was adjusted so that this row is coded only as an inter-continental emergence (inter_continental_emergence=Yes; first_detection reset from Yes to No) to avoid double-coding and to align with the definition that inter-continental emergence denotes first established occurrence in a new continent with in situ transmission. This event does not represent global first presence of Pd in bats, which clearly predates 1990 in Eurasia, so first_global_emergence and first_detection are appropriately set to No. Geography (continent North America, sub-region Northern America, USA [2006] and Canada [2010]) and the 2006–2012 time window are consistent with primary sources on the origin and early spread of WNS in eastern North America.([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/articles/what-is-white-nose-syndrome.htm?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Psoroptes ovis
EPP.common.name: Sheep scab
Host: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries)
Event.summary: At the beginning of the 21st century sheep scab had been pushed close to eradication in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, but from October 2010 the official veterinary service in the border municipality of Santana do Livramento began diagnosing new foci of ovine sarna (Psoroptes ovis) near the Caneleira area following farmer complaints.([pdfs.semanticscholar.org](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/db2f/54c10fca688c9114390ca28ebe255d56e92f.pdf)) During 2011–2012, intensified surveillance documented at least 11 additional scab foci along the Coxilha Negra and other localities on the dry border with Uruguay, with fences on the Uruguayan side covered in wool and repeated reinfestation of Brazilian flocks despite whole‑flock ivermectin treatment and quarantine of affected farms.([seapi.rs.gov.br](https://seapi.rs.gov.br/upload/arquivos/201612/02101318-inftec-35-caracterizacao-da-ovinocultura-em-santana-do-livramento.pdf)) By early 2013 these outbreak clusters had been brought under operational control through coordinated treatment and movement restrictions, but the border zone remained vulnerable to further incursions, and a severe outbreak on a 121‑sheep farm in São Vicente do Sul around 2017 illustrates that Psoroptes ovis has become re‑established more broadly in Rio Grande do Sul.([seapi.rs.gov.br](https://seapi.rs.gov.br/upload/arquivos/201612/02101318-inftec-35-caracterizacao-da-ovinocultura-em-santana-do-livramento.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive cross‑border grazing and animal movements along a long, largely unfenced dry frontier with Uruguay; differing official scab treatment protocols (two‑dose ivermectin in Rio Grande do Sul versus single‑dose regimens in Uruguay) and variable adherence to whole‑flock treatment; high stocking densities on native pasture; and reliance on reactive case management rather than coordinated preventive control, all of which allowed repeated reintroduction and spread of Psoroptes ovis between neighbouring flocks and across the international boundary.([seapi.rs.gov.br](https://seapi.rs.gov.br/upload/arquivos/201612/02101318-inftec-35-caracterizacao-da-ovinocultura-em-santana-do-livramento.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: No novel parasite strain, host expansion or acaricide resistance was reported in these outbreaks; they are therefore interpreted as re‑occurrence in a region that had nearly eliminated scab, driven primarily by husbandry and transboundary movement factors.([seapi.rs.gov.br](https://seapi.rs.gov.br/upload/arquivos/201612/02101318-inftec-35-caracterizacao-da-ovinocultura-em-santana-do-livramento.pdf))
Review: Decision: review – This event has been added because the 2010–2012 Santana do Livramento outbreaks, linked to contemporaneous cases across the Uruguayan border and followed by later foci in Rio Grande do Sul, represent one of the best‑documented and more impactful post‑1990 sheep scab resurgences outside Europe; the 2010–2012 time span reflects the main documented cluster, but continued lower‑level circulation is likely yet poorly quantified, so classification as a regional re_occurrence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) and inclusion of both Brazil and Uruguay should be checked by regional experts.([seapi.rs.gov.br](https://seapi.rs.gov.br/upload/arquivos/201612/02101318-inftec-35-caracterizacao-da-ovinocultura-em-santana-do-livramento.pdf))

EPP.scientific.name: Psoroptes ovis
EPP.common.name: Sheep scab
Host: Beef cattle (Belgian Blue breed, Bos taurus)
Event.summary: During the winters of 2016–2019, investigators visited 16 Belgian Blue beef farms in Flanders (Belgium) and the neighbouring Dutch province of Zeeland where psoroptic mange in housed cattle persisted despite correctly administered injectable macrocyclic lactone (ML) treatments and confirmed active Psoroptes ovis infestations on all farms.([assets-eu.researchsquare.com](https://assets-eu.researchsquare.com/files/rs-9599/v3/a3c62f0f-fbe7-49b1-a0e8-c74a29d1692b.pdf?c=1632767314&utm_source=openai)) In vivo trials showed that mite populations on 12 of the 16 farms failed to clear after two standard treatment rounds and met quantitative criteria for ML resistance, while broader surveys indicated that about 74% of Belgian Blue farms in northern Belgium had mange problems and many farmers regarded the disease as difficult or impossible to control.([assets-eu.researchsquare.com](https://assets-eu.researchsquare.com/files/rs-9599/v3/a3c62f0f-fbe7-49b1-a0e8-c74a29d1692b.pdf?c=1632767314&utm_source=openai)) These findings marked the emergence of multi‑drug‑resistant psoroptic mange as a major endemic health and welfare problem in Belgian Blue cattle in Western Europe, with sporadic export‑linked outbreaks reported in other countries, and triggered calls for improved diagnostics, alternative acaricides and breeding for reduced susceptibility.([backoffice.biblio.ugent.be](https://backoffice.biblio.ugent.be/download/8705139/8705144?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high stocking densities and close contact in housed beef systems; intensive selection for double‑muscled Belgian Blue cattle, which appear immunologically predisposed to severe psoroptic mange compared with other breeds; and decades of frequent, sometimes sub‑optimal use of ML products (e.g. underdosing, long intervals, partial treatment of groups) for mange and other parasites, creating strong selection pressure for resistance.([backoffice.biblio.ugent.be](https://backoffice.biblio.ugent.be/download/8749176/8749178?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Confirmed development and spread of Psoroptes ovis populations with reduced sensitivity or resistance to multiple ML compounds (ivermectin, doramectin, moxidectin), supported by pharmacodynamic and genetic studies showing altered expression of detoxification genes in resistant mites; this clearly fits the definition of re‑emergence driven by antimicrobial resistance rather than simple re‑occurrence.([assets-eu.researchsquare.com](https://assets-eu.researchsquare.com/files/rs-9599/v3/a3c62f0f-fbe7-49b1-a0e8-c74a29d1692b.pdf?c=1632767314&utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: review – This new event captures the large and well‑documented problem of macrocyclic lactone‑resistant psoroptic mange in Belgian Blue cattle in Belgium and the Netherlands, which likely ranks among the most impactful modern P. ovis episodes in cattle; coding as re_emergence (due to acquired ML resistance) in Western Europe and limiting the country list to Belgium and the Netherlands is justified by current data, but precise estimates of the number of affected herds and the wider European distribution of resistant mites should be confirmed in future expert review.([assets-eu.researchsquare.com](https://assets-eu.researchsquare.com/files/rs-9599/v3/a3c62f0f-fbe7-49b1-a0e8-c74a29d1692b.pdf?c=1632767314&utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Ranavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Ranavirosis
Host: Multiple wild amphibian species (e.g. Rana sylvatica, Lithobates pipiens, Ambystoma tigrinum, Hyla spp.); primarily larval and metamorphic stages
Event.summary: Between 1996 and 2001, the USGS National Wildlife Health Center recorded at least 64 amphibian morbidity and mortality events across the United States, many involving mass die‑offs of larvae or metamorphs in ponds where ranavirus infection was confirmed, with mortality often exceeding 90%. These outbreaks affected numerous frog and salamander species over a broad geographic range from the northeastern U.S. to the upper Midwest and western states, and similar Ambystoma tigrinum virus epizootics were documented in Canadian prairie salamander populations. Together, these events showed that ranaviruses were widely distributed in North American amphibian communities by the late 1990s and could cause recurrent, severe larval mortality.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High host densities in breeding ponds; environmental stressors such as drought, crowding and contaminants; and anthropogenic translocation of amphibians (e.g. bait salamanders and bullfrog trade) that redistributed FV3‑ and ATV‑like lineages within the continent. Internal mechanisms: highly virulent FV3‑ and ATV‑like strains capable of causing systemic infection and rapid mortality in larvae, with evidence for strain variation and adaptation influencing host range and severity, consistent with re‑emergence in previously affected North American subregions.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: This row appropriately aggregates the 1996–2001 North American ranavirus mass‑mortality events and classifies them as re‑emergence in a region where ranaviruses were already known since the 1960s. The main correction is to replace the vague 'Canada [late 1990s]' with a concrete start year 'Canada [1997]', reflecting early documented tiger salamander die‑offs in Saskatchewan and other provinces; the rest of the description, geography and sources are suitable for retention.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Ranavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: Ranavirosis
Host: Cultured American bullfrog (Lithobates catesbeianus) tadpoles and juveniles in ranaculture facilities
Event.summary: In the early to mid‑2000s, Brazilian frog farms raising American bullfrogs began reporting acute, farm‑wide die‑offs of tadpoles with edema, hemorrhages and multi‑organ necrosis; laboratory investigation of major outbreaks between 2003 and 2005 demonstrated infection with an FV3‑like ranavirus (Rana catesbeiana ranavirus, RCV‑BR) and ruled out toxic causes, implicating introduced bullfrogs as the likely source of the virus. A subsequent large outbreak in 2012 in São Paulo state again caused heavy mortality and yielded a frog virus 3 strain whose whole genome confirmed close relationship to North American FV3 and evidence of recombination. These linked episodes represent the first confirmed establishment of amphibian ranavirus in South American aquaculture, with repeated heavy production losses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and expansion of ranaculture using non‑native American bullfrogs imported from North America; high‑density rearing and movement of stock among farms without adequate biosecurity; lack of early diagnostic capacity and regulatory oversight. Internal mechanisms: introduction of highly virulent FV3‑like strains into a naïve region and host community; possible viral adaptation and recombination during circulation in captive bullfrogs, as suggested by genomic analyses of Brazilian FV3‑like isolates.
Review: Decision: review. Rationale: Mass mortality of farmed bullfrogs in Brazil is correctly identified as the first major South American ranavirus episode and merits inclusion, but the original row mis‑timed the earliest events and over‑used the 'first_detection' and 're_emergence' flags. Based on Mazzoni et al. (2009) and later genomic work, the main production crashes occurred from 2003–2005 with another prominent outbreak in 2012, so the event year has been revised to '2003–2012' and the country annotation to 'Brazil [2003]; Brazil [2012]'. Per project definitions this represents inter‑continental emergence of ranavirosis into South America; 'first_detection' and 're_emergence' should both be set to 'No'.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.
