EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella pullorum, Bacillary white diarrhoea
Host: Broiler quails on a large commercial farm, with other poultry and game birds present on the same multi-site operation
Event.summary: In late 2018 and again in July 2019, a large broiler quail farm in western France experienced recurrent outbreaks of pullorum disease, with the second episode occurring in a different building about eight months after the first. The 2019 outbreak began with high mortality in 8‑day‑old quails in one room (about 16% cumulative mortality over two weeks) and later affected slightly older birds in an adjacent room, and laboratory investigations isolated Salmonella Gallinarum biovar Pullorum and S. Infantis from sick birds. Whole‑genome sequencing showed that S. Pullorum isolates from the two episodes were closely related, supporting resurgence from on‑farm reservoirs rather than a new introduction; intensive culling, cleaning, disinfection and pest control (including management of lesser mealworm beetles) were implemented and no spread to other farms in the surrounding free‑range poultry area was documented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: multi‑age production and the presence of multiple avian species (broiler and laying quails, broiler chickens, ornamental poultry, pheasants, partridges) on the same multi‑site operation, along with incomplete cleaning and disinfection between batches, created opportunities for environmental persistence and re‑exposure. Internal mechanisms: the ability of S. Pullorum to persist in manure, within lesser mealworm beetles and in chronically infected birds, combined with efficient horizontal transmission in dense broiler quail flocks (Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation), allowed recurrence of disease without evidence of a fundamentally new strain.
Review: retain – Added the recurrent 2018–2019 pullorum disease outbreaks on a large broiler quail farm in western France, as documented by Le Bouquin et al. (2021) and an ANSES case summary. These episodes involved tens of thousands of birds and required extensive investigation and remediation, clearly qualifying them as among the largest well-characterized PD outbreaks in Europe since 1990. Geography (Europe – Western Europe – France), host description and classification as a re‑occurrence within an already affected country are appropriate; the linked 2018 and 2019 episodes are treated as a single epidemiologically connected event in line with the project’s definition of linked episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonellosis
Sub.regions: Europe: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; North America: Northern America; Asia: Western Asia; Oceania: Australia and New Zealand
Host: Primarily cattle; also pigs, poultry (especially turkeys), and sheep
Event.summary: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, a multidrug‑resistant clone of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium definitive phage type 104 (DT104), resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, streptomycin, sulfonamides and tetracycline (ACSSuT), expanded rapidly in cattle and other livestock in the United Kingdom and neighboring European countries. Through trade in animals and animal products and other routes, this DT104 clone spread across Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe and was recognized in multiple livestock species by the mid‑1990s. By 1996, the same multidrug‑resistant DT104 strain had emerged in cattle and humans in Canada, the United States, Israel and, shortly afterward, Australia and New Zealand, becoming a major cause of disease and prompting international control efforts in the late 1990s and early 2000s before incidence declined following interventions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification of cattle, pig and poultry production, high use of therapeutic and growth‑promoter antimicrobials in food animals, and extensive trade in live animals and animal products facilitated selection and rapid international dissemination of the DT104 clone. Internal mechanisms: Acquisition and stabilization of a multidrug‑resistance cassette (R‑type ACSSuT) associated with class‑1 integrons and the Salmonella genomic island SGI1 increased fitness under antimicrobial pressure and contributed to re‑emergence, and some sublineages developed additional quinolone resistance during the late 1990s.
Review: Review – Event is real and appropriately framed as the global emergence of multidrug‑resistant Salmonella Typhimurium DT104 in livestock. Geography has been corrected by adding Asia/Western Asia because Israel is listed among affected countries, and the event‑type flags were adjusted to reflect an inter‑continental re‑emergence of a multidrug‑resistant clone (inter_continental_emergence = Yes; intra_continental_emergence = No; re_emergence = Yes) in line with the mostly mutually exclusive classification rules.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonid alphavirus
EPP.common.name: SAV
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (Scotland) [2006]
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) in seawater (marine SAV2 infections)
Event.summary: Around 2006, marine infections of Atlantic salmon with Salmonid alphavirus genotype 2 (SAV2), previously mainly associated with sleeping disease in freshwater rainbow trout, were first identified in seawater farms in north‑west Scotland, particularly in Shetland and Orkney. In 2010, the first detections of marine SAV2 in Norway were reported from pancreas‑disease outbreaks in Atlantic salmon, and sequence analyses showed Norwegian marine SAV2 strains to be closely related to Scottish marine SAV2 viruses, consistent with recent translocation between the two areas. During the late 2000s and early 2010s, marine SAV2 caused notable PD outbreaks at affected Scottish and some Norwegian sites but remained more spatially restricted than SAV1 in Ireland and Scotland or SAV3 in Norway, and enhanced surveillance, movement controls and vaccination helped limit its broader establishment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement of infected fish or eggs and shared supply chains between Scottish and Norwegian salmon industries, together with high local farm densities and waterborne spread within fjords and island archipelagos, likely facilitated the jump of SAV2 from freshwater trout systems into marine salmon sites and its subsequent spread between regions. Internal mechanisms: the capacity of SAV2 to replicate efficiently and cause pancreas disease in marine‑reared Atlantic salmon represents both novel strain/genotype behaviour in this production niche and host/life‑stage expansion from rainbow trout in freshwater, fitting the definition of re‑emergence rather than simple re‑occurrence.
Review: retain – the event correctly represents the emergence of marine SAV2 infections in Atlantic salmon in Scotland and their subsequent introduction into Norway, a pattern that is epidemiologically and genetically distinct from earlier SAV1 and SAV3 outbreaks. Years and countries are consistent with sequence‑based studies and WOAH/OIE subtype‑distribution tables. I have kept the classification as re‑emergence (new host and production niche for SAV2) and not marked this as intra‑continental emergence because the spread occurred between countries within the same UN Northern Europe sub‑region, which under the project’s rules does not qualify as a separate intra‑continental event. Event‑level sources have been focused on molecular epidemiology and official surveillance reports.

EPP.common.name: Scabies, Sarcoptic mange
Host: Alpine chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra rupicapra), with Alpine ibex (Capra ibex) and other sympatric ungulates as secondary hosts
Event.summary: In October 1995, sarcoptic mange was first recorded in Alpine chamois in the Province of Belluno (Dolomites, northeastern Italy), marking the start of a new epizootic wave in this mountain region. Over subsequent years, the outbreak spread westward, reaching Bolzano Province in 1997 and Trento Province by 2000, and caused high mortality and demographic collapse in several chamois populations while also affecting sympatric Alpine ibex. By the mid‑2000s, after roughly a decade of intense impact, mange had become established and largely endemic across much of the regional chamois metapopulation, with episodic flare‑ups but reduced overall mortality compared to the initial epizootic front.

Drivers: High densities and connectivity of Alpine chamois across contiguous alpine massifs facilitated progressive spread once mange was introduced, and climatic conditions in high‑elevation habitats (cool, moist periods) favored mite survival off‑host. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic reflects geographic expansion of a host‑taxon–adapted Sarcoptes scabiei strain among largely naive chamois subpopulations, with possible spillover between chamois and Alpine ibex, consistent with re‑emergence driven by geographic range expansion of an existing strain and traits that permit efficient transmission in caprine hosts in alpine environments.

EPP.scientific.name: Sarcoptes scabiei
EPP.common.name: Scabies, Sarcoptic mange
Host: Endangered San Joaquin kit fox (Vulpes macrotis mutica), with likely involvement of domestic dogs and possibly other canids as reservoir or source hosts
Event.summary: In spring 2013, sarcoptic mange caused by Sarcoptes scabiei was first documented in an urban subpopulation of endangered San Joaquin kit foxes in Bakersfield, California, where this disease had not previously been reported in the subspecies. Between 2013 and about 2020, the epidemic expanded to encompass the entire Bakersfield urban population and, by early 2019, was detected in a satellite kit fox population in the town of Taft, leading to at least 90 clinically confirmed cases and substantial additional undetected mortality, with camera‑based indices indicating an approximate 50% decline in kit fox abundance in Bakersfield. Following intensive monitoring and some treatment and collar‑based interventions, reported case numbers dropped sharply around 2020, but mange remains an ongoing management concern with potential for re‑emergence or further spread to other fragmented kit fox populations.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Urbanization has concentrated San Joaquin kit foxes at high densities around anthropogenic food and water sources, while dense networks of artificial dens and frequent contact with domestic dogs and possibly red foxes created opportunities for cross‑species transmission and rapid intra‑population spread; small, fragmented populations and the endangered status of the subspecies amplify conservation impact. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and epidemiological data support a canine‑derived S. scabiei strain that adapted to San Joaquin kit foxes and spread between foxes, representing host expansion (spillover from domestic or other canids) and efficient fox‑to‑fox transmission, consistent with re‑emergence driven by host expansion and enhanced transmission in a new, highly susceptible canid host.
Internal mechanism tags: Host Expansion (Spillover from domestic/other canids to kit foxes); Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent, within North America).
Review: retain – High‑impact mange epidemic in an endangered canid with clear onset (Bakersfield, March 2013), documented spread to Taft by early 2019, and strong evidence for a ~50% decline in the urban Bakersfield population based on camera detections, as reported by FWS, Cypher et al., Foley et al., and related studies. Location (USA, Northern America), host, and timing match these sources, including first Taft detection in 2019. Classification as re‑emergence (new host expansion of a canine‑derived Sarcoptes strain in an already mange‑affected continent) is appropriate; imported cases without onward transmission are not involved, so no intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence applies. No corrections to event fields or URLs recommended.

EPP.scientific.name: Scrapie prion
EPP.common.name: PrPsc, Scrapie agent
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2002]
Host: Sheep (with later detection in goats in some countries)
Event.summary: From 2002, implementation of EU‑mandated active TSE surveillance in small ruminants, including abattoir and fallen‑stock testing, led to the detection of atypical/Nor98‑like scrapie across Great Britain and many EU member states. Between roughly 2003 and 2007, atypical cases were reported from an expanding set of Northern, Western and Southern European countries, and in some areas they accounted for a substantial proportion of diagnosed scrapie relative to classical disease. Despite this wider recognition, atypical scrapie has generally remained a low‑prevalence, sporadic infection of older sheep, without large flock‑level epidemics but with a now well‑documented pan‑European distribution.
Mechanism.or.driver: Internal mechanism – Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence (continent‑wide recognition and circulation of the atypical/Nor98 prion strain within European sheep populations). Possible Geographic Range Expansion (inherent) of this strain within already scrapie‑endemic regions. Drivers – Regulatory and technological drivers, particularly EU Regulation 999/2001 and associated active surveillance with rapid TSE tests, generated the sampling intensity and laboratory sensitivity needed to detect atypical cases widely across Europe.
Review: review – Corrected two issues: (1) removed Falkland Islands from the country list and restricted this episode to European countries, because the Falkland case represents a separate Southern Hemisphere event rather than part of the EU surveillance wave; and (2) set intra_continental_emergence to false, since atypical scrapie represents a new strain emerging in regions where scrapie was already endemic and, per the scheme rules, such strain changes should be coded as re_emergence rather than intra‑continental emergence. Per‑country start years remain approximate and should be cross‑checked in any future refinement.

EPP.common.name: PrPsc, Scrapie agent
Host: Sheep (atypical/Nor98 scrapie; isolated cases)
Event.summary: In 2009, brain tissue from a New Zealand sheep submitted as presumed negative control material for European scrapie rapid‑test evaluations yielded discordant test results and was ultimately confirmed, via detailed western blotting and immunohistochemistry, as atypical/Nor98 scrapie – the first recognised scrapie case of any form in New Zealand. EPP.scientific.name: Taylorella equigenitalis
EPP.common.name: CEM organism
Host: Horses (stallions and mares at a single Lusitano stud farm)
Event.summary: In 2008, Portugal documented its first outbreak of contagious equine metritis when a Lusitano stallion recently imported from Germany and two mares at the same stud farm tested positive for Taylorella equigenitalis on routine pre‑breeding examination. Comprehensive testing of all 30 equids on the premises identified four additional infected horses (three mares and one stallion), but no evidence of spread beyond the affected stud or into the wider Portuguese horse population. All culture‑positive animals underwent standard topical treatment and repeated culture testing, and subsequent national surveillance of more than 2,000 genital swabs from other farms failed to detect further cases, indicating this was a self‑limited introduction event.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growing international trade in Lusitano horses and importation of a breeding stallion from Germany with a false‑negative or incomplete CEM status provided the pathway for introduction of Taylorella equigenitalis into Portugal, while concentration of breeding at a single stud and initial lack of comprehensive screening allowed several additional horses to become infected before detection. Internal mechanisms: The ability of T. equigenitalis to persist in carrier stallions and mares with mainly subclinical or transient infertility favoured silent spread within the stud prior to testing, but no new genotype, host jump or antimicrobial resistance pattern was reported in relation to this episode.
Review: review – This event accurately captures Portugal’s first confirmed CEM outbreak and should be retained as a key intra‑continental emergence in Southern Europe. However, in line with the event‑type definitions, I changed first_detection from true to false because global first detection occurred in 1977 in the UK; the Portuguese episode instead represents spread of an established pathogen into a previously unaffected country within Europe, appropriately coded as intra_continental_emergence. I also simplified the sub_regions field to Southern Europe and left Germany only in the countries field as the epidemiological source, and focused the sources on the Open Veterinary Journal case report (including its PMC version), which provides the primary quantitative description of this outbreak.

EPP.scientific.name: Taylorella equigenitalis
EPP.common.name: CEM organism
Host: Horses (primarily Icelandic and Fjord breeds)
Event.summary: From 2019 through 2023, Denmark recorded multiple cases of Taylorella equigenitalis infection in horses, with contagious equine metritis recognised as the only WOAH‑listed equine disease present in the country during this period and 16 cases confirmed in 2023 alone, mainly in Icelandic and Fjord breeds. These detections, arising in breeding populations monitored through CEM surveillance linked to stud activity and international trade, represented a renewed and more sustained occurrence of CEM in Denmark following earlier sporadic isolations in 2001–2003. Danish authorities revised national procedures for handling CEM‑positive horses in 2023, imposing mandatory treatment, movement restrictions and a prohibition on breeding use until infected animals had completed prescribed treatment and three consecutive series of negative tests, contributing to declining annual case numbers after 2020 and apparent containment within monitored subpopulations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Ongoing intra‑European movement and breeding of horses, particularly in Nordic leisure and native breeds, together with increased surveillance that both detected and clustered cases, maintained a background risk of re‑introduction and local circulation of Taylorella equigenitalis. Internal mechanisms: Chronic or subclinical carriage in stallions and some mares, with efficient venereal transmission, allowed persistent low‑level circulation and occasional flare‑ups; there is no evidence from available data that these Danish cases were associated with a distinct, more virulent or resistant strain compared with other European T. equigenitalis populations.
Review: review – The Danish 2019–2023 series is well supported by national 'Animal Health in Denmark' reports and is large enough (including 16 cases in 2023) to warrant inclusion as a major modern episode in a previously affected country. I retained the event but clarified in the summary that Denmark had documented T. equigenitalis in 2001–2003, so this episode is correctly coded as a re‑occurrence rather than a first detection or intra‑continental emergence. I also noted the specific breeds affected and kept Denmark as a single‑country, multi‑year linked episode, which aligns with the guidance for recurrent, epidemiologically continuous events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria spp.
EPP.common.name: Theileriosis
Host: Cattle (Bos indicus and Bos taurus crossbreds)
Event.summary: In 2003, following importation of zebu cattle from Tanzania, East Coast fever caused by Theileria parva was introduced into Grande Comore in the Union of Comoros, an island previously free of the disease. The infection, carried by Rhipicephalus appendiculatus ticks on Muguga‑cocktail‑vaccinated cattle, spread rapidly during 2003–2004 and caused a severe epidemic that decimated the island’s cattle population, with participatory assessments later estimating livestock losses on the order of 10% or more. Subsequent control measures, including restrictions on cattle imports, intensified tick control and adaptation of husbandry practices, reduced incidence, but T. parva and its vector became established and the island remains at risk of recurrent outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement of live cattle from Tanzania without adequate pre‑movement screening for T. parva or tick infestation; use of Muguga‑cocktail‑vaccinated animals that carried vaccine‑strain parasites into a naïve island cattle population; suitable island climate for establishment of Rhipicephalus appendiculatus and limited local veterinary capacity to recognise and contain a new tick‑borne disease. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of existing Muguga‑cocktail genotypes rather than a novel strain, but into an immunologically naïve host population and new ecosystem, leading to marked local geographic range expansion and high transmission intensity (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent); Enhanced Transmission via abundant vector–host contact).
Review: retain – Well‑documented, high‑impact introduction of East Coast fever to Grande Comore with major cattle losses; geography (Eastern Africa, Comoros) and classification as re-occurrence at subregion level (disease long‑present elsewhere in Eastern Africa) are consistent with the protocol. Tanzania is appropriately noted as the infection source rather than a new emergence location; no structural changes recommended.

EPP.scientific.name: Theileria spp.
EPP.common.name: Theileriosis
Countries: Viet Nam [2014] (aborted dairy heifers imported from Australia)
Host: Cattle (imported pregnant dairy heifers)
Event.summary: In 2014, an outbreak of oriental theileriosis occurred in pregnant dairy heifers imported from Australia to Viet Nam, with abortions and clinical signs prompting investigation of both the affected heifers in Viet Nam and animals from the same shipment before export and after arrival in Taiwan. Multiplex tandem PCR on 112 cattle samples showed Theileria orientalis DNA in about 72% of animals, with very high prevalences and parasite loads in aborted heifers in Viet Nam and in cohorts shipped to Taiwan, and genotyping revealed Chitose and Ikeda types closely related to Australian outbreak strains. The episode, which linked severe disease in imported cattle in Asia to infection acquired in Australia, highlighted the risk of moving subclinically infected T. orientalis Ikeda/Chitose carriers through live‑cattle trade and led to calls for stricter pre‑export screening and biosecurity measures for oriental theileriosis.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance trade in pregnant dairy heifers from eastern Australia to Viet Nam and Taiwan without prior molecular screening for T. orientalis genotypes; transport stress and periparturient immunosuppression that likely precipitated clinical disease and abortion in infected heifers; presence or potential presence of competent Haemaphysalis vectors in destination countries. Internal mechanisms: High burdens of virulent Ikeda and Chitose genotypes in exported animals (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and long‑distance dissemination), which are strongly associated with clinical oriental theileriosis and abortion, demonstrating the capacity of these genotypes to cause transboundary disease even when infection is acquired pre‑export.
Review: review – Newly added event capturing the first reported outbreak of oriental theileriosis in imported cattle, with severe disease in heifers shipped from Australia to Viet Nam and high infection levels in animals sent to Taiwan. Classified as re-emergence (spread of pathogenic Ikeda/Chitose genotypes into additional production systems within Asia via trade) rather than inter-continental emergence, because T. orientalis was already established in both source and destination continents. Recommended to retain as a major transboundary emergence episode, but timing (2014) and country listing (Viet Nam plus Taiwan region under China) should be double-checked against full-text data.

EPP.common.name: TBEV

Event.summary: From 1993 onwards, the Baltic states and adjacent parts of northeastern Poland experienced a sudden and sustained surge in human tick-borne encephalitis incidence, with national case rates increasing several-fold compared with the 1980s. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania all saw sharp step-changes in 1992–1993, and in some counties incidence rose more than 10–30-fold, elevating the region to one of the highest-burden TBE areas in Europe. Elevated incidence persisted through the late 1990s, with marked spatial heterogeneity across counties, before stabilising at a high but fluctuating level under the influence of vaccination and public health measures.

Internal mechanisms: No single novel viral strain was identified as causal; the episode is interpreted primarily as ecological and socio-economic amplification of established European-subtype TBEV transmission cycles.
Review: review - Retained as a major high-incidence episode for the Baltic states and northeastern Poland. Corrected the emergence-type classification by setting intra_continental_emergence from true to false, because the virus and human disease were already established in these subregions and the main signal was a sharp resurgence in incidence, not first spread into new subregions. Re-occurrence remains true, reflecting socio-economic and ecological drivers of resurgence.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: TBEV
Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus ticks; wild rodents
Event.summary: During the 1990s and 2000s, many Central and Eastern European countries, especially Czechia, Slovakia, Slovenia, parts of Poland and Hungary, and selected alpine and pre-alpine regions of Austria and Croatia, reported sustained increases in TBE incidence compared with the 1970s–1980s. In Czechia, national data showed a marked rise in annual TBE cases from the early 1990s through 2008, and similar trends were documented in neighbouring countries as established enzootic foci intensified and new local foci appeared. By the late 2000s, incidence had stabilised at a higher level with pronounced year-to-year variability driven by climate and host dynamics rather than a single outbreak wave.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Warmer winters and earlier springs, changes in forest management and deer abundance, increased outdoor recreation and mushroom or berry picking, and reduced pesticide use collectively expanded suitable habitat and host availability for Ixodes ticks and increased human exposure. Internal mechanisms: No dominant novel genotype was linked to this regional trend; instead, the event reflects a broad geographic range expansion and intensification of existing European-subtype TBEV foci (geographic range expansion – inherent) under changing environmental and human-behavioural conditions.
Review: review - Event retained as a broad regional resurgence in Central and Eastern Europe. Cleaned the sub_regions field to use only UNSD categories (Eastern Europe; Southern Europe) instead of the previous free-text mixture, and set intra_continental_emergence from true to false because the countries involved were already within known endemic subregions; the main feature was a long-lasting increase in incidence (re-occurrence) and expansion of local foci rather than first entry into a new subregion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: TBEV
Host: Humans (food-borne and tick-bite associated TBE); small ruminants (goats, sheep, cows as virus source in milk); Ixodes ricinus ticks
Event.summary: Between 2007 and 2016, Slovakia reported the highest documented occurrence of alimentary (food-borne) tick-borne encephalitis in Europe, with multiple outbreaks linked to consumption of unpasteurised goat, sheep or cow milk and cheese, including a large outbreak in eastern Slovakia in 2013 that affected dozens of people. Similar but generally smaller food-borne TBE outbreaks occurred in the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and other countries during this period, highlighting alimentary transmission as a clinically important complement to tick-bite exposure in endemic areas. Most outbreaks subsided rapidly once contaminated dairy products were withdrawn from sale and pasteurisation or boiling of milk was reinforced, although sporadic alimentary events have continued to be reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cultural practices involving consumption of raw milk and artisanal cheeses from small ruminants grazing in endemic forest-edge pastures created opportunities for alimentary TBEV transmission; limited awareness of this route and lack of systematic pasteurisation in some rural settings allowed multi-person outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: The events involved European-subtype TBEV strains capable of surviving and remaining infectious in milk and dairy products; the prominence of alimentary outbreaks represents functional re-emergence via a different transmission route (enhanced transmission through food) rather than a novel genotype, and in some foci may reflect high viral loads in livestock following intense tick exposure.
Review: review - Retained as a distinct re-emergence episode characterised by large alimentary outbreaks, with Slovakia as the main hotspot. Sub_regions was restricted to Eastern Europe because all listed countries fall in this UNSD subregion. The emergence classification was adjusted to re_emergence only (re_occurrence set to false) to reflect the prominence of a re-emerging transmission route (food-borne infection) involving established European TBEV strains, rather than a generic resurgence driven mainly by external factors.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: TBEV
Countries: Norway (coastal Agder & Telemark, and western coast) [2015]
Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus ticks; wildlife reservoirs (rodents, deer)
Event.summary: In the mid‑2010s, Nordic countries documented expansion of human TBE cases into new coastal and higher-latitude foci, including increasing incidence along the Norwegian and Swedish coasts and newly recognised foci in Denmark beyond the long-known endemic island of Bornholm, where autochthonous cases in 2018–2019 highlighted spread to mainland Zealand and Jutland. Case counts in Norway, Sweden and Finland rose over 2015–2019 compared with earlier years, although absolute numbers remained lower than in Baltic or Central European hotspots. These northern foci have persisted, with interannual variability linked to climate and small-mammal population cycles and ongoing gradual spread northwards along the Scandinavian coastline.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Warmer temperatures, longer vegetation seasons and milder winters at higher latitudes have improved overwinter survival and seasonal activity of Ixodes ticks; changes in deer and rodent populations and human outdoor behaviour (recreation, second homes, forestry work) have increased human–tick contact. Internal mechanisms: Expansion represents geographic range expansion of existing European TBEV lineages into newly suitable northern habitats (geographic range expansion – inherent) rather than emergence of novel variants.
Review: review - Retained as a major intra-continental range expansion episode into new foci in the Nordic countries. Kept the focus on spread into new geographic areas (intra_continental_emergence = true) and set re_occurrence to false to comply with the rule that re-occurrence should not co-occur with intra-/inter-continental emergence; the main signal is establishment of new northern and western foci rather than mere resurgence in long-recognised localities.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: TBEV
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus and Ixodes persulcatus ticks; wildlife reservoirs
Event.summary: Between 2018 and 2020, EU/EEA countries experienced two of the highest regional TBE peaks on record. In 2018 they reported 3,212 cases (over 3,000 confirmed), with particularly high incidence in Lithuania, Czechia, Germany, Slovenia and Sweden, and Germany alone recording around 583 cases. After a moderate year in 2019, notification rates rose again in 2020 to 3,817 reported cases (3,734 confirmed), despite possible under-ascertainment during the COVID-19 pandemic. These peaks reflected synchronised amplification of TBEV activity across many established European foci rather than a single outbreak constrained to a few countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Favourable weather for ticks (warm, humid spring and summer), high rodent and deer densities, intensive human outdoor activity in forests and rural areas during climatically favourable seasons, and suboptimal vaccination coverage in several high-incidence countries (especially in the Baltics and parts of Central Europe) likely increased human exposure and disease burden. Internal mechanisms: The 2018 and 2020 peaks exemplify how climate variability and host–vector dynamics can trigger major regional re-occurrence within existing enzootic cycles without requiring the emergence of a fundamentally new viral variant.
Review: review - Retained as a major multi-country re-occurrence episode capturing record-high regional case totals. Updated the year field from a single year (2018) to 2018–2020 and clarified in the summary that both 2018 and 2020 represent EU/EEA-wide peaks, with 2019 as an intermediate year. Emergence classification remains re_occurrence only, as there is no evidence that these peaks reflected spread into new subregions or continents.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Event.summary: Between 2018 and 2020, EU/EEA countries experienced two of the highest regional TBE peaks on record. In 2018 they reported 3,212 cases (over 3,000 confirmed), with particularly high incidence in Lithuania, Czechia, Germany, Slovenia and Sweden, and Germany alone recording around 583 cases. After a moderate year in 2019, notification rates rose again in 2020 to 3,817 reported cases (3,734 confirmed), despite possible under-ascertainment during the COVID-19 pandemic. These peaks reflected synchronised amplification of TBEV activity across many established European foci rather than a single outbreak constrained to a few countries.

Internal mechanisms: The 2018 and 2020 peaks exemplify how climate variability and host–vector dynamics can trigger major regional re-occurrence within existing enzootic cycles without requiring the emergence of a fundamentally new viral variant.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus encephalitidis
EPP.common.name: TBEV
Host: Humans; Ixodes ricinus and Ixodes persulcatus ticks; wild rodents
Event.summary: Between 2019 and 2023, the Baltic countries reported 4,361 surveillance-confirmed TBE cases (Estonia 583, Latvia 1,055, Lithuania 2,723), corresponding to incidences of approximately 8.8, 11.2 and 19.4 per 100,000 person‑years, respectively, making them the highest-incidence TBE countries in Europe. Despite recommendations for universal vaccination of residents older than one year, more than 98% of TBE cases occurred in unvaccinated individuals, indicating persistent gaps in vaccine uptake. By 2023, incidence remained high but somewhat stabilised, with public health programmes emphasising vaccination, tick-bite prevention and enhanced awareness among populations and clinicians.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High environmental suitability for ticks and rodent reservoirs, extensive human use of forests and rural landscapes for work and recreation, and low to moderate vaccine coverage contributed to sustained high incidence; socio-economic patterns and health-seeking behaviour also influence under- and over-reporting. Internal mechanisms: The burden reflects endemic circulation of European TBEV strains rather than new variants; the re-occurrence at very high incidence in 2019–2023 underscores how incomplete vaccination and favourable ecologic conditions can maintain high disease impact in long-established foci.
Review: retain - Event appropriately captures the very high recent TBE incidence and vaccine-impact assessment in the Baltic states, based on detailed national surveillance and vaccine-effectiveness data. Classification as re_occurrence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence or re_emergence) is consistent with a resurgence and persistence of disease in long-established endemic foci driven mainly by vaccination gaps and favourable ecology.

EPP.scientific.name: Tilapinevirus tilapiae
EPP.common.name: Tilapia lake virus disease
Host: Farmed Nile tilapia and red tilapia hybrids in cages, ponds and hatcheries; some affected broodstock and seed stocks
Event.summary: In 2015–2016, tilapia farms in several provinces of Thailand experienced severe outbreaks with 80–90% cumulative mortality in juvenile and grow‑out fish, and laboratory investigations confirmed TiLV as the etiologic agent, marking its first recognized emergence in mainland South‑eastern Asia. Retrospective and prospective testing soon showed that genetically related TiLV strains were present in outbreaks and surveillance samples from other South‑east Asian countries, including Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, and in Chinese Taipei, often linked to substantial farm‑level losses and disruption of seed supply chains. As awareness grew, affected countries, FAO, NACA and WOAH issued alerts, and national services rolled out PCR‑based diagnostics, movement controls and improved farm‑level biosecurity; despite these measures, TiLV became established across much of the regional tilapia industry.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and high connectivity of tilapia farming in South‑eastern and parts of Eastern Asia; intense trade in live fry, fingerlings and broodstock among hatcheries and grow‑out farms; and initially limited awareness or diagnostic capacity enabled fast dissemination of TiLV once it entered the region. Internal mechanisms: TiLV displayed efficient horizontal transmission and high virulence in multiple Oreochromis species and hybrids across diverse production systems, supporting its classification as an intra‑continental emergence into new Asian sub‑regions driven by geographic range expansion and enhanced transmission rather than major viral attenuation or host change.
Review: review – Retained as a major intra‑continental emergence event into South‑eastern Asia, but sub_regions have been corrected to include both South‑eastern Asia and Eastern Asia because Chinese Taipei/Taiwan lies in Eastern Asia. Countries and approximate start years are consistent with outbreak and OIE notification reports, but the exact naming of "Taiwan Province of China" should be harmonised with the project’s Country sheet in a subsequent manual review.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Tilapinevirus tilapiae
EPP.common.name: Tilapia lake virus disease
Host: Farmed and wild Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) in and around Lake Victoria (cages, ponds and open lake)
Event.summary: From about 2015, producers around Lake Victoria began reporting unexplained mortalities in cage‑ and pond‑reared Nile tilapia, prompting regional investigations in the Tanzanian and Ugandan sectors of the lake. PCR‑based surveys of fish sampled from the Tanzanian part of Lake Victoria in 2015 and from the Ugandan part in 2016 confirmed TiLV infection in both farmed and wild tilapia, and phylogenetic analyses linked these East African viruses closely to strains from Israel and Thailand; later reviews report that the virus has spread throughout the lake ecosystem, including Kenyan waters. TiLV is now considered established in the Lake Victoria basin, and riparian states have launched surveillance plans, farmer training and biosecurity guidance, although eradication from this large, interconnected freshwater system is viewed as unrealistic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid growth of cage and pond aquaculture on Lake Victoria, transboundary hydrological connections, and frequent movement of live tilapia between hatcheries and farms around the lake created multiple opportunities for TiLV introduction (most likely from earlier African or Asian foci) and subsequent dissemination within the shared water body. Internal mechanisms: TiLV’s ability to infect both farmed and wild Nile tilapia and to persist in open freshwater systems underpins its geographic range expansion and environmental maintenance in Lake Victoria, with no clear evidence so far of major genetic adaptation specific to East African populations.
Review: review – Event retained as the key intra‑continental emergence of TiLV into Eastern Africa via Lake Victoria. Countries and years have been adjusted to reflect sample collection years reported for Tanzania (2015) and Uganda (2016); Kenya is kept in the country list with an estimated start year of 2018 based on later syntheses indicating spread throughout all riparian states, but there is less direct primary surveillance data than for Uganda and Tanzania. This row should be reviewed by regional experts to confirm whether Kenya should remain explicitly listed and whether the start year is appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Tilapinevirus tilapiae
EPP.common.name: Tilapia lake virus disease
Host: Wild and farmed Nile tilapia and tilapia hybrids in rivers, reservoirs and aquaculture systems in northern coastal and Amazonian regions
Event.summary: By late 2017, Peruvian authorities received reports of unusual mortalities in cultured and wild tilapia in northern and Amazonian regions, prompting emergency surveillance targeting TiLV. EPP.scientific.name: Tilapinevirus tilapiae

Host: Farmed Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) in ponds and cages; farmed Mozambique tilapia (O. mossambicus) and tilapia in polyculture; feral tilapia and hatchery broodstock in parts of India and Bangladesh

EPP.scientific.name: Tilapinevirus tilapiae
EPP.common.name: Tilapia lake virus disease
Host: Farmed Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) in commercial pond and recirculating systems; some imported live tilapia stocks
Event.summary: In 2017, TiLV was detected in Mexican tilapia aquaculture and formally reported to the World Organisation for Animal Health in 2018, indicating that the virus had reached Central America and was present in multiple production facilities across several states. Internal mechanisms: TiLV maintained its pathogenic phenotype under North American farm conditions, and genome analyses showed close relatedness to Asian lineages, indicating recent introduction with limited divergence and demonstrating the virus’s capacity for inter‑continental spread without the need for major adaptive change.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis
Host: Domestic pigs; hunted wild boar (Sus scrofa)
Event.summary: Between 2006 and 2013, national surveillance in Spain documented Trichinella larvae in both domestic pigs and wild boar, primarily T. spiralis and T. britovi, with 384 infected pigs (0.0001%) and 1,399 infected wild boar (~0.2%), confirming ongoing domestic and especially sylvatic circulation. In 2014, Trichinella pseudospiralis was isolated from a wild boar hunted in Girona Province, Catalonia, marking the first detection of this non-encapsulated species in the Iberian Peninsula. This finding expanded the known European range of T. pseudospiralis and highlighted that areas previously regarded as low risk could harbour non-encapsulated Trichinella, detectable only through artificial digestion and molecular typing.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growth of wild boar populations, expansion of recreational hunting, and demand for free-range/organic pig production increased contact between domestic pigs, wild boar and wildlife carcasses, maintaining Trichinella transmission. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion and/or first recognition of T. pseudospiralis in Iberian wild boar, representing re-emergence of the genus in the region via a new non-encapsulated species; detection depended on improved diagnostic and molecular tools rather than an obvious change in parasite biology.
Review: Decision: review. The original coding as intra-continental emergence has been corrected to re-emergence only, in line with project rules that new species or genotypes in regions where the genus is already endemic should not be labelled inter- or intra-continental emergence. The event is important for documenting the first Iberian detection of T. pseudospiralis and sustained Trichinella circulation in Spanish pigs and wild boar, but involves only a single known non-encapsulated-species isolate and no very large animal or human outbreaks; it may fall below the global top ten by impact and should be retained only if species-range expansions are prioritized alongside large epidemics.

EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis
Host: Wild boar (Sus scrofa); occasionally free-range pigs
Event.summary: From roughly 2013 to 2016, Italy recorded several trichinellosis outbreaks linked to wild boar hunted in regions previously classified as negligible risk for Trichinella, including a well-described outbreak in southern Italy in which consumption of undercooked wild boar sausages led to dozens of human cases caused by T. britovi. EPP.scientific.name: Trichinella spp.
EPP.common.name: Trichinellosis
Host: Backyard pigs used for traditional figatelli sausages; wild boar (background source in Corsica)
Event.summary: In 2015, three human trichinellosis cases were reported in south-eastern France after consumption of raw figatelli sausages produced in Corsica from pork contaminated with Trichinella britovi, despite long-standing EU-mandated carcass testing. Investigations showed that pigs had been slaughtered illegally and the figatelli label carried insufficiently visible warnings that the product must be thoroughly cooked, allowing infected meat from backyard pigs or wild boar to enter artisanal processing chains. Following the outbreak, French authorities tightened labelling requirements for figatelli and reinforced veterinary controls and surveillance for Trichinella in Corsican outdoor pigs and wild boar.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cultural preference for eating raw or rare figatelli, gaps in labelling and enforcement of Trichinella testing in small-scale Corsican pig systems, illegal slaughter, and potential mixing of meat from free-range pigs and wild boar enabled the parasite to persist in localized production niches even as industrial pork was essentially Trichinella-free. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain was identified; this episode represents a localized re-occurrence of T. britovi in Corsican backyard pig/wild-boar systems, with risk amplified by human behaviour and regulatory lapses rather than parasite evolution.
Review: Decision: review. The event description is supported by national French and ECDC sources, but the original classification has been adjusted to re-occurrence only (re_emergence set to No) because no parasite change was documented; the outbreak was driven by illegal slaughter, inadequate labelling and traditional consumption of raw figatelli. With only three confirmed human cases and a very local animal reservoir, this event is more important as a regulatory case study than as a top-ten global impact episode and is therefore flagged for review when prioritising events.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas foetus
EPP.common.name: Bovine trichomoniasis, Tritrichomonas foetus
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe
Host: Predominantly beef cattle herds using natural mating in affected EU Member States
Event.summary: From 2012 to 2016, World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH/OIE) notifications summarised by EFSA recorded bovine trichomoniasis in several EU Member States, with Spain reporting disease limited to one or more zones throughout the period, France reporting disease present nationally, and Portugal, Hungary, Poland and Italy reporting infection limited to zones in particular years. These notifications, together with earlier sporadic reports from Spain and other European countries, indicate that pockets of Tritrichomonas foetus infection persisted in beef‑cattle regions across Southern, Western and Eastern Europe at a time when most dairy herds were free of the parasite due to widespread artificial insemination. The episode represents re‑occurrence and formal recognition of geographically limited trichomoniasis foci across multiple European subregions, prompting its assessment under the EU Animal Health Law and highlighting trade‑related risks linked to movement of infected breeding cattle within the Union.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement and trade of live breeding cattle between Member States, combined with pockets of beef production that rely heavily on natural mating and retain older, potentially infected bulls, favoured the maintenance and dissemination of T. foetus within Europe; the absence of EU‑wide mandatory trichomoniasis testing for cattle movements meant infected bulls could be introduced into otherwise free herds. Internal mechanisms: available evidence points to typical bovine T. foetus genotypes rather than novel variants; parasite persistence was driven by its capacity for chronic colonisation of the bull preputial mucosa and efficient venereal transmission, with spatial spread shaped more by management and trade networks than by intrinsic changes in transmissibility or virulence.
Review: Review – EFSA’s assessment and earlier literature make clear that bovine trichomoniasis had been present in multiple European countries long before 2012 and was largely suppressed—but not eradicated—by artificial insemination, so WOAH notifications between 2012 and 2016 represent persistence and re‑occurrence of localized foci rather than first spread into new European subregions; intra_continental_emergence has therefore been changed from Yes to No, re_occurrence from No to Yes, the countries list has been restricted to Member States with documented bovine reports (removing the Netherlands, where recent monitoring describes T. foetus as not detected in cattle), and the host description was simplified to cattle to avoid conflation with wildlife or non‑bovine trichomonads.([efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2017.4992?utm_source=openai))

Host: Predominantly beef cattle herds using natural mating in affected EU Member States
Event.summary: From 2012 to 2016, World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH/OIE) notifications summarised by EFSA recorded bovine trichomoniasis in several EU Member States, with Spain reporting disease limited to one or more zones throughout the period, France reporting disease present nationally, and Portugal, Hungary, Poland and Italy reporting infection limited to zones in particular years. These notifications, together with earlier sporadic reports from Spain and other European countries, indicate that pockets of Tritrichomonas foetus infection persisted in beef‑cattle regions across Southern, Western and Eastern Europe at a time when most dairy herds were free of the parasite due to widespread artificial insemination. The episode represents re‑occurrence and formal recognition of geographically limited trichomoniasis foci across multiple European subregions, prompting its assessment under the EU Animal Health Law and highlighting trade‑related risks linked to movement of infected breeding cattle within the Union.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: movement and trade of live breeding cattle between Member States, combined with pockets of beef production that rely heavily on natural mating and retain older, potentially infected bulls, favoured the maintenance and dissemination of T. foetus within Europe; the absence of EU‑wide mandatory trichomoniasis testing for cattle movements meant infected bulls could be introduced into otherwise free herds. Internal mechanisms: available evidence points to typical bovine T. foetus genotypes rather than novel variants; parasite persistence was driven by its capacity for chronic colonisation of the bull preputial mucosa and efficient venereal transmission, with spatial spread shaped more by management and trade networks than by intrinsic changes in transmissibility or virulence.
Review: Review – EFSA’s assessment and earlier literature make clear that bovine trichomoniasis had been present in multiple European countries long before 2012 and was largely suppressed—but not eradicated—by artificial insemination, so WOAH notifications between 2012 and 2016 represent persistence and re‑occurrence of localized foci rather than first spread into new European subregions; intra_continental_emergence has therefore been changed from Yes to No, re_occurrence from No to Yes, the countries list has been restricted to Member States with documented bovine reports (removing the Netherlands, where recent monitoring describes T. foetus as not detected in cattle), and the host description was simplified to cattle to avoid conflation with wildlife or non‑bovine trichomonads.([efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2017.4992?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas gallinae
EPP.common.name: Trichomonosis
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [2005]
Host: Primarily European greenfinch (Chloris chloris) and Eurasian chaffinch (Fringilla coelebs); other garden passerines occasionally affected; reservoir in local columbids (e.g. feral pigeons, doves).
Event.summary: In spring–summer 2005, a novel, highly pathogenic lineage of Trichomonas gallinae was first recognised causing trichomonosis in British finches, with carcasses of greenfinches and chaffinches submitted from gardens across England and Wales. In 2006–2007, reports of sick and dead finches at feeding stations surged and post-mortems showed trichomonosis as the dominant cause of infectious mortality, leading to an estimated loss of about 1.5 million breeding greenfinches and marked declines in chaffinch survival across Great Britain and later in Ireland. Through the late 2000s the epidemic became endemic with recurring seasonal outbreaks but somewhat lower incident numbers, and greenfinch populations partially stabilised at a much reduced level.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density aggregation at garden feeding stations promoted oral–oral transmission via contaminated food and water; widespread supplementary feeding and cool, moist conditions at feeders favoured parasite survival; lack of prior exposure in finches left them immunologically naive. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – molecular typing identified a single clonal “finch epidemic strain” of T. gallinae distinct from most columbid strains; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – this strain showed efficient transmission in passerines via shared food and water sources; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – infection caused severe necrotic ingluvitis and rapid mortality, producing strong population-level impacts; Host Expansion (Spillover) – pathogen spilled over from columbids into finch species where it had not previously caused recognised epidemics.
Review: Decision: Retain. This is correctly captured as a major re-emergence event driven by a clonal finch epidemic strain causing unprecedented population declines of greenfinches and chaffinches in the British Isles.([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0012215&utm_source=openai)) The 2005–2010 window appropriately covers the initial emergence and the years of peak epidemic impact; Ireland’s first major mortality in 2007 is consistent with surveillance data. Emergence type is correctly set to re-emergence only (not intra-/inter-continental), since T. gallinae was long endemic in European columbids before jumping into passerines.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas gallinae
EPP.common.name: Trichomonosis
Host: European greenfinch (Chloris chloris) and Eurasian chaffinch (Fringilla coelebs), with spillover to other local finches; likely maintained in sympatric columbids.
Event.summary: Around 2008, finch trichomonosis emerged in southern Fennoscandia, with marked mortality and subsequent declines in European greenfinch and to a lesser extent chaffinch populations, following its initial establishment in Britain. From 2008 to roughly 2011, surveillance and molecular studies documented rapid spread of the same finch epidemic strain across Finland, Sweden and Norway, and by 2009 disease and excess finch mortality were reported at feeders in Denmark, accompanied by strong reductions in breeding and wintering greenfinch numbers in affected regions. After the initial wave, finch trichomonosis became established but less explosively epidemic, contributing to long-term depressed finch populations in Northern Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Seasonal migration of chaffinches and other finches between Britain and Fennoscandia transported infected birds and seeded new foci; shared high-density feeding at winter gardens and feeders in Northern Europe promoted local amplification. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – molecular analyses showed Fennoscandian finches carried an identical ITS/SSU rRNA finch epidemic strain to that in Britain, implying a single successful lineage with high transmissibility; Host Expansion (Spillover) – maintenance in migrating finches allowed colonisation of previously less-exposed Northern European passerine communities; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – traits of the epidemic strain facilitated persistence and spread into cooler northern climates when suitable host densities were present.
Review: Decision: Review. This event correctly represents the major extension of the finch epidemic strain into Fennoscandia and associated greenfinch declines.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21935745/?utm_source=openai)) However, two corrections were necessary: (i) Norway’s first confirmed finch trichomonosis cases occurred in 2008, not 2009, so the country year has been updated; and (ii) the intra_continental_emergence flag has been set to false, because T. gallinae was already endemic in Northern European columbids and this episode reflects re-emergence via host expansion and spread of a particular clonal lineage, not first presence of the parasite in a new subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Trichomonas gallinae
EPP.common.name: Trichomonosis
Host: Wild columbids: European turtle dove (Streptopelia turtur), stock dove (Columba oenas), wood pigeon (Columba palumbus), collared dove (Streptopelia decaocto), with pathogenic lineages capable of causing mortality and spillover to raptors and finches.
Event.summary: In the early 2010s, systematic molecular surveys across western and southern Europe revealed very high prevalence of Trichomonas gallinae in wild columbids, including turtle doves and stock doves, in Germany, Spain, Italy and Malta, with many birds infected by pathogenic lineages previously associated with mortality in columbids, raptors and finches. During this period, concern grew that trichomonosis was contributing to declines in already vulnerable species such as the European turtle dove, particularly along key migration flyways linking breeding grounds in western and central Europe with staging areas in the Mediterranean and winter quarters in Africa. Following these findings, trichomonosis was increasingly integrated into conservation assessments and management planning for European columbids, although infection remained widespread and endemic across much of the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Agricultural intensification and landscape change reduced food resources and potentially weakened columbid populations; high congregation at watering and feeding sites on migration flyways and in agricultural landscapes facilitated transmission; long-distance migration linked breeding and wintering areas, allowing continental‑scale dissemination; supplementary feeding of gamebirds and doves in some areas further increased contact rates. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – multiple genetic lineages were identified, including pathogenic “lineage A/B” (genotype B) shared with UK columbids and finches; Host Expansion (Spillover) – circulation of pathogenic lineages in columbids increased the risk of spillover into raptors and passerines; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – dominance of widely distributed pathogenic lineages indicates successful adaptation for broad geographic spread and use of multiple columbid hosts.
Review: Decision: Review. This row is best interpreted as a re-emergence/re-recognition of widespread, often pathogenic T. gallinae lineages in European columbids, with potential additive impacts on already declining turtle dove populations, rather than as an intra-continental emergence event; the intra_continental_emergence flag has therefore been set to false.([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1132905621/34)) The 2010–2015 window and listed countries reflect the timing and geography of key molecular surveys rather than discrete outbreak years, and should be regarded as approximate; nevertheless the event is retained because of its significance for conservation planning and the demonstration that highly pathogenic genotypes (including the finch epidemic-linked lineage) are widespread along major flyways.

EPP.scientific.name: Trypanosoma brucei
EPP.common.name: Nagana, Animal African trypanosomiasis, AAT
Host: Beef and dairy cattle (Bos taurus and Bos indicus crossbred herds); additional mortality recorded in wild marsh deer (Blastocerus dichotomus), but quantified impact is for cattle.
Event.summary: From 1995 to the late 1990s, large outbreaks of bovine trypanosomosis caused by Trypanosoma vivax swept through the Brazilian Pantanal wetlands and adjoining Bolivian lowlands. The first recognised cases occurred in 1995 in cattle near Poconé in the northern Pantanal, where herds showed fever, anemia, abortions, severe weight loss and deaths, and parasitological surveys confirmed high T. vivax prevalence. In 1996–1997 the disease spread widely through wetland provinces of Santa Cruz and Beni in Bolivia, with contemporaneous reports attributing up to 150,000 cattle deaths—around 5% of Beni’s 5‑million‑head herd—and marked production losses across affected ranches, prompting emergency treatment campaigns and economic analyses that estimated the total cost of the 1995 outbreak complex at roughly 4% of affected brood‑cow value (around US$160 million). Following intensive chemotherapeutic control and adjustments to grazing and trade practices, overt mortality declined and T. vivax became established as an endemic constraint in the Pantanal–Beni cattle systems rather than a short‑lived epizootic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and long‑distance movement of infected cattle from northern Brazil, where T. vivax was already present, into the previously unaffected Pantanal, together with extensive droving of large herds along wetland trails and the very high abundance of biting tabanid flies during the rainy season, created ideal conditions for rapid mechanical transmission between herds across the Brazil–Bolivia border. Naïve cattle populations with no prior immunity, sparse veterinary infrastructure in remote ranching areas, and delayed recognition of trypanosomosis as the cause of disease all amplified the scale and impact of these outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not pinpoint a novel parasite genotype; instead, the episode reflects the expansion and amplification of an established T. vivax lineage into new wetland ecosystems via mechanical transmission, so it is best classified as a very large re‑occurrence/recrudescence of AAT within the South America sub‑region rather than as first detection or an inter‑/intra‑continental emergence event.
Review: review – new event added. The 1995–1997 Trypanosoma vivax epizootic in the Brazilian Pantanal and Bolivian lowlands caused very large cattle losses (local reports of ~150,000 deaths in Beni and an estimated economic impact of ~US$160 million) and is widely cited as a major AAT event, clearly qualifying for inclusion among the top post‑1990 emergence episodes. Classified as a re‑occurrence within the South America sub‑region because T. vivax had been present elsewhere on the continent for decades and there is no strong evidence of a novel strain; mechanical transmission and cattle movements are the dominant drivers. Event should be retained but cross‑checked against any separate EPP entry that may exist for T. vivax to avoid double counting.

EPP.scientific.name: Vairimorpha apis
EPP.common.name: Nosema apis, Nosema ceranae
Host: Apis mellifera
Event.summary: From 1999 onwards, Spanish laboratories began receiving increasing numbers of diseased Apis mellifera samples with nosemosis, and retrospective molecular diagnostics later showed that most infections, even in archived samples from 1999–2002, were due to Nosema ceranae rather than Nosema apis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2075036/?utm_source=openai)) Between about 2000 and 2005, N. ceranae prevalence rose sharply in Spain and neighboring European countries such as France, Switzerland and Germany, coinciding with widespread reports of colony depopulation, poor productivity and increased winter mortality.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022201107000511?utm_source=openai)) By 2004–2005, N. ceranae had become the predominant Nosema species in many affected European apiaries, and severe colony losses in Spain and parts of Western Europe effectively marked the recognized emergence of N. ceranae‑driven nosemosis on the European continent.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large‑scale movement and trade of queens and colonies within Europe; intensification of beekeeping; climatic conditions in Mediterranean and temperate Europe that favored long transmission seasons; interactions with other stressors such as Varroa destructor, viruses and nutritional stress. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and successful colonization of A. mellifera; enhanced transmission compared with N. apis (reduced seasonality, ability to maintain high infection levels year‑round); increased virulence/pathogenicity manifested as rapid depopulation and colony weakening; geographic range expansion from an Asian origin into Europe.
Review: retain – This event captures the well‑documented emergence of N. ceranae‑associated nosemosis in Spain and adjacent Western/Southern European countries around 1999–2005, with correct continent/sub‑region coding and appropriate classification as an inter‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence of nosemosis due to a new parasite species. The timing and impact align with longitudinal Spanish data and early European surveys, so no structural changes were made.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2075036/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.common.name: Nosema apis, Nosema ceranae
Host: Apis mellifera
Event.summary: From 1999 onwards, Spanish laboratories began receiving increasing numbers of diseased Apis mellifera samples with nosemosis, and retrospective molecular diagnostics later showed that most infections, even in archived samples from 1999–2002, were due to Nosema ceranae rather than Nosema apis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2075036/?utm_source=openai)) Between about 2000 and 2005, N. ceranae prevalence rose sharply in Spain and neighboring European countries such as France, Switzerland and Germany, coinciding with widespread reports of colony depopulation, poor productivity and increased winter mortality.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022201107000511?utm_source=openai)) By 2004–2005, N. ceranae had become the predominant Nosema species in many affected European apiaries, and severe colony losses in Spain and parts of Western Europe effectively marked the recognized emergence of N. ceranae‑driven nosemosis on the European continent.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large‑scale movement and trade of queens and colonies within Europe; intensification of beekeeping; climatic conditions in Mediterranean and temperate Europe that favored long transmission seasons; interactions with other stressors such as Varroa destructor, viruses and nutritional stress. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and successful colonization of A. mellifera; enhanced transmission compared with N. apis (reduced seasonality, ability to maintain high infection levels year‑round); increased virulence/pathogenicity manifested as rapid depopulation and colony weakening; geographic range expansion from an Asian origin into Europe.
Review: retain – This event captures the well‑documented emergence of N. ceranae‑associated nosemosis in Spain and adjacent Western/Southern European countries around 1999–2005, with correct continent/sub‑region coding and appropriate classification as an inter‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence of nosemosis due to a new parasite species. The timing and impact align with longitudinal Spanish data and early European surveys, so no structural changes were made.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2075036/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Vairimorpha apis
EPP.common.name: Nosema apis, Nosema ceranae
Host: Apis mellifera
Event.summary: In the mid‑2000s, Nosema ceranae was first molecularly confirmed in Nosema‑positive Apis mellifera worker samples from eastern Canada and the central United States, demonstrating that the parasite had recently colonized temperate Northern American honey bee populations.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17897670/?utm_source=openai)) During 2006–2010, additional surveys across many U.S. states revealed high prevalence of N. ceranae, often coinciding with reports of unexplained colony depopulation and heavy winter losses during the period when colony collapse disorder (CCD) was first recognized.([ars.usda.gov](https://www.ars.usda.gov/research/publications/publication/?seqNo115=248454&utm_source=openai)) By about 2010, N. ceranae had become the predominant Nosema species in much of the USA and Canada, with most Nosema‑positive samples containing N. ceranae alone and only a small minority harboring N. apis or mixed infections.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation and interstate movement of colonies and package bees within North America; extensive migratory pollination services that facilitate pathogen spread among regions; co‑stressors including Varroa mites, viral infections, pesticides and nutritional stress that may amplify disease impact. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and global spread of N. ceranae into Northern American A. mellifera populations; enhanced transmission and persistence leading to high within‑colony prevalence; possible increased virulence contributing to rapid adult mortality and colony depopulation; partial ecological replacement of N. apis by N. ceranae.
Review: review – Mexico was removed from this event because the project’s Country sheet assigns Mexico to the Central America sub‑region under the South America continent; this North American event now covers only the USA and Canada and its start year has been adjusted to 2006 to match the first molecular detections there. The summary was rewritten to focus on U.S. and Canadian data, and a Mexico‑specific source was moved to the South/Central America event below. Classification as an inter‑continental emergence of N. ceranae into Northern America with concurrent re‑emergence of nosemosis is still appropriate.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17897670/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Vairimorpha apis
EPP.common.name: Nosema apis, Nosema ceranae
Host: Apis mellifera (Africanized and European lineages)
Event.summary: Retrospective molecular studies of archived Africanized Apis mellifera drones from southern Brazil revealed that Nosema ceranae had been present there since at least 1979, decades before its formal description, indicating an undetected long‑term presence in South America.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201113001286?utm_source=openai)) Later work on historical Africanized bee samples in Mexico showed that N. ceranae had parasitized A. mellifera in Central America since at least 1995, while from the mid‑2000s onward surveys in Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Colombia and Ecuador documented widespread N. ceranae infections in managed honey bee colonies, often co‑occurring with or supplanting N. apis.([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.3896/IBRA.1.50.2.09?utm_source=openai)) By about 2015, N. ceranae was recognized as a common and sometimes dominant Nosema pathogen across much of South and Central America, with high infection prevalence but variable association with overt colony losses depending on local climate, bee lineage and co‑stressors.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive movements and admixture of Africanized and European A. mellifera stocks in South and Central America; limited veterinary oversight of bee movements; warm climates that favor year‑round brooding and pathogen transmission; co‑exposure to pesticides, deforestation and habitat changes that can stress colonies. Internal mechanisms: Long‑standing host adaptation of N. ceranae to Africanized A. mellifera, followed by wider geographic expansion and recognition; enhanced transmission and chronic infection dynamics enabling decades of largely silent spread; re‑emergence of nosemosis as N. ceranae reached higher prevalence and interacted with additional stressors, sometimes displacing N. apis as the main Nosema species.
Review: review – This event was expanded to cover both South America and Central America (Mexico), reflecting the project’s geography where Central America is a South America sub‑region, and the event period was updated to 1979–2015 to capture retrospective detections in Brazil (1979 samples) and Mexico (1995 samples) while still emphasizing the main emergence wave after 2000. The countries list now includes Mexico [1995], and the re_occurrence flag was set to false to avoid prohibited co‑occurrence with inter‑continental emergence; re_emergence remains true because a new Nosema species altered disease dynamics in regions previously dominated by N. apis. Sources were updated to include both the Brazilian retrospective study and later Mexican work showing long‑term presence of N. ceranae in Africanized bees.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022201113001286?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

Event.summary: By the mid‑2000s, Nosema ceranae was detected in Apis mellifera colonies in New Zealand as part of a global survey, indicating that the parasite had reached Oceania and become established in local honey bee populations.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022201107000511?utm_source=openai)) Within a few years, N. ceranae was also confirmed in Australian honey bee colonies, with molecular studies documenting its presence alongside N. apis and other pathogens across multiple states.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022201112000560?utm_source=openai)) Through the late 2000s and early 2010s, N. ceranae became widespread in major beekeeping regions in Australia and New Zealand, although the severity of clinical disease and association with overt colony losses varied with climate, bee stocks and co‑infections.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of queens and bee packages from Europe and the Americas into Australia and New Zealand; regional movements of managed colonies for pollination and honey flows; warm temperate climates that can support nearly continuous brooding and pathogen replication. Internal mechanisms: Inter‑continental geographic range expansion into Oceania; efficient oral–fecal transmission via shared food, comb and water sources; potential increased virulence compared with N. apis under some environmental conditions; ongoing displacement of N. apis as the dominant Nosema species in parts of the region.
Review: retain – Evidence from global surveys and regional studies supports first establishment of N. ceranae in New Zealand and then Australia in the mid‑2000s, with correct assignment to Oceania (Australia and New Zealand) and appropriate classification as inter‑continental emergence plus re‑emergence. No geography or type‑coding changes were required; only top‑level references were checked against primary literature.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022201107000511?utm_source=openai))
