EPP.scientific.name: Vairimorpha apis
EPP.common.name: Nosema apis, Nosema ceranae
Sub.regions: Northern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Apis mellifera
Event.summary: Following its initial emergence in Southern and Western Europe, Nosema ceranae continued to spread across Northern and Eastern European honey bee populations from the early 2000s onward, with longitudinal surveillance in northeast Germany documenting a continuous increase in N. ceranae prevalence over more than a decade without complete replacement of N. apis.([apidologie.org](https://www.apidologie.org/articles/apido/pdf/2010/03/m09154.pdf?utm_source=openai)) During this period, N. ceranae infections became common in countries such as Germany, Denmark, Poland, Czechia, Hungary and Romania, often in the context of multifactorial colony losses where Nosema was one of several stressors.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7302437/?utm_source=openai)) By the mid‑2010s, N. ceranae was established across most European subregions, fundamentally altering the epidemiology of nosemosis in A. mellifera by reducing seasonality and promoting more chronic, year‑round infection patterns.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Ongoing intra‑European trade and movement of queens, nucleus colonies and production colonies; exposure to pesticides, habitat changes and variable nutrition that may have increased bees’ susceptibility; interactions with Varroa mites and viral infections. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion within Europe from initial foci in the southwest into cooler temperate climates; enhanced transmission and persistence facilitating establishment in Northern and Eastern Europe; re‑emergence in previously affected subregions driven by a novel Nosema species with distinct epidemiology; partial but not universal displacement of N. apis, altering the temporal pattern and impact of nosemosis.
Review: review – Germany is classified as Western Europe in the project’s Country sheet, yet this event also includes Denmark (Northern Europe) and several Eastern European countries; I therefore added Western Europe to the sub_regions field so that all listed countries are represented by their correct UNSD sub‑regions. The event otherwise appropriately captures intra‑continental spread and re‑emergence of N. ceranae within Europe, supported by long‑term German surveillance and broader European distribution data.([apidologie.org](https://www.apidologie.org/articles/apido/pdf/2010/03/m09154.pdf?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Vairimorpha apis
EPP.common.name: Nosema apis, Nosema ceranae
Host: Apis mellifera (indigenous and imported lineages)
Event.summary: In the early 2010s, surveys of indigenous honey bees in Saudi Arabia using microscopy and PCR detected both Nosema apis and Nosema ceranae, with N. ceranae reported for the first time in the country and mapped across multiple regions.([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1128/AEM.00270-07?utm_source=openai)) Around the same time, Iranian investigators reported the first molecular detection of N. ceranae in Apis mellifera colonies in Iran, adding to evidence that the parasite had spread into Western and Southern Asia and the broader Middle East.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22347302/?utm_source=openai)) Over the following years, N. ceranae became recognized as a widespread component of the pathogen complex affecting honey bees in this region, though its specific contribution to colony losses has varied among studies and often interacts with other stressors.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional movements and importation of queens and colonies between Western/Southern Asian countries and from Europe/Asia; arid and semi‑arid climates that can stress colonies and modulate disease expression; co‑occurrence of other pathogens and pesticide exposures. Internal mechanisms: Intra‑continental geographic range expansion of N. ceranae from Eastern and Central Asia into Western and Southern Asia; establishment in locally adapted A. mellifera populations; host expansion and possible strain diversification suited to hot, dry conditions; re‑emergence of nosemosis in areas where only N. apis had previously been known.
Review: review – Iran is assigned to Southern Asia in the project’s geographic scheme, whereas Saudi Arabia lies in Western Asia; the sub_regions field was therefore expanded to "Western Asia; Southern Asia" so that both countries are correctly represented. The event’s interpretation as intra‑continental spread and re‑emergence of nosemosis driven by N. ceranae in the Middle East/West Asia remains valid and is supported by first‑detection papers from Saudi Arabia and Iran and regional reviews.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22347302/?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Vairimorpha apis
EPP.common.name: Nosema apis, Nosema ceranae
Host: Apis mellifera intermissa; Apis mellifera adansonii
Event.summary: Around the late 2000s, Nosema ceranae was first reported infecting African honey bee subspecies when molecular and microscopic surveys detected the parasite in Apis mellifera intermissa colonies in Algeria, providing the earliest confirmed record of N. ceranae in North Africa.([sfamjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://sfamjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1462-2920.14103?utm_source=openai)) Shortly thereafter, a PCR‑based study in Benin showed that only N. ceranae (and not N. apis) was present in sampled Apis mellifera adansonii colonies, revealing the parasite’s arrival in West Africa and documenting its prevalence in local apiaries.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/254861124_Determinants_et_contraintes_de_la_production_du_miel_dans_le_Nord-Ouest_du_Benin_Cas_des_communes_de_Natitingou_et_de_Tanguieta?utm_source=openai)) Over 2009–2012, these findings, together with continent‑wide disease inventories, established that N. ceranae had recently invaded African A. mellifera lineages, although infection remained patchy and was not yet clearly linked to large‑scale colony collapses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected colonies, queens and beekeeping equipment from Europe and other regions into North and West Africa; increasing long‑distance trade and translocation of colonies; environmental changes and agricultural intensification that may stress local honey bee populations and facilitate novel pathogen establishment. Internal mechanisms: Inter‑continental geographic range expansion of N. ceranae into African A. mellifera subspecies (A. m. intermissa and A. m. adansonii); host adaptation to African lineages; re‑emergence of nosemosis in regions previously affected mainly by N. apis, now involving a second Nosema species with different chronicity and seasonality.
Review: review – A new event was added to represent the first confirmed presence of N. ceranae in African honey bees, based on reports from Algeria (A. m. intermissa) and Benin (A. m. adansonii) around 2009–2011 and syntheses showing that, at the time, these were the only well‑documented African records. This event is coded as an inter‑continental emergence of N. ceranae into Africa with re‑emergence of nosemosis due to a new parasite species. The precise start year and country‑specific dates may be refined as additional historical data are uncovered, but the inclusion of an African first‑detection event is necessary to capture a major geographic expansion of this EPP.([sfamjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://sfamjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1462-2920.14103?utm_source=openai))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Alphavirus venezuelanense
EPP.common.name: VEEV
Host: Humans; equines (horses, donkeys, mules)
Event.summary: Beginning in April 1995 in Falcón State, an epizootic of Venezuelan equine encephalitis caused by subtype IC virus swept east and west through much of northern Venezuela in largely unvaccinated equine populations, producing extensive equine deaths and tens of thousands of human febrile and neurologic illnesses. By mid‑1995 the epidemic crossed the border into La Guajira Department of northern Colombia, where household surveys and clinical surveillance estimated roughly 75,000–100,000 human infections, including several thousand neurologic cases and hundreds of deaths, alongside substantial equine mortality and major socio‑economic disruption. Large‑scale emergency equine vaccination with live‑attenuated TC‑83 and inactivated vaccines, movement restrictions, vector‑control efforts and seasonal reductions in mosquito densities curtailed transmission, and the epidemic subsided by late 1995 with only residual activity into early 1996.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: After about 20 years without major epizootics, large cohorts of unvaccinated horses accumulated across northern Venezuela and adjacent Colombia; unusually heavy rains and humid conditions in 1995 increased mosquito vector densities, and movement of viremic equids and humans along trade and travel routes facilitated spread into La Guajira. Weaknesses in routine equine vaccination and vector control allowed rapid amplification once epizootic virus was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and phenotypic analyses indicate that the 1995 epidemic virus belonged to an epizootic IC lineage closely related to enzootic ID strains from the region and to viruses from the 1992–1993 Venezuelan outbreak, with mutations associated with high equine viremia and efficient mosquito transmission; this supports classification as viral re‑emergence of an equine‑virulent lineage rather than simple recurrence of long‑silent epizootic strains.
Review: retain – 1995 Venezuela–Colombia epidemic is a key high‑impact event with scale and geography consistent with primary sources (≈75,000–100,000 human cases and extensive equine mortality in northern Venezuela and La Guajira, Colombia); classification as re‑emergence of subtype IC virus in a previously affected sub‑region is appropriate and no geographic or type‑coding corrections are needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
EPP.common.name: WNV, West Nile encephalitis virus
Sub.regions: Northern America; Caribbean; Central America; South America
Host: Wild birds (especially corvids and other passerines), zoo and captive birds, horses, humans, domestic dogs and cats, other incidental mammals
Event.summary: In 1999, West Nile virus was detected for the first time in the Western Hemisphere during an outbreak of encephalitis and extensive bird deaths in New York City, marking the introduction of the virus into North America. Over the next several years, the introduced lineage 1 strain spread rapidly via migratory birds and competent Culex vectors across the continental United States, into Canada, Mexico, the Caribbean and parts of Central and northern South America, leading to massive mortality in wild birds and more than 27,000 documented equine infections alongside tens of thousands of human cases. By around 2004 the virus had become established across much of the Americas, with incidence declining from early epidemic peaks but with continued endemic seasonal transmission in birds, horses and humans.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Probable translocation of an infected bird or mosquito via air or ship travel to New York, followed by rapid spread along bird migratory routes and through abundant urban and rural Culex breeding sites in temperate and subtropical climates. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a lineage 1 NY99 genotype highly adapted to naïve North American bird species and local Culex mosquitoes, enabling efficient bird–mosquito–bird transmission and rapid geographic range expansion; subsequent minor genetic changes (e.g. WN02 genotype) improved local adaptation but did not constitute a new lineage for emergence-type classification.
Review: review – Retain as a key event describing the introduction and hemispheric spread of WNV in the Americas; geography, timing and hosts are appropriate, and inter_continental_emergence remains correctly set to true. However, first_detection has been set from true to false because WNV was detected in animals and humans decades earlier in Africa and Europe; this episode represents first detection in the Americas, not in the host system globally. Source URLs already include detailed primary and review articles and were not otherwise modified.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense

Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Humans, horses, wild birds and sentinel poultry
Event.summary: Following the 2004–2008 introduction of lineage 2 into Central Europe and the 2010 epidemic in Greece, West Nile virus activity expanded between 2010 and 2013 across Southern and Eastern Europe, including Italy, the Balkans, Romania, parts of European Russia and Austria, with multiple human and equine outbreaks. During these years, both lineage 1 and lineage 2 strains circulated, causing clusters of neuroinvasive disease in humans and horses and repeated detection in birds and sentinel poultry in new regions within affected countries. While annual case numbers varied with climate and vector abundance, by 2013 WNV had become entrenched along much of the Danube and Po river basins and Mediterranean coastal lowlands, and subsequent control efforts focused on targeted vector management and equine vaccination in high‑risk areas rather than eradication.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive wetland and riverine habitats, irrigation agriculture and warming summers facilitated Culex breeding and viral overwintering, while bird migration enabled stepwise spread between river basins and coastal zones in Southern, Eastern and parts of Western Europe. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation and geographic expansion of both lineage 1 and lineage 2 viruses, with lineage 2 in particular showing strong adaptation to local ecosystems, representing re‑emergence driven by established but spreading strains rather than a completely novel lineage during this period.

First, WNV was already present in both Eastern and Southern Europe before 2010, so intra_continental_emergence has been set to false and the event kept as re_emergence. Event.summary: In 2012, more than a decade after West Nile virus became established in North America, the United States experienced one of its largest resurgence years, with 5,674 reported human cases and 286 deaths, accompanied by increased detection of equine and avian infections in many states and parts of Canada. EPP.scientific.name: White spot syndrome virus
EPP.common.name: WSSV
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (mainly Litopenaeus vannamei and P. stylirostris)
Event.summary: Origin: In January 1999, WSSV was first detected causing white spot disease in farmed shrimp in Nicaragua, Honduras and Guatemala; within months it was found in farms in Panama and spread into major shrimp-farming areas of Ecuador, where by April 1999 it triggered an explosive epidemic. Development: Between 1999 and 2001 the virus disseminated rapidly throughout Central and South American shrimp industries (including the other listed countries), causing acute pond die-offs and, for example, an estimated 42% loss of production capacity in Ecuador alone (about 63,000 tonnes and US$280 million in the first year) and massive job losses regionally. End: By the early 2000s, WSSV had become endemic in much of Latin American shrimp aquaculture; Brazil and Venezuela initially remained exceptional by imposing strict bans on live crustacean imports, while affected countries rebuilt production via improved management, domesticated SPF stocks, and selective breeding for disease tolerance rather than eradication of the virus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-volume transboundary movement of live broodstock and post-larvae of L. vannamei and P. stylirostris from multiple Latin American sources with limited health certification; rapid expansion and intensification of shrimp farms in estuarine systems; weak early-warning and contingency planning for exotic viral diseases. Internal mechanisms: Highly virulent WSSV genotypes capable of causing nearly 100% mortality within 3–10 days post-onset; efficient transmission via water and carcasses that allowed entire farm clusters and coastal embayments to be infected during a single production cycle.
Review: Decision: Retain. This episode is widely recognized as one of the largest and most economically devastating WSSV pandemics, affecting most shrimp-farming countries in Central and South America from 1999 onward. The list of countries and timing (1999–2001) matches FAO and review sources; coding as an inter‑continental emergence into the South America continent (as defined in the project’s country list, including Central America) is appropriate. No changes to geography or classification were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: White spot syndrome virus
EPP.common.name: WSSV
Host: Farmed penaeid shrimp (primarily Penaeus monodon and Fenneropenaeus indicus) in semi‑intensive coastal ponds
Event.summary: Origin: In late August 2011, the first officially reported African outbreak of white spot disease occurred at a large shrimp farm near Quelimane in Zambezia Province, Mozambique, followed in May 2012 by a confirmed WSSV outbreak in a semi‑intensive shrimp farm in southwestern Madagascar along the Mozambique Channel. Development: These linked outbreaks caused heavy mortalities and severe economic losses, described as nearly crippling the regional shrimp industry, and triggered emergency responses including movement bans, culling of stock, and rapid establishment of surveillance and coastal barrier measures against further spread. End: Despite control efforts, subsequent studies demonstrated WSSV’s continued presence in farms and wild crustaceans in the Mozambique Channel, indicating that the virus had become established in the region’s coastal ecosystems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of WSSV into previously WSSV‑free Eastern African coastal systems, most likely via infected live shrimp or contaminated products from the Indian Ocean/Red Sea region; absence of prior surveillance and contingency plans; concentration of shrimp farms along the Mozambique Channel with shared hydrodynamics that facilitated rapid regional dissemination. Internal mechanisms: High virulence and environmental stability of WSSV, enabling efficient spread through farm effluents and wild crustacean populations; likely common origin of circulating genotypes in Mozambique, Madagascar and parts of the Middle East, as suggested by genotyping work.
Review: Decision: Review. WOAH and subsequent virological studies confirm major WSD outbreaks in Mozambique (2011) and Madagascar (2012) with heavy economic losses and establishment of WSSV in the Mozambique Channel. However, given strong evidence that Egypt had already experienced large WSD outbreaks since 2009, this episode is no longer treated as the first African occurrence. It is reclassified as an intra‑continental emergence into a new African subregion (Eastern Africa), with 'inter_continental_emergence' set to No, and the duplicated 'Eastern Africa; Eastern Africa' subregion entry has been simplified to a single 'Eastern Africa'.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans and non-human primates; Haemagogus/Sabethes forest mosquitoes; risk of urban Aedes aegypti involvement in fringe areas
Event.summary: Around 2007–2009, yellow fever virus activity surged in several South American countries, with intense sylvatic transmission in parts of Brazil and Bolivia and smaller human outbreaks in Paraguay and northeastern Argentina, accompanied by widespread non-human primate die‑offs. Human cases occurred both in rural forested zones and, in Paraguay, in and around the metropolitan area of Asunción, raising concerns about urban yellow fever re‑establishment for the first time in decades. Coordinated emergency vaccination campaigns, enhanced surveillance of human and primate cases and focused vector control in high‑risk municipalities curtailed transmission and prevented sustained urban cycles.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Deforestation, agricultural expansion and human encroachment into forest habitats increased contact with infected sylvatic mosquitoes and primates; movement of unvaccinated people between forested areas and towns infested with Aedes aegypti created opportunities for peri‑urban and limited urban transmission, particularly in Paraguay. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses indicate circulation of established South American genotypes; the episode is best characterised as re-occurrence with geographic range fluctuations of existing lineages rather than emergence of a distinct new strain.
Review: review – Kept as a multi-country South American episode because Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina experienced increased human cases and extensive epizootics; however, case numbers (on the order of hundreds regionally) are smaller than in the 1995 Peru epidemic, Brazil 2016–2018, Angola/DRC 2015–2016 or Sudan 2012. Event type has been corrected from re-emergence to re-occurrence (no evidence for intrinsic viral change), and the country name has been standardised to “Bolivia (Plurinational State of)” to match the provided list.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans; predominantly urban Aedes aegypti cycle with contribution from sylvatic reservoirs
Event.summary: In December 2015, yellow fever cases were detected in Luanda, Angola, heralding the country’s largest outbreak in 30 years and the biggest African epidemic since at least the early 1990s, which spread to many Angolan provinces and into urban areas of neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo. By late 2016, more than 7,000 suspected cases, 962 confirmed cases and almost 400 deaths had been reported across Angola and DRC, and viraemic travellers exported cases to Kenya, China, Morocco and other countries without seeding sustained local transmission. Massive emergency vaccination campaigns using standard and fractional dosing, combined with intensified vector control and global coordination under the newly launched Eliminate Yellow Fever Epidemics (EYE) strategy, eventually interrupted transmission and ended the epidemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid unplanned urbanization in Luanda and Kinshasa with high densities of Aedes aegypti, low vaccination coverage in many districts, intense intra‑African and international travel of unvaccinated workers, and limited global vaccine stockpiles all contributed to explosive spread and exportation. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses linked outbreak viruses to lineages previously circulating in Angola, indicating resurgence of existing strains; enhanced transmission resulted from dense human–vector contact and human mobility rather than documented increases in virulence or vaccine escape.
Review: retain – Confirmed as one of the largest and most disruptive modern yellow fever epidemics (≈7,334 suspected cases, 962 confirmed, ~393 deaths), depleting the global vaccine stockpile and directly triggering the EYE strategy; it clearly belongs in the top 10. Sub-regions have been narrowed to Middle Africa, reflecting that sustained transmission occurred in Angola and DRC, while Kenya, China and Morocco are correctly kept in the country list as imported cases without reclassifying the event as inter-continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: Plague bacillus
Host: Humans; small mammals (especially Mastomys spp. and Rattus rattus) in the Western Usambara (Lushoto) and other foci; fleas (Xenopsylla spp. and others).
Event.summary: In north‑eastern Tanzania, particularly the Western Usambara Mountains (Lushoto District), human plague re‑intensified from 1990 onward after earlier control successes, with 364 cases reported in 1990 and a major national peak of about 1,293 cases and 60 deaths in 1991. Through the mid‑1990s, annual epidemics continued in high‑altitude villages, with further large waves in 1994–1997 (approximately 444, 831, 947 and 504 cases respectively), affecting dozens of communities and generating thousands of cases over the decade despite repeated control efforts. Expanded surveillance, community education, rodent and flea control, and better access to antibiotics gradually reduced case numbers and case‑fatality rates after the late 1990s, though the Lushoto focus has remained a persistent natural plague hotspot with recurrent seasonal outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Settlement and cultivation of steep highland slopes, traditional grain storage inside houses, poor housing construction with earth floors, and sleeping on the floor promoted close contact between humans, rodents and fleas in Western Usambara villages; recurrent seasons of favourable temperature and humidity for flea survival, combined with limited access to timely care, allowed explosive plague waves. Internal mechanisms: Studies from Lushoto indicate that persistent transmission in local rodent‑flea systems, rather than introduction of new strains, underlies the repeated outbreaks; enhanced transmission within these established enzootic foci explains the large multi‑year epidemics rather than major genetic change in Y. pestis.
Review: review: New event added because repeated large epidemics in the Western Usambara (Lushoto) focus and other Tanzanian districts in the 1990s (notably ~1,293 cases in 1991 and hundreds of cases per year in 1994–1997) clearly place Tanzania among the most affected countries globally in this period. Classified as re‑occurrence within an established Eastern African focus; there is no evidence for first detection, or for intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or strain‑level re‑emergence. Years and case magnitudes are taken primarily from WHO compilations and Tanzanian retrospective analyses; this multi‑year aggregation is justified by the continuous, closely linked epidemic behaviour in the same focus, but experts may wish to split individual peak years into separate rows if more temporal resolution is desired.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: Plague bacillus
Host: Humans; commensal rats and domestic guinea pigs (reservoir/bridge hosts); fleas.
Event.summary: After decades with little reported activity, bubonic plague re‑emerged in northern Peru in 1992, with about 120 human cases in rural districts, and then expanded dramatically in 1993 when roughly 611 cases and 31 deaths were notified across 122 localities in Piura, Lambayeque and La Libertad. Transmission continued in 1994 with an additional ~420 cases and 19 deaths, affecting both coastal and Andean communities where rodents and guinea pigs were kept inside homes and rat die‑offs preceded human illness. Intensified surveillance, insecticide campaigns, rodent control, improved clinical management, and long‑term control programmes in these departments led to a marked decline in annual case numbers after the mid‑1990s, although low‑level transmission and sporadic outbreaks have persisted in traditional plague foci.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rural poverty, crowding, storage of grain and other foodstuffs inside dwellings, and the widespread practice of rearing and slaughtering guinea pigs and other small mammals indoors created ideal conditions for rodent and flea proliferation and human exposure; lapses in sustained vector‑control and environmental management after earlier eradication efforts allowed the pathogen to re‑establish in domestic settings. Internal mechanisms: Available evidence indicates reactivation of long‑standing natural plague foci in Andean and coastal Peru, with no clear signal of novel genotypes or host shifts; the resurgence is best explained by intensified transmission in pre‑existing rodent–flea cycles rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: review: New event added because the early‑1990s Peruvian outbreaks (120 cases in 1992; ~611 in 1993; ~420 in 1994) represent the principal modern re‑emergence of plague in South America and clearly rank among the highest‑impact post‑1990 episodes by case and death counts. Classified as re‑occurrence in an established South American plague focus; there is no evidence of first detection, inter‑continental spread, or strain‑level re‑emergence. The time window and affected departments follow WHO/PAHO summaries; more detailed national data could be used in a future iteration to distinguish separate sub‑epidemics within this 1992–1994 episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: Plague bacillus
Host: Humans; endemic rodent reservoirs (e.g. Rattus rattus and Malagasy rodents); fleas (Xenopsylla cheopis and others).
Event.summary: From the mid‑1990s Madagascar experienced a dramatic resurgence of plague, with annual suspected case counts rising to about 1,147 in 1995, 1,629 in 1996 and peaking at roughly 2,863 cases and 176 deaths in 1997, mainly in the central highlands. These multi‑year epidemics manifested as recurrent seasonal waves of mainly bubonic plague in rural highland districts, occasionally extending towards larger towns, and were preceded by rodent die‑offs and high flea indices around houses and grain stores. With support from the Institut Pasteur de Madagascar and international partners, surveillance and laboratory confirmation improved, antibiotic treatment and community education were scaled up, and vector and reservoir control campaigns were re‑established, stabilising incidence by the early 2000s though Madagascar has continued to report hundreds of cases annually.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Socio‑economic decline, reduced investment in plague surveillance and vector control, encroachment of agriculture and housing into rodent habitats, and climatic conditions favouring flea survival collectively enabled explosive spread from long‑standing enzootic foci into human populations in the highlands. Internal mechanisms: Available genotyping suggests that these epidemics largely involved existing Y. pestis lineages circulating in Madagascar; the main internal process was enhanced transmission efficiency and geographic expansion of established rodent–flea cycles rather than emergence of novel strains or host shifts.
Review: retain: This multi‑year episode represents the single largest concentration of human plague globally in the 1990s, with annual case counts in Madagascar far exceeding those of other countries; it is unquestionably within the top‑10 events by impact. The event is correctly coded as re‑occurrence in an endemic focus rather than first detection or re‑emergence, and the time span and sub‑region (Eastern Africa) align with WHO and Institut Pasteur de Madagascar analyses. No structural changes were made beyond confirming figures against WHO compilations.

EPP.common.name: Plague bacillus
Host: Humans; peridomestic and wild rodents; fleas.
Event.summary: During the 1996–1997 transmission season, the southern African plague belt experienced a pronounced regional upsurge, including a large bubonic outbreak in Namwala District, Southern Province, Zambia, where roughly 267 human cases and 26 deaths occurred between December 1996 and February 1997, and major epidemics in neighbouring Malawi and Mozambique. Malawi reported an outbreak totalling about 582 cases and 11 deaths in 1997 across Nsanje, Chikwawa and Ntchisi districts, while Mozambique notified approximately 825 cases and 18 deaths the same year, with most cases clustered in Mutarara and other districts after years of lower activity. These concurrent epidemics in adjacent countries prompted WHO‑supported responses with intensified case‑finding, antibiotic treatment, rodent and flea control, and community risk communication, after which reported case numbers declined markedly in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High rodent densities associated with seasonal agricultural production, poor rodent‑proofing of grain stores and dwellings, and favourable climate for flea survival drove epizootics in the border regions of Zambia, Malawi and Mozambique, while limited access to health care and weak early surveillance allowed human outbreaks to grow large before recognition. Internal mechanisms: Investigations in Namwala and affected districts documented infection in multiple rodent and flea species but did not identify major new genotypes; the events are best interpreted as amplification and geographic spread of long‑standing plague foci under conducive environmental and socio‑economic conditions rather than pathogen evolution.

EPP.scientific.name: Yersinia pestis
EPP.common.name: Plague bacillus
Host: Humans; rodents (reservoirs); fleas (vectors).
Event.summary: Beginning in August 2017 Madagascar experienced an unprecedented nationwide plague epidemic, with WHO and partners reporting roughly 2,119–2,417 suspected, probable and confirmed cases and 171–209 deaths by late November, about two‑thirds of which were pneumonic and many arising in urban centres including Antananarivo and Toamasina. The outbreak appears to have started from bubonic cases in the central highlands but rapidly evolved into urban pneumonic transmission with widespread person‑to‑person spread, extensive contact tracing, and international concern, and lower‑level transmission continued into early 2018 before returning to the country’s usual seasonal pattern of mainly rural bubonic plague. A massive national and international response—encompassing prophylactic antibiotics for thousands of contacts, infection‑prevention‑and‑control measures in health facilities, enhanced laboratory support, aggressive vector and reservoir control and sustained risk communication—ultimately interrupted urban pneumonic chains and curtailed the epidemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Endemic plague foci in Madagascar’s central highlands, seasonal increases in rodent and flea populations, heavy human mobility between rural highland communities and major coastal and capital cities, overcrowded urban housing, and weak infection‑prevention‑and‑control in health facilities collectively enabled rapid seeding and amplification of urban pneumonic transmission. Internal mechanisms: No entirely new genotype was demonstrated, but the outbreak highlighted how existing Y. pestis lineages can cause large‑scale human‑to‑human transmission when social and infrastructural conditions allow, effectively expanding the pathogen’s realized geographic and contact range without fundamental evolutionary change.
Review: retain: The 2017–2018 Madagascar epidemic is the largest urban pneumonic plague outbreak recorded in recent decades and is unquestionably among the most consequential post‑1990 emergence events globally by both case count and international concern. Its classification as re‑occurrence in an endemic focus (rather than re‑emergence or inter‑continental spread) is consistent with WHO and ECDC assessments, given the lack of evidence for a novel strain or sustained transmission outside Madagascar. No structural corrections to this row were needed beyond confirming case and death ranges against multiple situation reports.

EPP.scientific.name: Acroptilon repens
EPP.common.name: hardheads, Russian knapweed, Turestan thistle
Host: Perennial forage crops and rangelands (alfalfa, hayfields, pastures) and disturbed rights‑of‑way in western and central United States and southern/central Canada
Event.summary: During the 1990s, Russian knapweed expanded eastward and northward from core western U.S. populations into additional Great Plains and interior states and continued to increase in density where it was already present, while also spreading within Canadian prairie provinces and British Columbia. By the 2000s it was formally listed as a noxious weed in numerous U.S. states and Canadian provinces, with national and provincial agencies recognizing it as a serious invasive threat to forage production and ecosystem health. Through the late 2000s and around 2010, coordinated noxious‑weed, biocontrol and integrated weed management programs helped slow further spread in some jurisdictions, but the species remained widely established across Northern America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued movement of contaminated seed and hay between regions, road and rail corridors, and disturbance from cultivation and infrastructure development facilitated colonization of new areas within Northern America; formal policy recognition as a noxious weed generally followed after the biological invasion had already expanded. Internal mechanisms: Clonal expansion via rhizomes and long‑lived root systems, combined with allelopathy and strong competitive ability under semi‑arid conditions, enabled persistence and densification of stands once introduced into new landscapes.
Review: review – The episode of broader North American spread and policy recognition is real and important, and the emergence‑type coding as re‑occurrence (not intra‑ or inter‑continental) is appropriate because this is further spread within the already invaded Northern America sub‑region. However, Canada’s per‑country date was incorrect: Russian knapweed was introduced to Canada in the early 1900s, not the mid‑1990s.([inspection.canada.ca](https://inspection.canada.ca/en/plant-health/seeds/seed-testing-and-grading/seeds-identification/rhaponticum-repens?utm_source=openai)) I have changed the Countries field from “Canada [1995]” to “Canada [1990]” to indicate that this re‑occurrence episode is considered to begin (approximately) at the start of the 1990s rather than representing first arrival. This event overlaps strongly with Event 1 in both time and space; I therefore recommend retaining it but marking it for possible future merging with Event 1 into a single North American re‑occurrence episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia artemisiifolia
EPP.common.name: annual ragweed, common ragweed, ragweed, low ragweed, Roman wormwood, short ragweed, small ragweed
Host: Primarily annual arable and forage crops (sunflower, maize, soybean, cereals) and fallow land/road verges in agricultural landscapes
Event.summary: From around 1990, common ragweed populations already present in parts of the Pannonian Basin and south‑east Europe expanded explosively, colonizing large areas of arable land and disturbed habitats in Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, southern Russia and Ukraine and causing severe yield losses and allergenic pollen exposure. This expansion continued through the 1990s and 2000s, with ragweed becoming one of the most abundant weeds in many fields and along transport corridors, leading to some of the highest airborne ragweed pollen concentrations recorded in Europe and large increases in hay fever and asthma. By about 2010, the invasion front had reached cooler northern limits in Eastern Europe and the Black Sea region, with further spread slowing as populations approached climatic limits, prompting wide‑scale monitoring and control programmes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: profound socio‑economic and land‑use changes following political transitions in Eastern Europe in the late 1980s–1990s (farm restructuring, field abandonment, reduced weed control), expansion of road and rail networks and increased movement of contaminated grain and birdseed, and lack of effective regulation of seed impurities all facilitated rapid spread and build‑up of dense populations. Internal mechanisms: strong ruderal life‑history traits (high seed production and long‑lived seed bank), plus inherent tolerance to a wide range of soils and disturbance regimes, promoted dominance; no specific new strain is implicated, so this is classified as re‑occurrence driven mainly by external factors rather than documented genetic change.
Review: retain – This row correctly captures the major 1990–2010 invasion episode in the Pannonian Basin and neighbouring Black Sea regions, which multiple studies identify as Europe’s main ragweed hotspot with extremely high pollen loads and widespread crop impacts; the spatial focus (Eastern and Southern Europe) and classification as re-occurrence driven predominantly by land-use and socio-economic change, rather than first occurrence or documented strain change, are appropriate and supported by EFSA, EPPO and regional invasion histories.

Internal mechanisms: pre‑adapted invasive traits (high fecundity, persistent seed bank) and broad climatic tolerance allowed establishment across a wide precipitation and temperature gradient; while some local adaptation is likely, there is currently limited direct evidence for region‑specific novel genotypes, so this episode is best treated primarily as intra‑continental emergence into previously uncolonized Asian subregions rather than as a documented re‑emergence driven by genetic change.

Event.summary: Around the early 2000s, common ragweed, already naturalized elsewhere in Africa, was documented as part of the non‑native flora in Egypt and recorded as casual or locally established in Algeria and Morocco, indicating the presence of self‑sustaining foci in Mediterranean North Africa. Over the 2000s and 2010s the species persisted and likely expanded locally in irrigated and disturbed habitats, and by the late 2010s it was recorded for the first time from the wild flora of Tunisia, confirming its spread along the southern Mediterranean coast and the presence of multiple naturalized foci in the northern African subregion. By 2022, international alerts recognized common ragweed as part of the non‑native flora of Tunisia and broader North Africa, prompting concern about its future spread into additional agroecosystems and the potential emergence of new allergy hotspots on the African continent.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction via contaminated seed, ornamental plantings and other trade pathways from Europe and Asia, combined with irrigated agriculture and disturbed roadside and urban habitats in Mediterranean North Africa, facilitated establishment; limited awareness and management allowed persistence and gradual spread. Internal mechanisms: there is currently no clear evidence of distinct African genetic lineages or novel adaptive traits; the invasion appears to be driven mainly by propagule pressure and suitable climate rather than demonstrated evolutionary change, so this episode is treated as an intra‑continental emergence within Africa rather than a first inter‑continental emergence.
Review: review – This event was originally misclassified as an inter-continental emergence for Africa and described as marking the first establishment of ragweed on the continent; herbarium and floristic data show A. artemisiifolia has been naturalized in South Africa since at least 1896, and also listed as naturalized in Southern Africa and Egypt, so the North African episode represents spread into a new African subregion (Northern Africa) rather than first arrival on the continent. The event type has therefore been corrected to intra-continental emergence and the summary rewritten to remove the claim of first African establishment; the countries and timing (Egypt and neighbouring states with a later confirmed record in Tunisia in 2018) remain broadly consistent with EPPO and regional botanical sources but should be fine-tuned if more precise first-record dates become available.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia confertiflora
EPP.common.name: weakleaf bur ragweed, weakleaf burr ragweed, ragweed
Host: Field crops (e.g. cotton, watermelon), orchards (avocado, date), degraded pastures, roadside and riparian vegetation
Event.summary: Around 1990, Ambrosia confertiflora was first recorded in Israel near Zichron Yaakov and is reported as having been introduced to Palestine in the same period, most likely via contaminated seed mixtures for poultry and aquaculture imported from the southern USA and Mexico. From an initial focus near Shechem (Nablus) in the northern West Bank, the species spread rapidly along Nahal Shechem and downstream to the Alexander River, invading cultivated areas, riverbanks and nature reserves such as Wadi Qana. By about 2000 it had formed dense stands across parts of Samaria and the coastal plain, displacing native vegetation, invading agricultural land and establishing itself as a serious invasive weed in Israel and the occupied Palestinian territory.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction as a contaminant in imported seed mixes for poultry or aquaculture from the United States into the Nablus/Shechem area, followed by downstream dispersal along streams (Nahal Shechem, Alexander River) and facilitated by road construction, soil movement and intensive agriculture in the coastal plain and Jordan Valley. Additional spread was promoted by the absence of early coordinated control and by frequent disturbance along rivers, roads and in orchards and field crops. Internal mechanisms: high fecundity with production of numerous barbed achenes, efficient hydrochory (seed transport in rivers and wadis), vegetative spread from perennial rootstocks, and tolerance of a wide range of semi‑arid to mesic conditions, giving strong competitive ability in disturbed habitats and inherent capacity for geographic range expansion once introduced.
Review: review – Retain this event as the first well‑documented inter‑continental emergence of Ambrosia confertiflora into Asia (Israel and the State of Palestine), with large ecological and agricultural impacts. Corrected misclassification of the “first_detection” flag (now false, since global first detection predates 1990 in its native range) and standardized the country list to match the UN/Excel country list, setting both Israel and State of Palestine to [1990] based on national reports that date introduction into Palestine to 1990. Added Palestinian national‑report sources for introduction year and flagged the event for expert review mainly regarding the exact start year of widespread field detection in the West Bank, but recommend retaining the event and its classification as an inter‑continental emergence episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia confertiflora
EPP.common.name: weakleaf bur ragweed, weakleaf burr ragweed, ragweed
Host: Riverside and wadi vegetation, degraded pastures, orchards (avocado, citrus, date), summer field crops (cotton, watermelon), urban and peri‑urban wasteland
Event.summary: From the late 1990s into the 2000s, Ambrosia confertiflora underwent a massive expansion on both sides of the Green Line, especially along the Alexander River, Wadi Tirza and through Samaria into the northern Jordan Valley, where dense monospecific stands developed. During the 2000s and early 2010s the species spread further west into the Hefer Valley and the coastal plain and eastwards along wadis, invading orchards, pastures, summer field crops and protected areas while becoming one of the most harmful invasive plants documented in Israel and the occupied West Bank. By around 2017, infestations extended to additional regions including parts of Lower Galilee and the Negev, prompting coordinated national management plans and surveillance, although persistent populations remained entrenched along rivers, roadsides and agricultural landscapes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Ongoing downstream transport of achenes in rivers and irrigation canals, movement of contaminated soil and machinery, expansion of irrigated agriculture and orchards, and lack of early coordinated management allowed rapid build‑up of seed banks and spread along linear corridors. Road and infrastructure development, together with repeated soil disturbance in orchards and row crops, further facilitated establishment and local dominance. Internal mechanisms: very high seed production with durable seed banks, vigorous clonal growth from perennial rootstocks, and ecological plasticity across semi‑arid to mesic habitats, leading to a dramatic increase in abundance and extent without evidence for a novel genotype; resurgence is therefore attributed mainly to external drivers (re‑occurrence) rather than evolutionary change in the weed.
Review: review – Retain this event as a major re‑occurrence episode representing the rapid expansion and intensification of the invasion in Israel and the State of Palestine from about 2000 to 2017, with extensive ecological and agricultural impacts and national‑level management responses. No change was made to the emergence‑type classification (re_occurrence = true, others = false), which is appropriate because the species was already present in Western Asia and no new genotype or host shift has been documented; this is a resurgence within the same sub‑region driven by external factors. The country string was standardized by replacing the vague “[2000s]” with “[2000]” for the State of Palestine to match the requested format; this year should be interpreted as the approximate onset of the large‑scale expansion phase rather than first introduction. Because the split between the 1990‑2000 and 2000‑2017 episodes is somewhat arbitrary along a continuum of spread, this event is flagged for expert review of the temporal boundaries, but it should be retained as one of the largest documented emergence episodes for this species.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia trifida
EPP.common.name: great ragweed, Texan great ragweed, giant ragweed, tall ragweed, blood ragweed, perennial ragweed, horseweed
Sub.regions: Eastern Europe; Southern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Primarily riverbanks and floodplains, roadsides and disturbed land, with localized invasion of maize and sunflower fields; major producer of allergenic pollen affecting nearby human populations
Event.summary: After scattered earlier records in the 19th and 20th centuries, giant ragweed expanded conspicuously in Central and Eastern Europe from about 2000 onward, with particularly rapid spread documented in parts of European Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Hungary and the western Balkans along major river systems and transport corridors. During the 2000s and 2010s, populations increased in agricultural landscapes of Italy and France as well, where dense stands formed in some sunflower and maize fields and produced heavy pollen loads contributing to allergic disease. By the 2010s and early 2020s, Ambrosia trifida was recognized as an emerging invasive ragweed in Europe, added to the EPPO Alert list in 2014 and to the EPPO A2 List in 2019, and first detected as a naturalised invasive population in additional countries such as Montenegro in 2024, prompting regional risk assessments and coordinated early‑warning and control programs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Repeated introduction as a contaminant in grain and seed, increased river traffic and road transport, and regional climate warming favoring warm‑summer annuals all promoted establishment and spread; disturbance of riparian zones, road verges and abandoned fields provided ideal habitats, while limited early awareness of this species (compared to common ragweed) delayed targeted control. Internal mechanisms: strong competitive ability in fertile, disturbed soils, prolific seed production, and potential for long‑distance dispersal along rivers and human transport routes supported range expansion; European field studies suggest shifts in morpho‑functional traits that may enhance invasiveness in some invaded sites, supporting classification as re‑emergence in addition to intra‑continental spread.
Review: review – Retain: this row appropriately aggregates the main European invasion episode since ca. 2000, which, although still locally distributed, spans multiple sub‑regions and has significant agronomic and allergenic impacts where dense populations occur. The event has been re‑typed to intra‑continental emergence + re‑emergence (with re‑occurrence set to No) to reflect spread into new European sub‑regions (Southern and Western Europe) alongside evidence of trait shifts in invaded populations, while respecting the rule that re‑occurrence should not co‑occur with intra‑continental emergence. Countries and timing were checked against EPPO and the 2021 European monograph, including confirmation of the first record for Montenegro in 2024.([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/epp.12661?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis spiraecola
EPP.common.name: black bean aphid
Host: Citrus spp. (sweet orange, clementine, satsuma, lemon and other citrus); occasionally other fruit trees and ornamentals in the same orchards
Event.summary: From the 1980s into the 1990s, Aphis spiraecola rapidly built up in Mediterranean citrus orchards in Spain, Italy, Greece and southern France, where it had previously been absent from citrus or regarded as a minor species compared with Aphis gossypii. Through the 1990s–2000s it displaced A. gossypii as the dominant citrus aphid across much of the western Mediterranean, including the Algarve region of Portugal, causing chronic infestations of spring flushes, leaf curling and increased concern about Citrus tristeza virus spread. By the 2010s A. spiraecola was entrenched as the key citrus aphid in most Mediterranean coastal citrus zones and is now managed primarily through conservation biological control, monitoring and selective insecticides rather than broad‑spectrum sprays.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of irrigated citrus along Mediterranean coasts, relatively mild winters, and insecticide programmes that disrupted natural enemies more than A. spiraecola are thought to have favoured this species over A. gossypii and other aphids in citrus systems. Internal mechanisms: High performance of A. spiraecola on clementine and sweet orange, together with differences in parasitoid and predator complexes compared with A. gossypii, allowed it to attain much larger populations and become an important Citrus tristeza virus vector in Mediterranean citrus.
Review: review – Retain this event as a major Mediterranean citrus emergence episode but with corrections. Turkey was removed from the country list to keep the event strictly within Europe according to the UNSD continent/sub‑region scheme, and France was added to justify inclusion of Western Europe. The emergence‑type classification has been changed from re-emergence to re-occurrence, because the shift reflects a resurgence and dominance change in an already infested subregion driven mainly by agronomic and ecological factors (citrus intensification, insecticide use, natural enemy disruption) rather than documented genetic change in the aphid. Years and countries are consistent with Mediterranean citrus aphid literature but should be double‑checked against regional sources.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis spiraecola
EPP.common.name: black bean aphid
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Apple (Malus domestica), pear (Pyrus spp.), citrus (where present), and numerous ornamentals and shrubs (e.g. Spiraea spp.) in orchards and urban landscapes
Event.summary: Beginning around 2000, Aphis spiraecola was first confirmed as established in Germany and then spread north and east from its earlier Mediterranean strongholds into more temperate parts of Western, Eastern and Northern Europe. Over the 2000s–2010s, first records were documented from Hungary, Bulgaria, Serbia, the Baltic states, the United Kingdom, Kosovo, Slovakia, Czechia and Denmark, mainly in apple orchards and ornamental plantings, with the species often behaving as an invasive green apple aphid. By the late 2010s A. spiraecola had become widespread across much of Europe on apple and other Rosaceae, coexisting with or locally displacing the native Aphis pomi and requiring inclusion in pest monitoring and integrated pest management thresholds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased intra‑European trade in nursery stock, ornamentals and planting material, together with gradual climate warming that favoured overwintering and survival in more northerly climates, facilitated stepwise colonisation of new European subregions. Internal mechanisms: Inherent geographic range expansion capacity and host versatility (use of apple and other Maloideae as secondary hosts, with host-alternating or anholocyclic life cycles) enabled A. spiraecola to establish and persist under Central and Northern European conditions once introduced.
Review: review – Retain as a major intra-European range-expansion episode but adjust classification. The event remains an intra-continental emergence, because it documents spread into new European sub-regions (Western, Eastern, Northern Europe) from long-established Mediterranean populations. The previous re-emergence flag has been removed, as there is no clear evidence that genetic changes (rather than introductions and climate suitability) are the primary drivers. Country first-record years match Borbély et al. (2021) and the distribution summary on Wikipedia but should be cross-checked against national faunistic records.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Host: Apple (Malus domestica), pear (Pyrus spp.), citrus (where present), and numerous ornamentals and shrubs (e.g. Spiraea spp.) in orchards and urban landscapes
Event.summary: Beginning around 2000, Aphis spiraecola was first confirmed as established in Germany and then spread north and east from its earlier Mediterranean strongholds into more temperate parts of Western, Eastern and Northern Europe. Over the 2000s–2010s, first records were documented from Hungary, Bulgaria, Serbia, the Baltic states, the United Kingdom, Kosovo, Slovakia, Czechia and Denmark, mainly in apple orchards and ornamental plantings, with the species often behaving as an invasive green apple aphid. By the late 2010s A. spiraecola had become widespread across much of Europe on apple and other Rosaceae, coexisting with or locally displacing the native Aphis pomi and requiring inclusion in pest monitoring and integrated pest management thresholds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased intra‑European trade in nursery stock, ornamentals and planting material, together with gradual climate warming that favoured overwintering and survival in more northerly climates, facilitated stepwise colonisation of new European subregions. Internal mechanisms: Inherent geographic range expansion capacity and host versatility (use of apple and other Maloideae as secondary hosts, with host-alternating or anholocyclic life cycles) enabled A. spiraecola to establish and persist under Central and Northern European conditions once introduced.
Review: review – Retain as a major intra-European range-expansion episode but adjust classification. The event remains an intra-continental emergence, because it documents spread into new European sub-regions (Western, Eastern, Northern Europe) from long-established Mediterranean populations. The previous re-emergence flag has been removed, as there is no clear evidence that genetic changes (rather than introductions and climate suitability) are the primary drivers. Country first-record years match Borbély et al. (2021) and the distribution summary on Wikipedia but should be cross-checked against national faunistic records.

EPP.scientific.name: Aphis gossypii
EPP.common.name: cotton aphid, melon aphid, puceron du melon
Host: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) in major production regions of Brazil and Argentina, with additional foci in Paraguay
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through about 2010, cotton blue disease caused by cotton leafroll dwarf virus (CLRDV) and transmitted persistently by Aphis gossypii became the most important viral disease of cotton in Brazil and Argentina, with the virus confirmed as a distinct polerovirus and the aphid identified as its main vector. During this period, epidemics repeatedly affected large areas of South American cotton, with susceptible cultivars suffering severe stunting, blue‑green foliage and boll loss, and reported yield reductions of up to roughly 70–80% in badly affected fields, prompting heavy reliance on aphid control and deployment of Cbd gene‑based resistant varieties. In the 2000s, widespread use of these resistant cultivars was partly undermined by the emergence and spread of an atypical CLRDV strain that broke Cbd resistance, so national breeding and management programs shifted toward stacking resistance and refining vector and virus management, reducing—but not eliminating—the frequency of catastrophic outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and regional spread of CLRDV and later an atypical recombinant strain into intensive cotton production zones, planting of highly susceptible and then single‑gene (Cbd) resistant cultivars over large areas, and climatic conditions favoring high Aphis gossypii populations allowed repeated, landscape‑scale epidemics; aphid management often depended on insecticides with limited effectiveness against a persistently transmitted virus. Internal mechanisms: No clear genetic change in A. gossypii is implicated; instead, the key biological factor is its intrinsic efficiency as a persistent vector of CLRDV combined with its high reproductive rate and ability to persist on alternate hosts, making this best classified as a re‑occurrence of vector impact driven by viral evolution and agronomic choices rather than by novel aphid biotypes.
Review: review – added as a major South American cotton blue disease / CLRDV epidemic vectored by Aphis gossypii; years (1990–2010) and inclusion of Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay are approximate and should be cross‑checked, but multiple sources document CLRDV as the main viral disease of cotton in the region with yield losses up to about 80% and near‑ubiquitous field incidence, making this clearly one of the top global A. gossypii impact events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactericera cockerelli
EPP.common.name: potato/tomato psyllid
Host: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) and other solanaceous crops (e.g. tomato, pepper) in northern Mexico and the south‑western/central United States
Event.summary: In the mid‑1990s, a new potato disorder later termed zebra chip was first observed in commercial fields near Saltillo, Mexico, and by around 2000 similar symptoms appeared in potato fields in south Texas, USA. Over roughly 2000–2006 the disease intensified and became economically important, causing serious yield and quality losses in Texas and then in additional south‑western and central U.S. potato‑growing areas while remaining closely associated with high populations of the native potato/tomato psyllid. By the mid‑2000s, zebra chip and its B. cockerelli vector were recognized as a major production problem across much of northern Mexico and the western/central United States, prompting substantial research investment and major changes in insecticide use and crop management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and geographic expansion of irrigated potato production in warm regions of northern Mexico and the southern United States, availability of year‑round solanaceous hosts, and movement of infested planting material and equipment facilitated high psyllid densities and rapid spread of the new disorder. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and spread of Candidatus Liberibacter solanacearum (CLso), a previously undescribed phloem‑limited bacterium vectored by B. cockerelli, converted a long‑known foliar pest into the driver of a severe tuber disease, representing a re‑emergence of the psyllid’s impact through a novel pathogen association and increased virulence/pathogenicity in potato relative to historical psyllid yellows.
Review: retain (minor correction). Event represents the primary modern emergence of zebra chip associated with B. cockerelli and CLso in Mexico and the southern/central USA, clearly one of the globally most impactful episodes (large yield and quality losses, tens of millions of dollars in damages). The event year has been slightly extended from 1994–2005 to 1994–2006 to reflect documentation that severe economic impacts in Texas continued through 2005–2006. Countries, continents and sub-regions correctly reflect Mexico (South America | Central America) and the United States (North America | Northern America). Classification as re-emergence (new pathogen association greatly increasing impact of a long-established pest) without first-detection or intra-/inter-continental emergence is appropriate. Sources (Crosslin et al. 2010 Plant Health Progress; Nebraska Extension EC1905; reviews of zebra chip disease and B. cockerelli) are relevant and sufficient for this major event.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactericera cockerelli
EPP.common.name: potato/tomato psyllid
Host: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) and other solanaceous crops
Event.summary: From about 2009, large zebra chip outbreaks associated with dense populations of Bactericera cockerelli were documented in commercial potato fields in Honduras and subsequently in neighboring Central American countries, building on earlier reports from Mexico and Guatemala. Over the early 2010s, the psyllid–CLso complex spread and became established across key highland potato‑growing areas of Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua and El Salvador, causing severe foliar symptoms, yield reductions and tuber quality defects at times affecting most plants in infested fields. By the mid‑2010s, zebra chip associated with B. cockerelli and CLso was considered widespread and economically important in multiple Central American countries, raising regional concern for the sustainability of potato and other solanaceous crop production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional trade and movement of seed potatoes and other planting material, limited vector control capacity, and continuous or overlapping potato cropping systems facilitated dissemination of the psyllid and CLso within the Central American highlands; suitable cool highland climates supported high vector and pathogen pressure. Internal mechanisms: The outbreaks reflect the spread of existing CLso haplotypes A and B within established B. cockerelli populations rather than the emergence of new genotypes; the main mechanism is high inoculum pressure and efficient transmission by the psyllid, leading to a pronounced resurgence of disease severity in areas where psyllids had historically been present but zebra chip had not previously caused such large, multi-country epidemics.
Review: retain with corrections – review. This event appropriately captures a major regional resurgence of zebra chip in Central America but required several adjustments. (i) Country start years have been refined to better match available evidence: Honduras [2009] (severe outbreaks documented by 2009), Guatemala [2009] (disease known earlier but large regional epidemics evident by late 2000s), Nicaragua [2011] and El Salvador [2012] (following EPPO reporting of first CLso/B. cockerelli findings). (ii) Under the UNSD-based scheme, these countries all lie in the South America | Central America sub-region, so no intra-continental emergence flag is used, consistent with guidance not to treat spread to additional countries within the same sub-region as intra-continental emergence. (iii) The event is re-classified as re-occurrence only (re-emergence set to false): the available literature indicates regional spread of existing CLso haplotypes A/B and increased disease incidence driven mainly by external drivers (trade, cropping systems), without clear evidence for new genotypes or other intrinsic changes in B. cockerelli in this period. Sources remain broadly appropriate (APS feature articles, Nebraska extension profile, scientific reviews and regional proceedings), but more precise local reports (e.g. EPPO Reporting Service items for Nicaragua and El Salvador) could be added in a later refinement.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Zeugodacus cucurbitae
EPP.common.name: melon fly
Sub.regions: Western Africa; Middle Africa; Northern Africa
Host: Cucurbit crops (e.g., cucumber, melon, pumpkin, squash) and other local hosts
Event.summary: From 1999 onwards, melon fly was detected for the first time in multiple West and Central African countries where it had previously been absent, beginning with Gambia and Côte d’Ivoire and then rapidly appearing across the Sahelian and Guinean zones. Surveys using cuelure traps and fruit sampling during the early 2000s showed that the species became established and locally abundant on cucurbits and some other hosts throughout these new areas. By around 2006, Z. cucurbitae was widespread and regarded as a major cucurbit pest across much of Western and parts of Central and North‑eastern Africa, with ongoing management challenges but no clear continent‑wide eradication or containment.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increasing regional trade and movement of infested cucurbit fruit and vegetables, weak quarantine at land borders, and expansion of irrigated vegetable production facilitated the rapid spread from long‑infested eastern Africa and Indian Ocean islands into West, Middle and North‑eastern Africa. Internal mechanisms: the species’ broad host range, high reproductive rate, and strong dispersal capacity underpinned its capacity for geographic range expansion within Africa (geographic range expansion – inherent).
Review: Review – Retain this as a key intra‑continental emergence episode for Africa. Corrected sub_regions to include Northern Africa because Sudan is classified there in the UN/Excel scheme, and standardised the country list to use the official country names from the “Country” sheet (e.g. Côte d’Ivoire, Democratic Republic of the Congo). Event years and country‑specific first records match De Meyer et al. 2015 and associated sources. Classification as intra‑continental emergence (spread from previously infested Eastern Africa into new African sub‑regions) is appropriate and should be kept.

EPP.scientific.name: Zeugodacus cucurbitae
EPP.common.name: melon fly
Host: Field‑grown cucurbits (melon, cucumber, pumpkin, squash) in smallholder and peri‑urban systems
Event.summary: Following initial detections in West and Central Africa around 1999–2004, melon fly populations built up substantially in the 2000s in irrigated vegetable zones of countries such as Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Guinea, Mali, Niger and Senegal. Field surveys and fruit sampling during this decade showed high infestation rates in cucurbit fields, with melon fly becoming one of the dominant cucurbit‑infesting tephritids in several regions. By the end of the 2000s, recurrent heavy infestation episodes and associated yield losses had turned the species into a key constraint on cucurbit production in many West African production basins, with farmers resorting to frequent insecticide applications and other ad hoc control measures.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of irrigated dry‑season vegetable production, monocropping of cucurbits near towns, and limited access to integrated pest management options created conditions for recurrent outbreaks; informal regional trade in fruits likely redistributed populations among countries. Internal mechanisms: strong competitive ability relative to native Dacus species on cultivated cucurbits and broad host use contributed to its dominance and repeated high‑density outbreaks (enhanced transmission/establishment; geographic range expansion – inherent).
Review: Retain – This row captures the shift from initial introduction (late 1990s) to recurrent, high‑impact infestations in key West and Central African cucurbit production basins during the 2000s. Countries, timing and impact are consistent with Vayssières et al. 2007 and subsequent work. Classification as re_occurrence (dramatic increase in incidence within already invaded West/Middle African sub‑regions) is appropriate. There is some temporal and geographic overlap with the 1999–2006 invasion row, but the focus here on outbreak intensity and yield loss justifies keeping it as a separate high‑impact episode; this should simply be noted when using the dataset to avoid double‑counting impacts.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Host: Wide range of cultivated and wild fruit hosts; major damage reported in guava, mango, Polynesian chestnut and other tree fruits on affected islands
Event.summary: Beginning in the early 1990s Bactrocera dorsalis invaded multiple Pacific islands where it had previously been absent. Around 1992 the fly was recorded in Nauru, where it became a serious pest before being eradicated by a coordinated male‑annihilation and bait‑spray campaign completed by the late 1990s. In July 1996 B. dorsalis was discovered on Tahiti in French Polynesia and rapidly spread to Moorea and other Society Islands, and in the same period it was first reported from Palau; on several islands it quickly displaced or added to existing polyphagous fruit flies and caused heavy damage to guava, mango and other fruit crops. Eradication was achieved in some locations (e.g. Nauru), whereas in French Polynesia the pest became established and long‑term classical biological control with the parasitoid Fopius arisanus was implemented to reduce but not eliminate B. dorsalis populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increasing shipping and air traffic, and informal movement of fresh fruit between Asian source regions and remote Pacific islands, provided repeated opportunities for the introduction of infested fruit; once established, continuous fruiting of multiple hosts and limited quarantine capacity on small islands favoured spread within and between islands. EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Host: Mixed fruit orchards (citrus, persimmon, stone fruits, grape) in Campania (Italy) and potential hosts near wholesale markets and airports in Austria and France where adults were trapped
Event.summary: Between 2012 and 2018, nine adult Bactrocera dorsalis sensu lato were captured in methyl‑eugenol traps at several sites around Vienna, Austria, and identified as interceptions with no evidence of establishment.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-6656?utm_source=openai)) In 2018, a dedicated survey in mixed fruit orchards in Campania (Southern Italy) captured seven male B. dorsalis in methyl‑eugenol traps at Nocera Inferiore and Palma Campania, representing the first confirmed field detections of this species in European orchards and prompting emergency phytosanitary measures and delimiting zones.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6316371/?utm_source=openai)) From 2019 onwards, France reported sporadic male captures near the Rungis wholesale market, Orly airport and in a citrus orchard in Var, leading to increased surveillance and local regulatory actions; to date all findings are considered transient incursions linked to imported fruit, with no confirmed long‑term establishment anywhere in Europe.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/DACUDO/distribution/FR?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growing imports of tropical and subtropical fruits from Africa and Asia, passenger‑borne movement of infested fruit, and concentration of trade through major hubs (Rungis, airports, wholesale markets) have repeatedly introduced B. dorsalis into Europe, where Mediterranean and some temperate microclimates are potentially suitable for establishment.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12470648/?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The species’ capacity to survive in a range of subtropical climates and its strong male response to methyl eugenol underpin both its invasion risk and the feasibility of early detection at very low densities; however, current evidence suggests repeated short‑lived incursions rather than sustained in situ transmission, so no emergence‑type category is ticked for this episode.
Review: Decision: review. The European detections are important as first records on this continent, but they mostly consist of isolated trap captures near trade hubs and one small cluster of males in Italian orchards, with no confirmed established populations. In line with the project’s exclusion of imported cases without in situ transmission from inter‑continental emergence, inter_continental_emergence was changed from Yes to No, and the event is now treated as a high‑priority detection/incursion episode without any emergence‑type flag set.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/DACUDO/distribution/FR?utm_source=openai)) The year range was also adjusted to 2012‑2022 to encompass the Austrian interceptions and later French captures, and the countries list was limited to Austria, Italy and France where well‑documented official reports exist. Because the borderline between transient incursions and genuine establishment remains under close scrutiny, this row should be revisited as more surveillance data accumulate.
