EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Host: Diverse cultivated and wild fruits (including mango, citrus, guava and other tropical fruit crops)
Event.summary: In 1996, Bactrocera dorsalis was first recorded on Mauritius, an Indian Ocean island off the African coast, where an intensive area-wide campaign combining bait sprays and male annihilation led to official declaration of eradication in 1999. From 2005 onwards, the species invaded the Comoros and then spread stepwise to Mayotte in 2007 and Madagascar by 2010, where it became the dominant fruit fly in many mango-growing areas, while Mauritius experienced at least two further incursions in 2013 and 2015, the latter leading to widespread establishment, and Réunion recorded its first invasion around 2017. Together these invasions produced a pattern of repeated long-distance introductions from Asia and from the African mainland, island hopping, occasional successful eradications and eventual establishment on most major south-west Indian Ocean islands, with substantial chronic fruit losses and increased insecticide use.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: human‑mediated movement of infested fruit between Asia, East Africa and the south-west Indian Ocean islands, dense tourism and trade links (air and sea traffic), and highly suitable tropical climates with abundant host fruit. Internal mechanisms: introduction of invasive genotypes capable of founding new island populations from few individuals, leading to strong founder effects and genetic bottlenecks, followed by rapid demographic expansion; genomic work supports two distinct invasion pathways (a western route via East Africa into Comoros–Mayotte–Madagascar and an eastern route directly from Asia into Mauritius and Réunion). Repeated eradications and reintroductions on Mauritius illustrate both the species’ high colonisation ability and the possibility of local elimination under intensive area‑wide management. (Supported by Deschepper et al. 2023 and EPPO/NPPO reports for Mauritius and other islands.)
Review: review – Event retained but reclassified to better match the definitions: treated as inter-continental emergence because the 1996 Mauritius incursion is the first confirmed occurrence of B. dorsalis on the African continent, and re_emergence is kept to reflect repeated reintroductions and distinct invasion pathways; intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence flags were removed to maintain the mostly mutually exclusive structure of event types. The sub-region label was standardised to the UNSD term ‘Eastern Africa’. Country sequence and eradication/reintroduction history are consistent with EPPO reports and Deschepper et al. (2023), but finer dating for Comoros, Mayotte, Madagascar and the status of Réunion after 2017 should be double-checked against national reports.

Host: Diverse cultivated and wild fruits (including mango, citrus, guava and other tropical fruit crops)
Event.summary: In 1996, Bactrocera dorsalis was first recorded on Mauritius, an Indian Ocean island off the African coast, where an intensive area-wide campaign combining bait sprays and male annihilation led to official declaration of eradication in 1999. From 2005 onwards, the species invaded the Comoros and then spread stepwise to Mayotte in 2007 and Madagascar by 2010, where it became the dominant fruit fly in many mango-growing areas, while Mauritius experienced at least two further incursions in 2013 and 2015, the latter leading to widespread establishment, and Réunion recorded its first invasion around 2017. Together these invasions produced a pattern of repeated long-distance introductions from Asia and from the African mainland, island hopping, occasional successful eradications and eventual establishment on most major south-west Indian Ocean islands, with substantial chronic fruit losses and increased insecticide use.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: human‑mediated movement of infested fruit between Asia, East Africa and the south-west Indian Ocean islands, dense tourism and trade links (air and sea traffic), and highly suitable tropical climates with abundant host fruit. Internal mechanisms: introduction of invasive genotypes capable of founding new island populations from few individuals, leading to strong founder effects and genetic bottlenecks, followed by rapid demographic expansion; genomic work supports two distinct invasion pathways (a western route via East Africa into Comoros–Mayotte–Madagascar and an eastern route directly from Asia into Mauritius and Réunion). Repeated eradications and reintroductions on Mauritius illustrate both the species’ high colonisation ability and the possibility of local elimination under intensive area‑wide management. (Supported by Deschepper et al. 2023 and EPPO/NPPO reports for Mauritius and other islands.)
Review: review – Event retained but reclassified to better match the definitions: treated as inter-continental emergence because the 1996 Mauritius incursion is the first confirmed occurrence of B. dorsalis on the African continent, and re_emergence is kept to reflect repeated reintroductions and distinct invasion pathways; intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence flags were removed to maintain the mostly mutually exclusive structure of event types. The sub-region label was standardised to the UNSD term ‘Eastern Africa’. Country sequence and eradication/reintroduction history are consistent with EPPO reports and Deschepper et al. (2023), but finer dating for Comoros, Mayotte, Madagascar and the status of Réunion after 2017 should be double-checked against national reports.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Sub.regions: Eastern Africa; Middle Africa; Western Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Primarily mango, but also citrus, guava, papaya and many other cultivated and wild fruit crops (over 250 host plants documented in Africa).
Event.summary: In 2003, an unknown Bactrocera species later synonymised with B. dorsalis (B. invadens) was first detected on the coast of Kenya, signalling the start of a major invasion from Asia into the African mainland and rapidly damaging mango and other fruit crops. Over the following decade, the species spread quickly from East Africa across much of Central, West and parts of Southern Africa, becoming the dominant fruit fly in many mango-producing regions and displacing native Ceratitis species, with severe yield losses, increased insecticide use and trade disruptions. By the mid‑2010s, B. dorsalis was established across most of tropical sub‑Saharan Africa, with only some southern fringe areas remaining free or under transient incursion status, and it continues to cause chronic high infestation levels and high management costs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: repeated introductions from Asia (probably from the Indian subcontinent) followed by intense intra‑African trade in fresh fruit, weak phytosanitary controls, extensive plantings of highly suitable hosts (especially mango) and favourable tropical climates across large areas of sub‑Saharan Africa. Internal mechanisms: introduction of an invasive genotype within the B. dorsalis complex (historically described as B. invadens) with very broad host range and high reproductive capacity, leading to competitive displacement of native fruit flies and very rapid geographic range expansion into a previously unoccupied continent. (Summarised from Lux et al. 2003, Drew et al. 2005, African invasion syntheses and EPPO distribution data.)
Review: review – Event retained as the main Africa-wide mainland invasion episode but reclassified as intra-continental emergence only: it captures spread from initial African foci (post‑Mauritius) into additional African UN sub-regions (Middle, Western and Southern Africa). Inter_continental_emergence and re_emergence flags were removed because first continental occurrence is already represented by the 1996 Mauritius event, and this wave reflects subsequent within-continent expansion rather than reappearance in a previously known sub-region. The country list and approximate dates are broadly consistent with EPPO and regional reviews, but some southern fringe countries (e.g. Botswana, Eswatini) with more recent detections are not listed and could be added in a future refinement if judged among the top-impact events.

EPP.scientific.name: Bemisia tabaci
EPP.common.name: sweetpotato whitefly
Host: protected and open-field vegetables (tomato, cucurbits), cotton, ornamentals
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, MEAM1 (B) biotype populations of Bemisia tabaci spread from their presumed Middle Eastern origin into Mediterranean Europe, first causing serious outbreaks in greenhouse vegetables and ornamentals in Spain and Italy. Over the next few years the invasive biotype became established across southern European countries including Greece and Portugal, where it caused major yield losses and outbreaks of begomovirus diseases. By the mid‑1990s, MEAM1 was widely established and gradually integrated into regional management programs, though it remained an important vector and pest.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive greenhouse vegetable and ornamental production, high pesticide inputs, and trade in infested planting material and ornamentals facilitated spread around the Mediterranean. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype (MEAM1) with expanded host range and higher fecundity, increased insecticide resistance, and strong vector competence for begomoviruses, leading to much greater impact than previously resident Bemisia populations.

EPP.scientific.name: Bemisia tabaci
EPP.common.name: sweetpotato whitefly
Host: protected horticultural crops (tomato, cucurbits, ornamentals)
Event.summary: In the early 2010s, a MED Q2 subgroup of Bemisia tabaci, originating from the eastern Mediterranean, was reported invading and spreading within Southern Europe, including Italy and Spain where Q1 lineages had previously dominated greenhouse crops, and later France. Between about 2010 and 2015, Q2 established and, in some areas, began to replace Q1, coinciding with reports of increased insecticide resistance and control failures in protected horticultural systems. As growers and regulators introduced stricter phytosanitary measures and updated integrated pest management programs, populations of the most resistant biotypes were partially suppressed, though MED remained the dominant whitefly in Mediterranean greenhouses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-intensity greenhouse production with heavy reliance on chemical control, frequent cross-border movement of ornamentals and vegetable transplants, and climatic suitability for year‑round Bemisia survival. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and spread (MED Q2 subgroup) with particularly high resistance to several insecticide classes and strong fitness under greenhouse conditions, leading to re-emergence and intensification of Bemisia problems even where MED Q1 was already established.

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici; barley (Hordeum vulgare) also affected in the same production systems
Event.summary: Around 1998, soon after strobilurin (QoI) fungicides were introduced in European cereals (from 1996), airborne and field samples from northern Germany revealed wheat powdery mildew populations with very high resistance factors to trifloxystrobin, indicating the first documented QoI resistance in Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici. Over 1998–2000, QoI-resistant isolates rapidly increased to high frequencies in northern Germany and were also detected at appreciable frequencies in France, Belgium, Denmark, and the United Kingdom, compromising control where QoI fungicides were heavily relied upon and raising concerns for barley powdery mildew as well. After this rapid selection phase, QoI-resistant mildew became established across affected regions, and disease management shifted toward mixtures, alternative modes of action, and resistance management guidelines to slow further resistance expansion.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Rapid and widespread adoption of QoI fungicides on wheat and barley, often in repeated applications, produced strong selection for resistant mildew genotypes; large, aerially connected cereal production areas in western and northern Europe facilitated spread.
Internal mechanisms: Emergence of QoI-resistant mutants (e.g., in cytochrome b) with little fitness penalty, followed by swift clonal propagation and wind-borne dispersal (Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation for efficient aerial spread).
Review: review – Event corresponds to first detection and rapid rise of QoI-resistant Bgt in northern Germany in 1998 and parallel increases in nearby European countries, supported by Heaney et al. 2000 and MDPI’s fungicide-resistance review. Countries were expanded from a vague 'Germany; other North German regions' to explicit countries (Germany, France, Belgium, Denmark, UK) with approximate late-1990s start-years, and the episode is retained as a re-emergence (fungicide resistance) rather than an intra-/inter-continental emergence. A human curator should verify the additional country list and refine start-years using detailed monitoring data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Wheat (Triticum spp.) – Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici
Event.summary: From about 2000 through the mid‑2000s, European wheat powdery mildew populations showed a continent‑wide rise in virulence against the resistance gene Pm8, which had been widely introgressed into commercial cultivars via the 1BL.1RS rye translocation. As Pm8-virulent pathotypes spread through multiple European subregions, formerly resistant winter wheat varieties in countries such as Germany, Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia, Poland and France became increasingly susceptible, contributing to more frequent mildew epidemics and greater reliance on fungicides. By the mid‑2000s, Pm8 was largely regarded as ineffective across much of Europe, and breeding programs began shifting toward new resistance sources and gene pyramids to cope with the re-emergence of mildew damage.
Mechanism.or.driver:
Drivers: Large-scale cultivation of cultivars carrying Pm8 over diverse European environments created uniform selection pressure; high connectivity of cereal production areas via long-distance spore dispersal allowed rapid spread of successful virulent genotypes.
Internal mechanisms: Stepwise accumulation and selection of virulence to Pm8, followed by spread of diverse, highly virulent lineages across different European subregions (Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity).
Review: review – Event captures the continent-wide loss of Pm8 effectiveness in European wheat, supported by Eastern/Central European virulence surveys and recent AvrPm8 work. Intra-continental emergence has been reset to 'No' because new virulence on an existing pathogen in the same subregions fits the re-emergence definition, and the vague 'other European wheat-growing countries' entry was replaced by a set of key countries (Germany, Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia, Poland, France) with approximate early-2000s start-years. These country start-years and the exact list should be checked and refined against national survey data, but the event itself is retained as a major post-1990 Bgt episode.

EPP.scientific.name: Bradybaena similaris
EPP.common.name: Asian trampsnail
Countries: Argentina (Entre Ríos – southernmost South American record) [2019]
Host: Peridomestic vegetation, gardens, and agricultural plantations (including various crops in northeastern and east-central Argentina)
Event.summary: Although Bradybaena similaris had a historical record from Misiones Province in the mid-20th century, a 2019 BioInvasions Records study documented nine new localities in Misiones and the first confirmed record in Entre Ríos Province, representing the southernmost occurrence of the species in South America. Surveys in urban and rural sites, including residential gardens, waterfalls, and agricultural plantations, showed that the snail was now widespread and established in northeastern Argentina and extending into temperate east-central areas, lengthening its latitudinal range by about one degree and appearing in places where it had previously gone undetected or misidentified. Internal mechanisms: Broad environmental tolerance and high colonization ability allow the species to persist in both subtropical Misiones and cooler temperate Entre Ríos, supporting continued geographic range expansion within Argentina.
Review: Review – retain with reclassification and clarification of historical context. The BioInvasions Records article confirms that B. similaris had an earlier record in Misiones (1956) and that the 2019 work adds numerous new localities plus a new southernmost record in Entre Ríos, implying both filling of distribution gaps and a modest latitudinal range extension. Because Argentina (and the broader South American subregion) were already known to harbor the species, this episode represents renewed spread and increased detection within a previously affected subregion, not a first introduction or documented genetic/phenotypic shift. EPP.scientific.name: Bremia lactucae
EPP.common.name: lettuce downy mildew
Host: Lactuca sativa (open‑field and protected lettuce)
Event.summary: In 2016, lettuce producers across north‑western Europe experienced unusually frequent and severe downy mildew outbreaks, including on cultivars carrying the then‑recommended set of Bremia resistances, and numerous isolates were collected for analysis. The International Bremia Evaluation Board Europe (IBEB‑EU) determined that one virulence profile was widely distributed across France, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Scandinavia and Belgium, and in 2017 officially designated this new race as Bl:33EU. By late 2017 Bl:33EU was recognized as the most widespread race in Europe, and its establishment led to revisions of resistance descriptions and a push for new cultivars effective against Bl:33EU as well as strengthened chemical and hygiene measures to manage the elevated disease risk.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: extensive European trade in lettuce seed and seedlings, dense year‑round production, and conducive cool, humid weather allowed rapid spread of a single successful race across multiple countries. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:33EU combined a virulence spectrum able to overcome many deployed Dm genes; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity and Enhanced Transmission – its performance and spread across many production areas indicate superior fitness relative to many localized races it replaced.
Review: Decision: Retain. The description of Bl:33EU as a widely distributed race first evaluated from 2016 isolates and denominated in 2017, with confirmed presence in France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, Scandinavia and Belgium, is consistent with IBEB‑EU communications. Treating this as a re‑emergence event (new, more virulent race of an existing pathogen) without intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence is appropriate, and the country and sub‑region assignments follow the press release wording; no structural changes are required.

Event.summary: During the 2016–2017 seasons, extensive sampling by IBEB‑EU across European lettuce fields recovered over 1000 B. lactucae isolates, many representing previously unrecognized virulence profiles associated with local outbreaks. Among these, two virulence types were repeatedly found over large distances and multiple production zones; after formal testing, in 2018 IBEB‑EU denominated them as new races Bl:34EU and Bl:35EU, with Bl:34EU detected widely across France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, Austria, Switzerland, Italy, Spain, Portugal and Scandinavian countries, and Bl:35EU predominant in France and parts of southern Netherlands, southern UK and south‑west Germany. Both races contributed to serious disease episodes in susceptible cultivars, and their spread required updates to resistance labeling and emphasized the need for integrated control beyond single‑gene resistance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: pan‑European movement of lettuce seed and transplants, and favorable cool, moist conditions in 2016–2017 facilitated dispersal of successful races; strong selection from widespread use of similar resistance gene combinations and fungicide programs. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – races Bl:34EU and Bl:35EU exhibited virulence patterns distinct from Bl:33EU and prior races; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – Bl:35EU, in particular, was described as a more aggressive variant of Bl:33EU able to break additional resistance sources; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – rapid colonization of many European subregions within a few seasons.
Review: Decision: Review. This row appropriately aggregates the emergence of Bl:34EU and Bl:35EU, which IBEB‑EU denominated in April 2018 on the basis of 2016–2017 surveys, and the listed countries match the union of territories reported for these races (Bl:34EU widely spread across western, southern and northern Europe; Bl:35EU mainly France plus parts of the Netherlands, UK and Germany). Because the 'countries' field does not distinguish which race occurs where and the bracket years [2016] are approximate for both, the event should be retained but marked for review if a future version separates Bl:34EU and Bl:35EU into more race‑specific, country‑level records.

EPP.scientific.name: Bremia lactucae
EPP.common.name: lettuce downy mildew
Host: Lactuca sativa (field lettuce, particularly in Mediterranean regions)
Event.summary: From the late 2010s, French and Mediterranean lettuce producers reported recurring downy mildew problems in cultivars with up‑to‑date resistance, and IBEB‑EU surveillance identified a distinct virulence profile that had been present for several years in France and was increasingly found in Spain, Portugal and Italy. On 1 June 2021 IBEB‑EU formally denominated this profile as the new race Bl:37EU, with the type isolate FR19064 representative of a widely distributed, highly virulent population in these southern European countries. After its official recognition, Bl:37EU became a key target for breeders and resistance screening, and guidance to growers stressed the need to combine cultivars resistant to Bl:37EU with strict hygiene and fungicide programs to mitigate frequent outbreaks in Mediterranean lettuce production.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of lettuce production in Mediterranean winter areas with conditions highly favorable to downy mildew and heavy reliance on genetic resistance led to strong selection for virulent pathotypes; regional trade in plant material facilitated spread among France, Spain, Portugal and Italy. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:37EU represented a new virulence profile not covered by existing differential sets; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – its broad distribution and impact in resistant cultivars suggest enhanced ability to overcome multiple resistance factors; Enhanced Transmission – genetic traits enabling persistence and spread under Mediterranean conditions.
Review: Decision: Review. The event has been updated to reflect IBEB‑EU’s denomination of Bl:37EU on 1 June 2021, with an event window of 2018–2021 chosen to capture the period during which this virulence pattern was present and epidemiologically important in France, Spain, Portugal and Italy. Country bracket years were adjusted from [2016] to [2018], which better matches the 'several years' of prior occurrence mentioned in IBEB‑EU communications. Classification as re‑emergence only (new virulence profile in an existing European population) remains appropriate, but the start year and precise national spread should be validated against detailed monitoring data.

EPP.scientific.name: Bremia lactucae
EPP.common.name: lettuce downy mildew
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe
Host: Lactuca sativa (diverse lettuce market types across Europe)
Event.summary: By the early 2020s, continuing surveillance by IBEB‑EU documented further shifts in European B. lactucae populations, with many local outbreaks and increasing reports of disease in cultivars carrying resistance to earlier races, particularly in both southern and northern lettuce‑growing regions. In 2023, after evaluating isolates collected in 2021–2022, IBEB‑EU officially identified and named three additional races, Bl:38EU, Bl:39EU and Bl:40EU, noting that Bl:38EU occurred more frequently in southern Europe, Bl:39EU in northern Europe, and Bl:40EU across the whole continent. These newly recognized races contributed to renewed downy mildew pressure in affected areas until breeders confirmed that many newer varieties with broad resistance (e.g. Bl:29‑40EU notation) remained effective, and growers adjusted cultivar choice and integrated control measures accordingly.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: ongoing continent‑wide lettuce production with strong dependence on single‑race resistance and fungicides, plus favorable cool and humid periods, maintained high selection pressure for new virulence combinations; pan‑European movement of seedlings and seed disseminated successful races between regions. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – three distinct races (Bl:38EU, 39EU, 40EU) with differing regional prevalence; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – Bl:40EU in particular established across Europe; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – ability of some new races to infect cultivars resistant to the previously dominant race set (Bl:16‑37EU).
Review: Decision: Review. The summary has been clarified to state that IBEB‑EU denominated Bl:38EU, Bl:39EU and Bl:40EU in 2023 on the basis of isolates collected in 2021–2022, consistent with the official press release. The country list and sub‑regions represent a reasonable union of areas where the three races are reported to be most frequent (Bl:38EU in southern, Bl:39EU in northern, Bl:40EU across Europe), but the bracket years [2021] are approximations rather than documented first‑detection years for each country. The event should be retained as a major recent re‑emergence episode, but national timing and impact could be refined in future updates.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Bremia lactucae
EPP.common.name: lettuce downy mildew
Host: Lactuca sativa (open‑field and protected lettuce)
Event.summary: From 2022 onward, IBEB‑EU surveys began to detect a new Bremia lactucae virulence pattern in a growing share of European lettuce isolates, reaching about 3% of isolates in 2023 and 10% in early 2024. After a formal evaluation process, on 1 July 2024 IBEB‑EU denominated the French isolate REQ2301723 as the type isolate of race Bl:41EU, reporting repeated findings of this race in France, Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. Bl:41EU breaks several widely used resistance genes, including R53, R55 and R56, and rapidly became a major focus for breeders and advisors as a new threat to both open‑field and protected lettuce across western and northern Europe.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: highly intensive lettuce production across western and northern Europe, reliance on similar combinations of resistance genes and fungicide programs, and extensive intra‑European trade in seed and young plants created conditions for rapid spread and selection of a new, broadly adapted virulence type. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – Bl:41EU represents a distinct virulence profile, different from races Bl:38–40EU and able to overcome multiple contemporary resistance factors; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity and Enhanced Transmission – its rapid rise in frequency and repeated detection across several countries indicate strong fitness under current European production and climate conditions.
Review: Decision: Review. This new event records the emergence of race Bl:41EU as described in the 2024 IBEB‑EU press release, which reports first occurrence of the underlying virulence pattern in 2022, increasing frequencies in 2023–early 2024 and official denomination on 1 July 2024, with confirmed presence in France, Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and the UK. The 2022–2024 window and bracket years [2022] are approximations aimed at capturing the period when Bl:41EU became epidemiologically important; as additional surveillance data become available, national start years and impact assessments should be refined. Classification as re‑emergence only is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia serpens
EPP.common.name: serpent spurge, matted sandmat
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Asia
Host: Weed of flower beds, pavements, cemeteries, irrigated gardens, roadsides and other urban/peri‑urban ruderal sites; locally in crop fields and plastic‑tunnel horticulture
Event.summary: From the early 2000s onward, floristic surveys documented Euphorbia serpens spreading south‑ and east‑ward from its earlier Western and Central European range into new parts of Europe and adjacent Western Asia. First national records were published for Switzerland (2004), Greece and Crete (2007), Turkey (2007), Cyprus (2010), Italy (2010, with additional regional records by 2015), Hungary (2013), Bulgaria (2016) and Romania (2018), typically as a weed of flower beds, pavements, container plantings and other warm, disturbed urban habitats.([plant-journal.uaic.ro](https://www.plant-journal.uaic.ro/docs/2018/12.pdf?utm_source=openai)) By the late 2010s authors concluded that E. serpens subsp. serpens was in an active phase of expansion of its secondary (alien) range across south‑eastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, though still mainly confined to ruderal and horticultural settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increasing trade in ornamental plants and potting substrates, movement of contaminated soil and construction materials, and road/rail traffic across the Mediterranean basin and Balkans supplied propagules to new cities and river valleys; many records are explicitly linked to imported container plants and recently built urban green spaces.([plant-journal.uaic.ro](https://www.plant-journal.uaic.ro/docs/2018/12.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Warming climates in parts of Europe may also favor this C4 annual. Internal mechanisms: rapid germination, multiple generations per season, prostrate mat‑forming growth, and tolerance of trampling and heat allow E. serpens to exploit irrigated, nutrient‑rich ruderal sites and expand geographically wherever propagules arrive.
Review: review – Retain as a major multi‑country intra‑continental emergence episode. I corrected the 'sub_regions' field to use only UNSD categories (Western Europe, Southern Europe, Eastern Europe, Western Asia) and removed the informal 'South‑eastern Europe' label, but left the classification as 'intra_continental_emergence = true' since the event clearly represents spread into new European and West‑Asian subregions. Evidence and years follow Sîrbu & Şușnia (2018) and the EPPO reporting note.

EPP.scientific.name: Chilo suppressalis
EPP.common.name: striped riceborer
Host: Rice (Oryza sativa) and associated wetland grasses in European rice-growing landscapes
Event.summary: In 2010, Chilo suppressalis was first reliably recorded from two localities in the Great Hungarian Plain, representing a new addition to the central/eastern European lepidopteran fauna and indicating spread within Europe from earlier foci in France and Spain. A few years later, in 2014, the species was documented from Nazaré on the Atlantic coast of Portugal, adding Portugal to the list of European countries where this rice borer is established or considered invasive. Following these detections, national and regional entomological and plant-health reports began treating C. suppressalis as an emerging invasive rice pest in the newly colonized areas, with monitoring and risk assessment emphasizing the potential for further spread into other suitable European rice-growing regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued expansion of C. suppressalis within Europe is associated with irrigated rice and wetland habitats in southern and eastern Europe, facilitated by irrigation networks, warm summers and movement of infested plant material or larvae in rice straw; climate-change-related warming may also improve overwintering success at higher latitudes. Internal mechanisms: The species’ diapause and cold-hardiness traits and its ability to exploit flooded rice and reed habitats support geographic range expansion, but there is no clear evidence of new genotypes specific to these invasions; this episode is therefore coded as intra-continental geographic expansion rather than a re-emergence based on biological change.
Review: Decision: review. The event correctly captures post‑2000 spread of C. suppressalis into new European countries (Hungary and Portugal) and appropriately codes this as intra-continental emergence. I standardized the countries field to “Hungary [2010]; Portugal [2014]” and pruned the source list to emphasize primary faunistic records (microlepidoptera.hu for Hungary; SHILAP and distribution syntheses for Portugal and broader Europe) plus the CAPS datasheet, removing Wikipedia-based sources which are less authoritative. The biological and management implications (invasive status, potential spread into other rice areas) are broadly correct, but national plant-health records could be consulted to refine impact magnitude and confirm whether earlier, overlooked records exist.

EPP.scientific.name: Cucumber mosaic virus
EPP.common.name: cucumber mosaic cucumovirus
Host: Solanum lycopersicum (tomato); Capsicum annuum (pepper); Cucumis melo and other cucurbits
Event.summary: From the late 1980s into the early 1990s, vegetable production in parts of Spain, Italy and France experienced severe epidemics of systemic tomato necrosis caused by cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) strains carrying necrogenic satellite RNAs, with the most intense phase around 1990–1992. In eastern Spain and southern Italy in particular, CMV–satRNA complexes caused systemic death of tomato plants and necrotic fruit, with reports that roughly 80% of tomato plants were lost over about 70% of the growing area and some fields suffered complete crop failure, and associated damage was also reported in pepper and cucurbit crops. The epidemic declined after growers and researchers deployed a mix of control measures, including withdrawal of the most susceptible cultivars, the use of attenuating satellite RNAs and other cross‑protection strategies, improved aphid management and sanitation, and by the mid‑1990s the incidence of necrogenic satRNAs in CMV populations in Spain had fallen sharply.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensive open‑field and protected vegetable production along the Mediterranean coast, high densities of aphid vectors, and the presence of numerous CMV‑susceptible weed and crop hosts created strong inoculum pressure and facilitated rapid CMV spread; limited availability of CMV‑resistant tomato cultivars and dense plantings exacerbated the impact. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity were central, as specific necrogenic satellite RNAs (e.g. D‑satRNA and related CARNA‑5 variants) associated with existing CMV strains converted otherwise moderate infections into lethal systemic necrosis and fruit necrosis, effectively transforming CMV into a far more destructive pathosystem in tomato; the CMV–satRNA complexes also maintained effective transmission by aphids, so there was no trade‑off between virulence and spread.
Review: review – Added to capture the large CMV–necrogenic satellite RNA epidemics in tomato (and associated damage in peppers and cucurbits) in eastern Spain and parts of Italy and France, which caused reported losses of ~80% of tomato plants over much of the growing area and total crop failure in some fields. The event window is set to 1990–1992 to reflect the peak of these epidemics while respecting the 1990+ cut-off, even though the outbreak began in the late 1980s, and the country list is restricted to those with published evidence of necrogenic CMV–satRNA epidemics. Classified as re-emergence because CMV was already endemic in Southern Europe and the key novelty was the emergence and spread of highly virulent necrogenic satellite RNAs associated with existing CMV strains. Human review is recommended to confirm that the temporal bounds and country coverage match the intended episode granularity.

EPP.scientific.name: Cydia pomonella
EPP.common.name: codling moth
Host: Apple and pear orchards in western United States (Washington, Oregon, California, Utah) and adjacent Canadian pome-fruit regions (British Columbia)
Event.summary: In the early 1990s, monitoring in apple and pear orchards in western U.S. states showed that codling moth populations had evolved substantial resistance to the organophosphate insecticide azinphos-methyl after decades of intensive use, causing control failures and high fruit damage. Through the 1990s, resistance levels in some Washington and Utah orchards were strongly associated with prior insecticide selection pressure, and cross-resistance to several other insecticide classes was observed, leading to widespread concern and economic losses. By the late 1990s, this crisis drove large-scale adoption of pheromone-based mating disruption and integrated pest management programs across Washington, Oregon, California and neighboring British Columbia, which gradually reduced reliance on high-rate organophosphate sprays and restored better control.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Prolonged, intensive use of organophosphate insecticides (especially azinphos-methyl) and other broad-spectrum chemistries in western North American orchards, combined with relatively limited early resistance-management practices, created strong selection pressure; tightening regulatory scrutiny of organophosphates also constrained options. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – codling moth populations evolved resistance to azinphos-methyl with documented resistance ratios in multiple orchards, and cross-resistance to carbamates, chlorinated hydrocarbons and pyrethroids; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – not relevant; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – not primary here; this event reflects mainly resistance evolution and consequent resurgence in damage.
Review: review – Field surveys in Washington and Utah during 1991–1992 documented significant azinphos-methyl resistance in many codling moth populations, and subsequent work linked this to long-term organophosphate use and helped trigger large-scale adoption of mating disruption and IPM in western North America. The event description, geography (USA plus adjacent British Columbia) and classification as re-emergence (resistance-driven resurgence in a long-infested region) are appropriate. A key peer‑reviewed source (Knight et al. 1994, J Econ Entomol, doi:10.1093/jee/87.2.285) has been added to strengthen the evidence base; otherwise no structural corrections are needed and the event should be retained as one of the major post‑1990 episodes.([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jee/article-pdf/87/2/285/19237572/jee87-0285.pdf?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Cydia pomonella
EPP.common.name: codling moth
Host: Organic and integrated apple orchards (and other pome fruits) heavily reliant on CpGV-based biopesticides in southwest Germany and southeast France.
Event.summary: Around 2003, an organic apple orchard in southwest Germany reported serious codling moth damage despite repeated applications of commercial Cydia pomonella granulovirus (CpGV) formulations based on the Mexican isolate CpGV‑M, and similar failures were soon observed in France. Laboratory bioassays on larvae collected in 2003–2005 confirmed an at least 1000‑ to >60,000‑fold reduction in susceptibility to CpGV‑M compared with susceptible strains, marking the first documented field resistance of any insect to a commercial baculovirus product. Over 2003–2006, resistant field populations were reared and characterized (e.g. CpR/CpRR1 in Germany and RGV in France), and genetic studies showed that this "type I" resistance was dominant and largely linked to the Z sex chromosome, explaining its rapid rise and severe control failures in affected organic orchards.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Nearly two decades of intensive CpGV‑M use in European organic and low‑input orchards, often as the cornerstone control tactic, created strong selection pressure; high codling moth pressure in some orchards and limited rotation with alternative effective modes of action compounded this pressure. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – evolution of high-level resistance to CpGV‑M, with 1,000–100,000‑fold resistance factors; Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity – not applicable to the pest, though resistance forced selection and deployment of more virulent CpGV genotypes; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – emergence of resistant codling moth genotypes carrying a Z‑linked, dominantly inherited resistance trait (type I CpGV resistance) that sharply reduced mortality from CpGV‑M.
Review: retain – This event accurately captures the first documented field resistance of any insect to a commercial baculovirus (CpGV-M), originating in an organic apple orchard in southwest Germany around 2003 and shortly thereafter in France, with extremely high resistance ratios and clear evidence of dominant, Z-linked inheritance. The geographic scope, timing and classification as re-emergence (resistance-driven resurgence in previously well-controlled orchards) are well supported by primary literature and need no correction.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630735/?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Dasineura gleditchiae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie du févier, honeylocust podgall midge
Host: Gleditsia triacanthos in nurseries and urban plantings
Event.summary: By 1997, Dasineura gleditchiae had spread from earlier foci in the Netherlands, Italy and other countries into Luxembourg and the Czech Republic, where it was recorded on honeylocust in urban sites and nurseries. In 2000 it was detected in a tree nursery in Burgenland, Austria, indicating further Central European expansion via traded planting material. Over this period, infestations in nurseries and roadside plantings caused repeated galling of new leaves, reducing the ornamental value of honeylocust and prompting localized control measures, but the midge became established across these countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: intensive intra‑European movement of nursery stock and ornamental honeylocust between the Netherlands, Italy and Central European countries, along with increased use of honeylocust as an avenue and park tree in Luxembourg, Czechia and Austria. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion (inherent) within Europe combined with strong colonization potential of a multivoltine, host‑specific gall midge able to exploit young honeylocust foliage in nurseries and urban landscapes.
Review: Review – The timing and countries (Luxembourg 1997, Czechia 1997, Austria 2000) agree with EPPO’s reconstruction of spread and are correctly assigned to Western and Eastern Europe. Because both sub‑regions already had D. gleditchiae (Netherlands and Switzerland for Western Europe; Hungary for Eastern Europe), this episode represents further spread within existing sub‑regions, not intra‑continental emergence. I changed 'intra_continental_emergence' from 'true' to 'false'; no other flags were altered. Retain as a multi‑country Central/Western European expansion episode, noting that first records for other nearby countries (e.g. Poland, Slovakia, Serbia, Croatia, Bulgaria) are not explicitly represented here.

EPP.scientific.name: Blumeria graminis
EPP.common.name: grass mildew
Host: Triticale (×Triticosecale) – hybrid cereal of wheat and rye
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, breeders and pathologists in France and Germany began to report unusual powdery mildew infestations on triticale, a cereal hybrid that had previously been regarded as largely free of this disease, with first official trial infections documented around 2001 and subsequent observations in Belgium and Poland. As triticale acreage in Europe nearly doubled after 2000, mildew epidemics became increasingly frequent and severe, with reports from Central Europe of yield losses approaching one quarter of the crop in susceptible varieties and a first major national epidemic in Switzerland in 2005, leading to routine fungicide treatments and a shift in breeding priorities toward mildew resistance. By the mid-2000s, powdery mildew was widely recognised as a significant and economically important disease of triticale across Western and parts of Eastern Europe, marking the establishment of a new host–pathogen combination within the B. graminis complex.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia glyptosperma
EPP.common.name: ridgeseed spurge, ribseed sandmat
Host: Ruderal and arable-land vegetation including disturbed field margins, railway verges, urban wasteland and riverine alluvial sands in Eastern Europe.
Event.summary: From 1997 onwards, Euphorbia glyptosperma was recorded for the first time in Eastern Europe when naturalized populations were collected in multiple regions of south-eastern European Russia (Volgograd, Saratov, Astrakhan, Kalmykia, Dagestan and neighbouring areas), mainly along railways, roadsides and disturbed steppe margins. In 2005 the species was discovered in Romania along a railway near Ciurea (Iași County), and by 2009–2011 it had spread to additional Romanian sites around Galați and onto alluvial sands along the lower Siret River, while a small population was photographed in 2011 in northern Crimea, confirming its presence in Ukraine. By roughly 2017, floristic syntheses treated E. glyptosperma as a naturalized alien across parts of Eastern Europe, though still largely confined to disturbed and riverine sandy habitats.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance human-mediated dispersal with contaminated cereal or other seed lots and via transport infrastructure (railways, ports and major roads) appears to be the primary pathway into south-eastern European Russia, Romania and Crimea, with secondary spread along river corridors such as the lower Siret. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the species’ annual life cycle, high seed production, tolerance of drought and nutrient-poor, disturbed substrates, and ability to exploit man-made habitats (ballast, levees, urban ruderal sites) facilitate its colonization of new areas within Europe; there is no clear evidence for novel genotypes or herbicide resistance specific to Eastern European populations.
Review: review – Event retained but corrected: (i) start year adjusted from 2005 to 1997 to reflect earlier collections in south-eastern European Russia; (ii) the Russian Federation entry now explicitly notes collections from 1997–2006; and (iii) the event summary was updated to integrate Russian, Romanian and Crimean records into a single Eastern Europe intra-continental emergence episode. Classification as intra-continental emergence (new UNSD subregion within Europe) remains appropriate, but an expert should confirm whether additional Eastern European countries beyond Russia, Romania and Crimea/Ukraine need to be incorporated or split into separate episodes.

EPP.scientific.name: Hemileia vastatrix
EPP.common.name: coffee rust fungus
Host: Coffea arabica (primarily); some Coffea canephora in mixed systems
Event.summary: From 2008, Colombia began experiencing unusually severe coffee leaf rust epidemics that caused an average 31% drop in national coffee production between 2008 and 2011 compared with 2007, as rust spread widely in susceptible arabica plantings under unusually wet and cool conditions and high input costs limited effective control. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) In 2012–2013, the epidemic extended and intensified across Central America, southern Mexico and several Caribbean countries (notably Jamaica and the Dominican Republic), where regional coffee output fell by roughly 16–20% relative to pre‑epidemic harvests, many smallholder farms reported 30–50% yield losses, and severe outbreaks were also reported in Peru and Ecuador by 2013, prompting phytosanitary emergencies and large‑scale renovation programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8271816/?utm_source=openai)) From about 2014–2015 onward, national and regional control efforts, farm‑level renovation and pruning, and some recovery in prices gradually reduced epidemic intensity and allowed production to partially rebound, although the pathogen remained endemic and rust continued to cause chronic losses in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers (external): Multiple analyses attribute the 2008–2013 'Big Rust' wave to a conjunction of prolonged periods of unusually high rainfall and reduced diurnal temperature range in parts of the Andes and Mesoamerica that favoured rust infection and survival; sustained low or volatile coffee prices and/or rising input costs that reduced profitability and led farmers to cut back on fertilization, fungicides and renovation; aging, densely planted, rust‑susceptible arabica stands, including high‑altitude farms where rust had previously been minor; and weakened public extension and research systems that limited early warning and coordinated response. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: The epidemic largely reflected massive build‑up and spread of existing rust populations in susceptible varieties; while very large pathogen populations and widespread planting of cultivars carrying single major resistance genes (e.g. Catimor derivatives and Lempira) were associated with increased genetic diversity and breakdown of resistance in some countries, subsequent race analyses have not identified a single novel hyper‑virulent lineage uniquely responsible for the crisis, so the event is best classified as a dramatic re‑occurrence driven primarily by external socio‑economic and climatic factors.
Review: Decision: review. This event is correctly retained as a single linked, multi-country 'Big Rust' episode spanning Colombia (from 2008) and, from 2012–2013, most of Central America, southern Mexico, Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, Peru and Ecuador, in line with regional syntheses that describe a continuous wave of high-intensity epidemics rather than isolated outbreaks. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12571-015-0446-9?utm_source=openai)) I have (i) adjusted the event year from 2008–2014 to 2008–2013 to match the period in which the main epidemic peaks are consistently reported, while recognising that severe losses in parts of Peru and Ecuador continued into 2014–2015; and (ii) refined the country list to name Jamaica explicitly and to avoid an unsourced catch‑all reference to 'other Caribbean producers (e.g. Haiti)', for which comparable epidemic‑scale documentation could not be found. ([apsnet.org](https://www.apsnet.org/members/community/newsroom/releases/Pages/BigRusts_PhytoReview.aspx?utm_source=openai)) Classification as a re-occurrence (with intra- and inter-continental emergence marked 'No') remains appropriate, because the fungus was already long established in the affected subregions and current evidence points to climatic and management drivers plus incremental race diversification rather than a single new hyper‑virulent strain. Given the complexity of this regional crisis, the revised year range and country list should be reviewed by a coffee‑rust expert before final adoption.

EPP.scientific.name: Hemileia vastatrix
EPP.common.name: coffee rust fungus
Countries: United States of America – Hawaii: Maui [2020]
Host: Coffea arabica (commercial and backyard coffee in Hawaii)
Event.summary: In October 2020, coffee growers and extension agents in Maui and on Hawai‘i Island observed characteristic yellow-orange leaf lesions that were confirmed by state and federal laboratories as coffee leaf rust, marking the first known establishment of Hemileia vastatrix in Hawaii and the first in situ spread of the pathogen in the Northern America continent as defined in this project. ([hdoa.hawaii.gov](https://hdoa.hawaii.gov/blog/main/nr20-17-clrconfirmedonhawaiiisland/?utm_source=openai)) Over late 2020 and early 2021, the disease rapidly spread within infected islands and was subsequently detected on O‘ahu and Lana‘i, and by mid‑2021 confirmations on Kaua‘i and Moloka‘i meant that all major Hawaiian coffee‑growing islands were affected, threatening a coffee industry valued at tens of millions of dollars annually and increasing production costs through new fungicide and sanitation requirements. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2309-608X/8/2/189?utm_source=openai))

([apsjournals.apsnet.org](https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PDIS-09-23-1869-PDN?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera glycines
EPP.common.name: soybean cyst nematode
Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event.summary: From about 1996 onwards, soybean cyst nematode re‑emerged as the most damaging pathogen of soybean across the United States and Ontario, Canada, with national disease‑loss surveys consistently ranking SCN above all other soybean diseases. Analyses of loss data for 1996–2016 estimated cumulative yield losses approaching US$32 billion in the United States alone—more than US$1.5 billion annually—driven in part by SCN populations able to reproduce on widely used PI 88788‑based resistant cultivars and by expanded soybean acreage. By the late 2010s SCN was endemic across most of the U.S. soybean belt and a large share of Canadian soybean land, and management shifted toward more diverse resistance sources, nematode‑protectant seed treatments and intensive outreach, although substantial, often “hidden” yield losses continue each year.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion and intensification of soybean cultivation in the U.S. and Canada, frequent soybean‑after‑soybean rotations, and heavy reliance on a narrow set of resistance sources increased selection pressure and allowed SCN populations to build to damaging densities. Internal mechanisms: Evolution and spread of virulence phenotypes capable of reproducing on PI 88788 and related resistance genes, combined with long‑term cyst survival and efficient belowground transmission, produced a large‑scale re‑emergence in terms of economic impact despite the nematode’s long‑standing presence in North America.
Review: Review: Retain as a key global re‑emergence episode with the largest documented economic losses. Corrected type classification by setting re_occurrence=No and re_emergence=Yes, reflecting that heightened impact was driven largely by virulence evolution and intensification rather than a simple resurgence. Simplified the countries field to “United States of America [1996]; Canada [1996]” to match event‑sheet formatting, while the 1996–2016 window remains aligned with published loss estimates. Sources (Tylka & Marett distribution/loss analysis, University of Minnesota Extension, CFIA risk documents and EPPO) appropriately support the magnitude and extent of this episode, though Canadian‑specific loss figures could be added in a later refinement.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera glycines
EPP.common.name: soybean cyst nematode
Host: Glycine max (soybean)
Event.summary: Around 2001, soybean cyst nematode was officially recognized as a quarantine pest in Iran after being detected in commercial soybean fields in the Dasht‑e‑Naz area of Mazandaran province, and subsequent surveys soon found it in multiple locations in neighbouring Golestan. In 2002, H. glycines was reported for the first time in India from soybean fields in Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, while a 2008 survey showed that SCN was already widespread in northern Iran’s main soybean‑producing districts, with high juvenile and egg densities indicative of significant yield‑loss potential. These detections marked the first confirmed establishment of SCN in the Southern Asia subregion, leading to quarantine regulation, resistance screening of local cultivars and progressive integration of SCN management into soybean production systems in both countries, although infested fields remain difficult to clean once established.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of irrigated soybean cultivation in northern Iran and central India, movement of seed and farm machinery from already infested regions, and limited prior awareness or diagnostic capacity allowed SCN to establish and spread before it was widely recognized. Internal mechanisms: Multiple generations per season under warm conditions, a relatively broad host range within legumes and long‑term survival of eggs in cysts supported establishment and high population densities, representing a geographic range expansion of Asian lineages into a previously uninfested UNSD subregion.
Review: Review: New event added to represent the early‑2000s introduction and spread of SCN into Southern Asia (Iran and India), which does constitute an intra‑continental emergence into a new UNSD subregion of Asia. Classified as intra_continental_emergence=Yes because Asia was already infested in Eastern and South‑eastern Asia; no re_occurrence or re_emergence flags are used. The 2001–2008 period spans first official recognition in Iran, first report in India and the detailed Iranian distribution survey; sources include Iranian quarantine and resistance studies, the Nematology distribution paper and EPPO records for India. Exact first‑detection dates at field level and quantitative loss estimates remain areas where further regional expert review would be valuable.

EPP.scientific.name: Ipomoea imperati
EPP.common.name: beach morningglory, beach morning-glory
Countries: Italy – Sicily (San Leonardo River mouth on the Catania–Syracuse coast) [2001]
Host: Coastal sandy-beach and dune plant communities (embryonic and shifting dunes with Ammophiletea vegetation in Spain, Italy, Balearic Islands and Madeira)
Event.summary: From the early 2000s, Ipomoea imperati re-appeared and expanded within Southern Europe, first through rediscovery of a small but persistent Sicilian population at the mouth of the San Leonardo River and subsequent records along the Calabrian Tyrrhenian coast, following earlier extinction of mainland Italian populations.([biodiversityjournal.com](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2021/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04_899-903.pdf)) In parallel, Spanish botanists documented the species as an alien strandline plant along Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, with a 2005 note reporting it as a new adventive in Doñana National Park and a 2015 study describing incipient naturalized stands of 300–750 m² on Cádiz dunes at Barbate and Algeciras, already rated as high-risk invaders of Natura 2000 dune habitats.([biolveg.uma.es](https://www.biolveg.uma.es/abm/Volumenes/vol40/40_Garcia_de_Lomas_Ipomoea.pdf)) Over the 2010s–early 2020s, additional dense mats of 1,500–3,000 m² were recorded at Castilnovo and Los Lances (Tarifa) and the species was newly reported as part of the alien flora of the Balearic Islands, while three small but nearly monospecific dune populations were found along the south‑western Sicilian coast; by 2025, I. imperati remained localized but clearly expanding within selected Spanish and Italian dune systems and subject to active monitoring and control in some protected areas, with no indication that the invasion episode has yet ended.([biodiversityjournal.com](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2021/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04_899-903.pdf))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Repeated introductions and secondary spread along heavily used Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts via ornamental or landscaping plantings, beach restoration works, shipping and tourism-related activities have increased propagule pressure of Ipomoea imperati in Spain, Italy, Balearic Islands and Madeira, while intense disturbance and fragmentation of dune systems (walkways, parking areas, beach bars, residential development) create open sandy microsites that favor establishment and clonal expansion.([biolveg.uma.es](https://www.biolveg.uma.es/abm/Volumenes/vol40/40_Garcia_de_Lomas_Ipomoea.pdf)) External management responses (inclusion in national invasive-plant atlases, targeted removal in Doñana and other Andalusian sites) both reflect and influence the trajectory of this episode.([juntadeandalucia.es](https://www.juntadeandalucia.es/medioambiente/contenidoExterno/Pub_renpa/boletin69/parques/parques7.html?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – buoyant seeds, vegetative stolons and a deep, robust rhizome system enable long-distance hydrochorous dispersal along coasts and rapid local mat formation on embryonic and shifting dunes; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – tolerance of salt spray, burial and sand movement makes the species particularly well adapted to colonize disturbed dune fronts; Competitive exclusion of some native strandline and foredune species arises from its dense, nearly monospecific mats, which can smother other vegetation and stabilize sand in ways that alter natural dune dynamics.([biodiversityjournal.com](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2021/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04_899-903.pdf))
Review: REVIEW – Retain this event but with substantial corrections. (1) Changed the event type from intra-continental emergence + re-emergence to re-occurrence only, because Ipomoea imperati has long been present in the Southern Europe subregion (e.g. historical Italian and eastern Mediterranean records) and there is no evidence of a novel strain or host shift; the post‑2000 spread in Spain and reappearance in Italy represent renewed incidence within an already affected UNSD subregion, not movement into a new subregion or biological re-emergence.([biodiversityjournal.com](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2021/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04_899-903.pdf)) (2) Adjusted the time span from 2005–2021 to 2001–2025 to reflect the first modern Sicilian record (Turrisi 2001), earlier Spanish coastal records synthesized by Sanz Elorza et al. (2001, 2004), the 2005 Doñana adventive report, subsequent Cádiz xenophyte populations (2011–2015) and new Andalusian and Balearic localities documented up to 2023–2025.([biolveg.uma.es](https://www.biolveg.uma.es/abm/Volumenes/vol40/40_Garcia_de_Lomas_Ipomoea.pdf)) (3) Simplified and standardized the countries field, removing nested subnational descriptions that belong in the event summary and aligning country assignments with the UNSD Southern Europe list while still indicating key coastal areas and first-record years. (4) Pruned and updated event-level source URLs to prioritize primary floristic and invasion-ecology papers (Garcia-de-Lomas et al. 2015; Garcia-de-Lomas et al. 2024; Caldarella et al. 2021; Cennamo et al. 2013), Macaronesian and Balearic alien-flora notes, the Andalusian invasive-plant control portal, and POWO for range context, while de-emphasizing duplicate ResearchGate copies and general Wikipedia summaries.([biolveg.uma.es](https://www.biolveg.uma.es/abm/Volumenes/vol40/40_Garcia_de_Lomas_Ipomoea.pdf)) (5) Overall, this episode clearly qualifies as one of the main modern emergence events for this species but should be re-checked by a coastal weed specialist for completeness of country list and precise dating of earliest Spanish records.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.common.name: pea leafminer

Host: Glasshouse lettuce and ornamentals (Netherlands, Belgium, Northern Europe); outdoor and greenhouse vegetables including cucumber, beans, peas, lettuce and other leafy vegetables (Southern Europe)
Event.summary: After its first European detection on glasshouse lettuce in the Netherlands in 1987, Liriomyza huidobrensis expanded rapidly in the early 1990s into Belgium, Italy, Spain and Greece, where it was first reported from multiple greenhouse and field vegetable crops by 1991–1992. The invasion triggered severe outbreaks in protected horticulture and in some outdoor vegetable systems, leading to substantial yield losses and widespread reports of control failures across Western and Southern Europe. Through the mid-1990s, intensive development of biological control and integrated pest management in European glasshouses gradually reduced outbreak intensity, and the pest is now typically present at lower prevalence but remains an economic concern in protected cultivation.

Internal mechanisms: Pre-existing insecticide resistance in Peruvian-origin populations and broad host range enabled rapid population buildup; strong dispersal in protected environments supported geographic expansion within Europe.
Review: review: Retain this as a major event but reclassify it as an inter-continental emergence (first establishment of L. huidobrensis in Europe) rather than intra-continental spread, broaden the event window to 1990–1995 to better reflect early 1990s spread, and specify Spain [1992] and Greece [1992] using primary European sources; Wikipedia has been removed from the event’s sources in favor of EPPO reports and peer-reviewed literature, and a reviewer should confirm alignment with the 1990+ rule and whether any other high-impact European countries warrant explicit mention.

EPP.scientific.name: Liriomyza huidobrensis
EPP.common.name: pea leafminer
Sub.regions: Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia
Host: Potato, brassicas, beans, peas, lettuce and various highland vegetables and ornamentals in cool tropical highland production zones
Event.summary: Beginning in the early 1990s, Liriomyza huidobrensis spread from Western Asia and Europe into East and Southeast Asia, with early detections reported in China by 1993 and in Indonesia in 1994 on highland potatoes in West Java, followed soon by Viet Nam, Sri Lanka, Peninsular Malaysia and the Philippines. Once established in highland vegetable-growing areas, the fly reached outbreak densities on potatoes, brassicas and other vegetables, causing extensive mine damage, reduced yields and frequent control failures across multiple Asian countries. Through the late 1990s and early 2000s, national IPM programs promoting parasitoids, cultural control and more selective insecticides began to moderate damage levels, although the pest remains one of the most important leafminers in Asian highland vegetable systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of international trade in seed potatoes, ornamentals and vegetable seedlings from Europe and the Americas, coupled with expansion of highland vegetable production in Asia, facilitated repeated introductions and spread; indiscriminate insecticide use eliminated natural enemies and favored leafminer outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Pre-adaptation to cool highland climates and wide host range enabled colonization of tropical highlands; insecticide-resistant lineages from Peru supported high population densities under chemical control regimes.
Review: retain: This event appropriately summarizes the 1990s expansion from Western Asia into East, South-eastern and Southern Asia (China, Indonesia, Viet Nam, Sri Lanka, Malaysia and the Philippines), with dates and host systems consistent with EPPO and Weintraub et al. (2017); emergence is correctly coded as intra-continental spread within Asia, and no substantive corrections were required.

EPP.common.name: vegetable leafminer, mineuse maraichère
Host: Tomato in India; cotton and later vegetables in Thailand, with additional damage on other vegetables locally

EPP.scientific.name: Liriomyza sativae
EPP.common.name: vegetable leafminer, mineuse maraichère
Host: Lowland cucurbits and legumes (especially cucumber, French beans and yard‑long bean) and other vegetables in Indonesia’s lowland production zones, later spreading eastwards
Event.summary: From 1996 onwards, Liriomyza sativae emerged as a new and highly damaging pest in lowland vegetable systems in Indonesia, first recorded attacking cucumbers, tomatoes and yard‑long beans in Karawang (West Java) and then spreading to other lowland areas in South and Central Kalimantan, where French beans and yard‑long beans suffered damage levels up to about 60–70%. EPP.scientific.name: Obolodiplosis robiniae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) in urban trees, shelterbelts and plantations; occasionally ornamental Robinia spp.
Event.summary: Around 2002, Obolodiplosis robiniae was first detected in eastern Asia, with sudden appearance of characteristic leaf-margin galls on black locust in Japan and the Republic of Korea, representing the first established populations of the species outside North America. By 2004 the gall midge was recorded in China (Qinhuangdao City, Hebei Province) and then rapidly spread across multiple provinces, infesting roadside trees and plantations. The event marked a major inter-continental invasion from North America into Asia and set the stage for further expansion and local outbreaks in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: International trade in live plants and nursery stock of Robinia pseudoacacia, including asymptomatic material carrying eggs or early-instar larvae in young leaflets, is considered the primary pathway for trans-Pacific introduction and rapid regional spread; extensive planting of black locust in East Asia (for shelterbelts, afforestation, and ornamentals) provided abundant habitat. Internal mechanisms: High reproductive rate and multiple generations per growing season, together with good dispersal ability of adults, promoted rapid population build-up; genetic studies indicate substantial genetic variation in Chinese populations consistent with multiple introductions and/or large founding populations, facilitating successful colonization and spread.
Review: Decision: review. This event correctly captures the first established populations outside North America in East Asia (Japan and Republic of Korea in 2002; China in 2004) and is appropriately classified as an inter-continental emergence into Asia. Country dates and interpretation are supported by Kodoi et al. 2003 for Japan and Korea and by Yang et al. 2006 and subsequent genetic work for China. The source list has been refined to emphasize primary East Asian references rather than a European-focused review; otherwise no changes to timing, geography or event-type flags are required.

EPP.scientific.name: Obolodiplosis robiniae
EPP.common.name: cécidomyie gallicole du robinier, locust gall midge
Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; Northern Europe
Host: Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) in urban landscapes, roadsides, shelterbelts and plantations; ornamental Robinia cultivars in parks and gardens
Event.summary: In July 2003 Obolodiplosis robiniae was first reported in Europe from Paese near Padua in northeastern Italy, where heavy galling of black locust foliage was observed, and by 2004–2006 it had spread into Central and Eastern Europe, including Czechia, Slovenia, Hungary, Slovakia, Croatia, Germany and Ukraine. Between 2006 and 2010 the gall midge rapidly colonized much of Western and Northern Europe, with first records from countries such as the Netherlands, Switzerland, Austria, France, Poland, Serbia, Romania, the United Kingdom, Luxembourg, Sweden, Denmark, Spain and additional Balkan and Russian localities, often causing conspicuous defoliation of amenity and roadside black locust. Although densities later declined in some regions due to parasitoid build-up, the species has remained widely established across Europe and now occupies most areas where black locust is planted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The primary driver was continent-wide movement of infested nursery and landscaping stock of Robinia pseudoacacia, combined with the widespread use of this invasive tree in forestry, erosion control and ornamental plantings across Europe; human-assisted jump dispersal was followed by natural spread along road networks and river corridors. Internal mechanisms: The midge’s host specialization on an already widely invasive tree, its multivoltine life cycle and ability to exploit young foliage, and the initial absence or low abundance of specialized natural enemies in Europe allowed rapid population growth and dispersal; later, introduction and spread of the parasitoid Platygaster robiniae contributed to natural regulation but did not prevent continent-wide establishment.
Review: Decision: review. This row appropriately represents the inter-continental emergence of O. robiniae into Europe and its rapid spread across Southern, Central, Eastern, Western and Northern Europe, in line with Duso & Skuhravá 2003, Skuhravá et al. 2007, EPPO RS 2008/202 and later syntheses. The countries list has been updated to include Hungary [2006] and Romania [2007], which are explicitly reported as early, often heavily infested areas, and reordered slightly while retaining approximate entries (≤2010) for Albania, North Macedonia and the Russian Federation where only regional summaries are available. Event-type flags remain correct (inter-continental emergence only) and the episode is clearly among the largest global emergence events for this species.

EPP.scientific.name: Panicum dichotomiflorum
EPP.common.name: western witchgrass, fall panicum, fall panicgrass, fall panic
Host: Weed in disturbed sites, moist road verges, waste ground and arable field margins
Event.summary: Around 2001, fall panicum was first discovered in Slovenia near Lendava, close to the Hungarian border, representing spread from previously invaded Central European countries where it was already established. In 2003, systematic flora mapping in Hungary recorded the species for the first time as a new element of the Hungarian adventive flora, with populations in western, southern and northern parts of the country on disturbed, periodically wet soils. Over the next few years the grass persisted at multiple scattered Hungarian localities, remaining locally common in disturbed habitats but still in an early invasive phase.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Stepwise spread from established populations in Austria, Croatia and other Central European countries along river valleys, transport corridors and disturbed land; likely introduction via contaminated grain, birdseed mixtures, and vehicle or rail traffic. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) from Western/Southern Europe into Eastern Europe and the Pannonian Basin, facilitated by the species’ annual life cycle, prolific seed production and tolerance of moist, disturbed soils; no specific novel strain or resistance mechanism was reported.
Review: Decision: retain. Independent floristic sources confirm first national records near Lendava (Slovenia, 2001) and multiple Hungarian localities from 2003 onward, and these countries fall in different UNSD sub‑regions (Southern vs Eastern Europe); therefore classification as an intra‑continental emergence into a new European sub‑region is appropriate. No changes were required to continent, sub‑regions, timing or emergence‑type flags, and the event plausibly represents one of the largest post‑1990 spread episodes for this species in Europe.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (urban and peri-urban populations in Luanda and other Angolan provinces; urban and peri-urban populations in Kinshasa and surrounding provinces of DRC)
Event.summary: In December 2015, an urban yellow fever outbreak began in Viana municipality of Luanda, Angola, and over 2016 spread to all provinces, causing more than 4,000 suspected cases and over 100 deaths, largely in unvaccinated urban populations. The virus was exported to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where autochthonous urban transmission occurred in Kinshasa and border provinces during 2016, and infected travelers carried the Angolan strain to several non-endemic countries, including China, although no sustained transmission was documented outside Africa. A massive emergency vaccination campaign—using dose-fractionation to stretch limited global supplies—combined with vector control and intensified surveillance ultimately interrupted urban transmission in Angola and DRC by late 2016, with mop-up activities continuing into 2017.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large, densely populated urban centers with low yellow fever vaccination coverage and extensive Aedes aegypti infestation; high population mobility between rural and urban areas and across borders; global vaccine stockpile limitations that necessitated fractional dosing; concurrent global attention to Zika diverting some resources and focus. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses showed the outbreak strain was closely related to viruses from a 1971 Angolan outbreak, indicating reactivation and spread of existing Central African lineages rather than emergence of a novel genotype, though efficient urban amplification via Aedes aegypti represented a critical internal transmission mechanism. Imported cases to Asia and elsewhere remained part of this linked outbreak and did not generate independent inter-continental emergence events because no local onward transmission occurred.
Review: Review: Subregion coding has been corrected to Middle Africa only; there was no confirmed autochthonous transmission in West African countries during this episode, and Angola plus DRC are both classified as Middle Africa in the Country sheet. The event was previously labelled as intra-continental emergence, but yellow fever had long been endemic in Middle Africa, so this is better classified as a major re-occurrence in an already affected subregion, driven by low urban vaccination coverage and vector ecology. Accordingly, intra_continental_emergence was changed from Yes to No while retaining re_occurrence = Yes. Source list has been refocused on WHO, ECDC and peer-reviewed outbreak analyses; the Wikipedia synthesis is no longer needed as a primary reference for this row.
