EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
EPP.common.name: Yellow fever virus
Host: Humans (populations in multiple high-risk districts across West and Central/Middle Africa)
Event.summary: From late 2020 through 2021, multiple yellow fever outbreaks were detected across West and Middle Africa, beginning with confirmed clusters in Guinea and Senegal despite prior nationwide preventive mass vaccination campaigns, and followed by outbreaks and confirmed cases in Nigeria, Togo and Gabon and then at least nine countries in 2021, including Cameroon, Chad, Central African Republic, Côte d’Ivoire, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ghana, Niger, Nigeria and Republic of the Congo. These episodes represented a region-wide resurgence in areas with known historical transmission but, in some instances, recent vaccination efforts, with cases occurring in hard-to-reach districts with weak surveillance and substantial population movement, raising concerns about undetected spread to neighboring countries. Intensified implementation of the Eliminate Yellow Fever Epidemics (EYE) strategy—through reactive vaccination, catch-up campaigns, risk communication, and surveillance strengthening—gradually contained distinct outbreaks, though yellow fever remains a serious ongoing threat in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent immunity gaps even after mass vaccination (e.g. missed populations, nomadic groups), health system weaknesses in conflict-affected or remote areas, population displacement and cross-border movements, and environmental conditions conducive to Aedes spp. vectors; COVID-19 disruptions likely affected routine immunization and surveillance, compounding risk. Internal mechanisms: The pattern indicates resurgence of endemic regional YFV lineages across multiple countries rather than emergence of a single new strain; no clear evidence suggests major changes in virulence or transmissibility, so the main mechanism is re-occurrence driven by external programmatic and ecological factors.
Review: Review: This row appropriately treats the 2020–2021 multi-country upsurge in West and Middle Africa as a linked regional resurgence. Subregion coding has been corrected to “Western Africa; Middle Africa” to match the listed countries; references to a generic “Central Africa” and “Eastern Africa” in the sub_regions field were inconsistent with the Country sheet and have been removed. Because all affected countries lie within historically endemic subregions and there is no evidence of new continental spread or a unique genotype, intra_continental_emergence has been changed from Yes to No while retaining re_occurrence = Yes. Country list now matches the main WHO West & Central Africa summary, with explicit start years for each country; smaller East African outbreaks in 2020 (e.g. Ethiopia, Uganda, South Sudan) remain outside this particular multi-country West/Middle Africa episode.

EPP.common.name: desert locust

Event.summary: From late 1992, desert locust populations along the Red Sea coasts of Eritrea, Sudan, Saudi Arabia and Yemen became gregarious following above‑average rains and formed swarms that initiated a regional upsurge. Over 1993–1994, successive generations spread west into Sahelian West Africa (e.g. Mauritania) and east across the Arabian Peninsula into India and Pakistan, causing significant damage to crops and pasture across multiple African and Asian countries before extensive control operations and deteriorating breeding conditions reduced populations. By mid‑1994, the upsurge had collapsed as dry conditions returned in key breeding areas and intensive ground and aerial control campaigns suppressed remaining swarms.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Unusually heavy and sustained rainfall along the Red Sea coastal plains and adjacent deserts in 1992 created persistent green vegetation, allowing multiple overlapping breeding cycles and gregarization; limited early warning capacity and delayed large‑scale control enabled populations to expand and spread across the Sahel and into Southwest and South Asia. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of host shift, novel genotype, or resistance—expansion was driven by favorable moisture and vegetation enabling normal migratory and reproductive behavior over a wide area (geographic range expansion mediated by climate rather than inherent trait change).

Sub-regions were updated to include Northern Africa (Sudan and Egypt belong to this UN sub-region) and to make explicit coverage of Eastern and Western Africa and Western/Southern Asia. The duplicate, non-standard entry “Sudan (inland Sahel zones) [1993]” was removed so that each country appears once with a single start year. Host: Rainfed and irrigated cereals (millet, sorghum, wheat), pulses, horticultural crops and rangeland/forest vegetation across Sahelian, Maghreb, Red Sea and Mediterranean agro‑ecosystems
Event.summary: From late 2003, unusually heavy summer rains in the western Sahel allowed desert locust populations in Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Senegal and neighbouring countries to build up rapidly and gregarize, initiating the largest upsurge in West and North Africa since the late 1980s. Through 2004, swarms multiplied and spread across most of Western Africa and into Northern and Middle Africa, causing extensive crop and pasture losses, and then moved north and east into the Maghreb, the Canary Islands and parts of Southern Europe (Spain, Portugal, Greece) as well as Western Asia (including Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia and Syria). Massive international control operations and the onset of drier conditions by 2005 reduced locust densities, and the plague gradually collapsed, although lingering impacts on food security persisted in vulnerable Sahelian countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Above‑normal rainfall and resulting persistent green vegetation in the Sahel in 2003 triggered rapid population growth, while delays in early intervention due to limited resources and institutional weaknesses allowed the situation to escalate into a full plague; high poverty and dependence on rainfed agriculture in the Sahel and Maghreb greatly amplified the food security impact. Internal mechanisms: no evidence of novel genotypes or resistance driving the upsurge—the scale reflected favourable climatic conditions and the species’ inherent capacity for long‑distance migration; however, high mobility and reproductive potential allowed rapid geographic range expansion across West/North Africa, parts of Southern Europe and the Near East once control lagged behind population growth.

EPP.scientific.name: Spodoptera frugiperda
EPP.common.name: fall armyworm, "légionnaire d’automne"
Host: Maize (Bt and non-Bt), primarily Zea mays
Event.summary: Around 2006, unexpectedly severe damage by fall armyworm was observed in Cry1F Bt maize in Puerto Rico, marking the first documented case of field-evolved resistance of S. frugiperda to a Bt maize event and leading to withdrawal of TC1507 maize there. During the early 2010s, subsequent monitoring and bioassays documented high levels of Cry1F resistance in fall armyworm populations in mainland USA (Florida, North Carolina) and in Brazil, with larvae surviving on Bt maize plants in the field. This resistance has persisted in Puerto Rico despite removal of Cry1F maize and contributed to reduced efficacy of single-toxin Bt hybrids across parts of the Americas, driving shifts to pyramided Bt traits and integrated resistance-management strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive and continuous planting of single-toxin Cry1F Bt maize hybrids (TC1507 and related events) in warm tropical and subtropical production systems with high fall armyworm pressure; inadequate refuge compliance in some areas; year-round cultivation enabling multiple pest generations. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance – field-evolved resistance to the Cry1F Bt toxin (and cross-resistance to some other Cry1 toxins) mainly via changes in midgut receptors such as ABCC2 and reduced Cry1F binding, increasing larval survival and damage on Bt maize.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (retain, with modifications). Changes made: (1) Updated Event Year from "2006" to "2006-2013" so the row clearly covers the linked Cry1F resistance episode in Puerto Rico, southeastern USA and Brazil, consistent with reports of initial field-evolved resistance in Puerto Rico from 2006 onward and subsequent confirmations in Florida/North Carolina and Brazil around 2012–2013.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22537834/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Corrected continent and sub-region fields to follow the UNSD scheme: Puerto Rico is placed under South America | Caribbean, the United States under Northern America | Northern America, and Brazil under South America | South America. (3) Refined country-year annotations to Puerto Rico [2006–2008], USA [2012–2013], and Brazil [2013], which better matches the timing of documented resistance detections. Event-type classification as re-emergence (due to evolution of Bt resistance in an already established pest within its native continental range) and not as intra- or inter-continental emergence is appropriate and has been retained. Rationale: This is clearly one of the most impactful post-1990 events for FAW because it marks the first field-evolved resistance to a Bt maize event globally and triggered major changes in resistance management; it should be kept as a major re-emergence episode but flagged for the minor structural corrections above.

EPP.scientific.name: Spodoptera frugiperda
EPP.common.name: fall armyworm, "légionnaire d’automne"
Sub.regions: Western Africa; Middle Africa; Eastern Africa; Southern Africa
Host: Primarily maize (Zea mays), but also sorghum, millet and other cereals and some vegetable crops
Event.summary: In early 2016, fall armyworm was detected for the first time outside its native Americas on São Tomé and Príncipe and nearly simultaneously in maize fields in southwestern Nigeria, Benin and Togo, where severe outbreaks on maize were initially misattributed to indigenous Spodoptera species and then confirmed as S. frugiperda by morphological and molecular diagnosis. Over 2016–2018 the pest spread rapidly across Western and Middle Africa into Eastern and Southern Africa, becoming established in most sub-Saharan countries and causing extensive damage to smallholder maize and other staple crops. By 2018, fall armyworm infestations and associated yield losses had stabilized at high levels across much of the region, prompting FAO and partners to launch the Global Action for Fall Armyworm Control and national IPM programs to reduce its impact.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Accidental introduction of S. frugiperda from the Americas to West Africa, likely via trade or transport of infested plant material or contaminated cargo; favorable tropical and subtropical climates with year-round host availability (maize and other cereals); widespread monoculture maize, limited early detection capacity, and constrained access to effective, safe control tools in many smallholder systems. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – strong flight capacity (on the order of tens of kilometres per night) and broad host range facilitated rapid colonization across diverse African agro-ecological zones; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – adaptation of invasive populations to local climatic regimes and cropping calendars, enabling continuous breeding and spread across Western, Middle, Eastern and Southern Africa.
Review: Decision: REVIEW (retain, with corrected event-type classification). Changes made: (1) Adjusted emergence-type flags so that this episode is coded solely as an inter-continental emergence (first establishment in Africa outside the native Americas), with first_detection and intra_continental_emergence set to "false". This follows the rule that event types should generally be mutually exclusive, and that spread within Africa to additional sub-regions (Western, Middle, Eastern, Southern Africa) is considered part of the same inter-continental invasion episode rather than separate intra-continental events.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5082806/?utm_source=openai)) (2) Confirmed that the listed countries and years (Nigeria, Benin, Togo, Sao Tome and Principe in 2016; Zambia, DRC and others in 2016–2017; East and Southern African countries mainly in 2017–2018) are consistent with EPPO, IPPC and FAO reporting, though additional African countries experienced outbreaks in the same period. (3) Continent and sub-region fields already matched the UNSD classification and were left unchanged. Rationale: This is unequivocally one of the largest FAW emergence events globally in terms of area affected, yield loss and number of countries, and should definitely be retained; the corrections concern only the technical coding of the emergence type.

Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long-distance migration of moths from already infested regions (likely via the Arabian Peninsula and/or eastern Africa into the Indian subcontinent), aided by monsoon wind systems; intense regional and cross-border trade in plant products; continuous availability of host crops in tropical and subtropical agro-ecosystems; limited initial awareness and preparedness among farmers and extension systems. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – high dispersal ability, broad thermal tolerance and polyphagy allowed colonization across diverse Asian climates and cropping systems; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – rapid build-up of populations in multi-cropping systems, with some evidence of adaptation to local cropping calendars and possibly differing host-use patterns between the so-called ‘rice’ and ‘corn’ strains.

EPP.common.name: fall armyworm, "légionnaire d’automne"
Host: Maize, sorghum and other cereals; some vegetable and forage crops
Event.summary: In late January 2020, fall armyworm was detected for the first time in Oceania on the Torres Strait islands of Saibai and Erub (Australia), with subsequent confirmations on mainland Queensland and then other northern states, marking its arrival in the region. Between 2020 and 2022, fall armyworm spread through key maize- and sorghum-growing regions of northern and eastern Australia and, via wind-assisted migration, reached New Zealand where initial eradication efforts gave way to long-term management once the pest proved widespread, leading to emergency regulatory responses and rapid deployment of biological and chemical control options across affected countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Natural migration of moths from already infested parts of Southeast Asia via prevailing winds and island stepping-stones into northern Australia, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands and later New Zealand; high connectivity through regional trade and movement of plant materials; favorable tropical and temperate climates and extensive maize and sorghum production in northern Australia and parts of Oceania. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) – the invasive populations’ broad climatic tolerance enabled establishment in new subtropical and temperate environments in Oceania; Enhanced Transmission/Vector Adaptation – rapid build-up in local maize and sorghum systems led to persistent populations requiring new biological control and biopesticide approaches (e.g. nucleopolyhedrovirus-based products and parasitoid wasps) for sustainable management.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
EPP.common.name: Zika virus
Host: Humans (general population; pregnant women; Guillain–Barré syndrome patients)
Event.summary: Beginning in October 2013, French Polynesia experienced a large Zika virus outbreak across its archipelagos, with over 8,000 suspected cases and an estimated attack rate near 10% of the population, representing the largest Zika outbreak to that date and the first where neurological complications such as Guillain–Barré syndrome were clearly recognized. In 2014, travel from French Polynesia seeded outbreaks in other Pacific islands including New Caledonia and the Cook Islands and led to introduction of Zika virus to Easter Island, part of Chile, marking the first documented autochthonous transmission in South America. By 2015, the Pacific outbreaks waned as herd immunity accumulated and control efforts intensified, but the virus had established a foothold in the Pacific that likely facilitated subsequent spread to mainland South America.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increasing air and maritime travel among Pacific islands (tourism and cultural links) that moved infected persons from French Polynesia to other islands; high densities of competent Aedes vectors in tropical island settings; limited prior population immunity across the Pacific; constrained vector-control capacity in small island health systems. Internal mechanisms: Efficient vector-borne transmission by Zika’s Asian lineage; recognition for the first time of a strong association with Guillain–Barré syndrome and later congenital malformations, reflecting either intrinsic neurotropism of the circulating strain or improved ascertainment of severe outcomes; geographic range expansion from Polynesia to Melanesia and into South American territory (Chile, via Easter Island).
Review: review – Event correctly captures the large French Polynesia–centred Pacific outbreak and the first documented autochthonous transmission in South America (Easter Island/Chile). The previous classification set both intra- and inter-continental emergence to “Yes”, which is inconsistent with the rule that only re-emergence can co-occur; it has been corrected to inter-continental emergence only, and the Chile entry in the country list has been standardized (Chile [2014] with Easter Island detail moved to the narrative).

Event.summary: In early 2015, Brazil confirmed autochthonous Zika virus transmission, likely introduced from the Pacific by travellers, and over the following months the virus spread explosively through Brazil with an estimated 1.5 million infections and an unprecedented surge in microcephaly and other congenital central nervous system malformations in infants. EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (across tropical and subtropical urban areas in the Americas)
Event.summary: In 2019, the Region of the Americas recorded its largest dengue epidemic on record to that date, with PAHO reporting more than 3 million cases and over 1,500 deaths, heavily affecting Brazil, Central America, Mexico, and several Caribbean nations. Following a relatively quiet 2017–2018, large susceptible populations, favorable climatic conditions, and persistent Aedes aegypti infestations allowed all four serotypes to circulate and drove explosive transmission across multiple countries. Intensive regional and national responses—including emergency vector control, risk communication, and strengthened clinical management—helped keep the overall case‑fatality rate below 1%, but transmission remained high into early 2020 before declining and later resurging in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cyclical build‑up of susceptible populations, El Niño–linked and other climatic anomalies increasing mosquito breeding and survival, rapid urbanization with inadequate water and waste services, and high human mobility across borders; constrained vector‑control capacity limited sustained impact. Internal mechanisms: Co‑circulation of all four DENV serotypes and shifting serotype dominance likely increased the probability of severe disease in previously exposed individuals, but no single novel strain has been clearly singled out; the event primarily represents a large-scale regional re‑occurrence.
Review: Retained without changes in emergence typing. This is clearly a major re_occurrence in a long‑endemic region, with >3 million cases and >1,500 deaths in the Americas and co‑circulation of all four serotypes. It remains an important benchmark event despite being surpassed in overall global burden by 2024.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
EPP.common.name: Dengue virus
Host: Humans (populations across tropical and subtropical urban areas in the Region of the Americas)
Event.summary: In 2024, dengue transmission reached unprecedented levels globally, with WHO receiving reports of about 14.4 million cases and 11,201 deaths across all six regions; more than 90% of these cases occurred in the Region of the Americas, where Brazil alone reported over 10 million cases and more than 6,000 deaths, and other Latin American countries such as Argentina, Mexico, Colombia, Paraguay, Peru, Guatemala and Honduras also experienced very large epidemics. These surges followed earlier peaks in 2019 and 2023 and were driven by favorable climatic conditions, rapid urbanization, widespread Aedes aegypti infestations and high mobility of people and virus lineages. Intensive international and national responses—including emergency vector control, updated clinical guidance, and deployment or pilot use of dengue vaccines in some countries—aimed to reduce severe disease and deaths, but the 2024 Americas outbreak nonetheless marked the highest regional and global dengue burden ever recorded.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term global and regional trends including urbanization, climate change increasing geographic and seasonal suitability for Aedes mosquitoes, resumption and intensification of international and regional travel after COVID‑19, persistent deficiencies in water and waste infrastructure, and limited scalable vector‑control tools; demographic growth has expanded populations at risk. Internal mechanisms: Hyperendemic circulation of all four DENV serotypes with shifting regional dominance and extensive serotype mixing increases the likelihood of severe outcomes among previously exposed individuals, but no single novel genotype explains the 2024 surge; the event reflects very large‑scale re‑occurrence and continued geographic expansion within a long‑affected region.
Review: Retained and scope clarified. The original entry treated this as a single "Global" event, which conflicts with the requirement not to merge events across continents; here the focus is explicitly on the Region of the Americas, which accounted for >90% of the ~14.4 million global cases and over 10 million cases in Brazil alone in 2024. The episode is correctly classified as re_occurrence, with no evidence of a new continent, new host system or clearly novel viral lineage. Separate 2024 events could be added for Asia and Africa if finer spatial detail is required.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Host: Humans (residents using the municipal drinking‑water supply in Cranbrook, British Columbia)
Event.summary: From early June to mid‑July 1996, the unfiltered, chlorinated surface‑water supply serving Cranbrook, British Columbia became contaminated with Cryptosporidium, most likely via livestock manure runoff entering the watershed, causing a community‑wide outbreak. Official investigations documented 29 laboratory‑confirmed and about 100 clinical cases, but Health Canada and provincial assessments estimate that roughly 2,000 residents experienced cryptosporidiosis, making this one of the largest documented drinking‑water Crypto outbreaks in Canada. A boil‑water advisory, temporary control measures, and subsequent investment in improved filtration and multi‑barrier treatment gradually eliminated oocysts from the distribution system and ended the outbreak, and the event contributed to stronger source‑water protection and treatment requirements in British Columbia.

Because detailed peer‑reviewed epidemiologic descriptions are limited and some later literature focuses instead on a smaller 2004 California waterpark outbreak, this row should be checked by a human reviewer against primary CDC and state reports before deciding whether to retain it as one of the top global events.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Host: Humans (residents of North Battleford using the municipal drinking‑water system)
Event.summary: In March–April 2001, failures at one of North Battleford’s surface‑water treatment plants in Saskatchewan allowed Cryptosporidium‑contaminated water from the North Saskatchewan River to enter the municipal distribution system, producing a large waterborne outbreak. Internal mechanisms: the environmental persistence of C. parvum oocysts and very low infectious dose, coupled with widespread community exposure via municipal tap water, explain the large number of illnesses; the outbreak reflects re‑occurrence linked to infrastructure vulnerability rather than emergence of a new parasite genotype.

The original version mischaracterized 1,907 illnesses as laboratory-confirmed; Canadian and research reports distinguish between 25–275 stool-confirmed infections, ≈1,900 clinically defined cases in case-series analyses, and an estimated 5,800–7,100 symptomatic residents. The revised summary describes this range without over‑stating confirmation rates, while maintaining classification as a major re‑occurrence event. EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Host: Humans (patrons of the Seneca Lake State Park interactive sprayground and their close contacts)
Event.summary: In summer 2005, a massive outbreak of gastrointestinal illness due to Cryptosporidium occurred among users of an interactive sprayground at Seneca Lake State Park in upstate New York, when recycled spray water stored in underground tanks became contaminated with oocysts and was inadequately disinfected. By late August, state health authorities had identified over 2,000 reported cases across more than 20 counties, with later summaries and litigation documents indicating that at least 3,000–3,800 people developed cryptosporidiosis and several hundred had confirmed infection, making this one of the largest recreational‑water cryptosporidiosis outbreaks on record. The sprayground was closed for the season, extensive hyperchlorination and system redesign were undertaken, and New York subsequently mandated ultraviolet disinfection and stricter design and operating standards for spraygrounds, after which no comparable large‑scale recurrence at the site was reported.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: design of the sprayground with recirculated water stored in holding tanks, lack of effective filtration and protozoa‑targeted disinfection, very high use by diaper‑aged children, and delayed recognition of an outbreak, all of which allowed amplification of contamination and exposure over weeks. Internal mechanisms: high oocyst shedding by infected children, extreme chlorine resistance of Cryptosporidium, and a very low infectious dose enabled explosive spread once the recirculation system was contaminated; there is no evidence of a novel strain or altered host range, so the event reflects re‑occurrence in a particularly high‑risk recreational setting.

Multiple public health and legal sources converge on Seneca Lake 2005 as a very large sprayground‑associated cryptosporidiosis outbreak with thousands of cases and major regulatory consequences, so it clearly belongs among the most impactful Crypto events. However, reported case counts (≈1,700–3,800 symptomatic, ≈400–425 confirmed) vary between sources; a reviewer should select a consistent numeric summary and confirm that the wording and references align with the preferred figures.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Host: Humans (urban and peri‑urban residents using the Galway municipal water supply; visitors and tourists)
Event.summary: In March 2007, Galway City and surrounding areas in western Ireland noted a sharp increase in cryptosporidiosis cases that was quickly linked to contamination of public drinking‑water supplies sourced from Lough Corrib, with C. hominis identified as the main agent. A prolonged boil‑water notice affecting about 120,000 people remained in place for roughly five months while authorities managed 242 laboratory‑confirmed cases and an estimated several hundred additional unreported illnesses, carried out environmental investigations, and invested in upgraded treatment barriers and source‑water controls. The outbreak abated once contaminated sources were controlled, new treatment infrastructure (including UV disinfection) was installed, and oocyst levels in treated water declined, though the event had substantial economic and reputational costs for the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: heavy reliance on a large surface‑water source subject to agricultural and sewage contamination, combined with treatment works that lacked adequate barriers for protozoa and were not designed to address Cryptosporidium specifically, and the absence of routine monitoring systems capable of early detection. Internal mechanisms: a human-adapted C. hominis subtype spread efficiently via municipal tap water, but no new genotype was identified; the outbreak is best understood as a re‑occurrence linked to infrastructure and catchment pressures rather than parasite evolution.
Review: review – Existing row retained but flagged. Galway 2007 is clearly the largest documented cryptosporidiosis outbreak in Ireland and had very high economic impact, but by case numbers (≈240 confirmed, ≈740 estimated total) it is smaller than several other events now included (Kelowna, North Battleford, Seneca Lake, etc.). The summary has been lightly updated to reflect current estimates and costs. If the dataset must be strictly limited to ten global events, this row is a candidate for removal despite its local importance.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Host: Humans (vacationers and residents using a small mountain drinking‑water supply)
Event.summary: In August 2019, an outbreak investigation in a small municipality in the Tuscan‑Emilian Apennines of north‑eastern Italy identified cryptosporidiosis among 114 exposed vacationers and residents, with approximately 75–80 laboratory‑confirmed cases and high attack rates among visitors. Microbiological and environmental studies implicated a small spring‑fed drinking‑water system serving the mountain community, where low but epidemiologically significant levels of Cryptosporidium parvum oocysts were detected following intense rainfall that likely washed contamination from human or animal sources into the supply. A boil‑water advisory, provision of alternative water, and technical improvements to the small water system were implemented; once these measures were in place and contamination decreased, no further large clusters were reported, and the episode was recognized as only the second documented waterborne Crypto outbreak in Italy.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: heavy rainfall in a mountainous catchment overwhelming a small, minimally treated spring‑water system, allowing contamination with Cryptosporidium from nearby human or livestock fecal sources, and limited treatment capacity to remove oocysts before distribution. Internal mechanisms: the low infectious dose of C. parvum and partial immunity patterns (more severe disease among immunologically naïve tourists than among locals) amplified the outbreak impact without evidence for a new strain or change in host range, so the event is best characterized as a re‑occurrence.

This well‑described Italian outbreak is notable as only the second documented waterborne Crypto event in Italy and had a high attack rate in a small community, but with ≈75–80 cases it is not among the very largest outbreaks worldwide. EPP.scientific.name: Cryptosporidium spp.
EPP.common.name: Cryptosporidium parasites
Host: Humans (residents and visitors using the Queenstown municipal drinking‑water supply; particularly younger adults frequenting the central business district)
Event.summary: In September 2023, health authorities in Queenstown, New Zealand detected an unusual increase in cryptosporidiosis cases, mainly in younger adults, and subsequently linked the outbreak to the municipal drinking‑water supply served by the Two Mile and Kelvin Heights treatment plants, which lacked a validated protozoa barrier. Over the following weeks, more than 60 confirmed and additional suspected cases were reported, prompting a town‑wide boil‑water notice, alternative water provision, and intensive environmental investigations that pointed toward human fecal contamination of the distribution system. The outbreak gradually declined as the boil‑water advisory, short‑term treatment upgrades, and behavior changes took effect, and regulators required rapid installation of protozoa barriers and longer‑term infrastructure improvements before all boil‑water notices could be lifted.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: absence of effective protozoa treatment barriers (e.g., UV or advanced filtration) in the main Queenstown water treatment plants despite serving a rapidly growing tourism hub, likely human sewage intrusion into the distribution network, and possible contributions from heavy rainfall and aging infrastructure. Internal mechanisms: chlorine resistance and low infectious dose of Cryptosporidium allowed sustained waterborne transmission once oocysts entered the network; there is no evidence of a novel strain or host expansion, and impact was driven primarily by infrastructure and contamination pathways.
Review: review – Existing row retained but flagged. The Queenstown 2023 outbreak is not among the largest in terms of case numbers, but it is a recent, well‑documented example of a drinking‑water Crypto event in New Zealand with clear infrastructure and regulatory implications. Sources and classification as a re‑occurrence are appropriate. A reviewer should decide whether to prioritise its inclusion for temporal and geographic completeness if the dataset is narrowed to the ten highest‑impact events globally.

EPP.scientific.name: Hepatovirus A
EPP.common.name: Hepatitis A virus
Host: Humans (restaurant patrons consuming raw imported scallops at Genki Sushi and their close contacts)
Event.summary: In 2016, Hawaii experienced a large hepatitis A outbreak linked to consumption of raw frozen bay scallops imported from the Philippines and served at Genki Sushi restaurants on Oahu and Kauai, ultimately resulting in 292 confirmed cases, over 70 hospitalisations and substantial economic disruption. The outbreak was first recognized in June 2016 when clusters of hepatitis A were detected in Oahu residents without travel history; subsequent investigations and a case–control study implicated raw scallops served at a sushi chain, and HAV was detected in implicated scallop lots. Closure of affected Genki Sushi outlets, embargo and recall of the imported scallops, intensive post-exposure prophylaxis for exposed patrons and contacts, and extensive risk communication led to a gradual decline in new cases, with the outbreak declared over in early 2017.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of HAV-contaminated raw frozen scallops from a foreign supplier; service of these scallops uncooked in sushi to large numbers of customers; low baseline immunity in Hawaii’s adult population; and challenges in rapid traceback due to long HAV incubation and complex food service operations. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of unusual viral genetic characteristics; the outbreak was driven by a classic foodborne common-source exposure amplified by popular restaurant venues.
Review: retain – This 2016 Hawaii outbreak (292 confirmed cases, 51–80 hospitalisations depending on source) is widely cited as one of the largest post-vaccine-era foodborne HAV outbreaks in the U.S. and was missing from the original dataset. It clearly qualifies as a top-tier emergence event in terms of case numbers and public health/economic impact. Added here as a distinct re-occurrence event in Northern America; year span set to 2016–2017 to reflect that illnesses continued into early 2017 even though exposure was in 2016. ([marlerclark.com](https://marlerclark.com/news_events/settlements-determined-in-genki-sushi-hepatitis-a-outbreak?utm_source=openai))

EPP.scientific.name: Paracoccidioides spp.
EPP.common.name: paracoccidioidomycosis
Host: Humans (rural workers, migrants, and indigenous populations including Suruí people)
Event.summary: Beginning around 1997, a pronounced increase in paracoccidioidomycosis cases was documented in Rondônia in Brazil’s Western Amazon, particularly in the southeastern part of the state. Case series, mortality data, and skin‑test surveys showed that this region had rapidly become a new hyperendemic focus, with incidence estimates in some localities reaching several tens of cases per 100,000 inhabitants per year. Through the 2000s the area remained a sustained hotspot, although later data suggest some gradual decline in incidence after the peak period.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid deforestation of primary forest, settlement schemes, road building, cattle ranching, and expansion of coffee and other crops brought large numbers of non‑immune migrants and indigenous residents into recently disturbed forest soils. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) of P. brasiliensis complex into the Western Amazon and establishment of stable transmission cycles in agro‑forestry mosaics; no specific single genotype has been identified as the sole driver, so the event is interpreted primarily as spatial expansion rather than strain‑level emergence.
Review: retain – Rondônia’s emergence as a hyperendemic area from 1997 onward is clearly documented and commonly cited as a major epidemiologic shift. Time frame and geography are appropriate, and classification as intra‑continental emergence into a new Amazonian sub‑region matches the definitions. No corrections to event coding were necessary; sources are relevant primary and review articles.

EPP.scientific.name: Paracoccidioides spp.
EPP.common.name: paracoccidioidomycosis
Host: Humans (children and adolescents 10–16 years with acute/subacute infant‑juvenile paracoccidioidomycosis)
Event.summary: Between 2010 and 2012, clinicians in Northeast Argentina, historically an area with high incidence of chronic adult paracoccidioidomycosis but very few juvenile cases, detected several children and adolescents with acute/subacute disseminated disease. This represented an unusual cluster of the infant‑juvenile form in a region where only one such case had been reported in the previous decade. The cluster was temporally linked to the preceding 2009 El Niño–Southern Oscillation event and to major environmental changes in the Paraná River valley associated with the Yacyretá hydroelectric dam, and was characterized by severe systemic presentations requiring intensive management. After this period, juvenile cases have continued to be monitored, but no comparable explosive cluster has been described.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional climatic anomalies (strong El Niño‑related rainfall and flooding around 2009), extensive deforestation, agricultural expansion, and long‑term hydrological and ecological changes due to the Yacyretá dam altered soil moisture and vegetation in Northeast Argentina, likely increasing airborne dispersal of Paracoccidioides propagules and exposure of children and adolescents. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain was identified; available data suggest the same Paracoccidioides lineages circulating in the area, so the event is best interpreted as re‑occurrence (a sharp increase in a previously rare clinical form) driven by environmental and social factors rather than intrinsic fungal change.
Review: retain – This event was missing from the original dataset and has been added because the 2010–2012 infant‑juvenile cluster in Northeast Argentina is repeatedly highlighted in the literature as a notable emergence of acute/subacute PCM linked to climatic and anthropogenic change. Classified as re‑occurrence (increase of a rare clinical form in a long‑endemic sub‑region) rather than intra‑continental emergence, since the area was already endemic for adult PCM. Time window, geography, and drivers follow the Medical Mycology case series and related Argentine epidemiologic reviews; sources are appropriate primary and review articles. Recommended to retain as one of the major post‑1990 emergence events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Paracoccidioides spp.
EPP.common.name: paracoccidioidomycosis
Host: Humans (mainly young adults and adolescents with acute/subacute paracoccidioidomycosis)
Event.summary: During December 2015–December 2016, a reference center in Rio de Janeiro state diagnosed eight acute/subacute cases of paracoccidioidomycosis among residents of municipalities bordering the newly built Raphael de Almeida Magalhães Highway (Arco Metropolitano). This represented a more than five‑fold increase over the expected annual number of acute cases from the area, in a state where PCM was already endemic. The temporal and spatial clustering of cases near segments of highway constructed between 2008 and 2014, together with environmental sampling that detected Paracoccidioides DNA in soils along the road, supported interpretation as an outbreak linked to massive earthworks and deforestation. After completion of the most intense construction phases and with time for the exposed cohort to pass through the incubation window, incidence rates of new acute cases declined toward background levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large‑scale civil engineering for the Arco Metropolitano (2008–2014), including deforestation and removal of large volumes of soil in Atlantic forest remnants, generated dust plumes and altered local microclimates; a strong El Niño event in 2015–2016 further increased rainfall and soil humidity, conditions known to favor sporulation and aerial dispersion of Paracoccidioides conidia. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype has been uniquely associated with this cluster; it is best interpreted as re‑occurrence driven by intense environmental disturbance and increased inhalational exposure, rather than intrinsic fungal evolution.
Review: review – Corrected the event years to 2015–2016 (matching the documented diagnostic period for the Baixada Fluminense outbreak) and adjusted the country field to Brazil [2015]; original entry used 2014–2016, which blurred construction and clinical periods. Added two key sources: a study detecting Paracoccidioides DNA in soils along the highway and a Rio de Janeiro cohort describing temporal changes in acute PCM incidence, both reinforcing the environmental‑disturbance interpretation. Classification as re‑occurrence (in an already endemic state) without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence remains appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Paracoccidioides spp.
EPP.common.name: paracoccidioidomycosis
Host: Humans (rural populations including farmers, fishers, and other workers in the Tocantins‑Araguaia basin)
Event.summary: In the mid‑2010s, a detailed clinical and eco‑epidemiological investigation in the Tocantins‑Araguaia basin in northern Brazil identified 106 new paracoccidioidomycosis cases over 27 months, corresponding to more than 47 cases per year. This incidence ranked northern Tocantins and surrounding areas of Goiás, Pará, and Maranhão as a novel hyperendemic zone for the disease, in contrast to previous perceptions of only sporadic cases. The study led to calls for making PCM a notifiable disease in the region and for intensified surveillance and diagnostic capacity. Transmission remains active, and the basin is now recognized as part of Brazil’s northern endemic belt.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid land‑use change in the Tocantins‑Araguaia basin, including deforestation of riparian forests, expansion of cattle and soybean production, road construction, hydro‑agricultural projects, and population inflows to new rural settlements, increased soil disturbance and human contact with Paracoccidioides reservoirs. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion (inherent) and consolidation of Paracoccidioides spp. in newly disturbed agro‑ecosystems; molecular assays could not fully discriminate species in this area, but there is no evidence that a single novel lineage alone explains the hyperendemicity.
Review: retain – The Tocantins‑Araguaia basin has been clearly defined as a new hyperendemic area with very high incidence (≈47 cases/year at a single reference hospital), and is widely cited as a major recent geographic expansion of PCM. The time window and geography in the original entry are consistent with the available data and with the linked eco‑epidemiologic study. Classification as intra‑continental emergence into a previously under‑recognized northern sub‑region is appropriate. No changes beyond minor wording; sources remain suitable.

EPP.scientific.name: Paracoccidioides spp.
EPP.common.name: paracoccidioidomycosis
Host: Humans (adult male rural resident with chronic mucocutaneous paracoccidioidomycosis)
Event.summary: In 2016, a man from a mountainous rural area of Ceará state, in Brazil’s semi‑arid Northeast, was diagnosed with autochthonous chronic paracoccidioidomycosis despite no travel to known endemic regions. Earlier reviews had characterized this part of Ceará as having very low endemicity with no confirmed local cases, so the report was interpreted as expansion of the recognized geographic range of Paracoccidioides within Brazil. Since publication in 2019, clinicians in the region have been alerted to consider PCM in differential diagnoses, although no large cluster from this microregion has yet been documented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely related to localized environmental and land‑use changes (e.g., small‑scale agriculture, soil disturbance, and possibly microclimatic shifts in mountainous semi‑arid zones) combined with increased clinician awareness and access to mycological diagnosis in Northeastern Brazil. Internal mechanisms: Possible geographic range expansion or detection of a previously cryptic focus of Paracoccidioides in a new Brazilian sub‑region; there is no evidence for a novel strain, so the event is treated as intra‑continental emergence rather than classic re‑emergence.
Review: retain – The Ceará case is clearly framed in the primary report as the first autochthonous PCM from a mountainous area previously considered non‑endemic, justifying intra‑continental emergence into a new Brazilian sub‑region. Time, place, and interpretation are consistent with the literature. Because this is a single case rather than a cluster, its inclusion is justified mainly by its geographic significance; however, it still falls within the top tier of distinct emergence events for this pathogen. No coding changes were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus louisense
EPP.common.name: St. Louis encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (neuroinvasive encephalitis cases), with underlying transmission in passerine birds and Culex mosquitoes
Event.summary: During 25 weeks in 1990–1991, central and south Florida experienced a major epidemic of St. Louis encephalitis, with approximately 222 laboratory‑diagnosed human cases and at least 14 deaths, representing the last large, classic SLEV outbreak in the United States. The epidemic developed over the late summer and autumn as intense bird–mosquito transmission in rural citrus groves and nearby communities led to widespread human neuroinvasive disease, particularly among older adults. Aggressive mosquito control, public health education to reduce evening outdoor exposure, and the seasonal decline in vector populations helped end transmission by early 1991, after which SLEV activity returned to low, sporadic levels in Florida.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: A combination of climatic conditions (wet–dry rainfall cycles followed by heavy summer rains), expansion of flood‑irrigated citrus agriculture, and high densities of Culex nigripalpus and susceptible avian hosts created ideal conditions for explosive amplification and human spillover during 1990–1991. External factors such as land‑use change and mosquito habitat creation in irrigation furrows were key drivers, consistent with a re‑occurrence of an endemic lineage. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a novel SLEV genotype or major phenotypic shift was found; the epidemic is best interpreted as amplification of established lineage II strains, driven by environmental and demographic factors rather than viral evolution.
Review: review – updated Event Year to 1990–1991 to match the documented 25‑week Florida epidemic spanning late 1990 into early 1991 and clarified that approximately 222 laboratory‑diagnosed cases occurred across 28 counties. Replaced a generic ScienceDirect overview with the Florida‑specific epidemic analysis (Meehan et al. 2000) while retaining US‑wide and re‑emergence reviews; classification as re‑occurrence in an already endemic sub‑region without evidence of a new genotype remains appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus louisense
EPP.common.name: St. Louis encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (neuroinvasive encephalitis), with supporting evidence of transmission in local birds and Culex mosquitoes
Event.summary: In August 2001, an outbreak of St. Louis encephalitis centered on Monroe and West Monroe, Louisiana, led to about 63 reported human cases and prompted a state emergency alert. The epidemic evolved rapidly over several weeks during peak mosquito season, with many cases recognized only after substantial transmission had already occurred. Intensified vector control, public health messaging to reduce evening mosquito exposure, and seasonal declines in mosquito abundance brought the outbreak under control by late summer, after which SLEV activity in Louisiana again became sporadic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Warm, humid late‑summer conditions and abundant Culex quinquefasciatus breeding habitats in urban and peri‑urban areas, combined with delayed recognition of the outbreak and limited prior immunity in older adults, facilitated sustained transmission before control measures were escalated. Internal mechanisms: Available reports and molecular data do not indicate emergence of a distinct new genotype or strain; the event reflects ecological amplification of endemic virus rather than virologically driven re‑emergence, consistent with classification as a re‑occurrence.
Review: review – event timing and location (Monroe area, Ouachita Parish, Louisiana, 2001) and a scale of roughly 63 human cases agree with Louisiana Department of Health descriptions; classification as a re‑occurrence in an already endemic sub‑region without evidence of a novel strain is appropriate. Replaced Wikipedia with the state Saint Louis encephalitis manual while retaining Louisiana morbidity and annual reports as primary documentation, which strengthens source quality.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus louisense
EPP.common.name: St. Louis encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (encephalitis and meningoencephalitis), Culex pipiens/quinquefasciatus complex mosquitoes, local wild and domestic birds
Event.summary: From January to May 2005, Córdoba Province, Argentina, experienced the first large documented outbreak of St. Louis encephalitis in the country, with 47 laboratory‑confirmed and probable human cases and nine deaths after decades of only sporadic detections. The outbreak began with clusters of neurologic disease in Córdoba City and spread through urban neighborhoods as infected Culex mosquitoes amplified genotype III SLEV in naïve bird populations. Intensive vector control, public advisories to reduce mosquito exposure, and the seasonal decline in mosquito abundance ended the outbreak by late autumn, although virologic and serologic studies showed that SLEV continued to circulate silently in birds and mosquitoes in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Urban expansion, local environmental conditions conducive to Culex breeding, and high densities of susceptible eared doves and other urban‑adapted birds facilitated explosive amplification once genotype III SLEV was introduced; limited prior human awareness and surveillance delayed recognition of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses identified re‑emergence of genotype III SLEV in Córdoba after at least 26 years of absence, and experimental work showed higher virulence and higher viremias in birds and mice compared with non‑epidemic strains, consistent with re‑emergence driven by a more pathogenic genotype.
Review: retain – event timing, location (Córdoba Province, Argentina), case and death counts, and characterization as re‑emergence driven by introduction of a more virulent genotype III strain are consistent across CDC and peer‑reviewed sources; no corrections to geography or event‑type coding are needed.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus louisense
EPP.common.name: St. Louis encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (encephalitis cases), Culex mosquitoes and local birds as transmission reservoirs
Event.summary: In 2006, following the 2005 Córdoba epidemic, a new outbreak of Saint Louis encephalitis was reported in Paraná Province, Argentina, indicating spread of the emergent Argentine genotype III SLEV lineage into additional central regions. Neurologic cases occurred in residents after the summer mosquito season began, with epidemiologic evidence supporting local bird–mosquito amplification rather than isolated importations from Córdoba. Strengthened vector control, heightened clinical awareness, and the seasonal decline in mosquito populations brought the outbreak under control within the same season, confirming that the genotype III lineage had become established more broadly in central Argentina.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional bird movements and possible movement of infected vectors or hosts from Córdoba, along with warm, humid conditions and standing water that supported Culex populations, facilitated geographic spread to Paraná Province; human disease reflected spillover after enzootic cycles were established. Internal mechanisms: The outbreak is attributed to the same re‑emergent, more virulent genotype III lineage first identified in Córdoba, representing geographic expansion of an epidemic genotype with enhanced fitness in local ecological settings rather than de novo evolution in Paraná.
Review: retain – recognition of a 2006 outbreak in Paraná Province linked to the post‑2005 genotype III lineage, location within Argentina’s central region, and classification as re‑emergence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) are consistent with CDC and PAHO syntheses; case numbers remain incompletely documented but the event clearly qualifies as one of the major Argentine SLEV outbreaks after 2005.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus louisense
EPP.common.name: St. Louis encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (dengue‑like febrile illness, meningoencephalitis, and hemorrhagic manifestations), Culex mosquitoes, local birds in an urban setting with intense concurrent dengue transmission
Event.summary: In the first half of 2006, during a large dengue virus serotype 3 outbreak in São José do Rio Preto (northwest São Paulo State, Brazil), investigators identified the first recognized community outbreak of Saint Louis encephalitis in the country, detecting SLEV RNA in six patients whose serum or cerebrospinal fluid had initially tested negative for dengue and yellow fever viruses. These SLEV‑infected patients presented with dengue‑like febrile illness, including three cases of viral meningoencephalitis and three with hemorrhagic signs, revealing that SLEV was co‑circulating with dengue in a densely populated urban center. As the dengue epidemic waned, vector control efforts intensified and arboviral transmission declined, but the outbreak highlighted that SLEV infections in Brazil were being missed and that SLEV could cause both neurologic and hemorrhagic disease during large arboviral seasons.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very high levels of dengue virus transmission (>15,000 suspected dengue cases) and associated vector control efforts focused primarily on Aedes aegypti created a context in which other arboviruses, including SLEV transmitted by Culex species, circulated largely unrecognized; urban crowding and year‑round mosquito breeding in water‑holding containers facilitated human exposure. Internal mechanisms: Molecular characterization indicated that the Brazilian outbreak strains were closely related to SLEV genotype V, which had been present in South America for decades; no clear evidence of a novel variant was identified. The episode is therefore best interpreted as re‑occurrence of pathogenic genotype V in humans, with clinical recognition improved by molecular diagnostics, rather than emergence of a new SLEV genotype.
Review: review – newly added event capturing the 2006 São José do Rio Preto community outbreak in Brazil, which primary sources describe as the first documented SLEV outbreak in the country with six RT‑PCR–confirmed human cases (three meningoencephalitis, three with hemorrhagic signs) during a large dengue‑3 epidemic. Classified as re‑occurrence (rather than first detection or inter‑continental emergence) because SLEV and human infections were already known from Brazil; the key impact is the shift from isolated infections to a recognizable outbreak and demonstration of hemorrhagic manifestations.
