EPP.scientific.name: Orthoflavivirus louisense
EPP.common.name: St. Louis encephalitis virus
Host: Humans (23 confirmed infections, predominantly neuroinvasive disease), Culex mosquitoes, wild and peridomestic birds
Event.summary: In summer 2015, Maricopa County, Arizona, experienced a notable outbreak of St. Louis encephalitis with 23 confirmed human cases, most neuroinvasive, and at least one to two deaths, occurring concurrently with a large West Nile virus outbreak. The outbreak began in July with detection of SLEV‑positive mosquito pools and rapidly progressed to clusters of human encephalitis cases in metropolitan Phoenix as a newly introduced genotype III lineage, closely related to Argentine strains, amplified in local bird–mosquito cycles. Intensive vector‑control interventions, public health messaging, and the seasonal decline of mosquito populations by October curtailed transmission, but subsequent phylogeographic work showed that the introduced genotype III lineage persisted and seeded onward spread across the western United States.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Urban heat islands, irrigated landscapes, and abundant Culex vectors and avian hosts in metropolitan Phoenix, together with low recent human exposure to SLEV, created favorable conditions for amplification once the virus was introduced; co‑circulation with West Nile virus underscored shared ecological drivers and strained surveillance systems. Internal mechanisms: Sequencing demonstrated that the Arizona outbreak strain belonged to genotype III, previously restricted to Argentina, representing cross‑continental introduction of a more virulent lineage with evidence of enhanced neuroinvasiveness and efficient transmission in local vectors and hosts, consistent with re‑emergence via novel genotype introduction rather than resurgence of historical US strains.
Review: retain – the 2015 Maricopa County outbreak is correctly dated, geographically located, and described in terms of human impact (~23 confirmed cases, including transplant‑associated infections) and linkage to an introduced genotype III lineage of South American origin; classification as re‑emergence via novel genotype introduction, without intra‑/inter‑continental emergence at the species level, is appropriate and well supported by phylogeographic analyses.

EPP.scientific.name: Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Duck herpesvirus 1, Duck plague virus
Host: Numerous captive duck and goose species in zoological and ornamental collections kept under enforced indoor housing
Event.summary: In 2005, an outbreak of duck viral enteritis occurred in multiple species of captive ducks and geese in Germany after flocks were moved indoors under strict biosecurity because of the regional threat of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1; within weeks, birds developed severe disease and high mortality, and duck plague virus was confirmed as the cause.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Enforced in-house keeping of normally free-ranging waterfowl due to H5N1 concerns greatly increased stocking density and contact rates, likely allowing latent carriers to seed explosive transmission in naïve birds, while shared indoor water and fomites amplified virus spread. Internal mechanisms: The causative strain (later characterized as DEV 2085) showed virulent field-virus genomic features but no evidence of being a new species or continent-level introduction; this fits re-occurrence of DVE under altered husbandry rather than emergence of a novel agent.
Review: retain – Added as a key European event: the 2005 Germany outbreak in numerous captive duck and goose species, temporally linked to H5N1-driven indoor confinement, is one of the more severe and well-characterized DVE epizootics in Europe. Correctly coded as re-occurrence in Europe/Western Europe, Germany, with impact likely involving many hundreds of birds; flock numbers should be verified from the Kaleta et al. 2007 full text for precise impact comparison.

EPP.scientific.name: Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Duck herpesvirus 1, Duck plague virus
Host: Chara-Chemballi breed domestic ducks (Anas platyrhynchos domesticus local indigenous type) in a commercial flock of 4,500 adults
Event.summary: An outbreak of duck plague in a commercial flock of 4,500 Chara-Chemballi ducks in Kadavakathi village near Tenkasi, Tamil Nadu, resulted in the death of about 2,000 birds (44.4% mortality), with affected ducks showing typical clinical signs and necropsy lesions; PCR amplification of the DEV polymerase gene confirmed duck viral enteritis virus infection.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Recent long-distance movement of a large flock purchased from Kerala, transport stress during hot weather, and exposure to contaminated local water sources likely contributed to virus introduction and explosive within-flock spread. Internal mechanisms: Histopathology and molecular testing indicated infection with virulent Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1 similar to other field strains in India; no novel genetic traits were reported, so this is best interpreted as a high-impact re-occurrence in a susceptible indigenous breed rather than emergence of a new variant.
Review: retain – Added because this single-farm outbreak caused 2,000 deaths among 4,500 Chara-Chemballi ducks (44.4% mortality), making it one of the more severe, well-documented duck plague events in India after 1990. Correctly classified as re-occurrence in Asia/Southern Asia, India. Event year is set to 2019, matching the case-report publication year; the paper does not explicitly state the outbreak year, so this timing should be confirmed against the full text if precise temporal ordering is critical.

EPP.scientific.name: Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1
EPP.common.name: Duck herpesvirus 1, Duck plague virus
Host: Commercial hemp ducks (approximately 5,000 birds around 310 days of age) on an intensive farm
Event.summary: In December 2021, a severe duck plague outbreak occurred on a farm with about 5,000 hemp ducks in Qingyuan, Guangdong Province, China, causing high mortality among adult birds; pathological investigation and genomic analysis identified field strain DP-GD-305-21 as the causative duck enteritis virus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Large, single-age cohort of adult ducks kept under intensive conditions, with potential gaps in vaccination and contact with contaminated water or fomites, enabled rapid farm-wide spread once virus was introduced. Internal mechanisms: Whole-genome sequencing showed DP-GD-305-21 to be a virulent Chinese field strain closely related to other CHv/CV-like viruses, with several point mutations across genes such as UL12, UL41, UL47 and LORF11; these changes may influence virulence or antigenicity, but current evidence mainly supports continued circulation of an established virulent lineage rather than emergence of a wholly new subtype.
Review: retain – Added as a recent high-impact Chinese farm outbreak involving roughly 5,000 adult ducks with detailed pathological and genomic characterization; correctly located in Asia/Eastern Asia, China. Classified here as re-occurrence of virulent Chinese field lineages, but given documented gene-level differences from earlier strains, future work could justify re-emergence status if these mutations are shown to alter virulence or vaccine responsiveness.

EPP.scientific.name: Border disease virus
EPP.common.name: BDV, Pestivirus D
Host: Sheep (Composite ewe flocks; many persistently infected lambs)
Event.summary: In 2019, two large commercial Composite ewe flocks in the South‑Western Slopes region of New South Wales experienced unexpectedly poor reproductive performance, with one property scanning only 69.9% of 3,500 maiden ewes pregnant and then marking just 1,922 lambs, implying loss of more than 500 lambs between scanning and marking. Diagnostic work identified resorbing fetuses, stillbirths and many weak or 'hairy' lambs, and BDV RNA was detected by BDV‑specific qRT‑PCR in most of 10 examined aborted or stillborn lambs, while a high proportion of surviving hairy lambs were BDV‑positive by pestivirus antigen ELISA. Cross‑sectional serosurveys across age groups revealed high BDV antibody prevalence in some cohorts and many still‑susceptible breeding ewes in others, and in a monitored group of 120 persistently infected lambs, only 21 were alive at 5 months and 14 at 12 months, illustrating the substantial cumulative reproductive and post‑weaning losses associated with this outbreak.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12961243/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: joining maiden ewes at a young age under drought conditions, together with intensive confinement feeding in drought lots, placed large numbers of immunologically naïve breeding sheep together during the critical early gestation window for fetal BDV infection; limited historic recognition of BDV in Australian sheep and the focus on BVDV in cattle meant BDV was not an early diagnostic priority. Internal mechanisms: establishment of BDV infection with transplacental spread leading to widespread fetal death, stillbirths and the birth of many persistently infected hairy lambs that shed virus efficiently, driving large‑scale flock‑level reproductive loss and poor lamb survival, even though the virus itself appears to belong to existing BDV lineages rather than a novel genotype.
Review: Retain: Newly added, high‑impact re‑occurrence event showing large‑scale BDV‑associated reproductive loss in Australian sheep, with thousands of ewes at risk and well‑documented fetal and lamb outcomes. Classified as re_occurrence driven by management and demographic factors rather than a new genotype or region.

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic haematopoietic necrosis virus
EPP.common.name: EHNV
Host: Wild juvenile European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis); other susceptible native and introduced fishes in the upper Murrumbidgee system were at risk of exposure but disease was only confirmed in redfin during this event.
Event.summary: In December 2009, EHNV was confirmed in juvenile redfin perch from a fish‑kill event in Blowering Dam, a major impoundment in the upper Murrumbidgee River catchment of New South Wales that had experienced earlier, largely anecdotal EHN outbreaks in the late 1980s and early 1990s.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) The 2009 detection involved conspicuous disease in redfin but did not result in documented clinical cases in native fishes, and subsequent basin‑wide surveys indicated that EHNV remained restricted to the known endemic focus rather than spreading into other catchments. This event nonetheless highlighted ongoing circulation of EHNV in one of the Murray–Darling Basin’s largest headwater reservoirs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistent redfin populations in Blowering Dam, angler‑mediated movement of live bait and fishing gear, and the dam’s large volume and cool‑water regime, which favour dense redfin assemblages, set the stage for periodic EHN outbreaks when environmental conditions and host demography allowed.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: As in other reservoirs, EHNV’s capacity to remain at low prevalence between outbreaks, coupled with high case‑fatality in juvenile redfin, leads to episodic but sometimes dramatic mortality events without necessarily leaving strong serological signatures in surviving fish.
Review: REVIEW – retain event but adjust classification. The 2009 Blowering Dam episode is well supported by the 2007–2011 surveillance work and subsequent syntheses as a re‑occurrence within the upper Murrumbidgee endemic area; there is no evidence that it involved a novel strain or first detection in a new UNSD sub‑region, so re_emergence has been set to false while re_occurrence remains true.([usgs.gov](https://www.usgs.gov/diseases-of-aquatic-organisms/viral-diseases-wild-fish?items_per_page=6&page=0&utm_source=openai)) Location, timing and host information are consistent with available sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Epizootic haematopoietic necrosis virus
EPP.common.name: EHNV
Host: Wild European/redfin perch (Perca fluviatilis) in Talbingo Reservoir, in which infection with EHNV was detected by qPCR in a small number of sampled fish; no overt clinical disease or large‑scale fish kill was reported at the time of detection.
Event.summary: In early 2025, targeted disease surveillance carried out under the Snowy 2.0 Biosecurity Risk Management Plan detected epizootic haematopoietic necrosis virus in redfin perch from Talbingo Reservoir using quantitative PCR, marking the first confirmed presence of EHNV in this major Snowy Mountains storage.([snowyhydro.com.au](https://www.snowyhydro.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Snowy-2.0-Biosecurity-Risk-Management-Plan_Annual-Report-for-the-Financial-Year-ended-30-June-2025.pdf)) All sampled fish appeared externally healthy and only two positive detections were obtained among more than 250 individuals, so the event is best interpreted as detection of subclinical infection rather than a visible epizootic. Nonetheless, the finding triggered a revision of the surveillance program to focus on preventing spread into upstream Tantangara Reservoir, which is currently considered redfin‑ and EHNV‑free but supports habitats of high conservation value including Macquarie perch and stocky galaxias.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The long‑standing presence of redfin perch in Talbingo Reservoir, combined with regional movements of anglers and potential water transfers associated with Snowy 2.0 infrastructure, created a realistic pathway for EHNV introduction from known endemic areas in the upper Murrumbidgee and other Murray–Darling catchments.([snowyhydro.com.au](https://www.snowyhydro.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Snowy-2.0-Biosecurity-Risk-Management-Plan_Annual-Report-for-the-Financial-Year-ended-30-June-2025.pdf)) Internal mechanisms: EHNV’s ability to persist at low prevalence without overt disease, together with its potential to spread via infected fish or contaminated water, motivates precautionary surveillance and control efforts even when only subclinical infections are detected.
Review: REVIEW – newly added surveillance‑based emergence event. The WOAH Quarterly Aquatic Animal Disease report for Q1 2025 and the Snowy 2.0 Biosecurity Risk Management Plan annual report both document qPCR‑confirmed EHNV infection in wild redfin from Talbingo Reservoir and describe associated changes to surveillance priorities, but they do not report a conspicuous fish kill or clinical disease.([rr-asia.woah.org](https://rr-asia.woah.org/app/uploads/2025/07/Australias-QAAD-Q1-2025.pdf)) The event is therefore classified as a re‑occurrence (detection of infection in a new reservoir within the same UNSD sub‑region) with high confidence in occurrence but uncertain short‑term impact; it is included because of its clear management importance and demonstration of northward range expansion within the Snowy–Murrumbidgee system.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Equine arteritis virus
EPP.common.name: EAV, Equine arterivirus
Host: Warmblood breeding horses (stallions, mares and foals) on a single Warmblood breeding farm in Pennsylvania
Event.summary: In spring 1996, an imported Warmblood stallion that was a known carrier of equine arteritis virus seeded an extensive outbreak of equine viral arteritis on a Warmblood breeding farm in Pennsylvania, USA. Over several weeks, clinical EVA was recorded in 23 horses on the farm (four stallions, seven mares and 12 foals), with one late‑term abortion and three foal deaths, as virus spread from the carrier stallion to in‑contact stallions, mares and foals via both venereal and respiratory routes. Emergency vaccination of clinically unaffected horses with modified‑live vaccine, strict on‑farm biosecurity, and management of carrier stallions eventually curtailed the outbreak but highlighted the risk posed by imported Warmblood carriers to North American sport‑horse breeding operations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Importation of a persistently infected Warmblood stallion from Europe into a susceptible Warmblood breeding herd, combined with intensive on‑farm breeding and close stabling of stallions, mares and foals, enabled rapid venereal and aerosol spread; prior absence of EVA vaccination and limited screening of imported stallions amplified the risk. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced Transmission – selection of a single EAV variant from the carrier stallion’s semen that was efficiently transmitted both vertically and horizontally on the farm; Genetic Stability – molecular analyses showed the outbreak strain remained highly stable as it spread through mares and foals, indicating that re-occurrence was driven by introduction and management factors rather than emergence of a markedly divergent genotype.
Review: retain – This Warmblood breeding‑farm outbreak (23 clinical cases, foal deaths and abortion) is explicitly highlighted in major reviews as a notable international EVA event and is likely among the top 10 post‑1990 outbreaks by impact. New row added and classified as a re-occurrence within an already endemic US subregion, driven by introduction of a carrier stallion; no evidence supports inter- or intra-continental emergence.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Wild rodents and hares, mosquitoes and other biting insects, humans (especially rural residents and people engaged in outdoor work or recreation)
Event.summary: In 2000, Finland experienced its largest recorded tularemia epidemic, with 926 laboratory-confirmed human cases nationwide and an annual incidence of about 18 per 100,000 inhabitants, centred in northern and western health districts. The outbreak coincided with high mosquito abundance and favourable summer weather, leading to widespread ulceroglandular disease after mosquito bites as well as some pneumonic cases associated with farm work and exposure to contaminated hay dust. As vector populations declined seasonally and awareness campaigns on personal protection and case recognition were implemented, case numbers fell back to baseline, but surveillance has since documented recurrent regional epidemics, confirming persistent enzootic F. tularensis subsp. holarctica foci.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Warm, wet summers promoting mosquito proliferation, abundant rodent and hare hosts, and extensive human outdoor and agricultural activity in endemic areas increased contact with infected vectors and contaminated aerosols. Internal mechanisms: The epidemic reflects re-occurrence and amplification of established F. tularensis subsp. holarctica lineages in Finland, without clear evidence of a novel strain or host jump, though with notable spread into additional Finnish districts within the same Northern Europe sub-region.
Review: review – new high-impact event added. The 2000 Finnish epidemic (926 cases) is one of the largest modern tularemia outbreaks worldwide and clearly belongs among the top events for this pathogen. Classified as re-occurrence in an already endemic Northern European sub-region, driven by high mosquito densities and outdoor exposure, with no evidence of a new lineage or host shift. Recommended for inclusion among the core top-10 emergence events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Wild rabbits and small rodents, questing ticks (e.g., Dermacentor spp.), humans (landscapers, outdoor workers)
Event.summary: From May to October 2000, Martha’s Vineyard, Massachusetts, experienced a notable cluster of tularemia cases associated with outdoor landscaping work, in an area where tularemia had previously been rare but where infected lagomorphs and small rodents were found. Environmental and veterinary investigations demonstrated an epizootic of Francisella tularensis subsp. tularensis in rabbits and other small mammals with evidence of aerosolization of contaminated dust during mowing and brush-cutting, leading to unusually frequent pneumonic disease in humans. Following public health advisories, modifications to landscaping practices, and increased awareness and tick control, the incidence of severe pneumonic cases declined, though tularemia has remained endemic in local wildlife with sporadic human cases reported annually.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of small mammals and ticks in peri‑residential landscapes, intensive mechanical mowing and brush cutting that aerosolized contaminated dust, and increased human recreational and occupational exposure contributed to efficient transmission. Internal mechanisms: Enhanced transmission via environmental aerosolization of a highly virulent type A strain (F. tularensis subsp. tularensis), representing a change in dominant exposure route and effective host–environment interface rather than an entirely new genotype, and best classified as re-occurrence within an existing North American focus.
Review: review – event retained as a key North American episode due to its unusual concentration of pneumonic tularemia and its importance for understanding aerosol transmission, but emergence-type classification was corrected. Co-classification as both re_occurrence and re_emergence conflicted with the project rules and available evidence; the event is better interpreted as re-occurrence driven by environmental and behavioral factors without a demonstrated new strain. No changes to geography or timing were required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Wild hares and rodents (voles and other small mammals), mosquitoes and other biting arthropods, humans
Event.summary: In the summer of 2000, Sweden reported an exceptionally large tularemia season with numerous human cases and evidence of widespread epizootics in hares and small mammals, extending well beyond the historically endemic northern river-lake foci into central and southern municipalities. The outbreak coincided with favorable conditions for mosquito vectors and high rodent and hare densities, suggesting efficient vector-borne amplification of Francisella tularensis subsp. holarctica in new landscapes within the country. As vector activity declined with seasonal change and targeted public health messaging reduced human exposure to biting insects and sick wildlife, incidence decreased, but tularemia has since recurred periodically in many of these newly affected districts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climatic and hydrological conditions that favored mosquitoes and other biting arthropods, alongside high densities of susceptible hares and rodents near lakes and rivers, promoted explosive vector-borne transmission and spread into new ecological regions of Sweden. Internal mechanisms: Predominantly ecological and vector-driven geographic range expansion of established F. tularensis subsp. holarctica lineages into previously low-risk parts of Sweden, representing re-occurrence and spatial spread within an already endemic Northern European sub-region rather than intra-continental emergence at the continental scale.
Review: review – event retained as a major Nordic outbreak with documented spread into new Swedish municipalities, but the emergence classification was corrected. Because tularemia was already well established in Northern Europe and in Sweden prior to 2000, the event does not meet criteria for intra-continental emergence and is better described as re-occurrence with geographic expansion in an endemic sub-region. Added a more specific Swedish 2000 outbreak source (EID case-control study) and aligned mechanism text with the revised classification.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Wild hares and rodents, mosquitoes and other biting arthropods, humans
Event.summary: In 2003, Sweden reported 698 human tularemia cases, the largest national outbreak since 1967, with most infections acquired in long-recognised endemic foci in the north-central river valleys and northern coastal areas. The epidemic peaked in late summer and early autumn, coinciding with high mosquito activity, and epidemiologic investigations indicated that mosquito bites and outdoor activities near lakes and rivers, where infected hares and small mammals were abundant, were key risk factors for Francisella tularensis subsp. holarctica transmission. As temperatures fell and mosquito populations declined, human incidence dropped, but this outbreak confirmed that Sweden’s enzootic foci were capable of producing recurrent large mosquito-borne epidemics, leading to strengthened surveillance and public education on vector avoidance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Warm, wet conditions that favoured mosquito breeding, abundant susceptible wildlife near watercourses, and intensive outdoor recreation and farming combined to increase human exposure to infected vectors. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a novel bacterial genotype; instead, the outbreak reflects re-occurrence and amplification of established F. tularensis subsp. holarctica lineages within long-standing Swedish foci, with some geographic spread into additional municipalities in the same Northern Europe sub-region.
Review: review – new high-impact event added. The 2003 Swedish epidemic (698 human cases) is one of the largest modern tularemia outbreaks and provides an important example of recurrent, mosquito-driven epidemics in long-established Northern European foci. Classified as re-occurrence in an endemic sub-region, not first detection or intra-continental emergence. Recommended for inclusion among the top-impact events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Francisella tularensis
EPP.common.name: Rabbit fever
Host: Common ringtail possums (Pseudocheirus peregrinus) and possibly other native wildlife; humans scratched or bitten by infected possums or exposed while handling wildlife or contaminated material
Event.summary: In 2011, two women in western Tasmania developed ulceroglandular tularemia after close contact with injured common ringtail possums, and Francisella tularensis subsp. holarctica (biovar japonica) was confirmed by culture and molecular typing, representing the first documented F. tularensis infections in Australia and in the Southern Hemisphere. Retrospective investigations subsequently identified F. tularensis DNA in archived ringtail possum tissues from possum die-offs in 2002–2003, suggesting that the bacterium had been present in Australian wildlife for some time but had gone undetected because tularemia was not previously considered endemic. Following recognition of these cases, Australian public health and wildlife authorities added tularemia to national notifiable disease lists, developed clinical and laboratory guidelines, and initiated targeted wildlife and human surveillance, which to date have not revealed large epizootics but confirm a focal presence of the pathogen.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased clinical awareness and laboratory capability, plus closer interaction between people and native wildlife (e.g., handling injured possums), enabled detection of a pathogen that likely circulated cryptically in local ecosystems. Internal mechanisms: Demonstrates geographic range expansion of F. tularensis subsp. holarctica to Oceania and adaptation to a new marsupial reservoir (common ringtail possums), fitting an inter-continental emergence event for this host system–continent combination, even though the lineage appears closely related to strains circulating in other parts of the Northern Hemisphere.
Review: review – event retained as the first confirmed F. tularensis subsp. holarctica occurrence in Australia and the Southern Hemisphere, appropriately classed as inter-continental emergence. The earlier 2003 Northern Territory foot-wound isolate was later reclassified as F. hispaniensis and therefore is not treated as a tularemia event here. First_detection was set to false to reserve that category for the global first description of the pathogen, and the host list, countries field, and summary were revised to emphasise the well-documented ringtail possum-associated cases in Tasmania.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Sprivivirus cyprinus
EPP.common.name: Spring viraemia of carp virus
Host: Goldfish (Carassius auratus) maintained in a lake in São Paulo State, Brazil (ornamental cyprinids).
Event.summary: In 1998, an outbreak of haemorrhagic disease in goldfish kept in a lake in São Paulo State, Brazil, was investigated and SVCV was identified as the causative agent, confirming spring viraemia of carp in South America for the first time. The event, which involved clinically affected goldfish likely derived from international ornamental fish trade, represented the first confirmed occurrence of SVCV in the Americas and outside its long‑recognised European range. The outbreak was controlled by culling and sanitary measures at the affected site, and no further confirmed SVCV outbreaks in Brazilian finfish have been reported, but the episode triggered increased surveillance and highlighted the risk of inter‑continental spread via ornamental fish.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: international movement of ornamental cyprinids, probably from SVCV‑endemic regions, with limited pre‑import testing and biosecurity at the receiving site allowed introduction of the virus into a Brazilian lake. Internal mechanisms: the virus involved appears to belong to the classic SVCV genogroup I, with no evidence of a novel genotype; the key biological factor was SVCV’s ability to cause acute haemorrhagic disease in susceptible cyprinids introduced into naïve environments rather than viral innovation.
Review: review – New row added to capture the 1998 SVCV outbreak in goldfish in a São Paulo lake, which OIE and CFSPH identify as the first confirmed occurrence of SVCV in the Americas and thus the inter‑continental emergence of SVCV into the South America continent. Classified as first_detection and inter_continental_emergence; magnitude of fish losses is not fully quantified in accessible summaries, so key outbreak details should be cross‑checked directly against Alexandrino et al. 1998 before final use.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Sprivivirus cyprinus
EPP.common.name: Spring viraemia of carp virus
Host: Wild common carp (Cyprinus carpio) inhabiting Tecocomulco Lagoon, a natural, apparently hydrologically isolated freshwater lagoon in central Mexico.
Event.summary: In October 2015, ten wild common carp showing septicaemia, exophthalmia, moderate abdominal distension and external and internal haemorrhages were collected from Tecocomulco Lagoon, a closed freshwater system in central Mexico with no previous reports of SVCV. Laboratory investigation using cell culture, semi‑nested RT‑PCR, gene sequencing and electron microscopy confirmed infection with SVCV genogroup Ia, representing the first confirmed detection of SVCV in Mexico and documenting its presence in a natural water body in Central America. Although no large‑scale fish kill was reported, the finding extended the known southern range of SVCV in the Americas and led Mexican authorities to inform SENASICA and recommend enhanced surveillance and stricter controls on carp movements and ornamental fish imports.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: the precise route of introduction into Tecocomulco Lagoon is unknown, but likely involved previous human‑mediated translocation of infected carp for stocking, movements of contaminated equipment, or introduction via susceptible ornamental cyprinids or possibly waterfowl, reflecting regional trade and stocking practices. Internal mechanisms: the Mexican isolate showed typical SVCV molecular features and clustered within genogroup Ia alongside North American and Asian isolates, indicating geographic range expansion of an existing lineage into a new subregion of the Americas rather than evolution of a novel genotype; the confined lagoon setting highlighted how even hydrologically isolated systems can harbour exotic fish viruses once introduced.
Review: review – Kept as the first confirmed detection of SVCV in Mexico, supported by the 2019 Journal of Fish Diseases case report; however, event‑type coding has been corrected. Because SVCV had already been reported from Brazil (1998) within the same South America continent, this episode is now classified as first_detection and intra_continental_emergence (new Central America subregion) rather than inter_continental_emergence. The summary also clarifies that no mass mortality was documented, and the event is important primarily for range extension.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Sprivivirus cyprinus
EPP.common.name: Spring viraemia of carp virus
Countries: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region [2020]
Host: Cyprinid fishes (likely carp and related species) in aquaculture and/or ornamental trade in Hong Kong SAR, China.
Event.summary: In the second quarter of 2020, infection with spring viraemia of carp virus was officially reported from Hong Kong SAR, China, via the WOAH Regional Representation for Asia and the Pacific, indicating detection of SVCV in local cyprinid stocks. The notification reflects continued circulation and geographic spread of SVCV within East Asia’s ornamental and food‑fish carp sectors rather than a wholly new introduction, as SVCV had been reported from mainland China for more than a decade. Following notification, veterinary authorities in Hong Kong SAR emphasised surveillance, movement control, and strengthened biosecurity in aquaculture and ornamental facilities to prevent further dissemination within the territory and to trading partners.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: dense ornamental and food‑fish carp trade networks between mainland China and Hong Kong SAR, high farm and holding densities, and complex cross‑boundary supply chains favour repeated introductions and local circulation of SVCV. Internal mechanisms: the event is best interpreted as continued circulation of established Asian genogroup Ia strains within the Eastern Asia subregion, with no evidence for a novel genotype; thus the main mechanisms involve regional geographic range maintenance and trade‑mediated spread rather than viral innovation.
Review: review – Retained as a WOAH‑notified detection of SVCV in Hong Kong SAR in 2020, supported by the Asia–Pacific Quarterly Aquatic Animal Disease report, but event‑type coding has been corrected. Because Hong Kong SAR and mainland China are both in the Eastern Asia subregion, this detection cannot be classified as intra‑continental emergence; it is now coded solely as re_occurrence within an already affected subregion. Geography and timing otherwise match the WOAH report, and inline markdown citations were removed from the mechanism text.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.
Country: China, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera tryoni
EPP.common.name: Queensland fruit fly
Host: Backyard and commercial fruit crops (including stone fruit, citrus and other common host fruits) in infested suburbs of Perth
Event.summary: In February 1989, Queensland fruit fly was detected breeding in backyard tomatoes and other host fruits in the Perth suburb of Dalkeith, representing the first established population of this species in Western Australia and a serious threat to the state’s Qfly‑free horticultural industries. The Western Australian Department of Agriculture implemented an intensive 10‑month eradication program over roughly 300 km² of metropolitan Perth using protein bait sprays, male‑lure bait blocks and releases of hundreds of millions of sterile male flies, combined with strict movement controls on host produce. After no further wild Qfly were detected for more than a year, the program was declared successful in late 1990 and Western Australia regained its Queensland‑fruit‑fly‑free status, which has since been maintained through ongoing early‑warning trapping and rapid responses to new incursions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The incursion was attributed to human‑mediated movement of infested host fruit from Qfly‑endemic eastern Australia into Perth, facilitated by increasing interstate travel and trade and the availability of highly suitable backyard and commercial host trees in the city’s Mediterranean climate. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence that this outbreak involved a novel strain or adaptive change in the pest; rather, it demonstrated that existing eastern Australian Qfly populations can survive and reproduce in marginal but favourable microclimates when introduced, and that eradication is feasible using area‑wide integrated management and sterile insect technique.
Review: review – New event added because the 1989–1990 Perth incursion and eradication program is widely documented as a major Qfly emergence episode (∼A$5 million program over about 300 km²). It begins slightly before the nominal 1990 cut‑off but most of the response and the declaration of eradication occurred in 1990; recommended to keep as one of the top-impact events but flagged for final decision on the start‑year rule.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera tryoni
EPP.common.name: Queensland fruit fly
Host: Commercial orchards and backyard fruit trees (especially citrus and stone fruits) in and around Loxton North in the Riverland horticultural district
Event.summary: In 1990, a Queensland fruit fly outbreak was detected in the Riverland region at Loxton North when larvae were found in locally grown fruit and the detection met South Australia’s formal outbreak definition, marking the first modern fruit fly outbreak in this high‑value production area. Authorities established an outbreak area around Loxton North with intensive trapping, bait spraying and fruit stripping, and imposed movement restrictions on host produce in and around the affected zone to protect the Riverland Pest Free Area and its export markets. After a focused eradication campaign and a period without further detections, the Loxton North population was eliminated and the Riverland again qualified as fruit‑fly‑free, a status later recognised in interstate and international market access protocols.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Historical PIRSA accounts indicate that Riverland outbreaks are rare and usually result from infested fruit being carried across the South Australia–Victoria border despite quarantine controls, rather than from natural spread, and the 1990 Loxton North event fits this pattern; high densities of irrigated citrus and stone fruit around Loxton North meant that any introduced flies could build up rapidly if not detected. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence that the 1990 outbreak involved a novel strain, resistance or host shift; it is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence of an existing pest in a previously pest‑free production area, driven by lapses in compliance with movement restrictions and successfully eradicated using the standard South Australian eradication program.
Review: review – New event added to capture the 1990 Loxton North outbreak, which PIRSA identifies as one of only two Riverland fruit fly outbreaks between 1957 and 2013 and therefore a historically important emergence episode; however, detailed public data on affected host crops and exact quarantine dates are limited, so these aspects should be checked against South Australian outbreak records.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera tryoni
EPP.common.name: Queensland fruit fly
Host: Backyard and nearby orchard fruit trees (mixed host fruits typical of Riverland town blocks, including stone and pome fruits and citrus) in the Lyrup area
Event.summary: In 2013, a second rare Queensland fruit fly outbreak was recorded in South Australia’s Riverland, near the town of Lyrup, again temporarily disrupting the region’s long‑standing pest‑free status. Following detection of infested fruit, PIRSA implemented its standard eradication protocol, establishing an outbreak area and surrounding suspension zone, intensifying trapping and baiting, and restricting the movement of host fruit from affected properties. The Lyrup outbreak was eradicated within the following season and the Riverland’s Qfly‑free status was restored, but the episode highlighted the continuing risk of incursions despite the Yamba roadblock and other border controls and foreshadowed the much larger series of outbreaks beginning in 2020–2021.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Official historical summaries attribute the very infrequent Riverland outbreaks, including the 2013 event near Lyrup, to occasional failures of border quarantine and inadvertent importation of infested fruit from neighbouring states, rather than to natural spread from established populations, against a backdrop of highly susceptible irrigated orchards. Internal mechanisms: As with other Riverland incursions before 2020, there is no evidence for genetic change, host shifts or resistance in the flies involved; the episode is best described as a re‑occurrence of an existing pest in a previously pest‑free production area driven by human‑assisted dispersal.
Review: review – New event added because PIRSA’s Yamba Roadblock history explicitly lists a Queensland fruit fly outbreak near Lyrup in 2013 as one of only two Riverland outbreaks prior to 2014, suggesting it was a significant emergence episode. Publicly available detail on the size, duration and precise locality of this outbreak is sparse, so the narrative is partly inferred from standard SA outbreak protocols and should be checked against PIRSA’s original outbreak notice and internal reports.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera tryoni
EPP.common.name: Queensland fruit fly
Host: Backyard and urban fruit trees (mixed hosts including stone fruit and other common garden fruit species) in metropolitan Adelaide
Event.summary: On 25 December 2014, Biosecurity SA declared a Queensland fruit fly outbreak in the Adelaide suburb of West Croydon after larvae were found in backyard fruit, marking renewed incursion of the pest into South Australia’s otherwise fruit-fly-free mainland status. Authorities immediately established a 1.5 km quarantine zone with strict controls on movement, disposal and treatment of fruit and vegetables, and mounted bait-spotting and hygiene programs in affected streets. After a standard eradication period with no further detections, the outbreak was declared eradicated in 2015 and Adelaide’s fruit-fly-free status was restored.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction was attributed to infested fruit brought from endemic eastern Australian states by travellers, combined with abundant backyard host trees in inner suburbs and high summer temperatures favouring development. Internal mechanisms: No specific genetic or phenotypic changes were implicated; the event represents re-occurrence driven by human-assisted dispersal rather than adaptive evolution.
Review: retain – Localised but economically relevant Adelaide metropolitan outbreak; dates, location and control measures align with ABC and PIRSA documentation, and classification as re‑occurrence is appropriate since Qfly was already present in the broader Australia and New Zealand sub‑region and the event reflects re‑introduction rather than new geographic sub‑region colonisation.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera tryoni
EPP.common.name: Queensland fruit fly
Host: Urban backyard and small-scale horticultural fruit trees including Citrus spp. and Prunus spp. in central Auckland
Event.summary: In February 2015, an isolated population of Queensland fruit fly was detected in the central Auckland suburb of Grey Lynn, representing New Zealand’s first confirmed local breeding population of this species rather than a single trapped adult. Biosecurity New Zealand initiated a large-scale emergency response, including intensive male-lure trapping, baiting, fruit stripping and strict movement controls on host produce within the controlled area, and the population was classified as transient and under eradication. No further Qfly life stages were detected after March 2015, and the outbreak was officially declared eradicated on 4 December 2015, with New Zealand’s status updated to ‘Absent: pest eradicated’ in subsequent IPPC and EPPO records, although later single-fly detections (for example Devonport 2019 and Mt Roskill 2026) have prompted new but much smaller responses.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The most likely driver was accidental introduction via infested fruit or luggage from eastern Australia or Pacific islands, with high propagule pressure due to close travel links, combined with favourable summer conditions in Auckland’s mild climate and dense host availability in suburban gardens. Internal mechanisms: There is no evidence of novel genotypes or adaptive traits specific to this event; rather, the incursion reflects geographic range expansion via human-mediated dispersal into a previously pest-free but climatically marginal part of the wider Australia and New Zealand sub-region, and is best classified as a re-occurrence in that sub-region.
Review: review – Corrected the event period from “2015–2017” to “2015” because IPPC and EPPO records state that no Qfly life stages were detected after March 2015 and eradication was declared on 4 December 2015, with the pest status update published in 2017; reclassified the episode from intra‑continental emergence to re‑occurrence since Qfly was already present elsewhere in the Australia and New Zealand sub‑region and no evolutionary change was involved. A general-purpose Wikipedia link has been removed in favour of official MPI and IPPC documentation.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cryphonectria parasitica
EPP.common.name: chestnut blight fungus
Host: Castanea sativa (sweet chestnut)
Event.summary: In July 2023, mortality of sweet chestnut trees was reported in the parc châtaigneraie in the Akfadou mountain range of Tizi Ouzou, Algeria, where affected trees showed crown dieback with persistent withered leaves, trunk and branch cracks and cankers with orange pycnidial stromata and mycelial fans under the bark; morphological and DNA sequence analyses of EF‑1α and β‑tubulin genes confirmed Cryphonectria parasitica as the causal agent. Pathogenicity tests on detached chestnut twigs reproduced canker development and yielded the same fungus, and forestry archives indicated that the infected groves had originally been established with planting material from the Cévennes region of France, pointing to introduction via infected stock. This outbreak constitutes the first report of chestnut blight in Algeria and only the second documented African country record after Tunisia, representing a re‑occurrence and geographic expansion of the disease within the Northern Africa subregion and prompting calls for broader surveys and strengthened phytosanitary measures.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of infected chestnut planting material from France to establish groves in Tizi Ouzou, combined with suitable cool, humid montane conditions and a lack of prior targeted surveillance for C. parasitica in Algerian chestnut stands. Internal mechanisms: high virulence of the introduced C. parasitica lineage on C. sativa and efficient production of asexual spores on trunk cankers, enabling local spread within the small chestnut park and posing a risk of further dissemination to other plantings in North Africa.
Review: review – Newly added event reflecting the first confirmed occurrence of C. parasitica in Algeria (and second known African country record); classified as re_occurrence within Northern Africa because Tunisia was already affected, and summarised primarily from the 2025 Plant Disease note and EPPO distribution update; recommended for follow‑up once national survey data on spread and impact become available.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Diaphorina citri
EPP.common.name: Asian citrus psyllid
Host: Citrus spp. (orange, mandarin, tangelo) and ornamental Murraya spp.
Event.summary: In January 1998, Diaphorina citri was found in high numbers on backyard citrus in Guadeloupe, representing the first record for the Caribbean basin and warning of a new invasive vector threat. Over the following years the psyllid spread to multiple neighboring Caribbean islands, colonizing both citrus and ornamental hosts and greatly expanding its range within the region. By the mid‑2000s, D. citri was broadly established in Caribbean citrus areas, prompting long‑term biological control and surveillance programs.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional trade and informal movement of citrus and Murraya plants among Caribbean islands, combined with favorable tropical climate and year‑round flushing of citrus vegetation, promoted establishment and rapid dispersal. Internal mechanisms: Inherent geographic range expansion ability of D. citri in warm, humid climates and high reproductive rates on new flushes of citrus, enabling rapid population buildup and colonization of new islands once introduced.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Diaphorina citri
EPP.common.name: Asian citrus psyllid
Host: Citrus spp. (especially lime and sweet orange) in commercial and backyard plantings
Event.summary: By around 2008, Oman was reported as being fully invaded by Diaphorina citri, adding to existing infestations in neighboring countries of the Arabian Peninsula and placing its citrus industry at high risk for both huanglongbing and witches’ broom disease of lime. In the ensuing years the psyllid became widespread in Omani citrus‑growing areas, where it acted as a vector for HLB in a region already burdened by other serious citrus diseases, leading to increased tree decline and management costs. The event evolved into a persistent regional problem as coordinated control programs attempted to limit further disease spread and maintain citrus production in the face of dual vector‑borne disease pressures.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Regional movement of infested citrus material and natural spread from already infested neighboring countries, combined with expansion of citrus cultivation in arid environments relying on irrigation, provided new habitats for D. citri; limited early surveillance delayed detection until the pest was widespread. Internal mechanisms: Efficient vectoring of CLas in an environment where susceptible citrus and other phloem‑limited pathogens (e.g., witches’ broom) were present, along with the insect’s capacity to exploit irrigated oases and orchards in otherwise harsh climates, contributed to significant re‑emergence of citrus disease problems in western Asia.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Maconellicoccus hirsutus
EPP.common.name: hibiscus mealybug
Host: Ornamental and landscape plants (notably Hibiscus rosa‑sinensis and other ornamental shrubs) and, to a lesser extent, fruit crops such as grapevine and guava in urban and peri‑urban settings
Event.summary: Surveys in 2010 revealed that hibiscus mealybug was present throughout Cyprus, mainly on ornamental hibiscus in private gardens and garden centres but also occasionally on grapevine and guava, representing a major new outbreak focus in the eastern Mediterranean part of the pest’s native/long‑established Asian range. The finding, formally reported in 2011, triggered official control and intensive surveillance, as the pest became widely established in urban and tourist areas and raised concern about potential spread to mainland Mediterranean agriculture and the wider EPPO region. During the first half of the 2010s, management in Cyprus focused on containment, monitoring and promotion of biological control to limit damage in city parks, gardens and nearby crops.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-185?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction with infested ornamental plants imported from already infested parts of the Middle East or wider Asian range; high densities of susceptible ornamentals in coastal resort and urban landscapes; Mediterranean climates with mild winters and warm summers that favour survival and reproduction. Internal mechanisms: Continued geographic range expansion at the fringes of a long‑established range; broad host spectrum allowing establishment on common ornamental and fruit species even at low initial densities; initially limited presence of specialised natural enemies at the point of introduction, increasing the likelihood of establishment and rapid population growth.
Review: review – This event corresponds to the well‑documented discovery and rapid spread of M. hirsutus on Cyprus and is important because it marks establishment in the eastern Mediterranean and within the EPPO region, but the original row had major geographical and classification errors. Cyprus is classified as Asia/Western Asia in the provided country list, not Europe/Southern Europe, so continent and sub‑region have been corrected accordingly.([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PHENHI/distribution/CY?utm_source=openai)) Because the pest was already widespread in Asia (including several other Western Asian countries) long before 2010, this outbreak is better described as a re‑occurrence (regional resurgence on a new island within an already infested sub‑region) rather than an inter‑continental emergence, so the inter‑continental flag has been set to false and re‑occurrence to true. The event has also been re‑dated to 2010–2015 to reflect the first-record year documented by the Cyprus NPPO and EPPO RS 2011/069. Recommended action: retain as a major episode but keep flagged for expert review, especially regarding whether later detections in Greece and Türkiye should be treated as an extension of this same Mediterranean episode or as separate minor events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoebolavirus sudanense
EPP.common.name: Sudan virus
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In late July 2012, Uganda’s Ministry of Health reported clusters of severe illness and deaths in Kibaale District in western/mid‑western Uganda, and laboratory testing at the Uganda Virus Research Institute confirmed Sudan virus as the cause of the outbreak. The epidemic caused roughly two dozen cases with a high case‑fatality ratio, with transmission occurring mainly among household contacts and in healthcare settings before heightened control measures were implemented. Aggressive case isolation, contact tracing, public communication, and partner support brought the outbreak under control within weeks, and Uganda was declared Ebola‑free later in 2012 after the required 42‑day period without new cases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: close contact in households and during funerals, limited early infection‑prevention and control in peripheral health facilities, and delayed recognition of Ebola contributed to spread within the district; mobility between neighbouring villages facilitated local dissemination. Internal mechanisms: virus characterization identified Sudan virus consistent with previously known lineages, with no clear evidence of novel virulence or resistance traits; the event is best interpreted as a re‑occurrence in a country with prior Sudan virus outbreaks rather than a fundamentally new variant‑driven emergence.
Review: retain – Event accurately represents the 2012 Kibaale Sudan virus outbreak as documented by WHO, CDC and ECDC, with correct geography (Uganda, Eastern Africa) and appropriate classification as a re‑occurrence in a country with prior Sudan virus activity. Case numbers are presented approximately (“roughly two dozen cases”), which is consistent with small differences between WHO and CDC summaries; no corrections to timing, location or emergence type were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoebolavirus sudanense
EPP.common.name: Sudan virus
Host: Humans
Event.summary: In November 2012, Uganda detected new cases of Ebola haemorrhagic fever in Luweero District, and laboratory analysis confirmed Sudan virus as the aetiologic agent; additional linked patients were later identified in Luweero and Kampala Districts. This outbreak involved 7 cases (6 laboratory‑confirmed and 1 probable) and 4 deaths, with infections mainly linked through household exposure and health‑facility contacts before stringent infection‑prevention measures were implemented. After rapid deployment of response teams, reinforcement of infection‑prevention and control, and systematic contact follow‑up in affected districts, no additional transmission chains were identified and the event was declared over following the standard 42‑day observation period without new cases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: likely new zoonotic spillover or a short, initially undetected transmission chain in Luweero, with subsequent limited spread in family and healthcare settings and potential amplification risk due to proximity to Kampala; strengthened national surveillance capacity allowed relatively quick detection and response compared with earlier outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: virus typing indicated Sudan virus consistent with previous Ugandan strains, with no clear signal of novel genetic traits or resistance; thus the episode is treated as a re‑occurrence of Sudan virus disease in an already affected subregion rather than a mechanistically distinct re‑emergence.
Review: review – Retain this event but refine the description and sources. Case numbers in the summary have been aligned with WHO Disease Outbreak News (7 cases: 6 confirmed, 1 probable; 4 deaths) instead of the earlier vague “about seven cases with four fatalities”, and WHO DONs from 17, 23 and 30 November 2012 have been added to the source list to better document the episode. Geography (Uganda, Eastern Africa) and classification as a re‑occurrence remain appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoebolavirus sudanense
EPP.common.name: Sudan virus
Countries: Uganda [2022 – Mubende, Kassanda, Kyegegwa, Kagadi, Bunyangabu, Kampala, Wakiso, Jinja, Masaka and others]
Host: Humans
Event.summary: On 20 September 2022, Uganda declared an outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Sudan virus after a 24‑year‑old man from Madudu sub‑county in Mubende District tested positive at the Uganda Virus Research Institute following several unexplained community deaths. The outbreak spread across central and western Uganda with major transmission foci in Mubende and Kassanda and additional cases reported from districts including Kyegegwa, Kagadi, Bunyangabu, Wakiso, Kampala, Jinja and Masaka, resulting in 142 laboratory‑confirmed and 22 probable cases and 55 confirmed deaths before control measures took full effect. After 42 days with no new cases following the last patient’s outcome in late November 2022, national authorities and WHO declared the outbreak over on 11 January 2023.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: suspected new spillover from a wildlife reservoir into a rural community, followed by human‑to‑human spread amplified in households, traditional burial practices, and health facilities where infection‑prevention and control measures were initially imperfect; population mobility from rural epicentres to trading hubs and to Kampala facilitated wider geographic dissemination. Internal mechanisms: genomic sequencing indicated the outbreak strain was closely related to the Nakisamata Sudan virus detected in Luwero in 2011, supporting a new spillover of a related lineage rather than continuation of earlier human transmission chains; no clear evidence of markedly increased transmissibility, virulence, or treatment resistance was identified, so under the project definitions this episode is treated as a large re‑occurrence rather than a mechanistic re‑emergence.
Review: review – Event is correctly included as one of the most impactful Sudan virus outbreaks, but several corrections were required. The emergence type has been recoded from re‑emergence to re‑occurrence because WHO, CDC and genomic analyses describe the virus as closely related to the 2011 Nakisamata lineage without evidence that viral evolution (e.g. substantially increased transmissibility or resistance) drove the outbreak; repeated zoonotic spillover and contextual factors better explain transmission. Case and death counts in the summary have been updated to the final official figures (142 confirmed and 22 probable cases with 55 confirmed deaths), and wording in the mechanism section was adjusted to reflect these interpretations. Geography and timing were left unchanged.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoebolavirus sudanense
EPP.common.name: Sudan virus
Countries: Uganda [2025 – Kampala, Wakiso, Mbale, Luwero, Jinja and other affected districts]
Host: Humans
Event.summary: On 30 January 2025, Uganda’s Ministry of Health declared an outbreak of Sudan virus disease after post‑mortem samples from a 32‑year‑old nurse who died at Mulago National Referral Hospital in Kampala tested positive for Sudan virus in three national reference laboratories. Subsequent investigation and enhanced surveillance identified additional epidemiologically linked infections among healthcare workers and community contacts in Kampala and in districts connected to the index case’s movements, including Wakiso, Mbale, Luwero and Jinja, culminating in 12 confirmed and 2 probable cases and 4 deaths by late April 2025. Rapid activation of mortality surveillance, contact tracing, isolation and infection‑prevention measures, together with launch of a ring‑vaccination trial of a Sudan virus candidate vaccine, contained the outbreak, and the Ministry of Health declared it over on 26 April 2025 after 42 days with no new cases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: the index case was a mobile healthcare worker who sought care at multiple facilities in Kampala, Wakiso and Mbale and also visited a traditional healer while symptomatic, creating opportunities for nosocomial and community exposure before Sudan virus disease was suspected; urban density and inter‑district travel along major transport corridors increased the potential for spread, although strong preparedness and rapid response meant that high‑risk contacts were quickly traced, monitored and isolated. Internal mechanisms: genomic analysis of virus from the index case confirmed Sudan virus and showed close clustering with sequences from the 2012 Luweero outbreak rather than with the 2022 Mubende lineage, indicating an independent spillover from a wildlife reservoir or shared ecological focus rather than continuation of the 2022 transmission chain; no specific mutations associated with increased virulence or resistance have been implicated, so the event is best classified as another re‑occurrence of Sudan virus disease in Eastern Africa.
Review: review – New event added to capture the 2025 Sudan virus disease outbreak centred on Kampala, which was missing from the original profile despite being one of only a small number of documented SVD outbreaks and therefore within the “top 10” events by default. Classification as a re‑occurrence (not intra‑/inter‑continental emergence or mechanistic re‑emergence) follows WHO and CDC descriptions and genomic analyses indicating an independent spillover closely related to the 2012 Luweero lineage rather than continuation of the 2022 outbreak. Geography (Uganda, Eastern Africa), host system (humans), case counts (12 confirmed, 2 probable, 4 deaths) and end date are based on WHO Disease Outbreak News, CDC outbreak summaries and recent peer‑reviewed/technical reports.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Plasmodium spp.
EPP.common.name: malaria parasites
Host: Humans (Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum)
Event.summary: After malaria had been reduced to only a few hundred cases a year in Tajikistan by 1990, civil war, economic collapse and the cessation of vector control led to a rapid resurgence of Plasmodium vivax and re‑establishment of local Plasmodium falciparum transmission from 1991 onward, especially in southern districts bordering Afghanistan. Official notifications rose from hundreds of cases in the early 1990s to 2,411 cases in 1994 and 29,794 cases in 1997, with contemporaneous estimates suggesting 200,000–500,000 infections that year as returning refugees and cross‑border movements seeded transmission into vulnerable communities. Beginning in 1998, intensive national and international control efforts—including renewed indoor residual spraying, mass radical treatment with primaquine, and establishment of specialized anti‑malaria centres—rapidly reduced incidence, halving reported cases by 1999 and setting the country on a trajectory that ultimately led to elimination.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Armed conflict and population displacement, breakdown of health‑care and surveillance systems, suspension of mosquito‑control operations because of financial and logistical constraints, shortages of trained public‑health staff, and expansion of irrigated agriculture in arid southern valleys (creating Anopheles breeding sites) created ideal conditions for malaria resurgence once parasites were reintroduced from Afghanistan. Internal mechanisms: Available data do not implicate new parasite genotypes or antimalarial drug resistance as the primary cause; this episode is best characterized as a large‑scale re-occurrence of P. vivax and P. falciparum malaria in an area where transmission had previously been nearly eliminated.
Review: review – new large resurgence episode added. Justification: Malaria control collapse during Tajikistan’s civil war led to one of the largest documented post-elimination resurgences, with 29,794 officially reported cases and estimated 200,000–500,000 infections in 1997. Classified as re-occurrence in Central Asia (no evidence that parasite evolution or new drug resistance was the primary driver). Start and end years (1991–1999) chosen to bracket the period of sharp increase and subsequent decline; recommend expert review of exact temporal bounds and whether to split early vs peak years into separate rows.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Staphylococcus aureus
EPP.common.name: Staphylococcus aureus infection
Countries: United States of America [2002, Michigan; 2002, Pennsylvania]
Host: Humans (severe invasive infections including chronic wound infection and bacteremia)
Event.summary: In the summer of 2002, Michigan reported the first documented human infection worldwide with vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (VRSA), followed shortly by a second case in Pennsylvania, both in patients with chronic wounds and prior vancomycin exposure. Over the subsequent few years, additional VRSA cases were detected sporadically in the United States, all associated with severely ill patients and prior exposure to vancomycin and vancomycin-resistant enterococci. By the mid‑2000s, intensive infection-control measures and careful stewardship limited VRSA to rare, isolated cases, preventing broader dissemination despite the grave implications of vancomycin resistance in S. aureus.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: prolonged vancomycin therapy for chronic MRSA infections, co-colonization or co-infection with vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE), and healthcare settings where multidrug-resistant organisms coexisted. Internal mechanisms: acquisition of the vanA gene cluster from enterococci via horizontal gene transfer, leading to high-level vancomycin resistance, representing antimicrobial resistance escalation and novel genotype emergence within S. aureus, with potential for increased treatment failure.
Review: retain – VRSA remains exceedingly rare but the first two clinical infections in Michigan and Pennsylvania (2002) were globally significant as proof that high-level vancomycin resistance could transfer into S. aureus. Countries were reformatted to keep “United States of America” as the country name with state-level detail in brackets, and Wikipedia was replaced with primary clinical descriptions from NEJM and CDC/JAMA; classification as re_emergence (new resistance mechanism in an endemic pathogen) without inter-continental flags is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus hendraense
EPP.common.name: Hendra virus
Host: Humans (horse trainer, stable worker, horse owner/trainer) infected after close contact with clinically ill or recently dead horses infected with Hendra virus
Event.summary: In September 1994, a novel severe respiratory disease outbreak in thoroughbred racehorses in Hendra, a suburb of Brisbane, led to infection of a 49‑year‑old horse trainer (fatal pneumonic illness) and a 40‑year‑old stable worker (self‑limited influenza‑like illness), marking the first recognised human cases of Hendra virus. Subsequent retrospective investigations linked a second focus in Mackay, north Queensland, where two horses had died in August 1994 and a 36‑year‑old horse trainer who assisted with necropsy later developed aseptic meningitis and then fatal encephalitis 13 months after exposure, with Hendra virus confirmed as the cause. The episode ended after infected horses were euthanised, extensive tracing and surveillance of exposed humans showed no further infections, and the novel virus was isolated and characterised as a new henipavirus with flying foxes identified as the wildlife reservoir in later studies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Initial emergence reflected ecological interfaces between pteropid flying fox reservoirs and high‑density racehorse stabling in peri‑urban southeast Queensland, with likely exposure of horses to bat urine, faeces or birthing products and intense unprotected human contact with severely ill or dead horses during training and necropsy. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) from bats to horses and then to humans, and enhanced transmission linked to high viral loads in acutely ill horses, but no evidence of a distinct new strain or adaptive genetic change within this initial emergence window.
Review: Retain – Verified against NSW Health’s human-case summary and other official and review sources: the 1994 Hendra (Brisbane) and 1995 Mackay human infections together represent the first recognised human emergence of Hendra virus, all within Queensland, Australia; timing, locations, host description and classification as both first_global_emergence and first_detection are consistent with the literature, and there is no evidence of additional, larger pre‑2000 human events or inter-/intra-continental spread that would alter this record.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus hendraense
EPP.common.name: Hendra virus
Host: Humans (veterinarian) infected after extensive exposure to blood and respiratory secretions during necropsy of a horse presumed to have died of Hendra virus infection
Event.summary: In late 2004, a veterinarian in her 20s in Cairns, north Queensland, performed a post‑mortem examination on a horse that was subsequently presumed, on clinical and epidemiologic grounds, to have had Hendra virus infection, resulting in extensive unprotected exposure to blood and respiratory secretions. About a week after exposure, she developed a mild influenza‑like illness and seroconverted to Hendra virus without progression to severe disease, while three other exposed individuals remained well and seronegative. The event concluded after public health follow‑up showed no secondary human transmission, and intensified infection‑control guidance for veterinarians and surveillance for equine cases in Queensland and northern New South Wales was implemented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued bat‑to‑horse spillover risk in tropical and subtropical Queensland combined with high‑risk veterinary procedures (post‑mortem examination of an undiagnosed horse without full respiratory protection) enabled a rare horse‑to‑human transmission event; recognition of this case prompted tighter infection‑control protocols for equine necropsy and suspect Hendra cases. Internal mechanisms: No evidence of a new strain or altered virulence; disease pattern suggests typical zoonotic infection in a single highly exposed host without onward human transmission.
Review: Retain – NSW Health’s case summary documents a single serologically confirmed human infection in a Cairns veterinarian in late 2004 after necropsy of a presumptive Hendra-infected horse; year, location, host description and exposure circumstances in this record match those details. Classification as re_occurrence (in the same sub-region, with no evidence of a new strain or new geographic area within Oceania) and not as intra-/inter-continental emergence is appropriate, and the listed sources are relevant and sufficiently specific for this event.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus hendraense
EPP.common.name: Hendra virus
Countries: Australia [2008 Redlands (Thornlands area), suburban Brisbane, Queensland]
Host: Humans (two veterinary staff: veterinarian and veterinary nurse/technician) infected while caring for and performing invasive procedures and necropsies on multiple horses with acute neurological and respiratory disease due to Hendra virus in a veterinary hospital setting
Event.summary: In July 2008, a veterinary hospital at Redlands, a suburb of Brisbane, Queensland, experienced an outbreak in which four horses with acute neurological signs tested positive for Hendra virus and a fifth became ill under quarantine, representing an intense focal equine outbreak in an enclosed clinical setting. Two veterinary staff members who had conducted high‑risk procedures—including nasal cavity lavage and necropsy—on the infected horses developed acute influenza‑like illness followed by encephalitis and seroconversion to Hendra virus, with one surviving and the other dying from severe neurologic disease. The incident ended after the clinic was quarantined, infected horses were euthanised, exposed staff and contacts were monitored and some given ribavirin, and no further human infections or secondary human‑to‑human spread were detected.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The outbreak was driven by introduction of Hendra‑infected horses—likely infected via bat‑to‑horse spillover outside the clinic—into a high‑density veterinary hospital where intensive handling, aerosol‑generating procedures (nasal lavage, endoscopy, necropsy) and initially limited respiratory protection created multiple high‑dose exposure opportunities for staff, leading to the largest documented cluster of human cases. Internal mechanisms: Clinical description highlighted some ‘novel’ clinical features in horses and humans, but virologic characterisation did not demonstrate a distinct new genotype; the event is best interpreted as severe disease from the existing virus in an amplifying setting rather than strain‑driven re‑emergence.
Review: Retain – NSW Health’s case summary and the 2008 Redlands outbreak paper describe a veterinary hospital cluster in Redlands (Thornlands area) with two human infections (one fatal), matching the event year, location, host description and exposure setting recorded here. Classification as re_occurrence in the same sub-region (rather than re_emergence, because no distinct new genotype or host jump was demonstrated) is consistent with current evidence; all listed sources are relevant, though the ABC explainer and Wikipedia entry provide general background rather than primary epidemiologic detail.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus hendraense
