EPP.scientific.name: Chronic wasting disease prion
EPP.common.name: CWD prion
Countries: Republic of Korea [2010 re-emergence; 2016-2024 annual cases]
Host: Farmed elk; farmed red deer; farmed sika deer
Event.summary: After several years with no detected CWD following early-2000s control efforts, CWD reappeared in South Korea in 2010 in farmed cervids, indicating that the pathogen had persisted or been reintroduced. During 2016–2024, national surveillance documented recurring cases almost every year in multiple farmed elk, red deer, and sika deer herds across the country, with repeated depopulations and economic losses in the farmed deer industry. By the early 2020s, CWD had become an entrenched management problem for Korean farmed cervids, requiring ongoing testing, movement controls, and herd culling to limit further spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued commercial farming and movement of multiple cervid species within South Korea; incomplete elimination of prions from previously infected premises; economic incentives to expand or restock deer farms after earlier depopulations; possible reintroduction via imported animals or contaminated products. Internal mechanisms: Re-emergence driven by persistent environmental prion contamination on farms and efficient multi-species transmission among elk, red deer, and sika deer, supporting sustained transmission cycles despite control measures.
Review: review – Event retained as a major re‑emergence episode of CWD in South Korean farmed cervids after several apparently disease‑free years, but the event type has been simplified: 're_occurrence' is kept as true to reflect renewed transmission in an already affected country, while 're_emergence' is set to false because current evidence points mainly to persistence and re‑introduction of existing strains rather than clear pathogen change. No adjustments to geography, hosts, or timeline were required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Chronic wasting disease prion
EPP.common.name: CWD prion
Host: Wild mountain reindeer (Rangifer tarandus tarandus)
Event.summary: In March 2016, Norway diagnosed CWD in a free-ranging wild reindeer from the Nordfjella herd in southern Norway, representing the first detection of the disease in Europe and the first confirmed natural CWD case in reindeer. Intensive follow-up surveillance during 2016–2018 identified additional classical CWD cases within Nordfjella Zone 1, leading authorities to implement a drastic management campaign that culled the entire wild reindeer population in that zone to prevent further spread to other reindeer areas. By 2018, culling in Nordfjella Zone 1 had been completed and ongoing national surveillance indicated no further classical CWD cases in reindeer outside the original outbreak zone, though vigilance remained high.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Possible introduction of CWD prions into the Nordfjella landscape via historical importation of infected cervids or contaminated animal products from North America, or via environmental contamination from other prion sources such as scrapie in small ruminants grazing in the region; high local reindeer densities and seasonal aggregation facilitating within-herd transmission. Internal mechanisms: Establishment of a classical CWD strain capable of efficient transmission in wild reindeer, with environmental persistence of prions on shared ranges; disease dynamics in a migratory, herd-living host leading to rapid amplification once the pathogen became established.
Review: review – Event correctly describes the 2016 detection of classical CWD in the Nordfjella wild reindeer herd, the first recognized occurrence in Europe and globally the first natural infection in reindeer, and the subsequent eradication cull of Nordfjella Zone 1. To conform with the schema, 'first_detection' was set to false (global first detection predates this event), while 'inter_continental_emergence' remains true to mark first establishment of CWD in the European continent. No changes were needed for geography, timeline, or sources.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chronic wasting disease prion
EPP.common.name: CWD prion
Host: Wild moose (European elk, Alces alces)
Event.summary: In March 2018, Finnish authorities reported the country’s first CWD-like transmissible spongiform encephalopathy case in a 15‑year‑old wild moose found dead near Kuhmo in eastern Finland, representing the first such detection in the country and extending the known European distribution of cervid prion disease. Subsequent investigations concluded that this case resembled the atypical CWD-like prion pattern previously described in Norwegian moose rather than the classical, highly transmissible North American form, and intensified surveillance of cervids was implemented in Finland and neighboring EU member states. No large clusters or clear transmission chains were identified in Finland after this index case, but it established Finland as part of the European region where atypical cervid TSEs occur.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: EU- and nationally coordinated cervid surveillance programs that increased sampling intensity after CWD was detected in Norway; detection in an older moose possibly linked to age structure and longevity in local populations. Internal mechanisms: Likely spontaneous or low-transmissibility atypical prion strain in moose, similar to Nor16CWD reported in Norway, representing a re-emergent form of cervid prion disease in a new national population and host context; host expansion within Northern Europe from Norwegian to Finnish moose populations.
Review: review – The 2018 Finnish moose case near Kuhmo is retained as a key milestone showing that atypical cervid prion disease occurs beyond Norway. Event‑type flags have been revised so that 'first_detection' and 'intra_continental_emergence' are set to false (Europe was already affected and this is a new country within the same Northern Europe sub‑region), while 're_emergence' is set to true to reflect appearance of a Nor16CWD‑like, likely sporadic strain in a new national host population. Sources from the Finnish government, Yle, and veterinary reports remain appropriate.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Chronic wasting disease prion
EPP.common.name: CWD prion
Host: Wild mountain reindeer (Rangifer tarandus tarandus)
Event.summary: After the culling of the Nordfjella reindeer herd, Norway continued intensive surveillance and in 2020 identified a classical CWD case in a wild reindeer on the Hardangervidda plateau, home to Europe’s largest wild reindeer population, indicating that classical CWD had either spread beyond Nordfjella or arisen independently. This detection triggered renewed concern and risk assessments, as Hardangervidda supports many thousands of reindeer and is ecologically and culturally important, leading authorities to consider further targeted removals and strengthened monitoring. In the early 2020s, ongoing testing of Hardangervidda and other reindeer areas continued to search for additional cases to guide long-term management of CWD risk in Norway’s remaining wild reindeer populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Residual or previously unrecognized circulation of CWD prions in Norway’s interconnected reindeer ranges, potentially influenced by animal movements between management areas, shared grazing grounds, and historic livestock use of the same mountain pastures. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence of classical, transmissible CWD in a second major wild reindeer population, highlighting the capacity of this prion strain to persist and spread within reindeer metapopulations despite localized eradication efforts in Nordfjella; environmental persistence of prions in alpine ecosystems sustaining risk over multiple years.
Review: review – The detection of classical CWD in a Hardangervidda wild reindeer in 2020 is appropriately treated as a separate high‑impact event because it involves Europe’s largest wild reindeer population. Event‑type classification was simplified by setting 're_emergence' to false and keeping 're_occurrence' true, since available data indicate the same classical strain as in Nordfjella rather than a new variant; the episode is thus best interpreted as renewed occurrence in another population within the same Northern Europe sub‑region. Geography, timeline (2020 onward), and Norwegian Veterinary Institute sources remain valid.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Query fever
Host: Domestic goats (including imported goats), humans (farm workers, pub patrons and community)
Event.summary: In April 1993, an explosive Q fever epidemic occurred in the village of Jedľové Kostoľany in Nitra District, Slovakia, after an abortion storm in a large-capacity goat breeding center whose animals included stock imported from Bulgaria. A total of 113 persons developed Q fever, most infected indirectly when goat attendants repeatedly visited the local pub wearing contaminated work clothes, enabling aerosol spread of Coxiella burnetii to other patrons, while a smaller group acquired infection directly through occupational contact with the goats. After recognition of the outbreak, tracing of the coxiellosis epizootic in the goat herd and application of veterinary and public-health measures, no further waves of community transmission were reported from this locality.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movement and trade of goats, including importation from an endemic Bulgarian herd, introduced heavily infected animals into a Slovak village; lack of hygiene barriers between farm and community (e.g. workers visiting pubs in soiled clothing) created an unusual indoor aerosol transmission setting. Internal mechanisms: available reports do not identify a novel genotype or altered virulence; the outbreak is interpreted as re-occurrence of endemic Q fever in Eastern Europe facilitated by livestock movements and social-behavioural factors rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – Case numbers (113 human infections) and the unusual route of pub-based aerosol transmission from goat attendants’ contaminated clothing match the primary Slovak and Bulgarian reports.([cejph.szu.cz](https://cejph.szu.cz/artkey/cjp-199704-0007_An-explosive-outbreak-of-Q-fever-in-Jedlove-Kostolany-Slovakia.php?utm_source=openai))  Country, subregion and year are correct, and classification as re-occurrence (not intra-continental emergence) is appropriate because Q fever was already present in Slovakia and no new subregion or strain emergence is documented. No column changes required; event is clearly among the larger post‑1990 outbreaks.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Query fever
Host: Sheep (slaughtered in open municipal abattoir, primary source), cattle (possible contributing source), humans (town residents and abattoir‑adjacent workers)
Event.summary: From March to June 1996, the small Alpine town of Briançon in southeastern France experienced a large outbreak of acute Q fever with about 200 diagnosed human cases, many presenting with atypical pneumonia. Epidemiologic investigation linked illness to a municipal abattoir located in the town centre where infected sheep and cattle were slaughtered and waste was left uncovered, and helicopter traffic and local winds were thought to disperse contaminated aerosols over nearby residential areas. After the abattoir was closed or modified and infected animal waste was properly managed, incident Q fever cases declined and the urban epidemic came to an end.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Location of an open abattoir in the town centre, inadequate covering and disposal of infected sheep offal, and strong valley winds and helicopter downdrafts that favoured long-distance aerosol spread from slaughter activities to densely populated neighbourhoods. Internal mechanisms: no evidence for a novel Coxiella genotype or host jump was reported; this event is best viewed as a re-occurrence of endemic French Q fever under high‑risk slaughter and land‑use conditions.
Review: retain – Added as a new row because multiple reviews identify the 1996 Briançon urban/abattoir outbreak (~204 Q fever cases) as one of the largest European events in the 1990–2010 period.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC88923/?utm_source=openai))  France/Western Europe classification and timing (1996) follow standard UNSD groupings and outbreak reports. Treated as re-occurrence since Q fever was long endemic in France and the key drivers were abattoir siting and aerosolisation of slaughter waste, not first detection or spread to a new subregion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Query fever
Host: Sheep and goats grazing near town (probable main reservoirs), cattle (possible minor role), humans (residents of Etropole and nearby villages)
Event.summary: In spring 2002, the mountain town of Etropole in Sofia district, central-western Bulgaria, experienced a sizeable Q fever outbreak with roughly 120 laboratory-confirmed human cases, many presenting with atypical pneumonia. Cases clustered among residents living in a valley area below pastures where flocks of sheep and goats grazed and lambed, and serological surveys in local livestock indicated substantial C. burnetii circulation in these herds. As lambing ended and flock movements and grazing near the town were restricted, new human infections declined and the outbreak resolved without evidence of spread to other Bulgarian regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Town topography in a narrow valley with prevailing winds from surrounding slopes, outdoor lambing and grazing of infected sheep and goats close to residences, and dry conditions that favoured aerosolisation of birth products and contaminated dust; these features match patterns seen in other mountainous Q fever hotspots.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235756073_Q_fever_in_humans_and_farm_animals_in_four_European_countries_1982_to_2010?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: no novel strain or host expansion was highlighted; the event is a re-occurrence of endemic Bulgarian Q fever driven by livestock management and environmental factors.
Review: retain – Newly added because comparative analyses of Q fever in Bulgaria, France, Germany and the Netherlands list the Etropole 2002 outbreak (≈121 human cases) as one of the larger European events linked to livestock in the post‑1990 era.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235756073_Q_fever_in_humans_and_farm_animals_in_four_European_countries_1982_to_2010?utm_source=openai))  Year, location and livestock sources have been aligned with those summaries, and the event is correctly classified as re-occurrence rather than first detection or geographical emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Query fever
Host: Single lambing ewe and associated sheep flock at farmers’ market, humans (market visitors, stall holders and nearby residents)
Event.summary: In May 2003, health authorities in Soest district, Germany, detected an unusual cluster of atypical pneumonia among visitors to a spa-town farmers’ market where a pregnant ewe had lambed in a public petting area. Subsequent investigation identified 299 notified human Q fever cases linked to this event, with risk strongly associated with time spent near the ewe’s pen and short-distance crowding around the animal. After the market ended, the flock was removed and no continued local source existed, so case numbers declined and no broader geographic spread beyond this point-source outbreak was observed.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of a heavily infected pregnant ewe into a crowded farmers’ market created a classic super‑spreading scenario, with lambing and heavily contaminated bedding generating high loads of C. burnetii aerosols in a confined public space; the lack of awareness of Q fever risk in this non‑occupational setting meant no respiratory protection or separation from visitors. Internal mechanisms: genotyping did not implicate a special high‑virulence strain; this is a re-occurrence event driven by extreme exposure conditions to a single infected ewe rather than by pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – Added as a new row because the Soest 2003 farmers’ market outbreak with 299 notified Q fever cases is repeatedly cited as one of the largest community point‑source Q fever outbreaks in Europe and worldwide.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1618839/?utm_source=openai))  Germany/Western Europe classification and year are straightforward, and treatment as re-occurrence is appropriate since Q fever was endemic in Germany and the event reflects an intense single-source exposure, not spread to a new subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Query fever
Host: Sheep flock grazing and lambing on meadows near prison and urban neighbourhoods, humans (prisoners, prison staff, nearby residents and veterinary personnel)
Event.summary: Between January and early March 2003, a large Q fever outbreak struck the city of Como in northern Italy, initially recognised when multiple prisoners from a local facility were hospitalised with acute pneumonia. Active case-finding identified 133 persons with acute Q fever, including inmates, guards, nearby residents and veterinary staff, and epidemiologic investigation implicated a flock of sheep that had grazed and lambed on meadows adjacent to the prison and urban area as the most likely source. After the infected flock was treated and movement and grazing near the town were curtailed, environmental contamination fell and no further waves of Q fever were detected in Como.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Grazing and lambing of infected sheep directly adjacent to densely populated urban and prison settings enabled windborne and local aerosol spread from contaminated meadows to persons with no agricultural occupation; diagnostic vigilance and serologic screening then revealed the full scale of the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: available reports do not indicate emergence of a new Coxiella genotype or host range; this is a re-occurrence of endemic Italian Q fever precipitated by high‑risk land use and flock management.
Review: retain – Newly added because the Como 2003 outbreak with 133 acute Q fever cases in prisoners, staff and local residents is recognised as a major post‑1990 European epidemic linked to sheep grazing and lambing near an urban area.([wwwnc.cdc.gov](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/1/03-0467_article?utm_source=openai))  Italy/Southern Europe assignment and classification as re-occurrence (not first detection) follow national Q fever histories; no evidence suggests inter‑ or intra‑continental emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Query fever
Host: Flocks of sheep and goats grazing in and around town, humans (urban residents and nearby villagers)
Event.summary: From early May to early June 2004, the town of Botevgrad (Sofia district, western Bulgaria) experienced a large Q fever outbreak with 220 clinically and serologically confirmed human cases, producing attack rates of about 8 per 1,000 inhabitants in the town. Most patients had no direct contact with livestock, but flocks of sheep and goats routinely grazed along roads and in gardens within and around Botevgrad, and a major dust storm early in May likely dispersed contaminated particles over residential areas. Following public‑health advisories, restriction of small-ruminant grazing inside town limits, and the natural end of the lambing season, incidence fell and the urban epidemic was considered over by mid‑June.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High densities of sheep and goats grazing and lambing in and around an urban municipality, combined with a documented dust storm, created conditions for long-range airborne spread of C. burnetii from infected small ruminants into the town; most cases occurred in people without occupational animal contact.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/26331870_An_outbreak_of_Q_fever_in_Bulgaria?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: no novel strain or host expansion was reported; the event represents a dramatic re-occurrence of Q fever in an already endemic Bulgarian focus driven by land use and meteorological conditions.
Review: retain – Added as a new major event because the Botevgrad 2004 outbreak (220 cases) is described as Bulgaria’s largest Q fever epidemic in the preceding decades and is widely cited in comparative European analyses.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/26331870_An_outbreak_of_Q_fever_in_Bulgaria?utm_source=openai))  Bulgaria/Eastern Europe classification and 2004 timing are consistent with outbreak reports; re-occurrence is appropriate as the region had long-standing Q fever activity and this episode did not involve spread to a new continent or subregion.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Query fever
Host: Domestic sheep (flock grazing and lambing near town), humans (nearby residents and exposed persons)
Event.summary: In June 2005, a large Q fever outbreak was identified in the Jena suburb of Winzerla, Germany, when residents living adjacent to a meadow developed febrile respiratory illness later confirmed as C. burnetii infection. Investigation traced the source to an infected flock of sheep that had been grazing and lambing on pasture bordering residential areas, leading to massive environmental contamination with birth products, dust and aerosols carrying the bacterium, and a total of 331 human cases were reported. After removal or relocation of the flock, environmental decontamination and public health messaging, the outbreak declined and new cases subsided.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density sheep grazing and lambing very close to a suburban residential area, combined with dry and windy conditions, enabled windborne dispersal of contaminated aerosols over the town; lack of prior awareness of Q fever risk in suburban sheep farming allowed this practice to continue until after the outbreak. Internal mechanisms: no novel strain, resistance, or host expansion was reported; the event reflects re-occurrence driven by environmental exposure and land‑use patterns rather than pathogen evolution.
Review: retain – This row is consistent with detailed German reports describing the 2005 Jena-Winzerla outbreak (331 reported cases) as one of the largest Q fever epidemics in Europe, with sheep grazing and lambing immediately adjacent to housing as the main driver.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2870892/?utm_source=openai))  Continent/subregion mapping and classification as re-occurrence are appropriate; no corrections needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Query fever
Countries: Israel [2005, central Israel boarding high school]
Host: Humans (boarding high school students and staff); external animal reservoir not fully defined but likely regional livestock or other mammals, with contaminated aerosols recirculated indoors via air-conditioning
Event.summary: In June 2005, numerous febrile respiratory illnesses were reported among 322 students and employees of a boarding high school in an urban area of central Israel, and subsequent investigation identified a large Q fever outbreak that had begun about two weeks earlier. Overall, 187 of 303 interviewed individuals reported compatible illness and C. burnetii infection was serologically confirmed in 144 of 164 persons tested, with risk highest among boarding students and those dining regularly in the school cafeteria. Environmental sampling demonstrated C. burnetii DNA in dust from the dining hall air-conditioning system, suggesting that contaminated aerosols from an external animal source were drawn into and recirculated within the building; after the summer break and cleaning/disinfection of the ventilation system, no further school-associated cases were documented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-density boarding-school setting with shared dining facilities, combined with contamination of the air-conditioning system that likely drew in and recirculated aerosols originating from infected animals in the surrounding region, allowed extensive indoor exposure of susceptible students and staff; awareness of Q fever risk in this fully urban context was initially low.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20415568/?utm_source=openai))  Internal mechanisms: although later genotyping work in Israel has identified local Coxiella strains, this outbreak is not clearly driven by a novel genotype or host expansion, and is best classified as a re-occurrence of endemic Q fever presenting in an unusual urban/indoor transmission setting.
Review: retain – Added because the central Israel boarding-school outbreak (187 illnesses, 144 serologically confirmed Q fever infections) is a well-documented large epidemic and is repeatedly cited as a key example of urban/indoor Q fever transmission.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20415568/?utm_source=openai))  Continent and subregion (Asia/Western Asia) align with UNSD groupings; given long-standing endemicity of Q fever in Israel, classification as re-occurrence rather than first detection or inter-continental emergence is appropriate.

EPP.scientific.name: Coxiella burnetii
EPP.common.name: Query fever
Countries: Netherlands [2005 – first dairy goat abortions; 2007-2010 – large epidemic]
Host: Dairy goats (primary source), dairy sheep (minor role), cattle (background reservoir), humans (large community outbreak)
Event.summary: From 2005, C. burnetii was first diagnosed as a cause of abortion waves on Dutch dairy goat farms, and between 2005 and 2007 abortion storms were confirmed on multiple large dairy goat and a few dairy sheep farms in the southeastern Netherlands. In 2007 a community Q fever outbreak was recognized, which evolved into the world’s largest recorded Q fever epidemic between 2007 and 2010, with about 4,000 notified human cases, strongly clustered around intensive dairy goat farms with abortion problems and PCR‑positive bulk tank milk. After 2009–2010, a comprehensive control programme including mandatory vaccination of dairy goats and dairy sheep, movement restrictions, bulk tank milk PCR surveillance, and culling of pregnant animals on infected farms led to steep declines in both animal shedding and human cases, and the epidemic was brought under control by around 2011–2012, though endemic circulation in livestock persisted at lower levels.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of the Dutch dairy goat sector following changes in European cattle milk quotas and prior livestock disease crises led to very large herds kept in close confinement, often near densely populated villages; high stocking density and concentrated kidding seasons resulted in massive environmental contamination with C. burnetii in barns and surrounding areas; low baseline human seroprevalence created a highly susceptible human population, and meteorological conditions facilitated windborne dispersal of contaminated aerosols into nearby communities. Internal mechanisms: molecular typing showed that a single predominant C. burnetii genotype was responsible for most cases in dairy goats, sheep and humans in the epidemic area, consistent with a clonal expansion of an outbreak strain with efficient transmission in goats and to humans, representing a re-emergence driven by genotype amplification and enhanced transmission in an intensified production system rather than initial introduction of the species to the region.
Review: retain – This row accurately reflects the 2007–2010 Dutch epidemic, which all major reviews agree is the largest Q fever outbreak ever recorded with >4,000 notified human cases and extensive abortion storms in dairy goats.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0399077X14000535?utm_source=openai))  Western Europe subregion, time span and emphasis on intensive dairy‑goat farming as the driver are correct. Classifying this as re-emergence (clonal expansion of a predominant genotype in an already endemic country) is consistent with molecular epidemiology papers; no corrections to emergence type are required.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyvirus cyprinidallo3
EPP.common.name: Koi herpesvirus (KHV)
Countries: United States of America [2004 – Chadakoin River, New York State]
Host: Wild/feral common carp (Cyprinus carpio) in a riverine ecosystem (Chadakoin River, New York State)
Event.summary: In July 2004, a mass mortality event affecting only wild common carp occurred in the Chadakoin River in New York State, USA, where histopathology and virology identified an unusual CyHV‑3 strain associated with extensive gill and internal organ lesions. The outbreak caused substantial local ecological concern because previous KHV problems in North America had been largely confined to cultured koi and carp rather than free‑living riverine populations. Mortality ceased after the acute die‑off, but subsequent work on KHV latency in wild carp showed that surviving fish can harbor CyHV‑3 DNA without clinical disease, indicating potential for recurrent outbreaks driven by environmental triggers rather than fresh introductions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: presence of CyHV‑3‑infected carp in connected water bodies or culture facilities, suitable summer water temperatures and high local carp densities in sections of the river that favored efficient transmission and disease expression. Internal mechanisms: ecological expansion of CyHV‑3 from cultured to wild carp, establishment of latent infection in surviving wild fish and the potential for reactivation under stress or favorable temperature conditions, making this a re‑emergence event in a new ecological context within an already affected continent.
Review: retain – Event accurately describes the 2004 Chadakoin River wild carp mortality in New York State and appropriately classifies it as a re‑emergence episode driven by ecological expansion of CyHV‑3 into wild riverine carp, with geography and timing consistent with the primary J Wildl Dis report and later latency studies; no substantive corrections were required.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyvirus cyprinidallo3
EPP.common.name: Koi herpesvirus (KHV)
Countries: Iraq [2018 – central and southern governorates along the Euphrates and Tigris rivers]
Host: Farmed common carp (Cyprinus carpio) in freshwater ponds, cages and enclosures, with likely involvement of feral carp in connected river systems
Event.summary: In late 2018, central and southern Iraq experienced a massive die‑off of farmed common carp along stretches of the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, involving thousands of tons of fish from ponds, cages and enclosures. Diagnostic investigations by national authorities and international laboratories confirmed CyHV‑3 infection, and in some reports coincident detection of carp edema virus, in affected carp, linking the mortality to koi herpesvirus disease. The event had major economic and food‑security impacts on Iraq’s carp‑farming sector and raised concerns about water quality and co‑factors such as pollution and parasitic infections. Emergency responses, including culling and disposal of dead fish, temporary movement restrictions and investigations into environmental drivers, helped end the acute mortality, but CyHV‑3 is now recognized as circulating endemically in Iraqi carp farming systems with potential for future large outbreaks.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion and intensification of carp aquaculture in Iraq with high stocking densities, degraded water quality and pollutant loads in the Euphrates–Tigris basin, and regional movement of live carp without robust health certification, creating conditions for explosive KHVD when CyHV‑3 was introduced. Internal mechanisms: re‑occurrence of CyHV‑3 within the already affected Western Asia subregion, with high virulence under warm, stressful conditions and potential interaction with other pathogens (e.g. carp edema virus) and environmental stressors that exacerbated mortality, but without clear evidence of a novel viral genotype.
Review: review – Retain this outbreak as a major post‑2005 emergence event in Western Asia but classify it as re‑occurrence only, since available evidence from Iraq indicates mass mortalities driven by CyHV‑3 (often with carp edema virus) in a subregion where the virus was already present (e.g. Israel, Iran) and does not demonstrate a new strain or fundamental host‑range shift. Summary and impact were cross‑checked against Ababneh et al. 2020 (mass mortality in Iraq), Toffan et al. 2020 and subsequent regional analyses.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Fascioloides magna
EPP.common.name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Countries: Poland [2012, Lower Silesian Wilderness; 2015, Bory Zielonogórskie; 2016, Podkarpackie Province (farmed fallow deer)]
Host: Wild red deer; farmed fallow deer
Event.summary: After a single mid‑20th‑century record, Fascioloides magna was rediscovered in 2012–2013 in red deer faecal samples from the Lower Silesian Wilderness in south‑western Poland, confirming renewed local presence. In 2015 eggs were again detected in red deer in the nearby Bory Zielonogórskie forests, and by 2016 adult flukes were reported in farmed fallow deer in Podkarpackie Province in south‑eastern Poland, with mitochondrial genotyping linking these parasites to central European foci. Together, these findings documented both a re‑occurrence in historical Polish range and the establishment of an expanding second European natural focus involving multiple regions within Poland.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Movements of red deer between Czech/Slovak and Polish forest complexes, trade and movement of farmed deer, and suitable wetland and forest habitats enabled recolonisation of former range and establishment of a new farmed‑deer focus. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion within cervid hosts, with parasites genetically traceable to existing central European populations, allowed F. magna to re‑establish and persist in Polish wild and farmed cervids.
Review: retain – This episode represents a substantial re‑establishment and spread of F. magna within Poland, including creation of a genetically characterised second European natural focus with both wild and farmed hosts, and should be retained. Corrected the emergence‑type classification to re_occurrence only, because it reflects recolonisation and intensification within an already affected Eastern European subregion rather than a new subregion or strain. Manual review is advised to confirm that no additional intra‑continental emergence label is desired at a finer spatial scale (e.g. at the level of ‘natural focus’ rather than UN subregion).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Fascioloides magna
EPP.common.name: Fasciolosis (giant liver fluke; American liver fluke)
Host: European fallow deer (Dama dama) in hunting estates; background wild red deer populations in neighbouring countries
Event.summary: Between December 2021 and January 2023, livers and faecal samples from 72 fallow deer culled on 11 hunting grounds in Arad County, western Romania, were examined, and adult Fascioloides magna and eggs were confirmed by sequencing as the parasite, with four animals testing positive. This study provided the first documented report of F. magna in Romania and completed the chain of Danube and Pannonian foci spanning neighbouring Hungary and Serbia. By the time of publication in 2024, the Romanian focus was recognised as a new national occurrence of an invasive parasite in wild cervids, with concern about further spread into Carpathian deer populations and potential spillover to domestic ruminants.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Natural movement and management of fallow and red deer across the Romania–Hungary–Serbia border region, together with suitable wetland and forest habitats along the lower Mureș and Danube systems, facilitated incursion of F. magna into Romanian hunting grounds. Internal mechanisms: Continued geographic range expansion from existing central European natural foci into a previously unaffected country within the same Eastern European subregion, without evidence of a novel strain or host shift, best fits re_occurrence driven by host dispersal and habitat connectivity.
Review: retain – This is the first national report for Romania and an important extension of the Danube/Pannonian fascioloidosis belt into a new country, directly affecting wild fallow deer populations. Reclassified it as re_occurrence within Eastern Europe (new country in an already affected subregion) rather than first_detection or intra‑continental emergence, and removed re_emergence since no host shift or novel strain is implicated. Recommended for retention as a major event, with manual review to confirm that the national ‘first report’ status is adequately captured in narrative rather than via the first_detection flag.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus caprinae
EPP.common.name: PPR virus, PPRV
Countries: India [1994, first major spread beyond Tamil Nadu; nationwide endemic by the 2000s]
Host: Domestic goats and sheep (small ruminants); limited serological evidence also in other domestic ruminants
Event.summary: From 1994 through roughly 2010, PPRV spread from initial foci in Tamil Nadu and neighboring southern states to become endemic across most of India, with repeated village‑ and district‑level outbreaks and high mortality in naïve goat and sheep populations. The expansion produced thousands of officially recorded outbreaks and tens of thousands of reported deaths, with the heaviest burden between about 2000 and 2007, causing substantial production losses and major constraints on small‑ruminant development. These impacts prompted progressive rollout of a national PPR control and then eradication programme based on mass vaccination, after which reported outbreaks and deaths began to decline, although PPRV remains endemic in some areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth and intensification of small‑ruminant production, extensive movement and trade of sheep and goats (including live‑animal markets and long‑distance transport), and limited early diagnostic capacity allowed PPRV to spread widely before systematic control began; concurrent rinderpest eradication drew attention and resources, delaying targeted PPR control. Internal mechanisms: Circulating lineage IV strains established sustained transmission in large, immunologically naïve small‑ruminant populations, with high intrinsic transmissibility supporting endemic maintenance across diverse agro‑ecological zones rather than any single novel strain.
Review: Retain – this is clearly one of the globally most impactful PPR episodes, with thousands of outbreaks and ~95,000 reported deaths in India between 1995 and 2019, and a major shift from regional to nationwide endemicity.([nivedi.res.in](https://www.nivedi.res.in/Nadres_v2/pdf/Left_bar_articles/5.viruses.pdf)) The start year has been tightened from 1990 to 1994 and the end to 2010, to match evidence that PPR was largely confined to southern India until outbreaks spread northward after 1994 and that the pre‑control high‑burden period runs to about 2010.([nivedi.res.in](https://www.nivedi.res.in/Nadres_v2/pdf/Left_bar_articles/5.viruses.pdf)) One SciDirect citation that referred primarily to Ethiopia has been replaced with the India‑specific Viruses 2021 epidemiological analysis; other sources remain appropriate. Type‑of‑emergence is left as re‑occurrence (no new sub‑region or major new lineage), which is consistent with the definitions. Recommended decision: retain (with edits applied).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus caprinae
EPP.common.name: PPR virus, PPRV
Countries: Türkiye [1999, first official reports in southeastern, eastern and Mediterranean regions; spread to central, Aegean, Marmara and Thrace regions by 2004]
Host: Domestic goats and sheep
Event.summary: In 1999 Türkiye officially reported its first PPR outbreaks in southeastern, eastern and Mediterranean regions, documenting establishment of the virus in a previously unaffected national population within the already affected Western Asia sub‑region. Over the following years, the disease became widespread, with repeated outbreaks in central, Aegean and Marmara regions and eventual spread into Thrace near the Bulgarian and Greek borders, raising concerns about potential incursion into the European Union. By around 2004, extensive vaccination and control measures were in place and reduced outbreak frequency, although PPRV remained endemic in much of the country.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross‑border livestock movements and informal trade from endemic neighbouring countries, together with dense flocks and mixed farming systems, facilitated introduction of PPRV into naïve Turkish small‑ruminant populations and onward spread. Internal mechanisms: Existing lineage IV PPRV strains established in new ecological and husbandry settings; there is no clear evidence that a fundamentally novel, more virulent strain drove this episode, which instead reflects regional re‑occurrence and geographic expansion within Western Asia.
Review: Retain – this episode marks the major establishment of PPR in Türkiye, including spread into the Thrace region bordering EU Member States, and is widely emphasised as a key step in the westward advance of the virus.([fao.org](https://www.fao.org/4/y5932e/y5932e03.htm)) However, under the project definitions, intra‑continental emergence must involve spread to a new UN sub‑region, not simply a new country within Western Asia; PPR was already endemic in the Arabian Peninsula and other Western Asian countries by the 1980s.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6751262/)) Accordingly, the intra_continental_emergence flag has been set to false and re_occurrence set to true to reflect a major resurgence and geographic expansion within an already affected sub‑region. Sources (FAO EMPRES bulletin and molecular studies from Türkiye) are appropriate and retained. Recommended decision: retain (classification corrected; flag for review of categorisation details if needed).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus caprinae
EPP.common.name: PPR virus, PPRV
Countries: Mongolia [2016 domestic livestock in western provinces; 2016–2017 Mongolian saiga and other wild ungulates]
Host: Domestic sheep and goats; Mongolian saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica mongolica); Siberian ibex (Capra sibirica); goitered gazelle (Gazella subgutturosa); argali sheep (Ovis ammon)
Event.summary: In 2016 PPR was officially reported for the first time in domestic sheep and goats in western Mongolia’s Khovd and Gobi‑Altai provinces, followed within months by a devastating outbreak among critically endangered Mongolian saiga antelope and other wild ungulates in the same region. From late 2016 through early 2017, an estimated 50–80 percent of the Mongolian saiga population died, alongside confirmed infections and deaths in ibex, argali and goitered gazelles, making this one of the most severe wildlife PPR events recorded. Mongolia implemented emergency livestock vaccination, strict movement controls, targeted carcass collection and destruction, and enhanced wildlife monitoring; by late 2017 active outbreak activity had declined, although population surveys in early 2018 still reflected the massive saiga losses and long‑term demographic impacts.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction of PPRV likely via cross‑border movement of infected small ruminants from endemic neighbouring regions, combined with close spatial overlap of livestock and wild ungulates on winter ranges and around limited water sources, facilitated rapid spillover and sustained wildlife transmission; harsh winter conditions and nutritional stress may have exacerbated mortality. Internal mechanisms: Genetic analyses show that the Mongolian outbreak viruses belonged to lineage IV closely related to strains circulating in China, with evidence that PPRV circulated undetected in livestock before wildlife cases; this episode exemplifies re‑emergence driven by host expansion and enhanced transmission in novel wild hosts rather than emergence of a distinct new viral lineage.
Review: Retain – this is a globally important event for both livestock and biodiversity, with ~50–80% of the Mongolian saiga population lost and substantial mortality in other wild ungulates following introduction of PPR into Mongolia in 2016.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6924898/)) The event year range has been tightened from 2016–2018 to 2016–2017, reflecting that major livestock and wildlife outbreaks occurred during this period, while 2018 mainly captured post‑epidemic population assessments. The first_detection and intra_continental_emergence flags have been set to false: the event is country‑level first detection within a sub‑region (Eastern Asia) where PPR was already present due to the Tibet outbreaks, and first/global detection occurred decades earlier. Re_emergence remains true, capturing the major host‑range expansion into several wild species. Recommended decision: retain (with corrected dates and classification).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus caprinae
EPP.common.name: PPR virus, PPRV
Host: Domestic sheep (notably Tushuri breed) and goats in affected flocks
Event.summary: In early 2016 Georgia reported its first PPR outbreaks in sheep flocks located near Tbilisi, representing the first officially recognised incursion of PPRV into the South Caucasus and, from a WOAH regional perspective, into continental Europe. Laboratory investigation confirmed infection with lineage IV PPRV closely related to strains circulating in neighbouring countries in the Middle East and Central Asia. Aggressive stamping‑out, movement controls and ring surveillance limited the outbreak to a small number of flocks, and Georgia has not reported further confirmed PPR outbreaks since 2016, although the wider Caucasus region remains under heightened surveillance given ongoing circulation in surrounding countries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross‑border movement and trade of small ruminants, including transhumant flocks moving between Georgia and neighbouring endemic areas, likely introduced PPRV into previously free Georgian sheep populations; gaps in awareness and surveillance delayed early detection but rapid response once detected limited spread. Internal mechanisms: The viruses involved belonged to lineage IV, already widespread in Western and Central Asia; the episode reflects geographic range expansion of an existing lineage into a new country within an already affected sub‑region rather than emergence of a novel variant.
Review: Added – this 2016 outbreak in Georgia was missing from the original dataset, yet it is epidemiologically and policy‑wise important as the first officially recognised PPR incursion into the South Caucasus and the first detection in Europe in WOAH’s regional reporting (even though Georgia is classified under Western Asia in the UNSD scheme used here).([woah.org](https://www.woah.org/en/disease/peste-des-petits-ruminants/)) Because PPR was already endemic in Western Asia, the event is coded as re_occurrence rather than intra/inter‑continental emergence. The event summary emphasises its bridgehead role toward Europe while keeping continent/sub‑region labels consistent with the project’s country table. Recommended decision: retain as a major added event (flagged for review only if a strict cap of 10 events forces trade‑offs with other small but symbolically important incursions such as Bulgaria 2018).

EPP.scientific.name: Morbillivirus caprinae
EPP.common.name: PPR virus, PPRV
Countries: Bulgaria [2018, Burgas and Yambol regions near the border with Türkiye]
Host: Domestic sheep and goats in smallholder flocks; heightened concern for nearby wild small ruminants (no large confirmed wildlife die‑offs during this initial incursion)
Event.summary: In mid‑2018 Bulgaria confirmed several PPR outbreaks in small ruminant flocks in the Burgas region near the border with Türkiye, representing the first recognised incursion of PPRV into the European Union and into Eastern Europe as defined in this project. The outbreaks affected smallholder sheep and goat farms, with clinical disease and virological confirmation indicating local transmission rather than isolated imported cases. Bulgaria rapidly implemented EU‑supported control measures including culling of affected and at‑risk flocks, movement bans, intensive surveillance and zoning; by July 2018 no further cases were detected, and the incursion was declared successfully contained.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction from endemic areas in neighbouring Türkiye via informal cross‑border movements or trade of small ruminants, with local husbandry practices and close flock contact enabling limited spread before detection. Internal mechanisms: Genetic and epidemiological evidence indicates that the viruses involved were closely related to lineage IV strains circulating in the region; the event reflects inter‑continental geographic range expansion into a new regulatory and ecological context rather than emergence of a novel variant, and rapid control prevented broader establishment.
Review: Retain – although relatively small in animal numbers, this event is highly significant as the first confirmed PPR incursion into the EU and into the European continent under the UNSD country classification used here (Georgia 2016 being treated as Western Asia).([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3381390/)) The inter_continental_emergence flag is therefore appropriate and has been kept. The first_detection flag has been set to false, as global first detection occurred decades earlier. The event summary has been slightly edited to avoid ambiguous wording about ‘one of the first events on the European continent outside Türkiye’s European part’ and instead focuses on its role as the first EU/Eastern Europe incursion. Recommended decision: retain (with corrected emergence‑type flag and clarified wording).

EPP.scientific.name: Multiple pathogens
EPP.common.name: Varroosis, Tropilaelaps infestation, Foulbrood (Diseases of bees)
Countries: New Zealand [2000 – North Island; 2006 – northern South Island; 2008 – wider South Island]
Host: Managed western honey bee (Apis mellifera) colonies (feral and domestic)
Event.summary: On 11 April 2000, Varroa destructor was detected for the first time in New Zealand in an apiary near South Auckland, with surveys showing that a substantial proportion of upper North Island apiaries were already infested. Despite movement controls and initial eradication attempts, the mite spread progressively through the North Island and by 2006–2008 had been confirmed in the South Island, forcing a shift from eradication to long‑term management. The invasion caused extensive mortality of feral and unmanaged colonies, major production losses and substantial new management costs for beekeepers and crop sectors reliant on pollination.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: genetic and epidemiological investigations, together with official reports, indicate introduction via illegal importation of queen bees or other live bee material from Varroa‑infested regions, followed by rapid spread through local movements of hives and natural drifting and robbing behaviour between colonies. Internal mechanisms: host expansion from Apis cerana to A. mellifera, high reproductive rates within brood cells, and the mite’s role as an efficient vector of deformed wing virus and other viruses led to severe colony weakening and collapse in the previously Varroa‑free New Zealand beekeeping system.
Review: retain – Corrected the emergence‑type coding by setting ‘first_detection’ to false: Varroa destructor had been recognised and described as a honey bee parasite and was already widespread in Asia, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas before 2000. The New Zealand episode is correctly characterised as an inter‑continental emergence (first establishment in the Oceania region). Timing, geographic progression and impact are well supported by OIE and New Zealand government documents and peer‑reviewed analyses. Event should be retained; no further structural changes recommended.

EPP.scientific.name: Multiple pathogens
EPP.common.name: Varroosis, Tropilaelaps infestation, Foulbrood (Diseases of bees)
Countries: Australia [2022 – initial detection in sentinel hives at Port of Newcastle; 2022-2023 spread within eastern states]
Host: Managed western honey bee (Apis mellifera) colonies and feral colonies
Event.summary: In June 2022, Varroa destructor was detected for the first time in Australia in sentinel hives at the Port of Newcastle, New South Wales, ending the country’s long‑standing varroa‑free status. A large‑scale eradication programme was launched, including statewide movement bans on hives, destruction of tens of thousands of colonies in red zones and baiting of feral bees, but ongoing detections through 2022–2023 showed that the mite had spread widely within eastern New South Wales and into parts of Queensland, Victoria and South Australia. In September 2023 the National Management Group concluded that eradication was no longer technically feasible and agreed to transition to long‑term management, marking the beginning of a new era in which Varroa destructor is expected to become endemic across much of Australia with major implications for pollination‑dependent industries.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction likely occurred via accidental importation of infested bees or equipment despite strong biosecurity controls, with high volumes of international shipping and trade providing opportunities for breach. Before detection, extensive movement of hives for pollination and honey production within eastern Australia allowed the mite to disperse beyond the initial port area, complicating eradication. Internal mechanisms: Varroa destructor’s high reproductive rate in sealed brood, efficient transmission of deformed wing virus and other viruses, and the absence of evolved mite resistance in Australian A. mellifera stocks underpin rapid colony decline and necessitate adoption of intensive miticide and integrated pest‑management strategies as the mite becomes established.
Review: retain – Added this new event to capture the 2022–2023 Varroa destructor incursion and subsequent abandonment of eradication in Australia, which ends the last major honey‑producing region previously free of Varroa and has large projected impacts on beekeeping and pollination‑reliant agriculture. All six emergence‑type fields are set to false because Oceania already harboured Varroa destructor (New Zealand) and this episode represents spread to a new country within the same sub‑region rather than emergence in a new continent or sub‑region; it is also not a re‑occurrence or re‑emergence in Australia, which had no prior established Varroa populations. Strongly supported by Australian government outbreak reports and national media; event should be retained and treated as one of the most impactful recent episodes for this complex.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus medius/giganteus reservoir); occasional livestock contact (e.g. sick cow near index case)
Event.summary: In April–May 2001, a cluster of acute encephalitis cases occurred in Chandpur village, Meherpur District, north-western Bangladesh; retrospective investigations and serologic testing later confirmed Nipah virus infection, making this the first recognized NiV outbreak in Bangladesh. Most patients had close contact with the index case and some had contact with a sick cow, while subsequent animal investigations found serologic evidence of NiV infection in local Pteropus bats, supporting bat-to-human spillover with limited human-to-human transmission. The outbreak ended after the deaths of the small cluster and basic infection-prevention measures were introduced in the district hospital and community awareness increased, although NiV was not conclusively identified as the cause until 2003.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Human settlements and small-scale livestock keeping in close proximity to Pteropus bat roosts, intimate caregiving of severely ill patients in households and limited infection-prevention capacity in the Meherpur district hospital facilitated initial spillover and short transmission chains. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of the NiV-Bangladesh lineage into humans via bat contamination of food or the environment and efficient transmission among very close contacts; no intermediate amplifying livestock host (such as pigs) was identified.
Review: review – Original ChatGPT row incorrectly combined Meherpur (Bangladesh) and Siliguri (India) into a single cross-country event and labeled it as both intra-continental emergence and re-emergence; this row has been restricted to Meherpur only and coded as intra-continental emergence of NiV into Southern Asia without re-emergence. The event is historically important as Bangladesh’s first recognized NiV outbreak but is smaller than several later Bangladesh outbreaks; a human reviewer should decide whether to retain it in addition to the 10 largest events.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Host: Humans (patients, family caregivers, health-care workers, visitors); fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir, suspected)
Event.summary: During January–February 2001, a large outbreak of febrile encephalitis with high mortality occurred in several hospitals in Siliguri, West Bengal, India. Later testing of stored clinical specimens demonstrated Nipah virus infection genetically closer to Bangladesh strains than to Malaysia strains, and most cases had clear hospital-associated exposure, indicating extensive human-to-human transmission among patients, visitors and health-care workers. Transmission chains were interrupted after enhanced infection-prevention measures, isolation of suspected cases and the natural exhaustion of susceptible close contacts, and this episode became the first recognized NiV outbreak in India and one of the largest Nipah events globally.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Crowded referral hospitals, frequent patient transfers between facilities, lack of routine use of personal protective equipment and close contact between caregivers and severely ill patients created an environment conducive to nosocomial NiV spread. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of a NiV-Bangladesh–like lineage into India with demonstrated capacity for efficient person-to-person transmission via respiratory secretions in hospital settings; no domestic animal amplifying host was identified in this outbreak.
Review: retain – Added as a new row because the 2001 Siliguri outbreak (≈66 cases, ≈45 deaths) is one of the largest NiV outbreaks and the first recognized event in India; it was previously merged with the Meherpur event, which obscured its size and nosocomial nature. Coded as intra-continental emergence into Southern Asia with no re-emergence flag, consistent with its timing and genotype evidence.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir); probable indirect involvement of domestic animals and contaminated environment
Event.summary: In early 2004, Bangladesh experienced its largest recorded Nipah season when linked clusters of encephalitis occurred in Rajbari and neighbouring Faridpur Districts, with more than 60 cases and very high case fatality. Outbreak investigations implicated wintertime consumption of raw date-palm sap contaminated by fruit bats as the main route of bat-to-human transmission, followed by substantial household and caregiving-associated human-to-human spread. The epidemic waned after the end of the date-palm sap harvesting season, intensive public-health messaging to avoid raw sap and contact with sick individuals, and strengthened isolation and barrier precautions in local health facilities.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Seasonal harvesting and widespread consumption of raw date-palm sap accessible to feeding Pteropus bats, dense household contact networks during illness and funerals, and limited early isolation capacity in rural hospitals. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of the NiV-Bangladesh lineage with efficient person-to-person transmission; no strong evidence for a major genetic shift compared with earlier Bangladesh outbreaks, so re-occurrence within the same subregion is considered the dominant pattern.
Review: retain – Row updated to include both Rajbari and Faridpur districts and to reflect that the combined 2004 Bangladesh season involved >60 cases and high mortality; event is clearly among the largest NiV outbreaks and appropriately coded as re-occurrence in Southern Asia driven by date-palm sap exposure and close-contact transmission.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir); limited involvement of domestic animals
Event.summary: In early 2007, Bangladesh reported several Nipah clusters in Thakurgaon District in the northwest and in Kushtia/Pabna/Natore and Naogaon Districts, together accounting for about 18 cases and nine deaths. These geographically separated but temporally linked clusters reinforced the pattern of seasonal NiV re-occurrence in Bangladesh’s “Nipah belt” and highlighted the importance of both bat-to-human and human-to-human transmission routes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Ongoing winter consumption of fresh date-palm sap accessible to bats, household caregiving practices with intense contact with severely ill patients, and limited use of personal protective equipment in district hospitals enabled repeated spillover and short chains of transmission. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of NiV-Bangladesh lineage viruses causing severe encephalitis with high case fatality; available sequence data do not indicate a distinct new genotype compared with earlier Bangladesh outbreaks, so this is treated as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: retain – Added as a new row to capture the aggregated 2007 Bangladesh season (≈18 cases, 9 deaths across multiple districts), which WHO-derived outbreak tables list among the larger NiV outbreaks; coded as re-occurrence in Southern Asia without intra-continental or re-emergence flags, consistent with repeated seasonal outbreaks driven by date-palm sap consumption and close-contact transmission.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Countries: Bangladesh [2010 – Faridpur, Rajbari, Gopalganj, Madaripur Districts]
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir)
Event.summary: Between February and March 2010, Bangladesh experienced a substantial Nipah outbreak season centered on Faridpur, Rajbari, Gopalganj and Madaripur Districts, with about 16 recognized cases and 14 deaths. Epidemiologic investigations found that many primary cases had recently consumed raw or fermented date-palm sap, while several secondary cases arose from close contact with severely ill Nipah patients in households or health facilities. The outbreak subsided after the sap-harvesting season ended and after intensified public messaging and infection-prevention measures reduced high-risk exposures.
