Internal mechanisms: Ongoing transmission of NiV-Bangladesh lineage viruses causing severe encephalitis with high case fatality; genetic analyses from 2008–2010 outbreaks show moderate diversity within a single lineage rather than emergence of a clearly distinct new strain, supporting classification as re-occurrence.
Review: retain – Added because WHO- and CEPI-based outbreak tables list the 2010 multi-district Bangladesh outbreak (≈16 cases, 14 deaths) among the 10 largest Nipah events; coded as re-occurrence in Southern Asia with no intra-/inter-continental or re-emergence flags, in line with its epidemiology and sequence data.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Countries: Bangladesh [2011 – Lalmonirhat, Rangpur, Dinajpur, Rajbari and other affected districts]
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir)
Event.summary: In January–February 2011, Bangladesh experienced its largest documented Nipah season, with several clusters of encephalitis in northern districts such as Lalmonirhat, Rangpur and Dinajpur and additional cases in central districts including Rajbari, totaling about 44 cases and 40 deaths. Many primary case-patients reported drinking raw date-palm sap, and detailed field investigations identified extensive person-to-person transmission within households and some health-care–associated spread. The season ended after the sap-harvesting period and following intensified public-health messaging, contact tracing and isolation of suspected Nipah cases through the national sentinel surveillance system.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High seasonal availability and consumption of raw date-palm sap, geographic clustering of bat roosts in the so-called Nipah belt, and close household and hospital contacts with severely ill patients combined to produce Bangladesh’s largest recorded Nipah season. Internal mechanisms: Continued circulation of NiV-Bangladesh lineage with efficient human-to-human transmission in close-contact settings; no distinct new genotype has been defined relative to earlier Bangladesh viruses, so the pattern is best described as re-occurrence in a known high-risk subregion.
Review: retain – Added to capture the 2011 Bangladesh season (≈44 cases, 40 deaths), which is clearly one of the largest NiV outbreaks worldwide and a key driver of enhanced national Nipah surveillance; appropriately coded as re-occurrence in Southern Asia, not as intra-continental emergence or re-emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Countries: Bangladesh [2013 – Gaibandha, Natore, Rajshahi, Naogaon, Rajbari, Pabna, Jhenaidah, Mymensingh and other affected districts]
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir)
Event.summary: In January–February 2013, Bangladesh again reported multiple Nipah clusters across several northern and central districts, including Gaibandha, Natore, Rajshahi, Naogaon, Rajbari, Pabna, Jhenaidah and Mymensingh, with around 24 cases and 21 deaths. As in previous years, most primary cases had consumed fresh date-palm sap shortly before illness onset, and subsequent infections occurred among family caregivers and other close contacts. Strengthened event-based and sentinel surveillance enabled earlier recognition and targeted control efforts, which, together with the end of the sap-harvesting season, brought the season to a close.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Persistently popular consumption of raw date-palm sap in high-risk districts, close household care of gravely ill patients, and limited but improving infection-prevention in smaller health facilities maintained the conditions for recurrent NiV-Bangladesh outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: Ongoing circulation of NiV-Bangladesh lineage viruses with high case-fatality and capacity for limited chains of human-to-human transmission; no evidence of major viral change relative to earlier Bangladesh seasons, so this episode is treated as re-occurrence.
Review: retain – Added to represent the 2013 Bangladesh Nipah season (≈24 cases, 21 deaths), which ranks among the ten largest Nipah outbreaks by case numbers; coded as re-occurrence in Southern Asia with drivers and mechanisms consistent with earlier Bangladesh outbreaks.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Countries: Bangladesh [2014 – multiple districts including Manikganj, Magura, Faridpur, Rangpur, Shariatpur, Kushtia, Rajshahi, Dinajpur, Chapai Nawabganj, Naogaon]
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir)
Event.summary: During February 2014, Bangladesh experienced another dispersed Nipah season with smaller clusters and sporadic cases reported from about 13 districts, totaling roughly 18 cases and nine deaths. Most primary cases again reported drinking raw date-palm sap during the cool months, and several secondary infections occurred among caregivers and family members in affected communities. Compared with earlier seasons, improved surveillance and faster outbreak investigation facilitated earlier risk communication and patient isolation, helping to limit the overall size of the season.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued harvesting and consumption of unprotected date-palm sap and close contact with severely ill patients in homes and local facilities sustained recurrent Nipah transmission in known high-risk districts, even as awareness and surveillance improved. Internal mechanisms: Recurrent circulation of NiV-Bangladesh lineage viruses causing severe disease; no clear evidence for emergence of a fundamentally new viral genotype or host range, so this event is classified as re-occurrence.
Review: retain – Added because the aggregated 2014 Bangladesh season (≈18 cases, 9 deaths across many districts) is listed among the largest Nipah outbreaks in WHO/CEPI compilations; appropriately coded as re-occurrence in a known endemic subregion and helps capture the sustained burden of NiV-Bangladesh in the 2010s.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Countries: Philippines [2014 – Sultan Kudarat and South Cotabato Provinces, Mindanao]
Host: Horses; humans (horse owners, slaughterers, meat consumers); fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir)
Event.summary: In 2014, a henipavirus outbreak occurred in villages in Sultan Kudarat and South Cotabato Provinces on Mindanao Island, Philippines, when horses developed acute, often fatal neurologic and respiratory disease followed by severe illness in people who slaughtered sick horses or ate their meat. Seventeen human cases with high case fatality were documented, with evidence for horse-to-human and limited human-to-human transmission, and molecular analyses indicated infection with Nipah virus or a very closely related henipavirus, most similar to the Malaysia lineage. The outbreak was controlled after cessation of slaughter and consumption of sick horses, quarantine and movement restrictions on equids, and community education to avoid contact with ill horses and bats, with transmission chains burning out once these measures were in place.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Backyard and free-grazing horse management under fruit trees frequented by Pteropodidae bats, slaughter and consumption of visibly ill horses, and lack of initial awareness of henipavirus risks in both animal and human health sectors. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion and amplification in horses as intermediate hosts, with efficient horse-to-human transmission, and re-emergence of a NiV-Malaysia–like lineage in a new country within South-eastern Asia, justifying classification as re-emergence in a previously affected subregion.
Review: retain – Event accurately summarizes the 2014 Mindanao horse–human henipavirus outbreak, which WHO and EID describe as probable Nipah virus or a very closely related henipavirus and which involved 17 human cases; coded as re-emergence in South-eastern Asia due to reappearance of a Malaysia-like lineage with a new amplifying host (horses), and is among the ten largest Nipah outbreaks.

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Countries: India [2018 – Kozhikode and Malappuram Districts, Kerala]
Host: Humans; fruit bats (Pteropus medius reservoir, confirmed serologically); possible limited domestic animal exposure
Event.summary: In May 2018, Kerala state in southern India detected its first Nipah virus outbreak when an index case with encephalitis in Kozhikode was linked to multiple generations of infection among family members, other patients, companions and health-care workers across Kozhikode and neighboring Malappuram District. Laboratory investigations confirmed NiV infection and sequencing showed a NiV-Bangladesh–like lineage, while serologic surveys identified NiV-reactive Pteropus medius bats near the index case’s home. Aggressive contact tracing, strict isolation of cases, establishment of dedicated treatment and quarantine facilities, and extensive community risk communication contained the outbreak within about a month, with roughly 19–23 cases and a very high case-fatality ratio.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Dense and busy hospital environments where the first cases were not immediately recognized as Nipah, close caregiving contact in households, and bat roosts and orchards near human dwellings created opportunities for both bat-to-human spillover and nosocomial transmission. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence of NiV-Bangladesh–like virus in a new ecological setting in southern India with demonstrated capacity for sustained human-to-human transmission in clinical settings; genomic analyses show close relatedness to Bangladeshi strains, so despite the new geography this is best classified as re-occurrence within Southern Asia rather than emergence of a distinct new lineage.
Review: retain – Event correctly captures the size, geography and nosocomial nature of the 2018 Kerala outbreak and uses appropriate sources; emergence coding has been adjusted from re-emergence to re-occurrence in a known subregion because sequencing indicates a NiV-Bangladesh–like lineage without clear evidence of a novel strain, while the outbreak itself is among the ten largest Nipah events.

EPP.scientific.name: Porcine circovirus 2
EPP.common.name: Porcine circovirus-associated disease, PCVAD
Host: Domestic pigs in nursery and grower/finisher units in Ontario and Quebec, Canada
Event.summary: In late 2004, swine herds in Ontario experienced unusually severe PCVAD outbreaks characterized by higher mortality and more extensive lesions than previously typical PMWS cases, soon followed by similar problems in Quebec herds. Molecular investigations during 2005–2006 identified a new PCV2 variant (RFLP type 321, corresponding to genotype PCV2b) that rapidly became dominant in affected Canadian herds and was associated with more severe lymphoid and systemic lesions compared with the previously dominant RFLP 422 strains. After several years, widespread adoption of PCV2 vaccination and improved control measures markedly reduced clinical PCVAD incidence, although PCV2b and related variants remained endemic in Canadian pig populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High pig density in Ontario and Quebec, frequent movement of pigs between herds and regions, and limited prior vaccination created conditions for rapid expansion of a fitter viral variant; concurrent infections and production stressors further amplified disease severity. Internal mechanisms: Emergence and rapid spread of a novel PCV2b strain (RFLP 321) with distinct ORF2 (capsid) gene sequence and evidence of higher virulence—histological comparisons showed more severe lesions in pigs infected with RFLP 321 than with older strains—constitute a clear example of novel strain/genotype emergence and increased virulence; this episode is classified as both re‑occurrence (marked resurgence of disease in a previously affected subregion) and re‑emergence (due to genetic change in the virus).
Review: Decision: review. Correction made: consolidated duplicate Canada entries in the Countries field into a single entry (“Canada [2004, mainly Ontario and Quebec 2004–2006]”) while retaining the emphasis on Ontario/Quebec as the focus of this severe PCV2b-associated episode. Event timing, geography, and the dual classification as both re‑occurrence and re‑emergence (due to emergence and dominance of the PCV2b/RFLP 321 variant) remain consistent with the cited Canadian studies.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Teschovirus aphthovirus A
EPP.common.name: Porcine teschovirus, PTV
Host: Suckling piglets and young pigs on a large‑scale commercial farm in Henan Province
Event.summary: In June 2020, a severe disease outbreak struck a large‑scale pig farm in Henan Province, China, initially affecting suckling piglets, which showed severe diarrhea, lethargy, locomotor ataxia, nystagmus, hind‑limb paralysis and coma; mortality among suckling pigs reached about 38%, which is remarkably high for porcine teschovirus infections. Virological investigations identified a novel PTV‑2 strain (HeNZ1) as the primary etiologic agent, with viral RNA and lesions consistent with teschovirus encephalomyelitis in central nervous tissues and other major viral pathogens ruled out. After diagnosis, affected cohorts were culled or managed with supportive care and strict biosecurity, and the outbreak subsided, but the event highlighted the capacity of emergent PTV‑2 variants to cause high‑mortality encephalomyelitis in modern Chinese herds.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High‑throughput pig production with dense, highly susceptible piglet populations and frequent internal animal movements facilitated rapid dissemination of the novel PTV‑2 strain, while limited prior immunity to this genotype likely exacerbated losses. Internal mechanisms: Genome and capsid analyses showed that the HeNZ1 strain was genetically distinct from previously described PTV‑2 isolates and associated with unusually high mortality, indicating novel strain/genotype emergence combined with increased virulence/neurotropism and effective evasion of host innate immune responses.
Review: review – Corrected the event year from 2023 to 2020 and specified Henan Province as the location, in line with the outbreak description in the original BMC Veterinary Research article; classification as a high‑mortality re‑emergence event driven by a novel PTV‑2 strain is appropriate and supported by molecular and clinical data.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9810521/))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Teschovirus aphthovirus A
EPP.common.name: Porcine teschovirus, PTV
Host: Commercial pigs (including suckling piglets) in western Chinese production regions (Gansu)
Event.summary: In 2022, a pig farm in Gansu Province, western China, experienced an outbreak characterized by diarrhea with high mortality, respiratory distress, paralysis and neurologic signs in piglets, prompting virome analysis of diarrheic samples. A porcine teschovirus strain belonging to genotype 5 was enriched and subsequently isolated; experimental infections demonstrated that this PTV‑5 variant caused severe interstitial pneumonia, watery diarrhea, paralysis and high mortality in challenged pigs, confirming a highly pathogenic phenotype. After recognition of the new strain and implementation of stricter biosecurity and movement controls, the on‑farm outbreak was brought under control, but the episode underscored that highly pathogenic PTV variants can still emerge in modern Chinese production systems.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of intensive pig production into western regions such as Gansu, long‑distance movement of pigs and possibly contaminated fomites or feed ingredients, and high within‑farm stocking densities likely facilitated introduction and rapid amplification of the PTV‑5 strain. Internal mechanisms: Phylogenetic analyses showed that the Gansu isolate shared only about 90% identity with the most closely related known PTV strain and contained multiple mutant clusters in VP1, consistent with a distinct, highly pathogenic PTV‑5 variant; animal challenge studies confirmed markedly increased virulence and broader tissue tropism compared with typical low‑pathogenicity PTVs.
Review: review – Corrected the timing from 2023–2024 to 2022 and specified Gansu Province as the outbreak location, in accordance with the Virology paper describing a highly pathogenic PTV‑5 variant; the classification as a re‑emergent, highly virulent strain within an already endemic continent remains appropriate.([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39798333/))
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Ambrosia psilostachya
EPP.common.name: Cuman ragweed, western ragweed, perennial ragweed
Countries: Morocco [1994, first record near Settat; subsequent scattered records in northern and western Morocco]
Host: Weed of disturbed ruderal sites (roadsides, wasteland, field margins) and some agricultural or peri‑urban habitats in northern Morocco
Event.summary: In 1994 Ambrosia psilostachya was documented for the first time in Morocco near Settat, adding a new country‑level occurrence within the already invaded Northern Africa subregion where the species had been naturalized in Algeria since at least 1918. Floristic work and later syntheses confirm its persistence in disturbed and ruderal habitats, with additional scattered sites reported in subsequent decades but no evidence of continent‑scale explosive spread. By the 2000s it was recognised as one of several alien ragweed species contributing to local allergenic pollen and ruderal weed floras in Morocco, although its documented impacts remain more localized than those of common ragweed (A. artemisiifolia).
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Secondary introduction within North Africa, probably via regional trade, contaminated crop material or movement of soil and road‑building materials, followed by spread along roadsides and other disturbed habitats. Internal mechanisms: Perennial rhizomes and seed production allow small founder populations to persist and expand locally once introduced, but available data suggest relatively limited regional spread compared with major invasion foci elsewhere.
Review: Decision: review. Floristic and aeroallergen syntheses confirm that A. psilostachya was first recorded in Morocco in 1994 near Settat and that it remains present mainly as localized populations in disturbed habitats.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/394998562_Contribution_a_la_connaissance_de_la_flore_du_Maroc_notamment_de_plantes_exogenes_naturalisees?utm_source=openai)) However, Northern Africa already harboured established populations in Algeria from 1918, so the Moroccan record does not represent intra‑ or inter‑continental emergence, nor a clear subregional resurgence. The previous coding of re_occurrence=Yes has therefore been corrected to re_occurrence=No to match the project definitions (spread into a new country within an already affected subregion). Given the apparently modest spatial extent and impact relative to major invasions in Italy, France, Iran and India, this event is flagged for expert review as a potentially lower‑priority, country‑level record that may fall below the top ten global emergence events for this species.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Zeugodacus cucurbitae
EPP.common.name: melon fly
Countries: Mozambique [2013 first detection; 2021-2023 documented multi-province spread]
Host: Field‑grown cucurbit crops (cucumber, zucchini, pumpkin and related cucurbits)
Event.summary: After the first confirmed record of melon fly in Mozambique in 2013, a coordinated monitoring program from May 2021 to May 2023 surveyed cucurbit production areas in several northern and central provinces and found the species established with low to moderate populations across multiple regions. The surveys, motivated by the goal of establishing fruit production areas free of or with low prevalence of fruit flies, revealed that Z. cucurbitae was now widespread enough to pose a serious threat to cucurbit production, given published estimates of potential yield losses of 53–100% under heavy attack. By 2023, the pest was recognized as an emerging constraint on cucurbit production and a risk to trade, prompting recommendations for strengthened surveillance, movement controls on cucurbits and implementation of integrated pest management, though large‑scale population reductions had yet to be demonstrated.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: expansion of cucurbit cultivation in northern and central Mozambique and inter‑provincial movement of infested cucurbit fruits likely facilitated spread from initial northern foci; the lack of prior systematic monitoring delayed recognition of its broader distribution. Internal mechanisms: high fecundity, multiple generations per year and the ability to achieve very high infestation levels in cucurbit hosts under suitable conditions explain the substantial yield loss potential observed elsewhere and anticipated in Mozambique (geographic range expansion – inherent; enhanced transmission).
Review: Review – Retain this as a clearly documented re‑occurrence/reinforcement of melon fly populations in Mozambique following the 2013 first record, with strong evidence of geographic expansion and emerging production risk between 2021 and 2023. Sub_regions has been corrected to Eastern Africa only, as Mozambique belongs to that UN sub‑region in the project country list. Classification as re_occurrence (increasing incidence in a previously known sub‑region driven by external factors) is consistent with the definitions. There is partial overlap with the broader Eastern Africa high‑pressure row (2010–2023); users should treat this as a more detailed, Mozambique‑specific sub‑episode within that wider pattern.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Countries: French Polynesia [1996 (Tahiti); late 1990s–2000s spread to Moorea, Raiatea, Tahaa, Huahine and other Society, Marquesas and Austral Islands]
Host: Mango, guava, citrus, papaya and many other cultivated and wild fruits in orchards and backyard gardens
Event.summary: In July 1996, Bactrocera dorsalis was detected for the first time on Tahiti in French Polynesia, where it rapidly became the most damaging fruit fly species, displacing existing tephritids in many hosts. Over the following decade, the species spread from Tahiti to neighbouring Society Islands and then to other archipelagos within French Polynesia, including parts of the Marquesas and Austral Islands, causing heavy infestations in mango, guava, citrus and other fruits and triggering large-scale control efforts. An initial attempt at eradication on Tahiti and Moorea in 1997 was not fully successful, but subsequent area‑wide suppression and classical biological control with the parasitoid Fopius arisanus reduced B. dorsalis populations and fruit damage, even though the pest remains established across much of the territory.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: accidental introduction via infested fruit from other infested Pacific or Asian regions, followed by intense movement of fresh produce among islands and highly suitable tropical climates with extensive mixed-fruit plantings. Internal mechanisms: strong dispersal capacity, extreme polyphagy and competitive dominance over resident fruit fly species allowed B. dorsalis to become the primary frugivorous pest wherever it established; effective adaptation to local host plants and subsequent augmentation by parasitoid releases shaped long-term population dynamics rather than obvious emergence of novel genotypes. (Based on Pacific fruit-fly management syntheses and EPPO distribution data for French Polynesia.)
Review: review – New major event added for the invasion and spread of B. dorsalis in French Polynesia beginning in 1996, which is widely recognised as a devastating Pacific outbreak and a key source for regional biological-control case studies. Classified as intra-continental emergence because it represents first establishment in the Polynesia sub-region, after earlier presence in Micronesian islands. Timing and archipelago sequence are based on South Pacific Commission reports, EPPO distribution data and Pacific area-wide management literature and should be checked against primary island-level pest reports for finer dating.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Countries: South Africa [2010 onward; initially Limpopo Province with subsequent spread to additional districts]
Host: Citrus, mango, guava and other commercial and backyard fruit crops
Event.summary: Following several years of concern after B. dorsalis invaded East Africa, the species was first detected in methyl-eugenol traps near the Zimbabwe border in Limpopo Province, South Africa, in 2010, representing its arrival in a major temperate–subtropical fruit export economy at the southern edge of its African range. Initial eradication actions removed some local populations, but further detections in Limpopo and later in other provinces (e.g. parts of Mpumalanga, North West and Gauteng) showed ongoing reintroductions and gradual establishment in key citrus and mango regions despite intensive control. By around the mid‑2010s, official reports described B. dorsalis as present but under official control and restricted mainly to northern and north-eastern production areas, where it continues to pose a serious threat to export markets and requires permanent surveillance and area‑wide management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: southward spread of the African invasion front via movement of infested fruit from neighbouring countries, long-distance overland transport networks, and dense commercial orchards providing abundant hosts in a high-value export sector, together with climatic suitability in lowland subtropical zones. Internal mechanisms: typical B. dorsalis traits of high fecundity, broad host range and strong dispersal allow repeated reintroductions to found transient or semi-permanent populations in the Southern Africa sub-region; however, there is no clear evidence of major genetic change relative to earlier African populations, and the event is best interpreted as re-occurrence driven by propagule pressure rather than intrinsic evolutionary shifts. (Based on IPPC pest reports, EPPO distribution data and South African entomological studies.)
Review: review – Event retained as a distinct, high-impact episode in South Africa but reclassified as re-occurrence within the Southern Africa sub-region. B. dorsalis was already present in the Southern Africa sub-region (e.g. Namibia, Zimbabwe, Zambia) when first detected in South Africa in 2010, so it should not be coded as intra-continental emergence for the continent. Re_occurrence captures repeated detections and partial establishment in a previously affected sub-region driven by movement of infested fruit and trade. Dates, locations and status are consistent with IPPC and EPPO records and South African literature, but the end year of 2015 is approximate and could be updated to reflect more recent official pest-status changes.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bemisia tabaci
EPP.common.name: sweetpotato whitefly
Host: vegetables (tomato, eggplant, pepper), cotton, ornamentals
Event.summary: Bemisia tabaci was known from China since the 1940s but remained minor until introduction of the invasive MEAM1 (B) biotype in the 1990s, after which it became a significant pest; in 2003, the MED (Q) biotype was first detected in Yunnan Province and by 2005 it had invaded Jiangsu and other eastern regions. Between 2005 and 2008 MED rapidly established and displaced MEAM1 across much of Jiangsu, leading to severe infestations and virus problems on vegetables and cotton. Over the subsequent decade MED became the dominant cryptic species in many Chinese cropping systems, forcing repeated adjustments in insecticide and resistance‑management strategies.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of protected vegetable production, intensive insecticide use, and large-scale movement of planting material and ornamentals across provinces favoured introduction and spread of MED. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence (MED cryptic species) with strong insecticide resistance, higher fitness under chemical control regimes, and competitive superiority that allowed rapid displacement of MEAM1, as well as enhanced vector competence for begomoviruses.
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia serpens
EPP.common.name: serpent spurge, matted sandmat
Countries: China [1991 – first published records from Shanghai and Jiangsu; later widespread along roadsides and coastal sands in eastern mainland China and in Taiwan, where by the 2000s it was deliberately planted as orchard ground cover in pomelo and other citrus orchards in Tainan and nearby districts]
Host: Weed of sandy roadsides and coastal habitats in eastern China; deliberately managed ground‑cover and self‑sown weed in citrus and other orchards, melon fields and lowland farmland in the Taiwan region
Event.summary: Around 1991 Euphorbia serpens was reported for the first time from China, as a weed of open ground in Shanghai and Jiangsu Province, marking its arrival in the Eastern Asia subregion after earlier introductions elsewhere in Asia.([rheedea.in](https://rheedea.in/storages/submission/file/1297225154.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Subsequent floristic treatments and national databases describe the species as an American alien that has recently naturalized in western Taiwan and in lowland eastern China, where it occupies sandy roadside and coastal habitats.([tai2.ntu.edu.tw](https://tai2.ntu.edu.tw/species/415%20008%2009%200?utm_source=openai)) From the 2000s, Taiwanese agronomic extension materials promoted “匍根大戟” (E. serpens) as a low‑growing, easily managed ground‑cover in citrus and other orchards, especially in Tainan’s Madou district, and documented its rapid spread to near‑complete soil cover in some groves.([kmweb.moa.gov.tw](https://kmweb.moa.gov.tw/subject/subject.php?id=6274))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑distance introduction via contaminated seed, planting material and soil associated with trade, followed by regional promotion of grass‑covered orchards and reduced herbicide use in Taiwan, created strong propagule pressure and favorable management conditions for E. serpens in Eastern Asia.([rheedea.in](https://rheedea.in/storages/submission/file/1297225154.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Internal mechanisms: the species’ ability to root at stem nodes, its extremely low stature, rapid clonal and seed reproduction, and tolerance of trampling, drought and heat make it well suited both as a spontaneous weed in sandy coastal and roadside habitats and as a deliberately managed ground‑cover under tree crops, enabling substantial geographic and ecological range expansion without evidence of novel genotypes.
Review: review – New event added. It synthesizes the first published records of E. serpens in mainland China (Shanghai and Jiangsu in 1991) with evidence that the species has recently naturalized in Taiwan and is now widely used as a deliberate ground‑cover in citrus orchards. I classify it as 'intra_continental_emergence = true' because it represents spread of an already Asian alien into the Eastern Asia subregion and into new agro‑ecosystems. Exact arrival dates in Taiwan precede 1990 but the main agronomic adoption clearly intensified after 2000; users may wish to refine the start/end years based on additional regional data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine indica
EPP.common.name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Countries: Mexico [2016 – Veracruz and Puebla citrus region]
Host: Persian lime and orange citrus groves
Event.summary: Between roughly 2010 and 2016, intensive glyphosate use (3–4 applications per year for 15+ years) in Persian lime and orange groves in the Gulf of Mexico citrus region selected Eleusine indica populations with reduced glyphosate susceptibility, culminating in the first confirmed glyphosate‑resistant goosegrass in Mexico around 2016. Detailed physiological and molecular work on biotypes from Persian lime and orange groves in Martínez de la Torre, Veracruz, showed that resistant populations combined an EPSPS Pro106Ser mutation with EPSPS overexpression and reduced glyphosate translocation, giving resistance indices up to ~16 compared with susceptible biotypes. Subsequent management and economic analyses in nearby Persian lime groves documented that glyphosate‑resistant weeds (including goosegrass) substantially increased herbicide costs and forced growers to adopt alternative programmes based on glufosinate and residual herbicides, making this one of the most impactful Eleusine indica resistance episodes in Latin American perennial crops.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term near-exclusive use of glyphosate in Persian lime and orange groves in Veracruz and Puebla (4–6 applications per year at 720–1080 g ae ha−1) with little rotation of modes of action; economic incentives favouring cheap glyphosate over more expensive residual or diversified programmes; high perennial-crop value and year‑round groundcover producing continuous weed selection. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via an EPSPS Pro106Ser target‑site mutation plus EPSPS overexpression and non‑target‑site reduced translocation, conferring moderate‑to‑high glyphosate resistance in multiple goosegrass biotypes; Enhanced Transmission through seed dispersal within citrus orchards and along farm tracks.
Review: Decision: review – This new event was added because glyphosate-resistant Eleusine indica in Mexican citrus groves (Veracruz/Puebla) is well documented mechanistically (EPSPS Pro106Ser + overexpression and reduced translocation) and economically (resistant weeds significantly increase weed-control costs), and likely ranks among the top global Eleusine indica emergence episodes in perennial crops. I set the event window to 2016–2020 (first confirmed resistance around 2016, with management trials in 2014–2015 and ongoing impacts) and classified it as re-emergence driven by resistance evolution; subject-matter experts should confirm whether this timeframe and impact ranking are appropriate and whether to further refine the end year based on newer monitoring data.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Elsinoë fawcettii
EPP.common.name: citrus scab fungus
Host: Citrus spp. (especially satsuma mandarin and other susceptible cultivars in northern Uruguay)
Event.summary: From the mid-1990s, as Uruguay expanded export-oriented satsuma mandarin and other citrus production in its northern regions, citrus scab caused by Elsinoë fawcettii became a major constraint, with field trials reporting that up to 98% of fruit in untreated plots had to be rejected for the fresh market due to severe scab lesions. Intensive reliance on benzimidazole fungicides for scab control selected for resistant E. fawcettii strains, and by the late 1990s benzimidazole-tolerant populations were documented in northern Uruguay, causing frequent spray failures and serious quality losses. By around 2000, adoption of alternative fungicides and improved management reduced disease incidence in treated blocks to below about 1–8%, stabilising export quality but at the cost of more complex and expensive spray programmes.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid growth of export-oriented citrus production in northern Uruguay in the 1990s increased the area planted to susceptible satsuma mandarins and other cultivars, while humid conditions and dense canopies in commercial orchards favoured severe scab epidemics; heavy, repeated use of benzimidazole fungicides created strong selection pressure. Internal mechanisms: Antifungal resistance (emergence of benzimidazole-tolerant E. fawcettii strains documented by Bernal 2000 and cited in EFSA and EPPO assessments); associated shifts in pathogen population structure under fungicide selection pressure.
Review: Decision: Review (new high-impact event added). Rationale: EFSA pest categorisation and the EPPO datasheet report that in Uruguay, up to 98% of fruit in untreated plots had to be rejected because of citrus scab and that benzimidazole-tolerant strains of E. fawcettii were detected in the northern citrus area in the late 1990s, with Bernal (2000) providing primary evidence of resistance and fungicide trials. This clearly qualifies as one of the most impactful post‑1990 emergence episodes for this pathogen. The event is classified as re‑emergence because the pathogen was already present in Uruguay before 1990 and the key novelty is the evolution of fungicide-resistant strains and associated epidemic severity. The 1995–2000 period is inferred from the JICA citrus protection project window and the timing of Bernal’s 2000 report and should be checked against the original proceedings paper for more precise start and end years.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Elsinoë fawcettii
EPP.common.name: citrus scab fungus
Countries: Georgia [2015, western Black Sea citrus belt]
Host: Citrus spp. (mandarin, lemon, orange, grapefruit in western Georgia)
Event.summary: Between 2015 and 2017, systematic surveys in western Georgia documented citrus scab caused by Elsinoë fawcettii in nearly all surveyed orchards and citrus species, revealing widespread disease across the country’s humid Black Sea citrus belt. As the surveys progressed, high incidence and severity were reported across multiple municipalities, indicating that scab had become a major problem in this previously under‑documented citrus area of the EPPO region. Subsequent management actions focused on fungicide use, sanitation and regulatory attention helped to limit further spread beyond western Georgia, but citrus scab remains established there.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Favourable humid subtropical climate in western Georgia, expansion and intensification of citrus cultivation, and historically limited targeted control likely facilitated the build-up and high incidence of citrus scab; improved survey intensity in 2015–2017 also revealed the true extent of disease. Internal mechanisms: No specific novel strain or resistance mechanism was reported for Georgia; the event reflects increased incidence and documentation of existing E. fawcettii populations rather than demonstrated genetic change.
Review: Decision: Review (retain provisionally). EPPO distribution data indicate that E. fawcettii has been present in Georgia since at least the 1980s (CABI Disease Map 125, 1986), with the 2015–2017 surveys showing that the pathogen is now widespread and causing high incidence across western Georgia. On that basis, the episode is best interpreted as a resurgence or increased recognition of disease in an already infested subregion rather than a first detection or new continental spread, so classification as re‑occurrence (with other emergence types set to “No”) is reasonable. However, published sources provide limited quantitative information on temporal trends in incidence prior to 2015, so the extent to which this represents a true resurgence versus improved survey coverage should be confirmed by expert review; no changes were made to the original event coding, but the event is flagged for further scrutiny.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Elsinoë fawcettii
EPP.common.name: citrus scab fungus
Countries: Portugal (Azores Islands) [2021, São Miguel; 2023–2025, additional islands under eradication]
Host: Citrus deliciosa, Citrus limon, Citrus reticulata and other citrus in small orchards on São Miguel and other affected Azorean islands
Event.summary: In July 2021, an official survey on São Miguel Island in the Azores (Portugal) detected citrus plants showing typical scab lesions, and laboratory analyses confirmed Elsinoë fawcettii as the causal agent—representing the first confirmed occurrence of this pathogen in Portugal and in European Union territory. Subsequent delimiting surveys and EPPO reports documented additional outbreaks on São Miguel, and later on Faial and Santa Maria islands, but not yet in mainland Portugal, leading national authorities and the EU to treat the incursion as a quarantine emergency under eradication. Ongoing eradication efforts, movement restrictions on citrus plants, and regulatory surveillance from 2021 through at least 2025 aim to prevent establishment and further spread within the Azores and to avert introduction into mainland Mediterranean citrus‑growing regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via movement of infected planting material or nursery stock into the Azores, combined with humid island conditions and sprinkler irrigation that favour scab development; increased phytosanitary surveillance under EU citrus health regulations enabled its detection. Internal mechanisms: No novel strain or resistance mechanism has yet been specifically reported in this incursion; its significance lies in geographic range expansion of an already cosmopolitan pathogen into a previously unaffected continent (Europe) and regulatory region (EU/EPPO).
Review: Decision: Review (classification corrected). EPPO distribution records and EFSA’s earlier pest categorisation indicate that E. fawcettii was long present in other continents but absent from the EU/European continent until its first detection in the Azores in 2021, and EPPO Reporting Service 2022/021 explicitly labels this as the first report for Portugal and the EPPO region’s second confirmed country after Georgia. Accordingly, the event is correctly an inter‑continental emergence into Europe, not a global first detection. The original row incorrectly set the 'first_detection' flag to 'Yes'; this has been changed to 'No' because first detection in the citrus host system occurred decades earlier in the Americas, whereas this episode represents first detection only in a new continent. Geographic fields (Europe, Southern Europe, Portugal – Azores) and the time span 2021–2025, reflecting initial detection and subsequent outbreaks under eradication, are supported by New Disease Reports and EPPO/NPPO updates and have been retained.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia davidii
EPP.common.name: David's spurge; toothed spurge
Countries: Argentina [1983 detection in Azul district; widespread in central Buenos Aires Province by the 1990s and now present in additional provinces such as Córdoba and San Luis]
Host: Soybean (Glycine max), sunflower (Helianthus annuus), maize (Zea mays), wheat and other cereals
Event.summary: From the early 1980s, toothed spurge populations (now recognised as Euphorbia davidii) appeared in isolated soybean fields in the Azul district, central Buenos Aires Province, and by the early–mid 1990s the weed had spread across roughly 80–85% of the district’s cropland, becoming abundant in soybean, sunflower, maize and short‑cycle wheat. Through the 1990s and 2000s, demographic studies documented rapidly increasing field densities (often 20–200 plants m−2 and up to 300–900 plants m−2) and strong competitive effects, with about 30% soybean yield loss (≈700 kg ha−1) at 100 plants m−2 and significant reductions in pods per plant and other yield components. Into the 2010s and early 2020s, large and persistent soil seed banks (>20 000 seeds m−2) and variable sensitivity to glyphosate have made the species a chronic and difficult‑to‑control weed in conservation‑tillage soybean systems, prompting development of population‑dynamics models to support integrated management.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid expansion of soybean and other summer crops in central Argentina; adoption of no‑till and reduced tillage systems that favour annual broadleaf weeds with persistent seed banks; and heavy reliance on glyphosate in transgenic soybean, which selected for populations tolerant to typical label rates. Movement of contaminated grain, seed and machinery within the Pampas facilitated spread between districts. Internal mechanisms: very large, long‑lived soil seed bank and strong seed dormancy; high fecundity; and high competitive ability at relatively low densities leading to major yield losses. Populations show variable sensitivity to glyphosate, suggesting early evolution of reduced herbicide susceptibility, although fully confirmed resistance biotypes have not yet been documented.
Review: Review – Retain this as the primary high‑impact event for Argentina but reclassify it as re‑occurrence (resurgence of an already introduced alien in the South America sub‑region driven mainly by changes in cropping systems and herbicide regimes) rather than re‑emergence, because there is no clear evidence that a novel biotype or strain triggered the outbreak. The event period is extended from 1990–2015 to 1990–2024 to reflect continuing high densities and yield losses documented into the 2010s–2020s; countries, hosts and sources remain appropriate and the event is clearly among the top global emergence episodes for this species.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia davidii
EPP.common.name: David's spurge; toothed spurge
Countries: Hungary [2011, with farmer reports of presence since 2008]
Host: Maize
Event.summary: In late August 2011, E. davidii was detected for the first time in Hungary in a maize field at Igar (Fejér County), where it had initially been misidentified as E. dentata before taxonomic revision. During the subsequent seasons, surveys and weed‑vegetation studies recorded the species at additional maize and sunflower sites, with ground cover in some maize fields ranging from 0.1% to 30%, indicating substantial local infestations within the national cropping mosaic. By the mid‑2010s, Hungary regarded E. davidii as a newly established but spatially limited agricultural weed requiring monitoring and preventive measures to limit further spread from the initial outbreak area.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: introduction as a contaminant of maize seed or grain, as suggested by the Hungarian plant protection authorities, coupled with intensive maize production and climatic conditions suitable for late‑summer annual broadleaf weeds; absence of early detection allowed the first population to flower and set seed before control was implemented. Internal mechanisms: high fecundity and efficient seed dispersal within fields via tillage and harvest operations, and a life cycle synchronized with maize phenology, supporting re‑occurrence within the same Eastern Europe sub‑region rather than a single transient incursion (Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent)).
Review: Retain – This event accurately captures the first documented establishment and subsequent spread of E. davidii in Hungarian maize fields within the already invaded Eastern Europe sub‑region. Classification as re‑occurrence (rather than intra‑continental emergence) is consistent with earlier records from European Russia and Ukraine, and the sources (EPPO Reporting Service, Hungarian weed‑science article and EPPO datasheet) are appropriate. No structural changes are required beyond noting that farmers reported the weed from about 2008.

EPP.scientific.name: Frankliniella occidentalis
EPP.common.name: western flower thrips
Host: Greenhouse and open‑field vegetables (pepper, cucumber, tomato, lettuce, corn, tobacco), ornamentals and other horticultural crops
Event.summary: Western flower thrips was first intercepted in 2000 on flowers at an international floriculture exhibition in Kunming, Yunnan Province, and a self‑sustaining population was first reported in 2003 on protected crops near Beijing. Between 2003 and about 2010, the pest expanded rapidly from initial foci in Yunnan and Beijing to numerous provinces across China in both greenhouse and open‑field vegetable and ornamental systems, causing increasingly severe damage and virus transmission. By 2015, F. occidentalis was widespread across much of China, with repeated outbreaks on vegetables, ornamentals and tobacco and significant economic losses reported.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10231115/))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: international trade in cut flowers and ornamental plants introducing the pest via Kunming; explosive growth of protected vegetable and flower cultivation across China; human‑mediated movement of infested planting material between provinces; and broad climatic suitability across many regions for establishment. Internal mechanisms: multiple introductions and bridgehead effects producing genetically structured invasive populations; high fecundity and polyphagy; geographic range expansion facilitated by adaptation to diverse climates; development of insecticide resistance in some Chinese populations; and efficient transmission of TSWV and other tospoviruses, amplifying yield impacts.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10231115/))
Review: Decision: REVIEW. Event kept as one of the largest and best‑documented emergence episodes. Corrections: (i) intra‑continental emergence set to “No” because F. occidentalis was already present in the Eastern Asia subregion (e.g. Japan from 1990 and Republic of Korea from 1994) before its establishment in China, so spread into China represents expansion to an additional country within the same subregion rather than a new subregion. (ii) re‑emergence set to “No” because this is the first establishment of the species in China, not a resurgence in an area where it was previously established. The event is now classified purely as country‑level first detection, with regional spread described narratively.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Grapholita molesta
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit moth
Countries: South Africa [1990 Western Cape; rapid spread during the early 1990s to all major stone‑fruit regions]
Host: Peach and other stone fruits (Prunus persica and other Prunus spp.), and to a lesser extent pome fruits such as apple (Malus domestica), pear (Pyrus communis) and quince (Cydonia oblonga) in commercial orchards
Event.summary: Around 1990, Grapholita molesta was formally recorded for the first time in South Africa in Western Cape peach orchards, following an accidental introduction probably in the late 1980s on infested budwood. ([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3889)) The pest population rapidly built up in peach and other stone‑fruit plantings, with up to six generations per year and reported losses of up to about 60% of fruit in badly affected orchards, prompting intensive insecticide programmes and later mating‑disruption trials. ([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3889)) Through the 1990s the moth became established across all major stone‑fruit‑growing districts of South Africa, after which it was managed as a key quarantine and production pest but remained widespread in commercial orchards. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/aesa/article/101/1/197/8488))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction via illegal or inadequately controlled movement of infested peach budwood and possibly fresh fruit into Western Cape production areas; expansion and intensification of commercial Prunus orchards providing abundant hosts; initially limited surveillance and awareness delaying detection until populations were well established. ([gd.eppo.int](https://gd.eppo.int/reporting/article-3889)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) enabling survival and reproduction in Mediterranean‑type climates of Southern Africa, combined with multivoltinism and good local dispersal that allowed rapid build‑up once introduced.
Review: review – Retain as a major post‑1990 emergence event, but the original classification has been corrected: Africa already harboured G. molesta in North Africa and on islands before 1990, so the South African episode is an intra‑continental emergence (new sub‑region within Africa), not an inter‑continental one, and it is not a global first detection. Year, country and impact description were cross‑checked against Afromoths, EPPO Reporting Service articles and the CABI compendium, and event‑specific South African sources were added to the URL list; these adjustments should be checked by a regional specialist.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Grapholita molesta
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit moth
Countries: Russian Federation [2010 Krasnoyarsk kray and Republic of Khakassia, southern Siberia]
Host: Apples, pears and stone‑fruit trees (Prunus spp., Malus domestica, Pyrus communis) in private and institutional orchards, as well as larvae in imported fruit at wholesale markets
Event.summary: Between 2010 and 2012, pheromone‑trap monitoring in southern Siberia (Krasnoyarsk kray and Khakassia) detected Grapholita molesta for the first time in this cold continental region, with males captured both at fruit markets and in orchards and larvae found in fruits. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266737908_Obnaruzenie_vostocnoj_plodozorki_na_uge_Sibiri_Detection_of_the_oriental_fruit_moth_Grapholita_molesta_in_southern_Siberia)) Trap catches and larval findings showed that at least part of the population was completing its life cycle locally, indicating northward expansion beyond the pest’s historical climatic range within the Eastern Europe (Russia) subregion. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266737908_Obnaruzenie_vostocnoj_plodozorki_na_uge_Sibiri_Detection_of_the_oriental_fruit_moth_Grapholita_molesta_in_southern_Siberia)) Following these detections, quarantine phytosanitary zones were established and ongoing monitoring and regulatory measures were implemented to contain further spread and protect developing fruit industries in these Siberian areas. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266737908_Obnaruzenie_vostocnoj_plodozorki_na_uge_Sibiri_Detection_of_the_oriental_fruit_moth_Grapholita_molesta_in_southern_Siberia))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increased inflow of infested fruit into Siberian cities and markets from southern regions where G. molesta is common; gradual climate warming leading to milder winters and longer growing seasons, relaxing thermal limits on survival and development north of earlier range margins. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266737908_Obnaruzenie_vostocnoj_plodozorki_na_uge_Sibiri_Detection_of_the_oriental_fruit_moth_Grapholita_molesta_in_southern_Siberia)) Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) via the species’ capacity to survive at lower winter temperatures than previously recorded; enhanced transmission due to multiple generations in favourable microclimates within river valleys and orchards, allowing establishment from relatively few introductions; practical host expansion from peach‑dominated systems to mixed orchards of apples, plums and cherries under Siberian conditions.
Review: review – Event retained as a key example of re‑emergence at the cold climatic margin of the species’ range, but the emergence‑type coding has been adjusted so that only 're_emergence' is marked 'yes'; 're_occurrence' has been set to 'no' to respect the intended mutual exclusivity of categories (apart from re‑emergence co‑occurring with inter‑/intra‑continental emergence, which does not apply here). Continent and sub‑region coding (Europe/Eastern Europe, including the whole Russian Federation) were checked against the project’s geographical scheme, and the description now explicitly notes that this represents a northward extension within an already affected sub‑region.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Grapholita molesta
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit moth
Countries: Belgium [2021 confirmed male from Genk, Limburg, in a garden‑centre area]
Host: Larvae are expected to use cultivated stone‑fruit trees (Prunus spp.) and possibly pome fruits in gardens and small orchards, inferred from the species’ biology elsewhere; no major damage in Belgian commercial orchards has yet been documented.
Event.summary: Although Grapholita molesta had previously been intercepted in Belgium on imported fruit, its occurrence in the wild fauna remained unconfirmed until a male was reliably identified from a garden‑centre context in Genk (Limburg) in 2021, based on genitalia examination. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/363186555_Interessante_waarnemingen_van_Lepidoptera_in_Belgie_in_2021)) This record led to inclusion of the species in Belgian Lepidoptera catalogues as an exotic with a very limited distribution, indicating that the moth can at least survive locally in Western European climates where it had long been considered absent or extremely rare. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/318221368_Crop_Protection_Compendium_Oriental_Fruit_Moth_Grapholita_molesta_Busck_CABI_Compendium)) Since 2021, only sporadic records have been reported and no major damage outbreaks in Belgian commercial orchards have been documented, so the episode currently represents a marginal range extension rather than a major agricultural emergence. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/363186555_Interessante_waarnemingen_van_Lepidoptera_in_Belgie_in_2021))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Horticultural trade in infested fruits and ornamental or fruit‑tree planting material from regions in southern or central Europe where G. molesta is well established; availability of suitable host trees in gardens and small orchards that can act as stepping stones for establishment. Internal mechanisms: Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) to cooler, more maritime climates and the moth’s ability to maintain small, low‑density populations on scattered hosts, increasing the chance that repeated introductions eventually give rise to detectable local populations.
Review: review – Event retained as the first confirmed record of G. molesta in Belgium but downgraded in emergence‑type coding: Western Europe already had long‑established populations in neighbouring countries, so this should not be classified as intra‑continental emergence, and 'first_detection' is inappropriate because global first detection occurred much earlier; all emergence‑type flags are therefore set to 'no'. The sources from the Belgian Lepidoptera project and Phegea article adequately document the 2021 record; Wikipedia is kept only as a supplementary overview. Given the very limited impact so far, this event is flagged for possible exclusion if future work needs to focus strictly on the most consequential post‑1990 events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera zeae
EPP.common.name: corn cyst nematode
Countries: Portugal [2002 – Pego and São Facundo (Abrantes), and Granja (Coimbra) in central Portugal]
Host: Zea mays (maize); Ficus carica (fig)
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, Heterodera zeae was detected for the first time in Portugal in soil from maize fields and in the rhizosphere of a fig tree in central regions, representing the first confirmed occurrence of the species in Europe. Subsequent diagnostic work characterized three Portuguese populations from two maize fields and one fig tree, confirming identity by morphology and biochemistry and highlighting the species as a potential risk to European maize. The nematode has since been considered present but with limited known distribution in Portugal, and no large-scale maize production losses have yet been documented; monitoring and phytosanitary awareness continue to aim at preventing further spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Likely introduction via movement of infested soil or maize-associated planting material from already infested areas in Asia or North Africa, together with the climatic suitability of Mediterranean maize-growing regions. Trade and movement of nursery stock (including fig) provide additional potential pathways. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was reported; establishment in Portugal represents an inter-continental geographic range expansion of existing H. zeae lineages into Europe, supported by their adaptation to warm summer conditions and ability to persist for years as cysts in soil.
Review: retain – First European record in Portugal in 2002 and its interpretation as an inter-continental emergence into Southern Europe are well supported by the primary description and EPPO records. Countries, sub-region and timing are correct, and no reclassification or source replacement is required.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera zeae
EPP.common.name: corn cyst nematode
Countries: Afghanistan [2009 – Nangarhar Province, five wheat fields with a history of maize cultivation]
Host: Zea mays (maize – previous crop in sampled fields); Triticum aestivum (wheat, from whose rhizosphere the nematode was recovered)
Event.summary: During surveys in 2009 in Nangarhar Province, Afghanistan, cysts and second-stage juveniles of Heterodera zeae were recovered from soil samples collected in five wheat fields that had previously been planted with maize, and morphological and LSU rDNA analyses confirmed the identity of the nematode as corn cyst nematode. This represented the first confirmed record of H. zeae in Afghanistan and extended its known range within Southern Asia into irrigated cereal systems bordering Pakistan. Although detailed data on yield losses are not available, the finding demonstrated that H. zeae had established in local wheat–maize rotations and raised concern about further spread along regional trade and seed/soil movement pathways.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The most plausible introduction pathway is the movement of infested soil or plant material (e.g. machinery, seed lots with adhering soil, or contaminated fodder and manure) from neighbouring Pakistan or other infested countries, combined with the expansion of irrigated wheat–maize rotations in Nangarhar Province. Limited nematode surveillance and absence of targeted control would have allowed the pest to persist unnoticed until surveys were undertaken. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was reported; this episode reflects geographic re-occurrence and range extension of existing Southern Asian H. zeae lineages into additional parts of the same UNSD subregion.
Review: review – New event added to cover the first confirmed record of H. zeae in Afghanistan (Nangarhar, 2009), treated as a re-occurrence within the already affected Southern Asia subregion rather than a new intra-continental emergence. Geographic details and timing follow EPPO GD and Asghari et al. (2013). Because field-level impact is still poorly quantified, this event is flagged for expert review but retained as a notable range extension.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera zeae
EPP.common.name: corn cyst nematode
Host: Zea mays (maize)
Event.summary: In winter 2009, Heterodera zeae was detected for the first time in Greece in a soil sample collected from an organic maize field at Paleochori Kavallas, where previous maize crops had shown stunting and wilting symptoms consistent with nematode damage. Laboratory analysis combining morphological and molecular methods confirmed the presence of H. zeae, making this the second report of the species in Europe after Portugal and extending its known range within the Southern Europe subregion. The nematode’s distribution and economic impact in Greece remain under investigation, and so far the pest is regarded as present but localized, with surveillance recommended to limit further spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction and spread are most plausibly linked to the movement of contaminated soil on agricultural machinery, shared equipment, or possibly infested planting material from other parts of Southern Europe or from infested regions in Asia/North Africa, facilitated by repeated maize cultivation in the affected field. Organic production systems with limited chemical nematicide use may have allowed gradual build‑up of populations before detection. Internal mechanisms: No new strain has been reported; this event is best viewed as a geographic re-occurrence within Southern Europe of existing H. zeae lineages that can survive and reproduce under the warm summer conditions of northern Greece.
Review: retain – Event accurately reflects the first Greek record (Paleochori Kavallas, 2009) and its status as the second European record. Treating this as re-occurrence within the already affected Southern Europe subregion (following the earlier Portuguese record) rather than as a new intra-continental emergence is consistent with the subregion-based classification rules; no corrections needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera zeae
EPP.common.name: corn cyst nematode
Countries: Spain [2022 – Talavera de la Reina, Toledo Province, Castilla-La Mancha]
Host: Zea mays (maize)
Event.summary: In autumn 2022, Heterodera zeae was detected for the first time in Spain in a commercial maize field near Talavera de la Reina (Toledo, Castilla-La Mancha) during a targeted survey for maize-parasitic nematodes, where affected plants were noticeably stunted. Morphological and molecular analyses confirmed the nematode as H. zeae, leading to its official recognition in 2023 as a new record for Spain and an additional occurrence within Southern Europe. The infested field is under monitoring and phytosanitary scrutiny, and while broader distribution or large-scale yield losses in Spain have not yet been documented, the finding has prompted recommendations for surveys and hygiene measures to prevent further spread into other maize-growing areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: The introduction to Spain is most likely linked to movement of infested soil or maize-related planting material (seed lots with adhering soil, contaminated machinery, or possibly soil on traded commodities) from other H. zeae-infested regions, facilitated by intensive maize production and repeated cropping in central-western Spain. The field’s warm summer climate and maize monoculture favored undetected build‑up of cyst populations prior to the survey. Internal mechanisms: No new virulent strain was reported; the event reflects further geographic re-occurrence of H. zeae within the already affected Southern Europe subregion, with spread driven mainly by anthropogenic movement of infested soil and the nematode’s inherent ability to persist in warm soils as long-lived cysts.
Review: retain – Event faithfully reflects the first Spanish record (Talavera de la Reina, 2022; reported 2023) and treats it as a re-occurrence within Southern Europe rather than a separate intra-continental emergence, in line with the subregion-based scheme already used for Portugal and Greece. Sources and geographic details are appropriate; no corrections required.

EPP.scientific.name: Balamuthia mandrillaris
EPP.common.name: granulomatous amebic encephalitis
Sub.regions: South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Eastern Asia
Countries: Thailand [2004 – first recognized Southeast Asian case]
Host: Humans, including children and adults, often with chronic facial or limb skin lesions or sinus involvement preceding CNS disease.
Event.summary: From the mid‑1990s onward, Balamuthia mandrillaris infections were reported from several parts of Asia, including Japan and India, indicating that the pathogen was present in both temperate and tropical Asian environments. In 2002, China documented its earliest known Balamuthia infection, and in 2004 Thailand reported the first recognized Southeast Asian case, followed by additional sporadic cases over the remainder of the decade. By around 2010, Balamuthia had been recognized across multiple Asian subregions, though reports remained sporadic and case‑fatality rates exceeded 90%.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of advanced neuroimaging, neurosurgery, histopathology and molecular diagnostics in large Asian referral hospitals enabled recognition of Balamuthia among patients with previously unexplained brain lesions or chronic granulomatous skin disease; widespread environmental contact with soil and dust in agricultural and peri‑urban settings likely provided exposure opportunities. Internal mechanisms: No consistent evidence supports a distinct Asian lineage or novel virulence trait; the pattern is compatible with long‑standing environmental presence and rare opportunistic human infection that became visible as diagnostic capacity improved, i.e. documentation of geographic range rather than de novo evolutionary expansion.
Review: review – This remains the appropriate inter‑continental emergence episode for Asia, but the original row placed the first Thai case around 2001–2002 and implied Asian cases started only in the early 2000s. Published reports show that Japan and India had cases by the mid‑to‑late 1990s and that the first clearly documented Southeast Asian case from Thailand was in 2004. The event window has been widened to 1993–2010 (matching CDC’s statement that Asian cases have been reported since 1993), country annotations have been adjusted accordingly, and the inter‑continental emergence classification remains justified.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Borrelia miyamotoi
EPP.common.name: Borrelia miyamotoi disease
Countries: Austria [2018, imported infection after tick bite in the United States]
Host: Humans (immunocompromised and immunocompetent patients with tick exposure in Western and Northern Europe)
Event.summary: Following the Dutch index case, multiple countries in Western and Northern Europe reported autochthonous Borrelia miyamotoi disease between about 2015 and 2018, including neuroborreliosis-like CNS infections in Germany and Sweden and increasing numbers of systemic cases in France. A large French study of 824 patients with persistent polymorphic symptoms after tick bites identified 43 with B. miyamotoi DNA in blood, while additional single cases were documented in countries such as Norway and Poland and in Austria (where a European-type strain was detected in a patient reporting a tick bite in the United States). Together, these reports demonstrated that B. miyamotoi was widely established in Ixodes ricinus across Europe and capable of causing both acute febrile illness and meningoencephalitis in immunocompromised and immunocompetent persons, leading several centers to add B. miyamotoi testing to diagnostic algorithms for tick-associated fever and neuroborreliosis.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7059645/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Broad distribution and increasing densities of I. ricinus in Western and Northern Europe; high recreational and occupational exposure to ticks; and rising interest in non-Lyme tick-borne infections that prompted targeted PCR and GlpQ-based serology in patients with compatible syndromes. Internal mechanisms: Stable transovarial maintenance of B. miyamotoi in Ixodes populations and its ability to cause invasive CNS disease as well as persistent polymorphic symptom complexes; the emergence pattern here reflects geographic and diagnostic expansion of existing genotypes rather than appearance of a clearly novel strain.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7827671/?utm_source=openai))
Review: Decision: Review. Clarified that this multi-country episode represents extension of B. miyamotoi disease from the earlier Eastern and Western European foci into additional Western and Northern European settings, which supports 'intra_continental_emergence = true' at the UNSD subregional level. Expanded the country field to indicate that the Austrian case was probably imported after a tick bite in the United States (despite a European genotype) and to acknowledge other Western/Northern European countries with sporadic cases (e.g., Norway, Poland) that are not assigned separate rows. No further type flags were added. Because the included French cohort focuses on patients with chronic polymorphic symptoms and the clinical significance of B. miyamotoi DNA in that context is debated, this grouping and its interpretation as a major emergence event should be reviewed by a subject-matter expert.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Rotavirus spp.
EPP.common.name: rotaviruses
Continent: Europe; Asia; Africa; South America; Northern America; Oceania
Sub.regions: Eastern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia; Western Africa; Eastern Africa; South America; Northern America; Australia and New Zealand
Host: Humans (primarily infants and young children)
Event.summary: After a prototype G12 strain was described in the Philippines in 1990, G12 rotaviruses were rarely detected until they reappeared in 2002 in Thailand and the United States and then spread widely through the 2000s. By the mid‑2000s, G12 (often G12P[8] or G12P[6]) caused sizable fractions of hospitalizations in countries such as India, Hungary, Malawi and several Latin American and African sites, sometimes becoming a leading genotype in single seasons. Around 2010, G12 was established as a globally distributed human genotype, after which its prevalence fluctuated but it remained part of the dominant global genotype set into the early vaccine era.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High birth cohorts and intense transmission in low‑ and middle‑income countries, together with international travel and trade, promoted dissemination from initial foci in Asia to Africa, the Americas and Europe. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence via reassortment created G12 lineages with human‑adapted Wa‑like genomic constellations; phylogenetic analyses show a rapid expansion of specific G12 lineages that mirrors the earlier global emergence of G9.

EPP.scientific.name: Parvovirus spp.
EPP.common.name: CPV, FPV
Countries: Argentina [2003, CPV-2c first detected and increasingly common
Host: Domestic dogs (mainly puppies and young dogs) with severe hemorrhagic gastroenteritis.
Event.summary: From 2003, CPV-2c was first identified in dogs in Argentina and rapidly increased in frequency, becoming the predominant variant affecting domestic dogs there by about 2008. Over subsequent years, CPV-2c was documented in neighbouring Uruguay and then Brazil, where molecular surveys between 2008 and 2010 showed CPV-2c as the main circulating subtype in diarrhoeic dogs, indicating swift replacement of earlier CPV-2a/2b variants. This regional shift was accompanied by widespread outbreaks of severe gastroenteritis in puppies and young dogs and marked a major South American amplification phase of the global CPV-2c pandemic.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High proportions of unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated dogs, especially in low-income urban and peri-urban settings; dense dog populations and informal breeding and kennelling systems; substantial cross-border movement of dogs between Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil; limited early genomic surveillance. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – introduction and subsequent dominance of CPV-2c, which exhibited greater fitness than co-circulating CPV-2a/2b variants in local dog populations. Possible Increased Virulence/Pathogenicity or partial immune escape relative to existing vaccine strains was suggested by severe disease in some vaccinated or maternally immune puppies, although vaccines based on CPV-2b generally remained protective at the population level.
Review: Decision: review (retain event). Evidence from Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil confirms a rapid rise and regional predominance of CPV-2c between 2003 and 2010 with substantial clinical impact, justifying inclusion as a major emergence episode. I reinterpreted the event type from an “intra-continental emergence + re-emergence” combination to a pure re-emergence event, because canine parvovirus had been endemic in South America since the early 1980s and the project rules state that spread of a new antigenic variant of an existing EPP within a continent should not be coded as intra-continental emergence. The time window and affected countries are otherwise well supported by the cited molecular-epidemiology studies, but a human reviewer should confirm that separating this South American episode from the broader 2000–2015 CPV-2c event is the preferred granularity for the final dataset.

In the USA, an adoption-guarantee shelter experienced a 10-month series of confirmed and suspected FPV cases with high morbidity and mortality in kittens, while in north-western Italy a multi-year outbreak originating in a single large shelter generated 177 hospitalised FPV cases over three years and became effectively endemic. Event.summary: Phylogeographic analyses indicate that an “Asian” CPV-2c lineage originated in Asia around 2008 and remained largely confined there until roughly 2012, when it underwent a marked expansion in population size and geographic range. Over the following decade, viruses from this lineage became widespread and often predominant in many parts of Asia (including China, Viet Nam, Thailand, Myanmar and India), and were introduced repeatedly into Africa, Europe and North America, with documented establishment in countries such as Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Egypt, Italy, Romania and Canada. This lineage displaced earlier CPV-2 variants in many settings, contributed to numerous outbreaks and endemic cases of severe canine parvoviral enteritis and further diversified into regional sublineages, representing a second major CPV-2c-driven re-emergence wave superimposed on existing CPV endemicity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Increasing international and regional trade and movement of pet dogs (including import of dogs from Asian countries to Europe and Africa), rescue and rehoming chains, and informal dog movements; sustained pools of unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated dogs in many low- and middle-income regions; urbanisation and dense free-roaming dog populations; limited molecular surveillance delaying recognition of the lineage’s spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence – the “Asian” CPV-2c lineage harbours a characteristic constellation of VP2 and non-structural gene mutations (e.g. at residues 5, 267, 324 and 370) associated with enhanced receptor binding and possibly increased fitness, enabling it to outcompete earlier CPV-2a/2b and prototype CPV-2c strains in multiple regions.
