This row was added because multiple phylogenetic and molecular-epidemiology studies identify the emergence and transcontinental spread of the “Asian” CPV-2c lineage (originating around 2008 and expanding out of Asia after 2012) as a distinct and highly impactful evolutionary episode, associated with replacement of pre-existing CPV variants and large numbers of clinical cases in dogs across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America. Event.summary: Clinical feline panleukopenia (FPV infection) had become rare in Australia by the early 2010s, with no large reported outbreaks for roughly four decades, largely due to widespread vaccination. The timing and geography (eastern Australia 2014–2018, New Zealand 2016–2018, United Arab Emirates 2017) match well-documented large FPV epizootics after decades of low clinical incidence in these regions, clearly qualifying this as a major re-emergent episode. EPP.scientific.name: Sprivivirus cyprinus
EPP.common.name: Spring viraemia of carp virus
Countries: United States of America [2002 North Carolina koi farm
Host: Koi carp (Cyprinus carpio koi) in ornamental/farm settings; common carp (Cyprinus carpio) in wild lakes and river systems; other North American freshwater fishes experimentally or incidentally exposed.
Event.summary: In 2002, SVCV was detected for the first time in North America during a severe outbreak at a koi farm in North Carolina, where about 15,000 koi died and roughly 135,000 additional fish were culled during eradication efforts. In the same year, a major kill of wild common carp occurred in Cedar Lake, Wisconsin, and subsequent detections between 2003 and 2007 included wild carp in an Illinois water channel linked to Lake Michigan, pet and farmed koi outbreaks in Washington State and Missouri in 2004, asymptomatic infected common carp in Hamilton Harbour, Lake Ontario, Canada in 2006, and wild carp in the Upper Mississippi River near Minnesota and Wisconsin in 2007, indicating establishment and limited spread in wild and cultured cyprinids. Intensive surveillance, movement controls, and destruction of affected cultured stocks curtailed further spread in commercial aquaculture, though SVCV persists in some wild carp populations in the Great Lakes–Upper Mississippi basin.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: international trade in live koi and carp from endemic regions, inadequate pre‑import virological screening, and subsequent movement of infected fish within North America facilitated introduction and secondary spread of SVCV into wild and farmed cyprinid populations. Internal mechanisms: phylogenetic analyses show North American isolates cluster within genogroup Ia and are closely related to Asian strains associated with Chinese ornamental fish, suggesting recent introduction from Asia; SVCV’s capacity for subclinical infection and shedding in survivor carp and broad cyprinid host range enhanced its invasive potential in novel freshwater ecosystems.

Host: Mainly corn (maize) and soybean in the US Corn Belt, with resistant populations reported from maize and mixed row‑crop systems in affected states.
Event.summary: In the mid‑1980s, a velvetleaf biotype in Maryland maize fields was found to survive normal atrazine treatments because it could rapidly detoxify the herbicide via enhanced glutathione S‑transferase activity; this represented one of the earliest documented cases of metabolism‑based triazine resistance in a broadleaf weed. During the 1990s and early 2000s, additional atrazine‑resistant velvetleaf populations were confirmed in Wisconsin (1990), Minnesota (1991) and Michigan (2004), indicating that resistance had either evolved repeatedly under strong selection or spread among fields across parts of the US Corn Belt. These resistant biotypes caused localized control failures in maize and soybean, forcing growers to change herbicide programmes and integrate alternative modes of action and cultural controls, and, because the resistant biotypes showed little or no fitness penalty, resistance is expected to persist in affected seedbanks even where atrazine use declines.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Very intensive use of atrazine and related photosystem‑II–inhibiting herbicides in North American maize and soybean production created strong selection pressure on velvetleaf populations that were already widespread and economically damaging, with annual US yield losses and control costs for velvetleaf alone estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars by the 1980s. Internal mechanisms: Evolution of herbicide resistance via enhanced metabolic detoxification of atrazine (notably increased glutathione S‑transferase activity) and associated mechanisms, without a clear fitness cost, led to the emergence and spread of resistant biotypes in multiple US states; this is a clear example of re‑emergence driven by pesticide resistance rather than by a new introduction or host jump.
Review: Review – Added as a previously omitted but well‑documented major re‑emergence event for this species, based on the International Herbicide‑Resistant Weed Database and primary studies documenting atrazine‑resistant velvetleaf biotypes in Maryland (1984) and additional US states from 1990–2004. Classified as re‑emergence (pesticide resistance) rather than first detection or intra‑continental emergence, since the species was already widespread in North American crops. Impact is substantial in terms of control failures, management cost and contribution to long‑term seedbanks, but the exact spatial extent and yield loss remain only partially quantified; inclusion and event years should be reviewed by a weed‑science specialist when harmonising event rankings across species.

EPP.scientific.name: Plasmodium spp.
EPP.common.name: malaria parasites
Host: Humans (primarily Plasmodium falciparum in previously low‑transmission highland and semi‑arid populations)
Event.summary: During the 1990s, highland and semi‑arid districts in Eastern Africa, especially the western Kenya highlands, experienced recurrent malaria epidemics after decades of low transmission, with hospital data from Kericho tea estates showing nearly annual outbreaks from 1990 to 1997, attack rates around 50% and substantial malaria‑attributable mortality. These epidemics intensified in the mid‑ to late‑1990s and peaked during the 1997–1998 El Niño event, when unusually heavy rains and flooding in previously marginal areas such as Wajir in north‑eastern Kenya triggered explosive outbreaks that affected tens of thousands of largely non‑immune people. National malaria programmes and partners responded with emergency indoor residual spraying, strengthened epidemic detection and early‑warning systems, and expanded access to effective treatment, and by the early 2000s malaria incidence and epidemic frequency in many highland settings had declined again.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Climate variability (including El Niño and Indian Ocean Dipole–related warm, wet anomalies), land‑use change (deforestation, swamp cultivation and agricultural expansion), rapid population growth and migration between lowland endemic zones and highland settlements, antimalarial drug resistance (notably to chloroquine and later sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine), and weakening of vector‑control and health‑care systems all increased epidemic risk. Internal mechanisms: No single novel parasite genotype was identified as causal; these epidemics largely reflect geographic range re‑occupation and amplification of existing Plasmodium falciparum lineages in populations with low immunity and failing first‑line drugs, so they are best coded as re-occurrence rather than re-emergence.
Review: review – new high-impact resurgence episode added. Justification: 1990s highland and semi‑arid epidemics in Eastern Africa produced very large attack rates and substantial mortality in previously low‑transmission areas and are widely cited as a key example of climate‑ and drug‑resistance‑driven malaria re‑occurrence. Classified as re-occurrence (not intra-/inter-continental emergence) because Plasmodium falciparum was long established in Africa and no single novel genotype was identified; drivers are climate variability, land-use change, drug resistance and weakened control programmes. Country list and years are approximate and based on multi-country syntheses; should be checked by a human reviewer.

EPP.scientific.name: Plasmodium spp.
EPP.common.name: malaria parasites
Countries: Myanmar [2013, western and northern border regions with India and Bangladesh]
Host: Humans (Plasmodium falciparum with emerging artemisinin-partial resistance signatures along the Greater Mekong–South Asia interface)
Event.summary: During the 2010s, artemisinin-resistant Plasmodium falciparum that had first become established in the eastern Greater Mekong Subregion spread across Myanmar into its western and northern border regions abutting India, Bangladesh and China, with multiple Pfkelch13 mutant lineages documented there by 2013–2014. Subsequent therapeutic-efficacy and genetic studies identified candidate or confirmed resistance-associated kelch13 polymorphisms (such as G625R, A675V and others) and slowed parasite clearance in parts of eastern India and the northeastern states bordering Myanmar, as well as K13-independent artemisinin resistance in Bangladesh’s Chittagong Hill Tracts, raising concern that the historical east‑to‑west spread of antimalarial resistance could repeat. National malaria programmes and WHO responded with intensified molecular surveillance, cross-border coordination, and efforts to accelerate P. falciparum elimination in the eastern Greater Mekong to prevent fully resistant lineages from becoming entrenched in the high‑burden Indian subcontinent.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Human mobility across porous international borders, continued use of artemisinin-based therapies with variable quality and adherence, and the long-recognized pattern of antimalarial resistance originating in the Greater Mekong and spreading westward toward the Indian subcontinent. Internal mechanisms: Westward geographic expansion and diversification of Pfkelch13 mutant parasite lineages originally arising in the Greater Mekong (including C580Y, F446I and regional variants such as G625R and A675V), along with K13-independent mechanisms that reduce artemisinin susceptibility in Bangladesh, represent a re-emergence of multidrug-resistance dynamics at the GMS–South Asia frontier rather than first presence of Plasmodium falciparum in these areas.
Review: review – retain as a distinct phase of the artemisinin-resistance crisis but correct geography and emphasis. Changes made: (1) Sub-regions expanded to 'South-eastern Asia; Southern Asia' and countries redefined to focus on Myanmar (western/northern border areas), India (West Bengal and northeastern states) and Bangladesh (Chittagong Hill Tracts), where kelch13 polymorphisms or K13-independent artemisinin resistance have been documented, rather than implying well-established resistance across all of South Asia by 2012–2014. (2) 'Intra-continental emergence' set to No to comply with guidance that new drug-resistant strains should be coded as re-emergence, not intra-continental emergence; 're-emergence' remains Yes. (3) Time window adjusted to 2013–2019 to better match available molecular and therapeutic-efficacy data. Because evidence for clinically significant resistance outside the Greater Mekong during this period is heterogeneous and evolving, this row should be reviewed by a malaria drug-resistance specialist.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Plasmodium spp.
EPP.common.name: malaria parasites
Countries: Rwanda [2012, molecular detection of Pfkelch13 R561H and P574L]
Host: Humans (Plasmodium falciparum)
Event.summary: From 2012 to 2015, molecular surveillance in Rwanda detected Pfkelch13 R561H and P574L mutations in Plasmodium falciparum, suggesting local emergence of genotypes analogous to Southeast Asian artemisinin-resistance markers; by 2018–2019, therapeutic efficacy studies linked R561H to delayed parasite clearance and ring-stage survival assays confirmed reduced susceptibility to dihydroartemisinin in isolates from southern Rwanda. The prevalence and geographic distribution of R561H increased over time, indicating clonal expansion and establishment of partial artemisinin resistance within Rwanda’s parasite population, although artemether-lumefantrine remained clinically efficacious in most sites. National control programs responded by intensifying therapeutic-efficacy monitoring, updating treatment guidelines as needed, and strengthening vector control and surveillance to track further spread of resistance.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High ACT drug pressure in a setting of intense transmission, possible reductions in population immunity following earlier control successes, and limited capacity to rapidly change first-line regimens or fully enforce rational drug use created conditions favouring selection of resistant parasites. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence of Pfkelch13 R561H and related alleles in African parasite populations, conferring partial artemisinin resistance as shown by delayed clearance and in vitro survival assays; genetic analyses support independent evolution in Rwanda rather than simple importation from Southeast Asia.
Review: retain – event accurately summarizes the independent emergence and spread of Pfkelch13 R561H (and related mutations) in Rwanda and is a key African evolutionary milestone. Dates (first detection in 2012–2015, clinical association and in vitro confirmation by 2018–2019), geography (Eastern Africa; Rwanda), and classification as re-emergence only (new genotype in an endemic pathogen) match the cited clinical, genetic, and in vitro evidence. No structural corrections were necessary, though precise end year (2020) is somewhat arbitrary and reflects the period over which data are available.

EPP.scientific.name: Plasmodium spp.
EPP.common.name: malaria parasites
Countries: Uganda [2016, first detection of kelch13 mutations such as C469Y and A675V in northern Uganda]
Host: Humans (Plasmodium falciparum)
Event.summary: Beginning around 2016, surveillance in Uganda detected multiple Pfkelch13 mutations (including C469Y, A675V, R561H and others) associated with delayed parasite clearance, with some—particularly C469Y and A675V—increasing in frequency through 2020–2022 in northern and south‑western districts. Laboratory studies confirmed reduced in vitro susceptibility of C469Y and related mutants to artemisinin derivatives, and ex vivo data showed decreased susceptibility to lumefantrine in parasites from northern Uganda by 2021, indicating that partner-drug tolerance was also emerging. These findings demonstrate indigenous emergence and clonal expansion of partially artemisinin-resistant and partner-drug-tolerant P. falciparum lineages in East Africa, prompting calls for intensified resistance monitoring and potential future treatment policy adjustments, even though current first-line ACTs still retain good efficacy in most settings.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Wide-scale ACT deployment with limited therapeutic-efficacy monitoring, high malaria transmission intensity, heterogeneous access to treatment and occasional sub-therapeutic drug exposures together created strong selection pressure for resistance. Internal mechanisms: Novel strain/genotype emergence and rapid selection of multiple Pfkelch13 mutant alleles (C469Y, A675V and others) conferring partial artemisinin resistance, coupled in some foci with reduced partner-drug susceptibility (e.g., lumefantrine), representing a major re-emergence of multidrug resistance dynamics within African parasite populations.
Review: retain – event is well supported by genomic and phenotypic studies documenting independent emergence and rapid expansion of multiple kelch13 mutations (especially C469Y and A675V) and reduced lumefantrine susceptibility in Uganda. Classification as re-emergence (without intra-/inter-continental emergence) is appropriate since the episode reflects new resistant genotypes in an endemic parasite. Timeline (from first detection around 2016 through documented spread by 2020–2022) and geography (Eastern Africa; Uganda) are consistent with current evidence. No corrections required beyond confirming that ACTs have remained largely efficacious to date.

EPP.scientific.name: Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica
EPP.common.name: Salmonella enterica
Countries: Mexico [2008 – source farms for contaminated peppers]
Host: Humans (general population consuming fresh produce)
Event.summary: In 2008, a large multistate outbreak of Salmonella enterica serovar Saintpaul infections occurred in the United States, with illnesses also reported in Canada, initially linked to tomatoes and later to imported jalapeño and serrano peppers. From April to late August 2008, at least 1,400–1,500 laboratory‑confirmed cases were reported across 43 US states, the District of Columbia and Canada, making it the largest foodborne outbreak identified in the United States in the preceding decade, before traceback investigations implicated peppers grown on Mexican farms irrigated with contaminated water. Following public advisories, import alerts and recalls targeting Mexican peppers and related products, the outbreak subsided and case counts returned toward baseline.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Complex, cross‑border fresh‑produce supply chains with inadequate hygiene controls at farms and packing facilities, combined with widespread distribution of contaminated peppers and widespread consumption of raw produce without a kill step, allowed a single contamination event to seed cases across much of North America. Internal mechanisms: No fundamentally novel strain properties were reported; instead, the outbreak reflects the high transmissibility of Salmonella via mass‑distributed foods and its ability to persist on fresh produce surfaces under warm, humid conditions (Geographic Range Expansion in food supply chains rather than intrinsic climatic adaptation).
Review: Review: RETAIN with minor corrections and flag for review. Updated 'continent' to include both 'North America' and 'South America' and 'sub_regions' to 'Northern America; Central America', and added Mexico to the country list as the source of contaminated jalapeño and serrano peppers, to reflect that the outbreak involved human cases in the United States and Canada and production in Mexico.([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5734a1.htm?utm_source=openai)) Emergence type remains 're_occurrence' because the event represents a large foodborne outbreak due to external supply‑chain factors in a region where Salmonella is long endemic. Wikipedia is now supplemented by primary CDC MMWR reports and a peer‑reviewed outbreak analysis to better document scale, sources and control measures.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyclospora cayetanensis
EPP.common.name: cyclosporiasis
Countries: Peru [2005, as origin of imported fresh basil used in multiple Florida restaurants]
Host: Humans (restaurant patrons and catered-event attendees consuming dishes containing fresh basil or basil pesto)
Event.summary: From March through May 2005, Florida experienced a very large statewide outbreak of cyclosporiasis, ultimately involving approximately 600 laboratory-confirmed and clinically compatible cases among residents and visitors who had eaten at numerous restaurants and catered events. Epidemiologic investigations identified fresh basil, used in pesto, salad dressings and garnishes, as the common exposure across multiple clusters, and traceback linked the basil to a single farm in Peru that supplied a wide network of Florida restaurant distributors. The outbreak was controlled after implicated basil shipments were no longer in distribution and U.S. and Peruvian authorities implemented enhanced field sanitation and export controls, with cyclosporiasis incidence in Florida returning to its usual seasonal baseline.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-volume importation of fresh basil from Cyclospora-endemic Peru for use as a raw ingredient in salads, sauces and garnishes; use of contaminated irrigation and wash water on source farms; difficulty removing oocysts from delicate leafy herbs by routine washing; and widespread distribution of a single contaminated commodity through restaurant supply chains. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel parasite genotypes or increased virulence; the outbreak reflects extensive environmental contamination of basil rather than intrinsic biological change. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence in a previously affected North American subregion driven by food-safety and agricultural practices in a South American source region, with enhanced effective transmission through a widely used raw herb.
Review: retain: Added this previously omitted 2005 Florida basil outbreak, which involved roughly 600 cases and is clearly among the ten most impactful post-1990 events for Cyclospora. Countries and subregions were set to reflect Florida as the main exposure location and a single Peruvian farm as the basil source. Classified as re_occurrence because Cyclospora had been recognized in North America for a decade and no parasite change was documented; the impact is due to a new high-volume herb vehicle rather than first emergence.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyclospora cayetanensis
EPP.common.name: cyclosporiasis
Countries: Guatemala [2009, as probable source of imported sugar snap peas]
Host: Humans (Stockholm County residents consuming ready-to-eat salads containing imported sugar snap peas)
Event.summary: During May–June 2009, Stockholm County, Sweden, detected an outbreak of cyclosporiasis with 12 laboratory-confirmed and six probable cases among persons without recent travel to endemic countries, representing the first reported outbreak in Sweden and only the second documented foodborne outbreak of cyclosporiasis in Europe. A case–control investigation implicated consumption of a ready-to-eat salad containing imported sugar snap peas, and traceback identified Guatemalan-grown peas as the likely common source. The outbreak waned once the implicated product was no longer on the market, and no sustained onward transmission in Sweden was documented.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growing European imports of fresh sugar snap peas from Cyclospora-endemic Guatemala; minimal processing and frequent consumption of peas in raw or lightly cooked form; routine produce surveillance that did not include Cyclospora; and very low baseline awareness of this parasite among Scandinavian clinicians and laboratories. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for novel lineages or enhanced virulence; the event is best explained by contamination of peas in Guatemalan production or packing environments. Mechanism categories: Intra-continental emergence within Europe, as cyclosporiasis extended from previously affected Western European areas into Northern Europe, driven by globalized fresh-produce trade and environmental contamination in the source region.
Review: retain: Corrected this row to specify sugar snap peas imported from Guatemala as the most likely vehicle, added Guatemala as a source country, and clarified that this was the first outbreak reported in Sweden and the second in Europe. Classification as intra_continental_emergence (spread to a new European subregion following earlier emergence in Germany) is appropriate. Event size is modest but it is important for documenting European spread, so it should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyclospora cayetanensis
EPP.common.name: cyclosporiasis
Countries: Mexico [2013, as origin of implicated salad mix and cilantro]
Host: Humans (restaurant patrons and consumers of bagged salad mix and cilantro across many U.S. states)
Event.summary: Between June and August 2013, the United States experienced an unusually large cyclosporiasis season, with 631 laboratory-confirmed cases reported from at least 25 states, greatly exceeding recent annual totals. Epidemiologic investigations identified at least two major, independent foodborne outbreaks within this season: a multistate cluster in Iowa, Nebraska and neighboring states linked to a prepackaged salad mix containing romaine lettuce and other vegetables imported from Mexico, and a series of clusters in Texas and nearby states linked to fresh cilantro from Mexico served at multiple Mexican-style restaurants. After implicated lots of salad mix and cilantro were withdrawn from commerce and the growing season ended, case counts declined toward baseline.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High-volume importation and centralized processing of fresh salad mixes and herbs from Cyclospora-endemic regions of Mexico; distribution of these ingredients through national restaurant and institutional food-service chains; and improved national surveillance and analytic capacity that allowed linkage of sporadic cases across jurisdictions into coherent outbreaks. Internal mechanisms: No convincing evidence of new strains or increased virulence; the high case numbers reflect repeated contamination events in produce supply chains rather than parasite evolution. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence in a previously affected North American subregion, with enhanced effective transmission via ready-to-eat salads and cilantro distributed widely through industrial food networks.
Review: retain: Minor corrections were made to explicitly list Mexico as the produce source country and to align sub-region coding with the Country sheet (Northern America and Central America). Classification as re_occurrence remains appropriate because large, imported-produce–linked outbreaks had already occurred in North America in the 1990s and early 2000s. This event is one of the highest-burden seasons and anchors the modern era of large U.S. Cyclospora outbreaks, so it should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyclospora cayetanensis
EPP.common.name: cyclosporiasis
Countries: Mexico (Puebla state) [2014, as source of implicated cilantro]
Host: Humans (primarily restaurant patrons consuming dishes containing fresh cilantro)
Event.summary: In the summer of 2014, U.S. surveillance identified another large cyclosporiasis season, with approximately 304 reported cases from at least 19 states, most of them in Texas. Multiple restaurant-associated clusters were investigated in which fresh cilantro served in salsa and other dishes was the only exposure strongly associated with illness, and traceback by state and federal investigators pointed to cilantro grown in the Mexican state of Puebla as the common source for a multistate outbreak involving about 60 cases. For many additional 2014 cases, a specific vehicle was not confirmed, but illness onsets clustered in late spring and summer and case counts returned toward baseline as the implicated cilantro and other seasonal produce left the market.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued heavy importation of fresh cilantro from Puebla, Mexico, where repeated environmental and hygiene deficiencies at farms and packing facilities were documented; the use of surface and irrigation water vulnerable to human fecal contamination; difficulty washing Cyclospora oocysts from delicate herb surfaces; and increasing year-round use of cilantro in restaurant cuisine. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for new parasite lineages or enhanced virulence; the increased incidence reflects recurrent contamination of cilantro and potentially other produce items. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence in a known North American subregion driven by persistent weaknesses in herb production and regulatory oversight in the exporting region.
Review: retain: This new row fills a clear gap by capturing the sizeable 2014 U.S. cyclosporiasis season (≈300 cases) and the documented multistate outbreak tied to cilantro from Puebla, Mexico. It is classified as re_occurrence, in line with similar cilantro-associated events in 2013 and 2015. Numbers and vehicles are based on CDC surveillance summaries, state investigations and regulatory reports; precise counts by state may warrant further fine-tuning, but the event is clearly among the top ten in impact and should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyclospora cayetanensis
EPP.common.name: cyclosporiasis
Countries: Mexico (Puebla state) [2015, as origin of implicated cilantro]
Host: Humans (consumers of restaurant meals and other foods containing fresh cilantro across multiple U.S. states)
Event.summary: In 2015, U.S. health departments reported 644 cyclosporiasis cases from 32 states and New York City, of which about 394 were domestically acquired and most had onset between May and August. Among these, a 61-case multistate outbreak involving patrons of unrelated Mexican-style restaurants in Texas, Georgia and Wisconsin was epidemiologically linked to fresh cilantro imported from the Mexican state of Puebla, and additional clusters in Texas were also associated with cilantro from the same production region. Although many domestically acquired cases had no single confirmed vehicle, overall case numbers again substantially exceeded pre-2013 baselines and declined only after targeted import alerts, field-level interventions in Puebla, and the end of the cilantro growing season.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Ongoing importation of fresh cilantro from Puebla, Mexico, where inspections repeatedly uncovered poor sanitation, human fecal contamination risks, and inadequate worker hygiene; widespread use of cilantro as a raw garnish and salsa ingredient; and improvements in surveillance and clinician awareness that increased recognition of cases. Internal mechanisms: No evidence for a new Cyclospora strain or increased virulence; the pattern is consistent with recurrent environmental contamination of cilantro fields and rinsing water. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence in the same North American subregion, driven by persistent supply-chain and agricultural issues in a specific exporting region and enhanced exposure through high-frequency cilantro use in restaurant dishes.
Review: retain: This row already captured the key features of the 2015 U.S. season, but I adjusted the narrative to align with CDC-reported totals (~644 cases, 394 domestically acquired) and emphasized the 61-case multistate outbreak associated with cilantro from Puebla, Mexico. Classification as re_occurrence remains appropriate, and the event is one of the largest cilantro-linked seasons. Wikipedia is kept only as a secondary synthesis source alongside primary CDC MMWR reports; the event should be retained.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyclospora cayetanensis
EPP.common.name: cyclosporiasis
Countries: Mexico [2019, as origin of basil implicated in a multistate outbreak]
Host: Humans (people in multiple U.S. states consuming fresh basil and other salads or herbs)
Event.summary: In 2019, the United States again experienced a high-burden cyclosporiasis season, with 1,696 laboratory-confirmed non-travel-associated cases reported by late August from 33 states, the District of Columbia and New York City. Within this broader seasonal increase, a 132-case multistate outbreak affecting 11 states was traced to fresh basil imported from Mexico and served at several restaurants, while numerous additional clusters were associated with salads and other fresh produce but lacked a single confirmed vehicle. Although total case numbers did not surpass the 2018 peak, the 2019 season reinforced the pattern of recurrent large summertime waves driven by contamination of imported leafy greens and herbs. Illness incidence declined as the implicated basil and other suspect produce left the market and targeted advisories and inspections were implemented.

Internal mechanisms: No evidence for substantial genetic or phenotypic change in the parasite; increased incidence is attributable to environmental contamination of basil and other produce items. Mechanism categories: Re-occurrence in a known North American subregion driven by globalized fresh-produce trade and seasonal environmental suitability in source regions, with enhanced effective transmission via widely distributed basil and mixed salads.
Review: retain: Added this new row to capture the large 2019 U.S. cyclosporiasis season (~1,700 domestically acquired cases) and the 132-case multistate outbreak linked to basil imported from Mexico. EPP.scientific.name: Treponema pallidum
EPP.common.name: Syphilis
Sub.regions: Western Europe; Northern Europe; Southern Europe
Host: Humans, predominantly men who have sex with men (MSM), including many living with HIV; smaller contributions from heterosexual transmission and congenital cases
Event.summary: After historically low syphilis incidence in Western and Northern Europe in the mid‑1990s, outbreaks of infectious syphilis were reported from 1997 onward, initially in UK cities and soon in Ireland, the Netherlands, France, Norway and other EU/EEA countries, largely concentrated among MSM. Through the 2000s and 2010s, case notifications rose steadily in many Western and Central European states, with particularly sharp increases among MSM and in urban centers, reversing previous declines. Sub.regions: Southern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Europe
Countries: France [2000 – sharp rise in detected cases]
Host: Cattle (Bos taurus)
Event.summary: Around 2000–2001, several EU Member States experienced a marked rise in detected BSE cases, with France seeing rapidly increasing numbers and Germany, Spain, Denmark and Italy reporting their first clear domestic cases, triggering continent-wide public alarm. Active surveillance and mandatory testing of older slaughter cattle revealed that earlier controls had not fully prevented exposure in cohorts born during the 1990s, leading to what was widely perceived as a renewed ‘mad cow crisis’ in continental Europe. In response, the EU introduced stricter measures, including a comprehensive ban on MBM in feed for all farmed animals, systematic removal of specified risk materials and large-scale testing, after which incidence in affected birth cohorts progressively declined.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Partial or delayed implementation and enforcement of feed controls in some Member States; continued cross-border trade in MBM and rendered by-products; intensified active surveillance and testing that uncovered previously undetected infections; strong consumer reaction and political pressure across the EU, which accelerated harmonised risk‑management actions. Internal mechanisms: Re-occurrence of classical BSE in existing European subregions due to residual contaminated feed stocks and exposure of susceptible birth cohorts; no evidence for a fundamentally new strain, but continued low-level feedborne transmission until controls were fully effective.
Review: retain – This row appropriately represents the 2000–2001 EU-wide BSE ‘mad cow’ crisis. The event has been reclassified from re_emergence to re_occurrence, because the surge reflects renewed or newly detected transmission of the existing classical BSE strain in already-affected European subregions, driven by incomplete feed controls and enhanced surveillance, rather than by a change in the agent. The country list and narrative have been updated to highlight Germany, Spain, Denmark and Italy’s widely reported first domestic cases in 2000–2001 and the sharp contemporaneous increase in France, while grouping other affected EU states in a general clause to avoid mis-dating smaller outbreaks.

EPP.scientific.name: Cyvirus cyprinidallo3
EPP.common.name: Koi herpesvirus (KHV)
Sub.regions: Europe – Northern Europe; Europe – Western Europe; Asia – Western Asia; Northern America – Northern America
Countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland [1996 – archival confirmation of CyHV‑3 in wild and farmed carp from unexplained mortality events]
Host: Ornamental koi carp (Cyprinus carpio koi) and farmed/common carp (Cyprinus carpio) in ponds and intensive culture systems in Europe, Israel and the United States
Event.summary: Cyprinid herpesvirus 3 was present by 1996 in the United Kingdom, where retrospective testing of archived tissues from unexplained mass mortalities of wild and cultured carp revealed CyHV‑3 DNA, but the disease was not recognized as a distinct syndrome at the time. In 1997–1998, severe outbreaks with 80–100% mortality in koi and common carp were reported independently from Germany, Israel and the United States, and virological investigations showed that a single, previously undescribed herpesvirus was responsible for these contemporaneous events. Following depopulation, disinfection and ad‑hoc movement controls at affected facilities, acute mortalities subsided locally, but the virus established latent and subclinical infections in surviving carp and, aided by international trade in live koi, seeded further spread to other regions.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: rapid growth of the ornamental koi trade and international movement of live koi and common carp with minimal health screening, high stocking densities and frequent mixing at shows and in holding facilities, and water temperatures in the 18–28 °C range that favor CyHV‑3 replication and acute disease expression. Internal mechanisms: emergence of a novel carp herpesvirus (CyHV‑3) with high virulence and efficient direct-contact and waterborne transmission, the ability to establish latent infections in survivors, and a broad capacity to infect both cultured and feral carp, enabling silent dissemination followed by explosive outbreaks when conditions are permissive.
Review: review – Retain this event as the global first emergence of CyHV‑3 but extend it to 1996–1998 and add the United Kingdom as the earliest confirmed location, based on archival detections of CyHV‑3 in UK carp from 1996 and subsequent mass‑mortality outbreaks in Germany, Israel and the USA in 1997–1998. Updated subregions and country list to reflect UK (Northern Europe) and clarified that this episode is classified as first/global emergence only (not also as first detection or inter‑continental emergence), in line with definitions that reserve the first‑emergence category for genuinely new pathogens in the host system.

Event.summary: From the 1990s through the 2000s, human alveolar echinococcosis emerged in central‑eastern and Baltic Europe and in several western and southern European countries that had previously reported no or very few locally acquired cases, including Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, Lithuania, Latvia, Slovenia, Romania, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and parts of northern Italy. These new human reports coincided with confirmation of Echinococcus multilocularis in foxes and small mammals in many of the same countries, often first detected in the mid‑1990s or early 2000s, while in Denmark and Sweden the parasite was found only in wildlife with no confirmed autochthonous human cases during this period. Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued spread and densification of infected fox populations across Europe, facilitated by rabies vaccination, landscape change, agricultural intensification and high rodent prey densities, enabled colonization of new subregions and countries. Greater diagnostic awareness, improved imaging and serology, and the creation of national and multinational registries led to better identification and reporting of AE cases in countries where the disease had previously gone unrecognized or had been misdiagnosed. Internal mechanisms: The emergence mainly reflects colonization of new geographic areas by existing parasite lineages adapted to fox–rodent cycles; no single novel hyper‑virulent strain is required to explain establishment, though local genotypic differences and ecological contexts likely modulate human risk.
Review: Decision: review – This event appropriately captures the multi‑country emergence of human AE in central‑eastern, Baltic and parts of western Europe and should be kept, but several clarifications were needed. (1) Denmark and Sweden were annotated as ‘wildlife only’ because up to at least 2015 no confirmed autochthonous human AE cases had been reported there, even though infected foxes and rodents were found.([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304401715003763?utm_source=openai)) (2) The summary text was edited so that human emergence is not implied for Denmark and Sweden, but rather linked explicitly to Poland, the Baltic states, Hungary, Slovenia, Romania, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and northern Italy, in line with European registry data and the 2019 global review.([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2958541/?utm_source=openai)) (3) Event coding as ‘first_detection’ and ‘intra‑continental emergence’ was retained because, at the continental scale, these represent new European countries and sub‑regions acquiring documented human AE transmission. Given the complexity of overlapping time windows with the fox‑range expansion event and the core Alpine re‑occurrence, this row should be cross‑checked against country‑by‑country incidence tables before final use, but it clearly represents one of the major human AE emergence patterns.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Enterovirus suid 1
EPP.common.name: Swine vesicular disease virus, SVDV
Host: Domestic pigs (swine)
Event.summary: Following the 2006–2007 epidemic in northern Italy, SVDV continued to circulate at low levels in a few regions of Italy, causing sporadic outbreaks detected through the strengthened national surveillance and eradication programme. Between 2008 and 2015, these residual foci were repeatedly re‑ignited by illegal or poorly controlled pig movements, insufficient farm biosecurity and environmental persistence of the virus, prompting EU measures specifically targeting SVD in Italy and progressive enlargement of control zones. Implementation of enhanced surveillance, trace‑back and strict movement controls ultimately led to the last recorded clinical outbreak in Calabria in 2015, after which only seropositive pigs were detected (until 2017), and SVDV was subsequently declared eradicated from Italy and, by extension, from domestic pigs globally.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: continued movement of pigs from non‑compliant or illegal holdings, vehicles contaminated with manure or pork products, and the virus’s marked environmental stability allowed sporadic re‑introductions into Italian farms despite control programmes; policy tools such as EU Decision 2005/779/EC and intensified national measures were required to progressively close these gaps. Internal mechanisms: no fundamentally new genotypes were identified in this late phase; rather, persistence of existing Italian lineages and their ability to survive in the environment and in pork products underpinned recurrent flare‑ups (Re-occurrence driven by external factors and environmental persistence; geographic spread remained confined to already affected Italian subregions).
Review: retain – The 2008–2015 window, restriction to Italy, and characterization as low-level re-occurrence following the 2006–2007 epidemic are consistent with Italian eradication programme reports and WOAH/EU documentation, which show continued sporadic outbreaks through 2015 and only serological positives through 2017. No structural changes were needed, so this event is retained as-is apart from minor wording harmonization with updated Italy-wide eradication data.

EPP.scientific.name: Foot-and-mouth disease virus
EPP.common.name: FMDV, Aphthovirus
Sub.regions: Southern Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Asia; South-eastern Asia; Eastern Europe; Southern Europe; Northern Europe; Western Europe; Northern Africa; Southern Africa
Countries: China, Taiwan Province of China [1999 distinct from 1997 pig‑only strain]
Host: Cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, and other cloven‑hoofed livestock
Event.summary: From the early 1990s through 2001, a single genetic lineage of FMDV serotype O (topotype ME‑SA, PanAsia strain) that emerged in northern India expanded its range, first spreading across South Asia and the Middle East and then into East Asia, the Russian Federation, and parts of Africa. Between 1998 and 2001 this PanAsia strain caused widespread outbreaks across multiple Asian subregions, reached South Africa, and culminated in major incursions into previously FMD‑free or long‑free areas of Europe in 2001, including the large United Kingdom epidemic and additional outbreaks in Ireland, France, and the Netherlands, with millions of animals ultimately culled and severe trade disruption. Control relied on rapid slaughter policies, emergency vaccination in some settings, strict movement controls, and coordinated international surveillance, after which the pandemic wave subsided although related ME‑SA lineages remain endemic in parts of Asia and the Middle East.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Intensification and globalization of livestock production and trade; long‑distance movement of live animals and animal products across Asia, the Middle East, and into Europe; porous borders and informal trade networks; limitations in regional vaccination coverage and strain matching at the time of spread. Internal mechanisms: emergence of the highly successful O/ME‑SA PanAsia lineage with genetic changes in VP1 and related regions conferring enhanced fitness, broad host range, and strong transmissibility, enabling rapid geographic range expansion and repeated re‑emergence in regions that were previously disease‑free or had long intervals since the last FMD outbreaks.
Review: review – retained as a single linked episode describing the global spread of the O/ME-SA PanAsia lineage from India across South and West Asia into East Asia, parts of Africa and Europe, consistent with molecular and historical reconstructions([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC387408/?utm_source=openai)). Event_year was broadened from 1998–2001 to 1990–2001 to align with first detection of PanAsia in India. Subregions were expanded (adding South-eastern Asia and Southern Europe) to match the listed countries. Event-type flags were simplified to re_emergence only (intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence set to false) because FMDV itself was already established on all affected continents and subregions; the key feature is emergence and global dissemination of a highly fit new lineage rather than first presence of the virus in those areas.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Infectious salmon anemia virus
EPP.common.name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event.summary: From 1996 to 2003, ISA was first detected and then became epidemic in salmon farms in southwest New Brunswick, Canada, and subsequently in 2001 spread to farms in Cobscook and Passamaquoddy Bays in neighboring Maine, USA, marking the first major establishment of ISAV outside Europe. The virus spread through densely stocked sites in the Bay of Fundy–Quoddy region, leading to slaughter of hundreds of thousands of salmon and tens of millions of dollars in compensation and control costs on both sides of the border. Aggressive depopulation, fallowing, movement controls and increasingly strict biosecurity regulations gradually reduced outbreak frequency in Atlantic Canada and Maine, although ISA has persisted at low levels in the wider region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High farm density in the Bay of Fundy–Quoddy region, shared service vessels and equipment between Canadian and Maine farms, and strong tidal exchange created an area‑wide contact network that promoted rapid local spread once ISAV was introduced. Limited early surveillance and gaps in bay‑management zoning delayed containment, and cross‑border movements of well boats and fish further linked Canadian and U.S. sites. Internal mechanisms: Introduction of virulent European‑lineage ISAV to North America (likely via movements of fish or eggs) followed by efficient horizontal transmission; available evidence does not point to a novel North American genotype during this first inter‑continental emergence wave.
Review: review – Expanded this row to cover the whole 1996–2003 Bay of Fundy–Quoddy epidemic, which encompassed both New Brunswick (from 1996) and epidemiologically linked outbreaks in Maine (from 2001). According to the event definitions, this cross‑border, hydrodynamically connected episode should be treated as a single linked event with multiple countries listed and country‑specific start years, rather than split across separate rows. Reclassified the event type so that it remains the first inter‑continental emergence of ISA into North America (inter_continental_emergence = true) but no longer uses first_detection, which should refer to the first global detection in 1984. Mechanism text was updated to integrate hydrodynamic and cross‑border risk factors previously described in the Maine‑only row. The original Maine‑specific row is therefore recommended for exclusion to avoid double counting (see that row’s Review).
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Infectious salmon anemia virus
EPP.common.name: Salmon isavirus, ISAV, Infectious salmon anemia virus
Host: Farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
Event.summary: In 2012, new ISA outbreaks occurred in eastern Canada, with confirmation at a commercial aquaculture facility in Nova Scotia and the first recorded ISA outbreak in Newfoundland and Labrador, each leading to the destruction of hundreds of thousands of farmed salmon. The virus was contained largely to individual sites or local areas, but depopulation orders, movement controls and surveillance were implemented across affected provinces. These 2012 events marked a significant re‑occurrence of ISA in Atlantic Canada, after earlier Bay of Fundy epidemics, and triggered further tightening of federal–provincial fish‑health regulations and ongoing localized outbreaks in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued high farm densities in parts of Atlantic Canada, waterborne spread within embayments, and possible wildlife or equipment‑mediated transmission provided pathways for ISA re‑introduction into Nova Scotia and for first establishment in Newfoundland and Labrador; detection was aided by routine surveillance programs. Internal mechanisms: Re‑occurrence is attributed to spread of existing virulent ISAV lineages circulating in the North Atlantic rather than to a clearly identified new genotype; localized outbreaks demonstrate the virus’s capacity to persist in the broader region and re‑invade farms when biosecurity is insufficient.
Review: retain – The 2012 Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador outbreaks are accurately represented as a re‑occurrence of ISA within a long‑affected North Atlantic subregion, with the Newfoundland event also being the first provincial establishment. Event impact (hundreds of thousands of salmon culled and national regulatory response) justifies inclusion among the most important post‑2005 episodes. Country entries have been reformatted so that “Canada” matches the Country sheet, with provincial detail and starting year moved inside brackets.

EPP.scientific.name: Leishmania spp.
EPP.common.name: Leishmaniasis / Leishmaniosis (animal leishmaniosis)
Countries: French Guiana [2016 emergence of autochthonous canine L. infantum]
Host: Domestic dogs (including military working dogs) as reservoirs; humans at risk for zoonotic infection
Event.summary: In 2016, molecular surveys in Cayenne, French Guiana, identified autochthonous Leishmania infantum infection in local dogs with an estimated prevalence of about 3%, marking the first clear evidence of a local canine visceral leishmaniasis transmission cycle in this previously non‑endemic part of the Guiana Shield. Around the same time, military working dogs deployed from France to French Guiana and tested negative before deployment were found infected on return, further confirming local transmission in South America’s northeastern coastal region. Subsequent years saw continued detection of infected dogs and sandflies, although the focus remained geographically limited, and public health responses concentrated on vector control and monitoring of canine and human cases.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: environmental changes and urban/peri‑urban development in and around Cayenne creating suitable habitats for sandfly vectors; movement of domestic and working dogs between Europe and French Guiana; and limited prior surveillance masking earlier low‑level circulation. Internal mechanisms: geographic range expansion of L. infantum to a new part of the South American coast; host expansion and establishment of dogs as a local reservoir; and efficient transmission via competent local Lutzomyia vectors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11061994/))
Review.Comment: Bulk rejected from Dataset review: Adjudicate category (no Review text, Low confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Host: Domestic cattle; water buffalo locally
Event.summary: In August 2015, LSDV was first detected in the European Union in cattle in northern Greece near the Turkish border, marking the first recognized establishment of the virus on the European continent. During 2015–2017, the virus spread extensively through Greece and into multiple Balkan countries, with thousands of outbreaks reported and severe trade and production impacts. A coordinated mass vaccination campaign and movement controls across the Balkans and EU member states led to a sharp decline in outbreaks after 2017, with most affected countries regaining disease‑free status in subsequent years.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction from the infected Middle East/Türkiye region, likely via wind‑borne or mechanically transported vectors and/or short‑distance animal movements, followed by regional spread under favorable climatic conditions for vector flies and ticks. Substantial movements of cattle among Balkan states and to EU markets amplified dissemination before control measures were harmonized. Internal mechanisms: Viruses belonged to the classical field strain lineage; no major genetic shifts were necessary for establishment, but the virus showed efficient transmission by local vector species, highlighting vector‑adaptation compatibility with European climates.
Review: review – Retained as the first confirmed inter-continental emergence of LSDV into Europe, but the continent and sub-region fields were corrected from “Europe; Asia / Southern Europe; Eastern Europe; Western Asia” to “Europe / Southern Europe; Eastern Europe” because the outbreaks listed here occurred only in European territories (Balkans, European Thrace, European Russia). Emergence-type coding as inter-continental emergence (first occurrence in Europe) is consistent with EFSA and WOAH timelines.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Sub.regions: Eastern Europe; Central Asia; Western Asia; Eastern Asia
Host: Domestic cattle
Event.summary: From 2017 onwards, molecular surveillance in Russia and Kazakhstan identified multiple vaccine‑like recombinant LSDV strains emerging in cattle populations that had been vaccinated with live‑attenuated capripox vaccines. These recombinant viruses caused field outbreaks and then spread eastward, with related genotypes later detected in parts of Asia including western China and Mongolia during the first local LSD incursions. Control measures in affected countries were progressively adjusted, including review of vaccine strains and strategies, as outbreaks linked to these recombinants were brought under better control by around 2020.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Extensive use of live‑attenuated capripox vaccines in settings with concurrent circulation of field strains created ecological conditions favorable for recombination, while large cattle populations and imperfect vaccination coverage allowed onward spread. Internal mechanisms: Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via recombination between vaccine and field LSDV strains led to multiple distinct vaccine‑like recombinant lineages with field‑virus behavior; these represented genuine viral re‑emergence with altered genomes and in some cases possibly modified virulence or transmission potential.
Review: review – Event retained as a distinct re-emergence episode driven by vaccine–field strain recombinants, but the sub-region list was expanded to include Eastern Asia because recombinant-derived strains seeded initial outbreaks in western China and Mongolia. Emergence type remains correctly set to re-emergence (novel genotypes) without marking additional intra-/inter-continental spread, which is handled in separate geographic events.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Host: Domestic cattle
Event.summary: In August 2019, China reported its first LSD outbreak in cattle in Xinjiang, representing the first recognized establishment of the disease in East Asia, followed soon by further outbreaks in Inner Mongolia and other provinces. During 2020–2021, related outbreaks were detected in additional eastern Asian territories, including Taiwan (Kinmen) and Hong Kong SAR, and Mongolia, with trade disruptions and targeted culling in some affected herds. Intensive surveillance, quarantine of infected farms and rapid vaccination responses gradually contained many of these foci, though LSDV has since become established in parts of western China and neighboring areas.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction likely occurred via movement of infected cattle or vectors from Central Asian or Russian foci into north‑western China, with subsequent dissemination through domestic cattle trade networks and communal grazing. Rapid intensification of cattle production and long‑distance transport in China further facilitated spread. Internal mechanisms: Genomic analyses indicated that early Chinese isolates were closely related to vaccine‑like recombinants circulating in Russia and Kazakhstan, suggesting introduction of a recombinant strain; however, no clear evidence of substantially increased virulence compared with other field strains was reported.
Review: review – Retained as the major East Asian geographic expansion, but the country list was corrected: (i) Mongolia’s first outbreak is now dated to 2021 rather than “2019–2020”, (ii) the Republic of Korea was removed because its first LSD outbreak occurred only in October 2023, and (iii) Taiwan (Kinmen Island, 2020) was added as part of this wave. The ‘first_detection’ flag was set to false because global first detection of LSD in cattle dates to 1929; this event is best classified purely as intra-continental emergence into a new Asian subregion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Host: Domestic cattle; Asian water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) in some countries
Event.summary: Starting in 2019, LSDV was first reported in Bangladesh and then in neighboring parts of India, marking the initial recognized spread of the virus into South Asia. During 2020–2021, outbreaks were notified in Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan and Pakistan, with tens of thousands of affected cattle and buffalo and substantial milk yield losses across the region. Emergency vaccination campaigns, movement restrictions and farmer awareness programs gradually improved control by late 2021, though the virus became endemic in many South Asian cattle populations.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Cross‑border cattle trade and informal livestock movements from already infected areas in the Middle East and Central Asia into South Asia, combined with abundant vector populations in monsoon climates and dense smallholder cattle systems, underpinned rapid spread. Limited prior exposure meant high susceptibility in regional herds. Internal mechanisms: Viruses were closely related to recombinant vaccine‑like strains and field strains from the Middle East and Central Asia; range expansion into a naïve host population, rather than a major intrinsic change in virulence, explains much of the high impact.
Review: review – Kept as the main introduction and early spread of LSD into South Asia (Bangladesh 2019, India 2019–2020, Nepal/Bhutan/Sri Lanka 2020, Pakistan 2021), with intra-continental emergence correctly marked. The ‘first_detection’ flag was changed from true to false because first detection refers to the host system globally (1929), not to the subregion; otherwise the row aligns with WOAH and regional review timelines.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Host: Domestic cattle; water buffalo in parts of mainland Southeast Asia
Event.summary: From late 2020, LSDV spread for the first time into mainland Southeast Asia, with initial large outbreaks reported in Viet Nam and Myanmar, followed in 2021 by major epizootics in Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Malaysia. Morbidity in many affected herds exceeded 15–30%, with notable economic losses in smallholder and commercial beef and dairy systems throughout the Mekong region. Regional vaccination programs, movement controls and improved surveillance progressively reduced outbreak numbers by late 2021, although the virus continued its southward spread into Indonesia and other areas in 2022.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction from South Asia and China via formal and informal cattle trade, transboundary grazing and possibly wind‑borne or mechanically transported vectors, followed by rapid intra‑regional spread facilitated by dense cattle populations, limited prior immunity and warm, humid climates highly favorable to vector flies. Internal mechanisms: Viral genotypes in Southeast Asia were closely related to recombinant and field strains circulating in South and East Asia; enhanced transmission in this region was largely attributable to ecological suitability and host movement rather than documented new viral traits.
Review: review – This row is retained as the first major Southeast Asian wave but the event year was broadened from “2020–2021” to “2020–2022” to match the inclusion of Indonesia and Singapore (first affected in 2022). As with other regional spread events, the ‘first_detection’ flag was reset to false (global first detection is historical), while intra-continental emergence remains appropriate for the first occurrence in the South-eastern Asia subregion.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Lumpy skin disease virus
EPP.common.name: LSDV, Capripoxvirus bovis
Host: Domestic cattle; water buffalo in some affected districts
Event.summary: In 2022, South Asia experienced an exceptionally severe LSD epidemic, with India reporting widespread outbreaks across many states and the death of tens of thousands of cattle within a few months, alongside major production losses. Neighboring Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh also recorded large numbers of cases, often in regions that had seen only limited disease in earlier years. Accelerated rollout of homologous and heterologous LSD vaccines, stricter movement controls and heightened farmer awareness gradually brought the large 2022 wave under better control by early 2023, though the virus is now entrenched in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: High baseline prevalence following initial introduction in 2019–2021, intense livestock movement after easing of COVID‑19 disruptions, and warm, humid conditions that favored vector proliferation combined to trigger a large secondary epidemic wave. Gaps in early vaccination coverage and cold‑chain/logistics issues further allowed explosive spread. Internal mechanisms: Molecular analyses from India indicated that 2022 outbreak strains were distinct from earlier 2019 isolates and represented a separate genetic lineage circulating under vaccine and immune pressure, consistent with Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence; reports of more severe disease in some areas support classification as viral re‑emergence rather than simple re‑occurrence.
Review: review – This severe South Asian wave is retained as a major re-emergence episode, but the emergence coding was adjusted so only ‘re_emergence’ is true (re_occurrence was set to false) to respect the guideline that event types are generally mutually exclusive, with re-emergence reserved for episodes involving clear viral genetic change. Genomic work from India demonstrates that 2022 strains form a distinct lineage from 2019 isolates under vaccine/immune pressure, justifying re-emergence classification.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Henipavirus nipahense
EPP.common.name: NiV
Host: Domestic pigs; humans (pig farmers, abattoir workers); fruit bats (Pteropus spp. reservoir); companion animals (dogs, cats)
Event.summary: From late 1998, intensive pig farms in peninsular Malaysia experienced a new respiratory–neurological disease in pigs accompanied by highly fatal encephalitis among pig handlers, initially misdiagnosed as Japanese encephalitis. Movement of infected pigs spread infection between major pig-producing states and into abattoirs in Singapore, leading to roughly 265 human encephalitis cases with over 100 deaths and the culling of more than a million pigs. The epidemic ended after aggressive pig depopulation, movement bans, farm closures and slaughterhouse controls removed the amplifying host populations and stopped human exposure.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid intensification and high density of pig production, frequent live-pig movements between Malaysian states and to Singapore, and siting of pig farms under fruit trees created close interfaces between Pteropus fruit bats and pigs; early misattribution to Japanese encephalitis delayed targeted control. Internal mechanisms: Host expansion (spillover) of a bat-borne henipavirus into pigs and then humans; enhanced transmission through high-titer virus shedding in pigs acting as amplifying hosts; inherent ability of the Malaysia genotype to spread efficiently within pig herds and from pigs to humans through close contact.
Review: retain – Correctly represents the first recognized NiV emergence in pigs and humans in peninsular Malaysia with linked cases in Singapore; continent, sub-region and countries match UNSD classifications; event-type coding as first global emergence/first detection (without intra- or inter-continental flags) is appropriate and the outbreak is clearly one of the two largest Nipah events globally.

EPP.scientific.name: Pasteurella multocida
EPP.common.name: Avian cholera, Avian pasteurellosis (Fowl cholera)
Host: Free-range layer chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus), farmed ducks; wild birds (gulls and waterfowl) as reservoir hosts
Event.summary: Beginning with the first recorded outbreak of fowl cholera in Danish wild birds in 1996, a highly virulent Pasteurella multocida subsp. multocida clone circulated for nearly a decade among wild waterbirds in Denmark and Sweden and subsequently spilled into outdoor poultry. By 2001–2004, the same outbreak clone had established in commercial free‑range layer farms in Denmark, causing recurrent episodes of elevated mortality in flocks of several thousand birds despite vaccination and biosecurity measures, and was also linked to earlier outbreaks in farmed ducks. Molecular typing showed that isolates from wild birds (Denmark 1996, 2001, 2003; Sweden 1998) and from multiple Danish poultry flocks were virtually indistinguishable, indicating long‑term clonal persistence across wild and domestic hosts. Cholera incidence in Danish poultry declined after 2004, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability of expanding free‑range systems to infection from local avifauna.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/7185094_Clonal_stability_of_Pasteurella_multocida_in_free-range_layers_affected_by_fowl_cholera))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of free‑range and organic layer production in Denmark increased direct and indirect contact between domestic birds and infected wild waterfowl and gulls, while shared equipment, lack of strict hygiene barriers, presence of other domestic animals, and imperfect vaccination facilitated farm‑level transmission and persistence. Internal mechanisms: A specific P. multocida ssp. multocida clone, originally detected in Danish wild birds in 1996 and later in Swedish wild birds in 1998, showed high virulence for domestic poultry and gamebirds and remained genetically stable across years and hosts, consistent with re‑emergence driven by a successful, highly pathogenic genotype that expanded from wild birds into free‑range poultry.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/7185094_Clonal_stability_of_Pasteurella_multocida_in_free-range_layers_affected_by_fowl_cholera))
Review: review – Retain as a major emergence of a virulent clone linking wild birds and free‑range poultry, but broadened the event period from 2001–2004 to 1996–2004 and clarified the country field to reflect epidemiologically linked wild‑bird outbreaks in Denmark (1996, 2001, 2003) and Sweden (1998) that predated and seeded the poultry epizootics.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

Cholera incidence in Danish poultry declined after 2004, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability of expanding free‑range systems to infection from local avifauna.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/7185094_Clonal_stability_of_Pasteurella_multocida_in_free-range_layers_affected_by_fowl_cholera))
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Rapid expansion of free‑range and organic layer production in Denmark increased direct and indirect contact between domestic birds and infected wild waterfowl and gulls, while shared equipment, lack of strict hygiene barriers, presence of other domestic animals, and imperfect vaccination facilitated farm‑level transmission and persistence. Internal mechanisms: A specific P. multocida ssp. multocida clone, originally detected in Danish wild birds in 1996 and later in Swedish wild birds in 1998, showed high virulence for domestic poultry and gamebirds and remained genetically stable across years and hosts, consistent with re‑emergence driven by a successful, highly pathogenic genotype that expanded from wild birds into free‑range poultry.([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/7185094_Clonal_stability_of_Pasteurella_multocida_in_free-range_layers_affected_by_fowl_cholera))

EPP.scientific.name: Porcine circovirus 2
EPP.common.name: Porcine circovirus-associated disease, PCVAD
Countries: Brazil [2000, with spread from initial diagnosis in Santa Catarina to herds in the Southeast region and Rio Grande do Sul by 2002–2003]
Host: Domestic pigs in commercial herds, including farrow‑to‑finish operations
Event.summary: In the early 2000s, PMWS/PCVAD was first recognized in Latin America, with Brazil reporting cases from 2000 in Santa Catarina and subsequent outbreaks in the Southeast and Rio Grande do Sul by 2002–2003, and Mexico confirming its first PMWS cases in 2001 despite retrospective evidence of earlier silent PCV2 infection. During 2000–2004, affected Brazilian farms experienced increased mortality in four‑month‑old weaned pigs and typical histologic lesions and PCV2 antigen in lymphoid tissues, while Mexican herds showed longstanding PCV2 seropositivity but only newly emerging clinical PMWS with production impacts. EPP.scientific.name: Taylorella equigenitalis
EPP.common.name: CEM organism
Countries: Germany (source country of the imported stallion) [2008, source only]
Host: Horses (stallions and mares at a single Lusitano stud farm)
Event.summary: In 2008, Portugal documented its first outbreak of contagious equine metritis when a Lusitano stallion recently imported from Germany and two mares at the same stud farm tested positive for Taylorella equigenitalis on routine pre‑breeding examination. Comprehensive testing of all 30 equids on the premises identified four additional infected horses (three mares and one stallion), but no evidence of spread beyond the affected stud or into the wider Portuguese horse population. All culture‑positive animals underwent standard topical treatment and repeated culture testing, and subsequent national surveillance of more than 2,000 genital swabs from other farms failed to detect further cases, indicating this was a self‑limited introduction event.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Growing international trade in Lusitano horses and importation of a breeding stallion from Germany with a false‑negative or incomplete CEM status provided the pathway for introduction of Taylorella equigenitalis into Portugal, while concentration of breeding at a single stud and initial lack of comprehensive screening allowed several additional horses to become infected before detection. Internal mechanisms: The ability of T. equigenitalis to persist in carrier stallions and mares with mainly subclinical or transient infertility favoured silent spread within the stud prior to testing, but no new genotype, host jump or antimicrobial resistance pattern was reported in relation to this episode.
Review: review – This event accurately captures Portugal’s first confirmed CEM outbreak and should be retained as a key intra‑continental emergence in Southern Europe. However, in line with the event‑type definitions, I changed first_detection from true to false because global first detection occurred in 1977 in the UK; the Portuguese episode instead represents spread of an established pathogen into a previously unaffected country within Europe, appropriately coded as intra_continental_emergence. I also simplified the sub_regions field to Southern Europe and left Germany only in the countries field as the epidemiological source, and focused the sources on the Open Veterinary Journal case report (including its PMC version), which provides the primary quantitative description of this outbreak.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Corrected category.

EPP.scientific.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
EPP.common.name: oriental fruit fly
Host: Diverse cultivated and wild fruits (including mango, citrus, guava and other tropical fruit crops)
Event.summary: In 1996, Bactrocera dorsalis was first recorded on Mauritius, an Indian Ocean island off the African coast, where an intensive area-wide campaign combining bait sprays and male annihilation led to official declaration of eradication in 1999. From 2005 onwards, the species invaded the Comoros and then spread stepwise to Mayotte in 2007 and Madagascar by 2010, where it became the dominant fruit fly in many mango-growing areas, while Mauritius experienced at least two further incursions in 2013 and 2015, the latter leading to widespread establishment, and Réunion recorded its first invasion around 2017. Together these invasions produced a pattern of repeated long-distance introductions from Asia and from the African mainland, island hopping, occasional successful eradications and eventual establishment on most major south-west Indian Ocean islands, with substantial chronic fruit losses and increased insecticide use.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: human‑mediated movement of infested fruit between Asia, East Africa and the south-west Indian Ocean islands, dense tourism and trade links (air and sea traffic), and highly suitable tropical climates with abundant host fruit. Internal mechanisms: introduction of invasive genotypes capable of founding new island populations from few individuals, leading to strong founder effects and genetic bottlenecks, followed by rapid demographic expansion; genomic work supports two distinct invasion pathways (a western route via East Africa into Comoros–Mayotte–Madagascar and an eastern route directly from Asia into Mauritius and Réunion). Repeated eradications and reintroductions on Mauritius illustrate both the species’ high colonisation ability and the possibility of local elimination under intensive area‑wide management. (Supported by Deschepper et al. 2023 and EPPO/NPPO reports for Mauritius and other islands.)
Review: review – Event retained but reclassified to better match the definitions: treated as inter-continental emergence because the 1996 Mauritius incursion is the first confirmed occurrence of B. dorsalis on the African continent, and re_emergence is kept to reflect repeated reintroductions and distinct invasion pathways; intra_continental_emergence and re_occurrence flags were removed to maintain the mostly mutually exclusive structure of event types. The sub-region label was standardised to the UNSD term ‘Eastern Africa’. Country sequence and eradication/reintroduction history are consistent with EPPO reports and Deschepper et al. (2023), but finer dating for Comoros, Mayotte, Madagascar and the status of Réunion after 2017 should be double-checked against national reports.
