EPP.scientific.name: Euphorbia prostrata
EPP.common.name: prostrate spurge, prostrate sandmat, blue weed, ground spurge
Host: Weed of anthropogenic habitats: wastelands, lawns, parks, gardens, fields, fallow lands, sidewalks, roadsides, railway embankments and river banks
Event.summary: Around 2012 Euphorbia prostrata was first recorded from the Almaty Region of Kazakhstan, marking its documented arrival in Central Asia and showing that this American species had reached a previously uncolonised Asian sub-region. By 2018–2019 it was found as a weed in anthropogenic habitats in Uzbekistan and by 2018–2021 it was newly recorded in several localities in the Russian Federation, mostly along railway rights-of-way and urban disturbed sites. These findings together document a coordinated eastward and northward expansion across Central Asia and into continental parts of Russia, where the species is currently assessed as an alien of minor impact but clearly increasing its range.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Expansion of transport infrastructure, urbanization and trade across Central Asia and the Russian Federation has increased movement of contaminated soil, road materials and plant propagules, facilitating long-distance dispersal of ruderal aliens. Irrigation schemes, parks and gardens provide persistently disturbed, watered microsites in otherwise harsh continental climates. Internal mechanisms: Geographic range expansion through pre-adaptation to hot, dry, nutrient-poor and compacted substrates typical of anthropogenic sites, with enhanced transmission via persistent seed banks and accidental transport with gravel and railway ballast enabling stepwise spread along transport corridors.
Review: Review – Retain this episode as an intra-continental emergence, because it documents the first confirmed records in the Central Asia sub-region (Kazakhstan and later Uzbekistan) and new records in Russia, within continents where the species was already established elsewhere. I simplified sub_regions to 'Central Asia; Eastern Europe' (dropping the non-standard 'Eastern Europe – Russia') and removed re_emergence, which is not supported by evidence of strain change. The Botanica Pacifica paper plus POWO provide adequate support for timing and geography.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Check category (High confidence).

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine indica
EPP.common.name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Countries: United States of America [2010 – Mississippi, cotton]
Host: Cotton and other glyphosate-resistant row crops; some turfgrass systems
Event.summary: Around 2010, glyphosate‑resistant Eleusine indica was first confirmed in Mississippi cotton fields in the United States, following years of intensive in‑crop glyphosate use in glyphosate‑resistant cotton and soybean systems. Over the first half of the 2010s, additional glyphosate‑resistant goosegrass populations were detected in other southeastern states, including Tennessee soybean fields, alongside previously established dinitroaniline‑resistant biotypes in cotton and goosegrass resistance to various herbicides in turfgrass. By 2015–2016, work on a Tennessee goosegrass population showed that a Pro106Ser mutation in EPSPS alone could confer glyphosate resistance, illustrating a clear genetic mechanism and highlighting goosegrass as an emerging, multi‑herbicide‑resistant weed threat in US row crops and turf.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Long‑term reliance on glyphosate in glyphosate‑resistant cotton, soybean and maize with minimal diversification of weed control; historical dependence on dinitroaniline pre‑emergence herbicides in cotton; high selection pressure in warm‑season turfgrass under frequent herbicide applications. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence via EPSPS Pro106Ser and other mutations, plus earlier dinitroaniline resistance arising from altered microtubule targets; Enhanced Transmission through seed movement with farm machinery and in turf sod; Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as resistant biotypes adapted to both agricultural fields and managed turf environments.
Review: Decision: retain – USDA‑ARS and weedscience.org confirm first US glyphosate-resistant goosegrass in Mississippi cotton in 2010, followed by Tennessee cases with an EPSPS Pro106Ser mutation and numerous earlier dinitroaniline‑resistant populations in cotton and turf. Geography, timing and framing as a re-emergence via resistance evolution (not an inter‑continental spread event) are accurate; only minor clarifications to the country field (making Tennessee and turf systems explicit) were made for clarity.

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine indica
EPP.common.name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Host: Orchards (citrus and fruit trees), tea plantations, direct-seeded rice, sugarcane
Event.summary: From the early 2010s, Eleusine indica became a dominant weed in Chinese orchards and tea plantations, where heavy glyphosate use led to the evolution of glyphosate‑resistant populations with EPSPS overexpression and Pro106 mutations. Around 2020, a goosegrass population from direct‑seeded rice in Jiangsu was confirmed to have multiple resistance to cyhalofop‑butyl (ACCase inhibitor) and glyphosate, coinciding with a shift toward direct‑seeding practices and increased grass‑weed pressure. By the early 2020s, multiple‑herbicide‑resistant goosegrass populations were also reported in sugarcane and citrus in Guangxi Province, including combined resistance to glyphosate, paraquat and PS II inhibitors, causing serious control failures in perennial crop systems and threatening rice and sugarcane yields.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Transition to direct‑seeded rice and reduced tillage, favouring grass‑weed proliferation; intensive glyphosate, ACCase inhibitor and glufosinate/PS II herbicide use in orchards, tea and sugarcane; climatic suitability for C4 grasses in southern China; limited integration of non‑chemical weed management. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance via ACCase target‑site mutations (e.g. Asp‑2078‑Gly) conferring cyhalofop resistance, EPSPS overexpression and point mutations for glyphosate resistance, and EPSPS amplification plus non‑target‑site mechanisms underpinning multiple resistance to glyphosate, paraquat and PS II herbicides; Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence and Multiple Resistance (stacked resistance to several modes of action); Geographic Range Expansion (Inherent) as resistant biotypes spread within southern Chinese agro‑ecosystems.
Review: Decision: retain – Chinese studies document glyphosate-resistant goosegrass in orchards/tea, multiple resistance to cyhalofop-butyl+glyphosate in direct‑seeded rice (Jiangsu) and complex multi‑resistance in sugarcane and citrus in Guangxi, matching the crops, geography and mechanisms described. The event is correctly treated as a re-emergence via new resistant biotypes in an already widespread weed; no changes to event type or core structure were needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Eleusine indica
EPP.common.name: crowsfoot grass, "manienie aliI", silver crabgrass, wiregrass, Indian goosegrass, goosegrass, Indian goose grass, goose grass
Countries: Indonesia [2012 – oil palm nurseries and plantations]
Host: Oil palm plantations and nurseries; maize (corn) fields
Event.summary: By the early 2010s, Indonesian oil palm nurseries and plantations were reporting Eleusine indica becoming dominant after repeated herbicide use, with early work noting poor control by glyphosate and the need for alternative graminicides. In 2012–2019, glyphosate‑ and paraquat‑resistant goosegrass was confirmed in North Sumatra oil palm, and subsequent studies showed additional resistance to ammonium glufosinate and widespread multiple‑resistant populations in Riau and West Kalimantan. By 2023–2025, greenhouse screening of maize‑field populations across six major maize‑producing provinces found widespread atrazine resistance and emerging mesotrione resistance in goosegrass, indicating multiple resistance across PS II and HPPD inhibitors on top of previously documented glyphosate and paraquat resistance and raising concerns for both oil palm and maize productivity.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Monoculture oil palm with frequent non‑rotated use of glyphosate, paraquat and glufosinate in plantation inter‑rows; intensification of maize production with heavy reliance on atrazine–mesotrione mixtures; lack of crop and herbicide rotation; limited awareness of resistance principles among smallholders. Internal mechanisms: Antimicrobial/Pesticide Resistance and Novel Strain/Genotype Emergence with documented glyphosate and paraquat resistance indices up to ~4–6, confirmed glufosinate resistance in some biotypes, and greenhouse evidence of PS II (atrazine) and HPPD (mesotrione) resistance; involvement of both target‑site and metabolic (non‑target‑site) mechanisms; Enhanced Transmission through extensive seed production and local movement on contaminated machinery within plantation and maize landscapes.
Review: Decision: retain – Indonesian oil palm and maize studies consistently report glyphosate-, paraquat- and glufosinate-resistant goosegrass in North Sumatra, Riau and West Kalimantan and more recent atrazine/mesotrione resistance in maize across multiple provinces, justifying a single linked national event. The timing, geography and classification as re-emergence due to multiple herbicide resistance are appropriate; minor clarifications were added to the country field to make the provincial spread explicit but no re-typing was needed.

EPP.scientific.name: Heterodera zeae
EPP.common.name: corn cyst nematode
Countries: Thailand [1994 – Phraputthabat Field Crop Research Station, Lopburi Province, maize field]
Host: Zea mays (maize)
Event.summary: In the mid‑1990s, Heterodera zeae was detected for the first time in South‑eastern Asia in a maize field at the Phraputthabat Field Crop Research Station in Lopburi Province, Thailand, where cysts and juveniles were recovered from stunted plants and confirmed morphologically as corn cyst nematode. A little over a decade later, detailed morphological work on cysts and second-stage juveniles collected from maize roots on Madura Island (Java, Indonesia) in 2008 identified the same species, providing the first confirmed report for Indonesia and showing that H. zeae had a restricted but established distribution on maize in parts of South‑eastern Asia. Although large-scale regional yield losses have not yet been quantified, these findings extended the nematode’s range into a new Asian subregion with substantial maize cultivation and prompted calls for surveillance and hygiene measures to prevent wider spread.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Introduction into South-eastern Asia is most plausibly linked to anthropogenic movement of infested soil or maize-associated planting material (including soil adhering to seed, roots or machinery) from already infested areas in Southern Asia or Egypt, combined with expansion of maize cultivation in warm upland environments of Thailand and Indonesia. Climatic suitability (high soil temperatures) and repeated maize cropping support establishment even from small founder populations. Internal mechanisms: No novel genotype was reported; the event reflects geographic range expansion of existing H. zeae lineages into a new UNSD subregion within Asia, facilitated by the nematode’s inherent adaptation to hot conditions and longevity of cysts in soil.
Review: review – New intra-continental emergence event added to capture first detection of H. zeae in the South-eastern Asia subregion (Thailand, later Indonesia–Java). Classification as intra-continental emergence (new Asian subregion) with subsequent spread within that subregion is consistent with UNSD geography and EPPO distribution data. Economic impact remains poorly quantified, so the event is flagged for expert review but is retained as a major geographic expansion episode.
Review.Comment: Bulk accepted from Dataset review: Added category.

EPP.scientific.name: Ipomoea imperati
EPP.common.name: beach morningglory, beach morning-glory
Countries: Portugal – Madeira Archipelago [2002, if treated as alien rather than long-established].
Host: Coastal sandy-beach and dune plant communities (embryonic and shifting dunes with Ammophiletea vegetation in Spain, Italy, Balearic Islands and Madeira)
Event.summary: From the early 2000s, Ipomoea imperati re-appeared and expanded within Southern Europe, first through rediscovery of a small but persistent Sicilian population at the mouth of the San Leonardo River and subsequent records along the Calabrian Tyrrhenian coast, following earlier extinction of mainland Italian populations.([biodiversityjournal.com](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2021/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04_899-903.pdf)) In parallel, Spanish botanists documented the species as an alien strandline plant along Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, with a 2005 note reporting it as a new adventive in Doñana National Park and a 2015 study describing incipient naturalized stands of 300–750 m² on Cádiz dunes at Barbate and Algeciras, already rated as high-risk invaders of Natura 2000 dune habitats.([biolveg.uma.es](https://www.biolveg.uma.es/abm/Volumenes/vol40/40_Garcia_de_Lomas_Ipomoea.pdf)) Over the 2010s–early 2020s, additional dense mats of 1,500–3,000 m² were recorded at Castilnovo and Los Lances (Tarifa) and the species was newly reported as part of the alien flora of the Balearic Islands, while three small but nearly monospecific dune populations were found along the south‑western Sicilian coast; by 2025, I. imperati remained localized but clearly expanding within selected Spanish and Italian dune systems and subject to active monitoring and control in some protected areas, with no indication that the invasion episode has yet ended.([biodiversityjournal.com](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2021/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04/biodiversity-journal-2021-12-04_899-903.pdf))

(2001, 2004), the 2005 Doñana adventive report, subsequent Cádiz xenophyte populations (2011–2015) and new Andalusian and Balearic localities documented up to 2023–2025.([biolveg.uma.es](https://www.biolveg.uma.es/abm/Volumenes/vol40/40_Garcia_de_Lomas_Ipomoea.pdf)) (3) Simplified and standardized the countries field, removing nested subnational descriptions that belong in the event summary and aligning country assignments with the UNSD Southern Europe list while still indicating key coastal areas and first-record years. Event.summary: From the mid-2000s onward, Liriomyza huidobrensis expanded its range and impact within Asia, becoming widely established across many provinces of China, additional regions of India and Nepal, and further highland vegetable areas in Southeast Asia such as northern Viet Nam and upland parts of Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand. During this period, the fly caused repeated, sometimes region-wide outbreaks on potatoes and mixed vegetables, prompting intensified pesticide use and concern about resistance and yield losses. Over the late 2010s, regional IPM programs, parasitoid releases and better species diagnostics improved management, but the pest remains a key constraint in many Asian highland vegetable systems, especially where insecticide overuse persists.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: Continued expansion of irrigated highland vegetable production, climate conditions favorable for cool-adapted leafminers, and intra-Asian trade in planting material facilitated ongoing spread and range filling; widespread use of broad-spectrum insecticides suppressed parasitoids and drove recurrence of severe infestations. Internal mechanisms: High dispersal ability and broad host range supported colonization of remaining suitable climatic niches in Asia, while previously evolved insecticide resistance allowed persistence and resurgence under chemical control regimes.

Event.summary: In the early 1990s, Liriomyza sativae was first recognised in Africa, with presence confirmed in Zimbabwe by 1991 and subsequently in Cameroon and Sudan, where serious outbreaks occurred on vegetables and okra in the mid‑1990s. These early African foci involved heavy leaf mining and substantial yield and quality losses in vegetable crops – for example, Sudanese studies recorded infestation levels up to 48–86.5% on tomato and faba bean with yield losses around 44–45% – and signalled that the American leafminer complex had successfully established on the continent. By the late 1990s the species was established in several African countries and began spreading across tropical regions, becoming part of a broader invasive Liriomyza complex that increasingly threatened smallholder and export‑oriented horticulture.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: accidental introduction on infested cut flowers and vegetable consignments from previously invaded regions (Arabian Peninsula and/or the Americas), combined with expansion of irrigated vegetable and ornamental production for domestic and export markets in Africa; weak phytosanitary inspection capacity for small packages and cut flowers. (2006), and Zimbabwe was added as an earlier but limited presence documented by Martinez & Bordat and OEPP distribution lists. Event.summary: From 1996 onwards, Liriomyza sativae emerged as a new and highly damaging pest in lowland vegetable systems in Indonesia, first recorded attacking cucumbers, tomatoes and yard‑long beans in Karawang (West Java) and then spreading to other lowland areas in South and Central Kalimantan, where French beans and yard‑long beans suffered damage levels up to about 60–70%. Through the late 1990s and early 2000s, the species became established in multiple lowland vegetable belts and contributed to frequent, severe leafminer outbreaks that triggered intensive insecticide use; surveys documented heavy infestations on cucurbits and legumes while highland systems remained dominated by L. huidobrensis. By the early 2000s, L. sativae had also been recorded further east (e.g. Timor‑Leste in 2003 and West Papua by 2005), forming a South‑East Asian invasion bridge that later fed into island‑hopping spread towards Papua New Guinea and, ultimately, northern Australia, after which the pest became a routine management concern in many lowland vegetable production systems in the region.
Mechanism.or.driver: Drivers: increasing trade in cut flowers and fresh vegetables (including from Europe and other invaded regions) into Indonesia, combined with rapid expansion of irrigated lowland vegetable production, often with high pesticide use and limited biological control. Internal mechanisms: polyphagy and strong adaptation to hot lowland conditions enabling L. sativae to exploit cucurbits, beans and other vegetables where L. huidobrensis was less competitive; ability to complete many generations per year under tropical temperatures; and repeated selection for insecticide resistance under intensive spraying, which undermined chemical control and promoted persistent high‑level infestations.

This wave also underpins later spread to Timor‑Leste and West Papua, which are mentioned in the summary but not given separate rows because the available impact data are less detailed. The episode is coded as intra‑continental emergence within Asia, with approximate country‑specific years based on Indonesian field studies and regional invasion syntheses; these dates and the inclusion of Timor‑Leste should be checked by an expert against NPPO and national literature before finalisation.

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus cacheense

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus cacheense
EPP.common.name: Cache Valley virus
Countries: United States of America (Missouri ‚Äì northwest Missouri)
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) ‚Äì man in his 60s with diabetes, coronary artery disease and prior thymectomy for malignant thymoma

EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus cacheense
EPP.common.name: Cache Valley virus
Countries: United States of America (New York State ‚Äì rural Cuba, NY)
Host: Humans (Homo sapiens) ‚Äì 58-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia on rituximab maintenance therapy
Event.summary: In July 2016, a 58‚Äëyear‚Äëold man from rural Cuba, New York, with chronic lymphocytic leukemia receiving rituximab maintenance therapy developed subacute confusion, memory loss, gait instability and fatigue. EPP.scientific.name: Orthobunyavirus cacheense

EPP.scientific.name: Bandavirus heartlandense
EPP.common.name: Heartland virus
Countries: United States of America (Georgia ‚Äì Baldwin County; retrospectively recognized fatal case with local deer serology indicating circulation since at least 2001)
Host: Humans (adult resident with fatal tick-associated illness retrospectively attributed to Heartland virus) and wildlife (white-tailed deer as sentinel hosts with neutralizing antibodies)
Event.summary: In 2005, an adult resident of Baldwin County, Georgia died after a severe febrile illness with cytopenias that was initially unexplained but was later shown by retrospective molecular and serologic testing to have been caused by Heartland virus. Review: review ‚Äì new event added to capture the retrospectively recognized 2005 fatal human case in Georgia and deer serology showing exposure since at least 2001; this substantially alters the inferred timing of earliest human infection but does not change that the 2009 Missouri episode is the first prospective detection, so no emergence-type flag is set here pending expert review.

EPP.scientific.name: Bandavirus heartlandense
EPP.common.name: Heartland virus

EPP.scientific.name: Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1

EPP.scientific.name: Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1

EPP.scientific.name: Baylisascaris procyonis

EPP.scientific.name: Border disease virus

EPP.scientific.name: Border disease virus

EPP.scientific.name: Border disease virus

EPP.scientific.name: Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridium botulinum

EPP.scientific.name: Clostridium botulinum

Countries: United States of America (California ‚Äì Salton Sea)

EPP.scientific.name: Orthoebolavirus zairense

Host: Humans (community members, health-care workers)
Event.summary: In early 1995, Ebola virus disease re-emerged in Kikwit and surrounding areas of Bandundu Region (now Kwilu), Democratic Republic of the Congo, when clusters of severe febrile haemorrhagic illness were first recognized among patients and hospital staff. Review: Status: retained. Major Central African outbreak (~315 cases, high CFR) in a country and sub-region where Orthoebolavirus zairense was already established; classification as a re-occurrence without intra-/inter-continental emergence or re-emergence is appropriate and consistent with outbreak reconstructions.

The 2018 Equateur Province outbreak (54 cases, 33 deaths) is one of the larger Zaire ebolavirus events and the first documented incursion into a sizable urban center (Mbandaka) in western DRC; it was missing from the original dataset and is appropriately classified as a re-occurrence in Middle Africa.
